h: Threads and the bugs they cause
x: Threads, races, locks, deadlock, atomics, concurrent collections and synchronizers. By the end of this track you can read concurrent Java and Kotlin code and say what can go wrong: which line races, which pair of locks can deadlock, which wait can hang forever, which test proves nothing. You can fix each problem with the smallest correct tool: one atomic library call, a lock around the whole compound action, a concurrent collection, a synchronizer, or no sharing at all. And you can show the fix holds with a stress test that makes threads collide, and find the cause of a hang or a slowdown in production with thread dumps and Java Flight Recorder. You need everyday Java or Kotlin and nothing else. The track starts at what a thread is and builds up one idea per lesson: thread life and interruption, race conditions, synchronized, wait and notify, deadlock, explicit locks, atomics, concurrent collections, synchronizers, immutability and confinement, three classic problems, and testing. The memory model track comes next and explains why the visibility rules you use here work. Every lesson has a lab in labs/concurrency, in the package workbench.concurrency.lNN. From labs/, run ./gradlew :concurrency:test --tests 'workbench.concurrency.lNN.*': the tests fail on the starting code and pass when your fix is right. Reference answers are in src/solution, and ./gradlew :concurrency:solutionTest runs the same tests against them. The Try-it programs are in src/demo, in Java and Kotlin, and run with ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=<class>. The labs compile for JDK 21 and run on 21 or later; install JDK 25. A race condition is a result that depends on timing. Its two shapes are read-modify-write and check-then-act, and both need the compound action made atomic. Reach for fixes in this order: don't share (immutability, confinement, hand-off), then one atomic library call, then a lock around the whole compound action, reads included. synchronized and ReentrantLock give exclusion and visibility. Release explicit locks in finally, lock on private objects, keep critical sections short and never call alien code inside them. Waiting for a condition is always while (!condition) wait() or await(). Use notifyAll() with one wait set, or one Condition per kind of waiter. Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions. A global lock order removes circular wait; tryLock with random back-off removes no-preemption. jcmd Thread.print finds monitor and ReentrantLock cycles. Atomics are compare-and-set underneath: read, decide, CAS, retry. LongAdder for hot counters, AtomicLong for decisions, AtomicReference plus an immutable object for several fields. Concurrent collections make single calls safe. Use their atomic per-key methods, bound every queue, and don't read size() or iteration as a snapshot. Latches wait for events once, barriers meet every round, semaphores cap concurrency, phasers change size. Count down and release in finally, and give every wait a deadline. ThreadLocal values outlive the request on pool threads: remove them in finally, or use scoped values on JDK 25+. A concurrency test must make threads collide and check invariants with a timeout. Find hangs with thread dumps and contention with JFR.

h: Threads and the bugs they cause: cheat sheet
x: Threads Call What it does t.start() runs t on a new thread; t.run() runs it on the current one t.join() waits for t to end; everything t wrote is visible afterwards t.interrupt() asks t to stop; blocking calls throw InterruptedException and clear the flag setDaemon(true) the JVM may exit while this thread still runs Thread.stop() removed in JDK 26; cancellation is cooperative When you catch InterruptedException: rethrow it, or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and stop. The two shapes of race Shape Looks like Fix Read-modify-write count++, balance -= x, put(k, get(k) + 1) an atomic call, or a lock around read and write Check-then-act if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v), lazy init one call that checks and acts: putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, Set.add, a CAS A thread-safe class makes single calls atomic, never two calls in a row. Pick the tool You need Use A hot counter, read now and then LongAdder One exact value with read-modify-write AtomicLong: updateAndGet, accumulateAndGet, or a CAS loop Several fields that change together one lock around both, or an AtomicReference to an immutable record A per-key update in a shared map ConcurrentHashMap.merge, compute, computeIfAbsent A table replaced as a whole a volatile field holding an immutable map Read-mostly data updated in place ReentrantReadWriteLock (never upgrade read to write) A wait that can time out or be cancelled ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout), lockInterruptibly() Two kinds of waiters on one lock one Condition each, then signal() is enough Hand work to other threads a bounded BlockingQueue, such as ArrayBlockingQueue(n) Wait for N events, once CountDownLatch N threads meeting every round CyclicBarrier At most N at once Semaphore A group that changes size between phases Phaser A small list, rarely changed, often iterated CopyOnWriteArrayList Per-request context ThreadLocal with remove() in finally; ScopedValue on JDK 25+ Idioms An explicit lock: Java lock.lock(); // before the try try { balance -= cents; } finally { lock.unlock(); // first line of finally } Kotlin lock.withLock { // lock, try, finally unlock balance -= cents } A guarded wait: Java synchronized (lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); // a while, never an if return items.removeFirst(); } Kotlin lock.withLock { // ReentrantLock + Condition: Any has no wait() while (items.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await() items.removeFirst() } A compare-and-set loop: Java long prev; do { prev = max.get(); if (amount <= prev) return; // decide on what you read } while (!max.compareAndSet(prev, amount)); // write only if nobody changed it Kotlin var prev: Long do { prev = max.get() if (amount <= prev) return // decide on what you read } while (!max.compareAndSet(prev, amount)) // write only if nobody changed it A thread-local on a pool thread: Java CURRENT.set(tenant); try { handle(request); } finally { CURRENT.remove(); // pool threads are reused } Kotlin CURRENT.set(tenant) try { handle(request) } finally { CURRENT.remove() // pool threads are reused } semaphore.acquire() also goes before the try, and tryAcquire's result must be checked: permits have no owner, so a stray release() adds one. Locks synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility, and is reentrant. Lock on a private final object, never on a boxed number or a String literal. Keep critical sections short. Never call alien code (listeners, repositories, other services) while holding a lock. Every access to shared mutable state, reads included, goes through the same lock or atomic. Deadlock Condition Remove it with Mutual exclusion immutable data, one owner per resource Hold and wait take one lock at a time, or acquire(n) in one step No preemption tryLock(timeout), release and retry with a random back-off Circular wait one global lock order, such as lower id first Livelock: busy threads that make no progress (fix: randomness). Starvation: one thread never gets its turn (fix: fairness, shorter holds). Concurrent collections ConcurrentHashMap: no null keys or values; compute functions run under the bin's lock, so keep them short and never touch the map inside one; size() is an estimate; iterators never throw. ConcurrentModificationException is a fail-fast iterator check. One thread can trip it; concurrent collections never throw it. new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() is unbounded. Always pass a capacity. BlockingQueue Throws Special value Blocks Times out Insert add offer put offer(e, t, unit) Remove remove poll take poll(t, unit) Shut consumers down with one poison pill each, after every producer has finished, compared by identity. Kotlin differences Java Kotlin synchronized method @Synchronized synchronized (lock) { } synchronized(lock) { }, a standard library function volatile @Volatile lock(); try { } finally { unlock(); } lock.withLock { } read and write locks rw.read { }, rw.write { }: write releases read locks first, so re-check new Thread(r).start() thread { } wait() / notify() on any object Any has neither: use ReentrantLock and Condition checked InterruptedException not checked, but you still restore the flag computeIfAbsent getOrPut on a ConcurrentMap may run its default more than once Testing and diagnosis Stress tests: a start latch, more threads than cores, many operations, many rounds, an invariant after join(), and a timeout on every test. A pass is not a proof. No Thread.sleep to wait in tests: use a latch, a future, or polling with a deadline. jcstress: ACCEPTABLE, ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING (allowed, worth seeing), FORBIDDEN (fails the test). Command Shows jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l every thread's state and stack, owned j.u.c locks, Java-level deadlocks jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json f.json the same as JSON; state and lock fields from JDK 25 jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=r.jfr starts a flight recording jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter r.jfr waits for synchronized, with duration and previous owner In a dump, BLOCKED means waiting for a monitor; WAITING (parking) means a java.util.concurrent lock, latch, queue or semaphore. Take several dumps a few seconds apart to tell stuck from busy.

h: Threads and the bugs they cause: track quiz
x: What does this print? Java Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()), "settle-worker"); t.run(); Kotlin val t = Thread({ println(Thread.currentThread().name) }, "settle-worker") t.run() settle-worker main Nothing: a thread must be started first It throws IllegalThreadStateException run() is an ordinary method call, so the lambda runs on the calling thread, main. Only start() creates a new thread that then calls run(). Calling run() by mistake is a classic way to make concurrent code silently single-threaded. A worker loops while (true) { try { process(queue.take()); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("interrupted", e); } }. During shutdown, executor.shutdownNow() doesn't stop it. Why? shutdownNow() never interrupts threads take() ignores interrupts The exception clears the interrupt flag, the catch only logs it, and the loop carries on The worker must be a daemon thread take() throws InterruptedException and clears the flag. Logging is not handling: the loop goes round and blocks again. Restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and leave the loop, or let the exception propagate. Four Kafka consumer threads run if (!seen.contains(key)) { charge(msg); seen.add(key); } with seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(). A redelivered message arrives on two threads at once. What is the smallest correct fix? if (seen.add(key)) charge(msg);, removing the key again if the charge fails Make seen a volatile field Switch to Collections.synchronizedSet Add Thread.sleep(10) before the check It is check-then-act: both threads can pass contains before either adds. Set.add checks and inserts in one atomic step and returns false to the loser. volatile and a synchronized wrapper leave the gap between the two calls. Two unrelated classes each declare private static final Integer LOCK = 0; and use synchronized (LOCK). What happens? Each class gets its own lock, because the fields are private It doesn't compile The JVM copies the lock per class loader Both share one lock object, because boxing 0 returns the cached Integer; javac warns about synchronizing on a value-based class Integer.valueOf(0) comes from a cache shared by the whole JVM, so both fields point to the same object and unrelated code contends on, or deadlocks over, one monitor. Lock on a private final Object lock = new Object() instead. A consumer does synchronized (queue) { if (queue.isEmpty()) queue.wait(); return queue.remove(); } with two consumers and notifyAll(). What can go wrong? Nothing: notifyAll() makes if safe A woken consumer can find the queue empty again, because the other consumer took the item or the wake-up was spurious, and remove() throws wait() keeps the monitor, so the producer can never add notifyAll() wakes only one consumer Waking up only means "something may have changed". Another consumer can get the monitor first and take the item, and the JVM allows spurious wake-ups. Re-check in a while loop. transfer(from, to) locks from, then to. Transfers run in both directions between the same merchant accounts, and the service sometimes freezes. Which fix removes the deadlock? Make the balance fields volatile Use fair locks Always lock the account with the lower id first, whichever way the money moves Add a short sleep between the two locks Opposite orders make a cycle: each thread holds one account and waits for the other. One global order means nobody can hold the second lock while waiting for the first, so circular wait is gone. Fairness and sleeps only change the odds. Fifty threads update an account's balanceCents and lastUpdated together, and readers must never see one without the other. Which design is correct? One AtomicReference to an immutable record holding both, updated with updateAndGet, or one lock around both Two AtomicLong fields Two volatile fields A LongAdder for the balance and an AtomicLong for the time Each atomic protects one variable, so with two of them a reader can see the new balance with the old time. A CAS on a reference to an immutable pair, or a single lock, makes both fields change as one step. A test checks a counter with 2 threads x 1,000 increments and has passed for a year. Which version of the test could actually catch a lost update? The same test with @RepeatedTest(100) The same test run on a faster machine The same test with Thread.sleep(100) before the assertion 8 threads released together by a start latch, 100,000 increments each, over many rounds, with a timeout With 1,000 increments the first thread often finishes before the second starts, so repeating the same test repeats the same non-overlap. A start latch, more threads than cores, long runs and many rounds make the threads collide. The timeout keeps a deadlock from hanging the build. IssuerGate.call does try { permits.acquire(); return issuer.call(); } finally { permits.release(); } with new Semaphore(20). Requests are often cancelled while waiting for a permit. What happens over a day? Nothing: acquire() gives up cleanly Each interrupted wait still releases a permit it never took, so the limit drifts above 20 release() throws once permits exceed 20 The semaphore resets itself every hour acquire() throws InterruptedException inside the try, so the finally runs release() anyway. Permits have no owner, so each stray release adds one for good. Call acquire() before the try. A Quarkus handler sets MERCHANT.set(request.merchantId()) on a ThreadLocal only when the header is present, and never removes it. What does a request without the header see on a reused worker thread? null, because each request gets a new thread It throws IllegalStateException The merchant id of whichever request that thread served last A random merchant id from another thread Pool threads are reused, and a thread-local value stays on the thread until someone removes it. Set it, then remove() in finally, or use a scoped value on JDK 25 and later.

h: Threads from zero · A thread is one path through your code, inside a shared process
x: Run an empty main method and the JVM already has six Java threads: main, plus five helpers such as Reference Handler, Finalizer and Signal Dispatcher. The garbage collector has more threads of its own, and so does the JIT compiler, the part of the JVM that turns hot bytecode into machine code while the program runs. A thread dump, a printout of every thread and what it is doing, lists them all. You've been writing multithreaded programs all along. Two words matter here. A process is a running program with its own memory. Your payment service in its container is one process, and no other process can read its memory. A thread is one path of execution inside a process. It runs one statement after another, calls methods and returns from them. The threads of one process split their memory in a simple way: They all share the heap. Every object you create with new, and every static field, can be reached by every thread that has a reference to it. Each thread has its own stack. Local variables, method parameters and the chain of calls in progress belong to one thread only. Each thread also tracks its own position in the code. That split explains most of this track. Sharing the heap is what makes threads useful: one thread can put a Payment into a map and another can read it, with no copying and no network. It is also what makes them dangerous. Two threads can change the same object at the same moment, and lesson 3 of this track (Race conditions: why count++ lies) shows how that silently loses money. Local variables are safe, because no other thread can see them. So when you look at a piece of code and ask "is this thread-safe?", the first question is always: which of these values live on the heap, and can another thread reach them? Meet the threads you already have Run HelloThreads with the command below. Read the list of threads that exist before your code starts any. Which of them are daemon threads? (A daemon thread is one the JVM does not wait for when it exits. The last section of this lesson comes back to it.) Run it three more times. Does worker-a always print before worker-b? HelloThreads.java package workbench.concurrency.l01; /** Lists the threads the JVM already has, then starts two of your own. Run it a few times. */ public class HelloThreads { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("cores the JVM sees: " + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()); System.out.println("Java threads before main starts any:"); for (Thread t : Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet()) { System.out.println(" " + t.getName() + (t.isDaemon() ? " (daemon)" : "")); } Runnable task = () -> System.out.println("hello from " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); Thread a = new Thread(task, "worker-a"); Thread b = new Thread(task, "worker-b"); a.start(); // try changing these two calls to a.run() and b.run() b.start(); a.join(); // wait for both to finish before main goes on b.join(); System.out.println("main is done"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.HelloThreads labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l01/HelloThreads.java HelloThreads.kt package workbench.concurrency.l01 // Lists the threads the JVM already has, then starts two of your own. Run it a few times. fun main() { println("cores the JVM sees: ${Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()}") println("Java threads before main starts any:") for (t in Thread.getAllStackTraces().keys) { println(" ${t.name}${if (t.isDaemon) " (daemon)" else ""}") } val task = Runnable { println("hello from ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } val a = Thread(task, "worker-a") val b = Thread(task, "worker-b") a.start() // try changing these two calls to a.run() and b.run() b.start() a.join() // wait for both to finish before main goes on b.join() println("main is done") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.HelloThreadsKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l01/HelloThreads.kt You'll see main and five daemon helper threads (the order of the list changes). The two workers usually print in start order, but not always: the order is up to the scheduler, and nothing in the code promises it. Code that depends on that order is a bug waiting for a busy day. Threads in one process share the heap. Each thread has a private stack for its local variables and calls. A process is a restaurant kitchen. The heap is the shared fridge and counters: any cook can take an onion from the fridge or put a plate on the pass. Each cook (a thread) carries a private order ticket and a cutting board, which is their stack. The stoves are the cores: more cooks than stoves means cooks take turns, which is fine when most of them are waiting for water to boil (I/O), and pointless when they all need a stove (CPU work). The kitchen closes when the last non-daemon cook goes home, not when the head chef does. The analogy breaks in one place. Cooks see what the others are doing. Threads do not reliably see each other's changes unless the code uses the tools in the rest of this track.

h: Threads from zero · Cores run threads, and concurrency is not parallelism
x: A CPU core runs one thread at a time. (Hyper-threading lets one physical core run two, a little slower each.) Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() tells you how many the JVM may use, and inside a container it follows the CPU limit, so your pod with cpu: 2 reports 2. Your service has far more threads than cores. The operating system's scheduler handles that: it lets a thread run for a short slice of time, then saves its registers (the handful of values the core is working on) and switches to another one. This is a context switch. It happens thousands of times a second, which is why 200 threads on 4 cores all appear to make progress. Two words get mixed up here, so pin them down: Concurrency is about structure: several tasks are in progress at the same time. It works fine on one core, by taking turns. Parallelism is about hardware: several tasks run at the same instant, on different cores. A Kafka consumer that handles 12 partitions on 12 threads is concurrent. Whether it is parallel depends on the cores and on what the threads are doing. That last part is the one that matters for sizing. A thread that waits for a 120 ms response from the card issuer uses no core while it waits. So an I/O-bound service can usefully run many more threads than it has cores. A CPU-bound job, like scoring transactions with a fraud model, is different. Once every core is busy, adding threads adds only switching overhead. The demo below shows the wall: on a 4-core machine, 8 threads are no faster than 4. The executors track turns this into a sizing formula. For now, remember the shape: CPU-bound work wants about one thread per core, and waiting work can use many more. Find the core count by timing Before running, check your core count and predict the time for 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads. Run ParallelSum with the command below. Each run does the same 400 million additions, split across the threads. Compare the times. Where does adding threads stop helping? ParallelSum.java package workbench.concurrency.l01; /** Splits a CPU-bound job over 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads and times each run. */ public class ParallelSum { static final int N = 400_000_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("cores: " + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) timed(4); // warm-up runs, so the JIT has compiled the loop for (int threads : new int[] {1, 2, 4, 8}) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long result = timed(threads); System.out.printf("%d thread(s): %4d ms (checksum %d)%n", threads, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, result); } } static long timed(int threads) throws InterruptedException { long[] partial = new long[threads]; Thread[] ts = new Thread[threads]; int chunk = N / threads; for (int w = 0; w < threads; w++) { int slot = w, from = w * chunk, to = (w == threads - 1) ? N : from + chunk; ts[w] = new Thread(() -> { long sum = 0; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) sum += (i * 31L) % 7; // pure CPU work partial[slot] = sum; }); ts[w].start(); } long total = 0; for (int w = 0; w < threads; w++) { ts[w].join(); total += partial[w]; } return total; } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.ParallelSum labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l01/ParallelSum.java ParallelSum.kt package workbench.concurrency.l01 private const val N = 400_000_000 // Splits a CPU-bound job over 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads and times each run. fun main() { println("cores: ${Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()}") repeat(3) { timed(4) } // warm-up runs, so the JIT has compiled the loop for (threads in intArrayOf(1, 2, 4, 8)) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val result = timed(threads) println("%d thread(s): %4d ms (checksum %d)".format(threads, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, result)) } } private fun timed(threads: Int): Long { val partial = LongArray(threads) val chunk = N / threads val workers = List(threads) { w -> val from = w * chunk val to = if (w == threads - 1) N else from + chunk Thread { var sum = 0L for (i in from until to) sum += (i * 31L) % 7 // pure CPU work partial[w] = sum }.apply { start() } } workers.forEach { it.join() } return partial.sum() } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.ParallelSumKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l01/ParallelSum.kt On a 4-core Linux machine one run printed 510 ms, 257 ms, 121 ms and 125 ms. Each doubling halves the time until the threads outnumber the cores. After that the extra threads just take turns on the same cores. Your numbers will differ, but the bend in the curve sits at your core count. Take a thread dump of one of your Quarkus services (jcmd <pid> Thread.print) and count. You'll find event-loop threads, a pool of worker threads for blocking code, Kafka client threads, connection-pool housekeeping threads and the JVM's own helpers, often well over a hundred, on a pod with two cores. Most of them are waiting at any moment, which is why that works. The names tell you who is who, and that is why you name your own threads. The same picture explains a Kafka rule you may already follow: a KafkaConsumer must be used from one thread, so services that want more parallelism run several consumers, one per thread, each with its own partitions.

h: Threads from zero · start() makes a new thread, run() is just a method call
x: Here is the whole API you need for now: Java Runnable task = () -> settle(batch); // what to do Thread t = new Thread(task, "settlement-1"); // a thread that will do it t.start(); // ask the JVM to run it on a new thread t.join(); // wait here until it has finished Kotlin val task = Runnable { settle(batch) } // what to do val t = Thread(task, "settlement-1") // a thread that will do it t.start() // ask the JVM to run it on a new thread t.join() // wait here until it has finished Runnable is a functional interface with one method, void run(), so a lambda works. You can also subclass Thread and override run(), but don't. It ties the work to one way of running it, and the executors and virtual threads you'll meet later take a Runnable, not a Thread subclass. The classic first bug is calling run() instead of start(): Java t.run(); // compiles, works, and runs settle(batch) on the CURRENT thread Kotlin t.run() // same trap in Kotlin: an ordinary call on the current thread Nothing fails. Your tests pass. The code is just sequential, and the job is as slow as before. start() is the call that creates a thread: the JVM asks the operating system for a new thread, and that new thread then calls run(). A thread can be started only once. A second start() throws IllegalThreadStateException. Two more habits pay off from the start. Name your threads. When you read a thread dump at 2 a.m., settlement-1 tells you something and Thread-7 does not. Know what happens to exceptions. If run() throws, that thread ends and the JVM prints the stack trace to standard error. The thread that started it is not told. main carries on as if nothing happened. That is one reason the executors track hands you work through a Future, which carries the exception back to the caller. Last, join(). It waits for a thread to end, and it also makes everything the thread wrote visible to the thread that called join(). Lesson 2 of this track looks at it closely. Break it with run() In HelloThreads, change a.start() and b.start() to a.run() and b.run(). Predict the two "hello from" lines. Run it with the same command as the first Try it. Put the start() calls back, then add a second a.start(); right after the first. Run it again. With run(), both lines say hello from main: no new thread was created, and the joins return at once because the threads never started. With the double start(), main dies with IllegalThreadStateException, while worker-a still prints its line, because the first start worked.

h: Threads from zero · Every thread costs memory and time, and the JVM waits for them
x: A Thread you create this way is a platform thread: one Java thread backed by one operating system thread. That has a price. Memory first. Each platform thread gets its own stack, and on 64-bit Linux the JVM reserves 1 MB for it by default (java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version shows ThreadStackSize = 1024, in KB). The operating system commits that memory only as the stack grows, so a thread with shallow calls uses much less. But 10,000 threads still means 10 GB of reserved address space, 10,000 kernel threads, and a scheduler that has to share the cores among all of them. Somewhere along that road your service dies with an OutOfMemoryError that says it is unable to create a native thread. Then time. Creating, starting and ending a thread is a round trip to the kernel. The demo below measures it. On a busy 4-core Linux machine it printed about 130 microseconds per thread. For one 120 ms card-issuer call, that's noise. For a new thread per Kafka record at 5,000 records a second, it's most of a core spent on thread churn. This is why the executors track reuses threads in pools, and why the virtual threads track exists at all. The last rule in this lesson is about shutdown. The JVM exits when the last non-daemon thread ends, or when someone calls System.exit. Returning from main ends the main thread and nothing else. A worker that is still settling a batch keeps the JVM alive until it finishes. Threads are non-daemon unless you say otherwise. Lesson 2 of this track shows daemon threads and how to stop a thread that should not finish. Kotlin gives you a shorter way to write all this. thread { ... } from kotlin.concurrent creates a java.lang.Thread and starts it at once. Its parameters (start, isDaemon, name, priority) map straight onto the Java ones. It's the same thread with the same costs, and only the syntax changes. Measure a thread, then let main go first Run ThreadCost. It starts and joins 10,000 empty threads, three rounds in a row. Note the microseconds per thread. Now open MainEndsFirst (below). main starts a worker and returns at once. Predict: how many "settling batch" lines will print? Run it with ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.MainEndsFirst. MainEndsFirst.java package workbench.concurrency.l01; /** main returns at once. Does the program end? */ public class MainEndsFirst { public static void main(String[] args) { Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) { System.out.println("worker: settling batch " + i); try { Thread.sleep(300); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } } System.out.println("worker: all batches settled"); }, "settlement-worker"); worker.start(); System.out.println("main: returning from main()"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.MainEndsFirst labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l01/MainEndsFirst.java MainEndsFirst.kt package workbench.concurrency.l01 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // main returns at once. Does the program end? fun main() { thread(name = "settlement-worker") { // thread {} starts it straight away for (i in 1..5) { println("worker: settling batch $i") try { Thread.sleep(300) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { return@thread } } println("worker: all batches settled") } println("main: returning from main()") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l01.MainEndsFirstKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l01/MainEndsFirst.kt ThreadCost prints tens to a couple of hundred microseconds per thread, depending on your machine and how busy it is. MainEndsFirst prints main: returning from main() first, then all five batches and all batches settled. The JVM waited for the non-daemon worker, even though main was long gone. The most common real mistake is reading a worker's result before the worker has finished. Someone starts a thread that fills an array or a field, then reads it on the next line, or adds a Thread.sleep(100) "to give it time". It works on the developer's laptop and returns a half-filled result in production when the machine is busy. The fix is join(): it waits for the thread to end and guarantees you see everything it wrote. sleep guarantees neither.

h: Threads from zero · Java and Kotlin
x: Starting and joining workers in Java and Kotlin Java long[] partial = new long[4]; List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int w = 0; w < 4; w++) { int slot = w; Thread t = new Thread(() -> partial[slot] = sumSlice(slot), "ledger-worker-" + w); t.start(); // nothing runs until start() workers.add(t); } for (Thread t : workers) t.join(); // join() throws the checked InterruptedException KotlinThreads.kt package workbench.concurrency.l01 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The same slice-and-join idea as LedgerTotals, written with Kotlin's thread {} builder. fun main() { val amounts = LongArray(1_000) { it + 1L } val partial = LongArray(4) val chunk = amounts.size / partial.size val workers = List(partial.size) { w -> thread(name = "ledger-worker-$w") { // starts at once: start = true is the default var sum = 0L for (i in w * chunk until (w + 1) * chunk) sum += amounts[i] partial[w] = sum } } workers.forEach { it.join() } // join is the same java.lang.Thread method println("total = ${partial.sum()} on ${workers.map { it.name }}") } Kotlin's thread { } is a small standard-library function that builds a java.lang.Thread, sets its options and calls start() for you, unless you pass start = false. So the Java mistake of forgetting start() mostly goes away. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so join() needs no throws InterruptedException. The interruption rules still apply, and lesson 2 of this track covers them. In Java a lambda can only capture effectively final locals, which is why the loop copies w into slot. A Kotlin lambda captures the w parameter of List(4) { w -> } directly.

h: Threads from zero · Worked example
x: Split a settlement total across four threads You have one million settled amounts in a List<Long> and four cores. First decide the slices. Give each worker a contiguous range, and spread the remainder so sizes differ by at most one. int slices = Math.min(workers, amounts.size()); // no idle threads int base = amounts.size() / slices; int extra = amounts.size() % slices; // the first `extra` slices get one more val slices = minOf(workers, amounts.size) // no idle threads val base = amounts.size / slices val extra = amounts.size % slices // the first `extra` slices get one more Give each worker its own slot in an array. Worker 2 writes only partial[2]. No two threads write the same memory, so there is nothing to race on. long[] partial = new long[slices]; Thread[] threads = new Thread[slices]; val partial = LongArray(slices) val threads = ArrayList<Thread>(slices) Start every thread first. Ask yourself before reading on: what would happen if you called join() inside this same loop, right after start()? int from = 0; for (int w = 0; w < slices; w++) { int start = from, end = start + base + (w < extra ? 1 : 0), slot = w; // 1. each worker sums its own slice into its own slot threads[w] = new Thread(() -> { long sum = 0; for (int i = start; i < end; i++) sum += amounts.get(i); partial[slot] = sum; }, "ledger-worker-" + w); threads[w].start(); from = end; } var from = 0 for (w in 0 until slices) { val start = from val end = start + base + if (w < extra) 1 else 0 // 1. each worker sums its own slice into its own slot threads += thread(name = "ledger-worker-$w") { // thread {} also starts it var sum = 0L for (i in start until end) sum += amounts[i] partial[w] = sum } from = end } Joining inside the loop would wait for worker 0 before starting worker 1, so the workers would run one at a time. Start them all, then join them all. Only after the joins is it safe to read partial, because join() makes each worker's write visible here. // 2. wait for every worker for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); // 3. combine on the calling thread long total = 0; for (long p : partial) total += p; // 2. wait for every worker threads.forEach { it.join() } // 3. combine on the calling thread val total = partial.sum()

h: Threads from zero · Quiz
x: What does this print? Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()), "audit"); t.run(); audit main Thread-0 Nothing, because the thread was never started run() is an ordinary method call, so the lambda runs on the calling thread, which is main. No new thread exists. It would print audit only with t.start(). It does print something, because run() executes the code, just on the wrong thread. A batch job scores transactions with a fraud model. It is pure CPU work, with no I/O. The pod has 4 cores. Which thread count gives about the best throughput? 1 4 64 400 With pure CPU work, each core can run one thread at a time. Four threads keep all four cores busy. More threads only take turns on the same cores and add context-switch overhead. Large counts like 400 make sense only when most threads spend their time waiting. A worker thread throws a NullPointerException out of its run() method. What happens to main, which started it? main gets the NullPointerException at its next line The JVM shuts down main carries on. The worker ends and its stack trace is printed to standard error main gets it when it calls join() An uncaught exception ends only the thread that threw it. The default handler prints the stack trace, and nobody else is told. join() simply returns once the worker has ended. Carrying exceptions back to the caller is a job for Future, in the executors track. What is wrong with this loop? for (Runnable job : jobs) { Thread t = new Thread(job); t.start(); t.join(); } Nothing. It runs the jobs in parallel It runs the jobs one at a time, because each join waits before the next thread starts It deadlocks on the second job join() must be called before start() Each join() blocks until that thread ends, so the next thread starts only after the previous one is done. You pay for threads and get sequential execution. Start all threads in one loop, then join them in a second loop. A Kafka consumer service handles 12 partitions with 12 threads on a 2-core pod. Each record waits about 50 ms on Oracle. Which statement is true? It is concurrent: 12 records are in progress, at most 2 threads run at any instant, and most are waiting anyway It is parallel: all 12 threads run at the same instant It cannot work, because threads must not outnumber cores It is neither concurrent nor parallel Twelve tasks in progress at once is concurrency. With 2 cores, at most 2 threads run at the same instant, which is the parallel part. Because each thread spends most of its time waiting on the database, 12 threads on 2 cores is a sensible setup. The rule of one thread per core is for CPU-bound work.

h: Threads from zero · Key terms
x: Process A running program with its own memory, such as one JVM. Thread One path of execution inside a process, with its own stack, sharing the process heap. Heap The memory where objects and static fields live. Every thread can reach it. Core A piece of the CPU that runs one thread at a time. Context switch The OS pausing one thread and resuming another on the same core. Concurrency Several tasks in progress at once, taking turns or not. Parallelism Several tasks running at the same instant on different cores. Platform thread A Java thread backed one-to-one by an operating system thread. What do threads in one process share, and what does each thread have of its own? They share the heap: objects and static fields. Each thread has its own stack: local variables, parameters and the calls in progress. What happens if you call t.run() instead of t.start()? The code runs on the current thread, like any method call. No new thread is created, and nothing warns you. Concurrency vs parallelism, in one line each. Concurrency: several tasks in progress at the same time (works on one core). Parallelism: several tasks running at the same instant on different cores. When does the JVM exit? When the last non-daemon thread ends, or when something calls System.exit. Returning from main ends only the main thread. How much stack does the JVM reserve for a platform thread on 64-bit Linux by default? 1 MB (ThreadStackSize = 1024 KB). It is reserved address space, committed as the stack grows. Change it with -Xss. What happens when you call start() twice on the same Thread? The second call throws IllegalThreadStateException. A thread runs at most once. A worker thread throws an uncaught exception. Who finds out? Only that thread dies. The default handler prints the stack trace to standard error. The starting thread is not told.

h: Threads from zero · Go deeper
x: Since JDK 21 there is a builder API for threads, and it is worth knowing because the virtual threads track uses the same shape: Java Thread t = Thread.ofPlatform() .name("ledger-worker-", 0) // ledger-worker-0, ledger-worker-1, ... .start(task); Kotlin val t = Thread.ofPlatform() .name("ledger-worker-", 0) // ledger-worker-0, ledger-worker-1, ... .start(task) Thread.ofPlatform() gives you the same kind of thread as new Thread(...). Thread.ofVirtual() gives you a virtual thread, which is not tied to one OS thread and costs far less. That is a whole track of its own. If you want to see the threads the JVM keeps for itself, run jcmd <pid> Thread.print against any running Java process. Beyond the Java threads from the first Try it, you'll see entries such as VM Thread, the JIT compiler threads and the garbage collector's worker threads. These are threads inside the JVM itself. They don't show up in Thread.getAllStackTraces(), but they use cores and memory like any other. One more cost: a context switch is not free. The kernel saves and restores registers, and the new thread often finds the CPU caches full of the old thread's data. That is why the ParallelSum demo does not get faster past the core count, and why a thousand busy threads can run slower than ten.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · A thread is always in one of six states
x: Call t.getState() and you get one of six values of the Thread.State enum. Thread dumps print the same names, so learning them now pays off every time you debug a stuck service. State What the thread is doing NEW Created, but start() has not been called. RUNNABLE Running, or ready to run and waiting for a core. BLOCKED Waiting to enter a synchronized block that another thread holds. WAITING Waiting with no time limit: Object.wait(), join(), LockSupport.park(). TIMED_WAITING The same with a time limit: sleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms). TERMINATED run() has returned or thrown. Three of these surprise people. RUNNABLE does not mean "using a CPU". The Javadoc says the thread is executing in the JVM "but it may be waiting for other resources from the operating system such as processor." A thread waiting its turn for a core is RUNNABLE. So is a thread stuck in a socket read from Oracle, because the JVM only sees that it is inside native code. A thread dump full of RUNNABLE threads can still be a service that does nothing. BLOCKED is only for synchronized. A thread waiting for a ReentrantLock (lesson 7 of this track) is parked: the lock's own Java code puts it to sleep with LockSupport.park() until another thread wakes it, and the JVM reports that as WAITING. If you search a dump for BLOCKED to find lock contention, you'll miss every explicit lock. TERMINATED is final. A thread cannot be restarted. If you need the work done again, you create a new thread, or better, hand the task to a pool. Put a thread in every state Read ThreadStates below. For each show(...) line, predict the state before you run it. Run it with the command below. Find the line the waiter prints when it is interrupted out of wait(). Keep it in mind for the third section. ThreadStates.java package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** Puts threads into each of the six states and prints what getState() reports. */ public class ThreadStates { static final Object monitor = new Object(); static volatile boolean spin = true; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Thread sleeper = new Thread(() -> pause(2_000), "sleeper"); System.out.printf("%-24s%s%n", "before start():", sleeper.getState()); sleeper.start(); show(sleeper, Thread.State.TIMED_WAITING, "inside sleep(2000):"); Thread busy = new Thread(() -> { while (spin) Thread.onSpinWait(); }, "busy"); busy.start(); show(busy, Thread.State.RUNNABLE, "in a busy loop:"); Thread waiter = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (monitor) { try { monitor.wait(); // no timeout } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("waiter interrupted, flag now " + Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()); } } }, "waiter"); waiter.start(); show(waiter, Thread.State.WAITING, "inside wait():"); Thread blocked = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (monitor) { } }, "blocked"); synchronized (monitor) { // main holds the monitor... blocked.start(); // ...so this thread cannot enter show(blocked, Thread.State.BLOCKED, "entering a held lock:"); } spin = false; waiter.interrupt(); for (Thread t : new Thread[] {sleeper, busy, waiter, blocked}) t.interrupt(); for (Thread t : new Thread[] {sleeper, busy, waiter, blocked}) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-24s%s%n", "after join():", sleeper.getState()); } // getState() is a snapshot, so poll until the thread gets where we sent it static void show(Thread t, Thread.State expected, String label) throws InterruptedException { for (int i = 0; i < 200 && t.getState() != expected; i++) Thread.sleep(10); System.out.printf("%-24s%s%n", label, t.getState()); } static void pause(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo ${Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted}") } } } show(waiter, Thread.State.WAITING, "inside wait():") val blocked = Thread({ synchronized(monitor) { } }, "blocked") synchronized(monitor) { // main holds the monitor... blocked.start() // ...so this thread cannot enter show(blocked, Thread.State.BLOCKED, "entering a held lock:") } spin = false val all = listOf(sleeper, busy, waiter, blocked) all.forEach { it.interrupt() } all.forEach { it.join() } println("%-24s%s".format("after join():", sleeper.state)) } // getState() is a snapshot, so poll until the thread gets where we sent it private fun show(t: Thread, expected: Thread.State, label: String) { var i = 0 while (i++ < 200 && t.state != expected) Thread.sleep(10) println("%-24s%s".format(label, t.state)) } private fun pause(ms: Long) { try { Thread.sleep(ms) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.ThreadStatesKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l02/ThreadStates.kt You'll see NEW, TIMED_WAITING (in sleep), RUNNABLE (busy loop), WAITING (in wait()), BLOCKED (main is inside synchronized (monitor), so the thread can't get in) and finally TERMINATED. The waiter prints flag now false: the interrupt woke it, and the flag was cleared on the way out. A thread starts NEW, lives in RUNNABLE, leaves it to wait for a lock, a signal or a timer, and ends TERMINATED. Interrupting a thread is like putting a sticky note on a colleague's monitor that says "please wrap up". If they are asleep at their desk (in sleep or wait), the note wakes them. If they are busy typing, they see it only when they look up, so a good colleague looks up between tasks. The trap is that waking up removes the note: if they read it, shrug and go back to sleep, nobody knows the request was ever made. Restoring the flag means sticking the note back on the monitor for whoever comes next. The analogy breaks because a colleague can ask what you wanted. A thread that clears the flag has no way to recover the request.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Wait with join(), because sleep() only passes time
x: This code waits for a worker, and it is a race: Java worker.start(); Thread.sleep(100); // "should be enough" use(worker.result); // may still be unset Kotlin worker.start() Thread.sleep(100) // "should be enough" use(worker.result) // may still be unset Thread.sleep(ms) pauses the current thread for at least that long and promises nothing about any other thread. On a quiet laptop the worker finishes in 2 ms and the code works. On a loaded CI agent, or a pod sharing its node with a batch job, it doesn't. And even when the worker has finished, main is not promised to see result. The language gives sleep no synchronization meaning, so the JIT may compile both threads as if the other did not exist: it can keep a value in a register instead of memory, or move a read or a write. The memory model track shows a loop that never ends for exactly this reason. join() fixes both problems. It is how one thread waits for another to finish, and it comes in three forms: Java t.join(); // wait as long as it takes t.join(500); // wait up to 500 ms, then return either way boolean ended = t.join(Duration.ofMillis(500)); // JDK 19+: says whether it ended Kotlin t.join() // wait as long as it takes t.join(500) // wait up to 500 ms, then return either way val ended = t.join(Duration.ofMillis(500)) // JDK 19+: says whether it ended After a timed join, check t.isAlive() (or the boolean) to learn whether the thread ended or you simply stopped waiting. join() does a second job, and it matters more than the waiting. When join() returns, the calling thread is guaranteed to see everything the finished thread wrote. The java.util.concurrent docs put it this way: "All actions in a thread happen-before any other thread successfully returns from a join on that thread." Happens-before is the memory model's name for that guarantee. That is why the lab in lesson 1 of this track (Threads from zero) could read the partial array after the joins with no locks at all. Use sleep for what it is: a pause. A back-off between retries to the card issuer, or a poll interval. Since JDK 19 you can write Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(200)) if you like the unit in the type. Give up waiting, then wait properly Read JoinWithTimeout. The worker takes about 500 ms. Predict both printed lines. Run it. Change the timed join to fetch.join(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) and run again. What does ended say now, and how long did main wait? JoinWithTimeout.java package workbench.concurrency.l02; import java.time.Duration; /** join(timeout) gives up waiting; join() waits for the end and makes the result visible. */ public class JoinWithTimeout { static long rateCents; // plain field: join() is what makes the write visible public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread fetch = new Thread(() -> { sleepQuietly(500); // stands in for a 500 ms call to an FX-rate service rateCents = 10_842; }, "fx-fetch"); fetch.start(); boolean ended = fetch.join(Duration.ofMillis(100)); // JDK 19+: returns whether it ended System.out.println("after join(100 ms): ended=" + ended + ", alive=" + fetch.isAlive() + ", rate=" + rateCents); fetch.join(); // no timeout: wait for the end System.out.println("after join(): alive=" + fetch.isAlive() + ", rate=" + rateCents); } static void sleepQuietly(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.JoinWithTimeout labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l02/JoinWithTimeout.java JoinWithTimeout.kt package workbench.concurrency.l02 import java.time.Duration import kotlin.concurrent.thread // join(timeout) gives up waiting; join() waits for the end and makes the result visible. private var rateCents = 0L // plain field: join() is what makes the write visible fun main() { val fetch = thread(name = "fx-fetch") { try { Thread.sleep(500) // stands in for a 500 ms call to an FX-rate service } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } rateCents = 10_842 } val ended = fetch.join(Duration.ofMillis(100)) // JDK 19+: returns whether it ended println("after join(100 ms): ended=$ended, alive=${fetch.isAlive}, rate=$rateCents") fetch.join() // no timeout: wait for the end println("after join(): alive=${fetch.isAlive}, rate=$rateCents") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.JoinWithTimeoutKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l02/JoinWithTimeout.kt First run: ended=false, alive=true, rate=0, then alive=false, rate=10842. With a 2-second limit, ended=true and the rate is already there after about 500 ms: a timed join returns as soon as the thread ends, it does not wait out the full time. Every shutdown in your stack is an interrupt in the end. When Quarkus stops, or Kubernetes sends SIGTERM during a rollout, executors call shutdownNow(), which interrupts their worker threads. A Kafka consumer loop that catches InterruptedException around a sleep back-off and carries on will keep the pod alive until the grace period runs out and the kubelet kills it, possibly halfway through a batch of offset commits. A Temporal activity that retries a card-issuer call with Thread.sleep between attempts has the same problem. Search your code for catch (InterruptedException and check each one either rethrows or calls Thread.currentThread().interrupt().

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Interrupt is a polite request, and the flag is easy to lose
x: Java has no safe way to kill a thread. It has interrupt(), which asks. t.interrupt() sets a flag on t, and what happens next depends on what t is doing: If it is blocked in sleep, wait or join, or in a blocking call such as BlockingQueue.take(), that call throws InterruptedException. Otherwise nothing happens right away. The flag stays set until the thread looks at it. The thread looks with Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted(), which only reads the flag, or with the static Thread.interrupted(), which reads it and clears it. Use the first one unless you really mean to consume the request. Now the detail behind most interrupt bugs. Methods that throw InterruptedException clear the flag before they throw. So inside your catch block the flag is already false. If you log the exception and carry on, the request is gone. The loop around you never learns it was asked to stop, and executor.shutdownNow(), which works by interrupting, can't stop your task. The rule has two options. Let the exception propagate (declare throws InterruptedException), or restore the flag before you do anything else: Java try { Thread.sleep(backoffMillis); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // put the request back return; // then stop, or throw your own exception } Kotlin try { Thread.sleep(backoffMillis) // Kotlin compiles this without a try, so add one on purpose } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // put the request back return // then stop, or throw your own exception } The JDK's own engineers get this wrong too. JDK 23 fixed ImageIcon.loadImage to restore the flag, and JDK 24 fixed the same bug in FileSystemPreferences.lockFile(). From JDK 26 the Thread Javadoc has a section on interruption that states the rule above in so many words. One more case. A loop that never blocks, such as one that publishes batch after batch while the outbox is full, never meets an InterruptedException. It must check isInterrupted() itself, once per iteration or once per batch. Otherwise the interrupt cannot reach it. Watch the flag disappear Run InterruptFlag and read the five numbered lines. Comment out the line me.interrupt() in the catch block. Predict lines 2 to 5, then run again. Explain to yourself why line 4 prints true the first time and why line 5 then prints false. InterruptFlag.java package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** Watch the interrupt flag: set by interrupt(), cleared when sleep() throws, restored by you. */ public class InterruptFlag { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { Thread me = Thread.currentThread(); try { Thread.sleep(10_000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("1. caught InterruptedException, flag is now " + me.isInterrupted()); me.interrupt(); // restore it: comment this line out and run again System.out.println("2. after interrupt(), flag is " + me.isInterrupted()); } System.out.println("3. isInterrupted() only reads it: " + me.isInterrupted()); System.out.println("4. Thread.interrupted() reads AND clears: " + Thread.interrupted()); System.out.println("5. so now the flag is " + me.isInterrupted()); }, "worker"); worker.start(); Thread.sleep(200); worker.interrupt(); // a request, not a command worker.join(); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.InterruptFlag labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l02/InterruptFlag.java InterruptFlag.kt package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Watch the interrupt flag: set by interrupt(), cleared when sleep() throws, restored by you. fun main() { val worker = thread(name = "worker") { val me = Thread.currentThread() try { Thread.sleep(10_000) // Kotlin doesn't force this try/catch on you } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("1. caught InterruptedException, flag is now ${me.isInterrupted}") me.interrupt() // restore it: comment this line out and run again println("2. after interrupt(), flag is ${me.isInterrupted}") } println("3. isInterrupted only reads it: ${me.isInterrupted}") println("4. Thread.interrupted() reads AND clears: ${Thread.interrupted()}") println("5. so now the flag is ${me.isInterrupted}") } Thread.sleep(200) worker.interrupt() // a request, not a command worker.join() } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.InterruptFlagKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l02/InterruptFlag.kt With the restore: false, true, true, true, false. Line 1 is false because sleep cleared the flag. Line 4 consumes it, so line 5 is false. Without the restore, every line after the first prints false: the request was lost the moment the exception was caught. h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Daemon threads, and the stop button Java took away
x: A daemon thread is one the JVM will not wait for. When the last non-daemon thread ends, the JVM exits and any daemon threads stop wherever they are. Their finally blocks do not run. Java Thread flusher = new Thread(this::flushMetrics, "metrics-flusher"); flusher.setDaemon(true); // before start(), or you get IllegalThreadStateException flusher.start(); Kotlin val flusher = Thread(this::flushMetrics, "metrics-flusher") flusher.isDaemon = true // before start(), or you get IllegalThreadStateException flusher.start() // or in one go: thread(name = "metrics-flusher", isDaemon = true) { flushMetrics() } A new thread copies the daemon setting of the thread that created it, so threads started from main are non-daemon. The JVM's own helpers, like Finalizer and Signal Dispatcher from lesson 1 of this track, are daemons. Daemon threads suit background work you can afford to lose halfway: a cache refresher, a metrics flusher. They are the wrong choice for anything that writes to the ledger or commits a Kafka offset, because the JVM can cut them off between the write and the commit. So how do you stop a thread that would not finish on its own? You interrupt it, and it stops itself. Java once had a real stop button. Thread.stop() threw an error inside the target thread wherever it happened to be, which released its locks and left half-updated objects for other threads to find. It was deprecated in Java 1.2, made to always throw UnsupportedOperationException in JDK 20, and removed in JDK 26. suspend() and resume() were removed in JDK 23. Old code that still calls stop() fails with NoSuchMethodError on JDK 26 and later. That leaves cooperative cancellation as the only kind there is: interrupt asks, the thread checks, cleans up and returns. Every executor, framework and pool you use is built on that contract. A task that swallows an interrupt doesn't just ignore one request. It breaks shutdown for every layer above it. Lose a finally block Run DaemonDemo. Count the flushes and look for the finally line. Change setDaemon(true) to setDaemon(false) (in Kotlin, isDaemon = true to false) and run it again. Stop it with Ctrl+C when you have seen enough. Keep it non-daemon, and add metrics.interrupt(); metrics.join(); just before main's last println. Run it once more. DaemonDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l02; /** A daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive. Its finally block does not run either. */ public class DaemonDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread metrics = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int i = 1; ; i++) { System.out.println("metrics: flush " + i); Thread.sleep(200); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { System.out.println("metrics: finally block ran"); } }, "metrics-flusher"); metrics.setDaemon(true); // must be called before start(); try false metrics.start(); Thread.sleep(700); System.out.println("main: done, returning"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.DaemonDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l02/DaemonDemo.java DaemonDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l02 // A daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive. Its finally block does not run either. fun main() { val metrics = Thread({ try { var i = 1 while (true) { println("metrics: flush ${i++}") Thread.sleep(200) } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } finally { println("metrics: finally block ran") } }, "metrics-flusher") metrics.isDaemon = true // must be set before start(); try false metrics.start() // (or: thread(isDaemon = true) { ... }) Thread.sleep(700) println("main: done, returning") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l02.DaemonDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l02/DaemonDemo.kt As a daemon: four flushes, main: done, returning, and no finally block ran. The JVM exited under it. As a non-daemon it flushes forever, because nothing asks it to stop. With the interrupt and join, it stops at once and prints finally block ran before main finishes. That is a clean shutdown. The most common real mistake is the empty or log-only catch: catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("interrupted", e); } inside a loop. People write it because Java forces them to catch the checked exception and the quickest way to make the compiler happy is to log it. Because the flag is cleared when the exception is thrown, the stop request vanishes and the loop runs on. The fix is one line, Thread.currentThread().interrupt();, followed by leaving the loop, or declaring throws InterruptedException and letting it propagate.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Java and Kotlin
x: An interruptible polling loop in Java and Kotlin Java Thread relay = new Thread(() -> { Thread me = Thread.currentThread(); while (!me.isInterrupted()) { // poll the outbox and publish here try { Thread.sleep(50); // the compiler forces you to handle the checked exception } catch (InterruptedException e) { me.interrupt(); // restore the flag, so the loop condition sees it } } System.out.println("relay stopped, flag = " + me.isInterrupted()); }, "outbox-relay"); relay.start(); KotlinRelay.kt package workbench.concurrency.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A polling loop that follows the interruption protocol, in Kotlin. fun main() { val relay = thread(name = "outbox-relay") { val me = Thread.currentThread() while (!me.isInterrupted) { // property syntax for isInterrupted() // poll the outbox and publish here try { Thread.sleep(50) // no try/catch is forced on you in Kotlin... } catch (e: InterruptedException) { me.interrupt() // ...but the protocol is the same: restore the flag } } println("relay stopped, flag = ${me.isInterrupted}") } Thread.sleep(300) relay.interrupt() relay.join() println("relay alive after join: ${relay.isAlive}") } Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so Thread.sleep(50) compiles without any try/catch. That changes the failure mode. In Java the usual bug is an empty catch that swallows the interrupt. In Kotlin the usual bug is no catch at all: the InterruptedException escapes the lambda, the thread dies with a stack trace on standard error, and any cleanup after the loop never runs. Neither is a clean stop. The protocol is the same in both languages: catch it where you can do something sensible, restore the flag, and leave. isInterrupted reads as a property in Kotlin, and the static Thread.interrupted() still clears the flag.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Worked example
x: Make a retrying card-issuer call cancellable This retry loop calls the card issuer and backs off on timeouts. Read it and find where a shutdown request disappears. AuthResult authorize(AuthRequest req) { for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return issuer.authorize(req); } catch (IssuerTimeoutException e) { try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt); } catch (InterruptedException ie) { log.warn("interrupted during back-off", ie); // and loop again } } } } fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): AuthResult { var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { return issuer.authorize(req) } catch (e: IssuerTimeoutException) { try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt) } catch (ie: InterruptedException) { log.warn("interrupted during back-off", ie) // and loop again } } attempt++ } } The inner catch logs and loops. sleep cleared the flag before throwing, so nothing remembers the request, and the loop has no limit. If the issuer is down during a rollout, this thread retries until the pod is killed. Before reading on, decide what the method should do when it is interrupted. Restore the flag first, then stop retrying and tell the caller why. Wrapping the cause in your own exception is fine, as long as the flag is set before you throw. Add a retry limit while you're here. AuthResult authorize(AuthRequest req) { for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return issuer.authorize(req); } catch (IssuerTimeoutException e) { if (attempt == 3) throw e; // 1. bounded retries try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt); } catch (InterruptedException ie) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // 2. restore the request throw new AuthCancelledException(req.id(), ie); // 3. stop, and say why } } } } fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): AuthResult { var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { return issuer.authorize(req) } catch (e: IssuerTimeoutException) { if (attempt == 3) throw e // 1. bounded retries try { Thread.sleep(200L * attempt) } catch (ie: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // 2. restore the request throw AuthCancelledException(req.id, ie) // 3. stop, and say why } } attempt++ } } Now the caller, say an executor shutting down, sees the interrupt flag still set on its worker thread, and the payment is reported as cancelled instead of being retried forever. If authorize could simply declare throws InterruptedException, that would be even simpler: then there is nothing to restore.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Quiz
x: A thread is stuck inside ReentrantLock.lock(), waiting for another thread to release it. What does getState() return? BLOCKED WAITING RUNNABLE TIMED_WAITING ReentrantLock makes waiting threads park with LockSupport.park(), and a parked thread is WAITING. BLOCKED is reserved for threads trying to enter a synchronized block or method. That difference matters when you scan a thread dump for contention. What does this print? Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(5_000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()); } }); t.start(); t.interrupt(); true Nothing: the thread sleeps for 5 s and ends false It depends on whether interrupt() runs before sleep() starts If the interrupt arrives during the sleep, sleep throws and clears the flag. If it arrives before the sleep starts, sleep sees the flag, clears it and throws at once. Either way the catch block sees false. Timing changes when the exception comes, not what the flag says. A Kafka consumer loop wraps its back-off in try { Thread.sleep(500); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("interrupted"); } and keeps looping. What goes wrong at shutdown? Nothing, because the exception was logged The consumer stops, but its last batch is processed twice The JVM throws IllegalMonitorStateException shutdownNow() interrupts it, the catch clears the request, and the loop keeps running until the process is killed shutdownNow() stops tasks by interrupting them. The InterruptedException cleared the flag, and the catch block didn't restore it, so the loop never learns it should stop. Logging doesn't count as handling. Restore the flag and leave the loop. A daemon thread writes audit lines to a file and closes the file in a finally block. The last non-daemon thread ends. What happens to the daemon thread? The JVM waits for it to finish the current line The JVM exits, the daemon stops where it is, and its finally block does not run The JVM interrupts it and waits for the finally block It becomes a non-daemon thread and keeps the JVM alive The JVM does not wait for daemon threads and does not unwind their stacks when it exits, so finally blocks don't run. Audit output can be lost or truncated. Work that must complete belongs on a non-daemon thread that you stop with an interrupt and join. From Threads from zero: a loop starts each thread and joins it in the same iteration, t.start(); t.join();, for four threads. While the loop runs, how many of those four threads are alive at the same time? At most one All four Two: the current one and the next None, because join() stops them Each join() blocks the loop until that thread is TERMINATED, and only then does the next iteration start a new thread. So at most one of the four is ever alive. The fix is to start all four first and join them in a second loop.
