h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Key terms
x: Thread state What a thread is doing right now, one of the six values of Thread.State. join Wait for a thread to end. Afterwards you see everything it wrote. Interrupt flag A per-thread boolean that interrupt() sets to ask the thread to stop. InterruptedException Thrown by blocking calls when the thread is interrupted. The flag is cleared when it is thrown. Daemon thread A thread the JVM does not wait for at exit. It can stop mid-work. Cooperative cancellation Stopping a thread by asking it, and letting it check and clean up itself. A thread waits to enter a synchronized block another thread holds. What state is it in? BLOCKED. A thread waits in ReentrantLock.lock(). What state is it in? WAITING (or TIMED_WAITING for a timed tryLock). Explicit locks park the thread; BLOCKED is only for monitors. Besides waiting, what does t.join() guarantee? Everything t wrote before it ended is visible to the thread whose join() returned. sleep() gives no such guarantee. What happens to the interrupt flag when sleep() throws InterruptedException? It is cleared before the exception is thrown. Inside the catch block, isInterrupted() returns false. What are the two correct ways to handle a caught InterruptedException? Rethrow it (declare throws InterruptedException), or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and stop what you're doing. isInterrupted() vs Thread.interrupted()? isInterrupted() only reads the flag. The static Thread.interrupted() reads it and clears it. What is the status of Thread.stop() on JDK 26? Removed. It always threw UnsupportedOperationException from JDK 20, and old binaries that call it get NoSuchMethodError on 26+.

h: A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt · Go deeper
x: Not every blocking call listens to interrupts. sleep, wait, join, BlockingQueue.take and Lock.lockInterruptibly throw InterruptedException. A thread blocked on an NIO InterruptibleChannel is different: the Javadoc says the channel is closed, the flag is set and the thread gets a ClosedByInterruptException. So interrupting a thread that is writing to a FileChannel closes the file for everyone who shares that channel. Plain synchronized does not respond at all. A thread that is BLOCKED waiting for a monitor stays blocked when you interrupt it; only the flag changes. A platform thread reading a classic java.net.Socket stream may also sit there until data arrives. For those, set a timeout (a socket read timeout, tryLock with a timeout) so the thread wakes up regularly and can check its flag. Two smaller facts. Interrupts are part of the memory model too: if T1 interrupts T2, everything T1 did before the interrupt is visible to T2 once T2 sees the interrupt (by catching the exception or reading the flag). And JDK 27's Javadoc for interrupt() notes that interrupting a thread that is not alive still records the request in the reference implementation, so do not count on an interrupt before start() being dropped.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Two threads, one counter, the wrong answer
x: Here is the smallest broken program in this course. Two threads share one counter, and each adds one to it a million times. Java static volatile int count = 0; Runnable work = () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) count++; }; Thread a = new Thread(work), b = new Thread(work); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); System.out.println(count); // 2,000,000? Usually not. Kotlin @Volatile var count = 0 val work = { repeat(1_000_000) { count++ } } val a = thread { work() } val b = thread { work() } a.join(); b.join() println(count) // 2,000,000? Usually not. On my laptop five runs printed 1,851,852, then 1,633,408, then 1,920,984, then 1,599,468, then 2,000,000. Four wrong answers and one right one, from the same code. This is a race condition: the result depends on how the threads happen to interleave. Nothing crashed. No exception, no warning, no log line. The program just did arithmetic wrong, and it did it differently each time. Two details are worth knowing now. The field is volatile (@Volatile in Kotlin) only to keep the demo honest. Without it the JIT compiler may keep count in a CPU register for the whole loop and write it back once at the end, which makes the lost updates disappear on some runs. That does not fix anything. It just hides the bug. volatile does not make count++ safe either; the memory model track shows exactly why. The second detail matters more. Shrink the loop to 1,000 and every run prints the right answer. The first thread finishes before the second one even starts, so they never overlap. That is why races pass unit tests and fail under production traffic. A test that never makes threads collide proves nothing about thread safety. Watch the counter lie Open RaceDemo.java (or its Kotlin twin, RaceDemo.kt) in the labs project. Before you run it, write down the number you expect. Run it from labs/ with the command below. Note how many updates each run loses. Run it again with -Pargs=1000 added. Predict first: will small loops lose updates? RaceDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l03; /** Two threads each add 1,000,000 to a shared counter. Watch what comes out. */ public class RaceDemo { // volatile only stops the JIT from keeping count in a register, which would hide the race. // It does NOT make count++ safe. The memory model track explains why. static volatile int count = 0; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int perThread = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 1_000_000; for (int run = 1; run <= 5; run++) { count = 0; Runnable work = () -> { for (int i = 0; i < perThread; i++) count++; }; Thread a = new Thread(work), b = new Thread(work); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); System.out.printf("run %d: expected %,d, got %,d (lost %,d)%n", run, 2 * perThread, count, 2 * perThread - count); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l03.RaceDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l03/RaceDemo.java RaceDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l03 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // @Volatile only stops the JIT from keeping count in a register, which would hide the race. // It does NOT make count++ safe. The memory model track explains why. @Volatile private var count = 0 /** Two threads each add 1,000,000 to a shared counter. Watch what comes out. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val perThread = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 1_000_000 for (run in 1..5) { count = 0 val work = { repeat(perThread) { count++ } } val a = thread { work() } val b = thread { work() } a.join(); b.join() println("run %d: expected %,d, got %,d (lost %,d)".format(run, 2 * perThread, count, 2 * perThread - count)) } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l03.RaceDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l03/RaceDemo.kt With a million per thread, most runs lose tens or hundreds of thousands of updates, and the number changes every run. With 1,000 per thread you almost always get exactly 2,000, because each thread finishes before the other gets going. Same bug, no symptom. Picture two cashiers sharing one paper tally sheet. Each reads the total, adds their sale on a scrap of paper, and writes the new total over the old one. If both read 41 before either writes, both write 42 and one sale disappears from the books. The fix is to pass a single pen: whoever holds it does read, add and write before handing it over. The analogy breaks in one way: cashiers would notice the sheet changed under them. A CPU never notices. It writes 42 without complaint.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · count++ is three steps, not one
x: Why count++ lies: three steps, two threads, one lost update count++ looks like one operation. The JVM runs it as three. Here is the bytecode javac produces for it: getstatic count // read the current value onto the stack iconst_1 // push 1 iadd // add them putstatic count // write the result back A thread can be paused between any two of those instructions. The operating system can move it off the CPU, or another core can run the same instructions at the same moment. So this can happen: T1 reads count: 41. T2 reads count: 41. T1 adds one and writes 42. T2 adds one and writes 42. Two increments ran. The counter moved by one. This is a lost update, and the pattern behind it has a name: read-modify-write. You read a value, compute a new one from it, and write it back, while assuming nobody changed it in between. Once you know the shape, you see it everywhere: balance = balance - amount; map.put(key, map.get(key) + 1); total += invoice.amount(); list.add(x) on an ArrayList, which does size++ inside. None of these is safe when two threads run it on shared data. The fix is always the same idea: the read and the write must happen as one step that no other thread can split. That property is called atomic. The simulator below lets you play the scheduler. You pick which thread runs its next step. Try to make two increments end with count = 1. Then try to get 2. Notice that you need the threads to take turns on whole increments to get the right answer. See the three steps yourself Run the demo once (previous Try it) so Gradle compiles it. From labs/, run the javap command below. It prints the bytecode of the class. Find the lambda method (lambda$main$0) and the four lines that make up count++. terminal javap -c -p concurrency/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/concurrency/l03/RaceDemo.class Inside lambda$main$0 you'll see getstatic count, iconst_1, iadd, putstatic count. A thread can be paused between any two of them. Thread interference (The Java Tutorials) read Look for the daily spend limit check in a payment service: if (spentToday + amount <= limit) { approve(); spentToday += amount; }. Two authorizations for the same card arrive 3 ms apart on two Quarkus worker threads. Both read spentToday before either adds to it, and the card goes over its limit. The same shape appears in Kafka consumers with concurrency above 1, in in-memory metrics counters, and in Temporal activities that check "already done?" before doing work. Activities can be retried, so make that check a single atomic step, ideally a database insert guarded by a unique key.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Check-then-act: the race inside an if
x: The second shape of race hides in an if. You check a condition, then act on it, assuming the condition still holds. Java if (!owners.containsKey(seat)) { // check owners.put(seat, passenger); // act return true; } return false; Kotlin if (!owners.containsKey(seat)) { // check owners[seat] = passenger // act return true } return false owners is a ConcurrentHashMap. Every single call on it is thread-safe. The code still sells the same seat twice, because the gap between containsKey and put belongs to nobody. Two buyers can both see the seat as free, and both go on to buy it. The second put silently replaces the first owner, and both callers got true. This is the point most people miss: a thread-safe class does not make your code thread-safe. Each method is atomic. Two calls in a row are not. The gap is often much wider than one line. Here is a version you may have written: Java if (!processed.contains(msg.idempotencyKey())) { ledger.charge(msg); // 80 ms call to the card issuer processed.add(msg.idempotencyKey()); } Kotlin if (msg.idempotencyKey !in processed) { ledger.charge(msg) // 80 ms call to the card issuer processed += msg.idempotencyKey } Kafka redelivers a message after a consumer rebalance, and two consumer threads pick up both copies. Both check the set during the same 80 ms. The customer pays twice. Lazy initialization is the same shape: if (instance == null) instance = new Expensive(); can build two instances. The fix is to let one operation do both the check and the act, so there is no gap: Java return owners.putIfAbsent(seat, passenger) == null; // only one caller can see null Kotlin return owners.putIfAbsent(seat, passenger) == null // same JDK call from Kotlin Inside, the map does the lookup and the insert as one step on that key's slot, so no other thread can get in between. Lesson 9 of this track shows how. putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, merge and Set.add (which returns false when the element was already there) all exist for this reason. Across machines, the same idea is a unique constraint in the database: insert the key first, and let the second insert fail. Double-book a concert Run DoubleBookingDemo with the command below. Eight buyers race for 1,000 seats. Change the check and the put into one call: if (owners.putIfAbsent(seat, me) == null) sold.incrementAndGet() in either version (keep the spin loop before it). Run it again. DoubleBookingDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l03; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Eight buyers race for the same 1,000 seats using check-then-act on a ConcurrentHashMap. */ public class DoubleBookingDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Map<Integer, String> owners = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); AtomicInteger sold = new AtomicInteger(); Thread[] buyers = new Thread[8]; for (int b = 0; b < buyers.length; b++) { String me = "buyer-" + b; buyers[b] = new Thread(() -> { for (int seat = 0; seat < 1_000; seat++) { if (!owners.containsKey(seat)) { // check for (int i = 0; i < 300; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); // a slow step owners.put(seat, me); // act sold.incrementAndGet(); } } }); } for (Thread t : buyers) t.start(); for (Thread t : buyers) t.join(); System.out.printf("seats: 1,000 tickets sold: %,d double-booked: %,d%n", sold.get(), sold.get() - 1_000); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l03.DoubleBookingDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l03/DoubleBookingDemo.java DoubleBookingDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l03 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** Eight buyers race for the same 1,000 seats using check-then-act on a ConcurrentHashMap. */ fun main() { val owners = ConcurrentHashMap<Int, String>() val sold = AtomicInteger() val buyers = (0 until 8).map { b -> thread(start = false) { for (seat in 0 until 1_000) { if (!owners.containsKey(seat)) { // check repeat(300) { Thread.onSpinWait() } // a slow step owners[seat] = "buyer-$b" // act sold.incrementAndGet() } } } } buyers.forEach { it.start() } buyers.forEach { it.join() } println("seats: 1,000 tickets sold: %,d double-booked: %,d".format(sold.get(), sold.get() - 1_000)) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l03.DoubleBookingDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l03/DoubleBookingDemo.kt The first run sells a few hundred tickets too many (one run here printed 1,413 tickets for 1,000 seats). After the change it sells exactly 1,000, every run, with the same slow step still inside the loop. Both buyers check before either one writes. The gap between check and act is where the race lives.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · What a fix has to do
x: Every fix for a race does two jobs. It makes the compound action atomic, so no other thread can run in the middle of it. And it makes the result visible, so the next thread to look sees the new value and not an old copy. Visibility gets its own track later. For now, know that the tools below give you both. Here are your options, in the order I reach for them: Don't share. Give each thread its own counter and add them up at the end. Or keep the state inside one thread, such as one Kafka partition handled by one consumer. No sharing, no race. Use one atomic operation the library already has. AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet(), LongAdder.increment(), ConcurrentHashMap.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum), putIfAbsent, Set.add. These are fast and hard to get wrong. Lesson 8 shows how they work. Lock the whole compound action. Mark the method synchronized so only one thread at a time can run it. This works for any code, including the slow 80 ms charge, but every caller now waits in line. Lesson 4 is about synchronized. The lock must cover the read too. A synchronized setter with an unsynchronized getter is still broken. Taking the same lock is what makes a thread see the last owner's writes, so a reader that skips it can keep using an old value, for example a copy the JIT kept in a register, as in the first section. And it must cover the whole action. Locking containsKey and put separately just gives you two atomic steps with the same gap between them. For the counter, the cheapest correct fix is to put count++ inside a static synchronized void inc() method, or to swap the int for an AtomicInteger. Either way the demo prints 2,000,000 on every run. Fix RaceDemo two ways In RaceDemo, add static synchronized void inc() { count++; } and call inc() in the loop. Run it. Undo that. Change count to static final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger();, call count.incrementAndGet(), reset it with count.set(0) and print count.get(). Run it. Which one felt slower? Add long t0 = System.nanoTime(); before the threads start and print the elapsed milliseconds after the joins to check. Both versions print exactly 2,000,000 on all five runs. On a typical laptop the atomic version is faster than the synchronized one when two threads fight over the counter, though both are much slower than the broken version. Correct code that does real synchronization costs something. The most common mistake is trusting a thread-safe collection to make compound logic safe. ConcurrentHashMap, Collections.synchronizedMap and ConcurrentLinkedQueue make each method call atomic. They say nothing about two calls in a row. Code like if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) or map.put(k, map.get(k) + 1) is still a race. Reach for the single method that does the whole job: putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent, merge or compute.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Java and Kotlin
x: The same race and fix in Java and Kotlin HitCounter.java public class HitCounter { private int count; // broken: count++ is read, add, write public void hitBroken() { count++; } // fixed: one thread at a time public synchronized void hit() { count++; } public synchronized int total() { return count; } } HitCounter.kt class HitCounter { private var count = 0 // broken: compiles to the same read, add, write fun hitBroken() { count++ } // fixed: Kotlin has no synchronized keyword; use the annotation @Synchronized fun hit() { count++ } @Synchronized fun total(): Int = count } Kotlin's count++ on a var property compiles to the same three bytecode steps, so it races in exactly the same way. Kotlin has no synchronized modifier. You write @Synchronized on a function, or call the standard library function synchronized(lock) { ... } with an explicit lock object. java.util.concurrent.atomic works the same from both languages.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Worked example
x: Find and fix the race in an idempotency check A payment handler skips messages it has already processed. It runs on four Kafka consumer threads. Read it and look for the shape before reading on. class PaymentHandler { private final Set<String> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); void handle(PaymentMessage m) { if (seen.contains(m.idempotencyKey())) return; // check ledger.charge(m); // 80 ms seen.add(m.idempotencyKey()); // act } } class PaymentHandler { private val seen: MutableSet<String> = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() fun handle(m: PaymentMessage) { if (m.idempotencyKey in seen) return // check ledger.charge(m) // 80 ms seen += m.idempotencyKey // act } } It is check-then-act. Two copies of the same message, handled by two threads within the same 80 ms, both pass the contains check. Both charge the card. The set being concurrent does not help, because the race is between the calls, not inside them. Claim the key first, in one atomic call. Set.add returns false if the key was already there, so only one thread gets past this line. If the charge fails, release the claim so a retry can try again. void handle(PaymentMessage m) { if (!seen.add(m.idempotencyKey())) return; // check and act in one step try { ledger.charge(m); } catch (RuntimeException e) { seen.remove(m.idempotencyKey()); // let a retry have another go throw e; } } fun handle(m: PaymentMessage) { // 1. claim the key: add() returns false if it was already there if (!seen.add(m.idempotencyKey)) return try { ledger.charge(m) // 2. charge } catch (e: RuntimeException) { seen.remove(m.idempotencyKey) // 3. release on failure throw e } } That fixes the race inside one JVM. It does not survive a restart, and it does not cover two pods. In production the claim belongs in the database: insert the key into a table with a unique constraint before charging, and treat a duplicate-key error as "already processed". It is the same idea, one atomic step, moved to the place that all instances share. INSERT INTO processed_payment (idempotency_key, received_at) VALUES (?, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP); -- a second insert fails on the unique key

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Quiz
x: Two request threads run account.balance = account.balance - amount; on the same account at the same time. What can go wrong? Nothing, because one Java statement runs atomically One of the two debits can be lost, because both read the same starting balance The JVM throws an IllegalStateException The balance always goes negative It's read-modify-write. If both threads read 100 and debit 10, both write 90. One debit vanished. Java statements are not atomic just because they fit on one line. counts is a ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer>. Many threads run counts.put(k, counts.getOrDefault(k, 0) + 1). What is the smallest correct fix? Make the map field volatile Wrap the map with Collections.synchronizedMap Use counts.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum) Switch to a HashMap merge reads, computes and writes in one atomic operation on that key. volatile on the field only affects the reference to the map, and a synchronized wrapper still makes each call atomic on its own, leaving the gap between get and put. A test runs 2 threads that each call hit() 1,000 times, and checks the total is 2,000. It passed 100 runs in a row. What does that tell you? The counter is thread-safe Very little: the threads probably never overlapped The JIT fixed the race The test should use 1 thread instead A thread can finish 1,000 increments before the second thread starts. With no overlap, a racy counter gives the right answer. Use more threads, more iterations and a start latch so they run at the same time. A cache does if (cache.get(id) == null) cache.put(id, loadFromDb(id)); on a ConcurrentHashMap. Two threads ask for the same missing id together. What happens? Both may call loadFromDb, and the second put replaces the first value The second thread blocks until the first one finishes The map throws ConcurrentModificationException Only one thread can call get at a time, so it is safe It's check-then-act. Both see null, both load, both put. You pay for two database calls and callers may hold different objects. computeIfAbsent(id, this::loadFromDb) runs the loader at most once per key. From the last lesson: main starts thread t, which sets result = 42. When can main safely read result? Right after t.start() returns After t.join() returns After Thread.sleep(100) Any time, because int writes are atomic join waits for t to finish, and everything t wrote before it ended is visible to the thread whose join returned. sleep only makes it likely, not guaranteed. An atomic write still says nothing about when another thread sees it.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Key terms
x: Race condition A bug where the result depends on which thread runs when. Lost update Two threads read the same old value and both write, so one change disappears. Read-modify-write Read a value, compute a new one from it, write it back. Unsafe on shared data unless done atomically. Check-then-act Test a condition, then act on it, assuming it still holds. Unsafe if another thread can act in between. Atomic Happens as one indivisible step. Other threads see it either not started or fully done. Critical section A piece of code that only one thread at a time may run, because it touches shared state. What is a race condition? A bug where the result depends on the timing or interleaving of threads. It usually gives wrong results silently, not an exception. Why is count++ not atomic? It runs as three steps: read count, add one, write it back. Another thread can run between them, so two increments can produce one. Name the two shapes of race condition. Read-modify-write (count++, balance -= x) and check-then-act (if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)). Is if (!chm.containsKey(k)) chm.put(k, v) safe on a ConcurrentHashMap? No. Each call is atomic, but another thread can put between them. Use chm.putIfAbsent(k, v). Atomic fix for map.put(k, map.get(k) + 1) on a ConcurrentHashMap? map.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum) Why does a 2-thread x 1,000-iteration race test usually pass on broken code? The first thread often finishes before the second starts, so they never overlap. Use a start latch and many iterations.

h: Race conditions: why count++ lies · Go deeper
x: Two terms sound alike and mean different things. A data race is a precise term from the Java Language Specification, chapter 17. It happens when two threads access the same variable, at least one access is a write, and the two accesses are not ordered by a happens-before relationship. A program with a data race can see surprising values, because the compiler and CPU are allowed to reorder and cache unsynchronized accesses. A race condition is a logic bug: the program is wrong under some interleavings. You can have one without the other. The fixed SeatMap has no data race, but if the code first called putIfAbsent and then, in a separate step, charged a card and rolled back on failure, other threads could still observe a seat that is sold and then unsold. That is a race condition built entirely from thread-safe calls. Going the other way, String.hashCode() caches its result in a plain field that several threads may write at once. That is a data race, but a benign one: every thread computes the same value, and int writes cannot tear. long and double are the exception to that last point. JLS section 17.7 allows a write to a non-volatile long or double to happen as two separate 32-bit writes, so another thread could read half of an old value and half of a new one. 64-bit JVMs write them in one go in practice, but the spec does not promise it unless the field is volatile. You'll meet happens-before properly in the memory model track. For now, the rule of thumb holds: every access to shared mutable state, reads included, goes through the same lock or the same atomic variable.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · synchronized lets one thread in at a time, and shows it what the last one wrote
x: In lesson 3 of this track, count++ lost updates because two threads could run its read and its write at the same moment. A transfer that does a -= cents and then b += cents has the same problem, and the warm-up showed a second one: a reader that looks between the two lines. Both go away if only one thread at a time can run the code that touches the balances. Every Java object has a built-in lock called its monitor (or intrinsic lock). synchronized takes it on the way in and releases it on the way out, even if the block throws. Java private final Object lock = new Object(); void transfer(long cents) { synchronized (lock) { // take lock's monitor, or wait until it is free a -= cents; b += cents; } // release it } Kotlin private val lock = Any() fun transfer(cents: Long) { synchronized(lock) { // take lock's monitor, or wait until it is free a -= cents b += cents } // release it } A synchronized instance method is shorthand for synchronized (this) around the whole body. A static synchronized method locks the Class object, such as Ledger.class. You get two guarantees, and you need both. Mutual exclusion. While one thread holds a monitor, any other thread that tries to enter a block guarded by the same monitor waits, in the BLOCKED state from lesson 2 of this track. So the debit and the credit happen as one step, from the point of view of everyone else who takes that lock. Visibility. When a thread releases a monitor, everything it wrote before that becomes visible to the next thread that takes the same monitor. The memory model calls this a happens-before edge from the release to the next lock. Without it, a thread could keep reading an old balance from a register or a CPU cache. Both guarantees work only between threads that use the same monitor. A thread that reads a and b with no lock is not excluded and gets no visibility promise. It can read a after the debit and b before the credit, and report a total that is short by the amount in flight. Two auditors in the simulator below show the difference. Step T1 halfway through its transfer, then let T2 read. Then try the same trick on T3. Audit with and without the lock Run AuditDemo. A transfer thread moves 50 back and forth 200,000 times, always under the lock. The auditor adds a + b without it. Predict the count of wrong totals, then run it again with -Pargs=locked, where the auditor takes the lock too. AuditDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** A transfer thread moves money under a lock. An auditor adds up the two balances, with or without it. */ public class AuditDemo { static final Object lock = new Object(); // volatile only so the JIT re-reads the fields on every pass; it does not make the pair consistent static volatile long a = 1_000, b = 1_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean auditorLocks = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("locked"); Thread transfers = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) { synchronized (lock) { // debit and credit as one step a -= 50; b += 50; } synchronized (lock) { // and move it back a += 50; b -= 50; } } }); Thread auditor = new Thread(() -> { long audits = 0, wrong = 0; while (transfers.isAlive()) { long total; if (auditorLocks) { synchronized (lock) { total = a + b; } } else { total = a + b; // reads a, then b, while transfers may run in between } audits++; if (total != 2_000) wrong++; } System.out.printf("auditor %s the lock: %,d audits, %,d saw a total other than 2,000%n", auditorLocks ? "took" : "skipped", audits, wrong); }); transfers.start(); auditor.start(); transfers.join(); auditor.join(); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.AuditDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l04/AuditDemo.java AuditDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A transfer thread moves money under a lock. An auditor adds up the two balances, with or without it. private val lock = Any() // @Volatile only so the JIT re-reads the fields on every pass; it does not make the pair consistent @Volatile private var a = 1_000L @Volatile private var b = 1_000L fun main(args: Array<String>) { val auditorLocks = args.firstOrNull() == "locked" val transfers = thread { repeat(200_000) { synchronized(lock) { // debit and credit as one step a -= 50 b += 50 } synchronized(lock) { // and move it back a += 50 b -= 50 } } } val auditor = thread { var audits = 0L var wrong = 0L while (transfers.isAlive) { val total = if (auditorLocks) { synchronized(lock) { a + b } } else { a + b // reads a, then b, while transfers may run in between } audits++ if (total != 2_000L) wrong++ } println("auditor %s the lock: %,d audits, %,d saw a total other than 2,000" .format(if (auditorLocks) "took" else "skipped", audits, wrong)) } transfers.join() auditor.join() } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.AuditDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l04/AuditDemo.kt Without the lock, millions of audits see a total that is not 2,000 (one run here: 3,410,195 of 28,311,835). With the lock, zero, every run. The writer was correct all along. The reader was the bug. A monitor is a meeting room with one key on a hook. Whoever holds the key is inside, and everyone else waits in the corridor, which is the BLOCKED state. Before leaving, you write your results on the whiteboard, and the next person to take the key reads them: that is the visibility half. A string-literal lock is a key that several departments share without knowing it. Calling alien code under the lock is inviting a stranger into the room and waiting while they make a phone call. The analogy breaks at reentrancy: a thread that holds the key can walk back into the same room through another door, another synchronized method, without queuing. No real room works like that.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · A thread can take a lock it already holds
x: synchronized is reentrant: a thread that holds a monitor can enter another block on the same monitor without waiting. The JVM keeps a hold count per monitor. It goes up on each entry and down on each exit, and the monitor is free again when it reaches zero. You rely on this all the time without noticing: Java public synchronized void withdraw(long cents) { if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents; // canCover is synchronized too } public synchronized boolean canCover(long cents) { return balanceCents >= cents; } Kotlin @Synchronized fun withdraw(cents: Long) { if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents // canCover is synchronized too } @Synchronized fun canCover(cents: Long): Boolean = balanceCents >= cents Without reentrancy, withdraw would wait forever for a lock it already holds. The same goes for a subclass whose synchronized override calls super.withdraw(...), which is also synchronized on the same object. Reentrancy has a side effect worth knowing. It lets the same thread back in while your object is halfway through a change. Say a synchronized publish() method loops over its listeners, and one listener calls subscribe(), which is also synchronized. The lock lets it straight in, because it is the same thread. subscribe() adds to the list that publish() is iterating, and the loop dies with ConcurrentModificationException. The lock did its job. It just isn't designed to stop the thread that already holds it. You'll fix exactly this in the lab. Enter the same lock three times Read ReentrancyDemo. AuditedAccount.withdraw calls super.withdraw, which calls canCover. All three are synchronized on the same object. Predict whether it finishes, then run it. ReentrancyDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** A synchronized method calls another synchronized method on the same object. */ public class ReentrancyDemo { static class Account { private long balanceCents = 10_000; public synchronized void withdraw(long cents) { System.out.println("withdraw: holds the lock? " + Thread.holdsLock(this)); if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents; // takes the same lock again } public synchronized boolean canCover(long cents) { System.out.println("canCover: holds the lock? " + Thread.holdsLock(this)); return balanceCents >= cents; } } static class AuditedAccount extends Account { @Override public synchronized void withdraw(long cents) { System.out.println("audit: about to withdraw " + cents); super.withdraw(cents); // and again, through super } } public static void main(String[] args) { new AuditedAccount().withdraw(2_500); System.out.println("done: no thread waited for a lock it already held"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.ReentrancyDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l04/ReentrancyDemo.java ReentrancyDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l04 // A synchronized method calls another synchronized method on the same object. open class SavingsAccount { private var balanceCents = 10_000L @Synchronized open fun withdraw(cents: Long) { println("withdraw: holds the lock? ${Thread.holdsLock(this)}") if (canCover(cents)) balanceCents -= cents // takes the same lock again } @Synchronized fun canCover(cents: Long): Boolean { println("canCover: holds the lock? ${Thread.holdsLock(this)}") return balanceCents >= cents } } class AuditedSavingsAccount : SavingsAccount() { @Synchronized override fun withdraw(cents: Long) { println("audit: about to withdraw $cents") super.withdraw(cents) // and again, through super } } fun main() { AuditedSavingsAccount().withdraw(2_500) println("done: no thread waited for a lock it already held") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.ReentrancyDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l04/ReentrancyDemo.kt It prints holds the lock? true at each level and finishes. The thread entered one monitor three deep, and the hold count went 1, 2, 3 and back to 0. An @ApplicationScoped bean in Quarkus is one instance shared by every request thread, so any mutable field on it, such as an in-memory rate limiter or a cached OAuth token for the card issuer, needs a lock or an atomic. The same holds for a Temporal activity implementation: you register one object and the worker calls it from many threads at once. When you do lock, look at what runs inside: a synchronized method that calls Oracle or the issuer turns 200 worker threads into a queue of one. One version note for later: on JDK 21 to 23, a virtual thread that blocks inside synchronized pins its carrier thread. JDK 24 removed most of that (JEP 491), and the virtual threads track covers it.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Lock on a private final object that only you can reach
x: A lock protects state only if every thread that touches the state uses the same lock, and no unrelated code uses it for something else. The safest choice is boring: Java private final Object lock = new Object(); Kotlin private val lock = Any() It is private, so no other class can lock it and stall you. It is final, so it can never change under you. Here are the choices that go wrong, roughly in the order I've seen them in code reviews. A boxed number, like synchronized (count) on an Integer. count++ on an Integer field creates a new Integer object and points the field at it. So each thread may lock a different object, and nothing is excluded. Small values are also cached: Integer.valueOf(42) returns the same object everywhere in the JVM. javac knows, and prints warning: [synchronization] attempt to synchronize on an instance of a value-based class. A string literal, like synchronized ("lock"). Literals are interned, so every class in the JVM that writes "lock" gets the same object. Your token cache and someone's metrics library now share a lock. A field that is not final. If anyone reassigns it, threads before and after the change lock different objects. this, on a public class. It works, and synchronized methods do exactly this. But any caller can also write synchronized (account) { ... } and hold your lock for as long as they like. A private lock keeps that decision inside your class. One more, which is always wrong: synchronized (new Object()). Every thread creates its own object, so nobody ever waits and nothing is visible to anyone. It's a lock that protects nothing. Share a lock by accident Read SharedLiteralLock. TokenCache and Metrics are unrelated and each lock on "lock". Run it and read the metrics thread's state and how long it waited. In the lab you'll compile DeclineCounter, which locks on an Integer. Look for javac's [synchronization] warning in the Gradle output when you do. SharedLiteralLock.java package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** Two unrelated classes each lock on the string "lock". They are the same object. */ public class SharedLiteralLock { static class TokenCache { void refresh() { synchronized ("lock") { // looks private. It isn't. sleep(1_000); // a slow refresh } } } static class Metrics { void record() { synchronized ("lock") { // a different class, a different "lock"? System.out.println("metrics: recorded"); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread refresher = new Thread(() -> new TokenCache().refresh(), "token-refresh"); Thread metrics = new Thread(() -> new Metrics().record(), "metrics"); refresher.start(); Thread.sleep(100); // let the refresher take the lock first long t0 = System.nanoTime(); metrics.start(); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println("metrics thread state after 200 ms: " + metrics.getState()); metrics.join(); System.out.printf("metrics waited about %d ms for a lock it never shared on purpose%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); refresher.join(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.SharedLiteralLock labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l04/SharedLiteralLock.java SharedLiteralLock.kt package workbench.concurrency.l04 // Two unrelated classes each lock on the string "lock". They are the same object. private class TokenCache { fun refresh() { synchronized("lock") { // looks private. It isn't. Thread.sleep(1_000) // a slow refresh } } } private class Metrics { fun record() { synchronized("lock") { // a different class, a different "lock"? println("metrics: recorded") } } } fun main() { val refresher = Thread({ TokenCache().refresh() }, "token-refresh") val metrics = Thread({ Metrics().record() }, "metrics") refresher.start() Thread.sleep(100) // let the refresher take the lock first val t0 = System.nanoTime() metrics.start() Thread.sleep(200) println("metrics thread state after 200 ms: ${metrics.state}") metrics.join() println("metrics waited about ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms for a lock it never shared on purpose") refresher.join() } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.SharedLiteralLockKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l04/SharedLiteralLock.kt The metrics thread is BLOCKED after 200 ms and waits about 900 ms, the rest of the token refresh. Two classes that never mention each other contend on one lock, because both literals are the same interned String.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Keep critical sections short, and never call alien code inside one
x: Everything inside a synchronized block runs one thread at a time. So anything slow in there turns your thread pool into a queue of one. The demo below makes it concrete: eight threads each authorize five payments, and each card-issuer call takes 40 ms. With the call inside the lock, the 40 calls run one after another: about 1,600 ms. With only the bookkeeping inside the lock, the calls overlap: about 200 ms. The rule: put only the reads and writes of shared state inside the lock. Do the I/O, the parsing and the computing before or after. The worse version of the same mistake is calling alien code while you hold a lock. Alien means code you don't control: a listener, a callback, a method a subclass can override, a lambda someone passed in. You can't know what it does. It might make a 2-second HTTP call. It might hand work to another thread and wait for it, and if that thread needs your lock, you've built a deadlock. It might call back into your object on the same thread, where reentrancy lets it in halfway through your update. This bug is common enough that the JDK has fixed instances of it in itself. JDK 25 carries a fix titled "j.u.l.Handler classes create deadlock risk via synchronized publish() method". The fix has the same shape every time. Under the lock, change your own state and take a copy of whatever you need. Release the lock. Then call out. Java List<Listener> toNotify; synchronized (lock) { rates.put(pair, rate); // 1. our state, under the lock toNotify = List.copyOf(listeners); // 2. a snapshot to work from } for (Listener l : toNotify) l.onRate(pair, rate); // 3. alien code, no lock held Kotlin val toNotify = synchronized(lock) { rates[pair] = rate // 1. our state, under the lock listeners.toList() // 2. a snapshot to work from (the block's value) } for (l in toNotify) l.onRate(pair, rate) // 3. alien code, no lock held The cost is that a listener may now hear about rates in a slightly different order than another thread published them. That is almost always a price worth paying. Move the slow call out of the lock Read SlowCallUnderLock. Both versions update approvedCents under the lock. Only one also holds the lock during the 40 ms issuer call. Predict both times (8 threads x 5 calls x 40 ms), then run it. SlowCallUnderLock.java package workbench.concurrency.l04; /** Eight threads authorize payments. Each call to the issuer takes 40 ms. Where should the lock go? */ public class SlowCallUnderLock { static final Object lock = new Object(); static long approvedCents; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.printf("issuer call inside the lock: %,5d ms%n", run(true)); System.out.printf("issuer call outside the lock: %,5d ms%n", run(false)); } static long run(boolean callInsideLock) throws InterruptedException { approvedCents = 0; Thread[] threads = new Thread[8]; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < threads.length; i++) { threads[i] = new Thread(() -> { for (int p = 0; p < 5; p++) { if (callInsideLock) { synchronized (lock) { boolean ok = callIssuer(); // 40 ms while every other thread waits if (ok) approvedCents += 1_999; } } else { boolean ok = callIssuer(); // slow work with no lock held synchronized (lock) { // lock only the shared update if (ok) approvedCents += 1_999; } } } }); threads[i].start(); } for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); if (approvedCents != 40 * 1_999) throw new AssertionError("lost an update: " + approvedCents); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } static boolean callIssuer() { try { Thread.sleep(40); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return true; } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.SlowCallUnderLock labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l04/SlowCallUnderLock.java SlowCallUnderLock.kt package workbench.concurrency.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight threads authorize payments. Each call to the issuer takes 40 ms. Where should the lock go? private val issuerLock = Any() private var approvedCents = 0L // guarded by issuerLock fun main() { println("issuer call inside the lock: %,5d ms".format(run(callInsideLock = true))) println("issuer call outside the lock: %,5d ms".format(run(callInsideLock = false))) } private fun run(callInsideLock: Boolean): Long { approvedCents = 0 val t0 = System.nanoTime() val threads = List(8) { thread { repeat(5) { if (callInsideLock) { synchronized(issuerLock) { val ok = callIssuer() // 40 ms while every other thread waits if (ok) approvedCents += 1_999 } } else { val ok = callIssuer() // slow work with no lock held synchronized(issuerLock) { // lock only the shared update if (ok) approvedCents += 1_999 } } } } } threads.forEach { it.join() } check(approvedCents == 40L * 1_999) { "lost an update: $approvedCents" } return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } private fun callIssuer(): Boolean { Thread.sleep(40) return true } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l04.SlowCallUnderLockKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l04/SlowCallUnderLock.kt About 1,600 ms with the call inside the lock (40 calls in a row) and about 200 ms outside (5 rounds of 8 calls at once). Both versions get the total right. Only one of them can serve traffic. The most common real mistake is guarding one piece of state with two different locks. The classic case is a static field updated in a synchronized instance method: each instance locks itself (this), but all instances share the static field, so two instances update it at the same time with no exclusion at all. The same thing happens when one class guards a shared map with its own lock and another class touches the map with no lock or a different one. Fix it by giving the state exactly one lock object, declared next to the state, private static final Object LOCK for static state, and taking it everywhere the state is read or written.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Java and Kotlin
x: Locking in Java and Kotlin Java public class DeclineCounter { private final Object lock = new Object(); private int declines; public void recordDecline() { synchronized (lock) { // a keyword declines++; } } public int total() { synchronized (lock) { return declines; } } } public class HitCounter { private int hits; public synchronized void hit() { hits++; } // locks this public synchronized int total() { return hits; } } KotlinLocks.kt package workbench.concurrency.l04 class DeclineCounterKt { private val lock = Any() // a private lock object, like `new Object()` in Java private var declines = 0 fun recordDecline() { synchronized(lock) { // a standard-library function, not a keyword declines++ } } fun total(): Int = synchronized(lock) { declines } // it returns the block's value } class HitCounterKt { private var hits = 0 @Synchronized fun hit() { hits++ } // like a Java synchronized method: locks `this` @Synchronized fun total() = hits } fun main() { val declines = DeclineCounterKt() val hits = HitCounterKt() val threads = List(8) { Thread { repeat(100_000) { declines.recordDecline() hits.hit() } }.apply { start() } } threads.forEach { it.join() } println("declines = ${declines.total()}, hits = ${hits.total()}") } Kotlin has no synchronized keyword. synchronized(lock) { ... } is an inline standard-library function, and the compiler emits the same monitorenter/monitorexit bytecode as a Java block. Because it is a function, it returns the value of its block, so total() can be one expression. @Synchronized on a function sets the same ACC_SYNCHRONIZED flag as Java's modifier, so it locks this (or, in an object, the object itself). Any() makes a fine private lock. One gap shows up in the next lesson: Any has no wait() or notify(), so Kotlin code that needs them must use a java.lang.Object or, better, the explicit locks from lesson 7 of this track.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Worked example
x: Fix a refund limiter with the wrong lock and a slow call inside A refund service caps total refunds per process. It runs as two bean instances behind a router. Find every lock problem before reading on. public class RefundLimiter { private static long refundedCents; // shared by every instance private static final long LIMIT_CENTS = 5_000_000; public synchronized boolean tryRefund(long cents) { // locks `this` if (refundedCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false; riskTeam.notifyLargeRefund(cents); // HTTP call, about 300 ms refundedCents += cents; return true; } } class RefundLimiter { companion object { private var refundedCents = 0L // shared by every instance private const val LIMIT_CENTS = 5_000_000L } @Synchronized fun tryRefund(cents: Long): Boolean { // locks `this` if (refundedCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false riskTeam.notifyLargeRefund(cents) // HTTP call, about 300 ms refundedCents += cents return true } } Two problems. First, the method locks this, but the state is static. Two instances lock two different monitors and can both pass the limit check at once. Second, a 300 ms HTTP call runs inside the lock, so every refund waits for the previous one's call. Fix the lock first: one lock object for the one piece of state. private static final Object LOCK = new Object(); // 1. one lock for the static state private val LOCK = Any() // 1. one lock for the shared state, in the companion object Now shrink the critical section. Reserve the amount under the lock, so the check and the update are one step. Then release the lock and make the call. If the call fails and the refund should not go ahead, give the reservation back, under the lock again. Ask yourself: why must the check and the += stay inside the same block? public boolean tryRefund(long cents) { synchronized (LOCK) { // 2. check and reserve as one step if (refundedCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false; refundedCents += cents; } try { riskTeam.notifyLargeRefund(cents); // 3. slow call, no lock held return true; } catch (RuntimeException e) { synchronized (LOCK) { refundedCents -= cents; } // 4. undo the reservation throw e; } } fun tryRefund(cents: Long): Boolean { synchronized(LOCK) { // 2. check and reserve as one step if (refundedCents + cents > LIMIT_CENTS) return false refundedCents += cents } try { riskTeam.notifyLargeRefund(cents) // 3. slow call, no lock held return true } catch (e: RuntimeException) { synchronized(LOCK) { refundedCents -= cents } // 4. undo the reservation throw e } } Split the check from the += and you're back to lesson 3 of this track: check-then-act, with two threads both passing the check. The lock has to cover the whole compound action. What it must not cover is the 300 ms call, and now it doesn't. If the limit must hold across pods, the reservation belongs in the database, but the shape stays the same.

Line 2: static fields cannot be locked Line 4: += is not allowed inside synchronized Line 3: it locks this, but the state is static, so different instances don't exclude each other There is no bug, because the method is synchronized Each instance locks its own monitor, while all instances share feesCents. Two partitions' counters run += at the same time and lose updates. Static state needs one static lock: private static final Object LOCK, or a static synchronized method. A thread inside synchronized void withdraw() calls canCover(), which is also synchronized on the same object. What happens? It enters at once, because the monitor is reentrant It deadlocks waiting for itself It throws IllegalMonitorStateException It waits until withdraw() returns Java monitors are reentrant. The JVM sees that the current thread already owns the monitor and increments the hold count. Without reentrancy every synchronized method that calls another one on the same object would hang. Which of these is the safest object to lock on for a class's internal state? "ledger-lock", a string literal Integer.valueOf(1) this, on a public class that callers also hold references to private final Object lock = new Object() A private final object can't be locked by anyone else and can't change. String literals are interned and shared JVM-wide. Small Integer values are cached and shared, and javac warns about locking on them. this works, but any caller can lock it too and stall your methods. publish() is synchronized and calls each listener inside the lock. One listener makes a 2-second HTTP call. What do other threads notice? Nothing, since each listener runs on its own thread Every thread that needs the same lock, even just to read a rate, waits up to 2 seconds The HTTP call is cancelled because of the lock The JVM detects the slow call and releases the lock Listeners run on the publishing thread, inside its critical section. Anyone who needs that monitor queues behind the HTTP call. Copy the listener list under the lock, release it, then notify. From Race conditions: why count++ lies: setBalance() is synchronized, but getBalance() is a plain getter with no lock. Is the class thread-safe? Yes: only writes need a lock Yes, if the field is a long No: a reader that skips the lock gets no visibility promise and can see a stale value No, but only on 32-bit JVMs Visibility comes from unlocking and locking the same monitor. A reader that never takes the lock has no happens-before edge to the writer, so it may keep seeing an old balance. h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Key terms
x: Monitor (intrinsic lock) The lock every Java object has, taken and released by synchronized. Mutual exclusion Only one thread at a time can run the code guarded by a lock. Visibility Whether one thread is guaranteed to see what another thread wrote. Reentrant A thread can take a lock it already holds without waiting for itself. Critical section The code that runs while a lock is held. Alien method Code you don't control, such as a listener or callback, which can block or call back in. Value-based class A class like Integer whose instances may be shared or cached, so its identity is not yours to lock on. What two guarantees does synchronized give? Mutual exclusion (one thread at a time per monitor) and visibility (writes made before releasing a monitor are seen by the next thread that locks it). What does a synchronized instance method lock? A static synchronized method? The instance, this. The static one locks the class object, for example Ledger.class. What does it mean that Java monitors are reentrant? A thread that already holds a monitor can enter it again without waiting. The JVM counts the holds and frees the monitor when the count is back to zero. Why is synchronized (count) on an Integer field broken? count++ replaces the field with a new Integer, so threads lock different objects. Small values are also cached and shared JVM-wide. javac warns [synchronization]. Why never lock on a string literal? Literals are interned: every "lock" in the JVM is the same object, so unrelated code shares your lock. What does synchronized (new Object()) { ... } protect? Nothing. Each call locks a fresh object no other thread can see, so there is no exclusion and no visibility. What should you do before calling listeners or callbacks from a locked method? Update your state and copy what you need (for example List.copyOf(listeners)) under the lock, release it, then call them.

h: synchronized and intrinsic locks · Go deeper
x: How does HotSpot make synchronized cheap when there is no contention? It doesn't create a full monitor object for every lock. An uncontended lock is a small change in the object's header (lightweight locking). Only when threads really fight over it, or one calls wait(), does the JVM inflate it into a full ObjectMonitor with an entry queue and a wait set. The details keep changing between releases, which is a good reason not to depend on them. The LockingMode default became lightweight locking in JDK 23, the option was deprecated in JDK 24 and its code removed in JDK 26. JDK 27 switched on a separate table that maps objects to their monitors by default, and made compact object headers the default too. None of this changes what synchronized means. It only changes what it costs. If you want to see contention rather than guess at it, Java Flight Recorder records a jdk.JavaMonitorEnter event when a thread has to wait for a monitor, with the monitor's class and the previous owner. JDK 25 added jdk.JavaMonitorNotify and jdk.JavaMonitorStatistics. Lesson 13 of this track uses them. For virtual threads, JEP 491 in JDK 24 is the change to know: before it, a virtual thread blocked inside synchronized held on to its carrier thread, and since JDK 24 it doesn't in most cases.

h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · A guarded block waits for a condition without burning a core
x: A consumer thread has nothing to do until a payment arrives. The worst way to wait is to spin: Java while (!ready) { } // checks the flag as fast as the core can go Kotlin while (!ready) { } // the same spin in Kotlin The demo below measured it. To wait one second, the spinning thread used about 1,026 ms of CPU: a whole core, doing nothing useful. The thread that waited properly used 0 ms. (The spinner's flag also has to be volatile, or the JIT may read it once and loop forever. The memory model track explains why.) The proper way is a guarded block. You hold the lock, check the condition, and call wait() if it doesn't hold yet: Java synchronized (lock) { while (!ready) { lock.wait(); // give back the lock, sleep until woken, take the lock again } // here ready is true, and we hold the lock } Kotlin synchronized(lock) { // lock is a java.lang.Object here: Kotlin's Any has no wait() while (!ready) { lock.wait() // give back the lock, sleep until woken, take the lock again } // here ready is true, and we hold the lock } wait() does three things in order. It releases the monitor, so other threads can get in and change the state. It parks the thread in the monitor's wait set, in the WAITING state, using no CPU. And when the thread is woken, it takes the monitor back before wait() returns. The thread that changes the state calls notifyAll(), holding the same lock: Java synchronized (lock) { ready = true; lock.notifyAll(); // wake every thread waiting on lock } Kotlin synchronized(lock) { ready = true lock.notifyAll() // wake every thread waiting on lock } notifyAll() does not hand over the lock. The woken threads move to the monitor's entry set, the threads waiting to get in, where they show as BLOCKED and compete for the lock like any newcomer. None of them can run until the notifier leaves its block. You must hold the monitor of the object you call wait() or notifyAll() on. Call them outside synchronized (lock) and you get IllegalMonitorStateException at once. That rule protects you. The condition can only change while someone holds the lock, so a waiter can't check the flag, miss the change that happens next, and then wait forever. Spin vs wait Run BusyWaitDemo. Both threads wait one second for the same event. Predict the CPU time of each. In the waiter, delete the synchronized line around the while loop and its closing brace, so lock.wait() runs without the lock. Run it again. Put it back. BusyWaitDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.ThreadMXBean; /** Two threads wait one second for the same flag. One spins, one calls wait(). Compare their CPU time. */ public class BusyWaitDemo { static final Object lock = new Object(); static boolean ready; // guarded by lock static volatile boolean readyForSpinner; // the spinner can't use the lock, so it needs volatile public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread spinner = new Thread(() -> { while (!readyForSpinner) { } // busy-wait: checks the flag as fast as it can }, "spinner"); Thread waiter = new Thread(() -> { synchronized (lock) { while (!ready) { // guarded block: the condition, in a loop try { lock.wait(); // releases lock, parks until notified } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; } } } }, "waiter"); spinner.start(); waiter.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); // the authorization takes a second to come back ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long spinCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(spinner.threadId()) / 1_000_000; // measure while both still wait long waitCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(waiter.threadId()) / 1_000_000; readyForSpinner = true; synchronized (lock) { ready = true; lock.notifyAll(); // wake the waiter; it runs once we leave this block } spinner.join(); waiter.join(); System.out.printf("spinner used about %d ms of CPU to wait 1 s%n", spinCpu); System.out.printf("waiter used about %d ms of CPU to wait 1 s%n", waitCpu); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l05.BusyWaitDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l05/BusyWaitDemo.java BusyWaitDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two threads wait one second for the same flag. One spins, one calls wait(). Compare their CPU time. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() // java.lang.Object, because Kotlin's Any has no wait() private var ready = false // guarded by lock @Volatile private var readyForSpinner = false // the spinner can't use the lock, so it needs @Volatile fun main() { val spinner = thread(name = "spinner") { while (!readyForSpinner) { } // busy-wait: checks the flag as fast as it can } val waiter = thread(name = "waiter") { synchronized(lock) { while (!ready) { // guarded block: the condition, in a loop try { lock.wait() // releases lock, parks until notified } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() return@thread } } } } Thread.sleep(1_000) // the authorization takes a second to come back val mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() val spinCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(spinner.threadId()) / 1_000_000 // measure while both still wait val waitCpu = mx.getThreadCpuTime(waiter.threadId()) / 1_000_000 readyForSpinner = true synchronized(lock) { ready = true lock.notifyAll() // wake the waiter; it runs once we leave this block } spinner.join() waiter.join() println("spinner used about $spinCpu ms of CPU to wait 1 s") println("waiter used about $waitCpu ms of CPU to wait 1 s") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l05.BusyWaitDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l05/BusyWaitDemo.kt The spinner uses about a full second of CPU to wait one second. The waiter uses close to zero. Without the synchronized block, the waiter dies at once with IllegalMonitorStateException: you can only wait on a monitor you hold. A monitor is a meeting room with one key. People who want the room queue in the corridor (the entry set, BLOCKED). The one inside can decide they can't continue yet, hang the key back up and go to the lounge next door (the wait set, WAITING). When someone in the room changes things, they can call into the lounge: notify() sends one person back to the corridor, notifyAll() sends everyone. Nobody walks from the lounge straight into the room. They queue for the key again, and by the time they get in, the thing they waited for may be gone, which is why they must look again. The analogy breaks at spurious wakeups: people don't leave the lounge for no reason, but a Java thread is allowed to.

h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · Always wait in a while loop, never an if
x: When wait() returns, the condition you waited for may not hold. There are two reasons. The first is in the Javadoc for Object.wait: "A thread can wake up without being notified, interrupted, or timing out, a so-called spurious wakeup." It is rare. It is also allowed, and the Javadoc tells you to test the condition again and keep waiting if it is not met. The second reason happens all the time. notifyAll() wakes every waiter, but they take the lock back one at a time, and other threads may get in first. Two consumers wait on an empty queue. A producer adds one item and calls notifyAll(). Consumer 1 gets the lock first and takes the item. Consumer 2 gets the lock next, and the queue is empty again. If consumer 2 checked with if, it is already past its check: Java if (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait(); // checked once, before waiting return queue.removeFirst(); // NoSuchElementException Kotlin if (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait() // checked once, before waiting return queue.removeFirst() // NoSuchElementException With while, consumer 2 checks again, sees the empty queue and goes back to waiting. That is all a guarded block is: a while loop around wait(), with the condition as the loop test. The habit costs nothing, so make it unconditional. Every wait() sits inside while (!condition). In a code review, treat an if around wait() as a bug, even in code that has never failed. It has just never had two waiters at the same time yet. Steal a wake-up Read IfInsteadOfWhile. Both consumers are parked before main adds one item and calls notifyAll(). Run it and read both consumers' lines. Change if (queue.isEmpty()) to while (queue.isEmpty()). Predict what each consumer prints, then run it again. IfInsteadOfWhile.java package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; /** Two consumers wait on an empty queue. One item arrives. The guard is an `if`. */ public class IfInsteadOfWhile { static final Object lock = new Object(); static final Deque<String> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); static String take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { if (queue.isEmpty()) { // BUG: checked once, never again after waking lock.wait(); } return queue.removeFirst(); // throws NoSuchElementException if someone else took it } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Runnable consumer = () -> { try { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " took " + take()); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " failed: " + e); } }; Thread c1 = new Thread(consumer, "consumer-1"); Thread c2 = new Thread(consumer, "consumer-2"); c1.start(); c2.start(); while (c1.getState() != Thread.State.WAITING || c2.getState() != Thread.State.WAITING) { Thread.sleep(10); // wait until both are parked in wait() } synchronized (lock) { queue.addLast("auth-1"); // one item... lock.notifyAll(); // ...and both consumers wake up } c1.join(2_000); c2.join(2_000); if (c1.isAlive() || c2.isAlive()) { // with `while`, one consumer goes back to waiting System.out.println("one consumer is still waiting; giving it a second item"); synchronized (lock) { queue.addLast("auth-2"); lock.notifyAll(); } } c1.join(); c2.join(); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l05.IfInsteadOfWhile labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l05/IfInsteadOfWhile.java IfInsteadOfWhile.kt package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.util.ArrayDeque // Two consumers wait on an empty queue. One item arrives. The guard is an `if`. @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() private val queue = ArrayDeque<String>() private fun take(): String { synchronized(lock) { if (queue.isEmpty()) { // BUG: checked once, never again after waking lock.wait() } return queue.removeFirst() // throws NoSuchElementException if someone else took it } } fun main() { val consumer = Runnable { try { println("${Thread.currentThread().name} took ${take()}") } catch (e: Exception) { println("${Thread.currentThread().name} failed: $e") } } val c1 = Thread(consumer, "consumer-1") val c2 = Thread(consumer, "consumer-2") c1.start() c2.start() while (c1.state != Thread.State.WAITING || c2.state != Thread.State.WAITING) { Thread.sleep(10) // wait until both are parked in wait() } synchronized(lock) { queue.addLast("auth-1") // one item... lock.notifyAll() // ...and both consumers wake up } c1.join(2_000) c2.join(2_000) if (c1.isAlive || c2.isAlive) { // with `while`, one consumer goes back to waiting println("one consumer is still waiting; giving it a second item") synchronized(lock) { queue.addLast("auth-2") lock.notifyAll() } } c1.join() c2.join() } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l05.IfInsteadOfWhileKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l05/IfInsteadOfWhile.kt With if: one consumer takes auth-1, the other fails with java.util.NoSuchElementException. With while: one takes auth-1, the other re-checks, waits again, and takes auth-2 when main gives it a second item. Which consumer wins can change from run to run. You'll rarely hand-write wait() in a payments service, and when you do it should look like the buffer above. You meet guarded blocks all the time inside libraries. A connection pool with 20 connections makes the 21st request wait until a connection is returned. A KafkaProducer blocks send() for up to max.block.ms when its buffer memory is full. A Quarkus worker pool queues requests when every worker is busy. In a thread dump those threads show WAITING or TIMED_WAITING inside the library's code. Reading the stack tells you which condition they wait for, and that usually tells you which resource ran out.

h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · Prefer notifyAll, because notify wakes one thread, maybe the wrong one
x: notify() wakes one thread from the wait set, and you don't get to choose which. That is fine when every waiter waits for the same condition and any one of them can use the change. It breaks when one monitor has waiters for different conditions. A bounded buffer is the classic case. Producers wait for "not full", consumers wait for "not empty", and with a plain monitor they share one wait set. Picture a buffer with one slot, two producers and two consumers, all using notify(): The slot is empty, so both consumers wait. Producer 1 fills the slot and wakes consumer 1. Before consumer 1 gets the lock, both producers find the slot full and wait. The wait set now holds producer 1, producer 2 and consumer 2. Consumer 1 empties the slot and calls notify(), which happens to wake consumer 2, the wrong kind. Consumer 2 finds the slot empty and waits again. Consumer 1 loops, finds it empty too, and waits. Now all four threads wait for a signal nobody will send. No thread holds the lock, so it isn't a deadlock in the textbook sense, but the program has stopped just the same. The demo below gets there within a handful of items. So the default is notifyAll(). It wakes every waiter, each one re-checks its own condition in its while loop, and the ones that can't go on wait again. The price is extra wake-ups when many threads wait, which rarely matters next to a stalled pipeline. Use notify() only when both of these hold: every waiter waits for the same condition, and one change lets at most one of them proceed. If you need precise wake-ups for two kinds of waiters, give each kind its own Condition on a ReentrantLock. That is lesson 7 of this track. Stall a pipeline with notify() Run NotifyStall. Two producers and two consumers share a one-slot buffer that signals with notify(). Read the thread states it prints when progress stops. Run it again with -Pargs=all, which switches both signals to notifyAll(). NotifyStall.java package workbench.concurrency.l05; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** A one-slot buffer shared by 2 producers and 2 consumers.
