h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · A bounded buffer, by hand
x: Put the three rules together and you get the bounded buffer you'll write in the lab. A bounded buffer sits between producers and consumers. It holds at most capacity items, so a fast producer has to wait for slow consumers instead of filling the heap. That waiting is called backpressure. Java public class BoundedBuffer<T> { private final Object lock = new Object(); private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final int capacity; public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.size() == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait(); } items.addLast(item); // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll(); // 3. signal: the state changed } } public T take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait(); } T head = items.removeFirst(); lock.notifyAll(); return head; } } } Kotlin class BoundedBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) { @Suppress("PLATFORM_CLASS_MAPPED_TO_KOTLIN") private val lock = Object() // java.lang.Object: Kotlin's Any has no wait() private val items = ArrayDeque<T>() @Throws(InterruptedException::class) // so Java callers see it, as in the Java version fun put(item: T) { synchronized(lock) { while (items.size == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait() } items.addLast(item) // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll() // 3. signal: the state changed } } @Throws(InterruptedException::class) fun take(): T { synchronized(lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait() } val head = items.removeFirst() lock.notifyAll() return head } } } Each method has the same three parts. The guard is a while loop that waits until the method can proceed. The act changes the state, safely, because the condition holds and the lock is held. The signal wakes the other side, because the state they wait on just changed. A few choices in there are deliberate. The lock is a private object, not this. Any code that can reach an object can call wait() or notify() on it. With a private lock, only the buffer can signal its own waiters. Both methods signal with notifyAll(), because producers and consumers share one wait set, as the previous section showed. Both methods declare throws InterruptedException. wait() throws it when the waiting thread is interrupted, and the buffer can't know what the caller wants to do about that, so it lets the caller decide. That is the second option from lesson 2 of this track: propagate. In production you won't write this class. ArrayBlockingQueue does the same job, faster and with timeouts, and lesson 9 of this track covers it. You write it once so that put and take stop being magic, and so that a thread dump full of threads waiting inside a queue makes sense to you. Check your model before the lab. Delete the notifyAll() in take(). Two producers fill a buffer of capacity 2 and then wait in put(). A consumer takes one item. What happens next? (The producers stay in wait(): the take made room, but nothing woke them. The consumers drain the buffer and then wait too, until every thread is waiting.) wait() moves the owner to the wait set and gives the lock back. notify moves a waiter back to the entry set, where it must win the lock again, so it must re-check its condition. The most common real mistake is using wait() and notify() as a bare signal, with no condition to check: one thread calls lock.wait() "until the result is ready", another calls lock.notify() when it is. If the notify happens before the waiter starts waiting, the signal is lost and the waiter sleeps forever. This is a lost wake-up. It passes tests because the waiter usually gets there first. The fix is to always wait for a state, never for an event: set a field such as ready = true under the lock before notifying, and wait with while (!ready) lock.wait();. A notify that came early is then harmless, because the waiter sees ready and never waits.

h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · Java and Kotlin
x: A guarded buffer in Java and Kotlin BoundedBuffer.java public class BoundedBuffer<T> { private final Object lock = new Object(); private final Deque<T> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); private final int capacity; public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.size() == capacity) { // 1. guard: re-check after every wake-up lock.wait(); } items.addLast(item); // 2. act: condition holds, lock held lock.notifyAll(); // 3. signal: the state changed } } public T take() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { while (items.isEmpty()) { lock.wait(); } T head = items.removeFirst(); lock.notifyAll(); return head; } } } KotlinGuarded.kt package workbench.concurrency.l05 import java.util.ArrayDeque import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Kotlin's Any has no wait()/notify(). The idiomatic guarded block uses a Lock and a Condition. class KotlinBuffer<T>(private val capacity: Int) { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val changed = lock.newCondition() // one wait set, like a monitor's private val items = ArrayDeque<T>() fun put(item: T) = lock.withLock { while (items.size == capacity) changed.await() // same while-loop guard items.addLast(item) changed.signalAll() // same as notifyAll() } fun take(): T = lock.withLock { while (items.isEmpty()) changed.await() items.removeFirst().also { changed.signalAll() } } } fun main() { val buffer = KotlinBuffer<Int>(2) val consumer = thread { repeat(5) { println("took ${buffer.take()}") } } repeat(5) { buffer.put(it) } consumer.join() } Kotlin's Any does not expose wait(), notify() or notifyAll(). The Kotlin samples in this lesson get them by using a java.lang.Object as the lock, which works but earns a compiler warning that you have to suppress. The idiomatic replacement is a ReentrantLock with a Condition: withLock { } takes and releases the lock, await() plays the part of wait(), and signalAll() the part of notifyAll(). The rules don't change. Condition allows spurious wakeups too, so you still wait in a while loop. As a bonus, one lock can have several conditions, so producers and consumers can wait separately. Lesson 7 of this track builds on exactly that.

h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · Worked example
x: Wait for a settlement file, with a deadline A batch job must wait until the settlement file has arrived, but give up after 30 seconds. Here is the first attempt. What can go wrong? boolean awaitFile() throws InterruptedException { synchronized (lock) { if (!fileArrived) lock.wait(30_000); return fileArrived; } } fun awaitFile(): Boolean { synchronized(lock) { if (!fileArrived) lock.wait(30_000) return fileArrived } } It is the if bug in a new shape. A spurious wakeup, or a notifyAll() meant for some other condition on the same lock, returns early with fileArrived still false, after 2 seconds instead of 30. Simply putting wait(30_000) in a while loop is wrong too: every wake-up would start a fresh 30 seconds. The fix is to compute a deadline once and wait for what is left of it. The guard loop now checks the condition and the clock. Each pass waits only for the remaining time. boolean awaitFile(Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeout.toNanos(); // 1. fix the deadline once synchronized (lock) { while (!fileArrived) { // 2. guard on the condition long leftMillis = (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000; if (leftMillis <= 0) return false; // 3. out of time lock.wait(leftMillis); // 4. wait only for what's left } return true; } } fun awaitFile(timeout: Duration): Boolean { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + timeout.toNanos() // 1. fix the deadline once synchronized(lock) { while (!fileArrived) { // 2. guard on the condition val leftMillis = (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000 if (leftMillis <= 0) return false // 3. out of time lock.wait(leftMillis) // 4. wait only for what's left } return true } } The side that receives the file sets the state before it signals, both under the lock. If it runs before anyone waits, nothing is lost: the waiter sees fileArrived and never calls wait(). Why does the waiter use System.nanoTime() and not System.currentTimeMillis()? void onFileArrived() { synchronized (lock) { fileArrived = true; // state first lock.notifyAll(); // then the signal } } fun onFileArrived() { synchronized(lock) { fileArrived = true // state first lock.notifyAll() // then the signal } } nanoTime() only ever moves forward, so it measures elapsed time. currentTimeMillis() is wall-clock time, and NTP can move it backwards or forwards, which would stretch or cut the timeout.

h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · Quiz
x: What happens when this runs on its own? Object lock = new Object(); lock.notifyAll(); Nothing, since nobody is waiting It wakes every thread in the JVM that is waiting on any lock It throws IllegalMonitorStateException, because the thread doesn't hold lock's monitor It blocks until some thread waits on lock wait, notify and notifyAll require the caller to own the object's monitor, so they must run inside synchronized (lock). It doesn't matter that nobody is waiting. The check comes first. A thread wakes up from lock.wait() because another thread called notifyAll(). When does it run the line after wait()? Immediately, in parallel with the notifier After it gets the monitor back, which is at the earliest when the notifier leaves its synchronized block Only after every other woken thread has finished Never: it has to call wait() again notifyAll() doesn't release the lock. The woken threads move back to competing for the monitor, and wait() returns only once this thread owns it again. Other woken threads may get it first and change the state, which is why the condition must be re-checked. A one-slot buffer has 2 producers and 2 consumers, and both put and take call notify(). Each wait() is correctly inside a while. What can happen? Nothing bad, because the while loops make it safe Two consumers take the same item IllegalMonitorStateException All four threads end up waiting with nobody left to notify them The while loops protect against acting on a false condition, not against lost signals. If a consumer's notify() wakes the other consumer instead of a producer, that wake-up is wasted, and soon every thread waits. notifyAll(), or one Condition per kind of waiter, fixes it. A worker calls lock.wait() with no condition, "until the report is done". The reporting thread calls lock.notifyAll() when it finishes. Sometimes the worker waits forever. Why? notifyAll() only wakes threads that started waiting before it was called, so an early report is a lost wake-up wait() without a timeout is not allowed notifyAll() needs a second call to wake a thread The worker must call notify() itself A notification wakes only threads that are already waiting. If the report finishes first, the signal goes nowhere, and the worker then waits for a signal that already happened. Wait for a state: while (!done) lock.wait();, with done = true set before notifyAll(). From A thread's life: a consumer is parked inside lock.wait() and another thread interrupts it. Which is true? wait() returns normally and the interrupt flag stays set wait() throws InterruptedException at once, without retaking the monitor Nothing happens until someone calls notify() wait() retakes the monitor, then throws InterruptedException with the interrupt flag cleared Like sleep, wait reacts to an interrupt by throwing InterruptedException and clearing the flag. It retakes the monitor first, so your catch or finally block still runs inside the synchronized block. Restore the flag or let the exception propagate.

h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · Key terms
x: Guarded block Code that waits, under a lock, until a condition holds: while (!cond) lock.wait();. Wait set The threads parked in wait() on one monitor, waiting to be notified. Spurious wakeup A return from wait() with no notify, interrupt or timeout. Allowed by the spec. notifyAll Wake every thread in the monitor's wait set. They then compete for the lock. Lost wake-up A signal sent before anyone waits for it, so the waiter never hears it. Backpressure Making a fast producer wait when the consumer can't keep up, instead of buffering without limit. What three things does lock.wait() do? It releases lock's monitor, parks the thread in the wait set (WAITING), and retakes the monitor before it returns. Why must wait() always sit inside while (!condition)? Spurious wakeups are allowed, and another thread may change the state between the notify and the moment you get the lock back. What happens if you call wait() or notify() without holding that object's monitor? IllegalMonitorStateException, at once. Does notifyAll() release the lock? No. The woken threads compete for the monitor after the notifier leaves its synchronized block. When is notify() safe to use instead of notifyAll()? Only when every waiter waits for the same condition and each change lets at most one waiter proceed. What is a lost wake-up? A notify that happens before anyone waits. If the waiter has no condition to check, it then waits forever. Fix: wait for a state field, set before notifying.

h: wait, notify and guarded blocks · Go deeper
x: Timed waits are the same idea with a clock. wait(millis) returns when notified, interrupted, spuriously, or when the time is up, and it does not tell you which. That is why the worked example tracks its own deadline with System.nanoTime(). The JVM has bugs here too. JDK 26 carries a fix titled "Notification can be lost due to interrupt in Object.wait". That is a good reason to use the standard library's queues and synchronizers wherever you can: they are tested far harder than any guarded block you or I will write. Two observability notes. JFR has a jdk.JavaMonitorWait event, with the monitor's class, the thread that notified, the timeout and whether it timed out, and JDK 25 added a jdk.JavaMonitorNotify event. And on virtual threads, Object.wait() used to pin the carrier thread. Since JDK 24 (JEP 491) it no longer does in most cases. Finally, the history. wait/notify have been in Java since 1.0. java.util.concurrent arrived in Java 5 with Condition, BlockingQueue and friends, built by Doug Lea on a framework called AbstractQueuedSynchronizer. When you read the source of ArrayBlockingQueue, you'll find the same guard, act and signal parts as in this lesson, written with a ReentrantLock and two Conditions.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Two locks taken in opposite orders can stop forever
x: Two locks taken in opposite orders: the wait-for cycle, and one global lock order that breaks it Here is a transfer that looks careful. It locks both accounts, so the debit and the credit happen as one step: Java void transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) { synchronized (from) { synchronized (to) { from.debit(cents); to.credit(cents); } } } // thread 1: transfer(a, b, 100) thread 2: transfer(b, a, 50) Kotlin fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, cents: Long) { synchronized(from) { synchronized(to) { from.debit(cents) to.credit(cents) } } } // thread 1: transfer(a, b, 100) thread 2: transfer(b, a, 50) Each call is correct on its own. Together they can freeze. Thread 1 locks a. Before it locks b, thread 2 locks b. Now thread 1 waits for b, which thread 2 holds, and thread 2 waits for a, which thread 1 holds. Neither will ever let go, because each releases its first lock only after it gets the second. That is a deadlock: a set of threads where each one waits for something another one in the set holds. Nothing throws. Nothing logs. CPU use drops to zero, both threads sit in BLOCKED, and every request that needs either account joins the queue behind them. In a payment service, the first sign is usually a health check that times out and a pool with no free threads. The nasty part is timing. The bad interleaving needs both threads to take their first lock inside the same tiny window. A test that runs one transfer at a time never sees it. Under load, with thousands of transfers a second between the same busy merchant accounts, it is only a matter of when. The simulator lets you play the scheduler. Run T1 to the end, then T2, and both transfers finish. Then reset and give each thread one step first. Freeze two transfers Read DeadlockDemo. Each thread takes its first lock, sleeps 300 ms, then asks for the second. Run it. After one second, main asks the JVM which threads are deadlocked. Delete the sleep(300) line and run it a few times. Does it still deadlock every time? Without the sleep it deadlocks only sometimes, and often both transfers finish. That is the same bug, now hiding. The sleep only widens a window that is always there. Deadlock is two cars meeting head-on at a one-lane bridge: each waits for the other to back up, and neither will. Lock ordering is a rule that traffic always crosses from the north side first. Livelock is both drivers backing up at the same moment, then both driving forward again, over and over. Starvation is the car on a side road that never finds a gap in the traffic, while everyone else gets through. The analogy breaks in one useful way: real drivers eventually lose patience and do something different. Threads never do, unless you write the timeout and the random back-off into the code yourself.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Deadlock needs four conditions, so break one
x: A deadlock can only happen when all four of these hold at once. They are known as the Coffman conditions, after a 1971 paper. Mutual exclusion. A resource can be held by only one thread at a time. A lock is exactly that. Hold and wait. A thread holds one resource while it waits for another. No preemption. Nobody can take a resource away from the thread that holds it. It has to let go on its own. Circular wait. There is a cycle: T1 waits for T2, which waits for T1. Longer cycles count too. Remove any one and deadlock becomes impossible. In practice you pick from three moves. Break circular wait with a global lock order. If every thread that needs both a and b takes them in the same order, no thread can hold the second while waiting for the first, so no cycle can form. This is the fix you'll reach for most often, and the next section shows it. Break no-preemption with a timed tryLock. A thread that can't get its second lock in time gives back the first and tries again later. It preempts itself. Break hold-and-wait by needing only one lock: one coarse lock around both accounts, or an operation designed so it never holds one resource while asking for another. Mutual exclusion is the one you rarely remove, since it is the reason you took a lock. Sometimes you can design it away, with immutable data or one owner per account (lesson 11 of this track). The same four conditions apply to every kind of resource, not just Java locks: database row locks, connections from a pool, permits from a semaphore. The figure shows the cycle from the first section as a wait-for graph. Deadlock detectors, including the JVM's, look for exactly this loop. Test the model on a case with no Java locks. A pool has 20 database connections. Twenty request threads each hold one and ask the pool for a second. Which of the four conditions hold, and which move would you pick? (All four: a connection serves one thread, each thread holds one while it waits, the pool can't take one back, and every thread waits for a connection that another thread holds. Taking one connection per request breaks hold and wait. A timeout on the second, after which the thread gives back its first, breaks no preemption.) A wait-for graph. Each thread holds one lock and waits for the other's. The cycle is the deadlock. You'll meet the same cycle outside the JVM. Two ledger transactions that run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the same two account rows in opposite orders deadlock in Oracle. Oracle detects that, fails one statement with ORA-00060: deadlock detected while waiting for resource, and your service sees an exception. The fix is the one from this lesson: lock rows in id order, for example with a single SELECT ... WHERE id IN (...) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE. The other common one is pool deadlock: a Quarkus endpoint that takes a connection from a pool of 20, then calls a method that needs a second connection from the same pool. With 20 concurrent requests, every thread holds one connection and waits for another, forever. No Java lock is involved, so no detector will name it.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Fix it with a global lock order
x: Give every account a stable, unique key, and always lock the lower key first, whichever way the money moves: Java void transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) { Account first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to; // one order for everyone Account second = first == from ? to : from; synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { from.debit(cents); to.credit(cents); } } } Kotlin fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, cents: Long) { val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to // one order for everyone val second = if (first === from) to else from synchronized(first) { synchronized(second) { from.debit(cents) to.credit(cents) } } } Now transfer(a, b) and transfer(b, a) both lock a first. Whoever gets a gets to run. The other waits for a while holding nothing, which is plain contention, not deadlock. Three details make or break this. The key must be unique and must never change. An account id or an IBAN works. hashCode() does not: two different objects can share one, and then two threads may again disagree about the order. If you have no natural key, Java Concurrency in Practice shows a tie-breaker: compare System.identityHashCode, and on a tie take one extra global lock first. The rule must be global. Each method locking in a sensible-looking order is not enough. One method that locks account then customer, and another that locks customer then account, recreate the cycle. Put the ordering in one helper and make every caller use it. The order must survive calls you don't see. If you call a listener, a repository or any other alien code while you hold a lock, that code may take locks of its own in a different order. That is the rule from lesson 4 of this track again: copy what you need, release the lock, then call out. In the lab, Account has a ReentrantLock instead of using synchronized, so that part 2 can use tryLock. The ordering idea is the same. Same transfers, one order Read OrderedLocks. It runs 100,000 transfers in each direction between the same two accounts, with the ordering rule above. Predict whether it finishes, then run it. Break it on purpose: change move to lock from first and to second. Run it again, and stop it with Ctrl+C if it hangs. OrderedLocks.java package workbench.concurrency.l06; /** The same opposite transfers, with every thread taking the locks in one global order. */ public class OrderedLocks { record Acct(int id, long[] balance) {} public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Acct a = new Acct(1, new long[] {1_000_000}); Acct b = new Acct(2, new long[] {1_000_000}); Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) move(a, b, 1); }, "A-to-B"); Thread t2 = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) move(b, a, 1); }, "B-to-A"); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); t1.start(); t2.start(); t1.join(); t2.join(); System.out.printf("200,000 opposite transfers in %d ms, total still %,d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, a.balance()[0] + b.balance()[0]); } static void move(Acct from, Acct to, long cents) { Acct first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to; // lower id first, whatever the direction Acct second = first == from ? to : from; synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { from.balance()[0] -= cents; to.balance()[0] += cents; } } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.OrderedLocks labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l06/OrderedLocks.java OrderedLocks.kt package workbench.concurrency.l06 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The same opposite transfers, with every thread taking the locks in one global order. private class Acct(val id: Int, var balance: Long) fun main() { val a = Acct(1, 1_000_000) val b = Acct(2, 1_000_000) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val t1 = thread(name = "A-to-B") { repeat(100_000) { move(a, b, 1) } } val t2 = thread(name = "B-to-A") { repeat(100_000) { move(b, a, 1) } } t1.join() t2.join() println("200,000 opposite transfers in %d ms, total still %,d" .format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, a.balance + b.balance)) } private fun move(from: Acct, to: Acct, cents: Long) { val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to // lower id first, whatever the direction val second = if (first === from) to else from synchronized(first) { synchronized(second) { from.balance -= cents to.balance += cents } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.OrderedLocksKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l06/OrderedLocks.kt With ordered locks, 200,000 opposite transfers finish in well under a second and the total stays 2,000,000. Locking in argument order usually hangs within the first few thousand transfers. With no sleep to widen the window, it is down to luck, so on some runs it may survive a while.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Timed tryLock, and the livelock it can cause
x: Sometimes you can't impose an order, for example when you don't know all the locks up front. Then make sure no wait can last forever. ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout) gives up after the timeout and returns false. If you can't get both locks, let go of what you hold, wait a little, and try again: Java if (from.lock().tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { if (to.lock().tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { /* move the money */ return true; } finally { to.lock().unlock(); } } } finally { from.lock().unlock(); // couldn't get both: let go of everything } } Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1, 10)); // random back-off, then retry Kotlin if (from.lock().tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { if (to.lock().tryLock(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { /* move the money */ return true } finally { to.lock().unlock() } } } finally { from.lock().unlock() // couldn't get both: let go of everything } } Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1, 10)) // random back-off, then retry The random back-off matters more than it looks. Leave it out, or use a fixed sleep, and two threads can fall into lockstep: both take their first lock, both fail on the second, both release, both retry at the same moment, forever. That is livelock. The threads are busy, they change state all the time, and nothing gets done. A thread dump looks healthy, which makes livelock harder to spot than deadlock. The demo below shows a livelock with no locks at all. Two polite diners share one spoon, and each hands it over whenever the other is hungry. In one second they pass it about ten million times and nobody eats. The fix is to break the symmetry: random back-off, or a rule such as "after three polite turns, eat anyway". The third failure is starvation: the system makes progress, but one thread never does. A non-fair ReentrantLock (the default) lets a thread that just released the lock grab it again before a waiter wakes up. That is faster overall, but one unlucky thread can wait a long time. new ReentrantLock(true) hands the lock to the longest waiter instead. It costs throughput, and its Javadoc warns that fairness of locks does not guarantee fairness of thread scheduling. Starvation also happens when readers keep a read-write lock busy so a writer never gets in. Lesson 12 of this track comes back to that. Watch a livelock, then break the symmetry Run LivelockDemo. Both diners are hungry and both are polite. Read the count of handovers and meals. Run it again with -Pargs=fixed, where a diner eats anyway after three polite turns. LivelockDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l06; /** Two polite diners share one spoon. Each hands it over while the other is hungry. Try -Pargs=fixed. */ public class LivelockDemo { static volatile int spoonOwner = 0; // diner 0 or diner 1 static final boolean[] hungry = {true, true}; // written by its owner only, read by the other static volatile boolean stop; static final long[] handovers = new long[2]; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); Thread d0 = new Thread(() -> dine(0, fixed), "diner-0"); Thread d1 = new Thread(() -> dine(1, fixed), "diner-1"); d0.start(); d1.start(); d0.join(1_000); d1.join(1_000); stop = true; d0.join(); d1.join(); System.out.printf("spoon handed over %,d times; meals eaten: %d%n", handovers[0] + handovers[1], (hungry[0] ? 0 : 1) + (hungry[1] ? 0 : 1)); } static void dine(int me, boolean fixed) { int other = 1 - me; int politeTurns = 0; while (!stop) { if (spoonOwner != me) { // not my spoon: wait for it Thread.onSpinWait(); continue; } boolean otherHungry; synchronized (hungry) { otherHungry = hungry[other]; } if (otherHungry && (!fixed || politeTurns < 3)) { politeTurns++; handovers[me]++; spoonOwner = other; // "you first": both keep saying it continue; } synchronized (hungry) { hungry[me] = false; } // eat spoonOwner = other; // then pass the spoon on return; } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.LivelockDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l06/LivelockDemo.java LivelockDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l06 import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two polite diners share one spoon. Each hands it over while the other is hungry. Try -Pargs=fixed. @Volatile private var spoonOwner = 0 // diner 0 or diner 1 private val hungry = booleanArrayOf(true, true) // guarded by synchronized(hungry) @Volatile private var stop = false private val handovers = LongArray(2) fun main(args: Array<String>) { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" val d0 = thread(name = "diner-0") { dine(0, fixed) } val d1 = thread(name = "diner-1") { dine(1, fixed) } d0.join(1_000) d1.join(1_000) stop = true d0.join() d1.join() val meals = (if (hungry[0]) 0 else 1) + (if (hungry[1]) 0 else 1) println("spoon handed over %,d times; meals eaten: %d".format(handovers[0] + handovers[1], meals)) } private fun dine(me: Int, fixed: Boolean) { val other = 1 - me var politeTurns = 0 while (!stop) { if (spoonOwner != me) { // not my spoon: wait for it Thread.onSpinWait() continue } val otherHungry = synchronized(hungry) { hungry[other] } if (otherHungry && (!fixed || politeTurns < 3)) { politeTurns++ handovers[me]++ spoonOwner = other // "you first": both keep saying it continue } synchronized(hungry) { hungry[me] = false } // eat spoonOwner = other // then pass the spoon on return } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.LivelockDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l06/LivelockDemo.kt Without the fix: around ten million handovers in one second and meals eaten: 0. Both threads were RUNNABLE the whole time. With -Pargs=fixed: 6 handovers and 2 meals, done at once.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Read a deadlock from a thread dump
x: When a service freezes, take a thread dump before you restart it. The restart destroys the evidence. jcmd # lists Java processes with their PIDs jcmd <pid> Thread.print # every thread's state and stack, plus deadlock detection jstack <pid> prints the same dump. If the JVM finds a cycle of threads waiting for each other's locks, it says so at the end. This is real output from the demo, on JDK 21: Found one Java-level deadlock: ============================= "transfer-A-to-B": waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f70d4001870 (object 0x00000006f794b518, a java.lang.Object), which is held by "transfer-B-to-A" "transfer-B-to-A": waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f70d80012f0 (object 0x00000006f794b508, a java.lang.Object), which is held by "transfer-A-to-B" Java stack information for the threads listed above: =================================================== "transfer-A-to-B": at workbench.concurrency.l06.DeadlockDemo.move(DeadlockDemo.java:42) - waiting to lock <0x00000006f794b518> (a java.lang.Object) - locked <0x00000006f794b508> (a java.lang.Object) ... Found 1 deadlock. Read it from the bottom up. Each thread's stack shows what it holds (- locked <...>) and what it wants (- waiting to lock <...>), and the header names the owner of the lock it wants. The line numbers take you straight to the two synchronized blocks that lock in opposite orders. The detector also finds deadlocks on ReentrantLock. Then the dump says waiting for ownable synchronizer ... which is held by, and the stack shows parking to wait for instead of waiting to lock. Add -l (Thread.print -l) to list the java.util.concurrent locks each thread owns. For tooling, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json writes JSON. On JDK 21 each thread has only tid, name and stack. From JDK 25 it also has state, blockedOn, waitingOn, owner and the monitors each thread holds, which is enough to rebuild the wait-for graph. Inside the process you can ask the same question in code, which makes a cheap health check: Java long[] ids = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads(); // null if none Kotlin val ids: LongArray? = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads() // null if none Two limits to know. The detector only sees cycles of Java locks. Twenty threads that each hold a pooled database connection and wait for a second one are deadlocked too, but the dump just shows twenty threads waiting inside the pool. And there is no JFR event for deadlocks: you find them with thread dumps or ThreadMXBean. Take the dump yourself Run ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l06.DeadlockDemo -Pargs=wait. It deadlocks, prints its PID, and stays alive for 60 seconds. In a second terminal, run jcmd <pid> Thread.print with that PID. Find Found one Java-level deadlock and follow each thread's locked and waiting to lock lines to a line number. Run jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/dump.json and open the file. Which fields does each thread have on your JDK? terminal 2 jcmd # find the PID of DeadlockDemo jcmd <pid> Thread.print jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/dump.json The text dump ends with Found 1 deadlock. and points at DeadlockDemo.java:42 for both threads. The JSON has tid, name and stack per thread on JDK 21, and state and lock fields as well on JDK 25 and later. Thread.dump_to_file refuses to overwrite an existing file unless you add -overwrite. diagnosticCommand.hpp at jdk-27-ga: the jcmd Thread.* commands docs The most common real mistake is believing that each method's locking order is enough. Developers check that transfer always locks from then to and call it consistent, but "from first" is a different order for every pair of calls. The same trap appears across classes: OrderService locks the order then the customer, CustomerService locks the customer then the orders. The fix is one rule for the whole system, such as "lower id first", written once in a helper that every caller uses, plus a review rule that nothing calls alien code while holding a lock.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Java and Kotlin
x: Ordered locking in Java and Kotlin Java void transfer(Account from, Account to, long cents) { Account first = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to; Account second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock().lock(); try { second.lock().lock(); try { from.debit(cents); to.credit(cents); } finally { second.lock().unlock(); } } finally { first.lock().unlock(); } } Kotlin fun transfer(from: Account, to: Account, cents: Long) { val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to val second = if (first === from) to else from first.lock().withLock { // kotlin.concurrent.withLock: lock, try, finally unlock second.lock().withLock { from.debit(cents) to.credit(cents) } } } The idea is identical, and so is the deadlock risk: Kotlin adds no protection here. What differs is ceremony. Kotlin's withLock { } extension on Lock writes the lock(), try, finally unlock() for you, so you can't forget the finally. In Java the try/finally pairs are on you, and an unlock() in the wrong finally is a classic way to leak a lock. Both languages get the same dump from jcmd, since Kotlin compiles to the same ReentrantLock and monitor calls.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Worked example
x: Find a deadlock that hides behind a callback A ledger tells an audit log about every posting. A scheduler flushes the audit log every second, and the flush reads the ledger's balance. Each class looks fine on its own. Find the cycle. class Ledger { synchronized void post(Entry e) { entries.add(e); auditLog.record(e); // calls AuditLog while holding the Ledger lock } synchronized long balance() { return sum(entries); } } class AuditLog { synchronized void record(Entry e) { pending.add(e); } synchronized void flush() { long b = ledger.balance(); // calls Ledger while holding the AuditLog lock write(pending, b); pending.clear(); } } class Ledger(private val auditLog: AuditLog) { @Synchronized fun post(e: Entry) { entries += e auditLog.record(e) // calls AuditLog while holding the Ledger lock } @Synchronized fun balance(): Long = sum(entries) } class AuditLog { @Synchronized fun record(e: Entry) { pending += e } @Synchronized fun flush() { val b = ledger.balance() // calls Ledger while holding the AuditLog lock write(pending, b) pending.clear() } } A request thread in post holds the Ledger lock and wants the AuditLog lock. The scheduler thread in flush holds the AuditLog lock and wants the Ledger lock. That is the AB/BA cycle again, split across two classes. The dump would show it like this: "http-worker-7": waiting to lock <0x...a0> (a AuditLog), locked <0x...b8> (a Ledger) "audit-flusher": waiting to lock <0x...b8> (a Ledger), locked <0x...a0> (a AuditLog) You could impose an order, but the cleaner fix is to stop holding a lock while calling the other class. Each method keeps its own lock only around its own state. Before reading the fix, decide: which call in each method is the alien one? void post(Entry e) { synchronized (this) { entries.add(e); } auditLog.record(e); // 1. no Ledger lock held while calling out } void flush() { long b = ledger.balance(); // 2. read the balance before taking our own lock List<Entry> batch; synchronized (this) { batch = List.copyOf(pending); pending.clear(); } write(batch, b); // 3. slow I/O with no lock at all } fun post(e: Entry) { synchronized(this) { entries += e } auditLog.record(e) // 1. no Ledger lock held while calling out } fun flush() { val b = ledger.balance() // 2. read the balance before taking our own lock val batch = synchronized(this) { pending.toList().also { pending.clear() } } write(batch, b) // 3. slow I/O with no lock at all } Now no thread ever holds one of the two locks while asking for the other, so hold-and-wait is gone and no cycle can form. The balance written with the batch may be a moment older than the last entry. For an audit log that is fine; if it weren't, you'd need one lock over both, which is the coarse-lock fix.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Lab
x: Fix a transfer deadlock, then add a transfer that gives up labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l06/Transfers.java labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l06/Account.java ./gradlew :concurrency:test --tests 'workbench.concurrency.l06.*' Run the tests. Two transfer tests time out after 10 seconds: they deadlocked. The three tryTransfer tests fail with UnsupportedOperationException. Read Account. You don't change it. debit and credit throw unless you hold that account's lock. Part 1: fix Transfers.transfer so it always locks the account with the lower id() first. Keep the try/finally around each unlock(). Part 2: write tryTransfer. Loop until the deadline: tryLock the first account for 10 ms, then the second for 10 ms. If you get both, move the money and return true. If not, release what you hold, sleep a random 1 to 10 ms, and loop. Return false when time is up. Run the tests until all five pass, then run them twice more. A self-transfer (from == to) takes the same ReentrantLock twice. That is fine, because it is reentrant, as long as you release it twice. In part 2, put the from.lock().unlock() in a finally that runs whether or not you got to. The test checks that from is free after a failed attempt. ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(1, 10) gives a random back-off without sharing a Random between threads. All five tests in TransfersTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can explain the four conditions for deadlock, remove one with lock ordering or timed tryLock, tell deadlock from livelock and starvation, and find a deadlock in a thread dump.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Quiz
x: Which change makes transfer(from, to) safe from deadlock when transfers run in both directions? Mark the field that holds each balance volatile Always lock the account with the lower id first, then the other Add Thread.sleep(1) between the two locks Make transfer a synchronized instance method on each account One global order means no thread can hold the second lock while waiting for the first, so circular wait can't happen. volatile doesn't affect locking. A sleep just changes the odds. A synchronized method on the source account is still "lock from, then to", the same broken order. Two threads use tryLock with a fixed 5 ms sleep between attempts. A thread dump shows both RUNNABLE or TIMED_WAITING, their stacks change between dumps, and no deadlock is reported. Nothing has completed in a minute. What is this? A deadlock that the JVM failed to detect Starvation of one thread Livelock: they keep retrying in lockstep and both keep failing A GC pause The threads are active, they release and retake locks, and neither makes progress. That is livelock. With fixed sleeps they stay in step. A random back-off breaks the symmetry. It isn't deadlock, because nobody waits forever on a held lock, and it isn't starvation, because nobody else is progressing either. A service stops answering. You suspect a lock cycle. Which tool tells you for sure? A JFR recording, filtered on the jdk.Deadlock event The GC log Restarting the pod and watching whether it happens again jcmd <pid> Thread.print, which prints "Found one Java-level deadlock" with the threads and locks involved The thread dump's deadlock detector finds cycles on monitors and on ReentrantLock, and names who holds what. JFR has no deadlock event. Restarting destroys the evidence. Take the dump first. A report thread needs a ReentrantLock for 50 ms once a minute. Request threads take the same lock thousands of times a second and grab it again the moment they release it. The report sometimes waits for minutes. What is this, and what is one fix? Starvation; a fair lock, new ReentrantLock(true), gives the longest waiter the next turn Deadlock; order the locks Livelock; add random back-off A race condition; make the field volatile Everyone else makes progress and one thread never gets its turn: that is starvation. A non-fair lock lets a running thread barge back in ahead of waiters. A fair lock queues them in order, at some cost in throughput. Making the request path hold the lock for less time also helps. From wait, notify and guarded blocks: a one-slot buffer using notify() stalls with all four threads WAITING. Will jcmd Thread.print report a Java-level deadlock? Yes, every stall is reported as a deadlock No: no thread holds the monitor, they are all waiting for a notification that will never come Yes, but only with the -l flag No, because jcmd can't see WAITING threads The deadlock detector looks for threads blocked on locks held by each other. Threads in wait() hold nothing, and the monitor is free. They are stuck because a signal was lost, not because of a lock cycle, so the dump shows four WAITING threads and no deadlock section.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Explain it back
x: A teammate says: "We added tryLock(5, SECONDS) everywhere, so we can't have deadlocks any more." Explain what they got right, and what can still go wrong.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Key terms
x: Deadlock Threads that each wait for a resource another one holds, so none can ever proceed. Livelock Threads that keep reacting to each other, busy but making no progress. Starvation One thread never gets the resource it needs while others keep getting it. Lock ordering A rule that every thread takes locks in the same global order. Wait-for graph A picture of which thread waits for which. A cycle in it is a deadlock. Thread dump A snapshot of every thread's state and stack, from jcmd Thread.print or jstack. Deadlock condition 1: what is mutual exclusion? A resource can be held by only one thread at a time. Every lock has it. Deadlock condition 2: what is hold and wait? A thread holds one resource while waiting for another. Deadlock condition 3: what is no preemption? Nobody can take a resource away from the thread that holds it; only the holder can release it. Deadlock condition 4: what is circular wait? A cycle of threads, each waiting for a resource the next one holds: T1 waits for T2, T2 waits for T1. How does a global lock order prevent deadlock? Every thread takes locks in the same order (for example lower id first), so no cycle can form. It breaks circular wait. Deadlock vs livelock vs starvation, in one line each. Deadlock: threads wait forever for each other. Livelock: threads stay busy reacting to each other and make no progress. Starvation: others progress, one thread never gets a turn. What does jcmd <pid> Thread.print print when it finds a lock cycle? Found one Java-level deadlock:, then each thread, the lock it waits for and who holds it, then their stacks, ending with Found 1 deadlock.

h: Deadlock, livelock and starvation · Go deeper
x: The JVM's detector covers two kinds of lock. ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() looks for cycles on monitors and on ownable synchronizers such as ReentrantLock and the write lock of ReentrantReadWriteLock. The older findMonitorDeadlockedThreads() sees monitors only. Neither sees semaphores, latches, Object.wait(), futures waiting on each other or pooled connections, because none of those has a single owning thread the JVM could point at. That covers the common case of two thread pools waiting on each other. Task A runs on pool 1 and blocks on a Future from pool 2, while pool 2's only thread is blocked on a Future from pool 1. No lock is involved, so the detector stays silent. The dump still gives it away if you read the stacks: every pool thread is parked in FutureTask.get or CompletableFuture.join. Java Concurrency in Practice calls this thread-starvation deadlock. JSON thread dumps keep improving. JDK 25 added per-thread state, parkBlocker, blockedOn, waitingOn, owner and the monitors each thread owns. JDK 26 added java.util.concurrent lock information. JDK 27 added a formatVersion field. If you build tooling on these dumps, check that field and the JDK version first. Databases take the opposite approach to the JVM. Oracle detects deadlocks between sessions and breaks them by failing one statement. Your code must be ready to retry that transaction, ideally after ordering its row locks so the retry doesn't deadlock again.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · ReentrantLock is synchronized with the controls exposed
x: A thread waiting to enter synchronized has no way out. It can't give up after a timeout, and an interrupt doesn't reach it until it gets the monitor. When a batch job holds that monitor for 1.5 seconds, every API thread behind it waits 1.5 seconds too, and so does a shutdown that tries to interrupt them. ReentrantLock gives you the same guarantees as synchronized. Only one thread holds it at a time. Releasing it happens-before the next thread takes it, so the next owner sees every write the last owner made. And it is reentrant: the owner can take it again, and it counts the holds. What you give up is the automatic release. A synchronized block always lets go when it exits, even on an exception. A ReentrantLock lets go only when you call unlock(). So every use follows one idiom: Java private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); private final List<Entry> entries = new ArrayList<>(); // guarded by lock void post(Entry e) { lock.lock(); // before the try, never inside it try { entries.add(e); } finally { lock.unlock(); // first line of finally: runs even if add throws } } Kotlin private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val entries = mutableListOf<Entry>() // guarded by lock fun post(e: Entry) { lock.withLock { // kotlin.concurrent: lock(), try, finally unlock() entries += e } } lock() goes right before the try, not inside it. If it were inside and something failed before the lock was taken, the finally would release a lock you don't hold, and unlock() throws IllegalMonitorStateException. In Kotlin, withLock { } writes the whole pattern for you. In return you get controls that synchronized doesn't have: tryLock() takes the lock only if it is free right now, and returns false otherwise. tryLock(200, MILLISECONDS) waits at most 200 ms. You met it in the previous lesson as a deadlock breaker. lockInterruptibly() waits, but gives up with InterruptedException when the thread is interrupted. new ReentrantLock(true) makes a fair lock that hands over to the longest waiter. isHeldByCurrentThread() and getQueueLength() let you assert and monitor. Several Conditions per lock, which is the next section. A thread waiting in lock() is parked, so a thread dump shows it as WAITING, not BLOCKED (lesson 2 of this track). Expect that when you read dumps of services that use explicit locks. My rule: use synchronized for a short, simple critical section, and switch to ReentrantLock when you need one of these controls. The old reason to switch, pinning of virtual threads inside synchronized, mostly went away in JDK 24 (JEP 491). The virtual threads track covers that. Three ways to wait for a busy lock Read TryLockDemo. A batch thread holds the ledger lock (and a monitor) for 1.5 seconds. api uses tryLock(200 ms), report uses lockInterruptibly(), and legacy waits on the monitor with synchronized. Predict the order of the four output lines, and what getState() prints for report and legacy. Run it. Then change api to wait 2 seconds instead of 200 ms and run it again. TryLockDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** A batch holds the ledger lock for 1.5 s. Three threads want in, each in a different way. */ public class TryLockDemo { static final ReentrantLock ledger = new ReentrantLock(); static final Object monitor = new Object(); public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread batch = new Thread(() -> { ledger.lock(); try { synchronized (monitor) { // the batch holds the lock AND a monitor pause(1_500); } } finally { ledger.unlock(); } }, "batch"); batch.start(); Thread.sleep(100); // let the batch get in first Thread api = new Thread(() -> { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); The interrupt ends report's wait at once. legacy keeps waiting until the batch finishes, and only then sees interrupted=true. With a 2-second timeout, api gets the lock after the batch is done. ReentrantLock (Java SE 25 API) docs A ReentrantLock is a meeting room with a screen outside. You can queue for the room (lock), glance at the screen and leave if it's busy (tryLock), queue for at most two minutes (tryLock(timeout)), or leave the queue when your phone rings (lockInterruptibly). Conditions are separate waiting areas: people waiting for a projector don't get woken when a chair frees up. A read-write lock is a museum gallery: many visitors at once, but the cleaner needs it empty. A visitor can't become the cleaner without walking out first, and if they wait inside for the room to empty, they wait forever. The analogy breaks in one place: a person in the room always leaves eventually. A thread that forgets unlock() holds the room for the life of the process.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Condition gives each reason to wait its own queue
x: A monitor has one wait set. In lesson 5 of this track that forced notifyAll() on the bounded buffer: producers and consumers waited in the same place, so a single notify() could wake the wrong kind of thread and stall everything. A ReentrantLock can have as many wait sets as you like. Each call to lock.newCondition() makes one. await() plays the part of wait(): it releases the lock, parks, and takes the lock back before it returns. signal() and signalAll() play notify() and notifyAll(). Here is the producer side of the buffer: Java private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition(); // producers wait here private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition(); // consumers wait here public void put(T item) throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.size() == capacity) notFull.await(); // releases the lock while waiting items.addLast(item); notEmpty.signal(); // wake one consumer } finally { lock.unlock(); } } Kotlin private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val notFull = lock.newCondition() // producers wait here private val notEmpty = lock.newCondition() // consumers wait here fun put(item: T) = lock.withLock { while (items.size == capacity) notFull.await() // releases the lock while waiting items.addLast(item) notEmpty.signal() // wake one consumer } Only consumers ever wait on notEmpty, and one new item lets exactly one consumer proceed. Those are the two conditions under which lesson 5 said notify() is safe, and now they hold for each queue. So signal() is enough, and the other waiters stay asleep. The rules from lesson 5 still apply: You must hold the lock to call await() or signal(). Otherwise you get IllegalMonitorStateException. Wait in a while loop. The Condition Javadoc allows spurious wake-ups, and another thread can take the item between the signal and your return from await(). Don't call wait() or notify() on a Condition. In Java it is an object like any other, so notFull.wait() compiles. It uses the condition object's own monitor, which you don't hold, and throws IllegalMonitorStateException. Condition also has timed waits. awaitNanos(n) returns the time left, so a loop can keep waiting for the rest of a deadline. offer(item, timeout) in the lab uses it. Count the wasted wake-ups Read WakeupCount. It moves 20,000 items through a one-slot buffer with 4 producers and 4 consumers. It does this twice: once with one Condition and signalAll(), once with two Conditions and signal(). A wake-up is wasted when a thread wakes, re-checks its while condition, and has to wait again. Predict which version wastes more. Run it twice and compare the counts and the times. WakeupCount.java package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * 4 producers and 4 consumers move 20,000 items through a one-slot buffer, twice: * once with one Condition and signalAll(), once with notFull/notEmpty and signal(). * A wake-up is "wasted" when the thread wakes, re-checks, and has to wait again. */ public class WakeupCount { static final class Buffer { final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); final Condition notFull; final Condition notEmpty; final boolean shared; final ArrayDeque<Integer> items = new ArrayDeque<>(); long wasted; // guarded by lock Buffer(boolean oneCondition) { shared = oneCondition; notFull = lock.newCondition(); notEmpty = oneCondition ? notFull : lock.newCondition(); // same queue, or two } void put(int x) throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.size() == 1) { notFull.await(); if (items.size() == 1) wasted++; // woke up for nothing } items.add(x); if (shared) notEmpty.signalAll(); else notEmpty.signal(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } int take() throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (items.isEmpty()) { notEmpty.await(); if (items.isEmpty()) wasted++; } int x = items.remove(); if (shared) notFull.signalAll(); else notFull.signal(); return x; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (boolean one : new boolean[] {true, false}) { Buffer buffer = new Buffer(one); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { threads.add(new Thread(() -> { try { for (int n = 0; n < 5_000; n++) buffer.put(n); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } })); threads.add(new Thread(() -> { try { for (int n = 0; n < 5_000; n++) buffer.take(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } })); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (Thread t : threads) t.start(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-34s wasted wake-ups: %,9d (%d ms)%n", one ? With two conditions, the count drops to hundreds or a few thousand, and the run is several times faster. It isn't zero, because of barging: a running thread can grab the lock and the item before the signalled thread wakes up. That is why the while loop stays. One lock, one entry queue, and a separate wait queue per condition. await() leaves the lock and parks in its queue; signal() moves one waiter to the entry queue. Condition.java at jdk-25-ga (spurious wake-ups, await and signal) read A Quarkus payment service usually has two lock shapes. One is a per-key lock around a check-and-update, such as a card's daily spend, where tryLock(50 ms) lets a request fail fast with a retryable error instead of tying up a worker thread behind a stuck holder. The other is a read-mostly cache, such as FX rates or BIN ranges, refreshed by a scheduled job and read by every request. For the cache, a read-write lock works, but check whether the refresh replaces the whole map. If it does, a volatile reference to an immutable map needs no lock at all. In Kotlin services, prefer withLock, read and write, and remember that write inside read releases the read lock first, so re-check whatever made you decide to write.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · ReadWriteLock lets readers share, and never lets them upgrade
x: An FX rate cache is read 5,000 times a second and refreshed every 5 seconds. With a plain lock, every reader waits for every other reader, although readers never conflict. A ReentrantReadWriteLock has two locks inside: many threads can hold the read lock together, and the write lock is exclusive. It waits until no reader and no writer is inside. Java private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); private final Map<String, BigDecimal> rates = new HashMap<>(); // guarded by rw BigDecimal rate(String pair) { rw.readLock().lock(); // many threads can hold this at once try { return rates.get(pair); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } } void refresh(Map<String, BigDecimal> fresh) { rw.writeLock().lock(); // waits until no reader and no writer holds the lock try { rates.clear(); rates.putAll(fresh); } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } } Kotlin private val rw = ReentrantReadWriteLock() private val rates = HashMap<String, BigDecimal>() // guarded by rw fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal? = rw.read { // many threads can hold this at once rates[pair] } fun refresh(fresh: Map<String, BigDecimal>) = rw.write { // waits until no reader and no writer holds the lock rates.clear() rates.putAll(fresh) } The trap is the cache miss. The natural code checks under the read lock and, if the rate is missing, takes the write lock to load it: Java rw.readLock().lock(); try { BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair); if (r != null) return r; rw.writeLock().lock(); // waits for every reader to leave, this thread included: forever try { r = loader.apply(pair); rates.put(pair, r); return r; } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } Kotlin rw.readLock().lock() try { val r = rates[pair] if (r != null) return r rw.writeLock().lock() // waits for every reader to leave, this thread included: forever try { return loader(pair).also { rates[pair] = it } } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock() } } finally { rw.readLock().unlock() } That is a lock upgrade, and ReentrantReadWriteLock doesn't support it. The write lock waits for all readers to leave. This thread is a reader, and it won't leave until it gets the write lock. It waits forever, on its own. Two threads doing it at once wait for each other. Worse, the JVM's deadlock detector says nothing. Run the demo with -Pargs=hang and take a thread dump: main is WAITING (parking) in WriteLock.lock, there is no Found one Java-level deadlock, and Thread.print -l lists Locked ownable synchronizers: None. Read locks have no single owner, so the detector has no cycle to find. The fix: release the read lock, take the write lock, and check again, because another thread may have loaded the rate while you held nothing. Going the other way, a downgrade, is allowed: while holding the write lock, take the read lock, then release the write lock. A read-write lock pays off when reads are frequent, take a while, and writes are rare. For a map lookup that takes 50 ns, the extra bookkeeping can cost more than it saves. When the cache is replaced as a whole, a volatile reference to an immutable map is simpler and faster still. Lesson 11 of this track shows that pattern. Upgrade, then downgrade Run UpgradeDeadlock. It tries the upgrade with tryLock(1, SECONDS) so it can't hang, then does a downgrade. Run the Kotlin twin. Its last line puts write { } inside read { }. Predict: does it hang? Optional: run the Java one with -Pargs=hang. In a second terminal run jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l with the printed PID and look at main. Stop it with Ctrl+C. UpgradeDeadlock.java package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock; /** * One thread, one ReentrantReadWriteLock. Upgrading (read, then write) never succeeds. * Downgrading (write, then read, then release the write) is allowed. * Run with -Pargs=hang to use lock() instead of tryLock() and see the thread wait forever. */ public class UpgradeDeadlock { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); boolean hang = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("hang"); // 1. the "upgrade": ask for the write lock while still holding the read lock rw.readLock().lock(); try { System.out.println("holding the read lock, read holds = " + rw.getReadHoldCount()); if (hang) { System.out.println("calling writeLock().lock() ... (pid " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + ", Ctrl+C to stop)"); rw.writeLock().lock(); // waits for every reader to leave, us included } boolean got = rw.writeLock().tryLock(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // the same wait, with a time limit System.out.println("write lock while holding a read lock, after 1 s: " + got); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } // 2. the downgrade: write lock, then read lock, then let go of the write lock rw.writeLock().lock(); try { rw.readLock().lock(); // allowed: we are the only writer } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } try { System.out.println("downgraded: write locked = " + rw.isWriteLocked() + ", read holds = " + rw.getReadHoldCount()); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l07.UpgradeDeadlock labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l07/UpgradeDeadlock.java UpgradeDeadlock.kt package workbench.concurrency.l07 import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock import kotlin.concurrent.read import kotlin.concurrent.write // One thread, one ReentrantReadWriteLock. That makes it a release-then-acquire, not an atomic upgrade. rw.read { rw.write { println("kotlin write {} inside read {}: write locked = ${rw.isWriteLocked}, read holds = ${rw.readHoldCount}") } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l07.UpgradeDeadlockKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l07/UpgradeDeadlock.kt write lock while holding a read lock, after 1 s: false, then downgraded: write locked = false, read holds = 1. h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · StampedLock trades safety rails for speed
x: Even a read lock writes to shared memory: every reader increments and decrements the lock's count. On a hot path with many cores, that one cache line (the small block of memory that caches copy between cores, and that a core must own before it can write to it) bounces between them. StampedLock (JDK 8) adds a mode with no write at all, the optimistic read: Java long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead(); // 1. no lock, just a version number long b = bid, a = ask; // 2. copy into locals if (!lock.validate(stamp)) { // 3. a writer got in: the copies may be torn stamp = lock.readLock(); // 4. fall back to a real read lock try { b = bid; a = ask; } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp); } } return new Quote(b, a); // 5. use the locals only after validate Kotlin var stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead() // 1. no lock, just a version number var b = bid; var a = ask // 2. copy into locals if (!lock.validate(stamp)) { // 3. a writer got in: the copies may be torn stamp = lock.readLock() // 4. fall back to a real read lock try { b = bid; a = ask } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp) } } return Quote(b, a) // 5. use the locals only after validate tryOptimisticRead() returns a stamp, a version number of the lock (or 0 if a writer holds it). You read the fields into locals with no lock held. Then validate(stamp) asks: did any writer get in since that stamp? If not, your copies are consistent. If yes, you throw them away and read again under a real read lock. Between steps 2 and 3, the copies can be garbage: a new bid with an old ask. The Javadoc only promises that writes happen-before your reads if a later validate returns true. So the code between the stamp and the validation must not act on the values. No loops driven by them, no array index, no calls that could throw. Copy, validate, then use. The price of the speed is a list of things StampedLock doesn't do: It is not reentrant. A thread that holds the write lock and asks for it again waits for itself. It has no Conditions. Stamps are not tied to a thread, and you must pass the right stamp to unlockRead or unlockWrite. Use it for a small group of fields that are read on a hot path and written rarely, such as a quote's bid and ask, and only after a profiler shows the read-write lock is the cost. For most code ReentrantReadWriteLock, or no lock at all, is the better choice. Catch torn reads with validate() Read OptimisticRead. A writer keeps updating a quote, and ask is always bid + 2 once a write is done. The reader counts how many optimistic reads saw a quote where that isn't true. Predict: will any torn quote get past validate()? Run it. Then delete the validate check (treat every optimistic read as good) and count the torn quotes yourself. OptimisticRead.java package workbench.concurrency.l07; import java.util.concurrent.locks.StampedLock; /** * A writer keeps moving an FX quote; the ask is always bid + 2. A reader reads both fields * optimistically for one second and counts how often validate() caught a half-written quote. */ public class OptimisticRead { static final StampedLock lock = new StampedLock(); static long bid = 100, ask = 102; // guarded by lock; ask == bid + 2 when no write is in progress static volatile boolean done; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread writer = new Thread(() -> { long v = 100; while (!done) { long stamp = lock.writeLock(); try { bid = ++v; for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); // widens the half-written moment ask = v + 2; } finally { lock.unlockWrite(stamp); } } }); writer.start(); long reads = 0, failed = 0, tornCaught = 0, tornPassed = 0; long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++; long stamp = lock.tryOptimisticRead(); // 1. no lock taken, just a version number long b = bid, a = ask; // 2. copy the fields into locals boolean torn = a - b != 2; if (lock.validate(stamp)) { // 3. did a writer get in since step 1? if (torn) tornPassed++; // never happens } else { failed++; if (torn) tornCaught++; stamp = lock.readLock(); // 4. fall back to a real read lock try { b = bid; a = ask; } finally { lock.unlockRead(stamp); } } } done = true; writer.join(); System.out.printf("reads: %,d failed validate(): %,d torn quotes caught: %,d torn quotes that passed validate(): %d%n", reads, failed, tornCaught, tornPassed); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l07.OptimisticRead labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l07/OptimisticRead.java OptimisticRead.kt package workbench.concurrency.l07 import java.util.concurrent.locks.StampedLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A writer keeps moving an FX quote; the ask is always bid + 2. A reader reads both fields // optimistically for one second and counts how often validate() caught a half-written quote. private class Quote { val lock = StampedLock() var bid = 100L // guarded by lock; ask == bid + 2 when no write is in progress var ask = 102L } @Volatile private var done = false fun main() { val q = Quote() val writer = thread { var v = 100L while (!done) { val stamp = q.lock.writeLock() try { q.bid = ++v repeat(20) { Thread.onSpinWait() } // widens the half-written moment q.ask = v + 2 } finally { q.lock.unlockWrite(stamp) } } } var reads = 0L; var failed = 0L; var tornCaught = 0L; var tornPassed = 0L val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++ var stamp = q.lock.tryOptimisticRead() // 1. no lock taken, just a version number var b = q.bid; var a = q.ask // 2. copy the fields into locals val torn = a - b != 2L if (q.lock.validate(stamp)) { // 3. did a writer get in since step 1? if (torn) tornPassed++ // never happens } else { failed++ if (torn) tornCaught++ stamp = q.lock.readLock() // 4. fall back to a real read lock try { b = q.bid; a = q.ask } finally { q.lock.unlockRead(stamp) } } } done = true writer.join() println("reads: %,d failed validate(): %,d torn quotes caught: %,d torn quotes that passed validate(): %d" .format(reads, failed, tornCaught, tornPassed)) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l07.OptimisticReadKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l07/OptimisticRead.kt Thousands of reads fail validation each second, and many of those saw a torn quote (a new bid with an old ask). The last number, torn quotes that passed validate(), is always 0. Without the check, those torn quotes would have gone to the caller. The most common mistake is a lock() without a finally, or with code between lock() and try that can throw. One exception on a rare path, a validation error or a timeout from a downstream call, skips the unlock(). The lock is now held by a thread that has moved on. Every other thread parks in ReentrantLock.lock(), and a dump shows dozens of threads WAITING (parking) while Thread.print -l names an owner that is idle somewhere else. Nothing ever releases it. The fix is the idiom, every time: lock() on the line before try, unlock() as the first line of finally. In Kotlin, use withLock { } and the problem can't happen.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Java and Kotlin
x: A read-mostly cache in Java and Kotlin Java BigDecimal rate(String pair) { rw.readLock().lock(); try { BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair); if (r != null) return r; // 1. fast path under the read lock } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); // 2. let go BEFORE asking for the write lock } rw.writeLock().lock(); try { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, loader); // 3. re-check under the write lock } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } } Kotlin fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = rw.read { rates[pair] ?: rw.write { // write {} let go of our read lock first, so another thread may have loaded it: re-check rates.getOrPut(pair) { loader(pair) } } } The Java version must release the read lock before taking the write lock, or it hangs. The Kotlin version looks like an upgrade, and it doesn't hang, because the standard library's ReentrantReadWriteLock.write releases every read lock this thread holds, takes the write lock, and takes the read locks back afterwards. Its documentation warns that this upgrade is not atomic: another thread can write in the gap, so anything you checked before write must be checked again inside it. That is why both versions re-check (computeIfAbsent, getOrPut). Kotlin's helpers remove the ceremony, not the reasoning.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Worked example
x: A per-card lock that fails fast Authorizations for one card must run one at a time, because each one checks and then updates that card's daily spend. Different cards must not wait for each other. And if one holder gets stuck, other requests for that card should fail fast with a retryable error instead of tying up worker threads. Read the solution and its subgoal labels. class CardLocks { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, ReentrantLock> locks = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); <T> T withCard(String cardId, Duration maxWait, Supplier<T> action) throws InterruptedException { // 1. one lock per card, created at most once ReentrantLock lock = locks.computeIfAbsent(cardId, id -> new ReentrantLock()); // 2. wait a bounded time; an interrupt also ends the wait if (!lock.tryLock(maxWait.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { throw new CardBusyException(cardId); // 3. busy: fail fast, the client retries } try { return action.get(); // 4. critical section } finally { lock.unlock(); // 5. always release } } } class CardLocks { private val locks = ConcurrentHashMap<String, ReentrantLock>() fun <T> withCard(cardId: String, maxWait: Duration, action: () -> T): T { // 1. one lock per card, created at most once val lock = locks.computeIfAbsent(cardId) { ReentrantLock() } // 2. wait a bounded time; an interrupt also ends the wait if (!lock.tryLock(maxWait.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { throw CardBusyException(cardId) // 3. busy: fail fast, the client retries } try { return action() // 4. critical section } finally { lock.unlock() // 5. always release } } } Before reading on, explain to yourself: why does tryLock sit outside the try, when unlock() is inside the finally? Answer: if tryLock returns false or throws InterruptedException, this thread doesn't hold the lock. A finally that called unlock() would throw IllegalMonitorStateException and hide the real result. Only the code that runs while you hold the lock goes inside the try. Why not synchronized (cardId)? Two Strings with the same contents are often different objects, so two requests for the same card could each lock their own string and run together. Interned strings go the other way: unrelated code that locks the same literal shares your lock (lesson 4 of this track). And synchronized has no timeout. A map of real lock objects avoids all three problems. One problem remains: the map gains a lock for every card it ever sees, and never shrinks. With millions of cards that is memory you don't get back. Removing entries safely is harder than it looks, because a thread may be about to lock the entry you remove. The usual answer is lock striping: a fixed array of locks, chosen by hash. private final ReentrantLock[] stripes = new ReentrantLock[256]; { for (int i = 0; i < stripes.length; i++) stripes[i] = new ReentrantLock(); } ReentrantLock lockFor(String cardId) { return stripes[Math.floorMod(cardId.hashCode(), stripes.length)]; // two cards may share a stripe: fine } private val stripes = Array(256) { ReentrantLock() } fun lockFor(cardId: String): ReentrantLock = stripes[Math.floorMod(cardId.hashCode(), stripes.size)] // two cards may share a stripe: fine Two cards that share a stripe now wait for each other. That costs a little throughput and nothing in correctness. If you ever hold two card locks at once, for a transfer between cards, take the stripes in index order, as in lesson 6 of this track, and skip the second lock when both cards land on the same stripe.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Lab
x: A buffer with two conditions and a cache that doesn't hang labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l07/LockBuffer.java labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l07/FxRateCache.java ./gradlew :concurrency:test --tests 'workbench.concurrency.l07.*' Run the tests. All eight fail. The five LockBuffer tests hit UnsupportedOperationException. Two FxRateCache tests time out (the upgrade hang), and the snapshot test reports mixed refreshes. Part 1: write LockBuffer with one ReentrantLock and two Conditions, notFull and notEmpty. Check the capacity in the constructor. put and take follow the shape in the second section, with signal(). Write offer(item, timeout): the same as put, but wait with notFull.awaitNanos(remaining) and return false when the time runs out. Part 2: fix FxRateCache.rate. Release the read lock, take the write lock, and re-check before calling the loader, so the loader runs once per pair. Fix snapshot so it reads every pair under one read lock. Run the tests until all eight pass, then twice more. awaitNanos returns the nanoseconds still left (zero or less when time is up). Keep the returned value and pass it to the next awaitNanos in the loop. Use lock.lockInterruptibly() at the top of put, take and offer, so an interrupted thread doesn't wait for the lock either. await() already throws InterruptedException when interrupted. The cache's HashMap is fine as it is: every access to it happens under the read or the write lock. Only the order in which you take the locks is wrong. All eight tests in ExplicitLocksTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can use ReentrantLock safely (try/finally, tryLock, lockInterruptibly), give each kind of waiter its own Condition, and use a read-write lock without the upgrade deadlock.
