h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Quiz
x: A request handler needs the ledger lock, but must answer 503 if it can't get the lock within 50 ms. Which tool fits? synchronized (ledger) ledger.lockInterruptibly() ledger.tryLock(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) A volatile boolean busy flag checked before lock() tryLock with a timeout waits at most 50 ms and returns false if the lock is still taken. lockInterruptibly waits without a limit unless someone interrupts the thread. synchronized can't time out at all. A volatile flag checked before locking is check-then-act: the lock can be taken between the check and the lock() call. Kotlin code: rw.read { if (cache[k] == null) rw.write { cache[k] = load(k) } }. Two threads ask for the same missing key. What can happen? Both hang, because a read lock can't be upgraded load(k) can run twice, because write { } releases the read lock before it takes the write lock Nothing bad: write { } upgrades atomically It throws IllegalMonitorStateException Kotlin's write releases this thread's read locks, takes the write lock, and restores the read locks after. Both threads can see null, both release, and each then loads in turn. It doesn't hang, but it isn't atomic. Re-check inside write, for example with getOrPut. From wait, notify and guarded blocks: a teammate merges notFull and notEmpty into one Condition changed, but keeps changed.signal() in both put and take. With several producers and consumers, what can happen? Nothing changes: signal() always wakes the right kind of thread Items are lost It throws, because two methods can't share one Condition Everything can stall: a signal() meant for a consumer can wake a producer, which waits again, and no one signals the consumers With one queue for both kinds of waiter, signal() may pick the wrong kind. That thread re-checks, waits again, and the signal is gone. It is the same lost wake-up that made the one-monitor buffer need notifyAll(). With one condition, use signalAll(); with two, signal() is fine. With StampedLock, you call tryOptimisticRead() and copy bid and ask into locals. What must happen before you use them? Call validate(stamp); if it returns false, read them again under readLock() Nothing: the stamp guarantees a consistent read Call unlockRead(stamp) Call tryConvertToWriteLock(stamp) An optimistic read takes no lock, so a writer can change the fields while you copy them. validate tells you whether a writer got in since the stamp. Only after it returns true are the copies known to be consistent. There is nothing to release, because nothing was locked. A dump shows 40 worker threads WAITING (parking) in ReentrantLock.lock(). Thread.print -l says the lock is owned by kafka-consumer-3, whose stack shows it idle inside poll(). What is the most likely bug? A deadlock between the workers The lock is unfair, so the workers are starving A code path in the consumer took the lock and left without unlock(), for example on an exception with no finally poll() holds the lock internally The owner isn't waiting for anything you'd expect, and it isn't in the critical section. It has moved on while still holding the lock, which happens when an exception or an early return skips the release. An unfair lock would still hand over now and then, and a deadlock needs the owner to wait for a lock too.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Key terms
x: ReentrantLock An explicit lock with the same rules as synchronized, plus tryLock, timeouts, interruptible waits, fairness and conditions. Hold count How many times the owning thread has taken a reentrant lock. It must release it as many times. Condition A wait queue tied to a lock. await() releases the lock and waits; signal() wakes one waiter. Fair lock A lock that hands over to the longest-waiting thread instead of letting new arrivals barge in. Read-write lock A pair of locks: many threads may hold the read lock together; the write lock is exclusive. Lock upgrade Going from a read lock to a write lock while still holding the read lock. ReentrantReadWriteLock hangs if you try. Optimistic read A StampedLock read that takes no lock and checks afterwards, with validate, that no writer got in. Where do lock() and unlock() go relative to try/finally? lock() on the line right before try. unlock() as the first statement of finally. In Kotlin, lock.withLock { } does both. What does lock.tryLock(50, MILLISECONDS) do when another thread holds the lock? It waits up to 50 ms. It returns true (and you hold the lock) if it got it in time, false otherwise. It throws InterruptedException if interrupted while waiting. A thread waits in lockInterruptibly() and another thread interrupts it. What happens? And for a thread waiting to enter synchronized? lockInterruptibly() gives up at once with InterruptedException. The synchronized waiter keeps waiting until it gets the monitor; it only sees its interrupt flag afterwards. Why can a bounded buffer with notFull and notEmpty conditions use signal() instead of signalAll()? Each condition has only one kind of waiter, and one change (one item in, or one slot free) lets exactly one of them proceed. A thread holding the read lock of a ReentrantReadWriteLock calls writeLock().lock(). What happens? It waits forever. The write lock waits for every reader to leave, including this thread. Release the read lock first, then re-check under the write lock. After long s = lock.tryOptimisticRead() and copying fields into locals, what must you do? Call lock.validate(s). If it returns false, a writer got in: read the fields again under lock.readLock(). In Kotlin, what does rw.write { } do when called inside rw.read { }? It releases this thread's read locks, takes the write lock, and restores the read locks afterwards. It doesn't hang, but it isn't atomic: re-check inside the block.

h: Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock · Go deeper
x: ReentrantLock, ReentrantReadWriteLock, Semaphore and CountDownLatch are all built on one class, AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS). It keeps one int of state and a queue of waiting threads. For ReentrantLock the state is the hold count; for a semaphore it is the number of permits left; for a latch it is the count. A thread that can't proceed joins the queue and parks with LockSupport.park. That is why it shows as WAITING in a dump, with a line like parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync). A release unparks the next thread in the queue. In non-fair mode, the default, a thread that arrives just as the lock is released can take it before the queued thread wakes. That is barging, and it is why the two-condition buffer in the second Try it still wasted some wake-ups. It is also why non-fair locks have much higher throughput: waking a parked thread takes microseconds, and a running thread can take and release the lock many times in that gap. Fair mode closes the gap and pays the wake-up cost on every hand-off. Even on a fair lock, the untimed tryLock() barges: its Javadoc says it does not honor the fairness setting. ReentrantReadWriteLock splits its 32-bit state into two 16-bit halves, one for read holds and one for write holds. That is why its Javadoc caps it at 65,535 recursive write locks and 65,535 read locks. StampedLock also has tryConvertToWriteLock(stamp), which upgrades a read or optimistic stamp to a write stamp if no other thread is in the way, and returns 0 if it can't. It is the only upgrade in the JDK's locks, and it can fail, so you still need the fallback path. If you ever build your own synchronizer, subclass AQS and implement tryAcquire and tryRelease; its Javadoc has a small Mutex example. First check java.util.concurrent for one that already exists. Lesson 10 of this track covers the common ones.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · An atomic variable does read-modify-write in one step
x: Lesson 3 of this track promised to show how AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() fixes count++. Start with what you get: Java private final AtomicLong authorized = new AtomicLong(); // no lock needed void onApproved(long cents) { authorized.addAndGet(cents); // read, add, write: one indivisible step } long total() { return authorized.get(); // a volatile read: sees the latest value } Kotlin private val authorized = AtomicLong() // no lock needed fun onApproved(cents: Long) { authorized.addAndGet(cents) // read, add, write: one indivisible step } fun total(): Long = authorized.get() // a volatile read: sees the latest value An atomic variable holds one value and offers read-modify-write operations that no other thread can split. addAndGet reads, adds and writes as one step. Its get() and set() behave like reads and writes of a volatile field, so every thread sees the latest value. The method names tell you what comes back. incrementAndGet() returns the new value and getAndIncrement() the old one. The same pairs exist for add, update and accumulate. AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean and AtomicReference cover most needs, and AtomicIntegerArray and AtomicLongArray give you arrays of them. How does a library turn three steps into one without a lock? The CPU has instructions for it. On x86, HotSpot compiles getAndAdd to a single lock xadd instruction and compareAndSet to lock cmpxchg, and ARM64 has its own equivalents. While the instruction runs, the core keeps the variable's cache line to itself, so no other core can get in between the read and the write. No thread ever waits for another. If the scheduler pauses a thread, it is never in the middle of an atomic update: the instruction either happened or it didn't. So some thread always makes progress, which is what lock-free means. Compare that with a lock: a thread that is paused while holding it stops every thread that needs it. Atomics have one hard limit. Each one protects exactly one variable. Two atomics are not atomic together, and neither are two calls on the same atomic, as the warm-up showed. Predict from the mechanism. The operating system pauses thread A for 50 ms. With an AtomicLong, what do the other request threads do during those 50 ms? And with a lock that A held at that moment? (With the atomic, they keep updating: A was paused before or after its instruction, never inside it. With the lock, every thread that needs it waits the full 50 ms.) Compare-and-set is a git push that only succeeds if the remote is still at the commit you started from. If a teammate pushed first, yours is rejected; you pull, rebase your change onto theirs, and push again. Nobody locks the repository, and nobody's commit is lost. ABA is the remote going from commit X to Y and then being force-pushed back to X: your check passes, though history changed underneath you. A version stamp on the branch fixes that. The analogy breaks on cost: a rejected push costs you minutes, while a failed CAS costs nanoseconds, so a thread just tries again at once.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Compare-and-set is the primitive, and the loop is the pattern
x: Almost every atomic operation is built on compare-and-set (CAS). compareAndSet(expected, next) does this as one step: if the current value equals expected, store next and return true; otherwise change nothing and return false. That is enough to build any read-modify-write, with a loop. Here is the lab's max tracker: Java long prev; do { prev = max.get(); // 1. read if (amount <= prev) return; // 2. decide: nothing to do } while (!max.compareAndSet(prev, amount)); // 3. write only if max is still prev; else retry Kotlin var prev: Long do { prev = max.get() // 1. read if (amount <= prev) return // 2. decide: nothing to do } while (!max.compareAndSet(prev, amount)) // 3. write only if max is still prev; else retry Read the value. Decide what the new value should be. Then store it, but only if nobody changed the value since you read it. If someone did, your decision was based on old data, so throw it away and start again. The figure shows two threads that both read 41. T1's CAS wins. T2's fails, so T2 reads 42 and writes 43. Nothing is lost. Compare that with the broken tracker in the lab, if (amount > max) max = amount on a volatile field. It reads, decides, and then writes blindly, whatever happened in between. CAS turns the blind write into a conditional one. A failed CAS costs a retry, not a wait. With little contention, retries are rare. With many threads hammering one variable, threads keep failing and re-reading, and the variable's cache line bounces from core to core. The section on LongAdder deals with that cost. Watch CAS fail and retry Read CasRetries. Its increment() is a hand-written CAS loop that counts its own failures. Predict the failure count for 1 thread, then for 8 threads. Run it twice. Check that counter is always exact. CasRetries.java package workbench.concurrency.l08; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** A hand-written compare-and-set increment. Count how often the CAS fails as threads are added. */ public class CasRetries { static final AtomicLong counter = new AtomicLong(); // returns how many times compareAndSet failed before it worked static long increment() { long failures = 0; while (true) { long seen = counter.get(); // 1. read if (counter.compareAndSet(seen, seen + 1)) { // 2. write only if still `seen` return failures; } failures++; // 3. someone else won: retry } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int perThread = 1_000_000; for (int threads : new int[] {1, 2, 4, 8}) { counter.set(0); AtomicLong failed = new AtomicLong(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); // start them all together List<Thread> ts = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++) { ts.add(new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } long mine = 0; for (int n = 0; n < perThread; n++) mine += increment(); failed.addAndGet(mine); })); } for (Thread t : ts) t.start(); go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); System.out.printf("threads: %d counter: %,10d failed CAS: %,10d (%.2f per increment)%n", threads, counter.get(), failed.get(), failed.get() / (double) counter.get()); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.CasRetries labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l08/CasRetries.java CasRetries.kt package workbench.concurrency.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A hand-written compare-and-set increment. Count how often the CAS fails as threads are added. private val counter = AtomicLong() // returns how many times compareAndSet failed before it worked private fun increment(): Long { var failures = 0L while (true) { val seen = counter.get() // 1. read if (counter.compareAndSet(seen, seen + 1)) { // 2. write only if still `seen` return failures } failures++ // 3. someone else won: retry } } fun main() { val perThread = 1_000_000 for (threads in listOf(1, 2, 4, 8)) { counter.set(0) val failed = AtomicLong() val go = CountDownLatch(1) // start them all together val ts = List(threads) { thread { go.await() var mine = 0L repeat(perThread) { mine += increment() } failed.addAndGet(mine) } } go.countDown() ts.forEach { it.join() } println("threads: %d counter: %,10d failed CAS: %,10d (%.2f per increment)" .format(threads, counter.get(), failed.get(), failed.get() / counter.get().toDouble())) } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.CasRetriesKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l08/CasRetries.kt One thread never fails: nobody else changes the value. With more threads, failures climb into the tens of thousands or millions, and the number changes a lot from run to run. The counter is exact every time. Failures stay below one per increment here, because a core tends to get a run of increments done before another core takes the cache line away. Both threads read 41. Only one CAS can succeed. The loser reads the new value and tries again, so no update is lost. In a Kafka consumer with 12 partitions on 12 threads, a records-processed counter is a LongAdder, and the highest offset seen for a lag gauge is an AtomicLong with accumulateAndGet(offset, Math::max). A circuit breaker around the 120 ms card-issuer API keeps its state in an AtomicReference to an immutable record, as in the last section. A "close once" guard is closed.compareAndSet(false, true) on an AtomicBoolean. The spend limit in the worked example is correct inside one JVM. Across several pods it belongs in the database, and the shape is the same: UPDATE card SET spent = spent + ? WHERE id = ? AND spent + ? <= daily_limit, then check that one row changed. That is a compare-and-set in SQL.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · The update methods write the loop for you, and may run your function twice
x: You rarely need to write the loop yourself. updateAndGet(f) and accumulateAndGet(x, f) contain it: Java max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max); // the same loop, written for you balance.updateAndGet(b -> b + 100); // any pure function of the old value Kotlin max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max) // the same loop, written for you balance.updateAndGet { b -> b + 100 } // any pure function of the old value Inside, they read the value, call your function, and CAS. When the CAS fails, they call your function again with the new value. So your function can run more than once for one update, and some of its results are thrown away. That means the function must be a pure function of its input. No logging, no counters, no calls to other services, no reads of other shared state that might change. updateAndGet(b -> { audit.log(b); return b - cents; }) can log balances that the account never had. Do side effects after the call returns, using the value it returned. The get variants, getAndUpdate and getAndAccumulate, return the value from before the update. Use them when the caller needs to know whether its own update applied. The worked example uses exactly that to build a spend limit. Count the calls Read UpdateTwice. Four threads make 250,000 deposits each with updateAndGet, and the function counts how often it runs. Predict: will the function run exactly 1,000,000 times? Run it two or three times. UpdateTwice.java package workbench.concurrency.l08; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** updateAndGet retries your function when it loses a race. Count how often the function really runs. */ public class UpdateTwice { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { AtomicLong balance = new AtomicLong(); LongAdder calls = new LongAdder(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Runnable deposits = () -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 250_000; i++) { balance.updateAndGet(b -> { calls.increment(); // a side effect: imagine this sent a notification return b + 1; }); } }; Thread[] ts = {new Thread(deposits), new Thread(deposits), new Thread(deposits), new Thread(deposits)}; for (Thread t : ts) t.start(); go.countDown(); // all four start together for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); System.out.printf("updates: %,d times the function ran: %,d%n", balance.get(), calls.sum()); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.UpdateTwice labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l08/UpdateTwice.java UpdateTwice.kt package workbench.concurrency.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import kotlin.concurrent.thread // updateAndGet retries your function when it loses a race. Count how often the function really runs. fun main() { val balance = AtomicLong() val calls = LongAdder() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val ts = List(4) { thread { go.await() repeat(250_000) { balance.updateAndGet { b -> calls.increment() // a side effect: imagine this sent a notification b + 1 } } } } go.countDown() // all four start together ts.forEach { it.join() } println("updates: %,d times the function ran: %,d".format(balance.get(), calls.sum())) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.UpdateTwiceKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l08/UpdateTwice.kt The balance is exactly 1,000,000 every time. The function runs more often than that, a few percent more in runs here (for example 1,026,201 times). Each extra call is a lost CAS race whose result was thrown away. If that function had sent a notification, customers would have received tens of thousands of duplicates.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · LongAdder for hot counters, AtomicLong for decisions
x: A single AtomicLong that sixteen threads increment is one cache line that every core wants at the same moment. Each increment has to pull the line over to its core, and the cores spend their time passing it around. LongAdder (JDK 8) spreads the count over several cells. When threads collide, it moves them to different cells, so they mostly write to different cache lines. sum() adds the base value and all the cells together. Java private final LongAdder declines = new LongAdder(); void onDecline() { declines.increment(); } // threads mostly hit different cells long declinesSoFar() { return declines.sum(); } // adds the cells up: not a snapshot Kotlin private val declines = LongAdder() fun onDecline() = declines.increment() // threads mostly hit different cells fun declinesSoFar(): Long = declines.sum() // adds the cells up: not a snapshot The price is in sum(). It reads the cells one by one while other threads keep adding, and its Javadoc says plainly that the result is not an atomic snapshot: increments that happen during the sum might not be counted. The adder also uses more memory than one long. That gives a clean rule. Use LongAdder for statistics that many threads update and someone reads now and then: requests served, declines, records consumed. Use AtomicLong when the value drives a decision, such as a spend limit, a sequence number or a rate limit. There you need the exact current value and a compare-and-set against it, and LongAdder has neither. LongAccumulator does the same trick for any associative function, such as max, with the same caveat on reads. Race an AtomicLong against a LongAdder Read AdderVsAtomic: 8 threads each count 2,000,000 events, first on one AtomicLong, then on a LongAdder. Predict which is faster, and by roughly how much. Run it. Then change the thread count in time to 1 and run it again. AdderVsAtomic.java package workbench.concurrency.l08; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** 8 threads each count 2,000,000 events: once on one AtomicLong, once on a LongAdder. */ public class AdderVsAtomic { static long time(Runnable perThreadWork) throws InterruptedException { Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) ts[i] = new Thread(perThreadWork); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (Thread t : ts) t.start(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int n = 2_000_000; for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong(); LongAdder adder = new LongAdder(); long a = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) atomic.incrementAndGet(); }); long b = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adder.increment(); }); System.out.printf("round %d: AtomicLong %,d in %4d ms LongAdder %,d in %4d ms%n", round, atomic.get(), a, adder.sum(), b); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.AdderVsAtomic labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l08/AdderVsAtomic.java AdderVsAtomic.kt package workbench.concurrency.l08 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import kotlin.concurrent.thread // 8 threads each count 2,000,000 events: once on one AtomicLong, once on a LongAdder. private fun time(perThreadWork: () -> Unit): Long { val t0 = System.nanoTime() List(8) { thread { perThreadWork() } }.forEach { it.join() } return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 } fun main() { val n = 2_000_000 for (round in 1..3) { val atomic = AtomicLong() val adder = LongAdder() val a = time { repeat(n) { atomic.incrementAndGet() } } val b = time { repeat(n) { adder.increment() } } println("round %d: AtomicLong %,d in %4d ms LongAdder %,d in %4d ms".format(round, atomic.get(), a, adder.sum(), b)) } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.AdderVsAtomicKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l08/AdderVsAtomic.kt Both totals are exactly 16,000,000. With 8 threads, the LongAdder was 4 to 10 times faster in runs here (for example 400 ms against 66 ms). With 1 thread the gap shrinks or disappears, because there is no contention for the adder to avoid. LongAdder.java at jdk-25-ga (when to prefer it over AtomicLong) read

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · AtomicReference swaps a whole object at once
x: AtomicReference<V> does compare-and-set on a reference. Combine it with an immutable object and you can change several fields as one step: build a new object from the old one, then swap the reference. Java record Breaker(State state, int failures, Instant openedAt) {} // immutable private final AtomicReference<Breaker> breaker = new AtomicReference<>(new Breaker(State.CLOSED, 0, null)); void onFailure(Instant now) { breaker.updateAndGet(b -> b.failures() + 1 >= 5 ? new Breaker(State.OPEN, b.failures() + 1, now) // trip : new Breaker(b.state(), b.failures() + 1, b.openedAt())); } Kotlin data class Breaker(val state: State, val failures: Int, val openedAt: Instant?) // immutable private val breaker = AtomicReference(Breaker(State.CLOSED, 0, null)) fun onFailure(now: Instant) { breaker.updateAndGet { b -> if (b.failures + 1 >= 5) Breaker(State.OPEN, b.failures + 1, now) // trip else b.copy(failures = b.failures + 1) } } The CAS compares references with ==, not equals. That is what you want here, because every update builds a new object. The lab's Treiber stack uses the same idea on a linked list. A node never changes after it is built. To push, build a node that points at the current head, then CAS the head from that old head to the new node: Java void push(T item) { Node<T> top, node; do { top = head.get(); node = new Node<>(item, top); // build the new node off to the side } while (!head.compareAndSet(top, node)); // publish it only if head is still top } Kotlin fun push(item: T) { var top: Node<T>? var node: Node<T> do { top = head.get() node = Node(item, top) // build the new node off to the side } while (!head.compareAndSet(top, node)) // publish it only if head is still top } CAS has one blind spot, called ABA. It checks that the value is the same as when you read it, not that it never changed. If the head goes from node A to B and back to A while your thread is paused, your CAS succeeds, although the list behind A is now different. In Java, ABA needs reuse: a node pool, recycled objects, array indices or plain numbers. With freshly allocated nodes, the garbage collector never reuses A's memory while your thread still holds a reference to A, so the lab's stack is safe. When you do recycle, AtomicStampedReference pairs the reference with an int stamp that you bump on every change, so A with stamp 0 and A with stamp 3 no longer match. Play out ABA by hand Read AbaDemo. It plays two threads on one thread, step by step, so the bad interleaving happens every time. Nodes are recycled. Before you run it, predict the stack after T1's compareAndSet. Run it and compare the plain AtomicReference with the AtomicStampedReference. AbaDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l08; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference; /** * The ABA problem, played out by hand on one thread so it happens every time. * Nodes are recycled (mutable next), as in a pooled or off-heap structure. */ public class AbaDemo { static final class Node { final String name; Node next; Node(String name, Node next) { this.name = name; this.next = next; } } static String show(Node n) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (; n != null; n = n.next) sb.append(n.name).append(n.next != null ? " -> " : ""); return sb.length() == 0 ? "(empty)" : sb.toString(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Node c = new Node("C", null), b = new Node("B", c), a = new Node("A", b); AtomicReference<Node> head = new AtomicReference<>(a); System.out.println("start: " + show(head.get())); Node top = head.get(), next = top.next; // T1 starts a pop... System.out.println("T1 reads top=A, next=B, then is paused"); head.set(b); // T2 pops A head.set(c); // T2 pops B (B is now T2's) a.next = head.get(); head.set(a); // T2 pushes the recycled A System.out.println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: " + show(head.get())); boolean ok = head.compareAndSet(top, next); // T1 resumes: head is A again System.out.println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B) = " + ok); System.out.println("stack now: " + show(head.get()) + " (B was popped by T2: corrupted)"); System.out.println(); a.next = b; b.next = c; AtomicStampedReference<Node> stamped = new AtomicStampedReference<>(a, 0); int[] stampHolder = new int[1]; Node top2 = stamped.get(stampHolder); // T1 reads the node AND the stamp int stamp = stampHolder[0]; Node next2 = top2.next; System.out.println("T1 reads top=A, stamp=" + stamp + ", next=B, then is paused"); stamped.set(b, 1); // every change bumps the stamp stamped.set(c, 2); a.next = c; stamped.set(a, 3); System.out.println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: stamp is now " + stamped.getStamp()); boolean ok2 = stamped.compareAndSet(top2, next2, stamp, stamp + 1); System.out.println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B, stamp " + stamp + ") = " + ok2 + ", so T1 re-reads and retries"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.AbaDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l08/AbaDemo.java AbaDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l08 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference // The ABA problem, played out by hand on one thread so it happens every time. // Nodes are recycled (mutable next), as in a pooled or off-heap structure. private class AbaNode(val name: String, var next: AbaNode?) private fun show(start: AbaNode?): String = generateSequence(start) { it.next }.joinToString(" -> ") { it.name }.ifEmpty { "(empty)" } fun main() { val c = AbaNode("C", null) val b = AbaNode("B", c) val a = AbaNode("A", b) val head = AtomicReference(a) println("start: ${show(head.get())}") val top = head.get() val next = top.next // T1 starts a pop... println("T1 reads top=A, next=B, then is paused") head.set(b) // T2 pops A head.set(c) // T2 pops B (B is now T2's) a.next = head.get() head.set(a) // T2 pushes the recycled A println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: ${show(head.get())}") val ok = head.compareAndSet(top, next) // T1 resumes: head is A again println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B) = $ok") println("stack now: ${show(head.get())} (B was popped by T2: corrupted)") println() a.next = b; b.next = c val stamped = AtomicStampedReference(a, 0) val stampHolder = IntArray(1) val top2 = stamped.get(stampHolder) // T1 reads the node AND the stamp val stamp = stampHolder[0] val next2 = top2.next println("T1 reads top=A, stamp=$stamp, next=B, then is paused") stamped.set(b, 1) // every change bumps the stamp stamped.set(c, 2) a.next = c stamped.set(a, 3) println("T2 pops A, pops B, pushes A again: stamp is now ${stamped.stamp}") val ok2 = stamped.compareAndSet(top2, next2, stamp, stamp + 1) println("T1 resumes: compareAndSet(A, B, stamp $stamp) = $ok2, so T1 re-reads and retries") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l08.AbaDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l08/AbaDemo.kt With the plain reference, T1's compareAndSet(A, B) returns true and the stack becomes B -> C, although T2 had already popped B: the stack is corrupted. With the stamp, the same CAS returns false, because the stamp moved from 0 to 3, so T1 re-reads and retries. The most common mistake is building check-then-act out of atomic calls: if (counter.get() < limit) counter.incrementAndGet(). Each call is atomic and the pair is not, which is lesson 3's bug one level down. The second form is two atomics that must change together, such as count and totalCents for an average: a reader can see the new count with the old total. People make these mistakes because "I used AtomicLong" feels like "this is thread-safe". The fix is one compare-and-set that includes the check (a CAS loop, updateAndGet or getAndUpdate), and for several fields, one AtomicReference to an immutable record, or a lock.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Java and Kotlin
x: A max tracker with Java's atomics and Kotlin's Java (java.util.concurrent.atomic) class MaxTracker { private final AtomicLong max = new AtomicLong(Long.MIN_VALUE); void offer(long amount) { max.accumulateAndGet(amount, Math::max); // CAS loop inside } long max() { return max.get(); } } Kotlin (kotlin.concurrent.atomics) @OptIn(ExperimentalAtomicApi::class) class MaxTracker { private val max = AtomicLong(Long.MIN_VALUE) // kotlin.concurrent.atomics, not java.util fun offer(amount: Long) { max.update { prev -> maxOf(prev, amount) } // a CAS loop inside, like updateAndGet } fun max(): Long = max.load() } On the JVM most Kotlin code simply uses java.util.concurrent.atomic, and everything in this lesson works the same. Kotlin 2.1 added its own atomics in kotlin.concurrent.atomics, mainly for multiplatform code. The names differ (load, fetchAndAdd, update) and, as of Kotlin 2.4, they still need @OptIn(ExperimentalAtomicApi::class). The behavior is the same compare-and-set underneath. One thing does not change between the languages: @Volatile var count = 0 followed by count++ compiles happily in Kotlin and loses updates exactly like the Java version.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Worked example
x: A daily spend limit without a lock A card has a daily limit. tryAuthorize must approve only if the new total stays within it, and many request threads call it. Here is a first attempt with an AtomicLong. Look for the race before reading on. private final AtomicLong spent = new AtomicLong(); boolean tryAuthorize(long cents) { if (spent.get() + cents <= limit) { // check spent.addAndGet(cents); // act return true; } return false; } private val spent = AtomicLong() fun tryAuthorize(cents: Long): Boolean { if (spent.get() + cents <= limit) { // check spent.addAndGet(cents) // act return true } return false } Each call on spent is atomic. The pair is not: with 90 of 100 spent, two threads can both pass the check for 10 and both add, ending at 110. Making the variable atomic did not make the logic atomic. The check has to happen inside the compare-and-set. The CAS loop does the check on the value it is about to replace. If another thread changes spent in between, the CAS fails and the loop decides again on fresh data. boolean tryAuthorize(long cents) { while (true) { long before = spent.get(); // 1. read the current spend if (before + cents > limit) return false; // 2. decide on that value if (spent.compareAndSet(before, before + cents)) return true; // 3. commit, if unchanged } // 4. lost the race: re-read, decide again } fun tryAuthorize(cents: Long): Boolean { while (true) { val before = spent.get() // 1. read the current spend if (before + cents > limit) return false // 2. decide on that value if (spent.compareAndSet(before, before + cents)) return true // 3. commit, if unchanged } // 4. lost the race: re-read, decide again } The same thing with getAndUpdate. The function is pure: it looks only at s. Before reading the next step, explain to yourself why the second line compares before + cents with the limit, instead of checking whether the value changed. boolean tryAuthorize(long cents) { long before = spent.getAndUpdate(s -> s + cents <= limit ? s + cents : s); return before + cents <= limit; // did OUR update apply? } fun tryAuthorize(cents: Long): Boolean { val before = spent.getAndUpdate { s -> if (s + cents <= limit) s + cents else s } return before + cents <= limit // did OUR update apply? } getAndUpdate returns the value that its final, successful call of the function saw. If that value plus cents fits the limit, the function added cents, so this caller is approved. If it didn't fit, the function returned s unchanged and nothing was spent. Checking whether the value changed tells you nothing, because other threads change it all the time. And this is why LongAdder is the wrong tool for a limit: it has no compare-and-set, and its sum() isn't exact while others add.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Quiz
x: Sixteen Kafka consumer threads count processed records. A metrics scraper reads the count once a minute. Which is the best fit? A volatile long with count++ A synchronized increment method An AtomicLong with incrementAndGet() A LongAdder with increment() and sum() Many writers and a rare, approximate read is exactly what LongAdder is for: threads mostly update different cells, so they don't fight over one cache line. AtomicLong is correct but slower under this contention. synchronized is correct and slower still. volatile with ++ loses updates. What does this print? Java AtomicInteger n = new AtomicInteger(5); int a = n.getAndIncrement(); int b = n.incrementAndGet(); System.out.println(a + " " + b + " " + n.get()); Kotlin val n = AtomicInteger(5) val a = n.getAndIncrement() val b = n.incrementAndGet() println("$a $b ${n.get()}") 5 7 7 6 7 7 5 6 7 6 6 6 getAndIncrement returns the old value (5) and leaves 6. incrementAndGet makes it 7 and returns the new value (7). The final get() is 7. The name says the order: get then increment, or increment then get. balance.updateAndGet(b -> { audit.log("balance " + b); return b - cents; }) runs on many threads. What can go wrong? Nothing: updateAndGet runs the function exactly once per call The balance can lose a debit The audit log can contain balances that never became the real balance, because the function reruns when its CAS fails It throws IllegalStateException on contention On a failed CAS, updateAndGet calls the function again with the fresh value. Each failed attempt still ran audit.log. The balance itself is correct. Keep the function pure and log the returned value after the call. From synchronized and intrinsic locks: a class keeps count and totalCents for an average, and both must always change together. Which is a correct choice? Two AtomicLong fields, each updated with addAndGet One AtomicReference to an immutable record holding both values, or a synchronized method that updates both Two volatile long fields Two LongAdder fields Each atomic protects one variable. With two of them, a reader can see the new count with the old total. One lock around both updates, or one CAS on a reference to an immutable pair, makes the two fields change as one step. When is ABA a real risk for a compare-and-set in Java? On every AtomicReference CAS, even with freshly allocated nodes Only on ARM processors Never: the JVM prevents it When the same value can come back after changes: recycled nodes, object pools, array indices, plain counters CAS only checks that the value equals what you read. That is fooled only if the value can return to an earlier one. With new nodes, the garbage collector won't reuse a node's memory while any thread still references it, so it can't come back. Pools, indices and numbers can, and AtomicStampedReference adds a version to catch it.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Key terms
x: Atomic variable A variable whose read-modify-write operations happen as one indivisible step. Compare-and-set (CAS) Write a new value only if the current value is still the one you expected; report whether it worked. CAS loop Read, compute, try CAS, and start over if another thread changed the value first. Lock-free Some thread always makes progress, even if others are paused, because nobody holds a lock. Contention Many threads trying to update the same thing at the same moment. LongAdder A counter spread over several cells so threads rarely collide; its sum is not a snapshot. ABA problem A CAS that succeeds because a value changed and then changed back. What does ref.compareAndSet(expected, next) do? As one indivisible step: if the current value equals expected, it stores next and returns true. Otherwise it changes nothing and returns false. incrementAndGet() vs getAndIncrement(): what does each return? incrementAndGet() returns the new value. getAndIncrement() returns the old value. Both add one atomically. Why must the function passed to updateAndGet have no side effects? When its compare-and-set loses a race, updateAndGet calls the function again with the new value. It can run several times for one update. Hot counter, read rarely: AtomicLong or LongAdder? LongAdder: threads update separate cells, so there is far less contention. Use AtomicLong when the exact value drives a decision. Is LongAdder.sum() an exact snapshot while other threads add? No. It reads the cells one at a time, so increments made during the sum may be missed. What is the ABA problem? A CAS succeeds because the value is back to what you read (A to B to A), though it changed in between. Fix it with a version stamp: AtomicStampedReference. if (n.get() < limit) n.incrementAndGet(); on an AtomicInteger: safe? No. Two atomic calls with a gap between them is check-then-act. Do the check inside a CAS loop or updateAndGet.

h: Atomics and compare-and-set · Go deeper
x: An AtomicLong is a separate object. If you have a million Account objects that each need an atomic counter, that's a million extra objects, each with its own header. The JDK's own classes avoid this by putting a volatile long field in the class and doing CAS on the field in place. Two tools do that. AtomicLongFieldUpdater (and its Integer and Reference siblings) is the older one. VarHandle, since JDK 9, is the general one: Java private volatile long spent; private static final VarHandle SPENT; static { try { SPENT = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(Account.class, "spent", long.class); } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); } } boolean add(long expected, long next) { return SPENT.compareAndSet(this, expected, next); // CAS on this object's field } Kotlin class Account { @Volatile private var spent = 0L fun add(expected: Long, next: Long): Boolean = SPENT.compareAndSet(this, expected, next) // CAS on this object's field companion object { private val SPENT: VarHandle = MethodHandles.privateLookupIn(Account::class.java, MethodHandles.lookup()) .findVarHandle(Account::class.java, "spent", Long::class.java) } } VarHandle also offers weaker memory orderings (getAcquire, setRelease, plain and opaque access), which the memory model track covers in its last lesson. Two more details. The weakCompareAndSet family may fail even when the value matches. Inside a retry loop that doesn't matter, and on some ARM processors it can be cheaper. And a CAS loop is lock-free but not wait-free: one unlucky thread could, in theory, lose every race forever while others succeed. In practice that almost never happens, but it is why a hot CAS loop under extreme contention can be slower than a lock, which queues threads instead of letting them all retry at once. LongAdder exists because of exactly that case.

h: Concurrent collections · ConcurrentHashMap is atomic per key, not per map
x: totals.put(m, totals.get(m) + cents) on a ConcurrentHashMap loses money under load. Both calls are thread-safe, and the pair is still a read-modify-write race, like count++ in lesson 3 of this track. To see why one call is safe and two are not, look at how the map locks. ConcurrentHashMap is the map to use when threads share one. Reads never lock. A write locks only the bin that its key hashes to (one slot of the map's internal array, shared by every key whose hash lands there), so writes to different keys mostly run in parallel. A write into an empty bin doesn't lock at all: it uses compare-and-set, as in the previous lesson. Every single-key call is atomic, because a write does its whole job inside one bin lock or one CAS. Two calls in a row are two separate steps, and another thread's write can land between them. So the map offers methods that do a whole read-modify-write on one key in one call: putIfAbsent(k, v) inserts only if the key is missing. computeIfAbsent(k, f) computes and inserts only if missing, and runs f at most once. compute(k, f) and computeIfPresent(k, f) replace the value with f of the old one. merge(k, v, f) inserts v, or replaces the old value with f(old, v). replace(k, expected, next) is a compare-and-set on one key. The Javadoc of each compute method says "The entire method invocation is performed atomically." That sentence is the reason to use them: Java ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> settledCents = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); void onSettled(String merchant, long cents) { settledCents.merge(merchant, cents, Long::sum); // insert or add, atomically for this key } String issuerFor(String bin) { return issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, directory::lookup); // lookup runs at most once per BIN } Kotlin val settledCents = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long>() fun onSettled(merchant: String, cents: Long) { settledCents.merge(merchant, cents, Long::plus) // insert or add, atomically for this key } fun issuerFor(bin: String): String = issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, directory::lookup) // lookup runs at most once per BIN The figure shows why this scales. Two threads that update keys in different bins never meet. Two threads that update the same key take turns, which is exactly what you want. Two more rules. ConcurrentHashMap rejects null keys and values with NullPointerException. That is on purpose: when get(k) returns null, it always means "absent", so you never need a second call to tell "missing" from "mapped to null" (and a second call would be check-then-act). And Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()) is no substitute. It has one lock for the whole map, and the same gap between calls. Three maps, one count Read MapShootout. Eight threads record 800,000 payments across 1,000 merchants: on a HashMap with merge, on a ConcurrentHashMap with get-then-put, and on a ConcurrentHashMap with merge. Predict the total for each. Run it twice. MapShootout.java package workbench.concurrency.l09; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** 8 threads count 800,000 payments over 1,000 merchants, three ways. Only one way is right. */ public class MapShootout { static void run(String label, Map<String, Integer> counts, Consumer<String> countOne) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; String[] error = new String[1]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); for (int n = 0; n < 100_000; n++) countOne.accept("m-" + (n % 1_000)); } catch (Throwable e) { error[0] = e.getClass().getSimpleName(); } }); ts[i].setDaemon(true); // a corrupted HashMap can even loop forever ts[i].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(5_000); long total = 0; try { for (int v : counts.values()) total += v; } catch (Throwable e) { error[0] = e.getClass().getSimpleName(); } System.out.printf("%-32s total %,9d of 800,000 keys %,5d of 1,000%s%n", label, total, counts.size(), error[0] == null ? "" : " threw " + error[0]); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Map<String, Integer> plain = new HashMap<>(); run("HashMap.merge", plain, k -> plain.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)); Map<String, Integer> chm1 = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); run("ConcurrentHashMap get then put", chm1, k -> chm1.put(k, chm1.getOrDefault(k, 0) + 1)); Map<String, Integer> chm2 = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); run("ConcurrentHashMap.merge", chm2, k -> chm2.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.MapShootout labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l09/MapShootout.java MapShootout.kt package workbench.concurrency.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import kotlin.concurrent.thread // 8 threads count 800,000 payments over 1,000 merchants, three ways. h: Concurrent collections · Keep the function short, and never touch the map from inside it
x: The function you pass to compute, merge or computeIfAbsent runs while the map holds the lock for that key's bin. Three things follow from that. First, other writes to the same bin wait for your whole function. The Javadoc says so: "Some attempted update operations on this map by other threads may be blocked while computation is in progress, so the computation should be short and simple." An 80 ms call to the issuer directory inside computeIfAbsent makes every write that lands in that bin wait 80 ms. Reads are not blocked. For a cache that loads each key once, that is often fine. When it isn't, the worked example shows how to keep the slow work outside the map. Second, the function must not change the map. The Javadoc is blunt again: "The mapping function must not modify this map during computation." Memoized recursion is how people break this rule without noticing: Java long fib(int n) { if (n < 2) return n; return memo.computeIfAbsent(n, k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2)); // calls computeIfAbsent again, inside } Kotlin fun fib(n: Int): Long { if (n < 2) return n.toLong() return memo.computeIfAbsent(n) { k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2) } // calls computeIfAbsent again, inside } On JDK 21, ConcurrentHashMap throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update here, and HashMap throws ConcurrentModificationException. The JDK only catches some of these cases, so don't count on an exception. Compute the value outside the map, or build the table bottom-up. Third, if the function throws, nothing is stored and the exception reaches the caller, so the next call tries again. If it returns null, nothing is stored either. The lab relies on that. Break the rule on purpose Run RecursiveUpdate. It computes fib(30) with memoized recursion on a ConcurrentHashMap, then on a HashMap, then bottom-up. Read the exception messages. Which map tells you what you did wrong? RecursiveUpdate.java package workbench.concurrency.l09; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; /** Memoized Fibonacci where the mapping function calls back into the same map. The Javadoc forbids it. */ public class RecursiveUpdate { static Map<Integer, Long> memo; static long fib(int n) { if (n < 2) return n; return memo.computeIfAbsent(n, k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2)); // modifies the map from inside compute } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Map<Integer, Long> m : List.<Map<Integer, Long>>of(new ConcurrentHashMap<>(), new HashMap<>())) { memo = m; try { System.out.println(m.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": fib(30) = " + fib(30)); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(m.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": threw " + e); } } // the fix: build the table bottom-up, outside any compute call Map<Integer, Long> table = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(Map.of(0, 0L, 1, 1L)); for (int n = 2; n <= 30; n++) table.put(n, table.get(n - 1) + table.get(n - 2)); System.out.println("bottom-up: fib(30) = " + table.get(30)); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.RecursiveUpdate labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l09/RecursiveUpdate.java RecursiveUpdate.kt package workbench.concurrency.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap // Memoized Fibonacci where the mapping function calls back into the same map. The Javadoc forbids it. private lateinit var memo: MutableMap<Int, Long> private fun fib(n: Int): Long { if (n < 2) return n.toLong() return memo.computeIfAbsent(n) { k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2) } // modifies the map from inside compute } fun main() { for (m in listOf<MutableMap<Int, Long>>(ConcurrentHashMap(), HashMap())) { memo = m try { println("${m.javaClass.simpleName}: fib(30) = ${fib(30)}") } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println("${m.javaClass.simpleName}: threw $e") } } // the fix: build the table bottom-up, outside any compute call val table = ConcurrentHashMap(mapOf(0 to 0L, 1 to 1L)) for (n in 2..30) table[n] = table.getValue(n - 1) + table.getValue(n - 2) println("bottom-up: fib(30) = ${table[30]}") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.RecursiveUpdateKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l09/RecursiveUpdate.kt ConcurrentHashMap: threw java.lang.IllegalStateException: Recursive update, HashMap: threw java.util.ConcurrentModificationException, and bottom-up: fib(30) = 832040. Only the version that fills the table outside any compute call works. Most of these show up in a payment service within a week. A BIN or tenant-config cache is a ConcurrentHashMap with computeIfAbsent. Per-merchant totals for a settlement report are merge(merchant, cents, Long::sum), or computeIfAbsent(merchant, m -> new LongAdder()).increment() when the keys are hot. Webhook or fraud-rule listeners that change only at deploy time live in a CopyOnWriteArrayList. And the outbox relay that moves ledger entries from request threads to a single Kafka-producing thread is a BlockingQueue. Give it a capacity, and decide what a full queue means: block the producer, answer 503, or pause() the Kafka consumer that feeds it.

h: Concurrent collections · Weak iterators, estimated sizes, and what ConcurrentModificationException means
x: ConcurrentModificationException sounds like "two threads touched my collection". It means something narrower: this collection's own iterator noticed that the collection changed in a way the iterator didn't make. ArrayList and HashMap iterators are fail-fast. They keep a count of changes and check it on every next(). One thread is enough to trip it, as the warm-up showed. And the check is best effort: when two threads race, it may not fire at all, and you get lost entries or a damaged structure instead. Never treat the exception as a race detector. The concurrent collections have weakly consistent iterators. They never throw ConcurrentModificationException, and they reflect the collection at some point at or after the moment the iterator was created. A change made during the loop may or may not show up. The same goes for size(), isEmpty() and containsValue() on ConcurrentHashMap. While other threads update the map, they describe a moving target. The Javadoc calls them useful for monitoring and estimation, not for program control. if (map.size() < 10_000) map.put(k, v) is check-then-act on an estimate. CopyOnWriteArrayList takes the opposite trade. Every write copies the whole array. Every iterator walks the array as it was when the loop started, so iteration never locks and never throws. That is perfect for a list of webhook listeners that changes at deploy time and is iterated on every payment. It is terrible for a list that grows with traffic: adding the 100,000th element copies 100,000 references. CopyOnWriteArraySet works the same way, and ConcurrentSkipListMap is the concurrent sorted map. Trip a fail-fast iterator with one thread Read FailFast. It modifies an ArrayList, a ConcurrentHashMap and a CopyOnWriteArrayList while iterating over each one, all on the main thread. Predict what each line prints. In the copy-on-write loop, the body adds an item for every item it sees: does the loop ever end? Run it. FailFast.java package workbench.concurrency.l09; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; /** ConcurrentModificationException needs no second thread. And concurrent collections never throw it. */ public class FailFast { public static void main(String[] args) { // 1. one thread, an ArrayList, a remove inside for-each List<String> pending = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay-1", "pay-2", "pay-3", "pay-4")); try { for (String p : pending) { if (p.equals("pay-2")) pending.remove(p); // changes the list under its own iterator } } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("ArrayList, one thread: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); } // 2. the same with a ConcurrentHashMap: weakly consistent, never throws Map<String, Integer> open = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(Map.of("pay-1", 1, "pay-2", 2, "pay-3", 3, "pay-4", 4)); for (String k : open.keySet()) { if (k.equals("pay-2")) open.remove(k); if (k.equals("pay-3")) open.put("pay-5", 5); // may or may not show up in this loop } System.out.println("ConcurrentHashMap: no exception, now " + open.size() + " keys"); // 3. CopyOnWriteArrayList: the loop walks a snapshot taken when it started List<String> hooks = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c")); int seen = 0; for (String h : hooks) { hooks.add(h + "+"); // goes into a NEW array seen++; } System.out.println("CopyOnWriteArrayList: loop saw " + seen + " items, list now has " + hooks.size()); // 4. the single-thread fix for case 1: remove through the iterator, or removeIf pending = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay-1", "pay-2", "pay-3", "pay-4")); pending.removeIf(p -> p.equals("pay-2")); System.out.println("ArrayList.removeIf: " + pending); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.FailFast labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l09/FailFast.java FailFast.kt package workbench.concurrency.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList // ConcurrentModificationException needs no second thread. And concurrent collections never throw it. fun main() { // 1. one thread, an ArrayList, a remove inside a for loop var pending = mutableListOf("pay-1", "pay-2", "pay-3", "pay-4") try { for (p in pending) { if (p == "pay-2") pending.remove(p) // changes the list under its own iterator } } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println("ArrayList, one thread: ${e.javaClass.simpleName}") } // 2. the same with a ConcurrentHashMap: weakly consistent, never throws val open = ConcurrentHashMap(mapOf("pay-1" to 1, "pay-2" to 2, "pay-3" to 3, "pay-4" to 4)) for (k in open.keys) { if (k == "pay-2") open.remove(k) if (k == "pay-3") open["pay-5"] = 5 // may or may not show up in this loop } println("ConcurrentHashMap: no exception, now ${open.size} keys") // 3. The ConcurrentHashMap loop throws nothing and ends with 4 keys. h: Concurrent collections · BlockingQueue is the collection for handing work between threads
x: Lesson 5 of this track built a bounded buffer by hand. ArrayBlockingQueue is the production version, and every BlockingQueue offers the same four ways to add and remove: Throws Returns a special value Blocks Times out Insert add(e) offer(e): false if full put(e) offer(e, time, unit) Remove remove() poll(): null if empty take() poll(time, unit) Examine element() peek(): null if empty Pick the column by what the caller should do when the queue is full or empty. A request thread usually wants offer and an answer now. A dedicated consumer thread wants take and sleeps until there is work. Queues reject null because poll uses null to mean "empty". The implementations differ in ways that matter in production: ArrayBlockingQueue is bounded, backed by one array and one lock. LinkedBlockingQueue takes an optional capacity, and the default is Integer.MAX_VALUE. That is unbounded in practice. It uses separate locks for the head and the tail, so producers and consumers contend less. SynchronousQueue has no capacity at all. Each put waits for a take, and offer with no waiting taker returns false. PriorityBlockingQueue orders by priority and is unbounded. DelayQueue releases each element only when its delay has passed. A bounded queue gives you back-pressure. When the consumer falls behind, put makes the producer wait, or offer tells it to back off, so the system slows down instead of filling memory. drainTo(list, max) moves everything already queued in one call without waiting, which is how you batch. The lab's Batcher uses exactly that pair: poll with a timeout for the first entry, then drainTo for the rest. Fill a queue every way you can Read QueueMethods. It fills an ArrayBlockingQueue of 2, then tries add, offer, timed offer and put on the full queue. Predict each line, including the capacity of a LinkedBlockingQueue built with no arguments. Run it. q.put("e-1"); q.put("e-2"); // now full try { q.add("e-3"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("add: throws " + e); } System.out.println("offer: " + q.offer("e-3")); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); boolean timed = q.offer("e-3", 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); System.out.printf("offer(300 ms): %s after %d ms%n", timed, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); Thread producer = new Thread(() -> { try { q.put("e-3"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); producer.start(); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println("put: producer is " + producer.getState() + " until space opens"); System.out.println("take: " + q.take() + " (frees a slot)"); producer.join(); System.out.println("queue now: " + q); try { q.offer(null); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("offer(null): throws NullPointerException"); } System.out.println("new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() capacity: " + new LinkedBlockingQueue<String>().remainingCapacity()); System.out.println("SynchronousQueue.offer with no taker waiting: " + new SynchronousQueue<String>().offer("e-9")); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.QueueMethods labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l09/QueueMethods.java QueueMethods.kt package workbench.concurrency.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The four ways to add to a full BlockingQueue, and two queues that surprise people. fun main() { val q: BlockingQueue<String> = ArrayBlockingQueue(2) q.put("e-1") q.put("e-2") // now full try { q.add("e-3") } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("add: throws $e") } println("offer: ${q.offer("e-3")}") val t0 = System.nanoTime() val timed = q.offer("e-3", 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) println("offer(300 ms): $timed after ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms") val producer = thread { q.put("e-3") } Thread.sleep(200) println("put: producer is ${producer.state} until space opens") println("take: ${q.take()} (frees a slot)") producer.join() println("queue now: $q") // Kotlin won't even compile q.offer(null) on a BlockingQueue<String>; the JDK would throw NullPointerException println("LinkedBlockingQueue() capacity: ${LinkedBlockingQueue<String>().remainingCapacity()}") println("SynchronousQueue.offer with no taker waiting: ${SynchronousQueue<String>().offer("e-9")}") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l09.QueueMethodsKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l09/QueueMethods.kt add throws IllegalStateException: Queue full, offer returns false at once, the timed offer returns false after about 300 ms, and the producer in put is WAITING until take frees a slot. The no-argument LinkedBlockingQueue reports a capacity of 2,147,483,647. SynchronousQueue.offer returns false because nobody is waiting to take. BlockingQueue (Java SE 25 API) docs The most common real mistake is the unbounded queue. new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() looks harmless, and put never blocks, so it works in every test. Then the database slows down during an incident, the consumer falls behind, the queue grows to millions of entries, the garbage collector thrashes, and the pod is killed for running out of memory, taking every queued entry with it. Executors.newFixedThreadPool uses the same unbounded queue internally, which the executors track comes back to. The fix is to always pass a capacity and to decide, on purpose, what happens when the queue is full: put to slow the producer down, or offer to reject the work with a retryable error.

h: Concurrent collections · Java and Kotlin
x: Load-once caching in Java and Kotlin Java ConcurrentHashMap<String, String> issuers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); String issuerFor(String bin) { return issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, directory::lookup); // lookup runs at most once per BIN } Kotlin val issuers = ConcurrentHashMap<String, String>() fun issuerFor(bin: String): String = issuers.getOrPut(bin) { directory.lookup(bin) } // atomic put, but lookup may run several times fun issuerForOnce(bin: String): String = issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin) { directory.lookup(it) } // lookup runs at most once per BIN Kotlin's idiomatic getOrPut is the trap. The standard library has a special version for ConcurrentMap that uses putIfAbsent, so it never overwrites a value that is already there. But its documentation says the default function "may be invoked even if the key is already in the map". With 8 threads racing for one new key, the lookup ran 8 times in a check here, against once for computeIfAbsent. And if the variable's declared type is plain MutableMap, Kotlin picks the general getOrPut, which is a check followed by a put with no atomicity at all. Use computeIfAbsent when the loader is slow or must run once. Kotlin's type system does help in one place: ConcurrentHashMap<String, String> can't be handed a null value, so the NullPointerException that Java callers can hit becomes a compile error.

h: Concurrent collections · Worked example
x: Load once, without holding the bin for 80 ms The issuer directory takes 80 ms. This cache loads each BIN once, which is good. But while it loads, every other write that lands in the same bin waits, and the Javadoc asks for short functions. The goal: keep the map operation tiny and do the slow work outside it, while still loading each BIN once. String issuerFor(String bin) { return issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, directory::lookup); // 80 ms with the bin locked } fun issuerFor(bin: String): String = issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, directory::lookup) // 80 ms with the bin locked Cache the promise of a value instead of the value. The function inside computeIfAbsent now only creates a CompletableFuture that starts the lookup on another pool. That takes microseconds, so the bin is free again almost at once. Every caller for the BIN gets the same future and waits on it outside the map. private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>> issuers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); String issuerFor(String bin) { // 1. claim the BIN: the function only creates a future, so the bin is locked for microseconds CompletableFuture<String> f = issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin, b -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> directory.lookup(b), ioPool)); try { return f.join(); // 2. wait outside the map, with every other caller } catch (CompletionException e) { issuers.remove(bin, f); // 3. failed: forget THIS future so a retry loads again throw e; } } private val issuers = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>>() fun issuerFor(bin: String): String { // 1. claim the BIN: the function only creates a future, so the bin is locked for microseconds val f = issuers.computeIfAbsent(bin) { b -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ directory.lookup(b) }, ioPool) } try { return f.join() // 2. wait outside the map, with every other caller } catch (e: CompletionException) { issuers.remove(bin, f) // 3. failed: forget THIS future so a retry loads again throw e } } Before reading on, explain to yourself: why remove(bin, f) with two arguments, and not remove(bin)? Answer: between the failure and the remove, another thread may already have put a fresh future in place of the failed one. The two-argument remove deletes the entry only if it still maps to the future that failed. It is a compare-and-set on one key, and it keeps you from throwing away someone else's good load. This is the Memoizer from Java Concurrency in Practice, section 5.6, written with CompletableFuture. One gap is left: entries never expire, so a BIN that moves to a new issuer stays wrong until restart. A production service would use a caching library with expiry and asynchronous loading. Writing it once by hand tells you what that library does for you, and what to look for when it misbehaves.
