h: Concurrent collections · Quiz
x: From atomics and compare-and-set: 16 threads count events for about 200 hot merchant keys. Which is the best fit? HashMap<String, Long> with merge ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> with computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new LongAdder()).increment() ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> with put(k, get(k) + 1) Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()) with merge computeIfAbsent creates each adder once, and after that every increment goes to a LongAdder, which spreads hot keys over cells. merge on a ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> would also be correct, just with more contention on hot keys. A plain HashMap breaks, get-then-put loses updates, and a synchronized map serializes every thread on one lock. Why does ConcurrentHashMap throw NullPointerException for put(k, null)? So that get(k) == null always means the key is absent, with no second call needed Because nulls would corrupt its bins It doesn't: only null keys are rejected To save memory If null values were allowed, get returning null would be ambiguous, and telling "absent" from "mapped to null" would need containsKey too. Two calls is check-then-act, which another thread can break. Banning null removes the ambiguity. A cache uses map.computeIfAbsent(id, k -> loadAccount(k)), and loadAccount calls map.computeIfAbsent(parentId, ...) on the same map. What should you expect? It works, because the two keys differ A deadlock every time It breaks the documented contract; ConcurrentHashMap may throw IllegalStateException: Recursive update or misbehave A ConcurrentModificationException from the iterator The Javadoc says the mapping function must not modify the map. Whether the JDK detects it depends on where the keys land, so sometimes it throws Recursive update and sometimes it seems to work. Don't rely on either. Load the parent first, outside the compute call. A list of five fraud-rule listeners changes only at deploy time and is iterated on every one of 3,000 payments a second, from many threads. Which collection fits? ArrayList guarded by synchronized around every loop Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>()) ConcurrentLinkedQueue CopyOnWriteArrayList Reads vastly outnumber writes and the list is tiny, so copying the array on each rare write is cheap, and every iteration runs lock-free over a stable snapshot. The synchronized options make every payment take a lock for the whole loop. A queue would work for iteration, but it doesn't model a list you add to and remove from by identity as cleanly. A Kafka consumer thread puts records into new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() and a single writer thread inserts them into Oracle. During a slow-database incident, what happens? put blocks the consumer once the queue holds 10,000 records The queue grows without limit, because the default capacity is Integer.MAX_VALUE, until memory runs out put throws IllegalStateException when the queue is full The writer thread speeds up to match With no capacity, the queue never fills, so nothing pushes back on the consumer. Memory grows until the pod dies. Give the queue a capacity so put blocks the consumer (or offer fails), and pause the Kafka consumer when it does.

h: Concurrent collections · Explain it back
x: A teammate says: "We switched to ConcurrentHashMap, so our cache and counters are thread-safe now." Explain what that does and doesn't buy them, with one example of each.

h: Concurrent collections · Key terms
x: ConcurrentHashMap A thread-safe hash map that locks per bin for writes and never locks for reads. Bin One slot of a hash table; keys whose hashes land in the same slot share it. Fail-fast iterator An iterator that throws ConcurrentModificationException when it notices its collection changed; best effort only. Weakly consistent iterator An iterator that never throws and may or may not show changes made while it runs. CopyOnWriteArrayList A list that copies its whole array on every write so readers can iterate a stable snapshot without locks. BlockingQueue A queue whose put and take wait when it is full or empty, used to hand work between threads. Back-pressure Slowing or rejecting producers when consumers fall behind, instead of buffering without limit. What does ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent(k, f) guarantee? The whole call is atomic for that key: if k is absent, f runs at most once and its result is stored. Other updates to the same bin wait while f runs. Can a ConcurrentHashMap hold null keys or null values? No. Both throw NullPointerException, so get(k) == null always means "absent". What happens if the function passed to computeIfAbsent modifies the same map? It breaks the contract. ConcurrentHashMap may throw IllegalStateException: Recursive update; HashMap may throw ConcurrentModificationException; sometimes nothing is caught. Is ConcurrentHashMap.size() exact while other threads update it? No. It is an estimate of a moving target: fine for monitoring, wrong for decisions. What does a ConcurrentHashMap iterator do if the map changes during the loop? It never throws. It is weakly consistent: changes made during the loop may or may not appear. On a full ArrayBlockingQueue, what do offer(e) and put(e) do? offer(e) returns false at once. put(e) waits until there is space (and throws InterruptedException if interrupted). What is the capacity of new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()? Integer.MAX_VALUE: unbounded in practice. Pass a capacity to get back-pressure.

h: Concurrent collections · Go deeper
x: Since JDK 8, ConcurrentHashMap is an array of bins. An empty bin is filled with a compare-and-set, with no lock. An update to a non-empty bin takes the monitor of the bin's first node with synchronized. That is why a long compute function blocks other writers in the same bin but nobody else. computeIfAbsent on an empty bin first installs a placeholder, a reservation node, and holds its lock while your function runs. A nested call that runs into a reservation node in the same thread is how the map detects many recursive updates and throws Recursive update. A bin that collects 8 or more entries turns into a small red-black tree, as long as the table has at least 64 bins, so a bad hashCode degrades lookups to logarithmic time instead of linear. When the table grows, threads that try to write during the resize help move bins to the new table instead of waiting for it. The size is kept the way LongAdder keeps a count: a base value plus counter cells that threads update under contention. That is why size() can't be an exact snapshot while writers are busy, and why mappingCount(), which returns a long, is the method the Javadoc prefers. The map also has bulk operations that most people never find: forEach, search and reduce, each with a parallelismThreshold. settledCents.reduceValuesToLong(Long.MAX_VALUE, Long::longValue, 0L, Long::sum) sums all values on the calling thread; a small threshold such as 1 lets it split the work over the common fork-join pool. Like the iterators, these see a weakly consistent view, so a total taken while payments settle is close but not exact.

h: Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser · CountDownLatch waits for N events, once
x: A service that takes traffic before its caches are warm sends its first requests straight to Oracle. So the thread that opens the port has to wait until three loaders are done. join() from lesson 2 of this track can't do it if the loaders run on pool threads, because a pool thread doesn't end when its task does. A CountDownLatch starts at a count. Any thread can call countDown(). Threads that call await() wait until the count reaches zero, then all of them go on. You used two of them in lesson 3 of this track to make threads collide. Java CountDownLatch warmedUp = new CountDownLatch(3); // each warm-up thread, when it is done (in a finally): warmedUp.countDown(); // the thread that opens the service for traffic: if (!warmedUp.await(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { throw new IllegalStateException("caches not warm after 30 s"); } Kotlin val warmedUp = CountDownLatch(3) // each warm-up thread, when it is done (in a finally): warmedUp.countDown() // the thread that opens the service for traffic: if (!warmedUp.await(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { throw IllegalStateException("caches not warm after 30 s") } The latch waits for events, not for particular threads. One thread may count down three times, or three threads once each. It doesn't care. It is also one-shot. Inside, the count is one atomic int. countDown() lowers it with a compare-and-set, the call that takes it to zero wakes every waiting thread, and no method ever raises it again. So once the count reaches zero, it stays there. Every later await() returns at once, and extra countDown() calls do nothing. There is no reset. If you need the same gate every round, you want a barrier, the next section. Two habits keep latches from hanging services. Call countDown() in a finally, so a task that throws still counts. Otherwise the count never reaches zero and the waiter waits forever, WAITING in CountDownLatch.await in every thread dump. And prefer await(timeout, unit), which returns false if time ran out, so the caller can fail with a clear message instead of hanging. A latch also carries visibility: everything a thread did before countDown() happens-before await() returns in the waiting thread. That is why the caller can read the warm-up results without another lock. Open for traffic when the caches are warm Read LatchDemo. Three threads load three caches (200, 400 and 300 ms) and count down. main waits at most 2 seconds. Predict when ready is printed, and what an extra countDown() does after that. Run it, then run it again with -Pargs=stuck, where one load takes a minute. LatchDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l10; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A service warms three caches in parallel and opens for traffic when all three are loaded. * Run with -Pargs=stuck to make one warm-up hang. */ public class LatchDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean stuck = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("stuck"); String[] caches = {"bin-ranges", "fx-rates", "merchant-config"}; long[] loadMs = {200, 400, stuck ? 60_000 : 300}; CountDownLatch warmedUp = new CountDownLatch(caches.length); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < caches.length; i++) { String name = caches[i]; long ms = loadMs[i]; Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(ms); // pretend to load System.out.printf("%5d ms %s loaded%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, name); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { warmedUp.countDown(); // count down even if loading failed } }, "warm-" + name); t.setDaemon(true); t.start(); } boolean ready = warmedUp.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // never wait forever at startup System.out.printf("%5d ms ready=%s, count=%d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, ready, warmedUp.getCount()); // a latch is one-shot: once at zero, await() returns at once, forever if (ready) { warmedUp.countDown(); System.out.println("after another countDown(): count=" + warmedUp.getCount() + ", await returns at once: " + warmedUp.await(0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l10.LatchDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l10/LatchDemo.java LatchDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l10 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A service warms three caches in parallel and opens for traffic when all three are loaded. // Run with -Pargs=stuck to make one warm-up hang. fun main(args: Array<String>) { val stuck = args.firstOrNull() == "stuck" val caches = listOf("bin-ranges" to 200L, "fx-rates" to 400L, "merchant-config" to if (stuck) 60_000L else 300L) val warmedUp = CountDownLatch(caches.size) val t0 = System.nanoTime() for ((name, ms) in caches) { thread(isDaemon = true, name = "warm-$name") { try { Thread.sleep(ms) // pretend to load println("%5d ms %s loaded".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, name)) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } finally { warmedUp.countDown() // count down even if loading failed } } } val ready = warmedUp.await(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // never wait forever at startup println("%5d ms ready=%s, count=%d".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, ready, warmedUp.count)) // a latch is one-shot: once at zero, await() returns at once, forever if (ready) { warmedUp.countDown() println("after another countDown(): count=${warmedUp.count}, await returns at once: ${warmedUp.await(0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)}") } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l10.LatchDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l10/LatchDemo.kt The caches load at about 200, 300 and 400 ms, and ready=true, count=0 follows right after the slowest one. The extra countDown() leaves the count at 0, and await returns at once. With stuck, main prints ready=false, count=1 after 2 seconds instead of hanging forever. A CountDownLatch is a rocket countdown: when it reaches zero the launch happens, and you can't count down again. A CyclicBarrier is a tour group regrouping at every landmark: the bus leaves only when everyone is back, and the guide (the barrier action) does a head count each time. A Semaphore is a car park with 20 spaces and a sign showing how many are free; nobody checks which car leaves, so a car that never parked can still "leave" and the sign shows 21. A Phaser is a relay race where runners can join or drop out between legs. The analogy breaks at the tour bus: a guide would go looking for a missing tourist. A barrier just waits, forever, unless you gave await a timeout.

h: Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser · CyclicBarrier makes N threads meet, then all go on together
x: A CyclicBarrier waits for threads, not events. You give it a number of parties. Each thread calls await() when it reaches the meeting point and waits there until the last party arrives. Then all of them are released together, and the barrier resets itself for the next round. That is the cyclic part. Java CyclicBarrier endOfDay = new CyclicBarrier(4, () -> recordExposure(sum(shares))); // the barrier action // each of the 4 workers, for every simulated day: shares[me] = simulate(me, day); endOfDay.await(); // the 4th to arrive runs the action, then all 4 go on Kotlin val endOfDay = CyclicBarrier(4) { recordExposure(shares.sum()) } // the barrier action // each of the 4 workers, for every simulated day: shares[me] = simulate(me, day) endOfDay.await() // the 4th to arrive runs the action, then all 4 go on The optional barrier action runs once per round, on the last thread to arrive, before anyone is released. It's the place to combine results: each worker writes its own slot of shares before await(), and those writes are visible to the action and to every thread after the barrier. The figure shows two rounds. A barrier can break. If a waiting thread is interrupted, or its await(timeout) times out, or the barrier action throws, the barrier is broken: the thread that timed out gets TimeoutException, and every other waiter, now and later, gets BrokenBarrierException until someone calls reset(). That is deliberate. A round with a missing party can't complete, and failing all of them is better than leaving the rest waiting forever. But look at what doesn't break it: a thread that throws before it ever calls await(). The barrier can't know it's gone. The others wait, with plain await(), forever. So use the timed await in anything that runs in production. Latch or barrier? A latch is a gate opened by events ("three caches loaded"). A barrier is a meeting point for a fixed group of threads ("all four workers finished day 3"). Three rounds, then a missing worker Read BarrierDemo. Three workers simulate three days; the barrier action prints the day's exposure and the name of the thread that ran it. On day 4, worker 2 never arrives and the other two wait at most 300 ms. Predict what each of them prints. Run it twice. BarrierDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l10; import java.util.concurrent.BrokenBarrierException; import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; /** Three workers, three rounds, one barrier that resets itself. Then a round where one worker never shows up. */ public class BarrierDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { long[] shares = new long[3]; CyclicBarrier endOfDay = new CyclicBarrier(3, () -> // runs once per round, before anyone moves on System.out.printf(" day closed by %s: exposure %,d%n", Thread.currentThread().getName(), shares[0] + shares[1] + shares[2])); Thread[] workers = new Thread[3]; for (int w = 0; w < 3; w++) { int me = w; workers[w] = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int day = 1; day <= 3; day++) { Thread.sleep(50L * (me + 1)); // workers finish at different times shares[me] = 1_000L * day * (me + 1); endOfDay.await(); // wait for the other two } // day 4: worker 2 never arrives, the others give up after 300 ms if (me == 2) return; endOfDay.await(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { System.out.println(" " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + ": TimeoutException, barrier now broken"); } catch (BrokenBarrierException e) { System.out.println(" " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + ": BrokenBarrierException"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "worker-" + w); workers[w].start(); } for (Thread t : workers) t.join(); System.out.println("broken: " + endOfDay.isBroken()); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l10.BarrierDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l10/BarrierDemo.java BarrierDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l10 import java.util.concurrent.BrokenBarrierException import java.util.concurrent.CyclicBarrier import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Three workers, three rounds, one barrier that resets itself. Then a round where one worker never shows up. fun main() { val shares = LongArray(3) val endOfDay = CyclicBarrier(3) { // runs once per round, before anyone moves on println(" day closed by %s: exposure %,d".format(Thread.currentThread().name, shares.sum())) } val workers = List(3) { me -> thread(name = "worker-$me") { try { for (day in 1..3) { Thread.sleep(50L * (me + 1)) // workers finish at different times shares[me] = 1_000L * day * (me + 1) endOfDay.await() // wait for the other two } // day 4: worker 2 never arrives, the others give up after 300 ms if (me != 2) endOfDay.await(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { println(" ${Thread.currentThread().name}: TimeoutException, barrier now broken") } catch (e: BrokenBarrierException) { println(" ${Thread.currentThread().name}: BrokenBarrierException") } } } workers.forEach { it.join() } println("broken: ${endOfDay.isBroken}") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l10.BarrierDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l10/BarrierDemo.kt Three lines day closed by worker-2, with exposures 6,000, 12,000 and 18,000: worker 2 is the slowest, so it is always the last to arrive and runs the action. On day 4, one worker gets TimeoutException and breaks the barrier, and the other gets BrokenBarrierException. Which one gets which can change between runs. broken: true at the end. Each worker waits at the barrier until the last one arrives. The barrier action runs once per round, then all three start the next day together. In a Quarkus service, a latch shows up at startup (open for traffic after the BIN ranges and FX rates load) and in almost every concurrency test you write. A semaphore shows up in front of anything with a concurrency limit: a card-issuer API that throttles at 20 calls per client, a PDF generator, a Temporal activity that calls a partner with a strict rate limit. Remember the multiplication: the limit is per JVM, so 6 pods with 20 permits each is 120 calls at the partner. Barriers and phasers are rarer in request-handling code and common in batch jobs: an end-of-day exposure simulation or a reconciliation that runs in phases across worker threads.

h: Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser · Semaphore limits how many threads do something at once
x: A Semaphore holds a number of permits. acquire() takes one, waiting while none are left. release() gives one back. With 20 permits, at most 20 threads can be between the two calls. Java private final Semaphore issuerPermits = new Semaphore(20); Authorization authorize(Request r) throws InterruptedException { issuerPermits.acquire(); // before the try, like lock() try { return issuer.authorize(r); // at most 20 threads in here } finally { issuerPermits.release(); } } Kotlin private val issuerPermits = Semaphore(20) fun authorize(r: Request): Authorization { issuerPermits.acquire() // before the try, like lock() try { return issuer.authorize(r) // at most 20 threads in here } finally { issuerPermits.release() } } This is how you protect something that tolerates N users but not N + 1: a card-issuer API that throttles above 20 concurrent calls per client, a pool of 20 database connections, a CPU-heavy PDF renderer. tryAcquire(timeout, unit) waits a bounded time and returns false if no permit came free, so a request can fail fast instead of piling up. The idiom is the one from explicit locks: acquire() before the try, release() in finally. It matters even more here, because of the property from the warm-up: permits have no owner. A lock knows who holds it and throws if a stranger releases it. A semaphore is just a counter. Both of these bugs silently raise your limit: calling acquire() inside the try, so an interrupted wait still runs the release() in finally; ignoring the result of tryAcquire, then running the task and releasing anyway. The lab's IssuerGate has both. Every extra release is a permanent extra permit, and a limit of 20 drifts to 30 over a day of interrupts and timeouts. No exception, no log line. Two more points. A Semaphore limits one JVM: six pods with 20 permits each send up to 120 calls to the issuer, so divide the issuer's limit by your pod count. And new Semaphore(20, true) makes it fair, which stops a fast thread from grabbing permits ahead of threads that have waited longer. Five permits, twenty calls Read SemaphoreDemo. Twenty threads each make a 100 ms issuer call through a Semaphore(5), and the demo tracks the peak number in flight. Predict the peak and the total time. Run it. Then move issuer.acquire() to inside the try in the Java version: does anything change in this run? Why might it in production? SemaphoreDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l10; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 20 authorizations, 5 issuer permits, 100 ms per call. Then the bug that adds permits out of thin air. */ public class SemaphoreDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Semaphore issuer = new Semaphore(5); AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger(), peak = new AtomicInteger(); Thread[] requests = new Thread[20]; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < requests.length; i++) { requests[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { issuer.acquire(); // before the try try { peak.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); Thread.sleep(100); // the call to the issuer inFlight.decrementAndGet(); } finally { issuer.release(); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); requests[i].start(); } for (Thread t : requests) t.join(); System.out.printf("20 calls, peak in flight %d, took %d ms%n", peak.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); // permits belong to nobody: any thread can release, even one that never acquired Semaphore pool = new Semaphore(5); pool.release(); System.out.println("new Semaphore(5), then one stray release(): " + pool.availablePermits() + " permits"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l10.SemaphoreDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l10/SemaphoreDemo.java SemaphoreDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l10 import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // 20 authorizations, 5 issuer permits, 100 ms per call. Then the bug that adds permits out of thin air. private inline fun <T> Semaphore.withPermit(block: () -> T): T { acquire() // before the try try { return block() } finally { release() } } fun main() { val issuer = Semaphore(5) val inFlight = AtomicInteger() val peak = AtomicInteger() val t0 = System.nanoTime() val requests = List(20) { thread { issuer.withPermit { peak.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max) Thread.sleep(100) // the call to the issuer inFlight.decrementAndGet() } } } requests.forEach { it.join() } println("20 calls, peak in flight ${peak.get()}, took ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms") // permits belong to nobody: any thread can release, even one that never acquired val pool = Semaphore(5) pool.release() println("new Semaphore(5), then one stray release(): ${pool.availablePermits()} permits") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l10.SemaphoreDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l10/SemaphoreDemo.kt Peak in flight 5, total about 400 ms: four waves of five calls. The stray release() turns 5 permits into 6. Moving acquire() inside the try changes nothing here, because nobody interrupts the waiters. In production an interrupt during the wait (a cancelled request, a shutdown) would release a permit that was never taken. Semaphore (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser · Phaser and Exchanger, briefly
x: A Phaser is a barrier whose group can change size. Parties register() to join and arriveAndDeregister() to leave, and each phase waits only for the parties registered at that moment. Phases are numbered from 0, and you can override onAdvance(phase, parties) to run code between phases and to end the phaser by returning true. Java Phaser phaser = new Phaser(1); // the coordinator is a party phaser.register(); // each worker joins when it starts phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance(); // wait for everyone still registered phaser.arriveAndDeregister(); // leave; later phases wait for one party fewer Kotlin val phaser = Phaser(1) // the coordinator is a party phaser.register() // each worker joins when it starts phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance() // wait for everyone still registered phaser.arriveAndDeregister() // leave; later phases wait for one party fewer Use it when the number of workers isn't known up front or changes between phases: a settlement run where some workers only fetch and then leave, or a job that registers one party per file it discovers. If the group is fixed, a CyclicBarrier is simpler and says what it means. A phaser can also replace a CountDownLatch that you'd like to reuse. An Exchanger is the smallest synchronizer: two threads meet and swap one object each, for example a full buffer for an empty one. You will rarely need it. CountDownLatch and Semaphore are built on AbstractQueuedSynchronizer, like ReentrantLock. CyclicBarrier uses a ReentrantLock and a Condition inside, and Phaser and Exchanger park their threads with LockSupport directly. So a thread waiting in any of them is parked and shows as WAITING or TIMED_WAITING in a thread dump, with the synchronizer's class in its stack. And none of them has an owner the deadlock detector can see, so a cycle of threads waiting on semaphores or latches is never reported as a deadlock. A worker leaves halfway Read PhaserDemo. Three workers run three phases (fetch, net, post). Worker 2 leaves after the first phase. onAdvance prints each phase and the parties left. Predict the party count printed for each phase. Run it. PhaserDemo.java package workbench.concurrency.l10; import java.util.concurrent.Phaser; /** A settlement run in three phases. One worker leaves after the first phase; the Phaser just has fewer parties. */ public class PhaserDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String[] phases = {"fetch", "net", "post"}; Phaser phaser = new Phaser(1) { // 1 party: main, until it deregisters @Override protected boolean onAdvance(int phase, int parties) { System.out.printf(" phase %d (%s) done, %d parties%n", phase, phases[phase], parties); return phase == phases.length - 1 || parties == 0; // true ends the phaser } }; Thread[] workers = new Thread[3]; for (int w = 0; w < workers.length; w++) { int me = w; phaser.register(); // a new party joins workers[w] = new Thread(() -> { for (int p = 0; p < phases.length; p++) { if (me == 2 && p == 1) { phaser.arriveAndDeregister(); // worker 2 only fetches, then leaves return; } phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance(); // like a barrier, for this phase } }); workers[w].start(); } phaser.arriveAndDeregister(); // main stops taking part for (Thread t : workers) t.join(); System.out.println("terminated: " + phaser.isTerminated()); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l10.PhaserDemo labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l10/PhaserDemo.java PhaserDemo.kt package workbench.concurrency.l10 import java.util.concurrent.Phaser import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A settlement run in three phases. One worker leaves after the first phase; the Phaser just has fewer parties. fun main() { val phases = listOf("fetch", "net", "post") val phaser = object : Phaser(1) { // 1 party: main, until it deregisters override fun onAdvance(phase: Int, parties: Int): Boolean { println(" phase %d (%s) done, %d parties".format(phase, phases[phase], parties)) return phase == phases.lastIndex || parties == 0 // true ends the phaser } } val workers = List(3) { me -> phaser.register() // a new party joins thread(start = true) { for (p in phases.indices) { if (me == 2 && p == 1) { phaser.arriveAndDeregister() // worker 2 only fetches, then leaves return@thread } phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance() // like a barrier, for this phase } } } phaser.arriveAndDeregister() // main stops taking part workers.forEach { it.join() } println("terminated: ${phaser.isTerminated}") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l10.PhaserDemoKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l10/PhaserDemo.kt phase 0 (fetch) done, 3 parties, then phase 1 (net) done, 2 parties and phase 2 (post) done, 2 parties, then terminated: true. main registered itself first so no phase could finish before every worker had joined, then left. Worker 2's arriveAndDeregister counts as its arrival for phase 1 and shrinks every later phase. The most common real mistake is releasing a permit you never acquired. It happens in two ways: acquire() placed inside the try, so an interrupted wait still reaches the release() in finally, and tryAcquire(timeout) whose false result is ignored. Both look fine in review and in tests, because tests rarely interrupt waiters or exhaust permits. In production, each cancelled request or timeout adds one permit for good, and the limit that protected the issuer API slowly stops limiting. The fix is the lock idiom: acquire() on the line before try, and if (!tryAcquire(...)) that returns or throws before the try is entered.

h: Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser · Java and Kotlin
x: A permit helper in Java and Kotlin Java static <T> T withPermit(Semaphore s, Callable<T> task) throws Exception { s.acquire(); // before the try, like lock() try { return task.call(); } finally { s.release(); // exactly the permit we took } } Authorization a = withPermit(issuerPermits, () -> issuer.authorize(request)); Kotlin inline fun <T> Semaphore.withPermit(block: () -> T): T { acquire() // before the try, like lock() try { return block() } finally { release() // exactly the permit we took } } val a = issuerPermits.withPermit { issuer.authorize(request) } Both languages use the same java.util.concurrent classes, and both block a thread while it waits. Kotlin's difference is that an inline extension function makes the safe idiom read like a language feature: the lambda is inlined, so there's no allocation, return inside it works as usual, and nobody on the team writes the try/finally by hand again. The Kotlin standard library doesn't ship withPermit for java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; you write it once, as above. kotlinx.coroutines has its own Semaphore with a built-in withPermit that suspends the coroutine instead of blocking a thread. The coroutines track covers it.

h: Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser · Worked example
x: A parallel reconciliation that can't hang End-of-day reconciliation compares 4 ledger partitions against the bank statement. Each takes a few seconds, so it runs on 4 threads and waits for all of them with a latch. Read this first version. What happens if reconcile throws for one partition? CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(4); List<Mismatch> found = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); for (Partition p : partitions) { new Thread(() -> { found.addAll(reconcile(p)); done.countDown(); }).start(); } done.await(); report(found); val done = CountDownLatch(4) val found = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Mismatch>() for (p in partitions) { thread { found.addAll(reconcile(p)) done.countDown() } } done.await() report(found) The failing thread dies before countDown(). The count stays at 1, and await() waits forever. The job doesn't fail; it just never ends. A dump shows main WAITING in CountDownLatch.await and no worker threads at all, because they all finished or died. The fix has three parts: count down in finally, record the failure so it isn't lost, and never wait without a deadline. Here is the version that always ends, with subgoal labels. CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(partitions.size()); List<Mismatch> found = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); List<Throwable> failures = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); for (Partition p : partitions) { new Thread(() -> { try { found.addAll(reconcile(p)); // 1. do the work } catch (Throwable e) { failures.add(e); // 2. remember the failure instead of losing it } finally { done.countDown(); // 3. always count down } }, "recon-" + p.id()).start(); } if (!done.await(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 4. never wait forever throw new IllegalStateException("reconciliation still running after 10 min"); } if (!failures.isEmpty()) throw new IllegalStateException("partitions failed: " + failures); report(found); // 5. countDown happens-before await returns: all results visible val done = CountDownLatch(partitions.size) val found = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Mismatch>() val failures = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Throwable>() for (p in partitions) { thread(name = "recon-${p.id}") { try { found.addAll(reconcile(p)) // 1. do the work } catch (e: Throwable) { failures.add(e) // 2. remember the failure instead of losing it } finally { done.countDown() // 3. always count down } } } if (!done.await(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 4. never wait forever throw IllegalStateException("reconciliation still running after 10 min") } if (failures.isNotEmpty()) throw IllegalStateException("partitions failed: $failures") report(found) // 5. countDown happens-before await returns: all results visible Before reading on, explain to yourself: why can main read found after await returns without any lock? Answer: everything a worker did before countDown() happens-before await() returns in the thread that waited. found is still a CopyOnWriteArrayList, because the four workers add to it at the same time. In a real service you'd submit the four tasks to an ExecutorService and use invokeAll, which the executors track covers. A latch is one of the pieces such tools are built from.

h: Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser · Quiz
x: A service must not accept traffic until four independent caches have loaded, each on its own thread. Which tool fits best? CountDownLatch(4), counted down by each loader, awaited by the startup code CyclicBarrier(4) Semaphore(4) Exchanger You are waiting for four events, once. That is a latch. A barrier would make the four loader threads wait for each other, which they don't need to, and it is built for repeated rounds. A semaphore limits concurrency; it doesn't wait for completion. try { sem.acquire(); callIssuer(); } finally { sem.release(); } with new Semaphore(10). A thread is interrupted while it waits in acquire(). What happens? Nothing: acquire() gives up cleanly The thread gets the permit anyway acquire() throws, the finally releases a permit that was never taken, and the semaphore now allows 11 The semaphore throws IllegalMonitorStateException in release() acquire() throws InterruptedException, which still runs the finally. Permits have no owner, so release() simply adds one. Move acquire() above the try. Three workers use a CyclicBarrier(3) with plain await(). One worker throws an exception before it reaches await() in round 5. What do the other two do? They get BrokenBarrierException at once The barrier notices the dead thread and lets them through They get TimeoutException after a default timeout They wait forever The barrier only breaks when a waiting thread is interrupted or times out, or the action fails. A thread that never arrives is invisible to it, and plain await() has no timeout. Use await(timeout, unit) so the round fails instead of hanging. From deadlock, livelock and starvation: 20 request threads each take 1 permit from a Semaphore(20) that guards DB connections, then call a helper that takes another permit from the same semaphore. Under full load everything stops. What will jcmd Thread.print say? Found one Java-level deadlock naming the semaphore No deadlock report: semaphore permits have no owner, so the detector can't see the cycle; you see 20 threads WAITING in Semaphore.acquire It reports a livelock The threads show as BLOCKED This is hold-and-wait: every thread holds one permit and waits for a second. It is a real deadlock, but the JVM's detector only follows owned locks (monitors and ReentrantLock-style synchronizers). Parked threads show as WAITING, not BLOCKED. Acquire both permits at once with acquire(2), or don't take a second one while holding the first. A batch job processes files in rounds and the number of worker threads changes between rounds as files are discovered. Which tool fits? One CountDownLatch per round, created up front A CyclicBarrier with the maximum number of workers A Phaser, with workers registering when they start and deregistering when they finish A Semaphore A phaser's group can grow and shrink between phases, and each phase waits only for the parties registered then. A barrier's party count is fixed, so missing workers would hang it. Latches are one-shot and need their count known in advance.

h: Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser · Key terms
x: Synchronizer An object that makes threads wait for each other or for events, such as a latch, barrier or semaphore. CountDownLatch A one-shot gate that opens when a count reaches zero. CyclicBarrier A meeting point for a fixed number of threads that resets itself after each round. Barrier action Code a CyclicBarrier runs once per round, before releasing the threads. Semaphore A counter of permits that limits how many threads can do something at once. Permit One unit of a semaphore's count. It belongs to nobody. Phaser A reusable barrier whose set of parties can change between phases. A CountDownLatch has reached zero. What do later await() and countDown() calls do? await() returns at once. countDown() does nothing. A latch can't be reset. When does a CyclicBarrier's barrier action run, and on which thread? Once per round, on the last thread to arrive, before any waiting thread is released. What breaks a CyclicBarrier? A waiting thread being interrupted or timing out, the barrier action throwing, or reset(). Then every waiter gets BrokenBarrierException. What does release() do on a Semaphore when the caller never acquired a permit? It adds a permit anyway. Permits have no owner, so stray releases silently raise the limit. Where do acquire() and release() go relative to try/finally? acquire() on the line before try; release() in finally. With tryAcquire, check its result before entering the try. Latch or barrier: "start serving after 3 caches load" vs "4 workers finish day N before any starts day N+1"? The first is a latch (waiting for events, once). The second is a barrier (a fixed group meeting every round). What can a Phaser do that a CyclicBarrier can't? Change its number of parties between phases: register() to join, arriveAndDeregister() to leave.

h: Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser · Go deeper
x: CountDownLatch and Semaphore, like ReentrantLock, are thin layers over AbstractQueuedSynchronizer: an int of state and a queue of parked threads. For a latch the state is the count, and await parks until it is zero. For a semaphore it is the permits left. CyclicBarrier is a ReentrantLock with one Condition, and Phaser and Exchanger keep their own queues of parked threads. All of them park through LockSupport, which is why they show up the same way in a thread dump: WAITING (parking), with a line like parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore$NonfairSync). A few API corners are worth knowing. Semaphore.acquire(n) takes several permits in one step, which avoids the hold-one-wait-for-another deadlock from the quiz. drainPermits() takes all that are left, which is handy when you want to stop new work during a shutdown. acquireUninterruptibly() ignores interrupts, which you almost never want. CyclicBarrier.await() returns the arrival index (parties minus one for the first to arrive, zero for the last), so you can pick one thread to do extra work without a barrier action. Phaser supports tiering: you can build a tree of phasers so thousands of parties don't all contend on one. Its Javadoc caps a single phaser at 65,535 registered parties. On virtual threads (JDK 21), blocking in any of these is cheap: the virtual thread parks and its carrier thread runs something else. A Semaphore is in fact the standard way to limit concurrency once you start a virtual thread per task, because there is no pool size to do it for you. The virtual threads track comes back to that. In Kotlin coroutines, the equivalents suspend instead of blocking: kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore, Job.join() or awaitAll() for latches, and channels for most of the rest.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Immutable objects need no locks
x: The surest way to avoid a race is to have nothing to race on. If no thread can change an object after it is built, every thread can read it at any time, with no lock, no volatile and no atomics. Lesson 3 of this track listed "don't share" as the first fix to reach for. This lesson is about that fix. An object is immutable when all its fields are final and set in the constructor, it has no setters, every mutable thing it holds is copied in and never handed out, and this doesn't escape during construction. Records and Kotlin data classes with vals get you most of the way: Java public record Merchant(String id, int feeBps, Currency settlementCurrency) { // fields are final public Merchant withFeeBps(int newFee) { // "changes" return a new object return new Merchant(id, newFee, settlementCurrency); } } Kotlin data class Merchant(val id: String, val feeBps: Int, val settlementCurrency: Currency) // vals: final fields val cheaper = merchant.copy(feeBps = 180) // "changes" return a new object final fields also carry a guarantee from the memory model (JLS 17.5). A thread that gets a reference to the object after its constructor has finished sees the correct values of its final fields, even if the reference reached it through a data race. Non-final fields have no such promise. The memory model track covers why. The pattern that follows is the cheapest way to share data that changes now and then: keep an immutable snapshot behind a volatile reference and replace it whole. Java private volatile Map<String, BigDecimal> rates = Map.of(); // an immutable map, replaced whole void refresh(Map<String, BigDecimal> fresh) { rates = Map.copyOf(fresh); // build it completely, then publish it in one write } BigDecimal rate(String pair) { return rates.get(pair); // no lock: every map this field ever points to is immutable } Kotlin @Volatile private var rates: Map<String, BigDecimal> = emptyMap() // an immutable map, replaced whole fun refresh(fresh: Map<String, BigDecimal>) { rates = java.util.Map.copyOf(fresh) // build it completely, then publish it in one write } fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal? = rates[pair] // no lock: every map this field ever points to is immutable This is the FX cache from lesson 7 of this track without any lock. The refresher builds the new map off to the side, where no reader can see it, and publishes it with one volatile write. A reader that reads the field once sees one complete version. If a reader needs several values from the same version, it copies the reference into a local first and reads them all from that. Half-done refreshes, counted Read SnapshotSwap. A refresher moves four FX rates to a new version over and over. It updates a ConcurrentHashMap in place, and also publishes an immutable snapshot through a volatile field. For one second, the main thread reads all four rates from each and counts reads that saw two versions at once. Predict both counts. Run it. SnapshotSwap.java package workbench.concurrency.l11; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; /** * An FX rate table refreshed as a whole while readers price payments. Every refresh moves all * rates to the same new "version". A reader that sees two versions in one quote saw a half-done refresh. */ public class SnapshotSwap { static final String[] PAIRS = {"EURUSD", "GBPUSD", "USDJPY", "USDCHF"}; // 1. shared mutable map, refreshed in place (each put is thread-safe on its own) static final Map<String, Long> live = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // 2. an immutable map behind a volatile reference, replaced in one write static volatile Map<String, Long> snapshot = Map.of(); static volatile boolean done; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread refresher = new Thread(() -> { for (long version = 1; !done; version++) { for (String p : PAIRS) live.put(p, version); // readers can see a mix Map<String, Long> fresh = new HashMap<>(); for (String p : PAIRS) fresh.put(p, version); snapshot = Map.copyOf(fresh); // build fully, then publish once } }); refresher.start(); long mixedLive = 0, mixedSnapshot = 0, reads = 0; long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++; if (mixed(live)) mixedLive++; if (mixed(snapshot)) mixedSnapshot++; // one read of the reference: one version } done = true; refresher.join(); System.out.printf("reads: %,d mixed versions, shared mutable map: %,d immutable snapshot: %d%n", reads, mixedLive, mixedSnapshot); } static boolean mixed(Map<String, Long> rates) { Long first = rates.get(PAIRS[0]); for (String p : PAIRS) if (!java.util.Objects.equals(rates.get(p), first)) return true; return false; } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.SnapshotSwap labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l11/SnapshotSwap.java SnapshotSwap.kt package workbench.concurrency.l11 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import kotlin.concurrent.thread // An FX rate table refreshed as a whole while readers price payments. Every refresh moves all // rates to the same new "version". A reader that sees two versions in one quote saw a half-done refresh. private val PAIRS = listOf("EURUSD", "GBPUSD", "USDJPY", "USDCHF") // 1. shared mutable map, refreshed in place (each put is thread-safe on its own) private val live = ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long>() // 2. an immutable map behind a volatile reference, replaced in one write @Volatile private var snapshot: Map<String, Long> = emptyMap() @Volatile private var done = false private fun mixed(rates: Map<String, Long>): Boolean { val first = rates[PAIRS[0]] return PAIRS.any { rates[it] != first } } fun main() { val refresher = thread { var version = 1L while (!done) { for (p in PAIRS) live[p] = version // readers can see a mix snapshot = java.util.Map.copyOf(PAIRS.associateWith { version }) // build fully, then publish once version++ } } var mixedLive = 0L; var mixedSnapshot = 0L; var reads = 0L val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { reads++ if (mixed(live)) mixedLive++ if (mixed(snapshot)) mixedSnapshot++ // one read of the reference: one version } done = true refresher.join() println("reads: %,d mixed versions, shared mutable map: %,d immutable snapshot: %d".format(reads, mixedLive, mixedSnapshot)) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.SnapshotSwapKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l11/SnapshotSwap.kt The shared mutable map shows mixed versions in hundreds of thousands of reads (271,876 of 1,422,759 in one run here), although every single put and get was thread-safe. The immutable snapshot shows 0, every run. An immutable object is a printed price list: anyone can read it at the same time, and to change a price you print a new list and swap it on the wall. Confinement is a ledger kept in one clerk's desk; others pass notes to that clerk instead of writing in it. A hand-off through a queue is passing a folder across the counter: once it's handed over, you don't reach back to add a page. A ThreadLocal on a pool thread is a locker that the next shift inherits, with whatever the last person left in it, unless someone empties it at the end of every shift. The analogy breaks at the price list: a printed list can't be edited by a stranger, but a Java object with one unprotected List field can.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Records and data classes are only shallowly immutable
x: final freezes the reference, not the object behind it. A record that stores a caller's ArrayList or byte[] can change whenever the caller changes it, and so can anyone you hand the array to. The lab's FxQuote has exactly this problem. The fix is a defensive copy: copy mutable things on the way in, and, for arrays, on the way out too. Java public record Settlement(String merchantId, List<Payment> payments) { public Settlement { payments = List.copyOf(payments); // reassign the parameter: the field gets the copy } } Kotlin class Settlement(val merchantId: String, payments: List<Payment>) { val payments: List<Payment> = java.util.List.copyOf(payments) // a plain parameter, copied into a property } A few details decide whether the copy works. List.copyOf makes an unmodifiable copy: later changes to the source don't show, and add on the copy throws. Collections.unmodifiableList(list) is not a copy. It is a read-only view of the caller's list, so the caller's later changes show straight through it. Arrays can't be made read-only. Clone in the constructor, and clone again in the accessor, or keep the data in an immutable type instead. Elements must be immutable too. A copied list of mutable Payment objects is a new list of the same shared objects. Kotlin adds one trap of its own. List is a read-only interface, not an immutable list: a data class with val tiers: List<Tier> stores whatever MutableList the caller passed, and Java code, or a cast, can still change it. A data class also can't copy its constructor parameters, because those parameters are its properties. Use a plain class, as above, when you need the copy. In Java, BigDecimal, String, Instant, LocalDate, UUID and the boxed numbers are immutable already. Date, Calendar and arrays are not. Mutate a record from outside Read ShallowRecord. ShallowQuote keeps the caller's list and array; DeepQuote copies them in and out. A third reference is an unmodifiableList view. After construction, the caller changes its list and array, and a reader writes into the array it got from signature(). Predict all three lines. Run it, then run the Kotlin twin, which adds one more line. ShallowRecord.java package workbench.concurrency.l11; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; /** A record's fields are final. The objects they point to are not. */ public class ShallowRecord { record ShallowQuote(String pair, List<String> tiers, byte[] signature) {} record DeepQuote(String pair, List<String> tiers, byte[] signature) { DeepQuote { tiers = List.copyOf(tiers); // copy in signature = signature.clone(); } @Override public byte[] signature() { return signature.clone(); // copy out } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> tiers = new ArrayList<>(List.of("up to 10k at 1.0842")); byte[] sig = {7, 7, 7}; ShallowQuote shallow = new ShallowQuote("EURUSD", tiers, sig); DeepQuote deep = new DeepQuote("EURUSD", tiers, sig); List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(tiers); // a read-only VIEW, not a copy tiers.add("above 10k at 9.9999"); // the caller keeps changing its list... sig[0] = 0; // ...and its array shallow.signature()[1] = 0; // a reader scribbles on what it was given deep.signature()[1] = 0; System.out.println("shallow: " + shallow.tiers() + " signature " + Arrays.toString(shallow.signature())); System.out.println("deep: " + deep.tiers() + " signature " + Arrays.toString(deep.signature())); System.out.println("unmodifiableList view: " + view); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.ShallowRecord labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l11/ShallowRecord.java ShallowRecord.kt package workbench.concurrency.l11 // A data class's vals can't be reassigned. The objects they point to can still change. private data class LooseQuote(val pair: String, val tiers: List<String>, val signature: ByteArray) private class SealedQuote(val pair: String, tiers: List<String>, signature: ByteArray) { val tiers: List<String> = java.util.List.copyOf(tiers) // copy in: unmodifiable even through a cast private val sig = signature.copyOf() val signature: ByteArray get() = sig.copyOf() // copy out } fun main() { val tiers = mutableListOf("up to 10k at 1.0842") val sig = byteArrayOf(7, 7, 7) val loose = LooseQuote("EURUSD", tiers, sig) // List<String> is read-only, not immutable val sealed = SealedQuote("EURUSD", tiers, sig) val view = java.util.Collections.unmodifiableList(tiers) // a read-only VIEW, not a copy tiers.add("above 10k at 9.9999") // the caller keeps changing its list... sig[0] = 0 // ...and its array loose.signature[1] = 0 // a reader scribbles on what it was given sealed.signature[1] = 0 println("shallow: ${loose.tiers} signature ${loose.signature.contentToString()}") println("deep: ${sealed.tiers} signature ${sealed.signature.contentToString()}") println("unmodifiableList view: $view") (loose.tiers as MutableList<String>).add("added through a cast") // read-only interface, mutable object println("shallow after a cast: ${loose.tiers}") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.ShallowRecordKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l11/ShallowRecord.kt The shallow quote shows the extra tier and a signature of [0, 0, 7]: both the caller and a reader changed it. The deep quote still shows one tier and [7, 7, 7]. The unmodifiableList view shows the extra tier, because it's a view. In Kotlin, a cast to MutableList adds to the shallow quote's "read-only" list. Kafka already confines state for you: one partition is read by one consumer thread at a time, so per-partition state needs no locks, as long as you don't hand it to another thread. Events and commands on the bus should be immutable records, so a consumer can pass them to a worker pool without copying. Temporal runs a workflow's code one thread at a time, so workflow state is confined by design; activities run on an ordinary thread pool and get none of that protection. And look at every ThreadLocal in your Quarkus services, including the ones inside libraries: logging MDC, a tenant or merchant context, a security principal. Each one needs a finally that clears it, or a framework hook that does it for you. A merchant id that leaks from one request into the next is a reportable incident, not just a bug.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Confinement keeps mutable state on one thread
x: Mutable state is fine as long as only one thread can reach it. That is confinement, and you already use it every day. Stack confinement is the simplest: local variables live on one thread's stack. A StringBuilder or ArrayList created inside a method and never stored anywhere else needs no protection at all. Java String statementLine(Payment p) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); // local: no other thread can ever see it sb.append(p.id()).append(';').append(p.cents()); return sb.toString(); // only the immutable String leaves } Kotlin fun statementLine(p: Payment): String = buildString { // the builder is local: no other thread can see it append(p.id).append(';').append(p.cents) } // only the immutable String leaves Thread confinement is the same idea at a larger scale: one thread owns some state, and every other thread asks that thread to act on it. A Kafka consumer is the classic case. Each partition is read by one consumer thread at a time, so per-partition state such as the last processed offset or a running total can live in a plain HashMap that only that thread touches. Event loops work the same way. When work moves between threads, move ownership with it. A request thread builds a batch, puts it into a BlockingQueue, and never touches it again. The writer thread takes it and owns it from then on. Java List<Entry> batch = new ArrayList<>(); // owned by this thread fill(batch); queue.put(batch); // ownership moves to whoever takes it // from here on, this thread never touches batch again Kotlin val batch = ArrayList<Entry>() // owned by this thread fill(batch) queue.put(batch) // ownership moves to whoever takes it // from here on, this thread never touches batch again The queue does two jobs. It hands the object over, and it makes the hand-off visible: everything the producer did before put happens-before the consumer's take returns. The figure shows the moment ownership changes. The rule is all on the producer: once you've handed it over, it isn't yours. A producer that reuses the list for the next batch is sharing a mutable object with no synchronization at all, and the writer sees half-cleared batches. Hand over, or keep using? Read HandOff. A producer fills 5,000 batches of 100 entries and puts each into a queue. A writer thread checks that every batch it takes is complete and in order. Run it. Then run it with -Pargs=reuse, where the producer clears and refills one list instead of creating a new one. Run the reuse version a few times. Is the damage count the same each time? HandOff.java package workbench.concurrency.l11; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; /** * A request thread fills batches of 100 ledger entries and hands each one to a writer thread * through a queue. Run with -Pargs=reuse to reuse one list instead of handing over a new one. */ public class HandOff { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean reuse = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("reuse"); BlockingQueue<List<Integer>> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4); int batches = 5_000; int[] damaged = {0}; Thread writer = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int b = 0; b < batches; b++) { List<Integer> batch = queue.take(); // the writer owns this list now try { Object[] entries = batch.toArray(); boolean ok = entries.length == 100; for (int i = 0; ok && i < 100; i++) ok = entries[i].equals(((Integer) entries[0]) + i); if (!ok) damaged[0]++; } catch (RuntimeException e) { damaged[0]++; // a list changing under you can throw, too } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "ledger-writer"); writer.start(); List<Integer> shared = new ArrayList<>(); for (int b = 0; b < batches; b++) { List<Integer> batch = reuse ? shared : new ArrayList<>(100); batch.clear(); // with reuse: clears a list the writer may be reading for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) batch.add(b * 100 + i); queue.put(batch); // hand it over, and never touch it again } writer.join(); System.out.printf("%s: %,d batches handed over, %,d damaged%n", reuse ? "reused list" : "new list each time", batches, damaged[0]); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.HandOff labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l11/HandOff.java HandOff.kt package workbench.concurrency.l11 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A request thread fills batches of 100 ledger entries and hands each one to a writer thread // through a queue. Run with -Pargs=reuse to reuse one list instead of handing over a new one. fun main(args: Array<String>) { val reuse = args.firstOrNull() == "reuse" val queue = ArrayBlockingQueue<MutableList<Int>>(4) val batches = 5_000 var damaged = 0 val writer = thread(name = "ledger-writer") { repeat(batches) { val batch = queue.take() // the writer owns this list now try { val entries = batch.toTypedArray() val ok = entries.size == 100 && entries.indices.all { i -> entries[i] == entries[0] + i } if (!ok) damaged++ } catch (e: RuntimeException) { damaged++ // a list changing under you can throw, too } } } val shared = ArrayList<Int>() for (b in 0 until batches) { val batch = if (reuse) shared else ArrayList(100) batch.clear() // with reuse: clears a list the writer may be reading for (i in 0 until 100) batch.add(b * 100 + i) queue.put(batch) // hand it over, and never touch it again } writer.join() println("%s: %,d batches handed over, %,d damaged".format(if (reuse) "reused list" else "new list each time", batches, damaged)) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.HandOffKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l11/HandOff.kt With a new list each time: 0 damaged batches. With reuse: some batches arrive damaged (from about a dozen to a few hundred in runs here), and the count changes every run. A lucky run could even show 0, which is exactly why this bug survives testing. Ownership moves through the queue. Writes before put happen-before the take, and the old owner never touches the batch again.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · ThreadLocal gives each thread its own copy, and pools keep it forever
x: ThreadLocal<T> gives every thread its own value for the same variable. It has two common uses: a per-thread copy of an object that isn't thread-safe, and request context, such as the tenant or user, that deep code reads without passing it around. Logging MDC, the per-request fields your logger adds to every line, is usually a ThreadLocal underneath. The catch is where the value lives. Each Thread object has its own small map from ThreadLocal to value, and get() looks in the current thread's map. The Javadoc says a thread keeps its copy as long as the thread is alive. Pool threads live for days, and so does whatever you left on them. A value set for one request is still there when the same thread serves the next one. If the next request sets nothing, it runs as the previous customer. That's a data leak between merchants, in a payment system. The rule has no exceptions: set it, then remove it in finally. Java private static final ThreadLocal<String> TENANT = new ThreadLocal<>(); void handle(Request r) { TENANT.set(r.tenant()); try { process(r); // deep code calls TENANT.get() } finally { TENANT.remove(); // the pool thread goes back clean } } Kotlin private val TENANT = ThreadLocal<String>() fun handle(r: Request) { TENANT.set(r.tenant) try { process(r) // deep code calls TENANT.get() } finally { TENANT.remove() // the pool thread goes back clean } } Call remove(), not set(null). remove() deletes the thread's entry; set(null) keeps an entry that holds null. For non-thread-safe helpers, prefer an immutable replacement over a per-thread copy. DateTimeFormatter is immutable, so one shared instance replaces a ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat>. Per-thread copies also scale badly with virtual threads, where every task is a new thread with an empty copy. The virtual threads track goes into that. For request context, JDK 25 made scoped values final (JEP 506). A scoped value is bound for the duration of one call and is gone when the call returns, so there is nothing to forget: Java static final ScopedValue<String> TENANT = ScopedValue.newInstance(); // JDK 25+ void handle(Request r) { ScopedValue.where(TENANT, r.tenant()).run(() -> process(r)); // bound for this call only } Kotlin val TENANT: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() // JDK 25+ fun handle(r: Request) { ScopedValue.where(TENANT, r.tenant).run { process(r) } // bound for this call only } That code needs JDK 25 or later; on JDK 21 to 24 the API is a preview, so the labs, which compile for JDK 21, use ThreadLocal. Watch one customer's context leak into another's request Read ThreadLocalBleed. Six requests run one after another on a pool of one thread. The handler sets the user only when the request carries one. Predict what each request without a user runs as, in the leaky version and in the clean one. Run it. ThreadLocalBleed.java package workbench.concurrency.l11; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Six requests on a pool of one reused thread. The handler sets the user only when the request * carries one. A pool of 1 makes the bug happen every time; a pool of 200 makes it rare and random. */ public class ThreadLocalBleed { static final ThreadLocal<String> USER = new ThreadLocal<>(); static String leaky(String user) { if (user != null) USER.set(user); return "request(" + user + ") ran as " + USER.get(); } static String clean(String user) { if (user != null) USER.set(user); try { return "request(" + user + ") ran as " + USER.get(); } finally { USER.remove(); // leave the thread as you found it } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String[] requests = {"alice", null, "bob", null, null, "carol"}; for (Function<String, String> handler : java.util.List.<Function<String, String>>of(ThreadLocalBleed::leaky, ThreadLocalBleed::clean)) { ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); System.out.println("---"); for (String user : requests) System.out.println(" " + pool.submit(() -> handler.apply(user)).get()); pool.shutdown(); } } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.ThreadLocalBleed labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l11/ThreadLocalBleed.java ThreadLocalBleed.kt package workbench.concurrency.l11 import java.util.concurrent.Executors // Six requests on a pool of one reused thread. The handler sets the user only when the request // carries one. A pool of 1 makes the bug happen every time; a pool of 200 makes it rare and random. private val USER = ThreadLocal<String>() private fun leaky(user: String?): String { if (user != null) USER.set(user) return "request($user) ran as ${USER.get()}" } private fun clean(user: String?): String { if (user != null) USER.set(user) try { return "request($user) ran as ${USER.get()}" } finally { USER.remove() // leave the thread as you found it } } fun main() { val requests = listOf("alice", null, "bob", null, null, "carol") for (handler in listOf(::leaky, ::clean)) { val pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() println("---") for (user in requests) println(" " + pool.submit<String> { handler(user) }.get()) pool.shutdown() } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l11.ThreadLocalBleedKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l11/ThreadLocalBleed.kt Leaky: the first anonymous request runs as alice, and the next two run as bob, whoever that thread served last. Clean: every anonymous request runs as null, because remove() in finally put the thread back as it was. A pool of one makes it happen every time. With 200 threads it happens rarely and randomly, which is how it reaches production. JEP 506: Scoped Values read The most common mistake is setting a ThreadLocal and never clearing it, usually because the code was written and tested where each request seemed to get a fresh thread. On a pool, the value stays on the thread. The next request that doesn't set it reads the previous request's tenant, user or MDC fields, and the logs show one customer's id on another customer's payment. Unit tests rarely catch it, because each test usually runs on a fresh thread or in a fresh JVM. The fix is mechanical: every set is paired with a remove() in a finally, or replaced by a scoped value on JDK 25 and later. The lab's TenantScope goes one step further and restores the previous value, so nested calls work too.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Java and Kotlin
x: A deeply immutable value in Java and Kotlin Java record public record Settlement(String merchantId, List<Payment> payments) { public Settlement { payments = List.copyOf(payments); // reassign the parameter: the field gets the copy } } Kotlin class class Settlement(val merchantId: String, payments: List<Payment>) { val payments: List<Payment> = java.util.List.copyOf(payments) // a plain parameter, copied into a property } // a data class can't do this: its constructor parameters ARE the properties Both compile to a class with final fields, so both get the memory model's final-field guarantee. The difference is where the copy can go. A Java record's compact constructor may reassign its parameters before the fields are set, so payments = List.copyOf(payments) stores the copy. A Kotlin data class can't do that, because its primary-constructor parameters are the properties, so you use a plain class with a separate property, as here, or a private constructor and a factory. Kotlin's List type doesn't help as much as it looks: it's a read-only interface, and listOf or toList results can still be changed through a cast or from Java. java.util.List.copyOf gives you a list that is unmodifiable for everyone. Data class copy() is shallow too: the copy shares the same list.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Worked example
x: A shared constant that someone changed A payment service adds a card fee to every order. Money looks like a value, and CARD_FEE looks like a constant. Read it and find what changes, and for whom. public class Money { private long cents; private final Currency currency; public Money(long cents, Currency currency) { this.cents = cents; this.currency = currency; } public Money add(Money other) { // changes this object, then returns it this.cents += other.cents; return this; } public long cents() { return cents; } } static final Money CARD_FEE = new Money(30, EUR); // "a constant" Money total = order.amount().add(CARD_FEE); // also changes order.amount() class Money(private var centsValue: Long, val currency: Currency) { fun add(other: Money): Money { // changes this object, then returns it centsValue += other.centsValue return this } val cents: Long get() = centsValue } val CARD_FEE = Money(30, EUR) // "a constant" val total = order.amount.add(CARD_FEE) // also changes order.amount add changes the object it's called on. The line order.amount().add(CARD_FEE) changes the order's own amount. Somewhere else, CARD_FEE.add(surcharge) changes the fee for every request on every thread. And because cents is neither final nor volatile, other threads may see the old fee, the new one, or a mix, at different times. static final on the reference didn't make the object constant. Make Money a value: final fields, and operations that return a new instance. Now CARD_FEE can be read by 200 threads with no lock, and nobody can change it. public record Money(long cents, Currency currency) { public Money { Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency"); } public Money plus(Money other) { // 1. never change this; return a new value if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch"); return new Money(Math.addExact(cents, other.cents), currency); // 2. overflow fails loudly } } data class Money(val cents: Long, val currency: Currency) { operator fun plus(other: Money): Money { // 1. never change this; return a new value require(currency == other.currency) { "currency mismatch" } return copy(cents = Math.addExact(cents, other.cents)) // 2. overflow fails loudly } } Before reading on, explain to yourself why the record version needs no synchronization even though CARD_FEE is read by every request thread. Then look at the classic trap with immutable types, which catches people moving from mutable ones: calling the operation and ignoring the result. BigDecimal total = BigDecimal.ZERO; for (BigDecimal fee : fees) total.add(fee); // does nothing: the result is thrown away for (BigDecimal fee : fees) total = total.add(fee); // right var total = BigDecimal.ZERO for (fee in fees) total.add(fee) // does nothing: the result is thrown away for (fee in fees) total += fee // right: plus() returns a new BigDecimal Answer: the fields are final, set once in the constructor, and the object never changes, so every thread that can see the reference sees 30 EUR. There is nothing to race on. The price is an allocation per operation, which the JIT often removes when the object doesn't escape. For money, that trade is easy.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Lab
x: A deeply immutable quote and a tenant scope that cleans up labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l11/FxQuote.java labs/concurrency/src/main/java/workbench/concurrency/l11/TenantScope.java ./gradlew :concurrency:test --tests 'workbench.concurrency.l11.*' Run the tests. All six fail. The three FxQuote tests change the quote from outside, through the list you passed in, the list it returns, and its signature array. The three TenantScope tests run on a pool of one thread and find a tenant left over from an earlier call. Give FxQuote a compact constructor that replaces tiers with List.copyOf(tiers) and signature with a clone. Override signature() so it returns a clone, not the field. Fix TenantScope.runAs: remember the previous value, set the new one (or remove() for null), run the work in a try, and in finally put the previous value back (or remove() if there was none). Run the tests until all six pass. In a compact constructor you assign to the parameter (tiers = List.copyOf(tiers);), not to this.tiers. The record assigns the fields after your code runs. List.copyOf also rejects null elements, which is usually what you want in a quote. Restoring the previous value instead of always calling remove() makes nested calls work: an inner runAs must hand the thread back to the outer one, not wipe it. All six tests in DontShareTest pass. By the end you can remove shared mutable state instead of locking it: build deeply immutable objects, publish snapshots, keep state confined to one thread, hand objects over through a queue, and use ThreadLocal without leaking between requests.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Quiz
x: Which of these can be shared between threads with no synchronization at all? A record whose List<String> component is the caller's ArrayList A class with volatile fields and setters A final class whose private final fields are a String, an Instant and a BigDecimal, with no setters A record with an int[] component and the default accessor All three field types are immutable and the fields are final, so the object can never change and the final-field rule makes it visible correctly. The record with the caller's list and the record with an array can be changed from outside. volatile fields with setters make each write visible, but the object still changes under readers. A constructor stores this.items = Collections.unmodifiableList(items);. The caller later adds an item to its own items list. What does the object's list show? The original items only It throws UnsupportedOperationException in the caller The caller's add is ignored The new item too, because unmodifiableList is a view of the caller's list unmodifiableList only stops you from changing the list through that reference. It still reads the caller's list, so the caller's changes show through. List.copyOf makes a copy that nobody can change. From explicit locks: an FX rate table is replaced as a whole every 5 seconds and read 5,000 times a second. What is the simplest correct design? A ReentrantReadWriteLock around a HashMap A volatile field holding an immutable map, replaced with a freshly built Map.copyOf(...) on each refresh A ConcurrentHashMap refreshed with clear() and putAll() A synchronized getter and setter on a HashMap Readers never block, and each one sees one complete version, because the new map is built fully before one volatile write publishes it. The read-write lock also works, with more code and some cost on every read. clear plus putAll on a concurrent map lets readers see an empty or half-filled table. A Quarkus request handler does USER.set(request.user()) on a ThreadLocal when the request is authenticated, and never removes it. What does a later anonymous request on the same worker thread see? The previous request's user null, because each request gets a fresh thread An IllegalStateException A random user from another thread Worker threads come from a pool and are reused. The value stays on the thread until someone removes it, so the anonymous request runs as whoever that thread served last. Pair every set with remove() in finally. A producer puts an ArrayList of entries into a BlockingQueue, then calls clear() on the same list and refills it for the next batch. What does that do to the consumer? Nothing: take() returns a copy of the list Nothing: put made the list thread-safe The consumer can see a partly cleared or refilled batch, because the producer kept changing an object it had handed over put throws, because the list is already in the queue The queue hands over a reference, not a copy. put happens-before take only for what the producer did before the put. After that, the producer and consumer share one mutable list with no synchronization. Hand over a new list each time.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Explain it back
