h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Key terms
x: Immutable object An object whose state can't change after construction; safe to share without locks. Defensive copy Copying a mutable argument or return value so no one else can change your object through it. Shallow immutability Final references to objects that can still change, as in a record holding an ArrayList. Snapshot publication Replacing a whole immutable object through one volatile write, so readers see one complete version. Thread confinement Keeping mutable state reachable by only one thread. Ownership hand-off Passing an object to another thread, through a queue, and never touching it again. ThreadLocal A variable with a separate value per thread; values live as long as the thread unless removed. Scoped value A JDK 25 value bound for one call and its callees, gone when the call returns (JEP 506). What does a class need to be immutable? All fields final and set in the constructor, no setters, mutable components copied in and never handed out, and this doesn't escape during construction. What does the memory model guarantee for final fields? A thread that gets a reference to the object after its constructor finished sees the correct values of its final fields, even without synchronization. Is a record with a List component immutable? Only shallowly. Copy it in the compact constructor: items = List.copyOf(items);. Collections.unmodifiableList(list) vs List.copyOf(list)? unmodifiableList is a read-only view: the owner's later changes show through. List.copyOf is an unmodifiable copy that nobody can change. How do you share data that changes rarely, without locks? Build a new immutable snapshot, then publish it with one write to a volatile field (or an AtomicReference). Readers read the reference once. A pool thread runs a task that calls ThreadLocal.set and never remove(). What happens next? The value stays on the thread. The next task on that thread sees it if it doesn't set its own. What makes passing a mutable object through a BlockingQueue safe? put happens-before take, so the consumer sees everything done before the put, as long as the producer never touches the object again.

h: Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal · Go deeper
x: Each Thread object has its own small hash map for its thread locals, called ThreadLocalMap. The keys are weak references to the ThreadLocal objects, and the values are strong references. When a ThreadLocal itself becomes garbage, its key goes away, but the value stays in the map until a later get, set or remove on that thread happens to clean it up. On a pool thread that lives for days, that can be a long time. In application servers this is a famous leak: a value whose class came from a redeployed web application keeps that application's whole class loader alive. remove() avoids all of it. InheritableThreadLocal copies values from a parent thread to a child thread when the child is created. It does nothing useful with pools, because pool threads are created once, long before the request that submits work to them. Scoped values (JEP 506, final in JDK 25) fix the design problems rather than the symptoms. A binding is immutable: there is no set, so code deep in the call stack can't change the tenant under you. It has a clear lifetime: it ends when run or call returns, even on an exception. And it is cheap to share with child tasks: with structured concurrency, still a preview API in JDK 25, threads forked inside the scope see the same bindings without copying a map per thread. One immutability trap to know: an object is only safe to share through a data race if this didn't escape while the constructor was running. A constructor that registers this as a listener, or starts a thread that uses this, hands out the object before its final fields are guaranteed to be visible. Build first, register after. The memory model track's lesson on safe publication covers the full rules.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Producer-consumer: a bounded queue between two speeds
x: Most of the concurrent code in a backend is this shape. Something produces work at one speed, such as a Kafka consumer polling records or request threads accepting payments, and something else processes it at another speed, such as a writer that inserts into Oracle. A BlockingQueue sits between them. Bound the queue. A bounded queue is how a slow consumer pushes back on a fast producer: put waits when the queue is full, so the producer slows to the consumer's pace instead of filling memory. Lesson 9 of this track showed what the unbounded default does during an incident. The hard part is stopping. Consumers wait in take(), and take() never returns on an empty queue. Inside, it parks on the queue's own not-empty Condition (lesson 7 of this track), and only a put signals it. Once the producers are done, nothing ever will. The standard answer is a poison pill: a special element that means "no more work". Three rules make it work: Put the pills only after every producer has finished, so they land behind every real record. Put one pill per consumer. A pill is taken once. Compare against the pill by identity. A pill made with new String("PILL") is a unique object, so a real record that happens to read PILL is still a record. Java // consumer while (true) { String record = queue.take(); // waits while the queue is empty if (record == PILL) break; // identity: a record "PILL" is still a record settle(record); } // coordinator, after every producer has finished: for (int i = 0; i < consumers; i++) queue.put(PILL); // one pill per consumer Kotlin // consumer while (true) { val record = queue.take() // waits while the queue is empty if (record === PILL) break // identity: a record "PILL" is still a record settle(record) } // coordinator, after every producer has finished: repeat(consumers) { queue.put(PILL) } // one pill per consumer The figure shows the queue at shutdown: the last real records, then the pills. Each consumer drains records until it hits a pill, so no record is left behind and no consumer is left waiting. There are other ways to stop: interrupt the consumers, or have them poll with a timeout and check a flag. Interrupting is fast but drops whatever is still queued: take() checks the interrupt flag before it looks at the queue, so it throws even when records are waiting. Polling adds latency and a flag to get right. Pills are the clean choice when every queued record must be processed. The lab builds the whole pipeline. One pill per consumer, or not Read PoisonPills. Two producers put 1,000 records each into a queue of 4; three consumers take them. After the producers finish, main puts the pills. Run it. Note how many records each consumer handled. Run it with -Pargs=onepill. Predict how many consumers are still waiting after one second, and in which thread state. PoisonPills.java package workbench.concurrency.l12; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; /** * Two producers, three consumers, one bounded queue, shut down with poison pills. * Run with -Pargs=onepill to send a single pill instead of one per consumer. */ public class PoisonPills { @SuppressWarnings("StringOperationCanBeSimplified") static final String PILL = new String("PILL"); // compared by identity public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean onePill = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("onepill"); BlockingQueue<String> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4); List<Thread> consumers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int c = 0; c < 3; c++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { int done = 0; try { while (true) { String r = queue.take(); if (r == PILL) break; // this consumer stops; the others keep going done++; } System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " got its pill after " + done + " records"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "consumer-" + c); t.setDaemon(true); t.start(); consumers.add(t); } Thread[] producers = new Thread[2]; for (int p = 0; p < 2; p++) { int me = p; producers[p] = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) queue.put("settle-" + me + "-" + i); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); producers[p].start(); } for (Thread t : producers) t.join(); // 1. every producer is done... for (int c = 0; c < (onePill ? 1 : consumers.size()); c++) queue.put(PILL); // 2. ...then one pill each for (Thread t : consumers) t.join(1_000); List<Thread> stuck = consumers.stream().filter(Thread::isAlive).toList(); System.out.println("consumers still waiting: " + stuck.size() + (stuck.isEmpty() ? "" : " (" + stuck.get(0).getState() + " in take)")); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l12.PoisonPills labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l12/PoisonPills.java PoisonPills.kt package workbench.concurrency.l12 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two producers, three consumers, one bounded queue, shut down with poison pills. // Run with -Pargs=onepill to send a single pill instead of one per consumer. private val PILL = String(charArrayOf('P', 'I', 'L', 'L')) // a fresh object: compared by identity fun main(args: Array<String>) { val onePill = args.firstOrNull() == "onepill" val queue = ArrayBlockingQueue<String>(4) val consumers = List(3) { c -> thread(isDaemon = true, name = "consumer-$c") { var done = 0 while (true) { val r = queue.take() if (r === PILL) break // this consumer stops; the others keep going done++ } println("${Thread.currentThread().name} got its pill after $done records") } } val producers = List(2) { me -> thread { repeat(1_000) { i -> queue.put("settle-$me-$i") } } } producers.forEach { it.join() } // 1. every producer is done... repeat(if (onePill) 1 else consumers.size) { queue.put(PILL) } // 2. ...then one pill each consumers.forEach { it.join(1_000) } val stuck = consumers.count { it.isAlive } println("consumers still waiting: $stuck" + if (stuck > 0) " (${consumers.last { it.isAlive }.state} in take)" else "") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l12.PoisonPillsKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l12/PoisonPills.kt With one pill each, all three consumers report their pill, their counts add up to 2,000, and consumers still waiting: 0. The split changes from run to run. With onepill, one consumer stops and two are still waiting: consumers still waiting: 2 (WAITING in take). In a real service, that is a shutdown that never finishes. Records first, pills last, one pill per consumer. Each consumer stops at its own pill, after every real record has been taken. Producer-consumer is a kitchen pass: cooks put plates on a shelf with room for eight, and waiters take them. When the shelf is full the cooks wait, and at closing time the head chef puts one "kitchen closed" card on the shelf for each waiter. Dining philosophers is five people sharing five chopsticks; numbering the chopsticks and always grabbing the lower number first stops the standoff. Readers-writers is a museum room: visitors can share it, but the restorer needs it empty, and someone has to decide whether new visitors may keep walking in while the restorer waits at the door. The analogy breaks at the closing card: a waiter who finds it would tell the others. A consumer that takes a pill just stops, and the other consumers learn nothing.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Dining philosophers: five threads, five locks, one cycle
x: Five philosophers sit at a round table with one fork between each pair. To eat, a philosopher needs both neighbouring forks. Each one picks up the left fork, then the right. It works most of the time. Then, one day, all five pick up their left fork at the same moment. Each now waits for the right fork, which the next philosopher holds as a left fork. Nobody puts a fork down. That is the deadlock from lesson 6 of this track, with five locks instead of two: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and a circular wait around the table. It is also what transfers look like when each one locks two of many accounts. The simulator has three philosophers. Let them eat one at a time, then reset and give each one a single step first. There are two standard fixes, and each removes a different condition. Resource ordering removes the circular wait. Number the forks and always take the lower-numbered one first. Philosophers 0 to 3 still take left then right, but philosopher 4 needs forks 4 and 0, so it takes fork 0 first. Now a philosopher who holds a fork and waits always wants a higher-numbered one. A cycle would need someone to wait for a lower number than the one they hold, so it can't close, however many forks or accounts there are. Java int left = seat, right = (seat + 1) % n; ReentrantLock first = forks[Math.min(left, right)]; // the last philosopher reaches right first ReentrantLock second = forks[Math.max(left, right)]; Kotlin val left = seat val right = (seat + 1) % n val first = forks[minOf(left, right)] // the last philosopher reaches right first val second = forks[maxOf(left, right)] A waiter removes the chance that everyone holds one fork. Only four of the five may sit down at once. Four philosophers share five forks, so even if each seated one holds a fork, one fork is still free, and a seated philosopher next to it can pick it up and eat. A Semaphore(n - 1) is the waiter: Java seats.acquire(); // Semaphore(n - 1): one chair short, so someone can always eat try { eatWithBothForks(); } finally { seats.release(); } Kotlin seats.acquire() // Semaphore(n - 1): one chair short, so someone can always eat try { eatWithBothForks() } finally { seats.release() } A third fix, tryLock on the second fork with a random back-off, removes no-preemption, but brings back the livelock risk from lesson 6. Ordering is the one to use when you can number your resources. The waiter fits when you can't, or when you want to cap how many workers compete at all. Freeze the table, then fix it two ways Read Philosophers. Five philosophers try to eat 200 meals each, pausing 1 ms between their two forks. After 3 seconds, the demo asks the JVM which threads are deadlocked. Run it as is. Then run it with -Pargs=ordered and with -Pargs=waiter. Compare the meal counts, the times and the deadlock count. Philosophers.java package workbench.concurrency.l12; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * Five philosophers, five forks, 200 meals each. Run as is (left fork, then right), * with -Pargs=ordered (lower-numbered fork first) or -Pargs=waiter (at most 4 may sit down). */ public class Philosophers { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "naive"; int n = 5; ReentrantLock[] forks = new ReentrantLock[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) forks[i] = new ReentrantLock(); Semaphore seats = new Semaphore(n - 1); // the waiter: one chair short AtomicInteger meals = new AtomicInteger(); Thread[] ps = new Thread[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { int left = i, right = (i + 1) % n; int first = mode.equals("ordered") ? Math.min(left, right) : left; int second = mode.equals("ordered") ? Math.max(left, right) : right; ps[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int m = 0; m < 200; m++) { if (mode.equals("waiter")) seats.acquire(); try { forks[first].lock(); try { Thread.sleep(1); // reach for the other fork forks[second].lock(); try { meals.incrementAndGet(); } finally { forks[second].unlock(); } } finally { forks[first].unlock(); } } finally { if (mode.equals("waiter")) seats.release(); } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "philosopher-" + i); ps[i].setDaemon(true); ps[i].start(); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long deadline = t0 + 3_000_000_000L; // 3 s for the whole table for (Thread p : ps) p.join(Math.max(1, (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000)); long[] stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads(); System.out.printf("%s: %d of 1,000 meals in %d ms, deadlocked philosophers: %d%n", mode, meals.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, stuck == null ? 0 : stuck.length); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l12.Philosophers labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l12/Philosophers.java Philosophers.kt package workbench.concurrency.l12 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Five philosophers, five forks, 200 meals each. Run as is (left fork, then right), // with -Pargs=ordered (lower-numbered fork first) or -Pargs=waiter (at most 4 may sit down). fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "naive" val n = 5 val forks = Array(n) { ReentrantLock() } val seats = Semaphore(n - 1) // the waiter: one chair short val meals = AtomicInteger() val ps = List(n) { i -> val left = i val right = (i + 1) % n val first = if (mode == "ordered") minOf(left, right) else left val second = if (mode == "ordered") maxOf(left, right) else right thread(isDaemon = true, name = "philosopher-$i") { repeat(200) { if (mode == "waiter") seats.acquire() try { forks[first].withLock { Thread.sleep(1) // reach for the other fork forks[second].withLock { meals.incrementAndGet() } } } finally { if (mode == "waiter") seats.release() } } } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() val deadline = t0 + 3_000_000_000L // 3 s for the whole table ps.forEach { it.join(maxOf(1L, (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000)) } val stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads() println("%s: %d of 1,000 meals in %d ms, deadlocked philosophers: %d" .format(mode, meals.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, stuck?.size ?: 0)) } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l12.PhilosophersKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l12/Philosophers.kt As is: almost no meals (0 or 1 in runs here) and deadlocked philosophers: 5, found by ThreadMXBean because the forks are ReentrantLocks. Ordered and waiter: all 1,000 meals in about a second, and deadlocked philosophers: 0 (the waiter version was slightly faster in runs here). The Kafka-to-Oracle path in a payment service is producer-consumer: a poll loop produces records, a worker pool settles them, and a bounded queue between them is what keeps a slow database from turning into an out-of-memory crash. Shutdown is where it usually goes wrong. On SIGTERM the application gets a grace period (30 seconds by default in Kubernetes), and the pipeline has to stop polling, drain what is queued, commit offsets for what it finished, and stop. The worked example shows that order. Dining philosophers is any job that locks several resources at once: transfers that lock two accounts, a netting run that locks a merchant and a settlement batch. Readers-writers is every reference table you refresh while serving traffic.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Readers-writers: decide who waits
x: Many threads read a shared table and a few write it: BIN ranges read on every payment, refreshed once an hour. Readers can share; a writer needs the table to itself. The question is what happens when both are waiting, and each answer starves somebody. Readers first lets a new reader in whenever no writer is inside. With a steady stream of overlapping readers, the reader count never drops to zero, so the writer never gets in. The refresh starves. Writers first makes new readers wait as soon as a writer is waiting. The refresh gets in quickly, but under a stream of writers, readers starve. A fair policy serves threads in arrival order. Nobody starves, and throughput drops, because readers that could have shared now wait behind a writer that arrived first. The JDK's ReentrantReadWriteLock picks a middle path. In its default non-fair mode it doesn't promise an order, but a thread that asks for the read lock waits if the thread at the head of the queue wants to write. In practice that keeps a writer from being starved by a stream of new readers. Fair mode gives strict arrival order: Java new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); // non-fair: a new reader waits if a writer is next in line new ReentrantReadWriteLock(true); // fair: strict arrival order, lower throughput Kotlin ReentrantReadWriteLock() // non-fair: a new reader waits if a writer is next in line ReentrantReadWriteLock(true) // fair: strict arrival order, lower throughput The Try it shows the difference. A textbook readers-first lock, written with synchronized, makes a writer wait as long as the readers keep coming, while ReentrantReadWriteLock lets it in within a couple of milliseconds. Before choosing a policy, ask whether readers need a lock at all. If the writer replaces the whole table, the snapshot pattern from lesson 11 of this track lets readers read an immutable map with no lock and no waiting, and the question of who starves goes away. Oracle takes the same approach with multiversion reads: readers see a consistent older version and don't wait for writers. Starve a writer Read ReadersWriters. Four readers hold the lock for 2 ms at a time, overlapping, for 1.5 seconds. 100 ms in, one writer asks for the lock. The demo measures how long it waits, first with a hand-written readers-first lock, then with ReentrantReadWriteLock. Predict both waits. Run it. ReadersWriters.java package workbench.concurrency.l12; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock; /** * Four readers keep a rate table busy for 1.5 s, overlapping all the time. One writer wants in once. * How long does it wait with a hand-written readers-first lock, and with ReentrantReadWriteLock? */ public class ReadersWriters { interface RW { void readLock() throws InterruptedException; void readUnlock(); void writeLock() throws InterruptedException; void writeUnlock(); } /** The textbook readers-first lock: a reader may enter whenever no writer is INSIDE. */ static final class ReadersFirst implements RW { private int readers; private boolean writing; public synchronized void readLock() throws InterruptedException { while (writing) wait(); readers++; } public synchronized void readUnlock() { if (--readers == 0) notifyAll(); } public synchronized void writeLock() throws InterruptedException { while (writing || readers > 0) wait(); writing = true; } public synchronized void writeUnlock() { writing = false; notifyAll(); } } static final class Jdk implements RW { private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); public void readLock() { rw.readLock().lock(); } public void readUnlock() { rw.readLock().unlock(); } public void writeLock() { rw.writeLock().lock(); } public void writeUnlock() { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } } static long writerWaitMs(RW lock) throws InterruptedException { long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_500_000_000L; Thread[] readers = new Thread[4]; for (int i = 0; i < readers.length; i++) { readers[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { lock.readLock(); try { Thread.sleep(2); } finally { lock.readUnlock(); } // a 2 ms read } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); readers[i].start(); Thread.sleep(1); // stagger them so they overlap } Thread.sleep(100); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); lock.writeLock(); // the refresh wants in long waited = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; lock.writeUnlock(); for (Thread r : readers) r.join(); return waited; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("readers-first lock: writer waited " + writerWaitMs(new ReadersFirst()) + " ms"); System.out.println("ReentrantReadWriteLock: writer waited " + writerWaitMs(new Jdk()) + " ms"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l12.ReadersWriters labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l12/ReadersWriters.java ReadersWriters.kt package workbench.concurrency.l12 import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Four readers keep a rate table busy for 1.5 s, overlapping all the time. One writer wants in once. // How long does it wait with a hand-written readers-first lock, and with ReentrantReadWriteLock? private interface RwLock { fun readLock(); fun readUnlock(); fun writeLock(); fun writeUnlock() } // The textbook readers-first lock: a reader may enter whenever no writer is INSIDE. private class ReadersFirst : RwLock { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val changed = lock.newCondition() private var readers = 0 private var writing = false override fun readLock() { lock.withLock { while (writing) changed.await(); readers++ } } override fun readUnlock() { lock.withLock { if (--readers == 0) changed.signalAll() } } override fun writeLock() { lock.withLock { while (writing || readers > 0) changed.await(); writing = true } } override fun writeUnlock() { lock.withLock { writing = false; changed.signalAll() } } } private class Jdk : RwLock { private val rw = ReentrantReadWriteLock() override fun readLock() = rw.readLock().lock() override fun readUnlock() = rw.readLock().unlock() override fun writeLock() = rw.writeLock().lock() override fun writeUnlock() = rw.writeLock().unlock() } private fun writerWaitMs(lock: RwLock): Long { val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_500_000_000L val readers = List(4) { thread { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { lock.readLock() try { Thread.sleep(2) } finally { lock.readUnlock() } // a 2 ms read } }.also { Thread.sleep(1) } // stagger them so they overlap } Thread.sleep(100) val t0 = System.nanoTime() lock.writeLock() // the refresh wants in val waited = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 lock.writeUnlock() readers.forEach { it.join() } return waited } fun main() { println("readers-first lock: writer waited ${writerWaitMs(ReadersFirst())} ms") println("ReentrantReadWriteLock: writer waited ${writerWaitMs(Jdk())} ms") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l12.ReadersWritersKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l12/ReadersWriters.kt Readers-first: the writer waits about 1,400 ms, until the readers stop on their own. ReentrantReadWriteLock: about 1 to 2 ms, because new readers queue behind the waiting writer instead of overtaking it. jcstress samples, including Classic_01_DiningPhilosophers and Classic_02_ProducerConsumerProblem read The most common mistake is getting the poison pills wrong at shutdown: putting a single pill for several consumers, or putting the pills before every producer has finished. With one pill, the other consumers wait in take() forever and the shutdown hangs until the platform kills the pod, so whatever they were holding is lost. With pills sent too early, consumers stop while producers are still putting, the bounded queue fills, and the producers block forever instead. Both bugs pass every test that never shuts the pipeline down. The fix is the order in this lesson: stop the producers, join them, put one pill per consumer, then join the consumers with a deadline.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Java and Kotlin
x: Stopping consumers: pills in Java, a closed channel in Kotlin coroutines Java, BlockingQueue for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { pool.add(start(() -> { while (true) { String r = queue.take(); if (r == PILL) return; // each consumer needs its own pill settle(r); } })); } for (Thread p : producers) p.join(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) queue.put(PILL); // 4 consumers, 4 pills for (Thread c : pool) c.join(); Kotlin, kotlinx.coroutines Channel // a Channel can be closed, so there are no pills coroutineScope { val records = Channel<String>(capacity = 8) val producers = sources.map { src -> launch { for (r in src) records.send(r) } } repeat(4) { launch { for (r in records) settle(r) } } // each loop ends when the channel is closed AND empty producers.joinAll() records.close() // "no more records": consumers drain, then stop } With threads and a BlockingQueue, Kotlin code looks just like the Java version: the queue has no notion of "closed", so you still need one pill per consumer, compared with ===. The real difference comes with coroutines. A Channel can be closed: close() means no more elements, and every for (r in records) loop ends once the channel is closed and empty, however many consumers there are. That removes the whole class of pill-counting bugs. coroutineScope also waits for every consumer it launched, so there is no join loop to forget. The coroutines track covers channels properly.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Worked example
x: Shut a Kafka-to-database pipeline down without losing records A pipeline polls Kafka on two producer threads and settles records on four consumer threads, through a bounded queue. On SIGTERM, someone wrote this. What happens to the records already in the queue, and to the batch a consumer is halfway through? void shutdown() { for (Thread c : consumers) c.interrupt(); // stop now, whatever is in the queue for (Thread p : producers) p.interrupt(); } fun shutdown() { consumers.forEach { it.interrupt() } // stop now, whatever is in the queue producers.forEach { it.interrupt() } } Interrupting a consumer that waits in take() stops it at once, so everything still queued is dropped. A consumer in the middle of a database call may abort it halfway. And a producer may have polled records it never put. Because offsets were committed only for processed records, Kafka will redeliver what was lost, but the shutdown did a lot of work for nothing, and only idempotent settlement (lesson 3 of this track) keeps the redelivery safe. The orderly version, with subgoal labels. running is a volatile flag the producers check in their poll loops. void shutdown() throws InterruptedException { running = false; // 1. producers stop polling Kafka for (Thread p : producers) p.join(); // 2. wait until no producer can put again for (int i = 0; i < consumers.size(); i++) { queue.put(PILL); // 3. one pill per consumer, behind every real record } long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(30); for (Thread c : consumers) { c.join(Math.max(1, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(deadline - System.nanoTime()))); // 4. one deadline for all } for (Thread c : consumers) if (c.isAlive()) c.interrupt(); // 5. still busy: interrupt; Kafka redelivers } fun shutdown() { running = false // 1. producers stop polling Kafka producers.forEach { it.join() } // 2. wait until no producer can put again repeat(consumers.size) { queue.put(PILL) } // 3. one pill per consumer, behind every real record val deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(30) for (c in consumers) { c.join(maxOf(1L, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(deadline - System.nanoTime()))) // 4. one deadline for all } consumers.filter { it.isAlive }.forEach { it.interrupt() } // 5. still busy: interrupt; Kafka redelivers } Before reading on, explain to yourself: why must step 2 finish before step 3 starts? Answer: a pill put while a producer is still running can land in front of that producer's last records. A consumer that takes the pill stops; with all consumers stopped and the queue bounded, the producer then blocks in put forever, and the shutdown hangs on step 2 of the next attempt. Joining the producers first guarantees that every real record is already ahead of the pills. Step 5 is the safety net. If the database is down, the consumers can't drain the queue within the grace period. Interrupting them is then the right call: the records they didn't finish were never committed to Kafka, so another instance will process them after a rebalance. Orderly shutdown and idempotent processing work together; neither is enough alone.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Quiz
x: A coordinator puts the poison pills for 4 consumers right after starting the producers, without waiting for them. The queue is bounded. What can happen? Nothing: the pills wait at the back of the queue The consumers take the pills early and stop, the queue fills, and the producers block in put forever The pills are rejected because the queue is full Each consumer processes exactly one record Pills are ordinary elements in arrival order. Put early, they sit in front of records that producers add later. Consumers stop at them, nothing drains the queue any more, and the producers block once it is full. Join the producers first. Five philosophers each take the left fork, then the right one, and sometimes all deadlock. Which change removes the deadlock? Make every fork a fair ReentrantLock Add a random sleep before picking up the left fork Always take the lower-numbered fork first, so the last philosopher reaches right first Use synchronized instead of ReentrantLock With one global order, no cycle of waiting can form, so circular wait is gone. Fair locks change who gets a free fork next, not the cycle. A random sleep only makes the bad timing rarer. synchronized deadlocks exactly the same way. A hand-written readers-first lock protects a BIN table. Readers arrive constantly and overlap. The hourly refresh calls writeLock(). What happens? The refresh waits until the readers stop arriving, which may be never: writer starvation The refresh gets in within one read's duration The refresh throws IllegalStateException Readers and the writer take turns Readers-first admits a new reader whenever no writer is inside, so the reader count never reaches zero while readers overlap. The writer waits for a moment that never comes. ReentrantReadWriteLock makes new readers queue behind a waiting writer, and a snapshot avoids locking reads at all. From synchronizers: the waiter fix for five philosophers uses a Semaphore. Why new Semaphore(4) and not new Semaphore(5)? To save one thread With 4 seated, at least one of them can always pick up both forks, so the cycle can't involve all five A semaphore can't have more permits than threads Fairness requires one fewer permit than threads With five permits, all five can sit, each take a left fork and deadlock as before. With four, at most four hold a fork, and five forks between four people means at least one of them can take both. Permits limit how many compete, which is what breaks the cycle here. A consumer checks if (record.equals("POISON")) break;, and the pill is the literal "POISON". What is the risk? equals is too slow for a hot loop None: a real record never contains that text The pill might be garbage collected A real record with that text stops a consumer early and is never processed Merchant references and free-text fields can contain anything, including the pill's text. With equals, such a record shuts a consumer down and is silently dropped. A pill created as a unique object and compared with == (or === in Kotlin) can't be confused with data.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Key terms
x: Producer-consumer Threads that create work hand it to threads that process it, usually through a queue. Poison pill A special queue element that tells one consumer to stop. Back-pressure A full bounded queue making producers wait, so they slow to the consumers' pace. Dining philosophers The classic deadlock: each thread holds one resource and waits for its neighbour's. Resource ordering Taking locks in one global order so no cycle of waiting can form. Readers-writers Sharing data between many readers and a few writers, and deciding who waits. Writer starvation A writer that never gets in because readers keep holding the lock. Poison pills: how many, and when do you put them? One per consumer, and only after every producer has finished putting. Why compare a poison pill with == rather than equals? So a real record with the same text isn't mistaken for the pill. Make the pill a unique object, such as new String("PILL"). Why bound the queue between producers and consumers? So put makes producers wait when consumers fall behind (back-pressure), instead of buffering until memory runs out. Which deadlock condition does "always take the lower-numbered fork first" remove? Circular wait: with one global order, no cycle of waiting threads can form. How does a Semaphore(n - 1) "waiter" prevent the dining philosophers deadlock? At most n - 1 philosophers compete for n forks, so at least one can always get both. Readers-first lock: who starves? Writers. With overlapping readers the reader count never reaches zero, so the writer never gets in. What does non-fair ReentrantReadWriteLock do when a writer is waiting and a new reader arrives? The reader usually waits if the writer is at the head of the queue, so a stream of readers doesn't starve the writer.

h: Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers · Go deeper
x: Poison pills are one of several ways to stop consumers. Executors use interruption: shutdownNow() interrupts every worker, and tasks are expected to stop when interrupted, as lesson 2 of this track described. A poll(timeout) loop that checks a volatile flag is simple but makes shutdown wait for up to one timeout, and adds a flag that every loop must check. Kotlin channels and reactive streams have completion built in, which is why they need no pills. Kafka's own consumer has wakeup(), which makes a blocked poll() throw WakeupException, the usual way to stop a poll loop from another thread. The dining philosophers problem has more solutions than the two here. Chandy and Misra's solution passes "dirty" and "clean" forks between neighbours with requests, which avoids both deadlock and starvation and works across machines, at the cost of messages. A plain tryLock with back-off works, but needs randomness to avoid livelock. All of them are ways of removing one of the four conditions from lesson 6. Readers-writers shows up all over databases. Oracle uses multiversion read consistency: a query reads the version of each block as of when the query started, so readers don't wait for writers and writers don't wait for readers. That is the immutable-snapshot idea from lesson 11 applied to storage, and it's why the problem rarely appears at the SQL level. Writers still wait for other writers on the same rows. If you want to see these problems under a real stress harness, the jcstress samples include Classic_01_DiningPhilosophers and Classic_02_ProducerConsumerProblem. The next lesson shows how to run jcstress and read its results.

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · A concurrency test has to make threads collide
x: A race only shows up when threads overlap at the wrong moment. A test that doesn't force overlap is a single-threaded test with extra steps. Five habits turn it into a stress test: Hold every thread at a start latch and release them together. Lesson 3 of this track built this. Use more threads than cores, so the scheduler interleaves them. Run many operations per thread, so the threads overlap for a long time. Run many rounds with a fresh state each time. One round is one sample of the interleavings. Check an invariant when all threads are done: totals that must add up, an amount that must never be exceeded. Never assert on timings. The lab packs those habits into a small harness, shaped like jcstress: a setup that builds fresh state, an actor that every thread runs over and over, and an invariant checked after join(). The figure shows one round. Java record Round(RefundLedger ledger, AtomicLong approved) {} int failed = Stress.failingRounds(20, 8, 2_000, () -> new Round(new RefundLedger(Map.of("pay-1", 10_000L)), new AtomicLong()), // fresh state per round r -> { if (r.ledger().refund("pay-1", 1)) r.approved().incrementAndGet(); }, // every thread, over and over r -> r.approved().get() == 10_000 && r.ledger().refunded("pay-1") == 10_000); // must hold at the end assertThat(failed).isZero(); Kotlin class Round(val ledger: RefundLedger, val approved: AtomicLong) val failed = Stress.failingRounds(20, 8, 2_000, { Round(RefundLedger(mapOf("pay-1" to 10_000L)), AtomicLong()) }, // fresh state per round { r -> if (r.ledger.refund("pay-1", 1)) r.approved.incrementAndGet() }, // every thread, over and over { r -> r.approved.get() == 10_000L && r.ledger.refunded("pay-1") == 10_000L }) // must hold at the end assertThat(failed).isZero() Eight threads try 2,000 one-cent refunds each against 10,000 cents captured, so a correct ledger approves exactly 10,000. The racy ledger in the lab approves all 16,000. Two more rules keep these tests from hurting you. Put a timeout on every one, with JUnit's @Timeout or assertTimeoutPreemptively, so a deadlock fails the test in seconds instead of hanging CI for an hour. And remember what a pass means: this run found no failure. A stress test can prove that a race exists. It can never prove that one doesn't, which is why the design rules from earlier lessons matter more than any test. The same bug, tested two ways Read NaiveVsStress. It tests the racy counter from lesson 3 twenty times the usual way (2 threads, 1,000 hits, no start line), then twenty times as a stress test (8 threads, 100,000 hits, start latch). Predict how many runs of each fail. Run it two or three times. NaiveVsStress.java package workbench.concurrency.l13; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; /** The same racy counter, tested twice: the way most tests are written, and the way that finds the bug. */ public class NaiveVsStress { static final class Counter { volatile int count; // volatile only stops the JIT from hiding the race (lesson 3) void hit() { count++; } // the bug: read, add, write } // 2 threads, 1,000 hits each, no start line static boolean naiveRound() throws InterruptedException { Counter c = new Counter(); Thread a = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) c.hit(); }); Thread b = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) c.hit(); }); a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join(); return c.count == 2_000; } // 8 threads, 100,000 hits each, released together static boolean stressRound() throws InterruptedException { Counter c = new Counter(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int t = 0; t < ts.length; t++) { ts[t] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) c.hit(); }); ts[t].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); return c.count == 800_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int naiveFailed = 0, stressFailed = 0; for (int r = 0; r < 20; r++) if (!naiveRound()) naiveFailed++; for (int r = 0; r < 20; r++) if (!stressRound()) stressFailed++; System.out.println("naive test (2 threads x 1,000, no start line): failed " + naiveFailed + " of 20 runs"); System.out.println("stress test (8 threads x 100,000, start latch): failed " + stressFailed + " of 20 runs"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l13.NaiveVsStress labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l13/NaiveVsStress.java NaiveVsStress.kt package workbench.concurrency.l13 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import kotlin.concurrent.thread // The same racy counter, tested twice: the way most tests are written, and the way that finds the bug. private class RacyCounter { @Volatile var count = 0 // @Volatile only stops the JIT from hiding the race (lesson 3) fun hit() { count++ } // the bug: read, add, write } // 2 threads, 1,000 hits each, no start line private fun naiveRound(): Boolean { val c = RacyCounter() val a = thread { repeat(1_000) { c.hit() } } val b = thread { repeat(1_000) { c.hit() } } a.join(); b.join() return c.count == 2_000 } // 8 threads, 100,000 hits each, released together private fun stressRound(): Boolean { val c = RacyCounter() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val ts = List(8) { thread { go.await(); repeat(100_000) { c.hit() } } } go.countDown() ts.forEach { it.join() } return c.count == 800_000 } fun main() { val naiveFailed = (1..20).count { !naiveRound() } val stressFailed = (1..20).count { !stressRound() } println("naive test (2 threads x 1,000, no start line): failed $naiveFailed of 20 runs") println("stress test (8 threads x 100,000, start latch): failed $stressFailed of 20 runs") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l13.NaiveVsStressKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l13/NaiveVsStress.kt The naive test fails rarely, 0 to 6 runs of 20 here, and a different number each time. The stress test fails 20 of 20. Same code, same bug. Only the second test is worth having in CI. One round of a stress test: fresh state, all actors released together, join, check the invariant. Repeat for many rounds. A stress test is a crash test: you don't learn anything by driving the car gently around the car park; you build a fresh car, drive it into the wall at speed, inspect it, and do it again many times. Replacing sleeps with latches is the difference between "wait ten minutes, then check whether the pizza arrived" and "open the door when the bell rings". jcstress is a test track that drives millions of cars in slightly different ways and records every kind of damage. A thread dump is a photo of the traffic; JFR is the traffic camera's recording. The analogy breaks at the crash test: a car that survived a thousand crashes really is strong. Code that passed a thousand stress rounds may still have a race the test never hit.

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · Replace sleeps with latches, and guesses with deadlines
x: Thread.sleep in a test is a guess about how long something takes. On your laptop the guess is generous and the test is slow. On a busy CI machine the guess is too short and the test fails for no reason. Both are bad, and the second teaches the team to ignore red builds. Wait for the event itself, and use the timeout only as a deadline far above any real duration: Java // flaky: hopes 50 ms is enough on every machine, and is slow on all of them worker.submit(payment); Thread.sleep(50); assertThat(store.status(payment.id())).isEqualTo(SETTLED); // solid: wait for the event itself, with a deadline far above any real duration CountDownLatch settled = new CountDownLatch(1); store.onSettled(id -> settled.countDown()); worker.submit(payment); assertThat(settled.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue(); assertThat(store.status(payment.id())).isEqualTo(SETTLED); Kotlin // flaky: hopes 50 ms is enough on every machine, and is slow on all of them worker.submit(payment) Thread.sleep(50) assertThat(store.status(payment.id)).isEqualTo(SETTLED) // solid: wait for the event itself, with a deadline far above any real duration val settled = CountDownLatch(1) store.onSettled { settled.countDown() } worker.submit(payment) assertThat(settled.await(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue() assertThat(store.status(payment.id)).isEqualTo(SETTLED) The latch version is fast when things are fast and patient when the machine is slow. It also gives you a clear failure, "not settled within 10 s", instead of a wrong status. The same tools let you hold a thread at a known point, which makes many concurrency tests deterministic. Give the code under test a fake dependency that blocks on a latch: Java class BlockingIssuer implements Issuer { final CountDownLatch inCall = new CountDownLatch(1); final CountDownLatch release = new CountDownLatch(1); @Override public Result authorize(Request r) throws InterruptedException { inCall.countDown(); // 1. tell the test: a thread is inside the call release.await(); // 2. hold it here until the test says go return Result.APPROVED; } } Kotlin class BlockingIssuer : Issuer { val inCall = CountDownLatch(1) val release = CountDownLatch(1) override fun authorize(r: Request): Result { inCall.countDown() // 1. tell the test: a thread is inside the call release.await() // 2. hold it here until the test says go return Result.APPROVED } } Now the test can wait on inCall, then check what other threads see while one is known to be inside the call. With the IssuerGate from lesson 10 set to one permit, a second caller with a 100 ms limit must time out. Then the test opens release and checks the clean-up. No sleeps, no luck. When there's no hook to wait on, poll for the condition with a short sleep and an overall deadline, rather than sleeping once and hoping. Checking Thread.getState() until the threads you expect are BLOCKED or WAITING is a common way to know they have queued up. The worked example uses it. Make a test flaky on purpose Read SleepVsLatch. Eight threads burn every core, like a busy CI box. A background worker settles a payment in about 2 ms. One test sleeps 3 ms and checks; the other waits on a latch for up to 5 seconds. Each runs 100 times. Predict the failure counts. Run it, then change the sleep to 10 ms and run it again. SleepVsLatch.java package workbench.concurrency.l13; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A test checks that a background worker settles a payment. One version sleeps 3 ms and hopes; * the other waits on a latch. Both run 100 times while 8 threads keep every core busy, like a CI box. */ public class SleepVsLatch { static volatile boolean burn = true; // the code under test: settles on another thread, about 2 ms of work static Thread settleAsync(Runnable whenDone) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { long end = System.nanoTime() + 2_000_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait(); whenDone.run(); }); t.start(); return t; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread b = new Thread(() -> { while (burn) Thread.onSpinWait(); }); // a busy machine b.setDaemon(true); b.start(); } int sleepFailed = 0, latchFailed = 0; for (int run = 0; run < 100; run++) { boolean[] settled = {false}; Thread t = settleAsync(() -> settled[0] = true); Thread.sleep(3); // "should be enough" if (!settled[0]) sleepFailed++; // (a racy read too, which is the point) t.join(); } for (int run = 0; run < 100; run++) { CountDownLatch settled = new CountDownLatch(1); settleAsync(settled::countDown); if (!settled.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) latchFailed++; // waits exactly as long as needed } burn = false; System.out.println("sleep(3) then assert: failed " + sleepFailed + " of 100"); System.out.println("latch.await(5 s): failed " + latchFailed + " of 100"); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l13.SleepVsLatch labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l13/SleepVsLatch.java SleepVsLatch.kt package workbench.concurrency.l13 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.concurrent.thread // A test checks that a background worker settles a payment. One version sleeps 3 ms and hopes; // the other waits on a latch. Both run 100 times while 8 threads keep every core busy, like a CI box. @Volatile private var burn = true // the code under test: settles on another thread, about 2 ms of work private fun settleAsync(whenDone: () -> Unit): Thread = thread { val end = System.nanoTime() + 2_000_000 while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait() whenDone() } fun main() { repeat(8) { thread(isDaemon = true) { while (burn) Thread.onSpinWait() } } // a busy machine var sleepFailed = 0 var latchFailed = 0 repeat(100) { var settled = false val t = settleAsync { settled = true } Thread.sleep(3) // "should be enough" if (!settled) sleepFailed++ // (a racy read too, which is the point) t.join() } repeat(100) { val settled = CountDownLatch(1) settleAsync { settled.countDown() } if (!settled.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) latchFailed++ // waits exactly as long as needed } burn = false println("sleep(3) then assert: failed $sleepFailed of 100") println("latch.await(5 s): failed $latchFailed of 100") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l13.SleepVsLatchKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l13/SleepVsLatch.kt The sleep version failed in about a quarter of the runs here (24 and 32 of 100). The latch version failed 0 times. A 10 ms sleep fails less often, but it can still fail, and it makes every run slower. In a Quarkus service, keep stress tests in their own JUnit tag so the normal build stays fast, and run them on CI where machines are busy, since busy machines interleave more. Integration tests with Testcontainers, Kafka and Oracle check wiring, not thread safety; they run too few concurrent operations to find a race. When a pod stops answering, take three thread dumps before anyone restarts it: kubectl exec <pod> -- jcmd 1 Thread.print -l works when the JVM is PID 1. When latency creeps up without errors, start a JFR recording on the pod and look at JavaMonitorEnter and ThreadPark: a lock that every request waits on shows up as hundreds of events on the same class.

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · Let jcstress search the interleavings for you
x: Some bugs need millions of attempts and a weak-memory CPU to show up at all. A weak-memory CPU, such as ARM, may let other cores see one core's writes in a different order than it made them. jcstress is the OpenJDK harness for exactly that. It runs tiny tests millions of times, with careful control over how threads start and where state lives, and counts every outcome it sees. The latest tagged release is 0.16, from February 2023; the master branch is 0.17-SNAPSHOT. A test is a class with shared @State, two or more @Actor methods that run at the same time, and a result object, here II_Result with two int fields. @Outcome annotations say which results are allowed: import org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.*; import org.openjdk.jcstress.infra.results.II_Result; import static org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.Expect.*; @JCStressTest @Outcome(id = "1, 2", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "actor1 went first") @Outcome(id = "2, 1", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "actor2 went first") @Outcome(id = "1, 1", expect = ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING, desc = "both read 0: one increment lost") @State public class RefundCounterRace { int refunds; // shared state, fresh for every sample @Actor public void actor1(II_Result r) { r.r1 = ++refunds; } @Actor public void actor2(II_Result r) { r.r2 = ++refunds; } } It is a Java-only tool: tests are processed by an annotation processor at build time, so there is no Kotlin twin here. The outcome labels are the part to learn: ACCEPTABLE is a correct result. ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING is allowed but worth seeing, usually the race the test is about. Here, "1, 1" means both actors read 0: an increment was lost. FORBIDDEN must never happen. If jcstress observes it even once, the test fails. For each test jcstress reports every observed outcome with how many times it occurred and its label. Results depend on the hardware: x86 keeps stores in order, so some memory-model anomalies that ARM machines (Apple Silicon, AWS Graviton) show regularly may never appear on an Intel laptop. Interesting means allowed, not guaranteed to appear. The README documents a Maven archetype and no official Gradle setup, so try it in a separate Maven project. The jcstress samples on GitHub are a course in themselves; each has the outcomes it expects in its source. Run a jcstress test (optional, needs Maven and network) In a scratch folder outside the labs, generate a jcstress project with the archetype command below (from the jcstress README). Add RefundCounterRace from this section to the generated sources, build, and run only that test with -t. Find the line for outcome 1, 1. Then change int refunds to an AtomicInteger and both actors to incrementAndGet(), rebuild and run again. terminal mvn archetype:generate -DinteractiveMode=false -DarchetypeGroupId=org.openjdk.jcstress \ -DarchetypeArtifactId=jcstress-java-test-archetype -DgroupId=org.sample -DartifactId=test -Dversion=1.0 cd test # put RefundCounterRace.java next to the generated sample test, then: mvn clean verify java -jar target/jcstress.jar -t RefundCounterRace The first run reports 1, 2 and 2, 1 as acceptable and 1, 1 as interesting, observed some percentage of the time (the jcstress samples record a few percent for this kind of test; your count will differ). With AtomicInteger, 1, 1 is never observed. If you mark 1, 1 as FORBIDDEN in the racy version, the test fails. jcstress (README: archetype, running, modes) docs jcstress samples read

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · When it hangs, take dumps; when it's slow, record JFR
x: In production you debug with what the JVM can tell you about itself. Two tools cover most cases. A thread dump answers "where is every thread right now, and what is it waiting for". jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l prints each thread's state and stack, the java.util.concurrent locks it owns, and a deadlock report if there is a cycle (lesson 6 of this track). The state line is the first thing to read: What the dump says What the thread is doing RUNNABLE Running, ready to run, or blocked inside native I/O such as a socket read BLOCKED (on object monitor) Waiting to enter a synchronized block that another thread holds WAITING (parking) Parked by java.util.concurrent: a lock, latch, queue or semaphore; the parking to wait for line names it WAITING (on object monitor) Inside Object.wait() TIMED_WAITING The same, with a timeout, or in sleep One dump is a photo. Take three, a few seconds apart. A thread in the same frame each time is stuck; a thread that moves is busy. Thirty threads WAITING (parking) on the same lock in every dump send you looking for its owner, which -l names. For tooling, Thread.dump_to_file -format=json writes JSON; on JDK 21 it has only names and stacks per thread, and from JDK 25 it adds state and lock fields. Java Flight Recorder answers "what were threads waiting on over the last minute, and for how long". It is built into the JVM and cheap enough for production. jdk.JavaMonitorEnter records each wait to enter a synchronized block longer than a threshold, with the monitor's class, the duration and the previous owner. jdk.JavaMonitorWait covers Object.wait(), and jdk.ThreadPark covers ReentrantLock and the other java.util.concurrent waits. JDK 25 added jdk.JavaMonitorStatistics and jdk.JavaMonitorNotify. jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l # states, stacks, owned j.u.c locks, deadlocks jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json t.json # JSON; per-thread state and lock fields need JDK 25+ jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=locks.jfr jfr summary locks.jfr # how many events of each type jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter locks.jfr # who waited for which monitor, how long, after whom No JFR event reports deadlocks; for those, use a dump or ThreadMXBean. In a container the JVM is often PID 1, so jcmd 1 Thread.print inside the pod is the quickest start. Record contention with JFR Read JfrContention. It starts a JFR recording from inside the program, runs six threads for one second (three fight over a monitor, three over a ReentrantLock), then reads the recording back. Run it. Which event type does each kind of lock produce? Run jfr summary and then jfr print --events jdk.JavaMonitorEnter on the file the demo printed. Find previousOwner. JfrContention.java package workbench.concurrency.l13; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; import jdk.jfr.Recording; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedEvent; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile; /** * Records one second of lock contention with Java Flight Recorder, from inside the program, * then reads the recording back and summarizes it. The .jfr file is kept for the jfr tool. */ public class JfrContention { static final Object ledgerMonitor = new Object(); static final ReentrantLock batchLock = new ReentrantLock(); static void busy(long micros) { long end = System.nanoTime() + micros * 1_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Path file = Files.createTempFile("contention-", ".jfr"); try (Recording rec = new Recording()) { rec.enable("jdk.JavaMonitorEnter").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)); // waited > 1 ms for a monitor rec.enable("jdk.ThreadPark").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)); // parked > 1 ms (j.u.c locks) rec.start(); long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L; Thread[] ts = new Thread[6]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { boolean useMonitor = i % 2 == 0; ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (useMonitor) { synchronized (ledgerMonitor) { busy(3_000); } // hold it 3 ms } else { batchLock.lock(); try { busy(3_000); } finally { batchLock.unlock(); } } } }, (useMonitor ? "ledger-" : "batch-") + i); ts[i].start(); } for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); rec.stop(); rec.dump(file); } Map<String, long[]> byKind = new TreeMap<>(); // count, total ms for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { String what = switch (e.getEventType().getName()) { case "jdk.JavaMonitorEnter" -> "JavaMonitorEnter on " + e.getClass("monitorClass").getName(); case "jdk.ThreadPark" -> "ThreadPark on " + (e.getClass("parkedClass") == null ? "?" : e.getClass("parkedClass").getName()); default -> e.getEventType().getName(); }; long[] agg = byKind.computeIfAbsent(what, k -> new long[2]); agg[0]++; agg[1] += e.getDuration().toMillis(); } byKind.forEach((k, v) -> System.out.printf("%-70s %5d events, %6d ms waiting%n", k, v[0], v[1])); System.out.println("recording kept at " + file); } } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l13.JfrContention labs/concurrency/src/demo/java/workbench/concurrency/l13/JfrContention.java JfrContention.kt package workbench.concurrency.l13 import java.nio.file.Files import java.time.Duration import java.util.TreeMap import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import jdk.jfr.Recording import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Records one second of lock contention with Java Flight Recorder, from inside the program, // then reads the recording back and summarizes it. The .jfr file is kept for the jfr tool. private val ledgerMonitor = Any() private val batchLock = ReentrantLock() private fun busy(micros: Long) { val end = System.nanoTime() + micros * 1_000 while (System.nanoTime() < end) Thread.onSpinWait() } fun main() { val file = Files.createTempFile("contention-", ".jfr") Recording().use { rec -> rec.enable("jdk.JavaMonitorEnter").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)) // waited > 1 ms for a monitor rec.enable("jdk.ThreadPark").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(1)) // parked > 1 ms (j.u.c locks) rec.start() val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_000_000_000L val ts = List(6) { i -> val useMonitor = i % 2 == 0 thread(name = (if (useMonitor) "ledger-" else "batch-") + i) { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { if (useMonitor) synchronized(ledgerMonitor) { busy(3_000) } // hold it 3 ms else batchLock.withLock { busy(3_000) } } } } ts.forEach { it.join() } rec.stop() rec.dump(file) } val byKind = TreeMap<String, LongArray>() // count, total ms for (e in RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { val what = when (e.eventType.name) { "jdk.JavaMonitorEnter" -> "JavaMonitorEnter on " + e.getClass("monitorClass").name "jdk.ThreadPark" -> "ThreadPark on " + (e.getClass("parkedClass")?.name ?: "?") else -> e.eventType.name } val agg = byKind.getOrPut(what) { LongArray(2) } agg[0]++ agg[1] += e.duration.toMillis() } byKind.forEach { (k, v) -> println("%-70s %5d events, %6d ms waiting".format(k, v[0], v[1])) } println("recording kept at $file") } ./gradlew :concurrency:demo -Pmain=workbench.concurrency.l13.JfrContentionKt labs/concurrency/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/concurrency/l13/JfrContention.kt Two lines: JavaMonitorEnter on java.lang.Object for the synchronized threads and ThreadPark on java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync for the explicit lock, each with a hundred or more events and about a second of total waiting. jfr print shows each event's duration, monitorClass, previousOwner (the thread that held the monitor) and the waiting thread's stack. The most common mistake is fixing a flaky concurrency test by tuning it until it passes: a longer sleep, a retry annotation, a CI rule that reruns failures. Flakiness in a concurrency test is often the only symptom a real race ever shows before production. Every retry hides it a little better. The fix is to find out why the test is flaky. If the test guesses at timing, replace the sleep with a latch or a deadline-bounded wait. If the code is racy, the test just did its job, so fix the code and keep the test.

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · Java and Kotlin
x: The same stress test in Java and Kotlin Java (JUnit 6) @RepeatedTest(5) // a race test is a sample: take several @Timeout(10) // a deadlock fails the test instead of hanging the build void noRefundIsLost() throws Exception { RefundLedger ledger = new RefundLedger(Map.of("pay-1", 10_000L)); AtomicLong approved = new AtomicLong(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) { // more threads than cores Thread th = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } for (int i = 0; i < 2_000; i++) if (ledger.refund("pay-1", 1)) approved.incrementAndGet(); }); th.start(); threads.add(th); } go.countDown(); // the starting gun for (Thread th : threads) th.join(); assertThat(approved.get()).isEqualTo(10_000); // an invariant, not a timing assertThat(ledger.refunded("pay-1")).isEqualTo(10_000); } Kotlin (JUnit 6) @RepeatedTest(5) // a race test is a sample: take several @Timeout(10) // a deadlock fails the test instead of hanging the build fun `no refund is lost`() { val ledger = RefundLedger(mapOf("pay-1" to 10_000L)) val approved = AtomicLong() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { // more threads than cores thread { go.await() repeat(2_000) { if (ledger.refund("pay-1", 1)) approved.incrementAndGet() } } } go.countDown() // the starting gun threads.forEach { it.join() } assertThat(approved.get()).isEqualTo(10_000L) // an invariant, not a timing assertThat(ledger.refunded("pay-1")).isEqualTo(10_000L) } JUnit, AssertJ and the latches work the same from both languages. Kotlin removes ceremony: thread { } starts a thread in one line, List(8) { ... } collects them, and with no checked exceptions there is no try/catch around go.await(). Two details differ. Backtick test names read like specs. And AssertJ needs 10_000L in Kotlin: assertThat(aLong).isEqualTo(10_000) would pass an Int, which picks the Object overload and fails because Long 10,000 isn't equal to Integer 10,000. For coroutine code, Kotlin has a tool Java lacks: kotlinx-coroutines-test runs suspending code on virtual time, so tests of delays and timeouts run instantly and deterministically. The coroutines track covers it.

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · Worked example
x: Turn a flaky "loads once" test into a deterministic one This test is meant to prove that BinCache from lesson 9 loads a BIN once when eight callers ask together. Read it and decide what it actually tests. @Test void loadsOnce() throws Exception { AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger(); BinCache cache = new BinCache(bin -> { loads.incrementAndGet(); return "Northwind Bank"; }); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) new Thread(() -> cache.issuerFor("411111")).start(); Thread.sleep(100); // "they should be done by now" assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1); } @Test fun `loads once`() { val loads = AtomicInteger() val cache = BinCache { loads.incrementAndGet(); "Northwind Bank" } repeat(8) { thread { cache.issuerFor("411111") } } Thread.sleep(100) // "they should be done by now" assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1) } It tests the scheduler. The loader is so fast that the threads rarely overlap, so the racy get-then-put cache passes too. And on a slow machine the threads might not have run at all within 100 ms, so loads is 0 and a correct cache fails. The fix is to control the timing: hold the first load inside the loader until every caller is known to be waiting, then let it go. Here is the deterministic version, with subgoal labels. The loader blocks on a latch, and the test polls thread states, with a deadline, until all eight callers are parked. @Test @Timeout(10) void loadsOnceWhileOthersWait() throws Exception { AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger(); CountDownLatch inLoader = new CountDownLatch(1), release = new CountDownLatch(1); BinCache cache = new BinCache(bin -> { loads.incrementAndGet(); inLoader.countDown(); // 1. a caller is inside the loader try { release.await(); } // and stays there until we say go catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return "Northwind Bank"; }); List<Thread> callers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> cache.issuerFor("411111")); t.start(); callers.add(t); } assertThat(inLoader.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue(); awaitParked(callers, 8); // 2. all 8 are now waiting, inside or outside release.countDown(); // 3. let the load finish for (Thread t : callers) t.join(); assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1); // 4. one load served all eight } static void awaitParked(List<Thread> threads, int n) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(5); while (threads.stream().filter(t -> t.getState() == Thread.State.BLOCKED || t.getState() == Thread.State.WAITING).count() < n) { if (System.nanoTime() > deadline) throw new AssertionError("callers never queued up"); Thread.sleep(5); // polling with a deadline: never a bare guess } } @Test @Timeout(10) fun `loads once while others wait`() { val loads = AtomicInteger() val inLoader = CountDownLatch(1) val release = CountDownLatch(1) val cache = BinCache { loads.incrementAndGet() inLoader.countDown() // 1. a caller is inside the loader release.await() // and stays there until we say go "Northwind Bank" } val callers = List(8) { thread { cache.issuerFor("411111") } } assertThat(inLoader.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)).isTrue() awaitParked(callers, 8) // 2. all 8 are now waiting, inside or outside release.countDown() // 3. let the load finish callers.forEach { it.join() } assertThat(loads.get()).isEqualTo(1) // 4. one load served all eight } fun awaitParked(threads: List<Thread>, n: Int) { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(5) while (threads.count { it.state == Thread.State.BLOCKED || it.state == Thread.State.WAITING } < n) { check(System.nanoTime() < deadline) { "callers never queued up" } Thread.sleep(5) // polling with a deadline: never a bare guess } } Before reading on, explain to yourself why this version fails on the racy cache every time. Answer: with get-then-put, every caller misses and enters the loader, so all eight end up waiting on release inside it, and step 2 is satisfied. When the test opens the latch, all eight loads finish and loads is 8. With computeIfAbsent, one caller is inside the loader and the other seven are BLOCKED on the map's bin, so loads is 1. The outcome no longer depends on luck, only on the code.

x: Which change makes a test most likely to catch a lost update in a counter? Add Thread.sleep(10) before the assertion Release 8+ threads together with a start latch, give each many iterations, and repeat the round many times Run the test with -Xint Run the test first in the suite Lost updates need threads running the same code at the same moment, over and over. The latch lines them up, many iterations keep them overlapping, and many rounds take many samples. A sleep before the assertion changes nothing about overlap. A test does worker.submit(p); Thread.sleep(50); assertTrue(store.isSettled(p)); and fails about once in 50 CI runs. What is the best fix? Increase the sleep to 500 ms Mark the test to retry twice on failure Wait for the settled event with a latch (or poll with a deadline) and a generous timeout, then assert Disable it on CI The test guesses how long settling takes. Waiting for the event makes it as fast as the code and patient on a slow machine, and a timeout far above any real duration only trips when something is really wrong. A longer sleep is slower and still a guess; a retry hides real races too. A jcstress run shows outcome 1, 1 marked ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING and observed in 4% of samples. What does that mean? The test failed The outcome is allowed by the test's annotations but marks the interesting case, here the lost update, and it really happened in 4% of samples jcstress could not decide The outcome only appears on ARM Interesting outcomes are permitted results that the test author wants highlighted, typically the race being demonstrated. Only an observed FORBIDDEN outcome fails a test. The frequency depends on hardware and load, so another machine may show a different number, or none. From explicit locks: three thread dumps, 5 seconds apart, each show 30 threads WAITING (parking) with parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock$NonfairSync). What do you look at next? Which thread owns that lock: run Thread.print -l and find it under "Locked ownable synchronizers", then read its stack The GC log Restart the pod and see whether it happens again Nothing: WAITING threads are idle and harmless Waiters on an explicit lock are parked, so they show as WAITING, not BLOCKED, and three identical dumps say they're stuck, not busy. The owner explains why: it may be in a slow call while holding the lock, or it may have left without unlock(). -l lists the java.util.concurrent locks each thread owns. Payments are slow under load but nothing deadlocks. Which tool shows which monitors threads waited on, for how long, and which thread held each one before them? A single jcmd Thread.print ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() The GC log A JFR recording with jdk.JavaMonitorEnter events (and jdk.ThreadPark for java.util.concurrent locks) JavaMonitorEnter records each wait above a threshold with the monitor class, the duration and previousOwner, over the whole recording. A single dump is one instant. The deadlock check only finds cycles, and the GC log is about memory.

h: Testing and debugging concurrent code · Key terms
x: Stress test A test that runs code on many threads at once, many times, to make races show up. Invariant A fact that must hold whatever the interleaving, such as "refunds never exceed captures". Flaky test A test that passes or fails without any code change, often because it guesses at timing. jcstress The OpenJDK harness that runs tiny concurrent tests millions of times and counts each outcome. Outcome One possible result of a jcstress test, labelled acceptable, interesting or forbidden. Thread dump A snapshot of every thread's state and stack, from jcmd <pid> Thread.print. JFR Java Flight Recorder: low-overhead event recording built into the JVM, read with the jfr tool. Why hold the threads of a stress test behind a start latch? So they all begin at the same moment and overlap. Without it, early threads can finish before late ones start, and the race never happens. Why does every concurrency test need @Timeout or assertTimeoutPreemptively? So a deadlock or a lost wake-up fails the test in seconds instead of hanging the build. What is wrong with Thread.sleep(50) before an assertion in a test? It guesses at timing: flaky on busy machines, slow on idle ones. Wait for the event with a latch or a deadline-bounded poll instead. jcstress: what does ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING mean? The outcome is allowed, but the author flags it as worth seeing, usually the race the test demonstrates. jcstress: what happens if a FORBIDDEN outcome is observed even once? The test fails. How do you tell a stuck thread from a busy one with thread dumps? Take several dumps a few seconds apart. A thread in the same frame every time is stuck; one whose stack changes is busy. Which JFR events show lock contention? jdk.JavaMonitorEnter for synchronized (with monitor class, duration and previous owner), jdk.JavaMonitorWait for Object.wait(), jdk.ThreadPark for java.util.concurrent locks.
