h: The Java Memory Model
x: Visibility, reordering, happens-before, volatile, safe publication and VarHandles. By the end of this track you can explain why one thread may never see another thread's write, name the happens-before edge that makes a read safe, and choose between volatile, an atomic and a lock for any shared field. You can publish objects so other threads see them whole, write lazy initialization that builds exactly once, and read VarHandle memory modes and jcstress results without guessing. This is the theory under every concurrent class you use, and the reason "it passed on my machine" means so little. You need the first track: threads, race conditions, synchronized and atomics. Install JDK 25. The memory model has not changed since Java 5 (JSR-133), so everything here holds from JDK 21 to JDK 27; when a lesson mentions a newer feature, it says which JDK. The labs live in labs/jmm, one package per lesson (workbench.jmm.l01 to l06). They are in Java, and every code sample and Try-it demo also comes in Kotlin. Memory-model bugs rarely show up on demand, so the tests check code that is deterministic once it's right: a loop that must stop, an initializer that must run exactly once under contention, a handoff that must deliver every item. Generous time limits make a broken version fail instead of hanging the build. Run ./gradlew :jmm:test --tests 'workbench.jmm.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and ./gradlew :jmm:solutionTest to run the same tests on the reference answers. Lesson 6 shows how to go further with jcstress, which runs outside Gradle. The JIT may read a plain field once for a whole loop, and the CPU's store buffer lets a later read overtake an earlier write. Neither is a bug: the memory model allows both. A read is guaranteed to see a write only through a happens-before edge: the same lock, the same volatile field, start, join, or a java.util.concurrent handoff. Sleep is not an edge. volatile gives visibility and ordering for one variable, not atomic read-modify-write. Use atomics or LongAdder for counters, a lock or an immutable snapshot for several fields. Publishing an object is a write that can race. Publish through a volatile field, a static initializer, a final field or a j.u.c handoff, and prefer immutable objects, which survive any race. Final fields are seen as the constructor left them, but only if this didn't escape the constructor. Wire objects up after construction. Double-checked locking needs a volatile field. For statics the holder idiom is simpler; in Kotlin, by lazy is the same DCL. A failed holder never retries. VarHandle modes form a ladder: plain, opaque, acquire/release, volatile. Release/acquire hands data from one writer through one variable; only volatile gives one total order. Tests can't prove the absence of reordering. Write code that is correct by the rules, and use jcstress, ideally on ARM, for anything lock-free.

h: The Java Memory Model: cheat sheet
x: The one rule A write is guaranteed visible to a read in another thread only if the write happens-before the read. Without an edge you have a data race: stale values that may never update, writes that seem to arrive out of order, and torn long and double values. The edges you use The writer does The reader does Edge? anything, then leaves synchronized (m) enters synchronized (m) on the same m yes anything, then writes volatile v reads the same v and sees that write yes t.start() anything inside t yes anything inside t t.join() returns yes puts into a concurrent collection a get or take that returns it yes executor.submit(task) the task runs yes the task of a Future future.get() returns yes latch.countDown(), semaphore.release(), lock.unlock() latch.await(), acquire(), lock() returns yes Thread.sleep, a different lock, a different volatile field anything no Edges chain: if A happens-before B and B happens-before C, then A happens-before C. That's how a plain field written before a volatile write reaches the reader of that volatile. Pick the tool for a shared field Situation Use One writer, readers want the latest value (stop flag, status, config version) volatile / @Volatile Many writers update one number (count++, balance += x) AtomicLong, LongAdder, ConcurrentHashMap.merge Several fields must change together a lock, or one immutable object behind a volatile reference A whole object replaced at runtime (rate card, issuer config) immutable snapshot published with one volatile write One value per key, built once computeIfAbsent (not Kotlin's getOrPut) "First writer wins" compareAndSet volatile gives visibility, ordering of the plain writes before it, one order of all volatile accesses, and atomic 64-bit reads and writes. It does not make v++ atomic, does not protect the object it points to, and does nothing for a thread that doesn't read it. Safe publication and immutability Publish through one of: a static initializer; a volatile field or AtomicReference; a final field of a properly constructed object; a lock or a java.util.concurrent handoff. An immutable object (final class, final fields, mutable inputs copied, nothing mutable handed out, no escaping this) is safe through any race. Never let this escape a constructor: register listeners and start threads afterwards, in a factory, a start() method or @PostConstruct. Java public record IssuerConfig(String baseUrl, Duration timeout) {} // immutable private volatile IssuerConfig config = new IssuerConfig("https://issuer.example", Duration.ofMillis(800)); void refresh(Settings s) { config = new IssuerConfig(s.baseUrl(), s.timeout()); } // one volatile write IssuerConfig current() { return config; } // one consistent snapshot Kotlin data class IssuerConfig(val baseUrl: String, val timeout: Duration) // immutable @Volatile private var config = IssuerConfig("https://issuer.example", Duration.ofMillis(800)) fun refresh(s: Settings) { config = IssuerConfig(s.baseUrl, s.timeout) } // one volatile write fun current(): IssuerConfig = config // one consistent snapshot Lazy initialization Need Use Every request needs it anyway build it eagerly at startup One per JVM, construction can't fail holder class idiom, enum, Kotlin object Per instance, or must retry after a failure double-checked locking on a volatile field, Kotlin by lazy One per key computeIfAbsent Java private static final class Holder { static final BinTable INSTANCE = new BinTable(); } static BinTable instance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } // the JVM's class-init lock does the work private volatile SigningKey key; // volatile is not optional SigningKey key() { SigningKey k = key; // one volatile read on the fast path if (k != null) return k; synchronized (this) { if (key == null) key = vault.fetch("issuer-signing-key"); return key; } } Kotlin class BinTable private constructor() { private object Holder { val INSTANCE = BinTable() } companion object { fun instance(): BinTable = Holder.INSTANCE } } val key: SigningKey by lazy { vault.fetch("issuer-signing-key") } // SYNCHRONIZED: a volatile DCL Kotlin modes: SYNCHRONIZED (default, runs once, others wait, retries if it throws), PUBLICATION (may run on several threads, one result wins: only for cheap, side-effect-free work), NONE (one thread only). A holder whose initializer throws never retries: later calls get NoClassDefFoundError. VarHandle access modes Mode Methods Adds plain get, set nothing across threads opaque getOpaque, setOpaque each access really happens; untorn; eventually visible acquire/release getAcquire, setRelease writes before the release are seen after the matching acquire volatile getVolatile, setVolatile one total order of all volatile accesses compareAndSet and getAndAdd have volatile semantics. Release/acquire does not forbid the store-buffering result (each thread writes its own flag, both read the other's as 0); only volatile does. AtomicReference and friends offer the same modes without a lookup. In app code use volatile, the Atomic classes and java.util.concurrent. Test any lock-free code with jcstress, on ARM if you can, because x86 hides many ordering bugs.

h: The Java Memory Model: track quiz
x: A worker runs while (!stopped) { pollOnce(); }, where pollOnce is small enough for the JIT to inline and stopped is a plain boolean that another thread sets. In production the worker sometimes never stops. Why, and what's the fix? A CPU cache keeps the old value forever; call System.gc() to flush it The JIT may read stopped once and loop forever; make the field volatile Add Thread.sleep(10) to the loop, because sleeping forces a fresh read Use an AtomicBoolean, because boolean writes can tear Caches are coherent; the compiler is the problem. With no edge, the JIT may hoist the read out of the loop. A volatile read can't be hoisted. Sleep has no synchronization semantics, and a boolean can't tear. In which case is the reader guaranteed to see x = 42? The writer sets x, then writes volatile a; the reader reads volatile b, then x The writer sets x inside synchronized (lockA); the reader reads x inside synchronized (lockB) The writer sets x, then sleeps 100 ms; the reader sleeps 200 ms, then reads x The writer sets x, then calls latch.countDown(); the reader returns from latch.await() and reads x countDown happens-before a successful await on the same latch, and the write to x comes before countDown in program order. The other options use different variables, different locks, or sleep, which creates no edge at all. Fifty request threads increment and decrement volatile int inFlight. The dashboard drifts further from the truth every hour. What's the fix? Use an AtomicInteger (incrementAndGet, decrementAndGet) Make it volatile long so it can't overflow Add Thread.yield() after each update Read it inside a synchronized block on the dashboard side inFlight++ is a read, an add and a write. volatile makes each one visible but doesn't stop two threads from reading the same value, so updates get lost. An atomic does the whole update as one step. A config version number is written only by one refresher thread and read by every request thread. What is enough? A lock around every read and write An AtomicLong updated with compareAndSet A volatile long A plain long, because writes are rare With a single writer there is no read-modify-write race, so the only problem is visibility, and that's what volatile solves. It also makes the 64-bit write atomic. A lock and CAS work but buy nothing here; a plain long has no edge at all. record RateCard(String currency, Map<String, Long> fees) stores the caller's HashMap as it is. Is a RateCard safe to share between threads? Yes: record fields are final Not quite: the reference is final, but the caller can still change the HashMap; copy it with Map.copyOf in a compact constructor No: records can't be shared between threads Yes, as long as it's published through a volatile field Final fields freeze what the constructor stored, which is a reference to someone else's mutable map. Later changes through the caller's reference are ordinary racy writes. A defensive copy makes the record truly immutable. A Kafka listener's constructor calls container.register(this) and then sets its deserializer field. What can happen? Nothing: a constructor always runs to the end before anyone can use the object The compiler rejects this as an argument inside a constructor The container can deliver a record before deserializer is set, and the listener throws a NullPointerException Nothing, as long as deserializer is final this escaped before the constructor finished, so another thread (or a callback on the same thread) can use a half-built object. Final doesn't help: its promise starts when the constructor returns. Register after construction. Which of these lazy initializers can hand a caller a half-built object? Double-checked locking on a plain (non-volatile) field The holder class idiom Kotlin by lazy with the default mode ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent The lock-free first check reads the field with no edge to the write, so the reference can become visible before the constructor's writes. The holder relies on class-initialization locking, by lazy uses a volatile field, and computeIfAbsent publishes through the map. A static holder builds an issuer client whose constructor connects over the network. The issuer is down when the first request arrives. What do later calls get once the issuer is back? A fresh attempt: the holder retries on the next call The half-built client from the first attempt null NoClassDefFoundError on every call until the JVM restarts If a static initializer throws, the class is marked as failed and is never initialized again. The first caller gets ExceptionInInitializerError and everyone after it NoClassDefFoundError. Use a volatile DCL or Kotlin lazy, which retry, for anything that can fail. Two threads each set their own flag with setRelease, then read the other's flag with getAcquire. Can both read false? No: release/acquire keeps each write before the read that follows it Yes, even on x86; volatile accesses would forbid it Only on ARM Only if the flags are long fields Release keeps earlier accesses before the write, but a later read of a different variable may still pass it, and x86's store buffer does exactly that. Only volatile's single total order forbids both reading false. Many threads may try to record "the first failure reason", and only the first one should stick. Which tool fits? A plain String field setRelease through a VarHandle compareAndSet(null, reason) on an AtomicReference or a VarHandle A volatile String set with if (reason == null) reason = r; First writer wins is a read-modify-write, so it needs one atomic step. compareAndSet succeeds for exactly one caller and has volatile semantics. The volatile check-then-set is a race between the check and the set, and setRelease is just a write.

h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · A plain boolean can keep a loop running forever
x: Here is the smallest version of a bug that ships in real services. A worker thread loops until another thread asks it to stop. Java static boolean stop; // plain field Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { long spins = 0; while (!stop) { spins++; } System.out.println("worker saw stop"); }); worker.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); stop = true; // main asks the worker to stop Kotlin var stop = false // plain property val worker = thread { var spins = 0L while (!stop) { spins++ } println("worker saw stop") } Thread.sleep(1_000) stop = true // main asks the worker to stop Run it on JDK 21 or 25 and the worker never stops. Not after a second, not after an hour. main wrote true, and the worker keeps reading false. Now run the same program with java -Xint. That flag turns off the JIT (just-in-time) compiler, the part of the JVM that compiles hot bytecode to machine code while the program runs. Without it, the JVM runs every line in its bytecode interpreter. The worker stops at once. One run printed worker saw stop after 135,865,168 spins. That flag tells you where the bug lives. It is not in the CPU cache, which is the same with or without -Xint. It is in the JIT compiler. After the loop has run many thousands of times, C2, the optimizing compiler in HotSpot (the JVM that ships with OpenJDK), turns it into machine code. C2 sees that nothing inside the loop writes stop, and nothing in the loop talks to other threads. So it reads stop once, before the loop, keeps the value in a register (a slot inside the CPU core that holds a value the code is working on), and runs the rest as while (true). That is a legal optimization. The Java Memory Model (JMM) only promises that one thread sees another thread's write when something connects the two: a volatile field, a lock, Thread.join, and a few more you'll meet in lesson 2 of this track. A plain field has none of that, so the compiler may assume no other thread ever changes it. The fix is one word: Java static volatile boolean stop; Kotlin @Volatile var stop = false The JIT can't keep a volatile field in a register or move its read out of the loop. Every pass reads it again, and the JMM guarantees the write from main becomes visible. Hang a thread, then unhang it Read StopFlagDemo.java below. Predict: will the worker print worker saw stop? Run it from labs/ with the Gradle command below. It waits 3 seconds for the worker, then exits. Run the Java file with the JIT turned off: java -Xint jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l01/StopFlagDemo.java (from labs/). The source launcher only runs Java files; the Kotlin twin compiles to the same field read, so the result carries over. Make the field static volatile boolean stop; (in the Kotlin twin, put @Volatile on stop) and run the Gradle command again. Does it ever notice? */ public class StopFlagDemo { static boolean stop; // plain field: no volatile, no lock public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { long spins = 0; while (!stop) { spins++; } System.out.printf("worker saw stop after %,d spins%n", spins); }); worker.setDaemon(true); // so the JVM can exit even if the worker never stops worker.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); // give the JIT time to compile the loop stop = true; System.out.println("main set stop = true"); worker.join(3_000); System.out.println("worker still running 3 s later? " + worker.isAlive()); } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l01.StopFlagDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l01/StopFlagDemo.java StopFlagDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l01 import kotlin.concurrent.thread private var stop = false // plain field: no @Volatile, no lock /** A worker spins until main sets a plain boolean. Does it ever notice? */ fun main() { // daemon, so the JVM can exit even if the worker never stops val worker = thread(isDaemon = true) { var spins = 0L while (!stop) { spins++ } println("worker saw stop after %,d spins".format(spins)) } Thread.sleep(1_000) // give the JIT time to compile the loop stop = true println("main set stop = true") worker.join(3_000) println("worker still running 3 s later? ${worker.isAlive}") } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l01.StopFlagDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l01/StopFlagDemo.kt The first run prints main set stop = true and then worker still running 3 s later? true. With -Xint the worker prints how many times it spun and stops, because the interpreter reads the field on every pass. With volatile the compiled loop stops too, within a moment of main setting the flag. jcstress sample BasicJMM_04_Progress: spin loops on plain, volatile and opaque fields read Picture a cashier who checks the "store closing" sign once at the start of the shift, writes "open" on a sticky note, and from then on only looks at the note. The manager can flip the sign at 9 pm and the cashier keeps selling. That's the JIT and a register. Making the field volatile is a rule that says: look at the sign every single time. The analogy breaks on the hardware side. The store buffer is more like the manager holding the new sign for a few seconds before hanging it, while already walking on to the next task. That delay is short and always ends; the sticky note never updates.

h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · The JIT only promises that one thread can't tell
x: Every optimizer in the JVM follows one rule, often called as-if-serial: it may change your code in any way, as long as a single thread running it alone can't tell the difference. Reading stop once is fine by that rule. If no other thread exists, stop can't change during the loop. Here is the change C2 is allowed to make, side by side: // what you wrote // what the compiled code may do while (!stop) { if (!stop) { spins++; while (true) { spins++; } } } The same rule lets the JIT do other things you never see in one thread. It can merge two writes to the same field into one, drop a write nobody reads, or swap two writes to different fields. Each change is invisible to the thread that runs the code. Another thread, reading those fields at the same time, can see the effects. Now the part that makes these bugs survive code review. Put almost any method call inside the loop and the hang usually goes away. A Thread.sleep(10), a log line, a Thread.yield(), even Thread.onSpinWait(). C2 treats each of these as something that may have changed memory, usually because it can't see inside the call, so it reads stop again after it. That is luck, not a guarantee. The Java Language Specification says outright that sleep and yield have no synchronization effect, and a compiler may still read the field once. A later JDK might inline more, or a teammate might replace the log call with a counter, and the hang is back. The loop that has worked for two years is still broken. It just hasn't been compiled the wrong way yet. So don't reason about what HotSpot does today. Ask one question: is there a synchronization point between the write and the read? For a plain field, there isn't. Hide the bug without fixing it In StopFlagDemo (either language), remove volatile or @Volatile again so the flag is plain. Add Thread.yield() as the first line inside the while loop. Predict before you run: will the worker stop? Run the Gradle command from the previous Try it. The worker stops. Thread.yield() ends in a native call that HotSpot can't look inside, so the JIT re-reads stop after each call. The program is still incorrect by the JMM: nothing promises that re-read. Undo the change and keep volatile. Look at every background loop in your services that ends with a flag: a Kafka consumer thread with private boolean running = true and a shutdown hook that sets it to false, a Quarkus @Scheduled job that a health check pauses, a reconciliation worker that drains an in-memory batch. Most of them call poll() or do I/O inside the loop, which hides the bug on today's HotSpot. Then someone optimizes the loop to drain a local list first, the loop becomes tight, and a pod that used to stop in 200 ms hangs until Kubernetes kills it 30 seconds later. Make every cross-thread flag volatile or an AtomicBoolean, so the guarantee lives in the code and not in the JIT's mood.

h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · Caches agree with each other; store buffers let a core run ahead
x: Why the stop loop spins: the caches agree, the store buffer drains, the JIT keeps stop in a register The usual story is that each CPU core keeps its own copy of stop in its cache, and the copy goes stale. That story is wrong on every server CPU you'll deploy to. Caches run a coherence protocol: when one core writes a memory location, the other cores' copies are invalidated or updated, usually within nanoseconds. No cache keeps an old value forever. The hardware does reorder, though, through a different part of the core: the store buffer. When a core writes, it doesn't wait for the cache. It puts the write in a small queue and runs the next instruction. If the next instruction is a read of a different variable, that read can finish before the write leaves the queue. To another core, the write and the read look swapped. The classic test for this has two threads and two fields, both starting at 0: Java // thread A // thread B x = 1; y = 1; r1 = y; r2 = x; Kotlin // thread A // thread B x = 1 y = 1 r1 = y r2 = x In any order that keeps each thread's two lines in sequence, at least one thread reads a 1. Yet r1 == 0 && r2 == 0 happens: each thread's write is still in its own store buffer when the other thread reads. The jcstress suite measured it in 6.29% of samples on x86_64 with plain fields. With both fields volatile it never happened. The JMM forbids that outcome for volatile fields, so on x86 HotSpot follows each volatile write with an instruction that drains the store buffer before any later read. x86 only lets a later read pass an earlier write. ARM, which runs Apple Silicon laptops and AWS Graviton servers, also lets reads pass reads and writes pass writes. Code that never fails on an x86 build agent can fail on an ARM pod. Catch the CPU reordering Read ReorderDemo.java. It runs the two-thread test above about half a million times with plain fields, then with volatile fields. Run it with the Gradle command below and note the counts. Run the Java file in the interpreter: java -Xint jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l01/ReorderDemo.java. Predict first: the JIT is off now, so will the plain count drop to zero? ReorderDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l01; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.IntConsumer; /** * The store-buffering test. Thread A runs {@code x = 1; r1 = y;} and thread B runs {@code y = 1; r2 = x;}. * If the four lines ran in any order that keeps each thread's two lines in program order, * at least one thread would read a 1. Count the trials where both threads read 0. */ public class ReorderDemo { static final class Plain { int x, y; } static final class Volatile { volatile int x, y; } static final int TRIALS = 1 << 19; static final int BATCH = 32; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int run = 1; run <= 3; run++) { System.out.printf("run %d: both read 0 in %,7d trials with plain fields, %,d with volatile fields (of %,d)%n", run, plain(), withVolatile(), TRIALS); } } static int plain() throws InterruptedException { Plain[] s = new Plain[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Plain(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } static int withVolatile() throws InterruptedException { Volatile[] s = new Volatile[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Volatile(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads. A small spin barrier every BATCH trials // keeps the two threads on the same trial at about the same moment. static void race(IntConsumer a, IntConsumer b) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger doneA = new AtomicInteger(), doneB = new AtomicInteger(); Thread ta = new Thread(() -> runSide(a, doneA, doneB)); Thread tb = new Thread(() -> runSide(b, doneB, doneA)); ta.start(); tb.start(); ta.join(); tb.join(); } static void runSide(IntConsumer side, AtomicInteger mine, AtomicInteger other) { for (int batch = 0; batch < TRIALS / BATCH; batch++) { mine.set(batch); while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait(); // wait for the other thread for (int i = batch * BATCH; i < (batch + 1) * BATCH; i++) side.accept(i); } } static int bothZero(int[] r1, int[] r2) { int n = 0; for (int i = 0; i < r1.length; i++) if (r1[i] == 0 && r2[i] == 0) n++; return n; } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l01.ReorderDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l01/ReorderDemo.java ReorderDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l01 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.function.IntConsumer import kotlin.concurrent.thread /* * The store-buffering test. Thread A runs `x = 1; r1 = y` and thread B runs `y = 1; r2 = x`. * If the four lines ran in any order that keeps each thread's two lines in program order, * at least one thread would read a 1. Count the trials where both threads read 0. */ private class PlainPair { var x = 0; var y = 0 } private class VolatilePair { @Volatile var x = 0; @Volatile var y = 0 } private const val TRIALS = 1 shl 19 private const val BATCH = 32 fun main() { for (run in 1..3) { println("run %d: both read 0 in %,7d trials with plain fields, %,d with @Volatile fields (of %,d)" .format(run, plain(), withVolatile(), TRIALS)) } } private fun plain(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { PlainPair() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } private fun withVolatile(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { VolatilePair() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads. A small spin barrier every BATCH trials // keeps the two threads on the same trial at about the same moment. private fun race(a: IntConsumer, b: IntConsumer) { val doneA = AtomicInteger() val doneB = AtomicInteger() val ta = thread { runSide(a, doneA, doneB) } val tb = thread { runSide(b, doneB, doneA) } ta.join(); tb.join() } private fun runSide(side: IntConsumer, mine: AtomicInteger, other: AtomicInteger) { for (batch in 0 until TRIALS / BATCH) { mine.set(batch) while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait() // wait for the other thread for (i in batch * BATCH until (batch + 1) * BATCH) side.accept(i) } } private fun bothZero(r1: IntArray, r2: IntArray): Int = r1.indices.count { r1[it] == 0 && r2[it] == 0 } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l01.ReorderDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l01/ReorderDemo.kt With plain fields a large share of trials see both reads return 0 (runs here showed between 85,000 and 330,000 of 524,288, and it changes every run). With volatile fields the count is 0 every time. Under -Xint the plain count stays high: the interpreter doesn't reorder anything, so this one is the store buffer, not the compiler. Coherent caches carry the write to every core. The worker still spins, because its compiled loop reads a register copy. The store buffer only delays a write, for nanoseconds. jcstress sample BasicJMM_07_Consensus: the store-buffering test with plain, volatile and acquire/release read

h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · Three layers reorder your code, and the memory model is the contract
x: Three layers stand between your source and what other threads observe. javac barely changes order. It compiles statements to bytecode almost one for one. The JIT (C1, then C2 for hot code) hoists reads, merges and removes writes, and moves independent loads and stores around. The CPU runs ahead through store buffers, and on ARM it reorders more freely still. Each layer follows as-if-serial, so a single thread never notices. You can't control which layer does what, and you don't need to. The JMM is the contract that sits above all three. It names the operations that link threads: volatile reads and writes, taking and releasing a lock, thread start and join, and the classes in java.util.concurrent. If every read of shared data is linked to the write it needs by those operations, the JMM guarantees that your program behaves as if its lines ran in some single interleaved order. That property is called sequential consistency, and lesson 2 of this track shows how the links work. If you skip the links, you have a data race, and the guarantees mostly go away. You can see a stale value, a value that seems to arrive before the write that made it, or, for long and double, half of one write and half of another. This is why "it works on my machine" means so little here. Your test ran on one CPU family, with one JIT, under one load profile. A different JDK, a busier server or an ARM instance can expose a reordering your tests never saw. In one jcstress test, a thread writes x and then y, the compiler is told to keep that order, and another thread reads y and then x. On x86_64, seeing the new y with the old x never happened. On AArch64 (64-bit ARM) it happened in 0.68% of samples. Both results obey the same JMM. Write to the contract, and the hardware becomes someone else's problem. Check yourself: you run StopFlagDemo with -Xint on an ARM laptop, which reorders more than x86. Does the worker stop? It does. The interpreter reads stop from memory on every pass, and coherence brings the new value to the worker's core. ARM's extra freedom only changes the order in which writes to different fields become visible. Each write still arrives. The plain field is still a data race, though, so the fix stays volatile. The most common mistake is "fixing" a hung loop by adding Thread.sleep, a log statement or Thread.onSpinWait() to it, seeing it stop, and moving on. Each of those happens to make HotSpot re-read the field today, because the JIT can't see what the call does. None of them is a synchronization point in the JMM, and the JLS says so for sleep and yield. A future JDK or a small refactoring brings the hang back. The fix is to declare the flag volatile (or use AtomicBoolean), and keep any sleep only if you want the pause.

h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · Java and Kotlin
x: A stop flag in Java and Kotlin SettlementLoop.java public class SettlementLoop implements Runnable { private volatile boolean running = true; @Override public void run() { while (running) { settleNextBatch(); } } public void stop() { running = false; } } SettlementLoop.kt class SettlementLoop : Runnable { @Volatile private var running = true override fun run() { while (running) { settleNextBatch() } } fun stop() { running = false } } Kotlin has no volatile keyword. You put @Volatile on a var property, and the compiler marks its JVM backing field volatile, so the bytecode is the same as the Java version. A val can't be @Volatile, because it is never written after construction. A plain Kotlin var has exactly the same bug as a plain Java field: a while (running) loop compiles to a field read the JIT can hoist. AtomicBoolean from java.util.concurrent.atomic works the same in both languages.

h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · Worked example
x: Find the flags that freeze a standby pod Two pods run a ledger exporter, and leader election picks one of them. When the standby pod is elected, a callback thread calls onElected(). On shutdown, a hook thread calls stop(). In a failover drill the standby was elected, exported nothing, and then ignored SIGTERM until Kubernetes killed it. Find the shared state before reading on. class LedgerExporter implements Runnable { private boolean leader; // 1. written by the election callback thread private boolean running = true; // 2. written by the shutdown hook thread @Override public void run() { while (running) { // 3. both flags read in a hot loop if (leader) exportBatch(); } } void onElected() { leader = true; } void stop() { running = false; } } class LedgerExporter : Runnable { private var leader = false // 1. written by the election callback thread private var running = true // 2. written by the shutdown hook thread override fun run() { while (running) { // 3. both flags read in a hot loop if (leader) exportBatch() } } fun onElected() { leader = true } fun stop() { running = false } } Both flags are written by one thread and read by another, with nothing linking them. On the standby, leader stays false for hours, so the profile says exportBatch() never runs. C2 compiles the loop as if that branch were not there. What's left is two reads of plain fields that nothing in the loop writes, so C2 reads them once. A copy of this class run for this lesson exported 0 batches after onElected() and was still spinning 3 seconds after stop(). Make both flags volatile. Then stop the standby from spinning: it has nothing to do, so it should sleep between checks and leave the core to other work. class LedgerExporter implements Runnable { private volatile boolean leader; // 1. both flags cross threads: both volatile private volatile boolean running = true; @Override public void run() { try { while (running) { // 2. re-read on every pass if (leader) { exportBatch(); } else { Thread.sleep(50); // 3. a standby doesn't need a whole core } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // 4. treat an interrupt as a stop, too } } void onElected() { leader = true; } void stop() { running = false; } } class LedgerExporter : Runnable { @Volatile private var leader = false // 1. both flags cross threads: both @Volatile @Volatile private var running = true override fun run() { try { while (running) { // 2. re-read on every pass if (leader) { exportBatch() } else { Thread.sleep(50) // 3. a standby doesn't need a whole core } } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // 4. treat an interrupt as a stop, too } } fun onElected() { leader = true } fun stop() { running = false } } The sleep alone would also have hidden the hang, because HotSpot re-reads fields after it. That is why the volatile stays. The sleep is there to save CPU. The volatile is there for correctness, and it keeps working after the next refactoring.

A stop-flag loop hangs with the JIT on and stops under -Xint. What is the best explanation? The worker's CPU cache never receives the new value The compiled loop read the field once and keeps using a register copy The interpreter runs on a single core, so there is no second cache The main thread's write is still sitting in its store buffer Caches and store buffers are identical in both runs, so they can't explain the difference. Only the JIT changes. C2 hoisted the read out of the loop, which as-if-serial allows for a plain field. A store buffer drains in nanoseconds, so it can't cause a hang. h: Why your loop never stops: caches and reordering · Key terms
x: Visibility Whether and when a write by one thread can be seen by a read in another thread. Hoisting The JIT moving a read out of a loop because it believes the value can't change inside the loop. Store buffer A per-core queue of pending writes. It lets the core keep running before its writes reach the cache. Cache coherence The hardware protocol that keeps every core's cache in agreement about each memory location. As-if-serial Optimizers may change anything a single thread can't observe. Data race Two threads access the same variable, at least one writes, and no synchronization orders the two accesses. volatile A field modifier: reads and writes go to memory in order, and they link threads in the memory model. h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Happens-before is a promise about visibility, not about time
x: The memory model answers one question: when is a read in one thread guaranteed to see a write from another? The java.util.concurrent package documentation gives the answer in one sentence: "The results of a write by one thread are guaranteed to be visible to a read by another thread only if the write operation happens-before the read operation." Happens-before is a relation between two actions, such as a write of a field and a read of it. If the write happens-before the read, and no other write to that field races in, the read sees that value. If nothing orders them, the read may see the new value, an old one, or, as in lesson 1 of this track, never the new value at all. The name misleads people. Happens-before is not about wall-clock time. A write can run a full second before a read and still not happen-before it: that was the stop flag. In the other direction, the JVM may reorder two actions that are ordered by happens-before, as long as no thread can tell. The first rule is one you already rely on. Inside one thread, each action happens-before every later action of that thread. This is program order, and it's why single-threaded code reads as written. The rules in the next sections connect different threads. Chain them together and you have a proof that a particular read sees a particular write. When two threads access the same field, at least one of them writes, and no chain of happens-before orders the two accesses, the program has a data race. Data races are what the JMM is really about. Its main promise is called DRF-SC: a program with no data races behaves as if the threads' actions ran one at a time, interleaved, each thread in its own order. You can reason about it like the simulator in "Race conditions: why count++ lies". A program with a data race gets very few guarantees beyond that. So the working method is short. For every field that two threads share, name the edge between the write and the read. If you can't name one, you have a race. Check yourself: T1 sets a plain status = APPROVED at 10:00:00.000. T2 reads status a full second later, with no lock and no volatile on either side. Is T2 guaranteed to see APPROVED? No. A second of wall-clock time is not an edge, and you can't name a rule that links the write to the read. That makes it a data race, and the old value is a legal result. Think of a sealed courier envelope. Everything you put in before sealing it (the release) travels with it. The recipient gets those contents only by opening that same envelope (the acquire). Anything you write after sealing stays behind, and opening a different envelope gets you nothing. The analogy breaks in one place: nothing is copied. Both threads look at the same memory the whole time. An unopened envelope doesn't mean the writes haven't arrived; often they have. It means you have no promise that they have.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Locks and volatile link threads only through the same lock or the same field
x: A volatile write and a read of the same field make a happens-before edge; a different field makes none Two rules cover most of the code you write. The monitor rule: releasing a lock happens-before every later acquisition of the same lock. Leaving a synchronized block or method releases the monitor; entering one acquires it. Add program order on both sides, and everything T1 did before leaving synchronized (lock) is visible to T2 once it enters synchronized (lock). The volatile rule: a write to a volatile field happens-before every later read of that same field, where "later" means the read sees that write or a newer one. A volatile works like a lock without the mutual exclusion. The JLS calls the source of such an edge a release and the target an acquire. Leaving a monitor and writing a volatile are releases. Entering a monitor and reading a volatile are acquires. Every class in java.util.concurrent is built on the same pair. Both rules contain the word same, and that's where the bugs are. Java synchronized (paymentLock) { status = APPROVED; } // T1 releases paymentLock synchronized (auditLock) { s = status; } // T2 acquires auditLock: no edge Kotlin synchronized(paymentLock) { status = APPROVED } // T1 releases paymentLock synchronized(auditLock) { s = status } // T2 acquires auditLock: no edge Two different locks give you mutual exclusion on each one and no edge between them. Volatile works the same way: a write to a volatile version and a read of a volatile checksum give no edge. The most common shape of this bug is the half-synchronized class: a synchronized setter and a plain getter. The writer releases the lock, the reader never acquires it, so there's nothing to pair with. LedgerTotals in the lab is that class. One more: synchronized (new Object()) does nothing for other threads. No other thread can ever lock that object, so no edge can form. HotSpot knows it, too. Its escape analysis proves that no other thread can reach the object and removes the lock completely, and then the read inside is just a plain read. Same lock or own lock Read LockScopeDemo.java. The writer sets balance inside synchronized (LEDGER_LOCK). By default the reader locks a fresh new Object() (Any() in Kotlin) on every pass. Predict, then run the Gradle command below. Run it again with -Pargs=shared added, so the reader locks LEDGER_LOCK too. LockScopeDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l02; /** A writer sets a balance inside a lock. A reader spins until it sees it. Which lock does the reader need? */ public class LockScopeDemo { static final Object LEDGER_LOCK = new Object(); static long balance; // meant to be guarded by LEDGER_LOCK public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean shared = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("shared"); Thread reader = new Thread(shared ? LockScopeDemo::readWithLedgerLock : LockScopeDemo::readWithOwnLock); reader.setDaemon(true); // so the JVM can exit even if the reader never stops reader.start(); Thread.sleep(500); // let the JIT compile the reader's loop synchronized (LEDGER_LOCK) { balance = 12_000; // cents } System.out.println("writer set balance = 12000 inside synchronized (LEDGER_LOCK)"); reader.join(3_000); System.out.println("reader still spinning 3 s later? " + reader.isAlive()); } static void readWithOwnLock() { long seen; do { synchronized (new Object()) { // a lock no other thread can ever take seen = balance; } } while (seen == 0); System.out.println("reader (own lock) saw balance = " + seen); } static void readWithLedgerLock() { long seen; do { synchronized (LEDGER_LOCK) { // the same monitor the writer released seen = balance; } } while (seen == 0); System.out.println("reader (LEDGER_LOCK) saw balance = " + seen); } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l02.LockScopeDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l02/LockScopeDemo.java LockScopeDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread private val LEDGER_LOCK = Any() private var balance = 0L // meant to be guarded by LEDGER_LOCK /** A writer sets a balance inside a lock. A reader spins until it sees it. Which lock does the reader need? */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val shared = args.firstOrNull() == "shared" // daemon, so the JVM can exit even if the reader never stops val reader = thread(isDaemon = true) { if (shared) readWithLedgerLock() else readWithOwnLock() } Thread.sleep(500) // let the JIT compile the reader's loop synchronized(LEDGER_LOCK) { balance = 12_000 // cents } println("writer set balance = 12000 inside synchronized(LEDGER_LOCK)") reader.join(3_000) println("reader still spinning 3 s later? ${reader.isAlive}") } private fun readWithOwnLock() { var seen: Long do { seen = synchronized(Any()) { balance } // a lock no other thread can ever take } while (seen == 0L) println("reader (own lock) saw balance = $seen") } private fun readWithLedgerLock() { var seen: Long do { seen = synchronized(LEDGER_LOCK) { balance } // the same monitor the writer released } while (seen == 0L) println("reader (LEDGER_LOCK) saw balance = $seen") } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l02.LockScopeDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l02/LockScopeDemo.kt With its own lock the reader is still spinning 3 seconds later: there's no edge, the JIT removes the useless lock and reads balance once. With -Pargs=shared the reader prints balance = 12000 right after the writer, because the writer releases and the reader acquires the same monitor. T1's release of the monitor pairs with T2's acquire of the same monitor. Program order on both sides extends the edge to every write before the release and every read after the acquire. A Kafka listener in your authorization service parses a mutable AuthRequest with Jackson, submits it to a worker pool, and then calls req.setReceivedAt(Instant.now()) for latency metrics. The submit edge covers everything written before submit, and nothing after it, so once in a while the worker logs receivedAt=null. The same reasoning applies to Quarkus beans that fill a HashMap at startup for request threads to read. Whether an edge exists there depends on how the framework hands work to request threads, which you can't see from your code. A final field holding Map.copyOf(...), or a volatile field, puts the guarantee where you can read it.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Thread start and join are edges, and sleep is not
x: Two rules link a thread to the code that started it. Thread.start() happens-before every action in the started thread. Whatever the parent wrote before calling start() (the config, the list of partitions, the variables a lambda captured) the new thread sees. Every action in a thread happens-before another thread returns from join() on it. The same holds when another thread sees isAlive() return false. After join() returns, the parent sees every result the worker wrote, even into plain fields and plain arrays. A third rule matters for cancellation. When T1 calls t2.interrupt(), that call happens-before any thread noticing the interrupt through isInterrupted(), Thread.interrupted() or an InterruptedException. Thread.sleep() has none of this. Sleeping for 50 ms doesn't wait for the worker to finish. And even if the worker did finish in time, the sleep creates no edge, so a stale read is still legal. A sleep long enough to "always work" passes on your laptop and fails on a busy CI agent. The start edge covers only writes made before start(): Java Thread sender = new Thread(() -> send(config.endpoint())); sender.start(); config = loadConfig(); // after start(): no edge to the sender thread Kotlin val sender = thread { send(config.endpoint) } // thread {} calls start() for you config = loadConfig() // after start(): no edge to the sender thread The sender may see config as null or as the old value. This case comes back in lesson 4 of this track, where a constructor starts a thread before it has finished setting fields. Replace a sleep with a join Read SleepIsNotJoinDemo.java. The worker makes 20 calls of about 10 ms each, then writes total. Predict what main prints. Run it with the Gradle command below. Replace Thread.sleep(50) with worker.join() and run it again. Think it through: would Thread.sleep(5_000) be a correct fix? Which rule would it be missing? SleepIsNotJoinDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l02; /** main starts a worker that adds up merchant settlements, then sleeps and reads the total. */ public class SleepIsNotJoinDemo { static long total; // written by the worker, read by main public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Thread worker = new Thread(() -> { long sum = 0; for (int merchant = 0; merchant < 20; merchant++) { sum += fetchSettlement(merchant); // each call takes about 10 ms } total = sum; }); worker.start(); Thread.sleep(50); // "plenty of time" System.out.printf("after sleep(50): total = %,d (expected %,d)%n", total, 20 * 100_000L); } // stands in for a call to the settlement service static long fetchSettlement(int merchant) { try { Thread.sleep(10); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return 100_000; } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l02.SleepIsNotJoinDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l02/SleepIsNotJoinDemo.java SleepIsNotJoinDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l02 import kotlin.concurrent.thread private var total = 0L // written by the worker, read by main /** main starts a worker that adds up merchant settlements, then sleeps and reads the total. */ fun main() { val worker = thread { var sum = 0L for (merchant in 0 until 20) { sum += fetchSettlement(merchant) // each call takes about 10 ms } total = sum } Thread.sleep(50) // "plenty of time" println("after sleep(50): total = %,d (expected %,d)".format(total, 20 * 100_000L)) } // stands in for a call to the settlement service for one merchant private fun fetchSettlement(@Suppress("UNUSED_PARAMETER") merchant: Int): Long { Thread.sleep(10) return 100_000 } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l02.SleepIsNotJoinDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l02/SleepIsNotJoinDemo.kt The first run prints total = 0: the worker is a fifth of the way through. With join() it prints 2,000,000 every time, because join() waits for the worker to end and its edge makes the write visible. A 5-second sleep would print the right number on an idle machine, but it is still a data race: no rule links the worker's write to the read in main.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Transitivity, and the edges java.util.concurrent gives you
x: Edges chain. If A happens-before B and B happens-before C, then A happens-before C. That property is why one volatile or one lock can protect many plain fields. Java // loader thread // request thread rates = Map.copyOf(loaded); // A while (!ready) { } // C: sees true ready = true; // B Map<String, Long> r = rates; // D Kotlin // loader thread // request thread rates = loaded.toMap() // A while (!ready) { } // C: sees true ready = true // B val r = rates // D A comes before B in program order. B is a volatile write and C is a volatile read that sees it. C comes before D in program order. So A happens-before D, and the request thread sees the map, though rates is a plain field. This is often called piggybacking on the volatile. Two conditions are easy to miss. The plain writes must come before the release: if the loader wrote rates after setting ready, no edge would cover it. And the reader gets the edge only when its acquire actually sees the release. If C reads false and the code goes on to read rates anyway, nothing is promised. You rarely need to build these chains by hand. java.util.concurrent documents its own edges in its package docs. Among them: putting an object into any concurrent collection happens-before another thread accesses or removes it; submitting a Runnable or Callable to an executor happens-before the task starts; whatever a Future's task does happens-before Future.get() returns in another thread; countDown(), release() and unlock() happen-before a successful await(), acquire() or lock() on the same object in another thread. So a mutable Payment object handed to another thread through a BlockingQueue needs no volatile fields, as long as the producer stops writing to it after put. Prefer these edges to hand-rolled flags. A CountDownLatch blocks instead of spinning, responds to interrupts, and its edge is written down in its Javadoc. Name the edge For each snippet, name the happens-before edge that makes the last read safe, or write "none". (a) order.setAmount(500); executor.submit(() -> audit(order)); and the task reads order.getAmount(). (b) queue.put(payment); payment.setStatus(SENT); and the consumer calls queue.take().getStatus(). (c) T1: x = 1; v = 1; T2: if (w == 1) log(x); where v and w are different volatile fields. (d) T1: synchronized (ledger) { total += 5; } T2: synchronized (ledger) { log(total); }. (a) Executor submission: writes before submit happen-before the task. (b) None for the status: setStatus runs after put, so the consumer may see the old value. (c) None: the volatile write and read are on different fields. (d) The monitor rule on ledger, as long as T1's block ran first. java.util.concurrent package docs, "Memory Consistency Properties" (JDK 25 source) docs The most common mistake is locking only the writes. People think of locks as protecting data from concurrent changes, so they put synchronized on the setter and leave the getter plain because "reads don't change anything". But visibility needs both halves of the edge: the reader must acquire what the writer released. Guard the read with the same lock, or, if the read is a single field and the writes are already safe, make the field volatile.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Java and Kotlin
x: The same lock on both sides, in Java and Kotlin LedgerTotals.java public class LedgerTotals { private long total; // guarded by this public synchronized void add(long cents) { total += cents; } // hb: the unlock in add() pairs with the lock here public synchronized long total() { return total; } } LedgerTotals.kt class LedgerTotals { private val lock = Any() private var totalCents = 0L // guarded by lock fun add(cents: Long) { synchronized(lock) { totalCents += cents } } // hb: same lock object on both sides fun total(): Long = synchronized(lock) { totalCents } } Kotlin's synchronized(lock) { } is a standard library function, not a keyword. It is inlined and compiles to the same monitor enter and exit bytecode as a Java synchronized block, so it creates exactly the same edges. Kotlin code often locks a private val lock = Any() instead of this, which keeps outside code from taking your lock. Both languages give you @Synchronized or synchronized methods on this if you prefer that. CountDownLatch, executors and Future.get() give the same edges from either language.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Worked example
x: Find the missing edge in an executor handoff A Kafka listener thread parses a request and hands it to a worker pool. The worker logs latency from receivedAt, and about one log line in a thousand says receivedAt=null. List each write, each read, and the thread that does it. void onRecord(ConsumerRecord<String, String> rec) throws IOException { // listener thread AuthRequest req = mapper.readValue(rec.value(), AuthRequest.class); // 1. build a mutable object workers.submit(() -> authorize(req)); // 2. hand it to a pool thread req.setReceivedAt(Instant.now()); // 3. one more write, after the handoff } fun onRecord(rec: ConsumerRecord<String, String>) { // listener thread val req = mapper.readValue(rec.value(), AuthRequest::class.java) // 1. build a mutable object workers.execute { authorize(req) } // 2. hand it to a pool thread req.receivedAt = Instant.now() // 3. one more write, after the handoff } Draw the edges. Jackson's writes in step 1 come before submit in program order, and submit happens-before the task starts, so the worker sees them. The write in step 3 comes after submit, and no edge covers it. The worker's read of receivedAt is a data race. It usually reads the new value because the task starts a little later, which is why it fails only now and then. Put every write before the release, and stop touching the object after it. Then the one submit edge covers all of it. void onRecord(ConsumerRecord<String, String> rec) throws IOException { AuthRequest req = mapper.readValue(rec.value(), AuthRequest.class); req.setReceivedAt(Instant.now()); // 1. every write happens before the release workers.submit(() -> authorize(req)); // 2. submit carries them all to the worker // 3. no writes to req after this line } fun onRecord(rec: ConsumerRecord<String, String>) { val req = mapper.readValue(rec.value(), AuthRequest::class.java) req.receivedAt = Instant.now() // 1. every write happens before the release workers.execute { authorize(req) } // 2. the handoff carries them all to the worker // 3. no writes to req after this line } If the listener needs the worker's decision, Future.get() is the edge back: everything the task did happens-before get() returns. No field in AuthRequest or in the result needs to be volatile. Better still, make the request a record built once with all its fields, and the question of later writes can't come up. Future<Decision> f = workers.submit(() -> authorize(req)); Decision d = f.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // hb: the task's actions happen-before get() returns val f: Future<Decision> = workers.submit(Callable { authorize(req) }) val d = f.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // hb: the task's actions happen-before get() returns

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Quiz
x: setStatus writes inside synchronized (paymentLock). getStatus reads inside synchronized (auditLock). Is the getter guaranteed to see the latest status? Yes, because both methods are synchronized No: the edge exists only between releasing a monitor and a later acquire of the same monitor Yes, because entering any synchronized block refreshes all fields from memory No, because a field can't be read inside a synchronized block Two different monitors give no edge. The idea that any synchronized block refreshes everything comes from thinking of locks as memory barriers. The JMM only promises the edge for the same monitor, and the JIT is allowed to optimize accordingly. T1 runs x = 1; v = 1; where v is volatile and x is plain. T2 reads v and gets 0, then reads x. What can T2 see for x? Always 0, because T1 hasn't written v yet Always 1, because volatile flushes every earlier write Either 0 or 1: T2's read of v didn't see the write, so no edge covers x It throws, because reading a plain field next to a volatile is illegal The volatile edge forms only when the read sees the write. T2 saw 0, so it has no edge to T1's writes, and its read of x races with x = 1. T1 may well have already written x, which is why option 1 is wrong too. main fills a plain HashMap with 10,000 entries, then calls executor.submit(() -> lookup(map)) and never touches the map again. Is the task's read safe? Yes: submitting to an executor happens-before the task starts, and nobody writes after that No, because HashMap is not thread-safe Only if the map field is volatile Only if you switch to ConcurrentHashMap HashMap is unsafe for concurrent writes, but here all writes come before the handoff and none after. The submit edge makes them visible to the task. Volatile or ConcurrentHashMap would add cost and no safety. A worker thread writes result. Which of these does NOT give main a happens-before edge to that write? worker.join() returns future.get() returns, where the worker is the future's task latch.await() returns, after the worker wrote and then called latch.countDown() Thread.sleep(1_000) returns join, Future.get and the latch are all documented edges. sleep only passes time. The loop now has a happens-before edge to the writer Nothing: there is still no edge, HotSpot just happens to re-read the field onSpinWait makes the next read volatile onSpinWait flushes the writer's store buffer onSpinWait is a hint to the CPU, with no synchronization effect in the JMM.
