h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Key terms
x: Happens-before The memory model's ordering between two actions. If a write happens-before a read, the read sees it. Program order The order of actions within one thread, as the code is written. Release The sending end of an edge: leaving a lock, writing a volatile, countDown(), put into a concurrent queue. Acquire The receiving end of an edge: entering a lock, reading a volatile, await(), take from a concurrent queue. Data race Conflicting accesses to one variable from two threads with no happens-before edge between them. DRF-SC The JMM promise: a program free of data races behaves as if its threads were interleaved one action at a time. Piggybacking Relying on transitivity so one volatile or lock edge also publishes the plain writes made before it. When is a write in one thread guaranteed visible to a read in another? Only when the write happens-before the read. State the monitor rule of happens-before. Releasing a lock happens-before every later acquisition of the same lock. T1 writes inside synchronized (a). T2 reads inside synchronized (b). Is there an edge? No. The edge needs the same monitor on both sides. State the volatile rule of happens-before. A write to a volatile field happens-before every read of that same field that sees it (or a later write). What does Thread.start() guarantee to the new thread? Everything the parent did before calling start() is visible to the new thread. Writes after start() are not covered. Is Thread.sleep(100) a happens-before edge? No. Use join(), Future.get() or a latch. What is a data race? Two threads access the same variable, at least one access is a write, and no happens-before edge orders them.

h: Happens-before, the rules that matter · Go deeper
x: Two refinements are worth knowing once the basic rules feel natural. First, the JLS builds happens-before from a smaller relation called synchronizes-with. Each synchronizes-with edge links a release in one thread to an acquire in another: releasing a monitor to a later acquire of the same monitor, a volatile write to a read that sees it, start() to the first action of the new thread, a thread's last action to a join() that returns. Happens-before is then program order plus synchronizes-with, closed under transitivity. Apart from an edge into finalizers, that's the whole construction. All the synchronization actions in a run also fall into one total order, which is why two volatile writes are seen in the same order by every thread. Second, a lock is not a memory fence. It's tempting to picture synchronized as "flush everything on exit, reload everything on entry". The JMM promises less, and the JIT uses the difference. The jcstress sample AdvancedJMM_01_SynchronizedBarriers writes x and y in two back-to-back synchronized (this) blocks, and an observer that takes no lock reads them with volatile reads. On x86_64 the observer saw the new y with the old x in 207,479 of about four billion samples. The JIT had merged the two blocks into one (lock coarsening) and reordered the writes inside it. That is legal: only a thread that also locks this is owed the order. Aleksey Shipilëv's "Close Encounters of The Java Memory Model Kind" walks through more misreadings like these, each with a jcstress test.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · volatile gives you visibility and ordering
x: Declaring a field volatile gets you three things, and you've already used two of them in this track. Visibility. A volatile read sees the latest volatile write to that field. The JIT can't keep the value in a register or hoist the read out of a loop. That was the stop flag in lesson 1 of this track. Ordering. A volatile write is a release: plain writes that come before it in program order can't move after it. A volatile read is an acquire: plain reads after it can't move before it. That's the piggybacking from lesson 2 of this track. Java config = load(); // plain write: stays before the volatile write version = 42; // volatile write (release) if (version == 42) { // volatile read (acquire), in another thread use(config); // plain read: stays after it, and sees the config } Kotlin config = load() // plain write: stays before the volatile write version = 42 // @Volatile write (release) if (version == 42) { // @Volatile read (acquire), in another thread use(config) // plain read: stays after it, and sees the config } One order for all volatile accesses. Every thread agrees on a single order of all volatile reads and writes. That's what forbids the store-buffering outcome from lesson 1 of this track, where both threads read 0. Acquire and release alone don't forbid it; lesson 6 of this track shows the difference. The ordering only helps threads that both use the volatile. If thread A writes a volatile x and thread B writes a plain y, B's write can still sit in its store buffer while B reads x. The try-it below measures this. The cost is lower than people fear. On x86 a volatile read compiles to an ordinary load; the only cost is that the JIT can't optimize around it. A volatile write costs more, because HotSpot follows it with an instruction that drains the store buffer. On ARM, HotSpot uses dedicated load-acquire and store-release instructions. For a flag read on every request, the price is noise next to one database call. Make only one side volatile Read HalfVolatileDemo. It runs the store-buffering test three ways: no volatile, only x volatile, and both volatile. Predict the middle column before you run: does one volatile field save both threads? Run it with the command below. HalfVolatileDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l03; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.IntConsumer; /** * The store-buffering test from lesson 1 of this track, three ways: no volatile, only x volatile, * both fields volatile. Thread A runs {@code x = 1; r1 = y;} and thread B runs {@code y = 1; r2 = x;}. * Counts the trials where both threads read 0. */ public class HalfVolatileDemo { static final class Plain { int x, y; } static final class XOnly { volatile int x; int y; } static final class Both { volatile int x, y; } static final int TRIALS = 1 << 19; static final int BATCH = 32; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int run = 1; run <= 3; run++) { System.out.printf("run %d: both read 0 in plain: %,7d only x volatile: %,7d both volatile: %,d%n", run, plain(), xOnly(), both()); } } static int plain() throws InterruptedException { Plain[] s = new Plain[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Plain(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } static int xOnly() throws InterruptedException { XOnly[] s = new XOnly[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new XOnly(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } static int both() throws InterruptedException { Both[] s = new Both[TRIALS]; for (int i = 0; i < TRIALS; i++) s[i] = new Both(); int[] r1 = new int[TRIALS], r2 = new int[TRIALS]; race(i -> { s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y; }, i -> { s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x; }); return bothZero(r1, r2); } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads, in lockstep batches so they overlap. static void race(IntConsumer a, IntConsumer b) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger doneA = new AtomicInteger(), doneB = new AtomicInteger(); Thread ta = new Thread(() -> runSide(a, doneA, doneB)); Thread tb = new Thread(() -> runSide(b, doneB, doneA)); ta.start(); tb.start(); ta.join(); tb.join(); } static void runSide(IntConsumer side, AtomicInteger mine, AtomicInteger other) { for (int batch = 0; batch < TRIALS / BATCH; batch++) { mine.set(batch); while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait(); for (int i = batch * BATCH; i < (batch + 1) * BATCH; i++) side.accept(i); } } static int bothZero(int[] r1, int[] r2) { int n = 0; for (int i = 0; i < r1.length; i++) if (r1[i] == 0 && r2[i] == 0) n++; return n; } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l03.HalfVolatileDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l03/HalfVolatileDemo.java HalfVolatileDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l03 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.function.IntConsumer import kotlin.concurrent.thread /* * The store-buffering test from lesson 1 of this track, three ways: no @Volatile, only x @Volatile, * both fields @Volatile. Thread A runs `x = 1; r1 = y` and thread B runs `y = 1; r2 = x`. * Counts the trials where both threads read 0. */ private class NoVolatile { var x = 0; var y = 0 } private class XVolatile { @Volatile var x = 0; var y = 0 } private class BothVolatile { @Volatile var x = 0; @Volatile var y = 0 } private const val TRIALS = 1 shl 19 private const val BATCH = 32 fun main() { for (run in 1..3) { println("run %d: both read 0 in plain: %,7d only x @Volatile: %,7d both @Volatile: %,d" .format(run, plain(), xOnly(), both())) } } private fun plain(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { NoVolatile() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } private fun xOnly(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { XVolatile() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } private fun both(): Int { val s = Array(TRIALS) { BothVolatile() } val r1 = IntArray(TRIALS) val r2 = IntArray(TRIALS) race(IntConsumer { i -> s[i].x = 1; r1[i] = s[i].y }, IntConsumer { i -> s[i].y = 1; r2[i] = s[i].x }) return bothZero(r1, r2) } // Runs a(i) and b(i) for every trial on two threads, in lockstep batches so they overlap. private fun race(a: IntConsumer, b: IntConsumer) { val doneA = AtomicInteger() val doneB = AtomicInteger() val ta = thread { runSide(a, doneA, doneB) } val tb = thread { runSide(b, doneB, doneA) } ta.join(); tb.join() } private fun runSide(side: IntConsumer, mine: AtomicInteger, other: AtomicInteger) { for (batch in 0 until TRIALS / BATCH) { mine.set(batch) while (other.get() < batch) Thread.onSpinWait() for (i in batch * BATCH until (batch + 1) * BATCH) side.accept(i) } } private fun bothZero(r1: IntArray, r2: IntArray): Int = r1.indices.count { r1[it] == 0 && r2[it] == 0 } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l03.HalfVolatileDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l03/HalfVolatileDemo.kt Plain fields show both threads reading 0 in a large share of trials. With only x volatile the count drops but stays well above zero (tens of thousands here): thread B's write to plain y can still wait in its store buffer while it reads x. Only when both fields are volatile does the count go to 0. A volatile field is a number on the office whiteboard instead of in someone's notebook. Everyone reads the board directly, nobody copies it to a private note, and everyone sees the changes in the same order. But two people can still walk up, both read 41, both go back to their desks to add one, and both write 42. The board was always current; the update just wasn't one step. The analogy is weak in one place: a real whiteboard has no rule about the notes you wrote before updating it. A volatile write does: everything you wrote before it becomes visible to whoever reads the new value.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · volatile does not make count++ atomic
x: Here's the bug from the warm-up: Java private volatile int retries; void onRetry() { retries++; // read, add one, write: three steps } Kotlin @Volatile private var retries = 0 fun onRetry() { retries++ // read, add one, write: three steps } volatile makes the read fresh and the write visible. It does nothing about the gap between them. Two threads read 41, both add one, both write 42. Each of those six accesses was perfectly volatile. The research for this track measured it: 4 threads each ran v++ a million times on a static volatile int, and the total came out at 3,681,731 instead of 4,000,000. The same run with a plain int came out at 3,997,394. The plain counter looked less wrong in that run, and that proves nothing: the JIT can batch plain increments in a register, which changes how many get lost. Runs for this lesson saw the order flip. Both are broken. The fix is a single step that reads and writes as one: Java private final AtomicInteger retries = new AtomicInteger(); void onRetry() { retries.incrementAndGet(); // one atomic read-modify-write } Kotlin private val retries = AtomicInteger() fun onRetry() { retries.incrementAndGet() // one atomic read-modify-write } For a counter that many threads hit hard and that you only read now and then (metrics), LongAdder is faster still. A lock works too, and it's the only choice once the update touches more than one field. The same trap hides in any compound action on a volatile: if (balance >= amount) balance -= amount, max = Math.max(max, x), if (state == OPEN) state = CLOSED. Every one of them reads, decides and writes as separate steps. Count four ways Read VolatileCounterDemo. Four threads each add 1,000,000 to a plain counter, a volatile counter, an AtomicInteger and a LongAdder. Predict which of the four reach 4,000,000, and whether volatile loses fewer updates than plain. Run it twice with the command below and compare the runs. VolatileCounterDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l03; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** Four threads each add 1,000,000 to four kinds of counter. Which ones add up? */ public class VolatileCounterDemo { static int plain; static volatile int vol; static final AtomicInteger atomic = new AtomicInteger(); static final LongAdder adder = new LongAdder(); static final int THREADS = 4, PER_THREAD = 1_000_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("plain int", () -> plain++); run("volatile int", () -> vol++); run("AtomicInteger", atomic::incrementAndGet); run("LongAdder", adder::increment); System.out.printf("expected %,d each%n", THREADS * PER_THREAD); System.out.printf("plain %,d volatile %,d atomic %,d adder %,d%n", plain, vol, atomic.get(), adder.sum()); } static void run(String name, Runnable increment) throws InterruptedException { Thread[] ts = new Thread[THREADS]; for (int t = 0; t < THREADS; t++) { ts[t] = new Thread(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < PER_THREAD; i++) increment.run(); }, name + "-" + t); } for (Thread t : ts) t.start(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); // join: the final reads in main see every thread's writes } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l03.VolatileCounterDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l03/VolatileCounterDemo.java VolatileCounterDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l03 import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder import kotlin.concurrent.thread private var plain = 0 @Volatile private var vol = 0 private val atomic = AtomicInteger() private val adder = LongAdder() private const val THREADS = 4 private const val PER_THREAD = 1_000_000 /** Four threads each add 1,000,000 to four kinds of counter. Which ones add up? */ fun main() { hammer("plain Int") { plain++ } hammer("@Volatile Int") { vol++ } hammer("AtomicInteger") { atomic.incrementAndGet() } hammer("LongAdder") { adder.increment() } println("expected %,d each".format(THREADS * PER_THREAD)) println("plain %,d @Volatile %,d atomic %,d adder %,d".format(plain, vol, atomic.get(), adder.sum())) } private fun hammer(name: String, increment: () -> Unit) { val ts = List(THREADS) { t -> thread(name = "$name-$t") { repeat(PER_THREAD) { increment() } } } ts.forEach { it.join() } // join: the final reads in main see every thread's writes } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l03.VolatileCounterDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l03/VolatileCounterDemo.kt The atomic and the adder print exactly 4,000,000 every time. Plain and volatile both come out short, often by hundreds of thousands, and which of the two loses more changes from run to run. The volatile counter is not "more correct"; it's wrong in a different pattern. Look at hand-rolled circuit breakers and rate limiters in your services. A common shape is volatile int failures with failures++ on every issuer timeout and if (failures > 5) open() right after. Under a burst of timeouts from the card issuer, increments get lost and the breaker opens late, exactly when it should be fastest. Libraries such as SmallRye Fault Tolerance use proper atomics or locks for this; copy them, or use them. The good uses of volatile are just as common: a volatile RateTable current that a scheduler replaces every minute, a volatile boolean draining that a Quarkus shutdown observer sets, a volatile long lastPollMillis for a Kafka liveness check.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · When volatile is enough, and when you need more
x: Make every field of a payment volatile and it can still be captured twice. The capture code checks status == AUTHORIZED, adds the amount to captured, then sets status = CAPTURED. Two threads can both pass the check before either one sets the new status, and every read and write along the way is a correct volatile access. The simulator at the end of this section lets you do it by hand. So the useful question is which fields volatile is enough for. Volatile is the right tool when all of these hold: Only one thread writes the field, or every write sets a value that doesn't depend on the current one. The field isn't part of a rule that involves other fields. Readers need the latest value, nothing more. That covers more fields than you'd think: a shutdown flag, a status that one callback thread moves forward, a last-heartbeat timestamp, a Kafka lag gauge that one poller updates. It also covers a reference to an immutable object that one thread replaces whole, such as a rate table refreshed every minute. Readers grab the current table with one volatile read, and the table itself never changes. The moment a decision needs a read, then a write based on what you read, volatile stops being enough. One variable with many writers takes an atomic class (incrementAndGet, compareAndSet, updateAndGet). Several variables that must change together, or a check that spans them, take a lock. Shape of the field Tool One writer, readers need the latest value volatile Many writers, one variable, read-modify-write AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, LongAdder Two or more fields under one rule a lock around every read and write A whole immutable object, replaced now and then a volatile reference or AtomicReference One mixed pattern is worth knowing. If writes are rare and reads are hot, make the writes synchronized and the field volatile. Writers exclude each other through the lock, so += is safe, and readers pay only for one volatile read. Java private volatile long balance; public long balance() { return balance; } // readers: one volatile read public synchronized void apply(long delta) { balance += delta; } // writers: the lock makes += safe Kotlin @Volatile private var balance = 0L fun balance(): Long = balance // readers: one volatile read @Synchronized fun apply(delta: Long) { balance += delta } // writers: the lock makes += safe The simulator shows the limit. Both fields are volatile, yet the capture-once rule fails. Pick the tool Choose volatile, an atomic or a lock for each field, and say why in one line. (a) boolean maintenanceMode, flipped by an admin endpoint, read by every request. (b) int inFlight, incremented when a request starts and decremented when it ends, by request threads. (c) long dailyLimitCents and long spentTodayCents, checked together before each authorization. (d) Map<String, Rule> rules, replaced every minute by a refresher thread with a new map that nobody modifies. (a) volatile: writes don't depend on the old value. (b) An atomic (AtomicInteger or LongAdder): many writers doing read-modify-write. (c) A lock: one rule spans two fields and needs check-then-act. (d) A volatile reference to an immutable map, built with Map.copyOf before it is published.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · What volatile covers: one variable, all 64 bits, and nothing behind it
x: Three details trip people up once the basics are clear. First, long and double. The JLS (section 17.7) lets the JVM treat a write to a non-volatile long or double as two separate 32-bit writes. A racing reader could then see the high half of one value and the low half of another. Writes and reads of volatile long and double are always atomic, and so are references and every type of 32 bits or less. The jcstress suite shows torn longs on a 32-bit x86 JVM: a reader saw -4294967296 and 4294967295 when the only values ever written were 0 and -1. 64-bit HotSpot writes a long in one instruction, so you won't see tearing there, but the spec doesn't promise it. In practice this rarely matters on its own: a long that two threads share needs volatile for visibility anyway, and you get atomicity with it. Second, a volatile reference covers the reference and nothing inside the object. Writing fees.add(f) to a volatile List<Fee> fees is not a volatile write. It's a call on whatever list the field points to, with no edge for readers and no protection for the list. Replace the whole object instead: Java private volatile List<Fee> fees = List.of(); // volatile covers the reference only void replaceFees(List<Fee> fresh) { fees = List.copyOf(fresh); // one volatile write of an immutable list } Kotlin @Volatile private var fees: List<Fee> = emptyList() // @Volatile covers the reference only fun replaceFees(fresh: List<Fee>) { fees = fresh.toList() // one write of a copy nobody else holds } The jcstress sample AdvancedJMM_05_MisplacedVolatile shows the cost of getting this wrong. A volatile field held a holder object, but the new value went into a plain field inside the holder. On AArch64 a reader saw the new object's field still at 0 in 553 samples. Third, arrays. A volatile long[] makes the array reference volatile and leaves every element plain. For volatile elements, use AtomicLongArray, AtomicIntegerArray or AtomicReferenceArray: Java class BalanceBoard { private volatile long[] balances = new long[16]; // volatile reference, plain elements private final AtomicLongArray safe = new AtomicLongArray(16); // each element acts like a volatile void post(int account, long cents) { balances[account] = cents; // plain element write: no edge for readers safe.set(account, cents); // volatile element write: readers of safe.get() see it } } Kotlin class BalanceBoard { @Volatile private var balances = LongArray(16) // volatile reference, plain elements private val safe = AtomicLongArray(16) // each element acts like a volatile fun post(account: Int, cents: Long) { balances[account] = cents // plain element write: no edge for readers safe.set(account, cents) // volatile element write: readers of safe.get() see it } } Check yourself: a volatile Map<String, Long> limits holds a HashMap, and request threads call limits.put(card, cents). Does a reader that calls limits.get(card) see the new entry? Nothing promises it. The only volatile access is the read of the field. The put writes inside the map, and those writes are plain, so no edge reaches the reader. Two threads calling put at once can also break the HashMap itself. Use one writer that replaces the whole map with an immutable copy, or a ConcurrentHashMap. The most common mistake is reaching for volatile as the general fix for "thread-safety": a field is shared, so it gets the keyword. That works for flags and single-writer values, and quietly fails for counters, check-then-act and any rule that spans two fields, because volatile makes each access visible and ordered without joining them into one step. Before adding volatile, ask who writes the field and whether the new value depends on the old one. If several threads write, or the write depends on a read, use an atomic or a lock.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Java and Kotlin
x: A volatile snapshot reference in Java and Kotlin FraudRules.java public class FraudRules { // replaced whole, never mutated: one volatile read gives a consistent snapshot private volatile Map<String, Rule> rules = Map.of(); // one refresher thread public void refresh(Map<String, Rule> fresh) { rules = Map.copyOf(fresh); // build first, then publish with one volatile write } // many request threads public Rule ruleFor(String merchantCategory) { return rules.get(merchantCategory); } } FraudRules.kt class FraudRules { // replaced whole, never mutated: one volatile read gives a consistent snapshot @Volatile private var rules: Map<String, Rule> = emptyMap() // one refresher thread fun refresh(fresh: Map<String, Rule>) { rules = fresh.toMap() // a private copy, then publish with one volatile write } // many request threads fun ruleFor(merchantCategory: String): Rule? = rules[merchantCategory] } The pattern is identical: build a new map, publish it with one volatile write, and never touch it again. The difference is in the copy. Java's Map.copyOf returns a truly unmodifiable map (and rejects nulls). Kotlin's Map type is only a read-only view, so the safety comes from toMap() making a fresh LinkedHashMap that no other code holds. If you passed the caller's map straight through, someone with a MutableMap reference could still change it under the readers.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Worked example
x: Choose the tools for a circuit breaker A breaker in front of a card issuer opens after 5 failures in a row. Request threads call onFailure and onSuccess, and check allowRequest before each call. Every field is volatile. For each field, ask: who writes it, and does the write depend on a read? class IssuerBreaker { private volatile int consecutiveFailures; // written by request threads private volatile long openedAtMillis; // 0 means closed void onFailure(long now) { consecutiveFailures++; // 1. read-modify-write if (consecutiveFailures >= 5 && openedAtMillis == 0) openedAtMillis = now; // 2. check-then-act } void onSuccess() { consecutiveFailures = 0; } boolean allowRequest(long now) { long opened = openedAtMillis; return opened == 0 || now - opened > 30_000; } } class IssuerBreaker { @Volatile private var consecutiveFailures = 0 // written by request threads @Volatile private var openedAtMillis = 0L // 0 means closed fun onFailure(now: Long) { consecutiveFailures++ // 1. read-modify-write if (consecutiveFailures >= 5 && openedAtMillis == 0L) openedAtMillis = now // 2. check-then-act } fun onSuccess() { consecutiveFailures = 0 } fun allowRequest(now: Long): Boolean { val opened = openedAtMillis return opened == 0L || now - opened > 30_000 } } consecutiveFailures has many writers, and ++ depends on a read, so increments get lost and the breaker opens late. Line 2 reads the counter again, separately, and then reads and writes openedAtMillis: two threads can both see 5 and both set the time. openedAtMillis itself is fine as volatile for the readers in allowRequest, which need one value and nothing else. Make the counter atomic and decide on the value it returns. Each incrementAndGet returns a different number, so only one thread sees exactly 5 for each run of failures, and only that thread opens the breaker. class IssuerBreaker { private final AtomicInteger consecutiveFailures = new AtomicInteger(); // 1. many writers: atomic private volatile long openedAtMillis; // 2. readers need one value: volatile void onFailure(long now) { int n = consecutiveFailures.incrementAndGet(); // 3. one atomic step, and keep the result if (n == 5) openedAtMillis = now; // 4. only one thread sees n == 5 } void onSuccess() { consecutiveFailures.set(0); } boolean allowRequest(long now) { long opened = openedAtMillis; // 5. read the volatile once return opened == 0 || now - opened > 30_000; } } class IssuerBreaker { private val consecutiveFailures = AtomicInteger() // 1. many writers: atomic @Volatile private var openedAtMillis = 0L // 2. readers need one value: @Volatile fun onFailure(now: Long) { val n = consecutiveFailures.incrementAndGet() // 3. one atomic step, and keep the result if (n == 5) openedAtMillis = now // 4. only one thread sees n == 5 } fun onSuccess() { consecutiveFailures.set(0) } fun allowRequest(now: Long): Boolean { val opened = openedAtMillis // 5. read the volatile once return opened == 0L || now - opened > 30_000 } } Two habits made this work. Use the value the atomic call returns: calling incrementAndGet() and then get() would bring the check-then-act gap back. And read a volatile into a local once when you use it twice, as allowRequest does, so both uses see the same value. When the breaker grows a half-open state that must let exactly one trial request through while it also resets the counter, two fields change together, and that is the point to switch to a lock.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Lab
x: Choose volatile, atomic or lock for a payment session labs/jmm/src/main/java/workbench/jmm/l03/PaymentSession.java ./gradlew :jmm:test --tests 'workbench.jmm.l03.*' Run the tests once. Four of the five fail: two waiters never see a write, the attempt counter comes up short, and the money invariant breaks. Try the quick fix first: put volatile on every field and run the tests. Two still fail. Before reading on, say which two and why. Now go field by field. Read the comment that says who writes it and who reads it, choose volatile, an atomic or a lock, and add a one-line comment saying why. Keep every public signature as it is. Run the tests until all five pass, then twice more. status and lastHeartbeatMillis each have one writer, and the new value doesn't depend on the old one. attempts++ is read-modify-write with many writers. An AtomicInteger lets attempts() keep returning int. tryRefund reads capturedCents, which tryCapture writes. Guard both fields with one lock, and take it in the two getters too. A pair of AtomicLongs can't keep refunded <= captured. All five tests in PaymentSessionTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can say exactly what volatile guarantees, show why it doesn't make count++ safe, and choose between volatile, an atomic and a lock for any shared field.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Quiz
x: Many request threads run balance += amount on a volatile long balance. What can go wrong? Two threads can read the same balance and both write, so one amount is lost Nothing: volatile makes the whole statement atomic The 64-bit write can tear into two halves Readers may never see the new balance += is read, add, write. Volatile makes each step visible and ordered but leaves the gap between them. Tearing is ruled out because the field is volatile, and visibility is fine, which is what makes the bug easy to miss. Which of these fields is correctly protected by volatile alone? A request counter that every request thread increments A reference to an immutable RateTable that one scheduler thread replaces every minute limit and spent, which are checked together before every authorization A volatile ArrayList<Fee> that several threads add fees to One writer, a whole-object replace, and readers that need only the latest reference: that's exactly volatile's job. The counter needs an atomic, the pair needs a lock, and the volatile list protects only the reference while ArrayList.add races. In HalfVolatileDemo only x is volatile. Why do both threads still sometimes read 0? The volatile write to x is lost Volatile only works between two volatile fields of the same object Thread B's plain write to y can wait in its store buffer while B reads x, so B's own pair of accesses is not ordered The demo's barrier lets the threads run different trials Each thread's write-then-read must be ordered for the outcome to be ruled out. Thread A's volatile write is followed by a store-buffer drain, but thread B wrote a plain field, so nothing stops B's read from passing its own write. Make both fields volatile and the count drops to 0. A class has private volatile long[] balances. Thread A runs balances[3] = 500. Thread B later reads balances[3]. What is guaranteed? B sees 500, because the array is volatile B sees 500 or 0, but never a torn value B sees 500 once A releases the array Nothing about the element: only the array reference is volatile, so this is a plain write and a plain read Element accesses of a volatile array are plain accesses. There's no edge from A's write to B's read, and a plain long element may even tear under the JLS. Use AtomicLongArray when elements are shared. From lesson 2 of this track: T1 sets a plain fee = 25 and then the volatile ready = true. T2 sees ready == true and then reads fee. Why must T2 see 25? Because fee is an int, and int writes are atomic Program order, then the volatile write-to-read edge, then program order again: the edges chain, so the write of fee happens-before its read Because volatile writes flush all CPU caches It doesn't have to; T2 may see 0 This is piggybacking on the volatile. The write of fee comes before the release in T1's program order, and the read comes after the acquire in T2's. Atomicity only rules out half-written values; it says nothing about which value you see.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Explain it back
x: A teammate asks: "If volatile makes every read and write go to memory, why does volatile int retries; retries++ still lose updates?" Explain in your own words, and say what you would use instead.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Key terms
x: Visibility Whether a read in one thread sees a write from another. Atomicity An operation happens as one indivisible step that no other thread can split. Read-modify-write Read a value, compute a new one from it, write it back. Needs an atomic or a lock when shared. Torn read Seeing half of one write and half of another, possible for non-volatile long and double under the JLS. Single writer A field that only one thread ever writes. Volatile is enough for it. Snapshot publication Building a new immutable object and publishing it with one volatile write, instead of mutating the old one. LongAdder A counter that spreads increments over several cells. Fast under contention; its sum is not a snapshot. What does a volatile field guarantee? Visibility of the latest write, release/acquire ordering around each access, and a single order of all volatile accesses that every thread agrees on. Is count++ on a volatile int atomic? No. It's still a read, an add and a write. Use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() or LongAdder. When is volatile alone enough for a field? When one thread writes it (or writes don't depend on the current value), and the field isn't part of a rule with other fields. Two fields must change together under one rule. Volatile, atomic or lock? A lock, taken around every read and write of both fields. Can a write to a non-volatile long tear? The JLS allows it to be split into two 32-bit writes. A volatile long or double is always written and read atomically. volatile List<Fee> fees; Is fees.add(f) from two threads safe? No. Volatile covers the reference only. Replace the whole list with an immutable copy instead, or use a concurrent collection. Are the elements of a volatile long[] volatile? No, only the array reference. Use AtomicLongArray for volatile element access.

h: volatile: what it gives you and what it doesn't · Go deeper
x: Atomic classes are volatile fields with extra operations. AtomicInteger.get() and set() have the same memory effects as reading and writing a volatile int. What the class adds is atomic read-modify-write: incrementAndGet, compareAndSet, getAndUpdate, accumulateAndGet. The functional ones (updateAndGet and friends) retry a compare-and-set in a loop, so the function you pass may run more than once and must have no side effects. Why is the JLS rule for long and double still there, when 64-bit JVMs never tear? Because the JLS is written for every JVM, including 32-bit ones, and dropping the rule would force those JVMs to use more expensive instructions for every 64-bit access. The VarHandle Javadoc states the same rule for its plain mode: plain reads and writes are guaranteed bitwise atomic only for references and for primitive values of 32 bits or less. A related term you may meet is word tearing: a write to one field or array element changing a neighbor, as some CPUs would do for single bytes. Java forbids it outright. Every field and every array element is its own variable, so a byte[] shared between threads never corrupts the byte next to the one you wrote. Races on that array are still races, of course.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Publishing an object is a write, and it can race
x: Publishing an object means making a reference to it reachable from another thread: storing it in a shared field, a static, a collection, or handing it to code that runs elsewhere. Java RateCard card = new RateCard("EUR", fees); // 1. allocate, 2. run the constructor registry.current = card; // 3. publish: store the reference where others look Kotlin val card = RateCard("EUR", fees) // 1. allocate, 2. run the constructor registry.current = card // 3. publish: store the reference where others look Three things happen. The JVM allocates memory with every field at its default (0, false, null). The constructor writes the fields. Then the reference is stored. In the writing thread they happen in that order. A thread that reads current through a plain field has no edge to any of them. The JIT may store the reference before the field writes, and an ARM CPU may make the stores visible in any order. So the reader can see current != null and still read a null currency or a fee of 0. That's a partially constructed object, and no line you wrote creates one. It's not theory. The jcstress sample BasicJMM_08_Finals publishes an object with four plain int fields through a plain field. On x86_64 a reader saw the reference with some fields still 0 in about 18,000 out of 219 million samples. On AArch64 it saw just about every mix of zeros and real values. Unsafe publication has a second failure you already know from lesson 1 of this track: the reader may never see the reference at all, because the JIT may read the field once. That's the RateCardRegistry bug in the lab. There are two ways out. Publish through something that creates a happens-before edge, so the reference and the state travel together. Or make the object safe to see even through a race, which is what final fields do. The best code does both. Check yourself: lesson 1 of this track showed that x86 only lets a later read pass an earlier write, so its stores reach memory in order. Yet the x86_64 run of BasicJMM_08_Finals still saw half-built objects. Which layer did that? The JIT, the only one left. It may move the field stores after the store of the reference, or move the reader's loads, and the CPU then runs them in the order the JIT chose. With no edge, another thread can see the publishing store before the constructor's store. It finds a real object with a default value inside. Publishing an object is like hanging a new price board in the shop window. Hang it before you've finished writing and a passer-by reads half a board, with blanks where prices should be. Safe publication means hanging it only when it's done, in a window everyone looks through. Final fields are like boards printed at the factory: by the time anyone can see one, it's complete, whichever window it's in. The analogy breaks on escaping this: in a shop you'd notice someone reading over your shoulder, and in Java the reader can be your own constructor's callback, running on the same thread.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Four ways to publish safely
x: An object is safely published when the reference and the state it had at that moment reach the reader together. The standard idioms, from Java Concurrency in Practice: Initialize it in a static initializer. The JVM runs class initialization under a lock, and every thread that uses the class sees the result. Store it in a volatile field or an AtomicReference. Store it in a final field of an object that is itself properly constructed. Store it in a field guarded by a lock, or hand it over through java.util.concurrent: a concurrent map or queue, an executor, a future. Each gives the reader an edge you already know: the class-initialization lock, volatile write and read, the final-field rule (next section), the monitor rule, or a j.u.c handoff. Java class RateCardRegistry { static final RateCard DEFAULT = new RateCard("EUR", Map.of("VISA", 120L)); // 1. static initializer private volatile RateCard current = DEFAULT; // 2. volatile field private final ConcurrentMap<String, RateCard> byCurrency = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // 4. j.u.c handoff void publish(RateCard card) { current = card; byCurrency.put(card.currency(), card); } } Kotlin class RateCardRegistry { companion object { val DEFAULT = RateCard("EUR", mapOf("VISA" to 120L)) // 1. static initializer (companion object) } @Volatile private var current: RateCard = DEFAULT // 2. @Volatile property private val byCurrency = ConcurrentHashMap<String, RateCard>() // 4. j.u.c handoff fun publish(card: RateCard) { current = card byCurrency[card.currency] = card } } A Kotlin companion object is initialized when its class is loaded, with the same semantics as a Java static initializer, so idiom 1 works the same way. For anything you replace at runtime, use a volatile field or an AtomicReference. Use static final for constants. Don't add synchronized getters only to publish; a volatile read is cheaper and says what you mean. Safe publication covers the state the object had when you published it. If you change the object afterwards, each change needs its own synchronization. That's why the best objects to publish are the ones that never change. Safe or not? For each line, say whether a request thread is guaranteed to see the whole RateCard, and name the idiom or the missing edge. (a) static final RateCard DEFAULT = new RateCard(...), read by any thread. (b) private RateCard current;, set by the loader, read by request threads. (c) private volatile RateCard current;, set by the loader, read by request threads. (d) cards.put(id, card) on a ConcurrentHashMap, and request threads call cards.get(id). (a) Safe: the static initializer runs under the class-initialization lock. (b) Not safe: no edge, so a reader may see a half-built card or never see it at all. (c) Safe: volatile write, then volatile read. (d) Safe: putting into a concurrent map happens-before a get that returns it. Watch for constructors that wire things up. A Quarkus bean whose constructor calls scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::refresh, ...) before it has assigned its HTTP client will, now and then, run refresh with a null client. A Kafka listener that registers itself with a listener container from its constructor can receive a record before its deserializer is set. Move that wiring into a @PostConstruct method or an @Observes StartupEvent observer, which CDI calls after the bean is fully constructed. For data, prefer records and val-only Kotlin classes for anything you cache and share: rate cards, issuer configs, BIN tables. Publish each new version with one volatile write.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Final fields survive a data race
x: The memory model gives final fields one extra promise. The JLS (section 17.5) says, in short: a thread that can only see a reference to an object after its constructor has finished is guaranteed to see the correct values of that object's final fields. No volatile, no lock. It holds even when the reference reached the reader through a data race. The promise reaches through the field. If a final field points to an array or a map, the reader also sees its contents as they were at the end of the constructor. The JLS calls the end of the constructor the freeze. Java final class Quote { private final String scheme; // final: correct even through a race private final Map<String, Long> fees; // final: and the map's contents as of the constructor private long hits; // plain: a racing reader may see 0 Quote(String scheme, Map<String, Long> fees) { this.scheme = scheme; this.fees = Map.copyOf(fees); } } Kotlin class Quote(scheme: String, fees: Map<String, Long>) { private val scheme = scheme // val: a final field, correct even through a race private val fees = fees.toMap() // val: and the map's contents as of the constructor private var hits = 0L // var: a plain field, a racing reader may see 0 } In BasicJMM_08_Finals, making all four fields final removed every partial result on both x86_64 and AArch64: readers saw either no object or the complete one. HotSpot keeps that promise with a barrier. When a constructor writes a final field, the C2 compiler puts a store-store barrier at the end of the constructor: every write before it must complete before any store after it, and the store that publishes the reference always comes after. On x86 the barrier compiles to nothing, because the CPU keeps stores in order anyway; it only stops the JIT from moving stores across it. On ARM it is a real fence instruction. Two limits. Final fields don't make the reference visible: a reader spinning on a plain field may still never see your object. And the promise holds only if this doesn't escape before the constructor ends: a thread that gets the reference before the barrier gets no ordering at all. The next section shows how that happens. Put the pieces together and you get an immutable object: a final class, every field final, mutable inputs copied in the constructor, nothing mutable handed out, and no escaping this. You can share it through any race and no reader will ever see it half-built or changing. Java records and Kotlin classes with only val properties get you most of the way. They still store a caller's mutable list as it is, so copy it, for example in a record's compact constructor: record FeeSchedule(List<Fee> fees) { FeeSchedule { fees = List.copyOf(fees); } }. Find final in the bytecode Run both demos below once (the Java one, then the Kotlin one) so Gradle compiles them. From labs/, run javap -p 'jmm/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/jmm/l04/FinalFieldsDemo$Quote.class' and the same for FinalFieldsDemo$MutableQuote.class. Run javap -p jmm/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/jmm/l04/KQuote.class and the same for KMutableQuote.class. Predict before each command: which fields will say final? FinalFieldsDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l04; /** Where final fields come from in Java. Run javap on the compiled classes to see them. */ public class FinalFieldsDemo { // a record's components become private final fields record Quote(String scheme, long feeCents) {} // for contrast: plain, non-final fields static final class MutableQuote { String scheme; long feeCents; } public static void main(String[] args) { Quote q = new Quote("VISA", 120); MutableQuote m = new MutableQuote(); m.scheme = "MC"; m.feeCents = 135; System.out.println(q + " and a mutable quote for " + m.scheme); } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l04.FinalFieldsDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l04/FinalFieldsDemo.java FinalFieldsDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l04 /** Where final fields come from in Kotlin. Run javap on the compiled classes to see them. */ class KQuote(val scheme: String, val feeCents: Long) // val: a private final backing field class KMutableQuote(var scheme: String, var feeCents: Long) // var: a private, non-final backing field fun main() { val q = KQuote("VISA", 120) val m = KMutableQuote("MC", 135) m.feeCents = 140 println("${q.scheme} ${q.feeCents} and a mutable quote for ${m.scheme} ${m.feeCents}") } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l04.FinalFieldsDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l04/FinalFieldsDemo.kt The record and KQuote both show private final java.lang.String scheme; and private final long feeCents;. MutableQuote and KMutableQuote show the same fields without final, and the Kotlin one also has setters. A Kotlin val and a Java record component become the same thing in bytecode: a final field, with the JMM's final-field promise attached. jcstress sample BasicJMM_08_Finals: plain, opaque and final publication read

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Don't let this escape the constructor
x: The freeze happens when the constructor returns. Any code that gets hold of this before then can see the object half-built, and that includes code running on the same thread. this escapes when a constructor: registers the object as a listener or callback; starts a thread, or submits a task, that uses the object; creates a lambda or inner class that captures this and hands it out; calls a method that a subclass can override. Here's the first case. The bus replays its last event to every new subscriber, so onEvent runs inside subscribe, before the fields are set: Java class ChargebackAlerts implements Consumer<PaymentEvent> { private final long thresholdCents; private final Pager pager; ChargebackAlerts(EventBus bus, long thresholdCents, Pager pager) { bus.register(this); // the bus calls accept() right here... this.thresholdCents = thresholdCents; // ...before these fields are set this.pager = pager; } public void accept(PaymentEvent e) { if (e.amountCents() > thresholdCents) pager.page(e); // NullPointerException on pager } } Kotlin class ChargebackAlerts(bus: EventBus, thresholdCents: Long, pager: Pager) : Consumer<PaymentEvent> { init { bus.register(this) // the bus calls accept() right here... } private val thresholdCents = thresholdCents // ...before these properties are set private val pager = pager override fun accept(e: PaymentEvent) { if (e.amountCents() > thresholdCents) pager.page(e) // NullPointerException on pager } } Kotlin runs init blocks and property initializers in the order you write them, so the same bug is one misplaced init away. And Kotlin's null safety doesn't help: pager is declared non-null and still reads as null. Moving register to the last line of the constructor is not a fix. The final-field promise is tied to the end of the constructor, and a subclass constructor would still run after it. The fix is to keep constructors to assigning fields, and do the wiring after construction: in a static factory (create, then register), in a start() method, or in a @PostConstruct method that your CDI container calls once the bean is built. A thread that starts too early Read ThisEscapeDemo. The constructor starts a heartbeat thread, then resolves its endpoint, which takes about 50 ms. Predict both lines of output, then run it. Fix it: move the thread start out of the constructor into a start() method, and call start() from main after construction. Run it again. ThisEscapeDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l04; /** A constructor that starts a thread before it has finished setting its fields. */ public class ThisEscapeDemo { static final class HeartbeatSender { private final String endpoint; HeartbeatSender(String endpointName) { Thread beat = new Thread(this::sendHeartbeat, "heartbeat"); beat.start(); // `this` escapes to another thread here... this.endpoint = resolve(endpointName); // ...and this final field is set about 50 ms later } void sendHeartbeat() { System.out.println("heartbeat thread sends to: " + endpoint); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { HeartbeatSender sender = new HeartbeatSender("issuer-gateway"); System.out.println("constructor finished, endpoint = " + sender.endpoint); Thread.sleep(100); } // stands in for a DNS or service-registry lookup static String resolve(String name) { try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return "https://" + name + ".internal:8443"; } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l04.ThisEscapeDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l04/ThisEscapeDemo.java ThisEscapeDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l04 import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** A constructor that starts a thread before it has finished setting its properties. */ private class HeartbeatClient(endpointName: String) { val endpoint: String init { thread(name = "heartbeat") { sendHeartbeat() } // `this` escapes to another thread here... endpoint = resolve(endpointName) // ...and this val is set about 50 ms later } fun sendHeartbeat() { println("heartbeat thread sends to: $endpoint") // a non-null String that reads as null } } fun main() { val sender = HeartbeatClient("issuer-gateway") println("constructor finished, endpoint = ${sender.endpoint}") Thread.sleep(100) } // stands in for a DNS or service-registry lookup private fun resolve(name: String): String { Thread.sleep(50) return "https://$name.internal:8443" } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l04.ThisEscapeDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l04/ThisEscapeDemo.kt The first run prints heartbeat thread sends to: null, then the constructor finishes with the real endpoint. The heartbeat thread ran while the constructor was still resolving. In Kotlin the val endpoint: String is non-null by type and still reads as null. After the fix, the heartbeat prints the real URL: start() happens-before the thread's first action, and the field was set before start(). The most common mistake is calling a class immutable because its fields are final. private final List<Fee> fees assigned straight from the caller's ArrayList is a final reference to a list the caller can still change. A getter that returns that list lets every reader change it too. The final-field promise covers the list's state at the end of the constructor and nothing after. Copy mutable inputs in (List.copyOf, Map.copyOf), hand out only unmodifiable views, and make the class final so a subclass can't add mutable state.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Java and Kotlin
x: An immutable rate card in Java and Kotlin RateCard.java public final class RateCard { private final String currency; private final Map<String, Long> feesByScheme; public RateCard(String currency, Map<String, Long> feesByScheme) { this.currency = currency; this.feesByScheme = Map.copyOf(feesByScheme); // our own unmodifiable copy } public String currency() { return currency; } public Map<String, Long> feesByScheme() { return feesByScheme; } // safe to hand out } RateCard.kt class RateCard(val currency: String, feesByScheme: Map<String, Long>) { // our own copy, behind a read-only type val feesByScheme: Map<String, Long> = feesByScheme.toMap() } Kotlin classes are final by default and a val compiles to a private final field with a getter, so the Kotlin class is three lines. The difference is in the map. Map.copyOf in Java returns a truly unmodifiable map. Kotlin's Map is a read-only interface: toMap() gives you a private LinkedHashMap, and code that casts it to MutableMap could still change it. Inside your own code that's usually fine. If the object crosses a library boundary, wrap it with Collections.unmodifiableMap(...) or build it with Java's Map.copyOf.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Worked example
x: Publish a config snapshot from a scheduler A Quarkus bean refreshes the card issuer's settings every minute on the scheduler thread. Request threads read them for every call. Sometimes a call goes to the new URL with the old timeout. Find both problems. @ApplicationScoped public class IssuerConfigHolder { @Inject SettingsClient settingsClient; private IssuerConfig config = new IssuerConfig(); // 1. a mutable object in a plain field @Scheduled(every = "60s") void refresh() { // scheduler thread Settings s = settingsClient.fetch(); config.setBaseUrl(s.baseUrl()); // 2. changed in place... config.setTimeout(s.timeout()); // ...one field at a time } public IssuerConfig current() { return config; } // 3. request threads read it } @ApplicationScoped class IssuerConfigHolder(private val settingsClient: SettingsClient) { private var config = IssuerConfig() // 1. a mutable object in a plain property @Scheduled(every = "60s") fun refresh() { // scheduler thread val s = settingsClient.fetch() config.baseUrl = s.baseUrl // 2. changed in place... config.timeout = s.timeout // ...one field at a time } fun current(): IssuerConfig = config // 3. request threads read it } First, the refresh changes one shared object in place, field by field, with no lock, so a request can read the new URL next to the old timeout, a pair that was never configured. Second, nothing publishes config safely: the fields are plain and there is no edge from the scheduler thread to the request threads. Even a full lock around refresh wouldn't help readers that don't take it. Make the config immutable, build a whole new one on each refresh, and publish it with one volatile write. Readers then always get one consistent snapshot. public record IssuerConfig(String baseUrl, Duration timeout) {} // 1. immutable: final fields, no setters @ApplicationScoped public class IssuerConfigHolder { @Inject SettingsClient settingsClient; private volatile IssuerConfig config = new IssuerConfig("https://issuer.example", Duration.ofMillis(800)); @Scheduled(every = "60s") void refresh() { Settings s = settingsClient.fetch(); config = new IssuerConfig(s.baseUrl(), s.timeout()); // 2. build a new snapshot, 3. publish it } public IssuerConfig current() { return config; } // 4. one consistent snapshot per read } data class IssuerConfig(val baseUrl: String, val timeout: Duration) // 1. immutable: val only @ApplicationScoped class IssuerConfigHolder(private val settingsClient: SettingsClient) { @Volatile private var config = IssuerConfig("https://issuer.example", Duration.ofMillis(800)) @Scheduled(every = "60s") fun refresh() { val s = settingsClient.fetch() config = IssuerConfig(s.baseUrl, s.timeout) // 2. build a new snapshot, 3. publish it } fun current(): IssuerConfig = config // 4. one consistent snapshot per read } Why both changes? The record alone makes every snapshot safe to read even through a race, but a reader might keep an old reference for a long time. The volatile alone publishes the reference, but a mutable object behind it could still change under a reader. An immutable object behind a volatile reference fixes both. One habit completes it: a request calls current() once and keeps that snapshot for the whole call.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Quiz
x: registry.current is a plain field. The loader stores a RateCard whose fields are all final. What can a request thread that reads registry.current see? null, or a RateCard with correct field values; it may also keep seeing null for a long time A RateCard whose currency is still null Always the latest RateCard, because its fields are final A ClassCastException, because the object is half-built Final fields guarantee that whoever sees the reference sees the constructed values. They don't make the reference visible, so the reader can see null, an older card, or the new one, but never a half-built one. Option 3 is the common confusion between the two guarantees. Which of these publishes a new RateCard safely to request threads that call current()? A plain field, with publish marked synchronized and current() unsynchronized A volatile field A HashMap field that publish puts the card into A plain field, written after Thread.sleep(100) The volatile write in publish pairs with the volatile read in current(). The half-synchronized version has no acquire on the read side, a plain HashMap creates no edge, and a sleep is not an edge. A constructor sets all its final fields and then, as its last line, calls bus.register(this). Is that safe? Yes, all the fields are already set Yes, final fields make any publication safe No: the final-field promise starts when the constructor returns, so the bus's threads get no such promise, and a subclass constructor hasn't run yet No, register can't accept this inside a constructor The freeze happens at the end of the constructor, and this left before that. In practice it often works, which is why the bug survives review. Register from a factory method or @PostConstruct instead. A final class has private final List<Fee> fees;, set with this.fees = fees; from the caller's ArrayList, and no setters. Is it safe to share between threads? Yes, the field is final Yes, as long as it is published through a volatile field No, because List is an interface No: the caller still holds the ArrayList and can change it after the constructor, racing with every reader Final freezes the reference and the list's state at the end of the constructor. Later changes through the caller's reference are ordinary racy writes to an ArrayList. Copy it with List.copyOf in the constructor. From lesson 3 of this track: a field is volatile Map<String, Rule> rules. A refresher thread calls rules.put(k, v) on the existing HashMap, and request threads call rules.get(k). Is it safe? Yes, the field is volatile No: put is not a volatile write, it changes a HashMap that isn't safe for concurrent use Yes, if the map has fewer than 16 entries Only on x86 Volatile covers the reference. put never writes the field, so there's no edge, and HashMap can corrupt itself under concurrent access. Build a new map and assign it with one volatile write, or use a ConcurrentHashMap.
