h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Key terms
x: Publication Making a reference to an object reachable from another thread. Safe publication Publishing so the reader gets the reference and the object's state together, through a happens-before edge or final fields. Partially constructed object An object a thread can see before the constructor's writes are visible to it. Freeze The end of a constructor, after which final fields carry the JMM's special visibility promise. Immutable object Final class, final fields, copied inputs, nothing mutable handed out, no escaping this. Escaping this A constructor letting other code get a reference to the object before the constructor has finished. Defensive copy Copying a mutable input or output so outside code can't change your object's state. An object is published through a plain field. What can a reader that sees the reference observe? Default values (0, false, null) in its non-final fields, because the reference may become visible before the constructor's writes. What do final fields guarantee? A thread that sees the reference after the constructor finished sees the final fields, and what they point to, as the constructor left them, even through a data race. Do final fields make the reference to the object visible to other threads? No. You still need a safe publication channel, such as a volatile field, for readers to see the reference at all. Name a safe publication idiom that needs no volatile and no lock. A static initializer, such as static final RateCard DEFAULT = new RateCard(...). Class initialization runs under a JVM lock. A constructor calls bus.register(this). What's the fix? Make the constructor only assign fields, and register in a static factory or @PostConstruct, after construction. What does a Kotlin val compile to? A private final backing field (plus a getter). A var gives a non-final field. Is this.fees = fees; enough for an immutable class with a list? No. Copy it (List.copyOf(fees)), or the caller can still change the list under your readers.

h: Safe publication, final fields and escaping this · Go deeper
x: The final-field promise has a few edges worth knowing. It covers what the constructor set and what the final fields point to as of the freeze. Change a mutable object that a final field points to after the constructor, and those later changes get no promise. That's why "effectively immutable" objects (objects nobody changes after publication, though nothing stops them) still need safe publication, while truly immutable objects don't. Reflection can break final. Frameworks have long used deep reflection (Field.setAccessible(true) followed by set) to write final fields after construction, and the JMM gives such writes almost no guarantees. JDK 26 starts closing this door with JEP 500, "Prepare to Make Final Mean Final": by default it warns when deep reflection mutates a final field, and a later release is planned to make that an error unless you opt in. Serialization libraries and mocking tools are the usual sources of these warnings. Finally, the static-initializer idiom works because class initialization is itself a synchronization protocol. The JVM initializes each class once, under a lock, and any thread that then uses the class is guaranteed to see what the static initializer wrote. Lesson 5 of this track builds lazy initialization on exactly that. Aleksey Shipilëv's "Safe Publication and Safe Initialization in Java" separates the two ideas this lesson combines: safe publication (the channel) and safe initialization (final fields), and measures what each costs.

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Double-checked locking without volatile hands out half-built objects
x: Lazy initialization means building something on first use instead of at startup: a BIN table read from a 40 MB file, a connection to a card issuer, a signing key from a vault. The naive version is the check-then-act race from the first track: Java private static BinTable table; static BinTable binTable() { if (table == null) { // check table = new BinTable(); // act: two threads can both get here } return table; } Kotlin private var table: BinTable? = null fun binTable(): BinTable { if (table == null) { // check table = BinTable() // act: two threads can both get here } return table!! } It has two bugs. Two threads can both see null and both build a table, which wastes 50 ms, or opens two connections and leaks one. And it publishes the table through a plain field, so lesson 4 of this track applies: a reader can see the reference before the constructor's writes. Marking the method synchronized fixes both. It's correct, and often good enough. But every caller now takes the lock on every call, forever, for a value that never changes after the first one. Under load, all request threads line up on one monitor just to read a field. Double-checked locking (DCL) tries to skip the lock once the value exists: Java static BinTable binTable() { if (table == null) { // 1. first check, no lock synchronized (BinTable.class) { if (table == null) { // 2. second check, under the lock table = new BinTable(); } } } return table; // plain read on the fast path } Kotlin private val lock = Any() fun binTable(): BinTable { if (table == null) { // 1. first check, no lock synchronized(lock) { if (table == null) { // 2. second check, under the lock table = BinTable() } } } return table!! // plain read on the fast path } The lock and the second check do stop two builds. The fast path is the problem. A thread that finds table != null never takes the lock, so it has no happens-before edge to the write inside it. The JIT and the CPU may let the reference out before the constructor's field writes. That thread can return a table that is not null and still empty. The jcstress sample Singleton_07_BrokenNonVolatileDCL measured it. On AArch64, a singleton with a plain field came back non-null but without its data in about 1.8 million of 2.3 billion samples. When the singleton's field was final, it never failed, because final fields survive a race (lesson 4 of this track). That's why broken DCL often seems to work: many singletons happen to have only final fields, and x86 rarely shows the reordering. The simulator below lets you play the reordering yourself. jcstress sample Singleton_07_BrokenNonVolatileDCL, with its recorded results read Lazy init is the first person into the office making coffee. With no rule, three people arrive at once, see an empty pot, and brew three pots. A rule that everyone checks in at reception before touching the pot works, but then everyone queues at reception for every cup, all day. Double-checked locking says: look at the pot; if it's full, pour; if it's empty, go to reception, look again, and brew. It only works if the pot is see-through, which is what volatile gives you: you never pour from a pot that looks full but is still brewing. That's where the analogy breaks. In an office you can see the coffee brewing. In the JVM, without volatile, a half-built object looks exactly like a finished one.

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Double-checked locking works when the field is volatile
x: Make the field volatile and DCL is correct. That has been true since Java 5, when JSR-133 gave volatile its release and acquire meaning. DCL's real job is a lazy field per instance; for a static, the holder idiom in the next section is simpler. So here is the instance version: Java class BinTableProvider { private volatile BinTable table; BinTable table() { BinTable t = table; // 1. fast path: one volatile read if (t != null) return t; synchronized (this) { // 2. slow path: one thread at a time t = table; // 3. check again: another thread may have won if (t == null) { t = new BinTable(); table = t; // 4. volatile write publishes the finished table } return t; } } } Kotlin class BinTableProvider { @Volatile private var table: BinTable? = null fun table(): BinTable { table?.let { return it } // 1. fast path: one volatile read synchronized(this) { // 2. slow path: one thread at a time table?.let { return it } // 3. check again: another thread may have won val t = BinTable() table = t // 4. volatile write publishes the finished table return t } } } The edge is the one from lesson 3 of this track. The volatile write in step 4 is a release, and the volatile read in step 1 is an acquire. A thread that reads a non-null table sees everything the building thread wrote before step 4, including every field the constructor set. Three details matter. Read the field once, into a local. A final return table would be a second volatile read. That's still correct, but the local keeps the fast path to one read. Joshua Bloch's Effective Java (item 83) writes it the same way. Both checks matter. Drop the first and you've rebuilt the synchronized method. Drop the second and every thread that queued at the lock builds its own table, one after another. The Try it below shows that one. Null needs care. DCL uses null to mean "not built yet", so an initializer that returns null runs again on every call. Kotlin's lazy uses a private sentinel instead, a marker object that only means "not built yet", and the jcstress sample Lazy_03_Basic keeps a separate volatile boolean. If the initializer throws, nothing is stored, so the next caller tries again. Keep that in mind for the next section, because the holder idiom behaves differently. Break DCL two ways Run DclDemo (Java or Kotlin) with the command below. Eight threads ask for a signing key at the same moment, and loading it takes 50 ms. Delete the line marked try deleting this line. Predict the output, then run it. Put the line back. Remove volatile (@Volatile in Kotlin). Predict, then run. DclDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l05; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Eight threads ask a hand-written double-checked lazy for the same value at the same moment. Edit it and rerun. */ public class DclDemo { static final class LazySigningKey { private volatile Object key; // try: remove volatile private final AtomicInteger loads; LazySigningKey(AtomicInteger loads) { this.loads = loads; } Object get() { Object k = key; // 1. fast path: one volatile read, no lock if (k != null) return k; synchronized (this) { // 2. slow path: one thread at a time k = key; // 3. check again: another thread may have won if (k != null) return k; // (try deleting this line) loads.incrementAndGet(); sleep(50); // fetching a signing key from a vault k = new Object(); key = k; // 4. volatile write publishes the key return k; } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { for (int round = 1; round <= 3; round++) { AtomicInteger loads = new AtomicInteger(); LazySigningKey lazy = new LazySigningKey(loads); Set<Object> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(8), go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { ready.countDown(); try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(lazy.get()); }); t.start(); threads.add(t); } ready.await(); go.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("round %d: key loaded %d time(s), threads saw %d distinct key(s)%n", round, loads.get(), seen.size()); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l05.DclDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l05/DclDemo.java DclDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l05 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** Eight threads ask a hand-written double-checked lazy for the same value at the same moment. Edit it and rerun. */ private class LazySigningKey(private val loads: AtomicInteger) { @Volatile private var key: Any? = null // try: remove @Volatile fun get(): Any { val k = key // 1. fast path: one volatile read, no lock if (k != null) return k synchronized(this) { // 2. slow path: one thread at a time val again = key // 3. check again: another thread may have won if (again != null) return again // (try deleting this line) loads.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(50) // fetching a signing key from a vault val fresh = Any() key = fresh // 4. volatile write publishes the key return fresh } } } fun main() { for (round in 1..3) { val loads = AtomicInteger() val lazy = LazySigningKey(loads) val seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<Any>() val ready = CountDownLatch(8) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { ready.countDown() go.await() seen += lazy.get() } } ready.await() go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("round $round: key loaded ${loads.get()} time(s), threads saw ${seen.size} distinct key(s)") } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l05.DclDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l05/DclDemo.kt The correct version loads the key once per round, and all eight threads get the same key. Without the second check it loads 8 times and hands out 8 different keys: each thread that queued at the lock builds its own. Without volatile the output doesn't change at all. On an x86 laptop the missing edge almost never shows, so no run of this program can prove the code correct. That's the trap of broken DCL: you need a stress harness like jcstress, ideally on ARM, to see it fail. Lazy fields hide in every Quarkus service: an issuer client built on the first request, a BIN table, a JWT signing key fetched from a vault, a Kafka producer created when the first message goes out. CDI already makes @ApplicationScoped beans lazy: the container creates the instance once, on the first call through its proxy, so the bean itself is safe. Look instead at lazy state inside a bean, a field filled in by a getter. In Kotlin use by lazy; in Java use a volatile DCL field. Better still, if every payment needs the value, load it at startup with @Startup or a StartupEvent observer, so a failure shows at deploy time instead of on the first authorization. And keep holders away from anything that can fail, such as a Temporal activity's client: after one failed initialization, every retry of the activity on that worker fails with NoClassDefFoundError until the worker restarts.

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · The holder class idiom lets the JVM do the locking
x: For a static singleton you don't need DCL at all. The JVM already has a lazy, thread-safe, run-once mechanism: class initialization. The JLS (section 12.4) says a class is initialized right before its first active use: creating an instance, calling a static method, or reading a static field that isn't a compile-time constant. The JVM runs the static initializer once, under a per-class initialization lock, and every thread that uses the class afterwards sees what it wrote. That's the first safe publication idiom from lesson 4 of this track. The holder class idiom moves the instance into a nested class, so building it waits for the first call: Java public final class CardBinTable { private CardBinTable() { /* load 40 MB of BIN ranges */ } private static final class Holder { // not initialized until instance() touches it static final CardBinTable INSTANCE = new CardBinTable(); } public static CardBinTable instance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; // first call initializes Holder, once, under the JVM's lock } } Kotlin class CardBinTable private constructor() { private object Holder { // an object is initialized on first access val INSTANCE = CardBinTable() } companion object { fun instance(): CardBinTable = Holder.INSTANCE } } Your code has no volatile and no lock. The jcstress sample Singleton_09_Holder notes that in hot code the JIT will likely drop the initialization check, so instance() becomes a single field read. It has three limits. It only works for statics: one instance per class, never one per bean or per tenant. The constructor can't take arguments you only know at runtime. And it never retries. If the initializer throws, the first caller gets ExceptionInInitializerError and every later caller gets NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class CardBinTable$Holder, until the JVM restarts. A holder that connects to an issuer on first use turns one failed connection into a dead service. An enum gives you the same guarantee: enum BinTable { INSTANCE; ... } is built by the enum's static initializer. Effective Java recommends it for singletons because serialization and reflection can't create a second instance. In Kotlin, an object declaration is the same idea; the docs say its initialization is thread-safe and done on first access. One surprise: "lazy" here means on first use of the class, not of the instance. A plain static final INSTANCE in a class with other static methods is built the first time any of them runs. A Kotlin companion object is initialized together with its class. The holder exists to separate the two. The Try it shows exactly when each one is built. When is each singleton built? Read HolderIdiomDemo. It has three singletons: an eager static final, a holder, and an enum (an object in Kotlin). Each one prints a line when it's built. Before you run it, write down after which numbered step each built line will appear. Run it, Java first, then Kotlin. HolderIdiomDemo.java package workbench.jmm.l05; /** When does each singleton get built? Watch the order of the lines. */ public class HolderIdiomDemo { // eager: built when the class is initialized, by the first use of anything static in it static final class EagerBins { static final EagerBins INSTANCE = new EagerBins(); private EagerBins() { System.out.println(" EagerBins built"); } static int tableSize() { return 3; } } // holder idiom: built when Holder is initialized, by the first call to instance() static final class LazyBins { private LazyBins() { System.out.println(" LazyBins built"); } private static final class Holder { static final LazyBins INSTANCE = new LazyBins(); } static LazyBins instance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } static int tableSize() { return 3; } } // enum singleton: built when the enum class is initialized enum EnumBins { INSTANCE; EnumBins() { System.out.println(" EnumBins.INSTANCE built"); } static int tableSize() { return 3; } } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("1. call EagerBins.tableSize()"); EagerBins.tableSize(); System.out.println("2. call LazyBins.tableSize()"); LazyBins.tableSize(); System.out.println("3. call LazyBins.instance()"); LazyBins.instance(); System.out.println("4. call LazyBins.instance() again"); LazyBins.instance(); System.out.println("5. call EnumBins.tableSize()"); EnumBins.tableSize(); } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l05.HolderIdiomDemo labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l05/HolderIdiomDemo.java HolderIdiomDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l05 /** When does each singleton get built? Watch the order of the lines. */ // eager: a companion object is initialized together with its class private class EagerBins private constructor() { init { println(" EagerBins built") } companion object { val INSTANCE = EagerBins() fun tableSize() = 3 } } // holder idiom in Kotlin: a private nested object is initialized on first access private class LazyBins private constructor() { init { println(" LazyBins built") } private object Holder { val INSTANCE = LazyBins() } companion object { fun instance(): LazyBins = Holder.INSTANCE fun tableSize() = 3 } } // Kotlin's own answer: an object declaration, built on first access and thread-safe private object BinTable { init { println(" BinTable built") } fun tableSize() = 3 } fun main() { println("1. call EagerBins.tableSize()") EagerBins.tableSize() println("2. call LazyBins.tableSize()") LazyBins.tableSize() println("3. call LazyBins.instance()") LazyBins.instance() println("4. call LazyBins.instance() again") LazyBins.instance() println("5. call BinTable.tableSize()") BinTable.tableSize() } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l05.HolderIdiomDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l05/HolderIdiomDemo.kt EagerBins built appears right after step 1: calling a static method initialized the class, which built INSTANCE. LazyBins built appears only after step 3, the first instance() call, because tableSize() in step 2 never touched Holder, and it doesn't appear again in step 4. The enum (or Kotlin object) is built in step 5, the first time anything in it runs. Class initialization is lazy per class; the holder makes it lazy per instance. jcstress sample Singleton_09_Holder read

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Kotlin's by lazy is double-checked locking, in three modes
x: val x by lazy { ... } is the DCL from earlier, written once in the standard library. The property compiles to a private final kotlin.Lazy x$delegate field, and the getter calls its getValue(). The default mode is LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED. Its implementation class, SynchronizedLazyImpl, has a volatile value field, a fast path that reads it once, and a synchronized block with a second check. It adds three things to the hand-written version: a sentinel instead of null, so a null result is cached too; a retry, because the docs promise that an initializer that throws runs again on the next access; and it drops the initializer after the first run, so whatever the lambda captured can be collected. Java // Java has no by lazy: a DCL field stands in for SYNCHRONIZED, a compareAndSet for PUBLICATION final class IssuerGateway { private final Vault vault; private volatile SigningKey signingKey; private final AtomicReference<Map<String, String>> routes = new AtomicReference<>(); IssuerGateway(Vault vault) { this.vault = vault; } SigningKey signingKey() { SigningKey k = signingKey; if (k != null) return k; synchronized (this) { if (signingKey == null) signingKey = vault.fetch("issuer-signing-key"); return signingKey; } } Map<String, String> routes() { Map<String, String> r = routes.get(); if (r != null) return r; routes.compareAndSet(null, parseRoutes(ROUTES_JSON)); // losers throw their result away return routes.get(); } } Kotlin class IssuerGateway(private val vault: Vault) { val signingKey: SigningKey by lazy { // SYNCHRONIZED: runs once, others wait vault.fetch("issuer-signing-key") } val routes: Map<String, String> by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) { parseRoutes(ROUTES_JSON) // may run more than once; one result wins } } Mode The initializer runs Use it for SYNCHRONIZED (default) once; other callers wait on a lock anything expensive or with side effects PUBLICATION maybe on several threads at once; one result wins cheap, side-effect-free work NONE with no synchronization at all values that never leave one thread Keep the default unless you have a reason. PUBLICATION fits a cheap, pure initializer when you'd rather waste a little work than block. The losers' results are thrown away without cleanup, so never use it for something that opens a connection. NONE fits single-threaded hot code. Never put it on a property of a shared bean or singleton: the docs call the multi-threaded behavior unspecified, and the demo below shows eight threads getting eight different values. SYNCHRONIZED has two traps. The lock is held while the initializer runs, so a 120 ms issuer call inside lazy makes every concurrent caller wait 120 ms. And by default the lock is the Lazy object itself; the docs warn that synchronizing on it from your own code can deadlock. Race the three lazy modes For each mode, predict how many times the 50 ms initializer runs and how many distinct values eight threads see. Run the Kotlin demo with the command below, then the Java twin, which builds the three modes by hand. Change the sleep from 50 to 0 and run it a few times. Which numbers move? LazyModesDemo.kt package workbench.jmm.l05 import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** Eight threads read the same lazy value at the same moment, once for each LazyThreadSafetyMode. */ fun main() { for (mode in LazyThreadSafetyMode.entries) { val runs = AtomicInteger() val signingKey: Lazy<Any> = lazy(mode) { runs.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(50) // a slow initializer, like fetching a key from a vault Any() } val seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<Any>() val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await() seen += signingKey.value } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("%-12s initializer ran %d time(s), threads saw %d distinct value(s)".format(mode, runs.get(), seen.size)) } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l05.LazyModesDemoKt labs/jmm/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/jmm/l05/LazyModesDemo.kt LazyModesDemoJava.java package workbench.jmm.l05; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import java.util.function.Supplier; // Java has no `by lazy`. These are the closest Java equivalents of Kotlin's three LazyThreadSafetyMode values. /** Eight threads read the same lazy value at the same moment, once for each kind of lazy. */ public class LazyModesDemoJava { // like SYNCHRONIZED: double-checked locking, so the initializer runs once static Supplier<Object> synchronizedLazy(Supplier<Object> init) { return new Supplier<>() { private volatile Object value; @Override public Object get() { Object v = value; if (v != null) return v; synchronized (this) { if (value == null) value = init.get(); return value; } } }; } // like PUBLICATION: any thread may compute, and the first compareAndSet wins static Supplier<Object> publicationLazy(Supplier<Object> init) { AtomicReference<Object> ref = new AtomicReference<>(); return () -> { Object v = ref.get(); if (v != null) return v; ref.compareAndSet(null, init.get()); return ref.get(); }; } // like NONE: no synchronization at all, only safe on one thread static Supplier<Object> unsafeLazy(Supplier<Object> init) { Object[] box = new Object[1]; return () -> { if (box[0] == null) box[0] = init.get(); return box[0]; }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { race("SYNCHRONIZED", LazyModesDemoJava::synchronizedLazy); race("PUBLICATION", LazyModesDemoJava::publicationLazy); race("NONE", LazyModesDemoJava::unsafeLazy); } interface LazyFactory { Supplier<Object> make(Supplier<Object> init); } static void race(String name, LazyFactory factory) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger(); Supplier<Object> signingKey = factory.make(() -> { runs.incrementAndGet(); sleep(50); // a slow initializer, like fetching a key from a vault return new Object(); }); Set<Object> seen = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(signingKey.get()); }); t.start(); threads.add(t); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : threads) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-12s initializer ran %d time(s), threads saw %d distinct value(s)%n", name, runs.get(), seen.size()); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :jmm:demo -Pmain=workbench.jmm.l05.LazyModesDemoJava labs/jmm/src/demo/java/workbench/jmm/l05/LazyModesDemoJava.java SYNCHRONIZED: 1 run, 1 value. PUBLICATION: up to 8 runs (here all 8, because every thread started before the first finished) but 1 value, because the first compareAndSet won and everyone returns its result. NONE: 8 runs and 8 values, each thread keeping its own. With no sleep, PUBLICATION and NONE usually run fewer times, because some threads arrive after the first one finished. The bug in NONE didn't go away. The window got smaller. Pick the simplest idiom that fits. Most lazy values in a service should not be lazy at all. Kotlin docs: lazy properties docs LazyThreadSafetyMode (Kotlin API) docs The most common mistake is leaving volatile off double-checked locking, because the code obviously builds only one instance. It does build only one. The bug is on the fast path, which reads the field with no edge to the write, and it almost never shows on x86 test machines, so it survives years of green builds and then fails on ARM. The fix is one word: volatile on the field (@Volatile in Kotlin). Better still, don't hand-write DCL. Use the holder idiom for statics, by lazy in Kotlin, and computeIfAbsent for one value per key.

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Java and Kotlin
x: One lazy value per key: computeIfAbsent in Java, and the getOrPut trap in Kotlin IssuerClients.java class IssuerClients { private final ConcurrentMap<String, IssuerClient> clients = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); IssuerClient clientFor(String issuerId) { // connect runs at most once per absent key; other callers for that key wait for it return clients.computeIfAbsent(issuerId, this::connect); } private IssuerClient connect(String issuerId) { return new IssuerClient(issuerId); // opens a connection } } IssuerClients.kt class IssuerClients { private val clients = ConcurrentHashMap<String, IssuerClient>() // looks the same, isn't: two threads can both run connect() for one key fun clientForRacy(issuerId: String): IssuerClient = clients.getOrPut(issuerId) { connect(issuerId) } // the same guarantee as Java: call the JDK method fun clientFor(issuerId: String): IssuerClient = clients.computeIfAbsent(issuerId) { connect(it) } private fun connect(issuerId: String): IssuerClient = IssuerClient(issuerId) // opens a connection } Kotlin's getOrPut on a ConcurrentMap never replaces a value that is already there, but its docs say the lambda may run even if the key is already in the map. Two threads can both connect, every caller ends up with the same client, and the losing connection is dropped without being closed. computeIfAbsent is the JDK's atomic version: the function runs at most once per absent key. Its Javadoc asks you to keep that function short, because other updates to the map can block while it runs. For a slow connect, store a lazy in the map, clients.computeIfAbsent(id) { lazy { connect(id) } }.value, so the map is busy only while the cheap Lazy object is created.

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Worked example
x: Make a lazily loaded fraud-rules field safe A rules provider downloads fraud rules on first use. At startup a burst of 200 authorizations arrives at once. Name the two bugs, then choose an idiom before you read on. @ApplicationScoped public class FraudRulesProvider { @Inject RulesClient rulesClient; private FraudRules rules; // plain field public FraudRules rules() { // called by every request thread if (rules == null) { rules = rulesClient.download(); // 300 ms, and it can fail } return rules; } } @ApplicationScoped class FraudRulesProvider(private val rulesClient: RulesClient) { private var rules: FraudRules? = null // plain field fun rules(): FraudRules { // called by every request thread if (rules == null) { rules = rulesClient.download() // 300 ms, and it can fail } return rules!! } } First, check-then-act: every request in the first 300 ms sees null and starts its own download. Second, a plain field: a request thread can see the reference before the rules' fields. Now the idiom. Not the holder: the field belongs to a bean, and a failed download must be retried on the next request, not turned into NoClassDefFoundError. A volatile DCL field fits, and in Kotlin by lazy is that DCL. Write it with subgoal labels. In Kotlin the whole thing is one line, and the retry on failure comes from the standard library. @ApplicationScoped public class FraudRulesProvider { @Inject RulesClient rulesClient; private volatile FraudRules rules; // 1. volatile: the fast path needs the edge public FraudRules rules() { FraudRules r = rules; // 2. fast path: one volatile read if (r != null) return r; synchronized (this) { // 3. slow path: one download at a time r = rules; if (r == null) { // 4. check again: someone may have won r = rulesClient.download(); // if this throws, nothing is stored rules = r; // 5. publish the finished rules } return r; } } } @ApplicationScoped class FraudRulesProvider(private val rulesClient: RulesClient) { // SYNCHRONIZED by default: steps 1 to 5 of the Java version, plus a retry if download() throws val rules: FraudRules by lazy { rulesClient.download() } } Ask one more question: does every authorization need the rules anyway? Then lazy buys you a slow first request and a failure you find on the first payment instead of at deploy. Load the rules at startup and publish them through a volatile field, as in lesson 4 of this track. Keep lazy for values that some requests never need.

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Quiz
x: A double-checked singleton has a volatile field. A teammate removes volatile because "the write already happens inside synchronized", and CI stays green. What do you tell them? That's fine: leaving the synchronized block publishes the object to every thread A thread on the lock-free fast path has no edge to that write, so it can get a half-built object; CI's x86 machines just rarely show it It can now build two instances It will deadlock under contention Releasing a lock creates an edge only to threads that later take the same lock. The fast path takes no lock, so only a volatile read gives it an edge. The second check still prevents two builds, so option 3 is wrong, and the bug simply doesn't show on most x86 runs. A Quarkus bean needs its own HttpClient, built on first use. Building it fails when the issuer's DNS is down, and the next request should try again. Which idiom fits? The holder class idiom An enum singleton Double-checked locking on a volatile field, or Kotlin by lazy by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) The holder and the enum are static, one per JVM, and a failed class initialization is permanent: later calls get NoClassDefFoundError. DCL stores nothing when the initializer throws, so the next call tries again, and Kotlin's lazy documents the same retry. NONE is unsafe on a bean that many request threads share. Rates has static final Rates INSTANCE = new Rates();, a constructor that prints built, and a static method currency() that returns "EUR". main prints start, then prints Rates.currency(). What is the output? start, built, EUR start, EUR, and built only when INSTANCE is first read built, start, EUR, because static fields are set when the JVM starts start, EUR, built Calling a static method is an active use, so the JVM initializes Rates first, and that runs new Rates(). Class initialization is lazy per class, not per field. A holder class is how you make the instance wait for its own first use. A shared Kotlin object has val pool by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) { ConnectionPool(size = 20) }. A burst of requests arrives right after startup. What can happen? Nothing bad: PUBLICATION means the pool is published safely, so it's built once Different callers keep using different pools The callers deadlock Several threads can each open a pool of 20 connections; one pool is kept and the others are dropped without being closed PUBLICATION lets the initializer run on several threads at once and keeps one result, so everyone does end up with the same pool (option 2 is wrong). The extra pools were still created, and their connections leak. Anything with side effects belongs in the default SYNCHRONIZED mode. From lesson 4 of this track: a DCL singleton without volatile, but every field of the singleton is final. What can a thread on the fast path see? null, which sends it to the slow path, or the complete object; the code is still fragile, because one non-final field added later breaks it A half-built object, just like the non-final case Always null, so every call takes the lock Two different instances Final fields are seen as the constructor left them, even through a data race, so the race on the reference is benign. jcstress Singleton_07 shows no failures with final fields and failures without them. Relying on that is brittle; add volatile.

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Key terms
x: Lazy initialization Building a value on first use instead of at startup. Double-checked locking Check without a lock, then lock and check again before building. Correct only with a volatile field. Holder class idiom Keep the instance in a private nested class, so the JVM builds it on the first call, once, under its class-initialization lock. Class initialization The JVM running a class's static initializer once, before the class's first active use. Enum singleton A one-constant enum used as a singleton; serialization and reflection can't make a second one. Sentinel A private marker object meaning "not set yet", so a real null result can be cached too. LazyThreadSafetyMode Kotlin's choice for lazy: SYNCHRONIZED (once, others wait), PUBLICATION (maybe many runs, one result), NONE (one thread only). Why is double-checked locking without volatile broken? The fast path reads the field without the lock, so it has no happens-before edge to the write. A thread can see the reference before the constructor's writes and use a half-built object. What one change makes double-checked locking correct? Declare the field volatile (@Volatile in Kotlin). The volatile write publishes the finished object; the volatile read on the fast path sees it whole. In the holder class idiom, what does the locking? The JVM's class initialization. Holder is initialized once, under a JVM lock, the first time Holder.INSTANCE is read. A holder's initializer throws on the first call. What does the second call get? NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class ...$Holder. Class initialization never retries; only a JVM restart does. What does val x by lazy { ... } compile to, and which mode does it use? A private final kotlin.Lazy x$delegate field. The default mode is SYNCHRONIZED: double-checked locking on a volatile field. LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION vs SYNCHRONIZED? PUBLICATION may run the initializer on several threads at once and keeps one result. SYNCHRONIZED runs it once while the other callers wait. Kotlin concurrentMap.getOrPut(k) { connect() }: can connect() run twice for one key? Yes. It never replaces a value, but the lambda may run on two threads. computeIfAbsent runs it at most once per absent key.

h: Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders · Go deeper
x: A lazy object can itself be published through a race, and then its own fields matter. Kotlin's SynchronizedLazyImpl has a non-final initializer field, because it sets it to null after the first run. The jcstress sample Lazy_01_BrokenFactory shows what a non-final factory field costs. On AArch64, when the lazy object itself reached another thread through a plain field, that thread sometimes saw the factory as null and failed, and in one sample the factory ran twice. by lazy doesn't hit this in practice, because the compiler keeps the Lazy in a private final x$delegate field, and final fields are safe once the owner's constructor has finished. If you write your own lazy wrapper and also want to drop the initializer, Lazy_05_WrapperOneShot shows the fix: a final field pointing to a small wrapper that holds the factory. Class initialization has one more rule worth knowing. Reading a static final field that is a compile-time constant, such as static final int MAX_BINS = 3, does not initialize the class at all: javac copies the value into the caller. That's why a holder only triggers on fields like INSTANCE, whose value is computed at runtime. The JDK is growing its own answer. JDK 25 previewed stable values (JEP 502). JDK 26 renamed the idea lazy constants (JEP 526, second preview), and JDK 27 has a third preview (JEP 531). It is a JDK type for a value that is computed at most once and that the JIT may then treat as a constant, which a volatile field can never be. It is a preview API, so it needs --enable-preview and stays out of these labs, but it is worth following if you write libraries. Finally, the history. "The Double-Checked Locking is Broken" declaration, signed by memory model researchers and JVM engineers before Java 5, explains why no clever trick could save DCL under the old memory model. The JSR-133 memory model of Java 5 fixed it by giving volatile its acquire and release meaning, which is the fix you used today.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · A VarHandle puts the memory mode on each access
x: volatile puts the memory rules on the field: every read and write of it is a volatile access, whether that access needs the full rules or not. A one-producer queue that only needs its data to arrive in order still pays, on x86, for the store-buffer drain after every volatile write (lesson 3 of this track), millions of times a second. A VarHandle puts the rules on each access instead. VarHandles came in JDK 9 with JEP 193. (A JEP, or JDK Enhancement Proposal, is the public design document for one JDK feature.) A VarHandle is a typed handle to one field or array element, with one method per mode: get and set (plain), getOpaque and setOpaque, getAcquire and setRelease, getVolatile and setVolatile. It also has atomic updates such as compareAndSet, getAndAdd and getAndSet. Java final class SettlementSlot { private static final VarHandle ITEM; // 1. one handle per field, static final static { try { ITEM = MethodHandles.lookup() // 2. a lookup that can see the private field .findVarHandle(SettlementSlot.class, "item", Settlement.class); } catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); } } private Settlement item; // 3. a plain field: the mode goes on each access Settlement peek() { return (Settlement) ITEM.getAcquire(this); // 4. receiver first, cast the result } } Kotlin class SettlementSlot { private var item: Settlement? = null // 3. a plain field: the mode goes on each access fun peek(): Settlement? = ITEM.getAcquire(this) as Settlement? // 4. receiver first, cast the result companion object { // 1. one handle per field; 2. looked up inside the class, so it can see the private field private val ITEM: VarHandle = MethodHandles.lookup() .findVarHandle(SettlementSlot::class.java, "item", Settlement::class.java) } } Three details make this work. Keep the handle in a static final field. The JIT treats a static final as a constant, so it can compile ITEM.getAcquire(this) down to one load plus whatever barrier the mode needs. In Kotlin, a private val in the companion object compiles to exactly that field. The access methods are signature-polymorphic. The compiler records the argument types and the cast on the result as the call's real signature, and the VarHandle checks them when the call runs. Kotlin 2 does the same: the as cast sets the return type. Types that can't be converted fail at runtime, with WrongMethodTypeException or ClassCastException, not at compile time. The mode at the access wins over the declaration. The Javadoc says a plain get reads a field as plain "even if that field is declared volatile", and warns that mixing modes on one field needs "extreme care". So keep the field plain, and send every access through the handle. You don't need the boilerplate to use the modes. Since JDK 9, AtomicInteger, AtomicLong and AtomicReference have getPlain, getOpaque, getAcquire, setRelease and friends. The old lazySet (JDK 6) is setRelease under another name. What a VarHandle saves is the extra object: the mode works on a plain field of your own class. Check yourself: a field is declared volatile, and one hot loop reads it through ITEM.get(this). Is that read volatile? No. The mode at the access wins, so it is a plain read, and the JIT may hoist it out of the loop exactly as it did in lesson 1 of this track. JEP 193: Variable Handles read VarHandle (Java SE 25 API) docs Think of a shared notice board in a busy office. Plain writes are notes you scribble on your own pad and may never pin up. Opaque writes are pinned to the board eventually, and your notes on one topic go up in the order you wrote them, but notes on different topics can go up in any order. A release write is a sealed envelope pinned to the board: everything you wrote before sealing it is inside, and whoever opens it (the acquire) reads all of it. Volatile adds a clerk who stamps every envelope with one office-wide sequence number, so everyone agrees on the order. The analogy breaks on cost: in an office the clerk is slow and the envelope is cheap; on x86 the envelope is free and only the clerk's stamp, the volatile write, costs anything.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Four modes, from weakest to strongest
x: The VarHandle Javadoc defines the modes as a ladder. Each one keeps everything below it and adds one promise. Plain mode (get, set) is an ordinary field access. It's atomic for references and for values of 32 bits or less, and it promises nothing about what other threads see, or when. The JIT may read it once for a whole loop. That was the hang in lesson 1 of this track. Opaque mode (getOpaque, setOpaque) adds two things. It's atomic for long and double too. And it's coherent for that one variable: the JIT must really perform each read and write, in order, so a thread spinning on it eventually sees a new value. It orders nothing else. Other fields can still appear in any order. Acquire and release (getAcquire, setRelease) add one-way ordering. Nothing before a release write may move after it. Nothing after an acquire read may move before it. When an acquire read sees the value that a release write stored, the reader also sees everything the writer did before the release. That's the happens-before handoff from lesson 2 of this track, built from one variable. Volatile mode (getVolatile, setVolatile, or a volatile field) adds a single total order: all threads agree on one order of all volatile accesses. That's what forbids the store-buffering result, where each thread writes its own variable and then reads the other's as 0. Mode What can still go wrong plain a loop never sees the new value; a long tears opaque a reader sees the flag before the data it guards acquire/release two threads each write, then both read the other's old value volatile nothing on this list The jcstress samples show each step. In BasicJMM_04_Progress, a plain spin loop is allowed to hang and an opaque one is not. In BasicJMM_06_Causality, a reader may see the flag without the data with opaque accesses (0.68% of samples on AArch64, 0 on x86_64), and never with release/acquire. In BasicJMM_07_Consensus, acquire/release still lets both threads read 0 (6.18% in the recorded run), and volatile forbids it. On x86, plain, opaque, acquire and release accesses all compile to ordinary loads and stores; the modes mostly restrain the JIT. Only the volatile write adds an instruction that drains the store buffer. The Try it measures what that buys. Store buffering in four modes Read ModesDemo. It runs the store-buffering test from lesson 1 of this track once per access mode, 262,144 trials each. Predict, for each mode, whether any trial ends with both threads reading 0. Run it (Java or Kotlin). Then explain the opaque line: opaque stops the JIT from reordering, so who is reordering? Much of java.util.concurrent is built on them. Where this lesson pays off is in reviews and upgrades. When someone proposes replacing a volatile flag in a Kafka consumer loop with getOpaque to save time, you can say it saves nothing on x86 reads, and ask for a profile and a jcstress test first. When a JDK 24 or later upgrade starts printing warnings about sun.misc.Unsafe memory-access methods, you know the library's fix is a VarHandle (or, for off-heap memory, the foreign memory API), and that the warning comes from the dependency, not your code. h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Release/acquire is for handing data to another thread
x: Release/acquire has one job: handing over data from one thread to another. The writer does plain writes, then one release write. The reader does one acquire read, and if it sees the new value, it reads the data. Java // writer thread report.total = 1_250_000; // 1. plain writes of the data report.count = 42; READY.setRelease(report, true); // 2. release: the data can't move after this // reader thread if ((boolean) READY.getAcquire(report)) { // 3. acquire: nothing below moves above this publish(report.total, report.count); // 4. sees the data, because it saw the release } Kotlin // writer thread report.total = 1_250_000 // 1. plain writes of the data report.count = 42 READY.setRelease(report, true) // 2. release: the data can't move after this // reader thread if (READY.getAcquire(report) as Boolean) { // 3. acquire: nothing below moves above this publish(report.total, report.count) // 4. sees the data, because it saw the release } Four rules keep it correct. Pair them on the same variable. A release of ready and an acquire of done give you nothing, just as a volatile write and a volatile read of two different fields gave you nothing in lesson 2 of this track. The promise only holds when the acquire reads the released value, or a later one. A reader that still sees false learns nothing, which is fine: it tries again later. Release/acquire doesn't make read-modify-write atomic. When several threads may write, and the first should win, use compareAndSet. The Javadoc gives it volatile semantics: it reads the current value as getVolatile and, if that value is the expected one, writes as setVolatile. Weaker variants exist (compareAndExchangeAcquire, weakCompareAndSetRelease and others). The weak ones may fail even when the value matches, so they belong inside retry loops. Don't use it for "I write my flag, then check yours". That's the store-buffering shape from the previous section, and it needs volatile, or better a lock or a compareAndSet on one shared variable. Why bother, when a volatile field does all this? Because the write side is cheaper. On x86, a release write is a plain store, while a volatile write also drains the store buffer. For a queue that hands over millions of messages a second from one producer, that difference shows up in a profile. That's the whole case for this mode. Hand over transfers three ways Read HandoffDemo. One producer hands transfers to one consumer through a one-item slot for three seconds. There are three slots: ordinary field access, opaque, and release/acquire. Predict for each one: does it keep going, and does the consumer ever see a transfer with the wrong fields? Run it three times, adding -Pargs=plain, then -Pargs=opaque, then no argument (release/acquire). Try the Kotlin twin too. Opaque usually does the same on x86, but nothing orders the transfer's fields before the slot write, so on ARM it is allowed to deliver a transfer whose fields are still 0. h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · When you need them, and why only jcstress can test them
x: Almost never in application code. Prefer, in this order: a java.util.concurrent class (a BlockingQueue for handoffs, ConcurrentHashMap, CompletableFuture); then a volatile field or an Atomic class; then a lock. Reach for VarHandle modes only when three things are true: you're writing a low-level building block, a profiler shows the cost of volatile or of the extra Atomic object matters, and you will test it with jcstress. That describes the people who write java.util.concurrent itself (FutureTask and ConcurrentLinkedQueue both keep their state behind VarHandles), high-performance queue libraries, and almost nobody writing a Quarkus endpoint. It's also the supported way out of sun.misc.Unsafe. JDK 23 deprecated Unsafe's memory-access methods for removal (JEP 471), and JDK 24 prints a warning the first time code uses them (JEP 498). A library that still uses Unsafe is a library you'll be upgrading soon. The bigger problem is testing. A JUnit test can't prove any of this. Your test ran on one CPU family, after one JIT warm-up, under one load. A green run says that machine didn't produce the bad outcome that time. The lab's tests check behavior that is deterministic once the code is right; they can't catch a missing release on x86. jcstress, the OpenJDK concurrency stress harness, is the honest test. You write a @State class, two or more @Actor methods that run against each other, and an @Outcome for each result, marked ACCEPTABLE, ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING or FORBIDDEN. jcstress runs the actors on fresh state objects many millions of times, in several JVM configurations, and prints how often each outcome happened. A forbidden outcome that appears even once fails the test. Two habits make its results worth having. Read the outcome table, not just pass or fail: an interesting outcome at 0.01% is a real bug in production. And run it on ARM if you can, on an Apple Silicon laptop or a Graviton instance. x86 never lets one store pass another, so many ordering bugs simply can't show there. The Try it puts your lab slot under jcstress and shows exactly that. Put your slot under jcstress Optional, and it needs Maven and network access. Finish the lab first. Then create a jcstress project with the archetype command from the jcstress README: mvn archetype:generate -DinteractiveMode=false -DarchetypeGroupId=org.openjdk.jcstress -DarchetypeArtifactId=jcstress-java-test-archetype -DgroupId=org.sample -DartifactId=test -Dversion=1.0 In test/pom.xml, change <javac.target>1.8</javac.target> to 21. The archetype targets Java 8, and VarHandle needs JDK 9 or later. Copy Settlement.java and your SettlementSlot.java into test/src/main/java/org/sample/ and change their package line to package org.sample;. Replace ConcurrencyTest.java with the test below. Run mvn clean verify, then java -jar target/jcstress.jar -t SlotHandoffTest -m quick -v. Read the results table. Change your slot's setRelease and getAcquire to setOpaque and getOpaque. Predict, rebuild and run again. SlotHandoffTest.java package org.sample; import org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.*; import org.openjdk.jcstress.infra.results.J_Result; import static org.openjdk.jcstress.annotations.Expect.*; @JCStressTest @Outcome(id = "-1", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "The slot was still empty") @Outcome(id = "8400", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "Saw the whole settlement") @Outcome(id = "0", expect = FORBIDDEN, desc = "Saw the settlement but not its amount") @State public class SlotHandoffTest { final SettlementSlot slot = new SettlementSlot(); @Actor public void producer() { Settlement s = new Settlement(); s.amountCents = 8400; // a plain write... slot.offer(s); // ...then the release } @Actor public void consumer(J_Result r) { Settlement s = slot.poll(); // the acquire r.r1 = (s == null) ? -1 : s.amountCents; } } java -jar target/jcstress.jar -t SlotHandoffTest -m quick -v jcstress prints a table like the ones in its samples. On an x86_64 machine in quick mode, a run here showed -1 (empty) in about 65% of 199 million samples, 8400 in the other 35%, and 0 (Forbidden) in none: the test is OK. The all-opaque version also showed 0 forbidden samples on x86_64, in about 133 million. That doesn't make it correct. x86 never lets one store pass another; ARM does, and there the opaque slot is allowed to fail. jcstress is the tool that would show it, if you run it on the right machine. jcstress: the OpenJDK concurrency stress tests (README and samples) read JEP 498: Warn upon Use of Memory-Access Methods in sun.misc.Unsafe read The most common mistake is using a weaker mode than the pattern needs, because "acquire/release is what volatile does, only cheaper". It isn't. Release/acquire is enough to hand data from one writer to its readers through one variable. It is not enough for Dekker-style code, where each thread writes its own flag and then reads the other's: both threads can read the old value, on x86 too, and both enter the critical section. If two variables are involved, or several threads write, use volatile, compareAndSet or a lock. And whichever mode you pick, write a jcstress test before you trust it.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Java and Kotlin
x: The same release/acquire handoff with AtomicReference, in Java and Kotlin LatestBatch.java final class LatestBatch { private final AtomicReference<Batch> latest = new AtomicReference<>(); // writer: build the batch with plain writes, then release it void publish(Batch b) { latest.setRelease(b); } // readers: an acquire read sees the batch's fields as the writer left them Batch current() { return latest.getAcquire(); } // several writers racing to set the first batch: compareAndSet, volatile semantics boolean publishFirst(Batch b) { return latest.compareAndSet(null, b); } } LatestBatch.kt class LatestBatch { private val latest = AtomicReference<Batch?>(null) // writer: build the batch with plain writes, then release it fun publish(b: Batch) = latest.setRelease(b) // readers: an acquire read sees the batch's fields as the writer left them fun current(): Batch? = latest.getAcquire() // several writers racing to set the first batch: compareAndSet, volatile semantics fun publishFirst(b: Batch): Boolean = latest.compareAndSet(null, b) } Kotlin has no memory-mode syntax of its own on the JVM. @Volatile gives you volatile, and for every other mode you call the same JDK classes as Java. AtomicReference and friends have had getAcquire, setRelease, getOpaque and getPlain since JDK 9, so this is the readable way to use the modes: no lookup, no casts, one extra object per field. VarHandle calls also work from Kotlin, because the Kotlin compiler (2.4 in these labs) treats VarHandle methods as signature-polymorphic and takes the return type from the as cast. Use a VarHandle only when that extra object per instance matters, as it does for nodes in a queue with millions of entries.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Worked example
x: Choose the weakest mode for a consumer's record counter, then decide whether it's worth it A Kafka consumer thread counts the records it has processed. A metrics scraper reads the count every 15 seconds on another thread. Right now it uses an AtomicLong. Before reading on, list what the reader actually needs. final class ConsumerMetrics { private final AtomicLong processed = new AtomicLong(); void onRecord() { processed.incrementAndGet(); } // consumer thread, once per record long processed() { return processed.get(); } // scrape thread, every 15 s } class ConsumerMetrics { private val processed = AtomicLong() fun onRecord() { processed.incrementAndGet() } // consumer thread, once per record fun processed(): Long = processed.get() // scrape thread, every 15 s } Only one thread writes, so the increment doesn't have to be an atomic read-modify-write; that was the lesson of single-writer fields in lesson 3 of this track. The reader needs a long that isn't torn and that eventually moves. It doesn't read any other data based on the count, so it needs no acquire. That's exactly opaque: atomic for 64 bits, coherent, eventually visible. The weakest correct version uses the modes AtomicLong already has, with subgoal labels. final class ConsumerMetrics { private final AtomicLong processed = new AtomicLong(); void onRecord() { long next = processed.getPlain() + 1; // 1. the only writer can read its own value plainly processed.setOpaque(next); // 2. opaque: untorn and eventually visible } long processed() { return processed.getOpaque(); // 3. a recent, untorn value; orders nothing else } } class ConsumerMetrics { private val processed = AtomicLong() fun onRecord() { val next = processed.getPlain() + 1 // 1. the only writer can read its own value plainly processed.setOpaque(next) // 2. opaque: untorn and eventually visible } fun processed(): Long = processed.getOpaque() // 3. a recent, untorn value; orders nothing else } Now decide. On x86 this replaces one locked instruction per record with a plain store. At 5,000 records a second you will never see the difference; in a loop doing tens of millions a second, you might. The price is a rule nobody can see in the code: the moment a second thread calls onRecord(), counts are silently lost. Keep incrementAndGet() until a profiler points at it, and if many threads count, use LongAdder instead.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Lab
x: A settlement slot and a kill switch with acquire and release labs/jmm/src/main/java/workbench/jmm/l06/SettlementSlot.java labs/jmm/src/main/java/workbench/jmm/l06/KillSwitch.java ./gradlew :jmm:test --tests 'workbench.jmm.l06.*' Run the tests once. All seven fail: the TODOs throw, and KillSwitch has no VarHandle yet. Settlement is given and needs no changes. Write SettlementSlot.offer and poll with the given ITEM handle: an acquire read to look at the slot, and a release write to fill it or empty it. In KillSwitch, add a private static final VarHandle for the reason field, the same way SettlementSlot does. Write trip with compareAndSet, and isTripped and reason with acquire reads. Run the tests until all seven pass, then twice more. Then ask yourself which of these tests would still pass on x86 if offer used setOpaque, and what that means. VarHandle methods take the receiver first and need a cast on the result: (Settlement) ITEM.getAcquire(this), ITEM.setRelease(this, s). Why does offer check the slot with an acquire read and not a plain one? A plain read in the producer's spin loop may be read once and never again. The acquire also pairs with the consumer's release of null. REASON.compareAndSet(this, null, why) returns true only for the caller that found null. It has volatile semantics, so a later acquire read of the reason sees the winner's string. All seven tests in VarHandleModesTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can name the four access modes and what each one promises, write a release/acquire handoff and a compareAndSet flag with a VarHandle, and explain why app code almost never needs them and why only jcstress can test them.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Quiz
x: A shutdown hook sets a flag once. A hot loop on another thread checks the flag and only needs to stop eventually; the flag guards no other data. What is the weakest mode that is guaranteed to work? Plain Opaque Acquire/release Volatile Opaque guarantees each read really happens, so the loop eventually sees the write (jcstress BasicJMM_04 forbids a stuck opaque spin). Plain may be read once for the whole loop. Acquire/release and volatile also work but promise more than this loop needs. In app code you'd still write volatile, because it's one keyword and costs nothing extra on an x86 read. Writer: report.total = t; READY.setRelease(this, true);. Reader: if ((boolean) READY.getOpaque(this)) use(report.total);. What can the reader see? The flag as true, but an old total: a release only helps a reader that acquires Always the new total, because the writer used release A WrongMethodTypeException, because the modes don't match Never the flag as true, because opaque reads can't see release writes The ordering is a pair: release on the writer's side, acquire on the reader's. An opaque read sees the flag eventually, but nothing stops the reader's read of total from happening before it. Modes may be mixed without an exception (option 3), and opaque reads do see the value (option 4). Two settlement workers decide who runs the nightly batch: each does MINE.setRelease(this, true), then reads the other's flag with getAcquire, and runs the batch if it reads false. What's wrong? Nothing: release/acquire orders the write before the read It only fails on ARM It throws, because each VarHandle may only be used by one thread Both workers can read false and both run the batch, even on x86; this shape needs volatile, or better one compareAndSet or a database lock This is store buffering. Release keeps earlier accesses before the write but doesn't stop the later read of a different variable from passing it, and x86's store buffer does exactly that. Volatile forbids it through its single total order. In a real service, use one shared variable with compareAndSet, or a lock in the database both workers share. Where do VarHandle access modes belong? On every hot volatile field in a Quarkus service Instead of synchronized in request handlers In low-level building blocks like queues, after a profiler shows the cost, with jcstress tests Nowhere: they were deprecated with sun.misc.Unsafe VarHandles are the supported replacement for Unsafe, not deprecated with it (option 4). They only pay off in code that hands over millions of values a second, and they need jcstress because unit tests can't see reorderings. A request handler gets nothing from them that volatile, an Atomic class or a lock doesn't give it more clearly. From lesson 3 of this track: many threads run balance += amount on a volatile long balance. Someone suggests BALANCE.getAndAdd(this, amount) through a VarHandle instead. Does that fix it? No, a VarHandle has the same problem as volatile Yes: getAndAdd is one atomic read-modify-write, like AtomicLong.getAndAdd Only if a setRelease follows it Only on 64-bit JVMs Volatile makes each read and each write visible, but += is still a read and a write with a gap between them, so updates get lost. getAndAdd is a single atomic update with volatile semantics. In app code an AtomicLong or a LongAdder says the same thing more plainly.
