h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Key terms
x: VarHandle A typed handle to a field or array element whose methods read and write it in a chosen memory mode (JDK 9). Access mode The memory rules for one read or write: plain, opaque, acquire/release or volatile. Opaque A mode where each access really happens, untorn and in order for that variable, with no ordering of other variables. Acquire and release A paired mode: writes before the release are visible to a thread whose acquire read sees the released value. Signature-polymorphic method A method whose real signature comes from the call site's argument types and result cast, like VarHandle.get. Store buffering Each thread writes one variable, then reads the other's; both may read the old value unless the accesses are volatile. jcstress The OpenJDK harness that runs concurrent actors millions of times and checks every outcome against acceptable and forbidden ones. What does a VarHandle let you choose that a volatile field doesn't? The memory mode of each access (plain, opaque, acquire/release, volatile) on a plain field, plus atomic updates such as compareAndSet. What does opaque mode add over plain? Each access really happens, untorn and in order for that variable, so a spinning reader eventually sees a new value. It orders no other variables. A release write and an acquire read of the same variable: what does the reader get? If its acquire read sees the released value, it also sees every write the writer made before the release. What does volatile add on top of acquire/release? One total order of all volatile accesses. That forbids the store-buffering result where two threads both read the other's variable as 0. What memory semantics does VarHandle.compareAndSet have? Volatile: it reads the witness value as getVolatile and, on success, writes as setVolatile. Why keep a VarHandle in a static final field? The JIT treats a static final as a constant, so each call compiles down to a load or store plus the barrier its mode needs. Why can't a passing JUnit test show that release/acquire code is correct? It shows one machine didn't produce a bad outcome that time. jcstress runs the actors millions of times and fails on any forbidden outcome; x86 can't show many ARM bugs.

h: VarHandles and memory ordering modes · Go deeper
x: The VarHandle Javadoc maps the modes onto the C and C++ memory model, which helps when you read papers or Rust and C++ code: volatile is compatible with memory_order_seq_cst, acquire with memory_order_acquire, and release with memory_order_release. There are also static fence methods, VarHandle.fullFence(), acquireFence() and releaseFence(), documented as the matching atomic_thread_fence calls, plus loadLoadFence() and storeStoreFence(). Fences order a thread's accesses around a point without tying the order to one variable. They're even easier to misuse than modes. The jcstress samples AdvancedJMM_14_SynchronizedAreNotFences and AdvancedJMM_15_VolatilesAreNotFences show that synchronized blocks and volatile accesses don't work as fences either. Their guarantees hold only between threads that take the same lock, or when a volatile read actually sees the volatile write; you can't use them as free-standing barriers. VarHandles aren't only for fields. MethodHandles.arrayElementVarHandle(String[].class) gives you the modes on array elements, which a volatile array never could, because volatile there applies only to the array reference. MethodHandles.byteArrayViewVarHandle reads and writes an int or a long inside a byte[] with a chosen byte order and a chosen mode. If you want the model behind the modes in one sitting, Doug Lea's "Using JDK 9 Memory Order Modes" is the short guide to the modes, by the lead author of java.util.concurrent. Aleksey Shipilëv's "Java Memory Model Pragmatics" is the long version.

h: Thread pools and executors
x: ExecutorService, ThreadPoolExecutor internals, sizing, futures, CompletableFuture and ForkJoin. By the end of this track you can choose and configure a thread pool on purpose: predict where ThreadPoolExecutor puts each task, size a pool from measured wait and compute times with Little's law, and cap it at what the database or the issuer can take. You can cancel work that respects interruption, schedule periodic jobs that survive a failure, compose asynchronous calls with CompletableFuture (parallel lookups, per-call timeouts, fallbacks, fan-out), split CPU work with ForkJoinPool and parallel streams without starving the JVM, and run all of it in production with named threads, visible failures, carried request context, the right metrics and a clean shutdown. You need the first track (threads, race conditions, synchronized, interruption), and the memory model track helps. Install JDK 25. The labs compile with release 21, so they run on JDK 21 or later; where JDK 25 changed something, such as the default executor of CompletableFuture or ForkJoinPool gaining scheduling, the lesson says so and keeps that code out of the labs. The labs live in labs/executors, one package per lesson (workbench.executors.l01 to l09). They are in Java, and every code sample and Try-it demo also comes in Kotlin. Concurrency tests never rely on tight timing: they use latches, barriers, max-concurrency counters, virtual time and generous timeouts, so a broken solution fails (or times out after a few seconds) instead of hanging the build. Run ./gradlew :executors:test --tests 'workbench.executors.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, ./gradlew :executors:solutionTest to see the reference answers pass the same tests, and ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=<class> for the demos. A pool is a queue and a few reused threads. shutdown() only starts the stop; awaitTermination or close() waits. submit hides exceptions in the Future. ThreadPoolExecutor starts core threads, then queues, then grows to max only when the queue is full, then rejects. An unbounded queue makes max useless. Size CPU pools to the cores and I/O pools by cores x utilization x (1 + W/C), check with Little's law, and cap by the smallest downstream limit. cancel(true) and shutdownNow() only interrupt. Tasks must cooperate, and code that catches InterruptedException must rethrow it or restore the flag. Periodic tasks never overlap, fixed rate catches up while fixed delay doesn't, and one uncaught exception silently ends the schedule. CompletableFuture: start independent calls first, combine with thenCombine, flatten with thenCompose, and pass an executor for anything that blocks. Failures skip stages until a handler and often arrive wrapped in CompletionException. Timeouts and cancel end the wait, not the work. Give each fan-out call its own deadline and fallback. ForkJoin is for CPU work: fork one half, compute the other, then join. Parallel streams share the common pool with the whole JVM, so never block in them. In production: named threads, one wrapper that reports every failure with its request id and carries context, metrics on queue and rejections, no task waiting on its own pool, and an ordered shutdown.

h: Thread pools and executors: cheat sheet
x: Lifecycle Call What it does execute(r) runs r; an exception kills the worker and reaches its UncaughtExceptionHandler submit(c) returns a Future; an exception is stored in it and nothing is printed shutdown() rejects new tasks, lets queued and running ones finish, returns at once shutdownNow() also interrupts running tasks and returns the ones that never started awaitTermination(t, unit) waits until terminated or the timeout passes; returns a boolean close() (JDK 19+) shutdown(), then waits with no timeout; works with try-with-resources ThreadPoolExecutor: where a task goes Fewer than corePoolSize threads: start a new thread. Otherwise: offer it to the queue. Queue full: start a thread if below maximumPoolSize. Otherwise: reject. Queue Effect LinkedBlockingQueue() (fixed pool) unbounded: max is dead code, overload hides as memory and latency SynchronousQueue (cached pool) no queue: every burst becomes threads, up to max ArrayBlockingQueue(n) bounded: a full queue grows the pool, then rejects. Pushes back. Rejection: AbortPolicy throws (default), CallerRunsPolicy makes the submitter run it (back-pressure), DiscardPolicy and DiscardOldestPolicy lose work silently. keepAliveTime retires threads above core; allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) retires core threads too. Sizing Work Threads CPU-bound about availableProcessors() Waits on I/O cores x target utilization x (1 + wait / compute) Any Little's law: in flight = arrival rate x time in system The smallest limit downstream (a 20-connection DB pool, an issuer's rate limit) is the real ceiling. Give each dependency its own pool or semaphore: a bulkhead. Futures, cancellation and interruption get() throws ExecutionException (cause inside), CancellationException or InterruptedException; get(t, unit) adds TimeoutException and ends only your wait. cancel(true) on a FutureTask interrupts the worker. The task stops only if it blocks interruptibly or checks the flag. Catching InterruptedException clears the flag: rethrow it, or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). JDK 19: state(), resultNow(), exceptionNow(). invokeAll waits for all; invokeAny returns the first success and cancels the rest. Scheduling Method Next run starts schedule(task, d, unit) once, after d scheduleAtFixedRate at initialDelay + n x period; late runs catch up back to back scheduleWithFixedDelay delay after the previous run ends Runs of one task never overlap. One uncaught exception suppresses every later run, silently: catch RuntimeException inside the task. JDK 25: ForkJoinPool implements ScheduledExecutorService and adds submitWithTimeout. CompletableFuture You have Method T -> U thenApply T -> CompletableFuture<U> thenCompose two futures, (T, U) -> V thenCombine failure -> value / future exceptionally / exceptionallyCompose (JDK 12) both outcomes -> new result handle both outcomes, observe only whenComplete a deadline orTimeout (fails) / completeOnTimeout (default value), JDK 9 many futures allOf (waits for all, fails if any failed) / anyOf (first to complete, even a failure) No executor means ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). Up to JDK 24, a common pool with parallelism below 2 meant a new thread per task; JDK 25 always uses the common pool. Pass an executor for anything that blocks. A plain stage runs on the thread that completes the previous stage, or on the caller if it's already done. xxxAsync(fn, executor) moves it. Start independent calls before combining them, or they run one after the other. Exceptions thrown in a stage arrive wrapped in CompletionException; completeExceptionally and orTimeout store them raw. Unwrap before testing the type. orTimeout and cancel(true) don't stop the task. Give the client its own timeout. Block once, at the edge, with a timeout. Never join() an unfinished future inside a stage. ForkJoinPool and parallel streams compute(): below the threshold, loop; else split, left.fork(), right.compute(), then left.join(). Each worker owns a deque (push and pop at the top); idle workers steal the oldest task from the bottom. Common pool: availableProcessors() - 1 workers plus the caller, shared by parallel streams and default async tasks. In parallel streams: no shared mutable state, toList() keeps order, small or cheap inputs are faster sequential. Never block in the common pool. Put I/O on an executor built for waiting; ManagedBlocker is a patch. Production checklist Name threads: Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory() (JDK 21+). Report failures from both execute and submit in one wrapper, with the request id; don't rethrow. Carry ThreadLocal context (MDC, tracing): capture at submission, install in the worker, restore in finally. Watch queue size, active count against max, rejections (count them in the handler) and time in queue. No task may block on another task in the same bounded pool: compose, inline, or use a separate pool per stage. Shut down in order: stop intake, then pools upstream first, all within one deadline inside the grace period; log what shutdownNow() returns.

h: Thread pools and executors: track quiz
x: On JDK 21, try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { pool.submit(this::exportLedger); }. What happens at the closing brace? Nothing: the pool keeps running until the JVM exits close() calls shutdown() and waits for the export to finish close() calls shutdownNow() and interrupts the export It doesn't compile, because ExecutorService isn't AutoCloseable Since JDK 19, ExecutorService is AutoCloseable. close() shuts the pool down and waits, with no timeout, for submitted tasks to finish. It only falls back to shutdownNow() if the waiting thread is interrupted. new ThreadPoolExecutor(4, 32, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()) gets a burst of 1,000 slow tasks. How many threads does it run? 32, the maximum 4, and 996 tasks wait in the queue 1,000, one per task 4, and 996 tasks are rejected The pool grows past core only when the queue refuses a task, and an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue never refuses. The maximum of 32 is never reached, and nothing is rejected until memory runs out. An 8-core service spends 20 ms of CPU and 180 ms waiting on the database per request, and you want about 80% CPU. The database pool has 40 connections. How many threads should the request pool have? 8, one per core 64, from 8 x 0.8 x (1 + 180/20) About 40: the formula says 64, but only 40 can talk to the database at once 200, to be safe under bursts The formula gives 64 threads to keep the CPU at 80%, but every request needs a connection, and only 40 exist. Threads 41 to 64 would just wait for a connection. The smallest limit on the path is the real ceiling. A task loops over 10 million ledger rows and never blocks or checks the interrupt flag. You call future.cancel(true). What happens? The thread is stopped at once cancel returns false because the task is running cancel returns true and the future reports cancelled, but the loop runs to the end The task gets an InterruptedException at the next loop iteration cancel(true) only sets the interrupt flag. A task that never blocks interruptibly and never checks isInterrupted() doesn't notice. The Future is marked cancelled either way, so its result is lost even though the work finishes. An FX refresher runs with scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refresh, 0, 30, SECONDS). At 03:12 the provider returns a 502 and refresh throws. What do you see at 09:00? The rate from 03:11, and no log line about the failure A fresh rate: the scheduler retried 30 seconds later A stack trace in the logs every 30 seconds since 03:12 The scheduler shut down and the service failed its health check An exception that escapes a periodic task suppresses every later run, and it is stored in the ScheduledFuture that nobody reads. Catch RuntimeException inside the task and expose the age of the last success on a health endpoint. price() and rate() each block for 200 ms. Which version takes about 200 ms in total? supplyAsync(() -> price(), io).thenCombine(supplyAsync(() -> rate(), io), BigDecimal::multiply) supplyAsync(() -> price(), io).thenCompose(p -> supplyAsync(() -> rate(), io).thenApply(p::multiply)) supplyAsync(() -> price().multiply(rate()), io) supplyAsync(() -> price(), io).thenApplyAsync(p -> p.multiply(rate()), io) Only the first starts both calls before waiting for either. The others are asynchronous too, but each calls rate() after price() has returned, so they take about 400 ms. A quote call has orTimeout(300, MILLISECONDS), and the provider hangs for 30 seconds. What happens to the call's thread on the io pool? It is interrupted at 300 ms and returns to the pool It stays busy for the full 30 seconds; only the future completed at 300 ms The pool replaces it with a new thread It is cancelled before the call starts orTimeout completes the future with TimeoutException and never touches the task. Under load, abandoned calls fill the pool. Set a client-side timeout no longer than the future's deadline. A Quarkus service enriches payments with payments.parallelStream().map(p -> enrich(p, binService.lookup(p.bin()))).toList(), and each lookup takes 50 ms. Unrelated CompletableFuture timeouts start appearing elsewhere in the service. Why? Parallel streams use virtual threads, which pin on the lookup The stream's toList() locks the list while the futures run The common pool rejects tasks when the stream is busy The lookups block the common pool's workers, and executor-less CompletableFuture tasks need the same pool Parallel streams and default async CompletableFuture tasks share ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which has cores minus one workers. Blocking lookups hold those workers, so everything else queues behind them. Move the lookups to an IO executor. A request thread sets the MDC requestId and submits a ledger write to a pool whose tasks, through a wrapper, run with the submitter's MDC. The wrapper restores the worker's MDC in finally. Which problem does that finally prevent? The submitting thread losing its own MDC A later task on the same worker logging with this request's id The task's exceptions being swallowed Deadlock between the request thread and the worker Pool threads are reused. Without the restore, the worker keeps req-42 in its MDC, and the next task on that thread, possibly from another request or none at all, logs under the wrong id. The submitting thread's MDC is never touched by the worker. Pick the tool for each job on JDK 25: (1) total fees over 20 million rows in memory, (2) 2,000 concurrent calls to a card-issuer API, (3) a heartbeat to the issuer every 30 seconds. (1) a parallel stream or ForkJoinPool; (2) virtual threads or a bounded IO pool, capped by a semaphore at the issuer's limit; (3) a ScheduledExecutorService with fixed rate (1) virtual threads; (2) a parallel stream; (3) a loop with Thread.sleep(30_000) on the common pool All three on one newFixedThreadPool(200) (1) a single-thread executor; (2) supplyAsync without an executor; (3) java.util.Timer CPU work over in-memory data splits well across the cores. Thousands of blocking calls want cheap threads, limited by what the issuer accepts, not by a pool size. A heartbeat is a timetable, which is what fixed rate is for, on its own scheduler. Sleeping in the common pool, executor-less supplyAsync for I/O and Timer are each a bug from this track.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · A thread per task costs time and has no ceiling
x: Here is a measurement from ThreadPerTaskDemo below. Five thousand tiny tasks, each run on a brand-new thread, took between 0.5 and 1.5 seconds per round on a 4-core machine, depending on how busy it was. The same tasks on a pool of four reused threads took 6 to 25 ms. The work was identical. The difference is the threads. A Java platform thread wraps an operating system thread. Starting one means a system call, a new stack (on 64-bit Linux the JVM reserves 1 MB of address space per thread by default) and registration with the OS scheduler. When the thread ends, all of that is torn down again. For a task that runs for microseconds, the setup costs far more than the work. The second cost is worse, because it only shows up under load. Thread-per-task has no upper limit. If 3,000 authorization requests arrive at once, you get 3,000 threads. Something runs out first: the process thread limit, memory for stacks, or CPU time spent switching between threads that all want to run. In Java the first sign is often java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread, during your busiest hour. A thread pool fixes both problems. It creates a few threads once and keeps them. Each thread loops: take a task from a queue, run it, take the next one. The pool size caps how many tasks run at the same time, and the rest wait in the queue. Virtual threads, the subject of the "Virtual threads" track, make threads cheap to create, so the first cost mostly goes away for them. The second one does not. You still need a limit on how much work runs at once; with virtual threads you put that limit on the scarce resource instead of on the threads. Pay for 5,000 threads Predict first: for 5,000 tiny tasks, how many times slower is one new thread per task than a pool of 4? Twice? Ten times? A hundred? Run ThreadPerTaskDemo (Java or Kotlin, they do the same thing) with the command below. It runs two rounds. Run it again with -Pargs=10000 added. Does each column double? ThreadPerTaskDemo.java package workbench.executors.l01; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** 5,000 tiny tasks: one new thread per task, then the same tasks on a pool of 4 threads. */ public class ThreadPerTaskDemo { static final LongAdder work = new LongAdder(); static void task() { work.add(Long.toHexString(System.nanoTime()).length()); // a few nanoseconds of real work } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int tasks = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 5_000; for (int round = 1; round <= 2; round++) { // 1. a brand-new platform thread for every task long t0 = System.nanoTime(); CountDownLatch done = new CountDownLatch(tasks); for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) { new Thread(() -> { task(); done.countDown(); }).start(); } done.await(); long perTask = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; // 2. the same tasks on four threads that are created once and reused t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) pool.execute(ThreadPerTaskDemo::task); } // close() waits for all of them long pooled = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("round %d: %,d tasks new thread each: %,d ms pool of 4: %,d ms%n", round, tasks, perTask, pooled); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l01.ThreadPerTaskDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l01/ThreadPerTaskDemo.java ThreadPerTaskDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder private val work = LongAdder() private fun task() { work.add(System.nanoTime().toString(16).length.toLong()) // a few nanoseconds of real work } /** 5,000 tiny tasks: one new thread per task, then the same tasks on a pool of 4 threads. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val tasks = args.firstOrNull()?.toInt() ?: 5_000 for (round in 1..2) { // 1. a brand-new platform thread for every task var t0 = System.nanoTime() val done = CountDownLatch(tasks) repeat(tasks) { Thread { task(); done.countDown() }.start() } done.await() val perTask = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 // 2. the same tasks on four threads that are created once and reused t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> repeat(tasks) { pool.execute(::task) } } // close() waits for all of them val pooled = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("round %d: %,d tasks new thread each: %,d ms pool of 4: %,d ms".format(round, tasks, perTask, pooled)) } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l01.ThreadPerTaskDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l01/ThreadPerTaskDemo.kt On the machine this was written on, one thread per task took 0.5 to 1.5 seconds per round and the pool took 6 to 25 ms: 50 to 150 times faster. The pool's first round is the slowest because the JIT is still warming up. With 10,000 tasks the thread-per-task column roughly doubles, because the cost is paid per thread. The pool pays it four times in total. Thread Pools (The Java Tutorials) read A pool is a courier office. The couriers are the threads, hired once and kept. Parcels go into one in-tray (the queue), and whichever courier is free takes the next one. shutdown() is the sign on the door that says "no more parcels": the couriers still clear the tray. shutdownNow() hands the tray back to the customers and phones every courier on the road to come back. The analogy breaks at that phone call. A real courier hears it. A Java task hears an interrupt only if it checks for one or is blocked in a method that does.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Executor runs tasks, ExecutorService owns the threads
x: java.util.concurrent splits the idea into two interfaces. Executor has one method, void execute(Runnable task). It says nothing about threads. An implementation may run the task on the calling thread, on a new thread or on a pool, and code that takes an Executor doesn't care which. ExecutorService extends it with what a pool needs: submit (which returns a Future, a handle you can use to wait for the task's result), invokeAll and invokeAny, and the lifecycle methods shutdown, shutdownNow, awaitTermination and, since JDK 19, close. You rarely implement it. You get one from the Executors factory: Java ExecutorService fixed = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8); // 8 threads, unbounded queue ExecutorService single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); // 1 thread, tasks run in order ExecutorService cached = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); // grows without limit, idle threads die after 60 s ExecutorService vts = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // JDK 21: a new virtual thread per task Kotlin val fixed = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8) // 8 threads, unbounded queue val single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() // 1 thread, tasks run in order val cached = Executors.newCachedThreadPool() // grows without limit, idle threads die after 60 s val vts = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() // JDK 21: a new virtual thread per task The first three are built on ThreadPoolExecutor with different settings. Lesson 2 of this track takes it apart. Now the trap. execute and submit look interchangeable, and they handle failure in opposite ways. Here is what SwallowDemo prints for the same failing task sent both ways: --- execute --- charging on pool-1-thread-1 Exception in thread "pool-1-thread-1" java.lang.IllegalStateException: card issuer returned 502 --- submit --- charging on pool-1-thread-2 submit: nothing printed. isDone=true With execute, the exception escapes the task and kills the worker thread. The thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler prints the stack trace (that is the default handler's job), and the pool starts a replacement worker. That is why the second task runs on pool-1-thread-2. With submit, the pool wraps your task in a FutureTask, which catches the exception and stores it in the Future. Nothing is printed. The only way to see the failure is to call get(), which throws ExecutionException with your exception as its cause. If nobody calls get(), the failure is gone. So choose on purpose. Use execute for fire-and-forget work, so failures at least reach the handler. Use submit only when some code will call get(). Lesson 9 of this track shows how to log failures from both. Lose an exception on purpose Run SwallowDemo below and read the thread name printed for each run. Delete the whole --- get --- part (the println and the try block around f.get()). Predict: will any trace of the second failure remain? Run it again. SwallowDemo.java package workbench.executors.l01; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** The same failing task, sent once with execute and once with submit. Watch where the exception goes. */ public class SwallowDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { Runnable charge = () -> { System.out.println("charging on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); throw new IllegalStateException("card issuer returned 502"); }; System.out.println("--- execute ---"); pool.execute(charge); Thread.sleep(200); // give the stack trace time to print System.out.println("--- submit ---"); Future<?> f = pool.submit(charge); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println("submit: nothing printed. isDone=" + f.isDone()); System.out.println("--- get ---"); try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: " + e.getCause()); } } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l01.SwallowDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l01/SwallowDemo.java SwallowDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** The same failing task, sent once with execute and once with submit. Watch where the exception goes. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> val charge = Runnable { println("charging on " + Thread.currentThread().name) throw IllegalStateException("card issuer returned 502") } println("--- execute ---") pool.execute(charge) Thread.sleep(200) // give the stack trace time to print println("--- submit ---") val f = pool.submit(charge) Thread.sleep(200) println("submit: nothing printed. isDone=" + f.isDone) println("--- get ---") try { f.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: " + e.cause) } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l01.SwallowDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l01/SwallowDemo.kt The first run prints a stack trace for the execute failure, then the submit task runs on pool-1-thread-2 because the first worker died. The get() block prints the ExecutionException and its cause. Without that block, the second failure leaves no trace at all: the exception sits inside a Future nobody reads. Executors (Java SE 25 API) docs A Kafka consumer in a payment service often hands records to a fixed pool so slow ledger writes don't stall polling. When Kubernetes stops the pod, it sends SIGTERM and waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 seconds by default) before SIGKILL. That is your shutdown budget. Stop polling first, then shutdown() the pool, awaitTermination for about 20 seconds, then shutdownNow() and log what it handed back, and commit offsets only for records that finished. Quarkus manages its own worker pool, and a Temporal WorkerFactory stops its threads when you shut the factory down. The pools you create yourself, for a fan-out to card issuers or a nightly settlement job, are yours to close.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · shutdown() starts the stop, awaitTermination() waits for it
x: An ExecutorService moves one way: running, then shutting down (or stopping), then terminated. Two methods start that trip, and neither of them waits. shutdown() closes the door. New tasks are rejected with RejectedExecutionException. Queued tasks and running tasks carry on. The method returns at once. shutdownNow() closes the door and empties the room. It removes every queued task that has not started and returns them as a List<Runnable>. Then it interrupts the threads that are running tasks. An interrupt is a request, not a kill. A task blocked in sleep, wait or BlockingQueue.take wakes up with an InterruptedException. A task in a CPU loop that never checks the flag keeps running. Lesson 4 of this track covers that protocol. To wait for the end, call awaitTermination(timeout, unit). It returns true if the pool terminated in time and false if not. Together they make the shutdown idiom from the ExecutorService Javadoc (the timeouts are yours to pick): Java pool.shutdown(); // 1. no new work try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { // 2. let the backlog finish pool.shutdownNow(); // 3. interrupt the stragglers if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) log.error("pool did not terminate"); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { pool.shutdownNow(); // we were interrupted: stop now Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // and keep the flag for our caller } Kotlin pool.shutdown() // 1. no new work try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { // 2. let the backlog finish pool.shutdownNow() // 3. interrupt the stragglers if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) log.error("pool did not terminate") } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { pool.shutdownNow() // we were interrupted: stop now Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // and keep the flag for our caller } Since JDK 19, ExecutorService is AutoCloseable, so try-with-resources can do the waiting. close() calls shutdown() and waits until every task has finished. If the waiting thread is interrupted, it calls shutdownNow(), keeps waiting, and sets the interrupt flag again before it returns. There is no timeout, so close() blocks forever on a task that never ends. Use close() for a short-lived pool inside one method. Use the idiom for a long-lived pool that must stop within a deadline. Forget both and you get a different bug. The threads of newFixedThreadPool are not daemon threads, so they keep the JVM alive after main returns, waiting for tasks that will never come. Watch shutdown not wait ShutdownDemo queues six 300 ms settlement batches on two threads, then calls shutdown(). Predict the timestamp on the shutdown returned line, then run it. Run it again with -Pargs=now, which calls shutdownNow() after 100 ms instead. Predict how many batches settle. ShutdownDemo.java package workbench.executors.l01; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** shutdown, awaitTermination and shutdownNow on a pool of 2 threads with 6 queued 300 ms tasks. */ public class ShutdownDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static Runnable settle(int id) { return () -> { try { Thread.sleep(300); // a 300 ms call to the ledger log("settled batch " + id); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("batch " + id + " interrupted"); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean now = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("now"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2); for (int i = 1; i <= 6; i++) pool.execute(settle(i)); if (now) { Thread.sleep(100); List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow(); log("shutdownNow returned " + neverStarted.size() + " tasks that never started"); } else { pool.shutdown(); log("shutdown returned. isShutdown=" + pool.isShutdown() + " isTerminated=" + pool.isTerminated()); } try { pool.execute(settle(7)); } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { log("batch 7 rejected: the pool is shut down"); } boolean done = pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); log("awaitTermination returned " + done + ". isTerminated=" + pool.isTerminated()); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l01.ShutdownDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l01/ShutdownDemo.java ShutdownDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg)) private fun settle(id: Int) = Runnable { try { Thread.sleep(300) // a 300 ms call to the ledger log("settled batch $id") } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("batch $id interrupted") Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } /** shutdown, awaitTermination and shutdownNow on a pool of 2 threads with 6 queued 300 ms tasks. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val now = args.firstOrNull() == "now" val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2) for (i in 1..6) pool.execute(settle(i)) if (now) { Thread.sleep(100) val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow() log("shutdownNow returned ${neverStarted.size} tasks that never started") } else { pool.shutdown() log("shutdown returned. isShutdown=${pool.isShutdown} isTerminated=${pool.isTerminated}") } try { pool.execute(settle(7)) } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { log("batch 7 rejected: the pool is shut down") } val done = pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) log("awaitTermination returned $done. isTerminated=${pool.isTerminated}") } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l01.ShutdownDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l01/ShutdownDemo.kt With shutdown(), that line prints within a few milliseconds, batch 7 is rejected, and the six batches settle in pairs at about 300, 600 and 900 ms. Only then does awaitTermination return true. With now, batches 1 and 2 are interrupted in their sleep, shutdownNow hands back the 4 batches that never started, nothing settles, and the pool terminates at about 100 ms. shutdown() and shutdownNow() only start the trip. awaitTermination() or close() is how you wait for the end. ExecutorService (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · A pool is a queue and a few threads that loop
x: Strip away the options and a fixed pool is small enough to write in a lab. Each worker thread runs this loop: Java while (true) { Runnable task = queue.take(); // blocks while the queue is empty if (task == POISON) return; // shutdown: time to exit task.run(); } Kotlin while (true) { val task = queue.take() // blocks while the queue is empty if (task === POISON) return // shutdown: time to exit task.run() } execute puts the task on a BlockingQueue, and workers take it off. The queue does the hand-off between threads, and the number of workers is the limit on how many tasks run at once. Shutdown is the interesting part. Idle workers are blocked inside take(), so the pool has to wake them. One way is a poison pill: a marker task, one per worker, added behind every real task. A worker that takes a pill exits. The queue is first in, first out, so every task submitted before shutdown() runs before any worker sees a pill. shutdownNow() drains the queue instead, adds fresh pills, and interrupts the workers, so idle ones fall out of take() and busy ones get the request to stop. There is one race to get right, and it is the check-then-act shape from "Race conditions: why count++ lies". execute checks the shutdown flag, then queues the task. If shutdown() runs between those two steps, the task lands behind the pills and never runs, although the caller was told it was accepted. So both methods take the same lock, and the check and the queueing happen as one step. ThreadPoolExecutor solves the same problem with one AtomicInteger called ctl. It packs the run state into the top 3 bits and the worker count into the other 29, so a single compare-and-set can check and change both. The lab uses a plain lock instead. It is slower and much easier to read, which is the right trade when the goal is to see the moving parts. Check yourself: in the toy pool, shutdown() adds one pill instead of one per worker, and the pool has four workers. What happens? One worker takes the pill and exits. The other three stay blocked in take() forever, so awaitTermination returns false. They are not daemon threads, so the JVM never exits either. Calling shutdown() and treating the work as done. A settlement job runs pool.shutdown(); dataSource.close(); and the batches still running fail with connection errors. The name sounds final and the call returns quickly, so it reads like a wait. It only stops new submissions. Wait with awaitTermination (or close() on JDK 19 and later) before you release anything the tasks still use.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Java and Kotlin
x: Closing a pool in Java and Kotlin UseDemo.java (sketch) try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { List<Future<Integer>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (int n = 1; n <= 10; n++) { int k = n; futures.add(pool.submit(() -> k * k)); } int total = 0; for (Future<Integer> f : futures) { total += f.get(); // must handle InterruptedException and ExecutionException } System.out.println("sum of squares 1..10 = " + total); } // close(): shutdown, then wait for every task UseDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** Kotlin's use {} calls ExecutorService.close() (JDK 19+), which waits for the tasks to finish. */ fun main() { val total = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> val futures = (1..10).map { n -> pool.submit<Int> { n * n } } futures.sumOf { it.get() } // get() can still throw ExecutionException; Kotlin just doesn't force a catch } println("sum of squares 1..10 = $total") } Both versions end in ExecutorService.close(), so the waiting is the same. Kotlin's use is its try-with-resources, and it works on a pool because ExecutorService has been AutoCloseable since JDK 19 (on older JDKs, write the shutdown idiom in a finally). The real difference is checked exceptions. Java makes you deal with InterruptedException and ExecutionException from get(). Kotlin compiles without a catch, so a failed task surfaces as an exception you never planned for. If you later wrap a pool for coroutines with asCoroutineDispatcher(), the dispatcher needs closing too; closing it shuts the pool down.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Worked example
x: Stop a settlement job without losing batches A nightly job settles merchant batches on a pool of 4. Here is the end of main as first written. Decide what happens to batches still running when this code reaches dataSource.close(). for (Batch b : batches) pool.execute(() -> settle(b)); pool.shutdown(); dataSource.close(); // release the 20 DB connections log.info("settlement finished"); for (b in batches) pool.execute { settle(b) } pool.shutdown() dataSource.close() // release the 20 DB connections log.info("settlement finished") shutdown() returned at once. The log line lies, and dataSource.close() pulls connections away from batches that are still running, so they fail with connection errors. Nothing waited for anything. Wait, with a deadline. The job has a 10 minute slot, so give the backlog 9 of them, then interrupt and record what never started. Release shared resources only after the pool has terminated. pool.shutdown(); // 1. no new batches try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(9, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 2. let the backlog finish List<Runnable> unstarted = pool.shutdownNow(); // 3. interrupt, collect the rest log.warn("{} batches never started", unstarted.size()); pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { pool.shutdownNow(); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } dataSource.close(); // 4. only now pool.shutdown() // 1. no new batches try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(9, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { // 2. let the backlog finish val unstarted = pool.shutdownNow() // 3. interrupt, collect the rest log.warn("{} batches never started", unstarted.size) pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { pool.shutdownNow() Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } dataSource.close() // 4. only now If the job has no deadline, JDK 19's try-with-resources is shorter, and the order is right by construction: the block cannot end before the pool has terminated. try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) { for (Batch b : batches) pool.execute(() -> settle(b)); } // close() waits for every batch dataSource.close(); log.info("settlement finished"); Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).use { pool -> for (b in batches) pool.execute { settle(b) } } // close() waits for every batch dataSource.close() log.info("settlement finished")

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Lab
x: Build a tiny fixed pool labs/executors/src/main/java/workbench/executors/l01/TinyPool.java ./gradlew :executors:test --tests 'workbench.executors.l01.*' Run the tests. All eight fail with UnsupportedOperationException. Write execute: a null check, then, inside synchronized (lock), throw RejectedExecutionException if shutdown is set, otherwise queue.add(task). Write workerLoop: take() a task, return on POISON or on InterruptedException, run the task, and count a RuntimeException in failed instead of letting it escape. Write shutdown (under the lock: set the flag, add one POISON per worker) and awaitTermination (wait on the terminated latch). Write shutdownNow: under the lock, set the flag, drain the queue into a list, remove the pills from it and add fresh ones. Then interrupt every worker and return the list. Run the tests until all eight pass, then run them twice more. Why add pills in shutdownNow as well? A running task may swallow the interrupt. When it ends, its worker goes back to take(). Without a pill waiting there, that worker blocks forever and awaitTermination never returns true. BlockingQueue.drainTo(list) moves everything in the queue into list in one call, in queue order. The shutdownNow test checks that you return the very same Runnable objects, in the order they were queued. Don't wrap them. All eight tests in TinyPoolTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can say what a thread pool saves you, pick execute or submit on purpose, and shut a pool down without losing work or hanging the JVM.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Quiz
x: A Kafka handler does pool.submit(() -> ledger.post(entry)) and never keeps the Future. post throws a SQLException wrapped in a RuntimeException. What shows up in the logs? A stack trace from the default UncaughtExceptionHandler Nothing at all A RejectedExecutionException on the next submit A warning that the pool lost a worker submit wraps the task in a FutureTask, which catches the exception and stores it in the Future. Nobody calls get(), so nobody sees it. The stack trace from the default handler is what you'd get with execute, which is why that option is tempting. main creates Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2), runs three tasks that finish quickly, and returns without calling shutdown(). What happens to the JVM? It exits when main returns It exits once the three tasks are done It keeps running, because the two idle worker threads are not daemon threads It throws IllegalStateException because the pool was never shut down The JVM exits when the last non-daemon thread ends. The pool's workers are non-daemon and wait in take() for more work forever. A cached pool would let the JVM exit after 60 idle seconds, because its idle threads time out. A pool runs a task with a loop while (true) { score(next()); } that never checks the interrupt flag and never blocks. You call shutdownNow() and then awaitTermination(5, SECONDS). What does awaitTermination return? true, because shutdownNow stops the threads true, because the task is removed from the queue It throws InterruptedException false, because the interrupt is only a request and this task ignores it shutdownNow calls interrupt() on the workers. That sets a flag and wakes blocking calls. A loop that never checks the flag and never blocks runs on, so the pool cannot terminate and the wait times out with false. Which code waits until every submitted task has finished, with no timeout, on JDK 21? pool.shutdown(); try (pool) { ... } (try-with-resources, which calls close()) pool.shutdownNow(); pool.isTerminated(); close() (JDK 19+) calls shutdown() and then waits until the pool has terminated. shutdown() and shutdownNow() return at once, and isTerminated() only reports the state. From "Race conditions: why count++ lies": four tasks on a fixed pool each run total += amount 100,000 times on a shared long field. What is total after close() returns? Exactly 400,000 times amount, because the pool runs tasks one after another Often less, because the four workers run at the same time and lose updates Exactly right, because each task runs on a single thread Unknown, because the pool throws ConcurrentModificationException A pool of four runs four tasks at once on four threads, so total += amount is the same read-modify-write race as before. The pool changes who creates the threads, not the rules for shared state. Use a LongAdder, an AtomicLong, or give each task its own subtotal.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Explain it back
x: A new teammate asks what shutdown(), shutdownNow() and awaitTermination() each do, and in what order the payments service should call them when the pod gets SIGTERM. Explain it in your own words.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Key terms
x: Thread pool A set of threads created once that run many tasks, taking them from a queue. Executor Anything that can run a Runnable. It has one method, execute. ExecutorService An Executor that also returns Futures and can be shut down and waited for. Future A handle to a task's result that you can wait on, check or cancel. Poison pill A marker item put in a queue to tell the consumer that takes it to stop. Daemon thread A thread that does not keep the JVM alive. Pool threads usually are not daemon threads. Graceful shutdown Stop taking new work, let accepted work finish within a deadline, then release resources. Does shutdown() wait for running tasks to finish? No. It rejects new tasks and returns at once. Queued and running tasks carry on. Wait with awaitTermination or close(). What does shutdownNow() return? A List<Runnable> of the queued tasks that never started. It also interrupts the threads running tasks. A task sent with submit() throws. Where does the exception go? Into the Future. Nothing is printed. get() throws ExecutionException with it as the cause. A task sent with execute() throws. What happens? The worker thread dies, its UncaughtExceptionHandler runs (by default it prints the stack trace), and the pool starts a replacement. What does ExecutorService.close() do (JDK 19+)? shutdown(), then waits with no timeout until every task is done. If interrupted while waiting, it calls shutdownNow(), keeps waiting, then restores the interrupt flag. Why can a forgotten newFixedThreadPool keep the JVM running after main returns? Its worker threads are non-daemon and wait for new tasks forever.

h: Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown · Go deeper
x: ThreadPoolExecutor has five run states, not three: RUNNING, SHUTDOWN, STOP, TIDYING and TERMINATED. shutdown() moves it to SHUTDOWN. shutdownNow() moves it to STOP, from either of the first two. When the queue is empty and the last worker has exited, the pool moves to TIDYING, runs the protected terminated() hook (override it to log or release something), and then becomes TERMINATED. Threads blocked in awaitTermination wake only at that last step. The state and the worker count live together in one AtomicInteger called ctl. The top 3 bits hold the state and the low 29 bits hold the count. That is why the Javadoc caps a pool at about 500 million workers: (2^29) - 1. Packing both into one word lets execute check "still running?" and "room for one more worker?" and claim the slot with one compare-and-set, which is the same atomic check-and-act the lab gets from a lock. One more detail from the Executors Javadoc: newSingleThreadExecutor() is "guaranteed not to be reconfigurable to use additional threads", unlike newFixedThreadPool(1). The fixed pool is a plain ThreadPoolExecutor, so any code holding it can cast it and call setMaximumPoolSize. The single-thread executor is wrapped so nobody can. If your design depends on tasks running one at a time, in order, say so with newSingleThreadExecutor().

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Four rules decide where every task goes
x: Seven tasks through the four rules of ThreadPoolExecutor, then an unbounded queue that makes max useless Executors.newFixedThreadPool, newCachedThreadPool and newSingleThreadExecutor are all built on one class, ThreadPoolExecutor. Its main constructor takes five settings: Java new ThreadPoolExecutor( 2, // corePoolSize 4, // maximumPoolSize 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS, // keepAliveTime for threads above core new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2), // the work queue new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()); // what to do when everything is full Kotlin ThreadPoolExecutor( 2, // corePoolSize 4, // maximumPoolSize 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS, // keepAliveTime for threads above core ArrayBlockingQueue(2), // the work queue ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()) // what to do when everything is full Every call to execute walks the same four rules, in this order: Fewer than corePoolSize threads? Start a new thread for this task, even if other threads are idle. Otherwise, offer the task to the queue. The queue said no? Start a new thread, if that stays within maximumPoolSize. Still no room? Hand the task to the RejectedExecutionHandler. Read rule 3 again, because it surprises almost everyone. The pool grows past core only when the queue is full. Most people expect the opposite: use more threads first, queue when you run out. ThreadPoolExecutor prefers queuing because it keeps the thread count small. Extra threads are a relief valve for bursts, not the main capacity. Here is that pool taking seven 500 ms tasks, from PoolPuzzleDemo: task 1 accepted: threads=1 queued=0 task 2 accepted: threads=2 queued=0 task 3 accepted: threads=2 queued=1 task 4 accepted: threads=2 queued=2 task 5 accepted: threads=3 queued=2 task 6 accepted: threads=4 queued=2 task 7 REJECTED: threads=4 queued=2 Tasks 1 and 2 start core threads. Tasks 3 and 4 wait. Tasks 5 and 6 find the queue full and get extra threads. Task 7 finds everything full and is rejected with RejectedExecutionException. One more detail: tasks 5 and 6 run before tasks 3 and 4. A new thread takes the task that made it, not the oldest task in the queue. Even a pool with a first-in, first-out queue does not promise first-in, first-out execution. Predict a burst, then run it Without running anything, write down where tasks 1 to 7 go for new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 60, SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2)). Run PoolPuzzleDemo (the Java and Kotlin versions print the same) with the command below and compare with your notes. Look at the done on lines. Which tasks finished first, and on which threads? PoolPuzzleDemo.java package workbench.executors.l02; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionHandler; import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * Seven 500 ms tasks into new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, ...). Where does each one go? * Args: queue (bounded | unbounded | handoff) and policy (abort | caller | discard | oldest). */ public class PoolPuzzleDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String queueKind = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "bounded"; String policyKind = args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "abort"; BlockingQueue<Runnable> queue = switch (queueKind) { case "unbounded" -> new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(); case "handoff" -> new SynchronousQueue<>(); default -> new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2); }; RejectedExecutionHandler policy = switch (policyKind) { case "caller" -> new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy(); case "discard" -> new ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardPolicy(); case "oldest" -> new ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardOldestPolicy(); default -> new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy(); }; ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS, queue, policy); System.out.printf("core=2 max=4 queue=%s policy=%s%n", queueKind, policyKind); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 1; i <= 7; i++) { int id = i; Runnable task = () -> { try { Thread.sleep(500); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } System.out.printf(" task %d done on %s%n", id, Thread.currentThread().getName()); }; try { pool.execute(task); System.out.printf("task %d accepted: threads=%d queued=%d%n", id, pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getQueue().size()); } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { System.out.printf("task %d REJECTED: threads=%d queued=%d%n", id, pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getQueue().size()); } } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.printf("all done in %d ms, completed tasks: %d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.getCompletedTaskCount()); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l02.PoolPuzzleDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l02/PoolPuzzleDemo.java PoolPuzzleDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l02 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** * Seven 500 ms tasks into ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, ...). Where does each one go? * Args: queue (bounded | unbounded | handoff) and policy (abort | caller | discard | oldest). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val queueKind = args.getOrElse(0) { "bounded" } val policyKind = args.getOrElse(1) { "abort" } val queue = when (queueKind) { "unbounded" -> LinkedBlockingQueue<Runnable>() "handoff" -> SynchronousQueue<Runnable>() else -> ArrayBlockingQueue<Runnable>(2) } val policy = when (policyKind) { "caller" -> ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() "discard" -> ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardPolicy() "oldest" -> ThreadPoolExecutor.DiscardOldestPolicy() else -> ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy() } val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS, queue, policy) println("core=2 max=4 queue=$queueKind policy=$policyKind") val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (id in 1..7) { val task = Runnable { try { Thread.sleep(500) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } println(" task $id done on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } try { pool.execute(task) println("task $id accepted: threads=${pool.poolSize} queued=${pool.queue.size}") } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { println("task $id REJECTED: threads=${pool.poolSize} queued=${pool.queue.size}") } } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS) println("all done in ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms, completed tasks: ${pool.completedTaskCount}") } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l02.PoolPuzzleDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l02/PoolPuzzleDemo.kt Exactly the output above: two core threads, two queued, two extra threads, one rejection. Tasks 1, 2, 5 and 6 finish first at about 500 ms, then tasks 3 and 4 run on the core threads and finish at about 1,000 ms. Task 7 never runs. Every execute() call walks these four checks in order. The pool only grows toward max after the queue refuses a task. A ThreadPoolExecutor is a restaurant. The core threads are the permanent waiters. The queue is the waiting area by the door. Maximum pool size is how many temporary staff the manager may call in, and the manager calls them only when the waiting area is full, never just because the waiters look busy. The rejection policy is the door policy when the waiting area is packed and every temp is working: turn guests away (AbortPolicy), make the person at the door serve them himself (CallerRunsPolicy), or quietly lose a booking (the discard policies). The analogy breaks on fairness. A real restaurant seats people in arrival order. A new temp in this pool serves the guest who arrived last.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · An unbounded queue turns maximumPoolSize into dead code
x: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) is new ThreadPoolExecutor(n, n, 0, MILLISECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()). The queue has no capacity limit, so rule 2 always succeeds. Rule 3 never runs, so no extra thread is ever started, and rule 4 never runs either, so nothing is ever rejected. That sounds safe. It isn't. An unbounded queue hides overload instead of reporting it. Say your authorization service gets 400 requests a second and the pool can finish 300. The queue grows by 100 tasks every second. After ten minutes, 60,000 tasks are waiting, each holding its request in memory, and a new request waits more than three minutes before a thread even looks at it. The client gave up long ago, so the pool is now doing work nobody wants. The first alert you get is probably the heap. Setting a larger maximumPoolSize on such a pool changes nothing. new ThreadPoolExecutor(10, 100, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()) runs 10 threads, forever. The 100 is dead code. newCachedThreadPool() fails the other way. It is new ThreadPoolExecutor(0, Integer.MAX_VALUE, 60, SECONDS, new SynchronousQueue<>()). A SynchronousQueue has no capacity at all: an offer succeeds only if an idle thread is waiting to take it. Under a burst no thread is idle, so every task gets a new thread. Two thousand slow calls means two thousand threads. There is one shape that pushes back: a bounded queue with a finite maximum. Then rule 4 can fire, and overload turns into a visible event that you choose how to handle. The sizes come from lesson 3 of this track. The shape comes from this one. One edge case is worth knowing. With corePoolSize 0 and an unbounded queue, rule 1 never starts a thread and rule 3 never runs, so it looks as if nothing would ever execute. The pool special-cases this: after queuing, if it has no threads at all, it starts one. You get a single-threaded pool. Swap the queue Predict the thread count and total time for the same seven tasks with an unbounded queue. Then run the demo with -Pargs=unbounded. Do the same with -Pargs=handoff, which uses a SynchronousQueue. With unbounded, the pool never goes past 2 threads, all seven tasks are accepted, five of them queue, and the run takes about 2,000 ms (four rounds of 500 ms). With handoff, nothing ever queues: tasks 1 to 4 each get a thread and tasks 5, 6 and 7 are rejected, because max is 4 and a SynchronousQueue holds nothing. ThreadPoolExecutor (Java SE 25 API), section Queuing docs A Kafka consumer for card authorizations fans each record out to a pool so slow issuer calls don't block polling. If that pool is newFixedThreadPool(16), a slow issuer quietly fills an unbounded queue while offsets march on, and a crash loses everything in it. Give it a bounded queue. Then decide what overload means. If the consumer should slow down, CallerRunsPolicy makes the polling thread do the work, but watch max.poll.interval.ms (300,000 ms by default): if one run of work on that thread takes longer than that, the consumer is removed from the group and its partitions are reassigned. If overload should fail fast, keep AbortPolicy with a counting handler, pause the partition, and alert on the counter. Quarkus and Temporal size their own worker pools from configuration; the same four rules apply to the ones you build.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Rejection policies decide who pays when the pool is full
x: When rule 4 fires, the pool calls its RejectedExecutionHandler. The same handler runs for any task submitted after shutdown(). The JDK ships four: Policy What happens to the task Who notices AbortPolicy (the default) execute throws RejectedExecutionException the caller, at once CallerRunsPolicy the submitting thread runs it itself the caller, by being slowed down DiscardPolicy dropped nobody DiscardOldestPolicy the oldest queued task is dropped, then the new one is retried nobody AbortPolicy is the right default for request handling. The caller gets an exception it can turn into an HTTP 503 or a retry, and you can count it. CallerRunsPolicy is back-pressure in one line. While the submitting thread is busy running a task, it isn't submitting more, so the producer slows to the pool's speed. It suits a batch job that reads files and fans out work. It is a bad idea when the caller is a thread that must never block: an event-loop thread (one thread that serves many connections, so it must never wait on any one of them), or a Kafka consumer thread that has to call poll() again within max.poll.interval.ms. After shutdown() it drops the task silently. The two discard policies lose work without a trace. They have a nastier side with submit. A dropped FutureTask never runs, so its Future never completes, and a caller blocked in get() waits forever. Use them only for work that is truly optional, like a best-effort metrics flush. In production you usually want a custom handler: count the rejection for a metric, then fail fast with a message that says how full the pool was. The interface has one method, rejectedExecution(Runnable task, ThreadPoolExecutor pool), and the lab has you write it. Try the other three policies Run the demo with -Pargs="bounded caller". Find the line for task 7. Which thread ran it, and when was the accepted line printed? Run it with -Pargs="bounded discard" and then -Pargs="bounded oldest". Count the done lines and work out which task disappeared each time. With caller, task 7 runs on main, so main is stuck for 500 ms and prints "task 7 accepted" only after task 7 done on main. With discard, task 7 is "accepted" and simply never runs: six done lines, no error. With oldest, task 3 (the oldest queued task) vanishes and task 7 runs instead. Neither discard policy says a word about it.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Keep-alive, core time-out and prestarting threads
x: Threads above corePoolSize are temporary. If one sits idle for longer than keepAliveTime, it exits and the pool shrinks back toward core. Core threads stay, even if they are idle for a week. Two methods change that default. allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) applies the keep-alive to core threads as well, so an idle pool can shrink to zero threads. That suits a pool used for a nightly report: it holds no threads for the rest of the day. It needs a keep-alive greater than zero, or the call throws IllegalArgumentException. prestartAllCoreThreads() goes the other way. By default even core threads are created lazily, one per task, the first time tasks arrive. Prestarting creates them all up front, so the first burst after a deploy doesn't also pay for thread creation. The Javadoc also recommends it when you build a pool around a queue that already holds tasks, since a pool with no threads would never look at them. You can watch the whole lifecycle with the getters: getPoolSize() (threads alive now), getActiveCount() (threads running a task), getLargestPoolSize() (the high-water mark) and getQueue().size(). They are approximate while the pool is busy, which is fine for dashboards. Lesson 9 of this track turns them into metrics. For most request-handling pools I set core equal to max and rely on a bounded queue plus a rejection policy. A pool whose size changes under load is harder to reason about, and the extra threads arrive exactly when the machine is busiest. Keep core below max when bursts are short and rare, and you would rather absorb them than reject. Watch the pool shrink KeepAliveDemo runs a pool with core 2, max 4, a queue of 2 and a 300 ms keep-alive. It submits six 200 ms tasks, then prints the pool every 150 ms. Predict the thread count at the end, then run it. Run it again with -Pargs=core, which also calls allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true). KeepAliveDemo.java package workbench.executors.l02; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A pool grows to max under a burst, then shrinks back when threads sit idle longer than keepAlive. * Pass "core" to call allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) as well. */ public class KeepAliveDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2)); if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("core")) pool.allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true); System.out.println("before any task: threads=" + pool.getPoolSize()); for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) { pool.execute(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(200); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int tick = 0; tick <= 8; tick++) { System.out.printf("%4d ms: threads=%d active=%d queued=%d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getActiveCount(), pool.getQueue().size()); Thread.sleep(150); } System.out.println("largest pool size seen: " + pool.getLargestPoolSize()); pool.shutdown(); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l02.KeepAliveDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l02/KeepAliveDemo.java KeepAliveDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l02 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** * A pool grows to max under a burst, then shrinks back when threads sit idle longer than keepAlive. * Pass "core" to call allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) as well. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(2)) if (args.firstOrNull() == "core") pool.allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) println("before any task: threads=${pool.poolSize}") repeat(6) { pool.execute { try { Thread.sleep(200) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (tick in 0..8) { println("%4d ms: threads=%d active=%d queued=%d".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.poolSize, pool.activeCount, pool.queue.size)) Thread.sleep(150) } println("largest pool size seen: ${pool.largestPoolSize}") pool.shutdown() } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l02.KeepAliveDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l02/KeepAliveDemo.kt The pool starts with 0 threads, jumps to 4 during the burst, and drops back to 2 a few hundred milliseconds after the work ends. The largest pool size reported is 4. With core, it drops from 4 to 2 and then to 0, because the core threads now retire too. Raising maximumPoolSize to fix a slow pool that uses an unbounded queue. Someone sees newFixedThreadPool(8) falling behind, swaps in new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 64, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()), and nothing changes, because the pool only grows past core when the queue is full and this queue is never full. Either raise corePoolSize, or give the queue a capacity so the pool can grow and eventually reject.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Java and Kotlin
x: Configuring the same pool from Java and Kotlin AuthPool.java (solution) package workbench.executors.l02; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public final class AuthPool { private AuthPool() {} public static ThreadPoolExecutor create() { ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, // core: kept even when idle 8, // max: only reached once the queue is full 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, // idle threads above core retire after 30 s new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16), // bounded, so max and rejection can ever happen new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()); // the default, written out so readers see it pool.prestartAllCoreThreads(); // start the 4 core threads now, not on first use return pool; } } AuthPoolConfig.kt package workbench.executors.l02 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong val rejectedAuths = AtomicLong() // Java constructors take no named arguments in Kotlin, so the comments do that job. fun authPool(): ThreadPoolExecutor = ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, 8, // core, max 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, // keep-alive for threads above core ArrayBlockingQueue(16), // Runnable is inferred from the parameter type ) { _, pool -> // RejectedExecutionHandler, written as a trailing lambda rejectedAuths.incrementAndGet() throw RejectedExecutionException("rejected: queued=${pool.queue.size}") }.apply { prestartAllCoreThreads() } fun main() { val pool = authPool() println("threads before any task: ${pool.poolSize}") pool.shutdown() } The pool is the same Java object, but two things differ when you build it from Kotlin. Kotlin does not allow named arguments when calling a Java constructor, so seven positional numbers need comments in both languages. And Kotlin converts a lambda to a Java single-method interface, so the RejectedExecutionHandler can be a trailing lambda instead of a class. The getters read as properties (pool.queue, pool.poolSize). In coroutine code you rarely build one at all: Dispatchers.IO is already a shared pool capped at 64 threads (or the core count, if larger), and limitedParallelism(n) gives you a smaller limit on top of it.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Worked example
x: Trace a rebalance burst through the authorization pool This is the pool from the lab. After a Kafka rebalance, the consumer gets 30 authorizations at once, and each one waits about 200 ms on the issuer. Before reading on, write down how many threads start, how many tasks queue and how many are rejected. ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16), new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()); val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(16), ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy()) Apply the rules in order. Tasks 1 to 4 start the core threads (rule 1). Tasks 5 to 20 fill the queue of 16 (rule 2). Tasks 21 to 24 find the queue full and start extra threads, up to 8 (rule 3). Tasks 25 to 30 find everything full and are rejected (rule 4). threads = 8, queued = 16, rejected = 6 Six RejectedExecutionExceptions reach the consumer. If that thread doesn't catch them, it dies, and the records are redelivered after the next rebalance, which causes the next burst. Decide on purpose instead. Here the right answer is to slow the consumer down, so the burst drains at the pool's pace. ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16), new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy()); // the consumer thread runs overflow itself val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, 8, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(16), ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy()) // the consumer thread runs overflow itself Now tasks 25 to 30 run on the consumer thread, one after another: about 6 x 200 ms = 1.2 s during which the consumer can't poll. That is far below the 5 minute max.poll.interval.ms, so the trade is fine here. If one task could take minutes, it wouldn't be, and you would pause the partition instead.
