h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Quiz
x: new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 4, 60, SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10)) receives 8 tasks that each block for a minute. Where are they? 4 running, 4 queued 2 running, 6 queued 4 running, 2 queued, 2 rejected 8 running Tasks 1 and 2 start core threads. The other 6 fit in a queue of 10, so the queue never refuses and the pool never grows. The tempting answer, 4 running, assumes the pool uses its max before queuing. It is the other way round. A batch job reads 2 million ledger rows and submits one task per 1,000 rows. You want it to run no faster than the pool can keep up, without losing a batch and without a retry loop. Which handler fits? AbortPolicy DiscardOldestPolicy CallerRunsPolicy DiscardPolicy CallerRunsPolicy makes the reading thread run the overflow batch itself, so it stops reading while it works. That is back-pressure, and nothing is lost. AbortPolicy would make you write the retry loop, and both discard policies lose batches without telling anyone. A pool uses DiscardPolicy. A request thread calls pool.submit(task).get() while the pool is saturated. What happens? get() throws RejectedExecutionException get() returns null get() throws CancellationException get() blocks forever, because the dropped task never runs and its Future never completes DiscardPolicy drops the FutureTask without running or cancelling it. Nothing will ever complete that Future, so get() without a timeout waits forever. This is why the Javadoc suggests cancelling dropped tasks in a custom handler. A pool with core 4, max 16 and a bounded queue grew to 16 threads during a spike an hour ago. Traffic is quiet now. With default settings, how many threads does it have? 4, because idle threads above core retired after keepAliveTime 16, because threads are never removed 0, because idle threads retire 1, the minimum Keep-alive applies to threads above core, so the pool shrinks back to 4. It only goes to 0 if you call allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true). From "Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown": a producer thread keeps calling execute on a ThreadPoolExecutor with the default handler after another thread has called shutdown(). What does the producer see? The tasks run, because shutdown() lets queued work finish A RejectedExecutionException from each execute call Nothing: the tasks are silently dropped An IllegalStateException After shutdown(), new tasks go to the rejection handler, and the default AbortPolicy throws RejectedExecutionException. Only tasks that were already queued still run. With a discard policy or CallerRunsPolicy they would be dropped silently instead.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Explain it back
x: A teammate set maximumPoolSize to 64 on a pool built with new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() and says the pool "can scale to 64 threads under load". Explain why it can't, and what you would change.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Key terms
x: corePoolSize The number of threads the pool keeps, even when idle. maximumPoolSize The most threads the pool may run, reached only when the queue is full. Work queue The BlockingQueue where tasks wait for a free thread. Direct handoff A SynchronousQueue: no storage, a task passes straight to an idle thread or not at all. RejectedExecutionHandler The callback that decides what happens to a task the pool cannot take. Back-pressure Slowing the producer down when the consumer can't keep up, instead of piling up work. Keep-alive time How long an idle thread above core waits before it exits. In what order does ThreadPoolExecutor.execute try its options? Start a thread if below core; else queue; if the queue refuses, start a thread if below max; else reject. Why does newFixedThreadPool(8) never run more than 8 threads, whatever max you set? Its LinkedBlockingQueue is unbounded, so the queue never refuses a task, and the pool only grows past core when the queue refuses. What queue does newCachedThreadPool() use, and what is the risk? A SynchronousQueue (no capacity) with max Integer.MAX_VALUE, so every task that finds no idle thread gets a new thread. Threads grow without limit. What does CallerRunsPolicy do with an overflow task? The thread that called execute runs it, which slows that producer down. After shutdown it drops the task. A pool with DiscardPolicy drops a task sent with submit. What happens to future.get()? It blocks forever. The task never runs, so its Future never completes. What does keepAliveTime apply to by default? Only to threads above corePoolSize. Call allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) to let core threads retire too. When does a new extra thread pick up a queued task first? It doesn't. A thread started by rule 3 runs the task that triggered it, so later tasks can overtake queued ones.

h: Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection · Go deeper
x: Why does ThreadPoolExecutor queue before it grows? Its Javadoc lists three queuing strategies and is honest about each. A direct handoff (SynchronousQueue) "avoids lockups when handling sets of requests that might have internal dependencies", because a task never waits behind another task that it depends on, but it needs an unbounded max. An unbounded queue suits independent tasks and smooths bursts, but "admits the possibility of unbounded work queue growth". A bounded queue "helps prevent resource exhaustion" but "can be more difficult to tune": a large queue with a small pool keeps CPU use low and can give "artificially low throughput", while a small queue needs a larger pool. That first point comes back in lesson 9 of this track as pool-induced deadlock: tasks that wait for other tasks in the same bounded pool. Two more details for when you read pool code. First, core and max can be changed at runtime with setCorePoolSize and setMaximumPoolSize, which is how some frameworks resize pools from configuration without a restart. Second, ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor extends ThreadPoolExecutor but uses its own unbounded delay queue, so its max setting has no useful effect: it is a fixed pool of corePoolSize threads. Lesson 5 of this track covers it.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · CPU-bound work wants about one thread per core
x: Here is CpuBoundDemo on a 4-core machine. The job is 32 SHA-256 tasks with no I/O and no locks, run on pools of different sizes: availableProcessors() = 4 1 threads: 359 ms 2 threads: 171 ms 4 threads: 92 ms 8 threads: 96 ms 16 threads: 98 ms Doubling the threads halves the time until the thread count reaches the core count. After that, nothing improves. A core runs one thread at a time, so a fifth thread on four cores only gets CPU by taking it from one of the other four. You pay for context switches and colder caches and get no extra work done. So for CPU-bound work, size the pool to Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(). Goetz suggests one more than that, so the CPUs stay busy when a thread stalls on a page fault (a pause while the operating system fetches a page of memory). Either is fine. Fifty threads for hashing is not. Ask the JVM, not the hardware spec. On Linux the JVM's container support, on by default, reads the CPU limit from the container's cgroup (the kernel feature that enforces a pod's limits) when the JVM starts. So inside a container, availableProcessors() reports the CPU limit of the container, and a pod with a 2-CPU limit on a 64-core node sees 2. That is the number you want, because it's all the CPU the pod gets. You can override it with -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=N. In a payment service, CPU-bound work is the minority: signing and verifying, encrypting card data, parsing a large settlement file, scoring a fraud model in-process. Most request handling spends its time waiting, and that needs a different rule. Find where the curve goes flat Check how many cores your machine has. Predict the pool size after which CpuBoundDemo stops getting faster. Run it with the command below. CpuBoundDemo.java package workbench.executors.l03; import java.security.MessageDigest; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** The same CPU-bound job (32 hashing tasks) on pools of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 threads. */ public class CpuBoundDemo { // pure computation: SHA-256 over 16 MB, like signing a big settlement file. No I/O, no locks. static long hash(long seed) throws Exception { MessageDigest sha = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256"); byte[] block = new byte[16 * 1024]; block[0] = (byte) seed; for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sha.update(block); return sha.digest()[0]; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("availableProcessors() = " + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()); hash(1); // warm up the JIT once for (int threads : new int[] {1, 2, 4, 8, 16}) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long sum = 0; try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)) { List<Future<Long>> parts = new ArrayList<>(); for (int task = 0; task < 32; task++) { long seed = task; parts.add(pool.submit(() -> hash(seed))); } for (Future<Long> f : parts) sum += f.get(); } System.out.printf("%2d threads: %,5d ms (checksum %d)%n", threads, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, sum); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l03.CpuBoundDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l03/CpuBoundDemo.java CpuBoundDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l03 import java.security.MessageDigest import java.util.concurrent.Executors // pure computation: SHA-256 over 16 MB, like signing a big settlement file. No I/O, no locks. private fun hash(seed: Long): Long { val sha = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256") val block = ByteArray(16 * 1024) block[0] = seed.toByte() repeat(1_000) { sha.update(block) } return sha.digest()[0].toLong() } /** The same CPU-bound job (32 hashing tasks) on pools of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 threads. */ fun main() { println("availableProcessors() = " + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()) hash(1) // warm up the JIT once for (threads in listOf(1, 2, 4, 8, 16)) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val sum = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads).use { pool -> val parts = (0 until 32).map { task -> pool.submit<Long> { hash(task.toLong()) } } parts.sumOf { it.get() } } println("%2d threads: %,5d ms (checksum %d)".format(threads, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, sum)) } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l03.CpuBoundDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l03/CpuBoundDemo.kt The time roughly halves from 1 to 2 threads and from 2 to the core count, then stays flat or gets a little worse. If other programs are busy on the machine, or the laptop has slower efficiency cores, the curve flattens earlier: the pool only gets the CPU nobody else is using. Little's law is a supermarket. If 120 customers walk in every hour and each one spends half an hour inside, there are about 60 people in the shop at any moment. To serve more customers per hour without making anyone shop faster, you need room for more people inside, which for a pool means more threads. The checkouts are the downstream limit: add aisles all you like, and if there are four tills, people queue at the tills. The analogy breaks at the door. Shoppers who see a packed shop walk away. An unbounded queue in front of a pool never turns anyone away, so it fills up instead.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Work that waits: N × U × (1 + W/C)
x: Most backend tasks compute briefly and then wait: for the database, the card issuer, a Kafka acknowledgement. A waiting thread uses no CPU, so while it waits, another thread can use the core. That is why pools for I/O work need more threads than cores. Goetz's formula from Java Concurrency in Practice says how many: threads = cores x target CPU utilization x (1 + wait time / compute time) Take 8 cores, a target of 80 percent CPU, and an authorization that computes for 20 ms (parsing, validation, signing) and then waits 180 ms for the issuer: 8 x 0.8 x (1 + 180/20) = 64 threads. The ratio is what matters. A task that waits nine times longer than it computes leaves room for about ten such tasks per core. The formula is a starting point, and it can mislead you in three ways. First, you have to measure W and C. A timer around the downstream call gives you W, and the rest of the task's time is roughly C. JFR shows the same split. A guess like "it's mostly I/O" gives a number that looks precise and isn't. Second, it assumes waiting is free. Waiting on a remote call is. Waiting for a lock, or for a connection that every other thread also needs, is not: more threads just make a longer line for the same lock. Third, it sizes for CPU and knows nothing else. It can't tell that the issuer accepts only 50 concurrent connections from you, or that your database pool has 20. Those limits often decide the answer, and the last section of this lesson is about them. Size two pools by hand A refund service runs on 4 cores, targets 50 percent CPU, and each refund computes for 5 ms and waits 95 ms on the ledger. Work out the pool size. A report job on the same box computes for 40 ms and waits 10 ms per row. Work out its pool size too, then check both with PoolSizing.ioBound once you've done the lab. Refunds: 4 x 0.5 x (1 + 95/5) = 40 threads. Reports: 4 x 0.5 x (1 + 10/40) = 2.5, rounded up to 3. The report job is mostly CPU, so it gets about as many threads as the cores you're willing to give it. Write down the three numbers for your busiest path before you touch a pool setting: peak arrivals per second, average time per request, and the smallest limit it passes through. For card authorizations that is usually the issuer connection limit or the database pool, not CPU. Check what your Quarkus worker pool is set to (quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads) and what your datasource allows, and make sure the second is not far smaller than the first, or the extra worker threads only queue for connections. Temporal workers have a maximum number of concurrent activity executions. That is a pool size by another name, and the same arithmetic applies: activities per second times average duration. Put issuer calls behind their own bulkhead, so a slow issuer costs you authorizations and nothing else.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Little's law: in flight = arrival rate × time in system
x: Goetz's formula starts from CPUs. Little's law starts from traffic. It holds for any stable system, a supermarket or a thread pool: L = λ x W L is the average number of requests inside, λ (lambda) is the arrival rate and W is the average time each request spends inside. Your payment API gets 400 authorizations a second at peak, and each takes 250 ms end to end, so 400 x 0.25 = 100 requests are in flight on average. With one thread per request, that is 100 busy threads. If you have fewer, the extra requests wait somewhere. Turn it around to see what a pool can do. Solve for λ: 50 threads at 250 ms each finish at most 50 / 0.25 = 200 requests a second. If 400 arrive, 200 a second pile up in the queue. The waiting adds to W, so the queue grows without limit until memory or patience runs out. That is the unbounded-queue story from lesson 2 of this track, with numbers. LittlesLawDemo checks the law with 200 requests that each wait 50 ms: 5 threads: 97 req/s measured, 100 predicted by threads / W 10 threads: 191 req/s measured, 200 predicted by threads / W 20 threads: 376 req/s measured, 400 predicted by threads / W When the work is waiting, throughput is threads divided by latency. Faster CPUs would not help. More threads would, for as long as threads are the scarce thing. That argument, made in JEP 444 (the JDK Enhancement Proposal for virtual threads), is why virtual threads exist, and the "Virtual threads" track picks it up. Check Little's law Read LittlesLawDemo. Predict the throughput for 40 threads before you run it. Run it with the command below and compare each row with its prediction. LittlesLawDemo.java package workbench.executors.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; /** * 200 requests that each wait 50 ms on a downstream call, on pools of 5, 10, 20 and 40 threads. * Little's law predicts throughput = threads / 0.05 s. Pass "db" to make every request also hold * one of only 10 database connections while it waits. */ public class LittlesLawDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean db = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("db"); Semaphore connections = new Semaphore(10); // a 10-connection pool, when "db" is on int requests = 200; double latencySeconds = 0.050; for (int threads : new int[] {5, 10, 20, 40}) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads)) { for (int i = 0; i < requests; i++) { pool.execute(() -> { try { if (db) connections.acquire(); try { Thread.sleep(50); // the downstream call } finally { if (db) connections.release(); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); } } double seconds = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9; System.out.printf("%2d threads: %4.0f req/s measured, %4.0f predicted by threads / W%n", threads, requests / seconds, threads / latencySeconds); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l03.LittlesLawDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l03/LittlesLawDemo.java LittlesLawDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l03 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore /** * 200 requests that each wait 50 ms on a downstream call, on pools of 5, 10, 20 and 40 threads. * Little's law predicts throughput = threads / 0.05 s. Pass "db" to make every request also hold * one of only 10 database connections while it waits. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val db = args.firstOrNull() == "db" val connections = Semaphore(10) // a 10-connection pool, when "db" is on val requests = 200 val latencySeconds = 0.050 for (threads in listOf(5, 10, 20, 40)) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads).use { pool -> repeat(requests) { pool.execute { try { if (db) connections.acquire() try { Thread.sleep(50) // the downstream call } finally { if (db) connections.release() } } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } } } val seconds = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e9 println("%2d threads: %4.0f req/s measured, %4.0f predicted by threads / W".format( threads, requests / seconds, threads / latencySeconds)) } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l03.LittlesLawDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l03/LittlesLawDemo.kt 5, 10 and 20 threads land within a few percent of 100, 200 and 400 requests a second. 40 threads falls short of 800 (about 630 here), because 200 requests are only five rounds for 40 threads and the pool's start-up time is now a large part of the run. Little's law: if 400 requests arrive each second and each stays 250 ms, about 100 are inside at any moment.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · The downstream decides: connection pools and bulkheads
x: Little's law counts threads, but a request in flight holds other things too. Say every authorization writes to the ledger and holds one of your 20 database connections for 10 ms. The database path then tops out at 20 / 0.01 = 2,000 writes a second, whatever your thread count. Threads beyond that line up for a connection instead of a CPU. Run the demo with db and you see it: with only 10 connections, 20 and 40 threads are no faster than 10. So size from the scarcest resource backwards: the database pool, the issuer's contract (say 50 concurrent connections per merchant client), a fraud API's rate limit. HikariCP, a widely used JDBC connection pool, makes the same point for databases on its wiki page about pool sizing. It starts from a small formula, connections = (cores x 2) + effective spindle count, and tells you to load-test from there, because more connections than the database can serve make every query slower. Limits also need isolation. Say authorizations, refunds and balance lookups share one pool of 64 threads, and the issuer slows from 120 ms to 3 s. Little's law fills all 64 threads with stuck issuer calls within seconds. Balance lookups, which never touch the issuer, now time out too. A bulkhead stops that. It is a separate limit per dependency, named after the walls that keep one flooded compartment from sinking a ship. It can be a separate pool per downstream, or a Semaphore around the call, which is what you build in the lab. The issuer gets 50 permits. When they are gone, new issuer calls fail fast, and the rest of the service keeps its threads. Hit the connection ceiling Predict the four rows of LittlesLawDemo when every request also needs one of 10 connections. Run the demo again with -Pargs=db. 5 threads still give about 100 requests a second and 10 threads about 200. 20 and 40 threads also stay near 200: ten connections at 50 ms each allow 10 / 0.05 = 200 a second, and the extra threads just wait in connections.acquire(). About Pool Sizing (HikariCP wiki) read Raising the thread count when the bottleneck is downstream. Authorizations slow down, someone doubles the pool from 64 to 128 threads, and latency gets worse: the database pool still has 20 connections, so 108 threads now queue for them, each holding a request in memory. It happens because thread count is the knob that's easy to turn. Look at the scarce resource first (Hikari's pending-connections metric, the issuer's error rate), size the pool to that limit, and put a bulkhead in front of the slow dependency.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Java and Kotlin
x: A bulkhead in Java and with coroutines Bulkhead.java (solution, core of call) public <T> T call(Callable<T> work) throws Exception { // a waiting caller blocks its platform thread here if (!permits.tryAcquire(maxWait.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { throw new BulkheadFullException("bulkhead '" + name + "' is full"); } try { return work.call(); } finally { permits.release(); } } Bulkhead.kt (kotlinx.coroutines) import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withPermit class Bulkhead(private val name: String, maxConcurrent: Int) { private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent) // fail fast, like Duration.ZERO in the Java version suspend fun <T> tryCall(work: suspend () -> T): T { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw BulkheadFullException("bulkhead '$name' is full") try { return work() } finally { permits.release() } } // wait for a permit: the coroutine suspends and holds no thread while it waits suspend fun <T> call(work: suspend () -> T): T = permits.withPermit { work() } } Both protect the issuer the same way: at most N calls in flight. The difference is what waiting costs. The Java version blocks a platform thread in tryAcquire, so a thousand waiting callers are a thousand parked threads, which is why it needs a short maxWait. The coroutine Semaphore suspends, so a thousand waiting callers are a thousand small objects. kotlinx's Semaphore has no timed acquire; wrap the waiting call in withTimeout if you need a deadline.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Worked example
x: Size the authorization pool from measurements Measure first. Under a load test at the expected peak, the authorization path shows these numbers. Before reading on, estimate the pool size. peak arrivals 400 / s CPU per request 10 ms (parse, validate, sign) wait per request 140 ms (issuer call) cores 8 issuer contract 50 concurrent connections Little's law gives the concurrency the traffic needs: L = 400 x (0.010 + 0.140) = 400 x 0.15 = 60 requests in flight, so 60 threads if each request holds a thread for its whole life. Check the CPU. 400 requests x 10 ms = 4 CPU-seconds every second, so 4 of the 8 cores are busy: 50 percent. Goetz's formula at that utilization agrees: 8 x 0.5 x (1 + 140/10) = 60. The box can carry the load. Now the downstream. The issuer allows 50 concurrent connections, and each call holds one for 140 ms, so the issuer path tops out at 50 / 0.14 = 357 authorizations a second. That is below the 400 peak. A pool of 60 would leave 10 threads queued on the issuer's connections. So the real answer is: put issuer calls behind a bulkhead of 50, size the pool near 60 so the non-issuer work keeps moving, and treat 357 a second as the service's real capacity. Getting to 400 is now a business question (a bigger contract with the issuer, or a second merchant client), not a pool setting. Bulkhead issuer = new Bulkhead("issuer", 50, Duration.ofMillis(100)); ExecutorService auth = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(60); val issuer = Bulkhead("issuer", 50, Duration.ofMillis(100)) val auth = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(60)

It throws InterruptedException, which call may simply let through. Don't wrap the work's exception. The test checks it gets the very same IOException back. All nine tests in SizingTest pass. h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Quiz
x: A fraud-scoring job is pure CPU and runs on a pod with an 8-CPU limit. Someone raises its pool from 8 to 32 threads. What happens to throughput? It roughly quadruples About the same, or a little worse from context switching It doubles It deadlocks Eight CPUs can run eight threads at a time. The other 24 threads only take turns on the same CPUs. For work that waits, more threads help; for pure computation they don't. A refunds endpoint receives 300 requests a second, and each takes 400 ms. How many requests are in flight on average? 75 750 120 40 L = λ x W = 300 x 0.4 = 120. Dividing 300 by 4, or multiplying by 2.5, are the tempting slips. Write the units down: requests per second times seconds gives requests. A service runs on 4 cores, aims for full CPU use, and each task computes for 10 ms and then waits 90 ms. What does Goetz's formula give? 40 4 36 400 4 x 1.0 x (1 + 90/10) = 4 x 10 = 40. The tempting 36 comes from using W/C alone instead of 1 + W/C; the 1 accounts for the time each task spends on the CPU. Authorizations, refunds and balance lookups share one pool of 64 threads. When the card issuer slows down, balance lookups, which never call the issuer, start timing out. What is the best fix? Double the pool to 128 threads Switch the pool to an unbounded queue Use CallerRunsPolicy Put issuer calls behind their own limit (a bulkhead), so they can't use every thread Slow issuer calls fill every shared thread, so unrelated work starves. A bulkhead caps how many threads issuer calls may hold. Doubling the pool only delays the problem: Little's law fills 128 threads as surely as 64 when each call takes 3 s. From "Inside ThreadPoolExecutor: core, max, queue, rejection": a pool is new ThreadPoolExecutor(20, 200, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()). Traffic is 400 requests a second at 250 ms each. What happens? It grows to 200 threads, which is plenty It stays at 20 threads, finishes at most 80 a second, and the queue grows without limit It grows to exactly the 100 threads Little's law asks for It rejects the excess requests With an unbounded queue the pool never grows past core, so 20 threads at 250 ms finish 20 / 0.25 = 80 a second. Little's law needs 100 in flight. The other 320 a second pile up in the queue, which never refuses, so nothing is ever rejected either.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Explain it back
x: Your manager asks why you can't just set every pool to 500 threads "to be safe". Explain, using the core count, Little's law and the database pool.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Key terms
x: CPU-bound Work limited by computation. More threads than cores don't help. I/O-bound Work that mostly waits on the network or disk, so one core can serve many such tasks. Little's law Requests in flight equal arrival rate times time spent in the system. Throughput Work finished per unit of time, such as requests per second. Latency How long one request takes from arrival to completion. Bulkhead A per-dependency limit that keeps one slow dependency from using all the threads. Wait/compute ratio How long a task waits divided by how long it computes. It decides how many threads one core can feed. How many threads for a pool doing pure CPU work? About one per core: Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() (Goetz suggests one more). Goetz's pool-size formula for tasks that wait? threads = cores x target utilization x (1 + wait time / compute time). State Little's law. L = λ x W: requests in flight = arrival rate x average time in the system. 50 threads, each request holds a thread for 250 ms. Maximum throughput? 50 / 0.25 = 200 requests per second. Why don't threads beyond the database pool size speed up database-bound requests? Each request needs a connection. The extra threads just wait in line for one. What is a bulkhead? A separate concurrency limit per dependency (its own pool or a Semaphore), so one slow dependency can't take every thread. What does availableProcessors() return in a pod with a 2-CPU limit? The JVM reads the container's CPU limit, not the host's core count.

h: Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law · Go deeper
x: Why aim for 80 percent CPU and not 100? Queueing theory has a short answer. In the simplest model of a single server with random arrivals (M/M/1), the average time in the system is W = S / (1 - ρ), where S is the service time and ρ is utilization. At 50 percent busy, a request spends 2 x S in the system. At 80 percent, 5 x S. At 90 percent, 10 x S. At 99 percent, 100 x S. Real systems are not M/M/1, but the shape holds: latency grows slowly at first and then very fast as you approach full use. Headroom is what keeps the 99th percentile sane during a burst. Little's law has a subtle side that this lesson glossed over. The W in L = λ x W is the measured time in the system, including time spent queuing. If you add threads and requests now queue for a database connection instead of for a thread, W grows and throughput doesn't. That is exactly the debate on the loom-dev list before JEP 444 was finalized: more threads raise the ceiling only while threads are what requests wait for. Once the bottleneck moves downstream, the downstream sets λ. The last tool is measurement. Time the queue wait and the run time of each task separately (lesson 9 of this track does this with beforeExecute and afterExecute). If queue wait dominates, the pool is too small for its traffic. If run time grew, look downstream.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Callable returns a value, and Future is the claim ticket
x: Runnable.run() returns nothing and can't throw checked exceptions. Callable<V>.call() returns a V and may throw any Exception, which makes it the natural shape for "call the issuer and give me the answer". Hand one to submit and you get a Future<V> back at once, a claim ticket for a result that doesn't exist yet: Java Future<String> auth = pool.submit(() -> issuer.authorize(payment)); // returns at once String decision = auth.get(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // waits up to 200 ms Kotlin val auth: Future<String> = pool.submit<String> { issuer.authorize(payment) } // returns at once val decision = auth.get(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // waits up to 200 ms get() blocks until the task finishes. Then it returns the value, or throws ExecutionException with the task's exception as the cause, or CancellationException if the task was cancelled. It throws InterruptedException if your own thread is interrupted while it waits. A successful get() also gives you visibility: everything the task wrote before it finished is visible to the thread that got the result. Use get(timeout, unit) in request paths. Plain get() waits forever, and forever is how one slow dependency turns into a pile of hung request threads. You can also submit a plain Runnable. The Future<?> you get back returns null from get(), which is still useful: it tells you when the task finished and whether it threw. The part people miss is that a timeout ends your wait, not the task. TimeoutDemo shows it: 16 ms pool-1-thread-1 calling the issuer 216 ms main get timed out after 200 ms 648 ms pool-1-thread-1 issuer answered: APPROVED (and the charge went through) The caller gave up at 200 ms and probably told the customer the payment failed. The task kept going, and the issuer approved the charge 430 ms later. So when you stop waiting, decide what happens to the work: cancel it, or make sure its result still gets recorded somewhere a retry can find it. Give up on a slow issuer Run TimeoutDemo (either language). Note the time on the issuer answered line. Run it again with -Pargs=cancel, which calls cancel(true) after the timeout. Predict: does the issuer still answer? With cancel, the task prints "interrupted: giving up on the issuer" at about 215 ms, cancel(true) returns true, and the pool closes at once. Future (Java SE 25 API) docs A Future is the ticket from a dry cleaner. You can come back and wait at the counter (get), wait only until your lunch break ends (get with a timeout), or ask the shop how your shirt is doing without waiting (state). Cancelling is phoning the shop to say "don't bother". If they haven't started, the shirt never gets cleaned. If it is already in the machine, the clerk may or may not hear the phone, and either way your ticket now says "cancelled". The analogy breaks at the end: a real shop tells you whether the shirt got cleaned. A cancelled Future never tells you whether the work happened.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · cancel(true) sends an interrupt, nothing more
x: Future.cancel(boolean mayInterruptIfRunning) has two modes. cancel(false) stops a task that hasn't started, so it will never run, and leaves a running task alone. cancel(true) does the same and, if the task is running, calls interrupt() on the thread running it. That is all it does. Java has no safe way to kill a thread: Thread.stop was deprecated for decades, has thrown UnsupportedOperationException since JDK 20, and was removed in JDK 26. Cancellation is cooperative. An interrupt sets a flag on the thread. If the thread is blocked in a method that responds to interrupts (Thread.sleep, Object.wait, BlockingQueue.take, Future.get and others), that method wakes up and throws InterruptedException. Code that never blocks and never checks the flag doesn't notice anything. CancelDemo cancels three tasks 100 ms after they start: after cancel: isCancelled=true/true/true isDone=true/true/true sleeper: InterruptedException, stopping checker: saw the flag after 46 slices, stopping ignorer: finished all 400 slices anyway Read the first line again. All three futures report cancelled and done straight away. A Future changes state the moment you call cancel. It doesn't wait for the task to stop. The ignorer then ran to the end. If its work was posting to a ledger, the post happened, and the Future still says cancelled. Two rules follow. A long CPU loop should check Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() every so often, as the checker does. And a cancelled Future only tells you that nobody will get a result from it. It does not tell you the side effects didn't happen. cancel(false) has its own use. During a graceful shutdown you may want running settlements to finish but queued ones never to start: cancel the queued futures with false and let awaitTermination wait for the rest. cancel returns false if the task had already finished or was already cancelled, which tells you the cancel came too late. Cancel three kinds of task Run CancelDemo and match each line of output to one of the three tasks. Make the ignorer cooperate: add the same isInterrupted() check the checker has at the top of its loop. Predict how long the demo takes now, then run it. i < 2_000_000; i++) x = x * 31 + i; return x; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { Future<?> sleeper = pool.submit(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(5_000); System.out.println("sleeper: woke up normally"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println("sleeper: InterruptedException, stopping"); } }); Future<?> checker = pool.submit(() -> { long x = 0; for (int s = 0; s < 400; s++) { if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { System.out.println("checker: saw the flag after " + s + " slices, stopping"); return; } x = slice(x); } System.out.println("checker: finished all slices " + (x & 1)); }); Future<?> ignorer = pool.submit(() -> { long x = 0; for (int s = 0; s < 400; s++) x = slice(x); // never looks at the flag System.out.println("ignorer: finished all 400 slices anyway " + (x & 1)); }); Thread.sleep(100); for (Future<?> f : new Future<?>[] {sleeper, checker, ignorer}) f.cancel(true); System.out.printf("after cancel: isCancelled=%b/%b/%b isDone=%b/%b/%b%n", sleeper.isCancelled(), checker.isCancelled(), ignorer.isCancelled(), sleeper.isDone(), checker.isDone(), ignorer.isDone()); } // close() waits: the ignorer is still burning CPU System.out.println("pool closed"); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l04.CancelDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l04/CancelDemo.java CancelDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l04 import java.util.concurrent.Executors // about a second of CPU work, in slices private fun slice(start: Long): Long { var x = start for (i in 0 until 2_000_000) x = x * 31 + i return x } /** cancel(true) on three tasks: one that sleeps, one that checks the flag, one that never looks. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3).use { pool -> val sleeper = pool.submit { try { Thread.sleep(5_000) println("sleeper: woke up normally") } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println("sleeper: InterruptedException, stopping") } } val checker = pool.submit { var x = 0L for (s in 0 until 400) { if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted) { println("checker: saw the flag after $s slices, stopping") return@submit } x = slice(x) } println("checker: finished all slices ${x and 1}") } val ignorer = pool.submit { var x = 0L repeat(400) { x = slice(x) } // never looks at the flag println("ignorer: finished all 400 slices anyway ${x and 1}") } Thread.sleep(100) listOf(sleeper, checker, ignorer).forEach { it.cancel(true) } println("after cancel: isCancelled=%b/%b/%b isDone=%b/%b/%b".format( sleeper.isCancelled, checker.isCancelled, ignorer.isCancelled, sleeper.isDone, checker.isDone, ignorer.isDone)) } // close() waits: the ignorer is still burning CPU println("pool closed") } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l04.CancelDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l04/CancelDemo.kt First run: the sleeper and the checker stop within milliseconds, but the ignorer burns about a second of CPU and close() waits for it, so "pool closed" comes last. After your change the ignorer stops after a few dozen slices too, and the demo finishes in well under a second after the cancel. Every call your payment service makes to an issuer, a fraud scorer or a ledger API should have a deadline, and a timeout should lead somewhere on purpose. For an authorization, "we stopped waiting" is not "declined": return a pending status, keep the idempotency key, and let a reconciler ask the issuer what happened. In a Kafka consumer, a stuck downstream call that ignores interrupts blocks the partition and, through max.poll.interval.ms, eventually costs you the partition. In the Temporal Java SDK, an activity learns it was cancelled when it heartbeats, so an activity stuck in one long blocking call with no timeout of its own never finds out. And grep for catch (InterruptedException e) in your services: every one should rethrow or restore the flag.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · The interruption protocol: rethrow or restore
x: When a blocking method throws InterruptedException, it clears the thread's interrupt flag first. That one detail is behind most interrupt bugs. If you catch the exception and carry on, the request to stop is gone, and no code further up can see it. Here is how that bites. A helper sleeps between polls and swallows the exception, because "there's nothing useful to do here". The loop around it checks isInterrupted() correctly and still never stops, because the helper cleared the flag before the loop could look at it. That is the bug in the lab's StatementPoller, and neither shutdownNow() nor cancel(true) can stop it. The Thread Javadoc in JDK 26 states the rule in a new section on interruption: code that catches InterruptedException should rethrow it, or restore the interrupted status with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() before it continues or throws something else. So there are two correct moves: Java // 1. propagate: declare it and let it go up void settle(Batch b) throws InterruptedException { ledgerQueue.put(b); } // 2. you can't propagate (Runnable.run can't throw it): restore the flag public void run() { try { ledgerQueue.put(batch); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the request visible return; // and stop } } Kotlin // 1. propagate: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so simply don't catch it fun settle(b: Batch) { ledgerQueue.put(b) } // 2. if you do catch it: restore the flag override fun run() { try { ledgerQueue.put(batch) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() // keep the request visible return // and stop } } Wrapping is fine if you restore the flag first: catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new LedgerUnavailableException(e); }. Logging it and moving on is not. One more trap: whether a blocked network read notices an interrupt depends on the API. NIO channels (the java.nio.channels API) do: the JDK closes the channel and the read fails. A classic java.net.Socket stream read on a platform thread does not. Give every HTTP and database client its own timeout, and treat the interrupt as a second line of defence. Check yourself: a task catches InterruptedException from Thread.sleep, logs it, and loops back to sleep again. Does the second sleep throw at once? No. The flag was cleared when the first exception was thrown, so the second sleep waits its full time. Add Thread.currentThread().interrupt() to the catch and the second sleep throws immediately, because sleep checks the flag before it starts to wait.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Future.state(), invokeAll and invokeAny
x: Before JDK 19, asking a Future how it ended meant calling get() inside a try with three catch blocks. JDK 19 added state(), which never blocks, and two accessors for futures you already know are done: Java switch (f.state()) { case RUNNING -> log.info("still waiting on the issuer"); case SUCCESS -> record(f.resultNow()); // the value, no checked exceptions case FAILED -> log.warn("issuer failed", f.exceptionNow()); // the task's own exception, unwrapped case CANCELLED -> log.info("cancelled"); } Kotlin when (f.state()) { Future.State.RUNNING -> log.info("still waiting on the issuer") Future.State.SUCCESS -> record(f.resultNow()) // the value, no checked exceptions Future.State.FAILED -> log.warn("issuer failed", f.exceptionNow()) // the task's own exception, unwrapped Future.State.CANCELLED -> log.info("cancelled") } resultNow() throws IllegalStateException if the task isn't done or didn't succeed. exceptionNow() throws it if the task didn't fail, including when it was cancelled. Call them after checking state(), or on futures you know are finished. ExecutorService also has two bulk methods. invokeAll(tasks) runs every task and returns their futures once all are done. With a timeout, it cancels whatever hasn't finished by the deadline, so every future it returns is done. invokeAny(tasks) returns the result of the first task that succeeds, cancels the rest, and throws ExecutionException only if every task fails. That fits "ask three FX-rate providers and take the first good answer". In InvokeAnyDemo the fastest provider fails after 100 ms. invokeAny ignores that failure, returns the answer from the provider that succeeds at 200 ms, and interrupts the slowest. invokeAll with a 250 ms deadline returns one future of each kind: failed, succeeded and cancelled. Both bulk methods block the calling thread until they return, so call them from a thread that may wait, never from a task running on the same bounded pool. A pool of 3 whose tasks each call invokeAll with 3 subtasks on that pool can end up with every thread waiting for subtasks that have no thread to run on. Lesson 9 of this track calls that pool-induced deadlock. First answer wins Read the three providers in InvokeAnyDemo: alpha takes 300 ms, beta fails at 100 ms, gamma takes 200 ms. Predict what invokeAny returns and which provider gets interrupted. Predict the three states invokeAll reports with its 250 ms deadline, then run the demo. InvokeAnyDemo.java package workbench.executors.l04; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Three FX-rate providers with different speeds: invokeAny takes the first, invokeAll waits with a deadline. */ public class InvokeAnyDemo { static Callable<String> provider(String name, long millis, boolean fails) { return () -> { try { Thread.sleep(millis); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(" " + name + ": interrupted, cancelled"); throw e; } if (fails) throw new IllegalStateException(name + " is down"); return name + " EUR/USD 1.0842"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { List<Callable<String>> providers = List.of( provider("alpha", 300, false), provider("beta", 100, true), // fastest, but fails provider("gamma", 200, false)); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { System.out.println("invokeAny -> " + pool.invokeAny(providers)); Thread.sleep(50); System.out.println("invokeAll with a 250 ms deadline:"); List<Future<String>> all = pool.invokeAll(providers, 250, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); for (Future<String> f : all) { System.out.println(" " + f.state() + switch (f.state()) { case SUCCESS -> ": " + f.resultNow(); case FAILED -> ": " + f.exceptionNow().getMessage(); default -> ""; }); } } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l04.InvokeAnyDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l04/InvokeAnyDemo.java InvokeAnyDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l04 import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Future import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit private fun provider(name: String, millis: Long, fails: Boolean) = Callable { try { Thread.sleep(millis) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { println(" $name: interrupted, cancelled") throw e } if (fails) throw IllegalStateException("$name is down") "$name EUR/USD 1.0842" } /** Three FX-rate providers with different speeds: invokeAny takes the first, invokeAll waits with a deadline. */ fun main() { val providers = listOf( provider("alpha", 300, false), provider("beta", 100, true), // fastest, but fails provider("gamma", 200, false), ) Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3).use { pool -> println("invokeAny -> " + pool.invokeAny(providers)) Thread.sleep(50) println("invokeAll with a 250 ms deadline:") val all = pool.invokeAll(providers, 250, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) for (f in all) { val detail = when (f.state()) { Future.State.SUCCESS -> ": " + f.resultNow() Future.State.FAILED -> ": " + f.exceptionNow().message else -> "" } println(" ${f.state()}$detail") } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l04.InvokeAnyDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l04/InvokeAnyDemo.kt invokeAny returns gamma's rate: beta finished first but failed, and a failure doesn't count. Alpha prints "interrupted, cancelled". With the 250 ms deadline, invokeAll reports alpha CANCELLED (interrupted at the deadline), beta FAILED with "beta is down" and gamma SUCCESS. A Future starts RUNNING and ends in one of three states. state() tells you which without blocking. ExecutorService (Java SE 25 API): invokeAll and invokeAny docs Catching InterruptedException and carrying on, usually in a helper like sleepQuietly() or in a retry loop that "just tries again". It happens because the compiler forces a catch in Java, and the quickest way to make it compile is an empty block. The flag is cleared when the exception is thrown, so the stop request vanishes and shutdownNow() or cancel(true) silently stop working. Fix: propagate it, or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() in the catch and then stop or throw.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Java and Kotlin
x: Cancelling work: Future and interrupts vs coroutine cancellation CancelOne.java Future<String> f = pool.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(5_000); // wakes with InterruptedException on cancel(true) return "done"; }); Thread.sleep(100); f.cancel(true); // sends an interrupt to the worker thread // f.isCancelled() is true at once, whatever the task does next CancelOne.kt (kotlinx.coroutines) val job = scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) { delay(5_000) // suspends; resumes with CancellationException on cancel println("done") } delay(100) job.cancel() // no interrupt: delay() notices the cancellation itself // a blocking call ignores job.cancel() unless you wrap it: // runInterruptible { Thread.sleep(5_000) } Both models are cooperative, and both need the task to listen. Java delivers the request as a thread interrupt, which blocking methods and isInterrupted() checks pick up. Coroutines deliver it as a CancellationException at suspension points such as delay, await and withContext, with no interrupt at all, so a blocking Java call inside a coroutine doesn't notice unless you wrap it in runInterruptible. The interrupt rules from this lesson still apply to Kotlin code that runs blocking work on an executor. Watch runCatching there: it catches InterruptedException like any other exception, which makes it an easy way to swallow a stop request.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Worked example
x: Give up on a slow issuer without lying to the customer An authorization handler submits the issuer call to a pool and waits for it. Under normal load this works. What happens when the issuer starts taking 30 seconds? Future<String> auth = pool.submit(() -> issuer.authorize(payment)); return auth.get(); // waits as long as the issuer does val auth = pool.submit<String> { issuer.authorize(payment) } return auth.get() // waits as long as the issuer does Every request thread ends up parked in get(). Little's law from lesson 3 of this track does the rest: at 400 requests a second and 30 s each, you would need 12,000 threads. The service stops answering anything. Bound the wait, and cancel the work you stopped waiting for. Future<String> auth = pool.submit(() -> issuer.authorize(payment)); try { return auth.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // 1. bounded wait } catch (TimeoutException e) { auth.cancel(true); // 2. interrupt the issuer call return "PENDING"; // 3. don't claim it was declined } val auth = pool.submit<String> { issuer.authorize(payment) } return try { auth.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 1. bounded wait } catch (e: TimeoutException) { auth.cancel(true) // 2. interrupt the issuer call "PENDING" // 3. don't claim it was declined } Why PENDING and not DECLINED? The interrupt may arrive after the request already reached the issuer, and a classic socket read may not even notice it. The charge can still happen. Saying "declined" invites the customer to pay again, and then you have a double charge. Make the outcome findable. Send an idempotency key with the request, and on timeout hand the key to a reconciler that asks the issuer later what happened to it. A retry with the same key can't charge twice. String key = payment.idempotencyKey(); Future<String> auth = pool.submit(() -> issuer.authorize(payment, key)); try { return auth.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { auth.cancel(true); reconciler.checkLater(key); // "what happened to key X?" return "PENDING"; } val key = payment.idempotencyKey() val auth = pool.submit<String> { issuer.authorize(payment, key) } return try { auth.get(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { auth.cancel(true) reconciler.checkLater(key) // "what happened to key X?" "PENDING" }

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Quiz
x: A task calls a ledger API that posts a debit. The caller's get(500, MILLISECONDS) throws TimeoutException and the caller does nothing else. What happens to the debit? It is cancelled automatically when get() times out It may well still be posted, because the task keeps running It is rolled back by the executor The task receives the TimeoutException and stops The timeout is only about the caller's wait. The task has no idea anyone gave up, so it carries on and posts the debit. Only cancel(true) sends it a signal, and even that is just an interrupt. A worker runs while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { work(); try { Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("interrupted"); } }. The pool calls shutdownNow() while the worker sleeps. What happens? The worker stops at the next loop check The worker throws and the pool replaces it The worker logs a warning and keeps looping, because the exception cleared the flag shutdownNow() waits until the worker finishes sleep clears the interrupt flag when it throws. The catch only logs, so the while check sees a clear flag and loops forever. Restore the flag in the catch, or return from it. You call cancel(true) on a task that is in a long CPU loop and never checks the interrupt flag. What do you see? isCancelled() is true at once, and the loop runs to the end anyway isCancelled() stays false until the loop ends The thread is stopped immediately cancel returns false because the task is running The Future moves to CANCELLED as soon as cancel succeeds, and cancel returns true for a running task. The interrupt sets a flag the loop never reads, so the work continues. Java can't stop a thread from outside. You ask three FX-rate providers for EUR/USD and want the first successful answer, ignoring providers that fail, with the slower ones cancelled. Which tool fits? Submit each one and call get() on them in order invokeAll, then pick the first SUCCESS A single-thread executor, so they run one at a time invokeAny invokeAny returns the first task that completes successfully and cancels the rest. invokeAll waits for every provider, so you pay for the slowest. Calling get() in order waits for the first provider even if the third is faster. From "A thread's life: start, join, sleep, interrupt": thread t is in Thread.sleep(10_000). Another thread calls t.interrupt(). Inside t's catch block, what does Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() return? true, because the thread was just interrupted false, because throwing InterruptedException cleared the flag It throws IllegalThreadStateException true until sleep's 10 seconds are up Blocking methods clear the interrupt flag when they throw InterruptedException. That's why a catch block that neither rethrows nor calls Thread.currentThread().interrupt() loses the stop request.
