h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Key terms
x: Callable A task that returns a value and may throw a checked exception. Future A handle to a task's result: wait for it, check its state, or cancel it. Interrupt A request to a thread to stop what it is doing. It sets a flag and wakes blocking calls. Interrupt flag The per-thread boolean that interrupt() sets and InterruptedException clears. Cooperative cancellation Cancellation that works only if the task checks for it and stops itself. invokeAny Run several tasks and return the first successful result, cancelling the rest. What does cancel(true) do to a task that is already running? It calls interrupt() on the task's thread. The task stops only if it responds to the interrupt. You call cancel(true) and the task ignores the interrupt. What does isCancelled() return? true, immediately, even though the task keeps running to the end. Does future.get(timeout) stop the task when it throws TimeoutException? No. It only ends your wait. Call cancel(true) if the work should stop. What happens to the interrupt flag when sleep throws InterruptedException? It is cleared. Rethrow the exception or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(). What does invokeAny(tasks) return? The result of the first task that succeeds. It cancels the others, and throws ExecutionException only if all fail. What does resultNow() do on a future that failed? Throws IllegalStateException. Check state() first, or use exceptionNow() for FAILED.

h: Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption · Go deeper
x: Two methods read the interrupt flag and they are easy to mix up. Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() reads it and leaves it alone. The static Thread.interrupted() reads it and clears it. Use the second only when you are about to handle the interrupt yourself, for example to throw InterruptedException from your own blocking method: Java if (Thread.interrupted()) throw new InterruptedException(); // clear, then report by throwing Kotlin if (Thread.interrupted()) throw InterruptedException() // clear, then report by throwing How does cancel(true) find the thread? FutureTask remembers the thread that is running it. cancel(true) moves the task to a cancelled state and then calls interrupt() on that thread. Because the flag belongs to the thread and not to the task, a pool has to make sure an interrupt meant for one task doesn't hit the next one on the same worker. ThreadPoolExecutor does that: before each task, its worker clears any leftover interrupt, unless the pool itself is stopping after shutdownNow(). Virtual threads, in the "Virtual threads" track, use the same interrupt mechanism. A virtual thread blocked in sleep or a BlockingQueue responds exactly as described here, so everything in this lesson carries over.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Three ways to schedule work, and which jobs belong elsewhere
x: The older scheduler in the JDK, java.util.Timer, has a trap. It runs every task on one thread, and if one task throws, that thread dies and the whole Timer is cancelled: every other task on it stops too, and the next schedule call throws IllegalStateException. So skip Timer. JDK 5 replaced it with the ScheduledExecutorService interface and its implementation, ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor. A ScheduledExecutorService runs tasks later, or over and over. You get one from Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(n) or newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(), and three of its methods do nearly all the work: Java ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2); scheduler.schedule(this::expireHold, 15, TimeUnit.MINUTES); // once, after a delay scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::sendHeartbeat, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // on a timetable scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshFxRate, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // with a gap between runs Kotlin val scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2) scheduler.schedule(this::expireHold, 15, TimeUnit.MINUTES) // once, after a delay scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(this::sendHeartbeat, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // on a timetable scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshFxRate, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // with a gap between runs Each call returns a ScheduledFuture, a Future that also knows its remaining delay. Cancel it to stop a periodic task. For a periodic task, get() never returns normally: it waits until the task is cancelled or fails. The scheduler is a pool like any other, so shut it down, or its threads keep the JVM alive. Some schedules don't belong in the JVM at all. An in-process scheduler forgets everything when the pod restarts, and with three replicas every job runs three times. The settlement export each night, a monthly fee run, anything with business meaning: put those in a cron job, a scheduler with a database such as Quartz, or a Temporal schedule. The JVM scheduler is for in-process housekeeping, like refreshing a cache, sending heartbeats or expiring holds kept in memory. Pick the method For each job, choose schedule, scheduleAtFixedRate, scheduleWithFixedDelay, or "not in the JVM": (a) drop an idempotency key from an in-memory cache 10 minutes after it was stored; (b) send the issuer a heartbeat every 30 seconds, which it expects on a steady beat; (c) refresh FX rates from a provider whose calls sometimes take 20 seconds; (d) export the settlement file once a night. Write one sentence of reasoning for each before you read the answer. (a) schedule: it is a one-shot delay. (b) Fixed rate: the timing is the point. (c) Fixed delay: a slow call pushes the next one later instead of causing a burst of catch-up calls. (d) Not in the JVM: a restart loses the schedule and every replica would export the file. ScheduledExecutorService (Java SE 25 API) docs Fixed rate is a train timetable. Trains are due at 8:00, 8:10, 8:20. If the 8:10 leaves twenty minutes late, the next train leaves as soon as the line is clear, and the one after that too, until they are back on the printed times. Fixed delay is a shuttle bus that leaves ten minutes after the previous one gets back, so a late bus just makes every later one later. The analogy breaks on parallel tracks. Two trains can run at once on a busy line. Two runs of the same scheduled task never overlap, however late they are.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Fixed rate catches up, fixed delay never does
x: The two periodic methods measure the period from different places. scheduleAtFixedRate(task, initialDelay, period, unit) follows a timetable fixed in advance. Runs are due at initialDelay, then initialDelay + period, then initialDelay + 2 x period, and so on. scheduleWithFixedDelay(task, initialDelay, delay, unit) waits delay after each run ends, then starts the next one. While runs are short, you can't tell them apart. They split when one run is slow. Take a 100 ms period where the second run takes 250 ms and the others 10 ms. In the lab's model, which counts virtual milliseconds, the runs start at: fixed rate: 0, 100, 350, 360, 400, 500, 600 fixed delay: 0, 110, 460, 570, 680, 790, 900 RateVsDelayDemo shows the same shape with a few milliseconds of real-world noise. Both rows follow from what the executor does after each run. It puts a periodic task back in its queue only when the run returns, with a new due time. For fixed rate the new due time is the old due time plus the period. For fixed delay it is the current time plus the delay. A due time that is already in the past means "run as soon as a thread is free". Fixed rate never runs two executions at once. A late run starts as soon as the previous one ends, and then the overdue runs go back to back (runs 3 and 4 above) until the schedule is back on its timetable. By run 5 it is on time again. Fixed delay has no timetable to catch up with, so a slow run just pushes everything after it later. Pick fixed rate when the timing itself is the point: a heartbeat the issuer expects every 30 seconds, a metrics flush per interval. Pick fixed delay when the task calls something that can slow down, like an FX provider or a database, because you never want a provider that just recovered to be hit with a burst of catch-up calls. For most housekeeping in a service, fixed delay is the safer default. Neither method ever runs a task concurrently with itself, even on a scheduler with many threads. A task that takes 3 minutes on a 1 minute rate doesn't pile up three copies. It just runs late, every time. Watch a slow run Run RateVsDelayDemo and compare its start times with the fixed-rate row above. Run it again with -Pargs=delay. Before you do, predict when run 3 starts. RateVsDelayDemo.java package workbench.executors.l05; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** A 100 ms schedule whose second run takes 250 ms. Default: fixed rate. Pass "delay" for fixed delay. */ public class RateVsDelayDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean delay = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("delay"); ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(); AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger(); CountDownLatch sevenRuns = new CountDownLatch(7); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); Runnable sync = () -> { int n = runs.incrementAndGet(); long start = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; long work = n == 2 ? 250 : 10; // run 2 hits a slow ledger try { Thread.sleep(work); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } System.out.printf("run %d started at %4d ms, took %3d ms%n", n, start, work); sevenRuns.countDown(); }; ScheduledFuture<?> f = delay ? scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(sync, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) : scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(sync, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); System.out.println(delay ? "scheduleWithFixedDelay, 100 ms" : "scheduleAtFixedRate, 100 ms"); sevenRuns.await(); f.cancel(false); scheduler.shutdown(); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l05.RateVsDelayDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l05/RateVsDelayDemo.java RateVsDelayDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l05 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** A 100 ms schedule whose second run takes 250 ms. Default: fixed rate. Pass "delay" for fixed delay. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val delay = args.firstOrNull() == "delay" val scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor() val runs = AtomicInteger() val sevenRuns = CountDownLatch(7) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val sync = Runnable { val n = runs.incrementAndGet() val start = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val work = if (n == 2) 250L else 10L // run 2 hits a slow ledger try { Thread.sleep(work) } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } println("run %d started at %4d ms, took %3d ms".format(n, start, work)) sevenRuns.countDown() } val f = if (delay) scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(sync, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) else scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(sync, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) println(if (delay) "scheduleWithFixedDelay, 100 ms" else "scheduleAtFixedRate, 100 ms") sevenRuns.await() f.cancel(false) scheduler.shutdown() } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l05.RateVsDelayDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l05/RateVsDelayDemo.kt With fixed rate, runs 3 and 4 start within about 10 ms of each other, right after the slow run, and runs 5 to 7 are back on the 100 ms grid. With fixed delay, run 3 starts about 100 ms after run 2 ends (around 460 to 500 ms), and every later run is 110 ms after the one before. On a busy machine, all times drift a little later. The same slow second run under both modes. Fixed rate catches up with its timetable; fixed delay shifts everything later. Look for three schedules in a payment service. FX rates or BIN tables refreshed into memory: fixed delay, wrapped so a provider outage keeps the last good value, with the value's age exposed as a metric. A heartbeat or keep-alive to the issuer: fixed rate on its own scheduler, so a slow refresh can't delay it. In-memory expiry of authorization holds or idempotency keys: schedule per entry, or better, a cache with built-in expiry. Quarkus's @Scheduled is a different scheduler with its own rules (it has a concurrentExecution setting for overlapping runs), so check how it treats exceptions and overlap instead of assuming the JDK behavior carries over. Anything with business meaning, like the settlement export, belongs in a durable scheduler such as a Temporal schedule.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · One exception, and the schedule stops without a word
x: This sentence in the ScheduledExecutorService Javadoc causes more production surprises than any other in the package. A periodic task keeps running until it is cancelled, the executor terminates, or "an execution of the task throws an exception", and then: "Subsequent executions are suppressed." Nothing is logged. The re-queue step from the previous section happens only when a run returns normally. A run that throws leaves its exception in the ScheduledFuture, the same way submit hides exceptions, and the task never goes back in the queue. Almost nobody calls get() on a periodic task's future. Here is SilentDeathDemo, a health check every 100 ms that throws on its third run: health check 1 health check 2 health check 3 after 1 s: runs=3 isDone=true get() threw ExecutionException, cause: java.lang.IllegalStateException: ledger ping timed out Ten periods passed and three runs happened. In a real service, the FX rate quietly stops refreshing, a cache serves data that is days old, and the first sign is a customer complaint. The fix is to catch inside the task, so that no exception ever reaches the scheduler: Java scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { refreshFxRate(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("FX refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e); // report it, keep the schedule } }, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); Kotlin scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay({ try { refreshFxRate() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { log.warn("FX refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e) // report it, keep the schedule } }, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) Catch RuntimeException (or Exception if the body calls checked-exception code), not Throwable. An OutOfMemoryError or a StackOverflowError means the JVM itself is in trouble, and a schedule that hides it will keep failing politely. Let errors stop the task and alert on them. The lab wraps the pattern once, as SafeTask.wrap, so every periodic task in a service gets it. If you want to catch a dead schedule anyway, check future.isDone() from a health endpoint. For a periodic task that should run forever, done means dead. Kill a schedule, then save it Run SilentDeathDemo. Count the health checks before the after 1 s line. Run it with -Pargs=safe, which wraps the check in a try/catch. Predict the run count after one second. SilentDeathDemo.java package workbench.executors.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** A health check every 100 ms that throws on its third run. Pass "safe" to catch inside the task. */ public class SilentDeathDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean safe = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("safe"); ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(); AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger(); Runnable check = () -> { int n = runs.incrementAndGet(); System.out.println("health check " + n); if (n == 3) throw new IllegalStateException("ledger ping timed out"); }; Runnable task = !safe ? check : () -> { try { check.run(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(" caught and logged: " + e.getMessage()); } }; ScheduledFuture<?> f = scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(task, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); Thread.sleep(1_000); // ten periods System.out.println("after 1 s: runs=" + runs.get() + " isDone=" + f.isDone()); if (f.isDone()) { try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: " + e.getCause()); } } scheduler.shutdownNow(); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l05.SilentDeathDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l05/SilentDeathDemo.java SilentDeathDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l05 import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** A health check every 100 ms that throws on its third run. Pass "safe" to catch inside the task. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val safe = args.firstOrNull() == "safe" val scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor() val runs = AtomicInteger() val check = Runnable { val n = runs.incrementAndGet() println("health check $n") if (n == 3) throw IllegalStateException("ledger ping timed out") } val task = if (!safe) check else Runnable { try { check.run() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println(" caught and logged: ${e.message}") } } val f = scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(task, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) Thread.sleep(1_000) // ten periods println("after 1 s: runs=${runs.get()} isDone=${f.isDone}") if (f.isDone) { try { f.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println("get() threw ExecutionException, cause: ${e.cause}") } } scheduler.shutdownNow() } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l05.SilentDeathDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l05/SilentDeathDemo.kt The first run prints three health checks and then nothing for the rest of the second: isDone=true, and get() reveals the exception. With safe, run 3 prints "caught and logged" and the checks continue to about 10 or 11 in the second, with isDone=false.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor, and ForkJoinPool as a scheduler in JDK 25
x: newScheduledThreadPool(n) returns a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor: a ThreadPoolExecutor whose queue is ordered by due time. Its Javadoc says it "acts as a fixed-sized pool using corePoolSize threads and an unbounded queue", so the maximum pool size has no useful effect. That has three consequences worth knowing. A scheduler with one thread runs one task at a time. A refresh that hangs for a minute delays every other task on that scheduler by a minute, heartbeats included. Give slow periodic work its own scheduler, or let the scheduled task only hand the real work to another pool. Cancelled tasks stay in the queue until their due time by default. If you schedule and cancel a lot, for example one timeout per request, call setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true) so they don't pile up. After shutdown(), one-shot delayed tasks still run when they come due, but periodic tasks stop. Those are the defaults of setExecuteExistingDelayedTasksAfterShutdownPolicy and setContinueExistingPeriodicTasksAfterShutdownPolicy, and they matter when a service shuts down with holds still waiting to expire. JDK 25 adds a second scheduler you already have. ForkJoinPool now implements ScheduledExecutorService, so ForkJoinPool.commonPool() can schedule tasks too, with the same fixed-rate, fixed-delay and exception rules. It also gains submitWithTimeout, which cancels a task (or runs an action you pass) if it hasn't finished in time. This compiles only on JDK 25 or later, so it stays out of the labs: Java // JDK 25+ ForkJoinPool pool = ForkJoinPool.commonPool(); pool.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshFxRate, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); ForkJoinTask<Quote> quote = pool.submitWithTimeout(() -> fetchQuote(pair), 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, null); // a null timeout action means: cancel(true) if it isn't done after 300 ms Kotlin // JDK 25+ val pool = ForkJoinPool.commonPool() pool.scheduleWithFixedDelay(this::refreshFxRate, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) val quote: ForkJoinTask<Quote> = pool.submitWithTimeout({ fetchQuote(pair) }, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, null) // a null timeout action means: cancel(true) if it isn't done after 300 ms Keep blocking work off the common pool, scheduled or not. Every parallel stream and every default CompletableFuture in the JVM shares it, which lesson 8 of this track shows the hard way. Check yourself: one single-thread scheduler runs a heartbeat at a 30-second fixed rate and an FX refresh with a 5-second fixed delay. A refresh starts just after a heartbeat and hangs for 90 seconds. How many heartbeats go out during the hang, and what happens when it ends? None go out during the hang, because the only thread is busy. When the refresh returns, the three heartbeats that came due in the meantime run back to back, because their due times are all in the past. The next refresh starts 5 seconds after the hung one ended. A periodic task with no try/catch. It works in every test, then one run throws (a 502 from the FX provider, a null in a response) and the schedule stops for good. The scheduler logs nothing, so the first sign is stale data hours later. People expect it to behave like a loop that logs and carries on. Wrap every periodic task body in a try/catch for RuntimeException that reports the failure, and expose isDone() or the age of the last success on a health endpoint.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Java and Kotlin
x: A fixed-delay refresher: scheduler vs coroutine loop FxRefresh.java ScheduledFuture<?> refresher = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { rate = fetchRate(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("FX refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e); } }, 0, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // later refresher.cancel(false); // no more runs; a running fetch finishes FxRefresh.kt (kotlinx.coroutines) val refresher = scope.launch { while (isActive) { try { rate = fetchRate() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e // let cancellation through } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("FX refresh failed, keeping the last rate", e) } delay(5.seconds) // the gap is measured from the end of the run } } // later refresher.cancel() // stops at the next delay() Coroutines have no scheduler API. A loop with delay is a fixed-delay schedule, and a fixed rate needs you to compute the next due time yourself. The failure behavior differs in a useful way: an exception that escapes the JDK task disappears into the ScheduledFuture, while an exception that escapes launch propagates to the parent scope and its exception handler, so it is loud by default. Either way you catch inside the loop to keep it alive, and in Kotlin you rethrow CancellationException, or cancel() would be swallowed like any other exception.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Worked example
x: Why did the FX rate stop updating? Checkout prices in USD have used the same EUR/USD rate for six hours. The logs show no errors. Here is the refresher. Find the bug before reading on. scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate( () -> rate = fxProvider.eurUsd(), // throws on a 502 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate( { rate = fxProvider.eurUsd() }, // throws on a 502 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) Six hours ago the provider returned a 502 and eurUsd() threw. That run's exception went into the ScheduledFuture, which nobody holds, and every later run was suppressed. No log line, because nothing ever printed the exception. Fixed rate is a second, smaller problem: when the provider is slow, overdue runs fire back to back. Catch inside the task, keep the last good rate, count the failure, and switch to fixed delay so a slow provider never gets a burst of catch-up calls. ScheduledFuture<?> refresher = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { rate = fxProvider.eurUsd(); // 1. fetch lastSuccess = Instant.now(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { failures.increment(); // 2. count it for a metric log.warn("FX refresh failed, keeping {}", rate, e); // 3. keep the old rate } }, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); val refresher = scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay({ try { rate = fxProvider.eurUsd() // 1. fetch lastSuccess = Instant.now() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { failures.increment() // 2. count it for a metric log.warn("FX refresh failed, keeping {}", rate, e) // 3. keep the old rate } }, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) Make the next failure visible. A health check that reports the rate's age and whether the schedule is still alive turns six silent hours into one alert. boolean healthy = !refresher.isDone() && Duration.between(lastSuccess, Instant.now()).toMinutes() < 5; val healthy = !refresher.isDone && Duration.between(lastSuccess, Instant.now()).toMinutes() < 5

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Quiz
x: A task scheduled with scheduleAtFixedRate(task, 0, 1, SECONDS) takes 3 seconds every time. What happens? Three copies run at once, one starting each second Each run starts as soon as the previous one ends, so it runs back to back The scheduler skips the missed slots and waits for the next whole second The scheduler throws RejectedExecutionException Executions of one periodic task never overlap. Every run is overdue by the time the last one ends, so it starts immediately, and the task runs continuously. Missed slots are not skipped; they are run late. scheduleWithFixedDelay(task, 0, 10, SECONDS) runs a task that always takes 2 seconds. When do the first three runs start? 0, 10 and 20 seconds 0, 2 and 12 seconds 0, 8 and 16 seconds 0, 12 and 24 seconds The delay is measured from the end of each run: run 1 ends at 2 s, so run 2 starts at 12 s, ends at 14 s, and run 3 starts at 24 s. 0, 10, 20 is what fixed rate would give. A periodic cache refresh throws a NullPointerException on its 40th run. Nothing catches it. What do you observe? It stops for good, nothing is logged, and its future reports isDone() = true It logs the exception and runs again next period The scheduler thread dies and is replaced, and the task keeps running The scheduler shuts down Later executions are suppressed and the exception is stored in the ScheduledFuture. Nothing is printed, which is the dangerous part. The scheduler and its other tasks carry on as if nothing happened. A single-thread scheduler runs a 30-second heartbeat and a report job that sometimes takes 2 minutes. The issuer complains about missing heartbeats. What is the right fix? Raise the scheduler's maximum pool size Switch the heartbeat to fixed delay Give the report job its own scheduler, or have its scheduled task hand the work to another pool Wrap the heartbeat in a try/catch With one thread, the heartbeat can't run while the report is running. Maximum pool size does nothing on a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor, and fixed delay or a try/catch don't free the thread. Separate the slow job from the time-sensitive one. From "Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption": a periodic task is in the middle of a run when you call cancel(false) on its ScheduledFuture. What happens? The run in progress is interrupted and no more runs happen The run in progress finishes, and no more runs happen Nothing, because cancel(false) only affects tasks that have not started The run in progress finishes, and the schedule continues cancel(false) does not interrupt a running task, so the current run completes. Cancelling still marks the future cancelled, so the scheduler never queues the next run. cancel(true) would also interrupt the current run.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Key terms
x: ScheduledExecutorService An executor that can run tasks after a delay or periodically. Fixed rate Runs due at fixed times (start + n x period), caught up after a late run. Fixed delay A fixed gap between the end of one run and the start of the next. ScheduledFuture The handle for a scheduled task: cancel it, check isDone, read its remaining delay. Suppressed execution A periodic run that never happens because an earlier run threw. Delay queue A queue ordered by due time that releases each task only when it comes due. scheduleAtFixedRate vs scheduleWithFixedDelay: what is the period measured from? Fixed rate: from a timetable fixed at the start (initialDelay + n x period). Fixed delay: from the end of the previous run. A periodic task throws once, uncaught. What happens to later runs? They are suppressed forever. Nothing is logged; the exception is in the ScheduledFuture. Can two runs of the same periodic task overlap? No. A late run waits for the previous one to finish, on any number of threads. Why does maximumPoolSize do nothing on a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor? It is a fixed pool of core threads with an unbounded delay queue, so it never grows past core. What did JDK 25 add to ForkJoinPool for scheduling? It implements ScheduledExecutorService (schedule, fixed rate, fixed delay) and adds submitWithTimeout. Why avoid java.util.Timer? One thread for all tasks, and one task that throws kills that thread and cancels every task on the Timer.

h: Scheduled executors: fixed rate vs fixed delay · Go deeper
x: The clock is System.nanoTime(), not the wall clock. A periodic task is unaffected when NTP corrects the system time or daylight saving time starts, which is what you want for "every 30 seconds". It also means a ScheduledExecutorService can't express "at 02:00 local time". You can approximate it by computing the delay to the next 02:00 and calling schedule again after each run, but that is a sign the job belongs in a real scheduler. CompletableFuture has its own small scheduling helper, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(delay, unit), which returns an Executor that runs each task after a delay. Lesson 7 of this track uses its relatives, orTimeout and completeOnTimeout.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · The executor you pass to supplyAsync decides where the work runs
x: A CompletableFuture<T> is a Future you can attach the next step to. Something has to complete it. Usually that is supplyAsync, which runs a Supplier on an executor and completes the future with its result: Java CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> prices.priceEur(cartId), io); // starts now, on io CompletableFuture<Void> audit = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> auditLog.write(cartId), io); // no result Kotlin val price: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ prices.priceEur(cartId) }, io) // starts now, on io val audit: CompletableFuture<Void> = CompletableFuture.runAsync({ auditLog.write(cartId) }, io) // no result Both calls return at once. The work is already running, or waiting in io's queue. A client library can also hand you a future and call complete(value) on it later, when its response arrives. The payment gateway in this lesson's lab works that way. The second argument matters more than it looks. Leave it out and the task goes to the default async executor, which is ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). That pool has availableProcessors() - 1 threads, so 7 on an 8-core machine, and the whole JVM shares them: every parallel stream, and every library that calls supplyAsync without an executor. Put a 120 ms issuer call there and seven concurrent authorizations fill it. The eighth waits in a queue behind them, and so does every parallel stream in the service. The JDK version changes the small-machine case. Up to JDK 24, CompletableFuture checked the common pool's parallelism first. If it was below 2, which is what a container with 1 or 2 CPUs gets, it skipped the pool and started a brand-new thread for every async task. JDK 25 removed that special case: async methods without an executor now always use the common pool. So on a 2-CPU pod, the same line gives you unbounded threads on JDK 21 and a single shared thread on JDK 25. Both are wrong for a blocking call. The rule is short. Pass an executor to anything that blocks: a bounded pool sized the way lesson 3 of this track showed, or, on JDK 21 and later, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Keep the default for short CPU work. Find out who runs your task Run WhoRunsItDemo. Note the thread names with and without an executor. Run it again with -Pargs=1cpu, which sets the common pool's parallelism to 1, as on a 2-CPU container. Predict the names first. Does your JDK version change the answer? WhoRunsItDemo.java package workbench.executors.l06; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; /** Which thread runs supplyAsync? Pass "1cpu" to size the common pool the way a 2-CPU container does. */ public class WhoRunsItDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("1cpu")) { // must run before anything touches ForkJoinPool: a 2-CPU container gets parallelism 1 System.setProperty("java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism", "1"); } System.out.println("JDK " + Runtime.version().feature() + ", common pool parallelism " + ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism()); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { String who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).join(); System.out.println("supplyAsync(task) ran on " + who); } try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { String who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName(), io).join(); System.out.println("supplyAsync(task, io) ran on " + who); } } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l06.WhoRunsItDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l06/WhoRunsItDemo.java WhoRunsItDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l06 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool /** Which thread runs supplyAsync? Pass "1cpu" to size the common pool the way a 2-CPU container does. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "1cpu") { // must run before anything touches ForkJoinPool: a 2-CPU container gets parallelism 1 System.setProperty("java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism", "1") } println("JDK ${Runtime.version().feature()}, common pool parallelism ${ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism()}") repeat(3) { val who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { Thread.currentThread().name }.join() println("supplyAsync(task) ran on $who") } Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> repeat(3) { val who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ Thread.currentThread().name }, io).join() println("supplyAsync(task, io) ran on $who") } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l06.WhoRunsItDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l06/WhoRunsItDemo.kt Without an executor, every call runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-N; with io, on io-1 and io-2. With 1cpu on JDK 21, the no-executor calls run on Thread-0, Thread-1, Thread-2: a new thread for each task. On JDK 25 or later they all run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1. CompletableFuture (Java SE 25 API) docs A pipeline is like an order ticket in a restaurant kitchen: "when the steak and the sauce are both ready, plate them, then send the plate to table 4." Nobody stands at the grill waiting for the steak. Whichever cook finishes the last part reads the ticket and does the next step. That's thenCombine, and it's why the next step runs on whatever thread finished last. The analogy breaks on heavy steps. A real cook who finishes the sauce knows to pass a two-hour braise to someone else. A plain thenApply doesn't: the thread that completes the stage does the next step, however slow it is, unless you name an executor with the Async variant.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Map with thenApply, flatten with thenCompose, wait for two with thenCombine
x: Each of these methods takes a future, attaches a step, and returns a new future for the step's result. Pick by the shape of the function you have: You have Method You get T -> U, plain code thenApply CompletableFuture<U> T -> CompletableFuture<U>, another async call thenCompose CompletableFuture<U> a second future and (T, U) -> V thenCombine CompletableFuture<V> T -> void, a side effect thenAccept CompletableFuture<Void> If you know Optional or streams: thenApply is map and thenCompose is flatMap. Use thenApply with a function that returns a future and you get a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<AuthResponse>>, a future of a future that no one waits for. Here is an authorization. The card lookup (40 ms) and the fraud score (60 ms) don't depend on each other. The issuer call needs both, and its client is already asynchronous: Java CompletableFuture<Card> card = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> cards.find(token), io); CompletableFuture<Integer> risk = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fraud.score(token, amount), io); CompletableFuture<Decision> decision = card .thenCombine(risk, (c, score) -> new AuthRequest(c, amount, score)) // both, then build .thenCompose(issuer::authorize) // returns CompletableFuture<AuthResponse> .thenApply(resp -> resp.approved() ? Decision.APPROVE : Decision.DECLINE); Kotlin val card = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ cards.find(token) }, io) val risk = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fraud.score(token, amount) }, io) val decision: CompletableFuture<Decision> = card .thenCombine(risk) { c, score -> AuthRequest(c, amount, score) } // both, then build .thenCompose(issuer::authorize) // returns CompletableFuture<AuthResponse> .thenApply { resp -> if (resp.approved) Decision.APPROVE else Decision.DECLINE } Parallelism comes from where you call supplyAsync, not from thenCombine. Both lookups start on the first two lines, before anything is attached, so the slow part takes max(40, 60) = 60 ms. Write card.thenCompose(c -> supplyAsync(() -> fraud.score(...), io)) and the fraud call starts only when the card is back: 40 + 60 = 100 ms. Nothing warns you. The code is still asynchronous, just slower. If any step fails, the steps after it are skipped and the final future fails with that exception. The next lesson is about handling that. Side by side, or one after the other Run CombineDemo. The price and the FX rate each take 300 ms. Read the timestamps. Run it with -Pargs=chain, which fetches the rate inside thenCompose, after the price. Predict the total time before you run it. In the chain branch, change thenCompose to thenApply and run it again. Read what the compiler says about the type, then undo the change. CombineDemo.java package workbench.executors.l06; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.math.RoundingMode; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** The price and the FX rate take 300 ms each. Pass "chain" to fetch them one after the other. */ public class CombineDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %-6s %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().getName(), msg); } static BigDecimal priceEur() { sleep(300); // the cart service log("price is 100.00 EUR"); return new BigDecimal("100.00"); } static BigDecimal eurToUsd() { sleep(300); // the FX provider log("rate is 1.0842"); return new BigDecimal("1.0842"); } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean chain = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("chain"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> usd; if (chain) { // the rate call starts only when the price has arrived usd = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::priceEur, io) .thenCompose(p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::eurToUsd, io) .thenApply(p::multiply)); } else { // both calls start now and run side by side CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::priceEur, io); CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(CombineDemo::eurToUsd, io); usd = price.thenCombine(rate, BigDecimal::multiply); } log("pipeline built, nothing has arrived yet"); log("charge " + usd.join().setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) + " USD"); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l06.CombineDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l06/CombineDemo.java CombineDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l06 import java.math.BigDecimal import java.math.RoundingMode import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executors private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%4d ms %-6s %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().name, msg)) private fun priceEur(): BigDecimal { Thread.sleep(300) // the cart service log("price is 100.00 EUR") return BigDecimal("100.00") } private fun eurToUsd(): BigDecimal { Thread.sleep(300) // the FX provider log("rate is 1.0842") return BigDecimal("1.0842") } /** The price and the FX rate take 300 ms each. Pass "chain" to fetch them one after the other. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val chain = args.firstOrNull() == "chain" Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> val usd: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = if (chain) { // the rate call starts only when the price has arrived CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::priceEur, io) .thenCompose { p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::eurToUsd, io).thenApply { r -> p * r } } } else { // both calls start now and run side by side val price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::priceEur, io) val rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::eurToUsd, io) price.thenCombine(rate) { p, r -> p * r } } log("pipeline built, nothing has arrived yet") log("charge ${usd.join().setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)} USD") } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l06.CombineDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l06/CombineDemo.kt The default run prints the price and the rate at about 300 ms, on io-1 and io-2, and charges 108.42 USD right after. With chain the rate arrives at about 600 ms. With thenApply the code no longer compiles: the result is now a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>>, not a CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>. The checkout from the demo and the lab: two calls side by side, joined by thenCombine, then the gateway's own future flattened by thenCompose. An authorization path usually has a few independent lookups (token vault, fraud score, card limits) before one issuer call. Start them all with supplyAsync(..., io) and join them with thenCombine; the latency becomes the slowest lookup instead of the sum. Watch the edges. In a Kafka consumer, a handler that starts a pipeline and returns lets the consumer commit the offset before the charge happens, so a crash loses the message: wait for the future with a timeout, or commit when it completes. In a Temporal activity, return only after the future completes, because the activity's result is what Temporal records. In a Quarkus REST endpoint, return the CompletionStage and let the framework finish the response.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Which thread runs the next step
x: thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine and thenAccept take no executor. So who runs the function? If the previous stage is still running when you attach the step, the step runs on the thread that completes the previous stage. If the previous stage is already complete, the step runs right away, on the thread that called thenApply. Both cases follow from one detail of the class. Each CompletableFuture keeps a stack of the steps attached to it. The thread that completes the future, by returning from a supplyAsync task or by calling complete, then pops those steps and runs every one that has no executor of its own. A step attached after that has nothing to wait for, so thenApply runs it on the spot. WhichThreadDemo shows both cases, plus the two Async variants: 1. thenApply on a finished future: main 2. thenApply attached while running: io-1 3. thenApplyAsync(fn): ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 4. thenApplyAsync(fn, cpu): cpu-1 For cheap code this is fine, and it's what the plain methods are for. Multiplying a price by a rate or mapping a response to a Decision takes microseconds. It doesn't matter which thread does it, and skipping a hop to another pool saves a queue and a context switch. It goes wrong when the step is slow and the completing thread isn't yours. If a client library completes its future on its own I/O thread, your plain thenApply runs there. Vert.x-based clients in Quarkus typically complete on an event-loop thread, and a step that blocks for 50 ms there stalls every other request that loop serves. The same goes for a scheduler thread that completes a timeout. Every method has two Async variants: thenApplyAsync(fn) always submits the step to the default executor, the common pool, with the same problems as supplyAsync without an executor. thenApplyAsync(fn, executor) submits it to the pool you name. Use it to move heavy or blocking work off a thread you don't own. So the rule has three parts. Use the plain method for cheap steps. Use the Async variant with an executor when the step blocks or burns CPU. Don't use the Async variant without an executor for anything that blocks. Predict four thread names Read WhichThreadDemo and write down the thread you expect for each numbered line. Run it and compare. For line 2, explain why it isn't main, even though main called thenApply. WhichThreadDemo.java package workbench.executors.l06; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** Which thread runs the next stage? It depends on timing, and on the Async suffix. */ public class WhichThreadDemo { static String me() { return Thread.currentThread().getName(); } public static void main(String[] args) { try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()); ExecutorService cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("cpu-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<String> done = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("x"); System.out.println("1. thenApply on a finished future: " + done.thenApply(x -> me()).join()); CompletableFuture<String> slow = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { sleep(200); return "x"; }, io); CompletableFuture<String> attached = slow.thenApply(x -> me()); // attached while slow still runs System.out.println("2. thenApply attached while running: " + attached.join()); System.out.println("3. thenApplyAsync(fn): " + slow.thenApplyAsync(x -> me()).join()); System.out.println("4. thenApplyAsync(fn, cpu): " + slow.thenApplyAsync(x -> me(), cpu).join()); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l06.WhichThreadDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l06/WhichThreadDemo.java WhichThreadDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l06 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executors private fun me(): String = Thread.currentThread().name /** Which thread runs the next stage? It depends on timing, and on the Async suffix. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("cpu-", 1).factory()).use { cpu -> val done = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("x") println("1. thenApply on a finished future: " + done.thenApply { me() }.join()) val slow = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ Thread.sleep(200); "x" }, io) val attached = slow.thenApply { me() } // attached while slow still runs println("2. thenApply attached while running: " + attached.join()) println("3. thenApplyAsync(fn): " + slow.thenApplyAsync { me() }.join()) println("4. thenApplyAsync(fn, cpu): " + slow.thenApplyAsync({ me() }, cpu).join()) } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l06.WhichThreadDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l06/WhichThreadDemo.kt main, io-1, ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 and cpu-1. Line 2 runs on io-1 because the step was attached while the supply task was still sleeping, so the thread that completed it ran the step. If your machine paused main for more than 200 ms between the two lines, you would see main there instead, which is the whole point: timing decides.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · join, get, and the one place you may block
x: Sooner or later a thread needs the value: to write an HTTP response, to commit a Kafka offset, to assert in a test. CompletableFuture gives you two blocking calls. get() is the Future method from lesson 4 of this track. It throws the checked InterruptedException and ExecutionException, with the failure as the cause, and get(timeout, unit) adds TimeoutException. join() is unchecked: it throws CompletionException with the failure as the cause, or CancellationException. That makes it easy to use inside lambdas and streams. It has no timeout, and it ignores interrupts: a thread stuck in join() stays stuck until the future completes. getNow(fallback) and resultNow() (JDK 19) never block. The rule: build the whole pipeline without blocking, and block at most once, at the edge, on a thread that is allowed to wait, with a timeout: Java // a blocking REST endpoint: the request thread may wait, but not forever Decision d = authorize(token, amount).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); Kotlin // a blocking REST endpoint: the request thread may wait, but not forever val d = authorize(token, amount).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) Often you don't need to block at all. Quarkus REST resource methods can return a CompletionStage<T>, and the framework writes the response when it completes. Never call join() or get() inside a stage on a future that may still be running. (On a future you know is done, such as after allOf in the next lesson, join() returns at once.) The stage runs on a pool thread, and that thread now sits idle until another task finishes. With a few of those, a bounded pool runs out of threads, and if the awaited task is queued behind them on the same pool, nothing ever finishes. That is pool-induced deadlock, and the last lesson of this track has you fix one. When a stage needs another async result, that's what thenCompose and thenCombine are for. Spot the blocking calls Read this method. Mark every line that blocks a thread, and say which thread. Java CompletableFuture<Receipt> checkout(String cart) { BigDecimal price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> prices.priceEur(cart), io).join(); // A CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fx.rate("EUR", "USD"), io); return rate.thenApply(r -> { BigDecimal amount = price.multiply(r); String id = gateway.charge(cart, amount, "USD").join(); // B return new Receipt(cart, amount, "USD", id); }); } Kotlin fun checkout(cart: String): CompletableFuture<Receipt> { val price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ prices.priceEur(cart) }, io).join() // A val rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fx.rate("EUR", "USD") }, io) return rate.thenApply { r -> val amount = price * r val id = gateway.charge(cart, amount, "USD").join() // B Receipt(cart, amount, "USD", id) } } Sketch the fix with thenCombine and thenCompose. The lab asks you to write it for real. A blocks the caller for the whole price call, and because the rate call starts only after it, the two calls run one after the other. B blocks whichever thread completes rate (an io thread) for as long as the gateway takes. The fix starts both supplyAsync calls first, combines them with thenCombine, and calls the gateway inside thenCompose, so no thread waits anywhere inside checkout. The most common mistake is supplyAsync(() -> blockingCall()) with no executor. It works in tests, where nothing else uses the common pool. In production, the blocking calls hold the common pool's few threads, and every parallel stream and every other default-executor future in the JVM waits behind them. On a small container before JDK 25 it's worse in a different way: a new thread per task, with no limit. People leave the executor out because the one-argument version looks complete and the Javadoc's default sounds harmless. The fix is to always pass an executor for I/O. Search the codebase for one-argument supplyAsync( and runAsync( calls; each one should be short CPU work, or get an executor.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Java and Kotlin
x: Two lookups side by side, then an async call Authorize.java (CompletableFuture) CompletableFuture<Decision> authorize(String token, BigDecimal amount) { CompletableFuture<Card> card = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> cards.find(token), io); CompletableFuture<Integer> risk = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fraud.score(token, amount), io); return card .thenCombine(risk, (c, score) -> new AuthRequest(c, amount, score)) .thenCompose(issuer::authorize) .thenApply(resp -> resp.approved() ? Decision.APPROVE : Decision.DECLINE); } Authorize.kt (kotlinx.coroutines) suspend fun authorize(token: String, amount: BigDecimal): Decision = coroutineScope { val card = async(Dispatchers.IO) { cards.find(token) } // both start now val risk = async(Dispatchers.IO) { fraud.score(token, amount) } val request = AuthRequest(card.await(), amount, risk.await()) val resp = issuer.authorize(request).await() // suspends on the CompletableFuture if (resp.approved) Decision.APPROVE else Decision.DECLINE } The Java version is a chain of callbacks: each method attaches a step, and you think about which thread runs each one. The Kotlin version reads top to bottom. async starts the two lookups at once, await() suspends the coroutine without blocking a thread, and the await() extension from kotlinx.coroutines.future turns the issuer's CompletableFuture into a suspension point. The structure differs too. If the fraud call fails, coroutineScope cancels the card lookup and rethrows. thenCombine does nothing like that: the card lookup keeps running and its result is thrown away. The coroutines track covers the details.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Worked example
x: Turn a blocking authorization into a pipeline This handler takes 40 + 60 + 120 = 220 ms per request, and holds a thread for all of it. Before reading on, mark which calls depend on which. Decision authorize(String token, BigDecimal amount) { Card card = cards.find(token); // 40 ms int score = fraud.score(token, amount); // 60 ms AuthResponse resp = issuer.authorize(new AuthRequest(card, amount, score)).join(); // 120 ms return resp.approved() ? Decision.APPROVE : Decision.DECLINE; } fun authorize(token: String, amount: BigDecimal): Decision { val card = cards.find(token) // 40 ms val score = fraud.score(token, amount) // 60 ms val resp = issuer.authorize(AuthRequest(card, amount, score)).join() // 120 ms return if (resp.approved) Decision.APPROVE else Decision.DECLINE } The card lookup and the fraud score are independent. The issuer needs both. The decision needs the issuer. So the best case is max(40, 60) + 120 = 180 ms, and only if the two lookups start together. Start both first, on the io pool, because they block. // 1. start the independent blocking calls together CompletableFuture<Card> card = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> cards.find(token), io); CompletableFuture<Integer> risk = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fraud.score(token, amount), io); // 1. start the independent blocking calls together val card = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ cards.find(token) }, io) val risk = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fraud.score(token, amount) }, io) Join the two with thenCombine. Building the request is cheap, so the plain method is right. The issuer client returns its own future, so flatten it with thenCompose, and finish with a cheap thenApply. return card .thenCombine(risk, (c, score) -> new AuthRequest(c, amount, score)) // 2. wait for both .thenCompose(issuer::authorize) // 3. async call, flattened .thenApply(resp -> resp.approved() ? Decision.APPROVE : Decision.DECLINE); // 4. cheap mapping return card .thenCombine(risk) { c, score -> AuthRequest(c, amount, score) } // 2. wait for both .thenCompose(issuer::authorize) // 3. async call, flattened .thenApply { if (it.approved) Decision.APPROVE else Decision.DECLINE } // 4. cheap mapping The method now returns CompletableFuture<Decision> and blocks nothing. The blocking endpoint that calls it waits once, with a timeout. A reactive endpoint returns the future instead. Decision d = authorize(token, amount).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // 5. block once, at the edge val d = authorize(token, amount).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // 5. block once, at the edge

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Quiz
x: cards.findAsync(token) returns CompletableFuture<Card> and issuer.authorizeAsync(card) returns CompletableFuture<Auth>. What is the type of cards.findAsync(token).thenApply(issuer::authorizeAsync)? CompletableFuture<Auth> CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Auth>> Auth It doesn't compile thenApply wraps whatever the function returns, and this function returns a future. You get a future of a future, and nothing waits for the inner one. thenCompose flattens it to CompletableFuture<Auth>. price() and rate() each block for 200 ms. Which version finishes in about 200 ms? supplyAsync(() -> price(), io).thenCompose(p -> supplyAsync(() -> rate(), io).thenApply(p::multiply)) supplyAsync(() -> price().multiply(rate()), io) supplyAsync(() -> price(), io).thenApply(p -> p.multiply(rate())) supplyAsync(() -> price(), io).thenCombine(supplyAsync(() -> rate(), io), BigDecimal::multiply) Only the last one starts both calls before waiting for either. The other three are all asynchronous, but each runs rate() after price() has returned, so they take about 400 ms. Being async is not the same as running in parallel. Future f has already completed. Request thread http-7 calls f.thenApply(this::render). Which thread runs render? http-7, right away A common pool worker The thread that completed f A new thread When the previous stage is already complete, a plain thenApply runs the function at once on the calling thread. The thread that completed f finished its work earlier and plays no part. Only thenApplyAsync would hand it to a pool. A service on JDK 21 runs in a container with 2 CPUs. It calls supplyAsync(() -> blockingLookup()) with no executor, 300 times a second. What happens? The lookups queue up behind a single common pool thread They run on virtual threads They run on the calling threads Each lookup gets a new platform thread, with no upper limit With 2 CPUs the common pool's parallelism is 1, and before JDK 25 CompletableFuture didn't use the common pool when its parallelism was below 2. It created a thread per task instead. The first option is what JDK 25 does with the same code. Neither is acceptable for blocking work: pass an executor. From "Sizing a pool": a checkout runs the price call (100 ms) and the FX call (100 ms) side by side on io, and you get 200 checkouts a second. How many io threads are busy on average? 20 40 200 400 Little's law: L = lambda x W. Each checkout holds two io threads for 0.1 s, so the pool sees 400 calls a second x 0.1 s = 40 busy threads. Running the calls side by side cuts latency; it doesn't cut the number of threads you need. Size the pool above 40, and check that the downstreams accept that many calls.
