h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Key terms
x: CompletableFuture A Future you can complete by hand and attach further steps to. Stage One step in a pipeline: a future plus the function that produces it from earlier results. thenCompose Attach a step that returns another future, and get one flat future back. thenCombine Wait for two futures and merge their results with a function. Default async executor Where async methods run when you pass no executor: the common ForkJoinPool. Common pool One ForkJoinPool per JVM, with cores minus one threads, shared by parallel streams and default async tasks. thenApply vs thenCompose? thenApply maps with a plain function (T -> U). thenCompose flattens a function that returns a future (T -> CompletableFuture<U>), like flatMap. What does a.thenCombine(b, fn) do? Waits until both a and b complete, then applies fn(aResult, bResult). It starts nothing: a and b must already be running to overlap. Which executor does supplyAsync(task) use on JDK 25? ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), always. Up to JDK 24 it used a new thread per task when the common pool's parallelism was below 2. Which thread runs a plain thenApply step? The thread that completes the previous stage, or the calling thread if that stage is already complete. join() vs get() on a failed CompletableFuture? get() throws checked ExecutionException, join() throws unchecked CompletionException. Both carry the failure as the cause. Why pass an executor to supplyAsync for blocking calls? Without one, the calls hold common pool threads, which every parallel stream and default-executor future in the JVM shares.

h: CompletableFuture: composing async steps · Go deeper
x: The stack of steps from "Which thread runs the next step" has one more consequence. One slow thenApply delays every other plain step attached to the same future, because the completing thread runs them one after another. CompletableFuture implements two interfaces. Future gives you get and cancel. CompletionStage has the composition methods and nothing that completes or blocks. When you write an API, return CompletionStage<T>, or call minimalCompletionStage() (JDK 9), so callers can't call complete or obtrudeValue on your future and change a result you already computed. A caller who needs to block can still call toCompletableFuture().join(), which makes the blocking visible in their code. There are a few other ways in. completedFuture(v) and failedFuture(ex) (JDK 9) are handy in tests. new CompletableFuture<>() plus complete(v) bridges any callback API, for example a Kafka producer's send callback. And completeAsync(supplier, executor) (JDK 9) completes an existing future from a task, which is useful when you must hand out the future before you know which executor will do the work.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · A failure skips every step until a handler catches it
x: When a stage throws, its future completes exceptionally. Every thenApply, thenCompose and thenCombine after it is skipped: the function never runs, and its own future fails with the same cause. The failure travels down the chain until it reaches a handler. There are four: Method Runs on Changes the outcome? exceptionally(ex -> value) failure only yes, replaces the failure with a value handle((value, ex) -> result) success and failure yes, returns any result whenComplete((value, ex) -> ...) success and failure no, passes the outcome on exceptionallyCompose(ex -> future) failure only yes, with another future (JDK 12) Where you attach the handler decides what you recover. Put exceptionally at the end of a checkout and the conversion and charge steps are skipped; the only honest value left to return is "declined". Put it right after the FX call and it can return the last known rate, and every later step runs as if nothing went wrong. Recover as close to the failing call as you can, with a value that makes sense at that point. whenComplete is for logs and metrics. It sees both outcomes and hands the same one on. One detail: if its action throws after a success, the result becomes that failure; after a failure, the original failure wins. When the fallback is itself asynchronous, such as a second FX provider or a cache service with an async client, use exceptionallyCompose. It is to exceptionally what thenCompose is to thenApply: Java CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = live.rateAsync(pair) .exceptionallyCompose(ex -> backup.rateAsync(pair)); // JDK 12+ Kotlin val rate: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = live.rateAsync(pair) .exceptionallyCompose { backup.rateAsync(pair) } // JDK 12+ Move the handler Run ErrorPathDemo. The FX call throws. Before you run it, write down which of the numbered steps will print. Run it with -Pargs=early, which recovers the rate right after the call. Predict again, including what whenComplete sees. ErrorPathDemo.java package workbench.executors.l07; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.math.RoundingMode; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** The FX call fails. Which steps still run? Pass "early" to recover the rate right after the call. */ public class ErrorPathDemo { static BigDecimal liveRate() { throw new IllegalStateException("FX provider returned 502"); } static <T> T step(String what, T value) { System.out.println(what); return value; } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean early = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("early"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(ErrorPathDemo::liveRate, io); if (early) { rate = rate.exceptionally(ex -> { // recover the rate itself System.out.println("exceptionally sees: " + ex); return new BigDecimal("1.0800"); // the last known rate }); } CompletableFuture<String> result = rate .thenApply(r -> step("1. convert at " + r, new BigDecimal("100.00").multiply(r))) .thenApply(usd -> step("2. round to cents", usd.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN))) .thenApply(usd -> step("3. charge " + usd + " USD", "charged " + usd + " USD")) .whenComplete((v, ex) -> System.out.println("whenComplete sees: " + (ex == null ? v : ex))); if (!early) { result = result.exceptionally(ex -> { // recover at the end instead System.out.println("exceptionally sees: " + ex); return "declined: FX rate unavailable"; }); } System.out.println("result: " + result.join()); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.ErrorPathDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l07/ErrorPathDemo.java ErrorPathDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l07 import java.math.BigDecimal import java.math.RoundingMode import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executors private fun liveRate(): BigDecimal = throw IllegalStateException("FX provider returned 502") private fun <T> step(what: String, value: T): T { println(what) return value } /** The FX call fails. Which steps still run? Pass "early" to recover the rate right after the call. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val early = args.firstOrNull() == "early" Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> var rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::liveRate, io) if (early) { rate = rate.exceptionally { ex -> // recover the rate itself println("exceptionally sees: $ex") BigDecimal("1.0800") // the last known rate } } var result = rate .thenApply { r -> step("1. convert at $r", BigDecimal("100.00") * r) } .thenApply { usd -> step("2. round to cents", usd.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)) } .thenApply { usd -> step("3. charge $usd USD", "charged $usd USD") } .whenComplete { v, ex -> println("whenComplete sees: ${ex ?: v}") } if (!early) { result = result.exceptionally { ex -> // recover at the end instead println("exceptionally sees: $ex") "declined: FX rate unavailable" } } println("result: ${result.join()}") } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.ErrorPathDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l07/ErrorPathDemo.kt The default run prints no numbered steps: whenComplete and then exceptionally both see a CompletionException wrapping the 502, and the result is the declined message. With early, exceptionally fires first, then steps 1, 2 and 3 run with the 1.0800 rate, and whenComplete sees charged 108.00 USD, a success. CompletionStage (Java SE 25 API) docs You phone three exchange bureaus for a EUR/USD rate. allOf is waiting until all three have called back, and giving up on the whole thing if one of them called to say it's closed. anyOf is taking whoever calls back first, even if that call is to say they're closed. The safe pattern gives each call its own egg timer: when it rings, you write "no answer" next to that bureau, and when every line has a rate or a "no answer", you pick the best rate. The analogy breaks when you hang up. A clerk who hears you hang up stops working. A provider call in the JVM keeps running after your timeout, and it keeps a pool thread busy until it's done.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · CompletionException: the wrapper you sometimes get
x: Handlers don't always see your exception. They see one of two things, by a rule that surprises everyone once. If the exception was thrown inside a stage, by a supplyAsync task or a thenApply function, the future stores it wrapped in a CompletionException. A handler on that future, or on any later stage, gets the wrapper, with your exception as getCause(). If someone completed the future with completeExceptionally(ex), as orTimeout and many client libraries do, a handler attached directly to that future gets ex itself. One stage later it is wrapped again. The wrapper comes from the library catching your exception inside a stage; completeExceptionally stores exactly the exception it is given. WrapDemo prints all the cases: 1. handle() on the supplyAsync future CompletionException <- IllegalStateException 2. handle() on completeExceptionally IllegalStateException 3. handle() one stage later CompletionException <- IllegalStateException 4. handle() after orTimeout TimeoutException 5. get() throws ExecutionException <- IllegalStateException 6. join() throws CompletionException <- IllegalStateException The last two lines are the blocking calls from the previous lesson: get() throws ExecutionException and join() throws CompletionException, both with the original as the cause. So a handler that checks ex instanceof TimeoutException is right in one place and silently wrong one stage further down. Unwrap first, then decide: Java .exceptionally(ex -> { Throwable cause = (ex instanceof CompletionException && ex.getCause() != null) ? ex.getCause() : ex; if (cause instanceof TimeoutException) return lastKnownRate; throw new CompletionException(cause); // not ours to handle: keep failing }) Kotlin .exceptionally { ex -> val cause = if (ex is CompletionException && ex.cause != null) ex.cause!! else ex if (cause is TimeoutException) lastKnownRate else throw CompletionException(cause) // not ours to handle: keep failing } Rethrowing inside a handler is how you say "I looked, and this one isn't mine". The lab's unwrap does the same job in a loop, and also strips the ExecutionException that get() adds. On a completed future, exceptionNow() (JDK 19) hands you the unwrapped cause directly. Predict the wrapper Cover the output above. Read WrapDemo and write down, for each numbered line, what you expect it to print. Run it and check. For each line you got wrong, find whether the exception was thrown inside a stage or passed to completeExceptionally. WrapDemo.java package workbench.executors.l07; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Which exception does each handler see? Predict every line before you run it. */ public class WrapDemo { static String describe(Throwable ex) { String name = ex.getClass().getSimpleName(); return ex.getCause() == null ? name : name + " <- " + ex.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName(); } static void show(String label, CompletableFuture<?> f) { String seen = f.handle((v, ex) -> describe(ex)).join(); System.out.printf("%-42s %s%n", label, seen); } public static void main(String[] args) { IllegalStateException down = new IllegalStateException("502"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<String> supplied = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { throw down; }, io); CompletableFuture<String> completed = new CompletableFuture<>(); completed.completeExceptionally(down); CompletableFuture<String> timedOut = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> sleepThen(1000, "late"), io) .orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); show("1. handle() on the supplyAsync future", supplied); show("2. handle() on completeExceptionally", completed); show("3. handle() one stage later", completed.thenApply(String::trim)); show("4. handle() after orTimeout", timedOut); try { supplied.get(); } catch (ExecutionException | InterruptedException e) { System.out.printf("%-42s %s%n", "5. get() throws", describe(e)); } try { supplied.join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { System.out.printf("%-42s %s%n", "6. join() throws", describe(e)); } } } static String sleepThen(long ms, String value) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return value; } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.WrapDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l07/WrapDemo.java WrapDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l07 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit private fun describe(ex: Throwable): String { val name = ex.javaClass.simpleName return ex.cause?.let { "$name <- ${it.javaClass.simpleName}" } ?: name } private fun show(label: String, f: CompletableFuture<*>) { val seen = f.handle { _, ex -> describe(ex) }.join() println("%-42s %s".format(label, seen)) } /** Which exception does each handler see? Predict every line before you run it. */ fun main() { val down = IllegalStateException("502") Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> val supplied = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync<String>({ throw down }, io) val completed = CompletableFuture<String>() completed.completeExceptionally(down) val timedOut = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ Thread.sleep(1000); "late" }, io) .orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) show("1. handle() on the supplyAsync future", supplied) show("2. handle() on completeExceptionally", completed) show("3. handle() one stage later", completed.thenApply { it.trim() }) show("4. handle() after orTimeout", timedOut) try { supplied.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println("%-42s %s".format("5. get() throws", describe(e))) } try { supplied.join() } catch (e: CompletionException) { println("%-42s %s".format("6. join() throws", describe(e))) } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.WrapDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l07/WrapDemo.kt The six lines shown in the section. Lines 2 and 4 are the raw exceptions, because completeExceptionally and orTimeout store them as they are. Every exception that crosses a stage boundary, or was thrown inside one, arrives as a CompletionException. Authorization paths are full of fan-outs with deadlines: a fraud vendor that must answer in 150 ms or the payment goes to manual review, an issuer call with a 2 s budget, two FX providers where any recent rate will do. Give each dependency its own deadline and its own fallback, close to the call, and record which path each request took with whenComplete, so a dashboard shows when the fallback rate becomes the normal rate. Remember the second timeout in the client, or a slow vendor quietly fills your pool. Temporal's activity timeouts have the same limit one level up: when an activity times out, the worker keeps running the activity code until it heartbeats and learns it was cancelled. In Quarkus, MicroProfile Fault Tolerance's @Timeout and @Fallback do this job with annotations, and the same two-timeout question applies.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Timeouts end the wait, not the work
x: JDK 9 added two timeouts to CompletableFuture: Java quote.orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // fails with TimeoutException quote.completeOnTimeout(lastKnown, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // completes with a default Kotlin quote.orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // fails with TimeoutException quote.completeOnTimeout(lastKnown, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // completes with a default Both change the future you call them on and return it. If it hasn't completed when the time is up, a JDK timer thread completes it (on JDK 21 the thread is called CompletableFutureDelayScheduler). Plain stages attached to it then run on that timer thread, so keep them cheap. What neither one does is touch the task. The provider call keeps running on its io thread until it returns, and then its result is thrown away. KeepsRunningDemo gives a 600 ms call a 200 ms timeout: the future fails at 200 ms, and the call finishes at 600 ms anyway. cancel(true) on a CompletableFuture is no better. Its Javadoc says the mayInterruptIfRunning flag "has no effect in this implementation because interrupts are not used to control processing." The future completes with CancellationException and the task runs on. The source shows why. supplyAsync hands the executor a small task that points to the future, and the future keeps no reference to that task or to the thread running it. So cancel can only store a CancellationException as the result. There is no thread it could interrupt. That is the opposite of the FutureTask from submit, where cancel(true) interrupts the worker, as lesson 4 of this track showed. This matters under load. Take a 20-thread pool and a provider that hangs for 30 seconds. Each request gets its TimeoutException after 300 ms, right on time, but each call holds its thread for 30 seconds. After 20 requests the pool is full of calls nobody is waiting for, and new calls, even to healthy providers, queue behind them and time out too. So every remote call needs two timeouts. The one on the future is the caller's deadline. The one in the client (the HTTP client's request timeout, the JDBC query timeout) gives the thread back. Set the client's timeout no longer than the future's, and bound the pool per provider, as lesson 3 of this track did with bulkheads. Time out a call, then watch it finish Run KeepsRunningDemo. Read the thread names and timestamps. Run it with -Pargs=cancel, which calls cancel(true) at 200 ms instead. Predict: does the provider see an interrupt? KeepsRunningDemo.java package workbench.executors.l07; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** A 600 ms provider call with orTimeout(200 ms). Pass "cancel" to try cancel(true) at 200 ms instead. */ public class KeepsRunningDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %-31s %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().getName(), msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean cancel = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("cancel"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> quote = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { log("asking the slow provider"); try { Thread.sleep(600); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("interrupted: the call stops here"); throw new IllegalStateException(e); } log("provider answered, but nobody is listening"); return new BigDecimal("1.0842"); }, io); if (cancel) { Thread.sleep(200); log("cancel(true) returned " + quote.cancel(true)); } else { quote.orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } quote.handle((v, ex) -> { log("the future completed with " + (ex == null ? v : ex.getClass().getSimpleName())); return null; }).join(); } // close() waits for the provider call, which is still running log("pool closed"); } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.KeepsRunningDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l07/KeepsRunningDemo.java KeepsRunningDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l07 import java.math.BigDecimal import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%4d ms %-31s %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().name, msg)) /** A 600 ms provider call with orTimeout(200 ms). The provider still prints its answer at about 600 ms, and pool closed waits for it. With cancel, cancel(true) returns true and the future completes with CancellationException on main, but the line interrupted never prints: the call runs to 600 ms.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Fan-out: allOf waits for everyone, anyOf takes whoever finishes first
x: To ask three FX providers at once, start three futures and combine them. The JDK gives you two methods that combine futures, and neither does what you want on its own. allOf(f1, f2, f3) returns a CompletableFuture<Void>. It completes when all three have completed, and it has no results of its own: you read them from your futures with join(), which no longer blocks because they're all done. If any of them failed, allOf fails too, but only after the slowest one finishes. One provider that returns a 503 in 50 ms fails the whole call, 300 ms later. anyOf(f1, f2, f3) returns a CompletableFuture<Object> that completes like whichever future completes first. That includes a failure. A provider that fails fast beats two that answer correctly a little later. If what you want is the first successful answer, anyOf can't give it to you; the deeper section has a ten-line helper for that. The fix is to make each call unable to fail before you combine them. Give every call its own timeout, then turn any failure into "no answer": Java CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>> safe = ask(provider) .orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // this provider's deadline .handle((price, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(price) : Optional.empty()); Kotlin val safe: CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>> = ask(provider) .orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // this provider's deadline .handle { price, ex -> if (ex == null) Optional.of(price) else Optional.empty() } Now allOf over the safe futures can only succeed, and the step after it picks the best answer, or fails with a clear error when every provider was skipped. The timeout must sit on each call. Put one orTimeout on the allOf instead and one hung provider throws away the two good answers. That is the lab: a quote aggregator with a timeout per provider, a report for every skipped provider with its real cause, and the lowest price among those that answered. Three ways to fan out Read FanOutDemo: flaky fails at 50 ms, alpha answers at 100 ms, beta at 300 ms. Run it with -Pargs=any, then -Pargs=all, then -Pargs=safe. Before each run, predict the result and when it arrives. FanOutDemo.java package workbench.executors.l07; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.Optional; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** flaky fails at 50 ms, alpha answers at 100 ms, beta at 300 ms. Pass any, all or safe. */ public class FanOutDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> ask(String name, long ms, String price, ExecutorService io) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { sleep(ms); if (price == null) { log(name + " fails"); throw new IllegalStateException(name + " returned 503"); } log(name + " answers " + price); return new BigDecimal(price); }, io); } public static void main(String[] args) { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "all"; try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { List<CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>> asks = List.of( ask("flaky", 50, null, io), ask("alpha", 100, "1.0850", io), ask("beta", 300, "1.0842", io)); CompletableFuture<?> result = switch (mode) { // the first future to complete wins, even when it completes with a failure case "any" -> CompletableFuture.anyOf(asks.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)); // waits for all three, then fails because one of them failed case "all" -> CompletableFuture.allOf(asks.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) .thenApply(done -> asks.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).min(Comparator.naturalOrder()).orElseThrow()); // turn each failure into an empty Optional first, so allOf can't fail default -> { List<CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>>> safe = asks.stream() .map(f -> f.handle((price, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(price) : Optional.<BigDecimal>empty())) .toList(); yield CompletableFuture.allOf(safe.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) .thenApply(done -> safe.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).flatMap(Optional::stream) .min(Comparator.naturalOrder()).orElseThrow()); } }; result.handle((v, ex) -> { log(mode + ": " + (ex == null ? "result " + v : "failed with " + ex.getCause())); return null; }).join(); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.FanOutDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l07/FanOutDemo.java FanOutDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l07 import java.math.BigDecimal import java.util.Optional import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService import java.util.concurrent.Executors private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(msg: String) = println("%4d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg)) private fun ask(name: String, ms: Long, price: String?, io: ExecutorService): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ Thread.sleep(ms) if (price == null) { log("$name fails") throw IllegalStateException("$name returned 503") } log("$name answers $price") BigDecimal(price) }, io) /** flaky fails at 50 ms, alpha answers at 100 ms, beta at 300 ms. Pass any, all or safe. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "all" Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> val asks = listOf(ask("flaky", 50, null, io), ask("alpha", 100, "1.0850", io), ask("beta", 300, "1.0842", io)) val result: CompletableFuture<*> = when (mode) { // the first future to complete wins, even when it completes with a failure "any" -> CompletableFuture.anyOf(*asks.toTypedArray()) // waits for all three, then fails because one of them failed "all" -> CompletableFuture.allOf(*asks.toTypedArray()) .thenApply { asks.map { it.join() }.min() } // turn each failure into an empty Optional first, so allOf can't fail else -> { val safe = asks.map { f -> f.handle { price, ex -> if (ex == null) Optional.of(price) else Optional.empty() } } CompletableFuture.allOf(*safe.toTypedArray()) .thenApply { safe.mapNotNull { it.join().orElse(null) }.min() } } } result.handle { v, ex -> log("$mode: " + if (ex == null) "result $v" else "failed with ${ex.cause}") }.join() } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l07.FanOutDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l07/FanOutDemo.kt any fails at about 50 ms with flaky's 503, and alpha and beta keep running after the result is printed. all also fails with the 503, but only at about 300 ms, after beta answers. safe succeeds at about 300 ms with 1.0842, beta's price, because the failure became an empty Optional. Timestamps run a bit late on a busy machine. Each provider call gets its own deadline and a handle step, so allOf only ever sees answers or empty results. The common mistake is putting orTimeout on the future and thinking the slow call is handled. The caller does get its answer on time, so every test passes. In production a hung provider keeps each abandoned call on a pool thread for as long as the HTTP client is willing to wait, often 30 seconds or more. The pool fills with calls nobody is waiting for, and requests to healthy providers start timing out behind them. People make the mistake because the future and the work feel like one thing. They aren't: the future is a box for the answer. Set a client-side timeout no longer than the future's deadline, and give each provider its own bounded pool or semaphore.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Java and Kotlin
x: One provider call with a deadline: CompletableFuture vs coroutines Ask.java (CompletableFuture) CompletableFuture<Optional<Quote>> ask(QuoteProvider p, String pair) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> new Quote(p.name(), p.quote(pair)), io) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // the caller stops waiting... .handle((q, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(q) : Optional.empty()); // ...but p.quote keeps running on io until it returns } Ask.kt (kotlinx.coroutines) suspend fun ask(p: QuoteProvider, pair: String): Quote? = try { withTimeoutOrNull(300.milliseconds) { // null when time is up runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { // interrupts the thread on cancel Quote(p.name(), p.quote(pair)) } } } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e // never swallow cancellation } catch (e: Exception) { null // a failure becomes "no answer" } The shapes match: a deadline, then a failure turned into "no answer". The difference is what happens to the work. orTimeout only completes the future, and the provider call runs to its end. withTimeoutOrNull cancels the block, and runInterruptible turns that cancellation into Thread.interrupt() on the IO thread, so a blocking call that responds to interrupts stops and gives its thread back. In both languages, a call that ignores interrupts keeps its thread, which is why the client-side timeout still matters. Kotlin also makes you rethrow CancellationException by hand when you catch Exception; CompletableFuture has no such trap.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Worked example
x: Give the FX call a deadline and a fallback The checkout gets its rate from an async FX client. When the provider hangs, every checkout hangs with it. Before reading on, decide what should happen after 300 ms. CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate(String pair) { return fx.rateAsync(pair); // no deadline: a hung provider hangs the checkout } fun rate(pair: String): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = fx.rateAsync(pair) // no deadline: a hung provider hangs the checkout Give the live call a deadline, observe failures without changing them, then fall back to the rate cache, which has its own async client. The cache gets its own short deadline, because exceptionallyCompose starts a new call that the first timeout doesn't cover. CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate(String pair) { return fx.rateAsync(pair) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 1. the live call gets 300 ms .whenComplete((r, ex) -> { // 2. observe, don't change if (ex != null) metrics.count("fx.live.failed", unwrap(ex).getClass().getSimpleName()); }) .exceptionallyCompose(ex -> cache.rateAsync(pair) // 3. fall back, asynchronously .orTimeout(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)); // 4. the fallback's own deadline } fun rate(pair: String): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = fx.rateAsync(pair) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 1. the live call gets 300 ms .whenComplete { _, ex -> // 2. observe, don't change if (ex != null) metrics.count("fx.live.failed", unwrap(ex).javaClass.simpleName) } .exceptionallyCompose { // 3. fall back, asynchronously cache.rateAsync(pair).orTimeout(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 4. the fallback's own deadline } Why unwrap in the metric? The live client may complete its future with a raw exception, orTimeout stores a raw TimeoutException, and anything thrown inside a stage arrives wrapped. Without unwrapping, half your failures would be tagged CompletionException, which tells the on-call engineer nothing. One gap is left. After 300 ms the checkout moves on, but the live call still holds a thread and a connection. Give the HTTP request a timeout of its own, so the client gives up too. With the JDK client it is one line on the request. HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // 5. the client stops waiting too .build(); val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // 5. the client stops waiting too .build()

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Quiz
x: Each step prints its letter: supplyAsync(fails, io).thenApply(A).whenComplete(B).exceptionally(C).thenAccept(D), and the supplier throws. What prints? A, B, C, D B, C, D C, D B and C, then the pipeline fails A is skipped because its input failed. whenComplete runs on failure too but passes the failure on, so C runs and recovers, and D runs with the fallback value. Recovery in exceptionally makes everything after it see a success. supplyAsync(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("502"); }, io).exceptionally(ex -> ...). What is the class of ex? ExecutionException IllegalStateException RuntimeException CompletionException, with the IllegalStateException as its cause The exception was thrown inside a stage, so the future stores it wrapped in a CompletionException. ExecutionException is what get() throws at the blocking edge. You would get the raw IllegalStateException only if someone had called completeExceptionally with it. Quote calls run on a fixed pool of 20 threads with orTimeout(300, MILLISECONDS). A provider hangs for 30 s, and 100 requests arrive in one second. What happens? The first 20 time out at 300 ms but keep their threads; later calls queue behind them, so they time out too, even to healthy providers Every request times out at 300 ms and the pool stays free orTimeout interrupts the hung calls, so the threads come back at 300 ms The pool rejects the 21st request orTimeout completes the future but never touches the task, so each hung call holds its thread for 30 s. A fixed pool has an unbounded queue, so nothing is rejected: new calls just wait behind the hung ones until their own deadlines pass. A client-side timeout and a per-provider limit prevent it. You want a metric for every FX call, tagged success or failure, without changing what the caller receives. Which method fits? exceptionally handle whenComplete thenAccept whenComplete sees both outcomes and passes the original one on. handle sees both too, but you'd have to rebuild the outcome yourself (rethrowing the failure), which is easy to get wrong. exceptionally misses successes and thenAccept misses failures. From "Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption": the same blocking call, sleeping in Thread.sleep, runs twice: once via executor.submit(task) and once via CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, executor). You call cancel(true) on both futures. What happens? Both calls are interrupted Only the submit call is interrupted; the CompletableFuture one keeps sleeping Only the CompletableFuture call is interrupted Neither, because cancel only affects tasks that haven't started submit returns a FutureTask, whose cancel(true) interrupts the worker thread. CompletableFuture.cancel ignores the flag: it completes the future with CancellationException and leaves the task alone. Both futures report isCancelled() == true.

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Key terms
x: CompletionException The unchecked wrapper CompletableFuture puts around an exception thrown inside a stage. exceptionally Runs only on failure and replaces it with a value. handle Runs on success or failure and returns a new result either way. whenComplete Runs on success or failure to observe; passes the outcome on unchanged. orTimeout Fails the future with TimeoutException if it isn't done in time. The work keeps running. completeOnTimeout Completes the future with a default value if it isn't done in time. allOf / anyOf Combine many futures: wait for all of them, or take the first to complete. Which CompletableFuture handler sees a failure but can't change the outcome? whenComplete. It passes the original result or failure on. exceptionally and handle can replace it. A handler on a failed supplyAsync future: which exception does it get? A CompletionException, with the exception the task threw as getCause(). Does orTimeout stop the task? No. It completes the future with TimeoutException and the task keeps running, holding its thread. Does cancel(true) interrupt a CompletableFuture's task? No. The flag has no effect. The future completes with CancellationException; the task runs on. One of three futures fails at 50 ms, the slowest takes 300 ms. When does allOf complete? At 300 ms, exceptionally. allOf waits for all of them; it doesn't fail fast. What does anyOf give you if the fastest future fails? A failure. anyOf completes like the first future to complete, success or failure. When do you use exceptionallyCompose instead of exceptionally? When the fallback is itself a future, such as a call to a backup provider (JDK 12+).

h: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out · Go deeper
x: anyOf gives you the first to finish, not the first to succeed. When you want the first success, complete a future of your own from each success, and fail it only when every call has failed. complete returns false for every caller after the first, so the first success wins without a lock: Java static <T> CompletableFuture<T> firstSuccess(List<CompletableFuture<T>> calls) { // calls must not be empty CompletableFuture<T> first = new CompletableFuture<>(); AtomicInteger failed = new AtomicInteger(); for (CompletableFuture<T> call : calls) { call.whenComplete((value, ex) -> { if (ex == null) first.complete(value); // only the first one counts else if (failed.incrementAndGet() == calls.size()) first.completeExceptionally(ex); }); } return first; } Kotlin fun <T> firstSuccess(calls: List<CompletableFuture<T>>): CompletableFuture<T> { // calls must not be empty val first = CompletableFuture<T>() val failed = AtomicInteger() for (call in calls) { call.whenComplete { value, ex -> if (ex == null) first.complete(value) // only the first one counts else if (failed.incrementAndGet() == calls.size) first.completeExceptionally(ex) } } return first } Two smaller things are worth knowing. orTimeout and completeOnTimeout change the very future you call them on. If a client library hands the same cached future to several callers, one caller's timeout fails it for all of them. Call copy() (JDK 9) first and put the timeout on your copy. And when you need a delay without a timeout, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, MILLISECONDS, io) (JDK 9) returns an Executor that runs each task 500 ms after you submit it. It is handy for a retry with backoff: supplyAsync(this::call, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, MILLISECONDS, io)).

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · RecursiveTask: split until the piece is small, then loop
x: ForkJoinPool (JDK 7) is a pool built for one shape of work: a big CPU job that splits itself into smaller jobs of the same kind. You describe the job as a RecursiveTask<V>, which returns a value, or a RecursiveAction, which doesn't. Both have one method to write, compute(), and it nearly always has this shape: Java class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> { static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000; final long[] a; final int from, to; SumTask(long[] a, int from, int to) { this.a = a; this.from = from; this.to = to; } @Override protected Long compute() { if (to - from <= THRESHOLD) { // 1. small enough: just loop long sum = 0; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) sum += a[i]; return sum; } int mid = (from + to) >>> 1; // 2. split SumTask left = new SumTask(a, from, mid), right = new SumTask(a, mid, to); left.fork(); // 3. let another worker take the left half long r = right.compute(); // 4. do the right half here return left.join() + r; // 5. then collect the left half } } long total = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new SumTask(amounts, 0, amounts.length)); Kotlin class SumTask(val a: LongArray, val from: Int, val to: Int) : RecursiveTask<Long>() { override fun compute(): Long { if (to - from <= THRESHOLD) { // 1. small enough: just loop var sum = 0L for (i in from until to) sum += a[i] return sum } val mid = (from + to) ushr 1 // 2. split val left = SumTask(a, from, mid) val right = SumTask(a, mid, to) left.fork() // 3. let another worker take the left half val r = right.compute() // 4. do the right half here return left.join() + r // 5. then collect the left half } companion object { const val THRESHOLD = 10_000 } } val total = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(SumTask(amounts, 0, amounts.size)) The threshold is the one number you have to choose. Too big, and there are only a few pieces, so some workers sit idle at the end. Too small, and the cost of creating and scheduling task objects eats the gain. The ForkJoinTask Javadoc gives a very rough rule: a task should do more than 100 and less than 10,000 basic computational steps. Then measure. ForkJoin tasks are for CPU work on data you already have in memory: summing a ledger, sorting, searching, transforming a big array. They should not block on I/O or locks, for reasons the last section shows. Change the threshold Run WorkStealingDemo. It totals fees over 2,000,000 ledger entries, first on one thread, then on a ForkJoinPool with 4 workers. Note the speed-up and how many leaves each worker ran. Run it with -Pargs="right 500", then with -Pargs="right 1000000". Before each run, predict the number of leaves and how many workers will have any. WorkStealingDemo.java package workbench.executors.l08; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; import java.util.concurrent.RecursiveTask; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** Fees over 2,000,000 ledger entries on a 4-worker ForkJoinPool. Args: [right|wrong] [threshold]. */ public class WorkStealingDemo { static final Map<String, LongAdder> LEAVES = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); static long fee(long amountCents) { long h = amountCents; for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) h = (h * 31 + i) % 1_000_003; // stands in for real fee rules return amountCents * 29 / 1_000 + 30 + h % 2; } static final class Fees extends RecursiveTask<Long> { final long[] amounts; final int from, to, threshold; final boolean wrong; Fees(long[] amounts, int from, int to, int threshold, boolean wrong) { this.amounts = amounts; this.from = from; this.to = to; this.threshold = threshold; this.wrong = wrong; } @Override protected Long compute() { if (to - from <= threshold) { LEAVES.computeIfAbsent(Thread.currentThread().getName(), k -> new LongAdder()).increment(); long sum = 0; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) sum += fee(amounts[i]); return sum; } int mid = (from + to) >>> 1; Fees left = new Fees(amounts, from, mid, threshold, wrong); Fees right = new Fees(amounts, mid, to, threshold, wrong); left.fork(); if (wrong) { long leftFees = left.join(); // waits for the left half before starting the right one return leftFees + right.compute(); } long rightFees = right.compute(); // works on the right half while the left one can be stolen return left.join() + rightFees; } } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean wrong = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("wrong"); int threshold = args.length > 1 ? With 500 there are 4,096 leaves and it is still fast, a little slower from the extra tasks. With 1,000,000 there are only 2 leaves, so only 2 workers ever get work and the speed-up drops to about 2. ForkJoinTask (Java SE 25 API) docs A fork/join pool is a team splitting a stack of 2,000 invoices to check. Each clerk keeps a personal pile. When you split your pile, you put half on top of it and keep working on the other half yourself. A clerk with nothing to do walks over and takes the bottom of somebody else's pile, which is the biggest bundle, so nobody has to walk over often. The analogy breaks when a clerk picks up the phone to a supplier for ten minutes: in an office you'd notice and share out the pile, but the pool usually can't tell a thread is waiting, so that clerk's desk just stands empty.

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Work stealing, and why fork, compute, join is the only good order
x: A ThreadPoolExecutor has one shared queue. A ForkJoinPool gives every worker its own double-ended queue, a deque. fork() pushes the task onto the top of the current worker's deque. The worker also pops from the top, so it always works on the task it forked most recently: the smallest one, whose data is still in its cache. A worker whose deque is empty becomes a thief. It picks another worker and takes the task at the bottom of that worker's deque. That is the oldest task, forked highest up in the recursion, so it is the biggest piece of work available. The thief splits it on its own deque and stays busy for a long time. That's why WorkStealingDemo reports only a handful of steals for 64 leaves. join() doesn't simply park the thread. If the task is still on the worker's own deque, the worker pops it and runs it. If a thief took it, the worker helps by running other pending tasks while it waits. A fork/join pool doesn't need a spare thread for every task that is waiting on another. Now the order. Fork one half, compute the other on this thread, and only then join: Java left.fork(); // the left half becomes stealable long r = right.compute(); // this thread works while a thief can take the left half return left.join() + r; Kotlin left.fork() // the left half becomes stealable val r = right.compute() // this thread works while a thief can take the left half return left.join() + r Swap the last two steps, left.fork(); left.join(); right.compute(), and the worker waits for the left half before it even starts the right one. The two halves of every split run one after the other. left.compute() + right.compute() is the same thing written honestly: sequential code with extra objects. Both still give the right total, which is why the bug survives code review. invokeAll(left, right) is the library's shortcut for the correct order. Join too early Run WorkStealingDemo with -Pargs=wrong. It joins the left half before computing the right one. Compare the time with the one-thread line, and look at how the leaves are spread. Why can leaves land on two workers when nothing runs in parallel? Args: [right|wrong] [threshold]. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val wrong = args.getOrNull(0) == "wrong" val threshold = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 50_000 val amounts = LongArray(2_000_000) { i -> 100 + (i * 7919L) % 250_000 } val s0 = System.nanoTime() var expected = 0L for (a in amounts) expected += fee(a) // one thread, for comparison println("one thread: %,d ms".format((System.nanoTime() - s0) / 1_000_000)) ForkJoinPool(4).use { pool -> val t0 = System.nanoTime() val total = pool.submit(Fees(amounts, 0, amounts.size, threshold, wrong)).join() val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 TreeMap(leaves).forEach { (thread, n) -> println("%-24s %4d leaves".format(thread, n.sum())) } println("%s order, threshold %,d: %,d ms, %d steals, same total: %b".format( if (wrong) "wrong" else "right", threshold, ms, pool.stealCount, total == expected)) } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l08.WorkStealingDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l08/WorkStealingDemo.kt The wrong order takes about as long as one thread, sometimes a little longer. Most leaves run on one worker, with a few on a second one: sometimes a thief steals the forked half in the moment between fork and join, but then the first worker just waits for it, so the work still happens one piece at a time. Each worker pushes and pops at the top of its own deque. An idle worker steals from the bottom, where the oldest and biggest task waits. Good fork/join work in a payment service is CPU work on data already in memory: totalling fees over a day's ledger extract, building a settlement file, deduplicating a batch of idempotency keys, sorting a big reconciliation set. Bad work is anything that calls out: an issuer lookup, a database query or a Kafka send inside a parallelStream(). On an 8-core Quarkus pod that has 7 common pool threads shared by the whole service, and the stall shows up as unrelated CompletableFuture timeouts somewhere else. When you do turn on parallel(), check the container's CPU limit, because availableProcessors() follows it and a 2-CPU pod gets a common pool of one worker.

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Parallel streams run on the common pool, along with everything else
x: list.parallelStream() splits its source into pieces and runs them as fork/join tasks on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). The calling thread takes part too: in SharedStateDemo, main shows up next to the common pool workers. The common pool has availableProcessors() - 1 threads by default (you can change it with -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism). It is one pool for the whole JVM. Every parallel stream uses it, every CompletableFuture async method without an executor uses it (lesson 6 of this track), and from JDK 25 so does scheduling on the common pool (lesson 5). Whatever runs there competes with all of that. Three mistakes cover most parallel stream bugs. Writing to shared state races. forEach(p -> list.add(p)) on an ArrayList, or forEach(x -> total[0] += x), runs the same read-modify-write races as any other threads. The demo loses about half the ids, and the sum comes out wrong by billions. Let the stream build the result: toList(), collect(...), sum(), reduce(...). Each thread works on its own piece, and the stream combines the pieces at the end. Order isn't kept. forEach on a parallel stream runs in whatever order the threads get to the elements. toList() and forEachOrdered keep the source order, at some cost. Too little work makes it slower. Splitting, scheduling and combining cost time. A stream of 1,000 cheap elements is faster sequential. Sources that split badly, such as a LinkedList, Stream.iterate or lines from a file, give the pool little to share out. That comes from how a stream splits its source. An array or an ArrayList splits in half by index, in one step, and each half can go to another worker. A LinkedList has no middle to jump to. Its Spliterator, the object that does the splitting, walks the list from the front and copies the next 1,024 elements into an array, then the next 2,048, and so on, all on the one thread that splits. Measure both versions, ideally with JMH (the OpenJDK harness for microbenchmarks), before you keep parallel(). Collect from many threads Run SharedStateDemo. Before you do, predict the size of the shared list and whether the shared sum is right. Run it twice more. Which numbers change between runs, and which never do? h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Blocking calls starve the common pool
x: A ForkJoinPool tries to keep about parallelism threads running. When one of them blocks in Thread.sleep, a socket read or a JDBC call, the pool normally doesn't know, and that thread is simply gone until the call returns. With 7 workers on an 8-core pod, seven slow issuer lookups in a parallel stream take every common pool thread in the JVM. StarvationDemo runs four rounds of 300 ms lookups in a parallel stream. As soon as all the threads are busy, another thread submits a task that should take microseconds, through supplyAsync with no executor. It waits about 1.2 seconds, until the lookups are nearly done. In a service, that tiny task is somebody else's request. The fix is to keep I/O off the common pool. Run blocking calls on an executor built for waiting: a bounded pool sized for the downstream, or virtual threads, which the next track covers. Then combine the results with CompletableFuture. In the demo's io mode, the lookups finish in about 300 ms and the tiny task waits about 2 ms. There is also a patch for code you can't move. ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(blocker) tells the pool "this worker is about to block", and the pool may start a spare thread to keep its parallelism up. CompletableFuture uses it internally when a pool thread calls join(). In the demo's managed mode, spare workers appear (with names like commonPool-worker-10) and both numbers look good again. It is still a patch: every blocked call costs a whole platform thread, and the spares are capped. You may read that a parallel stream started inside customPool.submit(...) runs on customPool. It does today, but it is how the implementation behaves, not something the specification promises. Don't build on it. Starve the common pool Run StarvationDemo. Note how long the tiny task waits and which thread finally runs it. Run it with -Pargs=io, then with -Pargs=managed. Predict each time: how long do all the lookups take, and how long does the tiny task wait? Args: [blocking|managed|io]. */ public class StarvationDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static final int PARALLELISM = ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism(); static final AtomicInteger STARTED = new AtomicInteger(); static final CountDownLatch ALL_BUSY = new CountDownLatch(1); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static void lookup() { if (STARTED.incrementAndGet() == PARALLELISM + 1) ALL_BUSY.countDown(); // the common pool and main are all busy sleep(300); // a remote call } static void managedLookup() { try { // tells the pool this worker is about to block, so it can start a spare thread ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(new ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker() { boolean done; @Override public boolean block() { lookup(); done = true; return true; } @Override public boolean isReleasable() { return done; } }); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "blocking"; int lookups = (PARALLELISM + 1) * 4; // four rounds of work for the common pool and main log(mode + ": common pool parallelism " + PARALLELISM + ", " + lookups + " lookups of 300 ms"); Thread fx = new Thread(() -> { try { ALL_BUSY.await(); // start once the lookups are under way } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } long t = System.nanoTime(); String who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).join(); // a tiny task log("tiny task waited " + (System.nanoTime() - t) / 1_000_000 + " ms, then ran on " + who); }); fx.start(); if (mode.equals("io")) { try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(lookups)) { List<CompletableFuture<Void>> calls = IntStream.range(0, lookups) .mapToObj(i -> CompletableFuture.runAsync(StarvationDemo::lookup, io)) .toList(); calls.forEach(CompletableFuture::join); } } else { boolean managed = mode.equals("managed"); IntStream.range(0, lookups).parallel().forEach(i -> { if (managed) managedLookup(); else lookup(); }); } log("all lookups done"); fx.join(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l08.StarvationDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l08/StarvationDemo.java StarvationDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.stream.IntStream import kotlin.concurrent.thread private val T0 = System.nanoTime() private val parallelism = ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism() private val started = AtomicInteger() private val allBusy = CountDownLatch(1) private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg)) private fun lookup() { if (started.incrementAndGet() == parallelism + 1) allBusy.countDown() // the common pool and main are all busy Thread.sleep(300) // a remote call } private fun managedLookup() { // tells the pool this worker is about to block, so it can start a spare thread ForkJoinPool.managedBlock(object : ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker { var done = false override fun block(): Boolean { lookup() done = true return true } override fun isReleasable() = done }) } /** Blocking BIN lookups in a parallel stream while a tiny task needs the common pool. Args: [blocking|managed|io]. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "blocking" val lookups = (parallelism + 1) * 4 // four rounds of work for the common pool and main log("$mode: common pool parallelism $parallelism, $lookups lookups of 300 ms") val fx = thread { allBusy.await() // start once the lookups are under way val t = System.nanoTime() val who = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { Thread.currentThread().name }.join() // a tiny task log("tiny task waited ${(System.nanoTime() - t) / 1_000_000} ms, then ran on $who") } if (mode == "io") { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(lookups).use { io -> val calls = (0 until lookups).map { CompletableFuture.runAsync(::lookup, io) } calls.forEach { it.join() } } } else { val managed = mode == "managed" IntStream.range(0, lookups).parallel().forEach { if (managed) managedLookup() else lookup() } } log("all lookups done") fx.join() } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l08.StarvationDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l08/StarvationDemo.kt In the default mode the lookups take about 1.2 s (four rounds of 300 ms on the common pool plus main), and the tiny task waits about as long, because every common pool thread is asleep. With io the lookups take about 300 ms and the tiny task waits a few milliseconds. With managed the pool adds spare workers, so both drop again, and the tiny task runs on one of the extra threads. The most common mistake is putting blocking calls in a parallel stream: ids.parallelStream().map(client::fetch).toList(). It looks like a free speed-up and it is one in a laptop test, where nothing else needs the common pool. In production the calls hold the common pool's few threads, and every parallel stream and every executor-less CompletableFuture in the JVM waits behind them. People reach for it because parallelStream() is the shortest way to say "do these at once". For I/O, say it with an executor: supplyAsync(() -> client.fetch(id), io) for each id, then join them all at the edge.

x: Divide and conquer: RecursiveTask vs coroutines CountOver.java (ForkJoinPool) class CountOver extends RecursiveTask<Integer> { final long[] a; final long limit; final int from, to; CountOver(long[] a, long limit, int from, int to) { this.a = a; this.limit = limit; this.from = from; this.to = to; } @Override protected Integer compute() { if (to - from <= 10_000) { int n = 0; for (int i = from; i < to; i++) if (a[i] > limit) n++; return n; } int mid = (from + to) >>> 1; CountOver left = new CountOver(a, limit, from, mid); CountOver right = new CountOver(a, limit, mid, to); left.fork(); // stealable int r = right.compute(); // work here return left.join() + r; // then collect } } int flagged = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new CountOver(amounts, 500_000, 0, amounts.length)); CountOver.kt (kotlinx.coroutines) suspend fun countOver(a: LongArray, limit: Long, from: Int, to: Int): Int = if (to - from <= 10_000) { (from until to).count { a[it] > limit } } else coroutineScope { val mid = (from + to) ushr 1 val left = async { countOver(a, limit, from, mid) } // like fork() val right = countOver(a, limit, mid, to) // like compute() left.await() + right // like join() } val flagged = runBlocking(Dispatchers.Default) { countOver(amounts, 500_000, 0, amounts.size) } Kotlin can extend RecursiveTask exactly like Java (the Kotlin WorkStealingDemo does). The coroutine version keeps the same shape and the same order rule: start the left half with async, compute the right half in place, then await. Two things differ. Dispatchers.Default is kotlinx.coroutines' own shared thread pool, sized to the number of cores (at least two); it is not the common ForkJoinPool, so it doesn't compete with parallel streams. And await() suspends the coroutine instead of helping with other tasks, so the thread goes back to the dispatcher. Blocking calls are just as wrong on Dispatchers.Default as on the common pool; they belong on Dispatchers.IO.

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Worked example
x: Speed up a nightly fee report without breaking it The report totals fees per merchant over 4 million payments. Someone made it parallel. Before reading on, find what breaks. Map<String, Long> feesByMerchant = new HashMap<>(); payments.parallelStream().forEach(p -> feesByMerchant.merge(p.merchant(), fee(p), Long::sum)); // one HashMap, many threads val feesByMerchant = HashMap<String, Long>() payments.parallelStream().forEach { p -> feesByMerchant.merge(p.merchant, fee(p), Long::plus) // one HashMap, many threads } Many threads call merge on one HashMap. That loses updates, and a resize under concurrent writes can corrupt the map. Let the stream build the result instead: with groupingBy, each thread fills its own partial map and the stream merges them at the end. // 1. CPU work only, and the stream owns the result Map<String, Long> feesByMerchant = payments.parallelStream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Payment::merchant, Collectors.summingLong(this::fee))); // 1. CPU work only, and the stream owns the result val feesByMerchant: Map<String, Long> = payments.parallelStream() .collect(Collectors.groupingBy({ it.merchant }, Collectors.summingLong(::fee))) Next someone wants merchant names in the report, from a service that takes 20 ms per call. Calling it inside the parallel stream would block the common pool for 4 million calls. There are only about 3,000 merchants, so look the names up after the aggregation, once each, on an IO pool. // 2. IO goes to a pool built for waiting, once per merchant Map<String, CompletableFuture<String>> names = feesByMerchant.keySet().stream() .collect(Collectors.toMap(id -> id, id -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> merchants.name(id), io))); // 3. wait at the edge: the report job's own thread may block names.forEach((id, name) -> report.line(name.join(), feesByMerchant.get(id))); // 2. IO goes to a pool built for waiting, once per merchant val names = feesByMerchant.keys.associateWith { id -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ merchants.name(id) }, io) } // 3. wait at the edge: the report job's own thread may block names.forEach { (id, name) -> report.line(name.join(), feesByMerchant.getValue(id)) } Last question: is parallel() worth keeping? Time both versions on production-sized data, with JMH or at least a few warm runs. With a cheap fee and a few thousand payments the sequential stream often wins. Keep parallel() only where the numbers say so, and remember that the pod's CPU limit sets the common pool's size.
