x: Which compute() body lets the two halves run at the same time? left.fork(); long l = left.join(); return l + right.compute(); return left.compute() + right.compute(); left.fork(); long r = right.compute(); return left.join() + r; long r = right.compute(); left.fork(); return left.join() + r; Only the third one makes the left half stealable and then keeps this thread busy with the right half while a thief can run the left. The first and last both wait for one half before the other is available, and the second never forks at all. All four give the right answer, which is why the bug is easy to miss. An 8-core pod runs cardIds.parallelStream().map(issuer::lookup).toList(), and each lookup takes 120 ms. What is the biggest risk? None: parallel streams run on virtual threads The lookups occupy the common pool's 7 workers, so other parallel streams and executor-less CompletableFuture tasks in the JVM wait behind them The stream silently falls back to running sequentially because the calls block It throws, because blocking isn't allowed in a ForkJoinPool Parallel streams use the common pool's platform workers, which the whole JVM shares, and the pool can't tell that a worker is blocked. Nothing throws and nothing falls back: everything else that needs the common pool just waits. Run the lookups on an IO executor instead. List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(); payments.parallelStream().forEach(p -> ids.add(p.id())); runs over 100,000 payments. What do you get, most of the time? Fewer than 100,000 ids, or an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException All 100,000 ids, in the original order All 100,000 ids, in a scrambled order A ConcurrentModificationException, every time Several threads call add on one ArrayList, which isn't thread-safe: writes race on the size and the backing array, so ids get lost or the array index runs past the end. ConcurrentModificationException comes from iterating while modifying, not from this race. payments.parallelStream().map(Payment::id).toList() is correct and keeps the order. Pick the tool for each job: (1) total the fees over 20 million ledger rows already in memory; (2) make 300 calls to a card-issuer API. (1) virtual threads; (2) a parallel stream Both in one parallel stream (1) a single-thread executor; (2) supplyAsync without an executor (1) a parallel stream or a RecursiveTask; (2) an IO executor or virtual threads, combined with CompletableFuture In-memory CPU work splits well and wants about one thread per core, which is what the common pool gives you. Waiting on an API wants many threads that are cheap to block, and they must not be the common pool's. supplyAsync without an executor would put those calls right back on the common pool. From "CompletableFuture: composing async steps": one part of a service calls supplyAsync(task) with no executor, another uses parallelStream(). Do they compete for threads? No: CompletableFuture has its own default pool Yes: both use ForkJoinPool.commonPool() (on JDK 25 always, on JDK 21 whenever its parallelism is at least 2) Only when both run on virtual threads No: every parallel stream creates its own pool The default async executor is the common pool, and so is the pool behind parallel streams. Before JDK 25 the one exception was a common pool with parallelism below 2, where CompletableFuture used a thread per task instead. Either way, a blocking task in one slows down the other.

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Explain it back
x: Explain to a teammate how work stealing keeps four workers busy on a recursive ledger sum, and why left.fork(); left.join(); right.compute() gets no speed-up even though it forks.

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Key terms
x: ForkJoinPool A pool where each worker has its own deque and idle workers steal tasks from busy ones. RecursiveTask A fork/join task that returns a value; RecursiveAction returns nothing. Work stealing An idle worker takes a task from the far end of another worker's deque. Deque A double-ended queue: the owner uses one end, thieves the other. Threshold The size below which a task stops splitting and just loops. Common pool The JVM-wide ForkJoinPool behind parallel streams and default async tasks. ManagedBlocker A way to tell a ForkJoinPool a worker will block, so it can add a spare thread. In compute(), what is the right order of fork, compute and join? Fork one half, compute the other half on this thread, then join the forked half. Joining first runs the halves one after the other. Where does a ForkJoinPool worker take its own tasks from, and where does a thief steal from? The owner pushes and pops at the top of its deque (newest first). A thief takes from the bottom (oldest, biggest task). Default parallelism of ForkJoinPool.commonPool()? availableProcessors() - 1 (at least 1). Change it with -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism. Which threads run a parallel stream? Common pool workers plus the thread that started the stream. Why is a blocking call inside a parallel stream a problem for the whole JVM? It holds a common pool worker, and that pool is shared by every parallel stream and every executor-less CompletableFuture. What does ForkJoinPool.managedBlock do? Tells the pool that a worker is about to block, so the pool can start a spare thread to keep its parallelism up. How big should a fork/join leaf be, by the ForkJoinTask Javadoc's rough rule? More than about 100 and fewer than about 10,000 basic computational steps. Then measure.

h: ForkJoinPool, work stealing and parallel streams · Go deeper
x: The virtual thread scheduler that the next track covers is also a ForkJoinPool, a separate instance from the common pool. JEP 444 describes it as a work-stealing ForkJoinPool that operates in FIFO mode. FIFO mode exists for tasks that are submitted and never joined, like events or messages: you get it with the asyncMode argument of the four-argument ForkJoinPool constructor, and each worker then takes its own tasks oldest first instead of newest first. The common pool has a few more knobs, all system properties read once when the pool starts: java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism, .threadFactory, .exceptionHandler and .maximumSpares, which caps the spare threads that managedBlock can add. Calling close() or shutdown() on the common pool does nothing, so library code can't switch it off by accident. Why does availableProcessors() - 1 make sense? Because the thread that calls invoke or starts a parallel stream works too. Seven workers plus the caller keep eight cores busy. It also means that on a 2-CPU container the common pool has one worker, and before JDK 25 that was enough for CompletableFuture to stop using it (lesson 6). Parallel streams don't use RecursiveTask internally. They use CountedCompleter, a ForkJoinTask that counts pending subtasks and runs a completion action when the count reaches zero, so no thread ever waits in join(). You rarely need to write one yourself, but it is the reason a parallel stream can split deep trees without stacking up joins.

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Name your threads, and know where failures go
x: The default names are pool-3-thread-7. In a thread dump of a service with eight pools, that tells you nothing. Name them, and the name shows up in every log line that prints the thread, in every thread dump and in every profiler: Java ThreadFactory named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(); // JDK 21+: ledger-0, ledger-1, ... ExecutorService ledgerPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, named); Kotlin val named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory() // JDK 21+: ledger-0, ledger-1, ... val ledgerPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, named) Before JDK 21 you write a small ThreadFactory with an AtomicInteger, or use Guava's ThreadFactoryBuilder. Now failures. Lesson 1 of this track showed that execute and submit treat an exception differently, and in production the difference decides whether you ever hear about it. With execute, the exception escapes the task. The worker thread dies, its UncaughtExceptionHandler runs, and the pool starts a new thread in its place. The default handler prints a stack trace to System.err, outside your logging framework and its request ids. With submit, the FutureTask catches the exception and keeps it. Nothing is printed. If nobody calls get(), which is normal for fire-and-forget work, the failure is gone. So an UncaughtExceptionHandler on the thread factory covers only half the cases. To cover both, catch failures in one place that every task passes through. submit, invokeAll and CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, pool) all end up in execute, so a ThreadPoolExecutor subclass that overrides execute and wraps each task sees everything. Report the failure there, with the request id, and don't rethrow: rethrowing only kills the worker and prints the same stack trace a second time. The lab builds exactly that pool. Find out who hears about a failure Run FailureDemo. Its threads are named ledger-N and have an UncaughtExceptionHandler. Before you run it, predict for each case: does the handler print, and which thread runs the next task? FailureDemo.java package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadFactory; /** Named threads with an UncaughtExceptionHandler. Which failures does the handler see? */ public class FailureDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ThreadFactory factory = Thread.ofPlatform() .name("ledger-", 0) // ledger-0, ledger-1, ... .uncaughtExceptionHandler((t, e) -> System.out.println(" handler: " + t.getName() + " died of " + e)) .factory(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, factory)) { System.out.println("1. execute() a task that throws"); pool.execute(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("ledger row locked"); }); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println(" the next task runs on " + pool.submit(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).get()); System.out.println("2. submit() a task that throws"); Future<?> f = pool.submit(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("negative amount"); }); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println(" (nothing printed) the next task runs on " + pool.submit(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).get()); try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println(" only get() shows it: " + e.getCause()); } } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.FailureDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l09/FailureDemo.java FailureDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** Named threads with an UncaughtExceptionHandler. Which failures does the handler see? */ fun main() { val factory = Thread.ofPlatform() .name("ledger-", 0) // ledger-0, ledger-1, ... .uncaughtExceptionHandler { t, e -> println(" handler: ${t.name} died of $e") } .factory() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, factory).use { pool -> println("1. execute() a task that throws") pool.execute { throw IllegalStateException("ledger row locked") } Thread.sleep(200) println(" the next task runs on " + pool.submit<String> { Thread.currentThread().name }.get()) println("2. submit() a task that throws") val f = pool.submit<Unit> { throw IllegalStateException("negative amount") } Thread.sleep(200) println(" (nothing printed) the next task runs on " + pool.submit<String> { Thread.currentThread().name }.get()) try { f.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println(" only get() shows it: ${e.cause}") } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.FailureDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l09/FailureDemo.kt For execute, the handler prints ledger-0 died of ... ledger row locked, and the next task runs on ledger-1: the pool replaced the dead worker. For submit, nothing prints, the next task still runs on ledger-1, and the exception only appears when get() is called. Thread.Builder (Java SE 25 API) docs Running pools in production is like running a busy restaurant kitchen. Name tags on every cook (thread names) let you see who is stuck. An order ticket travels with each dish (the request context), and every cook throws the old ticket away before taking the next one. The board by the pass shows how many tickets are waiting (queue size) and how many customers were turned away (rejections). The deadlock is two cooks who each started a dish that needs a sauce, put the sauce order at the back of the queue, and stand waiting for it, while nobody is left to make sauce. The analogy breaks at closing time: a kitchen can tell customers to leave. A pool has to stop its own intake first, then let each station finish in order, and it gets one fixed deadline from the orchestrator.

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Carry the request context across the hand-off
x: SLF4J's MDC (a per-thread map of values, such as the request id, that your log pattern prints), the current tracing span and the authenticated principal usually live in ThreadLocals. When you hand a task to a pool, they don't come along. The worker's ThreadLocal is empty, or it still holds a value that an earlier task left behind. Then the ledger write you are trying to trace during an incident logs no request id at all, or the wrong one. The fix has three steps: capture the value on the submitting thread, install it on the worker before the task runs, and put the worker's old value back afterwards: Java static Runnable withRequestId(Runnable task) { String captured = RequestContext.get(); // 1. on the submitting thread return () -> { String previous = RequestContext.get(); RequestContext.set(captured); // 2. on the worker try { task.run(); } finally { if (previous == null) RequestContext.clear(); else RequestContext.set(previous); // 3. never leak } }; } Kotlin fun withRequestId(task: Runnable): Runnable { val captured = RequestContext.get() // 1. on the submitting thread return Runnable { val previous = RequestContext.get() RequestContext.set(captured) // 2. on the worker try { task.run() } finally { if (previous == null) RequestContext.clear() else RequestContext.set(previous) // 3. never leak } } } The capture must happen in the method that is called on the submitting thread. Read the ThreadLocal inside the lambda and you read the worker's value, which is the bug you set out to fix. The finally matters as much: pool threads are reused, so whatever a task leaves behind is the next task's context. Don't make every caller remember to wrap. Wrap once, in the executor that everyone uses, as the lab does. MicroProfile Context Propagation's ManagedExecutor, which Quarkus provides, does the same for the contexts it knows about. Virtual threads don't change any of this: a new thread starts with empty ThreadLocals, except inheritable ones. Scoped values, final in JDK 25, are the newer tool for request context, and the virtual threads track covers them. Lose a request id, then leak one Run ContextDemo. The main thread sets req-42 and submits three tasks to a pool with one thread. Predict all three lines before you look. For line 3, find the task that caused it. ContextDemo.java package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** A request id in a ThreadLocal, handed to a pool three ways. */ public class ContextDemo { static final ThreadLocal<String> REQUEST_ID = new ThreadLocal<>(); // capture on the submitting thread, install on the worker, always clean up static Runnable withContext(Runnable task) { String captured = REQUEST_ID.get(); return () -> { String previous = REQUEST_ID.get(); REQUEST_ID.set(captured); try { task.run(); } finally { if (previous == null) REQUEST_ID.remove(); else REQUEST_ID.set(previous); } }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { REQUEST_ID.set("req-42"); pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("1. plain task sees: " + REQUEST_ID.get())).get(); pool.submit(withContext(() -> System.out.println("2. wrapped task sees: " + REQUEST_ID.get()))).get(); // a task that sets the ThreadLocal itself and forgets to remove it pool.submit(() -> REQUEST_ID.set("req-7")).get(); REQUEST_ID.remove(); // the next caller has no request pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("3. next task sees: " + REQUEST_ID.get() + " (left over from an earlier task)")).get(); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.ContextDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l09/ContextDemo.java ContextDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.Executors private val requestId = ThreadLocal<String?>() // capture on the submitting thread, install on the worker, always clean up private fun withContext(task: () -> Unit): Runnable { val captured = requestId.get() return Runnable { val previous = requestId.get() requestId.set(captured) try { task() } finally { if (previous == null) requestId.remove() else requestId.set(previous) } } } /** A request id in a ThreadLocal, handed to a pool three ways. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> requestId.set("req-42") pool.submit { println("1. plain task sees: ${requestId.get()}") }.get() pool.submit(withContext { println("2. wrapped task sees: ${requestId.get()}") }).get() // a task that sets the ThreadLocal itself and forgets to remove it pool.submit { requestId.set("req-7") }.get() requestId.remove() // the next caller has no request pool.submit { println("3. next task sees: ${requestId.get()} (left over from an earlier task)") }.get() } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.ContextDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l09/ContextDemo.kt Line 1 prints null: the plain task runs on a pool thread that never saw req-42. Line 2 prints req-42, because the wrapper captured it on main. Line 3 prints req-7, left over from the earlier task that set the ThreadLocal and never removed it. The new caller had no request at all. In a payment service, a named pool per dependency (issuer-, ledger-, fraud-) turns a thread dump during an incident into a map: 40 issuer- threads in a socket read means the issuer is slow, not your code. Put the request id or idempotency key in the MDC at the edge, and make every pool carry it, so a ledger write logged on ledger-7 can be traced back to the authorization that caused it. Count rejections on the authorization pool and alert on them, because each one is a declined payment. Settlement and statement jobs are where pool-induced deadlock likes to live: nested fan-outs on one shared pool that only hang at month-end volume. On shutdown, pause the Kafka consumer before draining the pools, so no offset is committed for work that never ran, and remember that a Temporal worker factory needs its own shutdown call, so activities in flight can finish.

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Watch the queue, the active count, rejections and time in queue
x: A pool is a queue in front of a few threads, and it is the first place a slow dependency shows up. Four numbers tell you most of what you need. The queue size, getQueue().size(). A queue that keeps growing means tasks arrive faster than they finish. Little's law from lesson 3 of this track says the wait grows with it. The active count, getActiveCount(), compared with the maximum. A pool pinned at its maximum for minutes is saturated, and it's usually waiting on something downstream rather than working. Rejections. ThreadPoolExecutor doesn't count them for you. Wrap the RejectedExecutionHandler in one that increments a counter and then throws, as MetricsDemo does. Every rejection is a request you turned away, so alert on it. Time in queue. This is latency the caller feels and the task never measures. Record the time when a task is submitted, in the same wrapper that carries the context, and compare it when the task starts. The getters are approximate. The Javadoc says so, because the threads keep changing them while you read. That's fine for a dashboard and wrong for program logic. Micrometer's ExecutorServiceMetrics binds most of these numbers for you. Of the four, queue time and rejections are what your customers feel. A pool with an empty queue and no rejections is healthy, however busy its threads look. Read a pool's dashboard MetricsDemo sends 10 tasks of 300 ms to a pool with 2 threads and a queue of 4. Predict how many are rejected, and when the queue empties. Run it and read the table row by row. MetricsDemo.java package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** 10 tasks of 300 ms hit a pool of 2 threads with a queue of 4. Watch the numbers a dashboard would show. */ public class MetricsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { LongAdder rejected = new LongAdder(); ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4), Thread.ofPlatform().name("auth-", 0).factory(), (task, executor) -> { rejected.increment(); // count it, then fail like AbortPolicy throw new RejectedExecutionException("auth pool full"); }); for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { try { pool.execute(() -> sleep(300)); } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { // the caller would answer 503 here } } System.out.println(" ms threads active queued done rejected"); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) { System.out.printf("%4d %7d %6d %6d %4d %8d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getActiveCount(), pool.getQueue().size(), pool.getCompletedTaskCount(), rejected.sum()); sleep(200); } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.MetricsDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l09/MetricsDemo.java MetricsDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder /** 10 tasks of 300 ms hit a pool of 2 threads with a queue of 4. Watch the numbers a dashboard would show. */ fun main() { val rejected = LongAdder() val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(4), Thread.ofPlatform().name("auth-", 0).factory()) { _, _ -> rejected.increment() // count it, then fail like AbortPolicy throw RejectedExecutionException("auth pool full") } repeat(10) { try { pool.execute { Thread.sleep(300) } } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { // the caller would answer 503 here } } println(" ms threads active queued done rejected") val t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(6) { println("%4d %7d %6d %6d %4d %8d".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.poolSize, pool.activeCount, pool.queue.size, pool.completedTaskCount, rejected.sum())) Thread.sleep(200) } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.MetricsDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l09/MetricsDemo.kt Two tasks run, four wait in the queue and four are rejected right away (2 + 4 = 6 accepted). Every 300 ms two more finish: the queue goes 4, 2, 0 while done climbs 0, 2, 4, 6, and active drops to 0 after about 900 ms. The rejected count stays at 4. ThreadPoolExecutor (Java SE 25 API): hooks and monitoring docs

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Pool-induced deadlock: tasks that wait for tasks in the same pool
x: Here is a statement job that works in every test: Java pool.submit(() -> { Future<List<String>> lines = pool.submit(() -> ledger.lines(merchant)); // a task inside a task return render(merchant, lines.get()); // waits for it }); Kotlin pool.submit<String> { val lines = pool.submit<List<String>> { ledger.lines(merchant) } // a task inside a task render(merchant, lines.get()) // waits for it } With 20 threads and 5 merchants, it's fine. At month-end it gets 400 merchants. The first 20 statement tasks take all 20 threads. Each one submits its fetch, and the fetches join the back of the queue, behind 380 statement tasks. Every thread now waits for a task that can only run on a free thread, and no thread will ever be free. The CPU drops to zero. Nothing throws. A thread dump shows no "deadlock found" line, because no lock is involved: every thread is just WAITING in FutureTask.get. Java Concurrency in Practice calls this thread starvation deadlock. Three fixes, in the order I'd try them: Don't block inside the pool. Compose: supplyAsync(() -> ledger.lines(m), pool).thenApply(lines -> render(m, lines)). The render step runs as a callback when the fetch completes, so no thread waits. Only the caller joins at the end. Don't split what doesn't need splitting. If the statement task only waits for the fetch, do the fetch inline in the same task. Give each stage its own pool. Statement tasks may wait for a separate fetch pool, as long as fetch tasks never wait for the statement pool. That's a bulkhead from lesson 3. A cached pool with no thread limit also makes the hang go away, by starting a thread for every waiting task. That moves the problem to memory and to the database connection pool. join() inside a CompletableFuture stage is the same bug, which is why lesson 6 of this track warned against it. Hang a pool on purpose Run DeadlockDemo: two statement tasks on a pool of two threads, each waiting for a fast fetch on the same pool. Read the active and queued counts. Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which composes the fetch and the render with CompletableFuture. Predict how long it takes. DeadlockDemo.java package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; /** Two statement tasks on a 2-thread pool, each waiting for a fetch on the same pool. Pass "fixed" to compose instead. */ public class DeadlockDemo { static List<String> fetchLines(String merchant) { return List.of(merchant + "-1", merchant + "-2"); // fast: the problem isn't speed } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("stmt-", 0).factory()); try { if (fixed) { List<CompletableFuture<String>> statements = List.of("m1", "m2").stream() .map(m -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchLines(m), pool) .thenApply(lines -> m + ": " + lines.size() + " lines")) // nobody waits inside the pool .toList(); statements.forEach(s -> System.out.println(s.join())); return; } List<Future<String>> statements = List.of("m1", "m2").stream() .map(m -> pool.submit(() -> { Future<List<String>> lines = pool.submit(() -> fetchLines(m)); // queued behind us return m + ": " + lines.get().size() + " lines"; // waits for it })) .toList(); Thread.sleep(300); ThreadPoolExecutor tpe = (ThreadPoolExecutor) pool; System.out.printf("after 300 ms: active=%d, queued=%d, completed=%d%n", tpe.getActiveCount(), tpe.getQueue().size(), tpe.getCompletedTaskCount()); try { System.out.println(statements.get(0).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); } catch (TimeoutException e) { System.out.println("no statement after 2 s: both threads wait for fetches that can never start"); } } finally { pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupts the stuck get() calls } } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.DeadlockDemo labs/executors/src/demo/java/workbench/executors/l09/DeadlockDemo.java DeadlockDemo.kt package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException private fun fetchLines(merchant: String) = listOf("$merchant-1", "$merchant-2") // fast: the problem isn't speed /** Two statement tasks on a 2-thread pool, each waiting for a fetch on the same pool. Pass "fixed" to compose instead. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("stmt-", 0).factory()) try { if (fixed) { val statements = listOf("m1", "m2").map { m -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fetchLines(m) }, pool) .thenApply { lines -> "$m: ${lines.size} lines" } // nobody waits inside the pool } statements.forEach { println(it.join()) } return } val statements = listOf("m1", "m2").map { m -> pool.submit<String> { val lines = pool.submit<List<String>> { fetchLines(m) } // queued behind us "$m: ${lines.get().size} lines" // waits for it } } Thread.sleep(300) val tpe = pool as ThreadPoolExecutor println("after 300 ms: active=${tpe.activeCount}, queued=${tpe.queue.size}, completed=${tpe.completedTaskCount}") try { println(statements[0].get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { println("no statement after 2 s: both threads wait for fetches that can never start") } } finally { pool.shutdownNow() // interrupts the stuck get() calls } } ./gradlew :executors:demo -Pmain=workbench.executors.l09.DeadlockDemoKt labs/executors/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/executors/l09/DeadlockDemo.kt The default run shows active=2, queued=2, completed=0 after 300 ms, then gives up after 2 s with no statement, although each fetch takes microseconds. The fixed run prints both statements at once, on the same two threads. Both threads wait for fetches that sit in the queue behind them. The fetches need a free thread, and none will ever be free.

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Shut down in order, with a deadline
x: When Kubernetes stops a pod it sends SIGTERM, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 seconds unless you change it) and then kills the process. Everything in flight has to finish, or be recorded as lost, inside that window. The order matters: Java void stop() throws InterruptedException { intake.stop(); // 1. no new work comes in long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(20); // inside the 30 s grace period for (ExecutorService pool : List.of(authPool, ledgerPool)) { // 2. upstream first: auth feeds ledger pool.shutdown(); long left = Math.max(0, deadline - System.nanoTime()); if (!pool.awaitTermination(left, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow(); // 3. interrupt what is still running log.warn("{} tasks never started", neverStarted.size()); // 4. say what was lost } } } Kotlin fun stop() { intake.stop() // 1. no new work comes in val deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(20) // inside the 30 s grace period for (pool in listOf(authPool, ledgerPool)) { // 2. upstream first: auth feeds ledger pool.shutdown() val left = maxOf(0L, deadline - System.nanoTime()) if (!pool.awaitTermination(left, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) { val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow() // 3. interrupt what is still running log.warn("{} tasks never started", neverStarted.size) // 4. say what was lost } } } Stop intake first: pause the Kafka consumer, or fail the readiness probe so the load balancer stops sending requests. Otherwise new work keeps arriving at pools that are trying to drain. Then shut pools down upstream first. authPool's tasks submit into ledgerPool. Shut down ledgerPool first and the authorizations still running in authPool get a RejectedExecutionException when they try to post to the ledger, which turns a clean shutdown into half-finished payments. Give the whole sequence one deadline, shorter than the grace period, and share it between the pools. When a pool misses it, shutdownNow() interrupts what is still running and returns the tasks that never started. Log them, with request ids if your wrapper keeps them, so somebody can replay them. Don't forget the schedulers from lesson 5: after shutdown() their periodic tasks stop, which is what you want. In Quarkus, put this in a method that observes ShutdownEvent, or in a @PreDestroy method on the bean that owns the pools. Never leave a pool for garbage collection to clean up: its threads keep it alive. Check yourself: why does stop() share one 20-second deadline between the pools instead of giving each pool 20 seconds? Because the waits add up. Two pools at 20 seconds each can take 40, and Kubernetes kills the process at 30, in the middle of the ledger pool's drain, before the log.warn line can say what was lost. The most common mistake is fire-and-forget with submit: pool.submit(() -> audit.write(event)) with nobody keeping the Future. The audit write starts failing on a schema change, every exception sits in a Future that is garbage the moment it's created, and nothing is logged for days. People use submit because it's the method they know, and the failure path never runs in tests. Use execute for fire-and-forget work, or better, run every pool through a wrapper that reports failures from both execute and submit with the request id, the way the lab's ProductionPool does.

x: Carrying the MDC: an executor wrapper vs a coroutine context element MdcExecutor.java (SLF4J) static Executor withMdc(Executor delegate) { return task -> { Map<String, String> captured = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(); // 1. on the submitting thread delegate.execute(() -> { Map<String, String> previous = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(); if (captured != null) MDC.setContextMap(captured); else MDC.clear(); // 2. on the worker try { task.run(); } finally { if (previous != null) MDC.setContextMap(previous); else MDC.clear(); // 3. never leak } }); }; } CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> ledger.post(entry), withMdc(ledgerPool)); MdcCoroutine.kt (kotlinx-coroutines-slf4j) // MDCContext() copies the MDC now and installs it every time the coroutine // runs, on whichever thread that is, then restores the thread's own MDC scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO + MDCContext()) { ledger.post(entry) delay(100) // may resume on another thread log.info("posted") // the request id is still in the MDC } // the same idea for your own ThreadLocal scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO + requestId.asContextElement(value = "req-42")) { /* ... */ } The Java wrapper installs the context once, because a task stays on one thread from start to finish. A coroutine can move to another thread at every suspension point, so a wrapper around the whole coroutine wouldn't be enough. MDCContext() and asContextElement are thread context elements: the dispatcher installs the value each time the coroutine resumes on a thread and restores the thread's old value when it suspends. One trap: an MDC.put inside the coroutine is lost at the next suspension, because the element keeps reinstalling the map it captured. The kotlinx docs say to wrap the change in withContext(MDCContext()).

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Quiz
x: A report service uses a fixed pool of 4. Each report task submits two sub-queries to the same pool and calls get() on both. It passes every test and hangs at month-end with the CPU near zero. What happened? The sub-queries got slow, so the reports need more time Four report tasks hold all four threads, and each waits for sub-queries queued behind other reports, so nothing can ever finish Two report tasks locked each other's monitors The queue overflowed and the sub-queries were rejected This is pool-induced deadlock. The awaited tasks need a free thread, and all the threads are busy waiting for them. Slowness wouldn't drop the CPU to zero forever, no monitors are involved, and a fixed pool's queue is unbounded, so nothing is rejected. A request thread puts requestId=req-42 in the MDC and submits a task to a fixed pool. The task logs a line. With no context propagation in place, which request id is on that line? req-42, because pool threads inherit the MDC None, every time, because pool threads clear their MDC between tasks Whatever that pool thread last had: often none, sometimes a stale id from an earlier task The logging call throws, because the MDC isn't thread-safe The MDC is a ThreadLocal on the worker thread. That thread was created long ago and is reused, so it holds nothing, or whatever an earlier task put there and didn't clean up. Nothing clears it between tasks unless your wrapper does. Which number warns you first that a bounded ThreadPoolExecutor is falling behind, before it starts rejecting? getPoolSize() getCompletedTaskCount() getLargestPoolSize() getQueue().size() climbing, or the time tasks spend in the queue A queue that keeps growing means arrivals outpace completions, and every queued task's wait grows with it. Pool size is fixed in a fixed pool, the completed count only rises, and the largest pool size is history. When the queue is full, rejections start. Intake hands work to enrichPool, whose tasks submit to ledgerPool. The pod gets SIGTERM. In what order do you shut down? Stop intake, shut down enrichPool and wait for it, then shut down ledgerPool and wait for it Shut down ledgerPool, then enrichPool, then stop intake Call shutdownNow() on both pools at once to be quick Stop intake, then shut down ledgerPool first because it holds the money Upstream first. While enrichPool drains, its tasks still submit to ledgerPool, so ledgerPool must keep accepting work until then. Shutting it down first makes those submissions fail with RejectedExecutionException, and shutdownNow on both interrupts work that could have finished. From "Inside ThreadPoolExecutor": a ProductionPool has 4 threads and a queue of 100, with the default AbortPolicy. 200 slow tasks arrive at once. How many are rejected? 0 96 100 196 Four tasks start the four threads, the next 100 fill the queue, and core equals max, so the pool can't grow. The remaining 96 are rejected with RejectedExecutionException, which is what a bounded queue is for: the caller hears about the overload at once.

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Key terms
x: Thread factory The object a pool asks for new threads; it sets their names, daemon flag and exception handler. UncaughtExceptionHandler Code that runs when an exception escapes a thread's run method. MDC Mapped Diagnostic Context: per-thread key-value pairs that SLF4J adds to every log line. Context propagation Copying thread-local state such as a request id from the submitting thread to the worker. Pool-induced deadlock Every thread in a pool waits for a task that is queued in that same pool. Also called thread starvation deadlock. Graceful shutdown Stopping intake, letting in-flight work finish within a deadline, and recording what didn't. How do you name pool threads on JDK 21+? Pass Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory() to the executor. Threads are named ledger-0, ledger-1, ... Which pool failures reach an UncaughtExceptionHandler? Only tasks run with execute(). With submit() the exception is stored in the Future and nothing is printed. Why does an MDC value disappear when you hand a task to a pool? The MDC is a ThreadLocal, and the task runs on another thread. Capture it at submission and install it in the worker. Why must a context wrapper restore the worker's value in finally? Pool threads are reused. Whatever one task leaves behind is the next task's context. What is pool-induced deadlock? Tasks in a bounded pool block waiting for other tasks queued in the same pool; every thread waits and the awaited tasks never start. Name two fixes for pool-induced deadlock. Compose instead of blocking (supplyAsync(...).thenApply(...)), or give each stage its own pool so waits never point back into the same pool. In what order do you shut down chained pools? Stop intake, then shut down the upstream pool and wait, then the downstream one, all within one deadline.

h: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown · Go deeper
x: Why is the JVM's deadlock detector silent? jcmd <pid> Thread.print (and ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads) look for cycles of threads that each hold a lock another one needs: monitors from synchronized, and ownable synchronizers such as ReentrantLock. A thread waiting in Future.get() parks on the future, which has no owner, so there is no cycle to find. Names and stack traces are your only tools, which is one more reason to name threads. The ThreadPoolExecutor Javadoc shows a second way to catch failures: override the afterExecute hook, which runs on the worker after each task: Java @Override protected void afterExecute(Runnable r, Throwable t) { super.afterExecute(r, t); if (t == null && r instanceof Future<?> f && f.isDone()) { try { f.get(); } catch (CancellationException e) { t = e; } catch (ExecutionException e) { t = e.getCause(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } if (t != null) log.error("task failed on {}", Thread.currentThread().getName(), t); } Kotlin override fun afterExecute(r: Runnable, t: Throwable?) { super.afterExecute(r, t) var failure = t if (failure == null && r is Future<*> && r.isDone) { try { r.get() } catch (e: CancellationException) { failure = e } catch (e: ExecutionException) { failure = e.cause } catch (e: InterruptedException) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt() } } if (failure != null) log.error("task failed on {}", Thread.currentThread().name, failure) } It works, with two limits. It can't stop an execute failure from killing the worker, because the exception is rethrown after the hook runs. And it doesn't know the submitter's request id unless a wrapper stored it. That's why the lab wraps execute. Its sister hook, beforeExecute(Thread, Runnable), is the natural place to measure time in queue, and terminated() runs once when the pool has fully stopped.

h: Virtual threads
x: Project Loom from the inside: carriers, pinning, structured concurrency and scoped values. By the end of this track you can explain what a virtual thread is and what happens when it blocks, run blocking code with one virtual thread per task, cap what reaches a database or partner API with a shared Semaphore, find and fix the traps (pinning, ThreadLocal caches, CPU-bound work), and move a real pool-based service to virtual threads while measuring that it worked. You also meet the two Loom features around them: structured concurrency, still preview, and scoped values, final in JDK 25. You need the basics from the first track (starting, joining and interrupting threads, locks and semaphores) and from the executors track (ExecutorService, Future, and sizing a pool with Little's law). Install JDK 25, the current LTS. JDK 24 removed most pinning, and the advice changes with it, so the lessons always say which JDK a fact applies to. The labs live in labs/vthreads, one package per lesson (workbench.vthreads.l01 to l06). They compile for JDK 21 and use only final JDK 21 APIs, so they run on 21 and on 25. Lessons 1 to 5 have Java labs, and lesson 6 is in Kotlin. Run ./gradlew :vthreads:test --tests 'workbench.vthreads.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and use solutionTest to check the reference answers. The Try-it demos run with ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=.... Lesson 5's preview demos live in labs/vthreads/preview/ and run outside Gradle on JDK 25. A platform thread is an OS thread, so a server gets thousands, not millions. Little's law (in flight = rate × time) says how many a blocking service needs. A virtual thread is a Thread that unmounts from its carrier at blocking calls. Its stack waits on the heap, and a few carriers (one per core) run all of them. Virtual threads give scale, not speed: one request is no faster, and CPU-bound work gains nothing because there is no time slicing. Use one new virtual thread per task, usually through newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() in try-with-resources. Never pool them. Limit a scarce downstream with one shared Semaphore, held only around its calls, sized from what the downstream allows. On JDK 21 to 23, blocking inside synchronized pins the carrier. JDK 24 fixed it; on JDK 25 class initializers and native frames still pin. Find pins with JFR's jdk.VirtualThreadPinned. ThreadLocal caches become one object per task. Share immutable objects, and move request context to arguments or scoped values (final in JDK 25). Structured concurrency ties subtasks to a block, cancels siblings on failure and waits for all of them. StructuredTaskScope is preview until JDK 28. Migrating means writing down the limits the old pool gave you, keeping connection pools small, and measuring in-flight requests and queue lengths, not thread counts.

Limiting a downstream Java private final Semaphore issuerLimit = new Semaphore(20, true); // one per downstream, shared by all callers Auth authorize(Payment p) throws InterruptedException { issuerLimit.acquire(); // outside the try try { return http.authorize(p); // only the call that needs the limit } finally { issuerLimit.release(); } } Kotlin private val issuerLimit = Semaphore(20, true) // one per downstream, shared by all callers fun authorize(p: Payment): Auth { issuerLimit.acquire() // outside the try try { return http.authorize(p) // only the call that needs the limit } finally { issuerLimit.release() } } Use tryAcquire(200, MILLISECONDS) to fail fast with a 503 instead of waiting forever. Watch requests in flight, each semaphore's queue length, and the pool's pending connections. A growing queue with flat throughput marks the saturated downstream. Structured concurrency (JDK 25, preview) and scoped values (JDK 25, final) Java static final ScopedValue<String> TENANT = ScopedValue.newInstance(); Quote quote(String id) throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // fail fast by default Subtask<Customer> customer = scope.fork(() -> crm.find(id)); Subtask<Limit> limit = scope.fork(() -> limits.check(id)); // forks can read TENANT scope.join(); // JDK 25: FailedException; JDK 27: ExecutionException return new Quote(customer.get(), limit.get()); } // close(): no subtask left running } // caller: ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").call(() -> quote(id)); // call() may throw Kotlin val TENANT: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() fun quote(id: String): Quote = StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope -> // fail fast by default val customer = scope.fork(Callable { crm.find(id) }) val limit = scope.fork(Callable { limits.check(id) }) // forks can read TENANT scope.join() // JDK 25: FailedException; JDK 27: ExecutionException Quote(customer.get(), limit.get()) } // close(): no subtask left running // caller: ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(Runnable { quote(id) }) Preview code needs --enable-preview and the matching JDK. h: Virtual threads: track quiz
x: An endpoint receives 1,500 requests per second, and each one spends 200 ms waiting on a partner API. With one thread per request, about how many threads are busy at once? About 8 About 300 About 1,500 About 7,500 Little's law: in flight = 1,500/s × 0.2 s = 300. With thread-per-request, that's also the number of threads. 7,500 multiplies by 5 instead of 0.2, and 1,500 forgets the time. A virtual thread prints Thread.currentThread() before and after Thread.sleep(10). What can differ between the two lines? The thread id, because a new virtual thread continues the work Nothing can differ: a virtual thread stays on one carrier for life The carrier worker shown after the @; the virtual thread itself is the same The second print never happens, because sleep throws on a virtual thread currentThread() always returns the virtual thread, so its id stays the same. The sleep unmounts it, and when it wakes, any free carrier can mount it, so the ForkJoinPool-1-worker-N part of toString() can change. 10,000 virtual threads must call a fraud API that allows 50 concurrent calls. What do you use? -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full, and check that nothing is printed jstack <pid>, looking for blocked carriers A JFR recording with jdk.VirtualThreadPinned, printed with jfr print Thread.getAllStackTraces() from a debug endpoint The JFR event is on by default with a 20 ms threshold and records the stack. -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads was removed in JDK 24, so its silence proves nothing. jstack and getAllStackTraces() don't show parked virtual threads. Which statement about JDK 25 is true? Scoped values are final; StructuredTaskScope is still a preview API Both scoped values and StructuredTaskScope are final StructuredTaskScope is final; scoped values are still preview Both are still preview and need --enable-preview JEP 506 made scoped values final in JDK 25. So close() stops waiting while cleanup still runs. shutdownNow() interrupts without completing the futures. A service ran on a fixed pool of 20 threads with a 20-connection database pool. After moving to one virtual thread per request, the pool times out at every peak. What is the right fix? Raise the connection pool to 2,000 connections Go back to the fixed pool of 20 threads for all request handling Add a shared Semaphore(20) around the database calls only, with a tryAcquire deadline Raise the pool's connection timeout to several minutes The fixed pool was an unwritten limit on the database. h: The thread-per-request wall · A platform thread is an OS thread, and you only get thousands
x:
Before JDK 21, every java.lang.Thread was a thin wrapper around one operating system thread. The JDK now calls these platform threads. The mapping is one to one: new Thread(r).start() asks the kernel for a thread, and the kernel schedules it. That costs real resources. Each platform thread reserves a stack up front: 1 MB by default on 64-bit Linux (-Xss, or ThreadStackSize in java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal). The kernel commits the pages lazily, but it still keeps the reservation, guard pages and its own bookkeeping per thread. Starting a thread is a system call. Switching between thousands of runnable threads costs the kernel time and costs you CPU caches. So a JVM is comfortable with hundreds of platform threads, and survives a few thousand. Push to tens of thousands and you start fighting ulimits (the per-user limits the OS puts on processes and threads), memory and the scheduler. A million is out of reach. Servers have used one style for decades anyway: thread-per-request. Tomcat, the Quarkus worker pool, and every JDBC-based service give each request one thread for its whole life. The code is easy to read. A stack trace tells you the whole story of a request. A debugger steps through it line by line. ThreadLocal context such as the logging MDC or the current transaction just works, because the request never changes threads. The catch is in the phrase "whole life". The thread stays assigned to the request while the request waits for the database, the fraud service and the card issuer. A blocked thread does no work, but nobody else can use it. You run out of threads long before you run out of CPU. Count what a thread costs Run ThreadCostDemo with the command below. It starts 4,000 platform threads that all stay alive until it releases them, then does the same with 100,000 virtual threads. Before you look at the output, guess which run finishes first: 4,000 platform threads or 25 times as many virtual threads? Try -Pargs='5000 1000000' for a million virtual threads. Leave the platform count at 5,000 or less on a laptop. ThreadCostDemo.java package workbench.vthreads.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; /** * Starts N threads that all block on one latch, so they exist at the same time, * then releases them. First with platform threads, then with virtual threads. * *

Args: platform count, virtual count. Default: 4000 100000. * Keep the platform count at 5,000 or below on a laptop. */ public class ThreadCostDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { int platform = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 4_000; int virtual = args.length > 1 ? Picture a restaurant where each waiter is assigned to one table from the moment guests sit down until they pay. While the kitchen cooks, the waiter stands at the table and does nothing. With 20 waiters you serve 20 tables at once, however many seats are empty, and guests queue at the door. Async code is one waiter running between many tables with a notepad of what each table needs next. It works, but the notepad gets complicated. If the slow part is the cooking itself (CPU work) or a pantry with room for only 20 cooks (a connection pool), more waiters don't help.

h: The thread-per-request wall · Little's law tells you how many threads you need
x:
One formula explains the wall. Little's law says that in any stable system: L = λ × W requests in flight = arrival rate × time each request spends inside It holds for supermarkets, call centers and servers, whatever the details. With thread-per-request, every request in flight holds one thread, so L is also the number of threads you need. Take a payment authorization. It parses the request (2 ms of CPU), calls the fraud service (40 ms), calls the card issuer (120 ms), writes to the ledger (35 ms) and replies (3 ms). That is 200 ms per request, and only 5 ms of it uses a CPU. The figure below shows the shape. At peak the service gets 1,500 authorizations per second: L = 1,500/s × 0.2 s = 300 requests in flight = 300 threads The worker pool has 200 threads. Turn the formula around to get the most it can serve: λ max = L / W = 200 / 0.2 s = 1,000 requests per second The other 500 requests per second wait in the pool's queue. The queue grows every second, so latency grows every second, and CPU sits at a few percent. Dashboards show a slow service with idle machines. Now the issuer has a bad day and its calls take 1,200 ms. W becomes 1.28 s and the same 200 threads cap you at 156 requests per second. A slow dependency shrinks your throughput even though your own code did not change. That is how one slow downstream service takes down a whole thread-per-request fleet. You have two ways out. Make W smaller, which you often can't, because the issuer is not yours. Or make L cheaper: hold the request somewhere other than an expensive OS thread while it waits. Predict the wall, then hit it WallDemo runs 2,000 fake authorizations that each block for 100 ms, first on a fixed pool of 100 threads. Use Little's law to predict the pool's time before you run it. Run it with the command below. Ignore the virtual thread line for now. Predict again for a pool of 200, then run with -Pargs='200 2000 100'. Then try a 300 ms latency: -Pargs='100 2000 300'. h: The thread-per-request wall · The async workaround, and what it costs
x: The industry's first answer was to stop holding a thread while waiting. Async code hands the thread back at every wait and continues later on whatever thread is free: Java // blocking: one thread per request, held for all 200 ms Receipt authorize(Payment p) { Risk risk = fraud.check(p); // 40 ms Auth auth = issuer.authorize(p, risk); // 120 ms return ledger.record(p, auth); // 35 ms } // async: the thread goes back to the pool at every wait CompletableFuture<Receipt> authorizeAsync(Payment p) { return fraud.checkAsync(p) .thenCompose(risk -> issuer.authorizeAsync(p, risk)) .thenCompose(auth -> ledger.recordAsync(p, auth)); } Kotlin // blocking: one thread per request, held for all 200 ms fun authorize(p: Payment): Receipt { val risk = fraud.check(p) // 40 ms val auth = issuer.authorize(p, risk) // 120 ms return ledger.record(p, auth) // 35 ms } // async: the thread goes back to the pool at every wait fun authorizeAsync(p: Payment): CompletableFuture<Receipt> = fraud.checkAsync(p) .thenCompose { risk -> issuer.authorizeAsync(p, risk) } .thenCompose { auth -> ledger.recordAsync(p, auth) } CompletableFuture, Reactor's Mono and Flux, Vert.x and Quarkus's reactive stack all work this way. A handful of event-loop threads, about one per core, can keep thousands of requests in flight. It works, and it is why reactive stacks became popular. You pay for it in the code. Every library on the request path must be async too. JDBC is blocking, so you need a reactive driver. One blocking call on an event-loop thread stalls every request that shares that loop, and nothing warns you. The call stack stops meaning anything. When issuer.authorizeAsync fails, the stack trace shows pool worker frames and lambda names, not authorize calling issuer.authorize. A debugger can't step from one stage to the next. A profiler shows time in the event loop. Control flow turns into operators. A try/catch becomes exceptionally or onErrorResume. A loop with an early exit becomes a recursive chain. ThreadLocal context (the MDC, the security context, the transaction) does not follow the request from thread to thread, so you need a context propagation library. Kotlin coroutines get closest to the blocking style. A suspend function, which the compiler can pause at a wait and resume later on any thread, reads top to bottom. Coroutines still need suspend-aware libraries, though. A blocking JDBC call inside a coroutine blocks a real thread, and you are back to pool sizing with Dispatchers.IO, the coroutine library's shared pool for blocking calls. If your code is already reactive and works, keep it. Most payment services are plain blocking code on a pool, and rewriting them as async chains to save threads is a poor trade. Check yourself: an async service runs on 8 event-loop threads, and someone adds a blocking 50 ms JDBC call to one handler. How many of those requests can the service now serve per second? At most 160. Each loop thread is stuck for the whole 50 ms of every call, so Little's law with L = 8 and W = 0.05 s gives 8 / 0.05 = 160, however fast the CPU is. Every other request on those loops waits behind the blocked calls.

h: The thread-per-request wall · Virtual threads: cheap threads, same blocking code
x: JDK 21 took the other way out: make threads cheap. Virtual threads became a final feature in JDK 21 (JEP 444, the JDK Enhancement Proposal that defines them). A virtual thread is a normal java.lang.Thread, but the JDK schedules it, not the OS. It runs on a small pool of platform threads, about one per core. When it blocks on a socket read, a sleep or a lock, the JDK parks it, saves its stack on the heap, and lets another virtual thread use that platform thread. Lesson 2 of this track shows how. A virtual thread starts in a few microseconds and needs a small heap object that grows with its stack. A million of them fit on a laptop. So you keep the blocking authorize method and give every request its own virtual thread: Java try (ExecutorService perRequest = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (Payment p : incoming) { perRequest.submit(() -> authorize(p)); // blocking code, cheap thread } } // close() waits for every task Kotlin Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perRequest -> for (p in incoming) { perRequest.submit(Callable { authorize(p) }) // blocking code, cheap thread } } // use {} closes the executor, and close() waits for every task Little's law still holds. At 1,500 requests per second and 200 ms you still have 300 requests in flight. They just don't cost 300 OS threads anymore. If the issuer slows to 1.2 s, you have 1,920 in flight, and that is fine too. Be clear about what virtual threads do not change: One request is not faster. It still waits 200 ms. Virtual threads give you scale (more requests in flight), not speed. CPU-bound work gains nothing. With 8 cores, at most 8 virtual threads compute at once. Downstream limits stay. Your ledger database pool still has 20 connections. With the thread cap gone, 300 requests reach that pool at once, and the bottleneck moves there. Lessons 3 and 6 of this track deal with it. The lab makes the wall measurable: the same blocking handler on a fixed pool and on one virtual thread per task. Run the same wall on virtual threads Run WallDemo again and look at the second line this time. Run -Pargs='100 2000 300'. Predict first: does the virtual thread time triple like the pool's did? Run -Pargs='100 5000 100'. Predict both lines before you look. The virtual line finishes 2,000 requests in a little over 100 ms (one run here: 165 ms), because all 2,000 sleep at the same time. With 300 ms latency it takes a little over 300 ms: the time follows the latency of one request, not the number of requests. With 5,000 requests the pool needs about 5 s and the virtual run still takes well under a second. The most common mistake is reading "slow and idle" as a CPU or code problem. Latency climbs, throughput flattens, CPU is at 5%, so the team adds pods or raises the pool to 2,000 threads. More threads does lift the cap for a while, but each one reserves 1 MB of stack and adds scheduling work, and the extra requests often just pile up on the database pool instead. Do the arithmetic first: measure W, compute L = λ × W for the peak rate, and compare L with your thread pool and with every pool behind it. Then fix the resource that is actually full.

h: The thread-per-request wall · Java and Kotlin
x: Blocking code that scales: virtual threads vs coroutines Java 21+: virtual threads // plain blocking code, one cheap virtual thread per payment List<Receipt> authorizeAll(List<Payment> batch) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<Receipt>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (Payment p : batch) futures.add(perTask.submit(() -> authorize(p))); List<Receipt> receipts = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<Receipt> f : futures) receipts.add(f.get()); return receipts; } } Receipt authorize(Payment p) { Risk risk = fraud.check(p); // ordinary blocking HTTP call Auth auth = issuer.authorize(p, risk); return ledger.record(p, auth); // ordinary JDBC } Kotlin: kotlinx.coroutines // suspend functions: the compiler turns them into state machines suspend fun authorizeAll(batch: List<Payment>): List<Receipt> = coroutineScope { batch.map { p -> async { authorize(p) } }.awaitAll() } suspend fun authorize(p: Payment): Receipt { val risk = fraud.check(p) // must itself suspend to free the thread val auth = issuer.authorize(p, risk) return ledger.record(p, auth) // blocking JDBC here would block a real thread } Both read top to bottom, and both keep thousands of payments in flight on a few OS threads. The difference is where the magic lives. Kotlin does it in the compiler: only suspend functions can give the thread back, so every waiting call on the path has to be suspend-aware, and a blocking JDBC call needs withContext(Dispatchers.IO), which is a thread pool again. Virtual threads do it in the JDK at run time: any blocking JDK call (sockets, sleep, locks, BlockingQueue) parks the virtual thread, so existing JDBC drivers and HTTP clients work unchanged. You can mix the two: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher() runs coroutines on virtual threads, which helps when they call blocking libraries.

h: The thread-per-request wall · Key terms
x: Platform thread A Java thread that is one OS thread. Expensive, so you get thousands. Virtual thread A Java thread scheduled by the JDK on a few OS threads. Cheap, so you can have millions. Thread-per-request A server style where each request gets one thread for its whole life. Little's law In flight = arrival rate × time inside. L = λ × W. Throughput How many requests finish per second. Latency How long one request takes from start to end. Event loop A thread that runs many requests' callbacks in turn and must never block. State Little's law. L = λ × W: the number of requests in flight equals the arrival rate times the time each request spends in the system. 1,500 requests per second, 200 ms each. How many threads does thread-per-request need? 300 (1,500 × 0.2). 200 threads, each request holds one for 200 ms. What is the maximum throughput? 1,000 requests per second (200 / 0.2 s). Above that the queue grows, even with idle CPU. What is a platform thread? A java.lang.Thread backed one to one by an OS thread, with its own stack (1 MB reserved by default on 64-bit Linux). Do virtual threads make a single request faster? No. They give scale (more requests in flight at once), not speed. Each request waits just as long. In which JDK did virtual threads become final, and under which JEP? JDK 21, JEP 444. What happens when a handler on an event-loop thread makes a blocking JDBC call? It blocks the event-loop thread, so every other request on that loop stalls until the call returns.

h: The thread-per-request wall · Go deeper
x: Little's law needs only one assumption: the system is stable, meaning requests leave as fast as they arrive over the long run. It says nothing about the shape of the traffic or the order of service, which is why it works for a payments API as well as for a supermarket. It does not tell you what happens near the limit. As a pool approaches 100% busy, the queue does not grow smoothly. Short bursts above the average rate make requests wait, and the waits add up faster than the load. A pool that is busy 95% of the time has much longer queues than one at 80%, even though it is only a little busier. That is why capacity planning leaves headroom. It also explains why thread-per-request held on for so long. If W is 5 ms (an in-memory lookup), 200 threads give you 40,000 requests per second, and nobody needs async code. The wall only appears when W is dominated by waiting on other systems, which describes most microservices. JEP 444's motivation section makes this exact argument: the number of threads limits throughput long before CPU or network do. One honest question remains: why not shrink -Xss and run 20,000 platform threads? Some teams did. You still pay a system call per thread start, the kernel still schedules 20,000 threads, and too small a stack turns deep call chains into StackOverflowError. A virtual thread's stack lives on the heap and grows only as deep as the code actually goes, so you don't have to guess a size.

h: How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations · A virtual thread is a Thread plus a continuation
x: Thread.ofVirtual().start(task) returns an ordinary java.lang.Thread. Inside the JDK it is an instance of java.lang.VirtualThread, a package-private subclass. It holds two things a platform thread doesn't have: a continuation and a scheduler. A continuation is a paused piece of code: everything a computation still has to do, plus every stack frame it had when it stopped. The JDK has an internal class for it, jdk.internal.vm.Continuation, with two operations that matter. run() starts the code, or resumes it where it stopped. yield(), called from inside that code, stops it and returns control to whoever called run(), with the frames kept. The next run() carries on from the line after the yield(). cont = new Continuation(scope, () -> { a(); yield(); b(); }) cont.run() // runs a(), stops at yield(), returns here cont.run() // carries on with b() You can't call this class yourself: the jdk.internal.vm package is not exported. The virtual thread uses it for you. Its task is wrapped in a continuation, and when the task is about to block, the JDK calls yield(). The thread stops without ever blocking an OS thread. The scheduler decides which paused continuation runs next, and on which OS thread. To your code, a virtual thread is just a thread. Thread.currentThread() returns it. ThreadLocals work. interrupt() works, and sleep throws InterruptedException the same way. Stack traces show your frames. A few things differ, and they are all in the Thread Javadoc: virtual threads are always daemon threads, their priority is fixed, they have no name unless you give one, and Thread.getAllStackTraces() leaves them out. Check yourself: a virtual thread runs a task that sleeps three times and then returns. How many times does its continuation yield, and how many times does a carrier mount it? It yields three times, once per sleep. It is mounted four times: once to start, and once after each sleep ends. Think of carriers as desks in an office and virtual threads as workers who carry their papers in a briefcase. A worker sits at any free desk and spreads out the papers. When the worker has to wait for a phone call, they pack everything into the briefcase, put it on a shelf, and free the desk. When the call comes, they take the next free desk, which may be a different one, and carry on. There are only as many desks as cores, but there can be a million briefcases on the shelves. The analogy breaks in one place: a real worker can be told to leave the desk. A virtual thread that never waits for anything keeps its desk until it is done, because nobody makes it get up.

h: How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations · Carriers: a few platform threads run every virtual thread
x:
Virtual threads mount on carriers, unmount at a blocking call, and come back on any carrier The default scheduler is a ForkJoinPool that the JDK creates just for virtual threads. It is a different pool from ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), which parallel streams use. It runs in FIFO mode, so ready virtual threads run roughly in the order they became ready. Its worker threads are platform threads, and they have a special name: carrier threads. By default there is one per core (Runtime.availableProcessors()). You can change that with -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism=N. The pool may add carriers for a while when some operation blocks a carrier, up to jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize, which defaults to 256. Two words describe the life of a virtual thread on a carrier: Mount: a carrier takes a ready virtual thread from the queue and runs its continuation. The virtual thread's top frames are now on the carrier's stack, and the carrier is busy running your code. Unmount: the continuation yields at a blocking call. The frames go to the heap, and the carrier goes back to the pool to mount someone else. The carrier is invisible to your code. Thread.currentThread() returns the virtual thread, and the carrier's own ThreadLocals are not visible. The one place it shows is the virtual thread's toString(): VirtualThread[#22,payment-0]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3. The part after @ is the carrier. Treat that format as a debugging aid, not an API: it is not specified anywhere. A virtual thread that unmounts can come back on any carrier. That is normal, and it is why the JDK never lets your code see the carrier: a ThreadLocal on the carrier would leak between unrelated requests. x: Unmounting is not magic in the JVM. The JDK team rewrote the blocking parts of the class library to check whether the current thread is virtual, and to yield instead of blocking. Here is parkNanos from java.lang.VirtualThread, trimmed to its core: // simplified from java.lang.VirtualThread.parkNanos (JDK 25) void parkNanos(long nanos) { timeout = nanos; setState(TIMED_PARKING); boolean yielded = yieldContinuation(); // unmount: frames to the heap, carrier is free if (!yielded) { parkOnCarrierThread(true, nanos); // couldn't unmount: block the carrier instead } } The JDK schedules a timer that will unpark the thread, and yieldContinuation() unmounts it. When the timer fires, the virtual thread goes back into the scheduler's queue. These operations unmount a virtual thread: Thread.sleep and LockSupport.park, and everything built on park: ReentrantLock, Semaphore, CountDownLatch, BlockingQueue.take, Future.get, CompletableFuture.join. Socket I/O, including the JDK's HttpClient and JDBC drivers that use plain sockets. The JDK switches the socket to non-blocking mode and registers it with a poller (epoll on Linux), which unparks the virtual thread when data arrives. From JDK 24 (JEP 491), synchronized and Object.wait(). On JDK 21 to 23 these pin the carrier instead: the virtual thread stays mounted, and the carrier blocks with it. Lesson 4 of this track covers that. Some operations can't unmount. Most file I/O blocks inside the OS, so the JDK lets it take over the carrier ("capture") and adds a temporary extra carrier to make up for it. Blocking while a native method or a class initializer is on the stack pins the carrier. The last rule surprises people: there is no time slicing. A virtual thread that computes for two seconds without blocking keeps its carrier for two seconds. Other virtual threads wait for a free carrier. Virtual threads are cheap waiting, not cheap computing. Replace the sleep with real work In CarrierDemo.java, replace Thread.sleep(50); with a 50 ms busy loop: long end = System.nanoTime() + 50_000_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { }. The compiler will then complain about the unreachable catch, so remove the try and catch too. In CarrierDemo.kt the loop is val end = System.nanoTime() + 50_000_000; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { }, and Kotlin doesn't mind the leftover catch. Predict the total time with one carrier (-Pargs='8 1') and with the default number of carriers. Then run both. Look at the before and after carriers. Did any thread change carrier this time? With one carrier the 8 busy loops run one after another: about 400 ms. With 4 carriers it takes about 100 ms on an idle machine (8 loops / 4 carriers x 50 ms), more if other programs are busy. No thread changes carrier, because none of them ever blocks, so none of them unmounts. CPU work is limited by carriers, which means cores.

h: How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations · Stacks live on the heap
x:
A platform thread's stack is a fixed block of native memory reserved when the thread starts, 1 MB by default. A virtual thread's stack is different. When it unmounts, the JDK copies its frames off the carrier's stack into stack chunk objects on the Java heap. The chunk is only as big as the frames that are really there, and the garbage collector manages it like any other object. When the virtual thread mounts again, the JDK doesn't copy the whole stack back. It copies the top few frames, enough to continue. If your code returns into a frame that is still on the heap, the JDK copies more at that point. A thread parked deep inside a framework pays for its depth only once, when it parks. This is what makes a million virtual threads possible. A virtual thread parked at a shallow depth costs about 2 KB of heap in the demo below, including the Thread object. A thread parked 200 frames deep costs more, because each frame has to be stored. Deep framework stacks (a Quarkus REST call through several interceptors, a Hibernate query) are not free, but they are paid for in heap, which the GC can reclaim, not in reserved memory sized for the worst case. It also explains a design choice. Kotlin coroutines save only the locals of suspend functions, in objects the compiler generates. A virtual thread saves the whole real stack, so a blocking call deep inside a library that knows nothing about virtual threads can still unmount. The compare block below shows both. In the lab you build the other half: a tiny scheduler with a run queue, a timer queue and one carrier, which mounts and unmounts hand-written continuations. Weigh a parked virtual thread Run StackOnHeapDemo. It parks 10,000 virtual threads at call depth 1, measures the heap, releases them, then does the same at depth 200. Before you look: how many times bigger will the depth-200 number be? Run -Pargs=1000 for depth 1,000 and compare with the 1 MB a platform thread reserves. The most common mistake is believing a virtual thread runs on "its" OS thread, and writing code that depends on that: carrier-level ThreadLocal tricks, native libraries that keep state per OS thread, or logging the OS thread id to correlate requests. A virtual thread can resume on a different carrier after every blocking call, and the JDK hides the carrier on purpose. Correlate with the virtual thread (or better, a request id you pass along), and treat the carrier as an implementation detail you never touch.

x: Stackful virtual threads vs stackless coroutines Java: the JDK saves the real stack // any method can block, even deep inside an old library void settle(Payment p) throws InterruptedException { Auth auth = issuer.authorize(p); // blocking socket read: unmounts here Thread.sleep(Duration.ofMillis(30)); // unmounts here too ledger.record(p, auth); // plain JDBC over a socket: unmounts } // run it on a virtual thread; nothing in settle() knows Thread.ofVirtual().name("settle-", 0).start(() -> { try { settle(payment); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); Kotlin: the compiler builds a state machine // only suspend calls can pause; the compiler rewrites this function suspend fun settle(p: Payment) { val auth = issuer.authorize(p) // must be a suspend fun to free the thread delay(30) ledger.record(p, auth) // blocking JDBC here would block the thread } // roughly what the compiler generates (simplified): // class SettleContinuation(var label: Int, var auth: Auth?) // label 0: call authorize(p); label = 1; return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED // label 1: auth = result; call delay(30); label = 2; return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED // label 2: ledger.record(p, auth) Both pause in the middle of a function and continue later, possibly on another thread. Kotlin coroutines are stackless: the compiler turns each suspend function into a state machine and saves its locals in a generated continuation object, so only suspend calls can pause. Virtual threads are stackful: the JVM copies the real frames, so any blocking JDK call anywhere on the stack can unmount, including calls inside libraries compiled before virtual threads existed. The fibers in this lesson's lab are written by hand in the Kotlin style, with a label counter, so you can see what the JDK saves you from writing.

The socket reads inside fraud.check may unmount and remount it several times on their own. Unmount. sleep reaches parkNanos, which schedules a timer for 50 ms and calls yieldContinuation(). The JDK copies the frames into a stack chunk on the heap, and run() returns on worker-2. worker-2 goes back to the queue and mounts another virtual thread. No OS thread is blocked. Wake and remount. The timer fires and unparks auth-1, which puts its continuation back in the queue. Whichever carrier is free next, say worker-4, mounts it, copies the top frames back, and sleep returns.
