h: How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations · Key terms
x: Continuation Code that can pause at a point and resume later with its stack intact. Carrier thread A platform thread that runs virtual threads, one at a time. Mount / unmount Start running a virtual thread on a carrier / take it off the carrier at a blocking call. Scheduler The ForkJoinPool that decides which ready virtual thread a free carrier runs next. Stack chunk A heap object holding the saved frames of an unmounted virtual thread. Stackful vs stackless Saving the real call stack (virtual threads) vs saving only compiler-chosen locals (Kotlin coroutines). Time slicing Forcing a running thread off the CPU after a time slot. The OS does it to platform threads; nobody does it to virtual threads. What is a carrier thread? A platform thread (a worker of the virtual thread scheduler's ForkJoinPool) that runs a virtual thread while it is mounted. What happens when a virtual thread unmounts? At a blocking call its continuation yields: the frames are copied to the heap and the carrier goes back to run other virtual threads. How many carrier threads does the default scheduler use? One per core (availableProcessors()), set by jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism. It can add carriers temporarily, up to 256 by default. Does the JVM time-slice virtual threads? No. A virtual thread keeps its carrier until it blocks or ends. Where are a parked virtual thread's stack frames? On the Java heap, in stack chunk objects sized to the real stack depth. Is the virtual thread scheduler ForkJoinPool.commonPool()? No. It is a separate ForkJoinPool in FIFO mode. Parallel streams and default CompletableFuture async methods use the common pool. h: How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations · Go deeper
x: Three implementation details are worth knowing, because they explain behavior you will see in production. How sockets unmount. A socket used from a virtual thread is put in non-blocking mode. When a read would block, the JDK registers the socket's file descriptor with a poller (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS) and parks the virtual thread. The poller waits on all the registered sockets at once and unparks each virtual thread when its socket is ready. One OS-level wait covers thousands of connections, which is what event-loop frameworks do by hand. Why file I/O is different. Linux has no general non-blocking API for regular files that the JDK uses here, so a file read really blocks the OS thread. The JDK lets the virtual thread capture its carrier for the duration and asks the scheduler for a temporary extra carrier so the others keep running. That is why jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize exists. A service that does heavy file I/O on virtual threads can see the carrier count grow toward 256. Why FIFO. A ForkJoinPool normally runs a worker's own tasks last-in first-out, which is good for divide-and-conquer work. For virtual threads the JDK creates it in async mode, which is first-in first-out, so a virtual thread that became ready long ago runs before one that became ready a moment ago. That keeps latency fair across requests. The scheduler itself is not a public API in JDK 21 or 25. You can tune its size with the system properties, but you can't plug in your own scheduler. Libraries that need special scheduling still use platform threads.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · Five ways to start a virtual thread
x: JDK 21 has no new VirtualThread(). You start virtual threads through the Thread.Builder API or through an executor: Java // 1. a one-off, no name Thread a = Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> settle(p)); // 2. a builder, when you want a name in thread dumps Thread b = Thread.ofVirtual().name("auth-", 0).start(() -> settle(p)); // auth-0 // 3. created now, started later Thread c = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(() -> settle(p)); c.start(); // 4. a ThreadFactory, for libraries and frameworks that take one ThreadFactory vtf = Thread.ofVirtual().name("ledger-", 0).factory(); ExecutorService named = Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(vtf); // 5. what you'll use most: one new virtual thread per task ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); Kotlin // 1. a one-off, no name val a = Thread.startVirtualThread { settle(p) } // 2. a builder, when you want a name in thread dumps val b = Thread.ofVirtual().name("auth-", 0).start { settle(p) } // auth-0 // 3. created now, started later val c = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted { settle(p) } c.start() // 4. a ThreadFactory, for libraries and frameworks that take one val vtf = Thread.ofVirtual().name("ledger-", 0).factory() val named = Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(vtf) // 5. what you'll use most: one new virtual thread per task val perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() The builder with name("auth-", 0) numbers its threads: the first is auth-0, the next auth-1. A builder object is not thread safe, so build it in one place. The factory it returns is thread safe, so share that. Use the executor in normal code. It gives you Futures, it has a close() that waits, and every framework already knows how to take an ExecutorService. Use the builder when you start a single long-lived thread, such as a Kafka poll loop, and want a name you can find in a thread dump. Virtual threads have no name by default, which makes a dump of 50,000 of them hard to read. All of these return ordinary Thread objects. join, interrupt and isAlive work as usual, and isVirtual() tells you which kind you have. Start one of each Run BuildersDemo. Each line is printed from inside the new thread. Predict before you look: which ones have a name, and what is isDaemon() for each? Add .daemon(false) before .start(...) on the ofVirtual() line (in either file) and run again. What happens? BuildersDemo.java package workbench.vthreads.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadFactory; /** Every way to start a virtual thread in JDK 21+, with what each one prints. */ public class BuildersDemo { static void show(String how) { Thread t = Thread.currentThread(); System.out.printf("%-34s name=%-10s virtual=%-5s daemon=%s%n", how, "'" + t.getName() + "'", t.isVirtual(), t.isDaemon()); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // 1. the shortcut: start one now, no name Thread a = Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> show("Thread.startVirtualThread")); a.join(); // 2. the builder: name it, then start it Thread b = Thread.ofVirtual().name("auth-7").start(() -> show("Thread.ofVirtual().name().start")); b.join(); // 3. unstarted: create now, start later Thread c = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(() -> show("Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted")); c.start(); c.join(); // 4. a factory with numbered names, for code that wants a ThreadFactory ThreadFactory factory = Thread.ofVirtual().name("ledger-", 0).factory(); try (ExecutorService named = Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(factory)) { for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) named.submit(() -> show("newThreadPerTaskExecutor(factory)")); } // 5. the one you'll use most: a new virtual thread per task, closed with try-with-resources try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<String> f = perTask.submit(() -> { show("newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor"); return "approved"; }); System.out.println("future result: " + f.get()); } // close() waits for every task submitted above } } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l03.BuildersDemo labs/vthreads/src/demo/java/workbench/vthreads/l03/BuildersDemo.java BuildersDemo.kt package workbench.vthreads.l03 import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** Every way to start a virtual thread in JDK 21+, called from Kotlin, with what each one prints. */ private fun show(how: String) { val t = Thread.currentThread() println("%-34s name=%-10s virtual=%-5s daemon=%s".format(how, "'${t.name}'", t.isVirtual, t.isDaemon)) } fun main() { // 1. the shortcut: start one now, no name Thread.startVirtualThread { show("Thread.startVirtualThread") }.join() // 2. the builder: name it, then start it Thread.ofVirtual().name("auth-7").start { show("Thread.ofVirtual().name().start") }.join() // 3. unstarted: create now, start later val c = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted { show("Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted") } c.start() c.join() // 4. a factory with numbered names, for code that wants a ThreadFactory val factory = Thread.ofVirtual().name("ledger-", 0).factory() Executors.newThreadPerTaskExecutor(factory).use { named -> repeat(2) { named.submit { show("newThreadPerTaskExecutor(factory)") } } } // 5. the one you'll use most: a new virtual thread per task, closed with use {} Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> val f = perTask.submit(Callable { show("newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor") "approved" }) println("future result: ${f.get()}") } // close() waits for every task submitted above } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l03.BuildersDemoKt labs/vthreads/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/vthreads/l03/BuildersDemo.kt Only auth-7, ledger-0 and ledger-1 have names; the rest print an empty name. Every line says virtual=true daemon=true. The .daemon(false) edit doesn't compile, in Java or in Kotlin: Thread.ofVirtual() returns a Thread.Builder.OfVirtual, which has no daemon method, because virtual threads are always daemon threads. A semaphore is the stack of visitor badges at a building's front desk. The building (the card issuer) has room for 20 visitors, so there are 20 badges. Visitors who arrive when the stack is empty sit in the lobby, which is cheap, and the next one in line gets a badge when someone hands theirs back on the way out. A pool of 20 virtual threads is like hiring 20 escorts who each walk one visitor through the whole day, the coffee shop included, so visitors who only want coffee wait for an escort too. The analogy breaks at the lobby: a real lobby fills up, but parked virtual threads only cost heap, so the line can grow far longer than you'd want. That is why you set a wait limit.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · One task, one virtual thread, one try block
x: newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts a brand-new virtual thread for every task you submit. It keeps no threads around and has no queue. Its Javadoc says it plainly: the number of threads it creates is unbounded. Since JDK 19, ExecutorService is AutoCloseable. close() shuts the executor down and then waits until every submitted task has finished. So the shape of a fan-out is one try-with-resources block: Java List<Receipt> authorizeAll(List<Payment> batch) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { // 1. fork: start every call before waiting for any List<Future<Receipt>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (Payment p : batch) futures.add(perTask.submit(() -> issuer.authorize(p))); // 2. join: collect in input order List<Receipt> receipts = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<Receipt> f : futures) receipts.add(f.get()); return receipts; } // 3. close(): waits for any task still running } Kotlin fun authorizeAll(batch: List<Payment>): List<Receipt> = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> // 1. fork: start every call before waiting for any val futures = batch.map { p -> perTask.submit(Callable { issuer.authorize(p) }) } // 2. join: collect in input order futures.map { it.get() } } // 3. close(): waits for any task still running Create the executor where the work starts, and let it end where the work ends. A short-lived executor per request or per batch costs almost nothing, because it doesn't own any threads. It also means that when this method returns, no thread it started is still running. That property gets a name and a whole API in lesson 5 of this track. In a Kafka consumer the natural unit is the poll batch: one executor block per batch, one virtual thread per record, and the offset commit after the block closes, when every record has finished. Do this only for topics where records with the same key don't have to be processed in order, because the virtual threads finish in any order. Two details trip people up. Start every task before you call get() on any of them. A loop that submits one task and then waits on it runs your batch one call at a time, on 5,000 threads. And get() reports a failed task as an ExecutionException whose cause is the real exception. The other tasks keep running when one fails, and close() still waits for them. Cancelling them is also lesson 5's topic. This executor has no limit, and that is deliberate. A limit belongs somewhere else, which the next two sections show. Check yourself: a teammate submits each payment and calls get() on its future before submitting the next. With 5,000 payments and a 120 ms issuer, how long does the batch take, and how many calls are in flight at once? About 10 minutes (5,000 × 0.12 s), with one call in flight. That is Little's law with L = 1, and 5,000 virtual threads didn't help at all. Every downstream in a payment flow has a concurrency contract: the card network's API allows a fixed number of calls in flight per merchant, your Oracle pool has 20 connections, the fraud vendor rate-limits by client. On platform threads the request pool size was hiding those limits. On virtual threads, each one needs its own shared semaphore (or a library bulkhead, such as Resilience4j's, if you already use one) on the client object. In a Kafka consumer that fans out one virtual thread per record in a poll batch, the semaphore is what keeps a 500-record batch from opening 500 calls to the issuer at once.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · Don't pool virtual threads
x: Thread pools exist for two reasons: platform threads are expensive to create, so you reuse them, and a fixed pool caps how much work runs at once. Neither reason survives virtual threads. Creating a virtual thread costs about as much as creating a small object, so reuse saves almost nothing. And a pool is the wrong place for a cap, because it caps everything the task does, not just the one call that needs it. Here is the mistake, in code that compiles and runs fine: Java // anti-pattern: a pool of 20 virtual threads to protect a 20-connection database ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()); pool.execute(() -> { Risk risk = fraud.check(p); // 60 ms, needs no limit, but waits for a pool slot anyway ledger.record(p, risk); // 10 ms, the only call that needs the limit }); Kotlin // anti-pattern: a pool of 20 virtual threads to protect a 20-connection database val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()) pool.execute { val risk = fraud.check(p) // 60 ms, needs no limit, but waits for a pool slot anyway ledger.record(p, risk) // 10 ms, the only call that needs the limit } Each task holds a pool slot for 70 ms, so 1,000 payments take 1,000 / 20 × 70 ms = 3.5 s. If only the ledger call is limited, the fraud calls all overlap. The batch then takes about 60 ms plus 1,000 / 20 × 10 ms, about 0.56 s. Same database limit, six times faster. Pooled threads bring a second problem with them: ThreadLocals survive from one task to the next on a reused thread. Lesson 4 of this track covers that. The rule from JEP 444 is short. Never pool virtual threads. Create one per task, and put the limit on the resource. Pools are still the right tool for platform threads doing CPU work. A newFixedThreadPool(cores) for hashing, PDF rendering or signature checks keeps that work bounded and off the virtual thread scheduler. The rule is about virtual threads only. A pool vs a semaphore, same limit Read PoolVsSemaphoreDemo. Each request makes a 60 ms fraud call and a 10 ms ledger call, and the ledger allows 20 at once. Predict both times with the arithmetic above, then run it. Change DB_LIMIT to 50 and predict again. Which version speeds up more? PoolVsSemaphoreDemo.java package workbench.vthreads.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; /** * Each request calls the fraud service (60 ms, no limit) and then the ledger database * (10 ms, at most 20 at once). Two ways to respect the database limit: * a pool of 20 virtual threads, or one virtual thread per request plus a Semaphore(20). */ public class PoolVsSemaphoreDemo { static final int REQUESTS = 1_000; static final int DB_LIMIT = 20; static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { // A: the anti-pattern. The pool size limits the database, and also everything else. long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(DB_LIMIT, Thread.ofVirtual().factory())) { for (int i = 0; i < REQUESTS; i++) { pool.execute(() -> { sleep(60); // fraud check: needs no limit sleep(10); // ledger write: needs the limit }); } } System.out.printf("pool of %d virtual threads: %,5d ms%n", DB_LIMIT, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); // B: one virtual thread per request; the semaphore guards only the database call Semaphore db = new Semaphore(DB_LIMIT); long t1 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < REQUESTS; i++) { perTask.execute(() -> { sleep(60); // all 1,000 fraud checks overlap try { db.acquire(); // at most 20 inside the database } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; } try { sleep(10); } finally { db.release(); } }); } } System.out.printf("virtual thread per task + Semaphore(%d): %,5d ms%n", DB_LIMIT, (System.nanoTime() - t1) / 1_000_000); } } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l03.PoolVsSemaphoreDemo labs/vthreads/src/demo/java/workbench/vthreads/l03/PoolVsSemaphoreDemo.java PoolVsSemaphoreDemo.kt package workbench.vthreads.l03 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore /** * Each request calls the fraud service (60 ms, no limit) and then the ledger database * (10 ms, at most 20 at once). Two ways to respect the database limit: * a pool of 20 virtual threads, or one virtual thread per request plus a Semaphore(20). */ private const val REQUESTS = 1_000 private const val DB_LIMIT = 20 fun main() { // A: the anti-pattern. The pool size limits the database, and also everything else. val t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(DB_LIMIT, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()).use { pool -> repeat(REQUESTS) { pool.execute { Thread.sleep(60) // fraud check: needs no limit Thread.sleep(10) // ledger write: needs the limit } } } println("pool of %d virtual threads: %,5d ms".format(DB_LIMIT, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) // B: one virtual thread per request; the semaphore guards only the database call val db = Semaphore(DB_LIMIT) val t1 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> repeat(REQUESTS) { perTask.execute { Thread.sleep(60) // all 1,000 fraud checks overlap db.acquire() // at most 20 inside the database try { Thread.sleep(10) } finally { db.release() } } } } println("virtual thread per task + Semaphore(%d): %,5d ms".format(DB_LIMIT, (System.nanoTime() - t1) / 1_000_000)) } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l03.PoolVsSemaphoreDemoKt labs/vthreads/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/vthreads/l03/PoolVsSemaphoreDemo.kt The pool takes about 3.5 s (one run here: 3,584 ms) and the semaphore version about 0.6 s (586 ms). With a limit of 50 the pool drops to about 1.4 s and the semaphore version to about 0.26 s. Both respect the database limit; only the pool also slows down the work that has no limit.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · Limit the resource with a shared Semaphore
x:
A Semaphore holds a number of permits. acquire() takes one, and waits if none are left. release() gives one back and wakes a waiter. On a virtual thread, waiting in acquire() parks the thread, so 5,000 waiters cost 5,000 small heap objects and no OS threads. The pattern has three rules: Java final class IssuerClient { private final Semaphore inFlight = new Semaphore(20); // 1. one per resource, shared by all callers private final IssuerHttp http; IssuerClient(IssuerHttp http) { this.http = http; } Auth authorize(Payment p) throws InterruptedException { inFlight.acquire(); // 2. acquire outside the try try { return http.authorize(p); // only the call that needs the limit } finally { inFlight.release(); // 3. always give it back } } } Kotlin class IssuerClient(private val http: IssuerHttp) { private val inFlight = Semaphore(20) // 1. one per resource, shared by all callers fun authorize(p: Payment): Auth { inFlight.acquire() // 2. acquire outside the try try { return http.authorize(p) // only the call that needs the limit } finally { inFlight.release() // 3. always give it back } } } The semaphore lives with the resource, as a field on the client that every request uses. A semaphore created inside a request handler gives each request its own 20 permits and limits nothing. acquire() sits before the try, so a thread interrupted while waiting never releases a permit it didn't get. If it did, the limit would quietly grow to 21, then 22. Pick the number from the downstream side: the issuer's documented concurrency limit, or the size of the database connection pool. Then check it with Little's law. Twenty permits on a 120 ms call give at most 20 / 0.12 s = 167 calls per second. If payments arrive faster than that, the waiters pile up, and each one waits longer than the last. Waiting forever is rarely what you want in a payment API. tryAcquire(200, MILLISECONDS) returns false if no permit came in time, so you can answer with a fast 503 or a retry hint instead of a slow timeout. This pattern is usually called a bulkhead, after the walls that stop one flooded section from sinking a ship. A request that calls two limited downstreams uses two semaphores: take the issuer permit, release it, then take the ledger permit. Don't hold one permit while you wait for another. It ties up the first resource for nothing, and two code paths that take them in opposite orders can deadlock exactly like two locks. Shed load instead of queueing forever ShedLoadDemo sends 1,000 requests at once through a Semaphore(20) guarding a 50 ms call. Each request waits at most 200 ms for a permit. Predict how many get served. Hint: in 200 ms each permit can serve about 200 / 50 = 4 calls, plus the first round. Run it, then try -Pargs='20 50 2000' and -Pargs='100 50 200', predicting each first. ShedLoadDemo.java package workbench.vthreads.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** * 1,000 requests arrive at once. The issuer allows 20 calls in flight, each takes 50 ms. * A request waits at most 200 ms for a slot, then gives up (a fast 503 instead of a slow timeout). * *

Args: permits, call ms, max wait ms. Default: 20 50 200. */ public class ShedLoadDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { int permits = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 20; long callMs = args.length > 1 ? Long.parseLong(args[1]) : 50; long maxWaitMs = args.length > 2 ? Long.parseLong(args[2]) : 200; Semaphore issuer = new Semaphore(permits); AtomicInteger served = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger shed = new AtomicInteger(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) { perTask.execute(() -> { try { if (!issuer.tryAcquire(maxWaitMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { shed.incrementAndGet(); // no slot in time: fail fast return; } try { Thread.sleep(callMs); // the issuer call served.incrementAndGet(); } finally { issuer.release(); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); } } System.out.printf("permits=%d call=%d ms max wait=%d ms: served %d, shed %d, in %d ms%n", permits, callMs, maxWaitMs, served.get(), shed.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l03.ShedLoadDemo labs/vthreads/src/demo/java/workbench/vthreads/l03/ShedLoadDemo.java ShedLoadDemo.kt package workbench.vthreads.l03 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** * 1,000 requests arrive at once. The issuer allows 20 calls in flight, each takes 50 ms. * A request waits at most 200 ms for a slot, then gives up (a fast 503 instead of a slow timeout). * * Args: permits, call ms, max wait ms. Default: 20 50 200. */ fun main(args: Array) { val permits = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 20 val callMs = args.getOrNull(1)?.toLong() ?: 50 val maxWaitMs = args.getOrNull(2)?.toLong() ?: 200 val issuer = Semaphore(permits) val served = AtomicInteger() val shed = AtomicInteger() val t0 = System.nanoTime() Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> repeat(1_000) { perTask.execute { if (!issuer.tryAcquire(maxWaitMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { shed.incrementAndGet() // no slot in time: fail fast return@execute } try { Thread.sleep(callMs) // the issuer call served.incrementAndGet() } finally { issuer.release() } } } } println("permits=%d call=%d ms max wait=%d ms: served %d, shed %d, in %d ms" .format(permits, callMs, maxWaitMs, served.get(), shed.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l03.ShedLoadDemoKt labs/vthreads/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/vthreads/l03/ShedLoadDemo.kt With the defaults, about 100 requests are served (20 permits × 5 rounds; one run here served 94) and the rest are shed in about a third of a second. A 2 s wait serves about 20 × 41 = 820. With 100 permits and 200 ms, about 500 are served. Served requests = permits × (max wait / call time + 1), which is Little's law turned around. Thousands of virtual threads park cheaply at the semaphore. Only 20 at a time reach the issuer, and Little's law gives the resulting throughput. Semaphore (Java SE 25 API) docs The most common mistake is keeping the old habit of a fixed pool and just giving it virtual threads: newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()). It looks like a cheap upgrade and it does limit the database. It also limits every other part of each task, keeps an unbounded queue in front of the pool, and reuses threads, so ThreadLocal state leaks between tasks. The second most common is the opposite: dropping the limit entirely because "virtual threads are cheap", and then sending 5,000 concurrent calls to a downstream that allows 20. Use one virtual thread per task and one shared semaphore per scarce resource.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · Java and Kotlin
x: Fan out with a shared limit in Java and Kotlin FanOut.java + Bulkhead.java (lab solution, trimmed) public final class Bulkhead { private final Semaphore permits; public Bulkhead(int maxConcurrent) { permits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrent); } public <T> T call(Callable<T> work) throws Exception { permits.acquire(); try { return work.call(); } finally { permits.release(); } } } static final Bulkhead ISSUER = new Bulkhead(20); List<String> authorizeAll(List<String> ids) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<String>> fs = new ArrayList<>(); for (String id : ids) fs.add(perTask.submit(() -> ISSUER.call(() -> authorize(id)))); List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<String> f : fs) out.add(f.get()); return out; } } FanOutKotlin.kt package workbench.vthreads.l03 import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore // one limit for the whole service, shared by every caller of the issuer val issuerLimit = Semaphore(20) // acquire, run, always release: the Kotlin version of try/finally around a permit inline fun <T> Semaphore.withPermit(block: () -> T): T { acquire() try { return block() } finally { release() } } fun authorize(id: String): String { Thread.sleep(50) // the blocking issuer call return "auth:$id" } fun authorizeAll(ids: List<String>): List<String> = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> // use {} = try-with-resources ids.map { id -> perTask.submit(Callable { issuerLimit.withPermit { authorize(id) } }) } .map { it.get() } // in input order } fun main() { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val receipts = authorizeAll((1..1_000).map { "pay-$it" }) val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("${receipts.size} receipts, first ${receipts.first()}, last ${receipts.last()}, in $ms ms") } The Kotlin version is the same design: use {} is Kotlin's try-with-resources and works because ExecutorService is AutoCloseable since JDK 19, and an inline extension gives Semaphore a withPermit block. Callable { ... } picks the submit overload that returns a value; a bare lambda can be read as a Runnable. Watch the name clash: kotlinx.coroutines has its own Semaphore with a suspending withPermit, built for coroutines. Inside coroutines use that one, because java.util.concurrent.Semaphore.acquire() blocks the thread. On virtual threads, use the JDK semaphore. Run the Kotlin file with ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l03.FanOutKotlinKt.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · Worked example
x: Send a payout batch to the bank, 20 at a time The bank's payout API allows 20 concurrent calls per client and takes about 150 ms. A batch has 3,000 payouts, and each one also needs an account lookup that has no limit. Start with the limit, as a field on the client that every caller shares. final class BankClient { // one limit for the whole service, from the bank's API contract private final Semaphore inFlight = new Semaphore(20); } class BankClient { // one limit for the whole service, from the bank's API contract private val inFlight = Semaphore(20) } Guard only the bank call. The account lookup happens before acquire(), so 3,000 lookups overlap freely. PayoutResult send(Payout p) throws Exception { Account acct = accounts.lookup(p.accountId()); // 1. unlimited work first inFlight.acquire(); // 2. wait for a slot (parks a virtual thread) try { return bank.payout(acct, p); // 3. the only limited call } finally { inFlight.release(); // 4. always give the slot back } } fun send(p: Payout): PayoutResult { val acct = accounts.lookup(p.accountId) // 1. unlimited work first inFlight.acquire() // 2. wait for a slot (parks a virtual thread) try { return bank.payout(acct, p) // 3. the only limited call } finally { inFlight.release() // 4. always give the slot back } } Fan out one virtual thread per payout, and collect in order. The executor block guarantees that no payout is still running when the method returns. List<PayoutResult> sendAll(List<Payout> batch) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<PayoutResult>> fs = new ArrayList<>(); for (Payout p : batch) fs.add(perTask.submit(() -> send(p))); // 5. fork all List<PayoutResult> results = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<PayoutResult> f : fs) results.add(f.get()); // 6. join in order return results; } } fun sendAll(batch: List<Payout>): List<PayoutResult> = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> val fs = batch.map { p -> perTask.submit(Callable { send(p) }) } // 5. fork all fs.map { it.get() } // 6. join in order } Check the timing with Little's law before you ship it. The bank stage caps you at 20 / 0.15 s = 133 payouts per second, so 3,000 payouts take about 22.5 s no matter how many threads you start. If that is too slow, the fix is a higher limit agreed with the bank, not more threads.

x: 10,000 concurrent requests each call a fraud API that allows 50 concurrent calls. Which design is right? newFixedThreadPool(50) of platform threads for all request handling newFixedThreadPool(50, Thread.ofVirtual().factory()) A virtual thread per request, and one shared Semaphore(50) around the fraud call A virtual thread per request, and a new Semaphore(50) created inside each request handler The limit belongs to the fraud API, so put one semaphore on the client and share it. Both pools limit all request handling, not just the fraud call. A semaphore created per request gives every request its own 50 permits, which limits nothing at all. What does this print? try (var perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) perTask.submit(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName().isEmpty())); } System.out.println("done"); true three times, then done done first, then true three times false three times, then done, because each thread is named pool-1-thread-N Nothing: the tasks are cancelled when the block ends Virtual threads have no name by default, so getName() is empty. close() at the end of the try block waits for all three tasks before done runs. The pool-1-thread-N names belong to the platform threads of newFixedThreadPool. A Semaphore(20) guards a 50 ms call. 1,000 virtual threads reach acquire() at the same moment. About how long until the last one gets a permit? About 50 ms About 2.5 s About 50 s Never: 980 threads fail with an exception Twenty permits on a 50 ms call serve 400 calls per second, so 1,000 calls need about 2.5 s, and the last thread waits for nearly all of it. Nothing fails: acquire() waits as long as it takes. Use tryAcquire with a timeout if that wait is too long. You submit 1 million tasks to Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). How many threads can it create? As many as there are cores 256, the scheduler's maximum A pool the JVM sizes from the workload Up to 1 million: one new virtual thread per task, with no limit The Javadoc says the number of threads it creates is unbounded. The core count and the 256 cap describe carrier threads, which run the virtual threads. They don't limit how many virtual threads exist. From the lesson "Synchronizers: latch, barrier, semaphore, phaser": a developer writes try { sem.acquire(); call(); } finally { sem.release(); }. A thread is interrupted while it waits inside acquire(). What happens to the semaphore? Nothing: release() ignores threads that hold no permit acquire() retries automatically after the interrupt It gains a permit it never handed out, so the limit quietly grows by one release() throws IllegalMonitorStateException A Semaphore doesn't track who holds permits. release() always adds one, even from a thread that never acquired. Every interrupted waiter raises the limit by one. Put acquire() before the try so finally only runs after a permit was really taken.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · Key terms
x: Thread.Builder The JDK 21 API for creating threads: Thread.ofVirtual() and Thread.ofPlatform(). Thread-per-task executor An executor that starts a new thread for every task and never reuses one. Fan-out Starting many calls at once and then collecting all their results. Semaphore A counter of permits. acquire takes one or waits, release gives one back. Bulkhead A limit on how many calls may be inside one downstream at once, so one slow dependency can't use up everything. Load shedding Rejecting work quickly when you're over capacity, instead of letting it queue. Which executor gives every task its own new virtual thread? Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). It has no pool, no queue and no limit. What does close() on an ExecutorService do (JDK 19+)? It calls shutdown() and then waits until every submitted task has finished. Should you pool virtual threads? No. Create one per task, and limit the scarce resource with a shared Semaphore. Where does the Semaphore for a downstream API belong? One per resource, shared by all callers, for example a field on the API client. One per request limits nothing. Semaphore(20) guards a call that takes 100 ms. Maximum calls per second? 200 (20 / 0.1 s). Why put acquire() before the try and release() in finally? So a thread that fails to acquire never releases a permit it didn't get, and a thread whose call throws always gives its permit back. How do you make a semaphore wait fail fast? tryAcquire(timeout, unit) returns false if no permit arrives in time, so you can reject the request.

h: Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores · Go deeper
x: Concurrency limits and rate limits are different things. A semaphore limits how many calls are in flight. Many APIs instead publish a rate, such as 300 requests per second. Little's law connects the two only if the latency is stable: 20 in flight at 100 ms is 200 per second, but if the API slows to 400 ms, the same 20 permits give 50 per second, while a rate limiter would happily let 300 per second through and pile them up inside the API. If the contract is a rate, use a rate limiter. If it's connections or concurrent calls, use a semaphore. Some teams use both. Fair or not. new Semaphore(20) is non-fair: a thread that calls acquire() just as a permit is released can take it ahead of threads that have waited longer. That gives better throughput. new Semaphore(20, true) hands permits out in arrival order, which keeps the worst-case wait lower. For a payment API, where a few very slow requests hurt more than a little lost throughput, fair is often the better default. Very many waiters. Thousands of virtual threads parked on one semaphore are fine. Each release() wakes one waiter, and each waiter costs a parked virtual thread. With hundreds of thousands of waiters, the bigger problem is latency: the last waiter waits for everyone ahead of it. A bounded wait with tryAcquire keeps that under control and turns overload into fast, honest errors. Structured fan-out. The try-with-resources block guarantees that every thread the method started has finished when it returns. What it doesn't do is stop the other tasks when one fails. Lesson 5 of this track builds that behavior with plain executors, and then shows the JDK's own API for it.

h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · Pinning: when a virtual thread can't let go
x:
A virtual thread is pinned when it reaches a blocking call but can't unmount. It stays on its carrier, and the carrier blocks with it. For that time the carrier is a plain platform thread again, and you have one carrier fewer for everybody else. On JDK 21 to 23 the most common cause is a monitor. The JVM tracked monitor ownership per OS thread, so a virtual thread holding a synchronized lock could not leave its carrier. Here is the shape that hurts, from this lesson's lab: Java public synchronized BigDecimal rate(String pair) { // a monitor BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair); if (r == null) { r = ratesService.fetch(pair); // 100 ms socket read while holding the monitor rates.put(pair, r); } return r; } Kotlin @Synchronized // a monitor, exactly like Java's synchronized fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = rates.getOrPut(pair) { ratesService.fetch(pair) } // 100 ms socket read while holding the monitor On JDK 21 the thread holding the monitor pins its carrier for 100 ms. Every other caller that blocks trying to enter the monitor pins its carrier too. With 4 carriers, 4 waiting callers are enough to stop every virtual thread in the JVM, including requests that never touch the cache. It can get worse than slow. In 2024 Netflix described services on Java 21 that stopped answering completely. Every carrier was held by a virtual thread pinned in synchronized code, waiting for a lock. The virtual thread that had to run next to move things along was unmounted, waiting for a free carrier, and there never was one. The figure shows the shape. JDK 24 fixed this (JEP 491). Monitors were reworked so that a virtual thread can acquire, hold and release them independently of its carrier. synchronized and Object.wait() now unmount like ReentrantLock does. JDK 25 is the first long-term-support (LTS) release with the fix. So the advice depends on your JDK. On JDK 25, leave working synchronized code alone. On JDK 21, replace synchronized around blocking calls with a ReentrantLock, which has always parked virtual threads properly. That is the first half of the lab. Pin the only carrier Read PinningDemo. It runs with one carrier. A ticker wants to tick every 50 ms, while three virtual threads each block for 100 ms: inside synchronized, inside a ReentrantLock, or inside a class initializer. Check your JDK with java -version. Predict the longest gap between ticks and the number of pinned events for each scenario on that JDK. Run it. If you have both JDK 21 and JDK 25 installed, run it on both (point JAVA_HOME at each). On JDK 21 to 23, pinned virtual threads can hold every carrier while they wait for a lock, and the thread that needs to run next to release them never gets a carrier. JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning read Back to the office from the lesson on carriers: desks are carriers, and workers pack their papers into a briefcase and free the desk whenever they wait. Pinning is a worker who is handcuffed to the desk while waiting. On JDK 21 to 23, holding a synchronized lock was such a handcuff, and a few handcuffed workers waiting on each other could block every desk in the building. JDK 24 removed that handcuff. A ThreadLocal cache is a drawer in the desk that each worker fills with their own stationery: fine when the same 200 people work there every day, useless when every visitor is new. The analogy breaks for CPU work: a worker who is busy at the desk is not stuck, they are working. They just never get up, because nobody tells them to.

h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · What still pins on JDK 25, and how to see it
x: JEP 491 removed the big case. Two smaller ones remain: Native frames. If a virtual thread calls native code (a JNI method, or a downcall through the Foreign Function and Memory API), and that native code calls back into Java code that blocks, the virtual thread is pinned. The JVM can't move native frames to the heap. Class initializers. A virtual thread that blocks while running a static {} block (or a Kotlin object's init) is pinned, because the JVM runs class initialization through its own frames. The second one is easy to write by accident: Java class FeeTable { // runs inside <clinit>: an HTTP call here pins the first virtual thread that touches FeeTable static final Map<String, BigDecimal> FEES = loadFromConfigService(); } Kotlin object FeeTable { // runs inside <clinit>: an HTTP call here pins the first virtual thread that touches FeeTable val fees: Map<String, BigDecimal> = loadFromConfigService() } Move slow loading out of static initialization, into an explicit startup step or a lazily filled cache. File I/O is a related case that isn't called pinning. A file read blocks inside the OS, so the virtual thread keeps its carrier, and the scheduler adds a temporary carrier to make up for it. To find pinning, use JFR. The jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event is on by default in both built-in settings files, with a 20 ms threshold, and it records the stack of the pinned thread. On JDK 25 it also records the reason, the blocking operation and the carrier. java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=pin.jfr,settings=profile -jar payments.jar jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned pin.jfr In a running service, jcmd <pid> JFR.start settings=profile does the same. To catch shorter pins, add jdk.VirtualThreadPinned#threshold=5ms to the -XX:StartFlightRecording options. You'll find older advice to use -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full. That property worked on JDK 21 to 23 and was removed in JDK 24. On JDK 25 it is silently ignored, so a clean run with it proves nothing. Read a pinned event Run PinningDemo once through Gradle (previous Try it) so its class is compiled. From labs/, run the class initializer scenario with a JFR recording, then print the pinned events with the commands below. Find the stack frame that names SlowRatesTable. On JDK 25, also read the pinnedReason and carrierThread fields. terminal java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=pin.jfr,settings=profile \ -cp vthreads/build/classes/java/demo workbench.vthreads.l04.PinningDemo init jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned pin.jfr One jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event of about 200 ms. Its stack shows Thread.sleep called from the static initializer of PinningDemo$SlowRatesTable. On JDK 25 the event also says blockingOperation = "LockSupport.park", pinnedReason = "VM call to ...SlowRatesTable.<clinit> on stack" and which ForkJoinPool-1-worker was blocked. On JDK 21 you only get the stack, which is still enough. jdk.jfr.Recording (Java SE 25 API) docs If your Quarkus services still run on JDK 21, check before you turn on @RunOnVirtualThread: JDBC drivers, HTTP clients and logging appenders that use synchronized around socket I/O pin on JDK 21 to 23. Many libraries have since switched to ReentrantLock, but trust a JFR recording under load more than a changelog. On JDK 25 that whole class of problem is gone, which is the best argument for upgrading first. The ThreadLocal trap applies on every JDK: look for ThreadLocal.withInitial caches of formatters, MessageDigest, Cipher or buffers in payment code, and for CPU-heavy steps such as signing settlement files or generating statements, which belong on a bounded platform pool.

h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · ThreadLocal caches stop caching
x: ThreadLocal works on virtual threads. Each virtual thread has its own values, exactly like a platform thread. The trap is a ThreadLocal used as a cache: Java // SimpleDateFormat isn't thread-safe, so keep one per thread static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> FORMAT = ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'")); Kotlin // SimpleDateFormat isn't thread-safe, so keep one per thread val FORMAT: ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> = ThreadLocal.withInitial { SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSS'Z'") } On a pool of 200 platform threads this builds 200 formatters, once, and reuses them for millions of requests. With one virtual thread per request, every request is a new thread with an empty map. The "cache" builds a formatter, uses it once, and throws it away. A million requests now build a million formatters. Nothing fails. You see it as allocation and GC time. Per-thread buffers are worse, because they cost memory for as long as the thread lives. A 64 KB ThreadLocal<byte[]> scratch buffer was 13 MB on 200 threads. On 100,000 live virtual threads it is 6.4 GB. The fixes are ordinary: Use an immutable, thread-safe object and share it. DateTimeFormatter replaces SimpleDateFormat. This is the second half of the lab. If the object is expensive and not thread-safe, use a real cache or pool for that object (a ConcurrentHashMap, a small object pool), not one per thread. If it is cheap, just create it where you need it. ThreadLocal for request context (an MDC entry, a tenant id) still works within one virtual thread, but it doesn't flow into threads you start, and it never gets wiped unless you call remove(). Scoped values, final in JDK 25, are the cleaner tool for that, and lesson 5 of this track covers them. To find thread-local use in a migrated service, run it with -Djdk.traceVirtualThreadLocals=true. That is an unsupported diagnostic property, but it exists on JDK 21 and 25, and it prints a stack trace whenever a virtual thread sets a thread local. Count the formatters Read ThreadLocalCostDemo. h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · CPU-bound work gains nothing
x:
Virtual threads make waiting cheap. They do nothing for computing. There are as many carriers as cores, so at most that many virtual threads compute at once, which is exactly what a fixed pool of that size gives you. It is worse than "no gain", because there is no time slicing. A virtual thread that signs a large settlement batch for 3 seconds keeps its carrier for 3 seconds. Put four of those on a 4-core pod, and every HTTP request handled on virtual threads waits until one of them finishes, even requests that only need a millisecond of CPU. Keep heavy CPU work on a bounded pool of platform threads, and let the virtual thread wait for it: Java private final ExecutorService cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()); Receipt settle(Batch b) throws Exception { Signature sig = cpu.submit(() -> signer.sign(b)).get(); // heavy CPU on a bounded platform pool return ledger.record(b, sig); // blocking I/O stays on the virtual thread } Kotlin private val cpu = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()) fun settle(b: Batch): Receipt { val sig = cpu.submit(Callable { signer.sign(b) }).get() // heavy CPU on a bounded platform pool return ledger.record(b, sig) // blocking I/O stays on the virtual thread } The virtual thread parks in get(), so it holds no carrier while the signing runs. The CPU pool keeps the heavy work to its own threads, and the OS time-slices those threads against the carriers, so request handling keeps moving. The line is fuzzy for work that is a little of both. Parsing a 2 KB JSON body is fine on a virtual thread. Anything that runs for tens of milliseconds without blocking (hashing, compression, PDF rendering, big XML transforms) belongs on the CPU pool. Hash on virtual threads Read CpuBoundDemo. Each of 64 tasks hashes a 1 MB buffer 20 times: a fixed amount of pure CPU work. Predict which line finishes first: a pool sized to your cores, or one virtual thread per task. Run it, then run -Pargs='256 20' and predict again. CpuBoundDemo.java package workbench.vthreads.l04; import java.security.MessageDigest; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** * 64 CPU-bound tasks (each hashes the same 1 MB buffer many times, a fixed amount of work) * on a pool sized to the cores, then with one virtual thread per task. * *

Args: number of tasks, hash rounds per task. Default: 64 20. */ public class CpuBoundDemo { static final byte[] DATA = new byte[1 << 20]; public static void main(String[] args) { int tasks = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 64; int rounds = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 20; int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(); Runnable work = () -> hash(rounds); hash(rounds); // warm up the JIT once time("fixed pool of " + cores + " platform threads", Executors.newFixedThreadPool(cores), tasks, work); time("virtual thread per task", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), tasks, work); } static void time(String label, ExecutorService executor, int tasks, Runnable work) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (executor) { for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) executor.execute(work); } System.out.printf("%-34s %d tasks in %,5d ms%n", label, tasks, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } static byte[] hash(int rounds) { try { MessageDigest sha = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256"); byte[] out = null; for (int r = 0; r < rounds; r++) out = sha.digest(DATA); // pure CPU, never blocks return out; } catch (Exception e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); } } } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l04.CpuBoundDemo labs/vthreads/src/demo/java/workbench/vthreads/l04/CpuBoundDemo.java CpuBoundDemo.kt package workbench.vthreads.l04 import java.security.MessageDigest import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** * 64 CPU-bound tasks (each hashes the same 1 MB buffer many times, a fixed amount of work) * on a pool sized to the cores, then with one virtual thread per task. * * Args: number of tasks, hash rounds per task. Default: 64 20. */ private val data = ByteArray(1 shl 20) fun main(args: Array) { val tasks = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 64 val rounds = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 20 val cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() val work = Runnable { hashRounds(rounds) } hashRounds(rounds) // warm up the JIT once timeTasks("fixed pool of $cores platform threads", Executors.newFixedThreadPool(cores), tasks, work) timeTasks("virtual thread per task", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), tasks, work) } private fun timeTasks(label: String, executor: ExecutorService, tasks: Int, work: Runnable) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() executor.use { exec -> repeat(tasks) { exec.execute(work) } } println("%-34s %d tasks in %,5d ms".format(label, tasks, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } private fun hashRounds(rounds: Int): ByteArray { val sha = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256") var out = ByteArray(0) repeat(rounds) { out = sha.digest(data) } // pure CPU, never blocks return out } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l04.CpuBoundDemoKt labs/vthreads/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/vthreads/l04/CpuBoundDemo.kt Both lines take about the same time (around 1 s on 4 cores in one run here), and the virtual thread line is never meaningfully faster. On a busy machine it can even be slower. Four times the tasks take about four times as long on both. The work is limited by cores, and both setups use all of them. The most common mistake today is following advice written for JDK 21 on JDK 25. Teams rewrite every synchronized block in the codebase as ReentrantLock, which is churn with no benefit on JDK 24 and later, and they "check" for pinning with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full, which JDK 24 removed, so it prints nothing and looks like a clean bill of health. Know which JDK you run. On JDK 25, keep synchronized, keep a JFR recording with jdk.VirtualThreadPinned in staging and production, and fix the pins it actually reports, which are mostly slow static initializers and native code.

x: Taking the monitor out of the slow path Java: synchronized becomes ReentrantLock // JDK 21 to 23: this pins for the whole fetch public synchronized BigDecimal rate(String pair) { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, ratesService::fetch); } // any JDK: a j.u.c lock parks a waiting virtual thread instead private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); public BigDecimal rate(String pair) { lock.lock(); try { return rates.computeIfAbsent(pair, ratesService::fetch); // rates is a plain HashMap } finally { lock.unlock(); } } Kotlin: @Synchronized becomes withLock // JDK 21 to 23: @Synchronized and synchronized(lock) {} are monitors, and pin the same way @Synchronized fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = rates.getOrPut(pair) { ratesService.fetch(pair) } // any JDK: kotlin.concurrent.withLock does lock / try / finally / unlock for you private val lock = ReentrantLock() fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = lock.withLock { rates.getOrPut(pair) { ratesService.fetch(pair) } // rates is a plain HashMap } Kotlin has no synchronized keyword, but @Synchronized and the synchronized(lock) { } function both compile to the same JVM monitor instructions as Java, so they pin on JDK 21 to 23 in exactly the same way. The Kotlin fix is shorter, because the standard library's withLock extension writes the lock(), try and finally { unlock() } for you, and it is inline, so it costs nothing. Note what neither version does: it doesn't let two different pairs load in parallel. That needs a lock per key, and on JDK 25 it is the only reason left to change this code.

h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · Worked example
x: Find and fix a pin from a JFR recording (JDK 21) The quote service runs on JDK 21 with virtual threads. Under load, p99 latency jumps from 150 ms to several seconds while CPU stays low. Record a few minutes of the load test with JFR and print the pinned events. jcmd $(pgrep -f quote-service) JFR.start name=pins settings=profile duration=120s filename=pins.jfr jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned pins.jfr | head -40 Read the stack in the event. The pin lasts as long as the FX call, and the frame just above the blocking call is a synchronized method of your cache. jdk.VirtualThreadPinned { duration = 103 ms stackTrace = [ java.lang.VirtualThread.parkOnCarrierThread(boolean, long) ... sun.nio.ch.NioSocketImpl.read(byte[], int, int) ... com.example.quotes.FxRateCache.rate(String) <- synchronized ] } Replace the monitor with a ReentrantLock, keeping the same "load once" behavior. The lock still serializes loads, but a waiting virtual thread now parks and frees its carrier. private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); public BigDecimal rate(String pair) { lock.lock(); // 1. take the lock (parks, doesn't pin) try { BigDecimal r = rates.get(pair); if (r == null) { r = ratesService.fetch(pair); // 2. slow call: the thread can unmount here rates.put(pair, r); } return r; } finally { lock.unlock(); // 3. always release } } private val lock = ReentrantLock() fun rate(pair: String): BigDecimal = lock.withLock { // 1. take the lock (parks, doesn't pin) rates[pair] ?: ratesService.fetch(pair) // 2. slow call: the thread can unmount here .also { rates[pair] = it } } // 3. withLock always releases Verify with the same recording under the same load: zero jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events from FxRateCache, and p99 back near 150 ms. Then put the JDK 25 upgrade on the plan, so the next synchronized in a library doesn't need the same fix.

Rewriting them is the JDK 21 advice. -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads no longer exists on JDK 24+, so it would print nothing and prove nothing. A payment service hashes request bodies with a ThreadLocal<MessageDigest> cache. It moves from a 200-thread pool to one virtual thread per request and serves 1 million requests. About how many MessageDigest objects does it create? 200, the same as before One per carrier thread, so about the number of cores About 1 million, one per request One, because ThreadLocal values are shared between virtual threads Each virtual thread has its own thread-local map, and each request runs on a new virtual thread, so withInitial runs once per request. It finishes in about the same time, about 62 s, because only 8 can compute at once either way It finishes in about 50 ms, because all 10,000 run at once It finishes about 8 times faster It deadlocks, because virtual threads can't run CPU work There are 8 carriers, so at most 8 virtual threads compute at once: 10,000 × 50 ms / 8 = 62.5 s, the same as the pool. Virtual threads only help when tasks spend their time waiting. With no time slicing, they can also delay other virtual threads in the same JVM. Wrap every format call in synchronized One shared, immutable DateTimeFormatter A ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> A volatile SimpleDateFormat field An immutable object is safe to share with any number of threads, so it needs no per-thread copies and no locking. The ThreadLocal works on a pool but becomes one formatter per task on virtual threads. synchronized is correct but makes every caller wait in line. volatile makes the reference visible but leaves the formatter's internal state racy.
