h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · Key terms
x: Pinning A virtual thread stuck on its carrier during a blocking call, so the carrier blocks too. Monitor The lock behind synchronized and @Synchronized, built into every Java object. JEP 491 The JDK 24 change that lets virtual threads hold monitors without pinning. JFR Java Flight Recorder: the JVM's built-in, low-overhead event recorder. jdk.VirtualThreadPinned The JFR event recorded when a virtual thread blocks while pinned for longer than the threshold. Carrier capture A blocking call, such as a file read, that keeps the carrier; the scheduler adds a temporary carrier. ThreadLocal cache Keeping one copy of an object per thread to reuse it. Useless when every task gets a new thread. What does it mean that a virtual thread is pinned? It reaches a blocking call but can't unmount, so it stays on its carrier and the carrier blocks with it. Does blocking inside synchronized pin a virtual thread on JDK 25? No. Since JDK 24 (JEP 491) monitors don't pin. On JDK 21 to 23 they do. What still pins a virtual thread on JDK 25? Blocking while a class initializer or a native frame (JNI, or an FFM downcall that calls back into Java) is on its stack. How do you detect pinning on JDK 24 and later? The JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned (on by default, 20 ms threshold). -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads was removed in JDK 24. Why does a ThreadLocal cache stop working with one virtual thread per task? Each task runs on a new virtual thread with an empty thread-local map, so the cached object is built once per task and thrown away. Do virtual threads speed up CPU-bound work? No. At most one virtual thread per carrier (per core) computes at once, and there is no time slicing. Kotlin replacement for @Synchronized around I/O on JDK 21? private val lock = ReentrantLock() and lock.withLock { ... } from kotlin.concurrent.

h: Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps · Go deeper
x: Why monitors pinned in the first place. Before JDK 24, HotSpot recorded the owner of a monitor as the OS thread that held it. If a virtual thread could unmount while holding a monitor, another virtual thread mounted on the same carrier would appear to own it too. Rather than redesign monitors for JDK 21, the Loom team shipped with pinning and a warning. JEP 491 changed the JVM to record the virtual thread as the owner, so the thread can move freely. Object.wait() on JDK 21. A virtual thread in Object.wait() was pinned too, but the scheduler compensated by adding a temporary carrier, up to jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize. That kept wait-heavy code alive at the cost of extra OS threads. Blocking on monitor entry got no such help, which is why the deadlock in this lesson's figure was possible. Testing for pins. The lab's JFR test is a pattern you can copy into a service's integration tests: start a jdk.jfr.Recording with jdk.VirtualThreadPinned enabled, run a realistic slice of traffic on virtual threads, stop and dump the recording, and assert there are no events. Warm up first, so one-time class loading doesn't show up as a pin. On JDK 24 and later, such a test catches class initializer and native pins. On JDK 21, it also catches every synchronized around I/O. Inheritable thread locals. A new thread copies its parent's InheritableThreadLocal values by default, and that includes virtual threads. Creating a million virtual threads from a thread with large inheritable values copies them a million times. Thread.ofVirtual().inheritInheritableThreadLocals(false) turns the copy off for threads that don't need it.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · A failed fan-out keeps working after nobody cares
x: Here is the fan-out from lesson 3 of this track, inside a quote handler. It needs the customer record (a CRM call that takes 2 s on a bad day) and a credit limit check, which fails after 100 ms. Java try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<Customer> customer = perTask.submit(() -> crm.find(id)); // up to 2 s Future<Limit> limit = perTask.submit(() -> limits.check(id)); // fails at 100 ms return new Quote(customer.get(), limit.get()); } Kotlin Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> val customer = perTask.submit(Callable { crm.find(id) }) // up to 2 s val limit = perTask.submit(Callable { limits.check(id) }) // fails at 100 ms Quote(customer.get(), limit.get()) } The request is doomed at 100 ms, and it fails at 2 s. customer.get() waits the full 2 s before limit.get() gets to throw. Swap the two get() calls and it still takes 2 s, because close() waits for the CRM call and nothing tells that call to stop. Many services keep one executor in a field instead. Then the method fails at 100 ms, but the CRM call keeps running with nobody waiting for its answer. It holds an HTTP connection and maybe a semaphore permit. Under load these orphans pile up, and nothing in a thread dump says which request they belonged to. Three things are missing here: Failure doesn't cancel anything. To stop the siblings you must call cancel(true) on each other future, in every fan-out, on every error path. Lifetimes aren't tied to the code. A Future is a value you can store anywhere, so nothing promises that the threads a method started have ended when it returns. Context doesn't follow the work. A ThreadLocal set by the handler, such as the request id in your logging MDC, is empty in the subtasks. InheritableThreadLocal copies it into every new thread, and the copy goes stale. Structured concurrency fixes the first two with one rule: subtasks can't outlive the block that started them, the same way a local variable can't outlive its method. Scoped values, at the end of this lesson, fix the third. Watch the orphaned call Read LeakDemo. Variant A opens an executor per request in try-with-resources. Variant B uses one shared executor. For each, predict when the request fails and whether the CRM call finishes. Run it with the command below. Fix variant A by hand. Wrap limit.get() in a try, call customer.cancel(true) in the catch (ExecutionException e), then rethrow. Run it again. LeakDemo.java package workbench.vthreads.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; /** * A quote handler fans out two calls: a slow CRM lookup (2 s) and a credit-limit check * that fails after 100 ms. Watch what happens to the slow call once the request has failed. */ public class LeakDemo { static volatile long t0; static void log(String what) { System.out.printf("%,7d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, what); } static String customer() throws InterruptedException { try { Thread.sleep(2_000); // the slow CRM call log("customer: call finished, nobody needs the result"); return "ACME Ltd"; } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("customer: interrupted, stopped early"); throw e; } } static String limit() throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(100); throw new IllegalStateException("credit limit service: 503"); } // A: an executor per request, in try-with-resources static String quoteA() throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<String> customer = perTask.submit(LeakDemo::customer); Future<String> limit = perTask.submit(LeakDemo::limit); return limit.get() + " " + customer.get(); // throws at 100 ms... } // ...but close() waits for the CRM call } static final ExecutorService SHARED = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // B: one long-lived executor for the whole service static String quoteB() throws Exception { Future<String> customer = SHARED.submit(LeakDemo::customer); Future<String> limit = SHARED.submit(LeakDemo::limit); return limit.get() + " " + customer.get(); // throws at 100 ms, and returns } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("A: executor per request, closed by try-with-resources"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { quoteA(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { log("request failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } System.out.println("B: one shared executor"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { quoteB(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { log("request failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } Thread.sleep(2_500); // stay alive to see what B left behind SHARED.close(); } } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l05.LeakDemo labs/vthreads/src/demo/java/workbench/vthreads/l05/LeakDemo.java LeakDemo.kt package workbench.vthreads.l05 import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** * A quote handler fans out two calls: a slow CRM lookup (2 s) and a credit-limit check * that fails after 100 ms. Watch what happens to the slow call once the request has failed. */ @Volatile private var t0 = 0L private fun log(what: String) = println("%,7d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, what)) private fun customer(): String = try { Thread.sleep(2_000) // the slow CRM call log("customer: call finished, nobody needs the result") "ACME Ltd" } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("customer: interrupted, stopped early") throw e } private fun limit(): String { Thread.sleep(100) throw IllegalStateException("credit limit service: 503") } // A: an executor per request, closed by use {} private fun quoteA(): String = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perTask -> val customer = perTask.submit(Callable { customer() }) val limit = perTask.submit(Callable { limit() }) limit.get() + " " + customer.get() // throws at 100 ms... } // ...but close() waits for the CRM call private val shared = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() // B: one long-lived executor for the whole service private fun quoteB(): String { val customer = shared.submit(Callable { customer() }) val limit = shared.submit(Callable { limit() }) return limit.get() + " " + customer.get() // throws at 100 ms, and returns } fun main() { println("A: executor per request, closed by use {}") t0 = System.nanoTime() try { quoteA() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { log("request failed: ${e.cause?.message}") } println("B: one shared executor") t0 = System.nanoTime() try { quoteB() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { log("request failed: ${e.cause?.message}") } Thread.sleep(2_500) // stay alive to see what B left behind shared.close() } ./gradlew :vthreads:demo -Pmain=workbench.vthreads.l05.LeakDemoKt labs/vthreads/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/vthreads/l05/LeakDemo.kt A: the CRM call finishes at about 2,000 ms, and only then does the request fail, although the error was known at 100 ms. B: the request fails at about 100 ms, and the CRM call still finishes at about 2,000 ms, for a request that is long gone. After your fix, A prints customer: interrupted, stopped early and fails at about 100 ms. That fixes one fan-out. Every other fan-out in the service needs the same code on every error path. ExecutorService (Java SE 25 API) docs A structured scope works like a function call for concurrent work. A local variable can't outlive the method that declared it, and a subtask can't outlive the block that forked it. A ThreadLocal is a whiteboard on the thread's wall: anyone can write on it, nobody has to wipe it, and the next person to use the room reads whatever was left. A scoped value is a sealed envelope handed down the call chain and shredded when the call returns. The analogy breaks for subtasks: a scope's forks don't get their own envelopes, they all read the parent's. That is safe only because nobody can change the envelope and the scope ends before the call does.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · A scope ties every subtask to one block
x: A structured scope has three operations, and the code always has the same shape: Java try (var scope = new FailFastScope()) { // this lesson's lab Supplier<Customer> customer = scope.fork(() -> crm.find(id)); Supplier<Limit> limit = scope.fork(() -> limits.check(id)); scope.join(); // waits, or throws the first failure return new Quote(customer.get(), limit.get()); } // close(): no subtask is still running Kotlin FailFastScope().use { scope -> // this lesson's lab val customer = scope.fork { crm.find(id) } val limit = scope.fork { limits.check(id) } scope.join() // waits, or throws the first failure Quote(customer.get(), limit.get()) } // close(): no subtask is still running fork starts a subtask on a new virtual thread. join waits for the subtasks. close is the guarantee: when the block ends, every thread the scope started has ended, whether the block returned, threw or was interrupted. The policy here is fail fast: the first subtask to fail cancels the others, and join throws that failure at once. You build exactly this in the lab, on a plain newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Each forked task runs inside a wrapper. If the task throws, the wrapper records the failure with AtomicReference.compareAndSet(null, failure), so only the first one wins, and then cancels everything else. Cancel means interrupt. That stops code blocked in sleep, socket reads, locks and queues, which covers almost all blocking on virtual threads. A loop that computes and never checks the interrupt flag keeps running. Two details are easy to get wrong, and the tests check both. The siblings you interrupt fail too, with an InterruptedException. Those failures must not replace the real one. The compare-and-set already handles it, because the real failure got there first. close() must wait for threads, not for futures. Future.cancel(true) interrupts the thread and marks the future done at once. On JDK 21, newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor counts a task as finished as soon as its future is done, so close() can return while a cancelled task is still in its finally block, writing an audit row or releasing a permit. executor.shutdownNow() interrupts every thread and leaves the futures alone, so close() keeps waiting until each thread has really finished. That second bug looks right and passes most tests, which is the strongest argument for using the JDK's scope once you can. The figure shows the difference it makes. Check yourself: in your FailFastScope, the limit check fails at 100 ms. At that moment the customer call is blocked in a socket read, and a third subtask is in a 3-second loop that computes and never checks the interrupt flag. When does join() throw, and when does close() return? join() throws at about 100 ms with the limit failure. close() returns at about 3 seconds: the interrupt stops the socket read but not the loop, and close() waits for every thread. With a shared executor the failed request leaves its customer call running. In a scope the failure cancels it, and close() waits until it has ended. A quote or authorization endpoint in a Quarkus service often fans out to a CRM, a limits service and an FX provider. Today those calls usually go through CompletableFuture or an injected executor, and a failure in one leaves the others running and holding connections. On JDK 25 you can get fail-fast behavior now with a small scope like the lab's, and move to StructuredTaskScope when JDK 28 makes it final. The same rule fits a Temporal activity that fans out: when Temporal cancels or times out the activity, a scope makes sure its HTTP calls stop with it instead of finishing in the background. For context, look at your MDC: SLF4J's MDC is a ThreadLocal, so log lines written inside forked subtasks lose the correlation id unless you copy it in, and a pooled thread that skips MDC.clear() tags the next request with the wrong id.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · StructuredTaskScope: the JDK's scope, still preview
x: StructuredTaskScope is the JDK's version. Its current shape arrived in JDK 25 (JEP 505, the fifth preview). It is still a preview API in JDK 26 (JEP 525) and JDK 27 (JEP 533). JEP 543 makes it final in JDK 28, due in March 2027, with the JDK 27 API unchanged. Until then you need --enable-preview. A preview API is fully specified and implemented, but it can still change from one release to the next, which is why this course keeps it out of the Gradle labs. Here is the quote handler in the JDK 25 shape: Java Quote quote(String id) throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // fail on the first failure Subtask<Customer> customer = scope.fork(() -> crm.find(id)); Subtask<Limit> limit = scope.fork(() -> limits.check(id)); scope.join(); // JDK 25: throws StructuredTaskScope.FailedException return new Quote(customer.get(), limit.get()); } // close(): cancels what is left and waits for it } Kotlin fun quote(id: String): Quote = StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope -> // fail on the first failure val customer = scope.fork(Callable { crm.find(id) }) val limit = scope.fork(Callable { limits.check(id) }) scope.join() // JDK 25: throws StructuredTaskScope.FailedException Quote(customer.get(), limit.get()) } // close(): cancels what is left and waits for it It is your FailFastScope with stricter rules. Subtasks run on virtual threads. get() before join() throws IllegalStateException. Scopes must nest like blocks, and the JDK checks that you close them in order. A JSON thread dump (jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json) shows each scope's threads grouped under it, so you can see which request a thread belongs to. The policy is a Joiner that you pass to open. JDK 25 has four: Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(), the default: fail fast, and join() returns null. Joiner.allSuccessfulOrThrow(): fail fast, and join() returns the subtasks as a Stream<Subtask<T>>. Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow(): the first success wins, and the scope cancels the rest. Joiner.awaitAll(): wait for everything and never throw. You check each subtask's state(). A second argument configures the scope, for example a timeout: Java try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.<Rate>anySuccessfulResultOrThrow(), cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)))) { scope.fork(() -> fxPrimary.rate(pair)); scope.fork(() -> fxBackup.rate(pair)); return scope.join(); // the first rate back; the slower call is cancelled } Kotlin StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow<Rate>()) { cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) }.use { scope -> scope.fork(Callable { fxPrimary.rate(pair) }) scope.fork(Callable { fxBackup.rate(pair) }) scope.join() // the first rate back; the slower call is cancelled } If the timeout expires first, the scope cancels both calls and join() throws StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException. Expect small edits when you move JDKs. JDK 26 renamed anySuccessfulResultOrThrow to anySuccessfulOrThrow, and allSuccessfulOrThrow now returns a List<T> of results. In JDK 27 the built-in joiners make join() throw the ordinary checked ExecutionException, like Future.get(), instead of FailedException. Your lab scope already behaves that way. Articles from the JDK 21 era show new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure() and throwIfFailed(). That API is gone and doesn't compile on JDK 25. Run the scope on JDK 25 This one needs JDK 25 exactly, because --enable-preview only works for the JDK's own release. Check with java -version. It runs outside Gradle, as a single-file program, from labs/. Run ScopeDemo and compare its timeline with LeakDemo. Look at the [req-42] on the customer's line: the subtask can read the request's scoped value. Make limit() return "limit ok" after its sleep instead of throwing. Predict how long the request takes, then run it. Now open the scope with a timeout: StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow(), cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500))) (in Kotlin, open(Joiner.awaitAllSuccessfulOrThrow<Any>()) { cf -> cf.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) }). Predict, then run. ScopeDemo.java (JDK 25 preview) // JDK 25 only. StructuredTaskScope is a preview API in JDK 25 (JEP 505). From labs/: // java --enable-preview --source 25 vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.java // The quote handler from LeakDemo, written with a scope. Not part of the Gradle build. import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope; import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Joiner; // for the Try it import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Subtask; public class ScopeDemo { static final ScopedValue<String> REQUEST_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance(); static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String what) { System.out.printf("%,7d ms [%s] %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, REQUEST_ID.orElse("-"), what); } static String customer() throws InterruptedException { try { Thread.sleep(2_000); // the slow CRM call log("customer: call finished"); return "ACME Ltd"; } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("customer: interrupted, stopped early"); throw e; } } static String limit() throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(100); throw new IllegalStateException("credit limit service: 503"); } static String quote() throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // default joiner: fail on the first failure Subtask<String> customer = scope.fork(ScopeDemo::customer); Subtask<String> limit = scope.fork(ScopeDemo::limit); scope.join(); // throws FailedException at about 100 ms return limit.get() + " " + customer.get(); } // close(): every subtask has ended } static void handle() { try { log("quote: " + quote()); } catch (StructuredTaskScope.FailedException e) { log("request failed: " + e.getCause().getMessage()); } catch (StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException e) { log("request timed out"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, "req-42").run(ScopeDemo::handle); // subtasks see req-42 too log("done: the binding has ended, and no subtask is still running"); } } java --enable-preview --source 25 vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.java labs/vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.java ScopeDemo.kt (JDK 25 preview) // JDK 25 only. StructuredTaskScope is a preview API in JDK 25 (JEP 505), called here from Kotlin. // Needs the Kotlin command-line compiler. From labs/: // kotlinc vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.kt -include-runtime -d vthreads/build/scope-demo.jar // java --enable-preview -jar vthreads/build/scope-demo.jar // Not part of the Gradle build. In Kotlin code you would usually use coroutineScope instead. import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Joiner // for the Try it private val REQUEST_ID: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() private val t0 = System.nanoTime() private fun log(what: String) = println("%,7d ms [%s] %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, REQUEST_ID.orElse("-"), what)) private fun customer(): String = try { Thread.sleep(2_000) // the slow CRM call log("customer: call finished") "ACME Ltd" } catch (e: InterruptedException) { log("customer: interrupted, stopped early") throw e } private fun limit(): String { Thread.sleep(100) throw IllegalStateException("credit limit service: 503") } private fun quote(): String = StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope -> // default joiner: fail on the first failure val customer = scope.fork(Callable { customer() }) val limit = scope.fork(Callable { limit() }) scope.join() // throws FailedException at about 100 ms limit.get() + " " + customer.get() } // close(): every subtask has ended private fun handle() { try { log("quote: ${quote()}") } catch (e: StructuredTaskScope.FailedException) { log("request failed: ${e.cause?.message}") } catch (e: StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException) { log("request timed out") } } fun main() { ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, "req-42").run(Runnable { handle() }) // subtasks see req-42 too log("done: the binding has ended, and no subtask is still running") } kotlinc vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.kt -include-runtime -d vthreads/build/scope-demo.jar && java --enable-preview -jar vthreads/build/scope-demo.jar labs/vthreads/preview/ScopeDemo.kt First run: at about 100 ms the customer line says interrupted, stopped early, then request failed: credit limit service: 503, then the done line, with [-] because the binding has ended. When both succeed, the quote arrives after about 2,000 ms, since the default joiner waits for every subtask. With the 500 ms timeout, the customer is interrupted at about 500 ms and the request reports request timed out. In every case the done line comes last: the scope never leaves a subtask running. h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Scoped values: request context with a lifetime
x: Request context (a correlation id, a tenant, the authenticated merchant) travels down the call chain without being a parameter of every method. The usual tool is a ThreadLocal, and it has three problems: It is mutable. Any code can call set(), so the code that reads it can't tell where the value came from. It lives as long as the thread unless someone calls remove(). On a pooled thread, a forgotten value leaks into the next request. That is how one tenant's log lines end up tagged with another tenant's id. Its inheritance is a copy. InheritableThreadLocal copies values into each new thread. With a virtual thread per subtask, that's one copy per subtask, and a change in the parent never reaches the children. A scoped value is the replacement. It is final in JDK 25 (JEP 506), so it needs no flag. You bind it for the length of one call, everything inside that call can read it, and nobody can change it: Java static final ScopedValue<String> TENANT = ScopedValue.newInstance(); void handle(Request req) { ScopedValue.where(TENANT, req.tenant()).run(() -> process(req)); // bound only inside run() } static String ledgerKey(String account) { return TENANT.get() + ":" + account; // NoSuchElementException if nobody bound it } Kotlin val TENANT: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() fun handle(req: Request) { ScopedValue.where(TENANT, req.tenant).run(Runnable { process(req) }) // bound only inside run() } fun ledgerKey(account: String): String = TENANT.get() + ":" + account // NoSuchElementException if nobody bound it There is no set(). To use another value for a nested call, bind again with where(...).run(...). The outer value comes back when that call returns. isBound() and orElse(...) let library code handle the case where nothing is bound, and call(...) is the variant that returns a value and may throw. Scoped values flow into subtasks forked in a StructuredTaskScope. The child doesn't get a copy. It reads the parent's binding, which is safe because the binding can't change and the scope ends before the binding does. They do not flow into threads you start yourself or into executor tasks, so pass the value as an argument there. On JDK 25 that gives a clear split. Use scoped values for new request context today. Their flow into subtasks needs StructuredTaskScope, which is still preview. Keep ThreadLocal where a library requires it, like SLF4J's MDC, and clear it in a finally. ThreadLocal and ScopedValue side by side You need JDK 25 or later. Scoped values are final there, so this runs without --enable-preview. Read ScopedValueDemo and predict its six lines of output before you run it. Run it. Then, in part 1, move the work into a try and add TENANT_TL.remove() in a finally. Run it again. ScopedValueDemo.java (JDK 25) // JDK 25 or later. Scoped values are final in JDK 25 (JEP 506), so no flag is needed. From labs/: // java vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.java // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where ScopedValue is a preview API. import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class ScopedValueDemo { static final ThreadLocal<String> TENANT_TL = new ThreadLocal<>(); static final ScopedValue<String> TENANT = ScopedValue.newInstance(); // deep in the call chain: reads the context, never sets it static String ledgerLookup() { return "ThreadLocal=" + TENANT_TL.get() + ", ScopedValue=" + TENANT.orElse("unbound"); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // 1. a ThreadLocal set on a pooled thread and never removed try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { pool.submit(() -> { TENANT_TL.set("bank-a"); // forgot TENANT_TL.remove() return ledgerLookup(); }).get(); System.out.println("1. next task, same pool thread: " + pool.submit(ScopedValueDemo::ledgerLookup).get()); } // 2. a scoped value is bound for one call, and gone afterwards ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(() -> System.out.println("2. inside run(): " + ledgerLookup())); System.out.println(" after run(): " + ledgerLookup()); // 3. rebind for a nested call; the outer binding comes back when it returns ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(() -> { ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-b").run(() -> System.out.println("3. nested: " + ledgerLookup())); System.out.println(" outer again: " + ledgerLookup()); }); // 4. a thread you start yourself does not inherit the binding ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(() -> { Thread child = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println("4. plain thread: " + ledgerLookup())); try { child.join(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); } } java vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.java labs/vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.java ScopedValueDemo.kt (JDK 25) // JDK 25 or later. Scoped values are final in JDK 25 (JEP 506). Needs the Kotlin command-line // compiler. From labs/: // kotlinc vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.kt -include-runtime -d vthreads/build/sv-demo.jar // java -jar vthreads/build/sv-demo.jar // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where ScopedValue is a preview API. import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.Executors private val TENANT_TL = ThreadLocal<String>() private val TENANT: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() // deep in the call chain: reads the context, never sets it private fun ledgerLookup() = "ThreadLocal=${TENANT_TL.get()}, ScopedValue=${TENANT.orElse("unbound")}" fun main() { // 1. a ThreadLocal set on a pooled thread and never removed Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> pool.submit(Callable { TENANT_TL.set("bank-a") // forgot TENANT_TL.remove() ledgerLookup() }).get() println("1. next task, same pool thread: " + pool.submit(Callable { ledgerLookup() }).get()) } // 2. a scoped value is bound for one call, and gone afterwards // Runnable { } is optional; it shows this is the carrier's run, not Kotlin's run {} ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(Runnable { println("2. inside run(): " + ledgerLookup()) }) println(" after run(): " + ledgerLookup()) // 3. rebind for a nested call; the outer binding comes back when it returns ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(Runnable { ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-b").run(Runnable { println("3. nested: " + ledgerLookup()) }) println(" outer again: " + ledgerLookup()) }) // 4. a thread you start yourself does not inherit the binding ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(Runnable { val child = Thread.ofVirtual().start { println("4. plain thread: " + ledgerLookup()) } child.join() }) } kotlinc vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.kt -include-runtime -d vthreads/build/sv-demo.jar && java -jar vthreads/build/sv-demo.jar labs/vthreads/preview/ScopedValueDemo.kt Line 1 shows ThreadLocal=bank-a in a task that never set it: the value leaked from the previous task on the same pool thread. After your fix it shows ThreadLocal=null. The scoped value is bank-a inside run() and unbound after it, bank-b in the nested call and bank-a again after it. The plain virtual thread prints unbound, because only StructuredTaskScope forks see the parent's binding. JEP 506: Scoped Values read The most common mistake is copying StructuredTaskScope code written for a different JDK. new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure() with join().throwIfFailed() is the JDK 21 to 24 API and doesn't compile on JDK 25. JDK 25 code that catches FailedException stops compiling on JDK 27, where join() throws ExecutionException. And --enable-preview only works with the JDK's own release, so a preview API ties the whole build to one JDK version. Pin the JDK version in any code that uses the preview, and keep that code small and in one place. For production services on JDK 25, use a plain executor with explicit cancellation (or a small scope like the lab's), and switch to the JDK's scope when JDK 28 makes it final.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Java and Kotlin
x: Request context that follows the subtasks Java: ScopedValue plus a scope (JDK 25, scope in preview) static final ScopedValue<String> TENANT = ScopedValue.newInstance(); // final in JDK 25 Statement statement(Request req) throws Exception { return ScopedValue.where(TENANT, req.tenant()).call(() -> { // bound for this call try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // preview in JDK 25 Subtask<Customer> customer = scope.fork(() -> crm.find(req.customerId())); Subtask<Balance> balance = scope.fork(() -> ledger.balance(ledgerKey(req.account()))); scope.join(); return new Statement(customer.get(), balance.get()); } }); } static String ledgerKey(String account) { return TENANT.get() + ":" + account; // the fork reads the parent's binding } Kotlin: a coroutine context element // the coroutine carries the context, not the thread class Tenant(val id: String) : AbstractCoroutineContextElement(Tenant) { companion object Key : CoroutineContext.Key<Tenant> } suspend fun statement(req: Request): Statement = withContext(Tenant(req.tenant)) { // bound for this block val customer = async { crm.find(req.customerId) } val balance = async { ledger.balance(ledgerKey(req.account)) } // children inherit the context Statement(customer.await(), balance.await()) } suspend fun ledgerKey(account: String): String = (currentCoroutineContext()[Tenant]?.id ?: error("no tenant")) + ":" + account Both are immutable context that children inherit and that ends with the block. The difference is what carries it. A scoped value is bound to a thread's call stack, and only StructuredTaskScope forks inherit it. A coroutine context element is bound to the coroutine, so it survives a coroutine moving to another thread at a suspension point, and every child started with launch or async inherits it. That is why scoped values and ThreadLocals are the wrong tool inside suspending code: a coroutine can resume on a different thread, where the binding isn't there. In Kotlin coroutine code, put context in the coroutine context. Use ScopedValue from Kotlin only in plain blocking code on threads.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Worked example
x: Make an authorization fan-out fail fast An authorization needs a fraud score and the card's open-to-buy amount. Both are blocking HTTP calls. The code runs on a shared executor field, and the request id lives in a ThreadLocal for logging. Read it and list what goes wrong when the fraud call fails. Auth authorize(Payment p) throws Exception { REQUEST_ID.set(p.requestId()); // a ThreadLocal Future<Score> fraud = shared.submit(() -> fraudApi.score(p)); // 300 ms Future<Money> open = shared.submit(() -> cards.openToBuy(p)); // 80 ms return decide(fraud.get(), open.get()); } fun authorize(p: Payment): Auth { REQUEST_ID.set(p.requestId) // a ThreadLocal val fraud = shared.submit(Callable { fraudApi.score(p) }) // 300 ms val open = shared.submit(Callable { cards.openToBuy(p) }) // 80 ms return decide(fraud.get(), open.get()) } Three problems. If the card call fails, fraud.get() still waits up to 300 ms first. If the fraud call fails, the card call keeps running after authorize has thrown. And both subtasks log without the request id, because REQUEST_ID is set on the handler's thread only. On a pooled handler thread it is also never cleared. On JDK 25 without preview, use a scope that owns its threads, like the lab's FailFastScope, and pass the request id as an argument. Every subtask now ends before authorize returns, and the first failure cancels the other call. Auth authorize(Payment p) throws Exception { try (var scope = new FailFastScope()) { // 1. open: owns the subtasks String rid = p.requestId(); // 2. context as a plain argument Supplier<Score> fraud = scope.fork(() -> fraudApi.score(p, rid)); Supplier<Money> open = scope.fork(() -> cards.openToBuy(p, rid)); scope.join(); // 3. first failure cancels the other return decide(fraud.get(), open.get()); } // 4. close: nothing left running } fun authorize(p: Payment): Auth = FailFastScope().use { scope -> // 1. open: owns the subtasks val rid = p.requestId // 2. context as a plain argument val fraud = scope.fork { fraudApi.score(p, rid) } val open = scope.fork { cards.openToBuy(p, rid) } scope.join() // 3. first failure cancels the other decide(fraud.get(), open.get()) } // 4. close: nothing left running On JDK 25 with --enable-preview, the JDK's scope does the same job, and a scoped value carries the request id into both forks. No method signature has to change. static final ScopedValue<String> REQUEST_ID = ScopedValue.newInstance(); Auth authorize(Payment p) throws Exception { return ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, p.requestId()).call(() -> { // 1. bind the context try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // 2. fail-fast scope Subtask<Score> fraud = scope.fork(() -> fraudApi.score(p)); // forks read REQUEST_ID Subtask<Money> open = scope.fork(() -> cards.openToBuy(p)); scope.join(); // 3. FailedException on JDK 25 return decide(fraud.get(), open.get()); } // 4. close: nothing left running }); } val REQUEST_ID: ScopedValue<String> = ScopedValue.newInstance() fun authorize(p: Payment): Auth = ScopedValue.where(REQUEST_ID, p.requestId).call<Auth, Exception> { // 1. bind the context StructuredTaskScope.open<Any>().use { scope -> // 2. fail-fast scope val fraud = scope.fork(Callable { fraudApi.score(p) }) // forks read REQUEST_ID val open = scope.fork(Callable { cards.openToBuy(p) }) scope.join() // 3. FailedException on JDK 25 decide(fraud.get(), open.get()) } // 4. close: nothing left running } When you move to JDK 27 or 28, change the error handling where you call authorize: catch ExecutionException from join() instead of StructuredTaskScope.FailedException. The fork, join and close lines stay the same.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Lab
x: Build a fail-fast scope on an executor labs/vthreads/src/main/java/workbench/vthreads/l05/FailFastScope.java ./gradlew :vthreads:test --tests 'workbench.vthreads.l05.*' Run the tests once. All seven fail with UnsupportedOperationException. Read the class comment in FailFastScope: it lists the rules the tests check. Add the state as fields: an ExecutorService from Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), a CopyOnWriteArrayList<Future<?>>, an AtomicReference<Throwable> for the first failure and a volatile boolean joined. Write fork. Submit a Callable that runs task.call() in a try. In the catch, record the failure with compareAndSet(null, failure); if that wins, call executor.shutdownNow() to interrupt the siblings. Rethrow. Add the future to the list and return a Supplier that throws IllegalStateException until join() has run, then returns future.resultNow(). Handle a fork after cancellation: once the executor is shut down, submit throws RejectedExecutionException. Catch it and return a handle whose get() always throws IllegalStateException. Write join: call get() on each future in order, ignore ExecutionException and CancellationException, and stop as soon as a failure is recorded. Set joined, then throw new ExecutionException(failure) if there was one. Write close: shutdownNow(), then close() on the executor. Run the tests until all seven pass, then run them twice more. Why compareAndSet? The siblings you interrupt fail too, with InterruptedException. They fail after the real failure is recorded, so their compareAndSet(null, ...) returns false and they don't replace it. Don't cancel with future.cancel(true). A cancelled future counts as done at once, and on JDK 21 the executor then stops waiting for that thread while its finally block still runs. The close() test catches exactly that. shutdownNow() interrupts the threads and leaves the futures alone. catch (Throwable failure) { ...; throw failure; } compiles inside the submitted lambda: Java's precise rethrow knows task.call() can only throw an Exception. Future.resultNow() (JDK 19 and later) returns the result of a task that succeeded and throws IllegalStateException for one that failed or was cancelled, which is what a handle needs after join(). All seven tests in FailFastScopeTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can say what structured concurrency guarantees, build fail-fast fork and join on a plain executor, read the JDK 25 StructuredTaskScope API and what changes after it, and use scoped values instead of request-context ThreadLocals.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Quiz
x: You compile on JDK 25 with --enable-preview. Which fan-out compiles and fails fast? try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) { ...; scope.join().throwIfFailed(); } try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { ...; scope.join(); }, with callers catching StructuredTaskScope.FailedException try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { ...; scope.join(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { ... } try (var scope = Executors.newStructuredTaskScope()) { ...; scope.join(); } JDK 25 (JEP 505) uses the static open() factory, and its default joiner makes join() throw the unchecked FailedException. ShutdownOnFailure is the JDK 21 to 24 API and no longer exists. Catching the checked ExecutionException is the JDK 27 shape; on JDK 25 nothing in the try block throws it, so javac rejects the catch. There is no Executors.newStructuredTaskScope(). What does this print on JDK 25? static final ScopedValue<String> ID = ScopedValue.newInstance(); ScopedValue.where(ID, "a").run(() -> { ScopedValue.where(ID, "b").run(() -> System.out.print(ID.get())); System.out.print(ID.get()); }); System.out.print(ID.orElse("-")); bb- ab- ba- bab The inner where rebinds ID to b for the nested call only. When it returns, the outer binding a is back, and after the outer run() nothing is bound, so orElse gives -. There is no set() that could leave b behind, which is the difference from a ThreadLocal. Inside ScopedValue.where(TENANT, "bank-a").run(...), a handler submits a task to Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). What does TENANT.isBound() return inside that task? false: only subtasks forked in a StructuredTaskScope see the parent's binding true: every virtual thread inherits its creator's scoped values true, but only if the task starts before run() returns It throws IllegalStateException, because scoped values can't be read on virtual threads Scoped value bindings flow only into threads forked by a StructuredTaskScope, whose lifetime is guaranteed to fit inside the binding. A thread started by an executor could outlive the run() call, so it gets nothing. Pass the value as an argument there. The second option describes InheritableThreadLocal, which copies values into every new thread. You want an FX rate from whichever of two providers answers first, and the slower call cancelled. Which tool fits? CompletableFuture.anyOf(primary, backup) StructuredTaskScope.open() with the default joiner StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.allSuccessfulOrThrow()) StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow()) (JDK 25 name) anySuccessfulResultOrThrow (renamed anySuccessfulOrThrow in JDK 26) returns the first successful result and cancels the rest. CompletableFuture.anyOf completes with the first result but cancels nothing, so the slower call runs to the end. The default joiner and allSuccessfulOrThrow both wait for every subtask to succeed. From the lesson "Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption": a fail-fast scope cancels a sibling that runs while (true) { total = total.add(nextChunk(buffer)); }, pure computation that never blocks and never checks the interrupt flag. What happens to that sibling? It stops at once, because cancelling a subtask kills its thread It keeps running: cancellation only interrupts, and this loop never looks It stops at its next loop iteration, because virtual threads check the flag automatically The JVM throws InterruptedException inside add Cancellation in Java is cooperative. cancel(true), shutdownNow() and a scope's cancel all just set the interrupt flag. Blocking calls react by throwing InterruptedException; a loop that never blocks must check Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() itself. A scope's close() would wait for this loop forever.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Explain it back
x: A colleague says that try-with-resources around newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() already gives you structured concurrency. Explain what it gives you, what it is missing, and what StructuredTaskScope and scoped values add.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Key terms
x: Structured concurrency Concurrent subtasks are tied to the block that started them and can't outlive it. Scope The object that forks subtasks, joins them, and on close guarantees they have all ended. Fail fast The first failure cancels the remaining subtasks and is reported at once. Joiner The policy you pass to StructuredTaskScope.open: when join() returns and what it returns or throws. Scoped value A read-only value bound for the length of one call and visible to all the code that call runs. Preview API A complete JDK API that is not final yet. It needs --enable-preview and can change in the next release. What does structured concurrency guarantee when the block that opened a scope ends? Every subtask forked in the scope has finished. None is still running, whether the block returned, threw or was interrupted. In a fail-fast scope, what happens to the other subtasks when one fails? They are cancelled, which means interrupted. join() throws the first failure. What does join() throw on JDK 25 when a subtask fails in StructuredTaskScope.open()? StructuredTaskScope.FailedException (unchecked), with the subtask's exception as its cause. From JDK 27 the built-in joiners throw ExecutionException. Is StructuredTaskScope final in JDK 25? No. It is a preview API in JDK 25, 26 and 27 and needs --enable-preview. JEP 543 makes it final in JDK 28. Are scoped values final in JDK 25? Yes, since JDK 25 (JEP 506). They need no flag. Which threads can read a scoped value's binding? Code running inside where(...).run(...) or call(...), and subtasks forked in a StructuredTaskScope opened there. Not threads you start yourself and not executor tasks. Why can't a hand-built scope cancel with future.cancel(true) and rely on executor.close() to wait? A cancelled future is done at once, so on JDK 21 the executor stops waiting for that thread while it still runs its finally. Use shutdownNow(), which interrupts without completing the futures.

h: Structured concurrency and scoped values · Go deeper
x: Custom joiners. A Joiner has two hooks, onFork and onComplete, and a result() method that join() calls at the end. onComplete returns true to cancel the scope. That is enough for policies the built-in joiners don't cover, such as "stop once three of five ledger replicas agree" or "collect successes and ignore failures". onComplete runs on the thread of the subtask that just finished, so a joiner's state must be thread-safe. Check the Javadoc of the exact JDK you use, because JDK 26 changed the hook signatures slightly. Why CompletableFuture doesn't solve this. allOf waits for everything even after one future fails, and cancel(true) on a CompletableFuture doesn't interrupt the thread doing the work: it only completes the future. The lesson "CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out" builds fan-out that way; notice how much code its error handling needs compared with a scope. Kotlin already has this. In coroutine code, coroutineScope { async { } } gives the same guarantees without a preview flag: children can't outlive the scope, the first failure cancels the siblings, and cancellation reaches each child at its next suspension point. The coroutines track covers it. StructuredTaskScope matters most for Java code and for Kotlin code that blocks on threads. Scoped values and virtual threads. A ThreadLocal costs a map entry per thread, and with a million virtual threads that adds up, as lesson 4 of this track showed. A scoped value binding is attached to the call, not copied per thread, and its forks share it. That makes it the natural fit for one virtual thread per request with many short subtasks. Old articles. Before JDK 25 the API was StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure and ShutdownOnSuccess, subclasses you created with new. Scoped values had static helpers such as ScopedValue.runWhere, which were removed during the previews. If a snippet uses either, it was written for an older preview.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · The old pool was a limit you never wrote down
x: Here is the quote service from this lesson's lab, as it runs in production today. It handles requests on a fixed pool of 10 platform threads. Nobody remembers exactly why 10, but the database pool has 10 connections. Java public final class QuoteService implements AutoCloseable { // 10 platform threads, because the database pool has 10 connections private final ExecutorService workers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10); public Quote quote(QuoteRequest request) throws Exception { String tier = db.tier(request.customerId()); // 5 ms on a pooled connection BigDecimal rate = fx.rate(request.pair()); // 100 ms HTTP call return new Quote(request.customerId(), request.pair(), rate, fee(tier, request.amount())); } } Kotlin class QuoteService(private val db: CustomerDb, private val fx: FxApi) : AutoCloseable { // 10 platform threads, because the database pool has 10 connections private val workers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10) fun quote(request: QuoteRequest): Quote { val tier = db.tier(request.customerId) // 5 ms on a pooled connection val rate = fx.rate(request.pair) // 100 ms HTTP call return Quote(request.customerId, request.pair, rate, fee(tier, request.amount)) } } The obvious migration is one line: replace newFixedThreadPool(10) with newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). Do that in the lab and every test fails with connection pool: no connection after 30 ms. The pool did two jobs. It ran the requests, and it made sure that no more than 10 of them could ever reach the database. The second job was never written down anywhere, but it's the reason the connection pool never had to wait. Virtual threads take over the first job and drop the second. In a burst of 300 requests, all 300 now ask for a connection at the same moment, and the pool's 30 ms borrow timeout was tuned for 10 callers. So put the second job back, explicitly, around the one call that needs it: Java private final Semaphore dbPermits = new Semaphore(db.poolSize(), true); // one permit per pooled connection public Quote quote(QuoteRequest request) throws Exception { String tier; dbPermits.acquire(); try { tier = db.tier(request.customerId()); // only the database call waits its turn } finally { dbPermits.release(); } BigDecimal rate = fx.rate(request.pair()); // FX calls now overlap freely return new Quote(request.customerId(), request.pair(), rate, fee(tier, request.amount())); } Kotlin private val dbPermits = Semaphore(db.poolSize, true) // one permit per pooled connection fun quote(request: QuoteRequest): Quote { val tier = withDbPermit { db.tier(request.customerId) } // only the database call waits its turn val rate = fx.rate(request.pair) // FX calls now overlap freely return Quote(request.customerId, request.pair, rate, fee(tier, request.amount)) } Why not just raise the pool's timeout? You could, and requests would wait inside the pool instead. The semaphore is better for two reasons. Its queue is visible: queueLength is a gauge you can put on a dashboard. And the policy is yours: wait, or tryAcquire with a deadline that fits the request's budget and fails before any work is done. Meanwhile the FX calls, which never needed a limit, go from 10 in flight to about 200. Migrate in two steps Read MigrationDemo. 300 requests arrive at once. Each borrows one of 10 connections for a 5 ms query (the pool gives up after 30 ms), then makes a 100 ms FX call. Predict, for A (the old pool), B (a plain swap to virtual threads) and C (virtual threads plus a Semaphore(10)): total time, failed requests, and peak FX calls in flight. Run it. Then change C's semaphore to new Semaphore(3, true) (in Kotlin, Semaphore(3, true)) and predict the new time before running again. The question is not how many threads you have but where the waiting requests queue. The old pool is a restaurant with 10 waiters and a kitchen with 10 burners. Nobody planned it, but with 10 waiters there are never more than 10 orders at the kitchen at once. Moving to virtual threads is like giving every table its own waiter the moment it's seated. Drinks and bread arrive at once, which is the FX call overlapping. But at a peak, 300 waiters crowd the kitchen door. The semaphore is a ticket machine at that door with 10 tickets: waiters queue in an orderly line you can count, and the kitchen works at its pace. The analogy breaks on cost. Real waiters are paid, so nobody would hire 300 by accident. Virtual threads cost almost nothing, so the crowd at the door can grow very large before anyone notices.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · A migration checklist
x: Every migration I have seen needed the same handful of changes. Go through them in this order. Run JDK 25 first. On JDK 21 to 23, blocking inside synchronized pins the carrier, and JDBC drivers, HTTP clients and logging appenders do exactly that. On JDK 25, only class initializers and native frames still pin. Lesson 4 of this track has the details. Replace the pools that run blocking work with one virtual thread per task, through newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() or your framework's switch. Delete the old pool-size setting so nobody tunes it later. For each downstream the old pool protected, write the limit down. That means one shared Semaphore per downstream, sized from what that downstream allows, held only around its calls. Also look for downstreams with no limit at all, because now nothing slows the traffic in front of them. Leave the connection pool small. A database runs well with a few connections per CPU core of the database server, and more connections make it slower. Every pod multiplies the number: 30 pods with 20 connections each are 600 sessions on one Oracle instance. Hunt ThreadLocals. Caches become one object per request (lesson 4 of this track), and request context belongs in arguments or scoped values (lesson 5). Keep CPU-heavy steps on a bounded pool of platform threads. Signing a settlement file on a virtual thread holds a carrier for the whole time. Give every wait a deadline. With a pool, a slow downstream filled the queue and callers got rejected. With virtual threads, nothing pushes back, and parked requests pile up in the heap. Use tryAcquire with a timeout and HTTP client timeouts, and return a fast 503 when you're over budget. Item 3 is the one teams skip, because the code still works in tests. It only fails at the first real traffic peak. Audit a codebase From labs/, run the three searches below on the vthreads exercises. Each one looks for one checklist item. For each hit, name the checklist item and the fix. Run the same searches on a service you own (change the path), and note which hits are request handling, which are CPU work, and which are context. terminal # 2. pools that run blocking work grep -rnE "newFixedThreadPool|newCachedThreadPool|new ThreadPoolExecutor" --include=*.java --include=*.kt vthreads/src/main # 5. ThreadLocal caches and context grep -rnE "ThreadLocal" --include=*.java --include=*.kt vthreads/src/main # 1. monitors around I/O (matters on JDK 21 to 23) grep -rnE "synchronized" --include=*.java --include=*.kt vthreads/src/main Unless you already fixed them, the searches find this lesson's QuoteService with its newFixedThreadPool(10), the ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> in ReceiptStamp and the synchronized methods in FxRateCache from lesson 4, plus a comment or two. In a real service, expect more pools than you thought: many of them sit inside libraries and framework config, not in your own code. In a Quarkus service the datasource is an Agroal pool sized by quarkus.datasource.jdbc.max-size, and with @RunOnVirtualThread the worker pool no longer stands in front of it. Before you annotate the busiest endpoint, find out what used to cap it, and write that cap down as a semaphore. Do the same for each REST client: a card issuer that allows 150 calls in flight for your merchant, shared across 4 pods, means Semaphore(37) per pod. Size the Oracle side from the database, not from the thread count, and multiply by the number of pods. For a Kafka consumer moved to virtual threads, check how many records your framework now processes at once, and whether records with the same key still need to be handled in order. In a Temporal worker, the maximum number of concurrent activity executions is already an explicit limit. Size it from the downstreams the activities call, not from CPU.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Quarkus and Spring Boot: the switch is one line
x: Most services don't create their request threads themselves. The framework does, so the switch is in the framework. Quarkus has no global switch. You opt in per endpoint, or per class, with @RunOnVirtualThread, and Quarkus then runs each call on a new virtual thread: Java @Path("/quotes") public class QuoteResource { @Inject QuoteService quotes; @POST @RunOnVirtualThread // each call runs on a new virtual thread public Quote quote(QuoteRequest request) { return quotes.quote(request); // plain blocking code: JDBC, REST client, Kafka producer } } Kotlin @Path("/quotes") class QuoteResource(private val quotes: QuoteService) { @POST @RunOnVirtualThread // each call runs on a new virtual thread fun quote(request: QuoteRequest): Quote = quotes.quote(request) // plain blocking code: JDBC, REST client, Kafka producer } The annotation is io.smallrye.common.annotation.RunOnVirtualThread. The same annotation works on Reactive Messaging @Incoming methods, which is how a Kafka consumer handles records on virtual threads. Opting in one endpoint at a time is a good fit for a migration: you move the busiest blocking endpoint first and compare. Spring Boot 3.2 and later has one property for the whole application: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true With it, the embedded web server handles requests on virtual threads, and Spring's own task executors use them too. Neither framework adds the limits from the checklist. That's still your code. They also change what an old setting means. quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads sizes the worker pool, which @RunOnVirtualThread endpoints don't use, so it no longer caps them. If you relied on it as your database limit, that limit is gone, exactly like the pool in the lab. The Quarkus guide lists the traps it sees most, and you know all of them by now: libraries that pin on JDK 21, CPU-heavy endpoints that monopolize a carrier, and libraries that pool objects in ThreadLocals. Check yourself: a Quarkus service sets quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads=20, its datasource has 20 connections, and its busiest endpoint now has @RunOnVirtualThread. At a peak of 500 concurrent calls to that endpoint, how many can ask for a connection at the same moment? All 500. The worker pool's size doesn't apply to virtual-thread endpoints, so nothing stands in front of the datasource. A shared Semaphore(20) around the database calls puts the limit back. h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Measure it, and let Little's law find the bottleneck
x:
Measure before you switch, then again after, with the same load test. You need a baseline of throughput, p50 and p99 latency, error rate, CPU, heap and GC time. Without it, "it feels faster" is all you'll have. After the switch, one number stops meaning anything: the thread count. Fifty thousand virtual threads is normal and tells you nothing. Watch where requests wait instead: requests in flight in the service the queue length on each downstream semaphore the connection pool's pending and active counts (HikariCP's Micrometer metrics are hikaricp.connections.pending and hikaricp.connections.active) jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events from a JFR recording, as in lesson 4 of this track Little's law ties these together: requests in flight = throughput × time in the system. Use it both ways. To predict, multiply: 400 requests per second that spend 120 ms in the service means about 48 in flight. To find a bottleneck, divide a limit by the time each request holds it. Ten database permits held for 20 ms each serve at most 10 / 0.02 s = 500 requests per second. Below that rate the semaphore's queue stays near zero. Above it, the queue grows every second, latency grows with it, and throughput stays flat at about 500. A rising queue gauge with flat throughput is what a saturated downstream looks like, and it is the alert to set up. Roll out like any risky change. Switch one pod (or one endpoint in Quarkus), send it real traffic, and compare its numbers with the pods still on the old pool. Look at p99 latency and error rate first. Then check that heap and GC didn't jump, because parked virtual threads keep their stacks on the heap. Watch a downstream saturate Read MeasureDemo. Requests arrive at a steady rate. // one permit per pooled connection } public Quote quote(QuoteRequest r) throws Exception { String tier; dbPermits.acquire(); // outside the try try { tier = db.tier(r.customerId()); // only the database call holds a permit } finally { dbPermits.release(); } BigDecimal rate = fx.rate(r.pair()); // FX calls overlap freely return new Quote(r.customerId(), r.pair(), rate, fee(tier, r.amount())); } // 3. a gauge for the dashboard public int dbWaiting() { return dbPermits.getQueueLength(); } @Override public void close() { requests.close(); // 4. waits for requests in flight } } QuoteService.kt (the lab's solution) class QuoteService(private val db: CustomerDb, private val fx: FxApi) : AutoCloseable { // 1. one new virtual thread per request: no size to pick private val requests = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() // 2. the limit the old pool gave you by accident, now explicit private val dbPermits = Semaphore(db.poolSize, true) // one permit per pooled connection fun quote(r: QuoteRequest): Quote { val tier = withDbPermit { db.tier(r.customerId) } // only the database call holds a permit val rate = fx.rate(r.pair) // FX calls overlap freely return Quote(r.customerId, r.pair, rate, fee(tier, r.amount)) } // 3. a gauge for the dashboard fun dbWaiting(): Int = dbPermits.queueLength override fun close() = requests.close() // 4. waits for requests in flight private inline fun <T> withDbPermit(block: () -> T): T { dbPermits.acquire() // outside the try try { return block() } finally { dbPermits.release() } } } The migration is the same in both: the executor changes, and the limit becomes a semaphore around one call. Kotlin's version reads better because a small inline function with a lambda wraps acquire, try and release, and inlining means the lambda costs nothing at run time. Java has no equivalent without a functional interface, so the try/finally sits in the method. Two Kotlin traps: kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore has a withPermit too, but it suspends a coroutine and is not the java.util.concurrent.Semaphore your threads need. And Kotlin doesn't check exceptions, so nothing reminds you that acquire() can throw InterruptedException. It still can, and it must still sit outside the try.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Worked example
x: Size every limit with Little's law before the switch A card authorization service runs on 4 pods, and each pod gets 200 requests per second at peak. A request holds a database connection for 15 ms, calls the fraud API for 200 ms, and calls the card issuer for 120 ms. The issuer allows 150 calls in flight for your merchant, across all pods. Today each pod has a fixed pool of 50 threads and 10 connections. First question: is the thread pool the bottleneck today? time in the system W = 15 + 200 + 120 ms = 335 ms threads needed L = 200/s x 0.335 s = 67 the pool has 50, so at peak requests queue for a thread pool capacity 50 / 0.335 s = about 149 requests/s Yes. The pool tops out near 149 requests per second, below the 200 that arrive, so requests queue at peak. Virtual threads remove that limit. Now check each downstream with the same formula, because nothing caps them any more. database connections busy 200/s x 0.015 s = 3 pool of 10: fine issuer calls in flight 200/s x 0.120 s = 24 limit 150 / 4 pods = 37 per pod fraud calls in flight 200/s x 0.200 s = 40 no published limit: ask the fraud team virtual threads 67 at a time, a small amount of heap Write the limits in code: one shared semaphore per downstream, sized per pod, held only around that downstream's calls. final class Downstreams { // 1. issuer: 150 calls in flight for the merchant, shared by 4 pods final Semaphore issuer = new Semaphore(150 / 4, true); // 2. database: one permit per pooled connection final Semaphore db = new Semaphore(10, true); // 3. fraud: no limit yet; add one when the fraud team gives you a number } class Downstreams { // 1. issuer: 150 calls in flight for the merchant, shared by 4 pods val issuer = Semaphore(150 / 4, true) // 2. database: one permit per pooled connection val db = Semaphore(10, true) // 3. fraud: no limit yet; add one when the fraud team gives you a number } Predict where each limit starts to bite, by dividing permits by the time each request holds one. The issuer semaphore starts to queue at 37 / 0.12 s, about 308 requests per second per pod, and the database at 10 / 0.015 s, about 666. If one pod dies, the other 3 get about 267 per second each, still under 308. So the first alert to set is the issuer semaphore's queue length, and the capacity of the service is now about 300 requests per second per pod instead of 149.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Quiz
x: After the switch to virtual threads, p99 latency doubles at peak while throughput stays flat. Which metric tells you whether the database is the bottleneck? The number of live virtual threads The queue length on the database semaphore (or the pool's pending count), climbing at peak CPU usage of the carrier threads The number of ForkJoinPool worker threads A saturated downstream shows up as a queue that grows while throughput stays flat. Virtual thread counts grow with any slowdown and don't say where the time goes. Carrier CPU is low when everybody waits, and the scheduler's worker count stays near the core count. A pod handles 300 requests per second, and each request holds a database connection for 25 ms. On average, about how many connections are busy? About 8 About 25 About 75 About 300 Little's law: busy connections = arrival rate × holding time = 300/s × 0.025 s = 7.5. A pool of 10 is close to its limit at this rate, and 10 / 0.025 s = 400 requests per second is where it saturates. The other options mix up the holding time with a count, or assume every request holds a connection the whole time. In a Quarkus service, how do you run one blocking REST endpoint on virtual threads? Raise quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads to 10,000 Set spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true Annotate the endpoint method with @RunOnVirtualThread Return a Uni from the method Quarkus opts in per method or class with @RunOnVirtualThread, and each call then runs on a new virtual thread. The thread pool setting sizes platform worker threads. The spring.threads property is Spring Boot's global switch. Returning a Uni makes the endpoint reactive and runs it on the event loop, which must never block. After the migration, the connection pool reports timeouts at every peak. Which fix is right? Raise the pool's maximum size to 1,000 connections Go back to a fixed pool of 20 platform threads for all request handling Raise the pool's connection timeout to 5 minutes Put a shared Semaphore sized to the pool around the database work, and use tryAcquire with a deadline that fits the request's budget The semaphore restores the limit the old pool gave you, only around the database work, with a queue you can see and a deadline you choose. A huge pool overloads the database for every service that shares it. A fixed pool brings back the cap on everything, including calls that never needed it. A 5-minute timeout hides overload as very slow requests. From the lesson "Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps": your service runs on JDK 21, and its JDBC driver holds a synchronized lock while it reads from the socket. You move request handling to virtual threads. What is the main risk, and the simplest fix? Pinning: queries block their carriers, and a few slow ones can stall every virtual thread. Upgrade to JDK 25, or to a driver version that uses ReentrantLock Data races inside the driver, because virtual threads don't respect synchronized. Wrap every call in your own lock A ThreadLocal leak in the driver. Call remove() after each query No risk: a JDBC driver never blocks while it holds a lock On JDK 21 to 23, blocking while holding a monitor pins the carrier, and with as many carriers as cores, a few slow queries can hold all of them. JEP 491 fixed this in JDK 24, so JDK 25 is the cleanest fix. synchronized still gives mutual exclusion on virtual threads, so there is no new race.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Key terms
x: Implicit limit A cap on concurrency that nobody configured on purpose, such as a thread pool's size protecting a database. Bulkhead An explicit limit on calls to one downstream, usually a shared Semaphore, so it can't be overloaded. Connection pool A fixed set of open database connections that callers borrow and return. Callers wait, or time out, when all are in use. Little's law In a stable system, requests in flight = throughput × average time in the system. @RunOnVirtualThread The annotation that makes Quarkus run an endpoint or message handler on a new virtual thread per call. Load shedding Rejecting work quickly, for example with a 503, when a limit is full, instead of letting it wait without end. What limit does a fixed thread pool give you without saying so? No more than N requests can reach any downstream at once. Moving to virtual threads removes it. Where does the semaphore go when you migrate to virtual threads? Around the one downstream call that needs the limit, as one object shared by all requests, sized from that downstream. Should you grow the connection pool to match the number of virtual threads? No. The database decides how many connections help, roughly a few per database CPU core, and every pod multiplies the pool. Queue in front of the pool instead. How do you run a Quarkus REST endpoint on virtual threads? Annotate the method or class with @RunOnVirtualThread. Quarkus has no global switch. How do you switch a Spring Boot 3.2+ application to virtual threads? spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true Little's law in one line? Requests in flight = throughput × time in the system (L = λW). Which gauge shows a saturated downstream after the move? The queue on its semaphore (or the pool's pending count) growing while throughput stays flat.

h: Moving a blocking service to virtual threads · Go deeper
x: Admission control at the door. The lab's semaphore waits without a deadline, deep inside the request. In a payment API it's often better to decide at the start: try to take every permit the request will need, or a single "requests in progress" permit sized from Little's law, with a short tryAcquire deadline, and answer 503 at once if you can't. Then you never call the fraud API for a request that would later time out at the database. Pool timeouts versus semaphore waits. A pool's borrow timeout and a semaphore's deadline look alike, but they sit at different places. The pool timeout fires after the request has done part of its work and maybe holds other resources. A deadline at the semaphore, at the start of the call, fails before any of that. Keep the pool's timeout too, as a safety net for bugs in your own limits. Fairness and the tail. A fair semaphore serves waiters in arrival order. That costs a little throughput and keeps p99 close to p50 during a burst. A non-fair one lets a newcomer grab a permit that was just released, which helps the average and hurts the unlucky waiters. For payment latency the tail matters more. Thread dumps after the move. jstack shows carriers, not the thousands of parked virtual threads. jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json writes all of them, grouped by the executor or scope that owns them. Before an incident, practise finding the stack of one stuck request in such a dump. When not to migrate. A service that is CPU-bound, or that already runs fully reactive code on a few event-loop threads, gains little. The win is largest for services that block on I/O and are limited by their thread pool today. Little's law tells you which kind yours is: compare the threads you need (rate × time) with the threads you have.

h: Capstone: a payment ledger under load
x: Build one ledger in three sittings: correct under contention, on a pool you can reason about, then on virtual threads. In three sittings you build one working program: an in-memory payment ledger that applies transfers from many threads, never loses or creates money, never deadlocks, shuts down without dropping an accepted transfer, publishes balances that always add up, and serves 10,000 concurrent requests on virtual threads while a slow fraud service is held behind a bulkhead and a deadline. At the end you defend the design in a review, and you know which earlier lesson's mechanism decides each line of it. The capstone draws on every track of Part 1. Lesson 1 uses races, deadlock and lock ordering, immutability and stress testing from Threads and the bugs they cause. Lesson 2 uses ThreadPoolExecutor, Little's law and production shutdown from Thread pools and executors, and happens-before and safe publication from The Java Memory Model. Lesson 3 uses one-thread-per-request, semaphores, pinning and fail-fast scopes from Virtual threads. There is little new theory: each section shows what breaks if you choose differently, then names the earlier lesson that explains why. The lab lives in labs/ledger, one package per lesson (workbench.ledger.l01 to l03). Each lesson's starter code contains the previous lesson's solution, so you can start any sitting fresh. Lessons 1 and 2 are in Java; lesson 3 adds a Kotlin server on top of the same Java ledger, the way a Kotlin service calls a Java library. Run ./gradlew :ledger:test --tests 'workbench.ledger.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes; solutionTest runs the same tests against the reference answers. The tests check what production cares about (invariants under 8 threads, no lost transfer on shutdown, a bulkhead that holds at 10,000 requests), never timings. The Try-it demos run with ./gradlew :ledger:demo -Pmain=..., and two of them hang on purpose so you can read a thread dump: install JDK 25, and keep jcmd and jq at hand. Start from invariants: money is conserved, no balance goes below zero, a transfer is whole or not at all. Every lock and edge in the program protects one of them. Per-account ReentrantLocks taken in one global id order give parallel transfers without deadlock; the balance check lives inside the same critical section as the move. A transfer is an immutable, validated value, so any thread can see it whole; a reused mutable object handed to a pool delivers the wrong data. Stress tests collide threads behind a start latch and check every invariant, at the end and at the point where it can break. A pass is evidence, not proof. The ledger pool is sized by Little's law (8 threads, 80 slots), bounded, named, and rejects by counting and throwing; overflow becomes a visible 503, never a lost transfer. Shutdown drains within a deadline, then cancels and hands back what never started; the journal is written before apply, so an interrupt never leaves half a transfer. A consistent snapshot holds every account lock in order, copies, and publishes an immutable record through a volatile field; readers never lock. Requests run on one new virtual thread each, behind written-down limits: a shared fraud semaphore, the bounded ledger pool, and one deadline per request with a stand-in fallback. Fail-fast screening takes results in completion order and ends with shutdownNow() and close(), so no call outlives its request or keeps a permit. Thread dumps find what tests can't: a pool parked on its own futures in Thread.print -l, and 10,000 virtual threads grouped by container and stack in the JSON dump.
