Make the values that cross threads immutable, and validate them in the constructor. Lock several accounts only in one global id order; sort them when there are more than two. Keep the check inside the critical section that acts on it. Never block inside an account lock: journal, fraud calls and logging happen outside. Size pools and queues with Little's law, then check the downstream's own limit. Bound every queue; choose the rejection policy on purpose and count rejections. Shut down in order, with one deadline, and hand back what never ran. One new virtual thread per request; a shared semaphore per slow dependency. One deadline per request; cancel what you stop waiting for; a fallback that is a business rule. Fail fast in fan-outs, and let no subtask outlive its request. Test invariants under collision, with latches and counts, never with timings. Diagnostics Question Command Which pool is stuck, and on what? jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l: named threads, state, parking to wait for, Locked ownable synchronizers Is it a lock cycle? the same dump ends with Found one Java-level deadlock if it is Where are 10,000 virtual threads? jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/t.json (add -overwrite to replace a file) How are they spread? jq per container, then group stacks by the first frame of your code and uniq -c Is anything pinned? JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned (20 ms threshold by default) Versions: virtual threads final in JDK 21 (JEP 444); synchronized stops pinning in JDK 24 (JEP 491), first LTS JDK 25; JSON dumps carry state and virtual from JDK 25; StructuredTaskScope is preview in JDK 25 to 27 and final in JDK 28 (JEP 543).

h: Capstone: a payment ledger under load: track quiz
x: Two transfers run at once: acc-07 to acc-03, and acc-03 to acc-07. With the ledger's lock order, which lock does each take first? Each takes its from account first Both take acc-03 first Both take acc-07 first Whichever thread starts first decides The order is by id, whatever direction the money moves, so both lock acc-03 first. The second thread waits while holding nothing, which is contention, not deadlock. "from first" is the order that deadlocks. A stress test of a ledger that checks the balance before taking the locks reports total 500,000 and no negative balances at the end. Why did it miss the bug? Accounts went negative during the run and later credits topped them up before the final check The race can't happen on x86 The JIT removed the check Eight threads are too few to cause a race Each move was still atomic, so the total held, and the overdrafts healed before the end. Check an invariant where it can break as well: debit refusing an overdraft turns the race into an immediate failure. Peak traffic is 3,000 transfers a second and the journal write takes 4 ms. The storage allows 10 concurrent writes. What should the ledger pool's thread count be? 12, from Little's law 3,000 10: the journal's limit is lower than what Little's law asks for As many as the machine has cores Little's law asks for 3,000 x 0.004 = 12, but the journal handles 10 at once, so the 11th and 12th threads would only queue inside it. Size from the scarce resource: 10 threads give at most 10 / 0.004 = 2,500 a second, and the counting rejection handles the rest. Which rejection policy may silently lose a transfer that a caller was told was accepted? A counting policy that throws CallerRunsPolicy AbortPolicy DiscardOldestPolicy DiscardOldestPolicy drops the oldest queued task, which a caller already holds a future for, and that future never completes. A throwing policy rejects the new transfer before anyone is told it was accepted, and CallerRunsPolicy runs it on the submitter. A balances endpoint adds up the accounts one at a time, locking each account while it reads it. Transfers keep running. What can it report? Always the exact total, because every read holds a lock A total that is too high or too low, because a transfer can run between two reads An exception, because two locks are taken A total that is always too low Money can move from an account not yet read to one already read (counted in neither) or the other way (counted twice). Only holding every lock at once, in the global order, gives one instant. A thread dump shows every ledger- thread WAITING (parking) on a FutureTask inside your own statement method, and no deadlock report. What is wrong? Tasks waiting for other tasks queued in the same bounded pool A lock-order deadlock between two accounts The journal is slow The pool's threads are pinned Workers parked on futures of their own pool, with tasks still queued, is pool-induced deadlock. There is no lock cycle, so the detector reports nothing. Do the work inline, compose instead of blocking, or use a separate pool. Which design caps what the fraud service sees when 10,000 requests run on virtual threads? A fixed pool of 20 virtual threads for whole requests A Semaphore(20) created in each request handler newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() alone One Semaphore(20) field on the fraud client, shared by every request One shared semaphore limits only the fraud call. A pool of virtual threads caps the whole request, including the limits check and the ledger wait. A semaphore per handler limits nothing, and the per-task executor has no limit at all. During a fraud outage each call takes 2 s. The request stops waiting at its 300 ms deadline but never cancels the call, and uses a shared executor. What happens to the bulkhead? Nothing: every request answers in 300 ms It grows to fit the extra calls Its permits stay held by abandoned calls for 2 s each, so most new requests can't get one The calls are interrupted automatically A timeout ends the wait, not the work. Each orphaned call keeps its permit until the fraud service answers. Cancel the call at the deadline so its finally gives the permit back to the next request. The ledger must run on JDK 21 and serve virtual threads. Why are the account locks ReentrantLocks? On JDK 21 a virtual thread waiting to enter or blocking inside synchronized pins its carrier; ReentrantLock parks and frees it synchronized doesn't give visibility ReentrantLock makes the critical section faster Kotlin can't use synchronized JDK 24 (JEP 491) removed monitor pinning, but on JDK 21 to 23 contended or blocking synchronized code holds the carrier. ReentrantLock has always let a waiting virtual thread unmount. Either way, nothing slow belongs inside an account lock. jcmd <pid> Thread.print on the server during an outage shows no request threads at all. Where are they? They have all finished They are inside the carriers, under the name ForkJoinPool-1-worker-N They were garbage collected They are parked virtual threads, which Thread.print doesn't list; Thread.dump_to_file -format=json does A parked virtual thread is a stack on the heap, not an OS thread. Thread.print lists platform threads (plus mounted virtual threads from JDK 24). The JSON dump lists every thread, grouped by the container that started it.

h: Design the ledger and make it correct · Write the invariants down before the code
x: Here is the smallest ledger that can be wrong. Fifty accounts, no locks: Java long[] balance = new long[50]; // 10,000 cents each, 500,000 in total void transfer(int from, int to, long cents) { if (balance[from] >= cents) { // check balance[from] -= cents; // read, subtract, write balance[to] += cents; // read, add, write } } Kotlin val balance = LongArray(50) { 10_000L } // 500,000 cents in total fun transfer(from: Int, to: Int, cents: Long) { if (balance[from] >= cents) { // check balance[from] -= cents // read, subtract, write balance[to] += cents // read, add, write } } Run it on eight threads with 100,000 random transfers each, and the total is wrong by millions of cents. You know the mechanism from Race conditions: why count++ lies: -= is a read, a subtraction and a write, and two threads that read the same balance lose one of the two updates. Before you write the real ledger, write down what correct means. An invariant is a statement about the data that must be true whenever another thread can look. This ledger has three: Money is conserved: the sum of all balances never changes. No balance is ever below zero. A transfer happens whole or not at all: nobody sees the debit without the credit. Each invariant decides part of the design. Invariants 1 and 3 say the debit and the credit must be one step that no other thread can split, and that step spans two accounts. Invariant 2 says the balance check belongs inside that same step. A check in one step and a debit in another is check-then-act, the second race shape from that lesson. And "whenever another thread can look" tells you where to test: not only at the end of a run. The rest of this lesson builds the ledger so that every line of apply points at one of these three. That is the habit to keep for any shared state: invariants first, then the locks that protect them, then a test that tries hard to break them. Count what a lock-free ledger loses Open BrokenLedgerDemo (or its Kotlin twin). Before you run it, write down what you expect the total to be after each run. Run it with the command below. Note how far off each run is. Run it again with -Pargs=1000, so each thread makes only 1,000 transfers. The threads still start behind a latch. Predict first: will the total be right? With 1,000 per thread it is still wrong, by thousands: the latch releases all eight threads at the same moment, so even short runs collide. Without the latch, short runs often look correct because each thread finishes before the next one starts. Picture a vault room where every safe-deposit box has its own key on a numbered hook. A clerk who moves cash between two boxes must hold both keys while doing it, and the house rule says: take the lower-numbered key first. Two clerks who both need boxes 3 and 7 never end up each holding one key and waiting for the other; one of them waits at hook 3 with empty hands. One key for the whole room would also be correct, and every clerk would queue at the door. The analogy breaks in one place: a real clerk who opens a box and finds it short of cash stops. A thread checks only what your code tells it to check, at the moment you tell it, which is why the check has to sit inside the locks.

h: Design the ledger and make it correct · A transfer is a value, so make it immutable
x: A transfer crosses threads. An HTTP handler or a file importer builds it, a pool thread applies it, the journal writes it and a log line prints it. If any of them can change it, the others can see two versions of it. Here is that bug in its most common form. A batch importer parses a file into one reusable row object, to save allocations, and hands each row to a pool: Java TransferRow row = new TransferRow(); // mutable, reused for every line for (String line : file) { row.parse(line); // overwrites id, from, to, cents pool.execute(() -> ledger.apply(row)); // a worker reads row later } Kotlin val row = TransferRow() // mutable, reused for every line for (line in file) { row.parse(line) // overwrites id, from, to, cents pool.execute { ledger.apply(row) } // a worker reads row later } By the time a worker reads row, the parser has moved on. In this section's demo, 100,000 lines reached the ledger as about 11,000 different transfers, most of them applied several times. A few dozen rows carried the id of one line and the amount of another. That is a data race: the worker read the fields with no happens-before edge to the parser's later writes, so it could see any mix of them. The fix is a value that can't change. A Java record, or a Kotlin data class of vals, has final fields and no setters: Java public record Transfer(String id, String from, String to, long cents) { public Transfer { // compact constructor: runs before the fields are set Objects.requireNonNull(id, "id"); Objects.requireNonNull(from, "from"); Objects.requireNonNull(to, "to"); if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive"); if (from.equals(to)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("two different accounts"); } } Kotlin data class Transfer(val id: String, val from: String, val to: String, val cents: Long) { init { // runs on every construction, copy() included require(cents > 0) { "amount must be positive" } require(from != to) { "two different accounts" } } } Two things come with it. As Safe publication, final fields and escaping this showed, an object with only final fields that doesn't leak this is seen whole by any thread, however it gets there. And the checks run once, at construction, so a Transfer that exists is valid. The ledger never asks whether cents is negative or from equals to, and the lock-ordering code in the next section relies on two different accounts. Money is a long of cents. A double can't hold 0.10 exactly, and a ledger that drifts by fractions of a cent breaks invariant 1 with no thread involved. Reuse one row, then use a record Run ReusedTransferDemo. It parses 100,000 lines and hands each one to a pool of 4 threads. Predict first: how many different lines reach the ledger? Run it again with -Pargs=record, which builds a new immutable Transfer for each line. Java Language Specification, section 8.10: Record classes docs Your payment services lean on the same invariants, usually through the database: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on two account rows, a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint, a unique key on the transfer id. Row locks deadlock exactly like Java locks when two transactions lock the same two rows in opposite orders, and the database then fails one of them with a deadlock error. The fix is the same global order: lock the rows sorted by account id. An in-memory ledger like this one shows up in front of the database: a wallet balance cache, a per-merchant spend limit, the local state of a Temporal workflow. And a Kafka consumer that reuses one mutable DTO per record has the importer's bug the day someone hands records to a pool.

h: Design the ledger and make it correct · Per-account locks, taken in one global order
x: Invariants 1 and 3 need the debit and the credit to happen as one step. The simplest way is one lock for the whole ledger. It is correct, and it makes two transfers that share no account wait for each other. With one lock per account, a transfer between accounts 3 and 7 and another between 12 and 40 can run at the same time. Per-account locks bring back the bug from Deadlock, livelock and starvation: a transfer from A to B locks A and waits for B, while a transfer from B to A holds B and waits for A. The fix from that lesson applies as it is. Give every account a unique, stable key and always lock the smaller key first: Java public Outcome apply(Transfer t) { Account from = account(t.from()), to = account(t.to()); Account first = from.id().compareTo(to.id()) < 0 ? from : to; // 1. one order for everyone Account second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock().lock(); try { second.lock().lock(); try { if (from.balance() < t.cents()) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; // 2. check... from.debit(t.cents()); // 3. ...and act to.credit(t.cents()); return Outcome.APPLIED; } finally { second.lock().unlock(); } } finally { first.lock().unlock(); // 4. on every path } } Kotlin fun apply(t: Transfer): Outcome { val from = account(t.from); val to = account(t.to) val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to // 1. one order for everyone val second = if (first === from) to else from return first.lock.withLock { second.lock.withLock { if (from.balance < t.cents) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS // 2. check... from.debit(t.cents) // 3. ...and act to.credit(t.cents) Outcome.APPLIED } } // 4. withLock unlocks in finally } Each line traces back to an invariant. The order (1) removes the cycle that a deadlock needs. The check sits under both locks (2), so no other transfer can spend the same money between the check and the debit. Debit and credit share one critical section (3), so a thread that takes these locks never sees half a transfer. And finally (4) releases both locks on every path, including the early return for a refusal. The account id is a String compared with compareTo. It is unique and never changes, and that is all an order needs. hashCode() would not do: two accounts can share a hash code, and then two threads can disagree about which one comes first. Why ReentrantLock and not synchronized? Here they behave the same. The choice pays off in lesson 3 of this track: on JDK 21, a virtual thread waiting to enter a synchronized block holds on to its carrier thread, and a ledger serving 10,000 virtual threads will have waiters. What do per-account locks buy? Run the demo and count. With one lock, at most one transfer is ever in progress. With per-account locks, about as many as you have cores. Whether that also makes it faster depends on how much work sits inside the lock and on what else your machine is doing, so the demo prints both. Count the transfers in progress Run LockGranularityDemo. It runs the same 400,000 random transfers under one ledger-wide lock, then under per-account locks taken in id order. Each transfer does 50 steps of work inside its lock. Before you read the output, predict the last column, "most transfers in progress at once", for each strategy. Run it with -Pargs=0 (no work inside the lock) and with -Pargs=200. Compare the times, and explain any surprise. With per-account locks it shows about as many as your cores (4 or 5 on the 4-core machine used here; a thread paused by the OS inside a lock still counts). The times vary with your machine and its load. On the busy machine used here the per-account version was faster in some runs and slower in others, and with -Pargs=0 the single lock often won, because handing a lock from thread to thread costs more than the few instructions it guards. The total is 500,000 in every row: both strategies keep the invariants. T1 and T2 move money in opposite directions, and both lock acc-03 first. T2 waits for that lock while holding nothing, so no cycle can form. ReentrantLock (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Design the ledger and make it correct · A stress harness that tests every invariant
x: A stress test for the ledger has to make threads collide, then check every invariant. Testing and debugging concurrent code listed the habits: a start line so the threads overlap, more threads than cores, many operations, and checks after join(). The lab's harness runs 8 threads that each make 100,000 random transfers between 50 accounts: Java CountDownLatch ready = new CountDownLatch(threads), go = new CountDownLatch(1); List<Thread> workers = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < threads; i++) { int me = i; workers.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { ready.countDown(); try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } // the start line long ok = 0, no = 0; // counted in locals: nothing shared for (int n = 0; n < perThread; n++) { if (ledger.apply(randomTransfer(me, n)) == APPLIED) ok++; else no++; } applied[me] = ok; refused[me] = no; // one slot per thread })); } ready.await(); go.countDown(); // release them together... for (Thread w : workers) w.join(); // ...and wait for all of them Kotlin val ready = CountDownLatch(threads); val go = CountDownLatch(1) val workers = List(threads) { me -> thread { ready.countDown() go.await() // the start line var ok = 0L; var no = 0L // counted in locals: nothing shared repeat(perThread) { n -> if (ledger.apply(randomTransfer(me, n)) == APPLIED) ok++ else no++ } applied[me] = ok; refused[me] = no // one slot per thread } } ready.await(); go.countDown() // release them together... workers.forEach { it.join() } // ...and wait for all of them After the joins, the test checks: the total is still 500,000, no balance is negative, applied plus refused is 800,000 so no transfer vanished, and some transfers were refused, which proves the overdraft branch ran at all. That list has a hole, and this section's demo falls into it. Take a ledger that locks in id order but checks the balance before it takes the locks. Money is still conserved, because each move is atomic. Balances look fine at the end, because a later credit usually tops up an account that went negative. Yet while it ran, thousands of debits took an account below zero. An end-of-run check sees a healthy ledger. So check each invariant where it can break, as well as at the end. The lab's Account.debit throws IllegalStateException when a debit would overdraw, so a race that overdraws fails the stress test at once. The check costs one comparison, and in production it turns a silent loss into an error that pages someone. In a database, a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint does the same job. Then remember what a pass means. Eight threads and 800,000 transfers that find nothing make the ledger more believable. They don't prove it. The proof is the argument you can make for each invariant from the code, which is why you wrote the invariants down first. Find the bug that conserves money Read CheckOutsideLockDemo. Both ledgers lock accounts in id order. The first checks the balance, looks up a fee, then takes the locks and moves the money. The second takes the locks, then checks. Predict which invariants each version breaks, then run it. Find the line that counts overdrafts. Explain why the "negative at the end" column misses what it counts. CheckOutsideLockDemo.java package workbench.ledger.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * Two ledgers that both lock accounts in id order. One checks the balance before it takes the * locks, the other checks after. Run each under 8 threads and test every invariant. */ public class CheckOutsideLockDemo { static final int ACCOUNTS = 50; static final AtomicInteger overdrafts = new AtomicInteger(); // debits that left a balance below zero static final class Account { final int id; final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); long balance = 10_000; // guarded by lock Account(int id) { this.id = id; } long read() { lock.lock(); try { return balance; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } } // the bug: the check runs under from's lock, but that lock is released before the move static void checkFirst(Account from, Account to, long cents) { if (from.read() < cents) return; // check lookUpFee(); // a slow step, outside any lock locked(from, to, () -> move(from, to, cents)); // act, later } // the fix: check and act inside the same two locks static void checkInside(Account from, Account to, long cents) { lookUpFee(); // the same slow step, still outside the locks locked(from, to, () -> { if (from.balance >= cents) move(from, to, cents); }); } static void move(Account from, Account to, long cents) { from.balance -= cents; to.balance += cents; if (from.balance < 0) overdrafts.incrementAndGet(); // the invariant, checked at the moment it can break } // stands in for a call to a fee table; it widens the gap between check and act static void lookUpFee() { for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); } static void locked(Account a, Account b, Runnable body) { Account first = a.id < b.id ? Run each under 8 threads and test every invariant. */ fun main() { runVariant("check, then lock and move", ::checkFirst) runVariant("lock, then check and move", ::checkInside) } private fun runVariant(label: String, mover: (CheckedAccount, CheckedAccount, Long) -> Unit) { val accounts = Array(50) { CheckedAccount(it) } val go = CountDownLatch(1) val workers = List(8) { thread { val rnd = ThreadLocalRandom.current() go.await() repeat(100_000) { val a = rnd.nextInt(50) var b = rnd.nextInt(49) if (b >= a) b++ mover(accounts[a], accounts[b], 1 + rnd.nextLong(5_000)) } } } go.countDown() workers.forEach { it.join() } val total = accounts.sumOf { it.balance } val negative = accounts.count { it.balance < 0 } println(label) println(" total %,d %s, negative at the end: %d, overdrafts while running: %,d" .format(total, if (total == 500_000L) "(conserved)" else "(WRONG)", negative, overdrafts.getAndSet(0))) } ./gradlew :ledger:demo -Pmain=workbench.ledger.l01.demo.CheckOutsideLockDemoKt labs/ledger/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/ledger/l01/demo/CheckOutsideLockDemo.kt Both totals are 500,000 and neither ledger ends with a negative balance. The first one still overdrew accounts a few thousand times while it ran (3,537 times in one run here); the second never did. Each move was atomic, so invariant 1 held. Invariant 2 broke in the gap between the check and the locks, and later credits hid the evidence before the end. CountDownLatch (Java SE 25 API) docs The most common real mistake is checking the balance in one step and moving the money in another: read the balance (often under the account's lock), decide, then lock both accounts and transfer. Each step is thread-safe, so the code looks careful. It is check-then-act across two critical sections, and another transfer can spend the same money in between. It hides well, because money is still conserved and later credits cover the overdraft before any end-of-day report runs. The fix is to put the check inside the critical section that moves the money, and to guard the invariant where it can break: a debit that would overdraw throws.

h: Design the ledger and make it correct · Java and Kotlin
x: The ledger's apply in Java and Kotlin Ledger.java public Outcome apply(Transfer t) { Account from = account(t.from()); Account to = account(t.to()); Account first = from.id().compareTo(to.id()) < 0 ? from : to; Account second = first == from ? to : from; first.lock().lock(); try { second.lock().lock(); try { if (from.balance() < t.cents()) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; from.debit(t.cents()); to.credit(t.cents()); return Outcome.APPLIED; } finally { second.lock().unlock(); } } finally { first.lock().unlock(); } } Ledger.kt fun apply(t: Transfer): Outcome { val from = account(t.from) val to = account(t.to) val first = if (from.id < to.id) from else to val second = if (first === from) to else from return first.lock.withLock { second.lock.withLock { if (from.balance < t.cents) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS from.debit(t.cents) to.credit(t.cents) Outcome.APPLIED } } } Kotlin's withLock is an inline function that calls lock(), runs the block and calls unlock() in a finally, so the two nested try/finally blocks become two nested lambdas. Because it is inline, return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS inside the block returns from apply itself, and the locks are still released. from.id < to.id on strings calls the same compareTo as the Java version. The immutable Transfer differs only in style: a Kotlin data class of vals is exactly as shallow as a Java record. Both make the fields final, and neither copies a mutable list you pass in.

h: Design the ledger and make it correct · Worked example
x: Add a fee without breaking the invariants The product team wants a fee on each transfer, paid into a fee account. Money is still conserved: the sender pays cents + fee, the receiver gets cents and the fee account gets fee. Three accounts now change in one step. Here is the first attempt. Read it against the three invariants and the lock order before you go on. Outcome applyWithFee(Transfer t, long fee) { Account from = account(t.from()), to = account(t.to()); from.lock().lock(); to.lock().lock(); feeAccount.lock().lock(); try { if (from.balance() < t.cents()) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; from.debit(t.cents() + fee); to.credit(t.cents()); feeAccount.credit(fee); return Outcome.APPLIED; } finally { feeAccount.lock().unlock(); to.lock().unlock(); from.lock().unlock(); } } fun applyWithFee(t: Transfer, fee: Long): Outcome { val from = account(t.from); val to = account(t.to) from.lock.lock() to.lock.lock() feeAccount.lock.lock() try { if (from.balance < t.cents) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS from.debit(t.cents + fee) to.credit(t.cents) feeAccount.credit(fee) return Outcome.APPLIED } finally { feeAccount.lock.unlock() to.lock.unlock() from.lock.unlock() } } Two bugs. The locks are ordered by role, not by id: a transfer from acc-02 to acc-05 locks 02 then 05, while a transfer from acc-05 to acc-02 locks 05 then 02. That is the deadlock cycle again. And the check tests cents, but the debit takes cents + fee, so a sender with exactly cents left goes below zero. The lab's debit would throw; a plain field would quietly go negative. Sort every account the operation touches by id, lock them in that order, and release them in reverse. The same code works for two accounts, three, or a payroll batch of fifty. distinct() covers the case where the sender is the fee account itself, because a ReentrantLock taken twice must also be released twice. Outcome applyWithFee(Transfer t, long fee) { Account from = account(t.from()), to = account(t.to()); List<Account> touched = Stream.of(from, to, feeAccount) .distinct() .sorted(Comparator.comparing(Account::id)) // 1. one global order, any number of locks .toList(); touched.forEach(a -> a.lock().lock()); try { if (from.balance() < t.cents() + fee) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; // 2. check what is debited from.debit(t.cents() + fee); // 3. three changes, one critical section to.credit(t.cents()); feeAccount.credit(fee); return Outcome.APPLIED; } finally { for (int i = touched.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) touched.get(i).lock().unlock(); // 4. reverse order } } fun applyWithFee(t: Transfer, fee: Long): Outcome { val from = account(t.from); val to = account(t.to) val touched = listOf(from, to, feeAccount) .distinct() .sortedBy { it.id } // 1. one global order, any number of locks touched.forEach { it.lock.lock() } try { if (from.balance < t.cents + fee) return Outcome.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS // 2. check what is debited from.debit(t.cents + fee) // 3. three changes, one critical section to.credit(t.cents) feeAccount.credit(fee) return Outcome.APPLIED } finally { touched.asReversed().forEach { it.lock.unlock() } // 4. reverse order } } Check it against the invariants. Conservation: the sender loses cents + fee and the other two gain exactly that. No overdraft: the check and the debit use the same amount under the same locks. Whole or nothing: all three changes happen inside one set of locks. No deadlock: plain apply locks two accounts in id order and this method locks three in id order, so any two operations agree on which lock comes first. Where the fee account's id sorts among the customer ids doesn't matter. Only the rule matters.

h: Design the ledger and make it correct · Quiz
x: A teammate orders the two locks in apply by System.identityHashCode(account) instead of by account id. What can go wrong? Nothing: every object has a different identity hash code Two accounts can share a hash code, and then two transfers may lock them in opposite orders and deadlock The hash code changes when the GC moves the object, so the order changes Nothing serious: ReentrantLock detects the deadlock and throws Identity hash codes are not unique. On a tie neither account sorts first, so one thread may lock A first and another B first, which is the cycle. Java Concurrency in Practice breaks the tie with an extra global lock; a unique account id avoids the problem. The identity hash code stays the same for the object's life even when the GC moves it, and no lock detects a deadlock for you. This apply locks both accounts in id order, but first it calls if (balanceOf(from) < cents) return INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS;, which takes and releases from's lock. Eight threads stress it. Which invariant can break? A balance can go below zero Money is no longer conserved Two opposite transfers can deadlock None: every step holds a lock It's check-then-act: another transfer can spend the money between balanceOf and the locks. Each move is still atomic, so the total is conserved, which is exactly why a test that only checks totals passes. Locks taken in id order can't deadlock. "Every step holds a lock" is the trap: two atomic steps in a row are not one atomic step. record Transfer(String id, List<String> tags, long cents). The importer fills an ArrayList of tags, builds the record, submits it to a pool, then clears the list and reuses it for the next line. What can the worker see in tags()? The original tags, because records are immutable A copy, because records copy their components An empty or half-changed list, because the record holds the importer's list object Nothing: clear() throws UnsupportedOperationException Records are shallowly immutable. The field can't point at another list, but the list itself is the importer's ArrayList, and clearing it changes what the worker reads. Copy it in the compact constructor with tags = List.copyOf(tags), which also gives the record an unmodifiable list. Records never copy their components for you. The ledger's stress test passed 50 runs in a row on your laptop. What have you shown? The ledger is thread-safe The ledger is thread-safe on x86, but maybe not on ARM The JIT compiled the race away These runs found no failure; the argument that each invariant holds has to come from the code A stress test can show that a race exists, never that none does. Fifty clean runs with a start latch and many threads make a bug less likely. The proof is the reasoning: which lock guards which field, and why each invariant holds inside the critical section. Which change to the ledger breaks invariant 3, "a transfer happens whole or not at all"? Locking to first whenever to has the lower id Replacing the ReentrantLocks with synchronized blocks taken in the same order Debiting inside one locked block, releasing both locks, then crediting inside a second locked block Making Transfer a Kotlin data class instead of a Java record Between the two blocks, a thread that locks both accounts (a snapshot, an audit) sees the money gone from one account and not yet in the other, and an exception at that point loses it. The other changes keep debit and credit in one critical section: locking the lower id first is the rule itself, synchronized gives the same exclusion, and a data class is as immutable as a record.

h: Design the ledger and make it correct · Key terms
x: Invariant A statement about your data that must be true whenever another thread can look, such as "the total never changes". Global lock order One rule, such as "lower account id first", that every code path follows when it takes more than one lock. It makes a wait cycle impossible. Lock granularity How much data one lock guards: the whole ledger, or one account. Finer locks let more work run at once and need a lock order. Compact constructor A record constructor without a parameter list. It runs before the fields are assigned, so it can check or normalize the values. Stress harness A test driver that starts many threads at once, runs many operations, then checks the invariants. Overdraft A debit that takes a balance below zero. In this ledger it is a bug, so debit refuses it. Ledger invariant 1: what must the sum of all balances do? Never change. A transfer moves money between accounts; it never creates or destroys any. Why must the balance check sit inside the same locks as the debit? Otherwise it is check-then-act: another transfer can spend the money between the check and the debit, and the balance goes negative. What stops transfer(A, B) and transfer(B, A) from deadlocking when each takes two locks? A global lock order: always lock the account with the lower id first, whichever way the money moves. Why not order locks by hashCode()? Two accounts can share a hash code. On a tie, two threads may lock in opposite orders. Use a unique, stable id. How do you lock N accounts for one operation without deadlock? Sort them by id, lock in that order, release in reverse. distinct() first, if one account can appear twice. What does a record's compact constructor give a Transfer? Checks that run before the fields are set, so every Transfer that exists is valid. With final fields, any thread sees it whole. A stress test checks only the final state. What can it miss? Violations that heal: an account that went negative and was topped up later. Also check each invariant where it can break.

h: Design the ledger and make it correct · Go deeper
x: Two directions this design grows in real systems. The first is hot accounts. A merchant settlement account that receives a third of all transfers serializes them on its one lock, whatever the order. A common fix is to split it into a few sub-accounts, each with its own lock, credit a random one, and add them up for the balance. For a single account you could also drop the lock and use a compare-and-set loop, as Atomics and compare-and-set showed. The check becomes part of the loop: Java boolean debit(AtomicLong balance, long cents) { while (true) { long current = balance.get(); if (current < cents) return false; // the check is inside the loop if (balance.compareAndSet(current, current - cents)) return true; } } Kotlin fun debit(balance: AtomicLong, cents: Long): Boolean { while (true) { val current = balance.get() if (current < cents) return false // the check is inside the loop if (balance.compareAndSet(current, current - cents)) return true } } That is lock-free for one account. A transfer touches two, and two compare-and-sets in a row are not one atomic step: between them the money is in neither account, which breaks invariant 3. That is why locks are the simpler tool for transfers. The second is the database. A persisted ledger uses the same ideas with other tools: row locks taken in account id order, a CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint, and a unique key on the transfer id so a retried request applies once. Many ledgers never update a balance in place at all. They append immutable entries, one debit and one credit per transfer, and compute balances from them. That is double-entry bookkeeping, and invariant 1 becomes "the entries of every transfer sum to zero", which you can check one transfer at a time.

h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Every pool setting is a decision
x: Lesson 1's ledger is correct on any number of threads. Now it needs threads to run on. In production a transfer does more than change two numbers. It first appends to a journal, a write-ahead log on disk, so a crash can't lose a transfer that a caller was told was accepted. Say that write takes 5 ms. The ledger needs a pool for that work, and the default pools are each wrong in their own way. Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8) has an unbounded queue, so a slow disk turns into millions of queued transfers and an out-of-memory error. Executors.newCachedThreadPool() has no thread limit, so the same slow disk turns into thousands of threads. Build the pool yourself and write down a reason for each setting: Java PoolPlan plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(1_600, Duration.ofMillis(5), Duration.ofMillis(50)); // 8 and 80 ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( plan.threads(), plan.threads(), // core == max: no burst threads 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(plan.queueCapacity()), // bounded: a full queue pushes back Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), // ledger-0, ledger-1, ... in every dump new CountingAbortPolicy()); // counted, then thrown at the caller pool.prestartAllCoreThreads(); Kotlin val plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(1_600, Duration.ofMillis(5), Duration.ofMillis(50)) // 8 and 80 val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor( plan.threads(), plan.threads(), // core == max: no burst threads 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(plan.queueCapacity()), // bounded: a full queue pushes back Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), // ledger-0, ledger-1, ... in every dump CountingAbortPolicy()) // counted, then thrown at the caller pool.prestartAllCoreThreads() The sizes come from Little's law, from Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law: in flight = arrival rate x time in the system. At a peak of 1,600 transfers a second, each holding a thread for 5 ms, 1,600 x 0.005 = 8 transfers are in flight, so 8 threads. With fewer, the queue grows at every peak. With many more, you only add threads that wait on the same disk. The queue gets the same law. A busy pool finishes 1,600 transfers a second, so 80 queued transfers drain in 80 / 1,600 = 50 ms. If 50 ms is the longest a transfer should wait for a thread, 80 slots is the most the queue should hold. A queue of 10,000 would hide six seconds of waiting behind a client's timeout. Core equals max because extra threads would only add waiters on the same journal, and the pool grows past core only when the queue is full. Here, the right answer to a full queue is no. That makes the rejection policy the last decision. DiscardPolicy and DiscardOldestPolicy drop a transfer, so they are never right for money. CallerRunsPolicy makes the submitting thread write the journal itself: fine for a batch importer, wrong for an HTTP thread with a client waiting. For the API path, count and throw. The handler answers 503 with Retry-After, the client retries with the same transfer id, and the counter shows on the dashboard. Send a burst at the pool Run BurstDemo: 300 transfers of 5 ms each arrive at once at the pool above. Predict how many are accepted and how long submitting takes. Run it with -Pargs=callerRuns. Predict how many transfers the submitting thread runs itself, and how long submitting takes now. BurstDemo.java package workbench.ledger.l02.demo; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionHandler; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** * A burst of 300 transfers hits a pool sized with Little's law: 8 threads, 80 queue slots, 5 ms * per transfer. Pass "callerRuns" to swap the counting abort policy for CallerRunsPolicy. */ public class BurstDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean callerRuns = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("callerRuns"); AtomicInteger rejected = new AtomicInteger(); RejectedExecutionHandler policy = callerRuns ? new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() // the submitting thread runs it itself : (task, pool) -> { // count it, then throw at the caller rejected.incrementAndGet(); throw new RejectedExecutionException("ledger pool full"); }; ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(80), Thread.ofPlatform().name("ledger-", 0).factory(), policy); pool.prestartAllCoreThreads(); AtomicInteger ranOnCaller = new AtomicInteger(); String caller = Thread.currentThread().getName(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); int accepted = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 300; i++) { try { pool.execute(() -> { if (Thread.currentThread().getName().equals(caller)) ranOnCaller.incrementAndGet(); sleep(5); // the journal write }); accepted++; } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { // an HTTP handler would answer 503 with Retry-After here } } long submitMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); long doneMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%s: accepted %d, rejected %d, run by the submitting thread %d%n", callerRuns ? With CallerRunsPolicy nothing is rejected, but the submitting thread ran 24 transfers itself and submitting took about 130 ms instead of 4. While it writes a journal entry it can't submit, which is the back-pressure. If that thread were serving an HTTP request, its client would have waited all that time for other people's transfers. Little's law sizes both halves of the pool: 8 threads for the transfers in flight, 80 slots for 50 ms of waiting. Whatever doesn't fit is rejected and counted. ThreadPoolExecutor (Java SE 25 API) docs A pool is a bank branch with eight tellers and a waiting area with eighty chairs. When every chair is taken, the guard at the door tells the next customer to come back in a minute and makes a tally mark (the counting rejection). Hiring a teller for every customer, or letting the queue spill out into the street, only looks kind. At closing time the guard locks the door, the tellers finish the people already seated, and anyone still waiting at the deadline gets a numbered ticket for tomorrow instead of being sent home with nothing. The analogy breaks at the statement job: a real teller who needs a colleague's help walks over and asks. A pool thread that waits for a task in its own queue just stands at its desk, and so do all the others.

h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Shut down by draining, and account for every transfer
x: A deploy stops the ledger while transfers are queued, and each of them belongs to a caller who was told "accepted". So the rule for shutdown is this: when it ends, every accepted transfer has been applied, has failed with an error its caller saw, or has been handed back to you by id. None may vanish. pool.shutdownNow() on its own breaks that rule. It interrupts the running tasks and returns the queued ones as a List<Runnable>. Ignore the list and those transfers are gone. Worse, their futures never complete, so a caller blocked in get() waits forever. In this section's demo a bare shutdownNow() loses 992 of 1,000 transfers. The order from Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown fixes it: Java public ShutdownReport shutdown(Duration grace) throws InterruptedException { pool.shutdown(); // 1. no new transfers; the queue drains if (pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) return new ShutdownReport(true, List.of()); // 2. everything accepted was applied List<Transfer> neverStarted = new ArrayList<>(); for (Runnable r : pool.shutdownNow()) { // 3. interrupt, take back the queue TransferTask task = (TransferTask) r; task.cancel(false); // wakes a caller blocked in get() neverStarted.add(task.transfer()); } pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS); return new ShutdownReport(false, List.copyOf(neverStarted)); // 4. log them, or replay them } Kotlin fun shutdown(grace: Duration): ShutdownReport { pool.shutdown() // 1. no new transfers; the queue drains if (pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) return ShutdownReport(true, emptyList()) // 2. everything accepted was applied val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow().map { r -> // 3. interrupt, take back the queue val task = r as TransferTask task.cancel(false) // wakes a caller blocked in get() task.transfer } pool.awaitTermination(grace.toNanos(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) return ShutdownReport(false, neverStarted) // 4. log them, or replay them } Two details make this work. First, the queue must hold objects that know their transfer. pool.submit(callable) wraps your work in an anonymous FutureTask, so the lab's submit builds a TransferTask, a FutureTask subclass with a transfer() accessor, and hands it to execute. Then shutdownNow() gives you back transfers instead of mystery Runnables. Second, an interrupted task must leave nothing half-done. Each task writes the journal first and changes memory second. An interrupt during the write means the transfer was never applied: its future fails with the InterruptedException, and no balance changed. apply itself never blocks, so once it starts, it finishes. Size the grace period from the same numbers as the pool. A full queue of 80 drains in 50 ms, so a few seconds of grace fits easily inside the 30 seconds Kubernetes gives a pod by default. Lose transfers, then stop losing them Run ShutdownDemo -Pargs=naive: 1,000 accepted transfers, then a bare shutdownNow(). Read the lost column and the last line. Run it with no arguments (drain, 100 ms of grace), then with -Pargs='drain 5000'. Before each run, predict how many transfers are applied. h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Publish a snapshot nobody can tear
x: The balances endpoint wants every balance at once, and invariant 1 says they must add up to the opening total. Reading the accounts one at a time, each under its own lock, doesn't give you that: Java long sum = 0; for (Account a : accounts) { a.lock().lock(); try { sum += a.balance(); } finally { a.lock().unlock(); } // each read is safe... } // ...the sum is not Kotlin var sum = 0L for (a in accounts) { sum += a.lock.withLock { a.balance } // each read is safe... } // ...the sum is not A transfer from account 40 to account 3 can run after you read 3 and before you read 40. Then you counted that money in neither account. In the other direction you count it twice. In the demo, a large share of such sums were wrong, by up to 13,957 cents, although no transfer ever broke an invariant. A sum like that is torn: it mixes two moments. A consistent snapshot needs one instant at which no transfer is half done. Lock every account, in the same id order that apply uses so the snapshot can't deadlock with a transfer, copy the balances, then release: Java public BalanceSnapshot snapshot() { for (Account a : inLockOrder) a.lock().lock(); // 1. every lock, in id order try { Map<String, Long> copy = new HashMap<>(); long total = 0; for (Account a : inLockOrder) { copy.put(a.id(), a.balance()); total += a.balance(); } BalanceSnapshot s = new BalanceSnapshot(copy, total, ++version); // 2. immutable latest = s; // 3. volatile write: published whole return s; } finally { for (int i = inLockOrder.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) inLockOrder.get(i).lock().unlock(); } } Kotlin fun snapshot(): BalanceSnapshot { inLockOrder.forEach { it.lock.lock() } // 1. every lock, in id order try { val copy = inLockOrder.associate { it.id to it.balance } val s = BalanceSnapshot(copy, copy.values.sum(), ++version) // 2. immutable latest = s // 3. @Volatile write: published whole return s } finally { inLockOrder.asReversed().forEach { it.lock.unlock() } } } For 50 accounts this pauses transfers for microseconds, and readers call latestSnapshot() without taking any lock. Happens-before, the rules that matter asked you to name the edge for every shared field. Here they are: Field Why every reader sees it correctly Account.balance the account's lock: each release happens-before the next acquire accounts, inLockOrder final fields, set in the constructor, never changed version written only while every account lock is held latest volatile: its write happens-before every later read a snapshot's balances and total final fields of a record, holding a map that Map.copyOf made unmodifiable a Transfer in the pool immutable, and execute happens-before the task runs a transfer's outcome the task's completion happens-before Future.get() returns Writing latest before the locks are released keeps snapshots in version order: two snapshots can't overlap, because each needs every lock. Tear a snapshot, then make it whole Run TornSnapshotDemo. Four threads move money while the main thread adds up all 50 balances, one locked account at a time. Predict how many sums come out wrong. Run it with -Pargs=locked, where the reader holds every lock while it adds. h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Find a hung pool in a thread dump
x: Here is a bug that passes every test with a small batch. A month-end statement job runs on the ledger pool, and each statement asks the same pool for a balance: Java pool.submit(() -> { Future<Long> balance = pool.submit(() -> balanceOf(merchant)); // a task inside a task return merchant + ": " + balance.get(); // waits for it }); Kotlin pool.submit(Callable { val balance = pool.submit(Callable { balanceOf(merchant) }) // a task inside a task "$merchant: ${balance.get()}" // waits for it }) With 2 threads and 3 merchants, the first two statements take both threads. Each submits a balance lookup, which queues behind the third statement. Now both threads wait for tasks that need a free thread, and no thread will ever be free. Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown called this pool-induced deadlock. This section is about finding it in a running process. Start PoolHangDemo with a long hang, then dump its threads from a second terminal: jcmd # lists Java processes and their PIDs jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l # -l adds the java.util.concurrent locks each thread holds Here is the part that matters, from a real run on JDK 21, trimmed: "ledger-0" #19 [5741] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=1.33ms elapsed=1.74s ... waiting on condition java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking) at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method) - parking to wait for <0x00000006f79ef530> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask) at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/LockSupport.java:221) at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.awaitDone(java.base@21.0.12.1/FutureTask.java:500) at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.get(java.base@21.0.12.1/FutureTask.java:190) at workbench.ledger.l02.demo.PoolHangDemo.statement(PoolHangDemo.java:33) at workbench.ledger.l02.demo.PoolHangDemo.lambda$main$0(PoolHangDemo.java:21) ... at java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor.runWorker(java.base@21.0.12.1/ThreadPoolExecutor.java:1144) ... Locked ownable synchronizers: - <0x00000006f79650b8> (a java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker) "ledger-1" #20 [5742] prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.83ms elapsed=1.74s ... waiting on condition java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking) at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(java.base@21.0.12.1/Native Method) - parking to wait for <0x00000006f7602c18> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask) ... at workbench.ledger.l02.demo.PoolHangDemo.statement(PoolHangDemo.java:33) ... Locked ownable synchronizers: - <0x00000006f79bb838> (a java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker) Read each thread in the same order. The name says which pool: both ledger- threads are stuck, which is why the factory names them. The state, WAITING (parking), means java.util.concurrent parked them; a thread stuck on synchronized would say BLOCKED. The parking to wait for line names the object they wait on: a FutureTask, so they are inside get(). The first frame from your own code, statement at line 33, is that get() call. And under Locked ownable synchronizers each worker holds its own ThreadPoolExecutor$Worker, a lock a worker holds while it runs a task. Both threads are busy, and busy waiting. Notice what is missing: the dump never says Found one Java-level deadlock. The JVM's detector looks for cycles of monitors and ReentrantLocks, and here nobody holds a lock that anybody else wants. Every worker of one pool parked on a FutureTask of that same pool, with tasks still queued, is the signature to learn. The fixes come from that lesson: do the lookup inline, compose with thenApply instead of blocking, or give lookups their own pool. Take the dump yourself Run PoolHangDemo with -Pargs=60 so it stays hung for a minute. It prints its PID. In a second terminal, run jcmd <pid> Thread.print -l. For both ledger- threads, find the state, the parking to wait for line, the first frame from workbench.ledger, and the Locked ownable synchronizers. Then find main. Scroll to the end of the dump. Is there a deadlock report? Explain why not. Change statement to call balanceOf(merchant) directly instead of submitting it, and run the demo again. The most common mistake is an unbounded queue: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n), or a LinkedBlockingQueue with no capacity. People choose it because it is the default and because rejecting feels worse than waiting. Bound the queue from Little's law, and turn the overflow into a counted, visible rejection.

Kotlin shortens the FutureTask subclass to one line, because the constructor parameter work goes straight to the superclass in the class header, and a trailing lambda converts to the Java Callable. When you call pool.submit with a bare lambda, Kotlin has to choose between submit(Runnable) and submit(Callable); writing Callable { ... } says which you mean. In coroutine code, Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(8) caps parallelism like this pool, but it queues without a bound and never rejects, so it can't replace the back-pressure.

h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Worked example
x: Size the pool for a new peak The sales forecast for a promotion day is 4,000 transfers a second. Under load the journal's write takes 4 ms. You want no transfer to wait more than 100 ms for a thread. Start with Little's law, for both halves of the pool. // 1. peak rate, time each transfer holds a thread, longest acceptable queue wait PoolPlan plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(4_000, Duration.ofMillis(4), Duration.ofMillis(100)); // 2. 4,000/s x 0.004 s = 16 in flight; 4,000/s x 0.1 s = 400 waiting System.out.println(plan); // PoolPlan[threads=16, queueCapacity=400] // 1. peak rate, time each transfer holds a thread, longest acceptable queue wait val plan = PoolPlan.fromLittlesLaw(4_000, Duration.ofMillis(4), Duration.ofMillis(100)) // 2. 4,000/s x 0.004 s = 16 in flight; 4,000/s x 0.1 s = 400 waiting println(plan) // PoolPlan[threads=16, queueCapacity=400] Now check the downstream, as Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law insisted. The storage team says the journal volume handles 12 concurrent writes before each one slows down. With 16 threads, the extra 4 just queue inside the journal and make every write slower. The real ceiling is the journal's: 12 writes / 0.004 s = 3,000 transfers a second, whatever the forecast says. Size from the scarce resource, and let the rejection policy handle the rest. At 3,000 a second, 100 ms of queue is 300 slots. Above that rate the pool rejects and counts, and the API answers 503 with Retry-After. // 3. the journal takes 12 writes at once: that sets the threads, and the throughput PoolPlan capped = new PoolPlan(12, 300); // 12 / 0.004 s = 3,000 a second; 3,000 x 0.1 s = 300 slots LedgerService service = LedgerService.start(ledger, journal, capped); // 3. the journal takes 12 writes at once: that sets the threads, and the throughput val capped = PoolPlan(12, 300) // 12 / 0.004 s = 3,000 a second; 3,000 x 0.1 s = 300 slots val service = LedgerService.start(ledger, journal, capped) If 3,000 isn't enough, more threads won't help, because the journal is the bottleneck. Make each write do more: group commit (one disk flush for a batch of transfers) raises what 12 concurrent writes can carry. Then check shutdown again: 300 queued transfers on 12 threads at 4 ms drain in 100 ms, so a 5 s grace period still fits well inside Kubernetes' 30 s.

x: A teammate builds the ledger pool as new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 32, 60, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()). The journal slows from 5 ms to 500 ms per write. What happens? The pool grows to 32 threads and keeps up The pool stays at 8 threads and the queue grows without limit Transfers are rejected once 32 are running The pool shrinks back to 8 threads after 60 seconds The pool grows past core only when the queue refuses a task, and an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue never refuses. So the 32 is dead code, nothing is ever rejected, and every transfer waits behind a queue that only grows. Option 1 is what most people expect from "max 32". Peak traffic is 1,200 transfers a second, and each holds a ledger thread for 10 ms. How many threads does Little's law ask for? 12 120 1,200 10 In flight = 1,200/s x 0.010 s = 12. 120 would mean 100 ms per transfer, and 1,200 forgets the time entirely. After that, check that the journal can take 12 writes at once; if not, its limit is your ceiling. The snapshot refresher writes latest = new BalanceSnapshot(copy, total, v) to a plain field, not a volatile one, and request threads read latest without locks. What can a reader see? Always the newest snapshot, because reference writes are atomic A snapshot with some balances missing, because Map.copyOf copies lazily An exception, because two threads touch the same field An old snapshot, possibly for a long time, because no happens-before edge links the write to the read Without volatile nothing orders the refresher's write before the readers' reads, so the JIT may keep an old reference in a register, and a reader may not see a newer snapshot for a long time. The record's final fields make whatever snapshot a reader does see complete, so the risk is staleness, not a half-built map. Map.copyOf copies at once. Make the field volatile. Four statement tasks run on a 4-thread pool. Each submits a balance lookup to the same pool and calls get(). A dump shows all four workers WAITING (parking) on a FutureTask. Which fix does NOT work? Do the lookup inline in the statement task Compose with supplyAsync(lookup, pool).thenApply(render) and join only at the caller Give the pool a fifth thread Run the lookups on a separate pool that never waits for the statement pool A fifth thread only moves the hang to the fifth statement running at once, and at month-end there are hundreds. The other three remove the wait: inline needs no second task, composition never holds a thread while it waits, and a separate lookup pool can't be starved by statements. Which rejection policy fits the ledger pool when the submitting thread is an HTTP request thread with a client waiting? DiscardPolicy, because the client can retry A policy that counts and throws, so the handler answers 503 with Retry-After DiscardOldestPolicy, because the newest transfer matters most CallerRunsPolicy, so the request thread writes the journal itself A counted, thrown rejection tells the caller at once: the client retries with the same transfer id, and the counter shows the overload on a dashboard. The discard policies drop a transfer without telling anyone, and its future never completes. CallerRunsPolicy suits a batch importer; here it makes one client wait for other clients' journal writes.

h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Key terms
x: Bounded queue A queue with a fixed capacity. When it is full, new work is rejected instead of waiting without limit. Rejection policy What a ThreadPoolExecutor does with a task it can't take: throw, run it on the caller's thread, or drop it. Write-ahead journal A log the ledger writes to disk before it changes anything in memory, so a crash can't lose an accepted transfer. Graceful shutdown Stopping a service so that accepted work finishes, or is handed back, within a deadline. Torn read A result built from reads taken at different moments, matching no state the data was ever in. Pool-induced deadlock Every thread of a pool waits for tasks queued in that same pool, so none can run. No lock is involved. Thread dump Every thread's name, state and stack at one moment, printed by jcmd <pid> Thread.print. Little's law for the ledger pool's thread count? threads = peak rate x time each transfer holds a thread. 1,600/s x 5 ms = 8. How big should the ledger pool's queue be? Peak rate x the longest queue wait you accept: 1,600/s x 50 ms = 80 slots. A bigger queue only hides latency. Why is DiscardPolicy never right for the ledger pool? It silently drops a transfer, and the future of a dropped submit never completes, so a waiting caller hangs. What does shutdownNow() return, and what must you do with it? The queued tasks that never started. Cancel the futures so waiting callers wake up, then log or replay the transfers. Why is a sum of separately locked balance reads torn? A transfer can run between two reads and move money from an unread account to a read one, or back, so the sum mixes two moments. Thread-dump signature of a pool-induced deadlock? Every worker of one pool WAITING (parking) on a FutureTask inside get(), tasks still queued, and no "Found one Java-level deadlock". Why hand a TransferTask to execute and not submit? submit wraps it in another FutureTask, so shutdownNow() would return the wrapper instead of your task and its transfer.

h: Run it on a pool you can reason about · Go deeper
x: Locking every account costs time in proportion to the number of accounts, and it stops every writer while it copies. At 50 accounts that is microseconds. At five million accounts it is a pause your clients feel. Three designs avoid it. Snapshot per shard. Split the accounts into shards, route every transfer to one shard, and snapshot each shard on its own. The grand total is the sum of the shard totals, which is only consistent while no transfer crosses a shard. Copy-on-write state. Keep all balances in an immutable map behind an AtomicReference, and make every transfer a compare-and-set of a new map. Readers get a consistent snapshot for free with get(). Writers pay for the copy and retry when another writer won, so this fits read-heavy books with modest write rates. It is the snapshot idea from Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal, used for writes too: Java private final AtomicReference<Map<String, Long>> balances = new AtomicReference<>(Map.of("alice", 100L, "bob", 0L)); boolean transfer(String from, String to, long cents) { while (true) { Map<String, Long> now = balances.get(); // a consistent snapshot, for free if (now.get(from) < cents) return false; Map<String, Long> next = new HashMap<>(now); // copy, change two entries next.merge(from, -cents, Long::sum); next.merge(to, cents, Long::sum); if (balances.compareAndSet(now, Map.copyOf(next))) return true; // retry if another writer won } } Kotlin private val balances = AtomicReference(mapOf("alice" to 100L, "bob" to 0L)) fun transfer(from: String, to: String, cents: Long): Boolean { while (true) { val now = balances.get() // a consistent snapshot, for free if (now.getValue(from) < cents) return false val next = now + mapOf(from to now.getValue(from) - cents, to to now.getValue(to) + cents) if (balances.compareAndSet(now, next)) return true // retry if another writer won } } Event sourcing. Treat the journal as the truth and a snapshot as the result of applying it up to a position. You can build snapshots on a replica that reads the journal, and the live ledger never stops for them. For dumps, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json <file> writes the same information as JSON, which tools can group and count. Lesson 3 of this track uses it on 10,000 virtual threads.

h: Serve it with virtual threads · One virtual thread per request, and every limit written down
x: Lesson 2's pool runs the journal writes. Requests need threads too, and they spend almost all their time waiting: on the fraud service, on the limits service, on the ledger pool. The thread-per-request wall gave you the number: in flight = rate x time. At 2,000 requests a second and 150 ms each, 300 requests are in flight. When the fraud service slows to 2 s, 4,000 are. A platform thread per request would mean 4,000 OS threads, each with a 1 MB stack reserved, created at the worst possible moment. Virtual threads make that number cheap. A request that waits on a socket, a latch or a semaphore unmounts from its carrier, and its stack waits on the heap, as How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations showed. So the server starts one new virtual thread per request, and never pools them: Java List<Reply> serveAll(List<Transfer> requests) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perRequest = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<Reply>> replies = new ArrayList<>(); for (Transfer t : requests) replies.add(perRequest.submit(() -> handle(t))); // 1. start every request List<Reply> out = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<Reply> f : replies) out.add(f.get()); // 2. then wait, in order return out; } // 3. close() waits for all } Kotlin fun serveAll(requests: List<Transfer>): List<Reply> = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perRequest -> val replies = requests.map { t -> perRequest.submit(Callable { handle(t) }) } // 1. start every request replies.map { it.get() } // 2. then wait, in order } // 3. close() waits for all In a real service the framework starts the threads: Quarkus with @RunOnVirtualThread, Spring Boot with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true. What no framework does, as Moving a blocking service to virtual threads warned, is write your limits down. Unlimited threads mean unlimited calls to whatever sits behind them. So every scarce thing gets an explicit limit: the fraud service: one shared Semaphore of 20 permits, held only around the fraud call; the journal: lesson 2's bounded ledger- pool, 8 threads and 80 slots, which rejects with a 503 when it is full; each request: one deadline of 300 ms for all of its screening. The ledger pool stays a pool of platform threads on purpose. It isn't there to save thread creation. It is a limit with a queue and a rejection policy, around work you want bounded. Request threads wait for it with future.get(), and a parked virtual thread costs a little heap. Do the arithmetic before the load test The fraud bulkhead has 20 permits, and a fraud call normally takes 20 ms. How many fraud checks a second can it pass? Is that enough for 400 requests a second? For 2,000? During an outage each fraud call takes 2 s, but the request interrupts it at its 300 ms deadline. How many requests a second now get a permit at all, and what happens to the rest? Open TransferServer.handle in the lab. Find the one wait that has no timeout and explain why it has none. Twenty permits at 20 ms pass at most 20 / 0.02 = 1,000 checks a second: plenty for 400, not enough for 2,000, so at 2,000 a second you'd need about 40 permits, if the fraud vendor allows that many. In the outage each permit is held for 300 ms, so only about 20 / 0.3 = 67 requests a second get one; the rest wait for a permit until their deadline and get the stand-in rule. The next section's demo shows exactly that. The wait without a timeout is ledger.submit(t).get(): once the ledger pool has accepted a transfer the money may move, and a timeout would end the wait but not the transfer. Threads are free, so every limit sits on a resource: 20 permits for the fraud service, 8 threads and 80 slots for the journal, and one deadline per request. JEP 444: Virtual Threads read The server is a restaurant that seats every guest the moment they walk in, because chairs (virtual threads) cost almost nothing. What it rations is what sits behind the chairs. The sommelier (the fraud service) takes 20 guests at a time. The kitchen (the ledger pool) has 8 cooks and 80 order slips, and when the slips run out the door says "kitchen full, try again in a minute". Every guest is promised an answer within five minutes. A guest who has waited that long for the sommelier gets the house wine if the order is small and is asked to come back if it is large, and the sommelier is told to stop decanting for him. The analogy breaks at the chairs: a seated guest still takes floor space and a waiter's attention. A parked virtual thread takes a couple of kilobytes of heap and no thread at all until something wakes it.

h: Serve it with virtual threads · A bulkhead and a deadline for the slow fraud check
x: The fraud service is the slow, shared dependency. When it slows down, two things must not follow: every request waiting as long as it does, and every request piling onto it at once. A deadline stops the first, a bulkhead the second. The bulkhead is the shared semaphore from Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores, with one change: the wait for a permit is bounded by the time the request has left. Java <T> T call(long waitNanos, Callable<T> block) throws Exception { if (!inFlight.tryAcquire(waitNanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) // 1. outside the try throw new TimeoutException("no permit in time"); try { return block.call(); // 2. only the slow call holds it } finally { inFlight.release(); // 3. always given back } } Kotlin fun <T> call(waitNanos: Long, block: () -> T): T { if (!inFlight.tryAcquire(waitNanos, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) // 1. outside the try throw TimeoutException("no permit in time") try { return block() // 2. only the slow call holds it } finally { inFlight.release() // 3. always given back } } The deadline is one number, computed once per request: System.nanoTime() + budget. Every wait inside the request uses what is left of it: the wait for a permit and the wait for the fraud answer. When it runs out, the request stops waiting and falls back. The fallback is a business rule, borrowed from card processing, called stand-in: small transfers (up to 50.00 here) go through without a fraud answer, larger ones get a fast "try again". The limit is a risk decision, not a technical one. Stopping the wait is not enough. Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption made the point: a timeout on get ends your wait, not the task. A fraud call that runs on after its request has answered still holds a permit, and during an outage those orphans fill the bulkhead, so new requests can't get a permit even for a call that would succeed. So at the deadline the request interrupts the call. The interrupted call's finally gives the permit back, and the next request can use it. Give the fraud HTTP client its own timeout of the same length as well, so a call that ignores the interrupt still ends. In this section's demo, an outage that makes every fraud call take 2 s still answers every request within about 320 ms, and the fraud service never sees more than 20 calls at once. an interrupt ends it early } finally { inFlight.decrementAndGet() } return true } finally { permits.release() } } private fun screen(cents: Long, latencyMs: Long): String { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + BUDGET_NANOS Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perCall -> val call = perCall.submit(Callable { fraudCall(latencyMs, deadline) }) return try { if (call.get(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) "approved" else "declined" } catch (e: TimeoutException) { // our deadline passed first call.cancel(true) // interrupt the call: it holds a permit fallback(cents) } catch (e: ExecutionException) { // no permit before the deadline fallback(cents) } } } private fun fallback(cents: Long) = if (cents <= STAND_IN_CENTS) "stand-in" else "timed out" /** 400 requests a second for 3 seconds, each on its own virtual thread. In the outage, about a quarter of the requests get the stand-in rule (290 of 1,200 in one run), the rest time out, the fraud service never sees more than 20 calls, and the slowest reply is about 320 ms. Without the cancel, the verdicts look the same, but the slowest reply is about 2,300 ms: each request's executor closes at the end of use, and close() waits for the fraud call nobody cancelled. With a shared executor instead, the replies would be on time and the orphaned calls would hold their permits for the full 2 s. Semaphore (Java SE 25 API) docs This is the shape of a Quarkus payment endpoint with @RunOnVirtualThread: the request runs on a virtual thread and calls a fraud REST client, a limits client and the database. Quarkus adds neither the bulkhead nor the deadline. SmallRye Fault Tolerance's @Bulkhead and @Timeout are one way to declare them, and a shared Semaphore plus one deadline per request is another. Either way, size the bulkhead from the fraud vendor's concurrency limit and Little's law, and set the REST client's read timeout to the same budget. The stand-in limit is a risk decision: agree the amount with the risk team, and log every stand-in with its transfer id so it can be reviewed. During an incident, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json inside the pod tells you in a minute whether requests are stuck on your bulkhead or on something else.

h: Serve it with virtual threads · Fail fast when one check says no
x: Screening calls two services: the fraud service, slow and behind the bulkhead, and the account limits service, which is fast. Run them at the same time and a request costs the slower of the two, not the sum. The trap is in how you collect the answers. Structured concurrency and scoped values showed it: call get() on the futures in the order you started them, and a fast "no" waits behind a slow "yes". In this section's demo the limits check says no at 10 ms, and the request still answers at about 600 ms. Take the answers in the order they finish, and stop at the first no: Java Verdict screen(Transfer t) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + budget.toNanos(); // 1. one deadline for both checks ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); try { CompletionService<Boolean> done = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(perTask); done.submit(() -> fraudBulkhead.call(deadline - System.nanoTime(), () -> fraud.passes(t))); // 2. fork both done.submit(() -> limits.passes(t)); for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { Future<Boolean> next = done.poll(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS); if (next == null) return fallback(t); // 3. deadline passed: stand-in rule try { if (!next.get()) return Verdict.DECLINED; // 4. a check said no: fail fast } catch (ExecutionException e) { if (e.getCause() instanceof TimeoutException) return fallback(t); // no fraud permit in time return Verdict.DECLINED; // 4. a check failed: fail fast } } return Verdict.APPROVED; } finally { perTask.shutdownNow(); // 5. interrupt whatever still runs... perTask.close(); // ...and wait until those threads end } } Kotlin fun screen(t: Transfer): Verdict { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + budget.toNanos() // 1. one deadline for both checks val perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() try { val done = ExecutorCompletionService<Boolean>(perTask) done.submit { fraudBulkhead.call(deadline - System.nanoTime()) { fraud.passes(t) } } // 2. fork both done.submit { limits.passes(t) } repeat(2) { val next = done.poll(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) ?: return fallback(t) // 3. deadline passed: stand-in rule val passed = try { next.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { if (e.cause is TimeoutException) return fallback(t) // no fraud permit in time return Verdict.DECLINED // 4. a check failed: fail fast } if (!passed) return Verdict.DECLINED // 4. a check said no: fail fast } return Verdict.APPROVED } finally { perTask.shutdownNow() // 5. interrupt whatever still runs... perTask.close() // ...and wait until those threads end } } ExecutorCompletionService hands you each future as it completes, so the first no is seen at once, and so is the first exception. Either one declines the transfer. The finally is what makes it fail fast: shutdownNow() interrupts the check that is still running, and close() waits until its thread has really ended. That order matters, as the lab in that lesson showed: close() after shutdownNow() waits for threads, not for futures. So no check outlives its request, still holding a permit or writing a log line for a request that has already answered. This is structured concurrency built by hand from an executor. JDK 25 has StructuredTaskScope for exactly this job, but it is a preview API in JDK 25, 26 and 27, so it stays out of the labs. The deeper note shows the same screening with it. One rule binds every check: it has to stop when interrupted. sleep, locks, queues, latches and semaphores do. A check that computes in a loop and never looks at the interrupt flag keeps running, and close() waits for it, deadline or not. Collect in order, then fail fast Run FailFastDemo. One transfer, two checks: fraud answers yes after 500 ms, limits answers no after 10 ms. Predict when each half prints its verdict. In the fail-fast half, replace done.take() with the futures in submit order: keep the two futures that done.submit returns and call get() on them in that order. Run it again.
