h: Serve it with virtual threads · Keep the carriers free: nothing slow under an account lock
x: Lesson 1 chose ReentrantLock for the accounts, and this is where that choice matters. A virtual thread is pinned when it blocks but can't leave its carrier, as Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps showed. On JDK 21 to 23, blocking inside synchronized, or waiting to enter a synchronized block another thread holds, pins. JDK 24 fixed both (JEP 491), and JDK 25 is the first LTS with the fix. These labs compile for JDK 21 and must run there too, so the ledger uses ReentrantLock, which has always let a waiting virtual thread unmount. The lock type is the smaller half of the rule. The bigger half is that nothing slow happens while you hold an account lock. Here is what someone might write to make "journal and apply" one atomic step: Java synchronized (merchant) { // or merchantLock.lock() journal.append(t); // 20 ms of disk I/O while holding the lock merchant.credit(t.cents()); } Kotlin synchronized(merchant) { // or merchantLock.withLock { } journal.append(t) // 20 ms of disk I/O while holding the lock merchant.credit(t.cents) } The demo runs this with one carrier thread, 20 payments into one hot merchant account, and a ticker that wants to tick every 10 ms. With synchronized on JDK 21, the ticker missed 425 ms of ticks: the carrier was pinned the whole time, so nothing else ran. With ReentrantLock the ticker was fine, but the 20 payments still took 430 ms, one after another, because each held the lock for its whole disk write. That is Little's law again: a lock held for 20 ms lets through at most 50 payments a second. With the journal written first and the lock taken only for the credit, all 20 took 21 ms. So the rule from synchronized and intrinsic locks holds in its strongest form. Inside an account lock, read and write the accounts, nothing else. The journal write, the fraud call and any logging that might block happen outside. That is why lesson 2's LedgerService writes the journal before apply takes a single lock. To check a running service, keep JFR's jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event on; it records pins longer than 20 ms by default. The old -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads flag was removed in JDK 24. Pin a carrier, then free it Run LockScopeDemo (or LockScopeDemoJava). It forces one carrier thread and runs three versions of the same 20 payments. Predict both columns for each row before you look. Explain the second row: no pinning, so why are the payments still slow? If you have JDK 24 or later installed, run Gradle on it and run the demo again. Which number changes? runVariant("journal inside synchronized ", () -> { synchronized (merchantMonitor) { journalWrite(); merchantBalance += 100; } }); runVariant("journal inside ReentrantLock ", () -> { merchantLock.lock(); try { journalWrite(); merchantBalance += 100; } finally { merchantLock.unlock(); } }); runVariant("journal first, then the lock ", () -> { journalWrite(); merchantLock.lock(); try { merchantBalance += 100; } finally { merchantLock.unlock(); } }); } static void runVariant(String label, Runnable transfer) throws InterruptedException { longestGap = 0; Thread ticker = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { long last = System.nanoTime(); ReentrantLock took 433 ms with a 19 ms gap: the carrier was free, but the payments queued behind a lock held across I/O. Journal first took 21 ms with a 16 ms gap. On JDK 24 and later, JEP 491 lets a virtual thread that holds a monitor unmount, so the first row's gap should drop to the second row's, while its time stays near 430 ms: the fix removes the pinning, not the queue behind the lock. JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning read

h: Serve it with virtual threads · Read 10,000 virtual threads in a JSON dump
x: Lesson 2 found a hung pool with jcmd <pid> Thread.print. Run that on the server during a fraud outage and the request threads are not there. On JDK 21, Thread.print lists platform threads only. JDK 24 added the virtual threads that are mounted at that moment, which during an outage is almost none. A parked virtual thread is a stack on the heap, not an OS thread, so the classic dump never sees it. The dump for virtual threads is Thread.dump_to_file: jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/requests.json Here is the demo's dump of 10,000 parked requests on JDK 21, cut down to its shape: {"threadDump": { "processId": "29205", "runtimeVersion": "21.0.12.1+1-1-24.04.4-Ubuntu", "threadContainers": [ {"container": "<root>", "parent": null, "owner": null, "threadCount": "7", "threads": [{"tid": "1", "name": "main", "stack": ["java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep0(Native Method)", "..."]}, "..."]}, {"container": "java.util.concurrent.ThreadPerTaskExecutor@7cded998", "parent": "<root>", "owner": null, "threadCount": "10000", "threads": [ {"tid": "19", "name": "request-0", "stack": [ "java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:596)", "...", "java.base/java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch.await(CountDownLatch.java:230)", "workbench.ledger.l03.demo.ParkedRequestsDemoKt.handle(ParkedRequestsDemo.kt:14)", "..."]}, "...", {"tid": "10025", "name": "request-9999", "stack": [ "java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:596)", "...", "java.base/java.util.concurrent.Semaphore.acquire(Semaphore.java:318)", "workbench.ledger.l03.demo.ParkedRequestsDemoKt.handle(ParkedRequestsDemo.kt:12)", "..."]}]}, {"container": "ForkJoinPool-1/jdk.internal.vm.SharedThreadContainer@3ee32429", "parent": "<root>", "owner": null, "threadCount": "4", "threads": [{"tid": "20", "name": "ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1", "stack": ["..."]}, "..."]}, "... three empty containers ..." ]}} Threads sit in thread containers. A container is whatever started them: your executor, with its own entry and thread list, or <root> for ordinary platform threads such as main. The 10,000 requests are one container, the carriers another (ForkJoinPool-1, one worker per core). On JDK 21 each thread entry has only tid, name and stack. JDK 25 adds state, virtual, parkBlocker and carrier. The named factory, Thread.ofVirtual().name("request-", 0), is what gives you request-9999 instead of an empty name. Ten thousand stacks can't be read one at a time, so group them. Count threads per container, then count stacks by the frame where your code starts and the JDK frame just above it: jq -r '.threadDump.threadContainers[] | "\(.threads | length)\t\(.container)"' /tmp/requests.json jq -r '.threadDump.threadContainers[].threads[].stack | (map(startswith("workbench.")) | index(true)) as $i | select($i != null and $i > 0) | "\(.[$i-1]) <- \(.[$i])"' /tmp/requests.json | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn 9980 java.base/java.util.concurrent.Semaphore.acquire(Semaphore.java:318) <- workbench.ledger.l03.demo.ParkedRequestsDemoKt.handle(ParkedRequestsDemo.kt:12) 20 java.base/java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch.await(CountDownLatch.java:230) <- workbench.ledger.l03.demo.ParkedRequestsDemoKt.handle(ParkedRequestsDemo.kt:14) 1 java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Thread.java:509) <- workbench.ledger.l03.demo.ParkedRequestsDemoKt.main(ParkedRequestsDemo.kt:34) That is the outage in three lines: 20 requests are inside the fraud call, 9,980 wait for a fraud permit, and main sleeps. The bulkhead held, and the fraud service is the problem. A dump of 10,000 threads is about 12 MB, so write it to a file and read it with tools, never in a terminal. Dump 10,000 parked requests Run ParkedRequestsDemo (or ParkedRequestsDemoJava) with -Pargs=60. It starts 10,000 requests on named virtual threads that all wait for a fraud service that hangs, and prints its PID. In a second terminal, run jcmd <pid> Thread.print and look for request- threads. Run jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/requests.json, then the two jq commands from this section. To take a second dump, delete the file first or add -overwrite. Before you read the counts, predict them: how many requests are inside the fraud call, and how many wait for a permit? Thread dump JSON schema (JDK 25 source) docs The most common mistake is a timeout that ends the wait but not the work: future.get(300, MILLISECONDS) in a try, a fallback in the catch, and nothing that stops the call. Every request answers on time, so the dashboards look fine. People make it because get with a timeout reads like a deadline. Cancel what you stopped waiting for (cancel(true), or shutdownNow() on the request's executor), release the permit in the call's own finally, and give the client library a timeout of the same length as a backstop.

x: The request handler and the fan-in, in both languages TransferServer.java Reply handle(Transfer t) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException { Verdict verdict = screening.screen(t); if (verdict == Verdict.DECLINED) return new Reply(t.id(), Status.DECLINED, false); if (verdict == Verdict.TIMED_OUT) return new Reply(t.id(), Status.TIMED_OUT, false); Outcome outcome; try { outcome = ledger.submit(t).get(); // no timeout: the money may already be moving } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { return new Reply(t.id(), Status.BUSY, false); } Status status = outcome == Outcome.APPLIED ? Status.APPLIED : Status.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS; return new Reply(t.id(), status, verdict == Verdict.STAND_IN); } List<Reply> serveAll(List<Transfer> requests) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService perRequest = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<Future<Reply>> replies = new ArrayList<>(); for (Transfer t : requests) replies.add(perRequest.submit(() -> handle(t))); List<Reply> out = new ArrayList<>(); for (Future<Reply> f : replies) out.add(f.get()); return out; } } TransferServer.kt fun handle(t: Transfer): Reply { val verdict = screening.screen(t) if (verdict == Verdict.DECLINED) return Reply(t.id(), Status.DECLINED) if (verdict == Verdict.TIMED_OUT) return Reply(t.id(), Status.TIMED_OUT) val outcome = try { ledger.submit(t).get() // no timeout: the money may already be moving } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { return Reply(t.id(), Status.BUSY) } val status = if (outcome == Outcome.APPLIED) Status.APPLIED else Status.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS return Reply(t.id(), status, standIn = verdict == Verdict.STAND_IN) } fun serveAll(requests: List<Transfer>): List<Reply> = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { perRequest -> val replies = requests.map { t -> perRequest.submit(Callable { handle(t) }) } replies.map { it.get() } } The threads, executors and futures are the same JDK classes on both sides; what differs is how each language spells the edges. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so get()'s InterruptedException and ExecutionException need no throws clause; an interrupted request thread still throws out of handle. A try is an expression in Kotlin, which lets val outcome = try { ... } replace Java's assign-in-try. use on an ExecutorService is Kotlin's try-with-resources, and both call close(), which waits for every request. Kotlin's default argument (standIn = false) saves the third constructor argument that the Java record needs every time. In the lab, the Kotlin server calls the Java ledger from lesson 2 directly: same package, same module, and records' accessors such as t.id() work as ordinary methods.

Verdict.APPROVED : Verdict.DECLINED; } catch (TimeoutException e) { return Verdict.STAND_IN; } } Five problems, each from an earlier lesson. The pool caps the whole task, so in a fraud outage the limits checks queue behind stuck fraud calls: put the limit on the resource, not on a pool. Two timeouts of 300 ms in a row allow 600 ms: there is no single deadline. A fast no from limits waits behind the fraud answer: no fail-fast. On timeout nothing is cancelled, so the orphaned calls keep all 20 pool threads busy and the next requests time out before they even start. And every timeout becomes a stand-in, whatever the amount. The fix is the lab's screen. Each numbered comment answers one problem: a deadline computed once (1), the fraud call alone behind a shared semaphore whose wait uses the time left (2), the stand-in rule only for small amounts (3), completion order and an early return for fail-fast (4), and shutdownNow() plus close() so nothing outlives the request (5). fun screen(t: Transfer): Verdict { val deadline = System.nanoTime() + budget.toNanos() // 1. one deadline for both checks val perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() try { val done = ExecutorCompletionService<Boolean>(perTask) done.submit { fraudBulkhead.call(deadline - System.nanoTime()) { fraud.passes(t) } } // 2. fork both done.submit { limits.passes(t) } repeat(2) { val next = done.poll(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) ?: return fallback(t) // 3. deadline passed: stand-in rule val passed = try { next.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { if (e.cause is TimeoutException) return fallback(t) // no fraud permit in time return Verdict.DECLINED // 4. a check failed: fail fast } if (!passed) return Verdict.DECLINED // 4. a check said no: fail fast } return Verdict.APPROVED } finally { perTask.shutdownNow() // 5. interrupt whatever still runs... perTask.close() // ...and wait until those threads end } } Verdict screen(Transfer t) throws InterruptedException { long deadline = System.nanoTime() + budget.toNanos(); // 1. one deadline for both checks ExecutorService perTask = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); try { CompletionService<Boolean> done = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(perTask); done.submit(() -> fraudBulkhead.call(deadline - System.nanoTime(), () -> fraud.passes(t))); // 2. fork both done.submit(() -> limits.passes(t)); for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) { Future<Boolean> next = done.poll(deadline - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS); if (next == null) return fallback(t); // 3. deadline passed: stand-in rule try { if (!next.get()) return Verdict.DECLINED; // 4. a check said no: fail fast } catch (ExecutionException e) { if (e.getCause() instanceof TimeoutException) return fallback(t); // no fraud permit in time return Verdict.DECLINED; // 4. a check failed: fail fast } } return Verdict.APPROVED; } finally { perTask.shutdownNow(); // 5. interrupt whatever still runs... perTask.close(); // ...and wait until those threads end } } Check it against the lab's tests, which are the production behaviours you care about. A stuck fraud call ends at the deadline, is interrupted, and gives its permit back. A no from either check declines at once and interrupts the other. A full bulkhead means the fallback without calling the fraud service at all. And 10,000 concurrent requests never put more than 50 calls into the fraud service, while every APPLIED reply, replayed on the opening balances, gives exactly the ledger's final snapshot.

h: Serve it with virtual threads · Quiz
x: A colleague moves val permits = Semaphore(20) from the fraud client into handle(), so each request creates its own. What does the fraud service see during a spike of 5,000 concurrent requests? At most 20 calls at once, as before Up to 5,000 calls at once: every request has its own 20 permits At most 1 call at once An IllegalStateException from the second semaphore A semaphore limits only the threads that share it. One per request hands every request a full set of permits, so the limit is gone. Keep one per dependency, in a field that every request uses. The ledger runs on JDK 21 and apply uses synchronized on both accounts, held for microseconds with no I/O inside. Ten thousand virtual threads pay into the same merchant account. What can happen? Nothing bad: the critical section is too short to matter The JVM throws IllegalMonitorStateException under that much contention Virtual threads waiting to enter the merchant's monitor pin their carriers, so heavy contention can leave no carrier free for other requests Each virtual thread gets its own copy of the monitor On JDK 21 to 23, a virtual thread blocked entering a monitor can't unmount, so with one hot monitor every carrier can end up waiting at it, and requests that never touch the account stop too. JDK 24 fixed it (JEP 491). ReentrantLock parks its waiters and frees the carrier on every JDK. A short critical section makes each wait short; it doesn't make the pins harmless. call.get(300, MILLISECONDS) throws TimeoutException, the request answers with the stand-in rule, and the code does nothing else. What is the fraud call doing now? Still running and holding its bulkhead permit until the fraud service answers Cancelled, because get with a timeout cancels the task Interrupted, because its request thread moved on Finished, because its future is now done A timeout on get ends your wait, nothing more. Nobody told the task to stop, so it runs on and keeps its permit, and its future is not done. Cancel it with cancel(true), or shutdownNow() on its executor, so the call is interrupted and its finally releases the permit. In a hand-built fail-fast scope on JDK 21 you call cancel(true) on the slow check's future, then close() on the virtual-thread executor. Why can close() return while the check is still running its finally block? cancel(true) doesn't interrupt the thread close() never waits for tasks Virtual threads skip finally blocks after an interrupt The executor counts a task as finished once its future is done, and cancel marks the future done at once On JDK 21 the per-task executor tracks tasks by their futures, and cancel(true) completes the future immediately while the thread is still unwinding. shutdownNow() interrupts the threads and leaves the futures alone, so close() keeps waiting until each thread has really ended. That is why screen calls shutdownNow() and then close(). Why does TransferServer.handle wait for ledger.submit(t).get() with no timeout? Because the ledger pool is so fast that it never matters Because once the pool has accepted the transfer it may be applied, and a timeout would report a failure for money that moved Because Future.get has no timeout version Because virtual threads can't be interrupted while they wait The wait is already bounded by design: a full queue rejects at once with BUSY, and 80 queued transfers drain in about 50 ms. A timeout there would end the wait, not the transfer, so the client would retry a transfer that already happened. If you need a hard bound, answer 202 with the transfer id and let the client ask for the outcome.

h: Serve it with virtual threads · Key terms
x: Bulkhead A separate, shared limit on one dependency, so one slow service can't take every thread or connection. Deadline One point in time for the whole request. Every wait inside the request uses whatever is left of it. Stand-in A fallback for when a check can't answer in time: small amounts go through unchecked, larger ones are refused. Fail-fast fan-out Running several checks at once and stopping all of them at the first failure or no. Orphaned call Work that keeps running after the request that started it has already answered. Pinning A virtual thread that blocks but can't leave its carrier, so the carrier blocks with it. Thread container A group in a JSON thread dump: the executor or scope that started a set of threads. Why one new virtual thread per request, not a pool of virtual threads? Creating one is cheap, and a pool would cap the whole request. Cap the scarce resource with a shared semaphore instead. What must happen to a fraud call when its request's deadline passes? Interrupt it (cancel(true) or shutdownNow()), so it stops and its finally releases the bulkhead permit. A timeout alone leaves an orphan holding the permit. What makes a fan-out fail fast? Take results in completion order, stop at the first no or failure, then shutdownNow() to interrupt the rest and close() to wait for them. What is stand-in processing? A fallback rule: when a check can't answer in time, small amounts go through unchecked and larger ones are turned away. On JDK 21, what pins a virtual thread in ledger code? Blocking inside synchronized, or waiting to enter a contended synchronized block. ReentrantLock never pins. JDK 24 removed both cases (JEP 491). Why don't parked virtual threads appear in jcmd <pid> Thread.print? It lists platform threads, plus mounted virtual threads from JDK 24. Use jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json <file>. How do you make 10,000 stacks in a JSON dump readable? Group them: count threads per container, and count stacks by the frame where your code starts, with jq ... | sort | uniq -c.

Structured concurrency is the JDK's own version of screen. StructuredTaskScope is a preview API in JDK 25 (JEP 505) and still preview in JDK 26 and 27; JEP 543 makes it final in JDK 28 with the JDK 27 API. Here is the screening in the JDK 25 shape. The last lesson says plainly when you shouldn't use Reactor at all. You need the first track (threads, races, synchronized), the executors track (pools, CompletableFuture, Little's law) and the virtual threads track, because this one keeps comparing against them. Install JDK 25. The labs use Reactor 3.8.8 and reactor-test 3.8.8 and compile with release 21, so they run on JDK 21 or later. The labs live in labs/reactive, one package per lesson (workbench.reactive.l01 to l08). They are in Java, and every code sample and Try-it demo also comes in Kotlin, with Kotlin Flow and coroutine counterparts where they exist. Timing tests use virtual time, latches and max-concurrency counters rather than sleeps. Run ./gradlew :reactive:test --tests 'workbench.reactive.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, use solutionTest to check the reference answers, and run the demos with ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=.... Reactive Streams is a contract of four interfaces: the subscriber asks for n items, the publisher never sends more, and onError or onComplete ends the stream for good. Assembly builds a recipe; subscription runs it, once per subscriber for a cold publisher. Mono.just(call()) runs the call at assembly; fromCallable and defer run it per subscription. flatMap runs inners concurrently in completion order (256 at a time by default), concatMap one at a time in order, flatMapSequential concurrently in order, switchMap keeps only the latest. Mono.zip completes empty, silently, when one source is empty. Say what empty means on each source. For remote calls: a lazy source, a per-attempt timeout, retryWhen(Retry.backoff(...).filter(...)) (3 retries means 4 attempts), and a fallback for exhausted retries. Code runs on the thread that delivered the signal. publishOn moves what follows, subscribeOn moves the source; blocking calls go on boundedElastic, with subscribeOn on each inner. limitRate reshapes demand. For sources that can't slow down, pick a loss policy; onBackpressureBuffer() with no size only hides the backlog. share, replay(n).refCount() and cache differ in what late subscribers get and when they disconnect. Sinks need a retrying emit when several threads push. Test with StepVerifier and virtual time: always verify() with a timeout, and build the publisher inside the supplier. Use Reactor for streams and composed concurrency; for request and response over blocking libraries, virtual threads and imperative code are simpler.

x: The contract Signal Direction Rule onSubscribe(s) publisher to subscriber always first, exactly once request(n) subscriber to publisher demand; the publisher never sends more than requested onNext(item) publisher to subscriber zero or more, never null, one at a time onError(e) or onComplete() publisher to subscriber at most one, and nothing after it cancel() subscriber to publisher the only way a subscriber stops the stream java.util.concurrent.Flow is the same four interfaces in the JDK. Flux is 0 to N items, Mono is 0 or 1. Nothing happens until you subscribe You write The work runs Mono.just(call()) once, at assembly, before anyone subscribes Mono.fromCallable(() -> call()) once per subscription Mono.defer(() -> client.call()) once per subscription; client.call() returns a publisher A cold publisher does its work again for each subscriber. retry re-subscribes, so it needs a lazy source. Picking an operator You want Use a synchronous change per item map, filter async calls, any order, capped flatMap(call, n) (default n is 256) async calls, one at a time, in order concatMap(call) async calls, concurrent, in input order flatMapSequential(call, n) only the latest request matters switchMap(call) one result from several independent calls Mono.zip(a, b, c), with switchIfEmpty or defaultIfEmpty on each two live streams interleaved / one after the other Flux.merge / Flux.concat a value recomputed when any input changes Flux.combineLatest Source 3, 1, 2, item i takes i x 100 ms: flatMap gives 1, 2, 3 at 300 ms, concatMap gives 3, 1, 2 at 600 ms, flatMapSequential gives 3, 1, 2 at 300 ms. Errors, retries, timeouts Java Mono.defer(() -> issuer.authorize(id)) // a fresh call per attempt .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) // per attempt .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // 4 attempts: 0, 100, 300, 700 ms .filter(e -> e instanceof IssuerUnavailableException || e instanceof TimeoutException)) .onErrorResume(Exceptions::isRetryExhausted, e -> Mono.just("PENDING:" + id)); Kotlin Mono.defer { issuer.authorize(id) } // a fresh call per attempt .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) // per attempt .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // 4 attempts: 0, 100, 300, 700 ms .filter { e -> e is IssuerUnavailableException || e is TimeoutException }) .onErrorResume(Exceptions::isRetryExhausted) { Mono.just("PENDING:$id") } Errors are terminal. retry(n) makes n + 1 immediate attempts and rethrows the original error; Retry.backoff ends with RetryExhaustedException (jitter 0.5 by default). Skip a bad item inside a per-item Mono, not with onErrorContinue. Threads Scheduler Threads For none the thread that subscribed, or the one that delivered the item most operators Schedulers.parallel() one per core CPU work and timers; never block Schedulers.single() one cheap serial work Schedulers.boundedElastic() up to 10 x cores, then a queue of 100,000 blocking calls publishOn moves the operators after it. subscribeOn moves the source, wherever it is written; the one nearest the source wins. Wrap blocking calls as Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(boundedElastic()), with subscribeOn on each inner Mono. block() throws on parallel and single threads. -Dreactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticOnVirtualThreads=true (Reactor 3.6+, JDK 21+) runs boundedElastic on virtual threads. Backpressure Between you and the source The source sees subscribe(consumer) or block() alone Long.MAX_VALUE take(3) 3 limitRate(10) 10, 8, 8, ... flatMap(call, 4) 4, 1, 1, ... For a source that can't slow down, choose: onBackpressureBuffer(n) (keep n, then fail loudly), onBackpressureDrop(onDropped), onBackpressureLatest(), onBackpressureError(). All of them request unbounded upstream. Never use onBackpressureBuffer() without a size. Flux.create buffers without limit by default. Sharing and Sinks Operator A late subscriber gets Disconnects share() = publish().refCount() only new items when the last one leaves replay(n).refCount() the last n, then new ones when the last one leaves publish().autoConnect(n) only new items never cache() everything never Mono.cache(ttl) the value until it expires not applicable Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort() for a live hub that survives having no subscribers; onBackpressureBuffer() buffers but shuts down when its last subscriber leaves. From several threads, use emitNext(item, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1))); a bare tryEmitNext can return FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED and lose the item. Testing and debugging Java StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> poller.awaitFinal("p-1")) // build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() // before expectNoEvent .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(90)) .expectNext(SETTLED) .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); // nothing runs without verify() Kotlin StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { poller.awaitFinal("p-1") } // build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() // before expectNoEvent .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(90)) .expectNext(SETTLED) .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // nothing runs without verify() TestPublisher drives a source by hand; PublisherProbe proves a branch ran. checkpoint("name") labels errors cheaply, log() prints every signal, Hooks.onOperatorDebug() is a costly last resort. When to use it Request and response over JDBC or other blocking clients: virtual threads and plain code. Streams, demand, cancellation, loss policies, and many calls composed with timeouts and retries: Reactor. Kotlin: coroutines and Flow, bridged by kotlinx-coroutines-reactor.

h: Reactive programming: track quiz
x: A Flow.Subscriber calls request(2) in onSubscribe and never requests again. Its publisher has 100 items ready. What does the subscriber receive? All 100 items, because the publisher pushes what it has 2 items, then nothing until it requests more 2 items, then onComplete 2 items, then onError, because the rest were not requested Rule 1.1: a publisher sends no more onNext signals than were requested. A publisher that still has items to deliver doesn't complete; it waits for more demand. A stream with unmet demand simply stalls, which is what to look for when a pipeline hangs. Mono<Receipt> r = Mono.just(chargeCard(payment)); is built, but nothing ever subscribes to r. How many times is the card charged? Never: nothing happens until you subscribe Once Once per subscriber, so zero It depends on the scheduler Mono.just takes a value, so Java evaluates chargeCard(payment) before just is even called: the charge happens at assembly. "Nothing happens until you subscribe" is true of the work inside operators and fromCallable, not of arguments you compute yourself. Source 3, 1, 2; each item i is turned into a call that takes i x 100 ms. What does concatMap emit, and when is it done? 1, 2, 3, done at 300 ms 3, 1, 2, done at 300 ms 3, 1, 2, done at 600 ms 1, 2, 3, done at 600 ms concatMap runs one call at a time in source order, so it takes 300 + 100 + 200 = 600 ms. flatMap would give 1, 2, 3 at 300 ms (completion order), and flatMapSequential 3, 1, 2 at 300 ms (concurrent, but reordered). A merchant search box sends a lookup on every keystroke. Results of an older query must never overwrite newer ones. Which operator fits? flatMap concatMap switchMap flatMapSequential switchMap cancels the previous lookup as soon as a new keystroke arrives, so only the latest query can produce results. flatMap lets a slow old query land after a newer one; concatMap and flatMapSequential would wait for every old query in order. Mono.zip(fxRate, fee, limit): limit completes empty because the customer has no limit configured. What does the zip do? Fails with NoSuchElementException Emits a tuple with null for the limit Waits for a limit that never comes Completes empty, with no error, and cancels the other calls An empty source gives the zip nothing to combine, so it completes empty at once and cancels the rest. Nothing is logged. Put switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(...)) or defaultIfEmpty(...) on each source that can be empty. Mono.defer(() -> issuer.authorize(id)).retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0)) against an issuer that always fails. What happens? 3 calls, then the issuer's exception 4 calls at 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms, then RetryExhaustedException with the issuer's exception as its cause 4 calls 100 ms apart, then the issuer's exception An endless loop of calls The 3 counts retries, so there are 4 attempts, with waits of 100, 200 and 400 ms. When the retries run out, Retry.backoff signals RetryExhaustedException ("Retries exhausted: 3/3"). Plain retry(3) would also make 4 attempts, with no waits, and rethrow the original error. Flux.fromIterable(ids).flatMap(id -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> dao.load(id))).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) loads 50 rows, 20 ms each, with a blocking DAO. About how long does it take? About 20 ms: flatMap runs them all at once About 1 second: all 50 run in turn on one thread About 250 ms: one thread per core It fails: blocking is not allowed on boundedElastic subscribeOn on the outer Flux puts the whole subscription on one boundedElastic thread, and each fromCallable runs synchronously when flatMap subscribes to it, on that same thread. Put subscribeOn(boundedElastic()) on each inner Mono, and cap the fan-out with flatMap's concurrency. A WebSocket of audit events can't slow down. No event may be lost silently, and bursts of a few hundred are normal. Which line fits? events.onBackpressureBuffer() events.onBackpressureLatest() events.onBackpressureBuffer(1_000, e -> log.error("overflow at {}", e.id())) events.limitRate(100) A bounded buffer absorbs the bursts, and if the consumer falls further behind, it cancels the source, logs the overflowing event and fails, so the gap is visible. The unbounded buffer hides the backlog until memory runs out, onBackpressureLatest drops events silently, and limitRate changes requests that this source ignores. Twelve dashboards share one FX provider connection. A dashboard that opens late must show the current rate at once, and the connection must close when nobody watches. Which operator fits? rates.replay(1).refCount() rates.share() rates.cache() rates.publish().autoConnect(1) replay(1) hands a late subscriber the latest rate, and refCount() cancels the upstream when the last subscriber leaves. share() makes a late dashboard wait for the next tick; cache() and autoConnect never disconnect, and cache() keeps every rate forever. A test builds Mono<Status> poll = poller.awaitFinal("p-1"); in @BeforeEach, then runs StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> poll).thenAwait(Duration.ofMinutes(5))...verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)). It fails with "VerifySubscriber timed out". Why? Virtual time doesn't work with Mono thenAwait must be replaced with Thread.sleep verify needs a longer timeout, such as 5 minutes The Mono was assembled before virtual time was installed, so its timers use the real clock Operators such as interval, delay and timeout pick their scheduler at assembly. Built in @BeforeEach, the poller's timers run on the real parallel scheduler, and advancing the virtual clock does nothing. Call poller.awaitFinal("p-1") inside the supplier. A 5-minute real timeout would just make the test slow.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Pull, push, and the consumer that drowns
x: There are two ways to move data from a producer to a consumer. In pull, the consumer asks for the next item when it is ready: Iterator.next(), ResultSet.next(), KafkaConsumer.poll(). The consumer sets the pace. The cost is a waiting thread: while the next item isn't there yet, the consumer's thread sits and does nothing. In push, the producer calls the consumer when an item exists: a listener, a callback, CompletableFuture.thenAccept. Nobody waits. The cost is that the producer sets the pace, and the consumer has no way to say "slow down". Push breaks when the producer is faster than the consumer. Here is a shape that shows up in payment services: Java // the listener returns at once, so the poll loop keeps fetching void onMessage(PaymentEvent e) { ledgerWriter.execute(() -> ledger.write(e)); // a fixed pool: its queue has no limit } Kotlin // the listener returns at once, so the poll loop keeps fetching fun onMessage(e: PaymentEvent) { ledgerWriter.execute { ledger.write(e) } // a fixed pool: its queue has no limit } Kafka itself is pull, and this code turns it into push. The listener returns in microseconds, so poll() keeps fetching, and the executor's LinkedBlockingQueue grows. With 10,000 events a second coming in and 2,000 going out, the heap gains 8,000 objects every second. Nothing fails at first. Then the garbage collector runs all the time, latency climbs, and the pod is killed for running out of memory. Backpressure is the fix: the consumer tells the producer how much it can take, and the producer never sends more. Reactive Streams makes this part of the protocol. The subscriber calls request(n), and the publisher may then push at most n items. If items are ready, they arrive at once, as with pull. If they aren't, the publisher pushes them when they appear, as with push. The Reactor docs call this a push-pull hybrid. When the consumer can't keep up, a system has four honest options: slow the producer down, buffer up to a limit, drop items, or fail. An unbounded queue is a fifth option that only looks like a choice. Reactive Streams makes you pick one of the four on purpose. Lesson 7 of this track, "Backpressure in practice", shows how to pick in Reactor. Drown a ledger writer, then rescue it Read DrowningDemo below. It sends 100,000 events to a writer that needs 10 microseconds per event, first with plain push and then through a SubmissionPublisher with request(1). Predict for each version: how long will the producer take, and how many events will be waiting in memory when it finishes? Run it (Java or Kotlin, they print the same). Then change writeToLedger to wait 20,000 nanoseconds and run again. Which number changes in each line? DrowningDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l01; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Flow; import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** A fast producer and a slow ledger writer, first with plain push, then with demand. */ public class DrowningDemo { static final int EVENTS = 100_000; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { pushWithoutDemand(); pushWithDemand(); } // Plain push: the producer hands every event to the writer's executor. Its queue has no limit. static void pushWithoutDemand() throws Exception { ExecutorService writer = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); AtomicLong written = new AtomicLong(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < EVENTS; i++) { writer.execute(() -> { writeToLedger(); written.incrementAndGet(); }); } long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; long w = written.get(); System.out.printf("plain push: producer done in %,5d ms, ledger wrote %,6d, %,6d events waiting in memory%n", ms, w, EVENTS - w); writer.shutdownNow(); } // With demand: the writer asks for one event at a time. submit() blocks when the 256-slot buffer is full. static void pushWithDemand() throws Exception { AtomicLong written = new AtomicLong(); long maxLag = 0; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (SubmissionPublisher<Integer> publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<>()) { publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<Integer>() { Flow.Subscription s; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(1); } public void onNext(Integer event) { writeToLedger(); written.incrementAndGet(); s.request(1); } public void onError(Throwable t) { t.printStackTrace(); } public void onComplete() { } }); for (int i = 0; i < EVENTS; i++) { publisher.submit(i); // waits while the buffer is full maxLag = Math.max(maxLag, publisher.estimateMaximumLag()); } long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; long w = written.get(); System.out.printf("with demand: producer done in %,5d ms, ledger wrote %,6d, never more than %,d waiting%n", ms, w, maxLag); } TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(50); } // stands in for a 10-microsecond ledger write static void writeToLedger() { long until = System.nanoTime() + 10_000; while (System.nanoTime() < until) Thread.onSpinWait(); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l01.DrowningDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l01/DrowningDemo.java DrowningDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.Flow import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong private const val EVENTS = 100_000 /** A fast producer and a slow ledger writer, first with plain push, then with demand. */ fun main() { pushWithoutDemand() pushWithDemand() } // Plain push: the producer hands every event to the writer's executor. Its queue has no limit. private fun pushWithoutDemand() { val writer = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() val written = AtomicLong() val t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(EVENTS) { writer.execute { writeToLedger(); written.incrementAndGet() } } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val w = written.get() println("plain push: producer done in %,5d ms, ledger wrote %,6d, %,6d events waiting in memory".format(ms, w, EVENTS - w)) writer.shutdownNow() } // With demand: the writer asks for one event at a time. submit() blocks when the 256-slot buffer is full. private fun pushWithDemand() { val written = AtomicLong() var maxLag = 0L val t0 = System.nanoTime() SubmissionPublisher<Int>().use { publisher -> publisher.subscribe(object : Flow.Subscriber<Int> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s; s.request(1) } override fun onNext(event: Int) { writeToLedger(); written.incrementAndGet(); s.request(1) } override fun onError(t: Throwable) = t.printStackTrace() override fun onComplete() {} }) for (i in 0 until EVENTS) { publisher.submit(i) // waits while the buffer is full maxLag = maxOf(maxLag, publisher.estimateMaximumLag().toLong()) } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("with demand: producer done in %,5d ms, ledger wrote %,6d, never more than %,d waiting".format(ms, written.get(), maxLag)) } TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(50) } // stands in for a 10-microsecond ledger write private fun writeToLedger() { val until = System.nanoTime() + 10_000 while (System.nanoTime() < until) Thread.onSpinWait() } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l01.DrowningDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l01/DrowningDemo.kt With plain push the producer finishes in tens of milliseconds and almost everything is still queued (one run here: 40 ms, 1,347 written, 98,653 waiting). With demand the producer takes as long as the writer needs (1,805 ms here) and never more than about 256 events wait, which is the publisher's buffer. With a 20 microsecond write, the plain version leaves even more events queued, and the demand version simply takes about twice as long. Its memory stays flat. Think of a kitchen and a waiter. With plain push the kitchen sends out every plate the moment it is cooked, and the waiter stacks them on a side table that keeps getting longer. With pull the waiter walks to the pass and stands there until a plate is ready. Reactive Streams is the waiter saying "I can carry three": the kitchen sends up to three plates, at once if they are ready or as soon as they are, and never a fourth until the waiter asks again. The analogy breaks at the end of the shift: a real kitchen notices when the waiter quits, but a publisher only stops when the subscriber calls cancel().

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Reactive Streams: the contract in seven methods
x: Reactive Streams demand: the publisher sends only what the subscriber asked for Reactive Streams is a small spec: four interfaces, seven methods, and a list of numbered rules. Here is all of the API: Java public interface Publisher<T> { void subscribe(Subscriber<? super T> s); } public interface Subscriber<T> { void onSubscribe(Subscription s); void onNext(T item); void onError(Throwable t); void onComplete(); } public interface Subscription { void request(long n); void cancel(); } public interface Processor<T, R> extends Subscriber<T>, Publisher<R> { } Kotlin // the same four interfaces, written as Kotlin declarations interface Publisher<T> { fun subscribe(s: Subscriber<in T>) } interface Subscriber<T> { fun onSubscribe(s: Subscription) fun onNext(item: T) fun onError(t: Throwable) fun onComplete() } interface Subscription { fun request(n: Long); fun cancel() } interface Processor<T, R> : Subscriber<T>, Publisher<R> Every method returns void (Unit in Kotlin), so every call is a one-way message. Java's Subscriber<? super T> is Kotlin's Subscriber<in T>: a publisher of payments also accepts a subscriber of any supertype, such as a Subscriber<Object> that logs everything. A subscriber sees signals in one fixed order, which the spec writes as onSubscribe onNext* (onError | onComplete)?. That means one onSubscribe, then any number of onNext, then at most one terminal signal. After onError or onComplete, nothing else arrives. You will rarely write these by hand. Reactor, RxJava, Mutiny (the library behind Quarkus' reactive APIs) and the reactive database drivers all implement them, and the rules are why one library can subscribe to another. The rules you will actually meet: 1.1 A publisher never sends more onNext signals than were requested in total. 1.3 Signals to one subscriber are serial: never two at the same time. So a subscriber needs no locks for its own fields. 1.9 onSubscribe comes before any other signal. 2.13 Subscriber methods must return normally. The only exception allowed is a NullPointerException for a null argument. A subscriber that wants to stop must call cancel(), not throw. An exception from onNext lands in the publisher's delivery code, which can't hand it back to the subscriber, so the spec has the publisher treat the subscription as cancelled and report the error some other way, such as a log line. 2.8 A subscriber must accept onNext calls that arrive after it cancelled. Items already requested may still be on their way. 3.9 request(n) with n <= 0 must produce onError(IllegalArgumentException). 3.17 Demand of Long.MAX_VALUE may be treated as "unbounded". That is a subscriber saying it wants no backpressure at all. Rule 3.9 is a good place to see that the spec and a library can differ. The JDK's publisher follows it. Reactor's operators only log a bad request at DEBUG level and send nothing, so a broken subscriber just waits forever. A stream that silently stalls is the symptom to remember. Break rule 3.9 on purpose RequestZeroDemo has a subscriber that calls request(0) in onSubscribe. It subscribes to a JDK SubmissionPublisher and to a Reactor Flux.range(1, 3). Predict what each publisher sends back. Then run it. Change request(0) to request(2). Predict again: does each stream complete? RequestZeroDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l01; import reactor.adapter.JdkFlowAdapter; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import java.util.concurrent.Flow; import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** A subscriber that breaks rule 3.9 by calling request(0). Two publishers react differently. */ public class RequestZeroDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (SubmissionPublisher<Integer> jdk = new SubmissionPublisher<>()) { jdk.subscribe(new Rude("JDK SubmissionPublisher")); jdk.submit(1); } TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(300); Flow.Publisher<Integer> reactor = JdkFlowAdapter.publisherToFlowPublisher(Flux.range(1, 3)); Rude rude = new Rude("Reactor Flux.range"); reactor.subscribe(rude); TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(300); if (!rude.signalled) System.out.println("Reactor Flux.range: no signal at all, the stream just stalls"); } static final class Rude implements Flow.Subscriber<Integer> { final String name; volatile boolean signalled; Rude(String name) { this.name = name; } @Override public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { s.request(0); } // rule 3.9 says: must be > 0 @Override public void onNext(Integer item) { signalled = true; System.out.println(name + ": onNext " + item); } @Override public void onError(Throwable t) { signalled = true; System.out.println(name + ": onError " + t); } @Override public void onComplete() { signalled = true; System.out.println(name + ": onComplete"); } } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l01.RequestZeroDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l01/RequestZeroDemo.java RequestZeroDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l01 import reactor.adapter.JdkFlowAdapter import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import java.util.concurrent.Flow import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** A subscriber that breaks rule 3.9 by calling request(0). Two publishers react differently. */ fun main() { SubmissionPublisher<Int>().use { jdk -> jdk.subscribe(RudeSubscriber("JDK SubmissionPublisher")) jdk.submit(1) } TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(300) val reactor: Flow.Publisher<Int> = JdkFlowAdapter.publisherToFlowPublisher(Flux.range(1, 3)) val rude = RudeSubscriber("Reactor Flux.range") reactor.subscribe(rude) TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.sleep(300) if (!rude.signalled) println("Reactor Flux.range: no signal at all, the stream just stalls") } private class RudeSubscriber(private val name: String) : Flow.Subscriber<Int> { @Volatile var signalled = false override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) = s.request(0) // rule 3.9 says: must be > 0 override fun onNext(item: Int) { signalled = true; println("$name: onNext $item") } override fun onError(t: Throwable) { signalled = true; println("$name: onError $t") } override fun onComplete() { signalled = true; println("$name: onComplete") } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l01.RequestZeroDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l01/RequestZeroDemo.kt The JDK publisher follows rule 3.9 and prints onError java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: non-positive subscription request. Reactor prints nothing at all: the stream just stalls. With request(2), the JDK publisher sends its one item and then onComplete, because it was closed. Reactor sends 1 and 2 and then stops without completing, because nobody asked for 3. Unmet demand never times out by itself. Demand goes up as request(n), data comes down as onNext. The publisher never sends more than it is owed. Reactive Streams for the JVM: specification and rules docs Your Kafka consumers already pull, which is why a slow listener slows poll() and eventually triggers a rebalance. The danger is the moment you hand records to something that doesn't push back: an unbounded executor queue, a CompletableFuture.runAsync per record, or a reactive pipeline that calls request(Long.MAX_VALUE). The same applies to a Temporal activity that streams settlement rows into an in-memory list, or a Quarkus endpoint that relays an issuer's event stream to clients. Ask one question of each: when the next stage is slow, what makes the stage before it wait?

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · java.util.concurrent.Flow and SubmissionPublisher
x: Java 9 copied the four interfaces into the JDK as nested types of java.util.concurrent.Flow: Flow.Publisher, Flow.Subscriber, Flow.Subscription and Flow.Processor. Same methods, same rules, different package. Reactor works with org.reactivestreams.Publisher, so you bridge with JdkFlowAdapter (in reactor-core) or FlowAdapters (in the reactive-streams jar). The JDK ships one real implementation, SubmissionPublisher. You hand it items from ordinary code, and it delivers them to each subscriber asynchronously: Java try (var publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<PaymentEvent>()) { publisher.subscribe(new BatchingSubscriber<>(32, ledger::write)); for (PaymentEvent e : events) { publisher.submit(e); // blocks while this subscriber is 256 items behind } } // close(): subscribers get onComplete after their buffered items Kotlin SubmissionPublisher<PaymentEvent>().use { publisher -> publisher.subscribe(BatchingSubscriber(32, ledger::write)) for (e in events) { publisher.submit(e) // blocks while this subscriber is 256 items behind } } // close(): subscribers get onComplete after their buffered items The parts that matter: Each subscriber gets its own buffer. Its maximum size defaults to Flow.defaultBufferSize(), which is 256. Delivery runs on an Executor. On JDK 21 the default is ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). Pass your own executor for anything slow. submit(item) blocks the producer's thread when a subscriber's buffer is full. This is where backpressure turns into something an ordinary thread can feel. In the first Try it, submit is what slowed the producer down to the ledger writer's pace. offer(item, onDrop) never blocks. When a buffer is full it calls your drop handler, and returns a negative number for each drop. There is also an offer with a timeout. If a subscriber method throws, the publisher cancels that subscription. close() completes every subscriber. closeExceptionally(t) sends them onError(t). Blocking in submit is fine on a dedicated producer thread or a virtual thread. It is a bad idea on an event-loop thread (one thread that serves many connections, as the next section explains), where it stalls everything else on that loop. SubmissionPublisher is a good teaching tool and a decent in-process fan-out, but it has no operators. You can't map, retry or time out a Flow.Publisher without writing the code yourself. That is the job Reactor does, starting with lesson 2 of this track. Fill a two-slot buffer SaturationDemo builds a SubmissionPublisher with a buffer of 2 and a subscriber that never calls request. It then offers 10 items. Predict what each offer returns and how many items are dropped. Run it. Now replace the offer(...) call with publisher.submit(i) and keep the assignment to lag. Predict, then run it. Stop it with Ctrl+C. SaturationDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l01; import java.util.concurrent.Flow; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** A SubmissionPublisher with a 2-slot buffer and a subscriber that never asks for anything. */ public class SaturationDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("default buffer: " + Flow.defaultBufferSize()); AtomicInteger dropped = new AtomicInteger(); try (SubmissionPublisher<Integer> publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<>(ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), 2)) { publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<Integer>() { public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { } // never calls request(n) public void onNext(Integer item) { System.out.println("got " + item); } public void onError(Throwable t) { } public void onComplete() { } }); for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) { // offer() does not block. When the buffer is full it calls the drop handler instead. int lag = publisher.offer(i, (subscriber, item) -> { dropped.incrementAndGet(); return false; // false: don't retry, drop it }); System.out.printf("offer(%d) -> %d%n", i, lag); } System.out.println("dropped " + dropped.get() + " of 10, lag " + publisher.estimateMaximumLag()); } } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l01.SaturationDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l01/SaturationDemo.java SaturationDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l01 import java.util.concurrent.Flow import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** A SubmissionPublisher with a 2-slot buffer and a subscriber that never asks for anything. */ fun main() { println("default buffer: ${Flow.defaultBufferSize()}") val dropped = AtomicInteger() SubmissionPublisher<Int>(ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), 2).use { publisher -> publisher.subscribe(object : Flow.Subscriber<Int> { override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) {} // never calls request(n) override fun onNext(item: Int) = println("got $item") override fun onError(t: Throwable) {} override fun onComplete() {} }) for (i in 1..10) { // offer() does not block. When the buffer is full it calls the drop handler instead. val lag = publisher.offer(i) { _, _ -> dropped.incrementAndGet() false // false: don't retry, drop it } println("offer($i) -> $lag") } println("dropped ${dropped.get()} of 10, lag ${publisher.estimateMaximumLag()}") } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l01.SaturationDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l01/SaturationDemo.kt The first two offers return a lag of 1 and 2. Offers 3 to 10 each return -1, the drop handler runs eight times, and the last line is dropped 8 of 10, lag 2. Nothing is delivered, because nothing was requested. With submit the program hangs on item 3: the buffer is full, the subscriber never asks for more, and submit waits for space. That hang is backpressure reaching your thread. Flow (Java SE 25 API) docs SubmissionPublisher (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · What non-blocking buys you, and what it costs
x: Here is what blocking IO costs. A thread sends a request to the card issuer and waits 120 ms for the answer. During those 120 ms it holds about a megabyte of stack and does no work. A pool of 200 such threads can have 200 calls in flight. By Little's law that caps you at 200 / 0.12 s, about 1,670 calls a second, however idle the CPUs are. Non-blocking IO removes the wait. An event-loop thread (Netty, or the JDK's NIO selectors) hands the request to the operating system and moves on to other work. When the response bytes arrive, the loop runs a callback to continue. A handful of threads can keep thousands of calls in flight. Reactive libraries are the programming model for that callback world: a Mono is the one reply you are waiting for, a Flux is a stream of them, and demand travels with the data. It has real costs. The Spring Framework docs say it plainly: "Reactive and non-blocking generally do not make applications run faster." The gain is "the ability to scale with a small, fixed number of threads and less memory", and you only see it when calls have latency. You also pay with stack traces that show operator internals instead of your code, a learning curve the whole team has to climb, and one strict rule: nothing on an event loop may block. A single JDBC call on an event-loop thread stalls every request that loop serves. Virtual threads (JDK 21, JEP 444) changed the trade. A blocked virtual thread unmounts from its carrier, so blocking code no longer burns a platform thread per call. For request and response over JDBC, a plain blocking style on virtual threads is now the simpler default. Reactive still earns its place where the problem is a stream: backpressure, cancellation that travels upstream, rate-limited fan-out, retries and timeouts as composable operators. Lesson 8 of this track comes back to this choice with the Spring team's own words. Quick check: your service makes 3,000 issuer calls a second, and each waits 120 ms. How many calls are in flight at any moment, and how many threads does each model need for them? (Little's law gives 3,000 x 0.12 s = 360 calls in flight. Blocking IO needs 360 threads, one parked per call. An event loop needs a handful, because no thread waits for a reply.) Spring Framework reference: WebFlux overview (applicability and performance) read The most common mistake is asking for everything. subscription.request(Long.MAX_VALUE) in onSubscribe, or a Reactor subscribe(item -> ...) with no demand control, tells the publisher "no backpressure, please". People do it because it is the shortest code that works in a test with ten items. In production the slow stage then buffers without limit or drops data. Request a bounded batch and ask for more as you finish, as in the lab.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Java and Kotlin
x: A one-at-a-time Flow.Subscriber in Java and Kotlin OneAtATime.java publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<Payment>() { private Flow.Subscription s; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(1); // ask for the first item } public void onNext(Payment p) { ledger.write(p); // slow work s.request(1); // only now ask for the next } public void onError(Throwable t) { log.error("feed failed", t); } public void onComplete() { log.info("feed done"); } }); OneAtATime.kt publisher.subscribe(object : Flow.Subscriber<Payment> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s s.request(1) // ask for the first item } override fun onNext(p: Payment) { // non-null type: Kotlin itself throws NPE on null ledger.write(p) // slow work s.request(1) // only now ask for the next } override fun onError(t: Throwable) = log.error("feed failed", t) override fun onComplete() = log.info("feed done") }) The protocol code is the same in both languages; three Kotlin details change how it feels. lateinit var s replaces the nullable field you would otherwise check. object : Flow.Subscriber<Payment> is Kotlin's anonymous class. And because onNext(p: Payment) declares a non-null parameter, the Kotlin compiler adds a null check to it: a publisher that sends null gets a NullPointerException, which is exactly what rule 2.13 asks for, with no code from you. Don't confuse java.util.concurrent.Flow with kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow. The Kotlin one is a coroutine stream with no request(n) at all: emit suspends until the collector has finished with the item, so a producer can never run ahead. The Spring docs call Kotlin Flow push-based and Reactor's Flux a push-pull hybrid. The coroutines track covers Flow, and kotlinx-coroutines-reactive converts between the two with asFlow() and asPublisher().

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Worked example
x: Find the rule violations in a hand-written subscriber A teammate wrote this subscriber for a statement export. It reads rows from a reactive database driver and writes them to a file. Read it and look for broken rules before reading on. class ExportSubscriber implements Flow.Subscriber<Row> { private Flow.Subscription s; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); } public void onNext(Row row) { if (row.amount() == null) throw new IllegalStateException("bad row " + row.id()); file.append(row.toCsv()); } public void onError(Throwable t) { s.request(1); } // "try again" public void onComplete() { file.close(); } } class ExportSubscriber : Flow.Subscriber<Row> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s s.request(Long.MAX_VALUE) } override fun onNext(row: Row) { if (row.amount == null) throw IllegalStateException("bad row ${row.id}") file.append(row.toCsv()) } override fun onError(t: Throwable) = s.request(1) // "try again" override fun onComplete() = file.close() } Three problems. request(Long.MAX_VALUE) turns backpressure off (rule 3.17), so a slow disk makes the driver buffer rows. Throwing from onNext breaks rule 2.13: the publisher may cancel, log, or do something you didn't expect. And calling request from onError breaks rule 2.3: after a terminal signal the subscription is dead. Fix them one by one. Ask for one item at a time. Turn a bad row into a cancel plus a recorded error. Treat onError as the end. class ExportSubscriber implements Flow.Subscriber<Row> { private Flow.Subscription s; private boolean stopped; volatile Throwable failure; public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription s) { this.s = s; s.request(1); // 1. bounded demand } public void onNext(Row row) { if (stopped) return; // 2. rule 2.8: late items may still come if (row.amount() == null) { stopped = true; failure = new IllegalStateException("bad row " + row.id()); s.cancel(); // 3. stop by cancelling, never by throwing return; } file.append(row.toCsv()); s.request(1); // 4. ask for the next one when done } public void onError(Throwable t) { failure = t; file.close(); } // 5. terminal: just clean up public void onComplete() { file.close(); } } class ExportSubscriber : Flow.Subscriber<Row> { private lateinit var s: Flow.Subscription private var stopped = false @Volatile var failure: Throwable? = null override fun onSubscribe(s: Flow.Subscription) { this.s = s s.request(1) // 1. bounded demand } override fun onNext(row: Row) { if (stopped) return // 2. rule 2.8: late items may still come if (row.amount == null) { stopped = true failure = IllegalStateException("bad row ${row.id}") s.cancel() // 3. stop by cancelling, never by throwing return } file.append(row.toCsv()) s.request(1) // 4. ask for the next one when done } override fun onError(t: Throwable) { failure = t; file.close() } // 5. terminal: just clean up override fun onComplete() = file.close() } This is correct but chatty: one request(1) call per row. Each call crosses into the publisher, and some publishers do real work per request. The lab asks for the same correctness with demand in batches, which is what Reactor's own operators do internally.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Lab
x: A Flow.Subscriber that asks in batches labs/reactive/src/main/java/workbench/reactive/l01/BatchingSubscriber.java ./gradlew :reactive:test --tests 'workbench.reactive.l01.*' Run the tests once. All five fail with TODO errors, and the two SubmissionPublisher tests also time out after 3 seconds. Write onSubscribe: keep the subscription and call request(batchSize). If a subscription is already stored, cancel the new one and return. Write onNext: reject null, pass the item to the handler, count it, and call request(batchSize) again only when a whole batch has been handled. Make a throwing handler safe: catch it, cancel the subscription, record the error, count down done, and ignore any later onNext. Write onError and onComplete so await returns. Run the tests until all five pass. You need two more fields: an int counting items in the current batch, and a boolean that says you have cancelled. Signals are serial (rule 1.3), so plain fields are safe here. The request test expects exactly [4, 4, 4] for 10 items in batches of 4. If you see eleven requests, you are asking after every item. If you see [4], you never reset the counter. Objects.requireNonNull(item) is all rule 2.13 asks for on null. All five tests in BatchingSubscriberTest pass. By the end you can explain how Reactive Streams demand (request(n)) stops a fast producer from drowning a slow consumer, name the rules a subscriber must follow, and write a Flow.Subscriber that asks for items in batches.
