h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Quiz
x: A subscriber calls request(3) in onSubscribe and never calls request again. The publisher has 10 items ready. What does the subscriber receive? All 10 items, because the publisher has them ready 3 items, then onComplete 3 items, and then nothing until it requests more 1 item, because each onNext needs its own request Rule 1.1 caps onNext signals at the total requested. The publisher has more to send, so it may not complete either. It waits for more demand. Having items ready doesn't let a publisher exceed demand. Inside onNext, your handler fails to parse a row. What should the subscriber do? Throw the exception so the publisher can call onError Call subscription.cancel(), record the error, and return normally Call request(0) to signal a problem Ignore it and call request(1) to get the next row Rule 2.13 says subscriber methods must return normally. Cancelling is the only legal way for a subscriber to stop the stream. Throwing leaves the reaction up to the publisher (SubmissionPublisher cancels; other publishers may just log), and request(0) is itself a rule violation. A producer thread calls SubmissionPublisher.submit(event) in a loop. One subscriber is slow and its buffer of 256 is full. What happens? submit blocks until that subscriber has room submit drops the event and returns -1 submit throws IllegalStateException The event goes to the other subscribers only submit blocks while any subscriber's buffer is full, which slows the producer to the slowest subscriber's pace. offer is the method that drops instead (and returns a negative number). Pick offer with a drop handler if the producer must never wait. Which of these is the strongest reason to choose a non-blocking, reactive design for a service? Each request will finish faster It is easier to debug than blocking code It can keep thousands of slow calls in flight with a few threads and little memory It removes the need for timeouts The Spring docs say reactive code generally doesn't run faster. The gain is scale with a small, fixed number of threads, and it only shows when calls have real latency. Debugging is harder, not easier, and slow calls still need timeouts. From "How virtual threads work: carriers and continuations": a virtual thread calls a blocking card-issuer API over a socket and waits 120 ms. What does its carrier thread do during the wait? It blocks for 120 ms, like a platform thread The JVM creates a new carrier thread for the other virtual threads It unmounts the waiting virtual thread and runs other virtual threads The call throws, because virtual threads cannot block Blocking socket IO parks the virtual thread and frees the carrier to run other virtual threads. That is why blocking code on virtual threads scales without a reactive rewrite. The carrier pool doesn't grow to compensate for normal IO waits.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Explain it back
x: A teammate asks why the payments team bothers with request(n) when "a queue in between does the same job". Explain in your own words what demand gives you that an unbounded queue doesn't, and when a queue is fine.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Key terms
x: Backpressure A way for a slow consumer to tell a fast producer how much it can take, so the producer never sends more. Demand The number of items a subscriber has asked for with request(n) and not yet received. Publisher The source of a stream. It sends items to a subscriber, never more than the subscriber asked for. Subscriber The receiver of a stream. It gets onSubscribe, then onNext items, then onError or onComplete. Subscription The link between one publisher and one subscriber. It carries request(n) and cancel() upstream. Terminal signal onError or onComplete. After one of them the stream is over and nothing else arrives. Non-blocking IO IO where the thread hands the request to the OS and moves on, and a callback runs when the answer arrives. What does request(n) promise the subscriber? That the publisher will send at most n more onNext signals (rule 1.1). It may send fewer and then complete or fail. In what order can a Reactive Streams subscriber see signals? onSubscribe onNext* (onError | onComplete)?: one onSubscribe, any number of onNext, then at most one terminal signal. How does a subscriber stop a stream when its handler fails? It calls subscription.cancel() and returns normally. Throwing from onNext breaks rule 2.13. What does SubmissionPublisher.submit do when a subscriber's buffer is full? It blocks the calling thread until there is room. offer drops instead and calls your drop handler. What happens if you call request(0) on a Reactor Flux.range subscription? Nothing at all. Reactor only logs it at DEBUG and the stream stalls. Spec rule 3.9 (and the JDK's SubmissionPublisher) say it must signal onError(IllegalArgumentException). What does request(Long.MAX_VALUE) mean? Unbounded demand: "send everything, no backpressure" (rule 3.17). Is kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow the same as java.util.concurrent.Flow? No. The JDK one is the Reactive Streams protocol with request(n). Kotlin's is a coroutine stream whose backpressure is suspension of emit.

h: Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure · Go deeper
x: Three details that will help later. Why request takes a long. Demand adds up. A subscriber may call request(5) and then request(10) before any item arrives, and the publisher then owes 15. Rule 3.17 says a subscription must support demand up to Long.MAX_VALUE, and that total demand at or above 2^63 - 1 may be treated as unbounded. Reactor's subscribe(Consumer) uses exactly that: it requests Long.MAX_VALUE. Operators like limitRate and flatMap then turn that unbounded demand into bounded requests upstream, which is lesson 7 of this track. Rule 3.3 and reentrancy. request may be called from inside onNext (rule 3.2), and a synchronous publisher may respond by calling onNext again from inside that request (rule 3.10). Done naively, a stream of a million items becomes a stack a million frames deep. Rule 3.3 makes publishers bound that recursion, usually with a small trampoline loop. This is one reason writing a correct publisher is much harder than writing a subscriber, and why you should use a library's. The TCK. The Reactive Streams project ships a Technology Compatibility Kit: a set of tests that check a publisher or subscriber against the numbered rules. Library authors run it. Reactor's TestPublisher (lesson 8 of this track) borrows the idea for application tests: you can create a deliberately non-compliant publisher, for example one that ignores demand, and check that your code survives it. Processor. A processor is both a subscriber and a publisher, so it can sit in the middle of a chain. Reactor used to expose processors directly. It has phased them out in favour of Sinks, which you'll meet in lesson 8 of this track.

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Flux is zero to many, Mono is zero or one
x: Reactor has two publisher types, and the type tells you how many items to expect. A Flux<T> emits zero to many items, then maybe onComplete or onError. All three are optional: a Flux with no terminal signal is infinite, like Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1)). A Mono<T> emits at most one item and then completes, or emits only an error. It can never send an item and then an error. Mono<Void> means "tell me when it's done", for example after a ledger write that returns nothing. Java Flux<String> authorizations = Flux.just("auth-1", "auth-2", "auth-3"); Flux<Integer> attempts = Flux.range(1, 3); Mono<String> fxRate = Mono.just("EURUSD=1.08"); Mono<String> nothing = Mono.empty(); Mono<String> declined = Mono.error(new IllegalStateException("card declined")); Kotlin val authorizations: Flux<String> = Flux.just("auth-1", "auth-2", "auth-3") val attempts: Flux<Int> = Flux.range(1, 3) val fxRate: Mono<String> = Mono.just("EURUSD=1.08") val nothing: Mono<String> = Mono.empty() val declined: Mono<String> = Mono.error(IllegalStateException("card declined")) Both types implement org.reactivestreams.Publisher, so everything from lesson 1 of this track applies. The split exists for readers and for operators. A method that returns Mono<Receipt> promises one receipt or none, and Mono has operators that only make sense for one value, such as Mono.zip into a tuple. Some operators change the type: mono.concatWith(other) gives a Flux, while mono.then(other) gives a Mono. The simplest way to run one is subscribe with up to three lambdas: Java authorizations.subscribe( a -> process(a), // onNext e -> log.error("stream failed", e), // onError () -> log.info("all authorizations done")); // onComplete Kotlin authorizations.subscribe( { a -> process(a) }, // onNext { e -> log.error("stream failed", e) }, // onError { log.info("all authorizations done") }) // onComplete This form requests everything (Long.MAX_VALUE). Always pass the error lambda. If you leave it out and the stream fails, Reactor does not throw to your code. It logs ErrorCallbackNotImplemented at ERROR level and your method carries on, so a test that doesn't assert on the error passes happily. The cause is rule 2.13 from lesson 1 of this track: onError must return normally, so the subscriber that subscribe builds for you can't throw. With no error lambda it hands the error to Reactor's onErrorDropped hook, and the default hook only logs it. Reactive Streams forbids null items, and Reactor 3.8 enforces it: Mono.just(null) throws a NullPointerException, and so does a map whose function returns null. Use Mono.empty() for "no value". Kotlin catches this one earlier: Reactor 3.8 publishes JSpecify nullness annotations, so a Kotlin map { if (ok) x else null } doesn't even compile ("Return type mismatch: expected 'Any', actual 'String?'"). Watch the signals go by Read FirstFluxDemo. It subscribes to a Flux of three authorizations with log() in the chain, then to a failing Mono with no error callback. Predict the order of the lines, including the log() lines. What happens to the declined card? Run it. Then add an error lambda to the second subscribe and run it again. FirstFluxDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l02; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; /** A Flux and a Mono, subscribed with the three callbacks, with log() printing every signal. */ public class FirstFluxDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Flux<String> authorizations = Flux.just("auth-1", "auth-2", "auth-3"); authorizations .log() // prints each signal that passes this point .subscribe( a -> System.out.println("got " + a), // onNext e -> System.out.println("failed: " + e), // onError () -> System.out.println("done")); // onComplete Mono<String> declined = Mono.error(new IllegalStateException("card declined")); declined.subscribe(s -> System.out.println("got " + s)); // no error callback: watch what happens System.out.println("main carries on"); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.FirstFluxDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l02/FirstFluxDemo.java FirstFluxDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l02 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono /** A Flux and a Mono, subscribed with the three callbacks, with log() printing every signal. */ fun main() { val authorizations: Flux<String> = Flux.just("auth-1", "auth-2", "auth-3") authorizations .log() // prints each signal that passes this point .subscribe( { a -> println("got $a") }, // onNext { e -> println("failed: $e") }, // onError { println("done") }) // onComplete val declined: Mono<String> = Mono.error(IllegalStateException("card declined")) declined.subscribe { s -> println("got $s") } // no error callback: watch what happens println("main carries on") } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.FirstFluxDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l02/FirstFluxDemo.kt log() prints onSubscribe, then request(unbounded), then each onNext followed by your got ... line, then onComplete() and done. The protocol from lesson 1 of this track, live. The declined card prints main carries on and an [ERROR] ... Operator called default onErrorDropped - reactor.core.Exceptions$ErrorCallbackNotImplemented log line (the two may appear in either order, since one goes to stderr). Nothing is thrown at main. With an error lambda, your lambda prints the failure and the ERROR log line is gone. Building a pipeline is writing a recipe card. Flux.range(...).map(...) is "take three numbers, multiply each by 100": no food yet. Subscribing is cooking, and with a cold publisher every guest who orders gets their own dish cooked from scratch. Mono.just(fetchRate()) is different: you cooked the dish while writing the recipe, then serve the same plate to everyone who orders, even an hour later. The analogy breaks on side effects: a kitchen never charges a customer's card just because a second waiter read the same order, but a cold Mono subscribed twice does exactly that.

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Assembly writes a recipe, subscribe cooks it
x: Here is the single most important fact about Reactor: building a pipeline runs none of your code. Java Flux<Integer> fees = Flux.range(1, 3) .map(cents -> cents * 100); // nothing has run yet fees.subscribe(System.out::println); // now range and map run Kotlin val fees: Flux<Int> = Flux.range(1, 3) .map { cents -> cents * 100 } // nothing has run yet fees.subscribe { println(it) } // now range and map run There are three separate passes, and it helps to keep them apart. Assembly. Each operator call returns a new Flux that wraps the previous one. Flux.range(1, 3).map(...) is a FluxMap object holding a FluxRange object. Your lambda is stored, not called. The Reactor docs describe this as building "an abstract description of your asynchronous process". Subscription. When you call subscribe, Reactor walks the chain backwards. Your subscriber subscribes to map, which creates its own subscriber and subscribes to range. Then request(n) travels up the same chain to the source. Data. Only now does the source emit. onNext signals flow down through each operator to your lambda, and finally onComplete or onError. Three consequences follow. Code inside an operator runs at subscription time: maybe once, maybe once per subscriber, maybe never if nobody subscribes, and possibly on another thread (lesson 6 of this track). Operators never change the object you call them on, so a dropped return value is a silent no-op: amounts.filter(a -> a > 10); on its own line does nothing at all. And a method that returns a Mono can still do work before it returns, at assembly time, which looks lazy but isn't. That last one is the subject of the final section. Count what runs, and when AssemblyDemo counts how often map runs, before and after subscribe. Then it filters a list of amounts. Predict both counts and the amounts printed. Run it. Fix the filter so only amounts above 10 print. AssemblyDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l02; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Building a pipeline runs none of it. Subscribing runs all of it. */ public class AssemblyDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { AtomicInteger mapped = new AtomicInteger(); Flux<Integer> fees = Flux.range(1, 3) .map(cents -> { mapped.incrementAndGet(); return cents * 100; }); System.out.println("after assembly: map ran " + mapped.get() + " times"); fees.subscribe(f -> System.out.println("fee " + f)); System.out.println("after subscribe: map ran " + mapped.get() + " times"); // A classic bug: the result of filter() is thrown away, so the filter is never part of the chain. Flux<Integer> amounts = Flux.just(5, 50, 500); amounts.filter(a -> a > 10); amounts.subscribe(a -> System.out.println("amount " + a)); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.AssemblyDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l02/AssemblyDemo.java AssemblyDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l02 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** Building a pipeline runs none of it. Subscribing runs all of it. */ fun main() { val mapped = AtomicInteger() val fees: Flux<Int> = Flux.range(1, 3) .map { cents -> mapped.incrementAndGet() cents * 100 } println("after assembly: map ran ${mapped.get()} times") fees.subscribe { f -> println("fee $f") } println("after subscribe: map ran ${mapped.get()} times") // A classic bug: the result of filter() is thrown away, so the filter is never part of the chain. val amounts: Flux<Int> = Flux.just(5, 50, 500) amounts.filter { a -> a > 10 } amounts.subscribe { a -> println("amount $a") } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.AssemblyDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l02/AssemblyDemo.kt after assembly: map ran 0 times, three fees, then after subscribe: map ran 3 times. All three amounts print, 5 included, because amounts.filter(...) returned a new Flux that nobody used. The fix is to subscribe to the result: amounts.filter(a -> a > 10).subscribe(...) in Java, amounts.filter { it > 10 }.subscribe { ... } in Kotlin. Three passes over the same chain: assembly runs no user code, subscription travels up, data travels down. Reactor reference: Introduction to reactive programming (source) docs Payment code is full of calls that must happen once per request and no more: issuer charges, ledger postings, Kafka sends. In a reactive client, check every place a Mono is subscribed: an explicit subscribe() for logging next to a framework that also subscribes, a block() in a test helper and another in the assertion, a retry wrapped around a Mono.just(client.call()). The same thinking applies outside Reactor. A Temporal activity is retried by the server, so it must be safe to run again. A cold Mono is the same idea in miniature: subscribing is "run it", and doing it twice runs it twice.

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Cold publishers run again for every subscriber
x: Most publishers you meet are cold: each subscriber gets its own run, from the start. Flux.range, Mono.fromCallable, an HTTP client's response Mono, a reactive database query: subscribe twice and the work happens twice. That is often what you want. The retry operator from lesson 5 of this track works by subscribing again, and a cold source gives it a fresh attempt. It also means two subscribers to an HTTP call each get their own response. It bites when you subscribe twice without meaning to. Payment code is where this hurts most: Java Mono<Receipt> charge = issuer.charge(request); // cold charge.subscribe(audit::record); // run 1: the card is charged return charge.block(); // run 2: charged again Kotlin val charge: Mono<Receipt> = issuer.charge(request) // cold charge.subscribe { audit.record(it) } // run 1: the card is charged return charge.block() // run 2: charged again block() is a subscription too: it subscribes and parks the calling thread until the value arrives. Each subscription is a separate charge at the issuer. The same thing happens when a controller subscribes to a Mono "to log it" and then returns it to a framework that subscribes again, or when a test calls block() twice on the same cold Mono. The fix is to build one chain and put the side effect inside it. doOnNext runs a side effect for each item and passes the item on unchanged: Java return issuer.charge(request) .doOnNext(audit::record) // runs once per subscription, inside the one chain .block(); Kotlin return issuer.charge(request) .doOnNext { audit.record(it) } // runs once per subscription, inside the one chain .block() If several consumers really do need the same single result, make the sharing explicit with cache() or share(). Those turn a cold publisher into a hot one that runs once and hands the result to everyone. They have sharp edges of their own, so they get lesson 8 of this track. A quick test for any Mono you didn't write: count subscriptions. Wrap it with doOnSubscribe(s -> counter.incrementAndGet()) and check the number after your code runs. The lab has you build exactly that helper. Charge a card twice by accident ColdDemo builds one charge Mono, subscribes once for an audit log and once with block() for the caller. Predict how many charges the issuer sees. Run it. Rewrite main as one chain: charge.doOnNext(r -> System.out.println("audit log: " + r)).block() in Java, or charge.doOnNext { println("audit log: $it") }.block() in Kotlin. Run it again. ColdDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l02; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** A cold Mono does its work again for every subscriber. Here the work is a card charge. */ public class ColdDemo { static final AtomicInteger charges = new AtomicInteger(); static Mono<String> charge(String paymentId) { return Mono.fromCallable(() -> { int n = charges.incrementAndGet(); System.out.println(" issuer: charging " + paymentId + " (charge #" + n + ")"); return "receipt-" + n; }); } public static void main(String[] args) { Mono<String> charge = charge("pay-42"); charge.subscribe(r -> System.out.println("audit log: " + r)); // subscriber 1 String receipt = charge.block(); // subscriber 2 System.out.println("returned to caller: " + receipt); System.out.println("charges made: " + charges.get()); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.ColdDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l02/ColdDemo.java ColdDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l02 import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private val charges = AtomicInteger() /** A cold Mono does its work again for every subscriber. h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Mono.just is eager; fromCallable and defer are lazy
x: Mono.just(x) holds a value you already have. That sounds harmless until x is a method call: Java Mono<String> rate = Mono.just(fx.fetchFxRate("EURUSD")); Kotlin val rate: Mono<String> = Mono.just(fx.fetchFxRate("EURUSD")) Java evaluates the argument before just is even called. So the remote call runs at assembly, on the caller's thread, exactly once. Every later subscriber gets the same captured value, however stale. If the call throws, the exception flies out of the method that builds the Mono, instead of arriving as onError where your error operators can see it. And a retry can never call the service again, because there is nothing to re-run. Two factory methods fix it, and they fit different shapes of work: You have Use When it runs A value already in hand Mono.just(value) at assembly, once A computation that returns a value (often blocking) Mono.fromCallable(() -> repo.find(id)) on each subscription Code that returns a Mono or reads state at subscribe time Mono.defer(() -> client.charge(sign(req))) on each subscription In Kotlin the same calls read Mono.fromCallable { repo.find(id) } and Mono.defer { client.charge(sign(req)) }. fromCallable also maps the edge cases into signals: a thrown exception becomes onError, and a null result becomes an empty Mono. Mono.fromSupplier is the same for code that throws no checked exceptions. defer is for when building the publisher itself does work: signing a request, reading Instant.now(), choosing a target from config. Wrapping it in defer moves all of that to subscription time. Watch for Mono.justOrEmpty(repo.find(id)). It handles null, but the call is still an eager argument. The same trap exists with Mono.fromFuture(cf): a CompletableFuture is already running when you pass it in, so use the Supplier overload, Mono.fromFuture(() -> client.sendAsync(req)), to start it per subscription. just, fromCallable, defer LazyDemo builds the same FX rate Mono three ways and subscribes to each twice. Before running, fill in a small table: calls at assembly and calls after two subscriptions, for each of the three. Run it and compare. Then change the defer line to use Mono.justOrEmpty(fetchFxRate()) inside the defer. Does that change anything? LazyDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l02; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Mono.just, fromCallable and defer, each subscribed twice. Count the calls. */ public class LazyDemo { static final AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); static String fetchFxRate() { calls.incrementAndGet(); return "EURUSD=1.08"; } public static void main(String[] args) { run("just", () -> Mono.just(fetchFxRate())); run("fromCallable", () -> Mono.fromCallable(LazyDemo::fetchFxRate)); run("defer", () -> Mono.defer(() -> Mono.just(fetchFxRate()))); } static void run(String name, java.util.function.Supplier<Mono<String>> build) { calls.set(0); Mono<String> rate = build.get(); int atAssembly = calls.get(); rate.block(); rate.block(); System.out.printf("%-13s calls at assembly: %d, after 2 subscriptions: %d%n", name, atAssembly, calls.get()); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.LazyDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l02/LazyDemo.java LazyDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l02 import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private val calls = AtomicInteger() private fun fetchFxRate(): String { calls.incrementAndGet() return "EURUSD=1.08" } /** Mono.just, fromCallable and defer, each subscribed twice. Count the calls. */ fun main() { run("just") { Mono.just(fetchFxRate()) } run("fromCallable") { Mono.fromCallable { fetchFxRate() } } run("defer") { Mono.defer { Mono.just(fetchFxRate()) } } } private fun run(name: String, build: () -> Mono<String>) { calls.set(0) val rate = build() val atAssembly = calls.get() rate.block() rate.block() println("%-13s calls at assembly: %d, after 2 subscriptions: %d".format(name, atAssembly, calls.get())) } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l02.LazyDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l02/LazyDemo.kt just: 1 call at assembly, still 1 after two subscriptions. fromCallable and defer: 0 at assembly, 2 after two subscriptions. justOrEmpty inside defer is still lazy, because defer delays the whole lambda, argument included. Outside defer, justOrEmpty(fetchFxRate()) would be eager like just. Reactor reference: Hot versus cold (source) docs The most common mistake is Mono.just(someCall()) where someCall() does real work: a remote call, a database read, Instant.now(), a random idempotency key. People write it because it reads like "a Mono of the result" and it passes tests that subscribe once. The call actually runs at assembly, once, on the caller's thread, and its exceptions skip your error handling. Use Mono.fromCallable(() -> someCall()) for a value, or Mono.defer(() -> ...) when the code returns a Mono.

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Java and Kotlin
x: Eager and lazy Monos in Java and Kotlin Rates.java // eager: fetchFxRate runs here, once, before just() is called Mono<Rate> eager = Mono.just(fx.fetchFxRate("EURUSD")); // lazy: the lambda runs on every subscription Mono<Rate> lazy = Mono.fromCallable(() -> fx.fetchFxRate("EURUSD")); // lazy: build a whole publisher per subscription Mono<Receipt> charge = Mono.defer(() -> issuer.charge(signer.sign(request))); Rates.kt // eager: fetchFxRate runs here, once, before just() is called val eager: Mono<Rate> = Mono.just(fx.fetchFxRate("EURUSD")) // lazy: the lambda runs on every subscription val lazy: Mono<Rate> = Mono.fromCallable { fx.fetchFxRate("EURUSD") } // lazy: build a whole publisher per subscription val charge: Mono<Receipt> = Mono.defer { issuer.charge(signer.sign(request)) } // lazy, written as a coroutine (kotlinx-coroutines-reactor): the block starts on each subscription val chargeCo: Mono<Receipt> = mono { issuer.chargeSuspending(signer.sign(request)) } The calls are the same Reactor API in both languages, and the trap is the same too, because it is plain argument evaluation: Kotlin evaluates fx.fetchFxRate("EURUSD") before Mono.just runs, exactly like Java. Kotlin's trailing lambdas make the lazy forms shorter (Mono.fromCallable { ... }), and kotlinx-coroutines-reactor adds mono { }, a cold Mono whose body is a coroutine: it starts on each subscription, and a null result gives an empty Mono. That is handy when a Kotlin service has to hand a Mono to Java code. Kotlin Flow has the same trap with different names: flowOf(call()) is eager, flow { emit(call()) } is lazy.

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Worked example
x: Make an issuer client method lazy This method signs a charge request and returns the issuer's response. It returns a Mono, so it looks lazy. Mark which lines run when charge(req) is called, and which run on subscribe. Mono<Receipt> charge(ChargeRequest req) { String nonce = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); SignedRequest signed = signer.sign(req, nonce); // HMAC with a one-time nonce log.info("charging {}", req.paymentId()); return issuerClient.send(signed); // a cold Mono: sends on subscribe } fun charge(req: ChargeRequest): Mono<Receipt> { val nonce = UUID.randomUUID().toString() val signed = signer.sign(req, nonce) // HMAC with a one-time nonce log.info("charging {}", req.paymentId) return issuerClient.send(signed) // a cold Mono: sends on subscribe } The nonce, the signature and the log line all happen at call time, once. Only the HTTP send happens on subscribe. Now add .retry(2) at the call site: each retry re-subscribes to the same send(signed) and replays the same nonce. An issuer that rejects reused nonces fails every retry with "replayed request", and the log shows one "charging" line for three attempts. Move the whole body into defer. Now every subscription, including every retry, builds a fresh nonce, signs again and logs again. Mono<Receipt> charge(ChargeRequest req) { return Mono.defer(() -> { String nonce = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); // 1. per attempt SignedRequest signed = signer.sign(req, nonce); // 2. per attempt log.info("charging {} (nonce {})", req.paymentId(), nonce); return issuerClient.send(signed); // 3. the cold call }); } fun charge(req: ChargeRequest): Mono<Receipt> = Mono.defer { val nonce = UUID.randomUUID().toString() // 1. per attempt val signed = signer.sign(req, nonce) // 2. per attempt log.info("charging {} (nonce {})", req.paymentId, nonce) issuerClient.send(signed) // 3. the cold call } Check it with a counter, the way the lab does: build the Mono, assert zero sign calls, subscribe twice, assert two. A test like this catches the next person who "simplifies" the method back to the eager version. Mono<Receipt> m = client.charge(req); assertThat(signer.calls()).isZero(); // nothing at assembly m.block(); m.block(); assertThat(signer.calls()).isEqualTo(2); // once per subscription val m = client.charge(req) assertThat(signer.calls()).isZero() // nothing at assembly m.block() m.block() assertThat(signer.calls()).isEqualTo(2) // once per subscription

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Quiz
x: What does this print? Flux<String> f = Flux.just("a", "b") .map(s -> { System.out.println("map " + s); return s.toUpperCase(); }); System.out.println("built"); map a, map b, built built only built, map a, map b Nothing Building the chain stores the lambda without calling it. Nobody subscribes to f, so map never runs and only built prints. The tempting first option is how Stream works with an eager terminal step; here there is no subscribe at all. issuer.charge(req) returns a cold Mono<Receipt> built with fromCallable. A handler does Mono<Receipt> r = issuer.charge(req); r.subscribe(audit::record); return r.block();. How many charges reach the issuer? One, because both use the same Mono object Two, one per subscription Zero, because subscribe and block cancel each other It depends on which thread runs first A cold publisher runs once per subscriber. subscribe and block are two subscriptions, so the callable runs twice. Sharing a Mono object shares the recipe, not the result. Put the audit in the chain with doOnNext, or use cache() if you really need to share a result. repo.find(id) is a blocking call that may return null. Which line gives a lazy Mono that runs the call per subscription and is empty on null? Mono.just(repo.find(id)) Mono.justOrEmpty(repo.find(id)) Flux.just(repo.find(id)).next() Mono.fromCallable(() -> repo.find(id)) fromCallable calls the lambda on each subscription and maps null to empty and exceptions to onError. justOrEmpty handles null too, but repo.find(id) is still an eager argument evaluated at assembly. Mono.just(null) would throw. You subscribe to Mono.error(new IllegalStateException("declined")) with only an onNext lambda. What happens? The exception is thrown out of subscribe to your code Reactor logs ErrorCallbackNotImplemented at ERROR level, and your code carries on Nothing at all: errors without a handler are ignored silently The JVM prints a stack trace and exits Without an error callback, Reactor routes the error to its onErrorDropped hook, which logs it at ERROR level. Your thread is not interrupted. That is why a test with no assertion on the error can pass even though the stream failed. From "Why reactive: push, pull and backpressure": you call flux.subscribe(item -> process(item)) with just the one lambda. What demand does that subscriber signal to the source? request(1) before each item request(256), then more in batches request(Long.MAX_VALUE): unbounded No request until the first item arrives The lambda form of subscribe requests everything, which the log() output shows as request(unbounded). That is rule 3.17's "effectively unbounded" demand: no backpressure from this subscriber. Lesson 7 of this track shows how operators like limitRate turn it back into bounded requests.

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Key terms
x: Flux A Reactor publisher of 0 to N items, optionally ending with complete or error. Mono A Reactor publisher of at most one item. Mono<Void> only signals completion or error. Assembly time When you call operators to build the chain. Only wrapper objects are created; none of your lambdas run. Subscription time When subscribe (or block) is called. The chain is linked up, demand goes up, and the source starts. Cold publisher A publisher that does its work again for each subscriber. Hot publisher A publisher that runs once and shares its items with whoever is subscribed. Lesson 8 of this track. Operator A method like map or filter that wraps a publisher and returns a new one. When does the lambda inside flux.map(...) run? At subscription time, once per item for each subscriber. Never at assembly, and never if nobody subscribes. Mono.just(fetch()) is subscribed three times. How many times does fetch() run? Once, at assembly, before just is even called. All three subscribers get the same value. What does Mono.fromCallable do with a thrown exception and with a null result? The exception becomes onError. null becomes an empty Mono (just onComplete). What is a cold publisher? One that does its work again, from the start, for every subscriber. Most Reactor sources are cold. amounts.filter(a -> a > 10); on its own line, then amounts.subscribe(...). Is anything filtered? No. Operators return a new Flux. The filtered one was thrown away, so amounts is unchanged. When do you pick Mono.defer over Mono.fromCallable? When the code returns a Mono (or other publisher), or must read state at subscription time, such as a nonce or Instant.now().

h: Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe · Go deeper
x: Two more eager traps look like the Mono.just one. Flux.fromStream(stream). A Java Stream can only be consumed once. The first subscriber drains it, and the second gets IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Use the supplier overload, Flux.fromStream(() -> repo.streamRows()), so each subscription gets a fresh stream. (Flux.fromIterable(list) is fine to subscribe many times, because a List can be iterated again.) Mono.fromFuture(future). A CompletableFuture represents work that has already started. Mono.fromFuture(client.sendAsync(req)) sends the request at assembly, and a retry re-subscribes to the same finished future. Mono.fromFuture(() -> client.sendAsync(req)) starts a new request for each subscription. This is the bridge you'll use most from code built with the executors track's CompletableFuture APIs. There is also a distinction between Mono.fromCallable and Mono.fromSupplier: the first accepts code that throws checked exceptions (a Callable may throw Exception), the second does not. Both are lazy and both treat null as empty. Finally, a word on block(). It subscribes, waits on the calling thread, and returns the value (or null for an empty Mono, or throws the error). It is the right tool at the edge of reactive code: a main method, a test, a blocking framework calling into a reactive client. Lesson 6 of this track explains why it throws on some Reactor threads, and why calling it in the middle of a pipeline defeats the point.

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · map and filter work one item at a time
x: map and filter are the operators you already know from java.util.stream, with one difference: they run when items arrive, not when you call them. map(f) is one item in, one item out, synchronously, on whatever thread delivered the item. Use it for pure, fast transformations: parse a message, convert cents to a Money, compute a fee. filter(p) keeps the items that match. It also takes care of demand for you: a dropped item doesn't use up the downstream's request, so the source is asked for more. In the Try it below, take(2) asks for 2 items, yet the source runs through 1 to 6 to find two that pass the filter. The most common map bug looks like this: Java Flux<Mono<String>> statuses = paymentIds.map(id -> issuer.fetchStatus(id)); // returns Mono<String> Kotlin val statuses: Flux<Mono<String>> = paymentIds.map { id -> issuer.fetchStatus(id) } // returns Mono<String> The function returns a Mono, so map gives you a Flux<Mono<String>>: a stream of recipes. Nothing subscribes to the inner Monos, so not one issuer call is made. The compiler is happy, the tests that only count items are happy, and the statuses are never fetched. When your function returns a publisher, you need one of the flattening operators below. The type checker is your friend here: if you see Flux<Mono<T>>, you used map where you needed flatMap. Two smaller rules. In Reactor 3.8 a map function may not return null; in Java the stream fails with NullPointerException: The mapper [...] returned a null value., and in Kotlin the null-returning lambda doesn't compile, thanks to Reactor's JSpecify annotations. Filter first, or use handle, which works like a map that may emit zero or one item for each input, so it can skip the inputs that have no value. And map must stay fast and non-blocking, because it runs inline on the delivering thread. A JDBC call inside map blocks that thread for every item. Lesson 6 of this track shows where blocking calls belong. Count the demand a filter sends MapFilterDemo filters the numbers 1 to 10 down to multiples of 3, maps them to amounts, and takes 2. A doOnRequest prints what the source is asked for. Predict how many requests the source sees and which amounts print. In Java, predict what the second pipeline does with the null; in Kotlin, read the comment that says why that line can't be written. Run it. Then change take(2) to take(4) and run again. MapFilterDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l03; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; /** map and filter are synchronous and work one item at a time. Watch the demand they send upstream. */ public class MapFilterDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Flux.range(1, 10) .doOnRequest(n -> System.out.println(" source asked for " + n)) .filter(amount -> amount % 3 == 0) // drops 1, 2, 4, 5, ... .map(amount -> "EUR " + amount * 10) .take(2) // we only want two .subscribe(s -> System.out.println("got " + s)); // Reactor 3.8: a mapper may not return null Flux.just("4111", "5500") .map(bin -> bin.startsWith("4") ? "VISA" : null) .subscribe(s -> System.out.println("scheme " + s), e -> System.out.println("error: " + e)); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.MapFilterDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l03/MapFilterDemo.java MapFilterDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l03 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux /** map and filter are synchronous and work one item at a time. Watch the demand they send upstream. */ fun main() { Flux.range(1, 10) .doOnRequest { n -> println(" source asked for $n") } .filter { amount -> amount % 3 == 0 } // drops 1, 2, 4, 5, ... .map { amount -> "EUR ${amount * 10}" } .take(2) // we only want two .subscribe { s -> println("got $s") } // Reactor 3.8 marks its API with JSpecify nullness, so in Kotlin a null-returning mapper doesn't compile: // .map { bin -> if (bin.startsWith("4")) "VISA" else null } // error: Return type mismatch: expected 'Any', actual 'String?'. // handle() is a map and a filter in one: emit when you have a value, skip otherwise. Flux.just("4111", "5500") .handle<String> { bin, sink -> if (bin.startsWith("4")) sink.next("VISA") } .subscribe({ s -> println("scheme $s") }, { e -> println("error: $e") }) } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.MapFilterDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l03/MapFilterDemo.kt The source is asked for 2 once, yet it emits 1 to 6, because filter tells it which items didn't count. You get EUR 30 and EUR 60. The Java version's second pipeline prints scheme VISA, then error: java.lang.NullPointerException: The mapper [...] returned a null value.. The Kotlin version uses handle, so it prints only scheme VISA: the null case was caught by the compiler instead. With take(4) the source is asked for 4 and runs to 10, but only three multiples of 3 exist, so you get three amounts and the stream completes. Think of a kitchen pass during a rush. flatMap is several cooks working different orders at once; plates go out as they're ready, so table 7 may get food before table 3. concatMap is one cook doing one order start to finish before reading the next ticket. flatMapSequential is several cooks, but the waiter holds finished plates until every earlier table has been served. switchMap is a customer who keeps changing their order: the cook bins the half-made dish each time. The analogy breaks on cancellation: a cook can stop at once, but a cancelled reactive call only promises you stop listening. The remote service may still finish the work.

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · flatMap subscribes to many inners at once
x: flatMap emits in completion order; concatMap and flatMapSequential keep input order flatMap(f) takes a function that returns a publisher, the inner, and does three things with it: For each source item it calls f and subscribes to the inner right away, without waiting for earlier inners to finish. It keeps up to concurrency inners subscribed at once. The default is 256. It merges all their items into one output, in the order they arrive. So the output order follows completion time, not input order. Its Javadoc says flatMap "does not necessarily preserve original ordering", and with real network calls it almost never does. Two facts about flatMap surprise people. First, flatMap does not create threads. If the inner is synchronous, such as Mono.fromCallable with no scheduler, the inners run one after another on the calling thread. The concurrency comes from inners that are themselves asynchronous: a non-blocking HTTP call, a Mono.delay, or a blocking call moved to another scheduler with subscribeOn (lesson 6 of this track). flatMap only subscribes to several of them before the first one finishes. Second, concurrency is also demand. flatMap(f, 4) asks the source for 4 items, then for 1 more each time an inner completes. That makes the concurrency argument a cap on in-flight calls: Java Flux<Score> scores = paymentIds.flatMap(id -> fraud.score(id), 4); // at most 4 calls at once Kotlin // the lambda stays inside the parentheses when another argument follows it val scores: Flux<Score> = paymentIds.flatMap({ id -> fraud.score(id) }, 4) // at most 4 calls at once Set it whenever the inner touches something shared. The default of 256 means up to 256 simultaneous calls to the fraud service, or 256 queries waiting on a connection pool of 20. Pick the number from the downstream's limit, not from a feeling. Each inner also gets a prefetch of 32: if an inner is a Flux, flatMap requests 32 items from it at a time. That rarely matters for Mono inners. One more behaviour to know now: if any inner fails, flatMap cancels the others and the whole stream fails. Lesson 5 of this track shows how to contain an error inside one inner. Where does flatMap's concurrency come from? FlatMapThreadsDemo runs flatMap with synchronous inners, then with Mono.delay inners, printing the thread for each result. Then it prints what flatMap and concatMap ask the source for. Predict the threads and the order in parts 1 and 2. Predict the request numbers in part 3. Run it. Then change part 3's concurrency from 2 to 3 and predict the new request line. h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Putting the order back: concatMap and flatMapSequential
x: When order matters, you have two choices with very different costs. concatMap(f) subscribes to one inner at a time. It asks the source for one item, waits for that item's inner to complete, then asks for the next. Output order is input order, and the total time is the sum of all the inner times. In Reactor 3.8 it does no prefetching on the source at all. flatMapSequential(f) subscribes to inners eagerly, like flatMap (concurrency 256, prefetch 32), but it holds back results from later inners until all earlier inners have finished. Output order is input order, and the total time is about the time of the slowest inner. The cost is memory, since results that finish early wait in a buffer, and head-of-line blocking: one slow first call holds back everything behind it. Here are the three on the same input, measured with virtual time (a test clock that skips the waits, lesson 8 of this track). The source emits 3, 1, 2 at once, and item i takes i x 100 ms: Operator Output Done at flatMap [1, 2, 3] 300 ms concatMap [3, 1, 2] 600 ms flatMapSequential [3, 1, 2] 300 ms Ordered output is not the only reason to pick concatMap. Pick it when each step must start after the previous one has finished. Ledger postings for one account are the classic case: posting 2 may only go out after posting 1 is acknowledged, because the ledger checks the balance, and after a failed posting nothing else may be sent. flatMapSequential gives you the right order in the output while sending all four postings at once, which is exactly what the ledger must not see. A short guide: You need Use Independent calls, any order flatMap(f, n) Output in input order, calls may overlap flatMapSequential(f, n) One at a time, each after the previous concatMap(f) Only the latest item matters switchMap(f) Measure the three operators OrderingDemo runs the source 3, 1, 2 through all three operators with real delays. Write down your prediction for each output and time, then run it. Change the source to Flux.just(1, 2, 3). Which operator's output changes, and which timing changes? Item i takes i x 100 ms. Same input, three operators. */ public class OrderingDemo { static Mono<Integer> slowCall(int i) { return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(i * 100L)).thenReturn(i); } public static void main(String[] args) { Flux.just(1).flatMap(i -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(1))).blockLast(); // warm up, so timings are fair run("flatMap ", src -> src.flatMap(OrderingDemo::slowCall)); run("concatMap ", src -> src.concatMap(OrderingDemo::slowCall)); run("flatMapSequential", src -> src.flatMapSequential(OrderingDemo::slowCall)); } static void run(String name, Function<Flux<Integer>, Flux<Integer>> operator) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); var out = operator.apply(Flux.just(3, 1, 2)).collectList().block(); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%s -> %s in about %d ms%n", name, out, Math.round(ms / 100.0) * 100); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.OrderingDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l03/OrderingDemo.java OrderingDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l03 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.time.Duration import kotlin.math.roundToLong private fun slowCall(i: Int): Mono<Int> = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(i * 100L)).thenReturn(i) /** Source 3, 1, 2. Item i takes i x 100 ms. With source 1, 2, 3 all three print [1, 2, 3]: the input order now matches the finishing order, so flatMap looks ordered. That is why order bugs hide in tests with uniform delays. concatMap still takes 600 ms, and the others still take 300 ms. The same three calls through three operators. Only flatMapSequential is both ordered and fast, and it pays with a buffer.

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · When only the latest matters: switchMap
x: switchMap(f) is for streams where a new item makes the old work pointless. Each time the source emits, switchMap cancels the inner for the previous item and subscribes to a new one. The checkout page is the payments example. The user picks EUR, then GBP 50 ms later. The quote for EUR is still in flight. With flatMap, both quotes eventually arrive, and if the EUR quote is slower, it arrives last and overwrites the GBP one on screen. That is a race with a real cost: the customer sees a price for the wrong currency. With switchMap, the EUR quote is cancelled the moment GBP is picked, and its result can never reach you. Java Flux<Quote> quotes = currencyPicks.switchMap(ccy -> fx.quote(ccy)); Kotlin val quotes: Flux<Quote> = currencyPicks.switchMap { ccy -> fx.quote(ccy) } Cancellation travels upstream through the inner, so a reactive HTTP client can abort the request it was making, and a Flux.interval inside stops ticking. Whether the far side stops its work depends on that service; cancelling only promises that you stop listening. Some details. switchMap requests an unbounded amount from its source, so it applies no backpressure upstream: every pick is seen, and older ones are simply dropped by cancelling. The stream completes when the source has completed and the last inner has completed. Search-as-you-type, "recompute when the config changes" and "show the latest balance" all have this shape. Kotlin Flow has the same operator under a different name: flatMapLatest, and mapLatest when the block returns a single value. The comparison below says how the other three map onto Flow. Cancel a stale lookup SwitchMapDemo simulates a user typing a card prefix: 41 at 100 ms, then 4111 at 200 ms. Each prefix starts a lookup that streams a suggestion every 60 ms, three in total. Predict which suggestions are shown, and when the first lookup is cancelled. Run it. Replace switchMap with flatMap and run it again. SwitchMapDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l03; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import java.time.Duration; /** Card number lookup as the user types: each new prefix cancels the lookup for the previous one. */ public class SwitchMapDemo { // a lookup that streams up to three suggestions, one every 60 ms static Flux<String> suggestions(String prefix) { return Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(60)) .map(n -> prefix + "-match" + n) .take(3) .doOnCancel(() -> System.out.println(" cancelled lookup for " + prefix)); } public static void main(String[] args) { Flux<String> typed = Flux.just("41", "4111").delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(100)); // at 100 ms and 200 ms var shown = typed .switchMap(SwitchMapDemo::suggestions) .doOnNext(s -> System.out.println("show " + s)) .collectList() .block(); System.out.println("all shown: " + shown); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.SwitchMapDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l03/SwitchMapDemo.java SwitchMapDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l03 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import java.time.Duration // a lookup that streams up to three suggestions, one every 60 ms private fun suggestions(prefix: String): Flux<String> = Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(60)) .map { n -> "$prefix-match$n" } .take(3) .doOnCancel { println(" cancelled lookup for $prefix") } /** Card number lookup as the user types: each new prefix cancels the lookup for the previous one. */ fun main() { val typed = Flux.just("41", "4111").delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(100)) // at 100 ms and 200 ms val shown = typed .switchMap { prefix -> suggestions(prefix) } .doOnNext { s -> println("show $s") } .collectList() .block() println("all shown: $shown") } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.SwitchMapDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l03/SwitchMapDemo.kt You see show 41-match0 (at 160 ms), then cancelled lookup for 41 when 4111 arrives at 200 ms, then the three 4111 suggestions: [41-match0, 4111-match0, 4111-match1, 4111-match2]. With flatMap nothing is cancelled, and the two lookups interleave: 41-match1 and 41-match2 show up between the 4111 suggestions, which is the stale-result race switchMap prevents. Kotlin docs: Asynchronous Flow (flattening flows) docs The most common mistake is reaching for plain flatMap for everything. It compiles, the tests pass with uniform fake delays, and in production two things go wrong. Order breaks: ledger postings or payment state changes arrive out of order as soon as latencies vary. And concurrency explodes: 256 simultaneous calls hit a service sized for 20. Decide on purpose: does order matter, must each call wait for the previous one, and what is the downstream's concurrency limit?

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Java and Kotlin
x: The four flattening operators in Java and Kotlin PaymentFlows.java // any order, at most 4 fraud calls in flight Flux<String> scores = paymentIds.flatMap(id -> fraud.score(id), 4); // one at a time, each after the previous one completes Flux<String> acks = postings.concatMap(p -> ledger.post(p)); // overlapping calls, output in input order Flux<String> rows = ids.flatMapSequential(id -> settlement.row(id), 4); // latest wins: a new pick cancels the previous quote Flux<String> quotes = picks.switchMap(ccy -> fx.quote(ccy)); PaymentFlows.kt // any order, at most 4 fraud calls in flight val scores = paymentIds.flatMap({ id -> fraud.score(id) }, 4) // one at a time, each after the previous one completes val acks = postings.concatMap { p -> ledger.post(p) } // overlapping calls, output in input order val rows = ids.flatMapSequential({ id -> settlement.row(id) }, 4) // latest wins: a new pick cancels the previous quote val quotes = picks.switchMap { ccy -> fx.quote(ccy) } Same operators, two syntax details. In Kotlin a lambda can only trail outside the parentheses when it is the last argument, so flatMap({ ... }, 4) keeps it inside. And Kotlin lambdas adapt to Reactor's Function<? super T, Publisher<? extends V>> parameter without fuss, so the switchMap typing problem the lab hints at in Java doesn't arise. The bigger difference is with Kotlin's own streams. In Kotlin Flow the default is sequential: a suspending map waits for each call, so it behaves like concatMap, and you opt in to concurrency with flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4), whose default is 16 rather than Reactor's 256. flatMapLatest and mapLatest are Flow's switchMap, and there is no flatMapSequential. In kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 those Flow operators still need @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class). FlowOperators.kt in the demo folder runs the same 3, 1, 2 example with Flow (-Pmain=workbench.reactive.l03.FlowOperatorsKt).

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Worked example
x: Fix a settlement job that floods the issuer A nightly job fetches the settlement status of every payment from the card issuer. The issuer's contract allows 10 concurrent calls per merchant. Last night the job got hundreds of 429 Too Many Requests responses. Read the pipeline. Flux<SettlementRow> report(Flux<String> paymentIds) { return paymentIds .flatMap(id -> issuer.settlementStatus(id)) // Mono<Status>, about 120 ms .map(SettlementRow::from); } fun report(paymentIds: Flux<String>): Flux<SettlementRow> = paymentIds .flatMap { id -> issuer.settlementStatus(id) } // Mono<Status>, about 120 ms .map { SettlementRow.from(it) } flatMap with no concurrency argument subscribes to up to 256 inners at once, and its first request to the source is 256. With 50,000 payment ids, the job keeps about 256 calls in flight the whole time. The issuer allows 10. Cap the in-flight calls at the contract's limit. By Little's law, 10 calls in flight at 120 ms each gives at most 10 / 0.12 s, about 83 calls a second, so 50,000 payments take about 10 minutes. That's the honest throughput of this contract. return paymentIds .flatMap(id -> issuer.settlementStatus(id), 10) // 1. never more than 10 in flight .map(SettlementRow::from); paymentIds .flatMap({ id -> issuer.settlementStatus(id) }, 10) // 1. never more than 10 in flight .map { SettlementRow.from(it) } The finance team then asks for the report in input order, so it diffs cleanly against yesterday's. Switching to concatMap would cut throughput to one call at a time, about 8 a second. flatMapSequential keeps the cap of 10 and restores the order, at the cost of buffering results that finish early. return paymentIds .flatMapSequential(id -> issuer.settlementStatus(id), 10) // 2. same cap, input order .map(SettlementRow::from); paymentIds .flatMapSequential({ id -> issuer.settlementStatus(id) }, 10) // 2. same cap, input order .map { SettlementRow.from(it) }

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Quiz
x: You need to enrich 10,000 transactions with merchant data. The merchant service allows 20 concurrent calls, and the output order doesn't matter. Which line fits? tx.map(t -> merchants.lookup(t)) tx.concatMap(t -> merchants.lookup(t)) tx.flatMap(t -> merchants.lookup(t), 20) tx.switchMap(t -> merchants.lookup(t)) flatMap with concurrency 20 keeps exactly as many calls in flight as the service allows. map would produce a Flux<Mono<...>> and make no calls. concatMap is correct but makes one call at a time, and switchMap would cancel all but the last lookup. issuer.fetchStatus(id) returns Mono<String>. What happens when you subscribe to ids.map(id -> issuer.fetchStatus(id))? Each status is fetched, one at a time You receive one Mono<String> per id, and no issuer call is made unless something subscribes to those Monos It doesn't compile All statuses are fetched in parallel map wraps each returned Mono as an item, giving Flux<Mono<String>>. A Mono is a recipe; nobody subscribes to these, so nothing runs. flatMap (or concatMap) is what subscribes to the inner publishers. Postings for one account must reach the ledger one at a time, each after the previous one is acknowledged. A teammate proposes flatMapSequential because "it keeps the order". What is wrong with that? Nothing, it is the right choice It sends all postings concurrently and only reorders the results It drops postings that finish out of order It cannot handle errors flatMapSequential subscribes to inners eagerly, so the ledger sees all postings at once. Only the output is reordered. concatMap is the operator that waits for each inner to complete before subscribing to the next. A switchMap inner is still running when the source emits a new item. What happens to that inner? It is cancelled, and its results never reach the output It finishes, and its results are emitted after the new inner's It is paused until the new inner completes switchMap waits for it before starting the new inner switchMap cancels the current inner and switches to a new one for each source item. That prevents a stale slow result from overwriting a newer one, which is what can happen with flatMap. From "CompletableFuture: composing async steps": which CompletableFuture method plays the same role as Reactor's flatMap for one async step? thenApply thenAccept thenCombine thenCompose thenCompose takes a function that returns another CompletableFuture and flattens it, just as flatMap subscribes to the publisher your function returns. thenApply is like map: given a function that returns a future, it produces a CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<T>>.

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Key terms
x: Inner publisher The Mono or Flux your function returns inside flatMap, concatMap or switchMap. Flattening Subscribing to inner publishers and merging their items into one output stream. Concurrency (flatMap) The maximum number of inners flatMap keeps subscribed at once, and its first request upstream. Prefetch How many items an operator requests ahead from a source so they are ready when needed. Head-of-line blocking One slow item at the front holds back items behind it that are already done. Virtual time A fake clock in tests (StepVerifier.withVirtualTime) that you move forward by hand, so delays take no real time. What is flatMap's default concurrency in Reactor? 256 inners at once (and a prefetch of 32 per inner). Its first request to the source is also 256. flatMap(f, 4): what does it request from the source? 4 at first, then 1 more each time an inner completes. So at most 4 inners are in flight. Does flatMap run inners on several threads? No. It only subscribes to several at once. Parallelism comes from inners that are themselves asynchronous (non-blocking IO, Mono.delay, subscribeOn). Source 3, 1, 2; item i takes i x 100 ms. Output of concatMap, and when does it finish? [3, 1, 2] at 600 ms: one at a time, in order. What does flatMapSequential trade for ordered output at flatMap speed? Memory: results that finish early are buffered until all earlier inners are done (and a slow first item holds back the rest). When does switchMap cancel an inner? As soon as the source emits a new item. Only the latest item's inner is kept. Kotlin Flow equivalent of Reactor's switchMap? flatMapLatest, or mapLatest when the block returns one value.

h: Transforming streams: map, flatMap, concatMap · Go deeper
x: Ordering per key with concurrency across keys. Postings must be ordered per account, but different accounts can be posted in parallel. The usual shape is groupBy plus concatMap inside a flatMap: Java postings.groupBy(Posting::accountId) .flatMap(account -> account.concatMap(ledger::post), 512) Kotlin postings.groupBy { it.accountId } .flatMap({ account -> account.concatMap { ledger.post(it) } }, 512) There is a trap. Each group stays open until the source completes, and flatMap only drains as many groups as its concurrency allows. The groupBy Javadoc says the concurrency of the subscriber "should be greater than or equal to the number of groups created". In a measured run, Flux.range(0, 1000).groupBy(i -> i % 300).flatMap(g -> g.reduce(0, Integer::sum), 10) simply hung; with concurrency 300 it completed. If the number of accounts is unbounded, partition by accountId.hashCode() % 32 instead and use concurrency 32, which is how a Kafka topic does it. Delaying errors. By default an error in any inner ends the whole stream. flatMapDelayError(f, concurrency, prefetch) and concatMapDelayError(f) let the other inners finish and report the error at the end. Use them for batch jobs where partial results are still useful, then decide what to do with the error. flatMapIterable. When your function returns a List (already in memory), flatMapIterable(order -> order.lines()) flattens it without creating inner publishers. handle. handle((item, sink) -> { if (ok(item)) sink.next(convert(item)); }) is a map and a filter in one step, and it lets you skip an item instead of returning null.

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Pairing by position: zip and Mono.zip
x: Flux.zip(a, b) waits until every source has emitted one item, combines those items, and repeats. It pairs by position: first with first, second with second. It completes as soon as any source completes, so the extra items of a longer source are dropped. Flux.zip(Flux.just(1, 2, 3), Flux.just("a", "b")) gives [[1,a], [2,b]], and the 3 is never used. In service code you'll use Mono.zip far more often, for fan-out: run several independent calls at once and combine the results. Java Mono<Quote> quote = Mono.zip(fx.rate("EURUSD"), fees.forMerchant(m), limits.forCustomer(c)) .map(t -> new Quote(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())); Kotlin val quote: Mono<Quote> = Mono.zip(fx.rate("EURUSD"), fees.forMerchant(m), limits.forCustomer(c)) .map { t -> Quote(t.t1, t.t2, t.t3) } Mono.zip subscribes to all of its sources immediately. If the FX rate takes 100 ms, the fee schedule 300 ms and the limit 200 ms, the quote is ready after 300 ms, not 600. There are typed overloads for up to eight sources (Tuple2 to Tuple8). If any source fails, the zip fails and cancels the others. That is usually what you want. The surprise is the other terminal signal. The Mono.zip Javadoc says it plainly: an "empty completion of any source will cause other sources to be cancelled and the resulting Mono to immediately ... complete". No error, no value. A customer with no limit configured makes the whole quote complete empty. A controller turns that into an empty 200 response, block() returns null, and the logs show nothing at all. Decide what "empty" means for each source and say it in code. Either it is an error: Java limits.forCustomer(c) .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(() -> new IllegalStateException("missing limit"))) Kotlin limits.forCustomer(c) .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error { IllegalStateException("missing limit") }) or it has a sensible default, such as fees.forMerchant(m).defaultIfEmpty(BigDecimal.ZERO). A Mono<Void> is always empty, so it can never take part in a zip; the last section shows the tool for that. Watch a quote disappear ZipDemo zips two Fluxes of different lengths, then zips three Monos where the limit is empty, then does it again with switchIfEmpty on the limit. Predict each line, including whether the slow FX call finishes or is cancelled. Run it. Then change the empty limit to Mono.just("500") and predict how long the zip takes. ZipDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l04; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; /** zip pairs by position. Mono Javadoc source, reactor-core 3.8.x (zip, zipDelayError, when, firstWithValue) docs Think of four ways to serve a table. merge brings each dish out the moment it is ready, from any cook. concat serves all the starters before the kitchen even begins the mains. zip waits until it has one plate from each of three cooks and carries them out together, and if one cook has nothing to make, no tray goes out at all. combineLatest is the drinks board above the bar: whenever any price changes, the whole board is redrawn with the newest prices. h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Interleave or take turns: merge and concat
x: Flux.merge(a, b) subscribes to every source at once and passes items on as they arrive, from whichever source has one. The output order is arrival order. It completes when all sources have completed, and by default the first error from any source ends it and cancels the rest. Flux.concat(a, b) subscribes to b only after a has completed. The output is all of a, then all of b. That makes it the right tool when the second source must not start early: settled entries before pending ones, cached rows before fresh ones, the first page before the rest. Java Flux<String> feed = Flux.merge(cardEvents, bankEvents); // both at once, as they arrive Flux<String> statement = Flux.concat(settled, pending); // pending only after settled completes Kotlin val feed: Flux<String> = Flux.merge(cardEvents, bankEvents) // both at once, as they arrive val statement: Flux<String> = Flux.concat(settled, pending) // pending only after settled completes The trap with concat is a first source that never completes. A live Kafka stream of card events never sends onComplete, so Flux.concat(cardEvents, bankEvents) never subscribes to the bank events at all. If the inputs are endless, you want merge. Flux.mergeSequential(a, b) sits in between. It subscribes to all sources at once, like merge, but emits them source by source, like concat, buffering what arrives early. It is the combining twin of flatMapSequential from lesson 3 of this track. Here are the three on the same inputs: card events at 30, 60 and 90 ms, bank events at 40, 80 and 120 ms. Operator Output Done at merge card-0, bank-0, card-1, bank-1, card-2, bank-2 120 ms concat card-0, card-1, card-2, bank-0, bank-1, bank-2 210 ms (bank starts at 90) mergeSequential card-0, card-1, card-2, bank-0, bank-1, bank-2 120 ms concat is late because the bank source starts its own 40 ms clock only when it is subscribed, at 90 ms. mergeSequential received bank-0 and bank-1 early, held them while the card events went out, and released both the moment the card source completed. Three ways to join two feeds MergeConcatDemo builds card events every 30 ms and bank events every 40 ms, three of each, and prints when each source is subscribed. For each combinator, predict when the bank source is subscribed, the output order and the total time. Run it. Then remove .take(3) from card() and predict what concat does. (Put it back afterwards; that run never ends, so stop it with Ctrl+C.) Timings drift by a few milliseconds, more on a busy machine. With an endless card source, concat prints card events forever and never subscribes to bank. The same two sources through three combinators. concat starts the bank source late; mergeSequential starts it early, holds b0 and b1 back, and releases them when the card source completes at 90 ms. A checkout or authorization service fans out constantly: FX rate, merchant fees, customer limits, a fraud score, all independent. Mono.zip keeps that fan-out at the speed of the slowest call, and the empty rule decides whether a misconfigured merchant becomes a clear error or a silent empty response. An operations dashboard that shows card events and bank callbacks in one feed is merge. A statement that lists settled entries before running the expensive pending query is concat. An exposure figure that must follow both the position and the FX rate is combineLatest.

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Recompute on every change: combineLatest
x: Flux.combineLatest(a, b, f) waits until every source has emitted at least once. After that, each new item from any source is combined with the most recent item from each of the others. Its Javadoc warns that elements "can and will be passed to the combinator multiple times", because the latest value stays in use until it is replaced. That is the shape of a derived value that must track several inputs. A customer's spending limit is stored in EUR, the checkout shows USD, and the EUR/USD rate moves: Java Flux<BigDecimal> usdLimit = Flux.combineLatest(limitsInEur, eurUsdRates, BigDecimal::multiply); Flux<Payment> inUsd = payments.withLatestFrom(eurUsdRates, Payment::convertedAt); // only payments trigger Kotlin val usdLimit: Flux<BigDecimal> = Flux.combineLatest(limitsInEur, eurUsdRates) { limit, rate -> limit.multiply(rate) } val inUsd: Flux<Payment> = payments.withLatestFrom(eurUsdRates) { p, rate -> p.convertedAt(rate) } // only payments trigger Compare it with zip on the same timeline. The limit is 1000 at 0 ms and 2000 at 300 ms. The rate is 1.10 at 100 ms, 1.20 at 200 ms and 1.15 at 400 ms. Operator Output zip 1100, 2400 combineLatest 1100, 1200, 2400, 2300 zip pairs the second limit with the second rate, so 2000 is multiplied by 1.20 even though 1.15 is the current rate by the end, and the rate change at 200 ms is never shown. combineLatest shows every state the inputs pass through. Two details. combineLatest stays silent until every source has emitted once, so an input that might never emit needs a starting value (rates.startWith(defaultRate)). And when only one side should trigger output, use withLatestFrom from the second line above: each payment is converted with the rate that is current when the payment arrives, and a rate change on its own emits nothing. zip versus combineLatest CombineLatestDemo multiplies a EUR limit by a EUR/USD rate with zip and with combineLatest, on the timeline from the section. Write down both outputs before you run it. Run it. Then swap combineLatest for limits().withLatestFrom(rates(), ...) (keep the multiply) and predict the output. } static Flux<BigDecimal> rates() { // 1.10 at 100 ms, 1.20 at 200 ms, 1.15 at 400 ms return Flux.just("1.10", "1.20", "1.15").map(BigDecimal::new) .zipWith(Flux.just(100L, 100L, 200L), (rate, wait) -> Mono.just(rate).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(wait))) .concatMap(m -> m);
