h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Choosing a combinator, and what errors do
x: Most combining questions come down to this table: You want Use One result from several independent calls Mono.zip, with switchIfEmpty or defaultIfEmpty on each source Items from several streams, as they arrive Flux.merge One stream after another, the next one started late Flux.concat Several streams started together, output stream by stream Flux.mergeSequential Item-by-item pairs Flux.zip A value recomputed from the latest of every input Flux.combineLatest Each item of one stream, enriched with the latest of another withLatestFrom Wait for several side effects that return Mono<Void> Mono.when The first of several sources to produce a value Mono.firstWithValue Mono.when(a, b) exists because Mono.zip and Mono<Void> don't mix: a Mono<Void> always completes empty, so zipping it completes the whole zip empty. Mono.when(ledger.write(a), audit.write(b)).then(Mono.just(receipt)) waits for both writes and then carries on. Mono.firstWithValue(providerA.rate(ccy), providerB.rate(ccy)) subscribes to both FX providers and takes the first rate that arrives, cancelling the slower call. Empty sources are skipped. That is the hedged-request pattern: it trades extra load for lower tail latency, so keep it for calls that are cheap for the other side. Every combinator in the table fails fast: the first error cancels the other sources. Each has a DelayError variant (Mono.zipDelayError, Flux.mergeDelayError, Flux.concatDelayError) that lets the other sources finish and reports the error at the end. Use those when partial work is still useful, such as a batch job that should process every file before reporting the bad one. The DelayError versions treat empty differently too: Mono.zipDelayError waits for the other sources to finish before it completes empty, instead of cancelling them. If a combinator surprises you, check two things: when does it subscribe to each source (all at once, or one after another), and what does it do when one source completes early or empty. Those two answers explain every row of the table. Quick check: Mono.zip(ledger.write(entry), fx.rate("EURUSD")), where the write is a Mono<Void> that completes after 20 ms and the rate takes 100 ms. What does the zip emit, when, and what happens to the rate call? (It completes empty at about 20 ms, because the write completed with no value, and it cancels the rate call that is still in flight. ledger.write(entry).then(fx.rate("EURUSD")) gives you the rate after the write.) Flux Javadoc source, reactor-core 3.8.x (merge, concat, mergeSequential, combineLatest, zip) docs The most common mistake is using Mono.zip without deciding what an empty source means. It works in every test that stubs all calls with values. In production one lookup returns nothing (a merchant without a fee schedule, a customer without a limit), and the whole result completes empty with no error and no log line. Put switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(...)) or defaultIfEmpty(...) on each source that can be empty, and add a test for the empty case.

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Java and Kotlin
x: Fan-out with Mono.zip and Mono.when in Java and Kotlin Checkout.java // three calls at once; ready when the slowest one is Mono<Quote> quote = Mono.zip( fx.rate("EURUSD").switchIfEmpty(missing("fx rate")), fees.forMerchant(m).defaultIfEmpty(BigDecimal.ZERO), limits.forCustomer(c).switchIfEmpty(missing("limit"))) .map(t -> new Quote(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())); // three side effects that return Mono<Void>: zip would complete empty Mono<Receipt> done = Mono.when(ledger.write(entry), audit.write(entry), kafka.send(event)) .then(Mono.just(receipt)); Checkout.kt // three calls at once; ready when the slowest one is val quote: Mono<Quote> = Mono.zip( fx.rate("EURUSD").switchIfEmpty(missing("fx rate")), fees.forMerchant(m).defaultIfEmpty(BigDecimal.ZERO), limits.forCustomer(c).switchIfEmpty(missing("limit"))) .map { t -> Quote(t.t1, t.t2, t.t3) } // `when` is a Kotlin keyword, so the method name needs backticks val done: Mono<Receipt> = Mono.`when`(ledger.write(entry), audit.write(entry), kafka.send(event)) .then(Mono.just(receipt)) The Reactor calls are the same. In Kotlin, tuple getters read as properties (t.t1), and core Reactor has no destructuring for tuples. when is a keyword in Kotlin, so Mono.when has to be written with backticks. Kotlin's own fan-out looks different: inside coroutineScope { } you start each call with async { } and then await() them, and the Reactor bridge awaitSingleOrNull() turns an empty Mono into null, which the compiler then forces you to handle. That makes the empty case hard to forget, while Mono.zip lets you forget it. The coroutines track covers async.

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Worked example
x: Make a checkout quote fail loudly instead of disappearing The quote endpoint fans out three lookups. It passed every test, and support reports that some merchants see an empty checkout page. Mono<Quote> quote(String m, String c) { return Mono.zip(fx.rate("EURUSD"), fees.forMerchant(m), limits.forCustomer(c)) .map(t -> new Quote(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())); } fun quote(m: String, c: String): Mono<Quote> = Mono.zip(fx.rate("EURUSD"), fees.forMerchant(m), limits.forCustomer(c)) .map { t -> Quote(t.t1, t.t2, t.t3) } New merchants have no fee schedule yet, so fees.forMerchant(m) completes empty. Mono.zip then completes empty and cancels the other two calls. The map never runs, the controller has nothing to render, and no error is logged. Decide per source: a missing fee schedule means "no fee", a missing FX rate or limit is a real error. Encode those decisions on each source, before the zip. Mono<Quote> quote(String m, String c) { return Mono.zip( fx.rate("EURUSD").switchIfEmpty(missing("fx rate")), // 1. empty becomes an error fees.forMerchant(m).defaultIfEmpty(BigDecimal.ZERO), // 2. or a sensible default limits.forCustomer(c).switchIfEmpty(missing("limit"))) .map(t -> new Quote(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())); // 3. only reached with all three } private static <T> Mono<T> missing(String what) { return Mono.error(() -> new IllegalStateException("missing " + what)); } fun quote(m: String, c: String): Mono<Quote> = Mono.zip( fx.rate("EURUSD").switchIfEmpty(missing("fx rate")), // 1. empty becomes an error fees.forMerchant(m).defaultIfEmpty(BigDecimal.ZERO), // 2. or a sensible default limits.forCustomer(c).switchIfEmpty(missing("limit"))) .map { t -> Quote(t.t1, t.t2, t.t3) } // 3. only reached with all three private fun <T : Any> missing(what: String): Mono<T> = Mono.error { IllegalStateException("missing $what") } Pin the behaviour with a test for the empty case, the one the original tests never had. StepVerifier.create(checkout.quote("m-1", "no-limit-customer")) .expectErrorMessage("missing limit") // 4. the case that used to complete empty .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); StepVerifier.create(checkout.quote("m-1", "no-limit-customer")) .expectErrorMessage("missing limit") // 4. the case that used to complete empty .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1))

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Quiz
x: Mono.zip(fraudScore, fxRate): the fraud call fails after 50 ms; the FX call would take 2 seconds. What happens? The zip waits 2 seconds, then fails The zip fails at about 50 ms and cancels the FX call The zip emits the FX rate with a null fraud score The zip retries the fraud call Combinators fail fast: the first error ends the zip and cancels the other sources. Waiting for the others is what Mono.zipDelayError does. Nothing is retried unless you add retry (lesson 5 of this track). A statement must show settled entries, then pending ones. The pending query is expensive and must not start until the settled list is complete. Which line fits? Flux.merge(settled, pending) Flux.mergeSequential(settled, pending) Flux.concat(settled, pending) Flux.zip(settled, pending) concat subscribes to pending only after settled completes. mergeSequential produces the same output order but subscribes to both at once, so the expensive query starts early. merge interleaves, and zip pairs entries that have nothing to do with each other. Card events and bank events are two endless Kafka streams. A dashboard uses Flux.concat(cardEvents, bankEvents). What does it show? Card and bank events, interleaved Only card events, forever Nothing until both streams complete Bank events first, because they are smaller concat waits for the first source to complete before subscribing to the second, and an endless stream never completes. The bank stream is never subscribed. merge is the combinator for live feeds. Limits: 1000 at 0 ms, 2000 at 300 ms. Rates: 1.10 at 100 ms, 1.20 at 200 ms. What does Flux.combineLatest(limits, rates, BigDecimal::multiply) emit? 1100, 2400 1100, 1200, 2400 1100, 1200 2200, 2400 Nothing until both have emitted (100 ms: 1000 x 1.10). Then every change from either side re-emits with the latest of the other: the rate change at 200 ms gives 1200, and the limit change at 300 ms gives 2000 x 1.20 = 2400. zip would give only 1100, 2400. From "CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out": you fan out three calls with CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b, c), and a fails at once. When does the allOf future complete? At once, exceptionally, and it cancels b and c Exceptionally, but only after b and c have also completed Normally, and you have to check each future yourself Never, because one future failed allOf completes when all of the given futures complete, and exceptionally if any of them did. It does not cancel the others. That is the opposite of Mono.zip, which fails at the first error and cancels the remaining sources.

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Key terms
x: Fan-out Starting several independent calls at once and combining their results. zip Combines one item from each source, position by position; completes when any source completes. merge Subscribes to all sources at once and emits their items in arrival order. concat Subscribes to each source only after the previous one has completed. combineLatest Emits a new combination whenever any source emits, using the latest item of each. DelayError variant A version of a combinator that lets the other sources finish before reporting an error. What does Mono.zip do when one of its sources completes empty? It completes empty right away (no value, no error) and cancels the other sources. How do you make an empty source fail inside a Mono.zip? Put .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(...)) on that source before zipping it (or defaultIfEmpty(x) if there is a sensible default). merge vs concat: when is the second source subscribed? merge: immediately, together with the first. concat: only after the first source completes. Flux.concat(endless, other): what happens to other? It is never subscribed, because endless never completes. When does combineLatest emit? Once every source has emitted at least once, and then on every new item from any source, combined with the latest of the others. Why can't you Mono.zip a Mono<Void>? It always completes empty, so the zip completes empty. Use Mono.when(...) to wait for side effects, then .then(...).

h: Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest · Go deeper
x: Zip in a chain. Mono.zipWith(other) zips two Monos without the static call, and Mono.zipWhen(value -> otherCall(value)) runs the second call after the first and gives you both results: handy when the second lookup needs the first one's answer, such as fetching a merchant and then that merchant's fee schedule. That is sequential on purpose, so it takes the sum of both times. Zipping a Flux with an index. flux.index() pairs each item with its position, which is often what people reach for zip with Flux.range to do. Many Monos of unknown count. For a list of calls, Mono.zip(listOfMonos, array -> ...) exists but hands you an Object[]. Usually Flux.fromIterable(ids).flatMap(this::lookup, n).collectList() is clearer: it caps concurrency, which Mono.zip cannot, and it returns results in arrival order (use flatMapSequential to keep the input order). Merge and backpressure. merge requests from all its sources at once, with a prefetch per source, and interleaves what comes back. merge asks each source for a small prefetch and requests more only as items move downstream, so a fast source can't flood a slow subscriber. Lesson 7 of this track looks at demand in detail. switchIfEmpty is lazy, the argument isn't. switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new IllegalStateException(...))) builds the exception object on every call, even when the source has a value. That is cheap but wasteful, and the stack trace points at assembly. The supplier form Mono.error(() -> new IllegalStateException(...)) builds it only when needed.

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · An error ends the stream for good
x: Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).map(i -> 8 / i) emits 8 and 4, then fails on the zero. The 4 is never divided. That is the Reactive Streams rule from lesson 1 of this track: onError is a terminal signal, and nothing comes after it. Reactor's error operators don't bend that rule. They can't resume the failed sequence. They catch the error signal on its way down and replace the rest of the stream with something else. The upstream is already finished. Java fees.onErrorReturn(-1) // emit one fallback value, then complete fees.onErrorResume(e -> cachedFees()) // switch to a fallback publisher fees.onErrorMap(ArithmeticException.class, e -> new IllegalStateException("bad fee table", e)) // translate it; still an error Kotlin fees.onErrorReturn(-1) // emit one fallback value, then complete fees.onErrorResume { cachedFees() } // switch to a fallback publisher fees.onErrorMap(ArithmeticException::class.java) { e -> IllegalStateException("bad fee table", e) } // translate it; still an error On the 8 / i stream, onErrorReturn(-1) gives [8, 4, -1]. The fallback takes the place of everything after the error, and the 4 is still lost. Each of the three has overloads that take an exception class or a predicate. Use them. onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> cachedRate()) recovers from the one failure you planned for and lets the others through. A fallback for every Throwable also hides the NullPointerException in your own mapper, and the dashboard shows cached data for a week before anyone notices. Position matters. An error operator only sees errors from operators above it. Put onErrorReturn(-1) before the map and the division by zero sails past it. doOnError(e -> log.warn(...)) is the side-effect version: it logs and passes the error on unchanged. One trap catches tests in particular. Flux.error(e).subscribe(v -> {}) returns normally. With no error consumer, Reactor reports the error to its onErrorDropped hook, which logs ErrorCallbackNotImplemented at ERROR level, and your code never hears about it. Always pass an error consumer to subscribe, or test with StepVerifier, which fails on an error you didn't expect. Four ways to handle a division by zero ErrorsDemo divides 8 by each of 1, 2, 0, 4 and handles the failure four ways: not at all, onErrorReturn, onErrorResume and onErrorMap. Write down what each line prints. Run it and compare. Does any version ever print a result for the 4? Add one more line: Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).onErrorReturn(-1).map(i -> 8 / i) (the operator before map), collected and blocked like the others. Predict first, then run it. ErrorsDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l05; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; /** An error ends the stream. The error operators replace what is left with something else. */ public class ErrorsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Flux<Integer> fees = Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).map(i -> 8 / i); // 8 / 0 throws fees.subscribe(v -> System.out.println("raw: " + v), e -> System.out.println("raw: error " + e)); System.out.println("onErrorReturn: " + fees.onErrorReturn(-1).collectList().block()); System.out.println("onErrorResume: " + fees .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(100, 200)) // switch to a fallback stream .collectList().block()); fees.onErrorMap(ArithmeticException.class, e -> new IllegalStateException("bad fee table", e)) .subscribe(v -> { }, e -> System.out.println("onErrorMap: " + e + " caused by " + e.getCause())); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.ErrorsDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l05/ErrorsDemo.java ErrorsDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l05 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux /** An error ends the stream. The error operators replace what is left with something else. */ fun main() { val fees: Flux<Int> = Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).map { i -> 8 / i } // 8 / 0 throws fees.subscribe({ v -> println("raw: $v") }, { e -> println("raw: error $e") }) println("onErrorReturn: " + fees.onErrorReturn(-1).collectList().block()) println("onErrorResume: " + fees .onErrorResume { Flux.just(100, 200) } // switch to a fallback stream .collectList().block()) fees.onErrorMap(ArithmeticException::class.java) { e -> IllegalStateException("bad fee table", e) } .subscribe({ }, { e -> println("onErrorMap: $e caused by ${e.cause}") }) } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.ErrorsDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l05/ErrorsDemo.kt The raw subscriber prints 8 and 4, then the ArithmeticException. onErrorReturn gives [8, 4, -1], onErrorResume gives [8, 4, 100, 200], and onErrorMap reports an IllegalStateException caused by the ArithmeticException. No line ever shows a result for 4: the error ended the source. Your extra line throws ArithmeticException from block(), because onErrorReturn only sees errors from operators above it. Reactor reference: Handling errors (source, 3.8.x) docs Retry with backoff is how you call a busy support line. You don't press redial fifty times a second: you wait a minute, then two, then four, and after a few tries you stop and send an email instead (the fallback). A timeout is hanging up on a line that rings forever. The analogy breaks in two places. The phone tells you "busy" and "no" apart for you, but in code you have to classify errors yourself, or you will redial a definite no. And when you hang up on a slow line, the other side never acted. A card issuer may have approved the payment just as your timeout fired.

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Skip a bad item inside the item, not on the stream
x: A Kafka consumer reads 10,000 settlement messages. Message 4,312 has a bad amount. You want to log it, park it on a dead-letter topic and carry on. onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty()) on the whole stream does stop the error, and it also stops the stream: on the demo input it gives [8, 4]. Everything after the bad item is gone, because the error ended the upstream before onErrorResume saw it. To survive a bad item, give each item its own small publisher and handle the error there: Java amounts.concatMap(i -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> 8 / i) .doOnError(e -> log.warn("skipping {}", i, e)) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty())) // only this item's Mono ends Kotlin amounts.concatMap { i -> Mono.fromCallable { 8 / i } .doOnError { e -> log.warn("skipping {}", i, e) } .onErrorResume { Mono.empty() } // only this item's Mono ends } This gives [8, 4, 2]. The inner Mono for the zero failed and was replaced by an empty one. The outer stream never saw an error. Use concatMap to keep the order and handle one item at a time, or flatMap when items may run concurrently. For the Kafka case, replace Mono.empty() with deadLetters.send(msg, e).then(Mono.empty()). Reactor also has onErrorContinue((e, item) -> ...), which produces the same [8, 4, 2] here. Don't use it. Its own Javadoc calls it "a specialist operator that can make the behaviour of your reactive chain unclear". It doesn't catch anything itself. It puts a marker in the subscriber context, which flows up the chain, and operators above it that know the marker drop the failing item instead of failing. That design has three consequences. It acts on operators above it, never below, so Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).onErrorContinue(...).map(i -> 8 / i) still fails. It only works with operators that support it. And it reaches into library code upstream that never expected an item to be skipped. Someone adds an operator above it six months later, and the error handling changes with no compile error. The inner-publisher version says what happens in the place where it happens. Skip the zero three ways SkipBadItemsDemo runs the same four amounts through onErrorResume on the whole stream, onErrorResume inside a per-item Mono, and onErrorContinue. Predict the three lists. Run it. Now move the onErrorContinue line above the map (so it reads amounts.onErrorContinue(...).map(i -> 8 / i)). Predict what happens, then run it. SkipBadItemsDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l05; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; /** Skipping bad items: handle the error inside each item's own Mono, not on the whole stream. */ public class SkipBadItemsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Flux<Integer> amounts = Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4); var whole = amounts.map(i -> 8 / i).onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty()).collectList().block(); System.out.println("onErrorResume on the stream: " + whole); var perItem = amounts .concatMap(i -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> 8 / i) .doOnError(e -> System.out.println(" skipping " + i + ": " + e.getMessage())) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty())) // only this item's Mono ends .collectList().block(); System.out.println("onErrorResume per item: " + perItem); var continued = amounts.map(i -> 8 / i) .onErrorContinue((e, item) -> System.out.println(" onErrorContinue dropped " + item)) .collectList().block(); System.out.println("onErrorContinue: " + continued); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.SkipBadItemsDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l05/SkipBadItemsDemo.java SkipBadItemsDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l05 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono /** Skipping bad items: handle the error inside each item's own Mono, not on the whole stream. */ fun main() { val amounts: Flux<Int> = Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4) val whole = amounts.map { i -> 8 / i }.onErrorResume { Mono.empty() }.collectList().block() println("onErrorResume on the stream: $whole") val perItem = amounts .concatMap { i -> Mono.fromCallable { 8 / i } .doOnError { e -> println(" skipping $i: ${e.message}") } .onErrorResume { Mono.empty() } // only this item's Mono ends } .collectList().block() println("onErrorResume per item: $perItem") val continued = amounts.map { i -> 8 / i } .onErrorContinue { _, item -> println(" onErrorContinue dropped $item") } .collectList().block() println("onErrorContinue: $continued") } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.SkipBadItemsDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l05/SkipBadItemsDemo.kt The whole-stream version prints [8, 4]: the 4 is lost. The per-item version prints [8, 4, 2] and logs the skipped zero. onErrorContinue also prints [8, 4, 2] in its original place. Moved above the map, it does nothing and block() throws ArithmeticException, because it only affects operators upstream of it. Flux Javadoc source: onErrorContinue (reactor-core 3.8.x) docs Your issuer client, your ledger client and your Kafka producer all need the same three decisions: which errors are worth another try, how long one attempt may take, and what happens when the tries run out. In a payment flow the last answer is rarely "fail": it is "pending, reconcile later", with the same idempotency key on every attempt so the issuer can spot repeats. Watch for stacked retries. A Temporal activity already has a retry policy (initial interval, backoff coefficient, maximum attempts, non-retryable error types), and Quarkus apps often add SmallRye Fault Tolerance @Retry on top. Put Retry.backoff(3, ...) inside an activity that Temporal retries 5 times and one bad minute at the issuer turns into 20 calls per payment. Pick one layer to own retries.

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Retrying means subscribing again
x: retry doesn't rewind anything. When an error reaches it, it subscribes to its upstream again: a new subscription, so a cold publisher (lesson 2 of this track) does its work again from the start. The failed sequence stays failed. retry(2) on a source that always fails makes three attempts, not two, and then passes on the original exception. It retries at once, with no pause. Against a card issuer that's already struggling, that is three calls inside a millisecond. For remote calls, use retryWhen with a Retry spec: Java issuerCall.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // 3 retries, waits double from 100 ms .filter(e -> e instanceof IssuerUnavailableException)) // only errors worth retrying Kotlin issuerCall.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // 3 retries, waits double from 100 ms .filter { e -> e is IssuerUnavailableException }) // only errors worth retrying Here is the arithmetic people get wrong. Retry.backoff(3, 100ms) means 3 retries, so 4 attempts. With jitter off, a source that always fails is called at 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms, and at 700 ms the chain fails with a RetryExhaustedException. Its message is Retries exhausted: 3/3, its cause is the last real error, and Exceptions.isRetryExhausted(e) recognises it. An error that the filter rejects is not retried and comes through unchanged. The defaults in Reactor 3.8: the wait doubles each time, the waits run on Schedulers.parallel(), and the jitter factor is 0.5. Jitter moves each wait by a random amount of up to half its length, never below the first wait. Keep it in production: a thousand clients that failed together shouldn't all come back in the same millisecond. Turn it off with .jitter(0) in tests that check times. Now the trap. retry re-runs only what happens at subscription time. Many hand-written clients do the work when you call the method and wrap the answer: return Mono.just(response) or Mono.error(e). Retrying that Mono re-subscribes to the same stored answer, four times, and never calls the issuer again. Wrap the call so it happens per subscription: Mono.defer(() -> issuer.authorize(id)). Reactor's WebClient is already lazy (each subscription sends a new request), but don't assume the same of every client. Count the attempts RetryDemo has four parts: a backoff that succeeds on the third call, retry(2) on a call that always fails, a backoff that runs out, and retry(3) on a Mono built from one eager call. For each part, write down the number of attempts, the times, and the final result. Run it and compare your numbers. In part 3, delete .jitter(0) and run the demo twice. Watch the times of attempts 2 to 4. RetryDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l05; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.util.retry.Retry; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** retry re-subscribes. What gets re-run depends on how the source was built. */ public class RetryDemo { static final AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); static long t0; // fails on the first two calls, succeeds on the third static String callIssuer() { int n = calls.incrementAndGet(); System.out.printf(" [%3d ms] attempt %d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, n); if (n < 3) throw new IllegalStateException("issuer busy"); return "APPROVED"; } static String alwaysFails() { callIssuer(); throw new IllegalStateException("issuer down"); } // a client that calls the issuer when the method is called, and wraps the answer in a Mono static Mono<String> eagerClient() { try { return Mono.just(callIssuer()); } catch (RuntimeException e) { return Mono.error(e); } } public static void main(String[] args) { // warm up Reactor and the formatter, so the first timings don't include class loading Mono.fromCallable(() -> 1).retryWhen(Retry.backoff(1, Duration.ofMillis(1))).block(); String.format("%3d", 0); start("1. fromCallable + retryWhen(backoff 50 ms, no jitter)"); System.out.println(" -> " + Mono.fromCallable(RetryDemo::callIssuer) .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0)) .block()); start("2. retry(2) on a source that always fails"); try { Mono.fromCallable(RetryDemo::alwaysFails).retry(2).block(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(" -> " + e); } start("3. backoff exhausted"); try { Mono.fromCallable(RetryDemo::alwaysFails) .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0)) .block(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(" -> " + e + "\n cause: " + e.getCause()); } start("4. retry(3) on a Mono built from one eager call"); AtomicInteger subscriptions = new AtomicInteger(); try { eagerClient().doOnSubscribe(s -> subscriptions.incrementAndGet()).retry(3).block(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println(" -> " + e + " after " + subscriptions.get() + " subscriptions"); } } static void start(String title) { System.out.println(title); calls.set(0); t0 = System.nanoTime(); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.RetryDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l05/RetryDemo.java RetryDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l05 import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import reactor.util.retry.Retry import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private val calls = AtomicInteger() private var t0 = 0L // fails on the first two calls, succeeds on the third private fun callIssuer(): String { val n = calls.incrementAndGet() println(" [%3d ms] attempt %d".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, n)) if (n < 3) throw IllegalStateException("issuer busy") return "APPROVED" } private fun alwaysFails(): String { callIssuer() throw IllegalStateException("issuer down") } // a client that calls the issuer when the function is called, and wraps the answer in a Mono private fun eagerClient(): Mono<String> = try { Mono.just(callIssuer()) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { Mono.error(e) } private fun start(title: String) { println(title) calls.set(0) t0 = System.nanoTime() } /** retry re-subscribes. What gets re-run depends on how the source was built. */ fun main() { // warm up Reactor and the formatter, so the first timings don't include class loading Mono.fromCallable { 1 }.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(1, Duration.ofMillis(1))).block() "%3d".format(0) start("1. fromCallable + retryWhen(backoff 50 ms, no jitter)") println(" -> " + Mono.fromCallable { callIssuer() } .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0.0)) .block()) start("2. retry(2) on a source that always fails") try { Mono.fromCallable { alwaysFails() }.retry(2).block() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println(" -> $e") } start("3. backoff exhausted") try { Mono.fromCallable { alwaysFails() } .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0.0)) .block() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println(" -> $e\n cause: ${e.cause}") } start("4. retry(3) on a Mono built from one eager call") val subscriptions = AtomicInteger() try { eagerClient().doOnSubscribe { subscriptions.incrementAndGet() }.retry(3).block() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println(" -> $e after ${subscriptions.get()} subscriptions") } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.RetryDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l05/RetryDemo.kt Part 1 calls at about 0, 50 and 150 ms and prints APPROVED. Part 2 makes 3 attempts in the same millisecond and rethrows issuer down. Part 3 calls at about 0, 50, 150 and 350 ms, then throws RetryExhaustedException: Retries exhausted: 3/3 with issuer down as the cause. Part 4 calls the issuer once and fails with issuer busy after 4 subscriptions: retry re-subscribed to the same stored error. Without jitter the waits are exactly 50, 100 and 200 ms; with the default jitter they change from run to run. Retry.backoff(3, 100 ms) with jitter off, against a call that always fails: four attempts, waits that double, and an exhausted error at 700 ms that a fallback can catch. h: Errors, retries and timeouts · A timeout turns silence into an error you can handle
x: A retry needs an error to react to. A card issuer that accepts the connection and then never answers sends no error at all. Your request waits, holding one of the 20 connections in the pool, until something gives up. With no timeout, nothing does. timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) signals a TimeoutException if no item arrives within 500 ms of subscribing (for a Flux, within 500 ms of the previous item), and it cancels the slow upstream. Its clock runs on Schedulers.parallel(), so it works under virtual time in tests. Where you put it decides what it limits: Java Mono.defer(() -> issuer.authorize(id)) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) // each attempt gets 500 ms .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).filter(this::worthRetrying)) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)); // the caller waits 2 s at most, in total Kotlin Mono.defer { issuer.authorize(id) } .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) // each attempt gets 500 ms .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)).filter(this::worthRetrying)) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)) // the caller waits 2 s at most, in total Above retryWhen, the timeout applies to each attempt. Its TimeoutException is one more error that the retry handles, if the filter lets it through. Below retryWhen, the timeout is a budget for the whole operation, waits included. With only the budget, one hanging attempt uses all 2 seconds and is never retried. Most remote calls want both. To swap in a fallback, use timeout(Duration, fallbackMono) or onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> ...). In payments, one fact matters more than the operators. A timeout tells you that you stopped waiting. It doesn't tell you the issuer said no. The authorization may have gone through on the other side while your client was giving up. So a retry must send the same idempotency key as the first attempt, so the issuer can recognise a repeat. And when the retries run out, the honest state is "unknown". Leave the payment pending and let reconciliation settle it, rather than marking it failed and letting the customer pay again. Per attempt or in total TimeoutDemo has a rate call that takes 300 ms. It applies a 100 ms timeout, then the same with a fallback, then a 100 ms per-attempt timeout with retries inside a 400 ms total budget. Predict each line, and how many attempts fit in the budget. Run it. In the last chain, delete the per-attempt .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)) and keep the 400 ms budget. Predict the result and the number of attempts, then run it. TimeoutDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l05; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.util.retry.Retry; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** timeout turns silence into an error you can handle. Where you put it decides what it limits. */ public class TimeoutDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Mono<String> slowRate = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(300)).thenReturn("live rate 1.08") .doOnCancel(() -> System.out.println(" slow call cancelled")); try { slowRate.timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)).block(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("timeout: " + e.getCause()); } String rate = slowRate.timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)) .onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> Mono.just("cached rate 1.07")) .block(); System.out.println("with fallback: " + rate); AtomicInteger attempts = new AtomicInteger(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { String r = Mono.defer(() -> { attempts.incrementAndGet(); return slowRate; }) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)) // per attempt .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(5, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0)) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(400)) // budget for the whole call .block(); System.out.printf("budget: got %s after %d attempts and %d ms%n", r, attempts.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.printf("budget: gave up after %d attempts and %d ms: %s%n", attempts.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName()); } } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.TimeoutDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l05/TimeoutDemo.java TimeoutDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l05 import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import reactor.util.retry.Retry import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** timeout turns silence into an error you can handle. Where you put it decides what it limits. */ fun main() { val slowRate: Mono<String> = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(300)).thenReturn("live rate 1.08") .doOnCancel { println(" slow call cancelled") } try { slowRate.timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)).block() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println("timeout: ${e.cause}") } val rate = slowRate.timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)) .onErrorResume(TimeoutException::class.java) { Mono.just("cached rate 1.07") } .block() println("with fallback: $rate") val attempts = AtomicInteger() val t0 = System.nanoTime() try { val r = Mono.defer { attempts.incrementAndGet(); slowRate } .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(100)) // per attempt .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(5, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0.0)) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(400)) // budget for the whole call .block() println("budget: got %s after %d attempts and %d ms".format( r, attempts.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println("budget: gave up after %d attempts and %d ms: %s".format( attempts.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, e.cause?.javaClass?.simpleName)) } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l05.TimeoutDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l05/TimeoutDemo.kt The plain timeout prints TimeoutException: Did not observe any item or terminal signal within 100ms and the slow call is cancelled. The fallback version prints cached rate 1.07. The budget run makes 3 attempts (at about 0, 150 and 350 ms) and gives up near 400 ms. Without the per-attempt timeout there is no error to retry, the single 300 ms call fits inside the 400 ms budget, and you get live rate 1.08 after 1 attempt. The most common mistake is a retry that doesn't choose. .retry() with no argument retries forever, at once, on every error. .retry(3) is better, but it still resends a declined card three times and retries the NullPointerException in your own mapper. People write it because the first failure they saw was a timeout, and a retry made it go away. The fix is retryWhen(Retry.backoff(n, firstWait).filter(...)), where the filter names the errors that a later attempt can fix (timeouts, 503s, connection resets) and everything else fails at once. Then check that the source is lazy, with Mono.defer if you are not sure, or the retries will never reach the server.

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Java and Kotlin
x: One retry policy as a Reactor chain and as a suspend function ResilientAuthorizer.java (Reactor) // Reactor: the policy is a chain of operators on a lazy Mono Mono<String> authorize(String paymentId) { return Mono.defer(() -> issuer.authorize(paymentId)) // a fresh call per attempt .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(500)) // per attempt .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) // waits of 100, 200, 400 ms .filter(e -> e instanceof IssuerUnavailableException || e instanceof TimeoutException)) .onErrorResume(Exceptions::isRetryExhausted, e -> Mono.just("PENDING:" + paymentId)); } ResilientAuthorizer.kt (coroutines) // Kotlin coroutines: the same policy as a plain loop in a suspend function suspend fun authorize(paymentId: String): String { var wait = 100.milliseconds repeat(4) { attempt -> // 1 call + 3 retries try { return withTimeout(500.milliseconds) { issuer.authorize(paymentId) } // per attempt } catch (e: IssuerUnavailableException) { // worth another try } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) { // so is a hang; a decline is not caught, so it reaches the caller } if (attempt < 3) { delay(wait); wait *= 2 } // 100, 200, 400 ms } return "PENDING:$paymentId" } Both versions make up to 4 attempts, give each 500 ms, wait 100, 200 and 400 ms between them, let a decline through and return PENDING at the end. In Reactor the policy is data: operators you can reorder, and a Retry spec you can pass around and reuse, and the result is still a lazy Mono that does nothing until subscribed. In the coroutine version the policy is ordinary control flow: a loop, try/catch, delay and withTimeout. That is easier to read and to step through in a debugger, but you write the loop yourself, and you must not swallow CancellationException by catching Exception too broadly (withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException, which is one). Kotlin Flow has retry and retryWhen operators too, and the coroutines track covers them.

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Worked example
x: Make a ledger write safe to retry A Kafka consumer posts each entry to the ledger service. Someone added retry() after a deploy caused a few 503s. Read it and list what can go wrong before reading on. Mono<Void> post(LedgerEntry entry) { return ledger.post(entry, UUID.randomUUID().toString()).retry(); } fun post(entry: LedgerEntry): Mono<Void> = ledger.post(entry, UUID.randomUUID().toString()).retry() Four problems. retry() with no limit retries forever and at once, so one bad entry stalls the whole partition. It retries a 400 (a bad entry) as eagerly as a 503. Nothing limits how long one attempt may hang. And the idempotency key is a fresh UUID per call of post. The retries of this one Mono reuse it, but when Kafka redelivers the message after a rebalance, post runs again with a new key, and the ledger has no way to see that it already booked the entry. The key has to come from the entry itself. Rebuild it in the order the lesson used: a lazy call, a per-attempt timeout, a filtered backoff, and a fallback for when the retries run out. LedgerErrors.isTransient returns true for timeouts, 503s and connection resets. Mono<Void> post(LedgerEntry entry) { String key = entry.idempotencyKey(); // 1. the entry's own key, never a new one return Mono.defer(() -> ledger.post(entry, key)) // 2. a fresh call per attempt .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // 3. no attempt waits forever .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(200)) // 4. 3 retries, jitter left on .filter(LedgerErrors::isTransient)) // a 400 or 409 is final .onErrorResume(Exceptions::isRetryExhausted, // 5. out of retries: park it e -> deadLetters.send(entry, e.getCause())); } fun post(entry: LedgerEntry): Mono<Void> { val key = entry.idempotencyKey // 1. the entry's own key, never a new one return Mono.defer { ledger.post(entry, key) } // 2. a fresh call per attempt .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // 3. no attempt waits forever .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(200)) // 4. 3 retries, jitter left on .filter(LedgerErrors::isTransient)) // a 400 or 409 is final .onErrorResume(Exceptions::isRetryExhausted) { e -> // 5. out of retries: park it deadLetters.send(entry, e.cause!!) } } Test the slow path with virtual time. The jitter is still on, so don't assert exact times: advance the clock further than any possible wait, then check the counts. Four attempts, one key, one dead letter. StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> poster.post(entry)) // build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(10)) // more than any jittered wait .verifyComplete(); // parked, not failed assertThat(ledger.keysSeen()).hasSize(4).containsOnly(entry.idempotencyKey()); assertThat(deadLetters.sent()).containsExactly(entry); StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { poster.post(entry) } // build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(10)) // more than any jittered wait .verifyComplete() // parked, not failed assertThat(ledger.keysSeen()).hasSize(4).containsOnly(entry.idempotencyKey) assertThat(deadLetters.sent()).containsExactly(entry)

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Lab
x: A card-issuer call with timeout, backoff and a fallback labs/reactive/src/main/java/workbench/reactive/l05/ResilientAuthorizer.java labs/reactive/src/main/java/workbench/reactive/l05/CardIssuer.java ./gradlew :reactive:test --tests 'workbench.reactive.l05.*' Run the tests once. All five fail. Read the Javadoc on ResilientAuthorizer: it lists five rules, and each test checks one of them. Look at ScriptedIssuer in ResilientAuthorizerTest. It chooses its answer when authorize() is called, not when the Mono is subscribed. Decide what that means for your retry before writing code. Write authorize as one chain: a lazy issuer call, a 500 ms timeout per attempt, retryWhen with Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(100)) and no jitter, a filter that lets declines through, and a fallback to "PENDING:" + paymentId only when the retries are used up. Run the tests until all five pass. Then read the virtual-time steps in each test: expectNoEvent(Duration.ofMillis(699)) followed by thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(1)) pins the result to exactly 700 ms. If "succeeds on the third attempt" fails and the issuer was called once, you called issuer.authorize(paymentId) directly. Retry then re-subscribes to the same failed Mono. Wrap it in Mono.defer. If the hanging-attempt test ends in a TimeoutException, either your timeout sits below retryWhen (so it limits the whole call) or your filter does not accept java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException. If the decline test receives PENDING:p-3, your fallback catches every error. Use the predicate overload: onErrorResume(Exceptions::isRetryExhausted, e -> ...). Retry.backoff(3, ...) gives 3 retries, so 4 attempts. jitter(0) makes the waits exactly 100, 200 and 400 ms. All five tests in ResilientAuthorizerTest pass. By the end you can recover from errors without pretending a stream continues, skip bad items safely, and wrap a flaky remote call in a per-attempt timeout, a filtered exponential backoff and a fallback, then prove the timing with virtual time.

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Quiz
x: What does Flux.just(5, 10, 0, 20).map(i -> 100 / i).onErrorReturn(-1).collectList().block() return? [20, 10, -1, 5] [20, 10, -1] [20, 10, 5] It throws ArithmeticException The division by zero ends the source, so 20 is never divided. onErrorReturn replaces the rest of the stream with one value and completes. The first option assumes the stream continues after the fallback, and the third is what per-item handling would give. An exchange-rate call sometimes hangs. Which chain retries a hanging attempt? (ofMillis and ofSeconds are Duration factories.) Mono.defer(this::rate).retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, ofMillis(100))).timeout(ofSeconds(2)) Mono.defer(this::rate).timeout(ofMillis(500)).retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, ofMillis(100))) Mono.defer(this::rate).retryWhen(Retry.backoff(3, ofMillis(100))) Mono.defer(this::rate).retry(3) Only a timeout above retryWhen turns each hanging attempt into an error that the retry can see. In the first option the timeout is a total budget: the first attempt hangs for 2 seconds and is never retried. The last two have no timeout, so a hang produces no error at all and nothing is retried. A Kafka consumer must log and skip messages whose amount fails to parse, and keep consuming. Which is the right shape? messages.map(this::parse).onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty()) messages.map(this::parse).onErrorContinue((e, m) -> log(m)) messages.concatMap(m -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> parse(m)).onErrorResume(e -> logAndSkip(m, e))) messages.map(this::parse).retry() Handling the error inside each message's own Mono ends only that inner Mono, so the outer stream keeps going. The first option ends the whole stream at the first bad message. onErrorContinue happens to work here, but it acts on operators upstream of it and can leak into library code; its Javadoc recommends the inner-publisher shape. retry() re-subscribes to the consumer forever and hits the same bad message again. issuer.authorize(id) always fails with IssuerUnavailableException. What does Mono.defer(() -> issuer.authorize(id)).retry(2).block() do? Calls the issuer 2 times, then throws RetryExhaustedException Calls the issuer 3 times, 100 ms apart, then throws IssuerUnavailableException Calls the issuer 3 times with no pause, then throws IssuerUnavailableException Calls the issuer once, because retry re-uses the first result retry(n) means n retries, so 3 attempts, all back to back, and it rethrows the original error. Pauses and RetryExhaustedException come from retryWhen(Retry.backoff(...)). Because of Mono.defer, each attempt really calls the issuer; without it, a client that does the work on call would be called once. From "Mono and Flux: nothing happens until you subscribe": a teammate writes Mono.just(issuerClient.authorizeBlocking(id)).retry(3). The call fails on the first try. How many times does the issuer receive a request? Once, and the exception is thrown before retry exists Four times Three times Zero times, because nothing is subscribed Mono.just takes a value, so Java evaluates authorizeBlocking(id) first, at assembly time. It throws right there, out of the line that builds the pipeline, and retry(3) is never even created. Even if it had returned a value, Mono.just would replay that same value to every subscriber. Use Mono.fromCallable or Mono.defer so each subscription makes the call.

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Key terms
x: Fallback What a stream switches to when an error arrives: a value, another publisher, or a different error. Retry Subscribing to the source again after an error, so a cold source does its work again. Exponential backoff Waiting longer before each retry, usually doubling: 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms. Jitter A random change to each backoff wait, so many clients that failed together don't retry at the same instant. RetryExhaustedException The error Retry.backoff and Retry.max signal when the retries run out; the cause is the last real error. Transient error A failure that a later attempt may not repeat: a timeout, a 503, a connection reset. Idempotency key A unique id sent with a request, so the server can tell a retry from a new request and do the work once. Flux.just(1, 2, 0, 4).map(i -> 8 / i).onErrorReturn(-1): what is emitted? 8, 4, -1, then complete. The error ended the source, so 4 is never processed. How do you skip one bad item in a Flux without ending the stream? Process each item in its own Mono inside concatMap/flatMap, and put onErrorResume on that inner Mono. Why is onErrorContinue discouraged? It acts on operators upstream of it (not downstream), only works with operators that support it, and can leak into library code. Its own Javadoc says so. retry(2) on a source that always fails: how many attempts, and which error? 3 attempts with no pause, then the original error. Retry.backoff(3, 100ms).jitter(0) on a source that always fails: attempts, timing, error? 4 attempts at 0, 100, 300 and 700 ms, then RetryExhaustedException ("Retries exhausted: 3/3") with the last error as its cause. Why can retry fail to call the server again? It re-subscribes. If the Mono was built from a call made at assembly (Mono.just(call()) or a client that calls eagerly), it replays the stored answer. Wrap it in Mono.defer. timeout above vs below retryWhen? Above: each attempt gets the time, and a timeout is retried. Below: one budget for the whole operation, waits included.

h: Errors, retries and timeouts · Go deeper
x: Transient errors. Retry.max(2).transientErrors(true) (also on backoff) counts retries in a row and resets the count after a successful onNext. That suits long-lived streams, such as a Kafka consumer, that fail now and then: each burst of failures gets its own budget instead of using up a lifetime total. The reference guide's example fails twice, emits, fails twice more and then succeeds: Retry.max(2).transientErrors(true) gets through, and plain Retry.max(2) runs out in the second burst. Other specs. Retry.fixedDelay(5, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) waits the same time between retries. Retry.indefinitely() never gives up, so pair it with a filter. Every spec has doBeforeRetry(signal -> ...) for logging the attempt number and onRetryExhaustedThrow(...) to choose the final error. The companion. retryWhen takes a function from a Flux<RetrySignal> (one signal per error) to a companion publisher. Each item the companion emits triggers one retry; if it completes, the sequence completes without error; if it errors, that error goes downstream. Retry.backoff is a ready-made companion built on Mono.delay, which is why its waits run on Schedulers.parallel() and why virtual time controls them. Repeat is the other loop. repeat re-subscribes after a successful completion, for polling. Reactor 3.8 added RepeatSpec for repeatWhen, the counterpart of Retry for repeats. Fatal errors. Reactor throws some errors straight up the stack instead of turning them into onError, such as OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError (see Exceptions.throwIfFatal). No error operator will catch those, and you shouldn't want one to.

h: Schedulers: publishOn, subscribeOn and blocking calls · Reactor runs on the thread that delivered the last signal
x: Reactor doesn't own a thread pool the way an ExecutorService does. Unless you say otherwise, the source runs on the thread that called subscribe(), and each operator runs on the thread that delivered the signal to it. Flux.range(1, 2).map(...).subscribe(...) called from main runs every step on main, and subscribe returns only when the range is done. Other threads appear when something asynchronous sits in the chain. A timer (Mono.delay, interval, delayElements, timeout, the waits of Retry.backoff) fires on Schedulers.parallel(), and the operators after it carry on there. An HTTP client delivers its response on its own I/O threads. In a flatMap over three timers, the three inners fire on three parallel workers, so the downstream sees items arrive on three different threads, still one at a time. Rule 1.3 from lesson 1 of this track holds: signals are serial even when the thread changes. When you want to choose the thread, you pass a Scheduler. It is close to an ExecutorService, and it is also a clock, which is how StepVerifier.withVirtualTime can fake time. Reactor 3.8 has four shared ones: Scheduler Threads Use it for Schedulers.immediate() the current thread a placeholder that changes nothing Schedulers.single() one shared thread cheap work that must stay serial Schedulers.parallel() one per CPU core CPU work and timers; never block here Schedulers.boundedElastic() up to 10 x cores, then a queue of 100,000 tasks blocking calls The threads of parallel and single are marked as non-blocking, and Reactor refuses block() on them (the last section). boundedElastic creates threads on demand up to its cap, reuses them, and drops a worker after 60 seconds idle. Past the cap, tasks wait in its queue. Past the queue, it throws RejectedExecutionException. You can build your own with Schedulers.newParallel, newBoundedElastic or fromExecutorService, and you then have to dispose() them. The reference guide still mentions Schedulers.elastic(), which no longer exists in 3.8: use boundedElastic(). A tour of the threads ThreadTourDemo prints the thread of each step in three chains: no scheduler at all, a chain after Mono.delay, and a flatMap over three timers. Predict each thread name before you run it. Run it. In part 3, add .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) right before the doOnNext (and import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers). Predict the threads, then run it again. ThreadTourDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l06; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; /** Where does each step run? Reactor stays on whatever thread delivered the last signal. */ public class ThreadTourDemo { static void where(String step) { System.out.printf(" %-26s on %s%n", step, Thread.currentThread().getName()); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("1. no scheduler anywhere"); Flux.range(1, 2) .doOnNext(i -> where("source emits " + i)) .map(i -> i * 10) .subscribe(i -> where("subscriber gets " + i)); System.out.println("2. after a timer (Mono.delay)"); Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10)) .doOnNext(t -> where("timer fires")) .map(t -> "ok") .doOnNext(v -> where("map after the timer")) .block(); System.out.println("3. flatMap over three timers"); Flux.range(1, 3) .flatMap(i -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10L * i)).thenReturn(i)) .doOnNext(i -> where("downstream gets " + i)) .blockLast(); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l06.ThreadTourDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l06/ThreadTourDemo.java ThreadTourDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l06 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.time.Duration private fun where(step: String) = println(" %-26s on %s".format(step, Thread.currentThread().name)) /** Where does each step run? Reactor stays on whatever thread delivered the last signal. */ fun main() { println("1. no scheduler anywhere") Flux.range(1, 2) .doOnNext { i -> where("source emits $i") } .map { i -> i * 10 } .subscribe { i -> where("subscriber gets $i") } println("2. after a timer (Mono.delay)") Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10)) .doOnNext { where("timer fires") } .map { "ok" } .doOnNext { where("map after the timer") } .block() println("3. flatMap over three timers") Flux.range(1, 3) .flatMap { i -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10L * i)).thenReturn(i) } .doOnNext { i -> where("downstream gets $i") } .blockLast() } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l06.ThreadTourDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l06/ThreadTourDemo.kt Part 1 runs entirely on main, and the source and subscriber alternate item by item. Part 2 runs on parallel-1, the timer's thread, including the map after it. Part 3 delivers the three items on three different parallel threads (for example parallel-2, parallel-3, parallel-4). After your change, all three arrive on single-1. Reactor reference: Threading and Schedulers (source, 3.8.x) docs Think of a bank branch. Requests are customers, and by default the clerk who greets a customer handles everything for them. publishOn is a ticket counter in the middle of the hall: from there on, a different clerk takes over. subscribeOn is the instruction at the front door saying which clerk opens the file in the first place, and it doesn't matter which wall the sign hangs on. boundedElastic is the back office with many clerks who are allowed to sit on the phone waiting for another bank; parallel is the few cashiers at the front, and if one of them waits on the phone, the queue stops. The analogy breaks at speed: a real clerk hand-off takes minutes, while a thread hop costs microseconds, which is still enough that you shouldn't add them for nothing.

h: Schedulers: publishOn, subscribeOn and blocking calls · publishOn moves what comes after it; subscribeOn moves the source
x: Two operators move work to another thread, and they move different things. publishOn(scheduler) sits in the data path. Items arrive from above on whatever thread, publishOn queues them (it prefetches 256 by default), and one worker of the scheduler hands them to the operators below. Everything after it, up to the next publishOn, runs on that worker. Everything before it is unaffected. Use it to get work off a thread that must stay free, or onto parallel for a CPU-heavy step. subscribeOn(scheduler) sits in the subscription path. When you call subscribe(), Reactor builds the chain of subscribers from the bottom up to the source (lesson 2 of this track). subscribeOn makes that subscribe call, and the request(n) calls after it, continue on the scheduler's thread. So the source starts producing there, and a synchronous source such as fromCallable or range runs there. Where you write it doesn't matter: Java Flux.range(1, 1) .doOnNext(i -> where("source")) // boundedElastic-1 .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) .doOnNext(i -> where("after publishOn")) // single-1 .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // written last, still moves the source .blockLast(); Kotlin Flux.range(1, 1) .doOnNext { where("source") } // boundedElastic-1 .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) .doOnNext { where("after publishOn") } // single-1 .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // written last, still moves the source .blockLast() With two subscribeOn calls, the one nearest the source wins. The other only adds a thread hop on the way up. Reactor's guide recommends writing subscribeOn right after the source, where a reader looks for it. Two limits. If the source is itself asynchronous, such as Mono.delay or an HTTP client, subscribeOn moves only the subscribe call: the items still arrive on the source's own threads. And after a publishOn below the source, the data path belongs to the publishOn scheduler, as the second line of output above shows. publishOn, subscribeOn, and two of them PublishSubscribeDemo runs three chains: publishOn in the middle, subscribeOn written after a publishOn, and two subscribeOn calls in a row. Predict the thread of every printed line. Run it. In part 3, swap the two subscribeOn lines so boundedElastic is nearest the source. Predict, then run it again. PublishSubscribeDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l06; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; /** publishOn moves what comes after it. subscribeOn moves the source, wherever you write it. */ public class PublishSubscribeDemo { static void where(String step) { System.out.printf(" %-22s on %s%n", step, Thread.currentThread().getName()); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("1. publishOn(single) in the middle"); Flux.range(1, 1) .doOnNext(i -> where("source")) .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) .doOnNext(i -> where("after publishOn")) .blockLast(); System.out.println("2. subscribeOn(boundedElastic) written last"); Flux.range(1, 1) .doOnNext(i -> where("source")) .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) .doOnNext(i -> where("after publishOn")) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) .blockLast(); System.out.println("3. two subscribeOn calls"); Flux.range(1, 1) .doOnNext(i -> where("source")) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.single()) // nearest to the source: this one wins .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // only adds a thread hop .doOnNext(i -> where("downstream")) .blockLast(); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l06.PublishSubscribeDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l06/PublishSubscribeDemo.java PublishSubscribeDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l06 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers private fun where(step: String) = println(" %-22s on %s".format(step, Thread.currentThread().name)) /** publishOn moves what comes after it. subscribeOn moves the source, wherever you write it. */ fun main() { println("1. publishOn(single) in the middle") Flux.range(1, 1) .doOnNext { where("source") } .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) .doOnNext { where("after publishOn") } .blockLast() println("2. subscribeOn(boundedElastic) written last") Flux.range(1, 1) .doOnNext { where("source") } .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) .doOnNext { where("after publishOn") } .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) .blockLast() println("3. two subscribeOn calls") Flux.range(1, 1) .doOnNext { where("source") } .subscribeOn(Schedulers.single()) // nearest to the source: this one wins .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // only adds a thread hop .doOnNext { where("downstream") } .blockLast() } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l06.PublishSubscribeDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l06/PublishSubscribeDemo.kt Part 1: the source on main, after publishOn on single-1. Part 2: the source on boundedElastic-1 although subscribeOn is written last, and after publishOn still single-1. Part 3: everything on single-1, because the subscribeOn nearest the source wins. After the swap, everything runs on a boundedElastic thread. publishOn splits the data path: before it, items run where the source runs; after it, on single. subscribeOn changes the thread of the subscription on its way up, so the source runs on boundedElastic even though subscribeOn is written near the end. In a Quarkus or Spring service you rarely pick the first thread. The HTTP server delivers requests on a few event-loop threads, and a reactive client delivers responses on its own I/O threads. The moment a chain calls Oracle through JDBC, an old card-scheme SOAP client or a file-based HSM wrapper, that call needs fromCallable plus subscribeOn(boundedElastic()), or the event loop stops serving everyone else while it waits. Size it against the real limit: boundedElastic allows 40 threads on a 4-core pod, but your Oracle pool has 20 connections, so cap the fan-out at 20. And when the reactive pipeline feeds a Kafka producer or a Temporal client that blocks, that call is a blocking call too.

h: Schedulers: publishOn, subscribeOn and blocking calls · Wrap a blocking call in fromCallable and subscribeOn(boundedElastic)
x: JDBC, a SOAP client, Files.readAllLines, an old vendor SDK: each holds its thread until the answer comes. Run one on parallel (one thread per core) and four slow calls on a 4-core pod stop every timer and every other pipeline that shares that pool. Reactor's FAQ gives the standard wrapper: Java Mono<BigDecimal> balance(String account) { return Mono.fromCallable(() -> ledgerDao.balance(account)) // lazy: runs per subscription .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()); // on a thread that may block } Kotlin fun balance(account: String): Mono<BigDecimal> = Mono.fromCallable { ledgerDao.balance(account) } // lazy: runs per subscription .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // on a thread that may block fromCallable makes the call lazy and turns a thrown exception into onError. subscribeOn puts the call on a thread that is allowed to block. As the FAQ says, subscribeOn does not subscribe to anything: it only says where the work runs once somebody subscribes. For many calls, the subscribeOn must sit on each inner Mono. This looks concurrent and isn't: Java Flux.fromIterable(accounts) .flatMap(a -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> ledgerDao.balance(a))) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()); // one thread runs every call, in turn Kotlin Flux.fromIterable(accounts) .flatMap { a -> Mono.fromCallable { ledgerDao.balance(a) } } .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // one thread runs every call, in turn flatMap subscribes to each inner on the thread it is running on, and a fromCallable runs right there, so the calls take turns on one thread: eight 100 ms calls take 800 ms. Move subscribeOn inside the flatMap, and the same eight take about 100 ms on eight threads. Then cap them with flatMap's concurrency argument, so the 20-connection pool in front of Oracle isn't asked for 40 connections at once. Since Reactor 3.6, boundedElastic can use virtual threads. On a JDK 21+ runtime, start the JVM with -Dreactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticOnVirtualThreads=true and the shared boundedElastic() runs every task on a new virtual thread (named loomBoundedElastic-N). The caps stay the same, and the Javadoc suggests raising reactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticSize when you turn it on. The property is read once, when the Schedulers class loads, so put it on the command line. The virtual threads track applies here too: on JDK 21 to 23, a driver that blocks inside synchronized pins its carrier. Eight blocking calls, three ways BlockingCallDemo makes eight ledger calls that each sleep 100 ms: with no scheduler, with subscribeOn on the outer Flux, and with subscribeOn on each inner call. Predict the time and the number of threads for each. Run it. Run it again with -Pargs=virtual added to the command. The demo then sets reactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticOnVirtualThreads before Reactor loads its schedulers. Look at the thread names and the virtual flag. BlockingCallDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l06; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; /** Eight blocking ledger calls of 100 ms each. Where you put subscribeOn decides how long they take. */ public class BlockingCallDemo { static final Set<Thread> threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); // a JDBC-style call: it holds the calling thread for 100 ms static BigDecimal balance(String account) { threads.add(Thread.currentThread()); try { Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return BigDecimal.TEN; } static void run(String title, Flux<BigDecimal> balances) { threads.clear(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long n = balances.count().block(); Thread one = threads.iterator().next(); System.out.printf("%-34s %d calls in %3d ms on %d thread(s), e.g. %s (virtual=%s)%n", title, n, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads.size(), one.getName(), one.isVirtual()); } public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("virtual")) { // must be set before Reactor's Schedulers class is first used; normally a -D JVM flag System.setProperty("reactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticOnVirtualThreads", "true");
