h: Schedulers: publishOn, subscribeOn and blocking calls · Keep block() at the edges
x: block() subscribes and parks the calling thread until the Mono finishes. On a parallel or single thread that is a bug, and Reactor checks for it: block(), blockFirst(), blockLast(), toIterable() and toStream() throw IllegalStateException: block()/blockFirst()/blockLast() are blocking, which is not supported in thread parallel-1. It shows up in code like the first line below, once the amount arrives from a timer, a timeout or a non-blocking client: Java usd.map(amount -> amount.multiply(fx.usdToEur().block())) // throws on a parallel thread usd.flatMap(amount -> fx.usdToEur().map(amount::multiply)) // composes instead Kotlin usd.map { amount -> amount.multiply(fx.usdToEur().block()) } // throws on a parallel thread usd.flatMap { amount -> fx.usdToEur().map(amount::multiply) } // composes instead The check is a safety net with holes in it. Mono.just(x).block() takes a shortcut for a value that is already there and doesn't check the thread at all, so a unit test whose stubs return Mono.just passes while staging fails. And the check only knows threads that implement Reactor's NonBlocking marker interface. A Kafka listener thread or an application worker thread isn't marked, so block() there works, and holds that thread until the answer comes. To find blocking calls the check misses, Reactor has a separate agent, BlockHound (not in the labs). It instruments the JDK and throws when a non-blocking thread calls something like Thread.sleep or a blocking socket read. So where is block() fine? In main, in a test (though StepVerifier is better), and at the edge where reactive code meets code that is blocking anyway, on a thread that is yours to block. On boundedElastic it is allowed, and it costs you one of a limited set of threads. Inside a pipeline there is always an operator that composes instead: flatMap, zipWith, then. When block() is refused BlockInParallelDemo multiplies a USD amount by an FX rate four ways: block() inside map, flatMap, block() on a Mono.just, and block() after publishOn(boundedElastic()). The amount arrives from Mono.delay, so on a parallel thread. Predict which lines fail. Run it. Change usd to Mono.just(new BigDecimal("100")) and run again. Predict line 1 first. BlockInParallelDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l06; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.time.Duration; /** block() on a Reactor parallel thread is refused. flatMap composes instead. */ public class BlockInParallelDemo { static Mono<BigDecimal> rate() { // a non-blocking FX lookup return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(20)).thenReturn(new BigDecimal("0.92")); } public static void main(String[] args) { // a timer emits on a parallel thread, just like a WebClient response emits on a Netty thread Mono<BigDecimal> usd = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10)).thenReturn(new BigDecimal("100")); try { usd.map(amount -> amount.multiply(rate().block())).block(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("1. block() inside map: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("2. flatMap instead: " + usd.flatMap(amount -> rate().map(amount::multiply)).block()); System.out.println("3. Mono.just(..).block() inside map: " + usd.map(amount -> amount.multiply(Mono.just(new BigDecimal("0.92")).block())).block() + " (a shortcut, not a permission)"); System.out.println("4. block() after publishOn(boundedElastic): " + usd.publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()).map(amount -> amount.multiply(rate().block())).block()); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l06.BlockInParallelDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l06/BlockInParallelDemo.java BlockInParallelDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l06 import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers import java.math.BigDecimal import java.time.Duration private fun rate(): Mono<BigDecimal> = // a non-blocking FX lookup Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(20)).thenReturn(BigDecimal("0.92")) /** block() on a Reactor parallel thread is refused. flatMap composes instead. */ fun main() { // a timer emits on a parallel thread, just like a WebClient response emits on a Netty thread val usd: Mono<BigDecimal> = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(10)).thenReturn(BigDecimal("100")) try { usd.map { amount -> amount.multiply(rate().block()) }.block() } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("1. block() inside map: ${e.message}") } println("2. flatMap instead: " + usd.flatMap { amount -> rate().map(amount::multiply) }.block()) println("3. Mono.just(..).block() inside map: " + usd.map { amount -> amount.multiply(Mono.just(BigDecimal("0.92")).block()) }.block() + " (a shortcut, not a permission)") println("4. block() after publishOn(boundedElastic): " + usd.publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()).map { amount -> amount.multiply(rate().block()) }.block()) } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l06.BlockInParallelDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l06/BlockInParallelDemo.kt Line 1 prints the block()/blockFirst()/blockLast() are blocking, which is not supported in thread parallel-1 message. Lines 2, 3 and 4 print 92.00: flatMap composes, Mono.just takes the scalar shortcut, and boundedElastic threads are allowed to block. With Mono.just as the amount, line 1 also prints 92.00, because map now runs on main. Same code, different thread, different result: that is why tests with Mono.just stubs miss this bug. BlockHound README read The most common mistake is putting subscribeOn(boundedElastic()) on the outer Flux of a flatMap and believing the calls now run in parallel. They run one after another on a single boundedElastic thread, so a batch of 200 lookups takes 200 times as long as one. People do it because subscribeOn "moves the work" and the code is shorter. The fix is to put subscribeOn on each inner Mono.fromCallable(...), ideally inside a small method like balance(account), and cap the fan-out with flatMap(this::balance, n).

h: Schedulers: publishOn, subscribeOn and blocking calls · Java and Kotlin
x: Choosing threads in Reactor and in coroutines StatementService.java (Reactor) // Reactor: say where each part of the chain runs Mono<Statement> statement(String account) { return Mono.fromCallable(() -> ledgerDao.lines(account)) // blocking JDBC call... .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // ...so the source runs here .publishOn(Schedulers.parallel()) // what follows runs here .map(lines -> pdf.render(lines)); // CPU-heavy rendering } StatementService.kt (coroutines) // Kotlin coroutines: switch the dispatcher around each block of work suspend fun statement(account: String): Statement { val lines = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { ledgerDao.lines(account) } // blocking JDBC call return withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { pdf.render(lines) } // CPU-heavy rendering } Reactor attaches threads to positions in a chain: subscribeOn picks where the source runs and publishOn picks where the rest runs. Coroutines attach them to blocks of code: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) runs the block on the IO dispatcher and comes back afterwards, so you read the thread switches top to bottom. The pools line up: Dispatchers.Default has one thread per core like parallel, and Dispatchers.IO is for blocking calls like boundedElastic. Kotlin Flow has one more twist: flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) changes where everything above it runs, which is closer to subscribeOn than to publishOn. kotlinx-coroutines-reactor bridges the two with Scheduler.asCoroutineDispatcher().

h: Schedulers: publishOn, subscribeOn and blocking calls · Worked example
x: Get a JDBC lookup off the I/O thread A payment-status endpoint takes the request as a Mono and looks the payment up in Oracle through a JDBC repository. Under load, every endpoint on the service slows down, not just this one. Find the cause before reading on. Mono<PaymentView> view(Mono<PaymentRequest> request) { return request .map(req -> repository.find(req.paymentId())) // JDBC, about 30 ms .map(PaymentView::from); } fun view(request: Mono<PaymentRequest>): Mono<PaymentView> = request .map { req -> repository.find(req.paymentId) } // JDBC, about 30 ms .map(PaymentView::from) The request arrives on one of the server's few event-loop threads, and map runs on whatever thread delivered the item. So the 30 ms JDBC call runs on the event loop. While it waits for Oracle, every other connection served by that loop waits too. Nothing throws, because the server's thread isn't one Reactor checks, and a unit test with Mono.just(request) runs it on the test thread and looks fine. Turn the lookup into its own inner Mono, wrapped and offloaded. The map after it now runs on the boundedElastic thread that finished the lookup, which is fine for a cheap conversion. A heavy step would get a publishOn(Schedulers.parallel()) first. Mono<PaymentView> view(Mono<PaymentRequest> request) { return request .flatMap(req -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> repository.find(req.paymentId())) // 1. wrap the blocking call .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())) // 2. run it off the I/O thread .map(PaymentView::from); // 3. continues on boundedElastic } fun view(request: Mono<PaymentRequest>): Mono<PaymentView> = request .flatMap { req -> Mono.fromCallable { repository.find(req.paymentId) } // 1. wrap the blocking call .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // 2. run it off the I/O thread } .map(PaymentView::from) // 3. continues on boundedElastic Pin it with a test. The trick is to make the request arrive on a non-blocking thread, the way production does, and record the thread the repository sees. @Test void lookupRunsOnBoundedElastic() { AtomicReference<String> thread = new AtomicReference<>(); repository.onFind(() -> thread.set(Thread.currentThread().getName())); Mono<PaymentRequest> request = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(5)) // 4. arrive on a non-blocking thread, .thenReturn(new PaymentRequest("pay-1")); // like the real server does StepVerifier.create(handler.view(request)).expectNextCount(1).verifyComplete(); assertThat(thread.get()).startsWith("boundedElastic-"); } @Test fun `lookup runs on boundedElastic`() { val thread = AtomicReference<String>() repository.onFind { thread.set(Thread.currentThread().name) } val request = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(5)) // 4. arrive on a non-blocking thread, .thenReturn(PaymentRequest("pay-1")) // like the real server does StepVerifier.create(handler.view(request)).expectNextCount(1).verifyComplete() assertThat(thread.get()).startsWith("boundedElastic-") }

h: Schedulers: publishOn, subscribeOn and blocking calls · Quiz
x: Where do A and B run? Java Flux.range(1, 3) .map(i -> i * 2) // A .publishOn(Schedulers.parallel()) .map(i -> i + 1) // B .subscribeOn(Schedulers.single()) .blockLast(); Kotlin Flux.range(1, 3) .map { i -> i * 2 } // A .publishOn(Schedulers.parallel()) .map { i -> i + 1 } // B .subscribeOn(Schedulers.single()) .blockLast() A on single-1, B on a parallel thread A on main, B on a parallel thread Both on single-1 A on a parallel thread, B on single-1 subscribeOn moves the subscription, so the synchronous range and the map right after it run on single-1, even though subscribeOn is written last. publishOn then moves everything below it to a parallel worker. The second option ignores subscribeOn; the last one mixes up which operator affects which direction. Mono.fromCallable(dao::load).subscribeOn(Schedulers.parallel()).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()). Where does dao.load run, and is that a problem? On boundedElastic, the last subscribeOn; fine On a parallel thread, the subscribeOn nearest the source; a problem if load blocks On both, one after the other On the calling thread, because two subscribeOn calls cancel out Only the subscribeOn nearest the source decides where the subscription reaches the source. The outer one adds a hop on the way up and nothing else. So a blocking load would run on one of the few parallel threads, which is the pool you must never block. A handler calls rates.current().block() inside a map. Its unit tests, which stub rates.current() with Mono.just(...), pass. In staging, where the item comes from a non-blocking HTTP client, it throws IllegalStateException. Why the difference? Staging runs a newer Reactor that bans block() everywhere In staging the map runs on a non-blocking thread, which Reactor checks; Mono.just(...).block() takes a shortcut and is never checked Mono.just is cold and the HTTP client is hot The unit tests forgot to call verify() In the tests everything runs on the test thread, and block() on a Mono.just returns the stored value without any check. In staging the item arrives on a thread marked non-blocking, so the real block() call is refused. Replace the block() with flatMap, and make test stubs emit on a non-blocking thread (for example via Mono.delay). You need the balances of 200 accounts from a blocking DAO, and the database pool has 20 connections. Which line fits? Flux.fromIterable(ids).flatMap(id -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> dao.balance(id))).subscribeOn(boundedElastic()) Flux.fromIterable(ids).flatMap(id -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> dao.balance(id)).subscribeOn(boundedElastic()), 20) Flux.fromIterable(ids).publishOn(boundedElastic()).map(dao::balance) Flux.fromIterable(ids).flatMap(id -> Mono.just(dao.balance(id)), 20) Each inner call carries its own subscribeOn, so up to 20 run at once on boundedElastic threads, matching the pool. The first option runs all 200 in turn on one thread. The third also runs them one by one, on one publishOn worker. The last calls the DAO while building each inner, on the caller's thread, so it blocks there. From "Pinning, ThreadLocals and other traps": you turn on the virtual-thread boundedElastic on JDK 21, and your JDBC driver blocks on socket reads inside synchronized methods. What happens during those reads? Nothing special: virtual threads always unmount when they block Each blocked virtual thread pins its carrier thread until the read returns, so carriers can run out Reactor detects it and moves the call to a platform thread The read throws IllegalStateException because boundedElastic is non-blocking On JDK 21 to 23, a virtual thread that blocks while holding a monitor can't unmount, so it holds its carrier (JDK 24 removed that limit, JEP 491). Reactor doesn't intervene. boundedElastic threads, virtual or not, are allowed to block, so there is no IllegalStateException either.

h: Schedulers: publishOn, subscribeOn and blocking calls · Key terms
x: Scheduler Reactor's source of threads, like an ExecutorService that is also a clock. publishOn Moves the operators after it onto a scheduler's thread. subscribeOn Moves the subscription, and so the source, onto a scheduler's thread. boundedElastic The shared scheduler for blocking calls: up to 10 threads per core, then a bounded queue. parallel scheduler The shared scheduler with one thread per core, for CPU work and timers. Never block on it. Non-blocking thread A thread marked with Reactor's NonBlocking interface; block() throws on it. BlockHound A Java agent from the Reactor team that detects blocking calls on non-blocking threads. With no scheduler anywhere, which thread runs a Reactor chain? The thread that called subscribe(). After a timer or an async client, the thread that delivered the item. What does publishOn(s) change? The thread of every operator after it (until the next publishOn), using one worker of s. What does subscribeOn(s) change? The thread of the subscription and request calls on their way up, so the source runs on s, wherever subscribeOn is written. Two subscribeOn calls in one chain: which one decides where the source runs? The one nearest the source. The other only adds a thread hop. How do you wrap a blocking call in Reactor? Mono.fromCallable(() -> blockingCall()).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) flatMap(x -> Mono.fromCallable(...)) followed by .subscribeOn(boundedElastic()): do the calls run concurrently? No. They run in turn on one boundedElastic thread. Put subscribeOn on each inner Mono. Mono.delay(d).map(x -> other.block()): what happens? IllegalStateException: block() is not supported on the parallel thread where the timer fired. Use flatMap.

h: Schedulers: publishOn, subscribeOn and blocking calls · Go deeper
x: ParallelFlux. For CPU-heavy work on many items, flux.parallel(4).runOn(Schedulers.parallel()).map(this::sign).sequential() splits the stream into 4 rails, runs each rail on its own parallel worker, and merges them back. Without runOn, the rails exist but share one thread. sequential() merges the rails as items finish, so the original order is lost. Tuning the shared schedulers. System properties set the sizes before the Schedulers class loads: reactor.schedulers.defaultPoolSize for parallel, reactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticSize (threads) and reactor.schedulers.defaultBoundedElasticQueueSize (queued tasks) for boundedElastic. Prefer a dedicated Schedulers.newBoundedElastic(20, 1_000, "oracle") per downstream, which works like a bulkhead from the executors track: one slow dependency can only exhaust its own threads. Dispose it on shutdown. publishOn prefetch. publishOn requests 256 items up front and then replenishes, so it also changes the demand the source sees. publishOn(scheduler, 32) lowers that. Lesson 7 of this track looks at demand in detail. Coroutines on a Reactor scheduler. kotlinx-coroutines-reactor has Schedulers.boundedElastic().asCoroutineDispatcher(), so coroutine code can share the same threads as the Reactor parts of a service.

h: Backpressure in practice · Demand is a number that travels up the chain
x: request(n) is the whole mechanism. A subscriber tells its publisher "I can take n more", the publisher sends at most n, and the subscriber asks again when it is ready. Lesson 1 of this track showed the contract. This lesson is about who sends those numbers in real code, and what happens when a source can't obey them. Most of the time it isn't you. subscribe(consumer), block() and blockLast() request Long.MAX_VALUE, which the spec treats as unbounded: send everything, as fast as you like. Then each operator between you and the source may change the number on its way up. Put doOnRequest right above an operator and you see what it sends: Between you and the source The source sees nothing (blockLast() alone) 9223372036854775807 take(3) 3 limitRate(10) 10, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8 publishOn(single()) 256, 192, 192, 192 flatMap(call, 4) 4, 1, 1, 1, 1 concatMap(call) 1, 1, 1, ... Operators with a queue inside (publishOn, limitRate, the inner queues of flatMap) prefetch a batch and refill it when about 75% of it has gone out. That keeps the source busy without unbounded buffering. When you need to control demand yourself, extend BaseSubscriber. Request a first batch in hookOnSubscribe, and more as you finish items: Java payments.subscribe(new BaseSubscriber<Payment>() { @Override protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) { request(2); } @Override protected void hookOnNext(Payment p) { post(p); request(1); } }); Kotlin payments.subscribe(object : BaseSubscriber<Payment>() { override fun hookOnSubscribe(s: Subscription) { request(2) } override fun hookOnNext(p: Payment) { post(p); request(1) } }) Now the part that matters. A source that honours request(n) simply produces less when nobody asks: Flux.range, a database cursor, a paged API client, a Kafka adapter that polls only on demand. Backpressure then works from end to end, and you never have to think about it. A source that can't slow down (a ticker, a WebSocket, a callback API bridged with Flux.create) has to put the extra items somewhere. The third section is about that choice. Watch the requests DemandDemo first runs a BaseSubscriber that asks for 2, then 1 more after each item. Then it puts doOnRequest above five different operators and prints what the source received. Before running, write down your guess for each of the five lines. Run it. Then change limitRate(10) to limitRate(10, 0) and predict the new line. DemandDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l07; import org.reactivestreams.Subscription; import reactor.core.publisher.BaseSubscriber; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.function.Function; /** Demand made visible: the requests that reach the source, for one subscriber and five operators. */ public class DemandDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("1. a subscriber that asks for 2, then 1 more after each item"); Flux.range(1, 4) .doOnRequest(n -> System.out.println(" request(" + n + ")")) .subscribe(new BaseSubscriber<Integer>() { @Override protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) { request(2); } @Override protected void hookOnNext(Integer item) { System.out.println(" got " + item); request(1); } }); show("2. blockLast() alone", Flux.range(1, 40), f -> f); show("3. take(3)", Flux.range(1, 40), f -> f.take(3)); show("4. limitRate(10)", Flux.range(1, 40), f -> f.limitRate(10)); show("5. publishOn(single())", Flux.range(1, 600), f -> f.publishOn(Schedulers.single())); Reactor reference: Introduction to reactive programming, on backpressure (source, 3.8.x) docs Think of a coffee bar. Real backpressure is the barista taking the next order only when a hand is free: the queue simply waits at the door, which is a source that honours request(n). limitRate is taking orders ten at a time instead of all at once. A source that can't slow down is a conveyor belt of cups that won't stop, and someone has to decide: stack them on a shelf of ten and call the manager when it's full (a bounded buffer that fails), let them fall off (drop), or keep only the last cup (latest). flatMap(call, 20) is a machine with 20 heads: never more than 20 brews at once. The analogy breaks at the shelf. A real shelf that overflows is easy to see. In Reactor, onBackpressureBuffer() with no size is a shelf you can't see, and it grows until the JVM runs out of heap.

h: Backpressure in practice · Use limitRate to turn one big request into small ones
x: A database cursor or a paging client that fetches "as many rows as were requested" does exactly that. Hand it the Long.MAX_VALUE of a plain subscribe or blockLast() (the first section), and it tries to fetch the whole table at once. limitRate(n) sits between a subscriber that asks for a lot and a source that should only be asked for a little. It requests n, then tops up by 75% of n each time 75% of the last batch has been delivered. Flux.range(1, 40).limitRate(10) sends 10, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8 upstream. Unlike take, it never cuts the stream short: every item still arrives, in batches. Use it when the size of the request changes what the source does. With limitRate(100) in front, the export still streams every row, but the cursor never has more than one batch of about 100 in flight: Java Flux<LedgerRow> export = cursor.rows(day) .limitRate(100) // the cursor sees 100, then 75 at a time .concatMap(uploader::send); Kotlin val export: Flux<LedgerRow> = cursor.rows(day) .limitRate(100) // the cursor sees 100, then 75 at a time .concatMap(uploader::send) limitRate(highTide, lowTide) sets both numbers. limitRate(10, 0) asks for exactly 10 and waits until all 10 have arrived before asking again (10, 10, 10, 10, 10), which suits an API that works in fixed pages. Its Javadoc says limitRate(n) is equivalent to publishOn(Schedulers.immediate(), n): the same prefetch-and-refill queue, without the thread switch. Know what it doesn't do. limitRate shapes demand; it doesn't make a slow consumer faster, and it can't help with a source that ignores demand. It also isn't a rate limit in the "per second" sense, despite the name: it counts items, not time. The last section shows how to protect a service you call, and why that isn't a per-second limit either. Quick check: predict the first three requests that Flux.range(1, 100) sees under .limitRate(20).blockLast(), and what changes with limitRate(20, 0). (20, then 15 and 15, because it tops up by 75% of 20. With a low tide of 0 it asks for 20 each time, and only after the whole batch has arrived.) limitRate sits between an unbounded request and a source that should be asked for little: the source sees 10, then 8 at a time, and every row still arrives. In payments the loss policy is a business decision, so make it in code where a reviewer can see it. An FX rate feed to a pricing screen wants onBackpressureLatest. Card authorizations and audit events must never be dropped silently, so they get a bounded buffer that fails loudly, plus a way to resume (Kafka offsets, the gateway's last acknowledged id). Metrics samples can be dropped. Calls out of your service are the other half: the issuer, the bank's settlement API and your Oracle pool each have a limit, and flatMap's concurrency should match the smallest of them. Quarkus's Mutiny has the same choices under onOverflow(), and the same reasoning applies.

h: Backpressure in practice · When the source can't slow down, choose what to lose
x: Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(1)) ticks once a millisecond, whatever you request. Put a screen behind it that takes 10 ms per tick and asks for one at a time, and the second tick fails the stream: OverflowException: Could not emit tick 1 due to lack of requests. Any source that can't be paused behaves like this, or worse, quietly piles items up: a WebSocket of FX prices, a multicast sink, a callback API. The onBackpressure operators make the choice explicit. Each one requests unbounded from the source, so the source never overflows, and then decides what to do with the items nobody downstream asked for: Operator Items with no demand Use it for onBackpressureBuffer(n) keeps up to n, then cancels the source and fails bursts you must not lose onBackpressureBuffer() keeps all of them almost nothing: the backlog grows until the heap runs out onBackpressureDrop(onDropped) drops them, calling onDropped samples, metrics, best-effort events onBackpressureLatest() keeps only the newest prices, positions, statuses: newer replaces older onBackpressureError() fails at once cases where falling behind is a bug Same ticker, same 10 ms screen, 20 frames. Drop showed ticks about 11 apart and threw away about 200. Latest also showed roughly every tenth tick, always the newest one at the moment the screen asked. onBackpressureBuffer(10) delivered ticks 0 to 11 in order, then failed with an overflow error once the buffer was drained. The unbounded buffer delivered 0 to 19 in order, which looks perfect, while the ticker had reached 204: more than 180 ticks were waiting in memory, and that number only grows. So the name misleads a little. None of these operators slows the source down. They are loss policies: they decide what to keep and what to give up. Real backpressure needs a source that honours request(n). When you have a choice of client or API, pick one that does. When you bridge a callback API yourself, make the same choice at the bridge: Flux.create(sink -> ..., FluxSink.OverflowStrategy.LATEST). The default strategy of Flux.create is BUFFER, the unbounded one. One ticker, five policies OverflowDemo runs a 1 ms ticker into a screen that asks for one tick at a time and takes 10 ms to draw each. It tries no strategy, then drop, latest, a buffer of 10 and an unbounded buffer, for 20 frames each. Predict, for each run, which ticks the screen gets and whether it ends with an error. Run it. For the last run, compare "ticker reached" with the number of ticks the screen got. Where are the others? h: Backpressure in practice · flatMap's concurrency protects the services you call
x: Demand also flows from your service toward the services it calls. Each inner publisher in a flatMap is an open request to somebody: the bank's settlement API, Oracle, the fraud service. And flatMap's default concurrency is 256. In the demo, the bank allows 20 open requests per client and answers in 50 ms. payments.flatMap(this::settle) over 200 payments opens all 200 at once: 20 settle and 180 come back as 429 Too Many Requests. payments.flatMap(this::settle, 20) keeps 20 open at a time, and all 200 settle in about 500 ms: ten rounds of 50 ms. The cap didn't slow down anything the bank would have accepted. It stopped 180 requests that were never going to work. Java Flux<Receipt> receipts = payments.flatMap(bank::settle, 20); // never more than 20 open requests Kotlin val receipts: Flux<Receipt> = payments.flatMap(bank::settle, 20) // never more than 20 open requests The source is backpressured too. flatMap requests 20 payments, subscribes to 20 calls, and requests one more payment each time a call finishes (the 4, 1, 1, 1, 1 pattern from the first section). So a Kafka adapter that polls on demand is never read faster than the bank answers. Pick the number from the smallest limit on the path, the downstream ceiling from the executors track: the bank's open-request limit, the connection pool, the fraud API's quota. Little's law connects them: 20 open requests of 50 ms each is at most 400 calls per second. A limit of so many calls per second is a different thing, because flatMap caps how many are open, not how many start per second. If the bank also had a per-second quota, you would add a rate limiter as well. concatMap is the extreme case, concurrency 1. Use flatMapSequential(call, 20) from lesson 3 of this track when you need the results in input order. Respect the bank's limit RateLimitDemo settles 200 payments against a fake bank that allows 20 open requests and refuses the 21st with a 429. Each refused call is skipped with onErrorResume, so the batch keeps going. Predict both lines: how many settle, how many are refused, and roughly how long each run takes. Run it. Then change the 20 in the second run to 25 and predict again. RateLimitDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l07; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.Function; /** 200 settlement calls against a bank that allows 20 open requests per client. */ public class RateLimitDemo { static final Semaphore openRequests = new Semaphore(20); static final AtomicInteger refused = new AtomicInteger(); // the bank: 50 ms per call, and a 21st concurrent request is refused with a 429 static Mono<String> bankCall(int id) { return Mono.defer(() -> { if (!openRequests.tryAcquire()) { refused.incrementAndGet(); return Mono.error(new IllegalStateException("429 Too Many Requests")); } return Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(50)).map(tick -> { openRequests.release(); // the response frees the slot return "receipt-" + id; }); }); } static void run(String title, Function<Flux<Integer>, Flux<String>> settle) { refused.set(0); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long settled = settle.apply(Flux.range(1, 200)).count().block(); System.out.printf("%-22s %3d settled, %3d refused with 429, in %3d ms%n", title, settled, refused.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } public static void main(String[] args) { bankCall(0).block(); // warm-up, so the timings below are fair // a refused call is skipped, so one 429 doesn't end the whole batch (lesson 5 of this track) run("1. flatMap(call)", f -> f.flatMap(id -> bankCall(id).onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty()))); run("2. flatMap(call, 20)", f -> f.flatMap(id -> bankCall(id).onErrorResume(e -> Mono.empty()), 20)); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l07.RateLimitDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l07/RateLimitDemo.java RateLimitDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l07 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.time.Duration import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private val openRequests = Semaphore(20) private val refused = AtomicInteger() // the bank: 50 ms per call, and a 21st concurrent request is refused with a 429 private fun bankCall(id: Int): Mono<String> = Mono.defer { if (!openRequests.tryAcquire()) { refused.incrementAndGet() Mono.error(IllegalStateException("429 Too Many Requests")) } else { Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(50)).map { openRequests.release() // the response frees the slot "receipt-$id" } } } private fun run(title: String, settle: (Flux<Int>) -> Flux<String>) { refused.set(0) val t0 = System.nanoTime() val settled = settle(Flux.range(1, 200)).count().block() println("%-22s %3d settled, %3d refused with 429, in %3d ms".format( title, settled, refused.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } /** 200 settlement calls against a bank that allows 20 open requests per client. */ fun main() { bankCall(0).block() // warm-up, so the timings below are fair // a refused call is skipped, so one 429 doesn't end the whole batch (lesson 5 of this track) run("1. flatMap(call)") { f -> f.flatMap { id -> bankCall(id).onErrorResume { Mono.empty() } } } run("2. flatMap(call, 20)") { f -> f.flatMap({ id -> bankCall(id).onErrorResume { Mono.empty() } }, 20) } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l07.RateLimitDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l07/RateLimitDemo.kt With the default concurrency of 256, all 200 calls open at once: 20 settle and 180 are refused, in well under a second. With a cap of 20, all 200 settle and none are refused, in about 500 ms (ten rounds of 50 ms). With 25, about 5 calls per round are refused, so you lose settlements while gaining nothing: the cap has to match the smallest limit on the path. The most common mistake is fixing an OverflowException with onBackpressureBuffer() and no size. The error goes away, the tests pass, and in production the buffer quietly holds everything the consumer hasn't caught up with, until a busy morning turns it into an OutOfMemoryError far from the cause. People reach for it because the name sounds like the fix. Decide instead what may be lost: give the buffer a size and a callback (onBackpressureBuffer(10_000, e -> log.error(...))) for data you must keep, onBackpressureLatest for values where newer replaces older, onBackpressureDrop for samples, and prefer a source that honours demand when you have the choice.

h: Backpressure in practice · Java and Kotlin
x: Loss policies and concurrency caps in Reactor and Kotlin Flow Feeds.java (Reactor) // Reactor: say what happens when the consumer can't keep up Flux<Tick> screen = ticks.onBackpressureLatest(); // keep only the newest Flux<AuditEvent> audit = events.onBackpressureBuffer(1_000); // hold 1,000, then fail loudly Flux<Receipt> receipts = payments.flatMap(bank::settle, 20); // at most 20 calls in flight Feeds.kt (Kotlin Flow) // Kotlin Flow: a slow collector suspends the emitter, unless a buffer sits between them val screen: Flow<Tick> = ticks.conflate() // keep only the newest val audit: Flow<AuditEvent> = events.buffer(1_000) // hold 1,000, then the emitter suspends @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) val receipts: Flow<Receipt> = payments.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 20) { p -> flow { emit(bank.settle(p)) } } // at most 20 at once Reactor's backpressure is a number sent upstream with request(n). Kotlin Flow's is suspension: emit() simply doesn't return until the collector is ready, so a cold flow can't overflow and has no demand numbers to reshape. The policies only matter when something puts a buffer between producer and collector: buffer, flowOn, or a hot callbackFlow or SharedFlow. conflate() keeps the newest, like onBackpressureLatest. buffer(1_000) suspends the emitter when full instead of failing, and buffer(n, BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST) or DROP_OLDEST drops. A callback API can't suspend, so inside callbackFlow you call trySend and must handle its failure: that is the place where Flow makes you choose. flatMapMerge(concurrency = 20) is the twin of flatMap(call, 20), and in kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 it still needs an opt-in.

h: Backpressure in practice · Worked example
x: Stop a fraud-scoring stream from eating the heap A service receives payment events from a gateway's listener API and scores each one with the fraud service. During the morning peak, heap use climbs for an hour and the pod is killed. The fraud team also reports bursts of 250 concurrent calls from this one client. Find both causes. Flux<PaymentEvent> events = Flux.create(sink -> gateway.onEvent(sink::next)); // push-only listener API events.flatMap(fraud::score) // about 30 ms per call .subscribe(scores::save); val events: Flux<PaymentEvent> = Flux.create { sink -> gateway.onEvent(sink::next) } // push-only listener API events.flatMap(fraud::score) // about 30 ms per call .subscribe(scores::save) Two defaults. Flux.create with no strategy uses BUFFER, which is unbounded: whatever the listener pushes while nobody is asking waits in memory. And flatMap without a number runs up to 256 scoring calls at once. The fraud API allows 50 per client, so most of the extra calls fail, and an error is terminal (lesson 5 of this track), so the stream can die as well as leak. Make each decision visible. Events must not be lost, but the gateway can replay from an event id, so a bounded buffer that fails is safe. The concurrency comes from the fraud API's limit. Flux.create((FluxSink<PaymentEvent> sink) -> gateway.onEvent(sink::next)) .onBackpressureBuffer(10_000, // 1. a bounded backlog... e -> log.error("backlog full at event {}", e.id())) // ...that says when it overflows .flatMap(fraud::score, 50) // 2. the fraud API's limit, not 256 .subscribe(scores::save, e -> gateway.resumeFrom(lastSavedId())); // 3. on overflow, replay from the last saved event Flux.create { sink: FluxSink<PaymentEvent> -> gateway.onEvent(sink::next) } .onBackpressureBuffer(10_000) { e -> // 1. a bounded backlog... log.error("backlog full at event {}", e.id) } // ...that says when it overflows .flatMap(fraud::score, 50) // 2. the fraud API's limit, not 256 .subscribe(scores::save) { gateway.resumeFrom(lastSavedId()) } // 3. on overflow, replay from the last saved event Now check the size with numbers, not hope. 50 calls in flight at 30 ms each finish at most about 1,666 scores per second (Little's law: 50 / 0.03 s). The morning peak sends 2,000 events per second, so the backlog grows by about 334 per second, and 10,000 slots last about 30 seconds. A burst of a few seconds fits. A peak that lasts an hour doesn't fit any buffer: it needs a faster consumer, more instances, or a source that can be told to wait. A buffer only absorbs bursts; it never fixes a consumer that is slower on average.

h: Backpressure in practice · Quiz
x: A nightly export does cursor.rows().limitRate(100).concatMap(upload). What requests does the cursor receive? One request for Long.MAX_VALUE 100, then 75 at a time 100, then nothing: limitRate stops after 100 rows 1 at a time, because of concatMap limitRate(100) requests 100 and tops up by 75 each time 75 have been delivered, however much the downstream asks for. Unlike take(100), it never ends the stream early. concatMap asks limitRate for one item at a time, but limitRate decides what reaches the cursor. A pricing screen shows the live EUR/USD rate from a feed that ticks 200 times a second. The screen redraws 10 times a second. Which policy fits? onBackpressureBuffer() onBackpressureBuffer(1_000) onBackpressureDrop() onBackpressureLatest() A rate is a value where newer replaces older: when the screen asks, it wants the newest tick. onBackpressureDrop would show whichever tick arrives after the screen asks, which is fresh too, but it may wait for the next tick and it throws away the newest one on hand. Both buffers would show stale rates, in order, getting further behind. Audit events arrive from a source that can't slow down. None may be lost silently, and bursts of a few hundred are normal. Which line fits best? events.onBackpressureBuffer() events.onBackpressureBuffer(1_000, e -> log.error("audit overflow at {}", e.id())) events.onBackpressureLatest() events.limitRate(100) A bounded buffer absorbs the normal bursts, and if the subscriber falls further behind, it cancels the source, logs the overflowing event and ends with an overflow error, so the gap is visible. The unbounded buffer never reports anything until memory runs out. onBackpressureLatest loses events silently. limitRate changes requests, which a source that ignores demand doesn't read. Flux.fromIterable(payments).flatMap(bank::settle) runs 300 settlements. The bank allows 20 open requests per client and answers the rest with 429. What happens, and what is the fix? All 300 settle, just more slowly; no fix needed flatMap opens up to 256 calls at once, most get a 429, and the first error can end the stream; use flatMap(bank::settle, 20) flatMap opens one call at a time; use flatMap(bank::settle, 20) to speed it up Add limitRate(20) before flatMap The default concurrency is 256, so far more than 20 requests are open at once, and an unhandled 429 is a terminal error. Capping flatMap at 20 matches the bank. limitRate(20) only changes how many payments are requested from the list at a time; flatMap would still subscribe to as many calls as it has payments, up to 256. From "Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law": flatMap(bank::settle, 20) and each call takes 50 ms. What is the most this can settle per second? 20 50 400 1,000 Little's law: in flight = rate x time, so rate = 20 / 0.05 s = 400 per second. To go faster you need more open requests (if the bank allows them) or faster calls. A per-second quota from the bank is a separate limit that a concurrency cap doesn't enforce.

h: Backpressure in practice · Explain it back
x: A teammate got OverflowException: Could not emit tick ... due to lack of requests and wants to add onBackpressureBuffer() because "that's what backpressure is for". Explain what backpressure really is in Reactor, why their fix is risky, and what you would ask before choosing a fix.

h: Backpressure in practice · Key terms
x: Demand How many more items a subscriber has asked for with request(n) and not yet received. Unbounded demand A request of Long.MAX_VALUE: send everything, as fast as you can. limitRate An operator that splits downstream demand into batches of n requested from upstream. Loss policy Buffer, drop, keep the latest, or fail: what to do with items a source pushes without demand. OverflowException Reactor's error for more items than were requested, from a source or a full bounded buffer. Concurrency cap The most inner publishers flatMap subscribes at once; 256 by default. What does subscribe(consumer) request from the source? Long.MAX_VALUE: unbounded demand, unless an operator in between reshapes it. Flux.range(1, 40).limitRate(10): what does the range see? request(10), then request(8) five times: it tops up by 75% of the batch. limitRate(100) vs take(100)? limitRate caps each request and still delivers every item. take caps the request and ends the stream after 100. Does onBackpressureDrop (or Buffer, Latest) slow the source down? No. They all request unbounded upstream and decide what to do with items nobody asked for. A slow subscriber finally requests 1. What does it get from onBackpressureLatest vs onBackpressureDrop? Latest: the newest item that arrived while it wasn't asking. Drop: nothing until the next item arrives after the request. What happens when onBackpressureBuffer(1000) overflows? It cancels the source, and after the subscriber drains the 1,000 held items, it ends with an overflow error. What is Flux.create's default overflow strategy? BUFFER: unbounded. Pass a FluxSink.OverflowStrategy (DROP, LATEST, ERROR) to choose.

h: Backpressure in practice · Go deeper
x: Sources that pull. Flux.generate calls your generator once per requested item, so it is backpressured by construction: good for paging through an API or reading a file line by line. Flux.create gives you a FluxSink for push APIs, and sink.onRequest(n -> ...) lets you pull n items from an API that supports it, which turns a push bridge into a real backpressured source. More buffer options. onBackpressureBuffer(maxSize, onOverflow, BufferOverflowStrategy.DROP_OLDEST) keeps the buffer bounded but evicts old items instead of failing (DROP_LATEST and ERROR are the other strategies). onBackpressureBuffer(Duration ttl, int maxSize, onEvicted) also evicts items older than the ttl, for data that goes stale. Prefetch everywhere. Many operators take a prefetch argument: flatMap(fn, concurrency, prefetch) sets how many items each inner is asked for (32 by default), concatMap(fn, prefetch) and publishOn(scheduler, prefetch) likewise. Smaller numbers mean less memory and more request round trips. Demand across the network. Reactive Streams demand stops at the process boundary. RSocket carries request(n) across the wire. HTTP has no request(n) of its own: a server streaming to a slow client relies on TCP flow control, and it is the server library's job to turn a full socket into lower demand on your Flux. Deprecated name. limitRequest(n) is deprecated in favour of take(n), which in 3.8 caps the upstream request at n by default.

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Cold sources run per subscriber; hot ones are shared
x: A cold publisher does its work again for every subscriber (lesson 2 of this track). That is right for an HTTP call per request. It is wrong for a WebSocket of FX rates that six dashboards open: six connections to the provider, six copies of the same ticks. A hot publisher produces whether or not anyone listens, and subscribers share what it produces from the moment they join. Reactor turns cold into hot with a few operators. They differ in two decisions: when to connect to the source, and what a subscriber that joins late receives. Operator Connects A late subscriber gets Disconnects share(), which is publish().refCount() at the first subscriber only new items when the last one leaves replay(n).refCount() at the first subscriber the last n items, then new ones when the last one leaves publish().autoConnect(n) when n have subscribed only new items never cache() at the first subscriber every item, from the start never In the demo a feed emits a rate every 100 ms and dashboard B joins at 250 ms. Cold, B opens a second connection and starts from the first rate. With share(), B gets only the rates from 300 ms on. With replay(1).refCount(), B immediately gets the 200 ms rate, then the live ones. With cache(), B gets all of them, including the two it missed, and the cache keeps every item for as long as the Flux lives. For a long-running feed that is a memory leak, so prefer replay(n) or cache(n). Mono.cache(ttl) is the right tool for a value that should be reloaded now and then, such as a fee schedule. Two details matter in production. publish follows the slowest subscriber: it requests from the source only what every subscriber can take, so one slow dashboard slows them all (combine it with a policy from lesson 7 of this track). And refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)) adds a grace period: when the last subscriber leaves, it waits 5 seconds before disconnecting, so a dashboard that refreshes the page doesn't make you reconnect to the provider. Five ways to share one feed HotColdDemo runs a cold feed (a rate every 100 ms, five rates) with dashboard A subscribing at once and B 250 ms later. It tries cold, share(), replay(1).refCount(), cache() and publish().autoConnect(2). For each run, predict the number of connections and what B receives. Run it. Then explain the autoConnect(2) line: why does A get all five rates, starting late? Reactor reference: Hot versus cold (source, 3.8.x) docs Reactor reference: Broadcasting to multiple subscribers with ConnectableFlux (source, 3.8.x) docs Cold is video on demand: everyone who presses play gets the film from the start, and the studio streams one copy per viewer. share() is live TV: one broadcast, and if you switch on late, you missed the start. replay(1) is live TV that shows you the last scene when you switch on. cache() is a recorder that keeps the whole broadcast forever, so every newcomer can watch from the beginning, and the recordings pile up. A sink is the studio's microphone, which only one presenter may speak into at a time. The analogy breaks at the end of the evening: a TV station keeps broadcasting to an empty room, while refCount switches the transmitter off when the last viewer leaves.

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Sinks push values in from ordinary code
x: Sometimes the values come from ordinary code: a Kafka listener callback, a webhook handler, a scheduled job. Sinks is Reactor's safe way to push them into a Flux. (Processors used to do this; Reactor has phased them out in favour of Sinks.) Java Sinks.Many<PaymentEvent> sink = Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort(); Flux<PaymentEvent> live = sink.asFlux(); // what subscribers see Sinks.EmitResult result = sink.tryEmitNext(event); // what the listener calls Kotlin val sink: Sinks.Many<PaymentEvent> = Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort() val live: Flux<PaymentEvent> = sink.asFlux() // what subscribers see val result: Sinks.EmitResult = sink.tryEmitNext(event) // what the listener calls Sinks.many().multicast() sends each item to the subscribers present at that moment, in three flavours. onBackpressureBuffer() buffers for slow subscribers and keeps items pushed before the first subscriber arrives for it. By default it also shuts down for good when its last subscriber leaves: a subscriber that comes later just receives onComplete. directBestEffort() keeps no buffer: a subscriber that isn't asking misses the item, and the sink keeps working with zero subscribers. directAllOrNothing() drops the item for everyone if one subscriber isn't ready. Then many().replay() keeps history for late subscribers (all(), limit(n), limit(Duration), latest()), many().unicast() allows exactly one subscriber, and Sinks.one() and Sinks.empty() carry a single value or a bare completion. The trap is threads. tryEmitNext never blocks and never retries. If two threads call it at the same moment, one of them gets EmitResult.FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED and its item is not emitted. This is rule 1.3 from lesson 1 of this track at work: a subscriber must never get two signals at once. The sink detects the overlap, and instead of breaking the rule, it fails the second call. Ignore the result and items vanish. In my runs of the demo, 8 threads emitting 10,000 items each delivered only a few thousand of the 80,000. Either check every result, or call emitNext(item, handler) with a handler that retries. Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) spins until the sink is free, for up to a second. Its Javadoc asks you not to keep and reuse it, so create one per call. Wrapping the emit in a lock works too. Who gets what from a sink SinksDemo pushes values into a multicast sink before and between two subscribers, checks two multicast flavours after every subscriber has left, fills a replay().limit(2) sink, tries two subscribers on a unicast sink, and finally lets 8 threads emit 10,000 items each, first with tryEmitNext, then with emitNext and busyLooping. Predict each line before you run it. For the race, guess how many of the 80,000 items arrive. Run it twice and compare the race numbers. Who receives what, and what happens with 8 threads? */ public class SinksDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Sinks.Many<Integer> multicast = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(); List<Integer> early = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); List<Integer> late = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); multicast.tryEmitNext(10); // nobody is subscribed yet multicast.asFlux().subscribe(early::add); After everyone left, the onBackpressureBuffer() sink only completes the new subscriber, while directBestEffort() delivers got 42. Replay with limit 2: [2, 3]. Unicast: the second subscriber fails with Sinks.many().unicast() sinks only allow a single Subscriber. The tryEmitNext race delivers only a few thousand of 80,000, with a different number each run; emitNext with busyLooping delivers all 80,000. Reactor reference: Sinks (source, 3.8.x) docs Picture a payment operations service. A Kafka consumer pushes authorization events into a sink, and dashboards follow them over server-sent events: that is a multicast directBestEffort sink with a thread-safe emit, because Kafka listener threads run concurrently and dashboards come and go. The FX rates come from one provider connection that a dozen screens share with replay(1).refCount(1, grace). The fee schedule is read from Oracle at most once every five minutes with Mono.cache(ttl). Every one of those has timing in it, so each gets a virtual-time test that runs in milliseconds in CI. And when a new service is plain request and response over Oracle, you build it on virtual threads instead.

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · StepVerifier checks the signals, and virtual time fakes the clock
x: A reactive test has to subscribe, check each signal in order, and fail when anything else happens. StepVerifier from reactor-test does that: Java StepVerifier.create(checkout.quote("m-1", "c-1")) .expectNext(expectedQuote) .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); Kotlin StepVerifier.create(checkout.quote("m-1", "c-1")) .expectNext(expectedQuote) .expectComplete() .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) Four rules, each learned from a test that lied: Nothing runs until verify() (or a shortcut such as verifyComplete() or verifyError()). A test that ends at expectComplete() never subscribes, and passes whatever the code does. verify() has no timeout by default, so a hung publisher hangs the build. Pass a Duration, or set StepVerifier.setDefaultTimeout(...) once. StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> ...) replaces Reactor's schedulers with a virtual clock, so a one-day delay is verified in milliseconds. Build the publisher inside the supplier: a Mono.delay built earlier has already picked the real clock, and the test times out. expectNoEvent(d) checks that nothing happens during d of virtual time. The subscription counts as an event, so put expectSubscription() first. For a source you drive by hand there is TestPublisher: call next(...), complete() or error(...) from the test, then check wasCancelled() or assertMinRequested(n). TestPublisher.create() respects demand like a real source and fails if pushed without it; createNoncompliant(...) breaks the spec on purpose (lesson 1 of this track). PublisherProbe answers a different question: was this branch subscribed at all? Use it to prove that a switchIfEmpty fallback ran, or didn't. All the virtual-time tests in this track's labs, from the backoff in lesson 5 to the bank calls in lesson 7, are built from these pieces. Break four StepVerifier rules StepVerifierDemo runs five small tests: one without verify(), a one-day delay under virtual time, expectNoEvent as the first step, a delay built outside the virtual-time supplier, and a TestPublisher driven by hand. (It runs from src/demo, so the lab's build adds reactor-test to the demo classpath.) Predict which ones pass, which fail, and with what message. Run it. In part 1, add .verify() to the end of the line and run again. h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Debugging: name the place with checkpoint, watch the signals with log
x: A stack trace from a reactive chain shows where the error was raised and how the subscription got there. It almost never shows where you wrote the operator that failed. In the demo, Flux.just(120, 80).single() inside a feeRow() method fails with IndexOutOfBoundsException: Source emitted more than one item. The top frame is Reactor's MonoSingle, and no frame of the trace is in feeRow(). Lesson 2 of this track explains why: feeRow() only assembled the chain and returned. By the time single() sees the second row, the data pass is running, and the frame of feeRow() is long gone. checkpoint("fee-row") marks a point in the chain. When an error passes through it, Reactor attaches a suppressed exception that reads Error has been observed at the following site(s): followed by *__checkpoint and fee-row. It is cheap, so put one at the edges of your own pipelines, named after what they do. checkpoint("fee-row", true) also records a stack trace when the chain is assembled, which points at the line in your code, at the cost of capturing that trace every time the chain is built. Hooks.onOperatorDebug() does that for every operator in the application. The reference guide calls it a last resort because of the cost. For production there is the reactor-tools agent (ReactorDebugAgent.init() as the first line of main), which adds the same information by instrumenting your classes when they load. It is a separate dependency and not in the labs. Java Mono<Integer> fee = feeRow(merchant).checkpoint("fee-row"); // name the place, cheaply Flux<Integer> rows = Flux.range(1, 5).log("rows").take(2); // print every signal at this point Kotlin val fee: Mono<Int> = feeRow(merchant).checkpoint("fee-row") // name the place, cheaply val rows: Flux<Int> = Flux.range(1, 5).log("rows").take(2) // print every signal at this point log("rows") prints every signal that passes that point: onSubscribe, request(2), onNext(1), onNext(2), cancel(). It is the quickest way to see this track's ideas in a real chain: the demand from lesson 7, the cancellation that take sends upstream, the thread each signal arrives on. It logs through SLF4J when that is on the classpath. Find the operator that failed DebugDemo runs a chain whose single() sees two fee rows, three times: plain, with checkpoint("fee-row"), and with checkpoint("fee-row", true). Then it puts log("rows") between a range and take(2). Run it. For each of the first three, find the information that tells you where the failing operator was written. Predict the log output first: which request and which last signal will it show? DebugDemo.java package workbench.reactive.l08; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.util.Arrays; /** Where did it fail? An operator error without help, with checkpoints, and the signals log() shows. */ public class DebugDemo { // assembled here, far away from where it is subscribed: the merchant has two fee rows, the code expects one static Mono<Integer> feeRow(String merchant) { return Flux.just(120, 80).single(); } static void show(String title, Mono<Integer> chain) { try { chain.block(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { boolean mentionsFeeRow = Arrays.stream(e.getStackTrace()).anyMatch(f -> f.getMethodName().equals("feeRow")); System.out.println(title); System.out.println(" " + e); System.out.println(" top frame: " + e.getStackTrace()[0]); System.out.println(" any frame in feeRow(), where single() was written? " + mentionsFeeRow); for (Throwable s : e.getSuppressed()) { s.getMessage().lines() .filter(l -> !l.isBlank() && !l.contains("#block")) .limit(4) .map(l -> l.replace("⇢", "->")) // Reactor prints an arrow here .forEach(l -> System.out.println(" " + l.strip())); } } } public static void main(String[] args) { show("1. no help", feeRow("m-1").map(fee -> fee + 1)); show("2. checkpoint(\"fee-row\")", feeRow("m-1").checkpoint("fee-row").map(fee -> fee + 1)); show("3. checkpoint(\"fee-row\", true)", feeRow("m-1").checkpoint("fee-row", true).map(fee -> fee + 1)); System.out.println("4. log(\"rows\") between a range and take(2)"); Flux.range(1, 5).log("rows").take(2).blockLast(); } } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l08.DebugDemo labs/reactive/src/demo/java/workbench/reactive/l08/DebugDemo.java DebugDemo.kt package workbench.reactive.l08 import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono // assembled here, far away from where it is subscribed: the merchant has two fee rows, the code expects one private fun feeRow(merchant: String): Mono<Int> = Flux.just(120, 80).single() private fun show(title: String, chain: Mono<Int>) { try { chain.block() } catch (e: RuntimeException) { val mentionsFeeRow = e.stackTrace.any { it.methodName.startsWith("feeRow") } println(title) println(" $e") println(" top frame: ${e.stackTrace[0]}") println(" any frame in feeRow(), where single() was written? $mentionsFeeRow") for (s in e.suppressed) { s.message.orEmpty().lines() .filter { it.isNotBlank() && "#block" !in it } .take(4) .map { it.replace("⇢", "->") } // Reactor prints an arrow here .forEach { println(" ${it.trim()}") } } } } /** Where did it fail? An operator error without help, with checkpoints, and the signals log() shows. */ fun main() { show("1. no help", feeRow("m-1").map { fee -> fee + 1 }) show("2. checkpoint(\"fee-row\")", feeRow("m-1").checkpoint("fee-row").map { fee -> fee + 1 }) show("3. checkpoint(\"fee-row\", true)", feeRow("m-1").checkpoint("fee-row", true).map { fee -> fee + 1 }) println("4. log(\"rows\") between a range and take(2)") Flux.range(1, 5).log("rows").take(2).blockLast() } ./gradlew :reactive:demo -Pmain=workbench.reactive.l08.DebugDemoKt labs/reactive/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/reactive/l08/DebugDemo.kt All three report IndexOutOfBoundsException: Source emitted more than one item with MonoSingle as the top frame, and no frame in feeRow(). The plain run gives no clue where it came from. The checkpoint run names fee-row. The run with true adds an assembly trace pointing at the main line where the checkpoint was written. The log shows onSubscribe, request(2), onNext(1), onNext(2) and cancel(): take(2) capped the demand and then cancelled the range. Reactor reference: Debugging Reactor (source, 3.8.x) docs

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · When reactive is still worth it
x: Reactor is not the default answer for new JVM code in 2026, and the Spring team says so itself. The Spring Framework reference still reads: "If you have a Spring MVC application that works fine, there is no need to change. Imperative programming is the easiest way to write, understand, and debug code." It warns about "the steep learning curve", tells you to "start small and measure the benefits", and adds: "We expect that, for a wide range of applications, the shift is unnecessary." Lesson 1 of this track quoted the same docs on speed: reactive doesn't make applications faster; it lets them scale with fewer threads when calls have latency. Virtual threads (final in JDK 21) took away most of the thread-count argument. Mark Paluch of the Spring team wrote in 2022, while they were still a preview: "The reasons to use asynchronous programming models go away in many cases if we start with the assumption that our code runs on Virtual Threads." The same post keeps a place for reactive: ReactiveX-style APIs "remain a powerful way to compose concurrent logic and a natural way for dealing with streams", and they are "the right approach for concurrent scenarios in which declarative concurrency (such as scatter-gather) matters." So here is the position I'd take for your services: For request and response over JDBC, JPA or other blocking clients, use virtual threads and plain imperative code. Don't rewrite a working Quarkus REST or Spring MVC service in Reactor. For streams (server-sent events, WebSockets, Kafka pipelines, anything where demand, cancellation and a loss policy matter), Reactor earns its complexity. For many calls composed with timeouts, retries and fan-out, Reactor's operators are hard to beat. Coroutines, or structured concurrency once it is final, are the imperative alternatives. In a stack that is already reactive end to end (WebClient, R2DBC, Reactor Netty), stay reactive and keep the few blocking calls on boundedElastic. In Kotlin, coroutines give sequential-looking code over the same runtime. kotlinx-coroutines-reactor bridges both ways (awaitSingle(), mono { }, Flow.asFlux()), and Spring maps Mono to suspend and Flux to Flow. The coroutines track builds on that. Quick check: one Quarkus endpoint reads a payment from Oracle over JDBC, calls the issuer once and returns. Another relays an issuer's live event stream to browsers that read at different speeds. Which one needs request(n), and why? (The second. The first waits for one reply, which a virtual thread does cheaply. The second has a fast producer and slow consumers, and only demand or a loss policy stops events piling up in memory for the slow ones.) Embracing Virtual Threads (Spring blog, Mark Paluch, 2022) read Spring Framework reference: Spring WebFlux overview, applicability and performance docs The most common mistake is calling tryEmitNext on a sink from several threads and ignoring the result. It looks safe because the sink is "thread-safe", and it is, in the sense that it detects the concurrent call and refuses it with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED instead of corrupting itself. The refused item is simply gone. In tests with one thread, everything arrives; in production, with four Kafka listener threads, events go missing with no log line. Use emitNext(item, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1))), or serialize the calls yourself, and write a test that emits from several threads at once.

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Java and Kotlin
x: A hot event hub and a shared feed in Reactor and Kotlin PaymentEvents.java (Reactor) // Reactor: a hub that listener threads push into, and a shared rate feed private final Sinks.Many<PaymentEvent> events = Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort(); void publish(PaymentEvent e) { events.emitNext(e, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(Duration.ofSeconds(1))); } Flux<PaymentEvent> live() { return events.asFlux(); } Flux<Rate> rates = provider.rates() .replay(1) // late subscribers get the latest rate .refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); // disconnect 5 s after the last one leaves PaymentEvents.kt (coroutines) // Kotlin coroutines: SharedFlow for events, StateFlow for "the latest value" private val events = MutableSharedFlow<PaymentEvent>(extraBufferCapacity = 1_000) fun publish(e: PaymentEvent) { check(events.tryEmit(e)) { "subscribers are too slow" } // thread-safe; suspend emit() waits instead } val live: SharedFlow<PaymentEvent> = events.asSharedFlow() val rates: StateFlow<Rate?> = provider.rates() .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null) // latest rate, stop 5 s after the last leaves The shapes match: a multicast sink is close to a MutableSharedFlow, and replay(1).refCount(1, grace) is close to stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null). The differences are in concurrency and lifetime. A MutableSharedFlow accepts emissions from any number of threads at once; its tryEmit fails only when the buffer is full, and emit suspends instead. A Reactor sink refuses concurrent emissions unless you retry or serialize. And stateIn and shareIn need a CoroutineScope: the shared upstream lives in that scope and is cancelled with it, which is structured concurrency. Reactor's sharing lives as long as subscribers keep it alive. StateFlow also always has a current value and skips values equal to the last one, which replay(1) does not. The coroutines track covers SharedFlow and StateFlow in detail.

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Worked example
x: Test a payment-status poller in milliseconds After a payment is sent to the bank, a poller asks for its status every 30 seconds until it is final, and gives up after 5 minutes. A real-time test would take 90 seconds for the happy path and 5 minutes for the timeout. Here is the code under test. Mono<Status> awaitFinal(String paymentId) { return Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) // poll every 30 s .concatMap(tick -> api.status(paymentId)) // one call at a time .filter(Status::isFinal) .next() // first final status, then stop polling .timeout(Duration.ofMinutes(5)); } fun awaitFinal(paymentId: String): Mono<Status> = Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(30)) // poll every 30 s .concatMap { api.status(paymentId) } // one call at a time .filter(Status::isFinal) .next() // first final status, then stop polling .timeout(Duration.ofMinutes(5)) The happy path: the fake API answers PENDING twice, then SETTLED. Under virtual time the polls happen at 30, 60 and 90 seconds of fake time. expectNoEvent(90 s) proves nothing came out earlier, and the settled status arrives exactly at 90 s. FakeStatusApi api = new FakeStatusApi(PENDING, PENDING, SETTLED); StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> new StatusPoller(api).awaitFinal("p-1")) // 1. build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() // 2. before any expectNoEvent .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(90)) // 3. silent until the third poll .expectNext(SETTLED) .verifyComplete(); assertThat(api.calls()).isEqualTo(3); val api = FakeStatusApi(PENDING, PENDING, SETTLED) StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { StatusPoller(api).awaitFinal("p-1") } // 1. build it inside the supplier .expectSubscription() // 2. before any expectNoEvent .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofSeconds(90)) // 3. silent until the third poll .expectNext(SETTLED) .verifyComplete() assertThat(api.calls()).isEqualTo(3) The timeout path: the payment never settles. Jump the clock to the deadline and expect the TimeoutException. Keep a real-time limit on verify as well, so a mistake makes the test fail in one second instead of hanging. FakeStatusApi stuck = new FakeStatusApi(PENDING); // pending forever StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> new StatusPoller(stuck).awaitFinal("p-2")) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMinutes(5)) // 4. jump to the deadline .expectError(TimeoutException.class) .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); // 5. a real-time safety net val stuck = FakeStatusApi(PENDING) // pending forever StepVerifier.withVirtualTime { StatusPoller(stuck).awaitFinal("p-2") } .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMinutes(5)) // 4. jump to the deadline .expectError(TimeoutException::class.java) .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) // 5. a real-time safety net Both tests run in a few milliseconds. If one of them hangs instead, look at where the poller is built: Flux.interval and timeout pick their scheduler when the chain is assembled, so a poller created before withVirtualTime runs on the real clock. The same goes for a Mono built once in a @BeforeEach and kept in a field.

If it reports crashed threads, you used EmitFailureHandler.FAIL_FAST, which throws on FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED. share() fails the late-subscriber test (no latest value); cache() and replay(1).autoConnect() fail the disconnect test (they never cancel upstream). h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Quiz
x: Two Kafka listener threads call sink.tryEmitNext(event) on the same Sinks.many().multicast() sink at the same moment, and ignore the return value. What can happen? Both events are emitted, in some order One call returns FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED and its event is never emitted The sink buffers the second event and emits it later The sink throws ConcurrentModificationException Reactor sinks detect concurrent emission and refuse it instead of blocking or queueing, so one of the two calls gets FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED. Ignoring the result loses that event silently. Use emitNext(event, EmitFailureHandler.busyLooping(...)), which retries, or serialize the calls. A test reads StepVerifier.create(service.refund("p-1")).expectNext("REFUNDED").expectComplete(); and passes. The refund code is in fact broken. Why does the test pass? expectComplete() ignores the value Nothing subscribes until verify() is called, so no expectation is ever checked StepVerifier only fails on errors, not on wrong values The refund runs on another thread, so its result arrives after the test ends expectComplete() only adds a step to the script. verify(), or a shortcut like verifyComplete(), is what subscribes and runs it. Add .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(1)) and the test checks the value and fails if it hangs. Dashboards share one FX provider connection. A dashboard that opens late must show the current rate at once, and the connection must close when nobody watches. Which operator fits? rates.share() rates.cache() rates.replay(1).refCount() rates.publish().autoConnect(1) replay(1) gives a late subscriber the latest rate, and refCount() connects on the first subscriber and cancels upstream when the last one leaves. share() gives late subscribers nothing until the next tick. cache() and autoConnect never disconnect, and cache() also keeps every rate forever. A team runs a Spring MVC service on JDBC that meets its latency targets. Someone proposes rewriting it with WebFlux "to make it faster". What do Spring's own docs say? Rewrite it: reactive code is faster for every workload If an MVC application works fine there is no need to change; reactive doesn't generally make applications faster Rewrite only the JDBC calls with Reactor and keep the controllers Switch to WebFlux but keep JDBC on the event loop The Spring reference says a working MVC application has no need to change, that blocking persistence APIs like JDBC point to MVC, and that reactive and non-blocking generally don't make applications run faster. With virtual threads, the thread-count argument for this kind of service is mostly gone too. The last option is the worst of both: JDBC on an event loop blocks every request it serves. From "Errors, retries and timeouts": a retry uses Retry.backoff(3, Duration.ofMillis(200)) with the default jitter. How should its virtual-time test check the slow path? expectNoEvent for exactly 1,400 ms, then expect the fallback Advance the clock well past the longest possible total wait, then check the result and the number of attempts Use real time with Thread.sleep(2_000) so the jitter is realistic It can't be tested while jitter is on With jitter each wait moves by up to half its length, so exact times are not fixed. Advancing well past the maximum (the worked example used 10 seconds) and then asserting the outcome and the count is stable. Exact-time assertions need jitter(0). Real sleeps make the test slow and still flaky.
