h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Key terms
x: Hot publisher A publisher that produces whether or not anyone subscribes; subscribers see what is produced while they listen. ConnectableFlux What publish() and replay() return: a shared Flux that subscribes to its source when it is connected. refCount Connect on the first subscriber, disconnect when the last one leaves (optionally after a grace period). Sink Reactor's thread-aware way to push values from ordinary code into a Flux or Mono. StepVerifier reactor-test's tool that subscribes to a publisher and checks its signals step by step. Virtual time A fake clock that replaces Reactor's schedulers in a test, so delays pass instantly. checkpoint An operator that labels a place in a chain so errors passing through it say where they came from. What is share() the same as, and what does a late subscriber get? publish().refCount(). A late subscriber gets only items emitted after it subscribed. Late subscriber on replay(1).refCount(): what does it get? The most recent item at once, then the live ones. The upstream is cancelled when the last subscriber leaves. Two threads call tryEmitNext on one sink at the same moment. What can happen? One gets EmitResult.FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED and its item is not emitted. Check the result or use emitNext(item, busyLooping(...)). What happens to Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer() when its last subscriber leaves? By default it shuts down: a later subscriber just receives onComplete. directBestEffort() keeps working. A StepVerifier chain without verify(): what runs? Nothing. verify() (or verifyComplete() etc.) is what subscribes and checks the steps. Why must the publisher be built inside the withVirtualTime supplier? Operators like delay, interval and timeout pick their scheduler at assembly. Built earlier, they use the real clock and the test hangs. What does checkpoint("fee-row") add to an error? A suppressed exception saying the error was observed at the checkpoint named fee-row. Cheap; checkpoint(name, true) also captures the assembly stack trace.

h: Hot and cold publishers, Sinks, and StepVerifier · Go deeper
x: Connecting by hand. publish() and replay() return a ConnectableFlux. Besides refCount and autoConnect, you can call connect() yourself once every subscriber is in place, and dispose the returned Disposable to disconnect. That suits a startup sequence that wires several consumers before any data should flow. Context instead of ThreadLocal. Because a chain hops threads, a ThreadLocal such as an MDC trace id doesn't follow it. Reactor's Context does: write it at the bottom with contextWrite(Context.of("traceId", id)) and read it upstream with Mono.deferContextual(ctx -> ...). It travels from the subscriber toward the source, so a contextWrite above the reader is invisible to it. With the Micrometer context-propagation library on the classpath, Hooks.enableAutomaticContextPropagation() (Reactor 3.5.3+) restores ThreadLocals such as the MDC around each operator; it isn't in the labs. BlockHound in tests. Calling BlockHound.install() at the start of a test run makes any blocking call on a non-blocking thread throw BlockingOperationError, which catches the JDBC call on an event loop from the schedulers lesson before production does. On JDK 13+ it needs -XX:+AllowRedefinitionToAddDeleteMethods. Backpressure in tests. StepVerifier.create(flux, 0) starts with no demand, and thenRequest(n) adds it step by step. That is how the lab of lesson 7 of this track checked which tick a slow subscriber receives.

h: Kotlin coroutines
x: Suspend functions, structured concurrency, dispatchers, cancellation, Flow and channels. By the end of this track you can write Kotlin coroutine code that a payments service can trust. You can say what suspend does and doesn't do, split a request into concurrent calls that take as long as the slowest one, and keep every coroutine inside a scope that waits for it, cancels it and hears about its failures. You can put blocking and CPU work on the right dispatcher, make loops and blocking calls respond to cancellation, and let independent work fail alone with a supervisor. You can build cold flows, share hot ones with StateFlow and SharedFlow, connect workers with channels, protect shared state with a Mutex, and test all of it on virtual time. And you can bridge coroutines to CompletableFuture, Reactor and virtual threads, and choose between the three for a given service. You need everyday Kotlin, and the earlier tracks help: threads, races and locks from the first track, executors and CompletableFuture from the executors track, virtual threads, and Reactor's cold and hot publishers. Install JDK 25. The coroutine library is kotlinx.coroutines 1.11.0 with Kotlin 2.4.21, and the lessons say which version a fact comes from, because several rules changed recently: passing a Job to a builder is deprecated since 1.11, and explicit backing fields became stable in Kotlin 2.4. The labs live in labs/coroutines, one package per lesson (workbench.coroutines.l01 to l11), all in Kotlin, with one Java test in lesson 11 that calls the Kotlin code from Java. Most stubs are buggy code with a KDoc that says what is wrong; a few are TODO()s. Run ./gradlew :coroutines:test --tests 'workbench.coroutines.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and solutionTest to check the reference answers. Nearly every test runs on virtual time with runTest, so a test of a 30-second backoff finishes in milliseconds. The Try-it demos run with ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=..., and almost every Kotlin demo has a Java twin showing the closest Java equivalent. suspend lets a function pause without blocking its thread; the dispatcher, not suspend, decides which thread runs it. Wrap callbacks with suspendCancellableCoroutine. Every coroutine lives in a tree: parents wait for children, cancellation flows down, failures flow up. coroutineScope for work the caller waits for, an owned scope for work that outlives a call, never GlobalScope. Blocking calls go on Dispatchers.IO (or a limitedParallelism view sized to the resource), CPU work on Default, and withContext switches and comes back. Cancellation is cooperative and travels as CancellationException: check in CPU loops, rethrow it from every catch-all, clean up with NonCancellable, and use runInterruptible for blocking calls. A failed launch or async cancels its parent at once. Supervisors (supervisorScope, SupervisorJob() in a scope's constructor) let children fail alone; handlers only work on roots. Flows are cold and sequential: flowOn moves the upstream, catch handles only upstream errors, onCompletion sees every ending. StateFlow is state (conflated, deduplicated); SharedFlow is events (configure its buffer); stateIn with WhileSubscribed shares one upstream. Channels hand each element to one receiver: worker pools, pipelines and callbackFlow bridges, with select for whichever comes first. Protect compound updates with a Mutex, not a one-thread view, and test timing logic on virtual time with runTest and injected dispatchers. Bridge to Java with future { }, await(), mono { } and awaitSingle(), and choose virtual threads, coroutines or Reactor per component.

h: Kotlin coroutines: cheat sheet
x: Builders and scopes You want Use Fire and forget inside a scope launch { } returns a Job A result later async { } returns a Deferred; await() it Several children, wait for all, fail together coroutineScope { } Children that fail alone supervisorScope { } Run a block on another dispatcher and come back withContext(dispatcher) { } Block a thread until done: main, tests, a blocking edge runBlocking { }, never inside suspend code Background work owned by a class CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler), cancelled when the owner closes Wrap a one-shot callback suspendCancellableCoroutine { } with invokeOnCancellation { } The tree: a parent completes only after its children; cancellation flows down; a failure (anything but CancellationException) cancels the parent and siblings, unless the parent is a supervisor. GlobalScope and CoroutineScope(...) created inside a function make orphans. Dispatchers Dispatcher For Size Dispatchers.Default CPU work; the default for launch and async one thread per core, at least 2 Dispatchers.IO blocking calls (JDBC, blocking SDKs) 64 at once (or cores, if more) Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n, "name") one blocking resource with its own budget n, added on top of IO's 64 Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(n) a CPU budget at most the core count executor.asCoroutineDispatcher() an existing pool or virtual threads; close it whatever the executor allows Dispatchers.Unconfined, Dispatchers.Main library code; UI threads not for server code Context: + merges elements, the right side wins; children inherit everything but the Job. Look the dispatcher up with ContinuationInterceptor (1.11). A ThreadLocal needs asContextElement(). Cancellation Situation Do A CPU loop ensureActive(), yield() or while (isActive) every few hundred items Catching around suspend calls rethrow CancellationException; runCatching and catch (e: Exception) catch it Suspending cleanup in finally withContext(NonCancellable) { release() } A deadline that is an expected outcome withTimeoutOrNull(d) { } ?: fallback A deadline that must fail the caller withTimeoutOrNull(d) { } ?: error("timed out"); withTimeout inside launch fails quietly A blocking call that should stop on cancel runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { }, plus the client's own timeout asFlow() over a long collection add .cancellable() Exceptions Builder Failure goes to launch child its parent at once async child its parent at once, whether or not anyone awaits root launch (in a scope you created, or a supervisor's child) the CoroutineExceptionHandler in its context, else the uncaught handler root async kept in the Deferred; await() rethrows it Handlers only work on roots. Put SupervisorJob() in a scope's constructor or use supervisorScope; launch(SupervisorJob()) detaches the child from the tree. The first exception wins, the rest are suppressed. Flow Rule Detail Cold the flow { } body runs once per collector, only when collected Sequential emit suspends until the collector is done; take(n) stops the producer Operators intermediate (map, filter, onEach, take) build; terminal (collect, toList, first) run Context flowOn(d) moves everything above it; emit inside withContext throws Errors catch sees only upstream; the collector's exceptions pass through; never try around emit Endings onCompletion { cause -> }: null, the error, or a CancellationException for an early stop Backpressure plain waits; buffer() runs ahead; conflate() keeps the latest; collectLatest cancels stale work Hot streams and channels Type Behavior StateFlow one current value; conflates; skips equal values; never completes SharedFlow broadcasts to every subscriber; replay, extraBufferCapacity, onBufferOverflow; default has no buffer, so tryEmit fails while a subscriber is busy stateIn / shareIn one shared upstream; SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000) starts with the first subscriber, stops 5 s after the last Read-only state val s: StateFlow<T> with field = MutableStateFlow(x) (Kotlin 2.4), or asStateFlow(); update with update { } or compareAndSet Channel a queue: each element to one receiver; rendezvous by default; close it, or for never ends Fan-out / fan-in N workers on one channel cap concurrency at N; close the results channel after joinAll() select first clause to complete wins (onAwait, onReceive, onTimeout); biased to the first callbackFlow trySend from the callback, end with awaitClose { unregister() } Shared state and testing Need Use One counter or value AtomicLong, AtomicReference, MutableStateFlow.update A compound update Mutex.withLock { }: suspends, fair, not reentrant; keep suspension outside it if you can limitedParallelism(1) serializes code only between suspension points: not a mutex Fast, exact timing tests runTest; currentTime, advanceTimeBy, runCurrent, advanceUntilIdle Delays in the code under test inject the dispatcher; Dispatchers.IO and Default stay real time A child that must start at once UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler) Endless work in a test backgroundScope; advanceUntilIdle ignores it Bridges and choosing From To Use CompletableFuture suspend future.await() (cancels the future); asDeferred().await() (doesn't) suspend CompletableFuture scope.future { } with an owned scope suspend Mono / Flux mono { } (cold), flux { }, flow.asFlux() Mono / Flux suspend / Flow awaitSingle(), awaitSingleOrNull(), publisher.asFlow() blocking Java caller suspend runBlocking { withTimeout(d) { } }, fine on a virtual thread Virtual threads for blocking Java code at scale; coroutines for Kotlin code that needs structured fan-out, cancellation and Flow; Reactor where a reactive stack already exists. One model per component, converted at its edges.

h: Kotlin coroutines: track quiz
x: Five coroutines in one runBlocking each call Thread.sleep(100) and print a line. About how long does the program take? About 100 ms, because coroutines run concurrently About 500 ms, because Thread.sleep blocks the one thread they share About 100 ms on a 4-core machine, 125 ms on 2 cores It doesn't compile: Thread.sleep is not allowed in a coroutine runBlocking runs its coroutines on the calling thread, and Thread.sleep blocks that thread, so the five sleeps happen one after another. delay(100) would suspend instead and the whole thing would take about 100 ms. What happens here? coroutineScope { launch { delay(100); throw IOException("ledger down") } launch { delay(1_000); println("risk done") } } risk done prints at 1 s, then the scope throws The exception is logged and the scope returns normally at 1 s At about 100 ms the second child is cancelled, risk done never prints, and the scope throws IOException Nothing is thrown, because launch swallows exceptions A failed child cancels its parent scope, which cancels the sibling and then rethrows the original exception once every child has stopped. Nothing waits for the full second. A Kotlin service calls a blocking JDBC repository from coroutines, and Oracle's pool has 20 connections. Where should the calls run? withContext(Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "oracle")) inside the repository On Dispatchers.Default, because it is the default withContext(Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(20)) Dispatchers.Unconfined, so they start immediately Blocking calls belong on IO, and a view of 20 matches the pool and adds to IO's 64 instead of competing with other blocking work. Default has one thread per core and must never block; a view over Default can't exceed the core count anyway. A poller runs while (true) { runCatching { checkStatus(); delay(5_000) } }. During shutdown its scope is cancelled. What happens? The loop ends at the next delay The JVM interrupts the thread and the loop ends The loop ends after the current status check The loop spins at full CPU: every delay throws at once and runCatching swallows it runCatching catches CancellationException like any other Throwable. The coroutine stays cancelled, so each delay throws immediately, gets swallowed, and the loop goes round again. Rethrow CancellationException, or keep the delay outside the catch. To stop one webhook failure from cancelling the ledger write in the same request, someone writes launch(SupervisorJob()) { webhooks.post(e) } inside coroutineScope. What did they get? A supervised child that the scope still waits for A child detached from the tree: the scope doesn't wait for it or cancel it, and its failure goes to a handler A compile error The same as supervisorScope A Job in a builder's context replaces the parent, so the coroutine becomes a child of a fresh SupervisorJob outside the request's tree. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 deprecates the pattern. Use supervisorScope { } or a supervisor scope owned by a long-lived component. records.map { parse(it) }.catch { emit(FALLBACK) }.collect { repo.save(it) }. repo.save throws SQLException. What does the caller of collect see? The SQLException Nothing: catch emits FALLBACK and the flow continues An IllegalStateException about exception transparency FALLBACK saved in place of the failed record catch only handles exceptions from above it. The save runs in the collector, below catch, so its exception passes straight through. Move the save into onEach above catch if the fallback should cover it. Payment transitions must reach both an audit writer and a notifier, and none may be lost when a Kafka listener thread publishes a burst of them. Which holder fits? MutableStateFlow<Transition?>(null) A cold flow { } that each consumer collects MutableSharedFlow<Transition>(extraBufferCapacity = 64), publishing with a checked tryEmit MutableSharedFlow<Transition>() with default parameters and tryEmit Events for several subscribers call for a SharedFlow, and a non-suspending publisher needs a buffer so tryEmit can hand values to busy subscribers. A StateFlow conflates events away, and a default SharedFlow has no buffer, so tryEmit fails whenever a subscriber is busy. A pricing coroutine recomputes a quote each time the cart total changes. A recompute takes 300 ms, totals change every 100 ms while the customer types, and only the latest total matters. Which operator fits? buffer() conflate() flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) collectLatest { } collectLatest cancels the computation in progress when a new total arrives, so stale work stops at once and only the latest is finished. conflate skips values but still finishes every computation it starts; buffer computes them all. Credits run on Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) and each does val b = balance; val c = fx.convert(amount); balance = b + c, where fx.convert suspends. Which change makes it correct? Mark balance as @Volatile Convert first, then do the read and the write together with no suspension between them (or hold a Mutex across all of it) Use Dispatchers.Default without the view Add yield() before the write A one-thread view serializes code only between suspension points, so credits interleave at fx.convert and overwrite each other. Removing the suspension from the critical part, or holding a Mutex across it, closes the gap. @Volatile and yield() don't. A Java caller holds f = facade.authorizeAsync(req), built with scope.future { authorize(req) }, and its orTimeout(800, MILLISECONDS) fires. What happens to the Kotlin coroutine? It is cancelled, because its future completed It keeps running, and the result is discarded Its thread is interrupted The whole facade scope is cancelled The coroutine started by future { } is cancelled when its future is cancelled or otherwise completed, and orTimeout completes that same future exceptionally. Only that coroutine stops; the scope and its other children carry on.

h: Suspend functions from zero · A suspend function can pause without blocking its thread
x: Most payment code has the same shape: call the card issuer and wait 120 ms, call the ledger and wait 30 ms, return. Nearly all of the time is waiting. With one thread per request, each thread spends that time parked and still holds its stack. The Kotlin docs put the cost plainly: a thread usually needs a few megabytes of memory, and a JVM typically handles a few thousand of them at once. A suspend function is a function that can pause in the middle and continue later, without holding a thread while it is paused. Java // Java equivalent: plain blocking calls on a virtual thread (JDK 21+); the JVM does the pausing Authorization charge(ChargeRequest req) { String token = vault.tokenize(req.pan()); // the virtual thread unmounts while it waits return issuer.authorize(token, req.amount()); // and here } Kotlin suspend fun charge(req: ChargeRequest): Authorization { val token = vault.tokenize(req.pan) // may pause here return issuer.authorize(token, req.amount) // and here } When charge pauses inside tokenize, the thread leaves and runs other work. When the vault answers, charge continues on the next line, possibly on a different thread. The code still reads top to bottom, with normal try/catch and normal return values. A coroutine is one running instance of such code: a piece of work that can be paused and resumed. You start one with a builder like runBlocking or launch (lesson 2 of this track). Two rules follow. You can call a suspend function only from another suspend function or from inside a coroutine. Plain code has nothing to resume, so the compiler refuses. Waiting must be done with a suspending call. delay(200) suspends: the coroutine is set aside and the thread is free. Thread.sleep(200) blocks: the thread stops, and every other coroutine that needs that thread waits too. The compiler accepts both, so nothing warns you. The Try it runs five coroutines on a single thread, main. Each waits 200 ms. With delay, the five waits overlap. With Thread.sleep, the one thread can only sleep for one of them at a time. Five waits on one thread Read SleepVsDelay.kt. All five coroutines run on main. Predict the total time with delay. Run it with the command below. Run it again with -Pargs=sleep added. Predict first, then watch how the five lines appear. SleepVsDelay.kt package workbench.coroutines.l01 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** Five coroutines share ONE thread and each waits 200 ms. Pass "sleep" to block instead of suspend. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val blocking = args.firstOrNull() == "sleep" val took = measureTimeMillis { runBlocking { // runs every coroutine below on the main thread repeat(5) { i -> launch { println("payment $i starts waiting on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") if (blocking) Thread.sleep(200) else delay(200) } } } } val how = if (blocking) "Thread.sleep" else "delay" println("5 waits of 200 ms with $how took $took ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.SleepVsDelayKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l01/SleepVsDelay.kt SleepVsDelayJava.java // Java equivalent of SleepVsDelay.kt: one thread, five 200 ms waits. // A non-blocking timer callback plays the role of delay; Thread.sleep blocks the one thread. package workbench.coroutines.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class SleepVsDelayJava { public static void main(String[] args) { boolean blocking = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("sleep"); ExecutorService oneThread = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "main-loop")); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<Void>> waits = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { int id = i; CompletableFuture<Void> done = new CompletableFuture<>(); oneThread.execute(() -> { System.out.println("payment " + id + " starts waiting on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); if (blocking) { sleep(200); // holds the only thread done.complete(null); } else { // a timer completes it later; the thread is free meanwhile CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, oneThread).execute(() -> done.complete(null)); } }); waits.add(done); } CompletableFuture.allOf(waits.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); oneThread.shutdown(); String how = blocking ? "Thread.sleep" : "a timer callback"; System.out.printf("5 waits of 200 ms with %s took %d ms%n", how, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } private static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.SleepVsDelayJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l01/SleepVsDelayJava.java With delay the run takes a little over 200 ms (278 ms here): the waits overlap on one thread. With Thread.sleep it takes over a second (1,078 ms here), and the five lines appear 200 ms apart, because each sleep holds the only thread. Same code, one word changed. The Java twin gives the same two numbers (225 ms and 1,025 ms here): a timer callback on a single-thread executor is the closest Java match for delay. A continuation is a bookmark with a sticky note. When a cook (a thread) reaches a step that needs the oven for 40 minutes, they don't stand at the oven. They put a bookmark in the recipe, write on the note which step comes next and which ingredients are already measured, and go cook something else. When the oven timer rings, any free cook can pick up the book, read the note, and carry on from that step. The recipe is the state machine, the step number is label, and the measured ingredients are the L$ fields. The analogy breaks in one place: in a kitchen the free cook picks up the book on their own. In a coroutine, the dispatcher decides who picks it up, and the callback that rings the timer is the only thing that can wake it.

h: Suspend functions from zero · A suspend function runs on whatever thread calls it
x: The most common wrong idea about coroutines is that suspend sends work to a background thread. It does not. The modifier adds the ability to pause and nothing else. Which thread runs the code is decided by the coroutine's dispatcher, a scheduler you will meet in lesson 4 of this track. Java // Java equivalent: the same plain method; in Kotlin the suspend modifier changed nothing int checksum(String digits) { int sum = 0; for (char c : digits.toCharArray()) sum = (sum * 31 + c) % 1_000_003; return sum; } Kotlin suspend fun checksum(digits: String): Int { var sum = 0 for (c in digits) sum = (sum * 31 + c.code) % 1_000_003 return sum // no suspension point anywhere } This function never suspends, so it runs start to finish on the caller's thread, exactly like a normal function. IntelliJ flags the modifier as redundant. Put a two-second CPU loop in a suspend function, call it from a request coroutine, and that request's thread is busy for two seconds. Marking it suspend changed nothing. The other half of the story: after a real suspension, the coroutine may continue on a different thread. A coroutine on Dispatchers.Default can start on worker-1, pause in delay, and resume on worker-3. Two things follow for your code. A ThreadLocal is not safe across a suspension point. The thread that resumes you may hold someone else's value. Logging MDC is a ThreadLocal, so this bites in real services. Lesson 4 of this track shows context elements, the coroutine way to carry such values. Memory visibility, on the other hand, is handled for you. Values a coroutine wrote before it suspended are visible after it resumes, even on another thread. You don't need @Volatile on locals that live across a delay. The reason is the hand-off. To resume you on another thread, the dispatcher submits your coroutine to its pool as a task, and the JDK's rule for executors applies: whatever a thread wrote before it submitted a task is visible to the thread that runs it (a happens-before edge, from the memory model track). That covers one coroutine's own state. Two coroutines that share a variable still need a lock or an atomic, which lesson 10 of this track covers. Watch coroutines change threads Read WhichThread.kt. Predict which thread computes the checksum. Run it. Look at the payment N ran on lines. Run it twice more. Do the thread sequences repeat? WhichThread.kt package workbench.coroutines.l01 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private fun where() = Thread.currentThread().name.removePrefix("DefaultDispatcher-") /** A suspend function that never suspends runs on its caller's thread, start to finish. */ suspend fun checksum(digits: String): Int { var sum = 0 for (c in digits) sum = (sum * 31 + c.code) % 1_000_003 return sum // no suspension point anywhere: plain code with a suspend label on it } fun main() = runBlocking { println("main coroutine runs on ${where()}") println("checksum ${checksum("4242424242424242")} computed on ${where()}") repeat(4) { id -> launch(Dispatchers.Default) { val seen = mutableListOf<String>() repeat(4) { seen += where() delay(20) // suspends; any free Default thread may resume it } println("payment $id ran on ${seen.joinToString(" -> ")}") } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.WhichThreadKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l01/WhichThread.kt WhichThreadJava.java // Java equivalent of WhichThread.kt: virtual threads also move between carrier threads. // A plain method runs on its caller's thread; a virtual thread that sleeps may wake up on another carrier. package workbench.coroutines.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; public class WhichThreadJava { static int checksum(String digits) { // the same code as the Kotlin suspend fun: it never pauses int sum = 0; for (char c : digits.toCharArray()) sum = (sum * 31 + c) % 1_000_003; return sum; } // a virtual thread prints as VirtualThread[#29]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3; keep the carrier part static String carrier() { String s = Thread.currentThread().toString(); int at = s.indexOf('@'); return at < 0 ? Thread.currentThread().getName() : s.substring(at + 1).replace("ForkJoinPool-1-", ""); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("main runs on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); System.out.println("checksum " + checksum("4242424242424242") + " computed on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); List<Thread> payments = new ArrayList<>(); for (int id = 0; id < 4; id++) { int pid = id; payments.add(Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { List<String> seen = new ArrayList<>(); for (int step = 0; step < 4; step++) { seen.add(carrier()); try { Thread.sleep(20); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } // unmounts; any carrier may resume it } System.out.println("payment " + pid + " ran on " + String.join(" -> ", seen)); })); } for (Thread t : payments) t.join(); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.WhichThreadJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l01/WhichThreadJava.java The checksum runs on main, the caller's thread. Each payment coroutine shows a sequence like worker-1 -> worker-1 -> worker-4 -> worker-3: after each delay any free Default worker may pick it up. The sequences change from run to run. The Java twin shows the same thing for virtual threads: after each Thread.sleep a virtual thread may continue on a different carrier. Your services talk to an issuer SDK, an HSM client, a fraud-scoring vendor and a tokenization vault. Several of them hand you a callback or a future. Wrap each one once, with suspendCancellableCoroutine or future.await(), and the rest of the code base gets plain sequential functions with normal try/catch. More important for payments: when the caller's timeout fires, the cancel reaches the vendor call, so you are not left with a charge in flight that nobody is waiting for. The same rule applies in a Kafka consumer or a Temporal activity written in Kotlin: a retry backoff written with Thread.sleep holds the thread and stalls every other coroutine scheduled on it. Use delay.

h: Suspend functions from zero · The compiler turns a suspend function into a state machine
x: A suspend function becomes a state machine with one small continuation object Coroutines need no special support from the JVM. They are a compiler feature plus a library. The Kotlin compiler rewrites every suspend function in continuation-passing style: it adds one hidden last parameter, a Continuation, and changes the return type to Any?. Here is what javap, the JDK tool that prints the contents of a compiled class, shows: // you write suspend fun chargeCard(pan: String): String // javap shows public static final java.lang.Object chargeCard(java.lang.String, kotlin.coroutines.Continuation<? super java.lang.String>); A Continuation is a callback that also carries the coroutine's context: interface Continuation<in T> { val context: CoroutineContext; fun resumeWith(result: Result<T>) }. The Object return is either the real result or a marker, COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, which means "I paused; I will call your continuation later". The body becomes a state machine. Each suspension point ends a state. The compiler generates one small class per suspend function (here StateMachineKt$chargeCard$1) with an int label for the next state and fields L$0, L$1 for locals that must survive a pause. Here is chargeCard from the demo, step by step: Label 0: store pan in the object, set label = 1, call tokenize(pan, this). If it returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, return that marker straight up the stack. The thread is now free. When the vault answers, someone calls resumeWith(token). That calls chargeCard again with the same object. A tableswitch (the bytecode for a switch over a small range of int values) on label jumps to state 1, which picks up the token and calls authorize. Label 2: take the result and return it to whoever is waiting. If tokenize does not suspend (a cache hit, say), it returns the token directly and the function carries on. Nothing is scheduled and no thread changes. This explains both the cost and the rules. A suspended coroutine is one small object holding a label and a few fields, not a thread stack, so you can have hundreds of thousands. And plain code cannot call a suspend function, because it has no continuation to pass in. Read the state machine with javap Run the demo once so Gradle compiles it: ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.StateMachineKt. From labs/, run the first javap command. Find the Continuation parameter and the Object return type on chargeCard. Run the second command. It prints the generated state class. Find label and the L$ fields. Run the third command and find the tableswitch. Predict first: how many cases will it have? terminal javap -p coroutines/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/coroutines/l01/StateMachineKt.class javap -p 'coroutines/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/coroutines/l01/StateMachineKt$chargeCard$1.class' javap -c -p coroutines/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/coroutines/l01/StateMachineKt.class | grep -A4 tableswitch chargeCard(java.lang.String, kotlin.coroutines.Continuation<? super java.lang.String>) returns java.lang.Object, and so do tokenize and authorize. The state class extends kotlin.coroutines.jvm.internal.ContinuationImpl and has int label, L$0, L$1 and result. The first tableswitch says 0 to 2: three states for two suspension points. Each suspension point ends a state. Suspending returns a marker and frees the thread; resuming calls the same function again, and the saved label says where to continue. KEEP: Kotlin coroutines design (continuations and state machines) read

h: Suspend functions from zero · Wrapping a callback API with suspendCancellableCoroutine
x: Most vendor SDKs in payments take a callback or return a future. suspendCancellableCoroutine turns a callback into a suspend function. It suspends the coroutine and hands you its continuation, and you resume it when the callback fires. Java // Java equivalent: complete a CompletableFuture from the callback, and pass cancellation back CompletableFuture<Integer> scoreAsync(Sdk sdk, String paymentId) { CompletableFuture<Integer> result = new CompletableFuture<>(); Runnable cancel = sdk.score(paymentId, result::complete); // 1. start; complete on callback result.whenComplete((v, e) -> { if (e != null) cancel.run(); }); // 2. timed out or cancelled: tell the SDK return result; } Kotlin suspend fun FraudSdk.scoreAwait(paymentId: String): Int = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont -> val cancel = score(paymentId) { s -> cont.resume(s) } // 1. start; resume on callback cont.invokeOnCancellation { cancel() } // 2. we were cancelled: tell the SDK } Three rules make a wrapper like this correct. Resume exactly once. Call resume with a value or resumeWithException with an error. A second resume on the same continuation throws IllegalStateException. Use the cancellable version. The standard library also has suspendCoroutine, and it works fine until someone cancels the caller. Then it can't react. The coroutine stays suspended until the SDK calls back, so a timeout fires late, and the SDK never hears that you gave up. In the Try it, a 100 ms timeout returns after a full second. Expect late replies. If the coroutine is cancelled first, a callback that arrives afterwards is ignored. kotlinx.coroutines calls this the prompt cancellation guarantee: a cancelled coroutine does not resume successfully, even if the value was already on its way. If that late value is a resource, such as a pooled session, pass a cleanup lambda: cont.resume(session) { _, late, _ -> late.close() }. The library calls it when the value can no longer be delivered. This tool is for callbacks that fire once. For listeners that fire many times you want callbackFlow (lesson 9 of this track). For a CompletableFuture you don't write any of this: future.await() in kotlinx-coroutines-core already does it (lesson 11 of this track). Make a timeout reach the SDK Read CallbackBridge.kt. The SDK answers after one second. The caller allows 100 ms. Predict how long withTimeout(100) takes to return. Run it. Change scoreAwait to use suspendCancellableCoroutine (import kotlinx.coroutines.suspendCancellableCoroutine). Keep the function the SDK returns: val cancel = score(paymentId) { s -> cont.resume(s) }, then add cont.invokeOnCancellation { cancel() }. Run it again. In the Java twin, run it, then add result.whenComplete((v, e) -> { if (e != null) cancel.run(); }); before return result; and run it again. CallbackBridge.kt package workbench.coroutines.l01 import kotlinx.coroutines.TimeoutCancellationException import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeout import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import kotlin.coroutines.resume import kotlin.coroutines.suspendCoroutine import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** A fraud-scoring SDK with a callback API. It answers after 1 second on its own thread. */ class FraudSdk { private val pool = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "fraud-sdk").apply { isDaemon = true } } fun score(paymentId: String, onScore: (Int) -> Unit): () -> Unit { val task = pool.schedule({ onScore(17) }, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS) return { println(" sdk: request for $paymentId cancelled"); task.cancel(false) } } } // Wrapped with suspendCoroutine: works, but cancellation cannot reach it. suspend fun FraudSdk.scoreAwait(paymentId: String): Int = suspendCoroutine { cont -> score(paymentId) { s -> cont.resume(s) } } fun main() = runBlocking { val sdk = FraudSdk() val took = measureTimeMillis { try { withTimeout(100) { sdk.scoreAwait("pay_981") } } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) { println(" timed out") } } println("withTimeout(100) returned after $took ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.CallbackBridgeKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l01/CallbackBridge.kt CallbackBridgeJava.java // Java equivalent of CallbackBridge.kt: wrap the callback SDK in a CompletableFuture. // The SDK answers after 1 second; the caller allows 100 ms. package workbench.coroutines.l01; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; import java.util.function.IntConsumer; public class CallbackBridgeJava { /** A fraud-scoring SDK with a callback API. It answers after 1 second on its own thread. */ static final class Sdk { private final ScheduledExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "fraud-sdk"); t.setDaemon(true); return t; }); Runnable score(String paymentId, IntConsumer onScore) { ScheduledFuture<?> task = pool.schedule(() -> onScore.accept(17), 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); return () -> { System.out.println(" sdk: request for " + paymentId + " cancelled"); task.cancel(false); }; } } // Wrapped as a future: the caller can time out, but nothing tells the SDK yet. static CompletableFuture<Integer> scoreAsync(Sdk sdk, String paymentId) { CompletableFuture<Integer> result = new CompletableFuture<>(); Runnable cancel = sdk.score(paymentId, result::complete); return result; } public static void main(String[] args) { Sdk sdk = new Sdk(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { scoreAsync(sdk, "pay_981").orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { if (e.getCause() instanceof TimeoutException) System.out.println(" timed out"); } System.out.printf("orTimeout(100) returned after %d ms%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); try { Thread.sleep(1_100); } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } // was the SDK told? } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l01.CallbackBridgeJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l01/CallbackBridgeJava.java First run: timed out after about 1,000 ms (1,014 ms here). The timeout did fire at 100 ms, but suspendCoroutine could not wake up until the SDK answered, and the SDK was never told. After the change: sdk: request for pay_981 cancelled, then timed out after about 100 ms (116 ms here). The Java twin returns at about 100 ms even before your change, because orTimeout completes the future by itself, but the SDK only hears about it once you add the whenComplete hook. suspendCancellableCoroutine (API reference) docs The common mistake is thinking suspend makes code non-blocking. People mark a function suspend, call JDBC or Thread.sleep inside it, and expect the thread to be free while it waits. It isn't. suspend only lets a function pause at suspending calls such as delay, await or a suspendCancellableCoroutine wrapper. A blocking call inside a suspend function still blocks the thread. Wait with delay, wrap callback APIs with suspendCancellableCoroutine, and move unavoidable blocking calls to Dispatchers.IO with withContext (lesson 4 of this track).

h: Suspend functions from zero · Java and Kotlin
x: Two calls in a row: CompletableFuture vs suspend ChargeService.java CompletableFuture<String> chargeCard(String pan) { return vault.tokenize(pan) // CompletableFuture<String> .thenCompose(token -> issuer.authorize(token)) // CompletableFuture<String> .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } ChargeService.kt suspend fun chargeCard(pan: String): String = withTimeout(2.seconds) { val token = vault.tokenize(pan) // suspend fun issuer.authorize(token) // suspend fun } Both versions free the thread while they wait. The Java version expresses "then" with callbacks: each thenCompose registers a lambda, errors arrive wrapped in CompletionException, and orTimeout only completes the outer future exceptionally. The vault and issuer calls keep running, because cancelling a CompletableFuture never interrupts the work behind it. The Kotlin version reads like blocking code: locals, try/catch and loops all work, and the compiler builds the callbacks for you. When withTimeout fires, it cancels the coroutine, and cancellation reaches the two calls if they are written to cooperate, as in section 4. On JDK 21+ you can also write the Java version as plain blocking calls on a virtual thread. Lesson 11 of this track has a guide for choosing between the two.

h: Suspend functions from zero · Worked example
x: Wrap a pooled-session SDK without leaking sessions An HSM vendor hands out sessions from a pool. acquire returns at once with a Ticket and calls you back later with a session or an error. Sessions must be closed. You want suspend fun HsmPool.acquireAwait(): Session. class Session(val id: Int) : AutoCloseable { override fun close() { /* back to the pool */ } } fun interface Ticket { fun cancel() } interface HsmPool { fun acquire(onReady: (Session?, Throwable?) -> Unit): Ticket } // Java equivalent: the same SDK shape final class Session implements AutoCloseable { @Override public void close() { /* back to the pool */ } } interface Ticket { void cancel(); } interface HsmPool { Ticket acquire(BiConsumer<Session, Throwable> onReady); } Start the request inside suspendCancellableCoroutine and resume exactly once from the callback: a value on success, an exception on error. suspend fun HsmPool.acquireAwait(): Session = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont -> // 1. start the request; the pool calls back on its own thread val ticket = acquire { session, error -> // 2. resume exactly once, with a value or an error if (error != null) cont.resumeWithException(error) else cont.resume(session!!) } } // Java equivalent: complete a CompletableFuture from the callback static CompletableFuture<Session> acquireAsync(HsmPool pool) { CompletableFuture<Session> result = new CompletableFuture<>(); // 1. start the request; the pool calls back on its own thread Ticket ticket = pool.acquire((session, error) -> { // 2. complete exactly once, with a value or an error if (error != null) result.completeExceptionally(error); else result.complete(session); }); return result; } If the caller times out, stop waiting for a session. invokeOnCancellation runs when the coroutine is cancelled while suspended here. // 3. our caller gave up: cancel the ticket cont.invokeOnCancellation { ticket.cancel() } // 3. our caller gave up (cancelled the future): cancel the ticket result.whenComplete((s, e) -> { if (result.isCancelled()) ticket.cancel(); }); One gap is left. The pool may hand out a session just after you were cancelled. The continuation ignores that late resume, and the session leaks. Use the resume overload that takes a cleanup lambda: the library calls it with the value it could not deliver. else cont.resume(session!!) { _, late, _ -> late.close() } // 4. late session: close it // 4. late session: complete() returns false when the future is already done, so close it else if (!result.complete(session)) session.close(); Self-check: why is step 4 needed even though step 3 cancels the ticket? (Cancelling is a request. The pool may already be calling you back on another thread, so the session can still arrive after you were cancelled.)

h: Suspend functions from zero · Quiz
x: This runs on one thread: runBlocking { repeat(3) { launch { Thread.sleep(100) } } }. About how long does it take? About 100 ms, because the three coroutines run concurrently About 300 ms, because each sleep blocks the only thread About 0 ms, because launch returns at once It does not compile: Thread.sleep is not allowed in a coroutine Thread.sleep blocks the thread, and runBlocking gives all three coroutines one thread, so they sleep one after another. With delay(100) they would overlap and finish in about 100 ms. The compiler happily accepts Thread.sleep here, which is why the bug survives code review. suspend fun parseStatement(json: String): Statement is pure CPU work with no suspending calls. A request coroutine on thread worker-2 calls it. Which thread runs the parsing? worker-2, the caller's thread A thread from Dispatchers.IO A new background thread for each call The thread is chosen at random by the JVM A suspend function that never suspends is ordinary code on the caller's thread. suspend does not move work anywhere. To run CPU work elsewhere you'd switch dispatcher explicitly with withContext(Dispatchers.Default), which lesson 4 of this track covers. How does suspend fun balance(accountId: String): Long look to a Java caller? long balance(String accountId) CompletableFuture<Long> balance(String accountId) Object balance(String accountId, Continuation<? super Long> continuation) void balance(String accountId, Consumer<Long> callback) The compiler adds a Continuation as the last parameter and changes the return type to Object, which holds either the result (boxed) or COROUTINE_SUSPENDED. That is why Java code can't simply call suspend functions; lesson 11 of this track shows the bridges (future {}). A callback SDK is wrapped with suspendCoroutine (not the cancellable version). The caller runs withTimeout(200) { sdk.callAwait() } and the SDK answers after 3 seconds. What happens? TimeoutCancellationException at 200 ms, and the SDK call is cancelled The call returns the SDK's value after 3 seconds; the timeout is ignored IllegalStateException, because the continuation was resumed twice The coroutine stays suspended until the SDK answers at 3 s, then throws TimeoutCancellationException; the SDK is never told The timeout cancels the coroutine at 200 ms, but a non-cancellable continuation cannot wake up until it is resumed. When the SDK answers at 3 s, the coroutine finds itself cancelled and throws. suspendCancellableCoroutine would resume at 200 ms and run invokeOnCancellation, where you cancel the SDK call. From the virtual threads track: a virtual thread calls Thread.sleep(200). What happens to its carrier thread? The carrier is blocked for the full 200 ms The virtual thread unmounts, and the carrier is free to run other virtual threads The JVM creates a new carrier to replace it sleep throws, because virtual threads cannot sleep When a virtual thread blocks in sleep, the JVM saves its stack and unmounts it, so the carrier runs other virtual threads. It is the same idea as a coroutine suspending, done by the JVM for any blocking call instead of by the Kotlin compiler for suspend calls.

h: Suspend functions from zero · Key terms
x: Coroutine One running piece of work that can pause and resume later, without holding a thread while paused. Suspend function A function marked suspend. It may pause at suspending calls and can only be called from a coroutine or another suspend function. Suspension point A call to a suspend function, where the caller may pause. It does not always pause, for example on a cache hit. Continuation The object that knows how to resume a paused coroutine: its context plus resumeWith(result). COROUTINE_SUSPENDED The marker a compiled suspend function returns to say it paused and will resume through the continuation. Continuation-passing style Compiling a function so it receives "what to do next" as an extra parameter, instead of returning to a waiting caller. Dispatcher The scheduler that decides which thread runs a coroutine, and which thread it resumes on. Does suspend run a function on a background thread? No. It only lets the function pause without blocking. The dispatcher decides the thread, and a suspend function that never suspends runs on its caller's thread. Inside a coroutine, what is the difference between delay(200) and Thread.sleep(200)? delay suspends the coroutine and frees the thread for others. Thread.sleep blocks the thread, so every coroutine waiting for that thread waits too. What does the compiler add to a suspend function's signature? A Continuation<T> as the last parameter. The return type becomes Any? (Object in Java). What does a compiled suspend function return when it pauses? The marker COROUTINE_SUSPENDED. The real result arrives later through continuation.resumeWith(...). Where does a suspended coroutine keep its local variables? In fields (L$0, L$1, ...) of a small state-machine object on the heap, next to an int label that says which state runs next. Why wrap a callback with suspendCancellableCoroutine and not suspendCoroutine? Only the cancellable one reacts to cancellation: it resumes the caller at once with CancellationException and runs invokeOnCancellation, where you cancel the underlying call. A callback fires after its coroutine was cancelled. What happens to cont.resume(value)? It is ignored (prompt cancellation guarantee). If the value is a resource, pass a cleanup lambda: cont.resume(value) { _, v, _ -> v.close() }.

h: Suspend functions from zero · Go deeper
x: Kotlin coroutines and Java virtual threads both rest on continuations, but they put them in different places. Kotlin's continuations are stackless. The compiler rewrites each suspend function into a state machine, and a suspended coroutine is a chain of those small state objects, one per suspend function still in progress. That is why suspend is part of the function type: every function between the coroutine and the suspending call must be compiled this way, or there is nowhere to save its state. People call this function coloring. It is also why coroutines work on any JVM version, on Android, and on Kotlin/JS and Native, where there is no Loom. Virtual threads use stackful continuations inside the JVM. When a virtual thread blocks, the JVM copies its stack frames to the heap and unmounts it from the carrier. Any blocking call, in any library, can pause it, with no change to the code and no coloring. The price is that the JVM decides when to pause, and code that holds a monitor or calls native code could pin the carrier on older JDKs (JDK 24 removed most pinning on synchronized, JEP 491). The KEEP also explains a detail you saw in javap: the state object is created once per call and reused across every suspension point in that call, so a function that suspends three times allocates one object, not three. And a suspend function whose suspending calls are all in tail position needs no state machine at all; it passes its continuation straight through. Read the "Implementation details" part of the KEEP (linked in sources) if you want the pseudo-Java the compiler generates, including how the generated invokeSuspend method re-enters the function.

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · launch starts a coroutine and hands you a Job
x: A coroutine builder is a plain function that starts a coroutine. You'll use four every day: launch, async, coroutineScope and runBlocking. They differ in what they give back and in whether the caller suspends or blocks. launch starts a coroutine and returns a Job at once. Use it for work whose result you don't need: write an audit row, publish an event, warm a connection. Java // Java equivalent: start a virtual thread, keep the handle, join it later Thread audit = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> auditLog.write(event)); // returns at once FxQuote quote = pricing.quote(pair); // carries on meanwhile audit.join(); // block until the audit is written Kotlin val audit: Job = launch { auditLog.write(event) } // returns at once val quote = pricing.quote(pair) // carries on meanwhile audit.join() // suspend until the audit is written A Job is a handle to the coroutine's lifecycle. You can check isActive and isCompleted, wait with join(), or stop it with cancel(). It holds no value. If the coroutine throws, the exception does not come back through the Job. It goes to the coroutine's parent, which lessons 3 and 6 of this track cover. launch is an extension function on CoroutineScope, so you can only call it where a scope exists: inside runBlocking, inside coroutineScope, or inside another coroutine. That restriction is on purpose. The scope becomes the new coroutine's parent, and the parent is what stops work from leaking. One detail surprises almost everyone. launch does not run its block immediately. It hands the block to the dispatcher and returns. Inside runBlocking, which has a single thread, the new coroutine gets to run only when the current coroutine suspends or finishes. So the line after launch usually runs first, and the Job already reports isActive = true for a block that has not started yet. Predict the order Read LaunchAndAsync.kt. Everything runs on the one thread that runBlocking owns. Write down the order in which the seven lines A to G will print. The letters are not a hint. Run it and compare. For each line you got wrong, find the suspension point that explains it. LaunchAndAsync.kt package workbench.coroutines.l02 import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** Predict the order of the lines before you run it. Everything runs on one thread. */ fun main() = runBlocking { println("A: before the builders") val audit = launch { println("C: audit starts") delay(100) println("F: audit written") } val price = async { println("D: price lookup starts") delay(50) 1_084_512L } println("B: builders returned, audit.isActive=${audit.isActive}") println("E: price is ${price.await()}") audit.join() println("G: audit.isCompleted=${audit.isCompleted}") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l02.LaunchAndAsyncKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l02/LaunchAndAsync.kt LaunchAndAsyncJava.java // Java equivalent of LaunchAndAsync.kt: one event-loop thread, tasks queue behind the running one. // Java has no suspension, so "await" becomes a callback (thenAccept) instead of a pause. package workbench.coroutines.l02; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class LaunchAndAsyncJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { ScheduledExecutorService loop = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "loop")); loop.execute(() -> { System.out.println("A: before the tasks"); CompletableFuture<Void> audit = new CompletableFuture<>(); loop.execute(() -> { // like launch: queued behind the running task System.out.println("C: audit starts"); loop.schedule(() -> { System.out.println("F: audit written"); audit.complete(null); }, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); }); CompletableFuture<Long> price = new CompletableFuture<>(); loop.execute(() -> { // like async System.out.println("D: price lookup starts"); loop.schedule(() -> price.complete(1_084_512L), 50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); }); System.out.println("B: tasks queued, audit.isDone=" + audit.isDone()); price.thenAccept(p -> System.out.println("E: price is " + p)) // like await, written as a callback .thenCompose(x -> audit) // like join .thenRun(() -> { System.out.println("G: audit.isDone=" + audit.isDone()); loop.shutdown(); }); }); loop.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l02.LaunchAndAsyncJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l02/LaunchAndAsyncJava.java A, B, C, D, E, F, G. B prints before C because launch and async only schedule their blocks, and the thread is still busy with main's body. The audit job is already isActive=true. C and D run when main suspends in await. E prints at about 50 ms, F at about 100 ms, and G after join. The Java twin prints the same order on a one-thread executor, but look at its shape: with no suspension, every "await" becomes a callback (thenAccept, thenCompose). A deli counter. launch is asking a colleague to restock the fridge: you don't wait and you expect nothing back. async is taking a numbered ticket: the order starts now, and you swap the ticket (await) for your sandwich later. Take three tickets at once and you wait for the slowest sandwich, not all three in a row. coroutineScope is the shift manager who won't close the till until every ticket issued during the shift has been served. runBlocking is standing at the counter, refusing to move until your order is done, while the queue behind you grows. The analogy breaks on one point: a real deli makes sandwiches in parallel with more staff. Coroutines get their overlap from waiting, so three calls on one thread still overlap, because none of them uses the thread while it waits for the network.

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · async returns a Deferred: start now, await later
x: async is launch with a result. It starts a coroutine and returns a Deferred<T> at once. A Deferred is a Job that will also hold a value. await() suspends until the value is ready and returns it, or rethrows the exception the coroutine failed with. What async buys you is concurrent decomposition: split one job into independent calls, start them all, then collect the answers. Java // Java equivalent: blocking calls on virtual threads, started together, joined afterwards List<FxQuote> allQuotes(String pair) { List<CompletableFuture<FxQuote>> pending = providers.stream() .map(p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> p.quote(pair), vthreads)) // 1. start all three .toList(); return pending.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList(); // 2. then wait for all } Kotlin suspend fun allQuotes(pair: String): List<FxQuote> = coroutineScope { val pending = providers.map { p -> async { p.quote(pair) } } // 1. start all three pending.awaitAll() // 2. then wait for all } Three providers that take 300, 120 and 200 ms answer in about 300 ms this way. One after another they take 620 ms. The classic mistake is to await too early: Java // Java equivalent of the same mistake: join right after starting FxQuote a = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> northbank.quote(pair), vthreads).join(); // waits 300 ms here FxQuote b = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fjord.quote(pair), vthreads).join(); // then starts this one Kotlin val a = async { northbank.quote(pair) }.await() // waits 300 ms right here val b = async { fjord.quote(pair) }.await() // and only then starts this one This compiles, runs and passes a functional test. It is also completely sequential. Concurrency lives in the gap between starting a Deferred and awaiting it, so start everything first and await afterwards. Prefer awaitAll() to map { it.await() }. Both return the results in list order. The difference shows up on failure: awaitAll fails as soon as any deferred fails, while the map version only notices when it reaches the failed one in the list. Don't use async when you don't need the value. An async that nobody awaits hides your intent, and in a supervisor scope it also hides the exception. Use launch. Sequential, concurrent, and accidentally sequential Read SequentialVsConcurrent.kt and predict both timings. Run it. In concurrent(), change the body to latencies.map { (p, ms) -> async { quote(p, ms) }.await() } and run again. Predict first. In the Java twin, make the same mistake: replace the body of concurrent with return LATENCIES.stream().map(e -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> quote(e.getKey(), e.getValue()), vthreads).join()).toList(); and run it. SequentialVsConcurrent.kt package workbench.coroutines.l02 import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.awaitAll import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis private suspend fun quote(provider: String, latencyMs: Long): String { delay(latencyMs) // stands in for a network call return "$provider:${latencyMs}ms" } private val latencies = listOf("northbank" to 300L, "fjord-fx" to 120L, "tidewater" to 200L) suspend fun sequential(): List<String> = latencies.map { (p, ms) -> quote(p, ms) } suspend fun concurrent(): List<String> = coroutineScope { latencies.map { (p, ms) -> async { quote(p, ms) } }.awaitAll() } fun main() = runBlocking { var result: List<String> val t1 = measureTimeMillis { result = sequential() } println("sequential: $result in $t1 ms") val t2 = measureTimeMillis { result = concurrent() } println("concurrent: $result in $t2 ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l02.SequentialVsConcurrentKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l02/SequentialVsConcurrent.kt SequentialVsConcurrentJava.java // Java equivalent of SequentialVsConcurrent.kt: blocking calls on virtual threads, // started together with CompletableFuture and joined afterwards. package workbench.coroutines.l02; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class SequentialVsConcurrentJava { static String quote(String provider, long latencyMs) { try { Thread.sleep(latencyMs); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } // a network call return provider + ":" + latencyMs + "ms"; } static final List<Map.Entry<String, Long>> LATENCIES = List.of(Map.entry("northbank", 300L), Map.entry("fjord-fx", 120L), Map.entry("tidewater", 200L)); static List<String> sequential() { return LATENCIES.stream().map(e -> quote(e.getKey(), e.getValue())).toList(); } static List<String> concurrent(ExecutorService vthreads) { List<CompletableFuture<String>> pending = LATENCIES.stream() .map(e -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> quote(e.getKey(), e.getValue()), vthreads)) // start all .toList(); return pending.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList(); // then wait } public static void main(String[] args) { try (ExecutorService vthreads = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<String> r1 = sequential(); System.out.printf("sequential: %s in %d ms%n", r1, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); long t1 = System.nanoTime(); List<String> r2 = concurrent(vthreads); System.out.printf("concurrent: %s in %d ms%n", r2, (System.nanoTime() - t1) / 1_000_000); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l02.SequentialVsConcurrentJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l02/SequentialVsConcurrentJava.java About 620 ms for the sequential version (642 ms here) and about 300 ms for the concurrent one (309 ms here). After your change, concurrent() takes about 620 ms too: each await runs before the next async starts. The Java twin behaves the same way (662 ms and 316 ms here, then about 620 ms with join inside the map). Concurrency happens between starting a Deferred and awaiting it. Start all three calls, then await: the total is the slowest call. Composing suspending functions (Kotlin docs) docs A payment details page in your Quarkus service needs the account (80 ms), the last 20 ledger entries (150 ms) and the risk flags (60 ms). Written as three suspend calls in a row, the page takes about 290 ms. Inside coroutineScope with three async calls, it takes about 150 ms, and if the ledger call fails, the other two are cancelled rather than left holding Oracle connections. Checkout is the same shape: FX quotes from several liquidity providers, a fraud score and a BIN lookup, all independent. Keep runBlocking at the edges. A blocking Kafka poll loop that hands each record to a suspend handler is one of the few places where it belongs.

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · coroutineScope waits for its children
x: coroutineScope is how a suspend function gets a scope to start children in. It creates a scope, runs the block, and then suspends until every coroutine started inside has finished. Only then does it return the block's value. Java // Java equivalent: an executor's close() waits for every task it accepted (JDK 19+) void warmUp() { try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { providers.forEach(p -> executor.submit(() -> p.quote("EURUSD"))); } // returns after the slowest provider has answered } Kotlin suspend fun warmUp() = coroutineScope { providers.forEach { p -> launch { p.quote("EURUSD") } } } // returns after the slowest provider has answered That gives your callers a strong promise: when a suspend function returns, the work it started is done. Nothing keeps running behind their back, holding a connection or writing to the ledger after the request has finished. Failure travels the same path in reverse. If one child fails, coroutineScope cancels the other children, waits for them to stop, and rethrows the exception to its caller. In allQuotes, a provider that throws at 50 ms makes the whole call fail at about 50 ms, and the two other requests are cancelled instead of left running. Lesson 3 of this track draws this tree of parents and children, and lesson 6 of this track is about the exceptions. coroutineScope suspends; it does not block. The thread is free while it waits. It is itself a suspend function, so you call it from suspend code, and you can nest it as deep as you like. The lab's quoteBoard puts allQuotes inside another coroutineScope: two currency pairs times three providers is six calls in flight at once, and the board is still ready in 300 ms. The builders so far, side by side: launch and async start a child and return at once, while coroutineScope runs a block and suspends until all of its children are done. You will rarely write launch or async without a coroutineScope (or a class-owned scope, lesson 3 of this track) around them. Quick check: warmUp() asks three providers that take 300, 120 and 200 ms, and the 120 ms one throws. When does warmUp return, and what happens to the other two calls? (It throws at about 120 ms. The scope cancels the 300 ms and 200 ms calls, waits for them to stop, and then rethrows the failure.)

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · runBlocking belongs at the edges: main and tests
x: runBlocking is the bridge from blocking code into coroutines. It starts a coroutine, blocks the current thread until that coroutine and all its children finish, and returns the result. The children run on that same blocked thread, in a small event loop. Use it at the edges only: fun main(), tests, and the rare framework callback that has to be blocking. For tests, runTest from kotlinx-coroutines-test is better, because it skips delays (lesson 10 of this track). For main, Kotlin also accepts suspend fun main(). Never call runBlocking from suspend code. The kotlinx.coroutines docs call it redundant there and warn that it blocks the thread. In a service it does real damage. Suspend code usually runs on a small shared pool, and runBlocking holds one of those threads for as long as the inner work takes, which is exactly what suspending was meant to avoid. It also ignores the caller's coroutine context, so the caller's cancellation and timeouts don't reach the work inside. The cause is in its signature: runBlocking is a plain function, not a suspend one, so its caller passes it no continuation and no context (lesson 1 of this track). It starts a fresh coroutine with no parent. The Try it runs eight 200 ms lookups on a pool of two threads. With delay, all eight overlap and finish in about 200 ms. With runBlocking { delay(200) } hidden inside the suspend function, each lookup holds a pool thread for its full 200 ms. Eight lookups on two threads need four rounds. If you find yourself reaching for runBlocking inside suspend code to "just call" another suspend function, you don't need it. Call the function directly. If you need several calls at once, that's coroutineScope with async. Starve a pool with runBlocking Read RunBlockingTrap.kt. Eight lookups share a pool of two threads. Run it as is (the good version). Note the time. Predict the time with runBlocking inside the suspend function, then run with -Pargs=bad. RunBlockingTrap.kt package workbench.coroutines.l02 import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import java.util.concurrent.Executors import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** A suspend function that "helpfully" calls runBlocking inside. Pass "bad" to use it. */ suspend fun lookupBad(id: Int): Int { runBlocking { delay(200) } // blocks the calling thread for 200 ms return id } suspend fun lookupGood(id: Int): Int { delay(200) // suspends; the thread serves other coroutines meanwhile return id } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val bad = args.firstOrNull() == "bad" // a pool with only two threads, like a small request pool Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2).asCoroutineDispatcher().use { pool -> val took = measureTimeMillis { runBlocking { withContext(pool) { repeat(8) { id -> launch { if (bad) lookupBad(id) else lookupGood(id) } } } } } println("8 lookups of 200 ms on 2 threads (${if (bad) "runBlocking inside" else "delay"}): $took ms") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l02.RunBlockingTrapKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l02/RunBlockingTrap.kt RunBlockingTrapJava.java // Java equivalent of RunBlockingTrap.kt: blocking on a future inside a task on a small pool. // Pass "bad" to join inside the task, like calling runBlocking inside suspend code. package workbench.coroutines.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.Executor; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class RunBlockingTrapJava { // a 200 ms lookup that completes from a timer: it holds no thread while it waits. // (If the timer completed on the same two-thread pool, the "bad" version would deadlock: // both threads blocked in join(), waiting for work that needs one of them.) static CompletableFuture<Integer> lookup(int id) { Executor after200ms = CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> id, after200ms); } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean bad = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("bad"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2); // a small request pool long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<Integer>> all = new ArrayList<>(); for (int id = 0; id < 8; id++) { int i = id; all.add(bad ? CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> lookup(i).join(), pool) // holds a pool thread for 200 ms : CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> i, pool).thenCompose(RunBlockingTrapJava::lookup)); } CompletableFuture.allOf(all.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); System.out.printf("8 lookups of 200 ms on 2 threads (%s): %d ms%n", bad ? "join inside the task" : "thenCompose", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); pool.shutdown(); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l02.RunBlockingTrapJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l02/RunBlockingTrapJava.java About 200 ms with delay (268 ms here). About 800 ms with runBlocking inside (849 ms here): each lookup holds one of the two threads for 200 ms, so the eight lookups run in four rounds of two. The Java twin shows the same cost for join() inside a pool task (219 ms vs 817 ms here). Its comment notes a worse outcome: if the lookup needed the same two threads to complete, both would wait forever. runBlocking (API reference, see the pitfalls) docs The most common builder mistake is awaiting each async right after starting it: val a = async { a() }.await(); val b = async { b() }.await(). The code looks concurrent and runs sequentially, so the latency is the sum. People write it because they read async as "run in the background" rather than "start a child that I will collect later". The fix is to start every async first, keep the Deferred values, and await them afterwards, preferably with awaitAll(). The runner-up mistake is GlobalScope.async or runBlocking inside suspend code to get a scope. Use coroutineScope { } instead.

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · Java and Kotlin
x: Three quotes at once: CompletableFuture vs async QuoteAggregator.java List<FxQuote> allQuotes(String pair) { List<CompletableFuture<FxQuote>> futures = providers.stream() .map(p -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> p.quote(pair), ioPool)) .toList(); return futures.stream() .map(CompletableFuture::join) // blocks until each one is done .toList(); } QuoteAggregator.kt suspend fun allQuotes(pair: String): List<FxQuote> = coroutineScope { providers.map { p -> async { p.quote(pair) } }.awaitAll() } Both start three calls and collect them in order. In Java, each supplyAsync takes a thread from ioPool for the whole call, and join blocks the caller's thread too. In Kotlin, the three children suspend while they wait, so they need no extra threads, and the caller suspends rather than blocks. Failure handling differs most. If one Java future fails, the others keep running to the end, and nobody cancels them (cancelling a CompletableFuture would not interrupt the work anyway). In Kotlin, coroutineScope cancels the remaining children as soon as one fails and rethrows the original exception. With virtual threads on JDK 21+, the Java version can block cheaply, but cancelling the siblings still needs structured concurrency, which is a preview API (see "Structured concurrency and scoped values" in the virtual threads track).

x: Make a payment details endpoint concurrent The endpoint makes three calls in a row. They don't depend on each other, so the 290 ms is all waiting. suspend fun details(id: PaymentId): PaymentDetails { val account = accounts.load(id) // 80 ms val entries = ledger.recent(id, 20) // 150 ms val flags = risk.flags(id) // 60 ms return PaymentDetails(account, entries, flags) } // Java equivalent: three blocking calls in a row PaymentDetails details(PaymentId id) { Account account = accounts.load(id); // 80 ms List<Entry> entries = ledger.recent(id, 20); // 150 ms List<Flag> flags = risk.flags(id); // 60 ms return new PaymentDetails(account, entries, flags); } Open a scope, start all three as children, then await. The function now takes as long as the ledger call, about 150 ms. suspend fun details(id: PaymentId): PaymentDetails = coroutineScope { // 1. start every independent call val account = async { accounts.load(id) } val entries = async { ledger.recent(id, 20) } val flags = async { risk.flags(id) } // 2. collect the answers PaymentDetails(account.await(), entries.await(), flags.await()) } // Java equivalent: start all three on virtual threads, then join PaymentDetails details(PaymentId id) { // 1. start every independent call var account = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> accounts.load(id), vthreads); var entries = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> ledger.recent(id, 20), vthreads); var flags = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> risk.flags(id), vthreads); // 2. collect the answers return new PaymentDetails(account.join(), entries.join(), flags.join()); } A new requirement: risk flags need the account's country. Keep that one dependency inside its own child, so the ledger call still runs alongside both. val account = async { accounts.load(id) } val entries = async { ledger.recent(id, 20) } // 3. a dependent call waits for its input inside its own child val flags = async { risk.flags(id, account.await().country) } var account = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> accounts.load(id), vthreads); var entries = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> ledger.recent(id, 20), vthreads); // 3. a dependent call runs once its input is there var flags = account.thenApplyAsync(a -> risk.flags(id, a.country()), vthreads); Self-check: the ledger call throws at 40 ms. What happens to the other two calls, and when does details fail? (The scope cancels the account and risk children, waits for them to stop, and rethrows the ledger exception at about 40 ms. Nothing is left running.)
