h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · Quiz
x: What does this print? runBlocking { launch { println("X") } println("Y") } X then Y Y then X Either order, it changes from run to run Only Y; the launched coroutine never runs launch schedules its block on runBlocking's single thread and returns. That thread is still running the outer block, so Y prints first. The child runs when the outer block finishes, and runBlocking waits for it before returning. Order is deterministic here because there is only one thread. About how long does this take? coroutineScope { val a = async { delay(300); 1 } val b = async { delay(200); 2 } a.await() + b.await() } About 200 ms About 500 ms About 300 ms About 0 ms, because async returns at once Both children start before the first await, so the delays overlap and the total is the longer one. 500 ms would be the sequential version. async does return at once, but await and the scope both wait for the children. fetchA takes 300 ms and fetchB 200 ms. How long does this take? val a = async { fetchA() }.await() val b = async { fetchB() }.await() About 500 ms: each await finishes before the next async starts About 300 ms: async runs them in parallel About 200 ms It does not compile, because await must be called later Calling await() right after async waits for that child before the next line runs, so nothing overlaps. Keep the Deferred values and await them after starting both. A suspend handler must publish a PaymentCaptured event and write an audit row, at the same time. It needs neither result, but it must not return until both are done. Which fits? GlobalScope.launch { publish() }; GlobalScope.launch { audit() } runBlocking { launch { publish() }; launch { audit() } } publish(); audit() coroutineScope { launch { publish() }; launch { audit() } } coroutineScope with two launch children runs them concurrently and returns only when both finish. GlobalScope returns at once and leaks the work. runBlocking blocks the handler's thread. Two plain calls are correct but sequential. From the executors track: CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b, c). b fails after 10 ms, while a and c take one second. When does the allOf future complete? As soon as b fails, after about 10 ms When all three have completed, after about one second, exceptionally After about one second, normally, with b's result left out Never: allOf hangs when one future fails allOf completes when all of its futures complete, and it completes exceptionally if any of them did. It does not cancel a and c when b fails. Compare coroutineScope with awaitAll(), which fails at 10 ms and cancels the two remaining children.

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · Key terms
x: Coroutine builder A function that starts a coroutine, such as launch, async, runBlocking or coroutineScope. Job A handle to a coroutine's lifecycle: check it, join it, cancel it. It holds no value. Deferred A Job that will also hold a result. await() returns it or rethrows the failure. CoroutineScope The thing you call launch and async on. It supplies the parent Job and context for new coroutines. Concurrent decomposition Splitting one task into independent calls, starting them together, and combining their results. Event loop The queue of coroutines that runBlocking runs one at a time on the thread it blocks. What does launch return, and where does its exception go? A Job, with no result. If the coroutine fails, the exception goes to its parent, not to whoever holds the Job. What does async return? A Deferred<T>: a Job that will hold a value. await() suspends until it is ready, then returns it or rethrows the failure. val a = async { f() }.await(); val b = async { g() }.await(): concurrent or sequential? Sequential. Each await finishes before the next async starts. Start both, then await. awaitAll() vs map { it.await() }? Same results in the same order, but awaitAll fails as soon as any deferred fails. The map version notices only when it reaches the failed one. When does coroutineScope { ... } return? After its block and every child started inside it have finished. If a child fails, it cancels the others and rethrows. Where is runBlocking allowed? At blocking edges: main, tests and blocking framework callbacks. Never inside suspend code, where it holds the thread and ignores the caller's context.

h: Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope · Go deeper
x: A Job moves through a small set of states. A job created with start = CoroutineStart.LAZY begins in New and starts only when you call start(), join() or await(). Every other job starts in Active. When its block finishes, a job is Completing while it waits for its children, then Completed. If it is cancelled or fails, it goes through Cancelling (children are being cancelled, finally blocks run) to Cancelled. isActive, isCompleted and isCancelled are views over these states. That is why launch reports isActive = true before its block has run a single line. Lazy async is a coroutine version of lazy {} for suspend work: val rates = async(start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) { loadRates() } starts nothing until the first await(). Be careful with it inside coroutineScope: a lazy child that nobody starts keeps the scope waiting forever, because the scope waits for all children, including those in the New state. The kotlinx.coroutines guide also has a section on "async-style functions", such as fun quoteAsync() = GlobalScope.async { ... }, and strongly discourages them. If the caller fails between starting and awaiting, the work keeps running in the background with nobody to collect it. Expose a suspend function instead, and let the caller decide what runs concurrently.

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Every coroutine has a parent, and a parent waits for its children
x: Every coroutine you start with launch or async gets a Job, and that job becomes a child of the job in the scope you called it on. Children can have children. The result is a tree, and the tree is the whole idea behind structured concurrency: concurrent work has the same nested shape as the code that started it. Java // Java equivalent: nested StructuredTaskScope (preview in JDK 25, JEP 505; needs --enable-preview) try (var details = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // a node, like coroutineScope details.fork(() -> accounts.load(id)); details.fork(() -> ledger.recent(id, 20)); details.fork(() -> risk.flags(id)); details.join(); // waits for all three subtasks } Kotlin runBlocking(CoroutineName("request")) { // root launch(CoroutineName("details")) { // child of request coroutineScope { // a node of its own async(CoroutineName("account")) { /* ... */ } async(CoroutineName("ledger")) { /* ... */ } launch(CoroutineName("risk")) { /* ... */ } } } } A scope is just a coroutine context that holds a job. The context is the small set of settings that travels with a coroutine: its job, its name, its dispatcher. Lesson 4 of this track takes it apart. launch reads the job from the scope's context and attaches the new coroutine to it. coroutineScope adds a node of its own between its caller and the children started inside it. The first rule of the tree: a parent cannot complete until all of its children have completed. When the body of a coroutine finishes, its job enters a waiting state ("completing") until every child is done. That is why coroutineScope returns only after the slowest child, and why runBlocking doesn't return while anything below it is still running. Completed children leave the tree, so job.children lists only the work that is still going. The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 docs spell out four rules for how lifecycles interact. The parent waits for its children. Cancelling the parent cancels the children. A child that fails with an exception cancels its parent (unless the parent is a supervisor, lesson 6 of this track). And a child that ends with CancellationException counts as cancelled, so the parent is not told. The next section is about the middle two. Print the tree Read JobTree.kt. Before running it, sketch the tree you expect to see at 100 ms, with names. Run it and compare with your sketch. Why does details appear twice? (Hint: what does coroutineScope inherit from its parent?) JobTree.kt package workbench.coroutines.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Job import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.job import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** Prints a Job and all of its children, indented. */ fun Job.printTree(indent: String = "") { // every coroutine is also a CoroutineScope, so we can read the name from its context val name = (this as? CoroutineScope)?.coroutineContext?.get(CoroutineName)?.name ?: "(coroutineScope)" println("$indent$name active=$isActive children=${children.count()}") children.forEach { it.printTree("$indent ") } } fun main() = runBlocking(CoroutineName("request")) { val details = launch(CoroutineName("details")) { coroutineScope { async(CoroutineName("account")) { delay(300) } async(CoroutineName("ledger")) { delay(300) } launch(CoroutineName("risk")) { delay(300) } delay(100) // give the children time to start println("tree at 100 ms, seen from the request coroutine:") this@runBlocking.coroutineContext.job.printTree() } } details.join() println("after join: request has ${coroutineContext.job.children.count()} children") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l03.JobTreeKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l03/JobTree.kt request has one child, details. Under it sits a second node also called details: that is the coroutineScope, which inherits its parent's context, name included. It has three children: account, ledger and risk. After join, the request has 0 children, because finished children leave the tree. coroutineScope (API reference) docs A family on a day out. The parent won't leave the park until every child is back at the car. If one child gets hurt, the parent calls everyone back and the trip ends, and the parent then tells whoever is waiting at home what happened. If a child simply decides they've had enough and sits in the car, nobody panics. GlobalScope is a child who wandered off with no parent at all: nobody will look for them at closing time. An owned scope is a school trip: the school, not any one parent, brings everyone home at the end of the day. The analogy breaks on timing. Real children come back when they hear the call. A coroutine only hears it at its next suspension point, so a child busy in a CPU loop keeps going until it pauses.

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Failure goes up, cancellation goes down
x: In the job tree, failure goes up and cancellation goes down Take the payment details endpoint from lesson 2 of this track: account, ledger and risk calls as three children of one coroutineScope. The ledger call throws IOException at 100 ms. Here is what the tree does, in order: The ledger child fails. It reports the exception to its parent, the scope. The scope's job is cancelled with that exception. A cancelled job cancels all of its children, so the account and risk calls are cancelled. Their finally blocks run. The scope waits until those children have actually stopped. coroutineScope rethrows the IOException to its caller, which can catch it like any exception. So a single failure takes down the whole subtree it belongs to, and then surfaces as one exception at the place that started the work. The total time is the time to the failure, about 100 ms, not the time of the slowest call. Nothing is left running in the background holding a connection. Cancellation only travels down. If the caller cancels the request (the client hung up, or a timeout fired), every coroutine below it is cancelled. A child that is cancelled does not cancel its parent. A child whose block ends by throwing CancellationException is treated the same way: it is "cancelled", not "failed", and the parent carries on. This is the default because it is almost always what a request needs. If one of three calls needed to build the response has failed, there is no response, so the other two calls are wasted work. When you do want siblings to survive each other's failures (sending a notification to email, SMS and push), you ask for it explicitly with a supervisor. That is lesson 6 of this track. One caution from the docs: cancellation reaches a coroutine only at a suspension point. A child stuck in a CPU loop or a blocking call finishes that first. Lesson 5 of this track shows how to cooperate. Watch one failure take down a scope Read FailureSpreads.kt. Predict which lines print, and at roughly what times. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=ok, so the ledger does not fail. Predict when coroutineScope returns. Run the Java twin, then run it with -Pargs=cancel. Compare what happens to the risk task. FailureSpreads.kt package workbench.coroutines.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.io.IOException /** One child fails at 100 ms. Watch what happens to its sibling and to the caller. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val ledgerFails = args.firstOrNull() != "ok" val t0 = System.nanoTime() fun log(msg: String) = println("[%4d ms] %s".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, msg)) try { coroutineScope { launch { delay(100) if (ledgerFails) { log("ledger: throwing IOException") throw IOException("ledger unavailable") } log("ledger: done") } launch { try { delay(1_000) log("risk: done") } finally { log("risk: finally block runs") } } log("scope body finished; the scope now waits for its children") } log("coroutineScope returned normally") } catch (e: IOException) { log("caller caught: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l03.FailureSpreadsKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l03/FailureSpreads.kt FailureSpreadsJava.java // Java equivalent of FailureSpreads.kt with a virtual-thread executor (JDK 21+, no preview APIs). // An executor has no parent-child tree: a failed task does not cancel its sibling unless you do it. // Pass "cancel" to cancel the sibling by hand, which is what coroutineScope does for you. package workbench.coroutines.l03; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.UncheckedIOException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; public class FailureSpreadsJava { static long t0; static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("[%4d ms] %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean cancelByHand = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("cancel"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService children = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<?> ledger = children.submit(() -> { sleep(100); log("ledger: throwing IOException"); throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("ledger unavailable")); }); Future<?> risk = children.submit(() -> { try { sleep(1_000); log("risk: done"); } finally { log("risk: finally block runs"); } }); try { ledger.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { log("caller caught: " + e.getCause().getCause().getMessage()); if (cancelByHand) risk.cancel(true); // interrupts the sibling } } // close() waits for every task, including the sibling nobody cancelled log("executor closed"); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException("interrupted", e); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l03.FailureSpreadsJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l03/FailureSpreadsJava.java The scope body finishes first, at a few ms. At about 100 ms the ledger throws, and within a few ms the risk child's finally runs and the caller catches ledger unavailable. risk: done never prints. (The first delay can read 150 ms or so on a cold JVM.) With -Pargs=ok, coroutineScope returns at about 1,000 ms, after the slowest child. The Java twin is the honest contrast: an executor has no tree, so after the ledger fails the risk task runs to risk: done at about 1,000 ms, and close() waits for it. With -Pargs=cancel you cancel the sibling by hand and its finally runs at about 100 ms (the last two lines can come in either order). coroutineScope does that step for you. One child fails. The scope cancels its siblings, waits for them to stop, and rethrows the failure to its caller. Two places in a payments service need this most. First, request fan-out: a payment details or checkout endpoint that calls three services should do so inside coroutineScope, so a failure or a client disconnect cancels the other calls and releases their Oracle connections. Second, partition-scoped background work in a Kafka consumer. Give each assigned partition a worker with its own scope, launch the per-partition jobs into it, and call shutdown() (cancel and join) in onPartitionsRevoked, before the offsets are committed and the partition moves to another pod. If those jobs ran in GlobalScope, two pods could settle the same batch during a rebalance. Anything that must survive a pod restart belongs in an outbox table or a Temporal workflow, not in a coroutine.

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · GlobalScope cuts work loose from the tree
x: GlobalScope is a scope with no job. A coroutine launched in it has no parent, so none of the rules above apply. Nothing waits for it, nothing cancels it, and its exception goes to the thread's uncaught exception handler, which usually means a log line nobody reads. Java // Java equivalent: a task on a shared, app-wide pool; nothing ties it to the request void startRefund(String id) { SHARED_POOL.submit(() -> refundSteps(id)); // returns at once; the refund is an orphan } Kotlin suspend fun startRefund(id: String) { GlobalScope.launch { refundSteps(id) } // returns at once; the refund is an orphan } The caller of startRefund thinks the refund is part of its request. It is not. When the client gives up and the request coroutine is cancelled, the refund keeps going. In a test, it keeps running after the test has finished and may fail the next one. At shutdown, it can still be writing when the connection pool closes. This is a leaked coroutine: work that outlives everything that knows about it. kotlinx.coroutines marks GlobalScope as @DelicateCoroutinesApi, so you have to opt in, and its docs call using it an antipattern. They also warn about the obvious workaround: CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch { } inside a function creates a brand-new root scope on every call and has every one of the same problems. The opt-in warning just doesn't fire. The fix depends on what you meant. If the caller should wait for the refund, call it directly, or use coroutineScope { launch { } } when it runs alongside other work. If the refund really should outlive the request, then something with a longer life has to own it: a component with its own scope, which the next section builds. In payments it often means something else again: write the refund to an outbox table or a Temporal workflow, so it survives a restart. An in-memory coroutine doesn't. There is one legitimate use: a coroutine that lives exactly as long as the whole application, such as a metrics reporter started in main. Cancel a request and watch the refund carry on Read LeakedWork.kt. The request is cancelled at 250 ms. Predict how many refund steps print after that. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which uses the coroutineScope version. Predict first. Run the Java twin both ways. It interrupts a request thread instead of cancelling a coroutine. LeakedWork.kt package workbench.coroutines.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.DelicateCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.GlobalScope import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private var start = 0L private fun ms() = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000 private suspend fun refundSteps(id: String) { repeat(6) { step -> delay(100) println(" [${ms()} ms] refund $id: step $step") } } /** Leaks: the refund belongs to GlobalScope, not to the request that started it. */ @OptIn(DelicateCoroutinesApi::class) suspend fun startRefundLeaky(id: String) { GlobalScope.launch { refundSteps(id) } } /** Structured: the refund is a child of the caller. */ suspend fun startRefund(id: String) = coroutineScope { launch { refundSteps(id) } } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val structured = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" start = System.nanoTime() val request = launch { if (structured) startRefund("r-17") else startRefundLeaky("r-17") delay(10_000) // the request goes on to do other things } delay(250) request.cancel() println("[${ms()} ms] request cancelled (client gave up)") delay(500) // keep the JVM alive a little to see what still runs println("[${ms()} ms] main done") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l03.LeakedWorkKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l03/LeakedWork.kt LeakedWorkJava.java // Java equivalent of LeakedWork.kt: a request thread hands the refund to a shared pool. // Interrupting the request (the client gave up) does not reach the pool's task. // Pass "fixed" to run the refund in the request's own thread, so the interrupt stops it. package workbench.coroutines.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class LeakedWorkJava { static final ExecutorService SHARED = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(r -> { // lives as long as the app Thread t = new Thread(r, "shared-pool"); t.setDaemon(true); return t; }); static long start; static long ms() { return (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000; } static void refundSteps(String id) throws InterruptedException { for (int step = 0; step < 6; step++) { Thread.sleep(100); System.out.printf(" [%d ms] refund %s: step %d%n", ms(), id, step); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean structured = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); start = System.nanoTime(); Thread request = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { try { if (structured) refundSteps("r-17"); // part of the request else SHARED.submit(() -> { refundSteps("r-17"); return null; }); // an orphan Thread.sleep(10_000); // the request goes on to other things } catch (InterruptedException e) { // the request was cancelled } }); Thread.sleep(250); request.interrupt(); System.out.printf("[%d ms] request interrupted (client gave up)%n", ms()); Thread.sleep(500); System.out.printf("[%d ms] main done%n", ms()); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l03.LeakedWorkJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l03/LeakedWorkJava.java With GlobalScope, steps 2 to 5 keep printing after request cancelled: the refund never heard about it. With -Pargs=fixed, the refund is a child of the request, so nothing prints after request cancelled except main done. The Java twin leaks the same way: interrupting the request thread does not reach a task on a shared pool. Its fixed version runs the refund on the request's own thread, so the interrupt stops it. GlobalScope (API reference: why it is delicate) docs

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · A class that starts background work owns a scope and closes it
x: Some work really does outlive a single call: a settler that works through card batches for one Kafka partition, an FX rate refresher, a cache warmer. The structured way to write it is a class that owns a scope, launches into it, and cancels it when its own life ends. Java // Java equivalent: the class owns an executor and shuts it down class BatchSettler implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // 1. the class's own pool private final Consumer<String> settle; BatchSettler(Consumer<String> settle) { this.settle = settle; } Future<?> submit(String batchId) { return pool.submit(() -> settle.accept(batchId)); // 2. every batch runs in it } @Override public void close() throws InterruptedException { pool.shutdownNow(); // 3. interrupt them all pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // and wait } } Kotlin class BatchSettler(context: CoroutineContext, private val settle: suspend (String) -> Unit) { private val scope = CoroutineScope(context + Job()) // 1. the class's own root fun submit(batchId: String): Job = scope.launch { settle(batchId) } // 2. every batch is a child suspend fun shutdown() = scope.coroutineContext.job.cancelAndJoin() // 3. cancel them all, wait } The scope's job is the parent of every batch. One call to cancel reaches all of them, and job.children tells you what is still running. The tree still exists. Its root is now the object, not a request. A few rules keep this honest. Tie the scope to a real lifecycle. Cancel it in @PreDestroy in a Quarkus bean, in onPartitionsRevoked for a Kafka partition worker, or in @AfterEach in a test. An owned scope that nobody cancels is just GlobalScope with extra steps. Create it once, as a field. A scope created inside a method is the orphan from the previous section. Pass the dispatcher (or the whole context) in. Production can use Dispatchers.IO, and tests can pass a test dispatcher and run on virtual time. The lab does exactly this. Choose cancel or cancelAndJoin on purpose. scope.cancel() is not a suspend function and returns at once, while children are still running their finally blocks. cancelAndJoin() waits until they have stopped, which is what you want before closing a connection pool. CoroutineScope(...) adds a Job() for you if the context has none, but write it out so readers see it. With a plain Job, one failed batch cancels the whole settler. Lesson 6 of this track swaps it for a SupervisorJob, so batches can fail on their own. Quick check: you call scope.cancel() and close the connection pool on the next line, while three batches still have a finally that returns a connection. What can go wrong, and which one change fixes it? (cancel() returns before those finally blocks have run, so they may hand connections back to a pool that is already closed. cancelAndJoin() waits for them first.) The most common mistake is reaching for GlobalScope.launch (or CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch inside a function) to "run this in the background" from a request. It compiles and seems to work, so it ships. The cost shows up later: work keeps running after the client has gone, tests interfere with each other, failures only appear as stray log lines, and shutdown races with in-flight writes. Decide who owns the work. If the caller should wait, use coroutineScope. If the work should outlive the call, give a long-lived component a scope it owns and cancels at the end of its life. If it must survive a restart, use durable storage, not a coroutine.

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Java and Kotlin
x: Fan-out that cannot leak: StructuredTaskScope vs coroutineScope PaymentDetails.java (preview in JDK 25, JEP 505: compile and run with --enable-preview) Details details(PaymentId id) throws InterruptedException { try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) { // default: fail on the first failure Subtask<Account> account = scope.fork(() -> accounts.load(id)); Subtask<List<Entry>> entries = scope.fork(() -> ledger.recent(id, 20)); scope.join(); // waits; throws StructuredTaskScope.FailedException if a subtask failed return new Details(account.get(), entries.get()); } // close() cancels unfinished subtasks and waits for them } PaymentDetails.kt suspend fun details(id: PaymentId): Details = coroutineScope { val account = async { accounts.load(id) } val entries = async { ledger.recent(id, 20) } Details(account.await(), entries.await()) } // returns only when both children are done; a failure cancels the other The idea is the same in both: subtasks cannot outlive the block that started them, the first failure cancels the siblings, and the caller gets one exception. In Java each subtask is a virtual thread running blocking code, and cancellation means interruption. In Kotlin each child is a coroutine, and cancellation reaches it at its next suspension point. The bigger practical difference is maturity. In JDK 25, StructuredTaskScope is a preview API that needs --enable-preview, and its shape has changed between previews (the JDK 21 to 24 previews used a different, subclass-based API). In Kotlin, every launch and async already joins the tree, including calls deep inside other suspend functions, and you get the guarantee without asking for it.

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Worked example
x: Give an FX rate refresher a scope it owns A Quarkus bean refreshes FX rates every 30 seconds. It was written with GlobalScope. After shutdown it keeps calling the rate provider against a closed connection pool, and in tests one instance's loop keeps running into the next test. class FxRateRefresher(private val rates: RateSource) { @OptIn(DelicateCoroutinesApi::class) fun start() { GlobalScope.launch { while (true) { rates.refresh(); delay(30.seconds) } } } } // Java equivalent of the bug: a static scheduler that nobody shuts down class FxRateRefresher { private static final ScheduledExecutorService SHARED = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(1); private final RateSource rates; void start() { SHARED.scheduleWithFixedDelay(rates::refresh, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } Give the class its own scope, created once, with the dispatcher passed in so tests can use a test dispatcher. A CoroutineName makes it easy to spot in thread dumps and debug output. class FxRateRefresher( private val rates: RateSource, dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO, ) : AutoCloseable { // 1. one scope per instance; its Job is the parent of everything we start private val scope = CoroutineScope(dispatcher + Job() + CoroutineName("fx-refresher")) // Java equivalent: one scheduler per instance, with a named thread class FxRateRefresher implements AutoCloseable { private final RateSource rates; // 1. the instance owns its scheduler private final ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(Thread.ofPlatform().name("fx-refresher").factory()); Launch into that scope. Catch failures of a single refresh inside the loop, so one bad response does not end the loop and, with a plain Job, cancel the whole scope. Rethrow CancellationException (lesson 5 of this track explains why). // 2. the loop is a child of the scope fun start(): Job = scope.launch { while (true) { try { rates.refresh() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("rate refresh failed", e) } delay(30.seconds) } } // 2. the refresh belongs to this instance's scheduler ScheduledFuture<?> start() { return scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> { try { rates.refresh(); } catch (Exception e) { log.warn("rate refresh failed", e); } // an escaping exception stops the schedule }, 0, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } Close the scope when the owner's life ends: @PreDestroy in the bean, @AfterEach in a test. cancel() returns at once; use cancelAndJoin() from suspend code when you must wait for the loop to stop. // 3. tie the scope to a real lifecycle override fun close() = scope.cancel() } @ApplicationScoped class RatesLifecycle(private val refresher: FxRateRefresher) { @PreDestroy fun stop() = refresher.close() } // 3. tie the scheduler to a real lifecycle @Override public void close() { scheduler.shutdownNow(); } } @ApplicationScoped class RatesLifecycle { @Inject FxRateRefresher refresher; @PreDestroy void stop() { refresher.close(); } } Self-check: a colleague suggests fun start() = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch { ... } to avoid the opt-in warning. Why is that no better? (Each call makes a new root scope that nothing holds on to. Nobody can cancel it, so it leaks exactly like GlobalScope.)

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Quiz
x: What happens here? coroutineScope { launch { delay(100); throw IOException("down") } launch { delay(1_000); println("done") } } done prints at 1 s, then the scope throws IOException The IOException is printed by the uncaught handler and the scope returns normally At about 100 ms the second child is cancelled, done never prints, and the scope throws IOException The scope returns normally at 1 s, because launch swallows exceptions The failed child cancels the scope's job, which cancels its sibling. The scope waits for the sibling to stop, then rethrows the original exception to its caller. Nothing waits for the full second. A child coroutine ends by throwing CancellationException. What happens to its parent and its siblings? Nothing: the child counts as cancelled, and the parent is not notified The parent is cancelled, and so are the siblings The parent rethrows the CancellationException to its caller The siblings are cancelled, but the parent keeps running A CancellationException means "I was cancelled", not "I failed". The child cancels its own children, but the parent keeps going. Only other exceptions travel up. Lesson 5 of this track shows why that makes swallowing it dangerous. A request handler calls GlobalScope.launch { reconcile(batch) } and returns. A minute later the service shuts down while the reconciliation is still running. What stops the reconciliation? The request's scope, which cancels it when the response is sent Quarkus, which cancels all coroutines on shutdown runBlocking at the top of the call stack Nothing in coroutines: it runs until it finishes or the JVM exits A GlobalScope coroutine has no parent, so no lifecycle reaches it. It stops when it finishes, or when the JVM dies, possibly halfway through. If it must be stopped cleanly, it needs an owner with a scope that is cancelled on shutdown. A Kafka partition worker starts a background flush loop when its partition is assigned. Where should the loop's coroutine live? In GlobalScope, because it outlives any single record In a scope owned by the partition worker, cancelled and joined in onPartitionsRevoked In runBlocking on the consumer's poll thread In a new CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO) created inside the assignment callback The loop lives exactly as long as the partition assignment, so the worker for that partition should own the scope and cancel it when the partition is revoked. A new scope created in the callback has no owner and leaks like GlobalScope. runBlocking would block the poll thread. From lesson 2 of this track: what does this return, and when? coroutineScope { launch { delay(200) } 42 } 42, at once, because launch returns immediately 42, after about 200 ms, when the child finishes Unit, because the last expression is launch It never returns, because nobody joins the child The block's value is 42, but coroutineScope returns only after every child has completed. You don't need join: waiting for children is the scope's job.

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Key terms
x: Structured concurrency Concurrent work forms a tree that matches the code: children can't outlive their parent, and failures and cancels follow the tree. Parent job The job a new coroutine attaches to. It waits for its children and cancels them when it is cancelled. Child coroutine A coroutine started in a scope. Its failure cancels its parent unless the parent is a supervisor. Scope A coroutine context that holds a job. New coroutines started in it become that job's children. GlobalScope A scope with no job. Coroutines started there have no parent and are not structured. Leaked coroutine A coroutine that keeps running after everything that cared about it has gone. When does a parent coroutine complete? Only after its own block and all of its children have completed. In a regular coroutineScope, one child throws IOException. What happens? The scope is cancelled, which cancels the other children. The scope waits for them to stop, then rethrows the IOException to its caller. A child ends with CancellationException. Is its parent cancelled? No. It counts as cancelled, not failed, so the parent is not notified. Which direction does cancellation travel in the job tree? Down only. Cancelling a parent cancels all of its children; cancelling a child leaves the parent alone. Why is GlobalScope.launch in a request handler a leak? The coroutine has no parent: nothing waits for it, nothing cancels it when the request ends, and its failure goes to the uncaught exception handler. How should a class that starts background coroutines be structured? Own one CoroutineScope(context + Job()) as a field, launch into it, and cancel it (or cancelAndJoin) when the owner's lifecycle ends.

h: Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree · Go deeper
x: An owned scope does not have to be a separate root. Job(parent) creates a job that is a child of another one, so CoroutineScope(dispatcher + Job(appJob)) gives you a component scope that is cancelled when the application job is cancelled. With a plain Job, the link also works upwards: a failure in the component cancels appJob too. That is usually not what you want for a long-lived component, which is one reason lesson 6 of this track reaches for SupervisorJob(parent). The tree is also how kotlinx.coroutines reports problems. When several children fail, the first exception wins, and the others are attached to it as suppressed exceptions. When you print a stack trace from a failed scope, look at the suppressed list before you conclude that only one thing went wrong. The kotlinx-coroutines-debug module can dump the live coroutines of a running JVM with their states and creation stacks (DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines()). It is not on this lab's classpath, but it is the tool to reach for when you suspect a leak in a real service. Without it, the cheap trick from the Try it, walking job.children from a known root, already tells you how much work a component still has in flight. Exposing inFlight per partition worker on a health or metrics endpoint is a cheap way to spot a stuck consumer.

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · A dispatcher picks the thread, and withContext switches it
x: suspend says nothing about threads (lesson 1 of this track). The dispatcher in a coroutine's context does: it decides which thread runs the coroutine each time it starts or resumes. kotlinx.coroutines ships four. Dispatchers.Default is a pool with one thread per CPU core, and at least two. launch and async use it when the context names no dispatcher. Dispatchers.IO is for calls that block a thread, such as JDBC or a blocking HTTP client. Up to 64 of them run at once. Dispatchers.Main is the UI thread on Android, JavaFX or Swing, and needs a UI module on the classpath. A Quarkus service has none, and using it throws IllegalStateException. Dispatchers.Unconfined has no thread of its own. The coroutine starts on the caller's thread and, after its first suspension, carries on on whatever thread resumed it. The docs say it should not be used in general code. runBlocking is the odd one out: it runs its coroutine on the thread that called it. To run one piece of work somewhere else, use withContext: Java // Java equivalent: CompletableFuture stages, each with its own executor CompletableFuture<byte[]> statementPdf(String accountId) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> store.loadRows(accountId), ioPool) // blocking JDBC call .thenApplyAsync(renderer::render, cpuPool); // CPU-heavy layout } Kotlin suspend fun statementPdf(accountId: String): ByteArray { val rows = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { store.loadRows(accountId) } // blocking JDBC call return withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { renderer.render(rows) } // CPU-heavy layout } withContext suspends the caller, runs the block on the other dispatcher, and then resumes the caller on its own dispatcher with the block's result. The code reads top to bottom. In the Java version every stage names its executor, and whatever you chain next runs where the last stage left off, not back where you started. withContext is also a scope, like coroutineScope in lesson 3 of this track. It waits for any children launched inside the block, and a failure inside it comes out as an exception in the caller. A switch is cheap but not free: the library queues a task on the other dispatcher, and the coroutine's state machine resumes there. Values you wrote before the switch are visible after it, even on another thread. The library provides that happens-before edge, so you don't need @Volatile for a coroutine's own locals. Print where each step runs Read WhereDoesItRun.kt. It turns on debug mode, which adds the coroutine's name and number to thread names. Predict the thread for each line. Run it. Look closely at the two Unconfined lines. Run it two or three times. Do Default and IO always print different workers? Run the Java twin and match each line to its Kotlin counterpart. WhereDoesItRun.kt package workbench.coroutines.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import java.util.concurrent.Executors private fun here() = Thread.currentThread().toString() fun main() { // debug mode adds " @name#id" to thread names. Set it before any coroutine starts. System.setProperty("kotlinx.coroutines.debug", "on") runBlocking(CoroutineName("statement")) { println("runBlocking ${here()}") withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { println("Default ${here()}") } withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { println("IO ${here()}") } withContext(Dispatchers.Unconfined) { println("Unconfined, before ${here()}") delay(10) // resumes on whatever thread finishes the delay println("Unconfined, after ${here()}") } Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "ledger-writer") }.asCoroutineDispatcher().use { single -> withContext(single + CoroutineName("ledger")) { println("single-thread exec ${here()}") } } Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher().use { vt -> withContext(vt) { println("virtual-thread exec ${here()}") } } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.WhereDoesItRunKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l04/WhereDoesItRun.kt WhereDoesItRunJava.java // Java equivalent of WhereDoesItRun.kt: in Java you pick an executor for each step yourself. package workbench.coroutines.l04; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class WhereDoesItRunJava { static String here() { return Thread.currentThread().toString(); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("main " + here()); // the common pool: one thread per core, the closest match for Dispatchers.Default CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("commonPool " + here()), ForkJoinPool.commonPool()).join(); // a cached pool grows for blocking work, roughly what Dispatchers.IO does (without the cap) ExecutorService cached = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("cached pool " + here()), cached).join(); cached.shutdown(); // a non-async stage runs on whichever thread completes the previous stage, like Unconfined CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> 1, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(10, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) .thenAccept(x -> System.out.println("thenAccept after timer " + here())) .join(); try (ExecutorService single = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "ledger-writer"))) { CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("single-thread exec " + here()), single).join(); } try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("virtual-thread exec " + here()), vt).join(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.WhereDoesItRunJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l04/WhereDoesItRunJava.java runBlocking prints main @statement#1. Default and IO print DefaultDispatcher-worker-N threads, and on some runs IO prints the same worker as Default: the two share one pool. Unconfined starts on main and, after delay, resumes on kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor, the thread that fired the timer. The single-thread executor prints ledger-writer @ledger#1 (the new name replaced the old one) and the virtual-thread executor prints a VirtualThread. In the Java twin, the thenAccept stage runs on whichever thread completed the timer stage, which is Java's version of Unconfined. Coroutine context and dispatchers (Kotlin docs) read A dispatcher is the dispatch desk at a delivery company. Default is a small team of in-house drivers, one per loading bay, who never sit idle. IO is a large pool of contract drivers who spend most of the day parked outside customers' buildings, waiting for someone to sign. A limitedParallelism view is a separate contract for one difficult customer: at most 20 drivers on that route, hired on top of the usual pool. The context is the delivery note stapled to each parcel: which desk, which customer, which tracking number, and every parcel split off from it gets a copy. The analogy breaks on idle drivers. A real driver waiting at a door can't be reassigned. A suspended coroutine gives its thread back at once, which is why only blocking calls need the IO desk at all.

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Default is for CPU work, IO is for blocking calls
x: Dispatchers.Default has as many threads as the machine has cores. On a 4-core pod that is 4. Run a 200 ms blocking query there and you hold one of those 4 threads for 200 ms while it does nothing. Four requests doing that at once take every thread, and all the CPU work in the service waits in the queue: JSON parsing, signature checks, and the coroutines of every other request. A blocking call belongs on Dispatchers.IO. Its limit is 64 (or the number of cores, if that is larger), set by the system property kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism. IO threads spend most of their time asleep in the kernel, waiting for Oracle or the issuer to answer, so 64 of them on 4 cores is fine. IO and Default share one pool of worker threads. When code on Default calls withContext(Dispatchers.IO), the docs say it "typically does not lead to an actual switching to another thread": the same worker keeps going, and the library counts it against IO's limit instead of Default's. What the split buys you is separate budgets. Blocking work can fill IO, and Default still has a thread for every core. Three rules follow. Never block on Default. Put withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around each blocking call at the lowest level, inside the repository or the client, so callers don't need to know the call blocks. Put long CPU work on Default: laying out a statement PDF, hashing a file of card numbers. A few microseconds of CPU work need no switch at all. Don't wrap calls that already suspend. A non-blocking HTTP client, a delay or a Channel.receive never holds a thread while waiting, so withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around them only adds a hop. The Java world has the same split under other names. The common ForkJoinPool is sized for CPU work, and blocking in it starves parallelStream() and every CompletableFuture.supplyAsync without an executor. Lesson 3 of the executors track sized a pool for each kind of work. Here the library gives you the two pools ready-made, and your job is to put each call in the right one. Starve Default with blocking calls Read BlockingOnDefault.kt. It starts 32 blocking calls of 200 ms, then asks Default to run a task that takes a microsecond. Predict how long that tiny task waits to start on your machine. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=io, which puts the blocking calls on IO. Predict first. Run the Java twin both ways. BlockingOnDefault.kt package workbench.coroutines.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** 32 blocking 200 ms calls, then one tiny CPU task on Default. Pass "io" to run the blocking calls on IO. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val onIo = args.firstOrNull() == "io" val blockingDispatcher = if (onIo) Dispatchers.IO else Dispatchers.Default val cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() var cpuWaitMs = 0L val took = measureTimeMillis { coroutineScope { repeat(32) { launch(blockingDispatcher) { Thread.sleep(200) } } // JDBC-style blocking calls delay(20) // let them start val asked = System.nanoTime() val heartbeat = async(Dispatchers.Default) { System.nanoTime() } // 1 microsecond of CPU work cpuWaitMs = (heartbeat.await() - asked) / 1_000_000 } } val where = if (onIo) "Dispatchers.IO" else "Dispatchers.Default" println("32 blocking calls on $where ($cores cores): $took ms") println("a tiny CPU task on Default waited $cpuWaitMs ms to start") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.BlockingOnDefaultKt -Pargs=io labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l04/BlockingOnDefault.kt BlockingOnDefaultJava.java // Java equivalent of BlockingOnDefault.kt: blocking calls on the common pool (sized for CPU work) // versus on a separate pool for blocking work. Pass "io" to use the separate pool. package workbench.coroutines.l04; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool; public class BlockingOnDefaultJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean onIo = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("io"); int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(); ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(64); // a pool sized like the common pool, so the demo behaves the same on every machine ForkJoinPool cpu = new ForkJoinPool(Math.max(2, cores)); var blockingPool = onIo ? io : cpu; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<Void>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) { calls.add(CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> sleep(200), blockingPool)); // JDBC-style blocking calls } Thread.sleep(20); long asked = System.nanoTime(); long started = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(System::nanoTime, cpu).join(); // tiny CPU task on the CPU pool CompletableFuture.allOf(calls.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); System.out.printf("32 blocking calls on %s (%d cores): %d ms%n", onIo ? "a 64-thread pool" : "the CPU pool", cores, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); System.out.printf("a tiny CPU task on the CPU pool waited %d ms to start%n", (started - asked) / 1_000_000); io.shutdown(); cpu.shutdown(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.BlockingOnDefaultJava -Pargs=io labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l04/BlockingOnDefaultJava.java On 4 cores, the 32 calls take about 1,600 ms on Default (8 rounds of 4) and the tiny task waits about 1,500 ms, because every Default thread is asleep in Thread.sleep. With -Pargs=io the calls take about 220 ms (all 32 at once) and the tiny task starts within a few milliseconds. Scale the numbers to your core count. The Java twin shows the same starvation with a ForkJoinPool sized like Default. In a Quarkus service, coroutines usually start on a worker or event-loop thread and then run wherever their dispatcher sends them. Give each blocking dependency a view sized to its real limit: Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "oracle") for an Agroal pool of 20 connections, and another for a blocking issuer SDK. Then a slow issuer can't take the threads the ledger queries need. Wrap the JDBC call itself in withContext(oracle) inside the repository, so a Kafka consumer coroutine on Default never blocks on Oracle. And if your logs rely on an MDC trace id, carry it in the context (MDCContext or asContextElement). Otherwise the half of a payment's log lines written after the first withContext will be missing it.

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · A limitedParallelism view gives each resource its own budget
x: IO's 64 is one budget for every blocking call in the JVM. That hurts when one resource is slow. Say the card issuer's client blocks, and its connection pool has 20 connections. When the issuer slows down, 64 coroutines can pile into issuer calls: 20 hold a connection, 44 hold an IO thread while they wait for one, and the ledger's JDBC calls, which need IO threads too, queue behind them. limitedParallelism makes a view of a dispatcher with its own limit: Java // Java equivalent: a separate pool per resource (a bulkhead) ExecutorService issuer = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofPlatform().name("issuer-", 0).factory()); ExecutorService reports = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(100, Thread.ofPlatform().name("reports-", 0).factory()); Kotlin val issuer = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "issuer") // at most 20 issuer calls at once val reports = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(100, "reports") // a batch export with its own budget A view owns no threads and needs no closing. It is a gate in front of its parent: at most 20 coroutines from the issuer view run at the same moment, and the rest wait in the view's queue without holding a thread. The name is optional. It arrived in kotlinx.coroutines 1.9, when the API became stable, and it is what toString() returns, which helps in logs. Views over IO are elastic: they don't take a share of IO's 64, they add to it. The KDoc's own example has a view of 100 for MySQL and one of 60 for MongoDB, and says the system may then run up to 64 + 100 + 60 blocking tasks at peak. So the view isolates the issuer both ways. It can't take more than 20 threads, and a burst of other IO work can't starve it either. Views over Default are different. A view can never exceed its parent's parallelism, so Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(100) still runs at most one task per core. And limitedParallelism(1) gives you a view that runs one task at a time, which is not the same as a lock. Lesson 10 of this track shows why. When you need a dispatcher that is not one of these, wrap an executor: executor.asCoroutineDispatcher(). That includes the virtual-thread executor from the virtual threads track, Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher(). kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 has no built-in virtual-thread dispatcher, so this is the supported route. A wrapped executor is yours to close: the dispatcher is AutoCloseable, and close() shuts the executor down. Three budgets for 400 blocking calls Read BlockingBudgets.kt. It runs 400 blocking calls of 200 ms on plain IO, on a view of 400 over IO, and on a virtual-thread executor. Predict the time and the peak for each. Run it. Change the view to Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(400) and run it again. Predict first. Run the Java twin. BlockingBudgets.kt package workbench.coroutines.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** 400 blocking calls of 200 ms each, on three different dispatchers. */ suspend fun runBlockingCalls(label: String, dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher) { val active = AtomicInteger() val peak = AtomicInteger() val took = measureTimeMillis { coroutineScope { repeat(400) { launch(dispatcher) { peak.accumulateAndGet(active.incrementAndGet(), ::maxOf) Thread.sleep(200) // a blocking issuer call active.decrementAndGet() } } } } println("%-32s %5d ms, peak %3d calls at once".format(label, took, peak.get())) } fun main() = runBlocking { runBlockingCalls("Dispatchers.IO", Dispatchers.IO) runBlockingCalls("IO.limitedParallelism(400)", Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(400)) Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher().use { vt -> runBlockingCalls("virtual-thread executor", vt) } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.BlockingBudgetsKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l04/BlockingBudgets.kt BlockingBudgetsJava.java // Java equivalent of BlockingBudgets.kt: the same 400 blocking calls on a 64-thread pool, // a pool that grows as needed, and one virtual thread per call. package workbench.coroutines.l04; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; public class BlockingBudgetsJava { static void runBlockingCalls(String label, ExecutorService pool) { AtomicInteger active = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger peak = new AtomicInteger(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (pool) { // close() waits for all 400 calls for (int i = 0; i < 400; i++) { pool.submit(() -> { peak.accumulateAndGet(active.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); try { Thread.sleep(200); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } // a blocking issuer call active.decrementAndGet(); }); } } System.out.printf("%-32s %5d ms, peak %3d calls at once%n", label, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, peak.get()); } public static void main(String[] args) { runBlockingCalls("fixed pool of 64", Executors.newFixedThreadPool(64)); runBlockingCalls("cached pool (grows)", Executors.newCachedThreadPool()); runBlockingCalls("virtual thread per task", Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.BlockingBudgetsJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l04/BlockingBudgetsJava.java Plain IO peaks at 64 calls at once, so 400 calls take 7 rounds, about 1,400 ms. The view of 400 runs all 400 at once in about 300 ms: it adds to IO's 64 instead of sharing it. The virtual-thread executor also peaks at 400. The view over Default peaks at your core count (at least 2) and takes far longer (about 20 s on 4 cores), because a view can't exceed its parent. The Java twin shows the same pattern with a fixed pool of 64, a cached pool and a virtual thread per task. Default and IO share one pool of threads but keep separate budgets. Views over IO add their own budgets on top of IO's 64. limitedParallelism (API reference) docs Dispatchers.IO (API reference: the 64 limit and elastic views) docs

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · The context is a set of elements, and + merges them
x: A coroutine context is a small immutable set of elements, at most one per key. You've met most of them already: the Job (the node in the tree from lesson 3 of this track), the dispatcher, CoroutineName, and CoroutineExceptionHandler (lesson 6). + combines two contexts, and when both have an element with the same key, the right side wins. val ctx = Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("capture") val renamed = ctx + CoroutineName("refund") renamed[CoroutineName] // CoroutineName(refund): the right side won renamed[ContinuationInterceptor] // Dispatchers.IO: untouched A new coroutine's context is built in three steps: the scope's context, then the context you pass to the builder (which overrides it), then a fresh Job that is a child of the scope's job. So children inherit the dispatcher, the name and anything else you add, but every child gets its own job. withContext(ctx) builds the context of its block the same way. Inside a suspend function, read an element with currentCoroutineContext()[Key]. The key is usually the element's companion object, which is why ctx[CoroutineName] reads so naturally. One change in kotlinx.coroutines 1.11: using CoroutineDispatcher as the key is deprecated, and later versions will reject it. Look the dispatcher up with ContinuationInterceptor. You can define your own element by extending AbstractCoroutineContextElement and giving it a companion Key. The lab does that to carry a payment's trace id into every coroutine that works on the payment. What does not follow a coroutine is a plain ThreadLocal. A coroutine that resumes on another thread sees that thread's value, which is how request ids and MDC log fields go missing after a withContext. asContextElement() turns a ThreadLocal into an element. The library sets the value on whichever thread runs the coroutine and restores the old value when the coroutine leaves. Java // Java equivalent: copy the ThreadLocal into the task by hand String captured = REQUEST_ID.get(); pool.submit(() -> { REQUEST_ID.set(captured); try { work(); } finally { REQUEST_ID.remove(); } }); Kotlin requestId.set("req-42") withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { requestId.get() } // null: another thread withContext(Dispatchers.Default + requestId.asContextElement()) { requestId.get() } // req-42 For SLF4J's MDC there is a ready-made element, MDCContext, in the kotlinx-coroutines-slf4j module, which is not on this lab's classpath. And CoroutineName shows up in thread names when the JVM runs with -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug (assertions with -ea turn it on too). That costs little, and it makes thread dumps readable. Merge contexts and lose a ThreadLocal Read ContextElements.kt. Predict the three lines about requestId. Run it. Add + CoroutineName("late") to the end of the renamed line and run again. Which name wins now? Run the Java twin, which copies the value by hand the way an MDC-propagating executor wrapper does. ContextElements.kt package workbench.coroutines.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.asContextElement import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlin.coroutines.ContinuationInterceptor private val requestId = ThreadLocal<String?>() fun main() = runBlocking { // 1. a context is a set of elements; + combines them, and the right side wins for the same key val ctx = Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("capture") val renamed = ctx + CoroutineName("refund") println("ctx[CoroutineName] = ${ctx[CoroutineName]}") println("renamed[CoroutineName] = ${renamed[CoroutineName]}") println("dispatcher by its key = ${renamed[ContinuationInterceptor]}") // 2. a ThreadLocal does not follow a coroutine to another thread requestId.set("req-42") println("main thread sees ${requestId.get()}") withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { println("on Default, plain ThreadLocal ${requestId.get()}") } // 3. asContextElement copies the value in and out whenever the coroutine runs on a thread withContext(Dispatchers.Default + requestId.asContextElement()) { println("on Default, asContextElement ${requestId.get()}") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.ContextElementsKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l04/ContextElements.kt ContextElementsJava.java // Java equivalent of ContextElements.kt: a ThreadLocal does not follow a task to a pool thread. // You copy it by hand (this is what MDC-propagating executor wrappers do). JDK 25 adds ScopedValue // (final in JDK 25, JEP 506), but the labs compile for Java 21, so this demo copies by hand. package workbench.coroutines.l04; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class ContextElementsJava { static final ThreadLocal<String> REQUEST_ID = new ThreadLocal<>(); // capture the caller's value now, install it around the task later, then restore static Runnable withRequestId(Runnable task) { String captured = REQUEST_ID.get(); return () -> { String previous = REQUEST_ID.get(); REQUEST_ID.set(captured); try { task.run(); } finally { REQUEST_ID.set(previous); } }; } public static void main(String[] args) { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) { REQUEST_ID.set("req-42"); System.out.println("main thread sees " + REQUEST_ID.get()); CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println("pool thread, plain ThreadLocal " + REQUEST_ID.get()), pool).join(); CompletableFuture.runAsync(withRequestId(() -> System.out.println("pool thread, copied by hand " + REQUEST_ID.get())), pool).join(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l04.ContextElementsJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l04/ContextElementsJava.java The name lookups print CoroutineName(capture), then CoroutineName(refund), and the dispatcher lookup prints Dispatchers.IO. The main thread sees req-42, the plain ThreadLocal on Default prints null, and the asContextElement version prints req-42. After your change the rightmost name, late, wins. The Java twin prints the same three requestId lines. asContextElement (API reference) docs The most common mistake is a blocking call on Default: a JDBC query, a blocking HTTP client, a Thread.sleep in a retry loop, inside a launch that inherited Default. It works in tests with one request at a time and falls over under load, when a handful of slow queries occupy every core's thread. People make it because nothing in the type system marks a call as blocking, and the code looks like any other function call. Wrap every blocking call in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) (or a view sized to the resource) inside the function that makes it, so the caller can't get it wrong. The opposite mistake is cheaper but still common: wrapping already-suspending calls in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) "to be safe", which adds a hop and hides which calls really block.

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Java and Kotlin
x: One request, two kinds of work: executors vs dispatchers StatementService.java class StatementService { private final ExecutorService io; // sized for blocking JDBC calls private final ExecutorService cpu; // sized to the cores StatementService(ExecutorService io, ExecutorService cpu) { this.io = io; this.cpu = cpu; } CompletableFuture<byte[]> statementPdf(String accountId) { return CompletableFuture .supplyAsync(() -> store.loadRows(accountId), io) // 1. block on an IO thread .thenApplyAsync(renderer::render, cpu); // 2. render on a CPU thread // the caller gets a future; whatever it chains next runs on a cpu thread } } StatementService.kt class StatementService( private val io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO, private val cpu: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.Default, ) { suspend fun statementPdf(accountId: String): ByteArray { val rows = withContext(io) { store.loadRows(accountId) } // 1. block on an IO thread return withContext(cpu) { renderer.render(rows) } // 2. render on a CPU thread } // the caller resumes on its own dispatcher with the bytes } Both versions keep the blocking call off the CPU threads, and both take the pools as constructor arguments so a test can pass its own. The difference is where the caller ends up. With CompletableFuture, the result is delivered on the thread of the last stage, and the caller either blocks on join() or keeps chaining callbacks that run who knows where. With withContext, the caller suspends, and when the block finishes it resumes on its own dispatcher, as if the call had been ordinary. You also own less: Dispatchers.IO and Dispatchers.Default are shared, process-wide pools that you never create or shut down, while the Java version needs two executors with a lifecycle.

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Worked example
x: Give a blocking issuer client a budget of its own A Kafka consumer captures card payments with a blocking issuer SDK. Each record is handled in launch on Default, on a 4-core pod. When the issuer slows to 2 s per call, consumer lag climbs and unrelated CPU work in the pod stalls. class CaptureHandler(private val issuer: BlockingIssuerClient, private val scope: CoroutineScope) { fun onRecord(record: CaptureRequest) { scope.launch { // scope uses Dispatchers.Default val result = issuer.capture(record) // blocks a Default thread for up to 2 s ledger.record(result) } } } // Java equivalent of the bug: blocking calls on the common pool, which is sized for CPU work class CaptureHandler { void onRecord(CaptureRequest record) { CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> issuer.capture(record)) // no executor: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() .thenAccept(ledger::record); } } First, get the blocking call off Default. Put the switch inside a small suspend wrapper around the SDK, so no caller can forget it. class SuspendingIssuer(private val sdk: BlockingIssuerClient) { // 1. the only place that knows this SDK blocks suspend fun capture(req: CaptureRequest): CaptureResult = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { sdk.capture(req) } } // Java equivalent: the wrapper picks the executor, so callers can't forget class AsyncIssuer { private final ExecutorService io = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); // 1. the only place that knows this SDK blocks CompletableFuture<CaptureResult> capture(CaptureRequest req) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> sdk.capture(req), io); } } IO allows 64 calls, but the SDK's pool has 20 connections. A slow issuer would let 64 coroutines take IO threads, and 44 of them would only be waiting for a connection, while ledger queries queue for IO threads. Give the issuer a view sized to its pool, and inject it so a test can pass a test dispatcher. class SuspendingIssuer( private val sdk: BlockingIssuerClient, // 2. a budget sized to the SDK's 20 connections, on top of IO's 64 private val dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(20, "issuer"), ) { suspend fun capture(req: CaptureRequest): CaptureResult = withContext(dispatcher) { sdk.capture(req) } } // Java equivalent: a bulkhead pool of exactly 20 threads for the issuer class AsyncIssuer implements AutoCloseable { // 2. a budget sized to the SDK's 20 connections private final ExecutorService issuerPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20, Thread.ofPlatform().name("issuer-", 0).factory()); CompletableFuture<CaptureResult> capture(CaptureRequest req) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> sdk.capture(req), issuerPool); } @Override public void close() { issuerPool.shutdown(); } } The handler no longer cares where the issuer runs. Its own work (mapping, a suspending ledger call) can stay on Default. fun onRecord(record: CaptureRequest) { scope.launch { val result = issuer.capture(record) // 3. suspends; no Default thread is held ledger.record(result) // back on Default } } void onRecord(CaptureRequest record) { issuer.capture(record) // 3. runs on the issuer pool .thenAccept(ledger::record); // and so does this stage, unless you pass an executor } Self-check: why not Executors.newFixedThreadPool(20).asCoroutineDispatcher() instead of the view? (It works, but it is a pool you must close, with 20 threads that sit idle between bursts. The view has no lifecycle, borrows threads from the shared pool only while calls run, and still caps the issuer at 20.)

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Quiz
x: A Quarkus endpoint handles 10 concurrent requests on a 4-core pod. Each one runs launch { repo.findPayment(id) } (a blocking 300 ms JDBC call) in a scope whose dispatcher is Default. At that moment a coroutine on Default needs 1 ms of CPU to check a signature. When does it run? At once, because Default and IO are separate thread pools Only once a Default thread finishes its blocking call, roughly 300 ms later At once, because kotlinx.coroutines moves blocking calls to IO for you Never: Default throws IllegalStateException when a thread blocks for too long All 4 Default threads are blocked inside JDBC calls, so the signature check waits in the queue until one returns. Nothing moves a blocking call for you, and nothing throws. Wrapping the query in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) keeps Default free. A nightly export makes 300 blocking calls to a reporting database whose pool has 100 connections. It must not slow down the service's other blocking calls. Which dispatcher fits? Dispatchers.IO Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(100) Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(100, "reports") Dispatchers.Unconfined A view over IO caps the export at 100, and because IO views are elastic it adds to IO's 64 instead of using them up. Plain IO would let the export take all 64 threads. A view over Default can't exceed the core count, and Default must never block anyway. What does this print? val ctx = CoroutineName("a") + Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("b") println(ctx[CoroutineName]?.name) b a a, b null, because the dispatcher replaced the name A context holds at most one element per key, and + lets the right side win. CoroutineName("b") replaces a. The dispatcher has a different key, so it sits beside the name without touching it. Inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("capture")) { ... } you call launch(CoroutineName("refund")) { ... }. What does the child coroutine's context contain? Default and refund, because launch uses Default unless told otherwise IO and capture, because the parent's context always wins IO and refund, and the same Job as the withContext block IO and refund, and a new Job that is a child of the block's job A child starts from its scope's context (IO and capture), then the builder's argument overrides it (refund), then it gets a fresh Job that is a child of the scope's job. The "Default unless told" rule only applies when the context has no dispatcher at all. From the executors track: each issuer call holds one of the issuer SDK's 20 connections. You give issuer calls their own pool of 64 threads. How many issuer calls can really make progress at once? 64 20 84 One per core The smallest limit on the path is the real ceiling. The other 44 threads sit waiting for a connection. That is why the issuer's dispatcher in this lesson is a view of exactly 20.
