h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Key terms
x: Dispatcher The context element that decides which thread runs a coroutine each time it starts or resumes. Dispatchers.Default The shared pool for CPU work: one thread per core, at least two. Dispatchers.IO The shared pool for blocking calls: up to 64 at once by default, using the same threads as Default. limitedParallelism view A dispatcher in front of another one that lets at most n of its tasks run at the same time. It owns no threads. withContext Runs a block with a changed context (often another dispatcher) and returns its result to the caller. Coroutine context The immutable set of elements a coroutine carries: job, dispatcher, name, exception handler, your own elements. Context element One entry in a context, found by its key, usually the class's companion object. How many threads does Dispatchers.Default have? One per CPU core, and at least two. What is Dispatchers.IO's default limit? 64 parallel blocking tasks, or the core count if that is larger. The kotlinx.coroutines.io.parallelism property changes it. Does Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(100) take 100 of IO's 64 threads? No. Views over IO are elastic and add to IO's budget: IO and the view together can run 64 + 100 blocking tasks. What does withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { load() } do to the calling coroutine? It suspends the caller, runs load() on IO, then resumes the caller on its own dispatcher with the result. ctx holds CoroutineName("a"). What name does ctx + CoroutineName("b") hold? b. One element per key, and the right side of + wins. Why does a ThreadLocal read null after withContext(Dispatchers.Default)? The block runs on another thread, which has its own value. Pass threadLocal.asContextElement() in the context to carry it along. In kotlinx.coroutines 1.11, which key looks up the dispatcher in a context? ContinuationInterceptor. Using CoroutineDispatcher as the key is deprecated.

h: Dispatchers and the coroutine context · Go deeper
x: Default and IO are two faces of one scheduler. On the JVM, kotlinx.coroutines runs a single pool of worker threads, and each task is marked as CPU work or blocking work. A worker running a blocking task doesn't count against Default's limit, so the scheduler can start another worker for CPU work. That is how a switch from Default to IO can stay on the same thread: the worker just changes which budget it is counted against. IO itself is a view of 64 over an unbounded blocking budget, which is why further views over IO can add to it. The docs say Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n) can safely replace the older newFixedThreadPoolContext(n). The old function creates n dedicated threads that you must close, and that idle between bursts. If you find it in a codebase, a view is almost always the better choice. Dispatchers.Unconfined has one legitimate niche: code that must react immediately on whatever thread delivered an event, such as some operator internals. To avoid stack overflows, nested unconfined coroutines form an event loop instead of calling each other recursively, which makes the order of execution surprising. Treat it as a library-writer's tool. A virtual-thread dispatcher (Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()) is an interesting option for code that blocks a lot, because each task gets a cheap virtual thread instead of an IO worker. It is not a free win. A virtual thread pinned by synchronized on JDK 21 to 23 (JEP 491 removed most pinning in JDK 24) still holds a carrier. Every time the coroutine resumes, the executor starts a new virtual thread for it, so you lose the scheduler's habit of keeping a coroutine on the same worker. And cancelling a coroutine blocked inside it still needs runInterruptible, which lesson 5 of this track covers. Lesson 11 of this track compares the options for a whole service.

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Cancellation is a request your code has to notice
x: Cancellation is a request: a coroutine stops only at a suspension point or a check job.cancel() doesn't stop a coroutine. It marks the job as cancelling, and that's all. The coroutine stops the next time it reaches a suspension point that checks: delay, withContext, await, join, a channel's send or receive, yield. That call throws CancellationException, the exception unwinds the stack, finally blocks run, and the job ends as cancelled. A coroutine that is already suspended notices at once: one waiting in delay(10_000) is resumed with the exception straight away. Code that never reaches such a point never notices. A CPU loop over two million card transactions runs to the end. So does a blocking call such as Thread.sleep or a JDBC query (section 4). This is cooperative cancellation. Java has the same model: Future.cancel(true) sets the interrupt flag, and a loop that never reads it keeps going. A CPU loop cooperates by checking now and then: Java // Java equivalent: read the interrupt flag yourself void scan(List<Txn> rows) { for (int i = 0; i < rows.size(); i++) { if (i % 1_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) throw new CancellationException(); score(rows.get(i)); } } Kotlin suspend fun scan(rows: List<Txn>) = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { for ((i, row) in rows.withIndex()) { if (i % 1_000 == 0) ensureActive() // throws CancellationException once cancelled score(row) } } You have three tools. ensureActive() throws if the job is cancelled. isActive returns a boolean, for loops that want to stop quietly: while (isActive) { ... }. yield() checks too, and also lets other coroutines waiting for the same dispatcher run, which matters when a long loop shares a small dispatcher. A check is just a read of the job's state, so it costs almost nothing, but once every few hundred rows is plenty. Watch which job you are checking. Inside launch { }, isActive and ensureActive() refer to that coroutine. A plain suspend function has no scope receiver, so write currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive(). In a lambda nested inside another scope, a bare isActive can quietly refer to the outer scope. Flow (lesson 7 of this track) has the same trap at a smaller scale. A flow { } builder checks on every emit, but asFlow() doesn't: Java // Java equivalent: a stream never reads the interrupt flag on its own IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5).forEach(i -> { if (i == 3) Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // ask to stop System.out.println(i); // prints 1 to 5 }); Kotlin (1..5).asFlow().collect { if (it == 3) cancel(); println(it) } // prints 1 to 5 (1..5).asFlow().cancellable().collect { if (it == 3) cancel(); println(it) } // prints 1 to 3 Cancel four CPU loops Read CancelABusyLoop.kt. Each loop would take about 1.5 s; the demo cancels it after 100 ms. Predict how long each one takes to stop. Run it. In the ensureActive() loop, change 1_000 to 10_000_000 and run it again. Predict first. Run the Java twin, which uses Future.cancel(true) and the interrupt flag. i++ } sum }, "ensureActive() every 1,000" to { var sum = 0L for (i in 0 until ROWS) { if (i % 1_000 == 0L) ensureActive() sum += checksum(i) } sum }, "yield() every 1,000" to { var sum = 0L for (i in 0 until ROWS) { if (i % 1_000 == 0L) yield() sum += checksum(i) } sum }, ) for ((label, loop) in loops) { val job = launch(Dispatchers.Default) { sink = loop() } delay(100) // let it get going val asked = System.nanoTime() job.cancelAndJoin() println("%-28s stopped %5d ms after cancel()".format(label, (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000)) } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.CancelABusyLoopKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l05/CancelABusyLoop.kt CancelABusyLoopJava.java // Java equivalent of CancelABusyLoop.kt: Future.cancel(true) only sets the interrupt flag. // A CPU loop stops only if it looks at the flag. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class CancelABusyLoopJava { static final long ROWS = 60_000_000L; static volatile long sink; // keeps the JIT from deleting loops whose result nobody reads /** Pure CPU work: a checksum over one fake card number. 60 million of them take about 1.5 s. */ static long checksum(long i) { long x = i; for (int k = 0; k < 20; k++) { x ^= x >>> 33; x *= -0xae502812aa7333L; x ^= x >>> 29; } return x; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Map<String, Runnable> loops = new LinkedHashMap<>(); loops.put("no check", () -> { long sum = 0; for (long i = 0; i < ROWS; i++) sum += checksum(i); sink = sum; }); loops.put("isInterrupted() every 1,000", () -> { long sum = 0; for (long i = 0; i < ROWS; i++) { if (i % 1_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) break; sum += checksum(i); } sink = sum; }); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); // one thread, so the no-op below waits for it for (var e : loops.entrySet()) { Future<?> f = pool.submit(e.getValue()); Thread.sleep(100); // let it get going long asked = System.nanoTime(); f.cancel(true); // sets the interrupt flag; the future reports "cancelled" at once // wait for the thread itself to come back: the no-op runs only once the loop has stopped pool.submit(() -> { }).get(); System.out.printf("%-28s stopped %5d ms after cancel(true)%n", e.getKey(), (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000); } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.CancelABusyLoopJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l05/CancelABusyLoopJava.java The loop with no check stops about 1,000 ms after cancel() (or more on a slow machine): it simply finished its work. The other three stop within a few milliseconds. With a check only every 10 million rows, that loop stops late, at its next check (10 million rows take a couple of hundred ms). The Java twin shows the same split: cancel(true) reports success at once, but the loop that never reads the flag keeps its thread busy until it ends. The same cancel reaches three coroutines. Only the ones at a suspension point or a check stop, and their finally blocks run. Cancellation and timeouts (Kotlin docs) read ensureActive (API reference) docs Cancelling a coroutine is like a manager putting a "stop, we're closing" note on each worker's desk. A worker who looks up between tasks (a suspension point) sees it, tidies up and goes home. A worker deep in a long calculation who never looks up keeps going until the calculation is done. A worker on hold with a supplier (a blocking call) can't see the desk at all until someone taps them on the shoulder, which is what runInterruptible does. runCatching is the worker who reads the note, throws it in the bin and starts the next task. NonCancellable is the exemption for tidying up: "finish putting the cash in the safe, then go." The analogy breaks in one place: binning the note doesn't make it go away. Every desk the worker sits at afterwards has the same note on it.

h: Cancellation and timeouts · CancellationException carries the cancel, so never swallow it
x: Cancellation travels as an exception, CancellationException (on the JVM it is java.util.concurrent.CancellationException). That is the point of it: it unwinds the stack, runs every finally and closes every use. It is also the danger. Any catch that catches it stops it. Java // Java equivalent: swallowing InterruptedException for (String id : batchIds) { try { settle(id); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log.warn("batch {} failed", id, e); failed.add(id); } // the cancel request is gone } Kotlin for (id in batchIds) { runCatching { settle(id) } // also catches CancellationException .onFailure { log.warn("batch $id failed", it); failed += id } } runCatching catches every Throwable. So do catch (e: Exception) and catch (e: Throwable), because CancellationException extends IllegalStateException. Here is what happens when the pod shuts down and cancels this run. The batch in progress is logged as failed. The loop moves to the next batch, which starts, hits its first suspension point, throws at once and is logged as failed too, and so on to the end of the list. Then the function returns normally, with a list of "failed" batches that never failed. In a while (true) polling loop it is worse: every delay throws at once, the exception is swallowed, and the loop spins at full CPU forever. The fix is to let it through. With runCatching, rethrow it first: .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it; ... }. With try, put catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } before the general clause. Better still, catch only what you expect, such as IOException or your client's error type, and let everything else propagate. The Java rule is the same: catch InterruptedException, restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt(), and stop. But the failure looks different, and the Try it shows how. A swallowed interrupt clears the flag, so the next sleep sleeps normally and the loop just runs to the end at its usual pace. A swallowed cancellation clears nothing. The job stays cancelled, every later suspension point throws at once, and the loop races to the end in a few milliseconds. So a coroutine that is cancelled cannot be talked out of it. Catching the exception only means the code after the catch runs inside a coroutine that is still cancelled. Swallow a cancel and count the damage Read SwallowedCancellation.kt. The poller is cancelled at 250 ms, after 3 attempts. Predict how many attempts run after the cancel, and how long cancelAndJoin takes. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which rethrows CancellationException. Run the Java twin both ways and compare how long shutdown takes. SwallowedCancellation.kt package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException /** Polls a settlement 20 times, 100 ms apart. A failed poll is logged and retried. */ suspend fun pollSettlement(rethrowCancellation: Boolean, onAttempt: () -> Unit) { repeat(20) { runCatching { onAttempt() // the HTTP call to the acquirer would go here delay(100) }.onFailure { e -> if (rethrowCancellation && e is CancellationException) throw e // swallowed: logged as a "failed poll", and the loop goes round again } } } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" var attempts = 0 var cancelledAt = -1 val poller = launch { pollSettlement(rethrowCancellation = fixed) { attempts++ } } delay(250) cancelledAt = attempts val asked = System.nanoTime() poller.cancelAndJoin() val ms = (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000 println(if (fixed) "runCatching + rethrow:" else "runCatching, swallowing:") println(" attempts before cancel: $cancelledAt, after cancel: ${attempts - cancelledAt}, cancelAndJoin took $ms ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.SwallowedCancellationKt -Pargs=fixed labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l05/SwallowedCancellation.kt SwallowedCancellationJava.java // Java equivalent of SwallowedCancellation.kt: catching InterruptedException and carrying on // swallows the cancel request, just as runCatching swallows CancellationException. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; public class SwallowedCancellationJava { static void pollSettlement(boolean restoreInterrupt, AtomicInteger attempts) { for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) { try { attempts.incrementAndGet(); // the HTTP call to the acquirer would go here Thread.sleep(100); } catch (InterruptedException e) { if (restoreInterrupt) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return; // stop: somebody asked us to } // swallowed: the flag is now clear, so the next sleep() sleeps normally } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); AtomicInteger attempts = new AtomicInteger(); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); pool.submit(() -> pollSettlement(fixed, attempts)); Thread.sleep(250); int cancelledAt = attempts.get(); long asked = System.nanoTime(); pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupts the poller pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - asked) / 1_000_000; System.out.println(fixed ? "catch + restore the flag:" : "catch, swallowing:"); System.out.printf(" attempts before cancel: %d, after cancel: %d, shutdown took %d ms%n", cancelledAt, attempts.get() - cancelledAt, ms); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.SwallowedCancellationJava -Pargs=fixed labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l05/SwallowedCancellationJava.java Swallowing: 17 attempts after the cancel, and cancelAndJoin returns within a few milliseconds, because every remaining delay threw at once. Fixed: 0 attempts after the cancel. The swallowing Java twin also runs 17 more attempts, but over about 1.7 s: catching the interrupt cleared the flag, so the later sleeps were normal sleeps. Restoring the flag and returning stops it at once. Cancellation reaches your payment code more often than you think. A Kafka rebalance revokes a partition, and its worker's scope is cancelled. A Quarkus shutdown cancels long-lived scopes in @PreDestroy. Every withTimeout on an issuer call is a cancel waiting to happen. Three things keep that safe. Never wrap a suspend call in runCatching or catch (e: Exception) without rethrowing CancellationException, or a shutdown turns into a list of fake failures. Release card holds, distributed locks and idempotency claims in finally with withContext(NonCancellable). And remember that an Oracle query running in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) ignores the timeout around it: use runInterruptible only if the driver responds to interrupts, and set Statement.setQueryTimeout either way. Temporal works on the same idea: an activity learns that it has been cancelled only when it heartbeats.

h: Cancellation and timeouts · A cancelled coroutine can't suspend, so cleanup needs NonCancellable
x: finally blocks run when a coroutine is cancelled, but they run inside a coroutine that is still cancelled. There, every suspension point throws CancellationException at once. Cleanup that suspends never gets past its first suspension: Java // Java equivalent: once the flag is set again, blocking cleanup fails at once String hold = issuer.placeHold(amount); try { awaitChallenge(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the cancel request, as you should } finally { issuer.releaseHold(hold); // blocks, sees the flag, throws InterruptedException } Kotlin val hold = issuer.placeHold(amount) try { awaitChallenge() // cancelled here } finally { issuer.releaseHold(hold) // suspends, so it throws at once: the hold stays on the card } The fix is one wrapper: finally { withContext(NonCancellable) { issuer.releaseHold(hold) } }. NonCancellable is a job that is always active. Inside that block, suspension points don't throw, so the release runs to the end. The coroutine itself stays cancelled. When the block finishes, the CancellationException carries on up the stack as before. Use it in exactly this shape: withContext(NonCancellable), in a finally (or a cleanup catch), around the cleanup call and nothing else. The docs warn against launch(NonCancellable) or async(NonCancellable). Passing a job to a builder replaces the parent, so the new coroutine leaves the tree from lesson 3 of this track: nothing waits for it and nothing can cancel it. And keep the cleanup short. Nothing will cancel it for you, so give a slow network call its own withTimeout inside the block. Cleanup that doesn't suspend needs nothing special. Closing a file, returning a JDBC connection to its pool, mutex.unlock() and semaphore.release() are ordinary calls and run fine in a cancelled coroutine. The same rule explains a quieter loss. If a coroutine is cancelled while it waits for a call that returns a resource, such as a pooled session, it resumes with CancellationException even if the resource was already on its way. The resource is never handed to your code, so your code can't close it. Lesson 1 of this track showed the fix on the callback side: the onCancellation lambda of resume releases it. Leave a hold on the card, then release it Read CleanupAfterCancel.kt. The payment is cancelled while it waits for a 3-D Secure challenge. Predict whether released hold-4250 prints. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which wraps the release in withContext(NonCancellable). Run the Java twin both ways. CleanupAfterCancel.kt package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.NonCancellable import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException private suspend fun releaseHold(id: String) { delay(50) // the network call to the issuer println(" released $id") } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" val payment = launch { val hold = "hold-4250" println(" placed $hold") try { delay(10_000) // waiting for the customer's 3-D Secure challenge } finally { try { if (fixed) withContext(NonCancellable) { releaseHold(hold) } else releaseHold(hold) } catch (e: CancellationException) { println(" release failed at once: ${e::class.simpleName}") throw e } } } delay(100) println(if (fixed) "cancel, release inside withContext(NonCancellable):" else "cancel, plain suspend call in finally:") payment.cancelAndJoin() println(" payment job finished, cancelled = ${payment.isCancelled}") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.CleanupAfterCancelKt -Pargs=fixed labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l05/CleanupAfterCancel.kt CleanupAfterCancelJava.java // Java equivalent of CleanupAfterCancel.kt: a thread that was interrupted can't make a blocking // cleanup call while its interrupt flag is set. Clear the flag for the cleanup, then restore it. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class CleanupAfterCancelJava { static void releaseHold(String id) throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(50); // the network call to the issuer System.out.println(" released " + id); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); pool.submit(() -> { String hold = "hold-4250"; System.out.println(" placed " + hold); try { Thread.sleep(10_000); // waiting for the customer's 3-D Secure challenge } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // keep the cancel request, as you should } finally { boolean wasInterrupted = fixed && Thread.interrupted(); // fixed: clear the flag for cleanup try { releaseHold(hold); } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(" release failed at once: InterruptedException"); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } if (wasInterrupted) Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // and put it back afterwards } }); Thread.sleep(100); System.out.println(fixed ? "interrupt, flag cleared around the release:" : "interrupt, plain blocking call in finally:"); pool.shutdownNow(); pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.println(" task finished"); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.CleanupAfterCancelJava -Pargs=fixed labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l05/CleanupAfterCancelJava.java Without the wrapper, release failed at once: JobCancellationException prints, and the hold is never released. With -Pargs=fixed, released hold-4250 prints about 50 ms after the cancel, and the job still finishes as cancelled. The Java twin fails the same way with InterruptedException, and the fix there is to clear the flag around the cleanup and restore it afterwards. NonCancellable (API reference) docs

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Timeouts are cancellation with a clock
x: withTimeout(d) { ... } runs the block and cancels it when d runs out. The cancellation is the ordinary kind: the block stops at its next suspension point, and withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException. withTimeoutOrNull(d) { ... } does the same and returns null instead of throwing. Java // Java equivalent: a fallback value when the future is late Decision decision = issuer.authorizeAsync(request) .completeOnTimeout(Decision.TIMED_OUT, 800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .join(); Kotlin val decision = withTimeoutOrNull(800.milliseconds) { issuer.authorize(request) } ?: Decision.TIMED_OUT // decline, or route to the fallback acquirer Prefer withTimeoutOrNull when a timeout is an outcome you expect. TimeoutCancellationException is a subclass of CancellationException, and that has a surprising effect. Inside launch, a timeout looks like an ordinary cancel, so the docs' own pitfall applies: a child that times out inside coroutineScope lets the scope finish normally, and nobody hears about it. If a timeout should fail the caller, turn it into a real error: withTimeoutOrNull(d) { ... } ?: error("issuer timed out"). A timeout is still cooperative, so it can't stop a blocking call. A thread blocked in Thread.sleep, a socket read or a JDBC call is not at a suspension point. withTimeout(300) { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { client.lookup(bin) } } waits for the whole call and only then throws, and the IO thread stays busy the whole time. If the blocking call is the entire block, with no suspension at all, the timeout is ignored and the late result comes back as if nothing had happened. For blocking code that responds to interrupts, use runInterruptible: Java // Java equivalent: give up after the timeout and interrupt the worker Future<String> f = io.submit(() -> binDirectory.lookup(bin)); try { return f.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); return null; } // interrupts the blocked thread Kotlin withTimeoutOrNull(300.milliseconds) { runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { binDirectory.lookup(bin) } // interrupted on cancel } runInterruptible runs the block on the dispatcher you give it. When the coroutine is cancelled, it interrupts that thread, and it turns the resulting InterruptedException back into a CancellationException. It only helps if the blocking call responds to interrupts. Thread.sleep, BlockingQueue.take and java.nio interruptible channels do. A classic socket read on a platform thread doesn't, and JDBC drivers vary, so set the client's own timeout too. Time out a slow issuer four ways Read TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt. The issuer takes 1.5 s and every call gets 300 ms. Predict the outcome and the time for each line. Run it. Delete the withContext(Dispatchers.IO) wrapper in the third case, leaving withTimeout(300) { Thread.sleep(1_500); "approved" }. Predict, then run. Run the Java twin and compare orTimeout with get plus cancel(true). TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt package workbench.coroutines.l05 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.TimeoutCancellationException import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.runInterruptible import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeout import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull /** Runs [block] and prints what came out and how long it took. */ private suspend fun timed(label: String, block: suspend () -> Any?) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() val outcome = try { "returned ${block()}" } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) { "threw TimeoutCancellationException" } println("%-50s %-36s after %5d ms".format(label, outcome, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) } fun main() = runBlocking { // the issuer takes 1.5 s; we give it 300 ms timed("withTimeout { delay }") { withTimeout(300) { delay(1_500); "approved" } } timed("withTimeoutOrNull { delay }") { withTimeoutOrNull(300) { delay(1_500); "approved" } } timed("withTimeout { withContext(IO) { sleep } }") { withTimeout(300) { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(1_500); "approved" } } } timed("withTimeoutOrNull { runInterruptible { sleep } }") { withTimeoutOrNull(300) { runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(1_500); "approved" } } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.TimeoutsAndBlockingKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l05/TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt TimeoutsAndBlockingJava.java // Java equivalent of TimeoutsAndBlocking.kt: a timeout on a CompletableFuture gives the caller // an answer on time, but nothing stops the blocking task. Future.cancel(true) interrupts it. package workbench.coroutines.l05; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; public class TimeoutsAndBlockingJava { static long t0; static String callIssuer() { try { Thread.sleep(1_500); // the issuer takes 1.5 s System.out.printf(" (the issuer call itself finished at %d ms)%n", ms()); return "approved"; } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.printf(" (the issuer call was interrupted at %d ms)%n", ms()); return "interrupted"; } } static long ms() { return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newCachedThreadPool()) { // 1. orTimeout: the caller gets a TimeoutException on time, the task runs on t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(TimeoutsAndBlockingJava::callIssuer, io).orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { System.out.printf("orTimeout(300 ms) caller got %s after %d ms%n", e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName(), ms()); } Thread.sleep(1_400); // wait, to see the abandoned task finish anyway // 2. Future.get with a timeout, then cancel(true): the blocked thread is interrupted t0 = System.nanoTime(); Future<String> f = io.submit(TimeoutsAndBlockingJava::callIssuer); try { f.get(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); System.out.printf("get(300 ms) + cancel(true) caller gave up after %d ms%n", ms()); } Thread.sleep(100); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l05.TimeoutsAndBlockingJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l05/TimeoutsAndBlockingJava.java The two delay cases end at about 300 ms: one throws, one returns null. The withContext(IO) case throws too, but only after about 1,500 ms, when the sleep is over. runInterruptible returns null at about 300 ms. After your change, the bare sleep returns approved after 1,500 ms: the block never suspended, so the timeout was ignored. In the Java twin, orTimeout gives the caller its exception on time while the abandoned call finishes at 1,500 ms anyway; cancel(true) interrupts it at about 300 ms. withTimeout (API reference: the pitfalls section) docs runInterruptible (API reference) docs The most common mistake is swallowing CancellationException with a catch-all: runCatching { }, catch (e: Exception) or catch (e: Throwable) around a suspend call, usually written to "log and keep going" in a batch or polling loop. It looks like good defensive code, and it works perfectly until the first shutdown or timeout. Then the loop either reports every remaining item as failed or spins at full CPU, and a cancelled job seems to hang or to finish with nonsense. The fix: rethrow CancellationException before handling anything else (if (e is CancellationException) throw e), or catch only the exception types you expect from the call.

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Java and Kotlin
x: Stopping a CPU loop: Future.cancel(true) vs Job.cancel() ReconciliationJob.java Future<Integer> f = pool.submit(() -> { int matched = 0; for (int i = 0; i < entries.size(); i++) { if (i % 1_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) { throw new CancellationException("reconciliation stopped at " + i); // 1. look at the flag } if (matches(entries.get(i))) matched++; } return matched; }); f.cancel(true); // 2. sets the worker's interrupt flag; the loop stops at its next check ReconciliationJob.kt val job = scope.async(Dispatchers.Default) { var matched = 0 for ((i, entry) in entries.withIndex()) { if (i % 1_000 == 0) ensureActive() // 1. throws CancellationException once cancelled if (matches(entry)) matched++ } matched } job.cancel() // 2. marks the job cancelled; the loop stops at its next check Both models are cooperative, and both loops need the same explicit check. The differences are in what carries the request. Java's interrupt is a flag on a thread. Catching InterruptedException clears it, so a swallowed interrupt is lost, and the request doesn't reach other threads the task started. A coroutine's cancellation is a state on its job. It stays set, it flows down to every child in the tree, and every suspension point checks it. The two also see different things: blocking JDK calls react to interrupts but not to job cancellation (bridge them with runInterruptible), while suspension points react to job cancellation and ignore the interrupt flag.

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Worked example
x: Make a chargeback poller stop cleanly A poller checks a chargeback's status every 5 s until the card scheme decides. It holds a lease (a row lock in Oracle) so only one pod polls each case. During a deploy, pods take 30 s to shut down, and leases stay locked until they expire. Find the three problems before reading on. suspend fun pollChargeback(id: String): Status { val lease = leases.acquire(id) try { while (true) { try { val s = scheme.status(id) if (s.isFinal) return s delay(5.seconds) } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("poll failed for $id", e) } } } finally { leases.release(lease) // suspend: a network call to Oracle } } // Java equivalent of the same bugs Status pollChargeback(String id) { Lease lease = leases.acquire(id); try { while (true) { try { Status s = scheme.status(id); if (s.isFinal()) return s; Thread.sleep(5_000); } catch (Exception e) { // also catches InterruptedException log.warn("poll failed for {}", id, e); } } } finally { leases.release(lease); // fails at once if the flag is set } } Problem 1: catch (e: Exception) swallows the CancellationException from delay, so a cancelled poller spins. Catch only the scheme client's error, and let cancellation through. while (true) { try { val s = scheme.status(id) if (s.isFinal) return s } catch (e: SchemeException) { // 1. only what we expect from the call log.warn("poll failed for $id", e) } delay(5.seconds) // outside the try: a cancel ends the loop } while (true) { try { Status s = scheme.status(id); if (s.isFinal()) return s; } catch (SchemeException e) { // 1. only what we expect from the call log.warn("poll failed for {}", id, e); } Thread.sleep(5_000); // InterruptedException now propagates } Problem 2: the lease release suspends in a cancelled coroutine, so it throws before it reaches Oracle. Wrap it in NonCancellable, with its own short timeout so a stuck database can't hold up shutdown. } finally { // 2. cleanup that suspends must run non-cancellable, and bounded withContext(NonCancellable) { withTimeoutOrNull(2.seconds) { leases.release(lease) } } } } finally { // 2. clear the flag for the cleanup, then restore it boolean interrupted = Thread.interrupted(); try { leases.release(lease); } finally { if (interrupted) Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } Problem 3: nothing bounds the whole poll. Give the caller a deadline, and treat running out as an expected outcome rather than an exception. // 3. the caller decides how long a poll may take val status: Status? = withTimeoutOrNull(10.minutes) { pollChargeback(id) } if (status == null) scheduleRetry(id) // still undecided: try again from the outbox later // 3. the caller decides how long a poll may take Future<Status> f = pool.submit(() -> pollChargeback(id)); try { handle(f.get(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)); } catch (TimeoutException e) { f.cancel(true); scheduleRetry(id); } Self-check: the timeout in step 3 cancels pollChargeback while it is suspended in delay. Trace what happens. (The delay throws TimeoutCancellationException, it passes the narrow catch, the finally releases the lease under NonCancellable, and withTimeoutOrNull turns the exception into null.)

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Quiz
x: val job = scope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) { while (true) { digest.update(nextBlock()) } }, where nextBlock() is a plain function. You call job.cancelAndJoin(). What happens? It returns at once, because cancel stops the coroutine It returns after the current loop iteration It never returns: the loop has no suspension point and never checks The caller gets a CancellationException thrown from cancelAndJoin Nothing in the loop looks at the job, so the cancel request is never noticed, and cancelAndJoin waits forever. Add ensureActive() or yield() to the loop, or loop on while (isActive). A coroutine was cancelled while it waited in delay. Its finally block must call the suspending lease.release(). Which line does that correctly? try { lease.release() } catch (e: CancellationException) { } withContext(NonCancellable) { lease.release() } launch(NonCancellable) { lease.release() } GlobalScope.launch { lease.release() } Inside withContext(NonCancellable) suspension points don't throw, so the release runs to the end, and the cancel carries on afterwards. Catching the exception just loses the release. launch(NonCancellable) and GlobalScope both start a coroutine outside the tree that nothing waits for, so shutdown can finish before the release does. What does this print? coroutineScope { launch { withTimeout(100) { delay(1_000) } } } println("done") done, after about 100 ms Nothing: coroutineScope throws TimeoutCancellationException done, after about 1,000 ms Nothing: the program hangs TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException, so the child counts as cancelled, not failed, and the scope completes normally. If a timeout must fail the caller, write withTimeoutOrNull(100) { ... } ?: error("timed out"). withTimeout(500) { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Thread.sleep(3_000) } }. How long does the caller wait, and what does it get? About 500 ms, then TimeoutCancellationException About 500 ms, then null About 3 s, then TimeoutCancellationException About 3 s, then the block's result The timer fires at 500 ms and cancels the coroutine, but Thread.sleep doesn't see it. When the sleep ends, withContext checks, finds the job cancelled, and the timeout surfaces as the exception. runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) would interrupt the sleep at 500 ms. From the executors track: a task is blocked in Thread.sleep(5_000) when someone calls future.cancel(true) on it. What happens to the task? Nothing until the sleep ends, then it carries on The thread is stopped and the task's finally blocks are skipped The future completes normally with null sleep throws InterruptedException at once, and the task can clean up and stop cancel(true) interrupts the worker thread, and sleep responds to interrupts by throwing. What the task does next is up to its code: restore the flag and stop, or swallow it and carry on. That is the Java version of runInterruptible.

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Key terms
x: Cooperative cancellation Cancelling only asks; the code stops when it next checks or reaches a suspension point. Suspension point A call to a suspend function such as delay, await or withContext. Library ones check for cancellation. CancellationException The exception that carries a cancel through the coroutine's code. Catching it without rethrowing breaks cancellation. NonCancellable A job that is always active. withContext(NonCancellable) lets cleanup suspend after a cancel. TimeoutCancellationException What withTimeout throws. It is a CancellationException, so a parent treats it as a cancel, not a failure. runInterruptible Runs blocking code on a dispatcher and interrupts its thread if the coroutine is cancelled. Does job.cancel() stop a CPU loop with no suspend calls? No. Cancellation is cooperative: the loop must call ensureActive() or yield(), or check isActive. What does a suspension point such as delay do in a cancelled coroutine? It throws CancellationException at once, without suspending. Why is runCatching { suspendCall() } risky inside a coroutine? It catches every Throwable, CancellationException included, so the coroutine carries on after it was cancelled. Rethrow CancellationException. How do you call a suspending cleanup function in finally after a cancel? withContext(NonCancellable) { release() } On timeout, what do withTimeout and withTimeoutOrNull do? withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException, a subclass of CancellationException. withTimeoutOrNull returns null. Can withTimeout stop a Thread.sleep(10_000) inside it? No. Blocking calls ignore cancellation. Wrap them in runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { ... } so the thread is interrupted. (1..1_000).asFlow().collect { ... }: does each element check for cancellation? No. asFlow() doesn't check. Add .cancellable(). A flow { } builder checks on every emit.

h: Cancellation and timeouts · Go deeper
x: A CancellationException doesn't always mean "I was cancelled". If you await() a Deferred that someone else cancelled, await throws CancellationException in your coroutine, even though your coroutine is fine. The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 KDoc calls this out as a legacy behavior that can't be changed compatibly: your coroutine then ends as "cancelled", so its parent isn't told and the work silently stops. If you catch it, check currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() in the catch. It throws only if your coroutine was cancelled, so after it you know the exception came from the thing you awaited, and you can turn it into a real error. The library also gives a prompt cancellation guarantee. If a coroutine is cancelled while suspended, it resumes with CancellationException even when the value it was waiting for had already arrived. withContext checks for cancellation both on entry and when its block returns. So val conn = withContext(io) { pool.borrow() } can lose a connection: the block borrowed it, the caller was cancelled in the meantime, and the result is thrown away. Borrow and release inside the same block, or use the onCancellation callback of CancellableContinuation.resume when you write the bridge yourself (lesson 1 of this track). Timeouts have one more subtle rule. The KDoc says cancellation on timeout "may happen at any time, even after the block finishes executing but before the caller gets resumed". So never write withTimeout { resource = open() } and expect resource to be either unset or yours. Open the resource outside the timeout, or close it in the block's own finally. Finally, runBlocking bridges in the other direction. If the thread blocked in runBlocking is interrupted, the coroutine is cancelled and runBlocking throws InterruptedException. That is how a coroutine-based Kafka handler called from a plain consumer thread can still be stopped by shutdownNow().

h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · launch and async both report a failure to their parent at once
x: A coroutine that ends with an exception other than CancellationException has failed, and a failed child tells its parent at once. With a regular job, the parent then does what lesson 3 of this track described: it cancels its other children, waits for them to stop, and fails with the same exception. That holds for launch and for async alike. The async half surprises people. Many expect a failure in async to wait in the Deferred until somebody calls await, the way a failed CompletableFuture waits for join. It doesn't: Java // Java equivalent: a failed future tells nobody until someone joins it CompletableFuture<Score> risk = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> riskScore(paymentId), pool); CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> postToLedger(paymentId), pool); Thread.sleep(500); // passed: the ledger task keeps running too risk.join(); // the failure shows up only here Kotlin coroutineScope { val risk = async { riskScore(paymentId) } // throws at 100 ms launch { postToLedger(paymentId) } delay(500) // never passed: the scope is cancelled at 100 ms risk.await() } At 100 ms the risk call fails, the scope cancels the ledger call, and coroutineScope throws the risk exception to its caller. The kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 KDoc says it directly: async follows the same rules, and only when the parent is a supervisor or there is no parent is the exception "only available through the returned Deferred". So a try around await does not protect the scope. By the time await would throw, the child has already cancelled the scope. runCatching { risk.await() } inside coroutineScope is a common bug, and it is one of the bugs in this lesson's lab. Where do launch and async differ, then? Only when a failure has nobody above it to tell. A launch at the root hands its exception to a handler, which the next section covers. An async at the root keeps it in the Deferred, and await rethrows it. That is the same split as execute and submit on a Java executor: execute sends a task's exception to the thread's uncaught exception handler, while submit keeps it in the Future for get. Fail an async that nobody awaits Read AsyncFailsWithoutAwait.kt. The risk call fails at 100 ms, and the body only awaits it at 500 ms. Predict which lines print, and when. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=supervisor, which uses supervisorScope. Predict first: when does the failure surface now, and what happens to the ledger child? Run the Java twin. throw IOException("risk service down") } // nobody awaits this yet launch { try { delay(1_000); log("ledger: done") } finally { log("ledger: finally") } } delay(500) log("body: still running at 500 ms, about to await risk") risk.await() } if (supervised) supervisorScope(body) else coroutineScope(body) log("scope returned normally") } catch (e: IOException) { log("caller caught: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.AsyncFailsWithoutAwaitKt -Pargs=supervisor labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l06/AsyncFailsWithoutAwait.kt AsyncFailsWithoutAwaitJava.java // Java equivalent of AsyncFailsWithoutAwait.kt: a failed CompletableFuture tells nobody. // The failure sits in the future until someone joins it, and the sibling task runs on. package workbench.coroutines.l06; The body's 500 ms line never prints. With -Pargs=supervisor, the failed async does nothing on its own. The body prints at 500 ms, await rethrows, and because the block itself threw, supervisorScope cancels the ledger child (ledger: finally) and rethrows. The Java twin is the contrast: nothing reacts at 100 ms, the caller sees the failure only when it joins at 500 ms, and the ledger task runs on to 1,000 ms. Coroutine exceptions handling (Kotlin docs) read Think of a coroutine family as a film crew on location. With a regular job, the crew is one unit: if the camera operator is injured, the director stops the shoot, sends everyone home and reports the incident to the studio. A supervisor is a courier depot instead. If one courier's van breaks down, the depot logs it and the other couriers finish their rounds, but when the depot closes for the night, everyone comes back. The exception handler is the depot's incident book: it records what went wrong after the fact and fixes nothing. launch(SupervisorJob()) is hiring a freelancer through a different agency. They do the work, but your depot doesn't know they exist and won't call them back at closing time. The analogy breaks at the start of the trip: a real crew member can see the director wave. A coroutine only hears about a cancel at its next suspension point.

h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · CoroutineExceptionHandler is a last resort, and only roots use it
x: CoroutineExceptionHandler is a context element that receives the exceptions nobody else handled. It is for logging and metrics. By the time it runs the coroutine has already finished, so there is nothing left to recover. The rule that trips people up: only root coroutines use it. A child passes its exception to its parent, all the way up to the root, so a handler installed on a child is never called. A handler takes effect in two places. One is a coroutine launched straight into a scope whose job is not a coroutine, such as CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + handler).launch { }. The other is a direct child of a supervisor, which handles its own failure the way a root does (next section). It never takes effect on async, because an async keeps its exception for await. Java // Java equivalent: the thread's uncaught handler sees execute() failures, never submit() ones Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler handler = (t, e) -> log.warn("task failed on {}", t.getName(), e); ExecutorService webhooks = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "webhooks"); t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler(handler); return t; }); webhooks.execute(() -> { throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("webhook 503")); }); // handler gets it Kotlin coroutineScope { launch(handler) { throw IOException("webhook 503") } // ignored: this is a child } // coroutineScope throws IOException val webhooks = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO + handler) webhooks.launch { throw IOException("webhook 503") } // a root: the handler gets it If there is no handler in the context, the library falls back to the JVM's last-resort path: handlers registered through ServiceLoader, then the thread's uncaught exception handler, which usually prints a stack trace to stderr. In a service that is one log line and nothing more. When several children fail at once, the first exception wins and the others are attached to it as suppressed exceptions. Read the suppressed list before you decide only one call failed. Handlers ignore CancellationException, since a cancel is not a failure. The practical upshot: install one handler on each long-lived scope you own, at the line where you create the scope, and use it to log and count. Don't sprinkle handlers on launch calls inside request code. There, a failure should reach the request, where an ordinary try around coroutineScope deals with it. Find out where a handler runs Read HandlerOnlyAtRoot.kt. It installs the same handler in three places. Predict which of the three prints handler got. Run it. In case 1, swap coroutineScope for supervisorScope and run it again. Predict first. Run the Java twin, which uses execute and submit on a pool with an uncaught exception handler. HandlerOnlyAtRoot.kt package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineExceptionHandler import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.io.IOException fun main() = runBlocking { val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { ctx, e -> println(" handler got: ${e.message} (from ${ctx[CoroutineName]?.name})") } println("1. handler on a child inside coroutineScope:") try { coroutineScope { launch(handler + CoroutineName("child")) { throw IOException("webhook 503") } } } catch (e: IOException) { println(" coroutineScope threw: ${e.message} (the child's handler was ignored)") } println("2. handler on a scope with a SupervisorJob, root launch:") val webhooks = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default + handler) webhooks.launch(CoroutineName("root-launch")) { throw IOException("webhook 503") }.join() println("3. the same scope, root async that nobody awaits:") val d = webhooks.async(CoroutineName("root-async")) { throw IOException("webhook 503") } delay(100) println(" nothing printed: the failure waits in the Deferred") try { d.await() } catch (e: IOException) { println(" await threw: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.HandlerOnlyAtRootKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l06/HandlerOnlyAtRoot.kt HandlerOnlyAtRootJava.java // Java equivalent of HandlerOnlyAtRoot.kt: execute() sends a task's exception to the thread's // uncaught exception handler (like a root launch and its handler), while submit() keeps it // inside the Future until someone calls get() (like a root async and await). package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.UncheckedIOException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class HandlerOnlyAtRootJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Thread.UncaughtExceptionHandler handler = (t, e) -> System.out.println(" handler got: " + e.getCause().getMessage() + " (on " + t.getName() + ")"); ExecutorService webhooks = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "webhooks"); t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler(handler); return t; }); Runnable failing = () -> { throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("webhook 503")); }; System.out.println("1. execute(): the exception reaches the thread's handler"); webhooks.execute(failing); Thread.sleep(100); System.out.println("2. submit() that nobody waits for:"); Future<?> f = webhooks.submit(failing); Thread.sleep(100); System.out.println(" nothing printed: the failure waits in the Future"); try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println(" get threw: " + e.getCause().getCause().getMessage()); } webhooks.shutdown(); webhooks.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.HandlerOnlyAtRootJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l06/HandlerOnlyAtRootJava.java Only case 2 prints handler got: webhook 503 (from root-launch). In case 1 the handler on the child is ignored and coroutineScope throws. In case 3 nothing prints until await rethrows. After your change, case 1 prints handler got too: a direct child of supervisorScope handles its own failure like a root, and the scope returns normally. The Java twin shows the same split: execute reaches the thread's handler, submit waits in the Future until get. CoroutineExceptionHandler (API reference) docs After a capture succeeds, a payments service usually fires several side effects: merchant webhooks, customer notifications, loyalty points, an analytics event. None of them should cancel the others, and none should fail the capture. If the request waits for them, wrap them in supervisorScope and turn each await into an outcome. If they run after the response, give a component one scope built with SupervisorJob(), Dispatchers.IO and a handler that logs with the payment id and increments a failure metric, and close it in @PreDestroy. The Kafka partition worker from lesson 3 of this track wants the same swap: with a SupervisorJob, one bad record no longer cancels every batch in the partition. And keep anything that must not be lost, such as the ledger write, out of fire-and-forget code entirely. It belongs in the request's own scope, or in an outbox table that a worker drains.

h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · A supervisor lets children fail alone
x: Sometimes siblings shouldn't care about each other. The payment is captured, and now an email, an SMS and a push notification go out. An outage at the SMS gateway must not cancel the email. That is the job of a supervisor: a job whose children can fail independently. A child's failure doesn't cancel its siblings or the supervisor. Cancellation still flows down, so cancelling the supervisor cancels every child. There are two ways to get one. supervisorScope { } is the supervisor version of coroutineScope, for work the caller waits for: Java // Java equivalent: futures are independent, so each one handles its own failure Map<Channel, CompletableFuture<Outcome>> sends = new EnumMap<>(Channel.class); senders.forEach((ch, s) -> sends.put(ch, CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> s.send(paymentId), pool) .handle((ok, e) -> e == null ? new Delivered() : new Failed(e.getMessage())))); CompletableFuture.allOf(sends.values().toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); Kotlin suspend fun notifyAll(paymentId: String): Map<Channel, Outcome> = supervisorScope { val sends = senders.mapValues { (_, s) -> async { s.send(paymentId) } } sends.mapValues { (_, d) -> try { d.await(); Outcome.Delivered } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { Outcome.Failed(e.message ?: e.toString()) } } } With async children, each failure stays in its Deferred, and await rethrows it where you can catch it. With launch children there is no await, so the failure goes to the handler in the context. supervisorScope doesn't install one, so without your own handler it lands in the uncaught exception handler. SupervisorJob() is the supervisor for a scope you own (lesson 3 of this track): CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO + handler). Every launch into that scope is a child that can fail alone, and its failure goes to the scope's handler. The library's own MainScope() is built the same way, from a SupervisorJob and the main dispatcher. One rule doesn't change. If the body of supervisorScope throws, the whole scope is cancelled, children included. Supervision covers the children, not the block itself, which is why the Try it in the first section cancelled the ledger child when await rethrew. Pick per call, not per service. A payment details endpoint that needs all three of its calls wants coroutineScope, so one failure cancels the rest at once. Notifications, cache warm-ups and optional enrichments want a supervisor. Three channels, one outage Read SupervisorDemo.kt. SMS fails at 50 ms, push takes 100 ms and email 300 ms. Predict the output with coroutineScope. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=supervisor. Predict first: what does the handler print, and when does the scope return? Run the Java twin and compare its default with Kotlin's default. SupervisorDemo.kt package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineExceptionHandler import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.supervisorScope import java.io.IOException private var started = 0L private fun log(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - started) / 1_000_000, msg)) // supervisorScope installs no handler of its own, so failed launch children need one in the context private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> log("handler: ${e.message}") } fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking(handler) { started = System.nanoTime() val supervised = args.firstOrNull() == "supervisor" val sendAll: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit = { launch { try { delay(300); log("email sent") } finally { log("email: finally") } } launch { delay(50); throw IOException("sms gateway down") } launch { try { delay(100); log("push sent") } finally { log("push: finally") } } } try { if (supervised) supervisorScope(sendAll) else coroutineScope(sendAll) log("scope returned normally") } catch (e: IOException) { log("caller caught: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.SupervisorDemoKt -Pargs=supervisor labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l06/SupervisorDemo.kt SupervisorDemoJava.java // Java equivalent of SupervisorDemo.kt: CompletableFutures are independent by default, like // children of a supervisor. Nothing cancels the siblings, so each future handles its own failure. package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.UncheckedIOException; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class SupervisorDemoJava { static long started; static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - started) / 1_000_000, msg); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { started = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { CompletableFuture<Void> email = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(300); log("email sent"); }, pool); CompletableFuture<Void> sms = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(50); throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("sms gateway down")); }, pool); CompletableFuture<Void> push = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { sleep(100); log("push sent"); }, pool); // each failure is handled where it happens; the siblings never hear about it CompletableFuture<Void> smsHandled = sms.exceptionally(e -> { log("handled: " + e.getCause().getCause().getMessage()); return null; }); CompletableFuture.allOf(email, smsHandled, push).join(); log("all three settled"); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.SupervisorDemoJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l06/SupervisorDemoJava.java With coroutineScope, email and push are cancelled at about 50 ms (their finally lines) and the caller catches sms gateway down. With -Pargs=supervisor, the handler prints at about 50 ms, push is sent at about 100 ms, email at about 300 ms, and the scope returns normally. The Java twin behaves like the supervisor without being asked: futures are independent, so each one has to handle its own failure. Same failure, two parents. A plain Job cancels the whole family; a SupervisorJob keeps the failure with the child that had it. supervisorScope (API reference) docs SupervisorJob (API reference) docs

h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · launch(SupervisorJob()) cuts the child loose
x: Here is the most common wrong fix. A merchant webhook in a capture handler keeps cancelling its siblings when the merchant's server is down, so someone writes: Java // Java equivalent: hand the task to some other, longer-lived executor try (var request = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { SHARED_POOL.submit(() -> webhooks.post(event)); // no longer part of this request request.submit(() -> ledger.record(event)); } Kotlin coroutineScope { launch(SupervisorJob()) { webhooks.post(event) } // meant as "make this child supervised" launch { ledger.record(event) } } It reads like "a supervised child". It is something else. A Job in a builder's context replaces the parent, so the new coroutine becomes the child of that fresh SupervisorJob, which has no parent of its own. The coroutine has left the tree. coroutineScope doesn't wait for it, cancelling the request doesn't cancel it, and its failure goes to a handler or the uncaught exception handler instead of to the request. It is GlobalScope from lesson 3 of this track, spelled differently. The builder docs say it plainly: passing a Job there breaks structured concurrency, and it doesn't throw "only for backward compatibility reasons". kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 goes further and deprecates the overload, so the compiler now warns: "Passing a Job to coroutine builders breaks structured concurrency, leading to hard-to-diagnose errors." The same rule applies to async and withContext. The one documented exception is withContext(NonCancellable) for cleanup, from lesson 5 of this track. Put the supervisor where it belongs. Inside a function, wrap the children in supervisorScope { }. For background work, give the owning class a scope built with SupervisorJob() in its constructor, and launch into that scope. Then the work is supervised and still owned: the scope waits for it, counts it and cancels it on shutdown. When you see launch(SupervisorJob()), launch(Job()) or async(SupervisorJob()) in a review, ask what the author wanted. Usually the answer is one of those two shapes. Cancel a request and watch the trap child survive Read SupervisorTrap.kt. The request is cancelled at 100 ms. Predict which of the two children prints after that. Run it. Look for the deprecation warning in the Gradle output when the demo compiles. Delete SupervisorJob() from the first launch and run it again. Run the Java twin, where the detached task lives on a shared executor. SupervisorTrap.kt package workbench.coroutines.l06 import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking private var since = 0L private fun stamp(msg: String) = println("%5d ms %s".format((System.nanoTime() - since) / 1_000_000, msg)) fun main() = runBlocking { since = System.nanoTime() val request = launch { // looks like "a supervised child". It is a child of a brand-new SupervisorJob instead, // so it has left the request's tree: nobody waits for it and nobody cancels it. launch(SupervisorJob()) { delay(300) stamp("trap child: still running, nobody cancelled me") } launch { try { delay(300); stamp("normal child: done") } finally { stamp("normal child: finally") } } } delay(100) request.cancelAndJoin() stamp("request cancelled and joined") delay(400) stamp("main done") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.SupervisorTrapKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l06/SupervisorTrap.kt SupervisorTrapJava.java // Java equivalent of SupervisorTrap.kt: a task sent to some other executor is not part of the // request. Shutting the request's executor down interrupts its own tasks, not that one. package workbench.coroutines.l06; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class SupervisorTrapJava { static long since; static void stamp(String msg) { System.out.printf("%5d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - since) / 1_000_000, msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { since = System.nanoTime(); ExecutorService shared = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); // what launch(SupervisorJob()) amounts to ExecutorService request = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); shared.submit(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(300); stamp("detached task: still running, nobody cancelled me"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { stamp("detached task: interrupted"); } }); request.submit(() -> { try { Thread.sleep(300); stamp("request task: done"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { stamp("request task: interrupted"); } }); Thread.sleep(100); request.shutdownNow(); request.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); stamp("request cancelled and joined"); Thread.sleep(400); shared.shutdown(); stamp("main done"); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l06.SupervisorTrapJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l06/SupervisorTrapJava.java The normal child's finally runs at about 100 ms and the request is cancelled and joined. Then, at about 300 ms, trap child: still running, nobody cancelled me prints: it was never part of the request's tree. After your change, neither child prints after the cancel. The Java twin shows the same leak with a task on a shared pool. (The warning appears only on the first compile; once the class is compiled, Gradle doesn't print it again.) The most common mistake is trying to contain a failure at the wrong place: wrapping await() in try or runCatching inside coroutineScope, or putting a CoroutineExceptionHandler on a child launch. Both look like error handling, and neither runs before the damage is done, because a failed child cancels its parent the moment it fails. The scope and its other children are already cancelled when your catch would run, and the handler on a child is never consulted. Decide first whether the siblings should share a fate. If they should, let the failure propagate and catch it around the whole coroutineScope. If they shouldn't, use supervisorScope (or a scope with a SupervisorJob), and then a try around each await or a handler on the scope does work.

h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · Java and Kotlin
x: A background sender: pool with an uncaught handler vs supervisor scope with a handler WebhookSender.java class WebhookSender implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "webhooks"); // last resort for task failures, like a CoroutineExceptionHandler t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> log.warn("webhook failed", e)); return t; }); void post(Event event) { pool.execute(() -> client.post(event)); // execute, not submit: failures reach the handler } @Override public void close() { pool.shutdownNow(); } } WebhookSender.kt class WebhookSender(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) { private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> log.warn("webhook failed", e) } // SupervisorJob: one failed post doesn't cancel the others or the scope private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler) fun post(event: Event): Job = scope.launch { client.post(event) } // a root child: failures reach the handler fun close() = scope.cancel() } The two defaults are opposite. A Java thread pool is a supervisor without being asked: tasks never cancel each other, so you only have to make sure failures are seen (execute sends them to the uncaught handler, submit hides them in a Future nobody reads). A coroutine scope with a plain Job fails together, which is right for a request and wrong for a background sender, so you opt in with SupervisorJob(). After that the shapes match: launch is execute and goes to the handler, async is submit and keeps its failure for await. What Kotlin adds is the tree. The scope still knows every child, so close() cancels the sends in flight, and code that calls post from a test can wait for them.

h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · Worked example
x: Undo a launch(SupervisorJob()) fix A capture handler posts a merchant webhook. The merchant's server was down, the webhook failure cancelled the ledger write, and someone fixed it like this. Tests became flaky (webhooks fire after the test has ended) and shutdown logs show webhooks posting into a closed HTTP client. Why? suspend fun capture(cmd: Capture) = coroutineScope { val result = issuer.capture(cmd) launch { ledger.record(result) } launch(SupervisorJob()) { webhooks.post(result.toEvent()) } // the "fix" result } // Java equivalent of the same fix: the webhook goes to a shared pool nobody owns CaptureResult capture(Capture cmd) throws Exception { CaptureResult result = issuer.capture(cmd); try (var request = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { request.submit(() -> ledger.record(result)); SHARED_POOL.submit(() -> webhooks.post(result.toEvent())); // the "fix" } return result; } The SupervisorJob() became the webhook's parent, so the webhook left the request's tree. Nothing waits for it and nothing cancels it. Decide what the author wanted. The response shouldn't wait for the merchant, so the webhook belongs to a long-lived owner. Give that owner a supervisor scope and a handler. class WebhookDispatcher(dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) : AutoCloseable { private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { ctx, e -> log.warn("webhook ${ctx[CoroutineName]?.name} failed", e) // 1. log with the payment id } // 2. supervised and owned: children fail alone, close() still reaches them private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler) fun post(event: Event): Job = scope.launch(CoroutineName(event.paymentId)) { webhooks.post(event) } override fun close() = scope.cancel() } // Java equivalent: the dispatcher owns its pool and its failure handler class WebhookDispatcher implements AutoCloseable { private final ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8, r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r, "webhooks"); t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, e) -> log.warn("webhook failed", e)); // 1. log return t; }); // 2. owned: close() reaches every task void post(Event event) { pool.execute(() -> webhooks.post(event)); } @Override public void close() { pool.shutdownNow(); } } The capture goes back to a plain structured scope. The ledger write must succeed or fail with the capture, so it stays a child. The webhook is handed to its owner. suspend fun capture(cmd: Capture): CaptureResult { val result = issuer.capture(cmd) ledger.record(result) // 3. part of the request: a failure fails the capture webhookDispatcher.post(result.toEvent()) // handed off: the owner deals with failures return result } CaptureResult capture(Capture cmd) { CaptureResult result = issuer.capture(cmd); ledger.record(result); // 3. part of the request webhookDispatcher.post(result.toEvent()); // handed off to its owner return result; } If the response must include whether the webhook got through, the request does wait, and the right shape is supervisorScope with an outcome per call instead. suspend fun captureAndNotify(cmd: Capture): Pair<CaptureResult, Boolean> = supervisorScope { val result = issuer.capture(cmd) ledger.record(result) // 4. waited for, but allowed to fail alone val hook = async { webhooks.post(result.toEvent()) } val delivered = try { hook.await(); true } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { false } result to delivered } Map.Entry<CaptureResult, Boolean> captureAndNotify(Capture cmd) { CaptureResult result = issuer.capture(cmd); ledger.record(result); // 4. waited for, but allowed to fail alone boolean delivered = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> webhooks.post(result.toEvent()), pool) .handle((ok, e) -> e == null) .join(); return Map.entry(result, delivered); } Self-check: in step 4, the ledger write throws. What happens to the webhook call? (Nothing yet: it hasn't started. The exception is thrown from the supervisorScope block itself, so the scope is cancelled and rethrows. A supervisor protects siblings from each other, not from a failing block.)

x: What happens here? coroutineScope { async { delay(100); throw IOException("risk down") } delay(1_000) println("after") } after prints at 1 s, and the exception is lost because nobody awaited the Deferred after never prints; at about 100 ms coroutineScope throws the IOException after prints at 1 s, then coroutineScope throws the IOException The uncaught exception handler prints the error, and after prints at 1 s A failed async child cancels its parent immediately, exactly like launch. The scope's own delay is cancelled, after never prints, and the scope rethrows the child's exception. The "waits in the Deferred" behavior is only for supervisors and roots. What does this do? val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> log.warn("failed", e) } coroutineScope { launch(handler) { throw IOException("webhook 503") } } The handler logs the error and coroutineScope returns normally The handler logs the error, then coroutineScope throws it too The handler is ignored and coroutineScope throws the IOException Nothing happens: the exception is swallowed by launch The launch is a child, and a child hands its exception to its parent. Only roots consult a handler, so this one is never called. The scope fails and rethrows the exception to its caller. A component sends merchant webhooks in the background for the whole life of the service. One failed webhook must not affect the others, failures must be logged, and shutdown must stop them. Which scope fits? CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO + handler), created once and cancelled on shutdown GlobalScope, with launch(handler) for every webhook CoroutineScope(Job() + Dispatchers.IO), with launch(SupervisorJob()) for every webhook supervisorScope { } around each webhook, called from the request A supervisor scope you own lets each webhook fail alone, routes failures to the handler, and still reaches every child on shutdown. GlobalScope and launch(SupervisorJob()) detach the webhooks so nothing can cancel them, and supervisorScope in the request makes the request wait for the merchant. No handler is installed anywhere. What happens? supervisorScope { launch { throw IOException("sms down") } launch { delay(100); println("push sent") } } println("done") push sent never prints; supervisorScope throws the IOException push sent prints, then supervisorScope throws the IOException Nothing prints: without a handler, the scope hangs The uncaught exception handler prints the IOException, then push sent and done print In a supervisor, a failed child doesn't cancel its sibling or the scope. A failed launch child has no await, so its exception goes to a handler, and with none installed it reaches the thread's uncaught exception handler, which prints it. The scope then returns normally after the slowest child. From lesson 5 of this track: a notifier loops over channels with try { sender.send(id) } catch (e: Exception) { log.warn("send failed", e) }. During shutdown its scope is cancelled while SMS is being sent. What happens? The loop stops at SMS, because CancellationException is not an Exception The cancel is logged as a failed send, and each remaining channel is attempted and "fails" at once The JVM interrupts the thread and the loop exits The scope's handler receives the CancellationException CancellationException extends IllegalStateException, so catch (e: Exception) catches it. The coroutine stays cancelled, so every later send throws at its first suspension point and is logged too. Rethrow CancellationException or catch narrower types. Handlers ignore cancellations.
