h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · Key terms
x: Failed coroutine A coroutine that ended with an exception other than CancellationException. It cancels its parent unless the parent is a supervisor. Root coroutine A coroutine with no parent coroutine above it, such as one launched straight into a scope you created. CoroutineExceptionHandler A context element that receives uncaught exceptions from root coroutines, for logging and metrics. Supervisor A job whose children fail independently. Cancellation still flows down to all of them. supervisorScope The supervisor version of coroutineScope, for a block of work the caller waits for. Suppressed exception An extra failure attached to the first one, when several children fail together. In a plain coroutineScope, an async child fails and nobody has called await. What happens? The scope is cancelled at once, its other children are cancelled, and the scope rethrows the child's exception. Where does a CoroutineExceptionHandler take effect? On root coroutines and direct children of a supervisor. Never on ordinary children, never on async. What does supervisorScope change compared with coroutineScope? A failed child doesn't cancel its siblings or the scope. Cancelling the scope still cancels every child. A launch child of supervisorScope fails. Where does its exception go? To the CoroutineExceptionHandler in its context, or to the thread's uncaught exception handler if there is none. What does launch(SupervisorJob()) { } inside a scope really do? The new SupervisorJob becomes the parent, so the coroutine leaves the scope's tree: the scope doesn't wait for it or cancel it. Where does SupervisorJob() belong? In the constructor of a scope you own: CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + dispatcher + handler). Inside a function, use supervisorScope { }. Three children fail at once. Which exception does the parent rethrow? The first one. The other two are attached to it as suppressed exceptions.

h: Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers · Go deeper
x: SupervisorJob(parent) takes an optional parent, and that link works in one direction. If the parent is cancelled or fails, the supervisor is cancelled with it. A failure of one of the supervisor's children doesn't travel up. That makes CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob(appJob) + dispatcher) a good shape for a component scope that should die with the application but never take it down. supervisorScope and SupervisorJob differ in one detail that bites in tests. supervisorScope waits for all its children, like coroutineScope, and rethrows if its own block throws. A scope built with SupervisorJob() never "completes" on its own: it is a long-lived container, and you end it with cancel(). That is why the lab's NotificationService has an explicit close(). The last-resort path on the JVM is pluggable. kotlinx.coroutines looks up CoroutineExceptionHandler implementations through ServiceLoader and calls each of them before the thread's uncaught exception handler. kotlinx-coroutines-test uses that hook to collect exceptions from coroutines that escape the test, and since 1.7 runTest fails at the end if any were collected, even from coroutines that are not children of the test. That is why the lab's stub fails loudly instead of printing a stack trace and passing. Finally, CancellationException again. Since a cancel is not a failure, it never goes to a handler, and a child that ends with it never cancels its parent. That is the rule that made the runCatching loop in lesson 5 of this track so dangerous, and it is also why withTimeout inside a launch fails quietly. Code that turns a timeout into a real error (withTimeoutOrNull(d) { } ?: error("timed out")) produces an IllegalStateException, which does travel up the tree.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · A flow is a recipe that runs once per collector
x: A cold Flow is a recipe: nothing runs until collect, and each collector runs it again A Flow<T> is a stream of values that you receive one at a time through a suspend call. The usual way to make one is the flow { } builder, where you call emit once per value: Java // Java equivalent: a cold Flux that asks for the next page once the previous one is in Flux<LedgerEntry> ledgerEntries(LedgerApi api, String accountId) { return api.page(accountId, null) // Mono<LedgerPage> .expand(p -> p.nextCursor() == null ? Mono.empty() : api.page(accountId, p.nextCursor())) .flatMapIterable(LedgerPage::entries); } Kotlin fun ledgerEntries(api: LedgerApi, accountId: String): Flow<LedgerEntry> = flow { var cursor: String? = null do { val page = api.page(accountId, cursor) // a suspend call to the ledger service page.entries.forEach { emit(it) } cursor = page.nextCursor } while (cursor != null) } Calling ledgerEntries(...) runs nothing. It returns a description of the work, like a recipe. The body runs when someone calls a terminal operator such as collect, and it runs again from the top for every collector. That is a cold flow. A Reactor Flux is cold in the same way (lesson 2 of the reactive track): nothing happens until you subscribe. Two properties follow from the design. A flow is sequential: emit is a suspend call that returns only when the collector has finished with the value, so the producer never runs ahead of the consumer. That is Flow's backpressure, and there is no request(n) in sight. And a collector that stops early stops the producer. take(3) cancels the flow after the third value, so the flow { } body never asks for a page it doesn't need. The other builders are shortcuts. flowOf(a, b, c) emits fixed values, and list.asFlow() or (1..n).asFlow() turn collections and ranges into flows. Remember from lesson 5 of this track that asFlow() doesn't check for cancellation between items, so add .cancellable() when a long one has to stop on time. channelFlow and callbackFlow are for producers that aren't plain sequential code, and lesson 9 of this track covers them. A flow returned from a function is almost always cold. The exceptions are the hot flows, StateFlow and SharedFlow, which keep running whether or not anyone collects. They are lesson 8 of this track. Collect a cold flow three times Read ColdFlow.kt. Predict every fetching page line, including the ones for take(3). Run it. Change take(3) to take(2) and run it again. Predict first: how many pages now? Run the Java twin, a Flux built the same way. ColdFlow.kt package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.take import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.toList import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** Three pages of two entries each, from a ledger API that takes 20 ms per page. */ fun entries(accountId: String): Flow<String> = flow { for (page in 0 until 3) { println(" fetching page $page of $accountId") delay(20) emit("e${page * 2 + 1}") emit("e${page * 2 + 2}") } } fun main() = runBlocking { println("building the flow") val flow = entries("acc-1") println("built; nothing fetched yet") println("first collect:") println(" got ${flow.toList()}") println("second collect:") println(" got ${flow.toList()}") println("take(3):") println(" got ${flow.take(3).toList()}") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.ColdFlowKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l07/ColdFlow.kt ColdFlowJava.java // Java equivalent of ColdFlow.kt: a Reactor Flux is cold too. Nothing runs until you subscribe, // every subscription starts again, and take(3) cancels the source when it has enough. package workbench.coroutines.l07; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class ColdFlowJava { static Flux<String> entries(String accountId) { return Flux.range(0, 3) .concatMap(page -> Mono.fromCallable(() -> { System.out.println(" fetching page " + page + " of " + accountId); return List.of("e" + (page * 2 + 1), "e" + (page * 2 + 2)); }).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(20)), 1) // prefetch 1: ask for one page at a time .flatMapIterable(entries -> entries); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("building the flux"); Flux<String> flux = entries("acc-1"); System.out.println("built; nothing fetched yet"); System.out.println("first subscribe:"); System.out.println(" got " + flux.collectList().block()); System.out.println("second subscribe:"); System.out.println(" got " + flux.collectList().block()); System.out.println("take(3):"); System.out.println(" got " + flux.take(3).collectList().block()); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.ColdFlowJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l07/ColdFlowJava.java Building prints nothing. Each full collection fetches pages 0, 1 and 2 again. take(3) fetches pages 0 and 1, because the third entry is on page 1, and the flow is cancelled before page 2. With take(2) only page 0 is fetched. The Java twin prints the same lines, because a Flux is cold too. Asynchronous Flow (Kotlin docs) read A cold flow is a recipe card, not a pot of soup. Writing the card (calling flow { } and chaining map and filter) cooks nothing. Each diner who orders (each collect) gets the recipe cooked from scratch, one plate at a time, and the cook doesn't start the next plate until the diner has taken the last one. A diner who says "that's enough" (take) stops the cooking. flowOn moves the cooking to another kitchen while the diner stays at the same table. catch is the cook's rule for kitchen accidents, such as serving a fallback dish when the oven breaks, and it has nothing to say about a diner who drops their plate. The analogy breaks on cost: a real kitchen would never cook the same meal twice for two diners, and a flow does exactly that unless you share it, which is lesson 8 of this track.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Intermediate operators build the pipeline, terminal operators run it
x: Operators come in two kinds. Intermediate operators such as map, filter, onEach, take and transform take a flow and return a new flow. They are plain functions, they return at once, and they run nothing. Terminal operators such as collect, toList, first, single, fold and count are suspend functions. They start the flow, consume it, and return when it ends. Java // Java equivalent: Reactor operators also only build; block() (or subscribe) runs them Flux<String> receipts = ledgerEntries(api, "acc-1") .filter(e -> e.amountCents() > 0) .map(e -> String.format("EUR %.2f", e.amountCents() / 100.0)); List<String> firstTen = receipts.take(10).collectList().block(); Kotlin val receipts: Flow<String> = ledgerEntries(api, "acc-1") // nothing runs yet .filter { it.amountCents > 0 } .map { "EUR %.2f".format(it.amountCents / 100.0) } val firstTen = receipts.take(10).toList() // now it runs By default all of it runs in one coroutine, one value at a time. The first entry travels through filter, through map and into the collector before the flow body produces the second. There are no queues between the stages and no extra threads. The few operators that add concurrency on purpose, such as buffer, flowOn and flatMapMerge, say so in their docs. A reusable operator is just an extension function, and it reads like a built-in: Java // Java equivalent: a function from Flux to Flux, applied with transform static Flux<LedgerEntry> settledOnly(Flux<LedgerEntry> entries) { return entries.filter(e -> e.status() == Status.SETTLED); } Flux<LedgerEntry> settled = ledgerEntries(api, "acc-1").transform(Ledger::settledOnly); Kotlin fun Flow<LedgerEntry>.settledOnly(): Flow<LedgerEntry> = filter { it.status == Status.SETTLED } val settled = ledgerEntries(api, "acc-1").settledOnly() transform { value -> ... } is the general form: it can emit zero, one or many values for each input. Watch for a terminal operator hiding in a function that ought to return a flow. suspend fun receipts(): List<String> = pipeline.toList() runs the whole export at the call and holds every line in memory. fun receipts(): Flow<String> leaves the caller free to stream, take the first ten, or stop on an error. Watch one value at a time Read OperatorOrder.kt. Predict the order of the emit, filter, map and collect lines. Run it. Add .take(1) just before .collect. Predict how many emit lines print now. Run the Java twin. OperatorOrder.kt package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.filter import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOf import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.onEach import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking fun main() = runBlocking { // amounts in cents; refunds are negative val pipeline = flowOf(4_250L, -990L, 12_000L) .onEach { println("emit $it") } .filter { it > 0 }.onEach { println(" filter passed $it") } .map { "EUR %.2f".format(it / 100.0) }.onEach { println(" map -> $it") } println("pipeline built: no line above has printed yet") pipeline.collect { println(" collect $it") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.OperatorOrderKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l07/OperatorOrder.kt OperatorOrderJava.java // Java equivalent of OperatorOrder.kt: a synchronous Flux also moves one item through the whole // chain before the source produces the next one, and nothing runs until subscribe(). package workbench.coroutines.l07; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; public class OperatorOrderJava { public static void main(String[] args) { // amounts in cents; refunds are negative Flux<String> pipeline = Flux.just(4_250L, -990L, 12_000L) .doOnNext(a -> System.out.println("emit " + a)) .filter(a -> a > 0).doOnNext(a -> System.out.println(" filter passed " + a)) .map(a -> String.format("EUR %.2f", a / 100.0)).doOnNext(s -> System.out.println(" map -> " + s)); System.out.println("pipeline built: no line above has printed yet"); pipeline.subscribe(s -> System.out.println(" subscribe " + s)); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.OperatorOrderJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l07/OperatorOrderJava.java The pipeline built line comes first. Then each amount goes all the way through before the next one is emitted: emit 4250, filter passed, map, collect, then emit -990, which stops at the filter, then the third amount. With take(1) only one emit prints: once the collector has its value, the flow is cancelled. The synchronous Flux in the Java twin prints the same order. Flow (API reference: operators, context, exceptions) docs Flows fit the streaming jobs in a payments platform. A statement export can stream ledger pages straight to the file instead of loading two million rows into a list. A settlement-file import can read the acquirer's file with a blocking reader under flowOn(Dispatchers.IO), map each line to a ledger posting, report progress in onCompletion, and turn a truncated file into one Aborted event with catch. Two habits keep them honest. Put work that can fail and must be covered by catch (such as saving each record) in onEach above the catch, then call collect() with no lambda. And keep blocking JDBC or file reads above a flowOn, never inside withContext around emit. For a JDBC cursor, opening and closing the connection inside the flow { } body means each collector gets its own connection, and onCompletion or finally releases it however the flow ends.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Move the upstream with flowOn, not with withContext around emit
x: A flow runs in the context of the coroutine that collects it. The docs call this context preservation, and it means the code that collects never has to wonder which thread its lambda runs on. It also rules out the obvious way to move a blocking source, such as the acquirer's settlement file read through a legacy blocking reader, to IO: Java // Java equivalent: Reactor has no such rule; subscribeOn moves the source to another scheduler Flux.<SettlementRecord>generate(sink -> { String line = reader.readLine(); if (line == null) sink.complete(); else sink.next(parse(line)); }) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()); Kotlin // wrong: emit from another context throws IllegalStateException ("Flow invariant is violated") flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(parse(reader.readLine()!!)) } } // right: flowOn changes the context of everything above it flow { while (true) emit(parse(reader.readLine() ?: break)) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) emit must run in the collector's context, and the builder checks every call. The reason is in the first section: emit calls the collector's code directly, so an emit inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO) would run the collector's lambda on an IO thread that the collector never asked for. flowOn(ctx) is the tool. It changes the context of the flow above it, the upstream, and leaves everything below it, the collector included, where it was. You can use it more than once, and each one covers the operators up to the previous flowOn. To do that, flowOn has to run the upstream in a separate coroutine, so when the dispatcher changes it puts a channel between the two halves. The KDoc says it buffers "similarly to buffer operator", with the default buffer size. The upstream can therefore run ahead of the collector by up to 64 values instead of exactly one. For a file read that is usually what you want. Reactor's nearest tools are subscribeOn, which moves the source, and publishOn, which moves what follows it (lesson 6 of the reactive track). The difference that matters is the subscriber. With Reactor, unless you add a publishOn, your subscriber runs on the scheduler's thread too. With flowOn, the collector always stays in its own context. So don't reach for flowOn to move the collector. If the collecting side blocks (it writes each line to a file, say), wrap the terminal call instead: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { flow.collect { writer.write(it) } }. Print which thread runs each stage Read FlowOnDemo.kt. Predict the thread for read, parse, format and save. Run it. Move .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) to just after the second map, before collect. Predict, then run. Run it with -Pargs=wrong to see the invariant check, then run the Java twin. FlowOnDemo.kt package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOn import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext private fun thread() = Thread.currentThread().name fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { if (args.firstOrNull() == "wrong") { try { flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit("pay-1,4250,EUR") } // emit from another context }.collect { println("collected $it") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("IllegalStateException: " + e.message!!.lines().first()) } return@runBlocking } flow { for (line in listOf("pay-1,4250,EUR", "pay-2,-990,EUR")) { Thread.sleep(50) // a blocking file read println("read on ${thread()}") emit(line) } } .map { println("parse on ${thread()}"); parse(it) } .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) // everything above this line runs on IO .map { println("format on ${thread()}"); "${it.first}: ${it.second} cents" } .collect { println("save on ${thread()} $it") } } private fun parse(line: String): Pair<String, Long> = line.split(",").let { it[0] to it[1].toLong() } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.FlowOnDemoKt -Pargs=wrong labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l07/FlowOnDemo.kt FlowOnDemoJava.java // Java equivalent of FlowOnDemo.kt: Reactor's subscribeOn moves the source to another scheduler, // and publishOn moves everything after it. Without a publishOn, the subscriber runs on that // scheduler's thread too, which is the difference from flowOn. package workbench.coroutines.l07; import java.util.List; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class FlowOnDemoJava { static String thread() { return Thread.currentThread().getName(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Flux.fromIterable(List.of("pay-1,4250,EUR", "pay-2,-990,EUR")) .doOnNext(line -> { try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } // a blocking file read System.out.println("read on " + thread()); }) .map(line -> { System.out.println("parse on " + thread()); return line.split(","); }) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // the source and the steps above run there .publishOn(Schedulers.single()) // the steps below move to another thread .map(f -> { System.out.println("format on " + thread()); return f[0] + ": " + f[1] + " cents"; }) .doOnNext(s -> System.out.println("save on " + thread() + " " + s)) .blockLast(); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.FlowOnDemoJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l07/FlowOnDemoJava.java read and parse run on a DefaultDispatcher-worker thread, while format and save run on main. After the move, format joins them on the worker, but save stays on main: no flowOn can move the collector. With -Pargs=wrong you get IllegalStateException: Flow invariant is violated. The Java twin needs subscribeOn for the source and publishOn to move the later steps to single-1. flowOn (API reference) docs

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Handle upstream errors with catch, and every ending with onCompletion
x: Flows promise exception transparency. An exception thrown downstream, by an operator below or by the collector, belongs to the downstream, and a flow must not catch it and carry on emitting. The error-handling operators are built around that rule. catch { e -> ... } handles exceptions from the flow above it. It can log, emit a fallback, or rethrow. Exceptions thrown below it, including inside collect { }, pass straight through to whoever called collect. Java // Java equivalent: onErrorResume only handles errors from above it; doFinally runs on every exit settlementRecords(file) .<ImportEvent>map(r -> new Imported(r.paymentId())) .doFinally(signal -> metrics.importEnded(signal)) .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(new Aborted(e.getMessage()))) .doOnNext(ledger::save) .blockLast(); Kotlin settlementRecords(file) // may throw IOException .map<SettlementRecord, ImportEvent> { ImportEvent.Imported(it.paymentId) } .onCompletion { cause -> metrics.importEnded(cause) } // sees every way the flow ends .catch { e -> emit(ImportEvent.Aborted(e.message ?: "error")) } // upstream failures only .collect { ledger.save(it) } // a failure here reaches the caller onCompletion { cause -> } is the flow's finally. It runs once, however the flow ends. cause is null after a normal end, the exception after a failure upstream or downstream, and a CancellationException when the collector stopped early, as take and first do. Unlike catch, it handles nothing: the exception carries on after it. Put it above catch to see the original error, or below to see only what got past. The classic way to break the rule is a try/catch around emit inside a builder. emit runs the downstream code, so that catch also catches the collector's exceptions. If it then emits again, the flow throws IllegalStateException ("Flow exception transparency is violated"). That is one of the bugs in this lesson's lab. Use catch instead, which knows where it sits. One more benefit of cold flows shows up here. retry(3) and retryWhen { cause, attempt -> ... } recover by collecting the upstream again, and that works only because the recipe can be run again from the top. Flow's error model is close to Reactor's. In both, a step that can fail goes above the error operator if you want it handled (onEach above catch, doOnNext above onErrorResume), and anything below it is the subscriber's problem. One difference makes Flow simpler: a failure in the collector is an ordinary exception thrown out of collect, so a plain try around the terminal call catches it. Fail upstream, then fail in the collector Read CatchDemo.kt. By default the file read fails after two lines. Predict every line of output, including what onCompletion prints. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=collector, where saving pay-2 throws instead. Predict first: does catch print anything? Run the Java twin both ways. CatchDemo.kt package workbench.coroutines.l07 import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.catch import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.map import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.onCompletion import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.io.IOException fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { val failIn = args.firstOrNull() ?: "upstream" // or "collector" val lines = flow { emit("pay-1,4250,EUR") emit("pay-2,-990,EUR") if (failIn == "upstream") throw IOException("settlement file truncated") emit("pay-3,120000,GBP") } try { lines .map { it.substringBefore(",") } .onCompletion { cause -> println("onCompletion: cause = $cause") } .catch { e -> println("catch: $e"); emit("ABORTED") } .collect { id -> println("collect $id") if (failIn == "collector" && id == "pay-2") throw IllegalStateException("ledger db down") } println("collect returned normally") } catch (e: Exception) { println("the caller got: $e") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.CatchDemoKt -Pargs=collector labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l07/CatchDemo.kt CatchDemoJava.java // Java equivalent of CatchDemo.kt: onErrorResume only handles errors from above it, like catch, // and doFinally runs on every way out, like onCompletion. An exception thrown in the subscriber's // own lambda is not an upstream error: no operator above it gets to "handle" it. package workbench.coroutines.l07; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.UncheckedIOException; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; public class CatchDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { String failIn = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "upstream"; // or "collector" Flux<String> lines = Flux.concat( Flux.just("pay-1,4250,EUR", "pay-2,-990,EUR"), failIn.equals("upstream") ? Flux.error(new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("settlement file truncated"))) : Flux.just("pay-3,120000,GBP")); try { lines .map(l -> l.substring(0, l.indexOf(','))) .doFinally(signal -> System.out.println("doFinally: signal = " + signal)) .onErrorResume(e -> { System.out.println("onErrorResume: " + e); return Flux.just("ABORTED"); }) .doOnNext(id -> { System.out.println("consume " + id); if (failIn.equals("collector") && id.equals("pay-2")) throw new IllegalStateException("ledger db down"); }) .blockLast(); System.out.println("blockLast returned normally"); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("the caller got: " + e); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l07.CatchDemoJava -Pargs=collector labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l07/CatchDemoJava.java Upstream failure: pay-1 and pay-2 are collected, onCompletion prints the IOException, catch prints it and emits ABORTED, which is collected, and collect returns normally. Collector failure: onCompletion prints the IllegalStateException, catch prints nothing, and the caller gets ledger db down. The Java twin matches: onErrorResume only handles the upstream error, and doFinally reports onError or cancel. catch covers the flow above it, never the collector. onCompletion sees every way the flow can end. catch (API reference) docs onCompletion (API reference) docs The most common mistake is treating .catch { } at the end of a chain as a try/catch around the whole pipeline, including the collect { } lambda. It isn't: catch handles only the flow above it, so an exception thrown while saving a record in collect sails past it and fails the caller. People expect otherwise because every other error handler they know wraps everything inside it. The fix is to move the work that can fail upstream of catch, the pattern the Kotlin docs show: records.onEach { ledger.save(it) }.catch { e -> log.warn("import failed", e) }.collect(). If the caller should see the failure instead, drop the catch and let it propagate.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Java and Kotlin
x: A settlement import: Flux vs Flow SettlementImport.java Flux<ImportEvent> importFile(LineReader reader) { return Flux.<SettlementRecord>generate(sink -> { // 1. a cold source, pulled on demand String line = reader.readLine(); if (line == null) sink.complete(); else sink.next(parse(line)); }) .subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // 2. the blocking read runs elsewhere .<ImportEvent>map(r -> new Imported(r.paymentId())) .doFinally(signal -> metrics.importEnded(signal)) // 3. every ending .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just(new Aborted(e.getMessage()))); // 4. upstream errors only } SettlementImport.kt fun importFile(reader: LineReader): Flow<ImportEvent> = flow { // 1. a cold source, plain sequential code while (true) emit(parse(reader.readLine() ?: break)) } .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) // 2. the blocking read runs elsewhere .map<SettlementRecord, ImportEvent> { ImportEvent.Imported(it.paymentId) } .onCompletion { cause -> metrics.importEnded(cause) } // 3. every ending .catch { e -> emit(ImportEvent.Aborted(e.message ?: "error")) } // 4. upstream errors only The shapes line up step for step, and both are cold. The source is where they differ most. Reactor needs a generator callback with an explicit sink, because a Flux source must answer request(n) from subscribers. A Flow source is an ordinary loop: emit suspends until the collector is ready, so backpressure comes from suspension. Threads differ too. subscribeOn moves the whole chain until a publishOn moves it again, so Reactor subscribers often end up on a scheduler thread. flowOn moves only the upstream, and the collector stays in its own coroutine context. The error operators are nearly identical: catch and onErrorResume both handle only what is above them, and onCompletion and doFinally both run on every ending.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Worked example
x: Stream a statement export instead of loading it A statement export loads every ledger entry for the month into a list, formats it, and writes the file. For a merchant with two million entries the pod runs out of heap, and nothing is written until all the pages are in. suspend fun exportStatement(accountId: String, out: Path) { val all = mutableListOf<LedgerEntry>() var cursor: String? = null do { val page = api.page(accountId, cursor) all += page.entries // every entry held in memory cursor = page.nextCursor } while (cursor != null) withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { Files.write(out, all.filter { it.amountCents != 0L }.map(::format)) } } // Java equivalent of the same design: collect everything, then write void exportStatement(String accountId, Path out) throws IOException { List<LedgerEntry> all = new ArrayList<>(); String cursor = null; do { LedgerPage page = api.page(accountId, cursor); all.addAll(page.entries()); // every entry held in memory cursor = page.nextCursor(); } while (cursor != null); Files.write(out, all.stream().filter(e -> e.amountCents() != 0).map(Export::format).toList()); } Make the source a cold flow. Only one page is in memory at a time, and the next page is fetched only when the writer has caught up. // 1. the source: pages on demand fun ledgerEntries(accountId: String): Flow<LedgerEntry> = flow { var cursor: String? = null do { val page = api.page(accountId, cursor) page.entries.forEach { emit(it) } cursor = page.nextCursor } while (cursor != null) } // 1. the source: pages on demand Flux<LedgerEntry> ledgerEntries(String accountId) { return api.page(accountId, null) .expand(p -> p.nextCursor() == null ? Mono.empty() : api.page(accountId, p.nextCursor())) .flatMapIterable(LedgerPage::entries); } Build the pipeline with intermediate operators, and write in the collector. The file write blocks, and it is on the collecting side, so it moves with withContext around the terminal call. flowOn wouldn't help: it never moves the collector. suspend fun exportStatement(accountId: String, out: Path) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { // 3. the collector's blocking writes run on IO Files.newBufferedWriter(out).use { writer -> ledgerEntries(accountId) .filter { it.amountCents != 0L } // 2. build: nothing runs yet .map(::format) .collect { line -> writer.write(line); writer.newLine() } // runs it, one line at a time } } void exportStatement(String accountId, Path out) throws IOException { try (BufferedWriter writer = Files.newBufferedWriter(out)) { ledgerEntries(accountId) .filter(e -> e.amountCents() != 0) // 2. build: nothing runs yet .map(Export::format) .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) // 3. the blocking writes run elsewhere .doOnNext(line -> write(writer, line)) .blockLast(); // runs it } } A half-written statement must not look finished. Delete it when the flow ends with an error. onCompletion sees the cause, and the exception still reaches the caller afterwards, which is what an export job should do. ledgerEntries(accountId) .filter { it.amountCents != 0L } .map(::format) .onCompletion { cause -> if (cause != null) Files.deleteIfExists(out) } // 4. no partial files .collect { line -> writer.write(line); writer.newLine() } ledgerEntries(accountId) .filter(e -> e.amountCents() != 0) .map(Export::format) .publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) .doOnNext(line -> write(writer, line)) .doOnError(e -> deleteQuietly(out)) // 4. no partial files .blockLast(); Self-check: a caller runs exportStatement(...) inside withTimeout(30.seconds) and the timeout fires halfway. Is the partial file deleted? (Yes. The timeout cancels the coroutine, so the flow ends with a CancellationException, cause is not null, and onCompletion deletes the file. It runs inside the pipeline, before use has closed the writer. Linux doesn't mind, but Windows refuses to delete an open file, so a finally around use is the more portable place for the delete.)

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Lab
x: A ledger flow, a settlement reader and an importer labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l07/LedgerModel.kt labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l07/LedgerFlows.kt ./gradlew :coroutines:test --tests 'workbench.coroutines.l07.*' Run the tests. Seven of eight fail. LedgerModel.kt holds the API, the reader and the event types. Write ledgerEntries with flow { }: ask for pages starting with cursor null, emit every entry, and stop when nextCursor is null. The three ledger tests check that it is lazy, cold and stops early. Fix settlementRecords: delete the withContext and add .flowOn(io) after the builder. Rewrite importReport as a chain: map each record to Imported, then onCompletion { onDone(it) }, then catch that emits Aborted(message). Run the tests until all eight pass. For ledgerEntries, a do { ... } while (cursor != null) loop inside flow { } is all you need. emit suspends until the collector is done, so take(3) cancels the loop before the next api.page call. map needs to know it produces the sealed type, not Imported, or catch can't emit Aborted into it. Write .map<SettlementRecord, ImportEvent> { ... }. Put onCompletion above catch: there it sees the upstream exception itself. Below catch it would see null, because catch turned the failure into a normal end. No try anywhere in importReport. A try around emit also catches the collector's exceptions, and that breaks exception transparency. All eight tests in FlowBasicsTest pass. By the end you can build a cold Flow with flow { }, tell intermediate operators from terminal ones, move blocking upstream work with flowOn, and handle errors with catch and onCompletion without breaking exception transparency.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Quiz
x: What does this print? val f = flow { println("start"); emit(1); emit(2) } println("built") f.collect { println(it) } f.take(1).collect { println(it) } built, start, 1, 2, start, 1 start, built, 1, 2, 1 built, start, 1, 2, 1 start, 1, 2, built, start, 1 Building the flow runs nothing, so built comes first. Each collect runs the body from the top, so start prints twice. take(1) cancels the flow after the first value, so the second run never emits 2. records.map { parse(it) }.catch { emit(FALLBACK) }.collect { ledger.save(it) }, and ledger.save throws SQLException on the third record. What happens? catch emits FALLBACK and the import carries on The SQLException reaches the caller of collect, and catch never sees it The flow retries the third record The exception is swallowed and collect returns normally catch only handles exceptions from the flow above it. save runs in the collector, below catch, so its exception passes through to the caller. Move the save into onEach above catch if the fallback should cover it. In runBlocking on the main thread: flow { A }.map { B }.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO).filter { C }.collect { D }. Where do A, B, C and D run? All four on IO A on IO; B, C and D on main A and B on IO; C and D on main A, B and C on IO; D on main flowOn changes the context of everything above it, the builder and the first map. Operators below it and the collector stay in the collector's context, which here is main. You collect flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(loadRates()) } }. What happens? It works, and the collector runs on IO too It deadlocks, because emit waits for the IO thread It works, and the collector stays on its own thread It throws IllegalStateException: the flow invariant is violated A flow must emit in its collector's context, and the builder checks every emit. Move the work with flow { emit(loadRates()) }.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) instead. From the reactive track: Flux<String> f = Flux.just("pay-1").map(id -> { log(id); return id; }); runs, and nobody ever subscribes to f. What is logged? pay-1, once, when map is called Nothing pay-1, once per operator in the chain An error, because a Flux must be subscribed A Flux is cold, like a Flow: assembling operators runs nothing, and the work starts only on subscribe. A Kotlin flow built the same way logs nothing until a terminal operator collects it.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Key terms
x: Cold flow A flow whose code runs only when collected, from the start, once per collector. Flow builder A function that creates a flow, such as flow { }, flowOf or asFlow. Intermediate operator An operator that returns a new flow without running anything, such as map or filter. Terminal operator A suspend function that runs the flow and consumes its values, such as collect or toList. Context preservation A flow runs in the collector's context; only flowOn changes the context of the part above it. Exception transparency A flow never catches and hides exceptions thrown by the code downstream of it. Upstream The part of a flow chain above a given operator, closer to the source. When does the body of a flow { } run? Each time a terminal operator collects it, from the top. Building the flow runs nothing. Intermediate vs terminal flow operator: what's the difference? Intermediate ones (map, filter, take) return a new flow and run nothing. Terminal ones (collect, toList, first) are suspend functions that run the flow. How does a flow get backpressure without request(n)? emit suspends until the collector has finished with the value, so the producer can't run ahead. What does .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) move? Everything above it in the chain. Operators below it and the collector stay in the collector's context. What happens if you call emit inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO) in a flow { }? The flow throws IllegalStateException: "Flow invariant is violated". Use flowOn instead. Does .catch { } handle an exception thrown inside collect { }? No. It only handles exceptions from upstream; the collector's exceptions pass through to the caller. What cause does onCompletion get when the collector uses take(1)? A CancellationException: the flow was stopped early. It gets null only after a normal end.

h: Flow basics: cold streams and operators · Go deeper
x: Why does a flow check emit so strictly? Because operators rely on it. Every operator in the chain runs in one coroutine and assumes that nothing else calls its downstream at the same time. If emit could be called from another coroutine or thread, map and filter would need locks. The checks for context and for exception transparency are what let ordinary sequential code be a correct stream operator. When you need to emit from several coroutines, use channelFlow { }. Its send is safe from any coroutine started inside the builder, because a channel sits between the producers and the collector. callbackFlow { } is the same thing for callback APIs, and it requires awaitClose { unregister() } at the end, or it throws when the block returns. Lesson 9 of this track uses both. The Flow interface itself is "not stable for inheritance", in the words of its KDoc: write flows with the builders, or extend AbstractFlow if you really need a class. That matters if you are tempted to implement Flow on a repository class. Two older guide examples are worth knowing, because the current Kotlin docs dropped them. A busy flow built with asFlow() doesn't check for cancellation between items, which lesson 5 of this track showed. And buffer(), conflate() and collectLatest change the sequential model on purpose. With a producer that takes 100 ms per item and a collector that takes 300 ms, three items take about (100 + 300) x 3 = 1,200 ms plain, about 100 + 300 x 3 = 1,000 ms with buffer(), and about 700 to 800 ms with conflate(), which skips the middle item. Lesson 9 of this track runs those numbers.

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · StateFlow is one current value, and it skips what you missed
x: A StateFlow<T> always has a value. You can read it with .value at any moment, and when you collect it you get the current value first, then each new one. It is hot: it exists and holds its value whether or not anyone collects, unlike the cold flows of lesson 7 of this track. That makes it the natural type for state such as a payment's status, a circuit breaker's state or the latest FX rate. Java // Java equivalent: a Reactor sink that replays its latest value, with repeats filtered out Sinks.Many<PaymentStatus> status = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(PaymentStatus.PENDING); status.tryEmitNext(PaymentStatus.AUTHORIZED); status.asFlux().distinctUntilChanged().subscribe(this::render); Kotlin val status = MutableStateFlow(PaymentStatus.PENDING) status.value = PaymentStatus.AUTHORIZED // set from any thread println(status.value) // AUTHORIZED status.collect { render(it) } // current value first, then each change; never returns Two rules make StateFlow cheap, and both surprise people. Updates are conflated: a slow collector doesn't get a queue of the values it missed, it gets the latest one when it is ready. Set 1, 2 and 3 in quick succession while a collector is busy and it sees 3 next, never 1 or 2. And it compares with equals. Setting a value equal to the current one does nothing, and no collector wakes up. With a data class, a new object with the same fields counts as equal. Both rules follow from what StateFlow is. Its KDoc describes MutableStateFlow(initial) as a shared flow with replay = 1 and DROP_OLDEST, seeded with the initial value and followed by distinctUntilChanged(). So StateFlow is for state, where only the latest value matters. It is the wrong type for events, where every one matters: payment transitions for the audit log, "send this receipt" commands, ledger postings. Conflation would drop some of them without a trace. Events need SharedFlow, which is the next section. One more thing to expect: collect on a StateFlow never returns. The KDoc says it plainly, "state flow never completes". Collect it in a coroutine you will cancel, or wait for one particular value with first: status.first { it == PaymentStatus.CAPTURED }. Watch a dashboard skip FX ticks Read StateFlowConflation.kt. Three ticks arrive while the dashboard is busy, then an equal rate is set again. Predict every dashboard shows line. Run it. Change Rate from a data class to a plain class and run it again. Predict first: what changes, and why? Run the Java twin, which needs three Reactor operators to get the same behavior. StateFlowConflation.kt package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineStart import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking data class Rate(val pair: String, val mid: Double) fun main() = runBlocking { val eurUsd = MutableStateFlow(Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0809)) val dashboard = launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { eurUsd.collect { rate -> println("dashboard shows ${rate.mid}") delay(100) // rendering is slow } } // three ticks arrive while the dashboard is busy rendering the first value eurUsd.value = Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0811) eurUsd.value = Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0812) eurUsd.value = Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0813) delay(150) println("setting an equal rate again (a new object, same fields)") eurUsd.value = Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0813) delay(150) println("value is ${eurUsd.value.mid}; the collector is still waiting, because a StateFlow never completes") dashboard.cancel() } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l08.StateFlowConflationKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l08/StateFlowConflation.kt StateFlowConflationJava.java // Java equivalent of StateFlowConflation.kt with Reactor: a sink that replays its latest value, // distinctUntilChanged for the equality rule, and onBackpressureLatest so a slow subscriber only // gets the newest value. StateFlow does all three by itself. package workbench.coroutines.l08; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class StateFlowConflationJava { record Rate(String pair, double mid) {} public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Sinks.Many<Rate> eurUsd = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(new Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0809)); Disposable dashboard = eurUsd.asFlux() .distinctUntilChanged() .onBackpressureLatest() .publishOn(Schedulers.single(), 1) // request one value at a time .subscribe(rate -> { System.out.println("dashboard shows " + rate.mid()); sleep(100); // rendering is slow }); Thread.sleep(20); // three ticks arrive while the dashboard is busy rendering the first value eurUsd.tryEmitNext(new Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0811)); eurUsd.tryEmitNext(new Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0812)); eurUsd.tryEmitNext(new Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0813)); Thread.sleep(250); System.out.println("setting an equal rate again (a new object, same fields)"); eurUsd.tryEmitNext(new Rate("EUR/USD", 1.0813)); Thread.sleep(150); dashboard.dispose(); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l08.StateFlowConflationJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l08/StateFlowConflationJava.java The dashboard shows 1.0809, then 1.0813: the two ticks in between are skipped. Setting the equal rate again prints nothing. With a plain class, equality falls back to identity, so the "equal" rate is a new value and the dashboard shows 1.0813 a second time. The Java twin prints the same two lines, using replay().latestOrDefault, distinctUntilChanged and onBackpressureLatest. StateFlow (API reference) docs A StateFlow is the departures board at a station. It always shows something, it shows only the latest state of each train, and if you look away while a platform changes twice, you see only the final platform. Nobody announces "still on time" again. A SharedFlow is the station's public address system. Every announcement goes to everyone standing there, people who arrive late hear nothing that was said before they came (unless the station repeats the last few, which is replay), and if the announcer talks faster than the slowest listener can follow, someone has to wait or a message gets cut. stateIn is putting one person in charge of phoning the control room and updating the board for everyone, instead of every passenger phoning in. The analogy breaks at the empty station: a real announcer stops talking when nobody is there, but a SharedFlow's emitter keeps going, and the announcements simply vanish.

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · SharedFlow is for events, and its buffer decides what gets lost
x: A MutableSharedFlow<T> broadcasts every value to every current subscriber. It has no current value. Three parameters decide what it keeps: Java // Java equivalent: a multicast Reactor sink with a buffer for slow subscribers Sinks.Many<Transition> transitions = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false); Sinks.EmitResult result = transitions.tryEmitNext(t); // FAIL_OVERFLOW when full Kotlin val transitions = MutableSharedFlow<Transition>( replay = 0, // late subscribers get no history extraBufferCapacity = 64, // room for values a slow subscriber hasn't read yet onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.SUSPEND, // when full: emit waits, tryEmit returns false ) replay is how many recent values a new subscriber gets first. extraBufferCapacity is room beyond that for values that slow subscribers haven't taken yet. onBufferOverflow decides what happens when all of it is full. SUSPEND, the default, makes emit wait for the slowest subscriber. DROP_OLDEST throws away the oldest buffered value, and DROP_LATEST throws away the new one. The two drop policies need some replay or buffer to work with. emit is a suspend function. tryEmit is its non-suspending twin for code that can't suspend, such as a Kafka listener callback, and it returns false when the value doesn't fit. Here is the trap. With the default parameters there is no buffer at all, so tryEmit fails whenever a subscriber is busy, and the value is lost unless you check the result. The lab's stub has exactly this bug. Give the flow a buffer, and check what tryEmit returns. A SharedFlow never completes either, and a value emitted while nobody subscribes goes nowhere, apart from the replay cache. If events must survive having no listener, you want something else: a Channel with one consumer (lesson 9 of this track), or a durable topic. Put side by side: StateFlow has a value, replays exactly one, conflates and skips duplicates. SharedFlow has no value, replays what you configure, and with a buffer and SUSPEND it delivers every event to every subscriber. Both are safe to emit into from many threads at once. Reactor's sinks are not by default: concurrent tryEmitNext calls can fail with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED. Find out which events get through Read SharedFlowEvents.kt. Each case calls tryEmit five times while the only subscriber needs 50 ms per event. Predict the five results and what is received, for each of the four configurations. Run it. Change the last case to MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1, extraBufferCapacity = 64). Does anything in that line change? Run the Java twin. SharedFlowEvents.kt package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineStart import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.BufferOverflow import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** Emits five events with tryEmit while one subscriber is busy, and reports what got through. */ suspend fun tryFive(label: String, events: MutableSharedFlow<String>) = kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope { val received = mutableListOf<String>() val auditor = launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { events.collect { delay(50); received += it } // the audit write takes 50 ms } val accepted = (1..5).map { events.tryEmit("e$it") } delay(400) auditor.cancel() println("%-40s tryEmit: %s received: %s".format(label, accepted, received)) } fun main() = runBlocking { tryFive("default (no replay, no buffer)", MutableSharedFlow()) tryFive("extraBufferCapacity = 2", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2)) tryFive("extraBufferCapacity = 2, DROP_OLDEST", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 2, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)) tryFive("extraBufferCapacity = 64", MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 64)) // replay: what a subscriber that arrives later gets first val replayed = MutableSharedFlow<String>(replay = 2) (1..5).forEach { replayed.emit("e$it") } // no subscribers yet println("a late subscriber to replay = 2 first gets: ${replayed.replayCache}") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l08.SharedFlowEventsKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l08/SharedFlowEvents.kt SharedFlowEventsJava.java // Java equivalent of SharedFlowEvents.kt with Reactor sinks: a multicast sink with a bounded // buffer refuses values when a slow subscriber can't keep up (FAIL_OVERFLOW instead of false), // and a replay sink keeps the last N values for late subscribers. Reactor sizes small buffers up // to its own minimum, so this twin sends 20 events instead of 5 to fill one. package workbench.coroutines.l08; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import reactor.core.Disposable; import reactor.core.publisher.Sinks; import reactor.core.scheduler.Schedulers; public class SharedFlowEventsJava { static void tryTwenty(String label, Sinks.Many<String> events) throws InterruptedException { List<String> received = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); Disposable auditor = events.asFlux() .publishOn(Schedulers.single(), 1) .subscribe(e -> { sleep(50); received.add(e); }); // the audit write takes 50 ms List<Sinks.EmitResult> results = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) results.add(events.tryEmitNext("e" + i)); Thread.sleep(1_200); auditor.dispose(); long ok = results.stream().filter(r -> r == Sinks.EmitResult.OK).count(); System.out.printf("%-26s tryEmitNext OK: %2d, FAIL_OVERFLOW: %2d received %2d events%n", label, ok, results.size() - ok, received.size()); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { tryTwenty("multicast, buffer of 2", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(2, false)); tryTwenty("multicast, buffer of 64", Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false)); Sinks.Many<String> replayed = Sinks.many().replay().limit(2); for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) replayed.tryEmitNext("e" + i); // no subscribers yet List<String> late = new ArrayList<>(); replayed.asFlux().subscribe(late::add).dispose(); System.out.println("a late subscriber to replay().limit(2) first gets: " + late); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l08.SharedFlowEventsJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l08/SharedFlowEventsJava.java Default: [false, false, false, false, false] and nothing received: no room at all while the subscriber is busy. Buffer of 2: two true, then false, and [e1, e2] received. Buffer of 2 with DROP_OLDEST: every tryEmit returns true, but only [e4, e5] arrive, because the older ones were dropped. Buffer of 64: everything gets through. The late subscriber to replay = 2 gets [e4, e5]. Adding replay = 1 changes nothing in that line: the subscriber was there from the start. The Java twin reports FAIL_OVERFLOW instead of false, and only after 9 events, because Reactor rounds small buffers up. A SharedFlow keeps replay plus extraBufferCapacity values. The newest are the replay cache; the older ones wait for slow subscribers. MutableSharedFlow (API reference: replay, buffer, overflow) docs In a payment service, StateFlow fits anything a page or a health check reads as "the current value": a payment's status for the status endpoint, the circuit breaker in front of the card issuer, the latest FX rates. SharedFlow fits in-process events, such as status transitions that an audit writer and a notifier both consume. Remember it is in memory only: an audit trail that must survive a pod restart still belongs in Kafka or an outbox table, with the SharedFlow as a fast in-process fan-out at most. Kafka listener threads can't suspend, so they publish with tryEmit, which means the flow needs a buffer and the result must be checked or turned into a metric. For a live ops dashboard or a server-sent-events endpoint in Quarkus, stateIn(appScope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial) gives every open connection the same feed from one upstream, and stops polling when nobody is watching.

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Turn one cold flow into a shared hot one with stateIn and shareIn
x: A cold flow runs once per collector. If three ops dashboards each collect a flow that polls the acquirer's settlement API, the API is polled three times. stateIn and shareIn run the upstream once, in a scope you give them, and share its values: Java // Java equivalent: one shared upstream that starts with the first subscriber // and stops 5 seconds after the last one leaves Flux<Long> capturedTotal = captures .scan(0L, Long::sum) .replay(1) .refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); Kotlin val capturedTotal: StateFlow<Long> = captures // a cold flow fed from Kafka .runningFold(0L) { total, cents -> total + cents } .stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initialValue = 0L) stateIn gives a StateFlow, so it needs an initial value. shareIn(scope, started, replay) gives a SharedFlow. The started argument decides when the shared upstream runs: SharingStarted.Eagerly starts at once, before any subscriber, and runs until the scope is cancelled. SharingStarted.Lazily starts with the first subscriber and then never stops. SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis) starts with the first subscriber and stops once the last one has been gone for stopTimeoutMillis. The default is 0. A few seconds is common, so a page reload or a quick reconnect doesn't restart the upstream. The scope owns the shared collection, so make it a long-lived scope you control, like the owned scopes of lesson 3 of this track. A request's scope would end the sharing when the request ends, and GlobalScope would never end it. In tests, backgroundScope plays that part. There is also a suspend overload, stateIn(scope) without started, which waits for the first value and keeps the upstream running for the life of the scope. Sharing doesn't make the upstream any less cold. When WhileSubscribed stops it and a new subscriber arrives later, the upstream runs again from the top: the poll loop restarts, and a runningFold starts again from its initial value. That is usually what you want for a live feed. For a total that must survive restarts, keep it somewhere durable and use the flow only to show it. Start and stop a shared poller Read StateInDemo.kt. It shares an FX poller with WhileSubscribed(300). Predict when polling started and polling stopped print. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=eagerly, then with -Pargs=lazily. Predict each first. Run the Java twin, which uses replay(1).refCount(1, 300 ms). h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Keep the mutable flow private and update it in one step
x: A class that owns some state should let callers read it and nobody else write it. Before Kotlin 2.4 that took two properties: Java // Java equivalent: a private sink and a public read-only view class PaymentTracker { private final Sinks.Many<PaymentStatus> status = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(PaymentStatus.PENDING); public Flux<PaymentStatus> status() { return status.asFlux(); } void authorize() { status.tryEmitNext(PaymentStatus.AUTHORIZED); } } Kotlin class PaymentTracker { private val _status = MutableStateFlow(PaymentStatus.PENDING) val status: StateFlow<PaymentStatus> = _status.asStateFlow() fun authorize() { _status.value = PaymentStatus.AUTHORIZED } } Kotlin 2.4.0 made explicit backing fields stable. They arrived as experimental in 2.3.0, whose release notes used exactly this case as their example. One property declares its public type and, separately, its field: class PaymentTracker { val status: StateFlow<PaymentStatus> field = MutableStateFlow(PaymentStatus.PENDING) fun authorize() { status.value = PaymentStatus.AUTHORIZED } // smart-cast inside the class } Outside the class, status is a StateFlow with no setter. Inside it, the compiler knows the field is a MutableStateFlow and smart-casts. One small difference remains. asStateFlow() returns a wrapper, so a caller can't cast it back to MutableStateFlow. An explicit backing field hides the type only at compile time. Both are fine in application code. In a library other teams build on, the wrapper is the stricter choice. Then write every change as one atomic step. count.value = count.value + 1 is a read-modify-write (lesson 3 of the threads track), and two threads running it together lose updates. count.update { it + 1 } retries with compare-and-set until it wins. status.compareAndSet(expected, new) moves only if the value is still expected and returns whether it did. That is how the lab's tracker makes sure two Kafka listener threads can't both capture the same payment: the loser's compareAndSet fails, it reads the new status, and the move is no longer allowed. The same habit applies to SharedFlow events. Emit from the method that changes the state, after the change has succeeded, so the event stream never describes a move that didn't happen. Lose cents with value = value + 1 Read StateUpdates.kt. Eight coroutines on Default each add a cent 100,000 times. Predict both totals. Run it twice. Run the Java twin, which does the same with an AtomicReference. StateUpdates.kt package workbench.coroutines.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.update import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** 8 coroutines on Default each add 1 cent to a shared StateFlow 100,000 times. */ suspend fun addCents(label: String, add: (MutableStateFlow<Long>) -> Unit) { val capturedCents = MutableStateFlow(0L) coroutineScope { repeat(8) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { repeat(100_000) { add(capturedCents) } } } } println("%-34s expected 800000, got %d".format(label, capturedCents.value)) } fun main() = runBlocking { addCents("value = value + 1") { it.value = it.value + 1 } // read-modify-write: loses updates addCents("update { it + 1 }") { it.update { cents -> cents + 1 } } // compare-and-set in a loop } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l08.StateUpdatesKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l08/StateUpdates.kt StateUpdatesJava.java // Java equivalent of StateUpdates.kt: the same read-modify-write race on an AtomicReference, // fixed the same way, with a compare-and-set loop (updateAndGet). package workbench.coroutines.l08; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import java.util.function.Consumer; public class StateUpdatesJava { static void addCents(String label, Consumer<AtomicReference<Long>> add) { AtomicReference<Long> capturedCents = new AtomicReference<>(0L); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) { for (int t = 0; t < 8; t++) pool.submit(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) add.accept(capturedCents); }); } System.out.printf("%-34s expected 800000, got %d%n", label, capturedCents.get()); } public static void main(String[] args) { addCents("set(get() + 1)", ref -> ref.set(ref.get() + 1)); // read-modify-write: loses updates addCents("updateAndGet(c -> c + 1)", ref -> ref.updateAndGet(c -> c + 1)); // compare-and-set in a loop } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l08.StateUpdatesJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l08/StateUpdatesJava.java value = value + 1 comes out far short of 800,000, and the number changes from run to run (one run here gave 259,299). update { it + 1 } gives exactly 800,000 every time. The Java twin loses updates with set(get() + 1) and gets 800,000 with updateAndGet, because they are the same race and the same fix. What's new in Kotlin 2.4.0 (explicit backing fields) read The most common mistake is using a StateFlow (or MutableSharedFlow() with default parameters) as an event bus. With StateFlow, two transitions in quick succession arrive as one, and repeating an event that equals the current value delivers nothing, so an audit log quietly misses entries. With a default SharedFlow, tryEmit from a non-suspending callback returns false whenever a subscriber is busy, and the event vanishes. Both look fine in a unit test with one fast collector. Decide what the stream carries. State, where only the latest matters, goes in a StateFlow. Events, where every one matters, go in a SharedFlow with extraBufferCapacity sized for bursts, SUSPEND overflow, and a checked tryEmit (or emit from a coroutine).

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Java and Kotlin
x: A payment tracker: Reactor sinks vs StateFlow and SharedFlow PaymentTracker.java class PaymentTracker { private final AtomicReference<PaymentStatus> current = new AtomicReference<>(PaymentStatus.PENDING); private final Sinks.Many<PaymentStatus> status = Sinks.many().replay().latestOrDefault(PaymentStatus.PENDING); private final Sinks.Many<Transition> transitions = Sinks.many().multicast().onBackpressureBuffer(64, false); public PaymentStatus currentStatus() { return current.get(); } // 1. a synchronous read public Flux<PaymentStatus> status() { return status.asFlux().distinctUntilChanged(); } public Flux<Transition> transitions() { return transitions.asFlux(); } boolean moveTo(PaymentStatus next) { PaymentStatus from = current.get(); if (!from.canMoveTo(next) || !current.compareAndSet(from, next)) return false; // 2. atomic move // 3. sinks reject concurrent emits (FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED), so serialize them synchronized (this) { status.tryEmitNext(next); transitions.tryEmitNext(new Transition(id, from, next)); } return true; } } PaymentTracker.kt class PaymentTracker(private val id: String) { val status: StateFlow<PaymentStatus> // 1. .value is a synchronous read field = MutableStateFlow(PaymentStatus.PENDING) val transitions: SharedFlow<Transition> field = MutableSharedFlow(extraBufferCapacity = 64) fun moveTo(next: PaymentStatus): Boolean { while (true) { val from = status.value if (!from.canMoveTo(next)) return false if (status.compareAndSet(from, next)) { // 2. atomic move check(transitions.tryEmit(Transition(id, from, next))) // 3. safe from any thread return true } } } } The Kotlin version needs fewer moving parts because StateFlow is both the holder and the stream: .value reads it synchronously, compareAndSet changes it atomically, and collectors see changes with conflation and de-duplication built in. Reactor has no single type for that, so the Java version keeps an AtomicReference for the value and a replaying sink for the stream, and must keep them consistent. The other real difference is concurrency. MutableStateFlow and MutableSharedFlow are documented as safe for concurrent emitters. Reactor's default sinks detect concurrent tryEmitNext calls and fail them with FAIL_NON_SERIALIZED, so the Java tracker serializes its emits.

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Worked example
x: Share one FX feed across every dashboard An ops dashboard shows live FX rates over server-sent events. Each open connection collects rates(), a cold flow that polls the provider every second. With 40 open tabs the provider sees 40 polls a second and starts rate-limiting the payment service too. fun rates(): Flow<FxRates> = flow { while (true) { emit(provider.latest()) // one HTTP call per collector per second delay(1.seconds) } } // in the SSE resource, once per connection rates().collect { send(it) } // Java equivalent of the same design: a cold Flux subscribed once per connection Flux<FxRates> rates() { return Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .concatMap(tick -> provider.latest()); // one HTTP call per subscriber per second } // in the SSE resource, once per connection return rates(); Decide the type first. A dashboard wants the latest rates, and a tab that missed a tick doesn't need it replayed, so this is state: a StateFlow. Share the upstream in a scope that lives as long as the service, and stop it when nobody watches. Five seconds of grace covers a tab reload. @ApplicationScoped class FxFeed(provider: FxProvider) : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO) // 1. the owner of the sharing val rates: StateFlow<FxRates?> = flow { while (true) { emit(provider.latest()); delay(1.seconds) } }.stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initialValue = null) // 2. one poll for all override fun close() = scope.cancel() // 3. ends with the bean } @ApplicationScoped class FxFeed { // 1. and 2.: one shared poll, started by the first subscriber, stopped 5 s after the last final Flux<FxRates> rates; FxFeed(FxProvider provider) { this.rates = Flux.interval(Duration.ZERO, Duration.ofSeconds(1)) .concatMap(tick -> provider.latest()) .replay(1) .refCount(1, Duration.ofSeconds(5)); } } Each connection now collects the shared StateFlow. A slow client gets the newest rates rather than a backlog, and a tick with unchanged rates (an equal data class) isn't sent at all. // in the SSE resource, once per connection: no extra poll fxFeed.rates.filterNotNull().collect { send(it) } // in the SSE resource, once per connection: no extra poll return fxFeed.rates.distinctUntilChanged().onBackpressureLatest(); Self-check: why not SharingStarted.Eagerly? (It would poll the provider every second from startup, even at night with no dashboards open, and never stop until shutdown. WhileSubscribed polls only while someone is watching.)

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Lab
x: A payment tracker and a live total labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l08/PaymentStatus.kt labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l08/PaymentTracker.kt labs/coroutines/src/main/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l08/LiveTotals.kt ./gradlew :coroutines:test --tests 'workbench.coroutines.l08.*' Run the tests. Five of seven fail. PaymentStatus.kt has the allowed moves; PaymentTracker.kt already uses explicit backing fields, so status is read-only outside the class. Give transitions a buffer: MutableSharedFlow(replay = 0, extraBufferCapacity = 64). The two transition tests should pass. Make moveTo atomic: in a loop, read status.value, check canMoveTo, call beforeMove, then status.compareAndSet(from, next). If the CAS fails, go round again. Emit the transition only after a successful CAS. In LiveTotals.kt, replace SharingStarted.Eagerly with SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis = 5_000). Run the tests until all seven pass. Inside the class, status smart-casts to MutableStateFlow, so status.compareAndSet(from, next) and transitions.tryEmit(...) compile without a cast. Check what tryEmit returns. With a buffer of 64 it should always be true here; check(...) turns a surprise false into a loud failure instead of a lost event. The race test holds both threads in beforeMove until both have read AUTHORIZED. With compareAndSet, the second one's CAS fails, it reads CAPTURED, and canMoveTo says no. The stateIn tests run on virtual time, so WhileSubscribed(5_000) takes no real time at all. All seven tests in HotFlowsTest pass. By the end you can choose between StateFlow and SharedFlow, configure replay, buffer and overflow so events aren't lost, share one upstream with stateIn and SharingStarted, and expose state read-only with an explicit backing field.

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Quiz
x: What does the collector print? val s = MutableStateFlow(0) launch { s.collect { println(it); delay(100) } } delay(10) s.value = 1; s.value = 2; s.value = 3 delay(200) s.value = 3 0, 1, 2, 3, 3 0, 1, 2, 3 0, 3 3 The collector prints 0 and is busy for 100 ms while 1, 2 and 3 are set. StateFlow conflates, so when it is ready it gets only the latest, 3. Setting 3 again is equal to the current value, so nothing is emitted. An audit writer collects val events = MutableSharedFlow<Transition>() and takes 50 ms per write. A Kafka listener thread calls events.tryEmit(t) while the writer is busy. What happens? tryEmit blocks the listener thread until the writer is ready tryEmit returns false and the transition is lost unless you check The transition is queued without limit tryEmit throws IllegalStateException With default parameters there is no buffer, so a non-suspending emit has nowhere to put the value while a subscriber is busy. tryEmit never blocks or throws; it returns false. Use extraBufferCapacity and check the result. Every chargeback event must reach both the email sender and the audit writer, which run all the time, and a burst of 50 events must not drop any. Which type fits? MutableStateFlow<Chargeback?>(null) MutableSharedFlow<Chargeback>(extraBufferCapacity = 64) with the default SUSPEND A cold flow { } that each consumer collects MutableSharedFlow<Chargeback>(replay = 1, onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST) Events go to several subscribers, and none may be lost, so a SharedFlow with room for bursts and SUSPEND fits. A StateFlow conflates events away, a cold flow would run once per consumer instead of broadcasting, and DROP_OLDEST discards events when a subscriber falls behind. A live settlement dashboard shares a polling flow with stateIn. A page reload must not restart the polling, and nothing should poll when no dashboard is open. Which started value fits? SharingStarted.Eagerly SharingStarted.Lazily SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed() SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000) WhileSubscribed(5_000) starts with the first subscriber and stops 5 s after the last leaves, so a reload within that window keeps it running. The default WhileSubscribed() stops at once, Lazily never stops, and Eagerly polls even before anyone opens a dashboard. From lesson 7 of this track: three dashboards each collect the same val rates = flow { while (true) { emit(poll()); delay(1_000) } }. How many times does poll() run per second? Three times: a cold flow runs once per collector Once: the flow is shared because it is the same object Once, but only for the first dashboard; the others get nothing It depends on the dispatcher A cold flow's body runs separately for every collector, even if they all hold the same Flow object. Sharing one upstream takes stateIn or shareIn.
