h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Key terms
x: Hot flow A flow that exists and produces values whether or not anyone collects it. StateFlow A hot flow with one current value; it conflates and skips equal values. SharedFlow A hot flow that broadcasts every value to every current subscriber. Conflation Keeping only the latest value for a slow consumer and dropping the ones in between. Replay cache The last few values a SharedFlow keeps and gives to each new subscriber first. SharingStarted The rule that tells stateIn or shareIn when to start and stop the shared upstream. Explicit backing field A Kotlin property whose field has a different, more specific type than the property itself. A StateFlow collector is busy while three new values are set. What does it see next? Only the latest one. StateFlow conflates: values a slow collector missed are skipped. What happens when you set a MutableStateFlow to a value equal to its current one? Nothing. It compares with equals, and an equal value emits nothing. MutableSharedFlow() with default parameters: what does tryEmit return while a subscriber is busy? false. There is no buffer, so the value is dropped. Add extraBufferCapacity and check the result. replay vs extraBufferCapacity in a MutableSharedFlow? replay: how many recent values a new subscriber gets first. extraBufferCapacity: extra room for values slow subscribers haven't taken yet. What does SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000) do? Starts the shared upstream with the first subscriber and stops it 5 s after the last subscriber leaves. How do you expose a StateFlow read-only with one property in Kotlin 2.4? An explicit backing field: val status: StateFlow<S> followed by field = MutableStateFlow(initial). How do you add 1 to a MutableStateFlow<Int> safely from many threads? flow.update { it + 1 }, which retries with compare-and-set. value = value + 1 loses updates.

h: StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams · Go deeper
x: MutableSharedFlow has a subscriptionCount: StateFlow<Int>. It is deliberately not conflated, so you can react to the first subscriber arriving or the last one leaving, for example to open and close a connection to a market-data feed. SharingStarted is an interface, and WhileSubscribed is written on top of exactly that count. A custom strategy can start sharing only during business hours, or only after a warm-up. WhileSubscribed has a second parameter, replayExpirationMillis, which defaults to Long.MAX_VALUE. It decides how long the last value stays in the replay cache after the upstream stops. Set it to 0 if a stale value is worse than none, for instance a rate that must never be shown once its feed is down. stateIn and shareIn keep a coroutine running in the scope you give them, so the scope's lifetime is the sharing's lifetime. If the upstream throws, that coroutine fails, the error goes up into the scope, and the StateFlow simply stops updating. Put a catch or retryWhen on the upstream, above stateIn, and decide what the subscribers should see while it recovers. kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 added two small helpers. SharedFlow.asFlow() returns a view that hides the hot-flow type, so callers can't rely on it being shared. And there is now an onSubscription overload on StateFlow that keeps the StateFlow type. Kotlin 2.1.20 also added common atomics such as AtomicInt in kotlin.concurrent.atomics, marked experimental. For plain counters shared between coroutines they are an alternative to a StateFlow you never collect, which lesson 10 of this track compares with Mutex.

h: Channels, select and pipelines · A channel is a queue between coroutines, and its capacity sets the pace
x: A Channel<T> is the coroutine version of a BlockingQueue. send puts an element in and receive takes one out, but where a blocking queue blocks a thread, a channel suspends a coroutine. Each element is received by exactly one receiver, which is the difference from a SharedFlow (lesson 8 of this track), where every subscriber gets every value. Java // Java equivalent: a bounded BlockingQueue, with an end marker because a queue can't be closed BlockingQueue<String> ids = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64); Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { for (String id : batchIds) putQuietly(ids, id); // blocks while the queue is full putQuietly(ids, END); }); for (String id = ids.take(); !id.equals(END); id = ids.take()) settle(id); Kotlin val ids = Channel<String>(capacity = 64) launch { for (id in batchIds) ids.send(id) // suspends while the buffer is full ids.close() // no more elements: the receiving loop will end } for (id in ids) settle(id) // receives until the channel is closed and empty The capacity decides how far a sender can run ahead of the receiver: Capacity send suspends when Like Channel.RENDEZVOUS (0, the default) no receiver is waiting SynchronousQueue Channel(n) n elements are already waiting ArrayBlockingQueue(n) Channel.BUFFERED 64 are waiting (a JVM property changes the default) ArrayBlockingQueue(64) Channel.UNLIMITED never: memory is the limit LinkedBlockingQueue Channel.CONFLATED never: a new element replaces the waiting one no JDK equivalent Rendezvous is the default for a good reason: it gives you backpressure for free, because a fast producer simply waits for the consumer. Add a buffer to absorb bursts. Be suspicious of UNLIMITED, which turns a slow consumer into an OutOfMemoryError some hours later. Close a channel when you are done sending. for (x in channel) ends only when the channel is closed and empty, so a receiver on a channel nobody closes waits forever. The produce { } builder takes care of it. It starts a coroutine that sends into a new channel, closes the channel when the block ends or fails, and returns it as a ReceiveChannel. It is still marked @ExperimentalCoroutinesApi, so it needs an opt-in. A channel is hot. Elements sit in it whether or not anyone receives, and a coroutine suspended in send never finishes until someone does. For a stream with a single consumer, a cold Flow is usually the better tool. Channels are for coroutines that hand work to each other. Five sends, four capacities Read ChannelCapacities.kt. The producer sends five ids as fast as it can, and the consumer needs 100 ms per id. Predict when each send returns, and what is received, for each capacity. Run it. Delete the channel.close() line and run it again. Predict first: what happens? Put the line back and run the Java twin, which uses three BlockingQueues. ChannelCapacities.kt package workbench.coroutines.l09 import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking /** A producer sends 5 batch ids as fast as it can; the consumer needs 100 ms per id. */ suspend fun run(label: String, channel: Channel<Int>) = coroutineScope { val t0 = System.nanoTime() fun ms() = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 val sendTimes = mutableListOf<Long>() launch { for (id in 1..5) { channel.send(id); sendTimes += ms() } channel.close() // no more ids: the consumer's for loop ends after the last one } val received = mutableListOf<Int>() for (id in channel) { delay(100); received += id } println("%-12s send() returned at %-26s received %s".format(label, sendTimes.toString() + " ms", received)) } fun main() = runBlocking { run("RENDEZVOUS", Channel(Channel.RENDEZVOUS)) run("capacity 2", Channel(2)) run("UNLIMITED", Channel(Channel.UNLIMITED)) run("CONFLATED", Channel(Channel.CONFLATED)) } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l09.ChannelCapacitiesKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l09/ChannelCapacities.kt ChannelCapacitiesJava.java // Java equivalent of ChannelCapacities.kt: blocking queues between two threads. SynchronousQueue // is a rendezvous, ArrayBlockingQueue(2) has capacity 2, LinkedBlockingQueue is unbounded. // The JDK has no conflated queue; Kotlin's CONFLATED channel keeps only the newest element. // A blocking queue has no close(), so the producer sends a marker (-1) at the end instead. package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue; public class ChannelCapacitiesJava { static void run(String label, BlockingQueue<Integer> queue) throws InterruptedException { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<Long> sendTimes = new ArrayList<>(); Thread producer = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { try { for (int id = 1; id <= 5; id++) { queue.put(id); sendTimes.add((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } queue.put(-1); // the end marker } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); List<Integer> received = new ArrayList<>(); for (int id = queue.take(); id != -1; id = queue.take()) { Thread.sleep(100); received.add(id); } producer.join(); System.out.printf("%-22s put() returned at %-26s received %s%n", label, sendTimes + " ms", received); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("SynchronousQueue", new SynchronousQueue<>()); run("ArrayBlockingQueue(2)", new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2)); run("LinkedBlockingQueue", new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l09.ChannelCapacitiesJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l09/ChannelCapacitiesJava.java Rendezvous: each send returns about 100 ms after the previous one, in step with the consumer. Capacity 2: the first three return at once (two buffered, one handed straight to the waiting receiver), then one every 100 ms. Unlimited: all five at once. Conflated: all five at once, but only [1, 5] is received, because each new id replaced the waiting one. Without close() the program never ends: the for loop waits for an id that will never come (stop it with Ctrl+C). The Java twin's three queues match the first three rows. Channels (Kotlin docs) read A channel is the hatch between a restaurant's kitchen and its dining room. With a rendezvous hatch there is no shelf: the cook holds the plate until a waiter takes it. A buffered hatch has a shelf with a fixed number of spots, and the cook waits only when the shelf is full. Fan-out is several waiters taking plates from the same hatch, each plate going to exactly one of them. Fan-in is several cooks passing plates through one hatch to one waiter. select is ringing two suppliers and going with whoever picks up first, then hanging up on the other. The analogy breaks at closing time: in a real kitchen the staff see the lights go off. A channel's receivers only learn that nothing more is coming when someone calls close(), and if nobody does, they wait at the hatch forever.

h: Channels, select and pipelines · Fan out to a fixed set of workers, fan in to one channel
x: Fan-out means several coroutines receive from the same channel. Each element goes to exactly one of them, and channels are fair: receivers waiting in line are served in the order they asked. So one channel plus N worker coroutines is a worker pool with a concurrency limit of N, and no thread pool is involved. Java // Java equivalent: a fixed pool takes tasks from its queue, a CompletionService collects results Map<String, String> settleAll(List<String> ids, int workers) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(workers)) { CompletionService<Map.Entry<String, String>> receipts = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool); for (String id : ids) receipts.submit(() -> Map.entry(id, settle(id))); Map<String, String> result = new HashMap<>(); for (int i = 0; i < ids.size(); i++) { var e = receipts.take().get(); result.put(e.getKey(), e.getValue()); } return result; } } Kotlin suspend fun settleAll(ids: List<String>, workers: Int): Map<String, String> = coroutineScope { val queue = produce { ids.forEach { send(it) } } // fan-out source val receipts = Channel<Pair<String, String>>() // fan-in val pool = List(workers) { launch { for (id in queue) receipts.send(id to settle(id)) } } launch { pool.joinAll(); receipts.close() } // close once every worker is done val result = mutableMapOf<String, String>() for ((id, receipt) in receipts) result[id] = receipt result } Fan-in is the reverse: many senders, one channel, one receiver. The hard part is knowing when to close the fan-in channel. Close it too early and a worker's send throws ClosedSendChannelException. Never close it and the receiving loop waits forever. A separate coroutine that does joinAll() and then close() is the usual answer. Everything sits inside coroutineScope, so the pipeline is structured (lesson 3 of this track). If one settle throws, the scope cancels the producer, the other workers and the closer, and rethrows. No coroutine is left waiting on a channel. Why not ids.map { async { settle(it) } }.awaitAll()? Because that starts all 10,000 calls at once, and the acquirer will not thank you. The worker pool caps them at N. A Semaphore would cap them too (lesson 10 of this track), but a pool of workers also gives each worker a natural home for its own state, such as one connection per worker. And it composes into multi-stage pipelines, with a channel between each stage: parse, then enrich, then post, each stage with as many workers as it needs. Spread 20 refunds over a pool Read FanOutFanIn.kt. Twenty refunds take 50 to 150 ms each. Predict the total time with 4 workers, and how the refunds spread across them. Run it, then run it with -Pargs=1 and -Pargs=10. Run the Java twin, a fixed pool with an ExecutorCompletionService. results.close() } val perWorker = mutableMapOf<String, Int>() for (r in results) perWorker.merge(r.substringAfter("by "), 1, Int::plus) println("$workers workers: ${perWorker.toSortedMap()}") } println("20 refunds took ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l09.FanOutFanInKt -Pargs=1 labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l09/FanOutFanIn.kt FanOutFanInJava.java // Java equivalent of FanOutFanIn.kt: a fixed pool takes tasks from its queue (fan-out), and an // ExecutorCompletionService hands back results in the order they finish (fan-in). package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorCompletionService; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom; public class FanOutFanInJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int workers = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 4; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(workers)) { ExecutorCompletionService<String> results = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool); for (int i = 1; i <= 20; i++) { String id = "refund-" + i; results.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextLong(50, 150)); // the issuer call return id + " by " + Thread.currentThread().getName(); }); } Map<String, Integer> perWorker = new TreeMap<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) perWorker.merge(results.take().get().split(" by ")[1], 1, Integer::sum); System.out.println(workers + " workers: " + perWorker); } System.out.println("20 refunds took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l09.FanOutFanInJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l09/FanOutFanInJava.java With 4 workers each one handles about 5 refunds, and the run takes roughly 20 x 100 ms / 4, about 500 to 700 ms. With 1 worker it takes about 2 s. With 10 workers it takes a few hundred ms, and each worker handles about 2. The Java twin spreads the work across its four pool threads the same way. One channel feeds four workers, so at most four calls run at once; a second channel brings their results back to one place. A worker pool over a channel is a good fit for settlement and refund batches: size the pool to what the acquirer allows (say, 8 concurrent calls), and the channel keeps everything else waiting without holding a thread. Rendezvous or small buffers keep memory flat when the acquirer slows down. select with onAwait and onTimeout is the shape of a hedged authorization or a fallback acquirer: take the first answer within 800 ms, otherwise route elsewhere, and cancel what you no longer need. callbackFlow is how a legacy listener API, such as a fraud engine's event callbacks or a JMS listener, becomes a Flow with clean unregistering. For a Kafka consumer, keep offset commits in order: a fan-out pool processes records out of order, so commit only what every worker has finished, or keep one worker per partition.

h: Channels, select and pipelines · Use select to wait for whichever happens first
x: select { } suspends until the first of several clauses can complete, runs that clause, and drops the rest. The clauses are things you can wait on: deferred.onAwait, channel.onReceive, channel.onSend(value) and onTimeout(ms). The classic payments use is hedging: ask two acquirers for a quote and take whichever answers first. Java // Java equivalent: anyOf completes with the first future, completeOnTimeout adds a fallback Object first = CompletableFuture.anyOf(north, east) .completeOnTimeout(defaultQuote, 500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .join(); north.cancel(true); east.cancel(true); // marks the futures; the HTTP calls may run on Quote quote = (Quote) first; Kotlin val quote = coroutineScope { val north = async { northAcquirer.quote(req) } val east = async { eastAcquirer.quote(req) } val first = select { north.onAwait { it } east.onAwait { it } onTimeout(500) { defaultQuote } // needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) } north.cancel(); east.cancel() // stop the losers first } Three details matter. select is biased: if several clauses are ready at the same moment, the first one listed wins, so list the source you prefer first. Stopping the losers is your job, just as with anyOf, but with coroutines the cancel actually reaches the losing calls at their next suspension point instead of only marking a future as cancelled. And the API status is mixed: in 1.11 the select builder compiles without an opt-in, while the guide still calls select expressions experimental and onTimeout needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class). Without the timeout clause, this is also what the lab's fastestQuote does, generalized to a list: select { calls.forEach { c -> c.onAwait { it } } }. select over the onReceive clauses of several channels can merge streams by hand. For most merging, Flow operators such as merge and combine are simpler and harder to get wrong. Keep select for "the first of these, then stop", and for the rare loop that must react to whichever of several channels has something. Hedge a quote across two acquirers Read SelectFirst.kt. North answers in 300 ms, east in 120 ms, and the budget is 500 ms. Predict the answer and the time. Run it. Run it with -Pargs=100, a 100 ms budget. Predict first. Run the Java twin both ways. SelectFirst.kt package workbench.coroutines.l09 import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.selects.onTimeout import kotlinx.coroutines.selects.select private var t0 = 0L private fun ms() = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) // onTimeout is experimental fun main(args: Array<String>) = runBlocking { t0 = System.nanoTime() val budgetMs = args.firstOrNull()?.toLong() ?: 500 val answer = coroutineScope { val north = async { delay(300); "north: 1.80%" } val east = async { delay(120); "east: 2.10%" } val result = select { north.onAwait { it } east.onAwait { it } onTimeout(budgetMs) { "no quote within $budgetMs ms: use the default acquirer" } } north.cancel(); east.cancel() // stop the losers result } println("after ${ms()} ms: $answer") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l09.SelectFirstKt -Pargs=100 labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l09/SelectFirst.kt SelectFirstJava.java // Java equivalent of SelectFirst.kt: CompletableFuture.anyOf completes with the first future to // finish, and completeOnTimeout supplies a fallback. Cancelling the losers is up to you. package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class SelectFirstJava { static String quote(String text, long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return text; } public static void main(String[] args) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long budgetMs = args.length > 0 ? Long.parseLong(args[0]) : 500; try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { CompletableFuture<String> north = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> quote("north: 1.80%", 300), io); CompletableFuture<String> east = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> quote("east: 2.10%", 120), io); Object answer = CompletableFuture.anyOf(north, east) .completeOnTimeout("no quote within " + budgetMs + " ms: use the default acquirer", budgetMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .join(); north.cancel(true); east.cancel(true); // only marks the futures; the tasks may run on System.out.printf("after %d ms: %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, answer); io.shutdownNow(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l09.SelectFirstJava -Pargs=100 labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l09/SelectFirstJava.java With 500 ms the answer is east: 2.10% after about 120 ms (a little more on a cold JVM), and north is cancelled. h: Channels, select and pipelines · Channels inside flows: callbackFlow, channelFlow and the backpressure operators
x: A flow is sequential, so emit may only be called from the flow's own coroutine (lesson 7 of this track). When values come from somewhere else, such as a listener API or several coroutines at once, callbackFlow and channelFlow put a channel inside the flow. Producers send or trySend into it, and the collector receives from it. callbackFlow is the bridge for listener APIs that call you many times: Java // Java equivalent: Flux.create with a sink, and onDispose for the cleanup Flux<PaymentEvent> events(PaymentEventBus bus) { return Flux.create(sink -> { Registration registration = bus.register(sink::next); sink.onDispose(registration::unregister); }); } Kotlin fun PaymentEventBus.events(): Flow<PaymentEvent> = callbackFlow { val registration = register { event -> trySend(event) } // called on the bus's thread awaitClose { registration.unregister() } // runs when the collector stops } awaitClose is not optional. It suspends until the collector goes away, then runs the cleanup. Without it the block returns right after registering, and callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException to stop you leaking the listener. From the callback, use trySend: it never blocks the caller's thread, and it fails if the buffer (64 by default) is full. For a callback that fires once, suspendCancellableCoroutine from lesson 1 of this track is the right tool. channelFlow is the same idea for your own coroutines: launch several producers inside it, and each one can send safely. The other place channels hide is the backpressure operators. Take the guide's numbers: a producer that needs 100 ms per item, a collector that needs 300 ms, three items. Pipeline The collector sees Time plain 1, 2, 3 about 1,200 ms: (100 + 300) x 3 buffer() 1, 2, 3 about 1,000 ms: the producer runs ahead conflate() 1, 3 about 700 ms: a busy collector skips to the latest collectLatest { } starts 1, 2 and 3, finishes only 3 about 600 ms: a new value cancels the old work buffer keeps everything and lets the producer run ahead into a channel. conflate keeps only the latest value, which suits prices and never suits payments. collectLatest cancels and restarts the collector's block for each new value, which suits "recompute the quote whenever the input changes". It is wrong for anything with side effects you can't take back, because the cancelled run may have done half its work. All three trade memory, completeness and freshness against each other, and the plain flow is the safe default. Reactor's onBackpressureBuffer, onBackpressureLatest and switchMap (lesson 7 of the reactive track) make the same three trades. Time four backpressure choices Read FlowBackpressure.kt. Predict what each of the four lines prints, and roughly how long it takes. Run it. In the conflate() line, change the collector's delay(300) to delay(50). Predict first: does it still skip a value? Run the Java twin with the Reactor counterparts. FlowBackpressure.kt package workbench.coroutines.l09 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.buffer import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.collectLatest import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.conflate import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis /** Three FX ticks, 100 ms apart. */ fun ticks(): Flow<Int> = flow { for (i in 1..3) { delay(100); emit(i) } } fun main() = runBlocking { // the collector takes 300 ms per tick (pricing a quote book) val plain = measureTimeMillis { ticks().collect { delay(300); print("$it ") } } println(" plain: $plain ms") val buffered = measureTimeMillis { ticks().buffer().collect { delay(300); print("$it ") } } println(" buffer(): $buffered ms") val conflated = measureTimeMillis { ticks().conflate().collect { delay(300); print("$it ") } } println(" conflate(): $conflated ms") val latest = measureTimeMillis { ticks().collectLatest { print("start $it, "); delay(300); print("done $it ") } } println(" collectLatest: $latest ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l09.FlowBackpressureKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l09/FlowBackpressure.kt FlowBackpressureJava.java // Java equivalent of FlowBackpressure.kt with Reactor: concatMap with prefetch 0 (ask for the // next tick only when the last one is priced) is close to a plain flow, onBackpressureBuffer to buffer(), onBackpressureLatest to conflate(), and switchMap // to collectLatest (a new tick cancels the work on the previous one). package workbench.coroutines.l09; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.function.Function; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class FlowBackpressureJava { /** Three FX ticks, 100 ms apart, produced only when asked for (like a cold flow). */ static Flux<Integer> ticks() { return Flux.range(1, 3).concatMap(i -> Mono.just(i).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(100)), 1); } /** Pricing a quote book: 300 ms per tick. */ static Mono<Integer> price(int i) { return Mono.just(i).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(300)).doOnNext(x -> System.out.print(x + " ")); } static void time(String label, Function<Flux<Integer>, Flux<Integer>> pipeline) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); pipeline.apply(ticks()).blockLast(); System.out.printf(" %-26s %d ms%n", label, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } public static void main(String[] args) { time("concatMap, prefetch 0:", f -> f.concatMap(FlowBackpressureJava::price, 0)); time("onBackpressureBuffer:", f -> f.onBackpressureBuffer().concatMap(FlowBackpressureJava::price, 0)); time("onBackpressureLatest:", f -> f.onBackpressureLatest().concatMap(FlowBackpressureJava::price, 0)); time("switchMap:", f -> f.switchMap(FlowBackpressureJava::price)); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l09.FlowBackpressureJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l09/FlowBackpressureJava.java Plain: 1 2 3 in about 1,200 ms. buffer(): 1 2 3 in about 1,000 ms. conflate(): 1 3 in about 700 ms. collectLatest: start 1, start 2, start 3, done 3 in about 600 ms. With a 50 ms collector, conflate() prints 1 2 3: it only skips values that arrive while the collector is busy, and now it never is. The Java twin prints the same values in about the same times with concatMap, onBackpressureBuffer, onBackpressureLatest and switchMap. callbackFlow (API reference) docs conflate (API reference) docs The most common mistake is a channel that nobody closes, or a callbackFlow without awaitClose. In the first case the receiving for loop never ends, so the coroutineScope around it never returns, and the request hangs with no error and no CPU use. In the second, callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException the first time it is collected, and the fix people reach for, an awaitCancellation() or a delay(Long.MAX_VALUE), keeps the flow open but never unregisters the listener. Use produce { }, which closes its channel when the block ends; close fan-in channels after joinAll(); and end every callbackFlow with awaitClose { unregister() }.

h: Channels, select and pipelines · Java and Kotlin
x: A capped worker pool: ExecutorService vs channel and coroutines RefundRunner.java List<String> refundAll(List<String> ids) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) { // 1. 8 threads = at most 8 calls CompletionService<String> done = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(pool); for (String id : ids) done.submit(() -> issuer.refund(id)); // 2. every task queued up front List<String> receipts = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < ids.size(); i++) receipts.add(done.take().get()); // 3. fan-in, in finish order return receipts; } // a failure surfaces at get(); the other tasks keep running until close() waits for them } RefundRunner.kt suspend fun refundAll(ids: List<String>): List<String> = coroutineScope { val queue = produce { ids.forEach { send(it) } } // 2. ids handed out one at a time val receipts = Channel<String>() val pool = List(8) { launch { for (id in queue) receipts.send(issuer.refund(id)) } } // 1. 8 workers launch { pool.joinAll(); receipts.close() } val result = mutableListOf<String>() for (r in receipts) result += r // 3. fan-in, in finish order result } // a failure cancels the producer and every worker, then rethrows Both cap the issuer at 8 concurrent refunds and collect results in the order they finish. The Java version spends 8 threads, which sit blocked while the issuer thinks, and it queues every task up front. The Kotlin version spends 8 coroutines, which suspend while waiting, and the rendezvous channel hands out ids only as workers free up, so a list of a million ids never sits in a task queue. The bigger difference is failure. In Java one failed refund shows up at get(), and the other tasks keep running until close() waits for them. In Kotlin the whole pipeline is one coroutineScope, so the first failure cancels the producer and every worker before the exception reaches the caller.

h: Channels, select and pipelines · Worked example
x: A three-stage settlement pipeline An acquirer's settlement file has 200,000 lines. Each line must be parsed, enriched with a BIN lookup (a blocking legacy client, 20 ms per call), and posted to the ledger in batches of 500. Doing it in one loop takes over an hour, almost all of it in BIN lookups. suspend fun importFile(reader: LineReader) { val batch = mutableListOf<Posting>() while (true) { val line = reader.readLine() ?: break val rec = parse(line) val bin = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { binClient.lookup(rec.cardBin) } // 20 ms, one at a time batch += Posting(rec, bin) if (batch.size == 500) { ledger.post(batch.toList()); batch.clear() } } if (batch.isNotEmpty()) ledger.post(batch) } // Java equivalent of the same single loop void importFile(LineReader reader) { List<Posting> batch = new ArrayList<>(); for (String line = reader.readLine(); line != null; line = reader.readLine()) { Record rec = parse(line); BinInfo bin = binClient.lookup(rec.cardBin()); // 20 ms, one at a time batch.add(new Posting(rec, bin)); if (batch.size() == 500) { ledger.post(List.copyOf(batch)); batch.clear(); } } if (!batch.isEmpty()) ledger.post(batch); } Stage 1 reads and parses on IO, into a small buffer. produce closes the channel when the file ends. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) suspend fun importFile(reader: LineReader) = coroutineScope { // 1. parse: one reader, a little ahead of the enrichers val records = produce(Dispatchers.IO, capacity = 100) { while (true) send(parse(reader.readLine() ?: break)) } void importFile(LineReader reader) throws Exception { // 1. parse: one reader thread, a little ahead of the enrichers BlockingQueue<Record> records = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100); Thread parser = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { for (String line = reader.readLine(); line != null; line = reader.readLine()) putQuietly(records, parse(line)); putQuietly(records, Record.END); }); Stage 2 fans out to 16 enrichers, the BIN service's limit. They fan in to one channel, closed when all 16 are done. // 2. enrich: 16 workers on IO, because the BIN client blocks val postings = Channel<Posting>(capacity = 1_000) val enrichers = List(16) { launch(Dispatchers.IO) { for (rec in records) postings.send(Posting(rec, binClient.lookup(rec.cardBin))) } } launch { enrichers.joinAll(); postings.close() } // 2. enrich: 16 threads, because the BIN client blocks BlockingQueue<Posting> postings = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000); ExecutorService enrichers = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16); for (int i = 0; i < 16; i++) enrichers.submit(() -> { for (Record rec = records.take(); rec != Record.END; rec = records.take()) postings.put(new Posting(rec, binClient.lookup(rec.cardBin()))); records.put(Record.END); // pass the end marker on to the next enricher return null; }); Stage 3 is a single writer, so ledger batches stay simple. When postings is closed and drained, the loop ends, and coroutineScope returns once every stage has finished. If any stage throws, the scope cancels the others. // 3. post: one writer, batches of 500 val batch = mutableListOf<Posting>() for (p in postings) { batch += p if (batch.size == 500) { ledger.post(batch.toList()); batch.clear() } } if (batch.isNotEmpty()) ledger.post(batch) } // 3. post: one writer, batches of 500 (the end of stage 2 needs its own marker or a latch) enrichers.shutdown(); List<Posting> batch = new ArrayList<>(); while (!(enrichers.isTerminated() && postings.isEmpty())) { Posting p = postings.poll(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); if (p == null) continue; batch.add(p); if (batch.size() == 500) { ledger.post(List.copyOf(batch)); batch.clear(); } } if (!batch.isEmpty()) ledger.post(batch); parser.join(); } Self-check: the ledger slows to a crawl. Trace what happens to memory and to the BIN service. (The writer falls behind, postings fills up to 1,000, the enrichers suspend in send, records fills up to 100, and the parser suspends too. Memory stays flat, and the BIN service sees fewer calls. Backpressure flows all the way back to the file read.)

h: Channels, select and pipelines · Quiz
x: val ch = Channel<String>(). A coroutine runs ch.send("batch-1"); println("sent"), and nothing ever receives from ch. What happens? sent prints at once, because send puts the element in a buffer send suspends forever, so sent never prints send throws IllegalStateException because nobody is receiving The element is dropped and sent prints The default capacity is rendezvous: send waits until a receiver takes the element. With no receiver it waits forever, and the coroutine never finishes. A buffered channel would accept it at once. Four workers each run for (id in ids) settle(id) on the same channel. The producer sends 40 ids and closes it. Which statement is true? Each id is settled exactly once, and at most 4 settle calls run at the same time Each id is settled four times, once per worker All 40 go to the first worker, because it started first The workers deadlock, because they compete for the same channel A channel is a queue: each element goes to one receiver, and fair receiving spreads the ids across the waiting workers. Four workers means at most four calls in flight. That is fan-out. What happens when this flow is collected? callbackFlow { bus.register { trySend(it) } } Events flow normally until the collector cancels Nothing is ever emitted, but the collector waits forever callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException, because the block returned without awaitClose The listener is unregistered automatically when the block returns callbackFlow requires the block to suspend in awaitClose { } until the collector stops. If the block returns while the channel is still open, it throws IllegalStateException, and the listener it registered is never unregistered. A pricing service recomputes a merchant's FX quote every time the amount in the checkout changes. A recompute takes 300 ms, and amounts change every 100 ms while the customer types. Only the latest quote matters, and a stale computation should stop. Which operator fits? buffer() conflate() Channel.UNLIMITED between input and pricing collectLatest { } collectLatest cancels the computation in progress when a new amount arrives, so only the latest is computed to the end. conflate skips values that arrive while busy but still finishes every computation it starts. buffer and an unlimited channel compute every stale amount. From the reactive track: which Kotlin Flow operator behaves most like Reactor's onBackpressureLatest()? buffer() conflate() collectLatest { } flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) Both keep only the newest value while the consumer is busy and hand it over when the consumer is ready. collectLatest is closer to switchMap, because it cancels the work in progress. buffer is onBackpressureBuffer.

h: Channels, select and pipelines · Explain it back
x: A teammate wants to settle 50,000 batches with batchIds.map { async { settle(it) } }.awaitAll(), and the acquirer allows 8 concurrent calls. Explain the problem and how a channel-based worker pool fixes it.

h: Channels, select and pipelines · Key terms
x: Channel A queue between coroutines: each element is received once, and send and receive suspend instead of blocking. Rendezvous A channel with no buffer: the sender waits until a receiver takes the element. Fan-out Several receivers on one channel, so each element is handled by exactly one of them. Fan-in Several senders into one channel, read by one receiver. produce A builder that starts a coroutine sending into a new channel and closes it when the block ends. select Waits for whichever of several clauses can complete first, and runs only that one. callbackFlow A flow builder with a channel inside, for turning listener callbacks into a Flow. What is the default capacity of Channel<T>(), and what does it mean for send? RENDEZVOUS (0): send suspends until a receiver takes the element. What does a Channel.CONFLATED channel do with a new element when one is already waiting? It replaces the waiting one. send never suspends, and a slow receiver gets only the newest. Several coroutines receive from one channel. How many of them get each element? Exactly one. That is fan-out, and it caps concurrency at the number of receivers. When does for (x in channel) stop? When the channel has been closed and every element in it has been received. Why must a callbackFlow block end with awaitClose { ... }? It keeps the flow open until the collector stops, then runs the cleanup. Without it, callbackFlow throws IllegalStateException and the listener leaks. Two select clauses are ready at the same moment. Which one wins? The one listed first: select is biased toward the first clause. conflate() vs collectLatest { } for a slow collector? conflate skips values that arrived while busy but finishes each one it starts. collectLatest cancels the block in progress when a new value arrives.

h: Channels, select and pipelines · Go deeper
x: actor { }, which older tutorials use to protect shared state with a channel of messages, is marked @ObsoleteCoroutinesApi: the KDoc says it will become obsolete when "complex actors" arrive. A plain coroutine looping over a channel you create does the same job without the warning. BroadcastChannel was deprecated in 1.7, and its deprecation level was raised in 1.9. Use SharedFlow (lesson 8 of this track) for one-to-many. The BUFFERED default of 64 comes from the JVM system property kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer. It is also the buffer flowOn, buffer(), channelFlow and callbackFlow use unless you pass a size. When you size a pipeline for memory, count those hidden buffers too. Channels also have trySend and tryReceive, which never suspend and return a ChannelResult. They are for code at the edge that can't suspend, like a listener callback, and trySendBlocking is the blocking variant for a plain thread that may wait. Since kotlinx.coroutines 1.11, ReceiveChannel.consumeTo(collection) drains a channel into a collection. The prime-sieve pipeline in the official channels guide is a fun read: each prime gets its own filtering coroutine, chained by channels, so the pipeline grows as it runs. It is a good picture of how cheap coroutines and channels are, and a poor model for production code, where a fixed number of stages with a known number of workers is far easier to monitor and to cancel.

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Coroutines on Default race like threads, and the same tools fix them
x: Coroutines on Dispatchers.Default run on several threads at once, so shared mutable state needs the same care as in the threads track. counter++ from 100 coroutines loses updates. @Volatile doesn't help, and the coroutines guide says so in as many words: "volatiles are of no help". A volatile write is atomic and visible, but read, add and write are still three steps. Pick the tool by the shape of the update. One value, changed in one atomic step: an atomic. AtomicLong.incrementAndGet(), AtomicReference.updateAndGet, or MutableStateFlow.update { } from lesson 8 of this track. They never suspend and never block. Kotlin 2.1.20 also added common atomics such as AtomicInt in kotlin.concurrent.atomics, as an experimental API; on the JVM the java.util.concurrent.atomic classes do the same job. Several steps that must happen together: a Mutex. State that one coroutine owns: confinement. Keep the map inside one coroutine and send it requests through a channel (lesson 9 of this track). Mutex is the coroutine lock: Java // Java equivalent: a ReentrantLock around the same read-modify-write private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); void credit(String account, long cents) { lock.lock(); try { balances.put(account, balances.getOrDefault(account, 0L) + cents); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } Kotlin private val mutex = Mutex() suspend fun credit(account: String, cents: Long) = mutex.withLock { balances[account] = (balances[account] ?: 0L) + cents } withLock takes the lock, runs the block in a try, and releases the lock in finally, the same idiom as Java's. The difference is what waiting costs. Mutex.lock() suspends the coroutine, so a credit waiting for the lock holds no thread. The KDoc gives the Mutex the memory semantics of a synchronized block, and makes it fair: waiters get the lock in the order they asked. Two warnings come with it. A Mutex is not reentrant. Its KDoc gives it two states, locked and unlocked, and unless you pass an owner token for debugging it keeps no record of who holds it, so a second lock can't tell its own holder from anyone else. (ReentrantLock records the owning thread, which would not work here: a coroutine may resume on another thread.) A coroutine that holds it and calls withLock again suspends forever, waiting for itself, so a transfer that calls credit while holding the lock deadlocks. Take the lock once, at the top. And the guide's measurements show that fine-grained locking, a lock or a dispatcher switch around every tiny increment, is slow. Lock around a meaningful unit of work, or use an atomic for a single number. Count a million payments five ways Read SharedCounter.kt. 100 coroutines on Default each count 10,000 payments. Predict which counters reach 1,000,000, and which is slowest. Run it twice. Run the Java twin, which uses 8 threads and a ReentrantLock. SharedCounter.kt package workbench.coroutines.l10 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withLock import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis private var plain = 0L @Volatile private var volatileCount = 0L /** 100 coroutines on Dispatchers.Default each count 10,000 captured payments. */ suspend fun count(label: String, increment: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit, read: () -> Long) { val ms = measureTimeMillis { coroutineScope { repeat(100) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { repeat(10_000) { increment() } } } } } println("%-28s %,9d of 1,000,000 in %4d ms".format(label, read(), ms)) } fun main() = runBlocking { count("plain var", { plain++ }, { plain }) count("@Volatile var", { volatileCount++ }, { volatileCount }) val atomic = AtomicLong() count("AtomicLong", { atomic.incrementAndGet() }, { atomic.get() }) val mutex = Mutex() var guarded = 0L count("Mutex.withLock", { mutex.withLock { guarded++ } }, { guarded }) val confined = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) var onOneThread = 0L count("withContext(limited(1))", { withContext(confined) { onOneThread++ } }, { onOneThread }) } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l10.SharedCounterKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l10/SharedCounter.kt SharedCounterJava.java // Java equivalent of SharedCounter.kt: the same counter on 8 platform threads. Coroutines on // Dispatchers.Default run in parallel, so they race exactly like threads do. package workbench.coroutines.l10; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; import java.util.function.LongSupplier; public class SharedCounterJava { static long plain = 0; static volatile long volatileCount = 0; static long guarded = 0; static void count(String label, Runnable increment, LongSupplier read) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8)) { for (int t = 0; t < 100; t++) pool.submit(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) increment.run(); }); } System.out.printf("%-28s %,9d of 1,000,000 in %4d ms%n", label, read.getAsLong(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } public static void main(String[] args) { count("plain field", () -> plain++, () -> plain); count("volatile field", () -> volatileCount++, () -> volatileCount); AtomicLong atomic = new AtomicLong(); count("AtomicLong", atomic::incrementAndGet, atomic::get); ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); count("ReentrantLock", () -> { lock.lock(); try { guarded++; } finally { lock.unlock(); } }, () -> guarded); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l10.SharedCounterJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l10/SharedCounterJava.java The plain and @Volatile counters come out short, by a different amount each run. AtomicLong, Mutex.withLock and the one-thread view all reach exactly 1,000,000. AtomicLong is fastest by far; the Mutex and the withContext switch for every increment take about a second, because each increment pays for a lock or a dispatch. The Java twin shows the same split, with ReentrantLock much cheaper than a Mutex here because these threads never suspend. Shared mutable state and concurrency (Kotlin docs) read Mutex (API reference) docs Shared state is the cash drawer at a shop. An atomic is a till that adds a sale in one press of a key. A Mutex is the key to the drawer: whoever holds it counts, takes and writes down, and the others wait their turn, without standing around blocking the aisle (they suspend). A one-thread view is a rule that only one cashier stands at the till at a time. That rule doesn't stop a cashier from walking off to phone the bank in the middle of counting, letting the next cashier count the same drawer. runTest is a rehearsal with a stage clock that jumps straight to the next cue, so a day of trading takes seconds. The analogy breaks on reentry: a shopkeeper holding the drawer key can open the drawer twice. A coroutine holding a Mutex that asks for it again waits for itself forever.

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · A one-thread view is not a mutex
x: A view such as Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) runs at most one of its coroutines at a time. That looks like a lock, and the KDoc has a heading of its own to say it isn't one: "limitedParallelism(1) is not a mutex!" The view guarantees that code between suspension points runs one coroutine at a time, with a happens-before edge from each to the next, so counter++ on it is safe. But the moment a coroutine suspends, the view's thread is free and the next coroutine runs. Any sequence that suspends in the middle is open to interleaving: Java // Java equivalent: one thread, but an async step in the middle CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> balances.getOrDefault(account, 0L), oneThread) .thenCombine(fx.toEurCentsAsync(amount, currency), Long::sum) // another credit runs meanwhile .thenAcceptAsync(after -> balances.put(account, after), oneThread); // writes over the other credit Kotlin withContext(oneAtATime) { val before = balances[account] ?: 0L val cents = fx.toEurCents(amount, currency) // suspends: another credit runs here balances[account] = before + cents // writes over the other credit } Play it out in the simulator: two credits, one thread, and a suspension in the middle of each. (The simulator lets you switch after any line. On the real view a switch can only happen at the suspending line, and that is enough to lose a credit.) There are two fixes. Move the suspension out of the critical part: convert first, then do the read and the write with nothing that suspends between them. On a one-thread view that is now safe, because nothing else can run in the middle. Or hold a Mutex across the whole sequence, which keeps other credits out even while the holder is suspended. The first is faster, because the conversions overlap. Use the second when the suspending call really must sit inside, for example a ledger check whose answer must not go stale before you write. The general rule is the one you learned for threads. A critical section is safe only if nothing else can run in the middle of it. For coroutines, "in the middle" means any suspension point, including the ones hidden inside functions you call. Interleave three credits, then lock them Read NotAMutex.kt. Predict the order of the read and write lines for the one-thread view, then for the Mutex. Run it. Look at the last part: why does the nested withLock time out instead of returning inner? Run the Java twin, where a single-thread executor interleaves the same way and ReentrantLock happily locks twice. NotAMutex.kt package workbench.coroutines.l10 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.joinAll import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withLock import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull fun main() = runBlocking { val oneAtATime = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) println("limitedParallelism(1):") List(3) { i -> launch(oneAtATime) { println(" credit $i: read balance") delay(20) // the FX call suspends: the single thread is free for someone else println(" credit $i: write balance") } }.joinAll() println("Mutex.withLock:") val mutex = Mutex() List(3) { i -> launch(Dispatchers.Default) { mutex.withLock { println(" credit $i: read balance") delay(20) // still suspends, but nobody else can enter the lock println(" credit $i: write balance") } } }.joinAll() println("Mutex is not reentrant:") val nested = withTimeoutOrNull(500) { mutex.withLock { withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { mutex.withLock { "inner" } } // the same coroutine tree locks again } } println(" nested withLock -> ${nested ?: "timed out after 500 ms: it waits for itself"}") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l10.NotAMutexKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l10/NotAMutex.kt NotAMutexJava.java // Java equivalent of NotAMutex.kt: a single-thread executor runs one task at a time, but an // async step (a CompletableFuture chain) lets the next task start before the first one has // written. A ReentrantLock held across the whole read-call-write keeps them apart, and unlike // Kotlin's Mutex it IS reentrant. package workbench.coroutines.l10; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; import java.util.stream.IntStream; public class NotAMutexJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ExecutorService oneThread = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(); System.out.println("single-thread executor:"); List<CompletableFuture<Void>> credits = IntStream.range(0, 3).mapToObj(i -> CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> System.out.println(" credit " + i + ": read balance"), oneThread) // the FX call is async: the thread is free while it waits .thenCompose(v -> CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> { }, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(20, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS))) .thenRunAsync(() -> System.out.println(" credit " + i + ": write balance"), oneThread) ).toList(); CompletableFuture.allOf(credits.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join(); oneThread.shutdown(); System.out.println("ReentrantLock around the whole credit:"); ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3)) { for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { int n = i; pool.submit(() -> { lock.lock(); try { System.out.println(" credit " + n + ": read balance"); Thread.sleep(20); // a blocking FX call, inside the lock System.out.println(" credit " + n + ": write balance"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } }); } } System.out.println("ReentrantLock is reentrant:"); lock.lock(); try { lock.lock(); // the same thread takes it again try { System.out.println(" nested lock -> inner (hold count " + lock.getHoldCount() + ")"); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } finally { lock.unlock(); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l10.NotAMutexJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l10/NotAMutexJava.java On the one-thread view, all three read balance lines print before any write balance: each credit suspended in the middle and let the next one in. With the Mutex, each credit reads and writes before the next one starts. The nested withLock times out after 500 ms, because a Mutex is not reentrant: the inner lock waits for the outer one, which waits for the inner one. The Java twin interleaves the same way on one thread, and its ReentrantLock reports a hold count of 2. limitedParallelism (API reference: "not a mutex") docs Most payment state lives in Oracle, where row locks and unique keys do this job, but services keep some state in memory: per-merchant rate-limit counters, a cache of FX rates, the in-flight totals of a settlement run. Counters belong in atomics. A compound update, such as checking a merchant's daily limit and then reserving the amount, needs a Mutex held across the check and the reservation, with any suspending call (the FX conversion, the fraud score) done before the lock if you can. Don't reach for limitedParallelism(1) as a lock: it serializes code only between suspension points. For tests, inject dispatchers everywhere (Quarkus beans can take a CoroutineDispatcher from a producer method), so a test passes StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) and a retry policy with a 30-second cap tests in milliseconds.

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Virtual time: runTest skips the delays
x: Testing coroutine code in real time is slow and flaky. A retry with waits of 100, 200 and 400 ms costs 700 ms per test, and a loaded CI machine turns 700 into 1,500 and your timing assertion into a coin toss. runTest from kotlinx-coroutines-test replaces the clock. Every delay in the test's coroutines is skipped, and a virtual clock jumps forward instead, keeping the order the delays would have produced. Java // Java equivalent: Reactor's StepVerifier with virtual time (reactor-test) @Test void waitsBetweenAttempts() { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> issuer.authorize(req) .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(2, Duration.ofMillis(100)).jitter(0))) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(300)) .expectNext(Decision.APPROVED) .verifyComplete(); } Kotlin @Test fun `waits 100 then 200 ms between attempts`() = runTest { val attempts = mutableListOf<Long>() retryWithBackoff(times = 3, initialDelay = 100.milliseconds, maxDelay = 1.seconds) { attempts += currentTime // virtual milliseconds if (attempts.size < 3) throw IOException("issuer 503") else "ok" } assertThat(attempts).containsExactly(0L, 100L, 300L) // in a few real milliseconds } runTest runs the body in a TestScope on a single-threaded test dispatcher, and currentTime reads the virtual clock. You can also drive the clock by hand: advanceTimeBy(ms) runs everything due before that point, runCurrent() runs what is due now, and advanceUntilIdle() runs everything queued. At the end, runTest waits for every child coroutine, so a test can't pass with work still pending. Three rules keep the clock honest. Only the test dispatcher's delays are virtual. Code that switches to Dispatchers.IO or Dispatchers.Default runs its delays in real time, and the test clock never sees them. That is why lesson 4 of this track injected the dispatchers: tests pass StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler), production passes the real ones. withTimeout inside runTest uses virtual time too. Combine it with real work on another dispatcher, and the scheduler, finding nothing of its own to do, can jump the clock forward and fire the timeout while the real work is still running. The lab tests in lesson 5 of this track use runBlocking for their blocking lookup for exactly that reason. The runTest timeout is wall-clock time: 60 seconds by default since kotlinx.coroutines 1.8 (it was 10 s in 1.7). Change it with runTest(timeout = 10.seconds) or the kotlinx.coroutines.test.default_timeout system property. In 1.11 the old dispatchTimeoutMs overloads are errors. Run five seconds of work in a blink Read VirtualTime.kt. It calls runTest from a plain main. Predict the virtual time of each log line, and how much real time the first runTest takes. Run it. Look at the last line: why did the clock stay at 0 while a real second went by? VirtualTime.kt package workbench.coroutines.l10 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.TestScope import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() { val realStart = System.nanoTime() fun real() = (System.nanoTime() - realStart) / 1_000_000 // runTest is meant for tests, but a plain main can call it too runTest { fun TestScope.log(what: String) = println("virtual %5d ms (real %4d ms) %s".format(currentTime, real(), what)) launch { delay(1_000); log("settlement file fetched") delay(200); log("file parsed") delay(2_000); log("ledger posted") } val fx = async { delay(3_000); log("FX rates fetched") delay(500); log("rates cached") } fx.await() log("await returned") } println("whole runTest took %d ms of real time".format(real())) runTest { val before = real() withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { delay(1_000) } // escapes the test scheduler println("withContext(Default) { delay(1_000) }: virtual $currentTime ms, real ${real() - before} ms") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l10.VirtualTimeKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l10/VirtualTime.kt The lines print at virtual 1,000, 1,200, 3,000, 3,200 and 3,500 ms, in that order, and await returned at 3,500. The real time stays well under a second, and most of it is the test library starting up. The last runTest reports virtual 0 ms and about 1,000 real ms: withContext(Dispatchers.Default) left the test scheduler, so its delay was a real one. runTest (API reference) docs

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Standard or Unconfined, and backgroundScope for work that never ends
x: runTest uses a StandardTestDispatcher by default. With it, launch only queues the new coroutine, and nothing runs until the test body suspends or advances the scheduler. Tests stay predictable, because you decide when each child runs. Production dispatchers don't run a child immediately either, so this is also the more honest default. UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler) enters a new coroutine at once and runs it to its first suspension, like Dispatchers.Unconfined. That is handy for a collector that must be subscribed before the next line emits, such as a test of a SharedFlow with no replay: Java // Java equivalent: StepVerifier subscribes first, then runs the action that emits StepVerifier.create(tracker.transitions()) .then(() -> tracker.moveTo(PaymentStatus.CAPTURED)) .expectNextMatches(t -> t.to() == PaymentStatus.CAPTURED) .thenCancel() .verify(); Kotlin backgroundScope.launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { tracker.transitions.collect { seen += it } // subscribed before the next line runs } tracker.moveTo(PaymentStatus.CAPTURED) If you mix dispatchers, give them all the same testScheduler. Two schedulers mean two clocks, and one of them will not move. backgroundScope is for coroutines that never finish on their own: a poller, a collector of a StateFlow, the sharing scope of a stateIn. runTest waits for every child before it returns, so an endless child in the test scope itself would hang until the 60-second timeout. Coroutines in backgroundScope are cancelled when the test body ends instead. Two details matter. advanceUntilIdle() stops once only background work is left (otherwise a poller would keep it busy forever), so drive background work with advanceTimeBy. And a failure in backgroundScope doesn't stop the test at once, but it is reported when the test ends, so the test still fails. This lesson's lab is written the way these rules suggest. The retry tests read currentTime to check each wait exactly, and the balance tests count how many conversions overlap instead of timing them. On the stub, one of those tests reports 0 virtual milliseconds: the stub's conversions ran on a real Default thread, outside the virtual clock. For flows there is also Turbine (app.cash.turbine, not on this lab's classpath), which adds flow.test { awaitItem() }. Its waits use a 3-second wall-clock timeout, not the virtual clock. Watch the two test dispatchers and a background poller Read TestDispatchers.kt. Predict the order in each of the two lists, and the poll count after each line. Run it. Move the poller from backgroundScope.launch to a plain launch, and add runTest(timeout = 3.seconds) (import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds). Predict, then run. TestDispatchers.kt package workbench.coroutines.l10 import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.UnconfinedTestDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceTimeBy import kotlinx.coroutines.test.advanceUntilIdle import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runCurrent import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() = runTest { // 1. runTest's default, StandardTestDispatcher: launch only queues the child val standard = mutableListOf<String>() launch { standard += "child ran" } standard += "after launch" runCurrent() // run what is due now println("StandardTestDispatcher: $standard") // 2. UnconfinedTestDispatcher: the child starts at once, up to its first suspension val unconfined = mutableListOf<String>() launch(UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) { unconfined += "child ran" } unconfined += "after launch" println("UnconfinedTestDispatcher: $unconfined") // 3. backgroundScope: for work that never ends, such as a rate poller var polls = 0 backgroundScope.launch { while (true) { delay(1_000); polls++ } } advanceTimeBy(5_500) println("polls after advanceTimeBy(5_500): $polls") advanceUntilIdle() println("polls after advanceUntilIdle(): $polls (background work doesn't keep it busy)") // when the test body ends, runTest cancels everything in backgroundScope } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l10.TestDispatchersKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l10/TestDispatchers.kt StandardTestDispatcher: [after launch, child ran] and UnconfinedTestDispatcher: [child ran, after launch]. The poller has run 5 times after advanceTimeBy(5_500), and still 5 after advanceUntilIdle(), which ignores background work. After your change, advanceUntilIdle() treats the poller as foreground work and runs it again and again, millions of virtual seconds' worth, until the 3-second wall-clock timeout stops everything with UncompletedCoroutinesError (an AssertionError): the test body did not run to completion. The most common mistake is protecting a sequence that suspends in the middle with something that only works between suspensions: a limitedParallelism(1) view, a single-threaded dispatcher, or synchronized around code that was refactored into a suspend function. It passes code review because it reads like a lock, and it passes tests that never make two coroutines overlap. Under load, two credits read the same balance, both suspend in the FX call, and one overwrites the other. The fix is to look for every suspension point inside the critical section. Move it out (compute first, then read and write with nothing in between), or hold a Mutex across the whole sequence and keep that sequence short.

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Java and Kotlin
x: A merchant limit check: ReentrantLock vs Mutex DailyLimits.java class DailyLimits { private final Map<String, Long> spent = new HashMap<>(); private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); boolean reserve(String merchant, long cents, long limit) { long risk = fraud.score(merchant, cents); // 1. the slow call, outside the lock (blocks a thread) lock.lock(); // 2. blocks the thread while waiting try { long already = spent.getOrDefault(merchant, 0L); if (risk > 80 || already + cents > limit) return false; spent.put(merchant, already + cents); // 3. check and reserve together return true; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } } DailyLimits.kt class DailyLimits { private val spent = HashMap<String, Long>() private val mutex = Mutex() suspend fun reserve(merchant: String, cents: Long, limit: Long): Boolean { val risk = fraud.score(merchant, cents) // 1. the slow call, outside the lock (suspends) return mutex.withLock { // 2. suspends while waiting, holds no thread val already = spent[merchant] ?: 0L if (risk > 80 || already + cents > limit) return@withLock false spent[merchant] = already + cents // 3. check and reserve together true } } } The shape is identical: do the slow call first, then check and reserve under one lock. Two things differ. Waiting for a ReentrantLock blocks a thread, while waiting for a Mutex suspends a coroutine, so a burst of 5,000 reservations doesn't need 5,000 threads. And the Java lock is reentrant while the Mutex isn't, so a helper that takes the Mutex again from inside withLock hangs instead of nesting. The Kotlin version has one extra trap that Java can't have: if someone later moves fraud.score inside withLock, it still works but holds the lock across a network call, and if they replace the Mutex with a one-thread dispatcher, it stops being correct at all.

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Worked example
x: Test a retry policy without waiting for it A capture client retries the issuer on IOException: up to 5 attempts, waits starting at 200 ms, doubling, capped at 2 s. The existing test uses real time and Thread.sleep. It takes 3 seconds, and it fails on CI about once a week. @Test fun `retries on 503`() = runBlocking { var calls = 0 val started = System.currentTimeMillis() val result = client.captureWithRetry(cmd) { calls++; if (calls < 4) throw IOException("503") else "ok" } assertThat(result).isEqualTo("ok") assertThat(System.currentTimeMillis() - started).isBetween(1_350L, 1_600L) // 200 + 400 + 800 = 1,400 } // Java equivalent of the flaky test: real sleeps, a timing window @Test void retriesOn503() { AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); long started = System.currentTimeMillis(); String result = client.captureWithRetry(cmd, () -> { if (calls.incrementAndGet() < 4) throw new UncheckedIOException(new IOException("503")); return "ok"; }); assertThat(result).isEqualTo("ok"); assertThat(System.currentTimeMillis() - started).isBetween(1_350L, 1_600L); } Move to runTest. The waits are delay calls on the test dispatcher, so they become virtual, and the test can check each attempt's exact virtual time instead of a window. @Test fun `waits 200, 400, then 800 ms between attempts`() = runTest { val at = mutableListOf<Long>() val result = client.captureWithRetry(cmd) { at += currentTime // 1. record virtual ms per attempt if (at.size < 4) throw IOException("503") else "ok" } assertThat(result).isEqualTo("ok") assertThat(at).containsExactly(0L, 200L, 600L, 1_400L) // 2. exact, and instant } // Java equivalent: Reactor's virtual time, if the client is built on Reactor @Test void waitsBetweenAttempts() { StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> client.captureWithRetry(cmd)) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(1_400)) // 1. advance the virtual clock .expectNext("ok") // 2. exact, and instant .verifyComplete(); } The test went back to real time when someone added withContext(Dispatchers.IO) around the HTTP call inside the client: its delay calls now ran on IO. Inject the dispatcher, and give the test the test scheduler's one. class CaptureClient(private val io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO) { suspend fun <T> captureWithRetry(cmd: Capture, call: suspend () -> T): T = withContext(io) { retryWithBackoff(times = 5, initialDelay = 200.milliseconds, maxDelay = 2.seconds) { call() } } } // 3. in the test val client = CaptureClient(io = StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)) // Java equivalent: inject the Scheduler, and give the test a virtual one class CaptureClient { private final Scheduler io; CaptureClient(Scheduler io) { this.io = io; } <T> Mono<T> captureWithRetry(Capture cmd, Mono<T> call) { return call.subscribeOn(io) .retryWhen(Retry.backoff(4, Duration.ofMillis(200)).maxBackoff(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).jitter(0).scheduler(io)); } } // 3. in the test VirtualTimeScheduler vts = VirtualTimeScheduler.getOrSet(); CaptureClient client = new CaptureClient(vts); Add the case people forget: cancellation during a wait must stop the retries. Virtual time lets you stop exactly between two attempts. @Test fun `a cancel during the backoff stops the retries`() = runTest { var calls = 0 val job = launch { client.captureWithRetry(cmd) { calls++; throw IOException("503") } } advanceTimeBy(300) // 4. attempts at 0 and 200 ms; now waiting until 600 ms job.cancel() advanceUntilIdle() assertThat(calls).isEqualTo(2) } @Test void cancelDuringBackoffStopsRetries() { AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> client.captureWithRetry(cmd, Mono.<String>fromCallable(() -> { calls.incrementAndGet(); throw new IOException("503"); }))) .expectSubscription() .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // 4. attempts at 0 and 200 ms .thenCancel() .verify(); assertThat(calls.get()).isEqualTo(2); } Self-check: suppose the helper wrapped both the attempt and the delay in one runCatching and retried on any failure. What would the cancel test report? (calls would be 5, not 2. After the cancel, each delay throws at once, runCatching swallows it as a failed attempt, and the loop races through the remaining attempts. The test catches it because it counts calls instead of timing them. Lesson 5 of this track showed the same trap.)

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Quiz
x: A merchant limit check runs mutex.withLock { if (spent + amount <= limit) { reserve(amount) } }, and reserve itself calls mutex.withLock { spent += amount }. What happens on the first reservation? It works: a coroutine may take a lock it already holds It throws IllegalStateException: the mutex is already locked It hangs: the inner withLock waits for the outer one, which never finishes The inner withLock is skipped, so spent never changes Mutex is not reentrant. The inner withLock suspends until the lock is free, but the lock is held by the same code waiting on it, so it never is. Take the lock once at the top and have reserve assume it is held. Which tool fits a per-merchant counter of approved payments, incremented by many coroutines on Default, where each update is just "add one"? A ConcurrentHashMap<String, AtomicLong> and incrementAndGet() A Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1) view around the whole handler A Mutex held across the handler's network calls @Volatile on the map field Each update is one atomic step on one value, so an atomic is the cheapest correct tool: it never suspends or blocks. A Mutex held across network calls serializes everything, and @Volatile on the field only covers the reference to the map, not the increments. Inside runTest, the code under test calls withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { delay(2_000) }. What does the test see? currentTime jumps by 2,000 and the test finishes at once The test fails at once, because Dispatchers.IO is forbidden in runTest currentTime jumps by 2,000, but only after advanceUntilIdle() The test waits about 2 real seconds, and currentTime doesn't move Only delays on the test dispatcher are virtual. withContext(Dispatchers.IO) leaves the test scheduler, so that delay is a real one, invisible to the virtual clock. Inject the dispatcher so the test can pass StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler). A test launches launch { while (true) { delay(1_000); poll() } } in the runTest body, checks the poll count after advanceTimeBy(3_500), and ends. What happens? The test passes; the loop is cancelled when the body ends The test hangs until the runTest timeout, because runTest waits for every child The loop never runs, because launch only queues it advanceTimeBy throws, because the loop never ends runTest waits for all children of the test scope before it returns, and this one never ends, so the test fails after the wall-clock timeout (60 s by default). Launch endless work in backgroundScope, which runTest cancels when the body ends. From lesson 5 of this track: a retry helper wraps each attempt in runCatching { block() } and retries on any failure. The caller is cancelled while an attempt is suspended in an HTTP call. What happens? The CancellationException counts as a failed attempt, and the helper goes on to the next one The retries stop at once, because runCatching never catches CancellationException The coroutine is killed and no finally blocks run The helper waits for the HTTP call to finish, then stops runCatching catches every Throwable, including CancellationException, so the cancel is logged and handled as a failed attempt. If the backoff delay sits outside the runCatching, it throws at once and ends the loop more or less by luck; if it sits inside, the loop races through every remaining attempt. Rethrow CancellationException before treating anything as retryable.
