h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Key terms
x: Mutex A coroutine lock: waiting suspends instead of blocking. Fair, and not reentrant. Critical section Code that must run without anything else touching the same state in the middle of it. Confinement Keeping mutable state reachable from only one coroutine or thread, so it needs no lock. Virtual time The test scheduler's clock. Delays advance it instantly instead of waiting. TestScope The scope runTest runs the test body in, with currentTime and a test dispatcher. StandardTestDispatcher A test dispatcher that queues tasks until the test lets the scheduler run. backgroundScope A scope inside runTest for endless work; it is cancelled when the test body ends. Does @Volatile make count++ safe across coroutines on Dispatchers.Default? No. It makes each read and write visible, but count++ is still read, add, write. Use an atomic or a Mutex. What does Mutex.withLock do while another coroutine holds the lock? It suspends the caller (no thread is blocked) until the lock is free, and the Mutex hands out the lock in arrival order. A coroutine holding a Mutex calls withLock on it again. What happens? It suspends forever: Mutex is not reentrant. Why is limitedParallelism(1) not a mutex? It runs one coroutine at a time only between suspension points. When one suspends, another runs, so a sequence with a suspension in the middle can interleave. What happens to delay(1_000) inside runTest? It is skipped: the virtual clock (currentTime) jumps forward by 1,000 ms, keeping the order of events. StandardTestDispatcher vs UnconfinedTestDispatcher for launch? Standard queues the new coroutine until the test yields or advances time. Unconfined starts it at once and runs it to its first suspension. Where do never-ending coroutines go in a runTest test? backgroundScope: they are cancelled when the test body ends, and advanceUntilIdle() doesn't wait for them.

h: Shared state and testing coroutines · Go deeper
x: Semaphore(permits) in kotlinx.coroutines.sync is the counting version of a Mutex: withPermit { } lets at most n coroutines in at once. It is the coroutine counterpart of the shared Semaphore from lesson 3 of the virtual threads track, and like the Mutex it suspends rather than blocks. Since 1.9 you can no longer cast a Mutex to a Semaphore; they are separate types. Mutex has an optional owner: lock(owner) and withLock(owner) record who holds it, and holdsLock(owner) checks it. Passing an owner turns a reentrant call into an immediate IllegalStateException instead of a silent hang, which is a cheap safety net in code where a helper might be called with the lock held. The test library has more knobs than this lesson uses. Several StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler, name = ...) instances can share one scheduler, so production code that takes two dispatchers (IO and CPU) can get two named test dispatchers with one clock. Dispatchers.setMain(...) and resetMain() swap the Main dispatcher for UI-style code. And runTest reports uncaught exceptions from coroutines it doesn't own at the end of the test, through a ServiceLoader hook, which is why a forgotten GlobalScope.launch that throws can fail an unrelated test. Finally, virtual time is not a load test. It proves that the order and the timing logic are right. It says nothing about how long the real FX service takes, how a real Mutex behaves with 5,000 waiters, or whether Oracle keeps up. Keep a few real-time integration tests, with generous margins, for that.

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Bridge CompletableFuture both ways with future { } and await()
x: Most of your Java code speaks CompletableFuture, and kotlinx.coroutines bridges it in both directions with nothing extra on the classpath. The old kotlinx-coroutines-jdk8 artifact was merged into the core library in 1.7. From a future to a suspend call, use await(): Java // Java equivalent: block a thread on the future, or chain on it int score = legacyFraudClient.score(req).join(); // blocks the caller CompletableFuture<Decision> d = legacyFraudClient.score(req).thenApply(this::decide); // or composes Kotlin suspend fun fraudScore(req: AuthRequest): Int = legacyFraudClient.score(req).await() // suspends until the future completes; no thread waits await() suspends without holding a thread. It rethrows the future's exception unwrapped, so you catch the IOException itself rather than an ExecutionException, and it has a fast path for a future that is already done. It also carries cancellation: if the awaiting coroutine is cancelled, it calls future.cancel(false). That is usually right, because nobody wants the answer any more. When the future is shared, or must finish anyway (a capture that has already gone to the issuer), use future.asDeferred().await(), which waits without cancelling it. From a suspend call to a future, use future { }: Java // Java equivalent: the Java caller's side, which is plain CompletableFuture code CompletableFuture<String> reply = facade.authorizeAsync(req) .orTimeout(800, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .thenApply(decision -> "pay-1: " + decision); Kotlin class AuthorizationFacade(private val service: AuthorizationService) : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) fun authorizeAsync(req: AuthRequest): CompletableFuture<Decision> = scope.future { service.authorize(req) } override fun close() = scope.cancel() } future { } is a builder like async: it starts a coroutine in the scope and hands its result back as a CompletableFuture. The link runs both ways. A Java caller's cancel(true), or an orTimeout that fires, completes the future, and that cancels the Kotlin coroutine. Give the facade a scope it owns, as in lesson 3 of this track, so closing the facade cancels everything still in flight. GlobalScope.future also compiles, and it leaks in exactly the way lesson 3 described. Cancel across the bridge Read FutureBridge.kt. Predict the three future cancelled lines. Run it. Run the Java twin. It is plain Java calling the Kotlin FraudFacade from the same file, so watch for the [kotlin] lines. In the Java twin, change orTimeout(50, ...) to orTimeout(500, ...) and run it again. Predict first. FutureBridge.kt package workbench.coroutines.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.cancel import kotlinx.coroutines.cancelAndJoin import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.future.asDeferred import kotlinx.coroutines.future.await import kotlinx.coroutines.future.future import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** Kotlin code with a Java-friendly face: every suspend call gets a CompletableFuture twin. */ class FraudFacade : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) suspend fun score(paymentId: String): Int { try { delay(200) // the fraud model return paymentId.length * 7 } catch (e: kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException) { println(" [kotlin] scoring $paymentId was cancelled") throw e } } fun scoreAsync(paymentId: String): CompletableFuture<Int> = scope.future { score(paymentId) } override fun close() = scope.cancel() } /** A Java-style future that takes 500 ms, and reports whether someone cancelled it. */ fun slowJavaFuture(): CompletableFuture<String> { val f = CompletableFuture<String>() CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).execute { f.complete("limits loaded") } return f } fun main() = runBlocking { println("1. await() on a Java future, then cancel the coroutine:") val f1 = slowJavaFuture() launch { f1.await() }.also { delay(100) }.cancelAndJoin() println(" future cancelled: ${f1.isCancelled}") println("2. asDeferred().await(), then cancel the coroutine:") val f2 = slowJavaFuture() launch { f2.asDeferred().await() }.also { delay(100) }.cancelAndJoin() println(" future cancelled: ${f2.isCancelled} (it still completes: ${f2.get()})") println("3. future { } for a Java caller, who cancels it:") FraudFacade().use { facade -> val f3 = facade.scoreAsync("pay-123") delay(50) f3.cancel(true) delay(50) println(" future cancelled: ${f3.isCancelled}") } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l11.FutureBridgeKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l11/FutureBridge.kt FutureBridgeJava.java // Java equivalent of FutureBridge.kt, from the Java side: plain Java calling the Kotlin // FraudFacade through its future {} methods. No Continuation, no runBlocking. package workbench.coroutines.l11; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; public class FutureBridgeJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (FraudFacade facade = new FraudFacade()) { System.out.println("1. compose two Kotlin calls like any futures:"); CompletableFuture<Integer> total = facade.scoreAsync("pay-1") .thenCombine(facade.scoreAsync("pay-22"), Integer::sum); System.out.println(" combined score: " + total.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); System.out.println("2. a Java timeout cancels the Kotlin coroutine:"); CompletableFuture<Integer> slow = facade.scoreAsync("pay-timeout") .orTimeout(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // fails the future after 50 ms try { slow.join(); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println(" java caller got: " + e.getCause()); } Thread.sleep(50); System.out.println("3. cancel(true) on the future the facade returned:"); CompletableFuture<Integer> cancelled = facade.scoreAsync("pay-cancel"); Thread.sleep(50); cancelled.cancel(true); Thread.sleep(50); System.out.println(" future cancelled: " + cancelled.isCancelled()); } } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l11.FutureBridgeJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l11/FutureBridgeJava.java Case 1 prints future cancelled: true: cancelling the coroutine cancelled the Java future it was awaiting. Case 2 prints false and the future still completes, because asDeferred().await() only waits. Case 3 prints [kotlin] scoring pay-123 was cancelled, then true. In the Java twin, the combined score is 77, and both the orTimeout and the cancel(true) produce a [kotlin] ... was cancelled line. With a 500 ms timeout the 200 ms score finishes first, so there is no timeout and no cancel line for it. Each neighbour of the coroutine world has a bridge in and a bridge out, and the async bridges carry cancellation both ways. future (API reference) docs await on CompletionStage (API reference) docs Think of three ways to run a busy restaurant. Virtual threads hire a cheap waiter for every table, and each one simply stands there while the kitchen cooks, which is fine because standing costs almost nothing. Coroutines have a few waiters who leave a numbered ticket at each table and come back when the order is ready; they also know which tickets belong to which party, so when a party leaves they tear up all its tickets at once. Reactor runs the room as a conveyor: orders move through fixed stations, and the conveyor only moves as fast as the last station can take plates. The bridges are the pass between the kitchen and the floor, where a ticket can become a plate and back. The analogy breaks on cost: in a real restaurant the conveyor is the expensive option to install, while in code the expensive part of Reactor is the reading, debugging and changing of the pipeline afterwards.

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Bridge Reactor with mono { }, awaitSingle and asFlow
x: Reactor speaks Mono and Flux, and the kotlinx-coroutines-reactor module (on this lab's classpath) bridges them. Java // Java equivalent: the Reactor side just sees ordinary Mono and Flux values Mono<Quote> north = quotes.quote(req); // built by mono { } in Kotlin Mono<String> both = Mono.zip(north, quotes.quote(otherReq)).map(t -> t.getT1() + " | " + t.getT2()); Flux<Double> ticks = fx.ticks(); // a Kotlin Flow through asFlux() Kotlin fun quote(req: AuthRequest): Mono<Quote> = mono { quoteSource.quote(req) } // suspend code as a Mono suspend fun quoteNow(req: AuthRequest): Quote = webClientQuote(req).awaitSingle() // a Mono in suspend code fun settlements(): Flow<Batch> = settlementFlux().asFlow() // a Flux as a Flow fun ticks(): Flux<Double> = fxTicks.asFlux() // a Flow as a Flux mono { } gives a cold Mono: the coroutine starts on subscription, once per subscriber, which is the contract every Reactor user expects (lesson 2 of the reactive track). A null result completes the Mono empty, and disposing the subscription cancels the coroutine. Its context may not contain a Job ("Mono context cannot contain job in it"), because the subscription owns the coroutine's life, not a scope. flux { } does the same for a stream, with send inside. In the other direction, awaitSingle() waits for exactly one value and throws NoSuchElementException for an empty Mono; awaitSingleOrNull() returns null instead. Publisher.asFlow() collects a Flux as a Flow: the Flow's suspension turns into Reactive Streams request(n) demand, and cancelling the collector cancels the subscription. Flow.asFlux() goes back, and the module's README describes the result as TCK-compliant: it passes the Reactive Streams test kit (TCK), which checks a publisher against the spec's numbered rules. Two things need care. Threads first: unless you pass a dispatcher, mono { } starts its coroutine on Dispatchers.Default, while the Reactor operators around it run wherever their schedulers put them. Then context: Reactor's Context, which WebFlux uses for things like trace ids, is visible inside the coroutine as a ReactorContext element. MDC thread locals are not, for the reason lesson 4 of this track gave. Quarkus users will meet Mutiny rather than Reactor. The shapes are the same (Uni is a Mono, Multi is a Flux), and Mutiny ships its own Kotlin coroutine bridges. Hand a coroutine to Reactor and back Read ReactorBridge.kt. Predict how many [kotlin] asking north lines print in part 1. Run it. Run the Java twin, which uses the same Kotlin quoteFor and tickFlux functions from plain Reactor code. In the Kotlin file, change awaitSingle() in part 2 to awaitSingleOrNull() and print the result. Predict first. ReactorBridge.kt package workbench.coroutines.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.take import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.toList import kotlinx.coroutines.reactive.asFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.reactive.awaitSingle import kotlinx.coroutines.reactor.asFlux import kotlinx.coroutines.reactor.mono import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import reactor.core.publisher.Flux import reactor.core.publisher.Mono import java.time.Duration /** A Kotlin suspend call, exposed to Reactor code as a cold Mono. */ fun quoteFor(acquirer: String): Mono<String> = mono { println(" [kotlin] asking $acquirer for a quote") delay(50) if (acquirer == "nobody") null else "$acquirer: 1.80%" } /** A Kotlin Flow of FX ticks, exposed to Reactor code as a Flux. */ fun ticks(): Flow<Double> = flow { for (i in 0 until 5) { delay(20); emit(1.0800 + i / 10_000.0) } } fun tickFlux(): Flux<Double> = ticks().asFlux() fun main() = runBlocking { println("1. mono { } is cold:") val m = quoteFor("north") println(" built the Mono; nothing asked yet") println(" awaitSingle() -> ${m.awaitSingle()}") println(" awaitSingle() again -> ${m.awaitSingle()}") println("2. an empty Mono:") try { quoteFor("nobody").awaitSingle() } catch (e: NoSuchElementException) { println(" awaitSingle() threw NoSuchElementException") } println("3. a Flux consumed as a Flow (cancelling the flow cancels the subscription):") val settlements = Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(10)).map { "batch-$it" }.doOnCancel { println(" [reactor] subscription cancelled") } println(" ${settlements.asFlow().take(3).toList()}") println("4. a Flow handed to Reactor as a Flux:") println(" ${tickFlux().map { "%.4f".format(it) }.collectList().block()}") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l11.ReactorBridgeKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l11/ReactorBridge.kt ReactorBridgeJava.java // Java equivalent of ReactorBridge.kt, from the Java side: Reactor code using the Kotlin // functions through their Mono and Flux faces. h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Give Java callers a face they can use
x: Java can see a suspend function, but it can't call it nicely. The compiler adds a Continuation parameter and changes the return type to Object (lesson 1 of this track showed the bytecode), so from Java the signature looks like this: Java // what Java sees for the same function: a Continuation parameter and an Object result public Object authorize(AuthRequest req, Continuation<? super Decision> $completion) Kotlin suspend fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): Decision You could implement Continuation by hand, but you would be rebuilding a coroutine builder, badly. Give Java callers one of three faces instead. A CompletableFuture method built with future { }, as in this lesson's lab. It is the default for Java code that composes asynchronously, such as a Quarkus REST resource that returns a CompletionStage. A Mono built with mono { }, for code that already lives in Reactor. A blocking method that wraps runBlocking { }, for Java callers that block anyway: a Temporal activity, a JUnit test, a Kafka listener thread, or any code running on a virtual thread. Blocking a virtual thread is cheap, so runBlocking on one is a fair bridge. It is still wrong inside suspend code or on an event-loop thread (lesson 2 of this track). Whichever you choose, name the faces so the difference shows: authorize for Kotlin, authorizeAsync or authorizeBlocking for Java. Keep the suspend function as the one real implementation and make the others thin wrappers, so the rules for retries and timeouts live in one place. @JvmOverloads, @JvmStatic and @JvmName take care of the rest of the Java-facing surface: default arguments, companion functions and clashing names. A blocking face needs a timeout of its own. runBlocking { withTimeout(2.seconds) { authorize(req) } } gives the Java caller an upper bound, and an interrupt of the calling thread cancels the coroutine and makes runBlocking throw InterruptedException. That is the bridge from Java's cancellation model to Kotlin's. The lab's Java test, JavaCallerTest.java, shows what a Java caller ends up writing against a future { } face: orTimeout, thenApply and get, with no Kotlin types in sight beyond the data classes. Quick check: two Java callers block on the issuer through different faces, and each caller's thread is interrupted while the call is in flight. Caller A uses authorizeBlocking, the runBlocking face. Caller B calls authorizeAsync(req).get(). Whose issuer call is cancelled? (Only A's. The interrupt reaches runBlocking, which cancels its coroutine. B's interrupt only makes get() throw InterruptedException. The future is still not complete, so the coroutine behind it keeps running until someone cancels the future or closes the facade.)

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Virtual threads, coroutines or Reactor: choosing for a payments team
x: All three solve the problem the virtual threads track opened with: a request spends most of its time waiting, and a platform thread per waiting request is too expensive. They solve it at different layers. Virtual threads make blocking cheap, so ordinary blocking code scales. Coroutines make waiting explicit with suspend, and add structured concurrency, cancellation and Flow. Reactor turns a request into a pipeline of operators with backpressure. The Try it below runs the same three calls each way, and each takes as long as the slowest call. Virtual threads (JDK 21+) Kotlin coroutines Reactor Your code looks like plain blocking Java or Kotlin sequential suspend functions chains of operators Blocking libraries (JDBC, old SDKs) the natural fit withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a VT dispatcher wrap them, move them to boundedElastic Fan-out with one deadline StructuredTaskScope, preview in JDK 25 coroutineScope, async, withTimeout Mono.zip, timeout Cancellation interrupts, if the code checks them flows down the job tree to every child a cancel signal up the chain Streams with backpressure none built in Flow Flux Debugging ordinary stacks and thread dumps debug mode and coroutine dumps operator traces, harder to read Java callers native through future { } or mono { } native Here is what I would do in a team that writes Quarkus services in Kotlin and Java, talks to Oracle over JDBC, consumes Kafka and runs Temporal workflows. Start with virtual threads for request handling that is mostly blocking calls. Quarkus has @RunOnVirtualThread, JDBC and the Temporal SDK are blocking APIs anyway, and since JDK 24 (JEP 491) synchronized no longer pins a virtual thread in most cases, so JDK 25 is a good base. Cap each downstream with a semaphore or a sized pool (lesson 3 of the virtual threads track). Use coroutines in Kotlin code that needs what virtual threads don't give you: fan-out with one deadline, cancellation that reaches every child, Flow pipelines, StateFlow-style shared state. Blocking calls inside still go through withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a virtual-thread dispatcher. Keep Reactor (or Mutiny) where a reactive stack already exists, or where you stream with backpressure end to end. Don't start a new, blocking-heavy service on it. Mixing them is normal, and cheap with the bridges from this lesson. What to avoid is several models in one call path for no reason: a coroutine that calls runBlocking, which calls a Mono, which blocks on JDBC. Pick one model per component, and convert at its edges. One request, three ways Read ThreeWays.kt and its Java twin. Each runs the same three calls (100, 300 and 200 ms) at once. Predict every time. Run both. In ThreeWays.kt, wrap the body of detailsWithCoroutines in withTimeout(250) { ... } and run it again. What happens to the calls still in flight? ThreeWays.kt package workbench.coroutines.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext import java.util.concurrent.Executors import kotlin.system.measureTimeMillis // one payment-details request: account (100 ms), ledger (300 ms) and risk (200 ms), done at once suspend fun detailsWithCoroutines(): List<String> = coroutineScope { val account = async { delay(100); "account" } val ledger = async { delay(300); "ledger" } val risk = async { delay(200); "risk" } listOf(account.await(), ledger.await(), risk.await()) } /** The same calls written as BLOCKING code, run on whatever dispatcher you pass. */ suspend fun detailsBlocking(vt: CoroutineDispatcher): List<String> = coroutineScope { val account = async(vt) { Thread.sleep(100); "account" } val ledger = async(vt) { Thread.sleep(300); "ledger" } val risk = async(vt) { Thread.sleep(200); "risk" } listOf(account.await(), ledger.await(), risk.await()) } fun main() = runBlocking { repeat(2) { detailsWithCoroutines() } // warm up val c = measureTimeMillis { println("coroutines: ${detailsWithCoroutines()}") } println(" took $c ms on ${Thread.currentThread().name.substringBefore(" @")}") Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher().use { vt -> val v = measureTimeMillis { println("blocking code on virtual threads: ${detailsBlocking(vt)}") } println(" took $v ms") } val b = measureTimeMillis { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { println("blocking code on Dispatchers.IO: ${detailsBlocking(Dispatchers.IO)}") } } println(" took $b ms") } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l11.ThreeWaysKt labs/coroutines/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/coroutines/l11/ThreeWays.kt ThreeWaysJava.java // Java equivalent of ThreeWays.kt: the same request with virtual threads (plain blocking code) // and with Reactor (operators, no blocking). Same total time: the slowest call. package workbench.coroutines.l11; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; public class ThreeWaysJava { static String call(String name, long ms) throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(ms); // a blocking client call return name; } static List<String> withVirtualThreads() throws Exception { try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<String> account = vt.submit(() -> call("account", 100)); Future<String> ledger = vt.submit(() -> call("ledger", 300)); Future<String> risk = vt.submit(() -> call("risk", 200)); return List.of(account.get(), ledger.get(), risk.get()); } } static List<String> withReactor() { return Mono.zip( Mono.just("account").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(100)), Mono.just("ledger").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(300)), Mono.just("risk").delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(200))) .map(t -> List.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())) .block(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { withVirtualThreads(); withReactor(); // warm up long t0 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.println("virtual threads: " + withVirtualThreads()); System.out.println(" took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.println("reactor: " + withReactor()); System.out.println(" took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); } } ./gradlew :coroutines:demo -Pmain=workbench.coroutines.l11.ThreeWaysJava labs/coroutines/src/demo/java/workbench/coroutines/l11/ThreeWaysJava.java Every version takes about 300 ms: the coroutines, the blocking code on a virtual-thread dispatcher, the blocking code on Dispatchers.IO, the plain virtual threads and the Reactor Mono.zip. With withTimeout(250), the program fails with TimeoutCancellationException at about 250 ms, and the ledger and risk calls still in flight are cancelled with it. Doing that in the Java virtual-thread version would take extra code to cancel the futures yourself. JEP 444: Virtual Threads read Reactor bridges: kotlinx-coroutines-reactor README read The most common mistake is bridging with blocking calls: runBlocking { } inside CompletableFuture.supplyAsync to give Java a future, or future.get() (even inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO)) to use a Java future from a coroutine. Both work in a demo, so they ship. Under load, each in-flight call pins a pool thread, and cancellation stops at the bridge: a Java caller's cancel(true) doesn't reach the coroutine, and a cancelled coroutine leaves the Java future running. The fix is the purpose-built bridges, which suspend instead of block and carry cancellation both ways: scope.future { } with a scope you own, future.await(), mono { } and awaitSingle().

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Java and Kotlin
x: One fan-out with a deadline: virtual threads vs coroutines PaymentDetails.java PaymentDetails details(String id) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService vt = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { Future<Account> account = vt.submit(() -> accounts.load(id)); // 1. three blocking calls, Future<List<Entry>> ledger = vt.submit(() -> ledgerClient.recent(id)); // one virtual thread each Future<Risk> risk = vt.submit(() -> riskClient.flags(id)); long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.toNanos(800); try { return new PaymentDetails( // 2. one shared deadline account.get(remaining(deadline), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS), ledger.get(remaining(deadline), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS), risk.get(remaining(deadline), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)); } catch (TimeoutException | ExecutionException e) { account.cancel(true); ledger.cancel(true); risk.cancel(true); // 3. cancel by hand throw e; } } // close() waits for every task } PaymentDetails.kt suspend fun details(id: String): PaymentDetails = withTimeout(800) { // 2. one shared deadline coroutineScope { val account = async { accounts.load(id) } // 1. three suspending calls, val ledger = async { ledgerClient.recent(id) } // one coroutine each val risk = async { riskClient.flags(id) } PaymentDetails(account.await(), ledger.await(), risk.await()) } // 3. a timeout or a failure cancels the other two automatically } Both take as long as the slowest call, and both are cheap: a virtual thread or a coroutine per call. The difference is how much of the structure you write yourself. In Java with virtual threads, the clients can stay blocking, which is the big win, but the shared deadline, the cancel-the-siblings-on-failure step and the cleanup are your code. JDK 25's StructuredTaskScope covers that, but it is still a preview API. In Kotlin, the deadline is withTimeout, the siblings are cancelled by coroutineScope, and the clients must suspend (or be wrapped in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) or a virtual-thread dispatcher). Pick the model that matches your clients: blocking clients favour virtual threads, suspending clients and complex fan-out favour coroutines.

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Worked example
x: Give a Java Temporal activity the Kotlin authorization service The authorization service is Kotlin, and its core is a suspend function with retries and timeouts. A Temporal activity written in Java must call it, and Temporal activities are blocking code. The activity can't call the suspend function directly. class AuthorizationService(private val issuer: IssuerClient) { suspend fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): Decision = retryWithBackoff(times = 3, initialDelay = 200.milliseconds, maxDelay = 2.seconds) { issuer.authorize(req) } } // what the Java activity sees: a Continuation parameter it can't sensibly supply public final class AuthorizationService { public final Object authorize(AuthRequest req, Continuation<? super Decision> $completion) { /* ... */ } } Add Java faces in a small Kotlin facade with its own scope. One returns a future, for Java code that composes; one blocks with its own timeout, for callers that block anyway. class AuthorizationJavaApi(private val service: AuthorizationService) : AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default) // 1. for Java code that composes futures fun authorizeAsync(req: AuthRequest): CompletableFuture<Decision> = scope.future { service.authorize(req) } // 2. for callers that block anyway, with its own upper bound fun authorizeBlocking(req: AuthRequest): Decision = runBlocking { withTimeout(10.seconds) { service.authorize(req) } } override fun close() = scope.cancel() } // Java equivalent of the same facade, if the service were a Java class returning futures final class AuthorizationJavaApi implements AutoCloseable { private final AuthorizationService service; AuthorizationJavaApi(AuthorizationService service) { this.service = service; } // 1. for Java code that composes futures CompletableFuture<Decision> authorizeAsync(AuthRequest req) { return service.authorizeAsync(req); } // 2. for callers that block anyway, with its own upper bound Decision authorizeBlocking(AuthRequest req) throws Exception { return service.authorizeAsync(req).get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } @Override public void close() { } } The activity uses the future face, so it can cancel the Kotlin work when Temporal cancels the activity. Temporal reports a cancel through the heartbeat, which throws. // the activity is Java; this is the Kotlin side it relies on: cancel(true) reaches the coroutine val f = api.authorizeAsync(req) f.cancel(true) // 3. cancels the coroutine inside AuthorizationService, retries included public Decision authorize(AuthRequest req) { CompletableFuture<Decision> f = api.authorizeAsync(req); try { while (true) { try { return f.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException stillWaiting) { Activity.getExecutionContext().heartbeat(null); } // 3. throws if cancelled } } catch (ActivityCompletionException cancelled) { f.cancel(true); // stops the Kotlin coroutine and its retries throw cancelled; } catch (InterruptedException | ExecutionException e) { throw Activity.wrap(e); } } A Reactor-based caller elsewhere gets its own face from the same function, and the retry rules still live in one place. // 4. a cold Mono for reactive callers fun authorizeMono(req: AuthRequest): Mono<Decision> = mono { service.authorize(req) } // 4. the reactive caller's side Mono<Decision> decision = api.authorizeMono(req) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)) .onErrorReturn(Decision.DECLINED); Self-check: why not implement authorizeAsync as CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { runBlocking { service.authorize(req) } }? (It blocks a common-pool thread for every call, the future has no link to the coroutine so cancel(true) stops nothing, and the work belongs to no scope, so close() can't stop it. That is the bug in this lesson's lab.)

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Quiz
x: A Java caller holds f = facade.authorizeAsync(req), where authorizeAsync is scope.future { authorize(req) }, and calls f.cancel(true). What happens to the Kotlin side? Nothing: cancel(true) only interrupts Java threads The coroutine is cancelled at its next suspension point The coroutine finishes, and its result is thrown away The whole scope is cancelled, with every other authorization The future from future { } is tied to its coroutine, and cancelling or completing the future cancels it. Only that coroutine is affected: the scope and its other children carry on, especially with a SupervisorJob. A coroutine does val s = fraudClient.score(req).await() and is cancelled while it waits. What happens to the Java future? It is cancelled with cancel(false), because nobody wants the answer any more It keeps running, and its result is discarded It is completed with null await() blocks until the future finishes, then throws await() cancels the future when the awaiting coroutine is cancelled. If the future must finish anyway (it is shared, or the work is already committed), use future.asDeferred().await(), which waits without cancelling. val q: Mono<Quote> = mono { quoteSource.quote(req) } is built, and then two different callers subscribe to q. How many times does quoteSource.quote run? Once, when mono { } is called Once, at the first subscription; the second subscriber gets the cached value Twice: the Mono is cold, so each subscription runs the coroutine Never, unless block() is called mono { } starts the coroutine on subscription, once per subscriber, like any cold Mono. Use .cache() on the Mono if you really want one call shared. A Java service handles 2,000 concurrent requests. Each one makes three blocking JDBC queries and one blocking HTTP call, and the team writes Java. Which model fits best? Rewrite it with Reactor, to avoid blocking Rewrite it in Kotlin with coroutines A platform thread pool of 2,000 threads Virtual threads, with a semaphore in front of the connection pool The code is blocking and Java, which is exactly what virtual threads make cheap: one per request, with no rewrite. A semaphore keeps the database pool from being overrun. Reactor and coroutines would mean rewriting every client for little gain, and 2,000 platform threads cost a lot of memory. From the virtual threads track: on JDK 21, a virtual thread blocks on a socket read while inside a synchronized block. What happens to its carrier thread? It is released, as with any blocking call It is pinned: it stays blocked with the virtual thread until the read returns The JVM throws IllegalStateException The virtual thread is moved to a new carrier On JDK 21 to 23, blocking while holding a monitor pins the virtual thread to its carrier, so the carrier blocks too. JEP 491 in JDK 24 removed most of that pinning, which is one reason to run virtual-thread services on JDK 25.

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Key terms
x: future { } A coroutine builder that returns the coroutine's result as a CompletableFuture. await() Suspends until a CompletableFuture completes, without blocking a thread. mono { } Turns suspend code into a cold Reactor Mono that runs once per subscription. awaitSingle() Suspends until a Mono emits its one value; throws if it completes empty. asFlow / asFlux Convert a Reactive Streams Publisher to a Flow, and a Flow to a Flux. Java face A thin wrapper that exposes a suspend function to Java as a future, a Mono or a blocking call. How do you wait for a CompletableFuture inside a coroutine without blocking? future.await() from kotlinx.coroutines.future. It suspends, unwraps the exception, and cancels the future if the coroutine is cancelled. How do you await a CompletableFuture without cancelling it when the coroutine is cancelled? future.asDeferred().await(). How do you return suspend code to Java as a CompletableFuture? scope.future { suspendCall() }, with a scope the class owns. Cancelling or completing the future cancels the coroutine. When does the coroutine inside mono { } run? On each subscription. The Mono is cold, a null result completes it empty, and disposing the subscription cancels the coroutine. What does awaitSingle() do on an empty Mono? It throws NoSuchElementException. awaitSingleOrNull() returns null instead. What does Java see for suspend fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): Decision? Object authorize(AuthRequest req, Continuation<? super Decision> completion): give Java a future, Mono or blocking face instead. Virtual threads or coroutines for a blocking JDBC-heavy Java service? Virtual threads: they make the existing blocking code cheap without a rewrite. Coroutines pay off for structured fan-out, cancellation and Flow in Kotlin.

h: Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads · Go deeper
x: kotlinx.coroutines 1.11 has no built-in virtual-thread dispatcher. Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher() is the supported route, and it gives every dispatch a fresh virtual thread. That makes it a good home for blocking calls inside coroutines, with two cautions. A coroutine blocked inside it still ignores cancellation unless the call is wrapped in runInterruptible, which interrupts the virtual thread. And the coroutine scheduler's habit of keeping a coroutine on one worker is lost, so code that relies on thread-local caches gets a new thread every time it resumes. CompletionStage.await() works for any CompletionStage, not just CompletableFuture, and Deferred.asCompletableFuture() goes the other way for a coroutine you already started with async. On the Reactor side, Deferred.asMono() and Job.asMono() give hot Monos for work that is already running, and Scheduler.asCoroutineDispatcher() lets coroutines run on a Reactor scheduler, which keeps thread usage in one place in a WebFlux service. The structured-concurrency story differs most across the three. Coroutines enforce it by default. Virtual threads get it through StructuredTaskScope, a preview API in JDK 25 (JEP 505) whose shape changed between previews. Reactor has no tree of tasks at all, only operator chains that cancel upstream. When you bridge, the tree ends at the bridge: a future { } coroutine belongs to the facade's scope, not to the Java caller, which is exactly why the facade must own and close that scope.

h: Servers and event loops: NIO, Netty, Vert.x and Jetty
x: Blocking vs non-blocking IO, NIO selectors, Netty pipelines and flow control, Vert.x and Quarkus event loops, Jetty 12, and zero-copy. By the end of this track you can explain what a blocked socket read costs and why ten thousand idle connections broke thread-per-connection servers, write a correct java.nio select loop, build and test Netty 4.2 pipelines with codecs, backpressure and leak detection, reason about Vert.x contexts, the event bus and the blocked-thread checker, predict which thread runs a Quarkus REST endpoint, configure Jetty 12's thread pool and virtual threads, and choose a server model for a payments service, down to what the kernel does with epoll, sendfile and io_uring. The track assumes no knowledge of NIO, Netty, Vert.x or Jetty. It builds each layer by hand first: a blocking server, then a select loop, then the same ideas in Netty, then the frameworks built on Netty. You need the basics from the first track (threads, locks, races), Little's law from the executors track ("Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law"), and the virtual threads track, which this one connects back to in lessons 1, 6, 7 and 8. Versions are pinned: JDK 21 or newer (install JDK 25, the current LTS), Netty 4.2.20.Final, Vert.x 5.2.3, Quarkus 3.40 and Jetty 12.1.14. The labs live in labs/nio, one package per lesson (workbench.nio.l01 to l08). Lessons 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 have Java labs; lessons 3, 6 and 8 are in Kotlin. Run ./gradlew :nio:test --tests 'workbench.nio.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and ./gradlew :nio:solutionTest to check the reference answers. Servers in the tests bind 127.0.0.1 on a free port, so nothing clashes with what you have running. The Try-it demos run with ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=..., in Java and Kotlin. A few steps use Linux tools (strace, epoll, io_uring); on macOS the same demos run on kqueue and say so. A blocked read holds its thread; thread-per-connection needs one thread per open socket, which is why ten thousand idle connections (C10K) broke it. Little's law sizes the threads a blocking design needs. A java.nio server reads and writes partially: keep unsent bytes, compact() instead of clear(), remove selected keys, and arm OP_WRITE only while bytes are pending, because Linux selectors are level-triggered. A Netty event loop is one thread that owns its channels for life. Netty 4.2 builds groups with MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup and an IoHandler factory, and blocking work is dispatched manually to your own executor. Frame before you decode, release every ByteBuf exactly once (last owner releases), catch leaks with PARANOID detection in tests, and turn auto-read off while a channel isn't writable. Vert.x puts contexts on Netty's loops: a handler never runs concurrently with itself, the event bus is best effort, the blocked-thread checker warns after 2 s, and executeBlocking is ordered per context unless you pass false. Quarkus REST picks the thread from the signature: reactive types and suspend run on the IO thread, plain values on a worker. Add @Blocking to JTA endpoints that return Uni, and use @RunOnVirtualThread with explicit downstream limits. Jetty 12 decides per task from the handler's declared invocation type: non-blocking on the selector thread, blocking with a reserved thread or handed off, optionally to virtual threads. Its pool queue must stay unbounded. Virtual threads hide an event loop inside the JDK's poller. Zero-copy (sendfile) and io_uring are kernel-level tools to measure, and every server model still needs a concurrency limit somewhere.

h: Servers and event loops: NIO, Netty, Vert.x and Jetty: track quiz
x: A thread-per-connection gateway has 6,000 terminals connected. They send 300 requests a second in total, each taking 100 ms. How many threads does the gateway hold? 30 300 About 6,000 One per CPU core Little's law gives 300 × 0.1 s = 30 requests in flight, but thread-per-connection keeps a thread on every open socket, busy or idle: about 6,000. That gap is the C10K problem in miniature. An NIO server burns one core at 100% with no traffic. Which change fixes it? Use direct buffers instead of heap buffers Register OP_WRITE only while a connection has unsent bytes Call selectNow() instead of select() Add a second selector thread A socket with free send-buffer space is always writable, and Linux selectors are level-triggered, so a permanent OP_WRITE makes every select() return at once. selectNow() would spin even harder. In Netty 4.2, a handler must call a blocking fraud-scoring SDK. What is the recommended way? pipeline.addLast(new DefaultEventExecutorGroup(8), "fraud", handler) Call it in the handler; Netty 4.2 loops are virtual threads Dispatch the call to your own executor and ctx.writeAndFlush the result from there Wrap the call in synchronized Netty 4.2 deprecated the per-handler EventExecutorGroup overloads and says to dispatch manually. Event loops are platform threads, and writeAndFlush from another thread is queued back onto the channel's loop. A Netty handler extends ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter, logs msg.readableBytes(), and then does nothing else with the ByteBuf. What is wrong? Nothing: the garbage collector frees it It leaks: it neither passes the buffer on nor releases it It double-releases the buffer It blocks the event loop ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter releases nothing. A handler that is the last to touch a buffer must release it (ReferenceCountUtil.release(msg)) or pass it on with ctx.fireChannelRead(msg). PARANOID leak detection reports it once the buffer is garbage-collected. A Netty proxy forwards from a fast client to a slow backend. The backend channel's isWritable() turns false. What should the proxy do? Turn off auto-read on the client channel until the backend channel is writable again Keep writing; Netty buffers it Close the backend channel Sleep in the handler until the backend catches up Writability is Netty's signal that the outbound buffer passed the high water mark. Stopping reads from the producer keeps the backlog in the kernel and TCP, not in your memory; sleeping would block the event loop. A Vert.x consumer wraps a 300 ms JDBC call in vertx.executeBlocking(callable). Six requests arrive at once. Roughly how long until all six are answered? About 300 ms About 600 ms About 1,800 ms, because executeBlocking is ordered per context by default Never: it deadlocks All six messages come from the consumer's one context, and the default executeBlocking runs calls from a context one after another. The event loop is free, but the queries are serialized. Pass false to let them overlap. In Quarkus 3.40, which endpoint blocks an IO thread? public Balance get(...) that calls JDBC @Blocking public Uni<Balance> get(...) that calls JDBC @RunOnVirtualThread public Balance get(...) that calls JDBC public Uni<Balance> get(...) that returns Uni.createFrom().item(jdbc.find(id)) A Uni return type puts the method on the IO thread, and jdbc.find(id) runs while the Uni is being built. The other three run on a worker or a virtual thread. A Jetty 12 health-check handler extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking, and someone adds a database ping to it. What happens under load? Jetty notices and moves it to a worker thread It runs on a selector thread in Produce-Consume mode, so other connections on that selector wait behind each ping It runs on a virtual thread Jetty rejects the handler at startup NonBlocking is a promise Jetty trusts: it runs the handler directly on the selector thread. Blocking there stalls the selector, which Jetty's docs call a risk of server lock-up. Change the superclass to Handler.Abstract. On JDK 21, what happens when a virtual thread calls socket.getInputStream().read() and no data has arrived? Its carrier thread blocks in the kernel until data arrives The JDK does a non-blocking read, registers the socket with its internal poller and parks the virtual thread; a poller thread unparks it when data arrives The JVM creates a new platform thread for the read The read throws, and the virtual thread retries in a loop NioSocketImpl keeps the socket non-blocking, gets EAGAIN, registers the file descriptor with the Poller (epoll, one-shot) and parks. On JDK 21 the pollers are platform threads such as Read-Poller; from JDK 22 on Linux they are mostly virtual threads. A service streams 500 MB settlement files to an internal archive over plain TCP. Which code sends them most efficiently, and what must it handle? Files.readAllBytes then one write; nothing else A loop of FileChannel.transferTo calls, because a call may transfer fewer bytes than asked Netty with io_uring, because it is always fastest A heap ByteBuffer of 500 MB transferTo to a socket becomes sendfile on Linux, so the bytes never pass through the JVM, and it can return early, so it belongs in a loop. Reading 500 MB into the heap wastes memory, and io_uring was not faster in this track's runs.

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · A blocked read holds a whole thread
x: Here is the core of every classic Java server. One thread accepts connections. Each connection gets a task that reads a line and writes it back. Java try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(8080)) { while (true) { Socket socket = server.accept(); // blocks until a client connects pool.execute(() -> echo(socket)); // one task per connection } } static void echo(Socket socket) { try (socket; var in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(socket.getInputStream(), UTF_8))) { var out = socket.getOutputStream(); String line; while ((line = in.readLine()) != null) { // blocks until the client sends a line out.write((line + "\n").getBytes(UTF_8)); } } catch (IOException e) { // the client went away } } Kotlin ServerSocket(8080).use { server -> while (true) { val socket = server.accept() // blocks until a client connects pool.execute { echo(socket) } // one task per connection } } fun echo(socket: Socket) { try { socket.use { s -> val reader = s.getInputStream().bufferedReader(UTF_8) val out = s.getOutputStream() while (true) { val line = reader.readLine() ?: break // blocks until the client sends a line out.write("$line\n".toByteArray(UTF_8)) } } } catch (e: IOException) { // the client went away } } The code is easy to read, and that is its strength. The cost hides in readLine(). Go one level down to see it. A socket is the kernel's object for one end of a TCP connection, and the kernel keeps a receive buffer for it: bytes that have arrived from the network but that your program hasn't read yet. read() copies bytes out of that buffer. If the buffer is empty, the kernel takes the calling thread off the CPU and parks it on the socket's wait list. When a packet arrives, the kernel appends its bytes to the buffer and wakes the parked thread, which then returns from read(). While the client thinks, or sits idle on a keep-alive connection (one it leaves open between requests), that thread can do nothing else. Two things surprise people the first time they look. The thread is not free to keep. A Java platform thread is a thin wrapper around one operating system thread, with its own stack, and Jetty's documentation puts it at about 1 MiB of native memory. The OS scheduler also has to track every one of them. And a thread dump hides the waiting. A platform thread blocked in a socket read reports RUNNABLE, because the JVM sees it running native code (SocketDispatcher.read0). A server with 2,000 idle connections shows 2,000 runnable threads and almost no CPU use. Vert.x's documentation makes the same point about every blocking API: while the thread waits for a result it can do nothing else, so a lot of concurrency needs a lot of threads. For a blocking server, the question is never how fast one request runs. It is how many threads you can hold, and how many your traffic needs. Count the threads Open ThreadPerConnectionDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin, ThreadPerConnectionDemo.kt). It connects 2,000 clients that never send anything: first to a server with a cached thread pool, then to one with a virtual thread per connection. Before you run it, write down two predictions: how many platform threads the first server holds, and what getState() returns for a handler stuck in read(). Run it from labs/ with the command below. Then run it again with -Pargs=5000 added. ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l01.ThreadPerConnectionDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l01/ThreadPerConnectionDemo.kt On my 4-core machine with JDK 21 the platform version went from 6 platform threads to 2,007, one per client plus the JVM's own, and the blocked handler reported RUNNABLE. The virtual version held the same 2,000 connections with 15 platform threads, and its blocked handler reported WAITING. With 5,000 clients the first number became 5,007 and the second stayed at 15. A thread-per-connection server is a restaurant that gives every table its own waiter for the whole evening. The waiter stands by the table while the guests read the menu, eat and talk, and serves nobody else. Forty tables need forty waiters even when only three tables want something. An event loop is one waiter walking the room who stops only at tables where someone raised a hand. The analogy breaks at the kernel: a real waiter has to scan the room, while epoll hands the event loop a list of exactly the tables with raised hands.

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Little's law counts the threads you need
x: The number of requests in a system equals the arrival rate times the time each one spends there: L = λ × W. That is Little's law, which you met in the executors and virtual threads tracks. With thread-per-request, L is also the number of threads you need. Take an authorization service. At peak it gets 800 requests a second. Each request spends 30 ms in your code and 120 ms waiting for the card issuer. That is 800 × 0.15 s = 120 requests in flight, so 120 busy threads, and a pool of 200 copes. If the issuer slows to 600 ms, the same traffic needs 800 × 0.63 s = 504 threads. Your CPU is no busier. The extra threads are all waiting. Thread-per-connection is worse than thread-per-request, because it pays for connections, not requests. A connection holds its thread for its whole life, including the idle time between requests. Picture 10,000 point-of-sale terminals that each keep a connection open and send one request every 10 seconds. That is 1,000 requests a second. At 150 ms each, Little's law says 150 are in flight. The thread-per-connection server still needs 10,000 threads, because 9,850 of them sit in read() waiting for their terminal's next request. That gap explains two defaults you may have seen in Tomcat's connector docs. maxThreads is 200 and caps simultaneous requests. maxConnections is 8,192 and caps open connections. The NIO connector's poller watches the idle sockets with select(), so a worker thread is needed only while a request is being processed. Threads follow requests in flight, not open sockets. Each extra platform thread costs a stack and a slot in the scheduler. When many threads are runnable, the OS also pays for context switches: saving one thread's registers and loading another's, with the CPU caches going cold in between. A few thousand works, as the demo showed. Tens of thousands is where servers in the late 1990s fell over, and it is still a bad place to be. Do the arithmetic before the incident A settlement service reads from Kafka and calls a ledger API: 300 calls a second, 40 ms in your own code, 260 ms waiting for the ledger. How many threads does thread-per-request need? The ledger has an incident and takes 2 s per call. Traffic stays the same. How many threads now? Open the lab test fixedPoolCapsConnections. Which of your two numbers would a fixed pool of 100 survive, and what would callers see in the other case? 300 × 0.3 s = 90 threads normally, and 300 × 2.04 s = 612 threads during the incident. A pool of 100 copes with the first. In the second, tasks queue behind busy threads, latency climbs past every client timeout, and the service looks down while its CPU is idle. The pool ran out of threads that were waiting, not threads that were working. Tomcat 11 HTTP connector attributes (docs source) docs Your Quarkus services already avoid thread-per-connection: Vert.x accepts and reads every connection on a few event-loop threads and borrows a worker thread only while a blocking endpoint runs. Thread-per-connection still hides in the code around them: a TCP client to a card network that keeps one reader thread per terminal, an ISO 8583 gateway written years ago, or a Kafka consumer you scaled by adding threads that each block on a 120 ms issuer call. Run Little's law on each one: requests per second times seconds per request gives threads in flight. Then compare that with the threads it actually holds while it waits.

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · C10K: ten thousand clients at once
x: In 1999 Dan Kegel wrote a page called "The C10K problem". The name is short for ten thousand concurrent clients. His argument was that the hardware of the day could already serve that many connections and the server software could not, because of how it used threads and system calls. The answer the industry settled on is the one this whole track is about: stop giving each connection a thread. Put many sockets in non-blocking mode, where a read on an empty receive buffer returns 0 bytes at once instead of parking the thread. Then ask the kernel one question: which of these sockets are ready right now? select and poll were the first system calls for that, and they take the whole list of sockets on every call, which gets slow with thousands of them. Linux added epoll and the BSDs and macOS added kqueue. Both keep the watched sockets inside the kernel and report only the ones that are ready. One thread can then watch thousands of connections and run code only for those with data. That loop (wait for ready sockets, serve each one a little, wait again) is called an event loop. That one idea has many names on the JVM: java.nio's Selector, which is epoll on Linux and kqueue on macOS (lesson 2). Netty's event loop: one thread running a selector and your handlers (lessons 3 and 4). Vert.x and Quarkus, which run on Netty (lessons 5 and 6). Jetty's ManagedSelector (lesson 7). The JDK's internal poller, which virtual threads use when they block on a socket (lesson 8). The price is the programming model. A thread that serves thousands of sockets must never block on any one of them. Every read has to return at once with whatever bytes are there, maybe none. Every write has to accept that only part of the buffer went out. Your code becomes a small state machine per connection, called whenever the kernel reports that something happened. The rest of this track is about writing that state machine well, or picking a framework that writes it for you. See the waiting threads in a dump Start the demo with 300 clients and hold the connections for 20 seconds: run the command below. While it holds the platform-thread version, run jcmd workbench.nio.l01.ThreadPerConnectionDemo Thread.print | grep -c NioSocketImpl.implRead in a second terminal. jcmd accepts the main class name instead of a pid. Run the same jcmd line again once the demo prints the virtual-thread section. Predict the count first. terminal ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l01.ThreadPerConnectionDemo -Pargs='300 20' The first count is 300: each handler's stack runs through NioSocketImpl.implRead down to SocketDispatcher.read0, and its state line says RUNNABLE. The second count is 0. Thread.print lists platform threads only, and the 300 virtual threads are parked off any thread. Lesson 8 shows how to find them. Thread per connection parks one thread on every socket. An event loop asks the kernel which sockets are ready and runs only those. C10k problem (Wikipedia) read

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Two ways out: fewer threads, or cheaper threads
x: There are two ways to serve 10,000 connections from one JVM. The first is the C10K answer: a few threads, each running an event loop over many non-blocking sockets. Netty, Vert.x and Quarkus work this way. It scales very far, and you pay with code that must never block. Call JDBC from an event loop and every other connection on that loop stops until the query returns. The second arrived in JDK 21: virtual threads (JEP 444). You keep the blocking code from the first section and change the executor. Java // echo() stays exactly as it was ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); Kotlin // echo() stays exactly as it was val pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() The demo showed the effect: 2,000 blocked readers on 15 platform threads. It works because the JDK runs an event loop for you. When a virtual thread's socket read would block, the JDK registers the socket with an internal poller built on epoll or kqueue, parks the virtual thread, and frees its carrier (the platform thread that was running it) for other work. Lesson 8 opens that poller up. Neither way makes a single request faster. Non-blocking IO and virtual threads buy concurrency per unit of memory, not latency. A request that waits 120 ms for the card issuer still takes 120 ms. Neither removes the limits behind your service either. If 10,000 virtual threads all want one of 20 database connections, 9,980 of them wait in the pool's queue. The virtual threads track shows how to cap that with a semaphore. My default for a new blocking service is virtual threads. I'd move to an event-loop framework when measurements say memory per connection or scheduling is the problem, or when the service already lives on one, as every Quarkus service does. Most payment services hit the limits of their downstreams long before either wall. Swap the executor, keep the code Finish the lab first, so BlockingEchoServer works. Read the test virtualThreadsScale. It passes Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() to the same server class that idleClientsHoldThreads runs on a cached pool. Change its client count from 500 to 1,500 (the loop bound and the isEqualTo(500)) and run only that test with --tests '*virtualThreadsScale'. Predict whether the platform-thread assertion still holds. It still passes. The platform-thread count grows by a few threads (carriers and poller threads) whether 500 or 1,500 connections are open, because a parked virtual thread holds no OS thread. Put the count back to 500 when you're done. JEP 444: Virtual Threads read The common mistake is sizing a blocking server by CPU: "we have 8 cores, so 16 threads is plenty." That rule is for CPU-bound work. A thread waiting on a socket uses no CPU, so the number comes from Little's law, and for thread-per-connection from the number of open sockets. The opposite mistake usually follows the first outage: raising maxThreads to 5,000 to ride out a slow downstream. Now a slow issuer fills 5,000 threads instead of 200, memory climbs, and the issuer receives 5,000 concurrent calls it can't serve either. Size from the traffic you expect, cap concurrency toward each dependency, and make idle connections cheap with an event loop or virtual threads.

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Java and Kotlin
x: One virtual thread per connection, in both languages VirtualEchoServer.java try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(8080); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { while (true) { Socket socket = server.accept(); pool.submit(() -> echo(socket)); // a blocked read parks the virtual thread } } VirtualEchoServer.kt ServerSocket(8080).use { server -> Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { pool -> while (true) { val socket = server.accept() pool.submit { echo(socket) } // a blocked read parks the virtual thread } } } The JDK does the work in both: ExecutorService is AutoCloseable since JDK 19, so Java's try-with-resources and Kotlin's use both shut the pool down and wait for running tasks. The difference worth knowing is coroutines. A Kotlin coroutine that calls the blocking readLine() does not suspend. It holds its dispatcher thread for the whole wait, so launch(Dispatchers.IO) { echo(socket) } is thread-per-connection again, capped by the IO dispatcher's 64 threads. Coroutines only free the thread when the IO call itself suspends, which is what Ktor and Vert.x's Kotlin APIs provide.

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Worked example
x: Size a terminal gateway with Little's law A gateway keeps one TCP connection per payment terminal: 6,000 terminals. Each terminal sends an authorization every 20 seconds. The gateway spends 15 ms of CPU and 135 ms waiting for the card switch per request. Today it runs one platform thread per connection. // 1. today: one platform thread per terminal connection ExecutorService pool = Executors.newCachedThreadPool(); while (true) { Socket terminal = server.accept(); pool.execute(() -> serveTerminal(terminal)); // loops: read request, call switch, reply } // 1. today: one platform thread per terminal connection val pool = Executors.newCachedThreadPool() while (true) { val terminal = server.accept() pool.execute { serveTerminal(terminal) } // loops: read request, call switch, reply } Apply Little's law to requests, then compare with connections. The gap is the cost of idle connections. arrival rate = 6,000 terminals / 20 s = 300 requests/s time in system = 15 ms + 135 ms = 0.15 s in flight = 300 x 0.15 = 45 requests threads held = one per connection = 6,000 threads idle threads = 6,000 - 45 = 5,955 waiting in read() Make idle connections cheap. A virtual thread parked in read() holds no OS thread, so the 5,955 idle connections cost a little heap each instead of a platform thread each. The serving code does not change. // 2. same serveTerminal(), cheap waiting ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // 2. same serveTerminal(), cheap waiting val pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() Now protect the switch. It allows 64 concurrent requests. The old design limited concurrency by accident, through thread count. Virtual threads remove that accident, so put the limit back on purpose, around the call that needs it. // 3. cap concurrency toward the switch, not the number of connections private final Semaphore switchSlots = new Semaphore(64); AuthResponse authorize(AuthRequest req) throws InterruptedException { switchSlots.acquire(); try { return cardSwitch.send(req); // 135 ms } finally { switchSlots.release(); } } // 3. cap concurrency toward the switch, not the number of connections private val switchSlots = Semaphore(64) fun authorize(req: AuthRequest): AuthResponse { switchSlots.acquire() try { return cardSwitch.send(req) // 135 ms } finally { switchSlots.release() } }

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Quiz
x: A thread-per-connection server has 3,000 clients with open connections. Together they send 600 requests a second, and each request takes 50 ms. How many threads does the server hold? 30 600 About 3,000 8, one per core Little's law gives 600 × 0.05 s = 30 requests in flight, which is what thread-per-request would need. Thread-per-connection keeps a thread on every open socket, so about 3,000. The 30 is the tempting answer, and the difference is the idle time between requests. A thread dump of a slow service shows 400 threads in SocketDispatcher.read0 with state RUNNABLE, and CPU is at 2%. What is going on? 400 threads are spinning on the CPU 400 threads are waiting for bytes on their sockets; native blocking reads show up as RUNNABLE The JVM is deadlocked The garbage collector has paused them A platform thread blocked in a socket read is inside native code, so the JVM reports it as RUNNABLE. Low CPU confirms they are waiting, not working. A deadlock would show BLOCKED threads waiting on monitors. Which change lets the lab's BlockingEchoServer hold 10,000 idle connections without 10,000 platform threads, with no change to handle()? Pass Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10_000) Run handle() inside CompletableFuture.supplyAsync Call socket.setSoTimeout(100) on every connection Pass Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() A virtual thread blocked in read() parks on the JDK's poller and frees its carrier, so idle connections hold no OS thread. A fixed pool of 10,000 is still 10,000 platform threads. supplyAsync runs on the common pool, which has about one thread per core, so most connections would never be served. A short timeout only makes reads fail. From the executors track: every thread of a 50-thread pool waits on a payment API that takes 2 s. What is the most this pool can finish per second, however much traffic arrives? 25 50 100 200 Turn Little's law around: throughput = threads / time per request = 50 / 2 s = 25 requests a second. Extra traffic only lengthens the queue. What do non-blocking IO and virtual threads change for a single request that waits 120 ms for the card issuer? It completes in well under 120 ms Not its latency: they let many more such requests wait at the same time, at a lower cost per wait It no longer needs a database connection It gets retried automatically when the issuer is slow Both techniques make waiting cheap, so one JVM can keep more requests in flight. The request itself still waits 120 ms for the issuer. Downstream limits such as connection pools stay exactly where they were.
