h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Key terms
x: Blocking IO A read or write that makes the calling thread wait until the operation can finish. Thread-per-connection A server design that gives every open socket its own thread for the socket's whole life. Thread-per-request A design where a thread is taken from a pool only while a request is being processed. Little's law In-flight items = arrival rate × time each item spends in the system. C10K Ten thousand concurrent clients on one server; the name of the scaling problem Dan Kegel described in 1999. Readiness notification The kernel tells you which sockets can be read or written now (select, poll, epoll, kqueue). Keep-alive connection A connection the client leaves open between requests, so it is idle most of the time. What does getState() report for a platform thread blocked in a socket read()? RUNNABLE. The wait happens in native code (SocketDispatcher.read0), so idle servers look busy in thread dumps. Little's law, in one line? Requests in the system = arrival rate × time in system (L = λ × W). With thread-per-request, that is the number of threads you need. Why does thread-per-connection need more threads than thread-per-request? A connection holds its thread while it sits idle between requests. Threads follow open sockets, not requests in flight. What is the C10K problem? Dan Kegel's 1999 name for serving ten thousand concurrent clients from one server. Thread-per-connection didn't scale there; non-blocking sockets with kernel readiness notification did. What does epoll (Linux) or kqueue (macOS) give a server? One call that returns only the sockets that are ready, so one thread can watch thousands of connections. Do virtual threads make a request faster? No. They make waiting cheap, so more requests can wait at once. A 120 ms issuer call still takes 120 ms. 2,000 virtual threads blocked in socket reads on a 4-core JDK 21 machine: about how many platform threads? About 15 (this lesson's demo): 4 carriers, a few JDK poller threads, and the JVM's own threads.

h: Blocking IO, threads and the C10K problem · Go deeper
x: "About 1 MiB per platform thread" needs one detail to be useful. On 64-bit Linux the default stack size (-Xss) is 1 MB, and the JVM reserves that much address space per thread. The kernel commits pages only as the stack actually grows, so 2,000 idle threads don't use 2 GB of RAM. They do use real memory for the pages they touched, kernel structures per thread, and a scheduler entry each. You can see the JVM's view with Native Memory Tracking. Start a JVM with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and run jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary. The Thread section shows how many threads exist and their reserved and committed stack memory. Run it on the demo while it holds 2,000 platform threads and again during the virtual-thread phase. The limit you hit first in production is often not memory. Containers and hosts cap the number of processes and threads per user or per cgroup (ulimit -u, the cgroup pids.max). When a JVM can't create a thread it throws OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread, a confusing name for a thread-count limit. Thread-per-connection is not always wrong. An internal service with 50 long-lived connections and steady traffic is simpler and faster to debug with one thread per connection, and the thread count never gets near any limit. The problem starts when connection count grows independently of the work, as with keep-alive clients, terminals and mobile apps.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · A ByteBuffer is a cursor with two marks
x: Everything in java.nio moves bytes through a ByteBuffer: a fixed block of memory with three numbers. capacity is its size. position is where the next put or get happens. limit is where reading or writing must stop. Most NIO bugs are one of these three numbers being wrong. A fresh buffer is in write mode: position 0 and limit equal to capacity. Each put moves position forward. Before you can read what you wrote, flip() sets limit to the current position and position back to 0. This section's demo walks a 16-byte buffer through the whole cycle: allocate(16) pos=0 lim=16 cap=16 remaining=16 put("hello") pos=5 lim=16 cap=16 remaining=11 flip() pos=0 lim=5 cap=16 remaining=5 get(2) -> "he" pos=2 lim=5 cap=16 remaining=3 compact() pos=3 lim=16 cap=16 remaining=13 put("XY") pos=5 lim=16 cap=16 remaining=11 flip() pos=0 lim=5 cap=16 remaining=5 readable content: "lloXY" compact() is the call server code needs most. It copies the unread bytes (llo) to the front and puts the buffer back in write mode right after them, so new data lands behind what you haven't used yet. clear() looks similar and does something else: it resets both marks and forgets everything, read or not. Forget flip() and nothing throws. A buffer of 8 with 2 bytes put has remaining() 6, so a write sends the 6 bytes after your data, whatever they happen to be. There are two kinds of buffer. allocate gives a heap buffer backed by a byte[]. allocateDirect gives memory outside the Java heap. The JDK's Javadoc says direct buffers have "somewhat higher allocation and deallocation costs" and recommends them for large, long-lived buffers used for native IO. They exist because the kernel reads and writes memory by address during a system call, and the garbage collector is allowed to move a byte[] on the heap. So the JDK copies a heap buffer through a temporary direct buffer on every channel read and write (sun.nio.ch.IOUtil does it). So allocate direct buffers once and reuse them. Netty's pooled allocators do exactly that for you. Predict the marks Open BufferDemo.java (or BufferDemo.kt). Cover the output above and predict pos and lim after compact(). Run it with the command below and check your prediction. Change b.compact() to b.clear() and run it again. What does readable content print now, and which bytes are gone? BufferDemo.java package workbench.nio.l02; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.US_ASCII; /** Walks a ByteBuffer through put, flip, get, compact and clear, printing its cursor after each step. */ public class BufferDemo { static void show(String step, ByteBuffer b) { System.out.printf("%-20s pos=%-2d lim=%-2d cap=%-2d remaining=%d%n", step, b.position(), b.limit(), b.capacity(), b.remaining()); } public static void main(String[] args) { ByteBuffer b = ByteBuffer.allocate(16); show("allocate(16)", b); b.put("hello".getBytes(US_ASCII)); show("put(\"hello\")", b); b.flip(); // write mode -> read mode: limit = position, position = 0 show("flip()", b); byte[] two = new byte[2]; b.get(two); show("get(2) -> \"" + new String(two, US_ASCII) + "\"", b); b.compact(); // move the unread "llo" to the front, back to write mode show("compact()", b); b.put("XY".getBytes(US_ASCII)); show("put(\"XY\")", b); b.flip(); show("flip()", b); byte[] rest = new byte[b.remaining()]; b.get(rest); System.out.println("readable content: \"" + new String(rest, US_ASCII) + "\""); ByteBuffer forgot = ByteBuffer.allocate(8); forgot.put((byte) 1).put((byte) 2); // no flip() before handing it to write() System.out.println("forgot flip(): remaining()=" + forgot.remaining() + ", so a write would send 6 stale bytes, not the 2 you put"); ByteBuffer heap = ByteBuffer.allocate(64), direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64); System.out.println("heap: isDirect=" + heap.isDirect() + " hasArray=" + heap.hasArray() + " " + heap.getClass().getName()); System.out.println("direct: isDirect=" + direct.isDirect() + " hasArray=" + direct.hasArray() + " " + direct.getClass().getName()); } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l02.BufferDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l02/BufferDemo.java BufferDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l02 import java.nio.ByteBuffer import kotlin.text.Charsets.US_ASCII /** Walks a ByteBuffer through put, flip, get, compact and clear, printing its cursor after each step. */ private fun show(step: String, b: ByteBuffer) = println("%-20s pos=%-2d lim=%-2d cap=%-2d remaining=%d".format(step, b.position(), b.limit(), b.capacity(), b.remaining())) fun main() { val b = ByteBuffer.allocate(16) show("allocate(16)", b) b.put("hello".toByteArray(US_ASCII)) show("put(\"hello\")", b) b.flip() // write mode -> read mode: limit = position, position = 0 show("flip()", b) val two = ByteArray(2) b.get(two) show("get(2) -> \"${String(two, US_ASCII)}\"", b) b.compact() // move the unread "llo" to the front, back to write mode show("compact()", b) b.put("XY".toByteArray(US_ASCII)) show("put(\"XY\")", b) b.flip() show("flip()", b) val rest = ByteArray(b.remaining()) b.get(rest) println("readable content: \"${String(rest, US_ASCII)}\"") val forgot = ByteBuffer.allocate(8) forgot.put(1).put(2) // no flip() before handing it to write() println("forgot flip(): remaining()=${forgot.remaining()}, so a write would send 6 stale bytes, not the 2 you put") val heap = ByteBuffer.allocate(64) val direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(64) println("heap: isDirect=${heap.isDirect} hasArray=${heap.hasArray()} ${heap.javaClass.name}") println("direct: isDirect=${direct.isDirect} hasArray=${direct.hasArray()} ${direct.javaClass.name}") } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l02.BufferDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l02/BufferDemo.kt With compact(): pos=3 lim=16, and the content ends as lloXY. With clear(): pos=0 lim=16 after the call, XY overwrites the first two bytes, and readable content prints just XY. The unread llo was dropped without an error. That is the bug in this lesson's lab. Three moments of one buffer: after writing hello, after flip() the readable bytes run from pos to lim, and compact() keeps the unread llo at the front. Level-triggered readiness is a doorbell that rings for as long as someone stands at the door. OP_READ asks "ring while a visitor is waiting": you answer, take the parcel, and it stops. OP_WRITE asks "ring while there is room in the outbox", and the outbox is nearly always empty, so it rings all day and you keep walking to the door for nothing. Ask for that ring only when you have a letter to post. The analogy breaks in one place: epoll doesn't ring on its own. Your loop asks it, and level-triggered means it answers yes every time you ask.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Non-blocking reads and writes move only what fits
x: Every TCP socket has two buffers inside the kernel. The receive buffer holds bytes that arrived from the network and that your program hasn't read yet. The send buffer holds bytes your program wrote that the kernel hasn't delivered to the other side yet. read and write never touch the network themselves: they copy between your ByteBuffer and these kernel buffers. Put a SocketChannel in non-blocking mode with configureBlocking(false) and those copies stop waiting. They do what the buffers allow right now and return. read(buf) copies whatever sits in the socket's receive buffer. That can be one byte, half a message, three messages, or nothing at all, in which case it returns 0. It returns -1 when the other side has closed its end. write(buf) is the call that bites. Its Javadoc says a socket channel in non-blocking mode "cannot write any more bytes than are free in the socket's output buffer". When the client reads slowly, the kernel's send buffer fills, and write sends part of your buffer or none of it. So every connection needs its own buffer for the bytes it hasn't sent yet. The pattern that handles both directions is four lines: Java int n = ch.read(buf); // append whatever arrived, maybe 0 bytes; -1 means the client is done buf.flip(); // switch to reading what we hold ch.write(buf); // send what the kernel accepts, maybe only part of it buf.compact(); // keep the unsent tail at the front, back to write mode Kotlin val n = ch.read(buf) // append whatever arrived, maybe 0 bytes; -1 means the client is done buf.flip() // switch to reading what we hold ch.write(buf) // send what the kernel accepts, maybe only part of it buf.compact() // keep the unsent tail at the front, back to write mode After compact(), buf.position() > 0 means bytes are still waiting. One run for this track echoed 8 MiB to a client with a 4 KiB receive buffer and counted 8 partial writes. With clear() in place of compact(), each of them would have dropped bytes. The read side has a twin rule: one read is not one message. TCP is a byte stream. A payment message sent with one write can arrive in three reads, and two messages can arrive in one. Anything more than raw echo needs framing, such as a length prefix or a delimiter. Lesson 4 builds one with Netty. One trap lives in the client. If a test client writes 8 MiB and only then starts reading, the echo stalls: the server can't send because the client isn't reading, so the server stops reading, so the client's write blocks. Clients of an echo server must read and write at the same time. The lab's tests use a writer thread for exactly this reason. Count the lost bytes Before you fix anything, run the lab tests with the command below. Read the failure for echoesEverything: how many of the 4,194,304 bytes came back? Run it twice more. Predict first: will the number be the same? terminal ./gradlew :nio:test --tests 'workbench.nio.l02.*' The echo comes back short, by a different amount every run (3,469,312, then 3,405,824, then 3,536,896 bytes in three runs here). How much gets lost depends on how often the kernel's send buffer was full at the moment the server wrote, which is timing. The idle test fails too, with a wakeup count in the hundreds of thousands. WritableByteChannel.write Javadoc (JDK 25 source) docs You won't write raw selectors in a Quarkus service, but you will debug their failure modes. A Vert.x or Netty process at 100% of one core with no traffic is often a loop that wakes without work to do. Netty itself fixed one in 4.2.20 (commit 06518dc): a timer due in under half a millisecond rounded the select timeout down to 0, so a loop with a pending timer polled the selector in a circle. Partial reads matter every time you parse a TCP protocol by hand, such as an ISO 8583 link to a card network: a message arrives in several reads, and only its length prefix tells you when you have all of it.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · A Selector tells one thread which channels are ready
x: A thread per connection versus one thread asking a Selector what is ready A Selector watches many channels at once. You register each channel with an interest set, the operations you care about (OP_ACCEPT, OP_READ, OP_WRITE), and select() blocks until at least one of them is ready. Each registration is a SelectionKey. It carries the interest set, the ready set that the selector fills in, and an attachment where you keep that connection's state. Java while (true) { selector.select(); // sleep until something is ready Iterator<SelectionKey> it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator(); while (it.hasNext()) { SelectionKey key = it.next(); it.remove(); // you must remove handled keys yourself if (key.isAcceptable()) { SocketChannel ch = server.accept(); ch.configureBlocking(false); ch.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ, new Conn()); } else { serve(key); // read, write, update the interest set } } } Kotlin while (true) { selector.select() // sleep until something is ready val it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator() while (it.hasNext()) { val key = it.next() it.remove() // you must remove handled keys yourself if (key.isAcceptable) { val ch = server.accept() ch.configureBlocking(false) ch.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ, Conn()) } else { serve(key) // read, write, update the interest set } } } The it.remove() line is not optional. The selector adds keys to the selected-key set and never takes them out. Leave a key in and the next pass handles it again with its old ready set. In this section's demo, one 6-byte message was handled as readable 7 times in 300 ms. For an accept key, that means calling accept() again and getting null back. The selector also comes with a threading rule. Its Javadoc says a selector is safe for concurrent use, but its selected-key set is not. The simple way to obey that is the one every framework uses: one thread owns a selector, runs its loop, and does all the work for its channels. Netty calls that thread an event loop. On Linux, Selector.open() returns sun.nio.ch.EPollSelectorImpl, a wrapper around epoll. On macOS you get a kqueue selector. The JDK registers sockets with epoll in level-triggered mode: as long as a socket is readable or writable, every select() reports it again. That one fact is behind the bug in the next section. Forget it.remove() Open StaleKeyDemo.java (or StaleKeyDemo.kt). A client sends exactly one 6-byte message, and the loop runs for 300 ms, once removing handled keys and once not. Predict how many times each version treats the channel as readable. Run it with the command below. StaleKeyDemo.java package workbench.nio.l02; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import java.nio.channels.SelectionKey; import java.nio.channels.Selector; import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel; import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel; import java.util.Iterator; /** One message arrives. How many times does the loop think the channel is readable? */ public class StaleKeyDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { run(true); run(false); } static void run(boolean removeHandledKeys) throws Exception { try (Selector selector = Selector.open(); ServerSocketChannel server = ServerSocketChannel.open()) { server.bind(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)); try (SocketChannel client = SocketChannel.open(server.getLocalAddress()); SocketChannel conn = server.accept()) { conn.configureBlocking(false); conn.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ); client.write(ByteBuffer.wrap("auth-1".getBytes())); // exactly one message ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(64); int loops = 0, handled = 0, bytes = 0; long end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L; while (System.nanoTime() < end) { selector.select(50); loops++; Iterator<SelectionKey> it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator(); while (it.hasNext()) { SelectionKey key = it.next(); if (removeHandledKeys) it.remove(); if (key.isReadable()) { // ready set from the last select that added the key handled++; buf.clear(); bytes += Math.max(0, conn.read(buf)); } } } System.out.printf("remove handled keys=%-5s loops=%d, handled as readable %d times, bytes read %d%n", removeHandledKeys, loops, handled, bytes); } } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l02.StaleKeyDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l02/StaleKeyDemo.java StaleKeyDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l02 import java.net.InetAddress import java.net.InetSocketAddress import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.nio.channels.SelectionKey import java.nio.channels.Selector import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel /** One message arrives. How many times does the loop think the channel is readable? */ fun main() { staleKeys(removeHandledKeys = true) staleKeys(removeHandledKeys = false) } private fun staleKeys(removeHandledKeys: Boolean) { Selector.open().use { selector -> ServerSocketChannel.open().use { server -> server.bind(InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)) SocketChannel.open(server.localAddress).use { client -> server.accept().use { conn -> conn.configureBlocking(false) conn.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ) client.write(ByteBuffer.wrap("auth-1".toByteArray())) // exactly one message val buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(64) var loops = 0 var handled = 0 var bytes = 0 val end = System.nanoTime() + 300_000_000L while (System.nanoTime() < end) { selector.select(50) loops++ val it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator() while (it.hasNext()) { val key = it.next() if (removeHandledKeys) it.remove() if (key.isReadable) { // ready set from the last select that added the key handled++ buf.clear() bytes += maxOf(0, conn.read(buf)) } } } println("remove handled keys=%-5s loops=%d, handled as readable %d times, bytes read %d" .format(removeHandledKeys, loops, handled, bytes)) } } } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l02.StaleKeyDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l02/StaleKeyDemo.kt With it.remove(): handled once, 6 bytes read. Without it: handled 7 times in 7 loop passes, still 6 bytes in total. h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Arm OP_WRITE only while bytes are waiting
x: A socket is writable whenever its send buffer has free space, which is nearly always. Combine that with level-triggered epoll and you get the classic NIO bug. Register OP_WRITE on every connection and select() never sleeps again: it returns at once, reports every idle connection as writable, and the loop goes around again. This section's demo measures it on one idle connection for 300 ms: Selector implementation: sun.nio.ch.EPollSelectorImpl idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ : 0 wakeups idle 300 ms, interest OP_READ | OP_WRITE: 431909 wakeups Zero against several hundred thousand, on a connection that sent nothing. Under strace the shape is just as clear: thousands of epoll_wait calls and a handful of epoll_ctl. In production it looks like a server at 100% of one core with no traffic. The rule is to register OP_READ by default and add OP_WRITE only while the connection has unsent bytes. When a write leaves bytes behind, arm it. When a later write drains them, drop it: Java boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0; // after compact(): unsent bytes at the front int ops = 0; if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_READ; // room left: keep reading if (pending) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_WRITE; // only while bytes wait key.interestOps(ops); Kotlin val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0 // after compact(): unsent bytes at the front var ops = 0 if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ // room left: keep reading if (pending) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE // only while bytes wait key.interestOps(ops) The OP_READ line is the other half of the same idea. When the buffer is full because the client reads slowly, stop reading from that client. Its bytes pile up in your socket's receive buffer, and TCP tells the client how much free space is left there (the TCP window). As the window shrinks to zero, the client's own writes stop. That is backpressure in two lines, and lesson 4 shows Netty's version of it: writability and AUTO_READ. In the 8 MiB run mentioned earlier, the server armed OP_WRITE only 4 times in 537 selects. Closing follows the same logic. A client can half-close a connection (shutdownOutput()): it says it will send nothing more but keeps reading. Your read then returns -1, yet the client still wants the rest of its echo. Close only once nothing is pending. Watch the spin Run SpinDemo (or SpinDemoKt) with the command below. Predict both numbers first. On Linux with strace installed, run it outside Gradle to count system calls: strace -f -c -e trace=epoll_wait,epoll_ctl java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo workbench.nio.l02.SpinDemo. the exact number depends on CPU speed). Under strace the loop slows down a lot, because strace stops the process on every system call, but the table still shows thousands of epoll_wait calls (4,315 in my run) against 5 epoll_ctl. On macOS the first line names the kqueue selector. The classic mistake is registering OP_WRITE together with OP_READ "so the loop can write whenever it needs to". On a level-triggered selector a socket with buffer space is always writable, so the loop spins at 100% CPU. The second classic is assuming one write sends the whole buffer and calling clear() after it, which silently drops bytes as soon as a client reads slowly. Write, compact(), check position() > 0, and arm OP_WRITE only then. Close on EOF only after the pending bytes are gone.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Java and Kotlin
x: The serve step in Java and Kotlin serve, Java private void serve(SelectionKey key) throws IOException { SocketChannel ch = (SocketChannel) key.channel(); Conn conn = (Conn) key.attachment(); if (key.isReadable() && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true; conn.buf.flip(); if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf); conn.buf.compact(); boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0; if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return; } int ops = 0; if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_READ; if (pending) ops |= SelectionKey.OP_WRITE; key.interestOps(ops); } serve, Kotlin private fun serve(key: SelectionKey) { val ch = key.channel() as SocketChannel val conn = key.attachment() as Conn if (key.isReadable && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true conn.buf.flip() if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf) conn.buf.compact() val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0 if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return } var ops = 0 if (!conn.eof && conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ if (pending) ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_WRITE key.interestOps(ops) } Both call the same JDK API, so behavior is identical: same partial writes, same level-triggered selector. The differences are surface ones that still trip people up. Kotlin has no |= for bit flags, so you write ops = ops or SelectionKey.OP_READ. Kotlin reads isReadable() and isAcceptable() as properties (key.isReadable), and the attachment is an untyped Any? that you cast with as Conn, just as Java casts from Object. Neither language helps you with the buffer's mode: flip() and compact() are runtime state, not types, so the compiler can't stop you from writing a buffer that is still in write mode.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Worked example
x: Trace one connection through a partial write The client sends 20 KiB and reads slowly. The server's buffer holds 16 KiB. First select(): readable. The server reads 16 KiB, flips, and the kernel accepts only 6 KiB of the write. read 16384 -> pos=16384 lim=16384 (buffer full) flip() -> pos=0 lim=16384 write -> 6144 -> pos=6144 lim=16384 (10240 bytes not sent) compact() -> pos=10240 lim=16384 (pending: 10240, room: 6144) interest = OP_READ | OP_WRITE Second select(): readable (the other 4 KiB arrived) and writable (the client read some). The server appends 4 KiB behind the pending bytes, then sends everything it holds. read 4096 -> pos=14336 lim=16384 flip() -> pos=0 lim=14336 write -> 14336 -> pos=14336 lim=14336 (all sent) compact() -> pos=0 lim=16384 (pending: 0) interest = OP_READ (OP_WRITE dropped: nothing to send) Now the client half-closes while the server still holds bytes. read returns -1, so stop reading, but keep OP_WRITE until the tail is gone. Close in the pass where pending reaches zero. // 1. remember EOF, don't close yet if (key.isReadable() && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true; // 2. send what we can, keep the rest conn.buf.flip(); if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf); conn.buf.compact(); // 3. close only when drained; otherwise ask for exactly what we need boolean pending = conn.buf.position() > 0; if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return; } key.interestOps((conn.eof ? 0 : SelectionKey.OP_READ) | (pending ? SelectionKey.OP_WRITE : 0)); // 1. remember EOF, don't close yet if (key.isReadable && ch.read(conn.buf) < 0) conn.eof = true // 2. send what we can, keep the rest conn.buf.flip() if (conn.buf.hasRemaining()) ch.write(conn.buf) conn.buf.compact() // 3. close only when drained; otherwise ask for exactly what we need val pending = conn.buf.position() > 0 if (conn.eof && !pending) { ch.close(); return } key.interestOps((if (conn.eof) 0 else SelectionKey.OP_READ) or (if (pending) SelectionKey.OP_WRITE else 0)) The lab's version adds one more condition: drop OP_READ while the buffer has no room left. Without it, a full buffer and a readable socket make the same spin as a stray OP_WRITE: select() says readable, read() copies 0 bytes into the full buffer, and the loop goes around again.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Quiz
x: A buffer of capacity 16 holds hello after five put calls. You call flip(), then get() twice, then compact(). Where are position and limit? position 0, limit 3 position 3, limit 16 position 2, limit 5 position 5, limit 16 compact() moves the 3 unread bytes (llo) to the front, sets position right after them (3) and limit back to capacity (16), ready for more writing. Position 2, limit 5 is the state before compact(). A non-blocking ch.write(buf) returns 4,096, and buf.remaining() was 16,384 before the call. What should the server do? Call write in a loop until everything is sent Throw an IOException: the client is broken Keep the 12,288 bytes with compact(), arm OP_WRITE, and go back to select() clear() the buffer and read the next message The kernel's send buffer is full. Looping would spin (later writes return 0) and hold up every other connection on this thread. Keep the bytes, ask the selector to say when the socket is writable again, and serve other connections meanwhile. Your NIO server uses one core at 100% with no traffic. Profiles show the loop thread in EPollSelectorImpl.doSelect over and over. What is the most likely cause? OP_WRITE stays in the interest set of idle connections The ByteBuffer is a heap buffer, not a direct one One selector has too many connections The JIT compiled the loop badly A level-triggered selector reports a writable socket on every call, and idle sockets are writable. Heap buffers cost a copy per IO, not a spin, and a busy selector would show real traffic. From lesson 1: 5,000 terminals keep connections open and each sends a 100 ms request every 10 s. How many threads sit blocked in read() on a single-selector NIO server, and on a thread-per-connection server? 0 on the NIO server, about 5,000 on the other About 5,000 on both 50 on both: Little's law decides 1 on the NIO server, 50 on the other NIO reads never block: the one loop thread waits in select(), not in read(). Thread-per-connection parks one thread per open socket. Little's law gives 50 requests in flight, but that only sets the thread count for thread-per-request designs. A handler calls ch.read(buf) and then parses one payment message from buf. Under load, parsing sometimes fails on a truncated message. What is wrong? The selector is edge-triggered and lost an event The buffer must be direct read must only be called while OP_WRITE is armed It assumes one read returns one whole message; TCP can split or merge messages, so it needs framing TCP delivers a byte stream. One read can hold part of a message or several messages. A length prefix or delimiter tells the parser when a message is complete; until then, keep the bytes and wait for the next read.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Key terms
x: ByteBuffer A fixed block of memory with a position, a limit and a capacity that NIO reads into and writes from. flip / compact flip() switches a buffer from writing to reading; compact() keeps unread bytes and switches back. Selector An object that waits until one of many registered channels is ready, so one thread can serve them all. SelectionKey One channel's registration with a selector: interest set, ready set and an attachment. Interest set The operations you ask the selector to watch for on a channel: accept, read, write. Level-triggered Readiness is reported on every check for as long as it is true, not once when it changes. Partial write A non-blocking write that sends only part of the buffer because the kernel's send buffer is full. What does flip() do to a ByteBuffer? Sets limit to the current position and position to 0: it switches from writing into the buffer to reading out of it. compact() vs clear()? compact() moves unread bytes to the front and continues writing after them. clear() resets both marks and forgets unread bytes. A non-blocking write(buf) sent fewer bytes than buf.remaining(). Why, and what next? The socket's send buffer had less free space. Keep the rest (compact()), arm OP_WRITE, and write again when the selector says the socket is writable. What happens if you never remove keys from selectedKeys()? They stay selected with their old ready set, so the loop handles the same event on every pass: 7 times in 300 ms for one message in this lesson's demo. Why does a permanently registered OP_WRITE make a selector spin? Linux epoll selectors are level-triggered, and a socket with send-buffer space is always writable, so every select() returns at once. How does an NIO server push back on a client that sends faster than it reads? It drops OP_READ while its buffer is full. Unread bytes fill the kernel buffer, the TCP window shrinks, and the client's writes slow down. Heap or direct ByteBuffer for socket IO? Direct, allocated once and reused. The JDK copies a heap buffer through a temporary direct buffer on every channel read or write, and direct buffers are costly to allocate.

h: NIO: buffers, channels and selectors · Go deeper
x: Level-triggered and edge-triggered are the two ways epoll can report readiness. Level-triggered, the default, reports a socket on every epoll_wait for as long as it is readable or writable. Edge-triggered (EPOLLET) reports it once, when it changes from not ready to ready, and then stays quiet until the next change. The JDK's EPollSelectorImpl never sets EPOLLET, so Selector is level-triggered on Linux. That is forgiving for reads (if you leave bytes unread, the next select() tells you again) and unforgiving for OP_WRITE. Edge-triggered code has the opposite trap: after a notification you must read until read returns 0, or you never hear about the leftover bytes. The JDK's virtual-thread poller, which lesson 8 looks at, uses a third mode, EPOLLONESHOT: report once, then disarm until the fd is registered again. That fits its job, which is to wake one parked thread once. Two more details from the JDK source. EPollSelectorImpl asks epoll_wait for at most min(fdLimit, 1024) events per call, so a selector with 10,000 ready sockets needs several calls to see them all. And Netty's NIO transport still carries a guard against selectors that return early with nothing selected: after 512 such returns in a row (io.netty.selectorAutoRebuildThreshold), it rebuilds the selector. That is the old "epoll spin bug" workaround, and the reason NioIoHandler counts empty wakeups. To see the system calls yourself on Linux, run any demo that only uses JDK classes outside Gradle with strace -f -c -e trace=epoll_wait,epoll_ctl java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo <class>. -c prints a count per system call when the process exits.

h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · An event loop is one thread that owns its channels
x: Netty is the select loop from the last lesson, written once and written well. Each piece you wrote by hand has a Netty name, and each fixes a bug you met there: Your loop in lesson 2 Netty Why it exists one thread running select() EventLoop, several in an EventLoopGroup one loop per core instead of one per server the Conn attachment Channel and its ChannelPipeline of handlers per-connection state and logic in small pieces flip() and compact() by hand ByteBuf, with separate read and write indexes no mode to get wrong (lesson 4) pending bytes and arming OP_WRITE the channel's outbound buffer Netty sets and clears OP_WRITE for you dropping OP_READ when full autoRead and writability backpressure as a setting (lesson 4) nothing: only the loop may touch the selector a task queue on every loop any thread can hand the loop work safely So an event loop is one thread that runs a selector over many channels, plus that queue of tasks. In Netty 4.2 you build a group by naming the IO handler, the transport-specific part: Java EventLoopGroup boss = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); // accepts connections EventLoopGroup workers = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory()); // serves them Channel server = new ServerBootstrap() .group(boss, workers) .channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class) .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { @Override protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) { ch.pipeline().addLast(new LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), new StringDecoder(UTF_8), new StringEncoder(UTF_8), new QuoteHandler()); } }) .bind(8080).sync().channel(); Kotlin val boss = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()) // accepts connections val workers = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory()) // serves them val server = ServerBootstrap() .group(boss, workers) .channel(NioServerSocketChannel::class.java) .childHandler(object : ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { override fun initChannel(ch: SocketChannel) { ch.pipeline().addLast(LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), StringDecoder(UTF_8), StringEncoder(UTF_8), QuoteHandler()) } }) .bind(8080).sync().channel() If you learned Netty 4.1, you wrote new NioEventLoopGroup(). Netty 4.2 deprecated it, along with its epoll and kqueue cousins, and javac -Xlint:deprecation says so: warning: [deprecation] NioEventLoopGroup in io.netty.channel.nio has been deprecated. The replacement is always MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup plus a factory: NioIoHandler, EpollIoHandler, KQueueIoHandler or IoUringIoHandler. The bootstrap still names the matching channel class. The boss group only accepts connections and hands each one to a worker loop, so one boss thread is plenty for one listening port. Small servers often pass a single group to .group(group) and let the same loops accept and serve. The lab does that, with one loop, so that you can see a blocked loop clearly. Without a thread count, a group gets two loops per core, so the demo prints 8 on a 4-core machine. Each new connection is registered with one loop, round-robin, and stays there for life: client port 59604 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-1, inEventLoop=true client port 59620 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-2, inEventLoop=true client port 59634 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-1, inEventLoop=true That pinning is why Netty handlers rarely need locks: every event for a channel runs on its loop's one thread, one after another. It is also why one slow handler hurts. Every other channel on that loop waits behind it. See which loop owns each connection Open EventLoopDemo.java (or EventLoopDemo.kt). It starts a server with one acceptor loop and two worker loops, then connects four clients one after another. Predict the thread name for the third and fourth client, and what inEventLoop() returns inside the handler. Run it. With one worker loop, all four land on the same thread. A channel pipeline is the mail line in an office. Letters come in at the door, one clerk opens the envelopes (the frame decoder), the next reads the handwriting (the string decoder), and the last one writes the answer. Replies go back down the same line the other way, and a typist (the encoder) turns them into print before they leave. The event loop is one worker who carries each letter through every station for a fixed set of mailboxes. The analogy breaks because real clerks work at the same time. In Netty one thread carries each message through every handler, which is exactly why one slow station stops the whole line.

h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · The pipeline: reads flow in, writes flow out
x:
Netty's event loop and pipeline: reads flow in, writes flow out, never block Every channel has a ChannelPipeline: a linked list of handlers between a head, next to the socket, and a tail. Two kinds of traffic move through it. Each handler gets a ChannelHandlerContext, usually called ctx: its own slot in the pipeline, with methods to pass an event to the next handler or to start a write from that slot. Inbound events start at the head and move toward the tail: channelActive when the connection opens, channelRead for each message, channelReadComplete after a batch of reads, and exceptionCaught when something fails. Inbound handlers transform the message on its way. In the quote server, the frame decoder turns a stream of bytes into one ByteBuf per line, and StringDecoder turns that into a String, so the last handler only ever sees whole lines. Outbound operations go the other way. write, flush and close start where you call them and move toward the head. StringEncoder sits on that path and turns your String back into bytes. So the order of addLast is the order inbound events see the handlers, and the reverse of the order writes see them. One detail decides which handlers a write passes. ctx.writeAndFlush(msg) starts at the current handler and goes toward the head, skipping everything after it. ctx.channel().writeAndFlush(msg) starts at the tail and passes every outbound handler. Inside a handler, use ctx unless you really want the whole pipeline. This section's demo puts a tap between the stages and feeds one line in pieces: writeInbound("hel") writeInbound("lo
wor") in, after framing : ByteBuf "hello" in, business sees : String "hello" out, to the wire : ByteBuf "HELLO
" 100-byte line -> TooLongFrameException: frame length (100) exceeds the allowed maximum (64) finish() = false The first fragment produced nothing: the decoder kept the bytes and waited for the end of the line. That is lesson 2's framing problem, solved once inside the pipeline. The 64-byte limit matters as much. Without it, a client that never sends a newline makes the decoder buffer forever. The demo uses EmbeddedChannel, which runs a pipeline with no socket and no real event loop. writeInbound pushes bytes in, readOutbound returns what the handlers wrote, and finish() says whether anything was left over. It is the fastest way to test a handler, and this lesson's lab uses it. Move the tap past the encoder Run PipelineDemo (or PipelineDemoKt) and match each printed line to a handler in the figure. In the EmbeddedChannel constructor, move the outbound tap so it comes right after new StringEncoder(UTF_8) instead of before it. Predict what out, to the wire prints now, then run it again. Reads travel from the head through the decoders to your handler; your writes travel back through the encoder to the head. One thread runs all of it. Every HTTP request to your Quarkus services arrives through a Netty pipeline: Vert.x runs its HTTP server on Netty event loops, so a blocked Vert.x event loop is a blocked Netty event loop. h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · Never block the event loop
x:
Handlers run on the event-loop thread. A handler that sleeps, waits on a lock, or calls JDBC holds that thread, and every other channel on the loop waits with it. This section's demo measures it with one event loop and two clients. Client A asks for SLOW, which sleeps 1 s to stand in for a database call. Client B asks for FAST 50 ms later: [blocking in the handler] event-loop lag probe: 1010 ms FAST reply after 1011 ms: FAST on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-2-1 [dispatch to app pool] event-loop lag probe: 0 ms FAST reply after 2 ms: FAST on app-blocking-pool The lag probe is a trick worth keeping: submit an empty task to the loop and time how long it waits to run. On a healthy loop it is close to 0. Netty 4.1 offered a shortcut: pipeline.addLast(executorGroup, "name", handler) ran one handler on a separate EventExecutorGroup. Netty 4.2 deprecated those overloads, and compiling the old call prints warning: [deprecation] addLast(EventExecutorGroup,String,ChannelHandler) in ChannelPipeline has been deprecated. The commit that did it (d64340b) says per-handler executors caused more problems than they solved and that it is "much better to dispatch it manually". Manual dispatch is three lines. Hand the slow part to your own executor and write the reply from there: Java @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { blockingPool.execute(() -> { // 1. leave the event loop String quote = quoteDao.findQuote(line); // 2. block here: JDBC, a 120 ms issuer call ctx.writeAndFlush(quote + "
"); // 3. safe from any thread }); } Kotlin override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { blockingPool.execute { // 1. leave the event loop val quote = quoteDao.findQuote(line) // 2. block here: JDBC, a 120 ms issuer call ctx.writeAndFlush("$quote
") // 3. safe from any thread } } Step 3 works because Netty checks inEventLoop() on every write. Called from another thread, the write becomes a task on the channel's own loop, so the pipeline still runs on one thread. If code in the executor needs the handler's own fields, hop back first with ctx.executor().execute(...), so that state stays confined to the loop. Size blockingPool like any blocking pool: Little's law and the downstream's limits from lesson 1, or virtual threads. Block the loop, then free it Open BlockingLoopDemo.java (or BlockingLoopDemo.kt). h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · What else Netty 4.2 changed
x: In Netty 4.2, ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT is no longer the pooled allocator most 4.1 code and blog posts assume: it is an AdaptiveByteBufAllocator, and a plain buffer(16) comes back as a direct AdaptiveByteBuf. The migration guide says most workloads should see less memory use and that it was designed to work well with virtual threads. -Dio.netty.allocator.type=pooled brings back the old pooled allocator if you need it. io_uring graduated from the incubator to a first-class transport. The package is now io.netty.channel.uring, the classes start with IoUring, and you use it like the others: MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup with IoUringIoHandler.newFactory() and the IoUring channel classes. Lesson 8 measures it against epoll. TLS clients now verify the server's hostname by default. Code that relied on the old behavior to connect to a test server with a mismatched certificate will start failing its handshake. netty-codec was split into smaller modules, and the minimum Java version is now 8. And Netty 4.1 and 4.2 cannot be on the same classpath. That one matters in practice: Vert.x 5.2.3 pins Netty 4.2.20.Final, so a library that drags Netty 4.1 jars in next to it fails at runtime in confusing ways instead of with a clear version conflict. Check ./gradlew dependencies for mixed io.netty versions before you debug anything else. The threading rules did not change. A channel still belongs to one loop, handlers still run on it, and blocking it is still the most common way to make a Netty service slow. Switch the transport In EventLoopDemo, change both groups to EpollIoHandler.newFactory() and the channel class to EpollServerSocketChannel.class (on macOS use KQueueIoHandler and KQueueServerSocketChannel). Run it. Predict first: do the thread names or the round-robin change? Now put the channel class back to NioServerSocketChannel.class but keep the epoll (or kqueue) factory. Predict what happens before you run it. With matching factory and channel class the output looks the same: same thread names, same round-robin, because the threading model doesn't depend on the transport. With a mismatch the bind fails at once with IllegalStateException: incompatible event loop type: io.netty.channel.SingleThreadIoEventLoop: an NIO channel can only register with a loop whose IO handler is NIO. That is why the 4.2 migration guide reminds you to configure the channel class as well as the factory. The common mistake is calling something blocking from a handler because "it's only a few milliseconds": a JDBC lookup, a CompletableFuture.get(), a synchronous HTTP client, even logging to a slow appender. A few milliseconds per message on a loop that serves 2,000 connections is a queue that never drains under load. The 4.1-era fix, addLast(eventExecutorGroup, handler), is deprecated in 4.2. Dispatch the blocking part to your own executor and call ctx.writeAndFlush with the result, or move the work to a non-blocking client.

h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · Java and Kotlin
x: Offloading a slow lookup from a Netty handler QuoteHandler.java final class QuoteHandler extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String> { private final Executor blocking; private final Function<String, String> lookup; QuoteHandler(Executor blocking, Function<String, String> lookup) { this.blocking = blocking; this.lookup = lookup; } @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { blocking.execute(() -> ctx.writeAndFlush(lookup.apply(line) + "\n")); } } QuoteHandler.kt class QuoteHandler( private val blocking: Executor, private val lookup: (String) -> String, ) : SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>() { override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { blocking.execute { ctx.writeAndFlush(lookup(line) + "\n") } } } At runtime these are the same class: Netty sees a SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>, and the Kotlin lambda becomes a Runnable through SAM conversion. Kotlin saves the constructor boilerplate and takes a function type where Java needs Function<String, String>. One Kotlin-only temptation is worth naming: calling runBlocking { } inside channelRead0 to use a suspend function. That blocks the event loop just like Thread.sleep. If you want coroutines, launch on a scope with its own dispatcher and call ctx.writeAndFlush from the coroutine, which is the same manual dispatch with a different executor.

h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · Worked example
x: Offload a handler without racing on its state A handler counts the authorizations it has served on each connection and calls a card issuer that takes 120 ms. It blocks the loop. The field served is safe only because one thread touches it. final class AuthHandler extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<AuthRequest> { private int served; // per-connection state @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, AuthRequest req) { AuthResponse res = issuer.authorize(req); // 120 ms, on the event loop served++; ctx.writeAndFlush(res.withSequence(served)); } } class AuthHandler : SimpleChannelInboundHandler<AuthRequest>() { private var served = 0 // per-connection state override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, req: AuthRequest) { val res = issuer.authorize(req) // 120 ms, on the event loop served++ ctx.writeAndFlush(res.withSequence(served)) } } Moving everything into the executor frees the loop but breaks the counter. Two requests on the same connection now run on two pool threads at once, and served++ is a read-modify-write race on a plain field. blockingPool.execute(() -> { AuthResponse res = issuer.authorize(req); served++; // two pool threads, one field: lost updates ctx.writeAndFlush(res.withSequence(served)); }); blockingPool.execute { val res = issuer.authorize(req) served++ // two pool threads, one field: lost updates ctx.writeAndFlush(res.withSequence(served)) } Do only the blocking call in the pool, then hop back to the channel's loop for everything that touches handler state. The loop is the lock. @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, AuthRequest req) { blockingPool.execute(() -> { AuthResponse res = issuer.authorize(req); // 1. block off the loop ctx.executor().execute(() -> { // 2. back on the channel's loop served++; // 3. confined state, no lock needed ctx.writeAndFlush(res.withSequence(served)); }); }); } override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, req: AuthRequest) { blockingPool.execute { val res = issuer.authorize(req) // 1. block off the loop ctx.executor().execute { // 2. back on the channel's loop served++ // 3. confined state, no lock needed ctx.writeAndFlush(res.withSequence(served)) } } } One thing the loop no longer gives you is order. Two requests on one connection can finish in either order, so replies can overtake each other. Either carry a correlation id the client matches on (most payment protocols do), or keep one request in flight per connection by turning off auto-read until the reply is written. h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · Key terms
x: EventLoop One thread that runs a selector over its channels plus a queue of tasks. EventLoopGroup A set of event loops; new channels are spread over them round-robin. IoHandler Netty 4.2's transport-specific engine inside a loop: NIO, epoll, kqueue or io_uring. ChannelPipeline The ordered list of handlers every event and write of a channel passes through. Inbound handler A handler for events coming from the socket, such as channelRead. Outbound handler A handler for operations going to the socket, such as write and flush. EmbeddedChannel A channel with no socket, for testing a pipeline synchronously. Netty 4.2 replacement for new NioEventLoopGroup()? new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory()), optionally with a thread count. The same pattern works with EpollIoHandler, KQueueIoHandler and IoUringIoHandler. Default number of event loops in a Netty group? 2 × available processors (property io.netty.eventLoopThreads): 8 on a 4-core machine. How long does a channel stay on its event loop? For its whole life. All its events run on that one thread, one after another. ctx.writeAndFlush(msg) vs ctx.channel().writeAndFlush(msg)? ctx starts at the current handler and goes toward the head. channel() starts at the tail and passes every outbound handler. Is ctx.writeAndFlush safe to call from a thread that isn't the event loop? Yes. Netty sees inEventLoop() is false and queues the write as a task on the channel's own loop. Why did Netty 4.2 deprecate addLast(EventExecutorGroup, ...)? Per-handler executors caused more problems than they solved. Netty now says to dispatch blocking work manually to your own executor. What is an event-loop lag probe? Submit an empty task to the loop and time how long it waits to run. Near 0 ms on a healthy loop; about the block time when a handler blocks.

h: Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline · Go deeper
x: Two details make manual dispatch work, and both are worth reading in Netty's source. First, every outbound call checks where it runs. AbstractChannelHandlerContext.write asks executor.inEventLoop(). On the loop, it calls the next handler directly. Off the loop, it wraps the write in a task and puts it on the loop's queue. That is why ctx.writeAndFlush from your pool is safe, and also why it is not free: each one is a task hand-off and a wake-up of the selector. Second, the loop interleaves IO and tasks. A Netty 4.2 loop is a SingleThreadIoEventLoop: it runs the IO handler (select and process ready channels), then drains its task queue, then selects again. Tasks you submit from other threads, writes from your pool, and timers all share the thread with IO. The 4.2 migration guide mentions hooks to measure how long IO processing and task processing take per loop run, for exactly this kind of tuning. When you dispatch, think about the order of replies on a connection, as the worked example showed, and about backpressure: if the pool is slower than the arrival rate, its queue grows without bound unless something stops reading. Lesson 4 covers AUTO_READ and writability, which are Netty's tools for that. To catch accidental blocking in tests, Netty ships an integration for BlockHound (Hidden$NettyBlockHoundIntegration in netty-common). BlockHound itself is a separate Java agent library. Installed in a test, it throws when code on a Netty event-loop thread calls a known blocking method such as Thread.sleep or a socket read.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Frame first, then decode
x: TCP delivers a stream of bytes, not messages (lesson 2). So the first job of any protocol pipeline is framing: finding where one message ends and the next begins. The payment link in this lesson's lab uses the most common framing for binary protocols, a length prefix: [ length: int32 ][ type: int8 ][ body: UTF-8 bytes ] length = 1 + body bytes Here is a frame decoder written by hand. Netty's ByteToMessageDecoder is a handler that keeps every byte that has arrived so far in one buffer (Netty calls it the cumulation) and calls your decode each time more bytes arrive. Your job is to take out whole frames and leave the rest for later: Java class HandMadeFrameDecoder extends ByteToMessageDecoder { @Override protected void decode(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, ByteBuf in, List<Object> out) { if (in.readableBytes() < 4) return; // 1. not even the length yet int length = in.getInt(in.readerIndex()); // 2. peek, don't consume if (length > 1020) throw new TooLongFrameException("frame too long: " + length); if (in.readableBytes() < 4 + length) return; // 3. body incomplete: wait for more in.skipBytes(4); out.add(in.readRetainedSlice(length)); // 4. one whole frame, no copy } } Kotlin class HandMadeFrameDecoder : ByteToMessageDecoder() { override fun decode(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, input: ByteBuf, out: MutableList<Any>) { if (input.readableBytes() < 4) return // 1. not even the length yet val length = input.getInt(input.readerIndex()) // 2. peek, don't consume if (length > 1020) throw TooLongFrameException("frame too long: $length") if (input.readableBytes() < 4 + length) return // 3. body incomplete: wait for more input.skipBytes(4) out += input.readRetainedSlice(length) // 4. one whole frame, no copy } } Each line follows a rule from the ByteToMessageDecoder Javadoc. Return without moving the reader index when a frame is incomplete. Use getInt(in.readerIndex()), not getInt(0), because the cumulation can still hold consumed bytes in front of the reader index. Hand the frame on as a slice, a view of the same memory, because readBytes(n) allocates a new buffer that someone must release. And never mark a ByteToMessageDecoder @Sharable: it keeps per-channel state. You don't have to write it. new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(1024, 0, 4, 0, 4) does the same job: frames of at most 1024 bytes, a length field at offset 0 that is 4 bytes long, no adjustment (the length counts only what follows it), and strip 4 bytes before passing the frame on. The figure shows each number on the wire. The next decoder sees exactly [type][body] and turns it into a PaymentMessage. On the way out, a MessageToByteEncoder<PaymentMessage> writes the three fields back. The maximum is a security setting. A client that sends a length of two billion would make a decoder without one buffer two gigabytes while it waits. With it, the demo's hostile frame fails at once with Adjusted frame length exceeds 1024: 5004 - discarded (5,000 plus the 4-byte length field). Feed a codec in awkward pieces Open CodecDemo.java (or CodecDemo.kt). It encodes two frames, 11 and 14 bytes long, and feeds them to a server pipeline cut at bytes 3, 9 and 14. Predict which of the four slices produce a reply, and which reply. Run it. Then change the cut at 9 to 11 and predict again. The four numbers after 1024 say where the length is, how long it is, how to adjust it, and how many bytes to strip before the next decoder. The outbound buffer is a bathtub with the drain open and two marks painted on the side. Your handler is the tap. The drain is the socket, and it empties only as fast as the client reads. When the water passes the high mark you turn the tap off (auto-read off), and when it falls below the low mark you turn it back on. Leave the tap running and the bathroom floods. The analogy breaks at the tap: turning it off doesn't waste water. The client's data waits upstream, in the kernel's buffers and the client's own send buffer, and TCP slows the client down for you.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · A ByteBuf has two indexes and a reference count
x: Netty's ByteBuf fixes the two things that made ByteBuffer painful in lesson 2. It has separate readerIndex and writerIndex, so there is no read mode, no write mode and no flip(). And it is reference-counted, so Netty can pool its memory. Pooling is the reason for the counting. Netty allocates direct memory, outside the Java heap, because the kernel can read it without a copy. Direct memory is costly to allocate, so Netty's allocator carves buffers out of big chunks and takes them back for reuse. The garbage collector can't do that hand-back: it frees an object at some unknown later time, when heap pressure says so, while a busy server needs the memory back the moment a message is done. So every ByteBuf carries a count. It starts at 1, retain() adds one, release() subtracts one, and at 0 the memory goes back to the pool. Touch the buffer after that and Netty throws: buffer(16): AdaptiveByteBuf direct=true readerIndex=0 writerIndex=0 refCnt=1 after writeInt+writeLong: writerIndex=12 readableBytes=12 after readInt: readerIndex=4 readableBytes=8 (no flip) retain(): refCnt=2 release() -> false, refCnt=1 release() -> true, refCnt=0 (memory goes back to the allocator) readLong() after release -> IllegalReferenceCountException: refCnt: 0 AdaptiveByteBuf comes from the adaptive allocator, the default since Netty 4.2. Who calls release()? Netty's wiki answers in one sentence: the party that accesses a reference-counted object last is responsible for destroying it. In a pipeline that works out as follows. A handler that passes a message on with ctx.fireChannelRead(msg) hands over ownership and must not release it. A handler that consumes a message and doesn't pass it on must release it. SimpleChannelInboundHandler does that for you after channelRead0 returns. A message you write belongs to Netty, which releases it once it is on the wire. A decoder that turns a buffer into something else releases the input. ByteToMessageDecoder and MessageToMessageDecoder do it for you. Get it wrong one way and you release twice: IllegalReferenceCountException, loud and immediate. Get it wrong the other way and you leak pooled memory that never comes back, quietly, until the service runs out of direct memory. Predict the count Open RefCountDemo.java (or RefCountDemo.kt). Cover the output above and predict refCnt after each line, and what release() returns each time. Run it. Then look at the composite part: addComponents(true, header, body) joins two buffers. Predict what body.refCnt() is after frame.release(). Reading after that throws IllegalReferenceCountException: refCnt: 0. The composite prints HDR:Payload: it shares memory with body, so the change made through body shows up without a copy. addComponents(true, ...) transferred ownership, so releasing the composite released both parts: header.refCnt=0 body.refCnt=0. Card networks and acquirer hosts often speak ISO 8583 over long-lived TCP connections, framed with a short binary length header in front of each message. That is LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder territory, as the worked example shows: a 2-byte length is (maxLength, 0, 2, 0, 2), and a length that counts its own two bytes needs a lengthAdjustment of -2. If such a gateway runs on Netty or Vert.x, a missing release() shows up weeks later as direct memory that only grows, until buffer allocations fail with an out-of-direct-memory error. Run the gateway's pipeline tests at PARANOID, and give every channel that forwards to a slower system writability-based backpressure.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · PARANOID leak detection catches leaks in tests
x: A leaked ByteBuf doesn't throw. Netty finds leaks after the fact with ResourceLeakDetector. It attaches a weak reference to each buffer it tracks, and when the garbage collector collects a tracked buffer whose count never reached 0, the detector logs a report. Tracking costs time, so by default (the SIMPLE level) Netty tracks about 1 buffer in 128. ADVANCED samples the same way but also records where the buffer was touched. PARANOID tracks every buffer with full records, and the Netty wiki recommends it for tests. Turn it on with -Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=paranoid, or in a test with ResourceLeakDetector.setLevel(Level.PARANOID). This is the start of the report from this section's demo, where a handler drops ten buffers without releasing them: [main] ERROR io.netty.util.ResourceLeakDetector - LEAK: ByteBuf.release() was not called before it's garbage-collected. See https://netty.io/wiki/reference-counted-objects.html for more information. Recent access records: #1: Hint: 'LeakDemo$1#0' will handle the message from this point. ... Created at: io.netty.buffer.AdaptiveByteBufAllocator.newDirectBuffer(AdaptiveByteBufAllocator.java:67) ... 10 buffers leaked; the listener saw 1 report(s): [ByteBuf] Read it from the bottom. Created at is where the buffer was allocated, and the access records show who touched it last: the hint names the handler that received it and never let go. Ten buffers leaked, yet there is one report, because the detector reports each distinct access path once. To fail a build on a leak you need two more pieces. ByteBufUtil.setLeakListener(...) gives you a callback per report, so a test can collect them. And detection needs a garbage collection followed by another allocation, because the detector checks its queue of collected buffers when it tracks the next one. The lab's last test does exactly that: Java for (int i = 0; i < 40 && leaks.isEmpty(); i++) { System.gc(); // collect the leaked ByteBuf objects Thread.sleep(20); ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT.buffer(8).release(); // the next allocation reports them } assertThat(leaks).isEmpty(); Kotlin var i = 0 while (i++ < 40 && leaks.isEmpty()) { System.gc() // collect the leaked ByteBuf objects Thread.sleep(20) ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT.buffer(8).release() // the next allocation reports them } assertThat(leaks).isEmpty() GC timing makes this check probabilistic, so pair it with a deterministic one: keep a reference to the buffer you pushed in, and assert refCnt() == 0 after the pipeline ran. The lab does both. Make a leak, then fix it Run LeakDemo (or LeakDemoKt). Predict first: ten leaked buffers, how many reports? Find the Hint: line in the report and match it to the handler in the code. Fix the handler by adding ReferenceCountUtil.release(msg); to channelRead, and run it again. h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Flow control: stop reading when you can't write
x: ctx.write(msg) never blocks, and a slow client never makes it fail. Netty puts the message in the channel's outbound buffer, a queue in your own process's memory, and moves it to the socket when the kernel's send buffer has room. That is handy, and it is also how a Netty service runs out of memory: if the peer reads more slowly than you write, the queue grows without limit. Netty tells you when the queue gets long. Each channel has two water marks, 32 KiB low and 64 KiB high by default (WriteBufferWaterMark). When the bytes waiting in the outbound buffer pass the high mark, channel.isWritable() turns false and Netty fires channelWritabilityChanged. When they drain below the low mark, isWritable() turns true and the event fires again. Two marks instead of one stop it from flipping on every write. Netty doesn't stop your writes when isWritable() is false. You have to act. For an echo server or a proxy, the action is lesson 2's: stop reading from whoever produces the data. setAutoRead(false) tells the event loop to stop reading that channel, which for the NIO transport means taking OP_READ out of its interest set: Java @Override public void channelReadComplete(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { ctx.flush(); if (!ctx.channel().isWritable()) ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(false); // stop reading } @Override public void channelWritabilityChanged(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { if (ctx.channel().isWritable()) ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(true); // drained: read again ctx.fireChannelWritabilityChanged(); } Kotlin override fun channelReadComplete(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { ctx.flush() if (!ctx.channel().isWritable) ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = false // stop reading } override fun channelWritabilityChanged(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { if (ctx.channel().isWritable) ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = true // drained: read again ctx.fireChannelWritabilityChanged() } This section's demo echoes 8 MiB to a client that writes fast and reads slowly. Without those two methods, the outbound buffer peaked at 1,905,344 bytes in one run and 1,332,000 in another, and a test run of the same code for this track saw 16,202,075: the whole payload. With them, the peak was about 129,000 bytes every time. In a proxy you wire it across two channels: the backend's writability switches the frontend's auto-read. Two more traps showed up while measuring this. Calling close() right after the last flush() lost 57,344 bytes that were still in the outbound buffer. Close from the write's future instead: ctx.writeAndFlush(last).addListener(ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE). And channelWritabilityChanged can fire inside your own flush() call, so a handler that writes from that event must cope with being called while it is already writing. Measure the queue Run BackpressureDemo (or BackpressureDemoKt) and note both peaks. Lower the water marks: add .childOption(ChannelOption.WRITE_BUFFER_WATER_MARK, new WriteBufferWaterMark(8 * 1024, 16 * 1024)) to the server bootstrap. Predict the new peak with backpressure: about a quarter of the old one? Run it and explain the number. Where in the handler is writability checked? peak is in the megabytes and changes every run; with it, about 129,000 bytes. With a 16 KiB high mark the peak only fell to 113,536 bytes in my runs, nowhere near a quarter. The handler checks isWritable() in channelReadComplete, which runs once after a whole batch of reads, so most of the peak is that one batch arriving before auto-read is switched off. Checking in channelRead as well would stop the batch early. WriteBufferWaterMark source, Netty 4.2 docs The common leak is a handler that does a little work on a buffer and then forgets whose it is. An audit or logging handler calls msg.copy() or msg.toString(UTF_8), passes a copy on, and never releases the original: that is this lesson's lab. The mirror image is a handler that extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<ByteBuf> and also calls ctx.fireChannelRead(msg): the base class releases the buffer when channelRead0 returns, so the next handler reads freed memory and gets IllegalReferenceCountException. Pass the same buffer on with ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter and fireChannelRead(msg), or call ReferenceCountUtil.retain(msg) before passing it on from a SimpleChannelInboundHandler.

x: The payment frame encoder and decoder PaymentFrameCodec.java class PaymentFrameEncoder extends MessageToByteEncoder<PaymentMessage> { @Override protected void encode(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, PaymentMessage msg, ByteBuf out) { byte[] body = msg.body().getBytes(UTF_8); out.writeInt(1 + body.length).writeByte(msg.type()).writeBytes(body); } } class PaymentFrameDecoder extends ByteToMessageDecoder { @Override protected void decode(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, ByteBuf in, List<Object> out) { int type = in.readByte(); out.add(new PaymentMessage(type, in.readCharSequence(in.readableBytes(), UTF_8).toString())); } } PaymentFrameCodec.kt class PaymentFrameEncoder : MessageToByteEncoder<PaymentMessage>() { override fun encode(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, msg: PaymentMessage, out: ByteBuf) { val body = msg.body.toByteArray(UTF_8) out.writeInt(1 + body.size).writeByte(msg.type).writeBytes(body) } } class PaymentFrameDecoder : ByteToMessageDecoder() { override fun decode(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, input: ByteBuf, out: MutableList<Any>) { val type = input.readByte().toInt() out += PaymentMessage(type, input.readCharSequence(input.readableBytes(), UTF_8).toString()) } } The runtime behavior is identical; the differences are names and types. Java's decoder parameter is called in, which is a keyword in Kotlin, so the Kotlin override renames it (input), which overriding allows. readByte() returns a Byte in Kotlin, and Kotlin never widens it to Int implicitly, so you write .toInt() where Java widens silently. The out list is a Java List<Object>, which Kotlin sees as MutableList<Any>. Getters such as isWritable() and isAutoRead() become properties (isWritable, isAutoRead = false) in Kotlin. Reference counting is the same in both: Kotlin's use {} does not help, because ByteBuf is not AutoCloseable.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Worked example
x: Frame an ISO 8583 style link with a 2-byte length An acquirer link sends each message behind a 2-byte big-endian length that counts only the bytes after it. Frames are at most 4,096 bytes. Ask four questions: where is the length, how long is it, what does it count, and do you keep it? wire: 00 08 | 30 31 30 30 61 75 74 68 (length 8, then "0100auth") offset: 0 the length starts the frame length: 2 bytes counts: what follows lengthAdjustment 0 keep: no initialBytesToStrip 2 That gives the decoder's arguments. LengthFieldPrepender is the matching encoder: it writes the length in front of every outbound buffer, so the business handler never deals with the header. ch.pipeline().addLast( new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, 0, 2), // 1. frame inbound, strip the header new LengthFieldPrepender(2), // 2. add the header outbound new Iso8583Codec(), // 3. bytes <-> messages new AuthorizationHandler()); ch.pipeline().addLast( LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, 0, 2), // 1. frame inbound, strip the header LengthFieldPrepender(2), // 2. add the header outbound Iso8583Codec(), // 3. bytes <-> messages AuthorizationHandler()) A second acquirer counts the 2 header bytes in the length: the same message arrives as 00 0a .... The decoder computes the frame size as header end plus the length value plus lengthAdjustment, so subtract the 2 bytes the value already includes. The prepender has a flag for the same convention. new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, -2, 2), // 10 - 2 = 8 body bytes new LengthFieldPrepender(2, true) // write 2 + body length LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, -2, 2) // 10 - 2 = 8 body bytes LengthFieldPrepender(2, true) // write 2 + body length Prove it with an EmbeddedChannel before you connect to anything: write one message out, feed the bytes back in split after the first byte, and expect the original. A wrong adjustment shows up here as a frame that never completes or one that swallows the next message's header. EmbeddedChannel ch = new EmbeddedChannel( new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, -2, 2), new LengthFieldPrepender(2, true)); ch.writeOutbound(Unpooled.copiedBuffer("0100auth", UTF_8)); ByteBuf wire = ch.readOutbound(); // 00 0a 30 31 30 30 61 75 74 68 ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(0, 1)); // half a header: nothing yet ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(1, wire.readableBytes() - 1)); wire.release(); ByteBuf frame = ch.readInbound(); // "0100auth" frame.release(); val ch = EmbeddedChannel( LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, -2, 2), LengthFieldPrepender(2, true)) ch.writeOutbound(Unpooled.copiedBuffer("0100auth", UTF_8)) val wire = ch.readOutbound<ByteBuf>() // 00 0a 30 31 30 30 61 75 74 68 ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(0, 1)) // half a header: nothing yet ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(1, wire.readableBytes() - 1)) wire.release() val frame = ch.readInbound<ByteBuf>() // "0100auth" frame.release()
