h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Quiz
x: LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(1024, 0, 4, 0, 4) has received the bytes 00 00 00 03 01 41. What does it pass to the next handler? Nothing yet: the length says 3 bytes follow and only 2 have arrived 01 41 All six bytes It throws, because the frame is shorter than 1024 The length field says 3 bytes follow; only 01 41 are there. The decoder keeps them in its cumulation and waits for one more byte. 1024 is a maximum, not a required size. A handler extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<ByteBuf>, and inside channelRead0 it calls ctx.fireChannelRead(msg) to pass the buffer on. What happens? It works: ownership moves to the next handler The base class releases the buffer when channelRead0 returns, so the next handler reads freed memory and fails with IllegalReferenceCountException Netty copies the buffer for the next handler The buffer leaks SimpleChannelInboundHandler releases the message after channelRead0, assuming you consumed it. Passing it on as well means two owners and one release too many. Call ReferenceCountUtil.retain(msg) before passing it on, or extend ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter. Your pipeline tests run at PARANOID and report no leaks. What does that tell you? The code has no leaks SIMPLE would have found more The allocator must be unpooled No tracked buffer that was garbage-collected during the run had a count above 0; paths the tests never ran stay invisible The detector only sees buffers that were allocated, tracked and collected while the tests ran. A leak on an error path the tests never exercise produces no report. PARANOID tracks more buffers than SIMPLE, not fewer. From lesson 3: on which thread does channelWritabilityChanged run, even when your writes come from an application thread pool? The channel's event loop thread A Netty IO thread from a separate pool The thread that called write Whichever thread is free Every event of a channel runs on the event loop it is registered with. A write from another thread is queued as a task on that loop, so the outbound buffer and its writability are only ever changed on the loop thread. A gateway reads authorizations from many terminals and forwards them to a slower card switch over one Netty channel. The switch channel's isWritable() turns false. What should the gateway do? Keep writing: Netty buffers it Close the switch channel and reconnect Turn auto-read off on the terminal channels until the switch channel is writable again Call Thread.sleep in the handler until it is writable Stop reading from the producers so the backlog stays in the kernel and in TCP, not in your memory. Writing anyway grows the outbound buffer without limit, and sleeping blocks the event loop for every other channel on it.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Explain it back
x: Explain why Netty's ByteBuf needs release() even though the JVM has a garbage collector, and how you would make sure a pipeline doesn't leak.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Key terms
x: Framing Finding where one message ends and the next begins in a byte stream. Length prefix A field before each message that says how many bytes the message has. Cumulation The buffer in which a ByteToMessageDecoder keeps bytes until a whole frame has arrived. Reference count A counter on a ByteBuf: retain adds one, release subtracts one, and at zero the memory goes back to the pool. Leak detector Netty's ResourceLeakDetector, which reports buffers that were garbage-collected without being released. Outbound buffer The queue in your process where a channel keeps written messages until the socket can take them. Water marks The high and low limits on the outbound buffer that switch isWritable() off and on. Auto-read Whether the event loop keeps reading a channel; turning it off is how Netty stops OP_READ. What do the arguments of LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(1024, 0, 4, 0, 4) mean? Max frame 1024 bytes; the length field is at offset 0 and 4 bytes long; adjustment 0 (it counts only what follows); strip the first 4 bytes before passing the frame on. Who releases a ByteBuf in a Netty pipeline? The party that touches it last. Passing it on with fireChannelRead or write hands over ownership; consuming it means releasing it. Why does ByteBuf need release() when the JVM has a garbage collector? Netty pools direct memory and must get it back as soon as a message is done. The GC frees objects at an unknown later time and can't return pooled chunks. SimpleChannelInboundHandler vs ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter: who releases? SimpleChannelInboundHandler releases the message after channelRead0 returns. ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter releases nothing; you pass the message on or release it. Netty's leak detection levels, in one line each? SIMPLE (default): about 1 in 128 buffers, no records. ADVANCED: same sampling, with access records. PARANOID: every buffer, with records; use it in tests. When does channel.isWritable() turn false, and when true again (defaults)? False when the outbound buffer passes the 64 KiB high water mark; true again when it drains below the 32 KiB low mark. How do you close a Netty channel without losing the last bytes? Close from the last write's future: ctx.writeAndFlush(last).addListener(ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE). close() right after flush() can drop bytes still in the outbound buffer.

h: Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks · Go deeper
x: A few ByteToMessageDecoder details explain behavior you will see in profiles. The default cumulator, MERGE_CUMULATOR, copies newly read bytes into one growing buffer. COMPOSITE_CUMULATOR adds them as components instead and avoids the copy, but the Javadoc warns it may be slower, because reading across component boundaries costs more. The decoder also compacts the cumulation after 16 reads (discardAfterReads), so a long-lived connection doesn't keep consumed bytes forever. setSingleDecode(true) makes it produce at most one message per read, which matters when you control reading yourself. That leads to FlowControlHandler. With auto-read off you call ctx.read() to ask for one more read, but a decoder can still emit many messages from that one read, because one read can contain many frames. Its Javadoc says FlowControlHandler "ensures that only one message per read() is sent downstream". Put it after your decoders when you need strict one-request-at-a-time processing per connection. On allocators: io.netty.allocator.type picks adaptive (the 4.2 default), pooled or unpooled. The adaptive allocator keeps several "magazines" of memory, picks one by thread id, and adds magazines when it sees contention. The older pooled allocator keeps per-thread caches, and its useCacheForAllThreads setting defaults to false, which suggests that buffers allocated on your own executor threads miss those caches. That last point is an inference from the property name and default, not something this track measured. Finally, production: leave the level at SIMPLE. It samples 1 buffer in 128, so a leak on a busy path still reaches the logs, while the other 127 buffers pay nothing for tracking.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Vert.x puts a context on top of Netty's event loop
x: A Vert.x context runs a verticle's handlers on one event-loop thread, so never block it Vert.x 5.2.3 runs on Netty 4.2.20. A Vertx instance starts a group of Netty event loops, twice the number of cores by default (8 on a 4-core machine), named vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 and up. Its HTTP server is a Netty pipeline like the one in lesson 3, and the stack trace later in this lesson ends in io.netty.channel.SingleThreadIoEventLoop.run, the same loop class. What Vert.x adds is a set of rules over those loops. The central one is the context: the home of a piece of code, which decides the thread that runs it. Most contexts are event-loop contexts, each tied to one event loop for life. When you register a handler, Vert.x remembers the current context, and every call of that handler runs there. The Vert.x docs promise that a handler is never executed concurrently and, worker verticles aside, always runs on the same event loop thread. That is lesson 3's Netty rule, one channel, one loop, extended to all your code: HTTP handlers, timers and event-bus consumers. The second change is the API. Vert.x 4 had two styles, callbacks and futures. Vert.x 5 kept only futures: every asynchronous method returns an io.vertx.core.Future, and the callback overloads are gone. Java // Vert.x 5: listen returns a Future server.listen(8080).onSuccess(s -> System.out.println("listening on " + s.actualPort())); // Vert.x 4 style no longer compiles: // server.listen(8080, ar -> ...) -> error: incompatible types: String is not a functional interface Kotlin // Vert.x 5: listen returns a Future server.listen(8080).onSuccess { s -> println("listening on ${s.actualPort()}") } // Vert.x 4 style no longer compiles: // server.listen(8080) { ar -> ... } the only two-argument listen left is listen(int, String) The Java error looks unrelated because the compiler matched the one remaining two-argument overload, listen(int, String), and complains that a String isn't a lambda. The same migration replaced executeBlocking(promise -> ...) with a version that takes a Callable and returns a Future. Hit the Vert.x 5 API change In ContextsDemo.java, add one line after Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx();: vertx.createHttpServer().listen(8080, ar -> {});. Predict whether it compiles. Then run the demo with the command below. Remove the line again. terminal ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.ContextsDemo Compilation fails with error: incompatible types: String is not a functional interface. The callback overload of listen no longer exists in Vert.x 5, so javac tries listen(int, String) and can't turn your lambda into a String. A Vert.x context is a desk with one chair. Everything registered at that desk (handlers, timers, event-bus consumers) is dealt with by whoever sits in the chair, one item at a time, so nobody at the desk needs to lock the drawers. An event-loop desk always has the same clerk; the event bus is the internal mail between desks; executeBlocking is sending a long errand to the back office and getting the result back on your desk. The analogy breaks for worker desks: different clerks can sit in a worker desk's chair on different days, though never two at once, which is why a worker verticle is still single-threaded but not tied to one thread.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Verticles: units you deploy, each with its own context
x: A verticle is a class you deploy into Vert.x, and deploying it gives each instance its own context. In Vert.x 5 you extend VerticleBase and return a Future from start(), so the deployment completes only when your setup has: Java public class AuthorizeVerticle extends VerticleBase { @Override public Future<?> start() { return vertx.eventBus().<JsonObject>consumer("payments.authorize", msg -> msg.reply(new JsonObject().put("status", "APPROVED")) ).completion(); // done when the consumer is registered } } vertx.deployVerticle(AuthorizeVerticle::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2)); Kotlin class AuthorizeVerticle : VerticleBase() { override fun start(): Future<*> = vertx.eventBus().consumer<JsonObject>("payments.authorize") { msg -> msg.reply(JsonObject().put("status", "APPROVED")) }.completion() // done when the consumer is registered } vertx.deployVerticle(::AuthorizeVerticle, DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2)) For two instances you pass a factory, because each instance must be its own object. In 5.2.3 that factory is a Supplier, though the docs still say Callable. Each instance gets its own event-loop context, usually on different loops, which is how one verticle class uses several cores. Inside one instance, code never runs on two threads at once, so its fields need no locks. The threading model in DeploymentOptions decides what kind of context a verticle gets. This section's demo prints where each kind runs: [EVENT_LOOP] start() on vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 eventLoopCtx=true workerCtx=false [WORKER] start() on vert.x-worker-thread-0 eventLoopCtx=false workerCtx=true [VIRTUAL_THREAD] start() on vert.x-virtual-thread-0 (virtual) eventLoopCtx=false workerCtx=false EVENT_LOOP, the default, must never block. A WORKER verticle runs on the worker pool (20 threads by default) and may block; it still never runs on two threads at once, though successive calls can land on different worker threads. VIRTUAL_THREAD is new in Vert.x 5 and needs Java 21: the verticle runs on virtual threads, and future.await() parks the virtual thread until the result arrives. It also runs one task at a time, with one catch from the docs: a field you read before an await() may have changed after it, because another task of the same verticle can run while you wait. Where does each verticle run? Open ContextsDemo.java (or ContextsDemo.kt). It deploys one verticle per threading model, then calls executeBlocking from an event-loop context. Predict the thread name in each line, and on which thread onSuccess runs after executeBlocking. Run it. ContextsDemo.java package workbench.nio.l05; import io.vertx.core.Context; import io.vertx.core.DeploymentOptions; import io.vertx.core.Future; import io.vertx.core.ThreadingModel; import io.vertx.core.VerticleBase; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Where does a verticle's code run? One verticle per threading model, plus executeBlocking. */ public class ContextsDemo { static String where() { Thread t = Thread.currentThread(); Context c = Vertx.currentContext(); return t.getName() + (t.isVirtual() ? " (virtual)" : "") + " eventLoopCtx=" + c.isEventLoopContext() + " workerCtx=" + c.isWorkerContext(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("default event loops: " + VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE + " (cpus=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + "), default worker pool: " + VertxOptions.DEFAULT_WORKER_POOL_SIZE); Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(); for (ThreadingModel model : List.of(ThreadingModel.EVENT_LOOP, ThreadingModel.WORKER, ThreadingModel.VIRTUAL_THREAD)) { await(vertx.deployVerticle(new VerticleBase() { @Override public Future<?> start() { System.out.println("[" + model + "] start() on " + where()); return Future.succeededFuture(); } }, new DeploymentOptions().setThreadingModel(model))); } vertx.runOnContext(v -> vertx.executeBlocking(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()) .onSuccess(name -> System.out.println("[executeBlocking] callable ran on " + name + ", onSuccess runs on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()))); Thread.sleep(300); await(vertx.close()); } static <T> T await(Future<T> f) throws Exception { return f.toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.ContextsDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l05/ContextsDemo.java ContextsDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l05 import io.vertx.core.DeploymentOptions import io.vertx.core.Future import io.vertx.core.ThreadingModel import io.vertx.core.VerticleBase import io.vertx.core.Vertx import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** Where does a verticle's code run? One verticle per threading model, plus executeBlocking. */ private fun where(): String { val t = Thread.currentThread() val c = Vertx.currentContext() return "${t.name}${if (t.isVirtual) " (virtual)" else ""} eventLoopCtx=${c.isEventLoopContext} workerCtx=${c.isWorkerContext}" } private fun <T> Future<T>.awaitIt(): T = toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) fun main() { println("default event loops: ${VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE} (cpus=${Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()}), " + "default worker pool: ${VertxOptions.DEFAULT_WORKER_POOL_SIZE}") val vertx = Vertx.vertx() for (model in listOf(ThreadingModel.EVENT_LOOP, ThreadingModel.WORKER, ThreadingModel.VIRTUAL_THREAD)) { vertx.deployVerticle(object : VerticleBase() { override fun start(): Future<*> { println("[$model] start() on ${where()}") return Future.succeededFuture<Unit>() } }, DeploymentOptions().setThreadingModel(model)).awaitIt() } // explicit types: an inferred Vert.x Future type carries vertx-codegen's @Nullable, which isn't on the classpath val task = Callable<String> { Thread.currentThread().name } vertx.runOnContext { vertx.executeBlocking(task) .onSuccess { name: String -> println("[executeBlocking] callable ran on $name, onSuccess runs on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } } Thread.sleep(300) vertx.close().awaitIt() } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.ContextsDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l05/ContextsDemo.kt The first line reports 8 event loops on 4 CPUs and a worker pool of 20. The three verticles start on vert.x-eventloop-thread-0, vert.x-worker-thread-0 and a virtual thread vert.x-virtual-thread-0. The executeBlocking callable runs on a worker thread, and onSuccess runs back on an event-loop thread: the context that called it. Each verticle instance has a context on one event loop. Contexts talk over the event bus, and blocking work goes to the worker pool and comes back to the same context. Every Quarkus service you run is a Vert.x application underneath: the HTTP layer is a Vert.x server on Vert.x event loops, and Quarkus's @ConsumeEvent sits on the same event bus. The blocked-thread warning in this lesson is the one you will see in a Quarkus log when an endpoint blocks an IO thread, with Quarkus-specific limits that lesson 6 covers. If a team writes plain Vert.x for a payment router or a ledger projection, make them pass false to executeBlocking for independent queries, set a send timeout on every event-bus request, and keep handlers idempotent, because the event bus will not redeliver a lost message.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · The event bus carries messages between contexts
x: The event bus is how verticles talk without sharing objects. There is one per Vertx instance, and an address is just a string such as payments.authorize. You can send in three ways: send(address, msg): to one consumer at that address, chosen round-robin. request(address, msg): to one consumer, and you get a Future of its reply. publish(address, msg): to every consumer at that address. This section's demo deploys two instances of a greeter and makes requests: request greet #0 -> hello dev0 from instance#1 on vert.x-eventloop-thread-1 request greet #1 -> hello dev1 from instance#2 on vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 request greet #2 -> hello dev2 from instance#1 on vert.x-eventloop-thread-1 request nobody -> NO_HANDLERS code=-1 message=No handlers for address nobody request fail -> RECIPIENT_FAILURE code=42 message=boom from instance#2 request silent (timeout 300 ms) -> TIMEOUT after 311 ms A request can fail in three ways, each delivered as a ReplyException with a failureType(). NO_HANDLERS means nobody listens at the address. RECIPIENT_FAILURE means the consumer called msg.fail(code, text), and you get its code and text. TIMEOUT means no reply arrived in time. The default timeout is 30 seconds, far too long for a payment path, so set one per request with new DeliveryOptions().setSendTimeout(...). The reply comes back on the requester's context, not the consumer's. A worker verticle that sends a request handles the reply on a worker thread; a virtual-thread verticle resumes on its virtual thread. Two properties keep the event bus from being a message broker. Delivery is best effort: there is no persistence and no retry, and the docs tell you to make handlers idempotent. And inside one JVM a message can be handed over by reference. With a custom local codec whose transform returns its argument, the consumer receives the very object you sent, so never change a message after you send it. Built-in codecs cover strings, numbers, Buffer, JsonObject and JsonArray; other types need a codec you register. Make every kind of reply happen Open EventBusDemo.java (or EventBusDemo.kt). Predict which instance answers each of the four requests, and how many lines publish prints. Run it. Change the silent request's timeout from 300 to 1,000 ms and run again. What changes, and what doesn't? EventBusDemo.java package workbench.nio.l05; import io.vertx.core.DeploymentOptions; import io.vertx.core.Future; import io.vertx.core.VerticleBase; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import io.vertx.core.eventbus.DeliveryOptions; import io.vertx.core.eventbus.EventBus; import io.vertx.core.eventbus.ReplyException; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Point-to-point, publish/subscribe and the three ways a request can fail. */ public class EventBusDemo { static final AtomicInteger IDS = new AtomicInteger(); public static class Greeter extends VerticleBase { final int id = IDS.incrementAndGet(); @Override public Future<?> start() { EventBus eb = vertx.eventBus(); eb.<String>consumer("greet", m -> m.reply("hello " + m.body() + " from instance#" + id + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName())); eb.<String>consumer("news", m -> System.out.println(" [news] instance#" + id + " got '" + m.body() + "'")); eb.<String>consumer("fail", m -> m.fail(42, "boom from instance#" + id)); return eb.<String>consumer("silent", m -> { /* never replies */ }).completion(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(); EventBus eb = vertx.eventBus(); await(vertx.deployVerticle(Greeter::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2))); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) System.out.println("request greet #" + i + " -> " + await(eb.<String>request("greet", "dev" + i)).body()); System.out.println("publish news:"); eb.publish("news", "release 1.0"); Thread.sleep(200); for (String address : List.of("nobody", "fail")) { try { await(eb.request(address, "x")); } catch (ExecutionException e) { ReplyException re = (ReplyException) e.getCause(); System.out.println("request " + address + " -> " + re.failureType() + " code=" + re.failureCode() + " message=" + re.getMessage()); } } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { await(eb.request("silent", "x", new DeliveryOptions().setSendTimeout(300))); } catch (ExecutionException e) { ReplyException re = (ReplyException) e.getCause(); System.out.println("request silent (timeout 300 ms) -> " + re.failureType() + " after " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); } System.out.println("default request timeout: " + DeliveryOptions.DEFAULT_TIMEOUT + " ms"); await(vertx.close()); } static <T> T await(Future<T> f) throws Exception { return f.toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.EventBusDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l05/EventBusDemo.java EventBusDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l05 import io.vertx.core.DeploymentOptions import io.vertx.core.Future import io.vertx.core.VerticleBase import io.vertx.core.Vertx import io.vertx.core.eventbus.DeliveryOptions import io.vertx.core.eventbus.ReplyException import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** Point-to-point, publish/subscribe and the three ways a request can fail. */ private val greeterIds = AtomicInteger() private class KtGreeter : VerticleBase() { val id = greeterIds.incrementAndGet() override fun start(): Future<*> { val eb = vertx.eventBus() eb.consumer<String>("greet") { m -> m.reply("hello ${m.body()} from instance#$id on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } eb.consumer<String>("news") { m -> println(" [news] instance#$id got '${m.body()}'") } eb.consumer<String>("fail") { m -> m.fail(42, "boom from instance#$id") } return eb.consumer<String>("silent") { /* never replies */ }.completion() } } private fun <T> Future<T>.await5(): T = toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) fun main() { val vertx = Vertx.vertx() val eb = vertx.eventBus() // a bare lambda is ambiguous here: Deployable is itself a single-method interface vertx.deployVerticle(::KtGreeter, DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2)).await5() repeat(4) { i -> println("request greet #$i -> ${eb.request<String>("greet", "dev$i").await5().body()}") } println("publish news:") eb.publish("news", "release 1.0") Thread.sleep(200) for (address in listOf("nobody", "fail")) { try { eb.request<Any>(address, "x").await5() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { val re = e.cause as ReplyException println("request $address -> ${re.failureType()} code=${re.failureCode()} message=${re.message}") } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() try { eb.request<Any>("silent", "x", DeliveryOptions().setSendTimeout(300)).await5() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { val re = e.cause as ReplyException println("request silent (timeout 300 ms) -> ${re.failureType()} after ${(System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000} ms") } println("default request timeout: ${DeliveryOptions.DEFAULT_TIMEOUT} ms") vertx.close().await5() } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.EventBusDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l05/EventBusDemo.kt The requests alternate between the two instances (1, 2, 1, 2 in my runs; the docs only promise a non-strict round-robin), each on its own event loop. publish prints two lines, one per instance, in either order. The failures come back as NO_HANDLERS, RECIPIENT_FAILURE with code 42, and TIMEOUT after about 300 ms. With 1,000 ms the timeout simply arrives later: the consumer still never replies. h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · The golden rule, and the catch in executeBlocking
x: Vert.x calls it the golden rule: don't block the event loop. Its docs list what counts: Thread.sleep(), waiting on a lock or a synchronized monitor, a long database operation, a complex calculation, spinning in a loop. They also give the budget: with one event loop and 10,000 HTTP requests a second, each request can take at most 0.1 ms. Vert.x checks the rule for you. A separate thread, vertx-blocked-thread-checker, wakes up every second and looks at each event loop. If the task a loop is running started more than 2 seconds ago, it logs a warning, and past 5 seconds it adds the blocked thread's stack trace. It measures one task at a time: each loop records when its current task began, and the checker compares that with the clock. So ten 300 ms blocking calls in a row hold a loop for 3 seconds and never produce a warning. This section's demo sleeps 6 seconds on an event loop: [vertx-blocked-thread-checker] WARN io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker - Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 has been blocked for 2891 ms, time limit is 2000 ms [vertx-blocked-thread-checker] WARN io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker - Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 has been blocked for 3891 ms, time limit is 2000 ms ... io.vertx.core.VertxException: Thread blocked at java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Thread.java:509) at workbench.nio.l05.BlockedThreadDemo.lambda$main$0(BlockedThreadDemo.java:13) ... at io.netty.channel.SingleThreadIoEventLoop.run(SingleThreadIoEventLoop.java:228) The first warning came at 2.9 s, not 2.0 s, because the checker only looks once a second. Search your logs for has been blocked for; the logger is io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker. The checker only reports. It never interrupts the blocked thread. For blocking work there is executeBlocking: it runs a Callable on the worker pool and completes a Future back on your context. Its catch is that it is ordered by default, so calls from the same context run one after another. The demo sends 4 concurrent HTTP requests, each doing a 500 ms fake JDBC call, to a server with one event loop: block-on-event-loop 4 requests x 500 ms -> 2201 ms, ran on [vert.x-eventloop-thread-0] executeBlocking-ordered 4 requests x 500 ms -> 2012 ms, ran on [vert.x-worker-thread-0] executeBlocking-unordered 4 requests x 500 ms -> 511 ms, ran on [vert.x-worker-thread-0, ..., vert.x-worker-thread-3] The ordered version freed the event loop for every other connection, but the four queries still ran single file, because every request to one server shares that server's context. Pass false when the calls are independent: executeBlocking(callable, false). And remember what the worker pool is: 20 threads by default, a bounded pool like the ones in the executors track. Behind a 20-connection JDBC pool, that is a thread-per-request design again. That is fine, as long as you size it like one. Three ways to make a slow call Open ExecuteBlockingDemo.java (or ExecuteBlockingDemo.kt). Predict the total time and the thread names for each of the three modes. Run it with the command below. Then run ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.BlockedThreadDemo and predict when the first warning appears and when the stack trace appears. Run it with -Pargs=2500 too: how many warnings now? ExecuteBlockingDemo.java package workbench.nio.l05; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions; import io.vertx.core.http.HttpServer; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.TreeSet; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** One event loop, an HTTP server, 4 concurrent requests that each make a 500 ms "JDBC call". Three ways. */ public class ExecuteBlockingDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (String mode : List.of("block-on-event-loop", "executeBlocking-ordered", "executeBlocking-unordered")) { Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(new VertxOptions().setEventLoopPoolSize(1)); Callable<String> fakeJdbc = () -> { Thread.sleep(500); return Thread.currentThread().getName(); }; HttpServer server = vertx.createHttpServer().requestHandler(req -> { switch (mode) { case "block-on-event-loop" -> { try { req.response().end(fakeJdbc.call()); // blocks the loop } catch (Exception e) { req.response().setStatusCode(500).end(); } } case "executeBlocking-ordered" -> // the default: ordered = true vertx.executeBlocking(fakeJdbc).onComplete(ar -> req.response().end(ar.result())); default -> vertx.executeBlocking(fakeJdbc, false).onComplete(ar -> req.response().end(ar.result())); } }).listen(0, "127.0.0.1").toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); java.net.http.HttpClient client = java.net.http.HttpClient.newBuilder() .proxy(java.net.http.HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build(); URI uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + server.actualPort() + "/"); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { calls.add(client.sendAsync(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())); } Set<String> threads = new TreeSet<>(); for (var call : calls) threads.add(call.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS).body()); System.out.printf("%-26s 4 requests x 500 ms -> %4d ms, ran on %s%n", mode, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads); vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.ExecuteBlockingDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l05/ExecuteBlockingDemo.java ExecuteBlockingDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l05 import io.vertx.core.Vertx import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions import java.net.URI import java.net.http.HttpRequest import java.net.http.HttpResponse import java.util.TreeSet import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.net.http.HttpClient as JdkHttpClient /** One event loop, an HTTP server, 4 concurrent requests that each make a 500 ms "JDBC call". Three ways. */ fun main() { for (mode in listOf("block-on-event-loop", "executeBlocking-ordered", "executeBlocking-unordered")) { val vertx = Vertx.vertx(VertxOptions().setEventLoopPoolSize(1)) val fakeJdbc = Callable { Thread.sleep(500) Thread.currentThread().name } val server = vertx.createHttpServer().requestHandler { req -> when (mode) { "block-on-event-loop" -> req.response().end(fakeJdbc.call()) // blocks the loop "executeBlocking-ordered" -> // the default: ordered = true vertx.executeBlocking(fakeJdbc).onComplete { ar -> req.response().end(ar.result()) } else -> vertx.executeBlocking(fakeJdbc, false).onComplete { ar -> req.response().end(ar.result()) } } }.listen(0, "127.0.0.1").toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() val client = JdkHttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(JdkHttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build() val uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:${server.actualPort()}/") val t0 = System.nanoTime() val calls = List(4) { client.sendAsync(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()) } val threads = TreeSet(calls.map { it.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS).body() }) println("%-26s 4 requests x 500 ms -> %4d ms, ran on %s".format(mode, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads)) vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.ExecuteBlockingDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l05/ExecuteBlockingDemo.kt About 2,000 ms on the event loop thread, about 2,000 ms on one worker thread with the ordered default, and about 500 ms across four worker threads with false (2,201, 2,012 and 511 ms in my run; this track's research run measured 2,814, 2,043 and 576). The blocked-thread demo warns between 2 and 3 seconds in, once a second after that, and adds the VertxException: Thread blocked stack trace after 5 seconds. A 2,500 ms sleep gives zero or one warning, depending on when the checker happens to look. Vert.x 5.2.3 core documentation: The Golden Rule (source) docs The common mistake is moving blocking code into executeBlocking and calling the job done. The event loop is free, so the warnings stop, but the default is ordered per context, and every request to one HTTP server or one consumer shares a context, so the calls still queue behind each other: 2,012 ms instead of 511 ms in this lesson's demo. Pass false for independent calls, or deploy a WORKER verticle with several instances. The second mistake is waiting for a result on the event loop, with toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(): if the result needs that same loop to complete, the thread waits for itself.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Java and Kotlin
x: A verticle that offloads a blocking query BalanceVerticle.java public class BalanceVerticle extends VerticleBase { @Override public Future<?> start() { return vertx.eventBus().<String>consumer("ledger.balance", msg -> vertx.executeBlocking(() -> LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body()), false) .onSuccess(msg::reply) // back on this verticle's context .onFailure(e -> msg.fail(500, e.getMessage())) ).completion(); } } vertx.deployVerticle(BalanceVerticle::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2)); BalanceVerticle.kt class BalanceVerticle : VerticleBase() { override fun start(): Future<*> = vertx.eventBus().consumer<String>("ledger.balance") { msg -> val query = Callable<Long> { LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body()) } vertx.executeBlocking(query, false) .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) } // back on this verticle's context .onFailure { e -> msg.fail(500, e.message) } }.completion() } vertx.deployVerticle(::BalanceVerticle, DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2)) Same Vert.x API, same threads at runtime. Two Kotlin wrinkles came up while building this lesson's demos. vertx.deployVerticle({ BalanceVerticle() }, options) does not compile in Kotlin: Deployable is itself a single-method interface, so a bare lambda matches both overloads. Use a constructor reference (::BalanceVerticle) or Supplier { BalanceVerticle() }. And some Vert.x 5 signatures carry a @Nullable type annotation from vertx-codegen, which is not on the classpath, so Kotlin can fail with "Type annotation class 'io.vertx.codegen.annotations.Nullable' of the inferred type is inaccessible" when it infers a lambda's type. Giving the Callable and the lambda parameter explicit types, as above, avoids it. Java ignores the annotation.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Worked example
x: Unblock a ledger verticle, step by step A balance consumer calls JDBC directly. It works in a demo with one request. Under load, every handler on the same event loop waits behind it, and the blocked-thread checker stays silent: it measures one task at a time, and each 300 ms query is under its 2-second limit. Short blocking calls are the kind that never show up in the logs. vertx.eventBus().<String>consumer("ledger.balance", msg -> { try { msg.reply(LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body())); // 300 ms on the event loop } catch (InterruptedException e) { msg.fail(500, "interrupted"); } }); vertx.eventBus().consumer<String>("ledger.balance") { msg -> msg.reply(LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body())) // 300 ms on the event loop } First attempt: executeBlocking with the default. The loop is free now, but six concurrent requests still take about 6 × 300 ms, because they all come from this consumer's context and the default is ordered. vertx.executeBlocking(() -> LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body())) // ordered: one at a time .onSuccess(msg::reply); vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Long> { LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body()) }) // ordered: one at a time .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) } Second attempt: unordered. The queries now overlap on the worker pool, and the replies still come back on the consumer's context. The lab's test checks both: total time under 1,000 ms for six queries, and an event-loop lag under 150 ms. vertx.executeBlocking(() -> LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body()), false) // independent calls .onSuccess(msg::reply) .onFailure(e -> msg.fail(500, e.getMessage())); vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Long> { LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body()) }, false) // independent calls .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) } .onFailure { e -> msg.fail(500, e.message) } Another design gives you a visible concurrency limit: make the whole verticle a worker and deploy as many instances as you want parallel queries. Each instance handles one message at a time on the worker pool, so four instances means at most four queries in flight, which you can match to the JDBC pool. vertx.deployVerticle(BlockingBalanceVerticle::new, new DeploymentOptions() .setThreadingModel(ThreadingModel.WORKER) // may block .setInstances(4)); // at most 4 queries at once vertx.deployVerticle(::BlockingBalanceVerticle, DeploymentOptions() .setThreadingModel(ThreadingModel.WORKER) // may block .setInstances(4)) // at most 4 queries at once

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Quiz
x: A verticle is deployed with setInstances(4) and default options. Its consumer increments a plain int field on every message. Is that safe? No: four threads can increment the same field at once Yes: each instance is its own object with its own context, and a context never runs two handlers at once Only if the field is volatile Only for WORKER verticles The factory creates four separate objects, so there are four separate fields, and each is only touched from its own context, one task at a time. volatile doesn't make ++ atomic anyway, and worker verticles have the same one-at-a-time rule. An HTTP handler wraps every database call in vertx.executeBlocking(() -> jdbc.query(...)). Under load, latency climbs while the database is idle and CPU is low. What is the most likely cause? executeBlocking is ordered by default, so calls from the server's context run one after another The worker pool has only one thread The event loop is blocked JDBC doesn't work on worker threads All requests to one server share its context, and the default executeBlocking serializes calls from a context. The default worker pool has 20 threads, and the event loop is free, which is why there are no blocked-thread warnings. Pass false. A log line says Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-3 has been blocked for 2412 ms, time limit is 2000 ms. What does Vert.x do to that thread? Interrupts it Replaces the event loop with a new one Nothing: it only logs, and adds a stack trace once the block passes 5 seconds Moves its handlers to another event loop The blocked-thread checker is an observer. It logs every second while the block lasts and includes the stack once it passes the warning-exception time (5 s by default). The handlers stay pinned to their loop, so everything on it keeps waiting. From lesson 3: Vert.x event loops are Netty event loops. Which Netty rule explains why a Vert.x handler doesn't need a lock for its own fields? A channel stays on one event-loop thread for life, and that thread runs its events one at a time Netty copies every message before delivering it Netty's event loops are virtual threads ByteBuf is reference-counted Vert.x extends Netty's one-channel-one-loop rule to contexts: everything registered on a context runs on its thread, one task after another. Confinement to one thread is what removes the need for locks. A ledger verticle must tell three other verticles (audit, metrics, notifications) about each posted entry and needs no answers. Which call fits? eventBus().send("ledger.posted", entry) eventBus().request(...) once per listener vertx.executeBlocking(...) around each notification eventBus().publish("ledger.posted", entry) publish delivers to every consumer at the address. send would reach only one of them, chosen round-robin, and request waits for replies nobody needs. Remember that delivery is best effort: if a notification must not be lost, the event bus is the wrong tool.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Key terms
x: Verticle A class you deploy into Vert.x; each deployed instance gets its own context. Context Where a piece of Vert.x code runs: one event loop, a worker, or a virtual thread, one task at a time. Threading model The kind of context a verticle gets: EVENT_LOOP, WORKER or VIRTUAL_THREAD. Event bus Vert.x's in-process messaging between verticles, addressed by strings, best effort. Worker pool The pool of threads (20 by default) that runs blocking work and worker verticles. executeBlocking Runs a Callable on the worker pool and completes a Future back on your context. Blocked-thread checker A Vert.x thread that warns when an event loop has been busy with one task for too long. How many event loops does a default Vertx instance create? 2 × available processors: 8 on a 4-core machine. What is a Vert.x context? The home of a piece of code: it fixes which thread runs it. A handler registered on a context always runs there, never concurrently with itself. When does Vert.x log a blocked event loop, and when does it add a stack trace (defaults)? A warning once a task has run more than 2 s (checked every 1 s); the stack trace after 5 s. It only logs. Why can executeBlocking(callable) still run your calls one at a time? It is ordered per context by default. Calls from the same context queue behind each other. Use executeBlocking(callable, false) for independent calls. The three failureType() values of a failed event-bus request? NO_HANDLERS (nobody listens), RECIPIENT_FAILURE (the consumer called fail), TIMEOUT (no reply in time; default 30 s). send vs request vs publish on the event bus? send: one consumer, round-robin. request: one consumer, and you get a Future of the reply. publish: every consumer at the address. How do you deploy 4 instances of a verticle in Vert.x 5? vertx.deployVerticle(MyVerticle::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(4)): a Supplier, so each instance is a new object.

h: Vert.x: event loops, verticles and the golden rule · Go deeper
x: Testing Vert.x code has its own traps, and vertx-junit5 exists because of them. A Vert.x callback runs on an event loop, after your test method has returned. If an assertion fails there, JUnit never sees it. The extension fixes that with VertxTestContext: the test passes only when you call completeNow() (or flag all checkpoints), and fails when you call failNow(...) or when an assertion inside tc.verify(() -> ...) throws. This track's research ran the same failing assertion both ways. Outside verify, the test ran into the timeout after about 2.6 seconds with "The test execution timed out. Make sure your asynchronous code includes calls to either VertxTestContext#completeNow(), VertxTestContext#failNow() or Checkpoint#flag()", and the real AssertionFailedError was only printed to the log. Inside verify, it failed in 0.059 seconds with the actual assertion message. So every assertion in a callback goes inside verify, or inside tc.succeeding(...) and tc.failing(...), which wrap it for you. Other details from the vertx-junit5 docs: the default timeout is 30 seconds, overridden per test with @io.vertx.junit5.Timeout (fully qualified, to avoid JUnit's @Timeout). A Vertx injected into a @BeforeAll method is shared by the class, one injected into @BeforeEach is shared by that test and its @AfterEach, and injected instances are closed for you. tc.checkpoint(n) gives a counter that must be flagged n times, handy for testing publish to several consumers. And in Vert.x 5, clients rely on Cleaner, so a client object that becomes unreachable can close its pool while a test still uses it. Keep clients in fields during tests.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · In Quarkus REST, the return type picks the thread
x: Every HTTP request to a Quarkus service is read on a Vert.x event loop, which Quarkus calls an IO thread. The Quarkus reactive architecture guide describes what happens next: the extension that dispatches the request decides whether to call your code right there on the IO thread, which avoids a thread switch, or on a worker thread, a thread from a normal bounded pool. For Quarkus REST (formerly RESTEasy Reactive) the decision comes from your method's signature. Everything in this lesson is pinned to Quarkus 3.40. A method that returns Uni, Multi, CompletionStage or a Reactive Streams Publisher, or a Kotlin suspend function, counts as non-blocking and runs on the IO thread. Anything else, such as a method that returns a Balance directly, runs on a worker thread. Java @Path("/balances") public class BalanceResource { @Inject LedgerRepository ledger; // JDBC, blocking @Inject ReactiveLedger reactiveLedger; // reactive SQL client, returns Uni @GET @Path("/{account}") public Balance balance(@PathParam("account") String account) { // plain value: worker thread return ledger.find(account); } @GET @Path("/{account}/live") public Uni<Balance> live(@PathParam("account") String account) { // Uni: IO thread return reactiveLedger.find(account); } } Kotlin @Path("/balances") class BalanceResource( private val ledger: LedgerRepository, // JDBC, blocking private val reactiveLedger: ReactiveLedger, // reactive SQL client, returns Uni ) { @GET @Path("/{account}") fun balance(@PathParam("account") account: String): Balance = // plain value: worker thread ledger.find(account) @GET @Path("/{account}/live") suspend fun live(@PathParam("account") account: String): Balance = // suspend: IO thread reactiveLedger.find(account).awaitSuspending() } Read the rule as a promise you make. A Uni return type tells Quarkus "this method won't block", so Quarkus skips the hop to a worker and saves its cost. Break the promise with a JDBC call inside and you are back in lesson 5: every other connection on that event loop waits. The worker pool is a bounded pool like the ones in the executors track. Quarkus runs blocking endpoints on its own executor, whose size quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads defaults to the larger of 8 × CPUs and 200 in 3.40: 200 threads on a 4-core machine. Predict the thread Without running anything, write down the thread for each Quarkus 3.40 endpoint: (a) public List<Payment> recent(), (b) public Uni<Payment> byId(...), (c) public CompletionStage<Receipt> refund(...), (d) Kotlin suspend fun capture(id: String): Receipt, (e) public Multi<Payment> stream(). Open the lab test DispatcherTest and find the test that encodes the same rules. Check your answers against it. (a) runs on a worker thread; (b), (c), (d) and (e) run on the IO thread. The one people get wrong is (d): a Kotlin suspend function is treated as non-blocking, so a blocking JDBC call inside it blocks an event loop, exactly like one inside a Uni method. Quarkus REST 3.40's dispatch decision, as this lesson's lab models it. The first rule that matches picks the thread. Quarkus REST guide at 3.40.1: execution model, blocking, non-blocking docs A Quarkus endpoint's return type is a label on a kitchen order. Orders marked "quick" (Uni, suspend) are handled by the waiter at the pass, the IO thread, who never leaves the floor for long. Orders without the label go to the back kitchen, the worker pool, which has a fixed number of cooks. @RunOnVirtualThread hires a temporary cook for each order, who sits down while the oven works and costs almost nothing while waiting. The analogy breaks at the label: a real waiter would notice a forty-minute stew. Quarkus trusts the label completely, so a slow dish marked "quick" blocks the waiter and every table behind them.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · @Blocking, @NonBlocking, and the @Transactional disagreement
x: When the signature guesses wrong, you annotate. @Blocking (from io.smallrye.common.annotation) sends a method to a worker even if it returns Uni. @NonBlocking keeps a method on the IO thread even if it returns a plain value. Both work on a method, on a class, or on your jakarta.ws.rs.core.Application subclass to change the default for the whole application. Filters follow their endpoint: under @Blocking they run on the worker, otherwise on the IO thread. Java @Blocking // returns Uni, but the body blocks: use a worker @GET @Path("/{account}/legacy") public Uni<Balance> legacy(@PathParam("account") String account) { return Uni.createFrom().item(ledger.find(account)); // the JDBC call runs right here } Kotlin @Blocking // returns Uni, but the body blocks: use a worker @GET @Path("/{account}/legacy") fun legacy(@PathParam("account") account: String): Uni<Balance> = Uni.createFrom().item(ledger.find(account)) // the JDBC call runs right here @Transactional is where the Quarkus documentation disagrees with itself. The Quarkus REST guide tagged 3.40.1 says a method or class annotated with jakarta.transaction.Transactional "will also be treated as a blocking method", because JTA is a blocking technology, and that an explicit @Blocking or @NonBlocking overrides this. The same guide on Quarkus's main branch says the opposite: since 3.35, @Transactional no longer makes a method blocking, the return type decides, and a Uni method that uses JTA needs an explicit @Blocking. The research for this track could not find the code that settles which is right for 3.40. So don't depend on either reading. Put @Blocking on every endpoint that uses JTA and doesn't return a plain value. It costs nothing when the rule already applies and saves you when it doesn't. When it doesn't, the failure is loud. Before it starts a transaction, Narayana's interceptor in 3.40.1 checks whether blocking is allowed and, on an IO thread, throws BlockingOperationNotAllowedException: "@Transactional cannot start a JTA transaction within a reactive pipeline. If the annotated method is intended to be blocking, ensure it is executed on a worker thread, for example by annotating it with @Blocking. ..." Read the rules both ways Take @Transactional public Uni<Void> post(Payment p). Where does it run under the 3.40.1 docs? Under the main-branch docs? What happens to the JTA interceptor in each case? Now @Transactional @NonBlocking public Uni<Void> post(Payment p). Where does it run, and what happens? Check the first answer against the lab test that mentions @Transactional. Under the 3.40.1 docs the first method runs on a worker and the transaction starts normally. Under the main-branch rule it runs on the IO thread, and the interceptor throws BlockingOperationNotAllowedException before your code runs. The second method runs on the IO thread under both readings, because an explicit annotation wins, so it always throws. In every case @Blocking would have given the same, working result, which is why it belongs on the method. A payments service on Quarkus with Oracle, JDBC and JTA is a blocking service, and that is fine: give its endpoints plain return types, put @Blocking on anything @Transactional that returns Uni or is suspend, and size the worker pool and the datasource pool together. Reach for Uni only where the whole call chain is reactive, such as a reactive SQL client or the Vert.x web client calling a card issuer. Kotlin teams need one extra rule: suspend does not mean "off the event loop". A suspend fun that calls a JDBC repository blocks an IO thread. When latency jumps while CPU is idle, search the logs for has been blocked for.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · What happens when you block an IO thread in Quarkus
x: Quarkus configures its Vert.x instance differently from plain Vert.x, and the differences change what your logs show. Setting Plain Vert.x 5 Quarkus 3.40 event loops 2 × CPUs CPUs, at least 2, at most one per 10 MB of max heap warn about a blocked loop after 2 s 2 s (quarkus.vertx.max-event-loop-execute-time) include the stack trace after 5 s 2 s (quarkus.vertx.warning-exception-time) threads for blocking work worker pool: 20 executor: quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads, max(8 × CPUs, 200) A comment in Quarkus's source explains the event-loop default: twice the number of cores used to be the recommendation, but matching cores 1:1 seemed more reasonable and saves memory. On a 4-core laptop that means 4 event loops instead of 8, so one blocked loop stalls a quarter of your connections. The stack-trace setting is the friendly difference. This section's demo builds a plain Vert.x instance with Quarkus's settings and blocks an event loop for 3 seconds. The first warning already carries the stack: plain Vert.x default event loops: 8, Quarkus 3.40 default: max(2, min(3420 MB / 10, 4 cpus)) = 4 [vertx-blocked-thread-checker] WARN io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker - Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 has been blocked for 2770 ms, time limit is 2000 ms io.vertx.core.VertxException: Thread blocked at java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Thread.java:509) at workbench.nio.l06.QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.lambda$main$0(QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java:30) In a real Quarkus service the line goes through Quarkus's own logging, so the prefix differs, but the message and the stack are Vert.x's. The first frame below Thread.sleep is your endpoint. Some Quarkus APIs don't wait for the checker. They test where they run and fail at once with BlockingOperationNotAllowedException, which extends IllegalStateException: the JTA interceptor from the previous section, and reading a request body as a blocking stream, which fails with "Attempting a blocking read on io thread". Go one level down and the test is simple. Quarkus asks its IO-thread detectors whether the current thread is an IO thread, and the Vert.x detector in 3.40.1 returns Context.isOnEventLoopThread(), the same call this lesson's lab uses. A fast exception in a test is a better way to find a blocking call than a slow event loop in production. Block an IO thread with Quarkus settings Open QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin). Predict the event-loop count it computes for your machine. Predict whether the first blocked-thread warning comes with a stack trace. Run it. Run it again with -Pargs=1500. How many warnings now, and why? QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java package workbench.nio.l06; import io.vertx.core.Context; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * A plain Vert.x instance configured the way Quarkus 3.40 configures its own, then blocked for 3 s. * Arg: sleep ms (default 3000). */ public class QuarkusLikeLoopDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { long sleepMs = args.length > 0 ? Long.parseLong(args[0]) : 3_000; int cpus = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors(); long maxHeapMb = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / (1024 * 1024); int quarkusLoops = (int) Math.max(2, Math.min(maxHeapMb / 10, cpus)); // VertxCoreRecorder.calculateDefaultIOThreads System.out.println("plain Vert.x default event loops: " + VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE + ", Quarkus 3.40 default: max(2, min(" + maxHeapMb + " MB / 10, " + cpus + " cpus)) = " + quarkusLoops); Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(new VertxOptions() .setEventLoopPoolSize(quarkusLoops) .setMaxEventLoopExecuteTime(2).setMaxEventLoopExecuteTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS) // Quarkus: 2 s, like Vert.x .setWarningExceptionTime(2).setWarningExceptionTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS)); // Quarkus: 2 s, Vert.x: 5 s vertx.runOnContext(v -> { System.out.println("[endpoint] on " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + ", Context.isOnEventLoopThread()=" + Context.isOnEventLoopThread()); try { Thread.sleep(sleepMs); // a JDBC call inside an endpoint that returns Uni } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } }); Thread.sleep(sleepMs + 300); vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l06.QuarkusLikeLoopDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l06/QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.java QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l06 import io.vertx.core.Context import io.vertx.core.Vertx import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** * A plain Vert.x instance configured the way Quarkus 3.40 configures its own, then blocked for 3 s. * Arg: sleep ms (default 3000). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val sleepMs = args.getOrNull(0)?.toLong() ?: 3_000L val cpus = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() val maxHeapMb = Runtime.getRuntime().maxMemory() / (1024 * 1024) val quarkusLoops = maxOf(2L, minOf(maxHeapMb / 10, cpus.toLong())).toInt() // VertxCoreRecorder.calculateDefaultIOThreads println("plain Vert.x default event loops: ${VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE}, " + "Quarkus 3.40 default: max(2, min($maxHeapMb MB / 10, $cpus cpus)) = $quarkusLoops") val vertx = Vertx.vertx(VertxOptions() .setEventLoopPoolSize(quarkusLoops) .setMaxEventLoopExecuteTime(2).setMaxEventLoopExecuteTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS) // Quarkus: 2 s, like Vert.x .setWarningExceptionTime(2).setWarningExceptionTimeUnit(TimeUnit.SECONDS)) // Quarkus: 2 s, Vert.x: 5 s vertx.runOnContext { println("[endpoint] on ${Thread.currentThread().name}, Context.isOnEventLoopThread()=${Context.isOnEventLoopThread()}") Thread.sleep(sleepMs) // a JDBC call inside an endpoint that returns Uni } Thread.sleep(sleepMs + 300) vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l06.QuarkusLikeLoopDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l06/QuarkusLikeLoopDemo.kt With a few gigabytes of max heap the memory cap doesn't bite, so the count equals your CPUs (4 here, against Vert.x's 8). The first warning, between 2 and 3 seconds in, already includes VertxException: Thread blocked and the stack, because the warning-exception time is 2 s. With a 1,500 ms block there is no warning at all: the checker only reports a task that has run longer than 2 seconds, so short blocks stay invisible in the logs.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · @RunOnVirtualThread: blocking code without the worker-pool cap
x: @RunOnVirtualThread tells Quarkus to run the method on a new virtual thread, instead of the IO thread or a worker. The code stays blocking-style, but waiting no longer holds a pooled thread: a JDBC call, or uni.await().atMost(...) on a Mutiny Uni, parks the virtual thread, and the JDK wakes it when the result is ready. This section's demo shows what the worker pool's cap costs. 200 requests arrive on one IO context, and each makes a 100 ms blocking call: worker pool (20 threads) 200 calls x 100 ms -> 1,037 ms on 20 distinct threads virtual thread per call 200 calls x 100 ms -> 113 ms on 200 distinct threads The Quarkus virtual threads guide compares the three models in one table, and its cons are the part to remember: Model Runs on Main cost plain return value worker thread the pool caps concurrency Uni and friends IO thread more complex code @RunOnVirtualThread a new virtual thread pinning, monopolization, inefficient object pooling Pinning means a virtual thread that can't unmount, so it holds its carrier thread while it waits. On Java 21 to 23 that happens when it blocks inside synchronized. JDK 24 removed that case (JEP 491), but native code can still pin, and the guide notes that pgjdbc drivers before 42.6.0 pin often on 21 to 23. Monopolization means CPU-heavy work that never blocks, so it keeps its carrier: virtual threads are for IO-bound work only. And libraries such as Jackson and Netty pool objects per thread, assuming a few long-lived threads; a new virtual thread per request defeats those pools. Two more things stay true. Virtual threads don't limit concurrency: 200 virtual threads sharing a 20-connection JDBC pool still queue at the pool, so put a semaphore or the pool's own limit in front of anything fragile. And the request still arrives on an IO thread. @RunOnVirtualThread works by moving your code off it. Pool cap versus virtual threads Open VirtualVsWorkerDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin). Predict both times before running. Run it. Give the worker pool 40 threads: change Vertx.vertx() to Vertx.vertx(new VertxOptions().setWorkerPoolSize(40)). Predict the new worker time, then run. VirtualVsWorkerDemo.java package workbench.nio.l06; import io.vertx.core.Context; import io.vertx.core.Future; import io.vertx.core.Promise; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** 200 requests arrive on one IO context; each makes a 100 ms blocking call. Worker pool vs a virtual thread each. */ public class VirtualVsWorkerDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(); // default worker pool: 20 threads Context server = vertx.getOrCreateContext(); // where the requests arrive Thread.Builder virtualThreads = Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-", 0); // used only on the server's thread for (boolean virtual : new boolean[] {false, true}) { Set<String> threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet(); List<Future<Object>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) { Promise<Object> done = Promise.promise(); server.runOnContext(v -> { Runnable blockingCall = () -> { threads.add(Thread.currentThread().getName()); try { Thread.sleep(100); // JDBC, a card-issuer call... } catch (InterruptedException ignored) { } done.complete(); }; if (virtual) virtualThreads.start(blockingCall); // like @RunOnVirtualThread else vertx.executeBlocking(() -> { blockingCall.run(); return null; }, false); // like @Blocking }); calls.add(done.future()); } Future.all(calls).toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.printf("%-26s 200 calls x 100 ms -> %,5d ms on %d distinct threads%n", virtual ? "virtual thread per call" : "worker pool (20 threads)", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads.size()); } vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l06.VirtualVsWorkerDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l06/VirtualVsWorkerDemo.java VirtualVsWorkerDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l06 import io.vertx.core.Future import io.vertx.core.Promise import io.vertx.core.Vertx import java.util.concurrent.Callable import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit /** 200 requests arrive on one IO context; each makes a 100 ms blocking call. Worker pool vs a virtual thread each. */ fun main() { val vertx = Vertx.vertx() // default worker pool: 20 threads val server = vertx.getOrCreateContext() // where the requests arrive val virtualThreads = Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-", 0) // used only on the server's thread for (virtual in listOf(false, true)) { val threads = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<String>() val t0 = System.nanoTime() val calls = List(200) { val done = Promise.promise<Any>() server.runOnContext { val blockingCall = Runnable { threads += Thread.currentThread().name Thread.sleep(100) // JDBC, a card-issuer call... done.complete() } if (virtual) virtualThreads.start(blockingCall) // like @RunOnVirtualThread else vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Any> { blockingCall.run(); "" }, false) // like @Blocking } done.future() } Future.all(calls).toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS) println("%-26s 200 calls x 100 ms -> %,5d ms on %d distinct threads".format( if (virtual) "virtual thread per call" else "worker pool (20 threads)", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads.size)) } vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get() } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l06.VirtualVsWorkerDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l06/VirtualVsWorkerDemo.kt About 1,000 ms on 20 worker threads (200 calls / 20 threads × 100 ms) and about 110 to 130 ms on 200 virtual threads. With 40 workers it drops to about 500 to 600 ms (534 and 598 ms in my runs): Little's law again, throughput = threads / time per call. The virtual version has no such cap, which is its strength and also why you add your own limit in front of a fragile downstream. Quarkus virtual threads guide docs The common mistake is converting a JDBC endpoint to return Uni "to make it reactive": return Uni.createFrom().item(repository.findById(id));. Quarkus sees Uni, runs the method on the IO thread, and findById blocks the event loop while the Uni is built. Nothing becomes reactive. The service just loses the worker thread that used to protect the event loop. Either keep the plain return type, add @Blocking, or switch the data access to a reactive client so the method really doesn't block.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Java and Kotlin
x: The lab's dispatch rules in Kotlin and Java DispatchRules.java final class DispatchRules { private static final Set<ReturnKind> NON_BLOCKING_RETURNS = EnumSet.of( ReturnKind.UNI, ReturnKind.MULTI, ReturnKind.COMPLETION_STAGE, ReturnKind.PUBLISHER, ReturnKind.SUSPEND); static Target target(Endpoint e) { Set<Marker> m = e.markers(); if (m.contains(Marker.RUN_ON_VIRTUAL_THREAD)) return Target.VIRTUAL_THREAD; if (m.contains(Marker.BLOCKING)) return Target.WORKER; if (m.contains(Marker.NON_BLOCKING)) return Target.IO_THREAD; if (m.contains(Marker.TRANSACTIONAL)) return Target.WORKER; return NON_BLOCKING_RETURNS.contains(e.returns()) ? Target.IO_THREAD : Target.WORKER; } } DispatchRules.kt object DispatchRules { private val nonBlockingReturns = setOf( ReturnKind.UNI, ReturnKind.MULTI, ReturnKind.COMPLETION_STAGE, ReturnKind.PUBLISHER, ReturnKind.SUSPEND) fun target(e: Endpoint): Target = when { Marker.RUN_ON_VIRTUAL_THREAD in e.markers -> Target.VIRTUAL_THREAD Marker.BLOCKING in e.markers -> Target.WORKER Marker.NON_BLOCKING in e.markers -> Target.IO_THREAD Marker.TRANSACTIONAL in e.markers -> Target.WORKER e.returns in nonBlockingReturns -> Target.IO_THREAD else -> Target.WORKER } } Both encode the same first-match-wins rules; Kotlin's when without a subject reads like the figure, Java uses early returns. The language difference that matters is in Quarkus itself: Java has no suspend, so a Java endpoint is non-blocking only through its return type, while a Kotlin suspend fun with a plain return type is non-blocking too and runs on the IO thread. One Kotlin trap from this lesson's lab: Vert.x 5's Future has a member await(), and in Kotlin a member always wins over an extension with the same name, so a test helper fun <T> Future<T>.await() is silently ignored. The lab's test calls its helper awaitResult() for that reason.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Worked example
x: Pick the thread for four payment endpoints A payment lookup reads Oracle through JDBC. Plain return type, so it runs on a worker. Nothing to add. @GET @Path("/payments/{id}") public Payment byId(@PathParam("id") String id) { // worker thread return payments.findById(id); // JDBC } @GET @Path("/payments/{id}") fun byId(@PathParam("id") id: String): Payment = // worker thread payments.findById(id) // JDBC A capture endpoint uses JTA and returns Uni because a client library wants one. Under the 3.40.1 docs @Transactional alone would send it to a worker; under the main-branch docs it would run on the IO thread and the interceptor would throw. Add @Blocking and both readings agree. @Blocking @Transactional @POST @Path("/payments/{id}/capture") public Uni<Receipt> capture(@PathParam("id") String id) { return Uni.createFrom().item(ledger.capture(id)); // JDBC inside a JTA transaction } @Blocking @Transactional @POST @Path("/payments/{id}/capture") fun capture(@PathParam("id") id: String): Uni<Receipt> = Uni.createFrom().item(ledger.capture(id)) // JDBC inside a JTA transaction A live feed of payment events comes from a reactive client and never blocks. Multi keeps it on the IO thread with no thread switch, which is the case the reactive model is built for. @GET @Path("/payments/events") public Multi<PaymentEvent> events() { // IO thread return eventStream.subscribe(); // non-blocking source } @GET @Path("/payments/events") fun events(): Multi<PaymentEvent> = // IO thread eventStream.subscribe() // non-blocking source A settlement report calls a slow SOAP service (2 s) that accepts at most 50 concurrent calls, and finance runs it in bursts of hundreds. The worker pool would cap throughput, so use a virtual thread per request, and put the downstream's limit back with a semaphore. private final Semaphore soapSlots = new Semaphore(50); @RunOnVirtualThread @GET @Path("/reports/settlement/{day}") public Report settlement(@PathParam("day") String day) throws InterruptedException { soapSlots.acquire(); // 1. respect the downstream's limit try { return soapClient.settlementFor(day); // 2. blocks: parks the virtual thread } finally { soapSlots.release(); } } private val soapSlots = Semaphore(50) @RunOnVirtualThread @GET @Path("/reports/settlement/{day}") fun settlement(@PathParam("day") day: String): Report { soapSlots.acquire() // 1. respect the downstream's limit try { return soapClient.settlementFor(day) // 2. blocks: parks the virtual thread } finally { soapSlots.release() } }

x: Simulate Quarkus's dispatch on plain Vert.x labs/nio/src/main/kotlin/workbench/nio/l06/Dispatcher.kt labs/nio/src/main/kotlin/workbench/nio/l06/Endpoint.kt ./gradlew :nio:test --tests 'workbench.nio.l06.*' Run the tests. Write Dispatcher.invoke: receive the request with server.runOnContext { ... }, then run the body there (IO thread), through vertx.executeBlocking(callable, false) (worker) or on a new virtual thread, and complete a Promise with the result or the failure. Run the tests until all seven pass. Then change false to the default and see which test fails, and why. Marker.BLOCKING in endpoint.markers reads naturally in Kotlin. val p = Promise.promise<T>(), then p.complete(value) or p.fail(e), and return p.future(). For the worker branch, vertx.executeBlocking(task, false).onComplete(p) passes the result straight on. Every request goes through the one server context, so an ordered executeBlocking would make the four 300 ms calls queue: that is what the overlap test catches. All seven tests in DispatcherTest pass. h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Quiz
x: In Quarkus 3.40 with no annotations, which endpoint runs on the IO thread? public Payment get(@PathParam("id") String id) public List<Payment> recent() public Uni<Payment> get(@PathParam("id") String id) public Response refund(...) Only the Uni return type marks the method as non-blocking. The other three return plain values, so Quarkus runs them on a worker thread. A Kotlin endpoint suspend fun capture(id: String): Receipt = repository.capture(id) calls a blocking JDBC repository. What happens under load? Nothing: suspend functions never block a thread It runs on the IO thread, so each JDBC call blocks an event loop; make it a plain function or call a non-blocking client Quarkus notices the JDBC call and moves it to a worker It runs on a new virtual thread Quarkus treats suspend like Uni: non-blocking, so it runs on the IO thread. suspend only frees the thread when the code inside actually suspends; a JDBC call blocks it. Quarkus can't see inside the method. A Quarkus log shows Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-2 has been blocked for 2105 ms, time limit is 2000 ms followed at once by a stack trace. Plain Vert.x would print the stack only after 5 s. Why here? Quarkus sets the warning-exception time to 2 s Quarkus lowers the blocked limit to 1 s Vert.x 5 changed its default to 2 s The stack means Quarkus killed the thread Quarkus's quarkus.vertx.warning-exception-time defaults to 2 s, the same as the blocked limit, so the first warning already carries the stack trace. Neither Vert.x nor Quarkus kills or interrupts the thread. From lesson 5: a Vert.x consumer calls vertx.executeBlocking(callable) without the second argument for every message. Six messages arrive at once, each needing 300 ms of blocking work. Roughly how long until all six are answered? About 300 ms About 1,800 ms About 600 ms Never: it deadlocks The default executeBlocking is ordered per context, and all six messages come from the consumer's one context, so they run one after another on the worker pool: 6 × 300 ms. Passing false lets them overlap. A report endpoint calls a blocking SOAP service that takes 2 s and allows 50 concurrent calls. Finance sends bursts of 500 requests. Which fits best? Return Uni and call the SOAP client inside it Plain return type, with the worker pool raised to 500 @NonBlocking, so it doesn't use a worker @RunOnVirtualThread, with a semaphore of 50 around the SOAP call The call blocks, so it must stay off the IO thread, which rules out Uni and @NonBlocking. Virtual threads make 500 waiting requests cheap, and the semaphore keeps the SOAP service at its limit of 50. A 500-thread worker pool would work, but costs 500 platform threads and still sends 500 concurrent calls downstream.
