h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Key terms
x: IO thread Quarkus's name for a Vert.x event-loop thread; it reads requests and writes responses. Worker thread A thread from Quarkus's bounded pool that may block, used for plain return types and @Blocking. @Blocking / @NonBlocking Annotations that override the thread Quarkus would pick from the method's signature. @RunOnVirtualThread Runs the endpoint on a new virtual thread instead of the IO thread or a worker. BlockingOperationNotAllowedException Thrown by guarded Quarkus APIs when blocking code runs on an IO thread. Pinning A virtual thread that can't unmount while it waits, so it holds its carrier thread. Monopolization CPU-heavy work on a virtual thread that never blocks, so it keeps its carrier. Which Quarkus REST return types run on the IO thread by default? Uni, Multi, CompletionStage, Publisher, and Kotlin suspend functions. Everything else runs on a worker thread. Where can you put @Blocking / @NonBlocking in Quarkus REST? On a method, a class, or a jakarta.ws.rs.core.Application subclass (which sets the app-wide default). Does @Transactional make a Quarkus REST method blocking? The 3.40.1 docs say yes, the main-branch docs say no (since 3.35). Add an explicit @Blocking to JTA endpoints that return Uni. Default number of Vert.x event loops in Quarkus 3.40? One per CPU, at least 2, and at most one per 10 MB of max heap: max(2, min(maxHeapMB / 10, cpus)). Why does a Quarkus blocked-thread warning come with a stack trace at 2 s? Quarkus sets quarkus.vertx.warning-exception-time to 2 s; plain Vert.x uses 5 s. What exception do guarded Quarkus APIs throw on an IO thread? BlockingOperationNotAllowedException (an IllegalStateException), e.g. from the JTA interceptor or a blocking body read. Three costs of @RunOnVirtualThread named by the Quarkus guide? Pinning (e.g. synchronized on Java 21 to 23, native code), monopolization by CPU-heavy work, and inefficient per-thread object pools.

h: Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads · Go deeper
x: A few details from the Quarkus 3.40 sources and docs help when you debug thread choices. Filters follow their endpoint. A @ServerRequestFilter runs on the worker for a @Blocking endpoint and on the IO thread otherwise, so a filter that does a blocking lookup (say, an API-key check against a database) blocks the event loop for every non-blocking endpoint. @ServerRequestFilter(nonBlocking = true) forces a filter onto the IO thread, which is only safe if it really never blocks. To check which thread runs your code, log Thread.currentThread().getName() or assert io.vertx.core.Context.isOnEventLoopThread() in a @QuarkusTest. Event-loop threads are named vert.x-eventloop-thread-N, and Quarkus's worker threads usually have executor-thread in their names. The Vert.x knobs live under quarkus.vertx.*: event-loops-pool-size, max-event-loop-execute-time, warning-exception-time and max-worker-execute-time (60 s). The old quarkus.vertx.worker-pool-size is deprecated in favor of quarkus.thread-pool.max-threads. Raising the event-loop count rarely helps a service that blocks: it only spreads the damage over more loops. Removing the blocking call is the fix. Finally, a version note on the @Transactional disagreement: the 3.40.1-tagged guide and the main-branch guide were both read for this track, and the code that applies the rule was not found. If you need certainty for your exact Quarkus version, write a @QuarkusTest that calls a @Transactional endpoint returning Uni and asserts which thread it ran on.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · A Jetty server is connectors, handlers and one thread pool
x: Jetty's documentation describes a Server as the component that links a collection of Connectors and a collection of Handlers, with threads from one ThreadPool doing all the work. Every thread you'll see in this lesson comes from that one pool. The connector you'll use is the ServerConnector. It has two kinds of threads. Acceptors (one by default) call accept() and hand each new socket on. A SelectorManager owns several ManagedSelectors, and each ManagedSelector is one thread running a java.nio Selector: the select loop from lesson 2, so epoll on Linux. By default there are max(1, min(cpus / 2, maxThreads / 16)) selectors, and the docs give a rule of thumb that one selector manages 1,000 to 5,000 sockets. Inside, each socket becomes an EndPoint that moves bytes and a Connection that parses a protocol (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, WebSocket). Java Server server = new Server(new QueuedThreadPool()); // one pool for everything ServerConnector connector = new ServerConnector(server); connector.setHost("127.0.0.1"); connector.setPort(8080); server.addConnector(connector); server.setHandler(new LedgerHandler(300)); server.start(); Kotlin val server = Server(QueuedThreadPool()) // one pool for everything val connector = ServerConnector(server).apply { host = "127.0.0.1"; port = 8080 } server.addConnector(connector) server.handler = LedgerHandler(300) server.start() The default pool is a QueuedThreadPool with at least 8 and at most 200 threads. The connector leases some of them for good: this section's demo, on 4 CPUs, shows 1 acceptor, 2 selectors and 3 leased threads. The pool must have room for those plus at least one thread for requests, and the docs suggest sizing maxThreads as the leased threads plus the threads you want for handlers. Two pool rules surprise people. The pool's queue must be unbounded. Jetty sometimes needs to run its own tasks to make progress (HTTP/2, for example, must write in order to read), and the docs warn that a rejected task can make the server grind to a halt. Limit load with a QoS handler instead. And a platform thread costs about 1 MiB of native memory, so 200 threads is a real number. Count what a default server starts Open JettyThreadsDemo.java (or JettyThreadsDemo.kt). From the formula above, predict the selector count on your machine with the default pool of 200. Run it and compare. Then predict the selectors for new QueuedThreadPool(12) on 4 CPUs. Ignore the last two lines for now; the third section explains them. JettyThreadsDemo.java package workbench.nio.l07; import org.eclipse.jetty.io.Content; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Handler; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Request; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Response; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Server; import org.eclipse.jetty.server.ServerConnector; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.Callback; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.VirtualThreads; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.QueuedThreadPool; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.ThreadPool; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpClient; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; /** What does a default Jetty 12 server start, and which thread runs a blocking vs a non-blocking handler? */ public class JettyThreadsDemo { static final HttpClient CLIENT = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build(); static String where() { Thread t = Thread.currentThread(); return t.getName() + " virtual=" + t.isVirtual(); } static class Blocking extends Handler.Abstract { // declares BLOCKING @Override public boolean handle(Request req, Response res, Callback cb) { Content.Sink.write(res, true, where(), cb); return true; } } static class NonBlocking extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking { // declares NON_BLOCKING @Override public boolean handle(Request req, Response res, Callback cb) { Content.Sink.write(res, true, where(), cb); return true; } } static Server start(ThreadPool pool, Handler handler) throws Exception { Server server = new Server(pool); ServerConnector connector = new ServerConnector(server); connector.setHost("127.0.0.1"); connector.setPort(0); server.addConnector(connector); server.setHandler(handler); server.start(); return server; } static String get(Server server) throws Exception { int port = ((ServerConnector) server.getConnectors()[0]).getLocalPort(); return CLIENT.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + port + "/")).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { QueuedThreadPool defaults = new QueuedThreadPool(); Server server = start(defaults, new Blocking()); ServerConnector c = (ServerConnector) server.getConnectors()[0]; System.out.println("cpus=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + " acceptors=" + c.getAcceptors() + " selectors=" + c.getSelectorManager().getSelectorCount()); System.out.println("QueuedThreadPool min=" + defaults.getMinThreads() + " max=" + defaults.getMaxThreads() + " started=" + defaults.getThreads() + " leased=" + defaults.getLeasedThreads()); System.out.println("[platform pool] BLOCKING handler -> " + get(server)); server.stop(); server = start(new QueuedThreadPool(), new NonBlocking()); System.out.println("[platform pool] NON_BLOCKING handler -> " + get(server)); server.stop(); for (boolean blocking : new boolean[] {true, false}) { QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(); pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("jetty-vt-")); server = start(pool, blocking ? new Blocking() : new NonBlocking()); System.out.println("[pool + virtual threads] " + (blocking ? "BLOCKING handler -> " : "NON_BLOCKING handler -> ") + get(server)); server.stop(); } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l07.JettyThreadsDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l07/JettyThreadsDemo.java JettyThreadsDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l07 import org.eclipse.jetty.io.Content import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Handler import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Request import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Response import org.eclipse.jetty.server.Server import org.eclipse.jetty.server.ServerConnector import org.eclipse.jetty.util.Callback import org.eclipse.jetty.util.VirtualThreads import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.QueuedThreadPool import org.eclipse.jetty.util.thread.ThreadPool import java.net.URI import java.net.http.HttpClient import java.net.http.HttpRequest import java.net.http.HttpResponse /** What does a default Jetty 12 server start, and which thread runs a blocking vs a non-blocking handler? */ private val client = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build() private fun where() = Thread.currentThread().let { "${it.name} virtual=${it.isVirtual}" } private class KtBlocking : Handler.Abstract() { // declares BLOCKING override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Sink.write(response, true, where(), callback) return true } } private class KtNonBlocking : Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() { // declares NON_BLOCKING override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Sink.write(response, true, where(), callback) return true } } private fun startServer(pool: ThreadPool, handler: Handler): Server = Server(pool).apply { addConnector(ServerConnector(this).apply { host = "127.0.0.1"; With a 12-thread pool the formula gives max(1, min(2, 12 / 16 = 0)) = 1 selector. Jetty also logs a few INFO lines when servers start and stop. Jetty 12.1 programming guide: HTTP server (connectors, acceptors, selectors) docs Jetty's adaptive strategy is a chef who also receives the deliveries. When a delivery arrives, the quickest thing is to cook it at once, while the ingredients are still warm, which is Produce-Consume. If the dish takes long (a blocking task), the chef first waves over a standby cook to take over receiving deliveries, then cooks: Execute-Produce-Consume. With no standby cook free, the order goes onto the kitchen's ticket rail for whoever is free next: Produce-Execute-Consume. The analogy breaks where Jetty trusts the order slip: a dish marked "quick" (NonBlocking) is always cooked at the door, even if it turns out to take an hour, and then nobody receives deliveries.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · The core Handler API is asynchronous
x: Jetty 12 rewrote the API at its center. In Jetty 11 a handler had a blocking signature built on Servlet types. In Jetty 12 it is boolean handle(Request request, Response response, Callback callback), and the migration guide spells out the new contract: return true to say you handled the request, and then complete the Callback, by succeeding or failing it, possibly long after handle has returned. Return false and Jetty moves on; with no other handler, the client gets a 404. A blocking handler is the simple case: do the work, write the response with Content.Sink.write(response, true, text, callback), which completes the callback once the bytes are written, and return true. A non-blocking handler reads the body without waiting for it: Java public class EchoHandler extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking { @Override public boolean handle(Request request, Response response, Callback callback) { Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete((body, failure) -> { if (failure != null) { Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure); return; } Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: " + body, callback); // completes the callback }); return true; // "I took this request"; the response finishes later } } Kotlin class EchoHandler : Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() { override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete { body, failure -> if (failure != null) { Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure) } else { Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: $body", callback) // completes the callback } } return true // "I took this request"; the response finishes later } } The request body is a Content.Source: you read it in Content.Chunks, which are slices of Jetty's network buffers, passed up without copying. The rule echoes Netty's reference counting from lesson 4: every chunk you read() must be released, except failure chunks, and a source must be read to the end or failed, or Jetty can leak its buffers. Helpers such as asStringAsync do the reading and releasing for you. The superclass is a declaration. Handler.Abstract says "I may block" (InvocationType.BLOCKING). Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking says "I never block", and Jetty uses that promise to pick a thread, as the next section shows. The Servlet API still exists, as a layer on top of this core. Jetty 12 ships it in separate environments named after Jakarta EE versions: ee8, ee9, ee10, and since 12.1 ee11, which brings Servlet 6.1. The docs list the core API's strengths as simple, minimal and asynchronous, with low overhead because you only configure what you use. Break the handler contract In JettyThreadsDemo, change the Blocking handler's body to just return false; (delete the Content.Sink.write line). Predict what the first GET prints. Put it back. Now think it through without running it: what does a client see if a handler returns true and never completes the callback? With return false the request finds no handler and Jetty answers with a 404 page, which the demo prints as the body. A handler that returns true and never completes the callback leaves the request open: the client waits until its own timeout or Jetty's idle timeout ends the connection. Returning true is a promise to finish the response exactly once. Jetty 11 to 12 migration guide (Handler API) docs You may run Jetty without choosing it: as the embedded server in a service, inside a test harness such as WireMock, or behind a framework. For a payments team the useful knobs are few. Declare honestly whether your handlers block. Size the QueuedThreadPool as leased threads plus request threads, and never give it a bounded queue. Use a QoS handler to shed load, not the pool. On JDK 21 or newer, turn on the virtual threads executor for a blocking service, and keep a real limit (the JDBC pool, a semaphore) in front of the database and the card issuer, because Jetty will now happily run 2,000 handlers at once.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · One strategy, three modes: who runs your handler
x: When a selector finds a readable socket, it produces a task: "run this connection's onFillable", which parses the request and calls your handler. Jetty's AdaptiveExecutionStrategy then decides which thread consumes that task, and it has three main modes, named in the Jetty docs: Produce-Consume (PC): the selector thread runs the task itself. No hand-off and warm CPU caches, but every other socket on that selector waits. The docs say this mode is equivalent to the event loop of Node.js or Netty. Produce-Execute-Consume (PEC): the task goes to the thread pool. No head-of-line blocking, but a hand-off, a queue and cold caches on another core. Execute-Produce-Consume (EPC): the selector thread runs the task, and a reserved thread, one the pool keeps idle and ready, takes over the selecting. Warm caches and no stall. The choice follows the task's invocation type. A NON_BLOCKING task runs in PC mode. A BLOCKING task runs in EPC mode when a reserved thread is available, and in PEC mode when none is. Jetty's source notes that this strategy used to be called "Eat What You Kill": the hunter eats what it caught. This section's demo reads the mode from each handler's own stack: default pool, BLOCKING -> qtp1636182655-25 :: AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.epcRunTask default pool, NON_BLOCKING -> qtp2144284609-37 :: AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.pcRunTask reservedThreads=0, BLOCKING -> qtp826865256-50 :: no strategy frame: dispatched to the pool virtual threads, BLOCKING -> jetty-vt-1 :: VirtualThread.run Now you can see why the handler's declaration matters. NonBlocking is a promise that lets Jetty run your code on the selector thread, exactly like a Netty event loop. Break the promise with a JDBC call and every connection on that selector stalls; the docs call it a risk of server lock-up. Containers combine their children's types, so one blocking handler anywhere in a handler tree makes the whole tree blocking. That's safe, but it costs the PC fast path. Compare that with the other servers you know. Netty-based servers, including Vert.x and Quarkus, run every handler in PC mode on the event loop, and offloading is your job. Tomcat's NIO connector watches sockets with a poller and processes requests on its executor threads (200 by default). Jetty sits in between: it chooses per task, from what your handler declares. Read the mode from the stack Open StrategyDemo.java (or StrategyDemo.kt). For each of the four setups, predict the mode: PC, EPC, PEC, or a virtual thread. Run it with the command below. Explain the third line: why does setReservedThreads(0) change the mode for a blocking handler? Read it from the handler's own stack. */ public class StrategyDemo { static final HttpClient CLIENT = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build(); static String mode() { List<String> methods = Arrays.stream(Thread.currentThread().getStackTrace()) .filter(f -> f.getClassName().contains("AdaptiveExecutionStrategy") || f.getClassName().contains("VirtualThread")) .map(f -> f.getClassName().replaceAll(".*\\.", "") + "." + f.getMethodName()) .collect(Collectors.toList()); String strategy = methods.stream().filter(m -> m.contains("RunTask") && !m.equals("AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.runTask")) .findFirst().orElse(methods.isEmpty() ? Read it from the handler's own stack. */ private val strategyClient = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build() private fun strategyMode(): String { val methods = Thread.currentThread().stackTrace .filter { "AdaptiveExecutionStrategy" in it.className || "VirtualThread" in it.className } .map { it.className.substringAfterLast('.') + "." + it.methodName } val strategy = methods.firstOrNull { "RunTask" in it && it != "AdaptiveExecutionStrategy.runTask" } ?: methods.firstOrNull() ?: "no strategy frame: dispatched to the pool" return "${Thread.currentThread().name} :: $strategy" } private fun modeHandler(nonBlocking: Boolean): Handler = if (nonBlocking) object : Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() { override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Sink.write(response, true, strategyMode(), callback); return true } } else object : Handler.Abstract() { override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Sink.write(response, true, strategyMode(), callback); return true } } fun main() { for (setup in listOf("default pool, BLOCKING", "default pool, NON_BLOCKING", "reservedThreads=0, BLOCKING", "virtual threads, BLOCKING")) { val pool = QueuedThreadPool() if (setup.startsWith("reservedThreads=0")) pool.reservedThreads = 0 if (setup.startsWith("virtual")) pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("jetty-vt-") val server = Server(pool) val connector = ServerConnector(server).apply { host = "127.0.0.1"; port = 0 } server.addConnector(connector) server.handler = modeHandler(setup.endsWith("NON_BLOCKING")) server.start() val uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:${connector.localPort}/") strategyClient.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()) // warm up the connection println("%-28s -> %s".format(setup, strategyClient.send(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body())) server.stop() } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l07.StrategyDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l07/StrategyDemo.kt Blocking on the default pool: epcRunTask. Non-blocking: pcRunTask, on the selector's own thread. With no reserved threads, a blocking task can't use EPC, because nobody could take over selecting, so it is dispatched to the pool and the handler's stack has no strategy frame at all (PEC). With virtual threads, the PEC path hands the task to a virtual thread, jetty-vt-1. A selector produces a task per ready connection; the adaptive strategy runs it in place, runs it in place while a reserved thread selects, or hands it off. h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Virtual threads in Jetty 12
x: Jetty 12 offers virtual threads in two ways, and they behave very differently. The first keeps the QueuedThreadPool and gives it a virtual threads executor: Java QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(12); pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("ledger-vt-")); Kotlin val pool = QueuedThreadPool(12) pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("ledger-vt-") When the strategy picks PEC for a blocking task, it sends the task to a virtual thread instead of a pool thread. Turning this on sets the reserved threads to zero by default, so blocking tasks always take that path. Acceptors, selectors and non-blocking tasks stay on platform threads. The demo in the first section showed it: the blocking handler ran on jetty-vt-0 and the non-blocking one on a qtp thread. The second is VirtualThreadPool, which replaces the pool. Despite its name, it doesn't pool virtual threads. It starts a new virtual thread for each task and limits how many tasks run at once with a semaphore, 200 permits by default. With it there are no qtp threads at all: the acceptor and the selectors run on it too. This section's demo sends 40 concurrent requests to a handler that blocks for 300 ms: QueuedThreadPool(max=12) 40 x 300 ms -> 1,681 ms, at most 10 in the handler at once QueuedThreadPool(max=12) + virtual 40 x 300 ms -> 326 ms, at most 40 in the handler at once VirtualThreadPool(maxThreads=8) 40 x 300 ms -> 2,122 ms, at most 7 in the handler at once Twelve platform threads minus the leased ones left about ten for requests. The virtual executor let all 40 wait at once. The VirtualThreadPool with 8 permits was slowest, because its permits cap concurrency below even the platform pool, and only 7 ever reached the handler at once, so at least one permit was held by something else at the time. One version note from the Jetty docs. Jetty dedicates a thread to each Selector, and up to Java 23, calling Selector.select() from a virtual thread pins its carrier; from Java 24 it doesn't. On 21 to 23, then, a server running everything on virtual threads loses one carrier per selector. That is one more reason to prefer the first option: QueuedThreadPool plus the virtual threads executor keeps selectors on platform threads and runs only your blocking handlers virtually. And as in every lesson of this track, virtual threads don't protect your downstream: 40 handlers at once means 40 JDBC calls at once. Three pools, one load Open JettyLoadDemo.java (or JettyLoadDemo.kt). Predict the time and the concurrency for each pool. Use Little's law: 40 requests, 300 ms each, and the number of threads that can run handlers. Run it. Change new VirtualThreadPool(8) to new VirtualThreadPool(64) and predict again before running. With 64 permits, the virtual pool lets all 40 requests run at once and finishes in about the same time as the virtual executor. The most damaging mistake is extending Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking because it sounds faster, then calling JDBC, a synchronous HTTP client or anything else that waits. The superclass is a promise: Jetty runs the handler on the selector thread in Produce-Consume mode, so every other connection on that selector waits behind your query, which is the event-loop failure from lessons 3 and 5. Extend Handler.Abstract for anything that might block. A close second is giving the QueuedThreadPool a bounded queue to protect the server: the docs say the queue must be unbounded, because Jetty's own progress depends on tasks that must not be rejected.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Java and Kotlin
x: An asynchronous echo handler in Java and Kotlin EchoHandler.java public class EchoHandler extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking { @Override public boolean handle(Request request, Response response, Callback callback) { Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete((body, failure) -> { if (failure != null) { Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure); return; } Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: " + body, callback); // completes the callback }); return true; // "I took this request"; the response finishes later } } EchoHandler.kt class EchoHandler : Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking() { override fun handle(request: Request, response: Response, callback: Callback): Boolean { Content.Source.asStringAsync(request, UTF_8).whenComplete { body, failure -> if (failure != null) { Response.writeError(request, response, callback, failure) } else { Content.Sink.write(response, true, "echo: $body", callback) // completes the callback } } return true // "I took this request"; the response finishes later } } The two are the same handler at runtime. The Kotlin version shows two small differences. The BiConsumer passed to whenComplete becomes a two-parameter lambda, and if/else replaces the early return, because a bare return inside a Kotlin lambda would return from handle itself and doesn't compile here (you'd need return@whenComplete). Kotlin also lets you write Jetty's setters as properties (server.handler = ..., pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = ...). The threading is identical: the lambda runs on whichever thread completes the body future, which can be a different thread from the one that called handle.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Worked example
x: Move a blocking ledger service onto virtual threads A Jetty service serves balances with a 300 ms JDBC query per request on a pool of 50. Under a burst of 400 requests the tail latency explodes. Little's law: about 45 threads can run handlers, so 400 requests need 400 / 45 × 0.3 s, about 2.7 s, to drain, while the CPU is nearly idle. QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(50); // about 45 left after leasing Server server = new Server(pool); server.setHandler(new LedgerHandler(300)); val pool = QueuedThreadPool(50) // about 45 left after leasing val server = Server(pool) server.handler = LedgerHandler(300) Keep the handler and give blocking tasks virtual threads. The pool keeps its platform threads for acceptors and selectors; every blocking handler gets a virtual thread, so the burst no longer queues for threads. QueuedThreadPool pool = new QueuedThreadPool(50); pool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("ledger-vt-")); val pool = QueuedThreadPool(50) pool.virtualThreadsExecutor = VirtualThreads.getNamedVirtualThreadsExecutor("ledger-vt-") Now the queue has moved to the database. 400 handlers all ask the connection pool, which has 20 connections. That is the right place for the wait, but give it a timeout, so a slow database turns into fast errors instead of 400 stuck requests. HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig(); config.setMaximumPoolSize(20); // the real concurrency limit config.setConnectionTimeout(500); // ms to wait for a connection, then fail val config = HikariConfig().apply { maximumPoolSize = 20 // the real concurrency limit connectionTimeout = 500 // ms to wait for a connection, then fail } Check the health endpoint is still cheap. It extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking, so it keeps running on platform threads in Produce-Consume mode, which the lab's last test asserts. If someone later adds a database ping to it, change its superclass in the same commit.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Quiz
x: A Jetty 12 handler extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking and calls a 200 ms REST client synchronously. What happens under load? Nothing special: Jetty moves it to a worker because the call blocks It runs on a selector thread in Produce-Consume mode, so other connections on that selector wait behind each call Jetty throws an exception because non-blocking handlers can't block It runs on a virtual thread, so blocking is free NonBlocking is a declaration Jetty trusts. It runs the task on the selector thread with no hand-off, like a Netty event loop. Jetty can't see that the call blocks, and virtual threads only get blocking tasks. A team gives Jetty's QueuedThreadPool a bounded queue of 1,000 tasks so it rejects work under overload. What do the Jetty docs say? Good practice: a bounded queue protects the heap Fine, as long as the bound is above maxThreads The queue must be unbounded: Jetty needs its own tasks to run to make progress, and rejecting one can stall the server; use a QoS handler instead Only HTTP/1.1 connectors support bounded queues Jetty submits internal tasks to the same pool, for example HTTP/2 must be able to write in order to read. A rejected internal task can stall connections. Limit concurrency with a QoS handler, which works at the request level. On a 4-CPU machine, new Server(new QueuedThreadPool(64)) with one default ServerConnector. How many selector threads? 1 2 4 8 max(1, min(cpus / 2, maxThreads / 16)) = max(1, min(2, 4)) = 2. Selector count follows CPUs and pool size, not connections. From lesson 2: a Jetty ManagedSelector wraps a java.nio.channels.Selector. Why does it run on its own dedicated thread? A selector's selected-key set isn't safe for concurrent use, so one thread owns each selector and its loop Selector.select() must run on the main thread Selectors are faster on platform threads The JDK allows only one selector per thread The Selector Javadoc says the selector is thread-safe but its key sets are not. One owner thread per selector is the pattern every framework uses: Netty's event loop, Vert.x's event loop, Jetty's ManagedSelector. You enable QueuedThreadPool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor(...) on JDK 21. Which of these runs on a virtual thread? The acceptor The ManagedSelector loops A Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking health check A Handler.Abstract handler that calls JDBC Only tasks the strategy runs in PEC mode, which are blocking tasks, go to the virtual threads executor. Acceptors, selectors and non-blocking handlers stay on platform threads, which also avoids selectors pinning carriers before Java 24.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Explain it back
x: A colleague says "Jetty is just a thread-per-request server like Tomcat". Explain what Jetty 12 actually does between reading a socket and calling a handler, and why a handler's superclass matters.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Key terms
x: Connector The Jetty component that accepts connections and turns bytes into protocol messages. Acceptor A thread that calls accept() and hands each new socket to a selector. ManagedSelector Jetty's wrapper around one java.nio Selector, run by one thread. Invocation type A task's or handler's declaration: BLOCKING, NON_BLOCKING or EITHER. Reserved thread An idle pool thread kept ready so a selector thread can hand off selecting and run a task itself. AdaptiveExecutionStrategy Jetty's per-task choice between running a task in place and handing it off (formerly Eat What You Kill). Callback The object a Jetty handler completes, by success or failure, when its response is done. What does a Jetty 12 ServerConnector run on threads? Acceptors (1 by default) that accept sockets, and ManagedSelectors, one thread each, running a java.nio select loop. Default number of selectors in a Jetty 12 ServerConnector? max(1, min(cpus / 2, maxThreads / 16)): 2 on 4 CPUs with the default 200-thread pool. The Jetty 12 core handler contract? boolean handle(Request, Response, Callback): return true if you handle it, then complete the callback exactly once, possibly after handle returns. false means "not mine". PC, EPC, PEC in one line each? PC: the selector thread runs the task. EPC: the selector thread runs it while a reserved thread takes over selecting. PEC: the task is handed to the pool (or a virtual thread). When does Jetty run a task in Produce-Consume mode? When the task is NON_BLOCKING, for example a handler that extends Handler.Abstract.NonBlocking. QueuedThreadPool.setVirtualThreadsExecutor vs VirtualThreadPool? The first sends only blocking tasks to virtual threads and keeps selectors on platform threads. The second runs everything on new virtual threads with a semaphore cap (200 by default). Why must Jetty's thread pool queue be unbounded? Jetty submits its own tasks to the pool to make progress (HTTP/2 must write to read); rejecting one can stall the server. Use a QoS handler to limit load.

h: Jetty 12: acceptors, selectors and thread pools · Go deeper
x: Three details from the Jetty 12.1 sources and docs round out the picture. There is a fourth mode. AdaptiveExecutionStrategy's Javadoc names Produce-Invoke-Consume for tasks whose invocation type is EITHER: they are run with Invocable.invokeNonBlocking, meaning the task is asked to proceed in a non-blocking way if it can. The selection order is PC for a non-blocking task, EPC if a reserved thread is available, PIC for EITHER, and PEC otherwise. Strategies also nest: the selector's strategy produces connection tasks, and an HTTP/2 connection runs its own strategy over its streams. Jetty also has the reverse problem of a declared handler. Request.demand(Runnable), which asks Jetty to call you back when more body content is available, treats a plain lambda as blocking. If your callback really is non-blocking, pass an Invocable.Task that declares so, or Jetty may hand it off to another thread for nothing. On sizing: each connector leases a thread per acceptor and per selector, and ReservedThreadExecutor leases its reserved threads, by default max(1, ceilToNextPowerOfTwo(min(cpus, maxThreads / 8))), or 0 once a virtual threads executor is set. The docs suggest maxThreads = leased threads + threads you want for handlers, and remind you that idle threads shrink back according to idleTimeout. Raising maxThreads to thousands is the old fix for blocking handlers; on JDK 21 or newer, the virtual threads executor is the cheaper one. HTTP/3 shows how far the connector abstraction stretches: Jetty implements HTTP/3 in Java but uses the native Quiche library for QUIC, through JNA, with a connector that has zero acceptors and a single selector over a DatagramChannel.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Zero-copy: let the kernel move the file
x: Sending a file the obvious way passes every byte through your process twice. read copies bytes from the kernel's page cache (its in-memory copy of recently used file pages) into your buffer, and write copies them back into the kernel's socket send buffer. With a heap ByteBuffer, the JDK adds another copy through a temporary direct buffer, as lesson 2 showed. Each call is also a system call: a switch from your program into the kernel and back. FileChannel.transferTo asks the kernel to do the whole move. On Linux, with a socket as the target, the JDK uses sendfile(2): the kernel sends pages from the page cache straight to the socket, and the bytes never enter your process. A run for this track sent 64 MiB to a loopback socket and counted system calls with strace: transferTo: sendfile 1 call copy through a 64 KiB heap buffer: read 2,119 calls, write 1,037 calls, no sendfile (the reads include the receiving side) Like write on a non-blocking socket, transferTo may move fewer bytes than you asked for. It returns how many it moved, so it lives in a loop: Java long sent = 0; while (sent < count) { sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, socket); // maybe partial } Kotlin var sent = 0L while (sent < count) { sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, socket) // maybe partial } Netty wraps the same idea in DefaultFileRegion: write one to a channel and the transport sends the file. The NIO transport calls FileChannel.transferTo, and the native epoll transport calls sendfile itself. When the socket buffer fills, sendfile fails with EAGAIN ("try again later"), and Netty waits for writability and resumes: lesson 2's partial-write logic again. Zero-copy has one condition: the bytes must leave exactly as they sit in the file. If the JVM encrypts them with TLS or compresses them, that work happens in your process, so the bytes have to come up into user space anyway. Tomcat's connector docs show the trade-off: for static files over 48 KiB it uses sendfile and skips compression. In payments, that makes zero-copy a tool for bulk transfers over plain internal links, such as settlement files and statement exports, where TLS ends at a proxy in front of the JVM. Count the system calls Run ZeroCopyDemo (or ZeroCopyDemoKt) with the command below. It sends a 64 MiB file twice: with transferTo, then through a 64 KiB heap buffer. Before looking at the times, predict how many transferTo calls the first pass makes. On Linux with strace, run it outside Gradle: strace -f -c -e trace=sendfile,read,write java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo workbench.nio.l08.ZeroCopyDemo, and find the sendfile line. Arg: MiB (default 64). */ public class ZeroCopyDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { long size = (args.length > 0 ? Long.parseLong(args[0]) : 64) << 20; Path file = Files.createTempFile("statement", ".bin"); try (RandomAccessFile raf = new RandomAccessFile(file.toFile(), "rw")) { raf.setLength(size); } try { for (String mode : new String[] {"transferTo", "copy"}) send(file, size, mode); } finally { Files.delete(file); } } static void send(Path file, long size, String mode) throws Exception { try (ServerSocketChannel listener = ServerSocketChannel.open() .bind(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0))) { Thread receiver = new Thread(() -> { // drains the socket, counts bytes try (SocketChannel in = listener.accept()) { ByteBuffer b = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1 << 20); while (in.read(b) >= 0) b.clear(); } catch (IOException e) { e.printStackTrace(); } }); receiver.start(); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); int calls = 0; try (FileChannel f = FileChannel.open(file); SocketChannel out = SocketChannel.open(listener.getLocalAddress())) { if (mode.equals("transferTo")) { long sent = 0; while (sent < size) { // may move less than asked: loop sent += f.transferTo(sent, size - sent, out); calls++; } } else { ByteBuffer b = ByteBuffer.allocate(64 * 1024); // heap: the JDK copies it again, via a direct buffer while (f.read(b) >= 0) { b.flip(); while (b.hasRemaining()) out.write(b); b.clear(); calls++; } } } receiver.join(); System.out.printf("%-10s %d MiB in %4d ms, %,d %s calls%n", mode, size >> 20, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, calls, mode.equals("copy") ? "read" : "transferTo"); } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l08.ZeroCopyDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l08/ZeroCopyDemo.java ZeroCopyDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l08 import java.io.IOException import java.io.RandomAccessFile import java.net.InetAddress import java.net.InetSocketAddress import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.nio.channels.FileChannel import java.nio.channels.ServerSocketChannel import java.nio.channels.SocketChannel import java.nio.file.Files import java.nio.file.Path import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** Sends a file over a loopback socket twice: FileChannel.transferTo (zero-copy) and read/write through a heap buffer. Arg: MiB (default 64). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val size = (args.getOrNull(0)?.toLong() ?: 64L) shl 20 val file = Files.createTempFile("statement", ".bin") RandomAccessFile(file.toFile(), "rw").use { it.setLength(size) } try { for (mode in listOf("transferTo", "copy")) sendFile(file, size, mode) } finally { Files.delete(file) } } private fun sendFile(file: Path, size: Long, mode: String) { ServerSocketChannel.open().bind(InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0)).use { listener -> val receiver = thread { // drains the socket, counts bytes try { listener.accept().use { input -> val b = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1 shl 20) while (input.read(b) >= 0) b.clear() } } catch (e: IOException) { e.printStackTrace() } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() var calls = 0 FileChannel.open(file).use { f -> SocketChannel.open(listener.localAddress).use { out -> if (mode == "transferTo") { var sent = 0L while (sent < size) { // may move less than asked: loop sent += f.transferTo(sent, size - sent, out) calls++ } } else { val b = ByteBuffer.allocate(64 * 1024) // heap: the JDK copies it again, via a direct buffer while (f.read(b) >= 0) { b.flip() while (b.hasRemaining()) out.write(b) b.clear() calls++ } } } } receiver.join() println("%-10s %d MiB in %4d ms, %,d %s calls".format(mode, size shr 20, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, calls, if (mode == "copy") "read" else "transferTo")) } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l08.ZeroCopyDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l08/ZeroCopyDemo.kt One transferTo call for all 64 MiB on loopback, against 1,024 read calls for the copy. The times are close and change from run to run (40 to 46 ms against 41 to 44 ms here), so a single run proves nothing about speed. strace shows the real difference: 1 sendfile call, against about a thousand write calls and twice as many read calls for the copying pass. A virtual thread's blocking read is a coat check. The virtual thread hands the poller a ticket (the socket's file descriptor) and leaves the counter, so the carrier, the clerk, can serve the next person in line. When the coat arrives (data on the socket), the poller calls the ticket number, and whichever clerk is free hands the coat back. Zero-copy is the opposite of a coat check: the parcel never comes to the counter at all, the warehouse ships it straight to the door. The analogy breaks at speed: a real coat check is slow, while parking and unparking a virtual thread is cheap, which is why 2,000 readers woke in 36 ms in this lesson's demo.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Readiness or completion: epoll and io_uring
x: Everything in this track so far uses readiness notification. epoll answers "which sockets are ready?", and then your loop makes the read or write system call itself: one call to wait, and one more per socket to move bytes. io_uring is a newer Linux interface that works by completion instead. Your program and the kernel share two ring buffers in memory. You put requests on the submission ring, such as "read up to 16 KiB from this socket into this buffer", the kernel does the work, and it puts results on the completion ring: "done, 4,096 bytes". One system call can submit and collect many operations, and the kernel, not your thread, moves the bytes. On the JVM you reach io_uring through Netty; the JDK's own selector and poller use epoll. Netty 4.2 moved io_uring out of the incubator into a first-class transport. Its package is io.netty.channel.uring, and you use it like the other transports: a MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup with IoUringIoHandler.newFactory(), and the IoUring channel classes. Netty checks the kernel when it loads, and IoUring.isAvailable() says whether it can run on this machine. Is it faster? Not reliably. This section's demo sends a 32 MiB DefaultFileRegion over every transport available: nio received 33,554,432 bytes in 29 ms epoll received 33,554,432 bytes in 18 ms kqueue unavailable: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError io_uring received 33,554,432 bytes in 65 ms The research for this track saw the same order (86 ms for epoll, 159 ms for io_uring in one run). Under strace, io_uring made no sendfile calls at all; the work went through 2,061 io_uring_enter calls, and Netty's history shows that it splices a file region instead. The transport is also still changing: Netty 4.2.20 itself contains several io_uring fixes. So measure your own workload before you switch. The switch is small, one factory and one channel class, which makes it cheap to try and cheap to undo. Every transport on your machine Predict which transports your machine supports: Linux has epoll and maybe io_uring; macOS has kqueue. Run TransportsDemo (or TransportsDemoKt). Run it twice and compare the times between runs, not only between transports. Netty 4.2 Migration Guide: io_uring graduated read Statement exports, settlement files and reconciliation reports are where zero-copy pays off in payments, provided TLS ends at the proxy or gateway in front of the JVM. For APIs, the choice of model matters more than the transport: most payment services are blocking stacks (Oracle, JDBC, JTA, vendor SDKs), and on JDK 21 or newer they can serve high concurrency on virtual threads, as long as every downstream sits behind an explicit limit. If your fleet still runs JDK 21, upgrading to the current LTS, JDK 25, brings both synchronized without pinning (JEP 491, from JDK 24) and virtual-thread pollers on Linux. Treat io_uring as an experiment to measure, not a default.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Under a virtual thread's blocking read: the JDK's own event loop
x: When a virtual thread calls socket.getInputStream().read() and no bytes have arrived, no OS thread blocks. The JDK's sources and a thread dump show what happens instead: The JDK's socket implementation, NioSocketImpl, keeps the socket in non-blocking mode, so the read returns at once with EAGAIN: nothing yet. It registers the socket's file descriptor with an internal Poller, which uses epoll with EPOLLONESHOT (report once, then disarm), and parks the virtual thread. Its carrier, the platform thread that was running it, moves on to other virtual threads. A poller thread waits in epoll_wait on every registered socket. When data arrives, it unparks the virtual thread, which is mounted on a free carrier and tries the read again. A jcmd thread dump of a parked reader shows that path: NioSocketImpl.read, then NioSocketImpl.park, Poller.poll, LockSupport.park and VirtualThread.park. Which threads do the polling depends on the JDK version. On JDK 21 the pollers are platform threads named Read-Poller and Write-Poller, plus Read-Updater and Write-Updater on Linux. This section's demo, on JDK 21, with 2,000 virtual threads blocked in read(): 2000 virtual threads blocked in read(); platform threads: 14 4 x ForkJoinPool-N-worker-N 1 x Read-Poller 1 x Read-Updater 1 x Write-Poller 1 x Write-Updater ... wrote 1 byte to each socket: all 2,000 readers woke and finished in 36 ms From JDK 22, Linux defaults to a mode the JDK source calls VTHREAD_POLLERS: one platform MasterPoller thread plus sub-pollers that are themselves virtual threads, scheduled like any other, which the source says "helps to integrate polling with virtual thread scheduling". That is the default on Linux in JDK 25, the current LTS; macOS keeps platform poller threads. From JDK 24, jcmd <pid> Thread.vthread_pollers lists the pollers. So virtual threads don't make event loops obsolete. They put one inside the JDK, so your code can stay blocking-style while an epoll loop does the waiting. Find the pollers Run PollerDemo (or PollerDemoKt). Predict the number of platform threads before you look. Run it with -Pargs=5000 and predict again: which names grow, if any? If you have JDK 25 installed, run the class with it directly: java -cp nio/build/classes/java/demo workbench.nio.l08.PollerDemo 2000 30, and while it holds, run jcmd <pid> Thread.vthread_pollers with the pid it prints. Which poller names appear? PollerDemo.java package workbench.nio.l08; import java.io.IOException; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.ServerSocket; import java.net.Socket; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.stream.Collectors; /** * N virtual threads each block in Socket.read(). Which platform threads exist meanwhile? * Args: [N, default 2000] [seconds to hold before releasing them, default 0] */ public class PollerDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int n = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 2_000; int holdSeconds = args.length > 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[1]) : 0; System.out.println("java " + System.getProperty("java.version") + ", cpus=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + ", pid=" + ProcessHandle.current().pid()); try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(0, n, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress()); ExecutorService readers = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { CountDownLatch connected = new CountDownLatch(n), done = new CountDownLatch(n); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { readers.submit(() -> { try (Socket s = new Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), server.getLocalPort())) { connected.countDown(); s.getInputStream().read(); // parks this virtual thread on the JDK poller } catch (IOException e) { e.printStackTrace(); } finally { done.countDown(); } }); } List<Socket> accepted = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) accepted.add(server.accept()); connected.await(); Thread.sleep(300); // let every reader reach read() Map<String, Long> platform = Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet().stream() // platform threads only .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(t -> t.getName().replaceAll("\\d+", "N"), TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting())); System.out.println(n + " virtual threads blocked in read(); platform threads: " + platform.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum()); platform.forEach((name, count) -> System.out.println(" " + count + " x " + name)); if (holdSeconds > 0) { System.out.println("holding " + holdSeconds + " s: try jcmd " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + " Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json"); Thread.sleep(holdSeconds * 1_000L); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (Socket s : accepted) s.getOutputStream().write(1); // data arrives: the poller unparks each reader done.await(); System.out.printf("wrote 1 byte to each socket: all %,d readers woke and finished in %d ms%n", n, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); for (Socket s : accepted) s.close(); } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l08.PollerDemo labs/nio/src/demo/java/workbench/nio/l08/PollerDemo.java PollerDemo.kt package workbench.nio.l08 import java.io.IOException import java.net.InetAddress import java.net.ServerSocket import java.net.Socket import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** * N virtual threads each block in Socket.read(). Which platform threads exist meanwhile? * Args: [N, default 2000] [seconds to hold before releasing them, default 0] */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val n = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: 2_000 val holdSeconds = args.getOrNull(1)?.toInt() ?: 0 println("java ${System.getProperty("java.version")}, cpus=${Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors()}, pid=${ProcessHandle.current().pid()}") ServerSocket(0, n, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress()).use { server -> Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().use { readers -> val connected = CountDownLatch(n) val done = CountDownLatch(n) repeat(n) { readers.submit { try { Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), server.localPort).use { s -> connected.countDown() s.getInputStream().read() // parks this virtual thread on the JDK poller } } catch (e: IOException) { e.printStackTrace() } finally { done.countDown() } } } val accepted = List(n) { server.accept() } connected.await() Thread.sleep(300) // let every reader reach read() val platform = Thread.getAllStackTraces().keys // platform threads only .groupingBy { it.name.replace(Regex("\\d+"), "N") }.eachCount().toSortedMap() println("$n virtual threads blocked in read(); platform threads: ${platform.values.sum()}") platform.forEach { (name, count) -> println(" $count x $name") } if (holdSeconds > 0) { println("holding $holdSeconds s: try jcmd ${ProcessHandle.current().pid()} Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json") Thread.sleep(holdSeconds * 1_000L) } val t0 = System.nanoTime() accepted.forEach { it.getOutputStream().write(1) } // data arrives: the poller unparks each reader done.await() println("wrote 1 byte to each socket: all %,d readers woke and finished in %d ms".format(n, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000)) accepted.forEach { it.close() } } } } ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l08.PollerDemoKt labs/nio/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/nio/l08/PollerDemo.kt On JDK 21, about 14 platform threads, the same with 5,000 readers: one carrier per core plus Read-Poller, Write-Poller and the two updaters. All readers wake within tens of milliseconds once data arrives. On JDK 25 on Linux, the platform list shows a MasterPoller instead of the read and write pollers and their updaters, because the sub-pollers are virtual threads and getAllStackTraces lists only platform threads; Thread.vthread_pollers shows them all. (The JDK 25 names come from the JDK source; this track ran its demos on JDK 21.) A virtual thread's blocking read is a non-blocking read plus park and unpark, driven by an epoll loop inside the JDK. sun.nio.ch.Poller source (JDK 25) read

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Choosing a server model for a payments service
x: After eight lessons the choice comes down to two questions: where does the waiting happen, and what limits it? If the service... Choose Watch out for uses JDBC, JTA and blocking SDKs, and is IO-bound thread-per-request on virtual threads: Quarkus @RunOnVirtualThread, Jetty's virtual threads executor a limit per downstream; pinning on JDK 21 to 23; CPU-heavy work has the same blocking stack and moderate traffic a bounded worker pool: Quarkus plain endpoints, Jetty's QueuedThreadPool size it with Little's law; the pool caps concurrency is async end to end (reactive SQL, async HTTP, streaming) an event loop: Vert.x, Netty, Quarkus Uni endpoints never block the loop; backpressure holds many idle long-lived connections (terminals, WebSockets) an event loop, or virtual threads if the per-connection work blocks memory per connection; idle timeouts sends large files unchanged zero-copy: transferTo, Netty's DefaultFileRegion no TLS or compression inside the JVM Two rules hold in every row. Concurrency needs a limit somewhere. An event loop limits it by never waiting, and a pool by its size. With virtual threads you have to add one, because 10,000 parked threads will make 10,000 calls to your card issuer the moment they wake. The lab for this lesson is exactly that bug. And the model doesn't change latency: a 120 ms issuer call takes 120 ms in every row. My default for a new payments service on Quarkus is plain blocking endpoints, moving to @RunOnVirtualThread when the worker pool becomes the limit, with JDBC and issuer calls behind explicit limits. Event loops and Uni earn their extra complexity when the whole stack is non-blocking or connection counts are very large. Whatever you choose, measure it: Little's law for threads, the lag probe and blocked-thread warnings for loops, and strace -c when you want to know what the kernel is really doing. Choose for three services A card-present gateway keeps 8,000 TCP connections from terminals; each sends one 200-byte message a minute and the work per message is a 3 ms in-memory check. Choose a model. A refund service: Quarkus, Oracle through JDBC with JTA, a blocking acquirer SDK at 400 ms, 150 requests a second at peak. Choose a model and say where the limits go. A nightly job sends 2 GB settlement files to an internal archive over plain TCP. Choose how to send them. The gateway is almost all idle connections and tiny non-blocking work: an event loop (Netty or Vert.x) fits, with an idle timeout and framing as in lesson 4. The refund service needs 150 × 0.4 = 60 requests in flight: plain blocking endpoints on the worker pool work, or @RunOnVirtualThread; either way, put @Blocking on JTA endpoints that return Uni, cap the acquirer SDK with a semaphore, and size the JDBC pool on purpose. The settlement job is zero-copy territory: FileChannel.transferTo in a loop (or Netty's DefaultFileRegion), since nothing has to change the bytes on the way. The common mistake is moving a blocking service to virtual threads and deleting the thread-pool limit with nothing in its place. The old pool of 200 threads was quietly protecting the database and the card issuer. Virtual threads remove that cap, so the next burst sends thousands of concurrent queries to a 20-connection pool or an issuer that allows 100 calls, and latency or error rates explode downstream. Put a Semaphore (or the client's own concurrency limit) around each fragile dependency, with a timeout on acquiring it, when you introduce virtual threads.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Java and Kotlin
x: A bounded zero-copy export on virtual threads StatementServer.export, Java private final Semaphore exportSlots = new Semaphore(maxConcurrentExports); // the database allows 4 void export(String day, SocketChannel out) throws Exception { exportSlots.acquire(); // waiting here parks the virtual thread try { Thread.sleep(QUERY_MILLIS); // the statement query try (FileChannel file = FileChannel.open(statements.resolve(day + ".csv"))) { FileSender.transferFully(file, 0, file.size(), out); // sendfile on Linux } } finally { exportSlots.release(); } } StatementServer.export, Kotlin private val exportSlots = Semaphore(maxConcurrentExports) // the database allows 4 fun export(day: String, out: SocketChannel) { exportSlots.acquire() // waiting here parks the virtual thread try { Thread.sleep(QUERY_MILLIS) // the statement query FileChannel.open(statements.resolve("$day.csv")).use { file -> FileSender.transferFully(file, 0, file.size(), out) // sendfile on Linux } } finally { exportSlots.release() } } Both use java.util.concurrent.Semaphore, and on a virtual thread acquire() parks without holding a carrier. A Kotlin team might reach for kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore with withPermit { } instead. That one only works inside coroutines and suspends rather than parks, so it fits a coroutine-based server, not this thread-per-connection one. FileChannel.transferTo is the same JDK call from both languages; Kotlin's use {} plays the part of Java's try-with-resources for the file channel.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Worked example
x: Design a statement-download service Requirements: at month end, 600 statement downloads a minute; each needs a 1.5 s database query and about 0.5 s to send its file. The database team allows 8 concurrent statement queries. Little's law first. arrival rate = 600 / 60 s = 10 requests/s time in system = 1.5 s + 0.5 s = 2 s in flight = 10 x 2 = 20 requests queries at once = capped at 8 -> requests wait for a slot, not for a thread Use one virtual thread per connection, so waiting for the query, for a slot or for a slow client costs no OS thread. Put the database's limit in a semaphore with a timeout, so an overloaded database turns into a fast error. private final Semaphore querySlots = new Semaphore(8); void export(String day, SocketChannel out) throws Exception { if (!querySlots.tryAcquire(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { // 1. wait for a slot, but not forever throw new IllegalStateException("statement service busy"); } try { renderStatement(day); // 2. 1.5 s query, parks the virtual thread } finally { querySlots.release(); // 3. free the slot before the slow send } sendFile(day, out); } private val querySlots = Semaphore(8) fun export(day: String, out: SocketChannel) { if (!querySlots.tryAcquire(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { // 1. wait for a slot, but not forever throw IllegalStateException("statement service busy") } try { renderStatement(day) // 2. 1.5 s query, parks the virtual thread } finally { querySlots.release() // 3. free the slot before the slow send } sendFile(day, out) } Send the file with zero-copy, in a loop, because transferTo can stop early when the client's socket is full. Releasing the query slot before this step matters: a slow client should hold a cheap virtual thread, not one of the 8 database slots. static int transferFully(FileChannel file, long position, long count, WritableByteChannel target) throws IOException { long sent = 0; int calls = 0; while (sent < count) { sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, target); // may be partial calls++; } return calls; } fun transferFully(file: FileChannel, position: Long, count: Long, target: WritableByteChannel): Int { var sent = 0L var calls = 0 while (sent < count) { sent += file.transferTo(position + sent, count - sent, target) // may be partial calls++ } return calls } Check the conditions before you promise zero-copy. If TLS terminates inside the JVM, the bytes must be encrypted in user space and transferTo gives you no zero-copy; send through a buffer and stop worrying about it. If an ingress proxy terminates TLS, the JVM's socket is plain and sendfile applies. Either way, the design's real limit is the 8 query slots, not the transfer method.

x: Export statements with zero-copy on virtual threads, within a limit labs/nio/src/main/kotlin/workbench/nio/l08/FileSender.kt labs/nio/src/main/kotlin/workbench/nio/l08/StatementServer.kt ./gradlew :nio:test --tests 'workbench.nio.l08.*' Run the tests. Two of three fail. The idle-connection test already passes: read it, it shows 300 parked virtual threads costing almost no platform threads. Write FileSender.transferFully: call file.transferTo in a loop until count bytes are sent, and return the number of calls. The first test feeds it a channel that accepts only 4 KiB per write, so a single call is never enough. Run the tests. The download test now fails on concurrency: all 20 exports ran at once. Fix StatementServer.export: add a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore with maxConcurrentExports permits, acquire() before measured { ... } and release() in a finally. Run the tests until all three pass. transferTo returns the number of bytes it moved this time; add it to the bytes sent so far and start the next call at position + sent. Acquire the permit outside measured { }, so that threads waiting for a permit don't count as running exports. Waiting in Semaphore.acquire() parks a virtual thread just like a socket read does: twenty waiting exports cost twenty parked virtual threads, not twenty OS threads. All three tests in StatementServerTest pass. By the end you can send files with zero-copy and handle partial transfers, explain readiness (epoll) versus completion (io_uring), describe how a virtual thread's blocking read waits on the JDK's poller in JDK 21 and later, and choose a server model for a payments service.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Quiz
x: A service sends 200 MB settlement files to a partner over HTTPS, with TLS handled by the JVM. Does FileChannel.transferTo give zero-copy here? No: the JVM encrypts the bytes in user space, so they must pass through your process Yes: on Linux transferTo always becomes sendfile Only with the io_uring transport Only if the file is read into a direct ByteBuffer first sendfile moves bytes from the page cache to the socket unchanged. TLS has to encrypt them first, and the JDK does that in your process, so the bytes come up into user space no matter which API you call. Zero-copy fits when TLS ends at a proxy in front of the JVM. file.transferTo(0, size, socket) returns a number smaller than size. What does that mean? An error occurred, and the socket should be closed The file is shorter than expected It moved only part of the data, for example because the socket buffer was full; call it again from the new position The kernel doesn't support sendfile Like a non-blocking write, transferTo moves what it can and reports how much. A single call is not a guarantee. Loop until the count is sent, as the lab's transferFully does. On JDK 21, 5,000 virtual threads are blocked in socket reads. Which threads wait in epoll_wait on their behalf? 5,000 platform threads, one per socket The ForkJoinPool carrier threads None: the kernel wakes virtual threads directly The JDK's poller threads (Read-Poller on JDK 21) The JDK registers each socket with its Poller, and the poller thread waits in epoll_wait for all of them. Carriers only run virtual threads that are ready, and the kernel knows nothing about virtual threads. From the virtual threads track: 10,000 requests run on virtual threads, and each calls a card issuer that accepts 100 concurrent calls. What protects the issuer? Nothing: virtual threads are cheap A Semaphore(100) around the issuer call A fixed pool of 100 virtual threads Setting jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism to 100 Virtual threads should not be pooled, and the scheduler's parallelism controls carriers, not how many virtual threads call the issuer. A semaphore around the call is the limit; the other 9,900 virtual threads park cheaply while they wait. A Quarkus payments API uses Oracle through JDBC and a blocking acquirer SDK, at 300 requests a second and 150 ms each. Which model fits best? Reactive Uni endpoints on the IO thread Plain blocking endpoints on the worker pool, or @RunOnVirtualThread, with explicit limits on JDBC and the acquirer The io_uring transport, because it is faster A Netty server with blocking handlers on the event loop The stack blocks, so it must not run on an event loop, which rules out Uni endpoints and blocking Netty handlers. Little's law gives 45 requests in flight, easy for a worker pool or virtual threads. The transport doesn't change the threading model.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Key terms
x: Page cache The kernel's in-memory copy of file pages that were read or written recently. System call A switch from your program into the kernel to ask for a service, such as read, write or sendfile. Zero-copy Moving data from a file to a socket without copying it through your process's memory. sendfile The Linux system call that sends file data to a socket inside the kernel. io_uring A Linux interface where programs submit IO requests on a shared ring and collect completions. Poller The JDK's internal epoll or kqueue loop that wakes virtual threads when their sockets are ready. EPOLLONESHOT An epoll flag: report the socket once, then stop until it is registered again. What does FileChannel.transferTo to a socket become on Linux? sendfile(2): the kernel sends pages from the page cache to the socket; the bytes never enter your process. When can't you use zero-copy for a file transfer? When the bytes must change on the way inside the JVM: TLS encryption done by the JVM, or compression. transferTo returned fewer bytes than you asked for. What next? Call it again from position + sent with the remaining count, in a loop, until everything is sent. epoll vs io_uring in one line each? epoll: tells you which sockets are ready, then you make the IO call (readiness). io_uring: you submit the IO on a shared ring and collect completions (completion). What happens when a virtual thread's socket read finds no data? NioSocketImpl gets EAGAIN, registers the fd with the JDK Poller (epoll, one-shot) and parks the virtual thread; a poller thread unparks it when data arrives. JDK 21 vs JDK 22+ (Linux) poller threads? JDK 21: platform Read-Poller/Write-Poller (plus updater threads). JDK 22+: one platform MasterPoller plus virtual sub-pollers (VTHREAD_POLLERS). With virtual threads, where must the concurrency limit come from? From you: a semaphore or the client's own pool around each downstream. Virtual threads themselves limit nothing.

h: Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model · Go deeper
x: Dan Kegel's C10K page, from lesson 1, compared ways to serve many clients. This track has now met each family on the JVM: readiness notification with a level-triggered Selector (lesson 2) and Netty's native epoll transport (lessons 3 and 4); completion-based IO with io_uring (this lesson); and one thread per client with blocking IO, which virtual threads made cheap again by running a readiness loop underneath. The JDK's poller has knobs, though you should rarely need them. On JDK 21, -Djdk.readPollers sets the number of read pollers (a power of 2, default 1); with 4, a thread dump shows four Read-Poller threads. From JDK 22, -Djdk.pollerMode selects the mode: 1 for SYSTEM_THREADS (platform pollers, the JDK 21 behavior) and 2 for VTHREAD_POLLERS. The JDK source after the current LTS adds a third mode, POLLER_PER_CARRIER (3), in JDK 27, while the Linux default stays VTHREAD_POLLERS. In VTHREAD_POLLERS mode on Linux, the number of read pollers defaults to the highest power of 2 not above the CPU count, capped at 32. Two smaller facts complete the picture. The JDK's Selector registers sockets level-triggered, while the poller uses one-shot registration: a selector serves the same socket again and again, while the poller wakes exactly one parked thread exactly once. And file IO is different from socket IO: a virtual thread reading a file does not go through the poller. As the virtual threads track explained, file operations capture the carrier while they run, which is one more reason zero-copy file sending is worth knowing about. To check any of this on your own JDK, jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json shows virtual threads and their stacks, and from JDK 24 jcmd <pid> Thread.vthread_pollers shows the pollers.

h: Capstone: a non-blocking quote service
x: A Netty service that fans out to three flaky providers with coroutines and answers inside a deadline. By the end of this track you have built one program: a TCP quote service on Netty 4.2. It fans every request out to three FX providers with Kotlin coroutines, answers within 300 ms with the best price (or the last good one, marked stale), cancels the provider calls when a client hangs up, and holds up under load with a bulkhead per provider, jittered retries for idempotent calls only, a hedge for the slow provider, load shedding at the door and an ordered shutdown. Its tests prove each of those properties by counting, never by timing: calls, permits, cancellations and virtual milliseconds. The track draws on all of Part 2. The server shell comes from "Servers and event loops: NIO, Netty, Vert.x and Jetty" (the event loop, the pipeline, codecs and writability). The fan-out comes from "Kotlin coroutines" (builders, the job tree, cancellation and timeouts, supervisors, select, virtual-time tests and the bridge to Java futures). "Reactive programming" supplies backpressure, Mono.zip and retries, and Reactor is the Java side of most comparisons. From Part 1 it uses Little's law, semaphores and the migration checklist of the virtual threads track. The last lesson ends with a design review: event loop or virtual threads for this service, and when you would switch. The lab is labs/quotes, one package per lesson (workbench.quotes.l01 to l03). Each lesson's starting code contains the previous lesson's solution, so you can start any sitting fresh. Lesson 1's lab is Java; lessons 2 and 3 are Kotlin, with lesson 1's Java server carried along. From labs/, run ./gradlew :quotes:test --tests 'workbench.quotes.lNN.*' until it passes; ./gradlew :quotes:solutionTest runs the same tests against the reference answers. Servers bind 127.0.0.1 on a free port, coroutine tests run on virtual time, and the Try-it demos run with ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=..., in Kotlin and in Java. The program is a TCP quote service: a Netty shell, a coroutine fan-out to three providers under a 300 ms deadline, and the guards that keep it up under load. The event loop never waits. Handlers hand futures back and finish in whenCompleteAsync(..., ctx.executor()), and a test proves the loop is free by counting calls and probe tasks. Auto-read is the only tap: read while writable and under 16 in flight, with FlowControlHandler holding lines already decoded. A best-of fan-out uses supervisorScope and withTimeoutOrNull per call, and rethrows only its own cancel. With no answer it serves a stale quote or fails clearly. scope.future { } in a SupervisorJob scope gives Java a future whose cancel reaches every provider call, so a hang-up stops the work. Each provider gets a bulkhead sized by Little's law. Only idempotent calls are retried, with jitter, and only the slow, idempotent provider is hedged. Shed at the door with tryAcquire and a clear ERR busy, and shut down in order: stop accepting, stop admitting, drain, cancelAndJoin, close. Event loop or virtual threads, the limits stay. Pick the model by where the waiting happens and by what the provider clients can do.
