Bulkhead permits come from the contract, admission comes from what the providers can answer before the deadline, and every retry and hedge counts as a call. Event loop or virtual threads Pick When event loop + coroutines (this design) the service lives on Netty, Vert.x or Quarkus; connections in the hundreds of thousands; you need auto-read, codecs and flow control; provider clients are non-blocking and a cancel must reach them one virtual thread per connection provider SDKs only block (JDBC, old SOAP clients); connections in the thousands; the team prefers plain Java either way bulkheads, deadlines, admission and an ordered shutdown stay. Virtual threads remove the pool and with it the one limit nobody wrote down Test recipes Count, don't time: hold quotes open with a controllable fake, then count calls, probe tasks, permits and cancellations. A 5-second wait only bounds how long a failure takes. Coroutines on virtual time: runTest, and pass StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) to the class that owns a scope. currentTime is exact; a delay on Dispatchers.Default is real. Pipelines without sockets: EmbeddedChannel(handlers), writeInbound, then runPendingTasks() before readOutbound() when replies are written from tasks. Real servers: bind 127.0.0.1 on port 0, read with a socket timeout, assert with latches, and always close the server in finally.

h: Capstone: a non-blocking quote service: track quiz
x: Which line in a Netty handler blocks the event loop? quote.whenCompleteAsync(callback, ctx.executor()) ctx.writeAndFlush(reply) called from a provider's thread source.quote(symbol).join() ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(false) join() holds the loop thread until the quote arrives, so every channel on that loop waits. The callback runs later as a task, a write from another thread is queued onto the loop, and changing auto-read returns at once. The handler turns auto-read off after 16 requests, yet it still receives 2,000 more requests from the bytes of one socket read. What is missing? A bigger high water mark A FlowControlHandler between the decoders and the handler A call to ctx.read() in channelRead0 TCP_NODELAY on the channel Auto-read stops the next socket read, not the lines the frame decoder already holds. FlowControlHandler keeps those decoded messages while auto-read is off and releases them as reading resumes. ctx.read() would do the opposite: ask for more. Why does this track's test for a free event loop count calls and probe tasks instead of asserting that a probe runs within 300 ms? On a busy build machine a healthy loop can miss a millisecond bar, while a blocked loop's counts are wrong at any speed Netty doesn't let you time tasks on an event loop Counting is faster to run Virtual time doesn't work for Netty, so nothing can be timed Timings depend on the machine's load; counts depend only on what the code did. A loop stuck in join() makes 1 call however fast the machine is, and the test's 5-second wait only bounds how long the failure takes to report. A quote needs any one of three providers' prices. Which scope runs the three calls? coroutineScope, so a failure cancels the rest GlobalScope, so the calls outlive a cancelled request runBlocking, so the event loop waits for the answers supervisorScope, so each call fails alone With supervisorScope a failed child keeps its exception for await, and the other calls carry on. coroutineScope is right when every answer is needed. GlobalScope leaks the calls, and runBlocking blocks the loop. Each call is async { withTimeout(300) { p.quote(s) } } in a supervisor fan-out, and the await rethrows every CancellationException. A provider is slow. What happens? The slow provider counts as no answer The request ends with TimeoutCancellationException, as if it had been cancelled The request waits for the slow provider The other providers are cancelled, but the request succeeds withTimeout signals with TimeoutCancellationException, a CancellationException, and the catch passes it up as if the whole request were cancelled. Use withTimeoutOrNull, and check ensureActive() before rethrowing a cancel. Lesson 1's Java handler cancels the future when the client hangs up. Which implementation of QuoteSource.quote turns that cancel into cancelled provider calls? CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> blockingBest(symbol), pool) CompletableFuture.completedFuture(runBlocking { best.quote(symbol) }) scope.future { best.quote(symbol) } in a scope the service owns GlobalScope.async { best.quote(symbol) }.asCompletableFuture() with no scope to close The future builder links both ways: cancelling the future cancels the coroutine, and the cancel travels down to the provider calls. supplyAsync's cancel stops nothing, runBlocking blocks the event loop before returning, and GlobalScope work has no owner to close it at shutdown. Which provider may be hedged? Northbank: indicative prices, so a repeat is harmless, and a slow tail worth cutting Fjord: firm quotes that reserve liquidity, because it is the slowest Every provider, after the same 80 ms None: hedging always doubles the load A hedge is a duplicate request, so only an idempotent provider qualifies, and it pays off only where the tail hurts. Hedging after about p95 costs about 5% more calls, not double. A firm quote is never repeated. Where does a provider's bulkhead permit belong? Around the whole retry loop, so a request holds one permit for all its attempts Around each single call, so a backoff wait holds nothing and a hedge needs its own permit Around the whole fan-out, one permit per request Nowhere: the deadline already limits the calls The permit limits calls in flight to the provider, so it wraps exactly one call. Around the retry loop it would be held through backoff waits, around the fan-out it would count requests instead of calls, and a deadline limits time, not concurrency. A burst of 500 requests meets a provider that can answer about 60 within the deadline. What does admission with tryAcquire change? It gets live answers to all 500, just later It cuts the live answers to almost none It makes the provider faster The same number of live answers, but the rest hear ERR busy at once instead of failing after the deadline Requests beyond what the provider can serve in time fail either way. Shedding makes them fail in a millisecond, early enough to try another instance, and nothing waits in a queue or on the event loop. In the demo, 50 requests got live answers in both runs. When should this service stay on an event loop instead of moving to one virtual thread per connection? When the provider SDKs only block When the team prefers plain Java and connections number in the thousands When it already runs on Netty or Vert.x, connections number in the hundreds of thousands, or the provider clients are non-blocking and a cancel must reach them Always: event loops are faster per request The event loop pays off for huge connection counts, protocol control and async clients. Blocking SDKs and plain Java favour virtual threads. Neither model makes a single request faster, and both still need the bulkheads, deadlines and admission.

Over three lessons you build one program: a small quote service. A client opens a TCP connection and sends a line such as 7 EURUSD. The service asks three FX providers for a price and answers 7 OK EURUSD 1.0842 northbank, the best price it got, within 300 ms. The providers are invented (Northbank, Eastgate and Fjord), and like real ones they are slow on a bad day and sometimes down. This lesson builds the server shell on Netty. Lesson 2 of this track adds the fan-out to the providers with coroutines and a deadline. Lesson 3 makes the whole thing hold up under load. One rule shapes every decision: the event loop never waits. As "Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline" showed, a channel is registered with one loop for its whole life, and that loop is a single thread that runs the handlers of every channel it owns. If a handler waits 100 ms for a provider, every connection on that loop gets 100 ms of silence. The protocol is lines of text. A client can be nc in a terminal, tests can write requests as strings, and LineBasedFrameDecoder does the framing. A binary protocol would use a length field instead, as "Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks" did, and nothing else in the design would change. Two details are deliberate. The decoder takes at most 64 bytes per line. Without a limit, a client that sends bytes and never a newline makes the decoder buffer forever. A longer line fails with TooLongFrameException. Every request carries an id, and every reply repeats it. A reply leaves when its quote arrives, so a fast quote overtakes a slow one and replies come back out of order. The client matches them by id. h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Hand the future back instead of waiting for it
x:
QuoteSource.quote(symbol) returns a CompletableFuture<Quote>. The first draft of the handler, which is the starting code of this lesson's lab, waits for it: Java @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { Request r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line); Quote q = source.quote(r.symbol()).join(); // the loop waits here ctx.writeAndFlush(QuoteProtocol.ok(r.id(), q)); } Kotlin override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { val r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line) val q = source.quote(r.symbol).join() // the loop waits here ctx.writeAndFlush(QuoteProtocol.ok(r.id, q)) } It answers correctly, and it passes a test with one client. This section's demo measures what it costs, with one event loop, ten clients and a provider that takes 100 ms. The tenth reply came after 1,072 ms, and the provider never saw more than one quote at a time. The loop asked for a quote, held its thread in join() until the answer came, and only then read the next request. The fix gives the future back to the loop and finishes later: Java CompletableFuture<Quote> quote = source.quote(r.symbol()); // 1. returns at once inFlight.add(quote); quote.whenCompleteAsync((q, e) -> { // 2. later, on this channel's loop inFlight.remove(quote); ctx.writeAndFlush(e == null ? ok(r.id(), q) : error(r.id(), e)); }, ctx.executor()); Kotlin val quote = source.quote(r.symbol) // 1. returns at once inFlight += quote quote.whenCompleteAsync({ q, e -> // 2. later, on this channel's loop inFlight -= quote ctx.writeAndFlush(if (e == null) ok(r.id, q) else error(r.id, e)) }, ctx.executor()) channelRead0 now returns in microseconds. The same demo answered all ten clients in 106 ms, with ten quotes waiting at once. The second argument decides which thread runs the callback. ctx.executor() is the channel's own event loop, so the callback runs there as a task, like every other event of this channel. That matters because the handler keeps state, the set of in-flight futures. With plain whenComplete, the callback would run on whatever thread completed the future, a provider's thread, while the loop adds to the same HashSet in channelRead0. That is the read-modify-write race from "Race conditions: why count++ lies". When every touch of handler state happens on the loop, you need no lock: the loop is the lock. ctx.writeAndFlush would be safe from any thread. The set is not. The interface carries the other half of the rule: quote must return at once and complete the future later. Lesson 2 meets that contract by starting a coroutine with scope.future { }. A runBlocking { } in its place would block the loop exactly like join(). How do you prove the loop is free? The lab in "Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline" timed a lag probe and asserted under 300 ms. That holds on a quiet laptop. On a build machine running eight builds on four cores, a healthy loop can miss 300 ms, and a broken handler can pass when the fake provider answers fast. This lab's test counts instead. It holds 100 quotes open, checks that the source saw 100 calls, then checks that the loop ran 50 empty tasks. A loop stuck in join() shows 1 call, on any machine and at any load. The 5-second limit in the test only decides how soon a failure is reported. Ten clients, one loop, two handlers Open BlockedLoopDemo.java (or the Kotlin twin). h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Auto-read is the only tap you control
x:
A client may pipeline: send 20,000 requests without waiting for a single reply. Two things then grow in the server's memory. Each request that waits for its quote is a future in the in-flight set. Each reply the client hasn't read yet sits in the channel's outbound buffer, because writeAndFlush never blocks ("Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks"). Nothing limits either one. Netty gives you one control: auto-read. While it is on, the loop reads the socket whenever bytes arrive. Turn it off and the loop stops reading that channel, the kernel's buffers fill, and TCP's window makes the client wait. The policy is one rule, applied after every new request, after every reply, and whenever writability changes: Java private void updateReading(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { boolean read = ctx.channel().isWritable() && inFlight.size() < MAX_IN_FLIGHT; ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(read); } Kotlin private fun updateReading(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { val read = ctx.channel().isWritable && inFlight.size < MAX_IN_FLIGHT ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = read } The cap of 16 bounds the futures one connection can hold. The writability check bounds the outbound buffer: isWritable() turns false above the high water mark, 64 KiB by default. There is a catch, and the demo shows it. Turning auto-read off stops the next socket read. It doesn't stop the lines the decoder already has. One read can bring 64 KB, a few thousand requests, and LineBasedFrameDecoder hands every one of them to the handler before the loop looks at auto-read again. FlowControlHandler, placed between the decoders and your handler, closes that gap. While auto-read is off it holds the decoded lines, and it releases them as reading resumes. The first one moves with the machine's load: on a busy machine the server's own loop choked on its growing queue and took fewer requests, but the queue still reached megabytes. The last peak is the 64 KiB high water mark (65,536 bytes) plus a few replies. Every client still got all 20,000 replies once it read them. The lab tests the cap directly: 40 pipelined requests against a source that holds every quote must produce exactly 16 calls. h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Close on purpose: say why, cancel what nobody will read, then stop
x: A connection ends in one of four ways, and each has its own code path. The client sends QUIT. The server writes BYE and closes from the write's future, with ctx.writeAndFlush("BYE\n").addListener(ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE). Closing right after flush() can drop bytes that are still in the outbound buffer; "Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks" lost 57,344 bytes that way. A line is too long. LineBasedFrameDecoder throws TooLongFrameException, and Netty passes it to the handler's exceptionCaught. The server answers ERR line too long and closes the same way. A client that sends 100 bytes where 64 are allowed is broken or hostile, and neither deserves a long conversation. The client hangs up. channelInactive runs on the loop, and the handler cancels every future still in its set. For a plain CompletableFuture that interrupts nothing, as "CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out" showed. It tells the source that nobody wants the answer any more. Lesson 2 turns that cancel into a coroutine cancel that reaches all three provider calls. The server shuts down. The order matters: Java @Override public void close() { stopAccepting(); // 1. close the listening socket connections.close().syncUninterruptibly(); // 2. close every open connection group.shutdownGracefully(0, 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // 3. then stop the loop threads .syncUninterruptibly(); } Kotlin override fun close() { stopAccepting() // 1. close the listening socket connections.close().syncUninterruptibly() // 2. close every open connection group.shutdownGracefully(0, 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // 3. then stop the loop threads .syncUninterruptibly() } stopAccepting() closes the listening socket first, so no new connection arrives while the rest shuts down. connections is a ChannelGroup: the server adds each new channel to it, and the group drops a channel again when it closes. Closing the group closes every open connection, each handler sees channelInactive and cancels its work, and only then does shutdownGracefully stop the loop threads. shutdownGracefully also closes the channels it still finds, but in this track's test runs that wasn't reliable: in about one run in three, a client still saw its connection open after the loops had stopped. Closing the connections yourself makes the order explicit. Lesson 3 of this track puts one more step between the first two lines: a short grace period in which quotes already in flight can still be answered. Check yourself before the lab: a client has two requests pending when close() runs. What does it read from its socket, and what happens to the two futures? (It reads end of stream, because its channel was closed. Both futures are cancelled in channelInactive.) WriteBufferWaterMark source, Netty 4.2 docs The most common mistake is blocking the event loop "just a little": join(), get(), block() or runBlocking in a handler, because the provider usually answers in 5 ms. It passes every test with one client and a fast fake. Under load, 5 ms per request on a loop that serves 2,000 connections is a queue that never drains, and a provider that stalls for 2 seconds freezes every connection on that loop. The runner-up is the half fix: whenComplete instead of whenCompleteAsync(..., ctx.executor()). It frees the loop but lets provider threads touch the handler's state. Return the future from channelRead0, and finish on the channel's own loop.

h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Java and Kotlin
x: The non-blocking handler in Java and Kotlin QuoteHandler.java (core) @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { QuoteProtocol.Request r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line); CompletableFuture<Quote> quote = source.quote(r.symbol()); inFlight.add(quote); updateReading(ctx); quote.whenCompleteAsync((q, e) -> { inFlight.remove(quote); if (ctx.channel().isActive()) { ctx.writeAndFlush(e == null ? QuoteProtocol.ok(r.id(), q) : QuoteProtocol.error(r.id(), e)); } updateReading(ctx); }, ctx.executor()); } @Override public void channelInactive(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { for (CompletableFuture<Quote> f : List.copyOf(inFlight)) f.cancel(true); inFlight.clear(); ctx.fireChannelInactive(); } QuoteHandler.kt (core) override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { val r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line) val quote = source.quote(r.symbol) inFlight += quote updateReading(ctx) quote.whenCompleteAsync({ q: Quote?, e: Throwable? -> // platform types: say they can be null inFlight -= quote if (ctx.channel().isActive) { ctx.writeAndFlush(if (e == null) QuoteProtocol.ok(r.id, q) else QuoteProtocol.error(r.id, e)) } updateReading(ctx) }, ctx.executor()) } override fun channelInactive(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { inFlight.toList().forEach { it.cancel(true) } inFlight.clear() ctx.fireChannelInactive() } At runtime these are the same handler: Netty sees a SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>, and the Kotlin lambda becomes a BiConsumer through SAM conversion. One Kotlin detail needs care. whenCompleteAsync comes from Java, so q and e arrive as platform types, and Kotlin won't stop you calling q.price when the future failed and q is null. Declare them Quote? and Throwable? so the compiler makes you check. Kotlin also tempts you with one thing Java doesn't have: runBlocking { } around a suspend call inside channelRead0. It blocks the loop exactly like join(). Lesson 2 of this track shows the bridge that doesn't: scope.future { }, which returns at once.

h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Worked example
x: Write the test that proves the loop is free, by counting Decide what to count. Hold every quote open, so a blocked loop stays blocked for the whole test, and count something the loop can only do while it is free: calls that reach the source. The fake keeps each future until the test releases it. final class FakeSource implements QuoteSource { private final List<CompletableFuture<Quote>> pending = new ArrayList<>(); // guarded by this private int calls; @Override public synchronized CompletableFuture<Quote> quote(String symbol) { calls++; // 1. count every call that reaches the source CompletableFuture<Quote> f = new CompletableFuture<>(); pending.add(f); // 2. hold it: a blocked loop stays blocked notifyAll(); return f; } } class FakeSource : QuoteSource { private val pending = mutableListOf<CompletableFuture<Quote>>() // guarded by this private var calls = 0 @Synchronized override fun quote(symbol: String): CompletableFuture<Quote> { calls++ // 1. count every call that reaches the source val f = CompletableFuture<Quote>() pending += f // 2. hold it: a blocked loop stays blocked (this as Object).notifyAll() return f } } Add a probe: hand the loop empty tasks and count how many ran. The 5-second wait only bounds how long a failure takes to report. The assertion is on the count, so a slow machine can't fail a healthy loop. static int probe(EventLoopGroup group, int tasks) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch ran = new CountDownLatch(tasks); for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) group.next().execute(ran::countDown); // 3. empty tasks ran.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // bounds the failure, it is not the assertion return tasks - (int) ran.getCount(); // 4. the assertion is on this count } fun probe(group: EventLoopGroup, tasks: Int): Int { val ran = CountDownLatch(tasks) repeat(tasks) { group.next().execute(ran::countDown) } // 3. empty tasks ran.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // bounds the failure, it is not the assertion return tasks - ran.count.toInt() // 4. the assertion is on this count } Spread 100 requests over 10 connections. One connection may hold only 16 requests (section 3), so 100 on one connection would test the cap instead of the loop. Assert both counts, then release the quotes and check that every id came back on the right connection. for (int c = 0; c < 10; c++) { // 10 connections x 10 requests Client client = new Client(server.port()); clients.add(client); client.send(requests(c * 10, 10)); } assertThat(source.awaitCalls(100)).isEqualTo(100); // 5. the loop asked for all 100 assertThat(probe(server.group(), 50)).isEqualTo(50); // 6. and still ran other work source.releaseAll(); for (int c = 0; c < 10; c++) assertThat(clients.get(c).readIds(10)).isEqualTo(ids(c * 10, 10)); val clients = List(10) { c -> // 10 connections x 10 requests Client(server.port()).also { it.send(requests(c * 10, 10)) } } assertThat(source.awaitCalls(100)).isEqualTo(100) // 5. the loop asked for all 100 assertThat(probe(server.group(), 50)).isEqualTo(50) // 6. and still ran other work source.releaseAll() clients.forEachIndexed { c, client -> assertThat(client.readIds(10)).isEqualTo(ids(c * 10, 10)) } Release the quotes in finally. A broken handler is stuck in join(); completing its future wakes the loop, so the server can close and the next test starts clean. Self-check: against the first-draft handler, which assertion fails, and with what number? (The first one: expected: 100 but was: 1. The loop took one request and has been waiting in join() ever since.)

h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Quiz
x: The server runs 8 event loops with 800 connections, and the first-draft handler calls source.quote(s).join(). One provider stalls for 2 seconds on a single request. Who waits? Only the client whose quote stalled All 800 clients: Netty runs one handler at a time for the whole server About 100 clients: every connection registered on the same loop as that request Nobody: join() parks the loop thread and Netty moves its channels to another loop Channels are spread over the 8 loops round-robin and stay where they were registered, about 100 per loop. The loop running join() can't read, decode or write for any of its channels for 2 seconds, while the other 7 loops carry on. Netty never moves a channel to another loop. A handler writes every reply with ctx.writeAndFlush and never looks at writability. A client pipelines thousands of requests and reads its socket slowly. Where do the unread replies pile up? In the client's receive buffer, which grows to fit Nowhere: writeAndFlush blocks the loop until the client reads In the kernel's send buffer, without limit In the channel's outbound buffer, in the server's own memory writeAndFlush never blocks. The kernel's buffers are small and fill first; after that Netty keeps the bytes in the channel's outbound buffer, in your heap or direct memory. In this lesson's demo that reached 2,487,339 bytes. Only reading less from that client stops it growing. QuoteHandler finishes each quote with whenCompleteAsync(callback, ctx.executor()). What goes wrong with plain whenComplete(callback)? The callback runs on the thread that completed the future, so it races the event loop on the in-flight HashSet writeAndFlush throws, because it may only be called on the event loop Nothing: the two behave the same The callback never runs, because the loop doesn't know about it whenComplete runs the callback on whichever thread completes the future, here a provider's thread, while the loop adds to the same set in channelRead0: a read-modify-write race on a plain HashSet. writeAndFlush itself is safe from any thread, which is why the bug is easy to miss. In Reactive Streams a subscriber paces the publisher with request(n). What plays that part between this server and one client? The 64-byte line limit Auto-read, switched on only while the channel is writable and fewer than 16 requests wait TCP's receive window on its own, with no code in the server The 64 KiB high water mark on its own Auto-read is the server's demand signal: it reads more only when it has room, and TCP carries the pause back to the client. TCP alone does nothing while the server keeps reading, because the bytes just move from the kernel into the server's heap. The water mark only reports a full buffer; your handler has to act on it. When a client hangs up, channelInactive calls cancel(true) on a pending future from a source that runs blocking calls with supplyAsync on a thread pool. What happens to the provider call? It is interrupted and stops at once The pool thread is stopped It runs to the end, and its result is dropped: cancel only completes the future The cancel fails, because the work has already started CompletableFuture.cancel completes the future with a CancellationException and doesn't interrupt the thread doing the work, whatever you pass. The call finishes and its result goes nowhere. To stop the work itself, the source has to react to the cancel, which is what lesson 2's coroutines do.

h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Explain it back
x: A colleague reviews your handler: "Why all this ceremony? The providers answer in 5 ms, so join() is fine, and Netty buffers writes for us anyway." Explain what join() costs on an event loop, why the callback runs on ctx.executor(), and why the server needs the auto-read rule.

h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Key terms
x: Event loop One thread that reads, decodes and writes for every channel registered with it, plus a queue of tasks. Pipelining A client sends many requests without waiting for the replies. In-flight request A request the server has read but not yet answered. Auto-read Whether the loop keeps reading a channel's socket. Off means the kernel's buffers fill and TCP makes the client wait. FlowControlHandler A Netty handler that holds already-decoded messages while auto-read is off. Correlation id An id the client puts on a request and the server repeats on the reply, so replies can arrive in any order. Probe task An empty task handed to an event loop to check that it still runs work. What does join() in a Netty handler cost? Every channel on that event loop waits until the future completes, not just the one that asked. Why finish with whenCompleteAsync(callback, ctx.executor())? The callback runs on the channel's own event loop, so the handler's state is only ever touched by one thread. When should the quote server read a connection? Only while the channel is writable and fewer than MAX_IN_FLIGHT (16) of its requests are waiting for a quote. What does FlowControlHandler add when auto-read is off? It holds messages the decoder already produced and releases them as reading resumes. Auto-read alone only stops the next socket read. Why count instead of time in a test that proves the loop is free? A healthy loop can miss a millisecond bar on a busy machine. A blocked loop's count (1 call, 0 probe tasks) doesn't depend on speed. Why does the quote protocol carry a request id? A reply leaves when its quote arrives, so replies can overtake each other. The client matches them by id. In what order does the server shut down? Stop accepting, close every open connection (a ChannelGroup; handlers cancel their in-flight work), then shutdownGracefully to stop the loop threads.

h: A Netty server that never blocks its loop · Go deeper
x: Three things a production shell adds to this one. An idle timeout. A client that connects and never sends a line holds a channel forever. IdleStateHandler fires an IdleStateEvent through userEventTriggered after a connection has been quiet for the time you set; close the channel there. TLS. An SslHandler goes first in the pipeline, before the frame decoder, and nothing after it changes. That is the payoff of keeping every concern in its own handler. Loop metrics. Every loop of a MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup is a SingleThreadEventExecutor, and pendingTasks() is the length of its task queue. In this server every reply is a task, so a queue that keeps growing is a loop that can't keep up. Export it per loop. Two limits of this lesson's design are worth knowing. The cap of 16 protects the server from one greedy client and does nothing against ten thousand polite ones: lesson 3 of this track adds a global admission limit that sheds load with a clear error. And whenCompleteAsync costs a task hand-off per reply even when the quote is already done. That is cheap next to a network round trip, and it buys the single-threaded handler state. Finally, the counting probe has a stronger cousin for tests: BlockHound, a separate Java agent library, throws as soon as code on a Netty event-loop thread calls a known blocking method such as CompletableFuture.join or Thread.sleep. Netty ships the integration for it (Hidden$NettyBlockHoundIntegration in netty-common).

h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · One request, three providers, one deadline
x: Lesson 1 left the server with a QuoteSource that must return a future at once. This lesson writes the source. For each request it asks Northbank, Eastgate and Fjord for a price, keeps the lowest, and answers within a deadline whatever the providers do. Lowest is what a customer buying the currency wants; a real dealing desk compares bid and ask, but the fan-out is the same either way. The shape is the concurrent decomposition from "Builders: launch, async, runBlocking, coroutineScope": start all three calls, then wait for them. With latencies of 120, 300 and 200 ms, one call after another takes 620 ms. Started together they take 300 ms, the time of the slowest: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: Mono.zip subscribes to all three sources at once Mono<List<Quote>> allPrices(String symbol) { return Mono.zip(northbank.quote(symbol), eastgate.quote(symbol), fjord.quote(symbol)) .map(t -> List.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())); } Kotlin suspend fun allPrices(symbol: String): List<Quote> = coroutineScope { providers.map { p -> async { p.quote(symbol) } } // 1. start all three .awaitAll() // 2. then wait: as long as the slowest } The deadline is the next decision. A price that arrives after 2 seconds is useless to a checkout page with a 300 ms budget. Give each call the deadline, start them together, and the whole request ends by the deadline: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: a timeout on each source, turned into "no answer" Mono<Optional<Quote>> inTime(Mono<Quote> call) { return call.timeout(DEADLINE) .map(Optional::of) .onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty())); } Kotlin providers.map { p -> async { withTimeoutOrNull(deadline) { p.quote(symbol) } } // null if p misses the deadline } withTimeoutOrNull is cancellation with a clock ("Cancellation and timeouts"). At the deadline it cancels the late call, which stops at its next suspension point, and returns null for it. Why one deadline per call, and not one withTimeout around the whole fan-out? Both bound the request. Around the whole fan-out, the timeout cancels everything and throws away the answers that did arrive: Northbank answered at 120 ms and Fjord at 200 ms, and you would still have nothing to send. Per call, only the late provider drops out, as the figure shows. Because all the calls start together, a per-call deadline is also a deadline for the request. Three ways to ask three providers Open FanOutDemo.kt. It runs on virtual time with runTest, so the clock is exact. The Java twin, FanOutDemoJava.java, does the same with Reactor in real time. Predict the three times and the three answer lists: one after another, all at once, and all at once with a 250 ms deadline. Run it. Then set deadline to 100 and predict the last line again. FanOutDemo.kt package workbench.quotes.l02 import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.awaitAll import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull // three invented providers: name, latency in ms, price private val providers = listOf(Triple("northbank", 120L, "1.0845"), Triple("eastgate", 300L, "1.0841"), Triple("fjord", 200L, "1.0843")) private suspend fun ask(name: String, ms: Long, price: String): String { delay(ms) return "$name $price" } /** One quote from three providers: one after another, all at once, and all at once inside a deadline. */ fun main() = runTest { // virtual time: delays are skipped, the clock still counts val deadline = 250L var t0 = currentTime val inTurn = providers.map { (n, ms, p) -> ask(n, ms, p) } println("one after another: ${currentTime - t0} ms $inTurn") t0 = currentTime val atOnce = coroutineScope { providers.map { (n, ms, p) -> async { ask(n, ms, p) } }.awaitAll() } println("async, all at once: ${currentTime - t0} ms $atOnce") t0 = currentTime val inTime = coroutineScope { providers.map { (n, ms, p) -> async { withTimeoutOrNull(deadline) { ask(n, ms, p) } } }.awaitAll() } println("with a $deadline ms deadline: ${currentTime - t0} ms $inTime") } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l02.FanOutDemoKt labs/quotes/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/quotes/l02/FanOutDemo.kt FanOutDemoJava.java // Java equivalent with Reactor: concat runs the calls in turn, Mono.zip subscribes to all three at once package workbench.quotes.l02; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; import java.util.Optional; /** One quote from three providers: one after another, all at once, and all at once inside a deadline. With a 100 ms deadline the last line takes 100 ms and all three answers are null: nobody was fast enough, which is the case section 3 handles. The Java twin prints similar times in real time (more on a busy machine), with Optional.empty where Kotlin prints null. All three calls start together and each gets the same deadline. The late call is cancelled at 250 ms, and the answers that arrived still count. withTimeoutOrNull (kotlinx.coroutines API) docs A dealer on an FX desk needs a price for a customer. She calls three banks at once on three phones and starts a kitchen timer. If one bank's line drops, she keeps listening to the other two; that is supervisorScope, where coroutineScope would hang up all three phones. When the timer rings she hangs up on whoever is still talking and quotes the best price she has. If nobody answered, she reads yesterday's price off the board with an "indicative" sticker on it. And if the customer walks away from the desk, she hangs up all three phones at once, which is the cancel travelling down the job tree. The analogy breaks at hanging up: a dealer's phone goes dead the instant she puts it down. A coroutine stops only at its next suspension point, so a provider client stuck in blocking IO keeps going until its call returns ("Cancellation and timeouts").

h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Let one provider fail alone, and tell your cancel from theirs
x: The first draft of BestQuote, the starting code of this lesson's lab, uses coroutineScope and withTimeout. Both are wrong for a quote, for reasons from earlier lessons. coroutineScope treats its children as one unit of work. When Northbank throws IOException at 50 ms, the scope cancels Eastgate and Fjord and rethrows ("Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers"). That is right for a payment details page that needs all three answers. A quote needs any one of them. supervisorScope lets each child fail alone: a failed async keeps its exception in its Deferred, and await hands it to you, where you turn it into "no answer". withTimeout signals a late call with TimeoutCancellationException, and that is a CancellationException. The usual rule, rethrow CancellationException so a cancel is never swallowed, now bites: one provider's timeout looks like a cancel of the whole request, and ends it. withTimeoutOrNull turns your own deadline into a plain null. But a provider can still throw TimeoutCancellationException from deep inside its own HTTP client, and this section's demo has one that does. So be precise and rethrow only when your coroutine was cancelled. ensureActive() makes exactly that check: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: each source handles its own error, so the zip never sees one Mono<Optional<Quote>> alone(Mono<Quote> call) { return call.map(Optional::of) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty())) // a failure stays with its provider .defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty()); // and so does an empty answer } Kotlin private suspend fun Deferred<Quote?>.awaitOrNull(): Quote? = try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() // we were cancelled ourselves: this rethrows null // only the provider's call ended that way } catch (e: Exception) { null // the provider failed: no answer from it } If the request itself was cancelled (the client hung up), ensureActive() throws and the cancel carries on up. If it returns, the cancellation belonged to the provider's call, and that provider simply has no answer. The demo runs the same three calls in three scopes: Scope Outcome coroutineScope, awaitAll fails at 50 ms: IOException: northbank 503 supervisorScope, rethrow every cancel fails at 100 ms: TimeoutCancellationException supervisorScope, rethrow only our cancel eastgate 1.0841 at 300 ms Reactor has no such trap, because cancellation there is not an error signal: you isolate each source with onErrorResume before Mono.zip. The compare block below puts the two whole fan-outs side by side. One failure, one timeout, three scopes Open FailAloneDemo.kt. Northbank fails at 50 ms, Fjord's own client times out at 100 ms, and Eastgate answers at 300 ms. Predict the outcome and the virtual time of each of the three attempts. Run it. Then, in callAll(), move async { fjord() } to the end of the list and predict the second line again. */ fun main() = runTest { attempt("coroutineScope, awaitAll") { coroutineScope { callAll().map { it.await() } } } attempt("supervisorScope, rethrow every cancel") { supervisorScope { callAll().map { it.naive() } } } attempt("supervisorScope, rethrow only our cancel") { supervisorScope { callAll().map { it.careful() } } } } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l02.FailAloneDemoKt labs/quotes/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/quotes/l02/FailAloneDemo.kt FailAloneDemoJava.java // Java equivalent with Reactor: a failed source fails Mono.zip unless each source handles its own error package workbench.quotes.l02; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.io.IOException; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.Optional; /** The same three calls zipped two ways: who survives a failure, and who survives a timeout? The naive supervisor fails at 100 ms with TimeoutCancellationException: it rethrew Fjord's timeout as if it were its own cancel. The careful one answers [null, null, eastgate 1.0841] at 300 ms. With Fjord last, the naive version waits for Eastgate first, then rethrows Fjord's exception: it fails at 300 ms instead of 100, and still throws away Eastgate's price. The Java twin shows the Reactor side: the raw Mono.zip fails on Northbank's error, and with onErrorResume on each call it answers with Eastgate at about 300 ms. Coroutine exceptions handling (Kotlin docs) read ensureActive (kotlinx.coroutines API) docs A checkout service fans out all the time: FX rates from several liquidity providers, a fraud score, merchant fees, a BIN lookup. Decide per call which scope it needs. Where any answer will do, as with several FX providers or several fraud vendors, use supervisorScope and a deadline per call. Where the response needs every answer, as with an account, its limits and its risk flags, use coroutineScope so that one failure cancels the rest at once. A Quarkus REST endpoint written as a Kotlin suspend fun runs on the event loop ("Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads"), so the fan-out inside it must suspend, never block. And keep the stale-price rule in mind for anything that moves money: an indicative price may be stale, but a price you book a payment at must be live and confirmed.

h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · When nobody answers, serve the last good quote and say it is stale
x: Sometimes all three providers miss the deadline: a network partition, or the minutes after a market opens. The service then has three options. It can wait longer, fail the request, or serve the last price it saw. Waiting longer breaks the deadline, which is the one promise the service makes. Failing is honest, and useless to a checkout page that only needs an indicative price. So BestQuote keeps the last live quote per symbol and serves it marked stale, 7 STALE EURUSD 1.0841 eastgate, and the client decides whether stale is good enough. Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: an empty Optional switches to the cache .flatMap(best -> best.map(Mono::just).orElseGet(() -> fromCache(symbol))) .doOnNext(q -> { if (!q.stale()) cache.remember(q); }) // only live answers refresh the cache Kotlin val best = answers.minByOrNull { it.price } if (best != null) { cache.remember(best) // only live answers refresh the cache return best } return cache.lastGood(symbol)?.asStale() // stale beats nothing ?: throw NoQuoteException(symbol) // the handler writes "7 ERR no quote for EURUSD" Two rules keep the cache honest. Only live answers go into it: if a stale answer could refresh the cache, one old price could be served forever. And with nothing cached, the request fails with NoQuoteException, which lesson 1's handler turns into 7 ERR no quote for EURUSD. A production cache would also have an age limit, so that a price from three seconds ago is served and one from last night is not. Check yourself: after an outage the providers recover, and on the next request Eastgate answers 1.0839 and Fjord 1.0842. What does the client get, and what does the cache hold for EURUSD afterwards? (OK EURUSD 1.0839 eastgate, and the cache now holds that live quote in place of the old one.)

h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Bind each request to its connection with scope.future
x: Lesson 1's handler calls quote on the event loop, and it cancels the future when the client hangs up. QuoteService connects that future to a coroutine: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: toFuture() subscribes, and cancelling the future cancels the subscription final class ReactorQuoteSource implements QuoteSource { @Override public CompletableFuture<Quote> quote(String symbol) { return best(symbol).toFuture(); // returns at once; cancel() reaches the zip } } Kotlin class QuoteService(context: CoroutineContext, private val best: BestQuote) : QuoteSource, AutoCloseable { private val scope = CoroutineScope(context + SupervisorJob()) // owned; failures stay per request override fun quote(symbol: String): CompletableFuture<Quote> = scope.future { best.quote(symbol) } // returns at once; cancel() reaches it override fun close() = scope.cancel() } scope.future { } starts a coroutine in the service's scope and returns a CompletableFuture at once, so the event loop never waits. The link works in both directions ("Coroutines meet Java: futures, Reactor, virtual threads"): when the coroutine finishes, the future completes, and when someone cancels the future, the coroutine is cancelled. The second direction is what binds a request to its connection. The client hangs up, channelInactive cancels the future, the future coroutine is cancelled, and the cancel travels down the job tree to the supervisorScope and its three provider calls ("Structured concurrency: scopes, jobs and the tree"). Each request is a small tree whose root is that coroutine, and the channel's lifetime bounds it. Why not give each channel its own CoroutineScope and cancel it in channelInactive? That works too, and it is the shape to pick when the handler itself is written in Kotlin. Here the Java handler from lesson 1 already keeps every pending future and cancels them on close, so a scope per channel would track the same requests twice. With future { }, the Java side holds the handle, the Kotlin side holds the tree, and neither needs to know how the other works. Two choices in the scope matter. The scope uses SupervisorJob. With a plain Job, one request that fails with NoQuoteException would cancel its parent, and with it every other request in flight; every later future would then come back cancelled at once. And the dispatcher is passed in. Production uses Dispatchers.Default. The tests pass a StandardTestDispatcher, so every delay and every deadline runs on virtual time, and a test that checks a 300 ms deadline takes a few milliseconds. The Java twin of this section's demo shows what you'd lose with a plain CompletableFuture built from three supplyAsync calls: cancelling the outer future cancels 0 of the 3 calls, and all three answer later with nobody listening. Hang up on a request Open HangUpDemo.kt. A request coroutine started with scope.future { } waits for three provider calls of 300, 400 and 500 ms. After 120 ms the demo cancels the future, as channelInactive would. Predict which calls print answered and which print cancelled, and how many coroutines are left in the scope. Run it, then run the Java twin, which builds the request from three supplyAsync calls. HangUpDemo.kt package workbench.quotes.l02 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.SupervisorJob import kotlinx.coroutines.async import kotlinx.coroutines.awaitAll import kotlinx.coroutines.cancel import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.future.future import kotlinx.coroutines.job import kotlinx.coroutines.supervisorScope import kotlin.coroutines.cancellation.CancellationException private val t0 = System.nanoTime() private fun ms() = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 private suspend fun call(name: String, latency: Long): String = try { delay(latency) println(" $name answered at ${ms()} ms") name } catch (e: CancellationException) { println(" $name cancelled at ${ms()} ms") throw e } /** A request coroutine behind a CompletableFuture. The client hangs up after 120 ms. */ fun main() { val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Default + SupervisorJob()) // the service's scope val request = scope.future { // what QuoteService.quote returns supervisorScope { listOf("northbank" to 300L, "eastgate" to 400L, "fjord" to 500L) .map { (name, latency) -> async { call(name, latency) } }.awaitAll() } } Thread.sleep(120) println("client hangs up at ${ms()} ms: the handler calls request.cancel(true)") request.cancel(true) Thread.sleep(600) println("at ${ms()} ms: coroutines still running in the scope: ${scope.coroutineContext.job.children.count()}") scope.cancel() } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l02.HangUpDemoKt labs/quotes/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/quotes/l02/HangUpDemo.kt HangUpDemoJava.java // Java equivalent with CompletableFuture: cancel() completes the future, but the calls behind it run on package workbench.quotes.l02; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** A request built from three supplyAsync calls. The client hangs up after 120 ms. */ public class HangUpDemoJava { static final long t0 = System.nanoTime(); static long ms() { return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } static String call(String name, long latency) { try { Thread.sleep(latency); System.out.println(" " + name + " answered at " + ms() + " ms, and nobody is listening"); return name; } catch (InterruptedException e) { System.out.println(" " + name + " interrupted at " + ms() + " ms"); return null; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { List<CompletableFuture<String>> calls = List.of( CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("northbank", 300), pool), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("eastgate", 400), pool), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> call("fjord", 500), pool)); CompletableFuture<List<String>> request = CompletableFuture.allOf(calls.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) .thenApply(v -> calls.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList()); Thread.sleep(120); System.out.println("client hangs up at " + ms() + " ms: the handler calls request.cancel(true)"); request.cancel(true); System.out.println("request cancelled: " + request.isCancelled() + ", calls cancelled: " + calls.stream().filter(CompletableFuture::isCancelled).count() + " of 3"); } // close() waits for the three calls, which finish anyway System.out.println("at " + ms() + " ms: all three calls have finished"); } } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l02.HangUpDemoJava labs/quotes/src/demo/java/workbench/quotes/l02/HangUpDemoJava.java All three calls print cancelled a few milliseconds after the hang-up, and the scope has 0 coroutines left: the cancel went from the future to the coroutine and down to its children. The Java twin reports calls cancelled: 0 of 3, and the three providers answer at about 300, 400 and 500 ms with nobody listening. CompletableFuture.cancel completed the outer future and stopped nothing. future (kotlinx.coroutines API) docs The most common mistake is building a best-of fan-out with coroutineScope and awaitAll(), then trying to rescue it with runCatching { deferred.await() } when one bad provider starts failing every quote. It doesn't work: in a plain scope, a failed child cancels its parent and siblings the moment it fails, long before your runCatching runs ("Exceptions: launch vs async, SupervisorJob, handlers"). The second version of the same mistake catches correctly but rethrows every CancellationException, and one provider's internal timeout then ends the request. Use supervisorScope, give each call withTimeoutOrNull, and in the catch rethrow only after currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() says the cancel was yours.

h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Java and Kotlin
x: The fan-out with Reactor's Mono.zip and with coroutines BestQuoteReactor.java // Reactor: errors, timeouts and empties become values at each source, then Mono.zip Mono<Quote> best(String symbol) { return Mono.zip(inTime(northbank.quote(symbol)), inTime(eastgate.quote(symbol)), inTime(fjord.quote(symbol))) .map(t -> Stream.of(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()) .flatMap(Optional::stream) .min(Comparator.comparing(Quote::price))) .flatMap(best -> best.map(Mono::just).orElseGet(() -> fromCache(symbol))) .doOnNext(q -> { if (!q.stale()) cache.remember(q); }); } Mono<Optional<Quote>> inTime(Mono<Quote> call) { return call.timeout(DEADLINE) .map(Optional::of) .onErrorResume(e -> Mono.just(Optional.empty())) // a failure or a timeout: no answer .defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty()); // an empty source would empty the zip } Mono<Quote> fromCache(String symbol) { Quote last = cache.lastGood(symbol); return last != null ? Mono.just(last.asStale()) : Mono.error(new NoQuoteException(symbol)); } BestQuote.kt class BestQuote( private val providers: List<Provider>, private val deadline: Duration, private val cache: QuoteCache = QuoteCache(), ) { suspend fun quote(symbol: String): Quote { val answers = supervisorScope { // 1. a failed call doesn't cancel the others providers .map { p -> async { withTimeoutOrNull(deadline) { p.quote(symbol) } } } // 2. late is null, not an exception .map { it.awaitOrNull() } // 3. failed is null too }.filterNotNull() val best = answers.minByOrNull { it.price } if (best != null) { cache.remember(best) return best } return cache.lastGood(symbol)?.asStale() ?: throw NoQuoteException(symbol) // 4. stale beats nothing } private suspend fun Deferred<Quote?>.awaitOrNull(): Quote? = try { await() } catch (e: CancellationException) { currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() // we were cancelled ourselves: this rethrows null // only the provider's call ended that way: no answer } catch (e: Exception) { null // the provider failed: no answer from it } } Both start the three calls together, give each its own deadline, turn a failure into "no answer", keep the lowest price and fall back to the cache. In Reactor every outcome becomes a value at the source: a timeout is an error signal you resume from, and an empty source is a third outcome you must name with defaultIfEmpty, or Mono.zip completes empty ("Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest"). Nothing runs until something subscribes, and cancelling the subscription cancels the three calls. In Kotlin the same policy is ordinary control flow: a scope, try/catch, minByOrNull. The scope guarantees that when quote returns, every call is either done or cancelled. The price of that directness is the CancellationException rule, which only coroutines have: a timeout is a cancel, so you must tell your own cancel from a provider's.

h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Worked example
x: Test the deadline and the hang-up on virtual time Make the providers controllable on the test clock. delay inside runTest uses virtual time, so a fake that delays 1,000 ms costs nothing, and recording cancellations in the catch tells the test exactly who was stopped. class FakeProvider( override val name: String, private val price: String, private val latency: Duration, private val cancelled: MutableList<String>, ) : Provider { override suspend fun quote(symbol: String): Quote { try { delay(latency) // 1. virtual time under runTest } catch (e: CancellationException) { cancelled += name // 2. record who was cancelled throw e } return Quote.live(symbol, price, name) } } // Java equivalent with Reactor: Mono.delay runs on Schedulers.parallel(), which virtual time replaces Mono<Quote> fake(String name, String price, Duration latency, List<String> cancelled) { return Mono.delay(latency) // 1. virtual time under StepVerifier .map(x -> Quote.live("EURUSD", price, name)) .doOnCancel(() -> cancelled.add(name)); // 2. record who was cancelled } Test the deadline. currentTime is the virtual clock, so the assertion can be exact: 300, not "under 400". A real-time version would take 300 ms per test and could fail on a busy build machine. @Test fun `a provider slower than the deadline is cancelled at the deadline`() = runTest { val best = BestQuote(listOf(northbank(120), eastgate(1_000), fjord(200)), deadline = 300.milliseconds) val quote = best.quote("EURUSD") assertThat(quote.provider).isEqualTo("fjord") assertThat(currentTime).isEqualTo(300) // 3. exact, and the test takes milliseconds assertThat(cancelled).containsExactly("eastgate") } // Java equivalent with Reactor: StepVerifier on virtual time StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> best("EURUSD")) // build the Mono inside the supplier .expectSubscription() .expectNoEvent(Duration.ofMillis(299)) .thenAwait(Duration.ofMillis(1)) // 3. exactly at the deadline .expectNextMatches(q -> q.provider().equals("fjord")) .verifyComplete(); assertThat(cancelled).containsExactly("eastgate"); Test the hang-up through QuoteService. Pass StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) as its context: the service's own scope then runs on the test clock too. runCurrent() runs what is due now, without moving the clock. @Test fun `cancelling the future cancels all three provider calls`() = runTest { val service = QuoteService(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler), slowBest) // 4. inject the test clock val future = service.quote("EURUSD") runCurrent() // the three calls have started future.cancel(true) // what channelInactive does runCurrent() assertThat(cancelled).containsExactlyInAnyOrder("northbank", "eastgate", "fjord") assertThat(service.inFlight).isEqualTo(0) } // Java equivalent with Reactor: cancelling toFuture() cancels the subscription at once CompletableFuture<Quote> future = source.quote("EURUSD"); future.cancel(true); // what channelInactive does assertThat(cancelled).containsExactlyInAnyOrder("northbank", "eastgate", "fjord"); Know where virtual time stops. A delay inside withContext(Dispatchers.Default) escapes the test scheduler and takes real time ("Shared state and testing coroutines"), which is why the service takes its dispatcher as a parameter. The two end-to-end tests in this lab use Dispatchers.Default and a real Netty server, so they assert only with latches: 6 provider calls started, 6 cancelled after the hang-up. h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Quiz
x: Inside supervisorScope, an async child throws IOException at 50 ms, while its two siblings run until 300 ms. Nobody has called await yet. What happens at 50 ms? The scope is cancelled and rethrows the IOException Nothing visible: the exception waits in that child's Deferred, and the siblings keep running The uncaught exception handler prints it, and the siblings are cancelled The two siblings are cancelled, but the scope itself keeps running In a supervisor, a failed child doesn't cancel its siblings or the scope. A failed async keeps its exception for await, which rethrows it when you get there. A handler is never used for async. In a plain coroutineScope, the first option would be right. Each provider call is async { withTimeout(300) { p.quote(s) } } inside supervisorScope, and the code that awaits it does catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }. One provider takes a second. What does the request get? The best of the other two prices, with null for the slow provider It waits a full second for the slow provider An IOException from the slow provider It ends with TimeoutCancellationException, as if the whole request had been cancelled withTimeout signals a late call with TimeoutCancellationException, a subclass of CancellationException. The catch rethrows it, so one provider's timeout ends the request. Use withTimeoutOrNull for your own deadline, and call currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() before deciding a cancel was yours. In the Reactor version, one provider's Mono completes empty: no value and no error. What does Mono.zip of the three do if that source has no defaultIfEmpty? It emits a tuple with an empty slot It fails with NoSuchElementException It completes empty at once and cancels the other two calls It waits for the other two and emits their pair Mono.zip needs one value from every source. When one completes empty there is nothing to combine, so the zip completes empty, with no error, and cancels the rest. The request would get no quote and no error. Mapping each source to Optional with defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty()) names the empty case. QuoteService.quote returned scope.future { best.quote(symbol) } to the handler, and the client hangs up, so channelInactive calls cancel(true) on it. What happens to the three provider calls? They are cancelled at their next suspension point: cancelling the future cancels the coroutine, and the cancel goes down the job tree Nothing: CompletableFuture.cancel never reaches the work behind a future Their threads are interrupted They finish, and their results go into the cache The future builder links both ways: the coroutine completes the future, and cancelling the future cancels the coroutine. From there cancellation travels down to the supervisorScope and its async children. A future made with supplyAsync is the case where the second option holds. Someone builds QuoteService's scope from context + Job() instead of SupervisorJob(). One request fails with NoQuoteException while 40 others are in flight. What happens? Only that request's future fails The other 40 are cancelled, the scope is cancelled, and every later request's future comes back cancelled at once The other 40 finish, but new requests fail Only requests for the same symbol are cancelled A failed child cancels a plain Job parent, and the cancelled parent cancels all its other children. A cancelled scope can't run new coroutines either: each new future completes with JobCancellationException at once. With SupervisorJob, each request's failure stays in its own future.

h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Key terms
x: Fan-out Starting several independent calls at once and combining what comes back. Deadline The time by which a request must answer, whatever its dependencies do. Supervisor scope A scope whose children fail alone; cancelling the scope still cancels them all. Stale quote The last live price for a symbol, served and labelled as old when no provider answers in time. future builder scope.future { }: starts a coroutine and returns a CompletableFuture linked to it both ways. Job tree The parent and child jobs of running coroutines; cancellation travels down it. Best-of fan-out: coroutineScope or supervisorScope? supervisorScope. Any one answer will do, so a failed call must not cancel the others. Why withTimeoutOrNull inside each async, not one withTimeout around the whole fan-out? Per call, only the late provider drops out. Around everything, the timeout cancels all calls and throws away answers that already arrived. Why is catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } wrong around a provider's await in this fan-out? A provider's own client timeout throws a CancellationException too, so rethrowing it ends the whole request. What does currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive() tell you inside a catch? It throws only if your own coroutine was cancelled. If it returns, the cancellation came from the call you awaited. What does cancel(true) on a future from scope.future { } do? It cancels the coroutine, and through the job tree every child the coroutine started. Why does QuoteService build its scope with SupervisorJob()? With a plain Job, one failed request cancels the scope and every other request, and later futures come back cancelled at once. May a stale quote refresh the cache? No. Only live answers go in; otherwise one old price could be served forever.

h: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline · Go deeper
x: Four refinements a production fan-out often adds. Propagate the deadline. The service knows that a request has, say, 180 ms left; the provider doesn't. Many RPC systems carry the remaining time in a header, so that the provider can give up too instead of finishing work nobody will read. With coroutines you compute it from a start time and pass it down; withTimeoutOrNull then wraps the remaining budget, not a fixed number. Answer early when the answer can't improve. If the request only needs a price within 0.5 pip of the best seen in the last second, it can return as soon as one such price arrives and cancel the rest. That is select over the onAwait clauses ("Channels, select and pipelines"), with the losers cancelled by hand. Put an age on the cache. Store the time with each quote and refuse to serve one older than a few seconds. Then a long outage ends in a clear error, not in a price from the morning. Mind the await legacy rule. The kotlinx.coroutines KDoc notes that await() on a Deferred that someone else cancelled throws CancellationException in your coroutine, even though your coroutine is fine. This lesson's ensureActive() check is the documented way to tell the two apart, and it is worth using anywhere you await work you didn't start. Lesson 3 of this track adds what the fan-out still lacks: a limit on how many calls each provider sees at once, retries for the calls that are safe to repeat, a hedge for the slowest provider, and load shedding when the whole service is full.

h: Hold up under load · A bulkhead for each provider, sized by Little's law
x: Lesson 2's fan-out sends every request to every provider at once. With a thousand requests in flight, Northbank sees a thousand concurrent calls, and its contract allows 10. Past that it answers 429, or slows down for everyone. The fix is a bulkhead: a limit on the calls in flight to one provider, so that one provider's limit doesn't become everybody's outage. In coroutines it is a Semaphore from kotlinx.coroutines.sync, the same tool "Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores" used from the JDK: Java // Java equivalent on virtual threads: java.util.concurrent.Semaphore, acquire before the try private Quote once(String symbol) throws IOException, InterruptedException { permits.acquire(); // blocks a cheap virtual thread try { return delegate.quote(symbol); } finally { permits.release(); } } Kotlin class GuardedProvider(private val delegate: Provider, maxConcurrent: Int /* ... */) : Provider { private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent) // kotlinx.coroutines.sync private suspend fun once(symbol: String): Quote = permits.withPermit { delegate.quote(symbol) } // suspends while all permits are out } withPermit suspends while no permit is free. It holds no thread, and the wait is cancellable, so lesson 2's deadline still applies: a call that waits too long for a permit is cancelled with the rest and counts as no answer. How many permits? Little's law ("Sizing a pool: CPU-bound, IO-bound and Little's law") says calls in flight equal arrival rate times time per call. If Northbank allows 10 calls at once and answers in 50 ms, it serves at most 200 calls a second. More permits add no capacity; they move the queue to Northbank's side, where you can't see it. Take the number from the provider's contract, and give each provider its own: Eastgate may allow 40, as the figure shows. Two placement rules matter. The permit goes around each single call, not around a whole retry loop: a call that waits out its backoff shouldn't hold a permit, and a hedge is a second call that needs one of its own. And the bulkhead lives in the provider's wrapper, not around the fan-out. A limit on requests can't protect a provider, because each request makes three calls. Forty requests, one provider, two limits Open BulkheadDemo.kt (virtual time) or BulkheadDemoJava.java (virtual threads, real time). Forty requests call a provider that answers in 50 ms. Predict the most calls in flight at once, and the time until all forty are answered, with no limit and with a limit of 4. Run it. Then change the limit to 8 and predict again from Little's law. How many calls does it see at once? */ fun main() = runTest { // virtual time, one thread: plain counters are safe here for (limit in listOf(null, 4)) { val permits = limit?.let { Semaphore(it) } var active = 0 var peak = 0 suspend fun call() { active++ peak = maxOf(peak, active) delay(50) // the provider thinks active-- } val t0 = currentTime coroutineScope { repeat(40) { launch { if (permits == null) call() else permits.withPermit { call() } } } } println("%-9s calls in flight at most: %2d all 40 answered after %3d ms".format( if (limit == null) "no limit" else "limit $limit", peak, currentTime - t0)) } } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l03.BulkheadDemoKt labs/quotes/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/quotes/l03/BulkheadDemo.kt BulkheadDemoJava.java // Java equivalent with virtual threads: one per request, and a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore as the bulkhead package workbench.quotes.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 40 requests at once to a provider that answers in 50 ms. How many calls does it see at once? Real time. */ public class BulkheadDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (Integer limit : new Integer[] {null, 4}) { Semaphore permits = limit == null ? null : new Semaphore(limit); AtomicInteger active = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger peak = new AtomicInteger(); Runnable call = () -> { peak.accumulateAndGet(active.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } active.decrementAndGet(); }; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService vthreads = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) { vthreads.submit(() -> { if (permits == null) { call.run(); return null; } permits.acquire(); // acquire before the try try { call.run(); } finally { permits.release(); } return null; }); } } // close() waits for all 40 System.out.printf("%-9s calls in flight at most: %2d all 40 answered after %3d ms%n", limit == null ? "no limit" : "limit " + limit, peak.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000); } } } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l03.BulkheadDemoJava labs/quotes/src/demo/java/workbench/quotes/l03/BulkheadDemoJava.java No limit: 40 calls at once, all answered after 50 ms. Limit 4: 4 at once, and 40 / 4 = 10 rounds of 50 ms, 500 ms. With a limit of 8 it is 5 rounds, 250 ms. The Java twin prints the same peaks in real time, with a few extra milliseconds of scheduling. The limit didn't make anything faster; it made the provider's load a number you chose. The finished service: admission at the door, one deadline for the fan-out, and a different set of guards for each provider. Semaphore (kotlinx.coroutines API) docs Picture the quote service as a restaurant on a Friday night with three suppliers. Each supplier has its own loading dock with a fixed number of bays: a truck that arrives when the bays are full waits outside (a bulkhead per provider). The host at the front door stops seating guests the kitchen can't serve before the theatre starts, and says so at once instead of letting them stand for an hour (shedding with ERR busy). A plate that comes out wrong is made again, but only when remaking is harmless; nobody runs the card twice (retry only idempotent calls). When one cook is slow, a second cook starts the same dish and the first plate out goes to the table (a hedge). At closing time the doors lock, the guests already eating finish, and the kitchen shuts after the last plate (an ordered shutdown). The analogy breaks at the hedge: a restaurant bins the second plate and eats the cost, while a provider counts both calls against your limit, which is why you hedge only the slow 5%.

h: Hold up under load · Retry only what is safe to repeat, and spread the retries
x: A transient failure, such as a 503 or a reset connection, often succeeds on a second try. But a retry is a second request, and the provider can't tell it from a new one. Northbank and Eastgate stream indicative prices, so asking twice changes nothing. Fjord's quotes are firm: each call reserves liquidity for two seconds and counts against our daily quota, and a retried firm quote reserves twice. So the decision belongs to the provider, as Provider.idempotent, false unless the provider says otherwise: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: the same decision before any retry operator is added Mono<Quote> quote(String symbol) { Mono<Quote> once = Mono.defer(() -> delegate.quote(symbol)); if (!delegate.idempotent()) return once; // a firm quote: exactly one call return once.retryWhen(Retry.backoff(2, Duration.ofMillis(50)).jitter(0.5) .filter(e -> e instanceof IOException)); } Kotlin override suspend fun quote(symbol: String): Quote { val once: suspend () -> Quote = { permits.withPermit { delegate.quote(symbol) } } if (!delegate.idempotent) return once() // a firm quote: exactly one call val attempt: suspend () -> Quote = if (hedgeAfter == null) once else ({ hedged(hedgeAfter, once) }) return retrying(backoff, random, attempt) } retrying is the backoff loop from "Shared state and testing coroutines" with one change, jitter. When Northbank blips, every request in flight fails in the same millisecond. Without jitter they all come back one backoff later, in the same millisecond again, and hit a provider that is still recovering. Multiplying each wait by a random factor between 0.5 and 1.5 spreads them out, which is what Reactor's Retry.backoff does by default ("Errors, retries and timeouts"): Java // Java equivalent on a virtual thread: the same factor, and a sleep that an interrupt ends double factor = 1 + jitter * (ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble() * 2 - 1); Thread.sleep((long) (nominal(n).toMillis() * factor)); Kotlin val factor = 1 + backoff.jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1) // 0.5 .. 1.5 for jitter 0.5 delay(backoff.nominal(n) * factor) // cancellable: the deadline still rules This section's demo has 1,000 clients that failed together and retry after a nominal 100 ms. Without jitter, all 1,000 retries land in one millisecond. With a jitter of 0.5 they spread over 50 to 150 ms, and no millisecond gets more than 18. Three more rules keep retries honest. Retry only errors that a later attempt might fix: here an IOException, never an unknown symbol. Keep every wait cancellable, so the deadline cuts off retries that can't finish in time; a retry after the deadline is work nobody will read. And count the calls: two retries means up to three calls per request, and Little's law applies to those as well. A thousand retries in one millisecond Open RetryJitterDemo.kt (or the Java twin, which computes the same waits without sleeping). A thousand clients failed together at 0 ms and retry after a nominal 100 ms. Predict how the retries spread over 25 ms buckets with no jitter and with a jitter of 0.5, and the most retries in any single millisecond. Run it. Then set the jitter to 0.1 and predict the busiest millisecond. When do the retries land? */ fun main() = runTest { for (jitter in listOf(0.0, 0.5)) { val random = Random(7) val retryAt = IntArray(1_000) val t0 = currentTime coroutineScope { repeat(1_000) { client -> launch { val factor = 1 + jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1) // 1 - jitter .. 1 + jitter delay(100.milliseconds * factor) retryAt[client] = (currentTime - t0).toInt() } } } val buckets = retryAt.groupBy { it / 25 * 25 }.toSortedMap() println("jitter $jitter: " + buckets.entries.joinToString(" ") { (from, hits) -> "$from-${from + 24} ms: ${hits.size}" }) println(" most retries in one millisecond: ${retryAt.groupBy { it }.values.maxOf { it.size }}") } } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l03.RetryJitterDemoKt labs/quotes/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/quotes/l03/RetryJitterDemo.kt RetryJitterDemoJava.java // Java equivalent: the same jitter formula with java.util.Random; the waits are computed, not slept package workbench.quotes.l03; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Random; import java.util.TreeMap; /** 1,000 clients fail together at 0 ms and retry after a nominal 100 ms. When do the retries land? */ public class RetryJitterDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { for (double jitter : new double[] {0.0, 0.5}) { Random random = new Random(7); Map<Integer, Integer> buckets = new TreeMap<>(); Map<Integer, Integer> perMs = new TreeMap<>(); for (int client = 0; client < 1_000; client++) { double factor = 1 + jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1); // 1 - jitter .. 1 + jitter int at = (int) Math.ceil(100 * factor); // delay rounds up to whole ms buckets.merge(at / 25 * 25, 1, Integer::sum); perMs.merge(at, 1, Integer::sum); } StringBuilder line = new StringBuilder("jitter " + jitter + ":"); buckets.forEach((from, hits) -> line.append(String.format(" %d-%d ms: %d", from, from + 24, hits))); System.out.println(line); System.out.println(" most retries in one millisecond: " + perMs.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).max().orElse(0)); } } } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l03.RetryJitterDemoJava labs/quotes/src/demo/java/workbench/quotes/l03/RetryJitterDemoJava.java No jitter: all 1,000 retries in the 100 to 124 ms bucket, and all of them in the same millisecond.
