With 0.1 the retries squeeze into 90 to 110 ms, and the busiest millisecond gets 58, three times as many: less jitter, less spread. Retry and RetryBackoffSpec source (reactor-core 3.8.x) docs The same guards sit in front of every payments dependency, with one difference that matters more than all the others: most payment calls are not idempotent. A card authorization, a capture or a refund must never be retried or hedged blindly, because the issuer can't tell a repeat from a new charge. Retry it only with the same idempotency key, and when the retries run out, mark it pending and reconcile, as "Errors, retries and timeouts" said. Reads are different: a balance, an FX rate or a BIN lookup can take a retry and a hedge. Give each issuer or acquirer its own bulkhead from its published limit, and pick one layer to own retries: a Temporal activity retry policy, SmallRye Fault Tolerance @Retry and a hand-written loop stacked on top of each other multiply the calls. During a Kubernetes rollout, the same shutdown order applies: fail the readiness check first so no new traffic arrives, drain within the termination grace period, then exit.

h: Hold up under load · Hedge the slow tail of one provider
x: Northbank answers in 40 ms most of the time, but one call in twenty takes 600 ms: a garbage-collection pause, or a slow replica. A retry doesn't help, because nothing failed; the call is just slow. A hedge does. If the first call hasn't answered by the time 95% of calls have, send one more identical call and take whichever answers first: Java // Java equivalent with Reactor: the delayed hedge is cancelled before it starts if the first call wins Mono<Quote> hedged(Duration after, Mono<Quote> call) { return Mono.firstWithValue(call, Mono.delay(after).then(call)); } Kotlin suspend fun <T : Any> hedged(after: Duration, call: suspend () -> T): T = coroutineScope { val first = async { call() } val early = withTimeoutOrNull(after) { first.await() } // stops the waiting, not the call if (early != null) return@coroutineScope early val second = async { call() } // the hedge val winner = select { first.onAwait { it }; second.onAwait { it } } coroutineContext.cancelChildren() // stop the loser winner } withTimeoutOrNull(after) { first.await() } stops waiting at the hedge time. It doesn't cancel first, which is a child of the coroutineScope, not of the timeout. Then select takes whichever deferred completes first ("Channels, select and pipelines"), and cancelChildren() stops the loser. Forget that line and coroutineScope waits for the slow call anyway, which undoes the hedge. In this section's demo, 200 Northbank quotes went from a p99 of 600 ms to a p99 of 120 ms, for 210 calls instead of 200. Hedging at the 95th percentile costs about 5% more calls. That cost decides where hedges go. Hedge only an idempotent provider, because a hedge is a duplicate request. Hedge only the provider whose tail hurts, here Northbank, at a time taken from its measured latency. And make the hedge take its own permit from the bulkhead. When Northbank is saturated, a hedge would only add to the queue that made it slow, so under full load the hedge waits for a permit, and the first call usually wins. The lab has a test for exactly that: with one permit, the hedge never runs alongside the first call. Cut Northbank's tail Open HedgeDemo.kt. Northbank answers in 40 ms, except every 20th call, which takes 600 ms. The demo asks for 200 quotes without a hedge, then with a hedge after 80 ms. Predict p50, p99, the slowest request and the number of calls for both runs. Run it. Then set the hedge to 30 ms, below Northbank's normal latency, and predict the number of calls. h: Hold up under load · Shed load at the door, then shut down in order
x: Bulkheads protect the providers. Nothing yet protects the service from more requests than it can answer within its deadline. Northbank takes 10 calls at a time at 50 ms each, so within 300 ms it can answer about 60 requests, and a burst of 500 leaves hundreds waiting for a permit until they fail at the deadline anyway. This section's demo measured it: 50 live answers, 450 misses, and 135,000 ms of waiting (summed over the requests that missed) that produced nothing. Load shedding turns those slow failures into fast ones. QuoteService admits at most maxInFlight requests, and the next one gets a failed future at once, which lesson 1's handler writes as 7 ERR busy: Java // Java equivalent: the same door with a java.util.concurrent.Semaphore public CompletableFuture<Quote> quote(String symbol) { if (!accepting) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new ShuttingDownException()); if (!admission.tryAcquire()) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new BusyException()); CompletableFuture<Quote> reply = best(symbol).toFuture(); reply.whenComplete((q, e) -> admission.release()); return reply; } Kotlin override fun quote(symbol: String): CompletableFuture<Quote> { if (!accepting) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(ShuttingDownException()) if (!admission.tryAcquire()) return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(BusyException()) // never waits val reply = scope.future { best.quote(symbol) } reply.whenComplete { _, _ -> admission.release() } // however the request ends return reply } With 50 admitted, the same burst got the same 50 live answers, and the other 450 clients heard busy within a millisecond, early enough to try another instance. tryAcquire never waits, so the event loop that calls quote never waits either. The permit comes back in whenComplete, however the request ends, including a cancel after a hang-up. Shutdown uses the same pieces, in the order "Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown" gave for thread pools: Java // Java equivalent for an executor-based service: the same order, from "Pools in production" void shutdown(Duration grace) throws InterruptedException { server.stopAccepting(); // 1. no new connections accepting = false; // 2. stop admitting pool.shutdown(); if (!pool.awaitTermination(grace.toMillis(), MILLISECONDS)) { // 3. drain, up to grace pool.shutdownNow(); // 4. interrupt the rest pool.awaitTermination(5, SECONDS); } server.close(); // 5. close connections, stop the loops } Kotlin suspend fun shutdown(grace: Duration): Int { accepting = false // 2. stop admitting val job = scope.coroutineContext.job withTimeoutOrNull(grace) { job.children.toList().joinAll() } // 3. drain, up to grace val left = job.children.count() job.cancelAndJoin() // 4. cancel the rest, wait for them return left } // QuoteApp: 1. server.stopAccepting(), then the above, then 5. server.close() Stop accepting connections. Stop admitting requests (ERR shutting down). Give the requests in flight a grace period to finish. Cancel what is left and wait for it with cancelAndJoin(), so that no coroutine outlives the service. Then close the connections and the loops. Lesson 1's ChannelGroup matters here: each connection is closed on its own loop, behind the reply that the drain just let through. Queue the burst, or shed it Open ShedDemo.kt. A burst of 500 requests meets a provider that takes 10 calls at a time, 50 ms each, under a 300 ms deadline. Predict the live answers, the misses, the requests shed as busy, and the time spent waiting for nothing, for both runs. Run it. Then admit 100 instead of 50 and predict the misses again. ShedDemo.kt package workbench.quotes.l03 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withPermit import kotlinx.coroutines.test.currentTime import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull /** * A burst of 500 requests. The provider takes 10 calls at a time, 50 ms each, and every request * has a 300 ms deadline. Queue them all, or shed what can't make the deadline? */ fun main() = runTest { for (maxInFlight in listOf(null, 50)) { val provider = Semaphore(10) val admission = maxInFlight?.let { Semaphore(it) } var live = 0 var late = 0 var busy = 0 var waitedForNothing = 0L coroutineScope { repeat(500) { launch { if (admission != null && !admission.tryAcquire()) { busy++ // answered "ERR busy" at once return@launch } try { val start = currentTime val answer = withTimeoutOrNull(300) { provider.withPermit { delay(50) } } if (answer != null) live++ else { late++; waitedForNothing += currentTime - start } } finally { admission?.release() } } } } println("%-14s live answers: %3d missed the deadline: %3d shed as busy: %3d ms spent waiting for nothing: %,d".format( if (maxInFlight == null) "queue them all" else "admit $maxInFlight", live, late, busy, waitedForNothing)) } } ./gradlew :quotes:demo -Pmain=workbench.quotes.l03.ShedDemoKt labs/quotes/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/quotes/l03/ShedDemo.kt ShedDemoJava.java // Java equivalent with virtual threads: Semaphore.tryAcquire() sheds, a timed tryAcquire is the deadline package workbench.quotes.l03; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** * A burst of 500 requests. The provider takes 10 calls at a time, 50 ms each, and every request * has a 300 ms deadline. Queue them all, or shed what can't make the deadline? Real time. */ public class ShedDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (Integer maxInFlight : new Integer[] {null, 50}) { Semaphore provider = new Semaphore(10); Semaphore admission = maxInFlight == null ? null : new Semaphore(maxInFlight); AtomicInteger live = new AtomicInteger(), late = new AtomicInteger(), busy = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicLong waitedForNothing = new AtomicLong(); try (ExecutorService vthreads = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 500; i++) { vthreads.submit(() -> { if (admission != null && !admission.tryAcquire()) { busy.incrementAndGet(); return null; } // ERR busy long start = System.nanoTime(); try { long deadline = start + TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.toNanos(300); if (provider.tryAcquire(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) { try { Thread.sleep(50); } finally { provider.release(); } if (System.nanoTime() <= deadline) { live.incrementAndGet(); return null; } } late.incrementAndGet(); waitedForNothing.addAndGet((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000); } finally { if (admission != null) admission.release(); } return null; }); } } System.out.printf("%-14s live answers: %3d missed the deadline: %3d shed as busy: %3d ms spent waiting for nothing: %,d%n", maxInFlight == null ? Admit 50: the same 50 live answers, 0 misses, 450 shed at once, and no wasted waiting. Admitting 100 gives the same 50 live answers, 50 misses and 15,000 ms of wasted waiting: past what the provider can serve in 300 ms, a bigger door only buys slow failures. h: Hold up under load · Design review: would one virtual thread per connection be simpler?
x: Here is the finished design next to the question every reviewer asks about it: wouldn't one virtual thread per connection, with plain blocking calls, be simpler? Concern This service One virtual thread per connection idle connections a few loop threads hold thousands one parked virtual thread each, a few KB waiting for providers suspended coroutines blocked virtual threads deadline and cancel structured: the cancel reaches every provider call interrupts, which some blocking clients ignore per-provider limits a Semaphore per provider a Semaphore per provider framing and backpressure Netty codecs, auto-read your own read loop; TCP does the pacing code shape futures at the Java edge, coroutines inside plain blocking Java Virtual threads ("The thread-per-request wall") make the right column cheap, and for many services they are the better choice. Switch when the providers only ship blocking SDKs, such as JDBC or an old SOAP client: this design would then need a blocking pool behind the coroutines, and you'd pay for two models. Switch when the team writes Java and connections number in the thousands. Stay on the event loop when the service already lives on Netty (Vert.x, Quarkus), when connections number in the hundreds of thousands, when you need the protocol control that auto-read and codecs give you, or when the provider clients are non-blocking and a cancel must reach them. Either way, the limits stay. Bulkheads, deadlines, admission and an ordered shutdown appear in both columns, because moving to virtual threads removes the pool, and with it the only limit nobody wrote down ("Moving a blocking service to virtual threads"). The question that picks the model is where the waiting happens ("Zero-copy, epoll, io_uring, and choosing a server model"). Here it happens in three provider calls per request, under a deadline, and both models can wait well. The most common load mistake is one retry policy for everything: every provider call, firm quotes and authorizations included, wrapped in the same retry(3) with no jitter. Under a short outage it sends synchronized waves of calls at a provider that is trying to recover, and for calls that aren't idempotent it does the work two or three times. The runner-up is an unbounded queue in front of a bounded resource: no admission limit, so a burst turns into hundreds of requests waiting for a permit until each one fails at its deadline, while the latency graph says the service is slow rather than full. Retry only idempotent calls, with jitter, inside the deadline, and shed at the door what you can't answer in time.

h: Hold up under load · Java and Kotlin
x: The guards around a provider with coroutines and on virtual threads GuardedProvider.java (virtual threads) // Java on virtual threads: the same guards around a blocking provider client final class GuardedProvider { private final BlockingProvider delegate; private final Semaphore permits; private final Backoff backoff; GuardedProvider(BlockingProvider delegate, int maxConcurrent, Backoff backoff) { this.delegate = delegate; this.permits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrent); this.backoff = backoff; } Quote quote(String symbol) throws IOException, InterruptedException { if (!delegate.idempotent()) return once(symbol); // 2. never repeat a firm quote for (int n = 1; ; n++) { try { return once(symbol); } catch (IOException e) { if (n > backoff.retries()) throw e; // out of retries double factor = 1 + backoff.jitter() * (ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextDouble() * 2 - 1); Thread.sleep((long) (backoff.nominal(n).toMillis() * factor)); // an interrupt ends it } } } private Quote once(String symbol) throws IOException, InterruptedException { permits.acquire(); // 1. every call holds a permit try { return delegate.quote(symbol); } finally { permits.release(); } } } Resilience.kt suspend fun <T> retrying(backoff: Backoff, random: Random, call: suspend () -> T): T { var n = 0 while (true) { try { return call() } catch (e: IOException) { if (++n > backoff.retries) throw e // out of retries val factor = 1 + backoff.jitter * (random.nextDouble() * 2 - 1) // 1 - jitter .. 1 + jitter delay(backoff.nominal(n) * factor) // so callers that failed together spread out } } } class GuardedProvider( private val delegate: Provider, maxConcurrent: Int, private val backoff: Backoff = Backoff(), private val hedgeAfter: Duration? = null, private val random: Random = Random.Default, ) : Provider { private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent) override val name: String get() = delegate.name override val idempotent: Boolean get() = delegate.idempotent override suspend fun quote(symbol: String): Quote { val once: suspend () -> Quote = { permits.withPermit { delegate.quote(symbol) } } // 1. every call holds a permit if (!delegate.idempotent) return once() // 2. never repeat a firm quote val attempt: suspend () -> Quote = if (hedgeAfter == null) once else ({ hedged(hedgeAfter, once) }) return retrying(backoff, random, attempt) // 3. a hedge per attempt } } The rules are the same in both: a permit around every single call, one call for a provider that isn't idempotent, and jittered retries for IOException only. What differs is what waiting and stopping cost. In Kotlin, withPermit and delay suspend, so a thousand requests waiting for a permit or a backoff hold no threads, and a cancel (the deadline or a hang-up) reaches them at once through the job tree. On virtual threads, acquire and Thread.sleep block, which is cheap too, and a cancel is an interrupt: it reaches the sleep and the semaphore, but only reaches the provider call if its client responds to interrupts. The Java version leaves the hedge out. On threads a hedge takes an ExecutorCompletionService, or JDK 25's StructuredTaskScope, still a preview API ("Structured concurrency and scoped values"), and the loser is stopped by an interrupt, which works only if its client responds to interrupts. Java code that can block on a virtual thread is shorter to read. Kotlin code gets the hedge and the deadline from the library.

h: Hold up under load · Quiz
x: In hedged, the first call is still running at 80 ms, so a second starts, and select returns the second call's answer at 110 ms. The author forgot cancelChildren(). When does hedged return? At 110 ms: select cancels the clause that lost When the slow first call finishes, because coroutineScope waits for every child At 110 ms, and the slow call keeps running in the background Never: the two calls deadlock on the permit select only picks the first clause to complete; stopping the losers is your job. The first call is still a child of the coroutineScope, and a scope returns only after all its children are done, so hedged returns when the slow call ends, which undoes the hedge. Nothing runs in the background, because the scope is structured. With Backoff(retries = 2, first = 50 ms, jitter = 0.5), or Reactor's Retry.backoff(2, Duration.ofMillis(50)), a call fails every time with IOException. How many calls does the provider see? 2 It depends on the jitter 3 4 Two retries after the first attempt: three calls, with waits of about 50 and 100 ms between them. Jitter moves when the retries happen, not how many there are. Count them when you size the bulkhead, because Little's law applies to every call. A provider's contract allows 10 calls at once, and it answers in 50 ms. How many calls per second can it serve, and how many permits should its bulkhead have? 200 per second, and 10 permits 500 per second, and 50 permits 10 per second, and 10 permits 200 per second, and 200 permits Little's law: in flight = rate x time, so 10 = rate x 0.05 s gives 200 calls a second. The bulkhead holds the contract's 10. More permits don't add capacity; they move the queue to the provider's side, where it slows everyone and you can't see it. After shutdown, the service must have no coroutines left. Which step guarantees it? scope.cancel(), which returns as soon as the cancel is sent job.cancelAndJoin(), which returns only after every child has finished withTimeoutOrNull(grace) around the drain Setting accepting = false before anything else cancel() only requests cancellation and returns while children may still be running their finally blocks; cancelAndJoin() waits until they have stopped. The grace period lets well-behaved requests finish, and accepting = false stops new ones from arriving, but neither stops what is already running. The providers only ship blocking Java SDKs, the service holds about 2,000 connections, and the team writes Java. A reviewer suggests one virtual thread per connection. What is the strongest argument for switching? Virtual threads make each request faster Virtual threads remove the need for per-provider limits Netty can't serve 2,000 connections With blocking SDKs this design needs a blocking pool behind the coroutines anyway, while virtual threads run the same calls in plain code, and 2,000 connections are easy for them The model should follow where the waiting happens. Blocking SDKs put the waiting on threads, so the event loop buys little here and costs a second model. Virtual threads give scale, not speed, and they remove the pool, so the bulkheads must be written down explicitly. Netty handles far more than 2,000 connections.

h: Hold up under load · Key terms
x: Bulkhead A limit on the calls in flight to one dependency, so that its limit can't sink the rest of the service. Idempotent call A call you can repeat without changing the outcome, such as reading a price. Jitter A random change to each retry wait, so clients that failed together don't retry together. Hedged request A second, identical request sent when the first is slower than usual; the first answer wins and the other is cancelled. Tail latency The slowest few percent of requests, such as p99: what the unluckiest users see. Load shedding Refusing work at the door, at once and with a clear error, when the service can't finish it in time. Graceful shutdown Stopping in order: no new work, let work in flight finish for a while, cancel the rest, then release resources. Where does a bulkhead's permit go? Around each single call to the provider: not around the retry loop (a backoff wait shouldn't hold a permit), and a hedge takes a permit of its own. How do you size a provider's bulkhead? From its contract's limit on concurrent calls. Little's law: permits / time per call = the most calls per second it can serve. Which calls may be retried or hedged? Only idempotent ones, where a repeat does no harm. A firm quote that reserves liquidity, like a card authorization, is called once. Why add jitter to retry waits? Clients that failed together would retry in the same millisecond. A factor between 0.5 and 1.5 spread 1,000 retries so that no millisecond had more than 18. When does a hedge start, and what does it cost? After about the provider's p95 latency. It adds about 5% more calls; in the demo it cut p99 from 600 to 120 ms. Why shed with tryAcquire instead of queueing? A request that can't make the deadline fails anyway. Shedding makes it fail in a millisecond with ERR busy, and nothing waits on the event loop. The quote service's shutdown order? Stop accepting, stop admitting, drain within the grace period, cancelAndJoin the rest, then close the connections and the loops.

h: Hold up under load · Go deeper
x: What a production version of this service would add, roughly in the order it would hurt to miss them. Metrics. Per provider: latency histograms (the hedge time comes from the p95), permits in use, calls retried, hedges sent and won, errors by type. Per service: requests admitted, shed and served stale, and the age of stale quotes. Without them, every number in this track (the 10 permits, the 80 ms hedge, the 50 in flight) is a guess. A circuit breaker. Retries help with blips; they make a dead provider worse. A breaker counts recent failures and, past a threshold, stops calling the provider for a while, then lets a few trial calls through. It sits outside the retry loop, so an open breaker fails fast instead of retrying. A retry budget. Cap retries as a share of all calls, for example 10%. During a long outage the budget runs out and the service stops multiplying its own load. Adaptive limits. Fixed permits are right only for the load they were measured under. Adaptive concurrency limits change the permits from observed latency, the way TCP's congestion control finds a window: when latency rises, the limit shrinks before the provider falls over. Deadline propagation and context. Send the time left with each provider call so that the provider can give up too, and carry the trace and request ids across the Netty-to-coroutine edge (asContextElement or MDCContext, as "Dispatchers and the coroutine context" showed), so that a slow quote can be found in the logs. Fair admission. One heavy client can still take most of the 50 slots. Per-client quotas at the door, on top of the global limit, keep a single caller from crowding out the rest. An operations story for shutdown. Fail the readiness check before the drain starts, so that the load balancer stops sending, and keep the grace period shorter than the platform's termination grace, or the platform kills the process mid-drain.

h: Kotlin generics, properly
x: Variance from first principles: out, in, projections, star projection, reified, KClass, and Java side by side. By the end of this track generics stop being a set of slogans you half remember. You can read any signature in your codebase, Kotlin or Java, and say what it accepts and why: List<out E>, Comparator<in T>, MutableList<*>, <T extends Comparable<? super T>>. You can decide, for each type parameter you write, whether it is out, in or invariant, by checking where it appears instead of guessing. You know what the JVM erases, what inline and reified bring back, when a KClass is enough and when you need a KType or a super type token, and you can build type-safe registries, event buses and result types that need no casts at the call site. You need to know the syntax of both languages, nothing more. The track starts from zero with type parameters, and every variance lesson repeats one picture: a producer hands values out, a consumer takes them in. Each lesson shows the compiler error for every wrong move, so you learn what the guard looks like when it fires. Install JDK 25; the labs compile with release 21 and use Kotlin 2.4.21, and the compiler messages quoted in the lessons are copied from that version. The labs live in labs/generics, one package per lesson (workbench.generics.l01 to l11). Most are Kotlin; lessons 3, 6 and 7 add a small Java exercise where the point is Java's arrays, wildcards or raw types, and lesson 8 has a Java test that calls your Kotlin code with a class token. Some tests check variance by reading the Java signature Kotlin generates, because out becomes ? extends there. From lesson 8 on, tests reach your inline functions through a Callers.kt file that you don't edit (lesson 8 explains why). Lesson 9's demos run with and without kotlin-reflect: add -Preflect to the demo command. Run ./gradlew :generics:test --tests 'workbench.generics.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, ./gradlew :generics:solutionTest to see the reference answers pass the same tests, and ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=<class> for the Try-it programs. A type parameter is a blank the caller fills in. It moves a ClassCastException from a far-away read to a compile error at the write. A class is not a type: String backs String and String?, List backs List<String> and List<Int>. Generic types are invariant unless declared otherwise. Producer out, consumer in: out T lets C<Sub> stand in for C<Super>, in T flips the arrow, and both shut one side. Java writes ? extends and ? super at every use. Variance limits which types flow, not whether state changes. Check positions with the sign rule when the intuition stops helping. Declare variance on the class when you can; project (MutableList<out T>, MutableList<in T>) when the class both reads and writes; split out a read-only out view when readers need flexibility. * means one unknown type argument: read as Any?, write nothing. It is not Any?, and it is not a raw type. The JVM erases type arguments. inline + reified brings the outer class back at each call site, Java can't call it, and nested arguments stay erased. KClass and Class describe classes; KType (from typeOf) describes full types. x::class is a KClass<out T>. Declaration details need kotlin-reflect. Recursive bounds give base classes a self type; T & Any removes null; @UnsafeVariance is a promise that a parameter is only compared; Nothing sits below every type. Type-safe containers tie the key to the value type (KClass<T>, Key<T> with a KType), keep the one unchecked cast private, and keep write keys invariant.

Substitution test: if I secretly hand you a C<CardAuthorized> where you expected a C<PaymentEvent>, can any call you make go wrong? No writes: out is safe. Only writes: flip it, in. out and in limit which types flow, not whether state changes: clear() works on MutableList<out T> and MutableList<*>. Function types are Function1<in P, out R>: a (PaymentEvent) -> Unit is a (CardAuthorized) -> Unit. java.util.Comparator and other Java interfaces are invariant in Kotlin: write Comparator<in T>. Where T may appear Position Sign out T in T return type, val + yes no parameter − no yes var, MutableList<T> anywhere 0 no no parameter of a parameter, f: (T) -> Unit − × − = + yes no parameter of the result, (): (T) -> Unit + × − = − no yes private members and plain constructor parameters are exempt; protected and internal are checked. @UnsafeVariance switches the check off for one use: only for parameters that are compared, never stored (List.contains). Declaration-site or use-site Every member only produces T (or only consumes it): declare out T (or in T) on the class, once. The class both reads and writes T: keep it invariant and project in each function that uses one side, MutableList<out T> or MutableList<in T>. Projecting an already-variant type gives a warning (List<out T>, redundant) or an error (List<in T>, conflicting). Variance on a function's own type parameter is an error. A type that does both but has readers that only read: split out a ReadX<out T> interface. Erasure and reified At run time a List<String> is a List. So is List<String>, is T and T() don't compile; check is List<*>, then check each element. as List<String> checks only the class and fails later, at a read (heap pollution). inline fun <reified T> copies the body into each call site with the real class: is T, as? T, T::class, filterIsInstance<T>(). Reified covers the outer class only (filterIsInstance<List<String>>() keeps every list), can't take Nothing or an erased T, and is invisible to Java (synthetic). Give Java a type: Class<T> overload. Kotlin 2.4: x::class on a nullable reified T is an error; use <reified T : Any>. h: Kotlin generics, properly: track quiz
x: fun <T> firstOrDefault(items: List<T>, default: T): T. What does val x = firstOrDefault(listOf(1, 2), "none") do? It doesn't compile: T can't be both Int and String It compiles with T = Any? and prints a warning It compiles: T is inferred as a common supertype of Int and String, so x is 1, typed Comparable<*> & Serializable It compiles and throws ClassCastException when x is used Inference looks for a type that both arguments fit, and Int and String share Comparable<*> and Serializable. That's legal, and usually not what you meant: val y: Int = firstOrDefault(listOf(1, 2), "none") fails with expected 'Int', actual 'Comparable<*> & Serializable'. An explicit type argument, firstOrDefault<Int>(...), turns the mistake into an error at the call. A helper must compare two values with < and also read .length. Which Kotlin signature allows both? fun <T : Comparable<T>> longer(a: T, b: T): T fun <T> longer(a: T, b: T): T where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> fun <T : CharSequence> longer(a: T, b: T): T fun <T : Any> longer(a: T, b: T): T Two bounds need a where clause, and the caller's type must satisfy both. Comparable<T> alone gives < but no length; CharSequence alone gives length but no <. Java writes the same thing as <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>>. val ids: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf("pay_1"). Which line compiles? val a: MutableList<Any> = ids val b: List<Any> = ids val c: MutableList<Any?> = ids val d: Array<Any> = ids.toTypedArray() Only the read-only List is declared out E, so only it is covariant. MutableList and Array are invariant in Kotlin because they can be written to; if they weren't, you could add an Int to a list of strings, which is exactly what Java arrays allow until an ArrayStoreException. Pick the variance for each: interface Feed<T> { fun next(): T }, interface Audit<T> { fun record(event: T) }, class Slot<T>(var item: T). out, in, invariant in, out, out out, out, out invariant, in, out Feed only returns T: a producer, out. Audit only takes T: a consumer, in. Slot has a var, which is read and written, so T sits in an invariant position and the class can be neither. What Java signature does Kotlin generate for fun <T> copyInto(from: MutableList<out T>, to: MutableList<in T>)? <T> void copyInto(List<T> from, List<T> to) <T> void copyInto(List<?> from, List<?> to) <T> void copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) <T> void copyInto(List from, List to) (raw types) Use-site projections are Kotlin's spelling of Java wildcards: out T is ? extends T and in T is ? super T, the same shape as Collections.copy. The lab for that lesson checks exactly this signature through Java reflection. Which function accepts a MutableList<String> and may call clear() on it? fun reset(l: MutableList<Any?>) fun reset(l: MutableList<Any>) fun reset(l: List<*>) fun reset(l: MutableList<*>) A star projection accepts a mutable list of any element type and still allows members that take no element, such as clear(). MutableList<Any?> and MutableList<Any> accept only lists of exactly that element type. List<*> accepts the list but has no clear(). Your Kotlin library exposes inline fun <reified T : Any> decode(json: String): T. A Java service in the same monorepo needs it. What do you add? @JvmStatic on the reified function Nothing: Java can call it with Decoder.<Payment>decode(json) A version that takes T as a raw Class and returns Object fun <T : Any> decode(json: String, type: Class<T>): T, and make the reified one delegate to it javac can't inline Kotlin code, so the reified function is a synthetic method it ignores. A Class-token overload works for both languages and can do a checked type.cast. Keeping the reified version as a one-line wrapper gives Kotlin callers the short form. Inside inline fun <reified T> describe(), called as describe<List<String>>(), what do T::class and typeOf<T>() keep? T::class is the class List; typeOf<T>() is the full List<String> Both keep List<String> Both give only List T::class doesn't compile for a generic T A KClass can only describe a class, and List<String> and List<Int> share one. typeOf builds a KType at the call site that includes arguments and nullability, and it works without kotlin-reflect. That difference is why a registry for Repository<Payment> and Repository<Refund> needs KType keys. In abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>>, why write protected abstract fun self(): B instead of return this as B in each setter? Because this as B doesn't compile Because abstract functions are faster Because self() is checked: a subclass that passes the wrong type argument fails to compile, while this as B compiles and throws ClassCastException at a later call Because Java can't call a function that returns B this as B is an unchecked cast; erasure makes it succeed inside the base class, and the failure shows up where a caller uses the result. Each subclass implementing self() = this lets the compiler check that this really is a B. Pick the types: (1) a function that only reads payments from a mutable buffer and may clear it; (2) a bus that stores handlers for CardAuthorized and accepts handlers for any PaymentEvent; (3) a key for a per-request List<String> attribute. (1) MutableList<out Payment>; (2) (CardAuthorized) -> Unit handlers stored behind a safeCast adapter, keyed by KClass<out PaymentEvent>; (3) an invariant Key<List<String>> that carries typeOf<List<String>>() (1) MutableList<Payment>; (2) handlers cast to (PaymentEvent) -> Unit; (3) Key<out List<String>> (1) MutableList<in Payment>; (2) a Map<String, Any> of handlers; (3) the class List::class as the key (1) MutableList<*>; (2) Consumer<CardAuthorized> in a raw list; (3) the string "currencies" Reading while still allowing clear() is an out-projection. Handlers consume, so a general handler fits, but storing a specific one needs an adapter rather than a cast. A key decides what may be written, so it must be invariant, and a KType keeps List<String> apart from other types with the same name. The other options each repeat a mistake from this track: in for reading, unchecked handler casts, an out write key, class keys for generic types, raw types and string keys.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · A cast from Any fails in the wrong place
x: Before generics, a container that could hold anything held Object in Java and Any in Kotlin. You put a value in, and you cast it back when you took it out. Here is a small settings holder written that way: Java class AnyBox { Object value; AnyBox(Object v) { value = v; } } static void configure(AnyBox box) { box.value = 978; // bug: the numeric code, not "EUR" } static String currencyLabel(AnyBox box) { String code = (String) box.value; // ClassCastException here return "Settles in " + code; } Kotlin class AnyBox(var value: Any) fun configure(box: AnyBox) { box.value = 978 // bug: the numeric code, not "EUR" } fun currencyLabel(box: AnyBox): String { val code = box.value as String // ClassCastException here return "Settles in $code" } The bug is in configure. Someone stored the ISO numeric currency code 978 where the rest of the code expects the letters "EUR". The compiler accepts it, because an Int is an Any. configure returns normally. Nothing fails until currencyLabel runs, maybe hours later, in a class another team owns. The stack trace points at the cast in the reader. The writer is not in it at all. That is the real cost of Any plus casts. The type check still happens, but it happens late, at run time, and in the wrong place. The error shows up at the read. The bug is at the write. Generics move the check to the write. Give the box a type parameter and say what it holds: Java class Box<T> { T value; Box(T v) { value = v; } } static void configure(Box<String> box) { box.value = 978; // now a compile error } Kotlin class Box<T>(var value: T) fun configure(box: Box<String>) { box.value = 978 // now a compile error } Both compilers now reject the bad line itself. javac says incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. kotlinc says: error: assignment type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'String' was expected. The reader needs no cast any more. box.value is already a String, so currencyLabel cannot throw a ClassCastException. The compiler messages in this track come from kotlinc 2.4.21. Gradle and IntelliJ print the same text with a capital first letter. Watch the cast fail far from the bug Run AnyBoxDemo with the command below (or its Java twin, AnyBoxDemoJava). Note which function the exception names. Make the box generic: change the class to class AnyBox<T>(var value: T) (Java: static class AnyBox<T> with a T value field), and change both functions to take AnyBox<String>. Leave main alone. Before you run it again, predict which line the compiler will reject. Then run it. Undo the change when you are done. AnyBoxDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l01.demo /** A settings box that holds Any. It compiles fine, and it fails far away from the bug. */ class AnyBox(var value: Any) // "module A": sets up the merchant's settlement currency fun configure(box: AnyBox) { box.value = 978 // the bug: the ISO numeric code instead of "EUR" } // "module B": reads the setting much later, in another class, maybe another team's code fun currencyLabel(box: AnyBox): String { val code = box.value as String // the cast fails HERE, not where 978 went in return "Settles in $code" } fun main() { val box = AnyBox("EUR") configure(box) println("configure() returned. Nothing has failed yet.") try { println(currencyLabel(box)) } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message}") println("thrown in: ${e.stackTrace.first()}") } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.AnyBoxDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l01/demo/AnyBoxDemo.kt AnyBoxDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l01.demo; /** Java twin of AnyBoxDemo.kt: a settings box that holds Object. It compiles, and fails far from the bug. */ public class AnyBoxDemoJava { static class AnyBox { Object value; AnyBox(Object value) { this.value = value; } } // "module A": sets up the merchant's settlement currency static void configure(AnyBox box) { box.value = 978; // the bug: the ISO numeric code instead of "EUR" } // "module B": reads the setting much later, in another class, maybe another team's code static String currencyLabel(AnyBox box) { String code = (String) box.value; // the cast fails HERE, not where 978 went in return "Settles in " + code; } public static void main(String[] args) { AnyBox box = new AnyBox("EUR"); configure(box); System.out.println("configure() returned. Nothing has failed yet."); try { System.out.println(currencyLabel(box)); } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("ClassCastException: " + e.getMessage()); System.out.println("thrown in: " + e.getStackTrace()[0]); } } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.AnyBoxDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l01/demo/AnyBoxDemoJava.java The first run prints configure() returned. Nothing has failed yet. and then ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String, thrown in currencyLabel. The function with the bug is not in the trace. After the change the build stops at compile time on box.value = 978: Kotlin says Assignment type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'String' was expected., javac says incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. The check moved from the reader to the writer. An Any box is an unlabeled crate in a warehouse. Anyone can put anything in it, and you find out what is inside when you open it at the far end of the building. A Box<String> is a crate with a label, and the loading dock refuses anything that does not match the label. You stop the wrong item at the door instead of at the other end. The analogy breaks in one place: a real label travels with the crate. On the JVM the label is removed after the loading dock, so the check happens at compile time only and the running program cannot read it.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · A type parameter is a blank the caller fills in
x: Read class Box<T> as: "Box has one blank in it, called T. Whoever uses Box fills the blank with a real type." T is the type parameter. The real type you put in, like String in Box<String>, is the type argument. Inside the class, T stands for whatever the caller chose. The class never finds out which one. Java class Box<T> { T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T replace(T newValue) { T old = value; value = newValue; return old; } } Box<String> currency = new Box<>("EUR"); Box<Long> limit = new Box<>(50_000L); currency.replace("USD"); // fine limit.replace("USD"); // error: String cannot be converted to Long Kotlin class Box<T>(var value: T) { fun replace(newValue: T): T { val old = value value = newValue return old } } val currency = Box("EUR") // Box<String> val limit = Box(50_000L) // Box<Long> currency.replace("USD") // fine limit.replace("USD") // error: actual type is 'String', but 'Long' was expected One class gives you many types: Box<String>, Box<Long>, Box<Payment>. The compiler checks each one on its own. To the compiler, Box<String> and Box<Long> are as different as String and Long. How does it check limit.replace("USD")? It substitutes. limit is a Box<Long>, so the compiler reads every T in Box as Long. For that call, replace is replace(newValue: Long): Long, and a String doesn't fit. Fill in the blank, then check the call as if the class had been written for Long all along. Do that in your head and you can predict any call on a generic class before the compiler does. Functions can have type parameters too. In Java the <T> goes before the return type. In Kotlin it goes right after fun, before the function name: Java static <T> T firstOrNull(List<T> items) { return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(0); } Kotlin fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T? = if (items.isEmpty()) null else items[0] <T> declares the blank. List<T> and T? use it, and the two uses are tied together. Pass a List<Payment> and you get a Payment? back, with no cast. Pass a List<String> and you get a String?. A function can have several type parameters, separated by commas: fun <T, K> indexBy(items: List<T>, key: (T) -> K): Map<K, T>. The single-letter names are a habit, not a rule: T for type, E for element, K and V for key and value, R for result. A method can also have a type parameter that its class does not have. In fun <C> mapSecond(f: (B) -> C): Duo<A, C> on a class Duo<A, B>, A and B belong to the class. C belongs to this one call, and the lambda you pass decides what it is. One fact to keep for later. At run time there is only one Box class. The <String> part exists for the compiler, and the JVM never sees it. Lesson 8 of this track, on type erasure, shows what that costs you. Fill the blank, then break it Run BoxDemo (or BoxDemoJava) with the command below to see it work. Uncomment the three wrong moves at the bottom of main, one at a time. For each one, write down the error you expect before you run. For the last one, decide how you would fix it without changing firstOrNull. BoxDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l01.demo /** One class with one blank, T. Each use fills the blank with a real type. */ class Box<T>(var value: T) { /** Puts [newValue] in and returns the old value. Both have type T. */ fun replace(newValue: T): T { val old = value value = newValue return old } } /** A generic function: <T> declares the blank, List<T> and T? use it. */ fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T? = if (items.isEmpty()) null else items[0] fun main() { val currency = Box("EUR") // Box<String> val limit = Box(50_000L) // Box<Long> val old = currency.replace("USD") println("currency was $old, now ${currency.value}") println("limit is ${limit.value}") println("first payment id: ${firstOrNull(listOf("pay_1", "pay_2"))}") // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // limit.replace("USD") // val wrong: Box<String> = Box(42) // val id: String = firstOrNull(listOf("pay_1")) } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.BoxDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l01/demo/BoxDemo.kt BoxDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l01.demo; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of BoxDemo.kt: one class with one blank, T. */ public class BoxDemoJava { static class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } /** Puts newValue in and returns the old value. Both have type T. */ T replace(T newValue) { T old = value; value = newValue; return old; } } /** A generic method: <T> before the return type declares the blank. */ static <T> T firstOrNull(List<T> items) { return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(0); } public static void main(String[] args) { Box<String> currency = new Box<>("EUR"); // diamond: javac infers <String> Box<Long> limit = new Box<>(50_000L); String old = currency.replace("USD"); System.out.println("currency was " + old + ", now " + currency.get()); System.out.println("limit is " + limit.get()); System.out.println("first payment id: " + firstOrNull(List.of("pay_1", "pay_2"))); // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // limit.replace("USD"); // Box<String> wrong = new Box<>(42); // String id = firstOrNull(List.<String>of()); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.BoxDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l01/demo/BoxDemoJava.java limit.replace("USD") gives Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'String', but 'Long' was expected. The Box line gives Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Box<String>', actual 'Box<Int>'. The last one gives expected 'String', actual 'String?': firstOrNull returns T?, so with T = String you get a String?. Declare id as String?, or add a default with ?: "none". In the Java twin the first two fail (String cannot be converted to Long, cannot infer type arguments for Box<>), and the third compiles: Java has no T?, so it hands you a null without warning. You write one generic class. The compiler checks each filled-in version as its own type. The JVM runs a single class. Payment services collect untyped bags: a Map<String, Any> of payment metadata, Kafka record headers read as bytes, a JSON blob from the card issuer parsed into a map. Every as String or as Long on a read is a place where a ClassCastException can show up far from the code that wrote the value. When you own the type, give it a type parameter or a real class (data class PaymentMetadata(val merchantId: String, val retries: Int)). When you do not own it, convert once at the edge, in the Kafka deserializer or the HTTP client, so everything behind that line is typed. The Kafka client already does this for you: a ConsumerRecord<String, PaymentEvent> hands you a typed value.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Inference fills in most type arguments for you
x: You rarely write type arguments in Kotlin. The compiler works them out from the values you pass. This is type inference, and Java does it too, with var and the diamond. Java var amounts = List.of(1200, 350, 99); // List<Integer> var box = new Box<>("EUR"); // Box<String> var fees = Map.of("EUR", 100, "USD", 250L); // Map<String, Number & Comparable<...> & ...> Kotlin val amounts = listOf(1200, 350, 99) // List<Int> val box = Box("EUR") // Box<String> val fees = mapOf("EUR" to 100, "USD" to 250L) // Map<String, Long> Look at the last line in each. Kotlin sees 250L in the same map and makes the literal 100 a Long, so both values fit Long. Java never changes a literal's type: 100 stays an Integer, and javac infers a long intersection type for the values instead. When the values really have different types, the compiler picks the closest type they share: Java var mixed = List.of(1, 2.5); // List<Number & Comparable<...> & Constable & ConstantDesc> var odd = List.of(1, "a"); // another intersection, of Serializable, Comparable and more Kotlin val mixed = listOf(1, 2.5) // List<Number & Comparable<*>> val odd = listOf(1, "a") // List<Comparable<*> & Serializable> Number & Comparable<*> is an intersection type: something that is both a Number and a Comparable. You cannot write that type in your own code, but the compiler uses it. When you see one, you have usually mixed types by accident. Sometimes there is nothing to infer from. emptyList() gets no values, so Kotlin has no clue what T should be: error: cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly. Java does not complain here. var none = Collections.emptyList(); quietly becomes a List<Object>, which is rarely what you meant. In both languages the fix is the same. Write the type argument at the call, or give the variable a type and let the compiler work backwards from it: Java var none = Collections.<String>emptyList(); List<String> alsoNone = Collections.emptyList(); Kotlin val none = emptyList<String>() val alsoNone: List<String> = emptyList() Each pair means the same thing. I use the first form inside expressions and the second for properties, where the declared type documents the API anyway. Kotlin builders infer too. buildList { add("idem_1"); add("idem_2") } is a List<String>, worked out from the add calls inside the lambda. Java has no such builder, so there you name the type up front: new ArrayList<String>(). Here is a trick you will use for the rest of this track. When you are not sure what the compiler inferred, assign the value to a type you know is wrong, such as val probe: Int = mixed in Kotlin or int probe = mixed; in Java. The error message prints the real type. Make the compiler tell you the type Open InferenceDemo.kt. For each of the six values, write down the type you think the compiler inferred. Uncomment probe1 only and run the demo. The build fails, and the message prints the inferred type. Comment it out again. Repeat for probe2 to probe6, one at a time. Count how many you predicted right. InferenceDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l01.demo /** * Make the compiler tell you what it inferred. Each probe assigns a value to an Int, * which is wrong on purpose. The error message prints the real, inferred type. * Uncomment ONE probe at a time, run, read the message, comment it out again. */ fun main() { val amounts = listOf(1200, 350, 99) val mixed = listOf(1, 2.5) val tags = listOf("card", null) val fees = mapOf("EUR" to 100, "USD" to 250L) val keys = buildList { add("idem_1"); add("idem_2") } val none = emptyList<String>() // val probe1: Int = amounts // val probe2: Int = mixed // val probe3: Int = tags // val probe4: Int = fees // val probe5: Int = keys // val probe6 = emptyList() println("compiled: ${amounts.size + mixed.size + tags.size + fees.size + keys.size + none.size} values") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.InferenceDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l01/demo/InferenceDemo.kt InferenceDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * Java twin of InferenceDemo.kt. Make javac tell you what `var` inferred: assign the value to an int, * which is wrong on purpose. Uncomment ONE probe at a time, run, read the message, comment it out again. */ public class InferenceDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { var amounts = List.of(1200, 350, 99); var mixed = List.of(1, 2.5); var tags = Arrays.asList("card", null); var fees = Map.of("EUR", 100, "USD", 250L); var keys = new ArrayList<String>(); // Java has no buildList: say the type up front keys.add("idem_1"); keys.add("idem_2"); var none = Collections.emptyList(); // no error in Java: what did it pick? // int probe1 = amounts; // int probe2 = mixed; // int probe3 = tags; // int probe4 = fees; // int probe5 = keys; // int probe6 = none; System.out.println("compiled: " + (amounts.size() + mixed.size() + tags.size() + fees.size() + keys.size() + none.size()) + " values"); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.InferenceDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l01/demo/InferenceDemoJava.java The messages say actual 'List<Int>', 'List<Number & Comparable<*>>', 'List<String?>', 'Map<String, Long>' and 'List<String>'. probe6 gives Cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly. Most people miss Map<String, Long> and the intersection type on the first try. The Java twin prints List<Integer>, List<INT#1> (javac's name for an intersection), List<String>, Map<String,INT#1> and ArrayList<String>, and probe6 shows List<Object>: Java picked Object for the empty list without a word.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Java says the same thing with different punctuation
x: Java has had generics since Java 5, and Kotlin compiles to the same JVM machinery. The ideas map one to one. Only the punctuation moves. Java class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } } static <T> T firstOrNull(List<T> items) { return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(0); } Box<String> box = new Box<>("EUR"); // diamond List<String> none = Collections.emptyList(); // inferred from the target List<String> same = Collections.<String>emptyList(); // explicit type argument Kotlin class Box<T>(private var value: T) { fun get(): T = value } fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T? = if (items.isEmpty()) null else items[0] val box = Box("EUR") // no diamond, no new val none: List<String> = emptyList() // inferred from the target val same = emptyList<String>() // explicit type argument Three differences matter in practice. In a Java method, <T> comes before the return type: static <T> T firstOrNull(...). In Kotlin it comes before the function name. The meaning is the same. Java also has no nullable types, so its firstOrNull returns a plain T that may be null, while Kotlin's says T?. Java needs the diamond <> on new, which tells javac to infer the type argument. Leave it out and new Box("EUR") is a raw type: Box with its generics switched off. Kotlin has no new and no raw types, so Box("EUR") is always a Box<String>. Java type arguments must be reference types. List<int> is an error (unexpected type, required: reference, found: int), so you write List<Integer>. In Kotlin you write List<Int>, and the compiler stores boxed java.lang.Integer objects for you. Raw types are why old Java code can still blow up. They exist so that code from before Java 5 keeps compiling. A raw List accepts anything, and javac only warns: warning: [unchecked] unchecked call to add(E) as a member of the raw type List The bad value then sits inside a List<String> until someone reads it. Why does the read fail and not the add? At run time the list holds plain Object references, so add(42) has nothing to check against. Where your code reads an element as a String, javac adds a hidden cast to String, and that cast is what throws. Lesson 8 of this track shows that cast in the bytecode. It is the AnyBox failure again, hidden inside a type that claims to be safe. When a Kotlin service gets a ClassCastException on a line with no cast in it, look for a raw type in the Java library underneath. Let a raw type smuggle in an Integer Run RawTypeDemo with the command below. Look for javac's Note: line near the top of the Gradle output. Predict: does ids.add(42) fail, or does something later fail? Change the parameter of legacyAppend from List ids to List<String> ids and run it again. Then undo it. (The Kotlin twin has no raw type to remove: it switches the check off with an unchecked cast instead, and fails the same way.) RawTypeDemo.java package workbench.generics.l01.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** A raw type switches the checks off. The bad value goes in quietly and fails on the way out. */ public class RawTypeDemo { // "List" with no <...> is a raw type: javac stops checking what goes in static void legacyAppend(List ids) { ids.add(42); // compiles, with an unchecked warning } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(); // diamond: javac infers ArrayList<String> ids.add("pay_1001"); legacyAppend(ids); System.out.println("size = " + ids.size() + ", nothing failed yet"); try { for (String id : ids) { // javac inserted a (String) cast here System.out.println(id.toUpperCase()); } } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("ClassCastException: " + e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.RawTypeDemo labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l01/demo/RawTypeDemo.java RawTypeDemo.kt // Kotlin twin of RawTypeDemo.java. Kotlin has no raw types; the closest way to switch the checks off // is an unchecked cast. The bad value goes in quietly and fails on the way out, exactly as in Java. package workbench.generics.l01.demo // MutableList<*> means "a list of something"; the cast pretends it is a list of anything private fun legacyAppend(ids: MutableList<*>) { @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") (ids as MutableList<Any?>).add(42) // compiles; without @Suppress Kotlin warns } fun main() { val ids: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf() // Kotlin infers nothing here: the type is declared ids.add("pay_1001") legacyAppend(ids) println("size = ${ids.size}, nothing failed yet") try { for (id in ids) { // the compiler inserted a cast to String here println(id.uppercase()) } } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l01.demo.RawTypeDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l01/demo/RawTypeDemo.kt Gradle prints Note: ... RawTypeDemo.java uses unchecked or unsafe operations. The program prints size = 2, nothing failed yet and PAY_1001, then a ClassCastException for the Integer. The add worked; the failure comes in the loop, where javac inserted a hidden cast to String. With List<String> ids the build fails at ids.add(42) with incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. Raw types (The Java Tutorials) read The common mistake is choosing Any or Map<String, Any> "to keep it flexible" and casting on every read. People do it because it compiles, and the first version has one writer and one reader who agree. Six months later there are five writers, and one of them stores an Int. The fix is to put the type in the signature: a type parameter when the content varies (Box<T>, Cache<V>), or a small typed class when the shape is fixed. If the values really are of several kinds, use a sealed interface, not Any.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Java and Kotlin
x: One generic box and one generic function, in both languages Box.java import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } T replace(T newValue) { T old = value; value = newValue; return old; } // <T> before the return type static <T> T firstOrNull(List<T> items) { return items.isEmpty() ? null : items.get(0); } static void use() { Box<String> box = new Box<>("EUR"); // diamond infers <String> Box raw = new Box("EUR"); // raw type: checks off List<String> none = Collections.<String>emptyList(); List<Integer> ints = List.of(1, 2); // no List<int> } } Box.kt class Box<T>(var value: T) { fun replace(newValue: T): T { val old = value value = newValue return old } } // <T> before the function name fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T? = if (items.isEmpty()) null else items[0] fun use() { val box = Box("EUR") // Box<String>, no diamond needed // there is no raw Box: Box without <...> must be inferable or it does not compile val none = emptyList<String>() val ints: List<Int> = listOf(1, 2) // Int works; stored as java.lang.Integer } The model is the same: one class, type parameters checked at compile time, one runtime class. Kotlin infers the type argument from constructor arguments without a diamond, and it has no raw types, so the unchecked-warning escape hatch that Java keeps for old code does not exist. Kotlin also accepts Int as a type argument, while Java forces you to write Integer. Both compile to boxed objects. One more difference shows in firstOrNull: Kotlin's return type says T?, so callers must handle null. Java's T can be null without saying so.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Worked example
x: Make an idempotency cache generic A payment API caches the response for each idempotency key, so a retried request gets the same answer. The first version stores Any, and every caller casts. Find the two places a wrong type could get in or out. class IdempotencyCache { private val responses = HashMap<String, Any>() fun put(key: String, response: Any) { responses[key] = response } fun get(key: String): Any? = responses[key] } // caller val cached = cache.get(key) as AuthorizationResponse? // cast on every read class IdempotencyCache { private final Map<String, Object> responses = new HashMap<>(); void put(String key, Object response) { responses.put(key, response); } Object get(String key) { return responses.get(key); } } // caller AuthorizationResponse cached = (AuthorizationResponse) cache.get(key); // cast on every read Decide what varies. The key is always a String. The response type changes per endpoint: authorizations, refunds, captures. So the response type becomes the type parameter, and the key stays a plain String. class IdempotencyCache<R> { private val responses = HashMap<String, R>() fun put(key: String, response: R) { responses[key] = response } fun get(key: String): R? = responses[key] } class IdempotencyCache<R> { private final Map<String, R> responses = new HashMap<>(); void put(String key, R response) { responses.put(key, response); } R get(String key) { return responses.get(key); } // null when absent } Fill the blank at the use site. Each endpoint gets its own cache with its own type. The cast is gone, and a wrong put is now a compile error. val authCache = IdempotencyCache<AuthorizationResponse>() val cached: AuthorizationResponse? = authCache.get(key) // no cast authCache.put(key, RefundResponse("rf_1")) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'RefundResponse', // but 'AuthorizationResponse' was expected. var authCache = new IdempotencyCache<AuthorizationResponse>(); AuthorizationResponse cached = authCache.get(key); // no cast authCache.put(key, new RefundResponse("rf_1")); // error: incompatible types: RefundResponse cannot be converted to AuthorizationResponse Add a helper that computes on a miss. It uses the class's R, so it needs no <R> of its own. Stop and answer: what would go wrong if you wrote fun <R> getOrPut(...) here? (A new R on the function would hide the class's R, and responses[key] = value would no longer type-check. The same happens in Java with <R> R getOrPut(...).) fun getOrPut(key: String, compute: () -> R): R { responses[key]?.let { return it } val value = compute() responses[key] = value return value } R getOrPut(String key, Supplier<R> compute) { R cached = responses.get(key); if (cached != null) return cached; R value = compute.get(); responses.put(key, value); return value; }

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Quiz
x: Payment metadata is a MutableMap<String, Any>. A retry handler stores meta["retries"] = "3". A report later runs val n = meta["retries"] as Int. What happens? A compile error on the line that stores "3" A ClassCastException on the line that stores "3" A ClassCastException on the as Int line, when the report runs n is 3, because Kotlin converts the string A String is an Any, so the store compiles and runs. The cast in the report is the first check, and it fails there. Casts never convert values. A typed field such as retries: Int would have made the store a compile error. Given fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T?, what does the compiler say about val id: String? = firstOrNull(listOf(1, 2))? Initializer type mismatch: expected 'String?', actual 'Int?' It compiles, and id is null It compiles, and id is "1" It compiles, then throws ClassCastException T is inferred from the argument as Int, so the call returns Int?. That does not fit in a String?. The type parameter ties the input and the output together, which is the whole point. Nothing is converted at run time. val none = emptyList() does not compile. Which line fixes it? val none = emptyList<String>() val none: List<String> = emptyList() Either of the two above Neither: emptyList needs an argument The compiler needs to know T. You can give the type argument at the call, or give the variable a type and let inference work backwards from it. Both produce a List<String>. Java: List raw = new ArrayList(); raw.add(7); List<String> names = raw; String s = names.get(0); What happens? A compile error on raw.add(7) It compiles with unchecked warnings, then throws ClassCastException on the names.get(0) line It compiles, and s is "7" ArrayStoreException on raw.add(7) Raw types turn the checks off, so javac only warns. The Integer sits in the list until the read, where javac inserted a cast to String. The failure appears far from the line that caused it, the same as with Any. From the race conditions lesson: a Kafka consumer does if (!seen.contains(key)) { charge(m); seen.add(key) }, where seen is ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet<String>(). Two copies of one message arrive on two threads. What is the smallest fix? Make the field seen volatile Replace seen with a Collections.synchronizedSet Call charge only after seen.add(key) returned true: if (seen.add(key)) charge(m) Make seen a MutableSet<Any> so both copies fit This is check-then-act. Each set call is atomic, but two calls in a row are not. add checks and inserts in one step and returns false for the second copy, so only one thread charges. volatile and a synchronized wrapper leave the gap between the two calls.
