h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Key terms
x: Type parameter The placeholder in a declaration, like T in class Box<T>. Type argument The real type that fills a type parameter, like String in Box<String>. Generic function A function with its own type parameters, such as fun <T> firstOrNull(items: List<T>): T?. Type inference The compiler working out type arguments from the values and the expected type. Intersection type A type that is two types at once, like Number & Comparable<*>. Inferred by the compiler; you cannot write it yourself. Diamond Java's <> on new, asking javac to infer the type arguments. Raw type A Java generic type used without type arguments, like plain List. The compiler stops checking it. In class Box<T>, what is T? A type parameter: a blank that each user of Box fills with a real type, such as Box<String>. Where does a bad value stored in an Any field get caught? At the cast in the code that reads it, at run time. The stack trace points at the reader, not at the writer with the bug. val e = emptyList() gives what error? cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly. Fix: emptyList<String>() or val e: List<String> = emptyList(). Where does <T> go in a Kotlin generic function, and in a Java one? Kotlin: before the name, fun <T> first(xs: List<T>): T. Java: before the return type, static <T> T first(List<T> xs). What does Java's diamond in new ArrayList<>() do? It tells javac to infer the type argument from the target type. Without it, new ArrayList() is a raw type. What does listOf(1, 2.5) infer to? List<Number & Comparable<*>>, an intersection type: the closest type that both Int and Double share. How do you see the type Kotlin inferred for x? Write val probe: Int = x. The compile error prints the actual type.

h: Generics from zero: type parameters · Go deeper
x: Two inference tools are worth knowing. A _ type argument lets you give some type arguments and infer the rest. If a function has two type parameters and only one can be inferred, write _ for the one the compiler can work out: runner.run<CardGateway, _>(). The Kotlin generics page has the full example. You can also widen a type on purpose. listOf(1, "a") infers an intersection type that you cannot name. If you really want a list of anything, say so: listOf<Any>(1, "a"). Now the type is List<Any> and it reads honestly in code review. One Java detail: the explicit type argument goes after the dot, Collections.<String>emptyList(), and it needs a receiver. Inside the same class you must write this.<String>helper() or MyClass.<String>helper(). In Java 8 and later you rarely need it, because target typing infers the argument from the variable you assign to. Finally, Kotlin's List<Int> holds java.lang.Integer objects, so a list of a million ints costs a million small objects. When that matters, use IntArray, which is a real int[].

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · An unbounded T can do only what Any? can do
x: A type parameter with no bound means "some type, I don't know which". So inside the function, T can do only what every type can do. In Java the default bound is Object. In Kotlin, "every type" includes the nullable ones, so the default bound is Any?. Java static <T> String describe(T x) { return "value=" + x + ", hash=" + Objects.hashCode(x); } describe("EUR"); // fine describe(978); // fine describe(null); // fine: any Java T accepts null Kotlin fun <T> describe(x: T): String = "value=$x, hash=${x.hashCode()}" describe("EUR") // fine describe(978) // fine describe(null) // also fine: T is inferred as Nothing? toString(), hashCode() and == work, because they exist on Any?. Anything more specific fails, even when every caller you have in mind would pass a String: Java static <T> int lengthOf(T x) { return x.length(); } // error: cannot find symbol: method length() Kotlin fun <T> lengthOf(x: T) = x.length // error: unresolved reference 'length'. The compiler is not being fussy. Someone could call lengthOf(42), and an Int has no length. A generic function must work for every type the caller is allowed to pick, so you can use only what all of them share. Comparison fails the same way. Java says cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T). Kotlin gives a stranger message: Java static <T> T bigger(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } // error: cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T) Kotlin fun <T> bigger(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b // error: candidate 'fun String.compareTo(other: String, ignoreCase: Boolean = ...): Int' // is inapplicable because of a receiver type mismatch. In Kotlin a > b means a.compareTo(b). The compiler looks for any compareTo it could use on a T, finds only the one on String, and tells you that one doesn't fit. When an error mentions some unrelated type's method, read it as "this operation is not defined for T". The null case surprises people coming from Java, where every T accepts null anyway and nobody thinks about it. In Kotlin, fun <T> f(x: T) accepts null too, because T can be String? or Nothing?. (Nothing? is the type Kotlin gives a bare null. Write val x = null, then val y: Int = x, and the error says actual 'Nothing?'.) Even an extension like fun <T> T.describe() can be called on null. If your function must not see null, you have to say so with a bound. Section 4 shows how. So the job of a bound is to promise more about T. The caller can pick fewer types, and in return your code can do more with the one they pick. Find the edge of an unbounded T Run UnboundedDemo (or UnboundedDemoJava). Note what describe(null) prints. Uncomment lengthOf, run, and read the error. Comment it out again. Uncomment bigger and run. Before you read the message, guess which type it will mention. UnboundedDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l02.demo /** An unbounded T is "some type, maybe nullable". You may only use what every type has. */ fun <T> describe(x: T): String = "value=$x, hash=${x.hashCode()}" // toString and hashCode work on Any? // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // fun <T> lengthOf(x: T) = x.length // fun <T> bigger(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b fun main() { println(describe("EUR")) println(describe(978)) println(describe(null)) // T is inferred as Nothing?, and null is allowed } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.UnboundedDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l02/demo/UnboundedDemo.kt UnboundedDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l02.demo; /** Java twin of UnboundedDemo.kt. An unbounded T is "some type": only Object's methods are available. */ public class UnboundedDemoJava { static <T> String describe(T x) { return "value=" + x + ", hash=" + java.util.Objects.hashCode(x); // Object's methods only } // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // static <T> int lengthOf(T x) { return x.length(); } // static <T> T bigger(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(describe("EUR")); System.out.println(describe(978)); System.out.println(describe(null)); // any Java T accepts null } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.UnboundedDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l02/demo/UnboundedDemoJava.java describe(null) prints value=null, hash=0: null is a legal T. lengthOf fails with Unresolved reference 'length'. bigger fails with a message about String.compareTo being inapplicable, because the only compareTo the compiler could find is String's. Neither error is about your callers. Both say T promises nothing beyond Any?. The Java twin fails both with cannot find symbol: Java's T promises nothing beyond Object. A bound is like the requirements line on a job posting. "Any person" (no bound) gets you many applicants, but you can't ask any of them to drive the van. "Must hold a driving licence" (an upper bound) shuts some people out, and in exchange you can hand the keys to whoever turns up. Two requirements (a where clause) shrink the pool to people who have both. The analogy breaks in one place: a real employer can interview the candidate and check. The compiler can only trust what the types declare. A class that happens to have a length method but does not implement CharSequence does not count.

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · An upper bound says what T must be
x: An upper bound says "T must be this type or a subtype of it". Java writes it with extends, even for interfaces. Kotlin writes it after a colon: Java static <T extends Comparable<T>> T maxOf2(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } maxOf2(1_200, 99); // 1200 maxOf2("EUR", "USD"); // USD Kotlin fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b maxOf2(1_200, 99) // 1200 maxOf2("EUR", "USD") // USD maxOf2(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 30)) Read T : Comparable<T> aloud as "T is something that can be compared with another T". Int is a Comparable<Int>, String is a Comparable<String> and LocalDate is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>. Kotlin accepts that last one because Comparable is declared in T, which lesson 5 of this track explains. Inside the function, a > b now compiles, because the bound guarantees a compareTo. The bound also rejects bad calls at the call site: Java maxOf2(1, "a"); // error: method maxOf2 cannot be applied to given types record Payment(String id, long cents) {} maxOf2(new Payment("pay_1", 500), new Payment("pay_2", 900)); // error: ... inference variable T has incompatible bounds // upper bounds: Comparable<T> lower bounds: Payment Kotlin maxOf2(1, "a") // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'String', but 'Int' was expected. data class Payment(val id: String, val cents: Long) maxOf2(Payment("pay_1", 500), Payment("pay_2", 900)) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Payment', // but 'Comparable<uninferred T (of fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2)>' was expected. The first call fails because the two arguments must be the same T. The second fails because Payment has no natural order. Should a payment compare by amount, by time or by id? The compiler won't guess. Make Payment implement Comparable<Payment> and the call compiles. Or, usually better, keep Payment plain and pass a Comparator where you need an order. The T appears twice in T : Comparable<T>, and that is on purpose. Comparable<T> says what T can be compared with. This is called a recursive bound, and it is the most common bound in practice. You'll see it again in Enum<E : Enum<E>> and in builder classes in lesson 10 of this track. The two compilers word their errors differently, but they say the same thing: Payment is not within the bound. One real difference shows up with LocalDate. In Java, LocalDate d = maxOf2(day1, day2) fails, because the strict bound forces T to be ChronoLocalDate. The JDK writes <T extends Comparable<? super T>> to fix that. Kotlin's plain T : Comparable<T> already returns a LocalDate. Bound T, then make Payment fit Run MaxDemo (or MaxDemoJava) and check the three results. Uncomment the maxOf2(1, "a") line, run, read the error, and comment it out. Uncomment the Payment line and run it. Then make Payment implement Comparable<Payment> by cents (override fun compareTo(other: Payment) = cents.compareTo(other.cents)) and run again. MaxDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l02.demo import java.time.LocalDate /** The bound T : Comparable<T> means "T can be compared with another T", so > is allowed. */ fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T): T = if (a > b) a else b data class Payment(val id: String, val cents: Long) fun main() { println(maxOf2(1_200, 99)) println(maxOf2("EUR", "USD")) println(maxOf2(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 30))) // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // println(maxOf2(1, "a")) // println(maxOf2(Payment("pay_1", 500), Payment("pay_2", 900))) } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.MaxDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l02/demo/MaxDemo.kt MaxDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l02.demo; import java.time.LocalDate; /** Java twin of MaxDemo.kt. The bound T extends Comparable<T> makes compareTo available. */ public class MaxDemoJava { static <T extends Comparable<T>> T maxOf2(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } // the JDK's own style: LocalDate is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>, not a Comparable<LocalDate>, // so only this version can return a LocalDate static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T maxOf2Flexible(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } record Payment(String id, long cents) {} public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(maxOf2(1_200, 99)); System.out.println(maxOf2("EUR", "USD")); System.out.println(maxOf2Flexible(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 30))); // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // System.out.println(maxOf2(1, "a")); // System.out.println(maxOf2(new Payment("pay_1", 500), new Payment("pay_2", 900))); // LocalDate later = maxOf2(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 30)); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.MaxDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l02/demo/MaxDemoJava.java The demo prints 1200, USD and 2026-11-02. The mixed call fails with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'String', but 'Int' was expected. The Payment call fails with Cannot infer type for type parameter 'T' and actual type is 'Payment', but 'Comparable<uninferred T ...>' was expected. Once Payment is comparable, it prints Payment(id=pay_2, cents=900). In the Java twin both bad calls fail with method maxOf2 ... cannot be applied to given types, and its extra wrong move shows why the JDK writes Comparable<? super T>: LocalDate later = maxOf2(...) fails with inference variable T has incompatible bounds. Bounds show up wherever your services compare or key things. A settlement cut-off window over LocalDate or Instant is a Window<T : Comparable<T>>. A generic retry policy that sorts attempts by time needs a comparable timestamp. An in-memory cache in front of the card issuer API, or a store of idempotency responses, should be Cache<K : Any, V : Any>, so a null from get always means "miss" and never "we cached a null". When you call a Java library from Kotlin, its <T> allows null, so a Kotlin wrapper with T : Any is the place to pin that down.

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · Two bounds need a where clause
x: A type parameter can have more than one bound. Angle brackets hold only one, so the rest go into a where clause after the signature. Java joins the bounds with &: Java static <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>> T shortestLabel(List<T> items) { T best = items.get(0); for (T item : items) { if (item.length() < best.length()) best = item; // CharSequence gives length() else if (item.length() == best.length() && item.compareTo(best) < 0) best = item; } return best; } Kotlin fun <T> shortestLabel(items: List<T>): T where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> { var best = items[0] for (item in items) { if (item.length < best.length) best = item // CharSequence gives .length else if (item.length == best.length && item < best) best = item // Comparable gives < } return best } T must satisfy every bound at once. A String is both a CharSequence and a Comparable<String>, so it fits. An Int is comparable but has no characters: error: cannot infer type for type parameter 'T'. Specify it explicitly. error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'CharSequence' was expected. You get two errors for one mistake. The first says the compiler gave up looking for a T. The second says why: an Int is not a CharSequence, so no T can meet both bounds. When "cannot infer type" appears next to a mismatch, read the mismatch first. It is the real reason. Here is one that surprises people: shortestLabel(listOf(StringBuilder("iban"), StringBuilder("bic"))) compiles. Since JDK 11, StringBuilder implements Comparable<StringBuilder>, so it sits in the overlap too. At most one bound may be a class. The others must be interfaces, because a JVM class has one superclass. Java also wants the class first: Java static <T extends Number & Exception> void amountOrError(T t) {} // error: interface expected here static <T extends Number & Comparable<T>> T clampToZero(T x) { ... } // fine: class first static <T extends Comparable<T> & Number> T wrong(T x) { ... } // error: interface expected here Kotlin fun <T> amountOrError(t: T) where T : Number, T : Exception {} // error: only one of the upper bounds can be a class. fun <T> clampToZero(x: T): T where T : Number, T : Comparable<T> = x // fine fun <T> anyOrder(x: T): T where T : Comparable<T>, T : Number = x // also fine Kotlin has no ordering rule. It just counts classes. Use where when the function needs two abilities that no single type in your code names. If you find yourself writing the same pair of bounds in five places, that pair probably wants to be one interface. A MerchantCode type that is a CharSequence and Comparable might be better modelled with a single interface of your own. Predict which calls fit both bounds Before running WhereDemo (or WhereDemoJava), decide whether the StringBuilder line compiles. Run it. Then uncomment sortedLabel(42, 7) and run again. Comment that out and uncomment amountOrError. Run, read the error, and comment it out again. WhereDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l02.demo /** Two bounds at once: T must be a CharSequence AND Comparable to itself. */ fun <T> sortedLabel(a: T, b: T): String where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> = if (a < b) "$a (${a.length}) then $b (${b.length})" else "$b (${b.length}) then $a (${a.length})" fun main() { println(sortedLabel("SEPA", "ACH")) println(sortedLabel(StringBuilder("iban"), StringBuilder("bic"))) // does this compile? predict first // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // println(sortedLabel(42, 7)) // fun <T> amountOrError(t: T) where T : Number, T : Exception {} } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.WhereDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l02/demo/WhereDemo.kt WhereDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l02.demo; /** Java twin of WhereDemo.kt. Two bounds at once, written with &. */ public class WhereDemoJava { static <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>> String sortedLabel(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) < 0 ? a + " (" + a.length() + ") then " + b + " (" + b.length() + ")" : b + " (" + b.length() + ") then " + a + " (" + a.length() + ")"; } // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // static <T extends Comparable<T> & CharSequence & Number> void tooMany(T t) {} // static <T extends Number & Exception> void amountOrError(T t) {} public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(sortedLabel("SEPA", "ACH")); System.out.println(sortedLabel(new StringBuilder("iban"), new StringBuilder("bic"))); // compiles? predict first // System.out.println(sortedLabel(42, 7)); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.WhereDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l02/demo/WhereDemoJava.java The demo prints ACH (3) then SEPA (4) and bic (3) then iban (4): StringBuilder is both a CharSequence and a Comparable<StringBuilder> on JDK 11 and later. sortedLabel(42, 7) fails with Cannot infer type for type parameter 'T' and actual type is 'Int', but 'CharSequence' was expected. amountOrError fails with Only one of the upper bounds can be a class. In the Java twin, sortedLabel(42, 7) fails with cannot be applied to given types, and both bad bound lists fail with interface expected here. Each bound shrinks the set of types a caller may pick. A where clause with two bounds allows only the overlap.

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · T : Any keeps null out
x: The default bound is Any?, so T can be a nullable type. Most of the time that is what you want. A Box<String?> is a fine thing to have. Sometimes it quietly breaks your API. Look at this cache. The Java version has the same problem, because HashMap happily stores null values: Java class Cache<K, V> { private final Map<K, V> entries = new HashMap<>(); void put(K key, V value) { entries.put(key, value); } V get(K key) { return entries.get(key); } // null means "no entry"... usually } Cache<String, String> lastError = new Cache<>(); lastError.put("pay_1", null); // "checked, no error" lastError.get("pay_1"); // null lastError.get("pay_9"); // null, but never stored Kotlin class Cache<K, V> { private val entries = HashMap<K, V>() fun put(key: K, value: V) { entries[key] = value } fun get(key: K): V? = entries[key] // null means "no entry"... usually } val lastError = Cache<String, String?>() lastError.put("pay_1", null) // "checked, no error" lastError.get("pay_1") // null lastError.get("pay_9") // null, but never stored With V = String?, get returns null for two different reasons, and the caller cannot tell them apart. The fix is the bound T : Any, which means "any type, but not a nullable one". Java has no such bound, so the closest it gets is a check at run time: Java void put(K key, V value) { entries.put(key, Objects.requireNonNull(value, "no null values")); // fails at run time } Kotlin class Cache<K : Any, V : Any> { ... } Cache<String, String?>() // error: type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'V (of class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>)' // must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'. Now V? in get always means "absent", because a stored value can never be null. The same bound helps functions that must return a real value: Java @SafeVarargs static <T> T coalesce(T... values) { for (T v : values) if (v != null) return v; throw new IllegalArgumentException("all values were null"); } String currency = coalesce(null, "EUR", "USD"); // the type says nothing about null Kotlin fun <T : Any> coalesce(vararg values: T?): T { for (v in values) if (v != null) return v throw IllegalArgumentException("all values were null") } val currency: String = coalesce(null, "EUR", "USD") // String, not String? The parameters are T? and the return type is T, and that difference is only meaningful because T itself can't be nullable. Pass a bare null to a T : Any parameter and you get null cannot be a value of a non-null type. So the rule I use is simple. Put T : Any on a type parameter when null already has a job in your API, such as "not found". Leave the default when holding a nullable value is fine, as in a Box<String?>. Java types carry no nullability. <T> in Java always allows null, and the best you can do is a run-time check or an annotation like @NonNull, which Kotlin reads when it calls the Java code. Lesson 10 of this track shows a related Kotlin tool, T & Any, for the rare case where you need both a nullable T and a non-null version of it in one signature. Make a null mean one thing Run NullBoundDemo (or NullBoundDemoJava). Look at the two lines it prints for pay_1 and pay_9. Change the Kotlin class header to class Cache<K : Any, V : Any> and run again. Java has no such bound: in the Java twin, uncomment the requireNonNull line instead and see that it fails only when it runs. Fix main so it compiles. How would you now record "checked, no error"? (One answer: store an empty string, or better, a small sealed interface CheckResult.) NullBoundDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l02.demo /** A tiny cache. get() returns null for "no entry". Is that always true? */ class Cache<K, V> { private val entries = HashMap<K, V>() fun put(key: K, value: V) { entries[key] = value } fun get(key: K): V? = entries[key] } fun main() { // V = String? is allowed, because the default bound of V is Any? val lastError = Cache<String, String?>() lastError.put("pay_1", null) // "we checked, there was no error" println("pay_1 -> ${lastError.get("pay_1")}") // stored null println("pay_9 -> ${lastError.get("pay_9")}") // never stored println("Can you tell those two apart? Neither can the caller.") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.NullBoundDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l02/demo/NullBoundDemo.kt NullBoundDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l02.demo; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Objects; /** Java twin of NullBoundDemo.kt. Java has no T : Any, so null stays ambiguous unless you check at run time. */ public class NullBoundDemoJava { static class Cache<K, V> { private final Map<K, V> entries = new HashMap<>(); void put(K key, V value) { entries.put(key, value); } // HashMap accepts null values V get(K key) { return entries.get(key); } // null: absent, or a stored null? } public static void main(String[] args) { Cache<String, String> lastError = new Cache<>(); lastError.put("pay_1", null); // "we checked, there was no error" System.out.println("pay_1 -> " + lastError.get("pay_1")); // stored null System.out.println("pay_9 -> " + lastError.get("pay_9")); // never stored System.out.println("Can you tell those two apart? Neither can the caller."); // Java's closest fix is a run-time check. Uncomment, run, and see where it fails. // Objects.requireNonNull(null, "cached values must not be null"); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l02.demo.NullBoundDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l02/demo/NullBoundDemoJava.java The first run prints pay_1 -> null and pay_9 -> null: a stored null and a missing entry look the same. With the bound, Cache<String, String?>() no longer compiles: Type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'V (of class Cache<K : Any, V : Any>)' must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'. From then on, get returning null can only mean "not there". The common mistake is leaving a type parameter unbounded and then returning T? to mean "absent", as in fun get(key: K): V?. It works in every test, because nobody stores a null. Then a caller writes Cache<String, Instant?> to remember "we checked and found nothing", and get can no longer tell "missing" from "stored null". People make this mistake because the default bound is invisible. The fix is to write V : Any whenever null has a job in your API, and to model "checked, nothing found" as a real value, not as a stored null.

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · Java and Kotlin
x: Bounds in Java and Kotlin Bounds.java import java.util.List; class Bounds { // one bound: extends, even for an interface static <T extends Comparable<T>> T maxOf2(T a, T b) { return a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; } // two bounds with &: the class (if any) must come first static <T extends CharSequence & Comparable<T>> T shortest(List<T> items) { T best = items.get(0); for (T item : items) { if (item.length() < best.length()) best = item; } return best; } // no way to say "not null": T may always be null static <T> T firstOrThrow(List<T> items) { return items.get(0); // could be null } } Bounds.kt // one bound: a colon fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T): T = if (a >= b) a else b // two bounds: a where clause, in any order, at most one class fun <T> shortest(items: List<T>): T where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T> { var best = items[0] for (item in items) { if (item.length < best.length) best = item } return best } // T : Any rules out nullable type arguments fun <T : Any> firstOrThrow(items: List<T>): T = items[0] // never null The bounds mean the same thing in both languages and compile to the same JVM bounds. Kotlin uses a colon and a where clause and does not care about order; Java uses extends and & and wants the class first. The real difference is nullability. Kotlin's default bound is Any?, so you can opt out of null with T : Any. Java has no nullable types, so every Java T allows null and only annotations can say otherwise. One small surprise: javap shows Kotlin's T : Comparable<T> as <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, because Kotlin's Comparable is declared in T. Lesson 5 of this track explains that ? super.

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · Worked example
x: Build a settlement window that works for any comparable type Settlement runs between a cut-off start and end. You want one class for amounts, dates and times. Start without a bound and see what breaks. class Window<T>(val start: T, val endInclusive: T) { operator fun contains(value: T) = start <= value && value <= endInclusive // error: candidate 'fun String.compareTo(...)' is inapplicable // because of a receiver type mismatch. } class Window<T> { final T start, endInclusive; Window(T start, T endInclusive) { this.start = start; this.endInclusive = endInclusive; } boolean contains(T value) { return start.compareTo(value) <= 0 && value.compareTo(endInclusive) <= 0; // error: cannot find symbol: method compareTo(T) } } Ask for exactly the ability you use. The body only compares, so the bound is T : Comparable<T>. Now <= resolves to compareTo. class Window<T : Comparable<T>>(val start: T, val endInclusive: T) { init { require(start <= endInclusive) { "start $start is after end $endInclusive" } } operator fun contains(value: T): Boolean = start <= value && value <= endInclusive } class Window<T extends Comparable<? super T>> { final T start, endInclusive; Window(T start, T endInclusive) { if (start.compareTo(endInclusive) > 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("start is after end"); this.start = start; this.endInclusive = endInclusive; } boolean contains(T value) { return start.compareTo(value) <= 0 && value.compareTo(endInclusive) <= 0; } } Use it with types that already fit the bound. LocalDate and Instant are comparable out of the box, so are Int and String. Self-check: why does Window(1, "z") fail? (Both values must be the same T, and there is no single T that is a Comparable<T> for both.) val cutoff = Window(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 6)) LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 4) in cutoff // true val limits = Window(1_000L, 50_000L) 75_000L in limits // false var cutoff = new Window<>(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 2), LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 6)); cutoff.contains(LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 4)); // true (needs the ? super T form for LocalDate) var limits = new Window<>(1_000L, 50_000L); limits.contains(75_000L); // false Make your own type fit. A Money value with an explicit order is a better fit than raw Long cents, and the window needs no change at all. data class Money(val cents: Long) : Comparable<Money> { override fun compareTo(other: Money): Int = cents.compareTo(other.cents) } val refundable = Window(Money(100), Money(500_00)) Money(42_00) in refundable // true record Money(long cents) implements Comparable<Money> { public int compareTo(Money other) { return Long.compare(cents, other.cents); } } var refundable = new Window<>(new Money(100), new Money(500_00)); refundable.contains(new Money(42_00)); // true

Which call does NOT compile? maxOf2(3, 7) maxOf2("EUR", "USD") maxOf2(LocalDate.now(), LocalDate.MIN) maxOf2(Payment("a", 5), Payment("b", 9)) where Payment is a plain data class Int, String and LocalDate are all comparable. A second bound for the same T goes into a where clause. The first option declares a second type parameter called Comparable, which is not what you meant, and & is Java's spelling, not Kotlin's. A teammate writes class Cache<K, V> { fun get(key: K): V? }. Another teammate creates Cache<String, Instant?>. What problem appears? Putting Number second gives interface expected here. The comma form declares a second type parameter, and the colon is Kotlin syntax. h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · Key terms
x: Upper bound A limit on a type parameter: "T must be this type or a subtype of it", written T : Comparable<T>. Default bound Any?, the bound a Kotlin type parameter has when you write none. where clause The place for extra bounds on a type parameter: where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T>. Recursive bound A bound that mentions the parameter itself, like T : Comparable<T>: T can be compared with another T. T : Any A bound that rules out nullable type arguments. Multiple bounds (Java) Java's <T extends A & B>; the class, if any, must come first. What is the default upper bound of a Kotlin type parameter? Any?. So an unbounded T accepts nullable types, and fun <T> f(x: T) can be called with null. fun <T> lengthOf(x: T) = x.length gives what error? unresolved reference 'length'. An unbounded T only has the members of Any?. How do you say "T can be compared with another T"? <T : Comparable<T>> in Kotlin, <T extends Comparable<T>> in Java. How do you give one type parameter two bounds in Kotlin? A where clause: fun <T> f(x: T) where T : CharSequence, T : Comparable<T>. Why does where T : Number, T : Exception fail? only one of the upper bounds can be a class. A JVM type has one superclass; the other bounds must be interfaces. What does class Cache<K : Any, V : Any> buy you? Neither type argument can be nullable, so get(): V? returning null always means "no entry". In Java's <T extends A & B>, which must come first? The class, if there is one. Interfaces follow after &. Otherwise javac says interface expected here.

h: Bounds and constraints: upper bounds, where, T : Any · Go deeper
x: Why does javap show Kotlin's fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T) as <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T maxOf2(T, T)? Because Kotlin declares Comparable<in T>, and when Kotlin writes a Java signature for a parameter of an in type, it adds ? super. That is also why Kotlin accepts LocalDate, which is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate> and not a Comparable<LocalDate>. Java's own Collections.max shows how messy this gets without declaration-site variance: Java public static <T extends Object & Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends T> coll) Kotlin fun <T : Comparable<T>> Iterable<T>.max(): T The Object & part is there for backward compatibility: it keeps the erased signature returning Object, as it did before Java 5. The ? super T lets a List<LocalDate> through. The ? extends T lets a collection of a subtype through. Kotlin's version gets the same flexibility from in and out declared once on Comparable and Iterable. Lessons 4 to 6 of this track build up to reading that Java signature with ease. One more bound rule: a type parameter bounded by another type parameter can't have extra bounds. fun <T, U> f(u: U) where U : T, U : Comparable<U> gives type parameter cannot have any other bounds if it's bounded by another type parameter.

h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · A class is not a type
x: String is a class. String and String? are two types. That difference is the whole lesson. A class is code: a declaration that exists at run time and that the JVM loads. A type is what the compiler checks: it says which values a variable may hold and which calls are allowed on it. Every class gives you at least two types, the plain one and the nullable one. A generic class gives you as many types as there are type arguments: List<String>, List<Int>, List<Payment?>, List<List<String>>. The two words have two matching relations, and they are not the same. Subclassing is about classes. CardPayment : Payment means the class CardPayment inherits from Payment. It is a fact about declarations. Subtyping is about types. A is a subtype of B when a value of type A can be used anywhere a B is expected, and nothing can go wrong. That is the substitution principle, and it is the test the compiler applies on every assignment and every argument. Usually the two agree. CardPayment is a subclass of Payment, and the type CardPayment is a subtype of the type Payment. Here are two cases where they come apart. The first one exists only in Kotlin, because Java types say nothing about null: Java String sure = "EUR"; String maybe = sure; // Java has no String?: every String may be null String back = maybe; // compiles, and may hand you a null later Kotlin val sure: String = "EUR" val maybe: String? = sure // fine: String is a subtype of String? val back: String = maybe // error: expected 'String', actual 'String?' There is only one class here, yet one type is a subtype of the other. A String can stand in for a String?, because a String? variable is allowed to hold a string. The reverse fails, because the value might be null. The second case is the classic one. MutableList<String> and MutableList<Any> share a class, and the JVM can't tell them apart. ids.javaClass == amounts.javaClass is true for a list of ids and a list of amounts. Even MutableList::class == List::class is true, because both are the JVM interface java.util.List. The difference between those types lives only in the compiler. The next section shows that the compiler has a very good reason to keep them apart. One class, many types Run ClassVsTypeDemo (or ClassVsTypeDemoJava) with the command below and read the comparisons. Uncomment val narrowed: String = maybe. Predict the error, then run. Comment it out and uncomment String?::class. Why can't a class literal be nullable? ClassVsTypeDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l03.demo /** Classes are what exists at run time. Types are what the compiler checks. They are not the same thing. */ fun main() { val ids: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf("pay_1") val amounts: MutableList<Int> = mutableListOf(1200) // the JVM sees one class for both lists println("same runtime class: ${ids.javaClass == amounts.javaClass} (${ids.javaClass.name})") // Kotlin's List and MutableList are one JVM interface, java.util.List println("MutableList::class == List::class: ${MutableList::class == List::class}") println("MutableList::class.java: ${MutableList::class.java}") // String and String? are two types of one class val maybe: String? = ids.firstOrNull() val sure: String = "EUR" val widened: String? = sure // String is a subtype of String?: always fine println("String? holds '$maybe', widened from String holds '$widened'") // Wrong moves. Uncomment ONE at a time, predict the error, then run. // val narrowed: String = maybe // val k = String?::class } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l03.demo.ClassVsTypeDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l03/demo/ClassVsTypeDemo.kt ClassVsTypeDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l03.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ClassVsTypeDemo.kt. The narrowing fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'String', actual 'String?'. The class literal fails with Type in a class literal cannot be nullable.: ? belongs to the type, and a class literal names a class. In the Java twin, the narrowing compiles (Java has no String?), and Class<List<String>> k = List.class fails with Class<List> cannot be converted to Class<List<String>>: a class literal never carries type arguments. Think of a shelf labeled "fruit". If I hand you a shelf of apples and you only take things off it, calling it a fruit shelf is honest: everything you take is fruit. If you are also allowed to put things on it, you might put a banana on my apple shelf, and the next person who expects an apple gets a banana. Read-only shelves can be relabeled upwards; read-write shelves can't. Java arrays are a shelf with a guard who checks every item you put on it and shouts when it is wrong. The analogy breaks at the label: on the JVM, a List's label is gone at run time, so there is no guard to shout, and the compiler has to stop you before the program runs.

h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · MutableList is not a MutableList
x: MutableList is not a MutableList : one list, two names, a crash on the read Here is the question the compiler asks. If it let you use a MutableList<String> where a MutableList<Any> is expected, could anything go wrong? Run the substitution test. Java asks the same question about List<String> and List<Object>: Java List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay_1")); List<Object> anything = ids; // suppose this compiled anything.add(42); // legal on a List<Object> String second = ids.get(1); // ClassCastException Kotlin val ids: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf("pay_1") val anything: MutableList<Any> = ids // suppose this compiled anything.add(42) // legal on a MutableList<Any> val second: String = ids[1] // ClassCastException anything and ids are the same list object. Through the Any view you can add an Int, and through the String view someone reads it as a String. So both compilers refuse the second line. javac says incompatible types: List<String> cannot be converted to List<Object>, and kotlinc says: error: initializer type mismatch: expected 'MutableList<Any>', actual 'MutableList<String>'. This rule is called invariance. MutableList<A> is a subtype of MutableList<B> only when A and B are the same type. It does not matter that String is a subtype of Any. The subtype arrow between the elements does not carry over to the lists. Every Java generic type is invariant in the same way. You can force the assignment anyway: in Java through a raw type, (List<Object>) (List<?>) ids, and in Kotlin with an unchecked cast, ids as MutableList<Any>. Kotlin warns with unchecked cast of 'MutableList<String>' to 'MutableList<Any>' and then does exactly what you asked. The 42 goes in, and the failure turns up later, on a read, as a ClassCastException in code that has no cast. That is the same late failure as lesson 1 of this track, and this time you switched off the compiler on purpose. Invariance annoys people in practice. You have a MutableList<CardPayment> and a function that takes MutableList<Payment>, and the call does not compile. The fix is never the cast. Ask what the function does with the list. If it only reads, it should take a List<Payment> (the last section explains why that works). If it adds, the compiler just caught a bug: it could have added a BankTransfer to your list of card payments. Switch off the guard and watch it fail Uncomment the step 1 line in InvarianceDemo (or InvarianceDemoJava) and run. Read the error, then comment it out again. Run the demo as it is. It forces the same assignment with an unchecked cast. Find the line that throws. Is it the line that added 42? The compiler refuses it. // val view: MutableList<Any> = ids // Step 2: force it with an unchecked cast. This compiles, with a warning. @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val anything = ids as MutableList<Any> anything.add(42) // fine for a MutableList<Any> println("ids has ${ids.size} elements, and nothing failed yet") try { val second: String = ids[1] // the compiler inserted a cast to String here println("second id: $second") } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l03.demo.InvarianceDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l03/demo/InvarianceDemo.kt InvarianceDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l03.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of InvarianceDemo.kt. What would go wrong if List<String> were a List<Object>? */ public class InvarianceDemoJava { @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay_1")); // Step 1: uncomment this line and run. javac refuses it. // List<Object> view = ids; // Step 2: force it through a raw type. This compiles, with an unchecked warning. The Java twin gives List<String> cannot be converted to List<Object> at step 1 and the same ClassCastException after the raw-type cast. Each arrow means "is a subtype of". A Kafka consumer collects a MutableList<CardAuthorized>, and a shared audit helper takes MutableList<PaymentEvent>: the call does not compile. Do not cast. If the helper only reads (it logs, sums or forwards events), change its parameter to List<PaymentEvent> and every caller works. h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · Java arrays said yes, and check every store at run time
x: Java made the other choice for arrays, back in Java 1.0. A String[] is an Object[]: Java String[] currencies = { "EUR", "USD" }; Object[] objects = currencies; // compiles: arrays are covariant objects[0] = 978; // compiles: an Integer is an Object // java.lang.ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer Kotlin val currencies: Array<String> = arrayOf("EUR", "USD") val objects: Array<Any> = currencies // error: initializer type mismatch: expected 'Array<Any>', actual 'Array<String>'. val forced = currencies as Array<Any> // a cast gets you there... forced[0] = 978 // ...and the same ArrayStoreException This is exactly the substitution that the previous section showed to be unsafe. Java allows it anyway and pays at run time. Every array remembers its element type, and the JVM checks every store into an array of references. When the value doesn't fit, it throws ArrayStoreException. The check costs a little on every store, and the error still comes at run time, possibly in a library far from the code that widened the array. That is why the rule is the way it is. An array knows its element type at run time, so the JVM can check late. A List<String> does not know its type argument at run time (lesson 8 of this track shows why), so nothing could check a late store. Java generics had to be invariant, and so are Kotlin's. Kotlin goes one step further and makes arrays invariant too, as the second snippet shows. Array<T> is a generic class like any other. So the ArrayStoreException can't happen in Kotlin code that uses Array<T>, unless you cast your way to it. If you really need to read an Array<Int> through an Array<Any> view, Kotlin has a safe way to say "read only", Array<out Any>, which lesson 6 of this track covers. You still meet covariant arrays from Kotlin, because Java APIs pass them around. Arrays.asList, varargs and toArray all hand out arrays whose runtime element type may be narrower than their static type. If a library writes into an Object[] you gave it, give it a real Object[]. Store an Integer into a String[] Run ArrayStoreDemo. Before it runs, predict whether objects[0] = 978 compiles and whether it runs. Uncomment List<Object> objectList = names; and run again. Compare the two answers Java gives. Run the Kotlin twin, ArrayStoreDemo.kt, then uncomment its val refused line. What did Kotlin need before it could fall into the same trap? ArrayStoreDemo.java package workbench.generics.l03.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java arrays are covariant, so the JVM must check every store. Java generics are invariant instead. */ public class ArrayStoreDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { String[] currencies = { "EUR", "USD" }; Object[] objects = currencies; // compiles: a String[] is an Object[] try { objects[0] = 978; // compiles too: an Integer is an Object System.out.println("stored 978"); } catch (ArrayStoreException e) { System.out.println("ArrayStoreException: " + e.getMessage()); } List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("EUR")); // Step 2: uncomment the next line and run. javac refuses it. // List<Object> objectList = names; System.out.println("currencies[0] is still " + currencies[0]); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l03.demo.ArrayStoreDemo labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l03/demo/ArrayStoreDemo.java ArrayStoreDemo.kt // Kotlin twin of ArrayStoreDemo.java. Kotlin arrays are invariant, so you need a cast to reach // the same trap. Once you do, the JVM's store check fires exactly as it does for Java. package workbench.generics.l03.demo fun main() { val currencies: Array<String> = arrayOf("EUR", "USD") // Step 2: uncomment the next line and run. Kotlin refuses it: arrays are invariant. // val refused: Array<Any> = currencies val objects = currencies as Array<Any> // forced: at run time a String[] really is an Object[] try { objects[0] = 978 // compiles: an Int is an Any println("stored 978") } catch (e: ArrayStoreException) { println("ArrayStoreException: ${e.message}") } println("currencies[0] is still ${currencies[0]}") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l03.demo.ArrayStoreDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l03/demo/ArrayStoreDemo.kt It prints ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer and then currencies[0] is still EUR: the array refused the store at run time. The list line does not compile: incompatible types: List<String> cannot be converted to List<Object>. Arrays check late, generics check early. The Kotlin twin prints the same ArrayStoreException, but only after a cast: its val refused: Array<Any> = currencies line fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Array<Any>', actual 'Array<String>'. h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · Why a read-only List is a List
x: After two sections of "no", here is a "yes" that seems to break the rule. Java needs a wildcard to say it: a ? in the angle brackets, which means "some type I don't name". Kotlin says it with a plain List<Any>: Java List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay_1")); List<? extends Object> view = ids; // compiles: a read-only view, spelled at the use site Kotlin val ids: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf("pay_1") val view: List<Any> = ids // compiles Run the substitution test again, on Kotlin's read-only List. What can a caller do with a List<Any>? Read elements, as Any. Ask the size. Iterate. There is no add and no set. Every element of a List<String> really is an Any, so every read through the Any view tells the truth. Nothing can go wrong, so the compiler allows it. That is the whole idea behind covariance: when a type only hands values out and never takes them in, its subtype arrow can follow the element type. Kotlin's List is declared as List<out E>, and the out is the promise that E only comes out. Lesson 4 of this track is about writing that promise yourself. Notice what view does not let you do. javac rejects view.add(42) with int cannot be converted to CAP#1. CAP#1 is javac's name for the unknown type behind the ?, and no int is known to fit it. Kotlin's List has no add at all: view.add(42) // error: unresolved reference 'add' on receiver of type 'List<Any>'. The list object is still mutable. ids.add("pay_2") works, and view sees the new element. The List<Any> type only removes the ways to write through this reference. At run time List and MutableList are the same java.util.List, so all of this is checked at compile time and costs nothing. Java has no read-only List type, which is why Java code writes List<? extends Object> at each use instead. Lesson 6 of this track maps those wildcards onto Kotlin. You now have the three answers a generic type can give to "is C<String> a C<Any>?": yes (covariant, like List), no (invariant, like MutableList and every Java generic), and "yes, then fail at run time" (Java arrays). The rest of this track explains when each answer is safe and how you choose it. Predict four lines Open ReadOnlyListDemo (or ReadOnlyListDemoJava). For lines 1 to 4, write down "compiles" or "error" before you run anything. Uncomment each line on its own, run, and check your answer. Comment it out again before the next one. ReadOnlyListDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l03.demo /** Predict which lines compile. Uncomment ONE at a time and run. */ fun main() { val ms: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf("a") val ints: Array<Int> = arrayOf(1, 2) val la: List<Any> = ms // compiles: List is read-only and covariant println("as List<Any>: $la, first is a ${la[0]::class.simpleName}") // val ma: MutableList<Any> = ms // 1 // val anys: Array<Any> = ints // 2 // la.add(42) // 3 // val back: List<String> = la // 4 println("ints: ${ints.joinToString()}") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l03.demo.ReadOnlyListDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l03/demo/ReadOnlyListDemo.kt ReadOnlyListDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l03.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ReadOnlyListDemo.kt. Java has no read-only List type, so it writes the read-only view as ? extends. */ public class ReadOnlyListDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> ms = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a")); Integer[] ints = { 1, 2 }; List<? extends Object> view = ms; // compiles: a read-only view, spelled at the use site System.out.println("as List<? extends Object>: " + view + ", first is a " + view.get(0).getClass().getSimpleName()); // List<Object> ma = ms; // 1 // Object[] anys = ints; // 2 // view.add(42); // 3 // List<String> back = view; // 4 System.out.println("ints: " + ints[0] + ", " + ints[1]); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l03.demo.ReadOnlyListDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l03/demo/ReadOnlyListDemoJava.java All four fail. 1: expected 'MutableList<Any>', actual 'MutableList<String>' (invariant). 2: expected 'Array<Any>', actual 'Array<Int>' (Kotlin arrays are invariant). 3: Unresolved reference 'add' on receiver of type 'List<Any>' (read-only). 4: expected 'List<String>', actual 'List<Any>': covariance goes up the arrow, never down. The Java twin differs on line 2 only: Object[] anys = ints compiles, because Java arrays are covariant. Lines 3 and 4 fail with cannot be converted to CAP#1 and List<CAP#1> cannot be converted to List<String>. The usual mistake is reaching for as MutableList<Payment> (or a raw type in Java) when the compiler rejects a MutableList<CardPayment>. It compiles with an unchecked warning, works in the test, and lets the callee add a different subtype into a list the caller thinks is homogeneous. The ClassCastException turns up later, on a read with no cast in sight. The fix is to look at what the callee does: if it only reads, take List<Payment>; if it writes, keep the types apart or make the function generic over the element type.

h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · Java and Kotlin
x: Invariance and arrays in Java and Kotlin Variance.java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; class Variance { static void demo() { List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); // List<Object> objects = names; // error: invariant List<? extends Object> view = names; // OK: a read-only view, written at the use site Object first = view.isEmpty() ? null : view.get(0); String[] currencies = { "EUR" }; Object[] objects = currencies; // OK: arrays are covariant objects[0] = 978; // compiles, throws ArrayStoreException } } Variance.kt fun demo() { val names: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf() // val objects: MutableList<Any> = names // error: invariant val view: List<Any> = names // OK: List is declared List<out E> val first: Any? = view.firstOrNull() val currencies: Array<String> = arrayOf("EUR") // val objects: Array<Any> = currencies // error: Kotlin arrays are invariant val readOnly: Array<out Any> = currencies // OK: you can read, not write } Both languages make generic types invariant, for the same reason: the type argument is gone at run time, so a bad write could not be caught later. The differences are in the exceptions to that rule. Java made arrays covariant and checks each store at run time. Kotlin makes arrays invariant like everything else. For the safe read-only case, Java asks you to write a wildcard (List<? extends Object>) at every use, while Kotlin's List declares out once, so a plain List<Any> parameter already accepts a List<String>. Kotlin's List and MutableList are the same java.util.List at run time; the split exists only for the compiler.

h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · Worked example
x: Why a list of card payments won't go into addProcessingFee A settlement job builds a MutableList<CardPayment>. A shared helper adds a fee line to a batch. The call does not compile. Before reading on, run the substitution test yourself: what could the helper do to the caller's list? interface Payment { val cents: Long } data class CardPayment(override val cents: Long) : Payment data class FeePayment(override val cents: Long) : Payment fun addProcessingFee(batch: MutableList<Payment>) { batch.add(FeePayment(batch.sumOf { it.cents } / 100)) } val cards: MutableList<CardPayment> = mutableListOf(CardPayment(1_200)) addProcessingFee(cards) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MutableList<CardPayment>', // but 'MutableList<Payment>' was expected. interface Payment { long cents(); } record CardPayment(long cents) implements Payment {} record FeePayment(long cents) implements Payment {} static void addProcessingFee(List<Payment> batch) { batch.add(new FeePayment(batch.stream().mapToLong(Payment::cents).sum() / 100)); } List<CardPayment> cards = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new CardPayment(1_200))); addProcessingFee(cards); // error: incompatible types: List<CardPayment> cannot be converted to List<Payment> Imagine it compiled. The helper adds a FeePayment to the caller's list. The caller later reads cards[1] as a CardPayment and gets a ClassCastException. The compiler's "no" was right, and an unchecked cast would only hide it. Split reading from writing. Computing the fee only reads, so that part takes a read-only List<Payment> (Java: List<? extends Payment>), which accepts the list of card payments. Adding the fee line is a decision the caller makes, with the right list. fun processingFee(batch: List<Payment>): FeePayment = FeePayment(batch.sumOf { it.cents } / 100) val fee = processingFee(cards) // compiles: List is covariant val ledgerLines: MutableList<Payment> = mutableListOf() ledgerLines.addAll(cards) ledgerLines.add(fee) // a list that is allowed to hold both static FeePayment processingFee(List<? extends Payment> batch) { return new FeePayment(batch.stream().mapToLong(Payment::cents).sum() / 100); } FeePayment fee = processingFee(cards); // compiles: ? extends makes it a read-only view List<Payment> ledgerLines = new ArrayList<>(); ledgerLines.addAll(cards); ledgerLines.add(fee); Check the result against the figure: MutableList<CardPayment> points to List<CardPayment>, which points to List<Payment>. Every arrow is a read-only one. The only list that receives a FeePayment is declared to hold any Payment.

h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · Key terms
x: Class A declaration that exists at run time, such as String or ArrayList. Type What the compiler checks: a class plus its type arguments and nullability, such as List<String>?. Subtype A is a subtype of B when an A can be used anywhere a B is expected. Substitution test Ask: if I secretly hand over a C<A> where a C<B> is expected, can any allowed call go wrong? Invariant C<A> is a subtype of C<B> only when A and B are the same. MutableList and all Java generics. Covariant C<A> is a subtype of C<B> whenever A is a subtype of B. Kotlin's List, Java arrays. ArrayStoreException What the JVM throws when you store a value into an array whose real element type doesn't accept it. What is the difference between subclassing and subtyping? Subclassing is about classes: one declaration inherits from another. Subtyping is about types: an A can be used wherever a B is expected. Is String a subtype of String?, or the reverse? String is a subtype of String?. A String? might be null, so it can't stand in for a String. Why can't a MutableList<String> be used as a MutableList<Any>? Through the MutableList<Any> reference you could add an Int, and a reader of the original list would get a ClassCastException. What does Object[] o = new String[1]; o[0] = 1; do? Compiles (arrays are covariant), then throws ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer at the store. Is a Kotlin Array<Int> an Array<Any>? No. Kotlin arrays are invariant: initializer type mismatch: expected 'Array<Any>', actual 'Array<Int>'. Why is a Kotlin List<String> a List<Any>? Read-only List has no add or set, so reading strings as Any can never go wrong. It is declared List<out E>. MutableList::class == List::class? true. Both are the JVM interface java.util.List; the read-only/mutable split exists only at compile time.

h: Subtyping, and why List is not List · Go deeper
x: Why could Java afford covariant arrays but not covariant generics? Arrays are reified: every array object carries its element type, so the JVM can check each store. Generic types are erased: an ArrayList<String> is just an ArrayList at run time, so no check is possible after compilation. Lesson 8 of this track is about erasure. Array covariance is also why Java has the odd "generic array creation" error. new List<String>[10] is rejected, because the array would remember only List, and its store check could not stop a List<Integer> from going in. In the lab's toy model, a generic class hands its arguments straight to its supertypes. Real Kotlin is more flexible: class StringMap<V> : HashMap<String, V>() fixes one argument and passes the other, and the compiler tracks that mapping for every supertype. The rules in the lab still hold; the real checker just does more bookkeeping. One more pair to keep apart: Nothing is a subtype of every type, and Any? is a supertype of every type. Lesson 10 of this track uses Nothing to explain why emptyList() fits every List<T>.

h: Covariance with out: producers · A producer only hands values out
x: A producer only hands values out, so the subtype arrow keeps its direction A producer is a type whose values of T only ever come out of it. A feed of payments, a page of search results, an iterator, a Supplier. You call it, and it hands you a T. Nothing about it takes a T in. Run the substitution test from lesson 3 of this track on a producer. Suppose some code expects a source of Payment, and you hand it a source of CardPayment. Every call it can make returns a CardPayment, and every CardPayment is a Payment. Nothing can go wrong. So it is safe to treat a Source<CardPayment> as a Source<Payment>. The compiler can't see that by itself. Generic types are invariant unless you say otherwise. In Kotlin you say otherwise on the declaration, once, with out. Java has no such keyword, so it says it at every use with ? extends: Java interface Source<T> { T next(); // null when empty } static long totalCents(Source<? extends Payment> source) { ... } Source<Card> cards = listSource(List.of(card1, card2)); totalCents(cards); // fine: the parameter says ? extends Source<Payment> plain = cards; // error: Source<Card> cannot be converted to Source<Payment> Kotlin interface Source<out T> { fun next(): T? // null when empty } fun totalCents(source: Source<Payment>): Long { ... } val cards: Source<CardPayment> = ListSource(listOf(card1, card2)) totalCents(cards) // fine: Source is declared out val plain: Source<Payment> = cards // also fine Remove the out and Kotlin behaves like Java's plain Source<T>: error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Source<CardPayment>', but 'Source<Payment>' was expected. This property is called covariance: the subtype arrow between the element types carries over, in the same direction, to the generic type. CardPayment is a subtype of Payment, so Source<CardPayment> is a subtype of Source<Payment>. The figure shows the two arrows side by side. Where you put out matters. Kotlin's out on the declaration is called declaration-site variance. You think about it once, when you write Source, and every user gets the flexible behaviour for free. Java's ? extends is use-site variance: every method that takes a source must remember to write it, and the ones that forget are stricter than they need to be. Lesson 6 of this track shows that Kotlin has the use-site form too, for types that can't be out everywhere. Take out away and watch the call break Run ProducerDemo (or ProducerDemoJava) with the command below. Both print the same totals. In ProducerDemo.kt, remove out from both interface Source<out T> and class ListSource<out T>. Predict which line fails, then run. Put out back. In the Java twin, uncomment the wrong move. Why does Java need ? extends on totalCents while Kotlin needs nothing there? Because Source is `out`, a Source<CardPayment> fits. */ fun totalCents(source: Source<Payment>): Long { var sum = 0L while (true) { val p = source.next() ?: break sum += p.cents } return sum } fun main() { val cards: Source<CardPayment> = ListSource(listOf(CardPayment("pay_1", 1_200, "4242"), CardPayment("pay_2", 350, "0005"))) println("card total: ${totalCents(cards)}") // a Source<CardPayment> used as a Source<Payment> val anything: Source<Any> = ListSource(listOf("EUR")) // Source<String> used as Source<Any> println("first of anything: ${anything.next()}") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l04.demo.ProducerDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l04/demo/ProducerDemo.kt ProducerDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l04.demo; import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of ProducerDemo.kt. Java has no `out` on a declaration, so Source<T> stays invariant * and every method that wants "a source of some kind of Payment" says so at the use site: ? extends. */ public class ProducerDemoJava { record Card(String id, long cents) implements Payment { public String getId() { return id; } public long getCents() { return cents; } } interface Source<T> { T next(); // null when there is nothing left } static <T> Source<T> listSource(List<T> items) { Iterator<T> it = items.iterator(); return () -> it.hasNext() ? it.next() : null; } // ? extends Payment: "a Source of Payment or of some subtype". Without it, a Source<Card> would not fit. static long totalCents(Source<? extends Payment> source) { long sum = 0; for (Payment p = source.next(); p != null; p = source.next()) sum += p.getCents(); return sum; } public static void main(String[] args) { Source<Card> cards = listSource(List.of(new Card("pay_1", 1_200), new Card("pay_2", 350))); System.out.println("card total: " + totalCents(cards)); Source<? extends Object> anything = listSource(List.of("EUR")); System.out.println("first of anything: " + anything.next()); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // Source<Payment> plain = cards; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l04.demo.ProducerDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l04/demo/ProducerDemoJava.java Both versions print card total: 1550 and first of anything: EUR. The Java wrong move fails with incompatible types: Source<Card> cannot be converted to Source<Payment>. Java's Source<T> is invariant, so each method that wants flexibility writes ? extends. Kotlin wrote out once on the interface. Covariance keeps the arrow: a Source of CardPayment is a Source of Payment, because a producer only hands values out. A covariant type is a vending machine. A machine that dispenses only cola can stand in for "a drinks machine": everyone who asks it for a drink gets a drink. What you must not do is let customers load their own cans into it. If the cola machine took returns, someone could load lemonade into it through the "drinks machine" label, and the next person who wanted cola would get lemonade. out is the rule that the machine has no loading slot for customers. The analogy breaks at one point: a real vending machine can still be emptied, restocked by staff or switched off. out says nothing about any of that. It only controls which type of can goes in through the public slot.

h: Covariance with out: producers · Every member has a position: in, out or invariant
x: A Source<out T> can't also have a fun push(item: T), and the substitution test shows why. out lets you pass cards, a Source<CardPayment>, where a Source<Payment> is expected. Through that view, push(BankTransfer(...)) type-checks, because a bank transfer is a Payment. Now a source that hands out card payments holds a bank transfer, and the next next() gives it to code that reads it as a CardPayment: a ClassCastException, far from the push. The compiler can't allow both the upcast and the parameter. With out, it keeps the upcast and rejects the parameter. out is a promise: "values of T only come out of this type". The compiler holds you to it by checking where T appears in each public member. Every place has a position: A return type is an out-position. The value flows out to the caller. A parameter type is an in-position. The value flows in from the caller. A var property is both at once, because it has a getter and a setter. That is an invariant position. In a class declared out T, T may appear only in out-positions. Try to break it, and the error names the position: Java // Java has no `out` on the declaration, so it checks the same rule where you USE the type: interface Producer<T> { T produce(); void consume(T item); } Producer<? extends Object> view = strings; Object out = view.produce(); // fine: T comes out view.consume("USD"); // error: String cannot be converted to CAP#1 Kotlin interface Producer<out T> { fun produce(): T // fine val latest: T // fine: a val only has a getter fun consume(item: T) // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position var current: T // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position } The full Kotlin message reads type parameter 'T' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position in type 'T (of interface Producer<out T>)'. Java's CAP#1 is javac's name for "the unknown subtype behind ? extends". Java can't promise any String fits it, so it refuses the call. Three special cases come up all the time in Kotlin. Constructor parameters are fine, as long as they are plain parameters or val properties. class Holder<out T>(val item: T, plain: T) compiles. Building the object puts a T in, but only once, when the real type is still known. A var constructor property is a var, so class Mutable<out T>(var item: T) fails with the invariant-position error. Private members are exempt. private var hidden: T and private fun replace(t: T) are allowed, because no outside code can call them with the wrong type. protected and internal members are checked like public ones. private set is not enough. var lastServed: T? = null; private set still fails, with occurs in 'invariant' position. The property is still a var. The fix is to split it: a private var for the class and a public val that reads it. The lab makes you do exactly that. Find the positions the compiler rejects Open PositionsDemo.kt. For the four numbered lines, predict the position the error will name: in or invariant. Uncomment each line on its own and run. Comment it out again before the next. Run PositionsDemoJava and uncomment its view.consume line. Where does Java report the same rule? PositionsDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l04.demo /** Which members may mention T in a class declared `out T`? Uncomment ONE line at a time and run. */ interface Producer<out T> { fun produce(): T // return type: out-position, fine val latest: T // val: out-position, fine // fun consume(item: T) // 1 // var current: T // 2 } class Holder<out T>(val item: T, plain: T, private var hidden: T) { // all three are fine private fun replace(t: T) { hidden = t } // private: exempt fun first(): T = item // protected fun keep(t: T) {} // 3 } // class Mutable<out T>(var item: T) // 4 fun main() { val h: Holder<Any> = Holder("EUR", "x", "y") println("Holder<String> used as Holder<Any>: ${h.first()}") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l04.demo.PositionsDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l04/demo/PositionsDemo.kt PositionsDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l04.demo; /** * Java twin of PositionsDemo.kt. Java cannot mark a declaration `out`, so the same rule shows up * where you USE the type: through a `? extends` reference you may call methods that return T, * and javac refuses calls that pass a T in. */ public class PositionsDemoJava { interface Producer<T> { T produce(); void consume(T item); // allowed in the declaration: Java checks the use site } public static void main(String[] args) { Producer<String> strings = new Producer<>() { String last = "EUR"; public String produce() { return last; } public void consume(String item) { last = item; } }; Producer<? extends Object> view = strings; // the Java spelling of "used as Producer<out Any>" Object out = view.produce(); // fine: out-position System.out.println("produced " + out); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // view.consume("USD"); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l04.demo.PositionsDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l04/demo/PositionsDemoJava.java 1 (fun consume(item: T)) and 3 (protected fun keep) fail with occurs in 'in' position. 2 (var current) and 4 (class Mutable<out T>(var item: T)) fail with occurs in 'invariant' position. The demo itself prints Holder<String> used as Holder<Any>: EUR. Java reports the rule at the call: String cannot be converted to CAP#1, because Java checks variance where you use a type, not where you declare it. Most read-side types in a payment service are producers: a page of results from the ledger API, a Feed of settlement records, a query result, a read-only snapshot of balances. Declare them out (or keep them as Kotlin Lists) and a Page<CardPayment> drops straight into reporting code that expects a Page<Payment>. In a Quarkus REST client written in Java you will see the same contract as List<? extends PaymentDto> in parameters. When you write a Kotlin library that Java services call, Kotlin adds those wildcards to parameters for you, so Java callers get the same flexibility.

h: Covariance with out: producers · List is Kotlin's answer to ? extends
x: You have used a covariant type every day: Kotlin's read-only List. Its declaration is public interface List<out E> : Collection<E>. That out is why a List<CardPayment> goes into any function that takes a List<Payment>, with no ceremony. Java static long sumCents(List<? extends Payment> payments) { // the wildcard is the flexible part long sum = 0; for (Payment p : payments) sum += p.getCents(); return sum; } static long sumCentsInvariant(List<Payment> payments) { ... } List<CardPayment> cards = new ArrayList<>(List.of(card1, card2)); sumCents(cards); // fine sumCentsInvariant(cards); // error: List<CardPayment> cannot be converted to List<Payment> Kotlin fun sumCents(payments: List<Payment>): Long = payments.sumOf { it.cents } fun sumCentsMutable(payments: MutableList<Payment>): Long = payments.sumOf { it.cents } val cards: MutableList<CardPayment> = mutableListOf(card1, card2) sumCents(cards) // fine: List is out sumCentsMutable(cards) // error: actual type is 'MutableList<CardPayment>', but 'MutableList<Payment>' was expected The two snippets line up exactly. Java's List<? extends Payment> and Kotlin's List<Payment> are the same contract: "a list I will only read from, of Payment or any subtype". Java's plain List<Payment> and Kotlin's MutableList<Payment> are the strict, invariant version. Kotlin keeps this promise when Java code calls it. When a parameter's type is declared out, Kotlin writes a ? extends into the Java signature. javap, the JDK tool that prints what a class file contains, shows it (package names shortened): public static final long sumCents(java.util.List<? extends Payment>); public static final long sumCentsMutable(java.util.List<Payment>); So Java callers can pass a List<CardPayment> to sumCents too. Kotlin skips the wildcard in two places: in return types, so Java callers don't have to handle wildcards, and when the type argument is a final class like String, where ? extends String would mean nothing. The lab's tests use this rule to check your out: they read the Java signature of your function and look for ? extends. Call a Kotlin function from Java Run ListOutDemo, then ListOutDemoJava. The Java one calls the Kotlin function sumCents with a List<CardPayment>. In each file, uncomment the wrong move(s) one at a time and run. From labs/, run the javap command: javap -p -cp generics/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.generics.l04.demo.ListOutDemoKt. Which parameter got a wildcard?
