h: Covariance with out: producers · out does not mean immutable
x: The most common wrong idea about covariance is that out means read-only, or immutable. It doesn't. out only limits which types can flow in. State can still change. This compiles and empties the shelf: Java List<CardPayment> cards = new ArrayList<>(List.of(card1, card2)); List<? extends Payment> view = cards; // "read-only" for the type only Payment taken = view.remove(0); // fine: remove hands a value out view.clear(); // fine: no T involved view.add(card3); // error: CardPayment cannot be converted to CAP#1 Kotlin class Shelf<out T>(private val items: MutableList<T>) { fun take(): T = items.removeAt(0) // changes state, only hands T out fun clear() = items.clear() // changes state, no T at all } val view: MutableList<out Payment> = mutableListOf(card1, card2) view.removeAt(0) // fine view.clear() // fine view.add(card3) // error: contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E)' Shelf holds a private MutableList<T>, which is allowed because private members are exempt. take() removes an item and still only hands a T out. clear() mentions no T at all. Both are legal in an out class. The Kotlin docs say it plainly: the only thing variance guarantees is type safety, and immutability is a different story. So when you need a class to be covariant but it also seems to need a method that takes a T, you have three honest options: Move the method out of the class as an extension function. fun <T> Feed<T>.nextOr(fallback: T): T declares its own T, so the class's variance rules don't apply. The standard library does this: plus(element: T) and getOrElse on List are extensions. Give the method its own type parameter, such as fun <R> map(f: (T) -> R): Page<R>. Here T sits inside the parameter of a function parameter, and two in-positions cancel out. Lesson 5 of this track shows why. Split the type in two: a covariant read interface and an invariant read-write one, like List and MutableList. There is also @UnsafeVariance, which switches the check off for one position. List.contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E) uses it, because contains only compares. It is a promise you make by hand, and lesson 10 of this track shows how to break it. Empty a covariant shelf Run ImmutableMythDemo (or ImmutableMythDemoJava). Before it runs, predict whether take() and clear() compile in a class declared out T. Uncomment the view.add line and run. Read which rule stops it. ImmutableMythDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l04.demo /** `out` limits which TYPES flow in. It does not stop state from changing. */ class Shelf<out T>(private val items: MutableList<T>) { // a private MutableList<T> is fine in an out class fun take(): T = items.removeAt(0) // changes state, still only hands T out fun clear() = items.clear() // changes state, mentions no T at all val size: Int get() = items.size } fun main() { val shelf: Shelf<Payment> = Shelf(mutableListOf(CardPayment("pay_1", 1_200, "4242"), CardPayment("pay_2", 350, "0005"))) println("took ${shelf.take().id}, ${shelf.size} left") shelf.clear() println("after clear: ${shelf.size} left") // The same is true of a use-site out projection: no add, but clear and removeAt still work. val view: MutableList<out Payment> = mutableListOf(CardPayment("pay_3", 99, "1111")) view.removeAt(0) println("view after removeAt: ${view.size} left") // view.add(CardPayment("pay_4", 10, "2222")) // uncomment: which rule stops this? } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l04.demo.ImmutableMythDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l04/demo/ImmutableMythDemo.kt ImmutableMythDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l04.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ImmutableMythDemo.kt. A ? extends view stops adds, not changes. */ public class ImmutableMythDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { List<CardPayment> cards = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new CardPayment("pay_1", 1_200, "4242"), new CardPayment("pay_2", 350, "0005"))); List<? extends Payment> view = cards; // read-only for the TYPE, not for the state Payment taken = view.remove(0); // compiles: remove hands a value out System.out.println("took " + taken.getId() + ", " + view.size() + " left"); view.clear(); // compiles: no T involved System.out.println("after clear: " + view.size() + " left, and cards has " + cards.size()); // view.add(new CardPayment("pay_4", 10, "2222")); // uncomment: which rule stops this? } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l04.demo.ImmutableMythDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l04/demo/ImmutableMythDemoJava.java It prints took pay_1, 1 left, after clear: 0 left and, in Kotlin, view after removeAt: 0 left. Variance never stopped the state from changing. The add fails with Receiver type 'MutableList<out Payment>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'. in Kotlin and CardPayment cannot be converted to CAP#1 in Java: only the in-position is blocked. Declaration-site variance (Kotlin docs) docs The common mistake is to read out as "immutable" and then trust a covariant type to protect shared state. A MutableList<out Payment> still has clear() and removeAt(), and a class Shelf<out T> can wrap a private mutable list. People make this mistake because the C# and Kotlin keywords sound like access rules. They are type rules. The fix is to keep two questions apart: "can a subtype stand in for the supertype here?" (variance) and "can anyone change this?" (expose a read-only interface, or copy). The other mistake is the reverse: giving up on out because one method takes a T. Move that method to an extension function, or split the type into a read interface and a write interface.

h: Covariance with out: producers · Java and Kotlin
x: A producer, declared once in Kotlin, spelled at each use in Java Feeds.java import java.util.List; interface Payment { long cents(); } record CardPayment(long cents) implements Payment {} // Java can't say "T only comes out" on the declaration interface Source<T> { T next(); } class Feeds { // every method that should accept subtypes must remember ? extends static long total(Source<? extends Payment> source, int n) { long sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += source.next().cents(); return sum; } static long sum(List<? extends Payment> payments) { return payments.stream().mapToLong(Payment::cents).sum(); } // forget it once and the method is stricter than it needs to be static long strict(Source<Payment> source) { return source.next().cents(); } } Feeds.kt interface Payment { val cents: Long } data class CardPayment(override val cents: Long) : Payment // say it once, on the declaration interface Source<out T> { fun next(): T } // plain types in every signature: Source and List are both covariant fun total(source: Source<Payment>, n: Int): Long { var sum = 0L repeat(n) { sum += source.next().cents } return sum } fun sum(payments: List<Payment>): Long = payments.sumOf { it.cents } // the compiler enforces the promise inside Source: // fun push(t: T) would fail with "declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position" The safety rule is the same in both languages: through a covariant view you may take values out but not put them in. The difference is who carries the burden. In Java the type stays invariant and every method signature has to say ? extends, so the flexibility depends on each author remembering. In Kotlin the author of Source says out once, the compiler checks every member of Source against it, and every signature that mentions Source<Payment> is automatically flexible. When Java calls that Kotlin code, Kotlin writes the ? extends into the parameter types for it.

h: Covariance with out: producers · Worked example
x: Make a settlement Feed covariant without losing a feature A settlement job reads payments from a Feed. Reporting code wants a Feed<Payment>, but the job has a Feed<CardPayment>. The feed only hands items out, so it should be covariant. Here it is before the change. class Feed<T>(items: List<T>) { private val queue = ArrayDeque(items) var lastServed: T? = null private set fun next(): T { val item = queue.removeFirst(); lastServed = item; return item } fun nextOr(fallback: T): T = if (queue.isEmpty()) fallback else next() } class Feed<T> { private final ArrayDeque<T> queue; private T lastServed; Feed(List<T> items) { queue = new ArrayDeque<>(items); } T next() { T item = queue.removeFirst(); lastServed = item; return item; } T nextOr(T fallback) { return queue.isEmpty() ? fallback : next(); } T lastServed() { return lastServed; } } Add out and read the errors. The compiler names two members. nextOr takes a T (in-position). lastServed is a var, so its type is in an invariant position, even with a private setter. In Java there is nothing to add to the class; each caller writes Feed<? extends Payment> instead. class Feed<out T>(items: List<T>) { // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position in type 'T?' var lastServed: T? = null private set // error: ... declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position in type 'T' fun nextOr(fallback: T): T = ... } // Java checks at the use site instead: static List<Payment> drainAll(Feed<? extends Payment> feed) { ... } Feed<? extends Payment> view = cardFeed; Payment p = view.next(); // fine view.nextOr(new BankTransfer(...)); // error: cannot be converted to CAP#1 Fix the property by splitting it: a private var (exempt) and a public val (an out-position). Callers still read lastServed, and nobody outside could set it before either. private var last: T? = null val lastServed: T? get() = last private T last; T lastServed() { return last; } // Java: a getter with no setter Fix nextOr by moving it out of the class as an extension. The extension declares its own T, so the class's out doesn't constrain it. Self-check: why is this safe? (At the call feed.nextOr(x), the compiler picks a T that fits both the feed and x. For a Feed<CardPayment> and a BankTransfer fallback, that T is Payment, and the result is typed Payment.) fun <T> Feed<T>.nextOr(fallback: T): T = if (hasNext()) next() else fallback val cardFeed: Feed<CardPayment> = Feed(cards) val p: Payment = cardFeed.nextOr(BankTransfer("pay_9", 0, "DE89...")) // T = Payment // Java: a static helper with its own <T> does the same job static <T> T nextOr(Feed<? extends T> feed, T fallback) { return feed.hasNext() ? feed.next() : fallback; } Payment p = nextOr(cardFeed, new BankTransfer("pay_9", 0, "DE89..."));

h: Covariance with out: producers · Quiz
x: Which member compiles inside class Feed<out T>? fun push(item: T) var current: T? = null with private set fun peek(): T? protected fun replay(item: T) A return type is an out-position, so peek(): T? is fine. push takes a T (in-position), and so does the protected replay: only private members are exempt. A var is an invariant position even when its setter is private. Kotlin: interface Source<out T> { fun next(): T }, interface Payment, and fun total(s: Source<Payment>). What does Java see as the parameter type of total? Source<Payment> Source<? extends Payment> Source<? super Payment> The raw type Source Kotlin turns a parameter of an out-declared type into ? extends, so Java callers can pass a Source<CardPayment> as well. It would skip the wildcard if Payment were a final class, and it never adds one to a return type. class Shelf<out T>(private val items: MutableList<T>) { fun clear() = items.clear() }. Does it compile, and what does it say about out? No: an out class can't hold a MutableList<T> No: clear() changes state, and out means immutable Yes: private members are exempt, and out restricts types, not state changes Yes, but only with @UnsafeVariance on items The MutableList<T> is private, so the variance check skips it, and clear() does not mention T at all. out guarantees that no wrongly-typed value gets in through the public API. It says nothing about whether the object can change. Java: static long sum(List<? extends Number> xs) and List<Integer> ints. Which line compiles inside sum? xs.add(5); Number first = xs.get(0); xs.add(null); is the only thing that fails Integer first = xs.get(0); Through ? extends Number you can read elements as Number. You can't add an Integer, because the list might really be a List<Double> (javac: cannot be converted to CAP#1). Reading as Integer fails for the same reason. add(null) actually compiles, since null fits any type. From "Subtyping, and why List is not List ": why does val x: MutableList<Any> = mutableListOf<String>() fail while val y: List<Any> = mutableListOf<String>() compiles? MutableList is a different class from List at run time Through x you could add an Int to a list of strings; List has no add, so y can only read Kotlin forbids Any as a type argument of mutable types mutableListOf returns a Java type that Kotlin can't widen That is the substitution test. A mutable view of the wider type could write a wrong value into the narrower list. A read-only view can't, which is exactly what List<out E> declares. At run time both are the same java.util.List.

h: Covariance with out: producers · Key terms
x: Producer A type whose T values only come out: iterators, sources, pages, read-only lists. Covariant C<Sub> is a subtype of C<Super>: the arrow keeps its direction. out Kotlin's keyword on a type parameter: "T only comes out of this type". Out-position A place where a value of T flows out: return types and val types. In-position A place where a value of T flows in: parameter types. Declaration-site variance Variance written once on the class (interface Source<out T>), as Kotlin does. Use-site variance Variance written where the type is used (Source<? extends Payment>), as Java does. What makes a generic type safe to declare out T? It only hands values of T out (return types, vals). It never takes a T in through a public member. With Source<out T>, is Source<CardPayment> a subtype of Source<Payment>? Yes. Covariance keeps the direction of the subtype arrow. Kotlin's out T on a declaration corresponds to what in Java? ? extends T, written at each use site, e.g. List<? extends Payment>. Why does var x: T fail in a class declared out T? A var has a setter, so T is in an invariant position. Even private set doesn't help; split it into a private var and a public val. Are constructor parameters allowed in a class declared out T? Plain parameters and val properties: yes. A var constructor property: no (invariant position). Does out make a type immutable? No. It only blocks T from flowing in. MutableList<out T> still has clear() and removeAt(). How do you keep a method like getOrElse(default: T) on a covariant type? Make it an extension function with its own type parameter: fun <T> Feed<T>.nextOr(fallback: T): T.

h: Covariance with out: producers · Go deeper
x: The rule "parameters are in-positions" has a twist when the parameter is itself a function. In fun <R> map(f: (T) -> R), T is the input of f. The page calls f and passes it a T, so the value flows out of the page into the caller's lambda. Two in-positions cancel out. That is why map is legal in Page<out T>, while fun replay(): (T) -> Unit (a function returned to the caller, which the caller will feed a T) is not. Lesson 5 of this track turns this into a sign rule. Kotlin is strict about inferred types too. In class E<in T> { private fun produce(): T? = null; fun use() = produce() }, the private produce is fine, but the public use() has the inferred return type T? and fails. Give public members of variant classes explicit types. Private members get one more rule, called private-to-this. Inside class C<out T>(private var t: T), the method fun copyFrom(o: C<@UnsafeVariance T>) { t = o.t } fails with cannot access 'var t: T': it is private/*private to this*/. A private member is only exempt when you reach it through this, because another instance o might really be a C<Subtype> seen as a C<T>. Finally, Kotlin leaves the wildcard out of Java signatures when the type argument is final. fun f(x: List<String>) is f(List<String>) in Java, because nothing can extend String. Use @JvmWildcard to force one, or @JvmSuppressWildcards to drop them.

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · A consumer only takes values in
x: A consumer only takes values in, so the subtype arrow flips A consumer is a type whose values of T only ever go in. An audit log, a Kafka producer, a metrics counter, a Comparator, an event handler. You hand it a T, and it hands nothing typed T back. Run the substitution test again, the other way round. Some code needs a sink for card authorizations. You hand it an audit log that accepts any payment event. Every call it can make passes a CardAuthorized, and the audit log takes every PaymentEvent, so it takes those too. Nothing can go wrong. So for a consumer, the more general type is the one that can stand in. A Sink<PaymentEvent> can be used where a Sink<CardAuthorized> is expected. The subtype arrow flips. This is contravariance, and Kotlin declares it with in. Java writes it at each use with ? super: Java interface Sink<T> { void accept(T item); } static void forwardAuthorizations(List<CardAuthorized> events, Sink<? super CardAuthorized> to) { ... } Sink<PaymentEvent> audit = e -> System.out.println("audit: " + e.getPaymentId()); forwardAuthorizations(auths, audit); // fine: the parameter says ? super Sink<CardAuthorized> strict = audit; // error: Sink<PaymentEvent> cannot be converted to Sink<CardAuthorized> Kotlin interface Sink<in T> { fun accept(item: T) } fun forwardAuthorizations(events: List<CardAuthorized>, to: Sink<CardAuthorized>) { ... } val audit: Sink<PaymentEvent> = AuditLog() forwardAuthorizations(auths, audit) // fine: Sink is declared in val cardSink: Sink<CardAuthorized> = audit // also fine The other direction fails, and it should. A Sink<CardAuthorized> might be a fraud checker that reads cents. Handing it a RefundIssued through a Sink<PaymentEvent> view would break it: error: initializer type mismatch: expected 'Sink<PaymentEvent>', actual 'Sink<CardAuthorized>'. The position rules are the mirror image of out. In a type declared in T, T may appear in parameters, and not in return types or vals. Add fun last(): T to Sink and the compiler says type parameter 'T' is declared as 'in' but occurs in 'out' position. The reason mirrors lesson 4. Through a Sink<CardAuthorized> view of the audit log, last() would promise a CardAuthorized, and the log may be holding a RefundIssued. The figure shows the two cases next to each other. Same element types, same "is a" arrow between them. A producer keeps the direction. A consumer reverses it. Pass a general sink where a specific one is needed Run SinkDemo (or SinkDemoJava). Every authorization goes through the audit log. Predict: does the wrong move at the bottom compile? Uncomment it and run. In SinkDemo.kt, remove in from interface Sink<in T> and run again. Which line breaks now? Put it back. Any sink that takes them will do. */ fun forwardAuthorizations(events: List<CardAuthorized>, to: Sink<CardAuthorized>) { for (e in events) to.accept(e) } fun main() { val audit: Sink<PaymentEvent> = AuditLog() forwardAuthorizations(listOf(CardAuthorized("pay_1", 1_200), CardAuthorized("pay_2", 350)), audit) val cardSink: Sink<CardAuthorized> = audit // a Sink<PaymentEvent> IS a Sink<CardAuthorized> cardSink.accept(CardAuthorized("pay_3", 99)) // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val back: Sink<PaymentEvent> = cardSink } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.SinkDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l05/demo/SinkDemo.kt SinkDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l05.demo; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of SinkDemo.kt. Java has no `in` on a declaration, so Sink<T> stays invariant and the * method that wants "a sink for card authorizations, or for anything more general" says ? super. */ public class SinkDemoJava { interface Sink<T> { void accept(T item); } static final Sink<PaymentEvent> AUDIT = e -> System.out.println("audit: " + e.getPaymentId()); // ? super CardAuthorized: "a Sink of CardAuthorized or of some supertype" static void forwardAuthorizations(List<CardAuthorized> events, Sink<? super CardAuthorized> to) { for (CardAuthorized e : events) to.accept(e); } public static void main(String[] args) { forwardAuthorizations(List.of(new CardAuthorized("pay_1", 1_200), new CardAuthorized("pay_2", 350)), AUDIT); Sink<? super CardAuthorized> cardSink = AUDIT; // the Java spelling of Kotlin's Sink<CardAuthorized> cardSink.accept(new CardAuthorized("pay_3", 99)); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // Sink<CardAuthorized> strict = AUDIT; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.SinkDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l05/demo/SinkDemoJava.java Both print audit: pay_1, audit: pay_2, audit: pay_3. The wrong move fails: Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Sink<PaymentEvent>', actual 'Sink<CardAuthorized>'. in Kotlin and Sink<PaymentEvent> cannot be converted to Sink<CardAuthorized> in Java. Without in, Kotlin rejects both forwardAuthorizations(..., audit) and val cardSink: Sink<CardAuthorized> = audit: an invariant Sink behaves like Java's plain Sink<T>. Producers keep the subtype arrow (out). Consumers flip it (in): the sink for the general type stands in for the sink for the specific one. A consumer is a recycling bin. A bin labeled "any recyclables" can stand in for a bin labeled "glass only": everyone who was going to drop glass into it still can. The reverse fails: if you hand out a glass-only bin as an "any recyclables" bin, someone drops cardboard in. So the bin with the wider label is the one that substitutes, which is the flip that in describes. The analogy breaks when you take things out: a real bin can be emptied and its contents inspected, but a Sink<PaymentEvent> seen as a Sink<CardAuthorized> gives you nothing typed back. Contravariant types are for putting values in, not for reading them.

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · Comparator: one ordering for many types
x: You already use the most common consumer: a comparator. A comparator only takes values, two at a time, and returns an Int. So a comparator written for a supertype works for every subtype: Java Comparator<PaymentEvent> byId = Comparator.comparing(PaymentEvent::getPaymentId); List<CardAuthorized> auths = new ArrayList<>(...); auths.sort(byId); // List<E>.sort(Comparator<? super E>) Comparator<? super CardAuthorized> forCards = byId; // fine Comparator<CardAuthorized> strict = byId; // error: Comparator<PaymentEvent> cannot be converted to Comparator<CardAuthorized> Kotlin val byId: Comparator<PaymentEvent> = compareBy { it.paymentId } val auths = listOf(CardAuthorized("pay_3", 1_200), CardAuthorized("pay_1", 350)) auths.sortedWith(byId) // sortedWith(comparator: Comparator<in T>) val forCards: Comparator<in CardAuthorized> = byId // fine val strict: Comparator<CardAuthorized> = byId // error: expected 'Comparator<CardAuthorized>', actual 'Comparator<PaymentEvent>' The last line surprises Kotlin developers. On the JVM, Kotlin's Comparator is java.util.Comparator, a Java interface, and Java interfaces have no declared variance. So Kotlin treats Comparator as invariant, exactly as Java does. The flexibility comes from the use site: the standard library declares sortedWith(comparator: Comparator<in T>), the Kotlin spelling of Java's ? super T. The JDK made the same choice everywhere. List.sort, Collections.sort, Stream.sorted and the TreeMap constructor all take a Comparator<? super E>. If you write your own ranking helper and forget the projection, it accepts only a comparator of the exact element type, and the shared byPaymentId comparator that the rest of the codebase uses no longer fits. Kotlin's own Comparable is different. It is declared interface Comparable<in T>, so the in is on the declaration. That is why lesson 2 of this track could call maxOf2 on LocalDate, which is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>: a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate> is a Comparable<LocalDate>. The rule of thumb for your own signatures: when a parameter is a comparator, a handler, a sink or a callback that receives your values, give it in (Kotlin) or ? super (Java). The lab's highest(items: List<T>, comparator: Comparator<in T>) is the shape to copy. Sort two kinds of event with one comparator Run ComparatorDemo (or ComparatorDemoJava). One Comparator<PaymentEvent> sorts both lists. Uncomment the strict line and run. Then change its type to Comparator<in CardAuthorized> (Java: Comparator<? super CardAuthorized>) and run again. Consumers are everywhere on the write side of a payment service: a Kafka producer wrapper that sends PaymentEvents, an audit log, a metrics recorder, a Comparator that orders settlement lines, a Temporal activity callback, a handler registered on an event bus. h: Contravariance with in: consumers · Function types: in on the left, out on the right
x: Function types are where producers and consumers meet. (P) -> R is Function1<in P, out R>: a function consumes its parameter and produces its result. So a function type is contravariant on the left of the arrow and covariant on the right: Java // Java's Consumer and Function are plain invariant interfaces, so say it at the use site: Consumer<PaymentEvent> auditAll = e -> System.out.println("audit " + e.getPaymentId()); Function<PaymentEvent, String> describe = e -> "event " + e.getPaymentId(); Consumer<? super CardAuthorized> onCard = auditAll; // fine Function<? super CardAuthorized, ? extends Object> label = describe; // fine Consumer<CardAuthorized> strict = auditAll; // error: cannot be converted Kotlin val auditAll: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit = { println("audit ${it.paymentId}") } val describe: (PaymentEvent) -> String = { "event ${it.paymentId}" } val onCard: (CardAuthorized) -> Unit = auditAll // fine: takes more general input val label: (CardAuthorized) -> Any = describe // fine: in on the left, out on the right val tooBroad: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit = onCard // error: expected '(PaymentEvent) -> Unit', actual '(CardAuthorized) -> Unit' This is why the lab's Dispatcher<CardAuthorized> accepts a handler written for every PaymentEvent without any extra work. Function types also explain the odd cases from lesson 4 of this track. Follow the value. In fun each(f: (T) -> Unit), the class calls f and hands it a T, so the T travels out of the class, even though it sits inside a parameter. In fun handler(): (T) -> Unit, the class hands a function to the caller, and the caller feeds it a T, so the T travels in. To get the same answer without tracing, give each position a sign: an out-position is +, an in-position is −. When one type sits inside another, multiply the signs. A plain parameter is −. The parameter of a function that is itself a parameter is − times −, which is +. Member in class C<…T> Where T sits Sign Legal under out T Legal under in T fun get(): T return + yes no fun put(t: T) parameter − no yes fun each(f: (T) -> Unit) parameter of a parameter − × − = + yes no fun handler(): (T) -> Unit parameter of the result + × − = − no yes fun putAll(xs: List<T>) List<out E> in a parameter − × + = − no yes You won't run this table often. Use it when an error points at a callback and the intuition stops helping. The Inbox interface in the demo has three members to test it on. Assign handlers, then test the sign rule Run HandlerDemo (or HandlerDemoJava) and uncomment the wrong move(s). Read the errors. In HandlerDemo.kt, look at the Inbox<in T> interface. Use the sign table to predict which of the three numbered members compile. Uncomment them one at a time and run to check your predictions. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val tooBroad: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit = onCard } /** The sign rule: uncomment ONE member at a time. Which are legal in a class declared `in T`? */ interface Inbox<in T> { fun accept(item: T) // in-position: fine fun acceptAll(items: List<T>) // List<out E> inside a parameter: in x out = in, fine // fun peek(): T // 1 // fun forEachPending(f: (T) -> Unit) // 2 // fun filterWith(p: (T) -> Boolean): Inbox<T> // 3 } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.HandlerDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l05/demo/HandlerDemo.kt HandlerDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l05.demo; import java.util.function.Consumer; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java twin of HandlerDemo.kt. h: Contravariance with in: consumers · PECS is out and in with Java spelling
x: Java programmers learn variance as PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. It comes from Effective Java (Item 31), and the Kotlin docs cite it as the background for out and in. The mapping is one to one: Role of the parameter Java Kotlin gives you T values (producer) ? extends T out T takes T values from you (consumer) ? super T in T both T T The JDK's copy method is the textbook case. src produces, dest consumes: Java // java.util.Collections: // public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) static <T> void copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) { for (T x : from) to.add(x); } copyInto(List.of(1_200, 350), numbers); // List<Integer> into a List<Number> copyInto(numbers, new ArrayList<Integer>()); // error: method copyInto cannot be applied to given types Kotlin fun <T> copyInto(from: List<T>, to: MutableList<in T>) { for (x in from) to.add(x) } copyInto(listOf(1_200, 350), numbers) // List<Int> into a MutableList<Number> copyInto(numbers, mutableListOf<Int>()) // error: actual type is 'MutableList<Int>', but 'MutableList<in Number>' was expected The Kotlin version needs only one projection, on to. from is a List, which is already out, so writing List<out T> would only earn a warning that the projection is redundant. When you design a signature, ask one question per parameter: does this parameter give me values of T, take values of T from me, or both? Give: out / ? extends. Take: in / ? super. Both: plain T. The wrong answer is rarely a compile error in your own code. It shows up later, as a caller who can't pass a perfectly good Comparator<PaymentEvent> and writes a cast to get around you. MutableList<in T> is a use-site projection: MutableList itself is invariant, and the function asks for a write-only view of it. Lesson 6 of this track is about those. Copy from a producer into a consumer Run PecsDemo (or PecsDemoJava). Both copy a list of ints into a list of numbers and a list of anything. Uncomment the wrong move and run. Say in one sentence why copying numbers into a list of ints must fail. PecsDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l05.demo /** Copy from a producer into a consumer: `from` only gives T, `to` only takes T. */ fun <T> copyInto(from: List<T>, to: MutableList<in T>) { // List is already out; MutableList gets a use-site in for (x in from) to.add(x) } fun main() { val amounts: List<Int> = listOf(1_200, 350) val numbers: MutableList<Number> = mutableListOf(2.5) val anything: MutableList<Any> = mutableListOf("EUR") copyInto(amounts, numbers) // T = Int; a MutableList<Number> accepts Ints copyInto(amounts, anything) println("numbers = $numbers, anything = $anything") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // copyInto(numbers, mutableListOf<Int>()) } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.PecsDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l05/demo/PecsDemo.kt PecsDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l05.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of PecsDemo.kt. Producer extends, consumer super: the JDK's own copy has both. */ public class PecsDemoJava { // the same shape as java.util.Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) static <T> void copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) { for (T x : from) to.add(x); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Integer> amounts = List.of(1_200, 350); List<Number> numbers = new ArrayList<>(List.of(2.5)); List<Object> anything = new ArrayList<>(List.of("EUR")); copyInto(amounts, numbers); // T = Integer, or Number: both work copyInto(amounts, anything); System.out.println("numbers = " + numbers + ", anything = " + anything); List<Number> slots = new ArrayList<>(Collections.nCopies(2, 0)); Collections.copy(slots, amounts); // the JDK version overwrites slots in place System.out.println("slots = " + slots); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // copyInto(numbers, new ArrayList<Integer>()); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l05.demo.PecsDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l05/demo/PecsDemoJava.java Both print numbers = [2.5, 1200, 350], anything = [EUR, 1200, 350], and Java also prints slots = [1200, 350] from Collections.copy. The wrong move fails with actual type is 'MutableList<Int>', but 'MutableList<in Number>' was expected (Kotlin) or method copyInto ... cannot be applied to given types (Java): a list of ints can't take the 2.5 that the source holds. Collections.copy (Java SE 25 API) docs The common mistake is writing a consumer parameter as plain T: fun register(handler: Comparator<CardAuthorized>) in Kotlin or void register(Consumer<CardAuthorized> handler) in Java. It compiles and works for the first caller. The second caller has a perfectly good Comparator<PaymentEvent> or Consumer<PaymentEvent> and gets a type mismatch, then writes a lambda adapter or a cast. People make the mistake because the plain type looks simpler and Kotlin's own Comparator is invariant on the JVM. The fix is to ask the PECS question for every parameter: if it only receives your values, write Comparator<in T> / Consumer<? super T>.

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · Java and Kotlin
x: A consumer, declared once in Kotlin, spelled at each use in Java Sinks.java import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; interface Sink<T> { // no declaration-site variance in Java void accept(T item); } class Sinks { // every consumer parameter must remember ? super static <T> void feedAll(List<? extends T> items, Sink<? super T> sink) { for (T item : items) sink.accept(item); } static <T> T highest(List<? extends T> items, Comparator<? super T> order) { T best = items.get(0); for (T item : items) if (order.compare(item, best) > 0) best = item; return best; } static <E> void subscribe(Consumer<? super E> handler) { /* store it */ } } Sinks.kt interface Sink<in T> { // say it once fun accept(item: T) } // Sink and List carry their variance, so these signatures stay plain fun <T> feedAll(items: List<T>, sink: Sink<T>) { for (item in items) sink.accept(item) } // java.util.Comparator is a Java interface: invariant, so project it here fun <T> highest(items: List<T>, order: Comparator<in T>): T { var best = items[0] for (item in items) if (order.compare(item, best) > 0) best = item return best } // function types are already Function1<in P, out R> fun <E> subscribe(handler: (E) -> Unit) { /* store it */ } The rule is identical: through a contravariant view you may put values in but get nothing typed back out. Java puts ? super on every consumer parameter; Kotlin puts in on the consumer's declaration once, and its function types are contravariant in their parameters out of the box. The one trap is Java interfaces used from Kotlin. Comparator, Consumer and every other Java interface have no declared variance, so Kotlin treats them as invariant and you need a use-site in (Comparator<in T>), exactly where Java needs ? super T. When Java calls Kotlin, a parameter of type Sink<PaymentEvent> shows up as Sink<? super PaymentEvent>.

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · Worked example
x: Design a dispatcher that accepts general handlers A payment service publishes CardAuthorized events. The fraud team writes a handler for card authorizations. The audit team writes one handler for every PaymentEvent. You want both to subscribe to the same dispatcher. Start by naming the role of each type: the event is produced by the dispatcher and consumed by the handler. interface PaymentEvent { val paymentId: String } data class CardAuthorized(override val paymentId: String, val cents: Long) : PaymentEvent val fraudCheck: (CardAuthorized) -> Unit = { check(it.cents) } val auditAll: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit = { log(it.paymentId) } interface PaymentEvent { String paymentId(); } record CardAuthorized(String paymentId, long cents) implements PaymentEvent {} Consumer<CardAuthorized> fraudCheck = e -> check(e.cents()); Consumer<PaymentEvent> auditAll = e -> log(e.paymentId()); Write the subscribe signature with the handler as a consumer of E. In Kotlin a function type already has in on its parameter, so (E) -> Unit is enough. In Java, Consumer<E> would reject the audit handler, so write Consumer<? super E>. class Dispatcher<E> { private val handlers = ArrayList<(E) -> Unit>() fun subscribe(handler: (E) -> Unit) { handlers.add(handler) } fun publish(event: E): Int { for (h in handlers) h(event) return handlers.size } } class Dispatcher<E> { private final List<Consumer<? super E>> handlers = new ArrayList<>(); void subscribe(Consumer<? super E> handler) { handlers.add(handler); } int publish(E event) { for (Consumer<? super E> h : handlers) h.accept(event); return handlers.size(); } } Wire it up. Both handlers subscribe to a Dispatcher<CardAuthorized>. Self-check before reading on: why can't the fraud handler subscribe to a Dispatcher<PaymentEvent>? (That dispatcher may publish a RefundIssued, and fraudCheck reads cents from a CardAuthorized.) val cards = Dispatcher<CardAuthorized>() cards.subscribe(fraudCheck) cards.subscribe(auditAll) // fine: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit is a (CardAuthorized) -> Unit cards.publish(CardAuthorized("pay_1", 1_200)) // 2 val all = Dispatcher<PaymentEvent>() all.subscribe(fraudCheck) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is '(CardAuthorized) -> Unit', // but '(PaymentEvent) -> Unit' was expected. var cards = new Dispatcher<CardAuthorized>(); cards.subscribe(fraudCheck); cards.subscribe(auditAll); // fine thanks to ? super E cards.publish(new CardAuthorized("pay_1", 1_200)); // 2 var all = new Dispatcher<PaymentEvent>(); all.subscribe(fraudCheck); // error: incompatible types: Consumer<CardAuthorized> cannot be converted to Consumer<? super PaymentEvent>

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · Quiz
x: interface Sink<in T> { fun accept(item: T) }. Which assignment compiles? val a: Sink<PaymentEvent> = cardSink where cardSink: Sink<CardAuthorized> val b: Sink<CardAuthorized> = auditSink where auditSink: Sink<PaymentEvent> Both Neither, unless Sink is declared out With in, the arrow flips: a sink of the supertype is a sink of the subtype. The reverse is unsafe: a card-only sink seen as a Sink<PaymentEvent> could be handed a refund. Which member can you add to interface Sink<in T>? fun last(): T val pending: List<T> fun acceptAll(items: List<T>) fun forEachPending(f: (T) -> Unit) acceptAll takes the items in: List<out E> inside a parameter is − × + = −, an in-position. last() and pending hand T out. In forEachPending, the T is the parameter of a parameter (− × − = +), so it is an out-position too. Kotlin: val byId: Comparator<PaymentEvent> = compareBy { it.paymentId }. Why does val c: Comparator<CardAuthorized> = byId fail? Comparators are covariant, so the arrow goes the other way Comparator is java.util.Comparator, a Java interface with no declared variance, so Kotlin treats it as invariant compareBy returns a raw type It doesn't fail; it compiles Kotlin can't add variance to a Java interface, so Comparator<A> and Comparator<B> are unrelated unless you project: Comparator<in CardAuthorized>. The standard library does that in sortedWith(comparator: Comparator<in T>). Kotlin's own Comparable is declared in T and behaves differently. Java: you write static void register(Consumer<CardAuthorized> handler). A teammate has a Consumer<PaymentEvent>. What is the right fix? Change the parameter to Consumer<? super CardAuthorized> Change the parameter to Consumer<? extends CardAuthorized> Ask the teammate to cast their handler Change the parameter to raw Consumer The handler consumes the events you pass it, so Consumer Super. ? extends would let you pass a consumer of some unknown subtype, which you could never call safely. A raw type turns off checking altogether. From "Covariance with out: producers": why is fun <R> map(f: (T) -> R): Page<R> allowed inside data class Page<out T>? Because map has its own type parameter, which exempts the whole method Because T is the parameter of f, which is itself a parameter: two in-positions make an out-position Because data classes skip the variance check It isn't allowed; it needs @UnsafeVariance The page calls f and passes it a T, so values of T flow out of the page. By the sign rule, − × − = +. A new type parameter R doesn't exempt anything: fun <R> bad(t: T): R would still fail.

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · Key terms
x: Consumer A type whose T values only go in: sinks, comparators, handlers. Contravariant C<Super> is a subtype of C<Sub>: the arrow flips. in Kotlin's keyword on a type parameter: "T only goes into this type". ? super T Java's use-site wildcard for a consumer: "T or any supertype of T". PECS Producer Extends, Consumer Super: the Java rule for choosing wildcards. Function1 The type behind (P) -> R: contravariant in the parameter, covariant in the result. Sign rule Out-positions are +, in-positions are −; multiply through nesting to find where T really sits. What makes a generic type safe to declare in T? It only takes values of T in (parameters). No public member returns a T. With Sink<in T>, which way does the arrow go between Sink<PaymentEvent> and Sink<CardAuthorized>? Sink<PaymentEvent> is a subtype of Sink<CardAuthorized>: the arrow flips. Kotlin's in T corresponds to what in Java? ? super T, written at the use site, e.g. Consumer<? super CardAuthorized>. Is (PaymentEvent) -> Unit a subtype of (CardAuthorized) -> Unit? Yes. Function types are Function1<in P, out R>, so a handler of the general type fits where a specific one is expected. Why must Kotlin code write Comparator<in T> instead of plain Comparator<T>? On the JVM, Comparator is the Java interface java.util.Comparator, which has no declared variance, so Kotlin treats it as invariant. What does PECS stand for? Producer Extends, Consumer Super (Effective Java, Item 31). In Kotlin: producer out, consumer in. Sign rule: where does T sit in fun each(f: (T) -> Unit)? Parameter of a parameter: − × − = +, an out-position. Legal under out T, illegal under in T.

h: Contravariance with in: consumers · Go deeper
x: Contravariance explains a detail of Kotlin's Comparable. It is declared public interface Comparable<in T>. So when Kotlin writes a Java signature for fun <T : Comparable<T>> max(a: T, b: T), the bound becomes <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, the same bound the JDK writes by hand in Collections.max. That is how LocalDate, a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>, gets through a bound that says Comparable<LocalDate>. The sign rule also covers type arguments of variant classes. Inside class C<out T>, a parameter of type Comparable<T> is allowed: the parameter is −, and Comparable's in is −, so T ends up in a + position. A parameter of type MutableList<T> is not allowed in either kind of class: an invariant argument is a 0, and anything times 0 stays 0, which is neither in nor out. C# uses the same keywords, in and out, for interfaces and delegates, which is where Kotlin borrowed them. Scala writes +T and -T, the signs from the table. One caution for Java interop: when Java calls a Kotlin function with a parameter handler: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit, it sees Function1<? super PaymentEvent, Unit>. A Java lambda fits that type, but it must return Unit.INSTANCE. Kotlin APIs meant for Java callers often take a Java functional interface instead, or are marked fun interface.

h: Use-site variance and type projections · MutableList and Array can't pick a side, so you project them
x: Lessons 4 and 5 of this track put the variance on the class: Feed<out T> only hands values out, Sink<in T> only takes them in. Many types can't do that. MutableList<E> has get(): E and add(element: E). Array<T> has get and set. T sits in both positions, so the class must stay invariant, and lesson 3 showed what goes wrong when Java arrays pretend otherwise. The trouble is that one function rarely uses both sides. Here is the copy example from the Kotlin docs, first without any variance: fun copyRow(from: Array<Any>, to: Array<Any>) { for (i in from.indices) to[i] = from[i] } copyRow(amounts, row) // amounts is an Array<Int> Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Array<Int>', but 'Array<Any>' was expected. Kotlin refuses for a good reason. If copyRow could see an Array<Int> as an Array<Any>, it could write a String into it. But copyRow never writes to from. It only reads. So you tell the compiler that, right where the type is used: Java // Java arrays are covariant, so Object[] already accepts an Integer[] static void copyRow(Object[] from, Object[] to) { for (int i = 0; i < from.length; i++) to[i] = from[i]; // the JVM checks each store } copyRow(amounts, row); // fine copyRow(amounts, new String[3]); // compiles, then throws ArrayStoreException Kotlin fun copyRow(from: Array<out Any>, to: Array<Any>) { for (i in from.indices) to[i] = from[i] // get() on Array<out Any> returns Any } copyRow(amounts, row) // fine: Array<Int> fits Array<out Any> copyRow(amounts, arrayOfNulls<String>(3)) // compile error: Array<String?> is not an Array<Any> Array<out Any> is a type projection. You haven't changed Array. You've asked for a narrower view of it, for one parameter: an array of some subtype of Any that this function will only read. Through that view get returns Any, and set is gone: from[0] = "EUR" Receiver type 'Array<out Any>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun set(index: Int, value: T): Unit'. Writing the variance where a type is used is called use-site variance. Java's wildcards are the same idea, and they are the only kind of variance Java has. Arrays are the odd case on the Java side: there are no wildcards for arrays, because every Java array has been covariant since Java 1.0 and the JVM checks each store at run time instead. Kotlin's Array<out Any> compiles to a plain Object[]. The figure shows the three ways to look at one invariant type. Copy ints into a row of Any Run ArrayCopyDemo and its twin ArrayCopyDemoJava. Compare the second line of the Java output with the Kotlin file's wrong move 3. In ArrayCopyDemo.kt, predict the error for each of the three wrong moves. Uncomment them one at a time and run. Remove out from copyRow's first parameter. Which line in main breaks now? Put it back. ArrayCopyDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l06.demo /** * The Kotlin docs' copy example. Array is invariant, because it has get AND set. * This function only reads `from`, so it asks for an out-projection of it. */ fun copyRow(from: Array<out Any>, to: Array<Any>) { for (i in from.indices) to[i] = from[i] // get() on Array<out Any> returns Any: fine // from[0] = "EUR" // wrong move 2: an out-projection has no set() } fun main() { val amounts: Array<Int> = arrayOf(1_200, 350, 99) val row = Array<Any>(3) { "" } copyRow(amounts, row) // Array<Int> fits Array<out Any> println(row.joinToString()) // Wrong move 1: without a projection, Array<Int> is not an Array<Any>. // val strict: Array<Any> = amounts // Wrong move 3: the bug Java only finds at run time. Kotlin stops it here. // copyRow(amounts, arrayOfNulls<String>(3)) } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l06.demo.ArrayCopyDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l06/demo/ArrayCopyDemo.kt ArrayCopyDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l06.demo; import java.util.Arrays; /** * Java twin of ArrayCopyDemo.kt. Java arrays are covariant, so Object[] already accepts an Integer[]. * There is no wildcard for arrays. The price: the JVM checks every store at run time. */ public class ArrayCopyDemoJava { static void copyRow(Object[] from, Object[] to) { for (int i = 0; i < from.length; i++) to[i] = from[i]; // each store is checked by the JVM } public static void main(String[] args) { Integer[] amounts = {1_200, 350, 99}; Object[] row = new Object[3]; copyRow(amounts, row); System.out.println(Arrays.toString(row)); try { copyRow(amounts, new String[3]); // compiles: a String[] is an Object[] } catch (ArrayStoreException e) { System.out.println("ArrayStoreException: " + e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l06.demo.ArrayCopyDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l06/demo/ArrayCopyDemoJava.java Kotlin prints 1200, 350, 99. Java prints [1200, 350, 99] and then ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer: the store into a String[] compiled and failed at run time. The Kotlin wrong moves fail at compile time: (1) Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Array<Any>', actual 'Array<Int>'., (2) Receiver type 'Array<out Any>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun set(index: Int, value: T): Unit'., (3) Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Array<String?>', but 'Array<Any>' was expected. Without out, the call copyRow(amounts, row) fails the same way as wrong move 1. One invariant MutableList, three views: plain (read and write, exact type only), out-projected (read only), in-projected (write only). Generics: type projections (Kotlin docs) docs Think of an invariant MutableList as a shared ledger book in the finance office. The book itself allows reading and writing. A use-site projection is a permission slip for one visit. An out-projection is a reading-room pass: you may read every entry, and you're told only that each one is "some kind of number", so you are not allowed to write anything in. An in-projection is the drop slot in the door: you can post an entry of the agreed kind, and if you peek through the slot you see only "something". The book never changes; only what this visitor may do changes. The analogy breaks in one place: a reading-room pass in real life also stops you from tearing pages out, but an out-projection does not. clear() and removeAt() still work, because a projection limits types, not mutation.

h: Use-site variance and type projections · An out-projection is a read view, and Java spells it ? extends
x: The projection you'll write most often is on MutableList. Here is a function that totals any mutable list of numbers: Java static double total(List<? extends Number> amounts) { double sum = 0; for (Number a : amounts) sum += a.doubleValue(); // reads come out as Number return sum; } total(cents); // a List<Integer> total(rates); // a List<Double> Kotlin fun total(amounts: MutableList<out Number>): Double { var sum = 0.0 for (a in amounts) sum += a.toDouble() // reads come out as Number return sum } total(cents) // a MutableList<Int> total(rates) // a MutableList<Double> Read MutableList<out Number> as "a mutable list of some subtype of Number, and I don't know which". That unknown is why writing is forbidden. The list might be cents, a MutableList<Int>. Adding 2.5 would put a Double into a list of ints. So both compilers refuse every call that takes the element type: amounts.add(0) Kotlin: Receiver type 'MutableList<out Number>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'. Java: incompatible types: int cannot be converted to CAP#1 Even add(0) fails, though 0 is a fine Int. The compiler doesn't know the list holds ints. CAP#1 is javac's name for that unknown: a captured type, a placeholder for "the one real element type of this particular list". Kotlin prints it as CapturedType(out Number), for example when you try val x: Int = amounts[0]. Nothing you can write is known to be a subtype of the placeholder, so nothing goes in. Members that don't take an E still work. size, isEmpty(), removeAt(0) and clear() all compile through the view, as lesson 4 showed. A projection limits which types flow in. It does not stop the list from changing. You need this only for invariant types. Kotlin's read-only List is already declared List<out E>, so a plain List<Number> parameter accepts a List<Int>. Write List<out Number> and the compiler warns that the projection is redundant. You'll see that warning in this lesson's lab. Total two lists, then try to add Run ReadViewDemo (or ReadViewDemoJava). One function totals a list of ints and a list of doubles. Uncomment the two wrong moves one at a time, predict, run. Change total's parameter to read-only List<Number> and run. Then change it to List<out Number> and look for a w: line in the build output. ReadViewDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l06.demo /** Totals any mutable list of numbers. It only reads, so it asks for an out-projection. */ fun total(amounts: MutableList<out Number>): Double { var sum = 0.0 for (a in amounts) sum += a.toDouble() // reads come out as Number // amounts.add(0) // wrong move 1: no add() through an out-projection return sum } fun main() { val cents: MutableList<Int> = mutableListOf(1_200, 350, 99) val rates: MutableList<Double> = mutableListOf(0.5, 1.25) println("cents: ${total(cents)}, rates: ${total(rates)}") val view: MutableList<out Number> = cents // the same projection on a variable view.removeAt(0) // still allowed: removeAt takes an Int, not a T println("after removeAt through the view: $cents") // Wrong move 2: no projection, so a MutableList<Int> is not a MutableList<Number>. // val strict: MutableList<Number> = cents } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l06.demo.ReadViewDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l06/demo/ReadViewDemo.kt ReadViewDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l06.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of ReadViewDemo.kt. ? extends at the use site is Kotlin's out-projection. */ public class ReadViewDemoJava { static double total(List<? extends Number> amounts) { double sum = 0; for (Number a : amounts) sum += a.doubleValue(); // reads come out as Number // amounts.add(0); // wrong move 1: no add() through ? extends return sum; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Integer> cents = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1_200, 350, 99)); List<Double> rates = new ArrayList<>(List.of(0.5, 1.25)); System.out.println("cents: " + total(cents) + ", rates: " + total(rates)); List<? extends Number> view = cents; // the same wildcard on a variable view.remove(0); // still allowed: remove(int) takes no T System.out.println("after remove through the view: " + cents); // Wrong move 2: no wildcard, so a List<Integer> is not a List<Number>. // List<Number> strict = cents; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l06.demo.ReadViewDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l06/demo/ReadViewDemoJava.java Both print cents: 1649.0, rates: 1.75 and then [350, 99]: removeAt (Java: remove(int)) worked through the read view. add(0) fails with Receiver type 'MutableList<out Number>' contains out projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'. (Java: incompatible types: int cannot be converted to CAP#1), and the strict assignment with expected 'MutableList<Number>', actual 'MutableList<Int>' (Java: List<Integer> cannot be converted to List<Number>). List<Number> compiles with no projection; List<out Number> compiles with the warning Projection is redundant: the corresponding type parameter of 'List<out Number>' has the same variance. Use-site projections show up at the edges of a payment service, where you pass mutable buffers around. A Kafka batch listener collects records into a MutableList<PaymentEvent> and hands it to helpers: the fee calculator only reads, so it takes MutableList<out PaymentEvent> (or better, a plain List), and the enrichment step only appends CardAuthorized lines, so it takes MutableList<in CardAuthorized>. Your own invariant classes get the same treatment: a Quarkus-managed Ledger<T> or a Cache<K, V> with get and put stays invariant, and the report that only reads asks for Cache<String, out Money>. On the Java side of the codebase, the same contracts are List<? extends PaymentEvent> and List<? super CardAuthorized>, the shape of the JDK's Collections.addAll(Collection<? super T> c, T... elements).

h: Use-site variance and type projections · An in-projection is a write view, and Java spells it ? super
x: Now flip the direction. This helper appends zero-amount placeholder lines. It only ever writes Ints: Java static void padWithZeros(List<? super Integer> target, int count) { for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) target.add(0); } padWithZeros(ints, 1); // List<Integer> padWithZeros(numbers, 2); // List<Number> padWithZeros(anything, 2); // List<Object> Kotlin fun padWithZeros(target: MutableList<in Int>, count: Int) { repeat(count) { target.add(0) } } padWithZeros(ints, 1) // MutableList<Int> padWithZeros(numbers, 2) // MutableList<Number> padWithZeros(anything, 2) // MutableList<Any> MutableList<in Int> means "a mutable list of Int or of some supertype of Int". Every such list accepts an Int, so add(0) is safe. Reading is the side that gets weaker. An element might be the 2.5 or the "EUR" that was already in the list, so the only thing the compiler can promise is Any? (Java: Object): val firstInt: Int = target[0] Kotlin: Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Int', actual 'CapturedType(in Int)'. Java: incompatible types: CAP#1 cannot be converted to Integer A MutableList<Double> is rejected at the call, because it can't take an Int: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MutableList<Double>', but 'MutableList<in Int>' was expected. The JDK's utility methods are written this way, and calling them from Kotlin is a good way to learn the mapping. Two of them from java.util.Collections, and the same contracts in Kotlin: Java public static <T> void fill(List<? super T> list, T obj) { /* ... */ } public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) { /* ... */ } Kotlin fun <T> fill(list: MutableList<in T>, obj: T) { /* ... */ } fun <T> copy(dest: MutableList<in T>, src: List<T>) { /* ... */ } Pass the wrong thing to the real Collections.copy from Kotlin, and the error shows how Kotlin reads Java's wildcards: java.util.Collections.copy(ints, listOf("a")) Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'List<String>', but '(Mutable)List<out Int!>!' was expected. Java's ? extends became out. The rule in the Kotlin docs is that Foo<? extends Bar> becomes Foo<out Bar!>! and Foo<? super Bar> becomes Foo<in Bar!>!. The ! marks a platform type (Kotlin can't tell whether Java allows null), and (Mutable)List means Kotlin can't tell whether Java will modify the list. It works the other way too: a Kotlin parameter MutableList<in T> compiles to Java's List<? super T>. The lab's tests check exactly that. h: Use-site variance and type projections · Declare variance once when you can, project when you must
x: You now have two places to put out and in, and the rule for choosing is short. If every public member of a class only produces T, declare out T on the class. If every member only consumes T, declare in T. You do it once and every caller benefits: nobody writes a projection, and a List<Int> simply is a List<Number>. This is declaration-site variance, and it's why Kotlin code has far fewer wildcards than Java code. If the class both reads and writes T, it stays invariant: MutableList, Array, a cache, a repository with save and findById. Then each function that only reads, or only writes, asks for a projection: Java static final class Ledger<T> { // reads and writes T: invariant private final List<T> entries = new ArrayList<>(); void record(T entry) { entries.add(entry); } T latest() { return entries.get(entries.size() - 1); } } static String latestId(Ledger<? extends PaymentEvent> ledger) { return ledger.latest().getPaymentId(); } static void recordCard(Ledger<? super CardAuthorized> ledger, String id, long cents) { ledger.record(new CardAuthorized(id, cents)); } Kotlin class Ledger<T> { // reads and writes T: invariant private val entries = mutableListOf<T>() fun record(entry: T) { entries += entry } fun latest(): T = entries.last() } fun latestId(ledger: Ledger<out PaymentEvent>): String = ledger.latest().paymentId fun recordCard(ledger: Ledger<in CardAuthorized>, id: String, cents: Long) = ledger.record(CardAuthorized(id, cents)) Java has no declaration-site variance, so every Java API works like Ledger. Each method that only reads or only writes must remember its wildcard, and the JDK has hundreds of them. Forget one and your own tests still pass. The first caller with a List<Integer> finds out. The Kotlin compiler also guards the line between the two kinds: You write The compiler says List<out PaymentEvent> warning: Projection is redundant: the corresponding type parameter of 'List<out PaymentEvent>' has the same variance. List<in PaymentEvent> error: Projection conflicts with variance of the corresponding type parameter of 'List<in PaymentEvent>'. Remove the projection or replace it with '*'. fun <out T> onFunction(t: T) error: Variance annotations are only allowed for type parameters of classes and interfaces. The last one catches people. Variance says when a C<A> can stand in for a C<B>. A generic function is not a type you can substitute, so out on its own type parameter has nothing to describe. Put the projection on a parameter's type instead, as copyInto does. The '*' in the second message is the star projection, the subject of the next lesson. Read and write one invariant ledger Run ChooseDemo (or ChooseDemoJava). latestId reads a ledger of cards; recordCard writes into a ledger of every event. Uncomment the wrong move in main, predict, run. At the bottom of ChooseDemo.kt, predict which of lines 1 to 3 is a warning and which are errors. Uncomment them one at a time to check. ChooseDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l06.demo interface PaymentEvent { val paymentId: String } data class CardAuthorized(override val paymentId: String, val cents: Long) : PaymentEvent data class RefundIssued(override val paymentId: String, val cents: Long) : PaymentEvent /** Reads AND writes T, so it can't be declared out or in. It stays invariant. */ class Ledger<T> { private val entries = mutableListOf<T>() fun record(entry: T) { entries += entry } fun latest(): T = entries.last() } // Only reads: ask for a read view. A Ledger<CardAuthorized> fits. fun latestId(ledger: Ledger<out PaymentEvent>): String = ledger.latest().paymentId // Only writes cards: ask for a write view. A Ledger<PaymentEvent> fits. fun recordCard(ledger: Ledger<in CardAuthorized>, id: String, cents: Long) = ledger.record(CardAuthorized(id, cents)) fun main() { val cards = Ledger<CardAuthorized>() val everything = Ledger<PaymentEvent>() everything.record(RefundIssued("pay_1", 500)) recordCard(cards, "pay_2", 1_200) recordCard(everything, "pay_3", 350) println("${latestId(cards)} ${latestId(everything)}") // Wrong move: the class is invariant, so the plain type still doesn't fit. // val strict: Ledger<PaymentEvent> = cards } // Predict each line, then uncomment it alone and run. // fun redundant(events: List<out PaymentEvent>) {} // 1 // fun conflicting(events: List<in PaymentEvent>) {} // 2 // fun <out T> onFunction(t: T) {} // 3 ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l06.demo.ChooseDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l06/demo/ChooseDemo.kt ChooseDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l06.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of ChooseDemo.kt. Java has only use-site variance, so every class is like Ledger: * invariant, with ? extends or ? super written by each method that only reads or only writes. */ public class ChooseDemoJava { static final class Ledger<T> { private final List<T> entries = new ArrayList<>(); void record(T entry) { entries.add(entry); } T latest() { return entries.get(entries.size() - 1); } } // only reads: ? extends static String latestId(Ledger<? extends PaymentEvent> ledger) { return ledger.latest().getPaymentId(); } // only writes cards: ? super static void recordCard(Ledger<? super CardAuthorized> ledger, String id, long cents) { ledger.record(new CardAuthorized(id, cents)); } public static void main(String[] args) { Ledger<CardAuthorized> cards = new Ledger<>(); Ledger<PaymentEvent> everything = new Ledger<>(); everything.record(new RefundIssued("pay_1", 500)); recordCard(cards, "pay_2", 1_200); recordCard(everything, "pay_3", 350); System.out.println(latestId(cards) + " " + latestId(everything)); // Wrong move: the class is invariant, so the plain type still doesn't fit. // Ledger<PaymentEvent> strict = cards; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l06.demo.ChooseDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l06/demo/ChooseDemoJava.java Both print pay_2 pay_3. The wrong move fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Ledger<PaymentEvent>', actual 'Ledger<CardAuthorized>'. (Java: Ledger<CardAuthorized> cannot be converted to Ledger<PaymentEvent>): the projections are on the functions, not the class. Line 1 compiles with the Projection is redundant warning. Line 2 fails with Projection conflicts with variance of the corresponding type parameter of 'List<in PaymentEvent>'. Line 3 fails with Variance annotations are only allowed for type parameters of classes and interfaces. The common mistake is declaring a parameter MutableList<Number> (Java: List<Number>) when the function only reads it. It works for the first caller, who happens to have a list of Number. The next caller has a MutableList<Int> and fixes the type error with ints.toMutableList<Number>(), an unchecked cast, or a second copy of the function. People make the mistake because the plain type looks simpler, and because "an Int is a Number" makes it feel like it should work. The fix is to ask what the function does with the list. Only reads and never modifies: take a read-only List<Number>. Reads and also removes or clears: take MutableList<out Number>. Only adds: take MutableList<in Int>. Reads and adds: keep the plain type.

h: Use-site variance and type projections · Java and Kotlin
x: The same copy and fill contracts with wildcards and with projections Transfers.java import java.util.List; import java.util.Queue; import java.util.Collection; final class Transfers { // dest only takes T, src only gives T: the shape of Collections.copy static <T> int copyInto(List<? extends T> from, List<? super T> to) { for (T x : from) to.add(x); return from.size(); } // only writes: ? super static <T> void fillWith(List<? super T> target, T value, int count) { for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) target.add(value); } // a read-only parameter still needs ? extends in Java static double sumAll(List<? extends Number> amounts) { double sum = 0; for (Number a : amounts) sum += a.doubleValue(); return sum; } } Projections.kt // MutableList is invariant, so each function projects it at the use site fun <T> copyInto(from: MutableList<out T>, to: MutableList<in T>): Int { for (x in from) to.add(x) return from.size } fun <T> fillWith(target: MutableList<in T>, value: T, count: Int) { repeat(count) { target.add(value) } } // List is declared List<out E>: no projection needed (one would only earn a warning) fun sumAll(amounts: List<Number>): Double { var sum = 0.0 for (a in amounts) sum += a.toDouble() return sum } For MutableList, the two versions say exactly the same thing: Kotlin's MutableList<out T> compiles to Java's List<? extends T>, and MutableList<in T> to List<? super T>, and Kotlin shows Java's wildcards back to you as out and in. The real difference is sumAll. Java has no read-only list type with declared variance, so every reading parameter needs ? extends. Kotlin's List carries out E on its declaration, so the plain type is already flexible and a projection on it is redundant. Arrays differ too: Java arrays are covariant with run-time store checks and take no wildcards, while Kotlin's Array<out T> is a compile-time projection that compiles down to a plain Java array.

h: Use-site variance and type projections · Worked example
x: Settle pending authorizations into a batch of any events A settlement job moves pending card authorizations into the outgoing batch, then clears the pending list. The first draft uses plain types. The batch the caller has is a MutableList<PaymentEvent>, because it also holds refunds. Read the error. fun settle(pending: MutableList<CardAuthorized>, batch: MutableList<CardAuthorized>): Long { var cents = 0L for (a in pending) { batch.add(a); cents += a.cents } pending.clear() return cents } val pending = mutableListOf(CardAuthorized("pay_1", 1_200), CardAuthorized("pay_2", 350)) val batch = mutableListOf<PaymentEvent>(RefundIssued("pay_0", 500)) settle(pending, batch) // error: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MutableList<PaymentEvent>', // but 'MutableList<CardAuthorized>' was expected. static long settle(List<CardAuthorized> pending, List<CardAuthorized> batch) { long cents = 0; for (CardAuthorized a : pending) { batch.add(a); cents += a.cents(); } pending.clear(); return cents; } List<CardAuthorized> pending = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new CardAuthorized("pay_1", 1_200), new CardAuthorized("pay_2", 350))); List<PaymentEvent> batch = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new RefundIssued("pay_0", 500))); settle(pending, batch); // error: incompatible types: List<PaymentEvent> cannot be converted to List<CardAuthorized> Name what each parameter does with CardAuthorized values. pending gives them to you (and is cleared, which takes no element). batch only receives them. So pending is a producer and batch is a consumer, for this function only. Both types are MutableList, which can't be declared out or in, so the variance goes on the parameters. Project each parameter. Self-check before reading the comments: why does pending.clear() still compile through an out-projection? (It takes no E, so it can't smuggle a wrong type in.) fun settle(pending: MutableList<out CardAuthorized>, batch: MutableList<in CardAuthorized>): Long { var cents = 0L for (a in pending) { // 1. read: each a is a CardAuthorized batch.add(a) // 2. write: the batch takes CardAuthorized or anything above it cents += a.cents } pending.clear() // 3. no E in clear(), so the read view allows it return cents } settle(pending, batch) // compiles: 1550, and batch holds the refund plus both cards static long settle(List<? extends CardAuthorized> pending, List<? super CardAuthorized> batch) { long cents = 0; for (CardAuthorized a : pending) { // 1. read: producer extends batch.add(a); // 2. write: consumer super cents += a.cents(); } pending.clear(); // 3. no T in clear() return cents; } settle(pending, batch); // compiles Check the result from the caller's side. The batch can now be a MutableList<CardAuthorized>, a MutableList<PaymentEvent> or a MutableList<Any>. The pending list can be a list of any subtype of CardAuthorized. If you later need settle to read back from the batch (say, to dedupe by payment id), that read returns Any? through the in-projection, and the compiler tells you so. At that point the parameter really is read and write, and it should go back to the plain type.

h: Use-site variance and type projections · Key terms
x: Type projection out or in written on one use of a type, giving a read-only or write-only view of it. Use-site variance Variance written where a type is used (a parameter, a variable). Java's wildcards and Kotlin's projections. Declaration-site variance Variance written once on the class (interface List<out E>), so every use gets it. Out-projection C<out T>: you can read T values; calls that take a T are forbidden. In-projection C<in T>: you can pass T values in; reads come back as Any?. Captured type The compiler's placeholder for the one unknown real type behind a projection or wildcard (CAP#1, CapturedType(out Number)). Platform type A type from Java whose nullability Kotlin doesn't know, shown as T! (and (Mutable)List for Java lists). What is a type projection? Variance written where a type is used, such as MutableList<out Number> in a parameter. It narrows that one use to reading or to writing; the class itself stays invariant. Through MutableList<out Number>, what do get and add do? get returns Number. add is forbidden: the real list might be a MutableList<Int>. Through MutableList<in Int>, what type does get return? Any?. The list may be a MutableList<Number> or MutableList<Any?>, so nothing more specific is safe. Does clear() compile on a MutableList<out Payment>? Yes. clear() takes no element, so a projection doesn't block it. Projections limit types, not mutation. How does Kotlin show Java's List<? extends Integer> and List<? super Integer>? As (Mutable)List<out Int!>! and MutableList<in Int!>!: ? extends becomes out, ? super becomes in. Declaration-site or use-site variance: how do you choose? If every member only produces T (or only consumes it), declare out (or in) on the class. If the class both reads and writes T, keep it invariant and project in each function that uses one side. What does fun f(l: List<in String>) give? An error: the projection conflicts with List's declared out E. (List<out String> gives only a warning: the projection is redundant.)

h: Use-site variance and type projections · Go deeper
x: Both compilers turn a wildcard or projection into a fresh captured type each time they check an expression: "the one specific type this list really has". That's why CAP#1 shows up in javac messages. Java can also capture a wildcard for a method call, which gives a well-known trick: you can't write l.set(i, l.get(j)) on a List<?>, but you can pass the List<?> to a private generic helper <T> void swapHelper(List<T> l, int i, int j), and inside the helper the element type has a name. The JDK chose not to bother. Collections.swap(List<?> list, int i, int j) assigns the list to a raw List and calls l.set(i, l.set(j, l.get(i))) under @SuppressWarnings, with a source comment saying that capturing the wildcard would need a supplementary private method. Kotlin captures projected arguments for calls too. Given fun <T> swap(l: MutableList<T>, i: Int, j: Int), the calls swap(star, 0, 1) with star: MutableList<*> and swap(view, 0, 1) with view: MutableList<out Number> both compile with kotlinc 2.4.21. Inside swap, T is the captured type, so values read from the list may be written back into the same list. You'll meet MutableList<*> properly in the next lesson. Arrays have one more twist. Because Java arrays carry no wildcards, Kotlin compiles Array<out Number> and Array<Number> both to Number[], and Array<in Number> to Object[]. From Java, those differences are invisible; the projection exists only for the Kotlin compiler. The door opens the other way too. Kotlin shows a Java Object[] parameter as Array<(out) Any!>!, so you may pass an Array<String> to it, as Java code could. That brings Java's covariance back: java.util.Arrays.fill(names, 42) with names: Array<String> compiles in Kotlin and throws ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer at run time.

h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · List<*> is a list of some type you don't know
x: A logging helper has to accept every list in the codebase: a List<String> of payment ids, a List<Int> of amounts, a List<Settlement>. It never needs to know the element type. Kotlin's way to say that is a star projection: Java static void logAll(List<?> items) { for (Object item : items) System.out.println(" " + item); // each item is an Object } logAll(ids); // List<String> logAll(cents); // List<Integer> Kotlin fun logAll(items: List<*>) { for (item in items) println(" $item") // each item is Any? } logAll(ids) // List<String> logAll(cents) // List<Int> Read List<*> as "a list of some specific type, and I don't know which". The list really does have one element type. You've chosen not to name it. Java writes the same idea as List<?>, the unbounded wildcard. What can you do with a list of an unknown type? Ask the same two questions as in the last lesson. Reading is safe, but all you know is that each element is something, so it comes out as Any?. Writing is not safe: the list might be a MutableList<Int>, so no String may go in. Kotlin doesn't even let null in, because the unknown type might be non-nullable: star.add("pay_3") Receiver type 'MutableList<*>' contains star projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'. star.add(null) Null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'CapturedType(*)'. val id: String = star[0] Initializer type mismatch: expected 'String', actual 'CapturedType(*)'. Java is more relaxed about one of these. add(null) compiles on a List<?>, because every Java reference type allows null. add("pay_3") fails with String cannot be converted to CAP#1, the captured type from lesson 6. Everything that doesn't take an element still works: size, isEmpty(), removeAt(0), clear(). So a function that empties any buffer can take a MutableList<*>. That's the drain function in this lesson's lab. Log and empty lists of any type Run StarListDemo and StarListDemoJava. Compare the last line of the Java output with Kotlin's wrong move 2. In StarListDemo.kt, predict the error for each of the three wrong moves. Uncomment them one at a time and run. In the Java twin, uncomment wrong moves 1 and 3. Which Kotlin error has no Java twin?
