Java also prints after add(null): [null]. Kotlin's wrong moves fail with Receiver type 'MutableList<*>' contains star projection which prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean'., Null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'CapturedType(*)'. and Initializer type mismatch: expected 'String', actual 'CapturedType(*)'. Java's fail with String cannot be converted to CAP#1 and CAP#1 cannot be converted to String. The add(null) error has no Java twin. Generics: star-projections (Kotlin docs) docs A star-projected list is a sealed shipping container whose manifest has been torn off. You know it holds one kind of goods, you just don't know which. You may unload items and handle each one as "some item", you may count them, and you may empty the container. You may not load anything in, because you can't know whether it matches what's inside. MutableList<Any?> is a different container, one labeled "mixed goods", which takes anything; a container of bananas is not a mixed-goods container, even though bananas are goods. The analogy breaks at the dock: a worker could open a box and read the label on the goods, but the JVM cannot recover a list's element type at run time at all. That is why is List<String> isn't allowed.

h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · What * stands for depends on how the parameter is declared
x: Take Source<out T : Number> first. A Source<*> might be a Source<Int> or a Source<BigDecimal>. Whichever it is, next() returns some Number, so Number is the most the compiler can promise. Now take Sink<in T>. A Sink<*> might be a Sink<String> or a Sink<CardAuthorized>. No value is accepted by every one of them, so the compiler allows none. Nothing is Kotlin's name for a type with no values, which is exactly that answer. Both answers come from the substitution question of lesson 4, asked about every type the star could stand for. So a * is shorthand for the safest projection that the declaration allows, and what it means depends on the declared variance. The Kotlin docs write it as three rules: For Source<out T : Number>, Source<*> means Source<out Number>. You can read, and reads keep the bound: you get a Number, not an Any?. For Sink<in T>, Sink<*> means Sink<in Nothing>. No value has type Nothing, so you can't pass anything in at all. For an invariant Box<T>, Box<*> means Box<out Any?> when you read and Box<in Nothing> when you write. (With a bound, Box<T : Payment>, reads would give Payment.) Java interface Source<T extends Number> { T next(); } interface Sink<T> { void accept(T item); } static Number peek(Source<?> source) { return source.next(); } // the bound survives the ? Sink<?> anySink = audit; anySink.accept("pay_1"); // error: String cannot be converted to CAP#1 anySink.accept(null); // compiles in Java Kotlin interface Source<out T : Number> { fun next(): T } interface Sink<in T> { fun accept(item: T) } fun peek(source: Source<*>): Number = source.next() // the bound survives the * val anySink: Sink<*> = audit anySink.accept("pay_1") // error: Receiver type 'Sink<*>' contains star projection which prohibits ... The invariant case shows the Nothing plainly. Assign to the property of a Box<*> and the compiler says what it expected: Assignment type mismatch: actual type is 'String', but 'Nothing' was expected. With several type parameters, each star is projected on its own. Map<*, *> reads keys and values as Any?. A function type (Int) -> String is Function1<in P, out R>, so Function1<*, String> is Function1<in Nothing, String>. You can't call it, because no argument fits, but you know any result would be a String. Function1<Int, *> is the opposite: you can call it with an Int, and the result is Any?. The same reasoning rules out comparing through a Comparable<*>: Receiver type 'Comparable<*>' contains star projection which prohibits the use of 'fun compareTo(other: T): Int'. The figure puts the three rules side by side. Read a Source<>, try to feed a Sink<> Before running StarRulesDemo, predict the static type of peek(amounts): Any?, Number or Int? Run it (or StarRulesDemoJava). Uncomment the three wrong moves one at a time. Which message mentions Nothing? StarRulesDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l07.demo /** out T with a bound: Source<*> means Source<out Number>. */ interface Source<out T : Number> { fun next(): T } /** in T: Sink<*> means Sink<in Nothing>. */ interface Sink<in T> { fun accept(item: T) } /** invariant T: Box<*> reads as Box<out Any?> and writes as Box<in Nothing>. */ class Box<T>(var item: T) fun peek(source: Source<*>): Number = source.next() // the bound survives the star fun peek(box: Box<*>): Any? = box.item fun main() { val amounts: Source<Int> = object : Source<Int> { override fun next() = 1_200 } val audit: Sink<String> = object : Sink<String> { override fun accept(item: String) = println("audit $item") } val box: Box<String> = Box("EUR") println("peek(source) = ${peek(amounts)}, peek(box) = ${peek(box)}") audit.accept("pay_0") // through the real type: fine val anySink: Sink<*> = audit // through *: nothing can be passed in val anyBox: Box<*> = box println("a Box<*> still reads: ${anyBox.item}") // Wrong moves. Uncomment one at a time, predict the error, then run. // anySink.accept("pay_1") // 1 // anyBox.item = "USD" // 2 // val n: Int = peek(amounts) // 3 } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l07.demo.StarRulesDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l07/demo/StarRulesDemo.kt StarRulesDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l07.demo; /** Java twin of StarRulesDemo.kt. Uncomment one at a time, predict the error, then run. // anySink.accept("pay_1"); // 1 // anyBox.item = "USD"; // 2 // Integer n = peek(amounts); // 3 } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l07.demo.StarRulesDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l07/demo/StarRulesDemoJava.java Both print peek(source) = 1200, peek(box) = EUR, audit pay_0 and a Box<*> still reads: EUR (Box<?> in Java). Java also prints audit null, because accept(null) is allowed through ?. The static type of peek(amounts) is Number: the bound survives the star. Kotlin errors: (1) Receiver type 'Sink<*>' contains star projection which prohibits the use of 'fun accept(item: T): Unit'., (2) Assignment type mismatch: actual type is 'String', but 'Nothing' was expected., (3) Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Int', actual 'Number'. Java: String cannot be converted to CAP#1 twice, then Number cannot be converted to Integer. A star is replaced by the safest projection: the bound for reading an out parameter, Nothing for writing an in or invariant one. Star projections are the honest type for data whose shape you only learn at run time. A webhook from a card issuer parsed with objectMapper.readValue(body, Map::class.java) comes back as a Map<*, *>, because Map::class.java is a Class<Map<*, *>>. Kafka record headers, Temporal payload converters and Quarkus config maps all hand you values of unknown element type. Log them with Map<*, *> and List<*>, check shapes with is Map<*, *>, and pull out typed values element by element with as?. A metrics helper that reports the size of any in-memory buffer takes a Collection<*>. On the Java side of the codebase, replace raw List and Map parameters with List<?> and Map<?, ?>.

h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · is not Any?, and it is not a raw type
x: Two other types look like "a list of anything", and both differ from *. MutableList<Any?> is a list whose element type is exactly Any?. You can add anything to it. But MutableList is invariant, so a MutableList<String> is not a MutableList<Any?>, and a function that takes one won't accept the other: Java static void addMarker(List<Object> list) { list.add("marker"); } static int sizeOf(List<?> list) { return list.size(); } addMarker(anything); // a List<Object>: fine sizeOf(ids); // a List<String>: fine addMarker(ids); // error: List<String> cannot be converted to List<Object> Kotlin fun addMarker(list: MutableList<Any?>) { list.add("marker") } fun sizeOf(list: MutableList<*>): Int = list.size addMarker(anything) // a MutableList<Any?>: fine sizeOf(ids) // a MutableList<String>: fine addMarker(ids) // error: actual type is 'MutableList<String>', but 'MutableList<Any?>' was expected. So choose by what the function does. If it adds arbitrary values, it needs a real MutableList<Any?> and can only take one. If it doesn't care about the element type, it takes MutableList<*> and accepts every mutable list. For read-only List the difference disappears: List is covariant, so List<Any?> and List<*> accept the same arguments. Java has a third option that Kotlin doesn't: the raw type. A raw List, with no angle brackets at all, switches generic checking off. It exists so that code written before Java 5 added generics still compiles: Java @SuppressWarnings({"rawtypes", "unchecked"}) static void addRaw(List list) { list.add(42); } addRaw(ids); // compiles: an Integer goes into a List<String> String last = ids.get(1); // ClassCastException here, far from the bug Kotlin // Kotlin has no raw types. A Java raw List arrives in Kotlin as List<*>, // so the same write is refused at compile time: fun addRaw(list: MutableList<*>) { list.add(42) } // error: ... prohibits the use of 'fun add(element: E): Boolean' The Kotlin docs say star projections are "very much like Java's raw types, but safe". In Java, write List<?> instead of a raw List whenever you mean "I don't know the type". It reads the same and keeps the checks on. Compare Any?, * and a raw type Run StarVsAnyDemo and StarVsAnyDemoJava. Find the line in the Java output where the raw type's damage shows up. Uncomment the wrong move in either file, predict, run. In StarVsAnyDemo.kt, change addMarker's parameter to MutableList<*>. Which line breaks now, and why? It can't add, but it can count. */ fun sizeOf(list: MutableList<*>): Int = list.size fun main() { val anything: MutableList<Any?> = mutableListOf(1_200, "EUR", null) val ids: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf("pay_1") addMarker(anything) // fine: it really is a list of Any? println("anything = $anything, sizeOf(ids) = ${sizeOf(ids)}, sizeOf(anything) = ${sizeOf(anything)}") // Read-only List is covariant, so here * and Any? accept the same arguments: val a: List<Any?> = ids val b: List<*> = ids println("a = $a, b = $b") // Wrong move. h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · Type checks need a star, then you check each element
x: JSON libraries, message headers and old Java APIs hand you values typed Any? or Map<*, *>. To use them, you check what they are. The first check most people write doesn't compile: if (amounts is List<Long>) println("a list of longs") Cannot check for instance of erased type 'List<Long>'. At run time a List<Long> and a List<String> are the same kind of ArrayList object, so the JVM can check the class and nothing more. Lesson 8 of this track explains erasure in full. For now the rule is: check with a star, then check each element you use. Java static List<Long> amountsIn(Object payload) { List<Long> out = new ArrayList<>(); if (payload instanceof List<?> list) { for (Object e : list) if (e instanceof Long l) out.add(l); // check every element } return out; } Kotlin fun amountsIn(payload: Any?): List<Long> { if (payload !is List<*>) return emptyList() return payload.mapNotNull { it as? Long } // payload is now a List<*>; check each element } After the !is List<*> line returns early, the compiler smart-casts payload to List<*> for the rest of the function. A when with is List<*> and is Map<*, *> branches does the same in each branch. Java's instanceof List<?> list (pattern matching for instanceof, final since Java 16) gives you the same kind of typed variable. Java's error for the bad check is Object cannot be safely cast to List<Long>. One full check does compile: when the compiler already knows the type argument. With c: Collection<String>, c is List<String> is fine, because only the class part needs checking at run time. The shortcut to avoid is payload as List<Long>. It compiles with an unchecked-cast warning and succeeds for any list at all. The ClassCastException comes later, at whichever line first reads a String as a Long. Checking the elements costs one line and fails in the right place. Better still, avoid the untyped route when you can. Ask the JSON library to bind the body to a data class, and the checking happens once, inside the library. Lesson 9 of this track shows how type tokens make that work for generic targets such as List<Settlement>. Pick apart an untyped webhook payload Run IsCheckDemo (or IsCheckDemoJava). The payload's amounts list contains a stray "oops". Uncomment the wrong move, predict, run. Replace it as? Long with it as Long and run again. Where does it fail, and is that where the bad data came from? IsCheckDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l07.demo /** A webhook payload arrives as Any? from a JSON library. Find out what it is. */ fun shape(payload: Any?): String = when (payload) { null -> "empty" is Map<*, *> -> "object with keys ${payload.keys}" // smart cast to Map<*, *> is List<*> -> "array of ${payload.size}" // smart cast to List<*> else -> "value $payload" } /** Safe: check every element instead of trusting the list's type. */ fun amountsIn(payload: Any?): List<Long> { if (payload !is List<*>) return emptyList() return payload.mapNotNull { it as? Long } // as? gives null for non-Longs } fun main() { val webhook: Any? = mapOf("id" to "pay_1", "amounts" to listOf(1_200L, "oops", 350L)) println(shape(webhook)) println(shape(listOf(1, 2, 3))) println(shape(42)) val amounts = (webhook as Map<*, *>)["amounts"] println("amounts = ${amountsIn(amounts)}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // if (amounts is List<Long>) println("a list of longs") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l07.demo.IsCheckDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l07/demo/IsCheckDemo.kt IsCheckDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l07.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Java twin of IsCheckDemo.kt. instanceof works with List<?> and Map<?, ?>, not with List<Long>. */ public class IsCheckDemoJava { static String shape(Object payload) { if (payload == null) return "empty"; if (payload instanceof Map<?, ?> map) return "object with keys " + map.keySet(); if (payload instanceof List<?> list) return "array of " + list.size(); return "value " + payload; } static List<Long> amountsIn(Object payload) { List<Long> out = new ArrayList<>(); if (payload instanceof List<?> list) { for (Object e : list) if (e instanceof Long l) out.add(l); // check every element } return out; } public static void main(String[] args) { Map<String, Object> fields = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // keeps key order, like Kotlin's mapOf fields.put("id", "pay_1"); fields.put("amounts", List.of(1_200L, "oops", 350L)); Object webhook = fields; System.out.println(shape(webhook)); System.out.println(shape(List.of(1, 2, 3))); System.out.println(shape(42)); Object amounts = ((Map<?, ?>) webhook).get("amounts"); System.out.println("amounts = " + amountsIn(amounts)); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // if (amounts instanceof List<Long>) System.out.println("a list of longs"); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l07.demo.IsCheckDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l07/demo/IsCheckDemoJava.java Both print object with keys [id, amounts], array of 3, value 42 and amounts = [1200, 350]: the stray string is skipped. The wrong move fails with Cannot check for instance of erased type 'List<Long>'. (Java: Object cannot be safely cast to List<Long>). With as Long, the run fails with ClassCastException: class java.lang.String cannot be cast to class java.lang.Long inside amountsIn, far from wherever the payload was built. The common mistake is writing Any? when you mean "unknown": fun logAll(items: MutableList<Any?>) or fun audit(fields: Map<Any?, Any?>). It looks maximally general, but MutableList and Map's key are invariant, so a caller's MutableList<String> or Map<String, Int> is rejected, and the caller ends up copying or casting to fit. The Java version of the same reflex is a raw List parameter, which compiles for everyone and silently turns checking off. The fix is to say what you mean: MutableList<*> / Map<*, *> in Kotlin and List<?> / Map<?, ?> in Java when you don't care about the type, and a real MutableList<Any?> only when you genuinely store arbitrary values.

h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · Java and Kotlin
x: Unknown type arguments: Kotlin's * and Java's ? Payloads.java import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.stream.Collectors; final class Payloads { static String describe(Object value) { if (value == null) return "nothing"; if (value instanceof String s) return "text " + s; if (value instanceof List<?> l) return "list of " + l.size(); // List<String> would not compile if (value instanceof Map<?, ?> m) return "map of " + m.size(); return "other"; } static String render(Map<?, ?> map) { // keys and values are Object return map.entrySet().stream() .sorted((a, b) -> String.valueOf(a.getKey()).compareTo(String.valueOf(b.getKey()))) .map(e -> e.getKey() + "=" + (e.getValue() instanceof Map<?, ?> m ? render(m) : e.getValue())) .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "{", "}")); } static int drain(List<?> buffer) { // not a raw List: checks stay on int n = buffer.size(); buffer.clear(); return n; } } Payloads.kt fun describe(value: Any?): String = when (value) { null -> "nothing" is String -> "text $value" is List<*> -> "list of ${value.size}" // List<String> would not compile is Map<*, *> -> "map of ${value.size}" else -> "other" } fun render(map: Map<*, *>): String = // keys and values are Any? map.entries .sortedBy { it.key.toString() } .joinToString(", ", "{", "}") { (k, v) -> "$k=${if (v is Map<*, *>) render(v) else v}" } fun drain(buffer: MutableList<*>): Int { // Kotlin has no raw types val n = buffer.size buffer.clear() return n } Kotlin's MutableList<*> compiles to Java's List<?>, and the two behave almost the same: reads give Any? / Object, writes of real values are refused, and members that take no element still work. Three things differ. Java lets you pass null through a ?; Kotlin refuses, because the unknown type might be non-nullable. Java still has raw types, which switch checking off; Kotlin has none, and shows a Java raw List as List<*>. And Kotlin works out what * means from the declaration's variance, so a star on an in parameter becomes in Nothing and a star on an out T : Number keeps the Number bound, while Java applies the same capture rules to every wildcard.

h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · Worked example
x: Render an untyped webhook payload for the audit log A card issuer's webhook is parsed into a map whose types you don't control. The first draft of the audit renderer asks for Map<Any?, Any?> to be "as general as possible". The parsed map in a test is a Map<String, Int>. Read the error. fun render(map: Map<Any?, Any?>): String = map.toString() val webhook: Map<String, Int> = mapOf("cents" to 1_200) render(webhook) // error: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Map<String, Int>', but 'Map<Any?, Any?>' was expected. static String render(Map<Object, Object> map) { return map.toString(); } Map<String, Integer> webhook = Map.of("cents", 1_200); render(webhook); // error: incompatible types: Map<String,Integer> cannot be converted to Map<Object,Object> Map<K, out V> is covariant in V but invariant in K, so Map<String, Int> is not a Map<Any?, Any?>. The renderer never puts anything into the map; it only reads. So it doesn't need to name either type. Use one star per type parameter. fun render(map: Map<*, *>): String = map.entries .sortedBy { it.key.toString() } // 1. keys are Any?: toString() works, even on null .joinToString(", ", "{", "}") { (k, v) -> "$k=$v" } static String render(Map<?, ?> map) { return map.entrySet().stream() .sorted(Comparator.comparing(e -> String.valueOf(e.getKey()))) // 1. keys are Object .map(e -> e.getKey() + "=" + e.getValue()) .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "{", "}")); } Payloads nest: the card field is itself a map. Check the value's shape with a star, and the smart cast gives you a Map<*, *> to recurse on. Self-check before reading the comment: why not v is Map<String, Any?>? (Type arguments are erased, so the compiler refuses that check.) fun render(map: Map<*, *>): String = map.entries .sortedBy { it.key.toString() } .joinToString(", ", "{", "}") { (k, v) -> val shown = if (v is Map<*, *>) render(v) else v.toString() // 2. smart cast to Map<*, *> "$k=$shown" } render(mapOf("cents" to 99, "card" to mapOf("scheme" to "visa", "last4" to "4242"))) // {card={last4=4242, scheme=visa}, cents=99} static String render(Map<?, ?> map) { return map.entrySet().stream() .sorted(Comparator.comparing(e -> String.valueOf(e.getKey()))) .map(e -> e.getKey() + "=" + (e.getValue() instanceof Map<?, ?> m ? render(m) : e.getValue())) // 2. pattern match .collect(Collectors.joining(", ", "{", "}")); } Now any map fits: Map<String, Int>, Map<String, Any?>, the Map<*, *> that a JSON library returns, or a map with Int keys. x: val star: MutableList<*> = mutableListOf("pay_1"). Which line compiles? star.add("pay_2") star.add(null) star.removeAt(0) val s: String = star[0] removeAt takes an index, not an element, so the star doesn't block it. Both add calls pass an element of the unknown type, which Kotlin refuses (even null, since the type might be non-nullable). A read gives only CapturedType(*), which is not known to be a String. interface Source<out T : Number> { fun next(): T } and fun f(s: Source<*>). What is the static type of s.next() inside f? Any? Number Nothing It doesn't compile: you can't call anything on a star projection For an out parameter with a bound, Source<*> means Source<out Number>, so reads keep the bound. Any? is what you'd get with no bound. Nothing is what a star gives on the writing side of an in or invariant parameter. You need a function that appends an audit marker string to whatever list a caller passes: a MutableList<String>, a MutableList<Any> or a MutableList<CharSequence>. Which parameter type fits? MutableList<*> MutableList<Any?> List<Any?> MutableList<in String> The function writes Strings and never reads, so it is a consumer: MutableList<in String> accepts lists of String or any supertype. A star forbids add. MutableList<Any?> accepts only lists of exactly Any?. List has no add at all. This is the "pick the right tool" contrast: * when you neither read typed values nor write, in when you write. Java: List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay_1")); List raw = ids; raw.add(42); Then String s = ids.get(1);. What happens? A compile error at raw.add(42) It compiles (with an unchecked warning) and throws ClassCastException at ids.get(1) It throws ArrayStoreException at raw.add(42) It runs fine and s is "42" A raw type turns generic checking off, so the Integer goes in. Erasure means the ArrayList can't notice. The cast that javac inserted at ids.get(1) fails, far from the bad write. ArrayStoreException is the array version of this check, which lists don't have. In Kotlin the same write fails to compile, because a raw List is seen as List<*>. From "Use-site variance and type projections": which signature lets copyAll copy a MutableList<Int> into a MutableList<Number>? fun <T> copyAll(from: MutableList<out T>, to: MutableList<in T>) fun copyAll(from: MutableList<*>, to: MutableList<*>) fun <T> copyAll(from: MutableList<T>, to: MutableList<T>) fun copyAll(from: MutableList<Any?>, to: MutableList<Any?>) from only gives values (out T) and to only takes them (in T), so T = Int works with a MutableList<Number> target. h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · Key terms
x: Star projection C<*>: a C of some type argument you don't know. Kotlin picks the safest projection for it. Unbounded wildcard Java's ? with no bound, as in List<?>: the Java twin of *. Raw type A Java generic type used with no type arguments at all (List). Generic checks are off for it. in Nothing What a star means on the writing side: only a Nothing could be passed, and no such value exists. Smart cast After if (x is List<*>), the compiler treats x as a List<*> without an explicit cast. Erased type A type argument that exists only at compile time. At run time a List<String> is just a List. What does List<*> mean? A list of one specific element type that you don't know or don't care about. Reads come out as Any?. Java's spelling is List<?>. Can you call add(null) on a MutableList<*>? Not in Kotlin: Null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'CapturedType(*)'. Java's List<?> does allow add(null). For interface Sink<in T>, what does Sink<*> mean? Sink<in Nothing>: no value fits, so you can't call accept at all. For interface Source<out T : Number>, what does Source<*> mean? Source<out Number>: reads give Number, because the bound survives the star. Why does fun f(l: MutableList<Any?>) reject a MutableList<String>? MutableList is invariant and Any? is a specific type argument. Use MutableList<*> if f doesn't need to add. How does Kotlin see a Java parameter of raw type List? As a star projection, List<*>, so Kotlin code can't write unchecked elements into it. payload: Any?. Why payload is List<*> and not payload is List<String>? Type arguments are erased at run time, so the JVM can only check the class. Check with a star, then check each element.

h: Star projection: when you don't know the type · Go deeper
x: Kotlin can still call a generic function with a star-projected argument. Given fun <T> swap(l: MutableList<T>, i: Int, j: Int), the call swap(star, 0, 1) with star: MutableList<*> compiles with kotlinc 2.4.21 and swaps the two elements. The compiler captures the unknown element type as T for that one call, so inside swap a value read from the list may be written back into the same list. Java does the same with a private helper method, the "capture helper" pattern; the JDK's Collections.swap(List<?> list, int i, int j) skips it and uses a raw type under @SuppressWarnings. The Map interface has a detail worth knowing. It is declared Map<K, out V>, invariant in K. So on a Map<*, *> the member get(key: K) would take in Nothing, and you could never look anything up. The standard library adds an extension, Map<out K, V>.get(key: K), so payload["amounts"] on a Map<*, *> still compiles and returns Any?. Stars also appear in class literals: Map::class.java is a Class<Map<*, *>>, and listOf(1)::class is a KClass<out List<Int>>. The class object of a generic class exists once for all type arguments, so it can't carry them. Lesson 9 of this track is about exactly that. And in Kotlin's own reflection, typeOf<List<*>>().arguments prints [*]: the star is part of the type, not an absence of one.

h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · Type arguments vanish when the code compiles
x: Lesson 7 hit a wall: is List<Long> doesn't compile. Here is why. Both compilers check type arguments and then remove them. At run time a List<String> and a List<Int> are the same kind of object: Java List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(); List<Integer> cents = new ArrayList<>(); System.out.println(ids.getClass() == cents.getClass()); // true: both are java.util.ArrayList Kotlin val ids = ArrayList<String>() val cents = ArrayList<Int>() println(ids.javaClass == cents.javaClass) // true: both are java.util.ArrayList This is type erasure. Java 5 added generics this way so that old and new class files could run on the same JVM. Kotlin compiles to the same JVM and inherits the rule. The compiler checks the type argument, and then it is gone: the object has no field that says String. Here is what both compilers leave in the class file. Each type parameter becomes its bound: a plain T becomes Object, and T : Comparable<T> becomes Comparable. So List.get returns an Object. Where your code needs a String, the compiler inserts a checkcast instruction to String right after the call. Run javap -c on any class that reads from a List<String> and you'll see it. That inserted cast is the line that throws in the last example below. Three things follow, and each has an error you'll meet: A type check can test only the class. x is List<String> fails with Cannot check for instance of erased type 'List<String>'., and is T fails the same way. Java says Object cannot be safely cast to List<String>. You can't create a T. Kotlin's T() gives Type parameter 'T' is not an expression. and Java's new T() gives unexpected type. A cast to a generic type checks only the class. This one compiles, with a warning, and it's the dangerous one: Java @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") List<String> lies = (List<String>) (Object) List.of(1_200, 350); lies.size(); // 2: the cast "worked" String first = lies.get(0); // ClassCastException: Integer cannot be cast to String Kotlin @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val lies = listOf(1_200, 350) as Any as List<String> lies.size // 2: the cast "worked" val first: String = lies[0] // ClassCastException: Integer cannot be cast to String The list now claims to hold strings and holds integers. That state is called heap pollution. The exception appears at the first read that needs a String, which may be in another class written by another team. Some generic information does survive. The signatures of declarations (a field's type, a method's parameters, a class's superclass) stay in the class file, and reflection can read them: Field.getGenericType() on a List<String> field returns java.util.List<java.lang.String>. What erasure removes is the type argument of each object. Lesson 9 puts the surviving part to work. Watch a cast succeed and a read fail Run ErasureDemo and ErasureDemoJava. Before you do, predict which of the three numbered steps throws. Uncomment wrong move 1 in either file, predict the error, run. Uncomment wrong move 2 (a top-level function) and run. Put both back. Generics: type erasure (Kotlin docs) docs Erasure is a warehouse that checks the packing list at the packing table and then throws it away. The box that goes on the truck says only "box". At the receiving dock, nobody can tell whether it holds shirts or shoes without opening it and looking at each item. A reified function is a mail merge: because each letter is printed separately for its recipient, each copy can carry the recipient's name. That is what inline buys you: one copy per call site, so the known type can be printed into each copy. The analogy breaks at nesting. A mail merge could print the whole address, but reified prints only the outer class: List<String> arrives as just List.

h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · inline and reified bring T back at each call site
x: Erasure removes T, and inline with reified writes the real class into each call site Kotlin has one way around erasure. Mark a function inline, and the compiler copies its body into every call site instead of calling it. At each call site the type argument is known, because isA<String>() is being compiled right there with String in plain sight. Mark the type parameter reified, and the compiler writes that real class into the copied body: Java // Java has no reified type parameters. The closest equivalent: pass the Class yourself. static boolean isA(Object x, Class<?> type) { return type.isInstance(x); } static <T> List<T> filterIsInstance(List<?> items, Class<T> type) { return items.stream().filter(type::isInstance).map(type::cast).toList(); } isA("pay_1", String.class); // true filterIsInstance(payload, String.class); // [pay_1, pay_2] Kotlin inline fun <reified T> Any?.isA(): Boolean = this is T // a real instanceof after inlining "pay_1".isA<String>() // true payload.filterIsInstance<String>() // [pay_1, pay_2]: the stdlib's reified filter Inside a reified function you get back what erasure took away: x is T, x as T and x as? T with a real check, T::class and T::class.java. The standard library relies on this for filterIsInstance<T>(), emptyArray<T>() and typeOf<T>(), which lesson 9 covers. The rules follow from how it works: You write Kotlin says fun <reified T> notInline(x: Any) = x is T Only type parameters of inline functions can be reified. fun <T> forward(x: Any) = x.isA<T>() Cannot use 'T' as reified type parameter. Use a class instead. classOf<Nothing>(TODO()) Cannot use 'Nothing' as reified type parameter. The second row matters in practice. A reified function can only be called with a type the caller knows. If the caller is itself generic with an ordinary T, its T is erased, so there is nothing to copy in. The requirement spreads upward: the caller must be inline with a reified T too, or it must pass a real class. The figure puts an erased call and an inlined one side by side. h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · Java passes a Class , and can't call reified functions
x: Before reified, the standard answer was a class token: pass the Class<T> as an argument and let it do the run-time work the erased T can't. Java APIs still look like this: entityManager.find(Payment.class, id), objectMapper.readValue(json, Payment.class). type.isInstance(x) is a checked is T, and type.cast(x) is a checked as T with no warning. Kotlin writes the token as Payment::class.java. Good Kotlin libraries offer both: a core that takes a Class<T> (or a KClass<T>) and works for everyone, plus a one-line reified wrapper for Kotlin callers: Java // Java calling the Kotlin functions in ClassTokenDemo.kt: BigDecimal zero = ClassTokenDemoKt.defaultOf(BigDecimal.class); // the Class-token core: fine BigDecimal viaReified = ClassTokenDemoKt.<BigDecimal>defaultOf(); // error: method defaultOf ... cannot be applied to given types Kotlin fun <T : Any> defaultOf(type: Class<T>): T = type.cast(defaults[type] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("no default for ${type.simpleName}")) inline fun <reified T : Any> defaultOf(): T = defaultOf(T::class.java) val zero: BigDecimal = defaultOf() // T inferred from the expected type Why can't Java call the wrapper? javac can't inline Kotlin code, so it has no way to supply T. Kotlin still writes a method for the wrapper into the class file, but flags it ACC_SYNTHETIC, and javac ignores synthetic methods. Read the error again: javac says defaultOf needs an argument, because the only defaultOf it can see is the Class-token one. A reified function with no such overload gives cannot find symbol. So if Java code will call your API, the Class-token version is not optional. One trap with tokens: Int::class.java is the primitive class int, but T::class.java for a reified Int is java.lang.Integer. A registry filled with one and queried with the other finds nothing. h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · What reified still can't do
x: Reified brings back the class at the call site, and only the class. Three limits are worth knowing. The type arguments of T itself are still erased. filterIsInstance<List<String>>() compiles without a single warning, and it keeps every list: Java // the Java version passes List.class: there is no List<String>.class List<List<String>> stringLists = filterIsInstance(batches, List.class); System.out.println(stringLists); // [[1200, 350], [pay_1]] String n = stringLists.get(0).get(0); // ClassCastException Kotlin val batches: List<Any> = listOf(listOf(1_200, 350), listOf("pay_1"), "pay_2") val stringLists = batches.filterIsInstance<List<String>>() // no warning println(stringLists) // [[1200, 350], [pay_1]] val n: String = stringLists[0][0] // ClassCastException The Kotlin docs say the same about their asPairOf<String, List<String>>() example: it "compiles but breaks type safety". After inlining, is List<String> is only instanceof List. Nothing and erased type parameters can't be reified, as the table above showed. And Kotlin 2.4 added an error about null. Inside inline fun <reified T> klassOf(x: T) = x::class, T may be a nullable type, so x may be null, and null has no class. Kotlin 2.3 warned about this; 2.4 refuses: Expression in class literal has nullable type 'T (of fun <T> klassOf)'. Use '!!' to make the type non-nullable. The fix is to say what you mean with <reified T : Any>, so callers can't pass null at all. T::class, the class literal of the type rather than of a value, is still allowed with a nullable bound. Java has no such check: x.getClass() on a null x throws NullPointerException at run time. So treat reified as a convenience for the outer class of a type: instance checks, casts and class tokens. When the full type matters, List<Settlement> and not just List, you need something that keeps the arguments. That's KType, in the next lesson. Find the edges of reified Run LimitsDemo (or LimitsDemoJava). Is the first line what filterIsInstance<List<String>>() promised? Uncomment wrong move 1 and run. Then uncomment wrong move 2: it compiles, so predict what happens when it runs. Uncomment the klassOf function at the bottom (3), read the Kotlin 2.4 error, then fix it by changing <reified T> to <reified T : Any>. LimitsDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l08.demo inline fun <reified T : Any> classOf(x: T) = x::class // T : Any, so x can't be null fun main() { // 1. Reified T is the outer class only. Nested type arguments are still erased. val batches: List<Any> = listOf(listOf(1_200, 350), listOf("pay_1"), "pay_2") val stringLists = batches.filterIsInstance<List<String>>() // compiles with no warning at all println("lists of strings? $stringLists") // 2. With a non-null bound, x::class is fine. println("classOf(\"pay_1\") = ${classOf("pay_1").simpleName}") // Wrong moves. Uncomment one at a time, predict the error, then run. // val nothing = classOf<Nothing>(TODO()) // 1 // val n: String = stringLists[0][0] // 2 (compiles: what happens at run time?) } // 3. Kotlin 2.4 turned this into an error: T may be nullable, and null has no class. // inline fun <reified T> klassOf(x: T) = x::class ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l08.demo.LimitsDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l08/demo/LimitsDemo.kt LimitsDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l08.demo; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of LimitsDemo.kt. The closest Java equivalent passes a Class token, and a Class token * has the same limit as a reified T: List.class stands for every List, whatever its elements. */ public class LimitsDemoJava { @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") static <T> List<T> filterIsInstance(List<?> items, Class<?> type) { return (List<T>) items.stream().filter(type::isInstance).toList(); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Object> batches = List.of(List.of(1_200, 350), List.of("pay_1"), "pay_2"); List<List<String>> stringLists = filterIsInstance(batches, List.class); // there is no List<String>.class System.out.println("lists of strings? " + stringLists); // getClass() on a value: a null receiver is only found at run time. Object maybe = null; try { System.out.println(maybe.getClass()); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("NullPointerException from getClass() on null"); } // Uncomment, predict, then run: it compiles, so what happens at run time? // String n = stringLists.get(0).get(0); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l08.demo.LimitsDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l08/demo/LimitsDemoJava.java Both print lists of strings? [[1200, 350], [pay_1]]: the list of ints got through. Kotlin then prints classOf("pay_1") = String; Java prints NullPointerException from getClass() on null. Wrong move 1: Cannot use 'Nothing' as reified type parameter. Wrong move 2 compiles and throws ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String (the same happens in the Java twin). Function 3: Expression in class literal has nullable type 'T (of fun <T> klassOf)'. Use '!!' to make the type non-nullable. With T : Any it compiles. Kotlin 2.4 compatibility guide (KTLC-370) docs The common mistake is a generic function that quietly casts: fun <T> decode(json: String): T = mapper.readValue(json, Any::class.java) as T, with @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") to silence the warning. It compiles, it "works" in the happy-path test, and when a payload has the wrong shape, the ClassCastException appears in whatever code first uses the result, often in another module. People write it because the compiler only warns, and because the cast looks like it checks something. It doesn't: with an erased T the cast checks nothing. The fix is to make the type real at run time: take a type: Class<T> and call type.cast(...), or make the function inline with a reified T and pass T::class.java to the library.

h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · Java and Kotlin
x: A parser registry: Class tokens in Java, Class tokens plus reified in Kotlin Parsers.java import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Function; final class Parsers { private final Map<Class<?>, Function<String, ?>> byType = new HashMap<>(); <T> void register(Class<T> type, Function<String, ? extends T> parser) { byType.put(type, parser); } // T is erased in here, so the caller hands over the Class <T> T parse(String text, Class<T> type) { Function<String, ?> parser = byType.get(type); if (parser == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("no parser for " + type.getSimpleName()); return type.cast(parser.apply(text)); // a checked cast: no warning } } // call site: Money m = parsers.parse("12.50 EUR", Money.class); Parsers.kt class Parsers { private val byType = HashMap<Class<*>, (String) -> Any>() fun <T : Any> register(type: Class<T>, parser: (String) -> T) { byType[type] = parser } // the same Class-token core, callable from Java fun <T : Any> parse(text: String, type: Class<T>): T { val parser = byType[type] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("no parser for " + type.simpleName) return type.cast(parser(text)) } // the Kotlin wrapper: the compiler writes Money::class.java into each call site inline fun <reified T : Any> parse(text: String): T = parse(text, T::class.java) } // call site: val m = parsers.parse<Money>("12.50 EUR") Both languages erase T inside parse, so both cores need the Class<T> argument, and both use Class.cast for a cast that really checks. The difference is at the call site. Kotlin can add an inline wrapper with a reified T, and the compiler fills in Money::class.java for the caller. Java can't use that wrapper: it is a synthetic method in the class file, and javac can't inline it. Note also that the wrapper calls only public members. A public inline function is copied into other modules, so it may not touch byType directly (public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API property).

h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · Worked example
x: Give a Kafka payload decoder a real type A consumer decodes JSON into payment events through a codec that, like most Java libraries, wants a class token: fun <T : Any> read(json: String, type: Class<T>): T. The first draft tries to hide the token behind a generic function. Read the error. fun <T : Any> decode(json: String): T = codec.read(json, T::class.java) // error: Cannot use 'T' as reified type parameter. Use a class instead. static <T> T decode(String json) { return codec.read(json, T.class); } // error: cannot select from a type variable Make the token explicit. This version works from Kotlin and from Java, and the codec does a checked conversion. fun <T : Any> decode(json: String, type: Class<T>): T = codec.read(json, type) val e = decode(json, CardAuthorized::class.java) static <T> T decode(String json, Class<T> type) { return codec.read(json, type); } CardAuthorized e = decode(json, CardAuthorized.class); Add the Kotlin convenience on top. Self-check before reading the comment: why must the wrapper be inline? (Only an inlined body is compiled at the call site, where T is known.) inline fun <reified T : Any> decode(json: String): T = decode(json, T::class.java) val e: CardAuthorized = decode(json) // T inferred from the expected type val r = decode<RefundIssued>(json) // Java can't call the reified wrapper; it keeps using the token version: RefundIssued r = decode(json, RefundIssued.class); Check the limit before you ship it. decode<List<CardAuthorized>>(json) compiles, but it passes List::class.java. The codec has no element type to bind to (Jackson, for example, fills such a list with LinkedHashMaps), and the first for (e: CardAuthorized in events) throws ClassCastException. For generic targets you need a token that keeps type arguments: typeOf<List<CardAuthorized>>() or a super type token, both in lesson 9.

h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · Key terms
x: Type erasure Removing type arguments after compile-time checking, so objects carry no <String> at run time. Unchecked cast A cast to a generic type that can check only the class. The compiler warns; the failure comes later. Heap pollution A variable of a generic type that refers to an object of the wrong type, such as a List<String> holding ints. inline function A function whose body the compiler copies into each call site. Reified type parameter A type parameter of an inline function whose real class is available in the copied body. Class token A Class<T> passed as an argument so code can check and cast to T at run time. Synthetic method A method the compiler writes into the class file but hides from javac, as Kotlin does with reified functions. What is type erasure? The compiler checks type arguments and then removes them. At run time a List<String> is just a List, with no record of String. Where does val l = listOf(1) as Any as List<String> fail? Not at the cast. It fails at the first read that needs a String, such as val s: String = l[0]. What do inline and reified do together? inline copies the function body into each call site. reified writes the caller's real class for T into that copy, so is T, as? T and T::class work. Can Java call inline fun <reified T : Any> parse(text: String): T? No. It is a synthetic method and javac can't inline it. Provide parse(text, type: Class<T>) as well. Does filterIsInstance<List<String>>() check the elements? No. Reified covers only the outer class; after inlining it is instanceof List, so a list of ints passes. Why is inline fun <reified T> klassOf(x: T) = x::class an error in Kotlin 2.4? T may be nullable, and null has no class. Write <reified T : Any>. Int::class.java vs T::class.java with a reified T = Int? The first is the primitive int; the second is java.lang.Integer. Use Int::class.javaObjectType for the boxed class.

h: Type erasure and reified type parameters · Go deeper
x: You can see the copy mechanism in the bytecode. Run javap -c -p on ClassTokenDemoKt.class (it is under generics/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/generics/l08/demo/ after you run the demo). The method kept in the class for defaultOf() has the flags ACC_PUBLIC, ACC_STATIC, ACC_FINAL, ACC_SYNTHETIC, and where T::class.java should be it loads Object.class next to a call to kotlin/jvm/internal/Intrinsics.reifiedOperationMarker. That marker tells the compiler where to write the real class when it inlines the body into a caller. In main, the call defaultOf<java.util.Currency>() has no call to defaultOf() at all: you'll find ldc class java/util/Currency followed by a call to the Class-token defaultOf. This is also why the lab routes test calls through Callers.kt. The inlined copy is fixed when the caller is compiled. Tests compiled once against src/main would keep a copy of your TODO stub forever, even when run next to the reference solution. Two more rules come from copying. A public inline function is copied into other modules, so it may only touch public API: reading a private field gives public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API property. That is the deep reason for the "Class-token core plus one-line reified wrapper" shape. And a lambda passed to an inline function is normally inlined too, so it can't be stored. If the function needs to keep it, say in a handler map, that parameter must be marked noinline. Lesson 11 of this track uses that for a typed event bus. Java's own answer to erasure for arrays is different: arrays are reified. Every String[] knows its component type at run time, which is why new T[1] is a compile error (generic array creation) and why Kotlin's arrayOf<T>() needs a reified T.

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · A class is not a type, and objects only know their class
x: Lessons 3 and 8 of this track gave you two facts. One class stands behind many types: the class String backs the types String and String?, and the class List backs List<String>, List<Int> and List<Payment>?. And at run time, erasure leaves each object with its class and nothing more. Kotlin's reflection API has a separate object for each idea. Most confusion about KClass comes from mixing them up: A KClass describes a class: String::class, CardAuthorized::class, List::class. It has no type arguments and is never nullable. Its interface is KClass<T : Any>. A Class is Java's object for the same class: String.class in Java, String::class.java in Kotlin. Every object can hand you its Class at run time. A KType describes a full type: the class, plus its type arguments, plus whether it is nullable. typeOf<List<String>?>() gives you one. Java Class<String> c = String.class; // Java's class object boolean same = new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass(); // true // Java has no KType. The closest thing is a java.lang.reflect.Type read from a declaration: Type t = Holder.class.getDeclaredField("ids").getGenericType(); // java.util.List<java.lang.String> Kotlin val k: KClass<String> = String::class // Kotlin's class object val c: Class<String> = String::class.java // the Java one, for Java APIs val t: KType = typeOf<List<String>?>() // List, with argument String, nullable val same = ArrayList<String>()::class == ArrayList<Int>()::class // true To pick the right one, ask what you need to know. "What kind of object is this?" is a question about a class, and a KClass or a Class answers it. "A list of what?" or "may it be null?" are questions about a type, and only a KType can answer them. One warning before you run anything. Without the kotlin-reflect library on the classpath, Kotlin prints these objects with a suffix: class java.lang.String (Kotlin reflection is not available) java.util.List<java.lang.String>? (Kotlin reflection is not available) Nothing is broken. toString() can't produce Kotlin names such as kotlin.String without the library, so it falls back to Java names and says so. Section 4 shows what the library adds. A Gradle project doesn't include it unless you ask; the kotlinc command-line compiler adds it by default, so the same code can print differently in the two. Meet the three objects Run ClassVsTypeDemo and read each line. Which of the three objects is printed with Java names and a suffix? Run it again with -Preflect added to the command, and compare the first and third lines. Run ClassVsTypeDemoJava. Which Kotlin line has no Java twin at all? ClassVsTypeDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l09.demo import kotlin.reflect.KClass import kotlin.reflect.KType import kotlin.reflect.typeOf fun main() { // 1. Three different objects. val k: KClass<String> = String::class // Kotlin's object for a class val c: Class<String> = String::class.java // Java's object for the same class val t: KType = typeOf<List<String>?>() // a full type: class, arguments, nullability println("KClass: $k") println("Class: $c") println("KType: $t") // 2. Different types, one class. println("ArrayList<String> and ArrayList<Int> share a class: ${ArrayList<String>()::class == ArrayList<Int>()::class}") println("String? is backed by the class String: ${typeOf<String?>().classifier == String::class}") println("but the types differ: ${typeOf<String>() == typeOf<String?>()}, ${typeOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<Int>>()}") // 3. What a KType knows that a KClass doesn't. println("classifier is List::class: ${t.classifier == List::class}, arguments: ${t.arguments.size}, nullable: ${t.isMarkedNullable}") } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ClassVsTypeDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l09/demo/ClassVsTypeDemo.kt ClassVsTypeDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l09.demo; import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType; import java.lang.reflect.Type; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of ClassVsTypeDemo.kt. Java has Class but no KType. The closest thing is * java.lang.reflect.Type, which you can read from a declaration (here, a field). */ public class ClassVsTypeDemoJava { static List<String> ids = List.of("pay_1"); // a declaration keeps its generic type public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Class<String> c = String.class; Type t = ClassVsTypeDemoJava.class.getDeclaredField("ids").getGenericType(); System.out.println("Class: " + c); System.out.println("Type: " + t + " (read from the field declaration)"); System.out.println("ArrayList<String> and ArrayList<Integer> share a class: " + (new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass())); System.out.println("the field's Type keeps its argument: " + ((ParameterizedType) t).getActualTypeArguments()[0]); // Java types carry no nullability, so there is no twin of typeOf<String?>(). } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.ClassVsTypeDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l09/demo/ClassVsTypeDemoJava.java Kotlin prints KClass: class java.lang.String (Kotlin reflection is not available), Class: class java.lang.String and KType: java.util.List<java.lang.String>? (Kotlin reflection is not available), then true, true, false, false and classifier is List::class: true, arguments: 1, nullable: true. With -Preflect the first line becomes class kotlin.String and the third kotlin.collections.List<kotlin.String>?. Java prints the class, the field's type java.util.List<java.lang.String>, true, and the argument class java.lang.String. Java has no twin for nullability in a type. A KType knows the class, the arguments and the nullability. Its classifier is a KClass, which converts to and from Java's Class. Objects can give you only their class. Reflection: class references and KType (Kotlin docs) docs Think of a car dealer's system. A KClass is a model name: "Corolla". A KType is a full order line: "Corolla, hybrid trim", or even "a Corolla, or no car at all", which is the nullable part. The factory stamps only the model name on each car. So a car in the lot, like an object at run time, can tell you its model and nothing about the order it came from. x::class is reading the stamp on a car you only knew as "some vehicle": the stamp names a model, and all the compiler could promise in advance was that it would be some kind of vehicle. The analogy breaks for typeOf. A real dealership keeps the order line in a file somewhere. In Kotlin a KType exists only where the compiler wrote it down, at a call site with a known or reified type, and never inside the object.

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · x::class is a KClass , for the reason lesson 4 gave
x: There are two ways to get a KClass. A class literal, CardAuthorized::class, names a class you know while writing the code, and its type is exact: KClass<CardAuthorized>. A bound class reference, event::class, asks a value for its class at run time, and its type has an out in it: Java PaymentEvent event = new CardAuthorized("pay_1", 1_200); Class<? extends PaymentEvent> c = event.getClass(); // what getClass() is declared to return Class<PaymentEvent> strict = event.getClass(); // error: Class<CAP#1> cannot be converted to Class<PaymentEvent> Kotlin val event: PaymentEvent = CardAuthorized("pay_1", 1_200) val k: KClass<out PaymentEvent> = event::class // the class of SOME PaymentEvent val strict: KClass<PaymentEvent> = event::class // error: expected 'KClass<PaymentEvent>', actual 'KClass<out PaymentEvent>' Why the out? The compiler knows that event is some PaymentEvent. When the program runs it turns out to be a CardAuthorized, but it could have been a RefundIssued. So the most the compiler can say is "the class of some subtype of PaymentEvent, I don't know which". That is exactly what out meant in lesson 4: a producer of some unknown subtype. Java says the same with ? extends; the Javadoc of Object.getClass() states that the result type is Class<? extends |X|>, where |X| is the erasure of the expression's static type. The out doesn't stop you from using the class. Everything that hands information out still works: event::class.simpleName, event::class == CardAuthorized::class, and cast, which gives you back a PaymentEvent. What you can't do is pass it where an exact KClass<PaymentEvent> is required. The compiler doesn't special-case final classes either: "pay_1"::class is a KClass<out String>. The other half of KClass<T : Any> is the bound. There is no class for a nullable type, because String? is backed by the class String. So KClass<String?> is an error, and so is asking a nullable value for its class: val kn: KClass<String?>? = null Type argument is not within its bounds: type parameter 'T (of interface KClass<T : Any>)' must be subtype of 'Any', but actual: 'String?'. val note: String? = ... note::class Expression in class literal has nullable type 'String?'. Use '!!' to make the type non-nullable. Write note?.let { it::class } instead, and you get a KClass<out String>?: null when there's no value to ask. Java has no compile-time check for this. note.getClass() throws NullPointerException when note is null. Ask values for their class Run ClassOfValueDemo (or ClassOfValueDemoJava). The loop variable is declared PaymentEvent; what does simpleName print? Uncomment the three wrong moves one at a time. Predict each error first. In the Java twin, uncomment the wrong move. h: KClass, Class and type tokens · KClass and Class are two views of the same class
x: On the JVM every KClass wraps a java.lang.Class, and you move between them with two properties. You'll do it often at the boundary with Java libraries: Java Class<CardAuthorized> c = CardAuthorized.class; boolean isCard = c.isInstance(event); // true CardAuthorized card = c.cast(event); // checked: ClassCastException if not String name = c.getSimpleName(); // "CardAuthorized" Class<?> runtime = event.getClass(); // the object's class Kotlin val k: KClass<CardAuthorized> = CardAuthorized::class val c: Class<CardAuthorized> = k.java // KClass to Class, for Java APIs val back: KClass<CardAuthorized> = c.kotlin // Class to KClass k.isInstance(event) // true val card: CardAuthorized = k.cast(event) // checked: ClassCastException if not val refund: RefundIssued? = RefundIssued::class.safeCast(event) // null instead of throwing k.simpleName // "CardAuthorized" event.javaClass // the object's Class, like Java's getClass() These are the KClass versions of the class-token tools from lesson 8. isInstance is a checked is, cast is a checked as, and safeCast is a checked as?. h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Names, checks and casts are free; describing a class needs kotlin-reflect
x: KClass has many more members: objectInstance, sealedSubclasses, isData, members, constructors, supertypes. Your code compiles against all of them, because they're declared in the standard library. But the code that answers them lives in a separate jar, kotlin-reflect (about 3.8 MB in 2.4.21), which a Gradle project doesn't have unless you add it. Without it they fail at run time: Origin::class.objectInstance KotlinReflectionNotSupportedError: Kotlin reflection implementation is not found at runtime. Make sure you have kotlin-reflect.jar in the classpath A rule of thumb that holds up: names, identity, instance checks, casts and typeOf are free; anything that lists or describes declarations needs kotlin-reflect. Works with the standard library alone Needs kotlin-reflect simpleName, qualifiedName, ==, .java, .kotlin objectInstance, sealedSubclasses, isData, isSealed isInstance, cast, safeCast members, constructors, typeParameters, supertypes typeOf<T>() with classifier, arguments, isMarkedNullable kotlin.reflect.full extensions such as createInstance() The kotlin.reflect.full extensions fail differently, with NoClassDefFoundError: kotlin/reflect/full/KClasses, because that class isn't in the standard library at all. Java reflection needs no extra jar, and it works on Kotlin classes too: Java CardAuthorized.class.getDeclaredFields(); // [cents, paymentId] Origin.class.getField("INSTANCE").get(null); // a Kotlin object is a static INSTANCE field Kotlin CardAuthorized::class.java.declaredFields // the same Java reflection, from Kotlin Origin::class.objectInstance // the Kotlin way: needs kotlin-reflect So when a Java-level answer is enough (fields, methods, annotations), go through .java and skip the dependency. When you need Kotlin-level facts (is this a data class, which subclasses does this sealed interface have, is this property nullable), add kotlin-reflect. Libraries that inspect Kotlin classes, such as Jackson's Kotlin module, pull it in for exactly this reason. Run one demo with and without kotlin-reflect Run ReflectDemo with the command below. Every line under -- needs kotlin-reflect fails. Note which error each one gives. Run it again with -Preflect at the end of the command. That flag adds kotlin-reflect to the demo's runtime classpath (see labs/generics/build.gradle.kts). Run ReflectDemoJava. Which of the Kotlin answers can Java reflection also give? h: KClass, Class and type tokens · KType keeps what KClass drops: typeOf and super type tokens
x: Now the problem this lesson's lab is built around. A service registry keyed by KClass works for PaymentGateway and FraudCheck. It can't hold a Repository<Payment> and a Repository<Refund> at the same time, because both have the class Repository, and the second registration silently replaces the first. You can't even write the class of the type you mean: val k = Repository<Payment>::class Only classes are allowed on the left-hand side of a class literal. A KType keeps the type arguments and the nullability. In Kotlin, typeOf<T>() gives you one. Java's answer is older and cleverer: Java // A super type token. An anonymous subclass's superclass signature survives erasure. abstract class TypeRef<T> { final Type type; protected TypeRef() { type = ((ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass()).getActualTypeArguments()[0]; } } Type t = new TypeRef<Map<String, List<Integer>>>() {}.type; // java.util.Map<java.lang.String, java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>> Kotlin val t: KType = typeOf<Map<String, List<Int>>>() t.classifier == Map::class // true t.arguments.size // 2: String and List<Int> typeOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<Int>>() // false typeOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<String>?>() // false: nullability counts The Java version is the idea Neal Gafter named super type tokens, and it's how Jackson's TypeReference and Gson's TypeToken work. Erasure removes type arguments from objects but not from declarations (lesson 8), and a class's declared superclass is a declaration. So you create a throwaway anonymous subclass, new TypeRef<...>() {}, and read its superclass back. The {} is the whole trick: without it there's no subclass, and javac says TypeRef is abstract; cannot be instantiated. It has one well-known hole. Inside a generic method, new TypeRef<List<T>>() {} records the type variable, and prints java.util.List<T>. typeOf is the Kotlin replacement. Through a reified parameter it keeps everything: inline fun <reified T> tokenOf() = typeOf<T>() called as tokenOf<List<String>>() gives the full List<String>. That is the difference from lesson 8, where T::class kept only List. It works without kotlin-reflect, apart from the toString() suffix, and KType equality is all a map key needs. When a Java library wants a java.lang.reflect.Type, convert with typeOf<List<CardAuthorized>>().javaType, which in 2.4.21 still needs @OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class). A super type token written in Kotlin also works, with a twist: it picks up Kotlin's declaration-site variance as wildcards. object : TypeRef<Map<String, List<Int>>>() {} prints java.util.Map<java.lang.String, ? extends java.util.List<? extends java.lang.Integer>>, because Map's V and List's E are declared out. javaType gives the plain form. Capture List two ways Run TypeTokenDemo and TypeTokenDemoJava. Compare the two super type token: lines. Find the line in the Java output where the token failed to capture the real type. Uncomment the wrong move in each file, predict, run. TypeTokenDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l09.demo import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType import java.lang.reflect.Type import kotlin.reflect.KType import kotlin.reflect.javaType import kotlin.reflect.typeOf /** A super type token written in Kotlin: the anonymous subclass remembers its superclass's type argument. */ abstract class TypeRef<T> { val type: Type = (javaClass.genericSuperclass as ParameterizedType).actualTypeArguments[0] } /** typeOf through a reified T keeps the whole type. T::class here would keep only the class. */ inline fun <reified T> tokenOf(): KType = typeOf<T>() @OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class) // KType.javaType still needs the opt-in in 2.4.21 fun main() { val t = typeOf<Map<String, List<Int>>>() println("typeOf: $t") println("arguments: ${t.arguments.size}, second is ${t.arguments[1]}") println("javaType: ${t.javaType}") println("tokenOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<String>>(): ${tokenOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<String>>()}") println("List<String> == List<Int> as KTypes: ${typeOf<List<String>>() == typeOf<List<Int>>()}") println("super type token: ${object : TypeRef<Map<String, List<Int>>>() {}.type}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val k = List<String>::class } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.TypeTokenDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l09/demo/TypeTokenDemo.kt TypeTokenDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l09.demo; import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType; import java.lang.reflect.Type; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Java twin of TypeTokenDemo.kt: the super type token, the trick behind Jackson's TypeReference. */ public class TypeTokenDemoJava { static abstract class TypeRef<T> { final Type type; protected TypeRef() { // getClass() is the anonymous subclass; its generic superclass is TypeRef<the type you wrote> type = ((ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass()).getActualTypeArguments()[0]; } } // the well-known hole: inside a generic method, the token captures the type VARIABLE static <T> Type listOf() { return new TypeRef<List<T>>() {}.type; } public static void main(String[] args) { Type t = new TypeRef<Map<String, List<Integer>>>() {}.type; System.out.println("super type token: " + t); System.out.println("arguments: " + Arrays.toString(((ParameterizedType) t).getActualTypeArguments())); System.out.println("inside a generic method: " + TypeTokenDemoJava.<String>listOf()); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // Type k = new TypeRef<String>().type; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l09.demo.TypeTokenDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l09/demo/TypeTokenDemoJava.java Kotlin prints the typeOf result java.util.Map<java.lang.String, java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>> (Kotlin reflection is not available), arguments: 2, ..., the same type as javaType without the suffix, true, false, and the Kotlin-written token java.util.Map<java.lang.String, ? extends java.util.List<? extends java.lang.Integer>>. Java prints its token as java.util.Map<java.lang.String, java.util.List<java.lang.Integer>>, its two arguments, and inside a generic method: java.util.List<T>: the hole. The wrong moves fail with Only classes are allowed on the left-hand side of a class literal. and TypeRef is abstract; cannot be instantiated. typeOf (Kotlin stdlib API) docs KClass (Kotlin stdlib API) docs The common mistake is keying generic things by class. A registry, cache or handler map uses KClass (or Java's Class) keys, someone registers a Repository<Payment> and later a Repository<Refund>, and the second silently replaces the first, because both have the class Repository. Nothing fails at registration. Much later, code that asks for the payments repository gets the refunds one, casts its elements to Payment, and throws ClassCastException far away. People make the mistake because KClass works perfectly for every non-generic service they registered first. The fix is to key by full type: a KType from typeOf<T>() in Kotlin, or a super type token's Type in Java. Use KClass keys only for types that have no type arguments.

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Java and Kotlin
x: A type-safe service registry in Java and Kotlin ServiceRegistry.java import java.lang.reflect.Type; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; final class ServiceRegistry { private final Map<Class<?>, Object> byClass = new HashMap<>(); private final Map<Type, Object> byType = new HashMap<>(); // Class<T> and T tied together: the compiler checks the pair <T> void register(Class<T> type, T impl) { byClass.put(type, impl); } <T> T get(Class<T> type) { Object impl = byClass.get(type); if (impl == null) throw new NoSuchElementException("no service for " + type.getSimpleName()); return type.cast(impl); // checked } // generic services: a super type token supplies the full type <T> void registerTyped(TypeRef<T> type, T impl) { byType.put(type.type, impl); } @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") // safe: only registerTyped puts values in <T> T getTyped(TypeRef<T> type) { return (T) byType.get(type.type); } } // registry.register(PaymentGateway.class, gateway); // registry.registerTyped(new TypeRef<Repository<Payment>>() {}, payments); ServiceRegistry.kt class ServiceRegistry { private val byClass = HashMap<KClass<*>, Any>() private val byType = HashMap<KType, Any>() // KClass<T> and T tied together: the compiler checks the pair fun <T : Any> register(type: KClass<T>, impl: T) { byClass[type] = impl } fun <T : Any> get(type: KClass<T>): T { val impl = byClass[type] ?: throw NoSuchElementException("no service for " + type.simpleName) return type.cast(impl) // checked, no kotlin-reflect needed } inline fun <reified T : Any> get(): T = get(T::class) // generic services: typeOf supplies the full type fun registerTyped(type: KType, impl: Any) { byType[type] = impl } fun getTyped(type: KType): Any = byType[type] ?: throw NoSuchElementException("no service for $type") inline fun <reified T : Any> registerTyped(impl: T) = registerTyped(typeOf<T>(), impl) @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") // safe: only registerTyped<T> puts values in inline fun <reified T : Any> getTyped(): T = getTyped(typeOf<T>()) as T } // registry.register(PaymentGateway::class, gateway); registry.get<PaymentGateway>() // registry.registerTyped<Repository<Payment>>(payments) Both are what Joshua Bloch calls a typesafe heterogeneous container (Effective Java, Item 33): one map holds values of many types, and the key carries the type, so get can return a T with a checked cast. The KClass half is a direct translation: KClass<T> for Class<T>, type.cast in both. The differences are at the call site and for generic types. Kotlin adds reified wrappers, so callers write get<PaymentGateway>() and registerTyped<Repository<Payment>>(repo). For generic types Java needs a super type token object at each call (new TypeRef<Repository<Payment>>() {}), while Kotlin's typeOf<T>() is computed from the reified T with no subclass and no hole for type variables. In both, the full-type half needs one unchecked cast, which is safe because the map is private and filled only through the typed register method.

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Worked example
x: Build the registry's KClass half, then find where it stops A first draft keys services by class and returns Any. It compiles, but every caller has to cast, and nothing stops a wrong registration. class ServiceRegistry { private val byClass = HashMap<KClass<*>, Any>() fun register(type: KClass<*>, impl: Any) { byClass[type] = impl } fun get(type: KClass<*>): Any? = byClass[type] } registry.register(PaymentGateway::class, AlwaysLowRisk()) // compiles: oops val gateway = registry.get(PaymentGateway::class) as PaymentGateway // ClassCastException here final class ServiceRegistry { private final Map<Class<?>, Object> byClass = new HashMap<>(); void register(Class<?> type, Object impl) { byClass.put(type, impl); } Object get(Class<?> type) { return byClass.get(type); } } registry.register(PaymentGateway.class, new AlwaysLowRisk()); // compiles: oops PaymentGateway gateway = (PaymentGateway) registry.get(PaymentGateway.class); // ClassCastException here Tie the key and the value together with one type parameter. Now PaymentGateway::class is a KClass<PaymentGateway>, so T is PaymentGateway and the implementation must be one. 2. Return a T with a checked cast. Self-check before reading on: why is type.cast safe here when as T in lesson 8 was not? (The KClass object is a real run-time value, so cast can really check.) fun <T : Any> register(type: KClass<T>, impl: T) { byClass[type] = impl } fun <T : Any> get(type: KClass<T>): T { val impl = byClass[type] ?: throw NoSuchElementException("no service for " + type.simpleName) return type.cast(impl) } registry.register(PaymentGateway::class, AlwaysLowRisk()) // error: Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'AlwaysLowRisk', but 'PaymentGateway' was expected. <T> void register(Class<T> type, T impl) { byClass.put(type, impl); } <T> T get(Class<T> type) { Object impl = byClass.get(type); if (impl == null) throw new NoSuchElementException("no service for " + type.getSimpleName()); return type.cast(impl); } registry.register(PaymentGateway.class, new AlwaysLowRisk()); // error: method register in class ServiceRegistry cannot be applied to given types; // reason: inference variable T has incompatible bounds Add the reified wrapper for Kotlin callers. It only touches the public get(type), as lesson 8 required of public inline functions. inline fun <reified T : Any> get(): T = get(T::class) val gateway: PaymentGateway = registry.get() // T from the expected type val fraud = registry.get<FraudCheck>() // Java keeps passing the class: PaymentGateway gateway = registry.get(PaymentGateway.class); FraudCheck fraud = registry.get(FraudCheck.class); Now try a generic service. Repository::class is a KClass<Repository<*>>, so the best get can return is a Repository<*>, and a second register(Repository::class, refunds) overwrites the payments repository without a word. Asking for Repository<Payment> explicitly fails at compile time: Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Repository<Payment>', actual 'Repository<*>'.
