h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Key terms
x: KClass Kotlin's run-time object for a class: CardAuthorized::class. No type arguments, never nullable. Class Java's run-time object for a class: CardAuthorized.class, or CardAuthorized::class.java from Kotlin. KType A full type at run time: class, type arguments and nullability. Made by typeOf<T>(). Class literal Name::class: the class you name in code. Its type is exact, KClass<Name>. Bound class reference value::class: the run-time class of a value, typed KClass<out DeclaredType>. kotlin-reflect The separate jar that answers questions about declarations: members, sealed subclasses, data classes. Super type token A Java trick that captures a full generic type through an anonymous subclass's superclass signature. Typesafe heterogeneous container One map holding values of many types, with the type as the key, so get can return a T safely. KClass or KType: which one knows that a value is a List<String>? and not just a List? KType (from typeOf<List<String>?>()). A KClass describes only the class: no type arguments, never nullable. Why is event::class a KClass<out PaymentEvent> when event: PaymentEvent? The real class is some unknown subtype of PaymentEvent, and out means exactly that. Java's getClass() returns Class<? extends PaymentEvent> for the same reason. Why is KClass declared KClass<T : Any>? There is no class for a nullable type: String? is backed by the class String. So KClass<String?> and nullableValue::class don't compile. How do you convert between KClass and Java's Class? k.java gives the Class; c.kotlin gives the KClass. A value's Class is x.javaClass. Without kotlin-reflect, what does Origin::class.objectInstance do? Throws KotlinReflectionNotSupportedError. Anything that describes declarations needs kotlin-reflect; names, checks, casts and typeOf don't. How do you get a runtime object for the full type List<String> in Kotlin? typeOf<List<String>>(), a KType. List<String>::class doesn't compile: only classes are allowed on the left of ::class. What is a super type token? An anonymous subclass, new TypeRef<List<String>>() {}, whose generic superclass is read back by reflection. It's how Jackson's TypeReference works.

h: KClass, Class and type tokens · Go deeper
x: Why doesn't a KType need kotlin-reflect, when so much else does? Because typeOf<T>() is mostly built by the compiler. At each call site it emits code that constructs the type from parts it already knows: the classifier (List::class), the arguments, the variance of each argument and the nullability flag. The standard library holds a small implementation of KType for that. Answering sealedSubclasses is different: it means reading Kotlin's own metadata out of the class file, and the reader for that metadata is what kotlin-reflect contains. KType also records variance and stars. typeOf<MutableList<out Number>>().arguments.single().variance is OUT, and typeOf<List<*>>().arguments prints [*]. So a registry keyed by KType treats MutableList<out Number> and MutableList<Number> as different keys, which is correct but can surprise you: the key must be written with exactly the same type on both sides. The docs page on reflection mentions that the kotlinc command-line compiler adds kotlin-reflect by default (you can opt out with -no-reflect). That's why a snippet that prints class kotlin.String in a quick command-line experiment prints class java.lang.String (Kotlin reflection is not available) inside your Gradle service. If you add kotlin-reflect to a service, add it on purpose: it's a 3.8 MB jar, and its first use loads and parses metadata, which costs a little time once per class. Last, the javaClass rule from section 3 has a reason. javaClass is an extension property on every type, and a KClass is a value like any other, so k.javaClass would mean the class that implements the KClass object, not the class it describes. The standard library declares a deprecated overload for exactly that receiver, and in 2.4.21 using it is an error. x.javaClass on ordinary values is unaffected.

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · A self type lets base-class setters return the subclass
x: Builders are where the plain generics of lessons 1 to 9 stop being enough. Put the common setters in a base class, add a subclass with its own setter, and the chain breaks as soon as a base setter runs: Java class PlainBuilder { protected long cents; PlainBuilder amount(long cents) { this.cents = cents; return this; } } class PlainCardBuilder extends PlainBuilder { PlainCardBuilder cardToken(String t) { ... } } new PlainCardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1"); // error: cannot find symbol Kotlin open class PlainBuilder { protected var cents = 0L fun amount(cents: Long): PlainBuilder { this.cents = cents; return this } } class PlainCardBuilder : PlainBuilder() { fun cardToken(t: String): PlainCardBuilder { ... } } PlainCardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1") // error: Unresolved reference 'cardToken' on receiver of type 'PlainBuilder'. amount returns a PlainBuilder, because that's all the base class knows about itself. The object is still a PlainCardBuilder, but the static type has lost it. The base class needs a way to say "I return whatever subclass I really am". The answer is a self type, written as a recursive bound: Java abstract class Builder<B extends Builder<B>> { protected long cents; B amount(long cents) { this.cents = cents; return self(); } protected abstract B self(); } final class CardBuilder extends Builder<CardBuilder> { CardBuilder cardToken(String t) { ...; return this; } @Override protected CardBuilder self() { return this; } } Kotlin abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> { protected var cents = 0L fun amount(cents: Long): B { this.cents = cents; return self() } protected abstract fun self(): B } class CardBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>() { fun cardToken(t: String): CardBuilder { ...; return this } override fun self() = this } Read B : Builder<B> as "B is a builder whose own B is B". The only types that fit are subclasses that name themselves, as CardBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>() does. Inside the base class, B stands for "my concrete subclass", so amount can return it. Substitute, as in lesson 1: for a CardBuilder, every B in the base class reads as CardBuilder, so CardBuilder().amount(1_200) has the static type CardBuilder, and .cardToken("tok_1") is in reach again. You met the shape already: lesson 2's T : Comparable<T> is a recursive bound, and Java's own Enum<E extends Enum<E>> is one too. Two details matter. The abstract self() keeps the code checked: each subclass returns this, and the compiler verifies it is a B. And the bound can't force honesty: class Liar : Builder<CardBuilder>() compiles. If you write self() as abstract, the liar must return a CardBuilder it doesn't have, which is where you'd notice. In pure Kotlin code you often don't need a builder at all. A data class with default arguments and copy covers most cases. Reach for self types when Java callers need a builder, or when you extend a Java class that already uses one. Break a builder chain, then fix it with B : Builder Run SelfTypeDemo (or SelfTypeDemoJava). Compare the static type and the run-time class on the first line. Uncomment wrong move 1, predict, run. Uncomment wrong move 2, the Liar class. It compiles. Add println(Liar().amount(5)::class.simpleName) below it and predict what prints. SelfTypeDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l10.demo // 1. Without a self type: the base setters return the base class, and the chain loses the subclass. open class PlainBuilder { protected var cents = 0L fun amount(cents: Long): PlainBuilder { this.cents = cents; return this } } class PlainCardBuilder : PlainBuilder() { private var token = "" fun cardToken(t: String): PlainCardBuilder { token = t; return this } fun build() = "card $cents with $token" } // 2. With a self type: B names "my own subclass", so the base setters return it. abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> { protected var cents = 0L fun amount(cents: Long): B { this.cents = cents; return self() } protected abstract fun self(): B } class CardBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>() { private var token = "" fun cardToken(t: String): CardBuilder { token = t; return this } override fun self() = this fun build() = "card $cents with $token" } fun main() { val lost: PlainBuilder = PlainCardBuilder().cardToken("tok_1").amount(1_200) // amount() returns a PlainBuilder println("after amount(): static type PlainBuilder, run-time class ${lost::class.simpleName}") println(CardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1").build()) // the chain keeps CardBuilder // Wrong moves. Uncomment one at a time, predict the error, then run. // println(PlainCardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1").build()) // 1 // class Liar : Builder<CardBuilder>() { override fun self() = CardBuilder() } // 2 (compiles: what does it break?) } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.SelfTypeDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l10/demo/SelfTypeDemo.kt SelfTypeDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l10.demo; /** Java twin of SelfTypeDemo.kt. The same recursive bound that java.lang.Enum uses: Enum<E extends Enum<E>>. */ public class SelfTypeDemoJava { static class PlainBuilder { protected long cents; PlainBuilder amount(long cents) { this.cents = cents; return this; } } static final class PlainCardBuilder extends PlainBuilder { private String token = ""; PlainCardBuilder cardToken(String t) { token = t; return this; } String build() { return "card " + cents + " with " + token; } } static abstract class Builder<B extends Builder<B>> { protected long cents; B amount(long cents) { this.cents = cents; return self(); } protected abstract B self(); } static final class CardBuilder extends Builder<CardBuilder> { private String token = ""; CardBuilder cardToken(String t) { token = t; return this; } @Override protected CardBuilder self() { return this; } String build() { return "card " + cents + " with " + token; } } public static void main(String[] args) { PlainBuilder lost = new PlainCardBuilder().cardToken("tok_1").amount(1_200); // amount() returns a PlainBuilder System.out.println("after amount(): static type PlainBuilder, run-time class " + lost.getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println(new CardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1").build()); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // System.out.println(new PlainCardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1").build()); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.SelfTypeDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l10/demo/SelfTypeDemoJava.java Both print after amount(): static type PlainBuilder, run-time class PlainCardBuilder and card 1200 with tok_1. Wrong move 1 fails with Unresolved reference 'cardToken' on receiver of type 'PlainBuilder'. (Java: cannot find symbol). The Liar compiles because the bound only asks for some builder, and Liar().amount(5) prints CardBuilder: a fresh object, not the liar you configured. Nothing forces a subclass to pass itself. A recursive bound lets the base class return its concrete subclass, so a chain keeps the subclass's own setters in reach. Generics: upper bounds (Kotlin docs) docs A self type is like a franchise operations manual. Head office writes it once, and every step ends with "hand the tray back to the counter of ______". When a restaurant joins, it writes its own name in the blank: that's CardBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>(). Every franchise then gets a manual that sends trays back to its own counter, without head office knowing any franchise by name. The analogy breaks in the same place the code does: a franchise could write another restaurant's name in the blank, and the manual can't stop it. The recursive bound only checks that the name belongs to some franchise.

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · T & Any says definitely not null
x: The default bound of a type parameter is Any? (lesson 2), so a plain T may be a nullable type. Sometimes you know that one particular value is not null, and you want the type to say so. Kotlin writes that as T & Any, a definitely non-nullable type: "T, with null taken out". Java // Java's types say nothing about null. The best you can do is a comment and a run-time check. static <T> T firstNotNullValue(List<T> items) { for (T item : items) if (item != null) return item; throw new NoSuchElementException("no non-null element"); } String first = firstNotNullValue(Arrays.asList(null, "eur", "usd")); Kotlin fun <T> List<T>.firstNotNullValue(): T & Any { for (item in this) if (item != null) return item // smart cast: item is T & Any here throw NoSuchElementException("no non-null element") } val first: String = listOf(null, "eur", "usd").firstNotNullValue() // T = String?, result String With T = String?, T & Any is String. With T = Payment, it's Payment. The compiler holds you to it: returning a plain T gives Return type mismatch: expected 'T (of fun <T> forget) & Any', actual 'T (of fun <T> forget)'. The Kotlin docs name the main use case: overriding Java methods whose generic parameters are annotated @NotNull. Kotlin reads @NotNull T in a Java interface as T & Any: Java public interface NotNullTransformer<T> { @NotNull T transform(@NotNull T value); } Kotlin class UpperCaser<T : CharSequence?> : NotNullTransformer<T> { override fun transform(value: T & Any): T & Any = ... } Two rules come with it. The left side must be a type parameter with a nullable bound; with T : Any there is no null to remove, and the compiler says Intersection types are supported only for definitely non-nullable types: left part must be a type parameter with nullable bounds. And the guarantee is Kotlin-only: Java sees <T> T firstNotNullValue(List<T>) with no trace of & Any. The docs also say that when you work only with Kotlin, you'll rarely need to write it, because inference handles it. Expect to type T & Any at the Java boundary and in small helpers. One more that earns its keep in a message handler: Java // Java: the null check happens, but the type can't record it static <T> T requireValue(T value, String name) { if (value == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException(name + " is required"); return value; } Kotlin fun <T> T.requireValue(name: String): T & Any = this ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("$name is required") val token: String = message.cardToken.requireValue("card token") // cardToken is a String? It turns an optional field of a Kafka message into a value the rest of the handler can use without !!. Take null out of a type Run NonNullDemo (or NonNullDemoJava). Open NotNullTransformer.java next to it: a Java interface with @NotNull. Uncomment wrong moves 1 and 2 in NonNullDemo.kt one at a time. Predict first. Uncomment function 3 at the bottom. In the Java twin, uncomment the oops line and run: what does Java catch, and when? NonNullDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l10.demo /** T may be nullable (String?), but the result is "T, definitely not null". */ fun <T> List<T>.firstNotNullValue(): T & Any { for (item in this) if (item != null) return item // smart cast: item is T & Any here throw NoSuchElementException("no non-null element") } /** The docs' example: fall back to a value that is known not to be null. */ fun <T> elvis(x: T, y: T & Any): T & Any = x ?: y /** Implements the Java interface in NonNullDemoJava.java, whose methods are annotated @NotNull. */ class UpperCaser<T : CharSequence?> : NotNullTransformer<T> { @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") override fun transform(value: T & Any): T & Any = value.toString().uppercase() as (T & Any) } fun main() { val currencies: List<String?> = listOf(null, "eur", "usd") val first: String = currencies.firstNotNullValue() // T = String?, result String val note: String? = null val shown: String = elvis(note, "no note") println("first = $first, shown = $shown") println("transformed = ${UpperCaser<String?>().transform("pay_1")}") // Wrong moves. Uncomment one at a time, predict the error, then run. // fun <T> forget(x: T): T & Any = x // 1 // val n: String = UpperCaser<String?>().transform(null) // 2 } // 3. & Any needs a type parameter whose bound is nullable. // fun <T : Any> pointless(x: T & Any) {} ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.NonNullDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l10/demo/NonNullDemo.kt NonNullDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l10.demo; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; import java.util.Objects; /** * Java twin of NonNullDemo.kt. Java types say nothing about null, so "T, but not null" can only be * a convention (or an annotation such as @NotNull), checked at run time. */ public class NonNullDemoJava { static <T> T firstNotNullValue(List<T> items) { for (T item : items) if (item != null) return item; throw new NoSuchElementException("no non-null element"); } static <T> T elvis(T x, T y) { return x != null ? x : Objects.requireNonNull(y); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> currencies = Arrays.asList(null, "eur", "usd"); String first = firstNotNullValue(currencies); String shown = elvis(null, "no note"); System.out.println("first = " + first + ", shown = " + shown); System.out.println("transformed = " + new UpperCaser<String>().transform("pay_1")); // Uncomment and run: it compiles in Java. What happens at run time? // String oops = elvis(null, null); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.NonNullDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l10/demo/NonNullDemoJava.java Both print first = eur, shown = no note and transformed = PAY_1. Kotlin's wrong moves: (1) Return type mismatch: expected 'T (of fun <T> forget) & Any', actual 'T (of fun <T> forget)'., (2) Null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'String'.: for T = String?, T & Any is String. Function 3: Intersection types are supported only for definitely non-nullable types: left part must be a type parameter with nullable bounds. The Java oops line compiles and throws NullPointerException from Objects.requireNonNull at run time. You meet self types in Java libraries before you write one. Testcontainers declares GenericContainer<SELF extends GenericContainer<SELF>>, which is why Kotlin test code for an Oracle or Kafka integration test sometimes needs class KGenericContainer(image: String) : GenericContainer<KGenericContainer>(image) just to use the fluent withEnv(...) chain. Card-issuer and banking SDKs in Java often ship builder hierarchies with the same shape. T & Any shows up when your Kotlin code implements a Java interface from such an SDK that marks generic parameters @NotNull. And Nothing is the honest return type for helpers like fun rejectPayment(reason: String): Nothing in a Temporal activity, which lets val card = request.card ?: rejectPayment("no card") type-check without a dummy value.

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · @UnsafeVariance: how List can take an E in contains
x: Here is a puzzle from lesson 4. List is declared interface List<out E>, and an out parameter can't appear in a parameter position. Yet you call list.contains(x) every day. The standard library's source (2.4.21) shows how: public operator fun contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E): Boolean public fun indexOf(element: @UnsafeVariance E): Int @UnsafeVariance "suppresses errors about variance conflict" for one type use. It is a promise from the author: this parameter is only compared, never stored, so a List<Int> seen as a List<Number> can't be damaged by it. contains(2.5) on that list just returns false. Why take an E at all, when Any? would need no annotation? Because the E lets the compiler catch nonsense checks. Java chose Object, and pays for it: Java Set<Long> paymentIds = Set.of(42L); paymentIds.contains(42); // false: 42 is boxed to an Integer, and Integer(42) != Long(42) List.of(1_200, 350).contains("1200"); // compiles, always false Kotlin val paymentIds: Set<Long> = setOf(42L) paymentIds.contains(42) // true: the literal 42 is typed as a Long here listOf(1_200, 350).contains("1200") // error: Type inference failed. The value of the type parameter 'T' must be mentioned in input types ... That first Java line is a real bug class: an int payment id looked up in a set of Longs, false every time. The annotation is called unsafe for a reason. It switches the check off, and the compiler believes you: Java // Java's way to break a ? extends view on purpose is an unchecked cast: List<? extends Object> view = ids; ((List<Object>) view).add(42); String lastId = ids.get(ids.size() - 1); // ClassCastException Kotlin class Ledger<out T>(first: T) { private val entries = mutableListOf(first) fun add(entry: @UnsafeVariance T) { entries.add(entry) } // stores it: a broken promise fun last(): T = entries.last() } val ids: Ledger<String> = Ledger("pay_1") val anything: Ledger<Any> = ids // fine: Ledger is out T anything.add(42) // compiles val lastId: String = ids.last() // ClassCastException Use @UnsafeVariance only on parameters that are read and compared (contains, indexOf, an equality check), never on ones that are kept. You might write it yourself on a read-only covariant type that offers a lookup, such as interface Page<out T> { fun indexOf(item: @UnsafeVariance T): Int }. To check that it's honest, follow the parameter through the body. If it only reaches ==, equals or hashCode, the promise holds. If it reaches a field, a collection or a callback that keeps it, remove the annotation and make the type invariant, or split it into a read view and a write view, as lesson 11 of this track does. Use the annotation well, then badly Run UnsafeVarianceDemo and UnsafeVarianceDemoJava. Find the line that compiles in Java and is rejected in Kotlin. Uncomment wrong move 1 in the Kotlin file, predict, run. Uncomment wrong move 2 (Ledger2) and read the error. That's the check @UnsafeVariance switched off in Ledger. UnsafeVarianceDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l10.demo /** Declared out, then the check is switched off for add(). It compiles. It is a lie. */ class Ledger<out T>(first: T) { private val entries = mutableListOf(first) fun add(entry: @UnsafeVariance T) { entries.add(entry) } fun last(): T = entries.last() } fun main() { // 1. The standard library uses @UnsafeVariance safely: contains only compares, it never stores. val amounts: List<Number> = listOf(1_200, 350) // List<Int> seen as List<Number> println("contains(350): ${amounts.contains(350)}, contains(2.5): ${amounts.contains(2.5)}") // 2. And because contains takes an E, the compiler can catch a nonsense check. // println(listOf(1_200, 350).contains("1200")) // wrong move 1 // 3. Used carelessly, the same annotation breaks type safety. val ids: Ledger<String> = Ledger("pay_1") val anything: Ledger<Any> = ids // fine: Ledger is out T anything.add(42) // compiles thanks to @UnsafeVariance try { val lastId: String = ids.last() println(lastId) } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message?.substringBefore(" (")}") } } // Wrong move 2: remove @UnsafeVariance from a copy of Ledger and read the error. // class Ledger2<out T> { fun add(entry: T) {} } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.UnsafeVarianceDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l10/demo/UnsafeVarianceDemo.kt UnsafeVarianceDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l10.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of UnsafeVarianceDemo.kt. Java's contains takes an Object, so it never needed the * annotation, and it can't catch a nonsense check. h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · Function types, Nothing and type aliases
x: Three more tools sit at the edges of the type system. Function types carry variance on both ends. (P) -> R is Function1<in P, out R> (lesson 5), so a composition helper accepts a more general second step and can hand back a more general result: Java // Function<T, R> is invariant, so the JDK writes the variance into the signature: // default <V> Function<T, V> andThen(Function<? super R, ? extends V> after) Function<String, Long> parseCents = s -> Long.parseLong(s.replace(".", "")); Function<Object, String> describe = x -> "<" + x + ">"; Function<String, String> pipeline = parseCents.andThen(describe); // <1250> for "12.50" Kotlin fun <A, B, C> andThen(first: (A) -> B, second: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> second(first(a)) } val parseCents: (String) -> Long = { it.replace(".", "").toLong() } val describe: (Any) -> String = { "<$it>" } // takes Any, not just Long val pipeline: (String) -> CharSequence = andThen(parseCents, describe) // <1250> for "12.50" Nothing is the bottom type: a subtype of every type, with no values at all. throw and TODO() have type Nothing, which is why val strict: Long = text.toLongOrNull() ?: fail("not a number") type-checks when fun fail(reason: String): Nothing. It also explains emptyList(): one shared List<Nothing> fits every List<Payment>, because List is out E and Nothing is below Payment. Lesson 11 uses the same trick for Either. Java has no bottom type. Collections.emptyList() is a generic method whose T is inferred at each call, and a Kotlin List<Nothing> reaches Java as a raw List. A type alias gives an existing type a shorter name, and it can be generic: Java // Java has no type aliases. The nearest thing, a functional interface, is a new, separate type. @FunctionalInterface interface Handler<E> { void handle(E event); } Kotlin typealias Handler<E> = (E) -> Unit // just a name: a Handler<E> IS an (E) -> Unit typealias Table<K> = MutableMap<K, MutableList<K>> val audit: Handler<CardAuthorized> = { println("audit ${it.paymentId}") } val plain: (CardAuthorized) -> Unit = audit // same type, no conversion Because an alias is only a name, it has the variance of what it stands for: a Handler<PaymentEvent> is a Handler<CardAuthorized>, exactly as with the function type. Aliases nested inside a class became Stable in Kotlin 2.3, with one limit: they can't mention the outer class's type parameters. Compose with variance, fail with Nothing Run FunctionTypesDemo (or FunctionTypesDemoJava, which also calls the JDK's own andThen). Uncomment the wrong move and read which type the compiler inferred for the pipeline. Change fail's return type from Nothing to Unit. Which line breaks, and why? FunctionTypesDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l10.demo /** A new name for a function type. Not a new type: a Handler<E> IS an (E) -> Unit. */ typealias Handler<E> = (E) -> Unit fun <A, B, C> andThen(first: (A) -> B, second: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> second(first(a)) } fun fail(reason: String): Nothing = throw IllegalArgumentException(reason) fun main() { // 1. Function1<in P, out R>: a more general second function fits. val parseCents: (String) -> Long = { it.replace(".", "").toLong() } val describe: (Any) -> String = { "<$it>" } val pipeline: (String) -> CharSequence = andThen(parseCents, describe) println("pipeline(\"12.50\") = ${pipeline("12.50")}") // 2. Nothing is a subtype of every type. val none: List<CardAuth> = emptyList() // emptyList() is a List<Nothing> here val cents: Long = "x".toLongOrNull() ?: 0L val strict: Long = "1200".toLongOrNull() ?: fail("not a number") // fail returns Nothing, so this is a Long println("none = $none, cents = $cents, strict = $strict") // 3. A type alias is only a name. val audit: Handler<CardAuth> = { println("audit ${it.id}") } val plain: (CardAuth) -> Unit = audit // same type, no conversion plain(CardAuth("pay_1")) // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val tooStrict: (Any) -> String = andThen(parseCents, describe) } data class CardAuth(val id: String) ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.FunctionTypesDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l10/demo/FunctionTypesDemo.kt FunctionTypesDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l10.demo; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java twin of FunctionTypesDemo.kt. Java's Function<T, R> is invariant, so the JDK writes the * variance into andThen's signature: andThen(Function<? super R, ? extends V> after). */ public class FunctionTypesDemoJava { static <A, B, C> Function<A, C> andThen(Function<A, ? extends B> first, Function<? super B, ? extends C> second) { return a -> second.apply(first.apply(a)); } static <T> T fail(String reason) { throw new IllegalArgumentException(reason); } // no Nothing: fake it with T public static void main(String[] args) { Function<String, Long> parseCents = s -> Long.parseLong(s.replace(".", "")); Function<Object, String> describe = x -> "<" + x + ">"; Function<String, CharSequence> pipeline = andThen(parseCents, describe); System.out.println("pipeline(\"12.50\") = " + pipeline.apply("12.50")); System.out.println("JDK andThen: " + parseCents.andThen(describe).apply("3.50")); List<CardAuth> none = Collections.emptyList(); // generic method: T inferred as CardAuth long strict = Long.parseLong("1200"); System.out.println("none = " + none + ", strict = " + strict); Consumer<CardAuth> audit = a -> System.out.println("audit " + a.getId()); // no type aliases in Java audit.accept(new CardAuth("pay_1")); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l10.demo.FunctionTypesDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l10/demo/FunctionTypesDemoJava.java Kotlin prints pipeline("12.50") = <1250>, none = [], cents = 0, strict = 1200 and audit pay_1; Java prints the same plus JDK andThen: <350>. The wrong move fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected '(Any) -> String', actual '(String) -> String'.: a function that needs a String input can't stand in for one that takes Any. With Unit, the strict line fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Long', actual 'Any'.: the elvis expression's type becomes the common supertype of Long and Unit. Nothing fits there because it is a subtype of Long. Type aliases (Kotlin docs) docs The common mistake in self-typed builders is the unchecked shortcut: @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") fun amount(c: Long): B { cents = c; return this as B } in the base class, with no self(). It works until someone copies a subclass and forgets to change the type argument: class WalletBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>(). That compiles, and WalletBuilder().amount(5) throws ClassCastException: class WalletBuilder cannot be cast to class CardBuilder at the call site, because erasure made the cast inside amount check nothing. People write the cast because it saves one override per subclass. The fix is an abstract protected abstract fun self(): B that each subclass implements as = this. Then the same copy-paste slip is a compile error: Return type mismatch: expected 'CardPaymentBuilder', actual 'WalletPaymentBuilder'.

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · Java and Kotlin
x: A self-typed builder hierarchy in Java and Kotlin PaymentRequestBuilder.java abstract class PaymentRequestBuilder<B extends PaymentRequestBuilder<B>> { protected long cents; protected String currency; B amount(long cents) { this.cents = cents; return self(); } B currency(String code) { this.currency = code; return self(); } protected abstract B self(); } final class CardPaymentBuilder extends PaymentRequestBuilder<CardPaymentBuilder> { private String token; CardPaymentBuilder cardToken(String token) { this.token = token; return this; } @Override protected CardPaymentBuilder self() { return this; } CardPayment build() { if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalStateException("amount must be positive"); return new CardPayment(cents, currency, "", token); } } // new CardPaymentBuilder().amount(1_200).currency("EUR").cardToken("tok_42").build(); PaymentRequestBuilder.kt abstract class PaymentRequestBuilder<B : PaymentRequestBuilder<B>> { protected var cents: Long = 0 protected var currency: String? = null fun amount(cents: Long): B { this.cents = cents; return self() } fun currency(code: String): B { currency = code; return self() } protected abstract fun self(): B } class CardPaymentBuilder : PaymentRequestBuilder<CardPaymentBuilder>() { private var token: String? = null fun cardToken(token: String): CardPaymentBuilder { this.token = token; return this } override fun self() = this fun build(): CardPayment { check(cents > 0) { "amount must be positive" } return CardPayment(cents, currency!!, "", checkNotNull(token)) } } // CardPaymentBuilder().amount(1_200).currency("EUR").cardToken("tok_42").build() The recursive bound is the same idea in both languages: B extends PaymentRequestBuilder<B> and B : PaymentRequestBuilder<B>, with each subclass passing itself and an abstract self() instead of an unchecked cast. Kotlin adds checks Java can't express: currency is a String?, so build() must deal with a missing value, and helpers like check and checkNotNull throw IllegalStateException with your message. The other three tools of this lesson have no Java twin: T & Any (Java types carry no nullability), @UnsafeVariance (Java has no declaration-site variance to suppress), and Nothing (Java has no bottom type). Java also has no type aliases. And in Kotlin you can often skip the builder entirely with a data class, default arguments and copy.

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · Worked example
x: Add a wallet payment to the builder hierarchy The lab's hierarchy has card payments and bank transfers. Product wants wallet payments too. The quickest path is copy and paste from CardPaymentBuilder, and that's how the classic bug gets in: the type argument still says CardPaymentBuilder. class WalletPaymentBuilder : PaymentRequestBuilder<CardPaymentBuilder>() { // copied, not changed private var walletId: String? = null fun walletId(id: String): WalletPaymentBuilder { walletId = id; return this } override fun self(): CardPaymentBuilder = this } // error: Return type mismatch: expected 'CardPaymentBuilder', actual 'WalletPaymentBuilder'. final class WalletPaymentBuilder extends PaymentRequestBuilder<CardPaymentBuilder> { // copied, not changed private String walletId; WalletPaymentBuilder walletId(String id) { walletId = id; return this; } @Override protected CardPaymentBuilder self() { return this; } } // error: incompatible types: WalletPaymentBuilder cannot be converted to CardPaymentBuilder The abstract self() caught it at compile time. With return this as B in the base class it would have compiled and failed later, at the first amount(...) call. Fix the declaration: the subclass passes itself. class WalletPaymentBuilder : PaymentRequestBuilder<WalletPaymentBuilder>() { private var walletId: String? = null fun walletId(id: String): WalletPaymentBuilder { walletId = id; return this } override fun self() = this // B is WalletPaymentBuilder: no cast final class WalletPaymentBuilder extends PaymentRequestBuilder<WalletPaymentBuilder> { private String walletId; WalletPaymentBuilder walletId(String id) { walletId = id; return this; } @Override protected WalletPaymentBuilder self() { return this; } // no cast Build: check the common fields with the base class's checkCommon(), then the wallet's own field. Self-check: why does amount(...) in the chain below return a WalletPaymentBuilder without any change to the base class? (Because B is filled with WalletPaymentBuilder in the declaration, and amount returns B.) fun build(): WalletPayment { checkCommon() val id = checkNotNull(walletId) { "wallet id is required" } return WalletPayment(cents, currency!!, reference, id) } } val p = WalletPaymentBuilder().amount(2_500).currency("EUR").walletId("wal_9").build() WalletPayment build() { checkCommon(); if (walletId == null) throw new IllegalStateException("wallet id is required"); return new WalletPayment(cents, currency, reference, walletId); } } WalletPayment p = new WalletPaymentBuilder().amount(2_500).currency("EUR").walletId("wal_9").build();

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · Quiz
x: abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> { fun amount(c: Long): B; ... } and class CardBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>(). What is the static type of CardBuilder().amount(1_200)? Builder<CardBuilder> CardBuilder Builder<*> B, which the compiler can't resolve outside the class amount returns B, and the subclass declaration fills B with CardBuilder. So at the call site the result is a CardBuilder, and its own methods are still available. That is the whole point of the recursive bound. fun <T> List<T>.firstNotNullValue(): T & Any. What is the type of listOf<String?>(null, "EUR").firstNotNullValue()? String String? Any String & Any? T is String?, and & Any removes the null: String? minus null is String. With T = Payment it would be Payment. That's why the result can go straight into a val code: String. Why can interface List<out E> declare fun contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E): Boolean without risk? Because the annotation makes the check happen at run time instead Because List is immutable, so nothing can be stored Because contains only compares the argument and never stores it, so a List<Int> seen as List<Number> can't be damaged Because E is erased, so variance doesn't apply at run time Variance protects against storing a wrong value. contains stores nothing; asking a list of ints whether it contains 2.5 just returns false. The annotation is a promise about that. It isn't a run-time check, and "immutable" isn't the reason: @UnsafeVariance on a storing method breaks even an immutable-looking class, as the Ledger demo shows. val parse: (String) -> Long and val describe: (Any) -> String. Does val p: (String) -> CharSequence = andThen(parse, describe) compile, with fun <A, B, C> andThen(first: (A) -> B, second: (B) -> C): (A) -> C? No: describe must be exactly (Long) -> String No: the result would be (String) -> String, which is not a (String) -> CharSequence Only with an explicit cast Yes: (Any) -> String is a (Long) -> String (in on the parameter), and (String) -> String is a (String) -> CharSequence (out on the result) Function types are Function1<in P, out R>. A function that accepts any value can stand in for one that accepts a Long, and a function that returns a String can stand in for one that returns a CharSequence. This is the "pick the right variance" check from lesson 5 applied twice in one call. From "Covariance with out: producers": class Ledger<out T> { fun add(entry: T) {} } doesn't compile. What does the compiler object to? T appears in an in-position (a parameter) in a class that declared it out add is public; it would compile if it were protected Classes declared out can't have functions with parameters Ledger needs a constructor that takes a T An out parameter may appear only in out-positions such as return types; a parameter is an in-position. protected members are checked too; only private ones are exempt. @UnsafeVariance would silence the error, and this lesson's demo shows what that costs when add stores the value.

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · Key terms
x: Recursive bound A bound that mentions the type parameter itself: T : Comparable<T>, B : Builder<B>. Self type A type parameter that stands for "my own concrete subclass", so base methods can return it. Definitely non-nullable type T & Any: the type parameter T with null taken out. @UnsafeVariance An annotation that switches off the variance check for one type use. A promise, not a check. Nothing Kotlin's bottom type: a subtype of every type, with no values. The type of throw and TODO(). Type alias A new name for an existing type, such as typealias Handler<E> = (E) -> Unit. Not a new type. What problem does abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> solve? Base-class setters can return B, the concrete subclass, so a chain like CardBuilder().amount(1).cardToken("t") keeps the subclass's methods. Why an abstract self(): B instead of return this as B? this as B is unchecked and fails late if a subclass passes the wrong type argument. An overridden self() = this is checked by the compiler. What does T & Any mean? T with null removed: a definitely non-nullable type. For T = String? it is String. What is the main use of T & Any? Overriding Java generic methods whose parameters or results are annotated @NotNull. How does List<out E> get away with contains(element: E)? The parameter is marked @UnsafeVariance. It's safe because contains only compares the element and never stores it. Why does val none: List<Payment> = emptyList() compile? emptyList() gives a List<Nothing>. Nothing is a subtype of every type, and List is out E, so it is a List<Payment>. Is typealias Handler<E> = (E) -> Unit a new type? No. It's only a name: a Handler<CardAuthorized> is an (CardAuthorized) -> Unit, with the same variance.

h: Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance · Go deeper
x: Recursive bounds go further than builders. java.lang.Enum is declared Enum<E extends Enum<E>> so that compareTo takes the same enum type, and EnumSet.noneOf(Class<E>) is bounded <E extends Enum<E>>. Kotlin's Enum<E : Enum<E>> is the same declaration. Lesson 2's fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T) is the most common recursive bound of all; the Java signature Kotlin generates for it is <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, because Kotlin's Comparable is declared in T. The standard library's use of @UnsafeVariance is easy to check. In the 2.4.21 sources (kotlin-stdlib-sources.jar, file Collections.kt) it appears on contains, containsAll and indexOf of List, and on AbstractCollection.contains. The contains("1200") error you saw comes from a second safety net: when the member contains(element: Int) doesn't accept a String, the compiler tries the extension Iterable<T>.contains(element: T), whose T is marked so that it must match the receiver's element type, and inference fails with the message you read. Two small facts about Nothing. The type of the literal null is Nothing?, which is why null fits every nullable type. And when a Kotlin function returns List<Nothing>, Java sees a raw List, because Java has no bottom type to write there. Type aliases can't create the distinct types people sometimes want from them. typealias PaymentId = String lets you pass any String where a PaymentId is expected. If you want the compiler to keep payment ids and refund ids apart, use a value class, @JvmInline value class PaymentId(val value: String), which is a real type with no wrapper object at run time in most uses.

h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Either: two out parameters and Nothing do the work
x: This lesson puts the whole track to work in four small designs. Each one uses a different tool, and the lab asks you to build all four. The first is a result type that is either a failure or a success: Java // Java 21: a sealed interface and records. Java has no Nothing, so Left carries an R it never uses. sealed interface Either<L, R> permits Left, Right {} record Left<L, R>(L value) implements Either<L, R> {} record Right<L, R>(R value) implements Either<L, R> {} static <L, R, R2> Either<L, R2> map(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super R, ? extends R2> f) { return switch (e) { case Left<L, R> l -> new Left<>(l.value()); // must rebuild: a Left<L, R> is not a Left<L, R2> case Right<L, R> r -> new Right<>(f.apply(r.value())); }; } Kotlin sealed interface Either<out L, out R> { data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing> data class Right<out R>(val value: R) : Either<Nothing, R> } fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.map(f: (R) -> R2): Either<L, R2> = when (this) { is Either.Left -> this // no rebuild needed is Either.Right -> Either.Right(f(value)) } Two tools from this track meet here. Either only hands values out, so both parameters are out (lesson 4). And Left fills the unused side with Nothing, the bottom type from lesson 10. Put together, a Left<String> is an Either<String, Nothing>, and because Nothing is a subtype of every type and R is out, it is also an Either<String, R2> for any R2. That's why is Either.Left -> this type-checks: the same object is a valid result for any success type. Java has neither tool, so its map must build a new Left every time. In payment code this is the shape of validation: fun validate(auth: Authorization): Either<RejectReason, ApprovedAuthorization>. A caller can map the success, fall back with getOrElse, or when over both cases, and because Either is sealed the compiler checks that both are handled. Unlike an exception, the failure is part of the signature. Covariance also makes results compose: an Either<String, Long> is an Either<Any, Number>, so a function that reports any failure and any numeric result accepts it. Remove the outs and almost everything breaks at once, including the Left and Right declarations themselves: Type parameter 'L' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position in type 'Either<L (of class Left<out L>), Nothing>'. A supertype is a position too. Fold, mapLeft, then remove out Run EitherDemo and EitherDemoJava. Compare how mapLeft handles the Right branch in each. In EitherDemo.kt, remove both outs from sealed interface Either (keep the ones on Left and Right). Predict how many lines break, then run. Put the outs back. EitherDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l11.demo /** Both parameters are out: an Either only hands values out. Left and Right fill the other side with Nothing. */ sealed interface Either<out L, out R> { data class Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing> data class Right<out R>(val value: R) : Either<Nothing, R> } /** Maps the failure side. `is Right -> this` type-checks because a Right<R> is an Either<Nothing, R>. */ fun <L, R, L2> Either<L, R>.mapLeft(f: (L) -> L2): Either<L2, R> = when (this) { is Either.Left -> Either.Left(f(value)) is Either.Right -> this } fun <L, R, T> Either<L, R>.fold(onLeft: (L) -> T, onRight: (R) -> T): T = when (this) { is Either.Left -> onLeft(value) is Either.Right -> onRight(value) } fun parseCents(text: String): Either<String, Long> = text.toLongOrNull()?.let { Either.Right(it) } ?: Either.Left("not a number: $text") fun main() { val ok = parseCents("1200") val bad = parseCents("12,00") println(ok.fold({ "error: $it" }, { "cents: $it" })) println(bad.mapLeft { it.uppercase() }) val wider: Either<Any, Number> = ok // out on both sides: String -> Any, Long -> Number println("wider = $wider") // Break it: remove both `out`s from `sealed interface Either` (keep them on Left and Right), // run, and read the errors in mapLeft and on the `wider` line. } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.EitherDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l11/demo/EitherDemo.kt EitherDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l11.demo; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java twin of EitherDemo.kt, with a sealed interface and records (Java 21 pattern matching). * Java has no Nothing, so Left must carry an R it never uses, and mapLeft must build a new Right. */ public class EitherDemoJava { sealed interface Either<L, R> permits Left, Right {} record Left<L, R>(L value) implements Either<L, R> {} record Right<L, R>(R value) implements Either<L, R> {} static <L, R, L2> Either<L2, R> mapLeft(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super L, ? extends L2> f) { return switch (e) { case Left<L, R> l -> new Left<>(f.apply(l.value())); case Right<L, R> r -> new Right<>(r.value()); // can't reuse r: it is an Either<L, R> }; } static <L, R, T> T fold(Either<L, R> e, Function<? super L, ? extends T> onLeft, Function<? super R, ? extends T> onRight) { return switch (e) { case Left<L, R> l -> onLeft.apply(l.value()); case Right<L, R> r -> onRight.apply(r.value()); }; } static Either<String, Long> parseCents(String text) { try { return new Right<>(Long.parseLong(text)); } catch (NumberFormatException ex) { return new Left<>("not a number: " + text); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Either<String, Long> ok = parseCents("1200"); Either<String, Long> bad = parseCents("12,00"); System.out.println(EitherDemoJava.<String, Long, String>fold(ok, l -> "error: " + l, r -> "cents: " + r)); System.out.println(mapLeft(bad, String::toUpperCase)); Either<? extends Object, ? extends Number> wider = ok; // Java: wildcards at the use site System.out.println("wider = " + wider); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.EitherDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l11/demo/EitherDemoJava.java Both print cents: 1200, the upper-cased failure (Left(value=NOT A NUMBER: 12,00) in Kotlin, Left[value=...] for the Java record) and wider = Right(value=1200). Kotlin's mapLeft returns this for a Right; Java builds a new Right. Without the outs you get six errors: Left and Right themselves (Type parameter 'L' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'invariant' position ...), mapLeft's when, two in parseCents, and Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Either<Any, Number>', actual 'Either<String, Long>'. Sealed classes and interfaces (Kotlin docs) docs The event bus is a post office sorting room. Letters (events) come in from every counter, which is the producing side. Each pigeonhole is labeled with a letter class, such as "registered", and each pigeonhole has clerks assigned to it, which is the consuming side. A clerk trained to handle any letter can be assigned to the registered pigeonhole: that's the (PaymentEvent) -> Unit handler under CardAuthorized::class. A clerk who only handles registered letters can't be given the general pile, so the office puts a checker in front of him who passes on only registered mail: that's the safeCast adapter. The analogy breaks at the checker. A real clerk would notice a wrong letter himself, but a Kotlin lambda can't: if you skip the adapter and cast the handler instead, the wrong event reaches it and fails with a ClassCastException inside the handler.

h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Split reading from writing: a covariant repository view
x: The second design is a repository. A full repository both takes entities (save) and returns them (findAll, findById), so it must be invariant, and an audit job that wants to read any repository can't accept a Repository<Merchant, Long> as a Repository<Entity<Long>, Long>. The fix is to split the interface by variance: put the reading half in its own covariant interface. Java interface ReadRepository<T> { List<T> findAll(); } // Java: invariant, so... static void printAll(ReadRepository<? extends Entity<?>> repo) { // ...each reader writes ? extends for (Entity<?> e : repo.findAll()) System.out.println("entity " + e.getId()); } Kotlin interface Entity<ID : Comparable<ID>> { val id: ID } interface ReadRepository<out T> { fun findAll(): List<T> } // only hands T out interface Repository<T : Entity<ID>, ID : Comparable<ID>> : ReadRepository<T> { fun save(entity: T): T // takes T in: invariant fun findById(id: ID): T? } fun printAll(repo: ReadRepository<Entity<*>>) { for (e in repo.findAll()) println("entity ${e.id}") } Now printAll accepts a Repository<Merchant, Long> and a Repository<Settlement, String>, because each one is a ReadRepository of its entity, and the read side is covariant. The full repository is still invariant, and the compiler still refuses val anyEntity: Repository<Entity<Long>, Long> = merchants with Initializer type mismatch. Nothing was weakened; the safe half was given its own name. The bounds are lesson 2's tools: ID : Comparable<ID> lets the in-memory implementation keep entities in a TreeMap sorted by id, and T : Entity<ID> ties each entity to its id type. The Kotlin docs give the same advice for reading and writing dictionaries: split the interface instead of casting. This is interface segregation, done by variance. Notice where the variance came from. You didn't decide that ReadRepository is covariant; you looked at its members, saw that each one only returns T, and the compiler agreed. That is the habit this track has been building: read the positions, and let them tell you. Audit any repository through its read view Run RepositoryDemo (or RepositoryDemoJava). One printAll reads merchants, settlements and a writable repository. Uncomment the wrong move in each file, predict, run. Remove out from ReadRepository in the Kotlin file. Which calls to printAll still compile? Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val anyEntity: Repository<Entity<Long>, Long> = writable } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.RepositoryDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l11/demo/RepositoryDemo.kt RepositoryDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l11.demo; import java.util.List; /** Java twin of RepositoryDemo.kt. Java's interfaces are invariant, so the reader writes ? extends. */ public class RepositoryDemoJava { interface ReadRepository<T> { List<T> findAll(); } static void printAll(ReadRepository<? extends Entity<?>> repo) { // every use must say ? extends for (Entity<?> e : repo.findAll()) System.out.println(" entity " + e.getId()); } public static void main(String[] args) { ReadRepository<Merchant> merchants = () -> List.of(new Merchant(2, "Bakery"), new Merchant(7, "Kiosk")); ReadRepository<Settlement> settlements = () -> List.of(new Settlement("s-1", 1_200)); System.out.println("merchants:"); printAll(merchants); System.out.println("settlements:"); printAll(settlements); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // ReadRepository<Entity<?>> strict = merchants; } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.RepositoryDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l11/demo/RepositoryDemoJava.java Both print the entities 2, 7 and s-1; Kotlin also prints entity 9 from the writable repository. The wrong moves fail with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Repository<Entity<Long>, Long>', actual 'Repository<Merchant, Long>'. (the full repository is invariant) and ReadRepository<Merchant> cannot be converted to ReadRepository<Entity<?>> in Java (no wildcard on the variable). Without out, none of the three printAll calls compile. These four shapes map straight onto a payment service. A Kafka consumer decodes each record and publishes it on an in-process bus, where the fraud check, the ledger writer and the audit log subscribe by event class, and the audit log takes every PaymentEvent. Validation of an incoming authorization returns Either<RejectReason, AuthorizedPayment> instead of throwing, so a Temporal workflow can branch on it without catching exceptions across the activity boundary. A reporting job that reads merchants and settlements from Oracle takes ReadRepository<Entity<*>>, while only the write path sees the invariant Repository. And per-request context in a Quarkus endpoint (the merchant id, the accepted currencies, the idempotency key) fits a typed-key container, so context[IDEMPOTENCY_KEY] comes back as a String with no cast.

h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · A typed event bus: events flow out, handlers take them in
x: The third design is the one in the figure: an event bus for a payment service. Events flow out of publishers, and handlers take them in. That's lessons 4 and 5 in one class. Java final class Router { private final List<Consumer<PaymentEvent>> adapters = new ArrayList<>(); <E extends PaymentEvent> void on(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> handler) { // Consumer Super adapters.add(event -> { if (type.isInstance(event)) handler.accept(type.cast(event)); }); } } Kotlin class EventBus { private val handlers = HashMap<KClass<out PaymentEvent>, MutableList<(PaymentEvent) -> Unit>>() fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: (E) -> Unit) { handlers.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() } .add { event -> type.safeCast(event)?.let(handler) } // the adapter } fun publish(event: PaymentEvent) { handlers[event::class]?.forEach { it(event) } } } Every piece has a reason. The map's keys are KClass<out PaymentEvent>, because that's the type of event::class (lesson 9). The handler can't go into the list as it is, and the compiler explains why: Argument type mismatch: actual type is '(E (of fun <E : PaymentEvent> on)) -> Unit', but '(PaymentEvent) -> Unit' was expected. A function that only takes CardAuthorized can't be handed a RefundIssued; function parameters are in. So the bus stores an adapter that takes any PaymentEvent, checks it with safeCast, and passes on only an E. The same in works in your favor at the call site: an audit handler of type (PaymentEvent) -> Unit can subscribe under CardAuthorized::class. For Kotlin callers, add the reified wrapper from lesson 8, with one new word: Java // Java callers pass the class: bus.subscribe(CardAuthorized.class, e -> fraudCheck(e)); // There is no Java equivalent of the reified, noinline wrapper. Kotlin inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(noinline handler: (E) -> Unit) = subscribe(E::class, handler) bus.subscribe<CardAuthorized> { fraudCheck(it) } A lambda passed to an inline function is normally inlined too, which means it doesn't exist as an object. This one gets stored in the map, so it has to stay an object: noinline says so. One limit to know: this bus routes by the exact class. A handler subscribed under PaymentEvent::class never runs, because no event's run-time class is the interface itself. The "Go deeper" part shows how to walk supertypes when you need that. Route events to typed handlers Run EventBusDemo (or EventBusDemoJava). The audit handler takes every PaymentEvent but is subscribed under CardAuthorized. Uncomment wrong move 1 inside Router.on (comment out the adapter line below it). Read the error. Restore it, then uncomment wrong move 2 in main. Why is a handler for one subtype refused for the supertype? EventBusDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l11.demo import kotlin.reflect.KClass import kotlin.reflect.safeCast interface PaymentEvent { val paymentId: String } data class CardAuthorized(override val paymentId: String, val cents: Long) : PaymentEvent data class RefundIssued(override val paymentId: String, val cents: Long) : PaymentEvent /** The smallest typed router: one list of adapters, each of which checks the event's class. */ class Router { private val adapters = mutableListOf<(PaymentEvent) -> Unit>() fun <E : PaymentEvent> on(type: KClass<E>, handler: (E) -> Unit) { // adapters.add(handler) // wrong move 1 adapters.add { event -> type.safeCast(event)?.let(handler) } // takes any event, passes on only an E } fun publish(event: PaymentEvent) = adapters.forEach { it(event) } } fun main() { val router = Router() val auditAll: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit = { println("audit ${it.paymentId}") } router.on(CardAuthorized::class) { println("fraud check ${it.cents}") } router.on(CardAuthorized::class, auditAll) // a handler for the supertype fits: in P router.on(RefundIssued::class) { println("refund ${it.cents}") } router.publish(CardAuthorized("pay_1", 1_200)) // events flow out of the publisher... router.publish(RefundIssued("pay_2", 500)) // ...and into the handlers that accept them // Wrong move 2. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // router.on(PaymentEvent::class) { e: CardAuthorized -> println(e.cents) } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.EventBusDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l11/demo/EventBusDemo.kt EventBusDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l11.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** Java twin of EventBusDemo.kt. The handler parameter says ? super E: Consumer Super. */ public class EventBusDemoJava { static final class Router { private final List<Consumer<PaymentEvent>> adapters = new ArrayList<>(); <E extends PaymentEvent> void on(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> handler) { adapters.add(event -> { // takes any event... if (type.isInstance(event)) handler.accept(type.cast(event)); // ...passes on only an E }); } void publish(PaymentEvent event) { adapters.forEach(a -> a.accept(event)); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Router router = new Router(); Consumer<PaymentEvent> auditAll = e -> System.out.println("audit " + e.getPaymentId()); router.on(CardAuthorized.class, e -> System.out.println("fraud check " + e.getCents())); router.on(CardAuthorized.class, auditAll); router.on(RefundIssued.class, e -> System.out.println("refund " + e.getCents())); router.publish(new CardAuthorized("pay_1", 1_200)); router.publish(new RefundIssued("pay_2", 500)); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.EventBusDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l11/demo/EventBusDemoJava.java Both print fraud check 1200, audit pay_1 and refund 500. h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Typed keys: one map, many value types, no casts at the call site
x: The last design is a container for values of many types, the kind of per-payment context a Quarkus request or a Temporal workflow carries around: the accepted currencies, the retry delays, the retry count. Lesson 9's registry used the type as the whole key. Here the key is a small object that carries a name and the full type of its value: Java record Key<T>(String name, Type type) { // Type from a super type token static <T> Key<T> of(String name, TypeRef<T> ref) { return new Key<>(name, ref.type); } } static final Key<List<String>> CURRENCIES = Key.of("currencies", new TypeRef<List<String>>() {}); <T> void set(Key<T> key, T value) { values.put(key, value); } @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") <T> T get(Key<T> key) { return (T) values.get(key); } // safe: only set puts values in Kotlin data class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType) inline fun <reified T> key(name: String) = Key<T>(name, typeOf<T>()) val CURRENCIES = key<List<String>>("currencies") operator fun <T> set(key: Key<T>, value: T) { values[key] = value } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") operator fun <T> get(key: Key<T>): T? = values[key] as T? // safe: only set puts values in val currencies: List<String>? = attributes[CURRENCIES] // no cast, no type argument at the call site The key's type parameter does the typing: attributes[CURRENCIES] is a List<String>? with no cast at the call site, and attributes[CURRENCIES] = 42 is a compile error (Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'List<String>' was expected.). The KType inside the key makes key<List<Long>>("retries") and key<Int>("retries") different keys, so two teams can't collide by picking the same name. Key<T> is invariant on purpose, and this is the last variance decision of the track. Declare it out T, and a Key<List<String>> becomes a Key<Any>. Then attributes[currencies] = 42 compiles, with T inferred as Any, and the next read of the currencies throws ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.util.List. A key is used to write as well as to read, so it can't be a producer. The one unchecked cast in get stays safe only as long as that holds. This is also a good place to stop adding generics. Four designs, two commented casts, one deliberately invariant key: if a design needs much more than that, a plainer one with a sealed class and a when is usually easier for the next engineer to read. Store typed attributes, then break the key Run TypedKeysDemo and TypedKeysDemoJava. Neither call site has a cast. Read LeakyKey in the Kotlin file: the same key with out T. Find the line where the bad value goes in, and the line where it fails. Uncomment the wrong move in each file. The invariant key stops at compile time what the leaky key let through. TypedKeysDemo.kt package workbench.generics.l11.demo import kotlin.reflect.KType import kotlin.reflect.typeOf /** Invariant on purpose: a Key<List<String>> is not a Key<Any>. */ data class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType) inline fun <reified T> key(name: String) = Key<T>(name, typeOf<T>()) class Attributes { private val values = HashMap<Key<*>, Any?>() operator fun <T> set(key: Key<T>, value: T) { values[key] = value } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") // safe: only set(Key<T>, T) puts values in operator fun <T> get(key: Key<T>): T? = values[key] as T? } /** The same thing with `out T`: it compiles, and it is broken. */ data class LeakyKey<out T>(val name: String, val type: KType) inline fun <reified T> leakyKey(name: String) = LeakyKey<T>(name, typeOf<T>()) class LeakyAttributes { private val values = HashMap<LeakyKey<*>, Any?>() operator fun <T> set(key: LeakyKey<T>, value: T) { values[key] = value } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") operator fun <T> get(key: LeakyKey<T>): T? = values[key] as T? } val CURRENCIES = key<List<String>>("currencies") val RETRIES = key<Int>("retries") fun main() { val attrs = Attributes() attrs[CURRENCIES] = listOf("EUR", "USD") attrs[RETRIES] = 3 val currencies: List<String>? = attrs[CURRENCIES] // typed by the key: no cast here println("currencies = $currencies, retries = ${attrs[RETRIES]}") val leaky = LeakyAttributes() val leakyCurrencies = leakyKey<List<String>>("currencies") leaky[leakyCurrencies] = 42 // compiles: T is inferred as Any try { val first: String? = leaky[leakyCurrencies]?.first() println(first) } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message?.substringBefore(" (")}") } // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // attrs[CURRENCIES] = 42 } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.TypedKeysDemoKt labs/generics/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/generics/l11/demo/TypedKeysDemo.kt TypedKeysDemoJava.java package workbench.generics.l11.demo; import java.lang.reflect.ParameterizedType; import java.lang.reflect.Type; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Java twin of TypedKeysDemo.kt. The key's type comes from a super type token; Java generics are invariant. */ public class TypedKeysDemoJava { static abstract class TypeRef<T> { final Type type = ((ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass()).getActualTypeArguments()[0]; } record Key<T>(String name, Type type) { static <T> Key<T> of(String name, TypeRef<T> ref) { return new Key<>(name, ref.type); } } static final class Attributes { private final Map<Key<?>, Object> values = new HashMap<>(); <T> void set(Key<T> key, T value) { values.put(key, value); } @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") // safe: only set(Key<T>, T) puts values in <T> T get(Key<T> key) { return (T) values.get(key); } } static final Key<List<String>> CURRENCIES = Key.of("currencies", new TypeRef<List<String>>() {}); static final Key<Integer> RETRIES = Key.of("retries", new TypeRef<Integer>() {}); public static void main(String[] args) { Attributes attrs = new Attributes(); attrs.set(CURRENCIES, List.of("EUR", "USD")); attrs.set(RETRIES, 3); List<String> currencies = attrs.get(CURRENCIES); // typed by the key: no cast here System.out.println("currencies = " + currencies + ", retries = " + attrs.get(RETRIES)); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // attrs.set(CURRENCIES, 42); } } ./gradlew :generics:demo -Pmain=workbench.generics.l11.demo.TypedKeysDemoJava labs/generics/src/demo/java/workbench/generics/l11/demo/TypedKeysDemoJava.java Both print currencies = [EUR, USD], retries = 3. Kotlin then prints ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.util.List: leaky[leakyCurrencies] = 42 compiled because out T let T be inferred as Any, and the read failed later. The wrong move fails with Argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Int', but 'List<String>' was expected. in Kotlin and method set in class Attributes cannot be applied to given types in Java. Reflection: typeOf (Kotlin docs) docs The common mistake in an event bus is casting the handler instead of wrapping it: handlers.add(handler as (PaymentEvent) -> Unit) under @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST"). It compiles, and every test that publishes the right event type passes. The first time an event of another class reaches that list, through a shared key, a supertype subscription or a bug in the routing, the handler receives it and throws ClassCastException: class RefundIssued cannot be cast to class CardAuthorized from inside its own body, far from the subscription that caused it. People write the cast because the adapter looks like extra ceremony, and because erasure makes the cast itself succeed. The fix is the adapter, { event -> type.safeCast(event)?.let(handler) }, which costs one line and makes the wrong event a no-op.

x: The typed event bus in Java and Kotlin EventBus.java import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Consumer; final class EventBus { private final Map<Class<? extends PaymentEvent>, List<Consumer<PaymentEvent>>> handlers = new HashMap<>(); // Consumer<? super E>: a handler for E or for any supertype of E <E extends PaymentEvent> void subscribe(Class<E> type, Consumer<? super E> handler) { handlers.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(event -> { if (type.isInstance(event)) handler.accept(type.cast(event)); // the adapter }); } int publish(PaymentEvent event) { List<Consumer<PaymentEvent>> list = handlers.getOrDefault(event.getClass(), List.of()); list.forEach(h -> h.accept(event)); return list.size(); } } // bus.subscribe(CardAuthorized.class, e -> fraudCheck(e)); EventBus.kt class EventBus { private val handlers = HashMap<KClass<out PaymentEvent>, MutableList<(PaymentEvent) -> Unit>>() // (E) -> Unit is already Function1<in E, ...>: a handler for any supertype of E fits fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: (E) -> Unit) { handlers.getOrPut(type) { mutableListOf() } .add { event -> type.safeCast(event)?.let(handler) } // the adapter } inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(noinline handler: (E) -> Unit) = subscribe(E::class, handler) fun publish(event: PaymentEvent): Int { val list = handlers[event::class] ?: return 0 for (h in list) h(event) return list.size } } // bus.subscribe<CardAuthorized> { fraudCheck(it) } The design is the same in both languages: keys from the event's run-time class, handlers stored behind an adapter that checks the class and casts, and a handler parameter that accepts supertypes. Where Java writes the variance at each use (Class<? extends PaymentEvent> keys, Consumer<? super E> handlers), Kotlin gets it from declarations: event::class is already a KClass<out PaymentEvent>, and a function type is already in on its parameter, so (E) -> Unit needs no projection. Kotlin also adds the reified wrapper, which needs noinline because the lambda is stored. Java callers can use the KClass version only through JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(CardAuthorized.class), so a bus meant for Java code should also offer a Class<E> overload.

x: Route a card-issuer webhook through all four designs A webhook body arrives. 1. Parse it into an Either instead of throwing, so the caller decides what a bad body means. fun parseWebhook(body: Map<*, *>): Either<String, PaymentEvent> { val id = body["id"] as? String ?: return Either.Left("missing id") val cents = (body["cents"] as? Number)?.toLong() ?: return Either.Left("missing cents") return when (body["type"]) { "auth" -> Either.Right(CardAuthorized(id, cents)) "refund" -> Either.Right(RefundIssued(id, cents)) else -> Either.Left("unknown type ${body["type"]}") } } static Either<String, PaymentEvent> parseWebhook(Map<?, ?> body) { if (!(body.get("id") instanceof String id)) return new Left<>("missing id"); if (!(body.get("cents") instanceof Number n)) return new Left<>("missing cents"); long cents = n.longValue(); Object type = body.get("type"); if ("auth".equals(type)) return new Right<>(new CardAuthorized(id, cents)); if ("refund".equals(type)) return new Right<>(new RefundIssued(id, cents)); return new Left<>("unknown type " + type); } Publish the successes on the bus. 3. Record the failures in the request's typed attributes. Self-check before reading the comment: why can Either.Right(CardAuthorized(...)) be returned where Either<String, PaymentEvent> is expected? (Right<CardAuthorized> is an Either<Nothing, CardAuthorized>, and both parameters are out.) val LAST_ERROR = key<String>("webhook.lastError") fun handle(body: Map<*, *>, bus: EventBus, context: Attributes): Int = when (val parsed = parseWebhook(body)) { is Either.Right -> bus.publish(parsed.value) // events flow out to the handlers is Either.Left -> { context[LAST_ERROR] = parsed.value; 0 } } static final Key<String> LAST_ERROR = Key.of("webhook.lastError", new TypeRef<String>() {}); static int handle(Map<?, ?> body, EventBus bus, Attributes context) { return switch (parseWebhook(body)) { case Right<String, PaymentEvent> r -> bus.publish(r.value()); case Left<String, PaymentEvent> l -> { context.set(LAST_ERROR, l.value()); yield 0; } }; } Wire the handlers once, at startup. The audit log is a (PaymentEvent) -> Unit and subscribes under both event classes; the fraud check only understands card authorizations. A nightly report reads merchants through the covariant ReadRepository<Entity<*>> view. Every type parameter in this flow has the variance its role demands, and the only casts are the two that are safe by construction: safeCast in the bus adapter and the unchecked cast inside Attributes.get. val auditAll: (PaymentEvent) -> Unit = { audit.write(it.paymentId) } bus.subscribe(CardAuthorized::class, auditAll) bus.subscribe(RefundIssued::class, auditAll) bus.subscribe<CardAuthorized> { fraud.check(it.paymentId, it.cents) } handle(mapOf("id" to "pay_1", "cents" to 1_200, "type" to "auth"), bus, context) // 2 handlers ran handle(mapOf("id" to "pay_2"), bus, context) // context[LAST_ERROR] == "missing cents" Consumer<PaymentEvent> auditAll = e -> audit.write(e.getPaymentId()); bus.subscribe(CardAuthorized.class, auditAll); bus.subscribe(RefundIssued.class, auditAll); bus.subscribe(CardAuthorized.class, e -> fraud.check(e.getPaymentId(), e.getCents())); handle(Map.of("id", "pay_1", "cents", 1_200, "type", "auth"), bus, context); // 2 handlers ran handle(Map.of("id", "pay_2"), bus, context); // LAST_ERROR is "missing cents"

h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Quiz
x: Which interface can safely be declared with out T? interface Repository<T> { fun save(entity: T): T } interface Cache<T> { var current: T } interface ReadRepository<T> { fun findAll(): List<T> } interface Key<T> { val name: String }, used as set(key: Key<T>, value: T) ReadRepository only hands T out. save takes a T, and a var is both read and written, so those must be invariant. The key is the subtle one: it has no T member at all, so out T would compile, but it is used to choose what may be written, and out would let set(key, 42) through. In the event bus, why can't subscribe simply do handlers[type]!!.add(handler) with handler: (E) -> Unit and a list of (PaymentEvent) -> Unit? Because lambdas can't be stored in a map Because (E) -> Unit is not a (PaymentEvent) -> Unit: function parameters are in, and a card-only handler can't take a refund Because E is erased, so the list can't hold it It can; the adapter is only for performance A (PaymentEvent) -> Unit must accept every event. A handler that only takes CardAuthorized doesn't, so the compiler refuses the add. The adapter takes any event and passes on only those that safeCast to E. The reverse direction works: a (PaymentEvent) -> Unit handler is a (CardAuthorized) -> Unit. Why does the reified subscribe need noinline on its handler parameter? Because reified functions can't take lambdas Because Java callers need it Because the handler is stored in the map, so it must exist as an object instead of being inlined Because noinline makes the type parameter reified Lambdas passed to an inline function are inlined too, so they don't exist as values. A lambda you store, return or pass on to a non-inline function must stay an object, which noinline requests. It has nothing to do with reified, which is about the type parameter. data class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType). Why include the KType when the key already has a name? So that key<List<Long>>("retries") and key<Int>("retries") are different keys and can't collide Because a data class needs at least two properties So that get can cast without an unchecked warning Because KType makes the key covariant With the name alone, two keys with the same name and different value types would share one slot, and reading one would return the other's value. The KType from typeOf<T>() makes them unequal. The cast in get is still unchecked; it is safe because only set puts values in. From "Star projection: when you don't know the type": a metrics helper reports the size of any in-memory buffer, a MutableList<CardAuthorized>, a MutableList<String> or anything else. Which parameter type fits best? MutableList<Any?> MutableList<in Any> MutableList<PaymentEvent> MutableList<*> The helper neither reads typed elements nor writes any, so a star projection says exactly that and accepts every mutable list. MutableList<Any?> accepts only lists whose element type is exactly Any?, and in Any accepts only lists of Any or Any?. (A plain Collection<*> would be even more general.)
