h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Key terms
x: Either A result that is a failure (Left) or a success (Right), declared out in both. Interface segregation by variance Splitting a type's reading half into its own covariant interface, so readers get flexibility the full type can't have. Adapter A small wrapper that turns one function type into another, here by checking the event's class first. noinline Marks a lambda parameter of an inline function that must stay an object, because it is stored. Typed key A key object that carries the type of its value, so a container can return that type without casts. Safe by construction An unchecked cast that can't fail, because a private invariant guarantees what was stored. Why is Left declared Left<out L>(val value: L) : Either<L, Nothing>? So one Left fits Either<L, R> for every R: Nothing is a subtype of every type, and Either is out in R. A repository both saves and returns T. How do you let read-only code accept a repository of any entity? Split out interface ReadRepository<out T> { fun findAll(): List<T> } and have the full Repository extend it. Readers take ReadRepository<Entity<*>>. What type do the keys of a class-keyed event bus have, and why? KClass<out PaymentEvent>, because event::class on a PaymentEvent has exactly that type. How do you store a (CardAuthorized) -> Unit in a list of (PaymentEvent) -> Unit? Wrap it: { event -> CardAuthorized::class.safeCast(event)?.let(handler) }. The adapter takes any event and passes on only a CardAuthorized. When does a lambda parameter of an inline function need noinline? When the function stores it, returns it or passes it to non-inline code, as subscribe does with its handler map. Why must a typed Key<T> be invariant? It decides what may be written. With out T, a Key<List<String>> could act as a Key<Any>, set(key, 42) would compile, and the next read would throw ClassCastException.

h: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus · Go deeper
x: Each design has a natural next step. The bus delivers only to the event's exact class. To deliver a CardAuthorized to handlers subscribed under PaymentEvent::class too, publish must walk the event's supertypes. Without kotlin-reflect you can do that through Java reflection: event.javaClass.interfaces and event.javaClass.superclass, converted with .kotlin. With kotlin-reflect, KClass.allSuperclasses lists them directly. Cache the result per class, since the walk is the same every time. Either gets more useful with flatMap, which chains steps that can each fail: fun <L, R, R2> Either<L, R>.flatMap(f: (R) -> Either<L, R2>): Either<L, R2>. Its Left branch returns this for the same reason map can. The standard library's own Result<out T> is also declared out, but its failure side is always a Throwable; Either lets the failure be a domain type such as RejectReason. Libraries such as Arrow ship a full Either. The repository can grow a write-only view too: interface WriteRepository<in T> { fun save(entity: T) }. A loader that writes Merchants can then accept a WriteRepository<Entity<Long>>. With both views, the invariant Repository is simply the type that is both. The typed keys can carry a default: class Key<T>(val name: String, val type: KType, val default: T), with get returning T instead of T?. Keep Key invariant when you do: default is read, but set still writes through the key.

h: Design patterns in Java and Kotlin
x: Creational, structural and behavioral patterns, what Kotlin makes unnecessary, and concurrency patterns. By the end of this track you can name the classic design patterns in the code you already run, and you know which ones modern Java and Kotlin have turned into a few lines: Strategy and Command into lambdas, State and Visitor into sealed types with an exhaustive switch or when, Builder into named arguments, Decorator into Kotlin by. You can also tell when a pattern still earns its class: adapters at the edge of your service, facades over multi-step jobs, framework proxies with rules of their own, and the concurrency patterns that keep a payment service up when the card issuer is not. The last lesson builds a circuit breaker and a bulkhead by hand, out of State, Decorator and compare-and-set. You need Kotlin data classes and lambdas. Records, sealed interfaces and pattern matching are explained where they first appear, and the modern Java data modeling track right after this one covers them in depth. The concurrency and memory model tracks help with lessons 1 and 11. Install JDK 25; the labs compile with release 21, so they also run on JDK 21. Kotlin samples use 2.4.21, and when guards need Kotlin 2.2 or later. The labs live in labs/patterns, one package per lesson (workbench.patterns.l01 to l11). About half are in Java and half in Kotlin, and every code sample and Try-it demo in the lessons comes in both languages. Most labs are refactors: the tests pin the behavior, and you change the shape. Run ./gradlew :patterns:test --tests 'workbench.patterns.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and ./gradlew :patterns:solutionTest to run the same tests against the reference answers. The concurrency tests use latches, counters and a fake clock, so they pass or fail the same way on every run. Patterns are vocabulary for recurring designs. In Java 21 and Kotlin, many of them are now a language feature: lambdas, sealed types with exhaustive switch/when, records and data classes, named arguments and by delegation. Creational: inject instances instead of hand-rolling singletons, name constructors with validating factories, use named arguments or a record plus builder, and remember that every copy (copy(), withers) is shallow. Structural: adapters translate a vendor's types and errors at the edge, facades own multi-step jobs, decorators add behavior behind the same interface (order matters), and proxies carry framework behavior with their own rules, self-invocation above all. Composite, State and Visitor become sealed types plus pure functions. Leave the default off the switch over your own types, and the compiler lists every place a new case needs a rule. Strategy, Command, Template Method and Chain of Responsibility become functions: lambdas, comparators, execute-around helpers and folded interceptor lists. Observer: return an unsubscribe handle and isolate listener failures; use SharedFlow for events and StateFlow for state. Memento and Command both give undo, by snapshot or by inverse. Concurrency patterns answer who owns the state and who waits: bounded producer-consumer queues, balking with compare-and-set, guarded suspension with futures, and one owner per piece of mutable state. Cheap threads don't make dependencies cheap: put a fail-fast bulkhead per dependency, a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing one, and one retry layer around idempotent calls.

h: Design patterns in Java and Kotlin: track quiz
x: A Quarkus service needs one shared FxRates cache. A teammate writes object FxRates { ... } and calls it directly from twelve classes. What is the main cost? It isn't thread-safe: two threads can create two instances Tests can't swap it for a fake, and its state leaks from one test to the next Kotlin creates a new instance per class that uses it It can't hold mutable state A Kotlin object is created once, safely, on first access, so thread safety isn't the problem. The cost is the hidden dependency: twelve classes reach for a global, so a test can't give them a fake, and anything one test caches is still there for the next. Make it an @ApplicationScoped bean and inject it. A Kotlin 2.4 data class Payout private constructor(...) is meant to be created only through a validating factory. What does payout.copy(amountMinor = -5) do? It doesn't compile, because copy() is private like the constructor It deep-copies the payout and rejects the negative amount It compiles: copy() stays public and skips the factory, though checks in init still run copy() isn't generated for a private constructor In Kotlin 2.4, a private primary constructor doesn't make the generated copy() private; you get a warning unless you add @ConsistentCopyVisibility. So copy() goes around the factory, and only rules in init still apply. That is why validation belongs in init. Name these four wrappers, in order: (1) a class that makes a vendor's SoapClient look like your PaymentGateway; (2) a PaymentGateway that wraps another and times authorize; (3) the object Spring injects so that @Transactional works; (4) one checkout() call over inventory, payments and email. Adapter, Decorator, Proxy, Facade Decorator, Proxy, Adapter, Facade Adapter, Proxy, Decorator, Bridge Facade, Decorator, Proxy, Adapter An adapter changes the interface to yours. A decorator keeps the interface and adds behavior. A proxy keeps the interface and controls access, here by wrapping calls in a transaction. A facade puts one simple entry point in front of several objects. Structure alone can't tell them apart; intent does. Notifications have four alert types and three channels, and both lists will grow. Which pattern keeps the code at N + M pieces instead of N x M classes? Composite Flyweight Adapter Bridge Bridge splits two dimensions that vary on their own: each alert holds a Channel and calls it, so a new channel works with every alert. Composite is for trees, Flyweight for sharing immutable instances, and Adapter for fitting one existing class to your interface. Every outbound PSP call must be timed and logged the same way, around a different call each time. What is the modern replacement for a Template Method base class here? A higher-order function, timed("psp.capture") { ... }, inline in Kotlin A Strategy map from call name to Runnable A Singleton that every call registers with A dynamic proxy around every lambda The skeleton is fixed and only the middle varies, which is execute around: one function that does setup and teardown and takes the varying step as a lambda. It composes, needs no subclass per call site, and can't hit the constructor-calls-hook trap. In Kotlin, inline removes the lambda object too. A ledger exposes "posting happened" notifications and the account's current balance as Kotlin flows. Which pairing is right? StateFlow for both SharedFlow for both SharedFlow for the postings, StateFlow for the balance StateFlow for the postings, SharedFlow for the balance Postings are events: two equal postings in a row are two real events, and a StateFlow would drop the second because it conflates by equals. The balance is state: collectors only need the latest value, which is exactly what StateFlow gives them, including late subscribers. A Java switch over a sealed PaymentState covers all five states with no default. A new Disputed state is added in a separately compiled jar, and a Disputed value reaches the old switch at runtime. What happens? It falls into the first case It returns null The JVM throws MatchException Nothing: the compiler rejected the old jar Exhaustiveness is checked at compile time against the subtypes known then. A subtype added later in separately compiled code is part of the runtime remainder, and Java throws MatchException for it (Kotlin throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException; a null state throws NullPointerException). Recompiling the switch turns it back into a compile error. When does the classic Visitor pattern still make sense in modern Java or Kotlin? Whenever a hierarchy has more than five subtypes For any sealed hierarchy you own Never: pattern matching replaced it completely For hierarchies that are open across modules, or libraries that hand you one, such as annotation processing or bytecode tools For a closed hierarchy you own, a sealed type plus switch or when gives Visitor's benefit (cheap new operations) without accept methods. Visitor still fits when the hierarchy isn't sealed or isn't yours: ElementVisitor in annotation processors, javac's Tree API, ASM's ClassVisitor. The card issuer is down, and every call hangs until a 2-second timeout. Which tool stops your request threads from each waiting those 2 seconds? A bulkhead of 50 A circuit breaker A retry with three attempts A bigger thread pool Once its failure threshold is reached, the breaker opens and rejects calls at once, with no network trip. A bulkhead only caps how many calls wait at the same time, so 50 of them still wait 2 seconds each. Retries multiply the waiting, and a bigger pool just lets more threads wait. Card.parse(raw) is a factory that returns a sealed CardResult with Valid and Invalid. What should the caller's when (or switch) look like? One branch per subtype and no else, so a new result type breaks the build here A single else branch, to be safe A try/catch around the call instead of a when An is Valid branch only, because invalid input throws A sealed result is a promise that the caller handles every outcome, and the compiler checks it only if there is no else. Add a Blocked result later, and every caller that needs to decide fails to compile. parse never throws for bad input; that's what Invalid is for.

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · A pattern is a name for a design you keep meeting
x: A design pattern is a name for a design that keeps showing up: the problem, the shape of the solution, and what it costs you. It is a word in a shared vocabulary. It is not a class template to paste. The 1994 "Gang of Four" book listed 23 patterns, written for C++ and Smalltalk. Java at the time had no lambdas, no records and no sealed types, and many of those patterns were workarounds for exactly that. The names are still worth knowing. In a code review, "put a decorator around the issuer client" is a whole design in a few words. And you need the names to recognise a pattern when a language feature or a framework hands it to you under another name. In Java 21+ and Kotlin 2.x, the 23 sort into three groups. This track follows them. The language absorbed them. Strategy, Command and Template Method become function values. State and Visitor become a sealed type plus an exhaustive switch or when. A sealed type lists all its subtypes in one place, so the compiler knows every case, and an exhaustive switch is one the compiler has checked covers them all. Builder mostly becomes Kotlin's named and default arguments. Singleton becomes an enum or a Kotlin object. Decorator becomes Kotlin's by delegation, where the compiler writes the forwarding methods for you. A framework absorbed them. Proxy lives inside Spring and Quarkus. Chain of Responsibility is a servlet filter chain or an HTTP client interceptor. Observer is Kotlin Flow, Reactor and java.util.concurrent.Flow. You still design them by hand. Adapter, Facade, Bridge, Composite, Mediator and Flyweight are about how you cut up your own domain, and no feature does that for you. The intent of an absorbed pattern survives. Strategy still means "swap the algorithm without touching the caller". What changed is the price. A strategy used to be an interface and three classes. Now it is a lambda in a map, so you use it ten times more often and stop calling it a pattern. Brian Goetz, Java's language architect, gave the strongest version of this in a 2018 design note on pattern matching: with powerful enough pattern matching, "the Visitor pattern is almost completely unnecessary". The same note says this does not make inheritance and virtual methods wrong. That is the position of this track too. Learn the intent, then reach for the cheapest feature that delivers it, and know when the feature is not enough. Find five patterns in the JDK Read main in PatternsYouAlreadyUse below (Java or Kotlin, they print the same). Write down what each of the six lines will print before you run anything. Run it from labs/ with the command below. Name the pattern behind each line: singleton, flyweight, read-through view (proxy) or strategy. Which line surprised you? PatternsYouAlreadyUse.java package workbench.patterns.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.Currency; import java.util.List; import java.util.Collections; /** Five patterns hiding in the JDK. Predict each line before you run it. */ public class PatternsYouAlreadyUse { record Payment(String id, long amountMinor) {} public static void main(String[] args) { // Singleton: one Runtime per JVM, no public constructor System.out.println("1. Runtime is a singleton: " + (Runtime.getRuntime() == Runtime.getRuntime())); // Flyweight: Integer.valueOf caches -128..127, Currency keeps one instance per code Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128; System.out.println("2. 127 == 127 (boxed): " + (a == b)); System.out.println("3. 128 == 128 (boxed): " + (c == d)); System.out.println("4. EUR == EUR (Currency): " + (Currency.getInstance("EUR") == Currency.getInstance("EUR"))); // Proxy/decorator view: unmodifiableList reads through to the list it wraps List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("p-1")); List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(ids); ids.add("p-2"); System.out.println("5. view after ids.add(\"p-2\"): " + view); // Strategy: a Comparator is an algorithm you pass in, and a lambda is enough to make one List<Payment> payments = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Payment("p-9", 500), new Payment("p-3", 12_000))); payments.sort(Comparator.comparing(Payment::amountMinor).reversed()); System.out.println("6. sorted by amount, desc: " + payments.stream().map(Payment::id).toList()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l01.PatternsYouAlreadyUse labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l01/PatternsYouAlreadyUse.java PatternsYouAlreadyUse.kt package workbench.patterns.l01 import java.util.Collections import java.util.Currency // Five patterns hiding in the JDK and the Kotlin standard library. Predict each line before you run it. private data class Payment(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long) fun main() { // Singleton: one Runtime per JVM, no public constructor println("1. Runtime is a singleton: " + (Runtime.getRuntime() === Runtime.getRuntime())) // Flyweight: a nullable Int is a boxed java.lang.Integer, and Integer.valueOf caches -128..127 val a: Int? = 127; val b: Int? = 127; val c: Int? = 128; val d: Int? = 128 println("2. 127 === 127 (boxed): " + (a as Any === b as Any)) println("3. 128 === 128 (boxed): " + (c as Any === d as Any)) println("4. EUR === EUR (Currency): " + (Currency.getInstance("EUR") === Currency.getInstance("EUR"))) // Proxy/decorator view: unmodifiableList reads through to the list it wraps val ids = mutableListOf("p-1") val view: List<String> = Collections.unmodifiableList(ids) ids += "p-2" println("5. view after ids += \"p-2\": $view") // Strategy: a Comparator is an algorithm you pass in; compareByDescending builds one from a lambda val payments = listOf(Payment("p-9", 500), Payment("p-3", 12_000)) println("6. sorted by amount, desc: " + payments.sortedWith(compareByDescending { it.amountMinor }).map { it.id }) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l01.PatternsYouAlreadyUseKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l01/PatternsYouAlreadyUse.kt It prints true, true, false, true, [p-1, p-2] and [p-3, p-9]. Line 3 surprises most people: Integer.valueOf only caches -128 to 127, so two boxed 128s are different objects. Line 5 shows that unmodifiableList is a view that reads through to the list it wraps. It blocks writes through the view, and it is not a copy. Most GoF patterns still have a job. What changed is who writes them: the language, a framework, or you. Pattern Matching for Java (Bierman and Goetz, design note) read A singleton is like the one cash vault in a bank branch. Everyone who needs cash goes to the same vault, and the manager makes sure nobody builds a second one. Lazy initialization is opening the vault only when the first customer asks. Double-checked locking is the manager glancing at the vault door from across the room, and only if it looks shut, walking over with the key and checking again, in case a colleague opened it in the meantime. The analogy breaks on testing: a bank can build a practice vault for training new staff, but a hard-coded getInstance() gives your tests no practice vault at all. That is why you inject it.

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Singleton in Java: enum, holder and double-checked locking
x: A singleton is a class with exactly one instance and one place to get it. The JDK has its own: the Runtime Javadoc says every Java application has a single instance of Runtime, and an application cannot create its own. The "one" is easy. The hard part is "one, created lazily, by many threads at once". The naive version is the check-then-act race from Race conditions: why count++ lies: Java static FxRates instance; static FxRates getInstance() { if (instance == null) instance = new FxRates(); // two threads can both see null return instance; } Kotlin private var instance: FxRates? = null fun fxRates(): FxRates { if (instance == null) instance = FxRates() // the same race in Kotlin return instance!! } If loading FxRates takes 20 ms and eight request threads arrive together, all eight see null and you build eight. Here are the correct versions, in the order I reach for them. Java enum IdGenerator { // 1. enum: the JVM makes exactly one INSTANCE INSTANCE; private final AtomicLong next = new AtomicLong(); long nextId() { return next.incrementAndGet(); } } final class FxRates { // 2. holder: lazy, no lock on the fast path private FxRates() { } private static final class Holder { static final FxRates INSTANCE = new FxRates(); } static FxRates getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } } Kotlin enum class IdGenerator { // 1. enum works the same in Kotlin INSTANCE; private val next = AtomicLong() fun nextId() = next.incrementAndGet() } class FxRates private constructor() { // 2. holder: a private object nested in the companion companion object { private object Holder { val INSTANCE = FxRates() } fun getInstance(): FxRates = Holder.INSTANCE } } The enum is what Effective Java (item 3) calls the preferred approach. Serialization and reflection can't make a second instance, and you write no locking code. Use it when the object is cheap or needed at startup anyway. The holder idiom is for an expensive object you want lazily. The JVM initializes the nested Holder class the first time anyone reads Holder.INSTANCE. Class initialization runs once, under a lock the JVM owns, so every later call is a plain static read. The third tool is double-checked locking (DCL), from Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders in the memory model track. The holder only works for static fields. When the lazy value lives in an instance field, such as one cache per merchant or a registry your DI container creates, DCL is the answer: Java private volatile Map<String, String> table; Map<String, String> table() { Map<String, String> t = table; // one volatile read on the fast path if (t == null) { synchronized (lock) { t = table; // re-check: another thread may have won if (t == null) table = t = load(); } } return t; } Kotlin @Volatile private var table: Map<String, String>? = null fun table(): Map<String, String> { table?.let { return it } // one volatile read on the fast path synchronized(lock) { table?.let { return it } // re-check: another thread may have won return load().also { table = it } } } Leave out volatile (@Volatile in Kotlin) and another thread can see a non-null reference to a map whose contents it can't see yet. That is the lab for this lesson. Build eight singletons by accident Predict: when eight threads call the racy getInstance together, how many FxRates get built? And with the holder? Run LazyRaceDemo with the command below. Delete the Thread.sleep(20) line in the constructor (FxRates in Java, SlowRates in Kotlin) and run it three more times. Did the race go away? LazyRaceDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l01; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.IdentityHashMap; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Eight threads ask for a "singleton" at the same moment. How many get built? */ public class LazyRaceDemo { static final AtomicInteger built = new AtomicInteger(); static final class FxRates { FxRates() { built.incrementAndGet(); try { Thread.sleep(20); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } // a slow load } } // broken: check-then-act on a plain static field static FxRates racy; static FxRates racyGet() { if (racy == null) racy = new FxRates(); return racy; } // initialization-on-demand holder: the JVM runs Holder's static init once, under its class-init lock static final class Holder { static final FxRates INSTANCE = new FxRates(); } static FxRates holderGet() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { report("racy check-then-act", LazyRaceDemo::racyGet); report("holder idiom ", LazyRaceDemo::holderGet); } static void report(String name, Supplier<FxRates> get) throws InterruptedException { built.set(0); Set<Object> seen = Collections.synchronizedSet(Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>())); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(get.get()); }); ts[i].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); System.out.printf("%s: constructor ran %d time(s), callers saw %d instance(s)%n", name, built.get(), seen.size()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l01.LazyRaceDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l01/LazyRaceDemo.java LazyRaceDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l01 import java.util.Collections import java.util.IdentityHashMap import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight threads ask for a "singleton" at the same moment. How many get built? private val built = AtomicInteger() private class SlowRates { init { built.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(20) // a slow load } } // broken: check-then-act on a plain top-level var private var racy: SlowRates? = null private fun racyGet(): SlowRates { if (racy == null) racy = SlowRates() return racy!! } // an object declaration: the JVM runs its static initializer once, under the class-init lock private object RatesHolder { val instance = SlowRates() } private fun holderGet(): SlowRates = RatesHolder.instance private fun report(name: String, get: () -> SlowRates) { built.set(0) val seen = Collections.synchronizedSet(Collections.newSetFromMap(IdentityHashMap<Any, Boolean>())) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await(); seen += get() } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("$name: constructor ran ${built.get()} time(s), callers saw ${seen.size} instance(s)") } fun main() { report("racy check-then-act", ::racyGet) report("object holder ", ::holderGet) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l01.LazyRaceDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l01/LazyRaceDemo.kt With the slow constructor, the racy version builds 8 instances and callers see 8 different objects. The holder (an object in the Kotlin twin) builds 1. Without the sleep, the racy count drops to 1, 3 or 4 and changes between runs. The race is still there; the window got smaller. A real config load is slow, which is why this shows up in production and not in your unit test. Runtime (Java SE 25 API) docs In a Quarkus payment service you rarely need getInstance(). The card-network config, the FX rate cache and the Kafka producer are @ApplicationScoped beans, so ArC makes one of each and injects them. Hand-written lazy state hides in smaller places: a per-merchant cache that loads fee schedules from Oracle on first use, a lazily built ObjectMapper in a shared library, a Temporal activity implementation that creates its issuer client the first time it runs. Each of those is a check-then-act waiting for two Kafka partitions to hit it in the same millisecond. Use the holder for statics, DCL or Kotlin lazy for instance fields, and keep the loader injectable so a test can count how many times it ran.

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Kotlin: object and lazy do the locking for you
x: Kotlin builds the singleton into the language. An object declaration defines a class and its one instance in a single step: Java // what the Kotlin compiler writes for that object, give or take public final class IdGenerator { public static final IdGenerator INSTANCE = new IdGenerator(); private final AtomicLong next = new AtomicLong(); private IdGenerator() { } public long nextId() { return next.incrementAndGet(); } } Kotlin object IdGenerator { private val next = AtomicLong() fun nextId() = next.incrementAndGet() } The Kotlin docs say the initialization of an object declaration is thread-safe and done on first access. Under the hood the compiler writes a class with a static INSTANCE field, set in its static initializer, as the Java twin shows. That is the same JVM mechanism as the holder idiom. Two details trip people up. A companion object is initialized when its outer class is loaded, like a Java static initializer. And companion members are not static. They are instance members of the companion object, so Java callers write Money.Companion.of(100) unless you mark the function @JvmStatic. For a lazy value inside a class, use by lazy. It has three modes, and they behave very differently: Mode What it does Use it for SYNCHRONIZED (default) takes a lock; the initializer runs once anything with side effects PUBLICATION no lock; racing threads may each run the initializer, the first stored value wins cheap, pure computations NONE no lock and no guarantee across threads values one thread owns PUBLICATION is the trap. If the initializer opens a connection pool or starts a Kafka consumer, eight concurrent first reads can open eight pools. Seven are thrown away, and nobody closes them. The default lazy is DCL written once, correctly, in the standard library. It also retries: if the initializer throws, the next access runs it again. In Kotlin, never write DCL by hand. Count the lazy initializer runs Read LazyModes.kt. The Java twin writes each mode by hand, which shows what the modes really do. Predict both lines of output: how many initializer runs, and how many distinct instances, for each mode? Run it with the command below. Add trial(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) at the end of main (in Java: trial("NONE", UnsafeLazy::new);) and run it again. Predict first. LazyModes.kt package workbench.patterns.l01 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Eight threads touch a lazy property for the first time, together. Count the initializer runs. class FxService(mode: LazyThreadSafetyMode, private val runs: AtomicInteger) { val rates: Map<String, Double> by lazy(mode) { runs.incrementAndGet() Thread.sleep(20) // pretend to load rates from a slow service mapOf("EUR/USD" to 1.08) } } fun trial(mode: LazyThreadSafetyMode) { val runs = AtomicInteger() val service = FxService(mode, runs) val seen = java.util.Collections.synchronizedSet(java.util.Collections.newSetFromMap(java.util.IdentityHashMap<Any, Boolean>())) val go = CountDownLatch(1) val threads = List(8) { thread { go.await(); seen += service.rates } } go.countDown() threads.forEach { it.join() } println("%-12s initializer ran %d time(s), callers saw %d instance(s)".format(mode, runs.get(), seen.size)) } fun main() { trial(LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED) trial(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l01.LazyModesKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l01/LazyModes.kt LazyModesJava.java package workbench.patterns.l01; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.IdentityHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Set; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** * Java has no `by lazy`, so here are the three Kotlin modes written by hand. * Eight threads read the value for the first time, together. Count the initializer runs. */ public class LazyModesJava { interface Lazy<T> { T get(); } // SYNCHRONIZED: double-checked locking; the initializer runs once static final class SynchronizedLazy<T> implements Lazy<T> { private final Supplier<T> init; private volatile T value; SynchronizedLazy(Supplier<T> init) { this.init = init; } public T get() { T v = value; if (v == null) { synchronized (this) { v = value; if (v == null) value = v = init.get(); } } return v; } } // PUBLICATION: no lock; every racer computes, compareAndSet keeps the first stored value static final class PublicationLazy<T> implements Lazy<T> { private final Supplier<T> init; private final AtomicReference<T> value = new AtomicReference<>(); PublicationLazy(Supplier<T> init) { this.init = init; } public T get() { T v = value.get(); if (v != null) return v; value.compareAndSet(null, init.get()); return value.get(); } } // NONE: a plain field, no guarantees across threads static final class UnsafeLazy<T> implements Lazy<T> { private final Supplier<T> init; private T value; UnsafeLazy(Supplier<T> init) { this.init = init; } public T get() { if (value == null) value = init.get(); return value; } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { trial("SYNCHRONIZED", SynchronizedLazy::new); trial("PUBLICATION", PublicationLazy::new); } static void trial(String mode, java.util.function.Function<Supplier<Map<String, Double>>, Lazy<Map<String, Double>>> make) throws InterruptedException { AtomicInteger runs = new AtomicInteger(); Lazy<Map<String, Double>> rates = make.apply(() -> { runs.incrementAndGet(); try { Thread.sleep(20); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return Map.of("EUR/USD", 1.08); }); Set<Object> seen = Collections.synchronizedSet(Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>())); CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] ts = new Thread[8]; for (int i = 0; i < ts.length; i++) { ts[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } seen.add(rates.get()); }); ts[i].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : ts) t.join(); System.out.printf("%-12s initializer ran %d time(s), callers saw %d instance(s)%n", mode, runs.get(), seen.size()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l01.LazyModesJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l01/LazyModesJava.java SYNCHRONIZED runs the initializer once and callers see 1 instance. PUBLICATION runs it 8 times, yet callers still see 1 instance, because only the first stored value is kept. NONE runs it 8 times and callers see 8 instances: each thread kept the map it built. No warning, no exception. Object declarations and expressions (Kotlin docs) docs LazyThreadSafetyMode (Kotlin API) docs

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Inject the instance instead of fetching it
x: Most singletons in a backend service should not be hand-rolled at all. Here is why, in one test you can't write: Java class PaymentPricer { long priceMinor(Payment p) { double rate = FxRates.getInstance().rate(p.currency(), "EUR"); // hidden, global return Math.round(p.amountMinor() * rate); } } Kotlin class PaymentPricer { fun priceMinor(p: Payment): Long { val rate = FxRates.rate(p.currency, "EUR") // FxRates is an object: hidden, global return (p.amountMinor * rate).roundToLong() } } To test priceMinor with a fixed rate of 1.10 you need to control FxRates, and you can't. The instance is global, built once per JVM, and loads real rates. A test that changes its state leaks into the next test, so the suite passes or fails depending on order. Nothing in the constructor of PaymentPricer even tells a reader that it calls an FX service. Pass the dependency in, typed as an interface: Java interface FxRates { double rate(String from, String to); } class PaymentPricer { private final FxRates rates; PaymentPricer(FxRates rates) { this.rates = rates; } long priceMinor(Payment p) { return Math.round(p.amountMinor() * rates.rate(p.currency(), "EUR")); } } // in a test: new PaymentPricer((from, to) -> 1.10) Kotlin fun interface FxRates { fun rate(from: String, to: String): Double } class PaymentPricer(private val rates: FxRates) { fun priceMinor(p: Payment): Long = (p.amountMinor * rates.rate(p.currency, "EUR")).roundToLong() } // in a test: PaymentPricer { _, _ -> 1.10 } Production still wants exactly one FxRates. Let the container make it. In Quarkus, an @ApplicationScoped bean is created once per application, on first use. In Spring, singleton is the default scope. You get one instance, lazy creation and shutdown hooks, and the class stays a plain class that a test can construct with new. A hand-written singleton still fits in a few places: stateless objects such as a comparator or a data object state in a sealed hierarchy, library code that can't assume a container, and state the JVM itself owns, like Runtime. Anything with I/O or configuration gets injected. The lab's CardNetworkRegistry follows that rule. It is not a static singleton. Its loader comes in through the constructor, so the tests can pass a slow fake loader and count its calls. A container would make one per application, and DCL inside keeps the lazy load safe when eight threads ask at once. Check yourself. Suppose the Kotlin object FxRates had a test hook, FxRates.override(1.10), and one test called it and never reset it. A test in another class runs later in the same JVM and prices a payment. Which rate does it get, and why? (1.10. The object is one static INSTANCE for the whole JVM, as the previous section showed, so its state outlives the test that set it. An injected fake goes away with its test.) Contexts and dependency injection (Quarkus CDI reference) docs The common mistake is lazy initialization through a plain field: if (cache == null) cache = load();. It passes every single-threaded test, so it looks harmless. Under load, two threads see null, both run load(), and if load() opens connections or registers listeners, one copy leaks. People write it because the race never shows in tests and the fix looks like over-engineering. The fix is one of three idioms: the holder class for a static, double-checked locking with a volatile field for an instance field, or Kotlin by lazy in its default SYNCHRONIZED mode.

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Java and Kotlin
x: One instance, and one lazy field, in Java and Kotlin FeeSchedules.java // singleton: the JVM's class-init lock does the work enum IdGenerator { INSTANCE; private final AtomicLong next = new AtomicLong(); long nextId() { return next.incrementAndGet(); } } // lazy instance field: double-checked locking final class FeeSchedules { private final Supplier<Map<String, Long>> loader; private final Object lock = new Object(); private volatile Map<String, Long> fees; FeeSchedules(Supplier<Map<String, Long>> loader) { this.loader = loader; } Map<String, Long> fees() { Map<String, Long> f = fees; if (f == null) { synchronized (lock) { f = fees; if (f == null) fees = f = Map.copyOf(loader.get()); } } return f; } } FeeSchedules.kt // singleton: the language makes it object IdGenerator { private val next = AtomicLong() fun nextId() = next.incrementAndGet() } // lazy instance field: the standard library does the locking class FeeSchedules(loader: () -> Map<String, Long>) { val fees: Map<String, Long> by lazy { loader().toMap() } // SYNCHRONIZED by default } A Kotlin object compiles to the same thing as a Java holder: a class with a static INSTANCE set in its static initializer, so the JVM's class-init lock guarantees one instance. by lazy replaces the whole DCL block (the volatile field, the lock object and the re-check), and it retries on the next access if the initializer throws. So Kotlin makes hand-written singletons and hand-written DCL unnecessary. It does not fix the design problem: a global object that does I/O is as hard to test as a Java static singleton, and the answer in both languages is to inject it.

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Worked example
x: Turn a static singleton into an injected bean, then make its lazy load safe A fee service reads merchant fee schedules through a global singleton. Before reading on, find what stops you from unit-testing feeMinor. class FeeService { long feeMinor(String merchantId, long amountMinor) { long bps = FeeSchedules.getInstance().bpsFor(merchantId); // global; loads from Oracle return amountMinor * bps / 10_000; } } class FeeService { fun feeMinor(merchantId: String, amountMinor: Long): Long { val bps = FeeSchedules.bpsFor(merchantId) // an object: global; loads from Oracle return amountMinor * bps / 10_000 } } The dependency is hidden and global. A test can't pass a fixed schedule, and anything the singleton caches leaks into the next test. Make the dependency visible: an interface, passed through the constructor. Now the test is one line. interface FeeSchedules { long bpsFor(String merchantId); } class FeeService { private final FeeSchedules schedules; // 1. the dependency is in the signature FeeService(FeeSchedules schedules) { this.schedules = schedules; } long feeMinor(String merchantId, long amountMinor) { return amountMinor * schedules.bpsFor(merchantId) / 10_000; } } // test: new FeeService(id -> 290).feeMinor("m-1", 10_000) == 290 fun interface FeeSchedules { fun bpsFor(merchantId: String): Long } class FeeService(private val schedules: FeeSchedules) { // 1. the dependency is in the signature fun feeMinor(merchantId: String, amountMinor: Long): Long = amountMinor * schedules.bpsFor(merchantId) / 10_000 } // test: FeeService { 290 }.feeMinor("m-1", 10_000) == 290L Production still wants one schedule table, loaded on first use. The container makes one bean. Inside it the table is an instance field, so the holder idiom can't help: Java uses DCL. Why must the field be volatile? Answer before you read the comment on it. The Kotlin bean is four lines, because by lazy is the DCL block. @ApplicationScoped class OracleFeeSchedules implements FeeSchedules { private final Object lock = new Object(); private volatile Map<String, Long> table; // 2. volatile: readers see the whole map public long bpsFor(String merchantId) { Map<String, Long> t = table; // 3. fast path: one read, no lock if (t == null) { synchronized (lock) { t = table; // 4. re-check under the lock if (t == null) table = t = loadFromOracle(); } } return t.getOrDefault(merchantId, 290L); } private Map<String, Long> loadFromOracle() { return Map.of("m-1", 250L); // SELECT merchant_id, bps FROM fee_schedule } } @ApplicationScoped class OracleFeeSchedules(private val db: FeeDb) : FeeSchedules { // 2-4. by lazy (SYNCHRONIZED) is the volatile field, the lock and the re-check in one line private val table: Map<String, Long> by lazy { db.loadSchedules() } override fun bpsFor(merchantId: String) = table[merchantId] ?: 290L }

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Lab
x: A lazy registry that loads once, and a harness that proves it labs/patterns/src/main/java/workbench/patterns/l01/CardNetworkRegistry.java labs/patterns/src/main/java/workbench/patterns/l01/Contention.java ./gradlew :patterns:test --tests 'workbench.patterns.l01.*' Run the tests. Seven of ten fail: the harness is a stub, and the registry runs its slow loader eight times when eight threads do the first lookup together. Write Contention.distinctInstances. Start the threads behind two latches (ready and go, as in Race conditions: why count++ lies), store each result in its own array slot, join every thread, then count the results in a set that compares with ==. Fix CardNetworkRegistry.table() with double-checked locking: a volatile field, a private lock object, and a re-check inside synchronized. Keep the Map.copyOf around the loader's result. Run the tests until all ten pass, then twice more. Collections.newSetFromMap(new IdentityHashMap<>()) is a Set that compares with ==. A HashSet would count eight empty lists as one. Read the volatile field into a local once at the top and return the local. The fast path then costs one volatile read. If the loader throws inside the synchronized block, the field is still null and the next caller tries again. You get that for free as long as you assign the field only after loader.get() returns. All ten tests in SingletonTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can say what a design pattern is and which ones modern Java and Kotlin absorbed, pick the right singleton form in each language, and prove a lazy instance is built once under contention.

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Quiz
x: A Kotlin class has val pool by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) { HikariDataSource(config) }. What can go wrong when traffic starts? Nothing, because the property is lazy Several threads can each open a pool; one is kept and the others are never closed Threads can see a half-built pool The first caller deadlocks PUBLICATION lets every racing thread run the initializer and keeps the first stored result. A pool opens connections when it is built, so the discarded pools leak them. Drop the mode argument: the default SYNCHRONIZED runs the initializer once. A half-built value is not the risk here; the store itself is safe, only the side effects repeat. You need a stateless, process-wide ID formatter in Java, and it's fine to build it at startup. Which form is simplest and still correct? An enum with one constant, INSTANCE Double-checked locking on a volatile static field A static field set inside getInstance() behind if (instance == null) A synchronized static getInstance() method An enum gives you exactly one instance, created when the class initializes, and serialization or reflection can't make another. DCL is for lazy instance fields and is overkill here. The plain if version races, and a synchronized getter is correct but takes a lock on every call for no benefit. Java code calls a Kotlin factory declared as class Money { companion object { fun of(minor: Long) = Money() } }. What does the Java caller write? Money.of(100) Money.INSTANCE.of(100) Money.Companion.of(100) new Money().of(100) Companion members are instance members of the companion object, which Java sees as a static field called Companion. Mark of with @JvmStatic if you want Money.of(100) to work from Java. INSTANCE is the field for an object declaration, not for a companion. A test passes alone and fails in the full suite. The class under test reads MetricsRegistry.INSTANCE.count("declines"). What is the likely cause and fix? JUnit runs tests in parallel, so add synchronized The enum gets created twice, so switch to the holder idiom The JIT caches the count, so make the field volatile The singleton keeps counts from earlier tests, so inject the registry and give each test its own A global singleton lives as long as the JVM, so one test's counts leak into the next and the result depends on order. Passing the registry through the constructor lets each test build a fresh one. An enum is never created twice, and visibility is not the problem when the tests run on one thread. From Lazy init done right in the memory model track: in double-checked locking, what goes wrong if the instance field is not volatile? Two instances can be created The synchronized block can deadlock Another thread can see a non-null reference to an object whose fields it can't see yet Nothing on x86, so it is safe in practice The re-check under the lock still prevents a second instance. The problem is the fast path, which reads the field without a lock. Without volatile there is no happens-before edge from the constructor's writes to that read, so a thread can see the reference before the fields. The JIT may reorder those writes on any CPU, x86 included, and the memory model allows it.
