h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Key terms
x: Design pattern A named, reusable shape for solving a design problem that keeps coming back. Singleton A class with exactly one instance and one way to get it. Holder idiom A nested static class whose static field holds the instance. The JVM creates it once, on first access. Double-checked locking Read a volatile field without a lock, and only lock (and check again) when it is still null. Object declaration Kotlin's built-in singleton: a class and its one instance, created thread-safely on first access. Lazy thread-safety mode How by lazy handles racing first reads: SYNCHRONIZED runs once, PUBLICATION may run many times, NONE promises nothing. What is a design pattern, in one sentence? A name for a recurring design: the problem, the shape of the solution and its trade-offs. Vocabulary, not a class template. Which Java singleton form does Effective Java call the preferred approach? A single-element enum: enum IdGenerator { INSTANCE; ... }. The JVM guarantees one instance, even across serialization and reflection. Why is the holder idiom lazy and thread-safe without a lock in your code? The JVM initializes the nested Holder class on the first read of Holder.INSTANCE, exactly once, under its own class-initialization lock. When do you need double-checked locking instead of the holder idiom? When the lazy value is an instance field (one per object, such as a per-merchant cache). The holder idiom only works for statics. by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) { init() }: how many times can init() run? Once per racing thread. The first stored value wins and every caller sees it, but the side effects repeat. Are Kotlin companion object members static on the JVM? No. They are instance members of the companion (Money.Companion.of() from Java) unless you mark them @JvmStatic. Why does an injected bean usually beat getInstance()? The dependency shows in the constructor, a test can pass a fake, and no global state leaks between tests. The container still makes only one.

h: Patterns in a modern language, and Singleton · Go deeper
x: The JDK is getting its own lazy constant, slowly. JDK 25 shipped StableValue as a preview API (JEP 502). JDK 26 renamed it LazyConstant (JEP 526, second preview), and JDK 27 still has it in preview (JEP 531). LazyConstant.of(() -> load()) promises that when several threads race, only one runs the computation. It can't hold null, and a failed computation is remembered: later calls throw without running it again. That is the opposite of Kotlin's lazy, which retries. Because it is a preview API that has already changed its name once, it stays out of this course's labs. If you want to try it, you need the matching JDK and --enable-preview. Serialization can break a class-based singleton. Deserializing a Serializable singleton creates a new object unless the class defines readResolve() to return the existing instance. The JVM handles enums specially, which is one reason Effective Java prefers them. Kotlin's data object gives a singleton a readable toString() and value-style equals. The Kotlin docs warn that serialization or reflection can still produce a second instance, so compare data objects with ==, never with ===. You'll use data object for states that carry no data, such as Pending in a payment state machine, in State and Chain of Responsibility (lesson 9 of this track).

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Static factory methods are constructors with names
x: A static factory method is a static method that returns an instance of its class, or of some class behind an interface. Effective Java opens with it (item 1: consider static factory methods instead of constructors), and the JDK is full of them: List.of, Duration.ofMinutes, Integer.valueOf, HttpClient.newHttpClient, Thread.ofVirtual. A constructor can do one thing: make a new object of exactly that class. A static factory can do four things a constructor can't. It has a name. Duration.ofMinutes(2) and Duration.ofSeconds(2) both take a long. Two constructors with the same parameter types can't exist, and new Duration(2) would say nothing anyway. It can return a cached instance. Integer.valueOf(100) hands back the same object every time. It can return any subtype, chosen from the input. List.of(1) and List.of(1, 2, 3) return two different private classes. EnumSet.noneOf picks a set backed by a single long when the enum has 64 constants or fewer, and a larger one otherwise. Callers never see the class names. The class it returns doesn't have to exist when the factory is written. DriverManager.getConnection(url) returns a Connection from whichever JDBC driver on the classpath accepts the URL, found through ServiceLoader. The Oracle driver in your service was written long after java.sql. The downsides are small. A class with only private constructors can't be subclassed, which pushes you toward composition and costs little. Factories are also harder to spot in an IDE than constructors, so stick to the usual names: of, from, valueOf, parse, newX, create. For your own value types, make this the default. Make the constructor private and offer Money.ofMinor(1250, "EUR") and Money.parse("12.50 EUR"). With the constructor private, every Money in the system went through your validation. Watch the JDK's factories choose Read FactoriesInTheJdk. For each of the first four lines, predict the class name you'll see. The Kotlin twin adds three lines for Kotlin's own listOf. Run it with the command below. Try EnumSet.noneOf(TimeUnit.class).getClass() in your IDE's auto-complete: can you type RegularEnumSet yourself? FactoriesInTheJdk.java package workbench.patterns.l02; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.EnumSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Static factories in the JDK pick the class for you. Predict each class name before you run this. */ public class FactoriesInTheJdk { public static void main(String[] args) { // the factory picks an implementation based on the input System.out.println("List.of(1) -> " + List.of(1).getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("List.of(1, 2, 3) -> " + List.of(1, 2, 3).getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("EnumSet of TimeUnit -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(TimeUnit.class).getClass().getSimpleName() + " (" + TimeUnit.values().length + " constants)"); System.out.println("EnumSet of scripts -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(Character.UnicodeScript.class).getClass().getSimpleName() + " (" + Character.UnicodeScript.values().length + " constants)"); // the factory can hand back a cached instance instead of a new one System.out.println("valueOf(100) twice -> same object? " + (Integer.valueOf(100) == Integer.valueOf(100))); System.out.println("Duration.ofSeconds(0) -> same as ZERO? " + (Duration.ofSeconds(0) == Duration.ZERO)); // and its name says what you get, which a constructor can't System.out.println("Duration.ofMinutes(2) -> " + Duration.ofMinutes(2)); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l02.FactoriesInTheJdk labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l02/FactoriesInTheJdk.java FactoriesInTheJdk.kt package workbench.patterns.l02 import java.time.Duration import java.util.EnumSet import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit // The same JDK factories called from Kotlin, plus Kotlin's own. Predict each class name first. fun main() { // JDK static factories pick an implementation from the input println("List.of(1) -> " + java.util.List.of(1).javaClass.simpleName) println("List.of(1, 2, 3) -> " + java.util.List.of(1, 2, 3).javaClass.simpleName) println("EnumSet of TimeUnit -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(TimeUnit::class.java).javaClass.simpleName + " (" + TimeUnit.entries.size + " constants)") println("EnumSet of scripts -> " + EnumSet.noneOf(Character.UnicodeScript::class.java).javaClass.simpleName + " (" + Character.UnicodeScript.entries.size + " constants)") // Kotlin's factory functions do the same (full names, since two of these are nested classes) println("listOf() -> " + listOf<Int>().javaClass.name) println("listOf(1) -> " + listOf(1).javaClass.name) println("listOf(1, 2, 3) -> " + listOf(1, 2, 3).javaClass.name) // a factory can hand back a cached instance, and its name says what you get println("Currency EUR twice -> same object? " + (java.util.Currency.getInstance("EUR") === java.util.Currency.getInstance("EUR"))) println("Duration.ofMinutes(2) -> " + Duration.ofMinutes(2)) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l02.FactoriesInTheJdkKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l02/FactoriesInTheJdk.kt List12 for one element and ListN for three. RegularEnumSet for TimeUnit (7 constants) and JumboEnumSet for Character.UnicodeScript (well over 64 constants). Both same object? lines print true, because the factories handed back cached instances. None of these classes are public, so you can't name them in your code. The factory is the only door. Kotlin's listOf plays the same game: EmptyList, Collections$SingletonList and Arrays$ArrayList, depending on how many elements you pass. DriverManager (Java SE 25 API) docs A static factory is the counter at a bank branch. You ask for "a debit card for this account", and the clerk decides which card stock, which network and which design you get. You never walk into the print room. An abstract factory is a branch that only issues matching sets: your card, PIN letter and online-banking token all come from the same issuer, so they work together. The analogy breaks on cost: a bank can add a new kind of card at one counter, but adding a new product to an abstract factory means teaching every family to make it.

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Factory Method: let someone else choose the class
x: The GoF Factory Method is a related idea with a confusingly similar name. A class needs to create something, but it shouldn't decide which concrete class. In the book's version, an abstract creator declares a creation hook and subclasses override it: Java abstract class CheckoutService { protected abstract PaymentGateway createGateway(); // the factory method final String pay(long amountMinor, String token) { return createGateway().charge(amountMinor, token); } } class AdyenCheckout extends CheckoutService { protected PaymentGateway createGateway() { return new AdyenGateway(); } } Kotlin abstract class CheckoutService { protected abstract fun createGateway(): PaymentGateway // the factory method fun pay(amountMinor: Long, token: String) = createGateway().charge(amountMinor, token) } class AdyenCheckout : CheckoutService() { override fun createGateway(): PaymentGateway = AdyenGateway() } That is one subclass per product, just to pick a constructor. Since Java 8, a function does the same job. A Supplier<PaymentGateway> (in Kotlin, a () -> PaymentGateway) is a factory, and a constructor reference is the shortest way to write one: Java record Checkout(Supplier<? extends PaymentGateway> gateways) { String pay(long amountMinor, String token) { return gateways.get().charge(amountMinor, token); } } new Checkout(AdyenGateway::new); // production new Checkout(FakeGateway::new); // test Kotlin class Checkout(private val gateways: () -> PaymentGateway) { fun pay(amountMinor: Long, token: String) = gateways().charge(amountMinor, token) } Checkout(::AdyenGateway) // production Checkout(::FakeGateway) // test When the choice depends on data (a config value, a tenant, the BIN of a card), put it in one static factory over a sealed product family: Java static PaymentGateway of(Provider p) { return switch (p) { // no default branch, on purpose case ADYEN -> new AdyenGateway(); case STRIPE -> new StripeGateway(); case FAKE -> new FakeGateway(); }; } Kotlin fun gatewayOf(p: Provider): PaymentGateway = when (p) { // no else branch, on purpose Provider.ADYEN -> AdyenGateway() Provider.STRIPE -> StripeGateway() Provider.FAKE -> FakeGateway() } Leave out default (or else in Kotlin). When someone adds KLARNA to the enum, this switch stops compiling, and the compiler points at the one place that needs a new gateway. With a catch-all branch that returns FakeGateway, the build stays green and real Klarna payments go to the fake. It is the factory bug I see most often in review. People mix up the two names, so keep them apart. A static factory is about how one class hands out its own instances. Factory Method is about who decides the concrete class: not the code that uses the object. You already write factory methods in your services under another name. A Quarkus @Produces method or a Spring @Bean method is a factory method that the container calls. It decides how to build the KafkaProducer or the issuer client, and the rest of the code injects only the interface. The container calls it when it creates the bean, not once per request, so a choice that depends on the current request (which network this card belongs to) still needs a factory you call yourself. Break a factory on purpose Run GatewayFactory with the command below. Add KLARNA to the Provider enum and run it again. Read the compiler error. Now add a catch-all as the last branch (default -> new FakeGateway(); in Java, else -> FakeGateway() in Kotlin), keep KLARNA, and run again. Where does Klarna's charge go? Undo both changes. GatewayFactory.java package workbench.patterns.l02; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** A factory method over a sealed family, and the same factory passed around as a function. */ public class GatewayFactory { enum Provider { ADYEN, STRIPE, FAKE } sealed interface PaymentGateway permits AdyenGateway, StripeGateway, FakeGateway { String charge(long amountMinor, String token); // the static factory: an exhaustive switch over the enum, with no default branch static PaymentGateway of(Provider p) { return switch (p) { case ADYEN -> new AdyenGateway(); case STRIPE -> new StripeGateway(); case FAKE -> new FakeGateway(); }; } } record AdyenGateway() implements PaymentGateway { public String charge(long amountMinor, String token) { return "adyen:" + token + ":" + amountMinor; } } record StripeGateway() implements PaymentGateway { public String charge(long amountMinor, String token) { return "stripe:" + token + ":" + amountMinor; } } record FakeGateway() implements PaymentGateway { public String charge(long amountMinor, String token) { return "fake:ok"; } } // the modern "factory method": the caller hands in how to make the product record Checkout(Supplier<? extends PaymentGateway> gateways) { String pay(long amountMinor, String token) { return gateways.get().charge(amountMinor, token); } } public static void main(String[] args) { for (Provider p : Provider.values()) { System.out.println(p + " -> " + PaymentGateway.of(p).charge(1_250, "tok_42")); } System.out.println("test checkout -> " + new Checkout(FakeGateway::new).pay(1_250, "tok_42")); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l02.GatewayFactory labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l02/GatewayFactory.java GatewayFactory.kt package workbench.patterns.l02 // A factory over a sealed family, and the same factory passed around as a function. enum class Provider { ADYEN, STRIPE, FAKE } sealed interface PaymentGateway { fun charge(amountMinor: Long, token: String): String companion object { // the factory: an exhaustive when over the enum, with no else branch fun of(p: Provider): PaymentGateway = when (p) { Provider.ADYEN -> AdyenGateway() Provider.STRIPE -> StripeGateway() Provider.FAKE -> FakeGateway() } } } class AdyenGateway : PaymentGateway { override fun charge(amountMinor: Long, token: String) = "adyen:$token:$amountMinor" } class StripeGateway : PaymentGateway { override fun charge(amountMinor: Long, token: String) = "stripe:$token:$amountMinor" } class FakeGateway : PaymentGateway { override fun charge(amountMinor: Long, token: String) = "fake:ok" } // the modern "factory method": the caller hands in how to make the product class GatewayCheckout(private val gateways: () -> PaymentGateway) { fun pay(amountMinor: Long, token: String) = gateways().charge(amountMinor, token) } fun main() { for (p in Provider.entries) { println("$p -> ${PaymentGateway.of(p).charge(1_250, "tok_42")}") } println("test checkout -> ${GatewayCheckout(::FakeGateway).pay(1_250, "tok_42")}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l02.GatewayFactoryKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l02/GatewayFactory.kt The first run prints one charge per provider and test checkout -> fake:ok. With KLARNA added, the build fails, pointing at the factory: javac says error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, and kotlinc says 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'KLARNA' branch or an 'else' branch. With a catch-all branch it compiles and prints KLARNA -> fake:ok: a customer's payment would go to the fake gateway, and nothing warns you. Card BIN routing is a factory: the first digits pick the network, and the network picks the issuer client, its base URL, its timeouts and its error mapping. Put that decision in one when over a sealed Network, return a sealed result for numbers you can't route, and inject the family factory as a function into your Quarkus resource or Temporal activity. Then a test passes a lambda that returns a fake family and records which network was asked for. For Kafka, a family of producer plus consumer plus serde, chosen once by a build profile, keeps the in-memory test setup from leaking into production config.

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Kotlin factories: companion, invoke and sealed results
x: Kotlin has no static, so its factories live in three other places. The companion object is the direct translation of a Java static factory. Make the constructor private and put the factory next to it: Java public final class Card { private final Network network; private final String last4; private Card(Network network, String last4) { this.network = network; this.last4 = last4; } public static CardResult parse(String raw) { /* validate, then new Card(network, last4) */ } } Kotlin class Card private constructor(val network: Network, val last4: String) { companion object { fun parse(raw: String): CardResult { /* validate, then Card(network, last4) */ } } } An operator fun invoke on the companion lets callers write what looks like a constructor call, Fee(290), while you run a factory that validates or returns a cached instance. Use it sparingly: readers expect Fee(290) to make a new object. The third shape is a top-level function named like the type. The Kotlin coding conventions allow a factory function to share the name of the abstract type it returns, and kotlinx.coroutines does exactly that: Job(), CoroutineScope(context) and MutableStateFlow(0) are functions that return a private implementation class. What a factory returns matters as much as where it lives. A parser that throws makes every caller remember a try. A factory that returns a sealed result makes the compiler remember for them: Java public sealed interface CardResult { record Valid(Card card) implements CardResult {} record Invalid(String reason) implements CardResult {} } switch (Card.parse(input)) { // no default case CardResult.Valid v -> charge(v.card()); case CardResult.Invalid i -> reject(i.reason()); } Kotlin sealed interface CardResult { data class Valid(val card: Card) : CardResult data class Invalid(val reason: String) : CardResult } when (val r = Card.parse(input)) { // no else is CardResult.Valid -> charge(r.card) is CardResult.Invalid -> reject(r.reason) } Add a third case later, say Expired, and every when without an else stops compiling until it handles it. Java 21 gives you the same check with a sealed interface, records and a switch with type patterns, as the Java twin shows. Throw exceptions for bugs and broken infrastructure. Return a sealed result for outcomes the caller is expected to handle, like a mistyped card number. Let the compiler find the missing case Run CompanionFactories (Kotlin, or its Java twin) with the command below and read the three parse lines. Add a fourth result: data class Blocked(val country: String) : IbanResult in Kotlin, or record Blocked(String country) implements IbanResult {} in Java. Predict what happens, then run. Fix it by adding a branch for Blocked to describe, not an else or default. CompanionFactories.kt package workbench.patterns.l02 // Three Kotlin factory shapes, and a factory that returns a sealed result instead of throwing. class Iban private constructor(val country: String, val digits: String) { override fun toString() = "$country****${digits.takeLast(4)}" companion object { // 1. a named factory in the companion: Iban.parse("...") fun parse(raw: String): IbanResult { val s = raw.replace(" ", "").uppercase() return when { s.length < 15 -> IbanResult.TooShort(s.length) !s.take(2).all(Char::isLetter) -> IbanResult.BadCountry(s.take(2)) else -> IbanResult.Ok(Iban(s.take(2), s.drop(2))) } } } } sealed interface IbanResult { data class Ok(val iban: Iban) : IbanResult data class TooShort(val length: Int) : IbanResult data class BadCountry(val prefix: String) : IbanResult } class Fee private constructor(val bps: Int) { override fun toString() = "Fee($bps bps)" companion object { private val standard = Fee(290) // 2. operator invoke: callers write Fee(290) and get the cached instance operator fun invoke(bps: Int): Fee = if (bps == 290) standard else Fee(bps) } } interface Ledger { fun post(entry: String) } // 3. a top-level function named like the interface, as kotlinx.coroutines does with Job() and CoroutineScope() fun Ledger(): Ledger = object : Ledger { override fun post(entry: String) = println(" ledger <- $entry") } fun describe(r: IbanResult): String = when (r) { // no else: the compiler checks every case is here is IbanResult.Ok -> "ok: ${r.iban}" is IbanResult.TooShort -> "too short (${r.length} chars)" is IbanResult.BadCountry -> "bad country code '${r.prefix}'" } fun main() { listOf("DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00", "DE89 3704", "12345678901234567890").forEach { println("parse(\"$it\") -> ${describe(Iban.parse(it))}") } println("Fee(290) === Fee(290)? ${Fee(290) === Fee(290)}") println("Fee(150) === Fee(150)? ${Fee(150) === Fee(150)}") Ledger().post("fee 29.00 EUR") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l02.CompanionFactoriesKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l02/CompanionFactories.kt CompanionFactoriesJava.java package workbench.patterns.l02; import java.util.List; /** The Java twin of CompanionFactories.kt: static factories, a cached instance, and a sealed result. */ public class CompanionFactoriesJava { static final class Iban { final String country, digits; private Iban(String country, String digits) { this.country = country; this.digits = digits; } @Override public String toString() { return country + "****" + digits.substring(digits.length() - 4); } // 1. a named static factory: Iban.parse("...") static IbanResult parse(String raw) { String s = raw.replace(" ", "").toUpperCase(); if (s.length() < 15) return new TooShort(s.length()); if (!Character.isLetter(s.charAt(0)) || !Character.isLetter(s.charAt(1))) return new BadCountry(s.substring(0, 2)); return new Ok(new Iban(s.substring(0, 2), s.substring(2))); } } sealed interface IbanResult {} // permitted subtypes: the records in this file record Ok(Iban iban) implements IbanResult {} record TooShort(int length) implements IbanResult {} record BadCountry(String prefix) implements IbanResult {} static final class Fee { private static final Fee STANDARD = new Fee(290); final int bps; private Fee(int bps) { this.bps = bps; } // 2. Java has no operator invoke, so the cached-instance factory needs a name static Fee of(int bps) { return bps == 290 ? STANDARD : new Fee(bps); } } interface Ledger { void post(String entry); // 3. a static factory on the interface returns a hidden implementation static Ledger create() { return entry -> System.out.println(" ledger <- " + entry); } } static String describe(IbanResult r) { return switch (r) { // no default: the compiler checks every case is here case Ok ok -> "ok: " + ok.iban(); case TooShort t -> "too short (" + t.length() + " chars)"; case BadCountry b -> "bad country code '" + b.prefix() + "'"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { for (String raw : List.of("DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00", "DE89 3704", "12345678901234567890")) { System.out.println("parse(\"" + raw + "\") -> " + describe(Iban.parse(raw))); } System.out.println("Fee.of(290) == Fee.of(290)? " + (Fee.of(290) == Fee.of(290))); System.out.println("Fee.of(150) == Fee.of(150)? " + (Fee.of(150) == Fee.of(150))); Ledger.create().post("fee 29.00 EUR"); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l02.CompanionFactoriesJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l02/CompanionFactoriesJava.java The first run prints ok: DE****3000, too short (8 chars) and bad country code '12', then true for the cached Fee with 290 bps and false for 150. Java has no operator invoke, so its twin needs a named factory, Fee.of(290). After adding Blocked, the build stops: kotlinc says 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Blocked' branch or an 'else' branch., and javac says the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. The compiler found the one place that needs the new case. Coding conventions: naming rules (Kotlin docs) docs Sealed classes and interfaces (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Abstract Factory: one choice for a whole family
x: Sometimes you create several objects that must match. A card network gives you an authorization API and a refund API, and a Visa auth code means nothing to Mastercard's refund endpoint. If every call site picks its own authorizer and its own refunder, sooner or later a code path that runs once a month pairs a Visa authorizer with a Mastercard refunder. Abstract Factory puts that choice in one place. One interface creates every product of the family, with one implementation per family: Java public interface CardNetworkClients { Network network(); Authorizer authorizer(); Refunder refunder(); static CardNetworkClients sandbox(Network network) { return switch (network) { case VISA -> new SandboxClients(Network.VISA, "https://sandbox.visa.example", "V"); case MASTERCARD -> new SandboxClients(Network.MASTERCARD, "https://sandbox.mastercard.example", "M"); }; } } Kotlin interface CardNetworkClients { val network: Network fun authorizer(): Authorizer fun refunder(): Refunder companion object { fun sandbox(network: Network): CardNetworkClients = when (network) { Network.VISA -> SandboxClients(Network.VISA, "https://sandbox.visa.example", "V") Network.MASTERCARD -> SandboxClients(Network.MASTERCARD, "https://sandbox.mastercard.example", "M") } } } Callers ask for the family once, clientsFor(card.network), and take both products from it. They can't mix families because they never pick a product directly. Each family here is one class built from settings, not a VisaAuthorizer plus a VisaRefunder. When the products are single-method interfaces, a family is just a class (or a Java record) of functions. The GoF diagram with two parallel class hierarchies is the worst case, not a requirement. The weakness runs the other way. Adding a family is cheap: one more implementation. Adding a product, say a Tokenizer, changes the interface and every family. And with a DI container you may not need to write the factory at all: Quarkus build profiles or Spring profiles can pick the Kafka messaging family in production and an in-memory one in tests. Write the factory yourself when the choice depends on runtime data, such as the card in this request. Check yourself. Card ops adds AMEX to Network. Where does the build fail, and which callers change? (It fails in sandbox, because its when and switch have no else or default, so you add an Amex branch with its own settings. No caller changes: callers only ask for a family and never name a product class.) Checkout asks for a family once. Both products come from that family, so a Visa auth code never reaches a Mastercard refund. The most common mistake is a factory switch or when with a default or else branch that returns something plausible, such as a fake or the most common implementation. It looks defensive. In practice it turns "you forgot to handle the new provider" from a compile error into a production incident. Write the switch over a sealed type or an enum with no default, so the compiler forces a decision for every new case. If some input really has no product, return a sealed Invalid result instead of guessing.

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Java and Kotlin
x: A validating factory that returns a sealed result Money.java public final class Money { private final long minor; private final String currency; private Money(long minor, String currency) { this.minor = minor; this.currency = currency; } public static Money ofMinor(long minor, String currency) { // named and validating if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount"); return new Money(minor, currency); } public sealed interface Parsed permits Ok, Bad {} public record Ok(Money money) implements Parsed {} public record Bad(String reason) implements Parsed {} public static Parsed parse(String text) { // "12.50 EUR" String[] parts = text.trim().split(" "); if (parts.length != 2) return new Bad("expected '<amount> <currency>'"); try { long minor = new BigDecimal(parts[0]).movePointRight(2).longValueExact(); return new Ok(ofMinor(minor, parts[1])); } catch (ArithmeticException | IllegalArgumentException e) { return new Bad("not an amount: " + parts[0]); } } } // caller: the compiler checks both cases are handled String shown = switch (Money.parse(input)) { case Money.Ok(Money m) -> "charge " + m; case Money.Bad(String why) -> "rejected: " + why; }; Money.kt class Money private constructor(val minor: Long, val currency: String) { companion object { @JvmStatic fun ofMinor(minor: Long, currency: String): Money { require(minor >= 0) { "negative amount" } return Money(minor, currency) } @JvmStatic fun parse(text: String): Parsed { // "12.50 EUR" val parts = text.trim().split(" ") if (parts.size != 2) return Parsed.Bad("expected '<amount> <currency>'") val minor = parts[0].toBigDecimalOrNull() ?.movePointRight(2) ?.runCatching { longValueExact() }?.getOrNull() ?: return Parsed.Bad("not an amount: ${parts[0]}") return if (minor < 0) Parsed.Bad("negative amount") else Parsed.Ok(Money(minor, parts[1])) } } } sealed interface Parsed { data class Ok(val money: Money) : Parsed data class Bad(val reason: String) : Parsed } // caller val shown = when (val p = Money.parse(input)) { is Parsed.Ok -> "charge ${p.money}" is Parsed.Bad -> "rejected: ${p.reason}" } The shape is the same: private constructor, named factories, a sealed result and an exhaustive switch or when at the call site. Java 21 deconstructs the result with record patterns (case Money.Ok(Money m)), Kotlin smart-casts it after is. The real difference is where the factory lives. Kotlin has no static: ofMinor is a method on the companion object, so Java callers would write Money.Companion.ofMinor(...) without @JvmStatic. Kotlin also gives you operator fun invoke and top-level factory functions, and its named arguments remove a lot of the constructor ambiguity that pushes Java code toward factories in the first place.

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Worked example
x: Replace ambiguous constructors with named factories A Refund class grew four constructors. Look at the last line and decide what it creates before reading on. public class Refund { public Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor) { ... } // partial public Refund(String paymentId) { ... } // full public Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor, String reason) { ... } // partial, with reason public Refund(String paymentId, String reason) { ... } // full, with reason } new Refund("p-1", "duplicate"); // ? class Refund { constructor(paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long) { ... } // partial constructor(paymentId: String) { ... } // full constructor(paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long, reason: String) { ... } // partial, with reason constructor(paymentId: String, reason: String) { ... } // full, with reason } Refund("p-1", "duplicate") // ? It's a full refund with a reason, but only the parameter types say so. Adding a chargeback reversal would mean a fifth constructor with another type mix. Give each kind a name, validate there, and make the constructor private so every Refund goes through a factory. public final class Refund { private final String paymentId; private final OptionalLong amountMinor; // empty = full refund private final String reason; private Refund(String paymentId, OptionalLong amountMinor, String reason) { this.paymentId = paymentId; this.amountMinor = amountMinor; this.reason = reason; } public static Refund full(String paymentId, String reason) { // 1. the name says what you get return new Refund(paymentId, OptionalLong.empty(), reason); } public static Refund partial(String paymentId, long amountMinor, String reason) { if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("partial refund needs a positive amount"); // 2. validate per kind return new Refund(paymentId, OptionalLong.of(amountMinor), reason); } } Refund.full("p-1", "duplicate"); Refund.partial("p-1", 500, "damaged item"); class Refund private constructor( val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long?, // null = full refund val reason: String, ) { companion object { fun full(paymentId: String, reason: String) = Refund(paymentId, null, reason) // 1. the name says what you get fun partial(paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long, reason: String): Refund { require(amountMinor > 0) { "partial refund needs a positive amount" } // 2. validate per kind return Refund(paymentId, amountMinor, reason) } } } Refund.full("p-1", "duplicate") Refund.partial("p-1", 500, "damaged item") Downstream, a full refund also releases the authorization hold. When the kinds behave differently, let the same factories return different records (or data classes) behind a sealed interface. Callers don't change, and code that handles refunds can switch over the two cases with the compiler checking it covers both. In Kotlin, @JvmStatic keeps Refund.full(...) working for Java callers, and Kotlin callers could also write Refund.Partial(paymentId = "p-1", amountMinor = 500, reason = "damaged"): named arguments already remove the ambiguity that started this. public sealed interface Refund permits FullRefund, PartialRefund { String paymentId(); static Refund full(String paymentId, String reason) { return new FullRefund(paymentId, reason); } static Refund partial(String paymentId, long amountMinor, String reason) { return new PartialRefund(paymentId, amountMinor, reason); // 3. the factory picks the record } } record FullRefund(String paymentId, String reason) implements Refund {} record PartialRefund(String paymentId, long amountMinor, String reason) implements Refund { PartialRefund { // 4. the invariant lives in the record if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive"); } } sealed interface Refund { val paymentId: String data class Full(override val paymentId: String, val reason: String) : Refund data class Partial(override val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val reason: String) : Refund { init { require(amountMinor > 0) { "amount must be positive" } } // 4. the invariant lives in the class } companion object { @JvmStatic fun full(paymentId: String, reason: String): Refund = Full(paymentId, reason) @JvmStatic fun partial(paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long, reason: String): Refund = Partial(paymentId, amountMinor, reason) // 3. the factory picks the class } }

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Quiz
x: Which of these can a static factory do that a constructor can never do? Return an instance of a subtype chosen from its arguments Validate its arguments Be called from another package Throw a checked exception Constructors can validate, be public and throw checked exceptions too. Only a factory can return a cached object or a different class, like List.of returning List12 or ListN depending on how many elements you pass. A factory has switch (provider) { case ADYEN -> ...; case STRIPE -> ...; default -> new FakeGateway(); }. A teammate adds KLARNA to the enum. What happens? A compile error in the factory A MatchException at runtime Klarna payments silently go to the fake gateway The switch throws NullPointerException The default branch catches every new constant, so the build stays green and Klarna gets the fake gateway. Without default, a switch expression over an enum must cover every constant, and adding KLARNA would be a compile error at exactly this line. Which Kotlin shape lets callers write Fee(290) while you return a cached instance? A secondary constructor operator fun invoke in the companion object An init block A data class with a default argument A constructor always makes a new object, whether primary or secondary. operator fun invoke(bps: Int): Fee on the companion turns Fee(290) into a function call that can return anything, including a cached instance. Readers expect a new object from that syntax, so use it with care. You have interface MessagingFactory { Publisher publisher(); Subscriber subscriber(); } with a Kafka family and an in-memory family. Now you need a DeadLetterQueue product too. What does that cost? Nothing: add one new class Only the Kafka family changes You have to switch to Factory Method The interface and every existing family change Abstract Factory makes new families cheap and new products expensive: every family must now produce a dead-letter queue, including the in-memory one used in tests. Weigh that before you add a product to the interface. From lesson 1 of this track: a Kotlin companion object holds a factory of(...) and val cache = loadCache(). When does loadCache() run? When the outer class is loaded, like a Java static initializer Lazily, the first time cache is read, under a lock Every time of is called At application startup, for every class on the classpath A companion object is initialized when its outer class is loaded, which matches a Java static initializer, so loadCache() runs then even if nobody reads cache. If you want it on first read, write val cache by lazy { loadCache() }.

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Key terms
x: Static factory method A static method that returns an instance, used instead of a public constructor. Factory Method (GoF) A creation hook that lets something other than the caller pick the concrete class. Now often a Supplier<T> or () -> T. Abstract Factory An interface that creates a whole family of matching objects, with one implementation per family. Product family Objects that must be used together, such as one network's authorizer and refunder. Sealed result A sealed set of outcomes (Valid, Invalid) returned instead of throwing. A switch or when must handle every case. Companion object A Kotlin object tied to a class, and the usual home for that class's factories. Name two things a static factory can do that a constructor can't. Return a cached instance, and return a subtype chosen from its arguments (List.of gives List12 or ListN). It also has a name. Why leave out default in a factory's switch over a sealed type or enum? So adding a new case is a compile error at the factory. With default, the new case silently takes the default branch. What replaced the GoF Factory Method's creator subclass in modern Java? A function: a Supplier<PaymentGateway>, usually written as a constructor reference such as AdyenGateway::new. Kotlin has no static. Where does a class's named factory usually live? In its companion object: companion object { fun parse(raw: String): CardResult }. What name may a Kotlin factory function have, by the coding conventions? The same name as the abstract type it returns, like fun Job(): Job or MutableStateFlow(0). When should a factory return a sealed result instead of throwing? When the failure is an outcome the caller is expected to handle, like a mistyped card number. Keep exceptions for bugs and broken infrastructure. Abstract Factory: what is cheap to add, and what is expensive? A new family is cheap (one implementation). A new product is expensive (the interface and every family change).

h: Factory Method and Abstract Factory · Go deeper
x: DriverManager is a factory whose products did not exist when it was written. On first use it asks ServiceLoader for every java.sql.Driver that a JAR on the classpath lists in a META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver file. getConnection(url) then offers the URL to each driver until one accepts it. You can build the same plug-in mechanism yourself: define an interface, list the implementations in META-INF/services/<interface name>, and call ServiceLoader.load(YourInterface.class). The module system adds provides ... with ... and uses ... declarations for the same thing. Effective Java lists conventional factory names, and sticking to them makes factories easy to find: from for a one-argument conversion (Date.from(instant)), of for aggregation (EnumSet.of(...)), valueOf, getInstance or instance, create or newInstance when each call returns a new object, getType and newType when the factory lives in another class (Files.newBufferedReader), and a bare type (Collections.list). From Java, a Kotlin companion factory is Money.Companion.parse(...). Annotate it with @JvmStatic and Java callers can write Money.parse(...). If a Java team consumes your Kotlin library, do it for every public factory. The same goes for @JvmOverloads on functions with default arguments, which you'll meet in Builder and Prototype (lesson 3 of this track).

h: Builder and Prototype · Named and default arguments replace most builders
x: A builder exists to fix the telescoping constructor: one constructor per combination of optional parameters, and call sites full of unlabeled literals. Java new ChargeRequest(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42", null, null, true, 2, 30_000); // which one is the timeout? Kotlin ChargeRequest(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42", null, null, true, 2, 30_000) // Kotlin allows the same mess The Java fix is the builder from Effective Java item 2: a mutable helper class with one method per field and a build() at the end. It works, and it costs you a second class that repeats every field. Kotlin removes the problem in the language. Parameters can have defaults, and callers can name them: Java // Java has no named or default arguments: the record keeps the rules, a builder supplies the defaults record ChargeRequest(long amountMinor, String currency, String token, String description, boolean capture, int maxRetries, long timeoutMs) { ChargeRequest { if (maxRetries < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("maxRetries must be >= 0"); } ChargeRequest withTimeoutMs(long ms) { return new ChargeRequest(amountMinor, currency, token, description, capture, maxRetries, ms); } } var req = ChargeRequest.builder(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42").maxRetries(2).build(); // the builder: next section var slower = req.withTimeoutMs(30_000); Kotlin data class ChargeRequest( val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String, val token: String, val description: String? = null, val capture: Boolean = true, val maxRetries: Int = 0, val timeoutMs: Long = 10_000, ) { init { require(maxRetries >= 0) { "maxRetries must be >= 0" } } } val req = ChargeRequest(amountMinor = 1_250, currency = "EUR", token = "tok_42", maxRetries = 2) val slower = req.copy(timeoutMs = 30_000) In the Kotlin version, every argument at the call site says what it is. Optional ones can be skipped, in any order. copy gives you a changed copy for free. And the init block runs for every construction, copy included, so nobody can skip the validation. That covers what most Java builders do. Java callers are the gap. Java has no named arguments, so they see one constructor with seven parameters. @JvmOverloads on the constructor generates the telescoping overloads for them (one per trailing default), which is better than nothing and worse than a builder. If a Java team will call the class a lot, give them a real builder. A rule of thumb for porting: if every call site of a Java builder sets two or three fields and leaves the rest at their defaults, the Kotlin version is a data class with defaults and nothing else. If call sites build the object across a loop or an if, keep a builder, as the next section explains. Check yourself. In the Kotlin ChargeRequest, what does req.copy(maxRetries = -1) do, and why? (It throws IllegalArgumentException. copy builds the new object through the primary constructor, so the init block runs again.) Functions: named and default arguments (Kotlin docs) docs Effective Java 3e source, item 2: the Builder read A builder is an order form at a card-printing desk: you tick the boxes you care about, leave the rest at their defaults, and the clerk checks the whole form before printing anything. Kotlin's named arguments are a form so short you fill it in at the counter. Prototype is photocopying a filled-in form and changing two fields. The analogy breaks on the shallow copy: a photocopy is a real, separate piece of paper, while copy() gives you a new form that still points at the same attached sheet of line items, so writing on the copy's attachment writes on the original's.

h: Builder and Prototype · When a builder still earns its place
x: Builders still win in four cases. The first is Java callers, as above. The second is validation that needs the whole object: "a statement descriptor is at most 22 characters, and only when capture is true" relates two fields. The third is construction spread across steps, such as headers added in a loop or 3-D Secure data added only for some cards; Kotlin's buildList { } and buildString { } are standard-library builders for exactly this. The fourth is nested data, which gets its own section next. The modern Java shape is a record that validates plus a small builder that only collects: Java record IssuerCall(String url, String method, Map<String, String> headers, Duration timeout, int maxRetries) { IssuerCall { // compact constructor: runs on every path Objects.requireNonNull(url, "url"); headers = Map.copyOf(headers); // immutable, and a copy if (maxRetries < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("maxRetries must be >= 0"); } IssuerCall withTimeout(Duration t) { return new IssuerCall(url, method, headers, t, maxRetries); } static Builder builder(String url) { return new Builder(url); } // Builder: fields with defaults, one setter each, and build() calls the constructor } Kotlin data class IssuerCall( val url: String, val method: String = "GET", val headers: Map<String, String> = emptyMap(), val timeout: Duration = Duration.ofSeconds(2), val maxRetries: Int = 0, ) { init { require(maxRetries >= 0) { "maxRetries must be >= 0" } } // runs on every path, copy() too } // no builder and no withers: named arguments and copy(timeout = ...) do both jobs The builder holds no rules. The rules live in the compact constructor, which build(), the wither withTimeout and a direct new IssuerCall(...) all go through. A compact constructor is a record constructor written without a parameter list. Its body runs first, and javac assigns the fields from the parameters after it, which is why headers = Map.copyOf(headers) changes what gets stored. Withers are how you get Prototype on a record: Java has no with syntax, so you write one small method per field you want to change. The Kotlin twin needs neither builder nor withers, and its init block plays the role of the compact constructor. The JDK's newer APIs follow the same idea of a builder that produces an immutable result: HttpClient.newBuilder(), and Thread.ofVirtual(), which returns a Thread.Builder. One builder bug deserves a name. If build() validates but the class also has a public constructor that doesn't, half the code base skips the rules. Put the rules in the type, never only in the builder. Find where the rules live Run RecordBuilderDemo with the command below and read the four lines. In the Java main, change .maxRetries(2) to .maxRetries(-1) (in Kotlin, maxRetries = -1). Predict: which line throws, and from where? Run it. Undo the change. RecordBuilderDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l03; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Objects; /** A record with a small builder: the record validates, the builder only collects. */ public class RecordBuilderDemo { record IssuerCall(String url, String method, Map<String, String> headers, Duration timeout, int maxRetries) { IssuerCall { // every path to an IssuerCall runs this Objects.requireNonNull(url, "url"); headers = Map.copyOf(headers); // really immutable if (maxRetries < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("maxRetries must be >= 0, was " + maxRetries); } IssuerCall withTimeout(Duration t) { // a hand-written "wither" return new IssuerCall(url, method, headers, t, maxRetries); } IssuerCall withMaxRetries(int n) { return new IssuerCall(url, method, headers, timeout, n); } static Builder builder(String url) { return new Builder(url); } static final class Builder { private final String url; private String method = "GET"; private final Map<String, String> headers = new LinkedHashMap<>(); private Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(2); private int maxRetries = 0; private Builder(String url) { this.url = url; } Builder method(String m) { method = m; return this; } Builder header(String k, String v) { headers.put(k, v); return this; } Builder timeout(Duration t) { timeout = t; return this; } Builder maxRetries(int n) { maxRetries = n; return this; } IssuerCall build() { return new IssuerCall(url, method, headers, timeout, maxRetries); } } } public static void main(String[] args) { IssuerCall call = IssuerCall.builder("https://issuer.example/authorize") .method("POST") .header("Idempotency-Key", "auth-7731") .maxRetries(2) .build(); System.out.println("built: " + call); System.out.println("faster copy: " + call.withTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(800)).timeout()); try { call.headers().put("X-Debug", "1"); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("headers: unmodifiable"); } try { call.withMaxRetries(-1); // the wither can't skip validation either } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("wither: " + e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l03.RecordBuilderDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l03/RecordBuilderDemo.java RecordBuilderDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l03 import java.time.Duration // The Kotlin twin of RecordBuilderDemo.java: no builder and no withers, because named arguments, // defaults and copy() do both jobs. The rules still live in one place: init. data class IssuerCall( val url: String, val method: String = "GET", val headers: Map<String, String> = emptyMap(), val timeout: Duration = Duration.ofSeconds(2), val maxRetries: Int = 0, ) { init { // runs for every construction, copy() included require(maxRetries >= 0) { "maxRetries must be >= 0, was $maxRetries" } } } fun main() { val call = IssuerCall( url = "https://issuer.example/authorize", method = "POST", headers = mapOf("Idempotency-Key" to "auth-7731"), maxRetries = 2, ) println("built: $call") println("faster copy: ${call.copy(timeout = Duration.ofMillis(800)).timeout}") // Map is a read-only type, so there is no put(). Force a cast and the map behind it refuses too: val write = runCatching { (call.headers as MutableMap<String, String>)["X-Debug"] = "1" } println("headers: ${if (write.isFailure) "unmodifiable" else "writable!"}") try { call.copy(maxRetries = -1) // copy() can't skip validation either } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("copy(): ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l03.RecordBuilderDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l03/RecordBuilderDemo.kt The first run prints the built call, PT0.8S for the faster copy, headers: unmodifiable and wither: maxRetries must be >= 0, was -1. With .maxRetries(-1) the program dies in build(), and the stack trace points into the record's compact constructor: the builder has no rules of its own, so it can't forget any. The Kotlin twin fails in the same place, its init block, and prints copy(): maxRetries must be >= 0, was -1 for the copy. HttpClient.Builder (Java SE 25 API) docs Payment requests to an issuer have a dozen optional fields: descriptor, 3-D Secure data, metadata, capture mode, retry policy. In Kotlin services, a data class with defaults and an init block is all you need. For a shared client library that Java services call, add a builder. Test fixtures are prototypes: one baseAuthorization copied per test with copy(amountMinor = 0). If that fixture holds a MutableList of line items, one test can poison every test after it. The same goes for a Quarkus @ApplicationScoped bean that hands out a default config object which callers then copy and modify.

h: Builder and Prototype · Type-safe builders: lambdas with receivers and @DslMarker
x: For nested data, Kotlin lets you write a builder that reads like a configuration file: Java // Java has no lambdas with receivers; the closest is a Consumer that receives the builder PaymentRequest req = paymentRequest(r -> { r.idempotencyKey("order-981-attempt-1"); r.lineItems(items -> { items.item("sku-1", 1_000); items.item("sku-2", 500); }); r.metadata("orderId", "981"); }); Kotlin val req = paymentRequest { idempotencyKey = "order-981-attempt-1" lineItems { item("sku-1", 1_000) item("sku-2", 500) } metadata("orderId", "981") } The trick is a lambda with receiver. paymentRequest takes a PaymentRequestBuilder.() -> Unit: a function that runs with a builder as this. Inside the braces, idempotencyKey and lineItems are members of that builder: Java static PaymentRequest paymentRequest(Consumer<PaymentRequestBuilder> block) { PaymentRequestBuilder b = new PaymentRequestBuilder(); block.accept(b); // the block gets the builder as a parameter return b.build(); } final class PaymentRequestBuilder { private String idempotencyKey; private final List<LineItem> items = new ArrayList<>(); void idempotencyKey(String key) { idempotencyKey = key; } void lineItems(Consumer<LineItemsBuilder> block) { LineItemsBuilder b = new LineItemsBuilder(); block.accept(b); items.addAll(b.build()); } PaymentRequest build() { /* validate, then copy into the request */ } } Kotlin fun paymentRequest(block: PaymentRequestBuilder.() -> Unit): PaymentRequest = PaymentRequestBuilder().apply(block).build() class PaymentRequestBuilder { var idempotencyKey: String? = null private val items = mutableListOf<LineItem>() fun lineItems(block: LineItemsBuilder.() -> Unit) { items += LineItemsBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun build(): PaymentRequest { /* validate, then copy into the request */ } } Gradle's Kotlin DSL, Ktor routing and kotlinx.html are built the same way. The Java shape, a Consumer per block, is what Spring Security's lambda configuration uses. The builder is still a builder: build() is the one place that sees every field, so it validates there. There is one trap. Inside lineItems { }, two receivers are in scope: the LineItemsBuilder and the outer PaymentRequestBuilder. So idempotencyKey = "x" written inside the inner block compiles and quietly sets the outer field. @DslMarker closes that hole: Java // Java needs no marker: each block names its builder, so reaching the outer one means typing r r.lineItems(items -> { items.item("sku-1", 1_000); r.idempotencyKey("x"); // compiles, but you can see it in review }); Kotlin @DslMarker annotation class PaymentDsl @PaymentDsl class PaymentRequestBuilder { ... } @PaymentDsl class LineItemsBuilder { ... } With both builders marked, the compiler only lets you call members of the nearest receiver without a prefix. Reaching the outer one needs an explicit label, this@paymentRequest.idempotencyKey, which nobody writes by accident. Build a DSL only when the data nests. A flat request with seven fields is clearer with named arguments, and a DSL would add two classes and a layer of indirection for nothing. The payoff comes with structure: line items under a payment, split payouts under a marketplace order, routing rules under a merchant. It also helps when many people write the same kind of configuration, because inside each block the IDE offers only that builder's methods. Make the inner block reach outside Run DslScope.kt with the command below. Uncomment the line reason = "oops" inside the refunds { } block. Predict, then run. Now delete both @RefundDsl lines above the two builder classes (keep the annotation class itself) and run again. What is the batch's reason? Restore the file. Then open the Java twin and uncomment batchB.reason("oops"): it compiles, but notice that you had to type the outer builder's name. DslScope.kt package workbench.patterns.l03 // A tiny refund-batch DSL. @DslMarker stops an inner block from reaching the outer builder by accident. @DslMarker annotation class RefundDsl data class Refund(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long) data class RefundBatch(val reason: String, val refunds: List<Refund>) @RefundDsl class RefundsBuilder { private val refunds = mutableListOf<Refund>() fun refund(paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long) { refunds += Refund(paymentId, amountMinor) } fun build() = refunds.toList() } @RefundDsl class RefundBatchBuilder { var reason: String = "unspecified" private var refunds: List<Refund> = emptyList() fun refunds(block: RefundsBuilder.() -> Unit) { refunds = RefundsBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun build() = RefundBatch(reason, refunds) } fun refundBatch(block: RefundBatchBuilder.() -> Unit): RefundBatch = RefundBatchBuilder().apply(block).build() fun main() { val batch = refundBatch { reason = "duplicate charge" refunds { refund("p-101", 1_250) refund("p-102", 990) // reason = "oops" // step 2 of the Try it: uncomment this line } } println(batch) println("total refunded: ${batch.refunds.sumOf { it.amountMinor }}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l03.DslScopeKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l03/DslScope.kt DslScopeJava.java package workbench.patterns.l03; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** * The Java twin of DslScope.kt. Java has no lambdas with receivers, so each block is a Consumer * that gets its builder as a named parameter (the style Spring Security uses for its config DSL). */ public class DslScopeJava { record Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor) {} record RefundBatch(String reason, List<Refund> refunds) {} static final class RefundsBuilder { private final List<Refund> refunds = new ArrayList<>(); RefundsBuilder refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor) { refunds.add(new Refund(paymentId, amountMinor)); return this; } List<Refund> build() { return List.copyOf(refunds); } } static final class RefundBatchBuilder { private String reason = "unspecified"; private List<Refund> refunds = List.of(); RefundBatchBuilder reason(String r) { reason = r; return this; } RefundBatchBuilder refunds(Consumer<RefundsBuilder> block) { RefundsBuilder b = new RefundsBuilder(); block.accept(b); refunds = b.build(); return this; } RefundBatch build() { return new RefundBatch(reason, refunds); } } static RefundBatch refundBatch(Consumer<RefundBatchBuilder> block) { RefundBatchBuilder b = new RefundBatchBuilder(); block.accept(b); return b.build(); } public static void main(String[] args) { RefundBatch batch = refundBatch(batchB -> { batchB.reason("duplicate charge"); batchB.refunds(r -> { r.refund("p-101", 1_250); r.refund("p-102", 990); // batchB.reason("oops"); // step 2 of the Try it: this compiles, but you have to name batchB }); }); System.out.println(batch); System.out.println("total refunded: " + batch.refunds().stream().mapToLong(Refund::amountMinor).sum()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l03.DslScopeJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l03/DslScopeJava.java The first run prints a batch with reason duplicate charge and total refunded: 2240. With the line uncommented, the build fails: 'var reason: String' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. Without the marker it compiles and prints reason=oops: the inner block silently rewrote the outer batch. Type-safe builders (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Builder and Prototype · Prototype: every copy is shallow until you make it deep
x: Prototype means making a new object by copying an existing one and changing a few fields. Payment code does this constantly: a recurring-charge template copied per merchant, a default config copied per tenant, a test fixture copied per test. Java's original mechanism, Cloneable, is broken by design. The interface has no clone method, so implementing it gives callers nothing to call. Object.clone() is protected and makes a shallow copy. To use it you override clone, call super.clone(), catch a CloneNotSupportedException that can't happen, and then fix every mutable field by hand. Skip it. Use a copy constructor, a static copy factory, or a wither on a record. Records make withers easy to write and Kotlin data classes generate copy(). Neither copies deeply. The Kotlin docs say it plainly: copy() creates a shallow copy, and references to other objects are shared. Java record Cart(String id, List<String> skus) { Cart withId(String newId) { return new Cart(newId, skus); } // a wither: shares the list } var c1 = new Cart("c1", new ArrayList<>(List.of("sku-1"))); var c2 = c1.withId("c2"); c2.skus().add("sku-2"); // c1.skus() is now [sku-1, sku-2] Kotlin data class Cart(val id: String, val skus: MutableList<String>) val c1 = Cart("c1", mutableListOf("sku-1")) val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2") c2.skus += "sku-2" // c1.skus is now [sku-1, sku-2] The fix is the same in both languages. Store collections you can't change (List.copyOf in a compact constructor in Java; a read-only List in Kotlin), and let withers build a new collection: copy(skus = skus + "sku-2"). Kotlin has a second trap. data class Email private constructor(val value: String) still gets a public copy(), so Email.of("anna@example.com").copy(value = "not-an-email") compiles and skips your factory. Kotlin 2.4 only warns, and the warning says it becomes an error in language version 2.5. Add @ConsistentCopyVisibility to make copy() as private as the constructor in the current release. Validation in an init block is safer still, because copy() runs it. Java records never had the private-constructor illusion: a record's canonical constructor can't be less visible than the record, so the rules belong in the compact constructor from the start. Spring both copy traps Read CopyTrap.kt (or its Java twin) and predict the three lines it prints. Run it. If Gradle recompiles the file, read the w: warnings too. Add @ConsistentCopyVisibility on the line above data class Email and run again. CopyTrap.kt package workbench.patterns.l03 // Two traps in data class copy(): it is shallow, and it ignores a private constructor. data class Cart(val id: String, val skus: MutableList<String>) data class Email private constructor(val value: String) { companion object { fun of(raw: String): Email { require("@" in raw) { "not an email: $raw" } return Email(raw) } } } data class Amount(val minor: Long) { init { require(minor >= 0) { "negative amount: $minor" } } } fun main() { // trap 1: copy() copies the reference to the list, not the list val c1 = Cart("c1", mutableListOf("sku-1")) val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2") c2.skus += "sku-2" println("c1.skus after changing c2: ${c1.skus}") // trap 2: the private constructor does not cover the generated copy() val email = Email.of("anna@example.com") val broken = email.copy(value = "not-an-email") println("copy() skipped the factory: $broken") // init blocks DO run on copy() val result = runCatching { Amount(5).copy(minor = -1) } println("Amount(5).copy(minor = -1): ${result.exceptionOrNull()?.message}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l03.CopyTrapKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l03/CopyTrap.kt CopyTrapJava.java package workbench.patterns.l03; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** The Java twin of CopyTrap.kt: record copies are shallow, and a factory can't hide a record's constructor. */ public class CopyTrapJava { record Cart(String id, List<String> skus) { Cart withId(String newId) { return new Cart(newId, skus); } // a hand-written wither: shares the list } record Email(String value) { // a record's canonical constructor is never more private than the record itself, // so this factory can always be bypassed with new Email(...) static Email of(String raw) { if (!raw.contains("@")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("not an email: " + raw); return new Email(raw); } } record Amount(long minor) { Amount { // compact constructor: every path runs it if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount: " + minor); } Amount withMinor(long m) { return new Amount(m); } } public static void main(String[] args) { // trap 1: the wither copies the reference to the list, not the list Cart c1 = new Cart("c1", new ArrayList<>(List.of("sku-1"))); Cart c2 = c1.withId("c2"); c2.skus().add("sku-2"); System.out.println("c1.skus after changing c2: " + c1.skus()); // trap 2: the factory validates, the canonical constructor doesn't Email broken = new Email("not-an-email"); System.out.println("new skipped the factory: " + broken); // the compact constructor DOES run on withers try { new Amount(5).withMinor(-1); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("new Amount(5).withMinor(-1): " + e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l03.CopyTrapJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l03/CopyTrapJava.java It prints c1.skus after changing c2: [sku-1, sku-2] (the copy shared the list), copy() skipped the factory: Email(value=not-an-email), and negative amount: -1, because init runs on copy(). The compiler warns that the non-public primary constructor is exposed via copy(). With @ConsistentCopyVisibility, the build stops with Cannot access 'fun copy(value: String = ...): Email': it is private. The Java twin prints the same story: the wither shares the list, new Email("not-an-email") skips the factory, and the compact constructor rejects -1. A shallow copy shares the list, so changing one cart changes both. Build a new list in the copy instead. Data classes: copying (Kotlin docs) docs The most common mistake is trusting copy() or a record wither to make an independent object when a component is mutable. A MutableList, a HashMap, an array or a mutable Date is shared between the original and the copy, so changing one changes both. It happens because the class looks immutable: every property is val, or it's a record. The fix is to store copies that can't change (List.copyOf in a compact constructor, read-only types and toList() in Kotlin), and to make withers build new collections instead of mutating the shared one.

h: Builder and Prototype · Java and Kotlin
x: A prototype that copies safely TenantConfig.java record TenantConfig(String tenantId, List<String> paymentMethods, Map<String, Long> dailyLimits) { TenantConfig { // every copy passes through here paymentMethods = List.copyOf(paymentMethods); dailyLimits = Map.copyOf(dailyLimits); } TenantConfig forTenant(String id) { // safe to share: nothing can change return new TenantConfig(id, paymentMethods, dailyLimits); } TenantConfig withMethod(String method) { // copy, change the copy, wrap again var methods = new ArrayList<>(paymentMethods); methods.add(method); return new TenantConfig(tenantId, methods, dailyLimits); } } var base = new TenantConfig("default", List.of("CARD"), Map.of("CARD", 500_000L)); var acme = base.forTenant("acme").withMethod("SEPA"); TenantConfig.kt data class TenantConfig( val tenantId: String, val paymentMethods: List<String>, // read-only types val dailyLimits: Map<String, Long>, ) val base = TenantConfig("default", listOf("CARD"), mapOf("CARD" to 500_000L)) val acme = base.copy( tenantId = "acme", paymentMethods = base.paymentMethods + "SEPA", // + builds a new list ) Kotlin generates copy() with named arguments, so it needs no withers, and + on a read-only List or Map returns a new collection. Java needs one hand-written wither per field. Both copies are shallow, and the safety comes from the components, not from the copy. There is one real difference: Java's compact constructor can replace the incoming list with List.copyOf, while a Kotlin data class property can't be reassigned in init. A Kotlin List parameter is only read-only, so a caller who passes a MutableList and keeps a reference can still change it. If that matters, take the list as a plain constructor parameter and store toList() in a property.

h: Builder and Prototype · Worked example
x: From a telescoping constructor to a record and builder, and to a Kotlin class Here is a call to an issuer charge request with eight positional arguments. Before reading on, say which argument is the statement descriptor, and which rule you'd expect ChargeRequest to enforce. new ChargeRequest(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42", "ACME*ORDER 981", null, true, 2, 30_000); ChargeRequest(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42", "ACME*ORDER 981", null, true, 2, 30_000) Put every rule in one place that all paths go through: the record's compact constructor in Java, the init block in Kotlin. The cross-field rule (a descriptor only on captured charges, and 22 characters at most) can only be checked where all fields are known. Kotlin also gets its defaults here, which is half of what a builder does. record ChargeRequest(long amountMinor, String currency, String token, String descriptor, String threeDsData, boolean capture, int maxRetries, long timeoutMs) { ChargeRequest { if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive"); // 1. single-field rules if (maxRetries < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("maxRetries must be >= 0"); if (descriptor != null && (!capture || descriptor.length() > 22)) // 2. cross-field rule throw new IllegalArgumentException("descriptor needs capture=true and at most 22 chars"); } } data class ChargeRequest @JvmOverloads constructor( val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String, val token: String, val descriptor: String? = null, // 3. defaults live in the signature val threeDsData: String? = null, val capture: Boolean = true, val maxRetries: Int = 0, val timeoutMs: Long = 10_000, ) { init { require(amountMinor > 0) { "amount must be positive" } // 1. single-field rules require(maxRetries >= 0) { "maxRetries must be >= 0" } require(descriptor == null || (capture && descriptor.length <= 22)) { // 2. cross-field rule "descriptor needs capture=true and at most 22 chars" } } } Java needs a builder that only collects and supplies defaults; its build() calls the canonical constructor, so the rules run there. Kotlin needs no builder: named arguments do the job, and @JvmOverloads gives Java callers some overloads. If Java teams call the Kotlin class often, add a builder for them too. static final class Builder { private final long amountMinor; private final String currency; private final String token; private String descriptor; private String threeDsData; private boolean capture = true; private int maxRetries = 0; private long timeoutMs = 10_000; // 3. defaults Builder(long amountMinor, String currency, String token) { this.amountMinor = amountMinor; this.currency = currency; this.token = token; // 4. required up front } Builder descriptor(String d) { descriptor = d; return this; } Builder maxRetries(int n) { maxRetries = n; return this; } Builder timeoutMs(long ms) { timeoutMs = ms; return this; } ChargeRequest build() { return new ChargeRequest(amountMinor, currency, token, descriptor, threeDsData, capture, maxRetries, timeoutMs); } } var req = new ChargeRequest.Builder(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42").descriptor("ACME*ORDER 981").maxRetries(2).build(); // 4. required values have no default, so the compiler insists on them val req = ChargeRequest(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42", descriptor = "ACME*ORDER 981", maxRetries = 2) val retryFaster = req.copy(timeoutMs = 2_000) // the "wither" is generated

h: Builder and Prototype · Lab
x: A validating payment DSL, and a prototype that stops leaking labs/patterns/src/main/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l03/PaymentRequestDsl.kt labs/patterns/src/main/java/workbench/patterns/l03/ChargeTemplate.java ./gradlew :patterns:test --tests 'workbench.patterns.l03.*' Run the tests. Twelve of thirteen fail: the DSL is all TODO, and ChargeTemplate leaks tags and metadata between copies. In PaymentRequestDsl.kt, write LineItemsBuilder: keep a private MutableList, and return toList() from build(). Write PaymentRequestBuilder: lineItems runs the block on a fresh LineItemsBuilder and keeps its items; metadata puts into a private map; build() validates with require and copies the collections into the PaymentRequest. Then write paymentRequest. Put @PaymentDsl on both builder classes. Fix ChargeTemplate.java: add a compact constructor that stores List.copyOf and Map.copyOf, and make the withers copy the collection, change the copy, and build a new template. Run the tests until all thirteen pass. require(condition) { "idempotency key is required" } throws IllegalArgumentException with that message when the condition is false. currency.matches(Regex("[A-Z]{3}")) checks for three capital letters. LineItemsBuilder().apply(block).build(): apply runs the lambda with the builder as this and returns the builder. In a record's compact constructor, tags = List.copyOf(tags); reassigns the parameter before the field is set. You don't write this.tags = .... All thirteen tests in PaymentDslTest and ChargeTemplateTest pass. By the end you can choose between named arguments, a Java record plus builder, and a Kotlin DSL builder, and make copies of templates that never share mutable state with the original.
