h: Builder and Prototype · Quiz
x: data class Fee(val bps: Int) { init { require(bps in 0..1_000) } }. What does Fee(290).copy(bps = 5_000) do? Returns Fee(5000), because copy() skips init Throws IllegalArgumentException, because copy() runs init Doesn't compile Returns Fee(290) unchanged copy() calls the primary constructor with the new values, so every init block runs again and require throws. That's why init is the safest place for a data class's rules. What copy() does skip is a validating factory, when the constructor is private. A Java team will call your Kotlin ChargeRequest(amountMinor, currency, token, descriptor = null, capture = true, maxRetries = 0) constructor from many places. What helps them most? Nothing; Java 21 supports named arguments Mark the class data Put @JvmStatic on the constructor Add @JvmOverloads, or give them a builder Java has no named or default arguments, so it sees one six-parameter constructor. @JvmOverloads generates overloads that drop trailing defaults, and a builder lets them set any subset by name. @JvmStatic applies to companion members, not constructors, and data changes nothing for Java callers here. A DSL has no @DslMarker. Inside lineItems { }, someone writes currency = "USD". LineItemsBuilder has no currency, but the outer PaymentRequestBuilder does. What happens? It sets the outer builder's currency Compile error: unresolved reference A runtime exception It declares a local variable Both receivers are in scope inside the inner lambda, so the compiler resolves currency on the outer builder and sets it. Nothing fails. With @DslMarker on both builders, that line becomes a compile error unless you write this@paymentRequest.currency. record Cart(String id, List<String> skus) {}. c1 was built with new ArrayList<>(List.of("a")). Then Cart c2 = new Cart("c2", c1.skus()); c2.skus().add("b");. What happens? c1 is unchanged, because records are immutable The add throws UnsupportedOperationException c1.skus() now contains b too It doesn't compile Records are only shallowly immutable: the field can't point elsewhere, but the ArrayList it points to can change, and c2 shares it. A compact constructor with skus = List.copyOf(skus); would give each record its own unmodifiable list, and the add would then throw. From Factory Method and Abstract Factory: you hide a data class's constructor (data class Email private constructor(val value: String)) and offer a validating Email.of(raw). In Kotlin 2.4, which line still creates an unvalidated Email? Email("x") in another file Email.of("a@b.example").copy(value = "x") Email.of("x") None: a private constructor covers every path The generated copy() stays public even when the constructor is private; Kotlin 2.4 only warns about it. So copy creates an Email your factory never saw. @ConsistentCopyVisibility makes copy() private, and an init check would run on copy() too. A direct constructor call from outside does not compile.

h: Builder and Prototype · Explain it back
x: A colleague says: "Kotlin data classes are immutable, so copy() gives us safe, independent templates." Explain where that's wrong, and how you'd make templates safe in Kotlin and in Java.

h: Builder and Prototype · Key terms
x: Telescoping constructor A chain of constructors, each adding one more optional parameter. Builder A helper that collects values step by step and makes the finished object in build(). Lambda with receiver A lambda whose this is a given object, written T.() -> R. DslMarker A meta-annotation for DSL marker annotations that limits implicit calls to the nearest receiver. Prototype Making a new object by copying an existing one and changing a few fields. Wither A method like withTimeout(t) that returns a copy with one field changed. Shallow copy A copy that shares the objects its fields point to, instead of copying them too. Does a Kotlin data class's init block run on copy()? Yes. copy() calls the primary constructor, so require checks in init run again. What is a lambda with receiver? A function type like Builder.() -> Unit. Inside the lambda, this is the Builder, so you call its members without a prefix. What does @DslMarker prevent? Calling a member of an outer DSL receiver implicitly from inside an inner block. Reaching it then needs an explicit this@label. Why is Cloneable considered broken? It declares no clone method, and Object.clone() is protected, shallow and throws a checked exception. Use copy constructors or withers. Is a Kotlin data class copy() deep or shallow? Shallow. A property that holds a mutable object, such as a MutableList, is shared by the original and the copy. Where does validation go for a Java record that has a builder? In the record's compact constructor, so build(), withers and direct new calls all run it. data class Email private constructor(...): is its copy() private in Kotlin 2.4? No. It stays public, with a warning. Add @ConsistentCopyVisibility to make it private.

h: Builder and Prototype · Go deeper
x: Effective Java's hierarchical builder solves a problem you may meet in a shared Java library: a Pizza.Builder that subclasses (NyPizza.Builder, Calzone.Builder) extend without losing the subclass type in a chain. It uses a recursive type parameter, Builder<T extends Builder<T>>, and an abstract self() method that each subclass implements as return this;. Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance in the generics track showed why that recursive bound works. In Kotlin you almost never need it, because named arguments and copy() remove the chain. Java has no with syntax for records yet. Project Amber has proposed one, derived record creation (JEP 468), where you would write something like point with { x = 3; }. Check its status on the JEP page before you plan around it. Until then, write withers for the fields that really change. People sometimes deep-copy an object graph by serializing and deserializing it, or with a reflection library. It works, it is slow, and it copies things you didn't mean to copy, such as a shared Clock or a connection. If you need a deep copy, the cleaner fix is usually to make the components immutable so a shallow copy is enough. Kotlin's buildList { add(...) }, buildMap { } and buildString { } are small standard-library builders with receivers. Use them when you build a collection with loops or conditions; the result is read-only once the block returns.

h: Adapter and Facade · Adapter: make their API fit your port
x: An adapter converts the interface of a class you can't change into the interface your code expects. In payments you write them all the time: the issuer gives you a SOAP SDK, a PSP gives you an HTTP client with its own types, and one acquirer still sends fixed-width files. Your payment logic should see none of that. It should see your own port, in your own words: Java interface PaymentGateway { String charge(long amountMinor, String currency, String token); } Kotlin fun interface PaymentGateway { fun charge(amountMinor: Long, currency: String, token: String): String } The adapter implements the port and holds the vendor object. All translation happens inside it, in both directions: your types into the vendor's on the way in, the vendor's results and errors into yours on the way out. Java record SoapGatewayAdapter(LegacySoapClient soap) implements PaymentGateway { public String charge(long amountMinor, String currency, String token) { String xml = "<txn amt='" + amountMinor + "' cur='" + currency + "' tok='" + token + "'/>"; try { String resp = soap.submitTxn(xml); return resp.substring(resp.indexOf("ref='") + 5, resp.lastIndexOf("'")); // vendor format ends here } catch (IOException e) { throw new GatewayUnavailable("issuer unreachable", e); // our exception, not theirs } } } Kotlin class SoapGatewayAdapter(private val soap: LegacySoapClient) : PaymentGateway { override fun charge(amountMinor: Long, currency: String, token: String): String { val xml = "<txn amt='$amountMinor' cur='$currency' tok='$token'/>" try { val resp = soap.submitTxn(xml) return resp.substringAfter("ref='").substringBefore("'") // vendor format ends here } catch (e: IOException) { throw GatewayUnavailable("issuer unreachable", e) // our exception, not theirs } } } The most common adapter bug is a leaky one. If IOException, the vendor's response codes or its DTOs show up in your service layer, every caller now depends on the vendor, and switching issuers means changing all of them. Java's checked exceptions help here, almost by accident. The port doesn't declare IOException, so javac won't let the vendor's exception escape the adapter. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the same leak compiles without a word. In Kotlin, the discipline is yours. When the port has one method, you don't need a class at all: a lambda or method reference is the adapter, in both languages. Let the vendor's exception leak Run SoapAdapterDemo in either language with the command below. Read the three lines. In the Java version, delete the try/catch in SoapGatewayAdapter.charge, keeping the two lines inside the try. Predict, then run. Do the same in the Kotlin version. Predict, then run. Restore both files. SoapAdapterDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l04; import java.io.IOException; import java.util.function.BiFunction; /** A legacy SOAP client adapted to our port, plus a lambda adapter for a one-method port. */ public class SoapAdapterDemo { // the port our payment code depends on interface PaymentGateway { String charge(long amountMinor, String currency, String token); } // a vendor client we can't change: XML in, XML out, checked IOException on failure static final class LegacySoapClient { String submitTxn(String xml) throws IOException { if (xml.contains("tok_down")) throw new IOException("SOAP fault: 503 Service Unavailable"); String token = xml.substring(xml.indexOf("tok='") + 5, xml.lastIndexOf("'")); return "<resp code='00' ref='R-" + token.toUpperCase() + "'/>"; } } static final class GatewayUnavailable extends RuntimeException { GatewayUnavailable(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); } } // the adapter: implements our port, holds the vendor client, translates both ways record SoapGatewayAdapter(LegacySoapClient soap) implements PaymentGateway { public String charge(long amountMinor, String currency, String token) { String xml = "<txn amt='" + amountMinor + "' cur='" + currency + "' tok='" + token + "'/>"; try { String resp = soap.submitTxn(xml); return resp.substring(resp.indexOf("ref='") + 5, resp.lastIndexOf("'")); // vendor format ends here } catch (IOException e) { throw new GatewayUnavailable("issuer unreachable", e); // our exception, not theirs } } } // for a one-method port, a lambda is the adapter static PaymentGateway fromFunction(BiFunction<Long, String, String> legacyCharge) { return (amount, currency, token) -> legacyCharge.apply(amount, token); } public static void main(String[] args) { PaymentGateway gateway = new SoapGatewayAdapter(new LegacySoapClient()); System.out.println("charged, ref " + gateway.charge(1_250, "EUR", "tok_42")); try { gateway.charge(1_250, "EUR", "tok_down"); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("caller sees " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } PaymentGateway quick = fromFunction((amount, token) -> "QUICK-" + amount); System.out.println("lambda adapter: " + quick.charge(990, "EUR", "tok_7")); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l04.SoapAdapterDemo amount, _, _ -> "QUICK-$amount" } println("lambda adapter: " + quick.charge(990, "EUR", "tok_7")) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l04.SoapAdapterDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l04/SoapAdapterDemo.kt Both versions print charged, ref R-TOK_42, caller sees GatewayUnavailable: issuer unreachable and lambda adapter: QUICK-990. Without the catch, Java refuses to compile: unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown. Kotlin compiles and prints caller sees IOException: SOAP fault: 503 Service Unavailable: the vendor's exception walked through your port. Functional (SAM) interfaces (Kotlin docs) docs An adapter is the travel plug you carry abroad: the hotel's socket stays the same, your charger stays the same, and the plug translates between them. A facade is the hotel's front desk: you ask for a taxi to the airport at six, and the desk deals with the taxi company, the wake-up call and the bill. You never call the taxi company yourself. The analogy breaks on errors: a travel plug either fits or it doesn't, but a software adapter must also translate the vendor's failures into yours, and a leaky one passes the foreign voltage straight through.

h: Adapter and Facade · Extension functions are Kotlin's light adapters
x: Kotlin has a lighter adapter for data: the extension function. The issuer SDK hands you a VendorTxn with fields called amt, ccyNum and respCd, and you want your own Receipt. Write the mapping once, as an extension on the vendor type: Java // Java has no extension functions: the same adapter is a static method static Receipt toReceipt(VendorTxn txn) { Currency currency = Currency.getAvailableCurrencies().stream() .filter(c -> c.getNumericCode() == Integer.parseInt(txn.ccyNum())) .findFirst().orElseThrow(); return new Receipt(txn.txnRef(), new BigDecimal(txn.amt()).movePointRight(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits()).longValueExact(), currency.getCurrencyCode(), txn.respCd().equals("00")); } List<Receipt> receipts = fromSdk.stream().map(Adapters::toReceipt).toList(); Kotlin fun VendorTxn.toReceipt(): Receipt { val currency = Currency.getAvailableCurrencies().first { it.numericCode == ccyNum.toInt() } return Receipt( reference = txnRef, amountMinor = BigDecimal(amt).movePointRight(currency.defaultFractionDigits).longValueExact(), currency = currency.currencyCode, approved = respCd == "00", ) } val receipts = fromSdk.map { it.toReceipt() } An extension function is not part of the class. It compiles to a static method that takes the receiver as its first parameter, which is exactly the Java twin. What changes is how the call reads, txn.toReceipt(), and where the IDE offers it: type txn. and it appears next to the vendor's own methods. Two rules keep these adapters honest. Keep them in your adapter package, next to the code that calls the SDK, and not in a shared utils file: they are part of the translation layer. And use them for data, not for behavior. An extension can't hold state, can't implement your port, and can't be replaced in a test. When you need something your service depends on, write a port and a class. The other light adapter in Kotlin is the fun interface. PaymentGateway { amount, _, _ -> legacy.pay(amount) } builds an adapter from a lambda, the same way a Java lambda implements a functional interface. Map vendor transactions to receipts Read ExtensionAdapters.kt (or its Java twin). Predict the three receipts, and look hard at the yen one. Run it with the command below. Add VendorTxn("T-1004", "0.05", "978", "05") to the list (new VendorTxn(...) in Java) and predict its amountMinor and approved before you run. ExtensionAdapters.kt package workbench.patterns.l04 import java.math.BigDecimal import java.util.Currency // A vendor DTO from the issuer SDK, with its names and units. class VendorTxn(val txnRef: String, val amt: String, val ccyNum: String, val respCd: String) // Our domain type. data class Receipt(val reference: String, val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String, val approved: Boolean) // An extension function is a lightweight adapter: it reads like a method on the vendor type, // lives in our code, and keeps the mapping in one place. fun VendorTxn.toReceipt(): Receipt { val currency = Currency.getAvailableCurrencies().first { it.numericCode == ccyNum.toInt() } return Receipt( reference = txnRef, amountMinor = BigDecimal(amt).movePointRight(currency.defaultFractionDigits).longValueExact(), currency = currency.currencyCode, approved = respCd == "00", ) } fun main() { val fromSdk = listOf( VendorTxn("T-1001", "12.50", "978", "00"), VendorTxn("T-1002", "1250", "392", "00"), VendorTxn("T-1003", "99.99", "840", "51"), ) fromSdk.map { it.toReceipt() }.forEach(::println) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l04.ExtensionAdaptersKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l04/ExtensionAdapters.kt ExtensionAdaptersJava.java package workbench.patterns.l04; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.Currency; import java.util.List; /** The Java twin of ExtensionAdapters.kt. Java has no extension functions, so the adapter is a static method. */ public class ExtensionAdaptersJava { // a vendor DTO from the issuer SDK, with its names and units record VendorTxn(String txnRef, String amt, String ccyNum, String respCd) {} // our domain type record Receipt(String reference, long amountMinor, String currency, boolean approved) {} // callers write toReceipt(txn), not txn.toReceipt(); the mapping still lives in one place static Receipt toReceipt(VendorTxn txn) { Currency currency = Currency.getAvailableCurrencies().stream() .filter(c -> c.getNumericCode() == Integer.parseInt(txn.ccyNum())) .findFirst().orElseThrow(); return new Receipt( txn.txnRef(), new BigDecimal(txn.amt()).movePointRight(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits()).longValueExact(), currency.getCurrencyCode(), txn.respCd().equals("00")); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<VendorTxn> fromSdk = List.of( new VendorTxn("T-1001", "12.50", "978", "00"), new VendorTxn("T-1002", "1250", "392", "00"), new VendorTxn("T-1003", "99.99", "840", "51")); fromSdk.stream().map(ExtensionAdaptersJava::toReceipt).forEach(System.out::println); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l04.ExtensionAdaptersJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l04/ExtensionAdaptersJava.java 1250 EUR approved, 1250 JPY approved (the yen has no minor unit, so "1250" stays 1250), and 9999 USD not approved. The new one is 5 EUR, not approved. The Kotlin call site reads it.toReceipt(); the Java one reads toReceipt(txn). Underneath, both are the same static method. Extensions (Kotlin docs) docs Your Quarkus services already have ports and adapters, even if nobody calls them that: a REST client interface for a PSP, a @ApplicationScoped bean that wraps the issuer SDK, a Kafka emitter behind a Notifier. Check where the vendor's vocabulary ends. A response code "05" in a Temporal activity, or a vendor exception caught in a REST resource, means the adapter is leaking. Temporal makes this concrete: activity retry policies decide on exception types, so translate vendor errors into your own retryable and non-retryable exceptions inside the adapter, where you know which is which. And a checkout facade is a natural Temporal workflow later, once the steps need durable retries.

h: Adapter and Facade · Facade: one call for a job with several steps
x: A facade gives callers one simple entry point to a subsystem. Checkout is the classic case: reserve stock, charge the card, post to the ledger, send a receipt. If every caller (the REST resource, the Kafka consumer for marketplace orders, the admin tool) makes those calls itself, each gets the order and the failure handling slightly different. Put the sequence in one class: Java record CheckoutFacade(Inventory inventory, Payments payments, Notifier notifier) { String checkout(String sku, long amountMinor, String token, String email) { if (!inventory.reserve(sku)) throw new IllegalStateException("out of stock: " + sku); // 1. reserve String receipt; try { receipt = payments.charge(amountMinor, token); // 2. charge } catch (RuntimeException e) { inventory.release(sku); // 3. undo the reservation throw e; } notifier.send(email, "paid " + receipt); // 4. tell the customer return receipt; } } Kotlin class CheckoutFacade( private val inventory: Inventory, private val payments: Payments, private val notifier: Notifier, ) { fun checkout(sku: String, amountMinor: Long, token: String, email: String): String { check(inventory.reserve(sku)) { "out of stock: $sku" } // 1. reserve val receipt = try { payments.charge(amountMinor, token) // 2. charge } catch (e: RuntimeException) { inventory.release(sku) // 3. undo the reservation throw e } notifier.send(email, "paid $receipt") // 4. tell the customer return receipt } } The facade owns two decisions: the order of the steps, and what a failure at each step means. Charging before reserving would take money for stock you don't have. A declined card must release the reservation. Those rules now live in one tested place, and each caller is one line. Nothing in either language replaces Facade; records and constructor injection only make it shorter. The risk is growth. A facade should orchestrate and nothing else: no amount maths, no vendor codes, no SQL. When it reaches forty methods, it has become the god service it was meant to hide, so split it by use case (CheckoutFacade, RefundFacade). One Java gotcha showed up while compiling this example. A record component can't be called notify: javac reports "illegal record component name", because the accessor notify() would clash with Object.notify(). The same goes for wait, hashCode, toString, getClass and the other no-argument Object methods. A Kotlin property named notify compiles to getNotify() and is fine. Break the facade's cleanup rule Run CheckoutFacadeDemo in either language and read the still reserved line. Remove the try/catch around the charge, so a decline no longer releases the stock. Predict the still reserved line, then run. Restore it. In the Java version only, rename the record component notifier to notify (and its use inside checkout). Compile. CheckoutFacadeDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l04; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.Set; /** A facade over inventory, payments and notifications: one call, the right order, cleanup on failure. */ public class CheckoutFacadeDemo { interface Inventory { boolean reserve(String sku); void release(String sku); } interface Payments { String charge(long amountMinor, String token); } interface Notifier { void send(String to, String message); } record CheckoutFacade(Inventory inventory, Payments payments, Notifier notifier) { String checkout(String sku, long amountMinor, String token, String email) { if (!inventory.reserve(sku)) throw new IllegalStateException("out of stock: " + sku); // 1. reserve String receipt; try { receipt = payments.charge(amountMinor, token); // 2. charge } catch (RuntimeException e) { inventory.release(sku); // 3. undo the reservation throw e; } notifier.send(email, "paid " + receipt); // 4. tell the customer return receipt; } } public static void main(String[] args) { Set<String> reserved = new HashSet<>(); Inventory inventory = new Inventory() { public boolean reserve(String sku) { return reserved.add(sku); } public void release(String sku) { reserved.remove(sku); } }; Payments payments = (amount, token) -> { if (token.equals("tok_declined")) throw new IllegalStateException("card declined"); return "R-" + amount; }; Notifier notifier = (to, message) -> System.out.println(" mail to " + to + ": " + message); CheckoutFacade facade = new CheckoutFacade(inventory, payments, notifier); System.out.println("receipt: " + facade.checkout("sku-1", 1_250, "tok_ok", "anna@example.com")); try { facade.checkout("sku-2", 990, "tok_declined", "anna@example.com"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("failed: " + e.getMessage() + "; still reserved: " + reserved); } } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l04.CheckoutFacadeDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l04/CheckoutFacadeDemo.java CheckoutFacadeDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l04 // A facade over inventory, payments and notifications: one call, the right order, cleanup on failure. interface Inventory { fun reserve(sku: String): Boolean; fun release(sku: String) } fun interface Payments { fun charge(amountMinor: Long, token: String): String } fun interface Notifier { fun send(to: String, message: String) } class CheckoutFacade( private val inventory: Inventory, private val payments: Payments, private val notifier: Notifier, ) { fun checkout(sku: String, amountMinor: Long, token: String, email: String): String { check(inventory.reserve(sku)) { "out of stock: $sku" } // 1. reserve val receipt = try { payments.charge(amountMinor, token) // 2. charge } catch (e: RuntimeException) { inventory.release(sku) // 3. undo the reservation throw e } notifier.send(email, "paid $receipt") // 4. tell the customer return receipt } } fun main() { val reserved = mutableSetOf<String>() val inventory = object : Inventory { override fun reserve(sku: String) = reserved.add(sku) override fun release(sku: String) { reserved.remove(sku) } } val payments = Payments { amount, token -> check(token != "tok_declined") { "card declined" } "R-$amount" } val notifier = Notifier { to, message -> println(" mail to $to: $message") } val facade = CheckoutFacade(inventory, payments, notifier) println("receipt: " + facade.checkout("sku-1", 1_250, "tok_ok", "anna@example.com")) try { facade.checkout("sku-2", 990, "tok_declined", "anna@example.com") } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("failed: ${e.message}; still reserved: $reserved") } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l04.CheckoutFacadeDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l04/CheckoutFacadeDemo.kt The first run mails a receipt for sku-1, then prints failed: card declined; still reserved: [sku-1]: the declined order gave sku-2 back. Without the catch, the line ends [sku-1, sku-2], so a declined card holds stock until someone notices. The rename gives error: illegal record component name notify. The Kotlin class can have a property called notify. JLS chapter 8.10: Record classes docs

h: Adapter and Facade · Ports and adapters: where the translation lives
x: Adapter and Facade both wrap something, and so do Decorator, Proxy and Bridge. Structure won't tell them apart. Intent will: Pattern Wraps Offers Why Adapter one object you can't change a different interface: yours make it fit your port Facade several objects a new, simpler interface hide a sequence of calls Decorator one object the same interface add behavior (Decorator and Proxy, lesson 5 of this track) Proxy one object the same interface control access (lesson 5 of this track) Bridge an implementation you pick your abstraction vary two dimensions (lesson 6 of this track) In a service built with ports and adapters (often called hexagonal architecture), you see Adapter and Facade on one picture. The payment logic sits in the middle and talks only to ports: CardAuthorizer, Ledger, Notifier. Adapters sit on the edge, one per technology: the issuer SDK adapter, an Oracle ledger, a Kafka notifier. The facade is the front door, where a REST resource or a Kafka consumer makes one call. That layout pays off twice. Switching issuers means writing one new adapter, and nothing in the middle changes. And the middle is tested with lambdas: new CheckoutFacade((pan, amount, currency) -> new Approved("A1"), ledger, notifier) needs no SDK, no database and no broker. Domain-driven design calls a thick layer of adapters an anti-corruption layer: the place where the vendor's model (response code "51", numeric currency "978", amounts as strings) is translated into yours, so it never spreads. If you find "51" in a service class, the layer has a hole. The lab is that layer in miniature: an adapter that keeps an issuer SDK's quirks to itself, and a facade that callers can use without knowing the steps. Check yourself. You switch issuers, and the new SDK throws TimeoutException where the old one threw IOException. In a service laid out this way, which files change? (Only the new issuer adapter, which catches the new exception and throws the same GatewayUnavailable. The facade, the payment logic and their tests don't change, because they never saw IOException either.) Callers make one call to the facade. Your code talks only to ports, and adapters on the edge translate to each vendor. The most common mistake is the leaky adapter: it wraps the vendor's method calls but lets the vendor's model through. The adapter rethrows SdkException (or wraps it in a RuntimeException that callers unwrap), returns the vendor's response code as a string, or exposes the vendor's DTOs in its method signatures. It happens because translating every code and error feels like busywork when there is only one vendor. Then the second issuer arrives, and every service that checks "51" has to change. Translate everything at the boundary into your own sealed results and exceptions, and test the adapter against a fake of the vendor class.

h: Adapter and Facade · Java and Kotlin
x: An anti-corruption adapter for a PSP webhook PspWebhookAdapter.java // the vendor's webhook body, with the vendor's names record PspWebhook(String type, String pspRef, String amtMinor, String ccy) {} // our model of what happened sealed interface PaymentEvent { record Captured(String paymentRef, long amountMinor, String currency) implements PaymentEvent {} record Refunded(String paymentRef, long amountMinor) implements PaymentEvent {} record Ignored(String why) implements PaymentEvent {} } final class PspWebhookAdapter { private PspWebhookAdapter() {} static PaymentEvent toEvent(PspWebhook w) { return switch (w.type()) { // vendor strings are an open set, so a default is right here case "charge.captured" -> new PaymentEvent.Captured(w.pspRef(), Long.parseLong(w.amtMinor()), w.ccy().toUpperCase()); case "charge.refunded" -> new PaymentEvent.Refunded(w.pspRef(), Long.parseLong(w.amtMinor())); default -> new PaymentEvent.Ignored("unhandled PSP event " + w.type()); }; } } PspWebhookAdapter.kt // the vendor's webhook body, with the vendor's names data class PspWebhook(val type: String, val pspRef: String, val amtMinor: String, val ccy: String) // our model of what happened sealed interface PaymentEvent { data class Captured(val paymentRef: String, val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String) : PaymentEvent data class Refunded(val paymentRef: String, val amountMinor: Long) : PaymentEvent data class Ignored(val why: String) : PaymentEvent } // the adapter as an extension: reads like a method on the vendor type fun PspWebhook.toEvent(): PaymentEvent = when (type) { // open set of vendor strings: else is right "charge.captured" -> PaymentEvent.Captured(pspRef, amtMinor.toLong(), ccy.uppercase()) "charge.refunded" -> PaymentEvent.Refunded(pspRef, amtMinor.toLong()) else -> PaymentEvent.Ignored("unhandled PSP event $type") } The translation is identical: vendor strings in, a sealed event of our own out. Kotlin writes it as an extension on the vendor type, so call sites read webhook.toEvent(); Java needs a static method on a holder class, so they read PspWebhookAdapter.toEvent(webhook). In bytecode they are the same static method. Both use a catch-all branch on purpose: vendor event types are an open set you don't control, unlike your own sealed types, where a missing case should break the build. Code that consumes PaymentEvent then switches over it with no default. Neither language makes Adapter unnecessary; Kotlin just makes the data-mapping kind cheaper to write.

h: Adapter and Facade · Worked example
x: Wrap a vendor FX feed behind a port, then test without it A pricing service calls a vendor FX feed directly. The feed returns strings like "EURUSD=1.0842;ts=1730000000" and throws a checked FeedException. Before reading on, list every vendor detail that leaks into priceInUsd. class Pricer { private final RateFeedClient feed = new RateFeedClient("https://fx.vendor.example"); long priceInUsd(long amountMinorEur) throws FeedException { String raw = feed.quote("EURUSD"); // vendor pair format BigDecimal rate = new BigDecimal(raw.substring(raw.indexOf('=') + 1, raw.indexOf(';'))); return new BigDecimal(amountMinorEur).multiply(rate).setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN).longValueExact(); } } class Pricer { private val feed = RateFeedClient("https://fx.vendor.example") fun priceInUsd(amountMinorEur: Long): Long { val raw = feed.quote("EURUSD") // vendor pair format; FeedException leaks unseen val rate = BigDecimal(raw.substringAfter('=').substringBefore(';')) return BigDecimal(amountMinorEur).multiply(rate).setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN).longValueExact() } } Four leaks: the pair format, the response format, the checked exception, and the hard-wired URL. Define the port in your words first. It says nothing about strings or vendors, and an empty result means "no rate right now". interface FxRates { Optional<BigDecimal> rate(String from, String to); // 1. our words: currencies in, a rate or nothing out } class Pricer { private final FxRates rates; Pricer(FxRates rates) { this.rates = rates; } OptionalLong priceInUsd(long amountMinorEur) { return rates.rate("EUR", "USD") .map(r -> new BigDecimal(amountMinorEur).multiply(r).setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN).longValueExact()) .map(OptionalLong::of).orElse(OptionalLong.empty()); } } fun interface FxRates { fun rate(from: String, to: String): BigDecimal? // 1. our words: currencies in, a rate or null out } class Pricer(private val rates: FxRates) { fun priceInUsd(amountMinorEur: Long): Long? = rates.rate("EUR", "USD")?.let { BigDecimal(amountMinorEur).multiply(it).setScale(0, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN).longValueExact() } } Now the adapter. Everything the vendor knows lives here: how pairs are spelled, how answers are packed, and which exception it throws. Why return empty instead of rethrowing on FeedException? Because the port promised "a rate or nothing", and the pricer decides what nothing means. final class VendorFxRates implements FxRates { private final RateFeedClient feed; VendorFxRates(RateFeedClient feed) { this.feed = feed; } public Optional<BigDecimal> rate(String from, String to) { try { String raw = feed.quote(from + to); // 2. our pair, their format return Optional.of(new BigDecimal(raw.substring(raw.indexOf('=') + 1, raw.indexOf(';')))); } catch (FeedException | RuntimeException e) { // 3. their failure, our answer return Optional.empty(); } } } class VendorFxRates(private val feed: RateFeedClient) : FxRates { override fun rate(from: String, to: String): BigDecimal? = try { val raw = feed.quote(from + to) // 2. our pair, their format BigDecimal(raw.substringAfter('=').substringBefore(';')) } catch (e: FeedException) { // 3. their failure, our answer null } catch (e: RuntimeException) { null } } Test the two halves separately. The pricer gets a lambda. The adapter gets a fake feed, a subclass of the vendor client that returns canned strings, which is how the lab tests its issuer adapter. // 4. the core, with no vendor at all assertThat(new Pricer((from, to) -> Optional.of(new BigDecimal("1.0842"))).priceInUsd(10_000)).hasValue(10_842); // 5. the adapter, against a fake of the vendor class RateFeedClient fake = new RateFeedClient("unused") { @Override public String quote(String pair) { return "EURUSD=1.0842;ts=1730000000"; } }; assertThat(new VendorFxRates(fake).rate("EUR", "USD")).contains(new BigDecimal("1.0842")); // 4. the core, with no vendor at all assertThat(Pricer { _, _ -> BigDecimal("1.0842") }.priceInUsd(10_000)).isEqualTo(10_842L) // 5. the adapter, against a fake of the vendor class (open in the SDK, or use an interface) val fake = object : RateFeedClient("unused") { override fun quote(pair: String) = "EURUSD=1.0842;ts=1730000000" } assertThat(VendorFxRates(fake).rate("EUR", "USD")).isEqualTo(BigDecimal("1.0842"))

h: Adapter and Facade · Lab
x: An issuer SDK adapter and a checkout facade labs/patterns/src/main/java/workbench/patterns/l04/IssuerSdkAdapter.java labs/patterns/src/main/java/workbench/patterns/l04/CheckoutFacade.java ./gradlew :patterns:test --tests 'workbench.patterns.l04.*' Read LegacyIssuerSdk.java, CardAuthorizer.java and Amounts.java. They are given; don't edit them. Run the tests: all ten fail. Write IssuerSdkAdapter.authorize. Call sdk.auth with Amounts.toDecimal and Amounts.numericCode, catch SdkException and return Unavailable(e.getMessage()), then split the response on | and map the code with a switch. Write CheckoutFacade.checkout as a switch over the AuthResult. Approved: post, send the receipt (catching a failing notifier), return Paid. Declined: send the notice, return Declined. Unavailable: return RetryLater. Run the tests until all ten pass. raw.split("\\|", -1) splits on a literal | and keeps the empty auth id in "51|". The pipe must be escaped, because split takes a regex. A switch over the sealed AuthResult with case AuthResult.Approved ok -> ... needs no default: the compiler checks all three cases. In a switch expression, use yield to return from a block. Wrap only the notifier call in try/catch. If the ledger post throws, let it propagate: an approved payment that isn't on the ledger is an incident, not something to swallow. All ten tests in AdapterFacadeTest pass. By the end you can wrap a vendor SDK in an adapter that keeps its types, codes and exceptions to itself, use Kotlin extension functions for light data adapters, and put a multi-step checkout behind a facade that owns the order and the failure rules.

h: Adapter and Facade · Quiz
x: Your issuer adapter catches SdkException and rethrows it wrapped in a RuntimeException. The checkout service catches that and checks getCause() instanceof SdkException to decide whether to retry. What's wrong? Nothing, since the exception is unchecked now The vendor type still leaks: the service depends on the SDK, so switching issuers breaks it A RuntimeException can't wrap a checked exception Retry decisions belong inside the vendor SDK Wrapping changed the exception's type, not who depends on it. The service still imports SdkException, so it's coupled to this vendor. Translate inside the adapter into your own result (Unavailable) or your own exception type that says retryable or not. A RuntimeException can wrap anything, so that option is simply false. Which statement about an adapter written in Kotlin is true? A vendor IOException thrown inside it can pass through your port without any compile error The compiler forces you to catch the vendor's checked exceptions Extension functions can implement your port interface fun interface ports can't be implemented with a lambda Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so nothing stops the vendor's IOException from reaching callers of your port. Java would refuse to compile the same adapter. Extensions can't implement interfaces, and a fun interface exists precisely so a lambda can implement it. Three call sites (a REST resource, a Kafka consumer and an admin tool) each reserve stock, charge the card, post to the ledger and send an email, each with slightly different failure handling. Which pattern fits? Adapter Decorator Facade Singleton A facade puts the sequence and its failure rules in one place, and each caller makes one call. An adapter changes one object's interface, a decorator adds behavior behind the same interface, and a singleton is about instance count, not about orchestrating steps. Which is the best use of a Kotlin extension function as an adapter? fun LegacyIssuerSdk.authorize(...), which callers use instead of a CardAuthorizer port A global fun Any.toJson() in a shared utils file An extension that caches vendor results in a top-level map fun VendorTxn.toReceipt(): Receipt, kept in the issuer-adapter package Mapping a vendor DTO to your own type is pure data translation, which is what extensions are good at, and keeping it in the adapter package keeps the vendor model contained. An extension on the SDK makes callers depend on the SDK and can't be swapped in a test. A global utils extension spreads everywhere, and caching in a top-level map is hidden shared state. From Factory Method and Abstract Factory: you now have one IssuerSdkAdapter for Visa's SDK and one for Mastercard's. Where should the choice between them live? In each REST resource, with an if on the card's BIN In one factory, a switch or when over the network with no default, injected into the facade Inside the facade's checkout, as string checks on the PAN In the adapters: each checks whether the card belongs to it Choosing which product to build is a factory's job: one exhaustive switch or when over a sealed or enum network, so adding a network is a compile error in one place. Spreading BIN checks over resources or the facade copies the rule, and adapters checking ownership turns every call into a guessing game.

h: Adapter and Facade · Key terms
x: Adapter A wrapper that makes an existing object fit the interface your code expects. Port An interface in your own words that your core code depends on, such as CardAuthorizer. Anti-corruption layer The adapters where a vendor's model is translated into yours, so it never spreads into your code. Facade One simple entry point that runs a multi-step job across several subsystems. Extension function A Kotlin function called like a method on a type it doesn't belong to; a static method underneath. Hexagonal architecture Core logic talks only to ports, and adapters on the edge connect each port to one technology. What does an adapter do? Makes an object you can't change fit the interface (port) your code expects, translating arguments, results and errors. What is a leaky adapter? One that lets the vendor's types, codes or exceptions (an SdkException, response code "51") reach your service code. A Kotlin adapter calls a method that throws IOException and has no catch. Does it compile? Yes. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the vendor's IOException passes through your port silently. Java would refuse. What does a Kotlin extension function compile to? A static method whose first parameter is the receiver. txn.toReceipt() is toReceipt(txn) in bytecode. What does a facade own? The order of the steps in a multi-step job, and what a failure at each step means. Not maths, vendor codes or SQL. Can a Java record component be named notify? No: "illegal record component name". Its accessor would clash with Object.notify(). The same goes for wait, hashCode, toString and the other no-arg Object methods. Adapter vs Facade, one line each? Adapter: one object, given a different interface (yours). Facade: several objects behind one new, simpler interface.

h: Adapter and Facade · Go deeper
x: The JDK has adapters you use daily. InputStreamReader adapts a byte stream into a character stream; its Javadoc calls it a bridge from byte streams to character streams, which shows how loosely the pattern names get used. Arrays.asList adapts an array into a fixed-size List that writes through to the array. Collections.enumeration and Enumeration.asIterator() (Java 9) adapt between the old and new iteration interfaces. The GoF book describes two kinds of adapter. An object adapter holds the vendor object and delegates to it, as in this lesson. A class adapter inherits from the vendor class and implements your interface at the same time. Java and Kotlin allow the second only when the vendor class is open, and it is usually worse: your adapter inherits every public method of the SDK, so callers can bypass your translation. Prefer the object adapter. Kotlin's by delegation (in Decorator and Proxy, lesson 5 of this track) can build an adapter that forwards most of an interface unchanged and overrides the few methods that need translation. That works when the two interfaces are almost the same, such as two versions of your own API. For a vendor SDK with a different model, write the translation out; it is the part that deserves a review. Facades and transactions mix badly in one way. If a Spring or Quarkus facade method is @Transactional and calls an external issuer inside the transaction, a 120 ms issuer call holds a database connection for 120 ms. With a pool of 20 connections, a slow issuer starves the database. Charge first, outside the transaction, then post to the ledger in a short one, and make the post idempotent so a retry can't double-post.

h: Decorator and Proxy · Decorator: same interface, one more behavior
x: A decorator wraps the same interface: the call goes in layer by layer, and the order of the layers changes the fee new DataOutputStream(new BufferedOutputStream(new GZIPOutputStream(out))) is three decorators around one stream. Each wrapper is an OutputStream too. Each adds one behavior (typed writes, buffering, compression) and passes the bytes on to the stream it wraps. The JDK's FilterInputStream Javadoc describes it plainly: it "wraps some other input stream, which it uses as its basic source of data, possibly transforming the data along the way". That is the whole pattern. A decorator implements the same interface as the object it wraps, does one extra thing, and forwards the call. Callers can't tell how many layers there are. Fees fit it well, because a fee is a base rule plus adjustments. In Java, a functional interface with default methods turns each adjustment into a one-line decorator. Each method returns a new lambda that calls the calculator it wraps: Java @FunctionalInterface interface FeeCalculator { long feeMinor(Payment p); static FeeCalculator percent(int bps) { return p -> p.amountMinor() * bps / 10_000; } default FeeCalculator plusFixed(long fixed) { return p -> feeMinor(p) + fixed; } default FeeCalculator crossBorder(String home, int extraBps) { return p -> feeMinor(p) + (p.country().equals(home) ? 0 : p.amountMinor() * extraBps / 10_000); } default FeeCalculator cappedAt(long cap) { return p -> Math.min(feeMinor(p), cap); } } FeeCalculator standard = FeeCalculator.percent(290).plusFixed(30).crossBorder("DE", 100).cappedAt(500); Kotlin fun interface FeeCalculator { fun feeMinor(p: Payment): Long } fun percent(bps: Int) = FeeCalculator { p -> p.amountMinor * bps / 10_000 } fun FeeCalculator.plusFixed(fixed: Long) = FeeCalculator { p -> feeMinor(p) + fixed } fun FeeCalculator.crossBorder(home: String, extraBps: Int) = FeeCalculator { p -> feeMinor(p) + if (p.country == home) 0 else p.amountMinor * extraBps / 10_000 } fun FeeCalculator.cappedAt(cap: Long) = FeeCalculator { p -> minOf(feeMinor(p), cap) } val standard = percent(290).plusFixed(30).crossBorder("DE", 100).cappedAt(500) In Kotlin the decorators are extension functions on a fun interface. Either way, every call returns a new calculator and leaves the one it wraps alone. Order matters. With standard, a domestic 100.00 EUR payment costs 3.20, a French one costs 4.20, and a French 1,000.00 EUR payment hits the cap at 5.00. Move cappedAt(500) before crossBorder and that last payment costs 15.00, because the surcharge now lands after the cap. Both chains compile. Only a test with a large cross-border payment tells them apart. Behavior decorators have the same issue. A retry decorator outside a logging decorator logs every attempt. Swap them and you log one call, however many attempts it took. Pick the order you want and pin it in a test. Stack two decorators in both orders Open DecoratorStack.java (or DecoratorStack.kt). The issuer fails twice, then approves. Logging records each call it sees; Retrying tries up to three times. Before you run it, write down how many log lines each of the two stacks produces. Run it with the command below. Then decide: if Logging fed your request-rate metric, which order would you want? DecoratorStack.java package workbench.patterns.l05; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Two decorators around a flaky issuer. Same pieces, two orders, two different behaviors. */ public class DecoratorStack { interface IssuerCall { String authorize(long amountMinor); } // the real client: fails twice, then succeeds static final class FlakyIssuer implements IssuerCall { private int calls; public String authorize(long amountMinor) { if (++calls <= 2) throw new IllegalStateException("issuer timeout #" + calls); return "A-" + amountMinor; } } // decorator 1: logs every call that passes through it record Logging(IssuerCall inner, List<String> log) implements IssuerCall { public String authorize(long amountMinor) { log.add("authorize " + amountMinor); return inner.authorize(amountMinor); } } // decorator 2: tries up to `attempts` times record Retrying(IssuerCall inner, int attempts) implements IssuerCall { public String authorize(long amountMinor) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return inner.authorize(amountMinor); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; } } throw last; } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> log = new ArrayList<>(); IssuerCall retryOutside = new Retrying(new Logging(new FlakyIssuer(), log), 3); System.out.println("Retrying(Logging(issuer)): " + retryOutside.authorize(1_250) + ", log lines: " + log.size()); log.clear(); IssuerCall logOutside = new Logging(new Retrying(new FlakyIssuer(), 3), log); System.out.println("Logging(Retrying(issuer)): " + logOutside.authorize(1_250) + ", log lines: " + log.size()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l05.DecoratorStack labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l05/DecoratorStack.java DecoratorStack.kt package workbench.patterns.l05 // Two decorators around a flaky issuer. Same pieces, two orders, two different behaviors. fun interface IssuerCall { fun authorize(amountMinor: Long): String } // the real client: fails twice, then succeeds class FlakyIssuer : IssuerCall { private var calls = 0 override fun authorize(amountMinor: Long): String { check(++calls > 2) { "issuer timeout #$calls" } return "A-$amountMinor" } } // decorator 1: logs every call that passes through it class Logging(private val inner: IssuerCall, private val log: MutableList<String>) : IssuerCall { override fun authorize(amountMinor: Long): String { log += "authorize $amountMinor" return inner.authorize(amountMinor) } } // decorator 2: tries up to `attempts` times class Retrying(private val inner: IssuerCall, private val attempts: Int) : IssuerCall { override fun authorize(amountMinor: Long): String { var last: RuntimeException? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return inner.authorize(amountMinor) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { last = e } } throw last!! } } fun main() { val log = mutableListOf<String>() val retryOutside = Retrying(Logging(FlakyIssuer(), log), 3) println("Retrying(Logging(issuer)): ${retryOutside.authorize(1_250)}, log lines: ${log.size}") log.clear() val logOutside = Logging(Retrying(FlakyIssuer(), 3), log) println("Logging(Retrying(issuer)): ${logOutside.authorize(1_250)}, log lines: ${log.size}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l05.DecoratorStackKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l05/DecoratorStack.kt Retrying(Logging(issuer)): A-1250, log lines: 3 and Logging(Retrying(issuer)): A-1250, log lines: 1. The outer decorator sees one logical call; the inner one sees every attempt. For a request-rate metric you want logging outside (one per request). For an issuer error-rate metric you want it inside, where the two failures are visible. FilterInputStream (Java SE 25 API) docs A decorator is a set of sleeves on a parcel: bubble wrap, then a box, then a shipping label. Each layer adds one thing, and the courier still handles it as one parcel. A proxy is the front desk of an office building: every visitor from outside signs in, gets checked and is sent up. The analogy holds for self-invocation, too: when someone already inside walks to the next office, they never pass the front desk. It breaks on judgment. A receptionist notices that the same visitor came in three times today; a proxy sees only one method name and its arguments, so it retries a charge as happily as a read unless you tell it which is which.

h: Decorator and Proxy · Kotlin's by writes the forwarding for you
x: A hand-written decorator for Map in Java must forward every method (get, put, remove, size, entrySet and many more) just to change one. Kotlin's class delegation writes the forwarding for you: Java // Java has no `by`. The short way is inheritance, and HashMap's internals decide what you count. class CountingMap<K, V> extends HashMap<K, V> { int puts; @Override public V put(K key, V value) { puts++; return super.put(key, value); } } Kotlin class CountingMap<K, V>(private val inner: MutableMap<K, V> = HashMap()) : MutableMap<K, V> by inner { var puts = 0 override fun put(key: K, value: V): V? { puts++; return inner.put(key, value) } } : MutableMap<K, V> by inner tells the compiler to generate every method of the interface as a call on inner, except the ones you override. The Kotlin docs call delegation "a good alternative to implementation inheritance". Now predict. After put("a", 1) and putAll(mapOf("b" to 2, "c" to 3)), what is puts? It is 1, and size is 3. The compiler forwards putAll to inner.putAll, and inner is a plain HashMap that has never heard of your override. The docs say so: overridden members "do not get called from the members of the delegate object". To count every insertion, override putAll too, and putIfAbsent, compute and merge. That surprise is also the benefit. With inheritance, the answer depends on how the parent class is written today. HashMap.putAll happens not to call put, so the Java count is also 1. HashSet.addAll does call add, so a set that counts in both methods counts each element twice. Effective Java item 18 is built on that bug. With by, the delegate never calls back into your code, so a JDK update can't change your count. The JDK has a read-only decorator you use often: Collections.unmodifiableList. It forwards reads and throws UnsupportedOperationException on writes. It is a view. Its Javadoc says queries "read through" to the list it wraps, so later changes to that list show up in the view. For a snapshot, use List.copyOf. Kotlin's List type is weaker still: a read-only interface on the same object, with no wrapper at all. Java List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(backing); backing.add("capture"); // view now shows it too view.add("refund"); // UnsupportedOperationException Kotlin val view: List<String> = backing // same object, read-only type backing += "capture" // view now shows it too (view as MutableList).add("refund") // works: nothing guards it Count what the delegate does behind your back Read CountingMapDemo.kt. Predict puts after one put and a putAll of two entries, and added after addAll of three elements. Run it with the command below. Now run the Java twin, CountingMapDemoJava, which uses extends HashMap and extends HashSet with the same overrides. Predict first: will the Java numbers match? CountingMapDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l05 // Decorators built with `by`: the compiler writes every forwarding method for you. class CountingMap<K, V>(private val inner: MutableMap<K, V> = HashMap()) : MutableMap<K, V> by inner { var puts = 0 private set override fun put(key: K, value: V): V? { puts++ return inner.put(key, value) } } class CountingSet<E>(private val inner: MutableSet<E> = HashSet()) : MutableSet<E> by inner { var added = 0 private set override fun add(element: E): Boolean { added++ return inner.add(element) } override fun addAll(elements: Collection<E>): Boolean { added += elements.size return inner.addAll(elements) // inner's addAll calls inner's add, never ours } } fun main() { val m = CountingMap<String, Int>() m["a"] = 1 // goes through our put m.putAll(mapOf("b" to 2, "c" to 3)) // forwarded to inner.putAll, which never calls our put println("CountingMap: puts=${m.puts}, size=${m.size}") val s = CountingSet<String>() s.addAll(listOf("x", "y", "z")) println("CountingSet: added=${s.added}, size=${s.size}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l05.CountingMapDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l05/CountingMapDemo.kt CountingMapDemoJava.java package workbench.patterns.l05; import java.util.Collection; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * The Java twin of CountingMapDemo.kt. Java has no `by`, so the short way is inheritance, * and then the result depends on how the parent class happens to be written. */ public class CountingMapDemoJava { static final class CountingMap<K, V> extends HashMap<K, V> { int puts; @Override public V put(K key, V value) { puts++; return super.put(key, value); } } // Effective Java item 18: HashSet.addAll calls add for each element, so this counts twice static final class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> { int added; @Override public boolean add(E e) { added++; return super.add(e); } @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { added += c.size(); return super.addAll(c); } } public static void main(String[] args) { CountingMap<String, Integer> m = new CountingMap<>(); m.put("a", 1); m.putAll(Map.of("b", 2, "c", 3)); // HashMap.putAll doesn't call put, today System.out.println("CountingMap: puts=" + m.puts + ", size=" + m.size()); CountingSet<String> s = new CountingSet<>(); s.addAll(List.of("x", "y", "z")); System.out.println("CountingSet: added=" + s.added + ", size=" + s.size()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l05.CountingMapDemoJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l05/CountingMapDemoJava.java Kotlin prints puts=1, size=3 and added=3, size=3: the delegate never calls your overrides, so you count exactly what you wrote. Java prints puts=1, size=3 but added=6, size=3, because HashSet.addAll calls add for each element and the override counts them a second time. With inheritance, your count depends on the parent's internals. Delegation (Kotlin docs) docs Collections.unmodifiableList (Java SE 25 API) docs Your Quarkus services run on proxies already: @Transactional, and the MicroProfile Fault Tolerance annotations such as @Retry and @Timeout, work through interceptors that ArC wires around your beans. Because ArC intercepts self-invocation, a Quarkus @Transactional method called from the same bean does run in a transaction, so a Spring habit of moving it to another bean is harmless there but a Quarkus habit of calling it directly breaks when the code moves to Spring. Temporal's Java SDK hands you activity stubs that are proxies of your activity interface: the call you write becomes a scheduled activity task. And a metrics or tracing wrapper around a Kafka producer, or around the card-issuer client that takes 120 ms, is a decorator: put it inside the retry if you want to see every attempt.

h: Decorator and Proxy · Dynamic proxies: one handler for every method
x: A decorator is written for one interface. A dynamic proxy is written once and works for any interface. java.lang.reflect.Proxy creates a class at runtime that implements the interfaces you name, and sends every call to one InvocationHandler: Java @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") static <T> T retrying(Class<T> iface, T target, int maxAttempts) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { Throwable last = null; for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) { try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { last = e.getCause(); // unwrap: the target's own exception } } throw last; }; return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler); } Kotlin inline fun <reified T : Any> retrying(target: T, maxAttempts: Int): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { _, method, args -> var last: Throwable? = null repeat(maxAttempts) { try { return@newProxyInstance method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { last = e.cause // unwrap: the target's own exception } } throw last!! } as T The handler gets the proxy, the Method being called and its arguments. It can run code before and after, and it decides whether to call the real object at all. A retry, a timer or an authorization check is written once and covers every method of every client. Two rules catch everyone the first time. First, method.invoke wraps whatever the target throws in an InvocationTargetException. Unwrap it with getCause() and rethrow that. If the wrapper escapes, the proxy sees a checked exception that charge never declared, and the caller gets an UndeclaredThrowableException wrapping an InvocationTargetException wrapping the real error. No catch (IllegalStateException e) in the caller will match it. Second, JDK proxies implement interfaces only. They can't extend a class. For classes, frameworks generate a subclass at runtime (Spring uses CGLIB), and a subclass can't override final methods. The Kotlin version is shorter for one reason: reified T lets the function read T::class.java itself, so callers write retrying(flaky, 3) and pass no Class object. Before you wrap a PSP client in this, know that it retries everything, charge included. If the first attempt timed out after the PSP took the money, the second attempt charges the card again. Retry only idempotent operations, or send an idempotency key the PSP deduplicates on. The worked example does exactly that. Break the retry proxy two ways Run RetryingProxyDemo (Java or Kotlin) and read the first two lines. In main, change retrying(PspClient.class, flaky, 3) to 2 attempts (retrying(flaky, 2) in Kotlin). Predict what the caller sees, then run. Keep 2 attempts. In the handler, replace last = e.getCause() with last = e (in Kotlin, last = e.cause becomes last = e). Predict the exception type, then run. Undo both changes. RetryingProxyDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l05; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** Dynamic proxies: a retrying proxy for any interface, and a tracing proxy that shows self-invocation. */ public class RetryingProxyDemo { interface PspClient { String charge(String token, long amountMinor); } interface Ledger { void post(String entry); void postTwice(String entry); } static <T> T retrying(Class<T> iface, T target, int maxAttempts) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { Throwable last = null; for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) { try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { // unwrap, or callers see a reflective wrapper last = e.getCause(); } } throw last; }; return iface.cast(Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler)); } static <T> T tracing(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> trace) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { trace.add(method.getName()); try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); } }; return iface.cast(Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, handler)); } public static void main(String[] args) { int[] calls = {0}; PspClient flaky = (token, amount) -> { if (++calls[0] < 3) throw new IllegalStateException("PSP 503"); return "ch_" + amount; }; PspClient psp = retrying(PspClient.class, flaky, 3); System.out.println("charge -> " + psp.charge("tok_42", 1_250) + " after " + calls[0] + " target calls"); System.out.println("proxy class: " + Proxy.isProxyClass(psp.getClass())); List<String> trace = new ArrayList<>(); Ledger real = new Ledger() { public void post(String entry) { } public void postTwice(String entry) { post(entry); post(entry); } // this.post(): skips the proxy }; tracing(Ledger.class, real, trace).postTwice("fee 3.20"); System.out.println("calls the proxy saw: " + trace); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l05.RetryingProxyDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l05/RetryingProxyDemo.java RetryingProxyDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l05 import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException import java.lang.reflect.Proxy // Dynamic proxies: a retrying proxy for any interface, and a tracing proxy that shows self-invocation. fun interface PspClient { fun charge(token: String, amountMinor: Long): String } interface Ledger { fun post(entry: String); post(entry) } // this.post(): skips the proxy } tracing<Ledger>(real, trace).postTwice("fee 3.20") println("calls the proxy saw: $trace") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l05.RetryingProxyDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l05/RetryingProxyDemo.kt The first run prints charge -> ch_1250 after 3 target calls and proxy class: true. h: Decorator and Proxy · Framework proxies and the self-invocation trap
x: Spring and Quarkus make your annotations work with proxies. When a bean has @Transactional, @Retryable or @Cacheable, the container doesn't hand out your object. It hands out a proxy that begins the transaction (or retries, or checks the cache) and then calls your object. Spring uses a JDK dynamic proxy when the bean implements an interface and a CGLIB subclass when it doesn't. Spring Boot may switch to class-based proxies by default, depending on its configuration. The proxy only sees calls that come through it. Look at this service: Java @Service class SettlementService { public void settleAll(List<String> batchIds) { for (String id : batchIds) settle(id); // really this.settle(id) } @Transactional public void settle(String batchId) { /* post to the ledger */ } } Kotlin @Service class SettlementService { fun settleAll(batchIds: List<String>) { for (id in batchIds) settle(id) // really this.settle(id) } @Transactional fun settle(batchId: String) { /* post to the ledger */ } } A REST resource calls settleAll on the proxy. settleAll has no annotation, so the proxy just forwards it. Inside, settle(id) is a plain call on the target object. The proxy never sees it, so no transaction starts. Spring's docs put it this way: "self invocation via an explicit or implicit this reference will bypass the advice." The same goes for private and final methods, which a proxy can't override. Spring's docs rank the fixes. Best: restructure so the call crosses a bean boundary (move settle to its own bean). Next: inject the bean into itself and call through that reference. Last: AopContext.currentProxy(), which they call "highly discouraged". Quarkus behaves differently. Its CDI container, ArC, supports "intercepted self-invocation", so the same code in a Quarkus service does start a transaction for each settle call. The Quarkus docs flag this as non-standard, because the CDI specification doesn't say whether self-interception should work. Code that moves between the two frameworks can change behavior without a single edited line. Kotlin adds one more trap. Classes and members are final unless marked open, and a CGLIB subclass can't override what is final. The kotlin-spring compiler plugin (a preset of all-open) opens classes that carry Spring annotations, so add it to every Kotlin Spring project. Quarkus transforms final classes for you, because quarkus.arc.transform-unproxyable-classes is true by default. Check yourself. In the Spring SettlementService, you move @Transactional from settle to settleAll and change nothing else. How many transactions does the REST call start now, and how many batches does each one cover? (One, covering all three batches. The outside call to settleAll goes through the proxy, so it starts a transaction. The inner settle calls still skip the proxy, so they run as plain method calls inside that one transaction.) Calls from outside go through the proxy. A call through this inside the bean goes straight to the target, so the transaction never starts. Spring Framework: proxying mechanisms (docs source) read All-open compiler plugin (Kotlin docs) docs The most common mistake is putting @Transactional (or @Retryable, or @Cacheable) on a Spring method that is only ever called from another method of the same bean. The code compiles, the tests with a mocked repository pass, and in production the inner call runs with no transaction, because this.settle() skips the proxy. People make it because the annotation sits right there on the method and looks like part of it, when it really lives in the proxy. The fix is to move the annotated method to its own bean, so the call crosses a proxy, or to put the annotation on the method the outside world calls. For Kotlin beans, also check that the kotlin-spring plugin is applied, or the proxy can't override the method at all.

h: Decorator and Proxy · Java and Kotlin
x: A timing decorator for a three-method port TimedGateway.java interface PaymentGateway { String authorize(String pan, long amountMinor); void capture(String authId); void refund(String authId, long amountMinor); } // one method changes; the other two are forwarded by hand final class TimedGateway implements PaymentGateway { private final PaymentGateway inner; private final Map<String, Long> nanos; TimedGateway(PaymentGateway inner, Map<String, Long> nanos) { this.inner = inner; this.nanos = nanos; } @Override public String authorize(String pan, long amountMinor) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return inner.authorize(pan, amountMinor); } finally { nanos.merge("authorize", System.nanoTime() - start, Long::sum); } } @Override public void capture(String authId) { inner.capture(authId); } @Override public void refund(String authId, long amountMinor) { inner.refund(authId, amountMinor); } } TimedGateway.kt interface PaymentGateway { fun authorize(pan: String, amountMinor: Long): String fun capture(authId: String) fun refund(authId: String, amountMinor: Long) } // `by inner` generates capture and refund; you write only what changes class TimedGateway( private val inner: PaymentGateway, private val nanos: MutableMap<String, Long>, ) : PaymentGateway by inner { override fun authorize(pan: String, amountMinor: Long): String { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return inner.authorize(pan, amountMinor) } finally { nanos.merge("authorize", System.nanoTime() - start) { a, b -> a + b } } } } The behavior is identical. What differs is who writes the forwarding: Java makes you type capture and refund, and Kotlin's by inner generates them. That has a second effect when the port grows. Add void voidAuth(String authId) to the interface and the Java decorator stops compiling until someone decides what it should do with the new method. The Kotlin one forwards it silently, untimed. Neither is wrong, but know which one you have. And remember that by has no open recursion: if the real gateway's capture calls its own authorize, that inner call is not timed. Kotlin makes the hand-written forwarding class unnecessary; it doesn't make Decorator unnecessary.

h: Decorator and Proxy · Worked example
x: Make a retry proxy safe for payments A teammate wrapped the PSP client in the generic retrying proxy from this lesson, with three attempts. The PSP sometimes answers a charge after 2 seconds, and the HTTP client gives up at 1.5 seconds. Before reading on, say what the customer sees on a slow day. interface PspClient { String charge(String token, long amountMinor); String status(String chargeId); } PspClient psp = retrying(PspClient.class, new HttpPspClient(), 3); psp.charge("tok_42", 1_250); // attempt 1 times out after the PSP has charged the card interface PspClient { fun charge(token: String, amountMinor: Long): String fun status(chargeId: String): String } val psp = retrying<PspClient>(HttpPspClient(), 3) psp.charge("tok_42", 1_250) // attempt 1 times out after the PSP has charged the card Attempt one timed out on our side, but the PSP finished it. Attempts two and three are new charges, so the customer pays two or three times. Retrying is only safe for idempotent operations. Make that visible in the interface: mark the methods that may be repeated. @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) // 1. keep the mark at runtime, so the handler can read it @Target(ElementType.METHOD) @interface Idempotent {} interface PspClient { String charge(String token, long amountMinor); // not marked: one attempt only @Idempotent String status(String chargeId); // a read: safe to repeat } @Target(AnnotationTarget.FUNCTION) @Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME) // 1. keep the mark at runtime, so the handler can read it annotation class Idempotent interface PspClient { fun charge(token: String, amountMinor: Long): String // not marked: one attempt only @Idempotent fun status(chargeId: String): String // a read: safe to repeat } The handler reads the mark before its loop. Unmarked methods get exactly one attempt. Why does method.isAnnotationPresent work here even though the annotation is on the interface, not on HttpPspClient? Because the Method the proxy receives is the interface's method. InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, args) -> { int attempts = method.isAnnotationPresent(Idempotent.class) ? maxAttempts : 1; // 2. ask the method Throwable last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return method.invoke(target, args); } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { last = e.getCause(); // 3. unwrap } } throw last; }; val handler = InvocationHandler { _, method, args -> val attempts = if (method.isAnnotationPresent(Idempotent::class.java)) maxAttempts else 1 // 2. ask the method var last: Throwable? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return@InvocationHandler method.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { last = e.cause // 3. unwrap } } throw last!! } Now make the charge itself safe to repeat. Most PSPs accept an idempotency key: a second request with the same key returns the first result instead of charging again. The key must come from the caller and stay the same on every attempt, so derive it from the order. A key generated inside the retry loop would be new on each attempt and protect nothing. interface PspClient { @Idempotent String charge(String idempotencyKey, String token, long amountMinor); // 4. the PSP deduplicates @Idempotent String status(String chargeId); } psp.charge("order-7781:charge", "tok_42", 1_250); // 5. same key on every attempt interface PspClient { @Idempotent fun charge(idempotencyKey: String, token: String, amountMinor: Long): String // 4. the PSP deduplicates @Idempotent fun status(chargeId: String): String } psp.charge("order-7781:charge", "tok_42", 1_250) // 5. same key on every attempt
