h: Decorator and Proxy · Key terms
x: Decorator A wrapper with the same interface as the object inside it, adding one behavior. Proxy A stand-in with the same interface that controls access to the real object: lazy, remote, transactional, retrying. Dynamic proxy A class generated at runtime by java.lang.reflect.Proxy that implements interfaces and routes every call to one handler. InvocationHandler The one method, invoke(proxy, method, args), that a dynamic proxy calls for every interface method. Class delegation (by) Kotlin syntax that generates forwarding methods for an interface to a delegate object. Self-invocation A bean calling its own method through this, which bypasses the framework's proxy. CGLIB proxy A runtime-generated subclass Spring uses to proxy a class without an interface; it can't override final methods. What makes a wrapper a decorator? It implements the same interface as the object it wraps, adds one behavior, and forwards the call. Callers can't tell it's there. Retry decorator outside a logging decorator, issuer fails twice then succeeds: how many log lines? Three. The inner decorator sees every attempt; the outer one sees one logical call. CountingMap : MutableMap by inner overrides put. After put once and putAll of two entries, what is puts? putAll is forwarded to inner, which never calls your override. What does Collections.unmodifiableList(list) give you? A read-through view: writes throw, but later changes to list show up. Use List.copyOf for a snapshot. In an InvocationHandler, why rethrow e.getCause() from InvocationTargetException? method.invoke wraps the target's exception. If the wrapper escapes, callers get UndeclaredThrowableException instead of the real error. Spring: @Transactional settle() called as this.settle() from the same bean. Transaction? No. Self-invocation goes to the target, not the proxy. (Quarkus ArC does intercept it.) Why does a Kotlin Spring project need the kotlin-spring plugin? Kotlin classes and members are final by default, and Spring's CGLIB subclass proxies can't override final members. The plugin opens Spring-annotated classes.

h: Decorator and Proxy · Go deeper
x: Resilience4j is a decorator library by design. Its README says it provides "higher-order functions (decorators)" for any functional interface, lambda or method reference, and that you can stack more than one. Supplier<String> guarded = CircuitBreaker.decorateSupplier(breaker, psp::charge) returns a new supplier that wraps the old one, and you can wrap that again with Retry.decorateSupplier. The order question from this lesson comes back: a retry outside the breaker retries rejected calls, and a retry inside it counts every attempt as a breaker call. The last lesson of this track builds a breaker by hand. Spring Framework 7.0 brought retry and concurrency limits into the core framework as annotations: @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit, switched on with @EnableResilientMethods. Both apply to "proxy-invoked methods", so self-invocation bypasses them exactly like @Transactional. @Retryable defaults to maxRetries = 3 after the first failure, which means four attempts in total, with a one-second delay. Spring 7 also added @Proxyable(INTERFACES) and @Proxyable(TARGET_CLASS) to choose the proxy type for a single bean. JDK proxy classes are final, extend java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and can be detected with Proxy.isProxyClass. Their names are unspecified, but names starting with $Proxy are reserved for them, which is why stack traces show $Proxy42.charge. A proxy also intercepts equals, hashCode and toString, so a proxy and its target are different objects to a HashSet unless the handler forwards those methods. Decorator and Proxy have the same structure. The difference is intent: a decorator adds behavior the caller asked for (compression, a surcharge), and a proxy controls access to the real object (a transaction, an authorization check, a lazily created connection). Collections.unmodifiableList sits on the line, which is a good sign that the names are for talking about designs, not for sorting classes into boxes.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Composite: a tree you price like a single rule
x: A merchant's fee plan is rarely one number. It's 0.30 plus 2.9%, plus a bundle of add-ons, and the bundle has rules of its own. Composite lets a group of rules and a single rule share one interface. A group answers by asking each of its children, so the code that prices a payment never checks whether it holds a leaf or a whole tree. The GoF version is an abstract Component class with add and remove methods that leaves must implement somehow. Java 21 and Kotlin replace it with a sealed type and one exhaustive switch: Java sealed interface Rule permits Flat, Percent, AllOf {} record Flat(long minor) implements Rule {} record Percent(int bps) implements Rule {} record AllOf(List<Rule> rules) implements Rule { AllOf { rules = List.copyOf(rules); } // immutable: copy what the caller passed } static long fee(Rule r, long amountMinor) { return switch (r) { // no default case Flat f -> f.minor(); case Percent p -> amountMinor * p.bps() / 10_000; case AllOf a -> a.rules().stream().mapToLong(x -> fee(x, amountMinor)).sum(); }; } Rule plan = new AllOf(List.of(new Flat(30), new Percent(290), new AllOf(List.of(new Flat(5))))); Kotlin sealed interface Rule { data class Flat(val minor: Long) : Rule data class Percent(val bps: Int) : Rule class AllOf(rules: List<Rule>) : Rule { val rules: List<Rule> = rules.toList() // immutable: copy what the caller passed } } fun fee(r: Rule, amountMinor: Long): Long = when (r) { // no else is Rule.Flat -> r.minor is Rule.Percent -> amountMinor * r.bps / 10_000 is Rule.AllOf -> r.rules.sumOf { fee(it, amountMinor) } } val plan = Rule.AllOf(listOf(Rule.Flat(30), Rule.Percent(290), Rule.AllOf(listOf(Rule.Flat(5))))) For a 100.00 payment, fee(plan, 10_000) is 30 + 290 + 5 = 325. The recursion follows the tree: AllOf adds up whatever its children return, and the children don't care who asked. The sealed type buys you two things. The switch has no default, so adding a Capped node makes javac report "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values" (kotlinc: "'when' expression must be exhaustive") at every place that prices or prints a plan. And a second operation over the same tree, such as describe, is just another function. The node classes don't change. Keep the tree immutable. List.copyOf in the compact constructor copies the caller's list, so a later edit to that list can't reach into a plan that is already in use. Kotlin's List is only a read-only view, so copy with toList(). An immutable tree can't grow a cycle, and threads can share it safely, which the last section relies on. Price a tree, then let the caller mutate it Open CompositeDemo.java (or CompositeDemo.kt). Before you run it, work out the two fees in your head. Run it with the command below and check your numbers. Note the last line. Remove the copy: in Java delete the compact constructor AllOf { rules = List.copyOf(rules); }; in Kotlin change = rules.toList() to = rules. Predict the last line, then run. CompositeDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l06; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** A fee plan as a tree. Leaves and groups share one sealed type, so one switch prices them all. */ public class CompositeDemo { sealed interface Rule permits Flat, Percent, AllOf {} record Flat(long minor) implements Rule {} record Percent(int bps) implements Rule {} record AllOf(List<Rule> rules) implements Rule { AllOf { rules = List.copyOf(rules); } // copy what we were given: the tree stays immutable } static long fee(Rule r, long amountMinor) { return switch (r) { // no default: a new node type breaks the build case Flat f -> f.minor(); case Percent p -> amountMinor * p.bps() / 10_000; case AllOf a -> a.rules().stream().mapToLong(x -> fee(x, amountMinor)).sum(); }; } static String describe(Rule r) { return switch (r) { case Flat f -> Long.toString(f.minor()); case Percent p -> String.format("%d.%02d%%", p.bps() / 100, p.bps() % 100); case AllOf a -> "(" + String.join(" + ", a.rules().stream().map(CompositeDemo::describe).toList()) + ")"; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Rule> bundle = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Flat(5))); Rule plan = new AllOf(List.of(new Flat(30), new Percent(290), new AllOf(bundle))); System.out.println("plan: " + describe(plan)); System.out.println("fee on 100.00: " + fee(plan, 10_000)); System.out.println("fee on 1,000.00: " + fee(plan, 100_000)); bundle.add(new Flat(1_000)); // someone edits the list they passed in System.out.println("after editing the source list: " + describe(plan)); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l06.CompositeDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l06/CompositeDemo.java CompositeDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l06 // A fee plan as a tree. Leaves and groups share one sealed type, so one `when` prices them all. sealed interface FeeRule { data class Flat(val minor: Long) : FeeRule data class Percent(val bps: Int) : FeeRule class AllOf(rules: List<FeeRule>) : FeeRule { val rules: List<FeeRule> = rules.toList() // copy what we were given: the tree stays immutable } } private fun fee(r: FeeRule, amountMinor: Long): Long = when (r) { // no else: a new node type breaks the build is FeeRule.Flat -> r.minor is FeeRule.Percent -> amountMinor * r.bps / 10_000 is FeeRule.AllOf -> r.rules.sumOf { fee(it, amountMinor) } } private fun describe(r: FeeRule): String = when (r) { is FeeRule.Flat -> r.minor.toString() is FeeRule.Percent -> "%d.%02d%%".format(r.bps / 100, r.bps % 100) is FeeRule.AllOf -> r.rules.joinToString(" + ", "(", ")") { describe(it) } } fun main() { val bundle = mutableListOf<FeeRule>(FeeRule.Flat(5)) val plan = FeeRule.AllOf(listOf(FeeRule.Flat(30), FeeRule.Percent(290), FeeRule.AllOf(bundle))) println("plan: ${describe(plan)}") println("fee on 100.00: ${fee(plan, 10_000)}") println("fee on 1,000.00: ${fee(plan, 100_000)}") bundle += FeeRule.Flat(1_000) // someone edits the list they passed in println("after editing the source list: ${describe(plan)}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l06.CompositeDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l06/CompositeDemo.kt plan: (30 + 2.90% + (5)), fees 325 and 2935 (30 + 2,900 + 5), and after editing the source list: (30 + 2.90% + (5)). Without the copy, the last line becomes (30 + 2.90% + (5 + 1000)): a plan already in use silently gained a 10.00 fee because someone edited the list they built it from. The root adds up what its children return. A nested group answers the same question, so one recursive function prices any plan. Sealed classes and interfaces (Kotlin docs) docs Think of a print shop. A job is either one sheet or a folder of jobs, and you price both by asking the same question: what does this cost? That's Composite. The paper stock is a flyweight: a hundred jobs say "A4, 90 g" and all point at one stock description, while each job brings its own page count, the extrinsic part. The job and the machine are a bridge: any job can go to the laser printer or the plotter. The analogy breaks on sharing. Two jobs can't print on the same physical sheet, but two payments can use the same fee plan object at the same instant, because nothing in it ever changes.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Bridge: two dimensions without N times M classes
x: Payment ops wants alerts: payment failed, fraud suspected, settlement late. Each must go out by SMS, email or Slack. Model that with inheritance (PaymentFailedSms, PaymentFailedEmail and so on) and you write nine classes. A fourth channel costs three more, each a near copy of its neighbors. Bridge splits the two dimensions. One side is the abstraction: what happened, the alert. The other is the implementor: how it travels, the channel. The alert holds a channel and calls it: Java interface Channel { void deliver(String to, String body); } // implementor: how it travels sealed interface Alert permits PaymentFailed, FraudSuspected { // abstraction: what happened void raise(String to); } record PaymentFailed(Channel channel, String paymentId) implements Alert { public void raise(String to) { channel.deliver(to, "payment " + paymentId + " failed"); } } record FraudSuspected(Channel channel, String last4, int score) implements Alert { public void raise(String to) { channel.deliver(to, "card ****" + last4 + " flagged, risk " + score); } } new PaymentFailed(sms, "pay_881").raise("on-call"); new PaymentFailed(email, "pay_881").raise("on-call"); // same alert, other channel: no new class Kotlin fun interface Channel { fun deliver(to: String, body: String) } // implementor: how it travels sealed interface Alert { fun raise(to: String) } // abstraction: what happened data class PaymentFailed(val channel: Channel, val paymentId: String) : Alert { override fun raise(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "payment $paymentId failed") } data class FraudSuspected(val channel: Channel, val last4: String, val score: Int) : Alert { override fun raise(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "card ****$last4 flagged, risk $score") } PaymentFailed(sms, "pay_881").raise("on-call") PaymentFailed(email, "pay_881").raise("on-call") // same alert, other channel: no new class Three alert types and three channels are now six small pieces, and a new channel is one more. Every alert works with it, because alerts only know Channel. Tests pass a recording lambda as the channel and check the text, with no SMS vendor in sight. In Kotlin the implementor side often shrinks to a function. With fun interface Channel, the lambda Channel { to, body -> slack.post(to, body) } is a whole channel. A plain function type, (String, String) -> Unit, works as well. Bridge is easy to confuse with Adapter, because both put an interface between two pieces of code. The difference is when and why. You design a bridge up front, because you know two things will vary on their own. You write an adapter afterwards, because a class you can't change has the wrong interface. They often meet: each channel is usually an adapter around a vendor SDK, like the issuer adapter in Adapter and Facade. Skip the bridge when only one dimension varies. If every alert goes by email, an alert with a Mailer field is plain composition, and calling it a pattern adds nothing. Add a channel without touching an alert Run BridgeDemo in either language and count the lines: 2 alert types times 2 channels. Add a Slack channel. Java: record Slack() implements Channel { public String deliver(String to, String body) { return "SLACK #" + to + ": " + body; } }, then add new Slack() to the list. Kotlin: private val slack = AlertChannel { to, body -> "SLACK #$to: $body" }, then add slack to the list. Predict how many lines print and how many alert types you had to edit. Run it. BridgeDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l06; import java.util.List; /** Alerts (what happened) and channels (how it travels) vary on their own: 2 + 2 classes, not 2 x 2. */ public class BridgeDemo { // the implementor side: how a message travels interface Channel { String deliver(String to, String body); } record Sms() implements Channel { public String deliver(String to, String body) { return "SMS to " + to + ": " + body; } } record Email() implements Channel { public String deliver(String to, String body) { return "EMAIL to " + to + ": " + body; } } // the abstraction side: what happened. Each alert HOLDS a channel instead of being one. sealed interface Alert permits PaymentFailed, FraudSuspected { Channel channel(); String raise(String to); } record PaymentFailed(Channel channel, String paymentId, String reason) implements Alert { public String raise(String to) { return channel.deliver(to, "payment " + paymentId + " failed: " + reason); } } record FraudSuspected(Channel channel, String last4, int score) implements Alert { public String raise(String to) { return channel.deliver(to, "card ****" + last4 + " flagged, risk " + score); } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Channel> channels = List.of(new Sms(), new Email()); for (Channel ch : channels) { System.out.println(new PaymentFailed(ch, "pay_881", "issuer declined (51)").raise("on-call")); System.out.println(new FraudSuspected(ch, "4242", 91).raise("risk-team")); } } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l06.BridgeDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l06/BridgeDemo.java BridgeDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l06 // Alerts (what happened) and channels (how it travels) vary on their own: 2 + 2 pieces, not 2 x 2. // the implementor side: one method, so a lambda is enough fun interface AlertChannel { fun deliver(to: String, body: String): String } private val sms = AlertChannel { to, body -> "SMS to $to: $body" } private val email = AlertChannel { to, body -> "EMAIL to $to: $body" } // the abstraction side: what happened. Each alert HOLDS a channel instead of being one. sealed interface PaymentAlert { val channel: AlertChannel fun raise(to: String): String data class PaymentFailed(override val channel: AlertChannel, val paymentId: String, val reason: String) : PaymentAlert { override fun raise(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "payment $paymentId failed: $reason") } data class FraudSuspected(override val channel: AlertChannel, val last4: String, val score: Int) : PaymentAlert { override fun raise(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "card ****$last4 flagged, risk $score") } } fun main() { val channels = listOf(sms, email) for (ch in channels) { println(PaymentAlert.PaymentFailed(ch, "pay_881", "issuer declined (51)").raise("on-call")) println(PaymentAlert.FraudSuspected(ch, "4242", 91).raise("risk-team")) } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l06.BridgeDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l06/BridgeDemo.kt Four lines before; six after, the last two starting SLACK #on-call and SLACK #risk-team. You edited zero alert types. In Kotlin the new channel was one lambda; in Java it was one small record. Functional (SAM) interfaces (Kotlin docs) docs Merchant onboarding probably stores fee plans as JSON or as rows in Oracle. Parse each plan into an immutable sealed tree once, cache it by plan id, and the pricing path in your Quarkus authorization service becomes a pure function, fee(plan, amount), that you test with no database. Your notification service is a bridge whether or not anyone named it: alert types from Kafka topics on one side, channel adapters around the SMS and email vendors on the other. And a Kafka consumer that deserializes a million payment events an hour builds a million "EUR" strings; mapping them to Currency.getInstance and enums at the edge leaves one object per value. In Java code, compare those amounts with equals or as primitive long, never == on Long.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Flyweight: share immutable objects instead of building new ones
x: Run Integer a = 127, b = 127; and a == b is true. Make both 128 and it's false. Integer.valueOf, which autoboxing calls, "will always cache values in the range -128 to 127, inclusive", so small values come from a shared pool and larger ones are new objects. That cache is a flyweight: many users share one immutable instance instead of each holding a copy. The JDK has more of them. The JVM interns string literals, keeping one String per literal, and s.intern() returns the pooled copy of any string. Currency "is designed so that there's never more than one Currency instance for any given currency", which is why it has no public constructor and you call Currency.getInstance("EUR"). Enums are flyweights by definition, and so are Kotlin's object and data object. The cache also explains one of the oldest bugs in Java payment code: Java Long settled = ledger.get("EUR"); // 25_000L, boxed when it went into the map Long expected = report.get("EUR"); // 25_000L, boxed separately if (settled == expected) { ... } // false: two different Long objects if (settled.equals(expected)) { ... } // true Kotlin val settled: Long? = ledger["EUR"] // 25_000L val expected: Long? = report["EUR"] // 25_000L if (settled == expected) { /* ... */ } // true: == calls equals() if (settled === expected) { /* ... */ } // false, and the compiler warns Java's == on objects compares references. With test amounts under 128 the cache makes it pass; with real amounts it fails. Kotlin's == calls equals, so you only meet this bug with ===, and on Long? kotlinc warns that "identity equality for arguments of types 'Long?' and 'Long?' is prohibited". You build your own flyweight with a canonicalizing factory: a private constructor and an of method that returns the pooled instance from a ConcurrentHashMap. Use computeIfAbsent. It checks and inserts in one atomic step, so eight threads asking for a new code at the same moment still get one instance. A get followed by a put on a miss is check-then-act, and under load it builds duplicates. Two more rules keep flyweights safe. They must be immutable, because every holder sees every change. And the pool must be bounded: interning merchant names from webhook payloads grows a map that never shrinks. Pool a known set, such as the merchant category codes in a reference table. Find out which objects are shared Read FlyweightDemo.java (or FlyweightDemo.kt) and predict all five lines before you run it. Run it with the command below. Break the pool: make Mcc.of return new Mcc(code) (Kotlin: make MccCode.of return MccCode(code)). Predict the last line, then run. FlyweightDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l06; import java.util.Currency; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Four flyweights: three from the JDK, one of our own. `==` asks "the same object?" */ public class FlyweightDemo { // our own: one shared instance per merchant category code static final class Mcc { private static final Map<String, Mcc> POOL = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private static final AtomicInteger BUILT = new AtomicInteger(); final String code; private Mcc(String code) { this.code = code; BUILT.incrementAndGet(); } static Mcc of(String code) { return POOL.computeIfAbsent(code, Mcc::new); } static int built() { return BUILT.get(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Integer a = 127, b = 127; Integer c = 128, d = 128; System.out.println("Integer 127 == 127: " + (a == b)); System.out.println("Integer 128 == 128: " + (c == d) + " equals: " + c.equals(d)); String parsed = new String("5411"); // a fresh object, like a field parsed from a message System.out.println("parsed == \"5411\": " + (parsed == "5411") + " after intern(): " + (parsed.intern() == "5411")); System.out.println("Currency EUR == EUR: " + (Currency.getInstance("EUR") == Currency.getInstance("EUR"))); Mcc first = Mcc.of("5411"), second = Mcc.of("5411"); System.out.println("Mcc 5411 == 5411: " + (first == second) + " instances built: " + Mcc.built()); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l06.FlyweightDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l06/FlyweightDemo.java FlyweightDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l06 import java.util.Currency import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger // Four flyweights: three from the JDK, one of our own. In Kotlin, `==` is equals(); `===` asks "the same object?" // our own: one shared instance per merchant category code class MccCode private constructor(val code: String) { init { built.incrementAndGet() } companion object { private val pool = ConcurrentHashMap<String, MccCode>() private val built = AtomicInteger() fun of(code: String): MccCode = pool.computeIfAbsent(code) { MccCode(it) } val instancesBuilt: Int get() = built.get() } } fun main() { // typed as Any so Kotlin boxes them, as Java does for Integer; === on Int? gets a compiler warning val a: Any = 127 val b: Any = 127 val c: Any = 128 val d: Any = 128 println("Integer 127 === 127: ${a === b}") println("Integer 128 === 128: ${c === d} ==: ${c == d}") val parsed = String(charArrayOf('5', '4', '1', '1')) // a fresh object, like a field parsed from a message println("parsed === \"5411\": ${parsed === "5411"} after intern(): ${parsed.intern() === "5411"}") println("Currency EUR === EUR: ${Currency.getInstance("EUR") === Currency.getInstance("EUR")}") val first = MccCode.of("5411") val second = MccCode.of("5411") println("Mcc 5411 === 5411: ${first === second} instances built: ${MccCode.instancesBuilt}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l06.FlyweightDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l06/FlyweightDemo.kt 127 is shared (true), 128 is not (false, though equals is true), a parsed "5411" is a different object until you call intern(), Currency hands out one EUR, and the pool gives one Mcc with instances built: 1. Without the pool the last line reads false instances built: 2. Integer.valueOf(int) (Java SE 25 API) docs Currency (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Share the tree, pass in the amount
x: Composite and Flyweight work well together. A platform with 40,000 merchants rarely has 40,000 fee plans. It has a dozen: standard, high-risk, marketplace and a few negotiated ones. Build each plan tree once at startup and let every merchant point at one of them, instead of parsing a plan per merchant per payment. The GoF book names the split that makes this work. Intrinsic state lives inside the shared object and is the same for every user: the rates and caps in the plan. Extrinsic state belongs to one use, so the caller passes it in: the payment amount. That's why fee takes the amount as an argument. A plan that kept "the current amount" in a field could not be shared, by two merchants or by two threads. Sharing across threads costs nothing here, because the trees never change. Records have final fields, List.copyOf returns an unmodifiable list, and an object that never changes can be read by 200 request threads at once with no lock, once it has been published safely (in a static final field, or set before the threads start). Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal in the concurrency track showed why that holds. The same thinking fits the small values on every payment: currencies, merchant categories, card networks, response codes. If the set is closed and known when you compile, an enum (Java) or enum class (Kotlin) is the flyweight, with no pool to write. Reach for a pooled factory only when the set is open but bounded, such as category codes loaded from a table. In the lab you build both halves: a five-node pricing composite with two operations, and a merchant-category flyweight that stays correct when eight threads ask for the same code at once. Check yourself. Merchants want to see "fees charged this month", and a teammate adds a var monthTotal to the shared root of the standard plan. What goes wrong, and where should the total live? (Every merchant on the standard plan points at that one root, so they all add to one total, and two request threads adding at once can lose an update. The total is extrinsic state: keep it per merchant, outside the tree.) The most common mistake is comparing boxed numbers with == in Java: if (entity.getAmountMinor() == expected) where both are Long. It passes every unit test, because test amounts like 100 or 50 sit inside the -128 to 127 cache and come back as the same shared object. In production a 250.00 payment is 25,000 minor units, the two Longs are different objects, and the check is false. People make it because == works on long, and nothing in the code shows the boxing. Use equals or Objects.equals(a, b), or better, keep amounts as primitive long in your domain types. In Kotlin, == already calls equals; only === has the bug, and the compiler warns on it.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Java and Kotlin
x: A flyweight that callers can't bypass CardBin.java // Not a record: a record's canonical constructor can't be private, // so `new CardBin(...)` would always bypass the pool. public final class CardBin { private static final Map<String, CardBin> POOL = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final String bin; // first six digits of the card number private final String issuer; private CardBin(String bin, String issuer) { this.bin = bin; this.issuer = issuer; } public static CardBin of(String bin, Function<String, String> issuerLookup) { return POOL.computeIfAbsent(bin, b -> new CardBin(b, issuerLookup.apply(b))); // built once per BIN } public String bin() { return bin; } public String issuer() { return issuer; } } CardBin.kt // A plain class: a private constructor holds, and there is no generated copy() to go around it. class CardBin private constructor(val bin: String, val issuer: String) { companion object { private val pool = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CardBin>() fun of(bin: String, issuerLookup: (String) -> String): CardBin = pool.computeIfAbsent(bin) { CardBin(it, issuerLookup(it)) } // built once per BIN } } Both use computeIfAbsent, so the lookup runs at most once per BIN even under contention. The real difference is what each language lets you hide. A Java record would be the natural value type, but javac rejects a private canonical constructor ("attempting to assign stronger access privileges; was public"), so anyone could call new and skip the pool: use a final class. In Kotlin, a data class with a private constructor still exposes a public copy() in 2.4.21 unless you add @ConsistentCopyVisibility, as Builder and Prototype showed, so a plain class is the safe choice there too. Kotlin also makes the flyweight's identity matter less: == calls equals, so the pool is about memory and one place to validate, not about making comparisons work. For a closed set, skip the pool and use an enum in either language.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Worked example
x: Turn an alert class explosion into a bridge The notification module grew by inheritance. Count the classes, then count what a WhatsApp channel would cost. abstract class Alert { abstract void send(); } class PaymentFailedSms extends Alert { void send() { sms.send(phone, "payment " + id + " failed"); } } class PaymentFailedEmail extends Alert { void send() { mail.send(address, "Payment alert", "payment " + id + " failed"); } } class FraudSuspectedSms extends Alert { void send() { /* the SMS code again */ } } class FraudSuspectedEmail extends Alert { void send() { /* the email code again */ } } // WhatsApp: PaymentFailedWhatsApp, FraudSuspectedWhatsApp, and one more per future alert abstract class Alert { abstract fun send() } class PaymentFailedSms : Alert() { override fun send() = sms.send(phone, "payment $id failed") } class PaymentFailedEmail : Alert() { override fun send() = mail.send(address, "Payment alert", "payment $id failed") } class FraudSuspectedSms : Alert() { override fun send() { /* the SMS code again */ } } class FraudSuspectedEmail : Alert() { override fun send() { /* the email code again */ } } // WhatsApp: PaymentFailedWhatsApp, FraudSuspectedWhatsApp, and one more per future alert Four classes for two alerts and two channels, and WhatsApp adds two more. Name the two dimensions: what happened decides the text, the channel decides the transport. Pull the transport out behind one interface, the implementor. interface Channel { void deliver(String to, String body); } // 1. the implementor side record SmsChannel(SmsVendor sms) implements Channel { // 2. one class per transport, public void deliver(String to, String body) { sms.send(to, body); } // usually an adapter } record EmailChannel(MailVendor mail) implements Channel { public void deliver(String to, String body) { mail.send(to, "Payment alert", body); } } fun interface Channel { fun deliver(to: String, body: String) } // 1. the implementor side class SmsChannel(private val sms: SmsVendor) : Channel { // 2. one class per transport, override fun deliver(to: String, body: String) = sms.send(to, body) // usually an adapter } class EmailChannel(private val mail: MailVendor) : Channel { override fun deliver(to: String, body: String) = mail.send(to, "Payment alert", body) } Each alert now holds a channel and builds only its text. Ask yourself: which alert type would change if the SMS vendor changed its API? None. Only SmsChannel would. sealed interface Alert permits PaymentFailed, FraudSuspected { void raise(String to); } // 3. the abstraction side record PaymentFailed(Channel channel, String paymentId) implements Alert { public void raise(String to) { channel.deliver(to, "payment " + paymentId + " failed"); } } record FraudSuspected(Channel channel, String last4, int score) implements Alert { public void raise(String to) { channel.deliver(to, "card ****" + last4 + " flagged, risk " + score); } } sealed interface Alert { fun raise(to: String) } // 3. the abstraction side data class PaymentFailed(val channel: Channel, val paymentId: String) : Alert { override fun raise(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "payment $paymentId failed") } data class FraudSuspected(val channel: Channel, val last4: String, val score: Int) : Alert { override fun raise(to: String) = channel.deliver(to, "card ****$last4 flagged, risk $score") } Test each side alone. A recording lambda is a complete channel, so alert tests need no vendor at all. WhatsApp is now one class, and no alert changes. List<String> sent = new ArrayList<>(); Channel recording = (to, body) -> sent.add(to + ": " + body); // 4. a fake channel in one line new PaymentFailed(recording, "pay_881").raise("on-call"); assertThat(sent).containsExactly("on-call: payment pay_881 failed"); val sent = mutableListOf<String>() val recording = Channel { to, body -> sent += "$to: $body" } // 4. a fake channel in one line PaymentFailed(recording, "pay_881").raise("on-call") assertThat(sent).containsExactly("on-call: payment pay_881 failed")

Run the tests: all eight fail. Write fee as one when (this) with five branches and no else. In MerchantCategory, add a private pool to the companion object and write of: reject unknown codes first, then return the pooled instance. Run the tests until all eight pass. Then add data class Discount(val bps: Int) : PricingRule to the sealed interface, read the two compiler errors, and delete it again. rules.sumOf { it.fee(amountMinor) } returns a Long when the lambda does, and an empty list sums to 0. rules.minOf { ... } works the same way for CheapestOf. joinToString(" + ", "(", ")") { it.describe() } takes a separator, a prefix and a postfix, and gives () for an empty list. "%d.%02d%%".format(bps / 100, bps % 100) turns 5 into 0.05%. requireNotNull(KNOWN[code]) { "unknown MCC: $code" } throws IllegalArgumentException. By the end you can model a fee plan as an immutable sealed tree priced by one exhaustive switch, split two independent dimensions with a bridge, and share immutable values through a thread-safe flyweight factory without falling for boxed ==.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Quiz
x: In Java, two totals are read from two maps: Long settled = ledger.get("EUR"); Long expected = report.get("EUR");. Each holds 25,000, boxed separately. What does settled == expected return on a standard JVM? true, because the values are equal false, because they are two different Long objects It doesn't compile It throws NullPointerException == on objects compares references. Long.valueOf shares instances only for -128 to 127, so two separately boxed 25,000s are different objects. With a test value of 100 the cache makes it pass, which is how this bug reaches production. Use equals, or primitive long. What fee does AllOf(Flat(30), CheapestOf(Percent(290), Flat(250))) charge on 10,000 minor units? 570 320 280 250 Percent(290) on 10,000 is 290 and Flat(250) is 250, so CheapestOf returns 250. AllOf adds the flat 30: 280. The tempting 320 prices the percentage and forgets that CheapestOf picks the minimum. You're designing payment notifications: four alert types today, three channels (SMS, email, Slack), and both lists will grow. Which structure fits? Alerts that hold a Channel interface, with one class or lambda per channel Twelve classes, one per alert and channel pair An adapter per alert type A singleton per channel that every alert extends Two dimensions that vary on their own are the case for Bridge: 4 + 3 pieces, and a new channel works with every alert. Twelve classes become fifteen with the next alert. An adapter fixes one mismatched interface, and extending a singleton puts the channel back into the class hierarchy. To save memory, a service puts every merchant name it receives in webhook payloads into a static ConcurrentHashMap pool and reuses the pooled string. What goes wrong over time? Two threads can get different instances for the same name Nothing: ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe The pool grows with every new name and never shrinks: a slow memory leak Pooled strings can't be compared with equals any more A flyweight pool must be bounded. Merchant names from outside are an open set, so the map keeps every name ever seen for the life of the JVM. Pool a known set (currencies, category codes from a reference table) or use a cache with eviction. Thread safety isn't the issue here; computeIfAbsent handles that. From Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal: a fee plan tree is built once at startup from records whose lists go through List.copyOf, kept in a static final field, and read by 200 request threads. What do the reads need? A synchronized block around each fee call The read side of a ReadWriteLock volatile on every record field Nothing: the tree is immutable and safely published Record fields are final, List.copyOf returns an unmodifiable list, and a static final field is published safely by class initialization. Nothing ever writes after that, so there is nothing to race on, and locks would only add contention.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Key terms
x: Composite A tree where groups and single items share one interface, so you handle both the same way. Leaf A node in a composite with no children, such as Flat(30). Bridge Splitting two independent dimensions so one side holds the other through an interface. Implementor In a bridge, the side that does the low-level work, such as a Channel that delivers messages. Flyweight A small immutable object shared by many users instead of copied for each. Intrinsic and extrinsic state Intrinsic state lives in the shared flyweight; extrinsic state comes from the caller with each use. Canonicalizing factory A factory that returns the one pooled instance for a key, such as Currency.getInstance("EUR"). What does Composite let you do? Treat a single item and a group of items through one interface. A group answers by asking its children, so callers never check which one they hold. Why leave default out of the switch that walks a sealed composite? So adding a node type is a compile error at every operation that handles the tree, instead of a silent fallback. What problem does Bridge solve? Two dimensions that vary on their own (alert type and channel) without N x M classes: the abstraction holds an implementor and calls it. Bridge or Adapter: which one is designed up front? Bridge. An adapter is retrofitted, to make a class you can't change fit your interface. Java: Integer a = 128, b = 128; What is a == b? false with default settings. Integer.valueOf caches only -128 to 127; 128 gives two different objects. Why must a flyweight be immutable? Every holder shares the same instance, so a change made by one would show up for all of them, on every thread. Why does a flyweight factory use computeIfAbsent instead of get then put? computeIfAbsent checks and inserts in one atomic step, so concurrent callers get one instance. get then put is check-then-act and can build duplicates.

h: Composite, Bridge and Flyweight · Go deeper
x: The GoF book spends pages on Composite's "transparency versus safety" choice: should add and remove live on the shared Component type, so leaves must throw, or only on groups, so callers must cast? A sealed type with immutable records ends the debate. There are no child-management methods at all: you build a new tree. Pattern matching gives each operation exact access to each node type, with no casts. Recursion over a tree is fine for fee plans a few levels deep. A tree built from outside input (a rules engine fed by a merchant portal, say) could be thousands of levels deep and throw StackOverflowError. Validate the depth when you build the tree, or walk it with an explicit stack. Composite also pairs with Visitor; lesson 10 of this track, Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento, shows why sealed types and pattern matching usually replace it. The Integer cache bounds are part of the contract: valueOf "will always cache values in the range -128 to 127, inclusive, and may cache other values outside of this range". The upper bound can be raised with the java.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high system property. That can make a boxed == bug disappear on one JVM and show up on another, which is one more reason never to rely on it. String interning has a GC cousin. G1's -XX:+UseStringDeduplication lets the collector make duplicate String objects share one backing array, with no code change. It saves memory for services that hold many equal strings (currency codes, country codes, status names) but doesn't make == work, because the String objects themselves stay distinct.

h: Strategy and Template Method · A strategy is a function you pass in
x: quotes.sort(Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::feeMinor)) is the Strategy pattern in one line. sort owns the algorithm for putting things in order. The comparator is the one decision it leaves to you, passed in as an object. GoF Strategy is exactly that: a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, picked by the client. In 1994 that meant an interface and a class per algorithm. Since Java 8, a lambda or a method reference is the class: Java record Quote(String psp, long feeMinor, long p95Millis) {} Comparator<Quote> cheapest = Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::feeMinor); Comparator<Quote> cheapestThenFastest = cheapest.thenComparingLong(Quote::p95Millis); quotes.sort(cheapestThenFastest); // sort is the context; the comparator is the strategy Kotlin data class Quote(val psp: String, val feeMinor: Long, val p95Millis: Long) val cheapest = compareBy<Quote> { it.feeMinor } val cheapestThenFastest = cheapest.thenBy { it.p95Millis } val ordered = quotes.sortedWith(cheapestThenFastest) // sortedWith is the context; the comparator is the strategy Comparator.comparing "accepts a function that extracts a Comparable sort key" and returns a comparator, and thenComparing chains a second one behind it. Nobody writes a class called FeeThenLatencyComparator any more. Kotlin's compareBy and thenBy do the same with function types, and any (Payment) -> Long already is a fee strategy, with no interface to declare. The JDK hands you strategies in more places than sorting. ThreadPoolExecutor takes a RejectedExecutionHandler that decides what happens when its queue is full (AbortPolicy, CallerRunsPolicy and two more), and Collectors.groupingBy takes the function that decides which group each element joins. Each time, the library owns the loop and asks you for one decision. A named type still helps in two cases. When the strategy has more than one method, such as a PSP client with authorize and refund, you have an interface with implementations, which is ordinary polymorphism. And a one-line @FunctionalInterface interface FeeStrategy { long fee(Payment p); } documents intent better than a bare ToLongFunction<Payment>, and reads better in stack traces. Watch for state. A lambda that captures and changes a field is a strategy with hidden memory, and two threads sorting with it at once will corrupt each other's results. Keep strategies pure: input in, answer out. Rank PSPs three ways Read StrategyDemo.java (or StrategyDemo.kt) and predict the three lines. Equal fees keep their original order, because the JDK's sort is stable. Run it with the command below. Add a fourth quote at the end of the list, new Quote("Bluefin", 25, 150) (PspQuote("Bluefin", 25, 150) in Kotlin). Predict all three lines again, then run. StrategyDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l07; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Three strategies for one decision: which PSP does the router try first? */ public class StrategyDemo { record Quote(String psp, long feeMinor, long p95Millis) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<Quote> quotes = List.of( new Quote("Northpay", 30, 200), new Quote("Adyx", 25, 900), new Quote("Kestrel", 30, 120)); // each value is a complete strategy: no class per algorithm Map<String, Comparator<Quote>> policies = new LinkedHashMap<>(); policies.put("cheapest", Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::feeMinor)); policies.put("fastest", Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::p95Millis)); policies.put("cheapest, then fastest", Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::feeMinor).thenComparingLong(Quote::p95Millis)); // sorted() is the context: it owns the algorithm and asks the strategy one question policies.forEach((name, order) -> System.out.println(name + ": " + quotes.stream().sorted(order).map(Quote::psp).toList())); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l07.StrategyDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l07/StrategyDemo.java StrategyDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l07 // Three strategies for one decision: which PSP does the router try first? data class PspQuote(val psp: String, val feeMinor: Long, val p95Millis: Long) fun main() { val quotes = listOf( PspQuote("Northpay", 30, 200), PspQuote("Adyx", 25, 900), PspQuote("Kestrel", 30, 120), ) // each value is a complete strategy: no class per algorithm val policies: Map<String, Comparator<PspQuote>> = mapOf( "cheapest" to compareBy<PspQuote> { it.feeMinor }, "fastest" to compareBy<PspQuote> { it.p95Millis }, "cheapest, then fastest" to compareBy<PspQuote> { it.feeMinor }.thenBy { it.p95Millis }, ) // sortedWith is the context: it owns the algorithm and asks the strategy one question policies.forEach { (name, order) -> println("$name: ${quotes.sortedWith(order).map { it.psp }}") } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l07.StrategyDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l07/StrategyDemo.kt cheapest: [Adyx, Northpay, Kestrel], fastest: [Kestrel, Northpay, Adyx], cheapest, then fastest: [Adyx, Kestrel, Northpay]. With Bluefin: [Adyx, Bluefin, Northpay, Kestrel], [Kestrel, Bluefin, Northpay, Adyx] and [Bluefin, Adyx, Kestrel, Northpay]. Three algorithms, zero classes: each strategy is one expression. Comparator (Java SE 25 API) docs Strategy is the route setting on a satnav: fastest, shortest, avoid tolls. The satnav still plans the trip; you swap the one rule it uses to rank roads. Template Method is a printed form with blanks: the form fixes the order of the questions, and each department fills in its own answers. Execute around is a waffle iron: it heats up, times the bake and switches off, and you pour in whatever batter you like. The analogy breaks at the waffle iron's plug. A real appliance can't forget to switch off, but a hand-written execute-around function can, which is why the teardown belongs in a finally block.

h: Strategy and Template Method · Refactor the if/else router, after pinning what it does
x: Every payments codebase has a method like LegacyRouter.fee: an if/else if chain on the payment method, with special cases added over the years. Before you touch it, pin what it does. Write a test that runs the old code and the new code over a grid of inputs (every method, amounts including 0 and 1, several countries) and asserts that they agree. Michael Feathers calls this a characterization test. It records today's behavior, bugs included, so the refactor can't change it by accident. Choose the grid for its edges, not its size. Include amount 0, amount 1 (where integer division rounds a percentage down to nothing), the home country and a foreign one, and every enum constant. Those are the places where a refactored rule most often drifts by a cent. Then pick one of two shapes: Java // open set: one lambda per method, in a map that config or plug-ins could fill static final Map<Method, FeeStrategy> STRATEGIES = new EnumMap<>(Map.of( Method.CARD, p -> 30 + p.amountMinor() * 290 / 10_000, Method.SEPA, p -> 25, Method.WALLET, p -> p.amountMinor() * 150 / 10_000)); // closed set: one switch, checked by the compiler static long fee(Payment p) { return switch (p.method()) { case CARD -> 30 + p.amountMinor() * 290 / 10_000; case SEPA -> 25; case WALLET -> p.amountMinor() * 150 / 10_000; }; } Kotlin // open set: one lambda per method, in a map that config or plug-ins could fill val strategies: Map<Method, (Payment) -> Long> = mapOf( Method.CARD to { p -> 30 + p.amountMinor * 290 / 10_000 }, Method.SEPA to { _ -> 25L }, Method.WALLET to { p -> p.amountMinor * 150 / 10_000 }, ) // closed set: one when, checked by the compiler fun fee(p: Payment): Long = when (p.method) { Method.CARD -> 30 + p.amountMinor * 290 / 10_000 Method.SEPA -> 25 Method.WALLET -> p.amountMinor * 150 / 10_000 } A map of strategies suits an open set: methods loaded from config, PSP plug-ins, rules a merchant can switch on. A switch or when with no default suits a closed set you own, like your Method enum. You see the difference the day someone adds CRYPTO to the enum. The switch stops compiling: "the switch expression does not cover all possible input values", or in Kotlin, "'when' expression must be exhaustive". The map compiles, ships, and throws on the first crypto payment: a NullPointerException from EnumMap.get in Java, or NoSuchElementException: Key CRYPTO is missing in the map from Kotlin's getValue. If you do choose a map for a closed set, add a startup check that every constant has an entry, so the failure moves from the first customer to the deploy. Neither shape needs a class per payment method. The lambdas are the strategies. Add a payment method and see who notices Run RouterDemo in either language: the map and the switch agree on all three methods. Add CRYPTO to the enum (PayMethod). Predict which part fails, and when, then run. Add the missing branch, case CRYPTO -> 0; in Java or PayMethod.CRYPTO -> 0 in Kotlin. Predict, then run again. Remove CRYPTO when you're done. RouterDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l07; import java.util.EnumMap; import java.util.Map; /** The same fee rules as a map of strategies and as a switch. Add a payment method and watch which one tells you. */ public class RouterDemo { enum PayMethod { CARD, SEPA, WALLET } record Pay(PayMethod method, long amountMinor) {} interface FeeStrategy { long fee(Pay p); } // open set: one lambda per method, in a map that config or plug-ins could fill static final Map<PayMethod, FeeStrategy> STRATEGIES = new EnumMap<>(Map.of( PayMethod.CARD, p -> 30 + p.amountMinor() * 290 / 10_000, PayMethod.SEPA, p -> 25, PayMethod.WALLET, p -> p.amountMinor() * 150 / 10_000)); // closed set: one switch, checked by the compiler static long feeSwitch(Pay p) { return switch (p.method()) { case CARD -> 30 + p.amountMinor() * 290 / 10_000; case SEPA -> 25; case WALLET -> p.amountMinor() * 150 / 10_000; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { for (PayMethod m : PayMethod.values()) { Pay p = new Pay(m, 10_000); System.out.printf("%-7s switch=%d", m, feeSwitch(p)); System.out.printf(" map=%d%n", STRATEGIES.get(m).fee(p)); } } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l07.RouterDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l07/RouterDemo.java RouterDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l07 // The same fee rules as a map of strategies and as a when. Add a payment method and watch which one tells you. enum class PayMethod { CARD, SEPA, WALLET } data class Pay(val method: PayMethod, val amountMinor: Long) // open set: one function per method, in a map that config or plug-ins could fill private val strategies: Map<PayMethod, (Pay) -> Long> = mapOf( PayMethod.CARD to { p -> 30 + p.amountMinor * 290 / 10_000 }, PayMethod.SEPA to { _ -> 25L }, PayMethod.WALLET to { p -> p.amountMinor * 150 / 10_000 }, ) // closed set: one when, checked by the compiler private fun feeWhen(p: Pay): Long = when (p.method) { PayMethod.CARD -> 30 + p.amountMinor * 290 / 10_000 PayMethod.SEPA -> 25 PayMethod.WALLET -> p.amountMinor * 150 / 10_000 } fun main() { for (m in PayMethod.entries) { val p = Pay(m, 10_000) print("%-7s when=%d".format(m, feeWhen(p))) println(" map=%d".format(strategies.getValue(m)(p))) } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l07.RouterDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l07/RouterDemo.kt With CRYPTO added, the build fails: javac says the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, kotlinc says 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'CRYPTO' branch or an 'else' branch. After you add the branch, three lines print and then CRYPTO switch=0 dies: Java throws NullPointerException because Map.get returned null, Kotlin throws NoSuchElementException: Key CRYPTO is missing in the map. The compiler found one gap; only a runtime crash found the other. Conditions and loops: when (Kotlin docs) docs Kafka already runs on strategies: the producer's partitioner.class names a Partitioner implementation, and the client calls it for every record. In your own services, the PSP router is the strategy you own: choose PSPs with a comparator over quotes, and price with a map or a switch depending on whether the set is yours. Temporal's RetryOptions is a back-off strategy passed as data. Execute around is the shape for everything that wraps a call in your Quarkus services: timing a PSP call, putting a payment id in the logging MDC for a block, running a block in a transaction. Write those as small higher-order functions, inline in Kotlin, instead of a base class every client must extend.

h: Strategy and Template Method · Template Method: a skeleton with holes for subclasses
x: Every call to a PSP needs the same wrapping: start a timer, make the call, note the outcome, record it. Template Method puts that skeleton in a base class as a final method and leaves holes, called hooks, for subclasses to fill: Java abstract class OutboundCall<T> { public final T execute() { // the skeleton: subclasses can't change it long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return doCall(); // hook 1: the varying step } finally { metrics.record(name(), System.nanoTime() - start); } } protected abstract String name(); // hook 2 protected abstract T doCall(); } final class CaptureCall extends OutboundCall<String> { protected String name() { return "psp.capture"; } protected String doCall() { return psp.capture(authId); } } Kotlin abstract class OutboundCall<T> { fun execute(): T { // final by default in Kotlin: subclasses can't change it val start = System.nanoTime() try { return doCall() // hook 1: the varying step } finally { metrics.record(name(), System.nanoTime() - start) } } protected abstract fun name(): String // hook 2 protected abstract fun doCall(): T } class CaptureCall(private val authId: String) : OutboundCall<String>() { override fun name() = "psp.capture" override fun doCall() = psp.capture(authId) } The base class owns the order, and because execute is final, no subclass can skip the timer. The JDK uses the shape: to build an unmodifiable list, you extend AbstractList and write only get and size; the rest of List is a skeleton built on those two hooks. Inheritance is the cost. A subclass depends on every detail of its parent, and a parent that changes when it calls its hooks can break subclasses it has never seen. That is the fragile base class problem. The sharpest edge is a base-class constructor that calls a hook. A subclass assigns its own fields only after the base constructor returns, so the hook runs on a half-built object. In Java, the field reads as null. In Kotlin, the same code reads null from private val psp: String, a property the type system promises is never null, and kotlinc compiles it without a warning. Never call an overridable method from a constructor. Compute such values lazily, or pass them up to the base constructor as arguments. Watch a hook run too early Read TemplateHookDemo.java (or .kt). The base constructor builds label by calling name(). Predict the label the template version prints. Run it with the command below and compare the two versions. Fix the template without changing ChargeCall: delete the label field and build the label inside execute() instead. Run again. TemplateHookDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l07; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Template Method's sharpest edge, and the execute-around function that avoids it. */ public class TemplateHookDemo { // classic Template Method: a final skeleton with hooks for subclasses abstract static class OutboundCall { private final String label; OutboundCall() { label = "outbound " + name(); // calls a hook before the subclass has set its fields } final String execute() { // the skeleton System.out.println(" start " + label); try { return doCall(); } finally { System.out.println(" end " + label); } } abstract String name(); // hook abstract String doCall(); // hook } static final class ChargeCall extends OutboundCall { private final String psp; ChargeCall(String psp) { this.psp = psp; } // runs AFTER OutboundCall() has called name() String name() { return "charge via " + psp; } String doCall() { return "ch_1250"; } } // execute around: the same skeleton as a function; the varying step is a parameter static <T> T outbound(String name, Supplier<T> body) { System.out.println(" start " + name); try { return body.get(); } finally { System.out.println(" end " + name); } } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("template: " + new ChargeCall("northpay").execute()); System.out.println("function: " + outbound("outbound charge via northpay", () -> "ch_1250")); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l07.TemplateHookDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l07/TemplateHookDemo.java TemplateHookDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l07 // Template Method's sharpest edge, and the execute-around function that avoids it. // classic Template Method: a skeleton with hooks for subclasses (Kotlin members are final unless open) abstract class OutboundCall { private val label = "outbound " + name() // calls a hook before the subclass has set its fields fun execute(): String { // the skeleton println(" start $label") try { return doCall() } finally { println(" end $label") } } abstract fun name(): String // hook abstract fun doCall(): String // hook } class ChargeCall(private val psp: String) : OutboundCall() { // psp is a non-null String... override fun name() = "charge via $psp" // ...and still reads as null here override fun doCall() = "ch_1250" } // execute around: the same skeleton as an inline function; the varying step is a lambda inline fun <T> outbound(name: String, body: () -> T): T { println(" start $name") try { return body() } finally { println(" end $name") } } fun main() { println("template: ${ChargeCall("northpay").execute()}") println("function: ${outbound("outbound charge via northpay") { "ch_1250" }}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l07.TemplateHookDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l07/TemplateHookDemo.kt The template prints start outbound charge via null: name() ran inside the base constructor, before ChargeCall had assigned psp. Kotlin prints the same null from a property declared as non-null String, with no compiler warning. The function version prints charge via northpay. After the fix, the template prints it too, because name() now runs only when the object is complete. AbstractList (Java SE 25 API) docs

h: Strategy and Template Method · Execute around: pass the hole in as a function
x: The modern answer keeps the skeleton and drops the subclass. Write the skeleton as a function and take the varying step as a lambda: Java static <T> T timed(String name, Metrics metrics, Supplier<T> body) { long start = System.nanoTime(); // setup try { return body.get(); // the caller's code } finally { metrics.record(name, System.nanoTime() - start); // teardown, always } } String captured = timed("psp.capture", metrics, () -> psp.capture(authId)); Kotlin inline fun <T> timed(name: String, metrics: Metrics, body: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() // setup try { return body() // the caller's code, inlined: no lambda object } finally { metrics.record(name, System.nanoTime() - start) // teardown, always } } val captured = timed("psp.capture", metrics) { psp.capture(authId) } This is execute around: the function runs the setup and the teardown, and calls your code in the middle. You use it every day. try-with-resources is execute around built into Java. Kotlin's standard library is full of it: use {} closes a resource, synchronized(lock) {} takes and releases a monitor, and measureTimeMillis {} times a block. Kotlin makes the function version cheaper than Java's. The compiler copies the body of an inline function, lambda included, into each call site, so no lambda object is created, and a return inside the block returns from the enclosing function. Java's Supplier has a different limit: it can't throw checked exceptions, so wrapping an SDK call that throws IOException needs your own functional interface with a throws clause. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so timed { sdk.call() } just works. Prefer the function. It composes (timed("psp.capture") { retrying(3) { psp.capture(id) } }), it needs no class per call site, and it can't hit the constructor trap, because there is no constructor. Keep Template Method for skeletons with many hooks, such as AbstractList, and make the template method final. Check yourself. psp.capture(authId) throws inside timed. Does the call still show up in the metrics, and does the caller see the exception? (Yes to both. The finally block records the time, and then the exception carries on to the caller as if timed weren't there.) The same skeleton both ways. Template Method fills the hole with a subclass; execute around takes it as a lambda from the call site. Inline functions (Kotlin docs) docs The most common mistake is adding default -> 0 (or else -> 0) to a switch over your own enum "to be safe". It feels defensive, and it silences the one check that mattered: when CRYPTO arrives, the compiler no longer lists the switches that need a rule, and crypto payments are priced at zero until finance notices. The map version has the same hole in a different place, a null lookup on the first crypto payment. For a closed set you own, leave the default out and let the build fail. Keep a default for open sets you don't control, such as config strings or vendor codes, and make it throw.

h: Strategy and Template Method · Java and Kotlin
x: An execute-around timer for SDK calls Psp.java // Supplier can't throw checked exceptions, so a wrapper for SDK calls needs its own interface @FunctionalInterface interface IoCall<T> { T call() throws IOException; } final class Psp { static <T> T timed(String name, Map<String, Long> metrics, IoCall<T> body) throws IOException { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return body.call(); } finally { metrics.merge(name, System.nanoTime() - start, Long::sum); } } static String captureOrNull(Map<String, Long> metrics, PspSdk sdk, String authId) throws IOException { String ref = timed("psp.capture", metrics, () -> sdk.capture(authId)); return ref.isEmpty() ? null : ref; // a lambda can't return from captureOrNull itself } } Psp.kt // inline: the block is pasted into the caller, so no lambda object and no checked-exception plumbing inline fun <T> timed(name: String, metrics: MutableMap<String, Long>, body: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return body() } finally { metrics.merge(name, System.nanoTime() - start) { a, b -> a + b } } } fun captureOrNull(metrics: MutableMap<String, Long>, sdk: PspSdk, authId: String): String? { val ref = timed("psp.capture", metrics) { sdk.capture(authId).ifEmpty { return null } // non-local return: leaves captureOrNull, the finally still records } return ref } The skeleton is identical: read the clock, run the caller's block, record in finally. Three things differ. Java's standard functional interfaces can't throw checked exceptions, so an SDK that throws IOException forces you to declare IoCall with a throws clause; Kotlin has no checked exceptions. Kotlin's inline copies timed and the block into each call site, so there is no lambda object, and return null inside the block returns from captureOrNull itself while the finally still runs. And an inline block may call suspend functions when the caller is a suspend function, which a Java lambda can't do. Neither language needs Template Method for this; the function is the whole pattern.

h: Strategy and Template Method · Worked example
x: Turn a back-off if/else into strategies, without changing behavior A retry helper reads the back-off policy name from config and decides the delay on every attempt. Spot two problems before reading on. // config: psp.backoff=exponential (or "fixed", "none") Duration delayBeforeRetry(String policy, int attempt) { if (policy.equals("fixed")) { return Duration.ofMillis(200); } else if (policy.equals("exponential")) { long ms = 100L << (attempt - 1); // 100, 200, 400, ... return Duration.ofMillis(Math.min(ms, 5_000)); } else if (policy.equals("none")) { return Duration.ZERO; } return Duration.ofMillis(200); // a typo in config silently means "fixed" } // config: psp.backoff=exponential (or "fixed", "none") fun delayBeforeRetry(policy: String, attempt: Int): Duration = if (policy == "fixed") { Duration.ofMillis(200) } else if (policy == "exponential") { val ms = 100L shl (attempt - 1) // 100, 200, 400, ... Duration.ofMillis(minOf(ms, 5_000)) } else if (policy == "none") { Duration.ZERO } else { Duration.ofMillis(200) // a typo in config silently means "fixed" } The policy is chosen again on every attempt, and a typo like exponentail quietly becomes "fixed". Fix neither yet. First pin today's behavior with a characterization test, so the refactor can't change a delay by accident. @ParameterizedTest @CsvSource({"fixed,1,200", "fixed,4,200", "exponential,1,100", "exponential,3,400", "exponential,9,5000", "none,2,0"}) void pinned(String policy, int attempt, long expectedMs) { assertThat(delayBeforeRetry(policy, attempt)).isEqualTo(Duration.ofMillis(expectedMs)); } @ParameterizedTest @CsvSource("fixed,1,200", "fixed,4,200", "exponential,1,100", "exponential,3,400", "exponential,9,5000", "none,2,0") fun pinned(policy: String, attempt: Int, expectedMs: Long) { assertThat(delayBeforeRetry(policy, attempt)).isEqualTo(Duration.ofMillis(expectedMs)) } Now give the decision a type with one method, and a factory for each policy. Each factory returns a lambda: a complete strategy. @FunctionalInterface interface Backoff { Duration delay(int attempt); // 1. one decision, one method static Backoff fixed(Duration d) { return attempt -> d; } static Backoff exponential(Duration base, Duration max) { return attempt -> { Duration d = base.multipliedBy(1L << (attempt - 1)); return d.compareTo(max) > 0 ? max : d; }; } Backoff NONE = attempt -> Duration.ZERO; } fun interface Backoff { fun delay(attempt: Int): Duration // 1. one decision, one method companion object { fun fixed(d: Duration) = Backoff { d } fun exponential(base: Duration, max: Duration) = Backoff { attempt -> minOf(base.multipliedBy(1L shl (attempt - 1)), max) } val NONE = Backoff { Duration.ZERO } } } Choose the strategy once, at startup. Here a default is right, because config strings are an open set you don't control, and it throws, so a typo fails the deploy. Point the pinned test at fromConfig(policy).delay(attempt): it still passes. static Backoff fromConfig(String name) { // 2. choose once, at startup return switch (name) { case "fixed" -> Backoff.fixed(Duration.ofMillis(200)); case "exponential" -> Backoff.exponential(Duration.ofMillis(100), Duration.ofSeconds(5)); case "none" -> Backoff.NONE; default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown psp.backoff: " + name); // 3. a typo fails the deploy }; } Backoff backoff = fromConfig(config.backoff()); // 4. the retry loop calls backoff.delay(n) fun fromConfig(name: String): Backoff = when (name) { // 2. choose once, at startup "fixed" -> Backoff.fixed(Duration.ofMillis(200)) "exponential" -> Backoff.exponential(Duration.ofMillis(100), Duration.ofSeconds(5)) "none" -> Backoff.NONE else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown psp.backoff: $name") // 3. a typo fails the deploy } val backoff = fromConfig(config.backoff) // 4. the retry loop calls backoff.delay(n)

h: Strategy and Template Method · Quiz
x: A team prices with Map<Method, FeeStrategy> built from config, and also has a switch over Method with no default in the invoicing code. Someone adds CRYPTO to Method. Which statement is true? The map fails to compile; the switch throws at runtime The switch fails to compile; the map compiles and fails on the first crypto payment Both fail to compile Both compile, and crypto payments cost 0 Only the switch tells the compiler which constants must be handled, so only the switch breaks the build. The map has no idea CRYPTO should be a key, so get returns null in production. With a map over a closed set, add a startup check that every constant has an entry. Quotes: Atlas (fee 30, p95 200 ms), Bluefin (fee 25, p95 900 ms), Cobalt (fee 30, p95 120 ms). In what order does Comparator.comparingLong(Quote::feeMinor).thenComparingLong(Quote::p95Millis) sort them? Bluefin, Cobalt, Atlas Bluefin, Atlas, Cobalt Cobalt, Atlas, Bluefin Atlas, Cobalt, Bluefin The first comparator puts the 25 fee first: Bluefin. Atlas and Cobalt tie on fee, so the second comparator breaks the tie by latency: Cobalt (120 ms) before Atlas (200 ms). The tempting "Bluefin, Atlas, Cobalt" ignores the tie-breaker and keeps the original order. A base class sets label = "outbound " + name(); in its constructor. The subclass ChargeCall(String psp) assigns this.psp = psp and implements name() as "charge via " + psp. What is the label of new ChargeCall("northpay")? It throws NullPointerException outbound charge via northpay outbound charge via null It doesn't compile The base constructor runs first and calls the overridden name() before ChargeCall has assigned psp, so psp is still null, and string concatenation turns null into "null". Nothing throws, which makes the bug easy to miss. Kotlin behaves the same even for a non-null val psp: String. At 30 call sites, code calls different PSP endpoints, and every call must be timed and logged in the same way. Which shape fits best? An abstract base class with a final execute() and one subclass per call site A Map<String, Runnable> holding all 30 calls A singleton that every call registers with A higher-order function, timed("psp.capture") { ... }, inline in Kotlin, wrapped around each call The skeleton is fixed and the middle varies per call site, which is execute around: one function, and each call site passes its own block. Thirty subclasses is Template Method's ceremony with its inheritance problems, and a map or a singleton doesn't wrap anything. From Decorator and Proxy: each method's base rule is a FeeCalculator stored in a Map<Method, FeeCalculator>. Ops now wants every fee capped at 5.00. Where does the cap go with the least code? Edit every lambda in the map to call Math.min(..., 500) Decorate each calculator once when you build the map: calculators.replaceAll((m, c) -> c.cappedAt(500)) Add a default -> 500 branch to the switch Make each strategy extend a CappedCalculator base class Strategies and decorators combine: the map picks the rule, and wrapping each rule in cappedAt(500) adds the cap once, in one place.
