h: Strategy and Template Method · Key terms
x: Strategy One interchangeable algorithm, passed in by the caller and used by the code that needs a decision. Characterization test A test that pins down what legacy code does now, so a refactor can't change it unnoticed. Template Method A base-class method that fixes the steps and lets subclasses fill in some of them. Hook An overridable method a template calls at a fixed point in its skeleton. Fragile base class When a change inside a parent class breaks subclasses that relied on how it worked. Execute around A function that wraps the caller's code with setup and teardown, taking that code as a lambda. Inline function A Kotlin function whose body, with its lambda arguments, is copied into each call site. In modern Java or Kotlin, what is a strategy usually written as? A lambda or method reference for a functional interface (Comparator, FeeStrategy), or a Kotlin function type such as (Payment) -> Long. You add a constant to an enum. What happens to a switch over it with no default, and to an EnumMap of strategies? The switch fails to compile. The map compiles, and get returns null for the new key at runtime. Map of strategies or exhaustive switch: which for a closed set you own? The switch (or when) with no default, so a new case is a compile error. Use the map for open sets: config, plug-ins. What is a characterization test? A test that records what existing code does today, bugs included, so a refactor can prove it changed nothing. What is Template Method? A final skeleton method in a base class that calls hook methods subclasses override. A base-class constructor calls an overridden method that reads a subclass field. What does it see? The field's default: null or 0, because the subclass constructor hasn't run yet. In Kotlin even a non-null val reads as null. What is execute around? A function that does the setup and teardown and takes the varying step as a lambda: try-with-resources, use {}, synchronized(lock) {}.

h: Strategy and Template Method · Go deeper
x: Strategy and State have the same structure: an object holds an interface and delegates to it. The difference is who chooses. The client picks a strategy and it stays put. A state object, or a transition function, picks the next state itself as events arrive. Lesson 9 of this track, State and Chain of Responsibility, builds the payment lifecycle that way. Java can do execute around without lambdas. Make the setup a constructor and the teardown close(), and try-with-resources does the rest: try (var t = metrics.timer("psp.capture")) { return psp.capture(id); }. This form lets checked exceptions pass through untouched and needs no functional interface, which is why many tracing and metrics libraries offer a closeable span or timer. The cost is that the caller must remember the try. Kotlin's inline has limits worth knowing. An inlined lambda can't be stored or passed to a non-inline function, because it doesn't exist as an object. Mark such a parameter noinline. If the lambda runs in another context (a different thread, a callback), mark it crossinline, which forbids non-local returns inside it. And large inline functions grow every call site, so keep them small: the skeleton inline, the heavy lifting in a normal function it calls. Spring's JdbcTemplate and TransactionTemplate carry the pattern's name, but they take your code as a callback, which is the execute-around shape from this lesson. The name stuck from an era when callbacks needed anonymous inner classes.

h: Observer and Command · Observer: tell the listeners, then stay out of their way
x: A posting hits the ledger, and four parts of the service care: the balance view, the receipt email, analytics and fraud scoring. If post calls all four directly, the ledger depends on every one of them, and a broken analytics endpoint makes postings fail. Observer inverts that. The ledger, the subject, keeps a list of listeners and tells each one what happened. It doesn't know who they are. Java final class EventBus<E> { private final List<Consumer<? super E>> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); AutoCloseable subscribe(Consumer<? super E> listener) { listeners.add(listener); return () -> listeners.remove(listener); // the handle that prevents leaks } void publish(E event) { for (Consumer<? super E> l : listeners) { try { l.accept(event); } catch (RuntimeException e) { log.warn("listener failed", e); // one bad listener must not starve the rest } } } } Kotlin class EventBus<E> { private val listeners = CopyOnWriteArrayList<(E) -> Unit>() fun subscribe(listener: (E) -> Unit): AutoCloseable { listeners += listener return AutoCloseable { listeners -= listener } // the handle that prevents leaks } fun publish(event: E) { for (l in listeners) { try { l(event) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { log.warn("listener failed", e) // one bad listener must not starve the rest } } } } No PaymentListener interface: Consumer<E> in Java and (E) -> Unit in Kotlin already say "something that takes an event". Each line here prevents a real bug. subscribe returns a handle, because a listener that is never removed is a lapsed listener: the bus holds a reference to it forever, so it can't be garbage collected and keeps reacting to events long after its owner is gone. The try/catch stops one failing listener from cancelling delivery to the ones after it. CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates over a snapshot, so a listener may unsubscribe while it is being called; with an ArrayList, that throws ConcurrentModificationException. Copy-on-write makes every subscribe expensive and every publish cheap, which fits listener lists. One property stays, whatever you do: delivery is synchronous. Every listener runs on the publishing thread, inside post. A 300 ms email call makes every posting 300 ms slower, and a listener that publishes another event starts a nested round of delivery before the first round is done. Keep in-process listeners fast, and hand slow work to a queue. Break a listener, then remove the safety net Read EventBusDemo.java (or EventBusDemo.kt). Three listeners subscribe; the second always throws. Predict the five lines it prints. Run it with the command below. Delete the try/catch in publish, keeping the l.accept(event) (l(event) in Kotlin) line. Predict, then run. Put it back. EventBusDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l08; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** A hand-rolled Observer: subscribe returns a handle, and one bad listener can't starve the rest. */ public class EventBusDemo { static final class EventBus<E> { private final List<Consumer<? super E>> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); AutoCloseable subscribe(Consumer<? super E> listener) { listeners.add(listener); return () -> listeners.remove(listener); // the handle that prevents leaks } void publish(E event) { for (Consumer<? super E> l : listeners) { try { l.accept(event); } catch (RuntimeException e) { // isolate each listener System.out.println(" (a listener failed: " + e.getMessage() + ")"); } } } } record Posted(String account, long amountMinor) {} public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { EventBus<Posted> bus = new EventBus<>(); bus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("ledger view got " + e)); bus.subscribe(e -> { throw new IllegalStateException("analytics dashboard is down"); }); AutoCloseable email = bus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("email sender got " + e)); bus.publish(new Posted("acc-1", 450)); email.close(); // unsubscribe bus.publish(new Posted("acc-1", 900)); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l08.EventBusDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l08/EventBusDemo.java EventBusDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList // A hand-rolled Observer: subscribe returns a handle, and one bad listener can't starve the rest. class EventBus<E> { private val listeners = CopyOnWriteArrayList<(E) -> Unit>() fun subscribe(listener: (E) -> Unit): AutoCloseable { listeners += listener return AutoCloseable { listeners -= listener } // the handle that prevents leaks } fun publish(event: E) { for (l in listeners) { try { l(event) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { // isolate each listener println(" (a listener failed: ${e.message})") } } } } data class PostedEvent(val account: String, val amountMinor: Long) fun main() { val bus = EventBus<PostedEvent>() bus.subscribe { println("ledger view got $it") } bus.subscribe { throw IllegalStateException("analytics dashboard is down") } val email = bus.subscribe { println("email sender got $it") } bus.publish(PostedEvent("acc-1", 450)) email.close() // unsubscribe bus.publish(PostedEvent("acc-1", 900)) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l08.EventBusDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l08/EventBusDemo.kt The ledger view and the email sender both get the 450 posting, with (a listener failed: analytics dashboard is down) between them. After email.close(), only the ledger view gets the 900 posting. Without the try/catch, the program prints the first ledger line and dies with IllegalStateException: analytics dashboard is down: the email sender never hears anything, and in a service the posting itself would fail. CopyOnWriteArrayList (Java SE 25 API) docs Observer is a newsletter: the publisher sends each issue to whoever is on the list, and every issue carries an unsubscribe link, which is the handle subscribe returns. Command is a restaurant order ticket. The waiter writes the order down instead of cooking it, puts it on the rail, and a cook works through the rail in order. A ticket can be voided before it's cooked, which is undo. Once the meal is served you can't un-serve it, so you comp a dessert, which is compensation. The analogy breaks on duplicates. A kitchen never cooks the same ticket twice by accident, but a message queue or a Temporal retry can deliver the same command twice, so the command itself must be safe to run again.

h: Observer and Command · Flows are observers with the bookkeeping done
x: Kotlin's coroutine library ships two ready-made subjects. A SharedFlow broadcasts every emitted value to every active collector. A StateFlow holds one current value: "a state flow is a hot flow", it "never completes", and each collector gets the current value first, then every change. Both are thread-safe, and both do the bookkeeping from the last section for you. There is no listener list to guard. Cancelling the collecting coroutine unsubscribes it, and each collector runs in its own coroutine, so one that fails doesn't stop the others. Java // Closest Java equivalent: the JDK's java.util.concurrent.Flow, with SubmissionPublisher as a hot publisher SubmissionPublisher<String> events = new SubmissionPublisher<>(); CompletableFuture<Void> done = events.consume(e -> System.out.println("got " + e)); // one subscriber events.submit("AUTHORIZED"); events.submit("AUTHORIZED"); // delivered again: a publisher has no idea of "same as last time" events.close(); // completes the stream; done completes after the last item Kotlin class PaymentStatus { private val _state = MutableStateFlow("NEW") val state: StateFlow<String> = _state.asStateFlow() // state: the latest value private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<String>() val events: SharedFlow<String> = _events.asSharedFlow() // events: every one, to every collector suspend fun on(event: String) { _events.emit(event) // with no buffer, waits until every current collector has taken it _state.value = event } } Keep the mutable flow private and expose the read-only type, as above. Use _state.update { ... } when the new value depends on the old one, because it is an atomic read-modify-write. The rule that matters for payments is in the StateFlow docs: values "are conflated using Any.equals comparison in a similar way to distinctUntilChanged", and "a slow collector skips fast updates". That is exactly right for state. A dashboard showing a payment's status needs only the latest one. It is wrong for events. Two 4.50 coffees on the same card, Posted("acc-1", 450) twice, arrive as one, and a slow consumer misses the updates in between. Use a SharedFlow for events, or a Channel when each item must go to exactly one consumer. Java has the interfaces but few implementations. java.util.concurrent.Flow holds the Reactive Streams types (Publisher, Subscriber, Subscription), and SubmissionPublisher is the one hot publisher in the JDK. In Reactor, a Flux is the same idea with backpressure, and Sinks.many().multicast() plays the role of a MutableSharedFlow. None of them drops equal values unless you ask with distinctUntilChanged(). Watch StateFlow drop an event Read StateVsShared.kt (or the Java twin, StateVsSharedJava.java). The same three updates go to a state holder and an event stream. Predict both lines. Run it with the command below. Kotlin: change val events = MutableSharedFlow<String>() to val events = MutableStateFlow("NEW") and run. Java: delete the if (Objects.equals(value, next)) return; line and run. Predict each first. StateVsShared.kt package workbench.patterns.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineStart import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.yield // The same three payment updates, observed through a StateFlow and through a SharedFlow. fun main() = runBlocking { val state = MutableStateFlow("NEW") // state: the latest value; equal values are dropped val events = MutableSharedFlow<String>() // events: every value, to every collector val fromState = mutableListOf<String>() val fromEvents = mutableListOf<String>() val collectors = listOf( launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { state.collect { fromState += it } }, launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { events.collect { fromEvents += it } }, ) for (update in listOf("AUTHORIZED", "AUTHORIZED", "CAPTURED")) { state.value = update events.emit(update) // suspends until every collector has taken it yield() } collectors.forEach { it.cancel() } println("StateFlow collector saw: $fromState") println("SharedFlow collector saw: $fromEvents") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l08.StateVsSharedKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l08/StateVsShared.kt StateVsSharedJava.java // Closest Java equivalent: the JDK's Flow API, where SubmissionPublisher delivers every event, plus a tiny // "latest value" holder that drops equal values the way Kotlin's StateFlow does. The JDK has no StateFlow. package workbench.patterns.l08; import java.util.List; import java.util.Objects; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.function.Consumer; public class StateVsSharedJava { /** Holds one current value and tells observers about changes; equal values are dropped. */ static final class LatestValue<T> { private final List<Consumer<T>> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); private T value; LatestValue(T initial) { value = initial; } synchronized void set(T next) { if (Objects.equals(value, next)) return; // StateFlow-style conflation by equals() value = next; observers.forEach(o -> o.accept(next)); } synchronized void observe(Consumer<T> o) { observers.add(o); o.accept(value); // new observers get the current value first } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { LatestValue<String> state = new LatestValue<>("NEW"); List<String> fromState = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); state.observe(fromState::add); List<String> fromEvents = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); CompletableFuture<Void> done; try (SubmissionPublisher<String> events = new SubmissionPublisher<>()) { done = events.consume(fromEvents::add); // a subscriber that gets every item for (String update : List.of("AUTHORIZED", "AUTHORIZED", "CAPTURED")) { state.set(update); events.submit(update); } } // close() completes the stream done.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.println("state holder saw: " + fromState); System.out.println("event publisher saw: " + fromEvents); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l08.StateVsSharedJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l08/StateVsSharedJava.java The state side prints [NEW, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED]: the initial value, then only real changes. The event side prints [AUTHORIZED, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED]: every event. With a StateFlow for events, the Kotlin event line becomes [NEW, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED], so the second authorization is gone and a fake NEW event appeared. Without the equality check, the Java state holder prints [NEW, AUTHORIZED, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED]: that one check is the whole difference. StateFlow (kotlinx.coroutines API) docs SubmissionPublisher (Java SE 25 API) docs A Kafka consumer group is a durable observer of a topic: it keeps its position in the log, so it can catch up after a crash, which no in-process listener can. Quarkus has the in-process kind built in through CDI events: Event<PaymentCaptured>.fire() on one side and an @Observes method on the other. Use those for fast, losable work, such as metrics and cache eviction. Anything that must not be lost, like a receipt, a ledger entry or fraud scoring, goes through an outbox row and Kafka. On the command side, every Temporal activity call is a command recorded in the workflow history and retried by policy, and your capture, refund and payout activities should all take an idempotency key.

h: Observer and Command · Command: a request you can store, queue and undo
x: Command turns a request into an object: what to do and with which arguments, as a value you can keep. Once a request is a value, you can queue it, log it, retry it and undo it. For a ledger, a sealed interface of records is the natural shape: Java sealed interface Command permits Deposit, Withdraw { void apply(Account a); void undo(Account a); } record Deposit(long amount) implements Command { public void apply(Account a) { a.balance += amount; } public void undo(Account a) { a.balance -= amount; } } record Withdraw(long amount) implements Command { public void apply(Account a) { if (a.balance < amount) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds"); a.balance -= amount; } public void undo(Account a) { a.balance += amount; } } final class CommandLog { private final Deque<Command> history = new ArrayDeque<>(); void run(Command c, Account a) { c.apply(a); history.push(c); } // record only after success void undoLast(Account a) { Command c = history.poll(); if (c != null) c.undo(a); } } Kotlin sealed interface Command { fun apply(a: Account) fun undo(a: Account) } data class Deposit(val amount: Long) : Command { override fun apply(a: Account) { a.balance += amount } override fun undo(a: Account) { a.balance -= amount } } data class Withdraw(val amount: Long) : Command { override fun apply(a: Account) { check(a.balance >= amount) { "insufficient funds" } a.balance -= amount } override fun undo(a: Account) { a.balance += amount } } class CommandLog { private val history = ArrayDeque<Command>() fun run(c: Command, a: Account) { c.apply(a); history.addFirst(c) } // record only after success fun undoLast(a: Account) { history.removeFirstOrNull()?.undo(a) } } Two details carry the pattern. First, run records the command only after apply succeeds. Record it first, and a rejected 1,000.00 withdrawal sits in the history, so the next undo "refunds" money that never left. Second, the commands are data. Withdraw(amount=30) prints well, compares by value, and can be serialized and written to a table. When a command needs no undo and no data, the class disappears. Runnable, Callable and () -> Unit are commands, and executor.submit(() -> settle(batchId)) hands one to a queue that a worker drains. Keep a named class when you need what a lambda can't give: equality, a readable log line, serialization, or a second method such as undo. Record the command too early Run UndoDemo in either language and read the three lines. In CommandLog.run, swap the two lines so the command is recorded before it is applied. Predict the history and the balance after one undo, then run. Swap them back. UndoDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l08; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; /** Commands as records, an undo log, and the one rule that keeps undo honest. */ public class UndoDemo { static final class Wallet { long balance; } sealed interface Command permits Deposit, Withdraw { void apply(Wallet w); void undo(Wallet w); } record Deposit(long amount) implements Command { public void apply(Wallet w) { w.balance += amount; } public void undo(Wallet w) { w.balance -= amount; } } record Withdraw(long amount) implements Command { public void apply(Wallet w) { if (w.balance < amount) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds"); w.balance -= amount; } public void undo(Wallet w) { w.balance += amount; } } static final class CommandLog { final Deque<Command> history = new ArrayDeque<>(); void run(Command c, Wallet w) { c.apply(w); // 1. apply first history.push(c); // 2. record only after it worked } void undoLast(Wallet w) { Command c = history.poll(); if (c != null) c.undo(w); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Wallet wallet = new Wallet(); CommandLog log = new CommandLog(); log.run(new Deposit(100), wallet); log.run(new Withdraw(30), wallet); try { log.run(new Withdraw(1_000), wallet); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("balance " + wallet.balance + ", history " + log.history); log.undoLast(wallet); System.out.println("after one undo: balance " + wallet.balance + ", history " + log.history); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l08.UndoDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l08/UndoDemo.java UndoDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l08 // Commands as data classes, an undo log, and the one rule that keeps undo honest. class Wallet { var balance = 0L } sealed interface WalletCommand { fun apply(w: Wallet) fun undo(w: Wallet) data class Deposit(val amount: Long) : WalletCommand { override fun apply(w: Wallet) { w.balance += amount } override fun undo(w: Wallet) { w.balance -= amount } } data class Withdraw(val amount: Long) : WalletCommand { override fun apply(w: Wallet) { check(w.balance >= amount) { "insufficient funds" } w.balance -= amount } override fun undo(w: Wallet) { w.balance += amount } } } class CommandLog { val history = ArrayDeque<WalletCommand>() fun run(c: WalletCommand, w: Wallet) { c.apply(w) // 1. apply first history.addFirst(c) // 2. record only after it worked } fun undoLast(w: Wallet) { history.removeFirstOrNull()?.undo(w) } } fun main() { val wallet = Wallet() val log = CommandLog() log.run(WalletCommand.Deposit(100), wallet) log.run(WalletCommand.Withdraw(30), wallet) try { log.run(WalletCommand.Withdraw(1_000), wallet) } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("rejected: ${e.message}") } println("balance ${wallet.balance}, history ${log.history}") log.undoLast(wallet) println("after one undo: balance ${wallet.balance}, history ${log.history}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l08.UndoDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l08/UndoDemo.kt rejected: insufficient funds, then balance 70 with a history of Withdraw 30 and Deposit 100, then after one undo: balance 100. With the lines swapped, the rejected Withdraw of 1,000 sits on top of the history, and the undo puts 1,000 back that never left: balance 1070.

h: Observer and Command · Commands that leave the process
x: Once a command is a record, it can leave the process, and most commands in a payment system do. The transactional outbox is a queue of commands that survives crashes. In the same database transaction that captures a payment, you insert a row saying "send receipt for payment 7781". A relay reads new rows and publishes them to Kafka, and a consumer executes them. Either both the capture and the command commit, or neither does, so a crash between the two can't lose the receipt. Temporal is built on the same idea. When a workflow calls a method on an activity stub, the SDK doesn't run your activity there. It records a command to schedule that activity, with its name and arguments, in the workflow's history, and a worker picks it up. If the worker dies, Temporal schedules it again, according to the retry options. Both deliver at least once. A stored command can run twice: the relay crashed after publishing but before marking the row sent, or the activity finished but its result was lost. So every command that leaves the process must be idempotent. Charge with an idempotency key, and make "send receipt 7781" a no-op the second time. Undo changes meaning too. In memory, undo puts the old state back. Across systems you can't un-send money. A captured payment is reversed by a new command, a Refund, with its own record, its own fees and its own failure modes. Sagas, including Temporal's, are lists of such compensating commands, run in reverse when a later step fails. Model a refund as a compensation, never as undo of a charge. Check yourself. The outbox relay publishes "send receipt for payment 7781" to Kafka, then crashes before it marks the row sent. It restarts. How many receipts does the customer get if the consumer just sends one per message, and what fixes it? (Two, because the relay publishes the row again. The consumer must remember which payment ids it has already sent a receipt for, and skip a repeat.) A command is data. Run now, it goes on an undo stack; stored, it goes through an outbox, Kafka or Temporal, and may run more than once. The most common mistake is using a StateFlow (or a "latest value" holder) for events. It looks like the obvious hot flow: it's thread-safe, it has a value, and the docs example is a counter. Then two identical postings, two equal status updates or two equal webhook notifications arrive in a row, and collectors see one. A slow collector also skips intermediate values, which for a payment can mean never seeing AUTHORIZED between NEW and CAPTURED. The rule: state goes in a StateFlow (only the latest value matters), events go in a SharedFlow or a Channel (each one matters). If a test emits two equal events and expects two, you'll catch it before production does.

h: Observer and Command · Java and Kotlin
x: A command queue drained by one worker LedgerWorker.java sealed interface LedgerCommand permits Deposit, Withdraw, Stop {} record Deposit(String account, long amountMinor) implements LedgerCommand {} record Withdraw(String account, long amountMinor) implements LedgerCommand {} record Stop() implements LedgerCommand {} // poison pill: a Java queue can't be closed final class LedgerWorker implements Runnable { private final BlockingQueue<LedgerCommand> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000); // bounded: put blocks when full private final Map<String, Long> balances = new HashMap<>(); // touched only by the thread running run() void submit(LedgerCommand c) throws InterruptedException { queue.put(c); } void stop() throws InterruptedException { queue.put(new Stop()); } @Override public void run() { try { while (true) { switch (queue.take()) { // commands are data: switch on them case Deposit d -> balances.merge(d.account(), d.amountMinor(), Long::sum); case Withdraw w -> balances.merge(w.account(), -w.amountMinor(), Long::sum); case Stop s -> { return; } } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } // start it after construction, never from the constructor: // Thread.ofVirtual().start(worker); LedgerWorker.kt sealed interface LedgerCommand { data class Deposit(val account: String, val amountMinor: Long) : LedgerCommand data class Withdraw(val account: String, val amountMinor: Long) : LedgerCommand } class LedgerWorker { private val queue = Channel<LedgerCommand>(capacity = 1_000) // bounded: send suspends when full private val balances = mutableMapOf<String, Long>() // touched only by the coroutine in start() fun start(scope: CoroutineScope): Job = scope.launch { for (c in queue) { // ends after stop(), once the queue is drained when (c) { // commands are data: when on them is LedgerCommand.Deposit -> balances.merge(c.account, c.amountMinor) { a, b -> a + b } is LedgerCommand.Withdraw -> balances.merge(c.account, -c.amountMinor) { a, b -> a + b } } } } suspend fun submit(c: LedgerCommand) = queue.send(c) fun stop() = queue.close() // a closed channel is the poison pill } The shape is the same: commands are sealed data, a bounded queue holds them, and one worker applies them in order, so the balances map needs no lock because only one thread or coroutine ever touches it. Two things differ. A Kotlin Channel can be closed, and for (c in queue) ends after the last queued command, so the Stop poison-pill command that Java needs disappears. And send suspends the coroutine when the queue is full, where Java's put blocks a thread; with virtual threads that blocking is cheap too, so the real gain is the built-in close. Neither language needs a Command class hierarchy with an execute() method: a sealed type plus an exhaustive switch or when in the worker does that job.

h: Observer and Command · Worked example
x: Take side effects out of the ledger's post method The ledger's post grew one call at a time. Before reading on, list what happens to a posting when the analytics service is down. void post(Posting p) { repository.insert(p); balances.add(p.account(), p.amountMinor()); receipts.send(p); // 300 ms SMTP call analytics.track(p); // throws when the dashboard is down fraud.score(p); } fun post(p: Posting) { repository.insert(p) balances.add(p.account, p.amountMinor) receipts.send(p) // 300 ms SMTP call analytics.track(p) // throws when the dashboard is down fraud.score(p) } The posting is already stored, but post throws, so the caller retries and may post twice. Fraud scoring is skipped, and every posting waits for SMTP. First split by what the work needs: the insert and the balance are the posting itself; the rest are reactions to it. void post(Posting p) { repository.insert(p); // 1. the posting itself balances.add(p.account(), p.amountMinor()); bus.publish(new Posted(p.account(), p.amountMinor())); // 2. everything else is a reaction } fun post(p: Posting) { repository.insert(p) // 1. the posting itself balances.add(p.account, p.amountMinor) bus.publish(Posted(p.account, p.amountMinor)) // 2. everything else is a reaction } Wire the reactions in one place at startup. The bus isolates failures, so a broken dashboard costs one log line. Which of these listeners can we afford to lose if the pod dies right after the insert? bus.subscribe(e -> metrics.increment("ledger.posted")); // 3. fast and losable: fine in-process bus.subscribe(e -> analytics.track(e)); // a missed event is a dashboard blip // receipts and fraud scoring are NOT subscribed here: see the next step bus.subscribe { metrics.increment("ledger.posted") } // 3. fast and losable: fine in-process bus.subscribe { analytics.track(it) } // a missed event is a dashboard blip // receipts and fraud scoring are NOT subscribed here: see the next step Receipts and fraud scoring must survive a crash, so they become stored commands: outbox rows written in the same transaction as the posting. A relay publishes them to Kafka, and each consumer handles a command at least once, so it must be idempotent. @Transactional void post(Posting p) { repository.insert(p); balances.add(p.account(), p.amountMinor()); outbox.insert(new OutboxRow("receipt.send", p.id())); // 4. same transaction: both commit or neither outbox.insert(new OutboxRow("fraud.score", p.id())); bus.publish(new Posted(p.account(), p.amountMinor())); // 5. in-process listeners: best effort only } @Transactional fun post(p: Posting) { repository.insert(p) balances.add(p.account, p.amountMinor) outbox.insert(OutboxRow("receipt.send", p.id)) // 4. same transaction: both commit or neither outbox.insert(OutboxRow("fraud.score", p.id)) bus.publish(Posted(p.account, p.amountMinor)) // 5. in-process listeners: best effort only }

x: An observable ledger and an undoable command stack labs/patterns/src/main/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l08/ObservableLedger.kt labs/patterns/src/main/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l08/CommandStack.kt ./gradlew :patterns:test --tests 'workbench.patterns.l08.*' Run the tests once: all eight fail. In ObservableLedger, add a private MutableSharedFlow<Posted> and a private MutableStateFlow(0L), and replace the two get() = TODO(...) getters with read-only views of them (= _events.asSharedFlow(), = _balance.asStateFlow()). Write subscribe with a list that tolerates removal during iteration, returning an AutoCloseable that removes the listener. Write post: update the balance atomically, call each listener inside its own try/catch, then emit the event. In CommandStack.kt, write apply and undo for Deposit and Withdraw, then run, undo and redo with two ArrayDeques. Run the tests until all eight pass. CopyOnWriteArrayList<(Posted) -> Unit>() gives you snapshot iteration. AutoCloseable { listeners -= listener } is the handle. _balance.update { it + amountMinor } is an atomic read-modify-write. A MutableSharedFlow with no replay delivers only to collectors that are already collecting, which is what the test sets up. In run, call cmd.apply(account) before you touch either deque: if it throws, nothing else runs. removeFirstOrNull() ?: return false handles the empty cases in undo and redo. h: Observer and Command · From memory
x: An event bus from memory Close this page. Write a generic EventBus<E> with subscribe and publish. It must survive a listener that unsubscribes itself during delivery and a listener that throws, and it must give every subscriber a way to leave. Then compare: which of the three did you miss?

h: Observer and Command · Quiz
x: A Kotlin service publishes payment events through a MutableStateFlow. The fraud model needs every Captured event. What will it miss? Nothing: StateFlow delivers every value An event equal to the previous one, and events a slow collector didn't get to in time Only events emitted before it started collecting, like any hot flow Events emitted from another thread StateFlow conflates by equals, so an event equal to the current value is never delivered, and a collector that falls behind only sees the latest value. Missing events from before you started collecting is true of a replay-0 SharedFlow too, but it isn't what makes StateFlow wrong here. StateFlow is thread-safe, so threads don't matter. A CommandLog.run pushes the command onto the history first and then applies it. The balance is 70. Withdraw(1000) fails with "insufficient funds". The user presses undo once. What is the balance? 70 40 1,070 1,000 The failed withdrawal was recorded before it threw, so it's on top of the history. Undoing it adds 1,000 that never left: 70 + 1,000 = 1,070. Recording only after apply succeeds keeps undo honest. A request-scoped object subscribes a listener to a singleton EventBus in its constructor and never closes the handle. What happens over a day of traffic? Memory grows, and every old request object keeps reacting to events Nothing: listeners are removed when the request ends The bus throws once it has too many listeners The listeners stop receiving events after a garbage collection The singleton's list holds a strong reference to each listener, and each listener's lambda captures its request object, so none of them can be collected, and all of them keep running on every event. That is the lapsed-listener leak. Return a handle from subscribe and close it when the owner's life ends. Fraud scoring must see every ledger posting, even if the pod crashes a millisecond after the posting commits. Which design fits? An in-process EventBus listener A StateFlow the scorer collects A MutableSharedFlow with replay = 1 An outbox row written in the posting's transaction and relayed to Kafka Anything in memory dies with the pod, so the in-process bus and both flows lose events written just before a crash. An outbox row commits with the posting or not at all, and the relay delivers it at least once, so the scorer must be idempotent. From StateFlow, SharedFlow and hot streams: a MutableSharedFlow<Posted>() (no replay, no buffer) emits three postings, and only then does a new collector start. What does the new collector see? All three postings None of the three; only postings emitted after it starts Only the last posting The first posting, then it waits A SharedFlow with replay = 0 keeps nothing for late subscribers: each emission goes to the collectors present at that moment. A StateFlow would hand the newcomer the latest value, and replay = 1 would replay the last posting.

h: Observer and Command · Explain it back
x: Explain to a teammate why the ledger's balance is a StateFlow but its events are a SharedFlow, using two 4.50 coffee purchases on the same card as your example.

h: Observer and Command · Key terms
x: Observer A subject keeps a list of listeners and notifies each one when something happens. Lapsed listener A listener nobody removed: it leaks memory and keeps reacting after its owner is gone. Hot flow A flow that exists and emits whether or not anyone collects, such as SharedFlow and StateFlow. Conflation Keeping only the latest value and dropping ones a collector didn't get to, or equal repeats. Command A request turned into a value: what to do, with which arguments, ready to store or queue. Compensation A new action that reverses the effect of an earlier one, such as a refund for a capture. Transactional outbox A table of outgoing messages written in the same transaction as the state change, then relayed. Why should subscribe return an AutoCloseable (or similar handle)? So the subscriber can leave. A forgotten listener stays referenced by the subject forever: the lapsed-listener leak. Why use CopyOnWriteArrayList for a listener list? It iterates over a snapshot, so a listener can unsubscribe during delivery without a ConcurrentModificationException. Writes are rare, reads are constant. What does a publish loop need around each listener call? A try/catch, so one throwing listener doesn't stop delivery to the others or fail the publisher. StateFlow or SharedFlow for payment events? SharedFlow (or a Channel). StateFlow drops values equal to the current one, and slow collectors skip updates. When does a command go on the undo history? Only after apply succeeds. Recorded earlier, a failed command gets "undone" and corrupts the state. Is a refund the undo of a charge? No. Money that moved can't be un-sent; a refund is a new compensating command with its own record and fees. Why must a command stored in an outbox or Temporal be idempotent? Delivery is at least once: a crash or a lost result can make it run twice.

h: Observer and Command · Go deeper
x: StateFlow is a special case of SharedFlow. Its docs describe it as a MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) combined with distinctUntilChanged(). Knowing the knobs helps when neither default fits. replay sets how many past values a new collector gets. extraBufferCapacity lets emit run ahead of slow collectors without suspending. onBufferOverflow decides what happens when that buffer is full: suspend the emitter, drop the oldest value or drop the newest. For payment events, the default (suspend) is the safe choice, because dropping is silent. Kotlin also has an observer for a single property: var status by Delegates.observable("NEW") { _, old, new -> log("$old -> $new") } calls the handler after every assignment, and Delegates.vetoable runs before the assignment and can reject it. They are handy for in-object state, and they are synchronous, like a hand-rolled listener list. Java has a history here. java.util.Observable and java.util.Observer shipped in Java 1.0 and were deprecated in Java 9. Observable is a class you must extend, its notification order is unspecified, and it isn't a good fit for concurrent code. Use a Consumer list, SubmissionPublisher or a reactive library instead. Undo for operations that can't be inverted, such as "apply discount rules" or "reformat the draft", doesn't fit the apply/undo pair. There, save a snapshot of the state before the command and restore it on undo. That is the Memento pattern, in lesson 10 of this track, Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento.

h: State and Chain of Responsibility · State as data: a payment lifecycle in sealed types
x: A payment moves from Created to Authorized to Captured, maybe to Refunded, and can end in Failed. The GoF State pattern gives each state its own class with one method per event: CreatedState.capture() throws, AuthorizedState.capture() returns a CapturedState. That is five classes with four methods each, and the rules for one transition live wherever its class happens to be. Java 21 and Kotlin let you write states and events as data and the rules as one function: Java sealed interface PaymentState permits Created, Authorized, Captured, Refunded, Failed {} record Created(String id) implements PaymentState {} record Authorized(String id, String authCode, long amount) implements PaymentState {} record Captured(String id, long amount) implements PaymentState {} record Refunded(String id, long amount) implements PaymentState {} record Failed(String id, String reason) implements PaymentState {} sealed interface PaymentEvent permits Authorize, Capture, Refund, Decline {} record Authorize(String authCode, long amount) implements PaymentEvent {} record Capture() implements PaymentEvent {} record Refund(long amount) implements PaymentEvent {} record Decline(String reason) implements PaymentEvent {} static PaymentState transition(PaymentState s, PaymentEvent e) { return switch (s) { // no default: a new state breaks the build case Created c -> switch (e) { case Authorize(var code, var amt) when amt > 0 -> new Authorized(c.id(), code, amt); case Decline(var reason) -> new Failed(c.id(), reason); default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Authorized a -> switch (e) { case Capture() -> new Captured(a.id(), a.amount()); case Decline(var reason) -> new Failed(a.id(), reason); default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Captured(var id, var amt) -> switch (e) { case Refund(var r) when r > 0 && r <= amt -> new Refunded(id, r); default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Refunded r -> throw illegal(s, e); // terminal case Failed f -> throw illegal(s, e); // terminal }; } Kotlin sealed interface PaymentState { data class Created(val id: String) : PaymentState data class Authorized(val id: String, val authCode: String, val amount: Long) : PaymentState data class Captured(val id: String, val amount: Long) : PaymentState data class Refunded(val id: String, val amount: Long) : PaymentState data class Failed(val id: String, val reason: String) : PaymentState } sealed interface PaymentEvent { data class Authorize(val authCode: String, val amount: Long) : PaymentEvent data object Capture : PaymentEvent data class Refund(val amount: Long) : PaymentEvent data class Decline(val reason: String) : PaymentEvent } fun transition(s: PaymentState, e: PaymentEvent): PaymentState = when (s) { // no else is PaymentState.Created -> when (e) { is PaymentEvent.Authorize if e.amount > 0 -> PaymentState.Authorized(s.id, e.authCode, e.amount) is PaymentEvent.Decline -> PaymentState.Failed(s.id, e.reason) else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is PaymentState.Authorized -> when (e) { PaymentEvent.Capture -> PaymentState.Captured(s.id, s.amount) is PaymentEvent.Decline -> PaymentState.Failed(s.id, e.reason) else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is PaymentState.Captured -> when (e) { is PaymentEvent.Refund if e.amount in 1..s.amount -> PaymentState.Refunded(s.id, e.amount) else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is PaymentState.Refunded, is PaymentState.Failed -> throw illegal(s, e) // terminal } Read it as a table. Each outer case is a state, each inner case is an event that state accepts, and everything else is illegal. Record patterns take fields out where you need them (Captured(var id, var amt)), and guards state what an event requires (when amt > 0). Kotlin's guards in when (is Refund if ...) became stable in Kotlin 2.2.0. The function is pure: old state and event in, new state out, no I/O. You test it without mocks, and replaying history is one fold: val current: PaymentState = events.fold(Created(id), ::transition), which is how the lab's replay works. Keep side effects out of it. If capturing needs the PSP, call the PSP first and feed its answer in as an event. h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Let the compiler keep the to-do list
x: Chargebacks arrive, and a captured payment now needs a Disputed state. Add the record to the sealed interface and compile, before you write a single rule: javac: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values kotlinc: error: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Disputed' branch or an 'else' branch. Every switch over the state type fails, and each error points at one place: the transition function, the status label in the API, the metrics tag, the admin screen. The compiler has written your to-do list. Work through it, and the feature is done when the build is green. That only works if you leave room for it. A default (or else) on a switch over your own sealed type means "and anything else", and the compiler believes you: Disputed falls into the default without a word. The inner switches in transition do use default, on purpose. Most (state, event) pairs are illegal, and listing each illegal pair adds nothing. So the rule is narrower than "never write default": never write it on the dimension you expect to grow. States grow. Here, the events within one state mostly don't. The check happens at compile time, so there is a gap at run time, which Brian Goetz's design notes call the remainder: null, and subtypes added after the switch was compiled. A switch on a null state throws NullPointerException. If a new subtype arrives from a separately compiled jar, Java throws MatchException and Kotlin throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException. You don't write code for those cases, but a deploy that mixes old and new jars can hit them. State and Strategy have the same structure: an object holds a value and behavior depends on it. The difference is who chooses. The caller picks a strategy, and it stays. A state machine picks its own next state as events arrive. Pull the rules into one pure transition function over sealed types, and the Oracle status column becomes a serialized state. h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Chain of Responsibility: pass it on, or answer now
x: A payment request passes logging, authentication, an idempotency check and fraud screening before any code charges the card. Each step may answer on its own (401, 409, "send to review") or pass the request on. That is Chain of Responsibility, and you use it every day. A servlet Filter gets the request and a FilterChain, and uses the chain "to invoke the next filter in the chain". OkHttp's Interceptor has one method, intercept(chain), and calls chain.proceed(request) to continue. Each link is a function of the request and next, the rest of the chain: Java Interceptor auth = (r, next) -> r.headers().containsKey("Authorization") ? next.proceed(r) // pass it on : new Response(401, "no token"); // answer now: the rest never runs Interceptor logging = (r, next) -> { Response res = next.proceed(r); // what follows runs on the way out log.info(r.path() + " -> " + res.status()); return res; }; Chain pipeline = chain(List.of(logging, auth, idempotency, fraud), chargeHandler); Kotlin val auth = Interceptor { r, next -> if ("Authorization" in r.headers) next(r) // pass it on else HttpResponse(401, "no token") // answer now: the rest never runs } val logging = Interceptor { r, next -> next(r).also { log.info("${r.path} -> ${it.status}") } // runs on the way out } val pipeline = chain(listOf(logging, auth, idempotency, fraud), chargeHandler) Code before next runs on the way in, code after it runs on the way out with the response, and not calling next at all is a short-circuit. Logging wraps everything; auth can stop a request before any later step sees it. The GoF version links handler objects with setNext(). You don't need that. A list of functions and a fold make the chain, as the comparison below shows, and the result is immutable, so one pipeline serves every request on every thread. The lab's FraudChain.build copies the list it is given for the same reason: a later edit to the caller's list must not change a chain that is already in use. Reorder two interceptors Read FilterChainDemo.java (or .kt). The third request has no token; the fourth is the client's fixed retry with the same idempotency key. Predict the four responses and the number of charges. Run it with the command below. Swap auth and idempotency in the list (List.of(logging, idempotency, auth)). Predict the last two responses and charges, then run. FilterChainDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l09; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Set; /** An OkHttp-style interceptor chain in front of a charge endpoint. The order of the list is behavior. */ public class FilterChainDemo { record Request(String path, Map<String, String> headers) {} record Response(int status, String body) {} interface Chain { Response proceed(Request r); } interface Interceptor { Response intercept(Request r, Chain next); } // fold the interceptors into one chain, from the last to the first static Chain chain(List<Interceptor> interceptors, Chain terminal) { Chain next = terminal; for (int i = interceptors.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Interceptor ic = interceptors.get(i); Chain rest = next; next = r -> ic.intercept(r, rest); } return next; } public static void main(String[] args) { int[] charges = {0}; Set<String> seenKeys = new HashSet<>(); Interceptor logging = (r, next) -> { Response res = next.proceed(r); // in: nothing; out: log the status System.out.println(" log: " + r.path() + " -> " + res.status()); return res; }; Interceptor auth = (r, next) -> r.headers().containsKey("Authorization") ? next.proceed(r) : new Response(401, "no token"); // short-circuit: stop here Interceptor idempotency = (r, next) -> seenKeys.add(r.headers().get("Idempotency-Key")) ? next.proceed(r) : new Response(409, "duplicate"); Chain handler = r -> { charges[0]++; return new Response(200, "charged"); }; Chain pipeline = chain(List.of(logging, auth, idempotency), handler); String token = "Bearer t0k"; System.out.println(pipeline.proceed(new Request("/pay", Map.of("Authorization", token, "Idempotency-Key", "order-7781")))); System.out.println(pipeline.proceed(new Request("/pay", Map.of("Authorization", token, "Idempotency-Key", "order-7781")))); System.out.println(pipeline.proceed(new Request("/pay", Map.of("Idempotency-Key", "order-7782")))); // token missing System.out.println(pipeline.proceed(new Request("/pay", Map.of("Authorization", token, "Idempotency-Key", "order-7782")))); // fixed and retried System.out.println("charges: " + charges[0]); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l09.FilterChainDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l09/FilterChainDemo.java FilterChainDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l09 // An OkHttp-style interceptor chain in front of a charge endpoint. The order of the list is behavior. data class HttpRequest(val path: String, val headers: Map<String, String>) data class HttpResponse(val status: Int, val body: String) fun interface Interceptor { fun intercept(r: HttpRequest, next: (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse): HttpResponse } // fold the interceptors into one function, from the last to the first fun chain(interceptors: List<Interceptor>, terminal: (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse): (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse = interceptors.foldRight(terminal) { ic, next -> { r -> ic.intercept(r, next) } } fun main() { var charges = 0 val seenKeys = mutableSetOf<String?>() val logging = Interceptor { r, next -> next(r).also { println(" log: ${r.path} -> ${it.status}") } // in: nothing; out: log the status } val auth = Interceptor { r, next -> if ("Authorization" in r.headers) next(r) else HttpResponse(401, "no token") // short-circuit: stop here } val idempotency = Interceptor { r, next -> if (seenKeys.add(r.headers["Idempotency-Key"])) next(r) else HttpResponse(409, "duplicate") } val handler = { _: HttpRequest -> charges++; HttpResponse(200, "charged") } val pipeline = chain(listOf(logging, auth, idempotency), handler) val token = "Bearer t0k" println(pipeline(HttpRequest("/pay", mapOf("Authorization" to token, "Idempotency-Key" to "order-7781")))) println(pipeline(HttpRequest("/pay", mapOf("Authorization" to token, "Idempotency-Key" to "order-7781")))) println(pipeline(HttpRequest("/pay", mapOf("Idempotency-Key" to "order-7782")))) // token missing println(pipeline(HttpRequest("/pay", mapOf("Authorization" to token, "Idempotency-Key" to "order-7782")))) // fixed and retried println("charges: $charges") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l09.FilterChainDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l09/FilterChainDemo.kt In order: 200 charged, 409 duplicate (the same key again), 401 no token, 200 charged, and charges: 2; logging prints a line for every request, rejected ones included. After the swap, the 401 request records its key before auth rejects it, so the fixed retry gets 409 duplicate and charges: 1: the customer's payment never goes through. Each step either passes the request on or answers it. The response comes back out through every step it passed, so logging sees all of them. h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Where chains go wrong
x: Chains fail in four ways, and each looks like a bug somewhere else. Order. Interceptors run in list order, and order is behavior. Put the idempotency check before auth, and a request rejected for a missing token has already used up its idempotency key, so the client's corrected retry gets 409 and the customer is never charged. Put logging after auth, and rejected requests never reach your logs. Pin the order with a test. Forgetting next. A handler that returns without calling next and without a real answer drops the request silently. In a servlet filter, the client gets an empty 200. Every path through a handler must either call next or return a deliberate response. Calling next twice. A retry wrapped around next.proceed(r) at the front of the chain repeats everything after it: the fraud check, the idempotency check and the charge. Put retries as close as possible to the call they retry, around the PSP client, not around the pipeline. Exceptions. When a later handler throws, the code after next.proceed(r) in earlier handlers never runs. Timers, MDC cleanup (removing the request's entries from the logger's per-thread context map) and metrics belong in finally. The same shape runs your Quarkus services. A CDI interceptor's @AroundInvoke method calls InvocationContext.proceed() to continue, and JAX-RS filters and CDI interceptors are ordered by @Priority. When a filter seems not to run, check its priority before you read its code. Check yourself. In the pipeline from the last section, fraud throws for one request. Does that request get a line from logging, which is first in the list? (No. logging writes its line after next.proceed(r) returns, and that call never returns. Wrap next.proceed(r) in try/finally and log in the finally, and the request shows up, with the exception still on its way out.) The most common mistake is a default (or else) branch on the outer switch over your own sealed state type. It is often added "to be safe" or to silence a warning while the type is young. From then on, a new state compiles without a word and quietly takes whatever the default does, usually "reject every event", so disputed payments get stuck and nobody notices until support does. Leave the default off the switch over states, and let each new state break the build at every place that needs a rule. Use default only on dimensions you don't expect to grow, such as the illegal events inside one state, or on open sets you don't control, such as vendor codes.

h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Java and Kotlin
x: Building the chain: an index walker and a fold RealChain.java // OkHttp's shape: an immutable chain object that knows its position interface Chain { Response proceed(Request r); } interface Interceptor { Response intercept(Request r, Chain next); } record RealChain(List<Interceptor> interceptors, int index, Function<Request, Response> terminal) implements Chain { RealChain { interceptors = List.copyOf(interceptors); // cheap after the first time: copyOf keeps an unmodifiable list } public Response proceed(Request r) { if (index == interceptors.size()) return terminal.apply(r); // past the last link return interceptors.get(index).intercept(r, new RealChain(interceptors, index + 1, terminal)); } } Chain pipeline = new RealChain(List.of(logging, auth, idempotency), 0, handler); Chain.kt // a function type replaces the Chain interface: the chain is just (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse fun interface Interceptor { fun intercept(r: HttpRequest, next: (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse): HttpResponse } fun chain(interceptors: List<Interceptor>, terminal: (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse): (HttpRequest) -> HttpResponse = interceptors.foldRight(terminal) { ic, next -> { r -> ic.intercept(r, next) } } // wrap from the last to the first val pipeline = chain(listOf(logging, auth, idempotency), handler) Both call the interceptors in the same order and both are immutable. The Java record walks an index and creates a small chain object per step per request; that object is a natural place to carry more context, which is why OkHttp's real chain also exposes the call, its timeouts and the connection. The Kotlin fold builds the nested closures once, and next is a plain function, so no Chain interface is needed. Java can fold too, with a loop from the last interceptor to the first, as the lab's FraudChain.build does. What both languages make unnecessary is the GoF handler base class with a mutable setNext() link.

h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Worked example
x: Add chargebacks to the payment lifecycle A captured payment can now be disputed. A dispute ends either won (back to Captured) or lost (a new terminal state, ChargedBack). Start with data only: the new states and events. sealed interface PaymentState permits Created, Authorized, Captured, Refunded, Failed, Disputed, ChargedBack {} record Disputed(String id, long amount, String caseId) implements PaymentState {} // 1. new states record ChargedBack(String id, long amount) implements PaymentState {} sealed interface PaymentEvent permits Authorize, Capture, Refund, Decline, OpenDispute, WinDispute, LoseDispute {} record OpenDispute(String caseId) implements PaymentEvent {} // 2. new events record WinDispute() implements PaymentEvent {} record LoseDispute() implements PaymentEvent {} sealed interface PaymentState { // ...the five existing states, plus: data class Disputed(val id: String, val amount: Long, val caseId: String) : PaymentState // 1. new states data class ChargedBack(val id: String, val amount: Long) : PaymentState } sealed interface PaymentEvent { // ...the four existing events, plus: data class OpenDispute(val caseId: String) : PaymentEvent // 2. new events data object WinDispute : PaymentEvent data object LoseDispute : PaymentEvent } Compile before writing any rule. Every switch over PaymentState in the service fails. Count them: that is the size of the feature. Why do none of the inner event switches fail? PaymentLifecycle.java:41: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values StatusLabels.java:12: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values LedgerMetrics.java:27: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (kotlinc: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is ChargedBack', 'is Disputed' branches or an 'else' branch.) The inner switches have a default, so the new events are simply illegal in the old states until you say otherwise. Now write the rules. Note the choice in step 5: no refund while a dispute is open, because the money may be going back through the card scheme already. case Captured(var id, var amt) -> switch (e) { case Refund(var r) when r > 0 && r <= amt -> new Refunded(id, r); case OpenDispute(var caseId) -> new Disputed(id, amt, caseId); // 3. captured payments can be disputed default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Disputed(var id, var amt, var caseId) -> switch (e) { case WinDispute() -> new Captured(id, amt); // 4. won: back to captured case LoseDispute() -> new ChargedBack(id, amt); // 5. lost: terminal; no refunds meanwhile default -> throw illegal(s, e); }; case Refunded r -> throw illegal(s, e); case Failed f -> throw illegal(s, e); case ChargedBack cb -> throw illegal(s, e); // 6. terminal is PaymentState.Captured -> when (e) { is PaymentEvent.Refund if e.amount in 1..s.amount -> PaymentState.Refunded(s.id, e.amount) is PaymentEvent.OpenDispute -> PaymentState.Disputed(s.id, s.amount, e.caseId) // 3. captured payments can be disputed else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is PaymentState.Disputed -> when (e) { PaymentEvent.WinDispute -> PaymentState.Captured(s.id, s.amount) // 4. won: back to captured PaymentEvent.LoseDispute -> PaymentState.ChargedBack(s.id, s.amount) // 5. lost: terminal; no refunds meanwhile else -> throw illegal(s, e) } is PaymentState.Refunded, is PaymentState.Failed, is PaymentState.ChargedBack -> throw illegal(s, e) // 6. terminal Fix the label and metrics switches the same way, then pin the new paths in tests. Because transition is pure, a whole dispute is one replay call with no PSP and no database. @Test void lostDisputeEndsChargedBack() { var events = List.<PaymentEvent>of(new Authorize("A-77", 5_000), new Capture(), new OpenDispute("CB-310"), new LoseDispute()); assertThat(replay("p1", events)).isEqualTo(new ChargedBack("p1", 5_000)); } @Test void noRefundWhileDisputed() { assertThatThrownBy(() -> transition(new Disputed("p1", 5_000, "CB-310"), new Refund(100))) .hasMessage("Refund not allowed in Disputed"); } @Test fun `a lost dispute ends charged back`() { val events = listOf(PaymentEvent.Authorize("A-77", 5_000), PaymentEvent.Capture, PaymentEvent.OpenDispute("CB-310"), PaymentEvent.LoseDispute) val end: PaymentState = events.fold(PaymentState.Created("p1"), ::transition) assertThat(end).isEqualTo(PaymentState.ChargedBack("p1", 5_000)) } @Test fun `no refund while disputed`() { assertThatThrownBy { transition(PaymentState.Disputed("p1", 5_000, "CB-310"), PaymentEvent.Refund(100)) } .isInstanceOf(IllegalStateException::class.java) }

h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Quiz
x: In transition, the outer switch (s) lists Created, Authorized and Captured, then ends with default -> throw illegal(s, e) instead of listing Refunded and Failed. Someone adds Disputed. What happens? The build fails at that switch It compiles, and every event on a disputed payment throws at runtime Disputed payments throw NullPointerException Disputed payments throw MatchException The default covers every state not listed, including ones that don't exist yet, so the compiler has nothing to report. Disputed falls into the default and rejects every event, which looks like a stuck payment in production. MatchException is only for subtypes the compiler couldn't know about; this one it could have flagged. The rule is case Refund(var r) when r > 0 && r <= captured -> new Refunded(id, r); followed by default -> throw illegal(s, e);. A Refund(6_000) arrives for Captured("p1", 5_000). What happens? It returns Refunded("p1", 6_000) It returns Refunded("p1", 5_000) It throws IllegalStateException("Refund not allowed in Captured") It doesn't compile, because the guard can be false When a guard is false, that case doesn't match, and the switch tries the next case: here the default, which throws. Guards are part of the pattern, so an over-refund is just one more illegal move. Nothing clamps the amount. A chain is [logging, idempotency, auth]. A request with idempotency key K and no token arrives, then the client fixes its token and retries with the same key K. What does the retry get? 200 charged 401 no token 500 server error 409 duplicate Idempotency runs before auth, so the first request records K and only then gets 401. The retry finds K already used and is stopped with 409, so the customer is never charged. With auth first, the rejected request never reaches the idempotency check, and the retry goes through. Someone adds a retry interceptor at the front of the chain that calls next.proceed(r) again when the response is a 5xx. What is the risk? Every later step runs again on each retry, including the fraud check and the charge Nothing: retries are always safe in a chain The retry can't reach the terminal step Only the logging step runs twice next is the whole rest of the chain, so retrying it repeats every step after the retry interceptor, the charge included. If the PSP took the money and then timed out, the retry charges again (or, with an idempotency check in the chain, returns a confusing 409). Retry around the PSP client call, with an idempotency key. From Strategy and Template Method: a PaymentState and a FeeStrategy both hold behavior behind an interface. What actually differs? Only strategies can be lambdas The client chooses a strategy and it stays; a state machine chooses its own next state as events arrive States must be classes, strategies must be functions A strategy can't depend on data Structurally they're the same: an object holds a value and behavior depends on it. The difference is control. You pick a fee strategy once per payment method and it doesn't change itself. A payment's state moves on its own, from Authorized to Captured, as the transition function processes events.

h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Key terms
x: State machine A set of states and the events that move between them; anything not listed is illegal. Transition function A pure function from the current state and an event to the next state. Guard An extra condition on a pattern case, such as when amt > 0; if false, the case doesn't match. Exhaustive switch A switch the compiler has checked covers every possible subtype or constant. Remainder The values an exhaustive switch can still meet at run time: null and subtypes compiled later. Chain of Responsibility A request passes along a list of handlers; each answers it or passes it on. Interceptor One link in a chain: it gets the request and the rest of the chain, and can act on the way in and out. What replaces the GoF State pattern's class-per-state in Java 21 and Kotlin? Sealed states and events as records or data classes, plus one pure transition(state, event) function with an exhaustive switch or when. Why leave default off the switch over a sealed state type? So a new state fails to compile at every switch that needs a rule. A default would silently absorb it. When is default fine inside a state machine? On the inner switch over events, where most (state, event) pairs are illegal. Never on the dimension you expect to grow. An exhaustive Java switch meets a sealed subtype compiled after it. What happens? And in Kotlin? Java throws MatchException; Kotlin throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException. A null state throws NullPointerException. Why keep the transition function pure? It's tested without mocks, and history becomes a fold: replaying events rebuilds the state. Side effects run outside it. In a chain of responsibility, what are a handler's two choices? Answer now (return a response or verdict), or pass the request on by calling next. Interceptors [a, b, c]: order on the way in, and on the way out? In: a, b, c, then the terminal step. Out: c, b, a.

h: State and Chain of Responsibility · Go deeper
x: Pattern matching for switch (JEP 441) and record patterns (JEP 440) both became final in JDK 21, so everything in this lesson compiles with --release 21 and no preview flags. In Kotlin, sealed subclasses must live in the same package and module as their parent, and guards in when with a subject became stable in 2.2.0. Keeping the transition pure doesn't mean the machine does nothing. A common shape returns the next state together with a list of effects to run, such as "call the PSP", "post to the ledger" or "send a receipt", as sealed records. A thin outer layer executes them and feeds the results back in as events. Tests then assert on the returned effects, not on mocks. Temporal workflows work in a similar spirit: workflow code decides, activities do the I/O, and the history of events lets Temporal replay the workflow to rebuild its state. Event sourcing takes replay to its end: store the events, not the state, and compute the state as a fold. Long histories get slow to replay, so systems store a snapshot every few hundred events and replay only what came after. That snapshot is a memento, from lesson 10 of this track, Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento. Chain of Responsibility also shows up per method, not only per request. A CDI interceptor's @AroundInvoke method receives an InvocationContext and calls proceed() to continue to the next interceptor or the bean itself. Transactions, metrics and fault-tolerance annotations in Quarkus are built this way, which is why the proxy rules from Decorator and Proxy still apply to them.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Visitor, the expression problem, and sealed types
x: Visitor lets you add operations to a fixed set of classes without editing those classes. Here is the classic form, for a tiny expression tree: Java interface ExprVisitor<R> { R visitNum(Num n); R visitAdd(Add a); R visitMul(Mul m); } sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul { <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v); } record Num(int value) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitNum(this); } } record Add(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitAdd(this); } } record Mul(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitMul(this); } } final class Eval implements ExprVisitor<Integer> { public Integer visitNum(Num n) { return n.value(); } public Integer visitAdd(Add a) { return a.l().accept(this) + a.r().accept(this); } public Integer visitMul(Mul m) { return m.l().accept(this) * m.r().accept(this); } } int result = expr.accept(new Eval()); // double dispatch: accept picks the case, visit picks the operation Kotlin interface ExprVisitor<R> { fun visitNum(n: Num): R; fun visitAdd(a: Add): R; fun visitMul(m: Mul): R } sealed interface Expr { fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>): R } data class Num(val value: Int) : Expr { override fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>) = v.visitNum(this) } data class Add(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr { override fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>) = v.visitAdd(this) } data class Mul(val l: Expr, val r: Expr) : Expr { override fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>) = v.visitMul(this) } object Eval : ExprVisitor<Int> { override fun visitNum(n: Num) = n.value override fun visitAdd(a: Add) = a.l.accept(this) + a.r.accept(this) override fun visitMul(m: Mul) = m.l.accept(this) * m.r.accept(this) } val result = expr.accept(Eval) // double dispatch: accept picks the case, visit picks the operation A new operation, such as printing, is one new visitor class. A new case, Neg, costs a method on the visitor interface, an accept on Neg, and an edit in every visitor anyone ever wrote. That trade-off is the expression problem. With ordinary virtual methods (an eval() on each record), a new case is cheap and a new operation touches every class. With Visitor it's the other way round. Plain Java and Kotlin can't make both cheap, so you pick the axis you expect to grow. In payment code, the axis that grows is usually operations. The instruction types (card, SEPA transfer, wallet payout) change rarely, while new validations, exports, reports and fee rules arrive all the time. That favors Visitor's side of the trade. Sealed types and pattern matching give you Visitor's side of the trade without its machinery: no accept, no visitor interface, one function per operation with a switch or when inside. The comparison below shows it in both languages. Brian Goetz puts it bluntly in the pattern-matching design notes: "if your language has sufficiently powerful pattern matching, the Visitor pattern is almost completely unnecessary". The same notes say this doesn't make virtual methods wrong. So, for a closed hierarchy you own, delete the visitor. Keep Visitor when the hierarchy is open across modules, or when a library hands you one: javax.lang.model.element.ElementVisitor in annotation processors, javac's Tree API, ASM's ClassVisitor. Add a case in both styles Run VisitorVsSwitch (Java or Kotlin) and check both results agree. Add a Neg case. Java: add Neg to permits and record Neg(Expr e) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v) { return v.visitNeg(this); } }. Kotlin: data class Neg(val e: Expr) : Expr { override fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>) = v.visitNeg(this) }. Build with the demo command. Fix each error the compiler gives you, build again, and keep a count of the places you edited. Expr): String = when (e) { is Num -> e.value.toString() is Add -> "(${show(e.l)} + ${show(e.r)})" is Mul -> "${show(e.l)} * ${show(e.r)}" } fun main() { val e = Add(Num(2), Mul(Num(3), Num(4))) println("${show(e)} = ${e.accept(Eval)} (visitor) = ${eval(e)} (when)") val zero = Mul(Num(0), e) println("${show(zero)} = ${eval(zero)}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo Add the 'is Neg' branch twice. javac reports them in rounds: cannot find symbol first; add visitNeg to ExprVisitor and you get Eval is not abstract and does not override abstract method visitNeg(Neg); implement that and the two switches fail with does not cover all possible input values.
