An iterator is a librarian fetching books one at a time from the stacks, so you can start reading before the last shelf is reached. A memento is a photo of a whiteboard before you erase it. A mediator is an air-traffic tower: planes talk to the tower, never to each other. The analogy breaks on the photo. A photo can't change after you take it, but a software memento that shares a list with the live object changes every time you edit, which is the bug the lesson's demo shows.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Iterator: let Kotlin write the state machine
x: Listing every refund from a PSP means walking a cursor-paginated API: fetch a page, hand out its items, follow the next cursor, stop when it's null. Loading every page into a list first wastes memory and makes the first item wait for the last page. An iterator hands them out one at a time. In Java you write its state machine by hand: Java static Iterator<String> refunds(Function<Integer, RefundPage> fetch) { return new Iterator<>() { private Iterator<String> current = Collections.emptyIterator(); private Integer cursor = 0; // null = no more pages public boolean hasNext() { while (!current.hasNext() && cursor != null) { // while, not if: skip empty pages RefundPage page = fetch.apply(cursor); current = page.items().iterator(); cursor = page.next(); } return current.hasNext(); } public String next() { if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException(); return current.next(); } }; } Kotlin fun refunds(fetch: (Int) -> RefundPage): Sequence<String> = sequence { var cursor: Int? = 0 while (cursor != null) { val page = fetch(cursor) // runs only when the consumer needs more yieldAll(page.items) cursor = page.next } } The Java version keeps two fields of state, and hasNext holds a classic bug: write if instead of while and an empty page in the middle ends the iteration early. Kotlin's sequence {} builder lets you write the loop you'd write for a list. yield and yieldAll suspend the block until the consumer asks for the next item, and the compiler builds the state machine. Nothing runs until someone iterates, and refunds(fetch).take(2).toList() fetches one page. Remember two properties. A sequence built this way is cold: each new iteration runs the block again from the top, so iterating twice fetches every page twice. And if the consumer stops early, the rest of the block never runs. The iterator {} docs warn that "finally blocks may be left unexecuted". Don't open a connection inside the block and close it in finally; open it at the call site with use {}. When you want your own type to work in a for loop, make it Iterable and build its iterator with iterator {}, the sibling of sequence {}: class RefundLog(...) : Iterable<String> { override fun iterator() = iterator { yieldAll(...) } }. Java has no generators. Stream.iterate(seed, hasNext, next) covers simple cases, but for paging, the hand-written iterator is still the clearest Java. Count the page fetches Run PagingDemo.kt (or its Java twin, PagingDemoJava). Before you run, predict how many GET lines each of the two calls prints. Kotlin: change take(2) to take(3) and predict the number of GETs. Java: in hasNext, change while to if and predict the all: line. Run, then undo the change. PagingDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l10 // Walk a cursor-paginated refunds API lazily. The sequence builder writes the iterator's state machine. data class RefundPage(val items: List<String>, val next: Int?) private val refundPages = mapOf( 0 to RefundPage(listOf("rf_1", "rf_2"), 1), 1 to RefundPage(emptyList(), 2), // an empty page in the middle 2 to RefundPage(listOf("rf_3"), null), ) fun refunds(fetch: (Int) -> RefundPage): Sequence<String> = sequence { var cursor: Int? = 0 while (cursor != null) { val page = fetch(cursor) // runs only when the consumer needs more yieldAll(page.items) cursor = page.next } } fun main() { val fetchPage = { cursor: Int -> println(" GET /refunds?cursor=$cursor"); refundPages.getValue(cursor) } println("first two: ${refunds(fetchPage).take(2).toList()}") println("all: ${refunds(fetchPage).toList()}") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l10.PagingDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l10/PagingDemo.kt PagingDemoJava.java package workbench.patterns.l10; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; import java.util.function.Function; /** Walk a cursor-paginated refunds API lazily. Java has no generators, so the iterator's state is written by hand. */ public class PagingDemoJava { record RefundPage(List<String> items, Integer next) {} static final Map<Integer, RefundPage> PAGES = Map.of( 0, new RefundPage(List.of("rf_1", "rf_2"), 1), 1, new RefundPage(List.of(), 2), // an empty page in the middle 2, new RefundPage(List.of("rf_3"), null)); static Iterator<String> refunds(Function<Integer, RefundPage> fetch) { return new Iterator<>() { private Iterator<String> current = Collections.emptyIterator(); private Integer cursor = 0; // null = no more pages @Override public boolean hasNext() { while (!current.hasNext() && cursor != null) { // while, not if: skip empty pages RefundPage page = fetch.apply(cursor); current = page.items().iterator(); cursor = page.next(); } return current.hasNext(); } @Override public String next() { if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException(); return current.next(); } }; } static List<String> take(Iterator<String> it, int n) { List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(); while (out.size() < n && it.hasNext()) out.add(it.next()); return out; } public static void main(String[] args) { Function<Integer, RefundPage> fetchPage = cursor -> { System.out.println(" GET /refunds?cursor=" + cursor); return PAGES.get(cursor); }; System.out.println("first two: " + take(refunds(fetchPage), 2)); System.out.println("all: " + take(refunds(fetchPage), Integer.MAX_VALUE)); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l10.PagingDemoJava labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l10/PagingDemoJava.java first two: fetches only page 0; all: fetches pages 0, 1 and 2 and prints [rf_1, rf_2, rf_3]. With take(3), three GETs run, because the third item sits behind the empty page. With if in Java, the iterator fetches the empty page, finds nothing and gives up: all: [rf_1, rf_2] after two GETs, and rf_3 is silently lost. Sequences (Kotlin docs) docs iterator {} builder (Kotlin API) docs The PSP clients in your services almost certainly page: refunds, disputes, payouts, settlement lines. Expose each as a Kotlin Sequence (or a Java Iterator) that fetches lazily, and the reconciliation job can stop at the first mismatch without downloading the rest. Mind that iterating twice hits the API twice. Memento is how a back-office tool offers undo on a draft refund batch, and how an event-sourced ledger keeps snapshots so that replay stays fast. Mediator is your checkout orchestration: inside one Quarkus service it can be a small router or a shared flow, and across services it is the Temporal workflow that sequences inventory, payment and shipping activities. Visitor shows up mostly when you write annotation processors or bytecode tools; in your own domain code, sealed types and switch or when replace it.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Memento: a snapshot you can hand back
x: An analyst editing a draft refund batch adds lines, sets a note, then wants to undo. Observer and Command undid a command by running its inverse. That works for "add 30". It doesn't for "apply the discount rules", which has no clean inverse. Memento saves a snapshot of the state before the change and puts it back on undo: Java final class Cart { private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(); private String coupon = ""; interface Memento {} // what callers hold: opaque private record State(List<String> items, String coupon) implements Memento {} Memento save() { return new State(List.copyOf(items), coupon); } // copy: later edits must not leak in void restore(Memento m) { State s = (State) m; items.clear(); items.addAll(s.items()); // copy back in: the memento stays intact coupon = s.coupon(); } } Kotlin class Cart { private val items = mutableListOf<String>() private var coupon = "" interface Memento // what callers hold: opaque private data class State(val items: List<String>, val coupon: String) : Memento fun save(): Memento = State(items.toList(), coupon) // copy: later edits must not leak in fun restore(m: Memento) { val s = m as State items.clear() items += s.items // copy back in: the memento stays intact coupon = s.coupon } } Three rules make it work. The snapshot must not share mutable parts with the live object: copy the list with List.copyOf or toList(), or later edits leak into the saved state. Restore must copy back in rather than point at the memento's list, so the same memento can be restored twice. And only the originator reads it. Callers get an opaque Memento to store and hand back, while the record with the data is private, so nothing else depends on the cart's insides. When the whole state is already an immutable record or data class, the pattern almost disappears: the state is its own memento, and an undo history is a List<State>. That is a strong argument for immutable aggregates. There are two costs. History grows with every checkpoint, so bound it; the lab keeps the newest N. And snapshots of large aggregates are expensive, which is why event-sourced systems store one every few hundred events and replay the rest. Let the snapshot share the list Run MementoDemo in either language and read both lines. In save(), store the live list instead of a copy: new State(items, coupon) in Java, State(items, coupon) in Kotlin. Predict the restored: line, then run. Put the copy back. MementoDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l10; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** A cart that can hand out a snapshot of itself and later put it back. */ public class MementoDemo { static final class Cart { private final List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(); private String coupon = ""; void add(String item) { items.add(item); } void coupon(String code) { coupon = code; } @Override public String toString() { return items + " coupon=" + coupon; } // callers see an opaque Memento; only Cart can read the State inside it interface Memento {} private record State(List<String> items, String coupon) implements Memento {} Memento save() { return new State(List.copyOf(items), coupon); // copy: later edits must not leak in } void restore(Memento m) { State s = (State) m; items.clear(); items.addAll(s.items()); // copy back in: the memento stays as it was coupon = s.coupon(); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Cart cart = new Cart(); cart.add("sku-1"); Cart.Memento before = cart.save(); cart.add("sku-2"); cart.coupon("AUTUMN10"); System.out.println("edited: " + cart); cart.restore(before); System.out.println("restored: " + cart); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l10.MementoDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l10/MementoDemo.java MementoDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l10 // A cart that can hand out a snapshot of itself and later put it back. class Cart { private val items = mutableListOf<String>() private var coupon = "" fun add(item: String) { items += item } fun coupon(code: String) { coupon = code } override fun toString() = "$items coupon=$coupon" // callers see an opaque Memento; only Cart can read the State inside it interface Memento private data class State(val items: List<String>, val coupon: String) : Memento fun save(): Memento = State(items.toList(), coupon) // copy: later edits must not leak in fun restore(m: Memento) { val s = m as State items.clear() items += s.items // copy back in: the memento stays as it was coupon = s.coupon } } fun main() { val cart = Cart() cart.add("sku-1") val before = cart.save() cart.add("sku-2") cart.coupon("AUTUMN10") println("edited: $cart") cart.restore(before) println("restored: $cart") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l10.MementoDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l10/MementoDemo.kt edited: [sku-1, sku-2] coupon=AUTUMN10, then restored: [sku-1] coupon=. Without the copy, the memento and the cart share one list. sku-2 lands in the "saved" state too, and restore then clears that shared list before copying from it, so you get restored: [] coupon=: worse than no undo at all.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Mediator in brief
x: A checkout touches inventory, payments, shipping and email, and each reacts to the others: missing stock means a refund, a captured payment means ship and send a receipt. If every service calls the ones it reacts to, four services need six links, and every new rule edits two of them. A mediator owns the coordination, and each colleague talks only to it: Java interface Colleague { void receive(String event); } final class CheckoutMediator { private final Map<String, List<Colleague>> routes = new HashMap<>(); void on(String event, Colleague c) { routes.computeIfAbsent(event, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(c); } void emit(String event) { routes.getOrDefault(event, List.of()).forEach(c -> c.receive(event)); } } mediator.on("payment.captured", shipping); mediator.on("payment.captured", email); mediator.on("stock.missing", payments); // payments refunds; inventory never calls payments directly Kotlin fun interface Colleague { fun receive(event: String) } class CheckoutMediator { private val routes = mutableMapOf<String, MutableList<Colleague>>() fun on(event: String, c: Colleague) { routes.getOrPut(event) { mutableListOf() } += c } fun emit(event: String) { routes[event].orEmpty().forEach { it.receive(event) } } } mediator.on("payment.captured", shipping) mediator.on("payment.captured", email) mediator.on("stock.missing", payments) // payments refunds; inventory never calls payments directly Mediator and Observer look alike. An observer is one subject telling many listeners about itself. A mediator sits between many parties and holds the rules about who reacts to what. In coroutine code, a MutableSharedFlow<CheckoutEvent> that all colleagues share is a natural mediator bus. Across services, the mediator becomes a message broker or a saga orchestrator: a Temporal workflow that calls the inventory, payment and shipping activities in order is a mediator with durable state. The risk is the god object. A mediator should route and sequence. When it starts computing fees or validating addresses, move that logic back to the colleague that owns it. Check yourself. A new rule arrives: when stock is missing, shipping must cancel the parcel it has booked. With the mediator above, what do you change? (One registration, mediator.on("stock.missing", shipping), plus shipping's own handling of that event. Inventory doesn't change, and it still knows nothing about shipping.) Without a mediator every service knows the others. With one, each knows only the hub, and the coordination rules live in one place. The most common Memento mistake is a shallow snapshot: save() stores a reference to the object's live mutable list (or an array, or a mutable nested object) instead of a copy. It happens because records and data classes look immutable, so new State(items, coupon) feels like a snapshot. It isn't: the record holds the same list the object keeps editing, so the "saved" state changes with every edit, and undo restores the present instead of the past. Copy every mutable part when you save (List.copyOf, toList()), copy again when you restore, and test it the way the lab does: save, edit, restore, edit again, restore again.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Java and Kotlin
x: Replacing a visitor: nested patterns in Java, guards in Kotlin Expr.java sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul {} record Num(int value) implements Expr {} record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {} record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {} static int eval(Expr e) { return switch (e) { case Num(var v) -> v; case Add(var l, var r) -> eval(l) + eval(r); case Mul(Num(var z), var r) when z == 0 -> 0; // nested record pattern: skip the right side case Mul(var l, var r) -> eval(l) * eval(r); }; } static String show(Expr e) { // a new operation: one new function, no class touched return switch (e) { case Num(var v) -> Integer.toString(v); case Add(var l, var r) -> "(" + show(l) + " + " + show(r) + ")"; case Mul(var l, var r) -> show(l) + " * " + show(r); }; } Expr.kt sealed interface Expr data class Num(val value: Int) : Expr data class Add(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr data class Mul(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr fun eval(e: Expr): Int = when (e) { is Num -> e.value is Add -> eval(e.left) + eval(e.right) is Mul if e.left == Num(0) -> 0 // no nested patterns in Kotlin: a guard says it is Mul -> eval(e.left) * eval(e.right) } fun show(e: Expr): String = when (e) { // a new operation: one new function, no class touched is Num -> e.value.toString() is Add -> "(${show(e.left)} + ${show(e.right)})" is Mul -> "${show(e.left)} * ${show(e.right)}" } Both delete the visitor interface and every accept method, and both make a new operation a single function. The difference is how far the patterns reach. Java 21 record patterns nest, so Mul(Num(var z), var r) when z == 0 matches "a multiplication whose left side is the literal 0" in one case, and binds the fields as it goes. Kotlin's when matches on type and smart-casts, but has no destructuring patterns, so the same rule is a guard (is Mul if e.left == Num(0)), which works because data classes compare by value. Guards in when are stable since Kotlin 2.2.0. In both, adding a case such as Neg breaks every function that switches over Expr, which is the compiler listing your work.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Worked example
x: Retire a visitor in four steps A fee-formula engine evaluates and prints expressions with a classic visitor. Product wants negation. Before reading on, list every file a Neg node touches in this design. interface ExprVisitor<R> { R visitNum(Num n); R visitAdd(Add a); R visitMul(Mul m); } sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul { <R> R accept(ExprVisitor<R> v); } // Num, Add, Mul: each record implements accept(v) by calling its own visitXxx(this) final class Eval implements ExprVisitor<Integer> { /* three visit methods */ } final class Show implements ExprVisitor<String> { /* three visit methods */ } // ...and any visitor another team wrote against ExprVisitor interface ExprVisitor<R> { fun visitNum(n: Num): R; fun visitAdd(a: Add): R; fun visitMul(m: Mul): R } sealed interface Expr { fun <R> accept(v: ExprVisitor<R>): R } // Num, Add, Mul: each data class implements accept(v) by calling its own visitXxx(this) object Eval : ExprVisitor<Int> { /* three visit methods */ } object Show : ExprVisitor<String> { /* three visit methods */ } // ...and any visitor another team wrote against ExprVisitor Neg needs a visitNeg on the interface, an accept on itself, and a new method in Eval, Show and every other visitor. The hierarchy is closed and ours, so retire the machinery first: drop accept and the interface, and write each operation as a switch. Behavior doesn't change; run the old tests. sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul {} // 1. no accept, no visitor interface record Num(int value) implements Expr {} record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {} record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr {} static int eval(Expr e) { // 2. each visitor becomes one function return switch (e) { case Num(var v) -> v; case Add(var l, var r) -> eval(l) + eval(r); case Mul(var l, var r) -> eval(l) * eval(r); }; } sealed interface Expr // 1. no accept, no visitor interface data class Num(val value: Int) : Expr data class Add(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr data class Mul(val left: Expr, val right: Expr) : Expr fun eval(e: Expr): Int = when (e) { // 2. each visitor becomes one function is Num -> e.value is Add -> eval(e.left) + eval(e.right) is Mul -> eval(e.left) * eval(e.right) } Now add the case, and compile before writing any logic. The errors are the to-do list: one per function that switches over Expr. sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul, Neg {} record Neg(Expr e) implements Expr {} // 3. the new case // javac: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (eval) // javac: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (show) data class Neg(val e: Expr) : Expr // 3. the new case // kotlinc: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Neg' branch or an 'else' branch. (eval) // kotlinc: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Neg' branch or an 'else' branch. (show) Fill in one branch per function. A brand-new operation, counting nodes for a complexity limit, is one more function, and no type changes at all. case Neg(var x) -> -eval(x); // 4. in eval case Neg(var x) -> "-" + show(x); // in show static int count(Expr e) { // 5. a new operation: one function return switch (e) { case Num n -> 1; case Add(var l, var r) -> 1 + count(l) + count(r); case Mul(var l, var r) -> 1 + count(l) + count(r); case Neg(var x) -> 1 + count(x); }; } is Neg -> -eval(e.e) // 4. in eval is Neg -> "-${show(e.e)}" // in show fun count(e: Expr): Int = when (e) { // 5. a new operation: one function is Num -> 1 is Add -> 1 + count(e.left) + count(e.right) is Mul -> 1 + count(e.left) + count(e.right) is Neg -> 1 + count(e.e) }

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Quiz
x: Your team owns a sealed PaymentInstruction hierarchy with five records, and keeps adding operations: validate, render, price, export. Which design makes each new operation cheapest? A classic Visitor with an accept method on each record An abstract method per operation on the sealed interface One function per operation with an exhaustive switch or when instanceof chains with a final else that throws Operations are the axis that grows, so you want operations to be single functions: a sealed switch gives that, with the compiler checking each one covers all five records. A Visitor gets the same trade-off with more machinery. Abstract methods make each new operation touch all five records, and an instanceof chain loses the compiler's check. A Java paging iterator has if (!current.hasNext() && cursor != null) in hasNext. Pages are [rf_1, rf_2], then an empty page, then [rf_3]. What does a full iteration return? [rf_1, rf_2] [rf_1, rf_2, rf_3] It throws NoSuchElementException It loops forever After rf_2, hasNext fetches the empty page once, finds nothing, and returns false, because if doesn't try again. The iteration ends early and rf_3 is never seen, with no error. while keeps fetching until it finds an item or runs out of pages. val refunds = pagedSequence(fetch) uses the sequence {} builder. The code calls refunds.count() and then refunds.first(). How many times is page 0 fetched? Once: a sequence caches its pages Twice: each terminal operation runs the block again from the top Never: sequences are lazy Once, but only if the pages are small A sequence from sequence {} is cold: every new iteration starts the block over. count() walks all pages and first() starts again from page 0. If you need the items twice, collect them once with toList(), or accept the second round of API calls. Draft.save() returns new State(lines, note), where lines is the draft's own ArrayList. The analyst saves, adds a line, and restores. What do they get? The draft as it was at save time An UnsupportedOperationException A ConcurrentModificationException The draft with the new line still in it, because the snapshot shares the live list The record holds a reference to the same list the draft keeps editing, so the new line is in the "saved" state too. Depending on how restore copies, you get the present back or even an empty list. Copy every mutable part on save (List.copyOf) and on restore. From Observer and Command: an analyst's draft supports undo for "add line" and for "apply discount rules", which has no simple inverse. Which approach handles both? A command stack where every command implements undo() A memento saved before each edit, restored on undo A StateFlow of the draft that collectors can rewind A Chain of Responsibility of undo handlers Command-based undo needs an inverse for every command, and "apply discount rules" doesn't have a clean one. A snapshot taken before any edit can always be restored, whatever the edit did. The two combine well: commands for the log, mementos for the undo. A StateFlow keeps only the latest value, so there is nothing to rewind to.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Key terms
x: Visitor One class per operation, with a method per case, called through accept on each element. Double dispatch Choosing code by two runtime types: accept picks the case, visit picks the operation. Expression problem No plain design makes both new cases and new operations cheap; you pick the axis that grows. Iterator An object that hands out a collection's elements one at a time without exposing how they are stored. Cold sequence A sequence whose work reruns for every iteration, from the start. Memento An opaque snapshot of an object's state that only the object can read and restore. Mediator A hub that holds the rules for how several parts react to each other, so they don't call each other. What is the expression problem, in one line each? Virtual methods: new cases are cheap, new operations touch every class. Visitor (or sealed + switch): new operations are cheap, new cases touch every operation. When does Visitor still fit in modern Java or Kotlin? For open hierarchies across modules, or when a library hands you one: ElementVisitor in annotation processors, javac's Tree API, ASM's ClassVisitor. Java pattern for "a multiplication whose left side is 0"? And Kotlin? Java 21: case Mul(Num(var z), var r) when z == 0. Kotlin: is Mul if e.left == Num(0) (no nested patterns). Why while, not if, in a paging iterator's hasNext? An empty page must not end the iteration; while keeps fetching until it finds an item or runs out of pages. Iterating a sequence {} twice: what happens to the work inside it? It runs again from the top: sequences built that way are cold. Collect with toList() if you need the items twice. Why can finally inside sequence {} or iterator {} fail to run? If the consumer stops early, the rest of the block never runs. Open resources at the call site with use {}. What makes a memento safe? It copies every mutable part on save, restore copies back in, only the originator can read it, and the history is bounded.

h: Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento · Go deeper
x: Kotlin's sequence {} is built on the same machinery as coroutines, but restricted. Its block runs on a SequenceScope, which allows only yield and yieldAll to suspend, so you can't call delay or another suspend function inside it. For asynchronous paging, where each page fetch is itself a suspending HTTP call, use flow {} and emit instead: a Flow is the suspending cousin of a sequence, cold in the same way, as you saw in Flow basics: cold streams and operators in the coroutines track. Java's Iterator has an optional remove(), and its Javadoc says iterators "allow the caller to remove elements from the underlying collection during the iteration with well-defined semantics". That's why iterator.remove() is safe inside a loop where list.remove(x) throws ConcurrentModificationException. For paging iterators, leave remove() unsupported, which is the default. Visitor and Composite often travel together: a visitor walks a composite tree. With sealed types, the walk is just recursion in each function, as in Composite, Bridge and Flyweight. If trees get deep enough to overflow the stack, an explicit stack in an iterator (or a sequence {} that pushes children) turns the recursion into iteration. Memento meets event sourcing in snapshots. An aggregate's state is the fold of its events. Replaying ten thousand events on every load is slow, so the store keeps a snapshot every few hundred events, and loading means restoring the newest snapshot and replaying what came after it. The snapshot format then becomes a contract between versions of your code, so give it a version field from the start.

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Hand-offs: producer-consumer, worker pools, thread-per-message
x: The safest way to share work between threads is to share a queue and nothing else. In producer-consumer, producers put work into a BlockingQueue, consumers take it out, and the queue does all the locking and waiting: Java BlockingQueue<Msg> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16); // bounded: a full queue makes the producer wait for (int c = 0; c < 4; c++) { pool.submit(() -> { while (true) { if (queue.take() instanceof Stop) return null; // poison pill: this consumer is done processed.incrementAndGet(); } }); } for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) queue.put(new Job(i)); for (int c = 0; c < 4; c++) queue.put(new Stop()); // one pill PER consumer Kotlin val channel = Channel<Int>(capacity = 16) // bounded: send suspends when full val workers = List(4) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { for (job in channel) processed.incrementAndGet() // ends when the channel is closed and drained } } repeat(1_000) { channel.send(it) } channel.close() // one call stops every worker Three rules from Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers still hold. Bound the queue: a full ArrayBlockingQueue(16) makes a fast producer wait, which is backpressure, while an unbounded queue hides overload until the heap runs out. Send one poison pill per consumer, because each pill stops exactly one. And don't swallow InterruptedException: it is how a pool tells its workers to stop. Kotlin's channel removes the pill: close() ends every for (job in channel) loop once the buffer is empty. Use a for loop in each worker, not consumeEach, which cancels the channel when its own loop ends. A worker pool is the same picture with the queue inside an ExecutorService. A fixed pool of platform threads still suits CPU-bound work. For blocking I/O, Java 21 brought back thread-per-message: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts a virtual thread for every task, and Kotlin launches a coroutine per message. Both make it trivial to send ten thousand concurrent requests to a PSP that accepts fifty, so thread-per-message always comes with a limit. That limit is the bulkhead, two sections down. Forget a poison pill Run ProducerConsumerDemo (Java or Kotlin) with the command below. Java: replace the pill loop with a single queue.put(new Stop());. Kotlin: delete channel.close(). Predict both numbers in the output line, then run. Put it back. ProducerConsumerDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l11; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** One producer, four consumers, a bounded queue, and one poison pill per consumer. */ public class ProducerConsumerDemo { sealed interface Msg permits Job, Stop {} record Job(int id) implements Msg {} record Stop() implements Msg {} public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int consumers = 4, jobs = 1_000; BlockingQueue<Msg> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16); // bounded: a full queue makes the producer wait AtomicInteger processed = new AtomicInteger(); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++) { pool.submit(() -> { while (true) { Msg m = queue.take(); if (m instanceof Stop) return null; // this consumer is done processed.incrementAndGet(); } }); } for (int i = 0; i < jobs; i++) queue.put(new Job(i)); for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++) queue.put(new Stop()); // one pill PER consumer pool.shutdown(); boolean finished = pool.awaitTermination(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.println("processed " + processed + " of " + jobs + ", all consumers finished: " + finished); if (!finished) { pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupt the ones still blocked in take() System.out.println("some consumers never got a pill and were still waiting in take()"); } } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l11.ProducerConsumerDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l11/ProducerConsumerDemo.java ProducerConsumerDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.joinAll import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds // One producer, four consumers, a bounded channel, and close() as the poison pill for all of them. fun main() = runBlocking { val jobs = 1_000 val channel = Channel<Int>(capacity = 16) // bounded: send suspends when full val processed = AtomicInteger() val workers = List(4) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { for (job in channel) processed.incrementAndGet() // ends when the channel is closed and drained } } repeat(jobs) { channel.send(it) } channel.close() // one call stops every worker val finished = withTimeoutOrNull(2.seconds) { workers.joinAll() } != null println("processed $processed of $jobs, all workers finished: $finished") if (!finished) { workers.forEach { it.cancel() } println("the workers were still waiting to receive: nobody closed the channel") } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l11.ProducerConsumerDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l11/ProducerConsumerDemo.kt processed 1000 of 1000, all consumers finished: true. With one pill, all 1,000 jobs are still processed, but after the two-second wait the line reads all consumers finished: false, and the demo reports that consumers were still waiting in take(). Three of the four never got a pill. In Kotlin without close(), the workers wait forever for the next element: all workers finished: false. In a service, that is a shutdown that hangs. BlockingQueue.java at jdk-25-ga (the producer-consumer example) read Channels (Kotlin docs) docs Picture a restaurant kitchen. The order rail is producer-consumer: waiters clip tickets on, cooks take them off, and a full rail tells the waiters to slow down. Each station has four burners, so a run on soup can't take the grill's burners: a bulkhead. When the fryer catches fire, someone hangs a sign saying "no fried food for ten minutes", and orders that need it are refused at the door instead of waiting forever: the breaker opening. When the dishwasher is already running, nobody starts a second one: balking. The analogy breaks on knowing why. A kitchen can see the fire. A breaker only counts failures, so you must tell it which errors mean "the dependency is sick" and which, like a declined card, mean the dependency is working perfectly.

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Who owns the state: the patterns you already know
x: Most of the remaining concurrency patterns answer one question: who owns this state, and what happens to callers who arrive at the wrong moment? You've met them all in earlier tracks: Pattern Problem Java 21+ Kotlin Taught in Immutable object share state with no locks records with List.copyOf data class with vals and copied lists Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal Active object one owner for mutable state a single-thread executor as a mailbox; methods return CompletableFuture a coroutine that owns the state and reads commands from a Channel Observer and Command (the command worker) Guarded suspension wait until a condition holds wait() in a while loop, or better CompletableFuture, CountDownLatch, Condition CompletableDeferred.await(), which suspends wait, notify and guarded blocks Balking don't start if it's already running AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true) the same, or Mutex.tryLock() Atomics and compare-and-set Read-write lock many readers, rare writers ReentrantReadWriteLock (no read-to-write upgrade), or an AtomicReference to an immutable snapshot the same Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock Future / promise a result that arrives later CompletableFuture with your own executor async and await inside coroutineScope CompletableFuture: composing async steps Balking is the one people get wrong most often. A settlement job that runs on a schedule, on retries and from an operator's button must never run twice at once. If it is already running, the right answer is to return at once, not to wait: Java final class SettlementJob { private final AtomicBoolean running = new AtomicBoolean(); boolean runIfIdle(Runnable settle) { if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return false; // balk: a run is in progress try { settle.run(); return true; } finally { running.set(false); } } } Kotlin class SettlementJob { private val mutex = Mutex() suspend fun runIfIdle(settle: suspend () -> Unit): Boolean { if (!mutex.tryLock()) return false // balk: a run is in progress try { settle() return true } finally { mutex.unlock() } } } The plain-boolean version, if (running) return; running = true;, is check-then-act and lets two runs overlap. And an AtomicBoolean protects one JVM only. With three pods, each pod has its own flag, so a run that must be unique across the fleet needs a database lock or a lease. Turn the balk into check-then-act Run SettlementJobDemo in either language: eight triggers fire at the same moment. Read the line. Replace the compareAndSet line with three lines: if (running.get()) return false;, then for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); (Kotlin: repeat(1_000) { Thread.onSpinWait() }), then running.set(true);. Run it four or five times and watch most runs at once. Then restore the compareAndSet. SettlementJobDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l11; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Balking: eight triggers fire at once, and the settlement run refuses to start while one is in progress. */ public class SettlementJobDemo { static final class SettlementJob { private final AtomicBoolean running = new AtomicBoolean(); boolean runIfIdle(Runnable settle) { if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return false; // balk: a run is already in progress try { settle.run(); return true; } finally { running.set(false); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { SettlementJob job = new SettlementJob(); AtomicInteger inside = new AtomicInteger(), mostAtOnce = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger ran = new AtomicInteger(), balked = new AtomicInteger(); Runnable settle = () -> { mostAtOnce.accumulateAndGet(inside.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); for (int i = 0; i < 2_000_000; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); // settling takes a moment inside.decrementAndGet(); }; CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] triggers = new Thread[8]; // the scheduler, a retry, an operator's button... for (int t = 0; t < triggers.length; t++) { triggers[t] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } if (job.runIfIdle(settle)) ran.incrementAndGet(); else balked.incrementAndGet(); }); triggers[t].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : triggers) t.join(); System.out.println("ran " + ran + ", balked " + balked + ", most runs at once: " + mostAtOnce); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l11.SettlementJobDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l11/SettlementJobDemo.java SettlementJobDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l11 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Balking: eight triggers fire at once, and the settlement run refuses to start while one is in progress. class SettlementJob { private val running = AtomicBoolean() fun runIfIdle(settle: () -> Unit): Boolean { if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return false // balk: a run is already in progress try { settle() return true } finally { running.set(false) } } } fun main() { val job = SettlementJob() val inside = AtomicInteger() val mostAtOnce = AtomicInteger() val ran = AtomicInteger() val balked = AtomicInteger() val settle = { mostAtOnce.accumulateAndGet(inside.incrementAndGet(), ::maxOf) repeat(2_000_000) { Thread.onSpinWait() } // settling takes a moment inside.decrementAndGet() Unit } val go = CountDownLatch(1) val triggers = List(8) { // the scheduler, a retry, an operator's button... thread { go.await() if (job.runIfIdle(settle)) ran.incrementAndGet() else balked.incrementAndGet() } } go.countDown() triggers.forEach { it.join() } println("ran $ran, balked $balked, most runs at once: $mostAtOnce") } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l11.SettlementJobDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l11/SettlementJobDemo.kt With compareAndSet, most runs at once is always 1, and usually ran 1, balked 7. With check-then-act, several triggers pass the check before any of them sets the flag, so most runs print 2 or 3 for most runs at once: two settlement runs over the same batch at the same time. It is the race from the concurrency track, inside a pattern. ReentrantReadWriteLock.java at jdk-25-ga (no read-to-write upgrade) read Your Kafka consumers are producer-consumer at the scale of a cluster: partitions are the queues, and a consumer per partition is the confinement that keeps per-account ordering safe. Your Quarkus services already speak these patterns through SmallRye Fault Tolerance's @CircuitBreaker, @Bulkhead, @Retry and @Timeout, which are interceptor-based, so they need calls that go through the proxy. Temporal brings its own retry policy for activities: don't add a second retry around the PSP call inside the activity, or one failure becomes nine calls. And breakers are per instance: with six pods, each pod has its own breaker and its own view of the issuer, so the fleet keeps probing a dead issuer six times as often as one pod would.

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Bulkhead: cap the calls to each dependency
x: Virtual threads make threads cheap. They don't make your dependencies cheap. The card issuer accepts 50 concurrent requests, the Oracle pool has 20 connections, and the fraud service slows to a crawl above 100. A bulkhead caps how many calls run against one dependency at once, so a slow dependency can use up its own share and nothing else. The name comes from ships: watertight walls keep one leak from flooding the hull. Java final class Bulkhead { private final Semaphore permits; Bulkhead(int maxConcurrent) { permits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrent); } <T> T call(Supplier<T> op) { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw new BulkheadFull(); // fail fast: don't queue behind slow calls try { return op.get(); } finally { permits.release(); // always, or the limit shrinks for good } } } Kotlin class Bulkhead(maxConcurrent: Int) { private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent) // kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore suspend fun <T> call(op: suspend () -> T): T { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw BulkheadFull() // fail fast: don't queue behind slow calls try { return op() } finally { permits.release() // always, or the limit shrinks for good } } } tryAcquire() makes the bulkhead fail fast: a call over the limit gets an error at once instead of waiting behind the slow ones. Resilience4j's semaphore bulkhead does the same by default (maxConcurrentCalls = 25, maxWaitDuration = 0). acquire() would wait, which turns the bulkhead into a limiter. That's fine for a batch job, and risky on a request path, where waiting requests pile up until the caller times out. Size each bulkhead to its dependency, not to your threads. A bulkhead of 30 in front of a 20-connection pool still queues ten callers inside the pool. With virtual threads, a semaphore is the natural limiter (Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores); a separate thread pool per dependency brings back the pools that virtual threads let you drop. Spring Framework 7 ships the same idea as @ConcurrencyLimit, applied through a proxy, so the self-invocation rule from Decorator and Proxy applies to it. Wait for a permit, or fail fast Run BulkheadDemo (Java or Kotlin). It sends 200 calls that each take 20 ms through a 20-permit semaphore, first with acquire() (wait), then with tryAcquire() (fail fast). Predict both lines first. Change the semaphore from 20 permits to 200 and run again. Predict most in flight before you look. Put it back to 20. BulkheadDemo.java package workbench.patterns.l11; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 200 virtual threads call a PSP that should see at most 20 at once: wait for a permit, or fail fast. */ public class BulkheadDemo { static void run(String mode, boolean failFast) throws InterruptedException { Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(20); AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger(), mostInFlight = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger done = new AtomicInteger(), rejected = new AtomicInteger(); long start = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) { ex.submit(() -> { if (failFast) { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) { rejected.incrementAndGet(); return null; } // bulkhead: reject now } else { permits.acquire(); // limiter: wait in line } try { mostInFlight.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); Thread.sleep(20); // the PSP takes 20 ms inFlight.decrementAndGet(); done.incrementAndGet(); } finally { permits.release(); } return null; }); } } // close() waits for all tasks long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%-10s done %3d, rejected %3d, most in flight %2d, about %d ms%n", mode, done.get(), rejected.get(), mostInFlight.get(), ms); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("wait", false); run("fail fast", true); } } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l11.BulkheadDemo labs/patterns/src/demo/java/workbench/patterns/l11/BulkheadDemo.java BulkheadDemo.kt package workbench.patterns.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger // 200 coroutines call a PSP that should see at most 20 at once: wait for a permit, or fail fast. suspend fun runBulkhead(mode: String, failFast: Boolean) { val permits = Semaphore(20) val inFlight = AtomicInteger() val mostInFlight = AtomicInteger() val done = AtomicInteger() val rejected = AtomicInteger() val start = System.nanoTime() coroutineScope { // waits for all 200 children repeat(200) { launch { if (failFast) { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) { rejected.incrementAndGet(); return@launch } // bulkhead: reject now } else { permits.acquire() // limiter: wait in line } try { mostInFlight.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), ::maxOf) delay(20) // the PSP takes 20 ms inFlight.decrementAndGet() done.incrementAndGet() } finally { permits.release() } } } } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000 println("%-10s done %3d, rejected %3d, most in flight %2d, about %d ms".format(mode, done.get(), rejected.get(), mostInFlight.get(), ms)) } fun main() = runBlocking { runBulkhead("wait", failFast = false) runBulkhead("fail fast", failFast = true) } ./gradlew :patterns:demo -Pmain=workbench.patterns.l11.BulkheadDemoKt labs/patterns/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/patterns/l11/BulkheadDemo.kt Waiting: done 200, rejected 0, most in flight 20, in a bit over 200 ms (ten waves of 20). Fail fast: about done 20, rejected 180, in about 20 ms. The exact split can vary slightly between runs. With 200 permits, most in flight jumps to 200 in both modes: nothing protects the PSP. h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Circuit breaker: State, Decorator and compare-and-set in one class
x: A circuit breaker's three states live in one AtomicReference, and compare-and-set picks the single probe A bulkhead limits how much a failing dependency can hurt you. A circuit breaker stops calling it for a while. After a run of failures the breaker opens, and calls fail at once without a network trip. That gives the issuer room to recover and gives your callers a quick answer instead of a two-second timeout. After a cool-down the breaker goes half-open and lets one probe through: success closes it, failure opens it again. The breaker is this track's capstone, because it is three earlier patterns in one class. Its states are sealed records with a transition, as in State and Chain of Responsibility. Its call(op) wraps any operation behind the same shape, as a decorator does. And its state lives in an AtomicReference that changes by compare-and-set, so a thousand request threads can share it without a lock: Java sealed interface State permits Closed, Open, HalfOpen {} record Closed(int consecutiveFailures) implements State {} record Open(Instant until) implements State {} record HalfOpen() implements State {} private final AtomicReference<State> state = new AtomicReference<>(new Closed(0)); // after a failed call: one pure transition, applied atomically state.updateAndGet(cur -> switch (cur) { case HalfOpen h -> new Open(clock.instant().plus(openFor)); // the probe failed case Closed(var n) when n + 1 >= threshold -> new Open(clock.instant().plus(openFor)); // trip case Closed(var n) -> new Closed(n + 1); case Open o -> o; // already open }); Kotlin sealed interface State { data class Closed(val consecutiveFailures: Int) : State data class Open(val until: Instant) : State data object HalfOpen : State } private val state = AtomicReference<State>(State.Closed(0)) // after a failed call: one pure transition, applied atomically state.updateAndGet { cur -> when (cur) { State.HalfOpen -> State.Open(clock.instant() + openFor) // the probe failed is State.Closed if cur.consecutiveFailures + 1 >= threshold -> State.Open(clock.instant() + openFor) // trip is State.Closed -> State.Closed(cur.consecutiveFailures + 1) is State.Open -> cur // already open } } Two choices make it testable and correct. Time comes from an injected Clock, so a test moves time forward 31 seconds at once instead of sleeping. And the move from open to half-open is a compareAndSet: when the cool-down ends and many threads arrive together, exactly one wins the right to probe, and the rest are still rejected. In production, use a library. Resilience4j 2.4.0 adds sliding windows, failure-rate and slow-call thresholds, metrics and events. Learn its defaults before you trust a test: minimumNumberOfCalls is 100, so a breaker that fails five calls in a unit test never opens, and waitDurationInOpenState is 60 seconds. And decide what counts as a failure. A declined card means the issuer is working fine, so it must not trip the breaker. Check yourself. The breaker opened at 10:00:00 with a 30-second cool-down. A test moves the fake clock to 10:00:31, and eight threads call at the same moment. How many calls reach the issuer, and what picks them? (One. Each thread tries the compareAndSet from Open to HalfOpen, and exactly one succeeds and runs the probe. The other seven find the state already changed and are rejected.) The breaker's three states. Only one probe runs in half-open; its result decides whether the breaker closes or opens again. Resilience4j CircuitBreakerConfig.java (defaults) read The most common mistake is retrying at every layer. The mobile app retries three times, the API gateway retries three times, the payment service's client retries three times, and Temporal retries the activity. One user tap becomes dozens of calls to an issuer that is already struggling, and the retries keep it down. It happens because each team adds a retry to make their own layer reliable, and nobody sees the product. Retry in one place, close to the call, only for idempotent operations or with an idempotency key, with backoff and jitter. Never retry a CallNotPermitted or a full bulkhead: those mean "stop", not "try again".

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Java and Kotlin
x: Guarded suspension: waiting for a 3-D Secure callback ChallengeResults.java // the request thread waits until the issuer's webhook arrives, or gives up after a timeout final class ChallengeResults { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>> pending = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); String awaitResult(String paymentId, Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException, TimeoutException { CompletableFuture<String> slot = pending.computeIfAbsent(paymentId, id -> new CompletableFuture<>()); try { return slot.get(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // blocks this thread until completed } finally { pending.remove(paymentId); } } // the webhook thread completes the guard; a callback that comes first is kept for the waiter void onCallback(String paymentId, String result) { pending.computeIfAbsent(paymentId, id -> new CompletableFuture<>()).complete(result); } } ChallengeResults.kt // the request coroutine waits until the issuer's webhook arrives, or gives up after a timeout class ChallengeResults { private val pending = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableDeferred<String>>() suspend fun awaitResult(paymentId: String, timeout: Duration): String { val slot = pending.computeIfAbsent(paymentId) { CompletableDeferred() } try { return withTimeout(timeout) { slot.await() } // suspends: no thread is held while waiting } finally { pending.remove(paymentId) } } // the webhook handler completes the guard; a callback that comes first is kept for the waiter fun onCallback(paymentId: String, result: String) { pending.computeIfAbsent(paymentId) { CompletableDeferred() }.complete(result) } } Both replace the hand-written wait() in a while loop with a one-shot promise, which can't miss a signal or wake up spuriously: complete happens once, and get or await returns as soon as it has. The difference is what waiting costs. CompletableFuture.get blocks a thread; on a virtual thread that is cheap, but it is still a thread per waiting payment. CompletableDeferred.await suspends the coroutine and holds no thread at all, and withTimeout cancels the wait cleanly. Java needs three checked exceptions in the signature; Kotlin needs none, and the timeout arrives as a TimeoutCancellationException. One gap is shared: a callback that arrives after the waiter gave up leaves an entry in the map, so a real version also expires old entries.

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Worked example
x: Put retry, breaker and bulkhead in the right order Three pieces from this lesson wrap one PSP charge. The order of the wrappers decides what happens on a bad day. Before reading on: with retry outermost, what does each retry attempt do while the breaker is open? Supplier<String> charge = () -> psp.charge("order-7781:charge", "tok_42", 1_250); // idempotency key Supplier<String> limited = () -> bulkhead.call(charge); // innermost: caps the calls in flight to the PSP Supplier<String> guarded = () -> breaker.call(limited); // then: stop calling a PSP that keeps failing String ref = retrying(3, guarded); // outermost: try again on transient failures val charge = Supplier { psp.charge("order-7781:charge", "tok_42", 1_250) } // idempotency key val limited = Supplier { bulkhead.call(charge) } // innermost: caps the calls in flight to the PSP val guarded = Supplier { breaker.call(limited) } // then: stop calling a PSP that keeps failing val ref = retrying(3) { guarded.get() } // outermost: try again on transient failures Each attempt hits the open breaker and gets CallNotPermitted in microseconds, which costs the PSP nothing. But a rejection isn't a transient failure, and retrying it is noise. Teach the retry to let fail-fast signals through untouched. static <T> T retrying(int attempts, Supplier<T> body) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return body.get(); } catch (CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted | Bulkhead.BulkheadFull e) { throw e; // 1. fail-fast signals: never retry them } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; // 2. a timeout or a 503: worth another attempt } } throw last; } inline fun <T> retrying(attempts: Int, body: () -> T): T { var last: RuntimeException? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return body() } catch (e: CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted) { throw e // 1. fail-fast signals: never retry them } catch (e: Bulkhead.BulkheadFull) { throw e } catch (e: RuntimeException) { last = e // 2. a timeout or a 503: worth another attempt } } throw last!! } Why is the bulkhead inside the breaker? An open breaker rejects before the bulkhead is reached, so a dead PSP never holds permits. Why is the retry outside? Each attempt is a separate breaker call, so three failed attempts count as three failures, and a PSP that is really down trips the breaker within one or two payments. Retrying inside the breaker would hide those failures from it. what each layer sees for one payment while the PSP returns 503: retry attempt 1 attempt 2 attempt 3 breaker Closed(0) -> (1) Closed(1) -> (2) Closed(2) -> Open (three failures trip it) bulkhead permit, released permit, released permit, released next payment: retry -> breaker rejects at once (CallNotPermitted) -> no PSP call, no permit Pin it in a test with a fake PSP that always fails and the lab's classes. The second payment must never reach the PSP. AtomicInteger pspCalls = new AtomicInteger(); Supplier<String> failing = () -> { pspCalls.incrementAndGet(); throw new IllegalStateException("PSP 503"); }; CircuitBreaker breaker = new CircuitBreaker(3, Duration.ofSeconds(30), clock); Bulkhead bulkhead = new Bulkhead(20); Supplier<String> pipeline = () -> breaker.call(() -> bulkhead.call(failing)); assertThatThrownBy(() -> retrying(3, pipeline)).hasMessage("PSP 503"); // 4. first payment: 3 attempts assertThat(breaker.state()).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.Open.class); assertThatThrownBy(() -> retrying(3, pipeline)).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted.class); assertThat(pspCalls.get()).isEqualTo(3); // 5. the second never left val pspCalls = AtomicInteger() val failing = Supplier<String> { pspCalls.incrementAndGet(); throw IllegalStateException("PSP 503") } val breaker = CircuitBreaker(3, Duration.ofSeconds(30), clock) val bulkhead = Bulkhead(20) val pipeline = { breaker.call { bulkhead.call(failing) } } assertThatThrownBy { retrying(3, pipeline) }.hasMessage("PSP 503") // 4. first payment: 3 attempts assertThat(breaker.state()).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.Open::class.java) assertThatThrownBy { retrying(3, pipeline) }.isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted::class.java) assertThat(pspCalls.get()).isEqualTo(3) // 5. the second never left

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Quiz
x: A Java pipeline has four consumer threads reading a BlockingQueue. After the last job, the producer puts a single Stop pill, then calls close() on the executor. What happens? All four consumers stop, because they all see the pill One consumer stops and the other three keep processing new jobs One consumer stops, three block in take() forever, and close() never returns The queue throws because a pill was taken twice take() removes the pill, so exactly one consumer sees it. The other three wait for the next item, which never comes, and ExecutorService.close() waits for them. Put one pill per consumer, or in Kotlin close the channel, which ends every for loop. A Quarkus service on virtual threads calls an issuer that allows 50 concurrent requests. Which limit fits best? A semaphore of 50 around the issuer call, with tryAcquire so extra calls fail fast A fixed pool of 50 platform threads for the whole service No limit: virtual threads are cheap A new CompletableFuture per call The limit belongs to the dependency, not to the service's threads, and with virtual threads a semaphore is the natural way to express it. A fixed pool of 50 throttles everything the service does, not just the issuer calls. "Virtual threads are cheap" is exactly how you send 5,000 requests to an issuer that takes 50. In a unit test, a Resilience4j 2.4.0 circuit breaker built with the default config fails five calls in a row, yet it stays CLOSED. Why? Resilience4j only counts checked exceptions as failures The default minimumNumberOfCalls is 100, so the failure rate isn't calculated yet Breakers only open after waitDurationInOpenState has passed The test needs a real clock With the defaults, the breaker needs at least 100 recorded calls before it computes a failure rate, so five failures change nothing. Set minimumNumberOfCalls and slidingWindowSize to small numbers in tests. All exceptions are recorded by default, and waitDurationInOpenState controls how long it stays open, not when it opens. A scheduled reconciliation job can also be started by an operator. If a run is already in progress, a second trigger should simply return. Which pattern is this? Guarded suspension Read-write lock Producer-consumer Balking Balking means: if the object isn't in the right state, return at once instead of waiting. Guarded suspension is the opposite, waiting until the condition holds, which here would queue a second run behind the first. Implement it with compareAndSet on an AtomicBoolean, and with a database lock or lease if it must be unique across pods. From Atomics and compare-and-set: when the cool-down ends, many request threads find the breaker Open with an expired until at the same moment. Why must the move to HalfOpen be a compareAndSet rather than a plain set? set is slower than compareAndSet So exactly one thread wins the right to probe; with set, every thread that saw the expired state would probe the PSP AtomicReference doesn't allow set on records compareAndSet makes the PSP call atomic Each thread read the same Open state. compareAndSet(open, halfOpen) succeeds for the first thread only, because after that the state is no longer the Open object the others read, so their CAS fails and they're rejected. A plain set lets all of them through to a PSP that may still be down. CAS makes the state change atomic, not the call itself.

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Key terms
x: Producer-consumer Producers put work on a shared queue and consumers take it off; the queue does the locking and waiting. Poison pill A special message that tells one consumer to stop. Active object An object whose method calls become messages run one at a time by its own thread, returning futures. Balking Returning at once instead of waiting when the object isn't in the right state, such as "already running". Guarded suspension Waiting until a condition holds, then going on; wait in a loop, or a future. Bulkhead A per-dependency cap on concurrent calls, so one slow dependency can't use up everything. Circuit breaker A wrapper that stops calling a failing dependency for a while, then probes to see if it recovered. Half-open The breaker state after the cool-down, where one probe call decides whether to close or reopen. Why bound a producer-consumer queue? A full bounded queue makes producers wait, which is backpressure. An unbounded one hides overload until memory runs out. N consumers stop on poison pills. How many pills? N, one per consumer: each take() removes one pill. In Kotlin, close() the channel instead. Balking or guarded suspension: which returns at once? Balking returns immediately if the object is busy. Guarded suspension waits until the condition holds. Bulkhead: tryAcquire or acquire? tryAcquire, so a call over the limit fails fast. acquire waits in line, which makes it a limiter. Release in finally either way. Circuit breaker: what happens in each state? Closed: calls pass and failures are counted. Open: calls are rejected at once. HalfOpen: one probe runs; success closes, failure reopens. Resilience4j 2.4.0 default minimumNumberOfCalls? A default breaker in a unit test that fails a handful of calls never opens. Which exceptions should a retry wrapper never retry? Fail-fast signals such as CallNotPermitted and a full bulkhead, and anything non-idempotent sent without an idempotency key.

h: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together · Go deeper
x: Resilience4j's breaker defaults, read from its source and printed by version 2.4.0: failureRateThreshold 50%, slowCallRateThreshold 100%, slowCallDurationThreshold 60 s, waitDurationInOpenState 60 s, permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState 10, minimumNumberOfCalls 100, and a count-based sliding window of 100 calls. Every exception counts as a failure unless you configure recordExceptions or ignoreExceptions. The project's README says Resilience4j 3 will require Java 21 and adds virtual-thread schedulers; it wasn't on Maven Central when this course was written, so the labs build the breaker by hand. Spring Framework 7 added @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit to the core framework, switched on with @EnableResilientMethods. @Retryable defaults to maxRetries = 3 after the first failure, so four attempts in total, with a one-second delay. Both work through proxies, so the self-invocation rule applies. Structured concurrency is the future-and-promise pattern with a lifetime. StructuredTaskScope forks subtasks, joins them, and cancels the rest when one fails, so no subtask outlives the method that started it. It is still a preview API in JDK 25, 26 and 27 (run with --enable-preview), which is why it stays out of the labs. Kotlin's coroutineScope has worked this way since the start: an async that fails cancels its siblings, and the scope waits for every child. The patterns in this lesson have distributed cousins. A database row lock or a lease is balking across pods. Kafka partitions are producer-consumer with ordering per key. A Temporal workflow is an active object with durable state: one logical thread per workflow, commands in, results out. The questions you ask stay the same: who owns the state, what waits, and what fails fast.

h: Modern Java data modeling
x: Records, sealed types, pattern matching and data-oriented programming, and where Project Valhalla is heading. By the end of this track you can model payment data the way modern Java intends: records whose compact constructors make invalid values impossible, sealed hierarchies the compiler can check, and pattern switches with nested record patterns and guards that take that data apart. You will know exactly where each guarantee stops (shallow immutability, null, subtypes added after compilation) and you can say, with versions, what Project Valhalla has and hasn't shipped. Every lesson sets the Java feature next to its Kotlin counterpart (data classes, sealed interfaces, when with guards, @JvmInline value class) and says honestly which side is better at what. You need only the syntax of both languages; the track starts from zero on records and sealed types. Install JDK 25. Records, sealed types, pattern switches and record patterns are all final in JDK 21, so the labs compile with --release 21. Anything newer is marked with its JDK: unnamed patterns (_) need JDK 22, flexible constructor bodies JDK 25, primitive patterns are still a preview, and value objects exist only as a preview in JDK 28 builds. The labs live in labs/modernjava, one package per lesson (workbench.modernjava.l01 to l04). Lessons 1 to 3 are in Java and lesson 4 is in Kotlin. Two of the lesson 2 tests run javac inside the test through javax.tools, so Gradle must run on a full JDK. Run ./gradlew :modernjava:test --tests 'workbench.modernjava.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and ./gradlew :modernjava:solutionTest to run the same tests on the reference answers. Demos for newer JDKs sit in labs/modernjava/preview (run them with java preview/File.java), and two compile-it-yourself experiments sit in labs/modernjava/javac. A record is a final, transparent carrier: javac generates fields, accessors, one canonical constructor and the Object methods from the header, so they can't drift apart. The compact constructor is the one door: new, factories, other constructors, withers and Java deserialization all go through it. Kotlin's init is the twin, but it can't normalize a parameter and Java deserialization skips it. Records are only shallowly immutable and their generated methods read fields: copy collections with copyOf, and mask secrets in toString, not in the accessor. A sealed type names its permitted subtypes; each one is final, sealed or non-sealed. On the class path they must share a package. A concrete sealed parent is a value of its own. A switch over a sealed type with no default is checked by the compiler, so adding a subtype turns every forgotten switch into a compile error. A default hides it. Record patterns take data apart in the case label. Cases run in order, guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, and javac rejects dominated cases, which kotlinc doesn't. Exhaustive is a compile-time promise: null needs case null, and a subtype added after compilation makes an old switch throw MatchException. Data-oriented code models closed domains as records and sealed types, validates at the edge, and writes operations as functions. It makes new operations cheap and new types loud. Project Valhalla's value objects are a preview in JDK 28, not in 25 to 27. Records are identity objects; JEP 468 withers are on hold; null-restricted types are still drafts.

Guards never count toward exhaustiveness. A null selector throws NullPointerException unless there is case null. default doesn't catch null. A nested type pattern (Point p) matches a null component; a nested record pattern (Point(var x, var y)) doesn't. No shared bag of nullable fields. Constructors refuse bad values; the type system refuses bad shapes. Parse untrusted input once, at the edge, into the model or a rejection. Trust the types behind the edge. Business operations are functions with one exhaustive switch each. Keep methods for open, plug-in hierarchies and for behavior about the value itself. Don't depend on record identity, so value (JDK 28 preview) can be a one-word change later.

h: Records: transparent carriers for data · A record is its components, and javac writes the rest
x: Here is a small value class written by hand, the way a lot of Java code still has them: Java public final class Money { private final long minor; private final String currency; // added in the last sprint public Money(long minor, String currency) { this.minor = minor; this.currency = currency; } public long minor() { return minor; } public String currency() { return currency; } @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Money m && m.minor == minor; // nobody updated this } @Override public int hashCode() { return Long.hashCode(minor); } @Override public String toString() { return "Money[minor=" + minor + "]"; } } Kotlin class Money(val minor: Long, val currency: String) { // currency added in the last sprint override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is Money && other.minor == minor // nobody updated this override fun hashCode() = minor.hashCode() override fun toString() = "Money(minor=$minor)" } It compiles, and new Money(1000, "EUR").equals(new Money(1000, "USD")) is true. A refund matcher that compares amounts now matches across currencies, and the log line doesn't even show the currency. The class says "these fields are the value" in four places, and the four drifted apart. A record says it once. You list its components, the values that make up the record, in the header, and javac writes the rest from that list: Java public record Money(long minor, String currency) {} Kotlin data class Money(val minor: Long, val currency: String) From that header javac generates a private final field per component, a public accessor per component (minor() and currency(), with no get prefix), a canonical constructor that takes the components in order, and equals, hashCode and toString. The class is final and extends java.lang.Record. Records have been final since JDK 16 (JEP 395), so everything in this lesson works on the JDK 21 the labs compile for. The Record Javadoc calls a record "a shallowly immutable, transparent carrier for a fixed set of values". Each part of that phrase is a rule you will run into. The component list is fixed: you can't add instance fields, and private int cache; in the body fails with field declaration must be static. Static fields, methods and nested types are fine. Transparent means the state is the API. Every component gets a public accessor, and equals and toString use every component. A record can implement interfaces but can't extend a class, because it already extends Record. And shallowly immutable means the fields are final while the objects they point to may not be. Section 3 is about that. The generated methods are not what you would write by hand. javap shows that equals, hashCode and toString are each a single invokedynamic instruction. invokedynamic is a call whose target the JVM decides at run time: the first time it runs, the JVM calls a bootstrap method, here java.lang.runtime.ObjectMethods.bootstrap, and links in whatever method that returns. javac passes it the component names as one string (minor;currency) and a direct getter for each private field, and the JDK builds the method bodies from that list. That is why the Javadoc says the exact hashCode algorithm and toString format may change: never parse a record's toString. kotlinc does it the older way and writes equals and hashCode out as ordinary bytecode in your class. A record is still an ordinary object with its own identity: every new makes a distinct object, and == and synchronized can tell it apart from an equal one. new Point(3, 4) == new Point(3, 4) is false, and synchronized on a record compiles and runs. Objects without identity are what Project Valhalla adds, as a preview feature scheduled for JDK 28. Lesson 4 of this track covers where that stands. Record (Java SE 25 API) docs JEP 395: Records read A record is like a line on a printed bank statement: date, amount, reference. Anyone can read every field, two lines with the same values mean the same thing, and to change one you print a new line. The bank checks the line before it prints it, which is the compact constructor's job. The analogy breaks at one point: a printed line can't point at anything that changes later, while a record's List component can be someone else's list that keeps growing after the record was made.

h: Records: transparent carriers for data · The compact constructor is the only way in
x: Validation in a static factory is easy to get around. Money.of(...) can check the amount all it likes, and new Money(-5, "eur") walks straight past it. A record gives you a place nobody can walk past. It has exactly one canonical constructor: the one whose parameters match the components. Every other constructor must call it first, and so does every static factory, every wither, and Java deserialization. That makes it the one place for validation and normalization. Write it in the compact form, with no parameter list: Java public record Money(long minor, String currency) { public Money { Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency"); if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount: " + minor); currency = currency.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT); // reassign the parameter } // javac assigns the fields here public Money(long minor) { this(minor, "EUR"); } // must delegate first } Kotlin data class Money(val minor: Long, val currency: String) { init { require(minor >= 0) { "negative amount: $minor" } require(currency == currency.uppercase()) { "currency must be upper case: $currency" } } constructor(minor: Long) : this(minor, "EUR") // must delegate first } In the compact form the parameters are ordinary local variables. You can reassign them, and javac copies their final values into the fields after your code runs. You can't touch the fields yourself: this.minor = minor; fails with cannot assign a value to final variable minor. A non-canonical constructor that doesn't start with this(...) fails on JDK 21 with constructor is not canonical, so its first statement must invoke another constructor of class Money. JDK 25 made flexible constructor bodies final, so there you may run plain statements, such as parsing "12.50 EUR", before the this(...) call. The Kotlin version shows a real difference. init runs on every construction, and copy() runs it too. But a data class can't change a constructor parameter before it becomes a property. It can reject "eur", but it can't turn it into "EUR". Normalizing moves into a factory function, and the public constructor still accepts the raw value. Deserialization is where the canonical constructor pays off. The Record Javadoc says the canonical constructor is invoked during deserialization, and that readObject and writeObject are ignored for records. An ordinary class needs a hand-written readObject to recheck its invariants, and most classes don't have one. A record gets the check for free. A Kotlin data class does not: Java deserialization never runs its init block, unless you mark the class @JvmRecord so it compiles to a real record. The Try it below tampers with a byte stream to show both. Go through every door Run CompactConstructorDemo. Read the last line of output before you read the code that produced it. Run the Kotlin twin, CompactConstructorDemoKt. Which tampered range got through? In the Java demo, add this.minor = minor; inside the compact constructor of Money and run again. Read the compiler error, then undo the change. If you have JDK 25, run java preview/FlexibleConstructor.java from labs/modernjava. Then run the same file with JDK 21 and read the two errors.
