Records in Kotlin: @JvmRecord docs Your Quarkus services already move records around: REST request and response bodies, Kafka event payloads, Temporal activity inputs. Each of those is a boundary where outside data becomes a value, and the compact constructor is where you check it once: three-letter currency codes, non-negative amounts, idempotency keys of the right length. After that, any Money the service holds is a valid one. Two places need care. A List component in a Kafka event must be copied, or a producer that reuses its buffer list changes events it has already handed off. And a record that holds a PAN, an IBAN or an access token must override toString, because the generated one prints every component into every log line and exception message that touches the record.

h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Equality and immutability go one level deep
x: equals on a record returns true when the other object is the same record class and every component is equal. For a reference component that means Objects.equals. For a primitive it means the wrapper's compare returns 0, which has two surprises for a double. A record holding NaN equals another one holding NaN, though NaN == NaN is false. And 0.0 and -0.0 are not equal, though 0.0 == -0.0 is true. Kotlin data classes behave the same way. Keep money in a long of minor units and neither will bite you. Arrays are worse. An int[] component compares by reference, so two records with equal arrays are not equal, and toString prints something like [I@1b6d3586. Use a List. A List component brings the real trap. The record holds a reference to whatever list the caller passed in, and if the caller keeps changing that list, the record changes too: Java record Batch(String id, List<String> paymentIds) {} var ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay_1", "pay_2")); var batch = new Batch("b-7", ids); var sent = new HashSet<>(Set.of(batch)); ids.add("pay_3"); sent.contains(batch); // false: the hashCode changed under the set Kotlin data class Batch(val id: String, val paymentIds: List<String>) val ids = mutableListOf("pay_1", "pay_2") val batch = Batch("b-7", ids) val sent = hashSetOf(batch) ids += "pay_3" batch in sent // false: the hashCode changed under the set The batch is still in the set. The set just looks for it in the wrong bucket. The fix is one line in the compact constructor: paymentIds = List.copyOf(paymentIds);. It makes an unmodifiable copy, and it throws NullPointerException for a null element. That is what you want for domain data, and a surprise for JSON lists that contain nulls. Kotlin's List<String> is a read-only view, not an immutable list, so a data class needs the same copy, made in a factory. Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal in the concurrency track made the same point about sharing between threads. Here the cost is a lost key, even on one thread. The last trap looks like a fix. To keep a card number out of the logs, someone overrides the accessor so card() returns ****1111. The logs don't change. The generated toString reads the field directly (that is what the getters in the bootstrap arguments are), so it still prints the full number. The override also breaks the record contract that new Masked(m.card()) equals m. Record patterns, which lesson 3 covers, do call the accessor, so different parts of your code now see different data. To hide a component, override toString, or keep the secret out of any record that gets logged. Lose a key, leak a card Predict the sent.contains line, then run ShallowDemo. Give Batch a compact constructor that copies its list, as SafeBatch does. Run it again. Run the Kotlin twin and look at the copy shares list line. Did copy() copy the list? h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Records, data classes and the missing copy()
x: Kotlin engineers reach for copy() first and find Java has none. A record that needs "the same refund with a smaller amount" gets a hand-written wither: Java record Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor, List<String> reasons) { Refund withAmount(long newAmount) { return new Refund(paymentId, newAmount, reasons); // through the canonical constructor } } Kotlin data class Refund(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val reasons: List<String>) val part = full.copy(amountMinor = 2_000) // generated, and it runs init Both go through validation, which is the point: there is no path to an invalid Refund. The cost on the Java side is typing, and it grows with the record. In a 2020 design draft, Brian Goetz pointed out that while a class has O(n) getters, it "could conceivably have O(2^n) withers", and asked that hand-written withers not become a best practice. Write withers only for the changes your domain actually makes. A language fix exists on paper. JEP 468, derived record creation, proposes refund with { amountMinor = 2_000; }. It would take the record apart, run the block, and call the canonical constructor with the result. It is a Candidate JEP, no JDK has shipped it, and in January 2026 Goetz wrote that it "has been 'on hold' for a while". Don't plan around it. The other differences matter more day to day. A data class may declare properties in its body, and Kotlin leaves those out of equals, hashCode, toString and copy(), so two objects that differ only there are equal. A record can't have body state at all. A data class can't be open, abstract or sealed, and a record is always final. Kotlin destructures with val (id, amount) = refund, through componentN() functions, while Java destructures with record patterns in switch and instanceof (lesson 3). Where the two languages meet, Kotlin reads a Java record's accessors as properties (money.minor), and @JvmRecord on a data class emits a real java.lang.Record that Java code sees as one. The Kotlin docs warn that adding @JvmRecord to an existing class is not a binary-compatible change, so decide when you create the class. Wither versus copy() Run WitherDemo and its twin WitherDemoKt. Compare the four lines each prints. Add a withPaymentId(String id) wither to the Java record and call it with " ". Should that be rejected? Add the check where every wither will get it. In WitherDemo.kt, add var note = "" to the body of RefundRequest, set full.note = "called twice", and print full == full.copy() and full.copy().note. reasons = List.copyOf(reasons); } Refund withAmount(long newAmount) { return new Refund(paymentId, newAmount, reasons); } Refund withReason(String extra) { var more = new java.util.ArrayList<>(reasons); more.add(extra); return new Refund(paymentId, amountMinor, more); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Refund full = new Refund("pay_81", 5_000, List.of("duplicate charge")); Refund part = full.withAmount(2_000).withReason("partial goodwill"); System.out.println("original: " + full); System.out.println("changed: " + part); System.out.println("same reasons list object: " + (full.reasons() == full.withAmount(1_000).reasons())); try { full.withAmount(-1); Withers and copy() both reuse the component references, which is safe here only because the list can't change. The blank-id check belongs in the compact constructor, so every wither inherits it. In Kotlin, full == full.copy() is true and the copy's note is empty: body properties are ignored by equals and not copied. Data classes (Kotlin docs) docs The common mistake is treating a record as deeply immutable and using it as a map or set key while one of its components is a mutable list or map. It works in tests, because nothing mutates the list there. In production a caller reuses its ArrayList, the record's hashCode changes, and HashMap.get returns null for a key that is still in the map. Copy every collection component in the compact constructor with List.copyOf, Set.copyOf or Map.copyOf, and don't use arrays as components.

h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Java and Kotlin
x: A validated money value in Java and Kotlin Money.java public record Money(long minor, String currency) { private static final Pattern ISO = Pattern.compile("[A-Z]{3}"); public Money { Objects.requireNonNull(currency, "currency"); currency = currency.trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT); // normalize in place if (!ISO.matcher(currency).matches()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad currency: " + currency); if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount: " + minor); } public Money plus(Money other) { if (!currency.equals(other.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch"); return new Money(Math.addExact(minor, other.minor), currency); } } Money.kt data class Money(val minor: Long, val currency: String) { init { require(ISO.matches(currency)) { "bad currency: $currency" } // can reject, can't normalize require(minor >= 0) { "negative amount: $minor" } } operator fun plus(other: Money): Money { require(currency == other.currency) { "currency mismatch" } return Money(Math.addExact(minor, other.minor), currency) } companion object { private val ISO = Regex("[A-Z]{3}") fun of(minor: Long, currency: String) = Money(minor, currency.trim().uppercase()) } } Both give you equals, hashCode and toString over all components, final fields, and a validation hook that every construction goes through, including Kotlin's copy(). Three things differ. Java's compact constructor can normalize a parameter before it becomes a field; a data class can only reject it, so normalizing lives in a factory and the public constructor stays open to raw input. Java deserialization rebuilds a record through its canonical constructor but skips a data class's init (@JvmRecord closes that gap). And Kotlin has copy() with named arguments, while Java has hand-written withers until JEP 468 ships, which it hasn't.

h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Worked example
x: Turn a mutable request class into a record A capture request in a payment service is a JavaBean: setters, a mutable list, and sixty lines of hand-written equals, hashCode and toString that nobody updated when currency was added. Any code can change it after it was checked. public class CaptureRequest { private String paymentId; private long amountMinor; private String currency; private List<String> lineItems = new ArrayList<>(); public void setAmountMinor(long amountMinor) { this.amountMinor = amountMinor; } public List<String> getLineItems() { return lineItems; } // hands out the live list // ... more setters, getters, equals, hashCode, toString } class CaptureRequest { var paymentId: String? = null var amountMinor: Long = 0 var currency: String? = null val lineItems: MutableList<String> = mutableListOf() // hands out the live list } Write the header. The components are the whole state, and every setter is gone. Recompile: each place that called a setter is now a compile error, which is your list of code that mutated a request after it was built. // 1. the components are the state public record CaptureRequest(String paymentId, Money amount, List<String> lineItems) {} // 1. the properties are the state data class CaptureRequest(val paymentId: String, val amount: Money, val lineItems: List<String>) Add the compact constructor. h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Key terms
x: Record component One of the values in a record's header. Each one gets a private final field and a public accessor. Canonical constructor The constructor whose parameters match the components in order. Every other way of making the record goes through it. Compact constructor The canonical constructor written without a parameter list. Its parameters are locals you can check and reassign; javac assigns the fields at the end. Accessor The generated public method that returns a component. It is named after the component: currency(), not getCurrency(). Shallow immutability The fields can't be reassigned, but the objects they point to may still change. Wither A method that returns a copy of a record with one component changed. Java has no generated ones. @JvmRecord A Kotlin annotation that compiles a data class to a real java.lang.Record. What does javac generate for record Point(int x, int y)? Private final fields, accessors x() and y(), a canonical constructor Point(int, int), and equals, hashCode and toString. The class is final and extends java.lang.Record. In a compact constructor, how do you normalize a component? Reassign the parameter: currency = currency.trim();. javac assigns the fields after the body. this.currency = ... doesn't compile. A record overrides its accessor to mask a card number. What does toString print? The full number. The generated toString, equals and hashCode read the fields, not the accessors. Override toString instead. record R(double d): is new R(Double.NaN).equals(new R(Double.NaN)) true? Yes. Primitive components compare with Double.compare, which treats NaN as equal to itself. And 0.0 doesn't equal -0.0. How do you make a record with a List component safe as a map key? Copy it in the compact constructor: items = List.copyOf(items);. The copy is unmodifiable and rejects null elements. Does Java deserialization run a Kotlin data class's init block? No, so a tampered stream can build an invalid object. A Java record, or a data class marked @JvmRecord, is rebuilt through its canonical constructor. Can you write refund with { amount = 200; } in Java today? No. Derived record creation (JEP 468) is a Candidate JEP, on hold as of January 2026, and in no JDK. Write withers by hand.

h: Records: transparent carriers for data · Go deeper
x: Two details round out the picture. A Java record can't hide its canonical constructor. The Record Javadoc says it "must provide at least as much access as the record class", and javac enforces it: Java public record Key(String v) { private Key { } } // error: invalid canonical constructor in record Key // (attempting to assign stronger access privileges; was public) Kotlin data class Key private constructor(val v: String) { companion object { fun of(raw: String) = Key(raw.trim()) } } // warning (Kotlin 2.4): non-public primary constructor is exposed via the generated 'copy()' method So validation must live inside the constructor, where nobody can bypass it. Kotlin lets you make a data class constructor private and force callers through a factory that normalizes, but copy() still exposes it. Kotlin 2.4.21 warns about this, says the warning becomes an error in language version 2.5, and offers @ConsistentCopyVisibility to make copy() as private as the constructor. The second detail is about what comes after records. In a January 2026 design note, "Data-Oriented Programming for Java: Beyond Records", Brian Goetz describes the cliff you fall off when a class is almost a record: one derived field or one private cache, and you are back to writing everything by hand. The note sketches carrier classes, written like class Point(int x, int y) { ... }: a normal class with a record-style state description. The language would require the canonical constructor and the accessors and give the class a deconstruction pattern, while the class declares its own fields and need not be final. It is a design note and no JEP exists yet, so treat it as a direction for now.

h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · A sealed type closes the list of direct subtypes
x: Any class, in any package, can implement an ordinary interface. So code that handles "each kind of command" can never know it handled them all: someone adds a Void command next week, it compiles, and the if/else chain that dispatches commands quietly skips it. Before JDK 17 the only fix was by hand: an abstract class with a package-private constructor, so that only classes in its own package can extend it. That closes the hierarchy, but the compiler still doesn't know the list, so it can't check a switch against it. A sealed type is a class or interface that names its permitted subtypes, the only classes allowed to extend it directly. Add sealed and a permits clause, and the list becomes part of the type: Java public sealed interface Command permits Authorize, Capture, Refund {} public record Authorize(String authCode, long amountMinor) implements Command {} public record Capture() implements Command {} public record Refund(long amountMinor) implements Command {} Kotlin sealed interface Command { data class Authorize(val authCode: String, val amountMinor: Long) : Command data object Capture : Command data class Refund(val amountMinor: Long) : Command } Sealed classes and interfaces have been final since JDK 17 (JEP 409). javac checks the list from both sides. A class that implements Command without being on it fails with class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Command (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause). javac also writes the list into the class file, as a PermittedSubclasses attribute (a table the JVM reads), and the JVM checks it when it loads a class. A subclass compiled against an older, unsealed Command fails to load with IncompatibleClassChangeError: class Void cannot implement sealed interface Command. You can leave permits out when every subtype is declared in the same source file as the sealed type. javac then takes the subtypes it finds there. Reflection shows the result: Command.class.isSealed() is true, and getPermittedSubclasses() returns the three records. Kotlin has no permits clause. Its rule is location: any class in the same package and the same module may extend a sealed type, and a class anywhere else fails with a class can only extend a sealed class or interface declared in the same package. With the JDK 21 target these labs use, kotlinc 2.4 writes the same PermittedSubclasses attribute as javac. So Java code sees a Kotlin sealed interface as sealed: a Java switch over it needs no default, and javac rejects a Java class that tries to implement it. Sealing restricts direct subtypes only. Refund.class.isSealed() is false, and what happens below each permitted subtype is the subject of the next section. Break the list on purpose Run SealedBasics (or SealedBasicsKt) with the command below. In the Java demo, uncomment static final class Void implements Command {} and run again. Read the error. Add Void to the permits clause and delete final from it. Run again. Then put final back. Now delete the whole permits ... clause and run. What does getPermittedSubclasses() print? In the Kotlin twin, uncomment class Void : Command. Does it compile? Why is that different from Java? SealedBasics.java package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Modifier; /** A sealed interface names its direct subtypes, and the JVM keeps that list. */ public class SealedBasics { sealed interface Command permits Authorize, Capture, Refund {} record Authorize(String authCode, long amountMinor) implements Command {} // records are final record Capture() implements Command {} record Refund(long amountMinor) implements Command {} // Step 2: uncomment this line and compile. // static final class Void implements Command {} public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Command.isSealed(): " + Command.class.isSealed()); for (Class<?> c : Command.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) { System.out.println("permits: " + c.getSimpleName() + (Modifier.isFinal(c.getModifiers()) ? " (final)" : "")); } System.out.println("Refund.isSealed(): " + Refund.class.isSealed()); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l02.demo.SealedBasics labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l02/demo/SealedBasics.java SealedBasics.kt package workbench.modernjava.l02.demo import java.lang.reflect.Modifier // Kotlin has no permits clause: the direct subtypes are the ones declared in this package and module sealed interface Command { data class Authorize(val authCode: String, val amountMinor: Long) : Command // final by default data object Capture : Command data class Refund(val amountMinor: Long) : Command } // Step 2: uncomment this line and compile. Then try it in another package. // class Void : Command /** kotlinc writes the same PermittedSubclasses attribute that javac does. */ fun main() { println("Command.isSealed(): ${Command::class.java.isSealed}") for (c in Command::class.java.permittedSubclasses) { println("permits: ${c.simpleName}" + if (Modifier.isFinal(c.modifiers)) " (final)" else "") } println("Refund.isSealed(): ${Command.Refund::class.java.isSealed}") } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l02.demo.SealedBasicsKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l02/demo/SealedBasics.kt The first run prints isSealed(): true, the three records marked (final), and Refund.isSealed(): false. The unlisted class fails with class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Command (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause). Listed but without a modifier, it fails with sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected. With no permits clause, javac infers all four from the file and prints Void too. In Kotlin, class Void : Command compiles: the list is whatever sits in the same package and module. JEP 409: Sealed Classes read A sealed type is like the list of settlement currencies in your merchant contract. The contract names them, so finance can write one procedure per currency and know the procedures are complete. Adding a currency means amending the contract, and then every procedure that branches on currency has to be checked, which is exactly what you want. A non-sealed branch is the clause that says "plus any currency a partner bank agrees to handle": you can't list those, but one procedure (send it to the partner) covers them all. The analogy breaks on enforcement: nobody stops a sales rep from quoting a currency that isn't in the contract, while javac and the JVM both refuse a subtype that isn't on the list.

h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · final, sealed or non-sealed: every branch has to choose
x: Every permitted subtype of a sealed type must say how its own branch ends, with exactly one of three modifiers. If a class says nothing, javac stops with sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected. An interface can't be final, so for one the message is sealed or non-sealed modifiers expected. final ends the branch. Records and enums are implicitly final, so a record needs no modifier, which is one reason sealed interfaces and records fit together so well. sealed continues the closed list one level down, with its own permits. non-sealed reopens the branch on purpose: anyone may extend it, in any package. Java public sealed interface PaymentMethod permits Card, BankTransfer, PartnerMethod {} public record Card(String network) implements PaymentMethod {} // final public sealed interface BankTransfer extends PaymentMethod permits Sepa, Swift {} // closed below public non-sealed interface PartnerMethod extends PaymentMethod { // open below String partnerId(); } Kotlin sealed interface PaymentMethod { data class Card(val network: String) : PaymentMethod // final by default sealed interface BankTransfer : PaymentMethod // closed below interface PartnerMethod : PaymentMethod { val partnerId: String } // open below } non-sealed sounds like it defeats the point of sealing. It doesn't, because the compiler still knows the shape of the tree. A switch covers the open branch with one case PartnerMethod p, and that case matches every partner class, including ones a partner team writes next year. Your switch stays exhaustive and the partner team stays free. Kotlin has no non-sealed keyword: a plain interface or an open class under a sealed parent plays the same role. So "sealed means final" is wrong: a sealed type has subtypes by definition, and a non-sealed branch can have any number. The trap that catches people in code review is a third one. A sealed class that isn't abstract is itself a possible value. With sealed class Fee permits Flat, Percent and no abstract, new Fee() is legal, so a switch with cases for Flat and Percent fails with the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. Make the parent abstract, or make it an interface. Kotlin avoids the trap entirely: its docs say a sealed class is always abstract. Reopen one branch, close the trap Run NonSealedDemo. GiftCard is partner code: which modifier lets it exist? Delete non-sealed from PartnerMethod, leaving a plain interface, and run. Read the error, then put it back. Delete abstract from sealed abstract static class Fee and run again. sealed: closed below record Sepa(String iban) implements BankTransfer {} record Swift(String bic) implements BankTransfer {} non-sealed interface PartnerMethod extends PaymentMethod { // non-sealed: here and compile. sealed abstract static class Fee permits Flat, Percent {} static final class Flat extends Fee { final long minor; Flat(long minor) { this.minor = minor; } } static final class The Kotlin twin can't show that trap, because its sealed class is always abstract. Each permitted subtype ends its branch: final has no subtypes, sealed keeps a closed list, non-sealed lets anyone in. A switch still needs only one case per branch. Sealed classes and interfaces (Kotlin docs) docs Payment services are full of closed lists: payment methods, authorization outcomes, dispute stages, ledger entry kinds, the event types on one Kafka topic. Make each of them a sealed interface of records, and the consumer that handles a topic becomes one switch with no default. The day someone adds RefundReversed to the event schema, the consumer, the projection that builds the read model and the metrics tagging all fail to compile until they handle it. That is better than finding out from a dead-letter queue. Keep each hierarchy in one package: on the class path, which is how Quarkus services usually run, javac won't let you split it.

h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · Where the subtypes may live
x: Sealing ties a hierarchy to one place, and Java and Kotlin draw the boundary slightly differently. In Java the permitted subtypes must be in the same module as the sealed type. A module here means a JPMS module: a set of packages described by a module-info.java. If your code isn't in a named module, the subtypes must be in the same package. A typical Quarkus or Spring service runs on the class path, in the unnamed module, so the package rule is the one you will meet. Split a sealed interface and its record across pay.api and pay.card and javac refuses: error: class PaymentMethod in unnamed module cannot extend a sealed class in a different package public sealed interface PaymentMethod permits pay.card.Card {} The wording is clumsy, since it names the sealed interface as the class doing the extending, but the rule is clear. Add a module-info.java that puts both packages in one module, and the same files compile. Kotlin's rule is the same package and the same module, whether or not you use JPMS modules. So for the code most of us write, the two languages agree: keep a sealed hierarchy in one package. That is rarely a burden. The subtypes are usually small records or data classes that read best next to each other, often nested inside the sealed type itself, which also lets Java infer permits. The restriction makes sense once you see what sealing promises. The author of a sealed type says "this is the complete list", and the compiler can only hold everyone to that if the whole list is compiled and shipped as one unit. A subtype in some other module could be released on its own schedule, and the list every switch was checked against would quietly go stale. Split a hierarchy across packages The folder labs/modernjava/javac/sealed-packages holds a sealed PaymentMethod in pay.api, a Card record in pay.card, and a module-info.java. Gradle doesn't compile it; you run javac yourself. Run the first command. Read the error and the line it points at. Run the second command, which adds the module descriptor. Predict, then check: move Card.java into pay/api/, change its package line to pay.api, change the permits clause to permits Card, and run the first command again. terminal cd labs/modernjava/javac/sealed-packages # 1. class path, unnamed module: two packages are not allowed javac -d ../../build/sealed-packages pay/api/PaymentMethod.java pay/card/Card.java # 2. one named module: two packages are fine javac -d ../../build/sealed-packages module-info.java pay/api/PaymentMethod.java pay/card/Card.java The first command fails with class PaymentMethod in unnamed module cannot extend a sealed class in a different package, pointing at pay.card.Card in the permits clause. The second compiles with no output, because both packages belong to module pay. After the move, the first command compiles too: on the class path, one package is enough.

h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · Let the compiler find every switch, and keep default out
x: Sealing pays off in a switch. Over a sealed type, javac knows every possible subtype, so a switch with one case per subtype is exhaustive (its cases cover every possible value) and needs no default. javac checks that the cases really do cover every subtype: Java static long ledgerImpact(Dispute d) { return switch (d) { // no default case Opened o -> -o.amountMinor(); case EvidenceSent e -> 0; case Won w -> 0; case Lost l -> -l.amountMinor(); }; } Kotlin fun ledgerImpact(d: Dispute): Long = when (d) { // no else is Dispute.Opened -> -d.amountMinor is Dispute.EvidenceSent -> 0 is Dispute.Won -> 0 is Dispute.Lost -> -d.amountMinor } Now the card schemes add an arbitration stage, and you add Arbitration to Dispute. Every switch over Dispute without a default stops compiling. On JDK 21 to 26 the error is the bare the switch expression does not cover all possible input values, pointing at the switch. JDK 27 adds the cases you're missing: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values return switch (d) { ^ missing patterns: Arbitration _ kotlinc has always been specific: 'when' expression must be exhaustive. Add the 'is Arbitration' branch or an 'else' branch. Either way, the build hands you the list of code to update. A default throws that list away. It means "and anything else", so Arbitration drops into it without a word and gets whatever the default returns. The OpenJDK team's 2026 guide to switching over sealed types has a section titled "By default, avoid default", because a default "sweeps errors, both present and future, under the rug". Use default only where you really mean "everything else", such as the illegal (state, event) pairs in a state machine, as State and Chain of Responsibility in the patterns track did. The same guide asks authors to say in the Javadoc why a type is sealed. It names two reasons: the type models a closed domain, like dispute stages, or the author only wants to control who implements it. Say which, and whether you expect to add subtypes, so the people switching over it know what to expect. Exhaustive also doesn't mean unbreakable at run time: a client compiled against the old list can still meet an Arbitration from a newer jar. Lesson 3 shows what happens then. Add a stage to the dispute flow Run DisputeSwitches once and look at the three functions: label, ledgerImpact and slaDays. Which one has a default? Add Arbitration to the permits clause and uncomment the Arbitration record. Before you run, predict which functions javac will report. Run it, then make it compile again by handling Arbitration where javac asked. What does slaDays return for an arbitration case now? Is that right? Do the same in the Kotlin twin, DisputeSwitchesKt. Preparing for Change: Safe Switching over Sealed APIs (OpenJDK Amber, 2026) read The usual mistake is adding default -> throw new IllegalStateException() to a switch over your own sealed type, "to be safe". It feels defensive, but it switches off the one check sealing gives you. When a new subtype arrives, the switch still compiles, the new case goes to the default branch, and you find out at run time, from a failed payment. Leave the default out and let the build fail. h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · Java and Kotlin
x: The dispute hierarchy in Java and Kotlin Dispute.java public sealed interface Dispute permits Opened, EvidenceSent, Won, Lost {} record Opened(String caseId, long amountMinor) implements Dispute {} record EvidenceSent(String caseId) implements Dispute {} record Won(String caseId) implements Dispute {} record Lost(String caseId, long amountMinor) implements Dispute {} static String label(Dispute d) { return switch (d) { // no default case Opened o -> "opened"; case EvidenceSent e -> "evidence sent"; case Won w -> "won"; case Lost l -> "lost"; }; } Dispute.kt sealed interface Dispute { data class Opened(val caseId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : Dispute data class EvidenceSent(val caseId: String) : Dispute data class Won(val caseId: String) : Dispute data class Lost(val caseId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : Dispute } fun label(d: Dispute): String = when (d) { // no else is Dispute.Opened -> "opened" is Dispute.EvidenceSent -> "evidence sent" is Dispute.Won -> "won" is Dispute.Lost -> "lost" } The idea is the same and so is the bytecode: both compilers write a PermittedSubclasses attribute, so each language sees the other's sealed types as sealed. Three things differ. Java names the subtypes in permits (or infers them from one source file) and makes every subtype choose final, sealed or non-sealed; Kotlin's list is whatever is declared in the same package and module, and subtypes are final unless you open them. Java's location rule is the module, or the package on the class path; Kotlin's is always package and module. And Kotlin has data object for a stateless case, where Java uses a record with no components or an enum.

h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · Worked example
x: Seal the events a Kafka consumer handles A ledger consumer handles three event types with an instanceof chain. Someone adds a fourth type, Adjusted, to the producer. This compiles with no warning, and the consumer starts throwing on the new events in production. public interface LedgerEvent {} void handle(LedgerEvent e) { if (e instanceof Posted p) post(p); else if (e instanceof Reversed r) reverse(r); else throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown event " + e); // Adjusted lands here } interface LedgerEvent fun handle(e: LedgerEvent) { if (e is Posted) post(e) else if (e is Reversed) reverse(e) else throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown event $e") // Adjusted lands here } Seal the event type and make each event a record in the same package. Records are final, so they need no modifier. // 1. close the list public sealed interface LedgerEvent permits Posted, Reversed, Adjusted {} public record Posted(String entryId, long amountMinor) implements LedgerEvent {} public record Reversed(String entryId, String reason) implements LedgerEvent {} public record Adjusted(String entryId, long deltaMinor) implements LedgerEvent {} // 1. close the list sealed interface LedgerEvent { data class Posted(val entryId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : LedgerEvent data class Reversed(val entryId: String, val reason: String) : LedgerEvent data class Adjusted(val entryId: String, val deltaMinor: Long) : LedgerEvent } Replace the chain with a switch that has no default. The chain could never be checked; the switch is checked on every build, and the else throw disappears because there is no "else" left. // 2. one case per event, no default void handle(LedgerEvent e) { switch (e) { case Posted p -> post(p); case Reversed r -> reverse(r); case Adjusted a -> adjust(a); } } // 2. one branch per event, no else fun handle(e: LedgerEvent) = when (e) { is LedgerEvent.Posted -> post(e) is LedgerEvent.Reversed -> reverse(e) is LedgerEvent.Adjusted -> adjust(e) } A switch statement with patterns must be exhaustive too, so the void version is checked just like the expression. Last, write down why the type is sealed, so the next person knows that adding an event is expected and that consumers must be updated, not given a default. /** * Every event on the ledger topic. Sealed because consumers must handle each one. * New events will be added: expect your switch to stop compiling, and handle the new case. */ public sealed interface LedgerEvent permits Posted, Reversed, Adjusted {} // 3. say why /** * Every event on the ledger topic. Sealed because consumers must handle each one. * New events will be added: expect your when to stop compiling, and handle the new case. */ sealed interface LedgerEvent // 3. say why

h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · Key terms
x: Sealed type A class or interface that lists which classes may extend it directly. Permitted subtype A class on a sealed type's list. It must be final, sealed or non-sealed. non-sealed The modifier that reopens one branch of a sealed hierarchy to any subclass. Exhaustive switch A switch whose cases cover every possible value of its selector, so it needs no default. PermittedSubclasses The class-file attribute that records a sealed type's list, checked by the JVM when a class loads. Unnamed module Where code on the class path lives when it has no module-info.java. Most services run here. Which modifiers can a permitted subtype of a sealed type have? Exactly one of final, sealed or non-sealed. Records and enums are implicitly final, so they need none. What does non-sealed do? It reopens that branch: anyone may extend it. A switch still covers the whole branch with one case for the non-sealed type. Why don't case Flat and case Percent cover sealed class Fee permits Flat, Percent when Fee isn't abstract? new Fee() is a possible value too. Make Fee abstract or an interface. Where may a Java sealed type's permitted subtypes live? In the same module. On the class path (the unnamed module), in the same package. Where may a Kotlin sealed type's direct subtypes live? In the same package and the same module. When can you leave out permits? When every subtype is declared in the same source file as the sealed type. javac infers the list. Why avoid default in a switch over your own sealed type? It stops the compiler from reporting the switch when a subtype is added. The new subtype silently takes the default branch.

h: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check · Go deeper
x: Sealing is enforced in three places, and it helps to know which one you are looking at. javac enforces it at compile time, with the errors in this lesson. The JVM enforces it at load time, from the PermittedSubclasses attribute. Compile final class B implements S against an old, unsealed S, then run it next to a newer S that is sealed and doesn't list B, and class loading fails with java.lang.IncompatibleClassChangeError: class B cannot implement sealed interface S. That stops a stray jar from smuggling a subtype into your hierarchy. And reflection reports it: Class.isSealed() and Class.getPermittedSubclasses(), both added with sealed classes, are what the tests in this lesson's lab use. None of the three stops you from adding a subtype yourself, and that is on purpose. The 2026 Amber guide calls adding a permitted subtype "a permissible and compatible evolution" of a sealed API. Clients compiled against the old list keep loading and running; only their switches change behavior. Recompiled, those switches fail to build. Not recompiled, they meet the new subtype at run time and throw MatchException. The guide calls this how Java balances "safety with resilience": you find out either at build time or loudly at run time, never silently. Lesson 3 runs that experiment, and shows that the same thing happens for an enum constant added after the switch was compiled. For Kotlin interop, one detail is worth checking in your own build. The PermittedSubclasses attribute only exists in class files for JDK 17 and later, so Java sees a Kotlin sealed type as sealed only when kotlinc targets 17 or higher. With the JDK 21 target the labs use, kotlinc 2.4 writes it, and javac rejects final class Bad implements Status {} against a Kotlin sealed Status with the usual not listed in its 'permits' clause error.

h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · A pattern switch is checked, an instanceof chain is not
x: Add a subtype: the pattern switch stops compiling, the instanceof chain stays silent A pattern is a test with a binding. Card c asks "is this value a Card?" and, if it is, gives you a new variable c of type Card. Pattern matching came to Java in steps. JDK 16 made instanceof patterns final (JEP 394): the type test and the cast become one, and the binding is in scope wherever the test is known to have passed. Java if (!(o instanceof Card c)) return "not a card"; return "last four: " + c.last4(); // c is in scope: the test can't have failed here Kotlin if (o !is Method.Card) return "not a card" return "last four: ${o.last4}" // smart cast: o is a Card from here on JDK 21 made pattern switch final (JEP 441), together with record patterns (JEP 440). It's tempting to read a pattern switch as a tidier if/else if chain. It is more than that, and the differences are the reason to prefer it: javac checks that it is exhaustive. An instanceof chain that forgets Wallet compiles without a word and falls into its final else. The switch that forgets it fails with the switch expression does not cover all possible input values. A pattern switch used as a statement must be exhaustive too, and the message then says switch statement. javac checks dominance: a case that can never match is a compile error (section 3). It has defined null rules (section 4). It compiles to one invokedynamic call to SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch, which picks the case, plus a synthetic arm that throws MatchException if no case matches at run time. Kotlin has had most of this for years. A when with a subject checks exhaustiveness over a sealed type, whether you use it as an expression or a statement, and smart casts merge the is check and the cast. With the JDK 21 target, kotlinc 2.4 even compiles that when to the same typeSwitch call; its fallback arm throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException instead. What Kotlin doesn't have is the subject of the next section. See which one the compiler catches Run PatternBasics (or PatternBasicsKt) with the command below. Delete the Wallet line from viaChain and run. Put it back, then delete the Wallet case from viaSwitch and run again. Which mistake did the compiler catch? From labs/, run javap -c -p modernjava/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/PatternBasics.class and find typeSwitch and MatchException in viaSwitch. Run the same javap on modernjava/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/PatternBasicsKt.class and look at viaWhen. PatternBasics.java package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; /** The same dispatch three ways: an instanceof chain, a guard clause, and a pattern switch. */ public class PatternBasics { sealed interface Method permits Card, Transfer, Wallet {} record Card(String network, String last4) implements Method {} record Transfer(String iban) implements Method {} record Wallet(String provider) implements Method {} // an if-chain: javac never checks that it covers every Method static String viaChain(Method m) { if (m instanceof Card c) return "card " + c.network() + " ****" + c.last4(); else if (m instanceof Transfer t) return "transfer from " + t.iban(); else if (m instanceof Wallet w) return "wallet " + w.provider(); else throw new IllegalStateException("unreachable?"); } // a pattern switch: javac checks that every Method is covered static String viaSwitch(Method m) { return switch (m) { case Card c -> "card " + c.network() + " ****" + c.last4(); case Transfer t -> "transfer from " + t.iban(); case Wallet w -> "wallet " + w.provider(); }; } // flow scoping: after the negated test returns, c is in scope for the rest of the method static String last4(Object o) { if (!(o instanceof Card c)) return "not a card"; return "last four: " + c.last4(); } public static void main(String[] args) { Method[] all = { new Card("VISA", "1111"), new Transfer("DE89370400440532013000"), new Wallet("Paywave") }; for (Method m : all) { System.out.println(viaChain(m) + " | " + viaSwitch(m)); } System.out.println(last4(all[0]) + ", " + last4("4111")); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.PatternBasics labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/PatternBasics.java PatternBasics.kt package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo sealed interface Method { data class Card(val network: String, val last4: String) : Method data class Transfer(val iban: String) : Method data class Wallet(val provider: String) : Method } // an if-chain: kotlinc never checks that it covers every Method fun viaChain(m: Method): String = if (m is Method.Card) "card ${m.network} ****${m.last4}" // smart cast: m is a Card here else if (m is Method.Transfer) "transfer from ${m.iban}" else if (m is Method.Wallet) "wallet ${m.provider}" else throw IllegalStateException("unreachable?") // when with a subject: kotlinc checks that every Method is covered fun viaWhen(m: Method): String = when (m) { is Method.Card -> "card ${m.network} ****${m.last4}" is Method.Transfer -> "transfer from ${m.iban}" is Method.Wallet -> "wallet ${m.provider}" } // a smart cast lasts for the rest of the function after a negated check returns fun last4(o: Any): String { if (o !is Method.Card) return "not a card" return "last four: ${o.last4}" } /** The same dispatch three ways: an if-chain, an early return, and a when. */ fun main() { val all = listOf(Method.Card("VISA", "1111"), Method.Transfer("DE89370400440532013000"), Method.Wallet("Paywave")) for (m in all) { println(viaChain(m) + " | " + viaWhen(m)) } println(last4(all[0]) + ", " + last4("4111")) } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.PatternBasicsKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/PatternBasics.kt Both versions print the same three lines and last four: 1111, not a card. Without its Wallet branch the chain still compiles, and the run crashes on the wallet with the chain's IllegalStateException. Without its Wallet case the switch doesn't compile: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (kotlinc: Add the 'is Wallet' branch or an 'else' branch.). In the bytecode, viaSwitch has invokedynamic ... typeSwitch and new java/lang/MatchException; the Kotlin viaWhen has the same typeSwitch call and new kotlin/NoWhenBranchMatchedException. JEP 441: Pattern Matching for switch read A pattern switch is the routing table in a card network's switch centre. Each row says "if the message looks like this, with these fields, send it there", and messages are checked against the rows from the top. Record patterns let a row look inside the message (BIN range, currency, merchant category) instead of only at its type, and a guard is an extra condition on a row. The network also proves that every possible message has a row, so nothing is dropped. The analogy breaks at the edges: a real routing table can fall back to a default route without anyone noticing a gap, while javac refuses a switch with a gap, and a message type invented after the table was built makes the Java switch throw instead of routing it somewhere.

h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Record patterns take the data apart in the label
x: A type pattern tests a type and binds one variable. A record pattern also takes the record apart, through its accessors, and each part can be a pattern too. Here are the first fee rules from this lesson's lab, next to the closest Kotlin. The when after each pattern is a guard, an extra condition that section 3 covers. Java return switch (charge) { case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card(var net, var corp), var r) when net == Network.AMEX -> bps(m, 350); case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card(var net, var corp), var r) when corp -> bps(m, 290); // ... }; Kotlin val m = charge.amount.minor return when (val method = charge.method) { // pick the nested part out first is Card if method.network == Network.AMEX -> bps(m, 350) is Card if method.corporate -> bps(m, 290) // ... } Read the Java label from the outside in. The selector, the value in switch (...), must be a Charge. Its amount() must match Money(long m, var ccy), which binds m and ccy. Its method() must be a Card, which binds net and corp. And region() binds to r. With var, javac infers each type from the record's components. Patterns are positional and type-checked: put String x where a record has an int and javac stops with incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. Generic records work too. Over sealed interface Result<T>, the case Ok<T>(var v) binds v as a T. Record patterns also work in instanceof, as in if (o instanceof Line(Point(var x, var y), var to) && x == 0). Kotlin has no record patterns. The closest tools are smart casts on nested properties, as in the twin above, and positional destructuring, val (from, to) = line, through component1() and component2(). Destructuring has a trap Java's patterns mostly avoid: it goes by position, not by name. With data class Payment(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long), the line val (amountMinor, id) = payment compiles without a warning and puts the id into amountMinor. Kotlin 2.3.20 added name-based destructuring as an Experimental feature, behind -Xname-based-destructuring; its name-mismatch mode warns about exactly this line. Java's record patterns are positional as well, but every component is type-checked, so most swaps fail to compile. Two var bindings of the same type can still be swapped silently, so keep the record header in front of you. Take a line apart Predict the third line of output, then run RecordPatterns. In describe, change Point(int x2, int y2) to Point(String x2, int y2) and run. Read the error, then undo it. Run the Kotlin twin, RecordPatternsKt, and read its last line. RecordPatterns.java package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; import java.util.List; /** Record patterns: take a record apart in the case label, nested as deep as you like. */ public class RecordPatterns { record Point(int x, int y) {} record Line(Point from, Point to) {} sealed interface Result<T> permits Ok, Err {} record Ok<T>(T value) implements Result<T> {} record Err<T>(String message, Throwable cause) implements Result<T> {} static String describe(Line line) { return switch (line) { case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(int x2, int y2)) when x1 == x2 -> "vertical at x=" + x1 + " len " + Math.abs(y2 - y1); case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when y1 == y2 -> "horizontal at y=" + y1; case Line(Point from, Point to) -> "diagonal " + from + "->" + to; }; } static <T> String show(Result<T> r) { return switch (r) { case Ok<T>(var v) -> "ok " + v; // T inferred for v case Err<T>(var msg, var cause) when cause != null -> "err " + msg + " caused by " + cause.getClass().getSimpleName(); case Err<T>(var msg, var cause) -> "err " + msg; }; } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Point(1, 0), new Point(1, 5)))); System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Point(0, 3), new Point(7, 3)))); System.out.println(describe(new Line(new Point(0, 0), new Point(2, 2)))); System.out.println(show(new Ok<>(List.of(1, 2)))); System.out.println(show(new Err<>("boom", new RuntimeException()))); Object o = new Line(new Point(0, 0), new Point(9, 9)); if (o instanceof Line(Point(var x, var y), var to) && x == 0 && y == 0) { // patterns in instanceof too System.out.println("from origin to " + to); } } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.RecordPatterns labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/RecordPatterns.java RecordPatterns.kt package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) data class Line(val from: Point, val to: Point) sealed interface Outcome<out T> { data class Ok<T>(val value: T) : Outcome<T> data class Err(val message: String, val cause: Throwable?) : Outcome<Nothing> } data class Payment(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long) // Kotlin can't take records apart in a when branch: match the outer type, then read the properties fun describe(line: Line): String { val (from, to) = line // positional destructuring via component1/2 return when { from.x == to.x -> "vertical at x=${from.x} len ${kotlin.math.abs(to.y - from.y)}" from.y == to.y -> "horizontal at y=${from.y}" else -> "diagonal $from->$to" } } fun <T> show(r: Outcome<T>): String = when (r) { is Outcome.Ok -> "ok ${r.value}" is Outcome.Err if r.cause != null -> "err ${r.message} caused by ${r.cause::class.simpleName}" // guard: Kotlin 2.2+ is Outcome.Err -> "err ${r.message}" } /** The Kotlin side: smart casts and positional destructuring instead of record patterns. */ fun main() { println(describe(Line(Point(1, 0), Point(1, 5)))) println(describe(Line(Point(0, 3), Point(7, 3)))) println(describe(Line(Point(0, 0), Point(2, 2)))) println(show(Outcome.Ok(listOf(1, 2)))) println(show(Outcome.Err("boom", RuntimeException()))) val o: Any = Line(Point(0, 0), Point(9, 9)) if (o is Line && o.from.x == 0 && o.from.y == 0) { // smart cast after the is check println("from origin to ${o.to}") } // destructuring goes by position, not by name: this compiles, with no warning, and swaps the values val (amountMinor, id) = Payment("p1", 500) println("swapped names: amountMinor=$amountMinor id=$id") } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.RecordPatternsKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/RecordPatterns.kt vertical at x=1 len 5, horizontal at y=3, diagonal Point[x=0, y=0]->Point[x=2, y=2], then ok [1, 2], err boom caused by RuntimeException and from origin to Point[x=9, y=9]. The String change fails with incompatible types: int cannot be converted to String. The Kotlin twin prints the same results with smart casts, and then swapped names: amountMinor=p1 id=500: positional destructuring put the id into amountMinor without a warning. One record pattern, three levels deep: the charge, its components, and the parts of each component, all bound in the case label. JEP 440: Record Patterns read Destructuring declarations (Kotlin docs) docs Most code that consumes payment events or issuer responses is a dispatch on shape: "a refund of a card payment over 500 EUR goes to manual review", "a decline with a retryable code goes back on the queue". Written as nested instanceof checks and casts, those rules hide gaps; written as one switch with record patterns, javac finds the missing shapes and the order of the rules is visible in one place. Two production habits follow from this lesson. Validate non-null at the edge (the REST resource, the Kafka deserializer) with Objects.requireNonNull, so switches never see null. And treat a MatchException in the logs after a deploy as "a service was built against an older version of a shared model jar": rebuild it, and the compiler will show you the cases to add.

h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Guards, order and dominance
x: Cases are tried from the top, and the first one whose pattern matches and whose guard is true wins. The guard is the when clause after the pattern. That makes order part of the meaning. A corporate AMEX card matches both of the first two lines below, so whichever comes first sets its fee: Java case CardCharge(var net, var corp, var amt) when net == Network.AMEX -> amt * 350 / 10_000; case CardCharge(var net, var corp, var amt) when corp -> amt * 290 / 10_000; case CardCharge(var net, var corp, var amt) -> amt * 30 / 10_000; Kotlin is Charge.Card if c.network == Network.AMEX -> c.amountMinor * 350 / 10_000 is Charge.Card if c.corporate -> c.amountMinor * 290 / 10_000 is Charge.Card -> c.amountMinor * 30 / 10_000 Guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, in either language. The compiler can't prove that a set of guards covers every value, so a family of guarded cases must end with an unguarded case of the same pattern. Delete the last line above and javac says the switch doesn't cover all possible input values, while kotlinc asks you to Add the 'is Card' branch. You can predict javac's verdict yourself. List the permitted subtypes of the selector's type. Cross off each one that has an unguarded case, or that sits under a sealed parent with an unguarded case. Inside record patterns, check combinations, not columns: for each subtype of the first component, the cases that start with it must between them cover the second component, and so on. With Pair(Red a, Red b) and Pair(Green a, Light b), the Red cases cover only Red in second place, so Pair(Red, Green) is missing. What is left over is what JDK 27 prints under missing patterns:. javac also rejects a case that can never be reached: this case label is dominated by a preceding case label. That happens when an earlier unguarded case already matches everything the later one could: case String s after case CharSequence cs, case Integer i when i > 0 after an unguarded case Integer i, a constant case 1 after case Integer i, or any pattern after default. A guarded case never dominates, which is why javac accepts the two guarded card rules in either order. Only your tests notice the difference. kotlinc has no dominance check at all: put the unguarded is Charge.Card first and it compiles without a warning, and every card pays 0.3%. Kotlin guards (is T if condition) have been stable since Kotlin 2.2; one limit is that a guard can't follow several conditions joined by commas. Several patterns can share one arm only if they bind nothing. On JDK 21 that rule makes such arms awkward: case Capture c, Refund r -> fails with illegal fall-through from a pattern, so you write two arms. JDK 22 made unnamed patterns final, and case Capture _, Refund _ -> is legal. _ also stands in for a component you don't need, as in case Authorize(var code, _). On JDK 21 it is a preview feature, and javac stops with unnamed variables are a preview feature and are disabled by default. Reorder the fee rules Run GuardsDemo and note the fee for the corporate AMEX card. Swap the lines marked // 1 and // 2. Predict which fee changes, then run. Undo. Move line // 3 above line // 1 and run. Do the same in GuardsDemoKt. Undo. Delete line // 3 and run both versions. h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Null, default and the remainder
x: switch has always thrown NullPointerException on a null selector, and a pattern switch keeps that rule unless you opt in with case null: Java return switch (currency) { case null -> "missing"; case "EUR" -> "euro"; default -> "other"; // default alone does not catch null }; Kotlin return when (currency) { // currency is a String? null -> "missing" "EUR" -> "euro" else -> "other" // without the null branch, null lands here } case null, default -> handles both in one arm. For most code, the OpenJDK guide on sealed switches prefers something simpler: reject null before the switch with Objects.requireNonNull, because a null that reaches business logic is a bug somewhere upstream. Kotlin settles the question in the type system. A when over a String? must handle null somewhere (kotlinc says Add the 'null' branch or an 'else' branch. if it doesn't), and nothing throws. Inside a record pattern, null follows a rule that surprises everyone once. A nested record pattern never matches null, but a nested type pattern that covers the whole component type does. So with case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when x1 == x2 first and case Line(Point from, Point to) second, a Line whose start is null skips the first case and lands in the second, with from bound to null. Change the second case to Line(Point(var a, var b), Point to) and javac still calls the switch exhaustive, but that Line now matches nothing and the switch throws MatchException. That points at the bigger limit: exhaustive is a compile-time promise. javac checks the switch against the subtypes it can see when it compiles. The values it can't see, which the Amber design notes call the remainder, are handled at run time. Compile a client against Status permits Active, Closed, then recompile only the hierarchy with a third status, Frozen, and run the old client: its switch throws java.lang.MatchException. An enum switch with no default does the same when it meets a constant added later. The old Kotlin when throws kotlin.NoWhenBranchMatchedException. You don't write code for the remainder, but in a deployment that mixes old and new jars, this is the exception you will see. Recompile the client and javac turns it back into a compile error. Feed a switch null, then a stranger Run NullDemo and NullDemoKt and compare their first lines. In the Java describe, change case Line(Point from, Point to) to case Line(Point(var a, var b), Point to) (and use a and b in the text). Predict: does it compile? What happens to the line with a null start? Run the separate-compilation experiment in labs/modernjava/javac/remainder. The five commands are at the top of Client.java. NullDemo.java package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo; /** What a switch does with null: at the top level, and inside a nested pattern. */ public class NullDemo { record Point(int x, int y) {} record Line(Point from, Point to) {} static String plain(String currency) { return switch (currency) { // the old rule: a null selector throws case "EUR" -> "euro"; default -> "other"; }; } static String withNull(String currency) { return switch (currency) { case null -> "missing"; // opt in to null case "EUR" -> "euro"; default -> "other"; }; } static String nullOrDefault(Object o) { return switch (o) { case String s -> "text " + s; case null, default -> "null or other"; // one arm for both }; } static String describe(Line line) { return switch (line) { case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when x1 == x2 -> "vertical"; case Line(Point from, Point to) -> "other line " + from + " -> " + to; // Point from also matches null }; } public static void main(String[] args) { try { System.out.println(plain(null)); } catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("plain(null): NullPointerException"); } System.out.println("withNull(null): " + withNull(null)); System.out.println("nullOrDefault: " + nullOrDefault(null) + " / " + nullOrDefault(42)); System.out.println("line, null start: " + describe(new Line(null, new Point(1, 1)))); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.NullDemo labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/NullDemo.java NullDemo.kt package workbench.modernjava.l03.demo data class Spot(val x: Int, val y: Int) data class Segment(val from: Spot?, val to: Spot?) // in Kotlin the type says whether null can arrive, and when compares with equals: null never throws fun plainWhen(currency: String?): String = when (currency) { "EUR" -> "euro" else -> "other" // null lands here } fun withNullWhen(currency: String?): String = when (currency) { null -> "missing" "EUR" -> "euro" else -> "other" } fun nullOrElse(o: Any?): String = when (o) { is String -> "text $o" else -> "null or other" } fun describeSegment(s: Segment): String { val from = s.from val to = s.to return when { from != null && to != null && from.x == to.x -> "vertical" else -> "other line $from -> $to" // you write the null case yourself } } /** What when does with null: the nullable type decides, and nothing throws. */ fun main() { println("plainWhen(null): ${plainWhen(null)}") println("withNullWhen(null): ${withNullWhen(null)}") println("nullOrElse: ${nullOrElse(null)} / ${nullOrElse(42)}") println("line, null start: ${describeSegment(Segment(null, Spot(1, 1)))}") } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l03.demo.NullDemoKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l03/demo/NullDemo.kt Java prints plain(null): NullPointerException; Kotlin prints plainWhen(null): other, because its when compares with equals and the type allowed null. Both print missing, then null or other twice, then a line whose start is null. After the change in step 2 the switch still compiles, and the null-start line throws java.lang.MatchException. The experiment prints active, priority 1, then sealed switch: java.lang.MatchException and enum switch: java.lang.MatchException from the old client; recompiling it gives two does not cover all possible input values errors. MatchException (Java SE 25 API) docs The mistake that ships is a guarded rule placed after a broader guarded rule, such as the corporate-card rate above the AMEX rate. Both cases are guarded, so javac accepts either order and reports nothing, and every corporate AMEX card is charged the corporate fee. People make it because they read the switch as a set of rules, when it is an ordered list. Write the most specific rule first, end each family with an unguarded case, and give every rule a test case that matches more than one guard, as the lab's ruleOrder test does.

h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Java and Kotlin
x: The fee rules in Java and Kotlin Fees.java static long fee(Charge charge) { return switch (charge) { case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card(var net, var corp), var r) when net == Network.AMEX -> bps(m, 350); case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card(var net, var corp), var r) when corp -> bps(m, 290); case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card c, var r) when r == Region.EEA || r == Region.UK -> bps(m, 30); case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Card c, var r) -> bps(m, 150); case Charge(var amount, BankTransfer(var instant), var r) when instant -> 50; case Charge(var amount, BankTransfer t, var r) -> 20; case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Wallet w, var r) when m < 1_000 -> 0; case Charge(Money(long m, var ccy), Wallet w, var r) -> bps(m, 100); }; } Fees.kt fun fee(charge: Charge): Long { val m = charge.amount.minor val r = charge.region return when (val method = charge.method) { is Card if method.network == Network.AMEX -> bps(m, 350) is Card if method.corporate -> bps(m, 290) is Card if r == Region.EEA || r == Region.UK -> bps(m, 30) is Card -> bps(m, 150) is BankTransfer if method.instant -> 50 is BankTransfer -> 20 is Wallet if m < 1_000 -> 0 is Wallet -> bps(m, 100) } } The rules, the order and the exhaustiveness check are the same in both: the first matching branch wins, guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, and neither version needs a default. The difference is where the data comes apart. Java's record patterns reach into Charge, Money and Card in the label and bind the parts. Kotlin can only test the type of the value it switches on, so the twin pulls method out first, switches on that, and reads charge.amount.minor by hand. javac also checks dominance, which kotlinc doesn't, and Java's switch has explicit null rules, where Kotlin leaves null to the type system.

x: Rewrite a refund router as one switch This code decides how a refund is paid back. It compiles, it has tests, and it has a bug the compiler can't see. Read it and look for a payment method it forgets. static String refundRoute(Event event) { if (event instanceof Refund r) { if (r.payment().method() instanceof Card c) { if (c.network() == Network.AMEX && r.amountMinor() > 50_000) return "manual review"; return "card refund"; } if (r.payment().method() instanceof BankTransfer) return "bank refund"; } return "ignore"; } fun refundRoute(event: Event): String { if (event is Refund) { val method = event.payment.method if (method is Card) { if (method.network == Network.AMEX && event.amountMinor > 50_000) return "manual review" return "card refund" } if (method is BankTransfer) return "bank refund" } return "ignore" } Name the shapes you care about, most specific first, and let each label take the event apart. Event is sealed (Refund, Capture) and so is Method, so the switch needs no default. static String refundRoute(Event event) { return switch (event) { // 1. the special case first case Refund(Payment(var id, Card(var net, var corp)), long amt) when net == Network.AMEX && amt > 50_000 -> "manual review"; // 2. then the general cases, one per method case Refund(Payment(var id, Card c), long amt) -> "card refund"; case Refund(Payment(var id, BankTransfer t), long amt) -> "bank refund"; // 3. events that need no refund case Capture c -> "ignore"; }; } fun refundRoute(event: Event): String = when (event) { is Refund -> when (val method = event.payment.method) { // 1. the special case first is Card if method.network == Network.AMEX && event.amountMinor > 50_000 -> "manual review" // 2. then the general cases, one per method is Card -> "card refund" is BankTransfer -> "bank refund" } // 3. events that need no refund is Capture -> "ignore" } That doesn't compile, in either language: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values (kotlinc: Add the 'is Wallet' branch). A refund of a wallet payment matches no case. The old chain had the same gap and returned "ignore", so wallet refunds were silently never paid. The compiler found the bug the tests missed. Add the case. case Refund(Payment(var id, Wallet w), long amt) -> "wallet refund"; // the case the chain forgot is Wallet -> "wallet refund" // the case the chain forgot On JDK 22 or newer, replace the bindings you never use with _, so a reader sees at a glance which parts each rule depends on. Kotlin's version already names only what it reads. // JDK 22+ case Refund(Payment(_, Card(var net, _)), long amt) when net == Network.AMEX && amt > 50_000 -> "manual review"; case Refund(Payment(_, Card _), _) -> "card refund"; case Refund(Payment(_, BankTransfer _), _) -> "bank refund"; case Refund(Payment(_, Wallet _), _) -> "wallet refund"; case Capture _ -> "ignore"; // Kotlin uses _ only for unused lambda parameters and destructured components val (_, amountMinor) = refund // skip the payment, keep the amount

h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Quiz
x: The switch is case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point(var x2, var y2)) when x1 == x2 -> "vertical"; case Line(Point from, Point to) -> "other";. What does it return for new Line(null, new Point(1, 1))? It throws NullPointerException "other", with from bound to null It throws MatchException "vertical" The nested record pattern Point(var x1, var y1) never matches null, so the first case is skipped. The type pattern Point from covers the whole component type, so it matches null and binds it. If the second case were also a record pattern, the switch would still compile and would throw MatchException for this line. Which pair of cases, in this order, does javac reject with this case label is dominated by a preceding case label? case Integer i -> ... then case Integer i when i > 0 -> ... case Integer i when i > 0 -> ... then case Integer i -> ... case Integer i when i > 0 -> ... then case 1 -> ... case Card c when c.corporate() -> ... then case Card c when c.network() == AMEX -> ... An unguarded case Integer i matches every Integer, so the guarded case after it can never run. A guarded case never dominates anything, which is why the other three orders compile. The last pair compiles but is probably a bug: corporate AMEX cards never reach the AMEX rule. Kotlin: data class Payment(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long). What does val (amountMinor, id) = Payment("p1", 500) do on Kotlin 2.4 with default settings? It fails to compile because the names don't match the properties It binds by name: amountMinor = 500, id = "p1" It compiles without a warning and binds amountMinor = "p1", id = 500 It compiles with a warning about swapped names Destructuring calls component1() and component2() in order, whatever you call the variables. Here the types even differ, but each variable just takes its component's type. Name-based destructuring exists only as an Experimental feature (2.3.20+, -Xname-based-destructuring). From lesson 1: record Masked(String card) overrides card() to return "****" plus the last four digits. For the card 4111111111111111, what does switch (m) { case Masked(var c) -> c; } return? 4111111111111111, because patterns read the field like toString does ****1111, because record patterns call the accessor It doesn't compile: records with overridden accessors can't be deconstructed null Record patterns extract components through the accessors, while the generated toString and equals read the fields. So this record shows ****1111 to patterns and the full number to toString: one more reason not to mask in the accessor. A switch over String currency has case "EUR" -> ... and default -> .... An upstream parser sometimes passes null. What does the OpenJDK sealed-switch guide prefer? Add case null to every switch that might see it Nothing: default already catches null Wrap the switch in try/catch for NullPointerException Reject null before the switch with Objects.requireNonNull(currency) default doesn't match null, so today the switch throws NPE. The guide allows case null but prefers Objects.requireNonNull before the switch: it fails where the bad value enters, with a clear message, instead of spreading null-handling into every switch.
