h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Key terms
x: Type pattern Card c: matches if the value is a Card, and binds it to c. Record pattern Card(var net, var corp): matches a Card and binds its components, which can be patterns too. Guard The when condition after a pattern (if in Kotlin). The case matches only if the guard is true. Dominance A case is dominated when an earlier case already matches everything it could. javac rejects it. Remainder The values an exhaustive switch doesn't cover at run time: nested nulls and subtypes added after compilation. MatchException What Java throws when an exhaustive switch meets a value from its remainder (since JDK 21). Unnamed pattern _ in a pattern: matches anything and binds nothing. Final from JDK 22. Do guarded cases count toward exhaustiveness? No, in Java or Kotlin. End each family of guarded cases with an unguarded case of the same pattern. When does javac say this case label is dominated by a preceding case label? When an earlier unguarded case already matches everything the later case could, such as case String s after case CharSequence cs, or case 1 after case Integer i. What does a pattern switch do with a null selector? It throws NullPointerException unless it has case null (or case null, default). default alone doesn't catch null. case Line(Point from, Point to) and the line's from is null. Does it match? Yes. A nested type pattern that covers the component's type matches null. A nested record pattern such as Point(var x, var y) doesn't. An old client's exhaustive switch meets a subtype added after it was compiled. What happens? Java throws MatchException; a Kotlin when throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException. Recompiling turns it into a compile error. How do you put several patterns in one switch arm? Only with unnamed patterns, from JDK 22: case Capture _, Refund _ ->. With named bindings javac says illegal fall-through from a pattern. Kotlin val (a, b) = payment: by name or by position? By position, through component1() and component2(). Swapped names compile without a warning. Name-based destructuring is Experimental since 2.3.20.

h: Pattern matching with switch and record patterns · Go deeper
x: Two newer features build on this lesson. Neither belongs in the labs, which compile for JDK 21. Primitive types in patterns have been a preview feature in every JDK from 23 to 27, and they are still a preview in the JDK 28 builds. They let a switch over an int use type patterns and guards, and let instanceof ask whether a value fits another primitive type exactly: Java // JDK 25: java --enable-preview --source 25 preview/PrimitivePatterns.java static String riskBand(int score) { return switch (score) { case 0 -> "no score"; case int s when s < 300 -> "high risk (" + s + ")"; case int s -> "low or medium risk (" + s + ")"; }; } Kotlin // Kotlin has always allowed conditions on any subject fun riskBand(score: Int): String = when { score == 0 -> "no score" score < 300 -> "high risk ($score)" else -> "low or medium risk ($score)" } Without the preview flags, JDK 25 stops with primitive patterns are a preview feature and are disabled by default. Treat the syntax as likely to change until it is final. The second feature is better error messages. JDK 27's javac lists what a non-exhaustive switch is missing, under a missing patterns: line, in the form Rect _ for a type and Pair(Red _,Green _) for a nested record pattern. That one change makes nested exhaustiveness errors much easier to read: on JDK 21 the same Pair switch only says it doesn't cover all possible input values, and you work out the missing combination yourself. One habit to avoid: don't write case _ when .... JDK 25's javac accepts it, but the JLS doesn't allow it, and a fix in JDK 28 development (JDK-8385488) makes javac reject it. Write default or a real type pattern instead.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Make illegal states unrepresentable
x: Here is how a card issuer's reply often arrives in a service: one class, every field optional. Java public class IssuerReplyDto { String status; // "APPROVED", "DECLINED" or "SOFT_DECLINE" String authCode; // only when approved Long amountMinor; // only when approved String declineCode; // only when declined Long retryAfterSeconds; // only on a soft decline } Kotlin data class IssuerReplyDto( val status: String?, // "APPROVED", "DECLINED" or "SOFT_DECLINE" val authCode: String?, // only when approved val amountMinor: Long?, // only when approved val declineCode: String?, // only when declined val retryAfterSeconds: Long?,// only on a soft decline ) Count what this type allows. Three statuses, times four optional fields that are each set or null, gives 48 shapes. Three of them make sense. The other 45, such as approved with no auth code, or approved with a decline code, can be built, serialized and passed around, and the comments are the only place that says which fields go together. Every consumer has to re-check that, and one of them won't: the capture job sends null as the auth code. Model the three outcomes instead, each with only its own fields: Java public sealed interface AuthResult permits Approved, Declined, RetryLater {} public record Approved(AuthCode code, long amountMinor) implements AuthResult {} public record Declined(DeclineReason reason) implements AuthResult {} public record RetryLater(Duration after) implements AuthResult {} Kotlin sealed interface AuthResult { data class Approved(val code: AuthCode, val amountMinor: Long) : AuthResult data class Declined(val reason: DeclineReason) : AuthResult data class RetryLater(val after: Duration) : AuthResult } Now there are three shapes, and "approved with a decline code" can't even be written down. The checks that are left move into the constructors: an AuthCode is six letters or digits, an approved amount is positive. That is what "make illegal states unrepresentable" means in practice. The types and the canonical constructors refuse the bad values once, so no consumer has to. Brian Goetz calls this style data-oriented programming: model the data as immutable records and sealed types, and write the logic as functions over them. He wrote it up in a 2022 InfoQ article, "Data Oriented Programming in Java". His 2019 design note on records and sealed types gives the vocabulary. A record is a product type: an Approved is a code and an amount, and its API models "the state, the whole state, and nothing but the state". A sealed interface is a sum type, "a discriminated union of a fixed set of types": an AuthResult is approved or declined or retry-later. Most messages a payment service handles have exactly this shape: a few alternatives, each a fixed set of fields. Count the shapes, then build a bad one Run IllegalStates (or IllegalStatesKt). Read the DTO consumer line: what will the capture job send to the issuer? In the Java demo, try to build an Approved with a decline code. There is no constructor for it: the shape doesn't exist. In the Kotlin twin, change AuthResult.Approved("", 4_200) to AuthResult.Approved(null, 4_200) and run. Which tool stopped you this time? shapes. */ public class IllegalStates { // the "bag of optionals" a JSON mapper gives you for the issuer's reply static final class IssuerReplyDto { final String status; // "APPROVED", "DECLINED" or "SOFT_DECLINE" final String authCode; // should be set only when approved final String declineCode; // should be set only when declined final Long retryAfterSeconds; // should be set only on a soft decline final Long amountMinor; // should be set only when approved IssuerReplyDto(String status, String authCode, String declineCode, Long retryAfterSeconds, Long amountMinor) { this.status = status; this.authCode = authCode; this.declineCode = declineCode; this.retryAfterSeconds = retryAfterSeconds; this.amountMinor = amountMinor; } } // a consumer of the DTO: it trusts that the fields match the In Kotlin, Approved(null, 4_200) doesn't compile at all, because the property is a non-null String: the type system did the constructor's job. Brian Goetz, Data Oriented Programming in Java (InfoQ, 2022) read Data-oriented code works like a payment network's message specification. A message is just fields with fixed meanings, the spec says which fields each message type carries, and every processor that reads the messages keeps its own logic (routing, risk, settlement) in its own system. Nobody ships behavior inside the message. A new processing step is easy to add, while a new message type means every processor updates its handling. The analogy breaks on enforcement: a spec is a document that a sender can violate, while a sealed type with validating constructors makes the bad message impossible to build in the first place.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Parse at the edge, then trust the types
x: The sealed model only helps if untrusted data can't get in around it. So the service converts raw input into the model in exactly one place, at its edge: the REST resource, the Kafka deserializer, the client for the issuer's API. Everything behind the edge works only with model values. Java static Parsed parse(IssuerReplyDto raw) { try { return switch (raw.status) { case "APPROVED" -> raw.authCode == null || raw.amountMinor == null ? new Rejected("approved without a code or an amount") : new Ok(new Approved(new AuthCode(raw.authCode), raw.amountMinor)); case "DECLINED" -> new Ok(new Declined(DeclineReason.fromCode(raw.declineCode))); case "SOFT_DECLINE" -> raw.retryAfterSeconds == null ? new Rejected("soft decline without retry-after") : new Ok(new RetryLater(Duration.ofSeconds(raw.retryAfterSeconds))); case null, default -> new Rejected("unknown status: " + raw.status); }; } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { return new Rejected(e.getMessage()); // a constructor refused a value } } Kotlin fun parse(raw: IssuerReplyDto): Parsed = try { when (raw.status) { "APPROVED" -> if (raw.authCode == null || raw.amountMinor == null) Rejected("approved without a code or an amount") else Ok(Approved(AuthCode(raw.authCode), raw.amountMinor)) "DECLINED" -> Ok(Declined(DeclineReason.fromCode(raw.declineCode))) "SOFT_DECLINE" -> if (raw.retryAfterSeconds == null) Rejected("soft decline without retry-after") else Ok(RetryLater(Duration.ofSeconds(raw.retryAfterSeconds))) else -> Rejected("unknown status: ${raw.status}") } } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { Rejected(e.message ?: "invalid reply") // a constructor refused a value } Two details make this work. The function never throws. A reply the model refuses comes back as Rejected with a reason, and the caller decides what that means (log it, alert, fail the payment safely) instead of an exception escaping from somewhere inside a mapper. And the constructors stay the final check: parse doesn't repeat the auth-code rule, it calls new AuthCode(...) and turns the refusal into a Rejected. Behind the edge, nothing re-validates. A method that takes an Approved knows it has a valid code and a positive amount, because no other kind of Approved can exist. Records, data classes and sealed types make this cheap: the model is a dozen lines, the edge is one function, and the compiler checks every switch in between. The lab builds exactly this for the issuer reply, in Kotlin, including the case the snippets above skip: an approved reply that also carries a decline code contradicts itself, and must be rejected. Predict what the edge does The issuer sends status: "APPROVED " (with a trailing space), auth code A1B2C3 and amount 4200. Which arm of parse takes it, and what does the capture job see? It sends a soft decline with retryAfterSeconds: 0. Does parse or a constructor produce the result? A teammate adds if (approved.amountMinor() <= 0) return; inside the capture job. Can that line ever run? The trailing space matches no status string, so case null, default returns Rejected("unknown status: APPROVED ") and the capture job never sees the reply: a strict edge turns a sloppy reply into a visible rejection instead of a capture with bad data. The zero wait gets past parse, because the field isn't null, and is refused by the RetryLater constructor once it has the range check (as the lab's does); the catch turns that refusal into Rejected. The teammate's line is dead code: an Approved with a non-positive amount can't be built, so the check can never be true. Look at the DTOs your Quarkus REST clients and Kafka consumers map into. Many are one class per endpoint, with a status field and a dozen nullable fields, and the rules about which fields go together live in if statements spread across services. Pick the one that causes the most defensive code (usually the issuer or acquirer response) and put a sealed model behind it. The DTO stays at the edge, where your JSON mapper keeps filling it. One parse function turns it into the model. Everything downstream, from the capture job to the retry scheduler to the Temporal workflow waiting for a soft decline to clear, switches over three records instead of re-checking strings. Valhalla needs nothing from you yet: keep your records free of identity tricks, and look again when JDK 28 is final and your frameworks support it.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Operations live outside the data
x: In classic object-oriented design, behavior lives in the classes: result.customerMessage(), result.nextStep(), result.metricTag(), each written three times across Approved, Declined and RetryLater. Data-oriented code keeps the records plain and writes each operation as one function with a switch: Java static String customerMessage(AuthResult r) { return switch (r) { case Approved a -> "Payment approved."; case Declined(var reason) when reason == DeclineReason.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS -> "Not enough funds. Try another card."; case Declined d -> "Payment declined."; case RetryLater(var after) -> "Your bank is busy. We'll try again in " + after.toSeconds() + " seconds."; }; } Kotlin fun customerMessage(r: AuthResult): String = when (r) { is Approved -> "Payment approved." is Declined if r.reason == DeclineReason.INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS -> "Not enough funds. Try another card." is Declined -> "Payment declined." is RetryLater -> "Your bank is busy. We'll try again in ${r.after.seconds} seconds." } Everything about customer messages sits in one function, the records don't depend on your translation code, and the next operation (a metrics tag, a ledger posting) is a new function that touches nothing else. That is one side of the expression problem, which Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento in the patterns track introduced. With methods on the classes, adding a type is local and adding an operation means editing every class. With sealed types and switches it is the other way round: a new operation is one function, and a new type breaks every switch until you handle it. Neither style makes both changes cheap, so choose by the change you expect more often. For payment data (authorization results, events, ledger entries, scheme messages) the set of types changes rarely and new operations keep arriving, so the data-oriented side wins. For open hierarchies that other teams extend, such as fraud checks or the PartnerMethod branch from lesson 2, keep an interface with methods. And behavior that is about the value itself, like Money.plus, belongs on the record. Keep business decisions out of the records; small methods that compute with the value itself can stay. Pay both costs Run ExpressionProblem (or ExpressionProblemKt). Write operation 3 where the comment says: isCustomerFacing, true for charges and refunds, false for fees. How many existing lines did you change? Add the Chargeback record (in Java, add it to permits too) and run. List the places the compiler asks you to change. Decide what a chargeback does to the balance and to the statement line, and handle it in each function. ExpressionProblem.java package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo; import java.util.List; /** Data in records, operations in functions. Add an operation, then add a type, and compare the cost. */ public class ExpressionProblem { sealed interface LedgerEntry permits Charge, Refund, Fee {} record Charge(String paymentId, long amountMinor) implements LedgerEntry {} record Refund(String paymentId, long amountMinor) implements LedgerEntry {} record Fee(String reason, long amountMinor) implements LedgerEntry {} // Step 3: add Chargeback to the permits clause, then uncomment this record. // record Chargeback(String paymentId, long amountMinor, String caseId) implements LedgerEntry {} // operation 1: how the entry moves the merchant's balance static long balanceDelta(LedgerEntry e) { return switch (e) { case Charge c -> c.amountMinor(); case Refund r -> -r.amountMinor(); case Fee f -> -f.amountMinor(); }; } // operation 2: the line on the merchant's statement static String statementLine(LedgerEntry e) { return switch (e) { case Charge(var id, var amt) -> "payment " + id + " +" + amt; case Refund(var id, var amt) -> "refund " + id + " -" + amt; case Fee(var reason, var amt) -> "fee " + reason + " -" + amt; }; } // Step 2: write operation 3 here, isCustomerFacing(LedgerEntry), as one more switch. public static void main(String[] args) { List<LedgerEntry> day = List.of(new Charge("pay_1", 10_000), new Fee("scheme fee", 35), new Refund("pay_1", 2_500)); long balance = 0; for (LedgerEntry e : day) { balance += balanceDelta(e); System.out.println(statementLine(e)); } System.out.println("balance " + balance); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l04.demo.ExpressionProblem labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l04/demo/ExpressionProblem.java ExpressionProblem.kt package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo sealed interface LedgerEntry { data class Charge(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : LedgerEntry data class Refund(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : LedgerEntry data class Fee(val reason: String, val amountMinor: Long) : LedgerEntry // Step 3: uncomment this class. // data class Chargeback(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val caseId: String) : LedgerEntry } // operation 1: how the entry moves the merchant's balance fun balanceDelta(e: LedgerEntry): Long = when (e) { is LedgerEntry.Charge -> e.amountMinor is LedgerEntry.Refund -> -e.amountMinor is LedgerEntry.Fee -> -e.amountMinor } // operation 2: the line on the merchant's statement fun statementLine(e: LedgerEntry): String = when (e) { is LedgerEntry.Charge -> "payment ${e.paymentId} +${e.amountMinor}" is LedgerEntry.Refund -> "refund ${e.paymentId} -${e.amountMinor}" is LedgerEntry.Fee -> "fee ${e.reason} -${e.amountMinor}" } // Step 2: write operation 3 here, isCustomerFacing(LedgerEntry), as one more when. /** Data in data classes, operations in functions. Add an operation, then add a type, and compare the cost. */ fun main() { val day = listOf(LedgerEntry.Charge("pay_1", 10_000), LedgerEntry.Fee("scheme fee", 35), LedgerEntry.Refund("pay_1", 2_500)) var balance = 0L for (e in day) { balance += balanceDelta(e) println(statementLine(e)) } println("balance $balance") } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l04.demo.ExpressionProblemKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l04/demo/ExpressionProblem.kt The demo prints three statement lines and balance 7465. Adding isCustomerFacing changed no existing line. The expression problem: each style makes one kind of change local and the other kind expensive. Sealed types at least make the compiler find every place to change.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Project Valhalla: what has shipped
x: Records are identity objects, and lesson 1 showed what that means. == compares references, you can lock on a record, and an array of Money is an array of references to separate heap objects. Project Valhalla's first feature lets a class give up identity: Java value record Money(long minor, String currency) {} // JDK 28 early-access builds, --enable-preview Kotlin @JvmInline value class AuthCode(val value: String) // Kotlin today: one property, compiled away The status is often misreported, so here it is precisely. JEP 401, Value Objects (Preview), together with JEP 539 (strict field initialization in the JVM), was integrated into the JDK mainline on 31 July 2026. JDK 27 had already branched off, so the feature ships in JDK 28, scheduled for 23 March 2027, and early-access builds of JDK 28 exist now. It is a preview: it needs --enable-preview and can still change. JDK 25, 26 and 27 don't have it. The Valhalla docs define value objects as immutable objects that lack identity, "distinguished solely by the values of their fields". == compares two value objects by their state, and identity operations such as synchronization fail with an exception. In return, the JVM may store them flat. In JDK 28 that means two optimizations. Flattening stores a value's fields directly inside the field or array element that holds it, with no separate object and no pointer. Scalarization lets JIT-compiled code keep the fields in registers and skip the allocation. Both have limits the docs spell out. Flattened values are read and written atomically and must allow null, so value objects with 64 bits or more of field data "cannot normally be flattened". Scalarization only happens once C2, the JIT's optimizing compiler, has compiled the code. Polymorphic variables, including those in generic APIs, aren't flattened. By the first rule, the Money above would not normally be flattened, since its long alone is 64 bits. Small records of a few int or short fields gain first. With the preview on, 28 JDK classes become value classes, among them Integer, Long, Optional, LocalDate, Instant and Duration. Synchronizing on an Integer, or putting one in a WeakReference, then throws IdentityException. Null-restricted types, the other thing people expect from Valhalla, are still draft JEPs. Kotlin's @JvmInline value class is an older, different trick. It holds one property and is erased to that property where the compiler can: a function taking an AuthCode compiles to one taking a String, under a mangled name. It is boxed when used as a generic T, an interface or a nullable type. Kotlin's design notes say the annotation leaves room for real Valhalla value classes later, but no such mode has shipped, so a Kotlin data class on JDK 28 is still an identity object. What to do today: don't depend on the identity of your records. No == between them, no synchronized on them, no identity-keyed maps. Then adopting value later is a one-word change. Look at identity, then at a Kotlin value class Run IdentityDemo. Which of its lines would change if Money were a value record? Run IdentityDemoKt. From labs/, run javap -p modernjava/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/modernjava/l04/demo/IdentityDemoKt.class. What parameter type does describeIban take? IdentityDemo.java package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo; /** Records are identity objects today. Here is what that identity looks like. */ public class IdentityDemo { record Money(long minor, String currency) {} public static void main(String[] args) { Money a = new Money(4_200, "EUR"); Money b = new Money(4_200, "EUR"); System.out.println("equals: " + a.equals(b) + ", ==: " + (a == b)); System.out.println("identity hash codes differ: " + (System.identityHashCode(a) != System.identityHashCode(b))); synchronized (a) { System.out.println("synchronized on a record: allowed, because it has an identity"); } // the Integer box cache lets identity leak into == for some values and not others Integer x = 127, y = 127, p = 128, q = 128; System.out.println("Integer 127 == 127: " + (x == y) + ", 128 == 128: " + (p == q)); // an array of records is an array of references to separate heap objects Money[] ledger = { a, b, a }; System.out.println("ledger[0] == ledger[2]: " + (ledger[0] == ledger[2]) + ", ledger[0] == ledger[1]: " + (ledger[0] == ledger[1])); } } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l04.demo.IdentityDemo labs/modernjava/src/demo/java/workbench/modernjava/l04/demo/IdentityDemo.java IdentityDemo.kt package workbench.modernjava.l04.demo data class MoneyAmount(val minor: Long, val currency: String) // Kotlin's value class today: one property, erased to that property wherever the compiler can @JvmInline value class Iban(val value: String) fun describeIban(iban: Iban): String = "IBAN ending ${iban.value.takeLast(4)}" /** Data classes are identity objects today; @JvmInline value classes are a compile-time trick. */ fun main() { val a = MoneyAmount(4_200, "EUR") val b = MoneyAmount(4_200, "EUR") println("==: ${a == b}, ===: ${a === b}") synchronized(a) { println("synchronized on a data class: allowed, because it has an identity") } val iban = Iban("DE89370400440532013000") println(describeIban(iban)) // compiled to a call taking a plain String val asAny: Any = iban // used as another type: boxed println("as Any, the object is a ${asAny::class.java.simpleName}") val inList = listOf(iban) // used as a generic T: boxed println("in a List, the element is a ${(inList[0] as Any)::class.java.simpleName}") } ./gradlew :modernjava:demo -Pmain=workbench.modernjava.l04.demo.IdentityDemoKt labs/modernjava/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/modernjava/l04/demo/IdentityDemo.kt equals: true, ==: false, different identity hash codes, a successful synchronized, Integer 127 == 127: true, 128 == 128: false, and ledger[0] == ledger[2]: true, ledger[0] == ledger[1]: false. With a value record, == would compare state, so a == b and ledger[0] == ledger[1] would be true, and synchronized would be refused. In Kotlin, javap shows describeIban-JSx-I4w(java.lang.String): the value class is erased to a String under a mangled name, and the demo shows it boxed back into an Iban when stored as Any or in a List. JEP 401: Value Objects (Preview) read Inline value classes (Kotlin docs) docs The common mistake is building the sealed model and then sneaking the old states back in: a shared details record with nullable fields inside each outcome, or a status enum stored next to the sealed type "for convenience". Now a Declined can carry status = APPROVED, and every consumer has to wonder which one is true. If two facts must agree, derive one from the other (a method computed from the type) or delete it. The opposite mistake is sealing an extension point, such as the interface partner teams implement, to get exhaustive switches; then every new partner needs a change in your module. Seal closed domains and leave plug-in points open.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Java and Kotlin
x: One model and one operation in Java and Kotlin AuthResult.java public record AuthCode(String value) { public AuthCode { if (value == null || !value.matches("[A-Z0-9]{6}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad auth code"); } } public sealed interface AuthResult permits Approved, Declined, RetryLater {} public record Approved(AuthCode code, long amountMinor) implements AuthResult { public Approved { if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive"); } } public record Declined(DeclineReason reason) implements AuthResult {} public record RetryLater(Duration after) implements AuthResult {} static String customerMessage(AuthResult r) { return switch (r) { case Approved a -> "Payment approved."; case Declined(var reason) when reason == DeclineReason.SUSPECTED_FRAUD -> "Payment declined. Please contact your bank."; case Declined d -> "Payment declined."; case RetryLater(var after) -> "Your bank is busy. We'll try again in " + after.toSeconds() + " seconds."; }; } AuthResult.kt @JvmInline value class AuthCode(val value: String) { init { require(value.matches(Regex("[A-Z0-9]{6}"))) { "bad auth code" } } } sealed interface AuthResult { data class Approved(val code: AuthCode, val amountMinor: Long) : AuthResult { init { require(amountMinor > 0) { "amount must be positive" } } } data class Declined(val reason: DeclineReason) : AuthResult data class RetryLater(val after: Duration) : AuthResult } fun customerMessage(r: AuthResult): String = when (r) { is AuthResult.Approved -> "Payment approved." is AuthResult.Declined if r.reason == DeclineReason.SUSPECTED_FRAUD -> "Payment declined. Please contact your bank." is AuthResult.Declined -> "Payment declined." is AuthResult.RetryLater -> "Your bank is busy. We'll try again in ${r.after.seconds} seconds." } The design is identical: a closed set of outcomes, each with only its own fields, constructors that refuse bad values, and an operation written as one exhaustive switch outside the data. Two things differ. Java's switch takes Declined apart in the label (Declined(var reason)), while Kotlin tests the type and reads r.reason after a smart cast. And AuthCode is a record in Java, which is a full object with identity, while Kotlin's @JvmInline value class is usually erased to a plain String. With JDK 28's preview, Java could write value record AuthCode(String value) and give up identity at the JVM level, which is something Kotlin's value class doesn't do today.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Worked example
x: From a payout webhook DTO to a closed model A payout provider calls your webhook with this body. Its docs say: a PAID event has an arrival date, a FAILED event has a reason, and a RETURNED event has the returned amount. The DTO encodes none of that. public record PayoutWebhookDto(String type, String payoutId, LocalDate arrivalDate, String failureReason, Long returnedMinor) {} data class PayoutWebhookDto(val type: String?, val payoutId: String?, val arrivalDate: LocalDate?, val failureReason: String?, val returnedMinor: Long?) Write one record per row of the provider's docs. Every field is required, so the record can't be half a PAID event. // 1. one record per valid combination public sealed interface PayoutEvent permits Paid, PayoutFailed, Returned {} public record Paid(String payoutId, LocalDate arrivalDate) implements PayoutEvent {} public record PayoutFailed(String payoutId, String reason) implements PayoutEvent {} public record Returned(String payoutId, long amountMinor) implements PayoutEvent { public Returned { if (amountMinor <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("returned amount must be positive"); } } // 1. one class per valid combination, with non-null properties sealed interface PayoutEvent { data class Paid(val payoutId: String, val arrivalDate: LocalDate) : PayoutEvent data class Failed(val payoutId: String, val reason: String) : PayoutEvent data class Returned(val payoutId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : PayoutEvent { init { require(amountMinor > 0) { "returned amount must be positive" } } } } Write the edge. It is the only code that looks at the DTO, and it checks that each type carries its own field. A null where the docs promise a value becomes a clear error here, not a NullPointerException three services later. // 2. the edge: DTO in, model out static PayoutEvent toEvent(PayoutWebhookDto d) { Objects.requireNonNull(d.payoutId(), "payoutId"); return switch (d.type()) { case "PAID" -> new Paid(d.payoutId(), Objects.requireNonNull(d.arrivalDate(), "arrivalDate")); case "FAILED" -> new PayoutFailed(d.payoutId(), Objects.requireNonNull(d.failureReason(), "failureReason")); case "RETURNED" -> new Returned(d.payoutId(), Objects.requireNonNull(d.returnedMinor(), "returnedMinor")); case null, default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown payout event: " + d.type()); }; } // 2. the edge: DTO in, model out fun toEvent(d: PayoutWebhookDto): PayoutEvent { val id = requireNotNull(d.payoutId) { "payoutId" } return when (d.type) { "PAID" -> PayoutEvent.Paid(id, requireNotNull(d.arrivalDate) { "arrivalDate" }) "FAILED" -> PayoutEvent.Failed(id, requireNotNull(d.failureReason) { "failureReason" }) "RETURNED" -> PayoutEvent.Returned(id, requireNotNull(d.returnedMinor) { "returnedMinor" }) else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown payout event: ${d.type}") } } Now the consumer. The old one was thirty lines of if ("PAID".equals(type) && arrivalDate != null). The new one is a switch with no default, so a new event type from the provider shows up as a compile error, not a silently ignored webhook. // 3. behind the edge: trust the types static void apply(PayoutEvent e, Ledger ledger) { switch (e) { case Paid(var id, var date) -> ledger.markSettled(id, date); case PayoutFailed(var id, var reason) -> ledger.reopen(id, reason); case Returned(var id, long amount) -> ledger.credit(id, amount); } } // 3. behind the edge: trust the types fun apply(e: PayoutEvent, ledger: Ledger) = when (e) { is PayoutEvent.Paid -> ledger.markSettled(e.payoutId, e.arrivalDate) is PayoutEvent.Failed -> ledger.reopen(e.payoutId, e.reason) is PayoutEvent.Returned -> ledger.credit(e.payoutId, e.amountMinor) }

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Quiz
x: Your issuer DTO has a status and four nullable fields, and the issuer's docs list three valid combinations. What does a sealed model with three records give you that careful validation in every consumer doesn't? Faster JSON mapping Invalid combinations can't be constructed, so no consumer can receive one Nothing, as long as every consumer validates Smaller objects on the heap With the sealed model the bad shapes don't exist, and the constructors refuse bad values once. Validating in every consumer works only until one consumer forgets, and the DTO keeps letting 45 nonsense shapes travel through the system. Neither the mapping speed nor the object size changes. Teams add a new fraud check every month, each in its own module, and every check answers score(payment). Which design fits? An enum listing all checks A sealed interface of records, scored by one switch in the risk module An interface FraudCheck with a score method that each team implements A sealed interface whose switch has a default branch for checks it doesn't know Here the set of types grows and the operation stays the same, and the types live in other modules: the object-oriented side of the expression problem. A sealed hierarchy would force every new check into the risk module and break its switch each month. A default would just hide the new checks. Which statement about Project Valhalla is accurate? JDK 25 LTS ships value classes as a preview Records became value objects in JDK 27 Null-restricted types such as String! are final in JDK 28 JEP 401 value objects are a preview feature of JDK 28; JDK 25, 26 and 27 don't have them JEP 401 was integrated after JDK 27 branched off, so it ships in JDK 28 (scheduled for March 2027) as a preview. Records are still identity objects; value record is only legal under that preview. Null-restricted types are still draft JEPs. From Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento: you replaced a Visitor over a sealed Expr with switch functions. Now a new node type, Pow, arrives. What does each design make you do? Visitor: add visitPow to the interface and to every visitor. Switches: every switch fails to compile until it handles Pow Visitor: nothing. Switches: nothing, because sealed types accept new records Visitor: one new class. Switches: one new function Both: only add the new record Visitor and sealed switches sit on the same side of the expression problem: adding a type is the expensive change in both. The difference is that the switches need no accept and no visitor interface, and the compiler points at each switch to fix. @JvmInline value class AuthCode(val value: String) and fun describe(c: AuthCode). What does the JVM see for describe(code) and for listOf(code)? Two ordinary AuthCode objects, like any class A String in both places describe takes a String under a mangled name, and the list holds a boxed AuthCode A Valhalla value object, flattened in both places Kotlin erases the value class to its one property where it can, so describe compiles to something like describe-XXXX(String). Used as a generic T, as in a List, it must be boxed into a real AuthCode object. None of this uses Valhalla: it is compile-time work, and it works on any JVM.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Explain it back
x: Your team lead asks: "Should we move our payment model to records and sealed types now, or wait for Valhalla to make it fast?" Answer in your own words: what the data-oriented style gives you today, where you would and wouldn't use it, and what Valhalla changes.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Key terms
x: Data-oriented programming Modeling data as immutable records and sealed types, and writing operations as functions that switch over them. Product type A type whose value is several values together, like a record: a code and an amount. Sum type A type whose value is one of a fixed set of alternatives, like a sealed interface: approved or declined. Illegal state A combination of field values that the domain says can't happen, such as approved with a decline code. Expression problem No design makes both new types and new operations cheap; you pick the side that matches how your code changes. Value object Valhalla's identity-free object: compared by its fields, and free for the JVM to copy or flatten. Preview in JDK 28. Flattening Storing a value object's fields directly inside the field or array that holds it, instead of a reference to a separate object. What does "make illegal states unrepresentable" mean in Java and Kotlin? Model each valid combination as its own record (or data class) under a sealed type, and check values in the constructors, so an invalid value can't be built. Record and sealed interface, in algebraic terms? A record is a product type: this and that. A sealed interface is a sum type: this or that. Where should untrusted input be validated? Once, at the edge: one parse function turns the DTO into the model or a rejection. Code behind the edge trusts the types. With sealed types and switches, what does adding an operation cost? And a type? An operation is one new function. A type breaks every exhaustive switch over the hierarchy, and the compiler lists each one. When do you keep an interface with methods instead of a sealed type? For open hierarchies that other teams extend (plug-ins, partner methods, fraud checks), and for behavior about the value itself, like Money.plus. Which JDK has JEP 401 value objects? JDK 28, as a preview feature (scheduled for March 2027; early-access builds now). Not JDK 25, 26 or 27. Why won't value record Money(long minor, String currency) normally be flattened in JDK 28? Flattened values must be read and written atomically and allow null, so values with 64 bits or more of field data aren't normally flattened. The long alone is 64 bits.

h: Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla · Go deeper
x: Brian Goetz's January 2026 design note, "Data-Oriented Programming for Java: Beyond Records", says where Amber goes next. It calls records, sealed classes and record patterns "the first feature arc of 'data-oriented programming' for Java", and announces the next arc: carrier classes and carrier interfaces. A carrier class is a normal class with a record-style state description in its header. It would declare its own fields and need not be final, yet still have a canonical constructor, accessors and a deconstruction pattern, so data that is almost a record (one cached field, one derived value) doesn't force you back to writing everything by hand. The note also describes reconstruction, the with expression from JEP 468, and points out how much its block resembles a compact constructor body: the component variables start with the old values, your block changes some of them, and the canonical constructor builds the new value, so the invariants still hold. Goetz explains that JEP 468 has been "on hold" until there was a path to extend it beyond records. The note also mentions an upcoming pattern assignment statement, for taking a record apart in an ordinary assignment. None of this is in a JDK or a JEP you can use. The design direction is useful anyway: it says the language will keep making "model the data with records and sealed types, switch over it" cheaper, so code written in that style today is code the platform is moving toward. On the Valhalla side, the next pieces on the project page are null-restricted storage, array enhancements, unifying primitives with classes, and a parametric JVM that can specialize generics. Only the first piece, value objects, has a JEP that has been integrated, and it is a preview.

h: Advanced Kotlin
x: Inline functions, value classes, delegation, type-safe DSLs, contracts, context parameters and compiler plugins. By the end of this track the Kotlin features you use every day stop being magic. For each one you can say what the compiler writes into the class file, and so predict how it behaves in a case nobody showed you: what an inline function pastes into its callers and why crossinline exists, where a value class is a plain long and where it becomes an object, which hidden fields by creates, how a lambda with receiver becomes a DSL, what a contract promises and why nobody checks it, how context parameters reach a function, and what the all-open, no-arg and serialization plugins change. Each lesson also shows what Java sees when it calls the same Kotlin code, because the two languages meet in the bytecode. You need the syntax of both languages and nothing else. The first lesson starts from what a lambda costs at run time. Every lesson shows the problem first, then the feature that fixes it, then the bytecode as javap prints it, then the trap. The compiler messages quoted in the lessons are copied from Kotlin 2.4.21. Install JDK 25; the labs compile with release 21. The labs live in labs/kotlin, one package per lesson (workbench.kotlin.l01 to l06). They are Kotlin, and each lesson adds a Java test that calls your Kotlin code the way a Java module would. Lessons 1 and 5 test inline functions through a Callers.kt file that you don't edit (lesson 1 explains why). The module already applies the kotlinx.serialization, all-open and no-arg plugins; lesson 6 puts them to work. Run ./gradlew :kotlin:test --tests 'workbench.kotlin.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, ./gradlew :kotlin:solutionTest to see the reference answers pass the same tests, and ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=<class> for the Try-it programs. To read bytecode, run javap -c -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo <class> after a demo has compiled. inline pastes a function and its lambdas into each caller: no lambda object, non-local returns allowed, but every caller carries a copy and a public body stays frozen in compiled clients. crossinline lets an inline function call a lambda from another execution context by forbidding return in it; noinline keeps a lambda as an object you can store. A value class is its underlying value where it's used as itself and a box everywhere else; functions that take one get mangled names, so give Java a validated door. by on a class forwards to an object captured once; by on a property is a hidden $delegate field plus getValue/setValue calls. lazy costs objects per instance. A DSL is lambdas with receivers (Function1 on the JVM) and builder classes; @DslMarker on the builder classes keeps calls on the nearest receiver. Contracts give callers smart casts and in-place lambdas; they are Experimental and trusted, never checked. Context parameters, Stable in 2.4.0, are arguments the compiler fills by type; on the JVM they are ordinary leading parameters. all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization change the class file at compile time: configure the exact jakarta annotations, mind no-arg's skipped initializers, and pin serial names. When in doubt, run javap: every feature in this track is visible there, and Java sees exactly that.

h: Advanced Kotlin: cheat sheet
x: Inline functions You write The compiler Java sees inline fun timed(block: () -> T) pastes the body and the lambda body into each caller an ordinary static method taking Function0 return in a lambda passed to an inline function a non-local return: leaves the enclosing function (Java lambdas can only leave themselves) return@forEach leaves only that lambda call continue in a loop noinline f: () -> Unit keeps f as a real object you can store or pass on Function0 crossinline f: () -> Unit lets you call f inside a Runnable, object or lambda; forbids return in it Function0 @PublishedApi internal fun helper() public in bytecode, so public inline bodies may call it a public method Inline small functions that take lambdas, or need reified or a non-local return. Not lambda-free functions: expected performance impact from inlining is insignificant. A public inline body is copied into clients at their compile time: changing it reaches a client only when the client is rebuilt. Not allowed: recursion (cannot be recursive) and local functions inside an inline function. Tests of inline functions must call them through code compiled with the solution, or they keep a copy of the stub. Value classes Use of @JvmInline value class Money(val cents: Long) Run time parameter, field, return value, a + b, a == b a plain long generic T, Money?, an interface it implements, Any, collections, println boxed: Money.box-impl(long) fun charge(m: Money) charge-<hash>(long): mangled, Java can't call it @JvmName("chargeFromJava") Java calls chargeFromJava(long), skipping init: validate again @JvmExposeBoxed (Experimental, @OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class)) a public constructor that runs init, boxed overloads One property only on the JVM: value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter. Multi-field value classes wait for Valhalla (JEP 401 is a preview in JDK 28). === is an error. A type alias is only another name; a value class is a new type. Keep override fun toString(): String with its explicit type: Kotlin 2.4.21 crashes on an inferred platform type there. Delegation Code Compiled to Trap class A(x: I) : I by x every I method forwards to a hidden private final I $$delegate_0 reassigning a var doesn't move it; equals/hashCode/toString not forwarded; the delegate never calls your overrides var p: T by d a p$delegate field, a static $$delegatedProperties KProperty[], accessors calling getValue/setValue one delegate object per property per instance val v by lazy { } a kotlin.Lazy v$delegate (SynchronizedLazyImpl by default) plus an initializer lambda two objects per instance, read through Lazy.getValue(); exceptions are not cached Delegates.observable / vetoable handler after / before the assignment vetoable never checks the initial value val host: String by map map["host"] on each read missing key fails on read: Key host is missing in the map. operator fun provideDelegate(thisRef, property) called once per property during construction the place to validate early Type-safe DSLs A.() -> B is Function1<A, B> on the JVM: the receiver is the first parameter, and Java passes b -> { ...; return Unit.INSTANCE; }. A DSL is builder classes plus fun entry(block: Builder.() -> Unit) = Builder().apply(block).build(). Validate single values at the call, cross-field rules in build(). @DslMarker on an annotation, that annotation on every builder class: only the nearest receiver is implicit, outer ones need this@label. On functions or properties it has no effect. buildList, buildMap, buildString: mutable receiver while building, read-only result, inline. Contracts and context parameters Feature Status in 2.4 Syntax JVM / Java Contracts Experimental: @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) contract { returns() implies (x != null); callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) } as the first statement no trace in bytecode; stored in Kotlin metadata Extended contracts Experimental, plus ExperimentalExtendedContracts for returnsNotNull(), holdsIn Context parameters Stable since 2.4.0, no flag context(tx: TxContext) fun note(line: String); _ plus contextOf<T>() leading parameters: context, then receiver, then the rest Explicit context arguments, callable references not stable: avoid -Xexplicit-context-arguments The compiler trusts contracts unconditionally: a lie compiles and fails as ClassCastException. Nothing: the discriminator is the simple class name Nothing: the plugin assigns stable numeric ids The "type" values change, because the default is the fully qualified class name, so old consumers can't decode new messages Serialization fails until you add a SerializersModule Without @SerialName, the discriminator value is the fully qualified class name.
