h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · inline pastes the function and its lambda into the caller
x: Kotlin's inline pastes the function body and its lambda into the caller: no Function0, no interface call, no unboxing Start with a helper that every service has: run a block of code and log how long it took. Java static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } } long fee = timed("fee", () -> amountMinor * 3 / 100); Kotlin fun <T> timedNotInline(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } val fee = timedNotInline("fee") { amountMinor * 3 / 100 } Count what one call costs. The lambda { amountMinor * 3 / 100 } uses a local variable from outside its braces, so it is a closure: the JVM builds a small object that holds a copy of amountMinor, and timedNotInline calls that object's invoke method. Kotlin creates the object with invokedynamic, the same instruction Java uses for its lambdas (the lesson "invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile" goes into it). And because the helper is generic, the Long result travels back as an Object and has to be unboxed, that is, turned from a java.lang.Long object back into a primitive long. That's one object, one call through an interface and one unboxing, on every call. The Kotlin docs name exactly these costs: function objects, captured closures and virtual calls. You could avoid all of it by hand, by pasting the helper's body into the caller: Java long start = System.nanoTime(); long fee; try { fee = amountMinor * 3 / 100; // the lambda's body, pasted in } finally { System.out.println("fee took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } Kotlin val start = System.nanoTime() val fee = try { amountMinor * 3 / 100 // the lambda's body, pasted in } finally { println("fee took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } Nobody writes that fifty times. inline asks the compiler to do the pasting for you. Write inline fun <T> timed(...) with the same body, and at every call site (every place in the code that calls it) the compiler copies the function's body, and the body of the lambda you passed, instead of making a call. javap, the JDK tool that prints a class file's bytecode, shows the difference in the demo below. The ordinary call site is seven instructions long: invokedynamic builds a Function0, invokestatic calls timedNotInline with it, and checkcast java/lang/Number plus longValue unbox the result. The inline call site has none of that. The multiply (lmul, ldiv) sits right inside feeInline, between two calls to System.nanoTime, just like the hand-pasted version. Read a bit further and you see the price. The finally block appears twice in feeInline, once for the normal exit and once for the exit by exception. That's real code growth, repeated in every caller, and the docs say it pays off only if you avoid inlining large functions. So inline is for small functions that take lambdas. The standard library is full of them: forEach, map, filter, let, apply, use, repeat, synchronized, require. Because they are inline, payments.map { it.amountMinor } costs about what a hand-written loop costs. The generics track used inline for one more reason: a reified type parameter exists only because the body is copied to a call site where the type is known. Java gets none of this. javac can't inline Kotlin code, so for Java InlineDemoKt.timed(...) is an ordinary static method that takes a Function0, and the Java lambda becomes an object like any other. Read the bytecode of an inline call Run InlineDemo (or InlineDemoJava) with the command below. Both print fee = 360. From labs/, run javap -c -p kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/InlineDemoKt.class. Find feeNotInline and feeInline. Before you look, predict which one contains invokedynamic and which one contains lmul. Then count the println calls inside feeInline. InlineDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo /** inline: the compiler pastes this body, and the lambda's body, into every caller. */ inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } /** The same function without inline: the caller builds a Function0 object and calls through it. */ fun <T> timedNotInline(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } fun feeInline(amountMinor: Long): Long = timed("inline") { amountMinor * 3 / 100 } fun feeNotInline(amountMinor: Long): Long = timedNotInline("not inline") { amountMinor * 3 / 100 } fun main() { println("fee = ${feeInline(12_000)}") println("fee = ${feeNotInline(12_000)}") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.InlineDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/InlineDemo.kt InlineDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; /** * Java twin of InlineDemo.kt. javac cannot inline Kotlin code, so for Java the inline function * timed() is an ordinary static method on InlineDemoKt that takes a Function0. */ public class InlineDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { // the Java lambda becomes a Function0 object; timed() calls its invoke() like any other method long fee = InlineDemoKt.timed("from Java", () -> 12_000L * 3 / 100); System.out.println("fee = " + fee); // the same idea written in plain Java: a Supplier and a call through it long same = timedJava("plain Java", () -> 12_000L * 3 / 100); System.out.println("fee = " + same); } static <T> T timedJava(String label, java.util.function.Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.InlineDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/InlineDemoJava.java feeNotInline is short: invokedynamic (a new Function0), invokestatic timedNotInline, then checkcast java/lang/Number and longValue to unbox the result. feeInline holds the arithmetic (lmul, ldiv) and two PrintStream.println calls, because the finally block was copied for both exits. Ignore the microsecond timings: one cold call measures class loading and lambda setup, not inlining. The bytecode is the evidence. The same helper with and without inline. The inline caller has no lambda object and no call, but it carries its own copy of the whole body. Inline functions (Kotlin docs) docs Inlining is a cook copying the recipe onto every order ticket instead of pinning one copy on the wall. Nobody walks to the wall, so each order moves faster, but every ticket gets longer. If the head chef fixes the recipe on the wall, tickets that were already printed still carry the old version: that's the frozen-body problem. The analogy breaks at crossinline. A cook can't accidentally walk out of the restaurant, but a lambda copied into a Runnable could try to return from a function that finished minutes ago, so the compiler has to forbid it.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · A bare return in an inlined lambda leaves the caller
x: Inside an ordinary lambda, a bare return doesn't compile. The error is 'return' is prohibited here. A lambda is an object with its own method, and that method can't make some other function return. An inlined lambda is different. Its body becomes part of the caller, so return can mean exactly what it says. Java static String firstDeclined(List<String> results) { for (String r : results) { if (r.startsWith("DECLINED")) return r; // Java needs a real loop to return early } return null; } static int countApproved(List<String> results) { int approved = 0; for (String r : results) { if (!r.startsWith("APPROVED")) continue; approved++; } return approved; } Kotlin fun firstDeclined(results: List<String>): String? { results.forEach { if (it.startsWith("DECLINED")) return it } // leaves firstDeclined return null } fun countApproved(results: List<String>): Int { var approved = 0 results.forEach { if (!it.startsWith("APPROVED")) return@forEach // leaves this lambda call only approved++ } return approved } The first return is a non-local return: it leaves the function that contains the lambda. It compiles only because forEach is inline. In the bytecode, firstDeclined is an Iterator loop with an areturn in the middle, and no lambda object exists at all. To leave only the current call of the lambda, add a label. return@forEach behaves like continue in a loop. Since Kotlin 2.2.0, break and continue also work inside a lambda passed to an inline function. The feature is stable, so you need no compiler flag. In the demo, break inside batch.forEach { } leaves the outer for loop, the way Java's labeled break outer does. Java has no non-local return. A Java lambda always compiles to a separate method, so return inside forEach(r -> { ... }) only ends that one call and the loop goes on. The demo's firstDeclinedBroken shows it: it always returns null. People who move from Java to Kotlin make the opposite mistake. They write return inside forEach to skip one element, and the whole function exits instead. Return, label, break Run NonLocalReturnDemo and then NonLocalReturnDemoJava. Before you run the Java one, predict what firstDeclinedBroken prints. Work out totalUntilVoid by hand from the three batches in main, then check your number against the output. Uncomment the wrong move at the bottom of main (a lambda stored in a val). Predict the error, run, then comment it out again. NonLocalReturnDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo /** A bare `return` inside forEach's lambda returns from firstDeclined: forEach is inline. */ fun firstDeclined(results: List<String>): String? { results.forEach { if (it.startsWith("DECLINED")) return it } return null } /** `return@forEach` leaves only the current lambda call, like `continue` in a loop. */ fun countApproved(results: List<String>): Int { var approved = 0 results.forEach { if (!it.startsWith("APPROVED")) return@forEach approved++ } return approved } /** Since Kotlin 2.2, `break` and `continue` work inside an inlined lambda too. */ fun totalUntilVoid(batches: List<List<Long>>): Long { var total = 0L for (batch in batches) { batch.forEach { amount -> if (amount < 0) break // leaves the for loop, not just the lambda total += amount } } return total } fun main() { val results = listOf("APPROVED pay_1", "DECLINED pay_2 insufficient funds", "APPROVED pay_3") println("firstDeclined = ${firstDeclined(results)}") println("countApproved = ${countApproved(results)}") println("totalUntilVoid = ${totalUntilVoid(listOf(listOf(1_000L, 250L), listOf(400L, -1L, 900L), listOf(75L)))}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val lookup = { r: String -> if (r.isEmpty()) return; r.length } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.NonLocalReturnDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/NonLocalReturnDemo.kt NonLocalReturnDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of NonLocalReturnDemo.kt. A Java lambda is always a separate method, so `return` * inside it only leaves the lambda. To return from the enclosing method you need a real loop. */ public class NonLocalReturnDemoJava { static String firstDeclined(List<String> results) { for (String r : results) { if (r.startsWith("DECLINED")) return r; // a loop, so return leaves the method } return null; } static String firstDeclinedBroken(List<String> results) { results.forEach(r -> { if (r.startsWith("DECLINED")) return; // leaves this lambda call only }); return null; // always reached } static long totalUntilVoid(List<List<Long>> batches) { long total = 0; outer: for (List<Long> batch : batches) { for (long amount : batch) { if (amount < 0) break outer; // Java's labeled break: Kotlin's non-local break total += amount; } } return total; } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> results = List.of("APPROVED pay_1", "DECLINED pay_2 insufficient funds", "APPROVED pay_3"); System.out.println("firstDeclined = " + firstDeclined(results)); System.out.println("firstDeclinedBroken = " + firstDeclinedBroken(results)); System.out.println("totalUntilVoid = " + totalUntilVoid(List.of(List.of(1_000L, 250L), List.of(400L, -1L, 900L), List.of(75L)))); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.NonLocalReturnDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/NonLocalReturnDemoJava.java Kotlin prints firstDeclined = DECLINED pay_2 insufficient funds, countApproved = 2 and totalUntilVoid = 1650 (1,000 + 250 + 400, then the -1 breaks out of the outer loop, so 900 and 75 are never added). Java's firstDeclinedBroken prints null. The wrong move fails with 'return' is prohibited here. (Gradle adds RETURN_NOT_ALLOWED): a lambda stored in a val is an object, so it can't return from main. What's new in Kotlin 2.2.0: non-local break and continue docs Your Quarkus services are full of small wrappers: timed("issuer.authorize") { client.authorize(req) } around a metrics timer, withMdc("paymentId", id) { ... } around logging, a retry around a card-issuer call that takes 120 ms and sometimes times out. Each one is a good inline candidate: a few lines, a lambda parameter, called on every request. The moment a wrapper hands the lambda to a Java API (executor.execute, CompletableFuture.supplyAsync, a transaction callback, Temporal's Async.function), its parameter needs crossinline. And if those wrappers live in a shared library that ten services use, a fix to an inline body reaches each service only when that service is rebuilt against the new version.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · When a lambda can't be pasted: noinline and crossinline
x: Inlining works only if the compiler can paste the lambda's body where you call it. Two things get in the way, and each one has its own modifier. The first is using the lambda as a value. An inlined lambda has no object behind it, so you can't store it in a field, add it to a list or pass it to an ordinary function. Try it and the compiler says illegal usage of inline parameter 'listener: (String) -> Unit'. Add 'noinline' modifier to the parameter declaration. noinline turns that one parameter back into a normal lambda object. The other parameters are still inlined. The second is calling the lambda from somewhere else: inside an object, a Runnable or another lambda. The docs call this "another execution context". That code runs later, maybe on another thread, when the caller may have returned long ago. A non-local return from there can't work, so the compiler stops you: cannot inline 'task: () -> Unit' here: it might contain non-local returns. Add 'crossinline' modifier to parameter declaration 'task: () -> Unit'. crossinline is a rule for the caller's lambda: no bare return inside it. With that rule in place, the compiler still pastes the lambda's body, now into a Runnable class it generates for that call site. In the demo, javap finds a class called ModifiersDemoKt$main$$inlined$runInBackground$1 with no Function0 field: the body of the caller's lambda is inside its run(). Java // Java lambdas already behave like crossinline ones: return leaves only the lambda static void runInBackground(Executor executor, Runnable task) { executor.execute(task); } runInBackground(pool, () -> System.out.println("settling batch 17")); Kotlin inline fun runInBackground(executor: Executor, crossinline task: () -> Unit) { executor.execute { task() } // task runs later, on a pool thread } runInBackground(pool) { println("settling batch 17") } // runInBackground(pool) { return } // error: 'return' is prohibited here. Both modifiers would make that function compile, so pick by what you do with the lambda. Use crossinline when you call it inside another lambda or object, because its body is still inlined into the new class. Use noinline when the lambda has to exist as a value you keep or hand on. Neither modifier changes the JVM signature: Java sees a Function0 either way. You'll need crossinline all the time at work. Plenty of Java APIs take a callback: Executor.execute(Runnable), CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(Supplier), a transaction template's execute(callback), Temporal's Async.function(...). Every inline Kotlin wrapper around one of them needs it. Make the compiler ask for each modifier Run ModifiersDemo (or ModifiersDemoJava, which calls the same Kotlin functions with plain Java lambdas). In ModifiersDemo.kt, delete noinline in subscribe. Predict the error, run, read it, then put it back. Delete crossinline in runInBackground, run, and put it back. Uncomment the last line of main and run. Why does the compiler refuse a return that it allowed in forEach? Predict without running: does inline fun once(block: () -> Unit) = run { block() } need crossinline? (run is itself inline.) Then add it to the file and check. ModifiersDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo import java.util.concurrent.Executor import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit val listeners = mutableListOf<(String) -> Unit>() /** noinline: `listener` is stored in a list, so it has to stay a real object. `log` is inlined. */ inline fun subscribe(log: (String) -> Unit, noinline listener: (String) -> Unit) { log("subscribing listener #${listeners.size + 1}") listeners += listener } /** crossinline: `task` runs inside a Runnable on another thread, so it may not return from the caller. */ inline fun runInBackground(executor: Executor, crossinline task: () -> Unit) { executor.execute { task() } } fun main() { subscribe({ println(it) }) { event -> println("listener got $event") } listeners.forEach { it("payment-captured") } val pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { Thread(it, "settlement-worker") } runInBackground(pool) { println("running on ${Thread.currentThread().name}") } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // Wrong moves, one at a time. Predict the error, run, then undo. // 1. Delete `noinline` in subscribe. // 2. Delete `crossinline` in runInBackground. // 3. Uncomment the next line. // runInBackground(pool) { return } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.ModifiersDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/ModifiersDemo.kt ModifiersDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; import kotlin.Unit; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * Java twin of ModifiersDemo.kt. noinline and crossinline leave no trace in the method signature: * Java sees plain Function0 and Function1 parameters. Every Java lambda already behaves like a * crossinline one, because `return` in a Java lambda can only leave the lambda. */ public class ModifiersDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { // subscribe(Function1<? super String, Unit>, Function1<? super String, Unit>) ModifiersDemoKt.subscribe( line -> { System.out.println(line); return Unit.INSTANCE; }, event -> { System.out.println("listener got " + event); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); ModifiersDemoKt.getListeners().forEach(l -> l.invoke("payment-captured")); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor(r -> new Thread(r, "settlement-worker")); // runInBackground(Executor, Function0<Unit>) ModifiersDemoKt.runInBackground(pool, () -> { System.out.println("running on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.ModifiersDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/ModifiersDemoJava.java The first run prints subscribing listener #1, listener got payment-captured and running on settlement-worker. Without noinline the build fails with illegal usage of inline parameter 'listener: (String) -> Unit'. Without crossinline it fails with cannot inline 'task: () -> Unit' here: it might contain non-local returns. The last line fails with 'return' is prohibited here.: by the time the Runnable runs on the pool thread, main may be somewhere else entirely. once compiles without crossinline: run is inline too, so block is still pasted into the caller's own code, and a return in it still has a function to leave. Swap run for an ordinary function that takes a lambda and the error comes back.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · When not to inline
x: inline has costs, and three of them show up in real code. The first is size. The body is copied into every caller, so a 40-line function called from 200 places becomes 200 copies. The compiler even warns when you inline a function that takes no lambdas: expected performance impact from inlining is insignificant. Inlining works best for functions with parameters of function types. The JIT already inlines small, hot methods at run time (the performance track covers how), so a lambda-free inline fun buys you nothing. The second is frozen bodies. A caller gets its copy of the body when the caller is compiled. In one test run, a client was compiled against version 1 of a small library, and then version 2 replaced the library jar without recompiling the client. The client printed inline=v1 plain=v2: the ordinary function ran the new code, and the inline one still ran the old copy. So if you publish a shared library, such as an internal payments SDK, treat a public inline body like a public signature. Changing it takes effect only when every client is rebuilt. The third is visibility, and it follows from the second. The body lands in other modules, so it may only use what those modules could use. Call a private function from a public inline one and you get public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API function. The fix is @PublishedApi internal: still hidden from Kotlin callers, but public in the bytecode, so the pasted copies can reach it. The helper's own body is not copied anywhere, so it can use private state freely. Java // Java has no internal or inline. The nearest shape: one public helper that callers reach public final class Tracing { private static final AtomicInteger COUNTER = new AtomicInteger(); public static String nextTraceId() { return "trace-" + COUNTER.incrementAndGet(); } } Kotlin inline fun <T> traced(operation: String, block: () -> T): T { val id = nextTraceId() // must be reachable from every caller's module println("[$id] start $operation") val result = block() println("[$id] end $operation") return result } @PublishedApi internal fun nextTraceId(): String = "trace-" + counter.incrementAndGet() private val counter = AtomicInteger() // fine: nextTraceId is not inline The compiler adds two hard limits. An inline function can't call itself (inline function 'fun recI(n: Int): Int' cannot be recursive.), and it can't contain a local function (local functions are not yet supported in inline functions.). Properties can be inline too, as long as the accessor has no backing field: val Long.asEuros: String inline get() = .... You'll mostly see that for a property with a reified type parameter. My rule: inline small functions that take lambdas, or that need reified or a non-local return. Leave everything else ordinary. If the inline body starts to grow, keep the inline part to a few lines and move the real work into a @PublishedApi internal function, which is compiled once. Break the visibility rule Run PublishedApiDemo, then PublishedApiDemoJava. In PublishedApiDemo.kt, change @PublishedApi internal fun nextTraceId() to private fun nextTraceId(). Predict the error and run the Kotlin demo. Put it back. Why can the Java twin call nextTraceId() directly, when Kotlin code in another module could not? PublishedApiDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger /** * A public inline function is pasted into callers, possibly in another module. So its body may * only use declarations those callers could use themselves. */ inline fun <T> traced(operation: String, block: () -> T): T { val id = nextTraceId() println("[$id] start $operation") val result = block() println("[$id] end $operation") return result } /** Not part of the Kotlin API, but public in the bytecode, so the pasted copies can call it. */ @PublishedApi internal fun nextTraceId(): String = "trace-" + counter.incrementAndGet() private val counter = AtomicInteger() // fine: nextTraceId is not inline, so its body is never copied /** An inline property: no backing field, and the getter is pasted into each caller. */ val Long.asEuros: String inline get() = "EUR " + (this / 100) + "." + (this % 100).toString().padStart(2, '0') fun main() { val refunded = traced("refund pay_7") { 1_999L } println("refunded ${refunded.asEuros}") // Wrong move. Change `@PublishedApi internal` on nextTraceId to `private`, predict, run. } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.PublishedApiDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/PublishedApiDemo.kt PublishedApiDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l01.demo; /** * Java twin of PublishedApiDemo.kt. `internal` is a Kotlin rule that javac does not know about. * In the bytecode nextTraceId() is public, so Java can call it, and traced() is an ordinary method. */ public class PublishedApiDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { long refunded = PublishedApiDemoKt.traced("refund pay_7", () -> 1_999L); System.out.println("refunded " + PublishedApiDemoKt.getAsEuros(refunded)); System.out.println("Java can call the internal helper too: " + PublishedApiDemoKt.nextTraceId()); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l01.demo.PublishedApiDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/PublishedApiDemoJava.java Both print [trace-1] start refund pay_7, [trace-1] end refund pay_7 and refunded EUR 19.99, and the Java twin also prints trace-2 from a direct call. With private, the build fails with public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API function. internal is a Kotlin rule; in the bytecode the function is public, and javac doesn't know the rule exists. Writing return inside forEach to skip one element. In Java, return in a forEach lambda skips to the next element, and many people carry that habit into Kotlin: Java batch.forEach(p -> { if (p.amountMinor() == 0) return; // Java: skips this payment, carries on ledger.post(p); }); Kotlin batch.forEach { p -> if (p.amountMinor == 0L) return // Kotlin: leaves the whole function ledger.post(p) } In Kotlin forEach is inline, so the bare return leaves the enclosing function, and every payment after the first zero-amount one is silently skipped. It compiles without a warning. Write return@forEach to skip one element, or use a plain for loop with continue, which reads better anyway.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · Java and Kotlin
x: Wrapping a callback API: Java Supplier vs Kotlin inline with crossinline Timing.java import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.Executor; import java.util.function.Supplier; final class Timing { static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.println(label + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } } // the caller's lambda is an object; supplyAsync gets a second lambda that calls it static <T> CompletableFuture<T> timedAsync(String label, Executor executor, Supplier<T> block) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> timed(label, block), executor); } } // call site: Timing.timedAsync("capture", pool, () -> gateway.capture(authId)); Timing.kt import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executor inline fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println("$label took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } // block runs inside the Supplier, another execution context: crossinline inline fun <T> timedAsync(label: String, executor: Executor, crossinline block: () -> T): CompletableFuture<T> = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ timed(label) { block() } }, executor) // call site: timedAsync("capture", pool) { gateway.capture(authId) } In Java the caller's lambda is always an object, and timedAsync wraps it in a second one for supplyAsync. In Kotlin the compiler pastes both timed and the caller's lambda into one Supplier class that it generates for that call site, so there is one object instead of two and no call through Supplier.get on the caller's code. The bigger difference is the rule on the caller: inside the Kotlin block a bare return is a compile error, while a Java lambda simply can't express one. Java code that calls the Kotlin timedAsync gets the ordinary compiled body and passes a Function0.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · Worked example
x: Write an inline transaction helper over a Java callback API A Java library (invented for this example) runs work inside a database transaction through a callback. You want Kotlin callers to write tx.transaction { ledger.post(entry) }. Start with the API and an ordinary Kotlin wrapper. public interface TxRunner { <T> T inTransaction(Callable<T> work); } // Java callers write the Callable themselves long balance = tx.inTransaction(() -> ledger.balanceOf("merchant-981")); interface TxRunner { fun <T> inTransaction(work: Callable<T>): T } // 1. an ordinary wrapper: it works, but each call builds a Function0 and a Callable fun <T> TxRunner.transaction(block: () -> T): T = inTransaction(Callable { block() }) The wrapper is one line and runs on every request, so make it inline. The compiler refuses, because block() is now called inside the Callable, which the library may run later or on another thread. // 2. add inline: the compiler stops here inline fun <T> TxRunner.transaction(block: () -> T): T = inTransaction(Callable { block() }) // error: cannot inline 'block: () -> T' here: it might contain non-local returns. // Add 'crossinline' modifier to parameter declaration 'block: () -> T'. // Java has no inline and no non-local return, so the question never comes up: // a return inside the Callable lambda only ends the Callable long posted = tx.inTransaction(() -> { ledger.post(entry); return 1L; }); Add crossinline. The caller's lambda is now pasted into a Callable class the compiler generates for each call site. In exchange, callers lose the non-local return: that's the rule crossinline enforces. // 3. crossinline: inlined into the generated Callable, no bare return allowed inline fun <T> TxRunner.transaction(crossinline block: () -> T): T = inTransaction(Callable { block() }) fun post(entry: JournalEntry) { tx.transaction { ledger.post(entry) } // tx.transaction { if (entry.isEmpty) return } // error: 'return' is prohibited here. } void post(JournalEntry entry) { tx.inTransaction(() -> { ledger.post(entry); return null; // Callable must return something }); } Check that it earns its place. It does: one line, a lambda parameter, called constantly. If it later grows logging, metrics and error mapping, keep the inline part to this one line and move the rest into a @PublishedApi internal function, so 300 call sites don't each carry a copy.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · Key terms
x: Inline function A function whose body the compiler copies into each call site, together with the bodies of the lambdas passed to it. Call site A place in the code that calls a function. With inline, this is where the copy of the body ends up. Non-local return A bare return inside an inlined lambda. It leaves the function that contains the lambda, not just the lambda. Labeled return return@forEach: leaves only the current call of the lambda, like continue in a loop. noinline Marks one lambda parameter of an inline function as an ordinary object, so you can store it or pass it on. crossinline Marks a lambda parameter that is called from another execution context. Non-local returns are forbidden in it. @PublishedApi Lets public inline functions use an internal declaration. The declaration is public in the bytecode. What does inline do to a function and the lambdas passed to it? The compiler copies the function body and each lambda body into the call site. No Function object is created and nothing is called through an interface. Inside fun f(), what does the return in list.forEach { if (it == 0) return } leave? The whole function f. It's a non-local return, allowed because forEach is inline. return@forEach would leave only that lambda call. When does the compiler ask for noinline? When you use an inline lambda parameter as a value: store it in a field, add it to a collection, or pass it to a non-inline function. When does the compiler ask for crossinline? When you call the lambda from another execution context, such as an object, a Runnable or another lambda. crossinline forbids non-local returns in the caller's lambda. Why is a public inline function's body part of your library's binary interface? Callers get a copy of the body when they are compiled. Change the body, and an old caller keeps running its old copy until it is recompiled. A public inline function calls a private helper. What happens, and what is the fix? Compile error: public-API inline function cannot access non-public-API function. Mark the helper @PublishedApi internal. What does Java see when it calls a Kotlin inline function? An ordinary static method that takes Function0/Function1 objects. javac inlines nothing. A reified inline function is synthetic, so javac can't see it at all.

h: Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns · Go deeper
x: Kotlin's inlining and the JIT's inlining are different tools. Kotlin inlines at compile time, across modules, before the JVM ever sees the code. That is the only kind that can make a non-local return or a reified type work, because both change what the code means. The JIT inlines at run time, only on hot paths, and can undo its choice (deoptimization) when its assumptions break. The lesson "Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics" in the performance track covers that side. The Kotlin docs say inlining pays off "especially at 'megamorphic' call-sites inside loops". The reason is in the profile the JIT keeps per call site. An ordinary forEach taking a Function1 has one invoke call site inside it. If 30 different lambdas flow through that one call site, the JIT sees 30 receiver classes there and can't inline any of them. With an inline forEach, each caller has its own copy of the loop, with exactly one lambda body pasted in. Nothing is left for the JIT to guess. A crossinline lambda leaves two classes behind. Run javap -p on the ModifiersDemoKt$... classes in kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/kotlin/l01/demo/: ModifiersDemoKt$runInBackground$1 implements java.lang.Runnable { final kotlin.jvm.functions.Function0<kotlin.Unit> $task; // used when Java calls the compiled body public final void run(); } ModifiersDemoKt$main$$inlined$runInBackground$1 implements java.lang.Runnable { public final void run(); // main's lambda body is pasted in here } The first is the template that the compiled runInBackground method uses when Java (or reflection) calls it: it holds the Function0. The second was generated for the one call site in main, with the lambda's body inside run(). Each inlined call site of a crossinline function gets a class like that, which is one more reason to keep these functions few and small. Finally, a reified inline function has no callable form at all, because its body makes no sense without a concrete type. Kotlin still writes a method into the class file, but marks it ACC_SYNTHETIC, and javac ignores synthetic methods. That's why Java code can't call filterIsInstance<T>()-style functions.

h: Value classes and what they compile to · A value class is a type at compile time and a long at run time
x: A Long parameter named amountMinor will accept an order id without complaint. Both are Long, so the compiler can't tell them apart. The classic fix is a small wrapper class, class Cents(val value: Long), and it works, but every amount is now an extra object on the heap. Kotlin's value class keeps the wrapper's type safety and, wherever it can, drops the object: at run time only the wrapped value, the underlying type (Long here), is left. Here is the wrapper in both languages: Java // Java's closest shape today: a record. It's a real object, allocated on every new. record Cents(long value) { Cents { if (value < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount: " + value); } } Kotlin @JvmInline value class Cents(val value: Long) { init { require(value >= 0) { "negative amount: $value" } } operator fun plus(other: Cents): Cents = Cents(value + other.value) override fun toString(): String = "$value cents" } fun charge(amount: Cents): String = "charged $amount" charge(199L) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Long', but 'Cents' was expected. The rules are short. On the JVM you write @JvmInline value class with exactly one property in the primary constructor. You may add init blocks, functions, secondary constructors and properties without backing fields (so no lateinit and no delegation). A value class can implement interfaces, can't extend a class, and is always final. At run time most of it disappears. javap -p on the demo shows what the compiler built: public static final java.lang.String charge-X49TzF8(long); // takes a plain long public static long constructor-impl(long); // Cents(...) runs init here public static final long plus-dpzqtSM(long, long); // a member, now static on longs public static final Cents box-impl(long); // used only when a box is needed Cents(150) compiles to a call to constructor-impl, which runs your init block and returns the same long. No object is created. plus turned into a static method that adds two longs. The Cents class still exists, with one long field, for the moments when a real object is needed. That's the next section. Compare a type alias. typealias CentsAlias = Long gives you a second name and nothing else: the docs say aliases are assignment-compatible with their underlying type, and value classes are not. In the demo, an orderId: Long goes straight into chargeAlias and compiles. Use aliases to shorten long generic types. Use value classes where mixing up two values would be a bug. You already use value classes from the standard library: UInt, ULong, kotlin.time.Duration and kotlin.Result are all declared this way, and javap shows the same box-impl and unbox-impl on each. See what Cents compiles to Run ValueClassDemo with the command below. From labs/, run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.ValueClassDemoKt workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.Cents. Find charge, constructor-impl and plus. Uncomment the wrong move in main, predict the error, and run. Comment it out again. Run ValueClassDemoJava. Before you do, predict its second line: Java calls chargeFromJava(-5L). Any Long is accepted where a CentsAlias is expected. */ typealias CentsAlias = Long fun charge(amount: Cents): String = "charged $amount" @JvmName("chargeFromJava") fun chargeJava(amount: Cents): String = "charged $amount" fun chargeAlias(amount: CentsAlias): String = "charged $amount (alias)" fun main() { val fee = Cents(150) + Cents(49) println(charge(fee)) val orderId: Long = 981 println(chargeAlias(orderId)) // compiles: an order id is a Long, so it is a CentsAlias too try { Cents(-1) } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { println("rejected: ${e.message}") } // Wrong move. Java has no value classes (Valhalla's are a JDK 28 preview), so it * sees what the bytecode holds: charge-<hash>(long), which javac can't call, and chargeFromJava(long). */ public class ValueClassDemoJava { // the closest Java shape today: a record, which is a real object with identity record CentsRecord(long value) { CentsRecord { if (value < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount: " + value); } } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println(ValueClassDemoKt.chargeFromJava(199L)); // Java passes a raw long, so Cents' init block never runs: System.out.println(ValueClassDemoKt.chargeFromJava(-5L)); System.out.println(new CentsRecord(199)); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // System.out.println(ValueClassDemoKt.charge(199L)); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.ValueClassDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l02/demo/ValueClassDemoJava.java The Kotlin demo prints charged 199 cents, charged 981 (alias) and rejected: negative amount: -1. javap lists charge-X49TzF8(long), chargeFromJava(long) and, on Cents, constructor-impl(long) and plus-dpzqtSM(long, long). The wrong move fails with argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Long', but 'Cents' was expected. The Java twin prints charged -5 cents: Java passed a raw long, so init never ran. The last section explains that door. Inline value classes (Kotlin docs) docs A value class is a label the compiler checks and then peels off. Inside Kotlin, the label Money stops you from putting an order id in the amount slot. At run time the label is gone and only the number travels, except when the number has to go somewhere that only takes objects, like a list. Then the compiler packs it in a box with the label printed on the outside. The analogy breaks at the border with Java: Java can't read the label at all, so it either can't call the function, or, through @JvmName, hands in a bare number that nobody checked.

h: Value classes and what they compile to · Boxed whenever it is used as another type
x: Value classes do get boxed, which means wrapped in a real Money object on the heap, the way Java wraps a long in a Long. The rule fits in one line of the docs: inline classes are boxed whenever they are used as another type. Java // Java's long and Long follow the same rule: a primitive where it can, a box when it must static Object asGeneric(Object x) { return x; } long minor = 1_999; Object boxed = asGeneric(minor); // autoboxed into a Long object List<Long> list = List.of(minor); // another Long object Kotlin fun <T> asGeneric(x: T): Any? = x // used as T: boxed fun asNullable(a: Amount?): Any? = a // used as Amount?: boxed fun asInterface(p: Priced): Any = p // used as Priced: boxed class Invoice(val amount: Amount) // used as Amount: stored as a long field Four cases box: a generic type parameter, a nullable type (Amount? must be able to hold null, and a long can't), an interface the class implements, and anything typed Any, which includes every collection and println. In the bytecode each one shows up as a call to Amount.box-impl(long) right before the call that needs the object. So a List<Money> holds one Money object per element. The docs draw the same comparison you'd draw: it's like Int being either a primitive int or a java.lang.Integer. Equality still works by value. a == Amount(1_999) compiles to equals-impl0(long, long), a comparison of two longs. Identity doesn't exist: a === b is a compile error, identity equality for arguments of types 'Amount' and 'Amount' is prohibited. That's stricter than Java, where Long a = 1_999L, b = 1_999L; a == b is false and the same code with 100L is true, because small boxes are cached. In practice, a value class saves the allocation wherever it's used as itself: fields, parameters, return values, arithmetic. That covers most domain code. A hot path that pushes millions of amounts through a List<Money> or a generic Map pays the same boxing as List<Long>. If that shows up in a profile, use a LongArray, as you would in Java. Uncomment the wrong move in BoxingDemo.kt and run it. Java has the same split for long and Long: a primitive where it can, * a box when the value is used as a generic type, a nullable, or Object. Kotlin forbids === on * value classes; Java lets you compare boxes by identity, and it goes wrong above 127. */ public class BoxingDemoJava { static Object asGeneric(Object x) { return x; } public static void main(String[] args) { long minor = 1_999; Object boxed = asGeneric(minor); // autoboxed to Long System.out.println("as Object: " + boxed.getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println("in a list: " + List.of(minor).get(0).getClass().getSimpleName()); Long a = 1_999L, b = 1_999L; System.out.println("a == b (identity): " + (a == b)); // two different Long objects System.out.println("a.equals(b): " + a.equals(b)); Long small1 = 100L, small2 = 100L; System.out.println("100L == 100L: " + (small1 == small2)); // cached box, so true } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.BoxingDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l02/demo/BoxingDemoJava.java The field in Invoice is a long. The Java twin prints false for a == b with 1,999 and true with 100: that's the Long cache, a trap Kotlin closes for value classes. Used as itself, a value class is its underlying long. Used as anything else, the compiler boxes it first. h: Value classes and what they compile to · Mangled names keep Java out, and @JvmName lets it back in
x: Look at that name again: charge-X49TzF8(long). The compiler adds a hash to every function that takes a value class. The docs call it mangling, and it does two jobs. It prevents clashes: describe(key: IdempotencyKey) and describe(raw: String) would both be describe(String) in the bytecode, and with mangling they become describe-<hash>(String) and describe(String). And it keeps Java away from functions that expect a valid value: a - can't appear in a Java method name. It reaches further than functions. A class with a value-class property gets a private constructor, plus a public synthetic one with an extra DefaultConstructorMarker parameter, and a mangled getter: the demo's Invoice has getAmount-hwXtt_M(). Java can't build it or read it by name. Members that return a value class are mangled too, so the lab's Money.Companion.parse becomes parse-LC5NfZc(String). A top-level function that only returns one is not: parseAmount(String) hands Java a plain long. For a single function, the quick fix is @JvmName: Java System.out.println(ValueClassDemoKt.chargeFromJava(199L)); // charged 199 cents System.out.println(ValueClassDemoKt.chargeFromJava(-5L)); // charged -5 cents: init never ran // ValueClassDemoKt.charge(199L); // error: cannot find symbol Kotlin @JvmName("chargeFromJava") fun chargeJava(amount: Cents): String = "charged $amount" Read the second Java line again. Java passes a raw long, and nothing runs init on the way in. @JvmName opens a door around your validation, so a function meant for Java should validate again, for example by building a fresh Cents(amount.value). Kotlin 2.2.0 added a fuller answer, @JvmExposeBoxed. It is still Experimental in 2.4, so you opt in with @OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class). On a class it adds a public constructor that runs init. On a function it adds a version that takes and returns the box, describeFee(Fee), next to the mangled describeFee-pUsR5hI(long). The compiler flag -Xjvm-expose-boxed does the same for a whole module. Java Fee fee = new Fee(125); // a real constructor: init runs System.out.println(ExposeBoxedDemoKt.describeFee(fee.doubled())); Kotlin @file:OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class) @JvmExposeBoxed @JvmInline value class Fee(val minor: Long) { init { require(minor >= 0) { "negative fee: $minor" } } fun doubled(): Fee = Fee(minor * 2) } @JvmExposeBoxed fun describeFee(fee: Fee): String = "fee of ${fee.minor} minor units" Frameworks see the same bytecode Java does. Anything that finds getters by name through reflection, such as a JSON mapper or an ORM reading an entity, will meet getAmount-hwXtt_M. Check how your libraries handle that before you put value classes in DTOs or entities. Open the door for Java, properly Run ExposeBoxedDemo, then ExposeBoxedDemoJava. Run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.Fee workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.ExposeBoxedDemoKt. Find the two doubled methods and the two describeFee methods. Delete the first line of ExposeBoxedDemo.kt (@file:OptIn(...)) and run. Put it back. With @JvmExposeBoxed, Java gets a real constructor that runs the * init block, and boxed overloads of doubled() and describeFee(). */ public class ExposeBoxedDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Fee fee = new Fee(125); // runs init: validation is back System.out.println(ExposeBoxedDemoKt.describeFee(fee.doubled())); try { new Fee(-1); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l02.demo.ExposeBoxedDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l02/demo/ExposeBoxedDemoJava.java Both print fee of 250 minor units, and the Java twin also prints rejected: negative fee: -1, so the public constructor ran init. javap shows doubled-etMGDqA(long) next to Fee doubled(), describeFee-pUsR5hI(long) next to describeFee(Fee), and a public Fee(long) constructor. h: Value classes and what they compile to · One field only, until Valhalla
x: Give a value class two properties and the compiler stops you: value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter. So Point(x, y) or Money(cents, currency) can't be value classes on the JVM in Kotlin 2.4, and there is no hidden flag for it. The limit comes from the JVM. Kotlin can erase a one-field class into its field because the JVM already has a long. A two-field value with no identity needs support from the JVM itself, which is Project Valhalla. JEP 401, value classes and objects for Java, is integrated into JDK 28 as a preview feature, and JDK 28 is still in development. The Kotlin team's design notes explain why @JvmInline is mandatory today: it marks the current compile-time trick, so that a plain value class without the annotation can later compile to real Valhalla value classes. They call multi-field value classes before Valhalla "all theoretical". No Kotlin release has a Valhalla mode yet. For now, the one-field limit shapes your design. An amount that carries its own currency stays a data class. Or you keep the currency elsewhere: many payment services give each account one currency, so the amount needs none of its own. Where do value classes pay off? IDs and keys (PaymentId, MerchantId, IdempotencyKey), amounts in minor units, and validated strings such as an IBAN: anywhere two Strings or two Longs could be swapped by accident. Validation runs once, in init, and the type is the proof that it ran. Where don't they? In APIs that Java code calls a lot, unless you add @JvmName overloads or @JvmExposeBoxed, and in classes that reflection-heavy frameworks read. Keep them in the Kotlin domain code and convert at the edges. Try a second field In ValueClassDemo.kt, change value class Cents(val value: Long) to value class Cents(val value: Long, val currency: String). Run the demo. Undo it. Which of your own types would you make a value class, and which would stay a data class? The build fails with value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter. Single-value concepts such as ids, keys and minor-unit amounts fit. Anything with two parts (amount plus currency, a card's expiry month and year) stays a data class for now. Believing a value class is never boxed, and then counting on it in a hot path that goes through generics. A Map<PaymentId, Money> or a List<Money> holds a boxed object per entry, exactly like List<Long>, and a nullable Money? field holds a reference to a box: Java List<Long> amounts = new ArrayList<>(); for (long m : rawAmounts) amounts.add(m); // one Long object per element Kotlin val amounts = ArrayList<Money>() for (m in rawAmounts) amounts += Money(m) // one Money object per element The value class still gives you type safety in those places, just not the allocation savings. Profile before you rely on them, and use a primitive array (LongArray) for large numeric batches.

h: Value classes and what they compile to · Java and Kotlin
x: An idempotency key: Java record vs Kotlin value class IdempotencyKey.java public record IdempotencyKey(String value) { public IdempotencyKey { if (value.length() < 8 || value.length() > 64) throw new IllegalArgumentException("idempotency key must be 8 to 64 characters"); if (!value.matches("[A-Za-z0-9_-]+")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad character in idempotency key: " + value); } } // every new IdempotencyKey(...) is an object with identity static Charge findCharge(IdempotencyKey key) { ... } // JVM: findCharge(IdempotencyKey) IdempotencyKey.kt @JvmInline value class IdempotencyKey(val value: String) { init { require(value.length in 8..64) { "idempotency key must be 8 to 64 characters" } require(value.matches(Regex("[A-Za-z0-9_-]+"))) { "bad character in idempotency key: $value" } } } // IdempotencyKey(...) runs init and returns the same String fun findCharge(key: IdempotencyKey): Charge? = TODO() // JVM: findCharge-<hash>(String) Both validate once at construction and both compare by value. The record is a real object: each new allocates, and a map keyed by it holds those objects. The value class is a String at run time wherever it is used as itself, so findCharge costs exactly what a String parameter costs. The price is on the Java side: Java sees findCharge-<hash>(String), which it can't call, and can't construct an IdempotencyKey at all without @JvmExposeBoxed. JEP 401, a preview in JDK 28, adds value record to Java: a record without identity, which gives the JVM room to flatten it.

h: Value classes and what they compile to · Worked example
x: Make a swapped argument a compile error, then give Java a safe door A refund call takes two Strings and a Long. Someone swapped the ids in a hotfix, and it compiled. static String refund(String merchantId, String paymentId, long amountMinor) { ... } refund(paymentId, merchantId, 1_999); // swapped: compiles, refunds the wrong thing fun refund(merchantId: String, paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long): String = TODO() refund(paymentId, merchantId, 1_999) // swapped: compiles, refunds the wrong thing Give each concept its own value class. The swapped call now fails to compile, twice, and nothing allocates: in the bytecode the function still takes two Strings and a long. @JvmInline value class MerchantId(val value: String) @JvmInline value class PaymentId(val value: String) @JvmInline value class Money(val cents: Long) // 1. one type per concept fun refund(merchant: MerchantId, payment: PaymentId, amount: Money): String = TODO() refund(payment, merchant, Money(1_999)) // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'PaymentId', but 'MerchantId' was expected. // error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'MerchantId', but 'PaymentId' was expected. // Java gets the same safety from records, at the cost of an object each record MerchantId(String value) {} record PaymentId(String value) {} static String refund(MerchantId merchant, PaymentId payment, long amountMinor) { ... } refund(payment, merchant, 1_999); // error: incompatible types: PaymentId cannot be converted to MerchantId Check the Java view. javap shows refund-<hash>(String, String, long): the Java module that also issues refunds can't call it any more. Don't reach for @JvmName here, because Java would pass raw values past every init. Add a Java entry point that takes the raw types and builds the value classes, so validation runs. // 2. a door for Java: raw types in, value classes (and their init blocks) inside fun refundFromJava(merchantId: String, paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long): String = refund(MerchantId(merchantId), PaymentId(paymentId), Money(amountMinor)) // javap: refund-<hash>(String, String, long) and refundFromJava(String, String, long) // 3. the Java module calls the plain name; a negative amount fails inside Money's init String result = RefundsKt.refundFromJava("m-981", "pay_7", 1_999L); Java can still swap the two strings in refundFromJava, so the door is a compromise: it validates values, it can't check names. That's why the type safety belongs in Kotlin and the door belongs at the edge, used by as few callers as possible.

Invoice(amount = m), where class Invoice(val amount: Money) m.cents * 2 Any? is another type, so the compiler calls Money.box-impl before audit. total takes Money as itself (two longs in the bytecode), Invoice stores a long field, and m.cents reads the long directly. The parameters are the underlying types, so it isn't refund(PaymentId, Money) either. Add @JvmName, a raw-typed entry point, or @JvmExposeBoxed for Java.
