h: Value classes and what they compile to · Key terms
x: Value class @JvmInline value class X(val v: T): its own type in Kotlin, its single property T at run time where possible. Boxing Wrapping the underlying value in a real object of the value class, done when it is used as another type. Name mangling The hash suffix, as in charge-X49TzF8, that the compiler adds to functions with value-class parameters. @JvmName Sets the JVM name of a function, which can remove the mangled suffix so Java can call it. @JvmExposeBoxed Experimental annotation (Kotlin 2.2+) that adds Java-callable boxed constructors and overloads. Type alias A second name for an existing type. It adds no type safety. Project Valhalla The OpenJDK project that adds value objects without identity to the JVM. JEP 401 is a preview in JDK 28. What does @JvmInline value class PaymentId(val value: String) compile to where it's used as a PaymentId? A plain String. PaymentId(...) calls the static constructor-impl, which runs init and returns the same String. When is a value class boxed? Whenever it's used as another type: a generic T, a nullable X?, an interface it implements, or Any (collections, println). Why does fun charge(amount: Cents) compile to charge-X49TzF8(long)? Mangling. It avoids clashes with overloads on the underlying type, and Java can't call a name with a - in it. What does @JvmName on a value-class function give Java, and what's the catch? A name Java can call. Java passes the raw underlying value, so init never runs: validate again inside. Type alias vs value class? An alias is another name, assignment-compatible with the original type. A value class is a new type: a Long won't go where Cents is expected. How many properties can a Kotlin value class have on the JVM? Exactly one: value class must have exactly one primary constructor parameter. More waits for Valhalla. What does @JvmExposeBoxed add, and what does it need? A public constructor that runs init, and boxed overloads Java can call. It's Experimental: @OptIn(ExperimentalStdlibApi::class).

h: Value classes and what they compile to · Go deeper
x: Two details that matter when you design with value classes. A value class can wrap a generic type: @JvmInline value class Box<T>(val value: T). The docs say the underlying type is then mapped to Any?, or to the upper bound of T, so at run time it's an Object field and you rarely save anything. Generic value classes help for type safety, not for speed. The second detail is a compiler bug worth knowing about. In Kotlin 2.4.21 (and 2.3.21) this crashes the compiler with Backend Internal error: Exception during IR lowering and a NoSuchElementException from the string-concatenation lowering: @JvmInline value class M(val c: Long) { override fun toString() = java.math.BigDecimal.valueOf(c, 2).toPlainString() } fun f(m: M) = "x $m" The trigger is the inferred return type: toPlainString() returns a Java platform type, String!. Write override fun toString(): String = ... and it compiles. It's a small, concrete argument for explicit return types on anything public: they keep platform types from leaking into your API, and here they also keep the compiler alive. Finally, the history of the keyword, which explains old code you'll still meet. Kotlin 1.5.0 made these classes stable with the value modifier plus @JvmInline on the JVM, and deprecated the old inline class spelling with a warning. The design notes give the reason for the split: @JvmInline names today's erasure trick, which leaves the plain value class free to mean a real Valhalla value class one day.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · Class delegation forwards to the object you passed in, once
x: Lesson 5 of the patterns track showed what by writes for you: every method of the interface, forwarded to the object you named, except the ones you override. It also showed the trap: putAll goes straight to the inner map and never sees your put override. Two more details matter once you put by into real classes. The first is that the delegate is captured once. class ConfigurableFees(var policy: FeePolicy) : FeePolicy by policy looks like it forwards to the policy property. javap shows two fields instead: private final FeePolicy $$delegate_0; // set from the constructor argument, never changed private FeePolicy policy; // the property you can reassign The generated feeMinor calls $$delegate_0. Assign a new policy and the property changes, but every call still goes to the old object: the demo prints after swap, policy = FlatFee(99), fee: 25. A hand-written Java decorator reads its field on every call, so swapping works there: Java final class ConfigurableFeesJava implements FeePolicy { private FeePolicy policy; ConfigurableFeesJava(FeePolicy policy) { this.policy = policy; } void setPolicy(FeePolicy policy) { this.policy = policy; } @Override public long feeMinor(long amountMinor) { return policy.feeMinor(amountMinor); // the current field, on every call } } Kotlin class ConfigurableFees(var policy: FeePolicy) : FeePolicy by policy // forwards to the FIRST policy val fees = ConfigurableFees(FlatFee(25)) fees.policy = FlatFee(99) fees.feeMinor(10_000) // 25: $$delegate_0 still holds FlatFee(25) If the target has to change at run time, write the forwarding yourself. Otherwise make the constructor parameter a plain parameter or a val, so nobody expects it to move. The second detail: equals, hashCode and toString are not forwarded. They come from Any, not from the interface. A Tags class that delegates MutableSet<String> prints as Tags@2752f6e2, and two Tags with the same elements are not equal. That breaks the Set contract, which says two sets with the same elements are equal, and a HashSet<Tags> will happily keep both. Override the three and forward them to the inner set when the wrapper should behave like what it wraps. With those two rules in mind, by is still the best tool for one job: wrapping a wide Java interface to change one or two methods. A DataSource that counts borrowed connections, a Kafka Producer that adds a trace header to every record: you write the methods you change, and the compiler writes the other twenty, with no chance of forgetting one when the interface grows a new method in the next library version. Swap a delegate and watch nothing happen Run ClassDelegationDemo. Before you read the second line, predict the fee after the swap. Run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.ConfigurableFees from labs/ and find both fields. Run ClassDelegationDemoJava, which swaps a hand-written Java decorator and then the Kotlin class from Java. In Tags, add override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is Set<*> && inner == other and override fun hashCode() = inner.hashCode(). Run again. ClassDelegationDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo interface FeePolicy { fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long): Long } class FlatFee(private val fee: Long) : FeePolicy { override fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long): Long = fee override fun toString(): String = "FlatFee($fee)" } /** `by policy` forwards to the object passed in at construction, stored in a hidden final field. */ class ConfigurableFees(var policy: FeePolicy) : FeePolicy by policy /** Delegating a Set forwards Set's methods, but not equals, hashCode or toString. */ class Tags(private val inner: MutableSet<String> = HashSet()) : MutableSet<String> by inner fun main() { val fees = ConfigurableFees(FlatFee(25)) println("fee: ${fees.feeMinor(10_000)}") fees.policy = FlatFee(99) // swap the policy... println("after swap, policy = ${fees.policy}, fee: ${fees.feeMinor(10_000)}") val a = Tags().apply { add("refund"); add("manual") } val b = Tags().apply { add("refund"); add("manual") } println("a = $a") println("a == b: ${a == b}, a.size = ${a.size}, \"refund\" in a: ${"refund" in a}") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.ClassDelegationDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/ClassDelegationDemo.kt ClassDelegationDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; /** * Java twin of ClassDelegationDemo.kt. Java has no `by`, so you write the forwarding yourself. * Written by hand, it reads the field on every call, so swapping the policy works. */ public class ClassDelegationDemoJava { static final class ConfigurableFeesJava implements FeePolicy { private FeePolicy policy; ConfigurableFeesJava(FeePolicy policy) { this.policy = policy; } void setPolicy(FeePolicy policy) { this.policy = policy; } @Override public long feeMinor(long amountMinor) { return policy.feeMinor(amountMinor); // reads the current field each time } } public static void main(String[] args) { ConfigurableFeesJava fees = new ConfigurableFeesJava(new FlatFee(25)); System.out.println("fee: " + fees.feeMinor(10_000)); fees.setPolicy(new FlatFee(99)); System.out.println("after swap, fee: " + fees.feeMinor(10_000)); // the Kotlin class, seen from Java: setPolicy changes the property, not the $$delegate_0 field ConfigurableFees kotlinFees = new ConfigurableFees(new FlatFee(25)); kotlinFees.setPolicy(new FlatFee(99)); System.out.println("Kotlin class after swap, fee: " + kotlinFees.feeMinor(10_000)); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.ClassDelegationDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/ClassDelegationDemoJava.java Kotlin prints fee: 25, then after swap, policy = FlatFee(99), fee: 25: the property moved, the calls didn't. javap lists private final ...FeePolicy $$delegate_0 and private ...FeePolicy policy. The Java decorator prints 99 after its swap, and the Kotlin class still prints 25 when Java swaps it. a == b is false until you add equals and hashCode, then true. Delegation (Kotlin docs) docs A delegated property is a flat with a building manager. You own the flat, but every request to get in or change something goes through the manager, who can keep a log, refuse a change, or fetch the keys only on the first visit. Visitors from outside (Java callers) see an ordinary front door, a getter and a setter. The analogy breaks at class delegation: there the manager is fixed on the day the building opens, and changing the name on the mailbox (the var) doesn't change who answers.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · A delegated property is a hidden field and two calls
x: A delegated property is a hidden delegate field plus a getter and setter that call getValue and setValue Property delegation shares the keyword and almost nothing else. Start without it. Say every change to an order's status must be logged, and you want the logging written once, in a small helper class you can reuse for any audited property. By hand, the property forwards its getter and setter to the helper: Java final class OrderJava { private final Box<String> status = new Box<>("NEW"); // the helper holds the value String getStatus() { return status.get(); } void setStatus(String s) { status.set("status", s); } // and logs every change } Kotlin class Order { private val statusBox = Audited("NEW") // the helper holds the value var status: String get() = statusBox.getValue(this, ::status) set(value) = statusBox.setValue(this, ::status, value) // and logs every change } ::status is a reference to the property itself, a KProperty, which knows its name, so the helper can log status without a string literal that could drift. That forwarding is all by does. The helper object is called the delegate. It needs only two functions with fixed names, getValue and setValue, and then by writes the getter and setter for you: Java // Java has no `by`: the helper is an ordinary class, and you write the forwarding above yourself final class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } void set(String name, T value) { System.out.println(" " + name + ": " + this.value + " -> " + value); this.value = value; } } Kotlin class Audited<T>(private var value: T) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> { override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = value override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) { println(" ${property.name}: ${this.value} -> $value") this.value = value } } class Order { var status: String by Audited("NEW") // the same forwarding, written by the compiler } getValue receives the owning object (thisRef) and a KProperty that describes the property, including its name. A val needs only getValue. You can write them as operator fun members or extensions on any class, or implement ReadOnlyProperty or ReadWriteProperty as here. The compiler's version matches your hand-written one with one change, shown in the figure. For each delegated property it adds a hidden field, status$delegate, typed as whatever the expression after by returns. Instead of a fresh ::status on every call, it builds one static array per class, $$delegatedProperties, with a KProperty object per property, filled once in the static initializer. Then getStatus() loads status$delegate, loads $$delegatedProperties[0], calls getValue, and casts the result to String. Java sees none of this. It sees getStatus() and setStatus(String), ordinary methods; the delegate field is private and the array is package-private. That suits frameworks that work through getters and setters. It's also a warning: a setter that logs, validates or audits looks exactly like a plain setter from the outside. A few kinds of delegate get no $delegate field: delegating to another property (by this::amountMinor), to a named object, to this, or to a constant. The docs list the cases. Everything else costs one extra object per delegated property, per instance. The operators don't have to live in the delegate's class. They can be extension functions, and that's how by settings works on a plain Map in the last section: the standard library declares getValue as an inline extension operator on Map, which looks up the key property.name. You can do the same for a type you don't own. An operator fun Headers.getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): String would let a class write val traceId: String by kafkaHeaders. Find the generated field and array Run PropertyDelegateDemo, then PropertyDelegateDemoJava, which calls the same Order through setStatus and lists its fields by reflection. From labs/, run javap -c -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.Order and read getStatus. Add var note: String? by Audited(null) to Order and set it in main. Predict the new fields before you run. PropertyDelegateDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo import kotlin.properties.ReadWriteProperty import kotlin.reflect.KProperty /** A hand-written delegate: getValue and setValue are all the compiler needs. */ class Audited<T>(private var value: T) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> { override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = value override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) { println(" ${property.name}: ${this.value} -> $value") this.value = value } } class Order { var status: String by Audited("NEW") var amountMinor: Long by Audited(0L) } fun main() { val order = Order() order.status = "AUTHORIZED" order.amountMinor = 4_250 println("status = ${order.status}, amountMinor = ${order.amountMinor}") println("fields the compiler generated:") Order::class.java.declaredFields.forEach { println(" ${it.type.simpleName} ${it.name}") } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.PropertyDelegateDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/PropertyDelegateDemo.kt PropertyDelegateDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Field; /** * Java twin of PropertyDelegateDemo.kt. Java sees getStatus and setStatus, ordinary methods, * and can't tell that a delegate sits behind them. */ public class PropertyDelegateDemoJava { // the hand-written Java shape: a field holding a helper object, and accessors that call it static final class Box<T> { private T value; Box(T value) { this.value = value; } T get() { return value; } void set(String name, T value) { System.out.println(" " + name + ": " + this.value + " -> " + value); this.value = value; } } static final class OrderJava { private final Box<String> status = new Box<>("NEW"); String getStatus() { return status.get(); } void setStatus(String s) { status.set("status", s); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Order order = new Order(); // the Kotlin class order.setStatus("AUTHORIZED"); // goes through status$delegate.setValue order.setAmountMinor(4_250L); System.out.println("status = " + order.getStatus() + ", amountMinor = " + order.getAmountMinor()); OrderJava hand = new OrderJava(); hand.setStatus("AUTHORIZED"); System.out.println("fields of the Kotlin Order, seen by reflection:"); for (Field f : Order.class.getDeclaredFields()) { System.out.println(" " + f.getType().getSimpleName() + " " + f.getName()); } } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.PropertyDelegateDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/PropertyDelegateDemoJava.java Both print the two changes, then the fields: KProperty[] $$delegatedProperties, Audited status$delegate and Audited amountMinor$delegate. getStatus is getfield status$delegate, getstatic $$delegatedProperties, iconst_0, aaload, invokevirtual Audited.getValue, checkcast String. Adding note adds a note$delegate field and a third array entry, not a second array. What the compiler writes for one delegated property: a field for the delegate, a shared KProperty array, and accessors that call the delegate. Delegated properties (Kotlin docs) docs Audit trails are the obvious fit in payments: a PaymentDraft whose status and amountMinor record every change for the compliance log, written once as a delegate instead of in every setter. Quarkus configuration usually arrives through @ConfigMapping interfaces, but code that reads a parsed Map (a merchant's routing rules from a JSON column, Kafka headers) can use map-backed properties, with provideDelegate to check the required keys when the object is built rather than on the first payment that needs them. And be careful with by on CDI beans: a bean that delegates an interface to a constructor argument keeps that argument forever. That's fine for an injected client, and wrong for anything you meant to swap at run time, such as a fee policy behind a feature flag.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · What by lazy costs: an object per instance and a call per read
x: by lazy is the delegate you use most, and the memory model track already took it apart: it is double-checked locking, SYNCHRONIZED by default, with PUBLICATION and NONE as the other modes (lesson 5 of that track). This section is about the bill. Java // Java's per-instance lazy field: volatile double-checked locking, by hand private volatile Double eurUsd; double eurUsd() { Double v = eurUsd; if (v == null) { synchronized (this) { v = eurUsd; if (v == null) eurUsd = v = rates.fetch("EURUSD"); } } return v; } Kotlin class FxQuote(private val rates: RateService) { val eurUsd: Double by lazy { rates.fetch("EURUSD") } // SYNCHRONIZED } Each FxQuote gets a private final kotlin.Lazy eurUsd$delegate field. The constructor fills it with a new SynchronizedLazyImpl (fields initializer, _value and lock), and the initializer lambda is a second object. Every read calls Lazy.getValue() through an interface, and for a Double it then unboxes with checkcast Number and doubleValue. There's no $$delegatedProperties array, because lazy never looks at the property. For one configuration object, none of that matters. For a class you create per payment, per Kafka record or per database row, it's two extra objects every time, for a value you may never read. Use lazy on long-lived objects: singletons, @ApplicationScoped beans, caches. For short-lived ones, compute the value in the constructor or make it a function. When only one thread can ever touch the object, lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) drops the lock and the class becomes UnsafeLazyImpl. The docs say it "doesn't incur any thread-safety guarantees and related overhead". Think of a parser or a report builder that lives inside one function call. Don't use it on anything a CDI container shares: an @ApplicationScoped bean is read from many request threads at once, and NONE gives you no guarantee that they all see one value. One behavior is easy to miss. lazy doesn't cache an exception. In the demo the first read throws rate service timed out, and the second read runs the initializer again and succeeds. For a remote call that's usually what you want. Count the initializer runs Run LazyDemo. Before you do, predict how many times the initializer runs over three reads when the first one throws. Run LazyDemoJava, which does the same with hand-written double-checked locking and then reads the Kotlin class from Java. Run javap -c -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.FxQuote and read getEurUsd. LazyDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo var rateCalls = 0 class FxQuote { /** Default mode: SYNCHRONIZED. The first reader runs the initializer under a lock. */ val eurUsd: Double by lazy { rateCalls++ if (rateCalls == 1) throw IllegalStateException("rate service timed out") 1.0842 } } fun main() { for (mode in LazyThreadSafetyMode.entries) { println("$mode -> ${lazy(mode) { 0 }.javaClass.name}") } val quote = FxQuote() try { quote.eurUsd } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("first read failed: ${e.message}") } println("second read: ${quote.eurUsd} (initializer ran $rateCalls times)") println("third read: ${quote.eurUsd} (initializer ran $rateCalls times)") println("field: ${FxQuote::class.java.declaredFields.joinToString { "${it.type.name} ${it.name}" }}") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.LazyDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/LazyDemo.kt LazyDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; /** * Java twin of LazyDemo.kt. Java has no lazy delegate. For a per-instance lazy field the usual * shape is double-checked locking on a volatile field, which is what Kotlin's SYNCHRONIZED mode does. */ public class LazyDemoJava { static int rateCalls = 0; static final class FxQuoteJava { private volatile Double eurUsd; // null means "not computed yet" double eurUsd() { Double v = eurUsd; if (v == null) { synchronized (this) { v = eurUsd; if (v == null) { rateCalls++; if (rateCalls == 1) throw new IllegalStateException("rate service timed out"); eurUsd = v = 1.0842; } } } return v; } } public static void main(String[] args) { FxQuoteJava quote = new FxQuoteJava(); try { quote.eurUsd(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("first read failed: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("second read: " + quote.eurUsd() + " (initializer ran " + rateCalls + " times)"); System.out.println("third read: " + quote.eurUsd() + " (initializer ran " + rateCalls + " times)"); // the Kotlin class from Java: getEurUsd() calls Lazy.getValue() on every read FxQuote kotlinQuote = new FxQuote(); try { kotlinQuote.getEurUsd(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("Kotlin FxQuote from Java, first read failed: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("Kotlin FxQuote from Java, second read: " + kotlinQuote.getEurUsd()); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.LazyDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/LazyDemoJava.java The three modes map to kotlin.SynchronizedLazyImpl, kotlin.SafePublicationLazyImpl and kotlin.UnsafeLazyImpl. The first read fails, the second succeeds, and the initializer ran 2 times, not 3: once the value is stored, reads stop calling it. The only field is kotlin.Lazy eurUsd$delegate, and getEurUsd is getfield, invokeinterface Lazy.getValue, checkcast Number, doubleValue. The Java version behaves the same. Delegated properties: lazy (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · The standard delegates, and provideDelegate for early checks
x: The standard library ships the delegates you'd otherwise write by hand. Delegates.observable(initial) { property, old, new -> } calls you after every assignment. Delegates.vetoable(initial) { property, old, new -> Boolean } calls you before it, and returning false keeps the old value. And a val can read from a Map: val host: String by settings looks up the key "host". A var does the same with a MutableMap. Delegates.notNull<Int>() covers what lateinit can't, a primitive: reading it before the first assignment throws Property size should be initialized before get. Java void setOwner(String owner) { // observable, by hand String old = this.owner; this.owner = owner; System.out.println("owner: " + old + " -> " + owner); } void setLimit(int limit) { // vetoable, by hand if (limit <= 100) this.limit = limit; } int port() { return (Integer) settings.get("port"); } // map-backed, by hand Kotlin var owner: String by Delegates.observable("<none>") { property, old, new -> println("${property.name}: $old -> $new") } var limit: Int by Delegates.vetoable(100) { _, _, new -> new <= 100 } val port: Int by settings // settings["port"], cast to Int The demo prints owner: <none> -> alice, owner: alice -> bob, limit after veto: 100 and limit after ok: 50. A map-backed property fails only when you read it: a missing key throws java.util.NoSuchElementException: Key port is missing in the map. That's late. For configuration you'd rather fail when the object is built, and that's what provideDelegate is for. If the object after by has an operator fun provideDelegate(thisRef, property), the compiler calls it once per property, while the owning object is being constructed, and keeps what it returns as the real delegate. The docs describe it as the way to get "the necessary validation right away". PropertyDelegateProvider { thisRef, property -> ... } creates one without a new class. In the demo, binding issuerUrl prints during Settings(), before anyone reads the property. The lab uses the same trick to register every audited property up front. Watch the standard delegates fire Run StdDelegatesDemo (or its Java twin). Predict the order of building Settings..., binding issuerUrl and built; ... before you look. Change the veto to new <= 40 and run. Predict both limit lines first. Remove "host" to "issuer.example" from the map. Predict which line fails, and when. StdDelegatesDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo import kotlin.properties.Delegates import kotlin.properties.PropertyDelegateProvider import kotlin.properties.ReadOnlyProperty class Payout { // observable: the handler runs after the assignment var owner: String by Delegates.observable("<none>") { property, old, new -> println("${property.name}: $old -> $new") } // vetoable: the handler runs before the assignment; false keeps the old value var limit: Int by Delegates.vetoable(100) { _, _, new -> new <= 100 } } class IssuerConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val host: String by settings // reads settings["host"] val port: Int by settings // reads settings["port"] } /** provideDelegate runs once per property, while the object is built: validation happens right away. */ fun requiredEnv(): PropertyDelegateProvider<Any?, ReadOnlyProperty<Any?, String>> = PropertyDelegateProvider { _, property -> println("binding ${property.name}") ReadOnlyProperty { _, _ -> "value of ${property.name}" } } class Settings { val issuerUrl: String by requiredEnv() } fun main() { val p = Payout() p.owner = "alice" p.owner = "bob" p.limit = 500 println("limit after veto: ${p.limit}") p.limit = 50 println("limit after ok: ${p.limit}") val config = IssuerConfig(mapOf("host" to "issuer.example")) println("host = ${config.host}") try { println("port = ${config.port}") } catch (e: NoSuchElementException) { println("port failed on access: ${e.message}") } println("building Settings...") val s = Settings() println("built; issuerUrl = ${s.issuerUrl}") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.StdDelegatesDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/StdDelegatesDemo.kt StdDelegatesDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l03.demo; import java.util.Map; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; /** * Java twin of StdDelegatesDemo.kt. Java writes each behavior into the setter or getter by hand. */ public class StdDelegatesDemoJava { static final class PayoutJava { private String owner = "<none>"; private int limit = 100; void setOwner(String owner) { String old = this.owner; this.owner = owner; // observable: assign, then notify System.out.println("owner: " + old + " -> " + owner); } void setLimit(int limit) { if (limit <= 100) this.limit = limit; // vetoable: check, then assign } int getLimit() { return limit; } } static final class IssuerConfigJava { private final Map<String, Object> settings; IssuerConfigJava(Map<String, Object> settings) { this.settings = settings; } String host() { return (String) get("host"); } int port() { return (Integer) get("port"); } private Object get(String key) { if (!settings.containsKey(key)) throw new NoSuchElementException("Key " + key + " is missing in the map."); return settings.get(key); } } // provideDelegate has no Java twin: Java validates in the constructor, which also runs at build time static final class SettingsJava { final String issuerUrl; SettingsJava() { System.out.println("binding issuerUrl"); issuerUrl = "value of issuerUrl"; } } public static void main(String[] args) { PayoutJava p = new PayoutJava(); p.setOwner("alice"); p.setOwner("bob"); p.setLimit(500); System.out.println("limit after veto: " + p.getLimit()); p.setLimit(50); System.out.println("limit after ok: " + p.getLimit()); IssuerConfigJava config = new IssuerConfigJava(Map.of("host", "issuer.example")); System.out.println("host = " + config.host()); try { System.out.println("port = " + config.port()); } catch (NoSuchElementException e) { System.out.println("port failed on access: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("building Settings..."); SettingsJava s = new SettingsJava(); System.out.println("built; issuerUrl = " + s.issuerUrl); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l03.demo.StdDelegatesDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l03/demo/StdDelegatesDemoJava.java building Settings... comes first, then binding issuerUrl while the constructor runs, then built; issuerUrl = value of issuerUrl. With new <= 40 both assignments are vetoed, so both lines print 100: the handler checks assignments, never the initial value. Without host, building IssuerConfig still works and the program fails on the config.host read with Key host is missing in the map. Swapping the target of class delegation at run time. class Router(var gateway: Gateway) : Gateway by gateway invites a feature flag to set router.gateway = newGateway: Java // the Java decorator people have in mind: it reads the field on every call @Override public String authorize(Payment p) { return gateway.authorize(p); } Kotlin class Router(var gateway: Gateway) : Gateway by gateway router.gateway = newGateway // the property changes; authorize() still calls the old gateway The assignment works, the property changes, and every call still goes to the gateway passed to the constructor, because the compiler copied it into a hidden final $$delegate_0 field. Nothing fails; the traffic simply never moves. If the target must change, write the forwarding methods yourself so they read the property each time, or forward to an AtomicReference<Gateway>.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · Java and Kotlin
x: An audited field: Java setters vs a Kotlin delegate PaymentDraft.java public final class PaymentDraft { private final ChangeLog log; private String status = "NEW"; private long amountMinor = 0; public PaymentDraft(ChangeLog log) { this.log = log; } public String getStatus() { return status; } public void setStatus(String s) { if (!s.equals(status)) log.record("status", status, s); // repeated in every setter status = s; } public long getAmountMinor() { return amountMinor; } public void setAmountMinor(long a) { if (a != amountMinor) log.record("amountMinor", amountMinor, a); amountMinor = a; } } PaymentDraft.kt class Recorded<T>(private var value: T, private val log: ChangeLog) : ReadWriteProperty<Any?, T> { override fun getValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>): T = value override fun setValue(thisRef: Any?, property: KProperty<*>, value: T) { if (value != this.value) log.changes += Change(property.name, this.value, value) this.value = value } } class PaymentDraft(val log: ChangeLog) { var status: String by Recorded("NEW", log) // the audit is written once, in Recorded var amountMinor: Long by Recorded(0L, log) } In Java the audit lives in every setter, and a new field without it is a silent gap that only review can catch. In Kotlin it's written once, in the delegate, and each property opts in with by. The property name comes from the KProperty the compiler passes in, so it can't drift from the field name the way a string literal can. The run-time price is one delegate object per property per instance, plus one static KProperty array per class. Java code calling the Kotlin class can't tell the two apart: it sees getStatus and setStatus either way.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · Worked example
x: A config object that fails at startup, not on the first payment Start with a map-backed config. It reads nicely, but a missing key is found only when someone reads the property, which may be the first payment routed to that acquirer at 2 a.m. final class RoutingConfig { private final Map<String, Object> settings; RoutingConfig(Map<String, Object> settings) { this.settings = settings; } String acquirer() { return (String) settings.get("acquirer"); } // null if missing long timeoutMs() { return (Long) settings.get("timeoutMs"); } // NullPointerException if missing } class RoutingConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val acquirer: String by settings // NoSuchElementException, but only when read val timeoutMs: Long by settings } Write a provider. provideDelegate runs once per property while the object is built, so it can check the key right away and hand back a delegate that only returns the value it read. fun <T> Map<String, Any?>.required(): PropertyDelegateProvider<Any?, ReadOnlyProperty<Any?, T>> = PropertyDelegateProvider { _, property -> // 1. check the key while the owning object is constructed require(property.name in this) { "missing config key '${property.name}'" } @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") val value = this[property.name] as T // 2. the real delegate just returns what was read ReadOnlyProperty { _, _ -> value } } class RoutingConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val acquirer: String by settings.required() val timeoutMs: Long by settings.required() } // Java does the same check in the constructor, one line per key RoutingConfig(Map<String, Object> settings) { this.acquirer = (String) require(settings, "acquirer"); this.timeoutMs = (Long) require(settings, "timeoutMs"); } private static Object require(Map<String, Object> m, String key) { if (!m.containsKey(key)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("missing config key '" + key + "'"); return m.get(key); } Build one with a key missing. It fails in the constructor, with the property's name in the message, because the name came from the KProperty the compiler passed in. RoutingConfig(mapOf("acquirer" to "acq-a", "timeoutMs" to 2_000L)) // fine RoutingConfig(mapOf("acquirer" to "acq-a")) // java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: missing config key 'timeoutMs' new RoutingConfig(Map.of("acquirer", "acq-a", "timeoutMs", 2_000L)); // fine new RoutingConfig(Map.of("acquirer", "acq-a")); // java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: missing config key 'timeoutMs' The cast is still unchecked: a "timeoutMs" to "2000" entry passes the check and fails later with a ClassCastException on the first read. If that matters, pass the expected class into required and check it with isInstance, the class-token trick from the generics track.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · Quiz
x: What does this print? class Fees(var policy: FeePolicy) : FeePolicy by policy val fees = Fees(FlatFee(25)) fees.policy = FlatFee(99) println(fees.feeMinor(10_000)) 25 99 An IllegalStateException 0 by policy reads the constructor argument once and stores it in $$delegate_0. The generated feeMinor calls that field, so the swap changes only the property. 99 is what a hand-written decorator that reads its field each call would print. Which fields does class Order { var status: String by Audited("NEW") } have in the bytecode? private String status private final Audited status$delegate, plus a static KProperty[] $$delegatedProperties One static Audited shared by every Order None: the delegate is inlined into getStatus Each delegated property gets a hidden field holding its delegate, typed as the delegate expression, and each class gets one static array of KProperty objects that the accessors pass to getValue and setValue. Nothing is shared between instances, and nothing is inlined. An AuthorizationEvent is created 2 million times a minute in a Kafka consumer. It has val summary: String by lazy { describe(this) }, which is read for about 1% of events. What's the best change? Keep it: lazy costs nothing until it's read Switch to lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.PUBLICATION) Mark the property @Volatile Make it a function or a getter, val summary get() = describe(this), computed on demand lazy allocates the Lazy object and the initializer lambda in the constructor, for every event, read or not. A getter without a backing field costs nothing until called. Changing the mode keeps both allocations; it only changes the locking. class IssuerConfig(settings: Map<String, Any?>) { val port: Int by settings }, and settings has no "port" key. When does it fail? When IssuerConfig is constructed At compile time Never: port reads as 0 When port is read: NoSuchElementException: Key port is missing in the map. A map-backed property is a lookup in its getter. Building the object only stores the map. To fail at construction, check the key in a provideDelegate, which runs while the object is built. From the memory model track: two threads read val rules by lazy { download() } for the first time at the same moment. What happens? download() may run twice, and each thread keeps its own result download() runs once; the other thread waits and sees the same value Nothing is guaranteed unless the property is @Volatile The second thread gets ConcurrentModificationException The default mode is SYNCHRONIZED: double-checked locking with a lock, so one thread runs the initializer and the other waits for it. The first option describes PUBLICATION, where several threads may run it but all see the first stored value.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · Key terms
x: Class delegation class A(x: I) : I by x: the compiler writes every method of I as a call on x, except the ones you override. Delegated property A property whose get and set are handed to another object with by. $delegate field The hidden field, such as status$delegate, that holds a property's delegate. KProperty A run-time description of a property (its name, its type), passed to getValue and setValue. Lazy The standard delegate that computes a value on first read and keeps it. Three thread-safety modes. provideDelegate An operator the compiler calls once per property at construction, to create or check the real delegate. Map-backed property val host: String by settings: reads settings["host"] each time the property is read. class Fees(var policy: FeePolicy) : FeePolicy by policy. After fees.policy = other, which object gets the calls? The original one. The compiler copied it into a hidden final field, $$delegate_0, at construction. Does class delegation forward equals, hashCode and toString? No. They come from Any, not from the interface. Override them yourself if the wrapper should behave like what it wraps. Which functions does a delegate for a var need? getValue(thisRef, property: KProperty<*>) and setValue(thisRef, property, value), as operators or via ReadWriteProperty. A val needs only getValue. What does the compiler generate for var status by Audited("NEW")? A status$delegate field holding the delegate, a static $$delegatedProperties array of KProperty, and accessors that call getValue/setValue on the delegate. What does by lazy cost per instance? A Lazy object (SynchronizedLazyImpl by default) and an initializer lambda, created in the constructor, plus an interface call, and unboxing for primitives, on every read. observable vs vetoable: when does each handler run? observable runs after the assignment. vetoable runs before it, and returning false keeps the old value. When does provideDelegate run? Once per property, while the owning object is being constructed, before any read. That makes it the place for early validation.

h: Delegation: class delegation and delegated properties · Go deeper
x: Delegating to another property is the one case worth knowing that has no $delegate field at all. It is useful when you rename a property and need the old name for a while: Java // Java keeps the old accessor by hand and marks it deprecated public long getAmountMinor() { return amountMinor; } @Deprecated public long getAmount() { return amountMinor; } Kotlin class Payment { var amountMinor: Long = 0 @Deprecated("Use amountMinor", ReplaceWith("amountMinor")) var amount: Long by this::amountMinor } javap -p on that class shows getAmount and setAmount, a static helper getAmount$delegate(Payment), and no amount$delegate field: the compiler reads and writes amountMinor directly. The IDE offers the ReplaceWith fix at every call site, so the rename can finish over a few releases. The other cases without a field, from the docs: a delegate that is a named object, this, a constant expression or an enum entry, and "a final val property with a backing field and a default getter in the same module". Everything else pays for one delegate object per property per instance. One more design note on class delegation. It composes well with the patterns track's decorators because the delegate never calls back into your class. With inheritance, HashSet.addAll calls add, so an override of add sees every element. With by, addAll goes to the inner set, and your add override is skipped. Neither is wrong, but only the by version is stable across JDK updates, because it doesn't depend on how the parent class happens to be written.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · A lambda with receiver is a function whose first parameter is this
x: A Java builder call repeats the builder's name on every line: b.debit(...), b.credit(...), b.memo(...). Kotlin DSLs drop that prefix, and the whole trick is one type. First a word: the receiver of a call is the object it's called on. In sb.append(x), sb is the receiver. Inside a class's own methods the receiver is this, and you can leave it out. A function type with a receiver, written A.() -> B, is a lambda that runs with an A as this. So inside its braces you call the A's members with no prefix, as if you were writing a method of A. apply, with and run in the standard library are built on it. Java // Java has no receiver lambdas. Its idiom: a Consumer that receives the builder as a parameter. static String receipt(Consumer<StringBuilder> block) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); block.accept(sb); return sb.toString(); } receipt(sb -> sb.append("captured ").append(1_999)); Kotlin fun receipt(block: StringBuilder.() -> Unit): String = StringBuilder().apply(block).toString() receipt { append("captured "); append(1_999) } // `this` is the StringBuilder To the JVM, StringBuilder.() -> Unit and (StringBuilder) -> Unit are the same thing: a kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<StringBuilder, Unit>. The receiver is just the first argument. That's why Kotlin lets you assign one type to the other, and why you can call a receiver lambda both ways, sb.withReceiver() or withReceiver(sb). The difference exists only in the compiler, which decides what this means inside the braces. It is also exactly what Java sees. Java calls receipt with a Function1, gets the builder as a parameter, and must end with return Unit.INSTANCE, because a Kotlin () -> Unit returns a real Unit object. Two more facts make DSLs work. A receiver lambda can take parameters too: Builder.(Int) -> Unit gets a this and an Int. And an extension function is a named lambda with receiver. fun EntryBuilder.payout(merchant: String, grossMinor: Long, feeBps: Int) can be called inside any EntryBuilder.() -> Unit block, which is how you add vocabulary to a builder you don't own. The worked example does that. Call a receiver lambda both ways Run ReceiverDemo, then ReceiverDemoJava. In ReceiverDemo.kt, try the reverse assignment: val back: (StringBuilder) -> Unit = withReceiver. Predict whether it compiles, then run. In the Java twin, delete return Unit.INSTANCE; from the first lambda and run. Read javac's complaint. ReceiverDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo // Two function types. Inside the first, the StringBuilder is `this`; in the second it's a parameter. val withReceiver: StringBuilder.() -> Unit = { append("EUR "); append(19.99) } val withParameter: (StringBuilder) -> Unit = { sb -> sb.append("EUR ").append(19.99) } /** An ordinary function that takes a lambda with receiver: the smallest possible DSL entry point. */ fun receipt(block: StringBuilder.() -> Unit): String = StringBuilder().apply(block).toString() fun main() { val sb = StringBuilder() sb.withReceiver() // call it like an extension function... withReceiver(sb) // ...or pass the receiver as the first argument println(sb) val swapped: StringBuilder.() -> Unit = withParameter // the two types are interchangeable println(receipt(swapped)) println(receipt { append("captured "); append(1_999) }) println("JVM type of withReceiver: ${withReceiver.javaClass.interfaces.joinToString { it.name }}") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l04.demo.ReceiverDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l04/demo/ReceiverDemo.kt ReceiverDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo; import kotlin.Unit; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** * Java twin of ReceiverDemo.kt. Java has no lambdas with receivers. A Kotlin * StringBuilder.() -> Unit is a Function1<StringBuilder, Unit> to Java: the receiver is the first parameter. */ public class ReceiverDemoJava { // Java's own idiom for the same job: a Consumer that gets the builder as a parameter static String receiptJava(Consumer<StringBuilder> block) { StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); block.accept(sb); return sb.toString(); } public static void main(String[] args) { String r = ReceiverDemoKt.receipt(sb -> { sb.append("captured ").append(1_999); return Unit.INSTANCE; // Kotlin's Unit is a real object here }); System.out.println(r); System.out.println(receiptJava(sb -> sb.append("refunded ").append(500))); StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); ReceiverDemoKt.getWithReceiver().invoke(sb); // a receiver lambda, invoked with the receiver as argument System.out.println(sb); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l04.demo.ReceiverDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l04/demo/ReceiverDemoJava.java Kotlin prints EUR 19.99EUR 19.99 (one call as an extension, one with the receiver as an argument), EUR 19.99, captured 1999, and JVM type of withReceiver: kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1. The reverse assignment compiles too. Without return Unit.INSTANCE, javac stops with incompatible types: bad return type in lambda expression and missing return value: Function1.invoke returns an Object, so a Java lambda for it has to return something. Type-safe builders (Kotlin docs) docs Function literals with receiver (Kotlin docs) docs A lambda with receiver is like being handed a form already clipped to a clipboard: inside the block you write on that form without saying which one. Nested blocks stack forms on top of each other, and without @DslMarker a field that doesn't exist on the top form gets written onto the form underneath, without anyone noticing. The marker says only the top form may be written on without naming it. The analogy breaks in a good way: a clerk finds the misfiled field after the forms are sent, while the compiler finds it before the code ever runs.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · A DSL is builder classes plus functions that take receiver lambdas
x: A type-safe builder has two pieces. A builder class holds the state and offers the vocabulary: properties to set and functions to call. An entry function creates the builder, runs your lambda on it and returns the result: Builder().apply(block).build(). Nesting is the same trick again: a builder function that takes another receiver lambda. Lesson 3 of the patterns track built a payment-request DSL this way, and the Kotlin docs build HTML from nothing more than classes, extension functions and function literals with receiver. You need no library. The standard library ships three small builders you can use today: Java List<Item> building = new ArrayList<>(); building.add(new Item("sku-1", 2, 999)); building.add(new Item("sku-2", 1, 500)); if (building.size() == 2) building.add(new Item("gift-wrap", 1, 0)); List<Item> items = List.copyOf(building); // freeze it with a copy String text = new StringBuilder().append("total=").append(2_498).toString(); Kotlin val items = buildList { add(Item("sku-1", 2, 999)) add(Item("sku-2", 1, 500)) if (size == 2) add(Item("gift-wrap", 1, 0)) // `this` is a MutableList } val totals = buildMap { for (i in items) put(i.sku, i.qty * i.unitMinor) } val text = buildString { append("total="); append(totals.values.sum()) } Inside buildList { }, this is a MutableList, so add, addAll and even size work. The result is typed List, and the demo shows it really is read-only: cast it back to MutableList, call add, and you get UnsupportedOperationException. That's what you want from a builder: mutable while you build, fixed once you're done. Java gets the same with List.copyOf, one copy later. buildList, buildMap and buildString are inline, so their lambdas cost nothing (lesson 1 of this track). Your own entry functions can be inline too. Most DSL entry points run a few times per request, so it rarely matters. Where does validation go? Check a single bad value at the call that passes it, so the error points at the wrong line: a debit of -100 fails inside debit. Check rules that span fields in build(), the one place that sees all of them: debits must equal credits. The lab does both. Use the standard builders Run BuildersDemo and BuildersDemoJava. They print the same four lines. In buildList { }, add println(this::class.simpleName) as the first line. Predict whether you'll see ArrayList, then run. Move the if (size == 2) line above the two add calls and run again. What changed, and why? Java builds a mutable collection, then copies it into an * unmodifiable one. buildList and buildString are inline-only Kotlin functions, so Java can't call them. */ public class BuildersDemoJava { record ItemJava(String sku, int qty, long unitMinor) {} public static void main(String[] args) { List<ItemJava> building = new ArrayList<>(); building.add(new ItemJava("sku-1", 2, 999)); building.add(new ItemJava("sku-2", 1, 500)); if (building.size() == 2) building.add(new ItemJava("gift-wrap", 1, 0)); List<ItemJava> items = List.copyOf(building); Map<String, Long> totals = new LinkedHashMap<>(); for (ItemJava i : items) totals.put(i.sku(), i.qty() * i.unitMinor()); String text = new StringBuilder() .append("total=") .append(totals.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum()) .toString(); System.out.println(items.stream().map(ItemJava::sku).toList()); System.out.println(totals); System.out.println(text); try { items.add(new ItemJava("late", 1, 1)); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("the copied list is read-only: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()); } } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l04.demo.BuildersDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l04/demo/BuildersDemoJava.java Both print [sku-1, sku-2, gift-wrap], {sku-1=1998, sku-2=500, gift-wrap=0}, total=2498 and a line saying the list is read-only. Inside the block, this is the standard library's own list builder class (it prints ListBuilder), not an ArrayList: that's how the result can become read-only without a copy. With the if first, size is 0, so no gift-wrap line is added. Payment services build nested data all day: a payout batch with entries and postings, routing rules per merchant, a test fixture for a Kafka event with its headers. A small DSL makes Quarkus tests and fixtures read like the data they produce, and it puts the validation (debits equal credits, every party has an IBAN) in one build() instead of in every test. Keep DSLs for nested data that many people write; a flat request with six fields is clearer with named arguments. Put @DslMarker in from the first day. Adding it later breaks every call site that was quietly reaching an outer builder, which is the point, but finding them in a hundred tests is a bad afternoon.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · @DslMarker makes only the nearest receiver implicit
x: Nesting creates a trap. Inside payer { } two receivers are in scope: the PartyBuilder and the outer PaymentRequestBuilder. Kotlin resolves an unqualified call against all of them, nearest first. So payee { } written inside payer { } compiles, because it finds payee on the outer builder. In the demo, without a marker, that misplaced line builds a second party and the program fails at run time with IllegalArgumentException: iban required for 'oops'. In a DSL without a required field, it would simply build the wrong request. @DslMarker closes the hole. Annotate an annotation class with it, then put that annotation on every builder class. From then on, inside a block only the nearest marked receiver is implicit: Java // Java needs no marker: each lambda names its builder, so reaching the outer one takes `r.` DslMarkerDemoKt.paymentRequest("PR-1", r -> { r.payer(p -> { p.setName("ACME Ltd"); r.setCurrency("EUR"); // deliberate, and visible in review return Unit.INSTANCE; }); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); Kotlin @DslMarker @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS, AnnotationTarget.TYPE) annotation class PaymentDsl @PaymentDsl class PartyBuilder { /* ... */ } @PaymentDsl class PaymentRequestBuilder(private val id: String) { /* ... */ } paymentRequest("PR-2") { payer { name = "ACME Ltd" payee { name = "oops" } // error: cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver this@paymentRequest.currency = "EUR" // an explicit label still works } } The full message is 'fun payee(block: PartyBuilder.() -> Unit): Unit' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. The label this@paymentRequest uses the name of the function that took the lambda, and nobody types it by accident. The rules are narrow, so learn them exactly. The docs say a marker counts only on classes, on the receiver types of function types (the TYPE target, as in @PaymentDsl PartyBuilder.() -> Unit) and on type aliases. On a function or a property it "has no effect". Marking a common superclass is enough, so a DSL with twenty builders can mark one base class. And extension functions on a marked builder still work inside its block, because they resolve against the nearest receiver. Watch the marker catch a misplaced call Run DslMarkerDemo (or its Java twin). Both print the same PaymentRequest, with currency EUR. Uncomment the wrong-move block at the end of main. Predict, then run. Now remove @PaymentDsl from both builder classes (keep the annotation class) and run again. Put the markers back, and move one @PaymentDsl onto the payer function instead of PartyBuilder. Does the error come back? DslMarkerDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo @DslMarker @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS, AnnotationTarget.TYPE) annotation class PaymentDsl data class Party(val name: String, val iban: String) data class PaymentRequest(val id: String, val currency: String, val payer: Party, val payee: Party) @PaymentDsl class PartyBuilder { var name = "" var iban = "" fun build(): Party { require(iban.isNotBlank()) { "iban required for '$name'" } return Party(name, iban) } } @PaymentDsl class PaymentRequestBuilder(private val id: String) { var currency = "EUR" private var payer: Party? = null private var payee: Party? = null fun payer(block: PartyBuilder.() -> Unit) { payer = PartyBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun payee(block: PartyBuilder.() -> Unit) { payee = PartyBuilder().apply(block).build() } fun build() = PaymentRequest(id, currency, checkNotNull(payer) { "payer missing" }, checkNotNull(payee) { "payee missing" }) } fun paymentRequest(id: String, block: PaymentRequestBuilder.() -> Unit): PaymentRequest = PaymentRequestBuilder(id).apply(block).build() fun main() { val req = paymentRequest("PR-1") { currency = "GBP" payer { name = "ACME Ltd"; iban = "GB33BUKB20201555555555" } payee { name = "Corner Shop" iban = "GB94BARC10201530093459" this@paymentRequest.currency = "EUR" // an outer receiver needs an explicit label } } println(req) // Wrong move. Uncomment the block, predict, run. Then remove @PaymentDsl from both builder // classes and run it again. // paymentRequest("PR-2") { // payer { // name = "ACME Ltd" // payee { name = "oops" } // iban = "GB33BUKB20201555555555" // } // } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l04.demo.DslMarkerDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l04/demo/DslMarkerDemo.kt DslMarkerDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l04.demo; import kotlin.Unit; /** * Java twin of DslMarkerDemo.kt. Java calls the same Kotlin DSL with Function1 lambdas. It needs no * marker: each block names its builder, so reaching the outer one means typing `r.` on purpose. */ public class DslMarkerDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { PaymentRequest req = DslMarkerDemoKt.paymentRequest("PR-1", r -> { r.setCurrency("GBP"); r.payer(p -> { p.setName("ACME Ltd"); p.setIban("GB33BUKB20201555555555"); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); r.payee(p -> { p.setName("Corner Shop"); p.setIban("GB94BARC10201530093459"); r.setCurrency("EUR"); // the outer builder, named explicitly return Unit.INSTANCE; }); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); System.out.println(req); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l04.demo.DslMarkerDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l04/demo/DslMarkerDemoJava.java With the markers, the build fails with 'fun payee(block: PartyBuilder.() -> Unit): Unit' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Without them it compiles, runs, and dies with IllegalArgumentException: iban required for 'oops', thrown while building the misplaced payee. With the marker on the function and not the class, the wrong move compiles again: a marker on a function has no effect, and PartyBuilder is no longer a marked receiver. With @PaymentDsl on both builders, only the nearest receiver is implicit inside payer { }. Reaching the outer builder needs an explicit label.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Calling a DSL from Java, and what became of context receivers
x: A Kotlin DSL works from Java, though it isn't pretty. Every Builder.() -> Unit parameter is a Function1<Builder, Unit>, so the Java caller writes b -> { b.debit(...); return Unit.INSTANCE; }, and the lab's LedgerFromJavaTest does just that. If Java callers matter, add a thin overload that takes a java.util.function.Consumer and give it its own name, so Kotlin callers never have to choose between two lambda types: Java JournalEntry e = LedgerKt.journalEntryJava("payout-981", b -> { b.debit("merchant:981", 12_000L); b.credit("bank:clearing", 12_000L); // a void lambda: no Unit.INSTANCE }); Kotlin fun journalEntryJava(id: String, block: Consumer<EntryBuilder>): JournalEntry = journalEntry(id) { block.accept(this) } // `this` is the EntryBuilder @DslMarker means nothing to Java. A Java lambda names its parameter, so the scope problem doesn't arise. DSLs were also the main reason for an experiment you'll still find in older code and blog posts: context receivers. Kotlin 1.6.20 shipped them as a prototype behind -Xcontext-receivers, and its release notes warned that the compiler would "produce pre-release binaries that cannot be used in production code". They let a function demand a receiver from its surroundings, as in context(Logger) fun audit(), so a DSL function could require being called inside some scope. Kotlin 2.2.0 replaced them with context parameters, and the 2.3.20 notes say it plainly: "Experimental context receivers are no longer supported and are replaced by context parameters." In Kotlin 2.4.21 the old syntax fails twice: context parameters must be named. Use '_' to declare an anonymous context parameter. and then unresolved reference 'log', because a context parameter is not a receiver in the body. The old flag fails too: experimental context receivers are superseded by context parameters. Remove the '-Xcontext-receivers' compiler argument and migrate to the new syntax. When you see either message, the fix is the next lesson: context parameters, stable since Kotlin 2.4.0. A check before you move on: a Java caller passes b -> { b.debit("merchant:981", 100L); b.credit("bank:clearing", 100L); } to journalEntry, with no return at the end. Predict what javac says, and why the same lambda is fine for journalEntryJava. (The answer follows from the two interfaces: Function1.invoke returns a value, and Consumer.accept returns void.) Putting the marker on the builder functions instead of the builder classes, or leaving one builder unmarked. @PaymentDsl fun payer(...) compiles and does nothing: the docs say a marker on a function or property has no effect. The scope check starts only when the receiver types themselves (the builder classes, or one common superclass) carry the annotation: Java // Java has no equivalent rule to get wrong: the outer builder is always reached by name r.payer(p -> { p.setName("ACME Ltd"); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); Kotlin @PaymentDsl fun payer(block: PartyBuilder.() -> Unit) { ... } // no effect at all @PaymentDsl class PartyBuilder { ... } // this is what the check needs Test your DSL by writing a misplaced call on purpose. If payee { } inside payer { } compiles, your marker isn't doing anything.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Java and Kotlin
x: A journal-entry builder: Java Consumer vs Kotlin lambda with receiver Journal.java public final class Journal { public static JournalEntry entry(String id, Consumer<EntryBuilder> block) { EntryBuilder b = new EntryBuilder(id); block.accept(b); // the builder arrives as a parameter return b.build(); } } JournalEntry e = Journal.entry("payout-981", b -> { b.memo("merchant payout"); b.debit("merchant:981", 12_000); b.credit("bank:clearing", 11_850); b.credit("revenue:fees", 150); }); Journal.kt fun journalEntry(id: String, block: EntryBuilder.() -> Unit): JournalEntry = EntryBuilder(id).apply(block).build() // the builder is `this` inside block val e = journalEntry("payout-981") { memo = "merchant payout" debit("merchant:981", 12_000) credit("bank:clearing", 11_850) credit("revenue:fees", 150) } Both compile to the same thing: a function object that receives the builder. On the JVM, Kotlin's EntryBuilder.() -> Unit is a Function1<EntryBuilder, Unit>, and Java's Consumer<EntryBuilder> plays the same role. The difference is only in the source: Kotlin makes the builder this, so the block reads like a list of statements, and nested blocks need @DslMarker to stop calls from reaching outer builders by accident. Java names the parameter every time, which is noisier but can never resolve a call against the wrong builder.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Worked example
x: Add vocabulary to the ledger DSL with an extension function Every merchant payout is the same three postings: debit the merchant's balance, credit the bank with the net amount, credit fee revenue. Written out each time, the arithmetic gets copied, and one day it's copied wrong. Journal.entry("payout-981", b -> { b.debit("merchant:981", 12_000); b.credit("bank:clearing", 12_000 - 150); b.credit("revenue:fees", 150); }); journalEntry("payout-981") { debit("merchant:981", 12_000) credit("bank:clearing", 12_000 - 150) credit("revenue:fees", 150) } Write an extension function on the builder. It works even if EntryBuilder lives in a library you can't edit, and inside a block it reads like a built-in word. // 1. compute the fee once, in one place fun EntryBuilder.payout(merchant: String, grossMinor: Long, feeBps: Int) { val fee = grossMinor * feeBps / 10_000 // 2. the three postings, always balanced debit("merchant:$merchant", grossMinor) credit("bank:clearing", grossMinor - fee) credit("revenue:fees", fee) } journalEntry("payout-981") { payout("981", 12_000, feeBps = 125) } // Java's version is a static helper that takes the builder as its first parameter, // which is exactly what the Kotlin extension compiles to static void payout(EntryBuilder b, String merchant, long grossMinor, int feeBps) { long fee = grossMinor * feeBps / 10_000; b.debit("merchant:" + merchant, grossMinor); b.credit("bank:clearing", grossMinor - fee); b.credit("revenue:fees", fee); } Check where it can be called. Inside entry { } it resolves against the nearest receiver, the EntryBuilder. Inside batch { } but outside an entry, it doesn't compile, so a payout can't be posted outside an entry by accident. batch("batch-17") { entry("payout-982") { payout("982", 8_000, 125) } // fine payout("983", 5_000, 125) // error: candidate 'fun EntryBuilder.payout(...): Unit' is inapplicable because of a receiver type mismatch. } Batches.batch("batch-17", bb -> { bb.entry("payout-982", b -> payout(b, "982", 8_000, 125)); // fine // payout(bb, "983", 5_000, 125); // error: incompatible types: BatchBuilder cannot be converted to EntryBuilder }); Run it: the entry has postings of 12,000 debit, 11,850 and 150 credit, and build() accepts it because the debits equal the credits. Integer division rounds the fee down, so the bank gets the extra cent. Whether that's right is a business rule, and it's now in one function you can test.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Quiz
x: What is the JVM type of a parameter declared as block: PartyBuilder.() -> Unit? kotlin.jvm.functions.Function0<Unit> kotlin.jvm.functions.Function1<PartyBuilder, Unit> java.util.function.Consumer<PartyBuilder> A generated interface named PartyBuilderBlock The receiver becomes the first parameter, so a receiver lambda with no other parameters is a Function1. That's why Java passes p -> { ...; return Unit.INSTANCE; }. Consumer is Java's idiom for the same job, not what Kotlin compiles to. Both builders carry @PaymentDsl. Which of these compiles inside payer { }? payee { name = "x" } currency = "GBP" this@paymentRequest.currency = "GBP" None of them With the marker, members of the outer PaymentRequestBuilder can't be reached implicitly, so payee { } and currency = ... are errors. An explicit label names the outer receiver on purpose, and that is allowed. You put @PaymentDsl on the functions payer, payee and paymentRequest, but not on the builder classes. What happens to payee { } written inside payer { }? It compiles and calls the outer builder's payee: a marker on functions has no effect A compile error: implicit receiver not allowed It always throws at run time A compiler warning, then it runs The docs say a DSL marker counts only on classes, receiver types in function types and type aliases. On functions or properties it has no effect, so the scope check never starts and the misplaced call resolves against the outer builder. What does buildList { add(1); if (size == 1) add(2) } return, and can you add to it afterwards? [1, 2], and casting it to MutableList lets you add [1], because size was read before add It doesn't compile: size isn't available inside the block [1, 2], and it's read-only: add after a cast throws UnsupportedOperationException Inside the block this is a MutableList, so size is 1 after the first add and the second element is added. The returned list is read-only even if you cast it, which is the point of a builder: mutable while building, fixed afterwards. From the patterns track: a ChargeRequest has six flat fields and no nested parts. What's the best way to build it in Kotlin? A type-safe DSL with @DslMarker A constructor with named and default arguments A Java-style builder with setters and build() A buildMap of field names to values Named and default arguments already give readable, checked construction for flat data. A DSL earns its two extra classes only when the data nests, like items under a request or postings under an entry.
