h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Key terms
x: Lambda with receiver A lambda in which one object is this, so its members can be called without a prefix. Function type with receiver A type such as A.() -> B. On the JVM, the receiver is the first parameter of a Function1. Type-safe builder Builder classes plus functions that take receiver lambdas, so nested data can be written as code the compiler checks. @DslMarker Meta-annotation for an annotation that marks DSL receivers. Inside a block, only the nearest marked receiver is implicit. Implicit receiver An object whose members you can call without naming it, such as this inside a receiver lambda. Labeled this this@paymentRequest: names an outer receiver by the function that introduced it. Context receivers An experimental feature (1.6.20) that let a function require a receiver from its scope. Replaced by context parameters. What is A.() -> B? A function type with receiver: inside the lambda, the A is this. On the JVM it's Function1<A, B>. Are StringBuilder.() -> Unit and (StringBuilder) -> Unit interchangeable? Yes. The receiver is just the first parameter: you can assign one to the other and call either as f(sb). What does @DslMarker change inside a nested block? Only the nearest receiver marked with that annotation is implicit. Outer marked receivers need an explicit this@label. Where must a DSL marker annotation go to have any effect? On the builder classes (or a common superclass), on receiver types of function types, or on type aliases. On functions or properties it does nothing. What does buildList { } give you? A MutableList as this while you build, and a read-only List as the result. It's inline, so the lambda costs nothing. How does Java call fun journalEntry(id: String, block: EntryBuilder.() -> Unit)? With a Function1<EntryBuilder, Unit>: b -> { b.debit(...); return Unit.INSTANCE; }. What happened to context receivers? A 1.6.20 prototype behind -Xcontext-receivers, replaced by context parameters in 2.2.0, and no longer supported since 2.3.20.

h: Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers · Go deeper
x: Context parameters, the subject of the next lesson, interact with implicit receivers, and Kotlin 2.4.21 is strict about it. The KEEP for context parameters uses this example: Java // No Java twin: Java has neither receivers nor context parameters. // The nearest idea is two parameters of the same type, where you must pick one by name. static void moo(Cow cow) { System.out.println("moo from " + cow.name()); } Kotlin class Cow(val name: String) { fun moo() = println("moo from $name") } with(Cow("receiver")) { context(Cow("context")) { moo() // which Cow? } } The with block makes one Cow an implicit receiver, and the context(...) block brings a second Cow into scope as a context argument. A bare moo() would resolve against the receiver, which is probably not what the author meant. Kotlin 2.4.21 reports an error: call to 'fun moo(): Unit' defined in 'Cow' uses an implicit receiver shadowed by a context parameter. Make the receiver explicit using 'this' or 'contextOf<Cow>()'. The type-safe builders page calls this a warning. The compiler you run is what counts, and here it is stricter than the page. A second detail: the TYPE target on the marker lets you mark one block without marking the class, as in fun payer(block: @PaymentDsl PartyBuilder.() -> Unit). That helps when the builder comes from a library you can't annotate. And when you design a DSL for others, keep each builder's surface small. Every public member is offered by the IDE inside the block, and every one of them is a word someone will eventually use in the wrong place.

h: Contracts and context parameters · Your own check functions teach the compiler nothing
x: The standard library's require(currency != null) makes currency usable as a String on the next line. Write the same check in your own function, and the compiler forgets it: Java // Java's type system doesn't track null at all, so the question never comes up static void requireCurrency(String currency) { if (currency == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency missing"); } requireCurrency(currency); System.out.println(currency.toUpperCase()); // compiles, as everything does Kotlin fun requireCurrencyPlain(currency: String?) { if (currency == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("currency missing") } requireCurrencyPlain(currency) println(currency.uppercase()) // error: only safe (?.) or non-null asserted (!!.) calls are allowed on a nullable receiver of type 'String?'. The feature that fails here is the smart cast: after a check such as if (x != null), the compiler treats x as the narrower type. It does that only for checks it can see in the current function. It never reads the body of a function you call, because that body may change, or live in another module. A contract closes the gap. It is a contract { } block, written as the first statement of a function, that states something about the function's behavior that callers may rely on. Two kinds matter in practice. returns() implies (currency != null) says: if this function returns normally, the condition holds. callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) says: the lambda runs exactly once, during this call, and is not stored. The other kinds are AT_MOST_ONCE, AT_LEAST_ONCE and UNKNOWN. Java // Java can't assign a local inside a lambda at all: // "local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final" String[] label = new String[1]; ContractsDemoKt.once(() -> { label[0] = "batch-17"; return Unit.INSTANCE; }); Kotlin @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun requireCurrency(currency: String?) { contract { returns() implies (currency != null) } if (currency == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("currency missing") } @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun <T> once(block: () -> T): T { contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) } return block() } val label: String once { label = "batch-17" } // allowed: the block runs exactly once This is how require, check, requireNotNull, run, let and apply work in the standard library. Contracts are still Experimental in Kotlin 2.4: the 2.4.0 notes say so, and without @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) every part of the block fails with this declaration needs opt-in. No compiler flag is needed, only the annotation. Take each contract away Run ContractsDemo (or ContractsDemoJava, which calls the same Kotlin functions). Wrong move 1: call requireCurrencyPlain(currency) instead of requireCurrency(currency). Predict the error, run, undo. Wrong move 2: delete the contract { callsInPlace(...) } line in once. once is still inline. Predict whether that is enough, run, undo. Wrong move 3: delete the @OptIn above isCaptured, run, undo. ContractsDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo import kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts import kotlin.contracts.InvocationKind import kotlin.contracts.contract sealed interface PaymentEvent data class Captured(val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : PaymentEvent data class Failed(val paymentId: String, val reason: String) : PaymentEvent fun lookupCurrency(merchant: String): String? = if (merchant.startsWith("m-")) "eur" else null /** Checks, but tells the compiler nothing. */ fun requireCurrencyPlain(currency: String?) { if (currency == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("currency missing") } /** The same check, plus a promise: if this returns, currency was not null. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun requireCurrency(currency: String?) { contract { returns() implies (currency != null) } if (currency == null) throw IllegalArgumentException("currency missing") } /** A promise about the receiver: a true result means this is a Captured. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun PaymentEvent.isCaptured(): Boolean { contract { returns(true) implies (this@isCaptured is Captured) } return this is Captured } /** A promise about the lambda: it runs exactly once, during this call. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun <T> once(block: () -> T): T { contract { callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) } return block() } fun main() { val currency = lookupCurrency("m-981") requireCurrency(currency) println("currency = ${currency.uppercase()}") // smart cast to String val event: PaymentEvent = Captured("pay_7", 1_999) if (event.isCaptured()) println("captured ${event.amountMinor}") // smart cast to Captured val label: String // a val, assigned inside a lambda once { label = "batch-17" } println("label = $label") // Wrong moves, one at a time. Predict the error, run, undo. // 1. Call requireCurrencyPlain(currency) instead of requireCurrency(currency). // 2. Delete the line `contract { callsInPlace(...) }` in once. // 3. Delete @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) above isCaptured. } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContractsDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l05/demo/ContractsDemo.kt ContractsDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo; import kotlin.Unit; /** * Java twin of ContractsDemo.kt. Java has no contracts. It has no null checks in the type system to * satisfy, its instanceof pattern binds a new variable instead of smart-casting, and a lambda may * not assign a local variable at all. */ public class ContractsDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { String currency = ContractsDemoKt.lookupCurrency("m-981"); ContractsDemoKt.requireCurrency(currency); // to Java: a void method, nothing more System.out.println("currency = " + currency.toUpperCase()); PaymentEvent event = new Captured("pay_7", 1_999); if (event instanceof Captured c) { // the pattern binds c: no promise needed System.out.println("captured " + c.getAmountMinor()); } // String label; once(() -> { label = "x"; ... }) would not compile: // "local variables referenced from a lambda expression must be final or effectively final" String[] label = new String[1]; ContractsDemoKt.once(() -> { label[0] = "batch-17"; return Unit.INSTANCE; }); System.out.println("label = " + label[0]); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContractsDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l05/demo/ContractsDemoJava.java The demo prints currency = EUR, captured 1999 and label = batch-17. Move 1 fails on currency.uppercase() with the nullable-receiver error. Move 2 fails with 'val' cannot be reassigned. and variable 'label' must be initialized.: being inline doesn't tell the compiler how many times the body calls block. Move 3 fails with this declaration needs opt-in. Its usage must be marked with '@kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts' or '@OptIn(kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts::class)'. KEEP-0139: Kotlin contracts read A contract is a signed statement from a colleague: "if my check returns, the field is filled in". The compiler files it and never opens the folder to see whether it's true, so a false statement passes every gate until the moment someone relies on it. A context parameter is the badge you wear inside a building: doors (functions) check that you have one of the right kind and let you through without asking for it again. The analogy breaks at the JVM: there the badge is just one more argument handed to every function, and Java has to hand it over in person.

h: Contracts and context parameters · The compiler trusts a contract and never checks it
x: A contract is a promise, and the compiler doesn't check the body against it. The design document, KEEP-139, says the compiler "trusts contracts unconditionally" and that the programmer is "responsible for writing correct and sound contracts". Formal verification is listed as a non-goal. So this compiles without a single warning: Java // Java's version of the same lie: a check that always says yes, and a cast that believes it static boolean lyingIsCaptured(PaymentEvent e) { return true; } if (lyingIsCaptured(failed)) { Captured c = (Captured) failed; // ClassCastException } Kotlin @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun PaymentEvent.lyingIsCaptured(): Boolean { contract { returns(true) implies (this@lyingIsCaptured is Captured) } return true // the lie } if (failed.lyingIsCaptured()) println(failed.amountMinor) // ClassCastException The smart cast to Captured lets failed.amountMinor compile. At run time the JVM still checks the cast it was given, and Failed is not a Captured: class ...Failed cannot be cast to class ...Captured. A contract can't make a wrong value right. It moves the cast from your code, where a reviewer sees it, into a promise inside another function. Look one level down and the reason is plain. javap -c on the honest isCaptured shows a null check on the receiver, then instanceof Captured and ireturn: no trace of the contract. The contract lives in the Kotlin metadata of the class file, which only the Kotlin compiler reads when it compiles a caller. Java callers never see it, and nothing at run time enforces it. The K2 compiler does catch some callsInPlace mistakes, as warnings. A block declared EXACTLY_ONCE but called twice gets wrong invocation kind 'EXACTLY_ONCE' for 'block: () -> Unit' specified, the actual invocation kind is 'AT_LEAST_ONCE'. A block declared in place but stored in a list gets leaked in-place lambda 'block: () -> Unit'. Nothing checks returns ... implies. And the block must come first: anything before it is contract should be the first statement. So write contracts the way the standard library does: tiny functions whose body is the condition itself, such as if (!condition) throw ..., so a reader can check the promise in one glance. Kotlin 2.2.20 added more Experimental forms (contracts on property accessors, returnsNotNull(), holdsIn). The last two need a second opt-in, ExperimentalExtendedContracts. Make a contract lie Run LyingContractDemo. Before you do, predict: compile error, a warning, or a run-time failure? Run LyingContractDemoJava, which tells the same lie in Java with a cast, then calls the Kotlin function. Run javap -c -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContractsDemoKt from labs/ and read isCaptured. Where is the contract? LyingContractDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo import kotlin.contracts.ExperimentalContracts import kotlin.contracts.contract /** A contract that lies. The compiler checks neither the promise nor the body. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun PaymentEvent.lyingIsCaptured(): Boolean { contract { returns(true) implies (this@lyingIsCaptured is Captured) } return true } fun main() { val failed: PaymentEvent = Failed("pay_8", "insufficient funds") try { if (failed.lyingIsCaptured()) println("captured ${failed.amountMinor}") } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message}") } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.LyingContractDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l05/demo/LyingContractDemo.kt LyingContractDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo; /** * Java twin of LyingContractDemo.kt. Java's version of the same lie is a helper that answers true * and a cast that trusts it. In both languages the cast is the line that fails at run time. */ public class LyingContractDemoJava { static boolean lyingIsCaptured(PaymentEvent e) { return true; } public static void main(String[] args) { PaymentEvent failed = new Failed("pay_8", "insufficient funds"); try { if (lyingIsCaptured(failed)) { Captured c = (Captured) failed; // Java makes you write the cast yourself System.out.println("captured " + c.getAmountMinor()); } } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("ClassCastException: " + e.getMessage()); } // the Kotlin function, seen from Java: just a boolean method, the contract is gone System.out.println("Kotlin lyingIsCaptured from Java: " + LyingContractDemoKt.lyingIsCaptured(failed)); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.LyingContractDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l05/demo/LyingContractDemoJava.java It compiles cleanly and fails at run time with ClassCastException: class workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.Failed cannot be cast to class workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.Captured. The Java twin fails the same way, then prints Kotlin lyingIsCaptured from Java: true: to Java it's a boolean method. In javap, isCaptured is a null check on the receiver, then instanceof and ireturn. The contract isn't in the bytecode at all. Payment validation code is full of checks that should narrow types: ensure(req.currency != null, "CURRENCY_MISSING") followed by code that uses the currency. A small contract-backed ensure gives you that without a !! on every line, and with a stable error code for the API response. Context parameters fit the values your Quarkus request handlers drag through every layer today: the transaction id, the merchant id for logs, an audit sink, a Clock your tests can freeze. A Temporal activity implementation could open one context(audit, TxContext(paymentId)) { ... } block and call ten helpers that never mention either. Keep injected services in constructors, where CDI puts them, and keep contracts tiny, because nobody checks them but you.

h: Contracts and context parameters · Context parameters: arguments the compiler passes for you
x: Some values have to reach almost every function in a request: a logger, the transaction id, a clock. Passed by hand, they turn every signature into plumbing: Java boolean authorize(Logger logger, TxId tx, Payment payment, String merchant) { ... } String checkout(Logger logger, TxId tx, Payment payment, String merchant) { boolean ok = authorize(logger, tx, payment, merchant); // pass both on, by hand audit(logger, "checkout " + tx.value()); return ok ? "APPROVED" : "DECLINED"; } Kotlin context(logger: Logger, tx: TxId) fun Payment.authorize(merchant: String): Boolean { logger.log("[${tx.value}] authorizing $amountMinor for $merchant") return amountMinor < 100_000 } context(logger: Logger, tx: TxId) fun checkout(payment: Payment, merchant: String): String { val approved = payment.authorize(merchant) // logger and tx flow on by themselves audit("checkout ${tx.value}") return if (approved) "APPROVED" else "DECLINED" } A context parameter is a parameter the caller doesn't write. You declare it in context(...) before fun, with a name and a type. At each call, the compiler finds a value of that type in the caller's surroundings and passes it: an enclosing function's own context parameter (as in checkout above), a context(console, TxId("tx-42")) { ... } block from the standard library, or an implicit receiver, such as the this of a with(console) { ... } block. The value it finds is called the context argument. Inside the function, you use the parameter by its name. If you don't need a name, write _ and read the value with contextOf<Logger>(). The docs describe them as dependencies that are "implicitly available in the surrounding context". On the JVM there is nothing implicit about them, as the figure shows. They become ordinary leading parameters: the context parameters first, then the extension receiver, then the value parameters. javap prints authorize(Logger, TxId, Payment, String), and Java calls it by passing all four. The status changed a lot in a short time. Context parameters were a preview in Kotlin 2.2.0 behind -Xcontext-parameters, and became Stable in 2.4.0, "except for context arguments and callable references". So in 2.4 you need no flag. The old flag now earns warning: the argument '-Xcontext-parameters' is redundant for the current language version 2.4., which tells you an older build file is still around. Follow a context through two calls Run ContextParamsDemo. Predict the six lines it prints for the two checkouts. Run ContextParamsDemoJava, which calls the same functions from Java with every argument spelled out. Run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContextParamsDemoKt and match each parameter to the figure. Uncomment the wrong move at the end of main (a call outside any context). Predict the error, then run. ContextParamsDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo interface Logger { fun log(msg: String) } class TxId(val value: String) data class Payment(val amountMinor: Long) /** Two context parameters, then an extension receiver, then an ordinary parameter. */ context(logger: Logger, tx: TxId) fun Payment.authorize(merchant: String): Boolean { logger.log("[${tx.value}] authorizing $amountMinor for $merchant") return amountMinor < 100_000 } /** Calls authorize and audit without passing the logger or the tx id: the context flows on. */ context(logger: Logger, tx: TxId) fun checkout(payment: Payment, merchant: String): String { val approved = payment.authorize(merchant) audit("checkout ${tx.value} ${if (approved) "approved" else "declined"}") return if (approved) "APPROVED" else "DECLINED" } /** An anonymous context parameter, read with contextOf. */ context(_: Logger) fun audit(event: String) = contextOf<Logger>().log("AUDIT $event") fun main() { val console = object : Logger { override fun log(msg: String) = println(msg) } context(console, TxId("tx-42")) { println(checkout(Payment(5_000), "coffee-shop")) println(checkout(Payment(250_000), "car-dealer")) } with(console) { audit("an implicit receiver works too") } // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict, run. // checkout(Payment(1), "kiosk") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContextParamsDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l05/demo/ContextParamsDemo.kt ContextParamsDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l05.demo; /** * Java twin of ContextParamsDemo.kt. Java has no context parameters. To Java they are ordinary * leading parameters: context parameters first, then the extension receiver, then the rest. */ public class ContextParamsDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Logger console = System.out::println; TxId tx = new TxId("tx-j"); // checkout(Logger, TxId, Payment, String) System.out.println(ContextParamsDemoKt.checkout(console, tx, new Payment(5_000), "coffee-shop")); // authorize(Logger, TxId, Payment receiver, String merchant) System.out.println(ContextParamsDemoKt.authorize(console, tx, new Payment(250_000), "car-dealer")); // audit(Logger, String) ContextParamsDemoKt.audit(console, "called from Java"); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l05.demo.ContextParamsDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l05/demo/ContextParamsDemoJava.java Each checkout prints [tx-42] authorizing ..., then AUDIT checkout tx-42 approved (or declined for 250,000), then APPROVED or DECLINED, and the last line is AUDIT an implicit receiver works too. javap lists authorize(Logger, TxId, Payment, String), checkout(Logger, TxId, Payment, String) and audit(Logger, String). The wrong move fails twice: no context argument for 'logger: Logger' found. and the same for tx: TxId. On the JVM, context parameters are plain leading parameters, followed by the extension receiver and then the ordinary parameters. h: Contracts and context parameters · Resolution rules, limits, and when to use them
x: The compiler resolves context arguments by type, so two values of the same type in the same scope are a problem. context(a, b) { use() } with two Loggers fails with multiple potential context arguments for 'l: Logger' in scope. The docs give the rule: if several compatible values exist at the same scope level, the compiler reports an ambiguity. A nearer scope still wins over an outer one: in context(a) { context(b) { note("x") } } the inner b is used. That's a reason to give context parameters specific types: a TxId class instead of a bare String, an AuditLog interface instead of (String) -> Unit. A few things are not allowed. Constructors can't have context parameters (context parameters on primary constructors are unsupported.). A property can have them only without a backing field, so it has to be a computed getter (property with context parameters cannot be initialized because it has no backing field.). And two parts are still not stable in 2.4: passing a context argument explicitly by name, behind -Xexplicit-context-arguments, and callable references such as ::checkout. Leave both alone in production code for now. One change in 2.3.20 can surprise you if you migrate older code. Overload resolution used to treat a declaration with context parameters as more specific than one without. The 2.3.20 notes say that rule no longer applies, so a pair of overloads that differed only by a context may become ambiguous. The JVM shape has two consequences. Java code can call these functions, as long as it passes every argument. And adding a context parameter to a public function changes its JVM signature, exactly like adding a parameter, so already-compiled callers break. Treat it as an API change. Where do they fit in a Quarkus service? Not for business dependencies: a PaymentRepository belongs in the constructor, where CDI injects it once. Context parameters suit values that belong to the current unit of work and are needed by many small functions: the transaction or trace id, an audit sink, a Clock for tests, the TxContext the lab uses. They are cheap, they are visible in every signature, and the compiler checks them, which a ThreadLocal or a static MDC never does. A check to finish: fun handle(req: AuthRequest) = with(AuditLog { println(it) }) { context(TxContext("tx-9")) { req.authorize(10_000) } }. Will it compile, and where does each context argument come from? (Answer: it compiles. The AuditLog comes from the implicit receiver of with, and the TxContext from the context(...) block. Each type has exactly one candidate.) Writing a contract that is almost true. A team adds returns(true) implies (this@isFinal is Settled) to isFinal(), which returns true for Settled and, after a later change, also for Cancelled. Every caller that wrote if (p.isFinal()) p.settledAt still compiles. It fails only at run time, with a ClassCastException, on the first cancelled payment: Java // Java makes the risky cast visible at every call site, where review can see it if (p.isFinal()) { Instant at = ((Settled) p).getSettledAt(); } Kotlin if (p.isFinal()) println(p.settledAt) // the cast is hidden in isFinal's contract The compiler trusts contracts unconditionally, so a change to the body never revisits the promise. Keep the body of a contract function identical to its promise (return this is Settled), and add a unit test that feeds each subtype through it.

h: Contracts and context parameters · Java and Kotlin
x: A validation helper with an audit trail: Java parameters vs Kotlin contracts and context parameters Authorize.java final class Authorize { static void ensure(boolean condition, String code, Supplier<String> message) { if (!condition) throw new PaymentRejected(code, message.get()); } static Decision authorize(AuditLog audit, TxContext tx, AuthRequest req, long limitMinor) { try { ensure(req.amountMinor() <= limitMinor, "OVER_LIMIT", () -> "over the limit"); ensure(req.currency() != null, "CURRENCY_MISSING", () -> "currency is required"); audit.record("[" + tx.txId() + "] approved " + req.currency().toUpperCase()); return Decision.APPROVED; } catch (PaymentRejected e) { audit.record("[" + tx.txId() + "] rejected " + e.code()); return Decision.rejected(e.code()); } } } Authorize.kt @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) inline fun ensure(condition: Boolean, code: String, lazyMessage: () -> String) { contract { returns() implies condition callsInPlace(lazyMessage, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE) } if (!condition) throw PaymentRejected(code, lazyMessage()) } context(audit: AuditLog, tx: TxContext) fun AuthRequest.authorize(limitMinor: Long): Decision = try { ensure(amountMinor <= limitMinor, "OVER_LIMIT") { "over the limit" } ensure(currency != null, "CURRENCY_MISSING") { "currency is required" } audit.record("[${tx.txId}] approved ${currency.uppercase()}") // smart cast Decision.Approved } catch (e: PaymentRejected) { audit.record("[${tx.txId}] rejected ${e.code}") Decision.Rejected(e.code) } The Java version compiles because Java doesn't track null, so req.currency().toUpperCase() is accepted whether or not the check ran. The Kotlin version compiles only because the contract tells the compiler that ensure returns only when its condition holds. Kotlin's ensure is inline, so the message lambda costs nothing on the happy path; Java builds a Supplier on every call. The audit log and transaction appear in Java's signature as two extra parameters that every caller passes on. In Kotlin they are context parameters, filled in by the compiler, and they still compile to exactly those two leading parameters, so Java can call the Kotlin authorize with authorize(audit, tx, req, limitMinor).

h: Contracts and context parameters · Worked example
x: Replace a ThreadLocal transaction id with a context parameter A service keeps the current transaction id in a ThreadLocal, so deep helpers can log it. It works until a helper runs on another thread, or a test forgets to set it, and then the log says tx=null. The compiler can't help, because nothing in the signature says the value is needed. final class Tx { static final ThreadLocal<String> CURRENT = new ThreadLocal<>(); } static void note(String line) { System.out.println("[" + Tx.CURRENT.get() + "] " + line); // null if nobody set it } object Tx { val current = ThreadLocal<String>() } fun note(line: String) { println("[${Tx.current.get()}] $line") // null if nobody set it } Make the need part of the signature. The helper declares a context parameter, and so does every function that calls it, until you reach the place that knows the transaction. class TxContext(val txId: String) // 1. the helper declares what it needs context(tx: TxContext) fun note(line: String) = println("[${tx.txId}] $line") // 2. callers in between declare it too, and never pass it by hand context(tx: TxContext) fun capture(paymentId: String) { note("capturing $paymentId") } // Java's honest equivalent: an explicit parameter on every function in the chain record TxContext(String txId) {} static void note(TxContext tx, String line) { System.out.println("[" + tx.txId() + "] " + line); } static void capture(TxContext tx, String paymentId) { note(tx, "capturing " + paymentId); } Open the context once, where the transaction starts: the Kafka listener or the REST resource. Forgetting it is now a compile error, no context argument for 'tx: TxContext' found., instead of a null in production logs. // 3. open the context where the transaction id is known fun onMessage(record: PaymentCommand) { context(TxContext(record.txId)) { capture(record.paymentId) } } // capture("pay_7") // error: no context argument for 'tx: TxContext' found. void onMessage(PaymentCommand record) { capture(new TxContext(record.txId()), record.paymentId()); } Check the price: each function in the chain gets one more JVM parameter, and nothing else. No ThreadLocal, no lookup, and the value follows the call, not the thread, so it survives a hop to another thread or a coroutine. Keep MDC for the logging library if it needs it, and fill it from the context at the edge.

h: Contracts and context parameters · From memory
x: Write ensureNotNull with a contract, from memory Close this page. Write ensureNotNull(value, code, lazyMessage) that returns the value as non-null, throws PaymentRejected when it's null, and gives callers a smart cast on the variable they passed. h: Contracts and context parameters · Quiz
x: What happens with this code? @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class) fun PaymentEvent.isCaptured(): Boolean { contract { returns(true) implies (this@isCaptured is Captured) } return this is Captured || this is Refunded } if (event.isCaptured()) println(event.amountMinor) A compile error: the body doesn't match the contract A compiler warning about an unsound contract It compiles; for a Refunded event the smart cast fails at run time with ClassCastException It compiles, and the smart cast is skipped when the contract is wrong The compiler trusts returns ... implies without checking it, so event.amountMinor compiles as if event were a Captured. At run time the JVM checks the cast it was given, and a Refunded is not a Captured. K2 warns only about some callsInPlace mistakes, never about implies. Which contract makes this compile? val total: Long withLedgerLock { total = ledger.sum() } println(total) callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE) in withLedgerLock callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.AT_MOST_ONCE) No contract: making withLedgerLock inline is enough returns() implies (block != null) A val must be assigned exactly once, and only EXACTLY_ONCE tells the compiler the assignment happens once, during the call. AT_MOST_ONCE allows zero runs, so total might be unassigned. Inline alone says nothing about how many times the body calls block: without the contract you get 'val' cannot be reassigned. How does Java call context(audit: AuditLog) fun note(line: String)? note(line), and the audit log comes from a ThreadLocal note(audit, line): the context parameter is the first JVM parameter note(line, audit) It can't: context parameters are Kotlin-only On the JVM, context parameters become ordinary parameters placed first, then the extension receiver, then the value parameters. Java has no context, so it passes the value itself. Inside context(primaryLog, backupLog) { note("x") }, both are AuditLog. What does the compiler do? Uses primaryLog, the first one listed Uses backupLog, the last one listed Passes both and lets note choose Reports multiple potential context arguments for 'audit: AuditLog' in scope. Context arguments are resolved by type. Two compatible values at the same scope level are an ambiguity, and the compiler refuses to guess. Give the two roles different types, or open the contexts in nested blocks so that one is nearer. From lesson 1: a test class was compiled against the stub of the public inline function ensure. You fix ensure and recompile only src/main. What does the old test class run when it calls ensure? Your new body, because it's on the classpath The stub's body, copied into the test class when the test was compiled Nothing: it fails with NoSuchMethodError Whichever version the class loader finds first An inline body is pasted into the caller at the caller's compile time, so the old test class holds its own copy of the stub. That's why the lab's tests call Callers.ensuring, an ordinary function compiled together with your code.

h: Contracts and context parameters · Key terms
x: Smart cast The compiler treating a variable as a narrower type after a check proves it, such as String? to String after != null. Contract A contract { } block that states a fact about a function's behavior for callers to rely on. The compiler trusts it. callsInPlace A contract effect: the lambda runs during the call (not stored), a given number of times. returns implies A contract effect: if the function returns (or returns a given value), a condition holds. Context parameter A parameter declared in context(...) that callers don't write; the compiler fills it by type from the surroundings. Context argument The value the compiler finds and passes for a context parameter at a call site. Opt-in @OptIn(...): your explicit agreement to use an Experimental API that may change. What is a Kotlin contract? A contract { } block, the first statement of a function, that tells the compiler something it can't infer: how a lambda is called, or what a normal return implies. What does returns() implies (x != null) give the caller? A smart cast: after the call returns normally, the compiler treats x as non-null. What does callsInPlace(block, EXACTLY_ONCE) allow in the caller? Initializing a val inside the lambda, because the compiler now knows the block runs exactly once during the call. Does the compiler verify a contract against the function body? No. It trusts it. A lying returns(true) implies (this is Captured) compiles and fails at run time with ClassCastException. What opt-in do contracts need in Kotlin 2.4? @OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class). They are still Experimental. No compiler flag is needed. Where can a context argument come from? From the caller's surroundings, matched by type: an enclosing function's context parameter, a context(a, b) { } block, or an implicit receiver such as with(x) { }. JVM signature of context(l: Logger, tx: TxId) fun Payment.authorize(m: String): Boolean? static boolean authorize(Logger, TxId, Payment, String): context parameters, then the receiver, then the value parameters.

h: Contracts and context parameters · Go deeper
x: Kotlin 2.4.0 added one more Experimental contract effect, returnsResultOf(), to help the new unused-return-value checker. It needs the flag -Xallow-returns-result-of, and the release notes warn that using it "produces pre-release binaries that earlier Kotlin compiler versions can't read". Keep it out of libraries that others consume. The extended contracts from Kotlin 2.2.20 behave in an interesting way on the 2.4.21 compiler. Their old -X flags (-Xallow-contracts-on-more-functions and friends) now print the argument '...' is redundant for the current language version 2.4., and a generic returns(true) implies (this is Ok<T>) or a holdsIn contract compiles without any flag. So they appear to be enabled by default from language version 2.3. They still need their opt-ins, though: returnsNotNull() without @OptIn(ExperimentalExtendedContracts::class) is an opt-in error. If you're migrating from context receivers, three differences bite. Context parameters must be named (or _), and a context parameter is not a receiver in the body, so log("x") becomes logger.log("x"). this@Logger is gone; use the name or contextOf<Logger>(). And classes can't declare a context any more, only functions and properties. Finally, a design note. The docs mention "simplified dependency injection" as a use. Treat that carefully in a CDI application. A context parameter is resolved at compile time, at each call site, from what is lexically in scope. CDI resolves beans at startup, from the whole application. They answer different questions: context parameters suit per-call values, and CDI suits long-lived services.

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Kotlin classes are final, and framework proxies need to subclass them
x: Quarkus, Spring and Hibernate add behavior to your classes with proxies: classes they generate that extend yours and override each method, to do something before and after calling super. A @Transactional method gets an overriding method that opens a transaction, calls yours and commits. Write such a subclass by hand and the problem shows at once: Java class AuditedSettlementService extends SettlementService { // error: cannot inherit from final SettlementService @Override public String settle(String batch) { return super.settle(batch); } } Kotlin class TimedSettlementService : SettlementService() { // error: this type is final, so it cannot be extended. override fun settle(batch: String): String = // error: 'settle' in 'SettlementService' is final super.settle(batch) // and cannot be overridden. } Kotlin classes and their members are final unless you write open. A framework that generates subclasses hits the same wall as your hand-written one, just later. You could write open on every bean and every method, and nobody keeps that up. A compiler plugin is a jar that the Kotlin compiler loads to change what it emits. The all-open plugin "makes classes and their members open at compile time without requiring the open keyword", for every class that carries an annotation you configure (or whose superclass does, or that uses a meta-annotation built on it). This lab module configures it for workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies. javap on the demo's SettlementService then shows public class and public java.lang.String settle(...), with no final. What it leaves alone is just as important: private members stay private, backing fields stay private final, and an unannotated PlainHelper stays public final class. kotlin-spring is all-open with a preset for Spring's annotations, such as @Component and @Transactional. Quarkus users need care. The quarkus preset inside the Kotlin 2.4.21 plugin lists only javax.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped and RequestScoped, but Quarkus 3 uses the jakarta namespace. In a test run, a jakarta-annotated bean compiled with that preset stayed public final class. Name the annotations yourself, as the Quarkus Kotlin guide does for jakarta.ws.rs.Path and jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped: // build.gradle.kts of a Quarkus 3 service plugins { kotlin("plugin.allopen") version "2.4.21" } allOpen { annotation("jakarta.ws.rs.Path") annotation("jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped") } Quarkus's CDI container can also transform many final classes at build time (quarkus.arc.transform-unproxyable-classes is true by default), but its Kotlin guide still configures all-open, and so should you. Open a class without writing open Run AllOpenDemo, then AllOpenDemoJava, which extends the same Kotlin class from Java. Run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.SettlementService from labs/. Which members are still final? Delete @OpenForProxies above SettlementService. Predict the errors, run, and put it back. AllOpenDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo import workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies import java.lang.reflect.Modifier /** Marked for all-open: the plugin makes the class and its members open at compile time. */ @OpenForProxies class SettlementService { val feeBps: Int = 125 fun settle(batch: String): String = "settled $batch at $feeBps bps" private fun secret(): Int = 42 // private stays private, and final } /** Not marked: final, like every Kotlin class by default. */ class PlainHelper { fun help(): String = "help" } /** What a framework generates at build or run time: a subclass that wraps every call. */ class TimedSettlementService : SettlementService() { override fun settle(batch: String): String { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return super.settle(batch) } finally { println(" settle took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } } fun describe(cls: Class<*>) { val methods = cls.declaredMethods.sortedBy { it.name }.joinToString { m -> val kind = when { Modifier.isPrivate(m.modifiers) -> "private" Modifier.isFinal(m.modifiers) -> "final" else -> "open" } "${m.name}:$kind" } println("${cls.simpleName}: ${if (Modifier.isFinal(cls.modifiers)) "final" else "open"} class; $methods") } fun main() { describe(SettlementService::class.java) describe(PlainHelper::class.java) val service: SettlementService = TimedSettlementService() println(service.settle("batch-17")) // Wrong move. Delete @OpenForProxies above SettlementService, predict, run. } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.AllOpenDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l06/demo/AllOpenDemo.kt AllOpenDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo; /** * Java twin of AllOpenDemo.kt. Java classes are open unless you write final, so Java can extend the * Kotlin class only because all-open removed its final. Remove the marker and javac says: * "cannot inherit from final SettlementService". */ public class AllOpenDemoJava { static final class AuditedSettlementService extends SettlementService { @Override public String settle(String batch) { System.out.println(" audit: settling " + batch); return super.settle(batch); } } public static void main(String[] args) { SettlementService service = new AuditedSettlementService(); System.out.println(service.settle("batch-17")); AllOpenDemoKt.describe(PlainHelper.class); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.AllOpenDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l06/demo/AllOpenDemoJava.java The demo prints SettlementService: open class; getFeeBps:open, secret:private, settle:open, PlainHelper: final class; help:final, a timing line and settled batch-17 at 125 bps. javap shows public class SettlementService, private final int feeBps and private int secret(): only the field keeps its final. Without the marker, the build fails with this type is final, so it cannot be extended. and 'settle' in 'SettlementService' is final and cannot be overridden., and the Java twin would get cannot inherit from final SettlementService. Each plugin reads an annotation at compile time and changes the class file: modifiers, a new constructor, or a whole new class. All-open compiler plugin (Kotlin docs) docs Quarkus guide: using Kotlin (all-open configuration) docs Compiler plugins are the print shop's finishing step. Your manuscript says "open for proxies" or "needs a blank form" in the margin, and the finisher acts on the note: it trims the final off, binds in an extra blank page (the no-arg constructor), or prints a matching order form for each document (the serializer). The reader of the finished book, the JVM, only sees the result. The analogy breaks with the blank page: a real finisher wouldn't hand you a form with required fields left empty, but no-arg does exactly that, which is why the initializer trap exists.

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · no-arg gives frameworks an empty constructor, and skips your initializers
x: Hibernate builds an entity the same way every time: call a constructor with no parameters, then set the fields from the row. Its documentation says an entity must "be a non-final class, with a non-private constructor with no parameters". A Kotlin class like LedgerRow(val id: String, var amountMinor: Long) has no such constructor. By hand, you'd add one: Java @Entity public class LedgerRow { @Id private String id; private long amountMinor; private String note = "default-note"; protected LedgerRow() { } // for Hibernate public LedgerRow(String id, long amountMinor) { this.id = id; this.amountMinor = amountMinor; } } Kotlin class LedgerRow(val id: String, var amountMinor: Long) { var note: String = "default-note" constructor() : this("", 0) // the hand-written version: invented defaults } The hand-written Kotlin constructor works, but it invents an empty id that any Kotlin caller can now create by mistake. The no-arg plugin generates the constructor for classes with an annotation you configure, and the docs say it's "annotated with @Deprecated at the HIDDEN level, so you can call it from Java but not from Kotlin". The demo shows both sides: Kotlin's LedgerRow() fails with no value passed for parameter 'id'., and Java's new LedgerRow() compiles, with only a deprecation note from javac. Now the trap. The generated constructor doesn't run property initializers. The option that would run them, invokeInitializers, is "disabled by default". So after new LedgerRow(), note holds null, even though Kotlin declared it a non-null String, and the first note.length in Kotlin code throws a NullPointerException. For a JPA entity that's usually fine, because Hibernate sets every mapped column right afterwards. For anything else, turn invokeInitializers on or give the property no initializer. For JPA, use kotlin-jpa rather than configuring no-arg yourself: it's no-arg with a preset for @Entity, @Embeddable and @MappedSuperclass, in both the javax.persistence and jakarta.persistence packages. Since Kotlin 2.3.20, the Gradle org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.jpa plugin also applies all-open with the JPA preset, so that, in the release notes' words, "lazy associations work as expected instead of causing eager loading". On older Kotlin versions you had to add all-open for entities yourself. Build an entity the way an ORM does Run NoArgDemo, then NoArgDemoJava. Predict blank.note before you look. Uncomment the wrong move in NoArgDemo.kt, predict, run, and comment it out again. In NoArgDemo.kt, add println(blank.note.length) at the end of main. Predict what happens, then run. NoArgDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo import workbench.kotlin.NoArgEntity /** no-arg adds a zero-argument constructor that only Java and reflection can call. */ @NoArgEntity class LedgerRow(val id: String, var amountMinor: Long) { var note: String = "default-note" } fun main() { // the way an ORM builds an empty entity before it fills in the columns val blank = LedgerRow::class.java.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() println("blank.amountMinor = ${blank.amountMinor}") println("blank.note is null: ${(blank.note as String?) == null}") // declared String, holds null println("normal note = ${LedgerRow("row-1", 100).note}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict, run. // val direct = LedgerRow() } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.NoArgDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l06/demo/NoArgDemo.kt NoArgDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo; /** * Java twin of NoArgDemo.kt. Java can call the generated constructor directly: it is hidden from * Kotlin with @Deprecated(level = HIDDEN), which javac doesn't enforce. */ public class NoArgDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { LedgerRow blank = new LedgerRow(); // compiles in Java System.out.println("blank.amountMinor = " + blank.getAmountMinor()); System.out.println("blank.note = " + blank.getNote()); // null: the initializer never ran System.out.println("blank.getId() = " + blank.getId()); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.NoArgDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l06/demo/NoArgDemoJava.java Both show amountMinor = 0 and a null note, and the Java twin also prints getId() = null: the generated constructor sets nothing and runs no initializer. The Kotlin call LedgerRow() fails with no value passed for parameter 'id'. and the same for amountMinor. The added line compiles, because note is declared String, and throws NullPointerException at run time. No-arg compiler plugin (Kotlin docs) docs Kotlin-jpa plugin (Kotlin docs) docs A Quarkus 3 payment service in Kotlin needs all three. All-open, configured with the jakarta annotations by name (jakarta.ws.rs.Path, jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped), so ArC and RESTEasy can subclass your beans and resources; don't trust a preset that knows only javax. kotlin-jpa for Hibernate entities, which on Kotlin 2.3.20 and later also opens them for lazy-loading proxies. And kotlinx.serialization for the PaymentEvent messages on your Kafka topics, with a @SerialName on every subtype so a package rename can't break consumers, and ignoreUnknownKeys = true so a producer can add a field without taking down every consumer.

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · kotlinx.serialization writes the serializer at compile time
x: Most JSON libraries on the JVM work by reflection: at run time they look at a class, find its constructor and properties, and guess how to fill them. Kotlin classes make that guessing harder, with default arguments and non-null types. kotlinx.serialization doesn't guess. "When you annotate a class with @Serializable, the Kotlin serialization plugin generates a KSerializer for that class." The demo's Posted gets a nested class, Posted$$serializer, that implements GeneratedSerializer<Posted> with real serialize and deserialize methods, plus Posted.serializer() on the companion object. Without the plugin, Posted.serializer() is unresolved reference 'serializer'. Java // Java's usual approach, with Jackson: annotations read by reflection at run time @JsonTypeInfo(use = JsonTypeInfo.Id.NAME, property = "type") @JsonSubTypes({ @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = Posted.class, name = "posted"), @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = Reversed.class, name = "reversed") }) public sealed interface LedgerEvent permits Posted, Reversed { String paymentId(); } String json = new ObjectMapper().writeValueAsString(events); Kotlin @Serializable sealed interface LedgerEvent { val paymentId: String } @Serializable @SerialName("posted") data class Posted(override val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String = "EUR") : LedgerEvent @Serializable @SerialName("reversed") data class Reversed(override val paymentId: String, val reason: String? = null) : LedgerEvent private val json = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } val text = json.encodeToString(events) // events: List<LedgerEvent> A sealed hierarchy is "closed polymorphism": the plugin knows every subclass at compile time, so it can write and read a "type" field, the class discriminator that tells a decoder which subclass an object is, with no registration. Three details decide what the JSON looks like. The discriminator is written only when the static type is the base: List<LedgerEvent> gets "type":"posted", and Json.encodeToString(p) with p typed Posted gets none. Its value is the fully qualified class name unless you set @SerialName, so without it a package rename changes your wire format. And the default Json leaves out properties that equal their default (encodeDefaults is off), writes nulls, and rejects unknown keys: Encountered an unknown key 'acquirer'. For events that cross a Kafka topic, that last default matters most. A consumer with the default Json breaks the day a producer adds a field, so set ignoreUnknownKeys = true. Build one Json instance and reuse it: the docs say instances "are immutable and thread-safe", and that reusing them improves performance. The JSON format is Stable; HOCON, ProtoBuf, CBOR and Properties are still Experimental. Read the JSON a sealed hierarchy produces Run SerializationDemo. Before you do, predict which lines will contain "type". Remove @SerialName("posted") from Posted and run again. What is the type value now? Run SerializationDemoJava, which uses the generated serializer from Java through Posted.Companion.serializer(). SerializationDemo.kt package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo import kotlinx.serialization.SerialName import kotlinx.serialization.SerializationException import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable import kotlinx.serialization.json.Json @Serializable sealed interface LedgerEvent { val paymentId: String } @Serializable @SerialName("posted") data class Posted(override val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String = "EUR") : LedgerEvent @Serializable @SerialName("reversed") data class Reversed(override val paymentId: String, val reason: String? = null) : LedgerEvent private val lenient = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } fun main() { val events: List<LedgerEvent> = listOf(Posted("pay_1", 1_999), Reversed("pay_1")) val text = lenient.encodeToString(events) println(text) println("round trip equal: ${lenient.decodeFromString<List<LedgerEvent>>(text) == events}") val p = Posted("pay_2", 1) println("static type Posted: ${Json.encodeToString(p)}") println("static type LedgerEvent: ${Json.encodeToString<LedgerEvent>(p)}") val newer = """{"type":"posted","paymentId":"pay_3","amountMinor":5,"acquirer":"acq-a"}""" println("lenient: ${lenient.decodeFromString<LedgerEvent>(newer)}") try { Json.decodeFromString<LedgerEvent>(newer) } catch (e: SerializationException) { println("default Json: ${e.message?.lineSequence()?.first()}") } println("generated serializer: ${Posted.serializer().javaClass.name}") } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.SerializationDemoKt labs/kotlin/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/kotlin/l06/demo/SerializationDemo.kt SerializationDemoJava.java package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo; import kotlinx.serialization.json.Json; /** * Java twin of SerializationDemo.kt. The plugin's output is ordinary bytecode, so Java can use it: * Posted.Companion.serializer() returns the generated KSerializer, and Json.Default does the rest. * Java code normally uses Jackson instead; this shows what the plugin generated. */ public class SerializationDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Posted p = new Posted("pay_2", 1L, "EUR"); String text = Json.Default.encodeToString(Posted.Companion.serializer(), p); System.out.println("Java, static type Posted: " + text); Posted back = Json.Default.decodeFromString(Posted.Companion.serializer(), text); System.out.println("decoded: " + back + ", equal: " + back.equals(p)); System.out.println("generated serializer: " + Posted.Companion.serializer().getClass().getName()); } } ./gradlew :kotlin:demo -Pmain=workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.SerializationDemoJava labs/kotlin/src/demo/java/workbench/kotlin/l06/demo/SerializationDemoJava.java The list prints [{"type":"posted","paymentId":"pay_1","amountMinor":1999},{"type":"reversed","paymentId":"pay_1"}]: no currency (it equals its default) and no reason (null, with explicitNulls = false). The static-type Posted line has no type; the LedgerEvent line has one. The lenient instance ignores acquirer, and the default one fails with Encountered an unknown key 'acquirer'. Without @SerialName the type becomes workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.Posted. The Java twin prints the same JSON and the class name Posted$$serializer. Serialize polymorphic classes (Kotlin docs) docs Customize the Json instance (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · KSP and kapt generate new source files instead
x: The three plugins above change the compiler's output from the inside. A second family of tools generates new source files from your annotations, the way Java annotation processors do: dependency injection (Dagger), database access (Room), mappers (MapStruct). kapt runs Java annotation processors on Kotlin code. The docs say it "generates stub files from Kotlin source code and then runs the Java annotation processors on those stubs". Those stubs are Java declarations of your Kotlin classes, written only so a Java processor can read them, and the migration guide calls them "expensive": they "significantly increase build time" and lose Kotlin-specific features. KSP is the Kotlin-native alternative, "a source code generation framework for Kotlin". Its processors read Kotlin declarations directly, and its README says they "can run up to 2x faster" than kapt. The limits are part of the design: KSP processors "can't examine expressions or statements, and they can't modify the source code". They only add new files. Two version facts matter in 2026. KSP2 "is no longer a compiler plugin" and is built on the same compiler APIs as IntelliJ IDEA. And since KSP 2.3.0, KSP1 is deprecated and "KSP version is no longer tied to the Kotlin compiler version", so a KSP release number no longer has to match your Kotlin version. My rule: use KSP whenever the library ships a KSP processor, and kapt only for processors that exist just for Java. Keep an eye on build time when you add kapt: every kapt module pays for the stub step on each build. A check to end on, and the answer follows from how the serialization plugin works: a module depends on the kotlinx-serialization-json library but doesn't apply kotlin("plugin.serialization"). You mark a class @Serializable and call Captured.serializer(). What happens, and at which stage? (It fails at compile time with unresolved reference 'serializer'.: the annotation compiles because it's in the library, but nobody generates the companion function.) Relying on a preset that doesn't match your annotations, and finding out from a proxy error at startup or, worse, from interceptors that silently don't run. With Kotlin 2.4.21 the all-open plugin's quarkus preset knows only javax.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped and RequestScoped, while Quarkus 3 code uses jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped: Java // in Java the question doesn't exist: classes are open unless you write final @ApplicationScoped public class FeeService { public long feeMinor(long amountMinor) { return amountMinor * 125 / 10_000; } } Kotlin @ApplicationScoped // jakarta.enterprise.context: not in the 2.4.21 quarkus preset class FeeService { // javap: public final class FeeService fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long): Long = amountMinor * 125 / 10_000 } The fix is to list the annotations you use, with their full jakarta names, in allOpen { annotation(...) }, and to check one bean with javap after any build change.

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Java and Kotlin
x: A proxy-ready service and entity: Java as written vs Kotlin with plugins Beans.java @ApplicationScoped public class FeeService { // open by default in Java public long feeMinor(long amountMinor) { return amountMinor * 125 / 10_000; } } @Entity public class PaymentEntity { // open by default @Id private String id; private long amountMinor; private String note = "default-note"; // runs in every constructor protected PaymentEntity() { } // the no-arg constructor, written by hand public PaymentEntity(String id, long amountMinor) { this.id = id; this.amountMinor = amountMinor; } } Beans.kt @ApplicationScoped // all-open configured for this annotation class FeeService { fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long): Long = amountMinor * 125 / 10_000 } @Entity // kotlin-jpa: no-arg + all-open for entities class PaymentEntity(@Id val id: String, var amountMinor: Long) { var note: String = "default-note" // skipped by the generated no-arg constructor } Java gets proxy-ready classes for free: classes and methods are open unless marked final, and you write the no-arg constructor yourself, where field initializers run as usual. Kotlin's defaults point the other way, so the plugins put back what frameworks need, at compile time, driven by annotations. The class files end up close to the Java ones, with one difference that bites: Kotlin's generated no-arg constructor skips property initializers unless you enable invokeInitializers, so note is null on a fresh instance, while Java's hand-written constructor runs note = "default-note".

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Worked example
x: Version a Kafka event without breaking consumers Version 1 of a payment event goes onto a topic. The consumer uses the default Json. Here are both sides, with the Java consumer using Jackson. // Java consumer with Jackson: by default it also fails on unknown properties ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper(); Captured c = mapper.readValue(record.value(), Captured.class); @Serializable @SerialName("captured") data class Captured(override val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long) : PaymentEvent val event = Json.decodeFromString<PaymentEvent>(record.value()) // the default Json: strict The producer team adds acquirer and deploys first. Every consumer with the default settings now fails on every message, because unknown keys "result in an error" by default. // producer v2 writes {"type":"captured","paymentId":"pay_7","amountMinor":1999,"acquirer":"acq-a"} Json.decodeFromString<PaymentEvent>(v2) // SerializationException: ... Encountered an unknown key 'acquirer' at path: $ mapper.readValue(v2, Captured.class); // Jackson: UnrecognizedPropertyException, unless FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES is turned off Configure the consumer once, in one shared instance: tolerate new keys, keep @SerialName stable, and add new fields with defaults so old messages still decode. // 1. one instance, reused: immutable and thread-safe val events = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } // 2. a new field gets a default, so v1 messages without it still decode @Serializable @SerialName("captured") data class Captured(override val paymentId: String, val amountMinor: Long, val acquirer: String? = null) : PaymentEvent ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper() .configure(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, false); Check the other direction. A v1 consumer that doesn't know a new subtype, say "type":"chargeback", still fails, and it should: ignoreUnknownKeys covers fields, not types. Deploy consumers before producers when you add a subtype.

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Quiz
x: A Quarkus 3 bean is annotated @jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped, and the build relies on the all-open plugin's built-in quarkus preset (Kotlin 2.4.21). What does javap show for the class? public class, with open methods public final class: the preset lists only the javax annotations A compile error: the preset rejects jakarta annotations public class, but every method is still final The preset in the 2.4.21 plugin names javax.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped and RequestScoped only. A jakarta-annotated class matches nothing, so the plugin leaves it alone. Configure annotation("jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped") explicitly. An entity built with the default no-arg plugin settings has var status: String = "NEW". What does status hold right after Hibernate calls the generated constructor, before it sets any column? "NEW" "" null, even though the type is String Nothing: the constructor throws because status isn't set The generated constructor doesn't run property initializers unless invokeInitializers is enabled, and it is off by default. Hibernate normally overwrites the field from the row; any other code that reads it first sees null in a non-null property. Captured is a @Serializable @SerialName("captured") subclass of a sealed PaymentEvent, and c is typed Captured. What does Json.encodeToString(c) produce? {"paymentId":"p","amountMinor":1}: no discriminator, because the static type isn't the base {"type":"captured","paymentId":"p","amountMinor":1} The fully qualified class name in a "type" field A SerializationException: sealed subtypes must be encoded as the base The docs say the type discriminator is included only when you use the base class as the static type. Encode c as a PaymentEvent (or inside a List<PaymentEvent>) to get "type":"captured". The fully qualified name appears only when there is no @SerialName. Your service needs generated mappers from an annotation processor that exists only for Java. Which tool runs it on Kotlin classes? KSP all-open kotlinx.serialization kapt kapt generates Java stubs from your Kotlin sources and runs Java annotation processors on them. KSP runs KSP processors, which a Java-only processor isn't. all-open and kotlinx.serialization change the compiler's output and don't run processors at all. From the patterns track: a framework proxy wraps FeeService, and inside FeeService, charge() calls this.audit(), where audit has an interceptor. With a Spring-style proxy that forwards to a separate target object, does the interceptor run for that inner call? Yes, because all-open made audit open No: this is the target, so the call never goes through the proxy Only if audit is private Only when the class is written in Java all-open makes the proxy possible; it doesn't route calls through it. A forwarding proxy calls the target, and inside the target this.audit() is a plain call on the target. That's the self-invocation trap from the Decorator and Proxy lesson, and it's the same in Java and Kotlin.
