h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Key terms
x: Compiler plugin A jar the Kotlin compiler loads to change what it emits, usually driven by annotations. Proxy A class a framework generates that extends yours and overrides methods to add behavior such as transactions. all-open Compiler plugin that makes annotated classes and their members open, without writing open. no-arg Compiler plugin that adds a zero-argument constructor, hidden from Kotlin, for frameworks that need one. kotlin-jpa no-arg with a preset for JPA annotations; since Kotlin 2.3.20 its Gradle plugin also applies all-open for them. Class discriminator The "type" field that tells a decoder which subclass a JSON object is. KSP Kotlin Symbol Processing: a framework for processors that read Kotlin declarations and generate new source files. kapt Runs Java annotation processors on Kotlin code by first generating Java stubs of the Kotlin classes. Why does a Kotlin bean need all-open (or open) for CDI or Spring proxies? Kotlin classes and members are final by default, and those proxies are generated subclasses that override your methods. What does all-open leave unchanged? Private members, backing fields (still final), and every class without a configured annotation. Quarkus 3 and the built-in quarkus all-open preset in Kotlin 2.4.21: what goes wrong? The preset lists only javax.enterprise.context annotations, so jakarta-annotated beans stay final. Name the jakarta annotations in allOpen { }. What does no-arg generate, and who can call it? A zero-argument constructor marked @Deprecated(level = HIDDEN): Java and reflection can call it, Kotlin code can't. Does no-arg's constructor run property initializers? Not by default (invokeInitializers is off), so a non-null property can hold null on a fresh instance. When does kotlinx.serialization write the "type" discriminator? Only when the static type is the polymorphic base, such as List<PaymentEvent>. Its value is the @SerialName, or else the fully qualified class name. KSP vs kapt in one line each? kapt runs Java annotation processors on generated Java stubs (slow builds). KSP processors read Kotlin symbols directly, up to 2x faster, and can only add files.

h: Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization · Go deeper
x: The presets inside the 2.4.21 all-open plugin, read from the plugin's own classes, say more than the docs page. spring lists @Component, @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, @SpringBootTest and also org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated, which the docs page leaves out. micronaut lists four AOP annotations, jpa lists Entity, Embeddable and MappedSuperclass in both namespaces, and quarkus lists only the two javax scopes. When a framework moves packages, presets lag behind, and listing annotations by name is the only setting you control. On the command line the same plugins take -P options, which helps when you test a hypothesis with plain kotlinc: -Xplugin=<allopen jar> -P plugin:org.jetbrains.kotlin.allopen:annotation=com.example.OpenForProxies, and for no-arg -P plugin:org.jetbrains.kotlin.noarg:invokeInitializers=true. Maven users add <plugin>all-open</plugin> to the Kotlin Maven plugin with the kotlin-maven-allopen dependency. Since Kotlin 2.3.20, kotlin-maven-noarg also includes kotlin-maven-allopen. kotlinx.serialization has more for event streams. Open polymorphism, where subclasses live in other modules, needs a SerializersModule that registers each one. classDiscriminator renames the "type" field if your schema already uses that name. coerceInputValues turns invalid values, such as an unknown enum constant, into the property's default instead of failing. And @JsonIgnoreUnknownKeys (Experimental) relaxes unknown keys for one class instead of the whole Json instance. Finally, the generated code is plain JVM bytecode, so it's fast and free of run-time reflection, which also makes it a good fit for GraalVM native images. The startup track covers why reflection is the hard part there.

h: Capstone: a typed event library
x: A sealed event model, a typed event bus and an API that reads well from Kotlin and from Java. By the end of this track you'll have built one working library: a typed, in-process event library for a payments service. It has a sealed model of payment events with value-class ids and amounts, and one parser at the edge that turns raw Kafka fields into that model or rejects them. It has an event bus that routes each event to the handlers of its class and of every supertype, accepts one general handler for any subscription, survives a failing handler, and runs middleware and timing decorators. And it has an API that reads well from both sides: a subscription DSL for Kotlin, and overloads, statics and a facade for Java, checked by a Java test. It draws on the whole of Part 3. The model comes from Modern Java data modeling (sealed types, pattern switches, parsing at the edge) and from the value classes of Advanced Kotlin. The bus is variance, reified type parameters and KClass from Kotlin generics, properly, put together with Observer, Chain of Responsibility and Decorator from Design patterns in Java and Kotlin. The API leans on inline functions and type-safe DSLs from Advanced Kotlin. Each lesson names the earlier lesson it relies on, so you can go back when a step doesn't stick. The labs live in labs/events, one package per lesson (workbench.events.l01 to l03). Each lab starts from the previous lab's solution, so you can begin at any lesson. Lessons 1 and 2 are written in Kotlin; lesson 3 adds a Java class, RefundDesk, and a Java test that uses the library the way a Java team would. Run ./gradlew :events:test --tests 'workbench.events.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and ./gradlew :events:solutionTest to check the reference answers. The tests use kotlin-reflect for two checks (sealedSubclasses and the variance of Handler); the library itself doesn't need it. Parse raw input once, at the edge, into a sealed model; return Ok or Rejected and never throw. Behind the edge, handlers trust the types. A when with no else over your own sealed type turns a new event type into a list of compile errors. A sealed middle level lets one branch, or one handler, stand for its leaves. Value classes make ids and amounts their own types at no cost where used as themselves; their init blocks make every instance valid. One field only, so Money is euro cents until it needs a currency. Route each event to its class and then its event supertypes, nearest first, from a per-class cache. Declare handlers in, store them behind casting adapters. Observer rules hold: return a handle, isolate each handler's exception and report it, iterate a copy-on-write snapshot. Delivery stays synchronous, so keep handlers fast. Concerns for every event once are a middleware chain built by a fold, where order is behavior. Concerns for one handler are decorators. Test time with a fake ticker. The subscription DSL collects and commits, uses reified on<E> with crossinline, and @DslMarker so nested blocks can't reach the wrong builder. Give Java Class<E> overloads, @JvmOverloads, @JvmStatic, @JvmField, @file:JvmName and a facade that builds the value classes, and test it from Java. In the design review, defend forced choices by their mechanism and write down the judgment calls with the condition that would undo them.

h: Capstone: a typed event library: cheat sheet
x: The model (lesson 1) [ ] Every event is a past-tense fact in one sealed hierarchy: PaymentEvent, with a sealed MoneyMovement in the middle for captures and refunds. [ ] Leaves are data classes (records in Java): final, compared by value, validated in init. [ ] Ids and amounts are value classes with init checks: PaymentId, Money (euro cents). Keep toString(): String explicit. [ ] Every operation is a when / switch with no else over your own sealed type. [ ] One edge function, parseEvent(fields): Parsed, returns Ok or Rejected and never throws. Rules live in the constructors; the parser turns their IllegalArgumentException into Rejected. [ ] Rejected goes to a dead-letter topic with its reason. Never retry it. Java sealed interface PaymentEvent permits PaymentAuthorized, PaymentDeclined, MoneyMovement { PaymentId paymentId(); } sealed interface MoneyMovement extends PaymentEvent permits PaymentCaptured, PaymentRefunded { Money amount(); } record PaymentCaptured(PaymentId paymentId, Money amount) implements MoneyMovement {} Kotlin sealed interface PaymentEvent { val paymentId: PaymentId } sealed interface MoneyMovement : PaymentEvent { val amount: Money } data class PaymentCaptured(override val paymentId: PaymentId, override val amount: Money) : MoneyMovement The bus (lesson 2) [ ] Registry keyed by KClass; dispatch keys = the event's class, then its event supertypes, nearest first, cached per class with computeIfAbsent. Java reflection (getInterfaces, getSuperclass) is enough: no kotlin-reflect. [ ] Delivery order is a promise: most specific key first, then wider ones; within a key, subscription order. Test it. [ ] fun interface Handler<in E : PaymentEvent>: a consumer, so in. Java sees Handler<? super E>. [ ] Store each handler behind an adapter Handler<PaymentEvent> { e -> handler.handle(type.cast(e)) }. [ ] subscribe returns a Subscription : AutoCloseable that removes exactly that adapter. Closing twice is harmless. [ ] catch (e: Exception) around each handler, reported to an injected ErrorHandler with the event. [ ] Each key's handlers in a CopyOnWriteArrayList: delivery iterates a snapshot, a handler may unsubscribe itself, publishers need no lock. [ ] Middleware (every event once: logging, dedupe) is a chain built once by foldRight over a copy of the list. Order is behavior. [ ] Per-handler concerns (timing) are decorators: same Handler<E>, record in finally, clock injected as a Ticker. Java <E extends PaymentEvent> AutoCloseable subscribe(Class<E> type, Handler<? super E> handler) { Handler<PaymentEvent> adapter = event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)); List<Handler<PaymentEvent>> list = registry.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()); list.add(adapter); return () -> list.remove(adapter); } Kotlin fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { val adapter = Handler<PaymentEvent> { event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)) } val list = registry.computeIfAbsent(type) { CopyOnWriteArrayList() } list += adapter return Subscription { list.remove(adapter) } } The API (lesson 3) [ ] The DSL collects in on and subscribes in commit, after the block: a block that throws subscribes nothing; one handle closes all, in reverse. [ ] inline fun <reified E> on(crossinline handler: (E) -> Unit): crossinline because the lambda runs inside a Handler object. [ ] @DslMarker on the builder classes; a check(!committed) for calls from inside handlers, which the marker can't see. [ ] Every reified or KClass function has a Class<E> overload that delegates with type.kotlin. [ ] @JvmOverloads on constructors with defaults, @JvmStatic on object members, @JvmField on companion constants, @file:JvmName on files of top-level functions. [ ] A facade (Events.captured(String, long)) that builds the value classes, so Java input is validated. Never @JvmName straight past init. [ ] Callbacks are fun interfaces with void/int methods, and the Java DSL entry takes a Consumer: no return Unit.INSTANCE. [ ] One Java test in the Kotlin module's build. Kotlin as written What Java gets Fix reified function invisible (synthetic) Class<E> overload KClass<E> parameter JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(X.class) Class<E> overload default arguments all-defaults and full constructors only @JvmOverloads object member, companion val INSTANCE.f(), Companion.getX() @JvmStatic, @JvmField value classes in a data class private constructor, mangled getters facade with plain types Design review questions Question Forced, or a judgment call? No else on sealed whens? forced: Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check Handler<in E>? forced: Contravariance with in: consumers Class<E> overloads? forced: Type erasure and reified type parameters Value classes plus a Java facade? judgment: undo if most callers are Java Money without currency? judgment: undo when a second currency arrives Synchronous, in-memory delivery? judgment: keep inside one service; durable events go through an outbox Unbounded DropDuplicates? judgment: undo; bound it or use a unique key in the handler's store

h: Capstone: a typed event library: track quiz
x: A capture arrives as raw fields with amountMinor = "0". Where is it refused, and what does the consumer see? In the ledger handler, which throws, and the consumer retries the record In PaymentCaptured's init; parseEvent returns Rejected with that message In parseEvent, by its own amount > 0 check, which returns null Nowhere: a zero capture is valid The rule lives in the constructor, once. The edge calls the constructor and turns its IllegalArgumentException into a Rejected, which the consumer sends to the dead-letter topic before any handler acts. summary, movesMoney and the metrics tag are whens over PaymentEvent with no else. Someone adds PaymentDisputed : PaymentEvent. What finds every place that must change? A run-time NoWhenBranchMatchedException in production A code search for PaymentCaptured The compiler: each of those whens fails until it handles disputes Nothing: when falls through to the last branch Exhaustiveness is checked at compile time, and with no else the new subtype is missing from each when. An else anywhere would swallow it silently. The run-time exception only happens when code compiled against the old model meets the new type. Why is Money a value class of euro cents with no currency field? Because a JVM value class can hold exactly one field, and this service settles in euros only Because value classes can't hold a Currency object Because Java callers can't read two fields Because data classes can't validate in init Until Valhalla, Kotlin's @JvmInline value class has one property. Amount plus currency would be a data class, one object per amount. The design review marks this as a judgment call to undo when a second currency arrives. Subscribed in this order: audit under PaymentEvent, movements under MoneyMovement, ledger then receipts under PaymentCaptured. You publish a capture. In what order do they run? audit, movements, ledger, receipts ledger, receipts, movements, audit receipts, ledger, movements, audit ledger, movements, audit, receipts Keys are visited nearest first: PaymentCaptured, then MoneyMovement, then PaymentEvent. Within one key, handlers run in subscription order, so ledger comes before receipts. In a Java class, Handler<PaymentEvent> audit = e -> ...; and then bus.subscribe(PaymentCaptured.class, audit); compiles. Why? Because Java generics are covariant Because subscribe casts its argument Because PaymentCaptured.class is a Class<PaymentEvent> Because Handler is declared in, so kotlinc writes Handler<? super E> into the Java signature Declaration-site in becomes a ? super wildcard in parameter types. A handler of any event can then stand in for a handler of captures, in Java as in Kotlin. Java generics are invariant without a wildcard. Of three handlers for a capture, the second throws IllegalStateException. What does publish return, and what happens to the error? 3; the bus reports it, with the event, to its ErrorHandler, and the third handler still runs 1; publish stops at the failure and rethrows 2; the failing handler isn't counted and the error is dropped It throws, after running all three Each call is wrapped in its own try, so one failure can't starve the rest, and publish counts the handlers it called. The bus doesn't decide what an error means: the injected ErrorHandler does. You want to know how long the receipts handler takes per event. Where does the timing go? A middleware, first in the list Inside publish, around deliver A decorator around the receipts handler: the same Handler<E>, timed in finally In the ErrorHandler Middleware and publish see one delivery to all of an event's handlers, so they'd add the ledger's time to the receipts' time. A decorator wraps exactly one handler, and with an injected Ticker its numbers are testable. A bus.subscriptions { ... } block declares two handlers and then throws because a config value is missing. How many handlers are subscribed afterwards? Two, and the caller has no handle to remove them One Two, removed again by a finally in the block None: the builder only subscribes after the block returns on only records a pending subscription, and commit runs after the block. So a failing block leaves the bus untouched, and a successful one returns a single handle for everything it declared. Java code needs a refund event for 5.00 on pay_7781. Which line compiles and validates? new PaymentRefunded(new PaymentId("pay_7781"), new Money(500)) Events.refunded("pay_7781", 500) new PaymentRefunded("pay_7781", 500L) PaymentRefunded.Companion.of("pay_7781", 500) The value classes' constructors and the data class constructor are private to Java (javac reports has private access or cannot find symbol). The @JvmStatic facade takes plain values and builds the value classes, so their init checks run. There is no Companion.of in this library. The business adds payments in pounds. Which change comes first? Make Money a data class of amount and currency, and add a currency field to the edge parser Add an else branch to every when so new currencies don't break the build Key the bus by currency as well as by class Add @JvmOverloads to Money The euro-only Money was a judgment call made cheap by the one-field rule. A second currency is exactly the condition that undoes it. The model changes, the parser learns the new field, and the compiler points at every place that used the old Money.

h: A sealed event model · What you'll build, and why it starts with the model
x: Over three lessons you'll build one small library: an in-process event library for a payments service. This lesson is the model, the types for every event the service can see. Lesson 2 of this track is the bus that routes those events to handlers. Lesson 3 is the API that Kotlin and Java code call. Each lab starts from the previous lab's solution, so you can pick up at any lesson. Start with what goes wrong without a model. The demo below has three handlers for messages from a Kafka topic, and each one reads the raw string fields itself: Java static void ledger(Map<String, String> fields) { if ("captured".equals(fields.get("type"))) { long cents = Long.parseLong(fields.get("amountMinor")); // parsing, deep inside a handler balanceCents += cents; } } Kotlin fun ledger(fields: Map<String, String>) { if (fields["type"] == "captured") { val cents = fields.getValue("amountMinor").toLong() // parsing, deep inside a handler balanceCents += cents } } Two bugs come out of three messages. A capture with "amountMinor": "12.50" throws NumberFormatException inside the ledger, after the audit handler has already logged it as a capture. And the receipts handler compares the type with "capture", a typo, so it never fires and nothing complains. Each handler parses and checks for itself, so each one can get it wrong in its own way, and the compiler can't help with any of it. The fix comes in three pieces, one per section. A closed set of event types, so the compiler knows every case; that's the tool from Sealed types: hierarchies the compiler can check. Small types for ids and amounts, so a bad value can't be built at all, from Value classes and what they compile to. And one function at the edge that turns raw fields into those types or refuses them, the idea from Data-oriented programming, and Project Valhalla. Behind that edge, no handler ever sees a string field again. Before you run the demo, predict which message fails, in which handler, and how many receipts get sent. Feel the stringly typed version fail Read StringlyDemo.kt (or StringlyDemoJava.java). Write down which message fails, in which handler, and how many receipts get sent. Run it with the command below. Find the line in the output that shows the bad message was already audited before it failed. Fix the typo in receipts and run again. Then answer: where would a check have to go so that pay_7782 never reaches audit at all? StringlyDemo.kt package workbench.events.l01.demo.stringly // Three handlers each read the raw fields of a message. Nothing checked the message first. var balanceCents = 0L var receiptsSent = 0 fun audit(fields: Map<String, String>) { println("audit ${fields["type"]} ${fields["paymentId"]}") } fun ledger(fields: Map<String, String>) { if (fields["type"] == "captured") { val cents = fields.getValue("amountMinor").toLong() // parsing, deep inside a handler balanceCents += cents println("ledger +$cents, balance $balanceCents") } } fun receipts(fields: Map<String, String>) { if (fields["type"] == "capture") { // a typo the compiler can't see receiptsSent++ } } fun main() { val messages = listOf( mapOf("type" to "captured", "paymentId" to "pay_7781", "amountMinor" to "1999"), mapOf("type" to "refunded", "paymentId" to "pay_7781", "amountMinor" to "500"), mapOf("type" to "captured", "paymentId" to "pay_7782", "amountMinor" to "12.50"), ) for (m in messages) { try { audit(m) ledger(m) receipts(m) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { println("FAILED $e") } } println("receipts sent: $receiptsSent") } ./gradlew :events:demo -Pmain=workbench.events.l01.demo.stringly.StringlyDemoKt labs/events/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/events/l01/demo/stringly/StringlyDemo.kt StringlyDemoJava.java package workbench.events.l01.demo.stringly; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** Three handlers each read the raw fields of a message. Nothing checked the message first. */ public class StringlyDemoJava { static long balanceCents = 0; static int receiptsSent = 0; static void audit(Map<String, String> fields) { System.out.println("audit " + fields.get("type") + " " + fields.get("paymentId")); } static void ledger(Map<String, String> fields) { if ("captured".equals(fields.get("type"))) { long cents = Long.parseLong(fields.get("amountMinor")); // parsing, deep inside a handler balanceCents += cents; System.out.println("ledger +" + cents + ", balance " + balanceCents); } } static void receipts(Map<String, String> fields) { if ("capture".equals(fields.get("type"))) { // a typo the compiler can't see receiptsSent++; } } public static void main(String[] args) { List<Map<String, String>> messages = List.of( Map.of("type", "captured", "paymentId", "pay_7781", "amountMinor", "1999"), Map.of("type", "refunded", "paymentId", "pay_7781", "amountMinor", "500"), Map.of("type", "captured", "paymentId", "pay_7782", "amountMinor", "12.50")); for (Map<String, String> m : messages) { try { audit(m); ledger(m); receipts(m); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("FAILED " + e); } } System.out.println("receipts sent: " + receiptsSent); } } ./gradlew :events:demo -Pmain=workbench.events.l01.demo.stringly.StringlyDemoJava labs/events/src/demo/java/workbench/events/l01/demo/stringly/StringlyDemoJava.java The third message prints audit captured pay_7782 and then FAILED java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "12.50", so the audit log already holds a capture the ledger never posted. receipts sent: 0, because of the typo; after the fix it's 1. The only place a check can stop pay_7782 before every handler is in front of all of them, which is the edge this lesson builds. The whole library. This lesson builds the model and the edge in front of it; lessons 2 and 3 add the bus and the API. Think of the mailroom of a bank. Every envelope is opened there, once. A clerk either fills in the right typed form (a transfer, a complaint, a change of address) and sends it to a desk, or returns the letter with a note saying what was missing. The desks behind the mailroom only ever see forms, so they never squint at handwriting. The analogy breaks at one point: a good clerk may guess what a messy letter meant. The edge function must never guess. A missing amount is a rejection, not a zero.

h: A sealed event model · A sealed interface lists every event the service can see

h: A sealed event model · Parse at the edge, then trust the types
x: The model refuses bad values, but bad values still arrive: from Kafka, from a webhook, from a database row someone edited by hand. So one function converts raw input into the model, in one place, at the edge of the service. It returns a result and never throws: Java static Parsed parse(Map<String, String> fields) { try { String type = field(fields, "type"); return switch (type) { case "captured" -> new Ok(new PaymentCaptured(new PaymentId(field(fields, "paymentId")), amount(fields))); // ... one case per type default -> new Rejected("unknown event type: '" + type + "'"); }; } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { return new Rejected(e.getMessage()); // a reader or a constructor said no } } Kotlin fun parseEvent(fields: Map<String, String>): Parsed = try { when (val type = field(fields, "type")) { "captured" -> Parsed.Ok(PaymentCaptured(PaymentId(field(fields, "paymentId")), amount(fields))) // ... one branch per type else -> Parsed.Rejected("unknown event type: '$type'") } } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) { Parsed.Rejected(e.message ?: "invalid event") // a reader or a constructor said no } Notice what parse does not do: it doesn't check the payment id's format or the sign of the amount. It calls PaymentId(...) and Money(...) and turns their refusal into a Rejected. The rules live in the constructors, once. A second copy of them in the parser would drift the first time someone edits one and not the other. Why a result instead of an exception? Because the caller has to decide what a bad message means, and an exception makes that decision for it. In a Kafka consumer, an exception that escapes the loop sends the consumer back to its last committed offset, so the same record fails again after every restart, and the partition behind it stops moving. A Rejected can go to a dead-letter topic with its reason as a header, add one to a metric and let the consumer commit the offset and move on. Never retry it: a malformed message stays malformed. Behind the edge, code trusts the types. A function that takes a PaymentCaptured has a valid id and a positive amount, because no other kind of PaymentCaptured can exist. There is no !!, no toLong() and no if (type == ...) anywhere in the handlers you'll write in lesson 2. The demo's parser knows only captures and refunds. h: A sealed event model · Java and Kotlin
x: The event model in Java and Kotlin Model.java (Java 21) record PaymentId(String value) { PaymentId { if (!value.matches("pay_[A-Za-z0-9]{4,24}")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid payment id: '" + value + "'"); } @Override public String toString() { return value; } } record Money(long minor) { Money { if (minor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must not be negative: " + minor); } @Override public String toString() { return BigDecimal.valueOf(minor, 2).toPlainString(); } } sealed interface PaymentEvent permits PaymentAuthorized, PaymentDeclined, MoneyMovement { PaymentId paymentId(); } record PaymentAuthorized(PaymentId paymentId, Money amount) implements PaymentEvent { PaymentAuthorized { if (amount.minor() <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("authorized amount must be positive: " + amount); } } record PaymentDeclined(PaymentId paymentId, DeclineReason reason) implements PaymentEvent {} sealed interface MoneyMovement extends PaymentEvent permits PaymentCaptured, PaymentRefunded { Money amount(); } record PaymentCaptured(PaymentId paymentId, Money amount) implements MoneyMovement { /* same check */ } record PaymentRefunded(PaymentId paymentId, Money amount) implements MoneyMovement { /* same check */ } static String summary(PaymentEvent e) { return switch (e) { // no default case PaymentAuthorized(var id, var amount) -> id + " authorized " + amount + " EUR"; case PaymentDeclined(var id, var reason) -> id + " declined: " + reason; case PaymentCaptured(var id, var amount) -> id + " captured " + amount + " EUR"; case PaymentRefunded(var id, var amount) -> id + " refunded " + amount + " EUR"; }; } Model.kt @JvmInline value class PaymentId(val value: String) { init { require(PATTERN.matches(value)) { "invalid payment id: '$value'" } } override fun toString(): String = value companion object { private val PATTERN = Regex("pay_[A-Za-z0-9]{4,24}") } } @JvmInline value class Money(val minor: Long) { init { require(minor >= 0) { "amount must not be negative: $minor" } } override fun toString(): String = BigDecimal.valueOf(minor, 2).toPlainString() } sealed interface PaymentEvent { val paymentId: PaymentId } data class PaymentAuthorized(override val paymentId: PaymentId, val amount: Money) : PaymentEvent { init { require(amount.minor > 0) { "authorized amount must be positive: $amount" } } } data class PaymentDeclined(override val paymentId: PaymentId, val reason: DeclineReason) : PaymentEvent sealed interface MoneyMovement : PaymentEvent { val amount: Money } data class PaymentCaptured(override val paymentId: PaymentId, override val amount: Money) : MoneyMovement { /* same check */ } data class PaymentRefunded(override val paymentId: PaymentId, override val amount: Money) : MoneyMovement { /* same check */ } fun summary(event: PaymentEvent): String = when (event) { // no else is PaymentAuthorized -> "${event.paymentId} authorized ${event.amount} EUR" is PaymentDeclined -> "${event.paymentId} declined: ${event.reason}" is PaymentCaptured -> "${event.paymentId} captured ${event.amount} EUR" is PaymentRefunded -> "${event.paymentId} refunded ${event.amount} EUR" } The shape is the same: sealed interfaces for the alternatives, final carriers for the leaves, validation in the constructor, and one exhaustive switch per operation. Three things differ. Kotlin's value classes compile to a String and a long wherever they're used as themselves, while Java's PaymentId and Money records are separate objects until value records arrive with Valhalla. Java names the subtypes in permits (or infers them within one file), while Kotlin requires them to share the package and module. And a data class's copy() runs init, so captured.copy(amount = Money.ZERO) throws; records have no copy. kotlinc writes the same PermittedSubclasses attribute that javac does, so Java code can switch exhaustively over this Kotlin model, which lesson 3 relies on.

h: A sealed event model · Key terms
x: Sealed hierarchy A type whose list of direct subtypes is closed and known to the compiler. Exhaustive when A when or switch with a branch for every possible subtype and no else, checked at compile time. Value class A one-field wrapper that is its own type in Kotlin and compiles to its field where it can. Edge The one place where raw input from outside the service becomes model values, or is refused. Dead-letter topic A Kafka topic that holds messages a consumer refused, with the reason, so they can be inspected or replayed. Remainder The cases an exhaustive switch can still meet at run time: null, and subtypes compiled after it. Why no else in a when over your own sealed type? Without it, a new subtype is a compile error at every when that must handle it. With it, the new subtype silently takes the else branch. What does a sealed middle level like MoneyMovement give you? One branch, is MoneyMovement, covers its leaves (captures and refunds), and code written against it doesn't break when siblings are added elsewhere. @JvmInline value class PaymentId(val value: String): what is a PaymentId field at run time? A plain String field. It is boxed only when used as another type: generic, nullable, interface or Any. Why is Money here euro cents, with no currency? A JVM value class holds exactly one field. Amount plus currency would be a data class, one object per amount, and this service settles in euros only. What does the edge function return for a malformed message? Parsed.Rejected(reason), never an exception. The caller routes it: dead-letter topic, log line, metric. Where does parseEvent check that a payment id is well formed? It doesn't. It calls PaymentId(raw), whose init checks, and turns the IllegalArgumentException into Rejected. An old service gets a message of a new event type as raw fields. What happens? Its parser's else branch returns Rejected("unknown event type"). Nothing crashes, so deploy consumers before producers.

h: A sealed event model · Go deeper
x: Three questions come up once a model like this is in production. How do events evolve? Adding a field with a default is safe for consumers that parse at the edge: old messages lack the field and get the default. Renaming a type or a field is not. Keep the old name in the parser for as long as old messages can arrive, and map it to the new type there, so the model itself never carries the history. If you serialize the model with kotlinx.serialization, as Compiler plugins: all-open, no-arg and kotlinx.serialization showed, pin each type's name with @SerialName for the same reason. Should the edge return Either instead of a sealed Parsed? Either<String, PaymentEvent> from Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus works, and composes with map and flatMap. A dedicated Parsed reads better at the call site (is Parsed.Rejected) and leaves room for a third case later, such as Ignored for event types a service deliberately doesn't handle. Kotlin's Result<T> is the wrong fit: its failure side is a Throwable, and a rejection is not an exception. What about the database? Rows you read back are untrusted input too. A column holding 'captured' and a nullable amount_minor is a raw map with a schema, and a migration or a manual fix can break it. Read rows through the same kind of edge function, or reuse parseEvent by turning each row into its field map. Java has one tool here that Kotlin lacks: since JDK 21 a pattern switch can take case null explicitly, while Kotlin rules out null at compile time by declaring the parameter non-nullable. Both end up with the same guarantee behind the edge.

h: A typed event bus · Route by the event's class, then walk up its supertypes
x: Generics workshop: a type-safe container and event bus built a bus that keys handlers by event::class. It has a hole you met in the warm-up: an audit handler subscribed under PaymentEvent::class never runs, because no event's run-time class is the interface itself. The same goes for a handler of MoneyMovement. Lesson 1 of this track made that middle level on purpose, so the bus has to honor it. There are two honest fixes. The first keeps one flat list of (type, handler) pairs and asks type.isInstance(event) of each. It is short and correct, and every publish checks every subscription: forty handlers, forty checks per event, almost all of them misses. The second keeps the registry keyed by KClass, as KClass, Class and type tokens did, and works out for each event class the list of keys to visit: the class itself, then each supertype that is an event, nearest first. Java static List<Class<?>> dispatchKeys(Class<?> type) { LinkedHashSet<Class<?>> found = new LinkedHashSet<>(); ArrayDeque<Class<?>> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(type)); while (!queue.isEmpty()) { Class<?> c = queue.removeFirst(); if (!PaymentEvent.class.isAssignableFrom(c) || !found.add(c)) continue; queue.addAll(List.of(c.getInterfaces())); if (c.getSuperclass() != null) queue.add(c.getSuperclass()); } return List.copyOf(found); } Kotlin private fun dispatchKeys(type: Class<*>): List<KClass<*>> = keyCache.computeIfAbsent(type) { val found = LinkedHashSet<Class<*>>() val queue = ArrayDeque<Class<*>>().apply { add(type) } while (queue.isNotEmpty()) { val c = queue.removeFirst() if (!PaymentEvent::class.java.isAssignableFrom(c) || !found.add(c)) continue queue.addAll(c.interfaces) c.superclass?.let(queue::add) } found.map { it.kotlin } } For PaymentCaptured the walk gives [PaymentCaptured, MoneyMovement, PaymentEvent], and publish looks up only those three keys. The breadth-first order is a promise to callers: specific handlers run before general ones, and within one key, in subscription order. Guava's EventBus routes the same way, to subscribers of "any type to which the event is assignable", and caches the flattened hierarchy per class. The walk uses Java reflection, getInterfaces() and getSuperclass(), which costs no extra jar. kotlin-reflect's allSuperclasses would also work, but that lesson's rule applies: describing a class needs the 3.8 MB kotlin-reflect at run time, and naming and casting don't. The answer never changes for a class, so computeIfAbsent caches it once per class. On a ConcurrentHashMap that call is one atomic step, so two threads publishing the first capture at once don't race to fill the cache. Guava EventBus source and Javadoc read Picture a newspaper's wire desk. A story about a football transfer goes to the football editor first, then to the sports editor, then to the chief editor, who wants everything: the most specific desk first, then each wider one. h: A typed event bus · Handlers only consume events, so declare them in
x: A handler only ever takes an event in. It never hands one back. That makes it a consumer, and Contravariance with in: consumers gave the rule: declare the type parameter in. Java @FunctionalInterface interface Handler<E extends PaymentEvent> { void handle(E event); } // Java: invariant <E extends PaymentEvent> Subscription subscribe(Class<E> type, Handler<? super E> handler) { ... } Kotlin fun interface Handler<in E : PaymentEvent> { fun handle(event: E) } fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { ... } Now an audit handler written for every event fits any subscription: bus.subscribe(PaymentCaptured::class, audit) compiles with audit: Handler<PaymentEvent>. Why a fun interface and not the function type (E) -> Unit? A function type is already in on its parameter, so variance would be free. But Java would see a Function1<? super E, Unit>, and every Java lambda would have to end with return Unit.INSTANCE. A fun interface with a void method takes a plain Java lambda. Lesson 3 is about exactly that surface. Inside the bus, handlers of different types share one map, so each one is stored behind an adapter that takes any PaymentEvent: Java Handler<PaymentEvent> adapter = event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)); Kotlin val adapter = Handler<PaymentEvent> { event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)) } The generics workshop used safeCast, so a wrong event became a no-op. h: A typed event bus · Observer rules: return a handle, isolate failures, iterate a snapshot
x: The bus is the subject from Observer and Command, so that lesson's three rules apply, and the lab tests each one. subscribe returns a handle. Subscription extends AutoCloseable, and closing it removes exactly the adapter that subscribe stored. Without a handle, a handler owned by a short-lived object stays in the map forever: a lapsed listener that keeps reacting to events and can't be garbage collected. One failing handler must not stop the others. deliver catches Exception around each call and reports it, with the event, to an ErrorHandler the bus was built with: Java for (Handler<PaymentEvent> handler : handlers) { // a snapshot: copy-on-write called++; try { handler.handle(event); } catch (Exception e) { onError.onError(event, e); // one failure must not starve the rest } } Kotlin for (handler in handlers) { // a snapshot: copy-on-write called++ try { handler.handle(event) } catch (e: Exception) { onError.onError(event, e) // one failure must not starve the rest } } It catches Exception, not Throwable: an OutOfMemoryError should still take the service down. And the bus doesn't decide what an error means. Guava's EventBus catches and logs, and its own Javadoc says that "is rarely the right solution for error handling". Here the service passes in its own ErrorHandler, which can count the failure and send the event to a retry topic. Each key's handlers live in a CopyOnWriteArrayList, so delivery iterates a snapshot. A handler may close its own subscription while it runs (a welcome email that fires once), and the loop carries on. With an ArrayList the next step of the loop throws ConcurrentModificationException. Copy-on-write makes subscribe copy the array, which is fine: subscriptions change at start-up, and events arrive all day. Those two collections also make the bus safe for many publishers with no lock of its own. ConcurrentHashMap guards the registry, and each list is replaced, never changed in place. The lab's load test runs eight publishers while another thread subscribes and closes in a loop, and counts every event. One rule doesn't change: delivery is synchronous. Every handler runs on the publisher's thread, which for a Kafka consumer is the poll loop. The design review in lesson 3 comes back to that. The demo runs the same three handlers on three buses. Predict what each run prints before you run it. One bad handler, three buses Read IsolationDemo. The first handler unsubscribes itself, the second always throws, the third sends a receipt. Each bus gets two captures. Predict the output of each of the three runs. Run it. h: A typed event bus · Middleware is a chain, timing is a decorator
x: Some extra behavior belongs to every event once: logging, tracing, dropping a Kafka redelivery. Some belongs to one handler: timing the ledger, retrying the receipt email. The first kind is a chain of responsibility around publish. The second is a decorator around one handler. They look alike, and choosing the wrong one gives the wrong numbers. The chain is the one from State and Chain of Responsibility. Each middleware gets the event and next, the rest of the chain, and either passes the event on or returns 0 to stop it. The bus builds the chain once, at construction, by folding a copy of the list from the right, so the first middleware wraps all the others and the last one wraps delivery: Java Next pipeline = this::deliver; for (int i = middleware.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Middleware m = middleware.get(i); Next rest = pipeline; pipeline = event -> m.intercept(event, rest); } Kotlin private val pipeline: Next = middleware.toList() .foldRight(Next(::deliver)) { m, next -> Next { event -> m.intercept(event, next) } } Order is behavior. With [dedupe, logging] a redelivery is dropped before anything logs it. With [logging, dedupe] it is logged and then dropped, which is what you want when you need to count redeliveries. Pick one and pin it in a test. The dedupe middleware itself is one line, if (seen.add(event)) next.proceed(event) else 0. add is the check and the act in one step, the fix from Race conditions: why count++ lies, so eight consumer threads can't all let the same capture through. Its "same event" is data-class equality: same type, same id, same amount. The decorator is the one from Decorator and Proxy: it implements the same Handler<E>, adds one behavior and forwards the call. Java static <E extends PaymentEvent> Handler<E> timed(Handler<E> inner, String name, Timings timings) { return event -> { long start = timings.ticker().nanos(); try { inner.handle(event); } finally { timings.record(name, timings.ticker().nanos() - start); } }; } Kotlin fun <E : PaymentEvent> Handler<E>.timed(name: String, timings: Timings): Handler<E> { val inner = this return Handler { event -> val start = timings.ticker.nanos() try { inner.handle(event) } finally { timings.record(name, timings.ticker.nanos() - start) } } } It records in finally, so a handler that throws is timed too, and the exception still reaches the bus's isolation. The clock is a Ticker you pass in. Tests use a fake one that moves forward by a fixed step on every read, so they check exact numbers with no sleeps and no flaky margins. A timing middleware couldn't do this job: it sees one delivery to all of an event's handlers, so it would add the ledger's 2 ms to the receipt email's 300 ms. In the demo, swap the first two middleware and predict what the redelivery prints. Reorder the chain Run ChainDemo and read the nesting of the > and < lines. Swap logging("outer") and dropDuplicates() in the list. Predict what the redelivery prints now, and run. Change tick() to add 90,000 instead of 40,000. Predict the ledger took line before you run. Virtual time keeps the output stable. */ default Handler timed(String name) { return event -> { long start = tick(); try { handle(event); } finally { System.out.println(" " + name + " took " + (tick() - start) / 1_000 + " us"); } }; } } static long clock = 0; static long tick() { clock += 40_000; return clock; } // every read moves the clock by 40 microseconds /** Chain of responsibility: each middleware passes the event on, or answers 0 itself. */ static Next chain(List<Middleware> middleware, Next deliver) { Next next = deliver; for (int i = middleware.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { Middleware m = middleware.get(i); Next rest = next; next = e -> m.intercept(e, rest); } return next; } static Middleware logging(String name) { return (event, next) -> { System.out.println(name + " > " + event.paymentId()); int called = next.proceed(event); System.out.println(name + " < " + event.paymentId() + ": " + called + " handler(s)"); return called; }; } static Middleware dropDuplicates() { Set<PaymentEvent> seen = new HashSet<>(); return (event, next) -> seen.add(event) ? next.proceed(event) : 0; } public static void main(String[] args) { Handler ledger = ((Handler) e -> System.out.println(" ledger posts " + e.paymentId())).timed("ledger"); Next pipeline = chain( List.of(logging("outer"), dropDuplicates(), logging("inner")), // Step 2: swap the first two e -> { ledger.handle(e); return 1; }); PaymentCaptured capture = new PaymentCaptured("pay_7781", 1_999); pipeline.proceed(capture); System.out.println("-- the same capture again (a Kafka redelivery)"); pipeline.proceed(new PaymentCaptured("pay_7781", 1_999)); } } ./gradlew :events:demo -Pmain=workbench.events.l02.demo.chain.ChainDemoJava labs/events/src/demo/java/workbench/events/l02/demo/chain/ChainDemoJava.java First run: outer >, inner >, the ledger lines, then inner < and outer < in reverse. The redelivery prints outer > and outer <: 0 handler(s): logged, then dropped. After the swap the redelivery prints nothing at all below the -- line. With 90,000 per read, ledger took 90 us: the decorator reads the clock twice, so the time is exactly one step. The common mistake is doing slow work inside a handler: an HTTP call to the email provider, a database write with retries. The bus makes publish look like fire-and-forget, so it feels free. It isn't: delivery is synchronous, so a 300 ms receipt call makes every capture 300 ms slower, and the Kafka consumer that published it falls behind. The fix is to keep handlers fast and hand slow work to something built for it: write a row to an outbox table in the same transaction, or put the work on a bounded executor. Then time each handler with the decorator, so the next slow one shows up in a metric before it shows up in the lag.

h: A typed event bus · Java and Kotlin
x: The bus in Java and Kotlin EventBus.java @FunctionalInterface interface Handler<E extends PaymentEvent> { void handle(E event); } @FunctionalInterface interface ErrorHandler { void onError(PaymentEvent event, Exception error); } @FunctionalInterface interface Next { int proceed(PaymentEvent event); } @FunctionalInterface interface Middleware { int intercept(PaymentEvent event, Next next); } final class EventBus { private final Map<Class<?>, List<Handler<PaymentEvent>>> registry = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final Map<Class<?>, List<Class<?>>> keyCache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private final ErrorHandler onError; private final Next pipeline; EventBus(List<Middleware> middleware, ErrorHandler onError) { this.onError = onError; Next next = this::deliver; for (Middleware m : List.copyOf(middleware).reversed()) { // reversed(): JDK 21 Next rest = next; next = event -> m.intercept(event, rest); } this.pipeline = next; } <E extends PaymentEvent> AutoCloseable subscribe(Class<E> type, Handler<? super E> handler) { Handler<PaymentEvent> adapter = event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)); List<Handler<PaymentEvent>> handlers = registry.computeIfAbsent(type, t -> new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>()); handlers.add(adapter); return () -> handlers.remove(adapter); } int publish(PaymentEvent event) { return pipeline.proceed(event); } private int deliver(PaymentEvent event) { int called = 0; for (Class<?> key : keyCache.computeIfAbsent(event.getClass(), EventBus::dispatchKeys)) { for (Handler<PaymentEvent> h : registry.getOrDefault(key, List.of())) { called++; try { h.handle(event); } catch (Exception e) { onError.onError(event, e); } } } return called; } private static List<Class<?>> dispatchKeys(Class<?> type) { /* breadth-first walk, as above */ } } EventBus.kt fun interface Handler<in E : PaymentEvent> { fun handle(event: E) } fun interface Next { fun proceed(event: PaymentEvent): Int } fun interface Middleware { fun intercept(event: PaymentEvent, next: Next): Int } class EventBus( middleware: List<Middleware> = emptyList(), private val onError: ErrorHandler = ErrorHandler.PRINT, ) { private val registry = ConcurrentHashMap<KClass<*>, CopyOnWriteArrayList<Handler<PaymentEvent>>>() private val keyCache = ConcurrentHashMap<Class<*>, List<KClass<*>>>() private val pipeline: Next = middleware.toList() .foldRight(Next(::deliver)) { m, next -> Next { event -> m.intercept(event, next) } } fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { val adapter = Handler<PaymentEvent> { event -> handler.handle(type.cast(event)) } val handlers = registry.computeIfAbsent(type) { CopyOnWriteArrayList() } handlers += adapter return Subscription { handlers.remove(adapter) } } inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(handler: Handler<E>): Subscription = subscribe(E::class, handler) fun publish(event: PaymentEvent): Int = pipeline.proceed(event) private fun deliver(event: PaymentEvent): Int { var called = 0 for (key in dispatchKeys(event.javaClass)) { for (handler in registry[key] ?: continue) { called++ try { handler.handle(event) } catch (e: Exception) { onError.onError(event, e) } } } return called } private fun dispatchKeys(type: Class<*>): List<KClass<*>> = keyCache.computeIfAbsent(type) { /* the walk */ } } The mechanism is identical: the same registry, the same walk, the same adapter, the same fold and the same catch. The differences are in who writes what. Java writes Handler<? super E> at the use site; Kotlin declares in once and kotlinc puts the wildcard into the Java signature. Kotlin gets default arguments on the constructor and a reified subscribe<E> for its own callers; Java callers get neither until lesson 3 adds @JvmOverloads and a Class<E> overload. And Kotlin's Next(::deliver) turns a function reference into a fun interface object, where Java writes this::deliver against its functional interface.

A Handler argument is an ordinary object, even when the caller writes it as a lambda, so there is nothing to inline and nothing that needs noinline. h: A typed event bus · Key terms
x: Dispatch keys The list of types a bus looks up for one event: its class, then its event supertypes, nearest first. Adapter A small wrapper that lets a Handler be stored as a Handler , by casting each event on the way in. Failure isolation Catching each handler's exception so that the other handlers still run. Lapsed listener A handler that was never unsubscribed, so the bus keeps it alive and keeps calling it. Middleware A link in a chain around publish that can pass an event on, change it or stop it. Virtual time A fake clock that tests move forward by hand, so timing can be checked exactly. Why does a bus keyed by event::class never call a handler subscribed under PaymentEvent::class? No event's run-time class is the interface itself. Delivery must also look up each supertype of the event's class. In what order does this bus call handlers? The event's own class first, then each event supertype, nearest first. Within one key, in subscription order. Why is the handler type Handler<in E>? A handler only consumes events. With in, a Handler<PaymentEvent> can stand in for a Handler<PaymentCaptured>. What Java signature does kotlinc give fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>) when Handler is in? subscribe(KClass<E>, Handler<? super E>): kotlinc turns declaration-site in into a ? super wildcard in parameters. Why a CopyOnWriteArrayList for each key's handlers? Delivery iterates a snapshot, so a handler can unsubscribe itself, and publishers need no lock. Each subscribe copies the array, which is fine because subscriptions rarely change. Middleware or decorator: per-handler timing? Decorator. Middleware wraps one delivery to all of an event's handlers; a decorator wraps one handler and implements its interface. Why does DropDuplicates test seen.add(event) instead of seen.contains(event)? add checks and inserts in one atomic step. Contains-then-add lets two threads pass the same event.

h: A typed event bus · Go deeper
x: Three extensions come up as soon as this bus meets real traffic. Asynchronous delivery. Give the bus an Executor and let deliver submit each handler call instead of making it. Two things change. Errors no longer come back to the publisher, so the ErrorHandler becomes the only place they surface. And ordering is gone: two captures for the same payment can run in either order on two pool threads. If order per payment matters, and in a ledger it does, route each payment id to one single-threaded lane, for example lanes[abs(id.hashCode() % lanes.size)], which is what a Kafka partition does for you between services. Bound the executor's queue, or a slow handler turns into an OutOfMemoryError. Generic events. This bus keys by KClass, which is enough because no event has a type parameter. If you ever publish an Envelope<PaymentCaptured>, the class key collapses every envelope into one, the problem from KClass, Class and type tokens. Key by KType from typeOf<T>() then, and know that the supertype walk gets harder: KType has no cheap "all supertypes" answer without kotlin-reflect. Guava's own verdict. Guava's EventBus Javadoc now opens with "We recommend against using EventBus", and its list of reasons reads like a review of any in-process bus: cross-references between producer and subscriber are hard to find, it gives little control of threading, it has no backpressure, and it doesn't propagate exceptions. Lesson 3's design review starts from that list. An in-process bus is still the right tool for decoupling modules inside one service, as long as handlers stay fast and the events that must survive a crash also go to an outbox.

h: An API for Kotlin and Java callers · A subscription DSL: one block, one handle
x: Wiring a service by hand looks like this: five subscribe calls, five handles to keep, and a config lookup between the third and the fourth. If that lookup throws, three handlers are live, nobody holds their handles, and the service starts half wired. The fix is the DSL shape from Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers: a builder that collects what the block declares, and an entry function that commits it all at once. Java // Java, through the Consumer entry point Subscription handle = Events.subscriptions(bus, timings, b -> { b.on(PaymentEvent.class, e -> audit.record(e)); b.on(PaymentCaptured.class, Handlers.timed(c -> ledger.credit(c), "ledger", timings)); b.on(PaymentRefunded.class, Handlers.timed(r -> ledger.debit(r), "ledger", timings)); }); Kotlin val handle = bus.subscriptions(timings) { on<PaymentEvent> { audit.record(it) } timed("ledger") { on<PaymentCaptured> { ledger.credit(it) } on<PaymentRefunded> { ledger.debit(it) } } } Each piece is a decision. on only adds a Pending(type, handler) to a list; commit subscribes them after the block has returned. So a block that throws subscribes nothing, and the caller gets back one Subscription that closes everything, in reverse order. Pending<E> keeps a type and its handler together, so the builder can hold a List<Pending<*>> and still subscribe each entry without a cast, using the star projection from Star projection: when you don't know the type. on<PaymentCaptured> { ... } is inline with a reified E, so it can pass E::class on, as in Type erasure and reified type parameters. Its body is on(E::class, Handler { handler(it) }), and the compiler stops you there: cannot inline 'handler: (E) -> Unit' here: it might contain non-local returns. Add 'crossinline' modifier. The lambda is called from inside another object, the Handler, which runs later, when no enclosing function is left to return from. Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns gave the choice: noinline would also compile but keeps a lambda object inside the Handler; crossinline pastes the body into the generated Handler class. One mistake the DSL can't prevent at compile time: calling on from inside a handler. The handler lambda has no receiver, so the builder is still in scope, and the call compiles. At run time it would register into a builder that has already committed, and the subscription would silently never exist. A check(!committed) in on turns that into an IllegalStateException at the first event, which the bus's isolation reports. Before you run the demo, predict the handler count it prints after the block that fails. With your eager on, the handle has nothing to close, so you get after close: 3 handlers, and the failed block leaves one more behind: handlers: 4. In the Java twin, Unit.INSTANCE appears only inside b.timed(...), which takes a Kotlin receiver lambda; the Consumer entry point needs none. Think of a bank branch with one vault and two counters. At the first counter, regulars speak the house shorthand and the teller fills in the forms for them: that's the Kotlin DSL. At the second, visitors fill in the standard printed forms themselves: that's the Java door, with its overloads and its facade. Both counters feed the same vault, under the same rules. The analogy breaks where a teller might bend a rule for a visitor who doesn't understand the form. The facade never may: Events.captured builds the same value classes and runs the same checks as the Kotlin path.

h: An API for Kotlin and Java callers · @DslMarker keeps a nested block from reaching out
x: Inside timed("ledger") { ... } two builders are in scope: the TimedGroup (nearest) and the SubscriptionsBuilder around it. Kotlin resolves a call against both, nearest first. TimedGroup has no timed, so this compiles: Java // Java has no implicit receivers: the same mistake must name the outer builder, b b.timed("ledger", g -> { g.on(PaymentCaptured.class, c -> ledger.credit(c)); b.timed("refunds", r -> { r.on(PaymentRefunded.class, e -> ledger.debit(e)); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); Kotlin timed("ledger") { on<PaymentCaptured> { ledger.credit(it) } timed("refunds") { on<PaymentRefunded> { ledger.debit(it) } } // reaches the OUTER builder } You meant "refunds, inside the ledger group". What you get is a sibling group: refunds are timed under refunds only, and the ledger dashboard silently misses them. The demo prints {ledger=1, refunds=1} where you expected the ledger to count two. Mark both builder classes with an annotation that is itself annotated @DslMarker, and the nested call stops compiling: 'fun timed(name: String, block: TimedGroup.() -> Unit): Unit' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. If you really want a sibling, say so with a label, this@subscriptions.timed("refunds") { ... }, which nobody types by accident. The rules are the ones from that DSL lesson: the marker counts on classes (or a common superclass), and has no effect on functions. Java never had this problem. Every Java lambda names its parameter, so reaching the outer builder takes b.timed, and a reviewer sees it. Java pays elsewhere: timed takes a TimedGroup.() -> Unit, which Java sees as Function1<TimedGroup, Unit>, so each block ends with return Unit.INSTANCE. That cost is why the Java entry point, Events.subscriptions, takes a java.util.function.Consumer, and why the lab's Java code times handlers with Handlers.timed(...) instead of a group. You meant "time refunds inside the ledger group". Run it. // timed("refunds") { on<PaymentRefunded> { println("ledger -${it.cents}") } } // Step 4: uncomment instead. The label says which builder you mean. // this@subscriptions.timed("refunds") { on<PaymentRefunded> { println("ledger -${it.cents}") } } } } bus.publish(PaymentCaptured("pay_7781", 1_999)) bus.publish(PaymentRefunded("pay_7781", 500)) println("timed groups: ${timings.calls}") } ./gradlew :events:demo -Pmain=workbench.events.l03.demo.dsl.MarkerDemoKt labs/events/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/events/l03/demo/dsl/MarkerDemo.kt MarkerDemoJava.java package workbench.events.l03.demo.dsl; import kotlin.Unit; /** Java has no implicit receivers: reaching the outer builder takes an explicit b. that a reviewer sees. */ public class MarkerDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Bus bus = new Bus(); Timings timings = new Timings(); JavaDsl.subscriptions(bus, timings, b -> { b.timed("ledger", g -> { g.on(PaymentCaptured.class, c -> System.out.println("ledger +" + c.getCents())); // Step 2 (Java): this is the same mistake, and it has to be written out: b.timed, not g.timed. b.timed("refunds", r -> { r.on(PaymentRefunded.class, e -> System.out.println("ledger -" + e.getCents())); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); }); bus.publish(new PaymentCaptured("pay_7781", 1_999)); bus.publish(new PaymentRefunded("pay_7781", 500)); System.out.println("timed groups: " + timings.getCalls()); } } ./gradlew :events:demo -Pmain=workbench.events.l03.demo.dsl.MarkerDemoJava labs/events/src/demo/java/workbench/events/l03/demo/dsl/MarkerDemoJava.java With the marker: 'fun timed(name: String, block: TimedGroup.() -> Unit): Unit' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. The labelled call compiles with the marker and gives the same map, now on purpose. The Java twin prints the same map. Mixed codebases are where this lesson pays. A Kotlin domain module holds the model and the bus, and older Java services (a reconciliation job, the support tool, a Temporal worker written with the Java SDK) consume it. Give them Events and the Class<E> overloads, and the Java code reads like any Java library. In Quarkus, a Java CDI bean calling a Kotlin object needs @JvmStatic or it writes INSTANCE everywhere. h: An API for Kotlin and Java callers · Design review: defend it, or undo it
x: A design review is where you find out which decisions you can defend. Here are the questions a sceptical reviewer asks about this library, with the answer I'd give. Disagree where your service differs. "Why value classes, if Java needs a facade?" Keep them. In the Kotlin model a swapped id and amount don't compile, and an invalid id can't exist. The facade costs one file. If most callers were Java, I'd undo it and use plain records with compact constructors. "Money has no currency." Undo it before a second currency arrives. Money(minor, currency) becomes a data class, one object per amount, and the edge gets a currency field to parse. The one-field rule of value classes made the first version cheap; it doesn't make it right forever. "Supertype dispatch will surprise people." Keep it, and document it. The sealed hierarchy makes the set of keys small, fixed and testable, and the order is a tested promise. The surprise to warn about: a PaymentEvent handler also receives every event type added next year. "in, adapters, casts: isn't that over-engineered?" Keep in: it is what lets one audit handler serve every subscription, from Kotlin and from Java. The single cast is checked by type.cast and guaranteed by the keys. "Delivery is synchronous and in memory." Keep it for decoupling modules inside one service. Undo it for anything that must survive a crash or reach another service: that goes to an outbox table and Kafka. Guava's own EventBus Javadoc now says "We recommend against using EventBus", and lists no backpressure, little control of threading and no exception propagation among the reasons. This bus fixes the last one with an ErrorHandler, and not the first two. "DropDuplicates remembers every event forever." Undo it as written. Bound it to a window of recent events, or move idempotency into the handler's own store with a unique key, which also survives restarts. "The DSL commits after the block. What if commit fails halfway?" Today subscribe can't fail. If it ever can, commit must close what it already opened before rethrowing. Notice the pattern in the answers. A choice is safe when an earlier lesson's mechanism forces it (in for a consumer, no else on a sealed when). It is a judgment call when it trades cost for safety (value classes, the facade, a currency-less Money). Those are the ones to write down, with the condition that would make you undo them. Write your own review notes Without looking back, list five design choices in the library you built across the three labs. For each, write one line: keep or undo, the earlier lesson whose mechanism decides it, and the condition that would change your answer. Pick the choice you're least sure about and write the test that would tell you you were wrong. A strong list mixes forced choices (no else on the sealed when, Handler<in E>, a Class<E> overload because Java can't call reified functions) with judgment calls (value classes plus a facade, euro-only Money, synchronous delivery, unbounded dedupe). The forced ones cite a mechanism; the judgment calls cite a condition, such as "undo when a second currency arrives" or "undo when a handler needs to survive a restart". Guava EventBus Javadoc: why Guava recommends against it read The common mistake is building the Java door by loosening the model. Someone adds @JvmName("capturedFromJava") to a function that takes PaymentId and Money, or swaps the model's value classes for raw String and Long "so Java can use it". The first lets Java pass a raw long that no init block ever checks: a negative capture gets through. The second brings back the swapped-argument bug for the Kotlin callers too. People do it because it's the quickest way to make javac stop complaining. The fix is a facade that takes plain values and builds the value classes, so every check still runs, and leaves the model alone.

The Kotlin version reads the domain types directly (it.paymentId, it.amount), uses on<E> with a reified type and a timed group whose handlers can't reach the outer builder by accident. The Java version passes Class tokens, gets plain String and long through the Events facade, and times handlers one by one with Handlers.timed, because a Kotlin receiver lambda would cost it a return Unit.INSTANCE. What doesn't differ is the safety: the same init blocks validate events built from Java, Handler<? super E> lets the Java audit handler fit any subscription, and javac can switch exhaustively over the Kotlin sealed model.

h: An API for Kotlin and Java callers · Worked example
x: Add subscribeOnce, with its Kotlin sugar and its Java door A welcome email must go out for a merchant's first capture only. Start with the core, in Kotlin, taking a KClass. The handle closes itself, and compareAndSet makes sure only one of eight publishing threads runs the handler, the balking idea from Concurrency patterns that tie it all together. One race needs care: an event can arrive before handle.set has run, so the code closes again after setting it. fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribeOnce(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { val fired = AtomicBoolean() val handle = AtomicReference<Subscription>() handle.set(subscribe(type) { event -> if (fired.compareAndSet(false, true)) { // 1. only the first event wins try { handler.handle(event) } // 2. do the work finally { handle.get()?.close() } // 3. stop further deliveries } }) if (fired.get()) handle.get().close() // an event won before the handle was set return handle.get() } // What Java sees for the core: a KClass parameter it can only reach the long way round. bus.subscribeOnce(JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(PaymentCaptured.class), c -> sendWelcome(c)); Add the Kotlin sugar: a one-line reified wrapper. No noinline or crossinline: its parameter is a Handler, not a function type, so there is nothing to inline. inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> subscribeOnce(handler: Handler<E>): Subscription = subscribeOnce(E::class, handler) bus.subscribeOnce<PaymentCaptured> { sendWelcome(it) } // Java can't see the reified wrapper: javac reports "no suitable method found for subscribeOnce" bus.subscribeOnce(c -> sendWelcome(c)); Add the Java door: a Class<E> overload that converts and delegates. Because Handler is declared in, Java sees Handler<? super E>, so a general handler fits too. fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribeOnce(type: Class<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription = subscribeOnce(type.kotlin, handler) bus.subscribeOnce(PaymentCaptured.class, c -> sendWelcome(Events.paymentId(c))); Last, pin it from both sides. A Kotlin test publishes the same capture from eight threads and checks one email. h: An API for Kotlin and Java callers · Key terms
x: Entry function The function that creates a builder, runs your block on it and returns the result, such as bus.subscriptions { }. @DslMarker An annotation for DSL marker annotations: inside a block, only the nearest marked receiver can be called implicitly. crossinline A modifier for a lambda parameter of an inline function that is called from another object or lambda; it forbids non-local returns. Facade for Java A small object of static functions that takes and returns plain Java types and builds the Kotlin types inside. @JvmOverloads Makes kotlinc generate one Java overload per trailing default parameter. @JvmStatic Makes a member of an object or companion a real static method, so Java needs no INSTANCE or Companion. Design review A meeting where you defend each design choice, say what forces it, and what would make you undo it. Why does the subscriptions builder collect first and subscribe at the end? A block that throws halfway then subscribes nothing, and the caller gets one handle that closes everything the block declared. Why must the lambda of inline fun <reified E> on(handler: (E) -> Unit) be crossinline? The body calls it from inside another object, the Handler, which runs later. crossinline forbids non-local returns so it can still be inlined there. What does @DslMarker stop, and what can't it stop? It stops implicit calls to an outer marked builder from an inner block. It can't stop a call from inside a handler lambda, which has no receiver: use a runtime check. Java can't call your reified subscribe<E>. What do you add? A Class<E> overload that delegates with type.kotlin. The reified function stays a one-line wrapper for Kotlin. A Kotlin constructor where every parameter has a default: what does Java get without @JvmOverloads? A no-argument constructor and the full one. @JvmOverloads adds the ones in between. Why a facade like Events.captured(String, long) instead of @JvmName on functions that take value classes? The facade builds the value classes, so their init checks run. @JvmName lets Java pass raw values straight past them. What does a Java caller get for free from Handler<in E> and a Kotlin sealed model? Handler<? super E> in every signature, and an exhaustive switch over the sealed types with no default.

h: An API for Kotlin and Java callers · Go deeper
x: A production version of this library would add, roughly in this order: Asynchronous lanes. An executor per handler group, with one single-threaded lane per payment id so events for one payment keep their order, and a bounded queue in front of each lane. That's also where backpressure lives: when a lane is full, the publisher waits or the event goes to a retry topic. Real metrics and tracing. Replace Timings with Micrometer timers named after the subscription, and carry the trace context from the Kafka record through publish into each handler, so a slow handler shows up in the trace of the request that caused it. Durability. Events that must survive a crash or reach other services go through a transactional outbox to Kafka, as Observer and Command described. The in-process bus stays for decoupling modules inside one service. Dead letters for the edge. Parsed.Rejected goes to a dead-letter topic with the reason, a counter, and a replay tool for after the fix. Versioned events. Stable type names with @SerialName if you serialize with kotlinx.serialization, and parser branches that map old names to new types. A checked public API. on<E> and subscribe<E> are public inline functions, so their bodies are compiled into every caller, and the @JvmOverloads overloads are part of the Java ABI. A binary-compatibility check in the build catches a change that would break callers compiled against the previous version. @JvmExposeBoxed once it is stable, if it also covers interface members. Until then, the Events facade is the Java door. One thing it should not add is reflection-driven registration with annotations, Guava style (@Subscribe on methods, found by scanning). Guava's own Javadoc lists the costs: subscribers are hard to find from the publisher, and reflection breaks under code shrinkers. Explicit on<E> calls keep every subscription visible in the code that owns it.

h: Class loading, bytecode and dynamic proxies
x: Class loaders and initialization, reading bytecode, invokedynamic, JDK and generated proxies, the ClassFile API and agents. By the end of this track you can say which loader defined a class and exactly when its static initializer runs, and read javap output for Java and Kotlin, including the invokedynamic call sites behind lambdas, string concatenation and records. You can write a JDK dynamic proxy that gets equals, exceptions and default methods right, build subclass proxies with Byte Buddy, and predict whether Spring, Quarkus ArC or Hibernate will intercept a given call, self-calls and Kotlin's final members included. You'll also read and generate class files with the ClassFile API, and change a loaded class under live objects with an agent. Proxies get the most room, in lessons 4 and 5, because they sit under every annotation your framework honours. You need Java and Kotlin, and nothing about the JVM's internals. The Decorator and Proxy lesson of the patterns track is a useful warm-up for lesson 4. Install JDK 25. The labs compile with release 21, so they run on JDK 21 or later. The ClassFile API is final only from JDK 24, so lesson 6 keeps that code in single-file programs under labs/bytecode/preview/ that you run with java File.java on JDK 24 or later. The labs live in labs/bytecode, one package per lesson (workbench.bytecode.l01 to l07). Lessons 1, 3, 4 and 6 are in Java, and lessons 2, 5 and 7 in Kotlin. Every sample and demo comes in both languages. The tests read the JVM's view of your code directly: class identity and initialization, the members javap would list, call counts through proxies, and a class-file reader checked against ASM. Lesson 7's tests attach an agent to the test JVM, which the build allows with -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading. Framework behaviour (Spring, Quarkus, Hibernate) comes from their documentation; the track simulates both proxy models with Byte Buddy rather than running the frameworks. A class is (binary name, defining loader). Loaders delegate parent-first; the same bytes defined by two loaders are two classes with separate statics. Loading, linking and initialization are separate and lazy. <clinit> runs once, in source order, under a lock: a throw poisons the class (NoClassDefFoundError forever), and two initializers that need each other can deadlock. javap shows the JVM's shape: a typed operand stack, a constant pool referenced by index, descriptors like (JI)J, and Kotlin lowered to getters, Companion, INSTANCE, $default and final members. invokedynamic links a call site once through a bootstrap method. Lambdas become hidden $$Lambda classes; the call site type shows what they capture. A JDK proxy is a generated final $ProxyN that boxes arguments and calls one handler. Answer Object methods by identity, run defaults with invokeDefault, unwrap InvocationTargetException, and never retry a default method as a whole. Subclass proxies need non-final classes and methods. Whether self-calls are intercepted depends on whether the proxy is the object (ArC, @SuperCall) or forwards to a target (Spring AOP). The ClassFile API (final in JDK 24) parses class files into lazy models, builds them from lambdas, verifies them, and transforms them as a flatMap over elements. The JDK builds its own proxies and lambdas with it. Agents get an Instrumentation: transformers see classes as they load, and retransformation swaps method bodies in place, never the class's shape. Dynamic loading warns since JDK 21.
