h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Every class has a defining loader, and it is part of the class's identity
x: Your compiled classes sit in jars and directories, and the JVM reads none of them until some code needs one. A class loader is the object that finds a class's bytes and turns them into a Class the JVM can run. Ask three classes who loaded them and you get three different answers: Java System.out.println(String.class.getClassLoader()); // null System.out.println(java.sql.Connection.class.getClassLoader()); // ...ClassLoaders$PlatformClassLoader@<hash> System.out.println(PaymentApp.class.getClassLoader()); // ...ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@<hash> Kotlin println(String::class.java.classLoader) // null println(java.sql.Connection::class.java.classLoader) // ...ClassLoaders$PlatformClassLoader@<hash> println(PaymentApp::class.java.classLoader) // ...ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader@<hash> The JDK has three built-in class loaders. The bootstrap loader is part of the JVM and loads java.base; the ClassLoader Javadoc says it is "typically represented as null". The platform loader loads the other Java SE and JDK modules, such as java.sql and java.net.http. The app loader (also called the system loader) loads your class path: your code, Quarkus, the Kafka client, the Kotlin standard library. Each one has the next as its parent: app, then platform, then bootstrap. JDK 21 and JDK 25 print the same chain. When code asks a loader for a class, the default loadClass does three things in order. It checks whether this loader already has the name (findLoadedClass). If not, it asks its parent, which asks its own parent first. Only when every parent fails does it call its own findClass. So java.lang.String always comes from the bootstrap loader, even if some jar on your class path contains a class with that name. This is parent-first delegation. It's why a stray jar can't replace a JDK class. The loader that finally calls defineClass is the class's defining loader, and it is part of the class's identity. At run time a class is the pair (binary name, defining loader). The binary name is the full name, such as com.acme.Money, or com.acme.Money$Rate for a nested class. Two loaders that each define com.acme.Money from the same bytes produce two classes that happen to share a name. You'll build exactly that in the lab, and section 4 shows what it does to a cast. Kotlin adds nothing special here. kotlin.Unit is an ordinary class in an ordinary jar, so the app loader defines it like any other library class. Who loaded what Before you run it, write down the loader and module you expect for String, java.sql.Connection, the demo class itself and kotlin.Unit. Run LoaderTour from labs/ with the command below, then run the Kotlin twin. Compare the two "classes loaded so far" numbers. Why might they differ? The chain is app -> platform -> bootstrap. Both programs report roughly a thousand loaded classes; the Kotlin one loads a few more because it touches more of the standard library. ClassLoader (Java SE 25 API) docs A class name is like an account number, and the defining loader is the bank. Account 4471 at two banks is two accounts with two balances, and a transfer form for one bank rejects the other bank's account even though the numbers match. Parent-first delegation is a branch that always asks head office whether it already holds the account before it opens a new one, so nobody can open a second "java.lang.String". The analogy breaks in one place: two copies of a class are not strangers. They come from the same bytes and share everything their parent loaded, such as String and the interfaces they implement, which is why a plugin can still be used through a shared interface.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Loading, linking and initialization are three steps, and only the last runs your code
x: How a class gets in: parent-first delegation, then loading, linking and initialization Loading a class and running its static {} block are separate events. Chapter 5 of the JVM specification splits the work into three phases, and HotSpot runs each one as late as it is allowed to. Loading finds the bytes (in a jar, a directory, or generated in memory) and turns them into a Class object with defineClass. Linking checks and prepares the class. Verification proves that the bytecode, the instructions the compiler wrote into the class file (lesson 2), is type-safe. Preparation creates the static fields and sets them to their defaults: 0, false, null. Resolution turns symbolic references in the constant pool, the class file's table of the names it uses, ("method charge in class Ledger") into direct ones, and may do it lazily, one reference at a time. Initialization runs the class's static initializer, which javac names <clinit>: every static field initializer and static {} block, in source order. Two small experiments show the gaps between the phases. A generated class with broken bytecode was accepted by ClassLoader.defineClass on JDK 25, and the VerifyError appeared only when code first asked for its methods. A class that referenced a deleted Helper class loaded and ran fine. It failed with NoClassDefFoundError only when the branch that used Helper executed. Initialization is the phase your code can see, and its triggers are precise. JLS section 12.4.1 lists them: creating an instance, calling a static method, assigning a static field, or reading a static field that is not a constant variable. Initializing a class first initializes its superclass. Reflection such as Class.forName(name) or a reflective static field read counts too. These do not initialize a class: reading a static final primitive or String that has a constant initializer, because javac copied the value into your class file; Limits.class, new Limits[3] and Class.forName(name, false, loader); reading an inherited static field through a subclass name: Child.parentValue initializes only Parent, the class that declares the field. The constant rule surprises people most. static final int MAX_MINOR = 500_000 is a constant variable. static final Integer CAP = 500_000 is not, because boxing calls Integer.valueOf. Reading the first leaves Limits alone. Reading the second runs <clinit>. Kotlin draws the same line between const val and a plain val. The initialization puzzle Read InitPuzzle (or InitPuzzle.kt). For each of the eight steps, write down whether a <clinit> line prints after it, and which one. Run it and check your list. Change CAP to static final int CAP = 500_000; (in Kotlin, make it const val). Predict step 4, then run again. InitPuzzle.java package workbench.bytecode.l01; /** Predict which steps run a static initializer. Each <clinit> prints one indented line. */ public class InitPuzzle { static class Parent { static int parentValue = 1; static { System.out.println(" Parent.<clinit>"); } } static class Child extends Parent { static { System.out.println(" Child.<clinit>"); } } static class Limits { static final int MAX_MINOR = 500_000; // a constant variable: javac copies 500000 into callers static final Integer CAP = 500_000; // boxed, so not a constant variable static { System.out.println(" Limits.<clinit>"); } } static class Lazy { static { System.out.println(" Lazy.<clinit>"); } static void touch() {} } interface Step { void run() throws Exception; } static void step(String what, Step s) throws Exception { System.out.println(what); s.run(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { step("1. read Child.parentValue", () -> { int v = Child.parentValue; }); step("2. new Child()", () -> new Child()); step("3. read Limits.MAX_MINOR", () -> { int v = Limits.MAX_MINOR; }); step("4. read Limits.CAP", () -> { Integer v = Limits.CAP; }); step("5. new Lazy[3]", () -> { Lazy[] a = new Lazy[3]; }); step("6. Lazy.class", () -> { Class<?> c = Lazy.class; }); step("7. Class.forName(name, false, loader)", () -> Class.forName("workbench.bytecode.l01.InitPuzzle$Lazy", false, InitPuzzle.class.getClassLoader())); step("8. Lazy.touch()", Lazy::touch); } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.InitPuzzle labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l01/InitPuzzle.java InitPuzzle.kt package workbench.bytecode.l01 // Kotlin has no static fields of its own. An `object` and a companion object compile to a // class with a static initializer, so the same JVM rules decide when the init blocks run. open class KParent { companion object { @JvmField var parentValue = 1 init { println(" KParent.<clinit>") } } } class KChild : KParent() { companion object { init { println(" KChild.<clinit>") } } } object KLimits { const val MAX_MINOR = 500_000 // a constant: kotlinc copies 500000 into callers val CAP: Int = 500_000 // a property: reading it goes through KLimits init { println(" KLimits.<clinit>") } } object KLazy { init { println(" KLazy.<clinit>") } fun touch() {} } private fun step(what: String, s: () -> Any?) { println(what) s() } /** Predict which steps run a static initializer. Each one prints one indented line. */ fun main() { step("1. read KParent.parentValue") { KParent.parentValue } step("2. KChild()") { KChild() } step("3. read KLimits.MAX_MINOR") { KLimits.MAX_MINOR } step("4. read KLimits.CAP") { KLimits.CAP } step("5. arrayOfNulls<KLazy>(3)") { arrayOfNulls<KLazy>(3) } step("6. KLazy::class.java") { KLazy::class.java } step("7. Class.forName(name, false, loader)") { Class.forName("workbench.bytecode.l01.KLazy", false, KLazy::class.java.classLoader) } step("8. KLazy.touch()") { KLazy.touch() } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.InitPuzzleKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l01/InitPuzzle.kt Step 1 prints only Parent.<clinit>: the field belongs to Parent. Step 2 prints only Child.<clinit>, because Parent is already done. Step 4 prints Limits.<clinit>, step 8 prints Lazy.<clinit>, and steps 3, 5, 6 and 7 print nothing. After the change, step 4 prints nothing too and Limits is never initialized at all. The Kotlin twin shows the same pattern with KParent, KChild, KLimits and KLazy. A class can be loaded and linked long before it is initialized. Only the triggers in the bottom box run its static initializer. JVM Specification SE 25, chapter 5: Loading, Linking, and Initializing docs JLS SE 25, section 12.4.1: When initialization occurs docs Picture an FX service that loads its rate table in a static initializer: static final RateTable RATES = RateTable.load(Path.of("rates.csv")). In a Quarkus test run the file isn't on the test path. The first test fails with ExceptionInInitializerError, and the next forty fail with NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class RateTable, which sends people looking for a missing dependency. The same class under Quarkus dev mode is defined again by a fresh Runtime ClassLoader on every reload, so a static cache in a parent-first library that keeps old RateTable objects pins the old classes in memory. Load data in a bean that the container starts, and keep statics to constants.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · A static initializer runs once, top to bottom, under a lock
x: <clinit> is ordinary code, with three properties that cause real outages. It runs in source order. In this class the constructor runs before the line that sets DEFAULT_BPS: Java public final class FeeSchedule { public static final FeeSchedule INSTANCE = new FeeSchedule(); // runs first private static final int DEFAULT_BPS = Integer.parseInt(System.getProperty("fees.default.bps", "350")); private final int fallbackBps = DEFAULT_BPS; // still 0 here } Kotlin class FeeSchedule private constructor() { val fallbackBps = DEFAULT_BPS // still 0 here companion object { @JvmField val INSTANCE = FeeSchedule() // runs first private val DEFAULT_BPS = System.getProperty("fees.default.bps", "350").toInt() } } The thread running <clinit> may read the class's statics while it is still running, so the constructor sees the default 0. Every unknown country now pays a 0 bps fee, and nothing throws. The JVM did exactly what the source says. With a constant initializer (= 350) the bug disappears, because javac inlines it. That's why this bug tends to arrive the day someone makes a constant configurable. The lab has it for you to fix. It runs once, and a failure is permanent. If <clinit> throws, the first caller gets ExceptionInInitializerError. The JVM marks the class as failed, and every later use from any thread gets NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class .... It never retries. On JDK 21 the cause of that second error even names the original exception and the thread it happened in. In a long log you often see the NoClassDefFoundError hundreds of times and the real cause once, near the top. It runs under a lock. One thread runs <clinit> and every other thread that needs the class waits. That lock is what makes the holder idiom from the memory model track safe, and it can deadlock. If FxRates's initializer reads Fees, Fees's initializer reads FxRates, and two threads start one each, each thread holds one class's lock and waits for the other's. The threads report RUNNABLE, not BLOCKED. ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() returns nothing, and jstack prints waiting on the Class initialization monitor for ... with no "Found one Java-level deadlock" section. Search thread dumps for that phrase when a service hangs at startup. Keep static initializers boring. Constants and small immutable maps are fine. File reads, network calls and reads of other classes' statics belong in a lazy method or in a bean that the container starts. Deadlock two classes Run InitDeadlockDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It starts two threads and waits one second. Read the state and top frame it prints for each thread, and what the deadlock detector says. Optional: run it with -Pargs=wait, then run the printed jstack command in a second terminal and search for Class initialization monitor. Fix it: make Fees.CARD_BPS a constant (static final long CARD_BPS = 108;, or const val in Kotlin) and run again. InitDeadlockDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l01; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.List; /** Two static initializers that need each other, started from two threads. */ public class InitDeadlockDemo { static class FxRates { static final long EUR_USD; static { pause(); EUR_USD = Fees.CARD_BPS + 108_000; } // needs Fees } static class Fees { static final long CARD_BPS; static { pause(); CARD_BPS = FxRates.EUR_USD / 1_000; } // needs FxRates } static void pause() { try { Thread.sleep(200); } catch (InterruptedException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Thread a = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(FxRates.EUR_USD), "rates"); Thread b = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Fees.CARD_BPS), "fees"); a.setDaemon(true); // daemon, so the JVM can still exit at the end b.setDaemon(true); a.start(); b.start(); Thread.sleep(1_000); for (Thread t : List.of(a, b)) { System.out.printf("%-5s state=%s at %s%n", t.getName(), t.getState(), t.getStackTrace()[0]); } long[] stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads(); System.out.println("deadlock detector: " + (stuck == null ? "found nothing" : stuck.length + " threads")); if (args.length > 0) { // -Pargs=wait gives you 30 s to run jstack System.out.println("jstack " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + " (search for 'Class initialization monitor')"); Thread.sleep(30_000); } } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.InitDeadlockDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l01/InitDeadlockDemo.java InitDeadlockDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l01 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Two objects whose initializers need each other, started from two threads. object KFxRates { @JvmField val EUR_USD: Long init { pausePlease(); EUR_USD = KFees.CARD_BPS + 108_000 } // needs KFees } object KFees { @JvmField val CARD_BPS: Long init { pausePlease(); CARD_BPS = KFxRates.EUR_USD / 1_000 } // needs KFxRates } private fun pausePlease() = Thread.sleep(200) fun main(args: Array<String>) { // daemon threads, so the JVM can still exit at the end val a = thread(name = "rates", isDaemon = true) { println(KFxRates.EUR_USD) } val b = thread(name = "fees", isDaemon = true) { println(KFees.CARD_BPS) } Thread.sleep(1_000) for (t in listOf(a, b)) { println("%-5s state=%s at %s".format(t.name, t.state, t.stackTrace[0])) } val stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads() println("deadlock detector: " + (stuck?.let { "${it.size} threads" } ?: "found nothing")) if (args.isNotEmpty()) { // -Pargs=wait gives you 30 s to run jstack println("jstack ${ProcessHandle.current().pid()} (search for 'Class initialization monitor')") Thread.sleep(30_000) } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.InitDeadlockDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l01/InitDeadlockDemo.kt Both threads show state=RUNNABLE with a top frame inside <clinit>, and the detector prints found nothing. The JVM exits only because the threads are daemons. In jstack each thread is in Object.wait() and waiting on the Class initialization monitor for the other class. After the fix, Fees no longer needs FxRates, so both threads print a number and the program ends normally.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Same bytes, two loaders: two classes
x: Because the loader is part of a class's identity, a custom loader can define its own copy of a class the app loader already has. Plugin systems, application servers and Quarkus dev mode do this on purpose. The usual tool is a child-first loader: for its own package prefix it calls findClass before it asks the parent. Java @Override protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException { synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name)) { Class<?> c = findLoadedClass(name); if (c == null && name.startsWith(prefix)) c = findClass(name); // child-first return c != null ? c : super.loadClass(name, resolve); // parent-first } } Kotlin override fun loadClass(name: String, resolve: Boolean): Class<*> = synchronized(getClassLoadingLock(name)) { var c = findLoadedClass(name) if (c == null && name.startsWith(prefix)) c = findClass(name) // child-first c ?: super.loadClass(name, resolve) // parent-first } Two such loaders over one class file give you two Class objects. Each has its own statics, and its static initializer runs once per loader. An object from one copy can't be cast to the other, even though the names match. The message is long, and worth learning to read: class ...TwoLoadersDemo$Counter cannot be cast to class ...TwoLoadersDemo$Counter (...$Counter is in unnamed module of loader 'plugin-1' @606d8acf; ...$Counter is in unnamed module of loader 'app') The same name twice with two loaders means isolation, not a missing jar. The Quarkus class-loading reference describes where you'll meet it: tests and dev mode use several loaders. Your application classes live in a Runtime ClassLoader that is recreated on every hot reload, on top of a Base Runtime ClassLoader that persists. The guide warns that marking a dependency "parent first" without also marking its dependencies can cause a LinkageError. (That comes from the Quarkus docs; this track didn't run dev mode.) The two "not found" errors fit the same picture. ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception from an explicit lookup by name, such as Class.forName or loadClass. NoClassDefFoundError comes from the JVM while it links or initializes code that was compiled against the class: either the class is missing at run time (the cause is then a ClassNotFoundException), or its static initializer already failed. Leaks have the same shape. A loader stays alive while anything reachable points at one of its classes or objects. In one experiment, a plugin instance added to a static list in a parent-loaded registry kept its whole URLClassLoader alive after close() and ten System.gc() calls, along with a 10 MB static array. Without the registration, the loader was collected. A persistent cache that holds an object from the previous Runtime ClassLoader pins every class of that old copy in the same way. Two Counters that aren't the same class Read TwoLoadersDemo. It loads Counter through two child-first loaders and calls hit() twice on the copy from plugin-1. Predict the three hits values and whether the cast at the end works. Run it (or the Kotlin twin) and find the two loader names in the exception message. TwoLoadersDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l01; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.InputStream; /** The same class file defined by two loaders: two classes, two sets of statics. */ public class TwoLoadersDemo { public static class Counter { public static int hits; public int hit() { return ++hits; } } /** Defines Counter itself (child-first); asks the parent for everything else. */ static class ChildFirst extends ClassLoader { ChildFirst(String name) { super(name, TwoLoadersDemo.class.getClassLoader()); } @Override protected Class<?> loadClass(String name, boolean resolve) throws ClassNotFoundException { if (!name.equals(Counter.class.getName())) return super.loadClass(name, resolve); synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name)) { Class<?> c = findLoadedClass(name); if (c != null) return c; try (InputStream in = getParent().getResourceAsStream(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class")) { byte[] bytes = in.readAllBytes(); return defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length); } catch (IOException e) { throw new ClassNotFoundException(name, e); } } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String name = Counter.class.getName(); Class<?> c1 = new ChildFirst("plugin-1").loadClass(name); Class<?> c2 = new ChildFirst("plugin-2").loadClass(name); System.out.println("same name: " + c1.getName().equals(c2.getName())); System.out.println("c1 == c2: " + (c1 == c2) + ", c1 == Counter.class: " + (c1 == Counter.class)); Object fromPlugin1 = c1.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(); c1.getMethod("hit").invoke(fromPlugin1); c1.getMethod("hit").invoke(fromPlugin1); System.out.printf("hits: plugin-1=%s, plugin-2=%s, app=%s%n", c1.getField("hits").get(null), c2.getField("hits").get(null), Counter.hits); try { Counter c = (Counter) fromPlugin1; // checkcast against the app loader's Counter } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println(e.getMessage()); } } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.TwoLoadersDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l01/TwoLoadersDemo.java TwoLoadersDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l01 class KCounter { fun hit(): Int = ++hits companion object { @JvmField var hits = 0 } } /** Defines KCounter itself (child-first); asks the parent for everything else. */ private class KChildFirst(name: String) : ClassLoader(name, KCounter::class.java.classLoader) { override fun loadClass(name: String, resolve: Boolean): Class<*> { if (name != KCounter::class.java.name) return super.loadClass(name, resolve) synchronized(getClassLoadingLock(name)) { findLoadedClass(name)?.let { return it } val bytes = parent.getResourceAsStream(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class")!!.use { it.readAllBytes() } return defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.size) } } } /** The same class file defined by two loaders: two classes, two sets of statics. */ fun main() { val name = KCounter::class.java.name val c1 = KChildFirst("plugin-1").loadClass(name) val c2 = KChildFirst("plugin-2").loadClass(name) println("same name: ${c1.name == c2.name}") println("c1 == c2: ${c1 == c2}, c1 == KCounter::class.java: ${c1 == KCounter::class.java}") val fromPlugin1 = c1.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() repeat(2) { c1.getMethod("hit").invoke(fromPlugin1) } println("hits: plugin-1=${c1.getField("hits").get(null)}, plugin-2=${c2.getField("hits").get(null)}, app=${KCounter.hits}") try { val c = fromPlugin1 as KCounter // checkcast against the app loader's KCounter } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println(e.message) } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l01.TwoLoadersDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l01/TwoLoadersDemo.kt same name: true, c1 == c2: false and c1 == Counter.class: false. The hits are plugin-1=2, plugin-2=0, app=0: three classes, three separate static fields. The cast fails with ... cannot be cast to class ...$Counter, and the parentheses name loader 'plugin-1' and loader 'app'. Quarkus: Class loading reference read The common mistake is reading NoClassDefFoundError as "a jar is missing" and adding dependencies until it goes away. Often the jar is fine: the class's static initializer threw once, earlier, and the JVM now refuses that class for the life of its loader. People make this mistake because the later error is the one that fills the log, and its name sounds like a class-path problem. The fix is to search the log for the first ExceptionInInitializerError (or read the cause of the NoClassDefFoundError on JDK 21 and later), fix what threw, and move I/O and configuration out of static initializers into lazy or container-managed code.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Java and Kotlin
x: When static initialization runs, in Java and Kotlin Limits.java class Limits { static final int MAX_MINOR = 500_000; // constant: copied into callers, no init static final Integer CAP = 500_000; // not a constant: reading it runs <clinit> static Limits defaults() { return new Limits(); } static { System.out.println("Limits init"); } } // Limits.MAX_MINOR -> nothing // Limits.CAP -> "Limits init" // Limits.defaults() -> "Limits init" (if not done yet) Limits.kt object Limits { const val MAX_MINOR = 500_000 // constant: copied into callers, no init val CAP: Int = 500_000 // private static field + getCAP() on the object fun defaults() = Limits init { println("Limits init") } } // Limits.MAX_MINOR -> nothing // Limits.CAP -> "Limits init" (goes through Limits.INSTANCE) // Limits.defaults() -> "Limits init" (if not done yet) Kotlin has no static, but an object compiles to a class with a public static final INSTANCE field and a static initializer that builds it, so the JVM rules are the same. Only const val (primitives and String) is inlined into callers like a Java constant variable. A plain val in an object becomes a private static field plus a getter, so reading it touches the class and runs its init blocks. Companion objects follow the same rules, and their init code lands in the outer class's static {} block, which is why the Kotlin FeeSchedule in section 3 reads 0 exactly like the Java one.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Worked example
x: Read a NoClassDefFoundError back to its cause A Quarkus test run shows this, forty times. Before reading on, decide: is a jar missing? java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class com.acme.fx.RateTable at com.acme.fx.QuoteService.quote(QuoteService.java:31) ... Caused by: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError: Exception java.lang.IllegalStateException: rates file missing: rates.csv [in thread "executor-thread-1"] No. "Could not initialize class" means the JVM found RateTable and already tried to initialize it. The cause (JDK 21 and later) points at the first failure. Here is the class. Each chunk of <clinit> runs once, in order. public final class RateTable { // 1. runs inside <clinit>: any exception here poisons the class for good static final RateTable CURRENT = load(Path.of("rates.csv")); static RateTable load(Path p) { if (!Files.exists(p)) throw new IllegalStateException("rates file missing: " + p); return new RateTable(/* parse 4,000 lines */); } } class RateTable private constructor() { companion object { // 1. runs inside RateTable's <clinit>: any exception here poisons the class for good val CURRENT: RateTable = load(Path.of("rates.csv")) fun load(p: Path): RateTable { check(Files.exists(p)) { "rates file missing: $p" } return RateTable(/* parse 4,000 lines */) } } } Move the I/O out of class initialization. A bean the container builds at startup fails once, with a clear stack trace, and a fixed file or a restart of the test fixes it. The class itself has no static state left to poison. @ApplicationScoped public class RateTableProvider { private volatile RateTable current; @PostConstruct void load() { // 2. ordinary code, ordinary exception current = RateTable.load(Path.of("rates.csv")); } public RateTable current() { return current; } // 3. no static state left to poison } @ApplicationScoped class RateTableProvider { @Volatile private lateinit var current: RateTable @PostConstruct fun load() { // 2. ordinary code, ordinary exception current = RateTable.load(Path.of("rates.csv")) } fun current(): RateTable = current // 3. no static state left to poison } If the value must stay static, make it lazy with a holder class (memory model track, lesson 5). A failure still poisons the holder, but only callers that need the table see it, and the error appears at the first real use instead of whenever some unrelated class touched RateTable.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Lab
x: Fix an initialization-order bug, then load one class twice labs/bytecode/src/main/java/workbench/bytecode/l01/FeeSchedule.java labs/bytecode/src/main/java/workbench/bytecode/l01/IsolatingLoader.java ./gradlew :bytecode:test --tests 'workbench.bytecode.l01.*' Run the tests once. Eight of ten fail: the unknown-country fee comes back as 0, and every loader test hits UnsupportedOperationException. In FeeSchedule, read the static fields from top to bottom as <clinit> runs them. Move one line so the constructor sees the real DEFAULT_BPS. Don't change any number. Ask yourself why currency() was right all along. In IsolatingLoader.findClass, read the class file through the parent with getParent().getResourceAsStream(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class"), then call defineClass(name, bytes, 0, bytes.length). Throw ClassNotFoundException when the stream is null. In loadClass, take getClassLoadingLock(name). Return findLoadedClass(name) if it isn't null. For names that start with the prefix, call findClass. For everything else, return super.loadClass(name, resolve). Run the tests until all ten pass. Then read castAcrossLoadersFails and find which loader names appear in the message. Constants such as "EUR" are inlined by javac, so their order doesn't matter. Integer.parseInt(...) is a method call, so DEFAULT_BPS is 0 until <clinit> reaches its line. If a test fails with LinkageError: attempted duplicate class definition, your loadClass defined the same name twice. Check findLoadedClass first. Don't call super.loadClass for prefix names before findClass: the parent would find the app's copy and you'd get the same Class from both loaders. All ten tests in ClassLoadingTest pass. By the end you can say which loader defines a class and why, predict exactly when a static initializer runs, and read a NoClassDefFoundError or a class that "cannot be cast to" itself for what it really means.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Quiz
x: class Parent { static int rate = 290; static { log("Parent"); } } and class Child extends Parent { static { log("Child"); } }. Fresh JVM: your code reads Child.rate. What is logged? Parent then Child Only Child Only Parent Nothing, because rate is static A static field reference initializes only the class that declares the field, even when you name it through a subclass. rate is declared in Parent, so only Parent runs. Parent then Child is what new Child() or a static method declared in Child would log. A service's logs show NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class com.acme.BinTable on every request since startup. What do you look for first? A bin-table jar missing from the image An earlier ExceptionInInitializerError (or the NCDFE's cause) showing what BinTable's static initializer threw A second copy of BinTable in another jar A JIT deoptimization of BinTable "Could not initialize class" means the JVM found the class and its initializer already failed once; the class stays failed for the life of its loader. The first failure was an ExceptionInInitializerError, and on JDK 21 the NCDFE's cause names it. A missing jar shows up as an NCDFE caused by ClassNotFoundException instead. A Quarkus test fails with class com.acme.Money cannot be cast to class com.acme.Money (com.acme.Money is in unnamed module of loader 'Quarkus Runtime ClassLoader' ...; com.acme.Money is in unnamed module of loader 'app'). What happened? Two different versions of Money were compiled The JVM's class cache is corrupt Money is missing a no-argument constructor Money was defined by two loaders, and an object from one copy met a variable typed with the other The same name with two different loaders is two different classes, even from identical bytes. The fix is to make sure both sides use the same copy, for example by not holding Money objects in something the app loader owns, or by adjusting what is loaded parent-first. Recompiling changes nothing, because the bytes were never the problem. At startup two threads hang. Both are RUNNABLE with a top frame in a <clinit>, and findDeadlockedThreads() returns null. What is the most likely cause? A class-initialization deadlock: two static initializers that need each other, started from two threads A busy loop, because the threads are RUNNABLE Lock contention on a synchronized method A full GC pause Threads waiting for another thread's class initialization show as RUNNABLE, and the JDK's deadlock detector doesn't report them. jstack gives it away with waiting on the Class initialization monitor for .... Break the cycle so one initializer no longer reads the other class's statics. From Lazy init done right: the holder idiom puts static final CardBinTable INSTANCE = new CardBinTable(); in a nested Holder class. Why doesn't the table get built when the outer class CardBinTable is initialized? Nested classes are loaded by a different class loader Holder is a separate class, and nothing initializes it until instance() reads Holder.INSTANCE The JIT removes unused static fields static final fields are always initialized lazily A nested class is its own class with its own <clinit>. Initializing the outer class doesn't touch it. The first read of Holder.INSTANCE is a non-constant static read, which triggers Holder's initialization once, under the JVM's class-init lock. That lock is also why the idiom is thread-safe without volatile.

h: Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization · Key terms
x: Class loader An object that finds class bytes and turns them into Class objects. The JDK has bootstrap, platform and app loaders. Parent-first delegation A loader asks its parent for a class before trying to find it itself. Defining loader The loader that called defineClass. It is part of the class's identity. Linking Verifying, preparing (static fields set to defaults) and resolving a loaded class, before it is initialized. The static initializer javac builds from static field initializers and static {} blocks, run once per class. Constant variable A final primitive or String with a compile-time constant initializer. javac copies its value into the code that reads it. Child-first loader A custom loader that defines certain classes itself before asking its parent, to isolate plugins or reloadable code. Which loader defines java.lang.String, and how does getClassLoader() show it? The bootstrap loader, built into the JVM. String.class.getClassLoader() returns null. In what order does the default loadClass look for a class? findLoadedClass (already defined here?), then the parent's loadClass, then its own findClass. Does reading static final int MAX = 500; from another class initialize the declaring class? No. It's a constant variable, so javac copied 500 into the caller. static final Integer MAX = 500; is not a constant and does initialize it. Your code reads Child.x, where static field x is declared in Parent. Which classes initialize? Only Parent, the class that declares the field. A static initializer throws. What do the first and the later uses of the class get? First use: ExceptionInInitializerError. Every later use: NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class .... The JVM never retries. How does a class-initialization deadlock look in a thread dump? Threads in RUNNABLE state, waiting on the Class initialization monitor for ..., and no "Found one Java-level deadlock" section. Two loaders define com.acme.Money from the same bytes. Is b.isInstance(objectFromA) true? No. A class is (name, defining loader), so these are two classes. A cast between them throws ClassCastException naming both loaders.

x: Three details that didn't fit above. Interfaces have their own initialization rule. Initializing a class initializes its superclass, but its superinterfaces only if they declare a default method. In one experiment, new Impl() for a class implementing WithDefault (which has a default method) and NoDefault (which doesn't) printed WithDefault.<clinit> and Impl.<clinit>, and NoDefault stayed uninitialized until code read one of its fields. HotSpot's InstanceKlass::initialize_impl follows the JVMS steps one by one, and its comments quote this rule. Lambdas are hidden classes. A lambda's class has a name like LoaderInfo$$Lambda/0x00007f2408000a08, isHidden() returns true, and Class.forName on that name throws ClassNotFoundException. LambdaMetafactory defines it with Lookup.defineHiddenClass (JDK 15) as a nestmate of the class that contains the lambda, which means it may use that class's private members. Lesson 3 of this track shows the call site that creates it. You can watch the phases. -Xlog:class+load=info prints a line per loaded class with its source, and -Xlog:class+init=info prints verification start and end and an Initializing '...' line per class. h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · The javap tool turns a class file back into readable instructions
x: javap ships with every JDK, and it reads .class files. Point it at your build output: javap -c -p bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class -c prints each method's bytecode, -p includes private members, and -v (verbose) adds the constant pool, stack and local-variable sizes, flags and the class-file version. Here is one method in Java and its Kotlin twin, both compiled by the labs build: Java static long feeMinor(long amountMinor, int bps) { return amountMinor * bps / 10_000; } Kotlin fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long, bps: Int): Long = amountMinor * bps / 10_000 javac kotlinc static long feeMinor(long, int); public static final long feeMinor(long, int); 0: lload_0 0: lload_0 1: iload_2 1: iload_2 2: i2l 2: i2l 3: lmul 3: lmul 4: ldc2_w #7 // long 10000l 4: sipush 10000 7: ldiv 7: i2l 8: lreturn 8: ldiv 9: lreturn The two compilers agree on almost everything. kotlinc put the top-level function in a class named StackDemoKt, made it public static final, and pushed 10000 as a short (sipush) that it then widens, where javac loads a ready-made long from the constant pool. That's a style difference between the compilers: both leave the same long 10000 on the stack. That is the right mental model for bytecode. It's the contract between your compiler and the JVM, and it's what every tool in this track reads or writes: the verifier, the JIT (the compiler inside the JVM that turns hot bytecode into machine code), java.lang.reflect.Proxy, Byte Buddy, agents. You'll rarely write it, but you'll read it whenever the source doesn't explain what happens at run time. A Kotlin property that Java can't see, a lambda that allocates, or a framework proxy that skips your method all show up in javap first. The class-file version tells you which compiler settings won. The labs compile with release 21, so javap -v prints major version: 65. JDK 25's javac without --release writes 69. kotlinc 2.4.21 run by hand with no -jvm-target writes 52, which is Java 8, and that changes how it compiles string templates (lesson 3). Read one method in two languages Run StackDemo once (command below) so Gradle compiles it, and run StackDemoKt for the Kotlin twin. From labs/, run javap -c -p bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class, then the same for bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemoKt.class. Find describe in both. Which instruction does Kotlin add before building the string, and why? StackDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l02; /** Small methods to read with javap: run the demo once so Gradle compiles it, then javap -c -p. */ public class StackDemo { /** Card fee in minor units: amount times basis points, divided by 10,000. */ static long feeMinor(long amountMinor, int bps) { return amountMinor * bps / 10_000; } static String describe(String currency, long amountMinor) { return amountMinor + " " + currency; } public static void main(String[] args) { long fee = feeMinor(125_000, 290); System.out.println(describe("EUR", fee)); // 3625 EUR } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l02.StackDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.java StackDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l02 // Small functions to read with javap: run the demo once so Gradle compiles it, // then javap -c -p on StackDemoKt.class (top-level functions live in a class named after the file). /** Card fee in minor units: amount times basis points, divided by 10,000. */ fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long, bps: Int): Long = amountMinor * bps / 10_000 fun describe(currency: String, amountMinor: Long): String = "$amountMinor $currency" fun main() { val fee = feeMinor(125_000, 290) println(describe("EUR", fee)) // 3625 EUR } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l02.StackDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.kt Both print 3625 EUR. In the Kotlin describe, the first three instructions are aload_0, ldc "currency" and invokestatic Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter: a public Kotlin function checks every non-null reference parameter on entry, so a Java caller passing null fails right there with the parameter's name. Both versions then build the string with invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants. The Kotlin class also has two main methods: your main() and a main(String[]) bridge that calls it. The javap command (JDK 25 tool docs) docs Bytecode is the kitchen ticket, and your Kotlin or Java source is the menu. The menu says "steak, medium, with the usual sides". The ticket the cook reads says "1 steak, MR, fries, salad, no butter", because the waiter filled in every default and translated the house terms. javap lets you read the ticket. When a dish comes out wrong, the ticket tells you whether the waiter (the compiler) or the cook (the JVM) did it. The analogy breaks because a real ticket is short and ad hoc, while bytecode is strictly typed and checked: the JVM's verifier refuses a ticket that asks for an int and hands over a String.

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · The operand stack: every instruction pops its inputs and pushes its result
x: The JVM is a stack machine. Each method call gets a frame with two areas: an array of local-variable slots, and an operand stack. Instructions don't name registers. They pop their inputs off the stack and push their result back. Here is feeMinor(125_000, 290) step by step. The parameters start in local slots. amountMinor is a long, and a long or double takes two slots, so it fills slots 0 and 1, and bps sits in slot 2. lload_0 pushes the long in slot 0: the stack holds 125000. iload_2 pushes the int in slot 2: 125000, 290. i2l pops the int and pushes it as a long, because lmul only takes two longs. lmul pops both and pushes 36250000. ldc2_w #7 pushes the long constant 10000 from constant-pool entry 7. ldiv pops two longs and pushes 3625. lreturn pops the long and returns it. The first letter of an instruction gives its type: i int, l long, f float, d double, a reference. iload and lload, iadd and ladd are different instructions, which is how the verifier proves type safety without running anything. The broken class from lesson 1 pushed a String and then ran ireturn. It loaded, then failed with VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack as soon as the JVM verified it. javap -v shows the frame sizes the compiler computed. For feeMinor it prints stack=4, locals=3. Two longs on the stack at once need four slots, and the locals need three. You've met this before: count++ on a field is getstatic, iconst_1, iadd, putstatic. That's four instructions, and another thread can run between any two of them. Reading the stack is how you see that a single line of source is not a single step. Predict two instructions Change feeMinor in StackDemo.java to return amountMinor * bps / 10_000 + 30; (and the same in StackDemo.kt). Before you compile, write down the instructions you expect between ldiv and lreturn, for javac and for kotlinc. Run both demos, then javap -c -p both classes and check. javac adds ldc2_w // long 30l and ladd. kotlinc adds bipush 30, i2l and ladd: it pushes the small int and widens it, as it did with sipush 10000. Both now print 3655 EUR. The operand stack after each instruction of feeMinor(125000, 290). Longs count as one entry here but take two stack slots. Your Quarkus services mix Kotlin and Java, and the boundary is where javap pays off. A Kotlin data class AuthorizationRequest(val amountMinor: Long, val currency: String = "EUR") looks friendly, but a Java Kafka deserializer has to pass the currency every time, and a Java mapper that calls getCurrency() on a field declared val isoCurrency fails to compile. A Kotlin companion val TIMEOUT_MS that Java reads as Config.Companion.getTIMEOUT_MS() can't go into a Java annotation, while const val can. When a Java teammate says "I can't call it", run javap -p on the Kotlin class and read the API they actually have.

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · The constant pool holds every name, and descriptors encode every type
x: Bytecode never contains a class name or a method name inline. invokestatic #15 means "the method described by constant-pool entry 15". javap -v prints the pool, and following the references shows how a call is spelled: #7 = Long 10000l #15 = Methodref #16.#17 // workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.feeMinor:(JI)J #16 = Class #18 // workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo #17 = NameAndType #19:#20 // feeMinor:(JI)J #19 = Utf8 feeMinor #20 = Utf8 (JI)J #21 = Fieldref #22.#23 // java/lang/System.out:Ljava/io/PrintStream; #27 = String #28 // EUR A Methodref points to a Class and a NameAndType, which point to Utf8 strings. There is no entry 8: a Long or Double entry uses two pool indexes, a quirk the JVM specification itself calls "a poor choice" in retrospect, and one every class-file reader must handle (lesson 6 has you write one). The string (JI)J is a method descriptor: parameter types in parentheses, then the return type. The grammar is short: Descriptor Type B C D F I J S Z byte, char, double, float, int, long, short, boolean Lpkg/Name; a reference type, with / instead of . [ before a type an array of it: [J is long[], [Ljava/lang/Class; is Class[] V void (return type only) So (Ljava/lang/String;J)Ljava/lang/String; is String describe(String, long). The two letters that trip people up are J for long and Z for boolean. The descriptor has no parameter names and no generics. List<String> and List<Payment> are both Ljava/util/List;. Generic types survive only in a separate Signature attribute that reflection reads, which is the erasure from the generics track seen from the class file. Resolution, the lazy linking step from lesson 1, is the JVM turning entries like #15 into a direct pointer the first time an instruction uses them. javap -v also shows a BootstrapMethods table when the class uses invokedynamic. StackDemo.describe has one, pointing at StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants with the recipe \u0001 \u0001. That's lesson 3. Walk the constant pool Run javap -v bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class | less from labs/. Find major version, then the Methodref for describe, and follow it to its Class and NameAndType entries. Decode describe's descriptor by hand, then find stack= and locals= for main. terminal javap -v bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class | grep -E 'major|Methodref|NameAndType|stack=' major version: 65 (release 21). describe is a Methodref to StackDemo with NameAndType describe:(Ljava/lang/String;J)Ljava/lang/String;, which reads String describe(String, long). The numbers after stack= are small (single digits): the compiler sizes each frame exactly.

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · What Kotlin compiles to
x: javap shows the JVM's view of a Kotlin class, not the Kotlin source. Learn to translate it back. Here is what javap -p shows for five shapes, compiled by kotlinc 2.4.21 in the labs build (the full output is the next Try it). A property becomes a private field plus accessors. var balanceMinor: Long with private set gives getBalanceMinor() and no setter method at all. A property named isEmpty keeps its name for the getter: isEmpty(). A lateinit var iban is a public field, plus a getter and setter. A companion object is a nested class Account$Companion and a field public static final Companion Companion on Account. Its members split three ways. A const val MAX_MINOR becomes public static final long MAX_MINOR on Account, a real constant Java can use in a switch. A plain val DEFAULT_CURRENCY becomes a private static field on Account, with the public getter on Companion. A function is a method on Companion only, unless you add @JvmStatic, which emits a static method on Account as well. An object Registry is a final class with a private constructor and public static final Registry INSTANCE, built in its static initializer. Top-level functions are static methods on a class named after the file (KotlinShapesKt). Default arguments compile to a second, synthetic method. greet(name: String = "Ana", punct: Char = '!') produces greet$default(String, char, int, Object). The int is a bitmask of the arguments the caller left out: 0: iload_2 // the mask 1: iconst_1 2: iand // bit 0 set: name was omitted 3: ifeq 9 6: ldc "Ana" 8: astore_0 ... bit 1 the same way for punct, then invokestatic greet(String, char) Java never sees the defaults. It calls greet("Bo", '?') with every argument, unless you add @JvmOverloads. A data class Payment adds component1(), component2(), copy, a static copy$default, and equals, hashCode and toString. Everything is final unless you write open, which is the root of the proxy problems in lesson 5. Kotlin keeps its own model of the class (nullability, which methods are properties, default values) in a @kotlin.Metadata annotation that javap -v shows as an encoded blob. The Kotlin compiler and kotlin-reflect read it. The JVM ignores it. What Java sees of five Kotlin shapes Read the five declarations at the top of KotlinShapes.kt. For Account, predict which members Account has and which Account$Companion has. Run KotlinShapesKt (command below). It prints each class's fields, constructors and methods. Run the Java twin, KotlinShapesJava, which calls the same classes from Java. Uncomment a.setBalanceMinor(5); and run it again. KotlinShapes.kt package workbench.bytecode.l02 import java.lang.reflect.Modifier // Five Kotlin shapes. main() prints the JVM members of each class, close to what `javap -p` shows. data class Payment(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long = 0) class Account(val owner: String) { var balanceMinor: Long = 0 private set // a getter, and no setter at all val isEmpty: Boolean get() = balanceMinor == 0L lateinit var iban: String // a public field, plus getter and setter companion object { const val MAX_MINOR = 10_000_000L // public static final on Account val DEFAULT_CURRENCY = "EUR" // private static on Account, getter on Companion @JvmStatic fun open(owner: String) = Account(owner) // static on Account AND on Companion fun create(owner: String) = Account(owner) // only on Companion } } object Registry { val accounts = mutableListOf<Account>() } fun greet(name: String = "Ana", punct: Char = '!') = "Hello $name$punct" fun main() { val classes = listOf( Payment::class.java, Account::class.java, Account.Companion::class.java, Registry::class.java, Class.forName("workbench.bytecode.l02.KotlinShapesKt"), ) for (c in classes) { println("${Modifier.toString(c.modifiers)} class ${c.name}") c.declaredFields.sortedBy { it.name }.forEach { println(" field ${Modifier.toString(it.modifiers)} ${it.type.simpleName} ${it.name}") } c.declaredConstructors.forEach { k -> println(" ctor (${k.parameterTypes.joinToString { it.simpleName }})" + if (k.isSynthetic) " synthetic" else "") } c.declaredMethods.sortedBy { it.name }.forEach { m -> println(" method ${Modifier.toString(m.modifiers)} ${m.name}(${m.parameterTypes.joinToString { it.simpleName }})") } } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l02.KotlinShapesKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l02/KotlinShapes.kt KotlinShapesJava.java package workbench.bytecode.l02; /** The Kotlin shapes from KotlinShapes.kt, called from Java: this is the API javap describes. */ public class KotlinShapesJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Payment p = new Payment("p-1", 1_250); // Java must pass every argument Payment q = p.copy("p-2", 99); // copy() takes all of them too System.out.println(p.getAmountMinor() + " " + p.component1() + " " + q); Account a = Account.open("ana"); // @JvmStatic: a real static method Account b = Account.Companion.create("bo"); // no @JvmStatic: through the Companion a.iban = "DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00"; // lateinit: a public field // a.setBalanceMinor(5); // does not compile: private set, no setter System.out.println(a.getBalanceMinor() + " " + a.isEmpty() + " " + b.getOwner()); System.out.println("max=" + Account.MAX_MINOR + " currency=" + Account.Companion.getDEFAULT_CURRENCY()); Registry.INSTANCE.getAccounts().add(a); // object: a singleton behind INSTANCE System.out.println(KotlinShapesKt.greet("Bo", '?')); // top-level function: static on the file class } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l02.KotlinShapesJava labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l02/KotlinShapesJava.java Account has public static final long MAX_MINOR, private static final String DEFAULT_CURRENCY, public String iban, getBalanceMinor() with no setter, isEmpty(), a static open(String) and a synthetic access$getDEFAULT_CURRENCY$cp(). Account$Companion has create, open and getDEFAULT_CURRENCY. Payment has the synthetic constructor ending in DefaultConstructorMarker and the static copy$default. The Java twin prints 1250 p-1 Payment(id=p-2, amountMinor=99) and three more lines; with the setter line uncommented the build fails, because the method doesn't exist. Calling Kotlin from Java (Kotlin docs) docs The common mistake is assuming Java sees Kotlin source structure: that a companion val is a static field, that default arguments work from Java, or that @Throws is optional. It's optional for Kotlin callers and required for Java ones: without @Throws(IOException::class), Java code can't even write catch (IOException e) around the call, because javac rejects catching a checked exception the method doesn't declare. People make the mistake because the Kotlin code compiles and its tests pass. The fix is to design the Java-facing API on purpose with const val, @JvmField, @JvmStatic, @JvmOverloads, @Throws and @JvmName, and to check it with javap -p or a Java test that calls it.

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · Java and Kotlin
x: One wallet API, written in Java and generated by Kotlin Wallet.java (what you'd write by hand) public final class Wallet { public static final long MAX_BALANCE_MINOR = 10_000_000L; private final String owner; private long balanceMinor; public Wallet(String owner) { this.owner = owner; } public static Wallet open(String owner) { return new Wallet(owner); } public long getBalanceMinor() { return balanceMinor; } public long deposit(long amountMinor) { return deposit(amountMinor, "EUR"); } public long deposit(long amountMinor, String currency) { balanceMinor += amountMinor; return balanceMinor; } } Wallet.kt (kotlinc generates the same members) class Wallet(val owner: String) { var balanceMinor: Long = 0 private set @JvmOverloads fun deposit(amountMinor: Long, currency: String = "EUR"): Long { balanceMinor += amountMinor return balanceMinor } companion object { const val MAX_BALANCE_MINOR = 10_000_000L @JvmStatic fun open(owner: String) = Wallet(owner) } } javap -p on the Kotlin class lists the same public members as the Java one, plus a few extras. There's a Companion field and class, open exists twice (static on Wallet, instance on Companion), and there's a static deposit$default with the bitmask, plus the @kotlin.Metadata annotation. Two real differences remain. kotlinc inserts Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter for every non-null reference parameter of a public function, so new Wallet(null) from Java fails at once with "parameter owner". And the class is final by default, so a subclass-based proxy can't extend it.

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · Worked example
x: Translate synthetic names in a Kotlin stack trace A Java batch job that calls a Kotlin library fails. Read the trace and name the Kotlin construct behind each frame before you go on. Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Parameter specified as non-null is null: method com.acme.wallet.Wallet$Companion.open, parameter owner at com.acme.wallet.Wallet$Companion.open(Wallet.kt) at com.acme.wallet.Wallet.open(Wallet.kt) at com.acme.batch.Reconcile.lambda$run$0(Reconcile.java:11) at java.base/java.lang.Iterable.forEach(Iterable.java:75) at com.acme.batch.Reconcile.run(Reconcile.java:10) Read it from the bottom. Reconcile.run is Java code that calls forEach with a lambda, and javac compiled the lambda's body into the private method lambda$run$0. The lambda calls the static Wallet.open. That static method exists only because of @JvmStatic, and its whole body forwards to Wallet$Companion.open, where the Kotlin code lives. accounts.forEach(a -> { // 1. this lambda body is the method lambda$run$0 Wallet w = Wallet.open(a.ownerName()); // 2. the @JvmStatic bridge w.deposit(a.amountMinor()); }); accounts.forEach { a -> // 1. a Kotlin lambda body is also a private static method (its name contains $lambda$) val w = Wallet.open(a.ownerName) // 2. Kotlin callers go straight to Companion.open w.deposit(a.amountMinor) } The top frame is the null check kotlinc put at the start of Companion.open. owner is a non-null String in Kotlin, but Java passed null, because a.ownerName() returned null for one account. The message names the method and the parameter, so you don't need a debugger. Fix it at the boundary, where the null enters. String owner = a.ownerName(); if (owner == null) { // 3. decide what a missing owner means here, before crossing into Kotlin rejected.add(a.id()); return; } Wallet w = Wallet.open(owner); // 3. or accept the null in the Kotlin API and decide there companion object { @JvmStatic fun open(owner: String?): Wallet = Wallet(requireNotNull(owner) { "account has no owner" }) } The same reading works for every synthetic name: copy$default and greet$default are default arguments, access$...$cp is a companion reaching a private static, INSTANCE is an object, and a $lambda$ or lambda$ suffix is a lambda body. Both Kotlin frames say (Wallet.kt) with no line number: each is stopped in code kotlinc added before your first line, a parameter check or a bridge.

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · Quiz
x: javap shows a static method body: iload_0, iload_1, imul, iconst_1, iadd, ireturn. What source produced it? return a * b + 1; with int a, b return a + b * 1; with int a, b return (a + 1) * b; with int a, b return a * (b + 1); with int a, b Trace the stack: push a, push b, multiply (ab), push 1, add (ab + 1), return. For a * (b + 1) the iconst_1; iadd would come right after iload_1, before imul. Which Java signature has the descriptor (Ljava/lang/String;[JZ)V? void m(String s, long j, boolean z) boolean m(String s, long[] js) void m(String[] s, int j, char z) void m(String s, long[] js, boolean z) Ljava/lang/String; is a String, [J is an array of long (J is long, not int), Z is boolean, and V after the parenthesis is the void return type. A Kotlin library has fun authorize(amountMinor: Long, currency: String = "EUR"): AuthResult. A Java caller writes client.authorize(1_250). What happens? It compiles and uses "EUR" It compiles, and currency is null at run time It doesn't compile: Java only sees authorize(long, String) and the synthetic authorize$default, unless the function has @JvmOverloads It throws NoSuchMethodError at run time Defaults live in the synthetic authorize$default method with its bitmask, which only kotlinc calls. @JvmOverloads makes kotlinc also emit authorize(long), which fills in the default for Java callers. Java code must use a Kotlin value in an annotation: @Timeout(Config.TIMEOUT_MS). In Kotlin it's companion object { val TIMEOUT_MS = 120L }. What's the right change? Add @JvmStatic to the property Make it const val TIMEOUT_MS = 120L Add @JvmField to the property Move it to a top-level val Annotation arguments must be compile-time constants. const val emits public static final long TIMEOUT_MS with a constant value on Config, which javac treats like a Java constant. @JvmField gives a public static field, but not a constant javac can put in an annotation. @JvmStatic gives a static getter, which is still a method call. From Race conditions: count++ on a static int compiles to getstatic count, iconst_1, iadd, putstatic count. Between which instructions can another thread change count and cause a lost update? Only between iadd and putstatic None: one line of Java runs atomically Between any two of them: after getstatic, the value on this thread's operand stack is a private copy Only before getstatic getstatic copies the field onto this frame's operand stack. From then on the thread computes with its own copy, and putstatic writes back whatever it computed. Any write by another thread after the getstatic and before the putstatic is overwritten.
