h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · Key terms
x: javap The JDK tool that prints a class file's members, bytecode and constant pool. Operand stack The per-call stack that bytecode instructions pop inputs from and push results onto. Local variable slots A per-call array holding parameters and locals; long and double take two slots. Constant pool The table in a class file that holds every name, type, string and number the bytecode refers to by index. Descriptor The compact type string of a field or method, such as (JI)J for long f(long, int). Class-file version The major version in a class file: 65 for Java 21, 69 for Java 25, 52 for Java 8. @kotlin.Metadata An annotation where kotlinc stores Kotlin-only information about a class, such as nullability and properties. Which javap flags show private members, bytecode, and the constant pool? -p for private members, -c for bytecode, -v for everything including the constant pool and stack/locals sizes. In a method descriptor, what do J and Z mean? J is long and Z is boolean. (I is int, V is void, Lpkg/Name; is a reference type, [ is an array.) How many local-variable slots does a long parameter take? Two. So in static long f(long a, int b), a is in slots 0 and 1 and b is in slot 2 (iload_2). Kotlin companion object { val X = 1 }: how does Java read X? And with const val? Plain val: Outer.Companion.getX(). const val: Outer.X, a public static final constant. What does kotlinc generate for fun greet(name: String = "Ana") besides greet(String)? A static greet$default(String, int, Object): the int is a bitmask of the omitted arguments. Java can't use the default unless you add @JvmOverloads. What does a Kotlin lateinit var iban: String look like to Java? A public field iban, plus getIban() and setIban(String). Where does Kotlin keep nullability and property information that the JVM doesn't model? In the @kotlin.Metadata annotation on each class, which kotlinc and kotlin-reflect read and the JVM ignores.

h: Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output · Go deeper
x: Three more things javap shows you. Inline functions are copied, not called. inline fun <T> measure(block: () -> T): T is still emitted as a static method, so Java can call it. But at each Kotlin call site kotlinc pastes the function body (System.nanoTime() calls and all) into the caller, and the lambda's code with it, so no Function0 object is created. A non-inline lambda such as val adder: (Int) -> Int = { it + 1 } compiles to an invokedynamic that LambdaMetafactory links (Kotlin 2.0 made that the default), with the body in a private static method like useAll$lambda$0. A reified T argument compiles to a plain ldc of the class: typeName<User>() becomes ldc class kt/User. The JVM target changes the output. With -jvm-target 21, string templates become invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants. With kotlinc's command-line default of 1.8, the same template becomes new StringBuilder, append, append, toString. The Kotlin 1.5.20 release notes describe the switch and the option -Xstring-concat=inline to turn it off. The labs pass jvmTarget = 21 in Gradle, so you see the indy version. Annotations you never wrote show up too. javap -v on a Kotlin class prints RuntimeVisibleAnnotations: kotlin.Metadata(mv=[2,4,0], k=1, ...) with two encoded arrays. mv is the metadata version and k=1 means a class. The d1 array is a protobuf that the kotlin-metadata-jvm library can decode. That annotation is how Kotlin reflection knows a JVM getBalanceMinor() is the property balanceMinor.

h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · An invokedynamic call site is linked once, by library code
x: Every other invoke instruction names its target: invokestatic StackDemo.feeMinor:(JI)J calls exactly that method. invokedynamic names only a method name, a type, and a bootstrap method that will decide the target. Here is the method reference IndyTour::add in javap -c -p, and the matching entry from javap -v: invokedynamic #15, 0 // InvokeDynamic #2:applyAsInt:()Ljava/util/function/IntBinaryOperator; BootstrapMethods: 2: REF_invokeStatic java/lang/invoke/LambdaMetafactory.metafactory:(...)Ljava/lang/invoke/CallSite; Method arguments: (II)I REF_invokeStatic workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.add:(II)I (II)I The type ()IntBinaryOperator says what this instruction does for the code around it: take nothing off the stack and push an IntBinaryOperator. How it gets one is not in your class file. The first time the instruction runs, the JVM calls the bootstrap method with a Lookup for your class (an object that carries your class's access rights), the name, the type and the static arguments listed above. The bootstrap method returns a CallSite, an object holding a target MethodHandle of exactly that type. A method handle is a typed reference to a method that the JVM can call directly, much like a function pointer. The JVM links the instruction to it. From then on, every execution calls the target directly, and the bootstrap method never runs again for that call site. LambdaMetafactory and StringConcatFactory both return a ConstantCallSite, whose target can never change, so the JIT can inline straight through it. MutableCallSite exists for language runtimes that need to relink later. invokedynamic arrived in Java 7 for other JVM languages, and javac first used it for lambdas in Java 8. The design moves the strategy out of your class files and into the JDK. The bytecode says "concatenate a long and a String with this recipe". How that's done is decided by the JDK you run on, so a newer JDK can do it better without you recompiling. Relink a call site by hand Read CallSiteDemo. It builds a MutableCallSite, calls through its dynamicInvoker(), changes the target, and calls again. Predict the three lines it prints, then run it (or the Kotlin twin). CallSiteDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l03; import java.lang.invoke.ConstantCallSite; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import java.lang.invoke.MethodType; import java.lang.invoke.MutableCallSite; /** A call site is a slot holding a target method handle. invokedynamic calls through one. */ public class CallSiteDemo { static String eur(long minor) { return String.format("%d.%02d EUR", minor / 100, minor % 100); } static String usd(long minor) { return String.format("$%d.%02d", minor / 100, minor % 100); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Throwable { MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup(); MethodType type = MethodType.methodType(String.class, long.class); MethodHandle eur = lookup.findStatic(CallSiteDemo.class, "eur", type); MethodHandle usd = lookup.findStatic(CallSiteDemo.class, "usd", type); MutableCallSite site = new MutableCallSite(eur); MethodHandle invoker = site.dynamicInvoker(); // what an invokedynamic instruction would call through System.out.println("linked to eur: " + (String) invoker.invokeExact(362_550L)); site.setTarget(usd); // relink: same invoker, new target System.out.println("relinked to usd: " + (String) invoker.invokeExact(362_550L)); ConstantCallSite fixed = new ConstantCallSite(eur); // what lambdas and string concatenation get try { fixed.setTarget(usd); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("ConstantCallSite.setTarget -> UnsupportedOperationException: linked for good"); } } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l03.CallSiteDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l03/CallSiteDemo.java CallSiteDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l03 import java.lang.invoke.ConstantCallSite import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles import java.lang.invoke.MethodType import java.lang.invoke.MutableCallSite // A call site is a slot holding a target method handle. invokedynamic calls through one. object Formats { @JvmStatic fun eur(minor: Long) = "%d.%02d EUR".format(minor / 100, minor % 100) @JvmStatic fun usd(minor: Long) = "$%d.%02d".format(minor / 100, minor % 100) } fun main() { val lookup = MethodHandles.lookup() val type = MethodType.methodType(String::class.java, Long::class.javaPrimitiveType) val eur = lookup.findStatic(Formats::class.java, "eur", type) val usd = lookup.findStatic(Formats::class.java, "usd", type) val site = MutableCallSite(eur) val invoker = site.dynamicInvoker() // what an invokedynamic instruction would call through println("linked to eur: " + invoker.invoke(362_550L) as String) site.target = usd // relink: same invoker, new target println("relinked to usd: " + invoker.invoke(362_550L) as String) val fixed = ConstantCallSite(eur) // what lambdas and string concatenation get try { fixed.target = usd } catch (e: UnsupportedOperationException) { println("ConstantCallSite.setTarget -> UnsupportedOperationException: linked for good") } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l03.CallSiteDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l03/CallSiteDemo.kt linked to eur: 3625.50 EUR, then relinked to usd: $3625.50 through the very same invoker, then a line saying ConstantCallSite.setTarget threw UnsupportedOperationException. An invokedynamic instruction calls through its call site the way the invoker does. Lambdas get the constant kind, linked for good. java.lang.invoke package (Java SE 25 API) docs An invokedynamic call site is a phone extension that isn't wired to anyone yet. The first time anyone dials it, the switchboard (the bootstrap method) reads the note taped to the phone, which is the static arguments, decides who should answer, and wires the extension straight to that desk. Every later call rings the desk directly, and the switchboard never hears about it again. For a lambda that captures nothing, the desk always hands back the same printed form. For one that captures, it fills in a fresh copy each time. The analogy breaks because real wiring can be redone at will; a lambda's call site is a ConstantCallSite, wired once for the life of the class.

h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · A lambda is a hidden class that LambdaMetafactory spins at first use
x: javac turns a lambda into two things: a private method holding the body, and an invokedynamic that produces the object. Java static IntUnaryOperator plus(int fee) { return x -> x + fee; } Kotlin fun plus(fee: Int): (Int) -> Int = { x -> x + fee } javac: invokedynamic #1:applyAsInt:(I)Ljava/util/function/IntUnaryOperator; private static int lambda$plus$1(int, int) // (fee, x): captures first bootstrap args: (I)I, lambda$plus$1:(II)I, (I)I kotlinc: invokedynamic #1:invoke:(I)Lkotlin/jvm/functions/Function1; private static final int plus$lambda$0(int, int) bootstrap args: (Ljava/lang/Object;)Ljava/lang/Object;, plus$lambda$0:(II)I, (Ljava/lang/Integer;)Ljava/lang/Integer; Read the call site type as a factory: (I)IntUnaryOperator means "give me the captured int, and I'll give you an operator". The body method takes the captured values first, then the lambda's own parameters. The three static arguments are the interface method's erased type, the body, and the interface method's type as this lambda uses it. Kotlin's Function1.invoke is erased to (Object)Object, so the third argument, (Integer)Integer, tells the metafactory to insert boxing and casts. At link time LambdaMetafactory generates a class named like IndyTour$$Lambda/0x00000007c0000a08. It's a hidden class, defined with Lookup.defineHiddenClass as a nestmate of IndyTour: a class allowed to use IndyTour's private members, which is how it may call the private body. Class.forName on its name throws ClassNotFoundException. Since JDK 24 the JDK writes these classes with the ClassFile API from lesson 6. The demo shows the allocation rule. A lambda that captures nothing is linked to a single shared instance, so greeter() == greeter() is true. A capturing lambda gets a new object each time the expression is evaluated, but every object shares one class. That's one small allocation per evaluation, not per call of the lambda. Kotlin compiles lambdas the same way, which has been the default since Kotlin 2.0. The release notes list what you give up: such a lambda isn't serializable, and its toString() is less readable. Function references differ. In the demo, ::addMinor stored as (Int, Int) -> Int compiled to an ordinary generated class, IndyTourKt$main$ref$1, and isHidden is false. Tour the lambdas Run IndyTour, then IndyTourKt. Compare the class names they print. From labs/, run javap -c -p bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.class | grep -E 'invokedynamic|lambda' and match each invokedynamic to a line of source. Do the same for bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTourKt.class, and run ls on that folder. Which Kotlin construct got a class file of its own? IndyTour.java package workbench.bytecode.l03; import java.util.function.IntBinaryOperator; import java.util.function.IntUnaryOperator; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** Lambdas, a method reference, string concatenation and a record: every one is an invokedynamic. */ public class IndyTour { record Fee(String currency, long amountMinor) {} static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } static Supplier<String> greeter() { return () -> "hello"; } // captures nothing static IntUnaryOperator plus(int fee) { return x -> x + fee; } // captures fee public static void main(String[] args) { IntBinaryOperator ref = IndyTour::add; Class<?> c = ref.getClass(); System.out.println("method ref: " + ref.applyAsInt(1_250, 30) + ", class " + c.getName()); System.out.println("hidden: " + c.isHidden() + ", nestmate of IndyTour: " + (c.getNestHost() == IndyTour.class)); try { Class.forName(c.getName()); } catch (ClassNotFoundException e) { System.out.println("Class.forName(its name): ClassNotFoundException"); } System.out.println("captures nothing: same object both times? " + (greeter() == greeter())); IntUnaryOperator p30 = plus(30), p45 = plus(45); System.out.println("captures fee: same object? " + (p30 == p45) + ", same class? " + (p30.getClass() == p45.getClass())); Fee fee = new Fee("EUR", 3_625); System.out.println("concat: " + fee.amountMinor() + " " + fee.currency() + ", record: " + fee); } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l03.IndyTour labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.java IndyTour.kt package workbench.bytecode.l03 // Lambdas, a function reference, a string template and a data class, compiled by kotlinc 2.4.21. data class KFee(val currency: String, val amountMinor: Long) fun addMinor(a: Int, b: Int) = a + b fun greeter(): () -> String = { "hello" } // captures nothing fun plus(fee: Int): (Int) -> Int = { x -> x + fee } // captures fee fun main() { val ref: (Int, Int) -> Int = ::addMinor val c = ref.javaClass println("function ref: ${ref(1_250, 30)}, class ${c.name}") println("hidden: ${c.isHidden}") val lambda = greeter() println("lambda class ${lambda.javaClass.name}, hidden: ${lambda.javaClass.isHidden}") println("captures nothing: same object both times? ${greeter() === greeter()}") val p30 = plus(30) val p45 = plus(45) println("captures fee: same object? ${p30 === p45}, same class? ${p30.javaClass == p45.javaClass}") val fee = KFee("EUR", 3_625) println("template: ${fee.amountMinor} ${fee.currency}, data class: $fee") } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l03.IndyTourKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour.kt Java: IndyTour$$Lambda/0x..., hidden: true, a nestmate of IndyTour, Class.forName fails, same object both times? true for greeter, and same object? false, same class? true for plus. Kotlin: the lambdas print IndyTourKt$$Lambda/0x... and hidden: true, but the function reference prints IndyTourKt$main$ref$1 and hidden: false. It's the IndyTourKt$main$ref$1.class file in the folder. Both programs also contain several makeConcatWithConstants call sites, one per string they build. The bootstrap method runs once per call site. After linking, the instruction calls the target directly. LambdaMetafactory (Java SE 25 API) docs What's new in Kotlin 2.0.0: lambdas via invokedynamic read In a Kafka consumer, batch.forEach(p -> ledger.post(p.id(), convert(p, rate))) creates one small Consumer per poll, capturing this and rate, and calls it once per record. That's nothing to worry about. A lambda created inside a per-record inner loop allocates per record, and only then is it worth a look. The same reading helps with framework code: Quarkus and Hibernate stack traces are full of $$Lambda frames, and those are hidden classes linked by LambdaMetafactory, not classes you can find on the class path. And if a library jar was built with an old Kotlin JVM target, its string templates are StringBuilder chains rather than invokedynamic. javap -v tells you which in five seconds.

h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · String concatenation, records and switches go through bootstrap methods too
x: Since JDK 9 (JEP 280), javac compiles + on strings to one invokedynamic per expression, linked by StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants. The constant parts travel as a recipe string, with \u0001 marking each argument: Java "concat: " + fee.amountMinor() + " " + fee.currency() + ", record: " + fee Kotlin "template: ${fee.amountMinor} ${fee.currency}, data class: $fee" invokedynamic makeConcatWithConstants:(JLjava/lang/String;Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String; recipe: concat: \u0001 \u0001, record: \u0001 The call site type lists the dynamic values in order. Here javac first turned the record into a String with String.valueOf, and kotlinc passed the data class object as is. Kotlin templates compile the same way when the JVM target is 9 or newer, which is what the labs use. With kotlinc's command-line default of Java 8, the same template becomes a StringBuilder chain. Records push the idea further. A record's toString, hashCode and equals are each two instructions and an invokedynamic. The bootstrap is java.lang.runtime.ObjectMethods.bootstrap (JDK 16), and its static arguments describe the record: ObjectMethods.bootstrap Method arguments: workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour$Fee currency;amountMinor REF_getField IndyTour$Fee.currency:Ljava/lang/String; REF_getField IndyTour$Fee.amountMinor:J The JDK builds the three methods from that description at first use. A Kotlin data class takes the other road: kotlinc writes the toString body itself, getfield currency, getfield amountMinor, then a concatenation invokedynamic. Both print the same kind of text. The record carries a description, while the data class carries finished code. Pattern-matching switch over a sealed type compiles to invokedynamic typeSwitch with java.lang.runtime.SwitchBootstraps. javac 21 also emits the constant form, condy (CONSTANT_Dynamic), for enum case labels in such a switch. A condy entry is a constant whose value a bootstrap method computes on first use, through ConstantBootstraps. Same idea, for values instead of calls. A record and a data class, side by side From labs/ (after running IndyTour and IndyTourKt once), run the two javap commands below. In the record, find which bootstrap method its toString uses and the string that lists its components. In the data class, find the recipe that toString passes to makeConcatWithConstants. terminal javap -v 'bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/IndyTour$Fee.class' | grep -A6 BootstrapMethods javap -v bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/bytecode/l03/KFee.class | grep -A3 BootstrapMethods The record's toString, hashCode and equals all use bootstrap 0, ObjectMethods.bootstrap, with the arguments IndyTour$Fee, currency;amountMinor and two REF_getField handles. The data class has only a StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants bootstrap, with a recipe like KFee(currency=\u0001, amountMinor=\u0001). Its hashCode and equals are plain bytecode that kotlinc wrote. JEP 280: Indify String Concatenation read

h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · You can call the bootstrap methods yourself
x: A bootstrap method is a public static method, so your code can call it too. That is today's lab. LambdaMetafactory.metafactory takes six arguments, and javap -v already showed you all of them: Java CallSite site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory( lookup, // 1. caller: must be able to see the body "get", // 2. interface method name methodType(Supplier.class), // 3. factory type: captured values -> interface methodType(Object.class), // 4. interface method type, erased lookup.findStatic(ByHandDemo.class, "banner", methodType(String.class)), // 5. body methodType(String.class)); // 6. interface method type as this lambda uses it Supplier<String> s = (Supplier<String>) site.getTarget().invoke(); Kotlin val site = LambdaMetafactory.metafactory( lookup, // 1. caller: must be able to see the body "get", // 2. interface method name methodType(Supplier::class.java), // 3. factory type: captured values -> interface methodType(Any::class.java), // 4. interface method type, erased lookup.findStatic(Banners::class.java, "banner", methodType(String::class.java)), // 5. body methodType(String::class.java), // 6. interface method type as this lambda uses it ) val s = site.target.invoke() as Supplier<String> The JVM supplies arguments 1 to 3 from the call site; the static arguments are 4 to 6. getTarget() is the factory. Calling it runs what the invokedynamic instruction would run on every execution: it takes the captured values and returns a lambda object. For a non-capturing lambda, call it once and keep the result. For a capturing one, keep the factory and call it once per object, which is the shape the lab tests for. The generated class is a nestmate of the lookup's class, so the hidden class in the demo is named ByHandDemo$$Lambda. StringConcatFactory.makeConcatWithConstants(lookup, name, type, recipe) works the same way and returns a call site whose target formats the arguments. Why do this outside a lab? You rarely need to. Code that has a Method in hand at run time, such as a serializer or a router, can turn it into an interface instance once and then call it at the speed of a lambda, instead of paying for Method.invoke on every call. Lesson 4 measures that cost against a JDK proxy. One lambda and one concatenation, by hand Read ByHandDemo. Match each of the six metafactory arguments to the javap -v listing in section 1. Run it (or the Kotlin twin) and read the class and call-site names it prints. The common mistake is guessing what a lambda costs instead of reading what it captures. People avoid lambdas in hot paths because "each lambda allocates". Then they miss the real allocation: a lambda that reads a field captures this, so it allocates on every evaluation, even though it looks like it captures nothing. The fix is to check the call site type in javap -c -p. ()Ljava/util/function/Supplier; captures nothing and is a shared instance. h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · Worked example
x: What does this consumer's lambda capture? A settlement consumer converts each payment with an FX rate and posts it. Before reading on: does the lambda capture anything, and how often does it allocate? class FxPoster { private final Ledger ledger; void handle(List<Payment> batch, long rateMicros) { batch.forEach(p -> ledger.post(p.id(), p.amountMinor() * rateMicros / 1_000_000)); } } class KFxPoster(private val ledger: KLedger) { fun handle(batch: List<KPayment>, rateMicros: Long) { batch.forEach { p -> ledger.post(p.id, p.amountMinor * rateMicros / 1_000_000) } } } Ask javap. The Java call site type is the list of captured values: this (because ledger is a field, read through this) and the long rate. The body became an instance method for the same reason. // 1. the factory: takes FxPoster and long, returns a Consumer invokedynamic #0:accept:(LFxPoster;J)Ljava/util/function/Consumer; // 2. the body: an instance method, the captured long first, then the element private void lambda$handle$0(long, FxPoster$Payment); So Java allocates one Consumer per call to handle, once per batch and not once per payment, and calls it once per element. The Kotlin version compiles to no lambda at all: forEach is an inline function, so kotlinc pasted the loop into handle. Its bytecode is Iterable.iterator, hasNext, next and a direct KLedger.post. Store the same lambda in a val first and Kotlin does what Java does: val post: (KPayment) -> Unit = { p -> ledger.post(p.id, p.amountMinor * rateMicros / 1_000_000) } batch.forEach(post) // 3. invokedynamic #0:invoke:(LKFxPoster;J)Lkotlin/jvm/functions/Function1; // private static final kotlin.Unit handleBoxed$lambda$0(KFxPoster, long, KPayment) Consumer<Payment> post = p -> ledger.post(p.id(), p.amountMinor() * rateMicros / 1_000_000); batch.forEach(post); // 3. same call site as before: invokedynamic accept:(LFxPoster;J)Ljava/util/function/Consumer; // Java has no inline functions, so a lambda passed to forEach is always an object The verdict: one small object per batch is noise next to a 120 ms ledger call, so leave the code as it is. The habit worth keeping is reading the call site type. When it starts with your class, the lambda holds this, which also keeps that object reachable for as long as the lambda lives.

h: invokedynamic: how lambdas and string concatenation compile · Key terms
x: invokedynamic A call instruction whose target a bootstrap method chooses the first time it runs. Bootstrap method A static method, named in the BootstrapMethods table, that links an invokedynamic call site and returns a CallSite. CallSite An object holding the method handle an invokedynamic calls. ConstantCallSite can't be relinked; MutableCallSite can. LambdaMetafactory The JDK bootstrap method that turns a lambda's body method into an object implementing a functional interface. Hidden class A class defined with Lookup.defineHiddenClass (JDK 15) that no class loader can find by name. Capture Values from the surrounding scope that a lambda stores, such as a local variable or this. Condy CONSTANT_Dynamic: a constant-pool entry whose value a bootstrap method computes on first use. When does an invokedynamic's bootstrap method run? Once per call site, the first time the instruction executes. It returns a CallSite, and later executions call its target directly. What does the call site type (I)Ljava/util/function/IntUnaryOperator; on a lambda mean? The lambda captures one int. The call site is a factory: give it the int, get an IntUnaryOperator. () -> "hello" is evaluated twice. Same object? Yes. A non-capturing lambda's call site returns one shared instance. What kind of class is Foo$$Lambda/0x..., and can Class.forName find it? A hidden class defined by LambdaMetafactory as a nestmate of Foo. Class.forName throws ClassNotFoundException. What is \u0001 in a makeConcatWithConstants recipe? A slot for the next dynamic argument. "paid \u0001 to \u0001" takes two values. Which bootstrap builds a record's toString, equals and hashCode? java.lang.runtime.ObjectMethods.bootstrap (JDK 16), given the record class, the component names and getter handles. Does Kotlin's list.forEach { ... } create a lambda object? No. forEach is inline, so kotlinc copies the loop and the lambda body into the caller.

x: Condy is easy to see. Compile this with javac 21 and run javap -v: Java sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {} record Circle(int r) implements Shape {} enum Square implements Shape { UNIT } static String name(Shape s) { return switch (s) { case Circle c -> "circle " + c.r(); case Square.UNIT -> "unit square"; }; } Kotlin // kotlinc compiles this `when` to an instanceof check and an enum comparison: no typeSwitch sealed interface Shape data class Circle(val r: Int) : Shape enum class Square : Shape { UNIT } fun name(s: Shape) = when (s) { is Circle -> "circle ${s.r}" Square.UNIT -> "unit square" } The switch becomes invokedynamic typeSwitch:(Ljava/lang/Object;I)I with SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch. Among its static arguments is a Dynamic constant-pool entry, shown as invoke:Ljava/lang/Enum$EnumDesc;, whose own bootstrap is ConstantBootstraps.invoke applied to Enum$EnumDesc.of. The enum label is built lazily, the first time the switch needs it, instead of forcing Square to initialize when the class loads. The lambda spinner changed tools recently. At jdk-23-ga, InnerClassLambdaMetafactory imports the JDK's internal copy of ASM; at jdk-24-ga it imports java.lang.classfile. Your class files didn't change at all. That's the point of invokedynamic: the JDK swapped its strategy underneath, and every lambda compiled since Java 8 picked it up.

h: Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy · Proxy.newProxyInstance generates a real class, and you can read it
x: A dynamic proxy: every call becomes one invoke with a Method and an Object array Start by writing a proxy yourself. This class does, for one interface, what the JDK will do for any interface. It holds one InvocationHandler, an object with a single method invoke(proxy, method, args) that receives every call: Java final class HandProxy implements FxQuotes { private static final Method QUOTE; // 1. looked up once static { try { QUOTE = FxQuotes.class.getMethod("quoteMicros", String.class); } catch (NoSuchMethodException e) { throw new NoSuchMethodError(e.getMessage()); } } private final InvocationHandler h; HandProxy(InvocationHandler h) { this.h = h; } @Override public long quoteMicros(String pair) { try { return (Long) h.invoke(this, QUOTE, new Object[]{pair}); // 2. box, ask the handler, unbox } catch (RuntimeException | Error e) { throw e; // 3. unchecked: as is } catch (Throwable t) { throw new UndeclaredThrowableException(t); // 4. undeclared checked: wrapped } } // ...the same for spreadMicros, equals, hashCode and toString } Kotlin class HandProxy(private val h: InvocationHandler) : KFxQuotes { override fun quoteMicros(pair: String): Long = try { h.invoke(this, QUOTE, arrayOf(pair)) as Long // 2. box, ask the handler, unbox } catch (e: RuntimeException) { throw e // 3. unchecked: as is } catch (e: Error) { throw e } catch (t: Throwable) { throw UndeclaredThrowableException(t) // 4. undeclared checked: wrapped } // ...the same for spreadMicros, equals, hashCode and toString companion object { private val QUOTE = KFxQuotes::class.java.getMethod("quoteMicros", String::class.java) // 1. once } } Each method finds its java.lang.reflect.Method once, puts the arguments in an Object[] (boxing turns the primitives into objects such as Long), asks the handler, and unboxes the answer. Writing that by hand for forty methods on six client interfaces is tedious and easy to get wrong, so the JDK writes it for you. In Decorator and Proxy you passed a handler to Proxy.newProxyInstance. At that moment the JDK generated a class like HandProxy, for whatever interfaces you listed. Here is what ProxyAnatomy reports about it, on JDK 21 and JDK 25 alike: class public final jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0 extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy, implements [interface ...ProxyAnatomy$FxQuotes] module jdk.proxy1, hidden: false fields [m0, m1, m2, m3, m4] methods [equals, hashCode, proxyClassLookup, quoteMicros, spreadMicros, toString] The Proxy Javadoc promises most of this. A proxy class is final, extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and implements exactly the interfaces you passed, in the same order. Its name is unspecified, but names starting with $Proxy are reserved for proxy classes, and Proxy.isProxyClass recognizes it. The module jdk.proxy1 and the counter in $Proxy0 are implementation details. Every generated method is HandProxy.quoteMicros, written directly in bytecode. This is quoteMicros(String) as JDK 25 generates it: {GEN} So every call loads the handler and the proxy, fetches the Method object that the static initializer looked up once (m0 to m2 are hashCode, equals and toString, then your interface methods), copies the arguments into a fresh Object[] (boxing primitives), and calls invoke. The result is cast back and unboxed. A null returned for a primitive return type becomes a NullPointerException at that unboxing step. The exception table is the whole exception contract. Error and RuntimeException pass straight through, and so do checked exceptions that the interface method declares. Anything else gets wrapped in UndeclaredThrowableException. quoteMicros declares nothing, so its last entry is any. The Kotlin twin prints the same shape for a Kotlin interface. Proxies are a JVM feature, and kotlinc's interfaces are ordinary JVM interfaces. Since JDK 23 the JDK's ProxyGenerator writes these classes with the ClassFile API; JDK 21 still used its internal copy of ASM, which is why the JDK 21 bytecode differs slightly in its exception handler. Take a proxy apart Read ProxyAnatomy (or ProxyAnatomy.kt). Before running it, predict which of the five calls in part 2 reach the handler. Run it. Check the class name, its fields and methods, and the list the handler saw. Look at part 3: why do {FxQuotes, Audited} and {Audited, FxQuotes} get different class names? The two orderings give $Proxy1 and $Proxy2, because the class implements its interfaces in the order you list them, so the cache keys on the order too. Proxy (Java SE 25 API) docs A JDK proxy is a receptionist for a list of phone extensions. Every call to one of those extensions goes to the receptionist, who writes a note (the Method and an Object[] of arguments) and hands it to one person, the handler, who decides what happens. Calls that staff make to each other inside the office never pass reception, which is self-invocation. A default method is a script taped to the desk: the handler can give the script to a staff member to read (forward it to the target), or read it out at reception itself (invokeDefault), in which case every call the script makes goes through reception again. The analogy breaks on identity. A receptionist knows they aren't the person you asked for, but a careless handler that forwards equals makes the proxy deny being itself.

h: Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy · What reaches the handler, and what the handler owes the caller
x: Three methods of Object reach the handler: hashCode, equals and toString, with method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class. The other public Object methods, such as getClass, wait and notify, are final, and the proxy doesn't override them. For hashCode and other no-argument methods, args is null, not an empty array. What you do with equals matters. The tempting handler forwards everything: Java InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> m.invoke(target, args); // equals too Kotlin val h = InvocationHandler { _, m, args -> m.invoke(target, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } // equals too Now proxy.equals(proxy) asks target.equals(proxy), and the target has never heard of the proxy, so the answer is false. equals is no longer reflexive. The ObjectMethodsDemo shows the symptom: after listeners.add(proxy), listeners.remove(proxy) returns false and the listener stays registered. A HashSet happens to survive, because HashMap compares references with == before it calls equals. That's luck, not correctness. Answer equals and hashCode by proxy identity (proxy == args[0], System.identityHashCode(proxy)), or decide on purpose how two proxies compare. The handler also owes the caller the right exceptions. The generated method rethrows unchecked exceptions and the checked exceptions its interface method declares. It wraps any other checked exception in UndeclaredThrowableException. Method.invoke adds a second layer: whatever the target throws arrives wrapped in InvocationTargetException. A handler must catch that and rethrow e.getCause(), or the caller sees UndeclaredThrowableException wrapping InvocationTargetException wrapping the real error. Kotlin makes the first rule easy to trip over. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so a Kotlin interface method declares none unless you write @Throws. Only interfaces can be proxied: passing a class fails with IllegalArgumentException: ... is not an interface. x: Decorator and Proxy showed the self-invocation trap: when the target calls this.authorize() inside its own method, this is the target, and the proxy never sees the inner call. Default methods give you a choice about that. If the handler forwards a default method with method.invoke(target, args), the default body runs on the target. Its this is the target, and its inner calls skip the proxy. DefaultMethodsDemo logs [totalMinor]. JDK 16 added InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args). It runs the interface's default body with this set to the proxy, so every call the body makes comes back through the handler: Java if (method.isDefault()) { return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args); // body runs with this = proxy } Kotlin if (method.isDefault) { return@InvocationHandler InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, *(args ?: emptyArray())) } Now the demo logs [totalMinor, balanceMinor, balanceMinor]. The proxy doesn't even need a target: a handler that answers the abstract methods itself and sends defaults to invokeDefault is a complete implementation. Calling invokeDefault on an abstract method throws IllegalArgumentException, and on a default method your code can't access it throws IllegalAccessException. Kotlin interfaces work too. With the labs' JVM target 21, kotlinc 2.4.21 compiles an interface function that has a body to a real JVM default method, plus a DefaultImpls class for older callers. method.isDefault is true and invokeDefault runs the Kotlin body (the Kotlin twin prints the same three calls). This choice decides whether a retry proxy is safe. Take default String authorizeAndCapture(pan, amount) { return capture(authorize(pan, amount)); }. Suppose your handler treats it like any other method and retries it whenever it fails. The first attempt authorizes, then the capture fails, so the handler retries the whole method, and the second attempt sends another authorization to the issuer. Run defaults through invokeDefault and retry only the abstract calls inside them. A failed capture is then retried as a capture, and the authorization that already succeeded stays at one. The lab tests exactly this. Count the handler calls Read DefaultMethodsDemo. Predict the handler saw list for both runs and the total for the target-less proxy. Run it (or the Kotlin twin). h: Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy · One class per loader and interface list, and a few nanoseconds per call
x: Generating a class is the expensive part, and the JDK does it once. Proxy caches proxy constructors per class loader, keyed by the ordered interface list. Ten thousand newProxyInstance calls with the same loader and interfaces generate one class and construct ten thousand small objects. Listing the same interfaces in a different order generates a second class, as ProxyAnatomy showed. Each class loader gets one dynamic module for its proxies. On the runs for this track, proxies for app-loader interfaces landed in jdk.proxy1, and a Runnable proxy created with the bootstrap loader (null) landed in jdk.proxy2. If any interface is package-private, the proxy class goes into that interface's package instead, and it isn't public (demo.$Proxy8 in one run). Calling Constructor.newInstance on a proxy class in a dynamic module throws IllegalAccessException. Use newProxyInstance, because Proxy.getProxyClass is deprecated. The per-call cost is the bytecode from section 1: an Object[], boxing, a virtual call to the handler, and whatever the handler does. One JMH run on JDK 25 (4 vCPUs, one fork, wide error bars) measured add(3, 4) like this: Call ns/op direct 0.83 Byte Buddy subclass with @SuperCall (lesson 5) 0.88 JDK proxy, handler calls method.invoke(target, args) 4.3 plain Method.invoke with boxing 11.8 Read the order, not the decimals. A few nanoseconds per call is nothing next to a 120 ms issuer call or a database round trip. It does show up in a loop that calls a proxied interface millions of times, and there a subclass proxy or plain code wins. You can save the generated class and read it yourself. -Djdk.proxy.ProxyGenerator.saveGeneratedFiles=true writes it to jdk/proxy1/$Proxy0.class under the current directory. On JDK 21 that just works. On the JDK 24, 25, 26 and 27 builds tested for this track, the JDK writes the first file and then newProxyInstance throws NullPointerException. The JDK source explains it: a return null; that used to sit inside a doPrivileged lambda now returns from generateProxyClass itself. The file is still written, so you can read it on any of them. Read the class the JDK wrote Run ProxyAnatomy once with Gradle so its classes exist. Then, from labs/, run the commands below. They work in a temporary directory, because the flag writes into the current one. On JDK 24 or later, expect a NullPointerException after the first file is written. Carry on with javap. Find quoteMicros and compare it with the listing in section 1. Then find the static initializer: where does it look up m3? terminal D=$PWD/bytecode/build/classes/java/demo cd "$(mktemp -d)" java -Djdk.proxy.ProxyGenerator.saveGeneratedFiles=true -cp "$D" workbench.bytecode.l04.ProxyAnatomy javap -c -p 'jdk/proxy1/$Proxy0.class' | less quoteMicros loads h, the proxy and m3, builds a one-element Object[], calls InvocationHandler.invoke, then checkcast Long and longValue. The static initializer calls Class.getMethod for hashCode, equals, toString, quoteMicros and spreadMicros (on JDK 21 it first loads each class with Class.forName) and stores them in m0 to m4. On JDK 21 the program also prints its normal output. On JDK 24 and later it stops with the NPE after writing $Proxy0.class. ProxyGenerator.java at jdk-25-ga (OpenJDK source) read The most common mistake is a handler that treats every Method the same way. It forwards equals, hashCode and toString to the target, which breaks reflexivity, so collections can't find or remove the proxy. It forwards or retries default methods as one unit, so their inner calls skip the retry and timing logic, or the whole sequence runs again. And it lets InvocationTargetException escape, so callers get UndeclaredThrowableException. People write it that way because the one-line m.invoke(target, args) handler works in the first test. The fix is a handler with four explicit cases in order: Object methods, default methods (invokeDefault), the methods you decorate, and an unwrapping catch.

x: A tracing proxy in Java and Kotlin Tracing.java @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") static <T> T tracing(Class<T> iface, T target, List<String> log) { InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> { if (m.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) { // 1. identity, not the target's return switch (m.getName()) { case "equals" -> proxy == args[0]; case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy); default -> "Tracing[" + target + "]"; }; } log.add(m.getName()); if (m.isDefault()) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args); // 2. this = proxy try { return m.invoke(target, args); // 3. args is null for no-arg methods } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw e.getCause(); // 4. the target's own exception } }; return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface}, h); } Tracing.kt inline fun <reified T : Any> tracing(target: T, log: MutableList<String>): T = Proxy.newProxyInstance(T::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(T::class.java)) { proxy, m, args -> val a = args ?: emptyArray() // 3. null for no-arg methods when { m.declaringClass == Any::class.java -> when (m.name) { // 1. identity "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy) else -> "Tracing[$target]" } else -> { log += m.name if (m.isDefault) InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *a) // 2. this = proxy else try { m.invoke(target, *a) } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! // 4. the target's own exception } } } } as T Same JVM mechanism, same four cases. The Kotlin version is shorter because reified T reads T::class.java itself, so callers write tracing(issuer, log). Two Kotlin-specific traps sit in it. args is a nullable Java array, null for methods with no parameters, so spreading it directly (*args) throws NullPointerException on hashCode(). And Kotlin interfaces declare no checked exceptions unless you add @Throws, so a Java client's IOException that the handler rethrows correctly still reaches Kotlin callers as UndeclaredThrowableException.

x: A test double for CardIssuerClient with no implementation class A test needs a CardIssuerClient that returns canned answers and records what was called, and you don't want to write a class with every method. A proxy with no target can do it. Start with the cases every handler needs. static CardIssuerClient fakeIssuer(Map<String, Object> answers, List<String> calls) { InvocationHandler h = (proxy, m, args) -> { // 1. Object methods: identity, so the fake behaves in collections if (m.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) { return switch (m.getName()) { case "equals" -> proxy == args[0]; case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy); default -> "FakeIssuer" + answers.keySet(); }; } // 2. default methods: run the real interface body, which calls back through this handler if (m.isDefault()) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args); // 3. abstract methods: record the call and return the canned answer calls.add(m.getName() + Arrays.toString(args)); if (!answers.containsKey(m.getName())) throw new UnsupportedOperationException(m.getName()); return answers.get(m.getName()); }; return (CardIssuerClient) Proxy.newProxyInstance( CardIssuerClient.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{CardIssuerClient.class}, h); } fun fakeIssuer(answers: Map<String, Any>, calls: MutableList<String>): CardIssuerClient = Proxy.newProxyInstance(CardIssuerClient::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(CardIssuerClient::class.java)) { proxy, m, args -> val a = args ?: emptyArray() when { // 1. Object methods: identity, so the fake behaves in collections m.declaringClass == Any::class.java -> when (m.name) { "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy) else -> "FakeIssuer${answers.keys}" } // 2. default methods: run the real interface body, which calls back through this handler m.isDefault -> InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, *a) // 3. abstract methods: record the call and return the canned answer else -> { calls += m.name + a.contentToString() answers[m.name] ?: throw UnsupportedOperationException(m.name) } } } as CardIssuerClient Use it. The interesting call is the default method: the fake has no code for authorizeAndCapture, yet the interface's own body runs and its two inner calls are recorded in order. A canned answer of the wrong type fails at the proxy's checkcast, with a ClassCastException from the generated method rather than from your handler. x: A teammate wants to wrap every issuer client in a JDK proxy that retries on timeouts. Explain what the JDK generates, the four cases their handler must handle, and the one retry rule that keeps a default method like authorizeAndCapture from charging twice.

h: Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy · Key terms
x: Dynamic proxy An object of a class generated at run time that implements given interfaces and sends every call to one handler. InvocationHandler The single invoke(proxy, method, args) method that receives every call made on a JDK proxy. UndeclaredThrowableException The unchecked wrapper a proxy throws when its handler throws a checked exception that the method doesn't declare. InvocationTargetException The wrapper Method.invoke puts around whatever the called method threw. Unwrap it with getCause(). invokeDefault InvocationHandler.invokeDefault: runs an interface's default method body on the proxy itself (JDK 16). Self-invocation A method calling another method of the same object through this, which bypasses any proxy in front of it. Dynamic module A module such as jdk.proxy1 that the JDK creates per class loader to hold proxy classes. What class does Proxy.newProxyInstance generate for one interface? A public final class such as jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0 that extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy and implements exactly the given interfaces, in order. Which Object methods reach an InvocationHandler? hashCode, equals and toString, with getDeclaringClass() == Object.class. Not getClass, wait or notify. What is args in invoke(proxy, method, args) for a method with no parameters? null, not an empty array. In Kotlin, use args ?: emptyArray() before spreading it. A handler throws a checked exception that the interface method doesn't declare. What does the caller get? UndeclaredThrowableException, with the checked exception as its cause. What does InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, m, args) do differently from m.invoke(target, args)? It runs the interface's default body with this = the proxy, so the body's inner calls come back through the handler. (JDK 16.) When does Proxy generate a new class? Once per class loader and ordered interface list. {A, B} and {B, A} are two classes. Why must a proxy answer equals itself? Forwarding it makes proxy.equals(proxy) ask target.equals(proxy), which is false, so lists can't find or remove the proxy.

h: Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy · Go deeper
x: Three corners of Proxy that the lesson skipped. Modules and visibility. If every interface is public and in an exported package, the proxy class is public, in an unconditionally exported but non-open package of a dynamic module. If any interface is non-public, the proxy class is non-public and goes into that interface's package and module, so all non-public interfaces must share one package. If an interface is in a package its module doesn't export, the proxy goes into a non-exported package of a dynamic module. In every dynamic-module case, Constructor.newInstance on the proxy class throws IllegalAccessException, which is why Proxy.getProxyClass is deprecated. What can fail at creation. newProxyInstance throws IllegalArgumentException when an element isn't a non-hidden, non-sealed interface, when an interface appears twice, when an interface isn't visible by name through the loader you pass (Class.forName(i.getName(), false, loader) != i), when two interfaces have a method with the same signature and incompatible return types, or when you pass more than 65,535 interfaces. The loader rule is the one you'll meet: in a Quarkus test or a plugin system, pass the loader that defined the interface (iface.getClassLoader()), not some other loader that has a second copy of it (lesson 1). The caches. Proxy keeps the constructors in a ClassLoaderValue, so the cache entry goes away with the loader. A second cache backs isProxyClass. And a ClassValue of ConcurrentHashMap<Method, MethodHandle> holds the method handles behind invokeDefault, so only the first call of each default method pays for the lookup. The saveGeneratedFiles crash from section 4 is easy to see in the source. At jdk-21-ga, generateProxyClass wrote the file inside AccessController.doPrivileged(new PrivilegedAction<>() { ... return null; }), and that return null belonged to the lambda. At jdk-24-ga, the release that permanently disabled the Security Manager, the doPrivileged wrapper is gone, and the same return null; now returns from generateProxyClass itself, so defineClass receives null bytes.

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · A subclass proxy wraps a class by overriding its methods
x: A JDK proxy needs an interface. Plenty of beans have none, so frameworks generate a subclass instead. Here is one written by hand, for the demo's SettlementService: Java class TimedSettlementService extends SettlementService { @Override public String settle(String batch) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { return super.settle(batch); // the original body, on THIS object } finally { log("settle", System.nanoTime() - t0); } } // audit() the same way; region() is final, so there is nothing to override } Kotlin class TimedSettlementService : KSettlementService() { // needs `open class` override fun settle(batch: String): String { // needs `open fun` val t0 = System.nanoTime() try { return super.settle(batch) // the original body, on THIS object } finally { log("settle", System.nanoTime() - t0) } } // audit() the same way; region() is final, so there is nothing to override } Every method the subclass overrides becomes a place to add behaviour, and super.settle(batch) runs the original body on the same object. Byte Buddy writes this class at run time, for any class and any set of methods: Java Class<? extends SettlementService> sub = new ByteBuddy() .subclass(SettlementService.class) .method(isDeclaredBy(SettlementService.class)) // which methods to override .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration() .filter(named("intercept")) .to(new InSubclass())) // who handles them .make() .load(SettlementService.class.getClassLoader()) .getLoaded(); Kotlin val sub: Class<out KSettlementService> = ByteBuddy() .subclass(KSettlementService::class.java) .method(isDeclaredBy(KSettlementService::class.java)) // which methods to override .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration() .filter { it.name == "intercept" } .to(KInSubclass())) // who handles them .make() .load(KSettlementService::class.java.classLoader) .loaded The demo prints the result: a public class named ...SettlementService$ByteBuddy$nsokwLlA (the suffix is random on every run) that declares settle, audit, and two accessors such as settle$accessor$cvePe5kh. The accessors are how the interceptor's @SuperCall Callable runs super.settle(...), the line you wrote by hand above. The interceptor receives @Origin Method for the method being called. Byte Buddy binds parameters by these annotations. A subclass can only intercept what it can override, and that sets the rules every subclass proxy lives by. A final class can't be subclassed at all. A final or private method isn't overridden, so it runs as written and nothing intercepts it: in the demo, region() just works, uncounted. And the subclass's constructor calls the superclass constructor, unless the framework skips it. Kotlin turns the first rule into a daily problem, because classes and members are final unless you write open. Byte Buddy refuses a plain Kotlin class with Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types. The Kotlin all-open compiler plugin "makes classes and their members open at compile time without requiring the open keyword", for classes carrying annotations you choose. Byte Buddy is the library most of the ecosystem uses for this; 1.18.17 is the current release. The older cglib's own README says it "is unmaintained and does not work well (or possibly at all?) in newer JDKs, particularly JDK17+" and points to Byte Buddy. Spring keeps working because it ships its own patched copy, repackaged as org.springframework.cglib, along with Objenesis. Generate a subclass, then try a Kotlin class Run TwoModelsDemo (or the Kotlin twin) and read the first two lines and the last line. In TwoModelsDemo.kt, make KotlinFinalService open: open class KotlinFinalService { open fun settle(...) }. Run either version again. From labs/, run javap -p bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/bytecode/l05/KSettlementService.class and find the one method that is still final. import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.Origin; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.RuntimeType; import net.bytebuddy.implementation.bind.annotation.SuperCall; import java.lang.reflect.Method; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.isDeclaredBy; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.named; /** The same subclass proxy, two models: the proxy IS the object, or the proxy forwards to a target. */ public class TwoModelsDemo { static final List<String> LOG = new ArrayList<>(); public static class SettlementService { static int constructed; public SettlementService() { constructed++; } public String settle(String batch) { return "settled " + batch + " (" + this.audit(batch) + ")"; } // self-call public String audit(String batch) { return "audited " + batch; } public final String region() { return "eu-west"; } } /** ArC-style: the generated subclass instance is the bean; @SuperCall runs the original body on it. */ public static class InSubclass { @RuntimeType public Object intercept(@Origin Method m, @SuperCall Callable<?> original) throws Exception { LOG.add("intercepted " + m.getName()); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Class<? extends SettlementService> sub = subclass(SettlementService.class, new InSubclass()); System.out.println("generated " + sub.getName()); The last line is Kotlin class without open: Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types: class ...KotlinFinalService; after adding open, that line disappears because make() succeeds. In javap, settle and audit are plain public, while region() is public final: kotlinc keeps a member final unless you mark it open, even inside an open class. Byte Buddy README (tutorial examples, Java version support) read All-open compiler plugin (Kotlin docs) docs Think of two ways to give a clerk a supervisor. In the first, the supervisor sits inside the clerk's own desk: every request, including the ones the clerk makes to themselves ("let me audit this first"), passes the supervisor. That's Quarkus ArC's intercepted subclass, and Byte Buddy's @SuperCall. In the second, the supervisor sits at a front counter and passes requests back to the clerk, who then talks to themselves in private. That's Spring's proxy. The analogy breaks on the front counter's own desk: a forwarding proxy is also a full copy of the clerk's class, with its own empty drawers. Anything it can't pass back, a final method, quietly runs at the counter, using those empty drawers.

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Where the real object lives decides whether self-calls are intercepted
x: Decorator and Proxy blamed self-invocation on proxies in general. The demo shows it's more specific than that. The same Byte Buddy subclass, built two ways, gives opposite answers for settle("B-17"), whose body calls this.audit(batch). In the first model, the generated subclass instance is the object. There's no separate target. The interceptor runs the original body through @SuperCall, on that same instance. When the body calls this.audit(...), this is the subclass, the call dispatches virtually to its override, and the interceptor runs again. The log reads [intercepted settle, intercepted audit]. In the second model, the subclass instance is only a front for a separate target object. By hand, it looks like this: Java class ForwardingSettlementService extends SettlementService { private final SettlementService target; ForwardingSettlementService(SettlementService target) { this.target = target; } @Override public String settle(String batch) { log("settle"); return target.settle(batch); // the body runs on the target } // audit() the same way } Kotlin class ForwardingSettlementService(private val target: KSettlementService) : KSettlementService() { override fun settle(batch: String): String { log("settle") return target.settle(batch) // the body runs on the target } // audit() the same way } The demo's Forwarding interceptor does the same with method.invoke(target, args). The body runs on the target, whose this is the target, so this.audit(...) is an ordinary call that the proxy never sees. The log reads [forwarded settle]. The demo also counts constructors: two, because the target was built once and the proxy subclass was built with newInstance, which runs the superclass constructor again. That's the "constructor called twice" that Spring's 3.2 documentation warned about. So "it's a subclass" doesn't settle the question. Ask where the state and the body run. If the proxy is the object, self-calls are intercepted, final methods still run on the real state, and fields are real. If the proxy forwards, self-calls skip it, and anything the proxy can't override runs on the proxy object itself, with whatever fields that object has. The lab tests this last point: a forwarding proxy's final method reads the proxy's own desk field ("unset"), not the target's ("London"). The frameworks you use pick different models. Spring AOP always forwards, whether it built a JDK proxy or a CGLIB subclass. Quarkus ArC intercepts with a generated subclass, and its documentation says self-interception works. The next two sections take them one at a time, from their documentation. This track ran neither framework; the Byte Buddy demo stands in for both models. Watch the two models disagree Run TwoModelsDemo again and compare the subclass model and forwarding model lines, and the constructor count. Predict what the subclass-model log shows if audit is final (in Java, add final; in Kotlin, remove open). Run it. Undo that. Then explain in one sentence why no change inside Forwarding.intercept could make it see the target's this.audit call. The forwarding interceptor only sees calls made on the proxy object, and the target's this.audit is a call on the target, so nothing the proxy does can see it. If the proxy is the object, a call on this goes through the interceptor again. If the proxy forwards, the target's own calls never leave the target. Moving a payments service from Spring Boot to Quarkus can change behaviour without one edited line. A @Transactional ledger method called from the same bean was silently non-transactional under Spring and becomes transactional under ArC, so a batch that used to commit row by row now commits per call, and lock times change. The reverse migration loses transactions instead. In Kotlin, the plugin setup decides whether a bean can be proxied at all: kotlin-spring (or a Spring Initializr project) for Spring, and all-open as the Quarkus Kotlin guide recommends, plus kotlin-jpa for Hibernate entities. Check the generated class with javap rather than trusting the annotation you can see.

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Spring AOP puts a JDK proxy or a CGLIB subclass in front of a separate target
x: Spring's reference documentation says it in one rule: "If the target object to be proxied implements at least one interface, a JDK dynamic proxy is used, and all of the interfaces implemented by the target type are proxied. If the target object does not implement any interfaces, a CGLIB proxy is created which is a runtime-generated subclass of the target type." Spring Boot changes the default. Its AopAutoConfiguration enables class-based proxies unless you set spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false (true in Boot 3.5.x and on main). So in a Boot application, expect CGLIB subclasses even for beans with interfaces. Spring Framework 7.0 adds @Proxyable(INTERFACES) and @Proxyable(TARGET_CLASS) to choose per bean. Either way, the proxy forwards to a separate target bean. Spring calls the code a proxy runs around a method advice, and a method that gets it is "advised". The rules follow from the previous section, and the docs list them for CGLIB proxies: "final classes cannot be proxied", "final methods cannot be advised", "private methods cannot be advised", and package-private methods in a parent class from another package can't be advised either. The constructor is no longer called twice, because Spring creates the CGLIB instance through Objenesis, which skips constructors. That also means a final method, which runs on the proxy object itself, sees a proxy whose fields were never initialized. For @Transactional the documentation spells out the consequences of proxy mode (the default): "only external method calls coming in through the proxy are intercepted", so self-invocation "does not lead to an actual transaction at runtime". The proxy must also be fully initialized, so don't rely on it in @PostConstruct. For class-based proxies, since Spring 6.0 protected and package-visible methods can be transactional too. Interface-based proxies need public methods declared in the interface. The documented ways out of self-invocation, best first: restructure so the call crosses a bean boundary, inject the bean into itself, or ("highly discouraged") AopContext.currentProxy(). AspectJ mode weaves the advice into your class instead, so there is no proxy at all. Kotlin adds one more requirement. The kotlin-spring compiler plugin is "a preconfigured wrapper around the all-open plugin". It opens classes annotated with @Component, @Async, @Transactional, @Cacheable and @SpringBootTest, and, through the @Component meta-annotation, @Service, @Repository, @Controller, @RestController and @Configuration. Projects from start.spring.io enable it by default. Without it, a Kotlin bean is a final class that CGLIB can't subclass. If you write open class by hand and forget open fun, you get the quieter failure: methods that are never advised. Read a class the way CGLIB would Open labs/bytecode/src/main/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l05/FxQuoteService.kt, the lab's starting point. Compile it with ./gradlew :bytecode:classes from labs/. Run javap -p bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/main/workbench/bytecode/l05/FxQuoteService.class. Mark each member: could a CGLIB subclass advise it? Then list what Spring would do with a @Transactional on quote. terminal ./gradlew :bytecode:classes javap -p bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/main/workbench/bytecode/l05/FxQuoteService.class public final class workbench.bytecode.l05.FxQuoteService and every method public final. Nothing can be advised, and the class itself can't be subclassed, so Spring couldn't build a CGLIB proxy for it at all. With kotlin-spring and a Spring annotation on the class, kotlinc would emit the class and its members without final. In the lab you add open by hand. Spring Framework reference: Proxying mechanisms docs kotlin-spring compiler plugin (Kotlin docs) docs

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Quarkus ArC generates its subclasses at build time, and Hibernate makes lazy ones
x: Quarkus's CDI container, ArC, generates its proxy classes while the application builds, not at startup. Its processor names them in comments in its own source: "Foo_Subclass extends Foo implements Subclass" for an intercepted bean, and "Foo_ClientProxy extends Foo implements ClientProxy" for a client proxy. Both are subclasses of your bean class, playing two roles. A client proxy stands in for a normal-scoped bean, one whose instance belongs to a scope such as @ApplicationScoped or @RequestScoped. The docs call it "an object that delegates all method invocations to a target bean instance". It's the forwarding model, used for laziness and scoping: the real instance is created on the first method call, which is also why the docs say to "never read or write a field of a normal scoped bean" from outside. A @Singleton bean has no client proxy. The intercepted subclass is the other model. The Quarkus CDI reference says: "Quarkus supports what is known as intercepted self-invocation or just self-interception - a scenario where CDI bean invokes its own intercepted method from within another method while triggering any associated interceptors." It calls this a non-standard feature, because the CDI specification doesn't define it. Given the generated Foo_Subclass extends Foo, the natural reading is that the subclass instance is the contextual instance (the bean object ArC created for that scope), so this.doSomething() dispatches to the intercepting override. That mechanism is an inference from the docs and the class names; this track didn't trace it in ArC's source. The behaviour is documented. A client proxy in front of an intercepted bean forwards to that subclass instance, so both apply at once. ArC also works around Kotlin's finality. quarkus.arc.transform-unproxyable-classes is true by default, and lets Quarkus proxy final classes and classes with final methods. The Quarkus Kotlin guide still configures all-open for @Path, @ApplicationScoped and JPA entities. Follow the guide, and check with javap and a test before assuming either is unnecessary. Private members are reached by reflection, so the docs recommend package-private instead. Hibernate's lazy proxies are generated at run time with Byte Buddy (ByteBuddyProxyFactory). A proxy "masquerades as a real entity", but holds no state until you call a method, and after the session ends that call throws LazyInitializationException. Its rules are the subclass rules: an entity "must be a non-final class, with a non-private constructor with no parameters", collection fields must use interface types, and "instanceof and typecasts do not work correctly" on a proxy for a polymorphic association, unless you pay for @ConcreteProxy. Your equals() "must be written to accommodate the possibility that the object passed to the equals() might be a proxy". For Kotlin entities, the kotlin-jpa plugin opens them and adds the no-argument constructor. Check yourself before the lab: a Payment loaded lazily through an association is a Hibernate proxy. What does payment.getClass() == Payment.class return, and what happens to an equals that starts with if (getClass() != o.getClass()) return false? (The first is false, because the object is an instance of the generated subclass, so that equals says a proxy and the real row differ.) The most common mistake is believing an interceptor annotation is part of the method, so it must apply on every call. It applies only when the call passes through generated code that can override the method. In a Spring bean that rules out self-calls, private methods, and in Kotlin every method you didn't mark open and the kotlin-spring plugin didn't open. People make it because the annotation sits right on the method, the code compiles, and unit tests that call the class directly can't tell the difference. The fix is to know which model your container uses, keep advised methods open and called from outside the bean (or rely on ArC's documented self-interception in Quarkus), and test through the container with an assertion on the effect, such as a rolled-back row.

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Java and Kotlin
x: A timing subclass proxy in Java and Kotlin TimedSubclass.java public class SuperCallTimer { @RuntimeType public Object intercept(@Origin Method m, @SuperCall Callable<?> original) throws Exception { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { return original.call(); // the original body, on this same object } finally { System.out.println(m.getName() + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) + " ns"); } } } // the service class is open by default in Java; final methods would be skipped FxQuoteService timed = new ByteBuddy() .subclass(FxQuoteService.class) .method(isPublic().and(isDeclaredBy(FxQuoteService.class))) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration() .filter(named("intercept")).to(new SuperCallTimer())) .make().load(FxQuoteService.class.getClassLoader()).getLoaded() .getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(); TimedSubclass.kt class SuperCallTimer { @RuntimeType fun intercept(@Origin m: Method, @SuperCall original: Callable<*>): Any? { val t0 = System.nanoTime() try { return original.call() // the original body, on this same object } finally { println("${m.name} took ${System.nanoTime() - t0} ns") } } } // FxQuoteService and each method must be `open` (or opened by all-open) val timed: FxQuoteService = ByteBuddy() .subclass(FxQuoteService::class.java) .method(isPublic<MethodDescription>().and(isDeclaredBy(FxQuoteService::class.java))) .intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration() .filter(named("intercept")).to(SuperCallTimer())) .make().load(FxQuoteService::class.java.classLoader).loaded .getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() The Byte Buddy calls are identical. The language changes what there is to intercept. A Java class and its methods are open unless marked final. A Kotlin class and its members are final unless marked open, so the same builder silently skips every Kotlin method you didn't open, and refuses the class outright if the class itself is final. Kotlin also needs an explicit type argument for isPublic<MethodDescription>(), because the matcher is generic. In both, filter(named("intercept")) stops Byte Buddy from considering the interceptor's other methods (equals, toString) as delegation targets, which otherwise fails with "Cannot resolve ambiguous delegation".

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Worked example
x: A @Transactional Kotlin method that never starts a transaction A Spring Boot service in Kotlin. Someone added open to the class so the proxy could be created, and the app starts fine. Before reading on: does settle run in a transaction when a controller calls it? @Service open class SettlementService(private val ledger: LedgerRepository) { @Transactional fun settle(batchId: String) { // no `open` ledger.post(batchId) } } // the Java equivalent of what kotlinc generated @Service public class SettlementService { private final LedgerRepository ledger; public SettlementService(LedgerRepository ledger) { this.ledger = ledger; } @Transactional public final void settle(String batchId) { // final: CGLIB can't override it ledger.post(batchId); } } Check the JVM shape. javap -p shows the class without final, which is why Spring could build its CGLIB subclass. settle is still public final void settle(java.lang.String). The Spring docs: "final methods cannot be advised". So the controller calls the proxy, the proxy can't override settle, and the inherited body runs on the proxy object, with no transaction. public class SettlementService { private final LedgerRepository ledger; public SettlementService(LedgerRepository); public final void settle(java.lang.String); // 1. final: never advised } It's worse than a missing transaction. The body runs on the proxy instance, not the target, and Spring creates CGLIB proxies through Objenesis, which skips constructors. On the proxy, ledger was never assigned. The forwarding test in this lesson's lab shows the same effect with Byte Buddy: a final method reads the proxy's own field, not the target's. Expect a NullPointerException on ledger, or silently wrong state. Fix it at the build, not one method at a time. The kotlin-spring plugin opens @Service and @Transactional classes and their members, so settle compiles without final. Then keep calls to settle coming from outside the bean, because the proxy still forwards and a self-call would still skip it. // build.gradle.kts plugins { kotlin("jvm") version "2.4.21" kotlin("plugin.spring") version "2.4.21" // all-open preset for Spring annotations }

x: Time a Kotlin class with Byte Buddy, two ways labs/bytecode/src/main/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l05/FxQuoteService.kt labs/bytecode/src/main/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l05/TimingProxies.kt ./gradlew :bytecode:test --tests 'workbench.bytecode.l05.*' Run the tests once. All six fail with NotImplementedError. In TimingProxies, write a private build(type, interceptor) that does ByteBuddy().subclass(type).method(isPublic<MethodDescription>().and(isDeclaredBy(type))).intercept(MethodDelegation.withDefaultConfiguration().filter(named("intercept")).to(interceptor)).make().load(type.classLoader).loaded.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance(). Write a SuperCallInterceptor(clock, sink) class with @RuntimeType fun intercept(@Origin method: Method, @SuperCall zuper: Callable<*>): Any?. Read the clock, call zuper.call(), read the clock, record, and on an exception record failed = true and rethrow it. Use it in subclassTimed. Run the tests. You should now get Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types. Open FxQuoteService and its three quote methods, but leave deskName final. Run again and watch the self-call test pass. Write a ForwardingInterceptor(target, clock, sink) whose intercept(@Origin method: Method, @AllArguments args: Array<Any?>) times method.invoke(target, *args) and unwraps InvocationTargetException. Use it in forwardingTimed. Run until all six pass. Cannot resolve ambiguous delegation ... to ... toString() or ... means Byte Buddy considered other methods of your interceptor. Keep the filter(named("intercept")). The fake clock moves 1 ms per read. quote should record 5ms in the subclass model (its own two reads, plus two for each inner call) and 1ms in the forwarding model. By the end you can build a subclass proxy with Byte Buddy, tell the two proxy models apart (the proxy is the object, or the proxy forwards to a target), and predict from that whether Spring, Quarkus ArC or Hibernate will intercept a call, including self-calls and Kotlin's final members.
