h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Quiz
x: A Spring Boot application has class FeeService implements FeeCalculator with a @Transactional method, and no AOP settings. What kind of proxy does Spring Boot give other beans by default? A JDK dynamic proxy, because the class implements an interface A CGLIB subclass of FeeService, because Boot sets proxyTargetClass=true unless spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false No proxy: @Transactional is applied by an agent A Byte Buddy subclass Spring Framework on its own would pick a JDK proxy for a bean with interfaces. Spring Boot's AopAutoConfiguration enables class-based proxies by default. Either kind forwards to a separate target, so the self-invocation rules are the same. Kotlin: @Service open class Payouts { @Transactional fun pay(id: String) { repo.save(id) } }, without the kotlin-spring plugin. A controller calls payouts.pay("p-1"). What happens? pay runs in a transaction Startup fails: Spring can't proxy the class pay is final, so the CGLIB proxy can't advise it. The body runs on the proxy object, without a transaction, where repo may be null It compiles to an interface-based proxy open class lets CGLIB subclass it, but each member is still final unless marked open. A final method is inherited unchanged, so calling it on the proxy runs the body on the proxy instance, which Spring created through Objenesis without running constructors. kotlin-spring opens the members as well. In a Quarkus @ApplicationScoped bean, settleAll() calls this.settle(id), and settle is @Transactional. Which statement matches the Quarkus documentation? The inner call is intercepted: ArC supports intercepted self-invocation, as a non-standard feature The inner call skips the interceptor, as in Spring It depends on quarkus.arc.transform-unproxyable-classes Quarkus rejects self-invocation at build time The Quarkus CDI reference says ArC supports self-interception: calling an intercepted method from another method of the same bean still triggers its interceptors. It's non-standard because the CDI spec doesn't define it. transform-unproxyable-classes is about final classes and methods, not self-calls. Which change makes a class usable for Hibernate's lazy proxies? Mark the entity final so Hibernate can inline it Declare collection fields as ArrayList instead of List Make equals compare getClass() of both objects Give the entity a non-private no-argument constructor and keep it non-final Hibernate generates a subclass of the entity, so the class must not be final and needs a non-private no-arg constructor. Collection fields must use interface types, because Hibernate puts its own collection classes there. A getClass() comparison in equals fails against a proxy, whose class is the generated subclass. From Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy: you call Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[]{FxQuoteService.class}, h) where FxQuoteService is a class with no interface. What happens? A subclass proxy is generated instead IllegalArgumentException: ... FxQuoteService is not an interface It works, but only public methods are dispatched UndeclaredThrowableException JDK proxies implement interfaces and extend java.lang.reflect.Proxy, so they can't extend your class. To intercept a class, a library must generate a subclass, which is what Byte Buddy, Spring's CGLIB, ArC and Hibernate do.

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Explain it back
x: A colleague says: "Spring uses a CGLIB subclass, and a subclass overrides methods, so self-calls must be intercepted." Explain why that's wrong, why Quarkus behaves differently, and what Kotlin adds to the picture.

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Key terms
x: Subclass proxy A generated subclass that overrides methods to add behaviour; it works for classes, not only interfaces. Byte Buddy A library for generating and changing classes at run time; Hibernate and many tools build on it. CGLIB An older bytecode library, now unmaintained; Spring ships its own patched copy for class-based proxies. Objenesis A library that creates objects without running constructors; Spring uses it for CGLIB proxy instances. Client proxy ArC's Foo_ClientProxy: a subclass that forwards each call to the real bean instance for its scope. Self-interception Intercepting a call a bean makes to its own method. ArC supports it; Spring's proxy mode doesn't. all-open A Kotlin compiler plugin that makes classes with chosen annotations, and their members, non-final. What can a subclass proxy never intercept? Anything it can't override: a final class (no proxy at all), final methods and private methods. Those run as written. Why does a plain Kotlin class fail with Byte Buddy, CGLIB or Hibernate? Kotlin classes and members are final by default. Byte Buddy says Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types. In the subclass model (proxy is the object), is a self-call this.audit() intercepted? Yes. this is the generated subclass, so the call dispatches to its overriding method and the interceptor runs. On a forwarding proxy (Spring style), where does a final method run? On the proxy object itself, with the proxy's own fields, which Spring's Objenesis-created proxies never initialized. Which proxy does Spring Boot use by default for a bean that implements an interface? A CGLIB subclass: Boot sets proxyTargetClass=true unless spring.aop.proxy-target-class=false. What does Quarkus ArC do about self-invocation of an intercepted method? It intercepts it (self-interception), a documented, non-standard CDI behaviour. Spring's proxy mode doesn't. Which Kotlin plugin opens Spring beans, and which opens JPA entities? kotlin-spring (an all-open preset) for Spring annotations; kotlin-jpa for entities, which also adds no-arg constructors.

h: Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors · Go deeper
x: Byte Buddy can also change a class instead of subclassing it. rebase(Clock.class) keeps the original method body under a new private name, now$original$..., and generates a new now that can call it. The Javadoc likens it to "creating a subclass where the subclass is later merged with the original class file". redefine(Clock.class) replaces now and discards the original body. Both produce a class with the original name, so you can only load them where the original isn't loaded yet, or rename them, or, in a running JVM, use an agent. That's lesson 7, where Byte Buddy's Advice comes in. Advice inlines your code into the existing method body instead of adding accessor methods and helper classes, which is what retransforming a loaded class requires. The subclass's helper methods have a cost you can see. Each intercepted method gets an $accessor$ twin so the interceptor can call the original, and @SuperCall creates a small Callable per call. In this track's single JMH run, a Byte Buddy subclass with @SuperCall measured about 0.9 ns per call against 0.8 ns direct, and the JDK proxy about 4.3 ns. The numbers are noisy and indicative only, but the order is clear. Quarkus can intercept some static methods too. The CDI reference allows an interceptor binding on a non-private static method, with three limits: only method-level bindings count, private static methods are never intercepted, and InvocationContext#getTarget() returns null. For producer methods whose result needs interceptors, InterceptionProxy generates, at build time, a subclass that intercepts and forwards. The class must not be final, must not have non-private final methods, and needs a non-private no-argument constructor. These are the subclass rules once again.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · A class file is a byte array with a fixed layout
x: Every tool in this track reads or writes the same format. That includes javap, the verifier, Proxy, LambdaMetafactory, Byte Buddy and agents. Here is the start of java/lang/Object.class on JDK 21, printed by this section's demo: ca fe ba be 00 00 00 41 00 7c magic minor major constant_pool_count The magic number 0xCAFEBABE marks a class file. The major version is 0x41, which is 65, and Java 21 wrote it. From Java 5 on, the Java version is the major version minus 44. Then comes constant_pool_count, and after it the constant pool itself, the table of names and constants from lesson 2. All numbers are big-endian. DataInputStream reads them, so the first fields take four lines: Java DataInputStream in = new DataInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)); int magic = in.readInt(); // u4: 0xCAFEBABE int minor = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2 int major = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2: 65 = Java 21, 69 = Java 25 int poolCount = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1 Kotlin val input = DataInputStream(ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)) val magic = input.readInt() // u4: 0xCAFEBABE val minor = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2 val major = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2: 65 = Java 21, 69 = Java 25 val poolCount = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1 The constant pool is harder. Each entry starts with a one-byte tag, and the tag decides how many bytes follow: a Utf8 entry has a length, a Class entry has two bytes, a Methodref has four. A Long or Double entry takes two pool indexes, which is why lesson 2's pool had no entry 8. After the pool come the access flags, then this_class, an index that points at a Class entry, then the superclass, interfaces, fields, methods and attributes. In the lab you write this walk yourself and check it against a real class-file library. That is the problem the ClassFile API solves. Any framework that generates or changes classes has to read and write this format exactly. The format also gains a major version with every JDK release, every six months, and sometimes new entry kinds or attributes. Until JDK 24 the JDK had no public library for it. Frameworks bundled ASM (Byte Buddy contains its own copy) and had to ship a new release for each new class-file version. The JDK carried a private copy of ASM too, and it's gone from the jdk-25-ga source tree. Read three class-file headers Before you run anything, predict the major version of ClassFileHeader.class (built by the labs), of java.lang.Object on the JDK you're using, and of kotlin.Unit in the Kotlin standard library. Run ClassFileHeader, then its Kotlin twin. If you have both JDK 21 and JDK 25 installed, run the Java version on each: java -cp bytecode/build/classes/java/demo:bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.bytecode.l06.ClassFileHeader. ClassFileHeader.java package workbench.bytecode.l06; import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream; import java.io.DataInputStream; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.InputStream; import java.util.HexFormat; /** The first ten bytes of three class files: magic, version and constant pool size. */ public class ClassFileHeader { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { show(ClassFileHeader.class); // compiled by the labs build with release 21 show(HeaderMarker.class); // compiled by kotlinc in the same build (from ClassFileHeader.kt) show(Object.class); // from the JDK you are running } static void show(Class<?> c) throws IOException { byte[] bytes; try (InputStream in = c.getResourceAsStream(c.getSimpleName() + ".class")) { bytes = in.readAllBytes(); } DataInputStream in = new DataInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)); int magic = in.readInt(); // u4 int minor = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2 int major = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2 int poolCount = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1 System.out.printf("%-34s %s magic=%X version=%d.%d (Java %d) pool entries=%d size=%d bytes%n", c.getName(), HexFormat.ofDelimiter(" ").formatHex(bytes, 0, 10), magic, major, minor, major - 44, poolCount - 1, bytes.length); } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l06.ClassFileHeader labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l06/ClassFileHeader.java ClassFileHeader.kt package workbench.bytecode.l06 import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream import java.io.DataInputStream import java.util.HexFormat /** A Kotlin class for the Java twin to read. */ class HeaderMarker /** The first ten bytes of three class files: magic, version and constant pool size. */ fun main() { show(HeaderMarker::class.java) // compiled by kotlinc in the labs build with jvmTarget 21 show(Unit::class.java) // the Kotlin standard library jar show(Any::class.java) // java.lang.Object, from the JDK you are running } private fun show(c: Class<*>) { val bytes = c.getResourceAsStream(c.simpleName + ".class")!!.use { it.readAllBytes() } val input = DataInputStream(ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)) val magic = input.readInt() // u4 val minor = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2 val major = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2 val poolCount = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1 println("%-34s %s magic=%X version=%d.%d (Java %d) pool entries=%d size=%d bytes".format( c.name, HexFormat.ofDelimiter(" ").formatHex(bytes, 0, 10), magic, major, minor, major - 44, poolCount - 1, bytes.size)) } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l06.ClassFileHeaderKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l06/ClassFileHeader.kt Every line starts with ca fe ba be. The labs' own classes (Java and Kotlin) are version=65.0 (Java 21), because the build uses release 21 and jvmTarget 21. java.lang.Object is 65 on JDK 21 and 69 on JDK 25, so the same program reports the JDK it runs on. kotlin.Unit is 52.0 (Java 8): the standard library is compiled for Java 8, so it runs everywhere. JVM Specification SE 25, chapter 4: The class File Format docs A class file is a filled-in form with a strict layout: boxes in a fixed order, a numbered glossary at the front (the constant pool), and every later box that needs a name writes a glossary number instead. Reading by hand means walking the glossary line by line, remembering that some entries take two lines. The ClassFile API is a clerk who reads the form into a folder of typed cards (models and elements), lets you hand back a new folder card by card (builders), and copies a form while you say "keep, drop, or replace" for each card (transforms). The analogy breaks at checking: a clerk would notice a nonsense answer. The builder writes whatever you hand it, and only verify asks whether the result is type-safe, never whether it's correct.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · The ClassFile API parses bytes into an immutable model
x: The package java.lang.classfile is the JDK's own class-file library. It was a preview feature in JDK 22 (JEP 457) and JDK 23 (JEP 466), and became final in JDK 24 (JEP 484). The labs compile with release 21, so this lesson's ClassFile API code lives in single-file programs under labs/bytecode/preview/, which you run with java File.java on JDK 24 or later. On JDK 21 they fail with package java.lang.classfile does not exist. Everything starts at ClassFile.of(). Its parse method turns bytes into a ClassModel: Java ClassModel cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes); System.out.println(cm.thisClass().asInternalName() + " major " + cm.majorVersion()); for (MethodModel m : cm.methods()) { long invokes = m.code() .map(code -> code.elementStream().filter(e -> e instanceof InvokeInstruction).count()) .orElse(0L); System.out.println(m.methodName().stringValue() + m.methodType().stringValue() + " invokes=" + invokes); } Kotlin val cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes) println("${cm.thisClass().asInternalName()} major ${cm.majorVersion()}") for (m in cm.methods()) { val invokes = m.code() .map { code -> code.elementStream().filter { it is InvokeInstruction }.count() } .orElse(0L) println("${m.methodName().stringValue()}${m.methodType().stringValue()} invokes=$invokes") } A model is an immutable description of one part of a class file. There are models for the class, each field, each method, and each method's code. The package documentation adds two properties. A ClassModel "is inflated lazily; most parts of the classfile are not parsed until they are actually needed". So a malformed method can parse fine and throw IllegalArgumentException only when you open it. Each model can also be read as a sequence of elements. A class's elements are its methods, fields and attributes. A method's code is a sequence of instructions, labels and other code elements. Each instruction is an object with a type you can match on, such as InvokeInstruction, ConstantInstruction or InvokeDynamicInstruction. The rest of the API is built on that: reading walks elements, building emits elements, and transforming maps elements to elements. Names and types come back as constant-pool entries (methodName() is a Utf8Entry, which is why the code calls stringValue()). When you build, you pass symbolic descriptions from java.lang.constant, such as ClassDesc.of("FeeRule") and MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), and the library creates the entries. Tour lesson 2's class with the ClassFile API This needs JDK 24 or later. From labs/, make sure lesson 2's demo was built (./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l02.StackDemo), then run the command below. The Kotlin twin needs kotlinc running on JDK 24 or later. Compare the constant-pool counts with the javap -v listing you read in lesson 2. describe builds a string and calls nothing else, yet its count is 0. Before reading on: which instruction does it contain, and why didn't the filter count it? ClassFileTour.java (JDK 24+) // JDK 24 or later (the ClassFile API is final since JDK 24, JEP 484). From labs/: // java bytecode/preview/ClassFileTour.java [path/to/Some.class] // With no argument it reads StackDemo.class from lesson 2 (run that demo once first), // or java.lang.Integer from the running JDK if the file isn't there. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile; import java.lang.classfile.ClassModel; import java.lang.classfile.MethodModel; import java.lang.classfile.constantpool.PoolEntry; import java.lang.classfile.instruction.InvokeInstruction; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; public class ClassFileTour { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Path p = Path.of(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class"); byte[] bytes = Files.exists(p) ? Files.readAllBytes(p) : Integer.class.getResourceAsStream("Integer.class").readAllBytes(); // 1. parse: an immutable model, inflated lazily as you ask for parts ClassModel cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes); System.out.println(cm.thisClass().asInternalName() + " extends " + cm.superclass().map(c -> c.asInternalName()).orElse("-") + ", major " + cm.majorVersion()); // 2. the constant pool, counted by kind of entry Map<String, Integer> kinds = new TreeMap<>(); for (PoolEntry e : cm.constantPool()) { kinds.merge(e.getClass().getInterfaces()[0].getSimpleName(), 1, Integer::sum); } System.out.println("constant pool: " + kinds); // 3. methods, and the invoke instructions inside each one for (MethodModel m : cm.methods()) { long invokes = m.code() .map(code -> code.elementStream().filter(e -> e instanceof InvokeInstruction).count()) .orElse(0L); System.out.println(" " + m.methodName().stringValue() + m.methodType().stringValue() + " invokes=" + invokes); } } } java bytecode/preview/ClassFileTour.java labs/bytecode/preview/ClassFileTour.java ClassFileTour.kt (JDK 24+) // JDK 24 or later, with kotlinc running on that JDK. From labs/: // kotlinc bytecode/preview/ClassFileTour.kt -jvm-target 21 -include-runtime -d build/cftour.jar // java -jar build/cftour.jar [path/to/Some.class] // With no argument it reads StackDemo.class from lesson 2, or java.lang.Integer from the JDK. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile import java.lang.classfile.instruction.InvokeInstruction import java.nio.file.Files import java.nio.file.Path fun main(args: Array<String>) { val p = Path.of(args.firstOrNull() ?: "bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class") val bytes = if (Files.exists(p)) h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Builders write a class from lambdas, and verify checks it before you load it
x: To generate a class you don't create builder objects yourself. You pass lambdas, and the library hands each one the builder for that level: a ClassBuilder for the class, a CodeBuilder for a method body. The CodeBuilder has one method per instruction, so a method body reads like the javap listings from lesson 2: Java byte[] feeRule = ClassFile.of().build(ClassDesc.of("FeeRule"), clb -> clb .withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_FINAL) .withMethodBody("fee", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob .lload(0) // the amount, slots 0 and 1 .ldc(290L) // basis points .lmul() .ldc(10_000L) .ldiv() .lreturn())); Class<?> c = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(feeRule); // load it next to this class Kotlin val feeRule = ClassFile.of().build(ClassDesc.of("FeeRule")) { clb -> clb.withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC or ClassFile.ACC_FINAL) clb.withMethodBody("fee", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC or ClassFile.ACC_STATIC) { cob -> cob.lload(0) // the amount, slots 0 and 1 .loadConstant(290L) // basis points (Kotlin: see below) .lmul() .loadConstant(10_000L) .ldiv() .lreturn() } } val c = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(feeRule) // load it next to this class fee(125000) returns 3625, the fee you computed by hand in lesson 2. MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass loads the bytes as a class in the same package and loader as the calling class. The builder writes what you tell it to, including nonsense. A method declared to return int that pushes a String builds without complaint. Lesson 1 showed what happens when you load such a class: defineClass can succeed and the VerifyError comes later. ClassFile.of().verify(bytes) runs the verifier's checks on the bytes before any of that, and returns a list of errors: verify(FeeRule): [] verify(Broken): [java.lang.VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack in Broken::answer() @2 (integer_type is not assignable from java/lang/String)] Kotlin has one trap here. ldc takes a java.lang.constant.ConstantDesc, and Java's String and Long implement that interface. Kotlin's String and Long types don't show it, so cob.ldc("forty-two") doesn't compile in Kotlin. Use loadConstant(310L), which has overloads for primitives, or pass a constant-pool entry: cob.ldc(cob.constantPool().stringEntry("forty-two")). h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · A transform is a flatMap over elements
x: Changing an existing class is where the element model pays off. The package documentation puts it in one sentence: "Transformation can be viewed as a 'flatMap' operation on the sequence of elements; for every element, we could pass it through unchanged, drop it, or replace it with one or more elements." A ClassTransform sees class elements, and a CodeTransform sees the instructions of one method. Inside a transform you hand each element to the builder: builder.with(element) passes it through, calling nothing drops it, and calling other builder methods replaces it. This one drops every debug... method and changes the rate constant in every method body: Java CodeTransform newRate = (cob, element) -> { if (element instanceof ConstantInstruction ci && Long.valueOf(290L).equals(ci.constantValue())) { cob.ldc(310L); // replace } else { cob.with(element); // pass through } }; ClassTransform transform = ClassTransform .dropping(e -> e instanceof MethodModel m && m.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug")) .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(newRate)); byte[] v2 = cf.transformClass(cf.parse(feeRule), ClassDesc.of("FeeRuleV2"), transform); Kotlin val newRate = CodeTransform { cob, element -> if (element is ConstantInstruction && element.constantValue().equals(290L)) { cob.loadConstant(310L) // replace } else { cob.with(element) // pass through } } val transform = ClassTransform .dropping { it is MethodModel && it.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug") } .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(newRate)) val v2 = cf.transformClass(cf.parse(feeRule), ClassDesc.of("FeeRuleV2"), transform) The result, FeeRuleV2, has only fee, and fee(125000) returns 3875. Everything the transform passed through is copied, and that's also the default: a transform that does nothing reproduces the class. The JDK writes its own generated classes with this API. ProxyGenerator switched from the internal ASM to java.lang.classfile in JDK 23, and the lambda spinner InnerClassLambdaMetafactory in JDK 24. So the $Proxy0 from lesson 4 and the $$Lambda classes from lesson 3 are built by the code you just ran. Who should use it? Tools that only need to run on JDK 24 and later can drop their ASM dependency, because the API always matches the JDK it runs on. Libraries that must support older JDKs can't do that. Byte Buddy, whose regular jar targets Java 8 and whose -jdk5 jar targets Java 5, keeps its bundled ASM and bridges to the ClassFile API when it's there (release notes for 1.16.0: "Include support for JDK Class File API"). With both constants replaced: 125000 x 310 / 1000 = 38750. With only dropping, FeeRuleV2 still loses debugTrace, but fee keeps the 290 constant and returns 3625 again. A transform walks the elements and decides, one at a time, to pass, drop or replace each one. The common mistake is treating verify (or a class that loads) as proof the generated code is right. The verifier checks types and stack shapes: that lreturn finds a long, that a method returns what its descriptor promises. A builder that leaves an extra value on the stack, pushes the wrong constant or forgets a division can still pass, as the ldiv experiment showed. People make the mistake because a VerifyError feels like the compiler's error checking. The fix is to test generated classes like any code: load them, call them with known inputs, and assert the results, as the lab's tests do against an independent reader.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Java and Kotlin
x: Reading a class's name in Java and Kotlin, by hand and with the API ThisClass.java // by hand (any JDK): walk the pool, then read this_class static String thisClass(byte[] bytes) { return ClassFileFacts.thisClass(bytes); // the lab's DataInputStream walk } // with the ClassFile API (JDK 24+) static String thisClassWithApi(byte[] bytes) { return ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).thisClass().asInternalName(); } ThisClass.kt // by hand (any JDK): walk the pool, then read this_class fun thisClass(bytes: ByteArray): String = ClassFileFacts.thisClass(bytes) // the lab's DataInputStream walk // with the ClassFile API (JDK 24+) fun thisClassWithApi(bytes: ByteArray): String = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).thisClass().asInternalName() Same bytes, same answer, and the API version is one line because the library does the pool walk for you, lazily. The language differences are small but real. Kotlin calls the API through ordinary SAM conversion for its Consumer and CodeTransform parameters, and uses or instead of | for access flags. Kotlin's mapped String and Long types don't expose Java's ConstantDesc, so ldc("...") needs a constant-pool entry or loadConstant instead. Compiling Kotlin against the API also needs kotlinc to run on (or point -jdk-home at) JDK 24 or later, whatever -jvm-target you choose.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Worked example
x: Find the jar that broke the deploy The payments service starts on JDK 21 and dies at once. Which part of the message tells you what to look for? Error: LinkageError occurred while loading main class com.acme.fx.RateTable java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: com/acme/fx/RateTable has been compiled by a more recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 69.0), this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 65.0 Class file version 69.0 is Java 25 (69 - 44). Something in the image was compiled for JDK 25. Here only one class is named, but a jar can mix versions, so check every class. Read each entry's header, with the lab's code. try (JarFile jar = new JarFile(path.toFile())) { jar.stream() .filter(e -> e.getName().endsWith(".class")) .forEach(e -> { try (InputStream in = jar.getInputStream(e)) { // 1. read magic, minor, major from the first 10 bytes ClassFileFacts.Header h = ClassFileFacts.header(in.readNBytes(10)); // 2. report anything newer than the runtime if (h.major() > 65) System.out.println(e.getName() + " -> Java " + ClassFileFacts.javaVersion(h.major())); } catch (IOException ex) { throw new UncheckedIOException(ex); } }); } JarFile(path.toFile()).use { jar -> jar.stream() .filter { it.name.endsWith(".class") } .forEach { e -> // 1. read magic, minor, major from the first 10 bytes val h = jar.getInputStream(e).use { ClassFileFacts.header(it.readNBytes(10)) } // 2. report anything newer than the runtime if (h.major() > 65) println("${e.name} -> Java ${ClassFileFacts.javaVersion(h.major())}") } } Two caveats. A multi-release jar keeps newer classes under META-INF/versions/25/, and those are allowed: the JVM only loads them on JDK 25. So skip that prefix, or you'll get false alarms. And module-info.class has a version too. When the culprit is your own module, the fix is in the build: compile with --release 21 (Gradle: options.release.set(21)) and jvmTarget = 21 for Kotlin, as the labs do, so the compilers also refuse JDK 22+ APIs.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Lab
x: Read the constant pool by hand labs/bytecode/src/main/java/workbench/bytecode/l06/ClassFileFacts.java ./gradlew :bytecode:test --tests 'workbench.bytecode.l06.*' Run the tests once. All seven fail. Read the class-file layout and the tag table in the Javadoc of ClassFileFacts. Write header: wrap the bytes in a DataInputStream, read the int magic and throw IllegalArgumentException (with "magic" in the message) if it isn't 0xCAFEBABE, then read three unsigned shorts. Write javaVersion as major - 44, rejecting anything below 49. Write a private pool walk: for i from 1 to count - 1, read the tag and either keep the value (readUTF() for tag 1, the name index for tag 7) or skip the right number of bytes. After a tag 5 or 6, add one to i. Write referencedClasses with the walk: the Utf8 string at each Class entry's name index. Write thisClass: after the walk, read access_flags, then this_class, and look up its name. Run the tests until all seven pass. The expected answers come from ASM, so a pass means your reader agrees with a production library on Java, Kotlin and JDK classes. A wrong byte count anywhere in the walk shifts everything after it, so the symptom is usually unknown constant pool tag far from the bug. Check the table entry for the last tag you handled. DataInputStream.readUTF() reads a two-byte length and then the bytes in the class file's own "modified UTF-8". That's exactly a Utf8 entry, so you don't decode anything yourself. Forgetting the extra index after Long and Double passes for some classes and fails for Fixture, which has both. All seven tests in ClassFileFactsTest pass. By the end you can read a class file's header and constant pool by hand, and with the ClassFile API (final in JDK 24) parse a class into a model, build a new class from builder lambdas, verify it before loading, and write a transform that drops or replaces elements.

x: A class file's major version is 61. Which is the oldest JDK that can load it? JDK 11 JDK 17 JDK 21 JDK 16 From Java 5 on, the Java version is major minus 44, so 61 is Java 17. A JVM loads class files up to its own major version: JDK 17 and later load it, and JDK 16 rejects it with UnsupportedClassVersionError. Your pool walk handles every tag but forgets that Long takes two indexes. What happens on a class with a long constant? Nothing: the second index is empty, so skipping it is optional readUTF throws immediately Every index after the long is off by one, and the loop reads one entry too many, past the end of the pool: names come out wrong, or the walk fails on an unknown tag Only the long's value is wrong You skipped the right number of bytes, but the numbering is off by one. Every later entry gets an index one too small, so a Class entry's name index points at the wrong string, and the loop expects one more entry than the file has, so it reads the access flags as if they were a tag. The symptom is far from the cause, usually an unknown tag or garbage names. That's why the lab's Fixture has both a long and a double. ClassFile.of().verify(bytes) returns an empty list for your generated class. What do you know? The class computes the right results The class has already been loaded The class will run on every JDK The bytecode is type-safe for the verifier, for example every return finds the type its descriptor promises, but it may still compute the wrong thing Verification checks types and stack shapes, not meaning. A fee method with a missing ldiv still verifies and returns the wrong number. A class verified today can also fail to load on an older JDK because of its version number. You want a build-time check, running on JDK 25, that fails if any class in your service references java/util/Random. Which tool fits best? ClassFile.of().parse(bytes) over every class file, checking the class entries in each constant pool A JDK dynamic proxy around every class A Java agent that retransforms every loaded class Class.forName on every class with initialization Every class a class mentions has a Class entry in its constant pool, so parsing the files is enough. No class needs to be loaded, initialized or run. Proxies intercept calls at run time, agents change loaded classes, and Class.forName runs static initializers, which is the last thing a build check should do. From Reading bytecode: javap shows #7 = Long 10000l and then #9 = InvokeDynamic ..., with no entry 8. Why? javap hides unused entries Entry 8 was optimized away by the JIT A Long (and a Double) entry takes two constant-pool indexes, so 8 is the second half of 7 Entry 8 is reserved for the class's own name The class-file format numbers 8-byte constants as two entries, and the next entry's index skips one. Any reader that walks the pool must add an extra step after each Long or Double, which is the bug the lab's fixture is designed to catch.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Explain it back
x: Explain to a teammate why a hand-written constant-pool walk is fiddly, what the ClassFile API's model, builder and transform each give you, and why the API's arrival in JDK 24 matters for frameworks.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Key terms
x: Magic number The first four bytes of every class file, 0xCAFEBABE. Major version The class-file version number; minus 44 it gives the Java version that wrote it. ClassFile API The JDK's own library for reading, writing and transforming class files, in java.lang.classfile, final in JDK 24. Model An immutable description of part of a class file (class, method, field, code), parsed lazily. Element One item in a model's sequence: a method of a class, or an instruction of a method's code. Transform A function that sees each element and passes it on, drops it, or replaces it while copying a class. ClassDesc A symbolic description of a class (from java.lang.constant) used when building, such as ClassDesc.of("FeeRule"). What are the first four fields of a class file? u4 magic 0xCAFEBABE, u2 minor version, u2 major version, u2 constant_pool_count. How do you get the Java version from a class file's major version? Subtract 44 (from Java 5 on): 52 is 8, 61 is 17, 65 is 21, 69 is 25. Which constant-pool entries take two indexes? Long (tag 5) and Double (tag 6). Since which JDK is java.lang.classfile a final API, and under which JEP? JDK 24, JEP 484. It was a preview in JDK 22 (JEP 457) and JDK 23 (JEP 466). In a ClassFile API transform, how do you keep, drop and replace an element? Keep: builder.with(element). Drop: don't pass it on. Replace: call other builder methods instead. What does ClassFile.of().verify(bytes) guarantee when it returns an empty list? That the bytecode passes the verifier's type checks. Not that it computes the right result. Why does cob.ldc("x") not compile in Kotlin? Kotlin's String type doesn't expose Java's ConstantDesc interface. Use cob.ldc(cob.constantPool().stringEntry("x")) or loadConstant for primitives.

h: Generating and transforming classes with the ClassFile API · Go deeper
x: Three details from the API's documentation and this track's runs. Models are lazy, and that can surprise you. parse reads little more than the header. A method's code is inflated when you ask for it, so a malformed method can parse fine and fail with IllegalArgumentException later, when you iterate its elements. If you run untrusted or generated bytes through the API, iterate or verify them up front. The ClassFile API and Byte Buddy are complements. Byte Buddy works at the level of types and methods (subclass this, intercept those methods with that delegate), and it runs on JDK 8. The ClassFile API works at the level of the class file (these instructions, that constant), and it needs JDK 24. Byte Buddy's README says that "as of 1.17.0, support will extend to new Java versions unless previously unknown class file features are discovered. This is possible through Byte Buddy's support of the Class File API." So on a new JDK, Byte Buddy can lean on the JDK's own reader and writer. ConstantPool is Iterable<PoolEntry>, not a collection, so Java needs StreamSupport to stream it, while Kotlin's Iterable extensions work directly: Java // JDK 24+: every Class entry a class references, with the API Set<String> names = StreamSupport.stream(ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).constantPool().spliterator(), false) .filter(e -> e instanceof ClassEntry) .map(e -> ((ClassEntry) e).asInternalName()) .collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new)); Kotlin // JDK 24+: every Class entry a class references, with the API val names = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).constantPool() .filterIsInstance<ClassEntry>() .map { it.asInternalName() } .toSortedSet()

h: Java agents and instrumentation · An agent is a class the JVM hands an Instrumentation object
x: Lessons 4 and 5 added behaviour by wrapping objects. That needs an interface or a non-final class, and it misses self-calls whenever the proxy forwards. It also only works on objects you create through the proxy. Sometimes you need more: timing a method inside a library jar, or tracing a framework class you don't construct yourself. An agent gets access to the class instead of the object. An agent is an ordinary class with a special entry point. The JVM calls it with a java.lang.instrument.Instrumentation, the JDK's handle for watching and changing classes. There are three ways to start one: java -javaagent:agent.jar[=args] calls the agent's premain(String args, Instrumentation inst) before your main. You can repeat the option, and the agents start in the order given. An executable jar can name an agent in its manifest with Launcher-Agent-Class. The JVM calls its agentmain before the application's main. A tool can attach to a JVM that is already running and load an agent jar. The JVM calls agentmain(String, Instrumentation). The next section covers this case. The agent jar's manifest names the class: Premain-Class or Agent-Class. Can-Retransform-Classes: true asks for the right to change classes that are already loaded. The first thing most agents do is register a ClassFileTransformer. The JVM calls its transform method with the bytes of every class it is about to define from then on, and the method returns either new bytes or null, which means "no change". The smallest useful agent changes nothing and only watches: Java public static void premain(String args, Instrumentation inst) { inst.addTransformer(new ClassFileTransformer() { @Override public byte[] transform(ClassLoader loader, String className, Class<?> redefined, ProtectionDomain domain, byte[] bytes) { System.out.println("[agent] loading " + className + " (" + bytes.length + " bytes)"); return null; // null: leave the class as it is } }); } Kotlin @JvmStatic fun premain(args: String?, inst: Instrumentation) { inst.addTransformer(object : ClassFileTransformer { override fun transform( loader: ClassLoader?, className: String?, redefined: Class<*>?, domain: ProtectionDomain?, bytes: ByteArray, ): ByteArray? { println("[agent] loading $className (${bytes.size} bytes)") return null // null: leave the class as it is } }) } The class files that transform receives are the bytes from lesson 6. An agent that wants to change a class rewrites them, with the ClassFile API on JDK 24 and later, or with a library such as Byte Buddy. A startup agent sees almost every class of your application, because nearly all of them load after premain returns. Note ClassFileTransformer uses an anonymous class above, not a lambda: both of its transform methods are default methods, so it isn't a functional interface. Watch a startup agent Read CountingAgent and AgentTarget. Predict which workbench/ classes the agent will report, and in which order relative to the two main: lines. Run StartupAgentDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It writes a jar that holds only a manifest with Premain-Class, then starts a second JVM with -javaagent:<jar>=payments. Find the arguments string, the number of classes already loaded when premain ran, and the total the transformer saw. StartupAgentDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l07; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.jar.Attributes; import java.util.jar.JarOutputStream; import java.util.jar.Manifest; /** Builds a one-line agent jar and starts a second JVM with -javaagent, so you can watch premain run. */ public class StartupAgentDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // 1. an agent jar needs a manifest naming the agent class; the class itself is on the class path Path jar = Files.createTempFile("counting-agent", ".jar"); Manifest manifest = new Manifest(); manifest.getMainAttributes().put(Attributes.Name.MANIFEST_VERSION, "1.0"); manifest.getMainAttributes().putValue("Premain-Class", CountingAgent.class.getName()); try (JarOutputStream out = new JarOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(jar), manifest)) { // no entries needed } // 2. java -javaagent:<jar>=payments -cp <this class path> AgentTarget String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); Process child = new ProcessBuilder(java, "-javaagent:" + jar + "=payments", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), AgentTarget.class.getName()) .redirectErrorStream(true) .start(); child.getInputStream().transferTo(System.out); System.out.println("child JVM exited with " + child.waitFor()); Files.delete(jar); } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l07.StartupAgentDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l07/StartupAgentDemo.java StartupAgentDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l07 import java.lang.instrument.ClassFileTransformer import java.lang.instrument.Instrumentation import java.nio.file.Files import java.security.ProtectionDomain import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.jar.Attributes import java.util.jar.JarOutputStream import java.util.jar.Manifest /** A startup agent: the JVM calls premain before main. It watches classes load and changes nothing. */ object KCountingAgent { @JvmStatic fun premain(args: String?, inst: Instrumentation) { println("[agent] premain args=$args, classes already loaded: ${inst.allLoadedClasses.size}") val seen = AtomicInteger() inst.addTransformer(object : ClassFileTransformer { override fun transform( loader: ClassLoader?, className: String?, classBeingRedefined: Class<*>?, domain: ProtectionDomain?, classfileBuffer: ByteArray, ): ByteArray? { seen.incrementAndGet() if (className?.startsWith("workbench/") == true) { println("[agent] loading $className (${classfileBuffer.size} bytes)") } return null // null means "no change" } }) Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(Thread { println("[agent] transformer saw ${seen.get()} class definitions") }) } } data class KPayment(val id: String, val amountMinor: Long) /** The program the startup agent watches. */ object KAgentTarget { @JvmStatic fun main(args: Array<String>) { println("main: started") val p = KPayment("p-1", 1_250) // KPayment is loaded here, on first use println("main: $p") } } /** Builds a one-line agent jar and starts a second JVM with -javaagent, so you can watch premain run. */ fun main() { // 1. an agent jar needs a manifest naming the agent class; the class itself is on the class path val jar = Files.createTempFile("counting-agent", ".jar") val manifest = Manifest().apply { mainAttributes[Attributes.Name.MANIFEST_VERSION] = "1.0" mainAttributes.putValue("Premain-Class", KCountingAgent::class.java.name) } JarOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(jar), manifest).use { } // no entries needed // 2. java -javaagent:<jar>=payments -cp <this class path> KAgentTarget val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val child = ProcessBuilder(java, "-javaagent:$jar=payments", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), KAgentTarget::class.java.name) .redirectErrorStream(true) .start() child.inputStream.transferTo(System.out) println("child JVM exited with ${child.waitFor()}") Files.delete(jar) } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l07.StartupAgentDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l07/StartupAgentDemo.kt [agent] premain args=payments, classes already loaded: ... comes first (several hundred JDK classes). Then the agent reports AgentTarget, then main: started, then AgentTarget$Payment just before it's used, then main: Payment[...]. At exit, transformer saw N class definitions, a few dozen. A record's first use also loads some JDK support classes. No warning appears: an agent named on the command line is not a dynamic load. java.lang.instrument package (Java SE 25 API) docs A proxy is a receptionist in front of one employee. An agent is the building manager, who has keys to every office. The manager can hand you a list of everyone who moves in (a transformer at startup), and can repaint an office while people are working in it (retransformation): the next person who walks in sees the new walls, and someone in mid-sentence finishes the sentence in the old room. What the manager can't do while the building is in use is add or knock down walls, which is the rule against new fields and methods. The analogy breaks on permission. Since JDK 21 the building logs a warning whenever a manager arrives after opening time, and one day the doors will stay shut unless you said yes at startup.

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Retransformation swaps method bodies under live objects
x: "An agent needs a restart" is false for method bodies. Instrumentation.retransformClasses(classes...) runs the registered transformers again on classes that are already loaded and installs the result in place. The Class object stays the same, so every existing instance and every reference to the class sees the new code. The demo shows it on a final class: clock.now() printed nothing extra before, and the same clock object prints the advice line after. The Instrumentation Javadoc lists what that does and doesn't mean: "If a retransformed method has active stack frames, those active frames continue to run the bytecodes of the original method. The retransformed method will be used on new invokes." "Redefining a class does not cause its initializers to be run. The values of static variables will remain as they were." "If this method throws an exception, no classes have been retransformed." The JVM Tool Interface (JVMTI, the native interface agents are built on) sets the limit on what may change: "The retransformation must not add, remove or rename fields or methods, change the signatures of methods, change modifiers, or change inheritance." Method bodies, the constant pool and attributes may change. So you can add timing code to settle(), but you can't add a long calls field to count with. The count has to live somewhere else, such as a public class the new code calls, which is what the lab's CallCounts is for. That limit also explains the other direction. A transformer that wants to add members can do it only when the class is first loaded, which means registering it before the class loads, usually through -javaagent. Quarkus's class-loading guide states the same rule for its own build-time transformers: "Once a class has been loaded it cannot be changed, so if a class is loaded before the transformers have been prepared this will prevent the transformation from working." Retransformation also needs permission. The agent's manifest must say Can-Retransform-Classes: true, and each transformer that should run again must be registered with addTransformer(transformer, true). isRetransformClassesSupported() reports whether this JVM and agent can do it. It's true for Byte Buddy's agent on JDK 21 to 27. Change a class under a live object Read LiveRetransformDemo (or the Kotlin twin). FxClock is final, and KFxClock is final because it's Kotlin. Before running it: will the after: call on the same clock print an advice line? Will you see a warning? Run it with the command below and read the output from top to bottom. LiveRetransformDemo.java package workbench.bytecode.l07; import net.bytebuddy.agent.ByteBuddyAgent; import net.bytebuddy.agent.builder.AgentBuilder; import net.bytebuddy.asm.Advice; import java.lang.instrument.Instrumentation; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.is; import static net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.named; /** Attach an agent to this running JVM and change a loaded class under a live object. */ public class LiveRetransformDemo { public static final class FxClock { // final: lesson 5's subclass proxies couldn't touch it public String now() { return "tick"; } } public static class TimingAdvice { @Advice.OnMethodEnter static long enter() { return System.nanoTime(); // copied to the start of now() } @Advice.OnMethodExit(onThrowable = Throwable.class) static void exit(@Advice.Origin("#t.#m") String where, @Advice.Enter long t0) { System.out.println(" [advice] " + where + " took " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) + " ns"); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0) { // -Pargs=allowed or -Pargs=blocked relaunch(args[0]); return; } FxClock clock = new FxClock(); System.out.println("before: " + clock.now()); Instrumentation inst = ByteBuddyAgent.install(); // self-attach: JEP 451 warns unless allowed System.out.println("retransform supported: " + inst.isRetransformClassesSupported()); new AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) .type(is(FxClock.class)) .transform((builder, type, loader, module, domain) -> builder.visit(Advice.to(TimingAdvice.class).on(named("now")))) .installOn(inst); System.out.println("after: " + clock.now() + " (the same object, no restart)"); } /** Runs this demo again in a child JVM with dynamic agent loading explicitly allowed or blocked. */ static void relaunch(String mode) throws Exception { String flag = mode.equals("blocked") ? "-XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading" : "-XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading"; String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); Process child = new ProcessBuilder(java, flag, "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), LiveRetransformDemo.class.getName()) .redirectErrorStream(true) .start(); System.out.println("child JVM with " + flag + ":"); child.getInputStream().transferTo(System.out); System.out.println("child exited with " + child.waitFor()); } } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l07.LiveRetransformDemo labs/bytecode/src/demo/java/workbench/bytecode/l07/LiveRetransformDemo.java LiveRetransformDemo.kt package workbench.bytecode.l07 import net.bytebuddy.agent.ByteBuddyAgent import net.bytebuddy.agent.builder.AgentBuilder import net.bytebuddy.asm.Advice import net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.`is` import net.bytebuddy.matcher.ElementMatchers.named /** Final, like every Kotlin class without `open`: lesson 5's subclass proxies couldn't touch it. */ class KFxClock { fun now() = "tick" } object KTimingAdvice { @JvmStatic @Advice.OnMethodEnter fun enter(): Long = System.nanoTime() // copied to the start of now() @JvmStatic @Advice.OnMethodExit(onThrowable = Throwable::class) fun exit(@Advice.Origin("#t.#m") where: String, @Advice.Enter t0: Long) { println(" [advice] $where took ${System.nanoTime() - t0} ns") } } /** Attach an agent to this running JVM and change a loaded class under a live object. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { // -Pargs=allowed or -Pargs=blocked relaunch(args[0]) return } val clock = KFxClock() println("before: ${clock.now()}") val inst = ByteBuddyAgent.install() // self-attach: JEP 451 warns unless allowed println("retransform supported: ${inst.isRetransformClassesSupported}") AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) .type(`is`(KFxClock::class.java)) .transform { builder, _, _, _, _ -> builder.visit(Advice.to(KTimingAdvice::class.java).on(named("now"))) } .installOn(inst) println("after: ${clock.now()} (the same object, no restart)") } /** Runs this demo again in a child JVM with dynamic agent loading explicitly allowed or blocked. */ private fun relaunch(mode: String) { val flag = if (mode == "blocked") "-XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading" else "-XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading" val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val child = ProcessBuilder(java, flag, "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.bytecode.l07.LiveRetransformDemoKt") .redirectErrorStream(true) .start() println("child JVM with $flag:") child.inputStream.transferTo(System.out) println("child exited with ${child.waitFor()}") } ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l07.LiveRetransformDemoKt labs/bytecode/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/bytecode/l07/LiveRetransformDemo.kt before: tick, then four WARNING: lines (next section), then retransform supported: true, then [advice] ...FxClock.now took ... ns printed from inside now(), then after: tick (the same object, no restart). The object was created before the agent existed, its class is final, and nothing was restarted. Retransformation changes the method body inside the existing class. Old objects use the new code on their next call. Instrumentation (Java SE 25 API) docs Agents already run in your services. APM and tracing tools usually arrive as -javaagent, and test libraries may self-attach. On JDK 21 and later, a self-attach in your CI logs the JEP 451 warning, and when the default flips, those builds fail. Find them now by running tests once without -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading. For debugging, the same mechanism lets you add timing to a slow method in a library you can't recompile, such as the client that calls a 120 ms card-issuer API, without a restart and without touching the code. Do it in staging, though: a retransformation applies to every caller in that JVM, including the ones handling real authorizations.

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Loading an agent into a running JVM prints a warning since JDK 21
x: The four lines in the demo's output are JEP 451, "Prepare to Disallow the Dynamic Loading of Agents", delivered in JDK 21: WARNING: A Java agent has been loaded dynamically (.../byte-buddy-agent-1.18.17.jar) WARNING: If a serviceability tool is in use, please run with -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading to hide this warning WARNING: If a serviceability tool is not in use, please run with -Djdk.instrument.traceUsage for more information WARNING: Dynamic loading of agents will be disallowed by default in a future release A dynamic load is any agent that arrives after startup, through the attach mechanism. ByteBuddyAgent.install() attaches to its own JVM, and so does any library that "self-attaches". The java.lang.instrument docs say "the JVM prints a warning on the standard error stream for each agent that it attempts to start in a running JVM", and name the HotSpot switch. -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading opts in and hides the warning. -XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading refuses the load, and then ByteBuddyAgent.install() throws IllegalStateException: Could not self-attach to current VM. An agent started with -javaagent doesn't warn: the startup demo in section 1 printed none. Today the default is still "allow, with a warning". In the jdk-25-ga source the flag is declared product(bool, EnableDynamicAgentLoading, true, ...), and runs for this track on JDK 21, 25, 26 and 27.0.1 all warned and loaded the agent. The last warning line says the default will change. When it does, every tool and test that self-attaches without the flag will fail at startup. So decide on purpose. If production uses an agent, an APM or a profiler, start it with -javaagent so it's there from the first class. If a test suite self-attaches, add the flag to the test JVM: the labs' Gradle build passes -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading to every test task, which is why the lab runs quietly. To find what would break, run your tests once without the flag and grep for the warning. One more warning can appear on JDK 25. In the research runs, Byte Buddy's AgentBuilder triggered WARNING: sun.misc.Unsafe::objectFieldOffset has been called by net.bytebuddy..., from JEP 498, which made the JDK warn about sun.misc.Unsafe memory access by default in JDK 24. Byte Buddy's release notes show it moving away from Unsafe (1.18.10: "Delay change of default for unsafe use to Java 26"), and the JDK 26 and 27 runs printed no such line. Allow it, then block it Run LiveRetransformDemo with -Pargs=allowed. It starts itself again in a child JVM with -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading. Run it with -Pargs=blocked, which uses -XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading. Predict the outcome first. Look at labs/build.gradle.kts and find the line that keeps the lab tests quiet. terminal ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l07.LiveRetransformDemo -Pargs=allowed ./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l07.LiveRetransformDemo -Pargs=blocked With allowed, the child prints the same lines as before but no WARNING: lines. With blocked, the child prints before: tick and then dies with java.lang.IllegalStateException: Could not self-attach to current VM using external process, exit code 1. In labs/build.gradle.kts, the shared test setup has jvmArgs("-XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading", "-Xshare:off"). JEP 451: Prepare to Disallow the Dynamic Loading of Agents read

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Byte Buddy's AgentBuilder writes the transformer, and Advice writes the bytecode
x: Writing a ClassFileTransformer that edits bytecode by hand means parsing, changing and re-emitting the class, with lesson 6's tools. Byte Buddy's AgentBuilder does the plumbing, and its Advice does the editing. This is the lab's solution, line by line: Java ResettableClassFileTransformer t = new AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() // 1. no new members: required to retransform .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) // 2. also rewrite classes already loaded .type(is(SettlementJob.class)) // 3. which classes .transform((builder, type, loader, module, domain) -> builder.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice.class).on(named("settle")))) // 4. what to change .installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install()); // 5. register and retransform now Kotlin val t = AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() // 1. no new members: required to retransform .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) // 2. also rewrite classes already loaded .type(`is`(SettlementJob::class.java)) // 3. which classes .transform { builder, _, _, _, _ -> builder.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice::class.java).on(named("settle"))) // 4. what to change } .installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install()) // 5. register and retransform now Advice is not a delegation. Byte Buddy copies the body of your @Advice.OnMethodEnter method into the start of the target method, and the @Advice.OnMethodExit body into every exit. That's why advice methods must be static, why they may only call public code (the copied code runs inside the target class), and why @Advice.Origin("#t.#m") can hand them the method's name as a constant. Nothing new is added to the class, so the result respects the retransformation rule. MethodDelegation from lesson 5 adds accessor methods and helper classes, so it only works on new classes or classes not yet loaded. The returned transformer's reset(inst, RETRANSFORMATION) puts the original bodies back. Because the advice runs inside the method, it sees every call, from anywhere: from other classes, from the class itself through this, and on final classes. Here are the three ways to intercept from this track side by side: needs this.method() calls final classes and methods JDK proxy (lesson 4) an interface not seen not relevant subclass proxy (lesson 5) an open class seen only if the proxy is the object can't intercept agent with Advice an agent seen fine The price is reach. An agent changes the class for every caller in that class loader, and starting one after startup warns, as section 3 showed. Use a proxy when you own the call path, and an agent when you need to change code you don't control. Check yourself before the lab: the lab's SettlementJob.settleAll calls settle three times on this. With the advice installed on settle, how many calls does CallCounts record when you call settleAll once? (Three: each inner call runs settle's new body, which begins with the copied advice.) Byte Buddy README (AgentBuilder and Advice examples) read The common mistake is expecting a transformer to see classes that are already loaded, or to add members to them. Someone writes an agentmain that calls addTransformer(t) and waits for transform to be called for a class the service loaded an hour ago. It never is, because a transformer sees class definitions that happen after it's registered. Or they add a field for a counter and the retransformation fails, because retransformation may only change method bodies. People make this mistake because the startup agent they copied did both and worked: at startup, nearly every class loads after premain. The fix is to register with addTransformer(t, true) and call retransformClasses, with Can-Retransform-Classes: true in the manifest, to keep the class shape unchanged (Byte Buddy: disableClassFormatChanges() and Advice), and to keep any state in a separate public class.

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Java and Kotlin
x: The counting advice in Java and Kotlin CountingAdvice.java public class CountingAdvice { @Advice.OnMethodEnter // copied to the start of the method static void enter(@Advice.Origin("#t.#m") String method) { CallCounts.hit(method); // must be public: this code runs in the target class } } // install it new AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) .type(is(SettlementJob.class)) .transform((b, type, loader, module, domain) -> b.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice.class).on(named("settle")))) .installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install()); CountingAdvice.kt object CountingAdvice { @JvmStatic // Advice needs a real static method @Advice.OnMethodEnter // copied to the start of the method fun enter(@Advice.Origin("#t.#m") method: String) { CallCounts.hit(method) // must be public: this code runs in the target class } } // install it AgentBuilder.Default() .disableClassFormatChanges() .with(AgentBuilder.RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) .type(`is`(SettlementJob::class.java)) .transform { b, _, _, _, _ -> b.visit(Advice.to(CountingAdvice::class.java).on(named("settle"))) } .installOn(ByteBuddyAgent.install()) Kotlin has no static, so the advice lives in an object with @JvmStatic, which makes kotlinc emit a real static method that Byte Buddy can copy. is is a Kotlin keyword, so the matcher must be written `is`(...). The bigger difference is in the target, not the agent. A Kotlin class is final by default, which blocked every subclass proxy in lesson 5, and an agent doesn't care: Advice edits the existing class instead of extending it. The advice's code is copied into the target class, so anything it calls (CallCounts, println) must be reachable from there, in Kotlin as much as in Java.

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Worked example
x: A transformer that never sees its class An engineer attaches an agent to a running staging service to log the bytes of IssuerClient, which loaded at startup. transform is never called for it. Read the agent and find out why before reading on. public static void agentmain(String args, Instrumentation inst) { inst.addTransformer(new LoggingTransformer("com/acme/IssuerClient")); // waits for transform(...) to be called for IssuerClient: it never is } @JvmStatic fun agentmain(args: String?, inst: Instrumentation) { inst.addTransformer(LoggingTransformer("com/acme/IssuerClient")) // waits for transform(...) to be called for IssuerClient: it never is } A transformer sees class definitions that happen after it's registered. IssuerClient was defined an hour ago, so nothing will define it again. To see it, ask the JVM to run the transformers again for that class. That needs three things: the manifest's Can-Retransform-Classes: true, registering the transformer as able to retransform, and the call itself. public static void agentmain(String args, Instrumentation inst) throws Exception { LoggingTransformer t = new LoggingTransformer("com/acme/IssuerClient"); inst.addTransformer(t, true); // 1. canRetransform = true for (Class<?> c : inst.getAllLoadedClasses()) { if (c.getName().equals("com.acme.IssuerClient")) { inst.retransformClasses(c); // 2. run the transformers again for it } } } @JvmStatic fun agentmain(args: String?, inst: Instrumentation) { val t = LoggingTransformer("com/acme/IssuerClient") inst.addTransformer(t, true) // 1. canRetransform = true inst.allLoadedClasses .filter { it.name == "com.acme.IssuerClient" } .forEach { inst.retransformClasses(it) } // 2. run the transformers again for it } Now transform is called with the class's current bytes and a non-null classBeingRedefined. If it returns changed bytes, they may only change method bodies, the constant pool and attributes. Returning a class with a new field makes retransformClasses throw, and then, as the Javadoc promises, no class was changed. Calls already inside IssuerClient methods finish on the old code, and the next calls run the new code. Byte Buddy packs all of this into the builder. RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION registers the transformer as retransform-capable and retransforms the matching loaded classes. disableClassFormatChanges() stops Byte Buddy from adding members. Advice changes only method bodies. That's why the lab needs five builder calls and no loop over loaded classes.

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Key terms
x: Java agent A class the JVM starts with an Instrumentation handle, through -javaagent, a launcher manifest or attach. Instrumentation The JDK interface that lets an agent add transformers, list loaded classes and retransform them. ClassFileTransformer A callback that receives each class's bytes before the JVM defines it and may return changed bytes. Retransformation Running transformers again on a loaded class and swapping in new method bodies, keeping the class's shape. Dynamic attach Loading an agent into a JVM that is already running; warned about since JDK 21 (JEP 451). Advice Byte Buddy's way of copying your enter and exit code into an existing method's body. JVMTI The JVM Tool Interface: the native interface for debuggers and agents, which defines what retransformation may change. Which method does the JVM call for an agent started with -javaagent, and when? public static void premain(String args, Instrumentation inst), before the application's main. What does a ClassFileTransformer.transform return to leave a class unchanged? null. Does retransforming a class run its static initializer again? No. Static fields keep their values, and existing instances are not changed. What may retransformation change, and what not? It may change method bodies, the constant pool and attributes. It may not add, remove or rename fields or methods, or change signatures, modifiers or the superclass. What prints the JEP 451 warning, and how do you silence it? Loading an agent into a running JVM (attach or self-attach). -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading silences it; -XX:-EnableDynamicAgentLoading blocks loading. Why must Byte Buddy advice methods be static and call only public code? Byte Buddy copies their bodies into the target method, so the code runs inside the target class. Two settings in Byte Buddy's AgentBuilder make a transformation safe for already-loaded classes. Which? .with(RedefinitionStrategy.RETRANSFORMATION) and .disableClassFormatChanges(), with Advice for the change itself.

h: Java agents and instrumentation · Go deeper
x: Retransformation and redefinition are two different calls. redefineClasses takes new class bytes you supply. retransformClasses asks the registered transformers to produce them, starting from the class's original bytes. Both follow the same JVMTI rule about the class's shape, and both need permission in the manifest (Can-Redefine-Classes, Can-Retransform-Classes). Byte Buddy's RedefinitionStrategy.REDEFINITION exists too, but RETRANSFORMATION cooperates better with other agents, because each transformer sees the result of the previous one. Agent order matters with more than one agent. With several -javaagent options, "the premain methods will be called in the order that the agents are specified", and each registered transformer sees the bytes produced by the ones before it. Two agents that both rewrite the same method, for example an APM agent and your own, can conflict. Test them together. This lesson closes the track's "integrity by default" thread. Recent JDKs warn before they forbid: dynamic agents since JDK 21 (JEP 451), sun.misc.Unsafe memory access since JDK 24 (JEP 498, default --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=warn), and reflective mutation of final fields since JDK 26 (JEP 500, default --illegal-final-field-mutation=warn). In the runs for this track, none of them had become a hard failure by JDK 27.0.1. To find what will break later, run your test suite once with the stricter settings: test JVM options for a "what will break later" run: --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=deny (JDK 24 and later) --illegal-final-field-mutation=deny (JDK 26 and later) and leave out -XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading

h: Memory and garbage collection
x: Heap, stacks and object layout, allocation, references, G1, ZGC and Shenandoah, GC logs, and hunting leaks. By the end of this track you can say where every byte of a JVM process lives, predict what an object costs, measure what a piece of code allocates, and explain how G1 and ZGC find and move live objects. You can read a GC log line by line, choose and configure a collector for a service on JDK 21, 25 or 27, size a heap so a pod is not OOM-killed, and find a leak, on the heap with a histogram and a heap dump or outside it with Native Memory Tracking. You don't need to know anything about garbage collection to start: lesson 1 begins with what the heap is. You do need to read Java and Kotlin, and two ideas from the threads track help: what a thread pool is, and why a ThreadLocal on a pool thread outlives the task. Install JDK 25, the current LTS. Defaults change between JDK 21, 25 and 27 (the collector a small container gets, the size of an object header, the ZGC flags), so the lessons always say which version a fact belongs to. JDK 26 and 27 behaviour comes from reading the JDK source, and the lessons say so. The labs live in labs/memory, one package per lesson (workbench.memory.l01 to l07). Lessons 1, 3, 5 and 7 have Java labs; lessons 2, 4 and 6 are in Kotlin. Run ./gradlew :memory:test --tests 'workbench.memory.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes. The tests are deterministic: they count allocated bytes with generous margins, wait for the GC with bounded loops on a ReferenceQueue, and count live objects with a class histogram. They need System.gc() to work, so never run them with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC. Many demos start a child JVM with the flags they want to show, so ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=... is all you type. Lesson 7's FFM demo needs JDK 22 or later and runs outside Gradle, from labs/memory/jdk25. -Xmx caps only the heap. Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, GC data and direct buffers come on top: 390 MB committed for a 256 MB heap in one measured process. An object costs a 12-byte header plus its fields, rounded up to 8. Compressed oops keep references at 4 bytes below 32 GB of heap; compact headers (JDK 25 opt-in, JDK 27 default) shrink the header to 8. Allocation is a pointer bump in a thread's TLAB; the allocation rate is what costs you. Count bytes with getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes, and treat escape analysis as a bonus you show in demos, never assert in tests. The GC keeps what roots can reach. Soft references go before an OOM, weak ones at the next GC, and Cleaner (not finalize()) is the safety net behind close(). Generational collectors copy the few survivors out of eden; write barriers and card tables keep young collections small. G1 adds regions, humongous objects, concurrent marking and mixed collections. ZGC moves objects while the application runs, using colored pointers and load barriers, so its pauses stay far below a millisecond; it pays in CPU, headroom and 8-byte references. With no flag, JDK 21 to 26 pick Serial unless the JVM sees 2 CPUs and 1,792 MB; JDK 27 picks G1. Keep G1 for most services, ZGC for tight pause budgets with spare cores, Parallel for batch, Epsilon for allocation-budget tests. A GC log line gives cause, heap before and after, and pause length. A pause line has Pause after GC(id) and ends in ms; the floor of young pauses and the after-value of a full GC show the live set. In a container the default heap is 25% of the limit. Size with MaxRAMPercentage, cap direct memory, and remember that going over the limit is a kernel kill with no Java error. Find heap leaks with a histogram, a heap dump and the dominator tree; find native growth with NMT's baseline and diff; give off-heap memory a lifetime with an FFM arena.

A Quarkus service has an 8 GB heap with G1. Which object is humongous? A 2.5 MB settlement file held in one byte[] A 1.5 MB JSON response held in one byte[] A HashMap with 100,000 entries A 1 MB direct ByteBuffer 8 GB / 2048 is 4 MB, so regions are 4 MB and anything over 2 MB is humongous: the 2.5 MB array. 1.5 MB is under the threshold. A HashMap is many small objects plus a table array well under 2 MB, and a direct buffer's bytes aren't on the heap at all. A ZGC log says GC(7) Major Collection (Allocation Rate) 342M(33%)->466M(46%) 0.119s. What happened? A 119 ms pause that made the heap grow A failed collection that will be retried A concurrent collection of 119 ms; the heap ended fuller because the application kept allocating while it ran A memory leak of 124 MB ZGC's collection lines show the concurrent cycle, not a pause; the pauses are separate Pause ... lines of hundredths of a millisecond. The application allocated during the cycle, which is why ZGC needs headroom. One line can't show a leak; the trend across many cycles can. A webhook relay runs on JDK 25 in a pod with 1 CPU and a 512 MiB limit, with no GC flag. Which collector does it run, and is that a problem? G1, the default everywhere; fine Serial, because the pod isn't server-class; often fine for a small single-CPU service ZGC, because the heap is small Parallel, because it has one CPU On JDK 21 to 26 the JVM picks G1 only with 2 or more CPUs and at least 1,792 MB. A heap leak; add -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError The GC pause goal was too long; lower MaxGCPauseMillis Kubernetes restarts JVMs after a fixed time The whole process went over the limit and the kernel killed it; size the heap with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage around 60 to 75 and cap direct memory Exit code 137 is SIGKILL from the OOM killer. No OutOfMemoryError was thrown, so no heap dump would be written. Young pauses end at 300, 340, 385, 430 and 470 MB over an hour, and a full GC goes 1400M->1180M(1536M). What do you do first? Take a class histogram and a heap dump, and find the biggest retained size in the dominator tree Turn on Native Memory Tracking Switch to ZGC Lower the pause goal A rising floor and a full GC that frees little mean the live heap is growing: a heap leak. Which choice does that without waiting for a GC?
