h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · -Xmx caps the heap, not the process
x: Every object your program creates with new lives in one area of memory, the heap. The garbage collector (GC) is the part of the JVM that finds objects nothing refers to any more and reuses their memory. -Xmx sets the largest size the heap may grow to. So it's natural to think -Xmx is the size of the process. It isn't. Start a JDK 21 service with -Xmx256m and turn on Native Memory Tracking (NMT), the JVM's own accounting of the memory it uses. In one such run, NMT reported 216 MB of heap committed. Committed means memory the operating system has really given the process, as opposed to address space that is only reserved for later. The whole process had committed 390 MB. The other 174 MB lived outside the heap, and -Xmx limits none of it. Here is where it went: Area Committed What lives there Java heap 216 MB every object you create with new Direct buffers and FFM memory 96 MB ByteBuffer.allocateDirect, Arena.allocate (that program asked for 96 MB) GC bookkeeping 45 MB card tables, remembered sets, marking bitmaps Shared class archive (CDS, class data sharing) 13 MB JDK classes, already parsed, mapped from a file Code cache 7 MB machine code from the JIT (just-in-time) compilers, which compile hot bytecode while the program runs Thread stacks 6 MB one stack per platform thread (71 of them) Metaspace 1 MB metadata for the classes loaded from your jars The heap is the part -Xmx caps and the GC cleans. Every object you create lands there. (Lesson 2 shows the one case where an object never gets created at all.) A virtual thread's stack is on the heap too, in stack chunk objects, while the thread is unmounted. Thread stacks live outside the heap. A thread's stack holds the local variables and return addresses of the methods it is running. Each platform thread reserves its stack, 1 MB by default on Linux x64, but only commits the pages it touches. That's why 71 threads committed only 6 MB. Metaspace holds class metadata: methods, bytecode, constant pools. It has no limit by default (MaxMetaspaceSize is unlimited), so a class loader leak grows it until the container runs out of memory. Direct buffers are memory that NIO asks for outside the heap. Netty and Vert.x, and so Quarkus, use them for socket reads and writes. Lesson 6 of this track fits all of this into a container limit, and lesson 7 measures it with NMT. For the rest of this lesson, we stay on the heap and look at what one object costs. List the memory areas of a JVM Read MemoryAreasDemo (or its Kotlin twin). It lists every memory pool the JVM reports, then creates a 64 MiB direct buffer. Predict: will the buffer show up in one of the heap pools? Run it from labs/ with the command below. Compare the max heap it prints with your machine's RAM. With no -Xmx, the JVM takes a quarter of it. A 4-byte seat number can name about 4 billion seats, which covers a 32 GB stadium, and the usher multiplies the number by 8 to find the seat. h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Every object starts with a 12-byte header
x: new Object() has no fields and still takes 16 bytes. On a 64-bit HotSpot JVM, every object starts with a header of two parts. The mark word is 8 bytes. It holds the identity hash code once something asks for it, the object's GC age (how many young collections it survived, in 4 bits, so at most 15), and the lock bits that synchronized uses. The class pointer says which class the object belongs to. It's compressed to 4 bytes by default. That's 12 bytes. The fields come next. Then comes padding: every object starts at a multiple of 8 bytes, so its size rounds up to a multiple of 8. new Object() is 12 bytes of header plus 4 of padding. An Integer puts its int in those 4 bytes, so it is also 16. A Long needs 8 more: 12 + 8 = 20, padded to 24. JOL (Java Object Layout, an OpenJDK tool) prints the real layout. Here is a payment class: Java class Payment { boolean captured; long amountMinor; byte status; String currency; int attempts; Object metadata; } Kotlin class Payment { var captured = false var amountMinor = 0L var status: Byte = 0 var currency: String? = null var attempts = 0 var metadata: Any? = null } JOL's output on JDK 21 (both classes print the same layout): OFF SZ TYPE DESCRIPTION VALUE 0 8 (object header: mark) N/A 8 4 (object header: class) N/A 12 4 int Payment.attempts N/A 16 8 long Payment.amountMinor N/A 24 1 boolean Payment.captured N/A 25 1 byte Payment.status N/A 26 2 (alignment/padding gap) 28 4 java.lang.String Payment.currency N/A 32 4 java.lang.Object Payment.metadata N/A 36 4 (object alignment gap) Instance size: 40 bytes The JVM chose the field order. It put the int right after the header, because a long must start at a multiple of 8. References take 4 bytes each. And 6 of the 40 bytes are gaps. A subclass that adds a String and a short still takes 40 bytes, because its fields fill those gaps. The rule that gets you close every time: header, plus the sum of the field sizes, rounded up to 8. The lab has you write it and check it against JOL. The overhead hurts most in small objects. A three-letter currency code as a String costs 48 bytes: a 24-byte String plus a 24-byte byte[] that holds 3 bytes of data. An ArrayList<Integer> with 1,000 numbers costs 20,976 bytes. An int[1000] costs 4,016. Print real layouts with JOL Before you run anything, write down your guess for Payment, Integer, Long, and the string "EUR" with its array. Run LayoutDemo (Java) or LayoutDemoKt (Kotlin, whose class is called KPayment). Ignore JOL's two warnings about attaching an agent: the layouts are still right. Find the padding in the printout. Then look at the last line: the JVM's own allocation counter, which measures the same thing without JOL. h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Compressed oops make references 4 bytes, up to 32 GB
x: A reference on a 64-bit machine should take 8 bytes. On HotSpot it usually takes 4, thanks to compressed oops (an "oop" is an ordinary object pointer). Every object starts at a multiple of 8 bytes, so the lowest 3 bits of every object address are zero. The JVM doesn't store them. It keeps a 32-bit number and shifts it left by 3 bits when it follows the reference. 2^32 slots times 8 bytes is 32 GB. As long as the maximum heap fits in that range, every reference field and every slot of an Object[] takes 4 bytes. Give the JVM -Xmx32g or more and it switches compressed oops off on its own. References go back to 8 bytes. These are JOL's numbers on JDK 21 with -Xmx40g: Object heap under 32 GB -Xmx40g Payment 40 48 String (shell) 24 32 "EUR" with its array 48 56 ArrayList<Integer> of 1,000 20,976 25,920 int[1000] 4,016 4,016 The list grew by 24%. So a 40 GB heap holds less data than its size suggests, and a jump from 31 GB to 40 GB can buy you almost nothing. The int[] didn't change, because it holds no references. There is a way past 32 GB: -XX:ObjectAlignmentInBytes=16 keeps 4-byte references up to 64 GB, because a 4-bit shift now reaches twice as far. The price is that every object pads to 16 bytes, so Payment is 48 bytes again. For a payments service I'd rather stay under 32 GB per JVM and run more instances. Class pointers are compressed separately, into a 1 GB compressed class space. That's why the header stays 12 bytes even when compressed oops are off. Turn compressed oops off Predict the new size of Payment and of the ArrayList<Integer> with 8-byte references. Run the demo again with -Pargs=-XX:-UseCompressedOops added to the command. The demo starts a child JVM with that flag. Run it once more with -Pargs=-Xmx40g instead. The JVM only reserves address space for the max heap, so this works on a small laptop. terminal ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l01.LayoutDemo -Pargs=-XX:-UseCompressedOops ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l01.LayoutDemo -Pargs=-Xmx40g Both runs print the same numbers. References are now 8 bytes, so Payment grows to 48 and its gaps grow to 6 bytes in one block. The String shell is 32, "EUR" 56, and the list 25,920 bytes. int[1000] stays at 4,016. The allocation counter says 48 bytes per Payment. -Xmx40g switched compressed oops off by itself.

h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Compact object headers shrink the header to 8 bytes
x: Project Lilliput, the OpenJDK project working on smaller object headers, shrinks the header to 8 bytes. With compact object headers, the class pointer moves into the mark word (as 22 bits), and the separate class word disappears. JDK Compact object headers 21 not available: the JVM rejects the flag 24 experimental (JEP 450): -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders 25 and 26 product option, off by default (JEP 519): -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders 27 on by default, per the JDK source; -XX:-UseCompactObjectHeaders turns it off The JDK 25 manual says the option saves "4 bytes per object (on average)". The word that matters is "average". Objects still pad to 8 bytes, so each one saves either 8 bytes or nothing: Object 12-byte header 8-byte header Payment 40 32 Long 24 16 HashMap$Node 32 24 Integer 16 16 String (shell) 24 24 The right-hand column comes from JOL's layout simulation, which follows the JDK 25 source. The research for this course could only run JDK 21, so treat it as a prediction you can check yourself on JDK 25. The saving grows with the number of objects, not with the size of the heap. A heap full of small DTOs, map entries and boxed numbers gains the most. A heap full of large byte arrays barely changes: for one heap dump made mostly of 2 KB arrays, JOL estimated only 1.3% less. On JDK 25 it's worth a load test: it's one flag, and you can remove it again. Watch for old agents or libraries that read fields through Unsafe with hard-coded offsets, because the first field now starts at offset 8, not 12. Check compact headers on JDK 25 This step needs Gradle running on JDK 25 or later (check with ./gradlew --version). On JDK 21 the child JVM stops with Unrecognized VM option 'UseCompactObjectHeaders', which proves the version table. Run the demo with -Pargs=-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders. Read the last line, which the JVM measures itself. JOL 0.17 is older than compact headers, so trust that line over JOL's printout. terminal (JDK 25) ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l01.LayoutDemo -Pargs=-XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders Per the JDK 25 source and JOL's simulation, the allocation counter should report 320,000 bytes, 32 per Payment, against 40 without the flag. The "JOL simulation" line prints 32 on every JDK, because it is a model, not a measurement. JEP 519: Compact Object Headers read Sizing memory by counting data instead of objects. A team estimates a cache of 1 million idempotency keys as "36-character keys plus 8-byte values, about 44 MB" and sets the heap accordingly. The real cost is about 144 MB, because each entry is four objects with their own headers and padding: a String, its byte[], a Long and a HashMap$Node, plus a slot in the table. The fix is to measure: JOL's GraphLayout.parseInstance(map).totalSize() in a test, or the allocation counter, before you trust any estimate.

h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Java and Kotlin
x: The same two fields in Java and Kotlin Refund.java class Refund { long amountMinor; // primitive: 8 bytes inside the object Long feeMinor; // reference: 4 bytes here, plus a 24-byte Long elsewhere (or null) } Refund.kt class Refund( var amountMinor: Long, // compiles to a long field: 8 bytes inside the object var feeMinor: Long?, // compiles to a java.lang.Long field: a reference plus a 24-byte box ) Both classes compile to the same two JVM fields and the same 24-byte layout, and JOL can't tell them apart. The difference is what the source shows you. Java names the box: Long with a capital L. Kotlin has one Long type and decides for you: it's a primitive long when it can be, and a boxed java.lang.Long when it is nullable (Long?) or a type argument (List<Long>). So in Kotlin, a single ? can add an object per value. val versus var changes nothing in size, and data class adds methods, not fields.

h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Worked example
x: Estimate a million-entry idempotency cache, then check it A payment API remembers which idempotency keys it has seen, mapped to the ledger entry it created. Keys are 36-character UUID strings. How much heap does it take at 1 million entries? // key: the request's idempotency key, value: the ledger entry id Map<String, Long> seen = new HashMap<>(); seen.put(request.idempotencyKey(), ledgerEntryId); // key: the request's idempotency key, value: the ledger entry id val seen = HashMap<String, Long>() seen[request.idempotencyKey] = ledgerEntryId List the objects one entry creates and size each with the rule: header + fields, rounded up to 8. The table is shared: 1 million entries is more than 0.75 of 2^20 slots, so HashMap grows its table to 2^21 slots of 4 bytes, 8 MB in all. String 24 header 12 + byte[] ref 4 + hash 4 + coder 1 + flag 1 = 22 -> 24 byte[36] 56 header 12 + length 4 + 36 bytes of data = 52 -> 56 Long 24 header 12 + long 8 = 20 -> 24 HashMap$Node 32 header 12 + hash 4 + key, value, next 3 x 4 = 28 -> 32 table slot ~8.4 2,097,152 slots x 4 bytes / 1,000,000 entries ------ ~144 bytes per entry, ~144 MB for the cache Check the estimate instead of trusting it. JOL walks the whole object graph from the map. On JDK 21, with random UUID keys, it counted 4,000,002 objects and 144,388,672 bytes: 144.4 per entry. The data itself is 36 + 8 = 44 bytes per entry, so two thirds of the cache is headers, references and padding. GraphLayout g = GraphLayout.parseInstance(seen); System.out.println(g.toFootprint()); // a table: count and bytes per class System.out.println(g.totalSize() / seen.size() + " bytes per entry"); val g = GraphLayout.parseInstance(seen) println(g.toFootprint()) // a table: count and bytes per class println("${g.totalSize() / seen.size} bytes per entry") Shrink it where the bytes are. The key costs 80 bytes as a String plus its array. A UUID object holds the same 128 bits in two long fields and takes 32 bytes. That one change takes about 48 bytes off every entry, a third of the cache. Bounding the cache's size matters even more, and lesson 7 does that. h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Key terms
x: Mark word The first 8 bytes of every object: hash code, GC age and lock bits. Class pointer The header field that says which class an object is. 4 bytes when compressed. Compressed oops 4-byte object references that the JVM shifts by 3 bits to reach up to 32 GB of heap. Object alignment Every object starts at a multiple of 8 bytes, so sizes round up to 8. Shallow size The bytes of one object alone: header, fields and padding, not the objects it points to. Metaspace Native memory for class metadata. Unlimited by default. Code cache Native memory for the machine code the JIT compilers produce. Compact object headers An 8-byte header with the class pointer folded into the mark word. Opt-in on JDK 25. How big is an object header on a default 64-bit JDK 21? 12 bytes: an 8-byte mark word and a 4-byte compressed class pointer. What does the mark word hold? The identity hash code (once computed), the GC age in 4 bits, and lock state bits. How many bytes does a Long take on a default JDK 21? 24: a 12-byte header plus 8 bytes of value is 20, padded to a multiple of 8. Up to which max heap do compressed oops work by default? Just under 32 GB: 2^32 references times 8-byte alignment. At -Xmx32g and above, references become 8 bytes. Does -Xmx limit thread stacks, metaspace or direct buffers? No. It caps only the Java heap. Everything else comes on top of it. What does -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders do, and where is it available? It shrinks the header to 8 bytes by moving the class pointer into the mark word. Experimental in JDK 24, opt-in in JDK 25, on by default in JDK 27 per the JDK source. Why can adding a field to a class cost 0 bytes? Objects pad to 8 bytes. A small new field can fill the padding: a subclass of the 40-byte Payment that adds a String and a short is still 40 bytes.

h: Where objects live: heap, stacks, metaspace and object headers · Go deeper
x: The mark word has a precise bit layout, and it changed between JDK 21 and 25. On JDK 21 a normal object's mark word is unused:25 hash:31 unused_gap:1 age:4 unused_gap:1 lock:2. On JDK 25 it is unused:22 hash:31 unused_gap:4 age:4 self-fwd:1 lock:2, and with compact headers the 22 unused bits become klass:22, the class pointer. 22 bits can name about 4 million classes, which is plenty. Four of the gap bits are marked in the source as reserved for Valhalla, the project that will bring value objects. You can watch the mark word change with JOL's ClassLayout.parseInstance(obj).toPrintable(). On JDK 21 a fresh object shows 0x0000000000000001 (non-biasable; age: 0). After System.identityHashCode(obj) the hash appears in the word: 0x00000077846d2c01 (hash: 0x77846d2c; age: 0). Inside a synchronized block on JDK 21, the word points to a lock record on the thread's stack: (thin lock: 0x00007f310cdfe928). Field packing has its own rules since JDK 15. The JVM fills the 4-byte gap after a 12-byte header with an int, a float or a reference, but never with a long, which must start at a multiple of 8. That's why a Long has 4 bytes of padding in the middle and an Integer has none. Subclass fields can fill gaps left by the superclass, as the lab's CardPayment shows. Two practical notes about JOL. It can't read record field offsets on JDK 21 unless you set -Djol.magicFieldOffset=true (the lab sets it in code before JOL starts). And without permission to attach to processes it prints warnings and guesses addresses, but the layouts and sizes it prints are still exact.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Allocating an object is a pointer bump
x: Allocation on the JVM is cheap, and the reason is the TLAB, the thread-local allocation buffer. New objects go into eden, the area of the heap where every object starts its life (lesson 4 covers the rest of the heap). Every thread shares eden, so if each new took memory from it directly, all threads would fight over one pointer. Instead, each thread claims a chunk of eden for itself and allocates inside it with no locking at all. In a JDK 21 trace of a small test JVM, each chunk was about 266 KB. Allocating inside a TLAB means bumping a "top" pointer. This is HotSpot's fast path, from the JDK 25 source: HeapWord* obj = top(); if (pointer_delta(end(), obj) >= size) { // does the object fit? set_top(obj + size); // bump the pointer return obj; } return nullptr; // no: take the slow path A compare, an add and a store. Then the JVM writes the header and zeroes the fields. In compiled code, the JIT inlines all of this into your method. The slow path runs when the object doesn't fit. Usually the TLAB is simply full, and the thread takes a fresh one from eden with one atomic update. Objects too big for a TLAB go straight into eden. G1, the default garbage collector, splits the heap into equal regions of 1 to 32 MB, and an object bigger than half a region is humongous: a 3 MB byte[] on a heap with 2 MB regions skips TLABs and eden entirely. Lesson 4 shows why that costs more. So the new itself is cheap. What you pay for is the rate. Every TLAB brings the next young collection closer: the GC run that empties eden once it's full. A service that allocates 1 GB a second fills a 500 MB eden twice a second, and with G1 every full eden means a young collection pause. The objects that are already dead cost almost nothing at that point, because a young collection copies only the survivors. Kotlin compiles to the same new bytecode, so all of this is identical in both languages. Count TLAB refills Read TlabDemo. It allocates 2,000,000 arrays of 40 bytes, 80 MB in all, in a child JVM that logs a TLAB summary at every GC. Predict: how many times will the main thread go back to eden for a fresh TLAB? Run it with the command below. Find GC(1) TLAB totals. Divide the bytes the pause freed by refills. TlabDemo.java package workbench.memory.l02; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; /** * Allocates 2,000,000 small arrays in a child JVM that logs a TLAB summary at every GC. * Each "refills" count is how often a thread went back to eden for a fresh buffer. */ public class TlabDemo { static volatile Object sink; public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length == 0) { for (String line : Jvm.lines(List.of("-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+tlab=debug"), TlabDemo.class.getName(), "allocate")) { System.out.println(line.replaceAll("\\s+", " ")); } return; } for (int i = 0; i < 2_000_000; i++) sink = new byte[24]; // 16-byte header + 24 bytes = 40 bytes each System.out.println("allocated 2,000,000 arrays of 40 bytes: 80,000,000 bytes"); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l02.TlabDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l02/TlabDemo.java TlabDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l02 import workbench.memory.Jvm @Volatile private var tlabSink: Any? = null /** * Allocates 2,000,000 small arrays in a child JVM that logs a TLAB summary at every GC. * Each "refills" count is how often a thread went back to eden for a fresh buffer. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { Jvm.lines(listOf("-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+tlab=debug"), "workbench.memory.l02.TlabDemoKt", "allocate") .forEach { println(it.replace(Regex("\\s+"), " ")) } return } repeat(2_000_000) { tlabSink = ByteArray(24) } // 16-byte header + 24 bytes = 40 bytes each println("allocated 2,000,000 arrays of 40 bytes: 80,000,000 bytes") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l02.TlabDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l02/TlabDemo.kt Something like GC(1) TLAB totals: thrds: 1 refills: 300 ... slow allocs: 0 ... waste: 0.3%, followed by Pause Young ... 61M->1M. One thread allocated about 60 MB with about 300 refills, so roughly 5,000 arrays took the fast path for every trip to the shared eden. slow allocs: 0 means no array had to bypass its TLAB. The exact counts change from run to run. Each thread allocates inside its own TLAB by bumping a pointer. Only a refill touches shared eden. threadLocalAllocBuffer.inline.hpp at jdk-25-ga: the fast path read A TLAB is a cashier's own cash drawer. Taking change from your own drawer needs no one's permission, so it's fast. When the drawer runs low, you walk to the vault and sign for a new bundle of notes: that's the slow path, and it's rare. A humongous object is a pallet that never goes in a drawer and goes straight to the warehouse floor. The analogy breaks at the end of the day: a cashier counts the money out, but the garbage collector never looks at the dead objects in a TLAB. It copies the few live ones and reuses the whole drawer.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Count bytes with the thread's allocation counter
x: HotSpot counts every byte each thread allocates. com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean, an extension of the standard ThreadMXBean, gives you the counter with getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() (since JDK 14): Java var threads = (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); byte[] receipt = new byte[1 << 20]; long bytes = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; // 1,048,592 Kotlin val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes val receipt = ByteArray(1 shl 20) val bytes = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before // 1,048,592 The Javadoc calls the number "an approximation". For code that runs once, it is exact to the byte in practice: 1 MiB of data plus a 16-byte array header gave 1,048,592 in 20 out of 20 runs on JDK 21. That makes it the best tool to test your model from lesson 1. A thousand uncached Long boxes allocate 24,000 bytes, exactly 1,000 times 24. There are two traps. The first call to anything pays for one-time setup. The first Long.valueOf builds the JDK's cache of the 256 boxes from -128 to 127, and that cost 7,440 bytes in the demo. The first string concatenation bootstraps itself and cost about 137 KB. Measure twice and trust the second number. The counter returns -1 on a virtual thread. If your Quarkus endpoint runs with @RunOnVirtualThread, measure its code in a test on a platform thread. In a test, the pattern is: call the code once on tiny input so its classes are loaded, measure one call on real input, and compare the bytes with what the result itself needs, plus a margin. A method that returns a long[500] needs 4,016 bytes. If it allocates 1.5 MB, something inside it is boxing. That comparison is deterministic, and it is exactly what the lab's tests do. The counter is for questions like "which step of this request allocates?" For the allocation rate of a whole running service, use JFR or the GC log. The performance track covers JFR, and lesson 6 of this track reads GC logs. Predict four allocation counts Read AllocationCounterDemo (or the Kotlin twin). Write down your prediction for each line, for the first run and the second. Run it with the command below. Explain each difference between the first and the second column. AllocationCounterDemo.java package workbench.memory.l02; import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; /** Counts the bytes a few small pieces of code allocate, twice each, using the JVM's per-thread counter. */ public class AllocationCounterDemo { static final ThreadMXBean THREADS = (ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); static volatile Object sink; // results escape here, so nothing is optimized away static long bytes(Runnable work) { long before = THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); work.run(); return THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; } static void show(String what, Runnable work) { long first = bytes(work); // the first run also pays for one-time setup long second = bytes(work); System.out.printf("%-34s %,10d %,11d%n", what, first, second); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.printf("%-34s %10s %11s%n", "bytes allocated by", "first run", "second run"); show("new byte[1 MiB]", () -> sink = new byte[1 << 20]); show("1,000 x Long.valueOf(i % 128)", () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sink = Long.valueOf(i % 128); }); show("1,000 x Long.valueOf(1_000 + i)", () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sink = Long.valueOf(1_000 + i); }); show("1,000 x \"pay-\" + i", () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) sink = "pay-" + i; }); Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println("on a virtual thread the counter says " + THREADS.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes())).join(); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l02.AllocationCounterDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l02/AllocationCounterDemo.java AllocationCounterDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l02 import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory private val THREADS = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as ThreadMXBean @Volatile private var sink: Any? = null // results escape here, so nothing is optimized away private fun bytes(work: () -> Unit): Long { val before = THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes work() return THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before } private fun show(what: String, work: () -> Unit) { val first = bytes(work) // the first run also pays for one-time setup val second = bytes(work) println("%-34s %,10d %,11d".format(what, first, second)) } /** Counts the bytes a few small pieces of code allocate, twice each, using the JVM's per-thread counter. */ fun main() { println("%-34s %10s %11s".format("bytes allocated by", "first run", "second run")) show("ByteArray(1 MiB)") { sink = ByteArray(1 shl 20) } show("1,000 x boxing (i % 128).toLong()") { for (i in 0 until 1_000) sink = (i % 128).toLong() } show("1,000 x boxing (1_000 + i).toLong()") { for (i in 0 until 1_000) sink = (1_000 + i).toLong() } show("1,000 x \"pay-\$i\"") { for (i in 0 until 1_000) sink = "pay-$i" } Thread.ofVirtual().start { println("on a virtual thread the counter says ${THREADS.currentThreadAllocatedBytes}") }.join() } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l02.AllocationCounterDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l02/AllocationCounterDemo.kt The 1 MiB array costs 1,048,592 bytes both times. Long.valueOf(i % 128) costs 7,440 bytes the first time (building the box cache) and 0 after, because every value comes from the cache. Long.valueOf(1_000 + i) costs 24,000 both times. String concatenation costs about 184,000 bytes the first time and about 48,000 after: 48 bytes per id. On the virtual thread the counter says -1. com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean (JDK 25 API) docs A settlement job that computes interchange fees with BigDecimal for 10 million card transactions allocates about 1.8 GB for the arithmetic alone, at 184 bytes per fee. The same fee in long minor units with basis points allocates nothing, and the worked example shows how to keep the exact rounding rule. In a Kafka consumer, look at the per-record path: the deserialized DTO, every boxed Long id, every log line built with String.format. When the young GC runs several times a second on a quiet topic, that path is where the bytes come from. And if the code runs under Quarkus @RunOnVirtualThread, measure it in a test on a platform thread, because the counter says -1 on a virtual one.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Escape analysis can delete an allocation
x: Sometimes new allocates nothing. C2, the JIT compiler that optimizes hot methods, runs escape analysis: after inlining (copying small methods into the method that calls them), it checks whether an object can be seen outside the method it is compiling. If it can't, C2 can skip the object and keep its fields in registers. That step is called scalar replacement. Java record Point(long x, long y) {} static long sumPoints(int n) { long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { Point p = new Point(i, i + 1); // p never leaves the method s += p.x() + p.y(); } return s; } Kotlin data class Point(val x: Long, val y: Long) fun sumPoints(n: Int): Long { var s = 0L for (i in 0 until n) { val p = Point(i.toLong(), i + 1L) // p never leaves the function s += p.x + p.y } return s } Call it ten times with n = 1,000,000 and count the bytes of each call. On JDK 21, the first rounds allocated a few megabytes (3 MB, then 19 MB in one run; the numbers change every run), and from round 4 or so, each round allocated 0 bytes. With -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis, every round allocated 32,000,000 bytes: a million 32-byte points. Look at the first rounds again. The interpreter and C1, the quick JIT compiler, allocate every object. The allocation only disappears once C2 has compiled the method, and when that happens depends on timing. So never assert "allocates nothing" in a unit test. It can pass on your laptop and fail in CI. The lab asserts only the allocations the code really needs. An object escapes when you store it in a field, an array or a collection, return it, or pass it to a method that C2 doesn't inline. C2 also won't scalar-replace an array with more than 64 elements (the EliminateAllocationArraySizeLimit flag). Escape analysis is a bonus you get in tight loops. It won't save a design that puts every amount into a HashMap<Integer, Long>, because the boxes live on inside the map. Watch an allocation disappear, then bring it back Run EscapeDemo. It runs the measurement in two child JVMs: one with default flags, one with -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis. Now make p escape. In the Java version add static Point last; to the class and last = p; inside the loop. In Kotlin add a top-level var last: KPoint? = null and last = p. Predict the new numbers, then run it again. Remove the change when you are done. EscapeDemo.java package workbench.memory.l02; import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.List; /** * Sums a million short-lived Points per round and counts the bytes each round allocates. * The demo runs the experiment twice, in child JVMs: with escape analysis, and without it. */ public class EscapeDemo { record Point(long x, long y) {} // 12-byte header + 16 bytes of fields: 32 bytes static long sumPoints(int n) { long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { Point p = new Point(i, i + 1); // p never leaves this method s += p.x() + p.y(); } return s; } public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length == 0) { System.out.println("== default flags: escape analysis on"); Jvm.run(List.of(), EscapeDemo.class.getName(), "measure"); System.out.println("== -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis"); Jvm.run(List.of("-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis"), EscapeDemo.class.getName(), "measure"); return; } ThreadMXBean threads = (ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); long checksum = 0; for (int round = 0; round < 10; round++) { long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); checksum += sumPoints(1_000_000); long bytes = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before; System.out.printf("round %d: %,12d bytes%n", round, bytes); } System.out.println("checksum " + checksum); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l02.EscapeDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l02/EscapeDemo.java EscapeDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l02 import com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory data class KPoint(val x: Long, val y: Long) // 12-byte header + 16 bytes of fields: 32 bytes fun sumPoints(n: Int): Long { var s = 0L for (i in 0 until n) { val p = KPoint(i.toLong(), i + 1L) // p never leaves this function s += p.x + p.y } return s } /** * Sums a million short-lived points per round and counts the bytes each round allocates. * The demo runs the experiment twice, in child JVMs: with escape analysis, and without it. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { println("== default flags: escape analysis on") Jvm.run(listOf(), "workbench.memory.l02.EscapeDemoKt", "measure") println("== -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis") Jvm.run(listOf("-XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis"), "workbench.memory.l02.EscapeDemoKt", "measure") return } val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as ThreadMXBean var checksum = 0L for (round in 0 until 10) { val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes checksum += sumPoints(1_000_000) val bytes = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before println("round %d: %,12d bytes".format(round, bytes)) } println("checksum $checksum") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l02.EscapeDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l02/EscapeDemo.kt With default flags, the first few rounds allocate megabytes and then the count drops to 0 and stays there. With -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis, every round allocates 32,000,000 bytes. After you add last = p, the default run also allocates 32,000,000 bytes in every round, because the point now escapes into a static field and C2 has to create it.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Hidden allocations in everyday code
x: Most of the allocation in a service doesn't come from your own new statements. It hides in boxing, in collection helpers and in string building. The lab's settlement batch is a typical case: Java Map<Integer, Long> totals = new HashMap<>(); for (int i = 0; i < merchantIds.length; i++) { totals.merge(merchantIds[i], amountsMinor[i], Long::sum); // boxes the key, the amount and the sum } Kotlin val totals = HashMap<Int, Long>() for (i in merchantIds.indices) { totals.merge(merchantIds[i], amountsMinor[i]) { a, b -> a + b } // the same three boxes } For 20,000 payments over 500 merchants this allocates 1,539,040 bytes, about 77 bytes per payment. Merchant ids above 127 become new Integer boxes, and every amount and every running sum becomes a new 24-byte Long. The caller only needs one total per merchant: a long[500] of 4,016 bytes. Index the array by merchant id and you get the same answer with no garbage. These are the usual suspects in payment code: Boxed collections: List<Long>, Map<String, Integer>, and in Kotlin anything typed Long? or used as a type argument. Helpers that copy: toList(), map {}, windowed, zip, and streams of boxed values. Strings: each "pay-" + i costs 48 bytes (a String and its array), and String.format also allocates a varargs array and boxes its arguments. BigDecimal arithmetic: a fee computed as amount.multiply(rate).setScale(2, HALF_EVEN) allocated 184 bytes per call in my measurement, even after warm-up. Lambdas that capture local variables, which create a new object each time the expression runs. Don't chase every allocation. A request that allocates 50 KB is fine. Fix the loops over large batches, and the code a profile shows behind a young GC that runs several times a second. Measure, change one thing, and measure again. A check before the lab: amounts.map { it * 2 }.sum() in Kotlin, or amounts.stream().map(a -> a * 2).toList() in Java, on a list of 10,000 amounts above 1,000 cents. Count the objects each one creates and estimate the bytes. (About 10,000 new 24-byte Long boxes and a 40 KB array for the new list, so roughly 280 KB. Summing over a LongArray creates nothing.) Pooling short-lived objects to "save allocation". It sounds thrifty, but for the collector it's the expensive choice. A temporary object that dies in eden costs almost nothing, because a young collection copies only survivors. A pooled object survives, so the collector copies it to survivor space and then to the old generation, and every young object you store into it later must be tracked by the write barrier (lesson 4). Pools also need locking and reset logic, and a missed reset leaks one request's data into the next. Allocate short-lived objects freely, remove boxing from big loops, and keep pools for things that are truly expensive to create: connections, threads and large direct buffers.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Java and Kotlin
x: A money type with and without an object Cents.java // Java: a record is always an object (escape analysis may remove short-lived ones) record Cents(long value) { Cents plus(Cents other) { return new Cents(value + other.value); } // a new 24-byte object } Cents total = new Cents(0); for (long a : amountsMinor) total = total.plus(new Cents(a)); Cents.kt // Kotlin: a value class is a plain long at runtime, unless it has to be boxed @JvmInline value class Cents(val value: Long) { operator fun plus(other: Cents) = Cents(value + other.value) // compiles to long + long } var total = Cents(0) for (a in amountsMinor) total += Cents(a) // no objects The Kotlin value class compiles to a raw long in fields, parameters and return types, so the loop allocates nothing even in the interpreter. The Java record is a real object each time; C2 may scalar-replace the short-lived ones in a hot loop, but you can't count on it. The Kotlin version boxes as soon as the value is used as a type argument, a nullable type or Any: a List<Cents> or a Cents? holds boxed objects again, just like List<Long> does.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Worked example
x: Take the allocation out of a fee calculation A card fee is 1.75% of the amount, rounded half-even to the cent. The settlement job calls this 10 million times a night. Measure it first: with the allocation counter around 10,000 calls, it allocates 1,840,000 bytes, 184 per call, and the number stays the same after warm-up. static final BigDecimal RATE = new BigDecimal("0.0175"); static long feeMinor(long amountMinor) { BigDecimal amount = BigDecimal.valueOf(amountMinor, 2); // a new BigDecimal BigDecimal fee = amount.multiply(RATE).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); // two more return fee.unscaledValue().longValueExact(); // and a BigInteger } val RATE = BigDecimal("0.0175") fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long): Long { val amount = BigDecimal.valueOf(amountMinor, 2) // a new BigDecimal val fee = (amount * RATE).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) // two more return fee.unscaledValue().longValueExact() // and a BigInteger } Do the same arithmetic in long. 1.75% is 175 basis points, so the exact fee in cents is amountMinor * 175 / 10_000. Integer division drops the remainder, so the rounding rule has to be written out: round up above half, and on exactly half, round to the even neighbour. This version is for amounts of zero or more; refunds go in as positive amounts. static long feeMinor(long amountMinor, int basisPoints) { // 1. scale: cents x basis points, exact in a long for any real payment long scaled = amountMinor * basisPoints; // 2. divide, keeping the remainder long fee = scaled / 10_000, rest = scaled % 10_000; // 3. round half-even, the same rule as RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN if (rest > 5_000 || (rest == 5_000 && fee % 2 == 1)) fee++; return fee; } fun feeMinor(amountMinor: Long, basisPoints: Int): Long { // 1. scale: cents x basis points, exact in a long for any real payment val scaled = amountMinor * basisPoints // 2. divide, keeping the remainder var fee = scaled / 10_000 val rest = scaled % 10_000 // 3. round half-even, the same rule as RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN if (rest > 5_000 || (rest == 5_000L && fee % 2 == 1L)) fee++ return fee } Prove the two agree before you switch. Compare them on every amount from 0 to 1,999,999 cents, which includes every exact-half case at this rate. The run behind this lesson found 0 mismatches. Then measure again: the long version allocated 0 bytes for 10,000 calls, in the interpreter and after warm-up. for (long amount = 0; amount < 2_000_000; amount++) { if (feeMinorBig(amount) != feeMinor(amount, 175)) throw new AssertionError("differs at " + amount); } for (amount in 0L until 2_000_000L) { check(feeMinorBig(amount) == feeMinor(amount, 175)) { "differs at $amount" } }

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Quiz
x: A test warms up parseAmount three times, then asserts it allocates 0 bytes. It passes on your laptop and fails in CI. What's the most likely reason? The CI machine has a smaller TLAB The zero depends on C2 having compiled the method with escape analysis, which depends on timing The allocation counter is less accurate on Linux CI runs the tests on virtual threads The interpreter and C1 allocate every object. The allocation only disappears once C2 compiles the method, and three calls rarely get it there; when it does happen depends on the machine and on what else is running. TLAB size doesn't change how many bytes are allocated. A virtual thread would make the counter return -1, not a small positive number. A service runs G1 with 2 MB regions. Which allocation does NOT happen in a TLAB? new Payment() new byte[1_024] new byte[1_500_000] for a settlement file Long.valueOf(1_000_000) In G1, an object bigger than half a region is humongous and never goes in a TLAB: 1.5 MB is more than half of 2 MB. The other three are small and take the bump-pointer fast path. The boxed Long is outside the cache range, so it is a fresh 24-byte object, but still a TLAB allocation. Which of these loops keeps allocating once C2 has compiled it? results.add(new Point(i, i + 1)); Point p = new Point(i, i + 1); sum += p.x(); totals[merchantId[i]] += amount[i]; sum += amount[i] * 175 / 10_000; Adding the point to a list makes it escape: it outlives the loop, so it has to exist on the heap. The local point that only feeds a sum can be scalar-replaced. The last two never create objects at all. In Kotlin, which of these holds 10,000 amounts without one box per amount? List<Long> Array<Long> MutableList<Long?> LongArray LongArray compiles to a JVM long[], with the values stored inline. List<Long>, Array<Long> (a Long[]) and any list of Long? hold references to java.lang.Long boxes, 24 bytes each for values outside the -128 to 127 cache. From the previous lesson: on a default JDK 21, how many bytes do 1,000 calls of Long.valueOf(1_000 + i) allocate? 0, because of the Long cache 8,000 16,000 24,000 Values from 1,000 up are outside the -128 to 127 cache, so each call creates a new Long. A Long is a 12-byte header plus 8 bytes of value, padded to 24. The allocation counter reports exactly 24,000. 8,000 counts only the values.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Explain it back
x: A colleague says: "Allocation is free on the JVM, so I never think about it." Explain in your own words what is true in that, and what is missing.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Key terms
x: Eden The part of the young generation where new objects are created. TLAB A chunk of eden that one thread allocates into without locking. Bump-pointer allocation Allocating by moving a 'top' pointer forward by the object's size. Allocation rate Bytes allocated per second. It decides how often young collections run. Escape analysis C2's check for whether an object can be seen outside the method being compiled. Scalar replacement Keeping a non-escaping object's fields in registers instead of creating the object. Boxing Wrapping a primitive in an object, such as long in java.lang.Long. What is a TLAB? A thread-local allocation buffer: a chunk of eden owned by one thread. Allocating inside it is a pointer bump with no locking. What happens when an object doesn't fit in the current TLAB? The slow path: the thread takes a fresh TLAB from eden (one atomic update), or a large object goes straight into eden. Which G1 objects never go into a TLAB? Humongous objects: anything bigger than half a region. How do you count the bytes a block of code allocates? Read com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() before and after, on a platform thread. Measure twice to skip one-time setup. What does getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() return on a virtual thread? -1. Measure on a platform thread. What is scalar replacement? C2 replaces an object that never escapes the compiled method with its fields in registers, so the allocation never happens. Why must a unit test never assert that code allocates 0 bytes? The interpreter and C1 allocate every object. The zero only appears after C2 compiles the method, which depends on timing.

h: Allocation, TLABs and escape analysis · Go deeper
x: The TLAB trace line has more in it than the debug summary. With -Xlog:gc+tlab=trace, each refill prints a line like this one from JDK 21: TLAB: fill thread: 0x00007f79d401a8a0 [id: 22952] desired_size: 266KB slow allocs: 0 refill waste: 4256B alloc: 0.99998 1024KB refills: 1 waste 0.0% gc: 0B slow: 0B desired_size is the TLAB size the JVM is aiming for this thread. It adapts to how fast the thread allocates and how many threads share eden. refill waste is the most free space the JVM is willing to throw away to start a new TLAB. When an object doesn't fit and less than that is left, the thread abandons the rest of its TLAB and takes a new one. When more is left, the thread keeps its TLAB, allocates that one object directly in eden, and counts a slow alloc. The abandoned tail of a TLAB is filled with a dummy object so the heap stays walkable, and the waste percentage counts those tails. Escape analysis helps with locks too. If an object never escapes, no other thread can ever lock it, so C2 can drop the synchronized blocks on it. A local StringBuffer, whose methods are all synchronized, is the classic example. Finally, the counter you used is per thread. getThreadAllocatedBytes(long[] ids) reads it for other threads too. For a whole service, JFR records allocation events at TLAB refills and at allocations outside a TLAB, with stack traces, so it can show which code allocates the most. The per-second rate from JFR or the GC log tells you whether allocation is a problem at all; the per-block counter then tells you where the bytes come from.

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Reachability is a ladder: strong, soft, weak, phantom
x: The garbage collector doesn't free the objects you stopped using. It frees the objects nothing can reach. It starts from the GC roots (the local variables on every live thread's stack, static fields, and references held by native code called through JNI), follows every reference, and keeps whatever it finds. Everything else is garbage. java.lang.ref lets you point at an object without holding it as tightly. Its package docs define a ladder: An object is strongly reachable if a chain of ordinary references leads to it. The GC leaves it alone. It is softly reachable if the only way to it goes through a SoftReference. The GC may clear that reference when memory gets tight. It is weakly reachable if the only way goes through a WeakReference. The next collection that finds it clears the reference. It is phantom reachable if only a PhantomReference is left. Its get() always returns null; it only tells you the object is gone. Otherwise it is unreachable, and its memory can be reused. Each reference object can carry a ReferenceQueue. "Some time after" the GC sees the referent drop to that rung, it clears the reference and puts it on the queue. That's the spec's own wording, and it promises no deadline. Java ReferenceQueue<byte[]> queue = new ReferenceQueue<>(); WeakReference<byte[]> weak = new WeakReference<>(new byte[1_000], queue); System.gc(); // a request, fine in a demo Reference<?> gone = queue.remove(500); // the same weak reference, once the GC cleared it Kotlin val queue = ReferenceQueue<ByteArray>() val weak = WeakReference(ByteArray(1_000), queue) System.gc() // a request, fine in a demo val gone = queue.remove(500) // the same weak reference, once the GC cleared it A word on System.gc(). It's a request. Its Javadoc promises nothing about how much it reclaims or when, -XX:+DisableExplicitGC turns it into a no-op, and some collectors run it concurrently. This lesson uses it only in demos, and in test helpers that keep asking until a queue delivers and give up after a timeout. Never put it in service code. Climb down the ladder Read ReferenceLadderDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It makes four 1,000-byte arrays: one strong, one soft, one weak, one phantom. Predict which survive a System.gc() and which references land on the queue. Run it with the command below. ReferenceLadderDemo.java package workbench.memory.l03; import java.lang.ref.PhantomReference; import java.lang.ref.Reference; import java.lang.ref.ReferenceQueue; import java.lang.ref.SoftReference; import java.lang.ref.WeakReference; /** One object on each rung of the reachability ladder, before and after a GC. */ public class ReferenceLadderDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { ReferenceQueue<byte[]> queue = new ReferenceQueue<>(); byte[] strong = new byte[1_000]; // a plain local: strongly reachable SoftReference<byte[]> soft = new SoftReference<>(new byte[1_000], queue); WeakReference<byte[]> weak = new WeakReference<>(new byte[1_000], queue); PhantomReference<byte[]> phantom = new PhantomReference<>(new byte[1_000], queue); System.out.printf("before GC: soft %s, weak %s, phantom.get() %s%n", soft.get() != null, weak.get() != null, phantom.get()); System.gc(); // a request; fine in a demo, never a guarantee System.out.printf("after GC: soft %s, weak %s, phantom.get() %s%n", soft.get() != null, weak.get() != null, phantom.get()); for (Reference<?> r; (r = queue.remove(500)) != null; ) { System.out.println("enqueued: " + r.getClass().getSimpleName()); } Reference.reachabilityFence(strong); // keep `strong` alive until here System.out.println("strong array still here: " + strong.length + " bytes"); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.ReferenceLadderDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l03/ReferenceLadderDemo.java ReferenceLadderDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l03 import java.lang.ref.PhantomReference import java.lang.ref.Reference import java.lang.ref.ReferenceQueue import java.lang.ref.SoftReference import java.lang.ref.WeakReference /** One object on each rung of the reachability ladder, before and after a GC. */ fun main() { val queue = ReferenceQueue<ByteArray>() val strong = ByteArray(1_000) // a plain local: strongly reachable val soft = SoftReference(ByteArray(1_000), queue) val weak = WeakReference(ByteArray(1_000), queue) val phantom = PhantomReference(ByteArray(1_000), queue) println("before GC: soft ${soft.get() != null}, weak ${weak.get() != null}, phantom.get() ${phantom.get()}") System.gc() // a request; fine in a demo, never a guarantee println("after GC: soft ${soft.get() != null}, weak ${weak.get() != null}, phantom.get() ${phantom.get()}") while (true) { val r = queue.remove(500) ?: break println("enqueued: ${r.javaClass.simpleName}") } Reference.reachabilityFence(strong) // keep `strong` alive until here println("strong array still here: ${strong.size} bytes") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.ReferenceLadderDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l03/ReferenceLadderDemo.kt Before the GC: soft true, weak true, phantom.get() is null (it always is). After it: soft is still true, because memory isn't tight; weak is false. The queue receives the WeakReference and the PhantomReference. The strong array is untouched. Each kind of reference is a weaker rung on the ladder: the GC clears soft ones under memory pressure, weak ones at the next collection that finds them, and phantom ones only report that the object is gone. java.lang.ref package docs at jdk-25-ga: the reachability definitions docs Think of the heap as a hotel. A strong reference is a guest with a booking: nobody touches the room. A soft reference is luggage in the storage room, kept until the room is full, then cleared all at once. A weak reference is a coat left in the lobby: it goes at the next sweep, however soon that is. A phantom reference is the checkout slip the front desk gets after a guest has left, so housekeeping knows to clean the room; the slip never lets you talk to the guest. Where it breaks: a hotel sweeps on a schedule. The GC sweeps when it needs memory, so you can't plan around when it comes.

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Soft references wait for memory pressure, with no promise of when
x: SoftReference sounds made for caches, and its Javadoc says so: "Soft references are most often used to implement memory-sensitive caches." The contract is thinner than it sounds. The JVM guarantees one thing: all soft references to softly reachable objects are cleared before it throws an OutOfMemoryError. Otherwise, in the Javadoc's words, "no constraints are placed upon the time" of clearing. HotSpot ties it to a flag, -XX:SoftRefLRUPolicyMSPerMB (default 1000), described as the "number of milliseconds per MB of free space in the heap" an unused soft referent may live. Here's what memory pressure looks like. A 64 MB heap holds a 40 MB rate table behind a soft reference, and then the code asks for another 40 MB: GC(5) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 42M->42M(64M) 4.230ms GC(6) Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 42M->1M(8M) 10.816ms after a 40 MB report: rate table cached: false G1 ran a full GC (a collection of the whole heap, with every thread stopped) that kept the soft referent and still had no room. Then it ran a second full GC that cleared the soft reference, and the allocation went through. The rate table is gone, and the next request has to reload it. That's the trouble with soft caches in a service. They empty in bulk, at the worst moment: when the heap is nearly full and the collector is already running full GCs. Then every request that missed reloads at once, against a database that is slow for the same reason. And a heap full of soft references always looks full, so you can't size it by watching it. Use a cache with an explicit size limit and expiry instead, and size the heap for it. Lesson 7 builds one. I'd keep soft references for data that is truly optional and cheap to rebuild, and I rarely find such data in payment code. Squeeze a soft cache Read SoftCacheDemo. It starts a child JVM with -Xmx64m -Xlog:gc, caches 40 MB behind a soft reference, then allocates 40 MB more. Predict: does the second allocation fail? Run it and read the GC lines between the two printouts. SoftCacheDemo.java package workbench.memory.l03; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.lang.ref.SoftReference; import java.util.List; /** A 40 MB soft-referenced "rate table" in a 64 MB heap, then another 40 MB allocation. Runs in a child JVM. */ public class SoftCacheDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length == 0) { Jvm.run(List.of("-Xmx64m", "-Xlog:gc"), SoftCacheDemo.class.getName(), "run"); return; } SoftReference<byte[]> rates = new SoftReference<>(new byte[40 << 20]); System.out.println("rate table cached: " + (rates.get() != null)); byte[] report = new byte[40 << 20]; // only fits if the GC clears the soft reference System.out.println("after a 40 MB report: rate table cached: " + (rates.get() != null) + ", report " + report.length + " bytes"); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.SoftCacheDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l03/SoftCacheDemo.java SoftCacheDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l03 import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.lang.ref.SoftReference /** A 40 MB soft-referenced "rate table" in a 64 MB heap, then another 40 MB allocation. Runs in a child JVM. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { Jvm.run(listOf("-Xmx64m", "-Xlog:gc"), "workbench.memory.l03.SoftCacheDemoKt", "run") return } val rates = SoftReference(ByteArray(40 shl 20)) println("rate table cached: ${rates.get() != null}") val report = ByteArray(40 shl 20) // only fits if the GC clears the soft reference println("after a 40 MB report: rate table cached: ${rates.get() != null}, report ${report.size} bytes") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.SoftCacheDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l03/SoftCacheDemo.kt No OutOfMemoryError. Between the two printouts you'll see Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 42M->42M(64M), which kept the soft referent, then a second Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 42M->1M(8M), which cleared it. The last line says the rate table is no longer cached. Two full GCs to empty one cache is the cost a soft cache hides. SoftReference source at jdk-25-ga: the clearing contract docs Payment services touch native resources more than you'd think: the bank's HSM client hands out session handles, a compression codec holds native buffers, Netty pools direct memory. Wrap each in a class that implements AutoCloseable, release it with try-with-resources, and register a Cleaner only as a safety net that logs a warning when it fires, because a cleaner that fires means some code path forgot to close. A fraud-rule engine that loads and unloads rules at runtime is the classic place for a weak listener registry. And a rates cache behind SoftReference is the classic place for a pager alert: it empties exactly when the heap is under the most pressure.

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Weak references let go as soon as nobody else holds on
x: A weak reference holds nothing up. Once only weak references lead to an object, the next GC that finds it clears all of them at once. In the research behind this course, a short loop of GC requests cleared a weak reference on every run, under every collector it tried. That makes weak references wrong for caches: a weakly held value lasts until the next GC, which on a busy service is milliseconds away. It makes them right for one job: attaching data to an object whose lifetime someone else controls, without making that object live longer. WeakHashMap is that idea as a map. The keys are weak and the values are strong. When a key becomes unreachable, its entry goes away the next time you call size(), get() or put(). Java Map<Session, CheckoutState> checkouts = new WeakHashMap<>(); checkouts.put(session, new CheckoutState("2 items")); session = null; // the session ends; after a GC, checkouts.size() is 0 Kotlin val checkouts = WeakHashMap<Session, CheckoutState>() checkouts[session] = CheckoutState("2 items") // when the session becomes unreachable, the entry goes after the next GC There's one trap, and the Javadoc warns about it: a value must not refer to its own key. If a SessionAudit value holds its Session, the map's strong value keeps the weak key alive, and the entry never goes away. The demo below fills two maps and shows one emptying and the other one stuck. The same idea gives you a listener registry that doesn't leak. A registry that keeps listeners in a plain list keeps every listener alive, plus everything each listener refers to, until someone remembers to unregister. Hold them through WeakReference instead, and a listener whose owner is gone simply disappears. The catch is the mirror image: a lambda registered inline, with no other reference to it, disappears too, at the next GC. Whoever owns a listener must keep a reference to it. The lab builds this registry. Watch a WeakHashMap empty, and one that doesn't Read WeakHashMapDemo. Both maps get one entry, and both keys are dropped. Only the audits value refers back to its key. Predict both sizes, then run it. WeakHashMapDemo.java package workbench.memory.l03; import java.util.Map; import java.util.WeakHashMap; /** WeakHashMap drops an entry when its key is unreachable, unless the value refers to the key. */ public class WeakHashMapDemo { record Session(String id) {} record CheckoutState(String cart) {} record SessionAudit(Session session, String note) {} // refers back to its own key public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { Map<Session, CheckoutState> checkouts = new WeakHashMap<>(); Map<Session, SessionAudit> audits = new WeakHashMap<>(); Session s1 = new Session("s-1"); Session s2 = new Session("s-2"); checkouts.put(s1, new CheckoutState("2 items")); audits.put(s2, new SessionAudit(s2, "opened")); s1 = null; // the sessions end: nothing else refers to them s2 = null; for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(20); } // demo only: ask for a few GCs System.out.println("checkouts left: " + checkouts.size()); // size() also removes cleared entries System.out.println("audits left: " + audits.size()); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.WeakHashMapDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l03/WeakHashMapDemo.java WeakHashMapDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l03 import java.util.WeakHashMap data class KSession(val id: String) data class KCheckoutState(val cart: String) data class KSessionAudit(val session: KSession, val note: String) // refers back to its own key /** WeakHashMap drops an entry when its key is unreachable, unless the value refers to the key. */ fun main() { val checkouts = WeakHashMap<KSession, KCheckoutState>() val audits = WeakHashMap<KSession, KSessionAudit>() var s1: KSession? = KSession("s-1") var s2: KSession? = KSession("s-2") checkouts[s1!!] = KCheckoutState("2 items") audits[s2!!] = KSessionAudit(s2, "opened") s1 = null // the sessions end: nothing else refers to them s2 = null repeat(5) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(20) } // demo only: ask for a few GCs println("checkouts left: ${checkouts.size}") // size also removes cleared entries println("audits left: ${audits.size}") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.WeakHashMapDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l03/WeakHashMapDemo.kt checkouts left: 0 and audits left: 1. The audit entry's value holds its Session strongly, so the weak key never becomes weakly reachable. That entry will stay for as long as the map does.

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Cleaner is the safety net, close() is the real path
x: finalize() was the first way to run code when an object died. Java 9 deprecated it, and since JDK 18 it has been deprecated for removal (JEP 421). A finalizer can bring its object back to life, finalizers run on one JVM thread in no set order and at no set time, and an object with a finalizer needs at least two collections before its memory is freed. You can check whether your service still depends on one: start it with --finalization=disabled (JDK 18 and later), and no finalizer runs. In the demo, 1,000 finalizable objects ran 1,000 finalizers by default and 0 with the flag. The replacement is java.lang.ref.Cleaner. You register an object with a cleaning action. When the object becomes phantom reachable, the cleaner's thread runs the action. register returns a Cleanable, and its clean() runs the action at most once and unregisters it. Java public final class NativeBuffer implements AutoCloseable { private static final Cleaner CLEANER = Cleaner.create(); // one thread for all buffers private final Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable; public NativeBuffer(NativeMemory memory, int bytes) { long handle = memory.allocate(bytes); cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, new Release(memory, handle)); } private record Release(NativeMemory memory, long handle) implements Runnable { public void run() { memory.free(handle); } // no reference to the buffer } @Override public void close() { cleanable.clean(); } // the normal path, safe to call twice } Kotlin class NativeBuffer(memory: NativeMemory, bytes: Int) : AutoCloseable { private val cleanable: Cleaner.Cleanable init { val handle = memory.allocate(bytes) cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, Release(memory, handle)) } // a nested class has no reference to the outer object; only an `inner` class does private class Release(val memory: NativeMemory, val handle: Long) : Runnable { override fun run() = memory.free(handle) } override fun close() = cleanable.clean() // the normal path, safe to call twice companion object { private val CLEANER: Cleaner = Cleaner.create() } } The rule people break: the action must not refer to the object it cleans. If it does, the object never becomes phantom reachable and the action never runs. A lambda that reads a field captures this: in () -> memory.free(handle), handle means this.handle. A non-static inner class in Java captures this too. The Cleaner Javadoc warns about both. And the cleaner is only a safety net. It runs some time after a GC, and maybe not at all before the JVM exits. Release resources with try-with-resources (use {} in Kotlin), and let the cleaner catch the ones somebody forgot. Switch finalization off Read FinalizerDemo. It creates 1,000 objects whose class overrides finalize(), asks for 20 GCs, and counts the finalizer calls, once with default flags and once with --finalization=disabled. Run it. Then think of one library in your service that might still use a finalizer, and how you would test without it. FinalizerDemo.java package workbench.memory.l03; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 1,000 objects with a finalize() method, in two child JVMs: default, and --finalization=disabled. */ public class FinalizerDemo { static final AtomicInteger finalized = new AtomicInteger(); static class LegacyHandle { @Override @SuppressWarnings({"removal", "deprecation"}) protected void finalize() { // deprecated for removal since JDK 18 finalized.incrementAndGet(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { if (args.length == 0) { System.out.println("== default flags"); Jvm.run(List.of(), FinalizerDemo.class.getName(), "run"); System.out.println("== --finalization=disabled"); Jvm.run(List.of("--finalization=disabled"), FinalizerDemo.class.getName(), "run"); return; } for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) new LegacyHandle(); for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(20); } System.out.println("finalized " + finalized.get() + " of 1000"); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.FinalizerDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l03/FinalizerDemo.java FinalizerDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l03 import workbench.memory.Jvm import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger private val finalizedCount = AtomicInteger() class KLegacyHandle { // Kotlin has no override for finalize(): you declare it, and the JVM calls it protected fun finalize() { finalizedCount.incrementAndGet() } } /** 1,000 objects with a finalize() method, in two child JVMs: default, and --finalization=disabled. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isEmpty()) { println("== default flags") Jvm.run(listOf(), "workbench.memory.l03.FinalizerDemoKt", "run") println("== --finalization=disabled") Jvm.run(listOf("--finalization=disabled"), "workbench.memory.l03.FinalizerDemoKt", "run") return } repeat(1_000) { KLegacyHandle() } repeat(20) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(20) } println("finalized ${finalizedCount.get()} of 1000") } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l03.FinalizerDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l03/FinalizerDemo.kt finalized 1000 of 1000 with default flags and finalized 0 of 1000 with --finalization=disabled. The objects were still collected in the second run; only the finalizers were skipped. Running your test suite with that flag shows whether anything depends on them. Cleaner source at jdk-25-ga: the rules for cleaning actions docs JEP 421: Deprecate Finalization for Removal read Using weak or soft references as a cache. Weak values are gone at the next GC, so the hit rate falls apart under load. Soft values stay until the heap is nearly full, so the heap always looks full, and then they're cleared in bulk during full GCs, which sends a wave of reloads to the database at the worst moment. People reach for them because "the GC manages the memory for me" sounds safer than choosing a size. The fix is to choose the size: a cache with a maximum number of entries and an expiry time, and a heap sized to hold it.

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Java and Kotlin
x: Who holds a reference to the outer object Exporter.java class Exporter { private final Path tempFile; // inner (the default in Java): holds Exporter.this class Cleanup implements Runnable { public void run() { deleteQuietly(tempFile); } } // static nested: holds only what you pass in static class SafeCleanup implements Runnable { private final Path file; SafeCleanup(Path file) { this.file = file; } public void run() { deleteQuietly(file); } } } Exporter.kt class Exporter(private val tempFile: Path) { // inner (you must ask for it in Kotlin): holds this@Exporter inner class Cleanup : Runnable { override fun run() = deleteQuietly(tempFile) } // nested (the default in Kotlin): holds only what you pass in class SafeCleanup(private val file: Path) : Runnable { override fun run() = deleteQuietly(file) } } The defaults are opposite. A class declared inside a class is inner in Java unless you write static, and nested in Kotlin unless you write inner. So a Java cleaning action written as a plain inner class silently holds the object it should clean, while the same code in Kotlin doesn't. Lambdas behave the same in both: one that reads a property or field captures this. Kotlin also has no override for finalize(): to write one you declare protected fun finalize(), which is one more reason not to.

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Worked example
x: Find why a WeakHashMap keeps growing A payment gateway keeps statistics per open TCP connection to the card network. It uses a WeakHashMap so that closed connections drop out by themselves. After a day the map holds 2 million entries. Read the code and look for a strong path back to the key. record ConnectionStats(NetworkConnection connection, AtomicLong authorizations) {} static final Map<NetworkConnection, ConnectionStats> STATS = new WeakHashMap<>(); static void recordAuthorization(NetworkConnection c) { STATS.computeIfAbsent(c, k -> new ConnectionStats(k, new AtomicLong())) .authorizations().incrementAndGet(); } data class ConnectionStats(val connection: NetworkConnection, val authorizations: AtomicLong) val STATS: MutableMap<NetworkConnection, ConnectionStats> = WeakHashMap() fun recordAuthorization(c: NetworkConnection) { STATS.computeIfAbsent(c) { k -> ConnectionStats(k, AtomicLong()) } .authorizations.incrementAndGet() } Follow the references from a GC root. The static field holds the map, the map holds its entries, and each entry holds its value strongly. The value holds the connection. So every closed connection is still strongly reachable from STATS, through its own stats object, and its weak key is never cleared. static STATS -> WeakHashMap -> Entry (weak key, STRONG value) -> ConnectionStats -> connection <- the key itself Break the strong path. The stats only need something to print in logs, so store the connection's id instead of the connection. record ConnectionStats(String connectionId, AtomicLong authorizations) {} // no path back to the key STATS.computeIfAbsent(c, k -> new ConnectionStats(k.id(), new AtomicLong())); data class ConnectionStats(val connectionId: String, val authorizations: AtomicLong) // no path back to the key STATS.computeIfAbsent(c) { k -> ConnectionStats(k.id, AtomicLong()) } Prove it with a test that doesn't trust timing: drop the connection, keep a weak probe with its own queue, ask for GCs until the probe arrives (with a limit), then check the map. size() removes cleared entries before it counts. NetworkConnection c = openTestConnection(); recordAuthorization(c); ReferenceQueue<Object> q = new ReferenceQueue<>(); WeakReference<Object> probe = new WeakReference<>(c, q); c = null; Reference<?> seen = null; for (int i = 0; i < 50 && seen == null; i++) { System.gc(); seen = q.remove(50); } // bounded wait assertThat(seen).isSameAs(probe); assertThat(STATS).isEmpty(); var c: NetworkConnection? = openTestConnection() recordAuthorization(c!!) val q = ReferenceQueue<Any>() val probe = WeakReference<Any>(c, q) c = null var seen: Reference<*>? = null for (i in 0 until 50) { System.gc(); seen = q.remove(50); if (seen != null) break } // bounded wait assertThat(seen).isSameAs(probe) assertThat(STATS).isEmpty()

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Lab
x: A Cleaner that runs, and a registry that forgets labs/memory/src/main/java/workbench/memory/l03/NativeBuffer.java labs/memory/src/main/java/workbench/memory/l03/WeakListenerRegistry.java labs/memory/src/main/java/workbench/memory/l03/NativeMemory.java ./gradlew :memory:test --tests 'workbench.memory.l03.*' Run the tests. Four of seven fail; the GC waits make the failing run take about ten seconds. NativeMemory stands in for a native library: read it, but don't change it. Fix NativeBuffer.close(): keep the Cleaner.Cleanable that register returns and call its clean(). A second close then does nothing. Find out why a forgotten buffer is never cleaned. Look hard at the lambda: what does handle mean inside it? Replace it with a static nested class or a record that holds only the NativeMemory and the handle value. Make WeakListenerRegistry hold WeakReference<L>. size() drops cleared references before counting. fire() drops them too, and holds a strong reference to each listener while it calls it. Run the tests until all seven pass, then twice more. A field read inside a lambda is this.field, so the lambda captures this. Copying the field to a local variable first would also work, but a small static class makes the rule visible to the next reader. list.removeIf(ref -> ref.get() == null) drops the cleared references. The tests never assume a GC happened. They ask for one up to 50 times and wait on a ReferenceQueue or a condition, so a correct solution passes in well under a second. Reference.reachabilityFence(rule) in a test keeps rule strongly reachable until that line, even if the JIT sees no later use of the variable. All 7 tests in ReachabilityTest pass, three runs in a row. By the end you can say when the GC clears each kind of reference, pick the right one (or none) for caches, listeners and native resources, and write a Cleaner that actually runs.

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Quiz
x: A WeakHashMap<Merchant, MerchantView> keeps growing even after merchants are removed everywhere else. MerchantView has a field Merchant merchant used for logging. What is the cause? WeakHashMap only removes entries after System.gc() Each value strongly refers to its own key, so the keys never become weakly reachable Merchant doesn't override equals and hashCode The map needs a ReferenceQueue to remove entries Values in a WeakHashMap are strong. A value that points back to its key gives the key a strong path from the map itself, so the GC never clears it. Normal GCs clear weak keys without any System.gc(), and the map already manages its own internal queue: size(), get() and put() remove stale entries. You need a cache of FX rate tables that a service reloads from the database on a miss. Which choice fits best? Map<String, WeakReference<RateTable>> Map<String, SoftReference<RateTable>> A cache with a maximum size and an expiry time, and a heap sized for it Map<String, PhantomReference<RateTable>> A bounded cache keeps exactly as much as you decided, and expiry keeps rates fresh. Weak values are gone at the next GC, so the hit rate collapses. Soft values stay until the heap is nearly full and then go in bulk during full GCs, sending all the reloads at once. A phantom reference can't even return its value. A class registers CLEANER.register(this, () -> codec.release(nativeHandle)), where codec and nativeHandle are fields. A request path forgets to call close(). What happens to the native memory? The cleaner frees it at the next GC The cleaner frees it when the JVM exits It is never freed, because the lambda captures this and the object never becomes phantom reachable The JVM throws an exception when the object is collected Reading codec and nativeHandle inside the lambda means this.codec and this.nativeHandle, so the lambda holds this. The cleaner holds the lambda, so the object stays strongly reachable forever: a leak of both the object and its native memory. The Javadoc also makes no promise that cleaners run at exit. A dependency you use still overrides finalize(). What's the cheapest way to find out whether your service relies on it before finalization is removed? Run the service and its tests with --finalization=disabled Run with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC Search the logs for Finalizer Call System.runFinalization() after each request --finalization=disabled (JDK 18 and later) stops every finalizer from running, which is exactly the world after removal. If tests and a load run pass, nothing depends on it. DisableExplicitGC only ignores System.gc(), and calling runFinalization makes the dependency worse. From the threads track: a task on a fixed pool of one thread does buffer.set(new byte[1 << 20]) on a ThreadLocal and never calls remove(). The task finishes. When can that 1 MiB array be collected? At the next GC, because the task is done Only when a later task on that same pool thread calls buffer.remove(), or the thread ends When the ThreadLocal object itself is garbage collected Never, while the JVM runs The value lives in the pool thread's own map, and a live thread is a GC root. In the research behind this course, a weak probe on the array stayed set after five System.gc() calls and cleared only after a task called remove() on the same pooled thread. The thread outlives every task, so the value does too.
