h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Key terms
x: GC root A starting point for reachability: a live thread's stack, a static field, a native reference. Strongly reachable Reachable through ordinary references. The GC never frees it. SoftReference A reference the GC clears when memory is short, at the latest before an OutOfMemoryError. WeakReference A reference the GC clears as soon as nothing stronger holds the object. PhantomReference A reference whose get() is always null; it reports that an object is gone. ReferenceQueue Where the GC puts reference objects after clearing them, so you can react. Cleaner Runs a cleanup action after an object becomes phantom reachable, or when you call clean(). Finalization The old finalize() mechanism. Deprecated for removal since JDK 18. What are GC roots? Where reachability starts: local variables on live threads' stacks, static fields, and references held by native code. When is a SoftReference guaranteed to be cleared? Before the JVM throws an OutOfMemoryError. At any other time, the spec promises nothing. When is a WeakReference cleared? By the next GC that finds its referent reachable only through weak references. What does PhantomReference.get() return? Always null. A phantom reference only tells you, through its queue, that the object is gone. In a WeakHashMap, what keeps an entry alive forever? A value that refers to its own key, directly or indirectly. Values are strong. Why might a Cleaner action never run? The action refers to the object it cleans (a lambda reading a field, a Java inner class), so the object never becomes phantom reachable. How do you test whether code still relies on finalizers? Run it with --finalization=disabled (JDK 18 and later): no finalizer runs.

h: Reachability: strong, soft, weak and phantom references · Go deeper
x: There's a race the Cleaner pattern can hit even when you follow the rule. The JVM may decide an object is unreachable earlier than the source suggests, even while one of its methods is still running. The Reference.reachabilityFence Javadoc describes it: the JIT can load a field's value early, the object is then no longer needed, and the cleanup thread can free a resource that the method is about to use. So a method that passes a native handle to native code should keep its object reachable until the call returns: Java public int compress(byte[] input) { try { return Codec.compress(handle, input); // native call that uses the handle } finally { Reference.reachabilityFence(this); // `this` stays reachable until here } } Kotlin fun compress(input: ByteArray): Int { try { return Codec.compress(handle, input) // native call that uses the handle } finally { Reference.reachabilityFence(this) // `this` stays reachable until here } } The lab's tests use the same method for the opposite reason: to keep a listener strongly reachable until the asserts are done. Its Javadoc also states a guarantee in the terms of the memory model track: actions in a thread before reachabilityFence(x) happen-before the garbage collector clears any reference to x, so a cleanup thread sees everything the method wrote. Two more details are useful. Phantom references used to keep their referent in memory until you cleared them; since JDK 9 the GC clears them automatically when it enqueues them, which is why Cleaner works without extra steps. And a Cleaner owns a daemon thread, so create one per library (a static final field), never one per object.

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · Most objects die young, so the heap has generations
x: Most objects die young: eden, survivor copies and promotion to the old generation A payment request allocates the parsed JSON, a few DTOs, some strings and the response, and all of it is garbage a few milliseconds later. A few objects live much longer: a cached merchant config, a pooled connection, the entries of an idempotency cache. That split has a name, the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. A real log shows how lopsided it is. In one generational ZGC minor collection on a test workload, eden held 27 MB of live objects and 470 MB of garbage. HotSpot's collectors split the heap to match. New objects go into eden, in the young generation. When eden fills, a young collection finds the few live objects there and copies them into a survivor space. Everything else in eden is reclaimed at once, and the collector never even looks at it. Each time an object survives, its age goes up by one; it lives in the 4 age bits of the mark word from lesson 1. After enough survivals (at most 15, set by MaxTenuringThreshold, and G1 lowers it when survivor space runs short), the object is promoted to the old generation, which is collected much less often. The payoff is that a young collection costs time in proportion to what survives, not to what was allocated. A 500 MB eden with 5 MB of survivors gives a short pause. The same eden with 200 MB of survivors, for example a large batch held in memory while it's processed, gives a long one, and those objects then fill the old generation too. That makes medium-lived objects the expensive kind. They survive a few young collections, get copied each time, get promoted, and then die in the old generation, where only a bigger collection can reclaim them. An idempotency cache with a 10-minute expiry is exactly that shape. Watch survivors age Read GenerationsDemo. It runs the lesson's service load (ServiceLoad.java: short-lived request garbage plus a growing cache) for one second, with G1's age table logged. Run it. For each Pause Young line, compare the heap before and after the arrow. Follow one number through the age table from GC(0) to GC(2). GenerationsDemo.java package workbench.memory.l04; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; /** * Runs the service load for one second with G1's age table logged, and prints the first four young * collections: how much of the heap each one freed, and how old the survivors are. */ public class GenerationsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { ServiceLoad.run(1, 0.30); return; } for (String line : Jvm.lines(List.of("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+age=trace"), GenerationsDemo.class.getName(), "load")) { if (line.matches(".*GC\\([0-3]\\) (Pause Young|- age).*")) System.out.println(line.replaceAll("\\s+", " ")); } } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.GenerationsDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l04/GenerationsDemo.java GenerationsDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l04 import workbench.memory.Jvm /** * Runs the service load for one second with G1's age table logged, and prints the first four young * collections: how much of the heap each one freed, and how old the survivors are. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { serviceLoad(1.0, 0.30) return } val firstFour = Regex(""".*GC\([0-3]\) (Pause Young|- age).*""") Jvm.lines(listOf("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+age=trace"), "workbench.memory.l04.GenerationsDemoKt", "load") .filter { firstFour.matches(it) } .forEach { println(it.replace(Regex("\\s+"), " ")) } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.GenerationsDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l04/GenerationsDemo.kt Each young pause frees most of what it found: 54M->4M means about 50 of the 54 MB were garbage. The age table shows the survivors getting older: the 812 KB at age 1 in GC(0) appears at age 2 in GC(1) and at age 3 in GC(2). Those are cache entries, the long-lived objects. Exact numbers change from run to run. G1 runs a warehouse of identical storage bays. New stock lands in the receiving bays. Every so often a crew moves the few boxes still wanted from receiving into long-term bays, then declares every receiving bay empty at once: that's a young pause. Now and then an inspector walks the long-term bays while work goes on and notes how full each one is: concurrent marking. Then the crew empties the emptiest long-term bays first, a few per shift, because they give back the most space for the least lifting: mixed pauses. A pallet too big for one bay gets several neighbouring bays to itself: a humongous object. Where it breaks: a real crew can move boxes while people work around them. G1 has to stop every thread before it moves anything, and that stop is your pause.

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · Collectors mark, copy or compact, and they stop the world to move objects
x: A garbage collector needs two steps to be correct, and you can write both in a few lines. Here's a toy one. Its heap is a map from an object id to the ids that object's fields point to: Java Set<Integer> mark(Collection<Integer> roots) { Set<Integer> live = new HashSet<>(); for (int root : roots) visit(root, live); return live; } void visit(int id, Set<Integer> live) { if (!live.add(id)) return; // already marked: this also ends cycles for (int next : refs.get(id)) visit(next, live); // follow every reference field } Set<Integer> sweep(Set<Integer> live) { Set<Integer> dead = new HashSet<>(refs.keySet()); dead.removeAll(live); refs.keySet().removeAll(dead); // their memory is free again return dead; } Kotlin fun mark(roots: Collection<Int>): Set<Int> { val live = HashSet<Int>() fun visit(id: Int) { if (!live.add(id)) return // already marked: this also ends cycles refs.getValue(id).forEach(::visit) // follow every reference field } roots.forEach(::visit) return live } fun sweep(live: Set<Int>): Set<Int> { val dead = refs.keys.filterTo(HashSet()) { it !in live } refs.keys.removeAll(dead) // their memory is free again return dead } Marking follows references from the roots and remembers every object it reaches. Sweeping frees the rest. Two things follow from the code. A cycle of objects that point at each other, with no root pointing in, gets freed: a tracing collector asks only whether a root can reach an object, never how many references it has. And the sweep visits every object, dead or alive, so its cost grows with the heap. (The recursion is a toy shortcut: a chain of 200,000 objects overflows a thread's stack. A real collector keeps its own mark stack, and so will your lab.) HotSpot replaces the sweep with better moves. Copying, also called evacuation, moves the live objects into empty space and then treats the whole old space as free. It never touches the dead objects, so its cost follows the live ones, and it compacts memory as a side effect. Mark-compact slides the live objects together inside the space they're in: no spare room needed, but several passes. Young collections copy, which is why G1 calls them evacuation pauses. G1's full GC is a mark-compact of the whole heap, the last resort. Moving an object is only safe while no thread is using it. So these steps run in a stop-the-world pause at a safepoint: a moment when every application thread is stopped at a known place, with its references where the collector can find and update them. Compiled code checks for a pending safepoint at method returns and in loops. Getting every thread there takes time of its own, and -Xlog:safepoint splits it out: Safepoint "G1CollectForAllocation", Time since last: 32350666 ns, Reaching safepoint: 3409 ns, Cleanup: 4274 ns, At safepoint: 1671830 ns, Leaving safepoint: 1364 ns, Total: 1680877 ns "Reaching safepoint" (3.4 microseconds here) is how long the slowest thread took to stop. "At safepoint" (1.67 ms) is the collector's work. When the first number is large, the collector is not your problem: some thread ran a long time without reaching a safepoint check. Separate stopping from collecting Run SafepointDemo. It logs every safepoint during one second of service load and prints the first five GC safepoints. For each line, compare "Reaching safepoint" with "At safepoint". Both are in nanoseconds. SafepointDemo.java package workbench.memory.l04; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; /** Logs every safepoint during one second of service load and prints the GC ones. */ public class SafepointDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { ServiceLoad.run(1, 0.30); return; } Jvm.lines(List.of("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:safepoint"), SafepointDemo.class.getName(), "load").stream() .filter(line -> line.contains("G1CollectForAllocation")) .limit(5) .forEach(System.out::println); } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.SafepointDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l04/SafepointDemo.java SafepointDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l04 import workbench.memory.Jvm /** Logs every safepoint during one second of service load and prints the GC ones. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { serviceLoad(1.0, 0.30) return } Jvm.lines(listOf("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:safepoint"), "workbench.memory.l04.SafepointDemoKt", "load") .filter { "G1CollectForAllocation" in it } .take(5) .forEach(::println) } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.SafepointDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l04/SafepointDemo.kt Reaching the safepoint takes a few thousand nanoseconds (a few microseconds), and the GC work at the safepoint takes one to five million (one to five milliseconds). The threads in this load stop quickly because their loops are short. A long "Reaching safepoint" would point at a thread that runs a long time between safepoint checks. A Quarkus payment API in a container with a 1 GiB memory limit gets a 256 MB heap by default, and so 1 MB regions. Any payload over 512 KB held in one array is humongous there: a big merchant's settlement CSV, a base64 PDF statement inside a JSON response, a Kafka batch read into one buffer. And the idempotency cache, whose entries live for minutes, is the classic medium-lived structure: each entry survives several young pauses, gets promoted, and has to wait for marking and mixed collections to be freed. When the after-values of young pauses keep rising and you see (Evacuation Failure), the heap is too small for that cache, or the cache has no bound (lesson 7).

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · Write barriers and card tables keep a young collection small
x: There's a catch in the young collection story. To decide which young objects are alive, the collector follows references from the roots. But old objects point at young ones all the time: the idempotency cache sitting in the old generation gets a new young entry with every request. If a young collection had to scan the whole old generation to find those pointers, it would cost as much as a full GC. The fix is to do the bookkeeping when the pointer is written. The heap is divided into cards of 512 bytes (G1 prints CardTable entry size: 512 at startup), and the card table has one byte per card. Every time your code stores a reference into a field, it also runs a few extra instructions, the write barrier, that mark the card holding that field as dirty: cache.entries[i] = newEntry; // the store you wrote card_table[address_of(field) >> 9] = DIRTY; // what the barrier adds (512 = 2^9) A young collection then scans the roots plus the dirty cards, not the whole old generation. G1 goes a step further: each region keeps a remembered set, the cards elsewhere in the heap that point into that region. "Merge Heap Roots" in G1's pause log is the step that folds those remembered sets into the roots for the pause. G1 has a second barrier for its concurrent marking, which section 5 describes. While the application keeps running during marking, it can move a reference out of an object the marker hasn't visited into one it already has. To catch that, the barrier records the old value before a reference is overwritten, so the marker still finds every object that was live when marking began. The technique is called snapshot-at-the-beginning (SATB), and the comment on G1's barrier class in the JDK 25 source calls it "a logging barrier to support snapshot-at-the-beginning marking". These barriers are the steady cost of a generational, concurrent collector: a few instructions on every reference store in your code, all the time. Lesson 5 shows that ZGC pays at reference loads instead. Reason it through before you move on. A Kafka consumer keeps a long-lived map of the last offset per partition, so the map sits in the old generation. For every record it replaces one partition's value with a new boxed Long. Which cards does the barrier dirty, and what does the next young pause scan? (Only the few cards holding the map entries whose value changed. The pause scans those cards and the roots, finds the new Longs, and never reads the rest of the old generation.)

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · G1 splits the heap into regions
x: G1 cuts the heap into equal regions and collects the most garbage first G1, the default collector, doesn't keep one big eden and one big old space. It cuts the heap into equal regions, and each region has a role for a while: eden, survivor, old, humongous or free. The roles move around. After a young pause, the evacuated eden regions are free, and next time any of them can become anything. The region size comes from the max heap. In the JDK 25 source it's the max heap divided by 2048, clamped between 1 MB and 32 MB, then rounded up to a power of two. A 1 GB heap gets 1 MB regions, the 3.4 GB default heap on a 13 GB machine got 2 MB, and -Xmx40g gets 32 MB. Regions explain one of G1's sharp edges. An object larger than half a region is humongous. It skips TLABs and eden and gets its own run of whole, contiguous regions, which count as old from the start. A 3 MiB byte[] is 3 MiB plus a 16-byte header, so with 1 MB regions it takes four regions, and nearly all of the fourth one is wasted. A burst of humongous allocations can start a concurrent cycle on its own (the log says G1 Humongous Allocation), and each one needs enough free regions in a row. G1 does reclaim dead humongous objects early: in the demo, the first young pause freed Humongous regions: 12->0. In payment services the humongous objects are usually whole payloads held in one array: a settlement file, a large JSON response, a PDF statement. If your log is full of G1 Humongous Allocation, stream those payloads instead of buffering them, or raise the region size with -XX:G1HeapRegionSize until they are under half a region. Count the regions of a humongous object Read HumongousDemo. It runs a 1 GB G1 heap, so regions are 1 MB, and allocates 3 MiB arrays with ordinary garbage in between. Predict how many regions each 3 MiB array takes, then run it. HumongousDemo.java package workbench.memory.l04; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.List; /** * Allocates 3 MiB "settlement files" in a 1 GB G1 heap, where regions are 1 MB, and prints the * region counts G1 logs for the first young pause. */ public class HumongousDemo { static volatile Object sink; public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { for (int i = 0; i < 40; i++) { sink = new byte[3 * 1024 * 1024]; // 3 MiB + a 16-byte header for (int j = 0; j < 20_000; j++) sink = new byte[200]; // some ordinary garbage in between } return; } for (String line : Jvm.lines(List.of("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx1g", "-Xlog:gc,gc+init,gc+heap=info"), HumongousDemo.class.getName(), "load")) { if (line.contains("Heap Region Size") || line.matches(".*GC\\(0\\) (Pause|.*regions).*")) { System.out.println(line.replaceAll("\\s+", " ")); } } } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.HumongousDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l04/HumongousDemo.java HumongousDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l04 import workbench.memory.Jvm @Volatile private var humongousSink: Any? = null /** * Allocates 3 MiB "settlement files" in a 1 GB G1 heap, where regions are 1 MB, and prints the * region counts G1 logs for the first young pause. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { repeat(40) { humongousSink = ByteArray(3 * 1024 * 1024) // 3 MiB + a 16-byte header repeat(20_000) { humongousSink = ByteArray(200) } // some ordinary garbage in between } return } val firstPause = Regex(""".*GC\(0\) (Pause|.*regions).*""") Jvm.lines(listOf("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx1g", "-Xlog:gc,gc+init,gc+heap=info"), "workbench.memory.l04.HumongousDemoKt", "load") .filter { "Heap Region Size" in it || firstPause.matches(it) } .forEach { println(it.replace(Regex("\\s+"), " ")) } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l04.HumongousDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l04/HumongousDemo.kt Heap Region Size: 1M, then the first young pause reports Humongous regions: 12->0. Twelve regions held three arrays, four regions each, because 3 MiB plus a 16-byte header doesn't fit in three. All three were already dead, so the young pause reclaimed them right away. G1 gives each equal region a role. Young pauses evacuate every eden and survivor region; mixed pauses also take the old regions with the most garbage. g1HeapRegion.cpp at jdk-25-ga: how G1 picks the region size read

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · G1's cycle: young pauses, concurrent marking, mixed collections
x: Most of the time G1 runs only young pauses. Each one evacuates all eden and survivor regions. In Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 14M->1M(256M) 12.723ms, 14 MB was in use before, 1 MB after, the committed heap is 256 MB, and the stop-the-world pause took 12.7 ms. The old regions fill up slowly with promoted objects. When old-generation occupancy crosses the initiating heap occupancy percent (IHOP: 45% to begin with, then adapted from what G1 observes), G1 starts a concurrent marking cycle. Here's one from a 1 GB heap, verbatim: GC(20) Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation) 556M->527M(1024M) 13.734ms GC(21) Concurrent Mark Cycle GC(21) Pause Remark 583M->583M(1024M) 0.835ms GC(21) Pause Cleanup 637M->637M(1024M) 0.379ms GC(21) Concurrent Mark Cycle 53.866ms GC(22) Pause Young (Prepare Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) (Evacuation Failure) 996M->760M(1024M) 43.391ms GC(23) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 981M->660M(1024M) 10.429ms The cycle starts inside a young pause (Concurrent Start). Marking then runs on a background thread for 54 ms while the application keeps working, with two short pauses to finish (Remark, Cleanup). Now G1 knows how much of each old region is live. The next young pause (Prepare Mixed) is the last young-only one. Then come the mixed pauses: all young regions plus a few old ones, the ones with the most garbage. That choice is where the name Garbage First comes from. Which old regions? From the JDK 25 source: only regions less than 85% live are candidates (G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent). G1 sorts them by efficiency, best first. It drops the cheapest ones as long as the garbage it leaves behind stays within 5% of the heap (G1HeapWastePercent). And each mixed pause takes at least an eighth of the candidates, so the work is done in at most 8 mixed pauses (G1MixedGCCountTarget). The lab has you write these rules. Two phrases in the log mean trouble. (Evacuation Failure) means G1 ran out of free regions to copy into and had to leave objects where they were. Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) is the fallback: the whole heap, mark-compact, everything stopped. Both say the heap is too small for the live data plus the allocation rate, and the 200 ms pause goal (MaxGCPauseMillis) can't fix that. Squeeze G1 until it struggles Read G1CycleDemo. It runs the service load for 3 seconds in a 256 MB heap, with the cache growing to 60% of it. It counts each kind of GC event and prints the first line of each kind, in the order they happened. Run it. Find the cycle from this section in the first lines: Concurrent Start, Remark, Cleanup, Prepare Mixed, Mixed. Run it again and compare the counts. G1CycleDemo.java package workbench.memory.l04; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.regex.Matcher; import java.util.regex.Pattern; /** * Runs the service load for 3 seconds in a child JVM with a tight 256 MB G1 heap, then counts each * kind of GC event and prints the first line of each kind. */ public class G1CycleDemo { // "GC(12) Pause Young (Mixed) (G1 Evacuation Pause) ..." -> "Pause Young (Mixed)" static final Pattern KIND = Pattern.compile("GC\\(\\d+\\) ((?:Pause \\w+(?: \\((?:Normal|Concurrent Start|Prepare Mixed|Mixed)\\))?)|Concurrent \\w+ Cycle)"); public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { ServiceLoad.run(3, 0.60); return; } List<String> log = Jvm.lines(List.of("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:gc"), G1CycleDemo.class.getName(), "load"); Map<String, Integer> counts = new TreeMap<>(); Map<String, String> firstLine = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // in the order they first happened int evacuationFailures = 0; for (String line : log) { Matcher m = KIND.matcher(line); if (!m.find() || line.endsWith("Cycle")) continue; // skip the "cycle started" half of a pair counts.merge(m.group(1), 1, Integer::sum); firstLine.putIfAbsent(m.group(1), line); if (line.contains("(Evacuation Failure)")) evacuationFailures++; Which of these is a humongous allocation? new byte[400_000] for a receipt image A HashMap with 30,000 entries new byte[700_000] for a settlement file chunk A String of 300,000 Latin-1 characters 2 GB / 2048 is exactly 1 MB, so regions are 1 MB and the humongous threshold is 512 KB. 700,000 bytes is over it. 400,000 bytes and a 300,000-character Latin-1 string (a 300 KB array) are under it. A HashMap is many small objects; with 30,000 entries its table has 65,536 slots, a 256 KB array. Why does a young collection not have to scan the whole old generation for pointers into eden? Old objects are never allowed to point to young objects The write barrier marks dirty cards when references are stored, and the collector scans only those The JIT moves such objects into the old generation right away G1 copies the old generation in every young pause Old-to-young pointers are normal, for example a cache in the old generation getting new entries. Every reference store runs a barrier that marks the 512-byte card it wrote to as dirty. A young pause scans the roots plus the dirty cards; in G1, remembered sets track which cards point into which region. A G1 log shows GC(42) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 1210M->1180M(1536M), then (Evacuation Failure) on the next pauses, then Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 1490M->1150M(1536M). What does it tell you? The pause goal is too high; set -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=50 The young generation is too small; the old generation is fine The application calls System.gc() About 1.15 GB is really live in a 1.5 GB heap, which leaves G1 too little room to copy The full GC's after-value is the live set: 1,150 MB of 1,536 MB. A young pause that frees only 30 MB, and copies that fail for lack of free regions, say the same thing. A smaller pause goal can't create free regions. A System.gc() call would show (System.gc()) as the cause. In Safepoint "G1CollectForAllocation" ... Reaching safepoint: 48000000 ns ... At safepoint: 2100000 ns, where would you look first? At the GC settings, because the collection took 48 ms At application code that runs a long time without a safepoint check At the heap size, because the heap is too small At the number of GC worker threads "Reaching safepoint" is the time the slowest thread took to stop: 48 ms here. The GC work itself, "At safepoint", took 2.1 ms. A long time-to-safepoint means some thread ran far without reaching a safepoint check, which no GC setting fixes. From lesson 2: why is a dead 3 MiB array cheaper for G1 than a 3 MiB array that survives several young pauses, even though both are humongous? Dead humongous objects can be reclaimed in a young pause without any copying; live ones keep their contiguous regions and fill the old generation Live humongous objects are copied in every young pause Dead humongous objects go into a TLAB There is no difference; G1 treats all humongous objects alike Humongous objects never go through TLABs or eden, and G1 never copies them. The demo showed a young pause freeing Humongous regions: 12->0 because the arrays were already dead. A live one keeps its regions as part of the old generation until it dies and a collection finds it.

h: How garbage collectors work: generations and G1 · Key terms
x: Young generation Eden plus survivor space, where new objects live until they die or are promoted. Promotion Moving an object that survived enough young collections into the old generation. Evacuation G1's word for copying live objects out of a region so the region can be freed. Safepoint A moment when every application thread is stopped at a known place, so the GC can move objects. Card table One byte per 512-byte card of heap, marked dirty when a reference in that card changes. Remembered set G1's per-region list of cards elsewhere in the heap that point into the region. Humongous object In G1, an object bigger than half a region, stored in its own contiguous regions. Mixed collection A G1 pause that evacuates the young regions plus some old regions with the most garbage. What does the weak generational hypothesis say? Most objects die young. Collectors use it by collecting a small young generation often and the old generation rarely. What does a young collection's pause time depend on? Mostly on how much survives and must be copied, not on how much garbage there is. What does a write barrier do in a generational collector? On every reference store, it marks the card (512 bytes in G1) that holds the field as dirty, so a young GC scans dirty cards instead of the whole old generation. How does G1 pick its region size by default? Max heap / 2048, clamped to 1 to 32 MB, rounded up to a power of two. When is an object humongous in G1? When it is bigger than half a region. It gets whole contiguous regions and skips TLABs and eden. Which old regions can a G1 mixed collection take? Regions under 85% live (G1MixedGCLiveThresholdPercent), best first, until the remaining garbage is within 5% of the heap. Two objects point at each other and nothing else points at them. Does a tracing GC free them? Yes. Marking only asks whether a root can reach an object, so an unreachable cycle is never marked and gets freed.

h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · ZGC moves objects while your code keeps running
x: Lesson 4's G1 log had a young pause of 16 ms, and almost all of it was "Evacuate Collection Set": copying live objects while every thread waited. That pause grows with the work. A service with a 32 GB heap full of cached risk scores has more to copy in each pause, and a full GC on that heap can stop it for seconds. For a fraud check with a 20 ms budget, that is an outage. ZGC moves objects while your threads keep running. The hard part is that a thread may be about to read a reference to an object the collector has just moved. ZGC solves that with two tricks. First, every reference stored in the heap carries a few metadata bits, its color. ZGC needs room for them, so it uses full 8-byte references: on JDK 21, PrintFlagsFinal shows UseCompressedOops false under ZGC, and lesson 1's 40-byte Payment takes 48 bytes. Second, the JIT inserts a load barrier after every load of a reference from the heap. It compares the reference's color with the color the collector currently calls good. Nearly always they match, and the cost is a test and a branch. When they don't, the object may have moved. The barrier then finds the new address (moving the object itself if the collector hasn't done it yet) and writes the fixed reference back into the field, so the next load of that field is fast again. So ZGC only stops your threads to handle their roots, briefly. Each generational ZGC collection has three pauses, and in the demo each took about 0.02 ms. The java manual says ZGC gives "max pause times of a few milliseconds" and that "pause times are independent of what heap size is used", for heaps from 8 MB to 16 TB. The versions matter. JDK 21 added generational ZGC as an option (-XX:+ZGenerational, JEP 439), JDK 23 made it the default (JEP 474), and JDK 24 removed the old single-generation mode (JEP 490). Read its log with care. In Minor Collection (Allocation Rate) 582M(57%)->226M(22%) 0.052s, the 0.052 s is the whole concurrent collection, not a pause. The pauses are the lines that say Pause Mark Start, Pause Mark End and Pause Relocate Start. Find the pauses in a ZGC log Read ZgcDemo. It runs two seconds of the service load from lesson 4 under generational ZGC (it adds -XX:+ZGenerational on JDK 21 and 22), then prints every line of the first minor collection. Predict before you run: will the pauses be longer than G1's young pauses in lesson 4, the same, or shorter? Will the collection time on the last line be longer or shorter than G1's pauses? Run it and match the Pause lines to the three red marks in the figure. JEP 439: Generational ZGC read zAddress.hpp at jdk-25-ga: ZGC's colored pointers read ZGC is a removal company that moves you to a new house while you keep living in it. They carry boxes while you work, and they leave a forwarding note on the old address of each box they move. Whenever you reach for something, you check the label first; if it carries an old address, you follow the note and fix the label so the next reach is direct. That label check is the load barrier. Twice a day the movers ask everyone to freeze for a moment while they check the hallway: those are the pauses. Where it breaks: real movers only slow you down while they're in the house. ZGC's label check runs on every reference you load, all day, whether a move is going on or not.

h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Low pauses cost CPU, headroom and memory
x: The manual is honest about the price: ZGC gives low pauses "at some throughput cost". You pay in three ways. CPU. Marking and relocating run on GC threads beside your threads, and the barrier's slow path runs on your own threads. In a pod with 2 CPUs, the GC threads take CPU away from request handling exactly when the service is busiest. Headroom. While a collection runs, your code keeps allocating. In one run a major collection went 342M(33%)->466M(46%): the heap was fuller at the end than at the start, because the application allocated at least 124 MB during the 119 ms cycle. If the heap fills before a collection finishes, ZGC has to make allocating threads wait. The log calls that an allocation stall, and it hurts more than a pause, because it hits exactly the threads doing the most work. Stalls should be zero. When they aren't, give ZGC a bigger heap or more CPU. Memory per object. With 8-byte references, every object that holds references is bigger, as above. Shenandoah, the other concurrent collector in OpenJDK, makes the same trade with a different design. It also marks and evacuates while your threads run, and the manual says its pause times "are not proportional to the size of the heap". Its default mode has a single generation. A generational mode is experimental in JDK 24 and a product mode in JDK 25 (-XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational). Not every vendor's build includes Shenandoah, so check that java -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -version starts before you plan on it. The demo runs the same second of load under five collectors. Predict the order of the "longest pause" column before you run it, and look at the shape of the results rather than the exact numbers: they change on every run and every machine. Run one load under five collectors Read CollectorCompareDemo. Each collector gets the same second of load in a 512 MB heap, in a fresh child JVM. The child reports the rounds of work it finished and the CPU time the whole process used, GC threads included. Predict the order of the longest pauses, from longest to shortest. Then run it. Run it again and see which columns stay stable and which jump around. h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Choose a collector with a table, not a hunch
x: Before you choose, know what you get when you choose nothing. On JDK 21 to 26, the JVM picks G1 only on a "server-class machine": at least 2 CPUs and at least 1,792 MB of memory, both as the JVM sees them inside the container. Anything smaller silently gets Serial. A Quarkus service in a pod with 1 CPU, or with a 1 GiB memory limit, has been running Serial all along unless someone named a collector. Per the JDK 27 source, JDK 27 picks G1 everywhere. Then the table. These are my defaults for payment services, not benchmark results: Collector Pick it when Watch out for Serial 1 CPU and a heap up to a few hundred MB full GCs that grow with the live data Parallel batch jobs, where total throughput beats any single pause long full-GC pauses on big heaps G1 most services: heaps from about 256 MB to tens of GB, pause budgets of tens of milliseconds (Evacuation Failure), Pause Full, humongous churn ZGC GC pauses must stay under about 10 ms, and there are cores to spare CPU in small pods, Allocation Stall, 8-byte references Shenandoah the same goals as ZGC, on a build that includes it vendor availability; generational only from JDK 24 Epsilon tests and benchmarks only the JVM dies when the heap is full, by design The flags change with the JDK: Collector JDK 21 JDK 25 G1, Serial, Parallel -XX:+UseG1GC, -XX:+UseSerialGC, -XX:+UseParallelGC the same Generational ZGC -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -XX:+UseZGC Generational Shenandoah not available -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational Epsilon -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC the same From JDK 24, -XX:+ZGenerational is an obsolete flag, so remove it when you move a service from 21 to 25. The lab turns both tables into code. See what the JVM picks in a small container Run the first command. -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1 makes the JVM believe it has one CPU, like a pod with a 1-CPU limit. Run the second one without the flag and compare. Predict what JDK 27 would print for the first command. terminal java -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1 -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E ' Use(Serial|G1|Parallel|Z|Shenandoah)GC ' java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E ' Use(Serial|G1)GC ' On JDK 21 to 26 the first command shows UseSerialGC = true {ergonomic} and UseG1GC = false: one CPU is not a server-class machine. Without the flag, on a machine with 2 or more CPUs and enough memory, UseG1GC = true {ergonomic}. h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Epsilon never collects, which makes it a test tool
x: Epsilon is a garbage collector that never collects. It hands out memory, and when the heap is full, the JVM stops: Terminating due to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space In production that would be useless. In a test it's a measuring tool, because under Epsilon the heap size is an allocation budget: if a code path finishes under -Xmx64m, it allocated less than 64 MB in total, a few of which went to starting the JVM. The demo runs lesson 2's two ways of summing settlement totals, over 5 million payments, each under a 64 MB budget. The primitive version finishes. The boxed version dies. It dies even when the JIT's escape analysis removes the temporary boxes for the key and the amount, because every running sum is a new 24-byte Long stored in the map, and Epsilon never frees the old one: at least 120 MB. Epsilon has two other honest uses: benchmarks that must not be disturbed by GC pauses, and very short jobs that exit before they could fill the heap. It's an experimental option on every JDK from 21 to 27, and the JVM is strict about the order of flags. Write -XX:+UseEpsilonGC -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions and it refuses to start: Error: The unlock option must precede 'UseEpsilonGC'. Put a code path on an allocation budget Read EpsilonDemo. Each version runs in a child JVM with Epsilon and a 64 MB heap. Predict which version finishes, then run it. EpsilonDemo.java package workbench.memory.l05; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * Epsilon never frees anything, so a heap of 64 MB is an allocation budget. Two versions of the same * settlement totals run against that budget, each in its own child JVM. */ public class EpsilonDemo { static final int PAYMENTS = 5_000_000, MERCHANTS = 500; static long boxedTotals() { Map<Integer, Long> totals = new HashMap<>(); // every sum is a new Long stored in the map: at least 24 bytes per payment, even when the JIT // removes the temporary boxes for the key and the amount for (int i = 0; i < PAYMENTS; i++) totals.merge(i % MERCHANTS, 1_000L + i % 9_000, Long::sum); return totals.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum(); } static long primitiveTotals() { long[] totals = new long[MERCHANTS]; for (int i = 0; i < PAYMENTS; i++) totals[i % MERCHANTS] += 1_000L + i % 9_000; // no objects long sum = 0; for (long t : totals) sum += t; return sum; } public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { long sum = args[0].equals("boxed") ? boxedTotals() : primitiveTotals(); System.out.println("finished inside the budget, total " + sum); return; } List<String> epsilon = List.of("-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions", "-XX:+UseEpsilonGC", "-Xmx64m"); for (String version : List.of("primitive", "boxed")) { System.out.println("== " + version); Jvm.lines(epsilon, EpsilonDemo.class.getName(), version).forEach(System.out::println); } } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l05.EpsilonDemo labs/memory/src/demo/java/workbench/memory/l05/EpsilonDemo.java EpsilonDemo.kt package workbench.memory.l05 import workbench.memory.Jvm private const val PAYMENTS = 5_000_000 private const val MERCHANTS = 500 private fun boxedTotals(): Long { val totals = HashMap<Int, Long>() // every sum is a new Long stored in the map: at least 24 bytes per payment, even when the JIT // removes the temporary boxes for the key and the amount for (i in 0 until PAYMENTS) totals.merge(i % MERCHANTS, 1_000L + i % 9_000) { a, b -> a + b } return totals.values.sum() } private fun primitiveTotals(): Long { val totals = LongArray(MERCHANTS) for (i in 0 until PAYMENTS) totals[i % MERCHANTS] += 1_000L + i % 9_000 // no objects return totals.sum() } /** * Epsilon never frees anything, so a heap of 64 MB is an allocation budget. Two versions of the same * settlement totals run against that budget, each in its own child JVM. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { val sum = if (args[0] == "boxed") boxedTotals() else primitiveTotals() println("finished inside the budget, total $sum") return } val epsilon = listOf("-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions", "-XX:+UseEpsilonGC", "-Xmx64m") for (version in listOf("primitive", "boxed")) { println("== $version") Jvm.lines(epsilon, "workbench.memory.l05.EpsilonDemoKt", version).forEach(::println) } } ./gradlew :memory:demo -Pmain=workbench.memory.l05.EpsilonDemoKt labs/memory/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/memory/l05/EpsilonDemo.kt primitive prints finished inside the budget. boxed prints Terminating due to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. Five million new Long sums need at least 120 MB, and nothing is ever freed. Change PAYMENTS to 1,000,000 and the boxed run may finish or fail depending on how soon the JIT removes the temporary boxes, which is why you shouldn't build a test right at the edge of the budget. Switching to ZGC because "it has the lowest pauses" in a pod that has no CPU to spare, then watching p99 latency get worse. ZGC's GC threads run alongside your request threads, the load barrier runs on every reference load, and if the collector falls behind, allocating threads stall. The man page says it plainly: low pauses "at some throughput cost". The fix is to decide with numbers: measure the G1 pauses you actually have in the GC log, compare them with your latency budget, and only switch when G1's pauses really break the budget and the pod has spare cores. After a switch, watch CPU, pause lines and allocation stalls.

h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Java and Kotlin
x: Report which collector runs, from inside the service GcReport.java // log once at startup, and on a timer if you like for (GarbageCollectorMXBean gc : ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans()) { log.infof("%s: %d collections, %d ms", gc.getName(), gc.getCollectionCount(), gc.getCollectionTime()); } GcReport.kt // log once at startup, and on a timer if you like ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans().forEach { gc -> log.infof("%s: %d collections, %d ms", gc.name, gc.collectionCount, gc.collectionTime) } The code is the same API in both languages; Kotlin reads the getters as properties. What differs is what the beans mean for each collector, measured on JDK 21. G1 reports G1 Young Generation, G1 Concurrent GC and G1 Old Generation. Generational ZGC reports ZGC Minor Cycles, ZGC Minor Pauses, ZGC Major Cycles and ZGC Major Pauses; Shenandoah reports Shenandoah Cycles and Shenandoah Pauses. The time of a "Cycles" bean is concurrent work, not stopped time. A dashboard that adds up every bean's time as "GC pause" makes ZGC look like the slowest collector of all, the same trap as reading the 0.052 s in its log as a pause.

A fraud scorer: 8 CPUs at 30% use, a 16 GB heap of cached features, and a 5 ms GC budget. A nightly settlement batch: 8 CPUs, 16 GB, and nobody waiting on a single request. h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Quiz
x: A JDK 25 service runs in a container with 2 CPUs and a 1.5 GiB memory limit, with no GC flag. Which collector does it run, and what changes on JDK 27? G1 on both, because G1 is the default collector Serial on JDK 25, because 1,536 MB is under 1,792 MB; G1 on JDK 27 Parallel on JDK 25, G1 on JDK 27 ZGC on JDK 27, because it became the default On JDK 21 to 26, G1 is chosen only on a server-class machine: 2 or more CPUs and at least 1,792 MB as the JVM sees them. 1.5 GiB is 1,536 MB, so this pod gets Serial without anyone noticing. Per the JDK 27 source, JDK 27 selects G1 in all environments. ZGC has never been the default. A team moves a service in a pod with 2 CPUs from G1 to ZGC. GC pauses drop below 0.1 ms, but p99 latency gets worse. What is the most likely reason? ZGC's pauses are longer than the log says ZGC doesn't support Quarkus The heap is now too large for the region size ZGC's concurrent GC threads and load barriers take CPU from request threads, and allocating threads may stall ZGC moves the work out of the pauses, not out of the process. With 2 CPUs, GC threads compete with request threads, every reference load runs a barrier, and if the collection can't keep up with allocation, threads stall waiting for memory. Look for Allocation Stall lines and CPU saturation. Which flags select generational ZGC on JDK 21? -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+UseZGC -XX:ZGCMode=generational -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseZGC On JDK 21, plain -XX:+UseZGC gives the old single-generation ZGC; -XX:+ZGenerational opts in to the generational one. JDK 23 made generational the default, and JDK 24 removed the old mode, so on JDK 25 -XX:+UseZGC alone is right and ZGenerational is obsolete. ZGC is not experimental, so it needs no extra flag. A test should prove that importing a 50,000-line settlement file allocates less than 200 MB in total. Which setup does that most directly? Run the import in a child JVM with -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC -Xmx200m and check that it finishes Run it with -Xmx200m and G1, and check there's no OutOfMemoryError Call System.gc() after the import and check Runtime.totalMemory() Run it with ZGC and check the pause times Epsilon never frees anything, so finishing inside a 200 MB heap means total allocation stayed under 200 MB (minus what JVM startup used). With G1, the import could allocate gigabytes and still fit in 200 MB, because the GC keeps freeing garbage. totalMemory() after a GC shows what's committed, not what was allocated. From lesson 4: G1's young pauses grow with the amount of live data they copy. Why don't ZGC's pauses grow the same way? ZGC copies live objects while the application runs, and its pauses only deal with thread roots ZGC never copies objects; it only marks them ZGC uses bigger regions, so there is less to copy ZGC skips the young generation G1 evacuates inside the stop-the-world pause, so the pause grows with the survivors. ZGC relocates concurrently: the load barrier lets application threads find, and even perform, the moves. What's left for the pauses is handling roots such as thread stacks, which is why they stay around hundredths of a millisecond. ZGC does copy, and it is generational since JDK 21.

h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Key terms
x: ZGC A collector that marks and moves objects while the application runs; its pauses don't grow with the heap. Load barrier A few instructions the JIT adds after each reference load, to catch and fix references to moved objects. Colored pointer A reference with metadata bits that tell ZGC's barrier whether it can be used as it is. Concurrent relocation Moving live objects while application threads keep running. Allocation stall An application thread waiting for memory because a concurrent collection hasn't freed enough yet. Shenandoah OpenJDK's other concurrent, low-pause collector; not included in every vendor's build. Server-class machine The JVM's test for picking G1 by default on JDK 21 to 26: 2 or more CPUs and at least 1,792 MB. Epsilon A collector that allocates but never frees. For tests and benchmarks only. In Minor Collection (Allocation Rate) 582M(57%)->226M(22%) 0.052s from ZGC, what is 0.052 s? The whole concurrent collection, not a pause. The pauses are the Pause Mark Start, Pause Mark End and Pause Relocate Start lines. What does ZGC's load barrier do? After every reference load, it checks the reference's color bits. If they're stale, it finds the object's new address, moving it if needed, and writes the fixed reference back into the field. What is a ZGC allocation stall? Threads blocked because the heap filled before the concurrent collection finished. It means the heap is too small or the GC is short of CPU. Generational ZGC per JDK version? JDK 21: opt-in with -XX:+ZGenerational. JDK 23: the default. JDK 24 and later: the only mode. Which collector does JDK 25 pick with no GC flag in a 1-CPU container? Serial. G1 needs a server-class machine: 2 or more CPUs and at least 1,792 MB. JDK 27 picks G1 everywhere. What is Epsilon good for? Tests and benchmarks: it never frees memory, so a heap size becomes an allocation budget. The JVM exits when the heap is full. Why must -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions come first? HotSpot refuses an experimental option that appears before it, with The unlock option must precede 'UseEpsilonGC'.

h: Low-pause collectors: ZGC, Shenandoah, and choosing a GC · Go deeper
x: The full -Xlog:gc* output of one generational ZGC minor collection on JDK 21 has more to read than the pause lines: GC(4) y: Using tenuring threshold: 4 (Computed) GC(4) y: Allocation Stalls: 0 0 0 0 GC(4) y: MMU: 2ms/97.4%, 5ms/99.0%, 10ms/99.3%, 20ms/99.5%, 50ms/99.8%, 100ms/99.8% GC(4) y: Eden 27M (3%) 470M (46%) 233 / 217 1 / 0 0 / 0 GC(4) y: Young Generation 582M(57%)->226M(22%) 0.052s MMU is minimum mutator utilization: 2ms/97.4% means that in every 2 ms window during this collection, the application got at least 97.4% of the time. It's a better latency number than pause length alone, because it also counts a burst of pauses close together. The Eden row shows the generational hypothesis from lesson 4: 27 MB live against 470 MB of garbage. Allocation Stalls should stay all zeros. A prefix tells you which generation a line is about: y: for the young collection of a minor GC, Y: and O: for the young and old parts of a major GC. ZGC also gives memory back to the operating system on its own: ZUncommit is on by default and returns memory that has been unused for ZUncommitDelay, 300 seconds by default. G1 can shrink its heap after a full GC (the soft-reference demo in lesson 3 went from 64M to 8M), and its periodic collection for idle services is off by default (G1PeriodicGCInterval is 0). That difference can matter in a container: a ZGC service's resident memory can fall after a traffic peak, while a G1 service may keep what it grew to.

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · -Xlog:gc prints one line per collection
x: One flag makes every collection print a line. Since JDK 9 the flag is -Xlog:gc, part of the unified logging system (older guides show -XX:+PrintGCDetails, which JDK 9 replaced). Here's a G1 young pause: [0.128s][info][gc] GC(0) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 14M->1M(256M) 12.723ms Read it left to right. [0.128s] is the time since the JVM started, [info] the log level, [gc] the tag. GC(0) numbers the collection; a concurrent cycle gets a number of its own, and the pauses inside it reuse that number. Pause Young is the event. (Normal) says it's young-only; Concurrent Start, Prepare Mixed and Mixed are the other kinds from lesson 4. (G1 Evacuation Pause) is the cause: eden was full. You'll also see G1 Humongous Allocation and System.gc() there. 14M->1M(256M) is the heap used before the pause, used after it, and the committed heap size. Last, 12.723ms is how long every application thread was stopped. -Xlog:gc*, with the star, turns on every GC tag: phases, region counts, metaspace and CPU time. That's ten to fifteen lines per pause, the detail lessons 4 and 5 used. For a service, write the log to rotating files with wall-clock times, so it survives restarts and can't fill the disk: -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m The colons separate the parts: what to log, where to write it, the decorations at the start of each line (time adds the date and time of day), and the rotation, here at most 5 files of 20 MB. When the current gc.log is full, the JVM moves it to a numbered file such as gc.log.0 and starts a new one. Leave it on in production. It's a few lines per collection, and in an incident it's the first thing you'll want. Write a GC log the production way Read GcLogFileDemo. It runs two seconds of the lesson 4 service load in a child JVM with a 256 MB heap and the rotating-file setting from this section, at 200 KB per file. Predict: how many files will there be, and will the last young pause leave more or less heap than the first? Run it, then open labs/memory/build/gc-logs/gc.log and find a Pause Young line with its date and time. GcLogFileDemo.java package workbench.memory.l06; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import workbench.memory.l04.ServiceLoad; import java.io.IOException; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.stream.Stream; /** * Runs two seconds of service load in a child JVM that writes its GC log the way a production service * should: to rotating files, with timestamps. Then it does the three checks you do first on any GC log. */ public class GcLogFileDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { if (args.length > 0) { ServiceLoad.run(2, 0.55); return; } Path dir = Files.createDirectories(Path.of("build", "gc-logs")); // labs/memory/build/gc-logs under Gradle try (Stream<Path> old = Files.list(dir)) { for (Path f : old.toList()) if (f.getFileName().toString().startsWith("gc.log")) Files.delete(f); } String logging = "-Xlog:gc*:file=" + dir.resolve("gc.log") + ":time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=3,filesize=200k"; Jvm.lines(List.of("-XX:+UseG1GC", "-Xmx256m", logging), GcLogFileDemo.class.getName(), "load"); lines.addAll(Files.readAllLines(f)); } } // the three checks: full GCs, evacuation failures, and the heap left after young pauses System.out.println("Pause Full lines: " + lines.stream().filter(l -> l.contains("Pause Full")).count()); The first young pause goes 14M->1M, the last ones stay near 200 MB after the pause: the floor rose as the cache filled. The counts change from run to run. The java command, JDK 25 man page source: -Xlog docs A container's memory limit is a moving truck of fixed size. The heap is the big wardrobe, and -Xmx decides how big a wardrobe you buy. But the truck also has to carry the boxes nobody counts: metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, the GC's own bookkeeping. Buy a wardrobe as long as the truck and the boxes don't fit, and the driver (the kernel) refuses to drive and throws everything out, with no note left behind. Where it breaks: a truck is loaded once. A JVM keeps loading boxes while it runs, so the overflow can come hours after it started.

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · Turn a log into a few numbers
x: Three hundred log lines are hard to judge by eye. A few numbers say most of it: the number of pauses and their total time; divided by the elapsed time, that's the share of time your threads were stopped; the longest pause, which is what your p99 latency feels; the number of full GCs and evacuation failures, which should be zero in a healthy G1 service; the heap after the last full GC, the live set at that moment, which is the number you size a heap from; the trend of the after-values of young pauses: a floor that keeps rising means the live set is growing. Computing them has two traps. Not every line with a duration is a pause. Concurrent Mark Cycle 53.866ms ran beside the application, and G1's Evacuate Collection Set: 15.51ms is a phase inside a pause you've already counted. ZGC's Minor Collection ... 0.052s is a whole concurrent cycle. One rule works for every HotSpot collector: a pause line has Pause right after GC(id) (ZGC puts y:, Y: or O: in between) and ends with a duration in ms. The second trap is (System.gc()), which has parentheses inside its parentheses and breaks the obvious regular expression. The lab builds a parser with that rule and tests it on lines copied from real JDK 21 runs of all five collectors. Check yourself on the G1 cycle from lesson 4: seven lines, starting with Pause Young (Concurrent Start) and ending with Pause Full (System.gc()) 974M->1M(1024M). How many of them are pauses, and what does the last one tell you? (Six are pauses: Concurrent Start, Remark, Cleanup, Prepare Mixed, Mixed and the full GC. The two Concurrent Mark Cycle lines are not. The full GC's after-value, 1 MB, is the live set at that moment, because the program had finished its work and called System.gc().) Before a payment service moves to Kubernetes, check three things. Its JVM flags: a hard-coded -Xmx that equals the pod limit is a time bomb, and the absence of any flag means a 25% heap that may be far too small. Its GC log: it should go to rotating files with time decorations, so an incident at 3 a.m. has a log to read. And its exit codes: a pod that restarts with 137 and nothing in the log was killed by the kernel for native memory, not by a heap problem, and a heap dump won't explain it. For a Quarkus service with Netty's direct buffers, set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize on purpose instead of inheriting the heap size.

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · The JVM sizes its heap from the container limit
x: On Linux the JVM reads the container's limits: the cgroup memory limit and the CPU quota. UseContainerSupport is on by default in every JDK from 21 to 27. Without heap flags, the max heap is 25% of the memory limit (MaxRAMPercentage, default 25). A pod with a 1 GiB limit gets a 256 MB heap. That's a cautious default: three quarters of the pod stays free unless your service uses it outside the heap. -XX:MaxRAMPercentage changes the share. With 75, the same pod gets 768 MB. Prefer it over a fixed -Xmx, because the heap then follows the limit when someone resizes the pod. Watch the top end: in a 64 GB pod, 75% is 48 GB, and compressed oops switch off (lesson 1). -XX:InitialRAMPercentage sets the starting heap. It was 1.5625% on JDK 21 to 25, and per the JDK source it is 0 on JDK 26, where the JVM starts from a small minimum and grows. To see what the JVM detected, run java -XshowSettings:system -version inside the container. On the machine used for this course's research it printed Provider: cgroupv1, Effective CPU Count: 4 and Memory Limit: 13.35G. -Xlog:os+container=debug shows the detection step by step, which helps when the numbers look wrong. The demo can't create a container, so it uses -XX:MaxRAM, which tells the JVM how much memory to plan for, as a stand-in for a limit. That works on JDK 21 to 25. JDK 26 deprecated MaxRAM, and per the JDK source JDK 27 removed it; there, try the same flags in a real container (docker run --memory=1g). Watch the heap follow the limit Predict the max heap for limits of 1, 2 and 4 GiB, with defaults and with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75. Run HeapSizingDemo (JDK 21 to 25). Each line comes from a child JVM started with -XX:MaxRAM as the limit. If you have Docker, run docker run --rm --memory=1g eclipse-temurin:25 java -XshowSettings:system -version and find the memory limit it reports. h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · -Xmx equal to the limit gets the pod killed
x: Here's the configuration that looks right and fails: a pod with a 1 GiB limit and -Xmx1g. Lesson 1 already showed why it can't work: the heap is only part of the process. In the demo below, a JVM with a 256 MB heap, a 64 MB direct buffer and 56 threads had 378 MB resident in RAM. Scale that to -Xmx1g, and the process needs well over 1 GiB once its heap is in use. The failure doesn't look like a Java error. When a process goes over its cgroup limit, the Linux kernel's OOM killer ends it with SIGKILL. There's no OutOfMemoryError, no heap dump and nothing in the application log. Kubernetes reports OOMKilled and exit code 137 (128 plus signal 9). The pod can run fine for hours first, because Linux counts only the pages a process has touched, and the heap touches its pages bit by bit as it fills. The demo uses -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch to touch the whole heap at startup; without it, the same process showed 113 MB resident. So budget the whole process: the heap, plus direct buffers, plus metaspace and code cache, plus a stack for each thread, plus GC bookkeeping, plus headroom. Direct buffers need an explicit cap. Unless you set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, the JDK allows direct buffers up to the max heap size, so a service could in theory ask for twice its heap. Netty-based stacks such as Quarkus use direct memory for network I/O. My starting point for a payments pod is -XX:MaxRAMPercentage between 50 and 75, a -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize that fits what the I/O layer needs, and a bounded number of threads. Then measure under load with Native Memory Tracking, which lesson 7 covers, and adjust. Compare the heap with the whole process Read FootprintDemo. Its child JVM has -Xmx256m -Xms256m -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch, allocates a 64 MiB direct buffer and starts 50 threads, then prints what the JVM reports next to what Linux says is resident. Predict the resident number before you run it. Run it. Then remove -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch from the demo and run it again. FootprintDemo.java package workbench.memory.l06; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.lang.management.MemoryMXBean; import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; /** * A child JVM with -Xmx256m that does what services do: a 64 MiB direct buffer (think Netty) and 50 * threads. It then compares what the JVM reports with what the operating system says it uses. */ public class FootprintDemo { static final long MB = 1024 * 1024; public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length == 0) { // AlwaysPreTouch touches every heap page at startup, like a service that has run for a while Jvm.run(List.of("-Xmx256m", "-Xms256m", "-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch"), FootprintDemo.class.getName(), "child"); return; } ByteBuffer direct = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect((int) (64 * MB)); CountDownLatch never = new CountDownLatch(1); for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { try { never.await(); if (Files.exists(status)) { // Linux only Files.readAllLines(status).stream().filter(l -> l.startsWith("VmRSS")).forEach(l -> System.out.printf("resident in RAM %,5d MB (what the container limit counts)%n", Long.parseLong(l.replaceAll("\\D+", "")) / 1024)); Without AlwaysPreTouch the resident number drops to about 113 MB, because the heap's pages aren't touched yet; a running service gets there anyway as its heap fills. On macOS the demo can't read the resident size and says so. Setting -Xmx to the container's memory limit, or -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=100, because "the heap should get all the memory". The heap is the only part of the process -Xmx caps. Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, GC bookkeeping and direct buffers all come on top, so the process outgrows the limit and the kernel kills it, often hours after a deploy, with no Java error at all. People make the mistake because the heap is the only memory the JVM's error messages talk about. The fix: size with a percentage, between 50 and 75 for most services, cap direct memory, and confirm with Native Memory Tracking under real load.

Evacuate Collection Set is a phase inside a young pause, whose own Pause Young line already counts it. A JDK 21 service runs in a pod with a 2 GiB memory limit and no heap flags. The demo showed the same arithmetic for 1, 2 and 4 GiB. To use more, set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage, for example 60 or 75. Over ten minutes, a service's young pauses end at 310M, 355M, 402M, 447M and 495M, and a full GC finally goes 1490M->1210M(1536M). What is going on? The live set keeps growing, which points to a leak or an unbounded cache The young generation is too small; raise it G1's pause goal is too strict Nothing: G1 always lets the heap fill before collecting The after-values of young pauses are what survives, and their floor rises about 45 MB a pass. Even a full GC can only free 280 MB of 1,490 MB: 1.2 GB is really live. A bigger heap only delays the moment it fills; lesson 7 finds what's holding the memory. A pod has a 1 GiB limit. Which flag should you add first? -Xmx1g -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=100 -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize with a value that fits the I/O layer -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, to catch the OOM kill Without MaxDirectMemorySize, direct buffers may grow up to the max heap size, here 768 MB on top of a 768 MB heap in a 1 GiB pod. Capping it makes the budget real. -Xmx1g and 100% make the pod's problem worse, and a heap dump is never written when the kernel kills the process. From lesson 5: a ZGC service logs Allocation Stall (http-worker-12) 41.210ms lines during peaks. What do they mean? Normal ZGC pauses, which are always about 40 ms Application threads waited for memory because the heap filled before the concurrent collection finished The JIT stopped to compile a method A full GC ran ZGC's pauses stay well under a millisecond. A stall means a thread asked for memory and had to wait, because the application allocated faster than ZGC could reclaim. The fixes are more heap headroom or more CPU for the GC threads, or less allocation.

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · Key terms
x: Unified logging The JVM's logging system since JDK 9, configured with -Xlog. Decorations The bracketed fields at the start of each log line: time, uptime, level, tags. Live set The objects that are really still in use. A full GC's after-value shows it. Container support The JVM reading cgroup limits so it sizes itself to the container, not the host. MaxRAMPercentage The share of the memory limit the JVM uses as its max heap. Default 25. Resident memory (RSS) The pages of a process that are really in RAM: what a container limit counts. OOM killer The Linux kernel feature that kills a process that goes over its memory limit. In GC(0) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 14M->1M(256M) 12.723ms, what are 14M, 1M and 256M? Heap used before the pause, heap used after it, and the committed heap size. How do you recognize a pause line in any HotSpot GC log? Pause right after GC(id) (ZGC adds y:, Y: or O: in between), and a duration in ms at the end. What GC logging setting suits production? -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m: rotating files with wall-clock times. What max heap does a JVM pick in a container by default? 25% of the container's memory limit (MaxRAMPercentage = 25). Why does -Xmx equal to the container limit get the pod killed? Metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, GC data and direct buffers come on top of the heap, so the process goes over the cgroup limit and the kernel kills it. What does exit code 137 with OOMKilled mean for a JVM pod? The kernel's OOM killer sent SIGKILL. No OutOfMemoryError, no heap dump, nothing in the log. What is the default limit for direct buffers? The max heap size, unless you set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize.

h: Reading GC logs and sizing the heap in containers · Go deeper
x: Three settings change around the JDK versions this course covers, all read from the JDK source. InitialRAMPercentage was 1.5625 on JDK 21 to 25 and is 0 on JDK 26, where the JVM computes the initial heap from a minimum size instead. A service that used to start with a heap of 1/64 of its limit now starts smaller and grows, so expect a few more young pauses in the first seconds unless you set -Xms or -XX:InitialRAMPercentage yourself. MaxRAM is deprecated on JDK 26 and obsolete on JDK 27, together with the switches that forced or blocked "server-class" behaviour. On 27, test heap sizing in a real container. -XX:+UseContainerSupport is on in every version from 21 to 27, and -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=N overrides the CPU count the JVM detects. That count matters more than it looks: lesson 5 showed that on JDK 21 to 26 a single CPU silently means Serial GC, and the number of GC worker threads follows it too. Two flags help with Java's own OutOfMemoryError, the one that happens inside the limit: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError writes a heap dump (lesson 7 reads one), and -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError makes the JVM exit, so Kubernetes restarts a pod that would otherwise limp on with threads that died halfway through their work. Both are off by default, and neither helps with a kernel OOM kill.

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · A Java leak is memory that stays reachable
x: In C, a leak is memory nobody can reach any more. In Java it's the opposite: the garbage collector frees everything unreachable, so a Java leak is memory that stays reachable from a GC root after the program is done with it. The GC is doing its job. Your code still holds the reference. Here's the classic one in payment services, an idempotency cache with no eviction: Java static final Map<String, CachedResponse> IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); static CachedResponse handle(String requestId) { return IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE.computeIfAbsent(requestId, id -> new CachedResponse(id, 1_999, new byte[2_048])); } Kotlin val IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CachedResponse>() fun handle(requestId: String): CachedResponse = IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE.computeIfAbsent(requestId) { id -> CachedResponse(id, 1_999, ByteArray(2_048)) } Every request adds an entry, and nothing ever removes one. Lesson 6 showed the symptom in a GC log: the after-values of young pauses rise pass after pass, full GCs free less and less, and in the end the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError or spends its time in Pause Full. The same shape shows up in four places, over and over: maps and caches without a bound or an expiry; ThreadLocal values on pooled threads that nobody removes (the threads track showed a pool thread keeping one forever); listeners and callbacks registered and never unregistered (lesson 3's weak registry is one fix); class loaders that can't be unloaded, which shows up as metaspace growth and GC causes like Metadata GC Threshold, mostly in dev mode and test suites that reload code. The first tool is a class histogram: a count of live objects per class. jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram prints it after a full GC, so it counts only reachable objects. For the cache above, after 20,000 requests: num #instances #bytes class name (module) 1: 52255 43124072 [B (java.base@21.0.12.1) 2: 32139 771336 java.lang.String (java.base@21.0.12.1) 3: 22615 723680 java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap$Node (java.base@21.0.12.1) 4: 20000 640000 workbench.memory.l07.LeakDemo$CachedResponse [B means byte[]. The histogram tells you what fills the heap. It can't tell you who holds it. 20,000 of something you didn't expect to keep is the clue to follow next. Leak, count, dump Read LeakDemo. Its first child JVM handles 20,000 requests with the cache above, prints the top of the class histogram and writes a heap dump. Its second child has -Xmx64m -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError and handles requests until the heap is full. Predict: which class tops the histogram, and how many CachedResponse objects are alive? Run it.
