The heap is a set of loads hanging from hooks in the ceiling, the GC roots, by ropes that are references. Some loads hang from one rope; others are tied to two hooks. Cut the rope above the cache and 44 MB of receipts fall, because every rope to them ran through it. Cut a rope above something that also hangs from another hook, and nothing falls. Retained size is the weight that falls. Where it breaks: real ropes are cut once. In a heap, your code ties new ropes on every request, so you find the rope in a dump, but you fix it in the code that keeps tying it.

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · A heap dump and its dominator tree show who holds it
x: From a heap dump to the leak: retained size and the dominator tree A heap dump is a file with every object on the heap and every reference between them, in the HPROF format. You can get one three ways: jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/app.hprof from a running JVM. Its help text says "Impact: High": it does a full GC first (unless you pass -all) and pauses the JVM while it writes. -gz compresses the file, and JDK 24 and later add -parallel for more writer threads. -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError with -XX:HeapDumpPath=..., so the JVM writes one at the moment it runs out. It's off by default. It's also a manageable flag, so jcmd <pid> VM.set_flag HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError true turns it on in a running JVM. HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean.dumpHeap(path, true) from code, which is what the demo uses. Open the dump in Eclipse MAT (Memory Analyzer). Two sizes matter. The shallow size of an object is its own bytes, lesson 1's header-plus-fields. Its retained size is everything that would be freed if that one object were gone: the object plus everything reachable only through it. You can compute retained size by hand on a small graph, and doing it once makes MAT's numbers obvious. Look at the figure. The static field holds the map, the map holds a table, the table holds 20,000 nodes, each node holds a key and a response, and each response holds a 2 KB receipt. Every path from a root to a receipt goes through the map, so the map dominates the receipts, and they are in its retained set. Add it up: 20,000 receipts at 2,064 bytes, 20,000 keys at 80, 20,000 responses at 32, 20,000 nodes at 32 and the table: about 44 MB. The shared "EUR" string is different. A currency catalog reaches it too, so removing the map wouldn't free it, and it isn't in the map's retained set. MAT's dominator tree lists objects by retained size, biggest first. For a leak like this one, the map should sit at the top with about 44 MB, and its path to a GC root names the static field that holds it. (I couldn't run MAT for this course, so that's what the dominator tree's definition predicts for this dump, not a screenshot.) The histogram said "byte arrays". The dominator tree says "this map, held by this field". Find the holder in Eclipse MAT Download Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT) from the Eclipse website and open labs/memory/build/heapdumps/leak.hprof from the previous demo. Before you click anything, predict the top entry of the dominator tree and its retained size from the figure. Open the dominator tree. Then, on the biggest entry, use "Path to GC Roots" to find the field that holds it. From the definition and the histogram, the ConcurrentHashMap should top the dominator tree with a retained size of about 44 MB, almost all of it in 2 KB byte[] receipts. Its path to a GC root should end at the static field IDEMPOTENCY_CACHE of LeakDemo. If your top entry is something else, compare its retained size with the histogram's byte counts and follow its path to the root the same way. Everything below the map is reachable only through it, so it is the map's retained set. The shared string has another root, so the map doesn't retain it. Eclipse MAT help: dominator tree docs Eclipse MAT help: shallow and retained heap docs In a payment platform the usual suspects are easy to list. Idempotency caches and duplicate-detection maps that never evict. Per-merchant maps keyed by something that is created per request. A ThreadLocal buffer on Kafka consumer or worker threads that nobody removes. A Temporal or Kafka listener registered for each new tenant and never removed. And outside the heap: a Netty-based client that allocates direct buffers per call without releasing them, or a native HSM or compression library. Decide which half to look at from the GC log first. A rising floor means a heap dump and the dominator tree. A flat floor with a growing pod means NMT with a baseline and a diff.

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Native Memory Tracking finds growth outside the heap
x: Sometimes the heap is fine and the process still grows. The GC log shows a flat floor, a heap dump shows nothing odd, and the pod still gets OOM-killed (lesson 6). The memory is outside the heap, where heap dumps can't see. Native Memory Tracking (NMT) is the JVM's account of its own native memory. It's off by default. Start the JVM with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then ask a running process: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary scale=MB In the demo, a JVM with a 256 MB heap committed 294 MB at startup. After it allocated one 64 MiB direct buffer and started 100 threads, it had committed 369 MB. NMT shows where the difference went: Other went from nothing to 64 MB (the direct buffer), and Thread went from 1 MB to 11 MB committed, with 121 MB reserved, because each new thread reserves about 1 MB of stack but touches only a little of it. For a slow leak, take a baseline and compare later: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff scale=MB The diff marks every change: in one test, Other (reserved=100MB +100MB, committed=100MB +100MB) after 100 direct buffers of 1 MiB. A growing Other points at direct buffers or native code; a growing Thread at threads you start and never stop; a growing Class or Metaspace at class loaders. Direct buffers deserve one more level of detail. A ByteBuffer.allocateDirect call creates a small object on the heap that owns the native memory, and a phantom-reference cleaner, the same idea as lesson 3's Cleaner, frees that memory after the GC collects the small object. So native memory waits for a garbage collection, and a big, quiet heap may not collect for a long time. Unless you set -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize, the limit for all of it is the max heap size. Set it, and a leak fails loudly instead of quietly: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Cannot reserve 67108864 bytes of direct buffer memory (allocated: 0, limit: 33554432), with a stack trace that points at the code. Watch native memory move Read NmtDemo. Its first child runs with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and prints NMT's summary before and after a 64 MiB direct buffer and 100 threads. Its second child allocates 64 MiB of direct memory under -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=32m. Predict which NMT categories change, and by how much. Then run it. Then a direct buffer that doesn't fit under -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize. */ public class NmtDemo { static final Pattern CATEGORY = Pattern.compile("^-?\\s*(Total|[A-Z][\\w ]+?):? \\(?reserved=(\\d+)MB, committed=(\\d+)MB"); static String nativeMemory() throws Exception { // the same as: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary scale=MB return (String) ManagementFactory.getPlatformMBeanServer().invoke( new ObjectName("com.sun.management:type=DiagnosticCommand"), "vmNativeMemory", new Object[] {new String[] {"summary", "scale=MB"}}, new String[] {String[].class.getName()}); h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Arenas give off-heap memory a lifetime you control
x: The Foreign Function and Memory API (FFM), final since JDK 22 (JEP 454), gives off-heap memory a lifetime you control. Memory comes from an arena, and the arena decides when it's freed: Arena Lifetime Closed by Threads Arena.global() until the JVM exits nobody any Arena.ofAuto() until the GC finds it unreachable the GC any Arena.ofConfined() until you call close() you, from the owner thread the owner only Arena.ofShared() until you call close() you, from any thread any A confined arena in try-with-resources frees its memory at the closing brace. No GC is involved, so there's nothing to wait for. And if code uses a segment after its arena is closed, it gets an IllegalStateException ("Already closed"), not a crash or silently corrupted memory as with freed memory in C. Java try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) { MemorySegment ledger = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024); // 32 MiB off-heap ledger.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0, 1_999); } // freed here Kotlin Arena.ofConfined().use { arena -> val ledger = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024) // 32 MiB off-heap ledger.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0, 1_999) } // freed here Native segments count against the same limit as direct buffers. Per the JDK 25 source, allocating one reserves memory through the same accounting as ByteBuffer.allocateDirect, and on JDK 21's preview of the API, a 32 MiB segment under -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m failed with Cannot reserve 33554432 bytes of direct buffer memory. The labs compile for JDK 21, where FFM is still a preview, so this lesson's FFM demo is a single file that runs outside Gradle on JDK 22 or later. Free 32 MiB at a closing brace (JDK 22 or later) This one runs outside Gradle and needs JDK 22 or later, ideally 25. Check with java -version. From labs/, run java memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java. The Kotlin twin needs kotlinc: the commands are at the top of ArenaDemo.kt. Predict the three numbers it prints, then run it. Run it again with -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m placed right after java. ArenaDemo.java (JDK 22 or later) // JDK 22 or later: the Foreign Function and Memory API is final since JDK 22 (JEP 454). Written for JDK 25. // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where this API is a preview. From labs/: // java memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java // java -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java import java.lang.foreign.Arena; import java.lang.foreign.MemorySegment; import java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout; import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; public class ArenaDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { long before = directBytes(); // the JDK may already hold a little MemorySegment escaped; try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) { // 1. one owner thread, closed by try-with-resources MemorySegment ledger = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024); // 2. 32 MiB outside the heap for (long i = 0; i < ledger.byteSize() / Long.BYTES; i++) { ledger.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, i, i * 100); // 4 million longs, and no objects } System.out.println("entry 1,000 holds " + ledger.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 1_000)); System.out.printf("inside the arena: %+d MiB of direct memory%n", (directBytes() - before) >> 20); escaped = ledger; } // 3. freed here, not by the GC System.out.printf("after close(): %+d MiB of direct memory%n", (directBytes() - before) >> 20); try { escaped.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0); // 4. use after free is an exception, not a crash } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("reading after close() throws: " + e.getMessage()); } } // native segments are counted, and limited, together with direct ByteBuffers static long directBytes() { return ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean.class).stream() .filter(p -> p.getName().equals("direct")) .mapToLong(BufferPoolMXBean::getMemoryUsed).sum(); } } java memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java labs/memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.java ArenaDemo.kt (JDK 22 or later) // JDK 22 or later: the Foreign Function and Memory API is final since JDK 22 (JEP 454). Written for JDK 25. // Needs the Kotlin command-line compiler. From labs/: // kotlinc memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.kt -include-runtime -d memory/build/arena-demo.jar // java -jar memory/build/arena-demo.jar // java -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=16m -jar memory/build/arena-demo.jar // Not part of the Gradle build, because the labs compile for JDK 21, where this API is a preview. import java.lang.foreign.Arena import java.lang.foreign.MemorySegment import java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout import java.lang.management.BufferPoolMXBean import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory // native segments are counted, and limited, together with direct ByteBuffers fun directBytes(): Long = ManagementFactory.getPlatformMXBeans(BufferPoolMXBean::class.java) .filter { it.name == "direct" } .sumOf { it.memoryUsed } fun main(args: Array<String>) { // args unused; one main keeps every launcher happy val before = directBytes() // the JDK may already hold a little val escaped: MemorySegment Arena.ofConfined().use { arena -> // 1. one owner thread, closed by use {} val ledger = arena.allocate(32L * 1024 * 1024) // 2. 32 MiB outside the heap for (i in 0 until ledger.byteSize() / Long.SIZE_BYTES) { ledger.setAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, i, i * 100) // 4 million longs, and no objects } println("entry 1,000 holds ${ledger.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 1_000)}") println("inside the arena: %+d MiB of direct memory".format((directBytes() - before) shr 20)) escaped = ledger } // 3. freed here, not by the GC println("after close(): %+d MiB of direct memory".format((directBytes() - before) shr 20)) try { escaped.getAtIndex(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, 0) // 4. use after free is an exception, not a crash } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("reading after close() throws: ${e.message}") } } kotlinc memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.kt -include-runtime -d memory/build/arena-demo.jar && java -jar memory/build/arena-demo.jar labs/memory/jdk25/ArenaDemo.kt entry 1,000 holds 100000, then +32 MiB of direct memory inside the arena and +0 MiB after close(), and reading after close() throws: Already closed. With the 16 MB limit, arena.allocate fails with OutOfMemoryError: Cannot reserve 33554432 bytes of direct buffer memory. These outputs come from JDK 21's preview of the same API; the methods used here are the same in the final API of JDK 22 and later. JEP 454: Foreign Function & Memory API read Arena source at jdk-25-ga: the four kinds of arena docs Taking a heap dump to explain an OOM-killed pod. The kernel killed the process because the whole process outgrew its limit, and the heap was often fine: a heap dump shows only the heap, so it looks healthy and the team concludes the problem is random. People make the mistake because the heap is the only memory most tools show. The fix is to read the evidence in order: if the GC log's floor is flat, turn on -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, take a baseline, and diff it after the growth; cap -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize so a direct-buffer leak becomes an OutOfMemoryError with a stack trace instead of a silent kill.

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Java and Kotlin
x: A bounded LRU cache in Java and Kotlin LruCache.java final class LruCache<K, V> { private final Map<K, V> map; LruCache(int maxEntries) { // true = access order: get() moves an entry to the end, so the eldest is the least recently used map = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) { @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > maxEntries; } }; } synchronized V get(K key) { return map.get(key); } synchronized void put(K key, V value) { map.put(key, value); } } LruCache.kt class LruCache<K, V>(private val maxEntries: Int) { // true = access order: get() moves an entry to the end, so the eldest is the least recently used private val map = object : LinkedHashMap<K, V>(16, 0.75f, true) { override fun removeEldestEntry(eldest: MutableMap.MutableEntry<K, V>?): Boolean = size > maxEntries } @Synchronized fun get(key: K): V? = map[key] @Synchronized fun put(key: K, value: V) { map[key] = value } } Both build on the same JDK class, and both need the lock: LinkedHashMap isn't thread-safe, and in access order even get changes the map. Java overrides removeEldestEntry in an anonymous subclass; Kotlin does it with an object : expression, and its eldest parameter is nullable because the JDK doesn't annotate it. Kotlin returns V? from get, which makes the cache miss visible in the type. In a real service you'd often reach for a cache library with size limits and expiry, but the leak fix is the same idea in every form: decide a maximum and make the structure enforce it.

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Worked example
x: From OOMKilled to the line that leaks An invented settlement API restarts with exit code 137 every two days. Start with the GC log, because it decides which half of memory to look at. Here the young pauses end at about 300 MB, day after day: the live heap is flat. A heap dump would look healthy, so don't start there. GC(9120) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 1490M->301M(1536M) 9.420ms GC(9121) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 1488M->298M(1536M) 9.112ms Measure native memory. Restart one instance with NMT, take a baseline once it's warm, and diff a few hours later. Only one category moved. java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary ... -jar settlement-api.jar jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline # four hours later jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff scale=MB - Other (reserved=812MB +544MB, committed=812MB +544MB) (malloc=812MB +544MB #9310 +6480) Name the suspect. Other growing by thousands of mallocs is direct buffers or native code. The JDK's direct buffer pool confirms it: its count and size keep climbing. Find who allocates direct buffers per request. Here it's a report generator that keeps one per merchant report in a map and never removes them. // 1. the leak: one direct buffer per report, kept forever private final Map<String, ByteBuffer> reportBuffers = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); ByteBuffer bufferFor(String reportId) { return reportBuffers.computeIfAbsent(reportId, id -> ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1 << 20)); } // 1. the leak: one direct buffer per report, kept forever private val reportBuffers = ConcurrentHashMap<String, ByteBuffer>() fun bufferFor(reportId: String): ByteBuffer = reportBuffers.computeIfAbsent(reportId) { ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(1 shl 20) } Fix the lifetime, then add a guard. Give each report its memory for exactly as long as it's being written, with a confined arena (JDK 22 or later), or remove the buffer from the map when the report is done. Then cap direct memory, so the next leak of this kind fails as an OutOfMemoryError with a stack trace instead of a silent kill. void writeReport(String reportId, Report report) { try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) { // 2. memory lives exactly as long as the report MemorySegment buffer = arena.allocate(1 << 20); report.renderInto(buffer); upload(reportId, buffer); } // 3. freed here, no GC needed } // and on the command line: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m fun writeReport(reportId: String, report: Report) { Arena.ofConfined().use { arena -> // 2. memory lives exactly as long as the report val buffer = arena.allocate(1 shl 20) report.renderInto(buffer) upload(reportId, buffer) } // 3. freed here, no GC needed } // and on the command line: -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=128m

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Quiz
x: A class histogram after a full GC shows 2.1 million byte[] instances using 4.3 GB. What does that tell you about the leak? What fills the heap, but not who holds it: you need the dominator tree of a heap dump That byte[] is the leaking class, and the fix is to allocate fewer arrays That the leak is in native memory Nothing, because the histogram counts garbage too Byte arrays sit under strings, buffers, receipts and serialized payloads alike, so the histogram can't name the owner. GC.class_histogram runs a full GC first and counts only live objects. The dominator tree ranks objects by what they keep alive, and the path to a GC root names the field. In a heap dump, a MerchantRegistry object has a shallow size of 24 bytes and a retained size of 1.2 GB. What does that mean? The registry object itself is 1.2 GB The registry is referenced 1.2 billion times If the registry became unreachable, about 1.2 GB would be freed with it The dump is corrupt: retained size can't exceed shallow size by that much Shallow size is the object's own header and fields. Retained size adds everything reachable only through it, its retained set. A small object at the top of a big map routinely retains gigabytes. That's exactly the object to look at. A pod's young pauses end at a flat 400 MB, but NMT's summary.diff after six hours shows Thread (reserved=2150MB +1900MB, committed=210MB +185MB). What is leaking? Heap objects Metaspace Direct buffers Threads: code keeps starting threads, each with its own stack, and never ends them About 1,900 MB more reserved stack is roughly 1,900 new threads at about 1 MB each, with a little of each stack touched. Look for an executor created per request and never shut down, or threads started per connection. Direct buffers would show in Other, and metaspace in Class and Metaspace. Your service allocates a 1 MiB off-heap buffer per report. Which choice frees each buffer as soon as its report is written, without waiting for a GC? ByteBuffer.allocateDirect and drop the reference Arena.ofConfined() in try-with-resources, allocating the segment from it Arena.ofAuto() Arena.global() A confined arena frees its memory when close() runs, at the end of the try block. A dropped direct buffer and an automatic arena are freed only after the GC finds them unreachable, which on a quiet heap can take a long time. The global arena is never freed. From the threads track: a worker pool's tasks call TENANT.set(request.tenant()) on a ThreadLocal and never call remove(). Which leak pattern is this, and what does a heap dump show as the GC root? An unbounded cache; the root is a static map A value kept alive by a long-lived pool thread; the root is the live thread itself A class loader leak; the root is the class loader Not a leak, because ThreadLocal values are weak Each thread keeps its own ThreadLocal values, and a pool thread lives as long as the pool. A started, unfinished thread is a GC root, so the last value each thread saw stays reachable. The ThreadLocal key is weak inside the thread's map, but the value is strong. The fix is remove() in a finally block.

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Key terms
x: Class histogram A count of live objects and their bytes, per class. Heap dump A file (HPROF format) with every object on the heap and every reference between them. Retained size The memory that would be freed if one object became unreachable. Dominator Object X dominates Y if every path from a GC root to Y goes through X. Native Memory Tracking The JVM's own accounting of the memory it uses outside the heap. Direct buffer A ByteBuffer whose bytes live in native memory, freed after its heap object is collected. Arena In the FFM API, the owner of off-heap memory that decides when it's freed. MaxDirectMemorySize The limit for direct buffers and native segments. Defaults to the max heap. What is a memory leak in Java? Memory that stays reachable from a GC root after the program is done with it, so the GC may not free it. What does jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram show, and what does it miss? Live objects per class, after a full GC: what fills the heap. It doesn't show who holds them. Shallow size vs retained size? Shallow: the object's own bytes. Retained: everything freed if that object went away, the object plus all it alone keeps reachable. How do you get a heap dump at the moment of an OutOfMemoryError? -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=.... It's manageable, so jcmd <pid> VM.set_flag HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError true works on a running JVM. How do you find slow native memory growth? Start with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, run jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory baseline, then later jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary.diff. When is a direct ByteBuffer's native memory freed? After the GC collects the small buffer object on the heap and its Cleaner runs. On a quiet heap that can take a long time. When does a confined FFM arena free its memory? When close() runs, for example at the end of try-with-resources. No GC is involved.

h: Hunting memory leaks: heap dumps, native memory and off-heap · Go deeper
x: A few details make leak hunting faster. A histogram is cheap enough to take twice. Take one, wait ten minutes under load, take another, and compare instance counts: the class whose count only goes up is your lead, even before you have a dump. jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram -all skips the full GC and counts unreachable objects too, which is useful when you can't afford the pause and dangerous when you forget the flag. Heap dumps are large: about the size of the live heap, here 50 MB for 44 MB of leak. GC.heap_dump -gz=1 compresses while writing. Writing a dump pauses the JVM, so in a cluster take it from one instance after you've taken it out of the load balancer. MAT's GC roots have kinds, and the kind is a clue. A System Class root means a static field. A Thread root, "a started, but not stopped, thread" in MAT's words, means something reachable from a live thread: its stack or its thread-locals. JNI Global means native code is holding a reference. Class loader leaks look different from object leaks. Each redeploy or hot reload creates a new class loader with new classes. If anything from outside still references one object of an old class, for example a JDBC driver registered in a global list, a ThreadLocal on a shared thread or a static cache in a library, the whole old class loader and every class it loaded stay in metaspace. NMT shows Class and Metaspace growing, and GC logs show collections with the cause Metadata GC Threshold. In production Quarkus rarely reloads, but dev mode and long test suites do. Finally, jol-cli can estimate how a heap dump's objects would lay out under other JVM settings. For the 50 MB dump from this lesson's research, it estimated 1.3% less with compact object headers and 3.2% more without compressed references: a dump full of 2 KB arrays gains little from smaller headers, as lesson 1 predicted.

h: JIT, profiling and benchmarking
x: Tiered compilation, inlining and deoptimization, JMH, false sharing, JFR, async-profiler and flame graphs. By the end of this track you can say what the JVM does with your code after javac or kotlinc is done with it: which tier runs a method, what C2 inlines and bets on, and why it sometimes throws compiled code away. You can write a JMH benchmark that measures your code instead of the optimizer, spot false sharing and fix it with padding or LongAdder, record and query a running JVM with JDK Flight Recorder, read a flame graph from async-profiler without being fooled by it, and run a performance investigation from a p99.99 complaint to a fix you can prove to the byte. You don't need to know anything about JIT compilers or profilers to start: lesson 1 begins with bytecode. You do need the memory model track's first lesson (why a loop on a plain field can hang) and the first track's lesson on atomics and LongAdder. Install JDK 25, the current LTS. Thresholds and inlining limits are the same from JDK 21 to 27, and every lesson says which JDK a newer feature needs (JFR method timing and CPU-time sampling are JDK 25; compact object headers are on by default in JDK 27). async-profiler is a separate download for lesson 6. The labs live in labs/performance, one package per lesson (workbench.performance.l01 to l07). Lessons 1 and 6 have Kotlin labs; the rest are Java, because JMH benchmarks are Java classes here. The tests never time anything: they parse real JVM output, read class files and object layouts, record and read JFR files, and count allocated bytes. Run ./gradlew :performance:test --tests 'workbench.performance.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and solutionTest to check the reference answers. Demos run with ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=.... Many start a second JVM with the flags the lesson is about, so you see real -XX:+PrintCompilation, -XX:+PrintInlining and JFR output. HotSpot runs every method in the interpreter first, then C1 with profiling (about 200 calls) and C2 (about 5,000 more). OSR compiles long loops mid-run. Every new JVM starts cold. -XX:+PrintCompilation lines read: time, id, flags, tier, method, OSR index, bytecode size, message. JDK 25 says why code was made not entrant. C2 inlines within a bytecode budget (35 bytes at sites that aren't hot, 325 at hot ones) and only for one or two receiver types per call site. What it never saw becomes an uncommon trap; when one fires, the code is thrown away and recompiled. A nanoTime loop measures the optimizer. JMH, with returned results, non-final @State inputs, warm-up, forks and a baseline, measures your code. -prof gc B/op is steady enough for CI; time isn't. Caches move 64-byte lines. Threads writing neighbouring fields can slow each other badly (false sharing); pad with a class chain, check with JOL, or use LongAdder. JFR records GC, JIT, locks, samples and your own events on one timeline. Start it with -XX:StartFlightRecording or jcmd, query it with jfr view, read it with RecordingFile, stream it with RecordingStream. async-profiler samples stacks without safepoint bias in cpu, wall, alloc and lock modes. In a flame graph width is samples and the x-axis is alphabetical; wide exposed tops are where time goes. An investigation goes symptom (the tail), JFR (what and which line), flame graph (who calls), one fix, re-profile, JMH proof, allocation budget test.

h: JIT, profiling and benchmarking: cheat sheet
x: How HotSpot runs your code (JDK 21 to 27) Tier Runs the code Reached after 0 interpreter, counts calls and loop back-edges start 3 C1 with full profiling (branches, receiver types) about 200 calls (Tier3InvocationThreshold) 4 C2, optimized with the profile about 5,000 more calls (Tier4InvocationThreshold) OSR a running loop compiled and entered mid-loop about 60,000 back-edges (tier 3), 40,000 more (tier 4) Tier 1 is C1 for trivial methods; tier 2 is C1 with counters only, used when C2 has a backlog. Thresholds grow when compile queues are long. CompileThreshold (10,000) applies only with -XX:-TieredCompilation. Code cache: 240 MB reserved, three heaps; check with jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache. Reading PrintCompilation 40 10 % 4 Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) made not entrant: uncommon trap ms id flags tier method OSR bci bytecode size message (reason on JDK 25) Flags: % OSR, s synchronized, ! exception handler, b blocking, n native. Reasons on JDK 25: not used and OSR invalidation of lower levels are routine; uncommon trap means a C2 bet failed. Timestamps and ids change every run. What C2 bets on Rule Value Inline at a call site that isn't hot callee at most 35 bytes of bytecode (MaxInlineSize) Inline at a hot site (25% or more of the caller's calls) at most 325 bytes (FreqInlineSize) Types inlined per call site 2 (TypeProfileWidth); with more, only a type with 90% or more Uncommon trap kinds unstable_if (untaken branch), class_check (unseen type) Diagnose with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining and -Xlog:deoptimization=debug. Keep cold paths out of hot methods: Java static long requireAmount(long cents) { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents); // 21 bytes, inlines anywhere return cents; } Kotlin fun requireAmount(cents: Long): Long { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents) // 21 bytes, inlines anywhere return cents } final doesn't make calls faster; the number of receiver types does. Prefer JDK intrinsics (Math.addExact, Arrays.equals, Long.bitCount) over hand-written loops. JMH rules Java @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Fork(2) public class FeeBench { long amountCents = 123_456; // non-final input @Benchmark public long fee() { return FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents); } // result returned @Benchmark public void baseline() { } // the floor } Kotlin @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Fork(2) open class FeeBench { // JMH subclasses it var amountCents = 123_456L // non-final input @Benchmark fun fee(): Long = FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents) // result returned @Benchmark fun baseline() {} // the floor } Return results or Blackhole.consume them; never read inputs from final constant fields; never @Fork(0); compare with a baseline. -prof gc gives gc.alloc.rate.norm (B/op): stable enough for CI, unlike ns/op. Defaults in 1.37: 5 forks, 5 + 5 iterations of 10 s. Caches and false sharing Lines are 64 bytes. Two threads writing fields on one line slow each other down (false sharing); how much depends on the hardware. Pad hot fields at least 64 bytes apart with a class chain, check with JOL (ClassLayout.parseClass(X.class)), assert distances, not offsets. @Contended needs -XX:-RestrictContended and --add-exports for your own classes. For counters, use LongAdder. JFR java -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=rec.jfr,settings=profile -jar app.jar jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=x settings=profile # on a running JVM jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=x filename=x.jfr jfr summary rec.jfr jfr view hot-methods | allocation-by-site | gc-pauses | contention-by-site | deoptimizations-by-reason rec.jfr jfr print --events workbench.IssuerCall --stack-depth 3 rec.jfr default.jfc stays on; profile.jfc for short investigations. Custom events extend jdk.jfr.Event (begin, end, shouldCommit, commit); read files with RecordingFile, live events with RecordingStream. A custom event's setting on the command line needs a +: +workbench.IssuerCall#threshold=30ms. JDK 25: method-timing=, report-on-exit=, experimental jdk.CPUTimeSample on Linux. Recordings contain environment variables; JDK 27 can redact them. async-profiler and flame graphs asprof -d 30 -f cpu.html <pid> # CPU (use -e ctimer if perf_events is blocked) asprof -e wall -t -d 30 -f wall.html <pid> # waiting: I/O, locks, sleep, per thread asprof -e alloc -d 30 -f alloc.html <pid> # who allocates asprof -e lock -d 30 -f lock.html <pid> # contended locks asprof -d 30 -o collapsed -f out.collapsed <pid> # text: "a;b;c 42" Width = samples (inclusive), root at the bottom, left to right is alphabetical, never time. Wide exposed tops are self time; follow them down to the first frame in your code. getStackTrace-based profilers suffer from safepoint bias; async-profiler doesn't. The investigation loop Symptom: p99.9/p99.99 and GC count, not the average. JFR: gc-pauses, then allocation by the first frame in your code and its line. Flame graph: who calls it. Fix one thing; profile again (the order of costs changes). Prove it with JMH -prof gc; keep it with an allocation budget test (getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes), with a margin.

h: JIT, profiling and benchmarking: track quiz
x: Which compiler produced this line, and why is there an @ 4? 45 10 % 4 Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) C1, because % marks a profiled compile C2, compiling a running loop (OSR) entered at bytecode index 4 The interpreter, at line 4 of the source C2, inlining 4 callees Tier 4 is C2. % marks on-stack replacement: the loop was hot while the method was still running, so C2 compiled a version entered at the loop header, bytecode index 4. Bytecode indexes aren't source lines. A 60-byte (bytecode) validator is called on about 1 in 10 invocations of its caller. Will C2 inline it there? No: below 25% of the caller's calls the limit is 35 bytes, so it's "too big" Yes, everything under 325 bytes is inlined Only if the method is final Only in the interpreter C2 uses 325 bytes only when the call runs on at least 25% of the caller's invocations. Otherwise MaxInlineSize (35) applies. Moving the cold path into its own method is the usual fix. You must decide in a pull request whether a new JSON mapper allocates less than the old one, and keep it that way in CI. Which tool fits? A unit test timing 1,000 calls with System.nanoTime() -XX:+PrintCompilation A JMH benchmark with -prof gc, then an allocation budget test async-profiler in wall mode JMH with -prof gc gives bytes per operation with an error near zero, and a test using the per-thread allocation counter keeps the number from growing. A hand-made timing loop measures the optimizer, and wall mode answers a different question. A JMH benchmark reads its input from private final long amount = 12_345; and scores the same as an empty benchmark. Why? JMH can't read private fields The benchmark forgot @Fork Private fields are always cached in registers javac copies the constant into the method and C2 folds the calculation into a constant A final field with a constant initializer is a compile-time constant in Java, so the method contains ldc2_w 12345, and C2 can compute the result once. Use a non-final @State field. Two worker threads each update their own volatile long counter in the same small object, and the job is slower with two threads than with one. JOL shows the fields at offsets 16 and 24. What's the first thing to try? Make the fields non-volatile Add synchronized to both updates Put the counters at least 64 bytes apart (a class chain), or use one LongAdder per counter, then measure Use AtomicLong for both fields in the same object 8 bytes apart is one cache line, so every write takes the line from the other core: false sharing. Padding or LongAdder cells separate them. Removing volatile changes visibility, not layout, and an AtomicLong field is just a reference to an object that may sit next to the other one. Production pods show p99 spikes and you can't install anything on them. Which first step gives you GC pauses, lock waits and allocation for the last few minutes? jcmd <pid> JFR.dump from a continuous recording, then jfr view gc-pauses, contention-by-site and allocation-by-site Restart with -XX:+PrintCompilation Attach async-profiler Run JMH on the pod JFR is built into the JDK, and a continuous recording can be dumped without stopping the JVM. Its views answer all three questions from one file. Your custom JFR event fills four fields from expensive lookups before commit(). Most of the time no recording is running. What should the code check first? event.isEnabled() after commit event.shouldCommit() after end(), and fill the fields only if it returns true FlightRecorder.isAvailable() on every call Nothing: JFR skips disabled events before the fields are computed shouldCommit() is true only if some recording enables the event and the duration passes its threshold. Java evaluates your field values before commit() is called, so JFR can't skip that work for you. In a flame graph, Pattern.compile is drawn to the left of String.format at the same level. Which statement is true? Pattern.compile ran first Pattern.compile is the slower of the two Their order is alphabetical; only the widths carry information String.format called Pattern.compile Flame graphs sort frames alphabetically at each level; the x-axis is not a timeline. Width is the number of samples, and a callee is drawn above its caller, never beside it. A profiler built on Thread.getStackTrace() charges a lot of time to a method that only calls other methods. async-profiler doesn't. What's going on? async-profiler skips small methods The JIT inlined the method away getStackTrace uses wall-clock time Safepoint bias: getStackTrace sees threads only at safepoint polls, so time is charged where the thread can stop, not where it ran Reading another thread's stack needs that thread at a safepoint, and polls sit at method returns and loop back-edges. async-profiler interrupts the thread with a signal and walks the stack at the exact instruction. After hoisting a regex into a static final field, the fee method's allocation drops from about 2,000 to 200 bytes per call. What does the investigation loop say to do next? Stop: a 10x improvement is enough Profile again: the remaining 200 bytes now have a new top line (here the Matcher per call), fix that if the budget needs it, and stop when what's left is real work Increase the heap so GC runs less Rewrite the method in Kotlin Each fix changes the order of costs. In this track's investigation, the Matcher behind the hoisted pattern became the top line only after round 1; replacing the regex left 72 bytes, all of it the BigDecimal parse that is the actual job.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Every method starts in the interpreter and earns its way to C2
x: From the interpreter to C1 to C2, and back when a bet loses javac and kotlinc don't produce machine code. They produce bytecode: compact instructions for the JVM, stored in .class files, such as iload_2 (push local variable 2) or ladd (add two longs). HotSpot, the JVM in every OpenJDK build, turns bytecode into machine code for your CPU while the program runs. The part that does it is the JIT (just-in-time) compiler. Compiling late sounds wasteful, but it lets the JIT see what your code really does, which types and branches actually occur, and optimize for exactly that. Nothing is compiled when a class loads. Every method starts in the interpreter, a loop inside the JVM that reads one bytecode instruction at a time and carries it out. While it runs, the JVM counts how often the method is called and how often its loops jump back to the top (the back-edges). When the counts are high enough, a compiler thread turns the method into machine code in the background. The next call runs that code instead. There are two compilers. C1 compiles quickly and optimizes a little. C2 compiles slowly and optimizes hard, using a profile of what the code really did. Tiered compilation, on by default, uses both, in five levels: Tier Runs the code Notes 0 interpreter counts calls and loop back-edges 1 C1, no profiling for trivial methods such as getters 2 C1 with counters only used when C2 has a backlog 3 C1 with full profiling records branch counts and the receiver types at each call 4 C2 compiles with the profile that tier 3 collected The normal path is 0, then 3, then 4. A method gets C1 with profiling after about 200 calls (Tier3InvocationThreshold) and C2 after about 5,000 more calls at tier 3 (Tier4InvocationThreshold). Loop iterations add to the count. When the compile queues are long, the JVM raises these thresholds on the fly, so treat them as orders of magnitude. The defaults are the same in every release from JDK 21 to JDK 27. Tier 1 and tier 2 are side roads. A trivial method goes to tier 1 and stays there, because the HotSpot source says C2 would "yield the same code". Tier 2 skips most of the profiling, and the same source says it runs about 30% faster than tier 3, so the JVM uses it while C2 is busy. Old blog posts say a method is compiled after 10,000 calls. That is CompileThreshold, and it applies only when you turn tiered compilation off with -XX:-TieredCompilation. Here is a function that the JVM will run at three different speeds during one short program: Java static long feeCents(long amountCents) { return (amountCents * 29 + 500) / 1000 + 30; // 2.9% + 30 cents, rounded } Kotlin fun feeCents(amountCents: Long): Long = (amountCents * 29 + 500) / 1000 + 30 // 2.9% + 30 cents, rounded Watch the same batch get faster Predict: WarmupDemo times the same batch of 20,000 fee calculations 12 times. Will batch 12 take as long as batch 1? Run it with the command below and note when the time drops. Run it again with -Pargs=int, which restarts it with -Xint (interpreter only), then with -Pargs=c1 (-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1, C1 only). WarmupDemo.java package workbench.performance.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Times the same batch of fee calculations 12 times in a row. * No argument: normal tiered JVM. "int": interpreter only (-Xint). "c1": stop at C1 (-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1). */ public class WarmupDemo { static final long[] AMOUNTS = new long[20_000]; // 2.9% + 30 cents, rounded half up, in cents static long feeCents(long amountCents) { return (amountCents * 29 + 500) / 1000 + 30; } static long batch() { long total = 0; for (long a : AMOUNTS) total += feeCents(a); return total; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "tiered"; if (mode.equals("int")) { relaunch("-Xint"); return; } if (mode.equals("c1")) { relaunch("-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1"); return; } for (int i = 0; i < AMOUNTS.length; i++) AMOUNTS[i] = 500 + (i * 7919L) % 250_000; long check = 0; for (int round = 1; round <= 12; round++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); check += batch(); long micros = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000; System.out.printf("batch %2d: %,6d us%n", round, micros); } System.out.println("(checksum " + check + ")"); // use the result, so the JIT can't drop the work } // start a second JVM with extra flags and the same classpath, and show its output static void relaunch(String flag) throws Exception { String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, flag, "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), WarmupDemo.class.getName(), "tiered")); System.out.println("running with " + flag); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { out.lines().filter(l -> !l.startsWith("Picked up")).forEach(System.out::println); } p.waitFor(); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l01.WarmupDemo labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l01/WarmupDemo.java WarmupDemo.kt package workbench.performance.l01 // Kotlin twin of WarmupDemo.java: times the same batch of fee calculations 12 times in a row. // No argument: normal tiered JVM. "int": interpreter only (-Xint). "c1": stop at C1 (-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1). private val amounts = LongArray(20_000) // 2.9% + 30 cents, rounded half up, in cents fun feeCents(amountCents: Long): Long = (amountCents * 29 + 500) / 1000 + 30 fun batch(): Long { var total = 0L for (a in amounts) total += feeCents(a) return total } fun main(args: Array<String>) { when (args.firstOrNull() ?: "tiered") { "int" -> return relaunch("-Xint") "c1" -> return relaunch("-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1") } for (i in amounts.indices) amounts[i] = 500 + (i * 7919L) % 250_000 var check = 0L for (round in 1..12) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() check += batch() val micros = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000 println("batch %2d: %,6d us".format(round, micros)) } println("(checksum $check)") // use the result, so the JIT can't drop the work } // start a second JVM with extra flags and the same classpath, and show its output private fun relaunch(flag: String) { val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") println("running with $flag") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, flag, "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l01.WarmupDemoKt", "tiered").redirectErrorStream(true).start() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filterNot { it.startsWith("Picked up") }.forEach(::println) } p.waitFor() } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l01.WarmupDemoKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l01/WarmupDemo.kt With the defaults, the first four or so batches take a few hundred microseconds each, then the time falls to tens of microseconds once compiled code takes over the loop. One run here went from about 500 us to 60 us. With int every batch stays near 500 us. With c1 it also gets fast, a little behind the default on this tiny function. The drop comes around batch 4 or 5, not batch 2: batch() is called only 12 times, so it's the loop that gets compiled, as the OSR section explains. Your numbers will differ, the shape won't. Think of a card-payment risk engine. A new merchant starts in manual review: every transaction is checked by hand, slowly (the interpreter). After a couple of hundred transactions the merchant moves to automatic approval with full logging, so the team can see what normal looks like (C1 at tier 3, collecting the profile). After a few thousand, a tuned fast path takes over that trusts the merchant's history (C2). If something the history never showed happens, the merchant goes back to review and a new model gets built (an uncommon trap, then a recompile). The analogy breaks in two places. A risk team keeps its history across restarts, while a JVM forgets everything when the process ends. And the JIT doesn't weigh risk at all: it bets that what it saw is all there is.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Reading -XX:+PrintCompilation line by line
x: -XX:+PrintCompilation prints one line each time a compile finishes, and another when the JVM stops using compiled code. These are real lines from the small program Hot (in the Try it below) on JDK 21: 40 8 % 3 Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) 40 9 3 Hot::longLoop (27 bytes) 40 10 % 4 Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) 42 8 % 3 Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) made not entrant 79 14 2 Hot$Square::area (10 bytes) 88 18 4 Hot::total (42 bytes) Read the third line from left to right. It finished 40 ms after the JVM started. Its compile id is 10. The % says it's an OSR compile (on-stack replacement, the next section's topic), the 4 says C2 did it, and @ 4 says the compiled code is entered at bytecode index 4. The last number, (27 bytes), is the size of the method's bytecode, not of the machine code. Lesson 2 shows why that number matters: inlining limits are counted in these bytes. The five characters after the id are attribute flags: % for OSR, s for a synchronized method, ! for a method with an exception handler, b for a blocking compile and n for a native wrapper. A real s line looks like 58 25 s 3 Flags::syncInc (9 bytes). The compile id ties lines together. The fourth line repeats id 8 with made not entrant: the JVM stopped using that code, and new calls won't enter it. Most of these lines are routine. Tier 3 code is retired as soon as a tier 4 version takes over. On JDK 25 the JVM also prints the reason, after a colon: made not entrant: OSR invalidation of lower levels // C2 OSR code replaced the C1 OSR code made not entrant: not used // a newer compile of the method replaced it made not entrant: uncommon trap // a C2 assumption failed (lesson 2) Two warnings before you go hunting in logs. First, the timestamps and ids change from run to run: in three identical runs, the first OSR compile of longLoop landed at 40, 47 and 60 ms. The compile policy depends on queue lengths, so never diff two logs line by line. Second, the JDK's own methods (String::hashCode, Object::<init>) are compiled too, so filter by your package. Read the log of a running program Read Hot. Predict which of longLoop, total and Square::area will reach tier 4, and which will be compiled with %. Run it. The demo starts a second JVM with -XX:+PrintCompilation and keeps only the lines for this lesson's classes. Find the compile id of the first tier 4 compile of total, then the later line where that id is made not entrant. What did the program do just before? Run the Kotlin twin and compare the (N bytes) sizes. Add -Pargs=all to either one to see every line the JVM prints. Hot.java package workbench.performance.l01; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Watch HotSpot compile this program. Run without arguments: it starts a second JVM with * -XX:+PrintCompilation and prints only the lines about this lesson's classes. * Pass "all" to see every line, including the JDK's own methods. */ public class Hot { interface Shape { double area(); } record Square(double s) implements Shape { public double area() { return s * s; } } record Circle(double r) implements Shape { public double area() { return Math.PI * r * r; } } record Tri(double b, double h) implements Shape { public double area() { return 0.5 * b * h; } } static double total(Shape[] shapes) { double sum = 0; for (Shape s : shapes) sum += s.area(); // one call site: first only Squares, later three types return sum; } static long longLoop() { // called once, but the loop runs 50 million times: OSR long acc = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 50_000_000; i++) acc += (i ^ (i >>> 3)); return acc; } static void work() { System.out.println(longLoop()); Shape[] squares = new Shape[1000]; for (int i = 0; i < squares.length; i++) squares[i] = new Square(i); double r = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) r += total(squares); // only Square seen so far Shape[] mixed = new Shape[999]; for (int i = 0; i < mixed.length; i++) mixed[i] = switch (i % 3) { case 0 -> new Square(i); case 1 -> new Circle(i); default -> new Tri(i, i); }; for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) r += total(mixed); // two new types reach the same call site System.out.println(r); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { work(); return; } boolean all = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("all"); // the same as: java -XX:+PrintCompilation -cp <classpath> workbench.performance.l01.Hot child String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), Hot.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { out.lines() .filter(line -> all || line.contains("l01.Hot") || !line.contains("::")) .filter(line -> !line.startsWith("Picked up")) .forEach(System.out::println); } p.waitFor(); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l01.Hot labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l01/Hot.java Hot.kt package workbench.performance.l01 // Kotlin twin of Hot.java: the same program, so you can compare what the JIT does with Kotlin bytecode. // Run without arguments: it starts a second JVM with -XX:+PrintCompilation and prints the lines // about this file's classes. Pass "all" to see every line. interface KShape { fun area(): Double } class KSquare(private val s: Double) : KShape { override fun area() = s * s } class KCircle(private val r: Double) : KShape { override fun area() = Math.PI * r * r } class KTri(private val b: Double, private val h: Double) : KShape { override fun area() = 0.5 * b * h } fun total(shapes: Array<KShape>): Double { var sum = 0.0 for (s in shapes) sum += s.area() // one call site: first only squares, later three types return sum } fun longLoop(): Long { // called once, but the loop runs 50 million times: OSR var acc = 0L for (i in 0 until 50_000_000) acc += (i xor (i ushr 3)) return acc } fun work() { println(longLoop()) val squares = Array<KShape>(1000) { KSquare(it.toDouble()) } var r = 0.0 repeat(20_000) { r += total(squares) } // only KSquare seen so far val mixed = Array(999) { when (it % 3) { 0 -> KSquare(it.toDouble()); 1 -> KCircle(it.toDouble()); else -> KTri(it.toDouble(), it.toDouble()) } } repeat(20_000) { r += total(mixed) } // two new types reach the same call site println(r) } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") { work(); return } val all = args.firstOrNull() == "all" // the same as: java -XX:+PrintCompilation -cp <classpath> workbench.performance.l01.HotKt child val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l01.HotKt", "child").redirectErrorStream(true).start() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { all || it.contains("l01.HotKt") || it.contains("l01.K") || !it.contains("::") } .filterNot { it.startsWith("Picked up") } .forEach(::println) } p.waitFor() } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l01.HotKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l01/Hot.kt longLoop gets % lines at tier 3 and then tier 4 before the program prints 1251976370825152. total reaches tier 4, then that compile is made not entrant right after the Circle and Tri objects appear, and a new tier 4 compile with a higher id follows. On JDK 25 you also see the reasons. The Kotlin twin compiles to almost the same bytecode: 27 bytes for longLoop and 43 for total, against 42 in Java. One OSR line from PrintCompilation, column by column. The size is bytecode, not machine code. Your authorization endpoint on Quarkus has a p99 target of 150 ms. Every deploy, the dashboard shows a short bump: new pods answer their first requests slower than old ones did. That's the interpreter and C1 running code that the old pods ran in C2, plus the compiler threads competing with request threads for the pod's CPUs. Before you tune anything, check that the bump goes away within a minute or two. If it matters, warm the pod with synthetic authorizations before the readiness probe passes, or try the JDK 25 AOT cache in a staging environment. Don't load-test a pod that has just started and compare it to one that has been running for an hour.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · OSR compiles a loop while it is still running
x: longLoop is called once. It never gets near 200 calls, yet it was the first method compiled. If the JVM only counted calls, a method stuck in a long loop would stay in the interpreter forever. So it also counts back-edges. When one loop has jumped back about 60,000 times (Tier3BackEdgeThreshold), the JVM compiles a version of the method that starts at the loop. It then moves the running frame, with its local variables, into that code. This is on-stack replacement (OSR). C2 does the same at tier 4 after about 40,000 more back-edges (Tier4BackEdgeThreshold). The @ 4 points at the loop header. javap -c shows it: static long longLoop(); 0: lconst_0 1: lstore_0 2: iconst_0 3: istore_2 4: iload_2 // loop header: the OSR code is entered here 5: ldc #13 // int 50000000 7: if_icmpge 25 // loop exit test ... 22: goto 4 JDK 25 tells the rest of the story. These are real lines for the same method: 23 14 % 3 workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) 23 16 % 4 workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) 25 14 % 3 workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) made not entrant: OSR invalidation of lower levels 40 16 % 4 workbench.performance.l01.Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) made not entrant: uncommon trap The first made not entrant is housekeeping: once the C2 OSR code exists, the JVM retires the C1 one. The second is more interesting. When the loop ends at 40 ms, the C2 code throws itself away. -Xlog:deoptimization=debug says why: trap_bci=7 osr_bci=4 unstable_if reinterpret. Bytecode 7 is the exit test. While C1 profiled the loop, the exit branch had never been taken, so C2 didn't compile the exit at all. It put an uncommon trap there instead: a small stub that sends the frame back to the interpreter if the branch it never saw ever runs. It ran once, at the very end. That cost nothing here, and it's the JIT's betting habit in miniature. Lesson 2 is about those bets. OSR matters to you for one practical reason. A benchmark written as one long loop in main measures OSR code and its quirks, not the code your service runs after warm-up. JMH, in lesson 3, avoids that trap. Find the loop and the trap Run the Hot demo once so Gradle compiles it. From labs/, print the bytecode of longLoop with the first command below. Find index 4 and index 7. Run the second command. It starts Hot directly with the deoptimization log on. Find the longLoop line and the total lines. terminal javap -c -p -cp performance/build/classes/java/demo workbench.performance.l01.Hot | grep -A 20 'long longLoop' java -Xlog:deoptimization=debug -cp performance/build/classes/java/demo workbench.performance.l01.Hot child Index 4 is iload_2, the top of the loop, and index 7 is if_icmpge 25, the exit test. The log has one line for longLoop with trap_bci=7 osr_bci=4 unstable_if, printed when the loop ends, and several lines for total with trap_bci=27 class_check maybe_recompile. Bytecode 27 in total is the area() call. That second kind of trap is the topic of lesson 2.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Compiled code lives in the code cache, and every new JVM starts cold
x: Machine code needs somewhere to live. HotSpot keeps it in the code cache, a memory region outside the Java heap. With tiered compilation the default is 240 MB reserved (ReservedCodeCacheSize), split into three heaps. -XX:+PrintCodeCache on JDK 25 shows them: CodeHeap 'non-profiled nmethods': size=120036Kb used=2Kb max_used=2Kb free=120033Kb CodeHeap 'profiled nmethods': size=120028Kb used=5Kb max_used=5Kb free=120022Kb CodeHeap 'non-nmethods': size=5696Kb used=1253Kb max_used=1267Kb free=4442Kb CodeCache: size=245760Kb, used=1260Kb, max_used=1274Kb, free=244497Kb An nmethod is HotSpot's name for one compiled method. Tier 2 and tier 3 code goes into 'profiled nmethods'. Tier 1 and tier 4 code goes into 'non-profiled nmethods'. Stubs and adapters, the glue the interpreter and compiled code need, live in 'non-nmethods'. If one heap fills, the JVM warns CodeHeap 'non-profiled nmethods' is full. Compiler has been disabled., stops starting new compiles and schedules a clean-up so it can start again later. Until then, methods that aren't compiled stay in the interpreter. You can check a live JVM with jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache. Do that before you raise the size. The bigger cost for a service is that every JVM learns from scratch. Nothing from yesterday's process survives a restart. After a deploy, the first thousands of requests to a new pod run in the interpreter and in C1, and the hot paths reach C2 only after they've been called thousands of times. The compiler threads also share the pod's CPUs with your request threads. So a new pod is slower for a while after it starts, and a rolling deploy shows up as a bump in p99 latency. There are two usual fixes. You can send synthetic warm-up traffic to the pod before its readiness probe passes, so real users never hit the cold code. Or, on JDK 25, you can record a training run into an AOT cache: JEP 515 adds method profiles to that cache, so the next JVM starts with the profiles from the training run instead of an empty one. The startup track covers the AOT cache. One rule follows for every measurement in this track. A number taken in the first seconds of a JVM measures the interpreter and C1, plus the compiler's own work. Measure after warm-up, or say clearly that you measured a cold start. Look inside the code cache Run the first command. It starts a JVM that does nothing and prints the code cache at exit. Run the second one, which prints the code cache after Hot has run. Compare the used= numbers. Optional: start any demo that runs for a while, find its pid with jcmd -l, and run jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache against it. terminal java -XX:+PrintCodeCache -version java -XX:+PrintCodeCache -cp performance/build/classes/java/demo workbench.performance.l01.Hot child Three heaps of about 117 MB, 117 MB and 5.6 MB, 240 MB in total. With -version, only a few KB of compiled methods are used. After Hot, the two method heaps hold more, because Hot and the JDK methods it called were compiled. Even then it's a tiny part of 240 MB. JEP 515: Ahead-of-Time Method Profiling read The common mistake is timing code once, cold, and trusting the number. Someone writes a unit test that calls formatAmount with System.nanoTime() around it, sees 2 ms, and rewrites the method. They measured the interpreter, class loading and the compiler's own startup. The same call takes nanoseconds after warm-up. The fix is to measure after warm-up, with many iterations, and in a separate JVM from the one that ran other tests. Doing that by hand is full of traps, which is why lesson 3 uses JMH. Java long t0 = System.nanoTime(); format(amount); // first call: interpreter, class loading long coldNanos = System.nanoTime() - t0; Kotlin val t0 = System.nanoTime() format(amount) // first call: interpreter, class loading val coldNanos = System.nanoTime() - t0

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Java and Kotlin
x: The JIT sees bytecode, not Java or Kotlin Hot.java static double total(Shape[] shapes) { double sum = 0; for (Shape s : shapes) sum += s.area(); return sum; } // PrintCompilation: Hot::total (42 bytes) // OSR entry: @ 11 Hot.kt fun total(shapes: Array<KShape>): Double { var sum = 0.0 for (s in shapes) sum += s.area() return sum } // PrintCompilation: HotKt::total (43 bytes) // OSR entry: @ 14 Both loops compile to an indexed loop over the array with one invokeinterface call, so HotSpot treats them the same way: same tiers, same OSR, same throw-away when new shape types arrive. The only visible difference is a byte of bytecode and a different loop index. A Kotlin top-level function lives in a class named after the file (HotKt), and that's the name you'll grep for in logs. Where Kotlin really changes what the JIT sees is in inline functions and boxing, which come up in lesson 2.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Worked example
x: Read a PrintCompilation log for one method Start by filtering. The JVM compiles hundreds of its own methods, so keep only the lines for your package and the program's own output. java -XX:+PrintCompilation -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main | grep 'com.acme' Find the OSR lines first. A % means a loop was hot enough to compile while it ran. Here Hot::longLoop got C1 OSR code (tier 3) and then C2 OSR code (tier 4) within the same millisecond. 40 8 % 3 Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) 40 10 % 4 Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) 42 8 % 3 Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) made not entrant Follow one compile id from birth to retirement. Id 18 is the first C2 version of total. It's made not entrant at 106 ms, and id 25 replaces it at the same moment. Ask what the program did just before: that's when the new shapes appeared. 88 18 4 Hot::total (42 bytes) 106 18 4 Hot::total (42 bytes) made not entrant 106 25 4 Hot::total (42 bytes) Self-check: which compile of total is running at the end of the log? Answer: id 25, the last tier 4 compile whose id never appears again with made not entrant. That's the rule the lab asks you to code. On JDK 25, read the reason. not used and OSR invalidation of lower levels are routine. uncommon trap on a tier 4 line means C2 made a bet and lost. A few of those during warm-up are normal. The same method trapping again and again in a long-running service is worth a look. 60 27 4 Hot::total (42 bytes) made not entrant: uncommon trap

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Lab
x: Parse PrintCompilation output labs/performance/src/main/kotlin/workbench/performance/l01/PrintCompilation.kt ./gradlew :performance:test --tests 'workbench.performance.l01.*' Run the tests once. All eight fail with NotImplementedError. The fixtures in PrintCompilationTest are real JDK 21 and JDK 25 output from Hot. Write parse(line). Return null when the line isn't a compile line. Otherwise fill every field of CompileEvent: time, id, the five flag characters, tier, method, OSR index, bytes, and the message. Make it handle (native) instead of (N bytes), a missing tier column (-XX:-TieredCompilation), and both made not entrant and made not entrant: <reason>. Write parseAll, then deoptimizedFromC2 (tier 4 lines that were made not entrant) and runningInC2 (normal tier 4 compiles whose id never shows up as made not entrant). Run the tests until all eight pass. Then run the Hot demo with -Pargs=all, paste a few lines into a test of your own, and check your parser on them. The layout is fixed: time, spaces, id, one space, exactly five flag characters, one space, then the tier digit and a space only when tiered compilation is on. A regex such as ^\s*(\d+)\s+(\d+) ([%s!bn ]{5}) (?:([0-4-]) )?\s*(\S+)... gets you most of the way. Kotlin's MatchResult.destructured gives you the groups as strings. toIntOrNull() turns an empty optional group into null for free. For the reason, take what follows made not entrant, drop a leading colon and spaces, and use null when nothing is left. runningInC2 needs two passes: first collect every compile id that was made not entrant, then keep tier 4, non-OSR lines whose id isn't in that set. All eight tests in PrintCompilationTest pass. By the end you can say which tier is running a method, read every column of a -XX:+PrintCompilation line, and explain OSR and why a fresh JVM is slow.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Quiz
x: A batch job calls rebuildBalances() once, and it loops over 3 million ledger rows. What does -XX:+PrintCompilation most likely show for it? Nothing, since it is called only once One tier 4 line after 10,000 calls Lines with % and @ <bci>: OSR compiles of its loop at tier 3, then tier 4 A single tier 1 line, because it is called rarely The JVM counts loop back-edges as well as calls. After about 60,000 back-edges it compiles an OSR version of the method at tier 3, and C2 follows at tier 4. "Called once" only rules out normal, call-triggered compiles. On JDK 25, which line says that C2 code was thrown away because one of its assumptions failed? 42 22 2 Hot$Square::area (10 bytes) made not entrant: not used 25 14 % 3 Hot::longLoop @ 4 (27 bytes) made not entrant: OSR invalidation of lower levels 47 27 4 Hot::total (42 bytes) 60 27 4 Hot::total (42 bytes) made not entrant: uncommon trap Tier 4 plus uncommon trap means C2 hit a case it had compiled as "never happens" and handed the frame back to the interpreter. not used and OSR invalidation of lower levels are housekeeping: a newer or better compile replaced older code. The last line is a compile, not a retirement. What does (42 bytes) at the end of a PrintCompilation line measure? The size of the machine code C2 produced The size of the method's bytecode The stack frame size of the method How much memory one call allocates The JVM prints method->code_size(), the bytecode length. Machine code is usually much larger. It matters because the inlining limits in lesson 2 are measured in bytecode bytes. A teammate's warm-up script calls the authorization endpoint exactly 10,000 times "because HotSpot compiles after 10,000 calls". On JDK 25 with default flags, what's wrong with that reasoning? Nothing, 10,000 is the default threshold Tiered compilation uses about 200 calls for tier 3 and about 5,000 more for tier 4, loops count too, and the thresholds grow when compile queues are long, so no fixed call count guarantees C2 HotSpot only compiles methods marked final C2 is off by default since JDK 21 10,000 is CompileThreshold, used only with -XX:-TieredCompilation. With tiered compilation the triggers are different, and they scale with compiler load. Warm up until latency settles, not to a magic number. In the memory model track, a loop on a plain boolean running field spun forever, but it stopped when run with -Xint. In this lesson's terms, why? The interpreter re-reads the field on every iteration. The hang appears only after C2 (often via OSR) compiles the loop and keeps the value in a register -Xint makes every field volatile -Xint turns off the CPU caches The interpreter runs every thread on one core Under -Xint the method never leaves tier 0, and the interpreter loads the field each time. The JIT is allowed to read a non-volatile field once and hoist it out of the loop. A hot loop reaches C2 through OSR even when the method is called once, which is exactly when the hang starts.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Explain it back
x: A teammate asks why the first load test against a freshly deployed pod gave much worse numbers than the second one, five minutes later, with no code change. Explain it in your own words, using the tiers.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Key terms
x: Interpreter Tier 0. Runs bytecode one instruction at a time and counts calls and loops. C1 The fast, lightly optimizing JIT compiler. At tier 3 it also collects the profile. C2 The slow, heavily optimizing JIT compiler (tier 4). It uses the profile to make bets. Tiered compilation Using the interpreter, C1 and C2 in sequence, on by default. OSR (on-stack replacement) Compiling a running loop and moving the live frame into the new code mid-loop. Profile (MDO) Per-method data the JVM records while profiling: branch counts, types seen at calls. Code cache Memory outside the heap that holds compiled code, 240 MB reserved by default. Made not entrant Compiled code the JVM has retired: new calls no longer enter it. Which compiler runs a method at tier 3, and what does it add? C1, with full profiling: call and loop counters plus branch counts and receiver types at each call site. C2 uses that profile. Which compiler runs a method at tier 4? C2, compiling with the profile that tier 3 collected. In a PrintCompilation line, what do % and @ 4 mean? % marks an OSR compile. @ 4 is the bytecode index of the loop where the compiled code is entered. What is the number in (27 bytes) on a PrintCompilation line? The method's bytecode size. Inlining limits are measured in these bytes. Roughly when does a method reach tier 3 and tier 4 on JDK 21 to 27? About 200 calls for tier 3, then about 5,000 calls at tier 3 for tier 4. Loop iterations count too, and the bar rises when compile queues are long. What does made not entrant mean? The JVM stopped using that compiled version; new calls won't enter it. JDK 25 prints the reason, such as not used or uncommon trap. How big is the code cache by default, and how do you inspect it on a live JVM? 240 MB reserved with tiered compilation, in three heaps. jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache.

h: From bytecode to machine code: interpreter, C1, C2 · Go deeper
x: PrintCompilation is the summary. For the full story, run with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+LogCompilation, which writes an XML log of every compile decision, and open it in JITWatch, a log viewer for HotSpot's JIT. Its wiki says to add -Xlog:class+load=info so it can build its class model. To see the machine code too, add -XX:+PrintAssembly, which needs the hsdis disassembler library. A few jcmd commands help on a live JVM: Compiler.queue shows what's waiting to be compiled, Compiler.codelist lists the compiled methods, and Compiler.codecache shows the heaps. The number of compiler threads is chosen from the CPU count: -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal showed CICompilerCount = 3 on a 4-CPU machine. -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 (C1 only) compiles less and peaks lower. The HotSpot source describes it as mostly for testing. Keep it out of production. JDK 25 added two JEPs aimed at warm-up. JEP 514 makes the AOT cache easier to create, with -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot on a training run and -XX:AOTCache=app.aot on later runs. JEP 515 stores method profiles in that cache, so a new JVM can start compiling hot methods with C2 sooner. I tried it on WarmupDemo packed into a jar (the cache refuses a directory on the classpath): the training run wrote an 11 MB cache, and in the next run the batches were fast from batch 3 instead of batch 5. That's one run on one machine, but the direction is the point. Compiling the code ahead of time is a separate, later step: JEP 544 is in the mainline for JDK 28, which isn't released yet. The startup track goes through all of this. One more thing you may read about: "made zombie". Older JDKs printed that when retired code was finally freed. JDK 25 doesn't print it, so treat articles that show it as describing an older JVM.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Inlining copies the callee into the caller, inside a bytecode budget
x: Inlining means C2 pastes the body of a called method into the caller and compiles them as one piece. Saving the call is the small win. The big win is that C2's other optimizations work inside one compiled unit, and now they can see both sides of the call: escape analysis (proving an object never leaves the method, so it needn't be allocated on the heap), constant folding (computing results from known values at compile time) and loop optimizations such as unrolling. A method that isn't inlined is a wall C2 can't see through. C2 decides per call site (one call instruction in the bytecode), using the callee's bytecode size (the (N bytes) from lesson 1). The rule in HotSpot's bytecodeInfo.cpp is short. C2 divides how often the call site ran by how often the caller was invoked. If the call runs on at least 25% of the caller's invocations (InlineFrequencyRatio), the site counts as hot and the limit is 325 bytes (FreqInlineSize). Otherwise the limit is 35 bytes (MaxInlineSize). There is also a depth limit of 15 levels, and a callee that is already compiled into more than 2,500 bytes of machine code (InlineSmallCode) is refused. These values are the same from JDK 21 to JDK 27. The budget counts every byte, including code that almost never runs. Here is a guard that checks an amount on every refund. It builds its error message inline: Java static long requireAmountInline(long cents) { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d", MAX_CENTS, cents)); } return cents; } Kotlin fun requireAmountInline(cents: Long): Long { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) { throw IllegalArgumentException("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d".format(MAX_CENTS, cents)) } return cents } The Java version is 49 bytes. Move the message into its own method and the hot method shrinks to 21: Java static long requireAmount(long cents) { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents); // hot path: 21 bytes return cents; } static IllegalArgumentException badAmount(long cents) { // cold path, its own method return new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d", MAX_CENTS, cents)); } Kotlin fun requireAmount(cents: Long): Long { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents) // hot path: 21 bytes return cents } fun badAmount(cents: Long) = // cold path, its own function IllegalArgumentException("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d".format(MAX_CENTS, cents)) In the demo below, each guard runs on 1 call in 8, so neither site is hot. This is the real C2 output: @ 15 ...InliningDemo::requireAmountInline (49 bytes) too big @ 30 ...InliningDemo::requireAmountSplit (21 bytes) inline (hot) Don't read too much into inline (hot). It's simply the message C2 prints when it inlines and has nothing more specific to say. The JDK's own code uses this split all the time: a small check, and a separate method that builds the exception. See C2 refuse the big guard Run InliningDemo. It starts a second JVM with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining and keeps the lines about refund. Find the decisions under the tier 3 compile (C1 says callee is too large) and under the tier 4 compile (C2 says too big). Run the Kotlin twin. Compare the size of requireAmountInline in both languages.
