In Java the sizes are 49 and 21 bytes. In Kotlin the inline-message version is 66 bytes: Kotlin's "...".format(...) is an inline function, so kotlinc pastes its body (an array copy and a null check) into the caller. The split version is 21 bytes in both. bytecodeInfo.cpp: C2's inlining rules (JDK 25) read Think of a routing switch at a payment processor. If almost every transaction it has seen is Visa, it keeps a fast lane wired straight to the Visa network and sends anything else to a slow manual desk. Two networks still fit: two fast lanes. When it has seen five networks with no clear winner, it stops keeping fast lanes and looks up each transaction's route in a table. That's a megamorphic call site. When the first Amex arrives at a switch wired only for Visa, it goes to the manual desk, and the switch gets rewired with Amex in mind (an uncommon trap, then a recompile). The analogy breaks on cost: a real switch pays for each manual review, while the JVM pays once per trap and then rebuilds the fast path.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · C2 bets on the receiver types it has seen
x: A call through an interface, like rule.fee(amount), could go to any implementation. C2 can only inline it if it knows which one. The object a method is called on is the receiver, so at tier 3 C1 records the receiver types it sees at every call site, and C2 reads that profile. One type seen: C2 inlines that type's method behind a cheap class check. This is a monomorphic call site. Two types: it inlines both behind two checks (bimorphic). The profile keeps two types per site (TypeProfileWidth = 2). With three or more, C2 inlines only a type that has at least 90% of the calls (TypeProfileMajorReceiverPercent). Otherwise the site is megamorphic: C2 emits a plain virtual call (look up the method in the receiver's class at run time, then jump to it) and inlines nothing. -XX:+PrintInlining shows the switch. These are real lines for the area() call in lesson 1's Hot program, before and after the new shapes arrived: @ 27 Hot$Square::area (10 bytes) inline (hot) \-> TypeProfile (977323/977323 counts) = Hot$Square @ 27 Hot$Shape::area (0 bytes) virtual call The cost is more than the call. MegamorphicBench feeds one call site with 1, 2 or 3 fee-rule types, in batches of 1,024. In several runs on the shared 4-vCPU VM used for this course, one type took 0.2 to 0.4 µs per batch, two types 0.4 to 0.7 µs, and three types 3 to 4 µs. The error bars were wide on that noisy machine, but the jump at three types showed up in every run. With the calls inlined, C2 can optimize the whole loop. With a virtual call per element, it can't. Notice what didn't matter. The fee-rule classes in the benchmark are final, and so are the records in Hot. C2 inlined Square::area because the profile said every receiver was a Square, not because of a modifier. Kotlin classes are final by default, and that doesn't change anything here either. What changes speed is how many types reach one call site. Count the types at a call site Predict the three numbers before you run: ns per batch with 1, 2 and 3 types. Run MegamorphicBench. It's a JMH benchmark (lesson 3 explains JMH). Each case runs in a fresh JVM, so each starts with a clean profile. It takes about 10 seconds. Run it with -Pargs='1 4'. Does a fourth type cost more than the third? The Kotlin twin runs 1, 3 and 4 types. Three types cost several times more, around ten times on the course VM. Four types cost about the same as three: once the site is megamorphic, it's a virtual call either way. Expect wide error bars on a laptop with other work running. Payment code is full of interfaces with a handful of implementations: PaymentMethod, FeeRule, RiskCheck, Kafka Deserializers. When a hot loop in your settlement job calls through one of them and three or more implementations reach the same call site, that call becomes a virtual call and the loop around it loses its optimizations. You won't see that in a code review. You'll see it in a profile (lessons 5 and 6) or in a JMH run. Also expect a short burst of deoptimizations when a new payment method goes live, since the first wallet payment trips traps compiled for cards only. That burst is fine. A steady stream hours later is a signal to check jfr view deoptimizations-by-reason.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · When a bet loses: uncommon traps and deoptimization
x: C2 compiles what the profile showed and nothing else. A branch that was never taken and a receiver type that never appeared don't get compiled code. In their place C2 puts an uncommon trap: a stub that hands the running frame back to the interpreter if that "impossible" case ever happens. When a trap fires, the JVM deoptimizes: it rebuilds an interpreter frame from the compiled frame and carries on there. The compiled code is made not entrant. The method goes back to profiling, now with the new case in its profile, and gets compiled again. The figure shows the cycle. DeoptDemo triggers both common kinds. It settles batches of card charges, then one refund appears, then SEPA and wallet payments arrive: Java long fee = methods[i].feeCents(amounts[i]); // bytecode 20: which types has it seen? if (refund[i]) net -= amounts[i]; // bytecode 31: has this branch ever been taken? else net += amounts[i] - fee; Kotlin val fee = methods[i].feeCents(amounts[i]) // which types has it seen? if (refund[i]) net -= amounts[i] // has this branch ever been taken? else net += amounts[i] - fee The real log on JDK 25, trimmed to the important parts: phase 2: one refund per batch ... DeoptDemo.settle(...) trap_bci=31 unstable_if reinterpret 81 23 4 ...DeoptDemo::settle (62 bytes) made not entrant: uncommon trap phase 3: SEPA and wallet payments arrive ... DeoptDemo.settle(...) trap_bci=20 class_check maybe_recompile 93 25 4 ...DeoptDemo::settle (62 bytes) made not entrant: uncommon trap unstable_if means a branch C2 had compiled as never taken: the refund. class_check means a type check failed at a call it had inlined for cards only. Each time, a new tier 4 compile follows within a few milliseconds. This is normal, and cheap when it happens a few times. HotSpot also limits how often one method can go around the cycle (PerMethodRecompilationCutoff is 400 recompiles). Expect a burst of deoptimizations after a deploy, or when a new payment method gets its first traffic. A steady stream of them in a service that has been up for hours is worth a look. JFR has a ready-made view for it, deoptimizations-by-reason, which lesson 5 uses. Trip a branch trap and a type trap Predict: in which phase will the first made not entrant for tier 4 code appear, and with which reason in the deoptimization log? Run DeoptDemo. It starts a second JVM with -XX:+PrintCompilation -Xlog:deoptimization=debug. Match each trap_bci to a line of settle (bytecode 20 is the feeCents call, 31 is the if (refund[i]) test). Then run the Kotlin twin: its bytecode indexes differ, the story doesn't. feeCents(amountCents: Long): Long } class CardFee(private val bps: Long) : PaymentMethod { override fun feeCents(amountCents: Long) = amountCents * bps / 10_000 } class SepaFee(private val flat: Long) : PaymentMethod { override fun feeCents(amountCents: Long) = flat } class WalletFee(private val bps: Long, private val flat: Long) : PaymentMethod { override fun feeCents(amountCents: Long) = amountCents * bps / 10_000 + flat } fun settle(methods: Array<PaymentMethod>, amounts: LongArray, refund: BooleanArray): Long { var net = 0L for (i in amounts.indices) { val fee = methods[i].feeCents(amounts[i]) // call site: which types has it seen? if (refund[i]) net -= amounts[i] // branch: has it ever been taken? else net += amounts[i] - fee } return net } private fun work() { val n = 1_000 val methods = Array<PaymentMethod>(n) { CardFee(290) } val amounts = LongArray(n) { 1_000L + it } val refund = BooleanArray(n) var total = 0L println("phase 1: card charges only") repeat(3_000) { total += settle(methods, amounts, refund) } println("phase 2: one refund per batch") refund[500] = true repeat(3_000) { total += settle(methods, amounts, refund) } println("phase 3: SEPA and wallet payments arrive") for (i in 0 until n step 3) methods[i] = SepaFee(35) for (i in 1 until n step 3) methods[i] = WalletFee(150, 10) repeat(3_000) { total += settle(methods, amounts, refund) } println("done, checksum $total") } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") return work() val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-Xlog:deoptimization=debug", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l02.DeoptDemoKt", "child") .redirectErrorStream(true).start() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { "DeoptDemoKt::settle" in it || "DeoptDemoKt.settle" in it || it.startsWith("phase") || it.startsWith("done") } .map { it.replace(Regex(" pc=.*"), "") } // drop machine addresses .forEach(::println) } p.waitFor() } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l02.DeoptDemoKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l02/DeoptDemo.kt Phase 1 compiles settle up to tier 4, including an OSR version. Phase 2 prints unstable_if at trap_bci=31 and retires the tier 4 code, then recompiles. Phase 3 prints class_check at trap_bci=20, retires it again and recompiles. On JDK 25 the PrintCompilation lines end in made not entrant: uncommon trap; on JDK 21 they just say made not entrant. C2 compiles only what the profile saw. An unseen case hits an uncommon trap, the code is retired, and the method is profiled and compiled again.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Intrinsics: JDK methods the JIT swaps for hand-written code
x: Some JDK methods never run as their Java code once they're hot. HotSpot has hand-written machine code, or hand-written compiler IR (the compiler's internal form of a program), for them. These are intrinsics. In the JDK source they carry @IntrinsicCandidate, whose Javadoc says the method "may be (but is not guaranteed to be) intrinsified". PrintInlining marks them: java.lang.Long::bitCount (61 bytes) (intrinsic) java.lang.Math::addExact (32 bytes) (intrinsic) java.util.Arrays::equals (43 bytes) (intrinsic) Those are real lines from IntrinsicsDemo. Long.bitCount is 61 bytes of shifts and masks in Java, and on x86 C2 replaces it with one POPCNT instruction. Arrays.equals on byte arrays ends up in ArraysSupport.vectorizedMismatch, which reads 8 bytes at a time even in its Java version, and is an intrinsic as well. The bytecode size doesn't matter for an intrinsic, because that Java code isn't what runs. The practical rule: in hot code, call the JDK method instead of writing the loop yourself. For money in cents, Math.addExact and Math.multiplyExact give you overflow checks that throw ArithmeticException, and both are intrinsics. A hand-written loop that compares two idempotency keys byte by byte gives up the 8-bytes-at-a-time path that Arrays.equals gets for free, and it's more code to get wrong. Kotlin gets the same intrinsics, because its standard library calls these JDK methods. ByteArray.contentEquals calls java.util.Arrays.equals, and Long.countOneBits() calls java.lang.Long.bitCount: Java long total = Math.addExact(a, b); // ArithmeticException on overflow boolean same = Arrays.equals(keyA, keyB); int flags = Long.bitCount(riskMask); Kotlin val total = Math.addExact(a, b) // ArithmeticException on overflow val same = keyA.contentEquals(keyB) // calls java.util.Arrays.equals val flags = riskMask.countOneBits() // calls java.lang.Long.bitCount List the intrinsics in a hot loop Run IntrinsicsDemo. It prints the PrintInlining lines for the three JDK methods it calls. Run the Kotlin twin, which uses contentEquals and countOneBits instead of calling Arrays and Long directly. Optional: run the Java demo's child JVM yourself with -XX:+PrintInlining and grep for intrinsic to see how many others the JDK uses on its own. IntrinsicsDemo.java package workbench.performance.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.TreeSet; /** * Calls three JDK methods that HotSpot replaces with hand-written machine code. Run it: a second * JVM starts with -XX:+PrintInlining and the demo lists the intrinsic decisions for them. */ public class IntrinsicsDemo { static long totalCents(long[] cents) { long sum = 0; for (long c : cents) sum = Math.addExact(sum, c); // throws on overflow instead of wrapping return sum; } static boolean sameKey(byte[] a, byte[] b) { return Arrays.equals(a, b); // compares many bytes per step } static int riskFlags(long mask) { return Long.bitCount(mask); // one POPCNT instruction on x86 } static void work() { long[] cents = new long[1_000]; Arrays.fill(cents, 1_999); byte[] k1 = new byte[64], k2 = new byte[64]; long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) { s += totalCents(cents); if (sameKey(k1, k2)) s++; s += riskFlags(i); } System.out.println("checksum " + s); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { work(); return; } String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), IntrinsicsDemo.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); TreeSet<String> seen = new TreeSet<>(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { out.lines() .filter(l -> l.contains("intrinsic")) .filter(l -> l.contains("Math::addExact") || l.contains("Arrays::equals") || l.contains("Long::bitCount")) .map(l -> l.replaceFirst("^\\s*@ \\d+\\s+", "")) // drop the indent and the call-site index .forEach(seen::add); } p.waitFor(); seen.forEach(System.out::println); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l02.IntrinsicsDemo labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l02/IntrinsicsDemo.java IntrinsicsDemo.kt package workbench.performance.l02 // Kotlin twin of IntrinsicsDemo.java. The Kotlin standard library calls the same JDK methods, // so the same intrinsics apply: contentEquals calls Arrays.equals, countOneBits calls Long.bitCount. fun totalCentsKt(cents: LongArray): Long { var sum = 0L for (c in cents) sum = Math.addExact(sum, c) // throws on overflow instead of wrapping return sum } fun sameKeyKt(a: ByteArray, b: ByteArray) = a.contentEquals(b) fun riskFlagsKt(mask: Long) = mask.countOneBits() fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") { val cents = LongArray(1_000) { 1_999 } val k1 = ByteArray(64) val k2 = ByteArray(64) var s = 0L for (i in 0 until 200_000) { s += totalCentsKt(cents) if (sameKeyKt(k1, k2)) s++ s += riskFlagsKt(i.toLong()) } println("checksum $s") return } val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l02.IntrinsicsDemoKt", "child") .redirectErrorStream(true).start() val seen = sortedSetOf<String>() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { "intrinsic" in it } .filter { "Math::addExact" in it || "Arrays::equals" in it || "Long::bitCount" in it } .mapTo(seen) { it.replaceFirst(Regex("""^\s*@ \d+\s+"""), "") } // drop the indent and call-site index } p.waitFor() seen.forEach(::println) } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l02.IntrinsicsDemoKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l02/IntrinsicsDemo.kt Both programs print the same three lines, each ending in (intrinsic): Long::bitCount, Math::addExact and Arrays::equals. Kotlin's standard library functions disappear entirely: they are inline, so the call in the bytecode is already the JDK method. The common mistake is adding final to classes and methods to make calls faster. Part of the confusion is that final does matter for fields, as lesson 3 shows. For calls, C2 decides from the type profile. It inlined Square::area because every receiver it saw was a Square, and the third record type still turned the call into a virtual call, final or not. Kotlin's final-by-default classes behave the same way. If a profile shows a hot megamorphic call, measure it with JMH first. Then reduce the number of types that reach that one call site, or keep the hot callee small so it inlines wherever the type is known.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Java and Kotlin
x: The same guard, before and after the split InliningDemo.java // before: 49 bytes, "too big" at a site that isn't hot static long requireAmountInline(long cents) { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d", MAX_CENTS, cents)); } return cents; } // after: 21 bytes, inlined static long requireAmount(long cents) { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents); // hot path: 21 bytes return cents; } static IllegalArgumentException badAmount(long cents) { // cold path, its own method return new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d", MAX_CENTS, cents)); } InliningDemo.kt // before: 66 bytes, "too big" at a site that isn't hot fun requireAmountInline(cents: Long): Long { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) { throw IllegalArgumentException("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d".format(MAX_CENTS, cents)) } return cents } // after: 21 bytes, inlined fun requireAmount(cents: Long): Long { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents) // hot path: 21 bytes return cents } fun badAmount(cents: Long) = // cold path, its own function IllegalArgumentException("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d".format(MAX_CENTS, cents)) After the split, both languages compile requireAmount to the same 21 bytes, and C2 treats them the same. Before the split, the Kotlin version is 66 bytes against Java's 49. Kotlin's String.format extension is an inline function, so kotlinc copies its body into the caller: an Arrays.copyOf of the arguments and a null check. Kotlin inline removes a call at compile time, but the pasted bytecode counts against the JIT's budget for the method that received it. Use inline for small higher-order functions, and keep big bodies out of hot methods in either language.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Worked example
x: Find out why a hot method isn't inlined, and fix it A refund handler is slower than expected in a profile. Start the service with the diagnostic flags and look for your method in the inlining log. java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main | grep requireAmount C2's line names the method, its bytecode size and the reason. too big means the call site isn't hot and the callee is over 35 bytes. hot method too big would mean a hot site and a callee over 325 bytes. @ 15 com.acme.pay.Guards::requireAmount (49 bytes) too big Look at what the 49 bytes are. javap -c -p shows the boxing calls, the varargs array and String.format that build the message. All of that is the cold path. javap -c -p -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Guards | grep -A 30 'long requireAmount' Move the cold path into its own method and return the exception from it, so the hot method still ends in throw. Self-check before reading on: why return the exception instead of throwing it inside the helper? (Answer: with throw badAmount(cents), javac and the reader can see that the method ends there. A helper that throws by itself looks like an ordinary call that returns.) static long requireAmount(long cents) { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents); // hot path: 21 bytes return cents; } static IllegalArgumentException badAmount(long cents) { // cold path, its own method return new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d", MAX_CENTS, cents)); } fun requireAmount(cents: Long): Long { if (cents <= 0 || cents > MAX_CENTS) throw badAmount(cents) // hot path: 21 bytes return cents } fun badAmount(cents: Long) = // cold path, its own function IllegalArgumentException("amount must be between 1 and %d cents, got %d".format(MAX_CENTS, cents)) Run the same command again. h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Quiz
x: C2's inlining log shows @ 15 Guards::requireAmount (49 bytes) too big inside a refund handler. Which change is most likely to get it inlined? Mark requireAmount as final Move the message building into a separate method so requireAmount is under 35 bytes Raise the heap size with -Xmx Wrap the call in a lambda too big means the site isn't hot, so the 35-byte limit applies, and the cold message code is most of the 49 bytes. A static method is already statically bound, so final changes nothing, and the heap has nothing to do with inlining. A call site has seen CardFee (50%), SepaFee (30%) and WalletFee (20%). What does C2 compile there? Three inlined bodies behind three type checks CardFee inlined, the rest as a virtual call A plain virtual call, with nothing inlined Nothing: the method stays at tier 3 The profile holds two types per site, and with more than that C2 needs one type with at least 90% of the calls to inline it. 50% isn't enough, so the site is megamorphic and becomes a virtual call. A deoptimization log line reads trap_bci=31 unstable_if reinterpret. What happened? Bytecode 31 is a branch C2 compiled as never taken; it was taken, so the frame went back to the interpreter and the method will be recompiled The JVM ran out of code cache at bytecode 31 A class was loaded twice The method threw an exception at bytecode 31 unstable_if is the trap C2 places on a branch the profile never saw taken. When it runs, the JVM deoptimizes the frame and the code is made not entrant. class_check would be the type-based version. The inlining log shows java.lang.Long::bitCount (61 bytes) (intrinsic). What does that tell you? The method was too big to inline C2 replaced the call with hand-written code, so the 61 bytes of Java don't run in that compiled code The method was compiled to 61 bytes of machine code The method runs in the interpreter An intrinsic replaces the method body with code HotSpot ships for it, a single POPCNT on x86 for bitCount. The size in the line is still the Java bytecode size, which is irrelevant once the intrinsic applies. PrintCompilation shows DeoptDemo::settle (62 bytes). Using what lesson 1 said about that number, can C2 inline settle into a caller that calls it on only 1 invocation in 10? Yes, 62 bytes of machine code is small No: 62 bytes of bytecode is over the 35-byte limit for a site that isn't hot Yes, any method under 325 bytes is always inlined No, methods with loops are never inlined (62 bytes) is the bytecode size. A call on 1 invocation in 10 is below the 25% bar, so the 35-byte MaxInlineSize applies and 62 is too big. At a hot site the limit would be 325 and it could be inlined.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Explain it back
x: A colleague asks: "Why did our settlement loop get slower when we added a third payment method, even though the new class is tiny?" Explain it in your own words.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Key terms
x: Inlining Pasting a called method's body into the caller so C2 compiles and optimizes them together. Call site One specific call instruction in the bytecode. Profiles and inlining decisions are per call site. Monomorphic, bimorphic, megamorphic One, two, or too many receiver types seen at a call site. Type profile The receiver types and counts that tier 3 records at each call site. Uncommon trap A stub in C2 code for a case the profile never saw. Running it deoptimizes the frame. Deoptimization Turning a compiled frame back into an interpreter frame and retiring the compiled code. Intrinsic A JDK method that HotSpot replaces with its own hand-written code. Biggest callee (in bytecode) that C2 inlines at a call site it doesn't consider hot? 35 bytes (MaxInlineSize). When does C2 treat a call site as hot, and what's the size limit there? When the call runs on at least 25% of the caller's invocations. Then the limit is 325 bytes (FreqInlineSize). How many receiver types does C2 inline at one call site from the profile? Up to two. With more, only a type with at least 90% of the calls; otherwise it emits a virtual call (megamorphic). What is an uncommon trap? A stub C2 puts where the profile saw nothing, such as an untaken branch or an unseen type. If it runs, the frame is deoptimized and the code is made not entrant. Does marking a class final make calls to it faster in C2? Not by itself. C2 inlines from the receiver-type profile. What matters is how many types reach the call site. What does @IntrinsicCandidate on a JDK method mean? HotSpot may replace the method with hand-written machine code or compiler IR, as it does for Math.addExact and Arrays.equals. Why can a Kotlin function be bigger in bytecode than the same Java code? Calls to Kotlin inline functions, such as "...".format(x), are pasted into the caller by kotlinc, and that bytecode counts against the JIT's inlining budget.

h: Inlining, deoptimization and intrinsics · Go deeper
x: Inlining is what makes escape analysis work. C2 can only prove that an object never leaves a method if it can see every method the object is passed to. A Money value created in a hot method and passed to a callee that isn't inlined has escaped, so it gets allocated on the heap. The memory track looks at escape analysis from the allocation side. For experiments, -XX:CompileCommand=dontinline,com.acme.pay.Guards::requireAmount and -XX:CompileCommand=inline,... force a decision for one method, and the inlining log says force inline by CompileCommand. Use them to test a theory, not as a production fix. One result here surprised me. I expected a shared helper such as static long timed(LongSupplier work) to make its work.getAsLong() call megamorphic when three different lambdas pass through it. C2 inlined all three anyway. Once it had inlined timed into each caller, it knew the exact lambda class at each spot and didn't need the shared profile. Megamorphic sites come from types that C2 can't see at compile time, such as objects read from an array, a field or a collection. Other messages you'll meet in the log: inlining too deep (more than 15 levels, MaxInlineLevel), already compiled into a big method (a callee already compiled into more than 2,500 bytes of machine code), hot method too big (a hot site, over 325 bytes) and no static binding (C1 can't inline a virtual call). JITWatch shows the same information per method if the raw log gets too long.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · A nanoTime loop measures the optimizer, not your code
x: A nanoTime loop measures the optimizer: dead code, constant folding, and the loop JMH builds instead Here is the benchmark almost everyone writes first: Java long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) { Math.sqrt(x); // result discarded } long t1 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.printf("%.4f ns/op%n", (t1 - t0) / 1e8); Kotlin val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) { sqrt(x) // result discarded } val t1 = System.nanoTime() println("%.4f ns/op".format((t1 - t0) / 1e8)) It printed 0.0301, then 0.1299, then 0.0000 for every later round. A second loop that adds each result to a sum and prints the sum settled at about 1.9 ns per call. The JIT measured nothing in the first loop because, once C2 had compiled it, there was nothing left to measure. That is dead-code elimination: a computation whose result nobody uses can go. Dead code is one of several ways a hand-made loop lies: If the input is a constant, C2 can compute the answer at compile time, and you end up timing the load of one number. That's constant folding. The first rounds run in the interpreter and in OSR code, as lesson 1 showed, and a benchmark that is one long loop in main keeps measuring OSR code. The JIT unrolls loops and hoists work out of them. JMH's own sample on loops reports the measured cost of an addition falling "up to the point we do each addition with 1/20 ns, well beyond what hardware can actually do". A wrong benchmark can also print a believable number, which is worse. On JDK 21, the same discarded loop with Math.log instead of Math.sqrt was not eliminated: it reported 7 to 9 ns per call, drifting upward from round to round. It looks plausible and still measures an accident of how C2 compiles Math.log. Whether the JIT can remove a call depends on what it can prove, and you can't see that from the outside. Watch the work disappear Read NanoLoop. Predict both columns for round 1 and round 5. Run it. Then run the Kotlin twin. Change the discarded loop to Math.log(x) in either version and run it again. NanoLoop.java package workbench.performance.l03; /** * The benchmark everyone writes first: a loop timed with System.nanoTime(). * Round by round it measures the same thing, twice: once with the result thrown away, * once with the result added to a sum that gets printed. */ public class NanoLoop { public static void main(String[] args) { double x = 2.0; for (int round = 1; round <= 5; round++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) { Math.sqrt(x); // result discarded } long t1 = System.nanoTime(); double sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 100_000_000; i++) { sum += Math.sqrt(x + i); // result used } long t2 = System.nanoTime(); System.out.printf("round %d: discarded %.4f ns/op, used %.4f ns/op (sum %.1f)%n", round, (t1 - t0) / 1e8, (t2 - t1) / 1e8, sum); } } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l03.NanoLoop labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l03/NanoLoop.java NanoLoop.kt package workbench.performance.l03 import kotlin.math.sqrt // Kotlin twin of NanoLoop.java: the same naive nanoTime benchmark, with the result // thrown away and with the result used. fun main() { val x = 2.0 for (round in 1..5) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) { sqrt(x) // result discarded } val t1 = System.nanoTime() var sum = 0.0 for (i in 0 until 100_000_000) { sum += sqrt(x + i) // result used } val t2 = System.nanoTime() println("round %d: discarded %.4f ns/op, used %.4f ns/op (sum %.1f)" .format(round, (t1 - t0) / 1e8, (t2 - t1) / 1e8, sum)) } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l03.NanoLoopKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l03/NanoLoop.kt The discarded column starts near 0.03 ns and becomes 0.0000 by round 3; the used column stays near 2 ns. Kotlin does the same. With Math.log, the discarded loop typically reports several nanoseconds per call instead of zero: on JDK 21 x86_64 C2 doesn't remove that call. Neither loop tells you the real cost of the method. Benchmarking with a nanoTime loop is like timing a cashier by asking them to ring up the same item a million times while you watch. After the third time they stop scanning and type the total from memory, so you measure their memory. JMH is the mystery shopper: different baskets they can't predict (non-final inputs), every receipt checked (consumed results), a few practice rounds first (warm-up) and different shops on different days (forks). The analogy breaks because a cashier who stops scanning knows they're cutting corners. The JIT isn't cheating. Deleting unused work is its job, and your benchmark gave it permission.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · JMH builds the measuring loop for you
x: JMH is the OpenJDK project's microbenchmark harness: the code that calls your method, times it and reports the result. Version 1.37, from August 2023, is still the latest release. You write a method annotated @Benchmark. JMH's annotation processor generates the measuring loop around it at compile time, written to defeat the tricks above, and a runner executes it in fresh JVMs. A complete benchmark: Java @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) // 5 x 1 s, results thrown away @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) // 5 x 1 s, results kept @Fork(2) // two fresh JVMs public class FeeBench { long amountCents = 123_456; // input: a non-final field of the state object @Benchmark public long fee() { return FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents); // returned: JMH consumes it } } Kotlin @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1) @Fork(2) open class FeeBench { // JMH's generated code extends it, so it can't be final var amountCents = 123_456L // var: an input nobody can predict @Benchmark fun fee(): Long = FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents) } The Kotlin class has to be open because JMH's generated classes extend it, and the build needs a plugin such as kotlinx-benchmark to generate the JMH code for Kotlin classes. This course keeps its benchmarks in Java. What each piece does: @State(Scope.Thread): one instance per benchmark thread. Its fields are your inputs. @Setup: prepares state outside the measured time. Level.Trial, the default, runs it once per fork. @Warmup and @Measurement: iterations and their length. Warm-up results are thrown away. @Fork: how many fresh JVMs to run in. A new JVM has a clean profile, so one benchmark can't skew the next. @Fork(0) runs inside the JVM that launched it, which brings back every problem of the hand-made loop. @BenchmarkMode: Throughput (the default, operations per time), AverageTime, SampleTime or SingleShotTime. @Param: runs the benchmark once per value, as lesson 2's MegamorphicBench did with types. The JMH 1.37 defaults are 5 forks, each with 5 warm-up and 5 measurement iterations of 10 seconds: more than eight minutes per benchmark method. That's on purpose. The demos in this track use 100 to 300 ms iterations so they finish quickly. That's fine for seeing a trap and too short for deciding anything. You can run benchmarks from a main method with JMH's Runner and OptionsBuilder, as the demos do, or from a JMH uber-jar with command-line flags such as -f 2 -wi 5 -i 5 -prof gc. Five ways to measure one square root Read TrapsBench. Predict which of the five benchmarks will score about the same as baseline. Run it (under 10 seconds). Then run the Kotlin twin, which runs two of the five with JMH's full output so you can see the warm-up and measurement iterations go by. Change double x = 2.0; to final double x = 2.0; and run the Java version again. Which benchmark changes? TrapsBench.java package workbench.performance.l03; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.infra.Blackhole; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** The same Math.sqrt measured five ways. The iterations are far shorter than JMH's defaults, so treat the numbers as rough. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 100, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 100, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class TrapsBench { double x = 2.0; // input from a non-final @State field static final double CONSTANT = 2.0; // input the JIT knows at compile time @Benchmark public void baseline() { } // the harness on its own @Benchmark public void sqrtDiscarded() { Math.sqrt(x); } // result thrown away @Benchmark public double sqrtReturned() { return Math.sqrt(x); } // JMH consumes the return value @Benchmark public void sqrtBlackhole(Blackhole bh) { bh.consume(Math.sqrt(x)); } @Benchmark public double sqrtOfConstant() { return Math.sqrt(CONSTANT); } // folded before it runs public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var options = new OptionsBuilder() .include(TrapsBench.class.getName()) .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build(); System.out.printf("%-16s %10s %10s%n", "Benchmark", "ns/op", "error"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var s = r.getPrimaryResult(); System.out.printf("%-16s %10.3f %10.3f%n", r.getParams().getBenchmark().replaceAll(".*\\.", ""), s.getScore(), s.getScoreError()); } } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l03.TrapsBench labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l03/TrapsBench.java TrapsBench.kt package workbench.performance.l03 // JMH benchmarks must be Java classes in this lab (the annotation processor runs on Java only). // This Kotlin twin runs the same Java benchmark through JMH's Runner API, but with JMH's // normal output, so you can see every warm-up and measurement iteration as it happens. import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode fun main() { val options = OptionsBuilder() .include(TrapsBench::class.java.name + ".sqrt(Discarded|Returned)") // a regex: two of the five .verbosity(VerboseMode.NORMAL) .build() Runner(options).run() } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l03.TrapsBenchKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l03/TrapsBench.kt sqrtDiscarded and sqrtOfConstant land on top of baseline, around 0.3 to 0.5 ns on the course VM. sqrtReturned and sqrtBlackhole are around 2 ns. With final double x = 2.0, javac copies 2.0 into every method, so sqrtReturned drops to the baseline as well. The Kotlin twin's log shows # Blackhole mode: compiler (auto-detected ...) and ends with JMH's "REMEMBER: The numbers below are just data" warning. Each fork is a new JVM. Warm-up iterations are discarded; measurement iterations from every fork are combined into one score with an error. Before you swap Jackson for another JSON library in the payment API, or BigDecimal for long cents in the ledger, someone will write a quick test with System.nanoTime() and paste a number in the pull request. Ask for a JMH benchmark instead, kept in the repository: @State with realistic payloads read from fields, results returned, -prof gc on, several forks. Put the B/op number in the PR description, since it will mean the same thing on your laptop and in CI. Treat the ns/op number as a rough guide unless it came from a quiet machine. For a Quarkus service, benchmark the plain Java code (the mapper, the fee rule, the validator), not the HTTP endpoint, which is load testing and a different tool.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Consume every result and read inputs from non-final fields
x: Two rules fix most broken benchmarks. First, every result must reach JMH. The simplest way is to return it: JMH consumes return values. When there are two results, either combine them or pass each one to a Blackhole: Java @Benchmark public void feeAndTax(Blackhole bh) { bh.consume(FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents)); bh.consume(FeeMath.taxCents(amountCents)); } Kotlin @Benchmark fun feeAndTax(bh: Blackhole) { bh.consume(FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents)) bh.consume(FeeMath.taxCents(amountCents)) } JMH's sample on Blackholes also says: if you have one result, return it, and "Do not make your benchmark code less readable with explicit Blackholes!" On JDK 17 and later JMH detects compiler blackholes, where the JIT itself treats consume as "used, and nothing else". The log says so in its header, and JMH warns that results from different Blackhole modes aren't comparable. Second, inputs must come from non-final instance fields of the @State object. A final field with a constant initializer is a compile-time constant in Java, so javac copies the value into your method. javap on the lab's broken benchmark shows it: public long fee(); 0: ldc2_w #7 // long 123456l <- the field is gone, the number is baked in 3: invokestatic FeeMath.feeCents:(J)J 6: lreturn From there C2 can fold the whole fee calculation into one number. JMH's constant-folding sample puts it bluntly: "IDEs will say 'Look, this field could be final'. Don't. Trust. Them." A static final input has the same problem, which is what sqrtOfConstant shows. You can check both rules against a baseline. An empty @Benchmark method measures the harness alone (about 0.4 ns on the course VM). A benchmark that scores like the baseline is measuring nothing, whatever its name says. In a longer run on the same VM (2 forks of 5 one-second iterations), the empty baseline scored 0.365 ns/op, the discarded square root 1.09 and the constant one 0.545, while the returned square root and the Blackhole version took 3 to 6 ns. Short, noisy runs give different absolute numbers. Which benchmarks sit on the baseline stays the same. Check yourself: a benchmark returns amount.multiply(RATE), where RATE is a static final BigDecimal and amount is a non-final @State field. Can C2 fold the whole result into a constant? (No. RATE is known, but amount can change between calls, so the multiplication has to run.) JMHSample_08_DeadCode read JMHSample_10_ConstantFold read

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Measure allocation with -prof gc, because it doesn't wobble
x: Time is the noisiest thing you can measure. On a shared VM, the error bar on a short JMH run is often bigger than the score. Allocation is different: for the same code and input, a method allocates the same number of bytes every time. JMH's GC profiler (-prof gc, or addProfiler(GCProfiler.class) in code) reports it as gc.alloc.rate.norm, in bytes per operation. MoneyBench sums 2.9% fees over 100 card payments, once with BigDecimal and once with long cents. One run on the course VM: Benchmark ns/op error B/op error feeBigDecimal 3551.2 7675.7 15200.082 0.200 feeLongCents 106.2 271.4 0.002 0.006 The time error is more than twice the score. The allocation is exact: 15,200 bytes per call, 152 bytes per line, every time. BigDecimal is right for money, and every multiply, setScale and add returns a new object. The long version allocates nothing. A separate, longer run got the same 15,200 B/op, and with 10,000 lines it was 1,520,003 B/op: allocation grows exactly with the number of line items. That makes B/op the number to put in CI. A test can't assert "under 2 µs" without failing on a busy build agent, but it can assert "under 300 bytes per call", and lesson 7's lab does exactly that. Keep time measurements for quiet, dedicated machines, with several forks. JMH has more profilers. -lprof lists the ones your machine supports. -prof stack samples thread stacks: on the BigDecimal benchmark it put 48.4% of samples in BigDecimal.<init>. The perf family (perfnorm, perfasm) needs Linux perf and shows hardware counters and the generated assembly. Every JMH run ends with a reminder worth reading once: "The numbers below are just data. To gain reusable insights, you need to follow up on why the numbers are the way they are." Count the bytes Predict the B/op of each benchmark in MoneyBench, roughly. Run it (about 7 seconds). Compare the error columns for time and for bytes. Run the Kotlin twin. It writes the same two calculations in Kotlin (with * and += on BigDecimal) and counts bytes with the JVM's per-thread allocation counter instead of JMH. MoneyBench.java package workbench.performance.l03; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Setup; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.profile.GCProfiler; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.math.RoundingMode; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Fees for 100 card payments: BigDecimal against long cents, with JMH's GC profiler on. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 300, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 300, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class MoneyBench { BigDecimal[] amounts; long[] cents; @Setup public void setup() { // built once per fork, outside the measurement amounts = new BigDecimal[100]; cents = new long[100]; for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { cents[i] = 1_999 + i; amounts[i] = BigDecimal.valueOf(cents[i], 2); } } @Benchmark public BigDecimal feeBigDecimal() { // correct for money, and every operation allocates BigDecimal total = BigDecimal.ZERO; for (BigDecimal a : amounts) { // a new rate object per line, as plenty of real fee code does total = total.add(a.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.029")).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)); } return total; } @Benchmark public long feeLongCents() { // 2.9% in integer cents, rounded half up long total = 0; for (long c : cents) total += (c * 29 + 500) / 1000; return total; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var options = new OptionsBuilder() .include(MoneyBench.class.getName()) .addProfiler(GCProfiler.class) // the same as -prof gc on the command line .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build(); System.out.printf("%-14s %12s %10s %14s %8s%n", "Benchmark", "ns/op", "error", "B/op", "error"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var time = r.getPrimaryResult(); var bytes = r.getSecondaryResults().get("gc.alloc.rate.norm"); System.out.printf("%-14s %12.1f %10.1f %14.3f %8.3f%n", r.getParams().getBenchmark().replaceAll(".*\\.", ""), time.getScore(), time.getScoreError(), bytes.getScore(), bytes.getScoreError()); } } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l03.MoneyBench labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l03/MoneyBench.java MoneyBench.kt package workbench.performance.l03 // MoneyBench.java measures with JMH, which needs Java classes in this lab. This Kotlin twin runs // the same two fee calculations written in Kotlin and reads the JVM's per-thread allocation // counter around 100,000 calls: the same bytes-per-call idea as JMH's gc.alloc.rate.norm. // Allocation is steady enough to count this way. Time is not (remember NanoLoop). import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import java.math.BigDecimal import java.math.RoundingMode private val amounts = Array(100) { BigDecimal.valueOf(1_999L + it, 2) } private val cents = LongArray(100) { 1_999L + it } fun feeBigDecimal(): BigDecimal { var total = BigDecimal.ZERO for (a in amounts) { // a new rate object per line; the operators call multiply and add total += (a * BigDecimal("0.029")).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) } return total } fun feeLongCents(): Long { var total = 0L for (c in cents) total += (c * 29 + 500) / 1000 // 2.9% in integer cents, rounded half up return total } private val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean private var lastDecimal: BigDecimal? = null // results go somewhere the JIT can't ignore private var lastCents = 0L private inline fun bytesPerCall(calls: Int, block: () -> Unit): Double { repeat(50_000) { block() } // warm up first, so C2 code is measured val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes repeat(calls) { block() } return (threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before).toDouble() / calls } fun main() { val big = bytesPerCall(100_000) { lastDecimal = feeBigDecimal() } val small = bytesPerCall(100_000) { lastCents += feeLongCents() } println("feeBigDecimal: %10.3f B/op".format(big)) println("feeLongCents: %10.3f B/op".format(small)) println("(results: $lastDecimal, $lastCents)") } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l03.MoneyBenchKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l03/MoneyBench.kt feeBigDecimal allocates about 15,200 bytes per call with an error under 1 byte, while its time error is huge on a busy machine. feeLongCents allocates 0. The Kotlin twin prints exactly 15200.000 and 0.000 B/op: Kotlin's BigDecimal operators call the same methods and allocate the same objects. The most common mistake is a JMH benchmark that looks right and still measures nothing: a void method that discards its result, or an input in a final field with a constant initializer. Both compile, run and print a confident number, usually close to the baseline. The JIT removed or folded the work. The fix is mechanical. Return the result, or consume it in a Blackhole. Read inputs from non-final @State fields. Then add an empty baseline() benchmark and check that your real ones score clearly above it. Java private final long amountCents = 123_456; // javac copies 123456 into fee() @Benchmark public void fee() { FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents); } // and the result is dropped Kotlin const val AMOUNT_CENTS = 123_456L // kotlinc copies it too @Benchmark fun fee() { FeeMath.feeCents(AMOUNT_CENTS) } // and the result is dropped

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Java and Kotlin
x: Constants that get baked into the bytecode Java class Inputs { private final long amount = 123_456; // constant initializer: javac copies the value private final long fromCtor; // assigned in the constructor: a real field read long plain = 123_456; // what a benchmark input should be static final long RATE_BPS = 290; // copied by javac, and known to the JIT Inputs(long v) { fromCtor = v; } } Kotlin const val RATE_BPS = 290L // copied by kotlinc; RATE_BPS * 2 even becomes 580 open class Inputs(val fromCtor: Long) { // a real field read val amount = 123_456L // NOT copied: kotlinc reads the field var plain = 123_456L // what a benchmark input should be } Java copies any final field with a constant initializer into the code that uses it, instance fields included. Kotlin copies only const val. A Kotlin val amount = 123_456L compiles to getfield, as javap shows, so it isn't folded by kotlinc. Use var in a Kotlin benchmark anyway, because it says "input" to the next reader. Kotlin also folds arithmetic on constants at compile time: RATE_BPS * 2 compiled to ldc2_w 580. In either language, a benchmark that reads only constants measures the JIT's arithmetic, not yours.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Worked example
x: Turn a nanoTime test into a benchmark you can trust A pull request claims the new fee rule is "3x faster", based on this test. Spot the problems before reading on. @Test void newRuleIsFaster() { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) NewFeeRule.fee(12_345); // constant input, result dropped long newNs = System.nanoTime() - t0; t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) OldFeeRule.fee(12_345); long oldNs = System.nanoTime() - t0; assertTrue(newNs * 3 < oldNs); } @Test fun `new rule is faster`() { var t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(1_000_000) { NewFeeRule.fee(12_345) } // constant input, result dropped val newNs = System.nanoTime() - t0 t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(1_000_000) { OldFeeRule.fee(12_345) } val oldNs = System.nanoTime() - t0 assertTrue(newNs * 3 < oldNs) } Four problems: the results are dropped (dead code), the input is a constant (folding), the first loop warms up the JVM and the second inherits a warm JVM and a mixed profile, and a timing assertion in a unit test fails on a busy CI agent. Move the comparison to JMH, with the input in a non-final field. @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Fork(3) public class FeeRuleBench { long amountCents = 12_345; // 1. a non-final input @Benchmark public long oldRule() { return OldFeeRule.fee(amountCents); } // 2. returned @Benchmark public long newRule() { return NewFeeRule.fee(amountCents); } @Benchmark public void baseline() { } // 3. the floor to compare with } @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Fork(3) open class FeeRuleBench { var amountCents = 12_345L // 1. a non-final input @Benchmark fun oldRule(): Long = OldFeeRule.fee(amountCents) // 2. returned @Benchmark fun newRule(): Long = NewFeeRule.fee(amountCents) @Benchmark fun baseline() {} // 3. the floor to compare with } Add a @Param so the amount isn't one magic number, and turn on -prof gc so you get a stable second number. Self-check: why does @Param take strings? (Answer: JMH sets the field from text, one fork per value, so the values also show up in the results table.) @Param({"99", "12345", "9999999"}) long amountCents; @Param("99", "12345", "9999999") var amountCents = 0L Read the result with the error column, and check the baseline first. If newRule sits on the baseline, it measures nothing. If the error bars of the two rules overlap, "3x faster" isn't proven. And if newRule allocates 0 B/op where oldRule allocates 48, that's a result you can put in the PR whatever the timer says. Benchmark (amountCents) Mode Cnt Score Error Units FeeRuleBench.newRule 12345 avgt 15 ... ... ns/op FeeRuleBench.newRule:gc.alloc.rate.norm 12345 avgt 15 ... ... B/op

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Lab
x: Fix three broken benchmarks labs/performance/src/main/java/workbench/performance/l03/DeadFeeBench.java labs/performance/src/main/java/workbench/performance/l03/ConstantFeeBench.java labs/performance/src/main/java/workbench/performance/l03/ColdBatchBench.java ./gradlew :performance:test --tests 'workbench.performance.l03.*' Run the tests. Five of six fail; the sixth only checks that the classes are still JMH benchmarks. The tests never time anything: they call your benchmark methods and inspect them with reflection. DeadFeeBench: make fee() hand its result to JMH. ConstantFeeBench: make amountCents an input the compiler can't know. Keep the field name, because the test sets it to other values and expects fee() to follow. ColdBatchBench: move building the batch into a @Setup method that runs once per fork, and keep only the summing in totalFees(). Then give it real warm-up (at least 3 iterations) and at least one fork. Run the tests until all six pass. Optional: copy one fixed class into src/demo/.../l03, give it a main like TrapsBench's, and run it before and after your fix. For DeadFeeBench, changing void to long and adding return is the whole fix. A Blackhole parameter also passes, but one result reads better as a return value. For ConstantFeeBench, look at javap -c -p on the compiled class before and after. Before: ldc2_w 123456. After: getfield amountCents. In ColdBatchBench, add a long[] batch field and a @Setup(Level.Trial) public void buildBatch() method. Don't use Level.Invocation: it runs setup around every single call and distorts short benchmarks. @Fork(0) runs the benchmark inside the JVM that launched it, with that JVM's profile and garbage. Use at least 1, ideally 2 or more. All six tests in BrokenBenchmarksTest pass. h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Quiz
x: A benchmark method is public void fee() { FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents); }. It scores 0.4 ns/op, the same as an empty benchmark. What is the most likely reason? The fee calculation really takes 0.4 ns The result is discarded, so the JIT removed the calculation JMH's timer can't resolve anything under 1 ns The benchmark didn't fork A result nobody uses is dead code, and C2 deletes it. Return the value (JMH consumes return values) or pass it to a Blackhole. Matching the empty baseline is the giveaway. Which input declaration lets C2 fold FeeMath.feeCents(amountCents) into a constant in a Java benchmark? long amountCents = 123_456; in the @State class @Param("123456") long amountCents; private final long amountCents = 123_456; long amountCents; assigned in a @Setup method A final field with a constant initializer is a compile-time constant in Java, so javac writes ldc2_w 123456 into the method and C2 can compute the result once. The other three are real field reads that C2 can't predict. You must compare two JSON mappers in CI and fail the build on a regression. Which JMH number should the check use? The ns/op score gc.alloc.rate.norm (bytes per operation) The error column The number of warm-up iterations Allocation per operation is deterministic for the same code and input, with error bars near zero. Time on a shared CI agent has error bars that can exceed the score, so a time threshold fails at random. A colleague's benchmark uses @Fork(0) "to make it faster to run". What do they lose? Nothing, forks only matter for multi-threaded benchmarks A fresh JVM: the benchmark now shares the launcher's profile, heap and JIT state, so earlier code can change its result The warm-up iterations The ability to use @Setup With 0 forks the benchmark runs inside the JVM that started JMH. Its type profiles and compiled code are shared with whatever ran before, as lesson 2's MegamorphicBench showed by running each case in its own fork. From lesson 2: MegamorphicBench ran each @Param value (1, 2 and 3 types) in its own fork. What would likely happen to the 1-type result if all three ran in the same JVM, 3 types first? Nothing, each @Param value gets fresh compiled code The 1-type case would likely look slow too, because the call site's profile already holds three types It would get faster, because the JIT is already warm JMH would refuse to run The type profile belongs to the call site in the bytecode, not to the @Param value. After three types have been seen there, C2 compiles a virtual call, and the 1-type run inherits it. Forks give every case a clean profile.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Key terms
x: Dead-code elimination The JIT removing work whose result nothing uses. Constant folding Computing a result at compile time because the inputs are known constants. JMH The OpenJDK Microbenchmark Harness: generates and runs correct measuring loops. @State A JMH class whose fields hold benchmark inputs, with a scope such as one instance per thread. Fork A fresh JVM that JMH starts to run a benchmark in. Blackhole A JMH object that consumes values so the JIT must compute them. gc.alloc.rate.norm Bytes allocated per operation, reported by JMH's GC profiler. Why did a nanoTime loop around a discarded Math.sqrt(x) report 0.0000 ns/op? Dead-code elimination: C2 proved the result was unused and removed the call. How do you make sure JMH can't throw a benchmark's result away? Return it from the @Benchmark method, or pass it to Blackhole.consume (for several results). Why must JMH inputs be non-final @State fields? A final field with a constant initializer is copied into the method by javac (and static final values are known to the JIT), so C2 can fold the computation. What does @Fork(2) give you? Two fresh JVMs per benchmark, each with a clean profile and heap. @Fork(0) runs in the launcher's JVM. What does gc.alloc.rate.norm measure, and why is it useful in CI? Bytes allocated per benchmark operation (-prof gc). It is deterministic for the same code and input, so its error is near zero. In Kotlin, which property is copied into callers as a constant: val x = 5L or const val X = 5L? Only const val. A plain val in a class compiles to a field read.

h: Benchmarking with JMH, and the traps it saves you from · Go deeper
x: Three more JMH features are worth knowing before you need them. @State(Scope.Benchmark) shares one state object across all benchmark threads, and @Threads(4) or @Group runs several threads at once. That is how you measure contention, for example 4 threads incrementing one AtomicLong against a LongAdder. Lesson 4 talks about why those differ. Mode.SampleTime records a distribution of individual call times and prints percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9), which fits latency questions better than an average. Mode.SingleShotTime measures one call per iteration, which suits cold-start questions. JMH's padding is automatic for @State objects: the JMH false-sharing sample says "@States are automatically padded", but "This padding does not extend to the State internals". Fields inside your state object can still share a cache line, which is lesson 4's topic. If you want to see what C2 really did to a benchmark, -prof perfasm prints the hottest generated assembly next to the counters. It needs Linux perf and the hsdis disassembler. Without it, the cheap check is the one you already know: put an empty baseline next to every benchmark and be suspicious of anything that scores like it.

h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · Caches move memory in 64-byte lines
x: Your CPU never reads one long from memory. It moves a whole cache line, 64 bytes on x86. The Xeon VM used for this course reports it directly: /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/index0/coherency_line_size says 64. Each core has its own L1 and L2 caches (small, fast memories right next to the core), and the hardware keeps them coherent, as the memory model track said. Coherent has a price, though. A core that wants to write a line needs the only valid copy of it. Every other core's copy is invalidated, and the next time one of them reads the line, it has to fetch it again. Now look at what an ordinary object looks like in memory. JOL (Java Object Layout) reads the real field offsets from the running JVM: Java static final class Adjacent { volatile long card; volatile long sepa; } // JOL on JDK 21: 32 bytes; card at offset 16, sepa at offset 24 Kotlin class KAdjacent { @Volatile var card = 0L @Volatile var sepa = 0L } // JOL on JDK 21: 32 bytes; card at offset 16, sepa at offset 24 The first 12 bytes are the object header (an 8-byte mark word and a 4-byte class pointer), then 4 bytes of alignment gap, then the two fields, 8 bytes apart. The whole object is 32 bytes. Unless it happens to straddle a line boundary, both counters live on the same 64-byte line. For code that reads, that's good news: reading card brings sepa along for free. Arrays of primitives are fast to scan for the same reason. For two threads that each write their own field, it's bad news, and the next section shows why. Offsets depend on the JVM and its flags. On JDK 25 with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders (JEP 519) the header shrinks to 8 bytes and card moves to offset 8. JDK 27 turns compact headers on by default (JEP 534). So when you check a layout in a test, check the distance between fields, never absolute offsets. Read real layouts with JOL Run LayoutDemo. Ignore JOL's two # WARNING lines about attaching an agent. Before reading the output, predict the offset of sepa in each of the three classes. Look at the last entry: Striped64$Cell, the class LongAdder uses internally. Where is its only field? Run the Kotlin twin and compare. Each keeps their own money in their own compartment, so they never take each other's coins. But only one of them can have the drawer open at a time, so each sale waits for the other cashier to close it. That is false sharing: separate data, one physical unit. Padding gives each cashier their own drawer. LongAdder is the store manager's solution: one drawer per cashier, added up at closing time. h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · False sharing: two threads, two fields, one line
x: False sharing: two threads, two fields, one cache line bouncing between cores Put a thread on each counter. The card thread only writes card, the SEPA thread only writes sepa. They share no data, so there is nothing to lock and no race. But they share a line. Each write by core 1 invalidates core 2's copy of the line, and core 2's next write has to take the line back. The line bounces between the cores on almost every write. This is false sharing: the program shares nothing, the hardware shares a lot. FalseSharingDemo runs exactly that, 25 million increments per thread, first with the adjacent fields and then with the fields padded apart. On the shared 4-vCPU VM used for this course, one run printed this: round 1: adjacent 1,220 ms padded 247 ms round 2: adjacent 957 ms padded 225 ms round 3: adjacent 1,387 ms padded 206 ms That's a clear gap. But an earlier, more careful experiment on the same VM, with JMH running two threads per group, could not show any false-sharing effect: the error bars of padded and unpadded overlapped, and a second run reversed the order of the first. The Kotlin twin, run a few minutes after the Java one, showed a much smaller gap in one round. Whether you see the effect depends on whether your two threads land on different physical cores, on the CPU, and on what else the machine is doing. Two threads on hyperthreads (two hardware threads that share one physical core) share that core's L1 and L2, so there's no line to bounce. So don't promise anyone a speed-up from padding. The mechanism is certain, the size of the effect isn't, and the only way to know is to measure on the hardware you run on. When it does hit, it hits code that looks perfectly innocent: per-partition counters in a Kafka consumer, a stats object with one field per worker thread, an array of per-thread totals where the slots sit 8 bytes apart. Race two counters on one line Read FalseSharingDemo. Predict: will the adjacent run be slower, the same, or faster than the padded one on your machine? Run it, then run it again. Then run the Kotlin twin. If you see a big gap, check how many physical cores your machine has (lscpu on Linux, sysctl -n hw.physicalcpu on macOS). You may also see a small gap or none, depending on the CPU and where the scheduler puts the threads. All four counts always end at exactly 25,000,000: false sharing costs time, never correctness. Adjacent fields share a line, so every write by one core invalidates the other core's copy. Padded apart, each core keeps its own line. Look for objects that several threads write in a tight loop: a stats object with one counter per Kafka partition, an array of per-worker totals in a batch settlement job, hand-rolled request counters in a Quarkus filter. For metrics, use LongAdder (or a metrics library) instead of AtomicLong or a volatile field: it's correct under contention and pads its own cells. Reach for manual padding only when a profile or a JMH run on your production hardware shows the cost, and then pad the one or two objects involved, not every class. h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · Padding pushes hot fields onto separate lines
x: The fix is to keep at least 64 bytes between fields that different threads write. There are three ways, from least to most trustworthy. Padding fields in one class: put 8 or more unused longs between card and sepa. On today's HotSpot it works (sepa moved to offset 152), but JMH's false-sharing sample warns that this is "not versatile because JVMs can freely rearrange the field order, even of the same type". A class hierarchy: the same sample notes that "superclass fields are usually laid out first". So put each hot field and each block of padding in its own class, and chain them: Java abstract class CardCounter { volatile long card; } abstract class PadAfterCard extends CardCounter { long p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6, p7, p8; } abstract class SepaCounter extends PadAfterCard { volatile long sepa; } public final class SettlementCounters extends SepaCounter { public void addCard() { card++; } // only the card thread calls this public void addSepa() { sepa++; } // only the SEPA thread calls this } Kotlin abstract class CardCounter { @Volatile @JvmField var card = 0L } abstract class PadAfterCard : CardCounter() { @JvmField var p1 = 0L; @JvmField var p2 = 0L; @JvmField var p3 = 0L; @JvmField var p4 = 0L @JvmField var p5 = 0L; @JvmField var p6 = 0L; @JvmField var p7 = 0L; @JvmField var p8 = 0L } abstract class SepaCounter : PadAfterCard() { @Volatile @JvmField var sepa = 0L } class SettlementCounters : SepaCounter() { fun addCard() { card++ } // only the card thread calls this fun addSepa() { sepa++ } // only the SEPA thread calls this } This is what the lab asks for. @JvmField in the Kotlin version makes each property a plain public field, which keeps the layout obvious. @Contended: the JDK's own annotation, jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended, available since JDK 8. The JVM adds ContendedPaddingWidth bytes of padding, 128 by default, around each annotated field. JOL on a class with both fields annotated shows card at offset 144, sepa at 280, and a 288-byte object. Its Javadoc warns that it "will nearly always add significant space overhead to objects". There are two catches for your own classes. The JVM ignores the annotation outside the JDK unless you run with -XX:-RestrictContended: without the flag, JOL shows the same 16 and 24 as no annotation at all, with no warning. And it lives in an internal package, so compiling needs --add-exports java.base/jdk.internal.vm.annotation=ALL-UNNAMED. javac refuses that together with --release, with "exporting a package from system module java.base is not allowed with --release", so this course's labs, which compile with --release 21, can't use it. Every padding costs memory: 160 bytes instead of 32 here, and 288 with @Contended. That's nothing for one counter object and a lot for a million of them. Pad the few objects that several threads write in a hot loop, and nothing else. Check yourself: a class declares volatile long a;, then seven padding longs, then volatile long b;. JOL shows a at 16 and b at 80. Can they share a line? (No: 64 bytes apart. But another JVM may order the fields differently, which is why the lab's test reads the real offsets instead of trusting the source.) JMHSample_22_FalseSharing read

h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · LongAdder is the padding you should actually use
x: Hand padding is for library authors. For a counter in your service, the JDK already did the work. LongAdder (and LongAccumulator) extend Striped64, whose source explains the design: table entries are a "variant of AtomicLong padded (via @Contended) to reduce cache contention", because "Atomic objects residing in arrays will tend to be placed adjacent to each other, and so will most often share cache lines (with a huge negative performance impact) without this precaution". That's the value at offset 144 you saw in LayoutDemo. The cells are lazy. "When there is no contention, all updates are made to the base field." On the first failed compare-and-set, the table is created with 2 cells, and it doubles under more contention. Each thread then mostly updates its own cell, on its own cache line. sum() adds the base and the cells. As "Atomics and compare-and-set" said, sum() is not an atomic snapshot, so use LongAdder for counters you read now and then, such as metrics, and AtomicLong when the value drives a decision. Java public final class RequestMetrics { private final LongAdder count = new LongAdder(); private final LongAdder totalCents = new LongAdder(); public void record(long amountCents) { // called by every request thread count.increment(); totalCents.add(amountCents); } public long count() { return count.sum(); } // read by the metrics scraper } Kotlin class RequestMetrics { private val count = LongAdder() private val totalCents = LongAdder() fun record(amountCents: Long) { // called by every request thread count.increment() totalCents.add(amountCents) } fun count(): Long = count.sum() // read by the metrics scraper } AdderDemo shows the difference with four threads counting 10 million requests each. In one run on the course VM, AtomicLong took 640 to 760 ms per round and LongAdder about 200 ms. With an AtomicLong, all four cores fight over one line, and every failed compare-and-set retries. With a LongAdder, each core mostly works on its own padded cell. Like the false-sharing demo, the gap depends on the machine, and the Kotlin twin's run here showed a smaller one. AtomicLong against LongAdder Predict which one finishes first with four threads, and by how much. Run AdderDemo, then the Kotlin twin. Change THREADS to 1 and run again. Does LongAdder still win? i++) atomic.incrementAndGet(); }); LongAdder adder = new LongAdder(); long msAdder = time(() -> { for (int i = 0; i < PER_THREAD; i++) adder.increment(); }); System.out.printf("round %d: AtomicLong %,5d ms (%,d) LongAdder %,5d ms (%,d)%n", round, msAtomic, atomic.get(), msAdder, adder.sum()); With one thread, AtomicLong was faster on the course VM (about 70 ms against 110 ms). With no contention, LongAdder only touches its base field, its cells never exist, and its extra checks are pure cost. The common mistake is fixing a "slow counter" by making each thread write its own slot of a plain array, believing that no sharing means no contention. The slots are 8 bytes apart, so eight of them share one line, and the threads still fight over it. The other common mistake is padding with unused fields and never checking the result: the JVM may move fields, and an unused field doesn't stop it. Check with JOL, measure with a forked benchmark, or use LongAdder, which does both for you. A Kotlin var property is a private field plus a getter and setter; @JvmField exposes the field directly, and @Volatile makes it volatile. In both languages the padding fields are never read, and nothing in the language guarantees the order of fields within one class, which is why the hierarchy is the safer trick.
