A race: updates to p0 and p1 can be lost False sharing: the fields share a cache line, so the two cores keep invalidating each other's copy None: different fields never interact The object is too big to fit in a cache line 8 bytes apart means one 64-byte line. Each field has one writer, so nothing is lost, but every write takes the line away from the other core. That costs time, not correctness. You annotate two fields of your own class with @jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended, compile it, and run normally. JOL shows them at 16 and 24. Why? @Contended only works on JDK 27 The JVM ignores @Contended outside the JDK unless you run with -XX:-RestrictContended JOL can't see padding The fields must also be final RestrictContended is true by default, so the annotation only takes effect in JDK classes. With -XX:-RestrictContended the same class shows the fields at 144 and 280. The JVM prints no warning either way. A metrics counter is incremented by every request thread and read by a scraper every 10 seconds. Which is the best fit? A volatile long with count++ An AtomicLong A LongAdder A long field inside a synchronized method Many writers and rare reads is exactly what LongAdder is for: each thread mostly updates its own padded cell. AtomicLong is correct but makes all writers fight over one line. volatile with ++ loses updates. Your test checks that two fields are "at offset 16 and offset 88". It passes on JDK 21 and fails on JDK 27. What's the best fix? Pin the tests to JDK 21 Assert the distance between the fields (at least 64 bytes) instead of absolute offsets Turn off JOL on JDK 27 Add more padding until both pass JDK 27 turns compact object headers on by default, so every field moves by a few bytes. The distance between the two fields is what decides whether they share a line, and it doesn't depend on the header size. From the first track: two request threads call counter.incrementAndGet() on a shared AtomicLong 10 million times each. Then you switch to LongAdder.increment(). What changes in the result? Nothing: both count exactly; LongAdder usually gets there faster under contention LongAdder may lose some increments, but it's faster AtomicLong loses increments under contention LongAdder.sum() is always more up to date than AtomicLong.get() Both are exact once all writes finish. LongAdder spreads writes over cells so threads stop fighting over one cache line. Its sum() is not an atomic snapshot while writes are still happening, which is why decisions should use AtomicLong.

h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · Explain it back
x: Explain to a teammate why giving each consumer thread its own field in a shared stats object didn't make the counters fast, and what you'd do instead.

h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · Key terms
x: Cache line The unit a CPU cache moves around: 64 bytes on x86. Cache coherence The hardware keeping every core's copy of a line consistent, by invalidating copies on writes. False sharing Different data on one cache line, written by different cores, making the line bounce between them. Padding Unused bytes placed between fields so they land on different cache lines. @Contended A JDK-internal annotation that makes the JVM pad a field or class, 128 bytes by default. JOL Java Object Layout, a tool that prints the real field offsets and object sizes. LongAdder A counter that spreads contended updates over padded cells and sums them on read. How big is a cache line on x86? 64 bytes. Caches move whole lines, never single fields. What is false sharing? Threads writing different fields that sit on the same cache line, so the line keeps moving between cores. It costs time, not correctness. How far apart must two hot fields be to avoid sharing a 64-byte line? At least 64 bytes between their offsets. Why is a class hierarchy better than padding fields inside one class? HotSpot lays out superclass fields before subclass fields; within one class the JVM may reorder fields, even of the same type. What does @Contended need to work on your own classes? -XX:-RestrictContended at run time (otherwise it's silently ignored) and --add-exports java.base/jdk.internal.vm.annotation=ALL-UNNAMED to compile. How does LongAdder avoid false sharing? Under contention it spreads updates over Striped64.Cell objects, each padded with @Contended (JOL shows the value at offset 144). sum() adds them up. Why should a layout test assert distances, not offsets? Header sizes differ between JDKs and flags: compact object headers (default in JDK 27) move every field.

h: CPU caches, false sharing and @Contended · Go deeper
x: JMH protects you from one source of false sharing automatically. Its false-sharing sample says "@States are automatically padded", but "This padding does not extend to the State internals". Fields inside your @State object can still share a line, which is exactly what that sample demonstrates with several techniques side by side. To measure it on your own hardware, run that sample with several forks on a machine with real cores, and pin the threads to different physical cores if you can. Why does the JDK pad with 128 bytes when lines are 64? The flag ContendedPaddingWidth says how many bytes to pad, nothing more. A common explanation is that some CPUs prefetch the neighbouring line too, so a 64-byte gap can still let two hot fields interfere. That explanation isn't something this course could check against a primary source, so treat 128 as "the JDK's safe default" rather than a rule. Two other tools look at the same problem from the hardware side. perf c2c on Linux reports cache lines that bounce between cores (JMH wraps it as -prof perfc2c). And a CPU profiler such as async-profiler, in lesson 6, shows the symptom: lots of samples on a trivial line such as count++. There's also true sharing, which padding can't fix: many threads writing the same field, like an AtomicLong hit by every request. The only fixes there are to write less often or to split the value, which is what LongAdder does.

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · JFR records what the JVM was doing, and it's already in your JDK
x: Start with the problem. Authorizations are sometimes slow. The hand-made fix is a timer and a log line: log.info("issuer call took {} ms", ms). That gives you one number per call. It doesn't tell you whether a garbage collection paused every thread at that moment, whether the thread waited for a lock, or whether the code allocated 2 GB that second. JDK Flight Recorder (JFR) is a recorder built into HotSpot. It writes events, small timestamped records, about what the JVM is doing: GC pauses, JIT compilations, threads waiting on locks, sampled stacks of running threads (execution samples), sampled allocations, file and socket I/O, and more. Your own code can add events too. Everything lands in one timeline, in a compact binary format, kept in memory buffers and written to disk. You start a recording from the command line or on a live JVM: java -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=rec.jfr,settings=profile -jar app.jar jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=pay settings=profile # attach to a running JVM jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=pay filename=pay.jfr # copy what it has so far to a file jcmd <pid> JFR.stop name=pay The JVM answers with real lines like these (JDK 21): Started recording 1. No limit specified, using maxsize=250MB as default. Use jcmd 4971 JFR.dump name=1 to copy recording data to file. With filename= set, the file is written when the JVM exits. settings picks a configuration file. default.jfc is meant to stay on. profile.jfc, in the words of the java man page, "provides more data than the default configuration, but can have more overhead", so use it for shorter periods. The difference is in the details. In JDK 25, default samples thread stacks every 20 ms and allocations at up to 150 per second, and records lock waits of 20 ms or more. profile samples every 10 ms, records up to 300 allocation samples a second, and records lock waits from 10 ms. Record a busy payment service Read JfrDemo and skim PaymentWorkload next to it: four threads compute fees with BigDecimal, call a fake issuer that sleeps, and sometimes hold a shared lock for 15 ms. Predict which event type will be the most common in the recording. Run it. The demo starts a second JVM with -XX:StartFlightRecording and prints the path of the .jfr file. Run jfr summary on that file (the demo prints the command). JfrDemo.java package workbench.performance.l05; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Runs PaymentWorkload for 4 seconds in a second JVM started with * -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=build/perf05.jfr,settings=profile * and tells you where the recording is. */ public class JfrDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { PaymentWorkload.run(4); return; } Path file = Path.of("build", "perf05.jfr").toAbsolutePath(); String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), JfrDemo.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).inheritIO().start(); p.waitFor(); System.out.println("recording written to " + file); System.out.println("try: jfr summary " + file); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l05.JfrDemo labs/performance/src/demo/java/workbench/performance/l05/JfrDemo.java JfrDemo.kt package workbench.performance.l05 import jdk.jfr.Category import jdk.jfr.Description import jdk.jfr.Event import jdk.jfr.Label import jdk.jfr.Name import java.math.BigDecimal import java.math.RoundingMode import java.nio.file.Path import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of JfrDemo.java (with its workload and event in this one file). It runs the workload // for 4 seconds in a second JVM started with -XX:StartFlightRecording and writes build/perf05-kt.jfr. @Name("workbench.IssuerCall") @Label("Issuer Call") @Category("Workbench", "Payments") @Description("A call to the card issuer during authorization") class KIssuerCallEvent : Event() { @Label("Merchant") var merchant: String? = null // a Kotlin property: JFR records its field @Label("Amount (cents)") var amountCents = 0L @Label("Approved") var approved = false } private val ledger = Any() fun kFee(amount: String): Long = (BigDecimal(amount) * BigDecimal("0.029")).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN).unscaledValue().toLong() fun kCallIssuer(merchant: String, cents: Long): Boolean { val event = KIssuerCallEvent() event.begin() Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(2, if (merchant == "m_7") 40 else 12).toLong()) val approved = cents < 400_000 event.end() if (event.shouldCommit()) { // skip the field work when no recording wants it event.merchant = merchant event.amountCents = cents event.approved = approved event.commit() } return approved } fun kRunWorkload(seconds: Int) { val until = System.nanoTime() + seconds * 1_000_000_000L val workers = (0 until 4).map { w -> thread(name = "auth-$w") { var sink = 0L var i = 0 while (System.nanoTime() < until) { for (k in 0 until 2_000) sink += kFee("${100 + (k + i) % 9_000}.25") kCallIssuer("m_${i % 10}", 1_000 + (i * 7_919L) % 500_000) if (i % 25 == w) synchronized(ledger) { Thread.sleep(15) } // a ledger write under a shared lock i++ } if (sink == 42L) println() } } workers.forEach { it.join() } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") return kRunWorkload(4) val file = Path.of("build", "perf05-kt.jfr").toAbsolutePath() val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=$file,settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l05.JfrDemoKt", "child") .inheritIO().start().waitFor() println("recording written to $file") println("try: jfr summary $file") } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l05.JfrDemoKt labs/performance/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/performance/l05/JfrDemo.kt The JVM prints the two "Started recording" lines, then the demo prints the file path, about 400 KB after 4 seconds. In one run, jfr summary listed 1,746 workbench.IssuerCall events (the demo's own), 1,126 jdk.ObjectAllocationSample, 960 jdk.GCPhaseParallel and 530 jdk.ThreadSleep, but only 28 jdk.ExecutionSample, because the threads spend most of their time sleeping. JFR is the flight recorder in an aircraft. It's always on, records hundreds of instrument readings with timestamps, and costs little enough that nobody switches it off. When something goes wrong you pull the box and replay the minutes around it. Your custom events are the cockpit voice recorder: what the crew (your code) was doing, on the same clock as the instruments. The analogy breaks in one useful way: you can pull JFR's data from a running JVM with jcmd ... JFR.dump without stopping anything, and you can even subscribe to it live with RecordingStream.

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Ask the recording questions with jfr summary, view and print
x: The jfr tool ships with the JDK. Three of its subcommands cover most days. jfr summary rec.jfr lists every event type with its count and size. Read it first, to see what the recording holds. jfr view <view> rec.jfr prints a ready-made report. It arrived in JDK 21 with 74 views, and JDK 25 has 83. The ones you'll use most are hot-methods, allocation-by-site, gc-pauses, contention-by-site and deoptimizations-by-reason (lesson 2's uncommon traps, counted). Real output from the demo's recording: Contention by Site StackTrace Count Avg. Max. ------------------------------------------------------------- ----- ------- ------- workbench.performance.l05.PaymentWorkload.authorizeLoop(int, 7 15.5 ms 25.0 ms Allocation by Site Method Allocation Pressure ------------------------------------------------------- ------------------- workbench.performance.l05.PaymentWorkload.fee(String) 40.82% java.lang.StringLatin1.toChars(byte[]) 26.97% Each view is a query over events. jfr view --verbose allocation-by-site rec.jfr shows the columns it sums, and the JDK source defines it as SELECT stackTrace.topFrame AS S, SUM(weight) AS W FROM ObjectAllocationSample GROUP BY S ORDER BY W DESC. You can also pass an event type as the view, such as jfr view workbench.IssuerCall rec.jfr, and get a table of those events. On a live JVM, jcmd <pid> JFR.view hot-methods prints the same report without dumping a file (it works on JDK 21 as well). jfr print --events workbench.IssuerCall --stack-depth 2 rec.jfr prints events one by one, with every field and a short stack trace. Add --json for something a script can read. JDK Mission Control (JMC) is the desktop app for the same files: timelines, flame graphs of the samples, and automated analysis. It's developed in the openjdk/jmc project and downloaded separately from builds that several vendors publish. The jfr tool is enough for everything in this lesson. One warning before you send a recording to anyone. The demo's recording also holds 169 jdk.InitialEnvironmentVariable events and the full command line. For a payment service that can mean secrets. JDK 27 adds in-process redaction (JEP 536, -XX:FlightRecorderOptions:redact-argument=...). On older JDKs, check what's in the file first. Answer three questions from one file Using the file from the last Try it: which method allocates the most? Run jfr view allocation-by-site <file>. Where do threads wait for locks, and for how long at most? Run jfr view contention-by-site <file>. Which merchant has slow issuer calls? Run jfr view workbench.IssuerCall <file> and look at the Duration column, then jfr print --events workbench.IssuerCall --stack-depth 2 <file> | head -20. terminal (from labs/) jfr view allocation-by-site performance/build/perf05.jfr jfr view contention-by-site performance/build/perf05.jfr jfr view workbench.IssuerCall performance/build/perf05.jfr jfr print --events workbench.IssuerCall --stack-depth 2 performance/build/perf05.jfr | head -20 PaymentWorkload.fee(String) tops the allocation report (about 40% in one run). Contention shows authorizeLoop with a handful of waits averaging about 15 ms, the lock that one thread holds for 15 ms. The issuer table shows durations of a few ms for most merchants and up to about 40 ms for m_7, whose fake issuer is slower. Events go into a recording. A dump makes a .jfr file for the jfr tool, JMC or RecordingFile; RecordingStream reads the same events live. The jfr command, JDK 25 man page docs Run your Quarkus payment services with a continuous recording using default.jfc, maxage and maxsize set so it keeps the last hour or so. When the authorization p99 jumps, jcmd <pid> JFR.dump gives you the minutes around it without a restart, and jfr view gc-pauses and contention-by-site tell you quickly whether the JVM is involved. Add one custom event around each issuer call and each Kafka batch, with merchant, partition and outcome as fields, so you can line them up with GC and lock events. Before a recording leaves your network, remember it contains environment variables and command-line arguments, and on JDK 27 use the redaction options.

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Your own events put business context on the same timeline
x: A JFR event is a class that extends jdk.jfr.Event. Its fields are the data. Annotations give it a stable name and labels for the tools: Java @Name("workbench.IssuerCall") @Label("Issuer Call") @Category({"Workbench", "Payments"}) public class IssuerCallEvent extends Event { @Label("Merchant") String merchant; @Label("Amount (cents)") long amountCents; @Label("Approved") boolean approved; } IssuerCallEvent event = new IssuerCallEvent(); event.begin(); // 1. start the clock boolean approved = issuer.approve(merchant, cents); event.end(); // 2. stop it if (event.shouldCommit()) { // 3. false if no recording wants it event.merchant = merchant; event.amountCents = cents; event.approved = approved; event.commit(); // 4. write it, with a stack trace } Kotlin @Name("workbench.IssuerCall") @Label("Issuer Call") @Category("Workbench", "Payments") class KIssuerCallEvent : Event() { @Label("Merchant") var merchant: String? = null @Label("Amount (cents)") var amountCents = 0L @Label("Approved") var approved = false } val event = KIssuerCallEvent() event.begin() // 1. start the clock val approved = issuer.approve(merchant, cents) event.end() // 2. stop it if (event.shouldCommit()) { // 3. false if no recording wants it event.merchant = merchant event.amountCents = cents event.approved = approved event.commit() // 4. write it, with a stack trace } begin() and end() give the event its duration. commit() writes it, with the thread and a stack trace taken at that moment. shouldCommit() returns true only if some recording has the event enabled and the duration passes that recording's threshold, so you can skip filling in fields nobody will read. Kotlin needs nothing special: JFR records the fields behind Kotlin properties, and @Label on a property lands on the field. Compared with the log line from the first section, the event is structured (fields, not text to parse), off unless a recording asks for it, and filterable per recording: -XX:StartFlightRecording:+workbench.IssuerCall#threshold=30ms,... keeps only calls of 30 ms or more. The + is needed because your event isn't listed in the .jfc file. Without it, the JVM warns that the setting "doesn't exist" and ignores it. Above all, it sits on the same timeline as the GC pauses and lock waits, with the same thread names. The demo's events, as jfr view workbench.IssuerCall shows them: Start Time Duration Event Thread Stack Trace Merchant Amount (cents) Approved ---------- -------- ------------ ------------------------------------------------------ -------- -------------- -------- 18:05:59 9.94 ms auth-3 workbench.performance.l05.PaymentWorkload.callIssuer m_0 1,000 true 18:05:59 3.37 ms auth-2 workbench.performance.l05.PaymentWorkload.callIssuer m_0 1,000 true Reading events back in code is short. RecordingFile.readAllEvents(path) returns every event, and each RecordedEvent has getEventType().getName(), getDuration(), getString("merchant"), getBoolean("approved") and friends. That's the lab. Check yourself: you commit an event in a method that runs 50,000 times a second, and no recording enables it. What does shouldCommit() return, and what does it save you? (False. It saves the work of filling in the fields, and commit() would write nothing anyway.) Keep only the slow calls In JfrDemo.java, change the recording option to "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile,+workbench.IssuerCall#threshold=30ms" (note the +). Predict: out of about 1,700 issuer calls, roughly how many will be recorded now? Run the demo again, then jfr summary and jfr view workbench.IssuerCall on the new file. Only a few dozen workbench.IssuerCall events remain (43 in one run, against 1,744 without the threshold), all from m_7 and all 30 ms or longer, because only that merchant's fake issuer sleeps that long. The JVM's own events are unchanged. The threshold is a setting of the recording, not of your code.

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Stream events live, and what JDK 25 added
x: A recording file answers questions after the fact. jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingStream, available since JDK 14, delivers the same events to your code while the JVM runs: Java try (RecordingStream rs = new RecordingStream()) { rs.enable("workbench.IssuerCall").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(35)); rs.onEvent("workbench.IssuerCall", e -> System.out.printf("slow issuer call: %s, %d ms%n", e.getString("merchant"), e.getDuration().toMillis())); rs.startAsync(); // events arrive on a background thread PaymentWorkload.run(3); } Kotlin RecordingStream().use { rs -> rs.enable("workbench.IssuerCall").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(35)) rs.onEvent("workbench.IssuerCall") { e -> println("slow issuer call: ${e.getString("merchant")}, ${e.duration.toMillis()} ms") } rs.startAsync() // events arrive on a background thread kRunWorkload(3) } That's enough to turn JVM events into metrics or alerts inside the service, for example GC pause time per minute. Events arrive in batches after a short delay, so this is monitoring, not a callback on the hot path. JDK 25 added three profiling features. All of these ran here on JDK 25: Method timing and tracing (JEP 520). -XX:StartFlightRecording:method-timing=Work::fee,report-on-exit=method-timing counted and timed one method with no code change. It printed 21,282,793 invocations, an average of 0.000063 ms and a maximum of 7.54 ms. The filter can also be an annotation such as @jakarta.ws.rs.GET. CPU-time sampling (JEP 509), experimental and Linux only. Enable jdk.CPUTimeSample (for example jdk.CPUTimeSample#enabled=true,jdk.CPUTimeSample#throttle=10ms) and read it with jfr view cpu-time-hot-methods. It samples each thread by the CPU time it uses. In a 3-second run of one busy thread at 10 ms, it collected 276 samples, close to the 300 you'd expect. Cooperative sampling (JEP 518) changes how the JVM takes execution samples internally. You don't configure it. report-on-exit=<view> itself is also there in JDK 25 (JDK 21 rejects it), and it prints any view when the JVM exits: a profile in your CI log for free. Watch slow calls and GCs as they happen Run StreamingDemo and watch the output for 3 seconds. Predict before running the Kotlin twin: which merchant will show up, and roughly how slow? On JDK 25 only: run the workload with method timing, using the command in the note below, and compare the printed table with your expectations. // only the slow ones rs.enable("jdk.GarbageCollection"); rs.onEvent("workbench.IssuerCall", e -> System.out.printf("slow issuer call: %s, %d ms%n", e.getString("merchant"), e.getDuration().toMillis())); rs.onEvent("jdk.GarbageCollection", e -> System.out.printf("GC: %s, %.1f ms pause total%n", e.getString("name"), e.getDuration("sumOfPauses").toNanos() / 1e6)); rs.startAsync(); // events arrive on a background thread PaymentWorkload.run(3); Only m_7 appears, between 35 and 40 ms, because of the threshold and the fake issuer. For the JDK 25 step, run java '-XX:StartFlightRecording:method-timing=workbench.performance.l05.PaymentWorkload::fee,report-on-exit=method-timing' -cp performance/build/classes/java/demo workbench.performance.l05.JfrDemo child from labs/: it ends with a Method Timing table for fee. The common mistake is turning on profile.jfc in production "because more data is better", or starting a recording with no limits and never dumping it. profile doubles the sampling and lowers the lock thresholds, and the man page itself says it can have more overhead and belongs in short periods. A recording without maxage or maxsize falls back to a 250 MB default, so set limits that match how far back you need to look. The fix is a continuous default recording with limits, plus a short profile recording started with jcmd when you are investigating. Java // a continuous recording, started from code, keeping the last hour within 200 MB Recording r = new Recording(Configuration.getConfiguration("default")); r.setMaxAge(Duration.ofHours(1)); r.setMaxSize(200L * 1024 * 1024); r.start(); Kotlin // a continuous recording, started from code, keeping the last hour within 200 MB val r = Recording(Configuration.getConfiguration("default")) r.maxAge = Duration.ofHours(1) r.maxSize = 200L * 1024 * 1024 r.start()

x: A custom JFR event in Java and Kotlin IssuerCallEvent.java @Name("workbench.IssuerCall") @Label("Issuer Call") @Category({"Workbench", "Payments"}) public class IssuerCallEvent extends Event { @Label("Merchant") String merchant; @Label("Amount (cents)") long amountCents; @Label("Approved") boolean approved; } IssuerCallEvent event = new IssuerCallEvent(); event.begin(); // 1. start the clock boolean approved = issuer.approve(merchant, cents); event.end(); // 2. stop it if (event.shouldCommit()) { // 3. false if no recording wants it event.merchant = merchant; event.amountCents = cents; event.approved = approved; event.commit(); // 4. write it, with a stack trace } JfrDemo.kt @Name("workbench.IssuerCall") @Label("Issuer Call") @Category("Workbench", "Payments") class KIssuerCallEvent : Event() { @Label("Merchant") var merchant: String? = null @Label("Amount (cents)") var amountCents = 0L @Label("Approved") var approved = false } val event = KIssuerCallEvent() event.begin() // 1. start the clock val approved = issuer.approve(merchant, cents) event.end() // 2. stop it if (event.shouldCommit()) { // 3. false if no recording wants it event.merchant = merchant event.amountCents = cents event.approved = approved event.commit() // 4. write it, with a stack trace } The same event, recorded the same way. Kotlin properties work as event fields: a var compiles to a private field plus accessors, and JFR records the field. A Java annotation such as @Label placed on a Kotlin property goes to that field, because FIELD is the only one of its targets a property can use. @Category takes an array, written {"Workbench", "Payments"} in Java and as plain arguments in Kotlin. Both versions produce the same event type, workbench.IssuerCall, so the same jfr view works on either recording.

If the longest pause is a few ms, GC isn't your 200 ms. jfr view gc-pauses /tmp/auth-1402.jfr Second question: did threads wait on each other? contention-by-site lists monitors that threads waited on, with counts and the longest wait. A 180 ms max on a ledger lock would explain a lot. jfr view contention-by-site /tmp/auth-1402.jfr Third question: which calls were slow, and for whom? Your own event answers it, on the same clock. (The lock wait: it's inside your process and the issuer call may only look slow because the thread was waiting.) jfr print --events workbench.IssuerCall /tmp/auth-1402.jfr | grep -B3 -A6 'duration = [0-9][0-9][0-9] ms' Write the finding down with the evidence, and attach the views, not the raw file: the file contains environment variables and arguments.

Call begin() right before the issuer call and end() right after it. Fill the fields and commit() inside if (event.shouldCommit()). RecordingFile.readAllEvents(path) returns a List<RecordedEvent>. Filter on e.getEventType().getName(), then use e.getBoolean("approved"), e.getString("merchant") and e.getDuration(). Map.merge(merchant, 1L, Long::sum) counts per key in one line. A TreeMap keeps the result sorted, which makes failures easier to read. All five tests in FlightRecorderTest pass. By the end you can start and dump a JFR recording on a running JVM, answer questions with jfr summary, jfr view and jfr print, and add your own events that land in the same timeline as GC and locks.

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Key terms
x: JFR (JDK Flight Recorder) A recorder built into HotSpot that writes timestamped events about the JVM and your code. Event One timestamped record, such as a GC pause, a lock wait or one issuer call. Recording A running JFR session with its settings and limits, dumped to a .jfr file. Execution sample A periodic snapshot of a running thread's stack, used to find hot methods. Threshold A minimum duration below which a recording drops an event. JMC (JDK Mission Control) The desktop app for analysing .jfr files. RecordingStream An API that hands JFR events to your code while the JVM runs. How do you start a JFR recording on a JVM that's already running? jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=x settings=profile, and later jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=x filename=x.jfr. default.jfc or profile.jfc for a recording that stays on in production? default.jfc. profile.jfc samples twice as often and can have more overhead; use it for short investigations. Which jfr subcommand gives ready-made reports, and since which JDK? jfr view <view> file.jfr, since JDK 21. For example hot-methods, allocation-by-site, gc-pauses. What does event.shouldCommit() tell you? Whether a recording has this event enabled and the duration passes its threshold. If false, skip filling in the fields. How do you read events from a .jfr file in Java? RecordingFile.readAllEvents(path), then filter on e.getEventType().getName() and read fields with getString, getLong, getDuration. What does RecordingStream do? Delivers JFR events to callbacks inside the running JVM (since JDK 14), in batches after a short delay. Why check a .jfr file before sharing it? It contains environment variables and the command line. JDK 27 adds redaction (JEP 536).

h: JDK Flight Recorder and Mission Control · Go deeper
x: JFR's views are queries, and the JDK source keeps them in a file called view.ini. For example, hot-methods is SELECT stackTrace.topFrame AS T, COUNT(*), COUNT(*) FROM ExecutionSample GROUP BY T LIMIT 25, and deoptimizations-by-reason is SELECT reason, COUNT(reason) AS C FROM Deoptimization GROUP BY reason ORDER BY C DESC. jfr view --verbose shows which fields a view uses, which helps when you build your own analysis with RecordingFile. The demo recorded only 28 execution samples in 4 seconds. Its threads sleep most of the time, and the classic sampler records threads that are running Java code, not sleeping ones. Even so, 28 is fewer than a 10 ms period suggests, and this course couldn't pin down the sampler's exact rules in the source. That's one reason lesson 6 brings in async-profiler, which samples with signals and timers, and JDK 25 brought the CPU-time sampler. jfr has more subcommands: jfr configure builds a custom .jfc from options, jfr scrub writes a copy of a recording without chosen events, jfr assemble and jfr disassemble join and split chunk files, and jfr metadata lists every event type and field. To record a whole test run in CI, add -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=build/test.jfr to the test JVM's arguments. On JDK 25, report-on-exit=allocation-by-site prints the allocation report straight into the build log.

h: async-profiler and flame graphs · A sampling profiler is a loop that counts stacks
x: Take SlowFees.feeSlow, the fee calculation lesson 7 investigates. You want to know where its CPU time goes, call by call, without changing its code. You could add timers around every call, but timers change what they measure, and you'd need to know where to put them. A sampling profiler does something simpler. Every few milliseconds it looks at what each thread is executing, records the whole call stack, and counts how often each stack shows up. If a method is on top of the stack in 20% of the samples, the thread spent about 20% of its time there. You can build one in a dozen lines: Java Map<String, Long> stacks = new HashMap<>(); while (worker.isAlive()) { Thread.sleep(10); // 1. wait one sampling interval StackTraceElement[] st = worker.getStackTrace(); // 2. snapshot the thread's stack List<String> frames = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = st.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) // 3. root first frames.add(st[i].getClassName() + "." + st[i].getMethodName()); stacks.merge(String.join(";", frames), 1L, Long::sum); // 4. count identical stacks } Kotlin val stacks = HashMap<String, Long>() while (worker.isAlive) { Thread.sleep(10) // 1. wait one sampling interval val st = worker.stackTrace // 2. snapshot the thread's stack val key = st.reversed() // 3. root first .joinToString(";") { "${it.className}.${it.methodName}" } stacks.merge(key, 1L, Long::plus) // 4. count identical stacks } The output is the format every flame graph tool reads, collapsed stacks: one line per distinct stack, frames from the root to the top separated by ;, then the number of samples. java.lang.Thread.run;...SlowFees.feeSlow;java.math.BigDecimal.toPlainString;java.lang.Long.toString;java.lang.Long.getChars 45 Two words come up constantly. A frame's self time is the samples where it was on top of the stack, doing the work itself. Its inclusive time adds everything it called. feeSlow has almost no self time and a huge inclusive time: it does little itself and calls expensive things. PoorMansProfiler runs feeSlow on two threads for 4 seconds and samples them like this. One run took 702 samples. Its top frames were BigDecimal.<init> 15.0%, BigDecimal.toPlainString 15.0%, AbstractStringBuilder.ensureCapacityInternal 10.5% and Formatter.parse 9.5%. That looks like a usable answer. The next section shows why it isn't quite. Run a profiler you can read in one screen Read PoorMansProfiler and SlowFees.feeSlow. Predict the three methods that will be on top most often. Run it. It prints the top frames and writes build/poor-man.collapsed (relative to labs/performance). Open the collapsed file and find the line with the biggest count. Run the Kotlin twin and compare its top frames. Writes the samples as collapsed stacks, the text format * flame graph tools read, to build/poor-man.collapsed. */ public class PoorMansProfiler { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { long until = System.nanoTime() + 4_000_000_000L; Thread work = new Thread(() -> { try { SlowFees.hammer(2, until); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); work.start(); Map<String, Long> stacks = new HashMap<>(); // "frame;frame;frame" -> samples while (work.isAlive()) { Thread.sleep(10); for (Thread t : Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet()) { if (!t.getName().startsWith("fees-")) continue; StackTraceElement[] st = t.getStackTrace(); The top frames are spread over BigDecimal, StringBuilder, Formatter and regex methods. The Kotlin twin put 13.8% on its own kFeeSlow frame in one run, which is odd for a method that only calls other methods. Remember that oddity for the next section. A sampling profiler is a manager who walks past the team's desks every ten seconds and notes what each person is working on. After a day, the tally says where the time went, without anyone filling in a timesheet. Safepoint bias is a manager who only looks up when someone stands up from their desk: they see people at the coffee machine and the printer, and they never see the long stretches of typing. async-profiler is a camera that takes a snapshot at a random moment, wherever people are. The analogy breaks at the end: the camera also sees the cleaners and the building's machinery, the GC and JIT threads, which a real manager would ignore.

h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Safepoint bias: the hand-made profiler only sees threads where they can stop
x: Thread.getStackTrace() on another thread can't read that thread's stack at an arbitrary instruction. Compiled code keeps values in registers and has inlined frames, so the JVM can only describe a thread's stack at a safepoint: a point where it has recorded the full state of the frames. Compiled code checks for a request to stop at safepoint polls, which sit mostly at method returns and loop back-edges. So when the sampler asks, the thread runs on to the next poll and reports its stack there. The samples pile up on polls instead of where the CPU spends its time. A tight inlined loop without a poll looks free, and the method that contains the next poll gets the blame. That's why the Kotlin twin charged 13.8% to kFeeSlow itself. This is safepoint bias, and every profiler built on getStackTrace or the JVMTI GetAllStackTraces call has it. The same workload under async-profiler 4.6 gave a different picture. Its top frames were Formatter.format 17.7%, Long.getChars 14.9%, Pattern.compile 12.4% and BigDecimal.<init> 10.3%. Formatter.format didn't appear in the hand-made top six at all. And where the hand-made profiler charged 15% to toPlainString itself, async-profiler charged 14.9% to Long.getChars, a method toPlainString calls. async-profiler avoids the bias by interrupting each thread with a signal, driven by Linux perf_events or a timer, and walking the stack at the exact instruction where the signal landed. To make sense of JIT-compiled frames there, it reads HotSpot's internal structures: originally through AsyncGetCallTrace, a HotSpot-only function the profiler is named after, and since version 4.2 with its own walker by default. Because it works below the JVM, it also shows native frames, JVM frames (GC, JIT compiler threads) and kernel frames, which no Java-level profiler can see. JFR, from lesson 5, doesn't have the bias in its classic form either. In JDK 25 its sampler records where the thread was at the sampling moment and lets the thread finish the stack walk at its next safepoint (cooperative sampling, JEP 518). Check yourself: a method has one hot inlined loop and returns once at the end. Which method would a getStackTrace profiler blame for the loop's time? (Whichever frame reaches the next safepoint poll, often the loop's own back-edge or the caller after the return, not the instructions that burned the CPU.) Profile the same code with async-profiler Download async-profiler from its GitHub releases page (Linux x64 or arm64, or macOS) and unpack it. bin/asprof is the launcher. Run ProfileMe. It prints its pid and keeps four threads busy for 8 seconds. In a second terminal, within those 8 seconds: asprof -d 5 -f cpu.html <pid>. Open cpu.html in a browser. Compare its widest top frames with PoorMansProfiler's list. Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 8; System.out.println("pid " + ProcessHandle.current().pid() + ", running for " + seconds + " s"); System.out.println("attach with: asprof -d 5 -f cpu.html " + ProcessHandle.current().pid()); SlowFees.hammer(4, System.nanoTime() + seconds * 1_000_000_000L); System.out.println("done"); } } ./gradlew :performance:demo -Pmain=workbench.performance.l06.ProfileMe h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Reading a flame graph: width is samples, the x-axis is the alphabet
x: A flame graph is the collapsed stacks drawn as boxes. Each box is one frame. The root sits at the bottom, and each frame's callees are stacked on top of it. Three rules make it readable. Width is samples. A box's width is the number of samples with that frame on the stack at that position, which is its inclusive time there. Identical frames at the same depth under the same parent are merged into one box. The x-axis is not time. Boxes at the same level are sorted alphabetically. flamegraph.pl's own header says "The ordering on the x-axis has no meaning", and async-profiler's guide says a flame graph "does not preserve information on when a particular stack trace was taken". A box on the left didn't run first. Look at the tops. The part of a box with nothing above it is self time: the CPU was in that frame's own code. Wide tops are where to start. A wide box covered by its children is a caller, and the fix is usually in one of them. The figure is drawn from a real async-profiler CPU profile of the same fee code (its class was called PaymentSim in that run): 8,005 samples over 10 seconds, of which feeSlow covered 5,747 (71.8%). Its widest children are String.format (23.3% of all samples), Pattern.compile (17.6%), BigDecimal.toPlainString (11.5%) and the BigDecimal constructor (7.9%). Outside feeSlow, about 8% of the samples were G1 garbage collector threads and about 9% C2 compiler threads, and 608 samples were in __vdso_clock_gettime: the test harness calling System.nanoTime() around every request, so the measurement shows up in its own profile. async-profiler's HTML colours frames by type: green for compiled Java, aqua for inlined Java, light green for interpreted, yellow for JVM (C++) code, red for native and orange for kernel. Clicking a box zooms in, and the search field highlights every frame that matches. The same tools draw two useful variants: a reversed graph (--reverse) that merges stacks from the top frame down, which groups all callers of a hot leaf, and an icicle graph (--inverted) that hangs from the top. Read your flame graph like a profile Open cpu.html from the previous Try it. Type Pattern into the search field: what share of the samples matches? Click feeSlow to zoom in. Find the widest box that has nothing above it. Predict before checking: if you moved Pattern.compile(...) into a static final field, which boxes would disappear, and roughly how much narrower would feeSlow get? The search shows a match share in the bottom-right corner; in the profile the figure comes from, Pattern.compile and Pattern.matcher alone came to about 22% of all samples. The widest exposed tops sit inside Formatter, Pattern and BigDecimal. Hoisting the pattern removes the Pattern.compile tower (about 18% of samples) but keeps Pattern.matcher, which still allocates a Matcher per call. That's exactly what lesson 7 finds. The feeSlow part of a real 8,005-sample CPU profile. Widths are sample counts; small frames are grouped as "other" in this drawing. Interpreting a flame graph (async-profiler docs) read

h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Pick the mode: cpu, wall, alloc or lock
x: A flame graph shows samples of something. The mode decides what. async-profiler's main modes: Mode A sample means Use it for cpu (default) the thread was running on a CPU where CPU time goes wall the thread existed, running or not latency: where a request waits (I/O, locks, sleep) alloc the thread allocated memory who creates the garbage lock the thread waited to enter a lock contention cpu mode takes stacks from Linux perf_events. Those can be blocked, for example when /proc/sys/kernel/perf_event_paranoid is 2 or higher or in some containers. Then -e ctimer gives similar results from a timer, without kernel frames. wall samples every thread equally whether it runs, sleeps or blocks, and the docs recommend it per thread: asprof -e wall -t -i 50ms -f wall.html <pid>. For a payment API that is slow because it waits on an issuer, wall is the right mode and cpu is nearly empty. In alloc mode, "the top frame of every call trace is the class of the allocated object, and the counter is the heap pressure". It hooks into HotSpot when an object is allocated in a new TLAB (a thread's private allocation buffer) or outside one, and it doesn't disturb escape analysis: objects the JIT scalar-replaced never show up. On the slow fee code, an alloc profile here put 37.4% of the allocated bytes under Pattern.compile, 27.9% under String.format and 12.3% under toPlainString. The top frames were byte[], int[] and boolean[]: regex internals and string building. (The class names carry a short suffix in brackets; ignore it for now.) lock mode puts the class of the lock or monitor on top, and the counter is the nanoseconds spent waiting to enter it: asprof -e lock -t -i 5ms -f lock.html <pid>. You can also load the profiler at start-up instead of attaching later, which is handy in a container: -agentpath:/path/to/libasyncProfiler.so=start,event=cpu,file=cpu.collapsed,collapsed. -o collapsed writes collapsed stacks instead of HTML, which is what the lab reads. --all turns on every mode at once; the docs say it's not recommended for production. Who allocates, and who waits Start ProfileMe again. Attach in alloc mode: asprof -e alloc -d 5 -f alloc.html <pid>. Before opening it, predict the three widest children of feeSlow in the allocation graph. Start ProfileMe once more and attach with asprof -e wall -t -d 5 -f wall.html <pid>. How does it differ from cpu.html? terminal asprof -e alloc -d 5 -f alloc.html <pid> asprof -e alloc -d 5 -o collapsed -f alloc.collapsed <pid> # the same, as text asprof -e wall -t -d 5 -f wall.html <pid> In the allocation graph, Pattern.compile and String.format are the widest children of feeSlow, followed by toPlainString, and the top frames are array classes such as byte[] and int[]. The wall graph splits by thread (-t): the four fees- threads look much like the CPU profile because they never wait, while main sits in Thread.join the whole time. In a 3-second run here, main got 61 samples, exactly as many as each worker: wall mode samples every thread equally, and a CPU profile would ignore main completely. The most common mistake is reading a flame graph as a timeline: "first it validated the currency, then it formatted the log line". Boxes at the same level are in alphabetical order, so left and right say nothing about when or in which order. The second mistake is optimizing the widest box at the bottom of the graph. A wide box covered by its children (feeSlow here) spends its time in those children, and making it faster on its own changes nothing. Look for wide exposed tops, then follow them down to the first frame in your own code: that's the line to change. Java // what the profile points at: the frame in your code under the wide top if (!Pattern.compile("^[A-Z]{3}$").matcher(currency).matches()) { ... } Kotlin // what the profile points at: the frame in your code under the wide top require(Regex("^[A-Z]{3}$").matches(currency)) { "bad currency" }

h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Java and Kotlin
x: The hand-made sampler in Java and Kotlin PoorMansProfiler.java Map<String, Long> stacks = new HashMap<>(); while (worker.isAlive()) { Thread.sleep(10); // 1. wait one sampling interval StackTraceElement[] st = worker.getStackTrace(); // 2. snapshot the thread's stack List<String> frames = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = st.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) // 3. root first frames.add(st[i].getClassName() + "." + st[i].getMethodName()); stacks.merge(String.join(";", frames), 1L, Long::sum); // 4. count identical stacks } PoorMansProfiler.kt val stacks = HashMap<String, Long>() while (worker.isAlive) { Thread.sleep(10) // 1. wait one sampling interval val st = worker.stackTrace // 2. snapshot the thread's stack val key = st.reversed() // 3. root first .joinToString(";") { "${it.className}.${it.methodName}" } stacks.merge(key, 1L, Long::plus) // 4. count identical stacks } Both versions call the same JVM method, Thread.getStackTrace(), so both share its safepoint bias and its cost: each call stops the target thread briefly. The Kotlin twin's workload uses Regex, BigDecimal operators and the format extension, which call the same JDK classes, so its profile has the same hot spots with slightly different frame names, such as kotlin.text.Regex.<init> below Pattern.compile. Kotlin's frame names in profiles follow the compiled classes: top-level functions appear under the file class, such as ProfileMeKt.kFeeSlow.

x: From a profile to the line to change The authorization pods run hot. Attach to one for 30 seconds in CPU mode, as collapsed stacks so you can also grep them. asprof -d 30 -e cpu -o collapsed -f /tmp/auth-cpu.collapsed <pid> asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f /tmp/auth-cpu.html <pid> Find the widest self frames first: sort the collapsed lines by top frame. Here Pattern.compile and Formatter.format lead. awk '{n=$NF; $NF=""; k=split($0,f,";"); s[f[k]]+=n} END {for (x in s) print s[x], x}' /tmp/auth-cpu.collapsed | sort -rn | head -5 A JDK frame on top is rarely the thing to fix. Walk down each hot stack to the first frame in your own package. Self-check: why stop at your own frame and not at the JDK one? (You can't make Pattern.compile faster, but you can stop calling it per request.) java/util/regex/Pattern.<init> <- top, JDK java/util/regex/Pattern.compile <- JDK com.acme.pay.FeeService.fee <- first frame you own: the line to change Fix one thing, profile again, and compare widths. h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Quiz
x: A request is slow because each one waits 120 ms for the card issuer. The CPU flame graph of the service barely shows the request path. Which mode shows the wait? -e cpu with a shorter interval -e wall -t -e alloc -e lock wall samples every thread at the same rate whether it runs, sleeps or blocks, so a thread waiting on a socket shows up. CPU sampling only sees threads that are running, and the issuer wait isn't a Java lock, so lock won't show it either. In a flame graph, FeeService.fee is a very wide box, completely covered by String.format and Pattern.compile above it. Where is the time? In FeeService.fee's own code In the frames above it: fee has no self time, so its callees do the work Spread evenly over the graph In the frames below it Width is inclusive. A box with no exposed top has no self time. The fix is still in fee, because it's the frame in your code that calls String.format and Pattern.compile, but the CPU is in those callees. A profiler built on Thread.getStackTrace() blames 14% of the CPU on a method that only calls other methods. What's the most likely explanation? The method really does 14% of the work Safepoint bias: samples are taken where threads reach a safepoint poll, so time gets charged to wherever the next poll is Inlining makes the method slower The JIT removed the callees getStackTrace on another thread needs that thread at a safepoint, and polls sit at method returns and loop back-edges. Time spent between polls is charged to the frame where the thread stopped. async-profiler samples at the exact instruction instead. You profile with asprof -e alloc and see no Money objects, although the code creates one per payment. What could explain it? The alloc mode only shows arrays The JIT scalar-replaced the Money objects after escape analysis, so they were never allocated on the heap Allocation profiles only cover the main thread async-profiler can't see application classes async-profiler's docs say alloc mode doesn't disturb escape analysis and measures only real heap allocations. An object that never escapes its compiled method can be replaced by its fields in registers, so there's nothing to sample. From lesson 5: you need to know which methods allocate the most in a production pod, but you can't install async-profiler there. What's the closest built-in answer? jfr view allocation-by-site on a recording dumped with jcmd <pid> JFR.dump -XX:+PrintCompilation jcmd <pid> Thread.print A JMH benchmark with -prof gc JFR samples allocations as jdk.ObjectAllocationSample events with stack traces, and the allocation-by-site view groups them by top frame. It's built into the JDK, so nothing needs installing. JMH measures code in isolation, not the pod.

h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Key terms
x: Sampling profiler A profiler that records stacks at intervals and counts them, instead of timing every call. Collapsed stacks Text format: one line per distinct stack, frames joined by ;, then a count. Self time Samples where a frame was on top of the stack, running its own code. Inclusive time Samples where a frame was anywhere on the stack, including its callees. Safepoint A point where the JVM knows a thread's full state and can stop it or read its stack. Safepoint bias Profiling error from only seeing threads at safepoint polls. Flame graph Stacks drawn as boxes: root at the bottom, width = samples, alphabetical left to right. What does a line of collapsed stacks look like? root;caller;callee 42: frames from the root to the top separated by ;, then the number of samples. Self time vs inclusive time of a frame? Self: samples with the frame on top of the stack. Inclusive: samples with the frame anywhere on the stack. What is safepoint bias? Profilers that use getStackTrace/JVMTI only see threads at safepoint polls, so samples land on the next poll instead of where the CPU was. In a flame graph, what does the x-axis order mean? Nothing about time: frames at the same level are sorted alphabetically. Width is the number of samples. Which async-profiler mode shows where requests wait on I/O? wall (ideally with -t), which samples threads whether they run, sleep or block. What's on top of each stack in async-profiler's alloc mode? The class of the allocated object; the counter is the heap pressure. What do you do when async-profiler can't use perf_events (containers, perf_event_paranoid ≥ 2)? Use -e ctimer, which samples CPU with a timer, without kernel frames.

h: async-profiler and flame graphs · Go deeper
x: Before version 4.2, async-profiler took Java stacks with AsyncGetCallTrace, a HotSpot function that isn't part of any standard API. Its docs note that it "was broken several times even in minor JDK updates" and could crash the JVM, which is why 4.2 made its own walker over HotSpot's internal structures the default (--cstack vm). vmx mode goes further and interleaves Java and native frames in one stack. -a (or --ann) annotates frames by how they were compiled: _[j] for JIT-compiled methods, _[i] for inlined ones, _[0] for interpreted and _[1] for C1-compiled. That connects a profile back to lessons 1 and 2: a hot method stuck at _[0] or _[1] deserves a look with PrintCompilation. Differential flame graphs compare two profiles. Brendan Gregg's FlameGraph tools colour frames "red for more, and blue for less", which is a quick way to see what a change did. Make both profiles the same length and under the same load, or the comparison measures traffic, not code. async-profiler can also write JFR files (-o jfr) that JDK Mission Control opens, and convert them later with jfrconv. For CI, JMH's -prof async:libPath=<path to libasyncProfiler.so> runs it around a benchmark, so you get a flame graph of exactly the code you measured.

h: A performance investigation, start to finish · Start from the symptom: the tail and the GC, not the average
x: Here is the complaint, measured. Four threads call a card-fee calculation as fast as they can for 15 seconds, with a 256 MB heap, and every call is timed into a histogram. These are the research run's numbers on JDK 21: 604,529 calls/s p50 < 0.7 us p99 < 3.9 us p99.9 < 35.3 us p99.99 < 13.6 ms 130 GCs, 996 ms of GC time The average is excellent. One call in ten thousand takes over 13 ms, which in a payment API is the difference between a smooth checkout and a timeout somewhere upstream. jfr view gc-pauses on the same run said 129 pauses, 984 ms in total, median 2.98 ms. That's the first hypothesis: the slow calls are the ones that hit a pause, and the pauses happen because the code allocates. The code looks harmless: Java static long feeSlow(Payment p) { if (!Pattern.compile("^[A-Z]{3}$").matcher(p.currency()).matches()) // line 19 throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad currency"); BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal(p.amount()); BigDecimal fee = amount.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.029")).add(new BigDecimal("0.30")) // line 22 .setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); debug(String.format("payment %s merchant=%s amount=%s fee=%s", // line 24 p.id(), p.merchant(), amount.toPlainString(), fee.toPlainString())); return fee.unscaledValue().longValue(); } Kotlin fun ktFeeSlow(p: KtPayment): Long { require(Regex("^[A-Z]{3}$").matches(p.currency)) { "bad currency" } // a regex per call val amount = BigDecimal(p.amount) val fee = (amount * BigDecimal("0.029") + BigDecimal("0.30")) // constants per call .setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) ktDebug("payment %s merchant=%s amount=%s fee=%s" // formatted, then dropped .format(p.id, p.merchant, amount.toPlainString(), fee.toPlainString())) return fee.unscaledValue().toLong() } It returns the right fee. Three costs hide in it: a regex compiled on every call, two BigDecimal constants built on every call, and a DEBUG log line formatted on every call and then dropped because DEBUG is off. One caution before you change anything. The maximum latency stayed between 0.37 and 0.53 seconds in every version of this code, before and after the fixes. On a shared machine with four busy threads on four vCPUs, plus GC and JIT threads, the operating system sometimes doesn't schedule a thread for a while. Don't present the max as an effect of your fix. The percentiles are the evidence. Reproduce the symptom Read FeeVariants.feeSlow and FeeInvestigation. The demo starts a second JVM with -Xmx256m and a JFR recording, runs 4 threads for 3 seconds, then reads the recording. Predict: which line of feeSlow allocates the most? Run it with -Pargs=slow. Note the p99.99, the GC count and the top lines. Usage: -Pargs=slow (or hoisted, noregex). */ public class FeeInvestigation { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "slow"; if (args.length > 1 && args[1].equals("child")) { load(mode); return; } Path file = Path.of("build", "fees-" + mode + ".jfr").toAbsolutePath(); String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(java, "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:jfr+startup=warning", "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), FeeInvestigation.class.getName(), mode, "child") .inheritIO().start(); p.waitFor(); allocationByLine(file); } // the load: 4 threads, each timing every call into a fixed histogram (no allocation of its own) static void load(String mode) throws Exception { ToLongFunction<FeeVariants.Payment> fee = switch (mode) { case "slow" -> FeeVariants::feeSlow; case "hoisted" -> FeeVariants::feeHoisted; default -> FeeVariants::feeNoRegex; }; FeeVariants.Payment[] ps = FeeVariants.payments(4_096); long end = System.nanoTime() + 3_000_000_000L; long[][] hist = new long[4][]; List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++) { int id = t; Thread th = new Thread(() -> { long[] h = new long[20_001]; // 100 ns buckets up to 1 ms, then 100 us buckets up to 1 s long sink = 0; for (int i = id; System.nanoTime() < end; i++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); sink += fee.applyAsLong(ps[i & 4095]); long d = System.nanoTime() - t0; h[d < 1_000_000 ? (int) (d / 100) : (int) Math.min(20_000, 10_000 + (d - 1_000_000) / 100_000)]++; } hist[id] = h; if (sink == 42) System.out.println(); }); th.start(); threads.add(th); } for (Thread th : threads) th.join(); long[] h = new long[20_001]; for (long[] x : hist) for (int k = 0; k < h.length; k++) h[k] += x[k]; long total = 0; for (long n : h) total += n; long gcs = 0, gcMs = 0; for (GarbageCollectorMXBean gc : ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans()) { gcs += gc.getCollectionCount(); gcMs += gc.getCollectionTime(); } System.out.printf("%s: %,d calls/s p50 %s p99 %s p99.9 %s p99.99 %s GCs %d (%d ms)%n", mode, total / 3, pct(h, total, 0.5), pct(h, total, 0.99), pct(h, total, 0.999), pct(h, total, 0.9999), gcs, gcMs); } static String pct(long[] h, long total, double q) { long target = (long) Math.ceil(total * q), acc = 0; for (int k = 0; k < h.length; k++) { acc += h[k]; if (acc >= target) return k < 10_000 ? "<" + (k + 1) * 100 + "ns" : "<" + ((k - 10_000 + 1) * 100 + 1_000) + "us"; } return "?"; } // what `jfr view allocation-by-site` can't tell you: the line in YOUR code each sample came from static void allocationByLine(Path file) throws Exception { Map<String, Long> weight = new HashMap<>(); long total = 0; for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { if (!e.getEventType().getName().equals("jdk.ObjectAllocationSample") || e.getStackTrace() == null) continue; for (RecordedFrame f : e.getStackTrace().getFrames()) { if (f.getMethod().getType().getName().startsWith("workbench.performance.l07.FeeVariants")) { weight.merge(f.getMethod().getName() + " line " + f.getLineNumber(), e.getLong("weight"), Long::sum); total += e.getLong("weight"); break; // the first frame in our code is the one to change } } } long sum = total; System.out.println("allocation by line in FeeVariants.java (from " + file.getFileName() + "):"); weight.entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()).limit(5) .forEach(en -> System.out.printf(" %5.1f%% %s%n", 100.0 * en.getValue() / sum, en.getKey())); } } million calls per second on a laptop-class machine, p50 well under a microsecond, and a p99.99 hundreds or thousands of times the p50. Dozens of GCs or more in 3 seconds. The allocation by line puts lines 24 and 19 (String.format and Pattern.compile) at the top with about a third each, then line 25 (the toPlainString arguments) and line 22 (the constants). The latency numbers move a lot from run to run on a busy machine; the allocation shares hardly move. A performance investigation is like finding why a warehouse's late shipments come in bursts. You don't start by timing the average packer; you look at the late ones and notice they all coincide with the moments the floor is closed for cleaning (the GC pauses). Then you find what makes so much mess: a team that unpacks every box to check one label (the regex), another that prints a report nobody reads (the dropped log line). You fix one team, check the floor again, and only then notice the next mess that was hidden behind the first. The analogy breaks at the end: in a warehouse you'd stop at "less mess". In code you can measure the remaining mess to the byte and fail the build if it grows.

h: A performance investigation, start to finish · JFR names the allocation, and the first line in your code names the fix
x: jfr view allocation-by-site on the slow run answers "what allocates" in JDK terms: Formatter.parse 12.48% Pattern.compile() 10.34% PaymentSim.feeSlow 10.12% Arrays.copyOf 7.92% Pattern$BitClass.<init> 7.80% Matcher.<init> 7.44% That's real, and not yet useful: you can't change Formatter.parse. The view groups by the top frame, the method that did the allocating. What you want is the first frame in your own code under it. Each jdk.ObjectAllocationSample event carries a stack trace and a weight (how many bytes the sample stands for), so a few lines of RecordingFile, as in lesson 5's lab, can group by your file and line instead. FeeInvestigation does that. One run: allocation by line in FeeVariants.java (from fees-slow.jfr): 36.0% feeSlow line 24 String.format(...) for the dropped log line 32.6% feeSlow line 19 Pattern.compile(...) 19.1% feeSlow line 25 toPlainString() arguments for the log line 9.2% feeSlow line 22 new BigDecimal("0.029"), new BigDecimal("0.30") The research run's own parser got the same order: 34.7% on the regex line, 31.9% on String.format, 15.9% on the toPlainString arguments, 8.9% on the constants. More than half of all allocation is a log line nobody reads. A flame graph answers the next question: who calls the allocating code, and through which path. In lesson 6's allocation profile of the same code, Pattern.compile held 37.4% of the allocated bytes and String.format 27.9%. Two independent tools agree, which is the point of using both. JFR is built in and cheap enough to leave running. async-profiler gives you the full picture, native and JVM frames included, when you can attach it. The figure shows the loop this lesson follows. The step people skip is the dashed one. Compare the JDK view with the by-line view After the previous Try it, run the command below on the recording it wrote. Find the JDK frames from the view (Formatter.parse, Pattern.compile(), Matcher.<init>) in the by-line list. Which line of feeSlow does each one come from? terminal (from labs/) jfr view allocation-by-site performance/build/fees-slow.jfr jfr print --events jdk.ObjectAllocationSample --stack-depth 8 performance/build/fees-slow.jfr | head -30 The view lists JDK methods such as Formatter.parse, Pattern.compile(), Arrays.copyOf and Matcher.<init> at the top. In jfr print, each sample shows objectClass, weight and a stack where, a few frames down, FeeVariants.feeSlow appears with its line number: 24 under the Formatter frames, 19 under the Pattern and Matcher frames. The investigation loop: measure the tail, find the allocating line, fix one thing, prove it, re-profile, and stop when what is left is real work. Every Quarkus payment service has some version of this code: a validator that compiles a regex per request, BigDecimal constants created inline in fee or FX rules, a log.debug(String.format(...)) or string concatenation in a hot path with DEBUG off in production. When p99 or p99.99 of an endpoint drifts, run the loop: a JFR recording from one pod, gc-pauses and allocation by your own lines, an async-profiler flame graph if you can attach, one fix, a JMH benchmark with -prof gc for the PR, and an allocation budget test so the next refactoring can't silently bring the cost back. Put the JDK version next to the budget: allocation numbers changed between JDK 21 and 25 in this very example.

h: A performance investigation, start to finish · Fix one thing, then profile again
x: Round 1 fixes the three obvious costs: the pattern and the two constants become static final fields, and the log line is formatted only when DEBUG is on. The research run went from 604,529 to 3,355,692 calls per second, p99.99 fell from under 13.6 ms to under 35.6 µs, and the GC count from 130 to 79. Then profile again, because the picture has changed. FeeInvestigation -Pargs=hoisted here: allocation by line in FeeVariants.java (from fees-hoisted.jfr): 75.4% feeHoisted line 35 CCY.matcher(p.currency()).matches() 24.0% feeHoisted line 36 new BigDecimal(p.amount()) The research run put 94.8% on the same line. A precompiled Pattern still creates a new Matcher object on every call. That cost was there from the start, hidden under bigger ones. It only became the top line after round 1. Checking three letters doesn't need a regex at all, so round 2 replaces it with a plain loop: Java static final BigDecimal RATE = new BigDecimal("0.029"); // round 1: built once static final BigDecimal FIXED = new BigDecimal("0.30"); static boolean isCurrencyCode(String s) { // round 2: no regex for 3 letters if (s.length() != 3) return false; for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { char c = s.charAt(i); if (c < 'A' || c > 'Z') return false; } return true; } static long feeNoRegex(Payment p) { if (!isCurrencyCode(p.currency())) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad currency"); BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal(p.amount()); // the work that's left BigDecimal fee = amount.multiply(RATE).add(FIXED).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); if (debugEnabled) debug(String.format("payment %s merchant=%s amount=%s fee=%s", // round 1: guarded p.id(), p.merchant(), amount.toPlainString(), fee.toPlainString())); return fee.unscaledValue().longValue(); } Kotlin val KT_RATE = BigDecimal("0.029") // round 1: built once val KT_FIXED = BigDecimal("0.30") fun isCurrencyCodeKt(s: String) = s.length == 3 && s.all { it in 'A'..'Z' } // round 2: no regex fun ktFeeNoRegex(p: KtPayment): Long { require(isCurrencyCodeKt(p.currency)) { "bad currency" } val amount = BigDecimal(p.amount) // the work that's left val fee = (amount * KT_RATE + KT_FIXED).setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN) if (ktDebugEnabled) ktDebug("payment %s merchant=%s amount=%s fee=%s" // round 1: guarded .format(p.id, p.merchant, amount.toPlainString(), fee.toPlainString())) return fee.unscaledValue().toLong() } After round 2 the research run did 4,292,668 calls per second, p99.99 under 28.4 µs, and 37 GCs. The re-profile here shows 99.9% of what's left on one line, new BigDecimal(p.amount()), parsing the amount string. That's the actual job, so this is where to stop, unless a budget says otherwise. Parsing cents by hand would remove it, and would also add rounding and validation code that someone has to get right. Three habits come out of this. Fix one thing at a time, so you know what each change did. Profile after every fix, because the order of costs changes. And stop when the top of the profile is the work the code exists to do. Check yourself: in round 1 you hoist the Pattern but forget the log guard. Which line will lead the next profile?
