h: A performance investigation, start to finish · Key terms
x: Tail latency The slowest calls, measured by high percentiles such as p99.9 and p99.99. Allocation budget A test that fails if a method allocates more than an agreed number of bytes per call. Allocation sample weight How many bytes a JFR allocation sample stands for; summing it gives allocation pressure. Re-profile Measuring again after a fix, because the order of costs has changed. Hoisting Moving work that doesn't change, such as compiling a pattern, out of the per-call path. Boxing Wrapping a primitive such as a long in an object such as Long, which allocates. Which latency numbers show GC pauses hurting a few calls? The tail percentiles (p99.9, p99.99) together with the GC count and pause times, not the average. jfr view allocation-by-site shows JDK methods. How do you find your line? Walk each allocation sample's stack trace to the first frame in your own package and group by its method and line number, weighted by weight. Why profile again after each fix? The order of costs changes. Smaller costs, such as the Matcher behind a hoisted Pattern, only become the top line after the bigger ones are gone. When do you stop optimizing an allocation hot spot? When what's left is the work the code exists to do (here, parsing the amount) or when it fits the agreed budget. How do you measure allocation per call in a unit test? Warm up, then read com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() before and after N calls and divide by N. Why does a Kotlin (T) -> Long cost allocation in a hot loop? A function type is a generic Function1, so invoke returns an object and every Long result is boxed. Call directly, use inline, or a fun interface with a primitive return.

h: A performance investigation, start to finish · Go deeper
x: The research run also tried one thing worth knowing about latency numbers. Its histogram used fixed buckets (100 ns up to 1 ms, then 100 µs up to 1 s) in a preallocated array, so measuring added no allocation of its own. A latency recorder that allocates per sample would add exactly the garbage you're trying to measure. HdrHistogram is the usual library for this in production. The flame graph from lesson 6 showed 608 of 8,005 CPU samples in __vdso_clock_gettime: the harness calling System.nanoTime() around every request. Instrumentation has a cost, and on a 60 ns operation it's a large one. That's another reason the final proof is a JMH benchmark rather than the load harness. For logging in Quarkus, the cheapest disabled log call is one that does nothing before checking the level. JBoss Logging's debugf formats only when DEBUG is on, but the arguments are still evaluated and a varargs call still builds its array. In a hot path, the explicit if (log.isDebugEnabled()) guard is the version you can reason about. A profile will tell you if it matters. If you want to go below 72 bytes, the remaining cost is BigDecimal parsing. Amounts in cents as long, parsed directly from the request, allocate nothing (lesson 3's MoneyBench measured 0 B/op for the summing part). That trades allocation for code you must keep correct: rounding modes, scale validation, overflow with Math.multiplyExact. Take that trade only if the budget or the profile asks for it.

h: Startup and footprint
x: Why the JVM starts slowly, class data sharing, Project Leyden's AOT cache, GraalVM native image and CRaC. By the end of this track you can say where a JVM's start-up time and memory go, and measure both the way a load balancer and a container limit see them: time to first request from outside the process, and RSS from the OS. You can build and check a class data sharing archive on JDK 21 and a Project Leyden AOT cache on JDK 25, and you know the traps that make them silently useless, or, on JDK 25 builds before 25.0.4, run stale code. You can explain what GraalVM native image's closed world costs, write its reachability metadata for reflection and proxies, and spot static initializers that break when the build runs them. You can write CRaC checkpoint hooks in the right order, and pick between doing nothing, AppCDS, the AOT cache, native image and CRaC for a given service. You need no background on any of this; lesson 1 starts from what happens between typing java and the first line of main. Install JDK 25, at least 25.0.4: earlier JDK 25 builds can run old classes from an AOT cache after the JAR changes. The Leyden flags need JDK 24 or 25 and say so wherever they appear. Native image needs GraalVM or Mandrel, and CRaC needs a vendor build such as Azul Zulu's CRaC builds on Linux; those steps are marked optional, and everything else runs on a plain JDK. The labs live in labs/startup, one package per lesson (workbench.startup.l01 to l04). Lessons 1 and 3 are Java, lessons 2 and 4 Kotlin, and every sample and demo comes in both languages. Start-up numbers are noisy, so no test measures time or counts loaded classes. The tests load your classes in fresh class loaders and compare exact sets of class names, check JSON metadata against the GraalVM schema and against what the code really does, and drive a simulated checkpoint. Many demos start a second JVM with the flags you pass in -Pargs, because start-up has to be measured on a fresh process. A few Try-its run java directly on a JDK 25 against startup/build/classes/java/demo. Run ./gradlew :startup:test --tests 'workbench.startup.lNN.*' from labs/ until it passes, and ./gradlew :startup:solutionTest to run the same tests on the reference answers. Start-up repeats the same work on every launch: create the VM, load, parse and verify about 1,500 classes for a 300-class app, run static initializers, interpret until the JIT has profiles, and run the framework's start-up. Measure what users see: time to first request from outside, and RSS from ps or /proc. Create VM, the framework's started in, NMT committed memory and docker stats each miss part of it. <clinit> runs on first active use. The holder idiom (a nested class or Kotlin nested object) keeps expensive static work off the start-up path; a Kotlin companion object does not. CDS maps pre-parsed classes from an archive: the default one for JDK classes, AppCDS for yours. It saves parsing and verification, not initialization or JIT warm-up. The AOT cache (JDK 24+, one step on JDK 25) adds linked classes, resolved call sites and profiles. Require JDK 25.0.4+ and rebuild it with every JAR; check it in CI, run production in the default mode. A training run, an AOT cache and the native-image tracing agent all see only the code paths you exercise, so drive them with production-like traffic. Native image starts in milliseconds and uses less memory, but has no JIT (lower peak), needs metadata for reflection and proxies, and runs static initializers at build time in Quarkus. CRaC restores a warm process from an image. Close sockets and files before the checkpoint, reopen them after, mind the hook order and weak references, and recreate per-instance state. Default to the JVM with an AOT cache or AppCDS; choose native or CRaC only when start-up or memory per instance is the real limit and you accept their costs.

h: Startup and footprint: cheat sheet
x: Measure first Question Command or tool Where did each class come from? java -Xlog:class+load ...: source: shared objects file (archive), jrt:/ (parsed from the JDK), file: (class path), a class name (hidden class) How long did VM creation take? -Xlog:startuptime, last line Create VM, 0.03 secs. Nothing about your code What does the user wait for? Time to first request: launch the process, poll the endpoint from outside until 200 What is the footprint? RSS: ps -o pid,rss,args -p <pid>, /proc/<pid>/status (VmRSS, RssAnon, RssFile). Not docker stats, not heap used Where inside the JVM did memory go? -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, then jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary. Committed is not resident Class loading and initialization Loading parses a class into metaspace; linking verifies and prepares it; <clinit> runs on first active use (new, a static call, a non-constant static field, initializing reflection, a subclass). Holder idiom: put the expensive static field in a private nested class. Kotlin: a private nested object, or by lazy. A companion object's properties are static fields of the outer class and are built with it. Class data sharing (CDS) Kind Commands Since Default archive on unless -Xshare:off; lib/server/classes.jsa JDK 12 Dynamic AppCDS -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa, then -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa JDK 13 Static AppCDS -Xshare:off -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=app.classlist, -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedClassListFile=app.classlist -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa, then -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa Auto-created -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa (not for read-only containers) JDK 19 Rules: JARs only (no class directories), same class path or a prefix of it, a changed JAR is rejected. CDS saves parsing and verifying; it does not run static initializers or warm the JIT. Leyden AOT cache JDK What you get 24 JEP 483: -XX:AOTMode=record -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf, then -XX:AOTMode=create ... -XX:AOTCache=app.aot, then -XX:AOTCache=app.aot 25 JEP 514: one step, -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot. JEP 515: method profiles 26 JEP 516: full cache with any GC, including ZGC 27 -XX:AOTMode=required is the name for on 28 (in development) JEP 544: compiled code in the cache Require JDK 25.0.4+ or 26.0.2+ (JDK-8377932: earlier builds ran stale classes after the JAR changed). Rebuild the cache with every JAR, in the same build step. A cache is tied to the class path, the exact JDK build, OS and CPU, the GC (on JDK 25) and module options. A cache the JVM can't use leaves no archive at all, not even the default one. Production: no AOTMode (the default auto falls back safely). CI: -XX:AOTMode=on (required on 27+) with -Xlog:aot, looking for Opened AOT cache. Quarkus 3.40: quarkus.package.jar.aot.enabled=true trains during @QuarkusIntegrationTests; run java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -jar quarkus-run.jar. JDK 21: quarkus.package.jar.aot.type=app-cds. GraalVM native image { "reflection": [ { "condition": { "typeReached": "com.acme.EventDecoder" }, "type": "com.acme.PaymentAuthorized", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "long"] }, { "name": "paymentId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] }, { "type": { "proxy": ["com.acme.CardIssuerClient", "java.lang.AutoCloseable"] } } ] } File: META-INF/native-image/<groupId>/<artifactId>/reachability-metadata.json. Schema v1.2.0 top level: reflection, resources, foreign, comment only. Proxies are ordered interface lists; serialization is "serializable": true; constant arguments to Class.forName need no entry. Tracing agent: java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=<dir> .... Strict mode: --exact-reachability-metadata, -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit. Quarkus initializes all classes at build time. Fix with quarkus.native.additional-build-args=--initialize-at-run-time=a.B\\,c.D. Quarkus: @RegisterForReflection (targets for library classes, ignoreNested, serialization), @RegisterForProxy(targets = ...) in order, quarkus.native.resources.includes. CRaC java -XX:CRaCCheckpointTo=cr -jar app.jar # start, warm it up jcmd app.jar JDK.checkpoint # check the app's console: jcmd always says success java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=cr # restore, warm Hooks: org.crac.Resource (beforeCheckpoint, afterRestore), Core.getGlobalContext().register(r) in org.crac 1.5.0. Keep r in a field: the context holds weak references. Order: checkpoint in reverse registration order, restore in registration order. Everyone is told even if one throws; failures arrive as suppressed exceptions on CheckpointException. Open files and sockets fail the checkpoint (policy error). Socket reopen is not implemented. Choosing Constraint Pick Long-running, rarely restarted, nobody waits on start-up nothing JDK 21, no code changes dynamic AppCDS built with the image JDK 25.0.4+, no code changes, full peak throughput AOT cache trained by integration tests Milliseconds to start or memory per instance is the limit native image (about 59% lower peak in Quarkus's benchmark) Must start fast and warm, runtime under your control CRaC or Lambda SnapStart, with hooks

h: Startup and footprint: track quiz
x: Your new Quarkus pod logs started in 0.9s, but the load balancer only sends it traffic 2.4 s after the container starts. Which number should you work on, and how do you measure it? The 0.9 s, read from the log, because it is the framework's start-up The Create VM time from -Xlog:startuptime Time from launch to the first 200 from the readiness endpoint, measured from outside The time until C2 has compiled the hot methods Only the outside clock includes everything the load balancer waits for: the launcher, VM creation, class loading, framework start and the first request. The framework's log line starts late and stops early, and Create VM stops before your code runs. In Kotlin, class FxRates { companion object { val rates = loadRates(); fun source() = "ecb" } }. A health check calls FxRates.source(). Is loadRates() called? No, companion objects are lazy Yes: rates is a static field of FxRates, filled when FxRates is initialized, which this first call triggers Only on the first access to rates Only if rates is declared const Kotlin compiles companion properties to static fields of the outer class and initializes them in its <clinit>. Use a private nested object holding rates, or by lazy, to build them only when needed. NMT reports 290 MB committed, 216 MB of it heap, while VmRSS is 53 MB. What explains the gap? NMT double-counts the heap The JVM leaked native memory RSS doesn't include the Java heap Committed memory has been requested from the OS, but most of it, such as a fresh heap, has never been touched, so it is not resident Pages become resident only when something writes or reads them. A container is limited by resident memory, so RSS is the footprint; NMT tells you which part of the JVM asked for what. With -Xshare:off, java -version loads 440 classes and 0 come from an archive; without it, 405 load and all 405 are shared. Why did start-up get slower with sharing off? Each class now has to be found, parsed and verified by the JVM instead of being mapped ready-made from classes.jsa The JIT is disabled with sharing off The heap is smaller The JVM runs every static initializer twice The default CDS archive holds the JVM's internal form of about 1,300 JDK classes. Without it every class goes through the full load path, and the JVM generates at run time some classes the archive would have supplied, hence 440 instead of 405. A pipeline rebuilt pay.jar with a fix and reused last week's app.aot. Production runs JDK 25.0.2. What do you expect? A warning, then the fixed code without the cache The JVM refuses to start Possibly last week's classes, served from the cache with no error (JDK-8377932) The fixed code, with the full speed-up JDK 25.0.0 to 25.0.3 (and 26.0.0 to 26.0.1) did not check application JARs against the cache. 25.0.4 and later warn and run without the cache. Pin 25.0.4+ and rebuild the cache with every JAR. Someone adds -XX:AOTCache=/srv/app.aot to every pod's JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, but the file isn't in the image. What happens to start-up? Nothing changes: the JVM ignores the flag It gets slower than with no flag: the JVM runs with no archive at all, not even the default CDS archive The JVM refuses to start The JVM writes the cache at exit In the default auto mode the JVM prints an error and carries on, but with zero archived classes; in this track's run, a one-class program went from 542 shared classes to 0. Only -XX:AOTMode=on or required makes it exit, and only AOTCacheOutput writes a cache. Which entry correctly registers a JDK dynamic proxy over com.acme.LedgerClient and java.io.Closeable in schema v1.2.0? {"proxy": [["com.acme.LedgerClient", "java.io.Closeable"]]} at the top level {"reflection": [{"type": "com.acme.LedgerClient", "allPublicMethods": true}]} A proxy-config.json next to the file {"reflection": [{"type": {"proxy": ["com.acme.LedgerClient", "java.io.Closeable"]}}]} In v1.2.0 a proxy is a reflection entry whose type is an object with an ordered proxy list. The top level allows only reflection, resources, foreign and comment, and Quarkus 4.0 doesn't support the legacy separate files. Registering the interface itself doesn't define the proxy class. A Quarkus native service has static final String NODE_ID = UUID.randomUUID().toString().substring(0, 8); in an ordinary class, used to prefix ledger entry ids. Assuming the build succeeds, what do pods started from the same binary see? The same NODE_ID in every pod, computed once during the build A different NODE_ID per pod null A different value on every read Quarkus initializes all classes at build time by default, so the initializer runs once in the build and its result is stored in the image heap. Per-instance values belong in code that runs at start-up, or in a class marked --initialize-at-run-time. A service registers its ledger pool first and its Kafka consumer second with the CRaC global context. The consumer forgets to close its broker connection. What happens on jcmd app.jar JDK.checkpoint? jcmd reports an error and the JVM exits The checkpoint fails with the default error policy; the restore hooks run in registration order, and the app's console, not jcmd, shows the error The image is written and the connection is reopened after restore Only the consumer's hooks run Open sockets fail the checkpoint by default. The context still notifies everyone (consumer, then pool, before; pool, then consumer, after), collects the problems in a CheckpointException, and the process keeps running. jcmd prints success either way. An internal platform runs 120 small, lightly loaded Quarkus services per node, and memory per instance is what limits how many fit. Slower CI builds are acceptable. Which option fits best? The JVM with no changes An AOT cache on JDK 25 A native image for each service CRaC for each service Density is native image's strongest case: in Quarkus's benchmark, 95 MiB RSS against 304 MiB in JVM mode and 240 MiB with the AOT cache. Its lower peak throughput matters little for lightly loaded services. CRaC restores a full warm JVM, so it doesn't cut memory.

h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Start-up is work the JVM repeats on every launch
x: A generated test app with 300 classes loads 1,537 classes on JDK 21 before it finishes, with class sharing turned off. 301 come from the app's JAR. 911 come from the JDK's own modules. The other 325 are hidden classes: classes the JVM generates in memory at run time, with no class file, for lambdas and method handles. Your 300 classes are a fifth of the work. Here is what happens between typing java and the first line of your main. The java launcher, a small native program, loads the JVM library (libjvm.so on Linux) and asks it to create a VM. The JVM reserves the heap, generates its interpreter, starts its own threads, and initializes the core java.lang classes and the module system. Only then does the application class loader find your main class, and the real work starts. For every class your code touches, the JVM repeats the same steps on every launch. It finds the class file, parses it into its internal form in metaspace (native memory the JVM keeps for class data, outside the Java heap), verifies the bytecode (checks that it is type-safe), and later runs the class's static initializer. It runs your code in the interpreter, which executes bytecode one instruction at a time. The JIT compilers, the parts of the JVM that turn hot methods into machine code while the program runs, only start once they have profiles: counts of which methods, branches and types the code really uses. A framework adds its own start-up work on top: scanning the classpath for annotations, wiring beans by reflection, generating proxies, parsing config. Quarkus moves as much of that as it can to build time; its extension guide says to favor "doing work at build time ... as opposed to let the framework do work at startup time". Nothing of this survives the process. Stop the JVM and the next start does it all again. Only one thing is cached by default: the JDK ships an archive with about 1,300 of its own classes, already parsed, which the JVM maps from disk instead of parsing again. Lesson 2 of this track is about that archive and the bigger ones you can build. You can watch the loading happen. -Xlog:class+load prints one line per class, and the end of each line says where the class came from: [info][class,load] java.lang.Object source: shared objects file [info][class,load] java.util.regex.Pattern$Node source: jrt:/java.base [info][class,load] com.acme.pay.Main source: file:/srv/app.jar [info][class,load] com.acme.pay.Main$$Lambda/0x... source: com.acme.pay.Main shared objects file means the class was mapped from a class data sharing (CDS) archive, a file of classes the JDK has already parsed. jrt:/ means it was read and parsed from the JDK's modules file. file: is your classpath. A class name as the source marks a hidden class that this class defined at run time, usually a lambda. -verbose:class prints the same lines. That source: column turns "start-up is slow" into a histogram you can read. Check yourself before the Try it: a hidden class is generated in memory and has no class file. Why can its source: never start with file:? Count where your classes come from Read ClassSourcesDemo. It starts a second JVM with -Xlog:class+load, runs a little start-up work there (regex, java.time, a stream, String.format), and groups the log lines by source:. Predict: out of roughly 700 classes, how many come from the CDS archive? Then run it with the command below. Run it again with -Pargs=-Xshare:off added. This turns the archive off for the child JVM. Run the Kotlin twin (ClassSourcesDemoKt) once. Look at the file: line. ClassSourcesDemo.java package workbench.startup.l01.demo; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.time.LocalDate; import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; import java.util.regex.Pattern; import java.util.stream.Collectors; /** * Starts a second JVM with -Xlog:class+load, runs a little start-up work in it, and counts * where each loaded class came from. Extra arguments are passed to that JVM as flags. */ public class ClassSourcesDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("--work")) { work(); return; } List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(List.of(args)); // e.g. -Xshare:off cmd.addAll(List.of("-Xlog:class+load", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), ClassSourcesDemo.class.getName(), "--work")); Process child = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); Map<String, Integer> bySource = new TreeMap<>(); try (var lines = child.inputReader().lines()) { lines.filter(l -> l.contains(" source: ")) .forEach(l -> bySource.merge(bucket(l), 1, Integer::sum)); } child.waitFor(); int total = bySource.values().stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum(); System.out.printf("JDK %s, flags %s: %,d classes loaded%n", Runtime.version(), List.of(args), total); bySource.forEach((source, n) -> System.out.printf("%7d %s%n", n, source)); } /** Groups the "source:" field of a class+load line into a few buckets. */ static String bucket(String line) { String source = line.substring(line.indexOf(" source: ") + 9); if (source.equals("shared objects file")) return "shared objects file (the CDS archive)"; if (source.startsWith("jrt:/")) return "jrt:/ (the JDK's modules file, parsed now)"; if (source.startsWith("file:")) return "file: (your classes and JARs)"; return "other (hidden classes: lambdas, method handles)"; } /** A small taste of what services do at start-up: config, regex, dates, streams, lambdas. */ static void work() { Map<String, String> config = new TreeMap<>(); Pattern line = Pattern.compile("(\\w+(?:\\.\\w+)*)\\s*=\\s*(.*)"); for (String l : List.of("issuer.url = https://issuer.example", "pool.size = 20", "timeout.ms = 120")) { var m = line.matcher(l); if (m.matches()) config.put(m.group(1), m.group(2)); } String today = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 15).format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE); String summary = config.entrySet().stream() .map(e -> String.format("%s=%s", e.getKey(), e.getValue())) .collect(Collectors.joining(", ")); if (summary.isEmpty() || today.isEmpty()) throw new AssertionError(); } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l01/demo/ClassSourcesDemo.java ClassSourcesDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l01.demo import java.nio.file.Path import java.time.LocalDate import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter import java.util.TreeMap /** * Starts a second JVM with -Xlog:class+load, runs a little start-up work in it, and counts * where each loaded class came from. Extra arguments are passed to that JVM as flags. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "--work") { work() return } val cmd = buildList { add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()) addAll(args) // e.g. -Xshare:off addAll(listOf("-Xlog:class+load", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemoKt", "--work")) } val child = ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start() val bySource = TreeMap<String, Int>() child.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { " source: " in it }.forEach { bySource.merge(bucket(it), 1, Int::plus) } } child.waitFor() println("JDK ${Runtime.version()}, flags ${args.toList()}: %,d classes loaded".format(bySource.values.sum())) bySource.forEach { (source, n) -> println("%7d %s".format(n, source)) } } /** Groups the "source:" field of a class+load line into a few buckets. */ private fun bucket(line: String): String { val source = line.substringAfter(" source: ") return when { source == "shared objects file" -> "shared objects file (the CDS archive)" source.startsWith("jrt:/") -> "jrt:/ (the JDK's modules file, parsed now)" source.startsWith("file:") -> "file: (your classes and JARs, kotlin-stdlib too)" else -> "other (hidden classes: lambdas, method handles)" } } /** A small taste of what services do at start-up: config, regex, dates, collections, lambdas. */ private fun work() { val line = Regex("""(\w+(?:\.\w+)*)\s*=\s*(.*)""") val config = listOf("issuer.url = https://issuer.example", "pool.size = 20", "timeout.ms = 120") .mapNotNull { line.matchEntire(it)?.destructured } .associate { (key, value) -> key to value } .toSortedMap() val today = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 15).format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE) val summary = config.entries.joinToString(", ") { (k, v) -> "%s=%s".format(k, v) } check(summary.isNotEmpty() && today.isNotEmpty()) } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l01.demo.ClassSourcesDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l01/demo/ClassSourcesDemo.kt On JDK 21 on a shared Linux VM: 734 classes, 718 from the shared objects file, 8 from jrt:/, 7 hidden, and 1 from file: (the demo itself). With -Xshare:off: 767 classes, 747 parsed from jrt:/, 19 hidden, none shared. JDK 25.0.4 loaded 818 with 793 shared, and 831 with sharing off. The Kotlin twin loads 876, with 63 from file:, because the Kotlin standard library is a JAR on your classpath like any other. The java command (JDK 25 man page source): -Xlog and CDS docs Think of a shop that throws its stock away every night. Each morning someone unpacks every box, checks each item against the invoice, and puts it on a shelf before the first customer comes in. The lights going on is Create VM. The "open" sign is the framework's started in line. The first customer leaving with a receipt is the first 200, and that is the only moment the street cares about. A holder class is a box you leave sealed in the back until somebody asks for what is in it. The analogy breaks in one place: a real shop would keep its shelves stocked overnight. The JVM keeps nothing between runs unless you give it an archive, which is lesson 2.

h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Loading is lazy, and initialization is lazier
x: Loading a class and initializing it are two different events. The JVM loads a class when something needs its definition. It runs the class's static initializer, the method the bytecode calls <clinit>, only on the first active use: new, a call to a static method, a read or write of a static field that is not a compile-time constant, or a reflective call that asks for initialization. Initializing a subclass initializes its superclass first. Declaring a variable of the type does not initialize the class. Neither does Fees.class, which loads the class but runs no initializer. That rule decides what ends up on your start-up path. Here is a common shape: a table built in a static field. Java public final class BinTable { private static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build(); // runs in <clinit> public static String version() { return "bins-2026.11"; } public static String issuerOf(String pan) { return TABLE.get(pan.substring(0, 6)); } } Kotlin class BinTable { companion object { private val table = build() // also runs in BinTable's <clinit> fun version() = "bins-2026.11" fun issuerOf(pan: String) = table[pan.take(6)] } } The readiness check only logs version(). It still pays for the whole table, because calling any static method initializes the class, and the class's initializer builds the table. The Kotlin version has the same problem, and it surprises people. A companion object's properties compile to static fields of the outer class, and the outer class's <clinit> fills them. javap -p lists table as a private static final field of BinTable itself. The fix is the holder idiom: give the expensive field its own class. Java public final class BinTable { private static final class Holder { static final Map<String, String> TABLE = build(); // runs on first use of Holder } public static String version() { return "bins-2026.11"; } public static String issuerOf(String pan) { return Holder.TABLE.get(pan.substring(0, 6)); } } Kotlin object BinTable { fun version() = "bins-2026.11" fun issuerOf(pan: String) = Holder.table[pan.take(6)] private object Holder { val table = build() // a nested object is its own class } } Now version() touches only BinTable. The JVM loads and initializes Holder the first time issuerOf reads Holder.TABLE. It is also thread-safe without any lock in your code: the JVM initializes a class under its own lock (JLS 12.4.2), so if eight threads arrive at once, one runs the initializer and the others wait for it. In Kotlin, val table by lazy { build() } gives you the same laziness with a lock you can see. Lesson 5 of the memory model track, "Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders", shows why this is safe. Lazy is not always better. Moving the cost to the first request makes that request slow instead. Be lazy about work that many starts never need, such as admin tables or rarely used reports. Do the work early, on purpose, when every request needs it. Check the rule on a case the text didn't show: BinTable gets a public static final String VERSION = "bins-2026.11"; constant, and the readiness check reads BinTable.VERSION instead of calling version(). Does the table get built? (No. A compile-time constant is copied into the caller by javac, so reading it is not an active use of BinTable at all.) Every scale-out under load, every rolling deploy and every @QuarkusIntegrationTest JVM pays the whole start-up again, and a new pod is slowest at the moment traffic is highest. h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Three clocks, and only one is what users see
x: There are three start-up numbers, and people mix them up. The first is the JVM's own. -Xlog:startuptime prints the phases of creating the VM and ends with a line like Create VM, 0.0381310 secs. That is the JVM getting ready to run main. It says nothing about your code or your framework. The second is the framework's log line. Quarkus prints started in 0.968s. Listening on: http://localhost:8080. That number comes from inside the process, and every framework starts its clock at a slightly different place. The third is time to first request: from launching the process to the first successful response, measured from outside. This is the one that matters. A Kubernetes readiness probe, a load balancer and a user all see this clock and no other. It includes everything: the launcher, VM creation, class loading, framework start, and the first request itself, which loads more classes again (the HTTP handler path, JSON, your service code). On a shared 4-vCPU Linux VM, the demo below printed this for a tiny JDK HttpServer app on JDK 21: log : [0.031s][info][startuptime] Create VM, 0.0301657 secs log : started in 0.103s. Listening on: http://127.0.0.1:45969 first 200: 179 ms after launch, measured outside (15 attempts) 30 ms, 103 ms and 179 ms. The gap between the last two is the launcher, process creation, and the first request's own class loading. Even the first 200 is not the end. HotSpot has two JIT compilers: C1 compiles quickly with simple optimizations, and C2 compiles slowly into much faster code. Early requests run in the interpreter or in C1 code, and C2 only takes over a method after it has run often enough to be worth it. So time to first request and time to peak throughput are different numbers too. You can feel this when a new pod joins under load: it answers, but slowly, for a while. The performance track's first lesson, "From bytecode to machine code", goes into the tiers. Before the Try it, predict this: does -Xshare:off, which turns the CDS archive off, slow down Create VM too, or only the later clocks? Think about which classes the JVM loads while it creates itself. Read all three clocks Read FirstRequestTimer. It picks a free port, starts the same class as a service in a second JVM, polls /hello every 2 ms from outside, and stops the clock at the first 200. Run it with -Pargs=-Xlog:startuptime added to the command below. Note the three numbers. Predict what turning the archive off does to each clock, then run it with -Pargs='-Xlog:startuptime -Xshare:off'. h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Footprint is RSS, and the heap is only part of it
x: The same demo also reads the service's memory, and the numbers disagree by a factor of five. RSS : VmRSS: 53456 kB, RssAnon: 28824 kB, RssFile: 24632 kB NMT : Total: reserved=4901MB, committed=290MB NMT : Java Heap (reserved=3420MB, committed=216MB) Native Memory Tracking (NMT) is the JVM's own accounting. It says the JVM has committed 290 MB, 216 MB of it for the heap. The operating system says the process has 53 MB resident (RSS). Both are right. Committed memory is memory the JVM has asked the OS for. A page only becomes resident when someone touches it, and a fresh heap is mostly untouched pages. RSS is the number the container limit cares about. It is much more than the heap. It counts touched heap pages, metaspace and the class space, the JIT's code cache, GC data structures, thread stacks, the mapped CDS archive, the JDK's modules file, libjvm.so, direct buffers and malloc arenas. RssAnon is memory the process created for itself. RssFile is file-backed pages, such as the JDK's modules file and libjvm.so, and processes that map the same file can share them. For shared pages, Pss in /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup splits each one between the processes that map it. Measure it like this: ps -o pid,rss,args -p <pid> # RSS in kB, Linux and macOS grep -E 'VmRSS|RssAnon|RssFile' /proc/<pid>/status jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary # only if started with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary Don't use docker stats. The Quarkus guide on measuring performance says so in capitals: it "only measures a subset of the in-use resident pages", while a container is killed "based on its full RSS memory usage". It recommends ps -e -o pid,rss,args or docker top <id> -o pid,rss,args instead. One more trap: heap usage from your metrics dashboard is not footprint either. It leaves out everything in the list above, and it counts live objects, not the heap pages the GC has already touched. Check: a service starts with -Xms2g. Right after start-up, is its RSS about 2 GB? (No. The JVM commits 2 GB for the heap, but RSS grows only as the application and the GC touch those pages.) Committed is not resident Run FirstRequestTimer again with -Pargs=-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary. The demo asks the running service for its NMT summary with jcmd before it stops it. Compare the Total: committed line with VmRSS. Which one would a 512 MiB container limit compare against? On Linux, run cat /proc/self/status | grep Rss in a shell to see the same fields for cat itself. Then it reads the service's RSS. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.size > 1 && args[0] == "--serve") { serve(args[1].toInt()) return } val port = ServerSocket(0, 1, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress()).use { it.localPort } val cmd = buildList { add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()) addAll(args) // e.g. -Xlog:startuptime, -Xshare:off addAll(listOf("-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.startup.l01.demo.FirstRequestTimerKt", "--serve", port.toString())) } // 1. warm up our own HTTP client (nothing listens yet), then start the clock and the service val client = HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build() val hello = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:$port/hello")) .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).build() try { client.send(hello, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()) } catch (expected: IOException) { // refused: good, the client's own classes are loaded now } val t0 = System.nanoTime() val service = ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start() val serviceLog = CopyOnWriteArrayList<String>() thread(isDaemon = true) { service.inputReader().lines().forEach(serviceLog::add) } // 2. poll from outside every 2 ms until the first 200 var attempts = 0 var firstOk = -1L while (firstOk < 0 && System.nanoTime() - t0 < Duration.ofSeconds(5).toNanos()) { attempts++ try { if (client.send(hello, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).statusCode() == 200) { firstOk = System.nanoTime() - t0 } } catch (notUpYet: IOException) { Thread.sleep(2) } } // 3. footprint of the whole process, as the OS sees it, and the JVM's own accounting val rss = rss(service.pid()) val nmt = if (args.any { it.startsWith("-XX:NativeMemoryTracking") }) nmt(service.pid()) else emptyList() service.destroy() service.waitFor() println("JDK ${Runtime.version()}, flags ${args.toList()}") serviceLog.filter { "Create VM" in it || "started in" in it }.forEach { println(" log : $it") } println(" first 200: ${firstOk / 1_000_000} ms after launch, measured outside ($attempts attempts)") println(" RSS : $rss") nmt.forEach { println(" NMT : $it") } } /** Asks the running service for its Native Memory Tracking summary (needs -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary). */ private fun nmt(pid: Long): List<String> { val jcmd = Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "jcmd").toString() val p = ProcessBuilder(jcmd, pid.toString(), "VM.native_memory", "summary", "scale=MB") .redirectErrorStream(true).start() return p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { "Total:" in it || "Java Heap (" in it }.map { it.replace("-", "").trim() }.toList() } } /** RSS from /proc on Linux, from ps elsewhere. Both count the whole process, not just the heap. */ private fun rss(pid: Long): String { val status = Path.of("/proc", pid.toString(), "status") if (Files.exists(status)) { return Files.readAllLines(status) .filter { it.startsWith("VmRSS") || it.startsWith("RssAnon") || it.startsWith("RssFile") } .joinToString(", ") { it.replace(Regex("\\s+"), " ") } } val ps = ProcessBuilder("ps", "-o", "rss=", "-p", pid.toString()).start() return ps.inputStream.readAllBytes().decodeToString().trim() + " kB (ps)" } /** The service: one endpoint, and a Quarkus-style "started in" line, from the JVM's uptime. */ private fun serve(port: Int) { val server = HttpServer.create(InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port), 0) server.createContext("/hello") { exchange -> val body = """{"status":"AUTHORIZED","amountMinor":1250}""".toByteArray() exchange.responseHeaders.add("Content-Type", "application/json") exchange.sendResponseHeaders(200, body.size.toLong()) exchange.responseBody.write(body) exchange.close() } server.start() val uptimeMs = ManagementFactory.getRuntimeMXBean().uptime // since the JVM started println("started in %.3fs. Listening on: http://127.0.0.1:%d".format(uptimeMs / 1000.0, port)) } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l01.demo.FirstRequestTimerKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l01/demo/FirstRequestTimer.kt Here NMT reported committed=290MB with Java Heap ... committed=216MB, while VmRSS was about 53,000 kB. The JVM has reserved and committed far more than it has touched. The container limit counts resident memory, so RSS is the number to watch. On macOS the demo prints the ps value instead of the /proc breakdown. Quarkus: Measuring performance (RSS, not docker stats) read The common mistake is reading the wrong number and tuning against it. A team sees started in 0.9s in the Quarkus log and 180 MiB in docker stats and calls it done, while the readiness probe needs 2.5 s to see a 200 and the container's RSS is close to its limit. The framework's clock starts late and stops early, and docker stats counts only part of the resident pages. Measure time to first request from outside the process, read RSS from ps or /proc, and keep NMT for the question of where inside the JVM the memory went.

h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Java and Kotlin
x: A lazy table in Java and in Kotlin IssuerDirectory.java public final class IssuerDirectory { // eager: built in IssuerDirectory.<clinit>, on the first use of the class private static final Map<String, String> ALIASES = loadAliases(); // lazy: built in Holder.<clinit>, on the first read of Holder.BINS private static final class Holder { static final Map<String, String> BINS = loadBins(); } public static String version() { return "dir-v7"; } public static String issuerOf(String pan) { return Holder.BINS.get(pan.substring(0, 6)); } } IssuerDirectory.kt object IssuerDirectory { // eager: built in IssuerDirectory.<clinit>, on the first use of the object private val aliases = loadAliases() // lazy: Holder is its own class with its own <clinit> private object Holder { val bins = loadBins() } // also lazy, with a visible lock (LazyThreadSafetyMode.SYNCHRONIZED by default) val rates by lazy { loadRates() } fun version() = "dir-v7" fun issuerOf(pan: String) = Holder.bins[pan.take(6)] } Both compile to the same JVM mechanism: a static field filled in a class initializer, which runs once, on first active use, under the JVM's class-initialization lock. What differs is where Kotlin puts the fields. Properties of an object live in the object's class. Properties of a companion object live as static fields of the outer class, so touching the outer class at all builds them. A private nested object is the exact twin of Java's holder. by lazy is a library feature, not a JVM one: it allocates a Lazy object and takes a lock on first access, which costs a little but works for instance properties too, where the holder idiom cannot help.

h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Worked example
x: Find and fix a companion object that builds on start-up A readiness check calls FxRates.source() to report where the rates came from. Start-up got 400 ms slower after this class was added. Here it is, with the Java equivalent next to it. class FxRates { companion object { private val rates: Map<String, Double> = loadRatesFile() // 400 ms fun source() = "ecb-daily" fun rate(currency: String) = rates.getValue(currency) } } public final class FxRates { private static final Map<String, Double> RATES = loadRatesFile(); // 400 ms public static String source() { return "ecb-daily"; } public static double rate(String currency) { return RATES.get(currency); } } Check where the field lives with javap -p on the compiled class. The rates field sits on FxRates, not on the companion, and FxRates's static initializer fills it. So source() initializes FxRates, and that loads the file. $ javap -p build/classes/kotlin/main/com/acme/fx/FxRates.class public final class com.acme.fx.FxRates { public static final com.acme.fx.FxRates$Companion Companion; private static final java.util.Map<java.lang.String, java.lang.Double> rates; ... static {}; } Give the rates their own class. The readiness check now touches only FxRates. The first call to rate initializes Holder and pays the 400 ms once. object FxRates { fun source() = "ecb-daily" fun rate(currency: String) = Holder.rates.getValue(currency) // 1. its own class, so its own initializer private object Holder { val rates: Map<String, Double> = loadRatesFile() } } public final class FxRates { public static String source() { return "ecb-daily"; } public static double rate(String currency) { return Holder.RATES.get(currency); } // 1. its own class, so its own initializer private static final class Holder { static final Map<String, Double> RATES = loadRatesFile(); } } Prove it instead of trusting it. Start the service with -Xlog:class+load and grep for the class. After the fix, FxRates$Holder must not appear in the log until the first payment that needs a rate. $ java -Xlog:class+load -jar app.jar | grep FxRates [info][class,load] com.acme.fx.FxRates source: file:/srv/app.jar ... (readiness check passes, first payment arrives) ... [info][class,load] com.acme.fx.FxRates$Holder source: file:/srv/app.jar

h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Quiz
x: A Kubernetes readiness probe decides when your new pod gets traffic. Which number tells you how long that takes? The Create VM line from -Xlog:startuptime The framework's started in log line Time from launching the process until the readiness endpoint returns 200, measured from outside The time until C2 has compiled the hot methods The probe sees only the outside clock: launch to first successful response. Create VM stops before your code runs, and the framework's line is measured inside the process from wherever that framework starts counting. C2 compilation is about peak speed, which comes later still. A health check calls IssuerDirectory.version(). In Kotlin the class is class IssuerDirectory { companion object { val bins = loadBins(); fun version() = "v3" } }. Does the health check run loadBins()? No, companion objects are initialized lazily on first property access Yes: bins is a static field of IssuerDirectory, filled by its static initializer, which runs on this first use Only if the health check runs on a different thread No, because version() does not read bins Kotlin compiles a companion's properties to static fields on the outer class and initializes them in the outer class's <clinit>. Calling version() goes through IssuerDirectory.Companion, which initializes IssuerDirectory, which runs loadBins(). A private nested object or by lazy would keep it off this path. For one service you see: docker stats 180 MiB, NMT total committed 420 MiB, live heap after GC 90 MiB, ps -o rss 260 MiB. Which number is the footprint that counts against the container's memory limit? 180 MiB from docker stats 420 MiB committed 90 MiB of live heap 260 MiB of RSS RSS counts every resident page of the process, heap or not. Committed memory includes pages nobody has touched yet, live heap ignores metaspace, code cache, thread stacks and the rest, and the Quarkus guide warns that docker stats measures only a subset of the resident pages. Which of these runs the static initializer of class Fees (assuming nothing else has)? Class.forName("com.acme.Fees", false, loader) Declaring a local variable Fees f = null; Calling the static method Fees.version() Writing Fees.class to get its Class object Initialization happens on first active use, and a static method call is one. Class.forName with initialize=false loads the class without initializing it, a variable declaration needs neither, and a class literal gives you the Class object without running <clinit>. You run the same service with -Xshare:off. The number of loaded classes barely changes, but time to first request goes up by about 80 ms. Why? The JDK classes are now read and parsed from the modules file and verified, instead of mapped ready-made from the CDS archive The JIT is disabled with sharing off The heap is smaller, so the GC runs more The JVM now loads your classes twice -Xshare:off turns off the default CDS archive. The same classes still load, but each one now goes through finding, parsing and verifying in the JVM. In the demo the jrt:/ count jumped from 8 to 747. The JIT and the heap are not affected by this flag.

h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Explain it back

h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Key terms
x: Class loading Finding a class's bytes and turning them into the JVM's internal form in metaspace. Verification The check, done while linking, that a class's bytecode is type-safe before it runs. Static initializer (<clinit>) The method that sets a class's static fields and runs its static blocks, once, on first active use. Holder idiom Putting an expensive static field in a small nested class, so it is built on first use of that field only. Hidden class A class the JVM defines at run time with no class file, for example for a lambda. Time to first request From launching the process to the first successful response, measured from outside. RSS Resident set size: the memory pages of a process that are actually in RAM. NMT Native Memory Tracking: the JVM's own breakdown of the memory it has reserved and committed. What does each line of -Xlog:class+load tell you? The class name and its source:: shared objects file (CDS archive), jrt:/... (parsed from the JDK modules file), file:... (your classpath), or a defining class name for a hidden class such as a lambda. When does the JVM run a class's <clinit>? On first active use: new, a static method call, a read or write of a non-constant static field, initializing reflection, or initializing a subclass. Loading the class alone does not run it. Why is the holder idiom thread-safe with no lock in your code? The JVM initializes each class under its own initialization lock (JLS 12.4.2). One thread runs Holder.<clinit>; the others wait and then see the finished field. Is a Kotlin companion object property initialized lazily? No. It compiles to a static field of the outer class, filled by the outer class's <clinit>, so any first use of the outer class builds it. Use a private nested object or by lazy. What does the Create VM line of -Xlog:startuptime measure? Only the JVM's own creation, before main runs. Not class loading for your app, not framework start, not the first request. NMT says 290 MB committed and RSS is 53 MB. Which is resident memory? RSS. Committed memory has been requested from the OS, but untouched pages (most of a fresh heap) are not resident. Why not use docker stats for a JVM's footprint? It measures only a subset of the resident pages (Quarkus's measuring guide). Use ps -o rss, docker top <id> -o pid,rss,args or /proc/<pid>/status.

h: Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it · Go deeper
x: Loading is lazy, but not as lazy as the rule above suggests. Two things load classes you never called. The first is the verifier. To check that a method is type-safe, it sometimes needs to know whether one class is a subtype of another, for example when two branches produce different classes that meet at the same variable. To answer that, it loads both classes. A prototype of lesson 2's lab hit this: a test fixture whose static initializer read a field of its outer class pulled in the outer class, and verifying that class pulled in more. That is why the lab compares the exact set of classes your loader defined, taken from a run of the reference answer, and never a count of all loaded classes, which changes from one JDK build to the next. The second is the framework. Annotation scanning reads class files to find @Path or @ApplicationScoped, and reflection-driven dependency injection loads every bean class at start-up. This is the work Quarkus moves to build time. At build time it indexes the classes (Jandex), decides the wiring and generates plain bytecode that does it, so at run time there is no scanning and much less reflection. Its extension guide puts it as registering classes "at build time and generating code that registers them at static-init time instead of relying on reflection". Spring's AOT mode makes a similar move with a different design. If you want to see where a large app spends its start-up, -Xlog:class+load piped through sed -E 's/.*source: //' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head gives the same histogram as the demo, and the JFR jdk.ClassLoad event, which is off by default, records a stack trace for each load once you enable it. Measure first, then pick a fix from lessons 2 to 4.

h: Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache · The JDK already ships a class archive
x: Start with the cost. Turn sharing off and java -version alone makes the JVM find, parse and verify 440 classes before it prints one line. On a shared 4-vCPU VM that doubled the Create VM time from lesson 1, from about 27 ms to about 54 ms, and lesson 1's tiny service needed about 250 ms instead of about 180 ms to its first 200. Most JDK builds since JDK 12 avoid most of that work. They ship a class data sharing (CDS) archive, lib/server/classes.jsa, holding about 1,300 core JDK classes. The file does not contain class files. It contains the JVM's own internal structures for those classes, the ones it would otherwise build in metaspace, already parsed and verified, laid out as they sit in memory. At start-up the JVM memory-maps the file: it asks the OS to make the file part of its address space, so pages are read from disk only when they are touched. Then it fixes up the pointers and uses the classes as they are. This happens by default; -Xshare:off turns it off. java -version shows it. On JDK 21 that command loads 405 classes, and all 405 say source: shared objects file. With -Xshare:off it loads 440 classes and none are shared. The extra 35 are classes the JVM has to generate at run time when there is no archive to take them from. A JDK 21 package has two archives: classes.jsa (14.6 MB here) and classes_nocoops.jsa, for when compressed object pointers (32-bit object references, the default for heaps under 32 GB) are off. JDK 25 adds two _coh variants for compact object headers, a smaller object header layout that JEP 519 made a product feature in JDK 25 (still off by default). The JVM picks the archive that matches its flags. That tells you what CDS can and can't save. It saves the find, parse and verify steps from lesson 1. It does not run static initializers: those still run on first use, in the same order, so a class whose <clinit> takes 400 ms takes 400 ms with any archive. A test program that logs its initializer order printed identical output with and without a JDK 21 archive and a JDK 25 AOT cache. It also does nothing for the JIT, which still starts cold. Old articles also sell CDS as a way for JVMs on one host to share memory. Count on start-up time instead. Since JDK 21 the JVM maps archives at an alternative address by default (the log says ArchiveRelocationMode == 1), and patching the pointers writes to most pages, which makes them private. In one JDK 25 process, 11.5 MiB of the 14.4 MiB resident in the AOT cache's mapping were private dirty pages. Look at the default archive List the archives your JDK ships with the first command. Predict: with -Xshare:off, will java -version load more classes than with the archive, fewer, or the same number? Then count both with the next two commands. Run the last command to see which archive file the JVM opened. terminal ls -l "$JAVA_HOME"/lib/server/*.jsa java -Xlog:class+load -version 2>&1 | grep -c 'shared objects file' java -Xshare:off -Xlog:class+load -version 2>&1 | grep -c 'source:' java -Xlog:cds -version 2>&1 | grep -i opened On Ubuntu's JDK 21 build: two files, classes.jsa (14,581,760 bytes) and classes_nocoops.jsa; 405 shared classes; 440 classes with sharing off; and Opened archive .../lib/server/classes.jsa. On JDK 25.0.4: four files, including classes_coh.jsa and classes_nocoops_coh.jsa; 393 of 396 classes shared; 411 with sharing off. The java command, JDK 25: Class Data Sharing and the AOT cache (man page source) docs Without CDS, the JVM is a librarian who unpacks every book each morning, reads it, checks it for errors and only then shelves it. CDS is a bookcase that arrives already filled: you wheel it in and open the doors. The AOT cache is the same bookcase with the cross-references between books already filled in and sticky notes on the pages people read most. A training run is the day you watch which books people actually take. The analogy breaks at the worst place: a librarian would notice that the books in the wheeled-in bookcase are last year's edition. JDK 25 before 25.0.4 didn't.

h: Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache · AppCDS puts your own classes in the archive
x:
The default archive covers the JDK. AppCDS adds your own classes. It has been part of OpenJDK since JDK 10, and on JDK 21 it is the start-up gain you can have today without touching code. There are three ways to build one. The dynamic archive (JDK 13 and later) needs one training run. The JVM writes the archive when that run exits: java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main # training run java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main # every start after It stores only what the default archive lacks, so it is small: 1.47 MB for a 300-class app, where the static archive below was 12.9 MB because it holds the JDK classes too. The static archive takes three steps: record the class list, dump it, use it. java -Xshare:off -XX:DumpLoadedClassList=app.classlist -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main java -Xshare:dump -XX:SharedClassListFile=app.classlist -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp app.jar java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive (JDK 19 and later), used with -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa, folds this into your normal start command. If the file exists and came from the same JDK, the JVM uses it; if not, it writes one at exit. That is handy on a laptop and wrong for an immutable container: the file disappears with the pod, or the filesystem is read-only. Build the archive when you build the image. On JDK 21, on a shared 4-vCPU VM, the 300-class app's median CPU time fell from 349 ms with the default archive to 171 ms with a dynamic archive and 178 ms with a static one. Wall time fell from 333 ms to 196 ms and 191 ms. Your absolute numbers will differ. The halving is what carries over. The archive has rules. The class path must be JAR files, not directories of classes. The class path at run time must be the same as when the archive was made, or start with it. If a JAR changed after the archive was made, the JVM refuses the archive with warnings such as h21.jar timestamp has changed and size has changed, and runs normally from the JARs. It keeps using the default archive for the JDK classes. On JDK 21 this check works; keep that in mind for the last section. Check: in development you run the app with -cp build/classes/java/main:libs/*.jar and add -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa. What happens at exit? (JDK 21 refuses: Cannot have non-empty directory in paths. Package the classes into a JAR first, as the Try it does.) Climb the archive ladder Read ArchiveLadder. It packs its own package into startup/build/boot02/app.jar (CDS wants JARs), then runs the same small workload under each setup and counts the source: lines. Predict the "from archive" column for the dynamic AppCDS row, then run it. Run the Kotlin twin. Its class path is the app JAR plus kotlin-stdlib, and both go into the archive. Gradle runs demos on the JDK that runs Gradle. If that is JDK 21, run the class with a JDK 25 java to get the AOT cache row: java -cp startup/build/classes/java/demo workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadder. h: Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache · Leyden's AOT cache: train, assemble, run
x: Leyden's AOT cache: train, assemble, then start with the classes already loaded and linked Project Leyden is the OpenJDK project that moves start-up work out of production runs. Its first result is the AOT cache, built one JEP at a time: JDK What arrived 24 JEP 483: the AOT cache, with classes already loaded and linked; flags -XX:AOTMode, -XX:AOTConfiguration, -XX:AOTCache 25 (LTS) JEP 514: one-step -XX:AOTCacheOutput. JEP 515: method profiles from training, for faster warm-up 26 JEP 516: the full cache works with every GC, ZGC included 27 no Leyden JEP; -XX:AOTMode=required becomes the name for on 28, in development JEP 544: compiled code in the cache The java man page names three phases. In training you run the app with a representative workload, and the JVM records what it loaded and linked into an AOT configuration file. In assembly the JVM turns that file into the cache; your application does not run. In production you start with the cache. On JDK 25 one command does the first two: java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main # training + assembly, JDK 25+ java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main # production When training and assembly run in different pipeline stages, use the two-step form from JDK 24: java -XX:AOTMode=record -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -cp app.jar com.acme.pay.Main java -XX:AOTMode=create -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar The one-step command does the same underneath: after training it starts a second JVM with -XX:AOTMode=create, passing the settings through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. The cache holds more than an AppCDS archive. Normally the JVM resolves references lazily: the first time an instruction runs, it turns a symbolic name in the constant pool, such as java/util/Map.get, into a pointer to the real method. The first run of a lambda does more: its invokedynamic instruction calls a bootstrap method that generates the lambda's hidden class. The AOT cache stores the results of that work from the training run: classes already linked, those references and invokedynamic call sites already resolved (these modes switch on -XX:+AOTClassLinking), Java objects the JVM would build at start-up, such as its module graph, and on JDK 25 the method profiles, the counts that tell the JIT what is hot. The JVM loads and links every cached class before main runs, so it reports more classes loaded than without the cache, all from the archive. Code that training never ran gets none of this; it is resolved lazily, as before. On JDK 25 on the same VM, the 300-class app went from 504 ms of CPU to 81 ms, from 431 ms to 98 ms of wall time, and from 64 MiB to 42 MiB of max RSS. A JDK HttpServer app's median time to first request fell from 218 ms to 136 ms. Quarkus's perf lab measured time to first request of 4,417 ms in JVM mode and 1,859 ms with the cache, with peak throughput about 7% lower. Quarkus 3.40 wires it up for you. Set quarkus.package.jar.aot.enabled=true and it trains the cache while your @QuarkusIntegrationTests run and writes target/quarkus-app/app.aot; start with java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -jar quarkus-run.jar. Its aot-jar packaging leaves all class loading to the JDK's own loaders, because Leyden does not support custom class loaders yet. The docs add the rule the lab makes concrete: "The more representative your integration tests are of production traffic, the more effective the AOT cache will be." Make an AOT cache by hand (JDK 25+) Run ArchiveLadder once (previous Try it) so startup/build/boot02/app.jar exists. Then cd labs/startup/build/boot02 and use a JDK 25 java. Run the first command: training and assembly in one go. Find the Launching child process and Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS lines. Run the second command and look for Opened AOT cache. Predict the count from the third command, which names a file that doesn't exist. Then run it. terminal (JDK 25+) java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=pay.aot -cp app.jar workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadder --work java -XX:AOTCache=pay.aot -Xlog:aot -cp app.jar workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadder --work | grep Opened java -XX:AOTCache=nope.aot -Xlog:class+load -cp app.jar workbench.startup.l02.demo.ArchiveLadder --work | grep -c 'shared objects file' On 25.0.4.1 the first command printed Temporary AOTConfiguration recorded: pay.aot.config, Launching child process ... to assemble AOT cache pay.aot, a Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: ... -XX:AOTMode=create line, and AOTCache creation is complete: pay.aot ... bytes (about 11.5 MB). The second printed Opened AOT cache pay.aot. The third printed errors ending in Unable to map shared spaces, still ran the app, and counted 0 shared classes: a bad cache path also loses the default archive. Training records what the app loads and links, assembly writes the cache without running the app, and production maps it. x: A training entry point in Java and Kotlin TrainingMain.java /** Starts the service, drives every kind of request production sees, then exits so the JVM writes the cache. */ public final class TrainingMain { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { PaymentService service = PaymentService.start(); // the same wiring as production for (String fixture : List.of("authorize-eur.json", "authorize-usd.json", "refund.json", "capture.json")) { service.handle(Fixtures.load(fixture)); // real code paths, fake card issuer } service.stop(); System.exit(0); // JDK 24/25 write the training data when the JVM exits } } TrainingMain.kt /** Starts the service, drives every kind of request production sees, then exits so the JVM writes the cache. */ fun main() { val service = PaymentService.start() // the same wiring as production listOf("authorize-eur.json", "authorize-usd.json", "refund.json", "capture.json") .forEach { service.handle(Fixtures.load(it)) } // real code paths, fake card issuer service.stop() exitProcess(0) // JDK 24/25 write the training data when the JVM exits } The cache does not care which language produced the bytecode. What differs is the class path and the entry point. A Kotlin service has kotlin-stdlib (and often kotlinx-coroutines) as JARs on the class path, and they must be there in the same order in training and in production, or the cache is refused. The training entry point is TrainingMainKt, not TrainingMain. Kotlin 2.x compiles lambdas to invokedynamic, like Java, so the cache can pre-resolve those call sites in both. Before JDK 26 the training run has to exit to write its data, which is why both versions end the process; JDK 26 adds jcmd <pid> AOT.end_recording for long-running servers.

x: You add -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa, a dynamic archive, and run with -Xlog:class+load on JDK 21. Most JDK classes log source: shared objects file, but your own classes log source: file:/srv/app.jar. What does that tell you? The JVM rejected your dynamic archive and kept only the default one, so look for the warning that says why Everything works: app classes are always logged with their JAR Your classes are archived but -Xlog:class+load can't see that The default archive failed and your archive replaced it Archived classes log source: shared objects file, yours included. When JDK 21 rejects a dynamic archive (a changed JAR, a different class path) it warns and keeps the default archive underneath, so the JDK classes stay shared and only yours load from the JAR. The warning lines at the start of the output say which check failed. Your integration tests, which train the AOT cache, only send card authorizations. In production a refund arrives. What happens on the refund path? The refund fails with ClassNotFoundException The JVM throws away the whole cache Its classes load the usual way from the JAR, parsed and verified at that moment, so the first refund is slower The JVM retrains the cache in the background The cache contains what the training run loaded. Anything else loads the usual way, so the program is still correct, but those classes get no head start. That is why the training workload should look like production traffic, which is what the lab's missing function measures. A service runs ZGC on JDK 25. Its AOT cache was trained with the default G1. What do you get? The full speed-up, because the cache does not depend on the GC Only the method profiles A crash at start-up Nothing: the JVM can't use the G1-trained cache under ZGC and runs with zero archived classes On JDK 25 a G1-trained cache gave 0 archived classes under -XX:+UseZGC. Training under ZGC helps only partly. JDK 26's JEP 516 stores heap objects in a form every GC can load, so the full cache works with ZGC from 26 on. A platform team adds an APM agent to every pod through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS. Your service starts with -XX:AOTMode=on -XX:AOTCache=app.aot. What is the risk? None: on only means the cache is enabled If the agent's options are incompatible with the cache, the JVM exits at start-up instead of running without the cache The agent's classes get added to the cache The cache is rebuilt on every start on (required from JDK 27) is a fail-fast setting: if the cache can't be used, the JVM stops. The man page lists certain JVMTI options among the incompatible ones, and the JDK 27 page warns about exactly this case. In production leave the mode at the default auto, which falls back to running without the cache. A JDK 21 service runs in an immutable container with a read-only root filesystem. You want AppCDS with no code change. Which setup fits? -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive -XX:SharedArchiveFile=/app/app.jsa in the start command -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot in the start command A dynamic archive made at image build time with -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit, shipped in the image and used with -XX:SharedArchiveFile -Xshare:off, for predictable start-up AutoCreateSharedArchive writes the file at the exit of a run that had none, which fails on a read-only filesystem and is lost with a short-lived pod anyway. Building the archive during the image build gives every pod the same archive from its first start. -XX:AOTCacheOutput needs JDK 25.
