h: Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache · Key terms
x: CDS Class data sharing: classes stored pre-parsed in a .jsa file that the JVM maps at start-up. Default CDS archive The archive of about 1,300 JDK classes that ships in lib/server/classes.jsa and is used unless -Xshare:off. AppCDS A CDS archive that also holds your application's classes. AOT cache Leyden's archive (JDK 24+): classes loaded and linked ahead of time, heap objects, and from JDK 25 method profiles. Training run A run of the app with a representative workload that records what to put in the archive or cache. Assembly The step that turns the training data into the AOT cache; the application itself does not run. AOTMode The flag that sets how the JVM treats the cache: auto (default), record, create, on or required (27+), off. What work does a CDS archive save at start-up? Finding, parsing and verifying the archived classes: the JVM maps them ready-made from the .jsa file. Static initializers still run at first use. The two commands for a dynamic AppCDS archive (JDK 13+)? java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -cp app.jar Main, then java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp app.jar Main. The two commands for an AOT cache on JDK 25? java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -cp app.jar Main (training and assembly), then java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar Main. Which JDK builds can run stale classes from an AOT cache after the JAR changed? 25.0.0 to 25.0.3 and 26.0.0 to 26.0.1 (JDK-8377932). Fixed in 25.0.4, 26.0.2 and 27. -XX:AOTCache= names a missing or stale file, default mode. What do you get? The app runs with no archive at all, not even the default CDS archive, so it starts slower than with no flag. Where does -XX:AOTMode=on (JDK 27: required) belong? In CI, as a fail-fast check that the cache opens. Not in production, where an incompatible agent would stop the JVM from starting. From which JDK does the full AOT cache work with ZGC? JDK 26 (JEP 516). On JDK 25 a G1-trained cache gives nothing under ZGC, and a ZGC-trained one only part of the gain.

h: Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache · Go deeper
x: A few details that matter once you run this for real. The static archive is dumped in interpreter-only mode, as if -Xint were set, so the output is deterministic, bit for bit. For big class lists you can add -Xmixed to speed up the dump when you don't need that. You can also take an archive from a running process: jcmd <pid> VM.cds dynamic_dump app.jsa, if the process was started with -XX:+RecordDynamicDumpInfo, or jcmd <pid> VM.cds static_dump app.jsa. That suits a service whose real warm-up needs real traffic. To try flags without editing start scripts, JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa works, because the JVM reads that variable at start. In the AOT cache file names, %p and %t are replaced by the PID and the start time, as in -XX:AOTCacheOutput=pay%p.aot, so parallel training runs don't overwrite each other. The man page lags behind the code in one place: the JDK 25 page still says the cache holds "Java classes and heap objects" and that profiles will come in a future release, although JEP 515 shipped profiles in JDK 25. The JDK 28 development page lists classes, heap objects, execution profiles and compiled methods. What's next in Leyden, as of the JDK 28 development line: JEP 544 moves JIT compilation into the training run and ships the native code in the cache, while the JIT can still recompile in production. JEP 545 targets start-up and warm-up with ZGC. Neither is in a released JDK yet, so treat them as previews of where this is going, not as flags to use.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Native image builds a closed world
x: Lesson 2's AOT cache makes the JVM start faster, but it is still a JVM: it maps classes, links what training missed, interprets, and waits for the JIT. In Quarkus's benchmark below, the first request still took 1,859 ms with the cache. Native image removes that work from the start by doing it all in the build. native-image, from GraalVM or from Mandrel (the distribution "tailored for Quarkus"), takes your class path and builds one executable for one OS and CPU, in three steps. First it analyzes: starting at main, it follows every method call and field access it can see, and works out which classes can show up at each call. Second it runs static initializers where it can, and saves the objects they created into the image heap, a section of the executable that is mapped into memory at start-up. Third it compiles every reachable method to machine code. Code the analysis never reached is left out, and so are the JDK classes nothing uses. This is the closed-world assumption: everything the program will ever run is known when you build it. The binary runs on a small runtime, SubstrateVM, with no class loading, no bytecode verification, no interpreter and no JIT. That is why it starts fast and stays small. The Quarkus docs publish a tuned benchmark (Quarkus 3.34.3, JDK 25.0.2): JVM JVM + AOT cache Native (Mandrel) Time to first request 4,417 ms 1,859 ms 581 ms Peak throughput 13,265 tps 12,389 tps 5,411 tps RSS 304 MiB 240 MiB 95 MiB Build about 30 s build plus a training run 3 to 10 min, 4 to 8 GB of RAM Peak throughput is 59% lower. With no JIT there are no run-time profiles, and GraalVM's own docs say that "without profiling information, it is difficult to generate machine code of the same quality as a JIT compiler". Profile-guided optimization (PGO: building again with profiles recorded from a test run) narrows the gap, but "PGO is not available in GraalVM Community Edition". The default garbage collector is Serial, a single-threaded collector "optimized for low footprint and small Java heap sizes"; G1 is available only in Oracle GraalVM, on Linux. The other price is everything the analysis can't see: reflection, dynamic proxies, resources loaded by name, JNI (calls into native C code) and serialization. The analysis copes with constants. GraalVM works out reflective calls at build time "given that all the call arguments are constant", so Class.forName("com.acme.pay.Fees") with a literal just works. Class.forName(record.headers().get("type")) does not: the class name arrives with the Kafka message, and the build can't know it. You have to tell the build, or the call fails at run time. Current GraalVM throws MissingReflectionRegistrationError, which "extends java.lang.Error and should not be handled". A class name that only exists at run time Read DynamicLookupDemo. It calls a static no-argument method chosen by two strings. Run it as is, then with -Pargs='java.util.UUID randomUUID'. Any class on the class path works on the JVM. Ask yourself which classes a build would have to keep to support every possible argument. That is why the build needs a list. Optional, needs a GraalVM JDK: run the class with java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=build/ni -cp startup/build/classes/java/demo workbench.startup.l03.demo.DynamicLookupDemo java.util.UUID randomUUID and look at the JSON the agent wrote into build/ni. DynamicLookupDemo.java package workbench.startup.l03.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Method; /** * Calls a static, no-argument method chosen at run time, by class name and method name. * On the JVM any class on the class path works. A native image can only do this for the * classes and methods listed in its reachability metadata, so the demo prints that entry too. */ public class DynamicLookupDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String className = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "java.time.LocalDate"; String methodName = args.length > 1 ? args[1] : "now"; Class<?> type = Class.forName(className); // a name from data: the analysis can't see it Method method = type.getMethod(methodName); System.out.println(className + "." + methodName + "() = " + method.invoke(null)); System.out.println("A native image needs this in reachability-metadata.json:"); System.out.printf("{ \"reflection\": [ { \"type\": \"%s\", \"methods\": [ { \"name\": \"%s\", \"parameterTypes\": [] } ] } ] }%n", type.getName(), method.getName()); } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l03.demo.DynamicLookupDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l03/demo/DynamicLookupDemo.java DynamicLookupDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l03.demo /** * Calls a static, no-argument method chosen at run time, by class name and method name. * On the JVM any class on the class path works. A native image can only do this for the * classes and methods listed in its reachability metadata, so the demo prints that entry too. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val className = args.getOrElse(0) { "java.time.LocalDate" } val methodName = args.getOrElse(1) { "now" } val type = Class.forName(className) // a name from data: the analysis can't see it val method = type.getMethod(methodName) println("$className.$methodName() = ${method.invoke(null)}") println("A native image needs this in reachability-metadata.json:") println("""{ "reflection": [ { "type": "${type.name}", "methods": [ { "name": "${method.name}", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ] }""") } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l03.demo.DynamicLookupDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l03/demo/DynamicLookupDemo.kt The first run prints today's date and the entry { "type": "java.time.LocalDate", "methods": [ { "name": "now", "parameterTypes": [] } ] }. The second prints a random UUID and an entry for java.util.UUID and randomUUID. On the JVM both just work. A native image would work only for the class and method its metadata listed. The analysis follows calls from main. A class reached only through a name in the data is in the binary only if the metadata lists it. GraalVM: Reachability Metadata docs A JVM is a library with every book on the shelves: you can ask for any title, at any time. A native image is a printed booklet with only the pages someone proved you will read, bound in one cover. It is thin and opens instantly. But if your code looks up a page by a name that arrives in a message, the page has to be on the list you gave the printer, or it isn't in the booklet. Build-time initialization is the printer filling in the blanks on some pages before binding, so a date written there is the printing date. The analogy breaks on speed: a booklet is read faster than a library is searched, but a native binary runs hot code slower than a warmed JVM, because no one rewrites the pages after watching how you read.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Reflection and proxies need reachability metadata
x: You tell the build in reachability-metadata.json, placed in META-INF/native-image/<groupId>/<artifactId>/ on the class path. The current schema is v1.2.0, and its top level has four keys: reflection, resources, foreign and comment. Proxies, serialization and JNI all live inside reflection entries. A reflection entry names a type and the members your code uses: { "reflection": [ { "condition": { "typeReached": "com.acme.pay.EventDecoder" }, "type": "com.acme.pay.PaymentAuthorized", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, { "name": "paymentId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ] } A constructor is called <init>. Parameter types are fully qualified, primitives by name (long, int), and every method needs parameterTypes, even an empty one. Instead of listing members you can set allDeclaredConstructors or allPublicMethods, which keeps more code in the binary. The optional condition switches the entry on only once EventDecoder is reached at run time, which means just before its initializer starts; EventDecoder.class on its own doesn't count. A JDK dynamic proxy is a reflection entry whose type is an ordered list of interfaces: { "reflection": [ { "type": { "proxy": ["com.acme.pay.CardIssuerClient", "java.lang.AutoCloseable"] } } ] } The order is part of the proxy's identity: a proxy for (A, B) is a different class from one for (B, A). If the proxy gets serialized, add "serializable": true; the docs say proxies "can only be registered for serialization via the JSON files". Two warnings about documentation. The older schema, v1.1.0, had separate top-level jni and serialization sections, and some GraalVM prose still shows a top-level jni array; v1.2.0 rejects it. The current Quarkus main-branch docs say to use "a proxy section", which v1.2.0 also rejects. Check your file against the schema of the GraalVM you build with. You rarely write all of it by hand. The tracing agent watches a run on a normal JVM and writes what it saw: java -agentlib:native-image-agent=config-output-dir=build/ni-config -jar app.jar. Like an AOT training run, it only sees the code paths you exercise, so drive it with your integration tests and then read what it wrote. To make gaps fail loudly, build with --exact-reachability-metadata and run the tests with -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit. The order of proxy interfaces Read ProxyOrderDemo. It builds three proxies: (IssuerApi, AutoCloseable), (AutoCloseable, IssuerApi), and the first pair again. Predict the two same class lines before you run it. Run it, then the Kotlin twin. ProxyOrderDemo.java package workbench.startup.l03.demo; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.Arrays; /** Builds two JDK dynamic proxies from the same two interfaces, in opposite orders. */ public class ProxyOrderDemo { public interface IssuerApi { String authorize(String paymentId); } public static void main(String[] args) { InvocationHandler handler = (proxy, method, a) -> method.getName().equals("authorize") ? "APPROVED " + a[0] : null; ClassLoader loader = ProxyOrderDemo.class.getClassLoader(); Object first = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {IssuerApi.class, AutoCloseable.class}, handler); Object second = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {AutoCloseable.class, IssuerApi.class}, handler); Object again = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {IssuerApi.class, AutoCloseable.class}, handler); System.out.println("first : " + first.getClass().getName() + " " + names(first.getClass())); System.out.println("second: " + second.getClass().getName() + " " + names(second.getClass())); System.out.println("same class for (A, B) and (B, A)? " + (first.getClass() == second.getClass())); System.out.println("same class for (A, B) twice? " + (first.getClass() == again.getClass())); System.out.println(((IssuerApi) first).authorize("pay_81")); } static String names(Class<?> c) { return Arrays.toString(Arrays.stream(c.getInterfaces()).map(Class::getSimpleName).toArray()); } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l03.demo.ProxyOrderDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l03/demo/ProxyOrderDemo.java ProxyOrderDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l03.demo import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler import java.lang.reflect.Proxy /** Builds two JDK dynamic proxies from the same two interfaces, in opposite orders. */ interface IssuerApi { fun authorize(paymentId: String): String } fun main() { val handler = InvocationHandler { _, method, a -> if (method.name == "authorize") "APPROVED ${a[0]}" else null } val loader = IssuerApi::class.java.classLoader val first = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, arrayOf(IssuerApi::class.java, AutoCloseable::class.java), handler) val second = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, arrayOf(AutoCloseable::class.java, IssuerApi::class.java), handler) val again = Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, arrayOf(IssuerApi::class.java, AutoCloseable::class.java), handler) fun names(c: Class<*>) = c.interfaces.map { it.simpleName } println("first : ${first.javaClass.name} ${names(first.javaClass)}") println("second: ${second.javaClass.name} ${names(second.javaClass)}") println("same class for (A, B) and (B, A)? ${first.javaClass == second.javaClass}") println("same class for (A, B) twice? ${first.javaClass == again.javaClass}") println((first as IssuerApi).authorize("pay_81")) } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l03.demo.ProxyOrderDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l03/demo/ProxyOrderDemo.kt The first two proxies are different classes, jdk.proxy1.$Proxy0 and jdk.proxy1.$Proxy1, so same class for (A, B) and (B, A)? prints false. The repeat of the first pair reuses $Proxy0 and prints true. The JVM caches one proxy class per ordered interface list, which is why the metadata lists interfaces in order. Reachability metadata schema v1.2.0 (JSON schema) docs A Kafka consumer in a payments service is the classic native trap: the deserializer picks the event class from a header, Jackson creates it and calls its accessors by reflection, and a REST client to the card issuer is a dynamic proxy. In Quarkus the extensions register what they know about, and you add @RegisterForReflection to your event classes, or targets = [...] for event classes from a shared schema library you can't annotate. Look for static state that must differ per pod: an instance id for idempotency keys, a start timestamp in health output, a SecureRandom for nonces. Under build-time initialization they'd be the same in every pod, and some won't even build. Native pays off for scale-to-zero functions and for packing many small services on a node. For a consumer that runs all day at high throughput, the 59% lower peak in Quarkus's benchmark is usually the deciding number.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · The build is your program's first run
x: Class initialization is the other half of the story. GraalVM's docs give the numbers: "the simple 'Hello, World!' application requires more than 300 classes to be initialized", and in code compiled ahead of time, the check "is this class initialized yet?" on every access "can reduce performance by more than twofold". So the builder runs static initializers at build time where it can, and stores what they produced in the image heap. Plain GraalVM initializes most JDK classes at build time, and your classes only when it can prove that safe. An initializer that calls native code (System.out.println counts), makes a virtual call it can't pin to one target, or reaches a substituted method stays at run time. Quarkus goes further: "By default, Quarkus initializes all classes at build time." So your static initializer runs on the build machine, once, and its results are frozen into the binary: Java static final Instant STARTED_AT = Instant.now(); // the build's time, on every start static final Random JITTER = new Random(); // the builder refuses this one Kotlin val startedAt: Instant = Instant.now() // the build's time, on every start val jitter = Random() // the builder refuses this one The builder catches some of these. Quarkus lists two errors you are likely to meet: "Detected an instance of Random/SplittableRandom class in the image heap. Instances created during image generation have cached seed values", and "No instances are allowed in the image heap for a class that is initialized or reinitialized at image runtime: sun.security.provider.NativePRNG". Don't count on it for the rest. A timestamp, a hostname, a token fetched at start: whatever an initializer computes, every container started from that image sees the value from the build. The fix is to initialize that class at run time: quarkus.native.additional-build-args=--initialize-at-run-time=com.acme.pay.InstanceInfo\\,com.acme.pay.RetryJitter Quarkus needs the comma escaped. With plain native-image the options are --initialize-at-run-time= and --initialize-at-build-time=, and -H:+PrintClassInitialization reports what was initialized where. Better still, keep per-instance values out of static initializers, and compute them in a method that runs at start-up. Values that would be frozen at build time Read BuildTimeInitDemo. Two static fields are set in a class initializer. Run it twice and compare the output of the two runs. Now imagine the class was initialized at build time, the Quarkus default. Which line would be the same on every start of every pod, and which one would stop the build? BuildTimeInitDemo.java package workbench.startup.l03.demo; import java.time.Instant; import java.util.Random; /** * Static state computed in a class initializer. On the JVM it is computed again on every start. * In a native image built with build-time initialization (the Quarkus default), the initializer * runs once, inside the build, and every start of the binary sees the build's values. */ public class BuildTimeInitDemo { static final class InstanceInfo { static final Instant STARTED_AT = Instant.now(); // build-time init: the build's time, forever static final Random JITTER = new Random(); // build-time init: the native builder rejects it } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("started at: " + InstanceInfo.STARTED_AT); System.out.println("retry jitter ms: " + InstanceInfo.JITTER.nextInt(250)); } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l03.demo.BuildTimeInitDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l03/demo/BuildTimeInitDemo.java BuildTimeInitDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l03.demo import java.time.Instant import java.util.Random /** * Static state computed in a class initializer. On the JVM it is computed again on every start. * In a native image built with build-time initialization (the Quarkus default), the initializer * runs once, inside the build, and every start of the binary sees the build's values. */ object InstanceInfo { val startedAt: Instant = Instant.now() // build-time init: the build's time, forever val jitter = Random() // build-time init: the native builder rejects it } fun main() { println("started at: ${InstanceInfo.startedAt}") println("retry jitter ms: ${InstanceInfo.jitter.nextInt(250)}") } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l03.demo.BuildTimeInitDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l03/demo/BuildTimeInitDemo.kt On the JVM each run prints a new started at time and a new jitter value, because the initializer runs at every start. Initialized at build time, started at would print the build's timestamp forever, in every container. The Random in the image heap is one of the cases the builder refuses, with the "cached seed values" error. GraalVM: Class Initialization in Native Image docs

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Quarkus writes most of the metadata for you
x: In a Quarkus app you rarely touch the JSON. Quarkus extensions know what their libraries reflect on, and Quarkus generates reachability-metadata.json itself. Your part is the classes only your code knows about, and annotations are the way to declare them: Java @RegisterForReflection public record PaymentAuthorized(String paymentId, String currency, long amountMinor) { } @RegisterForReflection(targets = {IssuerResponse.class, IssuerError.class}) // a library's classes public class IssuerReflectionConfig { } @RegisterForProxy(targets = {CardIssuerClient.class, AutoCloseable.class}) // order matters public class IssuerProxyConfig { } Kotlin @RegisterForReflection data class PaymentAuthorized(val paymentId: String, val currency: String, val amountMinor: Long) @RegisterForReflection(targets = [IssuerResponse::class, IssuerError::class]) // a library's classes class IssuerReflectionConfig @RegisterForProxy(targets = [CardIssuerClient::class, AutoCloseable::class]) // order matters class IssuerProxyConfig @RegisterForReflection registers methods and fields by default, plus any nested classes unless you set ignoreNested = true. With targets it registers the listed classes and not the class it sits on, which is how you cover a library's classes that you can't annotate. serialization = true adds Java serialization. @RegisterForProxy takes the interfaces in order, and the Quarkus docs repeat that "the order of the specified proxy interfaces is significant". Resources go in application.properties: quarkus.native.resources.includes=templates/**,rates/*.csv. When you do need JSON, put it in src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image/<group-id>/<artifact-id>/; the current docs warn that Quarkus overwrites a file placed directly in META-INF/native-image/. The Quarkus 3.x guides still show the older separate files, reflect-config.json and proxy-config.json, while the 4.0 guides say those legacy files "are not supported". Write the unified reachability-metadata.json and the file survives the upgrade. ./mvnw verify -Dnative builds the binary and runs your @QuarkusIntegrationTests against it. Because a native build takes minutes and gigabytes, most teams run it in CI and develop in JVM mode. Quarkus's own advice is "Start with JVM mode. Move to native when you have a concrete need." Lesson 4 of this track turns that into a decision table. Check before the lab: your event classes live in a shared payment-events JAR that another team owns, so you can't annotate them. Which annotation do you add, and on which class? (@RegisterForReflection(targets = {...}) on any class in your own code, listing their classes; the class carrying the annotation is not registered itself.) Quarkus 3.40: Tips for writing native applications docs The usual mistake is copying a metadata snippet from an old blog post or from a different GraalVM version and trusting it. A top-level "proxy" or "jni" array, or a reflect-config.json dropped into a Quarkus 4 project, either fails schema v1.2.0 or is ignored, and the proxy or class it was meant to cover fails at run time in the one code path your smoke test didn't hit. Write proxies as reflection entries with "type": {"proxy": [...]}, prefer @RegisterForReflection and @RegisterForProxy in Quarkus, and run the native integration tests with -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit so a gap fails the build instead of a payment.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Java and Kotlin
x: The same event class registered from Java and from Kotlin PaymentAuthorized.java @RegisterForReflection public record PaymentAuthorized(String paymentId, String currency, long amountMinor) { } // the same thing by hand in reachability-metadata.json: // { "type": "com.acme.pay.PaymentAuthorized", // "methods": [ // { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, // { "name": "paymentId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } PaymentAuthorized.kt @RegisterForReflection data class PaymentAuthorized(val paymentId: String, val currency: String, val amountMinor: Long) // the same thing by hand: the accessor is a getter on the JVM // { "type": "com.acme.pay.PaymentAuthorized", // "methods": [ // { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, // { "name": "getPaymentId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } The annotation is the same, and Quarkus reads it the same way from both languages. What differs is the bytecode it describes. A Java record has an accessor named paymentId(). A Kotlin val paymentId compiles to a private field and a method named getPaymentId(). Hand-written metadata names JVM members, so the two entries differ even though the sources look alike. A non-null Kotlin Long is the primitive long in the constructor's signature; Long? would be java.lang.Long. Annotation arrays are {...} with .class in Java and [...] with ::class in Kotlin.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Worked example
x: Write the metadata for a Kafka event decoder Here is the decoder. Find every reflective call and, for each, the exact member it needs. Ignore code that uses classes by name in source, such as new or a direct method call: the analysis sees those. Object decode(ConsumerRecord<String, String> rec) throws ReflectiveOperationException { Class<?> type = Class.forName(new String(rec.headers().lastHeader("type").value())); // 1 Object event = type.getConstructor(String.class, String.class, long.class) // 2 .newInstance(rec.key(), currencyOf(rec), amountOf(rec)); audit.log(type.getMethod("paymentId").invoke(event)); // 3 return event; } fun decode(rec: ConsumerRecord<String, String>): Any { val type = Class.forName(String(rec.headers().lastHeader("type").value())) // 1 val event = type.getConstructor(String::class.java, String::class.java, Long::class.javaPrimitiveType) // 2 .newInstance(rec.key(), currencyOf(rec), amountOf(rec)) audit.log(type.getMethod("paymentId").invoke(event)) // 3 return event } Three needs: (1) the class by name, for every event type the topic can carry; (2) its (String, String, long) constructor; (3) its paymentId() method. Say the topic carries PaymentAuthorized and PaymentCaptured. Each gets one entry. The condition limits them to images where the decoder is used. { "reflection": [ { "condition": { "typeReached": "com.acme.pay.EventDecoder" }, "type": "com.acme.pay.PaymentAuthorized", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, { "name": "paymentId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] }, { "condition": { "typeReached": "com.acme.pay.EventDecoder" }, "type": "com.acme.pay.PaymentCaptured", "methods": [ { "name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "java.lang.String", "long"] }, { "name": "paymentId", "parameterTypes": [] } ] } ] } Put the file at src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image/com.acme/pay-events/reachability-metadata.json, the <groupId>/<artifactId> folder. In a Quarkus app, the annotation does the same job and moves with the class when someone renames it. That is the version to prefer. @RegisterForReflection public record PaymentAuthorized(String paymentId, String currency, long amountMinor) { } @RegisterForReflection public record PaymentCaptured(String paymentId, String currency, long amountMinor) { } @RegisterForReflection data class PaymentAuthorized(val paymentId: String, val currency: String, val amountMinor: Long) @RegisterForReflection data class PaymentCaptured(val paymentId: String, val currency: String, val amountMinor: Long) Prove it in CI. Build the native binary and run the integration tests against it with missing registrations turned into a hard exit. A new event type that nobody registered now fails the pipeline, not a refund at 3 a.m. ./mvnw verify -Dnative \ -Dquarkus.native.additional-build-args=--exact-reachability-metadata # and start the binary under test with -XX:MissingRegistrationReportingMode=Exit

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Lab
x: Write reachability metadata for a class and a proxy labs/startup/src/main/resources/META-INF/native-image/workbench/startup/reachability-metadata.json labs/startup/src/main/java/workbench/startup/l03/MetadataWriter.java ./gradlew :startup:test --tests 'workbench.startup.l03.*' Run the tests once. Eight of ten fail. Two MetadataFileTest checks pass already: the empty stub file has a valid shape. Read EventDecoder and IssuerClients. Write down every reflective call: which class, which constructor (with its parameter types), which methods, and which proxy interfaces in which order. Edit reachability-metadata.json by hand. Add one reflection entry for workbench.startup.l03.PaymentAuthorized with its <init> and the three accessors from EventDecoder.ACCESSORS, and one entry whose type is {"proxy": [...]}. Run MetadataFileTest until it passes. Implement MetadataWriter.reflection and MetadataWriter.proxy, so the same entries can be generated from Class objects. Run all ten tests. A method entry needs both keys, even with no parameters: {"name": "currency", "parameterTypes": []}. Class.getName() gives exactly the names the schema wants: java.lang.String for a class, long for a primitive. m instanceof Constructor<?> tells a constructor from a method. Class.isInterface() and a HashSet cover the two proxy rules. All ten tests in MetadataFileTest and MetadataWriterTest pass. By the end you can explain what the closed-world assumption costs, write reachability metadata for reflection and proxies by hand, use Quarkus's annotations instead, and spot static initializers that break when the build runs them.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Quiz
x: Code calls Proxy.newProxyInstance(loader, new Class<?>[] {A.class, B.class}, h) and elsewhere the same with {B.class, A.class}. On HotSpot, how many proxy classes exist, and what does that mean for native-image metadata? One class, so one proxy entry covers both Two classes, so you need two proxy entries, each with its own interface order None until the first method call Two classes, but metadata only needs the set of interfaces, not the order A proxy class is defined per ordered list of interfaces, so (A, B) and (B, A) are different classes; the demo prints $Proxy0 and $Proxy1. Native-image metadata describes proxy classes the same way, as an ordered list, so each order needs its own entry. Which of these calls needs a reachability metadata entry in a native image? Class.forName("com.acme.pay.Fees") with a string literal new Fees() Class.forName(rec.headers().lastHeader("type").value()) in a Kafka deserializer A lambda passed to stream().map(...) The analysis handles reflective calls whose arguments are constants, and it sees new and lambdas directly. A class name that arrives in a message header can't be known at build time, so the class and the members used on it must be listed. A Quarkus native service has static final Instant BOOTED = Instant.now(); in a class with default settings, and its health endpoint reports BOOTED. What do pods started on different days show? Each pod's own start time The same time in every pod: when the native binary was built The build fails with an image-heap error null, because static fields are not set in native images Quarkus initializes all classes at build time by default, so the initializer runs once inside the build and the Instant is stored in the image heap. The builder rejects some objects, such as a Random, but a timestamp is an ordinary value. Mark the class with --initialize-at-run-time or compute the value when the app starts. A colleague's reachability-metadata.json has a top-level "proxy": [["com.acme.Client", "java.io.Closeable"]] copied from an old example. With GraalVM's schema v1.2.0, what's the fix? Nothing, proxy is a valid top-level section Rename the file to proxy-config.json Move it into reflection as {"type": {"proxy": ["com.acme.Client", "java.io.Closeable"]}} Replace it with allPublicMethods: true Schema v1.2.0 allows only reflection, resources, foreign and comment at the top level. Proxies are reflection entries whose type is an object with a proxy list. Legacy files like proxy-config.json are not supported in Quarkus 4.0. A Kafka consumer runs all day on three pods at high throughput. Pods restart about once a week, and a six-second start-up hurts nobody. Which runtime fits best? A native image, for the smallest RSS The JVM, optionally with an AOT cache to trim start-up A native image with build-time initialization of everything CRaC, to restore a warmed snapshot This service lives on peak throughput and barely restarts, which is where the JIT wins: Quarkus's benchmark shows native at 59% lower peak. An AOT cache cuts start-up with no code change and costs only about 7% of peak in the same benchmark. Native and CRaC solve start-up problems this service doesn't have.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Key terms
x: Native image A standalone executable built ahead of time from your class path by GraalVM or Mandrel. Closed-world assumption The rule that all code a native image will run is known at build time. Reachability metadata The list of classes, members, proxies and resources the build must keep because only dynamic code uses them. Image heap Objects created at build time, stored in the executable and mapped at start-up. Build-time initialization Running a class's static initializer during the build instead of at each start. Tracing agent A JVM agent (-agentlib:native-image-agent) that records the reflection, proxies and resources a run uses. Mandrel A GraalVM-based distribution of native image tailored for Quarkus, without the polyglot parts. What is native image's closed-world assumption? All code is known at build time. The analysis keeps only what it can reach from main; anything used only through reflection, proxies or resource names must be declared in metadata. Where does reachability-metadata.json go? In META-INF/native-image/<groupId>/<artifactId>/ on the class path. How do you declare a JDK dynamic proxy in schema v1.2.0? A reflection entry: {"type": {"proxy": ["com.acme.Client", "java.io.Closeable"]}}, interfaces in the order the code uses. How is a constructor written in a methods entry? {"name": "<init>", "parameterTypes": ["java.lang.String", "long"]}: fully qualified class names, primitives by name. What does Quarkus do with static initializers in native mode by default? It runs them at build time. The values they compute are stored in the image heap and are the same on every start. How do you make one class initialize at run time in a Quarkus native build? quarkus.native.additional-build-args=--initialize-at-run-time=com.acme.Foo, escaping commas between classes as \\,. @RegisterForReflection(targets = {X.class}) on class Config: which class gets registered? X, not Config. That's how you register a library's classes you can't annotate.

h: GraalVM native image and Quarkus native · Go deeper
x: Some details for when you go native for real. Conditions are precise. "condition": {"typeReached": "com.acme.EventDecoder"} makes an entry active when that type is reached at run time, which the docs define as "right before the class-initialization routine starts for that type", or when one of its subtypes is reached. Writing EventDecoder.class does not reach it. Conditions mostly help library authors ship metadata that costs nothing in apps that never use the feature. Resources use globs: {"resources": [{"glob": "META-INF/**/*.properties"}, {"bundle": "com.acme.Messages"}]}. In Quarkus, use quarkus.native.resources.includes instead. The heap needs a limit. Without an explicit maximum, a native image sets the maximum Java heap to 80% of the physical memory size, according to the GraalVM memory docs. In a container, pass -Xmx (or -XX:MaximumHeapSizePercent) yourself. The default collector is Serial. --gc=G1 needs Oracle GraalVM on Linux, and --gc=epsilon never frees memory, which only makes sense for short jobs. PGO, in Oracle GraalVM only, is a three-step build: native-image --pgo-instrument ... builds an instrumented binary, you run it on a real workload so it writes a .iprof profile on exit, and native-image --pgo=app.iprof ... builds the optimized binary. That is the same idea as Leyden's training run, applied to compiled code. The JDK is moving toward some of these benefits without leaving the JVM. Lesson 2's AOT cache already ships linked classes and profiles, and JEP 544, in development for JDK 28, adds compiled code to the cache while keeping the JIT. Native image stays the option when the binary's size and start time, not the JVM's, are the limit.

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · A started JVM is still cold
x: Lessons 1 to 3 were about reaching the first request. There is a second wait after it. Run the same 20,000 card-number checks ten times in a fresh JVM, and on a shared 4-vCPU VM the first round took about 29 ms while round six and later took 2 to 3 ms. Nothing in the code changed between rounds. The JVM did. A fresh JVM runs every method in the interpreter and counts how often each one runs and how often each loop turns. When a method gets hot, C1 compiles it quickly, with light optimization, and keeps counting. When it stays hot, C2 compiles it again using the profile: which branches were taken, which classes arrived at each call. That climb is called warm-up, and every new JVM makes it again, on every pod, after every deploy and every scale-out. The tools in this track each attack part of it. AppCDS and the AOT cache get classes ready sooner. On JDK 25 the AOT cache also hands the JIT the profiles from its training run (JEP 515), so it can compile sooner, but the compiling still happens inside each new JVM; compiled code in the cache is JEP 544, still in development for JDK 28. A native image is compiled before it runs, so it never warms up, and it never reaches C2's profile-driven code either (lesson 3). CRaC takes a different route. It lets one JVM warm up, saves the whole running process to disk, and starts copies of it later, already warm. Before the Try it, predict the shape of the round times with -Xint, which turns the JIT off, and with -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1, which stops at C1. Watch a JVM warm up Read WarmupDemo. It starts a fresh JVM and runs ten rounds of 20,000 Luhn checks on 16-digit card numbers, printing each round's time. Run it as is. Note round 1 and round 10. Run it with -Pargs=-Xint and then with -Pargs=-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1, after writing down your prediction for each. Explain the three shapes with what C1 and C2 do. WarmupDemo.java package workbench.startup.l04.demo; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Runs the same work in 10 rounds in a fresh JVM and prints how long each round took. A fresh * JVM starts in the interpreter, then the JIT compiles the hot code. Extra arguments are passed * to that JVM as flags, for example -Xint (interpreter only) or -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 (C1 only). */ public class WarmupDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("--work")) { work(); return; } List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(); cmd.add(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()); cmd.addAll(List.of(args)); cmd.addAll(List.of("-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), WarmupDemo.class.getName(), "--work")); System.out.println("fresh JVM, flags " + List.of(args)); Process child = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).inheritIO().start(); child.waitFor(); } /** Ten rounds of 20,000 Luhn checks on card numbers, the check every PAN field gets. */ static void work() { long checksum = 0; for (int round = 1; round <= 10; round++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) { String digits = Long.toString(1_000_003L * i + round); String pan = "4000" + "0".repeat(12 - digits.length()) + digits; // a 16-digit PAN if (luhnValid(pan)) checksum += i; } long us = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000; System.out.printf("round %2d: %,7d us%n", round, us); } if (checksum == 42) System.out.println(); // keeps the JIT from dropping the work } static boolean luhnValid(String pan) { int sum = 0; boolean twice = false; for (int i = pan.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { int d = pan.charAt(i) - '0'; if (twice) { d *= 2; if (d > 9) d -= 9; } sum += d; twice = !twice; } return sum % 10 == 0; } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l04.demo.WarmupDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l04/demo/WarmupDemo.java WarmupDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l04.demo import java.nio.file.Path /** * Runs the same work in 10 rounds in a fresh JVM and prints how long each round took. A fresh * JVM starts in the interpreter, then the JIT compiles the hot code. Extra arguments are passed * to that JVM as flags, for example -Xint (interpreter only) or -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 (C1 only). */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "--work") { work() return } val cmd = listOf(Path.of(System.getProperty("java.home"), "bin", "java").toString()) + args + listOf("-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.startup.l04.demo.WarmupDemoKt", "--work") println("fresh JVM, flags ${args.toList()}") ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).inheritIO().start().waitFor() } /** Ten rounds of 20,000 Luhn checks on card numbers, the check every PAN field gets. */ private fun work() { var checksum = 0L for (round in 1..10) { val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in 0 until 20_000) { val pan = "4000" + (1_000_003L * i + round).toString().padStart(12, '0') // a 16-digit PAN if (luhnValid(pan)) checksum += i } val us = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000 println("round %2d: %,7d us".format(round, us)) } if (checksum == 42L) println() // keeps the JIT from dropping the work } private fun luhnValid(pan: String): Boolean { var sum = 0 var twice = false for (i in pan.indices.reversed()) { var d = pan[i] - '0' if (twice) { d *= 2 if (d > 9) d -= 9 } sum += d twice = !twice } return sum % 10 == 0 } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l04.demo.WarmupDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l04/demo/WarmupDemo.kt On a shared Linux VM: the default run went from about 29,000 us in round 1 to 2,100 to 3,400 us from round 6 on. With -Xint every round took 70,000 to 105,000 us and never got faster, because nothing is compiled. With C1 only, round 1 was about 18,000 us and later rounds stayed at 3,500 to 5,600 us: faster than the interpreter, slower than C2. Your numbers will differ; the shapes won't. JEP 515: Ahead-of-Time Method Profiling read Restarting a JVM is rebooting a laptop: every app starts from nothing and takes a while to get fast. Lesson 2's AOT cache is a faster reboot with the bookshelf already sorted. A native image swaps the laptop for a calculator built for one job: it is on instantly, but it can only do what it was built for. CRaC is hibernating the laptop with every app open and warm, then waking it. Before you hibernate, you close the network connections, because the other side won't wait for you. The analogy breaks in one place: you wake a laptop once, but you can restore one CRaC image into a hundred processes, and all hundred wake up with the same memory, the same counters and the same cached tokens.

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · CRaC saves a warm JVM to disk and brings it back
x: CRaC stands for Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint. A checkpoint writes a running JVM to disk; a restore starts a new process from that image. The OpenJDK implementation uses CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace), a Linux tool that freezes a process and writes its memory pages, each thread's CPU registers, and the kernel state it can describe into a directory of image files. A restore builds a new process from those files, and it continues at the instruction where the old one stopped. The heap, the loaded classes and the JIT's compiled code all come back as they were. The CRaC docs put it this way: "After the restore, Java runtime performance is also on-par with the one at the checkpoint." That mechanism also tells you what can't come back. A TCP connection lives partly in the kernel and partly on the other machine, and the card issuer's server dropped its side long before your restore. A file may have changed or moved. So the JVM and your code are told before and after, which is the "coordinated" part, and CRaC refuses to checkpoint while files or sockets are open. The flow has three commands: java -XX:CRaCCheckpointTo=cr -jar pay.jar # start; allows a checkpoint into the directory cr jcmd pay.jar JDK.checkpoint # after warm-up traffic: write the image, end the process java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=cr # later, any number of times: continue from the image One trap: the docs say "success is always reported in jcmd output, problems are reported in the console of the application". Read the application's log, not jcmd's "Command executed successfully". The CRaC project published these "time to first operation" numbers in 2020, from a JDK 14 CRaC build on a laptop: App Normal start Restored Spring Boot 3,898 ms 38 ms Micronaut 1,001 ms 46 ms Quarkus 980 ms 33 ms CRaC is not in mainline OpenJDK: there is no JEP, and the main repository has no CRaC commits. You get it from vendors. Azul ships it in its Zulu builds of JDK 17, 21 and 25 for Linux on x64 and ARM64, in the files with "-crac-" in the name; BellSoft ships CRaC builds of Liberica JDK 17 and 21. CRIU needs extra privileges, and restoring on a machine with a different CPU can fail unless you pin CPU features with -XX:CPUFeatures at checkpoint time. The image holds the whole heap, secrets included, so store it like a heap dump. Checkpoint and restore (optional, needs a CRaC JDK on Linux) If you have a CRaC build (for example a Zulu build with -crac- in its name), build any small service JAR and start it with the first command. Send it some requests. Run the jcmd command. Look at both terminals: jcmd's and the application's. Run the restore command and send a request at once. Compare how fast it answers with a normal start. Without a CRaC JDK, answer this from the mechanism instead: your service opened a log file in append mode and keeps it open. What does the checkpoint do, and why? terminal (CRaC JDK on Linux) java -XX:CRaCCheckpointTo=cr -jar pay.jar # in a second terminal, after some traffic: jcmd pay.jar JDK.checkpoint # later, as often as you like: java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=cr jcmd prints Command executed successfully whatever happened; the application's console shows any problem. If the checkpoint worked, the original process ends and cr is a directory of image files. The restore continues from the checkpoint and answers like a warm JVM. The open log file fails the checkpoint under the default error policy, because an open file descriptor can't be put in the image safely: the file might change or vanish before a restore. CRaC project documentation (README) docs For Quarkus services on Kubernetes, CRaC is rarely the first step: start with the AOT cache, which needs no code and no special JDK. CRaC and SnapStart fit where cold starts hit users directly, such as a card-tokenization function on Lambda that sits idle at night and must answer within the issuer's timeout on the first call. If you go there, every component with an outside connection needs hooks: the Oracle connection pool, the Kafka consumer (stop polling and close it before the checkpoint, create it again after restore), Temporal worker connections, the HTTP client to the card issuer. Then look for per-instance state created at start-up: an idempotency-key prefix, a node id for ledger entry ids, an OAuth token. In a restored copy those are shared with every other copy unless afterRestore makes new ones.

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Resources must let go before the snapshot
x: Your code takes part through two methods. In the org.crac library (version 1.5.0 is the latest release) a resource looks like this: Java public final class LedgerPool implements Resource { public LedgerPool() { Core.getGlobalContext().register(this); // the context only holds a weak reference } @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) { closeAllConnections(); } @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { reconnect(); } } Kotlin class LedgerPool : Resource { init { Core.getGlobalContext().register(this) // the context only holds a weak reference } override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) = closeAllConnections() override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) = reconnect() } org.crac mirrors the jdk.crac API of CRaC JDKs and finds the real implementation by reflection at run time. On a JDK without CRaC you can still register resources; only a checkpoint request fails. So the same JAR runs everywhere. The global context has documented rules. It calls beforeCheckpoint in the reverse order of registration and afterRestore in registration order. Components created later usually use the earlier ones: the Kafka consumer writes through the ledger pool, so it must stop first and start last. Every resource is told, even when another one throws, and the context collects the exceptions as suppressed exceptions on a CheckpointException. If the checkpoint fails, the restore notifications run at once, without an image, and the process keeps going. Open files and sockets fail the checkpoint by default. Their policy is error, which the CRaC docs describe as "just print error and fail the checkpoint". You can set other policies (ignore, close, reopen) in a file named by -Djdk.crac.resource-policies, but for sockets "the reopening part is not implemented, therefore will result in a runtime exception after restore". Close them yourself. The image is one copy of memory, and every restore starts from it. If you restore ten instances, anything generated before the checkpoint is the same in all ten: an instance id, a nonce counter, a cached access token. Recreate those in afterRestore. AWS Lambda SnapStart uses the same org.crac hooks, and AWS documents the same order. It is a separate implementation, though: the Quarkus guide warns that "SnapStart is not CRaC and can do things that would not work with others CRaC implementations", and it uses beforeCheckpoint to prime clients, so they are ready before the snapshot. Quarkus's SnapStart support also preloads and initializes the classes listed in META-INF/quarkus-preload-classes.txt before the snapshot, which moves lesson 1's class loading into the image. Restore time is limited, so keep afterRestore short. Hook order, and a forgotten socket Read HookOrderDemo. Three components register in the order a service creates them: the ledger DB pool, the Kafka consumer, the metrics reporter. Predict the order of the six hook lines, then run it. Run it with -Pargs=leak, where the reporter forgets to close its socket. Predict whether the restore hooks still run. HookOrderDemo.java package workbench.startup.l04.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * A toy checkpoint: three components register hooks in the order the service creates them. * Pass "leak" as an argument and the metrics reporter forgets to close its socket. */ public class HookOrderDemo { /** org.crac.Resource has the same two methods, each taking a Context argument. */ interface Resource { void beforeCheckpoint(); void afterRestore(); } static final List<Resource> registered = new ArrayList<>(); static final List<String> openSockets = new ArrayList<>(); static final class Component implements Resource { final String name; final boolean leaks; Component(String name, boolean leaks) { this.name = name; this.leaks = leaks; openSockets.add(name); // every component holds a connection registered.add(this); // and registers itself when it is created } public void beforeCheckpoint() { System.out.println(" beforeCheckpoint: " + name); if (!leaks) openSockets.remove(name); } public void afterRestore() { System.out.println(" afterRestore: " + name); if (!openSockets.contains(name)) openSockets.add(name); } } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean leak = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("leak"); new Component("ledger DB pool", false); // created first: the others use it new Component("Kafka consumer", false); new Component("metrics reporter", leak); System.out.println("checkpoint requested"); for (Resource r : registered.reversed()) r.beforeCheckpoint(); // last registered first if (openSockets.isEmpty()) { System.out.println(" -- snapshot written --"); } else { System.out.println(" -- checkpoint refused, still open: " + openSockets + " --"); } for (Resource r : registered) r.afterRestore(); // first registered first } } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l04.demo.HookOrderDemo labs/startup/src/demo/java/workbench/startup/l04/demo/HookOrderDemo.java HookOrderDemo.kt package workbench.startup.l04.demo /** * A toy checkpoint: three components register hooks in the order the service creates them. * Pass "leak" as an argument and the metrics reporter forgets to close its socket. */ private interface Hooks { // org.crac.Resource: the same two methods, plus a Context argument fun beforeCheckpoint() fun afterRestore() } private val registered = mutableListOf<Hooks>() private val openSockets = mutableListOf<String>() private class Component(val name: String, val leaks: Boolean) : Hooks { init { openSockets += name // every component holds a connection registered += this // and registers itself when it is created } override fun beforeCheckpoint() { println(" beforeCheckpoint: $name") if (!leaks) openSockets -= name } override fun afterRestore() { println(" afterRestore: $name") if (name !in openSockets) openSockets += name } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val leak = args.firstOrNull() == "leak" Component("ledger DB pool", false) // created first: the others use it Component("Kafka consumer", false) Component("metrics reporter", leak) println("checkpoint requested") registered.asReversed().forEach { it.beforeCheckpoint() } // last registered first if (openSockets.isEmpty()) { println(" -- snapshot written --") } else { println(" -- checkpoint refused, still open: $openSockets --") } registered.forEach { it.afterRestore() } // first registered first } ./gradlew :startup:demo -Pmain=workbench.startup.l04.demo.HookOrderDemoKt labs/startup/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/startup/l04/demo/HookOrderDemo.kt beforeCheckpoint runs for the reporter, the consumer, then the pool; the snapshot is written; afterRestore runs for the pool, the consumer, then the reporter. With leak the checkpoint is refused (still open: [metrics reporter]), and the restore hooks still run in the same order, so the service keeps working, as the real global context does when a checkpoint fails. The global context tells the newest component first at checkpoint and the oldest first at restore. CRaC: file descriptor policies docs Quarkus 3.40: AWS Lambda SnapStart configuration docs

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Choosing a start-up strategy
x: Here is the whole track in one table. The numbers come from the lessons: this track's own runs on a shared VM, Quarkus's perf-lab benchmark, and CRaC's 2020 results. Read them as directions, not promises. Nothing AppCDS (JDK 21) AOT cache (JDK 25.0.4+) Native image CRaC or SnapStart Code changes none none none; one property in Quarkus 3.40 metadata, build-time init fixes hooks for sockets, files, pools Start-up gain seen baseline about half the CPU about a sixth of the CPU; first request 218 to 136 ms first request 581 ms vs 4,417 ms first operation 33 ms vs 980 ms Peak throughput baseline same about 7% lower about 59% lower a warm JVM's RSS baseline a little lower 240 vs 304 MiB 95 vs 304 MiB a warm JVM's What it costs nothing an archive step in the build a training run; same JDK build, flags and JAR builds of 3 to 10 min and 4 to 8 GB a vendor JDK or Lambda, CRIU rights, image storage Start with the JVM and measure, as lesson 1 showed: time to first request from outside, RSS from ps. On JDK 25.0.4 or later, add the AOT cache trained by your integration tests. It is the cheapest gain in the table and changes no code. On JDK 21, build a dynamic AppCDS archive when you build the image. Do nothing more for services that rarely restart and that nobody waits on. Move to a native image when start-up in milliseconds or memory per instance is the real limit, for example scale-to-zero functions or many small services on one node, and the team accepts slow builds, metadata upkeep and lower peak throughput. Move to CRaC or SnapStart when new instances must be fast and warm at once, you control the runtime (Lambda, or a vendor CRaC JDK on Linux with CRIU rights), and you can make every connection pool, consumer and file handle checkpoint-safe. Check yourself with a case the table doesn't list: a nightly batch job on JDK 25.0.5 runs for 40 minutes, starts once a night, and is CPU-bound for the whole run. Which column wins? (Nothing, or at most the AOT cache. Its start-up is a rounding error next to 40 minutes, and native would cost it peak throughput every minute of the run.) The subtle mistake is registering a resource that nobody else holds. Core.getGlobalContext().register(new Resource() { ... }) compiles and works in a quick test, but the global context keeps only a weak reference, so the garbage collector can remove your anonymous resource at any time. Its hooks then never run: the checkpoint fails on the pool's open sockets, or worse, a restored process keeps a pool of dead connections. The CRaC best-practices guide gives the fix: store the resource in a field of the component it belongs to, and register that field.

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Java and Kotlin
x: A checkpoint-safe pool with org.crac in Java and Kotlin IssuerClientPool.java public final class IssuerClientPool { private final List<IssuerConnection> connections = new ArrayList<>(); // a field keeps the handler reachable: the global context only holds a weak reference private final Resource cracHandler = new Resource() { @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) { closeAll(); } @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { openAll(); } }; public IssuerClientPool() { openAll(); Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler); } private synchronized void openAll() { for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++) connections.add(IssuerConnection.open()); } private synchronized void closeAll() { connections.forEach(IssuerConnection::close); // nothing open in the image connections.clear(); } } IssuerClientPool.kt class IssuerClientPool { private val connections = mutableListOf<IssuerConnection>() // a property keeps the handler reachable: the global context only holds a weak reference private val cracHandler = object : Resource { override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) = closeAll() override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) = openAll() } // after cracHandler: Kotlin runs property initializers and init blocks top to bottom init { openAll() Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler) } @Synchronized private fun openAll() = repeat(20) { connections += IssuerConnection.open() } @Synchronized private fun closeAll() { connections.forEach { it.close() } // nothing open in the image connections.clear() } } The JVM sees the same thing from both: an object implementing org.crac.Resource, held strongly by the pool and weakly by the global context. Java's anonymous class and Kotlin's object : expression both compile to a small inner class, and Resource has two methods, so neither language can use a lambda for it. The Kotlin trap is order. Properties and init blocks run top to bottom. With the init block above cracHandler, a direct reference fails to compile ("variable 'cracHandler' must be initialized"), but the same reference made through a helper method compiles and registers null. Java runs all field initializers before the constructor body, so the Java version has no such trap. Kotlin sees the parameter as Context<out Resource>, which is Java's Context<? extends Resource>.

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Worked example
x: Make a Kafka-fed ledger service checkpoint-safe List what the service holds that lives outside the process: a ledger DB pool, a Kafka consumer that writes through the pool, and an instance id that prefixes every ledger entry id. The pool and the consumer hold sockets. The instance id is plain memory, which is the problem: every restored copy would get the same one. Give the consumer its hooks. It is created after the pool, so it is registered later, which makes the context stop it before the pool closes and start it after the pool is back. Keep the handler in a field. final class LedgerConsumer { private volatile KafkaConsumer<String, String> consumer = newConsumer(); private final Resource cracHandler = new Resource() { // 1. stop polling, commit, and close the broker connections @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) { stopPolling(); consumer.close(); } // 2. a new consumer joins the group again after restore @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { consumer = newConsumer(); startPolling(); } }; LedgerConsumer() { Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler); } } class LedgerConsumer { @Volatile private var consumer = newConsumer() private val cracHandler = object : Resource { // 1. stop polling, commit, and close the broker connections override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) { stopPolling(); consumer.close() } // 2. a new consumer joins the group again after restore override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) { consumer = newConsumer(); startPolling() } } init { Core.getGlobalContext().register(cracHandler) } } Make per-instance state after restore. The instance id moves out of a final field and into something afterRestore can replace, so two copies restored from one image never write the same ledger entry id. final class InstanceId implements Resource { private volatile String value = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); InstanceId() { Core.getGlobalContext().register(this); } // kept alive by whoever holds InstanceId String get() { return value; } @Override public void beforeCheckpoint(Context<? extends Resource> c) { } // 3. every restored copy gets its own id @Override public void afterRestore(Context<? extends Resource> c) { value = UUID.randomUUID().toString(); } } class InstanceId : Resource { @Volatile var value: String = UUID.randomUUID().toString() private set init { Core.getGlobalContext().register(this) } // kept alive by whoever holds InstanceId override fun beforeCheckpoint(c: Context<out Resource>) {} // 3. every restored copy gets its own id override fun afterRestore(c: Context<out Resource>) { value = UUID.randomUUID().toString() } } Test the checkpoint for real on a CRaC JDK, and read the application's console, because jcmd reports success either way. A refused checkpoint names what was still open. java -XX:CRaCCheckpointTo=cr -jar ledger.jar & # drive some traffic, then: jcmd ledger.jar JDK.checkpoint # prints "Command executed successfully" in any case # check the service's own log for errors, then restore and send a payment: java -XX:CRaCRestoreFrom=cr

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Quiz
x: On JDK 25, which of these brings back JIT-compiled machine code from a previous run, so hot methods are fast from the first request? An AOT cache made with -XX:AOTCacheOutput A dynamic AppCDS archive Restoring a CRaC checkpoint The default CDS archive A CRaC image holds the whole process memory, including the code cache, so a restored JVM is as warm as it was at the checkpoint. JDK 25's AOT cache holds classes, linked state, heap objects and method profiles that help the JIT start sooner, but the compiling still happens in each new JVM. Compiled code in the AOT cache is JEP 544, in development for JDK 28. A service registers, in this order, a ledger DB pool, a Kafka consumer and a metrics reporter. In which order does the global context call beforeCheckpoint? Pool, consumer, reporter Reporter, consumer, pool In parallel, on separate threads In an undefined order Checkpoint notification runs in reverse registration order, and restore notification in registration order. Components created later tend to use earlier ones: the consumer writes through the pool, so it must stop before the pool closes and start after it reopens. Nobody wrote hooks for the HTTP client's open connection to the card issuer. With the default settings of a CRaC JDK, what does a checkpoint request do? Saves the connection in the image; it works after restore Closes it silently and reopens it after restore Exits the JVM Fails the checkpoint with an error, runs the restore hooks, and leaves the process running The default policy for open files and sockets is error, which prints an error and fails the checkpoint. Restore notification then starts at once, without an image, and the service carries on. Even the reopen policy can't help a socket: the docs say reopening sockets is not implemented. One CRaC image is restored into 20 instances. Each instance builds idempotency keys from a random prefix chosen in a constructor before the checkpoint. What happens? All 20 instances use the same prefix, so their keys can collide Each instance gets its own prefix, because the restore reseeds memory The checkpoint fails because random numbers can't be saved The prefix is lost and becomes null A restore copies the image's memory as it was, so every instance starts with the same prefix. Recreate per-instance values like this in afterRestore. A Quarkus REST service on Kubernetes runs JDK 25.0.5, deploys several times a day, and peak throughput matters. The team wants faster pod start-up without code changes. Which option fits best? A native image CRaC with hooks for every resource The AOT cache, trained during the integration tests -XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive written to the pod's disk at run time The AOT cache needs no code change (one Quarkus property), keeps peak throughput within about 7% in Quarkus's benchmark, and on 25.0.4 or later it is rejected safely when the JAR changes. Native costs about 59% of peak throughput, CRaC needs hooks and a vendor JDK, and an archive written at run time is lost with each pod.
