h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Key terms
x: Warm-up The time after start-up during which the JIT is still compiling hot code, so the program runs slower than it will later. CRaC Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint: save a running JVM to disk and start copies of it later, already warm. Checkpoint The moment a running process is written to an image on disk. Restore Starting a new process from a checkpoint image; it continues where the old one stopped. CRIU Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace, the Linux tool CRaC uses to save and rebuild a process. Resource (org.crac) An object with beforeCheckpoint and afterRestore hooks, registered with a CRaC context. File descriptor policy The rule for an open file or socket at checkpoint time; the default, error, fails the checkpoint. Lambda SnapStart AWS Lambda's snapshot and restore of initialized Java functions, using the same org.crac hooks. What does CRaC do? Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint: it writes a running JVM's whole process to an image (with CRIU on Linux) and later starts new processes from it, warm, with heap, classes and JIT code as they were. In which order are CRaC hooks called? beforeCheckpoint in reverse registration order; afterRestore in registration order. What does CRaC do by default with an open file or socket at checkpoint time? Its policy is error: it prints an error and fails the checkpoint. The process keeps running. Why must you keep your org.crac Resource in a field? The global context holds only a weak reference. An unreferenced resource can be garbage-collected, and its hooks never run. Is CRaC part of mainline OpenJDK? No. There is no JEP. It ships in vendor builds such as Azul Zulu (17, 21, 25 on Linux, the -crac- files) and BellSoft Liberica (17, 21). jcmd pay.jar JDK.checkpoint prints "Command executed successfully". Did the checkpoint work? You don't know yet. jcmd always reports success; problems appear in the application's own console. Restored copies of one image share what? Everything in memory at the checkpoint: ids, counters, random seeds, cached tokens. Recreate per-instance values in afterRestore.

h: CRaC, and choosing a startup strategy · Go deeper
x: Three details for when you try CRaC for real. First, the threads. A resource can be called while other threads still use the component. The CRaC best-practices guide sorts components by how threads reach them: an unknown number of threads arriving at random, a known number of threads arriving periodically, or an event loop. For the first case it suggests a java.util.concurrent.locks.ReadWriteLock: borrowers take the read lock, and beforeCheckpoint takes the write lock and keeps it until afterRestore, so callers wait during the checkpoint instead of failing on a closed connection. Second, the policies. If a library holds a file you can't close, -Djdk.crac.resource-policies=<file> points at a policy file. Rules are separated by ---, match by type (file, pipe, socket, filedescriptor) and fields such as the path or port, and the first matching rule wins. ignore leaves the descriptor to CRIU, close closes it ("an attempt to use it after restore will fail"), and reopen reopens a file at the same position. Use policies as a temporary workaround; hooks in your own code are clearer. Third, the warm-up you capture. The CRaC docs describe the intended flow as a canary deployment: real traffic triggers class loading and JIT compilation, then you checkpoint, and the image becomes part of the release. A checkpoint taken after a synthetic warm-up only contains what that warm-up exercised, the same lesson as a training run in lesson 2. For Lambda, the Quarkus SnapStart guide also recommends -XX:+TieredCompilation -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, which trades peak speed for less compiling right after a restore. The C1-only run in this lesson's first Try it shows that trade.

h: Capstone: a tiny dependency injection container
x: Wire classes by reflection, add interceptors with proxies, then measure it and move the wiring to build time. Across three sittings you build one program: a small dependency injection container for a payment app. Lesson 1 wires classes by reflection: it finds the components from a list or a class path scan, picks each constructor, orders the graph with a readable cycle error, and gives every singleton exactly one instance when eight threads ask at once. Lesson 2 adds @Timed and @Retry, through a JDK proxy for components with interfaces and a Byte Buddy subclass for the rest, and refuses at start-up what Kotlin's final classes would otherwise break in silence. Lesson 3 measures the result per call with JMH and at start-up with -Xlog:class+load, looks inside the running container with a class histogram and a heap dump, then generates the same wiring as plain Java at build time and archives what is left with AppCDS and the AOT cache. At the end you can defend, with numbers you measured, why Spring wires at run time and why Quarkus and Micronaut moved the work to the build. The capstone draws on every track of this part: class loading, reflection and proxies from Class loading, bytecode and dynamic proxies; escape analysis, histograms and heap dumps from Memory and garbage collection; JMH and the JIT tiers from JIT, profiling and benchmarking; class counts, CDS and the AOT cache from Startup and footprint. The holder idiom and double-checked locking come from the memory model track. Each lesson names the earlier lesson it leans on, so you can go back for a mechanism when you need it. The labs live in labs/container, one package per lesson (workbench.container.l01 to l03). Lessons 1 and 3 are Java; lesson 2 is Kotlin, on top of lesson 1's Java container. Each lesson's starter code contains the previous lesson's solution, so you can start any sitting fresh. The tests check behaviour, never time: creation order, cycle messages, one instance under concurrent first access, retry counts, proxy identity, and a generated registry that wires the same graph as the reflective container. Run ./gradlew :container:test --tests 'workbench.container.lNN.*' from labs/, and ./gradlew :container:solutionTest for the reference answers. The demos run the reference container from src/solution, so they work before you finish a lab. Lesson 3's demos start child JVMs and take about ten seconds; its AOT cache commands need JDK 25.0.4 or later and say so. A container automates the wiring block of main: find the components, build each one from its constructor, and decide how many instances exist. Scan with getResources and Class.forName(name, false, loader); @Component needs RUNTIME retention, and every scanned class is loaded on every start. Pick the @Inject or only public constructor, skip Kotlin's synthetic ones, resolve by type, and order the graph depth-first post-order with a path that names any cycle. A singleton cell with double-checked locking on a volatile field builds one instance under concurrent first access; check-then-act and recursive computeIfAbsent don't. Interfaces get a JDK proxy (identity equals, invokeDefault, unwrap exceptions, annotations on the interface); classes get a Byte Buddy subclass that intercepts self-calls but not final members. Kotlin is final by default: open the class and methods, use all-open, or add an interface, and let the container refuse what it can't intercept instead of skipping it. Per call, proxies cost a few hundred bytes at most (B/op is the stable number); at start-up the reflective container loaded 2,207 classes against 991 for generated wiring. Generated wiring does the graph work in the build and wires with holders and new; it gives up run-time flexibility and a failed holder stays failed until restart. A class histogram says what is alive, a heap dump says who holds it; the container held its beans and Byte Buddy's loader, while JDK proxy classes and annotation instances stay for the life of the app loader. Archives and caches help most when little is made at run time: AppCDS skips proxies and custom-loader classes, so build-time wiring and an AOT cache work best together.

h: Capstone: a tiny dependency injection container: cheat sheet
x: The program in one picture ClassScanner (or a list) finds the components, Constructors picks one constructor each, BeanGraph orders them depth first, Container builds them lazily in SingletonCells, Interception wraps the ones with @Timed or @Retry, and RegistryGenerator writes all of it as Java at build time. Finding and building components Decision The lab's choice Why Which classes A list, or a scan with ClassLoader.getResources(packagePath) A scan loads every class in the package on every start Loading them Class.forName(name, false, loader) true runs every static initializer during the scan Seeing @Component @Retention(RUNTIME) The default CLASS retention is invisible to reflection JARs Need directory entries A files-only JAR scans as empty, with no error Constructor The @Inject one, or the only public one; never "the first" Reflection gives no order to rely on Kotlin Skip isSynthetic() constructors; don't default injected parameters All-default parameters add a no-arg constructor that also gets @Inject Parameters By type, interface to its one implementation Class files keep no parameter names without -parameters Order, cycles, scopes Creation order: depth-first post-order; each component after everything it needs; shared ones once. Cycle: keep the path you are inside; meeting a class on it again is the cycle. Report from the repeated class: Dependency cycle: Payouts -> Statements -> Payouts. Check the whole graph in the container's constructor; create objects lazily. Singleton: one per container. Not check-then-act on a map (duplicates), not recursive computeIfAbsent (Recursive update). A cell with double-checked locking on a volatile field; nested cell locks can't deadlock on an acyclic graph; a failed factory retries. Prototype: new on every get; a singleton that depends on it keeps the one it got. Interception Component Proxy Self-calls Breaks on Implements an interface JDK proxy around a separate target Not intercepted Annotations on the class, get(ImplClass) No interface Byte Buddy subclass, built with the real constructor arguments Intercepted final classes, final or private methods (Kotlin's default) Handler, in order: Object methods by identity; defaults through invokeDefault; the chain ending in method.invoke(target, args); unwrap InvocationTargetException. Chain: @Timed outside @Retry, so the time includes every attempt. Retry only listed failures, rethrow the original, and only calls that carry an idempotency key. Nested retries multiply. Kotlin: open class and methods, all-open (or kotlin-spring), or an interface. Refuse the rest at start-up. Measure Question Tool This app's numbers (JDK 21) Cost per call JMH with -prof gc, read B/op direct 0, generated 0, Byte Buddy 160, JDK proxy 208 Classes at start -Xlog:class+load, count by source: reflective 2,207, generated 991 Made at run time __dynamic_proxy__, __JVM_DefineClass__, hidden classes 30 proxies, 3 Byte Buddy classes, 123 hidden What is alive jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram 13 SingletonCell, 1 ByteArrayClassLoader, 119 proxy objects Who holds it jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump file.hprof, MAT path to GC roots cell, map, container, main's local Build time Run the same graph code in the build; a cycle fails the build. Holder class per singleton (lazy, thread-safe under the class init lock), factory per prototype, identity checks in get, interceptors written as source with chains from annotation values. Costs: a generator in the build, a component set fixed per artifact, holders that fail with NoClassDefFoundError until restart if a constructor throws, checked-exception constructors need wrapping. AppCDS and the AOT cache archive classes from JARs, not proxies (Unsupported location) or classes a custom loader defines. Generated wiring leaves almost nothing to make at start, and suits native image. Review questions for any container What does it do at start-up that depends only on the classes? Which of my methods are really intercepted, and how did I check? What allocates per call on the hot path, in B/op? How many classes does a cold start load, and how many are made at run time? What fails at build time, what at start-up, and what on first use?

h: Capstone: a tiny dependency injection container: track quiz
x: A teammate's scanner finds no components in production, though the same code finds twelve in the IDE. Production runs from a JAR built by a custom packaging step. What do you check first? Whether @Component has @Retention(RUNTIME) Whether the JAR has directory entries for the package Whether the classes are compiled with -parameters Whether the JIT has compiled the scanner getResources("com/acme/pay") finds a package in a JAR only through the directory's own entry. The IDE runs from a build directory, where every package is a real directory. A retention problem would fail in the IDE too. Kotlin: class FeeRules @Inject constructor(val bps: Int = 290, val currency: String = "EUR"). What does the lab's Constructors.pick do? Picks the primary constructor Picks the no-argument constructor Refuses: there are two @Inject constructors Picks the synthetic DefaultConstructorMarker constructor When every parameter has a default, kotlinc adds a public no-argument constructor, and it copied @Inject onto it. The synthetic one is filtered out, but two real marked constructors remain. Don't give injected parameters defaults. Eight request threads call get(FxRates.class) on a fresh container at the same moment. Which implementation builds exactly one FxRates? if (map.get(t) == null) map.put(t, create(t)) on a ConcurrentHashMap A recursive map.computeIfAbsent(t, this::create) A per-component cell: volatile read, then lock, read again, create synchronized only around map.put Check-then-act lets every thread that saw null create one, and a lock around put alone keeps that gap. A recursive computeIfAbsent may throw Recursive update when keys share a bin. The cell re-checks under its lock, so only the first thread runs the factory. CardIssuerClient is implemented by a final Kotlin class HttpIssuerClient, with @Retry on the interface method authorize. What does the lab's container do? Refuses: the class is final Wraps it in a JDK proxy; finality doesn't matter, and retries work Builds a Byte Buddy subclass Creates it without interception A component with an interface gets a JDK proxy, which only needs the interface. Finality only matters for subclass proxies. The bean is then a $ProxyN, so callers must ask for CardIssuerClient, not HttpIssuerClient. A forwarding proxy's handler sends equals to the target like every other method. What breaks? proxy.equals(proxy) is false, so ArrayList.remove(proxy) fails hashCode throws UndeclaredThrowableException Nothing, because collections compare references first The proxy class can't be generated The target is asked whether it equals the proxy, and it doesn't. HashSet happens to survive because HashMap compares references before calling equals; ArrayList doesn't. Answer equals and hashCode by proxy identity. Kotlin open class Payouts { @Timed fun pay(id: String) {} } is wired by a container that builds Byte Buddy subclasses without a start-up check. What happens on pay? Byte Buddy refuses the class It runs untimed, with no error, because pay is final It is timed, because the class is open A VerifyError when the subclass loads open on a class doesn't open its members. A subclass can't override a final method, so Byte Buddy leaves it alone and the annotation does nothing. The lab's container checks intercepted methods for final and refuses at start-up. Which number from ProxyCallBench belongs in a CI check that the issuer proxy hasn't become more expensive? ns/op of the JDK proxy row The ratio of the JDK proxy time to the direct time B/op (gc.alloc.rate.norm) with a small margin The number of JIT compilations On a shared machine the time error was larger than most scores, while bytes per operation came out the same on every run. Keep a margin, because a JDK upgrade or a longer chain can change what escape analysis removes. With a dynamic AppCDS archive on JDK 21, the reflective container still logs 30 __dynamic_proxy__ and 3 __JVM_DefineClass__ classes at every start. Why? The archive was built with the wrong JDK Those classes are made at run time and have no location an archive can verify AppCDS only stores JDK classes The training run was too short At dump time JDK 21 skips each proxy class with Unsupported location, and Byte Buddy's subclass is defined from bytes by its own class loader. Classes from JARs, Byte Buddy's own included, do come from the archive. After the reflective container is dropped and a GC runs, which of these is still loaded? The Byte Buddy subclass Byte Buddy's ByteArrayClassLoader The JDK proxy class for CardIssuerClient The SingletonCell objects Nothing outside the container pointed at the Byte Buddy object, its class or its loader, so the whole chain was collected. The JDK proxy class was defined in the application class loader and is cached by Proxy for that loader, so it stays as long as the application runs. Design review: a service starts once a week, runs for days, and loads payment-method plugins from a directory chosen at start-up. Which wiring fits best? Run-time wiring: the component set isn't known until start-up, and one slow start a week costs little Build-time wiring: it is always faster Native image: it starts fastest No container: wire everything by hand in main Build-time wiring needs the component set when you build, and plugins chosen at start-up break that. With one start a week, the 2,000-class start-up cost is paid rarely. Build-time wiring and native image pay off for services that start often or must meet a tight readiness budget.

h: Wire classes by reflection · A container is the main method that calls new, written once
x: Most services start with a block like this somewhere near main: Java IssuerConfig config = new IssuerConfig(); FxRates rates = new FxRates(); PaymentService payments = new PaymentService( new HttpIssuerClient(config), new FeeCalculator(rates), new Ledger()); Kotlin val config = IssuerConfig() val rates = FxRates() val payments = PaymentService( HttpIssuerClient(config), FeeCalculator(rates), Ledger()) That is dependency injection done by hand. Each class receives what it needs through its constructor and never calls new on its collaborators, so a test can pass in a fake issuer. The block has two jobs that get harder as the service grows: it must create things in the right order (config before the issuer client), and it must share the right instances (one rates for everyone). With six classes you do it in your head. With eighty, someone adds a constructor parameter and the block stops compiling in three places. A container does that block for you. It needs three decisions per class. Which classes take part? We call them components. How do you build one? Its constructor says what it needs. How many instances should exist? That is its scope. The smallest version is ten lines of reflection. type.getConstructors() returns the public constructors as Constructor objects. getParameterTypes() lists what each one needs, and newInstance(args) calls it, which allocates the object and runs the constructor exactly as new would. Build the parameters first, recursively, and you have a container: Java static Object build(Class<?> type) throws ReflectiveOperationException { Constructor<?> c = type.getConstructors()[0]; Object[] args = new Object[c.getParameterCount()]; for (int i = 0; i < args.length; i++) args[i] = build(c.getParameterTypes()[i]); return c.newInstance(args); } Kotlin fun build(type: Class<*>): Any { val c = type.constructors[0] return c.newInstance(*c.parameterTypes.map { build(it) }.toTypedArray()) } It works, and it is wrong in four ways you'll fix in this lesson. It takes "the first" constructor. It loops forever on a cycle. It has no list of components. And it never remembers anything, so it builds a new FxRates every time a constructor asks for one. Count the FxRates Read TinyContainerDemo (or the Kotlin twin). FeeCalculator and QuoteService both need an FxRates. Predict how many times new FxRates prints in each half. Run it from labs/. Give build a memory: add static final Map<Class<?>, Object> made = new HashMap<>();, return made.get(type) when it is there, and made.put(type, result) before returning. In Kotlin, made.getOrPut(type) { ... } does both. Run it again. TinyContainerDemo.java package workbench.container.l01.demo; import java.lang.reflect.Constructor; /** The smallest container that works: read a constructor, build its parameters first, then call it. */ public class TinyContainerDemo { public static class FxRates { public FxRates() { System.out.println(" new FxRates"); } } public static class FeeCalculator { public FeeCalculator(FxRates rates) { System.out.println(" new FeeCalculator"); } } public static class QuoteService { public QuoteService(FxRates rates) { System.out.println(" new QuoteService"); } } public static class PaymentService { public PaymentService(FeeCalculator fees, QuoteService quotes) { System.out.println(" new PaymentService"); } } static Object build(Class<?> type) throws ReflectiveOperationException { Constructor<?> constructor = type.getConstructors()[0]; // 1. the recipe is the constructor Class<?>[] needs = constructor.getParameterTypes(); Object[] args = new Object[needs.length]; for (int i = 0; i < needs.length; i++) args[i] = build(needs[i]); // 2. build what it needs first return constructor.newInstance(args); // 3. then the object itself } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("by hand:"); FxRates rates = new FxRates(); new PaymentService(new FeeCalculator(rates), new QuoteService(rates)); System.out.println("by reflection:"); build(PaymentService.class); } } ./gradlew :container:demo -Pmain=workbench.container.l01.demo.TinyContainerDemo labs/container/src/demo/java/workbench/container/l01/demo/TinyContainerDemo.java TinyContainerDemo.kt package workbench.container.l01.demo // The smallest container that works: read a constructor, build its parameters first, then call it. class KFxRates { init { println(" new KFxRates") } } class KFeeCalculator(rates: KFxRates) { init { println(" new KFeeCalculator") } } class KQuoteService(rates: KFxRates) { init { println(" new KQuoteService") } } class KPaymentService(fees: KFeeCalculator, quotes: KQuoteService) { init { println(" new KPaymentService") } } fun build(type: Class<*>): Any { val constructor = type.constructors[0] // 1. the recipe is the constructor val args = constructor.parameterTypes.map { build(it) } // 2. build what it needs first return constructor.newInstance(*args.toTypedArray()) // 3. then the object itself } fun main() { println("by hand:") val rates = KFxRates() KPaymentService(KFeeCalculator(rates), KQuoteService(rates)) println("by reflection:") build(KPaymentService::class.java) } ./gradlew :container:demo -Pmain=workbench.container.l01.demo.TinyContainerDemoKt labs/container/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/container/l01/demo/TinyContainerDemo.kt By hand, new FxRates prints once, because you passed the same rates twice. By reflection it prints twice: once for FeeCalculator and once for QuoteService. With the map it prints once. That map is a singleton scope in its simplest form, and section 4 shows why the plain version breaks under threads. A container is a kitchen's prep list. Every dish card lists what it needs, and the prep cook sorts the cards so stocks are made before the sauces that use them. A singleton is the one pot of stock that every dish ladles from; a prototype is a garnish made fresh for each plate. A card that needs a sauce that needs the same card is a cycle, and a good prep cook refuses it at the start of the shift, not at the first order. The analogy breaks at improvisation: a cook can make do when a card is unclear, while a container that guesses which constructor you meant is a bug.

h: Wire classes by reflection · Find the components: a list you write, or a scan of the class path
x: The simplest way to tell the container which classes take part is a list: new Container(List.of(PaymentService.class, Ledger.class, ...)). It is fast and obvious, and it is one more file to keep in step with the code. The usual alternative is to mark classes with an annotation and scan for them. A scan asks a class loader for the package's directory. loader.getResources("workbench/container/l01/app") returns one URL for every class path entry that contains that package. For a build directory it is a file: URL, and for a JAR it is a jar:file:/srv/app.jar!/workbench/... URL. You list the .class files under it and turn each file name into a binary class name. Then you load each class, and the flag you pass decides what runs. Class.forName(name, false, loader) loads and links the class without initializing it. As Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization showed, the one-argument Class.forName(name) also initializes it, so every static initializer in the package would run during the scan, components or not. After loading, c.isAnnotationPresent(Component.class) keeps the components. That only works because @Component has @Retention(RUNTIME). With the default retention, CLASS, javac writes the annotation into the class file, but the JVM never exposes it to reflection, and the scan finds nothing. A scan has a price. It loads every class in the package, including the ones that turn out not to be components. In ScanDemo, scanning an 11-class package loaded 272 classes: the 11, plus the JDK code for listing directories, streams and reading annotations. Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it showed that every class the JVM loads is found, parsed and verified on every launch. A large service scans thousands of classes at every start. Quarkus avoids this by indexing the classes when the application is built, which is where lesson 3 of this track ends up. One more trap, found while writing the demo. getResources finds a package inside a JAR only when the JAR has an entry for the directory itself. Most build tools write those entries, but a JAR built with "files only" gives the scan zero roots. Nothing fails; the container just has no components. Scan a package, then run its initializers by accident Read ScanDemo (or ScanDemo.kt). FeeTable and AuditTrail in the app package print a line from their static initializers. Predict: does either line print during the scan? Then run it. Set INITIALIZE = true and run it again. Then look at the last two lines: the same package in two JAR files. h: Wire classes by reflection · Pick one constructor, then walk the graph depth first
x: A container must never guess which constructor to call, because reflection gives you no order to rely on. The lab's rule is the one most containers use: if exactly one public constructor carries @Inject, use it; if there is only one public constructor, use that; otherwise refuse with a message that says what to do. Kotlin makes "only one public constructor" harder than it looks. class KotlinFees(val rates: FxRates, val bps: Int = 290) has two public constructors on the JVM: yours, and a synthetic KotlinFees(FxRates, int, int, DefaultConstructorMarker) that Kotlin callers use when they leave out bps. It is the $default trick from Reading bytecode: javap, the operand stack and Kotlin's output, applied to a constructor. Skip it with isSynthetic(). When every parameter has a default, kotlinc adds a third, a real public no-argument constructor, and in this track's run it copied @Inject onto that one too. The container then sees two marked constructors and refuses. Don't give injected parameters defaults. Parameters are resolved by type, not by name. Class files don't keep parameter names unless javac runs with -parameters (-java-parameters for kotlinc), so reflection reports arg0 and arg1. A parameter of interface type, such as CardIssuerClient, resolves to the one component that implements it. None or two is an error. Now the order. Visit a component, visit everything its constructor needs, and only then append the component to the list. This is a depth-first, post-order walk, and the result is a creation order in which every class comes after its dependencies. A shared dependency is appended once, because the walk skips classes that are already done. The same walk finds cycles. Keep a path: the components you are inside right now. If you reach a component that is on the path, you've come back to something that is still waiting for its own dependencies. Report the slice of the path from that component back to itself: Dependency cycle: Payouts -> Statements -> Reconciler -> Payouts The lab's container computes this order in its constructor. A cycle or a missing dependency then fails the deploy, not the first payment of the night. Creating the objects can still wait until someone asks for them. h: Wire classes by reflection · One singleton per container, even when eight threads ask first
x: A singleton component has one instance per container, created the first time someone needs it. A prototype component is created again on every request. Singleton is the default, and it is where the bugs are, because the first request often arrives on eight threads at once. The map from the first Try it is check-then-act, the race from Race conditions: why count++ lies. Every thread that reads null before the first put builds its own FxRates. In SingletonRaceDemo all eight threads did, and got eight different objects. ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent looks like the fix, but a container calls it recursively: building payouts means building ledger first, from inside the mapping function. The Javadoc forbids that: the function must not modify the map. In practice it works when the two keys land in different bins of the map's table and throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update when they share one. With Class keys the bin depends on identity hash codes, so the same container fails on some starts and not others. The JVM has its own lazy singleton, the holder idiom from Why the JVM starts slowly, and how to measure it: a nested class whose static final field is set on first use, under the class initialization lock. It is the best tool when you can write one holder class per singleton before compiling. A reflective container can't, because it learns its components at run time. Lesson 3 generates those holder classes. So the lab gives each singleton a cell that uses double-checked locking, the pattern Lazy init done right: double-checked locking and holders proved correct: Java T value = instance; // volatile read: no lock once it is built if (value == null) { synchronized (this) { value = instance; // someone may have built it while we waited if (value == null) instance = value = factory.get(); } } return value; Kotlin var value = instance // @Volatile var instance: T? = null if (value == null) { synchronized(this) { value = instance if (value == null) { value = factory(); instance = value } } } return value!! volatile is what makes the unlocked first read safe: a thread that reads a non-null reference also sees every write the constructor made before the reference was stored. Without it, a thread could see the reference and still read the new object's fields as zero. Building PaymentService holds its cell's lock while it builds FeeCalculator, which takes another lock. Nested locks usually mean deadlock risk. Here every lock is taken along an arrow of the graph, from a component to something it needs. Two threads could only wait for each other if the arrows formed a loop, and the constructor already rejected loops. One more difference from a holder: if the factory throws, the cell stays empty and the next get tries again. A static initializer that throws fails once and gives NoClassDefFoundError from then on. Race for the first FxRates Read SingletonRaceDemo (or the Kotlin twin). Each row releases eight threads at the same moment, and FxRates takes 20 ms to build. Predict the two numbers on each of the first two rows, and which computeIfAbsent line fails. Run it twice. Do the numbers change? Java gives you exactly the constructors you write. Kotlin's default arguments are compiled into an extra public synthetic constructor, and if every parameter has a default, into a real no-argument constructor as well, which receives the same annotations. So a container must filter isSynthetic() and must not be fooled by an @Inject that kotlinc copied. In both languages the class file keeps no parameter names by default, so the container resolves by type. The Kotlin class is also final, which is harmless here and becomes the main problem in lesson 2.

h: Wire classes by reflection · Worked example
x: Break a cycle the container reported The container refuses to start with Dependency cycle: Ledger -> AuditTrail -> Ledger. Here are the two constructors. Read them and ask what each one needs while it is being built, and what it only needs later, inside a method. @Component public class Ledger { private final LedgerStore store = new LedgerStore(); // hidden inside private final AuditTrail audit; public Ledger(AuditTrail audit) { this.audit = audit; } public void post(Entry e) { store.add(e); audit.record(e); } public long balance(String account) { return store.balance(account); } } @Component public class AuditTrail { private final Ledger ledger; public AuditTrail(Ledger ledger) { this.ledger = ledger; } public void record(Entry e) { if (ledger.balance(e.account()) < 0) alert(e); } } @Component class Ledger(private val audit: AuditTrail) { private val store = LedgerStore() // hidden inside fun post(e: Entry) { store.add(e); audit.record(e) } fun balance(account: String): Long = store.balance(account) } @Component class AuditTrail(private val ledger: Ledger) { fun record(e: Entry) { if (ledger.balance(e.account) < 0) alert(e) } } AuditTrail doesn't need a Ledger at all. It needs balances, which live in the ledger's store. Ledger needs the store to write to and the audit trail to notify. The loop exists because the store is hidden inside Ledger. Give the store its own component. Both classes depend on it, and the arrows no longer close a loop: LedgerStore is created first, then AuditTrail, then Ledger. @Component public class LedgerStore { public void add(Entry e) { /* ... */ } public long balance(String account) { /* ... */ return 0; } } @Component public class AuditTrail { private final LedgerStore store; public AuditTrail(LedgerStore store) { this.store = store; } public void record(Entry e) { if (store.balance(e.account()) < 0) alert(e); } } @Component public class Ledger { private final LedgerStore store; private final AuditTrail audit; public Ledger(LedgerStore store, AuditTrail audit) { this.store = store; this.audit = audit; } public void post(Entry e) { store.add(e); audit.record(e); } } @Component class LedgerStore { fun add(e: Entry) { /* ... */ } fun balance(account: String): Long = 0 /* ... */ } @Component class AuditTrail(private val store: LedgerStore) { fun record(e: Entry) { if (store.balance(e.account) < 0) alert(e) } } @Component class Ledger(private val store: LedgerStore, private val audit: AuditTrail) { fun post(e: Entry) { store.add(e); audit.record(e) } } If the two really do need each other at call time, production containers offer a lookup instead of an object: jakarta.inject.Provider<Ledger> in CDI, ObjectProvider<Ledger> in Spring. The constructor then receives something that finds the Ledger later, inside a method. The lab's container doesn't support that, on purpose. Reach for it after you've tried the split, not before.

Then instanceOf: the cell's get() for singletons, create for prototypes. Run the tests until all twelve pass, then twice more. In creationOrder, check done before path. h: Wire classes by reflection · Quiz
x: Your scanner calls Class.forName(name), with one argument, for every class in com.acme.pay. FeeTable has static final Map<String, Fee> ROWS = loadFromDisk(); and is never injected anywhere. When does loadFromDisk() run? Never, because nothing injects FeeTable During the scan, because the one-argument forName initializes every class it loads When the JIT compiles FeeTable Only if FeeTable is annotated @Component The one-argument Class.forName loads, links and initializes, so <clinit> runs during the scan for every class in the package, component or not. Class.forName(name, false, loader) loads and links without initializing. Being a component doesn't matter either way: the scan only checks the annotation after the class is loaded. A container resolves constructor parameters by name with Parameter.getName(). Gradle compiles PaymentService(CardIssuerClient issuer, Ledger ledger) with javac's default options. What names does the container see? arg0 and arg1 issuer and ledger CardIssuerClient and Ledger A NoSuchFieldException, because the names are private Method descriptors carry types, not names, and javac only writes a MethodParameters attribute when you pass -parameters (-java-parameters for kotlinc). Without it, reflection makes up arg0, arg1. That's why the lab resolves by type: the type is always in the descriptor. A service's container scans 4,000 classes at start-up, though only 300 are components, and none of the 4,000 has a static initializer. What does the scan add to every start? Nothing, because classes without static initializers are free Only the cost of calling 300 constructors Finding, parsing and verifying 4,000 classes, and reading their annotations A garbage collection to unload the 3,700 non-components Loading is the expensive part even without initialization: the JVM finds each class file, parses it into metaspace and verifies its bytecode, on every launch. The 3,700 non-components stay loaded; nothing unloads classes of the application loader. Initialization would add the static initializers on top. A teammate's SingletonCell uses double-checked locking, but the instance field is a plain field, not volatile. What can go wrong? Two threads can both run the factory The nested locks can deadlock Nothing on x86, so it is fine in production A thread can see a non-null reference and still read the new object's fields as zero The lock makes the factory run once. What the unlocked first read lacks is a happens-before edge to the constructor's writes: without volatile, the reference can become visible before the fields it points to. volatile on the field gives that edge. "It works on x86" describes one CPU and one JIT, not what the memory model allows. Ledger needs AuditTrail, AuditTrail needs PaymentService, and PaymentService needs Ledger. The container is built with the list [Ledger, PaymentService, AuditTrail]. What message does the lab's creationOrder throw? Dependency cycle: Ledger -> AuditTrail -> PaymentService -> Ledger Dependency cycle: PaymentService -> Ledger -> AuditTrail -> PaymentService A StackOverflowError, because the walk never ends Dependency cycle: Ledger -> PaymentService -> AuditTrail -> Ledger The walk starts at the first component in the list, Ledger, follows its constructor to AuditTrail, then to PaymentService, and then reaches Ledger, which is still on the path. The message is the path from the repeated class back to itself, in the order the walk went. Without a path the recursion would overflow the stack, which is what the ten-line container from section 1 does.

h: Wire classes by reflection · Key terms
x: Dependency injection A class receives the objects it needs, usually through its constructor, instead of creating them itself. Component A class the container creates and hands to others. Spring and CDI call the instances beans. Container The code that finds components, works out the order to build them in, builds them and keeps the shared ones. Scope How many instances of a component exist: one per container (singleton) or a new one per request (prototype). Creation order A list of all components in which each one comes after everything it depends on. Also called a topological order. Class path scan Finding classes by asking a class loader for a package directory and loading every class file in it. Double-checked locking Read a volatile field without a lock; only if it is empty, lock, read again, and build. Fast after the first call. What does Class.forName(name, false, loader) do that Class.forName(name) doesn't? It loads and links the class without initializing it, so no static initializer runs. A scanner should always pass false. Why does @Component need @Retention(RUNTIME)? With the default CLASS retention the annotation is in the class file, but reflection can't see it, so isAnnotationPresent returns false. Kotlin class Fees(val rates: FxRates, val bps: Int = 290): how many public constructors does getConstructors() return? Two: (FxRates, int) and a synthetic (FxRates, int, int, DefaultConstructorMarker) for default arguments. Filter with isSynthetic(). In what order does a container create components? Depth-first post-order: each component after everything its constructor needs. Shared dependencies appear once. How does a depth-first walk detect a dependency cycle? It keeps a path of the components it is still inside. Reaching one of them again is a cycle; the path from that component back to itself is the message. Why not build a container's singletons with a recursive ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent? The mapping function must not modify the map. If the inner key lands in the same bin, it throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update, and with Class keys that depends on identity hash codes. Why can nested SingletonCell locks not deadlock? Each lock is taken along a dependency arrow, from a component to what it needs. A deadlock would need the arrows to form a loop, and the container rejects cycles at start-up.

h: Wire classes by reflection · Go deeper
x: Spring creates singletons eagerly at the end of start-up by default, after the scan and the graph work, so that a constructor that throws stops the deploy too. The lab's container is lazy, like a CDI client proxy that creates its bean on the first method call. Neither is wrong; they put the same failure at different times. Spring can also resolve some cycles that the lab refuses. With field or setter injection it can hand out a reference to an object whose constructor has finished but whose fields aren't all set yet, from a cache of "early" singleton references. Constructor injection can never do that, because the object doesn't exist until its constructor's arguments do. That is one reason constructor injection is the recommended style: an impossible graph fails loudly. Since Spring Boot 2.6, even the setter-injection kind of cycle is refused unless you set spring.main.allow-circular-references=true. Three things a production container adds to this lesson's graph: qualifiers, when two components implement the same interface and the injection point must say which (@Named, @Qualifier); generic types, so that Repository<Payment> and Repository<Refund> are different dependencies (the lab compares erased classes only); and injection of lookups such as Provider<T>, which turn a hard edge into one that is followed at call time. Each one makes the graph work harder, and each one is easier to check at build time than at start-up, which is lesson 3's argument.

h: Add interceptors with proxies · An interceptor runs around a call, and proceed() is the call
x: Here is what timing and retries look like when every method does them itself: Java public String authorize(String pan, long amountMinor) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return http.authorize(pan, amountMinor); } catch (IssuerUnavailableException e) { if (attempt == 3) throw e; } } } finally { metrics.record("authorize", System.nanoTime() - t0); } } Kotlin fun authorize(pan: String, amountMinor: Long): String { val t0 = System.nanoTime() try { var attempt = 1 while (true) { try { return http.authorize(pan, amountMinor) } catch (e: IssuerUnavailableException) { if (attempt++ == 3) throw e } } } finally { metrics.record("authorize", System.nanoTime() - t0) } } Two lines of business logic, twelve lines of plumbing, copied into capture, refund and void. Decorator and Proxy moved the plumbing into a class that wraps the client, but you still write one decorator per interface. An interceptor is the plumbing written once, for any method. It receives an Invocation: the method's name, its arguments, and proceed(), which means "carry on with the call". Here is the lab's timer: Java public Object intercept(Invocation inv) { long start = clock.getAsLong(); boolean failed = true; try { Object result = inv.proceed(); failed = false; return result; } finally { log.record(inv.getName(), clock.getAsLong() - start, failed); } } Kotlin override fun intercept(inv: Invocation): Any? { val start = clock.asLong var failed = true try { return inv.proceed().also { failed = false } } finally { log.record(inv.name, clock.asLong - start, failed) } } Several interceptors form a chain. proceed() runs the next one, and after the last one it runs the real method. A retry interceptor is a loop that calls proceed() again after a listed failure. CDI's InvocationContext.proceed() and Spring's MethodInvocation.proceed() have exactly this shape. The order of the chain changes what you measure. With @Timed outside @Retry, the timer sees one call that took as long as all the attempts together. With @Timed inside, it records every attempt separately. The lab puts @Timed first, because the caller waited for all of it. The annotations themselves only mark methods: they need @Retention(RUNTIME) so the container can read them with getAnnotation, as @Component did in lesson 1. Swap the order of two interceptors Read ChainDemo (or the Kotlin twin). The "issuer" fails twice and then answers. A third interceptor prints each time the chain reaches it. Predict for each order: how many -> lines, and how many entries in the log? Run it. Then change RetryInterceptor(3, ...) to RetryInterceptor(2, ...) and predict what the first order prints. ChainDemo.java package workbench.container.l02.demo; import workbench.container.l02.CallLog; import workbench.container.l02.Interceptor; import workbench.container.l02.Invocation; import workbench.container.l02.RetryInterceptor; import workbench.container.l02.TimedInterceptor; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.function.LongSupplier; /** One issuer call that fails twice, sent through the same two interceptors in both orders. */ public class ChainDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { AtomicLong ticks = new AtomicLong(); LongSupplier clock = () -> ticks.addAndGet(10_000_000); // a fake clock: 10 ms per read Interceptor shout = inv -> { // a third interceptor, to watch proceed() System.out.println(" -> " + inv.getName()); try { return inv.proceed(); } finally { System.out.println(" <- " + inv.getName()); } }; for (String order : List.of("timed, retry", "retry, timed")) { CallLog log = new CallLog(); Interceptor timed = new TimedInterceptor(log, clock); Interceptor retry = new RetryInterceptor(3, List.of(IllegalStateException.class)); List<Interceptor> chain = order.startsWith("timed") ? List.of(timed, retry, shout) : List.of(retry, timed, shout); AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); System.out.println(order + ":"); Object result = new Invocation("Issuer.authorize", new Object[] {"4111111111111111"}, chain, () -> { if (calls.incrementAndGet() < 3) throw new IllegalStateException("issuer timed out"); // fails twice return "auth-1111"; }).proceed(); System.out.println(" result " + result + " after " + calls.get() + " calls, log " + log.calls()); } } } ./gradlew :container:demo -Pmain=workbench.container.l02.demo.ChainDemo labs/container/src/demo/java/workbench/container/l02/demo/ChainDemo.java ChainDemo.kt package workbench.container.l02.demo import workbench.container.l02.CallLog import workbench.container.l02.Interceptor import workbench.container.l02.Invocation import workbench.container.l02.RetryInterceptor import workbench.container.l02.TimedInterceptor import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.function.LongSupplier // One issuer call that fails twice, sent through the same two interceptors in both orders. fun main() { val ticks = AtomicLong() val clock = LongSupplier { ticks.addAndGet(10_000_000) } // a fake clock: 10 ms per read val shout = Interceptor { inv -> // a third interceptor, to watch proceed() println(" -> ${inv.name}") try { inv.proceed() } finally { println(" <- ${inv.name}") } } for (order in listOf("timed, retry", "retry, timed")) { val log = CallLog() val timed = TimedInterceptor(log, clock) val retry = RetryInterceptor(3, listOf(IllegalStateException::class.java)) val chain = if (order.startsWith("timed")) listOf(timed, retry, shout) else listOf(retry, timed, shout) var calls = 0 println("$order:") val result = Invocation("Issuer.authorize", arrayOf("4111111111111111"), chain) { if (++calls < 3) throw IllegalStateException("issuer timed out") // fails twice "auth-1111" }.proceed() println(" result $result after $calls calls, log ${log.calls()}") } } ./gradlew :container:demo -Pmain=workbench.container.l02.demo.ChainDemoKt labs/container/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/container/l02/demo/ChainDemo.kt Both orders print three ->/<- pairs, because the retry calls proceed() three times. With timed outside, the log has one entry, failed=false, 10 ms on the fake clock. With retry outside, it has three: two failed=true, one failed=false. With two attempts the call throws IllegalStateException: issuer timed out after two pairs, and the one log entry is recorded with failed=true on the way out. A JDK proxy is a receptionist in front of a specialist's office. Every visitor goes through the receptionist, who logs the time and sends them back in if the specialist was busy, but when the specialist walks down the corridor to ask a colleague a question, no receptionist sees it. A Byte Buddy subclass is the specialist with a habit built in: they log their own time, even for questions they ask themselves. A final Kotlin class is a specialist who refuses to learn new habits, and the honest thing is to say so at hiring time. The analogy breaks at retries: a receptionist would notice a patient being sent in twice, while an interceptor repeats whatever you annotated, harmful or not.

h: Add interceptors with proxies · A component with interfaces gets a JDK proxy, and the handler owes four answers
x: The container now decides, for each component, how its interceptors will run. If the component implements an interface, it gets a JDK proxy: Proxy.newProxyInstance generates a class that implements the interfaces and sends every call to an InvocationHandler, as Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy showed. The container creates the real object first, the target, and the proxy holds it. Spring Framework's documented rule is the same: "If the target object to be proxied implements at least one interface, a JDK dynamic proxy is used." (Spring Boot switches its default to subclasses, as Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors showed.) That lesson's handler rules come back as the four cases you write in the lab, in this order: equals, hashCode and toString arrive with method.declaringClass == Object. Answer them on the proxy, by identity. A handler that forwards equals to the target makes proxy.equals(proxy) false, and listeners.remove(proxy) quietly fails. A default method goes to InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args), so its body runs with this being the proxy and its inner calls come back through the handler. Every other method builds an Invocation with that method's chain and a target call, method.invoke(target, args). That target call catches InvocationTargetException and rethrows its cause, so the caller sees the issuer's own IssuerUnavailableException. Two consequences follow from "the proxy implements the interfaces". First, the bean is not a FakeIssuer. get(CardIssuerClient.class) works, but get(FakeIssuer.class) can't return a $Proxy5, so the lab's container refuses with a message naming the interface to ask for. Second, the handler only ever sees the interface's Method, so the annotations must be on the interface. @Timed on the class's method would never be read; the container refuses that at start-up too, rather than skipping it. Kotlin's final-by-default doesn't matter on this path. FakeIssuer in the tests is a plain, final Kotlin class, and that's fine: the JDK only needs the interface. Equals on two proxies Read ProxyIdentityDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It compares the container's proxy with one whose handler forwards every method to the target. Predict the three booleans on each line. Run it, and read the last line. h: Add interceptors with proxies · A class without interfaces gets a Byte Buddy subclass, so final is fatal
x: SettlementService has no interface, so the container generates a subclass with Byte Buddy, the "proxy is the object" model from Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors. Byte Buddy's subclass(type) copies the superclass's public constructors, so the container calls SettlementService$ByteBuddy$...(SettlementLedger) with the dependencies it resolved, and the original class is never instantiated on its own. There is one object. Each intercepted method is an override whose @SuperCall callable runs super.settle(...) at the end of the chain. A retry simply calls that callable again. Because the subclass is the bean, a self-call goes through it. settle calls this.audit(batch), this is the subclass, and audit's override runs its own chain. The figure shows both models side by side. A subclass can only intercept what it can override, and Kotlin makes that a daily problem. A Kotlin class is final unless you write open, and so is every member. On a final class Byte Buddy fails loudly: Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types. On an open class with a plain fun, it succeeds, and the method is simply not overridden. @Timed sits on it and does nothing. That silent case is why the lab's container calls check(component) for every component when it starts, and refuses a final class or a final or private intercepted method with a message that says what to change. There are three fixes. Write open on the class and on each intercepted method. Or let the all-open compiler plugin do it for classes that carry an annotation you choose; this lab's build opens classes marked @OpenForProxies: // container/build.gradle.kts plugins { kotlin("plugin.allopen") } allOpen { annotation("workbench.container.l02.demo.OpenForProxies") } kotlin-spring is the same plugin, preset to open @Component and its friends. The third fix is an interface, which moves the component to the JDK-proxy path where finality doesn't matter. Quarkus goes a fourth way: with quarkus.arc.transform-unproxyable-classes, on by default, it rewrites final classes at build time so it can subclass them. Each Byte Buddy class also gets its own class loader, a ByteArrayClassLoader, unless you choose another loading strategy. Lesson 3 counts what that costs. Watch a Kotlin class get refused, then opened Read FinalClassDemo.kt: two identical classes with a @Timed method, one marked @OpenForProxies. The Java twin, FinalClassDemoJava, does the same with a Java final class. Predict the final= flags on each line, and which class the container refuses. Run it. From labs/, run javap -p container/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/container/l02/demo/KOpenedFees.class and compare it with KFinalFees.class. h: Add interceptors with proxies · Retry the smallest call that is safe to repeat
x: A retry interceptor makes three promises. It only retries the exceptions the annotation lists: an IssuerUnavailableException is worth another try, a card number that fails the Luhn check is not. It counts attempts in total, so attempts = 3 means at most three calls. And when it gives up, the caller gets the original exception, not an UndeclaredThrowableException or an InvocationTargetException wrapped around it. The hard part is choosing which call to repeat. authorizeAndCapture is a default method that calls authorize and then capture. If the handler forwards it to the target and retries it as a whole, a capture that times out repeats the authorization too: the issuer sees a second hold on the customer's card. With invokeDefault, the default body runs on the proxy, and each inner call carries its own @Retry. The capture is retried as a capture. That is the default-method rule from Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and the lab tests it. Even a single call is only safe to repeat when the other side can recognize the repeat. A timeout doesn't tell you the issuer didn't capture; it tells you that you don't know. So retry a capture only if it carries an idempotency key, the same one on every attempt, which the issuer uses to drop duplicates. The interceptor can't know that; the person who writes @Retry on the method has to. Retries also nest. With a subclass proxy, a retried settle that calls a retried audit runs audit's body up to 3 x 3 = 9 times, as the warm-up asked. Put @Retry on the outermost call that is safe to repeat, or on the innermost one, and not on both. Retry the capture, not the authorization Read RetryDemo (or the Kotlin twin). The issuer's first capture times out. The first half uses the container's proxy; the second uses a handler that retries every method as a whole. Predict the list of calls the issuer sees in each half. Run it. fun main() { val c = Container(listOf(IssuerScript::class.java, FlakyIssuer::class.java)) val script = c.get(IssuerScript::class.java) script.captureFailures.set(1) val result = c.get(CardIssuerClient::class.java).authorizeAndCapture("4111111111111111", 12_000) println("container's proxy: $result, issuer saw ${script.seen}") println(" timed calls: ${c.callLog().names()}") val naiveScript = IssuerScript().apply { captureFailures.set(1) } val target = FlakyIssuer(naiveScript) val retryEverything = InvocationHandler { _, method, a -> callWithRetry(target, method, a) } // any method, defaults too val naive = Proxy.newProxyInstance(CardIssuerClient::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(CardIssuerClient::class.java), retryEverything) as CardIssuerClient println("retry the shell: ${naive.authorizeAndCapture("4111111111111111", 12_000)}, issuer saw ${naiveScript.seen}") } private fun callWithRetry(target: Any, method: Method, a: Array<Any?>?, attempt: Int = 1): Any? = try { method.invoke(target, *(a ?: emptyArray())) // the default body runs on the target } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { if (attempt == 3 || e.cause !is IssuerUnavailableException) throw e.cause!! callWithRetry(target, method, a, attempt + 1) } ./gradlew :container:demo -Pmain=workbench.container.l02.demo.RetryDemoKt labs/container/src/demo/kotlin/workbench/container/l02/demo/RetryDemo.kt Both halves return cap-auth-1111. Through the container the issuer sees [authorize, capture (timed out), capture], and the timed calls are authorize and capture: the default method itself is not timed. The naive handler gives [authorize, capture (timed out), authorize, capture]: one customer, two authorizations. The most common mistake is trusting that an annotation runs because it is on the method. Interception only happens when a call passes through generated code that can override or receive that method. A Kotlin method without open, a private method, a self-call on a forwarding proxy, an annotation placed on the class when the proxy only sees the interface: in each case the code compiles, the tests that call the class directly pass, and the timer or the retry never runs. People miss it because nothing fails. The fix is the lab's design: let the container check at start-up and refuse what it can't intercept, and test through the container with an assertion on the effect (a retry count, a log entry).

Java's default is overridable, so final is the exception you write; Kotlin's default is final, so open is. That single difference decides whether a subclass proxy can work, and on an open class with a plain fun it fails silently. The all-open plugin flips Kotlin's default for classes with an annotation you choose. Nothing differs for JDK proxies: both languages compile interfaces to ordinary JVM interfaces, and Kotlin interface functions with a body become JVM default methods that invokeDefault can run.

h: Add interceptors with proxies · Worked example
x: Add a third interceptor: @Audited Compliance wants every refund recorded with its arguments. Start with the marker. It needs RUNTIME retention and targets methods, like @Timed. @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Target(ElementType.METHOD) public @interface Audited { } @Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME) @Target(AnnotationTarget.FUNCTION) annotation class Audited Write the interceptor. It records the call before it proceeds, so an attempt that throws is in the audit trail too. It doesn't catch anything: failures are the retry's business, or the caller's. public final class AuditInterceptor implements Interceptor { private final List<String> trail; public AuditInterceptor(List<String> trail) { this.trail = trail; } @Override public Object intercept(Invocation inv) { trail.add(inv.getName() + Arrays.toString(inv.getArgs())); // 1. record first return inv.proceed(); // 2. then carry on } } class AuditInterceptor(private val trail: MutableList<String>) : Interceptor { override fun intercept(inv: Invocation): Any? { trail += inv.name + inv.args.contentToString() // 1. record first return inv.proceed() // 2. then carry on } } Decide where it goes in the chain. Outside @Retry, it records one entry per refund the caller asked for. Inside, it records every attempt. Compliance asked for every request sent to the issuer, so it goes inside: after the timer and the retry. List<Interceptor> chainFor(Method m) { List<Interceptor> chain = new ArrayList<>(); if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Timed.class)) chain.add(new TimedInterceptor(log, clock)); Retry r = m.getAnnotation(Retry.class); if (r != null) chain.add(new RetryInterceptor(r.attempts(), List.of(r.on()))); if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Audited.class)) chain.add(new AuditInterceptor(trail)); // 3. innermost return chain; } fun chainFor(m: Method): List<Interceptor> = buildList { if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Timed::class.java)) add(TimedInterceptor(log, clock)) m.getAnnotation(Retry::class.java)?.let { add(RetryInterceptor(it.attempts, it.on.map { k -> k.java })) } if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Audited::class.java)) add(AuditInterceptor(trail)) // 3. innermost } Teach the container that @Audited counts as intercepted, in isIntercepted, so check refuses a final audited method too. Then test through the container: a refund that times out once leaves two trail entries with the same idempotency key. If it leaves one, the interceptor is outside the retry; if it leaves none, the method was never overridden.

Byte Buddy throws Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types The call is timed, because the subclass overrides every method pay runs normally and is never timed, with no error anywhere The JVM throws VerifyError when the subclass loads The class is open, so subclassing works. pay has no open, so kotlinc made it final, and Byte Buddy can't override a final method; it skips it. You want to run this container in a GraalVM native image. Which part is the real obstacle? The JDK proxies: native image can't run java.lang.reflect.Proxy at all The singleton cells, because native image has no volatile Nothing: native image supports any code that runs on HotSpot The Byte Buddy subclasses: they are classes defined from bytes at run time, which a closed world can't contain Native image builds a closed world, so every class must exist at build time. After a test drops its last reference to the container, what keeps one of those loaders alive? Nothing it created: the loader can be collected with its class once no bean instance and no reference to the class is reachable The application class loader, which holds every child loader forever The JIT's code cache, which pins every class it compiled Metaspace, which is never collected A class keeps its loader alive and an object keeps its class alive, so the chain is: container, cell, bean, subclass, loader. Remove the root and the whole chain is unreachable, and a full GC can unload the class and free its metaspace. A bean is intercepted by a subclass. settle is @Timed and calls this.audit(), which is also @Timed. h: Add interceptors with proxies · Key terms
x: Interceptor Code written once that runs around many method calls, such as a timer or a retry. Interceptor chain The interceptors for one method, in order; each calls proceed() to hand on to the next, and the last hands on to the method. Target The real object behind a forwarding proxy, which the handler calls when the chain ends. Subclass proxy A generated subclass that overrides the intercepted methods and is itself the bean, so self-calls are intercepted. all-open A Kotlin compiler plugin that makes classes with chosen annotations, and their members, open instead of final. Idempotency key An ID sent with a request so the receiver can recognize a repeat and not do the work twice. What does proceed() do in an interceptor chain? It runs the next interceptor, or after the last one, the real method. A retry interceptor calls it again after a listed failure. Why put @Timed outside @Retry in the chain? Then it records one call that includes every attempt: the time the caller really waited. Inside, it records each attempt separately. The four cases of a decorating InvocationHandler, in order? Object methods by identity; default methods with invokeDefault; the chain ending in method.invoke(target, args); unwrap InvocationTargetException. Why can't a container return a JDK proxy for get(FakeIssuer.class)? The proxy class extends java.lang.reflect.Proxy and implements only the interfaces, so it is not a FakeIssuer. Ask for the interface. Kotlin open class S { @Timed fun pay() }: does a Byte Buddy subclass time pay? No, silently. pay is final because it isn't open, so the subclass can't override it. Three ways to make a Kotlin class interceptable by a subclass proxy? Write open on the class and the intercepted methods; use the all-open plugin (or kotlin-spring); or give it an interface and use a JDK proxy. When is it safe for an interceptor to retry an issuer call? When the failure is listed as retryable and the call carries an idempotency key, the same on every attempt, so the issuer can drop duplicates.

h: Add interceptors with proxies · Go deeper
x: Jakarta Interceptors, the spec behind CDI and Quarkus, has the same pieces under other names. An interceptor binding is an annotation like @Timed that is itself annotated @InterceptorBinding. The interceptor is a class with an @AroundInvoke method that takes an InvocationContext and calls ctx.proceed(). The order of the chain comes from @Priority on each interceptor class, with lower numbers running first. Spring AOP's equivalent is an AOP Alliance MethodInterceptor, whose invoke(MethodInvocation) also ends in proceed(), ordered by @Order or the Ordered interface. Annotations and proxies have a quieter interaction too. Java annotations are not inherited from interfaces: @Timed on CardIssuerClient.authorize is not visible through FakeIssuer.class.getMethod("authorize", ...). A JDK proxy hands the handler the interface's Method, so the lab's container sees it. A subclass proxy looks at the class's methods, so an annotation that lives only on an interface method would not be found there. Spring papers over this with its own annotation search, which walks interfaces and superclasses. The lab refuses the ambiguous case instead: annotations on the class of an interface-proxied component are an error. Byte Buddy can also load a generated class without a new class loader. ClassLoadingStrategy.UsingLookup with a MethodHandles.Lookup from the bean's package defines the subclass in the same loader and package as its superclass, which lets it override package-private methods and avoids one loader per class. The default used in the lab is the simplest one, and lesson 3's histogram shows what it leaves behind.

ProxyCallBench calls one fee calculation four ways. The bytes are exact and the same on every run, which is why they are the number to trust. Where do 208 bytes come from? The JDK proxy's generated method boxes the long argument and puts it in an Object[]. The handler builds an Invocation for each step of the chain and a lambda for the target call. Method.invoke boxes the result. The generated forwarding class does the same things in its source: new Object[] {p0}, new Invocation(...), a lambda. JMHSample_35_Profilers (the GC profiler) read Run-time wiring is a wedding caterer who arrives with raw ingredients and a recipe book, and starts cooking when the guests sit down. It works for any menu, even one changed that morning, and the guests wait. Build-time wiring is the caterer who cooks the day before and only reheats. Dinner is fast, and the menu is fixed the night before: a guest who arrives with a new allergy gets whatever was planned. AppCDS is a faster stove, and it helps both caterers, but only the second one has nothing left to cook. The analogy breaks at freshness: reheated code is exactly as good as fresh, and the JIT still warms it up after the start.

h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Move the wiring to build time: generate the registry
x: Everything the reflective container works out at start-up depends only on the classes, and the classes are fixed when you build. So do the work then. RegistryGenerator runs the same BeanGraph from lesson 1 at build time: it picks the constructors, orders the graph and checks for cycles, and a cycle now fails the build instead of the deploy. Then it writes a Java class that does the wiring with plain new calls. The lab's test compiles that class with javac, the way a build would. Each singleton gets a holder class. Lesson 1 promised it: Java private static final class FeeCalculator_Holder { static final FeeCalculator INSTANCE = new FeeCalculator(FxRates_Holder.INSTANCE); } Kotlin private object FeeCalculatorHolder { val INSTANCE = FeeCalculator(FxRatesHolder.INSTANCE) // a Kotlin object is a holder class too } The JVM initializes FeeCalculator_Holder the first time get touches it, once, under the class initialization lock from Class loading: loaders, delegation, linking and initialization. Its dependency is another holder, initialized first. There is no volatile, no lock after the first call, and no map: get is a list of if (type == FeeCalculator.class) checks. Prototypes get a factory method instead. Interceptors become source too. For CardIssuerClient the generator writes HttpIssuerClient_Proxy implements CardIssuerClient, and for SettlementService it writes SettlementService_Intercepted extends SettlementService, the same two models as lesson 2. It reads @Timed and @Retry now and writes their values into the code, INTERCEPTION.chain(true, 3, IssuerUnavailableException.class), so nothing reads an annotation at run time. Quarkus ArC does this with its generated _Subclass classes. Micronaut does the graph work in an annotation processor while javac runs, and Spring's AOT processing generates bean definitions as code ahead of time. You give up two things. The set of components is fixed when you build: nothing can scan a plugin directory at start-up or choose a bean from an environment variable without code the generator wrote for it. And a holder fails forever. If PaymentService's constructor throws on first use, the JVM marks PaymentService_Holder as failed, and every later get throws NoClassDefFoundError until you restart, where lesson 1's cell would simply try again. Read the class the generator writes Run GenerateDemo (or the Kotlin twin). It prints the registry the generator writes for the demo app, then tries a graph with a cycle. Find PaymentService_Holder. Which holders must the JVM initialize before it, and in what order? Find SettlementService_Intercepted.audit. Which line makes settle's self-call go through the chain? One $Proxy6 is the issuer proxy. One ByteArrayClassLoader holds the Byte Buddy subclass and its two helper classes, and one SettlementService$ByteBuddy$... is the bean. The other proxy objects are not beans. In this run $Proxy2, with 14 instances, is the @Component annotation, one instance per component class, and $Proxy8, with 42, is a proxy Byte Buddy uses to call JDK methods that don't exist on every Java version it supports (its JavaDispatcher). There were 119 proxy objects in all, and one of them was a bean. The histogram says what is alive, not who holds it. jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump <file> writes every object and reference to an HPROF file, 8 MB here. The JVM pauses while it writes, so on a production pod take it when you can afford a pause. In Eclipse MAT, "Path to GC Roots" on the SettlementService$ByteBuddy$... object should lead through SingletonCell.instance and the container's singletons map to the Container, held by a local variable of the main thread. The demo also proves it by letting go. It drops its only reference to the container and asks for a GC. Byte Buddy's class loader is collected, and with it the generated class: a class keeps its loader alive and an object keeps its class alive, so once the container was unreachable, the whole chain was. The JDK proxy class stays loaded, because it was defined in the application class loader and is cached by Proxy for that loader. The annotation instances stay too, cached with the classes and methods they annotate. The generated registry has a different root. Its singletons are static fields of holder classes, so they live as long as the class loader that loaded the registry. That is why the lab's tests load a fresh copy of the class for every test.
