h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Archive what is left: AppCDS on JDK 21, the AOT cache on JDK 25
x: Class data sharing and Project Leyden's AOT cache showed how to skip parsing and verifying classes at start-up. Apply it to both containers and the last two rows of StartupLadder appear: reflective, AppCDS 2145 2037 108 544 858 parsed from byte-buddy.jar 0, JDK proxies 30, defined from bytes 3, hidden 75 generated, AppCDS 882 847 35 143 362 parsed from byte-buddy.jar 0, JDK proxies 0, defined from bytes 0, hidden 35 AppCDS took Byte Buddy's 814 classes from the archive and nearly halved the reflective start. It could not take the classes made at run time. When the archive was written, JDK 21 printed Skipping jdk/proxy2/$Proxy3: Unsupported location for each of the 30 proxy classes, and the archived run still logs Byte Buddy's three classes as __JVM_DefineClass__: defined from bytes by its own class loader, at every start. So every start still generates and verifies them, and still runs the code that generates them. The generated registry has nothing of the kind: its only run-time classes are 35 hidden ones for lambdas. The AOT cache on JDK 25 goes further for the classes it can store: they arrive loaded and linked, with profiles from the training run. Use JDK 25.0.4 or later, as that lesson explained. The custom-loader limit stays: as Quarkus's AOT guide puts it, Leyden doesn't support custom class loaders yet, so Byte Buddy's classes are made at every start either way. The registry is also the shape native image wants (GraalVM native image and Quarkus native). It has no reflection to declare and no classes defined at run time, which a closed world can't contain. That is the whole argument for build-time wiring in one sentence: the less a start has to discover, generate and verify, the more of it a cache, an archive or a native build can do for you. Archive both starts Run StartupLadder once (section 2), so app.jar and classpath.txt exist in container/build/cap4. Run the two JDK 21 commands. Predict both numbers before you run them: how many classes does the archive refuse, and which run-time classes remain? If you have JDK 25.0.4 or later, run the last two commands with its java. terminal (from labs/) # from labs/, after StartupLadder has run once: it wrote app.jar and classpath.txt cd container/build/cap4 CP=$(cat classpath.txt) MAIN=workbench.container.l03.demo.StartupLadder # JDK 21 or later: a dynamic AppCDS archive for the reflective start java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=reflective.jsa -cp "$CP" $MAIN --reflective 2>&1 | grep -c 'Unsupported location' java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=reflective.jsa -Xlog:class+load -cp "$CP" $MAIN --reflective \ | grep -o 'source: __[A-Za-z_]*' | sort | uniq -c # JDK 25.0.4 or later: the one-step AOT cache for the generated registry java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=generated.aot -cp "$CP" workbench.container.l03.demo.gen.GeneratedStart java -XX:AOTCache=generated.aot -Xlog:aot -cp "$CP" workbench.container.l03.demo.gen.GeneratedStart | grep Opened On JDK 21 the first command prints 30: one Unsupported location warning per proxy class. The second prints 3 source: __JVM_DefineClass__, 75 source: __JVM_LookupDefineClass__ and 30 source: __dynamic_proxy__: the Byte Buddy classes, hidden classes and proxies that every start still makes, even with the archive. On JDK 25.0.4 or later the AOT cache commands should end with Opened AOT cache generated.aot. (this course's machine had only JDK 21, so that line comes from the start-up track's runs, not from this app). JEP 483: Ahead-of-Time Class Loading & Linking read The common mistake is measuring the wrong cost. Teams benchmark one proxied call, find a few nanoseconds, and conclude that proxies are free, while the start-up cost (thousands of classes loaded, generated, verified and interpreted before the first request) never appears in a microbenchmark. Others go the other way and remove a proxy from a component that makes one network call a second. People make it because JMH is the tool they know for performance. The fix is to measure both clocks, the way this lesson did: B/op from JMH for the hot path, and -Xlog:class+load counts plus time to the first request for the start, each on its own, before changing anything.

h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Java and Kotlin
x: A generated registry in Java and the same idea written by hand in Kotlin AppRegistry.java (generated, trimmed) public final class AppRegistry implements Registry { private static final class FxRates_Holder { static final FxRates INSTANCE = new FxRates(); } private static final class FeeCalculator_Holder { static final FeeCalculator INSTANCE = new FeeCalculator(FxRates_Holder.INSTANCE); } private static PaymentAttempt new_PaymentAttempt() { // a prototype return new PaymentAttempt(FeeCalculator_Holder.INSTANCE); } @Override public <T> T get(Class<T> type) { if (type == FxRates.class) return type.cast(FxRates_Holder.INSTANCE); if (type == FeeCalculator.class) return type.cast(FeeCalculator_Holder.INSTANCE); if (type == PaymentAttempt.class) return type.cast(new_PaymentAttempt()); throw new ContainerException("No component provides " + type.getSimpleName()); } } AppRegistry.kt (by hand) object AppRegistry { private object FxRatesHolder { val INSTANCE = FxRates() } private object FeeCalculatorHolder { val INSTANCE = FeeCalculator(FxRatesHolder.INSTANCE) } private fun newPaymentAttempt() = PaymentAttempt(FeeCalculatorHolder.INSTANCE) // a prototype @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") fun <T> get(type: Class<T>): T = when (type) { FxRates::class.java -> FxRatesHolder.INSTANCE FeeCalculator::class.java -> FeeCalculatorHolder.INSTANCE PaymentAttempt::class.java -> newPaymentAttempt() else -> throw ContainerException("No component provides ${type.simpleName}") } as T } Both compile to the same mechanism: one class per singleton whose static initializer builds it on first use, under the JVM's class initialization lock. A Kotlin object is that holder class, with its instance in a static INSTANCE field. The difference is who writes it. The Java one comes from a generator and is never edited; the Kotlin one is the kind of code Dagger generates, written by hand, which is fine for ten components and painful for eighty. You don't need by lazy here: it would work, but it adds a Lazy object per bean and a volatile read per access to do what the class initialization lock already does.

In the run-time container it is one filter before the graph is built, because the container learns its components at start-up anyway. List<Class<?>> components = new ArrayList<>(DemoApp.COMPONENTS); if ("mock".equals(System.getProperty("issuer"))) { components.remove(HttpIssuerClient.class); // decided at start-up components.add(MockIssuerClient.class); } Registry registry = new Container(components); val components = DemoApp.COMPONENTS.toMutableList() if (System.getProperty("issuer") == "mock") { components -= HttpIssuerClient::class.java // decided at start-up components += MockIssuerClient::class.java } val registry: Registry = Container(components) The generated registry has no start-up graph to change. One option is to generate one registry per profile and choose at the edge of the program. Each registry stays plain code, and the flag picks a class, not a graph. String source = RegistryGenerator.generate("com.acme.gen", "StagingRegistry", stagingComponents); // ...and ProductionRegistry from the production list, both at build time Registry registry = "mock".equals(System.getProperty("issuer")) ? new StagingRegistry() : new ProductionRegistry(); val source = RegistryGenerator.generate("com.acme.gen", "StagingRegistry", stagingComponents) // ...and ProductionRegistry from the production list, both at build time val registry: Registry = if (System.getProperty("issuer") == "mock") StagingRegistry() else ProductionRegistry() Check the costs. Two registries double the generated code and ship the mock in the production artifact. If the flag really is fixed per environment, a build-time property is cleaner: build the staging image with the staging list. Quarkus draws exactly this line between build-time configuration, fixed in the artifact, and run-time configuration, read at start-up. Write the decision down in one sentence a reviewer can check: "The issuer implementation is chosen per build, so each image wires one graph; a run-time property may change the issuer's URL and timeouts, never which class is wired." h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Quiz
x: You want CI to fail when someone makes the issuer proxy more expensive. Which number from ProxyCallBench should the check use? ns/op, with a 10% margin gc.alloc.rate.norm (B/op), with a small margin The score error, which must stay below 1 ns The number of forks Allocation per operation is the same on every run for the same code, while time on a shared CI machine can move by more than the score itself, as this lesson's runs did. Keep a small margin, because B/op can shift between JDK versions and JIT decisions. The generated Fees_Proxy allocates new Object[] {p0}, a boxed Long and an Invocation on every call, in its source. JMH reports 0 B/op for it. Why? JMH doesn't count objects smaller than 64 bytes The TLAB hides allocations from the GC profiler C2 inlined the whole call, and escape analysis removed the objects because none of them leaves the compiled method The objects are allocated off-heap Allocation in a TLAB is still allocation and still counted. What removed it is escape analysis after inlining: when every use of an object is inside one compiled method, C2 can replace it with its fields in registers. It only works once C2 has compiled the code and can see the whole call, which is why the reflective paths, where it can't, keep their 160 to 208 bytes. On JDK 21 you add a dynamic AppCDS archive to the reflective container's start. Which classes does every start still create at run time? None: the archive stores every class the training run loaded Only the application's own classes Byte Buddy's own classes from its JAR The JDK proxy classes, the classes Byte Buddy generates, and some hidden classes An archive holds classes the JVM can find again at a known location, such as a JAR on the class path. At dump time JDK 21 skips each proxy class with Unsupported location, and Byte Buddy's subclass is defined from bytes by its own class loader. Byte Buddy's JAR classes do come from the archive, which is why AppCDS still halved this start. A generated holder's constructor throws on first use because the issuer key is missing. Ops fix the configuration, and the next request calls get(PaymentService.class) again on the same JVM. What happens? NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class ...PaymentService_Holder, until the JVM restarts The holder retries and the request succeeds get returns null The JVM retries the static initializer after a back-off A static initializer runs once. When it throws, the JVM marks the class as failed, and every later use gets NoClassDefFoundError, for the life of its class loader. Lesson 1's SingletonCell stores nothing when its factory throws, so it retries. That is one real cost of build-time holders: keep their constructors free of I/O and configuration lookups. In a heap dump of the generated registry, what holds the PaymentService singleton? A SingletonCell in the registry's map The static field INSTANCE of the class PaymentService_Holder, which lives as long as its class loader Nothing: the JVM keeps holder instances off the heap The thread that first called get A holder's instance is a static field, and static fields belong to their class, which stays loaded while its class loader is reachable. The registry has no map and no cells. That is why the lab loads the registry in a new class loader for each test: the only way to get fresh singletons is a fresh copy of the classes.

h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Key terms
x: Build-time wiring Working out the dependency graph while the application is built and writing plain code that creates the components. Holder class A nested class whose static field holds one singleton; the JVM builds it on first use, once, under its class-init lock. Class histogram A count of live objects and bytes per class, after a full GC: jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram. Heap dump A file with every object on the heap and every reference between them, read with a tool such as Eclipse MAT. Path to GC roots The chain of references that keeps an object alive, from a root such as a thread's local variable or a static field. B/op Bytes allocated per benchmark operation, from JMH's GC profiler: steady enough to compare and to gate in CI. Which JMH number should a CI gate on proxy cost use? gc.alloc.rate.norm, bytes per operation, with a small margin. Time is too noisy on shared machines. Why can generated interceptor code show 0 B/op although its source allocates? C2 inlines the whole call, and escape analysis removes objects that never leave the compiled method. Name the -Xlog:class+load sources for classes made at run time. __dynamic_proxy__ (JDK proxies), __JVM_DefineClass__ (defined from bytes, as Byte Buddy does), and hidden classes such as lambdas. Why does reading annotations by reflection create classes? Each annotation instance is an object of a JDK proxy class generated for that annotation type. What makes a generated holder thread-safe without a lock in your code? The JVM runs a class's static initializer once, under the class initialization lock; other threads wait for it. What happens when a holder's constructor throws? ExceptionInInitializerError once, then NoClassDefFoundError on every later use until the JVM restarts. A SingletonCell would retry. Why can't AppCDS on JDK 21 archive a JDK proxy class? The class has no location an archive can check (Unsupported location); it is generated at run time.

h: Measure it, then make it start fast · Go deeper
x: What a production container adds to the one you built, roughly in the order you would need it: Lifecycle callbacks: @PostConstruct after injection and @PreDestroy on shutdown, run in reverse creation order so a Ledger closes after the PaymentService that writes to it. Qualifiers (@Named, @Qualifier) for two implementations of one interface, and resolution by generic type, so Repository<Payment> and Repository<Refund> are different dependencies. More scopes: per request, per session, per Kafka message, with a client proxy that forwards to the right instance for the current scope. Configuration injection, with type conversion and validation, split into build-time and run-time properties. Interceptor ordering by priority, decorators, and events between components. Lookup injection (Provider<T>, Instance<T>) for edges that must be followed at call time. Test support: replacing one component with a mock without rewriting the graph. Error messages that print the whole dependency path, not only the cycle. The way the generator runs matters too. This lab runs it as a separate step on compiled classes, which is close to what Quarkus does during its build. Dagger and Micronaut run theirs as annotation processors inside javac, so the generated classes are compiled with your code and IDEs can show them, but the processor sees source-level elements instead of loaded classes.
